# Patrologia Latina, volume 115 — English translation

## [Scan page 6]

### Patrologia

**Complete Course of Patrology**, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, and Economical Library of All the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers—whether Latin or Greek—from the Apostolic Age to the time of Innocent III (1216) for the Latins, and of the Council of Florence (1439) for the Greeks.

A chronological reprint of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have appeared during the first fifteen centuries of the Church, prepared according to the most accurate editions, collated with numerous manuscripts, most carefully corrected, and continuously elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and various readings; completed and augmented after all the principal editions published during the three best-known centuries.

Each work is provided with particular analytical indexes, and each volume with indexes of the authors and of the matters that follow; with chapters properly arranged within the text, and with titles in the upper margins of the individual pages distinguishing and indicating the subject matter.

The collection is enlarged by works both doubtful and apocryphal, as well as by works possessing some authority within ecclesiastical tradition; and is enriched with extremely full indexes of authors and works—alphabetical, chronological, statistical, synthetic, analytical, analogous, and covering every point of religion, whether dogmatic, moral, liturgical, canonical, disciplinary, historical, or any other, without exception.

Especially, however, it is furnished with two immense and comprehensive indexes: the first, of matters, by consulting which one may see at a glance whatever not only this or that Father, but also each individual Father, without a single omission, has written on any subject; the second, of Sacred Scripture, by which it is immediately apparent to the reader which Fathers, and in which passages of their works, have commented on the individual verses of the individual books of Sacred Scripture, from the first verse of Genesis to the last of the Apocalypse.

An edition of the greatest accuracy, easily preferable to all others, if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reproduced, and the very convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire course of the Patrology, together with the moderate price.

This one, methodical, chronological collection also gathers for the first time in our library six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, drawn from works and manuscripts belonging to every age, place, language, and form.

**Latin Series, First Section**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Innocent III.

Under the direction of J.-P. Migne, editor of the Universal Clerical Library, or Complete Course in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

Ahyto, Audradus, Aldricus, Leo IV, Benedict III, Angelomus, Saint Eulogius, Saint Prudentius.

## [Scan page 10]

### In the Year of the Lord 1650

## Ahyto, Bishop of Basel

### Notice by Acherius in the *Spicilegium*, volume I

We are bringing to light the work of the most noble Ahyto—called by others Haito, Heito, and Baido—bishop of Basel, after it had lain buried and neglected in the dust for more than eight hundred years. I owe the first indication of this monument to the distinguished Emeric Bigot, who, on returning from Rome to Paris, told me what antiquities he had discovered there and asserted that in the City there existed a *Capitulare* of Ahyto, bishop of Basel, consisting of twenty-four chapters and written in a very ancient hand. I was immediately inflamed with a keen desire for it; and not long afterward I expressed that desire in a letter to the most reverend Father Giovanni Bona, who by the splendor of his piety and learning illuminates the Catholic Church. He therefore took pains to satisfy me, as appears from the following letter sent by him to me:

> Most Reverend Father,
>
> More quickly than I had believed, I am sending you the *Capitulare* of Ahyto, bishop of Basel. I unexpectedly found it in the library of the most eminent Cardinal Barberini, and rejoiced like one who has found much spoil. Without delay I asked for it, obtained it, and gave it to a copyist to transcribe; this was done with the greatest fidelity. You will insert it in volume VI or VII of your *Spicilegium*, and say that you received it from the library of the most eminent Cardinal Francesco Barberini, Vice-Chancellor of the Holy Roman Church.
>
> In chapter 21 you will find *genupositum* used for “generation” or “degree of relationship,” an entirely obsolete word, except that *geniculum* is found used in the same sense in feudal usages.
>
> The Supreme Pontiff greatly praises your *Spicilegium*, and said that he especially approved the letters of distinguished men and whatever pertains to the history and ancient discipline of the Church; for these, he said, are singularly valuable, and the history contained in letters is the most certain of all. He then added that those who labor to rescue old works from the obscurity of libraries perform a more useful service to the republic of letters than those who compose new books: for new books, if they contain anything good, usually borrow it from the ancients.
>
> This judgment concerning studies, which I sincerely report to you as having come from the mouth of our most holy lord, I present without adding or taking away anything. May God grant you strength to gather more ears of this kind, for the honor of the monastic order and the benefit of the whole Church. This I pray from my heart.
>
> Rome, 10 September 1603.
>
> Your most obedient servant in Christ,  
> **D. Giovanni Bona**, of the Reformed Congregation of Saint Bernard,  
> General Abbot.

### Ahyto, or Haito, Bishop of Basel

### The Following Little Book

[This *Capitulare* also survives in manuscripts of the Vatican Library numbered 1446, 1447, and 1448.]

Many writers extol Ahyto for his holiness of life, learning, deeds, and embassy undertaken to the emperor of the Greeks.

The old *Annals of the Franks*, under the year 811, say:

> “After Arsatius—this was the name of the envoy of the emperor Nicephorus—had completed his mission and departed, envoys were sent from the emperor [Charlemagne] to Constantinople to confirm the same agreement: Haito, bishop of Basel, and Hugo, count of Tours.”

Einhard says the same in his *Annals* under the year 811, where the bishop of Basel is called Haito, apparently for Heito. The anonymous *Life of Charlemagne* has the very same words. The monk of Engolism also writes in the same life:

> “After envoys had been sent by the emperor to Constantinople to confirm the peace, Heito, bishop of Basel,” and so forth.

The *Annals of Fulda*, under the year 811, say:

> “The emperor sent his envoys to Constantinople, Haito, bishop of Basel,” and so forth.

Hermann the Lame, in his *Chronicle*, under the year 806, writes:

> “When Abbot Waldo of Reichenau had been transferred to govern the monastery of Saint-Denis, Heito, the ninth abbot, presided for seventeen years.”

Under the year 811:

> “Heito, abbot of Reichenau and bishop of Basel, was sent to Constantinople with Counts Hugo and Aio, and wrote his itinerary.”

Under the year 816:

> “The basilica of Saint Mary at Reichenau, built by Heito, abbot and bishop, was dedicated.”

Under the year 822:

> “When Heito, abbot and bishop of Reichenau, adopted a private and quiet life, Erlebald, the thirteenth abbot, presided for thirteen years.”

Finally, under the year 824:

> “At Reichenau, the monk Wetti, drawn from the body and restored to it, died after three days; Bishop Heito wrote his visions in prose, and Walafrid wrote them in heroic meter.”

Hepidannus, a monk of Saint Gall, in his *Annals*, which extend from the year of Christ 709 to 1044, writes:

> “In the year 802, Heito, bishop, is mentioned as distinguished at Charlemagne’s council.”

Under the year 810—or rather 811:

> “Heito crossed the sea,”

that is, he went as envoy by sea to Constantinople.

Under the year 820:

> “Heito the bishop is serving at Reichenau.”

In the *Chronicle of Saint Gall*, from the year 748 to 926, he is called Hatto, a corrupt form of Haito or Heito. It says that in the year 806 he succeeded Waldo as abbot of Reichenau, as Hermann also writes; and under the year 811:

> “Hatto crossed the sea.”

Under the year 822:

> “Hatto was succeeded in the government of Reichenau by Erlebald”—otherwise Erlebaldus—

and finally, under the year 836:

> “Bishop Hatto died.”

Most of these statements Hermann the Lame transferred into his own *Chronicle*.

## [Scan page 11]

## Ahyto, Bishop of Basel

### The Capitularies of Ahyto

These are the chapters that Ahyto, bishop of the Church of Basel and abbot of the monastery called Reichenau, established for the priests of his diocese, so that they might learn how they ought to govern themselves and the people entrusted to them chastely and justly, and confirm them in religion and divine worship.

1. First of all, the faith of priests must be examined: how they believe and teach others to believe. Examples must also be proposed, so that the Creator may be understood, however slightly, from the creature.

2. Secondly, it must be commanded that all learn the Lord’s Prayer, in which all necessities of human life are comprehended, and the Apostles’ Creed, in which the Catholic faith is contained in its entirety—both in Latin and in the vernacular—so that what we profess with the mouth may be believed and understood in the heart.

3. Thirdly, it must be made known that suitable responses to the priests’ salutations are to be learned. Not only clerics and priests devoted to God are to offer a response, but the whole devout people must respond with one voice.

4. Fourthly, the faith of Saint Athanasius must be learned by priests and recited from memory every Sunday at Prime.

5. Fifthly, they must know what the sacrament of baptism and confirmation is, and what the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood is; how visible creation is seen in these mysteries, while the invisible alone is supplied for the soul’s eternity—something contained in faith alone.

6. Sixthly, they must learn what is necessary for priests: the Sacramentary, Lectionary, Antiphonary, Baptismal Book, Computus, Penitential Canon, Psalter, and homilies for the Sundays and individual feasts throughout the year. If any one of these is lacking, the name of priest will scarcely remain in the man, for the Gospel warning is extremely dangerous:

> “If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit” (Matthew 15:14).

7. Seventhly, they must know the proper times for baptizing during the year: namely, Holy Saturday of Easter, so that the triple immersion in baptism may imitate the Lord’s three-day death, made glorious by the resurrection. Therefore this holy regeneration is to be celebrated by the whole Christian people through the eighth day. The other proper time for baptism is Holy Saturday of Pentecost.

If necessity arises, however, assistance may be given in danger at any time, for necessity scarcely recognizes a law. They must also have a vessel for the baptismal font that is never used for any other purpose.

8. Eighthly, the proper times of abstaining from work during the year must be announced: every Sunday from morning until evening, in honor of the Lord’s resurrection; but Saturday is to be a working day from morning until evening, lest they be caught up in Judaism.

The days of abstinence from work throughout the year are as follows: the Nativity of the Lord; Saint Stephen; Saint John the Evangelist; the Holy Innocents; the Octave of the Lord; the Epiphany; the Purification of Holy Mary; Holy Easter, as included in the preceding chapter; the three days of the Rogations; the Ascension of the Lord; Holy Saturday of Pentecost; Saint John the Baptist; the twelve Apostles, especially Saints Peter and Paul, who illumined Europe by their preaching; the Assumption of Holy Mary; the dedication of the basilica of Saint Michael the Archangel; and the dedication of any oratory or of any saint in whose honor that church was founded. The latter is to be announced only to those dwelling nearby, not generally to everyone.

When a fast has been proclaimed from the palace or from the house, all are to observe it generally. The remaining feasts of the year, such as those of Saint Remedius, Saint Maurice, and Saint Martin, are not to be imposed as days of rest, though they are not to be prohibited if the people wish to observe them chastely and with zeal for God.

9. Ninthly, the same priests must be commanded not to permit strange women to live with them, in accordance with the Council of Nicaea, except women concerning whom no suspicion of bad reputation can arise.

10. Tenthly, they are not to enter taverns, whether sitting there at home or occupied there on a journey. If they need to purchase something there, they should send their servants, have what is offered brought to another house, and receive it there faithfully with thanksgiving.

11. Eleventhly, they are not to attend secular lawsuits, stand surety, or keep dogs for hunting, hawks, falcons, or sparrowhawks; nor may they indulge in any game or spectacle. It is enough for them that the first Psalm says:

> “His delight is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he meditates day and night” (Psalm 1:2).

And what the Apostle commands:

> “No soldier entangles himself in civilian business, so that he may please the one who enlisted him” (2 Timothy 2:4).

**Editorial notes**

- “From memory”: that is, by heart, as Acherius correctly explains. We immediately added the words from a very ancient manuscript of Saint Gall, with which Baluzius compared the earlier edition.
- “In danger”: these words have been added from two manuscripts of Saint Gall.
- “In honor”: we have enclosed this in brackets, having added it from the same manuscripts. In one of them the reading is “in honor of the Sunday resurrection.”
- “From the palace”: concerning fasts proclaimed by our kings, see Gregory of Tours, book IX, chapter 21, and Charlemagne’s letter to Fastrada. Acherius correctly observes that the word subsequently printed as *a domo* is corrupt and should be read *a domino*; but he does not correctly explain it as “from the apostolic lord,” that is, the pope. It is more probably “from one’s own bishop.”

## [Scan page 12]

### Capitularies

12. Twelfthly, they must know that no one is to be ordained for money, and that no one ought to obtain possession of a church through gifts. If this has happened, both the person ordained and the ordaining bishop are to be deposed, for it is clear that those who do such things are afflicted with the heresy of Simon Magus.

Such a person is not to enter through the door into the sheepfold, according to the words of the Gospel; rather, climbing in by another way, he is a thief and a robber. Not only those who do this, but also those who consent to those doing it, are to be excommunicated.

13. Thirteenthly, no one is to dare receive a wandering cleric from another parish, allow him to remain with him, or permit him to celebrate Mass without our permission. Nor is anyone to assume the governance of another church or parish without our prior knowledge. Whoever acts otherwise is to be excommunicated.

14. Fourteenthly, they are not to celebrate the mysteries of the Mass in huts, unconsecrated churches, or houses, except perhaps for the sake of visiting those detained by illness. If they do so, they must know that they will be degraded for disobedience.

15. Fifteenthly, the tithe given by the faithful is to be called God’s census and therefore must be rendered in full. According to the canon of Toledo [Council of Toledo IX], one third of it ought to belong to the bishops. We do not wish to exercise this authority, but wish to receive only a fourth part of it, in accordance with the decrees of the Roman pontiffs and the observance of the Holy Roman Church.

If anyone is found contentious in this matter, whether cleric or layman, he is to be deprived of communion and judged by synodal censure.

16. Sixteenthly, each person must ensure that women do not approach the altar and that women dedicated to God are not involved in any ministry of the altar.

If altar cloths need to be washed, they are to be removed by clerics and handed over to the women at the chancel rail; there they are to be received back. Similarly, when offerings are presented by those women, the priests are to receive them there and carry them to the altar.

17. Seventeenthly, the priests themselves must preach by word and example to everyone that they are to accept no interest, neither a sescuplum (a one-and-a-half-fold return) nor one thing in exchange for another. For whoever does this is exceedingly faithless and rebellious against God’s commands. The prohibition is known to have been given equally to all Christians, but especially to priests, who ought to be the pattern and example of faith to everyone.

18. Eighteenthly, no one ordained or to be ordained is to migrate from his parish to another; nor is he to go to the thresholds of the Apostles for the sake of prayer while abandoning the care of his own church; nor to the palace for the purpose of lodging an appeal; nor, if suspended from communion, to receive communion from another without the permission and prior knowledge of his bishop.

If he does so, such communion, ordination, or migration is invalid. This must be announced to all the faithful, so that those who wish to go to the thresholds of the blessed Apostles for the sake of prayer may confess their sins at home and then depart, because they are to be bound or loosed by their own bishop or priest, not by a stranger.

19. Nineteenthly [Burchard, book III, chapter 198], nothing is to be read or sung in church except what is of divine authority or has been sanctioned by the authority of the orthodox Fathers.

They are not to venerate false names of angels, but only those named in prophetic and evangelical Scripture: Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael. Nor are they to make differing judgments in penitential cases, when one seeks to please one person by imposing less, and another by imposing more, flattering one and disparaging another. Rather, according to the quality of the person and the measure of the fault, the correction of punishment is to be administered.

20. Twentiethly, they must be admonished to consider that whatever is given by the faithful is redemption for sins. Therefore they are not to glory in such gifts, but should rather fear what is said in the Old Testament concerning priests:

> “They must bear the iniquity of the people.”

Therefore, with great fear, they must be solicitous for those whose gifts they share, because it is a great danger to become the judge of another’s life when one does not know how to govern one’s own.

21. Twenty-firstly, they must know and understand what the crime of incest is, and each must ensure in his own parish that it does not occur; and if it occurs, it must be corrected as quickly as possible.

No one is to take a wife or husband from his kinship as far as the fifth degree. If this has happened unknowingly, it is not to be readily believed, but examined by God’s judgment. They are not to be separated in the fourth degree, but are to remain in penance throughout all the days of their communion.

The same applies to a man who has two wives related to one another in the same way; a wife who has two husbands similarly related to one another; a godfather or godmother; a spiritual son or daughter from the font, confirmation, or religious dedication; another man’s wife while her husband is alive; or another woman’s husband while his wife is alive. No one may lawfully enter into marriage with such persons.

If persons are found in the first or second degree to have committed the crime of fornication, they must know that they have wholly lost the rights of marriage with another. If they are found in the third degree to have been polluted by such a crime, suitable penance must follow, but their marital rights are not to be denied them with respect to other persons.

Where slaves belonging not to one master but to different masters have been joined, such a union is not valid without the consent of both masters. Whatever is tolerated through negligence and is not corrected with whatever strength is possible: the person who consents to this negligence will be the author of the union.

Many more matters could be written concerning the crime of incest, such as a mother, a daughter, a stepmother, and almost countless others that do not occur to the mind for writing. Nevertheless, marital intercourse is forever forbidden between such persons and those similar to them.

22. Twenty-secondly, they must be admonished to know how to announce to the people what the works of mercy are, together with their fruits, as contained in the evangelical and apostolic writings, by which one reaches life; and what the works of iniquity are, together with their manifold fruits, by which one travels by the left-hand road toward eternal destruction.

They must avoid the crime of perjury in every way, for perjury is recognized as a crime when it is committed not only upon the Gospel or the relics of the saints, but also against the Truth who is God, if one lies.

**Editorial notes**

- “The marital rights of the other”: this is the reading of the cited manuscripts, more correctly than the earlier edition’s “the rights any further.”
- “Whatever is perceived through negligence”: Acherius emends the passage as follows: “Whatever is consented to negligently and is not corrected with whatever strength is possible.”
- “God’s census”: the cited manuscripts correctly read this; the earlier edition has “God’s census” in a corrupt form, and likewise “to God it is to be rendered in full.”
- “According to the decrees”: both manuscripts of Saint Gall read “according to your decrees.”
- “Whether cleric or layman”: the earlier edition reads “deacon,” but since that reading is corrupt, we have followed the two manuscripts frequently cited. At the end they read “he will be judged.”
- “Equally commanded”: the earlier edition reads “equally forbidden.”
- “They are not to venerate names”: Adalbert, bishop, was condemned at the Council of Soissons in the year 744 because he had inserted into his prayer the unknown names of seven angels.
- “Upon them”: we have added these words from two manuscripts of Saint Gall.
- “In the fifth degree”: the cited manuscripts read “into the fifth degree,” and below “into the fourth degree.” At the Council of Verberie, held in 752, as also in the Laws of the Ripuarians and the Laws of the Lombards, *geniculum* is used for “degree of relationship.”
- “But are to remain in penance”: the entire passage down to “the same applies” is found in neither manuscript of Saint Gall.

23. Twenty-thirdly, they must be admonished to know that they have been made the spouses of the churches over which they preside. Therefore they must devote the vigilance of their entire life to adorning them in every way and serving them continually.

24. Twenty-fourthly, they must in no way omit the canonical hours, whether nocturnal or diurnal. For just as the Roman Church sings the office, so must all who follow the same way of life do.

The rule of observing this form is taught not only by the New Testament but is also clear from the Old Testament, because the Prophet, inspired by the Holy Spirit, says:

> “Seven times a day I praise you” (Psalm 118:164).

And:

> “At midnight I rose to give thanks to you” (ibid., verse 62).

25. Twenty-fifthly, they must announce to the people that the spiritual sons and daughters whom they receive in baptism are their guarantors and sponsors in faith. On their behalf they renounce the devil, to whom they had previously been enslaved. Therefore they are to keep them under their care until they have reached adulthood and have explained and fulfilled for them the pledge of their faith and renunciation.

What they promised on their behalf, they must require from them in full by the same responses.

## [Scan page 13]

## Audradus of Sens, Chorepiscopus

### Historical Notice

Audradus, our subject, was first a priest and then chorepiscopus of Sens until the year 849, when all the chorepiscopi in Francia were deposed at the Council of Paris. He wrote a book *On Revelations* in the year 853, extracts from which may be read in André du Chesne. In it is mentioned the *Fountain of Life*, written in hexameters and addressed to Hincmar of Rheims; Oudinus first published it from a manuscript of the abbey of Floreffe, among the *Writers of Gaul and Belgium*. That learned man, however, was wholly mistaken when he attributed this little book to Hincmar himself, although he acknowledged Audradus as the author of the controversy. From that source we publish it. Audradus was also surnamed *Modicus*, was a kinsman of Burchard, bishop of Chartres, and attended the Council of Sens in 853.

(a) Lupus, letter 40, calls him his teacher.  
(b) Baronius, under the year 838, no. 6.  
(c) Oudinus, from a manuscript of the abbey of Floreffe, among the *Writers of Gaul and Belgium*.  
(d) The *Annals of Fulda*; Sigebert, chapter 94, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.

### Letter of Audradus the Chorepiscopus to Hincmar

You reveal, eloquent poet of noble intellect,  
that you have been nourished by sweet musical harmony.

While, blazing in spirit, you survey the pastures of virtue,  
while you bathe your eyes in the dew of springing water,

you hasten to the laurel shade and approach the pale ivy,  
and likewise the rich olive,  
giving your head a wondrous crown from the fountain.

At last, those whom you once saw going thirsty through the fields,  
wretched, you encouraged by your flourishing zeal,  
so that they might go to behold the shining temples  
of the Fountain of Life  
and ask from it, with prayers, gifts of salvation.

You also used such words, Hincmar,  
to admonish me, Audradus, whom you had long considered a dear friend:

“Live happily; now make use of our admonitions.  
Break your delays; hastening onward, come quickly  
to see all that you perceive.”

There a fountain, springing from the center of the seat,  
strikes the surrounding air,  
gives me abundant draughts of living flavors,  
and I shall go before you and open the gates.

### Poetic Fiction of Audradus, Bishop

Trusting these words, I hurried as a friend  
to examine the place;  
but, seeing the heights, I came.

Whether faith recoils from the telling,  
or whether it was the fiction of a brother,  
the report soon enclosed me in a holy mist.

Suddenly a summit appeared,  
and from its double edge, with rounded stone,  
surrounded the sacred fountain.  
If measured, it would have measured twice seven cubits.  
A white form shone in sevenfold shape upon the waters,  
and the East had veiled as many forms in mist.

While I was vainly tormented there for twelve hours,  
you remained at home, hiding your temples beneath peaceful branches.  
I began to accuse the faith of my deceptive friend,  
and tears were not lacking,  
since I had allowed you to go before me.

Shadows were already rising from the western regions;  
evening was coming, and Hesperus adorned the lands with his lamp.

With weeping I turned my conquered eyes through the walls,  
again and again asking the Lord with these prayers:

“O whoever you may be, guardian and ruler of this place,  
O deign to quench such great thirst in wretched me!”

At once a voice was carried through the air from the sacred seat:

“I am guardian of all things; I am the source of the living fountain.  
But without a vessel it denies its draughts to mortals.

Let there be for you such a figure as you may recognize:  
it must rise from the bottom with seven reeds,  
stand erect, and, distinguishing the summit,  
raise its tip;  
seven mouths indeed blaze from the top of its neck.”

“O how graciously he uttered these things in speech!  
At last he taught me what I should do in paternal language:

‘Run home and bring back with your hands what I command,  
dear child.  
But if poverty does not allow you to possess it,  
or if an envious stepmother has secretly stolen it by night,  
or if no hope of finding it remains at home—

[The text continues in the other column under the heading *Book of the Fountain of Life*.]

## [Scan page 14]

### Book of the Fountain of Life

When the young man, having brought these things in the commanded order,  
reports the commands, I recognize the instructions he has conveyed:

“Immortal glory to the Lord, and everlasting kingdom,  
who deigns to entrust twin salvations to me,  
and who has granted me to bathe my face in a living stream.

Hear the counsel: why are you being consumed by these breezes?  
A certain young man frequents you night and day  
and pours libations from a cup upon our altars.

To him we have given, in our green meadows,  
houses beneath which he may remain as commanded  
or be of benefit to his friends.

Already, like a swan, he circles his halls;  
he uses the bright waters under our guidance,  
whether, as a rich man, he loves to recline upon painted carpets.

Hasten, and report these words of mine to him:

‘Remember that the faithful have earned holy rest by hospitality.  
O young man, now and forever, farewell.

May he receive this with his ears;  
may he temper himself beneath woven, vine-covered dwellings;  
may he lay aside his thirst and his sleep in quiet through the night,  
and restore the fibers clinging through his inward parts.

And when day with its first light has cast down the shadows,  
let him soften clay and warm it in the first sunlight.  
Let him impress it with a form whose appearance he knows well;  
let him cover it with wax and bury the wax in sand.

Let him place harmless fires beside it,  
weigh it on a balance,  
and be pleased when the metals are weighed.

Let him remember what was entrusted to him  
and become mindful of profit,  
through which he triumphs in our springlike halls.

After everything, let him blow with both hands upon the bellows,  
empty the wax mold, and fill it with metal.

After some time, let him strip the vessel of its earthy casing,  
and smoke the new image with an iron hook;  
then let him bring the venerable pledge into your hands.

Remember to carry it here with you as you come.  
With it you will pour an offering to the fountain whose water springs toward the stars.

Moreover, it will reveal the reason why I fashion the figure from the vessel,  
and strengthen your doubtful minds with friendly words.

Meanwhile, let it dissolve the triple knot with song,  
which the molten metal will be able to loosen and adorn,  
when you place it here in your mind.

Thus I command you to fashion it:

The disk is distinguished by a double appearance of the moon,  
the dark and the bright driving away the shadows.  
One side turns the face of its light toward the earth,  
while the other half is held beneath darkness in the sky.

Finally, for twice seven days  
it pours forth a wondrous light upon the earth  
from its clustered face.

For—strange to say!—as the lights of Phoebus grow,  
the Fathers established the exceedingly solemn date of Easter.

But when it grows pale above,  
as soon as it begins to hide its light  
and its black form becomes faint upon the earth,  
they count three times seven days,  
which the suns must not exceed;  
yet within these a holy solemnity is rightly sought.

Let the number here explain holy Easter,  
or let it signify the moon;  
and it will be able to dissolve the triple knot.

Here remember this, young man;  
let them receive answers concerning the place.’”

The vine-covered houses yielded to a leafy covering.  
He receives the libations of our vow from the cup;  
there is no doubt that you brought us his commands.

“Give me your hand, beloved,  
and rest with me here tonight.  
Now enter, most faithful, the flourishing house.”

Alas! Let me now recall the deeds of the first parent,

consented to the lord of death, and brought upon the world  
and upon his children, and upon every succeeding offspring,  
the punishments he deserved—may he deserve them from the unjust lord.

The one who had offered Eve the evil of the forbidden tree,

and upon their descendants.  
Thus, when the human being willed it, he abandoned life for death.

Begin now with me the song of heavenly grace,

With the rod he raised the sign—apple and serpent—before the father: his offspring.  
He did not impose force upon them:  
they all perished voluntarily, one after another.

Christ likewise overcame chaos and departed from death.

For where light passed, there is eternal life,  
giving us the pattern that we can rise from darkness,  
provided that we celebrate the hour of his teaching,  
which the number of the moon marked with its gracious light.

Read what follows below if you wish to know these poems.

### Mystical explanation of Easter and of its days

Complete now with me the song of heavenly grace,  
of the eternal fountain, the Paschal calculation, and the hour.

Now hear, brother, what the unfolding of the knot is.

### The moon is distinguished by a twofold appearance

The world is distinguished in the moon’s twofold appearance,  
namely, dark and bright, driving away the darkness.

By this appearance it is said to be partly of the earth and partly of the heavens.

### The moon as a figure of humanity

The image of humanity, fashioned by the hands of the Creator,  
thus far instructs the human being, turned toward earthly things,  
to turn the light toward itself.

The moon, while it rolls its lights upon the earth,  
is held covered in darkness toward heaven.  
It gives the form of humanity, which, while seeking earthly things,  
turns the light of its understanding downward toward the earth.  
It also receives the praises of the crowd, rejoicing in their murmur,  
and, with its view of heaven obscured, is regarded as covered in darkness.

### The celebration of Easter is forbidden before the fifteenth day of the moon

In the meantime the solemn feast may be observed at the earliest,  
for the moon, with its gathered face, pours forth a wondrous light  
for twice seven days upon the earth.

During those days it is forbidden to seek the holy solemn feast.

These two periods signify the two times that precede Christ:  
the first before the law, the second under the law.

For earthborn people, weighed down by the burden of sin,  
wishing to confer the light of life upon themselves,  
unworthy of heaven, plunged their old age into darkness.  
Nor, with death not cast off, did they deserve to see Easter.

*Hosea 13:14.*

But when, pale above, it first begins to conceal its light,  
and its black form becomes mean upon the earth,  
count three sevens, which you must not exceed;  
within these it is permitted to seek the holy solemn feast.  

Thus, weeping, when he first begins to turn his life toward heaven  
and to be despised on earth,  
now bright in heaven, let him count that three times seven—  
the time in the world in which Christ’s grace shines—  
and, wholly converted in heart, seek  
the saving Easter, found by solemn reckoning.  
Leaping forth from the gloomy darkness of night,  
let him pass to the light which Christ bestowed upon the world,  
so that, God granting it, he may live blessed through the ages.

Complete now with me the song of heavenly grace,  
of the eternal fountain, the Paschal calculation, and the hour.

With God’s help, whose words you brought to me,  
revealing the mystery of faith under the name of Easter,  
I have explained it and have been able to untie the triple knot.  
I have also sung, perhaps, the two figures of the margin:  
the bright form which shines in seven spans  
and is varied by an equal number of intermingled black coverings.  
I have now also poured you forth, [reading uncertain], as a pledge of honour,  
in seven reeds, adorning [reading uncertain] three times with hours.

Whoever thirsts at this end strives in vain toward the shadows  
of the eternal fountain: this is the wisdom of the Father.  
For it will not enter dark hearts  
subject to sins, nor does the mind embrace it.  
But the Spirit of God, as a most worthy host,  
cleansing from vices, endows [the soul] with a sevenfold gift,  
and dedicates it as a fitting eternal dwelling to himself.  
One who thirsts for these waters can draw health-giving streams.  
Whoever has this vessel, let him hasten to the fountain’s waves,  
draw from them, and pour out an offering upon the sacred altars.  
By heavenly courses the sound becomes great for the world;  
he who covers this with sound instructed me in my inmost senses.  
These things, Audradus, I sing for you in sweet song:  
recount the dear pledges, as I often ask.  
Thus too, sweet friend, you will approach with a happy utterance  
the fountain sought through long struggle.  
Heavenly grace bestows the greatest gifts upon you.  
Remember me in these things when you pour offerings on the sacred altars;  
I beseech you, my brother, now be most blessed.

## Excerpts from the Book of Audradus the Modest

*(In du Chesne, *Scriptores rerum Francicarum*, vol. II, p. 390, from the manuscript codex of the most learned Jacques Sirmond.)*

### Chapter VIII

And behold, the Lord descended, and with him all the saints.  
He sat at the boundary of the ether and the air.

Then the sun was darkened for three continuous days,  
and the moon likewise during those nights;  
they gave no ray upon the earth during that period,  
although no cloud covered them.

The Lord ordered all the princes of the churches to come before him.  
They immediately appeared and worshiped him.

### Audradus of Sens, Chorepiscopus

**24**

### A

But when he had blessed them, he said:

> Whose fault is it, dearest brothers, that my inheritance,  
> which the Father redeemed with my blood,  
> is thus attacked and harassed?

Some of them said:

> Lord, it is the fault of the kings.

Then God said:

> Who are these kings? I did not know them; I did not appoint them.

They answered him:

> Louis, their father.

And he said:

> Where is he?

They brought him forward and said:

> Behold, he is here.

And the Lord said to him:

> Why have you placed such discord among your sons  
> that, because of it, my faithful are so severely harassed?

He answered:

> Lord, thinking that my elder son Lothair wished to obey you  
> and govern your Church according to your will,  
> I appointed him in my place to govern your people.  
>   
> But afterward, when I saw him rise up proudly against you  
> and refuse to agree to govern your people according to you,  
> I removed him. Then, seeing that the little one whom you gave me,  
> named Charles, was humble and obedient,  
> I understood that your gifts of mercy were in him.  
> Therefore I appointed him in place of the elder,  
> so that, humble and always obedient,  
> he might serve you according to your will  
> in the ministry of governing your people.

The Lord answered and said to those standing around him:

> Certainly he speaks the truth. He wished to remove the elder from the kingdom because of pride,  
> and he appointed the younger to reign because of humility and obedience.  
> Where are they?

They were immediately brought before him.

And the Lord said:

> Let Lothair, because he said, “I am,” be cast down.  
> Let Charles be established because of his obedience and humility.

I asked:

> What of the third?

Some of those standing nearby said:

> Lord, he took up arms against his father.

And while a severe judgment already threatened him,  
others of those standing nearby said:

> Lord, a good work has been found in him.  
> Although many have been consumed from your service on his account,  
> he nevertheless strives to acquire and substitute others for them from among foreign peoples.

At this the Lord said:

> Since a good work has been found in Lothair,  
> let him stand, and let him himself be established.

When the Lord had completed these things,  
he ascended above all the heavens to the right hand of the Father.

The anniversary day came, and the Lord’s word was fulfilled  
for Charles and his army.

For the enemies killed Vivianus and the beasts of the forest devoured him,  
and many churches were freed from their oppressors in that war,  
as the Lord had foretold.

The legate of the churches had reported this to King Charles  
through a certain Rothbernus, the king’s chamberlain,  
and had explained the whole text of the revelation.

But the king neglected to obey and, returning most dishonorably from Brittany,  
did not restore the churches to their proper order.

For this reason God brought the Northmen into Gaul  
to ravage them by land and sea,  
and the enormity of the evil-doers’ wickedness,  
like the wrath of God, began to boil up everywhere against these kings.

Then the legate of the churches remained before God  
for three continuous days and nights,  
on the third day without food or drink,  
praying that he might have mercy on his people  
and not withdraw the respite that had been granted.

Again the Lord, moved to pity, had mercy  
and in some measure mitigated the anger of his fury,  
still granting the interval of the truce.

---

### Chapter XV

It came to pass in the year 853,  
that is, in the ninth year of the truce, in the third month,  
that King Charles again summoned me to him.

In the presence of the princes of the churches—  
Wanilo, Hipomarus, Amalricus, and Leopardus,  
venerable archbishops—and of the most Christian queen Ermentrude,  
he began to inquire about all these matters,  
and whether I could in any respect be caught in a falsehood in my inquiry.

But I again recounted to him in the Lord’s speech  
everything that had been written above.

He began again and again to promise  
that within two months he would restore the church of Saint Martin,  
and the others that appeared to be exposed,  
to their proper order.

He did not fulfill this.

But, to provoke the Almighty’s anger still further,  
he summoned a certain deacon named Burchard,  
who belonged to the faction of King Lothair,  
and commended to him the Church of Chartres,  
so that he might be bishop there.

As though no cleric of more worthy reputation  
could be found in the kingdom,  
he said to Wanilo, archbishop of Sens,  
that he should ordain him bishop.

The same archbishop summoned me and said:

> I see that our king Charles has acted to provoke God’s anger  
> by summoning Burchard from Lothair’s faction  
> and appointing him pastor of the Church.  
> For throughout all the churches of this kingdom  
> a terrible reputation and report concerning him has spread.  
>   
> But if it might be possible that God’s anger should not be provoked,  
> because he is known to be zealous in secular affairs,  
> I beg you by every means to entreat God  
> that he may deign to show you  
> whether it can in any way be according to his will  
> that this Burchard should become a bishop.

He continued:

> For my part, if it could be so, I would gladly wish it.  
> For he is my kinsman.  
> Do therefore as I advise; and if God should deign to show you anything about it,  
> do not conceal it from me: I adjure you by the faith of God.

While I was praying as usual for the salvation of the brothers,  
and also for the matter mentioned above,  
behold, the Lord deigned to hear me.

Descending from heaven, he surrounded me  
with the radiance of his light where I was praying,  
and said:

> Cursed is the day on which Burchard will be a bishop.

Having said this, he returned to heaven.

One of the angels who had come with him remained at my right hand  
and said:

> Do you know what the Lord said?

I answered:

> Lord, I would like to know more clearly.

He said:

> On every day that Burchard is a bishop,  
> the wrath of God will drip down upon all the churches  
> until their ruin.  
>   
> Therefore the Most High forbids his ordainer  
> by excommunication from laying hands upon him  
> in episcopal blessing.

Having said this, he followed the Lord.

I, worshiping and giving thanks, reported everything  
to my archbishop, who immediately sent this oracle in writing  
to King Charles.

At the assembly of bishops who had gathered at Sens for this reason,  
and at the urging of the aforementioned archbishop,  
I reported it.

At first they refused to ordain this same Burchard as bishop,  
fearing so evident an oracle of God.

But afterward the king’s command,  
and the agreement of many bishops and princes of the kingdom, prevailed,  
and in the fourth month of the ninth year of the truce  
he was ordained bishop.

God’s anger immediately followed his ordination openly.  
In the following month, throughout the whole world,  
vineyards were struck by a burning wind,  
and storms, thunder, and dangers sent from heaven  
were unleashed beyond what can be described.

In that same year the Northmen, ascending the bed of the Loire,  
burned, in the ninth month,  
the monastery of Saint Martin of Tours  
and the basilica revered throughout the whole world,  
with no one able to prevent them.

The clerics of the blessed lord Martin, fleeing from there,  
carried his body with them  
to the monastery of monks called Cormery,  
subject to that same saint.

Then the pact that Christ had made with the kings  
was rendered void,  
because they had in no way turned themselves toward amendment,  
but had most openly turned toward provoking more wrath  
against themselves from God Almighty.

Therefore all peace was broken,  
and every evil, again seeming to revive,  
overflowed upon all the churches  
like an intolerable storm of the sea.

No one, faithful or unbelieving, could doubt  
that the wrath of God from heaven  
was shaking all the churches and the entire world  
everywhere and in every place.

Then the greater part of my embassy was made void,  
and all confusion and cursing began to overflow.

---

### Chapter XVIII

Hear me, brother.

This is the fountain from which, with much labor and study,  
you produced the venerable book  
which you aptly entitled *On the Fountain of Life*.

And the teacher said to me:

> Recognize that cup.  
> From it, indeed, you composed bright poems  
> in the aforesaid Book of the Fountain of Life.

And then God the Father began to recount everything from the beginning, grieving, and said:

> On the day, Son, on which, according to your humanity,  
> you rose from the dead,  
> you asked me, your almighty Father—  
> almighty Son, in all things equal and consubstantial with me—  
> and I gave you the nations as an inheritance.  
>   
> Now you see how those whom you redeemed are deserting you,  
> and how they have not feared to take up tyrannical arms  
> with military oath in the opposing faction  
> against you, who have known them  
> and taught them to worship you.  
>

> so that they might repent and recover from this wickedness,  
> while your saints entreated me, you, and our Spirit,  
> proceeding from me and you and in all things equal and consubstantial with us.  
>   
> They neglected them and counted all these things as nothing  
> in their pride.  
> Rather, they increased their works of wickedness; the following damaged words, concerning penitence, are uncertain.
