### Aldricus, bishop of Le Mans

### His writings: historical works, vol. II

## Deeds of Aldric, bishop of Le Mans, by his disciples

*(From Baluze, Miscellanea.)*

### I

The lord Aldric, bishop of the city of Le Mans,  
was, on his father’s side, by nation a Frank or Saxon,  
and on his mother’s side an Alemannian and Bavarian.

His father was named Sion, and his mother Gehildis.

The aforesaid bishop was born of royal stock  
and was begotten by very noble parents.

From infancy he was raised among bishops  
and was nobly and wisely instructed by them.

He willingly submitted himself to ecclesiastical disciplines  
and was appropriately and suitably incorporated into them.

When he was already twelve years old,  
his aforementioned father brought him to the palace  
and honorably commended him to the glorious Charles,  
king of the Franks, and to his son, lord Louis.

He was graciously received by him.

Adorned with every good custom  
and every gentle virtue, he became all things to all people,  
and, with the Lord’s favor, deserved to please both the king  
and all his nobles and servants.

During the day he served the king and his faithful affectionately;  
at night, secretly, he served the Lord  
with all his efforts, vigils, and prayers,  
and deserved to obtain divine grace.

It happened, however, that whenever he found an opportunity,  
he would secretly chant psalms and offer prayers  
in the church of Saint Mary built in the palace at Aachen.

One day, in the aforesaid church of Saint Mary,  
on the left side of the altar,  
while he was secretly chanting his psalms,  
he was inwardly admonished by divine inspiration  
to abandon secular military service  
and strive to serve the Lord alone.

He was still of tender age and was only beginning to enter puberty.

At first, fearing greatly that this suggestion  
might come from the devil,  
he earnestly prayed to God that, through the intercession  
of blessed Mary, in whose church he was praying,  
if the aforesaid desire was divinely present in his heart,  
God would make it clear to him through his mercy.

But if it were a diabolical impulse,  
he asked that this too be made known to him.

With all his strength, therefore,  
bending his knees and beating his breast  
before the altar of the aforesaid holy Mary,  
he prayed that he might deserve to do the Lord’s will in this matter,  
so that the devil might have no opportunity to deceive the young man.

Divinely strengthened in the good desire mentioned above,  
he was more firmly subjected to it  
and more fully confirmed.

Then he began with all his heart to ask God  
that, if the exhortation came from the devil,  
it might depart from him,  
but that, if it were divine grace,  
he might deserve to fulfill it fully  
according to God’s will.

In this intention, tormented in heart for nearly half a year,  
he was strengthened by angelic and divine consolation,  
and approached the king to beg  
that he might be permitted to abandon secular military service,  
join the spiritual militia,  
and be allowed to serve the Lord.

Nevertheless, he confessed this  
to no one except a single God-fearing friend,  
very close and dear to him,  
for he feared …

## [Scan page 21]

### Life of Aldric, Bishop of Le Mans

But if his parents and friends learned of this, they would not permit him to do it at all. When the king heard this, however, he was exceedingly saddened and promised to give him twelve or more counties if he would abandon the proposal and persevere in his secular service. But when Aldric heard this from the king, he replied that even if the king gave him half his kingdom, he would not on that account abandon his intention.

When the king saw that he could not turn him from his purpose, he granted him permission and a place wherever he might choose in his kingdom. Then, inspired by divine grace, Aldric asked that a place be given him in a certain city called Mediomatrici, also known by the name Metz; and he asked that a prebend be granted to him and only two clerics. The king granted this as well and promised to give him as much as he wished.

Having received permission from the king on these terms, he kissed him and hastened to the city already mentioned. There he was received graciously and devoutly by everyone. He was made a cleric by the bishop of that city, while the bishop and all the clergy sang divine blessings and chanted spiritual hymns. He was clothed in clerical garments and, after the episcopal and priestly imposition of hands and blessing, was placed among the brothers. [The text at this point is damaged and partially illegible.] Serving God day and night, he came to win many for the Lord.

He diligently learned Roman chant and grammar, as well as the order of sacred Scripture. By the gift of the Lord of all, he was thoroughly and most learnedly instructed in these subjects. After two years of his clerical service, he was ordained deacon by the bishop of that city, Gundulf, in the church of Saint Stephen. In that rank he served for nearly three years, striving daily to fulfill the office of the diaconate with extraordinary ability and learning.

After Gundulf, his aforementioned ordainer, had died, another bishop named Drogo—son of Charles, the most devout emperor—was appointed and ordained in the same city. Seeing the good purpose and zeal of the aforementioned Levite Aldric, which he displayed both in his ministry and toward everyone, Drogo began to urge him to become a priest.

The aforementioned deacon Aldric neither wished nor dared to reject the divine blessing to which he was repeatedly summoned by Drogo, bishop of that city and his aforementioned successor and ordainer. While he was nobly fulfilling the office of deacon, the clergy and people chose him, and he was ordained priest.

Growing ever stronger in virtuous deeds, and instructing many through his preaching and good exhortations, he deserved to win many—indeed innumerable people—for God and the holy Church. At length, when the brothers had chosen him, and when his bishop Drogo had urged and encouraged him—though reluctantly—he was elevated there to the position of senior cantor.

In the schools where he had already been appointed master, he wisely instructed many, indeed innumerable people, in the aforementioned arts, and deserved to produce great gain for the holy Church of God—indeed, to educate innumerable people in those arts.

> See the Bertinian Annals, year 632.

He was most learnedly trained in the aforesaid arts. When the aforementioned bishop, Lord Drogo, and all the clergy and people saw that he showed great zeal in these ministries and teachings and had produced many distinguished teachers and masters, they elevated him to a greater ministry, although reluctantly, and appointed him primicerius according to the Roman order. They ordered that the entire clergy, both of the city and of the monasteries, and of the whole diocese of that city, be subject to him, and they made him master of all.

Serving the Lord most zealously in these duties, he deserved to minister graciously to all good people. All good people loved him as they loved themselves, and whatever he commanded them they willingly did.

When the emperor of the Franks, Louis, heard of his reputation, he summoned him to himself and, in his palace, whether Aldric wished it or not, appointed him his senior priest and confessor. There, too, pleasing all the palatine nobles, he became, as was his custom, all things to all people; he was honored and venerated by everyone.

Thus they all loved him—if it may be said so—as they loved themselves, and in everything they willingly and wholeheartedly obeyed his commands as those of a superior. He lived nobly in the emperor’s palace for four months, serving him graciously, and could not obtain permission to escape from there even for a single day and return to his homeland.

The archbishop of that province, Landramn, together with Rorigo, count of the same diocese, and all the noblemen of that diocese, as well as all the palatine nobles, the clergy, and the people, chose him for the bishopric whose name is Le Mans. Through the staff of Landramn, metropolitan of the city of Tours and of the aforesaid diocese, the said bishopric was entrusted to him in the presence of the most glorious Emperor Louis, at the urging of Landramn and while everyone petitioned for it.

Aldric resisted this and did not wish to accept the aforesaid bishopric; nevertheless, although compelled, he accepted the sacred office when everyone urged him to do so. He was ordained by his aforesaid metropolitan and by the other noble and learned bishops who assembled for this purpose. Having been chosen by the clergy and people in the aforesaid city and in the mother church itself, he was consecrated bishop on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January [22 December], in the year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 832.

On the third day after his ordination, the aforementioned lord emperor, arriving in his city, gave thanks and praised the Lord because Aldric had now been ordained bishop. The aforesaid bishop therefore received the emperor Louis graciously and wisely, with psalmody, hymns, songs, crosses, and the other divine rites. Holding him by the hand, he led him to the church, praying at the altars, and commended him to the Lord in his prayers.

He strove to serve the aforementioned emperor and all his people nobly and graciously. There Lord Emperor Louis—

## [Scan page 22]

### Life

—solemnly celebrated the nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, while the aforesaid Bishop Aldric and his clergy most wisely and honorably performed the office.

The emperor remained in the same city for eight days. By his decree he restored to Aldric, to his cathedral church, to its clerics, and to the servants of the Lord serving there, to be possessed in the firmest right for perpetual times, a certain estate called Brogilus and Novavilla, together with all that belonged to it, which had formerly been taken away from that place and granted as a benefice.

### II

In the first year of his episcopate, the aforesaid bishop also succeeded, through his own work and good ingenuity, in bringing water by aqueduct into the aforementioned city of Le Mans, where no one had previously seen water arrive in this way. By the Lord’s help, he caused an adequate supply to be available to all who had previously suffered great need of water and could obtain it only with immense labor.

Previously, no one could buy even one or two half-measures of water within the city unless he paid a denarius to those who brought it from the Sarthe or from some spring, since they had no well there. For this reason water was so expensive.

In that same year he began to build a cloister where his canons could live regularly and canonically. Previously, as is reported, they had never been able to have a cloister; instead, wandering here and there through the city, sleeping and moving about by day and night, they had usually stayed in various dwellings. Because of this impediment they could not attend the divine office as they ought.

He gave them his own house in which they could live, together with its upper rooms, cellars, and other buildings that belonged to it. Nor was this enough for him: he also diligently built other houses around it, nobly and as the work required.

The aforesaid bishop was a very gentle and extremely wise man, learned in speech, retaining all the psalms in order by heart and refined by the most subtle exercise in their meanings. With his tongue devoted to reading, he was an exhorter to every good work. To his most flourishing people he continually preached salutary teachings concerning the Catholic and apostolic faith, preserving them undefiled forever, strengthening the hearts of the faithful.

He was a champion and very strong defender of the orthodox faith; a lover of poverty; gentle toward the needy and also solicitous for them; a redeemer of captives; a benefactor of orphans and widows, providing what was necessary; a lover of Christian religious observance and discipline. Affection for those who wished to live religiously and to possess the fear of God in their hearts dwelt within him.

He was a very gentle and gracious man, adorned with every goodness, beloved by all the clergy and the entire Christian people, slow to anger and quick to show mercy. He returned evil to no one for evil and did not exact vengeance according to merit. Rather, he was pious and merciful toward everyone, drawing all people to himself and dispersing no one.

With the Lord’s aid he deserved to gather a great flock into unity and to produce immense gain within the bosom of God’s holy Church, both within his own diocese and beyond it. He deserved to win many for the Lord.

In the aforementioned cloister, Bishop Aldric therefore built straight and double rows of buildings, in which he nobly and wonderfully constructed various dwellings for the brothers and for providing their necessities.

Moreover, in the same cloister he built from the foundations a church in honor of Saint Stephen. On the fifth day before the Ides of November [9 November] he solemnly consecrated it in honor of that Saint Stephen and of all the saints. On the very day of its consecration a wondrous sign appeared.

A certain priest had lost his gloves there while the aforesaid church was being consecrated. A certain cleric found them and wished secretly to carry them out of the new church. But he could not leave the church of Saint Stephen and all the saints, nor could he carry the gloves away with him, until, before many witnesses, he threw them down inside the church; then he escaped by fleeing.

In the aforesaid church he made six altars.

He placed the first above, in the middle of the apse, and consecrated it in honor of Saint Sophia. In the confession of that altar he placed relics of our Lord Jesus Christ, both from the sponge and from his own sandals.

The aforementioned bishop also made and consecrated a second altar in the upper and right-hand part of the church, in honor of Saint Stephen, Saint Vincent, Saint Gervasius, Saint Privatus, Saint Quirinus, Saint Nabor, and Saint Nazarius, martyrs of Christ; he decently placed their relics in it.

He made a third altar in the upper and left-hand part of the church and consecrated it in honor of Mary, the holy Mother of God; Saint Clement, bishop and martyr of the Roman Church; Saint Albinus; Saint Amandus; Saint Arnulf; Saint Martin; Saint Clement, first bishop of the city of Metz; Saint Audoenus; Saint Martial; Saint Benedict; Saint Paternus; and Saint Silvester, confessors of the Lord. With his own hands he decently placed the relics of these saints in the confession of that altar.

In the lower part and in the apse of the church he made and consecrated a fourth altar in honor of Saint Stephen and all the saints. With his own hands he decently placed and enclosed in it relics of Saint Stephen and many other saints.

In the lower right-hand part of the church he made a fifth altar and consecrated it in honor of Saint Paul, Saint James the apostle, and Saint Matthew the apostle and evangelist. In the confession of that altar he decently arranged and enclosed, with his own hands, relics of the aforementioned holy apostles.

In the lower left-hand part of the church he made a sixth altar and consecrated it in honor of Saint Theodore, Saint Julian, and Saint Lambert, martyrs of Christ. With his own hands he placed their relics in the confession of that altar.

### III

In the year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 834, in the thirteenth indiction, and in the thirty-second year of the reign of the most devout Emperor Louis, in the third year of the ordination of the aforesaid Bishop Aldric, the aforementioned bishop solemnly and decently dedicated the church already mentioned.

On the day of the Kalends of [the text is defective here], in the metropolitan city of Tours, with the consent and election of Landramn, archbishop of the aforesaid city of Tours, and of other bishops, many abbots and counts, and innumerable other prudent men, the most renowned Emperor Louis entrusted to the aforesaid Bishop Aldric the care of the city of Le Mans and the governance of the entire people of its diocese. May almighty God, to whom we humbly pray, grant him everlasting rest and eternal life with us.

In the aforementioned year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December [21 November], the aforesaid Bishop Aldric solemnly consecrated the apse of the mother and senior church of the city. He had founded it anew, wonderfully adorned and constructed it, and built its altar with marvelous workmanship.

He consecrated the aforesaid apse together with the altar already mentioned in honor of Saint Saviour, the holy Mother of God Mary, the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, and Saint Stephen. In that altar he decently placed and marvelously arranged with his own hands relics of the Saviour, of Mary his holy Mother, and of the bodies of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius and Saint Stephen.

He also reconciled and solemnly dedicated another part of the aforesaid mother and cathedral church, whose day of consecration was entirely unknown to everyone, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ the Saviour, the holy Mother of God Mary, the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, and Saint Stephen.

In the aforesaid church he constructed and founded anew ten altars, and on the day mentioned he consecrated them. He ordered the names of the saints in whose memory they were consecrated to be inscribed above them. Even today, those names can be found inserted separately and distinctly in each altar by anyone who investigates carefully.

He made an upper ambulatory running all around the church, in which he nobly constructed and consecrated five altars.

First, in the right-hand and eastern part of the ambulatory, he consecrated an altar in honor of Saint Martin, Saint Hilary, Saint Germanus, Saint Vedastus, Saint Domnolus, Saint Carilefus, and Saint Rigomer, confessors of Christ. He decently placed the relics of the aforementioned saints there with his own hands and according to ecclesiastical custom.

He consecrated another altar, placed in the same ambulatory in the middle of the aforesaid right-hand side, in honor of Saint Peter and Saint John the apostle and evangelist, Saint Andrew, and all the apostles, and placed their relics in the altar.

On the western side of the church, in the same upper ambulatory, he made and consecrated an altar in honor of all the saints, and with his own hands placed in it relics of many saints.

On the left-hand side of the church, in the left ambulatory, in the eastern part, he made and consecrated an altar in honor of Saint Dionysius, Saint Lawrence, Saint Remigius, Saint Medard, Saint Boniface, Saint Rusticus, and Saint Bleutherius, martyrs and confessors of Christ. He placed their relics in the altar with his own hands.

In the middle of the aforesaid left upper ambulatory he made and consecrated another altar in honor of Mary, the holy Mother of God, Saint Anastasis, Saint Genevieve, and all the holy virgins. He placed many relics of the holy virgins in it with his own hands.

Below, on the right-hand or eastern side of the church, he made and consecrated an altar in honor of Saint Ambrose, Saint Benedict, Saint Gregory, Saint Augustine, Saint Julian, Saint Jerome, and Saint Vigor, confessors of Christ. He decently placed their relics in it according to ecclesiastical custom.

Outside the choir, on the right-hand side of the church, he made and consecrated an altar in honor of Saint George, Saint Felix, Saint Symphorian, Saint Sixtus, Saint Tiburtius, and the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter. He decently placed their relics in it.

On the left-hand and eastern side of the church he made and consecrated an altar in honor of Saint Scholastica, Saint Agnes, Saint Lucy, Saint Leodegundis, Saint Afra, Saint Gertrude, and Saint Aldegundis, virgins of Christ. With his own hands he decently placed their relics in it.

Outside the choir, on the left-hand side of the church, he made and consecrated an altar in honor of Saint Agatha, Saint Felicitas, Saint Sabina, Saint Euphemia, Saint Perpetua, Saint Brigid, and Saint Genevieve, virgins of Christ. He decently placed their relics in it with his own hands.

In the middle of the church he made an altar on which he erected a crucifix of our Lord Jesus Christ, wonderfully fashioned in gold and silver. He decently placed that altar, situated in the middle of the church, in honor of the most holy Trinity, with his own hands.

The aforementioned Aldric, bishop of the aforesaid city of Le Mans, in the year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 835, in the twenty-third year of the reign of the most devout Emperor Louis, and in the third year of his own ordination, in the fourteenth indiction, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July [21 June], solemnly consecrated the western part of the aforesaid mother and cathedral church of the city of Le Mans. He had founded it anew, wonderfully adorned it, and brought it to completion.

In it he made an altar in honor of Saint John the Baptist, which he also solemnly consecrated on the aforesaid day of the Kalends in honor of Saint John the Baptist. He placed in it, with his own hands, relics of the aforesaid Saint John the Baptist and of many other saints.

## [Scan page 24]

He made another altar in the right-hand part of the western section of the church and consecrated it on the aforesaid day in honor of Saint Christopher, Saint Hippolytus, and Saint Salunias, martyrs of Christ. He decently placed their relics in the confession of that altar with his own hands.

On the left-hand side of the western part of the senior church, on the day mentioned above, he consecrated a third altar in honor of Saint Victurius, Saint Viventius, Saint Brixius, Saint Arveus, Saint Baudomarus, Saint Alminus, Saint Ulphacius, Saint Julian, the first bishop of that city, Saint Thuriau, Saint Pavasius, and Saint Liborius, confessors of Christ. He decently placed their relics in the aforementioned altar with his own hands.

On the eleventh day before the Kalends of July [21 June], the aforesaid Bishop Aldric was born from the womb of his mother. May almighty God, through the continual intercession of the saints mentioned above and of all the saints, grant him to live eternally and possess everlasting stability with them. Amen.

### IV

The aforesaid Bishop Aldric gave a certain estate to his canons, called Buxarias, together with everything belonging to it and with a forest called Pelicionis. From this, the aforesaid canons could more fully obtain their provisions, serve the Lord more delightfully, and eagerly devote themselves to praying for the aforementioned Emperor Louis and his wife Judith, for their royal children, for their entire army, and for Aldric, the bishop of that city. Thus they might rejoice in serving the Lord with greater delight and zeal.

Concerning the aforesaid estate, he stipulated and confirmed in his charter, which he made for his aforementioned canons concerning that estate, that the brothers and canons living in the city of Le Mans should receive a full meal on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January [22 December], when the senior mother and cathedral church of Le Mans, in honor of Saint Saviour, Mary his holy Mother, Saint Gervasius and Saint Protasius, and Saint Stephen, was solemnly dedicated by the aforementioned Bishop Aldric.

Likewise, he decreed that a full meal should be provided from the aforesaid estate for the aforementioned brothers and canons on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January, the day on which Aldric himself was canonically and solemnly consecrated in the aforesaid city and church by the most noble, learned, and holy bishops.

Likewise, he decreed that on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July [21 June], the aforementioned canons and servants of God should receive a full and excellent meal from the aforesaid estate. On that day Aldric was born from his mother’s womb, and the western part of the aforesaid mother and cathedral church was solemnly dedicated by the same bishop.

Likewise, on the Assumption of the holy Mother of God Mary, which falls on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September [15 August], when the aforesaid church was originally consecrated by Bishop Domnolus—but the day of its consecration had become entirely unknown to everyone—he decreed that, since it had now been renewed, reconciled, and consecrated in honor of the aforesaid holy Mother of God Mary, the saints Gervasius and Protasius, and Saint Stephen, a full meal should solemnly and canonically be provided for the aforementioned servants of God on the prescribed day before the Kalends.

For these five feasts he decreed that the aforementioned canons and servants of God should receive from the aforesaid estate, on each of the feast days, four measures of the finest bread, six excellent rams, two measures of the best wine, one measure of the best beverage, and the other provisions contained in the testament that he made concerning this matter.

### V

In the first year of the ordination and consecration of the aforesaid mother church and of the church of the city of Le Mans, many miracles appeared in the aforesaid church, with the Lord conspicuously granting them before the eyes of many people.

A certain man who was lame and weak in both feet came to the aforesaid church for the evening assembly. While the brothers were fulfilling their vows to the Lord and performing the evening offices, he was restored and healed in both feet before many witnesses. He deserved to receive his former gait, as though he had never been lame or weak.

Another man came to the morning assembly who had been mute from birth and deaf from the time of his nativity. While the canons and servants of God were most devoutly celebrating the morning assembly in the church of the holy Saviour, the holy Mother of God Mary, the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, and Saint Stephen, he fully recovered both hearing and speech there. He was able to speak and hear as though he had never been deaf or mute.

After this, a certain blind man came to the same church. While Mass was being most devoutly celebrated by the aforesaid Bishop Aldric, his fellow priests, and the other ministers, he deserved, by the Lord’s generosity, to receive full sight in the church. He saw as though he had never been blind.

Another man, possessed by a demon and grievously tormented by the devil, often wished to throw himself into fire, water, or other dangers. He was bound and tied with many ropes so that he could not injure anyone. When he came to the aforesaid church for the morning assembly, while the servants of God established there and the aforementioned bishop were intensely performing the divine offices, he was freed from the demon and completely healed, as though he had never been tormented by a demon.

Many other innumerable signs also appeared before witnesses in the aforesaid church, in the first year of his ordination, consecration, and reconciliation, and likewise in the following years. We have not inserted them here because of their number and because of the reader’s and hearer’s fatigue. Yet they were so numerous—whether in casting out demons, restoring the lame, returning hearing, or restoring sight, or in the other benefits of God—that, as I believe, two or three quires could scarcely contain them.

Many other sick people, suffering from fevers and other illnesses, were healed innumerably in the aforesaid church by the Lord’s generosity, and deserved to recover their former health and attain complete healing.

### VI

When the aforementioned Lord Aldric, bishop of the aforesaid city, received the bishopric on the fifth day before the Ides of November [9 November], through the generosity of the most devout Emperor Louis and with the consent and election of many noblemen, as has been stated above, certain rivals of the holy Church of God and of Aldric informed and firmly protested to the aforesaid Lord Emperor Louis that the abbey of Saint Vincent did not belong by right to the aforementioned bishop, but ought to be the imperial fisc of the aforesaid Lord Emperor Louis.

Emperor Louis therefore sent his vigorous and faithful agents to investigate and ascertain the truth: they were to determine whether it ought to be fisc property or whether it should belong by right and dominion to the aforesaid bishop.

Aldric was greatly distressed and saddened by this, because on such a pretext the aforesaid abbey of Saint Vincent might be lost from the right and dominion of the bishop and unjustly taken away. He had no acquaintances there and did not know the matter himself. He earnestly prayed to the Lord that, through his negligence, the abbey of Saint Vincent might not be lost from the right of the aforesaid Church or alienated.

The Lord heard him in this matter and greatly consoled him. With the Lord’s support he deserved to vindicate the property and retain it, by the firmest right, under the jurisdiction of his cathedral church. This was so even though, on the very day of his entry—when he first entered the city of Le Mans on the feast of Saint Martin—the investigation had been conducted. There he had witnesses who testified and confirmed that the abbey belonged by right to the bishopric assigned to him and ought to remain under its authority and jurisdiction.

He was unable at that time to find the charter which Lord Domnolus had made concerning the aforesaid abbey, when he enriched that monastery and the aforementioned church with the property of his cathedral see; the document had then been hidden from him. But after he had vindicated the matter and obtained the little monastery confirmed by imperial decree, he deserved, with the Lord’s assistance, to find and recover that charter.

For this reason we have decided to insert the aforesaid charter in this little work, so that, if—God forbid—in future times any dispute should arise concerning the aforesaid abbey and someone should wish to conceal the charter by some contrivance or evil design, a copy of it might be found in this work. Through it the faithful of that holy Church of God might have consolation, knowing that the abbey had never been lost from the right and jurisdiction of the aforesaid church.

Likewise, we have decided to insert here the charter which the aforementioned Lord Domnolus made concerning the estate belonging to the church of Saint Vincent and to the use of the brothers living there, with the consent of his canons and of other bishops and noblemen.

### VII

#### Copy of the gift and transfer which Lord Domnolus made to the church on the day of the dedication of the aforesaid church of Saint Vincent: of the estate of Tricione and Fraxinidus, of the small estate called Debuc, and of other small estates, properties, and territories belonging to his cathedral see

To the venerable Church of Le Mans and its clergy, Domnolus, bishop.

It was fitting for us to make a desirable intention known to your Charity, because, if your consent should approve the desire of our heart, we believe that nothing could ever overturn what we have jointly confirmed, through anyone’s opposition at any time. For the sake of the salvation of the people, as though to guard the city, we have dared—with God’s help and with yours—to bring here the relics of the lord and venerable martyr Saint Vincent through a presumptuous undertaking.

We have raised that place to the height of dignity; therefore we ask that it likewise be enriched by our gift. If your judgment should confer honor upon us, we ask that this little charter of donation be strengthened by your authority.

I therefore give, and wish to be understood to have given, in honor of the same Lord Vincent, the estate called Tricione, which Abundantius is known formerly to have held. Its boundaries run by the designated places as far as Confluentes, then to Bucias, along the Indua, as far as the boundary of Prohacense; adjoining the territory of Saturniacense. From there it proceeds by the road of Saturniacense as far as the field of Daulfus; then from the thicket of Censurius as far as the house of Mera; from there it reaches the field of Locogiacense, beginning from Tricione.

It includes everything that our deacon Mallaricus appears to have possessed during his lifetime by usufruct, with fields, meadows, pastures, woods, waters, and watercourses, and with the slaves bearing these names: Leudomadus with his wife Leudomalla and the infant Litomer; Leudolfus; likewise another Leudolfus; Chariobandus; Vinofleda; and Mogiana. It also includes the herd of horses which Allomer, residing within that boundary, appeared to guard.

Likewise, the estate of Fraxenetum, which the priest Ap[pius?] of blessed memory held, with the thickets of Marcilliacense, vineyards, woods, meadows, pastures, waters, and watercourses, together with ten resident dependants living there for the property of the Church.

All persons belonging to that house, whom the defender Deudoricus has obtained by designation to be possessed, are included, with the slaves bearing these names: Lanvonetus; Fredulus with his wife Taligia; Sesulfus; Castinus with his wife Leudomalla and his son Leudoghisilus; with his daughter Childegund; Puppa with her son Populonius; Leudomundus; and Leudomanda, together with all the freed persons of the aforesaid priest.

Likewise, the small estate at Buccis, which we received from the priest Eutelius, with the slaves who appear to work there; a meadow within the vineyards above the bank of the Sarthe, together with whatever Abundantius or the Church’s agents appear to have held; Chjldigisilus, a boy, with the herd of cattle which he himself— [the text breaks off here].

[scan page 26]

44

which he is seen to guard, together with the adjoining field beside the aforesaid meadow, which we made through our own labor: Sescismund with his wife Wiliare. All these things, by this deed of donation—which we unanimously asked the aforesaid deacon Aunulf to write—are established as having been transferred, so that the basilica under the stated name may have them and hold them; and whoever receives the dignity of that place shall claim them for himself by hereditary right, to possess them perpetually.

If at any time either the bishop of the city or any other person should wish to withdraw from the rule of the said basilica anything donated or transferred by us, let him receive a curse instead of a blessing and incur the offense of our Lord Jesus Christ and of all the holy martyrs; and, with the Lord’s help, let our will perpetually obtain firmness, [text corrupt: perhaps a reference to] the penalty of the Julian law.

Enacted in the city of Le Mans, in the eleventh year of the reign of our lord King Chilperic, on the day before the Nones of March.
