### XXXII

Here follows a copy of the imperial precept of Lord Louis concerning the aforesaid privilege of Saint Savior and of the monks, which the aforementioned Bishop Aldricus made for them with pious affection.

(See above, column 1271.)

### XXXIII

Here follows the account of the alms of the aforesaid Aldricus, bishop of the aforesaid city of Cenomanicum, explaining how he individually arranged what had been entrusted to him and ordained by this document that it should be given, in an orderly manner, to Christ’s male and female servants.

In the name of Saint Savior and in veneration of holy Mary, Mother of God, and of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius and of Saint Stephen, whose churches I appear, although unworthily, to have as my titular churches, I, Aldricus, unworthy and sinful bishop of the city of Cenomanicum and of the aforesaid church, wish it to be known to all the bishops, priests, deacons, subdeacons, and other ministers of the holy Church of God residing in our diocese and parish, and to all the faithful.

Considering the condition of human frailty, together with the permission of Lord Louis, the most pious emperor, and also with the consent of Ursmarus, metropolitan archbishop of the city of Tours, and of the other bishops of the neighboring provinces, and of the holy bishops of many other provinces, I began to consider, together with our canons and other parishioners, both priests and others serving divine worship, and with noble laymen—both our own and other free and good men—in what useful and reasonable manner, after my death, my small resources and what had been entrusted to me might be distributed for the benefit of the holy mother church and as my alms.

I did this lest, God forbid, anyone should seize, steal, or convert them to his own uses, as we know has already happened in many cases. Rather, let everything be distributed for the benefit of the holy Church, for the support of those serving us, for the provision of our clerics, both monks and canons, for the assistance of the laymen who appear to serve our church and us, and also for the feeding of the poor.

This distribution shall be made, by the counsel of the aforesaid metropolitan and through the hands of faithful priests or deacons and faithful laymen whom I shall have appointed and designated for this purpose, faithfully and reasonably, for the uses and needs named above, as we shall state below.

Whatever money of various kinds and clothing may at that time be found in our storehouse, let a full tenth part be distributed to the church which we built beside the river Sarthae, in the place formerly called Broilus Casalis, and which we, although unworthy, consecrated in honor of the Lord Savior and of holy Mary, Mother of God, and of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius and of Saint Stephen. Let it be given faithfully and charitably to the monks serving the Lord there.

Let a ninth part be given to the church which we built between the river Sarthae and the city wall, in which we have placed monks and decreed that they should live under the rule of Saint Benedict. We, although unworthy, canonically consecrated this church in honor of the aforesaid Lord Savior and of holy Mary, his Mother and the Mother of God and the Lord, and of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, and also of Saint Stephen. Since it appears to be subject to the mother church, let this ninth part be assigned without any delay, prohibition, or impediment to the monks, nuns, and the entire congregation serving the Lord there, faithfully and charitably.

Of the remainder of what is found in the storehouse, let four portions be made, according to the decrees of the canons: of gold, silver, other metals, utensils, clothing of various kinds, and all household goods.

One portion shall remain with the church entrusted to us; another shall be given as our alms to faithful poor persons; the third shall be given to the clerics, chaplains, and vassals; the fourth to the priests of the city, the monastery priests, the suburban priests, and the remaining parishioners, and to the deacons, subdeacons, other ministers, and clerics, as may best be arranged.

For this must be observed above all: everything must be done with charity.

### [Scan page 39]

Likewise, with the wine alone which may at that time be found both in the city and in its districts, let this be done as has been said: one tenth of the aforesaid wine shall be given to the monks, and a ninth part to the nuns living in the aforesaid places. Let the remainder be divided into four parts and distributed faithfully and charitably by the aforesaid men, or let it be distributed reasonably from the money found in our storehouse, as has been said.

Concerning all the remaining wine, and all the grain of every kind, and the legumes or hay stored in various places and in all our estates entrusted to us, we wish and earnestly request that ten equal portions be made and divided.

The first shall be faithfully kept for the mother church and for our successor whom the Lord shall choose.

The second shall be given to the vassals, chaplains, and servants who appear to serve the Lord and us in our residence, so that they themselves may not, God forbid, suffer want, but may have the means by which they can be supported and may be able, with God’s help, to remain usefully in service with our successor who will soon be appointed.

The third shall be given to the canons, servants of the holy mother church, and the nuns who offer daily offerings to the Lord in it, so that they may be pleased to offer their offerings to the Lord for me, a sinner, in future times.

The fourth shall be given to the monks who are in the monastery of Saint Calais and in the nunnery at Savonnières, and to the monastic nuns who are in the monastery at Intramnes.

The fifth shall be given to the monks who are in the monastery of Saint Savior, a little less than a mile from the city, above the river Sarthae; and to the monks who are in Saint Vincent near the city; and to the nuns who are in the monastery of Saint Savior and of Saint Mary and of Saint Gervasius, situated between the river Sarthae and the city wall.

The sixth shall be given to the congregations serving Christ faithfully in the other various monasteries, both in the parish of Cenomanicum and in the county of Angers, and in that of Tours and of Exmes, and throughout the other counties, insofar as ability and resources permit; let it be distributed with all reasonable discretion.

The seventh shall be distributed discreetly and reasonably to the priests, deacons, and other clerics of our parish who serve the Lord in the various churches, so that they may always desire to pray for me, the most wretched sinner, and offer sacrifices to the Lord continually. With bent knees I ask that they be urged to do this assiduously.

The eighth, as we have said, of the wine, grain of various kinds, legumes, and hay, shall be given reasonably and discreetly and entirely to the household servants living in our estates entrusted to us, who have worked for these things by their own labor, so that they may also be pleased to pray for me, a sinner. I ask that they be very frequently urged to do this.

The ninth and tenth parts of all the grain, wine, hay, and legumes shall be distributed entirely to the poor, widows, and orphans, faithfully, with complete discretion and charity.

For I ask all of you to deign to pray for me, so that, with the Lord’s approval, I may deserve to receive remission of all my sins and to have eternal life. Let it be so, let it be so.

As for the herds of animals, together with their herdsmen, and the herds of cows and oxen, pigs, sheep, and goats, which are at Bretil, in the county of Noviacum, and at Proliacum within the fifth estate, and at Novavilla above the river Sarthae, and at Cavania, and at Cepetum above the Sarthae, and at the estate of Bruonis in Belsa, and at another Proliacum on the river Viduus, we leave them to the church entrusted to us and to our successor, to be possessed, profitably used, and managed in their entirety.

In the whole bishopric I found fewer than twenty draft animals. Now, thanks be to God, I leave seven herds together with their herdsmen. Nor in the entire bishopric entrusted to us did I find, among all the livestock, as much as I now leave, with the Lord’s help, in one of the aforesaid little estates, apart from what I bought at my own expense and acquired by my own labor.

Therefore I humbly ask that no one find it harsh or objectionable if I give to my benefactors and donate to those serving me what I acquired by my sweat and bought at my own expense, and if, by offering it to the Lord as my alms, I order it to be faithfully distributed. I humbly ask that it be given to God’s servants and to the poor for the redemption of my many and innumerable sins.

Therefore, let the herds of draft animals, together with their herdsmen, and the herds of cows and oxen, pigs, sheep, and goats, which are at Alamaniscas, and the three herds of draft animals with their herdsmen, and the oxen of both kinds, pigs, sheep, and goats, which are at Drimiacum near Mantula and at Paciacum—in the estate, namely, over which David now has charge—be given in their entirety, without any delay or diminution, to our brothers and canons, faithfully and with all charity.

The herds of draft animals, together with their herdsmen, and the oxen of both kinds, pigs, sheep, and goats, which are within the monastery of Saint Calais, and at the estate of Floriacum, and at Conflentium, and at the estate of Maurus, and at Cotnnis, and at the estate of Martis, and at Rusciacum, and at Campo Sigalaici, and in that cell called Cantarnacum, and in the various dwellings built around the monastery, shall all be given in their entirety, without diminution or delay, to the monks serving the Lord in the monastery of Saint Calais, in the cell called Savonnières, and in the cell called Savonnières, for service to the Lord.

Third, the herds of draft animals, together with their herdsmen, and the oxen, cows, goats, and sheep which are at Hallay, and the four swine-yards situated in that same estate, both in the dwellings and in the other places where they appear to be, and the herds which are at Couré-Quadrice, in Saxon, shall all be given in their entirety—draft animals, oxen, cows, pigs, sheep, and goats—to the monks who serve the Lord in the church of Saint Savior above the river Sarthae, where that abbot appears to preside, with complete integrity and charity, without any hesitation, contradiction, or delay.

### [Scan page 40]

The herds of draft animals, together with their herdsmen, and the oxen of both kinds, pigs, sheep, and goats which are at Colonia beside the city, at the court called Villa, which Guadolduus now administers, at Carraria above the river Sarthae, and at Canon, shall be given in their entirety to the monks serving the Lord in the monastery of Saint Vincent.

The herds of draft animals, together with their herdsmen, and the cows, oxen, sheep, pigs, and goats which are at Gres and Fraxinidum, in Belsa, and at Semur, shall be granted without delay or diminution to the monks serving the Lord at Gres in the church of Saint Mary and Saint Almirus.

Of the horses mentioned above, I order that two of the best that may be found, properly equipped and adorned, be given to our aforesaid lord metropolitan; and two others, the next best that may be found, to Didanus, bishop of the city of Angers, well adorned with three draft animals [tribus jumentis; the precise construction is uncertain]. I entreat these holy bishops, if by the Lord’s mercy they survive me, to come at my death.

I earnestly ask that my soul be commended to the Lord through their holy prayers, and I humbly request that my body, together with my soul, be commended to the Lord in their prayers and that I be buried with their prayers.

I also earnestly entreat them all, and, prostrate at their feet, I ask them to pray for me and concerning me, that they may do for me, the most wretched sinner, what they wish their successors to do concerning them after their death, and that they may preserve and confirm this entire matter intact.

The herds of draft animals, together with their herdsmen, and the cows, oxen, sheep, pigs, and goats which are at Aviniacum, or at Casiliacum, and in that part of Paciacum over which Gundoldus now has charge, shall be given in their entirety, with the greatest charity and complete integrity and without any delay, to our sisters, the monastic nuns whom we have placed between the city wall and the river Sarthae in the church of the Lord Savior and of holy Mary, his Mother and ever-virgin, and of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius and of Saint Stephen, to live under the monastic order and under the rule of Saint Benedict.

The herds of draft animals, together with their herdsmen, and the oxen of both kinds, sheep, pigs, and goats which are at Rupiacum shall be given in their entirety, without any diminution or delay, to my brother Isaac and his son Rotgarius.

The herds of draft animals, together with their herdsmen, and the oxen of both kinds, pigs, sheep, and goats which are at Contrella, at Varennis, at Nuidonense, at Breuviacum in the county of Exmes, at Artinis above the river Liz, at Lancianum beyond the Loire, and at Vodelium, shall be distributed in their entirety, discreetly and reasonably, among the vassals who serve us in our residence and the clerics who serve the Lord in our chapel.

All the remaining herds of draft animals, oxen of both kinds, sheep, pigs, and goats which are in the cultivated lands and in the forest of Uvastina, in various dwellings and places, both above the river Liz and in the forest of Uvastica, and in Tricium, in various dwellings and places, and at Tauriaco, in the county of Bayeux, at Vetusvicus, at Celsriacum, at Nascas, at Cadarus, and at Colonia within the river Meduana, at Culcamia beyond the river Loire, at Callemare, at Mount Sodeoris, and in all the dwellings built there, and at Rivo Petrosus, and at Villa Nova in the county of Meaux, and at the estate of Macunus, at Bioca above the river Beuvron, and at Villena in the county of Paris, we implore and ask that they be distributed carefully and reasonably, with all fear and reverence, among our alms, priests, servants of God, or the poor; and we desire that everything be done with charity.

Concerning our horses, pack animals, mules, asses, and foals, which we still possess and without which royal and common service cannot easily be performed, let those to whom we entrust them arrange what should be done with them, both during my life and after my death.

Moreover, I order four good horses to be given for the place of my burial and to the brothers serving the Lord there. As for the remaining horses, I wish each of those who have been appointed and designated to carry out our alms to receive one as a blessing, so that they may be more willing to pray for me and to carry out the task entrusted to them.

Of the remaining horses, foals, mules, and asses, we order that three portions be made. One portion shall remain with the church entrusted to us and with our holy successor. Another shall be distributed carefully and reasonably among the clerics, vassals, servants, and household officials serving us. The third shall be faithfully and reasonably distributed as our alms, in whatever manner those entrusted with this may know and be able.

I also command and entreat them to act and distribute everything so carefully and reasonably that they will not fear rendering an account of it in the presence of our Lord Jesus Christ, and that they may not receive, God forbid, eternal condemnation, but an everlasting reward.

All those things which at the present time, as has been said, are found in the aforesaid places and estates, both within and outside them, I, with a devout mind and sound body, offer devotedly to the Lord God, for the great and excessive burden of my sins. Through this charter, which I dictated with a sound mind and ordered to be written according to the foregoing, and which I confirmed below with my own hand, I voluntarily and devoutly hand over the things written above to be fulfilled and faithfully carried out, just as this little page of the testament declares.

If anyone should presume to act otherwise, God forbid, with respect to the aforesaid possessions, insofar as he may be able and prevail, let him render an account of it to the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, to whom these things, prescribed for fulfillment and completion, have been devoutly offered and handed over. Before the tribunal of that eternal judge he shall on this account render the most grievous reckoning.

I first call upon my successor who will soon be appointed, whoever he may be, and, as though prostrate at his feet, I humbly entreat him to act concerning me and for me, the most wretched sinner, as he wishes his successors to act concerning him after his death, and to preserve and confirm this entire matter intact, just as …

# Aldric of Le Mans, Bishop

[The supplied text begins mid-sentence.] He wishes his possessions to be preserved after him. Therefore I humbly beseech that this little testamentary document be preserved in every respect; and if anyone should wish to act otherwise regarding what is inserted here, I beg that he correct him and provide every assistance to those whom he has expressly named for carrying this out, or to whom this business has been entrusted, so that they may complete these things without any impediment. But if—God forbid—he should act otherwise, let him render a trembling account of this before the tribunal of our Lord Jesus Christ.

I earnestly implore my holy successor, whoever the Lord may wish him to be, and all priests—both monks and canons—as well as all clerics and laypeople dwelling and residing in our diocese and parish, that on the anniversary of my death each year they diligently undertake to celebrate and faithfully pray for me, and devoutly sing vigils and Masses, so that, with the Lord’s favor, I may be worthy mercifully to receive remission of all my sins and indulgence, and may moreover be able to possess eternal life. Amen.

I also beseech my lord successor, by Almighty God, and I adjure all our brothers and fellow priests, that they faithfully urge him, if circumstances permit and if it pleases him, each year on the anniversary of the day of my death to provide from his own resources a full and good meal for the priests mentioned above, both monks and canons, and for the remaining clerics and the poor. But if this should prove burdensome or difficult for him—God forbid—then the meal which is now prepared and provided in the villa of Buxarias, which I willingly and most devoutly gave to our brothers and canons in a testament firmly ratified and confirmed by the privilege of the most pious lord Emperor Louis, and which I left to them for perpetual possession and enjoyment, on the day of my nativity and ordination: I ask that this meal be transferred entirely to the day of my death and anniversary, and that everything be done there in every respect as it is contained in the aforesaid testament, and that it be carried out most devoutly and faithfully as it is written in it. Thus, on that day, both priests and clerics and also the poor and needy who have prayed for me, a most wretched sinner, may have food and consolation, and may all devoutly pray there that I be granted eternal rest.

Moreover, I beg my aforesaid successor to preserve in every respect the testament which I made concerning the aforesaid villa of Buxarias for our brothers and canons, and to ensure that what it contains concerning the five meals for them and for the other priests, clerics, and poor be diligently fulfilled, so that at each of the festivals all may pray and say:

“Lord, grant eternal rest and eternal life to Aldric, our bishop. Amen.”

Regarding the matters just mentioned, therefore, let no one think that anything is mine except for improvement and canonical administration, since I have handed over to the Lord, through this present testament, everything that is mentioned and written in this document, in such a way that it may be used to fulfill and carry out the aforesaid provisions. I have firmly delegated it, and, as it is distinguished and inserted in this little document, I have ordered and requested with the greatest insistence that it be done. If anyone should act otherwise concerning the prescribed and offered things, insofar as he has the ability, or should handle them worse, let him bring a trembling account of his presumption before the tribunal of our Lord Jesus Christ.

I earnestly beseech everyone to act concerning everything written in this document in such a way that, in the sight of the Lord—God forbid otherwise—and with God’s grant, they may be worthy to possess eternal life together with the holy and elect of God. Amen.

## XL

### Concerning the dedication of the principal altar of the monastery of Anisola

In the year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 838, in the first indiction, in the twenty-fifth year of the reign of the lord Louis, most pious emperor, and in the sixth year of the ordination of Aldric, bishop of the city of Le Mans, on the fifth day before the Ides of May, the principal altar of the principal church of the monastery of Anisola was solemnly dedicated by the aforesaid Bishop Aldric in honor of the Lord Savior, of holy Mary, his mother, and of Saint Martin, the distinguished confessor.

On the aforesaid day before the Ides, the said Bishop Aldric was received with psalmody by the monks and the other noblemen in that monastery, after the aforesaid monastery of Anisola had been restored to him by the lord Emperor Louis. May the Lord grant him eternal life in answer to the prayers of those mentioned above and of all the saints. Amen.

> Hail, our bishop; all, Aldric, beseech you:  
> Now a lofty lord, now a humble father.  
> Behold, your fame proclaims the praises of a sacred deed  
> As far as the lofty homes of the Gauls.  
> You are the pious hope of your country, its solace and excellent strength,  
> Its strong wall and mighty shield.

## XLI

### Concerning the establishment and reception of hospices; the six bodies of saints brought into and placed in the bosom of the mother church, whose names are written here; the twelve bells placed in the bell towers of the mother church and sounded in succession at the several hours; and the consecration of bishops, priests, and those of the other orders, including nuns; and concerning commemorations of church dedications

The aforementioned Bishop Aldric endeavored to establish two hospices in the aforesaid city of Le Mans.

He strove to build one of them near the aforesaid city of Le Mans, on the river Sarthe, at the foot of the bridge of Saint Mary, because of the abundance of water and pasture. It was intended for the reception of bishops, counts, abbots, and all visitors. In it he also built a church, which he solemnly dedicated in honor of Saint Stephen, and he constructed and arranged other buildings for carrying out the aforesaid work, rationally, magnificently, and in an orderly manner.

He built the other hospice beside the mother church, that is, the principal church of the city, within the city, so that many poor and sick people, the blind and the lame, those burdened by other infirmities, and the needy might be received there, and so that food and bedding might be supplied to them adequately and prudently.

The aforesaid hospices were also nobly endowed by the said venerable Bishop Aldric from the resources of his own episcopal see. He canonically and rationally assigned to the aforesaid hospices, for the use of guests, pilgrims, the poor, and other visitors, villas or tithes, as is contained in the testaments made concerning them and inserted there, with the consent of many bishops and of his fellow priests. He confirmed these grants through testaments ratified by bishops, priests, other noblemen, and free men.

The aforesaid Aldric, venerable bishop of the said city, also found six bodies of saints that were being neglected in deserted churches, with regard to divine services, lights, and the other forms of divine worship. With the counsel of his fellow priests, he decently and appropriately placed them in the bosom of the church of his see and in the confession of the principal altar of that church. They were:

the body of Saint Julian, bishop of the aforesaid city and its first preacher;

that of Saint Thuribius, the aforesaid Bishop Julian’s successor;

that of Saint Pavacius, likewise bishop of the aforesaid city and an excellent preacher;

that of Saint Romanus, a distinguished priest and, as is reported, a nephew of Saint Julian and a minister of the holy Roman Church; some also attest that he was the brother of Saint Julia and of Saint Tevestina, the distinguished virgin, who built a small monastery of Saint Mary on the property of the principal church, with the assistance of Saint Innocent, bishop of the aforesaid city;

that of Saint Ada, also called Adrehildis, who, as it is read, at the urging of the aforesaid Saint Innocent came from the monastery of Saint Mary situated in the city of Soissons to the city of Le Mans, and there, in the aforesaid monastery of Saint Mary in the suburb of Le Mans, taught the rule of Saint Benedict and properly organized it;

a portion of the body of Saint Liborius, bishop and excellent confessor of the aforesaid city; and the greater part of the body of Saint Haduindus.

The aforesaid bodies of the saints were placed in the church which the aforesaid Bishop Aldric of the aforesaid city solemnly consecrated in honor of the Lord Savior, of holy Mary, his mother, of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, and of Saint Stephen, and also in veneration of all the saints. He solemnly, decently, and orderly placed the aforesaid bodies in the confession of the principal altar of that same church, as has been stated, with the intention that services, lights, and the other things pertaining to divine worship and the honor of the saints should be fully maintained there. Later, wherever the need to establish monasteries should require it, he would place the aforesaid bodies individually in each monastery, so that through their memories and evident intercessions divine worship might increase still more and the praise of God might be improved and multiplied in many ways, as subsequent events, with the Lord’s favor, are shown to have confirmed.

The same Aldric also endeavored to cast and install twelve bells of the finest metal in the aforesaid principal and mother church of the city. He placed them decently in the bell towers of that principal church and arranged that they should resound and ring marvelously and in an orderly fashion at each succession of the hours, so that through them he might decently and solemnly summon the people to church, and so that from them greater and manifold praise of the Lord might adorn and increase the church. Thus, amid well-sounding cymbals, all might constantly praise the Lord; and whenever their sweet sound resounded in the ears of the people, everyone might remember his sins and invoke the Lord’s mercy for them at each hour, so that they might be worthy to receive forgiveness and absolution, be made clean and pure from all the stains of sin, and attain everlasting glory.

The aforesaid Bishop Aldric was possessed of such distinction, honor, and affection that his reputation reached even the Roman See. The lord Gregory, the venerable apostolicus (pope) of the church of the Roman See, sent him from Rome to the region of Le Mans his priestly vestment, namely the vestment in which he had been clothed at Easter. He also sent him a pastoral staff, called a *ferula*, together with his letter, inviting him, if it were possible, to come to him. He granted that whatever petition and blessing he wished to receive from the See of Saint Peter, he would willingly and gladly send and grant it either in person or through his own messenger.

For the aforementioned bishop was the emperor’s counsellor and one of his foremost men; both the lord emperor and his magnates and the great men of the realm deferred to him, trusted him greatly, and declared themselves obedient and well-disposed toward him in all things.[^c0007-1] Yet he was greatly distressed because they kept him so often at court, and he was consequently unable to carry out his ministry as he wished and desired. For he was very often detained at court for almost a whole year and remained there, though unwillingly. Thus many things remained unfinished, both in his city and in his monasteries and parish; some were not even begun, although he prudently planned and eagerly wished to accomplish them for the completion of divine worship, the magnification of the praise of almighty God, and the benefit of the holy mother church.

The aforesaid Bishop Aldric performed sixty ordinations at various canonical times. He consecrated seven bishops, eight hundred priests, and nine hundred deacons, as well as subdeacons and the remaining orders as need required. Because of the length of the matter and the weariness of writer and reader, we have not inserted their names here, but in another schedule, in which we have set down more fully their names, witnesses, titles, dates, and the other particulars relevant to this matter. Whoever wishes to know these matters more fully may find them there; and if any dispute concerning their ordination should arise in future times, that schedule will fully show how, on what grounds, and to what titles they are known to have been ordained. Whoever wishes may find that schedule with the chief custodian of the mother and city church. The aforesaid pontiff also consecrated, at various canonical times, one hundred and twenty virgins among nuns and canonesses. In the monastery of Intramnes he canonically consecrated forty-five virgins as nuns. In the monastery of Saint Mary near the city on the river Sarthe, which he himself newly founded and adorned, he consecrated thirty-eight virgins as nuns, and seventeen other canonical virgins serving the Lord in various places.

## XLII

### Concerning the translation of the body of Saint Pavacius and the right arm of Saint Liborius

In the year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 840, in the third indiction, in the twenty-seventh year of the reign of Louis, most pious Augustus, and in the eighth year of Aldric, bishop of this parish and founder of this monastery, on the seventh day before the Ides of July, the body of Saint Pavacius and the right arm of Saint Liborius were solemnly translated by the aforesaid bishop and other bishops, priests, and the remaining sacred orders into this church of Saint Saviour. Here they were decently buried in a most noble shrine by the aforesaid bishops and priests, with signs following; through their prayers we ask to be delivered from all evils and to enjoy all good things eternally, with the help of him to whom belong honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

## XLIII

### Ordinance of Aldric, bishop of the city of Le Mans, concerning the lights and incense of the principal church of the city

It was established by Aldric, bishop of the city of Le Mans, that every night in the principal church three oil lamps should burn from Vespers throughout the night until morning, and, when the season required it, one wax candle. At Nocturns or Matins, ten oil lamps and five wax candles should burn every night: three before the principal altar; a fourth before the altar of the Holy Trinity or before the crucifix; and a fifth before the altar of Saint John.

The lamps made of oil should burn at the altars and in the places appointed: one between the principal altar and the episcopal throne; another before the steps of the principal altar; a third in the middle of the choir; a fourth at the exit of the choir; a fifth before the altar of Saint George, Saint Felix, Saint Symphorian, and the other saints whose names appear to be inscribed above it; a sixth before the altar of Saint Agatha, Saint Felicitas, Saint Sabina, and the other holy virgins whose names appear to be written above it; a seventh before the altar of the Holy Trinity; an eighth before the altar of Saint John the Baptist; a ninth before the altar of All Saints; a tenth before the altar of Saint Christopher, Saint Hippolytus, Saint Saturninus, and the other saints whose names appear to be written above it; and an eleventh before the altar of Saint Victor, Saint Brixius, Saint Arveus, and the other saints in whose honor it is known to have been consecrated.

On all Sunday nights and on the feasts of the twenty saints, it was established that more lights should be kindled and burn: thirty oil lamps and five wax candles.

The same provision applies on the feasts of Saint John the Apostle and Evangelist; the Holy Innocents; the octaves of the Lord; the octave of Epiphany; the feast of Saint Agnes; the feast of Saint Agatha; the feast of the Apostles Philip and James; the Finding of the Holy Cross; the feast of Saint Peter; likewise the feast of Saint Paul; the feast of Saint Lawrence; the Beheading of Saint John the Baptist; the feast of Saint Michael the Archangel; the feast of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle; the feast of Saint Matthew the Apostle and Evangelist; the feast of the Apostles Simon and Jude; the feast of All Saints on the Kalends of November; the feast of Saint Martin; the feast of Saint Cecilia, virgin and martyr; and the feast of Saint Andrew the Apostle.

These feasts are also to be celebrated with greater solemnity, namely Epiphany, the Purification of Saint Mary, the Ascension of the Lord, Pentecost, the dedication of the western part of the principal church and of the altar of Saint John the Baptist, which falls on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July, the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, the Assumption of Saint Mary, the Nativity of Saint Mary, the bishop’s feast, which is celebrated on the feast of Saint Thomas the Apostle, and the dedication of the mother and principal church’s own principal altar.

On these feasts it was established that the lights should burn threefold, namely ninety oil lamps and ten wax candles—one hundred or more, according to the opportunity and the space. Nevertheless, it was in no way permitted that there be fewer, but rather more. At the Nativity of the Lord, it was established that everything should be done with the solemnity appropriate to those days; and on the feast of Saints Gervasius and Protasius and of Saint Stephen, it should be done as well as possible.

The aforesaid bishop also established that incense of good fragrance should be offered at each altar and carried to the brothers gathered in the church and to the people coming to church for Matins, Mass, Vespers, and Compline. These things are to be performed most devoutly on each ordinary day, and more fully and solemnly on Sundays and feast days.

## XLIV

It also seemed fitting to insert in this document, which is known to have been written concerning certain acts of the bishops who lived in the city of Le Mans up to Aldric, bishop of that city, an account or memorandum of how the aforesaid Aldric, bishop of the aforementioned city, legally acquired before the lord Emperor Louis the monastery of Anisola, in which the distinguished confessor Saint Calais rests bodily. Thus, if any dispute concerning it should later arise, a copy of the aforesaid memorandum written in this document might be available for good men to read.

If anyone should at any time thereafter attempt to bring any claim concerning this matter against the aforesaid mother church and city church or against its successors, this document will show how the matter was vindicated, and he will not be able to vindicate whatever he seeks to claim. The vindication inserted below shall remain firm and stable for all time.

### Here begins the account, vindication, or memorandum of how the monastery of Anisola was canonically and legally vindicated by Bishop Aldric as belonging to the rights of the mother church of Le Mans before the lord Emperor Louis

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

In the time of Louis, most pious Augustus, the following claim or vindication was made concerning the monastery of Anisola between Bishop Aldric and Abbot Sigismund, who then held it.

The aforesaid Aldric asserted and proved by written documents and witnesses that the aforesaid monastery, with everything belonging to it, ought by right to belong to the church of his see; that his predecessors had founded a large part of it from the property of the mother church of Le Mans; that it ought to be subject to that mother church; and he affirmed this by law.

Sigismund, on the other hand, said that it ought to be the personal property of the lord emperor and not to belong to the aforesaid church. But he produced no genuine authority for this, except one letter which Pippin had made for a certain monk because of his hatred of Bishop Gauziolenus, so that the monastery would be subject to that monk and not to Gauziolenus. It was investigated and established that this had been done because of hatred of Gauziolenus.

For when Pippin was in the territory of Le Mans, returning from a certain persecution by his enemies and passing through that territory, the aforesaid Gauziolenus and his brother Harivius did not receive him. Instead, they shut themselves up within the city of Le Mans with all those whom they were able to gather with them and did not allow the lord King Pippin to enter. They attempted to harm him through their men; they killed his chamberlain in his presence while his army was encamped in the vineyard of Saint Peter near the city of Le Mans, and they wounded other men.

When the lord Pippin saw that he could accomplish nothing there, he devastated the whole region and began to proceed toward Francia. On that journey he came to the aforesaid monastery of Anisola and ordered the monks there not to render any obedience to the aforesaid Gauziolenus, since he was rebellious toward him, but to remain under his protection, or solely under his guardianship and authority.

At that time he gave them and their abbot Siebald a letter of such a kind that it is clear that this was done because of hatred of Gauziolenus, as has been said, and not for any other reason or because of any injustice. For Siebald himself then did not dare remain there, but traveled with Pippin as far as Francia.

Later, when Pippin realized that he had acted unjustly and had done this because of hatred of Gauziolenus, he ordered his son Charles, and charged him under oath, to restore the aforesaid monastery to the mother church of Le Mans, to which it rightly ought to belong, lest his soul suffer any harm on account of it.

Thus the lord Charles later acted: he restored it to Bishop Franco and confirmed it for the aforesaid mother church by his privilege. Many people are still alive who heard the lord Charles say that his father, the lord Pippin, had charged him to do this.

When the aforesaid monastery was restored by Bishop Franco, many were still living who had heard the lord Pippin order and charge Charles to do this.

Bishop Aldric had thoroughly investigated this account among truthful people and affirmed it before everyone through true and good witnesses. While Aldric and Sigismund were disputing in this way, the matter itself reached the lord emperor. He ordered that it be investigated firmly and that the truth be reported to him.

Before the dispute came before the lord emperor, however, their friends and good men wished to reconcile and bring them to agreement. Bishop Aldric obeyed their just requests, but Sigismund did not. Whatever his friends justly and reasonably advised him to do, the aforesaid Sigismund rejected.

The aforementioned Bishop Aldric offered him a rent from the monastery, as the predecessors of his aforesaid predecessors had done, and offered to let him hold it as his benefice. He did not wish to cause him any impediment concerning it throughout his lifetime, but permitted him to remain there quietly and peacefully with his monks.

The aforesaid Bishop Aldric, at the urging of the aforementioned friends and good men, also offered Sigismund another arrangement, so that, if he did not want this one, he might at least accept the other. He allowed him to hold two or three villas of his own choosing as his benefice and would demand from them neither service nor any gift, but would allow him to do whatever he wished with them.

Sigismund rejected all these proposals. Therefore, the aforesaid bishop began to seek his justice justly and reasonably, since he believed that he had a full and just claim in this matter.

The lord emperor ordered that this justice be investigated by Ebroin, bishop of the city of Poitiers; Erchenrad, bishop of the city of Paris; Count Rorigon; Altmar, seneschal of the empress Judith; and a royal envoy, together with other royal vassals.

But since the matter at that time did not reach a conclusion because of other necessities, and this was reported to the lord emperor, he ordered that the dispute be settled before him in his palace.

The lord emperor therefore ordered that both men bring their authorities and testimonies to his assembly at the palace of Aachen, which he held there during Lent with bishops, abbots, counts, and his other faithful men, so that the aforesaid dispute might be fully brought to an end there.

But Sigismund, although summoned to that assembly, did not arrive. For this reason the lord emperor summoned him again by letter to come after Easter. When he also refused this summons, he was summoned a third time, but did not come, nor did he send anyone to explain why he had failed to appear.

Then the lord emperor, seeing his disobedience and defiance, nevertheless waited another fifteen days after the third appointed assembly for him to come. But when he saw that Sigismund no longer wished to come or to settle his case justly—for he was not at all confident that he could do so reasonably and truthfully, and therefore did not wish to come to the assembly—the lord emperor asked his counselors, bishops, abbots, counts, and other faithful men what he ought to do about this, what advice they would give him, and what he should do concerning one so disobedient to his command.

Then all those of both orders replied:

“We have seen that this Bishop Aldric, your man, possesses royal authorities and privileges, both of your father and of your other predecessors, namely the kings of the Franks. In these documents, as has been read before us, it is written and recorded, and they have been confirmed by the actual hands of holy priests and kings, that the monastery of Anisola, concerning which this case is being heard, was given to the mother church of Le Mans, founded and adorned by the bishops of that mother church, and possessed by it according to law.

“The aforesaid bishop also has, as we see and hear, true and good witnesses of his own, who testify that these authorities are firm and genuine, and who affirm under oath that what they say is true.

“Moreover, they testify that within the lawful period the aforesaid mother church of the city of Le Mans had obtained lawful seisin of the aforesaid monastery, and that thirty years have not yet passed since it held lawful seisin of it. For this reason it was recently alienated, because Bishop Franco of the aforesaid church had obtained it for his relative Adalghysus, so that he might perform on his behalf the royal services and journeys which, because of his infirmity and old age, Franco was unable to perform.

“They also affirm that the same Franco retained for his own use, while he lived, certain small villas and certain vassals and household dependents, as they are called, from the aforesaid monastery. But after both men had died, there was no bishop then present in that see who would, at the proper time, bring this matter before the lord Emperor Louis. Thus it was given to another and removed from the aforesaid see on that account.

“The witnesses of Bishop Aldric also affirm through their authorities, and through your vassals and other truthful and good men, that what these monks say—that it is your personal property—is not true.

“They also say that, if it were your personal property, the property of that monastery would be protected according to Salic or Ripuarian law, as are the other places and properties that belong to you personally; and its dependents would not be divided, as is customary in that region with respect to other places and properties that are your personal possessions. But among them nothing has ever been preserved concerning these matters in the property of Saint Calais as is observed with the personal property of the lord emperor.

“For these reasons the aforesaid witnesses affirm and defend that the aforesaid monastery is not your personal property, nor anyone else’s, but belongs by right to the mother church of Le Mans, from whose property it was founded. In our view, they can make this claim reasonably and lawfully.

“The witnesses mentioned above also testify that all the bishops who were in the aforesaid city and in that see from the time of Saint Innocent, the second bishop and successor of Saint Victurius, and from the time of Saint Calais, the eminent confessor, had held the aforesaid monastery subject to them, with the exception of two. It has been truthfully investigated that their exception arose because of the aforesaid hatred and because of some negligence.

“They also testify that the aforesaid monastery pertains more to the right and subjection of the mother church than to your personal property or to any other claim. If any witnesses should come forward against them, they testify that they can prove them false, as you may order, and they firmly affirm this.

“Having carefully examined the aforesaid case, learning the truth of the matter, instructed by the authority of divine and secular law, and supported by full reasoning, we, your faithful men of both orders, judge and urge you to take it away from the one who has shown himself disobedient to you and who, summoned not once, twice, or three times to your assembly—”

[The supplied text ends mid-sentence.]

He refused to come, because he is known to be culpable and convicted on account of his absence; and by your authority and our judgment let the aforesaid monastery be restored to him, since it was not disobedient to you nor refused to come to your hearing, but was always present with its authorities and noble witnesses, and is fully and lawfully prepared to prove that the aforesaid monastery ought to belong to the church of its own see. Therefore, by firm authority, we judge that the aforesaid monastery, in its entirety, is to be restored to the aforesaid Bishop Aldric for the right of his see’s church.

Some of them, however, said:

“We cannot judge otherwise concerning ourselves, for if any one of us—even though no one is seeking him or bringing any charge—when summoned to your hearing, should refuse to come, unless illness or some legitimate necessity has detained him; and if some necessity or illness has detained him, unless he has sent you his advocate or a reasonable excuse, each one of us ought justly and with full reason to lose whatever he possesses from you. Therefore, just as we judge concerning ourselves, so we judge concerning him, because he did neither: he neither came himself nor took care to send word why he had absented himself.

“But these men who stand here present—namely Hagrano and Benedict and the others—say and wish to affirm, in whatever manner may please you, whether or not one of you should say otherwise, that they will fight him in single combat, or in court, if you wish, or establish the truth by oath: that the aforesaid Sigismund remained for no other reason, neither because of illness nor because of any other necessity, than that he did not wish to come lest he be convicted, because he believed that he had no justice or any just or reasonable cause in the aforesaid matter. These men proclaim this daily before you, before us, and before your other faithful followers, and they wish to prove it in whatever manner, as has been said, may please you and as they have been ordered.

“This has been proclaimed and investigated very frequently in public in this palace, in the hearing of us and your other faithful followers. Yet there is no one who wishes to contradict or resist them; rather, everyone says that they are speaking the truth, which also seems very likely to us.

“Thus, for fifteen days now, while awaiting another hearing, the third, which has been granted, he has sent neither his advocate nor his authorities, nor has he wished to offer any excuse for himself or for his contempt. Therefore, we judge according to the laws that he is already convicted and condemned on account of his absence and contumacy, so that his voice may no longer be heard in this matter.

“And so that we may confirm by the authority of the canons and the law what we say and judge, we ask that you order certain judgments relevant to this matter from the canons and laws to be read before you.”

Then the following judgments from the canons and laws were publicly read before all:

### Excerpt from the decrees of Pope Boniface, chapter II

“It is manifest that the person who does not use the opportunity to clear himself of a crime by an appointed and delegated judgment confesses it. For it makes no difference whether everything that has been said about him is proved in the present inquiry, since his very absence stands as a confession.” [Source citation: *Book V of the Capitularies*, c. 37; book VII, c. 43.]

Likewise, from the decrees of the same Pope Boniface:

“There is no doubt that the accused who evades judgment flees as a guilty person, just as the innocent seeks to be acquitted. For whoever thinks that he can evade judgment by delays confesses everything.”

Likewise, from the same author cited above:

“Care must be taken that, if anyone has neglected to appear, he does not gain a postponement of the judgment by his absence; rather, whatever is known to have sprung up wickedly must be torn out by the roots and corrected.”

### B

#### From the decrees of Pope Celestine

“For he is not free from suspicion who has refused to come to judgment and has delayed clearing himself, because his very absence is proof. Moreover, the truth will emerge if falsehood is displeasing. Indeed, the matter rightly concerns us if we favor error by silence.

“Therefore, those who are of this kind must be rebuked by every means, so that the truth about them may not be lulled to sleep by their cunning, but that their evasive sophistry may be most suitably and prudently exposed and corrected before all, and that what has hitherto been hidden and neglected may be restored.” [Source citation: Decree of Celestine I, chapter number illegible.]

### Excerpt from the decrees of Pope Innocent II

“Truth, though often assailed, will shine more brightly into the light, and destruction, when recalled to judgment, will be condemned more severely. For it is a divine fruit to review justice repeatedly, correct errors, and restore what has been taken away. Therefore our Lord and judge does not permit us to be idle concerning what he has granted us to exercise rather than neglect.” [Source citation: *Decrees of Innocent I*, c. 35.]

The following chapters, pertaining to the same matter, were brought forward by the wise counts and royal scabini, and were read out in judgment before all.

These chapters, which follow, have been taken from Roman law.

Emperor Valentinian, among other provisions, issued the following to Firminus, prefect of the praetorium and patrician:⁴

“If anyone summoned before a court refuses to appear, after the second or third summons let him know that he will incur the judgment imposed upon the contumacious; that is, whatever he would have been condemned to pay in court, had he been present, he shall pay to the plaintiff as though defeated.”

Issued on the seventh day before the Kalends of May at Rome, in the consulship of Herculanus, of clarissimus rank. [Source citation: *Novella unica on episcopal judgment*, in the Interpretation.]

### Five chapters on the effect of judgments and the limits of litigation, from Book V of Paul’s Sentences

“Anyone who, having been summoned by three judicial authorities, or called to judgment by three letters or three edicts, or summoned by a single peremptory summons—that is, one which terminates the case—and who refuses to present himself before the judge by whom he has been summoned, may be judged against as contumacious.” [Source citation: Paul, *Sentences*, book V, title 5, in the Interpretation.]

“Indeed, proceedings cannot be reopened by appeal whenever judgment has been given against a contumacious person.”

Likewise, from Theodosius, Book IV, concerning judgments issued after inquiry:

“Emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius to Clearchus, prefect: Whatever has been determined in a case while the parties were present shall possess the fullest force, nor may it be altered.”

Issued on the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Honorius VIII and Boethius.

The following judgment on the same Roman law is taken from Paul:

“For if such concessions are granted to judges, how much more widely and broadly are reins and restraints relaxed for kings and emperors, since defendants and accused persons are judged more severely in a charge of high treason than in any other kind of secular matter? For the honor of the head is the glory of the other members, and the disgrace of the head is the dishonor of the other members. Since all the members follow the head, let us speak, in comparison with our predecessors, according to the custom of the ancients.

“Just as we read that our predecessors confirmed and defined these matters not once or twice or three times, but very often, so the dishonoring and despising of elders and masters, and contempt for them, is an insult to their subjects and juniors; while the honor, exaltation, goodwill, and obedience shown to elders and masters are the honor and exaltation of their subjects and juniors. For the former are supported and exalted by the latter, and the latter by the former; the kingdom and the peoples are enlarged, their strength and justice increase, and the people are saved and exalted.

“But if anyone should presume to act against these provisions or to do anything by some stratagem, let him, condemned in all things and by all, be struck inwardly and outwardly by the sentence of punishment, so that no one may thereafter presume to do such things; and if anyone attempts to do so, let him likewise be condemned and not escape the sentence of punishment.”

Likewise, concerning what was stated above, if anyone delays coming to a hearing:

“If anyone, by evasion, goes here and there and delays coming to a hearing, especially if he has been summoned by judges, every provision must be made lest he lose his justice on such an occasion while seeking his right. Rather, let the person who delays coming to the hearing be judged as though convicted, and likewise culpable and convicted on account of his absence; thereafter let him be unable to recover this, but instead let him be assigned to the mines and other punishments, so that no one may again presume to do such things, and so that he may not profit from his cunning and absence by winning, nor rejoice at having evaded the matter, nor lose his justice.”

Issued on the ninth day before the Kalends of May.

Instructed by these and other authorities of the holy Fathers, the canons, and the laws, we judged reasonably, and judge again, that the aforesaid matters be restored, by your authority and your judgment, to Aldric, the aforesaid bishop, who was always fully prepared and present and never failed to appear in order to prove his right.

And if such firmness has thereby been established that may appear in the future, let the aforesaid church entrusted to him never thereafter suffer any harm, scandal, or charge on this account. And if anyone—which we do not believe—should thereafter wish to bring any claim or charge on this account against him or his successors, let him be unable to vindicate it, and let the voice of anyone attempting this be entirely disregarded. Rather, let this judgment now being rendered remain ratified for future times, and let your restoration remain firm and stable.

When these matters had been completed, we rendered this decision. Then the lord emperor, before those present, restored to Aldric, the aforesaid bishop, by their judgment and with full authority, the monastery of Anisolæ, in which the lord Carilephus rests bodily, for possession in future times under the right of the mother church of Le Mans, over which the aforesaid bishop presided. He gave him agents who would provide him with full investiture of it: namely Fulco, count of the palace; Arduin and Gaufridus, counts; and Folcrad, the royal vassal.

Afterward, as the lord emperor had ordered them, they solemnly gave full and lawful investiture in the very monastery to the aforesaid Bishop Aldric, before many witnesses, by the bells and doors of the principal church of that monastery, in which Saint Carilephus also rests bodily, and by the gates of the monastery itself.

This took place in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 838, in the second indiction, and in the fourth year of the reign of the aforesaid lord Louis, most pious emperor, and in the sixth year of the episcopate of the aforesaid Bishop Aldric. On the day before the Kalends of May, the aforesaid judgment was also conducted in the palace at Aachen; on that very day the same settlement was lawfully fulfilled by the aforesaid emperor and completed with full legal force.

Therefore it seemed desirable to commit this memorial to writing, so that, if any dispute should thereafter arise concerning how this matter was conducted, it might be clearly shown by this record; and so that, if anyone should attempt to bring any complaint on this account, he might in no way vindicate it.

This memorial was enacted and written in the palace at Aachen on the Kalends of May, in the sacristy of Saint Mary, while our Lord Jesus Christ reigns forever.

These charters and these decrees were publicly reread and recited before the lord emperor and Drogo, his brother and archchaplain, and also before his agents, whom the lord emperor had appointed to hear and determine this case; and before the bishops, counts, ministers, and judges who had been recorded, when this judgment was decided in the aforesaid palace, and when the aforesaid monastery was lawfully restored to the right of the aforesaid mother church of Le Mans and vindicated under the aforesaid title. They were as follows:

1. The tradition of Saint Carilephus, by which he handed himself over to Saint Innocent, bishop, with the permission and consent of King Childebert.

### XLIV

#### Copy of the letter which the lord Emperor Louis sent to Jonas, bishop of the city of Orléans, and to Henry, abbot, concerning the case of Aldric, bishop of the city of Le Mans, and his monks, concerning the monastery of Saint Carilephus, when the lord emperor restored it to him, with full legal process and to the church entrusted to him; and because certain monks, contrary to all canonical and regular authority, rashly departed from it and secretly carried away from there a considerable quantity of ecclesiastical property, including sacred golden and silver vessels

In the name of the Lord God and of our Savior Jesus Christ.

Louis, by the divinely granted mercy of God, Augustus emperor, to Jonas, venerable bishop, greeting.

We wish you to know that it has come to our attention that, when the monks departed rashly from the monastery of Saint Carilephus, they stripped that same monastery of ecclesiastical ornaments, both from the treasury and in the form of vessels, vestments, and books. Therefore we command you and Abbot Henry to investigate this with every diligence and to have the ecclesiastical property restored in its entirety to that church.

Farewell. In this matter, show the diligence which we confidently expect from you and which you recognize as our will.

### XLV

#### Likewise, a copy of another letter of the lord Emperor Louis concerning the aforesaid matter, to the persons named above

In the name of the Lord God and of our Savior Jesus Christ.

Louis, by the divinely granted mercy of God, Augustus emperor, to Jonas, venerable bishop, greeting.

We wish you to know that it has come to our attention that the monks have departed from the monastery of Saint Carilephus, seeking places belonging to others, forgetful of their own promise, in which they promised obedience and stability to the place of their profession, and renounced their own wills according to the rule of Saint Benedict. They have also forgotten the evangelical sentence in which we heard the Lord’s example:

“I have not come,” he said, “to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38).

They have likewise forgotten the apostolic sentence which says:

“Be subject to every human creature, whether to the king as supreme, or to governors as sent by him” (1 Peter 2:13).

They did this for no other reason than that their abbot appeared disobedient to us. We therefore took the same monastery away from that abbot and lawfully restored it to Aldric and to the church entrusted to him, just as it had been possessed and established by his predecessors, as the bearer of this letter will be able to tell you. It is too lengthy to insert everything in this letter concerning how the matter was reasonably conducted and decided. Nor do we find anything contrary to the authority of the canons in making monks subject to bishops.

Therefore we wish you to act as our agent, together with Abbot Henry, and to compel those monks, by the full authority of the canons, the rule, and our own authority, to return to their proper monastery. If any one of them should not obey you, we wish you to compel him to come into our presence at the next hearing which, with the Lord’s favor, we shall hold at Quierzy.

Farewell, and pray to the Lord for us.

### XLVII

#### Concerning the response of Emperor Louis and the judgment of his leading men against the decrees which the monks of the monastery of Anisolæ produced before him, when they came to plead against Bishop Aldric concerning the aforesaid monastery

When, in the palace at Aachen, in the twenty-fifth year of the reign of the lord Louis, most pious Augustus, a complaint concerning the monastery of Anisolæ and its property was brought and carefully examined before him and his leaders, both ecclesiastical and secular, at a general assembly, between Aldric, bishop of the city of Le Mans, and Sigismund, abbot of the same monastery, the aforesaid bishop produced, among other chartered documents and royal decrees, one decree which the lord Charles had ordered to be made, strengthened by his own hand and sealed below with his ring. By it he had restored the aforesaid monastery to Bishop Franco and to the church entrusted to him.

The aforesaid monks of Sigismund also produced a certain decree concerning their election, granting them permission to choose an abbot from among themselves, which they said had been written at the command of the lord Louis, most pious emperor.

To this the lord emperor replied:

“If I ordered this decree to be made, I did not know that the aforesaid monastery belonged to the bishopric of Le Mans, and I was unaware that my father had restored it there by his decree. But because you and your peers concealed this from me and advised me through fraud and evil contrivance to do this, the very decree which you say you instructed me to issue is weakened by your lie. For a case in which fraud intervenes has no force, but becomes all the more reprehensible.

“Therefore your decree cannot stand, because it is utterly destroyed by your lie and your fraud. For if we granted you only one election, we recognize that it was soon brought to an end, because Sigismund, whom you elected as your abbot, lost the aforesaid monastery through his own fault, since he proved disobedient and unfaithful to us.”

After saying these things, the aforesaid lord emperor asked all those standing around what seemed to them the more correct course in this matter. They replied—all the bishops, abbots, counts, and the remaining men alike:

“These later decrees which these monks produce cannot destroy the earlier ones held by Bishop Aldric and the church entrusted to him. Rather, the earlier decrees must prevail, and the later ones, which were obtained by fraud and evil contrivance, are invalidated and cannot stand, because an action in any matter in which fraud has intervened has no force.

“And so that what we testify may be confirmed by reason and law, we present to you certain testimonies from our authentic authorities.

“It has been established by the holy Fathers, good emperors, and the law that whatever a false petition has obtained from a prince, because fraud intervened, shall have no force.

“Likewise, elsewhere: ‘Whatever has been written contrary to law shall have no force, however it may have been obtained.’

“Likewise, elsewhere: ‘Those who bring false decrees of a prince shall be punished.’

“Likewise, elsewhere: ‘Fraud consists in acting one way while pretending another.’

“Likewise, elsewhere: ‘Whoever has employed fraud or fear so that property might pass to another shall be liable under an action for fraud.’

“Likewise, elsewhere: ‘There is evil fraud when someone, through falsehood, wishes to overturn what has previously been decided.’

“Likewise, elsewhere: ‘What has been lost through any circumstance of time, fraud, captivity, or fear caused by the power of greater persons must be restored by the judges presently in office and recalled to the authority from which it departed.’

“Likewise, elsewhere: ‘Whatever a true or false petition has obtained from a prince, because fraud intervened, shall have no force.’”¹

The fraud was great, because the aforesaid monks knew that the monastery belonged to the right of the church of the see of Le Mans: it is not yet thirty years since it was possessed by the bishops of that see. Concealing this and lying to you, they persuaded you to issue decrees to themselves without the consent of the aforesaid bishop of the see, to whom it justly belongs.

And it would be just that, if any layman had done this, he should suffer great loss; indeed, he would certainly be judged deserving of punishment by capital sentence. But since it was not laymen, but the aforesaid monks, who did this, it is fitting that they be restrained in such a way that no other monks thereafter presume to do similar things.

Therefore certain monks of the aforesaid monastery, together with the aforesaid Sigismund, their abbot, were condemned to exile. And thus the aforesaid monastery was confirmed to Bishop Aldric and to his bishopric, as is known from his decrees and as is contained in the other records of the charters.
