## VITA

### XLVIII

#### Memorial concerning how the monastery of Anisolæ was alienated from the right of the mother church of Le Mans after the death of Emperor Louis, most pious

If anyone wishes to know how the monastery of Anisolæ, together with its property, slipped from the right of the mother church of Le Mans after the death of Louis II, most pious emperor of the Franks, he may find something briefly set out in this memorial.

After the aforesaid lord Louis, most pious Augustus, died in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 840, a great sedition arose in his empire. Among its other evils there arose a certain tyrannical power in the county of Le Mans, which resisted Charles, his son, to whom the aforesaid emperor had given Neustria among his other territories, and which greatly harassed his faithful followers.

Sigismund, who had formerly been abbot of the aforesaid monastery of Anisolæ, joined this tyrannical power. Aldric, bishop of the church of Le Mans, who at that time held that monastery together with its property, faithfully adhered to his lord Charles. Although the aforesaid tyrannical power repeatedly summoned him to itself, and those exercising it promised to guarantee that he would not lose or have diminished the honors he possessed for the rest of his life, but would obtain even greater honors and whatever he might seek in that region if he joined them, he nevertheless did not withdraw from his purpose or from the aforesaid lord.

Rather, he remained steadfastly faithful to him and, to the extent of his power, assisted him; for his sake he abandoned all his possessions and followed him in every respect.

When the aforesaid sedition had ended, the said King Charles began to deliberate whether he should either drive the aforesaid tyrants from the borders or make them faithful to him. He sent his leading men to them, summoning them to come to him. They replied:

“We shall neither come to him nor be faithful to him unless, even if we are defeated, he grants us our lives, our limbs, and such honors as we now possess, however we may have acquired them, including the aforesaid Sigismund and the monastery of Anisolæ together with its property.”

Seeing that, because of the other seditions raging everywhere, this could not then be accomplished otherwise without great danger, the aforesaid lord King Charles consented to their requests. Among the other concessions, he granted Sigismund permission to have the aforesaid monastery, while he firmly promised the aforesaid Aldric and the church of his see that he would soon restore it.

For this reason the aforesaid monastery was then alienated from the right of the mother church of Le Mans—not lawfully vindicated, but tyrannically alienated.

### XLIX

As time passed, and the aforesaid Sigismund did not come to the aforesaid king, namely Charles, son of the emperor Louis, and after a great battle had been fought in the county of Auxerre between Charles and Lothar—in which victory was granted by the Lord God and our Savior to the aforesaid Charles—
## ALDRIC OF LE MANS

### [Scan page 51]

…and returning through the territory of Le Mans, while the aforementioned Sigemund still did not come to him, [the monastery] was restored on the Kalends of August at a place called Bona, on the River Liz, in the county of Le Mans, by the aforementioned lord Charles, according to law, to the aforesaid Bishop Aldric, by judgment of many noble and wise men: namely, the monastery of Anisol, with everything belonging to it. There, good and vigorous men were also sent to him, who, according to law, were to reinvest him with the monastery and with the mother church of Le Mans entrusted to him, and to provide him with full and lawful investiture, to be held lawfully by him in future times. This is shown to have been done under the pretext mentioned above on the third day before the Nones of the said month. Thus falsehood is subordinated to truth, and what was unjustly alienated is justly restored; these possessions have since been legally held by the aforesaid bishop and the ministers of his see, and are governed canonically and regularly.

### L

A copy of the formal letter which Drogo, archchaplain and archbishop of the city of Metz, canonically sent to Landramnus, archbishop of the city of Tours, so that, with his permission and at the command of the most pious lord Emperor Louis, he might ordain Aldric, cardinal priest of the aforesaid city of Metz and its chief priest, bishop of the mother church of Le Mans, as is set forth in the letter itself. The prologue of the aforesaid letter to the venerable Archbishop Landramnus is as follows:

“To his venerable brother in Christ and fellow bishop, Landramnus, archbishop, Drogo sends greetings in the Lord.

“I have learned that the lord emperor had granted the bishopric of the city of Le Mans to Aldric the priest, who was also our tonsured cleric, educated and a member of the clergy. But afterward, sending to us, he requested—as he ought—that I should give and grant to you and to your suffragan bishops, who were to be his ordainers, my consent and permission for his elevation to the episcopate. I consented to his request in such a way that, if by God’s will and that of the lord emperor you find him worthy and suitable for this office, as a holy servant of God’s Church, and if you decide accordingly—for he has displayed upright conduct among us—you are to know that, with our permission granted, you have the authority to complete the matter and consecrate him.

“I pray that you and all the brothers may be well, and that you remember me in your holy prayers of charity.”

### LI

A copy of the formal letter which Drogo, archchaplain and archbishop of the city of Metz, canonically sent to Aldric, cardinal priest of the aforesaid city of Metz and its primicerius (chief cleric), so that, with his consent and at the command of the most pious lord Emperor Louis, he might be ordained bishop of the mother church of Le Mans by his archbishop and the other bishops of the province. For the people had asked that he be ordained their bishop, and had sent him a letter for this purpose, so that, with the assistance and permission of the aforementioned Aldric, he might be ordained bishop of them and of the aforesaid Church. Accordingly, he sent them a canonical letter containing the following:

“To his beloved son Aldric, called bishop, Drogo, an unworthy archbishop, sends everlasting greetings in Christ.

“Let your Belovedness know that I am pleased that divine generosity has deemed worthy to confer upon you the honor which has been granted to you through imperial administration. But your Belovedness, as was proper, sent to me requesting that I send you a letter addressed to your metropolitan, granting him permission to ordain you. Now, although it would have been more fitting and honorable for both you and me that I should again respond in writing to a written request sent by you, nevertheless, lest my delay perhaps cause you some impediment in receiving the divine gift which, as I believe, has been granted to you, trusting in charity I have done as you asked.

“Therefore I have sent you two letters: one is addressed to your metropolitan, according to your request, granting him permission; the other is addressed to you, so that you may know that permission has been granted to you by us, and that we wished rather to rejoice in the increase of your honor than in any way to inflict injury upon you. Farewell always in the Lord, and take courage. Remember us always, and we ask that, through your charity, you henceforth keep unshaken the faith which you have always faithfully maintained toward us. Farewell again.”

### LII

A summary of the dues or full resources of the brothers serving God in the city of Le Mans, consisting of the possessions which Franco the elder and Aldric, their bishops, gave them, and which they confirmed by wills and royal charters.

The brothers’ men owe, in the principal wine-account, 402 measures of wine; from the wine-provision, 271 measures; from the hostilense, 149 silver shillings. Seven wethers are owed as pasture-dues, with seventy-six fleeces; forty-two `sogales` [probably goats]. Two [units] are owed, and five shillings as laudaticum. Ten [units] are owed as carnaticum; fifty-five rams without wool; and twenty-six shillings as lignarium. Nine [units] are owed as census; 101 shillings as inferenda and posturnum, or 180 shillings as sensaticum. There are owed from the provision, in wheat and rye, thirty-four measures and nine sextarii of `sufusum` [uncertain grain]; of oats, 444 measures; fifty-four assistance-services for the alvimanum; and every year 1,440 shingles.

### LIII

On the expulsion of Aldric, bishop of the city of Le Mans, and on the invasion and devastation of the mother church of Le Mans together with its possessions.

When the lord Louis, second emperor of the Franks—namely, the son of Emperor Charlemagne—died in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 840, in the third indiction and the twenty-seventh year of his reign, a certain tyrannical wickedness arose, among other evils, between the Loire and the Seine, and especially in the county of Le Mans, in which Aldric was then completing his eighth year in the dignity of the episcopate.

Although the aforementioned emperor divided his kingdoms among his three sons—namely, between Lothair, Louis, and Charles, placing Lothair in Middle Francia, Louis in East Francia, and Charles in Neustria and Aquitaine—and divided the remaining kingdoms and duchies among them, as is recorded in their annals, with the divine consent of their leaders, he entrusted the aforementioned pontiff to his aforesaid younger son Charles.

Aldric, the aforementioned pontiff, faithfully maintaining the allegiance due to the said Charles, was expelled in the aforesaid year from the aforementioned bishopric and from his own see by the faithless men of God’s holy Church and by his own people, through the aforesaid tyrannical power. Consequently, many works which he had begun to undertake in ecclesiastical and other matters for the love of God remained unfinished.

For the aforesaid episcopal see was then almost completely devastated and reduced, as it were, to nothing. He had begun a cloister for the canons, and the mother church in the middle of the city, from its foundations, together with its porticoes; he had also begun a paradise, and had completed most of it. Likewise, he had begun the buildings of five monasteries, together with their cloisters and other structures.

He had also gathered, for the support of that church and the refreshment of the poor, herds of livestock with more than eighty pack animals, and more than two hundred cows, sheep, goats, and pigs; he had sufficient grain, hay, and wine both for the use of the communities, guests, and poor, and for the needs of those serving him and the church entrusted to him.

But why should I say more? The aforesaid episcopal see and the possessions entrusted to it had been so well established, both in ecclesiastical and other matters, as they had not been since ancient days, or since the time within the memory of any human being. Yet these and its countless other goods—including the seven hospices which he had built for receiving and refreshing the poor and guests—were utterly devastated and destroyed by the aforementioned tyrants.

Because of these ambushes and many others, these and countless other good works which he wished and began to carry out in his episcopal see are no longer visible. The Lord will require them of those by whom they were overturned, devastated, and prevented, not of the man who wished to undertake and complete them, but was prevented, expelled, and forced to abandon them.

The aforesaid tyrants were descended from Heriveus and Wido, the earlier tyrants.

### LIV

Synod held by Aldric in the city of Le Mans.

“In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Aldric, an unworthy bishop of the mother church of Le Mans, sends greetings and everlasting glory to all the sacred orders entrusted to our pastoral care and to all the faithful.

“In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 840, in the third indiction and the twenty-seventh year of the reign of the lord Louis, most pious emperor, and in the eighth year of the ordination of the aforesaid Bishop Aldric—namely, on the fourth day before the Ides of May—the aforesaid pontiff assembled in the city of Le Mans a synod of all the priests and deacons and the other servants of God. After addressing, admonishing, and questioning them, the aforementioned Bishop Aldric began to discuss with them, at their request, what duty each person ought diligently to perform for his brothers, both living and released from the debt of death, and what each ought faithfully to fulfill for the aforesaid pontiff and for the flock of both orders entrusted to him.

“Considering and discussing this matter together under divine inspiration, we unanimously decreed, with good will and pure intention, that, as long as he lives, each priest of our order shall sing a Mass on Wednesday, together with the litany and offerings, for the aforesaid lord Bishop Aldric and for the people entrusted to him; and likewise on Friday. Whoever cannot do this shall sing fifty psalms, praying and beseeching the God of heaven that almighty God, according to his will, may grant our aforesaid pontiff to live this life, and that, when it pleases Him and the end of this life arrives, the heavenly gate may be opened to him and, at our supplication, a place among the company of the saints may be granted to him. Amen.

“Likewise, the aforesaid pontiff has promised to act for all of us, either personally or through someone appointed by him.

“Moreover, while discussing these matters on the aforesaid day before the Ides of May and in the aforementioned synod, we decreed among ourselves that, as long as he lives, each of us shall sing twelve Masses annually, with offerings and the other prayers, for his fellow brothers. Whenever one of us dies, the dean shall bring to the synod, at each appointed time, a list of the names of his juniors, and each of us shall complete twelve Masses for them, with offerings and the other prayers, as well as a vigil with nine psalms, the same number of lessons and responsories, and a matutinal synaxis faithfully for the deceased brothers.

“Thus let each person do this as he wishes it to be done for himself when the same event comes upon him, and as he will wish to render an account of this before the tribunal of the strict Judge—of what he has voluntarily promised here to do before God, before our pontiff, and before all of us.

“May almighty God grant that we act in such a way that, through these things, we may receive from the Lord our God not condemnation but a full recompense, and may have eternal life, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and is glorified, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.”

### LV

This is the Mass which is to be performed each week for the lord bishop and for all those entrusted to him, namely on Wednesday and Friday, together with the litany. After this follows the Mass which we are to sing for one another; after that follows the Mass which we are to sing for our deceased brothers.

#### Daily Mass

**Response:** Let my prayer enter.

Through the continual intercessions of holy Mary, Mother of God, and of your blessed apostles and martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, and of Saint Stephen, and of your other martyrs, confessors, virgins, and all your saints, we beseech you, Savior of the world: mercifully protect our pontiff Aldric; likewise protect those joined to him by family relationship and kinship, and defend from every wickedness all the men and women of both orders entrusted to him. Grant them to live according to your will, mercifully preserve the whole Christian people, and kindly grant eternal rest to the souls of all your male and female servants entrusted to him, and to all men and women who rest in Christ; graciously deem them worthy to be joined to the company of your saints. Through Christ, and so forth.

**Epistle to the Colossians.** Brothers, we do not cease praying and asking on your behalf.

**Response:** Lord, hear us.

**Response:** Do not overthrow.

**Gospel according to John.** At that time, Jesus, lifting his eyes to heaven, said: “Father, those whom you have given me, I wish that where I am, they also may be with me, so that they may see my glory which you have given me, because you loved me before the foundation of the world. Righteous Father, the world has not known you, but I have known you; and these have known that you sent me. I have made your name known to them, and I shall make it known, so that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them.”

**Offertory:** Hear, O God.

**Secret.** Lord, be appeased by these gifts, and, through the intercession of all your saints, protect our pontiff Aldric and all men and women entrusted to him, and defend the whole Christian people from every danger. Grant through these holy sacrifices the remission of all sins and eternal life to the souls of all your male and female servants entrusted to him who have died in Christ, and to all who have died in Christ.

**Preface.** It is truly fitting, and so forth. And we implore your clemency with poured-out prayers, that, through the intercession of the blessed and glorious ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God, your holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, Saint Stephen, and all your saints, our pontiff Aldric may be worthy to obtain forgiveness of all sins; that you may protect, under the guardianship of all your angels and saints, those men and women whom you have joined to him in the care of governance and united with him by family relationship and kinship, and the whole Christian people; and that, we pray, you may establish the souls of all your male and female servants entrusted to him who have died in Christ, and of all who have died in Christ, in the region of peace and light. Through Christ our Lord.

**Within the Canon.** Therefore, Lord, graciously accept this offering which we humbly offer to you for our pontiff Aldric, for the flock entrusted to him, for those joined to him by kinship and family relationship, and for the salvation of the whole Christian people. In your mercy grant that this devotion may benefit him and them for salvation, and that it may obtain eternal blessedness for the souls of all your male and female servants entrusted to him who have died in Christ, and for all who have died in Christ. And grant us our days, and so forth.

**At Communion:** Amen, I say to you.

**Post-Communion.** We beseech you, Savior of the world: may the reception of the divine sacrament purify our pontiff Aldric, together with the prayer of glorious holy Mary, Mother of God, and of all the saints. Everywhere extend your mercy to the flock entrusted to him, to those joined to him by family relationship and kinship, and to the whole Christian people; grant remission of all sins and eternal life to the souls of all your male and female servants entrusted to him who have died in Christ, and to all who have died in Christ. Through Christ, and so forth.

**Another.** Almighty and eternal God, through the pious and continual intercession of holy Mary, Mother of God, and of all your saints, mercifully protect our pontiff Aldric everywhere; defend him by your power from every adversity of body and soul; watch over the entire flock entrusted to him for governance; preserve the whole Christian people; and grant eternal rest to him and to all who rest in Christ. Through, and so forth.

#### Another Mass, which the aforesaid priests are to sing mutually for one another

God, who through the grace of the Holy Spirit have poured the gifts of charity into the hearts of your faithful, grant to your male and female servants of the various monasteries, titles, and places—to the priests, deacons, and all your other faithful, both men and women, whose memory we commemorate and whose names are contained in writing in these titles—health of mind and body for our brothers, sisters, and relatives, so that they may love you with all their strength and accomplish with complete love what pleases you. Through the Lord.

**Reading from the prophet Jeremiah.** If our iniquities testify against us, Lord, deliver us, we beseech you, for the sake of your name, because our apostasies are many. We have sinned against you; you are the expectation of Israel, its Savior in time of tribulation. But you are among us, Lord, and your holy name has been invoked over us. Do not abandon us, Lord our God.

**According to Matthew.** At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives,” and so forth.

**Secret.** Lord, graciously receive these gifts which we offer before the eyes of your majesty for our redemption and that of all the men and women whose memory we commemorate and whose names are written in these diptychs. Grant that we may all attain everlasting salvation. Through.

Almighty and eternal God, we implore the majesty of your mercy: graciously deign to grant forgiveness of sins to us and to all the men and women whose memory we commemorate and whose names are written in these diptychs, so that, freed from every bond of the enemy, we may cling to your commandments with all our heart and always love you alone with all our strength, and may be worthy at some time to attain the vision of your blessedness. Through Christ.

Therefore, Lord, graciously accept this offering which we offer to you for our sins and offenses, for all the men and women whose memory we commemorate, and whose names are written here, so that we may be worthy to obtain remission of all offenses, we beseech you.

As we partake of the divine mysteries, we beseech you, Lord, that these saving sacraments may benefit for prosperity and peace those men and women for whose love we have offered them before your majesty. Through Christ.

**Another.**

Grant to your male and female servants, Lord, we beseech you—to all the men and women whose memory we commemorate and whose names are written in these diptychs, and also to the other faithful of both sexes—steadfastness in your faith and sincerity, so that, strengthened in divine charity, they may not be torn away from its integrity by any temptations. Through Christ.

#### Mass for our deceased brothers and sisters

God, whose mercies are without number, receive our prayers for the souls of your male and female servants whose memory we commemorate and whose names are known to be written in these diptychs, and grant them a region of light and joy in the company of your saints. Through.

**Another.**

God, whose proper work is to show mercy and to hear the prayers of those who entreat you, be propitious to the souls of your male and female servants of the various monasteries and titles whose memory we commemorate and whose names are recorded here, so that, by your mercy, freed from the bonds of sins, they may be worthy to attain rest in eternal blessedness. Through.

**To the Thessalonians.** Brothers, we do not want you to be ignorant concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the others who…, and so forth.

**According to John.** At that time Jesus said to the crowds of the Jews: “Amen, amen, I say to you: the hour is coming, and is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live,” and so forth.

**Secret.** Lord, graciously regard these gifts, and grant that what we offer in supplication to the praise of your name may benefit for the forgiveness of all the men and women whose memory we commemorate and whose names are written here, and of all the deceased faithful. Through.

God, who have granted us in Christ, your only-begotten Son, our Lord, the hope of blessed resurrection, grant, we beseech you, that the souls for whom we offer this sacrifice of our redemption before your majesty may, through your mercy, be worthy to attain the rest of blessed resurrection with the saints. Through Christ.

Therefore, Lord, graciously accept this offering which we offer to you for the souls of all the men and women whose memory we commemorate and whose names are known to be written in these diptychs, and for all the deceased faithful, both men and women. Grant, we beseech you, that whatever they contracted through earthly conduct may be cleansed by these sacrifices, and that, freed from the bonds of death, they may be worthy to pass into life. And grant us our days, and so forth.

Be propitious, Lord, we beseech you, to all who rest in Christ, and may the souls of your male and female servants whose memory we commemorate and whose names are known to be written in these diptychs receive, through these purified sacrifices, forgiveness and eternal rest together. Through.

**Another.**

God, for whom it is possible to save all human beings without difficulty, grant such abundant perpetual mercy to the souls of your male and female servants of the various monasteries and titles whose memory we commemorate and whose names are recorded here, as you have granted them to belong to the grace of your Son, our Lord. Through.

**Another.**

God, life of the living, hope of the dying, salvation of all who hope in you, mercifully grant that the souls of your male and female servants whose memory we commemorate and whose names are written in these diptychs, freed from the darkness of our mortality, may rejoice in perpetual light with your saints. Through Christ.

### LVI

A copy of the precaria of the estate called Tridente, which Bishop Aldric made for Bavo, a royal vassal, during the time of Louis, the most pious Augustus.

“To the holy and venerable basilica of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, which is built within the city of Le Mans, and which Bishop Aldric appears to possess in lordship and governance, and to its community established in that basilica.

“I, Bavo, in the name of God, since I made the request and your will approved it, and with the permission of our lord Louis, glorious emperor, have been permitted by you to hold for our use the estates belonging to that basilica, whose names are Tridente and Vintleva, with all their entirety. This is on the condition that, as long as I live, I must hold and exercise lordship over them, and that after my departure, when God so commands, you shall cause them to return to the property of Saint Gervasius.

“And we have agreed that every year, for the winter feast of Saint Martin, I shall pay twenty-five silver shillings, or fully pay a tenth and a ninth of all revenue. If I should thereafter appear negligent or late, I must give security for it, and I must not for that reason lose the estates. Thus this precaria, written in one tenor, shall remain firm and stable for all time.”

Enacted publicly in the city of Le Mans, in the eighteenth year of the reign of the lord Louis, most glorious emperor, on the Nones—[the transmitted date reads: “Kalends of May”].

Signature of Bavo, royal vassal, who requested that this precaria be made. Signatures of Wido, Wulf, Heriveus, Serilo, Berilo, and Ebrulf, vicar. Hercheus. Signature of Adalbert Gislarnus, Adalgysus, Godofridus, and Jacobus. Deusdedit subscribed. Bobilo, subdeacon, wrote and subscribed.

### LVII

A copy of the charter of the lord Louis, most pious emperor, concerning the estate of Tridente, which the aforementioned emperor made for the mother church of Le Mans and for Aldric, bishop of that city.

[See the same work, column 1293.]

### LVIII

A copy of the precaria concerning Fraxinedo and Saint George in the county of Sées, and concerning the other estates of Saint Gervasius whose names are inserted in it, which Vulfingus holds and which Bishop Gauziolenus made for him in the first year of the reign of King Pippin.

“To the holy and venerable basilica of Saint Gervasius and Protasius, built within the city of Le Mans, where Bishop Gauziolenus appears to preside, and to its community established in that church.

“I, Vulfingus, in the name of God, since it is known how our lord Pippin, glorious king, ordered the estates of Saint George, Saint Gervasius, Fraxinedo, Flexobrachiale, Aciacum, and Saint George, with their appurtenances, and Aloniacum, Longa Filcaria, Camiacum, and Mundarias, to be restored to that church, and afterward, through the word of our lord Pippin, I made my request and your will approved that you permit me to hold those little estates as a usufructuary benefit from you, namely with their farms, houses, dwellings, buildings, slaves, resident dependants, freedmen, lands, vineyards, woods, meadows, pastures, and whatever appears to belong to those places.

“As long as I live, I may hold and exercise lordship over them as your beneficiary. I promise you that, as a payment for Saint Gervasius or for you, every year at the winter feast of Saint Martin I shall cause one pound of silver to be paid to Saint Gervasius or to the rectors of the churches. If I should be negligent or late in paying this census at the agreed time, I must give security for it; and, as long as I live, I must not lose the property.

“After my departure, when God so commands, you, the rectors of Saint Gervasius, shall cause those little estates, with all their appurtenances and whatever belongs or appears to belong to them, together with whatever I may bring there or improve, or however much may then be found there, to be restored to your lordship and power, without any judicial assignment or opposition from my heirs, so that you may do with them whatever you wish. This precaria shall remain firm as though it had always been renewed every five years.”

Enacted in the city of Le Mans in the first year of the reign of our lord Pippin, glorious king.

Sign of Vulfingus, who requested that this precaria be made. Signatures of Fulgobertus, Sichardus, and Viklenus. Salomon, requested to do so, subscribed. Aiglibertus subscribed. Signatures of Wanafredus and Gibolenus. Bertobodus subscribed. Beraldus wrote and subscribed.

The authentic charters and precarious grants of the earlier bishops concerning the estates listed below are preserved in the archive of the mother church of Le Mans; because of the length of the work, they have not been inserted in this document.

### LXI

A copy of the precaria which Bishop Franco made for Germundus concerning the estates of Fraxinedo, Flexobrachiale, Aciacum, and Saint George in the county of Sées, with their appurtenances, and Aloniacum, or Longa Filcaria, and Camiacum, together with Mundarias and everything belonging to them.

“To the holy and venerable basilica of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, built within the city of Le Mans, where Bishop Franco appears to preside, and to its community established in that church.

“I, Germundus, in the name of God, since it is known how our lord Charles, glorious king, ordered the estates of Saint Gervasius—Fraxinedo, Flexobrachiale, Aciacum, and Saint George, with their appurtenances, Aloniacum, Longa Filcaria, Camiacum, and Mundarias—to be restored to that church, and afterward, through the word of our lord Charles, glorious king, I made my request and your will approved that you permit me to hold those little estates as a usufructuary benefit from you, namely with their farms, houses, dwellings, buildings, slaves, resident dependants, freedmen, lands, vineyards, woods, meadows, pastures, and whatever appears to belong to those places.

“As long as I live, I may hold and exercise lordship over them as your beneficiary. I promise you that, as a payment for Saint Gervasius or for you, every year at the winter feast of Saint Martin I shall cause one pound of silver to be paid to you, for the benefit of Saint Gervasius and the rectors of the churches, or I shall fully pay a tenth or a ninth of all revenue.

“If I should thereafter appear negligent or late at the aforesaid agreed time, I must give security for it; and, as long as I live, I must not lose those properties. After my departure, when God so commands, you or the rectors of Saint Gervasius shall cause those little estates, with all their appurtenances and whatever belongs or appears to belong to them, together with whatever I may bring there or improve, or however much may then be found there, to be restored to your lordship and power, without any judicial assignment or opposition from my heirs, so that you may do with them whatever you wish. This precaria shall remain firm and stable as though it had always been renewed every five years.”

Enacted in the city of Le Mans in the thirty-first year of the reign of our lord Charles, glorious king, in the month of March.

### LX

**Copy of the precaria concerning the estate called Mansiones, in the district of Diablentica, which Bishop Merolus made for Vilibertus.**

To the holy Lord and venerable basilica of Saint Vincent the martyr, which is built outside the walls of the city of Le Mans, and which Bishop Merolus appears to possess and govern: I, Vilibertus, in the name of God—for it was my request and your will that decreed it, and by order of our lord Charles, the glorious king—have been permitted by you to hold for our use your estate belonging to the property of the monastery of Saint Vincent, situated outside the city and called Mansiones, with all its entirety and appurtenances in the district of Diablentica, on the following condition: that while I live I shall hold it and exercise dominion over it, and that after my departure from this life, when the Lord so wills, you shall cause it to return to the monastery of Saint Vincent.

And it has been agreed between us that each year, at the feast of Saint Martin in winter, I shall transfer to you ten silver solidi, or pay in full a tenth and a ninth of all the revenue. If I appear negligent or late in this matter, I must give security for it, and I must not forfeit the aforesaid estate. Rather, this precaria, as though it had always been renewed every five years, shall remain firm and stable.

Done in the city of Le Mans, in the forty-second year, while our lord Charles the glorious king was reigning, in the month of April. Witness of Vilibertus, who requested that this precaria be drawn up and made firm. Witness of Maginardus. Witness of Barifus. Witness of Girbertus. Witness of Enigrimus. Witness of Adelbertus. **Copy of the precaria which Bishop Merolus made for Vilibertus concerning the cell of Saint Frambaldus.**

And it has been agreed between us that each year, at the feast of Saint Martin in winter, I shall transfer six silver solidi, and if I appear negligent or late in this matter, I must give security for it. I must not forfeit the monastery itself; rather, this precaria, written in a single form, shall remain firm and stable at all times.

### LXII

**Copy of the precaria which Bishop Merolus made for Vilibertus concerning Belfaidus in the canonicate, and Senmurus, Ingranda, Vivillare, Fontanas, the little monastery, and Bragolium, with their appurtenances.**

To the holy Lord and venerable basilica of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, built within the city of Le Mans, where Bishop Merolus appears to preside, and to its congregation residing in that church: I, Vilibertus, in the name of God, since it is known that our lord Charles, the glorious king, ordered the estate of Saint Gervasius—namely the public settlement of Belfaidus with its appurtenances, the public settlement of Belfaidus with its appurtenances, Senmurus, Ingranda, Vivillare, Fontanas, the little monastery, Bragolium, or the public settlement of Auciacum, with all their entirety and appurtenances—to be restored to the aforesaid church; and afterwards, through the word of our lord Charles, the glorious king, my request was made and your will decreed that you should permit me, by your beneficence, to hold these little estates in usufruct, namely with manses, houses, buildings, slaves, tenant settlers, freedmen, lands, vineyards, woods, meadows, and pastures, and whatever appears to belong to or be connected with those places, for as long as I live, with your beneficence permitting me to hold and govern them.

And we promise you that, as recognition of Saint Gervasius or of yourselves, each year at the feast of Saint Martin in winter I shall transfer to you, for the portion of Saint Gervasius and of the rectors of the churches, one and a half pounds of silver, or pay in full a tenth and a ninth of all the revenue. If I appear negligent or late in this matter at the appointed time, I must give security for it; and while I live I must not forfeit these properties. After my departure from this life, when God so wills, you or the rectors of Saint Gervasius shall, without the authorization of any judge or opposition from my heirs, cause those little estates, with all their appurtenances and dependencies, and whatever I may have brought there or improved, or whatever may then be found there, to be restored to your ownership and power, so that you may do whatever you wish. This precaria, as though it had always been renewed every five years, shall remain firm and stable.

Done publicly in the city of Le Mans in the thirty-sixth year, while our lord Charles the glorious king was reigning, in the month of May. ### LXIII

**Copy of the letter which Lord Louis the emperor sent to Bishop Aldricus through his abbot and envoy Elisachor, ordering him to deliver the benefits and properties listed below to Bishop Aldricus or his envoys, and to restore his bishopric to him fully by imperial authority.**

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ. Louis, by the gracious mercy of God emperor Augustus, to Aldricus, venerable bishop and our faithful servant, greetings.

Let your diligence know that your envoy came into our presence and reported that certain vassals of ours—Chermundus, Vulfardus, Berchadus, Bodo, and his associate—hold benefits from your bishopric which had previously been alienated through precariae. Therefore we wish you, by our authority, to recover them until our presence, and always to take great care of our fidelity, just as we have known you to do until now.

For your aforesaid envoy has begged our piety to provide you with an envoy who would deliver to you and to the church entrusted to you the aforesaid properties and make a lawful investiture. Therefore we instruct Elisachor, our envoy, to make an investiture of the aforesaid benefits for you when he has been sent by us to those regions.

We also wish you, as soon as you can, to send to us a good and faithful envoy who will inform us how matters now stand concerning you and our other faithful servants, and what has been done regarding those cases which we ordered you to pursue. Fare well, and pray for us.

### LXV

**Settlement of Bethta with the monastery of Saint Vincent.**

It is known that Bethta, consecrated to God, conveyed or claimed for the basilica of Saint Vincent in the city of Le Mans a certain portion in the places called Soliacum and Mansio, the estate of Bariacum, and also Briscinum—property which her son Ermenfredus had left at his death and which had accrued to her by law—and received for it, as a price satisfactory and agreed upon, two hundred good, excellent, full-weight gold solidi.

When the venerable brother Patuinus, provost of that monastery, came with the sale itself, he brought it forward in a private conference for rereading while the parties were disputing among themselves—namely Berthofridus, Bodo with his wife Eudilane, or Bertholanda, and their children Ademarus and Johannes. They produced there a charter written in confused fashion which Bethta had made for those children of hers. It contained the provision that, while she lived, she had held the property jointly with her former husband Leogilisus, in two shares and her own third; and that after her departure, those children of hers should receive both the two shares and her third into their possession.

While they were disputing among themselves, good men appear to have brought them back to an agreement of peace. It was agreed between them that the fourth part which had been owed to the late Ermenfredus at Mansiones should be held permanently as adjudicated by the aforesaid children, Berthofridus and Bodo with his wife Eudilane or Bertholanda, against the venerable brother Patuinus, provost, and the monastery itself, insofar as they appear to possess anything there.

But with regard to the remainder, both at Soliaco and at Bariacum and Briscinum, whatever ought to have come to the late Ermenfredus, or whatever the aforesaid Bethta, also called Noberta, had transferred by title of sale to the aforesaid basilica against Berthofridus and Bodo together with their wife Eudilane and also Bertholanda—lands, houses, slaves, buildings, tenant settlers, meadows, pastures, vineyards, woods, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, connected and dependent property, and everything above-mentioned, however much the late Ermenfredus ought to have possessed in the aforesaid estates—the party of the monastery of Saint Vincent or its rectors must divide in equal measure with the men mentioned above.

Accordingly, it was agreed that three letters written in a single form should be made and received among them. This they did, so that neither party could withdraw from this agreement against the other. Whoever should presume to do so must lose his share to his counterpart and, in addition, must be compelled to pay to the fisc, with its associate, ten pounds of gold and twenty pounds by weight of silver; nor may he thereafter be able to assert any claim concerning it. These letters, which they made among themselves in good faith, with the stipulation inserted, shall remain firm and inviolable at all times.

Done at Soliaco in the matter itself, in the eleventh year of the reign of our lord Theodoricus, the glorious king, on the twelfth day of the present month of October. Bodo subscribed. Berthofridus subscribed in the name of Eudilane, his wife. Witness of Bertholanda, their kinswoman, who requested that this letter be drawn up. Diriceus, abbot, subscribed. ## 856

### MONK

### ON ANGELOMUS

*(Medieval and later Latin.)*

#### Historical Notice

Bernard Pez recently published the commentaries from a manuscript of the monastery of Saint Peter at Salzburg, in volume I of the *Anecdota*, Augsburg, 1721, folio; Angelomus prefixed to them a prologue in hexameter verse.

Angelomus, a Benedictine monk of Luxeuil in Burgundy, wrote to Lothair, and therefore before the year 855, when the emperor Lothair and Drogo, bishop of Metz, died (a), commentaries—or *Stromata*—on the *Song of Songs*. After the death of that same Drogo he composed *Stromata* on the books of Kings, collected from the Fathers and praised by Sigebert in chapter 86 and by Trithemius in chapter 266 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers* and *On Illustrious Benedictines*, book II, chapter 42. Trithemius also mentions his book *On the Divine Offices*.

The *Stromata* on the books of Kings, before the Roman edition of 1565, folio, I have seen published at Cologne in 1530, folio, by Eucharius Cervicornus, who writes in the preface: “Would that his remaining works, especially what he admits that he wrote on Genesis, still existed,” and so forth. We have determined that these are the works on Genesis.

(a) See Labbe, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, volume I, page 77.

### The Following Prologue to the Little Work of Angelomus the Deacon Begins

Reader, follow through the sequence of this excellent little book,  
which, with God dictating, I have been pleased to depict,  
so that it may disclose prose and also reveal mystical things to you;  
may it drive away harmful darkness from the harmful heart,  
and may you, as you read repeatedly, be able to pluck out  
life-giving meanings and sufficiently enrich the fibers of your mind.

Here the sacred little works of the history of Genesis are revealed.  
All that the ancient world’s foundations disclose—  
whatever God, who reigns in the heavenly citadel,  
created: the ethereal vault, the earth, and the waters—  
he transferred from formless matter into fitting forms,  
and whatever remains visible to sight and tangible to us,  
and whatever he had once created together with the Father  
by the powerful reason of the nourishing Spirit.

For they also recount the origins of our life,  
when they tell that the human being was placed in paradise,  
whence the savage, envious serpent dragged him down toward the Tartarean abode;  
he desired to seize the forbidden fruit, yet did not bear the wrath alone;  
but the human race, alas, suffered the punishments of Avernus,  
which he, falling, begot wholly from his own stock.

For six thousand years this race remained thrust down,  
until that Son of God descended from the court above,  
who wished to take the name of Adam and  
to release all his limbs, pitying the wretched man  
by bearing unworthy things,  
so that at last, weeping, he might attain the heavenly kingdoms  
which he could have lost without Christ through touching the apple.

Here are read the most illustrious deeds of the patriarchs,  
marked by exceedingly weighty mystical and figurative signs  
of Christ and of the gifts of our salvation.  
Here the sacred ornaments of the sacred law are seen,  
and the evangelical trumpet [*salpinx*, “trumpet”]  
sounds figuratively throughout the world.

Here the speech of the saints is woven, purer than gold,  
brighter than silver, more beautiful everywhere than amber;  
it reveals to us, figuratively, the rules of life.  
It draws out mystical things and promises the heights of heaven.  
For neither Doric Greek speech, nor Hebrew, nor the Latin language  
can express what this sacred little book retains in its bosom.

Come, then, traverse the shining paths gladly,  
so that you may receive, reader, so many sacred graces from this book,  
from which you may recognize Christ, the high-throned one,  
and may deserve, rejoicing, to ascend the threshold of heaven,  
where, seeing the Lord forever through the ages,  
you may enjoy the happy joy of many blessings.

Amen.

The verses end here.

### Likewise, a Preface to the Little Works on the Book of Genesis by Angelomus the Deacon

To the excellent Father, adorned with the flowers of virtue  
[Z., “Father, flourishing in virtues and adorned with moral excellence”]  
and with the splendor of wisdom, Leodricus the priest,  
Angelomus, humble Levite.

After we had explored, as far as we were able, with subtle inquiry and with the Lord’s generosity, the treasure chambers and treasures of the four Gospels—which rightly surpass all the pages of divine Scripture by their authority—under the permission and command of our distinguished lord the abbot, we eagerly absorbed spiritual understanding from the speech of the most learned priest Mellinus [Z., Mellicus], a man whose discourse was radiant and who proclaimed it throughout the whole Catholic Church.

At last, as you know, we approached the abysses of the Old Testament, with Christ as our guide, in obedience to the command of the aforesaid Father, although fearful. As eager investigators, we immersed the keel of our little vessel into the deep sea and the whirlpools of divine history.

For while, with the author of light breathing upon us, we carried the evangelical shield in our left hand and held the two-edged sword of the divine word in our right, we labored with the greatest exertion in proclaiming, once the burden had been lifted, the vast and mystical meanings, surrounded by testimonies from the divine writings. As we meditated upon them through fruitful comparison and entrusted to our memory the things which we had most willingly drawn from the teacher’s mouth, you began, amid conversations concerning the heavenly oracle, frequently and kindly to urge me to arrange in my own writing on parchment those things which seemed to be explained abundantly and wondrously by the authority of the divine writings and were stored in the treasure of the heart according to the weakness of my understanding, so that there might be something by which memory could be refreshed through frequent reading in the future.

Considering the weight of so great a task, I delayed doing so in every way, hiding myself. But while we were laboring at the work already begun—

* “Now first brought to light from the manuscript of the most famous monastery of Saint Peter at Salzburg, of the Order of Saint Benedict, carefully collated with the manuscript of the renowned monastery of Zwettl, of the Cistercian order.” Pez.

## [Scan page 60]

### ANGELOMUS OF LUXEUIL

We labored heavily at the work, with divine assent, in the burden of pastoral care, from which you could by no means excuse yourself, since you had been appointed for the salvation of others. When I saw you oppressed beneath so heavy a sickle, you proclaimed it with tearful mouth, because you could no longer imbibe the salutary words and honey of souls through continual meditation as before, you again summoned me by the authority of your command, not merely by suggesting as formerly but, in a certain way, attempting to order me, to explain in clear speech certain little works from the book of Genesis, especially the works of the six days, prepared by the Lord, according to the literal sense, which seemed exceedingly difficult, just as they had been handed down by the teacher.

You declared that their spiritual meaning, which in some places is greatly obscure, could be found elucidated in the books of the Fathers, especially by the most learned blessed Isidore; yet not all the mysteries contained in that aforesaid volume had been arranged by him. With unrestricted authority you commanded me to insert in their proper places both those matters that had been handed down to me and, more difficult still, those omitted by so great a teacher which I might myself be able to discover.

Fearing the severity of this injunction, I resolved in silent thought to give my assent. Yet although there were no other reasons, there are two above all which most strongly deterred me from this work.

First, I find myself unequal to the task, especially since I am furnished with no knowledge of the liberal arts and am adorned neither with the patterns of syllogisms nor with the figures of rhetorical devices, although I may have offered something as a preliminary. I am not supported by the flower of verbal learning, but am unlearned in expression and lacking in eloquence.

Second, the subject is clouded by such obscurity that scarcely anything seems to shine through to me. I therefore wonder why so great a man, having obtained not only the wisdom of the arts—though they are inept—but also the riches of the sacred Scriptures, should have thought it fitting to impose the burden of so great a task upon me, lacking in strength, by so sharp a command, so that you might be able to chant joyfully that epithalamium: “The king brought me into his wine cellar” (*Song of Songs* 1:4), and the rest.

Nevertheless, as I have said, reflecting that it was necessary for me to obey your commands, remembering that saying of the blessed Benedict: “Whoever hears you hears me,” and so forth (Luke 10:16), after long and much hesitation, weighing in my mind the insufficiency of my strength, I sought refuge, like a shipwrecked sailor tossed by stormy waves who finally reaches harbor through prayer. I confessedly sought that the giver of all things, the one hope, the Lord of the world, might grant strength, although I was unworthy, so that I could complete the task by the right path—or rather, with unblemished faith.

Finally, with him inspiring me, although I undertook the task fearfully, I nevertheless strove to obey your commands. I composed, in unpolished language, a few things concerning the works of the six days according to the historical sense, although figurative meanings are mingled with them, just as they had been handed down to me.

When I had already resolved to set down the final boundary with my last sentence and had decided to remain wholly silent about the matter thereafter, the teacher suddenly entered and addressed me with these words: “What is this, agreeable son? What is it that you are explaining with such zeal?” Since I could not conceal it, with my conscience as witness, I revealed it in a humble voice.

He, desiring to know it—as is characteristic of his keen and discerning mind—ordered me to reread before him whatever useful thing I had produced. When he had read it, he praised and approved it, so to speak, and also gave me a book of blessed Augustine written in lucid speech against the Manichaeans on this subject, so that I might verify the things I had arranged.

Having examined that book eagerly under Christ’s guidance, I found that it agreed not only in meaning but also, in certain places and syllables, in wording. Then [Z., “thereupon”] he commanded me, in language sweet as honey, not to be discouraged by laziness or grow weary, and not to abandon the work begun, but to attempt to complete it with diligent effort.

Reconsidering the matter, lest perhaps I should be ordered to produce it for some who were perfect, or at least for little ones, I took courage through divine assistance, encouraged by the prayers of you, Father, and of that same teacher, and relying upon the support of your prayers. I began to weave together the work commanded, although in uncultivated speech.

But so that no one might think that I had inserted material of my own invention, I gathered volumes of the holy Fathers from here and there [in the manuscript of Saint Peter, “gathered” is absent], so that I might strengthen what I wrote with their statements. From their great and deep rivers, so to speak, I diverted certain things into a small stream, inserting their principal and proper words.

Some things, for the sake of brevity, I wrote in my own words while following their meaning. Others, which I had learned by tradition but could not find in the volumes available to us, I ventured to append with examples, and I resolved to bring the little book to an end in this form, so that someone occupied by the many whirlpools of worldly affairs, who has no leisure to traverse the broad fields of the teachers, might quickly survey this little book, gathered together with great brevity.

I ask you to read it with careful examination and to adorn it with the ornaments of your own refinement and elegance, lest it produce disgust in the learned and a rougher style stain the ears of the wise.

But before this introduction reaches its end, it must be noted that in certain places, where the truth of the historical account is always being set forth, we have inserted spiritual and moral understanding; namely, wherever you instructed that the history should inculcate the truth of events and the faithfulness of the narrative, while spiritual understanding should lead to the secrets of heavenly figures and moral exhortation should invite the improvement of life.

Thus the reader, not pressed by history alone but captivated by spiritual—indeed moral—sweetness, may be able to find avenues of excuse; and, having begun to gather honeyed tastes from this, may more gladly strive to survey the teachers’ very broad fields. Farewell.

The preface ends here.

### The Text of the Little Work on Genesis Begins

“In the beginning God created heaven and earth.”

With divine grace assisting, which gives confidence to children and grants speech to the mute, I am about to describe a little work on the book of Genesis. Before I approach the composition [Z., “text”] of the historical narrative and the depths of the spiritual oracle, I wish to inquire why this volume is specially called *Genesis*, since many things are recalled in it which are not known to pertain to generation.

It is customary among the Hebrews to assign the names of books from their beginnings, just as Exodus and many others are named. Accordingly, *Bresith*, a Hebrew word, is rightly translated into Latin as *Genesis*, because at its beginning the creation of heaven and earth and the generation of human beings and animals are narrated.

Some also ask who is considered the author of this book. The question is superfluous, since the Holy Spirit is faithfully believed to be its author. No one could describe events that occurred before human beings existed unless the Holy Spirit dictated them and, through the voice of the writer, narrated to human beings what happened at the beginning.

It should nevertheless be understood that although it is written in the book, “Moses was exceedingly meek above all the people who dwelt on the earth” (Numbers 12:3), and that “the Lord spoke to Moses” and many similar statements occur, yet, as the teachers hand down and many examples confirm, Moses himself was the writer of the divine history. Scripture’s custom is that those who write speak of themselves in it as though of others, because they are moved by the Holy Spirit.

Next, some are also troubled by the question of why Moses wrote the history of the divine law in his own time, rather than having it written down earlier by someone else. The reason is that the first human beings before the Flood had knowledge of God, the natural law, and the wondrous works of God accomplished at the beginning. After the Flood, however, all these things had been handed over to oblivion, especially in the time of Moses, so that people plainly did not know what had happened previously [Z., “what had previously happened”].

Therefore philosophers, ignorant of the beginning of this world, said that the world was coeternal and coeval with God. Moses, perhaps hearing this—or because all these matters had been removed from human memory—thought it right, instructed by the divine Spirit, to set down the creation of heaven and earth and of the other creatures, and, at the Lord’s command, to hand over the written law to the children of Israel, so that he might instruct them more fully about God, lest they return to the idols of Egypt, and might show that the world had been created.

Since the law of good nature was no longer being observed as it had been among the first human beings, but had almost been abolished, the written law was described and given through Moses so that the good things already known might possess authority, the things that had begun to lie hidden might be brought to light, and the fear of discipline might correct those who sinned and restore faith in God.

Was Moses present when God created all things? Certainly not; it was the very coeternal Wisdom of God the Father, through whom all things were made. How, then, can we reconcile faith with this? The answer is that past events are often proved by future events, and future events by past ones, as is demonstrated in Daniel and shown in this book.

Moses, though himself a human being, wrote about that time when no human being yet existed. In the same way he also wrote about future events at a time when humanity existed, although those events were later shown to have been fulfilled in truth, as is made clear in the blessing of the patriarch Jacob. Jacob himself said in his prophecy: “The scepter shall not be taken from Judah…” (Genesis 49:10): things which had been foretold figuratively of Christ but are now believed to have been fulfilled in truth.

If he had not spoken of the true future, no one would have wished to believe what he wrote with certainty about the past. It is also asked where Moses published his books. Some say that he wrote Genesis and Exodus up to the words “Let us sing to the Lord” in Egypt, and the rest in the wilderness. Others assert that, after crossing the Red Sea, he wrote in the wilderness during the forty years; this can also be supported by reason.

These few remarks are enough for those who wish to know such matters. Now, with the Lord’s favor [Z., “generosity”], let us pass to the structure of the history. Moses says:

### Chapter One

**Verse 1: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.”**

First it must be noted that Scripture immediately reveals, in its first word, the eternity and power of God the Creator. When it says that he created the world at the beginning of time, it indicates that he himself existed perfectly and eternally before time. When it narrates that he created heaven and earth at the very beginning of creation, it declares the great speed of his operation: for him, to will and to do are one.

It is also plainly shown here that both were made by him simultaneously, although it is impossible for a human being to say how both were made. The phrase “In the beginning” can be understood in two ways.

First, it may mean “first of all,” that is, at the beginning of created things. The Seventy translators, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated it in the same way. In Hebrew it is written *Bresith*. Aquila interprets this as “in the chapter,” or—

[The supplied text ends here.]

[...] God’s will is greater than heaven and earth; and whoever asks this seeks something greater than God’s will, and can find nothing greater. Let human presumption therefore restrain itself and not seek what does not exist, lest it fail to find what does exist. If it desires to know God’s will, let it become God’s friend. For if someone wished to know the will of a person whose friend he was not, everyone would laugh at his shamelessness (Z: imprudence) or foolishness.

Nevertheless, we may suppose that this world was fashioned for humanity’s sake and made, in a certain sense, its house. Although it consists of different substances, it is nevertheless one (Z omits “is”), fitted with many members, so that from their reciprocal functions the things necessary for human beings might be produced.

Finally, when Scripture says, “God created heaven and earth,” some understand it simply. Sacred Scripture is their nest, but they have no wings with which to reach lofty things. When they hear of God, they suppose him corporeal, endowed with a mass of marvelous size and supreme power. Such people are not altogether to be despised; rather, one should implore the Lord to send his angel to restore them to the nest, so that they may grow feathers and receive the wings of spiritual understanding. Then they may understand God as incorporeal and invisible, lest, like featherless chicks, they be trampled by passers-by.

Others, however, endowed with the wisdom of a higher understanding (Z: “understanding of wisdom”), for whom divine Scripture is no longer, in a certain sense, a nest but fruit and food, fly joyfully among the branches of this tree. They attend to the fact that God himself is incorporeal and invisible, and understand that he created heaven and earth in the Son—that is, in his Word—not by a transitory utterance but by remaining eternally.

Accordingly (Z: “and now”), different people understand the words that follow, “heaven and earth,” in different ways. Some wish “heaven” to mean this visible sky, and “earth” this visible land from which all things are produced. Others wish “heaven” to mean the throne of God, withdrawn from all the changing movement of this world and reserved for the divine presence alone (Latin *solius*; Z: *solum*); we shall discuss this more fully in its proper place below.

Others understand “heaven” to mean spiritual creatures, that is, the angelic order, because on the first day God created this spiritual creation. Concerning it we read in the book of blessed Job: “When the morning stars praised me together and all the sons of God shouted for joy” (Job 38:7). In “earth,” however, they understand formless matter.

Others, indeed, understand by the terms “heaven and earth” the very formless matter from which heaven and earth were created. This is not without reason, since they were destined to be formed from it. For heaven is later said to have been made. The statement is like saying, when considering the seed of a tree, that it contains roots, trunk, branches, fruit, and leaves—not because they already exist there, but because they are destined to arise from it. That confused matter—or, according to Peter, “unconfused” (*inconfusa*, reading uncertain)—was, as it were, the seed of heaven and earth.

[Editorial note: Supply *creaturam*—“creation”—from manuscript Z.]

## Page 62 — In Genesis

For those who wish to understand by “heaven” this visible sky and by “earth” this visible land, if someone objects that God made something on the second and third days, they have no answer at all. Those who, as has been said, understand by “heaven” the spiritual orders and by “earth” the formless matter from which all things were formed likewise hold a correct view, and their interpretation should be accepted—provided that they are capable of discerning (Z: learning) what precedes in eternity, what precedes in time, what precedes by choice, and what precedes by origin.

For the two things placed first and last are the most difficult to understand. It is arduous, and exceedingly difficult to comprehend, how God in his eternity precedes all things—or, according to Peter, “proceeds” before them. The two things placed in the middle, however, are easily understood: in time, the flower precedes the fruit, while by choice the fruit precedes the flower. But how one thing precedes another by origin, as sound precedes song, is obscure.

It should nevertheless be observed that every song is a sound, but not every sound is a song. Sound, when formed, becomes song—and not merely song, but pleasant and sweet song. Thus sound precedes song by origin alone.

In the same way, formless matter does not precede formed creatures in eternity, as God precedes it. Nor does it precede them in time, since times did not exist before formed creatures. Nor does it precede them by choice, since it was inferior: formed creatures are more excellent than formless substance. But it precedes formed creatures by origin alone. For God created formless matter from nothing, and from it created all things, according to what is written in the Book of Wisdom: “For your hand, Lord, was not powerless, which created the world from formless matter” (Wisdom 11:18).

Hence the philosophers, as has already been said, unable to penetrate how divine Wisdom created the world from nothing, believed that the world was coeternal with God. They say this because they consider the craftsman’s material, not God. They say: “Wood assists the carpenter, silver the silversmith, and gold the goldsmith.” Although such craftsmen need these materials, they cannot create them. The Lord, however, needed none of these things; he created everything from formless matter, not outside himself like a craftsman—for a craftsman does not make wood but makes something from wood. The Almighty needed no assistance from anything he himself had not made in order to bring about what he willed; otherwise he would not be God.

But why is it said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” rather than, “In the beginning God said, ‘Let heaven and earth be,’” as it is said of the light, “God said, ‘Let there be light,’” and so forth? It is because at first it was necessary to comprehend and designate universally, under the name of heaven and earth, what he had made, and then to carry it out in its parts, as the account goes on to describe.

The text continues:

**Verse 2.** “But the earth was empty and void.”

When he had said above, “God created heaven and earth,” why is it now said, “But the earth was empty and void”? It is because the formless matter designated by the name “earth” was empty and void. It was empty—that is, unformed and not yet gathered together into its proper kinds. It was void because it was barren of producing fruits.

Hence another translation says, “Invisible and unformed.” It was invisible because of its darkness, and unformed because of its shapelessness, since it was still wholly covered by the abyss—that is, by an immense depth of waters.

From the statement, “But the earth was empty and void,” we may understand what sort of heaven is being considered first: it remains forever quiet, withdrawn from every changing condition of this world and abiding in the divine presence. For the heaven in which the luminaries are placed, and how and when it was made, is explained below.

That heaven, therefore, was not created empty and void like the earth, since it contributed nothing by way of creation; it was immediately filled with the most blessed hosts of angels. We have already spoken above of these angels, whom God created in the beginning, together with heaven and earth, to praise him, just as he himself says to blessed Job: “Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?” (Job 38:4). A little later: “When the morning stars praised me and all the sons of God shouted for joy?” (ibid.).

To one of these it is said: “How have you fallen from heaven?” and so forth (Isaiah 14:12). If he was still placed in heaven, how can he say, “I will ascend into heaven”? But since we read, “The heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord” (Psalm 113:16), although he was in heaven—that is, in the firmament—he wished to ascend into the heaven where God’s throne was.

Or, as we said above, “heaven” may mean either the angelic order itself or formless matter itself.

“And darkness was over the face of the abyss.” By the name “abyss” that formless matter is understood, because it was dark and deep. Scripture says, “And darkness,” and so forth. Why, then, are darknesses mentioned when no darknesses were previously said to have been created? If they were not created, are they eternal? Certainly not.

We must understand that darkness is not a substantial thing; rather, darkness properly means the absence of light. Just as silence is not a substance but the absence of sound, and nakedness is nothing other than the absence of clothing, so it is with darkness. Darkness is the deprivation of light, not a thing in itself. Wherever there is no light, darkness is said to be present.

It is therefore rightly said, “Darkness was over the face of the abyss,” because the formless matter mentioned above had not yet been illuminated and made manifest.

We may also say that God did not make any darkness in the water or in the air. Rather, in the distinct order of his providence, he first created the waters together with heaven and earth, and afterwards, when he willed, adorned them with the grace of light. We see him doing this even now, both in the water itself and in the air, through the daily rising and setting of the sun.

Here we should observe that, when he created two elements—water and earth—he also created two others: fire and air. He placed fire in iron and stones, since it had already been hidden in the bowels of the earth, as hot springs reveal (Z: produce). He placed air in the earth itself, and this is recognized by the fact that when the earth has been moistened and has received the sun’s warmth, it immediately exhales abundant vapors.

“And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters.” What does it mean that he was “borne”? Was it in the manner in which a bird is borne over the earth? Certainly not. He was borne not locally but in power, governing and sustaining the formless matter, just as the craftsman’s will is borne over the things being fashioned.

Hence another translation says, “He rested upon it” (Z: “brooded over it”), in the likeness of a bird brooding over eggs with the warmth of its body. This makes it clear that the passage concerns the Holy Spirit, not the spirit of this world, as heretics supposed. Just as a bird broods in order to bring forth its offspring in a formed state, so the Holy Spirit brooded over the formless substance so that he might create all things from it.

Nevertheless, we must ask why the waters are mentioned when they had not previously been said to have been created. Are they therefore eternal, as the Manichaeans suspected? No. They deceive themselves because they do not understand that the invisible substance itself is designated by the word “water.” It is appropriately called water because it was fluid and subject to the divine will, so that all things possessing moisture might be produced from it. Everything that is born and nourished grows and develops through the moisture of water.

We must understand, however, that the aforesaid formless substance is designated by the name “water” because we could know nothing about it unless sacred Scripture spoke in our customary manner. It is one thing, but it is distinguished by different names. If it were called by only one name, people would believe that it was only that one thing. It is therefore called by various names because all things were destined to be formed from it, so that what was unknown might be suggested to the inexperienced through familiar terms.

It is called heaven, earth, abyss, and water because all these things were destined to arise from it. Just as different kinds of tree are hidden in a small seed, so, as we have already indicated, everything was concealed in this formless matter.

It should also be observed that the whole Trinity is revealed at the beginning of this book. For the text continues:

**Verse 3.** “And God said: ‘Let there be light,’” and so forth.

What does “God said” mean? Did he speak with passing sounds? Certainly not. He is incorporeal, and if he speaks, does he speak in Hebrew, Greek, or Latin? No. By “God said,” Scripture does not mean the sound of words but what is understood through the sound (Z: “of speech”). With God there is pure understanding, without noise or the diversity of languages.

Therefore, for God to speak is for him to make, as it is written: “He spoke, and they were made,” and so forth (Psalm 148:5). The Word of God is his only-begotten Son, as John bears witness when he says: “In the beginning was the Word,” and so forth. Thus, when Scripture says that he spoke, it means that he made all things in his Word, who remains eternally.

When it says, “Let there be light,” this refers to the swiftness of divine power. If the luminaries that provide light are said to have been made on the fourth day, what does “Let there be light” mean? Was there perhaps already some light created above the firmament, by whose radiance the sun would be illuminated?

The name “light,” however, signifies the angelic order, which is certainly represented by the heaven mentioned above and is now called light. It was created in the beginning, but afterwards became light by turning toward the contemplation of the glory of its Creator. Therefore it is said, “Let there be light, and there was light.”

It is as though Scripture were saying plainly: “Let it turn continually toward contemplating me.” It was fitting that the angelic order, which by its dignity surpassed all creatures, should be called light by cleaving to the supreme Light, even though it had been created mutable. If it had been created immutable, those who fell through the sin of pride could never have fallen from that eternal vision. But because its nature was mutable, divine grace, when the others fell, made the remaining angels immutable through the generosity of its gift.

Some teachers, however, wish this to be understood simply, according to the historical sense. They say that this principal light shone in the upper regions of the same earth, which the daily light of the sun now customarily illuminates, and that by seeing it the most blessed angels began to enjoy blessedness.

Nor is it surprising that, by divine action, light could be reflected in the waters, since it is well established that human activity often makes them shine—namely, the activity of sailors who, when they have descended into the depths of the sea, pour oil from their mouths and thereby make the water around them transparent and bright. If a human being can accomplish such things through the oil of his mouth, how much more should we believe that God can create light through the Spirit proceeding from his mouth?

Read Bede’s *Hexaemeron*, the work of a modern teacher, if you wish to follow this interpretation.

For our part, we have decided to follow the statements of blessed Augustine, as we quoted earlier.

## Page 64 — Commentary

**Verse 4.** “And God saw that the light was good,” and so forth.

Why is it said, “God saw,” as though something new had happened, when he could not have created anything unless he had foreseen it? “God saw” is used for “he caused it to be seen.” Often what is produced is designated through the agent who produces it. Thus one speaks of a joyful house, a joyful letter, a pitcher pouring water into vessels, and other such expressions. Grammarians call this kind of figure metonymy.

Therefore, “God saw”—that is, “he caused to be seen”—how good the angelic creature was when it had been created by God. Or, by the statement “he saw,” Scripture may mean that, in predestination, he caused us to see how good the creature would be that was created by God.

In this way a future event is indicated through verbs in the past tense, just as he says to the apostles: “Everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:15), although the time had not yet come for him to do so.

When Scripture says, “And he divided the light from the darkness” (Z: “and the darkness”), it shows that a distinction was made between light and darkness, not that darknesses were made. It is like saying that we produce a voice by shouting, whereas we speak of silence without shouting, because silence is the cessation of the voice. Nevertheless, by a certain act of understanding we distinguish between the two, calling one voice and the other silence.

Just as it is rightly said that we make silence, so God is rightly said to make darkness, because he gives light—or withdraws it—to whomever he wills, at whatever times and in whatever places he wills. As Clement says: “Illuminating one part of the world,” he says, “he left another in darkness.” He spread light over the upper part of the world, where human habitation was destined to be, while leaving its lower regions in their ancient darkness.

If anyone wishes to accept this interpretation, we shall follow, as we began, blessed Augustine and attempt to preserve the master’s exposition.

“And God divided the light from the darkness,” and so forth. That is, he divided the heavenly citizens of the angels from the unclean spirits when Lucifer, turning away from the Creator and turning toward himself, supposing that he was sufficient for himself, was cast out with his followers from the heavenly places, through pride and without the help of his Creator. The others remained in their stability. He called these latter “day” and the former “night,” as the text continues: “And he called the light Day, and the darkness Night.”

For the ruin of those who fell became eternal, while the stability of those who remained was made permanent.

Some, however, say that the division of light from darkness signifies the distinction between formed and formless things, while the naming of day and night signifies a distribution by which it is shown that God leaves nothing in disorder.

When Scripture says that he “called” them, this means that he caused them to be called. He distinguished and ordered everything in such a way that things could be discerned and receive a name.

The text continues:

**Verse 5.** “And evening came and morning came, one day.”
