We must ask why “evening” and “morning” are mentioned when the sun was not yet in the firmament, so that evening would be produced by its setting and morning by its rising. Did the first, second, and third days perhaps have as much duration as the interval from sunrise to sunset and, after the sun’s circuit toward the north, its return to the east, so that by its radiance it might drive away the world’s darkness? Those who live in caves and prisons, although deprived of light, can nevertheless recognize such an interval through experience. This might perhaps be understood in that way, were it not for the addition of “evening and morning.”

It therefore remains that “evening” should be understood as the completion of the preceding work, and “morning” as the beginning of the work that follows. Scripture speaks according to our manner of expression so that the distinction among God’s works may be understood.

When it says, “Evening came and morning came, one day,” this may refer to the angelic creature. When it turned its gaze away from God and turned to contemplate the creature, it was, in a certain sense, evening. But when it turned back toward the Creator, so that in him it might understand the creature more clearly, it was morning.

If it had remained in contemplation of the creature, however, it would have been not only evening but also night.

“One day” is rightly added because of the unity of the angelic order, which cleaves so closely to the contemplation of the one God that it never turns its gaze away from that contemplation.

**Verse 6.** “And God said: ‘Let there be a firmament,’” and so forth.

By the name “firmament” the visible heaven is designated, now distinguished from that formless matter. Concerning it the text later says: “And God called the firmament heaven.”

But we must ask what sort of firmament divides the waters above from those below. Some say that the firmament is the airy heaven, from which birds are called “birds of heaven,” and that it divides the waters of the clouds from the waters of the rivers.

Others wish the starry or ethereal heaven to be understood, because it divides the waters above from those below. It is not incredible that invisible waters should exist above the firmament. If they exist, however, they are not fluid, since they do not flow like visible waters.

For this reason some suppose that they persist in a frozen solidity rather than in vaporous thinness, citing the star Saturn, which they say is extremely cold. They say that it is cold from these waters because it completes its course near the highest heaven in thirty years, although those who discuss weights may wish to deny this.

They do not say that these waters are located in distinct places like rivers, but that they surpass the heaven not by occupying places but by the dignity of their nature. For since heaven is the most beautiful of bodies, every invisible creature, as blessed Augustine says, surpasses even the beauty of heaven.

Thus, according to the opinion of that same outstanding teacher, there are waters above the heavens. He says: “But whatever and of whatever kind those waters may be, let us have no doubt that they are there; for the authority of this Scripture,” he says, “is greater than the capacity of every human intellect.”

As other teachers say, these waters covered the whole surface of the earth to such a height that they reached those places where, even now, they remain above the firmament of heaven and do not cease to praise the name of their Creator together with the heavens of heavens.

Finally, if someone wishes to deny this, then, if he created a human being as God did, he would place the appetite (*epithymia*) not in the head but in the stomach.

Nevertheless, we should not rashly decide this matter, since it lies beyond our sight.

Others understand the upper waters as the peoples of angels, concerning whom it is written: “And the waters that are above the heavens, let them praise the name of the Lord” (Psalm 148:4). They understand the lower waters as human beings dwelling on earth, concerning whom it is said: “The waters that you saw are peoples and nations.” The starry heaven, of course, separates them from one another.

## Page 65 — Angelo[m]us of Luxeuil, Monk

**Verse 9.** “And God said: ‘Let the waters under heaven be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear,’” and so forth.

If the whole world was full of waters, where were they gathered, unless in the place of which Scripture says, “Let them be gathered into one place”? It is as though it said: “Let that formless matter now distinguish and produce its own kinds; let the kind of water and the kind of earth appear.”

The gathering itself is the formation of the waters that we see and touch. When Scripture says, “Let the dry land appear,” what else should we understand than that matter received the visible form which this earth now has? It is rightly called dry land, because, just as fire properly has heat and water moisture, so earth has dryness.

**Verse 10.** “And he called the gatherings of waters seas.”

It should be observed that, according to the idiom of the Hebrew language, all gatherings of water—whether fresh or salt—are called seas.

But in the *Hexaemeron* of the aforementioned teacher Bede we read:

“It could have happened,” he says, “that the earth itself, sinking far and wide at the Creator’s command, provided concave regions in which the flowing waters could be received, so that the dry land might appear. It may also be understood and believed, not unreasonably, that the primordial waters were more diffuse, covering the earth like a mist, but that through their gathering they became denser and could be contained in the places assigned to them, while the dry land appeared elsewhere.”

He rightly says “into one place,” because through a continuous and unbroken flow they are joined to the Ocean and the Great Sea.

The text continues:

**Verses 11–13.** “Let the earth bring forth green grass,” and so forth, up to “whose seed is in itself.”

Why does Scripture say “in itself,” when many trees do not produce fruit in which they contain their seed? We should understand that, even if they do not contain it in the fruit, they contain it in the root from which they sprout.

“And God saw that it was good,” and so forth.

If grasses, the fruits of the earth, and fruit-bearing trees are good, and Scripture says, “God saw everything that he had made, and it was very good,” while finally adding, “God rested from all his works,” what are we to say about poisonous herbs and harmful trees?

The answer is that, when they were created, these harmful properties did not appear; rather, they received their nature at their origin so that they would have such properties in the future.

But what does Scripture mean when it says, “God saw that it was good”? It means that it pleased him in its goodness that it should remain what it was, just as it pleased him that what he had made should come into being.

What is meant by God’s saying to Adam concerning thorns and thistles, “Your earth will bring forth thorns and thistles for you,” unless it is meant to be understood that the statement was not made absolutely—“The earth will bring forth thorns and thistles”—but rather, “for you”? It is as though he said: “The things that previously brought forth food for the use of cattle and beasts now begin to produce thorns and thistles for you as an exercise in labor.”

If he had not sinned, the earth would never have produced those harmful things. It is therefore evident that after his sin the earth began to produce thorns.

Concerning poisonous and harmful herbs and trees, we should understand that they were created very good. If they do not provide food, they provide medicine. If they seem harmful to us, they are harmless to wild animals and birds, because they provide them with nourishment, even if they do not provide food for us.

Therefore, as Scripture says, every creature was created very good. But after the sin of the first parent, it came about that some trees appeared fruitless and sterile, and that poisonous herbs appeared, so that through them human beings might in a certain way contemplate their sin, be reminded to turn away from sins and turn toward God’s commandments, fear losing God’s cultivation, and fear appearing sterile in the field of the Church if they were not fruitful trees.

Or trees without fruit and harmful herbs were created so that no mysteries (Z: ministries) might be disclosed to the unworthy, and so that it might not be shown in what figure these things were spoken of concerning the future.

**Verses 14–19.** “And God said: ‘Let there be luminaries in the firmament of heaven,’” and so forth.

If the luminaries were made on the fourth day, why was “evening and morning” mentioned earlier, unless, as has already been said, evening is understood as the completion of the preceding work and morning as the beginning of the work that follows?

“And let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for years, and for days.”

This agrees with what the Lord says: “There will be signs in the sun and moon and stars” (Luke 21:25).

They are called signs because they signify something in the future. There are such signs in the stars that announce storms, rains, and wars, and some also show travelers at sea the way.

They are for seasons because by their changes they distinguish the seasons—spring, summer, autumn, and winter.

They are for days and years according to the courses of the sun and moon, since there are solar days and, according to the reckonings of astronomers, lunar days as well. Or this is because, before the luminaries were formed, there was nothing by which the hours of day and night could be marked.

For it is written: “He made the moon for seasons” (Psalm 103:19).

## Page 66 — Commentary

“But the sun knows its setting” (Psalm 103:19).

We must ask: if time begins here, and days begin to be marked by divisions and moments of hours, what are we to say about the interval that existed up to the fourth day? Were there no times? There were times in a certain sense, but that interval was not divided by the segments of hours as it is now. It passed without such divisions because there was no sun by which they could be distinguished.

Something similar happens even now when the sun is covered by a cloud and the times cannot be distinguished, although the interval of the day nevertheless passes.

**Verses 20–23.** “And God said: ‘Let the waters bring forth creeping living creatures, and birds,’” up to “And God blessed them, saying: ‘Increase and multiply,’” and so forth.

Here it is shown that creeping creatures and birds belong to one nature and one origin. But by the name “water” the air also is understood. Learned people classify it with water because it grows dense through the evaporation of waters and supports the flight of birds. If it did not possess a certain density, it could not sustain their flight.

Hence, in summer, when the weather is clear, it moistens the earth and drops appear. And if water possessed no solidity, it could not support the floating bodies of human beings or bear birds. Therefore, whatever is wave-like and flowing is assigned to fish, while whatever is dense and exhaled is assigned to birds.

That the air is dense and wind-bearing, and supplies breath, philosophers proved on Mount Olympus. They say that no wind is felt at its summit and no clouds gather there because, by its height, it rises above all this humid air in which birds fly. For this reason, they assert that birds cannot fly there.

They used to climb to its summit each year for the sake of sacrifices and write certain marks in the dust; the following year they found the marks intact. This could not happen if the place were exposed to winds or rains. They also applied moistened sponges to their nostrils so that they might draw in a thicker, customary breath, because the thinness of the air there did not provide normal inhalation.

They likewise asserted that they had never seen a bird in that place.

When Scripture says, “He blessed them, saying: ‘Increase and multiply,’” it bestows a blessing here for the first time, either because living creatures had been created, or because it was destined that through the water of baptism human beings would receive blessing.

**Verses 24–25.** “And God said: ‘Let the earth bring forth a living creature,’” and so forth, up to “And God saw that it was good.”

If God saw that it was good, what are we to say about the rottenness of trees and the illnesses of various creatures? The answer is that, when they were created, these illnesses did not appear; rather, they received at their origin the condition that they would have in the future.

But what does “God saw that it was good” mean? It means that it pleased him in its goodness that it should remain as it was, just as it pleased him that what he had made should come into being.

The text continues:

**Verse 26.** “Let us make humanity in our image and likeness.”

What does “Let us make humanity in our image” mean? It means that a rational creature was now being created, so that God might appear, in a certain sense, to make it with deliberation, and so that its nobility might be shown. Hence the plural, “Let us make.”

But why was it said above, “And God said: ‘Let there be …,’” while here it says, in the plural, “Let us make humanity in our image,” and so forth? It was to show that God is three in persons and one in the nature of the Godhead (Z: “one in divine nature”).

For this reason the text later says: “And God created humanity in his image,” and so forth.

Humanity is said to have been made in the image of God because it possesses an invisible and immortal soul by nature. But if the image of God is the rational faculty of the soul, while its likeness is the eternal life that he will give to all the elect, when what John says comes to pass—“We shall be like him,” and so forth (1 John 3:2)—this does not mean that they will become equal to the Godhead, but that they will be joined to eternity.

Alternatively, the image of God is in the inner human being, while likeness is found in conduct. Everyone possesses the image of God, but few possess his likeness. Those especially possess his likeness who imitate him and fulfill what he says: “Be holy, because I am holy,” and so forth (Leviticus 11:44).

The text continues: “And let him rule over the fish of the sea,” and so forth.

If all animals and birds were created so that they might be subject to humanity, why does humanity suffer harm from many beasts? A person may wish to drive away certain birds but be unable to do so; nor can he overcome beasts. Indeed, because of human weakness, he is often killed by them.

Although he cannot rule over all of them, nevertheless he is in no way ruled by beasts (Z: “he in no way rules beasts”). Whoever raises this objection is considering what humanity became after sin and does not consider what it was before it sinned.

Created in the image of God, humanity would have retained everything in subjection if it had remained within its proper order. But because it became a transgressor of God’s commandments, some things were granted for its benefit, while others were turned into a scourge, according to what God himself says through the prophet: “I am the Lord, making peace and creating evil” (Isaiah 45:7).

God appears to create evil when human beings suffer punishment from creatures that ought to have been subject to them.

If humanity had maintained its proper order, the beasts too would have preserved their obedience, as is shown in the case of blessed Daniel, to whom lions were subject even when they were hungry.

**Verse 27.** It should be observed that the fact that humanity was created in the image of God and appointed over the beasts is shown in the creation of humanity itself and of the creatures. Humanity was created upright so that it might contemplate heavenly things; beasts, by contrast, were created prone, so that they might display their obedience.

Therefore the Son of God (Z: “God the Son”) created humanity in his own image, and he created it in the image of the Father, because he himself is the image of God the Father, in whose image humanity too was created.

For, as has already been said, this refers to the inner human being (Z: “in the inner human being”), because humanity is rational, possesses a soul by nature, and was made immortal. Hence the Apostle says: “A man ought not to veil his head (Z: “his own head”), because he is the image of God; but a woman ought to veil …”

[Scan page 67]

…because a man strives toward heavenly things and contemplates divine realities, he ought not to veil his head—that is, to place the obstacle of sin before his mind. But if he ceases to meditate on divine things and turns excessively toward earthly matters, he is no longer called a man but a woman; and therefore he veils his head like a woman—that is, he places an obstacle before righteousness, lest, while he begins to think about permissible things, he burst forth into impermissible ones and spread himself wholly toward outward things, thereby offending God.

**“Male and female he created them.”** Why is it said that the female had already been created, when her formation is subsequently narrated, unless it is because he created her in the man by origin, since she was to be formed from the man?

God first created one male and one female, not as he created the animals and other things in plurality, but so that he might bind the human race to one another by an order of charity, since it would remember that it had arisen from one parent. Hence he formed the woman from the man’s side, so that he might declare that the earth was to be filled through their mutual union.

**Verse 28.** “And he blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it,” and so forth. Some understand this statement historically, others spiritually; but the better course is to understand it in both ways.

It should be known that it is not incredible that, according to God’s blessing, they could increase and multiply through sexual intercourse, if they had remained obedient to the divine commands—yet in such a way that their genitals would be moved by nature, not by any goading lustful desire. Thus as many chosen persons would have been born from them as must be chosen from all the nations for the restoration of the number of angels; and they would by no means have succeeded one another through death. Once the number of the elect had been completed, they would have passed from the bodily paradise to the heavenly one without death.

This seems impossible to some, since, they say, the sexual organs could not have moved without lust, given that the organs are moved by desire. But let them observe that not only in human beings but also in irrational animals certain members move while the others remain immobile—something they would not believe if they did not see it. Often, for example, when an animal’s skin is irritated by flies, the skin alone moves in order to drive them away, while the other limbs remain still. Likewise, one ear moves while the others remain at rest; and there are many other things that would seem incredible if they were not seen.

If such movements can occur in the limbs of irrational creatures, how much more could, by God’s blessing, the natural organs have been moved for procreation, without lust? And just as cultivation of the soil is undertaken for the production of crops, so Adam was able to beget offspring from that woman without lust.

Without abandoning the historical narrative, the passage may be referred to the fruitfulness of the soul: “Increase,” that is, multiply by augmenting virtues; “and fill the earth,” that is, make it fruitful through the virtues of the flesh; “and subdue it to the spirit”; and “rule over the beasts,” that is, over movements resembling beasts, which you have through intemperance [Z., “which you have through temperance”]. If these movements break out into destructive pleasures, they resemble beasts; but if they are governed, they become entirely tame. Hence Paul says: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh” (Gal. 5:24).

But it is asked for what useful purpose man received dominion over the fish, the birds, and the rest, or for what uses. He would not have eaten them if he had not sinned; in the first creation, the fruits of the trees alone were granted as food. Unless perhaps one should say that God foreknew that he would sin and, through sin, become mortal. Therefore he instituted from the beginning comforts by which man might be able to protect his frailty, whether food from these things or other necessities.

**Verses 29–30.** “And God said: Behold, I have given you every herb, and every tree,” and so forth, “so that they may be food for you, and for all the animals of the earth.”

How, then, are herbs and the fruits of trees said to have been given as food to all the animals of the earth and to the birds, when there are many beasts and birds that eat flesh and are not nourished by the crops of the earth, such as lions and others? Perhaps those things were specified which are eaten by such creatures; or, even though they eat flesh, they are nourished by these things because they eat the bodies of animals that feed on such herbs or fruits. Thus serpents, which dwell in sandy places, feed on the dead bodies of animals.

**Verse 31.** “And God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good.” Since many things were previously created and it was said of each one: “And God saw that it was good,” why is it said at the end, “and they were very good”? Is it not because, considered in their individual kinds, they are good, but joined together they are not merely good but very good in their totality?

For example, you praise the eye in a body by itself, and the other limbs individually; but when they are joined together so that there is one body, you call it not merely good but very good. Indeed, the totality of the body is praised to such an extent that, if any member is removed from it, the body is not merely useless but disfigured.

Or this is why, after the human being was created, it is not said individually, as it is of the other creatures, “God saw that it was good,” but after all the creatures had been made it was said, “and they were very good”: because they were created for the sake of man. Before this, each thing was, as it were, good individually; but once man, for whose sake they had been created, had been made, they were called very good, because all things were created for man’s adornment, while man was made for the glory and praise of his Creator.

## Chapter II

**Verse 1.** “Thus the heavens and the earth were completed, and all their array.” It is rightly said “the heavens” in the plural, because, according to the authority of Scripture, they are shown to be three: first, the airy heaven, from which the birds are called heavenly; second, the ethereal or starry heaven, where the luminaries are contained; and third, the spiritual heaven, which belongs properly to the angels. Concerning this the Apostle Paul says: “I know a man who was caught up to the third heaven” (2 Cor. 12:2). Shortly afterward he added that he was caught up into paradise. What he first called the third heaven, he repeated when he said “into paradise.”

[Scan page 68]

It should be known that the array of the spiritual heaven consists of angels, archangels, thrones, and so forth; the array of the ethereal heaven consists of the sun, moon, and stars; and the array of the airy heaven consists of clouds, winds, rains, and birds of various kinds. The adornment of the earth consists of the sea [Petr., “adornment in the air”], the ridges of the mountains, the valleys lying below, the broad [Z., dense] expanses of the plains, the alternations of the seasons, the forms of fruits, the courses of the waters, and so forth. It follows:

**Verse 2.** “And God completed on the seventh day his work which he had made, and he rested on the seventh day,” and so forth. According to the historical account, he completed the creation of the world in the number six because that number is read as perfect according to the principles of arithmetic, so that God might show that he had made all things perfect and very good.

But a deeper question is raised: what does it mean here that “he rested,” when he himself says in the Gospel: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17)? The teachers offer a threefold explanation of God’s rest.

First, when it says here “he rested,” it means that he ceased from creating new kinds of creatures, because thereafter he created nothing new by generation. Nevertheless, he continues to work by governing and sustaining his creature, which he had made from unformed matter.

Alternatively, “he rested” is said because it was destined that he through whom all things were made would, for our redemption, rest on the seventh day in the tomb [Z., “would rest”].

Or, by a transferred mode of expression, the statement may be referred to the members in relation to the head. For it is said, “God rested,” in place of “he caused [others] to rest,” because in him the elect attain perfect rest after this troubled life, which is figured by the six days, as though on the seventh day in the heavenly rest that meanwhile receives the souls of the elect, until at last the eighth day of the future resurrection arrives.

It is rightly said that God rested after the very good works, to show that the elect cannot reach the seventh day—that is, blessed rest—except after very good works. This also prompts the question why he wished to perform all his works over six days and to rest on the seventh, unless this number contains a great mystery.

For if it is divided into two, that is, into one and six, the unity of the Godhead, or the unity of charity, is signified by one; by six, the perfection of good works; and by seven, the eternal rest of souls. God therefore wished to perform his works over six days and rest on the seventh, showing that those who now display the unity of charity and the perfection of good works will attain heavenly rest, where they will contemplate the unity of the divine majesty—though the matter may be stated at a still deeper level.

The number six is also the first number perfect in operation and actuality, because in six days God created heaven and earth, and it is completed in its parts. For one, two, and three make six. The rest of the seventh day signifies that, before the creation of the world, God was perfect in himself by nature and power and eternally possessed rest in himself. But through the act of creation, creatures have perfection through him in their own natures, and a certain rest in the operation of obedience, especially rational creatures, which were created to rest in their Creator.

It follows:

**Verse 3.** “And he blessed the seventh day and sanctified it.” Why is it said of the Sabbath day, “God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it,” while we do not read that he said this of the other days? It was to show that, after the labors of the six ages of this world, the saints would rest in eternal Sabbath and blessed rest, as it will be said: “Come, you blessed of my Father,” and the rest (Matt. 25:34).

For this reason that day is read as having no evening, because the final rest of the saints will be everlasting. It is fittingly said that he sanctified and blessed it, because the saints receive eternal rest through the blessing of the Lord.

After these preliminary remarks, it should be noted that divine operation is distinguished in four ways. First, in the Word of God’s dispensation, all things are eternal. Second, he who lives forever created all things at once in unformed matter. Third, through the works of the six days, he distinguished various creatures. Fourth, from primordial seeds arise not unknown natures but known ones, which are repeatedly renewed so that they may not perish.

Thus far we have briefly gone through the historical account, although a few matters have been interspersed that seem to belong to the spiritual sense. We have omitted the spiritual interpretation for the sake of brevity. Anyone who wishes to know it should read the book of Isidore and survey the fields of the other teachers, because the history of divine law was not written without mystical meaning, as the Apostle Paul testifies when he says: “For the law has a figure of the good things to come” (Col. 2:17), not the very image of the things. And elsewhere: “All these things happened to them in a figure” (1 Cor. 10:11).

Explaining this also through the example of this history, where it is said, “For this reason a man will leave father and mother,” he showed that a sacrament was contained there when he said: “This is a great sacrament; but I speak of Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5:32).

We should therefore approach the history of the Old Testament and of the prophets in such a way that we neither seek a mystical meaning in everything nor restrict ourselves entirely to the historical sense, but recognize in some passages the mystical sense and in others the historical surface.

Wherever historical understanding is presented, it is presented only so that spiritual understanding may be contained within it, as in the construction of musical instruments. Wood is placed there, and strings are placed there as well, so that they may be contained within it and may sound sweetly. In the same way, history is set down so that, in joining things together, it may contain spiritual understanding. It follows:

**Verse 4.** “These are the generations of heaven and earth, when they were created, in the day when the Lord God made heaven and earth.” Here the works of God’s six days are recapitulated for the sake of those who said that the world was coeternal and maintained that it had always existed without a beginning, so that they may be silenced and utterly confounded.

But it must be asked what is meant by the statement, “in the day when he made heaven and earth,” since earlier he is read to have carried out all his works distinctly over six days. The meaning may be that the origin of all things was created at once in a substance that remained to produce various forms in their kinds, according to what is written: “He who lives forever created all things together” (Sir. 18:1).

The passage may also be understood at a deeper level. By “the day” in which he established the primordial creation, just as the Apostle says, “Behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2), he wished the whole period to be understood during which the saints labor in this life for eternal salvation. It follows:

[Scan page 69]

**Verse 5.** “And every shrub of the field before it arose on the earth, and every herb of the land before it sprouted.” How were the grass and vegetation of the field created before they arose? And if they had not yet appeared, how had they been made [Petr., “on the sixth [day]”]? The answer is that they were then created causally and originally, when it was said, “Let the earth bring forth green grass.” At that time the earth received the power of producing them; and within that power, as it were in roots, the things that were to arise in time had already been made.

He says fittingly, “every shrub of the field,” and so forth, in order to indicate the swiftness of God’s work: before any fruits had arisen from the earth by growing or sprouting, all the fields and hills were suddenly covered with grasses and trees. “For the Lord had not rained upon the earth, and there was no man to work the ground.” Why is the matter concerning man, who had already been made on the sixth day, recapitulated here? Because when God made every shrub of the field, it had not yet rained and man had not yet been made.

**Verse 6.** “But a spring rose from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth.” Here it is rightly asked: if the spring watered the extended surface of the fields and the whole surface of the earth, did it not water the summits of the mountains? And if it poured over the ridges and summits of the mountains, then it was not a spring but a flood.

But the statement, “A spring rose from the earth,” and what follows, has the same meaning as if he had said: It had not yet rained, but springs, bursting forth throughout the earth—whether in the level fields or on the summits of the mountains—watered their respective regions in their several places. He used “spring” in the singular instead of the plural, in the manner of Scripture, because of the unity of nature, since they all have one origin.

**Verse 7.** “Then God formed man from the mud of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life,” and so forth. Why did he form man from the mud of the earth, and not from an angelic creature? He wished to create him from the mud of the earth so that he might always preserve humility and not become proud, might see himself as dust and ashes after the example of Abraham, and might give thanks to his Creator because, although formed from such fragile material, he had been raised to such great grace that, if he were obedient to him, he would possess kingdoms with the angels of heaven.

“And he breathed into his face,” and so forth. God’s breathing into the face of the created man is the rational soul. But when it says that he breathed into his face the breath of life, a question arises: did God make the soul by breathing it in, or did he breathe into the body the soul that he had already made by giving it to the body?

In either case the meaning is one, and there is no real difficulty. Whether he made the soul by breathing, or, having created it, breathed it into the body by giving it to the body, we must nevertheless believe that the divine breath was not changed into a living soul but acted upon the living soul.

The soul does not share in the Godhead, nor did God create it from some breath of his own or from himself, so that we would be forced to say that God’s nature is mutable, like the soul, which at one time advances in wisdom, at another understands, and at another fails to understand. For if God had made the soul from himself, it could never have been vicious, mutable, or miserable.

It should also be known that the soul was not made from the visible elements. If it had been, it would have had some communion with them: solidity from earth, moisture from water, breath from air, and heat from fire. But since it lacks all these things, it is clear that it does not come from them, since it is shown to have nothing in common with them. Rather, as we said above, God created it from nothing, either by breathing it into existence or, having created it, breathing it into the body.

“And man became a living soul.” We should not understand this as referring to the spiritual man, who became a living soul, but still to the animal man. He became spiritual when, placed in paradise, he received the commandments of perfection. Therefore, after he sinned and was expelled from paradise, he remained such that he was animal. All who are born from him first become animal, until, reborn through the font of baptism, we attain the spiritual Adam, that is, Christ, through whom we become spiritual, according to what the Apostle Paul says: “It is not the spiritual that comes first, but the animal; afterward the spiritual” (1 Cor. 15:46).

**Verse 8.** “Now the Lord God had planted a paradise of delight,” and so forth. *Paradise* is interpreted as garden, delight, or pleasure. It should be known that paradise is mentioned in the divine books in four ways.

There is the paradise of which Moses speaks in this passage. In what place, province, or region it was situated is known to God alone, especially since it cannot be found anywhere in the whole world. Nevertheless, some maintain that it was placed in the East, saying that it was fitting for a place more delightful than all others to be planted in the more excellent part of the world. Hence some translated: “In Eden, toward the East.”

The world is also called paradise because of its adornment, as in Ezekiel, where the Lord speaks of the kingdom of the Assyrians: “The cedars were not higher than it in the paradise of God” (Ezek. 31:8).

A spiritual paradise is also mentioned, into which Paul says that he was carried: “I know a man who was caught up into paradise” (2 Cor. 12:2), that is, into heavenly delight.

According to the anagogical sense, paradise is the Church. Hence Solomon says in the Song of Songs: “A garden enclosed is my sister, a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain; your shoots are a paradise” (Song 4:12).

He says: “The Lord God had planted a paradise of delight from the beginning.” Some wish to understand “from the beginning” as from the beginning of the earth, that is, from the East. But if “from the beginning” means from the origin, or from the beginning of heaven and earth, as Symmachus and Theodotion translated it, then it signifies not the East but the origin and beginning. Thus it is understood that, before God made heaven and earth, he had established paradise.

Read the book of the Places of the blessed Jerome. For in Hebrew it is read: “The Lord God had planted a paradise in Eden from the beginning.” *Eden* is interpreted as delight. He rightly says “in Eden,” that is, in a place of delights. Hence, where the text says *voluptatis* (“of delight”), Symmachus translated it as “a flourishing paradise.”

[Scan page 70]

**Verse 9.** “And God brought forth from the earth every tree beautiful to see and pleasant to eat.” What, then, does it mean that he is said here to have brought forth from the earth a beautiful tree, and so forth, when above it says, “Let the earth bring forth green grass, and a fruit-bearing tree,” and so on?

It should be known that the beautiful tree is not said to have been brought forth because God created something new, but because, from the kinds that the earth had already produced on the third day, such trees subsequently arose and were produced from the power that the earth had previously received. Here too there is a recapitulation, just as above concerning man.

It follows: “And the tree of life in the middle of paradise.” Some wish to understand the tree of life only allegorically as divine wisdom, concerning which Solomon says: “She is a tree of life to those who take hold of her, and he who holds her fast is blessed” (Prov. 3:18). But we must believe that, just as the rock struck by Moses supplied water, although historically it signified Christ and was nevertheless a real rock, so too the tree of life, although it signified Christ, was nevertheless most evidently a bodily tree.

It is called the tree of life because, if the first parents had eaten from it, they would have been subject neither to illness nor to any failing of old age; and if they had remained obedient, they would not have died. Rather, through obedience their bodies would have been changed into spiritual bodies, as the bodies of the saints will be in the resurrection, and they would have passed from the earthly paradise to the heavenly one as immortals.

In the other trees there was food; in this one there was a sacrament. Likewise, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was not evil. God made all things good and could not establish anything evil in paradise. Why, then, is it called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil? It is called this not because the tree existed rationally in its own nature and possessed knowledge of good or evil, but because through it man could experience and know the difference between the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience.

Therefore the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil were created in paradise: through the former man could have been immortal, while through the latter he could become mortal. He used the tree of life as a kind of medicine, so that he might be incorruptible; but he used the tree of the knowledge of good and evil as a kind of poison, so that he might die.

**Verse 10.** “And a river went out from the place of delight to water paradise, and from there it is divided into four heads.” It should be known that this does not make the location of paradise evident, as though its place could be found by means of the rivers. Some say this, and blessed Augustine maintains that, although according to the testimony of Scripture they proceed from one spring, they flow beneath the earth, emerge in their appointed places after long courses, and remain hidden as rivers in the meantime.

**Verses 11–12.** “The name of one is Pishon; it is the river Ganges of India, which circles the whole land of Evilat, where gold is born; and the gold of that land is excellent. There also are bdellium and the onyx stone.”

Some say that bdellium is a most precious wood, while others say that it is a precious stone. Hence some translated “carbuncle” and “green stone” in place of bdellium and onyx.

Historically, *Pishon* is interpreted as “swelling,” because it swells when the wind rises; or as *os pupillae* (“mouth and pupil”), which is the better interpretation.

**Verse 13.** “The name of the second river is Gihon; it is the Nile River of Egypt, that is, the river which circles the whole land of Ethiopia.” Flowing from the East, supposedly from the roots of Mount Atlas, it turns toward the North, is increased by the autumn rains, and waters the plain of Egypt until it is hidden beneath the earth at the shore of the Red Sea; then, emerging again, it flows through Egypt toward the West.

It is interpreted as “dark,” because it runs through Ethiopia and Egypt; but “earth’s bounty,” or “fruitfulness,” is a better interpretation, because it makes men prosperous. This belongs more properly to the spiritual understanding.

**Verse 14.** “The name of the third river is the Tigris; it flows toward the Assyrians.” Because of its speed it received its name from the animal, and it is interpreted as “arrow.”

“The fourth river is the Euphrates, the river of Mesopotamia.” Scripture does not name the land through which it flows because the land it surrounds was near the land of the Jews and was known to them. It is interpreted as “fruitfulness.”

Thus far we have briefly described the historical account. From this point we shall try to insert briefly, especially because of the interpretations of the names, certain matters that pertain to the spiritual meaning, although this is contrary to the usual manner of our exposition.

The river that went out from paradise signifies our Lord and Redeemer, proceeding from the paternal source, from whom is the origin of all creatures. Concerning him the Psalmist says: “With you is the fountain of life”; and the Prophet says: “The Lord our God is a glorious river, leaping forth upon thirsty land” [Z., “the Lord our God is a glorious river”].

From him proceed four rivers that water paradise. These four rivers signify the four Gospels, which have their origin in the Lord Jesus Christ. Through them he waters his Church, which is figured by paradise, as we mentioned above when we discussed the threefold meaning of paradise.

[Scan page 71]

The interpretations of their names likewise correspond to the holy Gospels. Pishon, interpreted as *os pupillae* (“mouth and pupil”), signifies the Gospel of John: the mouth pertains to speech, and the pupil to sight. Because John, through the grace attributed to him, understood more deeply than the others, through the eye of the mind, the divinity of the Savior, he poured it forth in speech, saying: “In the beginning was the Word,” and so forth.

He circles the whole land of Evilat. The words immediately following *Evilat* are illegible in the supplied OCR, but the surviving exposition resumes by saying that its gold signifies spiritual wisdom. Solomon bears witness: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise.” There bdellium is found. If *bdellium* refers to a wood, it signifies the mystery of the cross, which is declared most fully in this Gospel; if it refers to the stone also called carbuncle, it signifies the excellence of divinity. The onyx stone, for which some codices have *prasinus*, “green stone,” signifies the Savior’s humanity, clearly declared in this Gospel. The text also associates the green stone’s unfading greenness and vigor with eternal life.

Gihon, interpreted as “the earth’s grace,” prefigures the Gospel of Matthew. That Gospel relates how the Lord, by his own grace and without any merits of ours requiring it, deigned to assume our earthly flesh. Isaiah speaks about this to the Jews: “The Lord God will put you to death and will call his servants by another name. Whoever is blessed upon the earth will be blessed in God, amen; and whoever swears on earth will swear by God, amen” (Isa. 65:15–16).

The Tigris, which flows toward the Assyrians and is said to mean “arrow,” signifies the Gospel of Mark, who embraces his Gospel in swift and brief discourse. It fittingly goes against the Assyrians, whose name is interpreted as “fierce,” or as demons, because it fights against the powers of the air that do not cease trying to take the human race captive.

The Euphrates, the river of Mesopotamia, is interpreted as “fruitfulness” and signifies the Gospel of Luke, which was composed at greater length. In it are recorded not only the birth of Christ but also the life of his forerunner and certain parables that are not found in the other Gospels.

Many also wished to understand these four rivers morally as signifying the four principal virtues: prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice.

Through Pishon prudence is understood. Prudence signifies contemplation of truth itself, which is removed from every human mouth because it is ineffable. Hence Pishon is interpreted as *os pupillae*, “mouth and pupil.” If one wished to express that contemplation, one would labor to bring it forth rather than actually bring it forth [Z., “you would bring it forth”], for Paul heard “ineffable words which it is not lawful for a man to utter” (2 Cor. 12:4). Evilat is accordingly interpreted as “giving birth” or “labor.” Through prudence and with labor, one brings forth the contemplation of truth rather than fully producing it, because no one can comprehend it completely.

There gold is born: the discipline of living, refined and shining free from every stain like pure gold. There bdellium is found, elsewhere inscribed as carbuncle. It signifies true truthfulness, which no falsehood overcomes, just as the flashing carbuncle is overcome by no darkness of night. The onyx stone, also called *prasinus*, “green stone” [Z. preserves the variant form *prasinus*], signifies eternal life through its greenness and vital force, because it does not wither.

Gihon, which circles all the hot and burning land of the Ethiopians, signifies [Z., “figures”] fortitude through the heat of action: a vigorous and tireless power that overcomes every sluggishness and reaches the fervor of love.

The third river, the Tigris, goes against the Assyrians and signifies temperance, which resists lust and restrains pleasurable desires. The unclean spirits are signified by the Assyrians, whose name is interpreted as “fierce,” or as demons; they endeavor to deceive the wretched by these desires, but this virtue overcomes them.

Of the fourth river, the Euphrates, Scripture does not say where it goes or what land it circles. It signifies justice, which extends to every part of the soul. Justice is the soul’s own order and equity, by which the other three virtues are joined harmoniously to one another; justice consists in this complete union and ordering.

It should be noted that philosophers and some teachers, following moral discipline, arrange the virtues as prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance. Prudence leads a person to knowledge of the truth; justice preserves love of God and neighbor; fortitude conquers adversity and despises death; temperance restrains vicious pleasures and moderates all things.

These are the four principal virtues: they adorn conduct, furnish merits, conquer the devil, and open heaven. The first understands, the second loves, the third gives victory, and the fourth imposes measure. Whoever has been instructed by the four Gospels and armed with these four virtues will fight effectively against the Assyrians, interpreted as demons, because they do not cease taking the human race captive in their struggle against the heavenly powers.

Whoever has a heart infused with these virtues is cooled from the heat of every carnal temptation and will dwell among the trees of paradise, that is, of the holy Church, and will receive the fruits of the trees and reach the tree of life. The fruitful trees of paradise are useful disciplines or holy people; the fruits of the trees are their conduct or works. The tree of life is wisdom herself, the mother of all good things, concerning whom Solomon says: “She is a tree of life to those who grasp her, and he who holds her fast is blessed” (Prov. 3:18).

Or it is the Holy of Holies himself, Christ; whoever stretches out his hand toward him will live forever.

It follows:

**Verse 15.** “Then the Lord God took the man and placed him in the paradise of delight.” Here it is shown that he had been created outside paradise. Some said that he was created in Hebron [Petr., “in the place of Hebron”], where he was also buried, and that he was suddenly placed there. But the divine history does not say this.

It says that he was placed there “to work it and to guard it.” What could he work, when there was not yet any weariness from labor? Or what could he guard, when there was no attacker or robber? Was it perhaps on account of the beasts? Certainly not, because harmful beasts did not exist until after sin.

But when it says that he was to work it and guard it, this does not refer to servile labor but to the exercise of joy and an honorable pleasure of the soul—just as a father, although he has no need, nevertheless exercises himself in labors for the sake of pleasure. Or he was placed there for this reason, so that he might work—[the supplied source ends incompletely].
and guard him—that is, that he should carry out the precepts of justice, persevere in the commandment, and guard himself lest he lose paradise.

Some explain it otherwise: “Therefore God took the man and placed him in paradise, to work it and guard it”—that is, so that God himself might work upon and guard the man: work upon him so that he would be just, and guard him so that he would be safe. In this sense the earth is said to be “worked” by human beings, not because they create it, but because they cultivate it so that it may bear fruit. Some have wished to reject this interpretation, saying that, if God guarded him, he would not have sinned.

It follows:

### Verse 16

“And he commanded him, saying: ‘From every tree of paradise you shall eat,’” and so forth.

It is asked how God spoke to Adam: either through a heavenly substance, as he now speaks to the angels; or through a bodily appearance, that is, through a form taken from the heavenly air, as formerly to the patriarchs; or by inspiring the mind, as he did to the prophets, according to what is written: “He spoke to me who was speaking within me.” But it should be understood that, before he sinned, God spoke to him through a heavenly substance, as to the angels; after he sinned, through a subordinate creature, that is, through an angel.

### Verse 17

“In whatever day you eat from it, you shall surely die.”

It is asked of which death this is said: whether bodily death, the death of the soul, or the death of Gehenna. But it should be understood that both deaths are intended, namely, of the soul and of the body.

The death of the soul occurs when, because of some sin, God—who is its life—abandons it [Z., “the soul, when God abandons it”]. The death of the body occurs when, because of some necessity, the soul abandons the body. For just as God is the life of the soul, so the soul is the life of the body. They merited bodily death by sinning, since they would have remained immortal had they not sinned. Although they would perhaps not have died immediately, but only after a long time, nevertheless, since the hope of immortality had already been lost, future death was called present, because it had already begun to be expected. Hence Symmachus translated: “You shall be mortal.”

Christ destroyed this twofold death of humanity by his single death. He died in the flesh alone for a time, but never in his soul, since he never sinned. We may also understand the death of Gehenna, by which the soul is now tormented, deprived of the fellowship of the saints, and which, after the judgment, it will endure together with the body once it has received it.

Therefore some, supported by the authority of Scripture, identify four deaths. The first, they say, is the death of the soul, which abandons its Creator. For when it abandons him, it sins. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Let the dead bury their dead” (Matt. 8:22). This statement presents two deaths, namely, of the soul and of the body. The third is the death suffered by the soul alone when it departs from this body [Z., “which the soul suffers when it departs from the body”]. The rich man in the underworld endured this death when he asked for a drop of water. The fourth occurs when the soul receives its body in the future and is cast into the fire, when the Lord will say: “Go into the eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41).

When Adam sinned, he died in his soul. This was the first death, the abandonment of God; three further deaths followed afterward.

### Verse 18

“God also said: ‘It is not good for man to be alone. Let us make him a helper like himself.’”

Here it is shown that woman was created for the man’s consolation and assistance, and therefore she ought to provide him consolation and be subject to him [Z., “so that she might provide him consolation and be subject to him”], according to the Apostle: “The woman does not have authority over her own body, but the man does” [Z., “does not have authority”].

It should, however, be asked why the Lord of the world began with a commandment. He did so lest man exalt himself through dominion, but should know, in observing the commandment, that he was subject to his Creator.

### Verse 19

“Therefore, having formed from the earth all the animals of the earth, he brought them to Adam,” and so forth.

This does not mean that he brought them by physical movement, as shepherds and hunters do, but that, by the hidden operation of his power, he willed them to come, so that Adam might see what he would call them. “See” means that he might discern and understand what he should call them.

### Verse 20

“Adam gave names to all the animals,” and so forth.

In the literal sense this shows how greatly man surpasses cattle and irrational animals: by his understanding he was able to distinguish everything and identify it by name, assigning names according to the qualities, habits, and dispositions of the beasts. The Lord bestowed this dignity upon him so that he might understand himself; and the better he recognized himself as superior to the animals, the more he would love the Creator [Z. adds: “the more he understood himself to be better than other living beings”].

But no helper like himself was found for Adam—that is, among all the animals no rational being was found except Adam alone.

Adam is interpreted as “man,” whether “earthly” or “red earth.” For the flesh was made from earth, and the soil was the material from which the human body was made. Spiritually, however, the fact that “red earth” is mentioned signifies Christ, who was to assume flesh from his seed and who is called the second Adam by the Apostle. His flesh was to be reddened by his own blood in the Passion [Z., “made ruddy”], according to what Isaiah asks: “Why, then, is your garment red?” and so forth (Isa. 63:2).

### Verse 21

“Therefore the Lord God cast a deep sleep upon Adam,” and so forth.

What does “he cast a deep sleep upon him” mean, in order to form the woman? Could God not have drawn out a rib from a man who was awake and formed the woman? Or perhaps Adam would have felt pain when the rib was removed, and therefore it was necessary for him to sleep? Who sleeps so deeply that bones can be torn from him while he remains unaware? Or did Adam not feel because God was removing it? The one who could remove it from a sleeping man could therefore have removed it without pain from one who was awake.

But the act was performed for the sake of the mystery. Woman was not formed from the earth like man, but from the side of a sleeping man, because it had been prefigured that Christ would sleep in death on the cross for the sake of the Church, and that from his side the fountain of our salvation would flow and the Church would be formed. “He filled the place with flesh for her.” What does this mean except that Christ gave his flesh in the Passion for the Church?

For from where was Adam weakened, from there the woman became strong [Z., “was made strong”]. Because Christ deigned to be weakened in the Passion, the Church was strengthened from that same source.

### Verses 22–23, etc.

“And the Lord God built the rib which he had taken from Adam into a woman,” and so forth, until it says: “She shall be called woman, because she was taken from man.”

How does he say that the woman was built here, when above he rested from all his work? He did not create new matter here, but expressed it in a form.

And Adam said: “This now is bone from my bones,” and so forth. He therefore called his wife woman, as the superior calls the inferior, and said: “This is bone from my bones,” and so forth. “Bone from my bones” may refer to strength, and “flesh from my flesh” to moderation. Allegorically, these two virtues are taught to belong to the lower part of the soul, which the prudent and rational mind governs.

“This one shall be called woman.” In some manuscripts it is found as: “This one shall be called a female.” The reason why she is called woman, because she was taken from man, does not sound equally in Greek and Latin; but the etymology is preserved in Hebrew [Z., “may it be preserved”]. A man is called *ish* and a woman *ishshah*. Thus she is rightly called *ishshah* from *ish*, “man.” This is what the passage says: “She shall be called woman, because she was taken from man.”

### Verse 24

“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and cling to his wife,” and so forth.

Here Adam first prophesied about Christ and the Church. Explaining this example, the Apostle Paul says: “This mystery is great; but I am speaking with reference to Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5:32). Whoever desires to understand this spiritually should diligently read the works of Augustine and Isidore.

He rightly says “in one flesh,” that is, in one will and agreement, or because one flesh is produced from two in their offspring.

### Verse 25

“Now both were naked, Adam namely and his wife” [Z., “naked”], “and they were not ashamed.”

This does not mean that they were unaware of their nakedness, but that nakedness was not yet shameful, because lust had not yet moved those members toward desire. If they had not sinned, they would not have been ashamed, as we see in infants: before the time of sexual desire and the movement of weakness arrives, they are not ashamed of nakedness.

Thus they were naked, as has been said, but were not ashamed, because they did not yet see another law in their members resisting the law of their mind and taking them captive under the law of sin (Rom. 7:23). They thought that nothing needed to be concealed, because they felt nothing that needed to be restrained.

After the sin, however, they were ashamed, because, through disobedience, the flesh in a certain way bore witness to shame; and by sinning they deserved that it should rebel against them.

# Chapter III

### Verse 1

“Now the serpent was more crafty than all the animals,” and so forth.

This does not mean that the serpent possessed any particular cunning or wisdom, but that the devil is understood through it, since he was acting deceitfully through the serpent. Aquila and Theodotion translated the term as “wicked” and “crooked,” so that cunning and craftiness rather than wisdom might be indicated.

Although the transgressing angel had been cast down from heaven through pride, he was nevertheless by nature more excellent and more cunning than all the animals. For although he lost his dignity, he did not lose his subtlety. The devil therefore chose for himself an animal suited to his nature—crooked and slippery—through which he might speak, so that by it his deceit and crookedness might be signified.

The serpent itself, however, could not speak, because it had not received this ability from the Creator. The devil took possession of it and used it as an instrument through which he could produce articulate sound in order to accomplish his malice. Through it he uttered words. But the serpent did not understand them, being without rational nature [Petr., “without reason”], just as a demoniac or a madman utters what he does not understand. It merely accomplished through him as much as he wished, and no more than the Creator permitted.

Hence some ask: if the serpent did not understand or perceive, how does it hear the words of enchanters, so that it comes out of its caves at their incantations? The answer is that, although animals lack understanding, they are not altogether without bodily senses. They possess sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. Therefore, although they hear the words of enchanters, they do not understand them. They do not obey through understanding; rather, when they come out of their caves at the incantations, they are compelled by the devil, with God’s permission.

It follows:

“He said to the woman: ‘Why did God command you not to eat from every tree of paradise?’”

He speaks to the woman because he saw that he could deceive the woman and not the man; or because he thought that the man alone had been created in the likeness of God and not the woman.

This raises the question why God permitted a human being to be tempted when he knew that the person would consent. The reason is that a human being would not have received great praise if he had been created in such a way that he could not do evil, but would have been like an animal. Rather, God created him with free choice, so that, if he persevered bravely in the commandments, he might be rewarded; but if he fell by consenting, he might be condemned, as happened.

Even today, throughout the whole human race, people are continually tempted through the devil’s ambushes, so that the virtue of the one who is tempted may be tested and the palm of the one who does not consent may appear more glorious.

### Verses 2–3

“To him the woman replied: ‘We eat from the fruit of the trees that are in paradise,’” and so forth.

Why did the woman answer the serpent’s question [Z., “the serpent”]? So that her transgression might be inexcusable, since she could in no way claim that she had forgotten the commandment, which she disclosed to the serpent.

### Verses 4–5

“But the serpent said to the woman: ‘You shall certainly not die. For God knows that on whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.’”

It was as though he had said: “It is not as you say. God has envied you his glory and dignity, and for that reason he gave you this command. He knows that, if you eat, you will be like him, knowing good and evil. I will give you better advice: eat, and your eyes will be opened,” and so forth.

He makes great promises in order to deceive more easily. He says: “Your eyes will be opened,” so that they would no longer wish to remain under God, just as he himself had refused to remain under him. “You must always seek new things and penetrate the knowledge of good and evil.”

It is worth asking why the devil was so hostile to human salvation. Clearly, it was because of his hatred of the Creator, his envy of humanity, and despair of his own salvation.

It follows:

### Verse 6

“The woman saw that the tree was good for food,” and so forth.

Why did the woman consider the tree after the serpent’s persuasion? She wanted to test whether there was anything deadly in it; and when she saw nothing of the sort, she tasted it with greater confidence. “She took of its fruit and ate, and gave some to her husband with her.”

The man therefore consented to the woman, as some think, because perhaps he did not see her dead from the food. It may also be that they thought the Creator had spoken symbolically when he said: “If you eat from it, you shall die,” and for that reason they ate.

### Verse 7

“He ate, and their eyes were opened.”

Why were they opened? Were they previously blind? Certainly not. Their eyes were opened not for seeing, but for distinguishing between the good which they had lost and the evil into which they had fallen. Or their eyes were opened toward one another for desiring one another, which immediately occurred as a punishment after the sin.

Guilt opened the eyes of desire, which innocence had kept closed. Here the passage shows how the devil rose up against the first human being through three temptations: gluttony, empty glory, and avarice. He tempted him through gluttony when he showed him the forbidden food of the tree and urged him to eat, saying: “Eat.” He tempted him through empty glory when he said: “You shall be like gods.” He tempted him through avarice when he added: “Knowing good and evil.”

Avarice is not only a desire for money, but also a desire for elevation. In this way the devil drew him toward pride, since he aroused in him an avarice for sublimity. Later he attempted to attack the second Adam, namely our Lord and Redeemer, with these same temptations, but he was overcome and defeated in the same ways.

We too are struck every day by these three suggestions: suggestion, pleasure, and consent. When we are tempted, we often slip into pleasure or even into consent, like our parents, because, having been propagated from the sin of the flesh, we carry within ourselves the source from which we endure the struggles of temptation.

But, as has been said, the Lord wished to be tempted according to the testimony of the Gospels, so that he might conquer our temptations by his own temptations and overthrow the enemy of the human race, together with the arrogance of his pride.

It should finally be noted that, before the transgression of the human being, before he had delivered himself over to death, the enemy had no power to approach the interior of man and implant hostile thoughts. But after he had ensnared him through the serpent, he received power to strike him inwardly.

In a metaphorical sense, the crafty serpent can signify the cunning of heretics, who, with illicit curiosity, urge people to touch the secrets of God that are removed from our senses, as though the serpent had said: “Why did God command you to possess knowledge that lies hidden?” You must always seek new things and penetrate the knowledge of good and evil.

They knew that they were naked and sewed together fig leaves, making themselves coverings, or girdles, or aprons, as another translation says.

They recognized that they were naked—that is, naked of the grace by which they had been clothed, so that the nakedness of the body would not confuse their minds by opposing the law of sin. They sewed fig leaves together, ashamed of the disobedience of their flesh. They rightly cover themselves with fig leaves [Z., “they were covered”]. The leaves of the fig signify the itching of the flesh, by which they were already burning after the sin.

They had lost the glory of simple chastity [Z., “of simplicity and chastity”], and therefore fled to the twofold origin of lust. The heat of the passion which they suffered in their minds was represented by fig leaves, since fig leaves are known to excite heat in the body; by covering both, they intensified it.

They say that, if one cuts the branches or leaves of a fig tree, a milky fluid flows out like poison, which inflames and burns human skin. Thus they signify the itching and heat of lust. Hence they think that they touched the forbidden fruit of this tree.

Others can understand the bitter leaves of the fig as signifying the bitter bitterness of punishment.

Spiritually, those cover themselves with fig leaves who embrace the harshness of the world, indulge the itching of carnal pleasure, and, deceived by heretical depravity and stripped of Christ’s grace, gather lies like fig leaves, making girdles of depravity when they lie about the Lord or the Church.

It follows:

### Verse 8

“And when they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in paradise at the breeze after midday,” and so forth.

What does it mean that, after the human sin, the Lord is said not to stand in paradise but to walk, except that he was showing that, when guilt intervened, he had withdrawn from the human heart? He also indicated by this the unstable expulsion of the pair from paradise into mortality.

Tropologically, God walks with those who do not remain steadfast in his commandments. Hence the words that follow: “at the breeze after midday.” Sacred Scripture often distinguishes the merits of situations by the condition of the time.

It rightly says “at the breeze after midday,” because the heat of charity had grown cold in them through the abundance of iniquity, and the more fervent light of truth had departed. As the darknesses of error approached, they were already constricting the sinful soul with the cold of its guilt, and under the shadow of sin it lay numb, as though beneath the chill of the breeze. Thus it is written of the same sinful human being that he followed a shadow.

Here it is shown that Adam, at midday, brought the death of transgression into this world. Therefore the Lord was crucified at the sixth hour for the life of the world—that is, when the sun was departing from the center of the world—and at that time he said to the thief: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

The order required by reason, or rather by divine mercy, was that, at the same hour when the Lord had then closed paradise against Adam in his sin, he should now open the gate of paradise to the repentant thief; and that, by the same means through which the first Adam had brought death to this world by sinning, the second Adam should destroy death by dying.

It should be asked, however, why the Lord wished to investigate the human sin himself rather than through an angel. The reason is that the merit of a single angel was insufficient for the redemption of the entire human race. Moreover, the devil had incurred no lesser crime in killing an angel than in killing the Creator.

Adam and his wife hid themselves in the midst of the tree of paradise. Literally, they hid themselves because they had chosen the concealment of their crime, whether from excessive shame or fear. But why “after midday”? Because, after the light of paradise and the happiness of this world had passed into the misery of the present age, they hid themselves [Z., “they hid themselves from the paradisiacal happiness of this age”].

Spiritually, the one who turns away from the Creator’s commandments and lives according to the errors and pleasures of his own will hides himself in the midst of the tree of paradise.

### Verse 9

“And the Lord God called Adam and said: ‘Where are you?’”

Did divine power not know where the servant had fled after his guilt? But because he saw him fallen into sin and hidden under sin as though from the eyes of truth, and because he did not approve the darkness of his error, he acts as though he does not know where the sinner is.

He both calls and seeks him, saying: “Adam, where are you?” By calling him, he gives a sign that he is summoning him to repentance. By seeking him, he openly indicates that he does not fail to know that sinners are rightly condemned. He therefore wished to admonish him by reproving him, so that he might consider where he was and from where he had fallen.

He says: “Where are you?”—as though he were plainly saying: “See from what great dignity you have fallen into what evil.”

The Lord reproved Adam while walking, as has been said, so that he might reveal his wickedness to his darkened mind not only through spoken words but also through visible actions. Thus the sinful man heard in words the evil he had committed; through the walking he perceived the instability of his mutability after losing the state of eternity; through the breeze, from which the warmth of charity had been expelled, he recognized his torpor; and through the setting of the sun he understood that he was drawing near to darkness.

It should be noted that, if previously he spoke with them [Z., omits “if”], perhaps as with the angels, it should now be believed that he appeared to them through a subordinate creature. For after the sin Adam could not see God in the substance of his divinity, but heard the words of reproof through an angel.

Yet it should be understood that God called him but did not immediately cast him out. Here it is shown figuratively that whoever falls away from faith or good works into his own deceit and desires should not despair, even if overwhelmed by the enormity of his crimes. God does not despise sinners, but still calls them to return through repentance, for he does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live (Ezek. 21:23). Therefore there should be no despair: even the wicked who have brought death upon themselves are called back to the hope of pardon.

### Verse 10

“And he said: ‘I heard your voice in paradise, and I was afraid because I was naked, and I hid myself.’”

He answered in a most pitiable manner, as though he could rightly be displeased at being naked, just as he had done before the sin. Before sinning, indeed, he did not notice his nakedness, because his attention was fixed on heavenly things. But because he thought that he could hide himself from God’s presence, the punishment of sin came upon him: he wished to hide from one from whom nothing can be hidden.

### Verse 11

“And God said to him: ‘Who told you that you were naked?’” and so forth.

God wished to examine his sin in this way so that he might look upon his guilt and, by confessing, recognize how far he had departed from the face of his Creator. But each of them chose the consolation of self-defense rather than confession. Hence it follows:

### Verse 12

“And Adam said: ‘The woman whom you gave me gave me from the tree, and I ate.’” He did not directly attribute the guilt to himself, but in a certain way to the woman whom the Lord had given him, and indirectly redirected his guilt toward the Creator, who had given him such a companion and thereby provided the occasion of sin.

From this the human race still draws the root of its bitterness. When someone is accused of his fault, he hides himself under the shadow of defenses, as though beneath fig leaves. In this concealment he hides not from the Lord, but the Lord from himself.

### Verse 13

“And the Lord God said to the woman: ‘Why have you done this?’ She answered: ‘The serpent deceived me.’”

The woman likewise attempted indirectly to turn the blame back upon the Creator, because he had permitted the serpent to enter there.

Behold: those who had heard from the deceiving devil, “You shall be like gods,” excuse their sin. When they were unable to become like God in divinity, they attempted, to increase their error, to make God like themselves in guilt.

Thus, as we described above, when they try to defend their sin, the man through the woman and the woman through the serpent cast away what they could have erased by the confession of humility. Hence even now it is the practice of sinners that, when guilt is exposed, it is defended, and the very means by which guilt should have been ended instead increases the debt [Z., “the sin is prolonged, so that, while the guilt is being committed, it is defended, and from the point at which it should have ended the debt is increased”].

Here it should be noted that every sin is committed in the heart in four ways, and is likewise completed in action in four ways. In the heart it is committed through suggestion, pleasure, consent, and the audacity of defense, as is shown here.

Suggestion comes through the adversary, pleasure through the flesh, consent through the spirit, and the audacity of defense through pride. The guilt that ought to have terrified the mind exalts it; and while it raises it by casting it down, it more grievously causes it to fall.

Thus the devil shattered the original uprightness of the human being through these four stages: the serpent persuaded, Eve took pleasure, Adam consented, and, when questioned, he refused through audacity to confess his guilt.

The same thing occurs daily in the human race, which was not unknown in the first parent. The serpent persuades because the hidden enemy secretly suggests evil to human hearts. Eve took pleasure because the carnal sense immediately submits to the serpent’s words in pleasure. Adam gave his assent because, while the flesh is carried away into pleasure, the spirit is also weakened and bent from its righteousness. When questioned, Adam refused to confess his guilt because the spirit, separated from truth through sin, becomes hardened in the audacity of its ruin.

Sin is also completed in action in four ways. First, hidden guilt is committed; afterward it is exposed before human eyes without shame for the debt; then it is brought into habit; and finally it is nourished either by the seductions of false hope or by the obstinacy of wretched despair.

This history of the first human being therefore manifests to us these forms of sin, whether they arise secretly in the heart or are openly perpetrated in action [Z., “are manifested”].

### Verse 14

“And he said to the serpent: ‘Because you have done this, you shall be accursed among all animals and beasts of the earth. You shall walk upon your breast and your belly.’”

The Seventy translators added “belly”; in the Hebrew only “breast” is found.

Behold: the serpent is not questioned, perhaps because he had not done this by his own nature or will, but the devil had acted through and by means of him. Consequently, the serpent himself is not questioned either, because the devil has no sin to confess and has absolutely no excuse to offer.

He immediately received the punishment of the curse—not the punishment reserved for the final judgment, which has been prepared for him and his angels, but the punishment spoken of here, by which he is allowed to have power over those who despise God’s commandments. His punishment on the day of judgment is greater because he rejoices in such misery.

He says: “You shall walk upon your breast and your belly.” By “breast” the pride of the mind is signified; by “belly” the desires of the flesh. Through these two things the devil creeps into those whom he wishes to deceive: either through earthly desire and lust, or through pride and insane teaching.

When someone commits lust in action, the serpent creeps into him from the belly. But when another turns over in his mind what he intends to commit, the serpent creeps into him from the breast. Since, however, one reaches the completion of actions through thought, the serpent is rightly described as first creeping upon the breast and afterward upon the belly.
