“And you shall eat earth”—that is, those whom you deceive through earthly desire shall belong to you—“all the days of your life,” that is, for the whole period during which you exercise this power, until the final day of judgment.

### Verse 15

“I will place enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed.”

The seed of the devil is perverse suggestion; the seed of the woman is the whole human race. By divine command these two seeds must maintain continual hatred toward one another, so that we may not do what the devil wishes, since he never wishes what will benefit us.

Although some wish “woman” to be understood as the mind, and “the seed of the woman” as the fruit of a good work, it may also appropriately be understood of the blessed Virgin Mary, from whom the Lord was born. Read Augustine and Isidore.

“She shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel.”

The head of the serpent is the thought of illicit suggestion. We must uproot it completely from the hearing of the heart through the whole intention and vigilant hand of careful reflection, and dash it against the rock, which is Christ.

The heel of the woman is the final period of our life, when the devil strives to attack us more fiercely. When he is detected at the beginning, he attempts to strike the heel. Even if he does not wound us through the suggestion of the first intention, he intends to deceive us at the end. If we resist him manfully, we shall receive the victory of perseverance together with our salvation.

It should be noted that, when it says, “You shall be accursed among all animals and beasts of the earth,” this refers to the devil, who is called accursed because he cannot repent. “Among all animals,” that is, among those that have preserved their own nature; and “among the beasts of the earth,” that is, among human beings, or the universal Church.

### Verse 16

“And to the woman he said: ‘I will multiply your labors,’” and so forth, until: “You shall be under your husband’s power,” and so forth.

What does “you shall be under your husband’s power” mean? Was she not under his power before the sin? Certainly she was, but under the kind of servitude that operates through love and casts out fear. Afterward, however, she was subject to the fear of conditional servitude, which operates through discipline [Z., “which”].

Spiritually, the woman signifies the mind. Therefore, when he says, “You shall bear children in pain,” this signifies that, when carnal pleasure wishes to overcome some evil habit, it suffers pains at the beginning and thus, through a better habit, gives birth to a good work as to children.

When he adds, “You shall be under your husband’s power,” and so forth, this signifies that carnal pleasure, which had struggled in pain in order to establish a good habit, is now made more cautious by those very pains; lest it fall, it obeys reason and willingly submits [Z., “serves”], as a wife obeys a husband giving commands.

### Verse 17

“But to Adam he said: ‘Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree,’” and so forth.

This does not signify, as many think, the work of cultivating the fields, but sins.

It is worth asking why, in Adam’s transgression, the Creator cursed the earth and not the waters. The reason is that the man ate against the prohibition from the fruit of the earth, whereas he did not drink from the waters; and because God predestined that, in the waters, he would wash away the sin which humanity contracted from the fruit of the earth.

Terrestrial animals have more of the curse than aquatic animals because they live more from the cursed earth than aquatic animals do. Therefore, after the resurrection, Christ wished to eat fish rather than a terrestrial animal.

Behold: through human sin the earth was cursed, so that it might bring forth thorns and poisonous plants, either as a punishment or as a discipline for mortals, and so that humanity might have original sin before its eyes and, thus admonished, eventually turn away from sins, as was said much earlier.

He says: “Cursed is the earth,” and so forth. Since we know with certainty that sacred Scripture prohibits cursing, what does it mean that now, for the sinful human being...

[scan page 77]  
**ANGELOMI, MONK OF LUXOVIUM**

**144**

[The opening words are corrupt in the supplied scan: “... by the curse of the earth ...”] But it should be known that Scripture mentions a curse in two ways: one which it approves, and another which it condemns. For a curse is pronounced either by the judgment of justice or by the passion of vengeance. The curse imposed upon the sinful man by the judgment of justice is approved, when he hears: “Cursed is the earth in your work.” But the curse imposed by the judgment of justice is again proclaimed when it is said to Abraham: “I will curse those who curse you.” On the other hand, the curse is not pronounced by the judgment of justice but by the passion of vengeance, as Paul’s admonition teaches when he says: “Bless, and do not curse” (Rom. 12:14). And again: “Nor shall those who curse inherit the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:10). God, therefore, is said to curse, and yet man is forbidden to curse, because what man does out of the malice of vengeance, God does only [Z.: “it says, ‘The malice of vengeance God does not do,’ etc.”] after examination and by the power of justice. When holy men pronounce a sentence of cursing, it does not burst forth from a desire for revenge but from the scrutiny of justice. For inwardly they perceive the subtle judgment of God, and they understand that the evils emerging outwardly ought to be struck by a curse; thus, in cursing, they do not sin, because they do not disagree with the eternal judgment.

Allegorically also, thorns are placed as a sign of sins. For he says:

**Verse 18.** — “The earth shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you.” This means plainly: “Your conscience will not cease to produce for you the pricks and goads of vices.” Yet, through the sentence imposed upon the man, our reason is reproved. Seduced by the desire of sin and removed from the paradise of blessedness, it bears the curses of earthly toil on account of sinful desire; it also bears the pain of temporal cares like thorns and thistles. Nevertheless, it is dismissed from the paradise of blessedness so that it may work the earth—that is, labor in this body and acquire for itself the merit of returning to the blessed life, signified by the name “paradise”—and may stretch out its hand to the tree of life and live forever. The stretching out of the hand properly signifies the cross, or the torment of repentance, through which eternal life is recovered. For he says:

**Verse 19.** — “You are dust, and you shall return to dust.” Another translation states it more clearly: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go.” The first man was created in such a way that, while he remained, time would pass away, but he himself would not pass away with time. He stood as the moments ran their course, because he was not advancing by growth toward the end of life. But when sin occurred, immediately, after offending the Creator, he began to go along with time; therefore he heard: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go.” Once the condition of immortality had been lost, the course of mortality swallowed him up, and as he was carried from youth into old age and from old age toward death, by passing he learned what he had been by standing.

We, because we are born from his lineage, retain the bitterness of the root as though in a young shoot. For, while infancy advances to childhood, childhood to adolescence, adolescence to youth, youth to old age, and old age passes into death, so, through these stages, he is driven by his growth toward decline.

**Note:** One manuscript has a corrupt passage in this place.

There are seven sins of Adam, and therefore seven punishments followed. Some people enumerate them as follows. The first sin was pride, because he loved to be in his own power more than in God’s. The second was sacrilege, because he did not believe God. The third was homicide, because by sinning he killed himself. The fourth was fornication spiritually [Z.: “spiritual fornication”], because he corrupted the integrity of his mind. The fifth was theft, because he touched the forbidden food. The sixth was greed, because he desired more than he ought. The seventh was gluttony, because he ate the forbidden fruit.

Although there were seven vices, seven punishments therefore followed. The first was the cursing of his earth; the second, expulsion from paradise; the third, arrival upon a lowly earth; the fourth, the death of his son; the fifth, labor; the sixth, bodily death; the seventh, his descent into [Z.: “to”] hell. Because he sinned seven times, he received seven acts of vengeance.

But here it is worthwhile to ask why the angel’s sin is concealed in silence in this book, while man’s is disclosed; and why the angel’s great crime was incurable, whereas man’s was curable. Perhaps because God predestined the angel’s sin to be punished, but predestined man’s to be healed. Moreover, because the angel was the inventor of his own crime, whereas man was deceived by another’s fraud. And just as the angel is more exalted in glory, so he is greater in his ruin. Man, however, the more fragile he is by nature, is the more readily inclined toward pardon.

**Verse 20.** — “And Adam called the name of his wife Eve, because she was the mother of all living.” Eve is interpreted as “life,” or “calamity,” or “woe.” “Life,” because she was the source of birth, and therefore she is called the mother of all. “Calamity” and “woe,” because through transgression she became the cause of dying; for from falling she received the name “calamity.” Others say that Eve was called both life and calamity because a woman is often the cause of salvation for her husband, and often of calamity and death.

Spiritually, in that she is interpreted as “life,” she signifies the Church, which is called the mother of the living—that is, of those who act rightly. Their opposites are sins, which are signified by the name “the dead.”

**Verse 21.** — “And the Lord God made for Adam and his wife tunics of skins, and clothed them.” What does it mean that he wove tunics of skins for them? It means that he was indicating that they were mortal.

**Verse 22.** — “Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil.” For he says, “like one of us.” He speaks as though God were saying this, either as a mockery directed against the offender, or as a warning intended to inspire fear, lest anyone should sin [Z.: omits “anyone”].

**COMMENTARY**

**145**

…because he was not only made in the way he wished to be made, but did not even preserve what he had been made. “Like one of us” is spoken in the plural because of the Trinity, as is also “Let us make man,” and the rest.

“Knowing good and evil,” namely, by experience, whereas God knows them through wisdom. “See, lest he perhaps take from the tree of life and live forever.” Therefore, in his mercy, God did not want him to take again from the tree of life, because, if he ate from it, he would remain immortal together with his sin, like the devil, as some maintain, and would not return through repentance. Hence they think that he had never eaten from the tree of life, because, they say, if he had eaten, he would not have sinned.

Alternatively: God wanted him to take from it and recover through repentance; and the wording is ambiguous. We speak in this way when we say: “That is why I warn you not to do again what you did,” although we want him to do it. And again: “That is why I warn you not to be good,” while certainly wishing him to be good. “That is why I warn you not to despair that you may be good.” In this way the Apostle says: “Lest perhaps God grant them repentance for the acknowledgment of the truth” (2 Tim. 2:25), although this is precisely what he desired.

**Verse 23.** — “And the Lord God sent him out from the paradise of pleasure, to work the earth from which he had been taken.” It may therefore be understood [Petr.: “to be done”] that man was dismissed into the labor of this life for this reason: so that at some time he might stretch out his hand to the tree of life.

**Verse 24.** — “And he cast Adam out.” There is no doubt that the Lord did this. “And he placed before the paradise of pleasure cherubim, and a flaming, turning sword, to guard the way of the tree of life.” It is not that God made Adam, whom he had cast out, dwell opposite the paradise of pleasure, but that, after casting him out, he placed cherubim and a flaming sword before the gates of paradise to guard it, so that no one could enter.

He fittingly placed cherubim, or a flaming and turning sword, to guard it—that is, through angelic ministry, a certain fiery guard [Z.: “a certain fiery custody”]. It is nevertheless properly called “turning,” because a time would eventually come when it could also be removed, namely, through the advent of the one who, through the mystery of his incarnation, opened the way to paradise for us. Before his advent, moreover, all the dead descended to the prison of hell, because man, who fell by himself, could not return to paradise except through the Lord.

Nevertheless, as some understand it, the passage can mean that Adam was placed before paradise, that is, positioned outside paradise, for the sake of the hope of repentance: so that, always looking upon the place of blessedness, he might perhaps repent and, through genuine amendment, return to the blessed life, which he spiritually called paradise. But—alas, what grief!—he did not wish to do so; he remained a sinner in his misery.

Furthermore, in the fact that he is said above to have received a tunic of skins, and is then set before paradise, where the cherubim and fiery sword were placed, this is allegorically signified [Z.: “this signifies”]: pleasures are withdrawn from carnal senses, that is, from those who live carnally. For just as skins are stripped from the body, so evil pleasures are stripped from the mind, and they pursue the divine law. When they turn toward God through the flaming sword—that is, through temporal tribulations—by recognizing and lamenting their sins, and through the cherubim—that is, through the fullness of knowledge, which is charity—they reach the tree of life, Christ, and live forever.

For “cherubim” is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge.” The turning sword, placed to guard the way of the tree of life, is understood as temporal punishments. No one can reach the tree of life except through these two things: endurance of hardships and fullness of knowledge, that is, through love of God and neighbor. “The fullness of the law,” says the Apostle, “is love” (Rom. 13:10).

**CHAPTER IV**

**Verse 1.** — “Now Adam knew Eve, his wife, and she conceived and bore Cain,” and the rest.

Cain is interpreted as “acquisition” or “possession.” Hence his mother, expressing his etymology, said: “I have possessed a man through God.” By some he is also called “lamentation,” because after Abel was killed, he too was killed and paid the penalty for his crime.

**Verse 2.** — “And again she bore his brother Abel.” Abel is interpreted as “mourning,” by which name it was signified that he would be killed. Likewise, according to some, it means “vanity,” because he was soon released and taken away.

Here it should be noted that two cities are spoken of, namely, the city of the devil and the city of God, which began to be built from the beginning of the world, as is shown here; likewise, there are two generations, the carnal and the spiritual. Hence Scripture gives us the rule that we should recognize two generations, of the wicked and of the good, as is established by many examples.

Cain, then, was born first from those two parents of the human race. He belonged to the city of the devil and to the carnal generation, of which Solomon says: “There is a generation that curses its father and does not bless its mother; a generation that is pure in its own eyes, yet is not washed from its filth,” and so forth (Prov. 30:11). The Gospel likewise says: “Brood of vipers” (Matt. 3:7), and: “All these things will be required of this generation,” along with many other passages.

Abel, born later, belonged to the city of God and to the spiritual generation. Hence the Apostle says: “Not first the spiritual, but the natural, and afterward the spiritual” (1 Cor. 15:46). Therefore, since each person arises from a condemned mass, everyone must first be evil and carnal from Adam. But if he progresses by being reborn in Christ, afterward he will be good and spiritual.

Thus, throughout the human race, these cities began to move through the world by being born and dying. The one born first represents the citizens of this age; hence he is recorded as having first built a city. The one born later, however, is a stranger in the world and belongs to the city of God, of which the Psalmist says: “The generation of the upright shall be blessed” (Ps. 112:2), and: “This is the generation of those who seek the Lord” (Ps. 24:6), and similar passages. By grace he is predestined, by grace cast out, by grace a stranger below, by grace a citizen above.

**Verses 3–5.** — “And it came to pass after many days that Cain offered gifts to the Lord from the fruits of the earth,” and the rest through: “The Lord did not look upon Cain and his gifts, and Cain was very angry, and his face fell.”

How could Cain have known that God had accepted his brother’s gifts and rejected his own, unless that interpretation of Theodotion is true, which says: “The Lord inflamed toward Abel and toward his sacrifice, but toward Cain and his sacrifice he did not inflame”? Hence it is believed that fire was sent from heaven and accepted that sacrifice, as is very often recorded to have happened when holy men offered sacrifices—for example, at the dedication of the temple under Solomon, and when Elijah built an altar on Mount Carmel.

**Verses 6–7.** — “And the Lord said to Cain: Why are you angry?” and the rest.

This means: Why are you angry, and, burning with envy against your brother, do you cast down your angry face toward the earth? “If you do well, will you not receive?” That is: If you offer the sacrifice with a pure mind, will you not receive it, since God looks favorably upon you and your sacrifice?

Or, as it is found in certain manuscripts: “If you do well, will not all your sin be forgiven?” Or, as Theodotion says: “Will it be accepted?” That is: “I will receive your gift, just as I received your brother’s.”

“But if you do evil, your sin will immediately be present at the door.” Or, as some manuscripts have it: “At once your sin will sit before the entrance.” That is, as you enter and leave, your sin will always accompany you, and the Lord will cease to guard your coming in [Z.: “your entrance”] and your going out.

“Your desire shall be beneath you,” with the implied addition, “if you wish”; “and you shall rule over it.” It is as though he had said more plainly: Since you possess free will, sin does not have dominion over you, but you have dominion over it [Petr.: “sin has no dominion over you, but you do,” and so forth], and it is in your power either to restrain it or to desire it. Nevertheless, I warn you that sin should not rule over you, but that you should rule over sin.

For the Septuagint translated it thus: “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned? Be still” [Z.: “your turning toward him will be”], “its turning will be toward you,” and the rest. But the sense in Hebrew is much different [Z.: “deeper”] from that in these translations. We are therefore compelled to linger longer over individual points.

A sacrifice is offered rightly when it is offered to the true God, to whom alone sacrifice must be offered. But it is not divided rightly when the place, time, the thing itself that is offered, or the one who offers and the one to whom it is offered, is not properly distinguished.

The Jews offer God the Father rightly by believing, but do not divide rightly by denying the Son. They offer the Old Testament rightly by receiving it, but do not divide rightly by rejecting the New. Likewise, someone who, through rapacity or through anything acquired by fraud, performs a work of almsgiving performs a good work, but with bad discernment.

It is therefore understood that God did not look upon Cain’s gift because Cain himself divided it badly. He offered rightly to God, to whom alone it should be offered, by presenting a good work; but he did not divide rightly, because he did not do it with a good will, giving something of his own to God but keeping himself for himself. This is what all do who follow not God’s will but their own—that is, those who live not with an upright heart but with a perverse one.

Or perhaps Cain kept the better things for himself and gave the worse to God, devising, as is thought, something based on human invention, and thus did not divide rightly. Abel, however, offered the best and natural things to God, and therefore his sacrifice was accepted.

Hence, in the Gospel, he is uniquely described as righteous, because three great marks of righteousness are said to have existed in him: virginity, priesthood, and martyrdom. In these he prefigured Christ.

We too offer rightly when, with good zeal, we perform a good work; but we do not divide rightly if we postpone discernment in a good work. For unless discernment is present, what is thought to be the cause of virtue becomes the guilt of a crime [Z.: “becomes guilty of a crime”].

He says: “Be still; you have sinned. But its turning will be toward you,” with “of sin” understood, “if you wish to repent” [Z.: “if you do not wish to repent”] “and to attribute to yourself what you have done.” From the statement “its turning will be toward you,” it can be understood that sin’s turning ought to be toward the man himself, so that he may know that he must attribute his sin to no one but himself. For this is the healing medicine of repentance and the plea for forgiveness.

A person then rules over sin if he does not delay in placing this before himself, but subjects sin through repentance.

**Verse 8.** — “And Cain said to Abel his brother: Let us go out.” He spoke to him deceitfully, and he did not rule over his sin. “And when they were in the field, he rose up against him and killed him.”

[The Latin is corrupt: “Behold: he who taught the first man death, he himself ... this second killing.”] If he had obeyed God when he heard, “You have sinned; be still,” or, as it is read in our translation, “If you do well, you will receive; but if you do not, your sin will be present at the door, and you will rule over it,” then, helped by the Lord, he would not have sinned.

Sin is present at the door when it knocks upon the thoughts. Desire is beneath, and man rules over it if, having perceived the wickedness of his heart, he is pressed to act quickly and, before it grows hard, subdues it in his resisting mind. Because Cain scorned to do this, he committed fratricide.

**Verses 9–10.** — “And the Lord said to him: Where is Abel your brother?” and the rest.

He asks not as one ignorant, but as a judge questioning the guilty person whom he is about to punish. Cain, to increase his condemnation, replied falsely and arrogantly: “I do not know. Am I my brother’s keeper?”

And the Lord said: “What have you done? Behold, the voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the earth.”

The question is how Abel’s blood cries to God. It cries to God because the guilt of that homicide appears before the sight of the just judge.

**Verses 11–12.** — “Now therefore you shall be cursed upon the earth, which has opened its mouth,” and so forth.

**149**

…namely, because Cain himself was bringing upon himself the condemnation of the first transgression [Z.: “his own condemnation of the first transgression”], and did not fear to add the crime of fratricide to original sin; therefore he was considered worthy of a greater curse.

**Verses 13–14.** — “And Cain said to the Lord: My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve forgiveness.”

Behold: he spoke in despair, which is the greatest sin. He did not confess his crime, but plunged into the evil of despair. Hence he added: “Behold, you cast me out today from the face of the earth, and from your face I shall be hidden, and I shall be a wanderer and a fugitive.”

Or, as the Septuagint translated it: “Groaning and trembling you shall be upon the earth. Everyone who finds me will kill me.” Thus he condemned himself in such a way that, by the shortcut of death, he might escape his present torments.

**Verse 15.** — “And the Lord said: By no means shall this be so; but whoever kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold.”

Here a very complicated question arises, because another translation renders it: “He shall exact seven acts of vengeance.” Before discussing the question, however, it seems proper to arrange the editions of the individual translators, by which the sense of Scripture may more easily be understood.

Aquila translated: “And the Lord said to him: Therefore everyone who kills Cain shall be avenged sevenfold.” Symmachus, however: “Therefore everyone who kills Cain shall pay seven weeks” [Z.: “Cain, after seven weeks, shall pay,” and so forth], or “he shall be avenged in the seventh.” The Septuagint, as has been said, and Theodotion have: “And the Lord said: Not so; everyone who kills Cain shall pay seven acts of vengeance.”

Let us now turn our style toward clarifying the question. After Cain had killed his brother and had been asked by the Lord where he was, he replied insultingly: “I do not know,” and so forth. For this reason he was condemned by a curse, so that he might live groaning and trembling upon the earth. Instead of begging for mercy, he multiplied sins upon sins and thought only of a crime that, in his opinion, could not be forgiven by the Lord.

Finally he replied to the Lord: “My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve forgiveness”—that is, “I have sinned more than I can deserve to be absolved.” “I am cast out,” he says, “today from your sight,” and, unable to bear even the light of his conscience because of his crime, “I shall be hidden and shall lie concealed. And whoever finds me will kill me.” Driven by the trembling of his body and the frenzy of his mind, he understood himself to be one who deserved to be killed.

But God, unwilling to end his torments by a shortcut of death or to hand him over to the punishment by which he had condemned himself, says: “It shall not be so”—that is, “You will not die as you think, nor will you receive death as a remedy. Rather, you will live until the seventh generation, and you will be tortured by the fire of your conscience, so that whoever kills you will, according to a twofold interpretation, either free you from the great torment in the seventh generation or free you from it altogether.”

It is not that the person who killed Cain would himself be subjected to seven acts of vengeance, but that the seven acts of vengeance which converged upon Cain over so long a time would be discharged upon the killer, who would kill the one whom life had left behind for punishment.

To make what we are saying clearer, let us draw an example from ordinary custom: a servant speaks to his master amid blows. “Because I burned down your house and squandered all your property, kill me.” The master replies: “You will not die as you wish, nor will you end your life by punishment. Rather, you will be kept alive for a long time, and you will live so miserably in this light that whoever kills you will do a service to the one killed, since he will free you from so many torments.”

According to the edition of the Septuagint, this seems to be the sense here.

As for Aquila’s “sevenfold” and Symmachus’s “he will pay seven weeks,” or “the seventh will exact vengeance,” the opinion of our predecessors is that Cain was killed by Lamech in the seventh generation. For Adam begot Cain; Cain begot Enoch; Enoch begot Irad; Irad begot Mehujael; Mehujael begot Methushael; Methushael begot Lamech, who killed Cain, as he later confesses: “For I have killed a man in my wound, and a young man in my bruise,” and so forth.

I think, therefore, that nothing obscure remains concerning Cain’s being killed in the seventh generation and, according to another translation, paying the penalty for his crime.

Others speculate variously about Cain’s seven acts of vengeance. They assert that the first was the sin of not dividing rightly; the second, that he envied his brother; the third, that he acted deceitfully when he said, “Let us go out”; the fourth, that he killed him; the fifth, that he insolently denied it: “I do not know”; the sixth, that he condemned himself: “My iniquity is greater than that I may be forgiven”; the seventh, that even after being condemned he did not repent, like the Ninevites and Hezekiah, king of Judah, who delayed an impending death by their tears.

They say that the most merciful God delayed punishment until the seventh generation so that Cain, compelled at least by his very evils and by the sorrow of a long life, might repent and deserve to be absolved. They say that this is the sense which we outlined above: whoever killed Cain would free him from his immense punishment and all his torments.

As for what our translator, following the Hebrew truth, rendered: “Whoever kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold,” some understand it in this way [Z.: “There are others who understand it thus”]: the number seven is very often placed in Holy Scripture for the fullness of any matter. Thus “he shall be punished sevenfold” means as though it said: “He who kills you will be punished with the gravest vengeance, since, despite being warned by the threat of such a great condemnation, he was unwilling to restrain his hands from shedding blood.”

Therefore the Lord inspired terror, lest anyone commit homicide. As far as the historical surface is concerned, let this explanation suffice, so that the discussion may not proceed at greater length.

Nevertheless, lest we seem to exceed the limits of the little book, we have postponed turning to the allegorical interpretation. But if you wish to learn more fully about the tropological meaning of the birth of the two sons and what Cain and Abel signify, now that the covering of the other teachers has been removed, read through their books. Therefore, so that, as we began, we may unfold the veils of history…
