**152**

With the Lord’s favor, let us open them. For the lawgiver Moses says: “And the Lord placed a sign on Cain,” and the rest. The Hebrews report that Lamech killed Cain, and that he confessed this to his wives.

“And the Lord placed a sign on Cain” [Z.: “as a sign”], and the rest. Hebrews and some believers make various conjectures about this sign; but Scripture indicates what he set upon Cain so that he should not be killed: namely, that he should always live trembling and groaning, a wanderer and fugitive, and should not dare [Z.: “hear”] to have a settled dwelling anywhere in the world. Perhaps for this reason he built a city, in which he might be preserved.

**Verse 16.** — “And Cain went out from the face of the Lord and dwelt in the land of Nod, east of Eden.”

The Septuagint translated it: “He dwelt in the land of Naid.” What the Septuagint translated as “Naid” is not found in Hebrew. Therefore Naid is not a land, as our common people suppose, but the sentence of God is fulfilled: he wandered here and there, a fugitive and a wanderer. Hence Naid is interpreted as “unstable,” “wandering,” “a place without a fixed dwelling,” or “agitation.”

**Verse 17.** — “And Cain knew his wife, and she conceived and bore Enoch.” Some say that the statement “he knew his wife” signifies that the vengeance would cease if he did not take a wife.

“And he built a city, and called its name after the name of his son Enoch.” Enoch is interpreted as “dedication.” For Cain afterward built a city in his name. Here Cain is first described as having built a city, so that it might plainly be shown that the one who was alienated from the solidity of the eternal homeland laid a foundation on earth. A stranger from the heights, he laid a foundation below; he fixed the station of his heart in earthly pleasure.

Hence in his line Enoch, whose name is interpreted as “dedication,” is born first; among the progeny of the elect, however, Enoch is remembered as being seventh. For the reprobate dedicate themselves by building themselves up in this life, which comes first; but the elect await the dedication of their building at the end of time, that is, in the seventh age.

Hence Paul bears witness that Abraham lived in tents because he was awaiting the city that has foundations, whose architect is the heavenly [Z.: “supernal”] builder.

**Verses 18–22.** — “And Enoch begot Irad,” and the rest, through: “And Methuselah begot Lamech, who took two wives; the name of one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah.”

Lamech is interpreted as “striking.” He struck and killed Cain. He was also the first to commit adultery, because he divided himself between two wives.

Here it should be noted that in the progeny of Seth no woman born there is named individually, whereas one is mentioned in the progeny of Cain. This signifies that the earthly city which Cain began will retain carnal generations until its end, generations that arise from the union of men and women [Z.: “that come about through the unions of husbands and wives”]. Hence, as a testimony, Zillah is interpreted as “his shadow.”

**Verse 23.** — “And Lamech said to his wives: I have killed a man in my wound, and a young man in my bruise.”

The Hebrews relate that Lamech killed Cain and confessed this to his wives. They say that Lamech was an archer, skilled in hunting; but in extreme old age his own eyes had grown dim, and he could not see clearly. He had a young guide who led him. One day, as he went through the forest to take wild animals in the hunt, the boy went ahead to show the way. When they had passed through a thicket, the youth saw Cain at a distance; unable to distinguish him, he thought that he was a beast [Z.: “he thought him to be a beast”], and said to Lamech: “I see a beast.” Lamech said: “Give me the bow, direct my hands there, and give me an arrow, so that I may shoot.” When his hands had been directed, he shot and struck Cain with the arrow. Feeling the body and beginning to touch what the missile had killed, he realized that he had killed Cain. Then, enraged, he turned the bow and struck the boy with it. This is what he said to his wives: “I have killed a man,” that is, Cain, “in my wound, and a young man in my bruise.”

We should understand the man and the young man as Cain himself: “man” because of his age and natural strength, and “young man” because of the foolishness and wanton instability of his character.

Nevertheless, Lamech spiritually interprets Christ, who killed Cain, that is, the devil. After killing him, he announces this to his wives—that is, to the two Churches over which he rules—and to whose word he commands them to listen.

Thus he says that he has killed a man, whom he calls the devil on account of his strength. “In my wound,” that is, by his death; and he calls him a young man on account of his wantonness and immortality. “In my bruise,” that is, not [Z.: omits “not”] without pain.

But it must be asked what Lamech meant when he said, after killing Cain: “Sevenfold vengeance shall be exacted from Cain, but from Lamech seventy-sevenfold.” This is said because the sin of homicide is recorded as having been avenged by the flood in the seventh generation.

Or, as the Jews relate, seventy-seven persons descended from Lamech and were found in the flood and destroyed. They say that vengeance was exacted from Lamech in this number because his line continued until the cataclysm.

But the crime of adultery, which Lamech was the first of all to commit with two wives, could be expiated only by the blood of Christ, who came into the world in the seventy-seventh generation, according to the Gospel of Luke. He took away the sin of the world, washed his garment in the blood of the grape, and trod the winepress alone.

**Verse 25.** — “And Adam again knew his wife, who conceived a son, and called his name Seth.”

Seth is interpreted as “resurrection” or “placement.” “Resurrection,” because he was born after his brother’s killing, as though he raised up his brother from the dead through a resurrection. “Placement,” because God placed him in the place of Abel.

Hence it is also said: “God has raised up for me another seed in place of Abel, whom Cain killed.” Or, as Aquila translated it: “God has placed for me another seed in place of Abel.”

Spiritually,…

[scan page 82]

## Commentary

Some indeed wish Adam and his wife to signify Christ and the Synagogue. From them was born a son, that is, the people of the Gentiles in faith, who is rightly called Seth, that is, “placed in truth.” What he says, “another seed in place of Abel,” signifies the good people of the New Testament in place of the patriarchs, prophets, and martyrs who were killed by the wicked faction of the Jewish people.

In the moral sense, Adam and his wife signify every holy person and the flesh; the son signifies perfect understanding; and “another seed in place of Abel” signifies good understandings in place of good things.

### Verse 26

“Seth also had a son, and called his name Enos” [Z.: “whom he called Enos”]. Just as Adam is interpreted as “man,” so Enos, according to the truth of the Hebrew language, means “man” or “male.” He bore this name appropriately. For it is written of him: “Then he began to call upon the name of the Lord”; or, as some translated it: “Then the beginning was made of calling upon the name of the Lord.”

Although most Hebrews think that at that time idols were first fashioned in the name and likeness of the Lord, some [Z.: “others”] have wished it to mean that this was said because Enos was the first to discover one of the ten names of the Lord by which he is called among the Hebrews.

But allegorically [Z.: “Nevertheless, allegorically”] the successors of the Christian people are signified, who call upon the name of the Lord, who is God.

## Chapter V

### Verses 1–4

“This is the book of the generation of Adam, on the day when God created man; he made him according to the likeness of God,” and so forth up to: “And he called their name Adam on the day when they were created.”

He says well, “and he called their names Adam,” that is, “man.” The name “man” applies equally to male and female.

### Verses 5–7

“All the time that Adam lived was nine hundred and thirty years, and he died.” According to the tropological interpretation, as some explain it, Adam’s nine hundred and thirty years signify the three laws, or faith, hope, and charity, or the stages of Christ’s life.

### Verses 8–9, 21

“Seth lived nine hundred and twelve years, and he died. Enos also lived, and after he had begotten Cainan [Z.: ‘after he begot Cainan’], nine hundred and five years, and he died.”

Cainan is called “lamentation” or “their possession.” For just as Cain means “possession,” so the derivative name Cainan means “their possession” [Z.: “the derived name Cainan means ‘their possession’”].

But in the fact that the years of Adam’s sons grow shorter, it was signified that the years of the human race thereafter would have to diminish. It follows:

### Verses 11–27

“Henoch begot Mathusalam, and he walked with God”—the phrase “in his way of life” is understood—“and he did not appear, because God took him.”

Henoch is interpreted as “dedication,” as we showed above. But it must be asked why he was preserved from death for so long, unless it was to show what all human beings could have been had they not sinned. Nevertheless, he will have to die, so that he may pay the debt owed by human nature, and so that no one may be incapable of dying—a thing Christ did not will.

Henoch begot Mathusalam, and all the days of Mathusalam were nine hundred and sixty-nine years, and he died.

Here arises a famous question, debated by many churchmen: according to careful calculation, Mathusalam is reported to have lived fourteen years after the Flood. For when Mathusalam was one hundred and sixty-seven years old, he begot Lamech. Again, when Lamech was one hundred and eighty-eight years old, he begot Noah. From Mathusalam’s birth to Noah’s birth, therefore, the total is three hundred and fifty-five years. The Flood occurred in Noah’s six-hundredth year of life; consequently, by calculating the figures in their parts, the Flood is shown to have occurred in Mathusalam’s nine-hundred-and-fifty-fifth year.

But since he is said above to have lived nine hundred and sixty-nine years, there is no doubt that he lived fourteen years after the Flood, as is found in the Septuagint. And how is it true that only eight souls were saved in the ark?

It therefore remains that, as in many other places, there is also an error here in the number. For in the Hebrew and Samaritan books, as blessed Jerome writes, it is recorded as follows:

“Mathusalam lived one hundred and eighty-seven years, and begot Lamech. Mathusalam lived, after he had begotten Lamech, seven hundred and eighty-two years, and begot sons and daughters. All the days of Mathusalam, as our translator rendered it, were nine hundred and sixty-nine years, and he died. Lamech lived one hundred and eighty-two years and begot Noah.”

From the day of Mathusalam’s birth, therefore, to the day of Noah’s birth there are three hundred and sixty-nine years. Add Noah’s six hundred years, since the Flood occurred in his six-hundredth year of life, and it follows that Mathusalam died in the nine hundred and sixty-ninth year of his life, in the very year when the Flood began.

Hence Mathusalam is interpreted as “he has died.” For how did they suppose [Z.: “suppose”] that he had been translated with his father and had escaped the Flood? For this reason he is expressly translated as “he has died,” to show that he did not live after the Flood but died in that same cataclysm, as I found in a certain volume.

For, as Scripture testifies, eight human beings alone escaped the Flood in the ark (1 Peter 3:20). But those who report that he lived fourteen years after the Flood incline more toward a spiritual interpretation: they interpret him as referring to Christ, because he alone is one whose life feels no age. In his elders also Noah seems to have experienced the Flood [Z.: “does not seem to have experienced it”].

### Verses 28–30

“Lamech lived one hundred and eighty-two years, and begot a son. He called his name Noah, saying: ‘This one will console us,’” and so forth.

Or, as some translated it: “This one will give us rest from all our works.”

Hence Noah is interpreted as “consolation” or “rest.” “Consolation,” because people were consoled in his days when they were destroyed by the Flood on account of their sin. “Rest,” because under him all former works ceased through the Flood, or because he provided rest for the animals in the ark.

[scan page 83]

The animals rested in the ark.

## Chapter VI

### Verse 2

“The sons of God saw the daughters of men, that they were beautiful,” and so forth.

By “the sons of God” he means the sons of Seth, and by “the sons of men” the offspring of Cain. But after the sons of Seth, overcome by desire, joined marriages with the daughters of Cain’s most degraded offspring, human beings of immense bodily size, proud in strength and uncultivated in character, were begotten from such a union—those whom Scripture calls Giants.

This displeased God, and he shortened the span of their lives. For the Greeks call them *Gigantes*, according to the etymology of the word, fancifully as though they were “earth-born,” that is, born from the earth, because the earth supposedly produced beings of immense bulk and like itself; for *gē* means “earth.”

Those who think that transgressing angels had intercourse with the daughters of men before the Flood, and that Giants were born from them—namely, extraordinarily large and powerful men by whom the earth was filled—are mistaken.

### Verse 3

“And God said: ‘My Spirit will not remain in man forever, because he is flesh,’” and so forth.

In Hebrew it is written: “My Spirit will not judge these men forever, because they are flesh.” The Spirit here signifies anger, and “flesh” signifies the frailty of human nature, as though he had said: “Since the human condition is fragile, I will not preserve them forever for punishment, but here I will repay them what they deserve.”

Therefore “anger” does not signify severity, as is frequently read in our books, but denotes God’s clemency, since the sinner is punished here according to his crime. Hence the angry God also says to certain people: “I will not visit their daughters when they have committed fornication, nor their daughters-in-law when they have committed adultery” (Hosea 2:14). And elsewhere: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with scourges; but I will not remove my mercy from them” (Psalm 88:39).

Moreover, lest he should seem cruel because he had not granted sinners a place for repentance, he added: “Their days shall be one hundred and twenty years”—that is, they would have one hundred and twenty years in which to do penance.

But because the human race of that time refused to repent, God did not wish to wait for the appointed time. He shortened the period by twenty years and brought in the Flood in the hundredth year.

The Spirit may also be understood as the soul. Thus, when he says, “My Spirit will not remain in man forever,” it is as though he had said: “The soul will not remain in the flesh forever, because man is not spiritual but fleshly.”

It follows:

### Verses 5–8

“God, seeing that the wickedness of men was great on the earth,” and so forth, up to: “It repented him that he had made man on the earth.”

It is asked what it means when God is said to have repented that he had made man, and again, that he was touched by inward grief of heart. Can repentance or grief of heart befall God?

It must be understood that God does not repent of his work or grieve as a human being does, for whom judgment concerning all things past is entirely fixed and whose present awareness is certain [F.: “foreknowledge”]. Rather, Holy Scripture uses familiar words intelligible to us and adapts itself to our smallness, so that through things known we may come to know things unknown.

### Verses 9–12

“These are the generations of Noah. Noah was a just and perfect man in his generations.”

If no one is without sin, how can anyone be perfect? Some are called perfect, not in the way in which they will be perfected—such as in that immortality in which they will be made equal to the angels of God—but as they can be perfect in this pilgrimage.

Hence the phrase “in his generation” was deliberately added, to show that he was just not according to consummate justice but according to the justice of his own generation. This is what is said in Hebrew: “Noah was a just man; he was perfect in his generations; he walked with God”—that is, he followed God’s footsteps.

### Verse 13

“God said to Noah: ‘The end of all flesh has come before me.’”

“All flesh” signifies all mortals except those who were to be saved in the ark. They were therefore preserved as a kind of seedbed of a second beginning.

It follows: “And I will destroy them together with the earth.”

How “together with the earth,” when the earth afterward remained? Teachers report that the earth’s vigor and fertility were much less after the Flood than before it. For this reason, they say, permission was then given to human beings to eat flesh, whereas before the Flood they had lived only on the fruits of the earth.

### Verse 14

“Make for yourself an ark from smoothed wood.”

Smoothed wood means strong and indestructible wood, of which another translation says “squared,” so that the ark would not be broken either by the force of the winds or by the inundation of the waters.

“And you shall coat it with pitch within and without.” Pitch is an extremely hot and exceptionally durable adhesive. Its property is that wood coated with it can be neither eaten by worms nor dissolved by the heat of the sun, the blasts of the winds, or floods of water.

### Verse 15

“The length of the ark shall be three hundred cubits, its breadth fifty cubits, and its height thirty cubits.”

What kind of appearance or shape, then, should we understand the ark to have had? It seems to have risen from the bottom with four corners, and these were gradually drawn inward toward the upper part until they narrowed to the space of one cubit.

For the text says that at its foundations it was three hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high, but that it narrowed toward the top into a pointed summit, so that its length and breadth there were one cubit.

Indeed, no shape could have been more suitable or appropriate for the ark than one in which a narrow ridge, as though forming a kind of roof, defended the top from the downpour of rain, while the squared stability of its bottom kept it firm in the water, so that it could be neither tilted nor sunk by the force of winds, the violence of waves, or the movements of the animals inside it.

### Verse 16

“You shall make compartments and three stories in it.”

Another translation says “two-storied in the lower parts” and “three-storied in the upper parts.” Thus we understand that there were five distinct areas of habitation in it.

Its lower places were assigned to dung and filth, so that the animals, and especially human beings, would not be troubled by the stench of excrement. The upper and adjoining chamber was assigned to preserving food for the animals.

The lower parts, which are said to have been two-storied, were divided for these purposes. The upper parts, called three-storied, were assigned first to the wild beasts, the harsher animals, and the serpents. Above these, suitable places served as stalls for gentler animals. Above everything, at the highest point, a dwelling was placed for human beings, since, just as man excels all animals in honor and wisdom, so he should excel them in position.

Thus five habitations are understood to have existed in it: the first for dung, the second for provisions, the third for wild animals, the fourth for tame animals, and the fifth for human beings.

“You shall make a window in the ark, and you shall complete it to the measure of one cubit at its summit.”

The window is ordered to be made at the summit [Z.: “on the summit”] of the ark so that there would be an opening through which he could send out birds to investigate whether the earth was dry.

“But you shall place the door of the ark below, in its side.” They report that the door said to have been made in the side was located so that the lower parts, which he called two-storied, lay beneath it, while the upper parts, which he called three-storied, took their name from the place of the door.

Through it the animals entered and were divided among their respective places according to the orderly arrangement described above.

But perhaps someone will ask whether the ark’s dimensions contain some mystery. They do indeed contain the perfect mystery of Christ’s body. Six times fifty is contained in three hundred, and ten times thirty likewise. For the human body, if you measure a man lying down, has a length six times its breadth and ten times its height.

The length of a man lying down is measured from the crown of the head to the feet, the breadth from side to side, and the height from the back to the belly. This figure appropriately applies to Christ because of the length of time for which he endures all things, the breadth of charity, and the height of the hope that is above.

It follows:

### Verse 19

“Of all clean animals take seven and seven into the ark; but of unclean animals, two and two, male and female. Likewise, of the birds of heaven, seven and seven, male and female, so that seed may be preserved upon the earth.”

What does “two and two” and “seven and seven” mean? Should we understand that four unclean animals and fourteen clean animals were brought in? Certainly not.

“Two and two” does not refer to four, but to male and female. For there were only two of the unclean animals, and only seven of the clean. He therefore placed the unclean animals in an even number, but the clean in an odd number, so that there would be animals from which to offer sacrifices to God.

There were rightly more clean than unclean animals because of their future use by the human race: there needed to be more that would be useful than harmful.

Of these animals it is said that “the breath of life was in them.” This refers not only to human beings but also to all other creatures that feed upon the vital breath.

It should be noted that some people are accustomed to ask whether the ark is described as having had enough capacity to contain so many and such great animals, together with suitable places for them and their food.

The Hebrews report that Moses, whom Scripture says was educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, used the number of cubits here according to the art of geometry, in which the Egyptians were especially skilled. They assert that a geometric cubit was worth as much as six of our cubits.

Read Origen on this matter, where he disputes against Apelles.

Finally, when Scripture reports that all the animals entered the ark, this did not happen because Noah gathered them, but because the Lord commanded it; compelled by his will, they came of their own accord to the ark in the prescribed number.

Some ask what should be understood concerning fish or birds [Z.: “creatures that live on high ground”] that can live in or upon the waters, or whether the smallest insects, flies, mice, lizards, and other such creatures were brought into the ark; whether their number was greater than the number specified, and where they would have been, if they were there.

Those troubled by these questions should be instructed to understand the statement as referring to creatures “that creep upon the earth.” It was not necessary to preserve in the ark those that can [Z.: “are accustomed to”] live in the waters—not only those submerged, such as fish, but also those that float upon them, such as many birds.

Moreover, when it says “male and female,” it certainly means that they were brought in for reproduction. Therefore it was not necessary for those creatures to be there that can be born without sexual intercourse, from various things or from the corruption of things. Or, if they were present, as they are accustomed to be in houses, they could have been there without any definite number.

Alternatively, if the most sacred mystery being enacted, and the figure of so great a reality, could not easily [according to the better reading in certain manuscripts: “with difficulty”] be fulfilled unless everything that, because its nature prevents it, cannot live in the waters were present there in that fixed number, this was not a matter for human care but for divine care.

Noah did not capture them and bring them in; he merely allowed those coming and entering to do so.

As for creatures that possess sex but cannot produce offspring, such as the mule and the hinny, it would be remarkable if they were there [Z.: “if they had been there”], and not rather their parents, namely the horse and the donkey, and whatever other creatures produce offspring through the joining of different kinds.

But this too pertained to the mystery, for this kind also has male and female. What should be understood concerning animals of different kinds that lived peacefully together and did not attack one another? Just as they were brought into the ark by God’s command, so they were preserved in the ark by God’s command.

They were either divided according to their kinds among separate chambers, or, if they remained together [Z.: “if they remained joined together”], they were nevertheless governed by God’s power. Read the fifteenth book of blessed Augustine’s *City of God*, where he discusses the ark at length.

Some also raise the question of how lions, eagles, and other creatures of this sort, which are accustomed to live on flesh, could have been fed in the ark.

Perhaps, as the teachers think, other animals besides the specified number were brought into the ark to serve as food for the others; or perhaps, by divine wisdom—or with God showing Noah—some food other than flesh was provided that would also be suitable as nourishment for such animals, which is more credible.

For we know that many animals for which flesh is food also eat fruit [Z.: “and fruits”].

What should be thought about the animals’ drink, of which Scripture says nothing? Some think that food or drink sufficient for one day was brought into the ark in such abundance that it would benefit the animals for many days, or perhaps for the whole year, which is more probable.

But let us set aside uncertain conjectures and grant divine power the ability to do with its creatures whatever it wished [Petr.: “whatever it wished to do”].

## Chapter VII

### Verses 1–19

“And the Lord shut him in from outside.”

How, after the door had been closed so that no human being remained outside the ark, could its outer door have been coated with pitch? Without doubt this was a divine work, so that the waters might not enter through the opening, which no human hand had protected.

It follows:

### Verse 20

“The water rose fifteen cubits above the mountains that it had covered.”

It is asked whether, if the water rose fifteen cubits higher, its height exceeded this turbulent air, which, as is said, is so high that neither clouds are seen nor wind is felt, as some suppose concerning Mount Olympus.

But it must be considered that, if the earth could intrude into the space of that tranquil ether, why could the water, by rising, not exceed that mountain and even that air?

Some nevertheless think that the earth was not then so uneven [Z.: “so even”], and that the mountains were not as high before the Flood as they are now.

### Verse 21

“All flesh that moved upon the earth perished, and all in whose nostrils was the breath of life on the earth died.”

If this is so, what should be said about animals whose nature cannot live always in dry places or always in wet places, such as otters and sea calves, and about the many kinds of birds that seek food in the waters but sleep, are nourished, and rest on dry land?

It must be said that divine power could sustain both kinds of nature until the Flood had passed, so that they could live either only in the wet or only in the dry. Unless perhaps places were prepared for them somewhere outside the ark where they could live in the waters and rest on dry land.

## Chapter VIII

### Verse 2

“God remembered Noah, and he brought a wind over the earth, and the waters diminished.”

This may be understood of the Spirit of whom it was said: “The Spirit of God was borne over the waters.” Then he was borne over them so that, when the waters had been gathered into one place, the earth might appear.

Now the Spirit is said to have been brought over the earth so that, when the waters of the Flood had been removed, he might reveal the face of the earth.

The word “spirit” may also be understood as “wind,” according to the Psalmist: “And a storm wind arose” (Psalm 106:25), by whose repeated blasts the waters were driven back.

### Verses 3–5

“The waters withdrew from the earth, going and returning.”

When it says, “The waters withdrew from the earth, going and returning,” the literal sense seems to be that all the courses of rivers and streams return through the earth’s hidden channels to the abyss, according to Solomon: “To the place from which the rivers flow, they return, so that they may flow again” (Ecclesiastes 1:7).

### Verse 6

“After forty days Noah opened the window, and sent out a raven, which went out and did not return.”

In Hebrew it is written: “Going out and returning, until the waters were dried up from the earth.” But, as our translation suggests, it did not return because either it was swallowed up and killed by the waters, or, finding some floating corpse, it was delighted to settle upon it. The dove, by contrast, naturally avoids such a thing; of it it is said: “When it found no place where its foot could rest, it returned to him in the ark.”

Nevertheless, it must be asked why the rain inundated the earth for forty days, and why Noah is again said to have opened the ark’s window after forty days.

This number forty spiritually signifies the tribulation of repentance. The fact that he opened the window after forty days signifies that heaven is opened by fasting.

For this reason Moses and Elijah, and also the Savior himself, consecrated fasts, as though fasting were necessary in three periods: before the Law, under the Law, and under grace.

It follows:

### Verse 11

“And it came to him toward evening, carrying an olive branch,” and so forth.

Why does it carry an olive branch, unless because it was foreshadowing the type of the Holy Spirit?

The dove, which represents the Holy Spirit, after the most dreadful bird had been driven away, flies back to Noah after the Flood as though to Christ after baptism, announcing peace to the world with branches of refreshment and light.

Before the description of this ark reaches its conclusion, however, it should be noted that, if God had made everything good, and even very good, why are some animals in it called clean and others unclean? Can anything unclean be good?

It must be understood that even what is called unclean is good in its own nature. It is considered unclean only by comparison with another, better nature.

Finally, an ox is better than a lion, because its nature is more suited to assisting human need. For the sake of man all animals were created; concerning him it is also said: “And let your terror and dread be upon all the animals of the earth.”

Therefore man was placed above the other animals in terror, both so that they might serve as a consolation for the vengeance already carried out, and so that the few human beings would not be oppressed by the greater number of beasts, and so that they would know that they ought to rule over irrational creatures, not rational ones.

Hence our first parents are read to have been shepherds of animals, not kings of men.

Spiritually, however, in what Noah says—“Make for yourself an ark”—the Father’s counsel to the Son may be understood concerning the taking on of flesh.

“From smoothed wood,” that is, from the Jews, fashioned according to the Law. Noah with his sons, in the uppermost place, is Christ with his apostles. The birds in the second place signify the saints; the cattle in the third represent the innocent; the beasts in the fourth indicate worldly people. The fifth place, with its dung, expresses hell.

Alternatively, these five places show the five ascents of the Church: catechumens, baptized persons, married persons, penitents, and saints.

The fact that the rain fell after seven days can signify the voluntary rain after the old Law, of which it is said: “You will set aside voluntary rain, O God,” and so forth (Psalm 67:10).

The fact that all the fountains of the abyss were broken open signifies the evangelists; the great abyss signifies the profundity of the Old Testament; and the cataracts of heaven signify the apostles.

But when he says, “The Lord shut him in from outside” [Z.: “the Lord shut him in”; another reading: “the Lord shut him in from outside”], he shows Christ protecting his Church from persecutors.

When he then says that all flesh was consumed, he guards against heretics who think that some escaped the Flood, as was believed concerning Mathusalam.

The words “going and returning” signify the vengeance and punishments inflicted upon persecutors and returning upon heretics.

The raven, sent out and not returning, represents the sinner or the devil, who does not return to the kingdom of Christ.

The dove, by contrast, which returned, signifies Adam, as some wish it to be understood, returning to paradise through Christ, if the reader is willing to accept this interpretation; or rather it signifies each just person returning to the Church, whose foot—that is, whose understanding—does not rest in this world.

The olive branch in the dove’s mouth signifies the confession of the Trinity in the mouth of every saint, together with green leaves, that is, perfect works.

### Verses 21–22

“I will not again strike every living thing, as I have done, for all the days of the earth. Seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, night and day shall not cease.”

“Seedtime and harvest” signify the teaching of the Scriptures. “Cold and heat” represent chastity and faith; “night and day” signify the Old and New Testaments.

Alternatively, by “seedtime and harvest” he indicates the teachers and writings [Petr.: “writers”] of heresy, and by “cold and heat” he indicates unbelief and the charity of faith. By “night and day” some wish heresies in both Testaments to be understood.

It follows:

## Chapter IX

### Verses 3–4

“As green herbs I have given you everything, except that you shall not eat flesh with its blood. For I will require the blood of your lives from the hand of every beast and from the hand of man,” and so forth.

How many have shed blood, yet their blood has not been poured out? Others have killed a man by poison or hanging, and their blood has not been shed. How, then, will the Lord pour out their blood, since the blood of the one who killed them has been shed [Petr.: “or, the blood of the one who killed him”]?

It is ridiculous to apply this to the resurrection as well as to this life. Therefore “the blood of man,” which is vital, by which he is invigorated, sustained, and lives, must be understood. Whoever sheds it, whether through scandal or through perverse teaching, will have it poured out on the day of judgment by the one who appeared to him to possess what was vital.

Historically, however, after the Flood the first consumption of flesh is granted to man, evidently because of the reduced fertility of the earth, as is believed, and because of human frailty.

### Verse 13

“I will set my bow in the clouds,” and so forth.

A sign of security is therefore given, because the Creator knew the fearful hearts of human beings, lest they should believe themselves to be destroyed again by a flood whenever they saw frequent inundations of rain. The same sign of security was fittingly placed in heaven, so that it might be seen by all and so that, in every tribulation, we might raise the eyes of our hearts to him who dwells in heaven.

But it is asked why it is given to human beings in different colours. It is for security and fear. Thus the bow displays at once the colour of water and of fire: it is partly azure and partly ruddy, so that it may bear witness both to the judgment that has occurred and to that which is to occur—that is, that the world will be burned by the fire of judgment. For the water of the Flood will not destroy it.

This raises for some the question whether there were rains before the Flood. They seem not to have existed, because a rainbow is formed only from the sun’s rays and a moist cloud. The earth could formerly have been made fertile by dew and by the irrigation of springs, as in Egypt.

### Verses 18–19

“The sons of Noah who came out of the ark were Shem, Ham, and Japheth,” and so forth, up to: “From these the whole human race was dispersed over the whole earth.”

From these men and their descendants the world was divided.

Shem, as is thought, received Asia. Let us give the historical interpretations of each name.

Shem is called “named,” because he received a name as a prophecy of his descendants. From him came the patriarchs, the apostles, and the people of God; from his stock also came Christ, whose great name extends among the nations from the rising of the sun to its setting.

Ham received hot Africa, and he too is named by a prophecy of the future. His descendants possess [Z.: “occupy”] that part of the earth which, because it is near the sun, is hotter. Hence Egypt to this day is called *Cam* in the language of the Egyptians.

Japheth received Europe. Japheth means “breadth.” From him the people of the Gentiles were born, and because the multitude of believers from the Gentiles is broad, Japheth was named from that breadth.

Fifteen nations were descended from Japheth, thirty from Ham, and twenty-seven from Shem. Together they make seventy-two, from whom seventy-two nations arose. Among them the Lord sent an equal number of disciples to preach.

### Verses 20–22

“Noah, a husbandman, began to work the earth, and he planted a vineyard. When he drank wine, he became drunk, and he was uncovered in his tent,” and so forth.

Why is so great a man said to have become drunk? Perhaps, as blessed Jerome, the interpreter of the heavenly Library, says, it was because he did not know how to become drunk with wine. For before the Flood, men are not read to have used wine [Petr.: “men are not read to have used wine”]. Hence it is said particularly of Noah: “He planted a vineyard.”

As some think, the uncovering of his thighs followed the drunkenness, because sexual desire often follows satiety.

But the fact that Noah’s sons, walking backward, covered their father’s nakedness, with their faces turned away, and so forth, can be understood morally.

We call “turned away” what we reject. What, then, does it mean that the sons, with their backs covered by a cloak, approach while turned away and cover their father’s nakedness, unless that good subjects are so displeased by the faults of their teachers that they nevertheless conceal those faults from others?

They carry the covering while turned away.

[scan page 87]

**ANGELUS OF LUXEUIL, MONK**

p. 164

**CHAPTER X**

**Verses 1–2.** These are the generations of Noah’s sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth. The sons of Japheth are Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, and the rest. As we indicated above, the seven sons of Japheth possessed the land in Asia from the Amanus and Taurus mountains, Coele-Syria, and Cilicia, as far as the river Tanais, as I have discovered in the books of blessed Jerome. In Europe, as far as Gades, they left their names to places and peoples; many of these were subsequently changed, while the rest remain as they were. Magog is Scythia; Madai, Media; Javan, Ionia—that is, Greece, whence also the Ionian Sea; Tubal, Iberia—that is, Spain, which some suppose to be Celtiberia, though others take it to be Italy; Meshech, Cappadocia. The Septuagint translators render Cappadocians as Cappadocians. Tiras is Thrace. Some have transferred Gog and Magog to the Gothic people, because all earlier learned men customarily called the Goths Getae rather than Gog.

**Verse 3.** The sons of Gomer: Ashkenaz, and Riphath, and Togarmah. The Greeks call Ashkenaz Rheginos [Z., Rennos], Riphath the Paphlagonians, and Togarmah the Phrygians.

**Verses 4–5.** The sons of Javan: Elishah, and Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim. From these the islands of the nations were divided in their lands, each according to its language, its families, and its nation. From the Ionians, that is, the Greeks, came the Eolians, who are called Aeolids; hence the fifth Greek language is called Aeolic. Finally, Josephus considers Tarshish to be Cilicia. Their capital city is therefore also called Tarsus, glorious through the apostle Paul. Kittim means the Citii [Z., the Scitii], from whom the city of Cyprus is still named. Dodanim means the Rhodians. Finally, as is found in the books of the *Antiquities*, almost all the islands and the shores of the whole world, and lands near the sea, were occupied by the Greeks as far as the Ocean—namely, from the Taurus and Amanus mountains, as we said above.

**Verse 6.** The sons of Ham: Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan. Cush is still called Ethiopia by the Hebrews; Mizraim is Egypt; Put is Libya, from whom the river of Mauretania is still called Put. Canaan, moreover, obtained the land that the Jews afterward possessed.

**Verse 7.** The sons of Cush: Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca. Seba, from whom come the Sabaeans, concerning whom Virgil says:

> “The Sabaean branch is rich in incense…”

Havilah are those dwelling in a more remote part of Africa, adjoining the wilderness of the Gaetulians. Sabtah is Sabathes, which is now called Astabar. Raamah and Sabteca gradually lost their ancient names, and it is unknown what names they now bear in place of the old ones.

The sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan [Z., “the son of Sheba, Dedan”; Vulgate, “the sons of Raamah, Sheba and Dedan”]. This Sheba is written with the letter *sin*, whereas the earlier name is written with *samekh*; from the latter, as we said, the Sabaeans were named. Sheba is therefore interpreted as Arabia. For in the seventy-first psalm, where we read, “The kings of the Arabs and of Sheba shall offer gifts,” the Hebrew has “the kings of Sheba”: the first name with *sin*, as Jerome says, and the second with *samekh*.

[scan page 88]

**COMMENTARY. IN GENESIS**

p. 166

Dedan, indeed, is an Ethiopian people in the western region.

**Verse 8.** Cush begot Nimrod. He began to be powerful on the earth, and he was a mighty hunter before the Lord, and so forth. This Nimrod first seized tyranny over the peoples and extended his kingdom into Babylon, because there the languages were confused and he built the tower. Babel is interpreted as “confusion.” He reigned in Erech, that is, Edessa; in Accad, which is now called Nisibis [Z., Nobitis; read “Nisibis”]; and in Calneh, which afterward, under King Seleucus, was called Seleucia. He is called a mighty hunter before the Lord—or, as it is found in certain manuscripts, “a mighty hunter against the Lord,” which seems better to us—for he was a suppressor and destroyer of earthly men. Thus, with his peoples, he raised a tower against the Lord, in which impious pride was signified: for the ruler’s domination is condemned in the language itself, so that it might not be understood as commanding a man to obey God’s command.

This conspiracy was dissolved when each person withdrew from the one whom he understood and joined himself only to the one with whom he could communicate; thus, with their languages divided, the nations were scattered across the lands. It follows:

**Verse 11.** From that land Asshur went out and built Nineveh, and Rehoboth the city, as it is found in certain manuscripts. From this land the empire of the Assyrians spread, who, from the name of Ninus, son of Belus, founded Nineveh, the great city, which the Hebrews call Nineveh. When it says, “He built Nineveh and Rehoboth the city,” we should not think that these were two cities; rather, since *Rehoboth* means “broad streets,” the text should be read: “He built Nineveh and the streets of the city.”

**Verses 13–14.** Mizraim begot the Ludim, the Anamim [Z., Ananim], the Lehabim, the Naphtuhim, the Pathrusim, and the Casluhim, from whom came the Philistines and the Caphtorim. Except for the Lehabim, from whom the Libyans were afterward named—previously they were called Putites—and the Casluhim, who afterward were called Philistines, whom we correctly call Palestinians, the other six peoples are unknown, because they were destroyed in the Ethiopian war until their former names passed into oblivion [Z., “their earlier names”]. They possessed the land from Gaza to the farthest borders of Egypt.

**Verses 15–18.** Canaan begot Sidon, his firstborn, and the Hittites, the Jebusites, the Amorites, the Girgashites, the Hivites, the Arkites, the Sinites, the Arvadites, the Zemarites, and the Hamathites. The firstborn of Canaan was Sidon [Z., Sidona], from whom the Phoenician city is called Sidon. Next came the Arkite, who founded Arcas, a town opposite Tripoli at the foot of Lebanon. The Arvadites were those who possessed the island of Aradus, separated by a short distance from the Phoenician shore. The Samarites are Emesa, a celebrated city of Coele-Syria. Hamath is called by both Syrians and Hebrews by the name it bore among the ancients. The Macedonians called it Epiphania.

**Verses 19–21.** The boundary of the Canaanites extended from Sidon, coming toward Gerar as far as Gaza; and it went toward Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, as far as Lasha. The remaining names are retained as proper names. It should only be noted that Lasha itself is what is now called Callirhoe, where hot waters burst forth and flow into the Dead Sea.

**Verse 22.** The sons of Shem: Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad, Lud, and Aram. These occupied the region from the Euphrates River through part of Asia as far as the Indian Ocean. Elam is the ancestor of the Elamites, the rulers of Persia. Concerning Asshur it has already been said that he founded the city of Nineveh. Arphaxad is the ancestor of the Chaldaeans; Lud, of the Lydians; and Aram, of the Syrians, whose capital is Damascus.

**Verse 23.** The sons of Aram: Uz, Hul, Gether, and Meshech. Uz was the founder of Trachonitis and Damascus; he held power over Palestine and Coele-Syria. Therefore the Septuagint translators, in the book of Job, where the Hebrew has “the land of Uz,” translated the region as the land of the Ausites. Hul is the ancestor of the Armenians. Gether is the ancestor of the Arcaeans or Carians. Meshech, whom the Septuagint translators called Mosoch, refers to those who are now called Maeonians.

**Verses 24–25.** Arphaxad begot Shelah [Z., Sela], and Shelah begot Eber. Eber had two sons: the name of one was Peleg, and the name of his brother was Joktan. Eber, from whom the Hebrews derive their name, imposed upon his son the name Peleg, which means “division,” because in his days the languages were divided at Babylon.

**Verses 26 and following.** Joktan begot Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, Hadoram, Uzal, Daebal [Z., Dedabal], Abimael, Sheba, Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab. I have not been able to discover the later names of these peoples. Either they are still called what they were at first, or it is unknown which names have been changed. They possessed the entire region of India from the river of Kabul, which is called Herat.

**CHAPTER XI**

**Verses 1–4.** The whole earth had one language and the same words, and so forth, until they said: “Come, let us make for ourselves a city and a tower whose summit may reach to heaven,” and so forth. They wished to build the tower of their pride in order to make their name famous before they were scattered, as Scripture testifies; or to investigate what was above heaven; or, as some think, to have a place to which they could flee, because they believed that the world would again be destroyed by a flood, as it had been previously.

But it may be asked whether it is credible that human beings could have been so foolish as to think that they could raise the height of any building to heaven. Since folly commonly follows pride, and wisdom humility, the tower is here placed as a symbol of pride. Because they attempted, in their folly and pride, to penetrate the heights, they were therefore confused.

Pride produced diversity of languages; the humility of Christ gathered the diversity of languages, so that those whom the tower had separated the Church might gather together. Concerning this dissolution we gave a brief account above, where we spoke of the division among the peoples. There we also mentioned Nimrod, who himself was the author of this tower and first began to rule over all human beings and to extend his kingdom.

Many are accustomed to ask whether the tower and the city were one work or two. Many judge that the tower was the citadel of the city of Babylon. History praises the extraordinary construction of this city: its excessive height was arranged in the form of a square on the plain, from corner to corner, and is said to have occupied sixteen thousand paces, with a circumference of sixty-four thousand [Z., sixty-three thousand], as the historian Herodotus says. Others, however, understand one tower, which they say they were especially attempting to raise among the others. They describe it as four thousand paces in height. Its summit, as the same authority says, narrows from a broad base toward a smaller upper section, so that the overhanging weight could more easily be supported by the broader lower parts. They also describe marble temples, golden statues, stone-paved streets shining with gold, and many other things that seem almost incredible. Hence Scripture says:

**Verse 5.** The Lord descended to see the city and the tower that the sons of men were building. Some say that all the towers of that city are signified by the singular number, just as one says “thousands” and understands “thousands of thousands.” Scripture then adds: “and they ceased building the city.” It follows:

**Verse 7.** “Come, therefore, let us descend and confuse their language there.” God’s “descent” means that he observes human actions or draws near to their understanding. Alternatively, he is said to descend both for assistance and for vengeance, when he gives care to the human race through the ministry of angels.

For the Lord says to the angels who were present, as blessed Gregory says: “Come, let us descend,” and so forth. They ascend insofar as they behold the Creator; they descend insofar as, by the examination of strict judgment, they restrain the creature who unlawfully raises himself there.

“Let us descend and confuse their language” therefore means that God shows them within themselves what ought rightly to be done, and that, through the force of an inward vision, he presents judgments to their minds and inspires them with hidden movements.

When he said in the plural, “Let us descend,” and then in the singular, “the Lord confused the language of the whole earth,” he wished to show, by the distinction of persons, the holy Trinity and, by the unity of its action, the unity of the divine majesty, just as at the beginning of the creation of humanity it was said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” so that the Trinity in persons and unity in the power of divinity might be believed.

**Verse 9.** Therefore its name was called Babel, because there the language of the whole earth was confused, and so forth. If God rested from all his works on the seventh day, how did such great diversity of languages suddenly appear? It should be understood that in this division of languages the Creator did not make something new; rather, he divided modes and forms of speaking among the various kinds of speech. Hence we find the same syllables and letters of the same power joined differently in the languages of different peoples; often, too, the same names or words signify one thing in one language and another in another. Where we say in the psalm, “with an iron rod” (Psalm 2:9), the Greek has *en rhabdo sidera* [ἐν ῥάβδῳ σιδηρᾷ]. Thus *sidera* in Latin does not signify “iron,” as it does in Greek, but “stars.” It should be noted, however, that this language remained only in the family of Eber, from whom the Hebrews were named: in that portion of humankind which remained God’s portion, and in which Christ was to be born. It was fitting that salvation should first be proclaimed to the world in the language through which death first entered the world. The title on the Savior’s cross also shows that this is the first of all languages.

**Verse 10.** These are the generations of Shem: Shem was one hundred years old when he begot Arphaxad, and so forth. Shem is repeated in order to show that Abraham derived his origin from his line, since it is the custom of the Hebrews to name only the firstborn.

**Verses 14–28.** Shelah also begot Eber, and so forth, until it says: “And Haran died before Terah his father in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldeans.” Eber is interpreted as “one who crosses over.” This signified the future Church, which crosses over from unbelief to faith and from vices to virtues.

But it must be asked what is meant by the statement concerning Haran, the brother of Abraham: “And Haran died before Terah his father in Ur of the Chaldeans.” *Ur* means “fire.” Hence in Hebrew it is written, “in Ur of the Chaldeans” (*Ur Chesdim* [F. *casdim*; Z., *cesi*]), that is, “in the fire of the Chaldeans.” The Chaldeans worship fire as a god.

Terah, as the Chaldeans relate [Z., “as the Hebrews also relate”], was sent with his sons by the Chaldeans into the fire because he refused to worship it. Haran was consumed in that fire. This is what is meant by saying that he died before the presence of Terah his father; we shall speak more fully of it below.

**Verse 29.** Abram and Nahor took wives. The name of Abram’s wife was Sarai, and the name of Nahor’s wife was Milcah, the daughter of Haran, the father of Milcah and the father of Iscah. Iscah herself was Sarai.

Finally, Haran, the son of Terah and brother of Abram and Nahor, begot two daughters, Milcah and Sarai, also called Iscah. Nahor took Milcah as his wife, and Abram took Sarai. At that time marriage between uncles and the children of their brothers had not yet been prohibited by law; among the first human beings, marriages had even been contracted between brothers and sisters.

**CHAPTER XII**

**Verse 1.** The Lord said to Abram: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house,” and so forth. It is asked why he commanded him to leave his land, since he had already left the land of his birth, that is, the land of the Chaldeans, with his father.

Unless, as some think, this departure does not concern a bodily departure but a departure of the mind, so that he would not retain the desire to return there after he had already left it bodily. Morally, as his example teaches us, we must leave our land—that is, the possessions of this world, or the earthly person—and our kindred, that is, our manner of life and former habits and vices, which have been joined to us from birth as though by blood relationship.

We must also leave the house of our father, namely every memory of this world, which is called the house of the devil, as in the psalm: “Forget your people and your father’s house” (Psalm 44:14). In this way, renouncing our former condition, we may be enlarged in the land that the same Lord shows us: in the people of God, in the congregation of the faithful, and in the land of the heavenly promise when the time comes for us to be brought into it.

It should be noted that two promises were made to Abraham. One was that he would possess the land of Canaan in his offspring, which is signified where it is said: “Go into the land that I shall show you,” and so forth. The other, far more excellent, was that he would be the father not of one Israelite nation alone but of all the nations that follow the traces of his faith. This is promised in the words: “In you all the nations shall be blessed.” Those who imitate Abraham’s faith shall be blessed in Abraham’s seed.

According to the historical sense, it is shown that many attain blessing through the examples of the saints. Moreover, when it says, “I will make you into a great nation,” it reveals the virtues. A great nation is the number of virtues.

Nevertheless, in a certain writer’s interpretation, the words “Go out from your land” are understood as follows: “Go out from your land,” that is, from the law of nature; “from your kindred,” that is, from the law of the letter; “from your father’s house,” that is, from the law of the New Testament; “into the land that I shall show you,” that is, into heaven, concerning which Isaiah says: “Your eyes shall see the land from afar” (Isaiah 33:17).

It should be observed that Abraham’s instability signifies the instability of that people [Z., “signified it”]. For his nation was to become greater through its instability than when it dwelt in its own land. Likewise, as some think, the Church will possess greater rewards through its journey—from its carnal dwelling and resurrection.

**Verse 4.** Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran. Here an irresolvable difficulty arises. If Terah, Abram’s father, was seventy years old when he begot Abram in the region of Chaldea, and afterward died at the age of two hundred and five in Haran, how is Abram now said to have departed from Haran after Terah’s death at the age of seventy-five, when, from Abram’s birth until his father’s death, the interval is shown to have been one hundred and thirty-five years [Z., “is shown”]?

Unless the Hebrew tradition we mentioned above is true: that Terah departed with his sons from the fire of the Chaldeans, and that Abram, surrounded by the Babylonian fire because he refused to worship it, was rescued by God’s help. Hence the Lord later said to him: “I am the Lord who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans.” From that time his days and the period of his life are reckoned, from the time when he confessed the Lord and despised the idols of the Chaldeans.

It may be that, since Scripture left the matter uncertain, Terah departed from Chaldea a few years before his death and came to Haran; or perhaps he came to Haran immediately after the persecution and remained there for a longer time. If anyone objects to this solution, let him seek another solution; then he will rightly reject what we have said.

**Verses 5–6.** He departed in order to go into the land of Canaan, and so forth. This was done as a figure of Christ, whose type Abram bore: Christ obeyed the Father even unto death.

When it is said, “Abram passed through to the place [Z., grove] of Shechem and to the bright valley,” it shows that Christ, through the patriarchs and prophets, came to the Church, which is *vallis illustris*, “the bright valley”—that is, fertile or outstanding in virtues and established in humility.

Hence it is appropriately added: “The Canaanite was then in the land.” This signifies worldly people and the Gentiles, although it may also be understood of the devil. Canaan is likewise interpreted as “their movement.”

**Verses 7–9.** “I will give this land to your seed,” according to the Psalmist’s words: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations,” and so forth (Psalm 2:8). There he built an altar, signifying the unity of faith in the Church.

He therefore pitched his tent with Bethel to the west and Ai to the east. Bethel is interpreted as “house of God.” It signifies the Jews, who had once been the house of God through knowledge, and who were, as it were, in the east while they were under the Law, that is, until the coming of Christ. But because of their unbelief they fell toward the west by refusing to believe in Christ.

Ai is interpreted as “chaos,” that is, an impassable abyss. It signifies the nations who were held in the abyss and depth of sins until the coming of Christ. Abandoning their error, they believed in Christ [Z., “in God”], who is the true East.

**Verses 10–20.** Abram went down into Egypt. He signifies Christ, who came into this world, according to what is written: “Behold, the Lord shall ascend upon a light cloud and enter Egypt” (Isaiah 19:1), in order to dwell there as a stranger. As he himself says in the Gospel: “Foxes have dens and the birds of heaven nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matthew 8:20).

A famine had become severe in that land, concerning which it is said: “I will send a famine upon you, not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of the Lord” (Amos 8:8).

Then follows the account of how Abram, when he went down into Egypt, said that Sarai his wife was his sister. He did not lie, because she was related to him by blood, as he himself says. Nevertheless, Pharaoh, king of Egypt, wished to take her as his wife; but when he learned by divine warning that she was his wife, he was greatly terrified and returned her unharmed.

Here it must be considered whether it was appropriate for Abram, so holy a man, to conceal that Sarai was his wife, and why he did not place his hope more fully in God, so that the king would not kill him. His action shows that a person ought not to tempt the Lord his God when he has something reasonable to do for the sake of his life. He did what he could for his own life; what he could not do, he entrusted to the one in whom he hoped, and to whom he commended his wife’s chastity.

His faith and hope did not fail him. For Pharaoh, terrified by God and afflicted with many subsequent evils, returned Abram’s wife to her husband with honor when he learned by divine revelation that she was unharmed.

But someone may ask how Sarai could remain undefiled if she had been seized by Pharaoh. The bodies of holy women are not stained by another’s violence, unless the will itself consents; and this can excuse Sarai, since she was living alone with the king in foreign places and could not resist. Yet an ugly necessity can also be excused for another reason. According to the book of Esther, any woman who had pleased the king was, among the ancients, anointed for six months with myrrh oil and for six months with various perfumes and women’s cosmetics, and only then was she brought into the king’s presence.

Thus it may have happened that, after Sarai had pleased the king, while her entrance to him was being prepared for a year and Pharaoh was giving many gifts to Abraham, Pharaoh was struck by the Lord while she still remained untouched by his intercourse.

**CHAPTER XIII**

**Verses 1–3.** Abram therefore went up from Egypt, he and his wife and everything he possessed, and Lot with him, toward the southern region. Abram was very rich in silver and gold. He returned by the route by which he had come, from the south to Bethel.

He is fittingly said to have gone up from Egypt toward the southern region, that is, toward the south; for he is not read to have turned at any point toward the west. But the following statement raises a difficulty: how could he have become very rich after leaving Egypt?

This is resolved by the Hebrew truth, where it is written: “Abram was exceedingly heavy.” He was weighed down by the burden of Egypt. Although this may seem to refer to the riches of livestock, gold, and silver, if they are Egyptian riches they are heavy for the holy man whose type he bore.

Finally, unlike the Septuagint, which reads “from where he had come into the wilderness as far as Bethel,” the Hebrew says: “He went by his route toward the south as far as Bethel.” He therefore departed from Egypt not to enter the wilderness, which he had left together with Egypt, but to come by the south, which is opposite the north, to the house of God, where his tent had been between Bethel and Ai.

In this ascent from Egypt Abram signifies our Lord and Redeemer, who, as we said above, descended into Egypt—that is, into this world—and, having completed the mystery of our redemption, ascended to the Father. Hence it is rightly said of Abram that he returned by the route by which he had come to Bethel from the south, because the only-begotten Son, in his preachers, will return at the end of the age to the Jewish people, according to the words: “When the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel shall be saved” (Romans 11:25).

**Verses 5–12.** Lot, who was with Abram, also had flocks of sheep, herds of cattle, and tents. The land could not contain them while they remained together, because their possessions were so great; and strife arose between the shepherds of Abram’s flocks and the shepherds of Lot’s flocks. Therefore they separated from one another.

Lot, whose name means “one who declines,” signifies the Jews, who declined from God by refusing to believe. Abraham, as we have often described him, signifies the Lord. Lot’s sheep and cattle signify the various peoples and assemblies of the Jews, composed of unbelievers.

Hence it is rightly said: “There was a quarrel between the shepherds of Abram’s flocks and the shepherds of Lot’s flocks.” By Abram’s shepherds the apostles of Christ are signified. By Lot’s shepherds the Sadducees and Pharisees are understood, for they quarreled greatly among themselves. But since “the Canaanite and the Perizzite then dwelt in the land,” they signify the unclean spirits who held power over the Jews. Lot may also signify the heretics, whom the Christian people cannot contain within the land—that is, within the Church.

But the shepherds of Christ and the deceivers of heretics, who claim to be shepherds, continually stir up quarrels and disputes among their sheep in the Church, and therefore they will be separated from one another.

Abram says to Lot: “Depart from me, I beg you. If you go to the left, I will hold to the right; if you choose the right, I will go to the left.” Here the Lord grants his brother—namely, the Jewish people, from whom he deigned to assume flesh—the freedom of choice.

The right signifies faith or the future life, concerning which the Church says: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song of Songs 2:6). The left signifies the present life, which the Jews chose. Hence it is said: “Lot lifted up his eyes and saw the whole region around the Jordan,” and so forth.

Alternatively, he rightly says: “If you go to the left, I will hold to the right,” and so forth, because on the day of judgment many of the Jews will believe in God, and many of those who believe will withdraw. This is what is meant by “I will go to the left.” For then Christ, like Abram, will turn toward the left in those believers who seemed to be his members.

If you wish to refer this to the heretics, then the Scripture’s statement will be fulfilled: “Depart from me, I beg you,” when he shall say to them: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matthew 25:41).

Accordingly it follows: “If you go to the left, I will hold to the right,” and so forth. The right is interpreted as worldly prosperity, which the heretics choose; the left, as unbelief or hell. That Abram chose the right signifies faith or the kingdom of the saints. That he chose the left signifies the breaking of his will, by which, in his members, he accommodates himself to those who love the present life—represented, as we said above, by the left.

Jordan, as some wish, shows in this passage the doctrine of the heretics, from which all things were watered, because in their own eyes their doctrine appears to water everything well. Therefore it is rightly added that they came to Segor. Segor is interpreted as “little.” Those who are deceived by heretics seem to themselves to possess great things, but they are held in smallness and misery and tend toward nothing.

**Verse 13.** The men of Sodom were very wicked and sinners before the Lord. Superfluously—
## COMMENTARY ON GENESIS

### [Scan page 92]

**COMMENT.**  
173

“Added, ‘before the Lord,’ as it is also found in the Septuagint; for the inhabitants of Sodom were evil and sinners among human beings.” He is called a sinner in the sight of God who can appear righteous before human beings, as is said in praise of Zechariah and Elizabeth, that they were both righteous in the sight of God; and in the Psalm it is said: “No living person shall be justified in your sight” (Psalm 142:2).

**Verses 14–17.** — “Then God said to Abram: ‘Raise your eyes and look from the place where you now are, toward the north and toward the south, toward the east and toward the sea, because all the land that you see I shall give to you and to your offspring.’” If only the land that he could then see, standing in one place, toward the four regions of the world, was being promised to him, the land of promise appears narrow. Yet not only that portion of land which he could see was promised. For it was not said, “I shall give you as much land as you see,” but, “I shall give you the land that you see,” since land farther away in every direction was also being given. Therefore he added: “Rise and walk through the land in its breadth and length,” so that by walking he might reach those places which, standing in one spot, he could not see with his eyes.

That land signified the land which his physical offspring would receive. The spiritual offspring, however, was going to possess the breadth of the whole world. When he said “toward the east and toward the sea,” what was meant? Holy Scripture, when speaking of the regions of the promised land, usually places the sea in the west, because the region of Palestine has the western sea. Nevertheless, as some think, Christ with the Church is spiritually said to raise his eyes from the world toward the four parts of the earth, by which the four Gospels are represented; and the whole earth is given to him, as elsewhere: “Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations,” and what follows (Psalm 2:8), “for ever,” that is, in the length of time.

### CHAPTER XIV

**Verses 1–6.** — Next it is related how the kings of the nations struck down the Rephaim in Ashtaroth-karnaim, and also the Zuzim with them, and the rest. “Rephaim” is interpreted as “giants”; “Zuzim” as “terrible and horrifying.” Ashtaroth, a city that is still so called today, signifies that the four kings killed giants and also the strong men of Arabia. Ashtaroth-karnaim signifies a certain land of giants on the heights of Sodom.

**Verse 7.** — “And returning, they came to the spring of Mishpat, which is Kadesh.” The spring of Mishpat is the spring of judgment, that is, Kadesh; it is named in anticipation, since it was called this only later. It signifies the place near the rock that is called the spring of judgment, because there God judged the people. “And they struck the whole region of the Amalekites, and the Amorite who dwelt in Hazazon-tamar.” This is the town that is now called Engedi, rich in balsam and palms, as I have found in the books of *Places*. “Hazazon-tamar” is interpreted as “city of palms.” For *tamar* means “palm.”

It follows:

**Verses 8–13.** — “And the king of Sodom went out, and the king of Gomorrah, and the king of Admah,” and so forth, up to: “Four kings against five.” The Valley of Siddim had many wells of bitumen. Therefore the king of Sodom and the king of Gomorrah turned their backs and fell there, while those who remained fled to the mountains. They carried away all their possessions, as well as Lot and his possessions, and the rest.

It should be noted that the Hebrews say that Bela, which is also Zoar, was the same as the place called Satis elsewhere in Scripture. They interpret it as “a trembling village,” because it was swallowed up by a third movement of the earth; and from the time when Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim were overthrown by divine fire, it was called “the little one,” since *Zoar* is translated as “little one.”

The Valley of Siddim, which is also called the wooded valley, as is written in this same book, where there had formerly been wells of bitumen, was, after God’s anger and the rain of sulfur, changed into the Dead Sea, which the Greeks call the “lake of bitumen.” This is asphalt. It is called the Dead Sea because it receives no kind of living creature; neither birds accustomed to the waters, nor oxen or camels, float there. Indeed, if the Jordan, swollen by rains, carries fish into it, they immediately die and float upon the thick waters.

It is said that a lighted lamp, if thrown upon it, floats without turning, but when its flame is extinguished it sinks; and that a vessel submerged by artifice, although it may be difficult to raise from the depths, will spring back immediately with everything living in it, even if it has been sunk and struck violently. Finally, Vespasian is said to have ordered people who did not know how to swim to be thrown into the depths with their hands bound, and all of them immediately floated to the surface.

The water itself is sterile and bitter, darker than other waters, and as though scorched, displaying the appearance of something burned [Z.: “burnt”]. It is certain that lumps of bitumen wander upon the waters of the black liquid. Those who approach in boats collect them; the bitumen clings, and is said not to be cut by iron at all. It yields only to menstrual blood or urine. It is useful for joining ships together and for treating human bodies.

The region still preserves the appearance of its punishment. For very beautiful apples grow there, producing in those who await them a desire to eat them; but if you pick them, they split open and dissolve into ash, raising smoke as though they were continually burning.

Certainly, during the summer days, an excessive vapor seethes across the stretches of the plain. Hence, through the accumulating evil of excessive dryness and parched soil [Z.: “dry earth”], the corrupted air inflicts pitiable illnesses upon the inhabitants.

Finally, these five kings, allegorically, signify the five bodily senses—sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch—overcome by the four kings who came from Babylon. The four kings are understood as the four principal vices: desire, joy, fear, and sadness. Through these four vices the devil conquered not only the people of Sodom, by whom the Gentiles were signified, but also Lot, whose name is interpreted as “one who turns aside,” by whom the Jews are signified, since they turned aside from the straight path of faith.

The wooded valley signifies the present world; the wells signify people submerged in the depths of vices; the bitumen signifies the gluing together of sins, by which they have been united in iniquity.
