This may also be understood in another way. The four kings who overcame the five can evidently signify vices opposed to virtues: heresy, paganism, hypocrisy, and avarice, which is the service of idols. They are called kings because they exercise a great measure of royal power [Z.: “of a king”].

The five kings who are overcome by them may be understood, as we said, as the five senses, since they too are called kings because our outer person is governed through them. They turn their backs until Abram, the exalted father, after conquering the four kings mentioned above, recovers the spoils and rescues his kinsman Lot—“the one who turns aside,” namely, the one who turns away from evil—from their power.

The fact that the five kings are said to withdraw from the four signifies that the opposing power chiefly persecutes those whom it previously held in slavery. The fact that the exalted Father, to whom we say in the Lord’s Prayer “Our Father,” is present in the number three hundred and eighteen signifies that this occurs through the elect, who are established in the persecution of virtues, founded on faith in the Trinity, possessing the fullness of the Decalogue, and rising with Christ on the eighth day, which follows the Sabbath.*

\* The passage is corrupt in both manuscripts.

**Verse 14.** — When Abram heard that his brother Lot had been captured, he counted the three hundred and eighteen trained servants. “Trained” means young men ready for battle and unmarried, concerning whom he later said, “except those who ate with the young men.” He pursued them as far as Dan. Dan is a town of Phoenicia now called Paneas, where one of the sources of the Jordan rises; it is called Dan, while the other is called Jor. From these two springs, which are not far from one another, joined into a single stream, the river is called Jordan. Just as one river is formed from two springs, so one name is formed from the two names [Z.: “is generated”].

**Verse 18.** — Next it is read how Abram met Melchizedek, king of Salem [Z.: “the king of Salem”].

Some people are accustomed to ask who this Melchizedek, king of Salem, was, whom the Apostle says (Hebrews 7:3) was “without father and without mother.” The Apostle therefore said that he was without father and without mother because Holy Scripture does not recount his genealogy.

Nevertheless, as I found in an ancient volume belonging to someone [Z.: “a certain person”], the Hebrews say that he was not without father and mother; rather, his father and mother are not mentioned by name, since he appears in the narrative only when he met Abram, and neither father nor mother is recorded of him in the divine Scriptures. His father, namely, was Melchi, and his mother Sedech. They say that his father Melchi died before Melchizedek was born. Likewise, his mother Sedech died in childbirth while Melchizedek was still in her womb; and from these two names their son was called Melchizedek. Therefore, as the Hebrews say, he was without father and mother because they had died before he was born.

They also transmit that this man, under another name, was Shem, the son of Noah. By calculating the years of his life, they show that he lived as far as Isaac, and that all the firstborn were priests, offering sacrifices to God and observing the ceremonies of the Law until the time of Aaron. These things, they say, were the birthright that Esau sold to his brother Jacob, and that Melchizedek, by right, received tithes from the victories of his great-grandson.

They further hold that Salem itself was the city later called Jerusalem. At first, they say, it was Jebus; afterward Salem; then Jerusalem. Later, after Solomon had more fully restored it, it was called Jerosolymis, as though “Jerusalem.” Others, however, say that Salem was not Jerusalem but the town of Satofoim [Z.: “Socaphoim”], which is still called Salem, and that Melchizedek’s palace appears to be there. Hence the passage: “Jacob crossed over into Salem, a city of the region of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan.”

From this the evangelist John says: “John was baptizing in Aenon near Salim, because there were many waters there” (John 3:23). It makes no difference whether it is called Salem or Salim, since the Hebrews very rarely use vowels in writing, and according to the will of readers and the diversity of regions they pronounce the same words with different sounds and accents [Z.: “they are pronounced”].

We set forth the opinions of different people, but leave it to the prudent reader to choose which of them is more truthful.

As far as the figure is concerned, however, this Melchizedek signifies Christ, according to the Apostle: Christ is without a mother in heaven and without a father on earth, offering to God for us on earth the bread of his body and the wine of his blood. To him it is said: “You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4). If anyone wishes to know this more fully, let him examine the writings of the blessed Jerome and Isidore.

It follows:

### CHAPTER XV

**Verses 2–4.** — “And Abram said: ‘Lord God, what will you give me? I shall go away without children, and the son of the steward of my house, this Damascus-born Eliezer,’” and the rest.

He did not say, “Lord God, what will you give me?” as though he doubted whether God’s promise would be fulfilled, but he was asking how it would come about. Yet it must be investigated who this Eliezer of Damascus was, concerning whom Abram said, “He will be my heir.”

He was evidently the son of Abraham’s steward, who later, as the Hebrews say, founded Damascus, gave his name to the city, and obtained kingship there. It should nevertheless be noted that where we have “the son of the steward,” some translators have “the son of Masech, my servant.” Aquila has “the son of the one who gives drink to my household.” Theodotion has “the son of the one who is over my house,” that is, the steward, who manages everything and distributes provisions to the household. He is called Damascus Eliezer.

Moreover, Eliezer is interpreted as “my God is a helper.” As we said, he founded Damascus.

It follows:

**Verses 5–6.** — “Receive the sky and count the stars, if you can.” And he said to him: “So shall your offspring be.”

Hence he says later: “Like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the seashore.” By the stars of heaven are understood the fewer, firmer, and brighter people; by the sand of the seashore, the great multitude of the weak and carnal.

**Verse 7.** — “I am the Lord who brought you out from Ur of the Chaldeans.” This is what we said shortly before: in the Hebrew it reads, “who brought you out from Chesdim,” that is, “from the burning of the Chaldeans.”

**Verses 8–9.** — “But he said: ‘Lord God, how can I know that I shall possess it?’” The Lord answered: “Take for me a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old she-goat [Codex: ‘threefold’], and a three-year-old ram; also a turtledove and a pigeon.” He took all these, divided them through the middle, and so forth.

What, then, was to be understood in that mystical sign concerning the posterity of Abraham’s race? Why were animals three years old to be taken? Why did he divide the animals but not the birds?

The animals three years old designate three periods of time in which the people grew to the height of their honor. From the time of the patriarch Abraham, through the promises, the people remained joined to God until the time of Moses. From the time of Moses the lawgiver, through receiving the Law from God, the manifestation of miracles, triumphs, and entry into the promised land, the people were glorified. From the time of David they were exalted through royal honor and the construction of the temple and the city of Jerusalem.

The ram signifies royal and priestly dignity; the heifer, the people serving under the letter of the Law; the she-goat, likewise, signifies that the people are sinful. The birds prefigured spiritual people chosen by God. The divisions of the animals show that schisms always exist among carnal people. The fact that he did not divide the birds signifies the peace and unity of spiritual people.

The terror that fell upon Abram around sunset signifies the terror on the day of judgment, which will separate spiritual people from carnal people, placing some on the right and others on the left. The birds that fly over the carcasses are demonic powers, which seek to perch upon carnal people; a devout teacher must drive them away by diligent admonition.

This method of allegory may also be understood in another way. The heifer signifies the people placed under a yoke; the she-goat signifies the sinful multitude of the nations; the ram signifies the leaders of the peoples. The animals three years old signify three periods, because this division—that is, the separation of the faithful from the unfaithful—took place in the third period.

The turtledove and the pigeon prefigure spiritual heirs from both peoples who will possess the future kingdom [Z.: “the future kingdom of God”]. The birds descending upon the carcasses are unclean spirits, who always seek to settle upon the minds of carnal people; a devout teacher must drive them away by diligent admonition, as we have shown above.

Hence it follows:

**Verses 10–12.** — “And Abram drove them away.”

They wish this to be understood morally. Often intrusive thoughts pollute the hearts of the righteous and touch them with delight in earthly things. But when they are quickly driven away by the holy hand of discernment, they are repelled like birds, lest the darkness of temptation cover the face of the heart, which it had already touched through illicit pleasure.

For often, during the very sacrifice of our prayer, intrusive thoughts force themselves upon us, capable of stealing or defiling what we offer to God while groaning within ourselves. Thus Abram, when he offered sacrifice at sunset, endured the birds settling upon it, but diligently drove them away lest they snatch away the sacrifice that had been offered.

So we, while offering holocausts to God on the altar of the heart, guard them from these unclean birds, lest evil spirits and perverse thoughts seize what our mind might profitably offer to the Lord.

**Verses 13–17.** — “And the Lord said to him: ‘Know beforehand that your offspring will be a sojourner in a land not its own; they will subject them to slavery and afflict them for four hundred years,’” and the rest.

This must not be understood as though the people of God were in that harsh slavery for four hundred years. Rather, because it is written, “In Isaac shall your offspring be called,” the years from the year of Isaac’s birth until the year of the exodus from Egypt are counted as four hundred and five.

When, therefore, you subtract twenty-five years—the period from the promise to the birth of Isaac—from four hundred and thirty, it is not surprising that Scripture wished to call the total of four hundred and five a full four hundred years. Scripture commonly names periods in such a way that whatever slightly exceeds or falls short of the complete number is not counted.

Thus the words “they will reduce them to slavery and harm them” are not to be referred to four hundred years, as though they held them in slavery for that entire period. Rather, the four hundred years refer to what was said: “Your offspring will be a sojourner in a land not its own.” Whether in the land of Canaan or in Egypt, that offspring was a sojourner before receiving the inheritance of the land promised by God. This occurred after they had been freed from Egypt.

A hyperbaton is therefore to be understood here, so that the order of the words is: “Know assuredly that your offspring will be a sojourner in a land not its own for four hundred years.” The intervening words—“they will reduce them to slavery and harm them”—are to be understood as not belonging to the four hundred years.

For it was toward the end of this period, namely after Joseph’s death, that the people of God began to undergo harsh slavery in Egypt.

But why is it said concerning Abraham’s descendants, “In the fourth generation they shall return here,” while in Exodus it is read: “In the fifth generation the children of Israel came up from the land of Egypt”?

Consider the genealogy of Levi. Levi begot Kohath; Kohath begot Amram; Amram begot Aaron; Aaron begot Eleazar; Eleazar begot Phinehas. Kohath entered Egypt with his father Levi. Again, Eleazar departed from Egypt with his father Aaron. From Kohath to Eleazar four generations are counted.

But according to Exodus, the children of Israel departed from the land in the fifth generation. Let the order of Judah be counted. Judah begot Perez; Perez begot Hezron; Hezron begot Aram; Aram begot Amminadab; Amminadab begot Nahshon; Nahshon begot Salmon.

Perez entered Egypt with his father Judah. Nahshon is described as the leader of Judah in the wilderness, and his son Salmon entered the promised land. Count from Perez to Nahshon, and you will find five generations.

### CHAPTER XVI

Next it is related how Abram went in to Hagar, an Egyptian maidservant, and begot a son by her. He called his name Ishmael, concerning whom it is said: “He will be a wild man; his hand will be against everyone,” and the rest.

How is Abram defended from the charge of adultery, since, while his lawful wife was alive, he joined himself to her maidservant? The Gospel law of one wife had not yet been promulgated. He also had a promise from God concerning the multiplication of his offspring [Petr.: *multiplicati*, “having been multiplied”], but he did not yet know from which wife this would occur, since he was later told that he would have a son by Sarah.

For this reason his intention to produce offspring was pious, since his intention to have intercourse was not lustful. Sarah also wished to have from her maidservant the child whom she could not have from herself. Both consented to the act, because both knew that Sarah was barren.

But how is it meant that everyone’s hand would be against Ishmael, or that his hand would be against everyone? The angel of the Lord found Hagar beside a spring of water in the wilderness, at the spring on the road to Shur, which leads through the desert, when she was hurrying to go to Egypt. He called his name Ishmael, because the Lord heard her humility.

Ishmael is interpreted as “hearing of God.” “He will be a wild man; his hand will be over everyone, and everyone’s hand over him, and he will dwell opposite the face of all his brothers.”

This signified that his offspring would dwell in the wilderness, namely the wandering Saracens, with uncertain settlements, who raid all the nations adjoining the desert at their side, and are attacked by everyone. It may also be understood as the fierce and wandering assault of unbelief, in the region of the Jews and heretics, who pitch their tents opposite the Church.

**Verse 13.** — “And Hagar said: ‘Indeed, here I have seen the back of the one who sees me.’” That is, of the angel. Through this is understood the incarnation of the Lord, just as it was said to Moses: “You shall see my back.”

**Verse 14.** — “Therefore she called that well the well of the living and seeing,” and the rest.

This well signifies the grace of baptism, or knowledge of the Scriptures. For all who are reborn to life live through the grace of baptism and see, enlightened by the grace of God. Some manuscripts have “of the one who is living and seeing,” because the more each person drinks in knowledge of the Scriptures by drinking deeply, the more he sees through understanding.

### CHAPTER XVII

**Verses 1–14.** — “And the Lord said to Abram: ‘Behold, my covenant is with you, and you shall be the father of a multitude of nations. Your name shall no longer be called Abram, but your name shall be Abraham, because I have made you the father of many nations.’”

The Hebrews say that God added to his name, which among them is the Tetragrammaton—that is, Jot and He and Vau and He—the letter He to the name of Abram and Sarah. For he was first called Abram, which is interpreted as “father of the exalted one,” and afterward he was called Abraham, “father of many.” The phrase “of nations” is not present but is understood in the name.

Nor is it surprising that, although among the Greeks and some others the letter *a* appears to have been added, we say that a Hebrew letter *he* was added. It is a characteristic of the language to write it with *e* but read it with *a*, just as conversely it writes with *a* and reads with *e*.

**Verse 15.** — “And God said to Abraham: ‘You shall not call your wife Sarai; Sarah shall be her name.’”

There were those who thought that Sarah was first written with one *r*, and that another *r* was later added, because *r* is the number one hundred among the Greeks. Accordingly, she was first called Sarai, written with *sin*, *resh*, and *yod*. When the *yod*, that is, the element *i*, was removed, *he* was added.

With the *yod*, that is, the element *i*, removed, *he* was added, which is read as *a*, and she was called Sarah. The reason for the change of name is that previously she was called “my princess,” the mistress of a single household; afterward she was called simply “princess.”

It should be noted, however, that different people read the word of this name, Sarah, differently. Some say that she was first called Sarai and afterward Sarah, because, as the blessed Jerome makes clear, among the Hebrews it is written with *sin*, *resh*, and *yod*, as we described above, almost without one *r*: it does not have two *resh* letters, but one. For that reason they think it should be read Sarai, and after the change Sarah.

Hence they believe that, if this is so, an ancient custom has remained in the Church: that Sarra was said to have acquired one *r* through the error of scribes; and in authoritative books you will always find it written in this way. Therefore the diligent poet, in his Paschal poem, wrote:

> “Now the wounded bowels of aged Sarah were withering.”

But others insist that Sarai, as you will find it in the very oldest volumes, should not be pronounced merely Sarai; rather, after the addition of the letter *he*, which is read as *a*, they maintain that she was subsequently called Sarah. For, they say, just as one letter was added to Abraham, so another was added to Sarah, as was shown above.

Accordingly, they report that Father Albinus, in the library which he corrected for Prince Charles—and which we ourselves carefully inspected there—took care to emend it so that there was one *r* in Sarah and two *a*’s. It is likewise read in some of our volumes, and we too think it should be read in that way.

Nevertheless, we leave the matter to the judgment of the prudent reader, whichever interpretation may seem preferable, since we would rather yield to another’s opinion than serve contentiousness.

“And he said to Abraham: ‘You shall therefore keep the covenant,’” and the rest, up to: “Every male among you shall be circumcised, and an infant eight days old shall be circumcised.”

Why did Abraham receive circumcision? Abraham’s circumcision was commanded so that he might be under the Law, just as Adam was forbidden to eat from the tree, in order that it might be tested whether he would fulfill the command or not.

Abraham believed that he would have a son through whose generation blessing would come to all nations, and in whose descendants an example of chastity and sobriety would remain. Therefore he received the sign of faith on that part of his body from which the son of faith, not of flesh, was to be born. The bodily part was not mutilated in a dishonoring way; rather, through the sign of faith he became more glorious.

Thus, to lose something for God is gain, not loss. Abraham, receiving the sign of his faith, was not disfigured but improved. If Adam had kept God’s covenant, Abraham would not have received this covenant. But because Adam first acknowledged the guilt of disobedience in this member, it was fitting that Abraham should receive in the same member the sign of obedience, so that it might be shown that the obedient would eventually beget children for life, whereas transgressors once begot children for death.

It should also be known that the religion and rite of circumcision, which took its beginning from the holy patriarch, had many forms and carried types of future realities. It was the sign of faith for Abraham and his offspring; a mark for chastising those who belonged to this offspring and faith, so that they might be cleansed from every pollution of flesh and spirit; and a prophecy of the Savior who would be born from this offspring.

He would cleanse us in the present through baptism from every pollution of deadly action, and in the future, through the resurrection, free us forever from all corruption of death. In particular, it pleased him to administer through this rite the gift of remission that would release the sin of Adam’s transgression, at the same time as the grace and Law were given to their author.

For the one who now says, “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5), was then saying: “The male whose flesh of the foreskin has not been circumcised, that soul shall perish from his people, because he has broken my covenant.”

It was not strictly the covenant of circumcision that the infant invalidated—for an infant, not yet able to discern, could not do so, whereas the elders who knew that it had to be observed could and should have kept it—but the covenant that God made with the first human being. Everyone who has lived even a single day on earth is convicted of having transgressed it, and it is therefore understood that he requires some remedy of salvation.

**Verses 19–20.** — Next it is related how a son is promised to Abraham, concerning whom he is told: “He will be born from you, and kings of peoples will arise from him.”

“Abraham fell on his face and laughed, saying in his heart: ‘Will a son be born to a man who is a hundred years old?’” and the rest, up to: “You shall call his name Isaac.”

It must be asked how it was said to Abraham concerning his son: “Nations and kings of peoples shall arise from him.” This did not come about according to earthly kingdoms, but must be understood according to the Church. Or was Esau also meant, since in the literal sense this was fulfilled in him?

It should be understood that he did not say, “Will a son be born to a man who is a hundred years old?” with a doubting spirit. These words do not show uncertainty and distrust, but the joy of one who marvels. Therefore, because Abraham laughed for joy, his son was called Isaac.

For this laughter should be understood in a good sense, as in the Gospel: “Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh” (Matthew 5:4). Isaac is interpreted as “laughter.” He was not called Isaac because of Sarah’s laughter, as some think, but because of Abraham’s laughter; and we approve this interpretation.

After Abraham laughed and Isaac was named, we later read that Sarah also laughed. This is why, in what follows, the Lord reproved Sarah when she laughed: Abraham too had laughed, but the Lord did not reprove him, because Abraham’s laughter was evidently one of wonder and joy, whereas Sarah’s was one of doubt and distrust. This could be judged by the one who knows the hearts of human beings.

Therefore Sarah, laughing in the same way, is rebuked; and immediately after being rebuked she becomes fruitful. Contrary to hope, she received through the divine promise what, on the basis of human reasoning, she had doubted she would possess.

It should also be noted here that in the Old Testament four people were named by their proper names before they were born: Ishmael, Isaac, Solomon, and Josiah, each for particular reasons. Whenever God either gives a name to a person or changes one, it is an indication of singular merit: that the person will become great.

Thus Abraham was called Abraham because he was going to be the father of many nations. Likewise, Jacob, because he saw God, merited being called Israel. King Josiah was named by God long before he was born because of the height of his outstanding virtue. Understand that the same should be thought concerning the others.

### CHAPTER XVIII

**Verses 1–2.** — “When Abraham had raised his eyes, while sitting in the valley of Mamre, he saw three men.” He spoke to these three as to one. Hence the question arises: since there were three, why does he address the Lord in the singular, saying, “Lord, if I have found favor in your sight, do not pass by your servant”?

Did he understand one of them to be the Lord and the others to be angels, or rather, sensing the Lord in the angels, did he address the Lord? It must therefore be understood that, sensing the Lord in the angels, he chose to speak to the Lord rather than to the angels.

At times God speaks through angels by means of images assumed from the air for a time before bodily eyes, as now with Abraham. He was able not only to see three men but also to receive them into an earthly dwelling and to provide food for their needs.

For unless angels, whenever they announce certain things to us on earth, assumed an aerial body for a time, they would certainly not appear to our external eyes, nor would they eat food with Abraham, unless they carried something solid made from a heavenly element.

Nor is it surprising that those who were received there are called sometimes angels and sometimes the Lord [Z.: “dominions”], because they are expressed by the name of the angels who outwardly mini—
[scan page 97]

## ANGELOMI LUXOVIENSIS

…were ministering; and by the title “Lord” it is shown that he presided inwardly over them, so that through the one [title] the authority of the presiding one, and through the other the office of those ministering, might become clear.

Spiritually, some wish these three men to be understood as our Lord, Moses, and Elijah; others as the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, as is read in what follows: “When Abraham led them on, one remained with him, and two were sent to Sodom.” Hence, by the one who remained [Z. adds: “with him”], they wish the Father to be understood; and by the two who were sent, the Son and the Holy Spirit, who are frequently said to have been sent by the Father.

The heat of the day and Abraham’s journey also signify the desire of the saints who longed for the coming of Christ, like Simeon and many others, of whom the Lord says to the apostles: “Many prophets and kings desired to see what you see,” and so forth (Luke 10:24).

Morally, what is suggested to us by this journey of Abraham except that, as the man and master of the house—that is, our spiritual understanding—he ought, in contemplating the Trinity, to go beyond the barriers of the flesh and, as it were, leave the door of the lower dwelling? But the care of the flesh, like a woman, should not appear outside or blush to be ostentatiously seen; rather, as if behind the man, under the discipline of the spirit, it should attend only to what is necessary, never allowing itself to be exposed shamelessly, but restraining itself modestly.

Yet, when it is often told not to presume upon itself and to transfer all its confidence into the hope of God, it despairs, and when its diligence ceases, it doubts that the supports of life can be present to it. Thus this same Sarah, hearing the promises of God, laughs; but when she laughs she is reproved, and once reproved she is immediately made fruitful. She who could not conceive while vigorous in youth conceived when broken by old age and her womb had withered [Z., “was withering”]. For when the care of the flesh desires to possess confidence in itself, it receives, contrary to hope, from the divine promise what it had doubted it would possess according to human reasoning. Hence Isaac, that is, “laughter,” is appropriately said to be begotten: when the mind conceives the confidence of heavenly hope, what else does it give birth to but joy?

### Verse 10

“Returning, he shall come to you at this time,” and so forth; that is, “I shall return to you at the time of life.” As though he had said, speaking in human fashion: “If I live, if life accompanies me.”

For some physicians report that, when the body of a man has already declined so far that, just as an older woman, although she still experiences menstruation, cannot conceive from a man of advanced age, she can conceive from a young man. Conversely, a woman who is of such advanced age that, although menstruation still flows, she cannot give birth by an older man, can do so by a younger one.

Hence some are also troubled by the question of how, when Abraham was near middle age according to the length of life then customary among human beings, and later had sons by Keturah, the Apostle could say that his body was “dead” (Romans 4:19), and proclaim as a miracle that he had begotten a child. But he called it “dead” in the sense that Abraham could no longer beget a child by a woman of advanced age. For if anyone were to take the Apostle’s words—“his body was dead”—literally, then, since he said “dead,” it would have to be understood that Abraham no longer even had a soul, but was a corpse.

### Verses 10–16

“And the Lord said: The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied, and their sin has become exceedingly grievous. I shall go down and see whether they have completed in deed the cry that has come to me.”

What is the cry of Sodom? Or what does it mean that the Lord said, “I shall go down and see whether they have completed in deed the cry that has come to me”? Sin accompanied by a voice is guilt in action; but sin accompanied also by a cry is guilt committed with freedom and boastfulness.

But when he said, “I shall go down and see,” and similar expressions, why does the almighty Lord, who knows everything, appear to doubt before the investigation, unless it is to set before us an example of seriousness, so that we do not presume to believe men’s evils before testing them?

And behold, he goes down through angels to investigate their evils, and immediately strikes the criminals. He who is patient, he who is mild, he of whom it is written, “But you, Lord, judge with tranquillity” (Wisdom 12:18), and of whom it is written again, “The Lord is patient”—when he finds them entangled in such great crimes, he appears to have set patience aside and does not wish to await the day of the final judgment for vengeance, but anticipates the day of judgment with the fire of judgment.

Behold: he appears to believe the evil only with difficulty when he hears of it, but then strikes without delay when, by investigation, he discovers it to be true. He thereby gives us an example that greater crimes are to be believed slowly when they are reported, but punished more quickly when they are truly recognized.

### Verse 27

“And Abraham said: Since I have once begun to speak to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes,” and so forth, until he says, “I shall not destroy it for the sake of ten.”

Why did Abraham call himself dust and ashes, although he had received such great promises from God? He tempered the sublimity of the promises with the submission of humility. It is plainly understood what position he considered himself to occupy: even while speaking with God, he judged himself to be dust and ashes.

If, therefore, he so despises himself after ascending even to the honor of divine conversation, one must carefully consider with what concern those should be regarded who have not attained to such a height, yet exalt themselves over the smallest matters.

It is usually asked whether what God said concerning Sodom—that he would not destroy the place if ten righteous persons were found there—was a special judgment concerning that city, or whether it should be understood generally, namely, that God spares any place in which even ten righteous persons are found.

We are not compelled to take this as referring to every place. Nevertheless, it could be said of Sodom in this way because God knew that not even ten were there. He therefore answered Abraham in such a manner that it might be signified that not even that number could be found there, to heighten the enormity of their wickedness [Z., “to excuse their wickedness”].

But it should be understood that, insofar as allegory is concerned, fifty signifies penitents; five times forty, those who walk by means of the four Gospels and restrain themselves from evil and do good through the five bodily senses. Twenty signifies those who possess the knowledge and observance of both Testaments. Thirty signifies those who stand in faith in the holy Trinity or in hope of future blessedness. In the number ten are those who humbly submit themselves under the mystery of the holy Cross and are found perfect in the love of God and neighbor, which is contained in the Decalogue.

The text continues:

[scan page 98]

## COMMENT. IN GEN.

…who possess knowledge and observance [of the two Testaments]. Thirty, moreover, designates those who stand in faith in the holy Trinity or in the hope of future blessedness. In the number ten are those who humbly submit themselves under the mystery of the holy Cross and are found perfect in the love of God and neighbor, which is contained in the Decalogue.

## CAPUT XIX

### Verses 1–2

“Two angels came to Sodom in the evening, while Lot was sitting at the gates of the city,” and so forth.

Why did Abraham, in the case of the three men, understand God or angels, and yet Lot again thought of them as men who required human food? Perhaps at first they believed them to be human beings; then, when they understood that God was speaking through them—since certain signs of divine majesty were present and appeared—they recognized afterward that they were angels, when they saw them ascend into heaven.

### Verses 3–7

“He compelled them strongly to turn in to him,” and so forth, until: “They surrounded the house, from boy to old man.”

Here one must consider how great is the virtue of hospitality. The angels are therefore said to have entered Lot’s house as though compelled to be his guests, so that Lot’s charity might be tested, proved, and rewarded, and so that it might be shown how great the goodness of hospitality is.

The angels entered the hospitable house in order to rescue their host. But the fire of judgment also entered the closed house together with the guests, in order to destroy the sinners within it. Guests, therefore, are not to be avoided but invited willingly. The old men ran together with the boys to commit the crime, appropriately, because the proverb says: “A young man, even when he grows old, will not depart from his ways” (Proverbs 22:6).

### Verses 8–9

“I have two daughters who have not yet known a man. I shall bring them out to you, and you may abuse them,” and so forth.

How can Lot be called righteous if he wished to surrender his daughters to so heinous a crime? Perhaps only because he judged the sin being committed against nature to be more wicked, by comparison, than what is committed in accordance with nature.

### Verses 10–18

“They closed the door, and they struck with blindness those who were outside and were trying to find it,” and so forth.

The Greeks have ἀορασία (*aorasia*), which may more accurately be rendered “inability to see”: it causes one not to see, not everything, but what ought not to be seen. By this *aorasia* those also were struck who were seeking Elisha.

Morally, what does it mean that, while the wicked are opposing him, Lot is brought back inside the house and protected, except that every righteous person, while enduring the assaults of the wicked, returns to his mind and remains undaunted?

The men of Sodom cannot find the door in Lot’s house because corrupters of minds discover no means of accusation against the life of the righteous. Struck with blindness, they go around the house, as do those who, driven by envy, scrutinize the deeds and words of others. But because the strong and praiseworthy action of the righteous life confronts them on every side, the wanderers grope at nothing but the wall.

### Verses 19–23

“And Lot said to them: I cannot be saved on the mountain, lest evil seize me and I die. Here is a city nearby to which I can flee; it is small, and I shall be saved in it,” and so forth, until:

“The Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah sulphur and fire from heaven, from the Lord, and he overthrew the whole region.”

It is asked why Lot, although he had been ordered to flee to the mountain, preferred Zoar so that he might be saved there, and then again migrated from Zoar to the mountain.

The Hebrews report that Zoar, having frequently been shaken by earthquakes, was first called Bela and afterward changed its name to Shallisha. Lot was afraid and said: “If, while the other cities were still standing, this one was so often overthrown, how much less will it be able to escape now in the common destruction?” This occasion of unbelief also gave the beginning to the intercourse with his daughters.

For he had seen the other cities destroyed and this one standing, and, having been snatched away by God’s aid [Z., “by stealth”], he ought not to have doubted what he had heard had been granted to him.

If God’s judgment is just, why were infants in Sodom burned together with their parents? So that the monstrous crime of the Sodomites might be recognized. Their sin reached even to the death of their children, lest any sign of their lineage remain. Was it not provided for them that, if they lived for a long time, they would not follow the examples of their parents and would suffer lighter torments in the future—or perhaps none at all—if they were killed in another’s cause?

For parents are guilty both on their own behalf and on behalf of their children. Thus the death of the children is the crime of the parents, and for that reason the children will become their parents’ accusers. It is some kind of benefit not to be guilty, though it is not glorious. It is useful not to be poor, even though one cannot be a king.

Morally, to flee burning Sodom is to avoid the fires of illicit flesh. The height of the mountains is the purity of the continent. Or, certainly, those are as if on a mountain who, although they engage in carnal intercourse, are not dissolved by any pleasure of the flesh beyond the legitimate union intended for the begetting of offspring.

To stand on the mountain is not to seek the fruit of propagation in the flesh; to stand on the mountain is not to cling carnally. But because there are many who abandon the crimes of the flesh and yet, once married, do not preserve solely the rights of legitimate intercourse, Lot indeed went out from Sodom but did not immediately reach the mountains. For a culpable life is abandoned, but the height of conjugal continence is not yet subtly maintained.

In the middle lies the city of Zoar, which saves the fugitive and the weak. For when married couples unite through lack of continence and flee the lapses of crime, they are saved by pardon. They find, as it were, a small city in which they are protected from the fires, because married life is not wondrous in virtues, but it is nevertheless secure from punishments.

Hence that same Lot says to the angel: “Behold, this city is nearby; I can flee to it. It is small, and I shall be saved in it. Is it not little, and shall my soul live in it?” It is called “nearby,” yet it is declared safe for salvation, because married life is neither far removed from the world nor excluded from the joy of salvation.

But married couples preserve their life in this activity as in a small city when they intercede for one another through continual prayers. Hence the angel rightly says to the same Lot: “Behold, I have accepted your prayer also in this matter, so that I will not overthrow the city for which you have spoken.” For—

[scan page 99]

## ANGELOMI

…because through prayer his entreaty is poured out before God, such a marriage is by no means condemned.

Concerning this prayer Paul also gives instruction, saying: “Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (1 Corinthians 7:5).

What is expressed by sulphur except the stench of the flesh, and what by fire except the ardor of carnal desire? When, therefore, the Lord had determined to punish the crimes of the flesh committed by the inhabitants of Sodom and Gomorrah, he marked the stain of the crime in the very character of the punishment. Sulphur has a stench, and fire has heat. Those, therefore, who had burned with perverse desires and the stench of the flesh [Z., “clung to the stench”] deserved to perish by sulphur at the same time, so that through a just punishment they might learn what they had done through unjust desire.

Why, in the days of Noah, is the world’s sin avenged by water, whereas the Sodomites are punished by fire? Because the sin of natural lust with women is condemned by the milder element, as it were; but the sin of lust against nature with men is avenged by the burning of a harsher element. There, the earth, having been washed by water, grows green again; here, having been burned by flames, it dries up in eternal sterility.

It is asked why vengeance from heaven came upon the impious inhabitants of those cities. Because the cry of the sinners is said to have ascended to heaven, they were therefore to be punished from heaven. Why were they punished by sulphurous fire? So that the most foul ardor of lust might be punished by the most foul ardor of flames.

### Verses 26–29

“His wife, looking back behind him, was turned into a pillar of salt.”

Why was Lot’s wife turned into a pillar of salt? For the seasoning of the faithful, because the punishment of the wicked is the instruction of the righteous.

### Verse 30

“Lot went up from Zoar and dwelt on the mountain, and his two daughters with him.” “He was afraid to remain in Zoar,” until: “Therefore Lot’s two daughters conceived by their father.”

By what reasoning can Lot’s daughters be excused from incest when they knowingly sought intercourse with their father, while he appears to have acted unknowingly?

It seems that Lot’s daughters had learned something about the consummation of the world, which was to come by fire, but, like young women who did not fully understand what they had learned, they did not know that, after the cities of Sodom had been destroyed by fire, a considerable span of the world still remained.

They supposed that something like what they had heard concerning the times of Noah had happened, and that, for the restoration of the mortal race, they alone had been preserved with their father. They therefore conceived a desire to restore the human race and thought that the beginning of the renewal of the age had to be made from themselves.

Although it seemed to them a grave sin to steal intercourse with their father, it nevertheless seemed a graver impiety to destroy, by preserving chastity, the hope of human posterity as they understood it.

For this reason they form the plan—in my judgment with the lesser guilt [Z. adds: “and with the greater justification”]—of softening and loosening their father’s grief or severity with wine. On successive nights they enter, and each receives conception from the man who is unaware. They do not repeat the act afterward [Z., “nor repeat it afterward”], nor do they seek it again.

Where is the guilt of lust? Where is the crime of incest proved? In what way can something that is not repeated in deed be attributed to vice?

If Lot is to be blamed as incestuous for this act, should he not also be blamed for this act to the extent that the ignorance produced by drunkenness deserves? For the eternal law also condemns this, which commands that food and drink be taken only for the health of the body.

Here one must consider more carefully how great an evil drunkenness is, and how greatly those should fear it for whom this evil is a habit rather than a crime. Drunkenness deceived the man whom Sodom did not deceive. He is burned by the flames of women whom the sulphurous flame did not burn. Lot was therefore deceived by circumstance, not by intention.

For this reason he stands midway between sinners and the righteous: he had descended from Abraham’s kindred, yet he had lived in Sodom. Indeed, his escape from Sodom, as Scripture indicates, pertains more to Abraham’s honor than to Lot’s merit.

“Lot therefore fled from Sodom,” and so forth.

We take Lot to have represented the Law, and his wife that people which, having departed from Egypt and been freed from the persecution of Pharaoh and, as it were, from the fires of Sodom, again desired the flesh, the pots of Egypt, onions, cucumbers, and melons; it looked back and perished in the wilderness, becoming even a memorial of desire.

There, therefore, the Law first destroyed that people, like Lot’s wife looking back, and left its wife behind. From there Lot came and dwelt in Zoar, of which he says: “This city is small, and I shall save my soul in it.”

Accordingly, insofar as the Law is concerned, the city is called both small and not small. For a city is named from the conduct of many, because it contains the lives of many within one place. Those, therefore, who live according to the letter of the Law have a small way of life. Nothing great is involved in observing Sabbaths and new moons, circumcision of the flesh, and distinctions among foods in a carnal manner; but to those who understand spiritually, it is not small but great.

Then Lot went up into the mountain and dwelt in a cave, he and his two daughters. The Law too should be understood to have gone up, because it acquired adornment through the Temple constructed at Jerusalem, when the house of God was indeed made a house of prayer; but evil inhabitants made it a den of thieves.

The prophet clearly describes Lot’s two daughters, saying that Oholah and Oholibah were two sisters, and that Oholah was Judah while Oholibah was Samaria (Ezekiel 23:4).

These daughters make their father drunk and induce sleep in him [Z., “and induce sleep in their father”], that is, they cover and overwhelm his spiritual sense. They draw from him only an understanding of the flesh, and from it they conceive and beget such sons as their father neither perceives nor acknowledges.

Such offspring also shall not enter the Church of God. “The Ammonite and the Moabite,” he says, “shall not enter the assembly of the Lord, even to the third and fourth generation and forever” (Deuteronomy 23:3). This signifies that the carnal generation of the Law shall not enter the Church of Christ [Z., “of God”], neither through the third generation, through the Trinity, nor through the fourth, through the Gospel, nor forever.

[scan page 100]

## COMMENT. IN GEN.

Morally, Lot signifies the rational sense and the manly spirit of those who strive to seize the citadel of contemplation; but his wife, who looks back, signifies the flesh devoted to desire. The two daughters signify the two principal vices, namely, pride and vain glory.

It should be observed that, when someone has escaped the fire of the world and avoided the conflagrations of the flesh, even after he has passed beyond Zoar, that is, the active life, which is civil, and has ascended to the height of knowledge and contemplation as though to a mountain, his two daughters—pride and vain glory—may lie in ambush for him. They are called daughters for this reason: they do not arise from outside us but lie in ambush in the cave of the heart, so that, while we sleep and are unaware, they may be able to beget in us offspring, namely, evil thoughts and actions.

There are some who seize the citadel of contemplation; but when they take these two daughters as wives, they are in a certain sense made drunk by them. Their minds are so alienated from God that, whatever children they beget—that is, whatever works they perform—do not bring them into the Church of the Lord, just as the Moabites and Ammonites do not enter it, neither through the third nor through the fourth generation. For neither knowledge of the Trinity nor understanding of the preaching of the Gospel will benefit them.

The text continues:

## CAPUT XX

### Verse 1

“Abraham departed from there into the southern land, dwelt between Kadesh and Shur, and sojourned in Gerar.”

Kadesh is a wilderness where there is a spring of judgment. Kadesh-barnea is in the desert, joined to the city of Petra in Arabia, where Miriam died and where Moses, after striking the rock, gave water to the thirsty people. As blessed Jerome says, her tomb, the tomb of Miriam, Aaron’s sister, is still shown there to the present day.

The princes of Amalek and Chedorlaomer were also killed there. Kadesh is interpreted as “holy” or “sanctifying,” and it was called the spring of judgment by anticipation, as we described above, because that place was afterward so named where Moses judged the people of the Lord.

Shur likewise has the same meaning. Gerar, or Gerara, as I have found it elsewhere, is so called from the name of a region beyond Daroma—for it was once the southern boundary of the Canaanites—and is a metropolitan city of Palestine. Scripture here testifies that it lay between Kadesh and Shur, that is, between two deserts: one of which joins Egypt, toward which the people came after crossing the Red Sea, while the other extends from Kadesh as far as the wilderness of the Saracens. There Abraham sojourned.

### Verses 2–11

“He said of Sarah his wife: ‘She is my sister.’ Therefore Abimelech, king of Gerar, sent and took her,” and so forth, until he says: “What have you done to us? In what have I sinned against you, that you have brought upon me and upon my kingdom a great sin?”

Why does God say to Abimelech, “I spared you, so that you should not sin against me”? So that it might be recognized that sin is committed against God when people do things which they suppose are to be regarded lightly as sins of the flesh.

Why did Abimelech not die at once when God said to him, “Behold, you shall die”? Certainly, God foretold what would without doubt have happened had Abimelech not guarded against sin by abstaining from it in response to this warning.

### Verses 12–15

Why did Abraham say a second time that Sarah was his sister? Because, after the earlier rebuke by Pharaoh, he was certain of God’s protection—that it could not be violated—yet uncertain of his own life, whether he would escape their hands. And it is remarkable that Sarah was the daughter of Haran, as Scripture testifies.

Therefore he said that she was his sister, either because Sarah was born from the seed of his father through his son, and Scripture also has the custom of calling cousins brothers and likewise sisters. Hence he appropriately said: “She is my sister.” Since Abraham and Haran had one father but not one mother, he added: “She is the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother.”

### Verses 16 and following

“Sarah said to Abimelech: ‘Behold, I have given a thousand pieces of silver to your brother; this shall be for you as a covering for the eyes of all who are with you,’” and so forth.

She rightly says, “This shall be for you as a covering for the eyes,” that is, for modesty or for the confusion of the face, “for all who are with you.” For there could be great shame in such a woman’s having been taken away from her husband.

And wherever you go, remember that you were exposed—understand, by me—and taken away from your brother.

So much for the historical sense. Spiritually, however, Abimelech, whose name is interpreted “my father is king,” signifies the wise men of this world, or an earthly kingdom, who, through human wisdom, insofar as it was granted to them, recognized God the Father as king of the whole creation.

Sarah signifies the Church. For Abraham is the only-begotten Son of the Father, who deigned to become a brother through grace.

The number one thousand signifies the perfection [Z., “persecution”] of the faith of the wise. Silver signifies knowledge of the Scriptures, through which they recognized that Sarah was Abraham’s wife, that is, that the Church was joined to the Lord through faith.

He says: “Behold, I have given a thousand pieces of silver to your brother,” who is the Son of God by nature and whose sister you are by grace. He appropriately said, “your brother,” because the wise have given the perfection of their faith, as though a thousand pieces of silver, to the Lord through knowledge of the holy Scriptures.

“For a covering,” he says, “for your eyes,” that is, for protection through the holy teachers. “Those who have come over from me to you,” as though he had said plainly: They have passed over from human wisdom to faith in you. They are, even to this day, a protection for the holy Church of God, especially those who have emerged from human wisdom and exalted learning.

“Remember that you were exposed,” because she remembers that the Church was formerly persecuted but remained unharmed.

Concerning Abimelech, king of the Philistines, we may also understand morally that he wished to take Sarah as his wife. How, then, did Abraham say that she was his sister, and why did God restrain Abimelech on her account?

I think, therefore, that Sarah, whose name is interpreted as “princess,” signifies strength of spirit. This virtue is joined to the wise man. Indeed, the Lord says: “Whatever she says to you, hear her voice in all that she counsels you.”

Abraham does not wish the virtue to be called his wife until—we should read [Z., “while” or “for”]—virtue cannot be shared with others and therefore cannot be called a wife. But when we have come to perfection, so that we are fit to teach others also, let us no longer enclose virtue and wife within our bosom; rather, let us join her as a sister to others who desire her. Hence it is written: “Say that wisdom is your sister” (Proverbs 7:4).

Accordingly, Abraham said that Sarah was his sister. Pharaoh once wished to possess Sarah, but not with a pure heart. Virtue, however, cannot accord with anything except purity of heart.

This Abimelech acts very differently from Pharaoh. It seems to me, therefore, that this Abimelech represents the diligent and wise men of the world who, although devoting themselves to philosophy and not attaining the complete and perfect rule of piety, nevertheless perceived God as the king of all.

Insofar as moral philosophy is concerned, they are shown to have devoted themselves even to the purification of the heart; but God did not permit them to touch this virtue. For this grace was being prepared to be handed over to the Gentiles, not through Abraham but through Christ.

God heals Abimelech, his wife, and his female slaves. We think these represent natural philosophy with its diverse and varied theories of the schools.

Meanwhile, Abraham desires to impart the gift [Z., “house”] of divine virtue to the Gentiles. But it is not yet time for the grace of God to pass from the former people to the Gentiles.

According to this allegory, Pharaoh, whose name is interpreted as “destroyer,” could not take Sarah, that is, virtue. Virtue therefore remains with Abraham, remaining in circumcision, until the time comes when, in Christ Jesus, perfect virtue passes over to the Church of the Gentiles.

Then the house of Abimelech and his female slaves give birth to sons for the Church. For this is the time when the barren woman gives birth, while Abraham—that is, the people—prays through the patriarchs and the prophets who prophesy.

Hence it is said there also: “Restore the wife to her husband, because he is a prophet, and he will pray for you, and you shall live.” Later he adds: “But when Abraham prayed, God healed Abimelech,” and so forth.

Abimelech wanted to receive Sarah as his wife. Why did Abraham say that she was his sister, and why did God restrain Abimelech on her account?

Then the house of Abimelech and his female slaves give birth to sons for the Church. For this is the time when the barren woman gives birth, while Abraham—that is, the people—prays through the patriarchs and prophets who prophesy.
