## CAPUT XX

### Verse 8

“Abraham made a great feast on the day when his son was weaned.”

Why did he make a great feast on the day Isaac was weaned, and not on the day of his birth or circumcision? Unless this is referred to some spiritual meaning, there is no solution to the question.

The exalted Father therefore made a feast when Isaac was taken from the breast, and there was great joy, because the supreme teacher rejoices over those who no longer need milk but spiritual food, whose senses have been trained through the capacity to receive it, and who possess discernment between good and evil. Of these Isaiah says: “He who is weaned from milk shall put his hand into the hole of the asp and into the den of the basilisk” (Isaiah 11:9).

But no feast of joy can be held over those of whom the Apostle says: “I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Corinthians 3:2).

Historically, however, it seems necessary to inquire after how many years children are usually weaned. Among the Hebrews there is disagreement: some assert that weaning is completed in the fifth year, others in the twelfth. Among us, however, this does not seem to be observed in the same way; a child is weaned in the third or fourth year, and sometimes in the fifth.

The text continues:

### Verses 9–13

“When Sarah saw the son of the Egyptian woman Hagar playing with Isaac, she said to Abraham: ‘Cast out this slave woman and her son,’” and so forth, until: “For in Isaac shall your offspring be called. But I shall also make the son of the slave woman into a great nation.”

This can be understood in two ways: either that the Jewish people would be numerous and rule in this world, or that those among them who believed in Christ would attain the glory of the heavenly kingdom.

It is worth noting what kind of play Sarah censures in Ishmael, the son of Hagar. The Hebrews express this in two ways. Either he committed idolatry, according to what is written elsewhere: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exodus 32:6); or he claimed the rights of the firstborn against Isaac, as though he were older, making a game of it.

Sarah could not tolerate this when she heard it. This is also demonstrated by her own statement: “Cast out this slave woman with her son,” and so forth.

### Verses 14–20

“Abraham rose early, took bread and a skin of water, placed it on her shoulder,” and so forth.

If Ishmael was thirteen years old when Isaac was born, and the years of weaning are added to his age, how can it be appropriate for a young man of such age to have sat upon his mother’s shoulders when it is said: “Abraham took bread and a skin of water, gave them to Hagar, placing them upon her shoulder, and the child, and sent her away”?

According to the idiom of the Hebrew language, every son is called an infant and a little child in comparison with his parents. The meaning is therefore this: Abraham placed the bread and the skin upon Hagar’s shoulder, and, having done this, gave the boy to his mother—that is, entrusted him to her hand, commended him to her, and so sent him out from the house.

This is made clear in what follows, where it is said: “Arise, take the child, and hold his hand”—not so that she might lift him from the ground as though he were lying there, but so that she might hold him by the hand as a companion. The fact that he is held by a parent’s hand shows the affection of concern.

What does it mean that the mother is said to have wept, while God is said to have heard the boy’s voice? The mother was lamenting not her own death but that of her son, and God spared the child for whom his mother’s weeping had been uttered.

How had Abraham planted a field by the Well of the Oath, if, in that land, as Stephen says, he had not received an inheritance, not even the space of a foot? One must understand this as the inheritance that God was going to give by his own gratuitous gift, not the land that was purchased for a price. It is understood—
## Angelomus of Luxeuil, Monk: Commentary on Genesis

### 194

The space around the well, however, is understood to belong to that purchase agreement in which the seven ewe-lambs had been given, when Abimelech and Abraham also swore an oath to one another.

Through Abimelech—that is, the kingdom or wisdom of this world—is understood that the depth of the holy Scriptures, or the grace of baptism, signified by the well, belongs especially to Abraham, that is, to the Lord Jesus Christ.

Therefore that place was called Beersheba because both swore there. There are two reasons why it was so called: either because Abimelech received the seven ewe-lambs from Abraham’s hand—for seven is called *sabee*—or because they swore there, since an oath is likewise called *sabee*. If we read the name above before this explanation, we should understand it to have been stated by anticipation, just as Bethel and Gilgal, which were called otherwise before the time when they received those names.

### Verse 21

“And he dwelt in the wilderness of Paran.”

Paran is now a town [Z., “Faron, a town,” etc.] joined to the Saracens across Arabia, who wander about in the desert. The children of Israel passed through this region when they moved their camp from Mount Sinai. It is across Arabia, as we have said, toward the southern plain, and lies from that place toward the east on a three-day journey. Ishmael is said to have dwelt there; hence the Ishmaelites who are now called Saracens.

### Verses 22–24

“At that time Abimelech and Phicol, the commander of his army, said to Abraham: ‘God is with you in all that you do. Therefore swear to me by God that you will not harm me, my descendants, or my stock, but according to the mercy that I have shown you, you shall act toward me and toward the land in which you have dwelt as a stranger.’”

Through Abimelech, the kingdom or wise men of this world are understood; through Phicol, the philosophers of this age [are understood]. Hence Abimelech is rightly interpreted as “my father is king,” while Phicol means “the mouth of all,” because of rational understanding, which is called logic and confesses God the Father of all, as Abimelech does; and because of moral understanding, which is called ethics and is in everyone’s mouth and concerns everyone. Since it expresses the similarity of common precepts, it circulates in everyone’s mouth, as this Phicol signifies.

These men come to Abraham because the kingdom, or the wise men and philosophers of this age, came to Christ through human understanding, recognizing through signs and miracles that God was with him in everything he did. Hence the statement: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5:19).

He says: “Therefore swear by God that you will not harm me,” because I have remained for so long in ignorance and unbelief; and my descendants, who will remain in human wisdom, and my stock, which meditates upon this understanding. “But according to the mercy that I have shown you,” that is, to your body, which is the Church, “you shall act toward me and toward the land in which you have dwelt as a stranger,” as it is written: “Foxes have dens and the birds of the air nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Luke 9:58).

“And Abraham said: ‘I will swear.’” This corresponds to: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Matthew 16:16).

“And Abraham reproved Abimelech because of the well of water, which his servants had seized by force,” because they had compelled many believers to turn aside to idols.

“And Abimelech answered: ‘I did not know who had done this thing. But you also did not tell me.’” Understand: neither through the Law nor through the Prophets.

“Then Abraham took sheep,” namely, the simple, “and oxen,” namely, teachers, “and gave them to Abimelech,” that is, to the followers of this world. “And the two of them made a covenant.”

“And Abraham set seven ewe-lambs of the flock apart,” and the rest.

The seven ewe-lambs signify the apostles, filled with the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. They are called ewe-lambs because they give birth to the members of Christ, whom they bring forth, although they were called by other names.

It should be noted, both from the earlier passages and from the present one, that Isaac was not born at the oak of Mamre but at Gerar, where Beersheba is still a town today. Not long ago this province was called Palaestina Salutaris, following the division of the Palestinian provinces [Peter, *Palestina*]. Scripture bears witness to this, saying: “And Abraham dwelt in the land of the Philistines.” “But Abraham planted a grove in Beersheba,” and the rest.

A grove consists of shady and fruitless trees. Such trees have broad and pleasant leaves, and they signify those whom the Lord chose from the Gentiles. They were instructed in the liberal arts and therefore seemed, as it were, great and expansive, yet they lacked the fruit of spiritual understanding. Abraham—that is, the Lord and our Redeemer—planted them in Beersheba, that is, inserted them into sacred Scripture, and through their eloquence adorned its surface with verbal richness [Z., “eloquence”].

## Chapter 22

### Verse 1

“God tested Abraham and said to him,” and the rest, until: “He called the name of that place: The Lord will see.”

It is commonly asked how it can be true that Abraham is said to have been tested by God, when James says: “God tests no one” (James 1:13). The answer is that, in the language of Scripture, *to test* is often used for *to prove*. The testing of which James speaks is understood as the testing by which each sinner is entangled. Hence the Apostle says: “Lest perhaps he who tests you should have tempted you” (1 Thessalonians 3:5).

Elsewhere also it is written: “The Lord tests you, to know whether you love him” (Deuteronomy 13:3). Here too the expression “to know” is used as though it said “to make you known,” because the strength of a person’s love is hidden from him unless it becomes known to him through experience.

Abraham, therefore, was tested so that he might be proved, justified, and crowned, and so that his obedience, tested by such an examination, might become known to later generations.

### Verse 2

When it says, “upon one of the mountains that I shall show you,” the Hebrews say that this was the mountain on which the Temple was later built, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, as it is also written in Chronicles: “And they began to build the Temple on Mount Moriah” (2 Chronicles 3:1).

### Verse 3

The name Moria is interpreted as “illuminating” or “shining,” because there is the *debir*, that is, the oracle of God.

### Verse 4

“On the third day,” and so forth.

It should be noted that from Gerar to Mount Moriah, that is, to the Temple precinct [Petr., “seat”], is a three-day journey, and consequently he is said to have arrived there on the third day. Some are therefore mistaken in thinking that Abraham was at that time dwelling at the oak of Mamre, since from there to Mount Moriah is scarcely a full day’s journey.

It is also asked why, in Abraham’s testing, God says: “Take your son, whom you love, Isaac.” Was it not so that, by the reminder of his love and the recollection of his name, the burden of the test might be increased, and the father’s affection might be tortured by remembering the promise, when God had previously said to him: “In Isaac shall your offspring be called”? It was as though, if he were killed, the whole hope of the promise would be frustrated.

And why did he not command him to kill his son immediately, but order him to take him with him for three days before offering him? It was so that the duration of the test might increase its severity. The journey was extended over three days, and throughout the entire period the father’s inward anguish increased. During all that long interval the father would look upon his son, take food with him, and watch the boy through the nights as he rested in his father’s arms, clung to his breast, and slept in his lap, so that at every moment the pain of killing his son would grow within the father’s affection.

### Verses 5–14

If Abraham was thinking with unwavering and firm resolve of slaughtering the boy as a burnt offering to the Lord, why did he say to his servants: “You wait here; I and the boy, when we have worshipped, will return to you”?

He therefore believed with an unwavering mind that he would kill him. In this there is a twofold cause for praise: both in the constancy with which he offered him and in his confidence in the resurrection [Petr., *in fiedere*] of the one to be raised. He knew with complete certainty that God could not lie, and that, even if the boy were killed, God’s promise would nevertheless remain secure.

Thus the apostle Paul had learned through the Holy Spirit what Abraham had held within himself. Praising his faith, he said: “By faith Abraham did not hesitate when he offered his only son, he who had received the promises, and from whom God was able to raise him even from the dead” (Romans 4:20).

From where did this ram come, which was sacrificed in place of Isaac? It is often asked whether it was suddenly created there from the earth or brought from elsewhere by an angel. This ram should not be considered imaginary but believed to have been real. Therefore the teachers judge it more likely that the angel brought it from elsewhere than that the Lord created it there after the six days of creation.

Why did Abraham call the name of that place “The Lord sees”? There is nowhere that the Lord does not see. “He saw” is used for “he appeared”; that is, he caused himself to be seen, just as in the statement: “Now I know that you fear God,” meaning, “I have caused it to be known.” This is a form of speech in which the effect is signified through the agent who produces it, as when we call cold “sluggish,” because it makes people sluggish.

But concerning the statement, “Therefore it is said to this day: On the mountain the Lord will see”—if people are ever found in distress and desire to be relieved by divine help, they say: “On the mountain the Lord will see,” that is, just as he had mercy on Abraham, so he will have mercy on us. For this reason people still customarily blow a horn as a sign of the ram that was given [Petr., singular: “blows”].

### Verses 16–19

“But the angel of the Lord called Abraham a second time from heaven, saying: ‘Because you have done this thing and have not spared your only son for my sake…’”

Did Abraham not spare his son because of the angel and not because of God? Either the name “angel” signifies Christ, who is undoubtedly God and is explicitly called by the prophet “the Angel of Great Counsel,” or the angel spoke in God and from God’s person, as often happens in the Prophets.

This seems even clearer in what follows, where we read: “And the angel of the Lord called Abraham again from heaven: ‘By myself I have sworn, says the Lord.’”

Why, after the second call to Abraham, were the same promises made again, with additions? It signifies that Abraham would have a twofold offspring: one carnal and the other spiritual. Therefore the Lord said to him: “So shall your offspring be as the stars of heaven and as the sand of the sea.” By the stars of heaven he intended spiritual offspring, and by the sand, carnal offspring.

When he said above, “By myself I have sworn, says the Lord,” he spoke in human fashion. Human beings swear by those greater than themselves; God has no one greater than himself, and therefore he swears by himself. But God’s swearing means that he confirms his promises with firmness.

Furthermore, when he said, “Your offspring shall possess the gates of their enemies,” this is understood spiritually. He said: “Your offspring shall possess”—that is, Christ, or all the faithful in the Church, whose father you will be through faith—“the gates of their enemies,” that is, the regions of the underworld, which were destroyed when the Lord died.

Alternatively, “he shall possess the gates” means sins, through which one goes to death. For he truly possesses the gates of his enemies who is not subjected to any suggestions of unclean spirits.

If anyone wishes to learn—or [Z., “learn additionally”]—this temptation more fully in its spiritual sense, let him take care to read the book of the aforementioned man, as we have often said. What follows is this.

### Verse 20

“After these things Abraham was told that Milcah also had borne sons to Nahor, his brother,” and the rest.

Why are the sons of Nahor, Abraham’s brother, named? Because something notable is later said to have happened either to them or to their descendants.

Thus of Cush, from whose stock Job descended, it is written at the beginning of his book: “There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job.” Some are therefore mistaken in thinking that Job was descended from Esau.

The second son born to Milcah was Buz, from whose race was Balaam, that diviner whom the Hebrews identify with Elihu in the Book of Job. At first he was a holy man and prophet of God; afterward, through disobedience and the desire for gain, he was blinded when he wished to curse Israel. He is called by a divine name, and it is said in the same book: “Then the wrath of Elihu, son of Barachel the Buzite,” that is, one descended from the root of this Buz, was kindled.

Kemuel was also the father of Damascus, for that city itself is called Aram and is mentioned under this name in Isaiah as belonging to Syria [Z., *Aroer*].

The fourth was Chesed, from whom the Chaldeans are called *Chasdim*. Bethuel was the father of Rebekah and Laban, the father of Leah and Rachel.

## Chapter 23

### Verse 1

“And Sarah lived one hundred and twenty-seven years and died in the city of Arba, which is Hebron; it is also Mamre.”

It is asked why one city is called by three names. Hebron is its proper and ancient name, and it was once founded by giants. Some, however, think that it should be read *Chebron*, with a *c* and an aspiration, like *cherubim*, rather than with a simple *c*. Read the interpretations of the Hebrew names by the blessed Jerome, and you will find that they are written with the Greek *chi*.

This city lies in a broad plain, twenty-two thousand paces distant from Aelia, that is, Jerusalem.

Arba—or, as it is read corruptly in some manuscripts, Arboc or Arbee—takes its name from the number four, because four patriarchs were buried there: Adam, the great father of the human race, as is shown more clearly in the Book of Joshua; Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Accordingly, as a certain person of our own time who came from Jerusalem reported, according to Bede, a modern teacher, the double cave that Abraham purchased lies one stadium eastward in a valley. The burials of the aforesaid patriarchs are enclosed by a square wall. Their heads face north, and each tomb is covered by a single stone, hewn in the manner of a basilica. The tombs of the three patriarchs are white, while Adam’s is darker and of poorer workmanship; Adam lies some distance from them, at the northernmost end of that wall.

The tombs of three women, smaller and of poorer construction, are also visible. Mamre is a hill, a thousand paces north of these monuments, very grassy and covered with flowers. It has a level plain on its summit, and on its northern side stands the trunk of Abraham’s oak, about two men’s heights, surrounded by a wall.

The city of Mamre received its name from one of Abraham’s allies. This, then, is the reason why the place is called by three names.

Then the text explains how Abraham purchased the double cave from Ephron the Hittite for four hundred shekels of silver, tested and accepted currency, and how Sarah was buried there.

Among the Hebrews the first form of Ephron’s name is written *Efron*, and the second *Efran*, after he was overcome by the price and agreed—although Abraham pressed him—to sell the tomb. The letter *vav*, which among them is read as *au* [read: *o*], was removed from his name, and he was called *Efran*. Scripture thus indicates that he was not a man of complete and perfect virtue, since he was able to sell the burial place of the dead.

Let those who sell tombs know, therefore—those who are not compelled to accept payment but extort it even from unwilling people—that they must change their name and understand how their merit is perishing, since even Ephron is secretly reproved by this fact: he accepted the payment unwillingly.

It should be known that the double cave can signify the active life and the contemplative life. Abraham represented the teachers. The four hundred silver shekels indicate the knowledge of the divine utterances, namely, of the Scriptures of both Testaments. For it is written: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested in the fire” (Psalm 12:6).

Thus one hundred, taken four times, can signify the fullness of the two lives, which is acquired and brought to completion through knowledge of the divine utterances [Z., “of the divine utterance”].

The silver is not inappropriately said to be tested and accepted currency. On public coinage the image and name of the king are found, and this signifies the Decalogue of the Law, in which both the knowledge of God and the name of the divine majesty are found.

Abraham therefore buried Sarah in the double tomb, because the soul that dies to the world so that it may live for God is received into the twofold life: the life of good works and the contemplation of divinity.

Let us speak more plainly, not inserting our own words, but making public the statements of the blessed Pope Gregory. That outstanding preacher says:

“What is signified to us by Abraham’s double tomb except that every perfect preacher hides his soul, dead to the desires of the present life, beneath the protection of good works and contemplation? Thus, withdrawn from carnal desire through the active and contemplative life, he lies hidden as though insensible, though previously he lived mortally by experiencing the desires of the world.

“Therefore the outstanding preacher says: ‘For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God’ (Colossians 3:3).

“The active life is a tomb because it covers those dead to evil works. But the contemplative life buries more perfectly, because it wholly separates a person from all the actions of the world.

“Whoever has already subdued the insults of the flesh within himself must still exercise his mind through the disciplines of holy activity. Whoever has already enlarged his mind through holy works must still extend it to the innermost secrets of contemplation.

“For a preacher is not perfect if, because of his devotion to contemplation, he neglects what must be done, or if, because of his insistence upon activity, he postpones what must be contemplated.”

## Chapter 24

### Verse 1

“Abraham was old, advanced in days.”

As Solomon says: “Gray hair is the understanding of human beings, and a spotless life is the age of old age” (Wisdom 4:9). And: “Rise before a gray head.”

### Verse 2 and following

“And he said to the older servant of his household, who was in charge of all that he had: ‘Place your hand under my thigh, that I may make you swear by the God of heaven and earth,’” and the rest.

What does “the God of heaven” have to do with Abraham’s thigh, except that a mystery is being indicated? By the thigh, offspring is understood. Therefore what was the meaning of that oath except that it signified that Christ would come in the flesh from Abraham’s line?

The Hebrews say that he swore by its sanctification, that is, by circumcision. But it is better understood that he swore by the offspring of Abraham, that is, by Christ, because the Lord himself, the God of heaven, was to come in the flesh, which is symbolized by the thigh.

### [Continuation]

How is Abraham’s servant not blameworthy in his request, despite the fault of augury? It is one thing to ask for something extraordinary, when the miracle itself signifies something; it is another to observe human errors through superstitious vanity in omens, auguries, and divinations. Such practices are covenants of demonic familiarity and are committed only with grave sin.

The former kind of request is therefore a confirmation and reckoning of faith directed toward God; the latter is an alliance of unbelief with the devil.

When Rebekah was departing and they said to her, “Our sister, may you increase to thousands upon thousands, and may your offspring possess the gates of their enemies,” were they prophets because they said what was to happen in the future? They were not prophets, nor did they make so great a wish merely out of vanity. But the [supplied: “blessing”] that God had promised Abraham could not remain hidden from them.

Then follows the account of how Isaac had gone out to meditate in the field. What was Isaac’s exercise, by which he is said to have exercised himself in the field toward evening? This exercise signifies prayer, in accordance with the passage in which the Lord prayed on the mountain. Isaac too was a type of the Lord.

What is the land of the South where Isaac lived when he returned with Rebekah, together with his father’s servant? The land of the South signifies Gerar, from which he had been brought by his father for sacrifice.

What is the *theristrum* with which Rebekah covered herself? The *theristrum* is the name even now given to a kind of Arab garment by which the women of that province veil themselves.

Spiritually, Abraham signifies God the Father—not as though God grows old, but because the prophecy concerning Christ and the Church had, as it were, already grown old through the passage of ages.

Isaac signifies the Lord Christ; the servant signifies prophetic or apostolic speech. Of him it is also said: “He was in charge of all the good things of your lord.” The apostles, who were rulers over the whole Church of God, were endowed with every virtue.

The camels signify those who believed from circumcision and who became teachers and helpers of the apostles. They are rightly said to number ten because of the Decalogue of the Law, although some wish to understand by the camels the preachers chosen from the Gentiles.

Alternatively, the camels signify the movements of the flesh, as Paul says: “I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind,” and so forth (Romans 7:23).

Or the old servant also bore the image of the Law, through which the bride of Christ, the Church, was betrothed. Rebekah herself signified this Church. Concerning her he is told: “You shall not take her from the daughters of the Canaanites.” The Canaanites are interpreted as “their movement,” that is, the hearts of the unstable. Hence the Psalmist says: “Do not let my feet be moved” (Psalm 121:3).

The passage continues: “But if she is unwilling to follow you, you will not be bound by the oath.” This is what the Lord says: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matthew 10:23).

[Something is missing here in both manuscripts.]

This woman was found in the evening—that is, in the sixth age—beside the spring, that is, the spring of baptism. She was found by the apostles. She placed the jar upon her arm, that is, she laid down her elevated eloquence and inclined herself toward humility; she received the ornaments of faith. She received golden earrings, namely, the meanings of Scripture, and the clear eloquence of silver. She followed the servant, that is, the holy preachers.

This is what we have briefly tasted in a running exposition. But we have endeavored to insert a fuller explanation by the blessed Pope Gregory, so that it may shine more clearly for readers.

Abraham says: “Place your hand under my thigh,” and the rest. What does it mean that Abraham commands the servant to place his hand under his thigh and swear by the God of heaven, except that the flesh of the one who was both Abraham’s son according to humanity and Lord according to divinity was to descend through that member?

Thus the boy is told: “Place your hand under my thigh and swear by the God of heaven,” as though he were plainly told: “Touch my son and swear by my Lord.” He is commanded to place his hand not upon the thigh but under the thigh, because from that thigh he was to descend who would be human, yet would come above all human beings.

Therefore it was not fitting for him to place his hand upon the thigh, because no flesh is above that flesh which the Only-Begotten of the Father united to himself for our redemption.

What does it mean that Isaac is forbidden to take a wife from the daughters of Canaan, except that no reprobate souls are joined to him of whom it is written: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17)?

The servant is commanded to bring a wife for the son from his kindred, because only the holy Church of the elect was to be joined to the Only-Begotten Son. Through predestination and foreknowledge, the Only-Begotten himself would not regard her as a stranger.

Who is the boy who is sent to bring back the wife, except the order of the prophets and apostles, together with all teachers? Whenever they bring the word of preaching to good minds in order to unite each soul to the Only-Begotten Son, they become, as it were, his stewards.

As he went, he carried with him all the good things of his master, because in the things they say about the Lord they display within themselves the riches of virtues. Thus they draw their hearers more quickly to follow God, since they show within themselves what they proclaim.

The same servant stood beside the spring and, according to the predetermined sign, proposed which girl should be chosen. The holy preachers consider the streams of sacred eloquence and, from them, select to whom or among whom they should entrust the words of their preaching; from those hearers they derive confidence in the certainty of their message.

He asked for a drink because every preacher thirsts for the soul of his hearer. But Rebekah offered him a drink because the holy Church of the elect satisfied the desire of her preachers through the faith of her virtue. Since she confessed the God whom she had heard, she offered her preacher the water of refreshment and cooled his spirit.

It should be noted that she placed the jar from her shoulder upon her arms, because that confession is pleasing which proceeds from good works. Or she offered water because she did not remain empty in what she believed. Immediately she strove to preach what she had heard, and by teaching she produced many preachers from herself.

Water in the jar is knowledge of preaching in due measure, because the holy Church studies not to know more than one ought to know, but to know with sobriety. The jar of water in her hands is the doctrine of preaching expressed in action. It offers drink not only to her companions but also to the camels, because it preaches the word of life not only to the wise but also to the foolish, in accordance with Paul’s words: “I am a debtor to the wise and to the foolish” (Romans 1:14).

Alternatively, water is given even to the beasts when it is determined how the care of the flesh should be maintained: it must not be indulged for the sake of pleasure, yet it must not be denied in necessities. Thus it is written: “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires” (Romans 13:14). Whoever forbids provision for the flesh in its desires plainly allows it in necessity, in accordance with the further statement: “No one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it” (Ephesians 5:29).

The servant gave Rebekah earrings and bracelets because every preacher adorns the hearing of the holy Church through obedience and her hands through the merit of good works.

The earrings weigh two shekels, while the bracelets weigh ten, because the first virtue of obedience consists in charity. Charity is distinguished in two commandments, namely, that God and one’s neighbor are to be loved. Right action is completed through the Decalogue, so that when good works have begun, no evil is thereafter committed.

Rebekah said that there was a spacious place in her father’s house for him to stay, because the holy Church showed that it knew the law of nature from the former people and received the preacher’s words in the broad bosom of charity.

For a teacher, a spacious place to dwell is the breadth of goodness in the heart of the hearer. Hence it is said to certain people: “Make room for us: we have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one; you are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections” (2 Corinthians 7:2).

It is as though he openly said to them: “Make a spacious place in your mind for receiving doctrine, but remain narrow when it comes to thinking about carnal things.”

That the house had abundant straw and hay was indicated because the holy Church, hearing the words of life, returned earthly support to the preachers. Paul, accepting such support as though it were nothing, said: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things?” (1 Corinthians 9:11).

Rebekah had a brother, Laban, who hurried out, looked at his sister’s earrings and bracelets, and summoned the servant inside. There are carnal people who are joined to the faithful. When they behold spiritual gifts, they are suspended in wonder and, even if not all the way to works, nevertheless admit the word of preaching into their souls so that they may receive the faith.

When they see good people shining with miracles, they do not reject what they hear about eternity, although they do not follow the holy Church of the elect in their conduct and remain in a carnal way of life.

Laban offered straw, hay, water, and bread. But the servant refused to accept them until he had first secured the matter of the marriage. There are many who are ready to support their teachers with temporal stipends, but the holy preachers refuse to receive temporal things unless they first obtain eternal ones.

If they do not find action in the hands of their hearers, they disdain to accept bodily support. Nor do they wash their feet with water, because they lift no one’s labor of desire through any consolation.

As soon as the servant had secured the matter of his master’s marriage, he brought out vessels of gold and silver and garments, which he gave to Rebekah. The teachers of the holy Church offer their people as many ornaments as they have taught them gifts of virtue.

She who had earlier received earrings and bracelets now receives vessels of gold and silver and garments. The holy Church, having first received faith, obedience, and works, later grows stronger in spiritual gifts. Filled with the spirit of prophecy and the grace of virtues, it learns through enlarged gifts.

The servant also gave gifts to her mother and brother. The Gentiles, from the time when the Church came to faith, grew in temporal glory after her conversion, just as we now see: Christians everywhere experience affliction, while various Gentiles glory in earthly power.

Her brothers too received gifts, because those who verbally hold the faith but do not follow their profession in their conduct and live carnally are customarily honored kindly by the faithful because they appear to be believers.

The mother and brothers received gifts, but they remained excluded from the share of the inheritance. Whether unbelievers or carnal people who remain within the profession of faith, they do not obtain a share in the eternal inheritance, although they do enjoy the glory of heavenly generosity temporarily.

Rebekah followed the man with her maidservants, because the holy Church has with it souls of lesser merit as companions. Even if some do not dwell in the chamber of contemplation through an ascent of the mind—such souls are like Rebekah’s maidservants, since they follow her conduct—they nevertheless do not ascend to the chamber of contemplation.

The same servant also had certain people in his company, because among the holy prophets there were some who lived well but did not possess the spirit of prophecy, and among the blessed apostles and teachers there were many who maintained a good life but did not produce words of preaching.

The servant hastened back to his lord because, when the holy preachers obtain the life of their hearers through preaching, they immediately give thanks to the one by whose gift they have received this success. They attribute nothing to themselves in that work, but everything to its Author.

At that time Isaac was walking along the road that leads to the well whose name is “Living and Seeing.” Who is the Living and Seeing One except almighty God, of whom it is written: “I live forever, says the Lord”? Of him it is again written: “All things are naked and open to his eyes” (Hebrews 4:13).

The well of the Living One is the depth of sacred Scripture, which he provided for our irrigation.

# ANGELOMUS, MONK OF LUXEUIL

## Commentary on Genesis

The almighty God granted [this]. What, then, is the [uncertain text: “way”] that leads to the well of the Living and Seeing One, except the humility of the Only-Begotten’s Passion, through which the depth of this well—that is, of the sacred Scriptures—was opened to us? For previously the streams of sacred Scripture spoke obscurely, but after the Passion of the Only-Begotten they have been opened to us.

What, then, did humility become for the faithful through his Passion, except the key of opening by which we have found the mystery of God’s drink, so that we might draw from the deep the water of knowledge? We recognize his Incarnation, Passion, death, resurrection, and ascension—events which, because we know them to have occurred, we now understand as things heard. Previously they could be read, but because he had not yet come, they could not be understood. Hence John says:

“He has conquered, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, to open the book and break its seals” (Rev. 5:5).

He opened the book and broke its seals who, by being born, dying, rising again, and ascending into heaven, disclosed to us the secrets of sacred Scripture.

It should be noted that Scripture does not say, “He was walking along the road that leads to the well,” but “he was walking back and forth” (*deambulabat*). Someone walks back and forth when, by going and returning, he repeatedly treads the road on which he walks. The Lord walked back and forth in the humility of his Passion, because he endured, repeatedly, now the insults of words from the Jews, now false testimony against himself, now slaps, now spitting, now a crown of thorns, and now the cross. To walk back and forth in the humility of the Passion, therefore, is to endure so many adversities and insults by undergoing them again and again in different ways.

What follows says that Isaac, when Rebecca came, lived in the southern land, because the Only-Begotten Lord and our Redeemer, when the Church came to him, dwelt in the minds of those born from the Jews who were held not by the coldness of sluggishness but by the fervor of charity. From that people came the prophetess Anna; from it came Simeon, who received the Lord into his arms.

He had gone out to meditate in the field. The field is understood as the world, as the Lord himself explains:

“The field is the world” (Matt. 13:38).

This is expressed in the fact that he deigned to appear visibly, as it is written:

“You went forth for the salvation of your people, to save your anointed ones” (Hab. 3:13).

Young men accustomed to warfare usually train themselves in arms. Isaac, therefore, went out to meditate in the field because the Redeemer, giving those who follow him the form of humility, displayed in himself examples of endurance and patience through the exercise of his Passion. Meditation on arms is the continual experience of sufferings. For he who endured blows from hands, the lance, and the cross allowed his Passion to be repeatedly enacted in himself even unto death.

We call sufferings weapons because through them we are freed from the hidden adversary, as the Lord himself says:

“By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke 21:19).

He went out to meditate in the field when the day was already declining, because he undertook the exercises of his Passion near the end of the world, as he speaks of the Crucified One through the Psalmist in figurative expression: “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Ps. 140:2).

When Rebecca saw Isaac, she descended from the camel, because the holier the Church recognizes her Redeemer, the more humbly she abandons the pursuits of bodily life and resists within herself the force of vice. Rebecca therefore descended when she saw Isaac, because, when the Gentile world recognized the Lord, it abandoned its vices and sought the lowliness of humility instead of the height of pride.

What does it mean that Isaac, seated upon the camel, saw Rebecca, except that the Church, coming from the Gentiles to her Redeemer, approached him while still relying upon vices and not yet attached to spiritual things but to animal impulses?

Nor should it trouble us that a servant also came with the camels, carrying his master’s riches. For even the holy preachers, although they already shine in understanding and proclaiming higher things through intellect and life, nevertheless still feel within themselves the opposition of the flesh. They see another law in their members resisting the law of their mind and taking them captive under the law of sin. They carry riches upon camels, because, lest the greatness of revelations exalt them, a goad of the flesh is given to them. They have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the excellence of the power may belong to God and not to them. Those, therefore, who speak heavenly things through the flesh and yet still feel within the flesh the contradiction caused by vice—what else are they doing than carrying riches upon the crooked backs of camels?

When Rebecca saw Isaac, she learned by asking the servant who that man was, because every day the holy Church understands through the words of the prophets and apostles what it ought to believe about its Redeemer.

She immediately covered herself with a cloak, because the more subtly she penetrates the mysteries of her Savior, the more deeply she is ashamed of her former life and blushes at having acted perversely. She took care to cover herself with a cloak because, when she saw the Lord, she was ashamed of the weakness of her conduct; and she who had previously been carried freely upon the camel, after descending, was then covered by modesty.

Therefore the Church, converted from its former pride, is addressed through the apostolic voice—as Rebecca descending from the camel and covering herself with a cloak:

“For what fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6:21).

Isaac brought her into his mother’s tent and took her as his wife, because the Lord loves the holy Church in the place of the Synagogue, from which he was born according to the flesh, and unites her to himself in love and contemplation. She who had previously been close through kinship—that is, known through predestination—afterward becomes united to him as a wife in continual love.

He loved her so greatly that he softened the grief caused by his mother’s death. For through the gain of the holy Church our Redeemer removed the sadness that could have arisen from the loss of the Synagogue: once Rebecca is joined to him, the grief over his mother’s death is taken away. For when the holy Church, coming from the Gentiles, is led to the chamber of contemplation, Judea is regarded as nothing.

We also wish to interpret the names themselves. Isaac is called “laughter,” while Rebecca is called “patience.” Laughter arises from joy, but patience from tribulation. Although the holy Church is already suspended in the contemplation of heavenly joy, it still bears and endures something sad [Petr.: “sadness”] from the burden of mortal flesh.

Isaac and Rebecca, then, are joined—that is, laughter and patience are mingled [Z.: “are mingled”]—because in the holy Church what is written is fulfilled:

“Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Rom. 12:12),

so that prosperity from contemplation may gladden her, while adversity from tribulation may still disturb her.

## Chapter XXV

### Verses 1–5

Next follows the account of how Abraham, after Sarah’s death, took another woman, namely Keturah, as his wife. Why did Abraham, after the promise made to him and the birth of Isaac—in whom God had promised him the multiplication of his offspring and the blessing of the nations—wish to take another wife?

It was not because of lack of continence, since he was already advanced in age. Rather, just as Hagar and Ishmael signify the carnal adherents of the Old Testament, so Keturah and her children signify heretics who consider themselves to belong to the New Testament. Yet both groups are called concubines. For Scripture says:

### Verse 6

“But to the sons of the concubines Abraham gave gifts.”

Only Sarah is always called his wife.

Who is this Keturah, and from what family did she come? Keturah is interpreted as “joined” or “life.” For this reason the Hebrews suspect that she was the same woman as Hagar, who, after Sarah’s death, passed from being a concubine into being a wife.

This view also seems to excuse Abraham’s already advanced age, so that an old man would not be accused of indulging in new marriages after his wife’s death. It is also reported that the sons born to Abraham from Keturah occupied Arabia as far as the shores of the Red Sea.

It is said that one of Abraham’s descendants, named Aser, led an army against Libya, settled there after defeating its inhabitants, and caused his descendants to call Africa by the name of their ancestor. It is also believed that other descendants of Abraham by Keturah occupied the regions of India [Z.: “they believe”].

### Verses 8–25

From this point follows the account of how Abraham, failing, died. How is it appropriate to say of Abraham, so holy a man, that he died “failing”? In the Hebrew text *deficiens*—“failing”—is not found; it was added by the translators of the Septuagint.

What does it mean that he is said to have been “full of days”? It means that he died full of the works of light and of the day.

What does Scripture mean when it says of the sons of Ishmael:

“They dwelt from Havilah to Shur, which is opposite Egypt”?

Havilah is the region around which the Pishon flows from paradise. It is named after a certain Havilah, a grandson of Noah, and is a wilderness opposite Egypt. Shur too is a wilderness between Kadesh and Bered, extending through the desert as far as the Red Sea and the borders of Egypt.

What does it mean that Ishmael fathered twelve princes? They either became rulers of regions or gave their names to tribes. This refers to the individual sons of Ishmael, whose firstborn was Nebaioth, after whom the entire region from the Euphrates to the Red Sea has been called Nabataea down to the present day; it is part of Arabia. Their families, towns, villages, fortified settlements, and tribes are likewise known by these names.

Among these are Kedar in the wilderness of Idumea, Tema to the south, and Kedemah toward the east.

What does it mean when it is said of Ishmael:

“He died in the presence of all his brothers”?

Does this mean that he was counted among his brothers? That is, he died in the hands of all his sons, with all his children surviving and none having been taken by death before him.

“Brothers” is used for “sons” also in Jacob’s words to Laban:

“Let it be placed before our brothers, so that they may judge between us.”

For we do not read that Jacob had any other brothers there except his children.

It is asked where Rebecca went to inquire of the Lord when the children in her womb collided. Perhaps she went to the place where Abraham had established an altar in order to pray; or perhaps even at that time there were certain men of God whom God could be asked through.

Should the Lord’s response to Rebecca be understood historically or allegorically?

“Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples will be divided from your body; one people will overcome the other, and the elder will serve the younger.”

In both ways. Spiritually, it is usually understood that Esau represents the elder people of God, namely Israel according to the flesh. Jacob represents Christ, propagated in the Christian people according to spiritual descent.

Yet this response is also found to have been fulfilled in its historical sense, when the people of Israel—that is, Jacob, the younger son—overcame the Idumeans, the nation descended from Esau, and made them tributary under David. Later, however, they rebelled and cast the Israelite yoke from their neck.

But we must ask what is meant by the earlier statement:

“Isaac entreated the Lord for his wife, because she was barren,” and so forth.

The things that holy men accomplish through prayer are so predestined that they are obtained through prayers. For even the predestination of the eternal kingdom has been arranged by the almighty God in such a way that the elect reach it through the labor of prayer [Petr.: omits “of prayer”], so that by asking they may merit to receive what the almighty God disposed before the ages to give them.

[Scan page 109]

This can readily be proved by a concise argument. Certainly we know that the Lord said to Abraham:

“In Isaac shall your offspring be called.”

He had also said to him:

“I have appointed you the father of many nations.”

Again he promised him:

“I will bless you, and I will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the shore of the sea.”

From this it is clearly established that the almighty God had predestined Abraham’s offspring to be multiplied through Isaac. Yet it is written:

“Isaac entreated the Lord for his wife, because she was barren,”

and the Lord heard him and granted Rebecca conception.

If, then, the multiplication of Abraham’s offspring through Isaac had been predestined, why did he take a barren wife? It is plainly evident that predestination is fulfilled through prayers, since the one in whom God had predestined Abraham’s offspring to be multiplied obtained through prayer the ability to have children.

### Verses 27–28

“Esau became a man skilled in hunting and a farmer; but Jacob was a simple man and lived in tents.”

Or, as another translation says, “he lived at home.”

What is signified by Esau’s hunting except the life of those who, spread out among external pleasures, follow the flesh? He is also described as a farmer because lovers of this world inhabit external things all the more as they leave their inner selves uncultivated.

Jacob, however, is said to be simple and to live in tents or at home. For all who refuse to scatter themselves among external cares remain simple in knowledge and dwell within their own conscience. To live in tents or at home is to confine oneself within the secrets of the mind and not dissipate oneself outwardly through desires, lest, while they gape after many things outside, they withdraw from themselves and become alienated through their thoughts.

### Verses 31–33

Finally, the account follows of how Esau sold his birthright to his brother Jacob for a dish of lentils.

What was the birthright that Esau sold to his brother Jacob? The Hebrews report that all firstborn sons performed the office of priests before Aaron was chosen for the priesthood, and that they possessed priestly garments in which they offered victims. These, they say, were the garments of Esau with which Rebecca clothed her son Jacob; their fragrance delighted the father and initiated the blessing.

This is the birthright that Esau lost because of the vice of gluttony. We should know, however, that the vice of gluttony attacks us in five ways.

Sometimes it anticipates the time of need. Sometimes it does not anticipate the time, but seeks more luxurious foods. Sometimes, although any food may be eaten, it demands that it be prepared more carefully. Sometimes it agrees with the quality and timing of the food but exceeds the proper measure of refreshment in the quantity consumed. At other times the thing desired is more contemptible, yet the person sins more seriously because of the very heat of his excessive desire.

We can display these occasions of vice more clearly if we support them with more evident examples. Jonathan incurred the sentence of death from his father’s mouth because, in tasting honey, he anticipated the appointed time for eating. The people led out of Egypt perished in the wilderness because, despising manna, they asked for meat, which they considered more luxurious.

The first fault of Eli’s sons arose because, at their behest, the priest’s servant wished to receive from the sacrifice not meat cooked in the ancient manner but raw meat, which he could prepare more carefully.

And when Scripture says to Jerusalem:

“This was the iniquity of Sodom, your sister: pride, fullness of bread, and abundance of ease” (Ezek. 16:49),

it plainly shows that she lost salvation because, with the vice of pride, she exceeded the proper measure of moderate refreshment.

Thus Esau lost the glory of the firstborn because he eagerly desired a food that seemed highly desirable—lentils—and, when he preferred them even to his birthright, showed how fiercely he burned with that appetite.

It is not the food but the appetite that is at fault. Hence we often eat more luxurious foods without guilt, while we taste more contemptible foods without an innocent conscience. Esau, whom we have mentioned, lost his primacy over lentils, while Elijah preserved the strength of his body in the wilderness by eating meat.

Therefore the ancient enemy, knowing that the cause of condemnation is not food but desire for food, subjected the first human being to himself not through meat but through an apple, and tempted the second not through meat but through bread. Thus Adam’s sin is often repeated even when what is consumed is poor and mean.

For it was not Adam alone who received the command of prohibition, that he might restrain himself from the forbidden apple.

## Chapter XXVI

Here the history is inserted [Petr.: “Here too the history is inserted”]. If the will of a righteous man is good, why did Isaac bless Jacob, whom he did not wish to bless, rather than Esau, whom he did wish to bless?

The will of a righteous man is good insofar as conscience is concerned; insofar as foreknowledge is concerned, however, it is free from error, for God alone judges future things. Accordingly, Isaac, being righteous and considering what was appropriate according to present human knowledge, thought that the elder son ought rather to be blessed by him.

But God, who knows hidden things, showed that the younger deserved the blessing, so that the blessing might be shown not to belong to human beings but to God. Hence it is said in Numbers to Moses and Aaron, the priests:

“Put my name upon the children of Israel: I, the Lord, will bless them” (Num. 6:27).

It is the priest’s role to bless; it is God’s role to grant the effect of the blessing. Thus Isaac understood through the prophetic spirit that the blessing had been predestined by God for the younger son.

He said:

“I have blessed him, and he shall be blessed.”

Spiritually, Isaac signifies the Jewish people, which, with eyes dimmed and prophesying in the present, did not recognize the Son, although it foresaw many things about him in the future. For the Jewish people, full of the spirit of prophecy yet blind, did not recognize in the present the one about whom it had foretold many future things.

To the accumulation of its condemnation, they despise him when born, though long beforehand they knew that he would be born, and also where he would be born. When questioned by Herod, they gave the place of his birth, namely Bethlehem, so that their knowledge itself would become for them testimony to their condemnation and for us assistance in believing.

## Commentary on Genesis

### Verses 12–16

“Isaac sowed in that land and found a hundredfold in that same year.”

Although he sowed seed in a foreign land, I do not think that the fertility of the crops was so great. I therefore consider preferable what is found in the Hebrew text and what Aquila also translated:

“And he found in that year a hundredfold reckoned.”

Since Scripture does not state what kind of crop had multiplied a hundredfold, it seems to me that it was showing the multiplication of all virtues in him.

The text continues:

“And the Lord blessed him, and the man became great, and he advanced, becoming greater, until he became exceedingly great.”

I do not know whether the fertility and multiplication of barley could make anyone glorious. Yet in certain manuscripts one finds:

“After this he sowed barley, and found a hundredfold.”

The fact that he sowed barley rather than wheat, and yet was blessed through it and became great, shows that he was not yet great; but after he had sown and gathered a hundredfold, he then became exceedingly great.

Barley is chiefly the food of animals and servants. Isaac, therefore, signifies the word of God. This word sows barley in the Law and wheat in the Gospels. The latter food is prepared for the more perfect and spiritual, while the former is prepared for the less instructed and the animal-like, because it is written:

“You will save both human beings and animals, Lord” (Ps. 35:7).

Yet in that very barley he found a hundredfold fruit. For you find in the Law martyrs, whose fruit is a hundredfold.

He sowed barley by expounding the Law and revealed that the Law is spiritual. Then he sowed wheat, namely the preaching of the Gospel. Hence first he satisfied five thousand people with five loaves, and afterward four thousand with seven loaves.

### Verses 17–22

Next he came to the valley of Gerar and lived there. In the Hebrew text, instead of “valley,” there is “torrent.” Isaac could not have lived in a valley. He lived beside a torrent after he had become great. Of this it is written:

“He shall drink from the torrent on the way” (Ps. 109:7).

Elijah also drank from it. But because Elijah was not perfect as Christ was, that torrent dried up. Our Lord, however, was also handed over at a torrent, dedicating our regeneration and the sacrament of baptism.

### Verses 23–29

After certain intervening matters, the history continues: he went up from that place to Beersheba, where the Lord appeared to him that same night, and so forth, until the passage says:

“When Abimelech, Ochozath his friend, and Phicol, the commander of the army, had come to that place,” and so forth.

And he said:

“I am the God of Abraham your father.”

As though he were saying: “Since I am the God of your father, I shall be merciful to you as I was to them.”

Spiritually, Isaac—that is, our Lord—extended his tent, namely the Church. He commanded his servants, that is, the apostles, to dig a well, namely apostolic teaching, with their own hands, that is, through their own writings.

What the different wells of Isaac, which his servants dug, signify is already frequently explained in the book of the aforementioned writer, if anyone wishes to know. The text continues:

### Verses 26–29

“When Abimelech, Ochozath his friend, and Phicol, the commander of the army, had come to that place, Isaac spoke to them,” and so forth.

It should be understood that this Abimelech, whom we previously said signifies philosophers and all learned men who, through philosophical education, grasped many things even from the truth, did not always have peace with Isaac. Sometimes he disagrees; sometimes he seeks peace. Philosophers neither always agree with the word of God nor are they always opposed to it.

Many philosophers write that there is one God who created all things. Some have even added that he made all things through his Word and that the Word of God governs all things. In this they agree with the Law and the Gospel.

They disagree with us when they say that matter is coeternal with God; when they deny that God cares for mortal things but confine his providence to the space above the lunar sphere; when they make the births of human beings depend upon the courses of the stars; and when they say that this world is eternal and will never be brought to an end.

There are other matters in which they disagree and agree. Therefore, according to this figure, Abimelech is sometimes described as being at peace with Isaac and sometimes as disagreeing with him.

It is not without purpose that two others are written to have come with Abimelech: Ochozath, his son-in-law, and Phicol, the commander of the army.

Ochozath is interpreted as “holding,” and Phicol as “the mouth of all.” Abimelech means “my father is king.” These three, as we showed much earlier, represent the whole of philosophy, which among them is divided into three parts: logic, physics, and ethics—that is, rational, natural, and moral philosophy.

The rational part is that which confesses God the Father of all things, as Abimelech does. The natural part is fixed upon and holds all things, relying upon the powers of nature; this is represented by Ochozath, whose name means “holding.” The moral part is in everyone’s mouth, pertains to everyone, and circulates in everyone’s speech because of the similarity of its common precepts; this is represented by Phicol, whose name means “the mouth of all.”

All these, instructed in such disciplines, come to the Law and say:

“We have seen that the Lord is with you, and therefore we said: Let there be an oath between us,” and so forth, until:

“We have sent you away in peace, increased by the blessing of the Lord.”

These three, who seek peace from the word of God and desire to reach an agreement and fellowship with it, may also represent the three Magi who came from the eastern regions, instructed by the books of their fathers and by the teaching of their ancestors. They said:

“We have seen the king who has been born, and we have seen that God is with him, and we have come to worship him.”

Someone of this kind, approaching the Law of God, necessarily says:

“I have sworn and determined to keep the judgments of your justice” (Ps. 118:106).

But when they ask, “Do not do us any harm,” and so forth, they seem thereby to seek the remission of sins and that they may not receive evils; they ask for a blessing, not a recompense.
