### Verse 30

“And he made them a feast.”

For it is certain that one who ministers the Word is a debtor to the wise and to the foolish.

## Chapter XXVII

### Verse 42

Rebecca said to Jacob:

“I have heard that your brother Esau is threatening to kill you.”

It is asked how Esau’s words were reported to Rebecca—those with which he threatened to kill his brother—when Scripture says that he spoke them in his own thought.

Unless the meaning is that we are being taught here that everything was divinely revealed to her [Z.: “to them”].

## Chapter XXVIII

### Verses 11–19, passim

From this point follows the account of how Jacob, sleeping on his journey, placed a stone beneath his head, fell asleep, and saw a ladder reaching from earth to heaven. He also saw the Lord leaning upon the ladder, and angels ascending and descending.

To sleep on a journey is, amid the passage of the present life, to rest from love of temporal things and to close the eyes of the mind against desire for visible things.

To behold ascending and descending angels is to contemplate the citizens of the heavenly homeland: either how lovingly they cling to their Creator above themselves, or with how much compassion of charity they descend to our weaknesses.

It should be noted very carefully that this man, while sleeping, sees angels and places his head upon a stone. For the one who ceases from external works and penetrates inwardly observes with attentive mind what is the principal thing in a human being: imitation of his Redeemer.

To place one’s head upon a stone is to cling in mind to Christ.

What does Jacob mean when he says:

“How terrible is this place! This is nothing other than the house of God and the gate of heaven”?

These words pertain to prophecy: it was destined to happen that in the promised land the true God would be feared and worshiped, that a tabernacle would be made for him, and that he—who is forever the blessed God of all things—would walk there with his feet.

We should understand “the gate of heaven” as an entrance through which believers may gain access to possess the kingdom of heaven.

Why did Jacob pour oil upon the stone that he set up as a monument? He did not do this as an act of idolatry. Neither then nor afterward did he habitually worship the stone or sacrifice to it. Rather, it was a sign established in a very clear prophecy concerning anointing. Hence Christ’s name derives from *chrism*.

Let us demonstrate this more clearly point by point.

Jacob saw the Lord leaning upon the ladder, saying to him:

“I am the God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac. The land on which you sleep I will give to you.”

“According to hope” is understood, and “to your offspring” according to fulfillment—that is, to Christ, in accordance with:

“Ask of me, and I will give you the nations” (Ps. 2:8).

Or his offspring signifies the apostles. “Your seed will be” that is, the faithful, “like the dust of the earth,” with “because of its multitude” [Z.: “greatness”] understood. “You will spread out to the west and to the east, to the north and to the south.”

We see this fulfilled because the Church of Christ has spread throughout the four regions of the world.

“And in you”—that is, in Christ, whom you prefigure—“and in your offspring”—that is, in the apostles—“all the tribes of the earth,” namely all the nations of the earth, “will be blessed.”

“I will be your guardian wherever you go.”

For God the Father guarded him, or his body, which is the Church.

“And I will bring you back to this land,” according to what Paul says:

“Blindness has happened in part to Israel. But when the fullness of time has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. 11:25).

When Jacob awoke from his sleep, he said:

“Truly, the Lord is in this place.”

He spoke prophetically, as we have already clearly demonstrated, because it was destined that the Lord would visibly appear in that same land.

“And I did not know it.”

He said this in the person of the Jewish people, who did not know that Christ had come upon earth for the salvation of the world.

The text continues:

“He called the name of the city Bethel.”

Bethel is interpreted as “house of God.” It signifies the Church, which is the house of God.

Previously the place was called Luz, which is interpreted as “almond tree.” It signifies Judea. Just as the almond tree sends out its leaves before all other trees, so Judea possessed knowledge of God and the Law before all the nations and flourished, as it were, in faith.

And just as the fruit of the almond contains three things within itself—skin, shell, and kernel—so sacred Scripture, which the people of Judea received, contains within itself a threefold understanding: physical, ethical, and logical—that is, historical, allegorical, and moral meaning.

## Chapter XXIX

### Verse 1

“Jacob therefore departed”—that is, the Lord Jesus Christ, whose type he represented in this passage—“for the land of the east,” namely to the Jewish people, who appeared to possess knowledge of the Law and of God. Of this the Prophet says:

“Behold the man; the East is his name” (Zech. 6:12).

### Verse 2

“And he saw a well in the field,” namely the depth of the Scriptures among the Jewish people, or the grace of baptism prefigured in the books of the Law and the prophets.

“And three flocks of sheep lying beside it.”

For the Jewish people was divided in three ways: into Pharisees, Sadducees, and the common people.

“For from it the flocks were watered”—that is, the Jews who hoped for the good things of the earth and were instructed by the sayings of the Old Testament; or the ancient fathers, understanding baptism in the books of the Law and the prophets [Z.: “not understanding”].

“And a great stone covered its mouth.”

The stone signifies Christ, who was hidden from unbelievers; or the hardness of the Law, by which spiritual understanding and the grace of baptism were concealed.

### Verses 3–6

“It was customary that, when all the sheep had been gathered, they would roll away the stone.”

For when the fullness of time arrived, so that the human race might be saved through the Only-Begotten, he deigned to reveal it; and then the hardness of the Law was made manifest. For it is written:

“Then he opened their minds, so that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:45).

—“After the flocks had been refreshed,” that is, the cre— [fragmentary]

### [Scan page 112]

...to the faithful nations. They placed one stone over the mouth of the well. For while the nations believed, the Jews remained in their unbelief, understanding neither Christ nor the depth of the Scriptures.

**Verse 7.** — Jacob said to the shepherds: “There is still much of the day remaining.” How does the Lord speak this to the preachers? He means that there is a great span of time from now until the future resurrection—a span not improperly compared with a day—for, while we remain in the brightness of faith, we may perform good works until the end of the age. Nor is it yet time to lead the flocks to the folds, that is, to the heavenly dwellings, since the faithful must first be perfectly instructed in knowledge of the faith. Hence it is also added:

“Give the sheep water before you.” That is, as though he were saying: “Instruct the simple in simplicity, and then lead them to pasture,” that is, to meditation on the Scriptures.

**Verse 8.** — They answered: “We cannot, until all the flocks have been gathered and we have removed the stone from the mouth of the well, so that we may water the flocks.”

They say rightly: “We cannot, until all the flocks have been gathered.” For the ancient preachers were unable to disclose either the depth of the Scriptures or the grace of baptism to others until the time came when all nations would be gathered through Christ to the depth of the Scriptures and to the fountain of baptism.

**Verse 9.** — “They were still speaking, and behold, Rachel was coming with her father’s sheep.” For she herself was leading the flock.

Rachel—which is interpreted as “sheep”—can signify the Church. She once led and now feeds the catholic people, coming with the faithful to Christ.

**Verse 10.** — “When Jacob saw her”—that is, the Lord, whose name means “supplanter”—“and knew that she was his cousin,” namely, the Church gathered from the nations, who became the daughter of the Synagogue, which is the sister of the only Son of God the Father and is called his daughter by grace; “and the sheep of Laban, his uncle,” that is, of the gentile people, from whom the Synagogue of the Jews first proceeded, from which the Lord deigned to assume flesh. Nevertheless, Laban signifies divine grace, whose sheep are all the elect.

“He removed the stone by which the well was closed,” that is, the hardness of the law by which spiritual understanding was shut in.

**Verse 11.** — “And having watered the flock”—that is, having refreshed the faithful people from the depth of the Scriptures, or from the reborn fountain of baptism—“he kissed her.” For afterward he was reconciled with his Church. “And, raising his voice, he wept.” He wept because he had taken pity on the human race.

**Verse 12.** — “And he disclosed to her that he was her father’s brother and the son of Rebekah.”

He rightly says that he disclosed that he was her father’s brother and Rebekah’s son, because the Lord deigned to become incarnate from the stock of the patriarchs and from the Synagogue of the Jews.

“And she hurried away and announced it to her father.” For the Church was not content solely with her own salvation, but strove to preach to the nations and to the wise men of this world.

**Verse 13.** — “When Laban heard that Jacob had come, he ran to meet him.” He ran in the steps of faith, “embraced him” with the arms of love and faith, and, “falling upon his neck, kissed him,” that is, he obtained fellowship in reconciliation and charity.

“He brought him into his house.” For through faith he prepared a dwelling for him in his mind, so that he might deign to dwell in him, according to what he himself says through the Prophet: “I will dwell in them and walk among them; I will be their father, and they shall be my sons,” says the Lord (II Cor. 6:16, 18).

Next follows the account of how Jacob, serving Laban, took two wives: first Leah, and second Rachel, for whom he served another seven years. It must be understood that some now mistakenly suppose that he took her as wife after another seven years; rather, he took her after seven days, the wedding feast of his first wife. For it follows: “And he went in to Rachel, and he loved Rachel more than Leah, and he served him another seven years.”

After this he took Leah’s maidservant, named Zilpah, and Rachel’s maidservant, Bilhah. From them he fathered twelve sons and one daughter. Leah bore Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun; Rachel, Joseph and Benjamin; Bilhah, Rachel’s maidservant, Dan and Naphtali; Zilpah, Leah’s maidservant, Gad and Asher. These are the twelve sons of Israel, the patriarchs.

Before extending our discussion farther, however, it is useful, for the sake of brevity, to give together the etymologies of their names, so that in a concise account we may show readers what they signify. They received their names from particular circumstances, so that the names might correspond either to certain future events or to circumstances already occurring.

While their spiritual mystery remains in them, we shall first pursue only the historical interpretations according to the letter, so that afterward we may be able to draw out their spiritual meanings more clearly.

Jacob is interpreted as “supplanter,” either because at birth he seized the heel of his emerging brother, or because he later deceived his brother by craft. Hence Esau said: “Rightly is his name called Jacob: for he has supplanted me this second time.”

Leah is interpreted as “laborious,” especially in childbearing. She experienced greater pains than Rachel in the fruitfulness of giving birth.

Rachel is interpreted as “sheep,” because Jacob first pastured Laban’s sheep for her sake.

**Verse 20.** — “And the days seemed to him few.” What does this mean, when a short time is usually more burdensome to lovers? It is said on account of the labor of servitude, which love made easy and light.

Reuben: “seeing a son,” or “son of vision.” When Leah bore him, she called his name Reuben, saying: “God has seen my humiliation.”

Simeon: “hearing,” or “heard.” Thus Leah said when she bore him: “Because the Lord has heard me.” Some interpret the name as “he has heard sorrow,” or as the name of a dwelling-place, which is spiritually appropriate.

Levi: “added,” or “taken up.” When Leah bore him, she said, without doubting her husband’s love: “Now my husband will be with me, because I have borne him three sons.”

Judah means “confession.” When Leah bore him, she gave praise to the Lord, saying: “Now I will confess to the Lord concerning this.” For this reason he was called Judah. His name therefore derives from confession, which is thanksgiving.

Issachar is interpreted as “reward.” For it is said: “There is a reward.” This was because Leah had bought from Reuben’s mandrakes the entrance of the man who was owed to Rachel. Hence, when he was born, Leah said: “God has given me my reward.”

Zebulun is interpreted as “dwelling-place.” Leah had borne this sixth son; therefore she said with confidence: “Now my husband will dwell with me.” Hence her son was called “dwelling-place.”

Naphtali means “wrestling,” or “comparison”; this is the reason for his name. When Rachel’s maidservant Bilhah had borne him, Rachel said: “God has made me dwell with my sister by wrestling.”

Dan is interpreted as “judgment.” When Bilhah bore him, Rachel, her mistress, said: “God has judged and, hearing me, has given me a son.” She expressed the reason for his name, so that, from the fact that the Lord had judged, she might give the maidservant’s son the name “judgment.”

Gad was named from “fortune,” or from “being equipped.” When Zilpah bore him, her mistress Leah said: “In fortune,” that is, “in readiness,” or “in event.” To state the matter more openly, the name is interpreted as “temptation” or “armed.”

Asher means “blessed.” When Zilpah bore him, Leah said: “I am blessed, and women will call me blessed.” From the fact that she was called blessed, she called him blessed according to the etymology of his name.

Joseph was named “increase” because his mother desired that another son be added to her.

For this reason Pharaoh called him *Saphaneth* in the Egyptian language. In Hebrew this sounds like “discoverer of hidden things,” because he revealed obscure dreams and foretold the famine. Yet because this name is given in Egyptian, its meaning must be sought according to that language. In Egyptian, *Saphaneth* is interpreted as “savior of the world,” because he delivered the whole earth from the imminent destruction of famine.

Benjamin is interpreted as “son of the right hand,” which signifies strength. The right hand is called *yamin*. His mother, dying, called him Benoni, that is, “son of my sorrow.” His father changed this and named him “son of the right hand.”

Dinah is translated as “cause.” For she became the cause of the conflict at Shechem.

Yet spiritually Jacob signifies either the Lord and our Redeemer, or perfect men who, desiring all things, wish to live in quietness in the life of contemplation. Rachel signifies the contemplative life; Leah, the active life.

Laban, whose name is interpreted as “whitening,” signifies the grace of almighty God, through which the remission of sins takes place, and to which perfect men serve for the sake of the contemplative life.

If you wish, reader, to know this more fully, examine with vigilant care the sayings of blessed Pope Gregory, the supreme preacher, and of Isidore, the energetic teacher; because of the limitation of our time, we have not wished to insert them here.

Nevertheless, Victorinus the martyr and other teachers wish these two wives of Jacob to be understood as the Synagogue and the Church. Leah, they say, being older, represented the Synagogue, because she first bore the people of God.

And what does it mean that she is said to be weak in the eyes [F.: “burdened”]? The law given through Moses was covered and sealed.

What is signified by the fact that Jacob is joined to her at night? It signifies that the Synagogue itself was joined to God in the darkness of the letter [Z.: “to the side”].

The crowd of her maidservants signifies, as some think, the multitude of patriarchs and prophets.

Rachel, however, younger and beautiful, at first barren and afterward fruitful, is an image of the Church. She is younger because she came later in time; beautiful because she is holy in body and spirit. Her eyes are beautiful because they were worthy to behold the Gospel.

She remained barren until the Synagogue had generated the people. She was joined to Jacob in the daytime because the Church of the nations is joined to Christ in the daylight of the New Testament. To her wedding the crowds of companions also gather, because through the holy apostles, who are her friends, the Church is incorporated into the Lord.

Jacob also had their maidservants and fathered sons by them, because in both peoples there are teachers who remain carnal and persist in the life of the old man; through their preaching, sons are generated for the Lord.

Hence Bilhah is interpreted as “grown old,” signifying those who are devoted to carnal perceptions but nevertheless proclaim spiritual things concerning the immutable substance of the Godhead.

Zilpah, interpreted as “open mouth,” represents those through whose preaching the mouth is opened while the heart does not follow. Of such people it is written: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matt. 15:8). And elsewhere: “What they say, do; but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23:2).

Why does Jacob serve for Rachel, while Leah is substituted, unless because the Lord, in order to take the Church, first joined the Synagogue to himself?

Let us see what sort of sons are born. From Leah are born Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and the others.

Reuben, who is interpreted as “seeing a son,” signifies a perfect teacher arising from the Synagogue of the Jews in faith. He is rightly called “seeing a son.” That works are signified by sons is attested by the Psalmist, who says among the blessings of the blessed man: “Your sons are like olive shoots around your table” (Ps. 127:4). And below: “And may you see your children’s children” (ibid., v. 7).

The one who fears the Lord cannot be blessed unless he has generated sons and received grandsons, since a better reward awaits the faithful virgin. But by sons, as we have said, works are signified; by sons’ sons, the fruits of works, that is, the eternal reward.

Finally, this Reuben, going out at the time of the wheat harvest, found mandrakes in the field, which he brought to his mother Leah, and so forth.

This signifies the holy apostles and the other preachers, who can go out into the field of preaching, proceed into public view, announce the word, fulfill it through works, and beget spiritual offspring.

The field may also signify the books of the law and the proclamations of the prophets. By the mandrakes, which have a good smell but a tasteless flavor, we may understand the Lord Jesus Christ: he has a good aroma among those who have believed in him, but is tasteless to those who remain in unbelief and who have formed a perverse opinion of him, according to what is written: “Some were saying, ‘He is good’; others said, ‘No, but he deceives the crowd’” (John 7:12).

### [Scan page 113]

But he went out rightly at the time of the wheat harvest, because they were sent to preach when the time had already come for the people to be gathered to faith, according to what is said of them: “Lift up your eyes and see the regions, because they are already white for harvesting” (John 4:35).

He brought them to Leah, his mother, because they first preached the Lord to the Synagogue, their mother. But through Leah he reached Rachel, because through the primitive Church Christ reached the Church of the nations.

Next comes Simeon. Simeon, who is interpreted as “hearing sorrow,” or, as some think, “the name of a dwelling-place,” signifies those who labor diligently here and grieve over their own sins and those of others, hearing whatever the preacher declares to them for repentance.

Hence he is rightly called “hearing sorrow,” or “the name of a dwelling-place,” so that by the quality of the name he might impress more clearly both what must be possessed here and what must be awaited profitably.

The joy of the heavenly dwelling-place will be given to those whose spirit here is saddened by fruitful repentance; to them it is also said: “Your sorrow will be turned into joy” (John 16:20).

Levi therefore follows Simeon; his name means “added.” By him we understand either those who purchase eternal things with temporal goods, as Solomon says: “The ransom of a man’s life is his wealth” (Prov. 13:8), or those who, by following God’s counsel, receive in this age a hundredfold with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life.

The saying also applies to them: “He who increases knowledge increases labor” (Eccl. 1:18). For the bitterness of tribulations was added to holy Jacob so that, once his reward had been tested, a more abundant recompense might be given.

**Judah.** Judah, who is interpreted as “confession” or “praise,” signifies those who persevere in a true confession of faith and render praises of thanksgiving to the Lord. Or he signifies those who truly confess their sins, because no one reaches the summit of good things without confession of evil; unless through confession we renounce evil deeds, we are not formed in righteousness.

**Issachar.** Issachar is interpreted as “reward.” He signifies those who, strengthened by patience, endure the temptations of the present life solely for the sake of the heavenly reward and are established by contemplation of the future reward, because they know, according to the Apostle, “that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18). The battle is fought more fruitfully where reward is hoped for.

**Dan.** Dan is interpreted as “judgment.” He seems, according to the meaning of his name, to signify eminent and exalted men who, living spiritually, know how to judge all things, according to what Paul says: “The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself judged by no one” (I Cor. 2:15).

**Zebulun.** Zebulun is interpreted as “dwelling-place of strength.” He designates those who lay down their lives for Christ, in whom the Lord performs and perfects the things we have mentioned above—namely, when strength is made perfect in weakness—so that the body, which is judged weak by its enemies and through whose substance they attempt to bring destruction even upon the soul, may experience itself unconquered because God strengthens it.

**Naphtali.** Naphtali, interpreted as “breadth,” signifies those who have been enlarged by generous works of mercy and, with an expanded heart, strive toward heavenly things. They seek care for the flesh not in desires but only in necessity, as the Apostle says: “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13:14).

**Gad.** Gad is interpreted as “temptation” or “armed.” He signifies those who are strong in the exercise of temptations. After they begin good works, they must be tested by greater temptations and girded for more serious battles, so that the strength of their faith may be proved. Solomon says: “My son, if you come to serve the Lord, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2:1).

Likewise the Psalmist says: “You have girded me for battle” (Ps. 17:40).

And since we call blessed those who have endured patiently:

**Asher.** Asher is interpreted as “blessed.” He prefigures those who patiently endure temptations, secure in the promise of heavenly reward and happy in the victory of their struggles. Hence Asher, that is, “blessed,” is placed after Gad in a very fitting order.

“Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life” (James 1:12). Because the patient are strengthened by the firm promise of this blessedness, they are not constricted; rather, rejoicing in hope and patient in tribulation, they sing with the Psalmist: “In tribulation you enlarged me” (Ps. 4:1). And again: “I ran in the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart” (Ps. 118:32).

**Joseph.** Joseph is interpreted as “increase” or “adding.” He signifies those who strive for the increase of spiritual substance and virtues. When this happy increase follows, the gifts of grace are bestowed upon them, and the glory of the heavenly gift is added besides, because beyond God’s commandments they offer something more, either in virginity or in the measure of their possessions.

**Benjamin.** Benjamin is interpreted as “son of the right hand.” He indicates those who do everything for this reason: that they may be placed at the right hand of the Judge.

Benjamin is rightly placed last, because when the last enemy, death, has been destroyed, the happiness of eternal inheritance will be given to the elect. Or each of the faithful may properly be called a son of the right hand; likewise the whole assembly of the Church, of which we sing: “The queen stood at your right hand, in a garment of gold, clothed in varied colors” (Ps. 44:10).

This Church, gathered from both peoples, like Jacob’s two wives, bore sons and Jacob served for them seven years.

Jacob’s seven years of service for the two wives therefore signify the time of the present life, which turns through seven days. In this time the Lord took the form of a servant, becoming obedient to the Father’s will even unto death.

He served for sheep; and our Lord says: “The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve” (Matt. 20:28).

He pastured sheep [Z.: “pastures them”]; and the Lord says in the Gospel: “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:14).

He took varied animals as his wages; Christ gathered to himself the diversity of the nations.

He cut three rods, stripped them of their bark, and placed them in the watering troughs, so that his sheep might multiply by looking at them. Our Lord likewise set before the faithful people, in the water of baptism, the names of the three Persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—so that whoever perceives this with a full heart may become God’s work.

**Another interpretation.** What does it mean to place green rods of almond and plane tree before the eyes of the flocks, except to offer the lives and teachings of the ancient fathers as an example to the peoples through the sequence of Scripture?

Because these are straight according to the test of reason, they are called rods. He strips away part of their bark, so that in what is stripped the inward whiteness may appear; and he preserves part of the bark, so that they may remain outwardly as they had been, in their greenness. The color of the rods becomes varied when the bark is removed in part and retained in part.

The teachings of the fathers who preceded us are set before the eyes of our consideration like varied rods. When we often flee from the literal meaning, we remove the bark, as it were; and when we often follow the literal meaning, we preserve the bark. When the bark of the letter is stripped away, the inner brightness of allegory is displayed; when the bark is retained, the green examples of the outward understanding are shown.

Jacob rightly placed them in the channels of water, because our Redeemer also fixed them in the books of the sacred knowledge by which we are inwardly imbued. The rams mating with the sheep while looking upon them signify that our rational spirits, when fixed upon their contemplation, are mingled with their various actions, so that they produce offspring of works corresponding to the examples of those who preceded them, which they see in the words of the commandments.

The offspring of good works has a varied color, because sometimes the bark of the letter is removed and the inner meaning is considered more sharply, while at other times the covering of the history is retained and the person is rightly formed in outward things.

Nevertheless, according to the historical account, we must ask how the offspring of different animals was produced by looking at the varied rods.

Jacob observed the time when the flocks went up and, in the heat of the day, went eagerly to drink. He placed variegated rods in the channels, and, having admitted the rams and he-goats, made the sheep and goats go up; while they drank eagerly and were mounted by the males, they conceived offspring such as the shadows of the rams and he-goats going up above them appeared in the reflection of the water.

The rods placed in the channels therefore also produced a varied color in the images. Nor is it surprising that this is the nature of conception in females: whatever they have seen—or conceived in their minds—in the final heat of pleasure in which they conceive, they produce offspring of that sort. The same thing is said to occur even among herds of mares in Spain.

Quintilian, in the controversy in which a matron was accused because she had borne an Ethiopian child, argues in her defense that conception has the nature we have described. Many similar things are also said to occur in the offspring of animals.

The same thing is reported to have happened to women, and it is found written in the books of the most ancient and most skilled physician Hippocrates. A woman who had borne a very beautiful child unlike both parents and their race would have been punished on suspicion of adultery, unless the physician mentioned had resolved the question. He advised them to inquire whether perhaps some such picture was in the bedchamber; when one was found, the woman was freed from suspicion.

**Verse 42.** — Why did Jacob wish the animals born in the earlier part of the season to be his and those born later to belong to Laban? Or why did he not, by this device, make all the animals his own?

Jacob, prudent and clever, preserved justice and equity even in this new method. If all the lambs and kids had produced varied offspring, there would have been some suspicion of fraud, and Laban would openly have opposed him out of jealousy.

Therefore he regulated everything in such a way that he himself received the fruit of his labor while Laban was not entirely dispossessed. Whenever the sheep and goats were first mounted, because the offspring is better, he placed the rods before them so that varied offspring might be born.

Whatever sheep and goats sought the male later, he did not place the rods before their eyes, so that animals of one color would be born. Whatever was born first belonged to him, because it was spotted and variegated; whatever came later belonged to Laban, because animals of a single color, whether black or white, were born.

Why should Jacob be accused of fraud in this matter? This event compels us to seek some prophetic and figurative meaning, although Jacob undoubtedly acted as a prophet. We must not believe that he did such a thing except by spiritual revelation.

How does Jacob say sixteen times that his father-in-law changed his wages? The meaning is that with each birth Laban changed the agreement. If he saw variegated animals being born, afterward he would say: “I want varied animals to be born to me in the future.” Again, when he saw animals of one color being born—for Jacob, hearing this, did not place the rods in the channels—he would say that he wanted animals of one color to be born to him in the future.

What more need be said? Up to ten times Laban always changed the arrangement of his animals for Jacob, and whatever he proposed should be born was turned into the opposite color.

So that ten periods of giving birth in six years may not seem incredible, read Virgil, where it is said: “The flocks twice heavy with offspring.” The nature of the Italian and Mesopotamian sheep is said to be the same.

Spiritually, Laban, who—as was read above—separated the spotted and variegated goats and sheep, he-goats and rams, while handing over the whole flock to his sons, signifies the Jewish people.

Hence Laban is interpreted as “whitening,” because this people is whitened in its own eyes by hypocrisy and pretense. Laban took the white and the black: the Jewish people, as we have said, is white in its own eyes through hypocrisy, but black because of the multitude of its sins.

### [Scan page 116]

His sons, the shepherds of Laban, signify the Pharisees and Sadducees, who appeared to preside over the Jewish people as though they were its leaders.

Jacob prefigured the Savior. The distance of three days between them signifies that, through faith in the holy Trinity—or in knowledge, speech, and action—they departed from the Lord.

### Chapter XXXI

**Verse 19.** — “At that time Laban had gone to shear his sheep, and Rachel stole her father’s idols.”

Where we now read “idols,” the Hebrew has *teraphim*, which Aquila interprets as “figures” or “images.” We have mentioned this so that we may know what *teraphim* means in the Book of Judges (Judg. 17–18).

**Verse 25.** — “Jacob had already pitched his tent on Mount Gilead.”

This does not mean that the mountain was called Gilead at that time; it is spoken by anticipation, as we have often said. It is called by the name by which it was later known.

**Verses 45–46.** — “Jacob therefore took a stone and set it up as a pillar, and said to his brothers: ‘Bring stones,’” and what follows.

The question is why Jacob set up a stone as a pillar. It must be carefully observed that such pillars were established as witnesses to each matter, not so that people might worship them as gods, but so that they might signify something to them.

**Verse 47.** — “Laban called it Jegar-sahadutha, and Jacob called it Galeed,” each according to the character of his own language.

In the Hebrew language, a heap is called *gal*, and testimony is *‘ed*. In the Syrian language, a heap is called *igar*, and testimony *sedutha*. Jacob therefore called the heap of testimony—namely, Galeed—in the Hebrew language; Laban called the same thing, that is, the heap of testimony, *igar sedutha* in the speech of his people. For he was a Syrian and had not changed the ancient language of the region of his ancestors in which he lived.

**Verse 53.** — “Jacob swore by the Fear of his father Isaac.”

What does it mean that he swore by the Fear of his father Isaac? It means that he swore by God, whom his father Isaac feared. This Fear was also commended above when he said: “The God of my father Abraham and the Fear of my father Isaac.”

### Chapter XXXII

**Verses 1–10.** — “Angels of God met him, and when he saw them he said: ‘These are the camps of God.’”

There is no doubt that there was a multitude of angels. In the Scriptures, the heavenly host is commonly called a “militia.”

**Verse 11.** — “And Jacob said to the Lord: ‘Deliver me from the hand of my brother Esau, for I fear him greatly.’”

People often ask how Jacob had faith when he feared his brother Esau so greatly. In the words of Jacob that follow, both human weakness and faithful piety are sufficiently apparent: he wished God both to deliver him and to fulfill what he had promised.

Nevertheless, by this example we are admonished that, although we believe that God will do what he has promised, we must still do what is required by human prudence for the protection of our salvation, lest by neglecting these things we seem to tempt God.

**Verse 22.** — “And he crossed the ford of the Jabbok.”

For it should not be read, as it is falsely found in certain manuscripts, “And Jacob crossed the ford of the Jabbok.” *Jabbok* is the proper name of the ford itself.

**Verses 23–29.** — “And when he had brought across everything that belonged to him, he remained alone. And behold, a man wrestled with him until morning,” and so forth, until he said: “No longer will your name be called Jacob, but Israel.”

How, then, did Jacob ask a blessing from the one whom he had defeated in wrestling?

This is a great prophecy concerning Christ. For Jacob is understood here in two ways: that is, as carnal and spiritual. Jacob prevailed against Christ, or rather seemed to prevail.

For this is manifested through those Israelites by whom Christ was crucified, and he is blessed by him in those Israelites who believed in Christ, among whom was the one who said: “For I too am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin” (Rom. 11:1).

Thus one and the same Jacob is both lame and blessed: lame in the breadth of the thigh, as though in the multitude [Z.: magnitude] of his race, concerning which it is said: “They have limped from their paths” (Ps. 17:46); but blessed in those of whom it is said: “The remnant has been saved according to the election of grace” (Rom. 11:5).

What is the reason for changing Jacob’s name, so that he should be called Israel? Various interpretations of this name are proposed. Blessed Jerome explained it as follows:

“The sense here is: ‘Your name shall not be called Supplanter,’ that is, Jacob, ‘but Prince with God,’ that is, Israel. For just as I am a prince, so you, who were able to wrestle with me, shall be called a prince. If you were able to wrestle with me—with God, or with an angel, since many interpret it in different ways—how much more with human beings? Therefore you need not fear wrestling with Esau.”

But what they interpret in the Book of Names—Israel as “a man seeing God,” or “a mind seeing God”—seems to me to have been interpreted with greater violence than truth; it is almost entirely a corruption of the language.

Morally, the angel signifies God, and Jacob, who contended with the angel, expresses the soul of every perfect man devoted to contemplation.

For the one who struggles in wrestling sometimes finds the one above him superior, and sometimes finds him with whom he is contending inferior. When the soul strives to contemplate God, it is placed, as it were, in a contest. At times it seems to prevail, because by understanding and sensing it tastes something of the uncircumscribed name; at other times it falls, because after tasting it, it again grows weak.

The angel is therefore, as it were, defeated when God is grasped by inward understanding. Yet we must note that, even when defeated, the angel seized Jacob’s sinew at the thigh and immediately made it wither, so that from that time Jacob limped on one foot.

For almighty God, when he is already known through desire and understanding, dries up every pleasure of the flesh in us; and he who previously, as if on two feet, in the…

## ANGELOMILUXOVIENSIS

… and we seemed to be seeking God and holding fast to the world; after recognizing God’s sweetness, one foot remains sound in us while the other limps. For it is necessary that, when the love of the world is weakened in us, the love of God alone grow strong. If we hold the angel, we limp on one foot, because, while the strength of inward love increases in us, the strength of the flesh undoubtedly grows weak. Everyone who limps on one foot relies upon that foot alone which he has sound, because the person whose earthly desire has now withered supports himself with all his strength on the one foot of love for God. He stands upon that foot, because he carries suspended from the earth the foot of love for the world, which he had been accustomed to place upon the ground.

And so, if we return to our own parents—that is, to our spiritual fathers—let us hold the angel on the way, so that by inward sweetness we may apprehend God. The contemplative life is indeed exceedingly lovely and sweet: it carries the mind above itself, opens heavenly things, shows that earthly things ought to be despised, reveals spiritual realities to the eyes of the mind, and hides bodily things. Hence the Church rightly says in the Song of Songs: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song 5:2). The heart that keeps watch sleeps, because, by advancing inwardly through contemplation, it rests from outward and restless activity. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXIII

### Verses 6–9

“And Jacob divided the children of Leah and Rachel, and of both the maidservants, and placed each maidservant and her children first; Leah and her children in the second place; and Rachel and Joseph last. And he himself, advancing, bowed prostrate to the ground,” and so forth.

Contrary to what most people think, he did not make three groups, but two. Indeed, where we read [textual note: the wording is corrupt in the supplied text], Aquila placed [the wording meaning] “so that he might make one troop of the maidservants with their little ones, and another of Leah and Rachel, who were free women, with their children”; and he made the maidservants go first, the free women second, while he himself went before both flocks to meet his brother and bow down before him.

### Verses 10–16

“And Jacob said: ‘For I have seen your face as though I were seeing the face of God,’” and so forth, “until my lord goes ahead of his servant, and I shall follow slowly in his footsteps.”

What does Jacob’s statement to his brother mean: “I have seen your face as though I were seeing the face of God”? Did the words of a frightened and troubled mind burst forth into such flattery? These are brotherly words, spoken with a kindly intention, since after the gracious reception his fear itself had passed away. Perhaps here we ought to understand the name of God as referring to angels, or to some holy person, according to the Apostle, who said: “Although there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, just as there are many gods and many lords” (1 Corinthians 8:5).

How did Jacob promise his brother that he would follow in his footsteps, when he was heading by another route? Perhaps he followed him for a time; or perhaps he first made the promise sincerely, but later chose something else after reconsidering the matter.

### Verse 17

“And Jacob came to Succoth, and built a house, and fixed up tents, and called the name of that place Succoth, that is, ‘Tents.’” Because he built tents for his flocks, he therefore called the name of that place “Tents.” Where we have “Tents,” the Hebrew reads *Sukkoth* [the supplied text gives *Sotheoth*]. Even today there is a city across the Jordan bearing this name, between the regions of Scythopolis.

### Verse 18

“And he passed over to Salem, a city of the Shechemites, which is in the land of Canaan,” and so forth.

A difficulty arises: how is Salem called a city, when Jerusalem, in which Melchizedek ruled, was earlier called Salem? Either, therefore, both cities bear the same name—as we can also find with many places in Judea, so that the same name of a city or place occurs in different tribes—or we should interpret the Salem now mentioned in place of Shechem as meaning “consummated” and “perfected,” while the Salem later called Jerusalem should be rendered in our language as “peaceful.” For, with a slight alteration of accent [Petrus: “of pronunciation”], both meanings are expressed by this word.

The Hebrews report that Jacob’s dislocated thigh became strong and was healed there; for this reason the same city received the name meaning “healed” and “perfected.”

## CHAPTER XXXIV

### Verses 1–4

“Dinah went out to see the women of that region,” and so forth, “and he soothed her sadness with flatteries.”

Dinah goes out to see the women of a foreign region when every mind, neglecting its own concerns and attending to the actions of others, wanders outside its proper character and order. Shechem, the ruler of the region, violates her, because the devil corrupts a mind found occupied with outward cares. “His soul was attached to her,” because he sees that she has been joined to him through iniquity. When the mind recovers from guilt and tries to mourn what it has done, the corrupter calls empty hopes and securities before its eyes, so as to take away the usefulness of sorrow; he then attaches himself to it and soothes its sadness with flatteries.

At one moment he speaks of the deeds of others as worse; at another, he says that what has been done is nothing; at another, he speaks of God as merciful; at another, he promises that there will still be time for repentance. Thus, while the deceived mind is led astray by these arguments, it is held back from the purpose of repentance, so that it perceives no good then, because it now feels no sorrow for evil, and later is overwhelmed more fully by punishments, although now it rejoices even in its sins.

### Verse 7

“Then it follows how Jacob’s two sons, Simeon and Levi, killed Hamor and Shechem as well,” and so forth.

How could Jacob’s two sons, by themselves, carry out such slaughter and devastation in a foreign land? There was no small multitude with Jacob, who had become exceedingly wealthy. Yet his sons are named in this action because they were the leaders and authors of the deed.

## CHAPTER XXXV

### Verses 1–29

“Jacob said: ‘Remove the foreign gods who are in your midst.’ And afterward they gave him all the foreign gods that they possessed, and the earrings that had been in their ears.”

Then it also follows how God appeared again to Jacob and blessed him; and afterward he departed from there and came in due course to the land that leads to Ephrath, and so forth, up to: “These are the generations of Esau.”

How did Jacob say to his household: “Throw away the foreign gods that are in your midst”? And again: “They therefore gave him all the foreign gods that they had, and the earrings that were in their ears”? If these were ornaments, they did not belong to idolatry. It must be understood that those earrings were amulets of foreign gods. For Scripture testifies that Rebekah received earrings from Abraham’s servant; this would not have happened if wearing earrings as ornaments had been forbidden. Therefore the earrings that were given together with the idols had been, as has been said, amulets of idols.

Why is it said a second time to Jacob: “You shall not be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name,” and he called him Israel? The angel by no means imposes a name upon him; rather, it is proclaimed that the name will be imposed by God. What is therefore promised as future is here said to have been fulfilled. The name is properly understood as referring to that promise in which God will be seen in a manner in which he was not previously seen by the fathers.

Where is Ephrath, where Jacob is said to have buried his wife Rachel? Ephrath and Bethlehem are names of the same city, with a similar interpretation. For one is translated “fruitful house” and the other “house of bread,” on account of that bread which is said to have descended from heaven.

But one may ask where the tower of the flock was, near which Jacob is said to have dwelt. It was near Bethlehem, where either the flock of the Lord’s angels sang at his birth, or Jacob pastured his own sheep and gave the place its name; or, what is more truly the case, where the mystery of future events was already being shown through prophecy [the supplied text reads *vaticinatio/vaticinio*].

What does it mean when Isaac is said to have “been consumed by age, died, and been gathered to his people”? How was he consumed, or to what people was he gathered? He was consumed by age, that is, perfected in age. He is gathered to the people of the angels, or to the people of holy souls, when those who finish this life pleasing God are joined to them. They are said to be gathered then when no anxiety of temptations or danger of sins remains. Scripture, contemplating this, says: “Before death, praise no one” (Ecclesiasticus 11:30).

## CHAPTER XXXVI

### Verses 7–8

How can Scripture say that after the death of his father Isaac Esau departed from the land of Canaan and lived on Mount Seir, when, as Jacob was coming from Mesopotamia, he is said to have sent messengers to his brother in the land of Seir and to have been living there at that time?

It is easy to suppose that, after his brother had departed for Mesopotamia, Esau later refused to live with his parents—either because he was troubled by the thought that he had been cheated of the blessing, or because of his wives, whose hatred was the greater or more influential cause. Often, too, a matter is included under a person’s name even though it does not properly belong to the name itself.

### Verses 9–14

“And Esau dwelt on Mount Seir; he is Edom. And these are the names of his sons: Eliphaz, the son of Adah, Esau’s wife,” and so forth, until it says: “These are their chiefs; he is Edom,” and these are the sons of Seir the Horrite, inhabitants of the land: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, and Anah.

Eliphaz, the son of Esau, is the very person who is mentioned in the book of blessed Job. Edom, Seir, and Esau are names of one man: he had three names and was called differently for different reasons. He is called Esau, that is, “red,” because of the cooking of the red lentil stew; he is so called because by eating it he lost his birthright. He is called Edom because of the redness of his body, which in Latin is called *sanguineus*, “blood-colored.” He is called Seir because he was shaggy and hairy. When he was born, he was hairy all over like a hide and lacked smoothness.

As for what follows—“and the Horrites who dwelt there,” or, as some copies have it, “the Chorrites”—after numbering Esau’s sons, the text goes back further and explains how many chiefs Esau had in the land of Edom from the race of the Horrites. In our language, the Horrites are interpreted as “free men.” Let us read Deuteronomy carefully, where it is written more clearly how the sons of Esau came and killed the Chorrites and possessed their land as an inheritance [Zwetlensis: “possessed their land as an inheritance”].

### Verses 22–23

“The sons of Lotan were Hori and Heman, and Lotan’s sister was Timna.” This is the Timna mentioned above: “Timna was the concubine of Eliphaz, the son of Esau’s firstborn, and she bore Amalek.” The Horrites are mentioned because Esau’s firstborn had taken a concubine from their daughters.

When the text says “Teman, Kenaz, Amalek,” and so forth, we should know that these names were afterward given to regions of the Idumaeans.

### Verse 24

“This is Anah, who found hot waters in the wilderness while he was pasturing the asses of Zibeon his father.”

The Jews assert that this Anah, Esau’s grandson, was the first to make herds of mares mount asses in the wilderness, so that a new kind of animal, contrary to nature, might be born from them: mules. They also say that wild asses were admitted to the female asses for this purpose, and that he himself discovered such a mating, so that the swiftest asses might be born from them.

[scan page 118]

## COMMENTARY ON GENESIS

… he saw that they were hated by his parents, and he began to dwell on Mount Seir. Then, after Jacob his brother had returned and harmony had been established between them, he too returned to his parents; and when they had buried their deceased father together, he departed again to Seir and there propagated the nation of the Idumaeans.

There were twelve sons of Jacob. When Benjamin is counted among them—as Scripture adds—these are called the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Mesopotamia of Syria [Zwetlensis: “of Syria”]. Since Benjamin plainly was born in Canaan, how can they then be said to have been twelve born in Mesopotamia?

There is no easier solution to this question than to understand the expression as a synecdoche. For when the greater or stronger part is involved, what does not properly belong to that name is customarily included under its name.

Why is it said a second time to Jacob: “You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name,” and he called him Israel?

The angel certainly does not then impose the name upon him; rather, what was to be imposed by God is proclaimed. What is therefore promised as future is here said to have been fulfilled. This name should properly be understood as referring to the promise in which God will be seen in a way in which he had not previously been seen by the fathers.

### Chapter XXXVI continued

Why did Esau, after the death of his father Isaac, leave the land of Canaan and dwell on Mount Seir, although, when Jacob was coming from Mesopotamia, he is said to have sent messengers to his brother in the land of Seir and to have been dwelling there at that time?

It may readily be supposed that, after Jacob had gone to Mesopotamia, Esau did not wish to live with his parents, either because of the distress caused by his belief that he had been deprived of the blessing, or on account of his wives, whose hatred was probably the stronger cause. Sometimes, however, what does not strictly belong to a name is nevertheless comprehended under that name.

### Chapter XXXV continued

What is the land of Ephrath, where Jacob is said to have buried Rachel his wife? Ephrath and Bethlehem are names of the same city, with similar interpretations: one means “fruitful house,” the other “house of bread,” on account of the bread said to have descended from heaven.

But where was the tower of the flock, near which Jacob is said to have lived? It was near Bethlehem, where either the flock of the Lord’s angels sang at his birth, or Jacob pastured his sheep and gave the place its name; or, more truly, where the prophecy of future events was already displaying its mystery.

What does it mean that Isaac is said to have “been consumed by age, died, and been gathered to his people”? He was consumed by age, that is, perfected in age. He was gathered to the people of angels or of holy souls, to whom those who finish this life pleasing God are joined. They are said to be gathered when no concern of temptations or danger of sins remains. Hence Scripture says: “Before death, praise no one” (Ecclesiasticus 11:30).

## CHAPTER XXXVI

### Verses 7–8

How does Scripture say that after the death of Isaac his father Esau departed from the land of Canaan and lived on Mount Seir, when, as Jacob was coming from Mesopotamia, he is said to have sent messengers to his brother in the land of Seir and to have lived there at that time?

It is readily supposed that, after his brother had departed for Mesopotamia, Esau did not wish to live with his parents, either because he was troubled by the thought that he had been cheated of the blessing, or because of his wives, whose hatred was the greater or more powerful cause.

### Verses 9–14

“Esau lived on Mount Seir; he is Edom.” These are the names of his sons: Eliphaz, son of Adah, Esau’s wife, and so forth.

Edom, Seir, and Esau are names of one man, who had three names and was called variously for particular reasons. He is called Esau, meaning “red,” because of the cooking of the red lentils from which he lost his birthright. He is called Edom because of the redness of his body, which in Latin is called *sanguineus*, “blood-colored.” He is called Seir because he was shaggy and hairy; when he was born, he was hairy all over like a hide and had no smoothness.

As for the Horrites—or Chorrites, as some copies read—after the sons of Esau have been listed, the text goes back and explains how many chiefs Esau had in Edom from the race of the Horrites, who in our language are interpreted as “free men.” Deuteronomy explains more plainly how the sons of Esau came and killed the Chorrites and took possession of their land as an inheritance.

### Verses 22–23

“The sons of Lotan were Hori and Heman, and Lotan’s sister was Timna.” This is the Timna mentioned above: “Timna was the concubine of Eliphaz, the firstborn son of Esau, and she bore Amalek.” The Horrites are mentioned because Esau’s firstborn took a concubine from their daughters.

When the text says “Teman, Kenaz, Amalek,” and so forth, we should understand that these names were later given to regions of the Idumaeans.

### Verse 24

“This is Anah, who found hot waters in the wilderness while he was pasturing the asses of Zibeon his father.”

The Jews say that this Anah, Esau’s grandson, was the first to make mares mount asses in the wilderness, so that mules, a new kind of animal contrary to nature, might be born. They say that wild asses were also admitted to the female asses for this purpose, and that he discovered such a mating, from which the swiftest asses were born. Human ingenuity forced a different animal into intercourse, and by this adulterous union produced another kind, just as Jacob, contrary to nature, brought about similarities of color.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

### Verse 2

“Joseph, when he was seventeen years old, was pasturing the flock with his brothers, still a boy, and he was with the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, the wives of his father. And he accused his brothers before his father of a very serious crime.”

What kind of crime was this? Some wish it to be understood as idolatrous superstition, as though they had worshiped an idol. Others interpret it as a crime like those of Sodom and Gomorrah.

Nevertheless, one may ask why the maidservants are here called wives, when above they are called concubines. Perhaps, according to the custom of Scripture, every concubine is a wife, but not every wife is a concubine. Sarah, Rebekah, Leah, and Rachel cannot be called concubines; Hagar, Keturah, Bilhah, and Zilpah, however, are called both wives and concubines.

### Verse 3

“And Jacob made Joseph a *tunicam polymitam*.” Some have interpreted *polymita* as “variegated,” while Aquila translated it as a tunic with *astragalon*, that is, a long, ankle-length tunic.

### Verses 9–24

“Joseph also dreamed another dream, and when he told it to his brothers he said: ‘I saw a dream: the sun, the moon, and eleven stars were worshiping me.’”

How was Joseph’s dream fulfilled, when he says that he saw the sun, moon, and eleven stars worshiping him, although it is clear that, while he was ruling in Egypt, his mother Rachel had died long before, and we do not even read that his father worshiped him?

In Christ, however, it is easy [one manuscript: “easier”] to understand the fulfillment of the dream, for Christ was given “the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow,” and so forth (Philippians 2:10).

### Verses 25–34

“They saw Ishmaelites traveling from Gilead, and their camels carrying spices, resin, and stacte to Egypt,” and so forth, “and they sold him to the Midianite merchants for twenty [Zwetlensis: thirty] pieces of silver.”

Why does Scripture call the Ishmaelites, to whom Joseph was sold by his brothers, also Midianites, since Ishmael was the son of Abraham by Hagar, whereas the Midianites descended from Keturah?

Scripture had said of Abraham that he gave gifts to the sons of his concubines—namely Hagar and Keturah—and sent them away from Isaac his son toward the eastern land. It should therefore be understood that they formed one nation.

Spiritually, the spices carried on the camels signify the two Laws: resin signifies the Law of the books, while stacte signifies the Law of the prophets. Camels signify teachers. The fact that Joseph was not rescued through Judah’s counsel signifies that Christ was not rescued, as regards the flesh, through the belated repentance of Judas Iscariot.

### Verse 35

“Jacob said: ‘I shall go down to my son mourning into the underworld.’”

How should we understand Jacob’s statement: “I shall go down to my son mourning into the underworld”? These are the words of a troubled and grieving man, exaggerating his misfortunes even further. Or he may have signified the grave by the name “underworld,” as though he had said: “I shall remain in mourning until the earth receives me, and the grave receives me as it receives him.”

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

### Verses 1–30

“At that time Judah went down from his brothers and turned aside to an Adullamite man named Hirah,” and so forth, until it says that his brother came out, with the scarlet thread in his hand, and he called him Zerah.

How could the story of Judah, his three sons, his wife, and Tamar have been completed within so few years? Joseph is believed to have been sold in the seventeenth year of his age. He spent thirteen years in Egypt before becoming known to Pharaoh. To these thirteen years were added seven years of abundance, making twenty years. Two more years are added, because Jacob entered Egypt with his sons in the second year of the famine. Thus twenty-two years are found during which Joseph was absent from his father and brothers. How could all these events have occurred in the intervening period?

Holy Scripture often presents many events by way of summary. It should be understood that these things began several years before Joseph was sold. As soon as Judah reached adolescence, he began to fall in love with the woman whom he took as his wife, before Joseph had been sold into Egypt.

Why does the text say of Tamar that she removed the garments of her widowhood? So that we might understand that from the time of the patriarchs widows had their own distinctive clothing, different from that of married women.

Why did Judah say: “She is more righteous than I”? Tamar sat at a crossroads, where a traveler ought to look carefully to determine which road to take, not wandering about in order to gratify the lust of shamefulness, but in order to receive children from her father-in-law. Her cause was more righteous than that of her father-in-law: his concerned lust, hers children. Therefore, in comparison with her, he had done the lesser evil.

If Perez received his name from “division,” because he had divided the membrane of the afterbirth, how did Zerah receive his name? Zerah means “rising” or “dawn.” Either he was so called because he appeared first, or because many righteous people were born from him, as we read in Chronicles.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

### Verse 1

“Joseph was therefore brought down into Egypt, and Potiphar, Pharaoh’s eunuch, bought him.”

Here one asks how Potiphar is later said to have had a wife. The Hebrews report that this man bought Joseph because of his extraordinary beauty for a shameful service; but when the Lord had dried up or taken away his virility, he was later chosen, according to the custom of the *hierophants*, for the priesthood at Heliopolis. His daughter was Aseneth [Zwetlensis: Asenath], whom Joseph later took as his wife.

## CHAPTER XL

### Verse 6

“After these things it happened that two eunuchs—the king of Egypt’s cupbearer and baker—sinned against their lord. Pharaoh was angry with them and sent them to the prison in which Joseph was confined,” and so forth, until Joseph says to his brothers: “I am Joseph, whom you sold into Egypt.”

Here we omit the spiritual interpretation, as we said earlier in the preface, and strive to pursue the historical understanding, lest we exceed the limits of the little work.

It is therefore asked, while preserving the spiritual interpretation, why foreign men were in prison with Joseph and saw omens of future events. They did so not because of the merits of their own minds, but so that Joseph might be magnified and the one who was hidden might be revealed.

What are the three branches? The three branches are three shoots.

Why did Pharaoh—or Herod—hold the days of his birth as festive holidays? Because they thought that the hour of their birth had ordained them for kingship. They performed a similar act of worship, so that those whose impiety was equal might also share one festival.

What does Pharaoh’s statement mean: “I thought that I was standing above the river”? It is like the statement found elsewhere in Genesis: “Behold, I am standing above the spring.” In the same manner the Psalm says: “He founded the earth upon the waters” (Psalm 23:2). People should not be forced to think that he literally founded the earth upon the waters. According to this manner of speaking, it is rightly understood that the earth is higher than the water; it is supported by those waters, so that earthly animals may dwell there.

How is the multitude of grain compared with the multitude of sand? Because, just as sand is innumerable, so the abundance of grain could not be comprehended by ordinary counting.

How should we understand, in the case of the holy man Joseph, that he had made his brothers drunk? In the idiom of the Hebrew language, drunkenness is used for satiety, as in: “You visited the earth and intoxicated it” (Psalm 64:10), and again: “They shall be intoxicated by the abundance of your house” (Psalm 35:9).

Why did Joseph mock his brothers so many times and hold them in suspense for so long before he wished to reveal himself? He troubled them not in order to avenge himself upon them, but to cleanse them from the guilt of the crime they had previously committed against him. Or rather, he delayed so that their joy might be increased when he revealed himself, and so that they might see the immense glory of the one whom they had believed themselves to have destroyed.

## CHAPTER XLVI

### Verse 5

“Jacob rose from the well of the oath, and went down into Egypt, he and his sons and his grandsons, his daughters and his granddaughters, and all his offspring together,” until it says: “All the souls of the house of Jacob who entered Egypt were seventy.”

How can it be said: “His sons and his daughters went down with him into Egypt,” when Jacob had no more than one daughter, Dinah? Either we should understand granddaughters to be signified by the name “daughters,” or the plural has been used for the singular, as in the statement: “He sent among them the dog-fly.”

When Scripture says: “All the souls that came forth from Jacob’s loins,” what should be said to those who use this testimony to affirm that souls are propagated from parents together with bodies? No one should doubt that “souls” is used for human beings, with the whole signified by a part.

### Verse 15

“These are the sons of Leah, whom she bore in Mesopotamia of Syria, together with Dinah: the souls of her sons and daughters were thirty-three.”

Were all these thirty-three souls born from Leah in Mesopotamia of Syria, when Jacob did not remain there with his father-in-law for more than twenty years, and seven years had passed before he took Leah as his wife? Therefore holy Scripture says that they all arose in Mesopotamia because their fathers arose there.

### Verses 26–27

“If the souls who came with Jacob into Egypt numbered sixty-six, and Joseph was found there with his two sons, how are the souls of the house of Jacob afterward said to number seventy?”

When Jacob himself, the father and root, is counted, they are understood to number seventy.

Although in Genesis we read that there were seventy souls of the house of Jacob, why is it said in the Acts of the Apostles that Jacob went down into Egypt with seventy-five souls? Luke could not have written anything contrary to the Scripture that had already been spread among the nations, especially since at that time the authority of the Seventy Translators was considered greater than that of Luke, who was unknown, insignificant, and regarded among the nations as unreliable.

This should be observed generally: whenever the holy apostles or apostolic men speak to peoples, they usually make use of testimonies that had already been circulated among the nations. Some, however, report that the evangelist, being a proselyte, did not know the Hebrew letters.

## CHAPTER XLVII

### Verses 3–31

The sons of Jacob, when asked what work they did, answered: “We are shepherds of sheep, as were our fathers,” and so forth, until the text says that Jacob called his sons and said to them: “Gather yourselves together, so that I may announce to you what will happen to you in the last days.”

The sons of Jacob, asked what work they had, replied: “We are shepherds of sheep, as were our fathers.”

Why do we read that the patriarchs were first shepherds of sheep, and not kings of nations? Because there is no doubt that servitude is just and dominion is just when animals serve human beings and human beings rule animals. For it was said when humanity was created: “Let us make the human being in our image and likeness, and let him have authority over the fish of the sea, the birds of the air, and all things that are upon the earth.” This implies that the rational creature ought to rule irrational life.

Either iniquity or adversity made one human being the slave of another. Iniquity did so, as it is written: “Cursed is Canaan; he shall be a servant to his brothers.” Adversity did so in Joseph’s case, when, sold by his brothers, he became a slave of a foreigner. Thus the first slaves to whom this name was applied in the Latin language were prisoners of war. For a person who had been overcome by another in war and preserved alive was called a *servus*, “slave”; *mancipia* were so called because they had been captured by hand.

[scan page 121]

## ANGELOMILUXOVIENSIS MONACHI

Why did Jacob wish to tell Joseph his son, as though he did not know, where and when he had buried Joseph’s mother? Perhaps he wished prophetically to recall that Joseph’s mother was buried where Christ was to be born.

What is the portion that Jacob gave to his son Joseph beyond his brothers, which he says he took from the hand of the Amorites with sword and bow?

He signifies the city that is called Shechem in Hebrew and, according to Greek and Latin declension, is called Sicima; many corruptly call it Sychar. It is now called Neapolis, a city of the Samaritans. *Shechem* in the Hebrew language is translated as “shoulder.” Thus the Seventy translated it.

When Jacob says that he possessed it “with his bow and sword,” he calls the bow and sword justice, by which the stranger and resident alien merited to be delivered from danger after Shechem and Hamor were killed. He feared, as we read above, that the neighboring towns and fortified places might rise against him because of the destruction of the allied city. “And the Lord did not give them over so that they might harm him.”

Or it may be understood as follows: “I shall give you Shechem, which I bought with my strength,” that is, with money, which I acquired through great labor and sweat. When he says “beyond his brothers,” he shows that he gave it to the tribe of Joseph without casting lots; and its mausoleum may still be seen there. It follows:

## CHAPTER XLVIII

### Verses 5–22

What does Jacob mean when he says: “Your two sons Ephraim and Manasseh, like Reuben and Simeon, shall be two tribes and be called by their own names”?

Just as Ephraim and Manasseh will be two tribes and produce two peoples, so they will inherit the land of promise, as my sons do [Zwetlensis supplies an alternative wording: “Your two sons Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, like Reuben and Simeon”]. The meaning is: just as Reuben and Simeon will be two tribes and will be called by their own names, so Ephraim and Manasseh will be two tribes, produce two peoples, and inherit the land of promise.

But the other sons whom you beget after my death shall be yours. They will be called by the names of their fathers in their inheritance. They will not receive land separately, nor have their own allotments, as the other tribes do; within the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh they will be mixed in as appendages of the people.

> Here the Zwettl manuscript ends.

## CHAPTER XLIX

### Verses 2–3

“Gather yourselves together and hear, sons of Jacob; hear Israel your father. Reuben, my firstborn, you are my strength, the beginning of my sorrow,” and so forth, until it says: “And he blessed each one with his proper blessings.”

What should be understood concerning the blessings with which the patriarch Jacob blessed his sons? Are they to be understood historically or allegorically, when he says: “Gather yourselves together, sons of Jacob, so that I may announce to you what will happen in the last days”?

These words appear to express allegory more than history. Both should be understood: history and allegory. History concerns the division of the promised land, whose divisions were to be seen by their descendants. Allegory concerns what would happen to Christ and the Church in the last days.

The foundations of history must first be laid, so that the summit of allegory may more suitably be placed upon the earlier structure.

### Verses 3–4

“Reuben, my firstborn, you are my strength, and the beginning of my sorrow; greater in dominion, poured out like water, do not increase. You climbed upon your father’s bed and defiled his couch.”

The sense is this: You are the firstborn, greater in power, and by the order of your birth you ought to have received the inheritance due to firstborn sons, the priesthood, and the kingdom. This is what the honor and surpassing strength indicated by the words convey.

Let us explain each point more clearly; the literal sense is evident. Blessed Jacob received his first son, Reuben, from Leah his wife. As the son of so great a father, Reuben ought to have conducted himself worthily; the birthright and kingdom should have belonged to him. Hence Jacob calls him his firstborn, as one to whom the gifts of the firstborn were due.

He also calls him “my strength,” because he ought to have directed the strength of the kingdom.

[scan page 122]

## Commentary

He did not utter these things in the indicative mood because he had foreseen or willed that they would happen in this way, but so that by these words he might exhort him to repentance, when he recalled from what great dignity he had fallen through sinning. Hence he also says, “the beginning of sorrow,” and what follows. For the beginning of that sorrow was this: after breaking the bonds of chastity, he rushed without restraint to violate his father’s wife. It must be believed that this act goaded him with no slight sorrow. But because you sinned and, like water that is not contained in any vessel, poured yourself out in the impulse of your will, therefore I command you not to sin further, but to remain among your brothers mourning the punishment of your sin, since you lost the rank of the firstborn. The beginning of sorrow, moreover, is every firstborn, because on his account the parents’ affections are first stirred.

### Verses 5–7

“Simeon and Levi are brothers; weapons of iniquity are their arms. Let my soul not enter their counsel, nor let my glory be united with their assembly; for in their fury they killed a man, and in their desire they undermined a wall. Cursed be their fury, because it was obstinate, and their anger, because it was harsh. I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.”

He signifies that it was not his counsel that they had killed Shechem and Hamor, men bound by treaty, contrary to the law of peace, and that during a time of friendship they had shed innocent blood; and that, carried away by a kind of fury and cruelty, they had overturned the wall of the guest-city. Hence he says, “Cursed be their fury, because it was obstinate,” and what follows.

“And I will scatter them in Israel.” Levi did not receive a possession of his own, but throughout all the tribes he had a few cities for dwelling [Cod.: “for dwellings”]. Concerning Simeon, however, it is written in your book that he too did not receive a separate lot as his first possession, but received something from the tribe of Judah. In Chronicles it is written more clearly that, when he had multiplied and had no place of possession, he went out into the wilderness.

### Verses 8–10

“Judah, your brothers will praise you; your hand will be upon the necks of your enemies; the sons of your father will adore you. Judah is a lion’s whelp; to the prey, my son, you have ascended [or, as it is written in Hebrew: ‘From captivity, my son, you have ascended’]; reclining, you have lain down like a lion and like a lioness: who will rouse him?”

Because *Judah* is interpreted as “confession” or “praise,” it is rightly written: “Judah, your brothers will confess to you,” or “will praise you.” Although this contains a great mystery concerning Christ, nevertheless, according to the literal sense, it signifies that kings would be generated from David’s stock and that all the tribes would adore him. For he does not say, “the sons of your mother,” but “the sons of your father.” What follows—“To the prey, my son, you have ascended”—shows that he would lead captive peoples; and according to the spiritual understanding, “you have ascended on high” means “you have led captivity captive,” or, as I think better, captivity signifies the Passion, and ascent the Resurrection.

### Verses 11–13

“Tying his colt to the vine and his she-ass to the choice vine.”

The colt of the she-ass on which Jesus sat signifies the people of the nations; he joined it to the vine of the apostles, who came from the Jews. Or, as it is written in Hebrew, he tied the she-ass on which he sat to *Sorech*, that is, to a choice vine—the Church gathered from the nations. When he says, “my son,” he turns his address to Judah, indicating that Christ would accomplish all these things.

As for the statement, “The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah, nor the ruler from his thighs, until he comes who is to be sent, and he himself will be the expectation of the nations,” it signifies that rulers from the tribe of Judah would not fail until the time when Christ was born. He, sent by the Father, is the expectation of the nations.

### Verses 14–15

“Issachar is a bony or strong ass, lying between the boundaries. He saw that rest was good and the land that it was excellent, and he placed his shoulder under the burden, and became subject to tribute.”

Since he had said concerning Zebulun that he would possess the broad shores of the sea and would reach Sidon and the remaining cities of Phoenicia, he now returns to the inland province. Issachar, who would possess the most beautiful region of Galilee beside Naphtali, is made by his blessing its inhabitant. He calls him a bony or strong ass, and says that he places his shoulder under the burden, because he would labor greatly in cultivating the land and transporting to the sea what was produced within his borders, while also carrying tribute to kings.

The Hebrews say that, metaphorically, this signifies that, meditating on the holy Scriptures day and night, he devoted himself to labor; and therefore all serve him, as though carrying gifts to a teacher.

### Verses 16–18

“Dan shall judge his people like one of the tribes of Israel. Let Dan be a serpent on the road and a horned serpent on the path, biting the horse’s hooves, so that its rider falls backward. I shall await your salvation, Lord.”

Samson, judge of Israel, was from the tribe of Dan. Thus Jacob now speaks as one seeing in the spirit Samson nourishing his hair, his Nazirite, triumphing over his enemies after slaughtering them. He compares him to a serpent or basilisk lying in ambush along the roads, allowing no one to pass through the land of Israel; and even if some rash man, trusting in his own strength as in the speed of a horse, should wish to plunder it like a bandit, he would not be able to escape.

He speaks throughout by the metaphor of the serpent and the horseman.
