Seeing, then, so strong a Nazirite of yours—one who died because of a prostitute and, by dying, killed our enemies—I thought, “O God, he is your Christ, your Son.” But because he died and did not rise, and Israel was again led captive, another Savior of the world and of my race must be awaited, that he may come for whom this has been reserved. He will be the expectation of the nations.

### Verse 19

“Gad, girded, will fight before him, and he himself will be girded afterward.”

This signifies that, when he returned after fourteen years to Reuben, to half the tribe of Manasseh, and to the sons whom he had left beyond the Jordan in possession, he would find a great battle against the neighboring nations and would fight bravely after defeating his enemies. Read the Book of Joshua and Chronicles.

### Verse 21

“Naphtali is a swift stag, giving words of beauty.”

Or, “Naphtali is an irrigated field”; for the Hebrew word *naphal* signifies both. It signifies that warm springs arise in this tribe, or that the waters of the Jordan flow into and irrigate the lake of Gennesaret. The Hebrews, however, wish “an irrigated field” and “words of beauty” to be prophesied on account of Tiberias, which seemed to possess knowledge of the Law. “A swift stag” indicates seasonal crops and the speed of a more fertile land.

But it is better if we refer everything to the teaching of the Savior, who taught this above all, as it is also written in the Gospel.

### Verses 22–26

“Joseph is a son who increases; Joseph is a son who increases and is beautiful in appearance. The daughters ran upon the wall; but they embittered him and quarreled with him, and, being envious, had arrows. Yet his bow remained strong, and the bonds of his arms and hands were loosened by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob. From there the shepherd went forth, the stone of Israel.”

“O son Joseph, you are so beautiful that all day long the crowds of Egypt’s girls look upon you from the walls, towers, and windows. They were envious of you and provoked your brothers to anger, having arrows of envy and being wounded by jealous darts. But you placed your bow and weapons of war in God, who is a strong defender; and your bonds, with which your brothers had bound you, were released and broken, so that from your seed the tribe of Ephraim might arise, strong, steadfast, and hard as a stone, unconquered, and also ruling the ten tribes of Israel.”

### Verse 27

“Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he eats the prey, and in the evening he divides the spoil.”

Because the prophecy is most clearly manifested in the apostle Paul, everyone can see that in his youth he persecuted the Church, while in his old age he became a preacher of the Gospel.

The Hebrews, however, say that the altar on which sacrifices were offered and at whose base the blood of victims was poured belonged to the territory of the tribe of Benjamin. They say, therefore, that this signifies that priests sacrifice victims in the morning and divide in the evening what they have collected from the people according to the Law. They place the bloodthirsty, ravenous wolf over the interpretation of the altar, and the division of the spoils over the priests, who, serving the altar, live from the altar.

This is the historical interpretation.

Spiritually, however, Reuben displayed the figure of the former people of the Jews, to whom the Lord says through the prophet: “Israel is my firstborn.” For, in accordance with what was due to the firstborn, the priesthood and kingship belonged to him. It is added, “my strength,” because from him came the strength of God, who is Christ.

But how is he himself the beginning of sorrows, unless because he continually inflicted injury upon God the Father, turning his back toward him and not his face? He was first in gifts, because to them first were entrusted the oracles of God, the legislation, and the covenant, or promise. He was “greater in rule,” certainly because of the greatness of his strength, since that same people ruled over the other nations in great abundance in this world.

Yet he was “poured out like water,” by sinning against Christ: like water that cannot be contained in a vessel, he burst forth in the outpouring of his will. This means that, after that people had been dispersed throughout the whole world, it was greatly diminished.

But why did he deserve such a fate? He adds: “Because you went up to your father’s bed.” The audacity of the firstborn people is indicated: they went up to their father’s bed and defiled it when they seized the Lord’s body, in which the fullness of divinity rested, and suspended it on the cross, staining it with iron.

“Simeon and Levi are brothers, weapons of iniquity are their arms.” By Simeon and Levi are understood the scribes and Pharisees and the priests of the Jewish people. The scribes of the Jews belonged to Simeon; from the tribe of Levi came the chief priests, who formed a council to seize Jesus by deceit and kill him.

Concerning this council he says: “Let my soul not enter their counsel.” For he recoiled from seeing such great crimes that the Jews would commit in the last times: “For in their fury they killed a man,” that is, Christ, of whom it is said, “Behold, a man; his name is Rising” (Zechariah 6:12); and elsewhere, “A woman shall encompass a man” (Jeremiah 31:22).

“They undermined a wall,” that is, they pierced with nails that spiritual and very strong wall which guards Israel. “Cursed be their fury, because it was obstinate”: namely, when, inflamed by fury and anger, they handed Christ over to Pontius Pilate, saying, “Crucify, crucify” (Luke 23:21). “And their anger, because it was harsh”: when they asked for the robber Barabbas and demanded that the Prince of Life be crucified.

“I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel”: some of them believed, while others remained in unbelief. Those are called “divided” who separate themselves from them and come to the faith. They are “scattered” because, after their homeland and temple had been overthrown, the unbelieving nation was dispersed throughout the world.

“Judah, your brothers will praise you.” Through this Judah the true confessor, Christ, is represented, who was born from his tribe according to the flesh. His brothers—namely, the apostles and all his co-heirs, who through adoption were made sons of God the Father and, by grace, brothers of Christ, although he is their Lord by nature—will praise him.

“Your hand shall be upon the necks of your enemies.” By those same hands, that is, by the wood of the cross, he both subdued his enemies and bent the opposing powers, according to what the Father promised him: “Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies as a footstool beneath your feet” (Psalm 110:1–2).

“The sons of your father will adore you,” because many of the sons of Jacob adore him, saved by the election of grace.

“Judah is a lion’s whelp,” when, being born as a little child, he became one of us.

“To the prey, my son, you have ascended”: that is, ascending the cross, you redeemed captive peoples, and, dying, rescued those whom the adversary had invaded. Finally, returning from the underworld, you ascended on high and led captivity captive.

“Reclining, you have lain down like a lion.” Most clearly Christ reclined in his Passion when, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit; or when, secure in the tomb, he rested as though in a kind of bodily sleep. But why “like a lion” and “like a lion’s whelp”? In his sleep he was a lion, because he did not die by necessity but by his own power, as he himself says: “No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10:18). What he added—“and like a lion’s whelp”—means that he died from where he had been born.

Christ rightly rested like a lion: he not only did not fear the bitterness of death, but even in death itself conquered the power of death. What does he mean by “Who will rouse him?” No one, except the one who himself says: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19).

“Let the ruler not fail from Judah,” and what follows. This clearly refers to Judah. For a long time, an unbroken succession of kings from his seed remained among the Jews until Christ was born. The same was stated above.

“Tying his colt to the vine.” His colt is the people from the nations, upon whom the work of the Law had never previously been imposed. He joined this people to the vine of the apostles, who are from the Jews. For “the vineyard of the Lord of Sabaoth is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5:7).

“And his she-ass to the vine.” He himself said, “I am the true vine” (John 15:1). To this vine, therefore, he tied his she-ass, namely the slow-moving Synagogue, weighed down by the burden of the Law.

“He will wash his robe,” or his flesh, “in wine,” in the blood of his Passion; or the holy Church in the wine that “will be poured out for many for the remission of sins.”

“And his garment in the blood of grapes.” The garment signifies the nations whom he joined to his body, as it is written: “As I live, says the Lord, unless I clothe myself with all these as with a garment.”

“His eyes are more beautiful than wine.” The eyes of Christ are the apostles and evangelists, who provide the light of knowledge to the Church. Their commands surpass the austerity of the wine of the former Law, because they are far more generous than the commandments of the Old Testament.

“And his teeth are whiter than milk.” The teeth are the holy teachers, who cut people away from error and, as though chewing them, transform them into the body of Christ [Cod.: “transmit them”]. By “milk” is signified the teaching of the Law, which nourished the carnal people like little children with a cup of milk.

These teeth have become whiter: they are the preachers of the Church, because they chew and distribute the strong and solid food of the word. Concerning them the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Solid food belongs to the mature” (Hebrews 5:14).

He rightly says that his teeth are whiter than milk. For all who are perfect and who explain the nourishment of Scripture, supplying the body of the Church with the subtle and refined understanding called spiritual, must be white and pure, free from every stain.

[Patrologia Latina, vol. 115, *In Genesis*.]

[scan page 123]

## Commentary of Angelomus, Monk of Luxeuil

[The supplied text resumes at an inherited source boundary.]

### Issachar

“Issachar is a strong ass.” Issachar, whose name is interpreted as “reward,” refers to the people of the nations, whom the Lord purchased at the price of his blood. He is called a strong ass because the Gentile people was formerly like a brute and lustful animal, incapable of reason, but is now strong, submitting its neck to the dominion of the Redeemer and bearing the yoke of Gospel discipline.

“This one, lying between the boundaries, saw that rest was good and the land excellent.” To lie between the boundaries is to rest in expectation of the end of the world, seeking none of the things that now lie between, but desiring the last things. The strong ass sees rest and the excellent land, because the simple Gentile people rises to the strength of good work in order to reach the homeland of eternal life. Hence he also places his shoulder under the burden: desiring to attain the promised rest, he gladly bears all the burdens of the commandments. Thus he became subject to tribute, offering faithful gifts and the offerings of good works to his King and Christ.

### Zebulun

“Zebulun will dwell on the shore of the sea and at the station of ships.” Zebulun, interpreted as “dwelling-place of strength,” signifies the Church, most strong in enduring every suffering. It dwells on the shore of the sea and at the station of ships, so that it may be a refuge for believers and point out the harbor of faith to those in peril. Against all the storms of this age it is established in immovable and unshaken firmness. It awaits the shipwreck of the Jews and the tempests of heretics, who are carried about by every wind: though it is beaten by their waves, it breaks the waves by which it is beaten; it is not shattered by the storms of their heresy, nor moved by any wind of schism.

“It stretches as far as Sidon,” that is, it reaches even to the nations. We also read in the Gospel that some of the apostles were called from there and that the Lord often taught in those places: “The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, the way of the sea beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations: the people that sat in darkness saw a great light” (Isaiah 9:1–2).

### Dan

“Dan shall judge his people like the other tribes of Israel. Let Dan be a serpent on the road and a horned serpent on the path,” and so forth. Some say that these words foretell that Antichrist will come from this tribe; others maintain that they are written of Judah, by whom Christ was betrayed, and understand the horseman and horse to signify the Lord with assumed flesh. They take his falling backward to mean that he would return to the earth from which he was taken. But because he rose on the third day, Jacob says, “I shall await your salvation, Lord,” just as he says through David: “You will not abandon my soul in hell” (Psalm 15:10).

Others apply this prophecy to Antichrist. They say that Antichrist will come from Dan because Dan is here called both serpent and biter. Accordingly, when the Israelite people took possession of the land by the division of the camp, Dan first pitched camp to the north, signifying him who said in his heart: “I will sit on the mount of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:13). Of him the prophet also says: “From Dan was heard the snorting of his horses” (Jeremiah 8:16).

He is called not only a serpent but also a *cerastes*; for *cerastae* is the Greek word for horns, and this serpent is said to be horned. Thus Antichrist’s coming is fittingly described: armed against the life of the faithful with the bite of pestilential preaching, he will also wield the horns of power.

Who does not know that a path is narrower than a road? Dan becomes a serpent on the road because he calls those whom he deceives into the broadness of the present life, and bites them on the road because he consumes with the venom of error those to whom he grants liberty. He becomes a horned serpent on the path because, when he finds persons faithful and constraining themselves to the narrow ways, he attacks them not only by the wickedness of crafty persuasion but also oppresses them by the terror of power, exercising, amid the anguish of persecution, the horns of power after the benefits of feigned sweetness.

Here the horse signifies this world, foaming in the course of passing times through its pride. Since Antichrist strives to seize the end of the world, this horned serpent is said to bite its hoof: to bite the hoof is to reach the end of the age by striking it. “So that its rider may fall backward.” The rider of the horse is anyone exalted in worldly dignities. He is said to fall backward, not upon his face, as Saul is remembered to have fallen. To fall upon one’s face is in this life to recognize one’s sins and bewail them in repentance; to fall backward, upon what one cannot see, is suddenly to fall from this life and not know to what punishments one is being led.

Since Judea, ensnared by its own error, awaits Antichrist instead of Christ, Jacob appropriately turns suddenly, in the voice of the elect, and says: “I shall await your salvation, Lord”: that is, unlike the unbeliever who awaits Antichrist, I faithfully believe in Christ, who will come for our redemption.

### Gad

“Gad, girded, will fight before him.” This girded Gad expresses the person of the Lord, who in the first advent of his humility comes to fight before the advent of Antichrist, girded most powerfully with the sword of his word upon his thigh. With it he divided enemies—son from father, daughter from mother, daughter-in-law from mother-in-law—as the Gospel says: “I came not to send peace on earth, but a sword” (Matthew 10:34).

“And he himself will be girded backward”: this shows the glory of our Lord in his second reign. When Antichrist comes, Christ will meet him backward, that is, after his footsteps, advancing with swift coming in order to kill him with the sword of his mouth. Gad is fittingly interpreted “robber,” because, from behind—that is, at the feet—he springs like a robber with sudden and rapid advent against Antichrist’s open assault.

Hence the Evangelist cries: “The day of the Lord comes as a thief in the night” (1 Thessalonians 5:2). Thus Christ is written to fight Antichrist both before and after him: before him in the hidden advent of humility, after him manifestly in the glory of majesty.

Moses plainly shows that this prophecy of the patriarch pertains especially to Christ: “Blessed,” he says, “in the breadth of Gad; he rested like a lion, and seized arm and crown, and saw his own dominion.” Let them therefore recognize who rested like a lion except Christ in his tomb; who broke the crown and arms of the mighty except our Redeemer, who humbled the power and pride of the exalted; and who saw his own dominion except him to whom were given dominion, honor, and kingdom?

### Asher

“Asher’s bread is rich, and he will provide delicacies for kings,” whom, as though sparing them, he gently entices.

But Asher, whose name signifies “riches,” is Christ, whose is the height of the riches of wisdom and knowledge. He became poor for us, although he was rich. His rich bread is his flesh, which is the food of the saints; whoever eats it will not die forever (John 6:51–52). Thus he also provides the kings with the delicacies of wisdom, that is, those who rule their own senses well, who master their vices, discipline their bodies, and subject them to service.

### Naphtali

Naphtali, whose name is interpreted as “expansion,” signifies the apostles and holy preachers, whose teaching has been spread throughout the breadth of the whole world. He is called “a swift stag” because the apostles and preachers, leaping swiftly like stags, transcend the entanglements of this world. Thus, meditating on lofty and exalted things, they give “words of beauty,” that is, they preach the teaching of the Lord the Savior to all nations.

### Joseph

“Joseph is a son who increases.” This prophecy, after the Ascension had been accomplished, presented the image of the Father’s voice, with which the Father addresses Christ returning to heaven after his victory: “Joseph, a son who increases,” namely among the nations. For when he had abandoned the people on account of the Synagogue’s unbelief, he enlarged for himself an innumerable people of the Church from all nations. David also sang this: “All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord” (Psalm 22:27).

“A son who increases and is beautiful in appearance.” His beauty is above all beauty, as it is also sung of him in the Psalms: “You are beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Psalm 45:3).

“The daughters ran upon the wall.” These are the nations, or the Churches, that believed in Christ. Kindled by Christ’s beauty, they run upon the solidity of faith as upon a wall, so that they may see the true bridegroom through contemplation and be joined and cling to him by the kiss of charity.

“But they rebuked him.” This happened when, calumniating him with false witnesses, they attempted to destroy the Holy One of the Lord, the people of the Synagogue.

“And, being envious, they had arrows.” No one shot arrows or any weapon of injury at Joseph, but this happened specifically in the case of Christ.

“His bow remained strong.” Christ placed his bow and weapons of war in God, who is a strong defender; by his power all the wickedness of the faithless is destroyed.

“And the bonds of his arms and hands were loosened.” These were the bonds with which his brothers bound him and led him to Pilate, or with which they suspended him on the wood of the cross. They were severed by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob, that is, by the hands of almighty God of Jacob, from whose mouth the Lord himself, the good shepherd, went forth—the stone and strength of believers in Israel.

[scan page 124]

## Commentary

“Your father’s God will be your helper.” Who assisted the Son except God the Father, who said, “Jacob is my servant; my soul will receive him”?

“And the Almighty will bless you with blessings from heaven above, with blessings of the abyss lying below.” For he subjected everything to him: heavenly things through the blessing of heaven, and earthly things through the blessing of the abyss lying below, so that he might rule over all angels and human beings.

“With the blessings of the breasts,” that is, either of the two Testaments, by one of which he was announced and by the other displayed; or with the blessings of Mary’s breasts, which were truly blessed, because that holy virgin herself supplied the Lord with milk from her body. Hence the woman in the Gospel says: “Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breasts that you sucked” (Luke 11:27).

“Blessed shall be the breasts and the womb.” The womb of that same mother is also blessed—the virginal womb, of course, which bore Christ the Lord for us. Concerning it the Father says through the prophet Jeremiah: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you” (Jeremiah 1:5).

“The blessings of your father have been strengthened by the blessings of your fathers.” The blessings, he says, of the Father—of the heavenly Father—which were given to you from the summit of heaven and from the abyss, have been strengthened, that is, have prevailed, over the blessings of your fathers. For the blessing of the Almighty Father in the Son prevailed beyond the entire merit of the holy patriarchs and prophets, so that none of the saints is equal to him.

“Until the desire of the eternal hills should come.” These hills are the saints who, prophesying Christ’s coming, awaited his incarnation with great desire. Concerning them the Lord says: “Many righteous people and prophets desired to see what you see” (Matthew 13:17). These saints are called hills because of the excellence of their holiness. They are also called eternal because they attain eternal life and do not perish with the world, but are believed to endure forever.

“Let all these blessings come upon the head of Joseph,” that is, let all these blessings be placed upon Christ, which he received when incarnate, and upon the crown of the Nazirite, of whom it is written: “He shall be called a Nazirite” (Matthew 2:23), that is, the Holy One of God among his brothers. For he is the head, exalted above all, of all the saints, whom he also calls his brothers in the Psalms.

### Benjamin

“Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he eats the prey, and in the evening he divides the spoil.”

By these words the apostle Paul is designated, born from the stock of Benjamin. In the morning he seized the prey, that is, at the beginning he devastated as many believers as he could. In the evening he divides the spoil, because, later becoming a believer, he distributed the sacred oracles to his hearers with wondrous exposition.

We read that one of the teachers brought to the city of Jerusalem what is written concerning Benjamin. Benjamin, he says, is interpreted as “son of sorrow.” By lot he received the place in which the earthly Jerusalem is situated, which now, because of unbelief, has been rejected and cast off. For this Jerusalem is designated in its children under the person of Benjamin.

Just as Benjamin receives the final blessing, so that same people will be saved last, after the fullness of the nations has entered. He said: “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf”—a wolf, that is, because that people shed the blood of prophets and righteous people. It is called ravenous because of its greed. It became ravenous from great hunger for the word of God and from starvation, because it too violently seized the kingdom of God.

“This one eats the prey in the morning.” The morning is understood as the time when he received the Law. At that time the first illumination of knowledge was given to the world. He eats in the morning because he still eats and meditates upon the Law that he received in the morning, although, by following the law of righteousness, he did not reach the law of faith.

“In the evening he divides the spoil.” The evening is the final time, when he will be converted. Then he will divide the food; then he will understand that the letter must be divided from the spirit; and then he will know that “the letter kills, but the spirit gives life.” Since, already illuminated by the Lord’s grace, he begins in the spiritual Law to divide and separate spiritual things from bodily things, therefore it is said that “in the evening he will divide the food”—something he had not previously done, though he had meditated on the Law throughout the day.

It is asked why Jacob made all those whom he begot from free women and maidservants equal in honor, sons, and heirs. It was to show that Christ the Lord grants heavenly rewards with equal honor and glory to all nations who, through faith, are reconciled to his body. “There is no distinction between Jew and Greek, barbarian and Scythian, slave and free,” because “Christ is all and in all” (Colossians 3:11).

For this reason our Savior and Lord assumed the form of a servant and served both free and slave, so that he might grant an equal gift of heavenly goods to all who believe in him. Nor is anyone more highly regarded by him because of nobility according to the flesh. Whoever obtains faith is not darkened by any stain of carnal birth.

That this would indeed happen is also signified through the prophet, when the Lord says: “In the last days I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh” (Joel 2:28).

The text continues.

## CHAPTER L

### Verse 23

“Joseph called his brothers and said to them: ‘After my death God will visit you, and he will bring you up from this land to the land which he swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Take my bones with you from this place.’”

Why did so great a man command that his bones be carried away from Egypt? It should not be believed that he gave this command without purpose. One who could prophesy did not give it thoughtlessly.

Since he was deeply devoted to the worship of God the Creator, and knew that he had received from him the power to govern Egypt in such great majesty, he did not wish honor to be offered to himself, but rather the honor due to the Creator. Therefore he desired that, after his death, the error should be removed: he perceived that the Egyptians, out of vanity, would offer him unlawful honor after death, since he was certain that the vanity of the common people venerates the dead as gods more than the living.

Thus, so that he might remain free from the Egyptians’ vain superstition, lest such things ever be done to the injury of God, he commanded …

[scan page 127]

## Angelomus

He commanded that his bones be carried out of Egypt—something that we find the apostles also followed, namely Paul and Barnabas. For when they saw that sacrifice was being offered to them, and knew that this was due to God, they tore their garments, saying: “What are you doing? We too are human beings, like you” (*Acts* 14:14). In this way they restrained the crowds.

If, however, anyone should wish to interpret this spiritually—namely, so that Joseph signifies the Lord and our Redeemer; Egypt, which is interpreted as “darkness,” signifies Judea because of its obscurity; his bones signify the powers of faith, which the Jews held unworthily, owing to the darkness of ignorance required by their unbelief; Joseph’s brothers signify the holy apostles, whose faith has been established in many places; and their land signifies the Church from the Gentiles, to whom they preached faith in the Savior—we do not wish to contradict him. Rather, without contention, we have decided to yield to his judgment.

## Expositions of Angelomus of Luxeuil

Since I was asked by many brothers, and also by certain prudent and noble men, to arrange some short work in volumes of the Books of Kings according to the learning of doctors and the teaching of my very learned master, I hesitated for a long time to do so. No work of the ancient authors, entirely expounded, was available among us for repeated reading and remembrance, especially on behalf of those who say—as I mentioned in the preface to this volume—that these books contain nothing other than the wars of kings and the deeds of many people.

I hesitated all the more because I was poor in learning, did not rely upon the elaboration of secular wisdom, and was, so to speak, unlearned in eloquence and of small talent. I could not say with the Psalmist: “From your commandments I have gained understanding.” Nor, I said, was I worthy for the angel to cleanse my lips with a burning coal from the altar, so that I might be able to explain the mysteries of Christ worthily.

Yet, while I resisted these excuses, they began to compel me by persuasive arguments—or rather, by urgent exhortations—not to refuse to write something in accordance with the modest capacity of my understanding and small talent, and according to what had been impressed upon me by my teacher. Since I could not continue to refuse, I finally resolved to give my consent and undertook to arrange at least some material, though rashly and fearfully, on the condition that they keep it more secretly within domestic walls and not give it to anyone to read, lest my ignorance and reckless boldness—

## The Monk of Luxeuil

For the book already demands its conclusion and seeks its final limit. Therefore, at the end, we humbly ask the reader that, if he considers this little work worthy of reading and finds anything useful in it, he not refuse to commend the author of the writing to the Lord, since whatever usefulness I have produced is his gift. But if he finds anything deserving of criticism, let him attribute it to our foolishness and weakness, since we have tried to write not through vanity or presumption, but rather under compulsion. And if he should find fault with its elaborate composition, let him know that prudent men seek in the Scriptures not ornamented language but usefulness, and that they prefer profitable statements to artificial words, since they know that things were not instituted for the sake of words, but words for the sake of describing things.

## Angelomus the Monk: Apologetic Preface to the Books of Kings

—were exposed to the readers and an opportunity furnished for the reproaches of those who criticize. For when I had begun writing the first book, so that, with God as author, I might gather hidden things from hidden sources, my shamelessness was exposed by my own example, and my foolishness was revealed to the sacred ears of the magnificent Drogo, that distinguished bishop than whom there is nothing nobler or wiser.

When he discovered this, he began, with liberating authority, to command me to take care not to leave the work I had begun unfinished, but to bring it intelligently to its conclusion. I was entirely unable to resist his praise, nor did I dare to oppose such authority—not only because he was the son of the outstanding Charles Caesar and the brother of the most gracious prince Louis, but also because he was a distinguished bishop and my excellent abbot.

Compelled by these necessities and driven on by praises of many kinds—or rather, trusting, as I may say, in the assistance of Christ, who gives confidence to the weak and speech to the mute—I dared to clarify the work I had undertaken. It must be understood, however, that in some places I have arranged the whole meaning as it was expounded by the doctors. In others, following their sense, I have inserted much in a concise style and reduced many matters to one. In still others, I have introduced in my own words what I did not find in the books of commentators but learned by listening attentively to my teacher.

I have also dared to insert a few things of my own, although they are few, which seemed appropriate to the reader and were supported by examples; and in the little book—

[scan page 128]

—I resolved, with Christ as guide, to bring the work to an end. In it, the person of the writer should not be considered, but the quality of the diction.

How many vigorous modern doctors there are, who have also left much to posterity, gathering monuments of the saints from their sayings! I do not say this because I think I can follow in their footsteps, especially since they drenched the fields of divine Scripture with the dew of heavenly nectar and left useful things for readers in future ages. I can scarcely, and only with difficulty, extract even the smallest things from their sayings and finally understand even the least of them. Yet, so that I should not appear ungrateful to the giver, although compelled, I have contributed as moderately as I could to those who instructed me.

It should also be noted for those who contend that this book contains little of a spiritual character that Scripture—as in many divine books—is recognized not only in three ways, according to Solomon’s statement, “Behold, I have described it for you three times,” but is also contained in many ways, as is written in the Book of blessed Job: “Would that God spoke with you and showed you the secrets of wisdom, and that his law were manifold.”

According to the testimony of the diligence of the doctors, these are recognized as sevenfold. They are the seven seals with which this book is proclaimed, according to the Apocalypse of John, to have been sealed, and which no one could open or loose except the Lion from the tribe of Judah, who holds the key of David and opened both the book and its seals.

The first is historical; the second allegorical; the third is a mode involving both. The fourth concerns the unchangeable essence of the divine Trinity, namely, when the sacred utterance speaks properly and when tropically. The fifth is parabolic, namely, when one thing is said but another is found written. The sixth concerns the twofold coming of the Savior, so that the first may not be understood in place of the second, nor the second in place of the first. The seventh is the mode by which we are instructed through divine commandments, so that a definite pattern for the life to be lived, and another figure signifying life, may regularly be made known.

It is now fitting to teach this by examples from this volume, so that those first instructed by these examples may know that many mysteries are contained in it.

The first, the historical mode, is found where nothing spiritual is contained, as Samuel says: “Obedience is better than sacrifice,” and in a thousand similar passages.

The second, the allegorical mode, is found where it is said that throughout all the borders of Israel a beautiful young girl was sought for King David, to sleep in his bosom and warm him, yet so chaste that, when she warmed him, she did not provoke him to lust. She signifies wisdom, which does not grow old even in the aged, but kindles her lovers, whose limbs are growing cold, with a greater fire.

The third, the mode involving both, is shown in David, where he is said to have looked imprudently upon Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, and to have sinned, so that it might be demonstrated that no one ought to look carelessly upon a woman according to the historical sense. In that deed, however, an allegorical meaning is also contained, as we have explained abundantly in its proper place.

The fourth mode is where the Divinity is intimated to us in sacred speech, sometimes properly and sometimes tropically. Properly, as Elijah says: “The Lord lives, in whose sight I stand”; and: “For you are God in heaven above and on earth beneath”; and: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Tropically, according to Micah: “I saw the Lord sitting, and all the host of heaven standing beside him,” and other such passages, which are customarily understood figuratively rather than literally when spoken of God.

The fifth is the parabolic mode, in which one thing is said while another is found in the sacred pages. This is what is said in the title of Psalm 34: “A psalm for David, when he changed his appearance before Abimelech and dismissed him,” whereas in this book he is reported to have done this before King Achish. When, therefore, he placed Abimelech in the place of Achish, he warned the reader, through the interpretation of the name itself, to penetrate more deeply into the hidden mystery, which we have set out below in its proper place.

The same mode applies to the statement: “The thorn-bush that is in Lebanon sent to the cedar that is in Lebanon, that it should give him its daughter,” and what follows.

As for the sixth mode, in which the twofold coming of Christ is contained, it is clear to everyone which was the first and which will be the future one; both are prefigured here.

The seventh mode, which retains the twofold character of the commandments, concerns the conduct of life, as in the example: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself”; for “whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law.” David fulfilled this not only in Jonathan but also in Saul, whom he loved although he was his enemy. Scripture says of this: “David lamented over Saul and over his son,” and what follows.

This same mode concerns the figurative life, namely, through the arrangement of the fleshly sacrifices and vessels. The sacrifices prefigured what the Apostle urges when he says: “Present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God.” The vessels likewise signified the chosen, occupied with divine duties.

Although this mode seems similar to the second, it is distinguished by the fact that the present mode concerns morals alone, whereas the second must also be referred to faith.

Although these modes are found here in many ways, nevertheless, following the familiar threefold division, we have tried first to touch upon the historical sense, which draws out the deeds; then to disclose the allegorical meaning, which builds up faith; and finally to append the moral sense, which shapes an upright life. Thus the lazy reader, oppressed by the weight of a single interpretation or burdened by the mass of history and allegory, may not find an excuse for negligence, but may instead, even with this poverty of ours, run joyfully through the broad fields of the learned.

## Prologue

If, reader, you wish to discern the typological senses which this flowering book contains, enter [the final word(s) of this couplet are uncertain in the supplied OCR].

Behold, the two sacred volumes of Kings contain two pairs of matters, which were formerly made manifest in the clothed speech of a learned sage.

Our pen has undertaken to join them together, trusting in Christ,  
and at last our hand wished to weave them.

Entering the fields and meadows of the devout,  
may it pluck flowers through the aid of the Most High.  
From these may you receive the fragrances of the divine stock,  
and may you rightly be able to gather good fruits.  
It brings dishes exceedingly beautiful to noble minds,  
from which the hunger of the soul is driven far away.  
The pure-white lilies, with red violets, are fragrant,  
and cinnamon, rose, and rue are equally fragrant.  
Here are contained the exceedingly sacred graces of Christ,  
which previously lay hidden for a long time beneath their covering.  
Here it sets forth the most holy deeds of the prophets  
and sings the many mystical words of many men.  
What David did, and what his illustrious offspring sang,  
this little book, reader, contains here in typological form.

Here the four-horsed chariot of the Gospel resounds in its hall,  
and thus proves that it possesses apostolic light.

There you will find the hidden treasures of the Fathers,  
and here their manifold riches are contained.  
For it unveils hidden things and at last discloses mysteries,  
bringing into the open whatever secret things they contain.

to live with the Lord, possessing the kingdoms of heaven.

Therefore gladly and swiftly traverse the paths of this work;  
feed upon its little pages: the bee bears you honey.  
Take these riches; despise the perishable things of the world;  
keep always on your lips what this book sings.  
Willingly leave the pale, foul contagions of the flesh;

Remember the author when you read these verses:  
“O God, say to ANGELOMI: ‘Have mercy on him.’”

## Preface to the First Book

We find in the authors of the divine Scriptures that there are twenty-two letters among the Hebrews, something no one who has read them is unaware of. According to their number, they also reckon twenty-two books. Among these is included this Book of Kings, which we are about to discuss. In their reckoning it is considered third in order after Judges.

Although some people—ignorant of spiritual understanding or devoted solely to human wisdom—say that in this volume nothing can be understood except the surface of the history, the wars of kings and the deeds of many people, nevertheless it appears to contain many mysteries of Christ and the Church in various ways.

For from the very beginning of Kings, the priesthood is changed to Samuel after Eli is rejected, and the kingdom is changed to David after Saul is rejected. This cries out that a new priesthood and a new kingdom, with the old rejected—the old having been a shadow of what was to come—would arrive in the Lord Jesus Christ.

Did not David himself, when he ate the bread of the Presence, which no one was permitted to eat except priests, foreshadow in one person the future union of both, namely, kingdom and priesthood in the one Jesus Christ?

Thus the succession of Samuel the priest prefigured the new and, as foretold, eternal priesthood, which is Jesus Christ, after the priest Eli had been rejected—that is, after the Jewish priesthood had been cast aside.

Samuel’s mother herself, who had previously been barren and later rejoiced in fertility, whose name is Anna—that is, “grace”—signifies the Christian religion itself and, finally, the grace of God, because Christ rises for us. She also signifies the Church, once barren but now fruitful, rejoicing in the praises of God.

There are innumerable matters of this kind, by which it is demonstrated that this book breathes forth spiritual flowers and shines with allegorical meanings. Of these, if the Lord grants it, we shall write in their proper places, each one according to what we see to agree with reason.

Let these few matters, briefly presented for those who know, suffice for now. In the end, with the Lord’s favor, we have decided to come to the sequence of the history. In it we shall first lay down, wherever it is appropriate—or rather, wherever it agrees with the subject—the foundations of the history, and afterward strive to insert the summit of spiritual understanding, as well as, in certain places, the harmony of moral sweetness, so that the reader may not be satisfied with the historical statements alone, but may profitably gather the melody of allegories and morals.

But it should first be noted that Kings is rightly placed after Judges, as we have said: either because now there are rulers of the Church, but afterward there will be a kingdom, or because judgment will come first and everlasting dominion will follow. For the sacred account says:

## Chapter One

“There was a certain man from Ramathaim Sophim, from Mount Ephraim, and his name was Elkanah, son of Jeroham, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph, an Ephraimite.”

Since in the prologue—or rather, in the introduction—we promised first to establish the foundations of the history and afterward the summit of allegory, inserting the harmony of morality wherever it should be pleasing, we therefore judge it fitting first to set forth the historical account of the generation of the holy prophet Samuel, so that afterward, with the Lord’s favor, we may be able to direct its allegory continuously.

His father Elkanah was from the tribe of Levi, but not from the line of Aaron the priest. That his father was from the tribe of Levi is most clearly demonstrated by the Books of Chronicles, where the line of descent is brought down to Levi. For he is said to have been the son of “Jeroham, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph, son of Elkanah, son of Mahath, son of Amasai, son of Elkanah, son of Joel, son of Azariah, son of Zephaniah, son of Tahath, son of Assir, son of Abiasaph, son of Korah, son of Izhar, son of Levi” (*1 Chronicles* 6), and so forth. His genealogy is shown here to agree with this. We shall try in what follows to bring this genealogy into harmony with the spiritual understanding.

His mother too is shown to have been from the tribe of Judah because he is called an Ephrathite. He is called an Ephrathite from Ephrath, the wife of Caleb, who is known to have been from the tribe of Judah; he is also so called from the city Ephrath—that is, Bethlehem—because Bethlehem was formerly called Ephrath. We also read that the patriarch Judah had a son called Shelah (*Genesis* 38). To Shiloh, therefore, Elkanah went up with his household on the appointed days, according to the law, to worship and sacrifice to the Lord of hosts.

But when Scripture says “at the appointed times,” it means the three festivals: Passover, Pentecost, and the solemnity of Tabernacles. Thus the Lord commanded in Exodus, saying: “Three times in each year you shall celebrate festivals for me” (*Exodus* 23). And again: “Three times a year every male of yours shall appear before the Lord your God, in the place that the Lord your God will choose” (*Exodus* 23).

Therefore, at that time the ark of the Lord was in Shiloh.

Shiloh is a city in the tribe of Ephraim, where the ark of the covenant and the tabernacle of the Lord remained from the time of Joshua son of Nun, after he had conquered the nations possessing the Promised Land, until the time of Samuel. For it is related in the Book of Joshua that the aforesaid leader, after lots had been cast there before the Lord, assigned the Promised Land to the individual tribes.

It is beyond doubt that, among all the tribes in which the Levites had settlements, Ramathaim was one of their dwelling places. It is the city called Arimathea in the Gospels, and the Gospels confirm that Joseph came from there (*Matthew* 27; *Mark* 15; *Luke* 23; *John* 19). It is a city in the region of Tamnitis, near Diospolis.

It should be noted that, according to the Hebrew truth, the name is not Ramathaim but Armatha or Armathaim, as we read in books of places. Likewise, in the interpretations of Hebrew names, Armathaim is found, which we do not hesitate to read in this way. Hence it is called Armathia, and it is interpreted as “two heights” or “their heights.”

“Two heights” is appropriate according to the historical sense, since the two tribes understood here are the royal and the priestly, namely Judah and Levi, from which his father and mother came.

“Sophim” is interpreted as “watcher” or “watchmen.” Here perhaps the prophets are understood, whose son Elkanah would be.

If anyone is troubled by the fact that he is called an Ephrathite, rather than an Ephraimite, let him observe that David too is later called the son of an Ephrathite (*1 Samuel* 17), although it is plainly evident that Jesse, David’s father, was not from Ephraim but from the tribe of Judah. Thus the same Elkanah is called an Ephrathite from Ephrath, rather than from Ephraim, as the context shows.

He lived among the citizens of Ephraim’s allotment, inhabiting the city of Ramathaim Sophim. For this reason Scripture mentions that he was from Mount Ephraim.

“Now he had two wives: the name of one was Anna, and the name of the second was Phenenna. Phenenna had children, but Anna had no children.”

Accordingly, Anna’s barrenness is appropriately mentioned, since her childbirth was destined to be renowned, like that of the earlier patriarchs. The intention was to introduce greater joy after prolonged sorrow because of the fertility received by the parents.

For just as Sarah, the legitimate wife whom the patriarch Abraham married first, was initially barren while the Egyptian Hagar bore a son; and just as Rachel, for whom Jacob served his father-in-law, was barren while her sister Leah bore children (*Genesis* 16; 29–30), so also Elkanah’s better wife, who bore the prophet, was at first barren and afterward, through the Lord’s grace, became fruitful, so that by such a birth the greatness of the future prophet might also be demonstrated.

“Now the man went up from his city at the appointed days to worship and sacrifice to the Lord of hosts at Shiloh,” and so forth.

Shiloh was in the tribe of Ephraim, where the ark of the covenant and the tabernacle of the Lord remained from the time of Joshua son of Nun until the time of Samuel.

Since Elkanah himself was a Levite, after offering the sacrifices he ate together with his wives, sons, and daughters.

“And he gave portions to Phenenna his wife, and to all her sons and daughters. But to Anna he gave one portion, sorrowful, because he loved Anna. Now the Lord had closed her womb. Her rival also afflicted her and troubled her greatly, so much so that she reproached her because the Lord had closed her womb,” and what follows.

When it says, “He gave portions to Phenenna his wife, and to all her sons and daughters,” these portions are understood as portions of the sacrifices, which he gave from the animals that had been sacrificed according to the custom of the law. Although the opinion of the Jews wishes the portions to be understood as garments, “he gave one portion to Anna, sorrowful.” She was sorrowful because the Lord had closed her womb.

When it adds, “Her rival also afflicted her,” and so forth, it demonstrates that just as Hagar, after conceiving, despised the barren Sarah, so Phenenna, fruitful in offspring, rivaled the barren Anna. For it is a consolation to the wicked to find fault with the lives of the good.

She wept and did not take bodily food with gladness; rather, according to the prophet, “My tears have been my bread day and night,” and she mingled her drink with weeping (*Psalm* 41).

“Anna rose after she had eaten in Shiloh and drunk, while Eli the priest was sitting upon his chair beside the doorpost of the temple.”

This Eli was the high priest and ruled the people of Israel after Samson. According to the book of the Hebrews, he ruled for forty years; according to the Septuagint interpreters, for twenty years.

“When she was bitter in soul, she prayed to the Lord, weeping abundantly, and made a vow, saying: ‘Lord of hosts, if you will look upon the affliction of your handmaid and remember me, and not forget your servant, and if you give your maidservant a male child, I will give him to the Lord all the days of his life,’” and what follows.

Perhaps she remembered the words of blessed Job, who said: “The one who is mocked by his friend, as I am, will call upon God and he will answer him, for he himself considers the labor and sorrow of his own” (*Job* 12). Of this it is written: “To you the poor man is abandoned; you are the helper of the orphan” (*Psalm* 9). The vows of the righteous are pleasing to him, and his eyes are upon their prayers.

[scan page 131]

“And so it happened that, while she multiplied her prayers before the Lord, Eli observed her mouth. Anna was speaking in her heart, and only her lips moved; her voice was not heard at all. Therefore Eli thought that she was drunk and said to her: ‘How long will you be drunk? Put away for a little while the wine with which you are soaked.’

“Anna answered: ‘Not so, my lord. I am an exceedingly unhappy woman, and I have drunk neither wine nor anything that can intoxicate; rather, I have poured out my soul in the sight of the Lord. Do not count your maidservant as one of the daughters of Belial, for out of the abundance of my pain and sorrow I have spoken until now.’”

“Belial” is interpreted as “without a yoke.”

Note that those who pursue drunkenness are called sons of Belial. Here is fulfilled what is written: “Man sees what is before his eyes, but God looks upon the heart” (*1 Samuel* 16), since Eli saw only the mouth of Anna as she prayed and did not hear her voice at all, but saw the movement of her lips and thought that she was drunk.

But she, because she lifted her heart upward and confessed to the Lord with her whole heart, was regarded by the Lord in her prayer, and he did not despise her petitions.

An excellent manner of praying has been given to us as an example: we should not form our prayers to the Lord through many words, but should believe that we shall be heard through contrition of heart and the outpouring of tears, because “a sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (*Psalm* 50).

This happens worthily if, when the prayer has been completed, we remain in the same course of righteousness. Hence it follows:

“And the woman went on her way and ate, and her face was no longer changed in different ways.”

“And it happened, after the cycle of days, that Anna conceived and bore a son, and she called his name Samuel, because she had asked him from the Lord.”

After the cycle of days—that is, after the return of the year—Anna bore a child and called his name Samuel. Samuel is interpreted as “petition of God,” or “his name is God,” because God was the author of his birth. He had been entreated by a barren woman and granted her a son who would be considered worthy to stand in the temple of God in his service all the days of his life.

Above he is called not merely “a man” but “one man,” because he was not wandering aimlessly in different directions, nor mobile and unstable, but was a firm and unshaken man who persevered.

Not only is the one who remains firm called “one man,” but all who are rightly ordered are called one: all who possess one wisdom, confess one Christ Jesus, and are filled with one Spirit of God. Every foolish person is not one but many. Hence Scripture says: “A fool is changed like the moon” (*Ecclesiasticus* 27). Although the moon appears to be one in substance, through its changes it is always itself another and different on different days. So sinners, who are changed from wisdom and knowledge and desire different things, become unstable in all their ways.

We have now briefly presented the historical account, but it is necessary finally to touch briefly upon the spiritual meaning.

This man Elkanah, whose name is interpreted as “possession of God,” bore the figure of the only Son of God, who is the true and special possession of God the Father. Of him Solomon says: “The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways” (*Proverbs* 8). And the Father says of him: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (*Matthew* 3 and 17). The same Son says in the Gospel: “The Father dwelling in me himself does the works” (*John* 14), and for this reason he is rightly called “one man.”

He is called “one,” not in the sense of number, but because he never becomes another from himself and therefore is never changed. Hence the Psalmist says: “But you are the same, and your years will not fail” (*Psalm* 101).

Armathaim Sophim, which is interpreted as “height” or “watchtower,” signifies the heavenly Jerusalem. Coming from there to us, he both taught that same contemplation and restored us to possess it through his death. Seated there at the right hand of the Father, he intercedes for us, according to the Apostle: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (*1 John* 2), and so forth.

He is rightly called the son of Jeroham, the son of Elihu, and the son of Suph, an Ephrathite.

Jeroham is interpreted as “merciful.” Elihu means “my God.” Suph means “pouring out.” These names, as it seems to us, are rightly referred to God the Father.

He is our mercy, because by his compassion it came about that the only-begotten Son, coming to us, redeemed us by his blood, according to what the Apostle says: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son for us” (*John* 3).

Laboring for us in his passion, he said: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (*Psalm* 21). Therefore he is called Suph, “pouring out,” because the Father poured him out from the bosom of his compassion from the heavenly places, so that he might empty and, in a certain sense, pour himself out, and set the human race free.

Hence Solomon says in the *Song of Songs*: “Your name is an ointment poured out” (*Song of Songs* 1). God’s name was poured-out ointment when, from the immensity of his divinity, he outwardly poured himself into our nature and made himself visible from what he had been as invisible.

For if he had not poured himself out, he would in no way have made himself known to us. Paul speaks of this outpouring: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself” (*Philippians* 2), and what follows.

What Paul calls “emptying,” Solomon called “pouring out.”

He is rightly called Ephrathite, for Ephrathite is interpreted as “fruitful.” This fits the only-begotten Son of God, for he is regarded as abounding in all the gifts and virtues of the Holy Spirit. Hence Isaiah says: “The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength” (*Isaiah* 11), and what follows.

It continues: “He had two wives: the name of one was Phenenna and the name of the second was Anna. Phenenna had children, but Anna had no children,” and what follows.

These two wives you should understand—

[The supplied source ends here, mid-sentence.]

[scan page 132]

## Expositions on the Books of Kings

Anna, that is, “grace,” and Phenennah, which is said to mean “conversion,” prefigured the image of two peoples, namely, the Church of the Gentiles and the Synagogue. For Phenennah prefigured the type of the Synagogue, which was first fruitful in children whom, through the preaching of the Law, it seemed to beget for God. But because it turned from the faith of the patriarchs and prophets to unbelief, it remains barren.

Anna, however, the barren woman—whose name is interpreted as “grace”—signified the Church of the Gentiles, which is known to have been redeemed by the grace of the holy Savior. Accordingly, the Apostle says: “For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God” (Ephesians 2). And again: “I will call the one who was not my people, ‘my people,’ and the one who had not obtained mercy, ‘the one who has obtained mercy’” (Romans 9), and so forth.

She is called barren, in accordance with what is written: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not suffer birth-pangs, because the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isaiah 54). Of her the Psalmist also says: “He makes the barren woman dwell in a house, a joyful mother of children” (Psalm 112).

This barren woman was barren of the fruitfulness of spiritual offspring, yet she did not cease to beget spiritual children for God through the font of baptism and the grace of the Holy Spirit. Concerning her, the Apostle says in the Song of Songs: “Our sister is little, and she has no breasts” (Song of Songs 8). What, then, shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be addressed? “She is little,” they say, because the mystery of preaching is not yet sufficient for her to undertake, so that she might be able to beget children from the inward mysteries or nourish them from her breasts.

What, then, does it seem to you, O Synagogue, should be done for our sister when she is to be addressed—that is, when she is to be led to faith through the mystery of the word—so that she who now appears barren may be able to beget spiritual children? While the Synagogue is silent, the Bridegroom, or the Apostles, answer what ought to be done: “If she is a wall, let us build upon her silver battlements,” that is, the knowledge of the divine Scriptures, so that she may be able not only to protect the weak but also to teach the unlearned, lest she remain barren forever.

Although she was then a wife in the predestination of divine grace, in accordance with what the Bridegroom says of her: “I have compared you, my beloved, to my mare in Pharaoh’s chariots” (Song of Songs 1)—that is, you were still serving inwardly in Pharaoh’s chariots, still running inwardly in paganism—but I considered what, through predestination, he made of you: “I have compared you to my mare,” that is, I considered you like my chosen ones.

Yet because the Bridegroom had not yet redeemed her with his own blood, nor betrothed her, she was considered barren, because she was not joined to him through faith. Rather, as we have said, the Synagogue seemed to give birth to children for him, as it were, through the Law.

We have touched on these matters briefly, as we have said; but in what follows, after certain passages that appear to have been interpolated into the history, we shall try to describe them more fully.

There were elsewhere two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, priests of the Lord. Since the historical sense is plain, let us turn it toward the spiritual understanding. Hophni, whose name is interpreted as “unshod,” without the madness of conversion, and Phinehas, whose name means “mute mouth,” signify the scribes and Pharisees of the Jews.

They are rightly called sons of Eli, who bore the type of the Jewish priesthood because of the carnal sacrifices of the Law and of their priesthood. For the scribes and Pharisees, seeking to establish their own righteousness, as the Apostle says (Romans 10), and refusing submission to God’s righteousness, did not wish to be subject to it or to receive the one whom the Law and the prophets had foretold would come. Thus, degenerating from the faith of the patriarchs and prophets and turning to the madness of unbelief, they deserved to have a mute mouth.

They were excluded from the true priesthood of Christ and from the confession of the true Priest, concerning whom it is written: “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: ‘You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek’” (Psalm 109).

And because they wished to claim for themselves the Church that properly belonged to Christ, who was the true Bridegroom, and did not wish to raise up the seed of faith in the name of their deceased brother—that is, of Christ—in accordance with what was written in the Law, they did not deserve to have a share in their lot.

Of them the Apostle says: “And with your feet shod in the preparation of the gospel of peace” (Ephesians 6). And through the prophet it is said: “How beautiful are the feet of those who announce good things” (Romans 10). Therefore they remained naked and unshod, deprived of the true faith and the dignity of the priesthood.

John feared to do this when he said: “I am not the Christ; after me comes one mightier than I, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to loosen” (John 1). It is as though he said: “I cannot uncover the footsteps of the Redeemer, because I do not presumptuously usurp the Bridegroom’s name.”

Because the scribes and Pharisees attempted to usurp this improperly—claiming for themselves the name of the Bridegroom, which belongs to Christ—and moreover despised him, indeed did not hesitate to spit in his face, their name is rightly called “the house of the unshod,” as it is written in the Law (Deuteronomy 25). Thus they remained naked of every dignity and unshod of the examples of the patriarchs and prophets.

Hence Shiloh is suitably applied to them, where they are said to have been priests. For Shiloh is interpreted as “his dismissal” or “petition.” Since they themselves petitioned Pilate to release Barabbas and hand Jesus over to them (Matthew 27), they were turned toward the madness of cruelty and cried out: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend” (John 19). And again: “Crucify him, crucify him” (Luke 23).

They were rightly dismissed and abandoned by God, stripped of every goodness, handed over to the Gentiles, and deprived of priesthood and kingdom; naked in the numbness of unbelief, they grew cold among the nations.

It follows: “Therefore Elkanah gave portions to Phenennah and to her sons and daughters. But to Anna he gave one portion, because he loved Anna.”

We have already explained above that Phenennah represented the Synagogue, which received from God portions with its sons and daughters, insofar as this pertains to the allegorical sense—namely, the temporal goods of the land of promise. Accordingly, the Psalmist says: “He gave them the lands of the nations, and they possessed the labors of the peoples,” so that they might observe his justifications and seek his law (Psalm 104). For to them were first entrusted the oracles of God, the legislation, the covenant, the restoration, and the rest.

Although she had been ungrateful, he gave Anna one sorrowful portion. For the portion that the Creator of all things bestowed upon Anna—that is, upon the Church of the Gentiles—may be understood as the natural understanding by which she was able to know God.

The outstanding preacher, describing this to the Romans, says: “For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that have been made” (Romans 1). His eternal power and divinity are also evident. Hence, speaking beforehand of the wise men of this world, he says: “Because what can be known of God is manifest among them” (ibid.). God manifested it to them, but he rightly calls her sorrowful, because the Lord had closed her womb.

For this reason she anxiously bore the fact that she could not spiritually beget children for God, since the time of his showing mercy had not yet come, when her barrenness would be opened and she would be made fruitful by spiritual grace.

Considering her fruitfulness from afar, Isaiah cried out: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear” (Isaiah 54), and so forth. After this barrenness, the Church was sorrowful, because she not only did not give birth to others but also regarded herself as barren through the grace of the Lord’s Incarnation and through the loss of the Law. Yet she was able to understand this through natural understanding.

Because the Lord loved her—not as she then was, but as she was to be in predestination—she understood this through natural understanding. But because the Synagogue did not know this predestination and future grace, it despised paganism and even pursued it with hatred.

He marvels at how the people of the Gentiles, cleansed by no mystery of circumcision and instructed by no admonitions of the prophets, suddenly rose from the lowest pleasures through the wilderness of paganism to the heights of virtue and to the embrace of the Bridegroom.

And he rightly says: “Like a column of smoke from the perfumes of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer”—that is, kindled by the fire of love or striving toward heavenly things with every effort of virtue.

Myrrh signifies the mortification of carnal pleasures; frankincense, the purity of prayers; and in the various powders of the perfumer is understood the fragrance of all virtues.

Elsewhere, therefore, the astonished Synagogue says: “I did not know it; my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Aminadab” (Song of Songs 6). It is as though she said: “I did not know, O Church of the Gentiles, that the gifts of spiritual grace were in you; but my soul troubled me because of the introduction of the New Testament and the evangelical chariot.”

For Aminadab is interpreted as “my willing people,” that is, Christ, who freely bestowed his grace upon the Church, which is already carried throughout the whole world.

But because the Church had not yet received that grace and remained barren and sorrowful, it is rightly added: “Her rival also afflicted and vexed her greatly, so that she reproached her because the Lord had closed her womb.”

No reader can doubt that the Synagogue of the Jews persecuted the Church of the Gentiles and, because of its worship of idols, despised and reproached it. Moreover, the primitive Church itself, still ignorant of the mystery of its salvation, wanted to rebuke Peter because he had entered Cornelius’s house and eaten with Gentiles. But when Peter recounted the divine grace bestowed upon them, they glorified God (Acts 11).

Regarding this contempt for idolatry, the Church from the Gentiles replied to the Synagogue, saying: “Do not consider that I am dark, because the sun has discolored me” (Song of Songs 1). It was as though she openly said: “I am dark because I am sinful, because my sun has discolored me”—that is, my Creator abandoned me when I was placed in error and withdrew the rays of his discipline.

“I have fallen into error,” she says, and therefore adds: “The sons of my mother fought against me” (ibid.). The sons of the mother are understood as the spirits of the world, because we and the angels were created by the one grace of God’s goodness and power. Since we are rational beings, we have, as it were, a fellowship of brotherhood.

But because the fallen angels, both before the Savior’s coming and daily, wage war against the Church of the Gentiles, she says: “The sons of my mother fought against me.” It is as though she said: “Because my Creator abandoned me in paganism, the sons of my mother fought against me.”

[scan page 133]

## Angelomus of Luxeuil, Monk

The Church says: “Do not despise me, O Synagogue, because, although I am dark in merit, I am beautiful through the grace of divine predestination.” But for this reason the Synagogue despises the Church: it considered what she was, but, as we have said, did not know what she would become.

Later, however, considering the Church, which by natural understanding, illuminated by divine grace, was coming to Christ, it says: “Who is this who comes up through the wilderness like a column of smoke, from the perfumes of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer?” (Song of Songs 3).

Thus it says: “Like a column of smoke from the perfumes of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer,” that is, kindled by the fire of love and striving toward heavenly things with every effort of virtue. By myrrh is understood the mortification of carnal pleasures; by frankincense, the purity of prayers; and by the various powders of the perfumer, the fragrance of all virtues.

Therefore elsewhere, astonished, the Synagogue says: “I did not know it; my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Aminadab” (Song of Songs 6). It is as though she said: “I did not know, O Church of the Gentiles, that the gifts of spiritual grace were in you, but my soul troubled me because of the introduction of the New Testament and the evangelical chariot.”

Aminadab is interpreted as “my willing people,” that is, Christ, who freely bestows his grace upon the Church, which is already borne throughout the whole world.

But because the Church had not yet received that grace and remained barren and sorrowful, it is rightly added: “She wept and did not take food.” Therefore her husband Elkanah said to her: “Anna, why are you weeping? Why do you not eat? Why is your heart afflicted? Am I not better for you than ten sons?”

For it says: “She wept and did not take food.” This is what blessed Job says, speaking of the same Church of the Gentiles, which desired the coming of its Redeemer: “Will the wild ass bray when it has grass?” (Job 6).

What is signified by the wild ass—that is, the untamed ass—if not the people of the Gentiles? As nature brought it forth outside the stalls of discipline, so it remained wandering in the field of its pleasures.

From the life of blessed Job we learn that many even among the Gentiles awaited the Redeemer’s coming. The grass of the wild ass, therefore, is this very Incarnation of the Mediator, by which the Gentiles themselves are now nourished.

For since it is said through the prophet: “All flesh is grass,” the Creator of the universe, taking flesh from our substance, willed to become grass, so that our flesh might not remain grass forever (Isaiah 40). The wild ass found grass when the people of the Gentiles received the grace of the divine Incarnation.

But because the life of the elect among the Gentiles was delayed, they groaned for a long time while awaiting their redemption and did not deserve to receive that grace by which they might be made fruitful and satisfied with the food of which the Lord says: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6).

It is rightly said: “Anna wept and did not take food.” And because the Church persevered in prayer for this grace of the Redeemer, at last he himself, through the mystery of his Incarnation, brought her consolation.

Hence it is said: “Anna, why are you weeping? Am I not better for you than ten sons?” Truly, I say, truly does the word of divine consolation speak: her husband, namely the Lord Christ, is better for the Church than ten sons.

Those ten sons signify the ones whom the Synagogue seemed to beget for God through the Law. Yet she loves him many times more—indeed, she loves the grace of evangelical preaching that was given through him more than those whom she bore carnally.

He loves the Church, and she is loved by him. For it is written: “My beloved is mine, and I am his” (Song of Songs 2).

The Church loves Christ so greatly that she not only despises everything for his sake, both the adversities and prosperities of the world, but also does not fear to die for love of him. Concerning this love, although it may be understood otherwise, the Song of Songs says: “Love is strong as death” (Song of Songs 8).

But because the Church persevered in the same grace and love that she had received, it is rightly said of her, after certain intervening words, that “her face was no longer turned in different directions.” For the Church was not changed in the knowledge of faith or in love of her Redeemer, nor could she, by turning aside in another direction, fall away from the grace of devotion that she had received.

As far as the historical sense is concerned, however, it is also rightly said: “Her face was no longer turned in different directions,” namely, because she did not doubt that she would obtain from God what she asked in faith, or because she remained in the true affection of compunction until she had obtained what she requested.

Here an example of prayer is given: whoever desires to be heard ought to persevere in the state in which he wishes to be found in prayer. If he once receives the grace of compunction through purity of mind, he ought to remain in that same purity of mind and not turn aside into any wantonness until he obtains the object of his will for which he asks.

Indeed, he must persevere until he receives the offspring of divine contemplation. If he desires this, it is not enough to experience compunction once; rather, he must be cleansed continually through the grace of compunction, in accordance with what the Psalmist says: “Establish a solemn day with frequent attendance, even to the horns of the altar” (Psalm 117).

The solemn day is compunction of our heart before the Lord. But the day is established with frequent attendance when the mind is continually moved to tears through love of the Lord.

If we were to ask, “How long?” he adds: “Even to the horns of the altar.” The horn of the altar is the exaltation of the inner sacrifice, that is, the contemplation of the divine vision.

Hence the soul, already pierced by love and longing, says in the Song of Songs: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song of Songs 1). For the soul kisses God as often as it is pierced by compunction in his love.

It says: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” It is as though it openly said: “Let the grace of his compunction touch me.” Or certainly, the kiss of his mouth is the perfection of inner peace. When we reach it, nothing more will remain for us to seek.

Therefore we ought to remain in the same grace of compunction like Anna and not turn our face in another direction until we attain the offspring of divine contemplation.

Up to this point we have tried to describe Elkanah, his two wives, their portions, and the other matters that we inserted, insofar as we were able to understand them and learned them from the transmitter. If anyone dislikes these interpretations and can find better ones, we have judged these worth following, because we have preferred to follow another’s understanding rather than serve obstinacy.

Having described these matters, we shall, with the Lord’s favor, turn our style to what follows. But first it should be noted that some, according to ethical discipline—that is, what they otherwise call the tropological sense—wish Elkanah, whose name is interpreted as “possession of the Lord,” to be understood as any holy and perfect preacher whose mind the Lord possesses.

By the two wives, Phenennah and Anna, they designate the active and contemplative life. Phenennah, fruitful in children and called “conversion,” designates the active life; Anna, barren and interpreted as “grace,” designates the contemplative life.

The active life consists in giving bread to the hungry, teaching the ignorant the word of wisdom, correcting the one who errs, recalling the proud neighbor to the way of humility, caring for the sick, and distributing whatever is useful to each person.

It is not improperly signified by fruitful Phenennah, whose name means “conversion,” because the active life has many actions by which it can assist its neighbors, toward which it must diligently turn.

It is fruitful in sons and daughters because it gives birth to works that, although strong, seem weak in comparison with contemplation. These works are signified by sons and daughters.

The contemplative life, however, consists in retaining the love of God and neighbor with the whole mind while resting from exterior action and clinging only to the desire for the Creator, so that the soul no longer wishes to do anything else but, having trampled all cares underfoot, burns with desire to see the face of its Creator.

This is signified by Anna, whose name means “grace,” but who is barren. She is rightly called barren because no one can penetrate contemplative life as it truly is. Or because no one is sufficient to preach fully what he experiences in it, so as to be able through preaching to beget many children.

Thus Anna, whose name means “grace,” is rightly taken as its figure, because no one is sufficient to attain it except through divine grace.

It is rightly described as having two wives, because no preacher is perfect unless he knows how to practice both lives. He must pass from the embraces of Phenennah to the embraces of Anna: he must first exercise himself in the active life so that, after begetting many children, he may afterward be bound more closely to the contemplative life, remain in its contemplation with his whole desire, and beget perfect works.
