He gives portions to these wives and to their sons and daughters because the highest man, whether he has created weak or strong works, always strives to labor more, bringing virtue upon virtue, so that perfection may eventually be attained in contemplation.

[scan page 135]

He who wishes to become God’s possession must have these two wives: first the active life, and afterward pass to the contemplative. Or, to put it differently, he must join to himself the nobler one, Anna, that is, grace.

For grace is first joined to a person through faith, as the Apostle says: “For by grace you have been saved through faith” (Ephesians 2). Phenennah is joined second, that is, to conversion, because after the grace of belief there must be the correction of conduct.

Phenennah first bears children, because the first fruits are offered through conversion. Unless we are converted, we cannot attain the embrace of Anna and beget children. For where the spirit of grace is, there God is said to be.

Hence Paul says: “Falling on his face, he will adore God, declaring that God is truly among you” (1 Corinthians 14). Therefore, unless works of conversion precede, we cannot beget the gifts of the divine Spirit.

This has been said beforehand, but it must be understood that God is found not only by the voice but also by the heart. Hence blessed Job says: “Who will grant me a hearer, so that the Almighty may hear my desire?” (Job 31). He does not say “my prayers,” but “my desire.” For the one who truly asks is not first in his voice, but in the thoughts of his heart.

Hence it is said to Moses: “Why do you cry out to me?” (Exodus 14), when he was saying nothing at all with his mouth. Hence Anna earlier was indeed silent with her mouth, yet poured forth all the voices of her desire. As it is written: “Anna was speaking in her heart, and only her lips were moving.”

For this reason the Lord says in the Gospel: “Enter into your room and, having closed the door, pray to your Father; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matthew 6).

He prays with the door closed in his room who, silent with his mouth, pours forth the affection of his mind in the sight of heavenly mercy. His voice is heard in secret when, through holy desires, he is silently answered.

Hence it is said: “The Lord has heard the desire of the poor.” And because Anna thus petitioned the Lord, she deserved to be heard for the child.

“She conceived and bore a son, and she called his name Samuel, because she had asked him from the Lord” (1 Samuel 1).

In the same way, the holy Church conceived in her heart, through natural understanding, the grace of faith and the mystery of the Incarnation, and deserved to give birth through the confession of her mouth. For, according to the Apostle: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10).

Hence the angel says to Cornelius: “Your prayers and your almsgiving have been heard in the sight of God” (Acts 10), and so forth.

“She called the child,” he says, “Samuel.” Samuel, whose name is interpreted as “his name is God,” was Anna’s firstborn, adorned with prophetic grace. Who else should be understood by him but the man who is the Lord—namely, our Redeemer?

For of him it is written: “The Almighty himself will come and save us” (Isaiah 35). He is also called a prophet, in accordance with what Moses says: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers; you shall hear him” (Deuteronomy 18; Acts 3, 7).

Samuel’s name therefore aptly agrees with Christ, because the whole Church confesses him to be both God and man. Concerning him it is added: “She took him with her after she had weaned him, with three calves, three measures of flour, and a vessel of wine, and brought him into the house of the Lord at Shiloh.”

He rightly says: “After she had weaned him,” because Anna, that is, the holy Church from the nations, first nourished the child whom she had conceived in her heart.

This child is Samuel, whose name may be understood as “God,” because where the spirit of grace is, there God is said to be. First she nurtured him with milk, whom she had conceived in her heart through the simple understanding of faith.

Concerning this the Apostle says: “I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Corinthians 3), because he taught and preached the mystery of the Incarnation and the Cross.

Hence the same outstanding preacher says again: “I judged that I knew nothing among you except the Lord Jesus Christ, and him crucified: to the Jews a stumbling block, but to the Gentiles foolishness” (1 Corinthians 2).

And rightly does he say, “with three calves.” For the three calves signify, as tradition has handed down to us, three periods: before the Law, under the examples of the patriarchs; under the Law, through the sayings of the prophets, by whom the Lord was prefigured and awaited by the Church; and in the third period, the time of grace.

When he appeared, the Church received faith by believing and in some manner presented the preaching, because it openly acknowledged its faith.

Hence it follows: “And with three measures of flour.” By the three measures of flour we should understand three virtues joined together in the unity of faith: faith, hope, and charity, which the Church offered in perfection.

Alternatively, the three measures of flour may be understood as the three sons of Noah, whom the believing Church brought to salvation and offered to God through confession.

Some also understand in the measures of flour the body of the Lord, and in the vessel of wine the mystery of his blood—mysteries that the Church celebrates daily by offering and receives as a model for imitation.

These are the gifts that the Church of the Gentiles offers for the child, showing that she has begotten a child—that is, that she has truly received the perfect faith of Christ—and that she wishes to demonstrate this faith through her works.

“And she brought him to Shiloh, into the house of the Lord.” When the primitive Church from the Synagogue of the Jews, which had been called the house of God, joined itself to the same perfect faith, to the mystery of Christ’s Incarnation, and to the triumph of the Cross, it entered the house of the Lord.

Concerning this it is said: “Holiness befits your house” (Psalm 92).

Let us also explain the matter according to the opinion of some. Where it says: “She brought him with her after she had weaned him, with three calves and three measures of flour,” the Hebrews say that the text does not contain “three measures” but “one ephah of flour.” They think that the Latin manuscripts have been corrupted and that she did not offer three measures contrary to the precept of the Law.

For there it is prescribed that a tenth of an ephah of fine flour be offered with each calf, two tenths with a ram, and one tenth with a lamb. This tenth was the tenth part of an ephah. Hence it may be understood that she could not offer three measures of flour with three calves, but rather nine tenths, from which, according to Hebrew measurement, one ephah is made.

Allegorically, however, the fact that he was brought to the house of the Lord before he was weaned signifies that Mother Church does not advance any of her children to the priesthood before she has educated them from the milk of infancy and the smallness of understanding and made them capable of spiritual doctrine.

“For everyone who partakes of milk,” says the Apostle, “is inexperienced in the word of righteousness” (Hebrews 5).

He offers him with three calves, a measure of flour, and a vessel of wine—that is, in the sacrifice of faithful confession, in the practice of good works, and in the grace of sacred instruction—fully instructed in the faith of the Holy Trinity.

Such a person can say with the prophet: “We shall render to the Lord the calves of our lips” (Hosea 14), and, remaining continually in the house of God, offer worthily the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood.

It follows: “And Anna prayed and said:”

## Chapter 2

“My heart has exulted in the Lord, and my horn has been exalted in my God.”

Here Anna most clearly seems to prophesy in her song, as we said above, the change from the Old Testament, or priesthood, to the New Testament, or priesthood, which is Christ. Some, however, say that she did not prophesy but merely praised God exultantly because she had obtained a son.

What does she mean, then, when she says:

“The bows of the mighty have been overcome, and the weak have been girded with strength; those who were previously full have hired themselves out for bread, and the hungry have been satisfied, until the barren woman bore seven, while she who had many children languished”?

Did she herself bear seven, although she was barren? When she said these things she had only one child; nor did she later bear seven sons, whether six in addition to Samuel, making Samuel the seventh, but rather three sons and two daughters.

Moreover, at that time no one yet ruled over that people. What she placed at the end—“he gives strength to kings, and exalts the horn of his Christ”—is therefore prophetic.

If she was not prophesying, let the Jews be silent, and let those many people be silent who think that these words refer historically only to the son she received.

Let Anna speak prophetically, foreseeing the fruitfulness of the Church in herself. Let the Church of Christ also speak—the city of the great King, full of grace and fruitful in offspring—and say: “My heart has exulted in the Lord.”

The heart of the holy Church does not exult in earthly matters, because someone may rejoice in the flesh without glorying in the joy of earthly things; rather, it exults in the Lord, in accordance with Paul’s admonition: “Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1).

Hence in the Song of Songs, in the voice of the elect, it is said: “We shall exult and rejoice in you” (Song of Songs 1). It is as though it openly said: “We shall exult and rejoice not in ourselves but in you,” because we recognize that we have arrived at the heights of contemplation through divine grace.

[scan page 136]

We take our hope in you for the forgiveness of sins, because we are weak. Hence it is rightly added: “And my horn has been exalted in my God.”

What, then, should we understand by the horn of the Church except its kingdom? For just as the horn rises above the flesh, so the kingdom of the holy Church transcends the adversities of this world and the desires of the flesh.

This kingdom is said to have been exalted in the Lord because it is raised everywhere by him. The primitive Church possessed this kingdom within the narrow boundaries of Judea, but now it is expanded and exalted among the Gentiles.

Hence the prophet says to it: “Enlarge the place of your tent, stretch out the curtains of your dwellings, strengthen your stakes, and extend the skins of your tents” (Isaiah 54). “You will penetrate to the right and to the left, and your offspring will inherit the nations.”

This has been enlarged and extended through the Apostle. The Church of the Gentiles received the kingdom of the Synagogue, and, rejoicing in its preachers, speaks in what follows, saying: “My mouth has been enlarged over my enemies.”

The holy preachers of the Church are therefore understood by this: their preaching or faith has been enlarged over its enemies, because it surpassed the knowledge of the scribes and heretics, and especially of its persecutors, in accordance with what had been promised to it through the prophet: “You will overcome the tongue that resists you in judgment” (Isaiah 54).

For the word of God is not bound in the narrow confines of persecutions, according to the Apostle (2 Timothy 2). The Church has rejoiced in the salvation of God.

“Salvation of God” means the Son of God. Simeon, receiving him in his arms, said joyfully: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, in peace, according to your word, because my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared before the face of all peoples” (Luke 2).

The patriarch Jacob also spoke of him, saying: “I shall await your salvation, O Lord” (Genesis 49).

Considering his magnificence and power, Anna says: “There is none holy like the Lord; indeed, there is none besides you, and there is none strong like our God,” and so forth.

She almost says: “There is none holy like the Lord,” because no one can compare with his holiness. She uses a distinction, as the Lord said: no one is like the Lord, who is holy and sanctifies, righteous and justifies.

The Psalmist considered this when he said: “Who among the clouds is equal to the Lord, or who is like God among the sons of God?” (Psalm 88).

Therefore it is rightly added: “There is none besides you, and there is none strong like our God.” No one becomes holy unless he has been sanctified by him. Nor can anyone even exist or possess any strength unless he has received it from him.

Hence the Apostle Paul says: “In him we live and move and exist” (Acts 17). The Truth himself says to his disciples: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15).

And although there are said to be many gods and many lords, none of them is by nature what God is. For what is a shadow in comparison with a body, or smoke in comparison with fire?

This he considered…

[Scan p. 137]

## Angelomus, Monk of Luxeuil

Abraham, when he was speaking with the Lord, says: “I shall speak to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes” (Genesis 18). In comparison with such great majesty, although he was rich, he recognized that he was nothing other than ash and dust.

The scribes, Pharisees, and the other worldly wise, however, disdain to consider these things. Therefore it is added concerning them:

“Do not multiply lofty words, boasting; let old things depart from your mouth,” and so forth.

Holy Church reproves the Jews and the wise of this age who exalt themselves against the knowledge of God, so that they may not become proud or think wrongly about God, but may think and speak humbly. For it is written: “The Lord is in heaven, and you are upon the earth” (2 Maccabees 15). Therefore let your words be few. Let, I say, the old things of the Law depart from their mouths—everything belonging to the old man, that is, to carnal conduct. But let them diligently seek the knowledge that comes from God; let them not boast in a human and carnal knowledge of the Law; let no empty speech come from their mouths; and let them know that no one can possess the knowledge of truth unless he has received it from God: “For he is the Lord of knowledge, and it is necessary that good thoughts be prepared by him.”

For it is written: “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit and withdraw from thoughts that lack understanding. For wisdom will not enter a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wisdom 1). The Spirit also searches the deep things of God (1 Corinthians 2).

But because the Jews, boasting in the Law, seeking higher things, and failing to know that God is the Lord of knowledge and the judge of consciences, despised acting rightly and were carnal in their wisdom, they fell from the arrogance of their pride and were humbled. For it follows:

“The bow of the mighty has been overcome, and the weak have been girded with strength.”

The word “bow” in sacred speech sometimes signifies the day of judgment, according to what is said through the Psalmist: “You have shown your people hard things; you have given us wine of compunction. You have given a sign to those who fear you, that they may flee from before the bow” (Psalm 59). At other times it signifies the sacred Scriptures, as the same Prophet says: “He bent his bow and prepared it, and in it he prepared vessels of death” (Psalm 7), and so forth. At other times the ambushes and intentions of the wicked are represented by it, as we read in the Psalm: “They have bent their bow to shoot bitter things” (Psalm 36).

Hence in this passage too it is said: “The bow of the mighty has been overcome.” For because the Jews were unwilling to bend the hardness of the Law, like the horns of a bow, toward the hearts of the New Testament, but wished to think carnally, and attempted by their perverse intentions to overcome the preaching of the Savior, thinking wrongly about him, despising his Church, and preparing their bow to shoot bitter things, they were cast down and humbled.

Well, therefore, is it said: “The bow of the mighty has been overcome.” That is, the perverse intention of the Jews, because they thought wrongly, has been weakened in the New Testament, having been brought forth from the Old Testament.

For because they boasted carnally in the Law and wished in a certain way to defend it, they were weakened; and the evil which they had intended to shoot from the quiver of their jealousy turned back upon themselves. The bow is turned against the one who draws it, because the wickedness of their evil intention, by which Jewish perfidy wished to exercise itself from the quiver of its jealousy, was turned back upon it. Condemned for the wickedness of its unbelief, it lost the grace of strength in which it boasted that it could fulfill the Law by human sufficiency without divine assistance. That same grace of strength was received, by the Lord’s gift, by those who had previously appeared weak among the nations, as is added:

“And the weak have been girded with strength.”

This refers to the peoples of the nations, who, presuming nothing upon their own virtues, have been strengthened in the Lord’s righteousness. In their voice the Psalmist speaks, saying: “Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak” (Psalm 6). Again: “Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me, for my soul trusts in you” (Psalm 56).

The gentile people were weak when they had been strangers to God’s covenant. Hence Solomon says concerning the same weakness of the nations: “The little hare is a feeble people that places its dwelling in a rock” (Proverbs 30). The feeble people are the faithful nation of the Gentiles, which, relying on none of its own strength, has learned to hope in the aid of its Redeemer. This is what it means to place its dwelling in a rock. “The rock,” says the Apostle, “was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10).

Under his protection, to avoid hostile attacks, it has learned to say to the Lord with the Psalmist: “Be to me a rock of strength and a fortified house, that you may save me” (Psalm 70).

Hence, concerning the rejection of the Jews and the salvation of the nations, it is fittingly added:

“Those who were previously filled with bread have hired themselves out, and the hungry have been satisfied.”

In Greek it is expressed thus: “Those full of bread have become few, and the hungry have crossed the land.”

“Those who were previously filled,” or “full of bread,” signify the Jews, who have become few. The oracles of God had been entrusted to them; these are signified by “bread,” with which they seemed previously to be satisfied. But because they were unwilling to understand spiritually, or to receive the one who said of himself, “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6), although he had bestowed many benefits upon them through signs and miracles, they proved ungrateful.

Therefore, while they were proud and earthly-minded, they were made less than they had been: in place of those same loaves they were driven from their own dwellings. Because they wished to defend the Law carnally, withdrew from believing in the Savior, and wanted to understand only earthly things in those loaves—that is, in the divine oracles—they lost both their place and their nation and the very oracles of God, according to the Lord’s threat: “The kingdom of God will be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matthew 21).

Hence the Apostles say: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but since you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13).

[Scan p. 138]

## Exposition of the Books of Kings—Book I

To these words it is added: “And the hungry have been satisfied.”

The hungry signify the Gentiles, who previously hungered for the bread of the word of God. But because the Jews were driven from their own dwellings and endured hunger, according to what had long before been spoken through the prophet—“I will send a famine among you, not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of God” (Amos 8)—the Gentiles began to be spiritually satisfied with that same food.

Hence it is expressed in Greek: “And the hungry have crossed the land.” For the nations, to whom the oracles of God passed, hungering greatly, savored not earthly things, as the Jews did, but heavenly things.

In the book of blessed Job it is written: “The hungry shall eat his harvest, and the armed man shall seize it, and the thirsty shall drink his riches” (Job 5). The harvest of the Jewish people had been the oracles of the sacred Law, from which they ought wisely to have been satisfied; yet they did not eat it. For although they held the Law literally, through the folly of their dullness they fasted from its meaning.

Therefore the hungry man eats his harvest, because the gentile people, by understanding the words of the Law, consumed what the Jewish people labored over without understanding. The Lord foresaw these hungry people of faith when he said through the Gospel: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matthew 5).

But because the Jewish people lost their harvest, it is rightly added how that people itself perished: “And the armed man shall seize it.” The ancient enemy seized the Jewish people as an armed man, because by the darts of deceitful suggestion he extinguished the life of faith in them, so that by the very means through which they believed they were clinging to God, they might oppose his ordering.

Of the same enemy it is said: “And the thirsty shall drink his riches.” Those who thirst for his riches drink them because the flowing stream of sacred speech, which the Jewish people had possessed in proud display, waters the minds of the Gentiles after their conversion.

Concerning them it is blessedly said:

“Until the barren woman bore very many, and she who had many sons became weak.”

In Hebrew and in the Septuagint, “seven,” rather than “very many,” is read. From this the Jews fabricate absurdities, asserting that when Samuel was born, the firstborn son of Peninnah died, and that as each of Hannah’s sons was born, one of Peninnah’s sons died. But because this cannot stand, we pass it over and hasten toward the deeper meaning.

For, as they say, the Greek likewise reads: “The barren woman bore seven, and she who had many children became weak.”

The barren woman who bore very many, or seven, signifies the Church from the Gentiles. Through the baptismal font and the gift of the Holy Spirit—called sevenfold because of its sevenfold operation, namely wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and the fear of God—she never ceases to beget many children.

Previously she was barren among the nations, but now she rejoices as fruitful in the Lord, according to what Isaiah had long before foretold: “The deserted and impassable land shall rejoice, and the wilderness shall exult and blossom like a lily” (Isaiah 35). This deserted land and wilderness first bore seven.

The number seven ordinarily signifies unity and the universality of perfection, because the whole is composed from the first odd and the first even numbers, that is, from three and four, as if from two different parts. Therefore the universe is represented by it: the holy Church, throughout the four quarters of the world, has brought forth peoples to the Lord in the unity of faith.

Concerning the same Church the same prophet says again:

“Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Galatians 4).

For a long time the Church, the mother of the Gentiles, was deserted by the Holy Spirit. Before the grace of regeneration she had no children; afterward, through God working within her, she bore nations and peoples. Hence it is added: “More than those of her who has a husband.”

This means the Synagogue, which, as though under the yoke of a husband, was weighed down by the burden of the Law. Or certainly it may refer to the one who, before she was cast out, believed that she possessed a husband; but after she was rejected and lost her husband, the Church became fruitful.

Hence Solomon says: “The almond tree shall blossom, the locust shall be fattened, and the caper shall be scattered” (Ecclesiastes 12). The almond tree shows its blossom before all other trees. What is signified by the blossom of the almond tree except the beginnings of the holy Church? In her preachers she opened the first flowers of virtues and preceded the holy ones who would come afterward, like succeeding trees, to bear the fruits of good works.

Then the locust is fattened, when heavenly grace is poured in; but immediately the caper is scattered, because when grace reaches the Gentiles, Judea, remaining in its barrenness, loses the order of right living.

Of her it is further added:

“And she who had many sons became weak.”

This means the Synagogue of the Jews and the earthly Jerusalem, which seemed carnally to beget many sons through the Law. Because she refused to receive the life-giving Spirit, she became weak through the letter that kills. Concerning this the Apostle Paul says: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3).

Because she wished to follow the surface of the letter, she lost spiritual understanding through unbelief and remained weak. This was prefigured in the Gospel when Peter cut off the ear of the servant of the high priest (Luke 22). The Jewish people, bound by improper obedience to the high priest, had been so subject to their persuasion that they were able to have Barabbas released and Jesus crucified (Matthew 27).

In the Lord’s Passion it lost the right ear—that is, the spiritual understanding of the Law—so that it hears the whole understanding of the letter with its left ear.

Hence in the Song of Songs the Bridegroom of the Church, whom he redeemed through the mystery of the Cross, speaks concerning the unbelief of the Synagogue: “Under the apple tree I raised you up” (Song of Songs 8), and so forth, as though he were saying: “Under the tree of the Cross I delivered you from eternal death.”

“But there your mother was corrupted; there she who bore you was violated”—that is, the greater part of the people, by denying me and choosing Barabbas, was rejected by me and became weak.

Concerning her it is rightly added:

“The Lord puts to death and gives life; he leads down to the underworld and brings back.”

He puts to death the one who had many sons, namely the Synagogue, and gives life to the barren woman, namely the Church of the Gentiles. Yet it may more suitably be understood that he gives life to the very ones whom he had put to death, repeating the same thought when he says:

“He leads down to the underworld and brings back.”

This is what the Apostle says: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3). Again: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above” (ibid.), and so forth.

But did he lead the same people down to the underworld and bring them back? This can without controversy be understood of the Head of the Church, that is, Christ, whose members are the faithful, with whom the Apostle said that our life is hidden. He descended to the underworld, and his soul was not abandoned there; rather, he soon rose from the dead, and the Father brought him back to himself (Psalm 15).

Concerning this it is further said:

“The Lord makes poor and makes rich; he humbles and exalts.”

The historical meaning is clear: he humbles the proud and exalts the humble (Luke 1). But at a higher level of understanding this may be taken of the Lord, who became poor for our sake by the will of the Father, because “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son for us” (John 3).

As Paul says: “He did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Romans 8). Indeed, he did so also by his own will, so that through his poverty he might make us rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom, which God promised to those who love him.

For he himself was enriched with the majesty of divinity, “because in him the whole fullness of divinity dwelt bodily” (Colossians 2). Isaiah also says of him: “The Spirit of the Lord rested upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; the Spirit of the fear of the Lord filled him” (Isaiah 11).

He was also humbled and exalted for our sake, as the Apostle says: “Christ became obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2). We have heard of his humility; let us hear also of his exaltation:

“Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (ibid.).

Concerning his exaltation it is further added:

“Raising the needy from the dust and lifting the poor from the dung heap.”

The Father raised the Son from the dust of the earth very quickly, as he himself asks through the Psalmist: “Raise me up, and I shall repay them,” so that his flesh would not see corruption (Psalm 40). Again, through the same Psalmist it is said: “You will not abandon my soul to the underworld, nor allow your Holy One to see corruption” (Psalm 16).

As has already been said, although he appeared poor and needy in the flesh, and in his poverty and humility overcame the proud devil—who is called king over all the sons of pride—the majesty of God the Father lifted him ineffably from the dung heap. Why did he do this? Do you ask why? Hear the answer: “That he may sit with princes and hold the throne of glory” (Matthew 19).

The princes are understood to be the holy Apostles, who will sit with Christ upon twelve thrones. But the Lord retains the throne of glory not only in his equality with the Father, sitting at the right hand of Majesty, according to what the Apostle says: “He sits at the right hand of Majesty on high” (Hebrews 1). Having become so much greater than the angels, as he has inherited a name more excellent than theirs, he will also hold the throne of glory, according to what he himself says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5).

“He will come in the glory of his Father to judgment, with angels and archangels, with thrones and dominions, and he will sit upon the throne of his glorious majesty, judging the world in righteousness” (Mark 8).

The princes too will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Matthew 19).

[Scan p. 139]

Hence Isaiah says: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people” (Isaiah 3). Solomon likewise says: “Her husband is noble at the gates, when he sits with the elders” (Proverbs 31).

The Lord, the husband of the holy Church, will therefore be noble at the gates of his city. Before the governor’s tribunal he appeared ignoble, but although even now he is considered contemptible by many, when the end of the age has come and the entrance to the heavenly homeland has been opened to the elect, he will then appear exalted to all.

He will hold the throne of glory without end, because “of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1). For it follows: “He himself shall rule from sea to sea” (Psalm 72), and so forth.

“For the foundations of the earth belong to the Lord, and he has set the world upon them.”

The four quarters of the world are understood by “the foundations of the earth”: east, west, north, and south, upon which he has set the world, because he has spread his Church everywhere.

Hence the Psalmist says: “From the rising of the sun to its setting, the name of the Lord is worthy of praise” (Psalm 113). Again it is written: “From the ends of the earth we have heard the praises of the righteous” (Isaiah 24). And again concerning the holy preachers: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 19).

Nevertheless, as some think, the foundations of the earth may themselves signify the preachers upon whose faith the Church has been established. Concerning them it is written: “Beneath him they are bent who carry the world” (Job 9). They are the ones who elsewhere are called columns, as it is written: “The columns of heaven tremble and quake at his nod” (Job 26)—namely, the holy preachers of the Church, upon whom the structure of the Church’s building rises, as another Scripture testifies, saying: “Whoever conquers, I will make him a column in the temple of my God” (Revelation 3).

For whoever is firmly established in God’s work with a right intention is raised up as a column in the structure of the spiritual building, so that, placed in this temple which is the Church, he may contribute both usefulness and beauty.

Hence, concerning the preaching of the saints, it is added:

“He will guard the feet of his holy ones, and the wicked will be silenced in darkness, for a man shall not be strengthened by his own power.”

Although the feet may signify the teachers, as it is said through Moses: “Those who draw near to his feet receive instruction from him” (Deuteronomy 33), nevertheless we may also understand by the feet of the saints the course of their action and the very work of preaching, by which the Lord directs them along the way of righteousness.

Concerning these preachers the Lord himself says: “Into whatever house or city you enter, and they do not receive you, when you leave that city, shake the dust from your feet” (Matthew 10; Mark 6).

Dust is the lightness of earthly thought. Even the highest preachers cannot be entirely free from it, since, being concerned for their hearers, they continually devote themselves to salutary cares. As they travel the roads of the world, they scarcely avoid touching the dust of the earth with their heel; but each day teachers hasten to wash away this dust of lightness by pouring out tears.

Hence, in the Song of Songs, when the Church was commanded to rise for the work of preaching, she answered the Bridegroom:

“I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?” (Song of Songs 5).

As though she were openly saying: “For your sake I have abandoned worldly business; how shall I return to it? I have washed away in secret acts of compunction and tears whatever I left behind in the course of preaching and in earthly thoughts; how shall I again defile myself with filthy stains?”

Although the elect fear this, their feet are guarded by God, so that they are not defiled by any filth of heretical wickedness or slip into any evil work. Hence it is said to holy souls through Ezekiel: “Their feet were straight feet” (Ezekiel 1).

The feet of the saints are called straight because their works have not been twisted toward the pursuit of iniquity, for they are preserved by the Lord amid the waves of this age.

But while they are guarded, the wicked, on the contrary—those who opposed their preaching—will be silenced in darkness. These are the Jews, who are wrapped in the darkness of unbelief and ignorance and are not worthy to contemplate the light of truth, because they believed that they could suffice for themselves without divine assistance.

Hence it follows:

“For a man shall not be strengthened by his own power.”

This means that a man is strong not by his own power but by divine strength; the man may be understood as the gentile people. Or it may be understood generally, because no one can perform good by his own powers or resist the devil. Indeed, if anyone tries to rise up against the Lord, he loses whatever good he seems to possess. This was demonstrated first in the angel and afterward in humanity.

For it is written: “Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, nor the rich man in his riches; but let him who glories glory in the Lord” (Jeremiah 9). Again it is said elsewhere: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and reject the understanding of the intelligent” (1 Corinthians 1).

This was most clearly demonstrated in the Jews, concerning whom it is added:

“The adversaries of the Lord will fear him, and he will thunder over them from heaven.”

The adversaries of the Lord are understood to be the same Jews, who said: “Let us put wood in his bread and eradicate him from the land of the living, so that his name may no longer be remembered” (Isaiah 53). Hence afterward they cried out: “Crucify him, crucify him” (John 19).

The Lord thundered from heaven over these adversaries—as some think—when through the Apostles he terrified their unbelieving hearts. By “heaven,” therefore, the Apostles themselves are understood, concerning whom the Psalmist says: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Psalm 19).

By “thunder,” however, are understood the threats of miracles and the terrors of signs. These were fulfilled when the Apostles began on the day of Pentecost to speak in various tongues of the mighty works of God, when the Holy Spirit appeared over them in the vision of fire.

When Peter preached, the Jews, struck as if by thunder and pierced in heart, said: “Brothers, what shall we do?” Then the Apostle Peter said: “Repent, therefore, and let each of you be baptized, and let your sins be blotted out” (Acts 2).

Hence it is written in Revelation: “From the throne proceeded flashes of lightning, voices, and thunder” (Revelation 4). This is what Mark says: “They went out and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word by the accompanying signs.”

When these thunders sounded, the enemies were terrified, and many of them were converted to the faith, according to Luke: “A great number of the priests were obedient to the faith.”

Through these heavens—or rather through the clouds which he filled with the Holy Spirit after he had ascended into heaven—the Lord thundered over his adversaries. Nevertheless, some wish the passage to be understood of the future judgment, when the unbelieving Jews, who wished here to establish their own righteousness, boasting in observance of the Law without the faith of Christ and refusing to submit to his righteousness, will be judged.

They will be condemned not only by the Lord whom they despised, but also by the Apostles, who are understood by the name “heaven,” as the Lord says: “You will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19).

Hence the Lord also says to the same Jews: “If I cast out demons by the prince of demons, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they shall be your judges” (Matthew 12).

Again it is said through the prophet: “The Lord will call judgment upon the fire; it will devour the great abyss and consume the portion of the house” (Amos 7).

Judgment will be called upon the fire when, in the judgment, the sentence of justice is displayed as punishment in eternal burning. It will devour the abyss because it will burn the wicked and incomprehensible minds of human beings, which now conceal themselves from people even under the sign of miraculous works. At the judgment they will say: “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name?” (Matthew 7), and so forth. But they will hear from the Lord: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity; I do not know who you are.”

With them, a portion of the house will also be consumed: the Jews who boasted of the ceremonies of their Law and of the number of their lineage, saying: “We have Abraham as our father” (John 8). Since they were formerly called the house of God, then the flame of Gehenna will burn them.

Hence it is not improperly added concerning both groups:

“The Lord will judge the ends of the earth.”

Although, according to the historical sense, this can be understood to mean that he judges all the ends of the earth, according to what the Psalmist says: “In his hand are all the ends of the earth” (Psalm 95), since he determines all things by his power, nevertheless the passage is understood of the future judgment, as we have said.

[Scan p. 140]

There, due recompense will come from the Lord upon the sons of Adam, when, according to the Apostle, “we must all appear before his tribunal, so that each may render an account according to what he has done” (2 Corinthians 5). Hence the Psalmist says: “He will repay each according to his works” (Psalm 62).

This will be when all the nations are gathered before him, and he will separate them from one another, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats (Matthew 25). The prophet says of this: “He has prepared his throne for judgment, and he himself will judge the world in righteousness; he will judge the peoples in justice” (Psalm 9).

This is the Lord Christ, who here endured his adversaries and their injustice by suffering, but there will truly show the wicked his righteousness.

By “the world” we ought to understand holy men, who are gathered from the universal Church as from the circle of a crown. These will be judged in equity, and abundant mercy will be granted to them because of the goodness of their faith and humility. They will hear: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you” (Matthew 25), and so forth.

By “the peoples,” however, sinners are to be understood—those who do not appear to have been freed from works of the devil. They will be judged with justice, because they will be condemned for the crime of their deeds. To them it will be said: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire.”

By these two words, “equity” and “justice,” he has described with marvelous brevity the quality of that judgment.

In that judgment, as we have said, the wicked Jews will be condemned more severely, because the Lord will judge the ends of the earth.

As far as the moral understanding is concerned, however, “the ends of the earth” signify the final state and intentions of human beings, which the Lord is said to judge.

Our merciful Creator does not abandon his work. Through his patience he tolerates human evils, and at times he releases them through conversion. When he regards hard and insensitive minds, he terrifies them now with threats, now with blows, now with revelations, so that those who had grown numb in the worst security may be softened by salutary fear.

For the Lord knows that the end of our life is subject to greater judgment, and therefore he purifies his elect more carefully at the end. Hence it is written here: “The Lord will judge the ends of the earth,” because he watches over our final moments as attentively as he weighs in them the beginnings of what follows.

And because, as has been said, he examines our works and intentions in various ways at the end, it is rightly said: “The Lord will judge the ends of the earth.” That is, he will judge the final state of a person, not according to what is changed for better or worse during the intervening time, but according to the state in which the one being judged is found at the end.

It follows:

“And he will give power to his king.”

The Lord gives power to his king because God the Father has everywhere given authority to his only-begotten Son, according to what Daniel says in his vision:

“I watched in the vision of the night, and behold, one like a son of man came with the clouds of heaven. He came to the Ancient of Days, and they presented him before him. And he gave him power, honor, and a kingdom; and all peoples, tribes, and tongues shall serve him. His power is an eternal power that shall not be taken away, and his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom that shall not be destroyed” (Daniel 7).

This is what the Apostle says:

“Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a man. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow” (Philippians 2), and so forth.

Hence Isaiah says: “His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace” (Isaiah 9). “He shall sit upon the throne of David and over his kingdom” (Luke 1).

Hence the angel says to Mary: “The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there shall be no end” (Micah 4).

Concerning him it is also rightly said: “And he will give power to his king”—namely to Christ, to whom the Father gave all things into his hands. Or “he will give power to his king” may mean the Christian people. He gives them strength, because they reign over the flesh like kings, and in the one who shed his blood for them they conquer the world.

“And he will exalt the horn of his Christ.”

What should we understand by the horn of Christ except his most firm and exalted power, which rises above all things? For Zechariah says: “He has raised up for us a horn of salvation” (Luke 1).

All bones are indeed covered with flesh; the horn projects beyond the flesh. Therefore the horn of salvation is called the kingdom of Christ the Savior, which surpasses all the joys of this age. In its symbolism, David or Solomon was consecrated to royal glory with the horn of oil.

Nevertheless, as some think, the power which the Son received from the Father specifically signifies the Church alone. Concerning this the Father speaks through the Psalmist, saying: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 2). He indicates its boundaries when he says, as was stated above: “The Lord will judge the ends of the earth.”

“‘The Father judges no one,’ he says in the Gospel, ‘but has given all judgment to the Son’” (John 5). And also: “He has given him power to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John 5).

Concerning this the Son himself says elsewhere: “I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain” (Psalm 2).

Concerning this authority he adds: “And he will exalt the horn of his Christ.”

They wish this to be referred to his body, which is the Church. For all who have been anointed with his chrism may rightly be called christs; yet, together with their Head, this entire body is one Christ.

The Son himself exalted the kingdom of this Christ—that is, of his body—insofar as he spread it everywhere, firmly established it in the faith, broke the kingdoms of the world, and caused them to be overcome.

Accordingly the Psalmist says: “I shall cut off all the horns of sinners,” that is, their kingdoms, “but the horns of the righteous shall be exalted” (Psalm 75). The horn of the righteous is the kingdom of the chosen people.

Although, as far as we have been able to understand, this interpretation is somewhat inartful, and for me—[sentence fragment continues beyond the supplied text].

## Commentary on the Books of Kings — Book I

had been handed down, we have explained how Hannah had prophesied about Christ, the Church of the Gentiles, and the rejection of the Synagogue. With these matters completed, by the Lord’s favor we now attempt at last to turn our pen to other subjects.

> Meanwhile Samuel was ministering in the temple of the Lord, girded with an ephod,

that is, with a linen shoulder-garment, which differs from the ephod worn by the high priest. It was made of four colors and was permitted for use by the lower ranks.

> And his mother made him a little tunic,

and so forth. The little tunic that his mother made for him signifies the simple teaching with which the minds of believers are to be clothed. To such persons Paul says: “And I gave you milk” (1 Cor. 3), and so forth. The linen shoulder-garment signifies chastity and continence together with good works. For whoever desires to undertake divine service must necessarily live chastely and continently, and thus exercise himself in good works.

> Now the sons of Eli were sons of Belial, not knowing the Lord, nor the priestly office toward the people; but whoever had sacrificed a victim, the priest’s servant came while the flesh was being boiled, and he had a three-pronged fork in his hand and put it into the cauldron or kettle,

and so forth, until it says:

> Thus the sin of the young men was very great before the Lord, for they drew people away from the sacrifice of the Lord.

Here, according to the allegorical sense, we can say nothing other than what follows from the moral understanding, which the careful teaching of the wise calls ethical: namely, how many people perish through an appetite for gluttony and by the sword of desire. So that the reader may clearly recognize their various forms, relying on the authority of divine Scripture we shall attempt to describe five modes, just as Pope Gregory also affirmed in his sayings.

Sometimes gluttony anticipates the time of eating; sometimes it does not anticipate the time, but seeks richer foods. Sometimes it demands that whatever is to be eaten be prepared with excessive care. Sometimes it observes the kind of food and the time appropriate for it, but exceeds the proper measure in the quantity consumed. Often what it desires is something mean or ordinary, yet even in this very wretchedness of desire it sins more grievously.

Jonathan earned the sentence of death from his father’s mouth because, in tasting honey, he anticipated the appointed time for eating. The people led out of Egypt perished in the wilderness because, despising manna, they asked for meat, which they considered more luxurious. The first fault of Eli’s sons, as the historical text here shows, arose when, at their request, the priest’s servant wished to take from the sacrifice not flesh cooked according to the ancient custom, but raw flesh, so that he could present it more carefully prepared.

And when it is said to Jerusalem:

> This was the iniquity of your sister Sodom: pride, fullness of bread, and abundance of ease [Ezek. 16],

it is plainly shown that she lost salvation because, through the vice of pride, she exceeded the measure of moderate refreshment. Esau lost the glory of his birthright because, in the great heat of desire, he craved humble food, namely lentils. By selling even his birthright for it, he showed how ardently he burned with appetite.

For it is not the food but the appetite that is at fault. Thus, we often take richer foods without guilt, and taste poorer ones without a clear conscience. Esau, whom we have mentioned, lost his birthright for lentils, whereas Elias preserved the strength of his body by eating meat in the wilderness. Therefore the ancient enemy, realizing that it was not food but desire that brought condemnation, subjected the first man to himself not through meat but through an apple, and tested the second not through meat but through bread.

Hence Adam’s fault is often committed even when what is eaten is mean and worthless. For Adam was not the only one to receive the command of prohibition, that he should refrain from the forbidden apple. Whenever God points out certain foods as harmful to our salvation, he forbids us from them, as though by a sentence. When we desire harmful things, what else do we touch except forbidden things?

Therefore we should take what the necessity of nature demands, not what the appetite for eating suggests. For if anyone strives to serve the pleasures of gluttony without restraint, he slips more gravely into the pit of vices. Falling from the state of uprightness, he is dragged toward the death of the soul and loses the good that he appeared to possess.

This is demonstrated in what follows concerning the sons of Eli. Through their appetite for gluttony they advanced to the accumulation of a greater sin, so that they slept with women and caused the Lord’s people to transgress. Thus they were not only expelled from the priesthood but also punished with death. For the text continues:

> Eli was very old, and he heard all that his sons were doing to all Israel, and how they slept with the women,

and so forth.

Although some wish this to be understood simply of adultery, as Josephus also says—that they inflicted insults upon the women who assembled for religious reasons, doing violence to some and persuading others with gifts—their life differed in no respect from the worst tyranny, as our teachers also affirm.

Nevertheless, the Hebrews say that they “slept with women” who attended at the entrance of the tabernacle because, after the period of menstruation or childbirth, when the sacrifice required by the Law had not yet been completed, they persuaded these women to return to their husbands and have intercourse with them. They are therefore said to have made them sleep with their husbands because they caused them to do so contrary to the commandment of the Law.

For a little later Eli says:

> This is not a good report that I hear, that you cause the Lord’s people to transgress.

The people therefore transgressed because they joined themselves to their wives before the sacrifice had been properly completed. Just as the priests extorted the flesh from the one who was sacrificing, so they also extorted the sacrifice from the one who was offering it. And just as, in offering the horns, they caused people to detract from the sacrifice of the Lord, so likewise they caused the people to transgress in joining themselves to their wives.

If anyone wishes to follow this interpretation, we leave him to his own judgment; we have decided to follow the former interpretation.

[scan page 143]

> If a man sins against a man, God may be appeased on his behalf; but if a man sins against God, who will pray for him?

Sin against a human being is not therefore the same as sin against God, because sinning against a human being, whatever the sin may be, admits of an easier remission. But sinning against God—that is, withdrawing from his worship—is the sin of impiety, and its remission is more difficult.

When someone sins against a human being, by placating the person he can make God favorable toward him. But when someone sins against God, who will pray for him? It is as though the text said: “Through whom could they make God, against whom they sinned, propitious to them?”

This must not, however, be understood to mean that no pardon is to be hoped for by those who have committed some offense in divine service, even if they perform worthy penance. Rather, forgiveness is more difficult and greater penance must be undertaken by those who offend in matters consecrated to God than by those who injure their neighbor in word or deed. For the greater the glory, the graver the offense.

Here it must particularly be observed that bishops and all who preside over the Christian people must consider more carefully how Eli’s sons sinned before the Lord by profaning the divine sacrifices, and how many people mocked the Lord’s sacrifice through them. Thus Eli the priest was condemned because he restrained their sins with too little severity.

He did restrain them, and he did rebuke them, but with the gentleness and mildness of a father, not with the severity and authority of a high priest. From this judgment priests should learn—as we began to say—that, for the sake of human favor or earthly advantage, they must not merely agree with or flatter those whom they govern in the sins by which they offend God. They must correct and amend them, not with gentleness or mildness, but with a hard and severe rebuke.

Otherwise, if they remain silent about the sins of their children—that is, the crimes of the people—they themselves will perish, and those who were not corrected will be punished together with those who govern them. Although they may be holy, the guilt of their subjects will nevertheless be charged to them because of their silence and the softness of their rebuke, if they fail to restrain them.

On the other hand, if they strive to rebuke guilt according to its measure with a harsh denunciation and do not neglect to heal the wounds of sinners with the antidote of their preaching, they should know that they will receive the crown of eternal reward. For it is written:

> Whoever converts a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins (Jas. 5).

Finally, in the Old Testament we read that Phinehas the priest, moved by zeal to appease the Lord’s anger, pierced the sinners before the people with a dagger, and thereby earned for himself both an everlasting name and an everlasting priesthood.

Because Eli did not wish to punish his sons’ sin with due severity, he not only lost the priesthood but was also punished with death, as we have said; the sacred history clearly demonstrates this in what follows. For it continues:

> A certain prophet of the Lord came to Eli the priest and said to him: Thus says the Lord: Did I not plainly reveal myself to the house of your father when he was in Egypt?

He calls the house of his prince Aaron, from whose stock Eli succeeded to the priesthood. The Lord says that he revealed himself to him when, in Egypt, he said:

> Go to meet Moses in the wilderness (Exod. 4).

There the Lord was first revealed to him, appointed him to obedience, and afterward chose not only him but also all the tribes for the priesthood. Hence it is said:

> I chose him from all the tribes of Israel for myself as priest, to go up to my altar, burn incense to me, and wear the ephod before me. And I gave to the house of your father all the sacrifices of the children of Israel. Why have you kicked away my victim and my gifts, which I commanded to be offered in the temple, and honored your sons more than me, so that you might eat the first portions of every sacrifice of my people Israel?

> Therefore, says the Lord God of Israel, speaking, I said that your house and the house of your father should minister in my sight forever. But now, says the Lord, far be this from me. Whoever glorifies me, I will glorify; but those who despise me will be held in dishonor.

> Behold, the days are coming when I will cut off your arm and the arm of your father’s house,

that is, the dignity and strength of the priesthood and the high priest. Hence it is also said:

> So that there will be no old man in your house,

that is, no high priest.

> And you will see your rival.

The rival of Eli’s house was Zadok, who, after Solomon expelled Abiathar, received the priesthood. Some, however, wish this to be understood of Samuel, as we read in the Books of Kings:

> Solomon expelled Abiathar, so that he would not be priest of the Lord, in order to fulfill the word of the Lord that he had spoken against the house of Eli (1 Kings 2).

> Nevertheless I will not completely cut off a man from you from my altar, but so that your eyes may fail and your soul may languish.

For this reason the Lord says that he will not entirely remove a man from Eli’s house from his altar, so that there would always be a man from Eli’s house in the house of the Lord who would replace another in the dignity of the priesthood; and, seeing himself deprived of that same dignity, his eyes would fail and his soul would languish from the excess of grief.

This prophecy, mystically concerning the change of the priesthood, was not fulfilled in Samuel, but was foreshadowed in the Lord Jesus Christ. For after the prophet Samuel there were priests from the line of Aaron, such as Zadok and Abiathar in the reign of David, and others afterward, before the time came when this change of priesthood had to be accomplished through Christ.

When he said:

> Speaking, I said that your house and the house of your father,

that is, Aaron, who was the first priest appointed, from whose descendants the others would follow,

> should minister in my sight forever. But now, says the Lord, far be this from me. Whoever glorifies me, I will glorify; but those who despise me will be held in dishonor,

behold, these are the days that were foretold.

[scan page 144]

They have now come. For there is no priest according to the order of Aaron. Whoever from his line is a man, when he sees the priesthood—or rather, the sacrifice of Christians—flourishing throughout the whole world while he himself is cast down, his eyes fail and his soul melts from the excess of grief.

Hence it follows:

> And I will raise up for myself a faithful priest according to my heart.

What the Prophet says to Eli in the person of God—

> I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who will act according to my heart and my soul; I will build him a faithful house, and he will walk before my Christ all his days—

must be understood, under the figure of Samuel, of the Lord the Savior, the supreme and true high priest.

For just as Samuel succeeded Eli in the priesthood after Eli’s death, being chosen not from the stock of Aaron but from another Levitical family—for he was the son of Elkanah, son of Jeroham, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph, son of Elkanah, son of Joel, son of Azariah, son of Zephaniah, son of Tahath, son of Asir, son of Asaph, son of Korah, son of Izhar, son of Kohath, son of Levi, son of Israel, as the Books of Chronicles relate—so the Mediator of God and human beings, in order to be our high priest, took flesh not from Levi but from another tribe, namely Judah.

He offered his own flesh to the Father as a lawful sacrifice for us. He left as heirs of his priesthood others than the race of Aaron: children, that is, of the grace of the New Testament, gathered not only from the Jews but from every nation of the Gentiles.

When God says, speaking in a human manner, “who will act according to my heart and my soul,” this can properly be understood of Samuel, who in all things obeyed God’s will as a man of God. But it can also be understood more profoundly of the Lord the Savior, because, as the only-begotten Son, he is conscious of all the Father’s secrets, according to what he himself openly testifies:

> I do nothing of my own accord, but as the Father taught me, so I speak (John 8).

And:

> He who sent me is with me, and he has not left me alone, because I always do what pleases him (John 8).

The Father builds for him a faithful house, and that house is us, if we hold firmly to the confidence and glory of hope to the end. This house will walk before his Christ, that is, before the supreme high priest, throughout all days, because the holy Church will never cease to advance until the end of the age through the increase of its members.

Otherwise, how could it be understood of Samuel that a faithful house was built for him, one that would walk before the Lord’s Christ—that is, before Samuel himself—throughout all days, when we read below that his sons turned away from his ways, declined into avarice, and perverted judgment? Unless perhaps in this place we understand his house as the people of Israel, who served the Lord throughout all the days of his priesthood. Concerning this people it is written:

> And all Israel rested after the Lord (1 Sam. 7).

And shortly afterward:

> The children of Israel removed the Baals and the Ashtaroth and served the Lord alone.

What follows is:

> It shall come to pass that whoever remains in your house will come to be prayed for and to offer a silver coin and a piece of bread.

This is not said properly of the house of this Eli, but of the house of that Aaron, from whose race there are still some who come and are converted. Of such people it is said:

> The remnant, according to the election of grace, has been saved (Rom. 11).

Of such remnants it is rightly understood that the one who is said to remain in your house “will come to be prayed for.” He is the one who believes in Christ, as happened in the times of the Apostles; this is also partly fulfilled in the present age and will be completed perfectly at the end of the world.

For although they are few, some every day come from the Jews to the Church, not only from the common people but also from the priestly stock.

> And when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved (Rom. 11).

Whoever among these is to be saved is the one who is said to remain. In the house of the priest Eli, which is perishing, he must take refuge in the Church and offer to the Christian priest a coin of confession of God, devoutly expressed in the Creed: brief in words, but outstanding in power.

Silver signifies the brightness of the heavenly word, just as the splendor of spiritual wisdom is often represented by gold. Let him also offer the bread of the saving sacrifice, having cast aside the flesh of legal victims, and let him say:

> Let me, I beg you, be assigned to one priestly portion,

that is, to the very people distinguished by Christ the priest. Peter says to them:

> You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood (1 Pet. 2).

When the text adds:

> That I may eat a morsel of bread,

it elegantly expresses the very kind of sacrifice. For the priest himself says:

> The bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world (John 6).

Because above he had said that he gave the house of Aaron food from the victims of the Old Testament, which were the sacrifices of the Jews, he now says that a morsel of bread is to be requested for eating, because this is the sacrifice of Christians in the New Testament.

## Chapter III

> The boy Samuel ministered to the Lord before Eli, and the word of the Lord was precious.

The text says, “the word of the Lord was precious.” It is called precious because it was rare, and prophecy was given only rarely. Everything rare is precious, because it is desired more greatly. Hence it is added:

> In those days there was no manifest vision.

Prophecy was not fully revealed. Because of the sins of the people and of those who governed the people, visions were no longer made manifest as they had been to their fathers.

This is the historical meaning. According to the spiritual meaning, however, it is rightly said:

> The boy Samuel ministered to the Lord before Eli.

The only-begotten Son of God, whom we have said is signified by Samuel—whose name is interpreted “the name of God”—appeared in the flesh in all things to have carried out the will of the Father. As he himself says:

> I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me (John 6).

Thus it is rightly added, “before Eli,” because he did not wish the priesthood of the Jews to cease immediately, before the true priesthood appeared. Hence it follows:

> And his word was precious,

because his preaching was beloved and precious to the faithful, but despised by unbelievers. Concerning them the text adds figuratively:

> It happened one day that Eli was lying in his place, and his eyes had grown dim so that he could not see the lamp of God before it was extinguished.

Because of extreme old age his eyes had grown dim, and he could not see the lamp of God while it was burning in the tabernacle, before daylight appeared, when the lamp was about to be extinguished, as Moses commands in the laws of Exodus (Exod. 27), so that the same lamp might burn until morning.

Alternatively, this may signify that Eli remained in his blindness until he was utterly extinguished together with his offspring—that is, until he was deprived of bodily life.

Mystically, Eli’s blindness signifies the blindness of the hearts of the Jews. The lamp of God is to be understood as our Lord. We know that in a clay lamp there is an exterior vessel and an interior light. Through the Prophet he says:

> My strength has dried up like a potsherd (Ps. 22).

What is meant by the potsherd except his body? In that vessel the light of divinity existed, and the flame of virtues and miracles shone forth.

When the rulers or priests of the Jews refused to believe in his virtues and miracles, the light of truth was extinguished in them. The text rightly says “before it was extinguished,” because they were unable to understand either by the radiance of the miracles that shone from him or by attentive reflection to grasp his teaching, until that priesthood, together with the temple and the people, was utterly overthrown.

Concerning them it is still said in the person of Eli:

> Therefore I swore to the house of Eli that the iniquity of his house will not be expiated by victims or offerings forever,

because the sin of the Jewish priests committed against Christ—that is, because they not only despised him but also crucified him—cannot be expiated forever by legal victims and sacrifices.

> Samuel was sleeping in the temple of the Lord, where the ark of God was. And the Lord called Samuel. He answered and said: Here I am,

and so forth, until it says:

> Samuel did not yet know the Lord, nor had the word of the Lord yet been revealed to him.

The fact that the Lord called Samuel three times prefigured that this boy would become a prophet, leader, and priest. Samuel is said not to know the Lord because the mystery of prophecy, or the word of the Lord, had not yet been revealed to him. In the ordinary sense he knew him, like everyone else.

> The Lord said to Samuel: Behold, I am about to do a thing in Israel such that whoever hears it, both his ears will tingle.

Here God’s threat is directed against Eli and his house, because, through the sin of Eli’s sons, the ark of God would be captured, Israel would fall, his sons would perish, and Eli’s house would be deprived of the priesthood of the house of the Lord. Because of this event, the ears of those who heard it would tingle with intense astonishment.

> Samuel grew, and the Lord was with him, and none of his words fell to the ground.

[scan page 145]

What is said about Samuel after he reported to Eli in the morning the words of the divine oracle that he had received during the night—“none of his words fell to the ground”—signifies that nothing of what he said was ineffective, but everything he foretold was fulfilled in events.

Words that are superfluous fall to the ground; they are to be regarded as worthless and trampled underfoot with universal contempt. Thus blessed Job also says:

> The light of my face did not fall to the ground (Job 29).

He had become accustomed to holding his face with such gravity that it was never relaxed into contemptible frivolity. Whenever he showed himself more cheerful to those present, he always did so for a useful purpose on their behalf.

Concerning this it is also added:

> All Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, knew that Samuel was a faithful prophet of the Lord.

By describing the boundaries of the land of Judah, he embraces the whole people together. Dan is a village four miles from Paneas on the road to Tyre; even today it is the northern boundary of the province of Judea. The Jordan River, bursting forth from that place, likewise received its name from it.

Beersheba is similarly a village in the southern part of Judea, thirty miles from Hebron. Thus it is said:

> And the word of Samuel came to all Israel.

His word concerned all Israel: they would be struck down by the Philistines because of the sins of Eli’s sons. Through divine revelation it became clear to him that this had been disclosed, as the outcome of events proved; therefore he was proclaimed a true prophet.

## Chapter IV

> Israel went out to meet the Philistines for battle and encamped beside the Stone of Help. The Philistines came to Aphek and drew up their battle line against Israel. When the battle was joined, Israel turned its back before the Philistines, and about four thousand men were struck down in the battle, scattered throughout the fields.

The literal sense is clear: the children of Israel suffered these things because of the sins of Eli’s sons. Accordingly, Aphek is rightly interpreted as “new fury” or “one who apprehends,” which aptly suits what happened. Those who deserved the Lord’s vengeance were apprehended by their enemies.

But what this signifies according to the allegorical sense must briefly be explained. Israel, whose name is interpreted “a man seeing God” or “strong with God,” signifies those who believe in God. The Philistines, whose name is interpreted “falling from the cup,” signify unclean spirits. Intoxicated by the cup of pride, they themselves fell from heavenly things and daily hasten to corrupt many human beings with their cup of malice.

Against them Israel—that is, the faithful—encamp beside the Stone of Help, so that they may not yield to the most unclean spirits and may be able to overcome them. The Stone of Help signifies the law of Christ, in which the true stone, Christ, is found. Concerning him it is written:

> The stone that the builders rejected (Ps. 118; Matt. 21),

and so forth.

The faithful remain beside it so that they may find Christ and say:

> Be for us a stone of help and a rock of refuge.

And also:

> Our help is in the name of the Lord (Ps. 124).

[scan page 146]

But while they remain beside the Stone—that is, while they meditate on the law of the Lord day and night, so that they may find the Savior their helper more fully—the Philistines come to Aphek and draw up their battle line against Israel.

Aphek is interpreted as “new fury.” It is rightly interpreted as new fury because, the more the unclean spirits see the faithful applying themselves to the divine laws and placing their hope in Christ, the more fiercely they are driven by the gall of their malice to construct new and harsher battles.

Thus the unclean spirits easily overthrow many who trust in their own virtues and glory in human wisdom, or who desire to receive the Law carnally, as the Jews understand it, and do not fear to despise the grace of the Gospel. For it follows:

> When the battle was joined, Israel turned its back before the Philistines, and about four thousand men were struck down in the battle, scattered throughout the fields.

The four thousand men who perished in this battle with the Philistines, in which the children of Israel engaged—that is, the believers from the primitive Church—are understood to be those who refused to accept the four Gospels.

> The people therefore sent to Shiloh, and brought from there the ark of the covenant of the Lord of hosts, who sits upon the cherubim. When the Philistines saw that the ark of the Lord had come into the camp, they were afraid, saying: God has come into the camp.

The ark that the children of Israel brought from Shiloh into battle signifies the two Testaments, which the faithful from the Jewish people carried over to the Gentiles. It is rightly called the ark of “the Lord of hosts, who sits upon the cherubim.”

“Cherubim” is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge,” which is found in the two Testaments, although the expression may also be referred to Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (Col. 2).

When the Philistines heard this—that is, the wise men of this world, or the unclean spirits themselves, about whom we spoke above—they trembled. The Apostles had begun to rain down words, to shine with miracles through the knowledge of both Testaments, and, as though thundering, to make the earth resound with a great cry and a loud noise through their preaching (Acts 2); and they believed that they would be overcome.

> They groaned, saying: Woe to us! There was no such rejoicing yesterday or the day before. Woe to us! Who will save us from the hand of these exalted gods? The Philistines fought, Israel was struck down, and each man fled to his tent.

Here too, in the statement that the ark was captured by foreigners, it was prefigured that the two Testaments, which we have said are signified by the ark, would be received by the Gentiles.

> The two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, also died.

By Hophni, whose name means “barefoot,” and Phinehas, whose name is said to mean “mute mouth,” we previously explained that the priesthood of the Jews was signified. Their deaths now signify the end of that priesthood.

They are rightly reported to have died after the ark had been captured, because, after the two Testaments had passed to the wise men of this world and to the Gentiles, the priesthood of the Jews came utterly to an end. It was exterminated as their sins demanded, and the priests themselves were killed by the Gentiles.

The Lord says this to Ezekiel:

> And you, son of man, take for yourself a sharp sword that cuts the hair, and take it and draw it over your head and your beard (Ezek. 5),

and so forth.

What does the sharp sword signify except the devastation of the Jews, which occurred under Vespasian and Titus? What do the hair of the head and the beard signify except the whole beauty and strength of that people? When the Jews lost all these things, those of them who had survived famine, pestilence, and the sword were scattered under the figure of hairs among all the nations, as though in every direction of the wind.

To make the higher meaning clearer, let us state it differently. He says:

> And you, son of man, take for yourself a sharp sword that cuts the hair,

and so forth.

In this action the judgment of the Redeemer is expressed. Appearing in the flesh, he shaved the head because he removed from the Jewish priesthood the mysteries of its commandments. The cut hair therefore signifies the subtlety of the mysteries; the head signifies the summit of the priesthood. He shaved the beard because, abandoning the kingdom of Israel, he cut away its adornment of virtue.

> A man from Benjamin came running and said to Eli: Israel has fled before the Philistines, and a great slaughter has taken place among the people. Moreover, your two sons have died, Hophni and Phinehas, and the ark of God has been captured. When he mentioned the ark of God, Eli fell backward from his seat beside the gate; his neck was broken, and he died.

Just as the death of the sons above signifies the end of the Jewish priesthood, so here the death of the father signifies that the Jewish high priesthood was irreparably overthrown, that its seat was left vacant, and that the glory of the priesthood and kingdom was extinguished, as we explained more fully above by an example.

This is what it means that he fell backward from his seat and died. Finally, after the priesthood had been extinguished and the seat of the high priesthood laid waste, the carnal Synagogue, adhering to it carnally, likewise immediately perished.

Its significance is indicated in what follows:

> His daughter-in-law, Phinehas’s wife, was pregnant and near the time of delivery. When she heard the news that the ark of God had been captured and that her father-in-law and her husband had died, she bowed down and gave birth. Sudden labor pains came upon her, and at the moment of her death those standing around her said: Do not be afraid, for you have given birth to a son,

and so forth.

Everything points toward what has been said above. For, as we have stated, Eli’s daughter-in-law, Phinehas’s wife, signified the carnal Jewish people. Joined to the carnal priesthood, she came to an end together with it and perished by divine judgment.

It must be observed, however, that she did not perish before giving birth to a living child. Likewise, the synagogue of the Jews did not perish completely before living children were born from it—that is, the primitive Church, which believed from that people.
