Therefore, rightly receiving no consolation from those who were consoling her, the Synagogue, despairing because of the humble believers, said:

[scan page 147]

“Glory has departed from Israel, because the ark of God has been captured.” This is what the Lord says: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. 21). Hence it should be noted that he called the child Ichabod. *Chabod* means “glory”; *Ichabod*, “glory has fallen.” This refers to those who emerged from the Synagogue without believing—people who could have been the Synagogue’s honor and glory if they had wished to believe in God and in their preaching. But because they scorned to do this, they lost that glory: for the holy preachers, despising them, came to the Gentiles. Hence the apostles say to them: “It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken to you first. But since you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, from now on we are turning to the Gentiles” (Acts 13).

## Chapter V

“The Philistines took the ark of God and carried it from Ebenezer to Ashdod. The Philistines took the ark of God and brought it into the temple of Dagon, setting it beside Dagon.”

“Ebenezer” means “stone of help.” It is the place where Samuel set up a stone between Mizpah and Shen. Ashdod—also called Azotus—is one of the five cities of the Allophyles; its name is interpreted as “burning of the fatherland.” It is fittingly called the burning of the fatherland, for where the idol Dagon stood, the arrival of the ark of God in Ashdod was the burning of the devil, the father of all enemies. Dagon is interpreted as “sad fish” (*piscis tristis*); it signifies the ancient enemy who, placed in the sea of this world, devours sinners.

“When they rose early the next day in Ashdod, behold, Dagon was lying facedown on the ground before the ark of the Lord,” and so forth. We have already said above that the ark signifies the two Testaments. The Philistines, however, are prefigured in this passage as the Gentiles. But when they carried the ark into their temple, their god Dagon fell, and both his palms and his head were cut off. What does it mean that, when the ark is placed beside Dagon, he is immediately thrown to the ground, except that, as soon as the Testaments of God reached the Gentiles, the idols that possessed the deceived world were immediately destroyed, and all the error of images collapsed, unable to endure the presence of God?

It should be noted, however, that those who set the ark beside Dagon, as though the ark of God had been made subject to him, represented the wise men of this world, who wished to subject the Testaments of God to their own knowledge. Those who restored Dagon to his place represented those who defended the worship of idolatry. The hands cut off from Dagon signified the mutilation of idolatrous work; his severed head signified the cutting off of the devil’s pride, from which sin had its beginning. That his members were found on the threshold occurred so that they might recognize the predetermined end of their idolatry. The threshold signifies the end of a journey, that is, the completion of an idol; or the threshold signifies faith, through which the worship of idolatry is destroyed.

This too has great significance: in the very ruin and breaking of Dagon, of all his shattered members they found only his back intact. The back signifies flight, that is, the abolition of idols. For whoever flees gives his back to his pursuers. Hence it is written concerning enemies: “You will make them turn their backs” (Ps. 21).

Where are the idols? They have perished; and if any remain, they hide them and flee. For the text continues:

“But the hand of the Lord was heavy upon the people of Ashdod, and he destroyed them, striking Ashdod and its territories in the most secret part of the buttocks,” and likewise the four remaining cities.

Here too a figure is presented. The fact that those who captured the ark of God were struck in their hind parts seems to signify this punishment: if some receive the Testament of God but love the life behind them, they will be tormented in their hind parts, from and for the sake of those things that, as the Apostle says, should be regarded as refuse (Phil. 3). Those who take up the divine Testament in such a way that, looking backward, they do not strip themselves of their former vanity, resemble those enemies who placed the ark of the covenant captive beside their idols.

Those old things fall even against the will of those who cling to them, because “all flesh is grass, and” the glory “of man is like the flower of grass. The grass withers, the flower falls,” but “the ark of the Lord remains forever” (Isa. 40): namely, the hidden meaning of the Testament and the kingdom of heaven, where the eternal Word of God is.

## Chapter VI

“Thus the ark of the Lord was in the region of the Philistines for seven months.” This period, because of the totality of the ages that run their course under the number seven, signifies that the Testament of the Lord will remain among the Gentiles until the consummation of the age.

Then the narrative proceeds to say that, after taking counsel, they offered five golden tumors, according to the number of their cities, to the ark. The literal sense is clear, yet the passage also has a meaning: it signifies certain people who repent after their idolatry. Those who offer golden tumors and golden mice to the ark of the Lord are those who, having recognized its power through the scourge, repent of their past sins and the worship of idols and, through true confession, give glory to God. Although compelled, they turn their zeal for life toward better things, recognizing that they rightly suffer the Lord’s scourges and blows.

It is therefore beyond doubt that the five cities of the Philistines represented the five bodily senses: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. Through these a person either fulfills God’s commandments by good conduct or, by wicked living, satisfies the devil. The text continues:

“Now therefore take and make one new cart and two milch cows, upon which no yoke has been placed; yoke them to the cart and shut up their calves at home. Then take the ark of the Lord and place it on the cart,” and so forth.

Although we pass over the historical sequence, which is sufficiently clear, so that no one may think we are indulging in mere play, let us explain what moral significance it bore, drawing not on our own opinions but on the sayings of the saints.

What did the cows of the Allophyles carrying the ark of God prefigure except the figure of holy and faithful people renouncing the world? They have drawn no yoke of sin, nor are they hindered from their religious purpose by any attachment to parents, nor by any action, as is said of the Levites through Moses: “Those who say to their father and mother, ‘I do not know you,’ and did not know [them]” (Deut. 33).

What was carried by these same cows represented the sacrament of Holy Scripture, which all the saints, in obedience, carry as though the ark of the Lord had been placed upon them. The cart on which the ark was carried indicated the mystery of Christ’s cross. Hence the Truth says: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. 16; Mark 8).

It should be noted that these cows are said to have been milch cows, for there are many who, inwardly set upon the way of God, are outwardly bound by carnal affections; yet they do not turn aside from the right path, because they carry the ark of God in their minds.

Behold, the cows proceed toward Beth-shemesh. Beth-shemesh means “house of the sun,” and the Prophet says: “But for you who fear God, the sun of righteousness shall rise” (Mal. 4). If, then, we are moving toward the dwelling of the eternal Sun, it is surely fitting that we should not turn aside from the way of God because of carnal affections.

We must consider with all our strength that the cows, placed beneath the cart of God, proceed while groaning; they utter lowings from their inmost being, and yet they do not deviate from the path. So holy preachers, and likewise all the faithful within the holy Church, ought to suffer with their neighbors through charity, yet not wander from the way of God through confession.

The Philistine rulers also followed them as far as the borders of Beth-shemesh. The people of Beth-shemesh were harvesting wheat in the valley. When they lifted up their eyes, they saw the ark and rejoiced at seeing it. The cart came into the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh and stopped there. There was a large stone there. They cut up the wood of the cart,” and so forth.

It has already been said above that Beth-shemesh is interpreted as “house of the sun.” But what other “house of the sun” can there be in this passage except the holy Church, illuminated by the Sun of righteousness? And what does it mean that the people of Beth-shemesh harvest grain in the valley except that the teachers of the Church handle the grain of God’s word in humility?

Who is the stone in the field of Joshua except Christ the Lord in his Church? The wood of the cart undoubtedly prefigured the mystery of Christ’s cross. To sacrifice the cows upon the stone is for the holy converts to mortify themselves to the world in imitation of Christ.

“These are the golden tumors which the Philistines returned as a guilt-offering to the Lord: one for Ashdod, one for Gaza, one for Ashkelon, one for Gath, one for Ekron.”

Ashdod is interpreted as “fire”; Gaza as “strength” or “riches”; Ashkelon as “weights” or “homicidal fire”; Gath as “winepress”; and Ekron as “sterility” or “eradication.”

Some understand the five cities of the Philistines as the five bodily senses. Among them, Ashdod is fittingly interpreted as “fire,” signifying that fire by which the hearts of wretched people are kindled. Concerning them it is written: “They are all adulterers, like an oven their hearts” (Hos. 7).

Gaza, which is called “strength,” signifies those who are strong in committing adultery; or “riches,” concerning which the Lord says: “The cares of riches choke the word” (Matt. 13). These are the riches in which the wicked place their trust.

Ashkelon, which means “weighed,” signifies the weight of malice by which the reprobate are oppressed; or the “homicidal fire” by which they commit murders in order to abound in riches. Concerning this it is said: “Iniquity sits in the talent of lead” (Zech. 5).

Then Gath rightly follows, which is interpreted as “winepress.” It signifies the tribulations of the present life, in which the elect and the reprobate are tormented.

Ekron, which is called “sterility” or “eradication,” signifies the sterility of the reprobate who persist in these vices; and if they persevere in them, they will be eradicated from the land of the living.

These five cities offer golden gifts when, instructed by the gold of spiritual understanding, they turn away through repentance from the vices admitted through the five bodily senses and submit themselves to the divine Testaments. Hence they must attend to death, where there is true sorrow and perpetual sterility, and thus restrain themselves from iniquities.

But as the historical account says:

“From the fortified city to the village without a wall, and as far as great Abel, upon which they placed the ark of the Lord.”

Great Abel is a city on the border of Israel. It is called “great Abel,” although it had previously been called Beth-shemesh, either because of the mourning over the men of Beth-shemesh that occurred there, or to distinguish it from the city of Abel-beth-maacah, concerning which the wise woman cried out to Joab: “Let them inquire in Abel” (2 Sam. 20).

Thus the passage should be understood as saying that from the fortified city to the village without a wall, and as far as great Abel, they gave the mice. “Upon which”—that is, upon the mourning—they placed the ark of the Lord, which had remained until that day in the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh, and it remained there until it was taken to Kiriath-jearim. And it struck seventy men of the people and fifty thousand of the common people,” and so forth.

## Chapter VII

“It came to pass that from the day when the ark of the Lord remained in Kiriath-jearim, the days multiplied. For it was the twentieth year, and all Israel’s house rested after the Lord.”

The statement that he struck seventy men of the people who were not of the Levitical stock, and fifty thousand of the common people, is taken indifferently as referring to one and the same event. For even from the one Greek word *laos* (λαός, “people”), both are customarily translated. There nevertheless appears to be a distinction, because in the first clause of the verse it is added that seventy men were struck; concerning the common crowd, however, it says fifty thousand men. This was so that the people might not be exposed to danger, since, as in Exodus 20, the people stood at a distance and prayed, while Moses alone ascended to the Lord.

Hence the Hebrew reads: “And he struck seventy men of the people and fifty thousand men.” These seventy men are understood as judges, seventy Hebrews, whose merits and glory are compared with fifty thousand men, just as it is said of David: “You are counted as one for ten thousand” (1 Sam. 18).

The statement, “From the day when the ark of the Lord remained in Kiriath-jearim, the days multiplied; for it was the twentieth year,” and so forth, should be reckoned up to the eighth year of David’s reign, when he brought it to Jerusalem amid the gathering of the people. For it is found below that, in the time of Saul, it had been taken from this city and brought to the camp while he was fighting against the Philistines. Thus it is written: “Saul said to Ahijah, ‘Bring the ark of God here’” (1 Sam. 14). The ark of God was there on that day with the Israelites.

Since it is established (2 Sam. 6) that David brought it to Jerusalem from the house of Aminadab, into which it is reported not to have been brought, it remains to understand that, in Saul’s days, it was brought back from the camp and remained in the aforesaid city, from which it would again be brought to Jerusalem during David’s reign.

The sense of the statement, therefore, is that from the day when the ark remained in Kiriath-jearim, it was the twentieth year, when it happened that it was transferred from there during Saul’s time for the sake of the war. Finally, after the twentieth year had been completed, it was transferred by Samuel to Mizpah. From Mizpah Samuel and Saul transferred it to Gilgal. From there Saul transferred it to Nob, from Nob to Gibeah, and from Gibeah to the house of Obed-edom at Aiud [reading uncertain]. From there he transferred it to Zion. From Zion Solomon transferred it into the Holy of Holies.

Alternatively, it was the twentieth year when all the house of Israel still rested after the Lord, having cast away their idols and serving him alone. The following statement refers to this: “The children of Israel removed the Baals and the Ashtaroth and served the Lord alone.”

No one who is interested in sacred history is unaware that this occurred during the entire period of Samuel’s rule, which, according to Josephus, lasted twelve years, and during the first period of Saul’s reign, which, according to the same historian, lasted twenty years.

Afterward, when the Spirit of the Lord had departed from Saul and an evil spirit troubled him—especially to persecute David, who was innocent and just—it was necessary that no part of his army or people should have become an accomplice in his wickedness.

Having established these points according to the historical sense, we shall attempt to explain mystically what it signifies that the ark came to Kiriath-jearim, that they brought it into the house of Aminadab at Gibeah, and that from the day it remained there the days multiplied.

Aminadab, into whose house the ark came, is interpreted as “spontaneous father.” He signifies the people of the Gentiles, to whom the Lord the Father bestowed the grace of the Testament. With the Psalmist they can say: “I will sacrifice to you freely and confess your name, O Lord, for it is good” (Ps. 53).

Gibeah means “hill,” and signifies the souls of the humble, concerning whom it is said: “Let the mountains receive peace for the people, and the hills righteousness” (Ps. 72). According to Augustine, mountains are the greater souls, while hills are the lesser.

Alternatively, Gibeah, where Eleazar, son of Aminadab, was appointed priest to guard the ark of the Lord, is interpreted as “hill” or “height.” Eleazar means “help.” It is fitting that he who guards the ark of the Lord is called “help,” because whatever good holy men possess they attribute not to themselves but to the Lord. Hence the Apostle says: “Through Christ we have such confidence toward God—not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as from ourselves; our sufficiency is from God” (2 Cor. 3), and so forth.

Kiriath-jearim, however, which is interpreted as “village of forests,” signifies the holy Church gathered from the multitude of the Gentiles. After the Testament remained in it, the righteous multiplied, being illuminated by it as by days.

Baalim means “having lords,” or “ascending,” or “higher.” The Israelites cast it out, together with Ashtaroth. It signifies the idols of the Gentiles, which believers from the Gentiles cast away after receiving the ark of the Testament.

Alternatively, if the old Israel is understood as “the man who sees God,” it removes from itself every work of evil spirits—for this is what Ashtaroth means. It removes boastfulness and pride, and thus serves God alone, because “there is no fellowship between light and darkness, nor any agreement between Christ and Belial” (2 Cor. 6).

“Samuel said: ‘Gather all Israel at Mizpah, that I may pray to the Lord for you.’ And they gathered at Mizpah, drew water, and poured it out before the Lord,” and so forth.

Here, if it does not seem presumptuous—for we do not fully understand the matter—we shall insert what Hebrew tradition holds, as we have read in certain manuscripts, concerning the drawing and pouring out of water.

They report that a curse had been collected in that water before the Lord. Just as under the Law a woman suspected of jealousy was tested by drinking water, so here the idolaters were tested by this water—namely, those who entirely denied having worshiped idols. They also report that whoever among the idolaters tasted this water had his lips adhere to one another so that he could not separate them. By this sign idolatry was detected, and the person was put to death.

The following passage also demonstrates this, where it says: “Samuel judged the children of Israel at Mizpah.” Here “judged” means that he handed the idolaters over to death according to the Law.

They also say that Moses tested the idolaters who had made the calf in this way: he seized the calf, burned it, crushed it to powder, scattered it in water, and gave the Israelites some of it to drink.

Leaving aside these fantasies, since we do not know whether they are true, we understand simply that it was fitting for such a sound-minded man to govern the people entrusted to him with justice and truth and the greatest prudence.

We shall briefly undertake to indicate what the figure signifies. Mizpah, where Israel was gathered and where they drew water before the Lord, is interpreted as “intention.” It signifies the holy Church, in which there is true intention. This can be understood more appropriately through Mizpah itself: the Church, gathered in the unity of the faith under the new priesthood, draws waters of tears and pours them out before the Lord through the satisfaction of repentance.

The fact that Samuel the prophet judged the Israelite people in the same place, that is, at Mizpah, seems to indicate that every spiritual preacher especially strives to teach those faithful whom he sees directing their intention toward contemplation and toward love of the heavenly homeland.

The Philistine rulers went up against Israel. When the children of Israel heard this, they were afraid of the Philistines and said to Samuel:

“Do not cease crying out to the Lord our God for us, that he may save us from the hand of the Philistines.”

Samuel took one suckling lamb and offered it as a whole burnt offering to the Lord.

This lamb, offered figuratively, brought victory to the people of God, because, when unclean spirits were overcome through Christ’s passion, peace was restored to the faithful. Hence sacred history continues:

“It came to pass that, while Samuel was offering the burnt offering, the Philistines began battle against Israel. The Lord thundered with a great roar against the Philistines on that day and terrified them,” and so forth.

The Lord thundered with a great roar when, through the holy apostles, he sent forth the sound of preaching, as it is written: “The Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High uttered his voice” (Ps. 18).

When the Lord thundered in this way, he terrified the Philistines, and they were struck down by the children of Israel. For the unclean spirits, overcome by the preaching of the saints, withdrew from their presence. This is explained more fully in ecclesiastical history.

Hence Beth-car, where they were struck down, is interpreted as “house of recognition” or “house of the lamb.” It prefigured the Church of him concerning whom John says: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1). In that Church, and from that Church, with the Lord’s favor, the unclean spirits were overcome.

It is fittingly said: “They pursued them as far as the place above Beth-car,” which is interpreted as “house of recognition,” because the preachers pursued them until all error had been cleansed away and God was truly recognized.

The text continues:

“Samuel took one stone and placed it between Mizpah and Shen; and he called its name Ebenezer,” and so forth.

This stone, which Samuel placed between Mizpah, interpreted as “intention,” and Shen, which means “teeth,” as a sign of victory, prefigured none other than our Lord Jesus Christ. According to the sayings of the prophets, he was placed between the discovery of the Old Testament and the preaching of the Gospel, and he grants help to his faithful as they fight against hostile powers.

He was prefigured in the stone because of his firmness; he was signified in the lamb because of his innocence, or because he was sacrificed for us.

The statement, “Thus far the Lord has helped us,” shows that whoever crosses beyond these boundaries, like heretics, does not deserve God’s help.

The statement, “There was peace between Israel and the Amorites,” was given to be understood in the future: after the hostile powers had been conquered and had withdrawn through the Lord’s passion, the people believing from both circumcision and uncircumcision were united in the city of faith.

Amorites is interpreted as “bitter” or “speaking.” The Apostle says: “You who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ. For he is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. 2), and so forth.

This is the Samuel who called upon God; as we read below, God heard him, and at harvest time he obtained rain. In the Holy Scriptures, rain signifies the words of the Gospel or of the Law. Moses likewise says: “Let my teaching be awaited like rain, and let my words descend like dew” (Deut. 32).

Christ therefore gave this rain to the world at harvest time, that is, when the Gentiles had to be gathered, so that, like grain into barns, they might be gathered within the Church’s embrace.

“Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life. Each year he went around Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah, and judged Israel in those places.”

It is not without a mystery that Samuel visited the places mentioned above and judged Israel. In this he represented the teachers of the holy Church. To make this clearer, let us explain it.

Bethel, interpreted as “house of God,” signifies the holy Church, which is called the house of God, in which the Lord has deigned to dwell by his grace, namely, in the minds of the elect. As he says: “I will walk among them and dwell in them” (2 Cor. 6; Lev. 26).

Gilgal, interpreted as “revelation,” likewise signifies the Church, concerning which the Lord says: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matt. 18), namely, through the grace of his revelation and the presence of his divinity.

Mizpah, interpreted as “intention,” follows fittingly, because in the holy Church of God mentioned above there is a pure intention in the minds of the elect, by which they always hunger and long for God.

In this Church the prophet Samuel judges the children of Israel—that is, as a faithful teacher, he makes judgments concerning the faithful in the Church.

It is therefore appropriately said that Samuel, returning, dwelt in Ramah, where his house was. This seems to indicate that every ecclesiastical teacher and spiritual man in the Church, although he delights to dwell always in the height of contemplation—for this is what Ramah means, being interpreted as “exalted mind”—nevertheless does not refuse, through acts of compassion, to descend to the weaker members of the Church.

He judges the people of Israel when, by his exhortation, he instructs and teaches the people entrusted to him to preserve the unity of faith and to practice the other virtues. Or, when he becomes a judge of another’s sins and exercises judgment in the house of God, he must not act with ill will, but according to what Holy Scripture reveals. Finally, he must return to the house of his own heart and conscience and offer sacrifices of good will to God.

## Chapter VIII

“All the elders of Israel gathered together and came to Samuel at Ramah. They said to him: ‘Behold, you are old, and your sons do not walk in your ways. Appoint a king over us to judge us,’” and so forth.

What did it signify that the elders of Israel, after rejecting Samuel the prophet, asked for a king, except what we recognize as fulfilled at the Savior’s coming? When the scribes and Pharisees rejected the Lord Jesus Christ, the true priest, and chose a king for themselves, they cried: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19).

Samuel, whose name is interpreted as “God,” rejected by the elders of Israel, signifies the Lord and Redeemer. Saul, whose name means “asked for” or “request,” because he is read to have been requested by the people, signifies Barabbas, whom they asked to have released for themselves.

Saul is read to have been the son of Kish, son of Abiel. Kish is interpreted as “hard” or “vomiting”; Abiel means “my father is God.” The interpretations of these names pertain to the hardness and vomiting forth of the malice of the Jews: although confessing God the Father, they denied the Son in his passion, saying: “Take this man away and release Barabbas to us,” not understanding that whoever denies the Son denies the Father who sent him.

## Chapters IX and X

“Samuel took a little flask of oil, poured it over his head, kissed him, and said: ‘Behold, the Lord has anointed you over his inheritance as ruler.’”

It should be understood that Saul did not always represent one and the same person. At times he represented the Jews, because of their pride and envy against God, as we touched upon above and shall demonstrate later. At times he represented our Lord Jesus Christ, because of the anointing of his kingship, the greatness of his stature, and his princely office. Concerning him Isaiah says: “The government was made upon his shoulder” (Isa. 9).

All the kings of Israel in former times were called, by reason of the sacrament of anointing, types of Christ the Savior. Hence David said to the man who pretended that he had killed Saul: “How were you not afraid to lay your hand upon the Lord’s anointed?” (2 Sam. 1).

It is fittingly said that Saul towered above all from the shoulder upward, in the spiritual sense, because Christ is our head above us. It is also fittingly said, “There was no one better than he”; and the Psalmist says: “Who shall be equal in the clouds, or who shall be like God, the Son of God?” (Ps. 89).

At times he represented the prince of this world, because of the arrogance of his heart and his oppression of the humble, as will be explained below. But in this passage, where he is read to have been anointed by Samuel, he designates Christ the Lord, that is, the Savior.

Just as Saul was taken up into the kingdom while seeking the missing she-asses of his father, so in a similar way our Lord and Savior, after being sent by his Father, deigned to come to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel and was established by him as king over all his people.

Thus he himself says: “I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain” (Ps. 2; Mark 23). This was prefigured by the she-asses because of simplicity, and by the sheep because of innocence.

The shoulder that Saul received, as was read above, signifies the authority that our Lord received. He is said to have been anointed by Samuel because the only-begotten Son is read to have been anointed with spiritual anointing by God the Father. Concerning him the Psalmist says: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you” (Ps. 45), and so forth.

We have not followed the sequence of the history here, but have attempted to set forth continuously its spiritual meaning. Since, however, we have passed over the historical account somewhat, we have decided to make a digression in order to explain it. Sacred history says:

“Saul said to his servant: ‘Come, let us go; what shall we bring to the man of God?’” and so forth.

Saul did not think that Samuel could indicate his father’s she-asses to him in any other way than through the price of divination. The servant spoke of this after hearing Saul say: “Bread has failed in our bags.”

“Behold, I have in my hand a quarter of a silver stater; let us give it to the man of God.”

Therefore he said: “What shall we bring to the man of God?”

When Saul was asking about the Seer, they answered:

“Hurry now, for today he came into the city, because there is a sacrifice of the people today on the high place.”

Here “sacrifice,” as some wish to understand it, means a meal that Samuel had prepared for the people at the Kalends, since the text continues:

“The people will not eat until he comes, because he will bless the sacrifice; afterward those who have been invited will eat.”

If someone wishes to understand this simply as referring to slaughtered victims and sacrifices, we do not prohibit it.

Samuel said to Saul:

“Go up before me to the high place, so that you may eat with me. In the morning I shall send you away, and I shall tell you everything that is in your heart.”

Here, if it is not displeasing, we presume to insert a Jewish tradition, as we have found it written. Saul had in his heart, as they themselves report, that he would become king, because he had seen in a vision that he was placed at the top of a tree; this vision was a royal sign.

Finally, he was not speaking only about the she-asses that he had lost, because when Samuel said, “I shall tell you everything that is in your heart,” he immediately joined the matter by means of the conjunction, adding:

“And as for the she-asses that you lost three days ago, do not be anxious, because they have been found. And to whom will belong all the best things of Israel? Will they not belong to you and to all your father’s house?”

Traditions of this kind among the Jews were produced from their apocryphal books, which they keep hidden with them and which are not found among our books. Because some accept them, this does not mean that they approve them; rather, they take from them what is necessary for confirmation.

The Apostle Paul does the same in his Epistles (Titus 1; 1 Cor. 15), drawing not only from the apocryphal books of the Hebrews but also from the works of Gentile poets and comic writers.

[scan page 152]

## Expositions on the Books

Where he saw it opportune, he brought forward examples—not in order to approve all their interpretations, but to insert what he saw was appropriate whenever necessary. Hence the Apostle Jude, in his Epistle, introduced an example from the same books, saying:

> “But Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied concerning these people, saying: ‘Behold, the Lord came with his holy myriads to execute judgment against all’” (Jude, ii [as printed]).

This was taken from the aforementioned books; but because it is true, it is not to be rejected. Nevertheless, not everything is to be approved; only what is necessary is to be accepted. In the same way, some traditions are to be adopted when occasion requires.

> “And when you have gone from there and gone farther”—and so on until he says—“three men ascending to God at Bethel will meet you.”

These men were going to Bethel for the sake of prayer, where Jacob had erected a stone.

> “After this, when you come to the hill of God, where there is a Philistine garrison…”

The hill of God was the place where the prophets lived.

> “And when you enter the city, you will meet a company of prophets coming down from the high place, prophesying themselves; and the Spirit of the Lord will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them, and you will be changed into another man. When all these signs have come upon you, do whatever your hand finds to do, because the Lord is with you; and the Spirit of the Lord will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them.”

The Jews say that he prophesied there concerning the future age, Gog and Magog, the rewards of the righteous, and the punishment of the wicked. Since he prophesied under the impulse of the Spirit of the Lord, there is no doubt that he prophesied concerning the coming of Christ and the salvation of humanity.

> “When all these signs have come upon you, do whatever your hand finds to do, because God is with you.”

It is as though he were saying: “By these signs you will be able to know that God has willed you to become king; therefore act royally in everything that must be done by you, because God is with you.”

> “When all who had known him yesterday and the day before saw that he was with the prophets and prophesying, they said to one another: ‘What has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?’ Another answered the other, saying: ‘And who is their father?’”

—and so forth.

He rightly says, with Saul prophesying together with the others, “And who is their father?” It is as though he were saying: “Who is greater than he in dignity and wisdom?” For one who is so learned and wise can very well associate with the prophets and be called their father—that is, their teacher. A teacher is called a father, just as Elisha calls Elijah his father, that is, his teacher: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its charioteer.” And in the Book of Job, Elihu calls Eliphaz “father,” that is, teacher, in these words:

> “My father, let Job be tested to the end” (Job 34).

The fact that Saul found everything as the seer had foretold signifies that everything happened to Christ as the books of the Law and the Prophets had formerly predicted—even if some wish these things to be understood of the Jews, to whom prosperity or adversity came just as had been foretold.

### Chapter XI

> “Now Nahash the Ammonite went up and began to fight against Jabesh-gilead. And all the men of Jabesh said to Nahash: ‘Make a covenant with us, and we will serve you.’ And Nahash the Ammonite answered them: ‘On this condition I will make a covenant with you, that I may put out the right eyes of all of you.’”

Since this is history, we shall undertake to unfold its spiritual meaning with the briefest explanation.

Nahash, whose name means “serpent,” signifies the devil—not only because he is slippery and crooked, but also because he deceived the first human being through the serpent. He goes up to fight against Jabesh, whose name means “sense,” because the devil is always trying to take away from human beings their understanding of divine kinship and goodness.

Gilead, which is called “a heap of testimony,” signifies those who have been instructed in the Church by the testimonies of the divine Scriptures. Nahash wants to tear out their right eyes; that is, he strives to take away the illumination of faith and preaching.

But Saul—that is, the Lord and our Redeemer—delivers them with his army: namely, with the assistance of his angels or preachers, who count the people at Bezek. Bezek means “poverty,” because in the poverty of the present life the Lord knows who are his; and with him there is a fixed number of the elect whom he raises up for battle against the devil.

We may apply this also to heretics, who are a people of sorrow because they do not possess the joy of the Holy Spirit. Their perversity makes this covenant with the people of the Church: that it may tear out their right eyes—that is, remove the understanding or vision of the sound orthodox faith. It wants them to have a left eye, that is, a perverse understanding and corrupt opinions.

But the faithful people heap together a mass of testimonies from the divine Scriptures, with which they may resist their enemies. They send throughout all the boundaries of Israel—that is, to the teachers of the Church—in order that these may bring them assistance and set the shield of faith against the enemy in opposition.

### Chapter XII

> “Then Samuel said to the people: ‘Come, and let us go to Gilgal and renew the kingdom there,’”

—and so forth until he says:

> “The Lord sent Jerubbaal and Bedan and Barak and Jephthah and Samuel, and delivered you from the hand of your enemies.”

Before we explain what precedes, we must say who this Jerubbaal and Bedan were. Jerubbaal is Gideon, who with three hundred men overcame the Midianites. Bedan, as some think, is Samson.

According to the higher meaning, however, Gilgal, where Samuel renewed the kingdom and reproved the children of Israel, means “revelation” and signifies the revelation and illumination of faith in the New Testament, where the old kingdom was changed into the new. We have already spoken above of this change, where we described Eli and his rejected sons, and the election of Samuel.

With the Lord’s favor, we shall speak later of Saul’s rejection and David’s establishment. But in the fact that Samuel reproved the children, according to the moral meaning he bore the type of spiritual teachers—those who do not have serious faults in themselves for which they must be reproved, but who strike at the sins of others without reluctance.

[scan page 153]

## Angélomus, Monk of Luxeuil

Solomon speaks of such men:

> “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven firmly in place” (Ecclesiastes 12).

He rightly says, “The words of the wise are like goads and like nails driven firmly in place,” because they do not know how to caress human sins or handle them with a soft hand of indulgence; rather, they correct them with the harsh rebuke of a severe admonition and drive into the erring the pain and wound of repentance.

Therefore, if someone’s speech does not prick but merely delights its hearers, it is not the speech of a wise man. Hence John rebuked the Jews who were boasting with a harsh denunciation, saying:

> “Brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matthew 3).

Finally, we can also indicate this interpretation by a brief inquiry into the passage in which he says, “The words of the wise are like goads,” and so forth. For they provoke people to conversion, and they are firm and do not err in any respect, because, inspired by the Holy Spirit in the prophets and apostles, they have come down to them. Therefore they are founded upon a solid root.

Hence the same verse adds:

> “They are given by the counsel of masters, from one shepherd”—

that is, they were spoken through the counsel of the prophets, and were inspired by one shepherd, namely the Holy Spirit.

Whoever is instructed by these words and illuminated by the divine Spirit can correct the sins of others, insofar as human frailty does not hinder him from restraining himself from sin. For he rightly reproves the evil of others who lives spiritually and cannot be reproached by anyone for his own offense. For it is written:

> “The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself judged by no one” (1 Corinthians 2).

One who judges others for their crimes must be innocent of every offense, just as Samuel is read to have been. Such men also bring rain from heaven—that is, the knowledge of preaching from the books of the prophets, of which it is written:

> “Judgment was set, and the books were opened” (Daniel 7).

They pour this knowledge into human hearts so that they may produce the fruit of faith and good works, and so that those who recognize that they have acted wickedly may be brought to fear.

Next follows the account of how Samuel, when questioned about his leadership and when the people entreated him, saying, “Do not cease praying for us,” answered:

> “Far be it from me before the Lord that I should cease praying for you.”

Here the perfect kindness of the saints, once displayed in Samuel, is shown—the kindness of which the Lord says:

> “Love your enemies, and pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matthew 5).

### Chapter XIII

> “Saul was the son of one year when he began to reign; and he reigned over Israel for two years.”

This is said not merely of Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul, but of Saul himself. For Saul was as innocent when he began to reign as a one-year-old son, and he persevered in innocence. Since he reigned for two years in that same innocence and humility, he is rightly said to have been like a son of one year.

The remaining years in which he reigned unworthily are not included in this reckoning. But if anyone wishes to understand the statement by anticipation as referring to Ish-bosheth, since it is later read that Ish-bosheth was forty years old when he began to reign and reigned for two years, and since the whole period from the death of Eli to Saul amounts to forty years, we do not forbid this interpretation, for it too can be understood.

> “And Jonathan struck the garrison of the Philistines that was in Geba. When the Philistines heard this, Saul sounded the trumpet throughout all the land, saying: ‘Let the Hebrews hear,’”

—and so forth.

What is said—“When the Philistines heard this, Saul sounded the trumpet”—is to be understood in this way: when the Philistines heard it, they were thrown into confusion; Saul sounded the trumpet. This trumpet was a sign of victory and an exhortation, so that the Hebrews might hear and know that, once the Philistines had been thrown into confusion, they had been overcome.

Therefore it follows:

> “And all Israel heard such news.”

> “Saul struck the garrison of the Philistines.”

When Israel learned these things, it was strengthened. Hence it also follows:

> “And Israel rose up against the Philistines.”

That is, Israel began to act bravely against them.

> “When the men of Israel saw that they were in a difficult position—for the people were hard-pressed—they hid themselves in caves, in hiding places, among rocks, and in pits and cisterns,”

—and so forth.

If Israel hid itself in the places mentioned, the question naturally arises: what is meant by the history’s adding:

> “But the Hebrews crossed the Jordan”?

We can understand this in no other way than by supposing that those who, terrified by fear of Saul, had withdrawn from him crossed over to the Philistines. Later, when they heard that the Philistines had fled, they joined their own people in battle.

What this means—that the fugitives returned and joined their own people in battle—we shall explain later.

> “While Saul was still at Gilgal, all the people who followed him were terrified. He waited seven days according to the appointed time of Samuel, but Samuel did not come to Gilgal. The people dispersed from him. Then Saul said: ‘Bring me the burnt offering and the peace offerings,’”

—and so forth until it says:

> “Samuel said to Saul: ‘You have acted foolishly and have not kept the commandment of the Lord your God that he commanded you,’”

and so forth.

Yet above he had already said:

> “You shall go down before me to Gilgal. I shall indeed come down to you, so that you may offer an offering and sacrifice peace offerings. You shall wait seven days until I come to you and show you what you are to do.”

Some think that Saul offered the burnt offering without blame, since Samuel, whom he had awaited, did not come to him within the appointed seven days. But whoever carefully distinguishes this passage will find that Saul was rightly blamed and reproved as disobedient.

Some distinguish the passage in this way:

> “You shall go down before me to Gilgal. I shall indeed come down to you.”

Then what follows is added:

> “To offer offerings and sacrifice peace offerings, you shall wait seven days until I come to you and show you what you are to do.”

Samuel therefore did not command Saul to await his arrival for seven days, but wished Saul to await him for those same seven days in order to offer offerings and sacrifice peace offerings. Saul did not do this, and therefore he is rightly blamed and branded with the epithet “foolish.” His offering was condemned because he transgressed the command of obedience and was not accepted by God.

Since he paid too little attention to the prophet’s command, he despised God, who was speaking through the prophet, as the Lord says:

> “Whoever listens to you listens to me, and whoever rejects you rejects me” (Luke 10).

Thus he heard:

> “But now your kingdom shall not endure. The Lord has sought for himself a man according to his heart, and the Lord has commanded him to be leader over his people, because you have not kept what the Lord commanded you.”

Saul’s rejection prefigured the future removal of the kingdom from the Jews. The fact that David was made his successor indicates that the Lord Jesus Christ, through the New Testament, was to reign in the Church and succeed the people of the Jews.

> “Now no ironsmith was to be found throughout all the land of Israel. For the Philistines had taken precautions, lest the Hebrews make a sword or spear. All Israel therefore went down to the Philistines, each to sharpen his ploughshare, his mattock, his axe, and his sickle. The edges of the ploughshares, mattocks, tridents, and axes were blunted,”

—and so forth.

The Philistines, who are also called Allophyles, although in many places in the holy Scriptures they signify different things in various allegorical ways, in this passage prefigure the bands of all heretics. United in impiety, they conspire against the Church of God. Trusting in the multitude of people who agree with them and in the powers of this world, they strive to strip the same Church of God of its faithful.

Many of the Church’s weaker members fear their multitude; having renounced the faith, they depart from the unity of the Church and join the same heretics. Others, hiding themselves in silence because they fear confessing their faith openly, lie concealed as though in caves and hollows of the earth.

The Philistines, who are said to be immensely numerous, clearly represent the teachers of all heretics. Because of their various sects, they are like horses of different colors, bound together by a single bond of impiety. With loosened reins they race across the fields of this world to deceive and oppress as many as they can.

The six thousand horsemen represent the proud men of the world who, swollen with carnal power, become the heretics’ assistants. The remaining multitude of the people signifies the vast common crowd, which the heretics deceive by cunning persuasion and draw to themselves.

The six hundred men who are said to have remained with Saul may represent Catholic men who cling to the Lord Christ through the unity of faith, like Saul, and who do not depart from him under any persuasion or terror of evil.

The ironsmiths allegorically signify spiritual men in the Church who, in a time of peace, when no one is disturbing them, become sluggish through mental security or negligence and grow dull in spiritual inquiry, as though they did not exist. Because they are not trained, they are never ready to answer the enemies of the faith.

The ploughshares, mattocks, and other tools spiritually indicate the testimonies and judgments of the sacred Law. In the peace of the Church, its priests use these testimonies solely for the instruction of the faithful people, as though for agriculture, according to the plain sense of the history.

If, however, at some time, with God’s permission, the wars of heretics should rise up against the Church, ecclesiastical men investigate these same testimonies with subtle inquiry and sharpen them with spiritual insight, as though turning tools into swords. Through them they overthrow the enemies of the faith, and defend both themselves and the other faithful from their persecution or persuasion.

The precepts and testimonies of the divine Law are tools in the peace of the Church and weapons in time of war.

To make the point clearer: in the peace of the Church, its bishops or priests, instructing the people entrusted to them in faith by simple preaching, do not set before them lofty or incomprehensible matters concerning God. Rather, they teach them simply to believe in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—one God, essentially one and true, but three in person.

But if some heretic, an advocate of the Sabellian party, should say, “Just as one deity is to be believed in God, so also one person, not three—that is, the Father himself is the Son and the Son himself is the Father, as Sabellius impiously taught,” what must the ecclesiastical men do? They must be able to prove from the sacred Scriptures themselves how almighty God is one in nature but three in persons.

Again, in a time of quiet, it is not appropriate for teachers of the Catholic Church to preach anything more to the peoples over whom they preside than that they should believe in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as of one substance and one deity; that the Son was ineffably begotten from the substance of the Father, without beginning, in every respect like and coequal with the Father; and that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son and is of one substance with those from whom he proceeds.

But if, against this true preaching, some advocate of the Arian party should say, “It is not as you preach; but just as you confess three persons in God, so you must believe three substances in him. The Son did not subsist from the substance of the Father but was created from nothing; likewise, the Holy Spirit is not to be believed to be God but a creature,” what will the ecclesiastical man do against such an impious preacher? He must bring forth proofs from both Testaments and sharpen the divine testimonies like tools, through which he may defend what he preaches and refute those who contradict him.

Again, in a tranquil time, it is not appropriate for the priests of the Church to preach anything more concerning the Son of God than that he is believed to be true God, ineffably begotten from the substance of the Father outside time, and true man, created and born in time from the substance of his mother for our redemption: of two substances but one person; consubstantial with the Father according to divinity and consubstantial with his mother according to humanity; one and the same in the singularity of his person.

Against this faith, if opposing parties arise, one may assert that the two natures in the Son of God are so confused and mingled that he constructs no distinction between God and man, but that what is divinity in him is also humanity, as the Eutychians and their like heretics impiously strive to defend.

Again, another may come forward who, while affirming two natures in him, wishes to assert two persons as well, as the Nestorians do. A third or fourth may arise: one who says that the same Son of God is truly God but was man only in appearance, as the Manichaeans and Priscillianists dared to say; another who contends that he was a mere man, without God, like the Photinians.

Still others may exist who say that he, the Son of God, assumed nothing from his mother and was not of the same nature as we are, but bore some imaginary flesh in the world. There are many others whom it would be too lengthy and unnecessary to enumerate.

What must ecclesiastical men do against all these enemies of the faith? They must file, sharpen, and clarify from both Testaments various judgments and testimonies, as though using different tools. Through these they may defend what they believe and preach, and either strike down their adversaries by piercing them or at least drive them into flight by terrifying them.

In this way the priests of God must act with complete vigilance against the various questions that arise in the Church through the vice of contention. They must also be watchful with every effort against the new inventions of heretics, lest the faith of the Church, like the foundation of a building, should slip and collapse under the assault of those heretics, as though struck by winds.

What Scripture says concerning the Israelite men—

> “All Israel therefore went down to the Philistines, each to sharpen his ploughshare, his mattock, and his axe,”

and so forth, may reasonably be understood to mean that the controversies of heretics are exercises for Catholics; the contention of evil people sharpens the understanding of the good; and the adversity of the impious is the left-handed weapon of the righteous.

The heretics, however, like the Philistines, take every precaution to prevent Catholic men from possessing spiritual weapons on their account.

### Chapter XIV

> “Now it happened one day that Jonathan the son of Saul said to his young armor-bearer: ‘Come, and let us cross over to the garrison of the Philistines that is beyond that place,’”

and so forth.

This statement depends upon what precedes.

Jonathan, whose name means “gift of a dove,” represented spiritual men filled in the Church with the gift of the Holy Spirit. Through such men the Lord disturbs, scatters, and puts to flight the assembly of heretics.

His armor-bearer prefigured their holy disciples, who follow their example and teaching and adhere to them indivisibly, as though carrying their weapons.

The fact that Jonathan and his armor-bearer went against the Philistines not through level and gentle places but by a rocky and steep route allegorically signifies that those priests who live within the Church and walk along the broad and spacious road of a dissolute life cannot oppose the enemies of the faith or fight them spiritually. Rather, this belongs to those who walk along the narrow and difficult way, between the Old and New Testaments and between prosperity and adversity, as though between two cliffs, advancing on the right and the left.

The route Jonathan proposed to his armor-bearer—that unless they were first challenged by the enemies, they should not cross over to them but remain at rest—typologically indicates to us through this sacred text that no Catholic should first take up the weapons of contention against heretics unless he has first been challenged by them to battle. For the wars of contention in the Church begin not with Catholics but rather with heretics.

The fact that Jonathan and his armor-bearer, in their first encounter with the Philistines, fought them not elsewhere but in a cultivated field, and struck down twenty enemies as first-fruits [the printed word is unclear], seems figuratively to signify that heretics yield and fall before those teachers who remain within the boundaries of the Church and do not depart from meditation on the Law, just as from cultivation.

Next follows:

> “But the Hebrews who had been with the Philistines yesterday and the day before, and had gone up with them into the camp, returned to be with Israel,”

and so forth until it says:

> “They reported to Saul that the people had sinned against the Lord by eating with the blood. He said: ‘You have acted treacherously. Roll a great stone to me now.’”

Before we undertake to unfold the spiritual figure, we must explain what Scripture means when it says of Jonathan:

> “His eyes were enlightened.”

What, according to the historical sense, does it mean that the people ate with the blood? What does sacred Scripture mean when it says:

> “Jonathan’s eyes were enlightened because he tasted the honey”?

Was he previously blind? Certainly not. His eyes were enlightened not for seeing, since he had seen before, but for discerning, because he had touched what was forbidden.

The same is reported of the first human beings: as soon as they tasted what had been prohibited, they are said to have had their eyes opened—namely, to discern between the good they had lost and the evil into which they had fallen.

Some, however, wish to understand the passage differently. They say that his eyes had been strained by excessive heat and by the exertion of battle and travel, and that, exhausted by excessive fasting, he had perhaps become weak not only in body but also in mind, where the eyes of the inner person are found.

[scan page 156]

Therefore, when he had tasted the taste of honey, he is said to have been enlightened because, they say, not only did his eyes begin to see more clearly after the restoration of his body, but his inner mind also became clearer, strengthened by the sweetness of the honey and more ready, with his strength renewed, to pursue his adversaries.

Hence he himself says:

> “My father has troubled the land. You yourselves have seen that my eyes were enlightened because I tasted a little of this honey. How much more if the people had eaten freely of the spoil of their enemies that they found!”

When he says, “My father has troubled the land,” he grew proud over the victory that had been achieved, and therefore reproved his father for the fast he had imposed.

Finally, what follows is:

> “The people, exhausted and turning toward the spoil, took sheep, oxen, and calves, and slaughtered them on the ground. And the people ate with the blood.”

The people did not make Saul’s oath void. Saul had said:

> “Cursed is the man who eats bread until evening, until I have avenged myself on my enemies.”

He said this because they had already obtained the victory. But they are said to have sinned against the Lord and to have eaten with the blood because, contrary to the precept of the Law, they ate before the evening sacrifice had been performed.

The practice was that, whenever homicide occurred among them, whether involving their own people or others, they were not to eat until the evening sacrifice had been offered for them. When a sanctuary was not present, the blood of the victims was commanded to be poured out upon the ground, while the victims’ flesh was eaten. But when the sanctuary was present, the blood of the victims was commanded to be poured upon the altar of the Lord.

Thus it is written in the Book of Deuteronomy:

> “You shall pour out the blood of your sacrifices upon the altar, but you may eat the flesh” (Deuteronomy 12).

Because this people did not do what was prescribed, they are said to have sinned against the Lord and therefore are said to have eaten with the blood.

Alternatively, they are said to have sinned against the Lord and to have eaten with the blood because, when they slaughtered the victims, they did not bring to the sanctuary for the priests, according to the command of the Law, the fat and the blood, even though they had a sanctuary with them.

When the sanctuary was absent, the blood of the victims was ordered to be poured upon the ground. This was the case with the victims that they slaughtered in their camps. But when the sanctuary was present, the blood of the victims was ordered to be poured upon the altar of the Lord.

There is also another possible interpretation. In former times, the Law mystically prescribed that no one in Israel should sacrifice a sheep, ox, goat, or any animal offered to the Lord in the camp, but that they should bring it all to the entrance of the tabernacle and slaughter everything there. Since they had not done this, they are said to have eaten indiscriminately by slaughtering with the blood.

Although this latter interpretation may please some, the earlier ones seem to us to agree more closely with the history. We do not state this in order to reject the latter interpretation or to prevent it from being understood, especially since it agrees with the spiritual meaning about which we shall speak in what follows. Rather, we leave our interpretation to the prudent reader, indicating our view so that, if it pleases him, he may favor us by agreeing with it. For, as I have said, this concerns the root of the historical account.

Behold, we have indicated the foundation of the history; now we shall unfold its spiritual meaning. First, however, we shall explain what it signifies that Jonathan, the son of Saul, while going into battle and observing the fast, saw honey upon the face of the field, extended the tip of his staff, dipped it into the honeycomb, and tasted it, whereupon his eyes were enlightened. We shall explain this so that afterward we may set out the remaining matters together.

As we said, Jonathan’s eyes were enlightened by tasting the honey, not for seeing, since he had seen beforehand, but for discerning, because he had touched what was forbidden. That occurrence, as with Adam, made him attentive and rendered him confused. What else does it express except that everyone who strives to serve God is warned to despise all such enticements of pleasure in the world?

For he cannot contend in spiritual strength against the Allophyles—that is, against the rulers of darkness—who still neglects to avoid such sweetness. “Honey dripping,” says Scripture (Proverbs 5), is found on the lips of the adulteress, signifying the delight of carnal pleasure.

According to the mystical understanding, Jonathan is thought to have tasted this honey and, when discovered by lot, to have been freed only with difficulty through the prayers of the people.

The matter described above also has a mystical meaning: after the Philistines, with the Lord’s assisting help, had been thrown into confusion, scattered, and put to flight, all those of the children of Israel who had remained attached to them returned again to their own Israelite people.

When the assembly of heretics, with the Lord cooperating, has been defeated, scattered, and put to flight by ecclesiastical men, and has yielded to the Catholics, those who had previously been taken away from the Church by force or perversion return again to the Church from which they had departed.

Yet many priests, still holding different opinions and having been led astray into various sects, decide that those whom they have been able to bring back to the Church from the heretics themselves—as though they were sheep or oxen—must be baptized again. In former times some priests had thought that those who converted from heresy to the Church should be baptized again, just as the heretical Donatists do.

It is unlawful, however, to baptize again those who have once been washed, or to administer a baptism that is not correct according to ecclesiastical rule to those converted from paganism.

Nevertheless, the Lord Christ, like Saul, recalls such people to the unity of the faith through ecclesiastical men, in the faith whose figure was represented by the great stone; Saul commanded all believers to be baptized.

The command that a sheep, ox, or any animal offered to the Lord should not be slaughtered in the camps but should all be brought to the entrance of the tabernacle, as we showed above, and slaughtered there, foreshadowed things to come.

For what the entrance was in the Law, the great stone is here; and this signifies unity of faith in Christ. Just as sheep, oxen, calves, and rams signify different people coming to the faith, so the slaughter of the animals indicates the washing of regeneration.

In this baptism, as with any animal, the old person dies and the new person rises again.

Those who kill the same believers, as though they were different animals, and eat them with the blood upon the ground are divided into various sects; in the unity of faith, as is fitting, they do not—[the supplied text breaks off].

### [Scan page 157]

**ANGELOMI, MONK OF LUXEUIL**

#### 303

They do not baptize them at all. They eat them, as it were, with the blood, when they join them to themselves without complete purification from sins. They consume them, as it were, when they make themselves one body with them. It follows:

> “But Saul built an altar to the Lord. Then he first began to build an altar to the Lord.”

The Hebrew does not have “first,” as we read in certain books. Hence the question arises: since it is read earlier that he built an altar when he was rebuked by Samuel, why is it said here, “Then he began first to build an altar to the Lord”? We must understand that he did build an altar, but because he built it disobediently, he is understood to have built it not for the Lord. Here, however, because he built it obediently and correctly, he is said to have built it for the Lord.

> “And Saul said to the people: Bring here all the corners of the people.”

By “the corners of the people” he calls the leaders of the people, around whom that same people clung, as though walls clung to stones here and there. Then it follows how Jonathan was discovered by casting lots. Hence Saul says:

> “May God do this to me and add this also, for you shall surely die, Jonathan.” And the people said to Saul: “Shall Jonathan then die, who has brought about this great salvation in Israel? This must not happen.” So the people rescued Jonathan, and he did not die.

Observe how much past good deeds avail against any slight offense. For if Jonathan’s past deeds had not helped him, he could never have escaped the evils that threatened him. God is not unjust, so as to forget anyone’s good works.

### Chapter XV

> “And Samuel said to Saul: The Lord sent me to anoint you as king over his people Israel. But now hear the voice of the Lord. Thus says the Lord of hosts: I have reviewed all that Amalek did to Israel, etc.,” until he says:
>
> “Do not spare him, and do not desire anything of his possessions, but kill from man to woman, and child and suckling, ox and camel and donkey.”

God is said to review the evils of the Amalekites, just as they had formerly been foretold through Moses in the Law. Therefore the Lord commands Israel to destroy even Amalek’s animals, so that no memory of him might remain in the animals either. For the Lord had said that he would wipe out the memory of Amalek from under heaven; therefore Saul is commanded to destroy him completely, from man to beasts. And because his memory was not completely erased, Saul’s sin and disobedience were the cause, as the following history shows.

Concerning this Amalekite it is said in the Book of Deuteronomy:

> “Remember what Amalek did to you on the way, when you were going out from Egypt: how he encountered you and struck down the hindmost of your people, who were exhausted and sitting down” (Deut. 25).

Here the Hebrews understand “the exhausted” to mean those who, according to the Law, were unclean and remained outside the camp. The Amalekites are said to have struck them down because, as they themselves relate, they cut off their circumcision and threw it up into heaven as an insult to God.

> “And Saul said to the Kenite: Go away, withdraw, and depart from Amalek, lest I involve you with him,” and the rest.

The Kenite himself was Jethro, Moses’ kinsman. The Kenites were descended from him; they had gone down to Amalek and lived with him, since he was their kinsman, and they held an inheritance in his land. The Kenite is said to have shown mercy to the children of Israel either because he had supported Moses in the land of Midian, or because he gave Moses counsel concerning the way in which he should govern the multitude of the people (Exod. 18).

> “It was announced to Samuel that Saul had come to Carmel and had erected for himself a triumphal arch.”

It was customary for kings, when they obtained a victory, to make an arch—that is, a structure of myrtle, palms, and olives, as some think—as a sign of victory. But if anyone wishes to understand it as an arch made of stones, on which he had depicted his victory in the manner of kings, we do not forbid it; indeed, we agree more readily, because we read in Solomon:

> “A wise king scatters the wicked and bends the arch over them” (Prov. 20).

Another translation has “millstone.” On it kings inscribed their praises and victories for eternal remembrance.

> “Then Samuel said to Saul: Let me be, and I will tell you what the Lord spoke to me during the night.” And he said to him: “Speak.” And Samuel said: “Were you not, when you were little in your own eyes, made head over the tribes of Israel?”

What is cast in the king’s teeth by this rebuke, except the pride with which he was puffed up? Anyone who has been placed in authority can turn this toward his own correction. Saul had formerly regarded himself as little in his own eyes, but, supported by temporal power, he no longer saw himself as little. Preferring himself to the rest because he could do more than all the others, he considered himself great above everyone. Yet, in a marvelous way, when he was little in his own eyes, he was great before the Lord; but when he appeared great to himself, he was little before God.

Often, while the mind is inflated by the abundance of those subject to it, it is corrupted into the excess of pride, with the very height of power serving as its enticement. This is said to have happened to Saul, to whom it is said:

> “Were you not, when you were little in your own eyes, made head over the tribes of Israel?”

It is as though he were told: “When you saw yourself as little, I made you great above the rest. But because you see yourself as great, you are regarded by me as little.”

Therefore, when Samuel rebuked him for not having obeyed the voice of the Lord, he answered from that very arrogance, saying:

> “Indeed, I heard the voice of the Lord, and I went on the way by which the Lord sent me.”

He added evil to evil, because he not only did not deign to acknowledge his fault, but also tried to defend it through pride; and by defending it he heaped it up. Finally, in what follows:

> “But the people took from the spoil sheep and oxen, the firstfruits of what had been killed, to sacrifice to the Lord their God at Gilgal.”

Here “firstfruits” means those things that were more valuable and better. It follows.
