### [Scan page 158]

#### 305

**COMMENTARY ON THE BOOKS OF KINGS—ON BOOK I**

> “And Samuel said: Does the Lord desire burnt offerings and sacrifices, and not rather that the voice of the Lord be obeyed? For obedience is better than sacrifices, and to listen than to offer the fat of rams. For to resist is like the sin of divination, and to refuse assent is like the crime of idolatry.”

Here we can say nothing other than the judgment of the supreme commentator, Pope Gregory, which he inserted in the books of the *Moralia* when explaining this passage morally in his treatment of the good of obedience. For he says:

“Obedience is rightly placed before sacrifices, because through sacrifices another person’s flesh is slaughtered, but through obedience one’s own will is put to death. The more quickly, therefore, someone appeases God, the more completely does he sacrifice himself before God’s eyes, restraining the pride of self-determination with the sword of the commandment.”

Conversely, disobedience is called the sin of divination, so that the nature of the virtue of obedience may be demonstrated. Thus, by contrast, it is shown more clearly what is thought of its praise. If resisting is like the sin of divination, and refusing assent like the crime of idolatry, obedience alone possesses the merit of faith; without it, anyone may be seen to be unbelieving.

Hence, in praise of obedience, Solomon says:

> “An obedient man speaks of victories” (Prov. 21).

An obedient man truly speaks of victories, because when we humbly submit to another’s voice, we conquer ourselves in our hearts. For what benefit is there in wishing indiscriminately to offer something to God while opposing his commands? No one can appease the Lord with gifts offered to him if he neglects to obey his orders. Since he does not need our goods, he is not nourished by our giving; and for this reason obedience is better than sacrifices. Whoever wishes may read more fully about it in the books of the *Moralia*.

> “And Saul said to Samuel: I have sinned, because I transgressed the word of the Lord,” and the rest, until he says:
>
> “And the Lord has rejected you from being king over Israel.”

The prophet rebukes the king for disobedience, because he did not take care to fulfill the command, and he foretold that the kingdom would be taken from him because he did not wish to follow the rectitude of God’s commands. And deservedly is he cast down from the summit of power who does not know how to hold authority rightly. For he holds authority rightly who subjects himself to his superior in humility for obedience, and places himself before his inferior in authority for teaching. If Saul had obeyed God’s commands, he would have ruled the people rightly.

> “And Samuel turned to go away; but he seized the hem of his cloak, and it was torn. And Samuel said to him: The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today and has given it to your neighbor, who is better than you.”

Observe the mystery: just as, in the Lord’s Passion, the high priest tore his garment (Matt. 26), so now King Saul is described as tearing the prophet’s garment. For through both powers—the royal, certainly, and the priestly—the tearing of the garment took place, to show that the stability of kingdom and priesthood could not remain among the Jewish people, who refused to receive the true king and priest coming to them, namely, the Lord Christ.

> “But the triumphator in Israel will not spare, and he will not be bent by repentance; for he is not a man, that he should repent.”

In the Hebrew it reads:

> “The triumphator of Israel will not lie.”

This triumphator is God, to whom every victory is rightly ascribed. He will not lie, because he grants to his servants what he promises them. He is not bent by repentance, because he does not repent of the good things he has bestowed; he is not changeable, but judges everything according to justice and truth.

> “And Saul said: I have sinned, but now honor me before the elders of my people and before Israel.”

It is as though he had said: “Honor me as king, so that I may go before you as king, and you may follow, while I worship the Lord your God.” By “the elders of his people” he means his own tribe; by “before Israel,” the other tribes of Israel.

But in saying, “Honor me before the elders of my people,” he spoke out of shame and under the control of pride, because he feared losing his honors. Therefore he did not obtain what he asked for when he said, “I have sinned,” and the rest. For whoever, under the appearance of confession, still fears losing human honors cannot obtain from God the forgiveness he requests with feigned humility. One cannot attain pardon in a confession of repentance where exaltation of mind takes precedence.

For what else is it than pride of heart to refuse to be reproved by people for the guilt of a crime? Through this pride the sinner, while refusing to displease human beings, excludes himself from the forgiveness he could have received from God. Feigned humility cannot obtain forgiveness from God.

But it should be noted that another edition has:

> “I will not return with you,” Samuel said, “because you have rejected the word of the Lord, and the Lord has rejected you from being king over Israel.” And Samuel turned his face to go away. Saul seized the hem of the double garment, and it tore. And Samuel said to him: “The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from your hand today and will give it to your neighbor who is good above you. Israel will be divided in two, and he will not turn away nor repent, because he is not like a man, that he should repent. He threatens, and does not remain.”

This is the one to whom it is said, “The Lord has rejected you from being king over Israel.” He “reigned forty years over Israel,” that is, for as long a period as David himself; and he heard this at the beginning of his reign.

Let us understand this to have been said because no one from his family was to reign, and let us refer it to the family of David, from which the Lord arose according to the flesh:

> “The mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2),

as blessed Augustine says. In the Greek copies also it is read:

> “The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from your hand,”

so that “from your hand” may be understood as meaning “from Israel.” For this man figuratively represented that people, which was destined to lose the kingdom; and the Lord Christ was destined to reign spiritually.

When it is said, “It shall be given to your neighbor,” this refers to kinship according to the flesh. Christ was from Israel according to the flesh, and so was Saul.

What has been added, “who is good above you,” can indeed be understood as “better than you,” as though it said: “Because he is good, therefore he shall be above you.” It accords with that other prophetic saying:

> “Until I place all your enemies beneath your feet” (Ps. 109).

Among these is Israel, from whose persecutor Christ took away the kingdom. Hence it is also said:

> “And Israel will be divided in two.”

That is, into Israel hostile to Christ and Israel adhering to Christ; into Israel belonging to the slave woman and Israel belonging to the free woman (Gal. 4). These two groups were at first together, until the barren woman, made fruitful through the grace of Christ, cast out the slave woman and her son (Gen. 21).

Because of Solomon’s sin, when his son Rehoboam was reigning, we know that Israel was divided in two and continued in that state until it was taken captive by the Chaldeans. But what has this to do with Saul? If something of this sort had been threatened, it should rather have been threatened to David, whose son Solomon was.

Finally, the Hebrews were not divided among themselves, but were scattered throughout the lands indiscriminately in the fellowship of the same error. That division, however, which God threatened under the person of Saul, who bore the figure of that kingdom and people, was threatened to that same kingdom and people:

> “Because he is not like a man, that he should repent. He threatens, and does not remain.”

That is, man threatens and does not remain. God is not one who repents as a man does. Wherever Scripture says that he repents, a change in circumstances is understood, while the divine foreknowledge remains unchangeable. Therefore, when he is said not to repent, this means that he does not change.

We plainly see that through these words a divine and insoluble judgment was pronounced concerning this division of the people of Israel: all who have passed over or will pass over to Christ will never be with the Israelites who remain enemies of Christ to the end of this life. They will remain perpetually in the division here foretold.

> “And Samuel said: Bring Agag, king of Amalek, to me.” And he was brought to him. “And Samuel cut Agag to pieces before the Lord at Gilgal.”

When Scripture records that holy men spared the enemies, some say that they are eager for human blood, because the righteous also struck their enemies so that none who could be saved was left by them. They do not understand that mysteries are represented under these words, and that what is indicated to us is rather that, when we fight against vices, we must leave none at all, but destroy everything, lest, if we spare them, it be counted against us as guilt, as is written concerning Saul, who kept the king of Amalek alive.

For how can anyone remain righteous if he still preserves some sin within himself, like Saul? But the saints, represented by Samuel, rage against their enemies—that is, against the vices of sinners—so that they do not allow any sin to remain unpunished.

> “Nevertheless Samuel mourned for Saul, because the Lord regretted that he had made Saul king over Israel.”

Here the perfect benevolence of the saints toward Saul is displayed in the prophet Samuel. Although he knew that Saul had sinned, he mourned for him out of the affection of his kindness. Paul likewise mourned for those who, after fornication and uncleanness, had not repented (2 Cor. 12).

### Chapter XVI

> “And the Lord said to Samuel: Fill your horn with oil and come, so that I may send you to Jesse the Bethlehemite; for I have provided a king for myself among his sons. Samuel did as the Lord commanded, and he anointed David, the youngest of his father’s sons, in the midst of his brothers. He was ruddy, handsome in appearance, and pleasing in face.”

Let us examine how this same David prophetically signified Christ. David means “strong of hand” or “desirable.” And what is stronger than that Lion of the tribe of Judah, who conquered the world? And what is more desirable than he, of whom it is said:

> “The Desired One of all the nations will come” (Hag. 2).

This David is anointed as a future king, announcing Christ through that anointing. For Christ is called from *chrism*, “anointing.”

After the seven older sons of Jesse had been rejected, the youngest in age was chosen for the kingdom. For when the Jewish priesthood and the kingdom of the earlier people were rejected—the people who observed the sabbath according to the Law—our Lord Christ, the head of the younger people, exercised an everlasting priesthood. He was anointed as king, whose kingdom has no end, and whom all nations, tribes, and languages will serve.

That he is said to have been anointed in the midst of his brothers refers to what the Prophet says of the Lord:

> “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44).

David was transferred from the pastoral office of tending sheep to the kingship. Our David, Jesus himself, was taken away from the sheep of the Jewish people and transferred to the kingdom of the nations. Christ is no longer among the Jewish people; he was taken away from them and now feeds the flocks of the nations.

> “So Samuel arose and went to Ramah. But the spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord troubled him.”

The question is raised concerning this evil spirit: if it is from the Lord, why is it evil? If it is evil, why is it from the Lord? But this sentence is contained in two words: in the Lord there is just power, and in the devil there is unjust power.

For the same spirit is evil through a most unjust will, and that same spirit is of the Lord through the just power it has received. Thus the devil is called the spirit of the Lord because of his ministry, since it is said that God makes good use even of spiritual evils, either for the condemnation of certain people, or for correction, or for testing.

Although he always desires affliction, nevertheless, if he does not receive power from our Creator, that same evil spirit cannot prevail in the matter of temptation. Therefore every will of the devil is unjust; yet, with God permitting it, every power is just.

It is rightly said, then, that an evil spirit from the Lord troubled him: “from the Lord,” namely, through the permission of just power; “evil,” through the desire of an unjust will. Although evil does not come from the Lord, power comes from no one except God.

The same is said elsewhere concerning the sleep of the Lord that had seized the soldiers

Thus he is called an evil spirit of the Lord, that is, a minister of God, sent to do to Saul what the Almighty judged that he ought to suffer. For that spirit, as has been said, was not God’s in the will by which it was evil; but as a creature created by God, and in the power which it had received—not from itself, but through the justice of the Lord of all—it was the Lord’s.

This has been said according to the historical sense. Tropologically, however, Saul prefigured the people of the Jews, who at the coming of the Savior were abandoned by God because of their impiety. They lost the Holy Spirit that they had once received and have been agitated to this day by an evil spirit—that is, by the devil’s falsehood.

> “Whenever the spirit of the Lord seized Saul, David took the lyre and played it with his hand; Saul was refreshed and felt better, and the evil spirit departed from him.”

This depends on what precedes. Here too, as above, the figure of the Savior is held before us. David was skilled in musical songs, and the Lord Jesus Christ daily resounds in the unity of the Church through varied harmonies in the exposition of the holy Scriptures, and modulates with mystical sweetness.

David, singing on the lyre, drove away the evil spirit; and Christ, through the power of his cross, crushed the demons and drove them from the hearts of believers. The power was not really in David’s lyre, but the mystery of Christ’s cross was mystically represented through the wood and the stretching of the strings; upon it also Christ’s Passion was sung.

David, the eighth and youngest brother, is chosen for the kingdom; and the Lord Jesus Christ emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and through the glory of his resurrection and the preaching of the Gospel—for the mystery of the number eight contains this meaning—obtained the kingdom among the nations.

David is described as handsome in face, because the Lord Jesus Christ is also “beautiful beyond the sons of men.” David is said to have been ruddy, and concerning our Savior the Prophet sings:

> “Who is this who comes from Edom?” (Isa. 63)

and the rest. The word is interpreted as “ruddy” or “blood-colored.”

Moreover, the moral lesson teaches us that when an unclean spirit invaded Saul, David’s lyre was taken up and calmed his madness. Often a proud or wealthy person must be soothed by the charm of exhortation, because hard wounds are often softened by gentle applications, and the fury of the insane is frequently brought back to health by a mediator who uses gentleness. When one condescends to such people in sweetness, the sickness of madness is eased.

Nor should we overlook the fact that, when an opposing spirit invaded Saul, David took up the lyre and calmed his madness. What is signified by Saul except the arrogance of the powerful? And what is suggested by David except the humble life of the saints? When Saul is seized by an unclean spirit, his madness is moderated while David sings, because when the minds of the powerful are turned into fury through exaltation, it is fitting that they be recalled to mental health, as though by the sweetness of a lyre, through the tranquility of our speech.

#### 310

### Chapter XVII

> “The Philistines gathered their forces for battle and assembled at Socoh,” and the rest.

Socoh is a town in the tribe of Judah, as is recorded in the books of *The Places*. Even today there are two villages on the road for travelers going from Eleutheropolis to Aelia, at the ninth milestone of the public road: one situated on a mountain and the other in the plain; they are called Socoh. The name is interpreted as “branch” or “twig.”

Azekah is a city of the Canaanites in the territory of the tribe of Judah, as far as which Joshua pursued the five kings. Even today it is called the village of Azekah, between Eleutheropolis and Aelia. Its name is interpreted as “fortress” or “trap.”

Domim, or Doma, in the tribe of Judah, is a large village in Daroma—that is, in the southern region—at the borders of Eleutheropolis, seventeen miles distant from it. Its name is interpreted as “silence” or “joy.”

> “Saul and the men of Israel were gathered together in the Valley of the Terebinth.”

“Terebinth” and “Sichim,” beneath which Jacob hid the idols near Neapolis. Hence Josephus reports that the Philistines camped between Socoh and Azekah. Against them Saul again led his army, and, establishing a camp on a certain mountain, forced the Philistines to abandon their former camp and come opposite the mountain that Saul had occupied. A mountain situated between them divided their army.

> “And a bastard went out from the camp of the Philistines, named Goliath,” and the rest.

Therefore, as we promised at the beginning, we wish to touch on the history little by little, so that afterward we may set forth the summit of spiritual understanding.

He is called a bastard because he was born from a giant father and a mother from Gath. David, however, was the son of an Ephratite man from Bethlehem of Judah, whose name was Jesse and who had eight sons.

The question is why he is said here to have had eight sons, when in Chronicles no more than seven are read. The matter is resolved as follows: he counts Nathan the prophet, the son of his son Shammah, whom he had raised and nourished among his sons as though he were a son. For before Samuel seven of his sons are read as having been brought, while the eighth was in the pastures. It is clear that Nathan was brought among them; he is also called Jonathan.

Concerning him it is said near the end of Samuel:

> “Jonathan, the son of Shammah, David’s brother, struck him down.”

It should be noted that wherever he is called a prophet, he is written as Nathan, not Jonathan.

> “And his father said to David: Go to your brothers; visit them to see whether they are well, and learn with whom they have been assigned.”

In the Hebrew it is written:

> “And you shall visit your brothers to see whether they are well, and take their pledges.”

In this passage the Hebrews understand “pledges” as a letter of divorce. According to the custom of that people, when they went out to battle they gave letters of divorce to their wives, so that if a husband happened to be captured in battle and led into captivity, his wife, after waiting three years, might marry another man if her husband did not return.

Let the prudent reader choose what he prefers; we have decided to keep to the simplicity of the historical account.

### [Scan page 161]

#### 319 / 311

> “And his brother said to David: Why have you come, and why have you left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your pride,” and the rest.

He says that he knows his brother’s pride and the wickedness of his heart. He did not doubt that David had been lifted up by swelling of heart because Samuel had anointed him king.

David was sent by his father to visit his brothers; likewise the Lord Christ says that he was sent by God the Father to the sheep that had perished, the house of Israel (Matt. 15).

David brought his brothers an *ephah* of roasted grain—that is, a measure of three portions—and the Lord Jesus Christ delivered the Decalogue of the Law to the people of the Jews.

> “David took the head of the Philistine and brought it to Jerusalem. But he placed his weapons in the tabernacle.”

The statement that David brought the Philistine’s head to Jerusalem anticipates what he did later. As for his weapons, that is, the Philistine’s, it should not be understood that he placed them in his own tabernacle, but in the tabernacle of the Lord. From that tabernacle he later received them from Abimelech the priest; therefore the word “his” has been added unnecessarily.

> “And Abner said: As your soul lives, O king, I do not know.”

According to that type of expression, this is said as in another passage:

> “Nabath blessed God and the king,”

that is, as though he had said: “May your soul not live, O king, if I know.” Alternatively: “May I see your death, if I know.” Or, as some wish, *si* is used in place of the adverb “not,” as in the Psalmist:

> “If they shall enter into my rest.”

That is, “They shall not enter.”

He says, “I know,” as though he had said, “I do not know.” He uses an oath by the life of the king and affirms that he does not know where David came from. Joseph also used this form when he said to his brothers:

> “By the life of Pharaoh, you shall not depart from here until your youngest brother comes.”

So much for the history, which we have touched on briefly as we promised. Now let us add the figures of spiritual realities.

The sacred narrative says:

> “The Philistines gathered their forces,”

and the rest. What are signified by the Philistines except hostile powers? And what is prefigured by Goliath of Gath except the devil, the head of all evils? From the beginning of the world he has fought against the people of God with his satellites, but before the coming of the true David—that is, the Redeemer of the human race—he could be conquered by no one.

Gath is the city of that same Goliath, and its name is interpreted as “winepress.” It therefore suggested the likeness of the present world or of hell, in which world and hell the devil trampled the human race, subject to sins, as in a winepress.

The enormous size, or height, of Goliath signified the devil’s pride. The number seven possesses the mystery of supreme rest; from that rest the same devil was excluded because of the merit of his pride and fell into this world, which is said to have been made in six days. And because he obtained dominion in this world over the creature that had abandoned God on account of sin, he proudly raised his head over the creature of the world itself.

Goliath’s weapons and all his armor demonstrated the devil’s impiety and wickedness, by which, warring against the human race, he had oppressed it under the heavy weight of sins. But Christ, through the new teaching that he handed down to his Church, commended the mystery of the Holy Trinity to all believers.

David brought ten portions of cheese to the commander, and the Lord Jesus Christ delivered the Decalogue of the Law to the Jewish people.

Goliath of Gath bore the person of the devil. Boasting from the height of his pride, he fought against the people of God throughout all the time that elapsed before the Savior’s coming. In the lowest part of this world, as though in a valley, he could be conquered by no one.

Eliab, David’s elder brother, whose name is interpreted “My God is father,” undoubtedly bore the type of the Jews. Although they falsely claim, through an erroneous opinion, to have God as their father, because they were jealous of the Lord Jesus Christ, his Son, they degenerated from the inheritance of the children of God and lost, through the merit of their fault, the firstborn privileges that rightly belonged to them.

David killed both the lion and the bear; and the Lord Jesus Christ will punish in judgment the devil, who secretly lies in wait for human beings and, before Christ and afterward, rages most openly.

David laid aside Saul’s armor, because Christ also rejected the bodily sacraments of the Law and the carnal wars that were not imposed upon the nations. We read about the burdens of the Law, but we do not observe them carnally.

He chose five very smooth stones from the stream and put them into his shepherd’s bag; and the Lord Christ took the five books of the Mosaic Law from the stream of this age. For mortal time flows and whatever enters the world passes away. It was in the stream as though in that people.

> “And he put them into the shepherd’s bag.”

For he himself is the true God, the shepherd of souls. The shepherd’s vessel in which, as some say, he used to milk signifies the divine grace joined to the Law, which is understood in the five stones and without which the Law is not fulfilled.

David is said to have been ruddy and handsome, because concerning the Lord Jesus Christ the Church says in the Song of Songs:

> “My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen from among thousands” (Song 5).

We have touched above upon his beauty.

Goliath challenged David to battle; likewise the devil’s pride, scorning Christ’s humility, was overthrown by him.

David’s staff, despised by the devil, bore the mystery of the Lord’s cross. David cast one stone from the five, because—[the supplied text ends here].
and Christ, who was announced from the Law, by singular power, through the unity of faith and his grace, overthrew the devil’s pride. He prefigured the founding of the Church, which, as though in a circle, is rolled through the volumes of time. David struck Goliath on the forehead and brought him down; likewise Christ, having conquered the devil, attached to himself those who had clung to the devil, separated them from his fellowship, and subjected them to his faith. For this was signified by the fact that Goliath, when struck, fell forward on his face. After striking Goliath, David took his sword; so did our David, who, when those whom the devil held in his power—and by whom he slaughtered darkened souls—believed, transformed their tongues against the devil. Thus Goliath is beheaded with his own sword. David carried Goliath’s sword to Jerusalem; likewise Christ transferred those whom he snatched from the devil’s power into his Church, for the defense of the altar of faith.

Saul asks Abner about David as though he were unknown: from what stock he descended, or whose son he was, although David had long before ministered to Saul and stood in his presence to drive away the evil spirit. Such, indeed, was the blindness of the Jews: they knew that the Lord Jesus Christ would come through the Law and the Prophets, and they could have recognized him, in his bodily presence, through the working of his miracles, as the Son of God; yet, as though they did not know him, they say to him: “Who are you? And where is your father?” (John viii).

In the moral sense, David held the type of the Lord, since his name is interpreted “strong of hand.” Goliath signifies the pride of heretics, who were overcome by the sword of rational faith. David came to battle with a shepherd’s bag, but David, overcoming that same Goliath, killed him with his own sword. The saints likewise do this: as members of the preceding David, they have deserved, through his condescension, to become what they are. When they conquer heretics who pride themselves on bringing forward the judgments of Holy Scripture, they defeat them with the very words and judgments that the heretics themselves utter, as though they were beheading the proud Goliath with his own sword.

## CHAPTER XVIII

“And it came to pass, when he had finished speaking to Saul, that the soul of Jonathan was bound to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul,” and the rest.

Jonathan, the son of Saul, whose soul was bound to David’s, seems to have signified those saints who, from the Jewish people, adhered through faith to the Lord Jesus Christ. Having received the grace of the Holy Spirit, they followed him for love of Christ, abandoning everything, as did the apostles and those who, in the Acts of the Apostles, sold all their possessions and brought the proceeds to the apostles’ feet (Acts ii).

But the fact that Jonathan stripped himself of his garments and weapons and clothed David seems to indicate that all the sacraments which had been stripped away—that is, the priesthood and preaching formerly bestowed upon the Jewish people—were to be transferred to Christ’s Church. Or, according to the higher sense, he rightly gave everything from his tunic to his belt, because believers likewise strove to devote to Christ every possession they could have in this world, turning everything into profit for him.

“Now when David returned after striking down the Philistine, women came out from all the cities of Israel, singing and dancing to meet King Saul with timbrels of joy and with sistrums; and the women, playing, sang and said: ‘Saul has struck down a thousand, and David ten thousand.’ But Saul was exceedingly angry, and this saying displeased him. He said: ‘They have given David ten thousand, and to me they have given a thousand. What remains for him but the kingdom alone?’ Therefore Saul did not look upon David with right eyes from that day onward.”

This is understood as follows: envy flared up in Saul against David; likewise, the Jewish people, joined together to their own ruin by rivalry, conspired against Christ the Lord. When they heard Christ preached in the churches—the one whom they had handed over to death—and saw believers rejoicing in praises of his victory, because he had triumphed over the ancient enemy, they were gravely offended.

“On the following day an evil spirit from God seized Saul, and he prophesied in the midst of his house. David was playing with his hand as on each day,” and the rest.

When it says, “an evil spirit from God seized Saul,” he was acting in the manner of those possessed. “And he prophesied.” In this passage, to prophesy must be understood as nothing other than reporting what belonged to another.

As for what follows concerning David—“He went out and came in before the people”—it should be understood in this way: when they went out to battle, he went out first before them in royal fashion, and then returned.

“Now Michal, Saul’s daughter, loved David. And it was reported to Saul, and it pleased him. Saul said: ‘I will give her to him, that she may be a stumbling-block to him and that the hand of the Philistines may be against him,’” and the rest.

Finally, Saul thought that David could be killed by these two dangers: either through the treachery of his daughter, by whom Saul saw that he himself was greatly loved, or because of the foreskins of the Philistines, to obtain which David was about to go to war against the Philistines. Hence he also says:

“Today my son-in-law shall be mine in two ways.” And Saul commanded his servants: “Speak secretly to David, saying: ‘Behold, you please the king, and all his servants love you,’” and so forth.

He says that David would become his son-in-law in two ways because David had already brought the foreskins of the Philistines for Merob, whom Saul gave to Adriel the Meholathite, and afterward two hundred for Michal. Although it is not explicitly said that Saul gave David the foreskins of the Philistines for Merob, anyone who reads and examines what precedes and follows will find that David gave Saul the foreskins of the Philistines twice. For above Saul had said: “Let not my hand be against him, but let the hand of the Philistines be against him.” Below he says:

“The king has no need of a bride-price, except a hundred foreskins of the Philistines, to take vengeance on the enemies of the king.” And Scripture adds:

“But Saul was thinking of throwing David into the hands of the Philistines.”

This is how we have arranged the meaning of the passage, following an interpretation devised by some commentators. If anyone does not wish to accept it, we do not object; but if he follows a better interpretation, we have resolved to rejoice gladly with him.

But let us state what seems to us. He aptly says, “Today my son-in-law shall be mine in two ways”: namely, because David had overthrown so huge a giant and was thereby worthy of such great valor that he should become the king’s son-in-law; this is one way. The other was the condition he proposed to him: that he should bring a hundred foreskins of the Philistines. David brought not only a hundred but even two hundred. From the very undertaking by which he was thought likely to perish for the kingdom, he was led to a more glorious triumph. Such is the history.

Moreover, in the figurative sense, Saul’s cunning pretense of exposing David to danger, and David’s being led to a more glorious triumph by the very undertaking in which he was thought likely to perish for the kingdom, signify that the Jews, when they attempted to kill Christ against God’s will, brought about the salvation of the Gentiles by the very means through which they believed they would extinguish him. For David’s bringing the foreskins of foreigners and thus receiving Saul’s daughter in marriage signified that Christ would not first betroth the Synagogue to himself unless he went forth glorious among the Gentiles. First he cut away among the nations the pollution of the flesh in both sexes, and afterward made the Synagogue his people. For, as it is written, after the fullness has entered in, then all Israel will be saved (Romans xi).

He brought a double number—that is, two hundred foreskins—either because he gained more from Jews and Gentiles, or because the number of the Gentile people acquired is greater than that of believing Jews. Saul’s hatred for David increased so greatly that the king, seeking relief for his spirit, tried to pin David to the wall with a spear while he was playing psalms.

What does it mean that, when an adverse spirit attacked Saul, David’s cithara, once taken up, soothed his madness? Saul signifies the pride of the Jews; David, the humility of Christ. Therefore, when Saul is seized by an unclean spirit, David’s singing moderates his frenzy: when the mind of the Jews is driven into fury through blasphemy, it is fitting that it be recalled to health through the tranquillity of evangelical speech, as though by the sweetness of a cithara.

Some understand Saul’s attempt to fasten David to the wall with a spear, and David’s evasion while the spear, having inflicted no wound, was driven into the wall, as follows: while Christ preached the Gospel, the Jews planned to inflict death upon him; but when he departed from them alive for the salvation of the Gentiles, their malice wounded only the hardness of their own minds.

With this purpose in mind, Saul had been accustomed to go to the field, where it had also been agreed that David should be killed, as Jonathan informed David.

Saul sent guards to David’s house to watch him and kill him in the morning. When Michal, David’s wife, had announced this to David, saying: “Unless you save yourself this night, tomorrow you will die,” she lowered him through the window. He departed and fled, and so was saved. When Saul’s messengers came, they found an image laid upon David’s bed, with a goatskin at its head.

Let us therefore hear what this signifies: Saul had sent men to watch David so that they might kill him. This does not refer to the Lord’s cross, but nevertheless it pertains to his Passion. Christ was crucified, died, and was buried. That tomb was like a house, to guard which the kingdom of the Jews sent guards when it placed guards at Christ’s tomb.

How was the house guarded, if David signifies Christ, so that Christ might be killed, when he was not killed in the tomb of Christ but on the cross? This is therefore referred to Christ’s body, because to kill Christ meant to remove the name of Christ. For no one would have believed in Christ if the lie of the guards, who were bribed to say, “While we were sleeping, his disciples came and stole him away” (Matthew xxviii), had prevailed.

Thus, to wish to kill Christ meant to extinguish the name of his resurrection, so that a lie might be preferred to the Gospel. But just as Saul could not accomplish that purpose when he sought to kill David, so the kingdom of the Jews could not erase the memory of Christ.

Those, however, who wished to presume upon Christ by means of Saul’s power—that is, the kingdom of the Jews—stumbled upon the stone of stumbling, as upon an image, and a kid appeared to them as a lamb: for they found no sin in the one whom they persecuted as a sinner.

“It was reported to Saul by those who said: ‘Behold, David is in Naioth in Ramah.’” Naioth is a place in Ramah, where David was staying. Ramah, in the tribe of Benjamin, is Saul’s city, six miles from Aelia, northward toward Bethel. There is another in the tribe of Asher.

Naioth is interpreted “beauty,” and Ramah “height.” These names of the places therefore fit the events accomplished there: they possess both the words of the prophets and the exaltedness of knowledge and the beauty of expression.

“He also stripped off his garments and prophesied before Samuel with the others; and he fell naked all that day and all that night. Hence the proverb arose: ‘Is Saul also among the prophets?’”

A major question arises here, since earlier it is written: “And Samuel did not see Saul until the day of his death,” whereas here Saul is said to have prophesied before Samuel.

The Hebrews solve this question in two ways. Either Samuel did not see him because, when Saul was thrown among the band of prophets, Samuel hid himself so that Saul would not see him; or he did not see him clothed in royal attire, which he had worn. Hence it is said: “He did not see him until the day of his death,” with “clothed in royal attire” understood.

His stripping should likewise be understood not as removing all his garments, but only his royal garments.

The same question is asked: how did those who had been sent to seize and lead the man to his death become worthy of being made such by the Spirit of God? Saul himself, who had sent them and who came seeking to shed innocent blood, also received that Spirit and prophesied.

As far as the literal sense is concerned, it is astonishing that a rejected man should suddenly prophesy, although many similar instances of the gift of prophecy are recorded among wicked men: Balaam, for example, whom Scripture does not conceal to have been condemned by divine judgment, nevertheless possessed prophecy.

The words written in the Gospel also bear witness to this interpretation. Many will say on that day: “Lord, Lord, we ate and drank in your name, and in your name we prophesied, and in your name we performed many miracles.” To them he will say: “I do not know you; depart from me, workers of iniquity” (Luke xiii).

Mystically, however, what else does this example of Saul and his messengers signify—those who began to prophesy after they had been sent to persecute David—than certain heretics who possess something good from the gift of the Holy Spirit, such as the books of the Law and the Gospel and the sacrament of baptism, yet persecute Christ in his members?

When they come to the Catholic Church, nothing in them is to be violated or treated as though they possess nothing that should be handed over. Nevertheless, they must not for that reason presume upon salvation. We do not reject what they have received, nor do we condemn it; but we must recognize the unity and fellowship bound together by charity, without which whatever they possess—even if it is holy and venerable—they themselves are nevertheless nothing.

They have become all the more unworthy of the reward of eternal life because they have not used well the gifts they received in this transitory life.

The Jews may also fittingly be represented in this passage. While they desire what is hostile to Christ, they carry in their mouths the sacraments of the Law and the Prophets as testimony to Christ, and, together with the Church, dispute from the Scriptures as though with prophets, just as those men prophesied with the prophets.

Whom did Saul, persecuting and prophesying, prefigure except the Jewish scribes and Pharisees? They carry in their mouths the sacraments of the Law and the Prophets, which were spoken concerning Christ as testimony to him, and dispute about the Holy Scriptures with ecclesiastical men.

The statement that Saul stripped himself and prophesied naked unmistakably prefigured this: the Jewish people, whose person Saul represented, stripped of the garment of faith and the dignity of the priesthood, and deprived of the glory of the kingdom, carried on their lips the words of the Law and the Prophets that bear witness to Christ, yet, blinded by the envy of their malice, persecuted the same Christ the Lord about whom they prophesied without understanding.

## CHAPTER XX

“And Jonathan said to David: ‘The Lord be with you, as he was with my father. And if I live, you will show me the mercy of the Lord.’”

What he says—“The Lord be with you, as he was with my father”—seems to me capable of being understood as though he had said plainly: “May the Spirit of the Lord remain with you, as he was formerly with my father, and may he make your kingdom as exalted as he made my father’s kingdom.”

“And if I live, you will show me the mercy of the Lord,” namely, so that I may be buried in your kingdom.

“But if I am dead, you will not remove your mercy from my house forever.”

What follows—“when the Lord has cut off the enemies of David, every one of them, from the earth”—and shortly afterward, “and the Lord will seek from the hand of David’s enemies,” was inserted by anticipation. The author first interposed a later event: this happened much afterward, when, after Saul had been killed, the kingdom was transferred to the house of David. Those who had unjustly persecuted him in innocence were then punished by a just divine vengeance.

At that time the Lord sought from the hand of David’s enemies why they had afflicted a holy man; they were then compelled to give an account of the hatreds with which they had raged against him for so long. The same may also be understood of Absalom, Sheba the son of Bichri, and David’s other enemies.

Alternatively: if you wish to know what the Lord sought from the hand of David’s enemies, it may perhaps—unless I am mistaken—be understood from the preceding statement, where it was said that Jonathan had made a covenant with the house of David. It may mean that the Lord sought this covenant from the hand of David’s enemies: that is, why they were unwilling to make peace with him through the covenant by which they saw that the Lord was with him.

The reason this sentence appears to have been inserted here by anticipation is that it might establish the truth of Jonathan’s testimony, which he gave concerning the time when the Lord would cut off David’s enemies, each one, from the earth. For David’s enemies were cut off from the earth, not because David himself took vengeance on his adversaries, but because the Lord judged on his behalf.

It is rightly added:

“Jonathan continued to make David swear, because he loved him as his own soul; for he loved him as his own soul.”

This means that those who embraced the perfect love of God according to the Law loved David, and that David delivered him unharmed from the destruction of his enemies. Even if death had prevented him from possessing the kingdom with David, as he had hoped, he nevertheless received, without any opposition, a share in the heavenly kingdom with him—the glory of his virtues having distinguished him for a time, since he too was an imitator of virtue.

“Jonathan came into the field beside the place appointed by David,” and the rest.

What does it mean that Jonathan, wishing to preserve David while he was hiding in the field beside the stone, shot two arrows as a signal, which the young boy, unaware of what had happened, gathered and carried back into the city? It signifies that God the Father had hidden his only-begotten Son, whom he had determined to send for the salvation of the human race, within the letter of the Law, where no one understood him.

David was hidden in the field; Christ was hidden in the world. “He was in the world,” John says, “and the world did not know him” (John i). He sat beside the stone because he was written on the tablets of the Law. For Saul, hating him and sitting amid the banquet, judged him to be a man marked for death; and the Jewish people, feasting at Passover, deliberated about Christ’s death.

“When morning came, Jonathan went into the field beside the place appointed by David, and the young boy was with him.” He shot one arrow, and he shot another. And God the Father, when the morning of faith dawned, first brought forth the testimony of the Law concerning Christ, and afterward sent the Prophets to bear witness to his coming.

Hence Habakkuk says: “Your arrows will go forth in your name” (Habakkuk iii), and the rest.

Jonathan’s boy gathered the arrows and brought them to his master, entirely unaware of what was happening. So too the Jewish people, carrying the books of the Law and the Prophets as though they had been divinely written, did not understand them; they did not recognize the one whom Moses and the Prophets had prefigured, although he was present among them.

## CHAPTER XXI

“David came to Nob, to Achimelech the priest, and Achimelech was astonished that David had come alone,” and the rest.

Achimelech was Aiah, son of Ahitub, son of Phinehas, son of Eli. Achimelech asked whether David and his young men, whom he had said he had appointed to a certain place, were clean.

David answered enigmatically in the plural concerning himself, saying: “The vessels of the young men were holy,” namely, free from marital intercourse.

When he says, “This way is polluted,” and in Hebrew it reads, “This way is common,” it should be understood as though he were saying: The Law commands that an outsider must not eat from these things, and you ask whether the young men are clean. Even if they were clean, they ought by no means to eat them. Therefore the way is common, because you are asking in a common manner.

“But today it will be sanctified in the vessels.” He says that it will be sanctified in the vessels—that is, in their minds—because they would not have eaten from them unless bodily necessity and danger to life had compelled them.

David is not, however, explicitly said to have eaten those loaves, as the Hebrews report. But read the Gospel, where the Lord speaks to the Jews about this passage, saying:

“Have you never read what David did when he was in need and was hungry, he and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God under Abiathar the high priest and ate the loaves of the Presence, which it was not lawful for anyone to eat except the priests, and gave them also to those who were with him?” (Mark ii).

But it must be asked why Achimelech the priest is read here as the one from whom David received the loaves, whereas the Lord names Abiathar in the Gospel.

The fact that the Lord calls Abiathar the high priest in place of Achimelech contains no discrepancy. Both were there when David came and asked for and received the loaves: Achimelech, the high priest, and Abiathar, his son.

After Saul killed Achimelech together with eighty-five men of his priestly household, Abiathar fled to David and became his companion throughout his exile. Later, when David was reigning, Abiathar himself attained the rank of high priest and remained in that office throughout the whole period of David’s reign. He became much more distinguished than his father. For this reason he was worthy that the Lord should make mention of him, even while his father was alive, as though he were the high priest.

Some interpret the earlier statement—“This way is polluted, but it will be sanctified in the vessels”—in this way: the journey is made polluted because I pretend that I have been sent by the king, and I do this because of the necessity of death; but it will be sanctified in those for whose sake I am also fleeing, because I do not lie merely for the sake of my own danger. They themselves will be saved because of this matter.

So much for the historical account. Let us now touch upon the spiritual meaning.

David, fleeing from Saul, went to Achimelech the priest. Achimelech is interpreted “My king is coming.” Likewise Christ, avoiding the persecution of the Jews, whose type Saul represented, passed over to the apostles, to whom the meaning of the name Achimelech applies: they were those whom the Lord, the King of kings, graciously called brothers, saying, “Go, tell my brothers” (Matthew xxviii). With them he also partook of the desired food: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover” (Luke xxii).

David came alone to Achimelech, and Christ was left alone in his Passion. When David says, “I appointed them and them a place for my young men,” he indicated what the Lord taught his apostles before his Passion: “After I have risen, I will go before you into Galilee.”

David asked Achimelech for five loaves but received one, because the unity of the Law is contained in the five books of Moses.

David took Goliath’s sword, because Christ the Lord also took away the devil’s weapons: “For he himself, being strong, plundered the strong man’s goods” (Matthew xii).

David confessed that he had come to Achimelech by a polluted way, because Christ the Lord also passed undefiled amid the unclean actions of the Jews.

When he says, “But today it will be sanctified in my vessels,” he indicated that the holy apostles, who were the Lord’s vessels, would sanctify their hearts through purifying faith, away from the contagion of the Jews.

Meanwhile, while David was fleeing from Saul, he wished to hide with a certain king of Gath named Achish. But when David’s glory had been mentioned, he feared that the man to whom he had fled might plot something against him out of envy, and so he feigned madness. As though seized by frenzy, he changed his expression; saliva flowed down his beard, he collapsed into their hands, and he fell at the doors of the gate.

King Achish said: “Why have you brought this man to me? Were there not enough madmen among us?” And so he dismissed him.

Achish is interpreted “How is it?” This signifies ignorance, and the speech of one who wonders but does not recognize. This was fulfilled among the Jewish people. Although they saw Christ, they did not recognize him; before them he changed his mouth and departed.

At that time the carnal ordinance of the Law was established there, and there was also a sacrifice according to the order of Aaron. Later he himself instituted a sacrifice from his body and blood according to the order of Melchizedek.

He therefore changed his mouth: he changed it in the priesthood and in the commandments, giving another covenant and abolishing the carnal observance. Then he collapsed into their hands, when they seized and crucified him.

“And he fell at the door of the gate,” that is, he humbled himself. This means that he fell as far as the door of our faith. The door of the gate is the beginning of faith: from there the Church begins and advances toward vision, so that, by believing what it does not see, it may deserve to enjoy it when it begins to see him face to face.

The saliva that, in that apparent madness, ran down his beard is explained by the Apostle, who says:

“Jews demand signs and Greeks seek wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified: to the Jews a stumbling-block, and to the Gentiles foolishness; but to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. For what is foolishness of God is wiser than human beings, and what is weakness of God is stronger than human beings” (1 Corinthians i).

Do not consider the saliva as such; consider that it ran down over the beard. For just as weakness is shown in saliva, so strength is shown in the beard. He therefore concealed his strength beneath the body of his weakness. What was weak outwardly appeared like saliva, while the divine power within was covered as though by a beard.

## CHAPTER XXII

“David fled to the cave of Adullam, where all his brothers and all his father’s household came down to him and visited him; and all who were in distress, oppressed by debt, and bitter in spirit gathered to him, and he became their leader.”

What does it mean that, while David remained in the cave, all his brothers and all his father’s household came to him, except that our Redeemer, after accomplishing his Passion and the redemption of the human race, first established the Church in Judaea from the people of Israel, from the nation in which he had deigned to assume flesh?

His brothers—that is, the apostles—and his father’s household—that is, those who had believed in him from the synagogue—came to him. All who were in distress and oppressed by debt gathered to him. This is what he himself said when he invited them to come to him:

“Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew xi).

Moreover, all who recognize that they are distressed by the fault of their sins and do not possess the breadth of charity, and who are oppressed by alien debt—that is, by the burden of sins which they paid to the devil when they presented their members to serve iniquity unto iniquity—must be bitter in spirit. That is, they must worthily repent of their past offenses and come to David, our desired one, so that he may become their leader.

For he is the one appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead: “Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace, whose kingdom shall have no end; his power shall rule from sea to sea, an eternal power, and his kingdom shall not be given to another” (Isaiah ix).

“Then the prophet Gad said to David: ‘Do not remain in the stronghold; go instead into the land of Judah.’”

In a remarkable way Gad the prophet is introduced here, although no mention of him had been made earlier. He is introduced here just as the prophet Elijah is introduced where it says: “And Elijah the Tishbite, from the inhabitants of Gilead, said…”

Thus Gad the prophet spoke to David from the mouth of the Lord, telling him not to remain among the nations and in a polluted land, but to return to the land of Judah and there, according to the Lord’s will, endure the persecution of his enemies.

“Then Doeg the Edomite said to Saul: ‘I saw David, the son of Jesse, at Nob,’” and the rest.

As far as the spiritual meaning is concerned, Doeg the Edomite—who, as it is read in Hebrew, had bound himself by a vow, according to the Jews’ account, to remain for a time in the tabernacle of the Lord and devote himself to prayer—represents the person of Judas the betrayer. Through him the devil brought these things about, so that, after Christ had been betrayed, the Church would afterward suffer persecution, many disciples of Christ and priests would be killed, and they would endure the gravest persecutions for his name.

Thus, against those by whom Christ had been received, the devil brought tribulations and death. “All who desire to live piously in Christ,” as the Apostle says, “will suffer persecution” (2 Timothy iii). And the Lord says: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (John xv).

Doeg, whose name is interpreted “anxious” and Edom “earthly” or “bloody,” may therefore, when his name is taken as a prefiguration of future things, signify the person of those who think about earthly matters and live carnally, and who persecute Christ in his members.

## CHAPTER XXIII

“Now at that time, when Abiathar, the son of Abimelech, had fled to David, he had come down with him, carrying the ephod,” and so forth.

That ephod was the one which Moses had made at the Lord’s command, as well as the breastplate, in which were instruction and truth. Through it David consulted the Lord and said:

“If the men of Keilah will deliver me into Saul’s hands, and if he will come down, as your servant has heard?” And the Lord said: “He will come down.”

It was as though he were saying: If this is the case, Saul will come down, and the men of Keilah will deliver you into his hands. In this way he indicated their intention.

The men of Keilah rightly signified the infidelity or inconstancy of the Jews, since, although David had rescued them from the hands of the Philistines, they proved ungrateful for his kindness and, constantly ungrateful toward the piety of our Redeemer, plot against him by conspiring with the powers of this world.

Keilah is interpreted “cast at the sling,” or “exalted for itself.” And it is written in the Psalm: “The wicked walk around” (Psalm xi). Elsewhere: “A fool changes like the moon” (Ecclesiasticus xxvii).

Hence what follows concerning the Ziphites:

“David was then in the wilderness of Ziph, in the forest,” and so forth, up to: “The Ziphites came to Saul, saying: ‘Behold, David is hiding among us.’”

Ziph is a rugged, dark, or misty mountain, where David stayed near Carmel, which is called Carmel in the Scriptures. It is still called that today as a village of the Jews; from there came Nabal the Carmelite. But ...
and a descendant of Caleb was called Ziph. Read [this in] Paralipomenon (1 Par. xi). Therefore, as was said above concerning the men of Keilah, so also concerning the Ziphites, who betrayed David to Saul and plotted his death with him: [Ziph] is interpreted as “flowering” or “blossoming.” They signify the Jews, who desired that he should germinate in an earthly kingdom and were discussing his death among their rulers—how they might seize the Savior after he had been betrayed by his disciple and hand him over to the governor for execution (Matt. xxvi). They also signify all the faithless, who, while seeking prosperity and while this present age prospers for them, betray the Lord Christ dwelling in his members to the powers of this age. Hence “flowering” is aptly interpreted, since they betray the Lord Christ dwelling in his members before the powers of this world.

## Chapter XXIV

Next it follows that, when Saul was pursuing David and seeking to capture him in the wilderness of En-gedi, David entered a cave and hid there. But the king, unexpectedly caught in the ambush, fell into what he had devised against an innocent man. For it is written: “He who digs a pit for his neighbor will himself fall into it” (Prov. xxvi). David, however, repaying good for evil, did not kill his enemy but cut off a piece of the king’s cloak as testimony; for it was easier to destroy an adversary caught in an ambush than to deceive him.

What, then, does it mean that this man, fleeing from Saul’s presence, hid in a cave? Why did he hide, except so that he might be concealed and not found? What does entering a cave mean except being covered by the earth? For he who is in a cave is covered by the earth, so that he is not seen. Jesus, however, bore the earth—that is, the flesh which he had received from the earth—and in it he concealed himself, so that God would not be found by the Jews. “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. ii).

Why, then, did they not find the Lord of glory? Because he had covered himself with a cave, that is, he placed before them the weakness of the flesh; and he concealed the majesty of his divinity beneath the covering of his body, as in the hiding place of a cave. Thus, not recognizing God, they persecuted a human being; and he could die only in a human being, and could be crucified only in a human being, because he could be seized only in a human being. He therefore set the earth before those who wickedly sought him, and kept God safe from those who wickedly sought him.

Thus, according to the flesh, he fled into a cave from Saul’s presence, because he suffered—concealing himself from the Jews to such an extent that he died. But why did he wish to remain patient unto death, fleeing from Saul’s presence into a cave? For the cave may be understood as the lower part of the earth. And certainly what is manifest and known to all is that his body was placed in a tomb cut out of rock. That tomb was the cave to which our David fled from Saul’s presence; for the Jews persecuted him until he was placed in the cave.

But what does it mean that Saul, the persecutor, entered the cave to relieve himself, except that the Jews brought forth, like a foul odor, the malice conceived in their minds against Christ? They displayed in their deeds the harmful thoughts they had entertained among themselves when they killed Christ.

David nevertheless did not wish to kill Saul. Although he had him in his power, hidden in a secret cavern, he preferred to preserve him rather than kill him. So also Christ, while he was in the cave—that is, in the flesh—had the persecuting people in his power, yet did not kill them. For it had been written concerning them by the prophet: “Do not kill them” (Ezek. ix).

David merely cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak in silence, to show prophetically that Christ had not killed the Jews but had taken from them only a portion of their royal glory. For the cutting off of the cloak signifies the amputation of the kingdom. Saul himself also demonstrated this elsewhere when he sinned through disobedience. When he was asking pardon and entreating Samuel to return with him to appease God, Samuel refused and turned his face away to depart. Saul seized the hem of his garment and tore it. Samuel then said to him: “The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from your hand today and will give it to your neighbor, and Israel will be divided into two peoples.”

This king, therefore, figuratively bore the person of Israel, because the people were going to lose the kingdom while persecuting Christ. But since we have treated this sentence at length above, according to the exposition of the teachers, we shall now repeat it briefly.

David, ceasing from Saul’s persecution, hid in a cave. Likewise, Christ the Lord, concealing his divinity beneath the cave of the flesh, withdrew from the hearts of the Jews. Saul came to relieve himself; the cloak was cut off, and he was dishonored. Likewise, after the Jewish people had poured out against the Lord Christ the wickedness they had conceived in their minds, crying, “Crucify him, crucify him,” they were stripped of the garment of faith, royal dignity, and even priesthood; and thus they were killed—but preserved for those among that people who would believe in Christ at the end of the world.

In another sense, according to the moral interpretation: whom does Saul signify except evil rulers? And whom does David signify except good subjects? For Saul’s relieving his bowels signifies wicked superiors extending the malice conceived in their hearts into the operation of a foul deed, and displaying outwardly through their actions the harmful thoughts they have entertained.

Their deeds, although most detestable, are not to be struck down by the sword of the mouth of humble subjects, even when they are judged rightly deserving of reprehension. Hence David was afraid to strike, because the minds of subjects, abstaining from every plague of detraction, do not destroy the life of their superiors with any sword of the tongue, even when they criticize imperfection rightly.

If at times, because of weakness, they can scarcely restrain themselves from reproving some extreme and outward evils of their superiors, they nevertheless speak humbly, as though cutting off a piece of the cloak: while harmlessly and secretly detracting, as it were, from the dignity of their rulers, they soil the garment of the king set over them. Yet they return to themselves and rebuke themselves most severely, even for the slightest tearing of the word.

Hence it is rightly written there:

“After this David struck his heart,” and so forth.

The deeds of superiors are not to be struck with the sword of the mouth, even when they are rightly judged deserving of correction. If the tongue slips against them even in the smallest matters, it must be restrained through the affliction of repentance, so that the person may return to himself. And when he has diminished the authority of his superiors, let him dread the judgment of the one who has been placed over him; for when we sin against our superiors, we oppose the ordering of the one who placed them over us.

Thus Moses also, when he learned that the people were complaining against himself and Aaron, said: “For what are we?” (Exod. xvi). “Your murmuring is not against us, but against the Lord.”

## Chapter XXV

“Now there was a certain man in the wilderness of Maon, and his property was in Carmel,” and so forth. This history can, as some think, possess a mystical meaning.

Nabal, a harsh, extremely wicked, and malicious man, can represent the Jewish people, some of whom, intoxicated by a cluster of gall and bitterness, were “stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart,” as blessed Stephen says: always resisting the Holy Spirit, following a hard and carnal understanding of the Law, and having become foolish. The interpretation of Nabal’s name suits them well, for Nabal is interpreted as “mad” or “foolish,” as Abigail said to David: because they rejected the coming Christ, who through the apostles was seeking from them the sustenance of faith and good works, saying: “We do not know where this man is from. We are disciples of Moses” (John xi).

Abigail, however, a most prudent and beautiful woman, represented that part of the people who, converted from the Jews to the faith, had deserved to please God. Her name is interpreted as “the exultation of my father.” Hence also the Lord says: “I confess to you, Father of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. xi). And again: “There will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents” (Luke xv), and the rest.

David, that is, our Lord, repeatedly pleading in the prophets and apostles for the salvation of the Jewish people, offered to it, in a spirit of pious devotion, an acceptable offering of good works. After the death of her husband, who perished in the folly of his foolishness, he took her into marriage; and he presented to himself a bride without spot or wrinkle.

The fact that the same Nabal is said to have died ten days after the time when David had been reproached is to be understood as a figure: the Jewish people, to whom it was said, “Hear, foolish people,” after rejecting the Lord and transgressing the Decalogue of the Law, fell into the Gospel and died in its sin (Jer. v).

It follows:

“Abigail said to David: ‘For if a man has risen up at any time pursuing you,’” and so forth.

By a most beautiful comparison, he distinguishes the condition of the righteous and the reprobate according to their respective destinies. He calls the souls of the righteous “living,” thereby indicating, conversely, that the souls of the reprobate have been overtaken by spiritual death. He compares the former to a bundle and the latter to a stone from a sling.

A bundle is tied together so that it may be held and preserved. A stone is placed in a sling so that it may be thrown. Thus the elect in this age are confined by the pressures of tribulations so that, warned by them, they may be joined more closely to one another in mutual charity; and, united with one another by the hand of their Redeemer, may be preserved forever.

The reprobate, however, the more broadly they are permitted in this life to indulge their own pleasures, as though released into freedom, the farther they are cast away in the future from the glory of the divine vision, so that it is rightly said of them: “They themselves have been driven out from your hand.”

He wonderfully describes the providence of the omnipotent One when he says that the soul of a holy man is guarded by God as in a bundle of the living. For just as it is very easy for anyone to preserve a small bundle of grass or hay held in his hand, so the power of our Lord and Savior preserves without difficulty all the elect throughout the world, from the beginning to the end of the age, so that none of them may perish in any way.

Accordingly, he himself speaks of them in the Gospel under the figure of sheep: “They follow me,” he says, “and I give them eternal life, and they will never perish. No one will snatch them from my hand” (John x).

Just as a single bundle is tied with whatever bonds may be used, so the entire company of the saints is bound together by one and the same end, hope, and charity, and is surrounded by the one protection of God.

The meaning is clear: David’s soul, although guarded from pursuing enemies, was always in the lot of the living. His enemies, however, amid the adversities pressing upon them, were like a stone whirled in a sling—shaken by unstable motion and destined to be cast out from their own boundaries, or even removed from human affairs.

Morally, what does Abigail indicate to us by the manner of her entreaty, except that we correct angry people more successfully if we withdraw during the very disturbance of their anger? In agitation they do not know what they are hearing; but when they have returned to themselves, they receive words of exultation all the more willingly as they are more calmly ashamed of having been endured.

To a mind drunk with fury, everything right that is said appears perverse. Hence Abigail rightly concealed Nabal’s fault while he was drunk, but rightly disclosed it after the wine had been digested. He could recognize the evil he had done precisely because he had not heard it while drunk.

According to the historical sense, Abigail said to David:

“When the Lord has done for my lord all the good that he has spoken concerning you, and has appointed you ruler over Israel, this will not be a cause of anguish or a stumbling-block of heart for you.”

This is understood as follows: “This will not be a cause of anguish for you”—that is, so that you should now shed Nabal’s blood and afterward have cause to weep and repent.

“Saul gave Michal, his daughter and David’s wife, to Phalti son of Laish, who was from Gallim.” As the Hebrews report, Phalti did not have intercourse with her; for if he had, David would never afterward have taken her back, since the Law strictly prohibits such intercourse.

“Phalti,” they say, “from Gallim,” that is, “from inundation.” The inundation is understood as the Law. For he was a teacher of the Law, from Gallim—that is, from “revelation” [the reading is uncertain]. When Michal is given to him by Saul, “Phalti” is interpreted as “escaping”; when she is taken away from him, “Phaltiel,” that is, “escaping from God,” is used—namely, because God protected him so that he would not touch her and become a transgressor of the Law.

Although it is read in what follows that Phalti went along with her when she was being brought back to David, weeping, they nevertheless say that afterward he rejoiced greatly because God had freed him from touching her. Since this appears to be a Jewish assertion, we do not approve it in every respect, but leave it to the judgment of the reader.

## Chapter XXVI

“The Ziphites came to Saul, saying: ‘Behold, David is hiding among us.’” What they signify has already been explained abundantly above.

The event is then recounted: when David was fleeing from Saul, he entered the king’s camp, found him sleeping, and neither struck nor killed him, but took only the spear that was near his head and the cup, while everyone slept.

“He went out from the camp and crossed to the summit of the mountain.”

What does this mean? The Jews were following Christ, but by persecuting him they were asleep, because they were not watchful in heart. Hardness of heart is a kind of sleep. They sleep in the old life and do not awaken in the new.

Christ came and did not kill them, but took away from them the cup of water—that is, the grace of the Law. He took away the royal scepter, namely the power of the kingdom, which they regarded as a great thing and by which they protected themselves temporally, and which they wielded against God through unbelief.

Then our victorious David entered their camp. Returning, he rose beyond it to the height of the mountain of heaven.

## Chapter XXVII

“David and his men went up, and they raided Geshur, Gezri, and the Amalekites. For these villages had been inhabited in the land from ancient times.”

These peoples were not under the power of Achish. They are said to have inhabited the land from ancient times because they had lived there peacefully and securely and had suffered no plundering by any enemy.

## Chapters XXVIII, XXIX, and XXX

“Meanwhile David was fleeing, and while he was proceeding with Achish, king of the Philistines, to battle against Israel, the Amalekites rose up and attacked Ziklag. They burned it and took captive everything that belonged to David and his men. When David returned to pursue the Amalekites, he found an Egyptian boy exhausted, whom the Amalekites had left sick on the road. David restored the boy, whom he had found, with food and made him the guide of his journey. Thus he pursued the Amalekites, found them feasting, and utterly destroyed them.”

The Amalekites are called “the people who lick.” By them the minds of worldly people are signified: while they delight only in temporal things, they lick, as it were, all earthly possessions by encircling them. Like a licking people, they seized plunder, since those who love earthly things increase their profits through the losses of others.

But what does it mean that the Egyptian boy, an Amalekite, was found exhausted on the road, except that the lover of the present age, covered by the blackness of his sin, is often abandoned by that same age when he is weak and despised, so that he cannot run along with it but grows sluggish, broken by adversity?

David found him because our Redeemer, truly strong of hand, sometimes converts those whom he finds despised by the glory of the world. He feeds them with his love and nourishes them with food, because he refreshes them with knowledge of the word. He chooses him as a guide of the journey because he also makes him his preacher.

Since he could not follow the Amalekites, he became David’s guide. The one whom the world had abandoned as unworthy not only receives God into his mind after conversion, but also, by preaching, carries him into the hearts of others.

With this guide, David found the Amalekite feasting and destroyed him: for through those who preach Christ, he destroys the joy of the world—that is, of those who had despised having them as companions.

The two hundred men who, exhausted, were left behind at the torrent with the baggage signify certain weak members of the Church, who cannot run along the way of God with the other spiritual men. Yet, by retaining the true faith and preserving good works through the active life, they receive from the most merciful David, that is, Christ the Lord, the reward of blessedness together with the others who are perfect.

“Samuel died, and all Israel mourned for him, and they buried him in Ramah, his city.”

Earlier it is said that he was buried in his house in Ramah—in his house, that is, among his family and kindred. The fact that he is here said to have died again, as the Hebrews say, is repeated because of his resurrection, so that the condemnation of Saul might also be shown to be just: Saul had died through sins and, having abandoned God, consulted a python contrary to the Law.

It follows:

“After Samuel’s death, the Philistines gathered against Israel. Saul consulted the Lord, but he did not answer him, neither by dreams nor by priests.”

The Hebrew has “neither by instruction nor by prophets.” The Lord answered through dreams, as the Hebrews assert; by fasting and praying they sought that a divine oracle should be given to them, and God revealed through dreams what was going to happen. Saul is expressly not said to have done this in the present passage.

“By instruction” means by the ephod, which the priest wore on his breast. Nor did he answer through prophets, because when they consulted him, the Lord did not answer them. These prophets are said to have been disciples of Samuel, and Saul joined himself to them when they prophesied and prophesied with them.

“Saul sought a woman who practiced divination, so that she might raise Samuel for him. When he had immediately been raised, he said to him: ‘Why have you disturbed me so that I should be raised?’” and so forth.

According to the historical sense, the question is whether the woman who practiced divination called the prophet himself from the underworld, or whether she displayed to Saul some imaginary illusion produced by the deceit of demons.

On this question, blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo, wrote as follows to Simplicianus, bishop of Milan:

“You ask, I say, whether an evil spirit could raise the soul of a righteous person and summon it, as it were, from the hidden repositories of the dead, so that it might be seen and speak with Saul. Is it not more astonishing that Satan himself took up the Lord and placed him upon the pinnacle of the temple? Whatever the manner in which he did it, it happened. In the same way, whether Samuel was raised remains hidden.

“Unless perhaps someone should say that the devil had easier permission to take up the living Lord wherever he wished to take him and place him wherever he wished than to raise the spirit of the dead Samuel from its dwelling places.

“If what happened in the Gospel troubles us because God wished and permitted it, it happened without any diminution of his power or divinity—just as he permitted himself to be seized, bound, mocked, crucified, and killed by the Jews themselves, although they were perverse and unclean and favored the works of the devil.

“It is not absurd to believe that, by some dispensation of the divine will, it was permitted that, not unwillingly or under the domination of magical power, but willingly and in obedience to the hidden dispensation of God—which was concealed from that divining woman and Saul— the spirit of holy Samuel should be brought forth and show itself to the eyes of the king who was destined to perish by divine judgment.

“Nevertheless, there may be another and easier interpretation of this event: we may believe that it was not truly the spirit of Samuel raised from its rest, but some phantom and imaginary illusion produced by the devil’s contrivance. Scripture therefore calls it by the name of Samuel because images are accustomed to be called by the names of the things whose images they are.

“Everything that is painted or fashioned is called by the names of the things whose images it is. When a painting of a man is seen, the proper name is applied without hesitation, and one says, ‘That is Cicero; that is Sallust; that is Achilles; that is Hector; this is the river Simois; that is Rome,’ although they are nothing other than painted images.

“Likewise, although the cherubim are heavenly powers, the figures fashioned from metal, which God commanded to be placed above the ark of the covenant to signify a great mystery, were also called cherubim. Again, when someone sees a dream, he does not say, ‘I saw an image of Augustine,’ but, ‘I saw Augustine,’ although at that time Augustine would have known nothing of what someone had seen.
