“It is therefore evident that it is not the people themselves but their images that are seen. Pharaoh likewise said that he had seen ears of grain and cattle in dreams, not images of ears of grain or cattle (Gen. xli).

“If, then, it is clearly established that images are called by the names of the things whose images they are, it is not surprising that Scripture says that Samuel was seen, even if perhaps an image of Samuel appeared through fabricated devices of the one who transforms himself into an angel of light and disguises his ministers as ministers of righteousness.

“If this moves you,” he says, “how could the words spoken to Saul have been predicted by an evil spirit? It may also seem astonishing how the demons recognized Christ, whom the Jews did not recognize.

“When God wishes even weak spirits to know something true—only temporal matters pertaining to this mortal life—it is easy and not incongruous for the omnipotent and just God, for the punishment of those to whom such things are foretold, to permit them to know beforehand the evil impending upon them before it arrives. Through the hidden arrangement of his mysteries, he may even impart some foreknowledge to such spirits, and they may announce to human beings what they have heard from angels.

“They hear only as much as the Lord and ruler of all commands or permits. Thus also the pythoness in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts xvi), with the apostle Paul and the evangelist bearing witness [the wording is corrupt].

“Yet they mix deceptions with what they say; and the truth which they were able to know, they announce not so much to teach as to deceive. Perhaps this is why, when that image of Samuel foretold to Saul that he would die, it also said that he would be with Samuel.

“That, however, is false. We read in the Gospel that the righteous and the wicked are separated after death by a great interval (Luke xvi): a great chasm is fixed between the proud rich man, who was already suffering torments in the underworld, and the one who had lain ulcerated at his gate and was already established in rest.

“Or, if Samuel said to him, ‘You will be with me’ because the words refer not to the quality of blessedness but to a common condition of death—since both were human beings, both could die, and the dead one foretold death to the living—then this passage can have its outcome according to either interpretation, without contradicting the faith.

“Unless, perhaps, by a deeper investigation it should be discovered clearly whether or not a human soul, after departing from this life, can be summoned by magical incantations and appear to the sight of the living, bearing even the features of its body, so that it can not only be seen but recognized; and, if it can, whether it is compelled or whether it deigns to appear, obeying the hidden mysteries of the supreme Law.

“If it should be judged impossible, then both senses cannot be admitted in the interpretation of this Scripture; when one is excluded, the imaginary likeness of Samuel, produced by a demonic ritual, must be understood.

“But since, whether this can happen or cannot happen, the deception of Satan and his ingenious activity in fabricating images continually watch in many ways to deceive human senses, we must for the present refrain from prescribing the results of more diligent investigations. Rather, let us suppose that something of this kind was done by the evil spirit through the ministry of that pythoness, since we are not permitted to devise and explain anything more extensive.”

These are the things that the most blessed Augustine wrote at that time concerning the pythoness and Samuel.

Since this kind of magical apparition is frequently read about in this book, it must be explained where the name comes from. Some say that it was discovered by Apollo Pythius and was called by his name. Others say that the Hebrew name agrees with this: they say that *python* means “of the abyss” [sic], and therefore think that *pythoness* and *pythons* should be read.

We, investigating the matter carefully, have found it written in both ancient and even modern volumes. Others, however, assert that the name comes from the serpent called *python*, from whose skin people practiced divination; hence they read *pythoness* and *pythons*. We leave the matter to the judgment of the prudent reader, to choose whichever explanation seems preferable.

This interpretation is placed after the preceding one according to the historical sense. We do this so that we may encompass the whole matter concerning Saul and the pythoness together.

## Chapter XXXI

“When the battle began, the Philistines struck Israel with a great slaughter, and Saul and Jonathan fell in the battle,” and so forth, until it says: “His armor-bearer himself fell upon his sword and died with him.”

The Hebrews say that this armor-bearer was Doeg the Idumean, who, seeing Saul dead, killed himself through fear of David.

“Saul died, and his three sons, and his armor-bearer, and all his men.”

These men are to be understood as his household servants. The three sons of Saul who were killed with him were Jonathan, Abinadab—who is also called Jesui—and Melchishua. Ish-bosheth, however, was at home. He is said to have been born in the year in which Saul was made king, and he is also said to have been forty years old when he began to reign. From this it is inferred that Saul reigned for forty years.

It must be asked why he is called Jesui in one place and Abinadab in another. Jesui is interpreted as “equal.” He is called “equal” because the sons are said to have been equal in merit to their father. Abinadab is interpreted as “my father [gave] freely.” For Saul their father, by acting wickedly, freely acquired for himself the fate that he should be killed together with his sons.

## Chapter II

The Amalekite who falsely told David that he had killed Saul was ordered to be killed because he had said that he had killed the Lord’s anointed and had not feared to lay his hand upon the Lord’s anointed; he himself was also called an Amalekite.

As I read in a certain volume, the Hebrews say that he was the son of Doeg the Idumean. For Amalekite and Idumean are one, as I have found: Esau’s firstborn son, who was also called Edom, was Eliphaz, and his son was Amalek.

Some Hebrews therefore maintain that the diadem and bracelet which he brought to David had been entrusted by his father Doeg to his son. Hence, they say, it is not to be believed that Saul had taken them into battle; rather, he had entrusted them to his friend, from whom the Amalekite himself received them.

If, however, someone thinks it credible that Saul had taken them into battle and that, after Saul died, the Amalekite had removed them from his head and arm and brought them to David for the sake of flattery and favor, we neither oppose nor prohibit that view, but leave it to his own judgment.

At a deeper level, however, we consider what it means that the Amalekite, who falsely claimed before David that he had killed King Saul, received the punishment of vengeance from him. Does it not mean that everyone who plots evil against his neighbor or rejoices in his destruction receives the punishment of just retribution from the heavenly Judge?

According to what is written: “Everyone who digs a pit will fall into it” (Prov. xxvi; Eccli. x). And: “He who strikes with the sword will perish by the sword” (Matt. vi). And again: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. i).

When these matters have been completed, the history follows concerning what David did. For it says:

“David lamented with this lamentation over Saul and over his son Jonathan. And he ordered them to teach the sons of Judah the song, as it is written in the Book of the Just,” and so forth.

In the Hebrew and in the true copies, it does not read “song” but *bow*, which also seems better to our teachers. For when it is written that he mourned Saul and Jonathan, who had been killed, “and ordered them to teach the sons of Judah the bow,” he did this because he already knew that the Philistines abounded in archers.

Alternatively: “David ordered them to teach the sons of Judah the bow,” that is, he ordered the kings of Judah to teach strength—namely, that they should be strong and attentive in the fear of the Lord and in the commandments of God, lest through disobedience they fall away from strength and from the fear of the Lord.

[scan page 172]

333

…just as Saul withdrew, and in the manner in which he had suffered defeat they might perish; and from the very place where Saul had been most grievously wounded by the blows of the Philistines, he taught them the same art of warfare and trained his own soldiers to defeat them. But concerning what follows, “as it is written in the Book of the Just,” they assert that this book can now be found nowhere, not even among the Hebrews themselves. Nor can the Book of the Wars of the Lord be found, which is mentioned in the Book of Numbers, nor Solomon’s songs, nor his most wise discussions concerning the nature of trees, herbs of every kind, animals of every kind, birds, reptiles, and fish.

Or, as is said in the Book of Chronicles: “The rest of Solomon’s earlier and later deeds are written in the words of Nathan the prophet, in the books of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the vision of Iddo the seer against Jeroboam son of Nebat,” together with many volumes of this kind, whose having been written Scripture indeed proves, but which are certainly not extant today.

For when Judaea was devastated by the Chaldaeans, the library that had been gathered in ancient times was also consumed by hostile fire, along with the other riches of the provinces. From it, the few books that are now contained in Holy Scripture were later restored through the diligence of Ezra, the pontiff and prophet. Hence it is written concerning him: “Ezra came up from Babylon, and he was a ready scribe in the law of Moses” (Ezra 7). “Ready,” that is, because he discovered forms of letters more readily written than those which the Hebrews had previously possessed. And in the letter of the king of the Persians we read: “Artaxerxes, king of kings, to Ezra the priest, the most learned scribe of the law of the God of heaven, greetings.”

There are nevertheless some who say that by this “Book of the Just” we should understand the book of the Hebrews itself, in which the just prophets are contained—namely, Samuel, Gad, and Nathan—and in which it is written how Saul, withdrawing through fear of the Philistines, perished through his disobedience.

“Glory, O Israel, over your mountains, those who were slain.” In Hebrew it reads, “over your heights.” The sense is: “O Saul, upon your heights, the glorious ones of Israel have been slain,” because, on account of the sin of your disobedience, they perished together with you. For disobedience was reckoned as idolatry, that is, as “the high places,” as in the Book of Samuel: “For obedience is better than sacrifices, and to listen than to offer the fat of rams” (1 Samuel 15). “For rebellion is like the sin of divination, and refusal to submit like the crime of idolatry.”

But when he says, “Do not announce it in Gath, nor proclaim it in the streets of Ashkelon,” and so forth, the prophet, astonished, lamented the sudden fall of the leaders of his people, and forbade anyone to rejoice over such a disaster or to spread its report throughout the cities of the enemies. Gath and Ashkelon are cities of the Philistines.

Thus far we have treated the historical meaning; now let us add what it signifies allegorically. For he says: “And David commanded them to teach the sons of Judah,” and what follows. The sons of Judah are understood as the faithful in the Church, confessing Christ the Lord. Concerning them the true David—that is, the Lord strong of hand—commanded that they be armed with the bow of divine understanding, lest, deceived by the blindness of ignorance, they fall into impiety, or, sluggish and lax before their enemies—that is, the unclean spirits—succumb after being deceived by some vice and fall irreparably into the perpetual death of the soul.

334

“Do not proclaim it in Gath,” and so forth. Gath, which is interpreted “winepress,” signifies the earthly city of Jerusalem, which killed the prophets and stoned those sent to it (Matthew 23). To its citizens—that is, the unbelieving Jews—the death of the Lord and of the holy apostles was an object of mockery. Therefore the true David, Christ the Lord, commands that his passion is by no means to be announced to them through evangelical preachers, since they preferred to be scoffers at Christ’s cross rather than its worshippers.

Then follows: “And David said: Mountains of Gilboa, let neither dew nor rain come upon you,” and so forth. Because of the fall of the mighty and the ruin of his people, he speaks as though indignantly to the very place of the slaughter, abhorring what had occurred there; yet this is not without a mystery of prophecy, as blessed Pope Gregory will shortly explain.

“Jonathan’s arrow never turned backward, and Saul’s sword did not return empty.” This indicates that Jonathan and Saul were, in their time, most warlike and brave in battle.

“Saul and Jonathan, lovely and comely in their life, were not divided even in death; swifter than eagles, stronger than lions.” He praises the beauty of their appearance and the constancy of their spirit, adding, in a hyperbolic figure, the likeness of eagle and lion.

“Daughters of Israel, weep over Saul, who clothed you in scarlet with delights and supplied golden ornaments for your adornment”—namely, from the spoils which he took from enemies.

“How have the mighty fallen in battle?” Understand: in their sin. “Jonathan and Saul, you were slain upon your heights,” as we said above. Thus, O Saul and Jonathan, you were slain “upon your heights,” that is, in the sin of your disobedience. This is the historical sense.

Spiritually, however, why does David, who did not repay evil to those who repaid him evil, curse the mountains of Gilboa when Saul and Jonathan fell in battle, saying: “Mountains of Gilboa, let neither dew nor rain come upon you; nor let there be fields of firstfruits, because there the shield of the mighty, the shield of Saul, was cast away, as though he had not been anointed with oil”?

What had the mountains of Gilboa done when Saul died, that neither dew nor rain should fall upon them and that the pronouncement of this sentence should dry them of every green shoot? But because Gilboa is interpreted “descent,” and through Saul, the anointed one who died, the death of our Mediator is represented, the mountains of Gilboa fittingly signify the proud hearts of the Jews. While they flow down amid the desires of this world, they united themselves in death to Christ, the Anointed One. Since the anointed king died bodily among them, they themselves are dried of every dew of grace.

It is rightly said of them: “They cannot be fields of firstfruits.” For the proud minds of the Hebrews bear no firstfruits, because at the Redeemer’s advent they remained, for the most part, in unbelief and refused to follow the beginnings of faith. The holy Church, indeed, made fruitful in its firstfruits by the multitude of the Gentiles, scarcely receives at the end of the world those Jews whom it finds, and, gathering the last, sets them forth as fruits left over. Isaiah says of these remnants: “Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved” (Isaiah 10; Romans 9).

The mountains of Gilboa may therefore be cursed by the prophet’s mouth so that, when the fruit dies as the land dries up, the possessors of the land may be struck by the loss of barrenness, receiving the sentence of the curse because, as their wickedness deserved, they admitted among themselves the death of the King.

In another sense, David, in the person of the saints, laments certain persons in the Church who, falling through pride and running with those who slip through the course of the present life, have been excluded from the spiritual light and have slipped—that is, been blinded. Resisting demons, they fall in the world, which is slippery—for, according to this interpretation, the mountains of Gilboa mean “slippery”—and, abandoning hope of recovery, destroy themselves with their own sword, that is, with the ruinous despair of escaping the ancient enemy, just as Saul died by falling upon his sword.

The Philistines, that is, malignant spirits, strip virtues from those whom they have slain and ascribe to their own strength the victory which occurs in such persons by God’s just permission. But our David, in his members—that is, in the elect and holy men—laments the fall of those who collapse. He does not rejoice in the destruction of the dying, but forbids such a report to be proclaimed in the cities of the Philistines; that is, he commands the faithful carefully to guard themselves and to arm themselves on every side with the shield of faith, clothed with the breastplate of righteousness, having the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, and to resist their adversaries, lest, shamefully overcome again, they give joy to their enemies.

**CHAPTER II**

“David therefore went up, with his two wives, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess and Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite; David also brought up, each with his household, the men who were with him, and they dwelt in the towns of Hebron.”

David’s ascent to Hebron with his two wives signifies the calling of the two peoples into the catholic Church. Hebron means “marriage,” and the holy Church alone is rightly called a marriage: it alone is the one bride of the heavenly King, of whom the Song of Songs says:

“There are sixty queens, eighty concubines, and maidens without number. My dove, my perfect one, is one; she is the only one of her mother, chosen by her who bore her.”

David brought there each man with his household, because each believer is called into that fellowship through the preaching of the Gospel. “There is no distinction of Jew and Greek, barbarian and Scythian, slave and free; but Christ is all things and in all.”

“The men of Judah came and anointed David there, that he might reign over the house of Judah.”

The men of Judah anoint David king, that he may reign over Judah’s house, because, when proud persons, despisers, and those who scorn God’s grace have been removed, all the elect rightly confess, through the good repute of sacred preaching and zeal for virtues, that Christ is King over all the people, and that he is the one to whom “all power has been given by the Father in heaven and on earth, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Philippians 2).

In another sense, after Saul’s death David is anointed and reigns, and transfers the ark of the covenant into his city, as is related below. Likewise, after the abolition of the Jewish kingdom and the cessation of its priesthood, the true David, Christ, received the kingdom in his Church, chosen from the Gentiles; and he transferred the ark of the covenant—that is, sacred Scripture—into the Church, which is his house.

[scan page 173]

335 — ANGELOMI LUXOVIENSIS MONACHI

“And it was reported to David that the men of Jabesh-gilead had buried Saul,” and what follows. How this happened is related more fully in the Book of Chronicles:

“When the men of Jabesh-gilead heard all that the Philistines had done to Saul, all the brave men rose, took the bodies of Saul and his sons, brought them to Jabesh, buried their bones beneath the oak that was in Jabesh, and fasted for seven days” (1 Chronicles 10).

Saul therefore died because of his iniquities, because he had transgressed the commandment of the Lord that he had ordered and had not kept it. Moreover, he had consulted a medium and had not hoped in the Lord. For this reason the Lord also killed him and transferred his kingdom to David son of Jesse.

Why does David repay the men of Jabesh-gilead with favor because they buried the bones of Saul and his sons, unless because our Redeemer is greatly pleased when someone consigns to oblivion, by condemning them, the evil deeds of those who died in their sins, and does not imitate the action that he knows displeased God, but chooses instead to do what he remembers the Lord commanded?

“Abner son of Ner, commander of Saul’s army, took Ishbosheth son of Saul, led him through the camps, and established him as king over Gilead, over the Geshurites, over Jezreel, over Ephraim, over Benjamin, and over all Israel.”

In Hebrew it reads, “He led him across to Mahanaim,” which is interpreted “camps.” He led him across, that is, beyond the Jordan, and established him as king at Mahanaim over Gilead and over the Geshurites. In Hebrew, however, it reads “over the Asshurites,” that is, over the tribe of Asher.

“But the house of Judah alone followed David.”

What does it mean that Saul’s son Ishbosheth, whose name is interpreted “man of confusion,” was established as king over all Israel with the assistance of Abner, whose name is interpreted “the father’s lamp,” while the house of Judah alone followed David? It means that, among the former people, only believers and those who truly confess God follow our David, that is, the Lord and Savior; among the rest, the error of confusion still reigns, instigated by the devil, who often transforms himself into an angel of light.

“And the number of the days that David dwelt, reigning in Hebron over the house of Judah, was seven years and six months.”

And rightly did David reign for seven years and six months in Hebron, which, as we said above, is interpreted “marriage,” or “vision of peace.” For our Savior reigns in the catholic Church, which is also his bride, throughout the whole time of this life, which proceeds according to the sixfold number of the days, in accordance with the saying: “Behold, I am with you all the days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28). After the completion of the number six, that is, after the perfection of good works, he will lead all his elect to the true Sabbath, that is, to eternal rest, where they will enjoy the perpetual vision of God.

Hebron, moreover, is a city in the tribe of Judah, once called Arbae, although it is incorrectly written Arboe in the Greek books. In our books, therefore, Arboe is written corruptly, whereas in Hebrew it reads Arbae, that is, “four,” because three patriarchs—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—were buried there, together with the great Adam, as is written in the Book of Genesis. Some suppose that Adam was buried at the place of Calvary, but that is false.

This same Hebron was formerly the metropolis of the Philistines and the dwelling-place of giants. Later it became David’s royal city in the tribe of Judah, a priestly city and a city of refuge. It lies about twenty-two miles to the south of Eleutheropolis. There the oak of Abraham, also called Mamre, was still shown until the reign of King Constantius, and his mausoleum can even now be seen.

Although a church has now been built there by our people, the place surrounding it is still worshipped by people of every nation as a terebinth, because Abraham once received angels as guests beneath it. This place was first called Arbae and later Hebron, taking its name from one of the four men, Caleb. Read the Book of Chronicles. It was founded seven years before the city of Tanis in Egypt.

“Abner son of Ner went out, with the servants of Ishbosheth son of Saul, from the camp at Gibeon. Joab son of Zeruiah and the servants of David also went out and met them beside the pool of Gibeon. When they had come together, they sat opposite one another, these on one side of the pool and those on the other. Abner said to Joab: ‘Let the young men arise and play before us.’ Joab answered: ‘Let them arise.’

“They arose, and twelve from Benjamin, on the side of Ishbosheth son of Saul, crossed over, together with twelve of David’s servants. Each seized his opponent by the head, thrust his sword into the side of the other, and they fell together. The name of that place was called the Field of the Strong at Gibeon. A very fierce battle arose on that day,” and what follows.

Josephus explains this passage as follows:

Abner advanced a very large chosen army to engage the tribe of Judah, for he was angry with those by whom David had been appointed king. Joab, sent by David, met him; he was the son of Zeruiah, David’s sister, and was descended from Sarvius. He had been appointed commander of the army against Abner. His brothers Abishai and Asahel, together with all David’s armed men, were also with him.

Coming to a certain spring in the city of Gibeon, Joab drew up his line for battle. When Abner said that he wished to test which side possessed the stronger army, the two agreed that twelve fighting men should be sent from each side. They advanced between the battle lines, where the others had remained at a distance from the fighting. The men of David, after laying aside their swords, seized the heads of their enemies and pierced their loins and sides with their own swords, until all twelve pairs had been killed as though by a single agreed action.

When these had fallen, the remaining armies also joined battle, and the struggle proceeded with great violence. Abner’s people were defeated and put to flight. Joab continued pursuing the fugitives, ordering his armed men to hasten after their tracks and not to cease killing them. Even the brothers of the slain greatly detested this conduct.

Among the pursuers, the younger Asahel was especially distinguished. He possessed such glory for the speed of his feet that he could outrun not only men but even horses. He pursued Abner in a straight course, turning neither to the right nor to the left. When Abner looked back, observed the force of his pursuer, and told him to take the weapons of one of the soldiers and cease pursuing him, Asahel would not withdraw from his attempt.

Abner again warned him to turn aside, lest he be forced to strike him and afterward be unable to face his brother Joab. When Asahel despised his words, Abner, while fleeing, was compelled to throw his spear backward; it suddenly pierced Asahel with a mortal wound.

Mystically, Abner, of the tribe of Benjamin and commander of Saul’s army, is understood to have challenged the servants of David who were with Joab, commander of the army of Judah, and to have killed Asahel, Joab’s brother, by striking him in the groin. Some interpret this as referring to Saul, who was not yet an apostle. He was of the tribe of Benjamin and, before he was seized by the Lord, is read as having challenged the apostles to battle and as having been present at the death of Stephen (Acts 6).

As for what Abner said to Asahel:

“Turn aside; do not follow me, lest I be compelled to pierce you through. If I raise my hand against you, I shall not be able to lift my face before Joab your brother.” But Asahel would not listen and would not turn aside. Therefore Abner struck him with the back of his spear in the groin, pierced him through, and he died in that same place. All who passed by the place where Asahel had fallen and died stopped there.

Morally, whom does Asahel typify but those whom fury violently seizes and drives headlong? They must be avoided all the more cautiously the more madly they are swept along. Hence Abner, whose name in our language means “the father’s lamp,” flees, because the tongue of teachers, which points out the heavenly light of God, when it sees someone’s mind borne over the precipices of fury, refrains from returning the darts of words against the angry; as though unwilling to strike its pursuer, it withdraws the force of rebuke.

But while the furious man does not cease, like Asahel, to pursue and rush upon it, it must happen that one who tries to restrain the madman is struck down by the very person whom he provokes to fury. The further corrupted words appear to say that, through a display of gentleness, the soul of the furious man is wounded from the side by the same arrows. Thus, when Abner stood against his pursuer, he pierced him not with a straight but with a reversed spear. For to meet an onset of reproof with the point of a sword is plain enough; but to strike a pursuer with a reversed spear is to inflict certain things upon one in a rage, as if sparing him and restraining his pride. Asahel therefore immediately falls: people who promise themselves peace while swelling with fury inwardly fall at once from that very tranquility to which they had raised themselves. Those, then, who recoil from the onset of their heat through the permission of gentleness are struck by this sword.

And what do the seven sons of David who were born to him in Hebron signify except the perfection of saints in faith, speech, and deed? They are daily begotten by Mother Church for her bridegroom, our Savior, and through spiritual marriage, by the grace of the Holy Spirit, are daily transformed into eternal life. From the sword-point [the intervening words are corrupt], sons of light arise.

“Abner answered Ishbosheth in anger: ‘Am I a dog’s head against Judah today, I who have shown mercy to the house of Saul your father, to his brothers and his neighbors, and have not delivered you into David’s hand, that today you should seek in me a charge concerning a woman?’”

That is, he says: “Because of you and because of your father’s house I am said to be a dog’s head against Judah, since I do not restore the house of Israel to David, whom I know is now king and will reign over the whole kingdom of Israel.” He calls himself a dog’s head—that is, something vile—because he was so regarded by the house of Judah, like a barking dog, and because he was commander of a troop, that is, of foolish men.

“And Abner cried to Joab and said: ‘Will your sword rage on unto slaughter?’” Joab’s response, as it is read in a certain disputation, is not clear. In Hebrew it reads: “Do you not know that bitterness will be at the end?” The sense is: “Do you not know what bitterness will come upon you because you are able to destroy your own people?”

**CHAPTER III**

“Now there was a long conflict between the house of Saul and the house of David. David, growing stronger and always advancing, while the house of Saul grew weaker daily.”

The house of David, then, which is the holy Church, grows stronger. The house of Saul, namely Babylon, the city of confusion, grows weaker daily. What else is the house of Saul, the proud and impious king, except that Babylon of confusion which leads the nations into prostitution and makes them fornicate in its prostitution?

There is a long conflict between the house of Saul and the house of David because the house of Saul persecutes what is according to the spirit, while the house of David is according to the spirit. The house of David advances all the more strongly in proportion as the house of Saul is more violently enraged against it through its persecutions. The latter, however, declines daily and wastes away in its iniquity; and at the end of the world, according to its merits, it will be cast with its king into the deepest abyss.

“These, then, were the sons of David who were born to him in Hebron. His firstborn was Amnon, by Ahinoam the Jezreelitess; after him came Chileab, by Abigail the widow of Nabal the Carmelite. The third was Absalom, son of Maacah, daughter of Talmai king of Geshur. The fourth was Adonijah, son of Haggith; the fifth was Shephatiah, son of Abital; the sixth was Ithream, by Eglah his wife. These were born to David in Hebron.”

It is asked why the other wives of David mentioned above are not named here, and why Eglah alone is called David’s wife. Eglah is Michal herself; she alone is here called his wife because in early youth she was first joined to David as his wife, and she is also said to have died in childbirth. Hence it is written later: “Therefore Michal, Saul’s daughter, had no son until the day of her death.”

“And Abner said to David: ‘Let me arise and gather to you all Israel, and make a covenant with you, that you may reign over all, as your soul desires.’ When David had dismissed Abner and he had departed in peace…” Abner came to David so that he might unite all Israel to his kingdom, but, David being unaware, Joab killed him treacherously. We shall speak more fully of this below, and explain it otherwise.

Others understand it thus: Abner, coming to David so that he might unite all Israel to his kingdom, was killed treacherously by Joab. Likewise Paul, the apostle to the Gentiles, who by his preaching strove to convert unbelievers to Christ’s faith, is recorded to have suffered very grave persecutions from the Jews. For just as Joab son of Zeruiah, Abner’s kinsman, continually lay in wait for Abner until death, so the Jews, the children of the synagogue, continually lay in wait for the apostle Paul, born from the same tribe of Benjamin, until, driving him out of Judaea, they compelled him to pass to the Gentiles (Acts 21).

Abner also brought this speech to the elders of Israel, saying:

“Yesterday and the day before yesterday you sought David to reign over you. Now, therefore, act, for the Lord has spoken to David, saying: ‘By the hand of my servant David I will save my people Israel from the hand of the Philistines and from all their enemies,’” and so forth.

What, then, does it mean that Abner exhorts all the people of Israel, so that, abandoning Ishbosheth son of Saul, they may come to David with a ready and devoted spirit, except that holy teachers, who are rightly called “the father’s lamp,” full of faith and knowledge, preach the Lord in all the nations and exhort them so that, rejecting the worship of idols and the confused error of religion, they may come with their author, abandoning the devil, to our David, who is truly strong of hand and marvelous, whom the prophet describes as desired by all nations, and may hasten to come without delay and strive perpetually to remain under his rule.

[scan page 176]

BOOK OF KINGS, BOOK II, CHAPTER III

Joab, who spoke deceitfully to Abner and struck him in the groin and killed him, signifies no other than the ancient enemy, who strives daily to overthrow the faithful by deceptive suggestions and attempts to kill them through harmful thoughts of lust. Joab is interpreted as “enemy” or “the same brother.” The devil is the head of all enemies; hence the Savior says to such people in the Gospel: “You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father” (John 8).

Our David is immune from this persecution because “God tempts no one. He himself is not a tempter of evils” (James 1), and because he wishes all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2). “Through the envy of the devil, death entered the whole world” (Wisdom 2), “and those who belong to his portion imitate him.”

The name and person of Joab may also suitably be transferred by interpretation to the Jewish people, who were always enemies of the preachers of the Gospel and persecuted the faith of Christ wherever they could. Concerning them Paul writes to the Thessalonians:

“For you, brothers, became imitators of the churches of God that are in Judaea in Christ Jesus, because you also suffered the same things from your own countrymen as they did from the Jews, who both killed the Lord Jesus and the prophets, persecuted us, and did not please God, and were hostile to all people, forbidding us to speak to the Gentiles so that they might be saved, thereby always filling up their sins. For the wrath of God has come upon them to the end” (1 Thessalonians 2).

Alternatively:

“And Joab struck Abner in revenge for the blood of Asahel his brother,” and so forth. What is signified by Joab, who is interpreted as “enemy” or “brother,” except the pride of the Jews and of heretics? What, however, is expressed by Abner, whose name is translated into Latin as “the father’s lamp,” except spiritual men and humble teachers of the Church?

Joab killed Abner treacherously at the gate because the enemies of the faith—that is, Jews and heretics—persecuted certain leaders of the Church even unto death in defense of the faith. For this reason, from the house of Joab, by which the impious people are signified, there does not cease one who suffers a discharge of semen—that is, one polluted by unclean thoughts and sordid deeds.

Likewise, there is a leper holding a staff; by this heretics are signified, corrupted by the thought of their falsehood. These heretics, while trying to defend their deception, revolve through the excess of their words, and, as though in a confusion of speech, conceal and enclose their lies within it. While with their contentious tongue they pierce the weak members of the Church with the sword of their mouth, they themselves first perish by the same sword of their impiety. And because they feed themselves on their falsehood, they fast empty of the bread of the word of God. Below we shall explain what is signified mystically, and now in another way:

“And the king of Israel, mourning for Abner, said: ‘Abner, you have not died as cowards usually die.’”

That is: “You did not perish in your folly, as cowards usually perish, because you were deceived by treachery.”

“Your hands were not bound, nor were your feet weighed down with fetters,” as are the hands of those who are usually bound and the feet of those who are usually shackled when they are captured in battle. Therefore you were killed by treachery, not by force.

But when David, excusing himself concerning the death of the innocent, says:

“I and my kingdom are innocent before God forever of the blood of Abner son of Ner; may it come upon the head of Joab and upon all his father’s house: neither may there cease from the house of Joab one who suffers a discharge of semen, or a leper who holds a staff, or one who falls by the sword, or one who lacks bread,”

he denotes the treachery and misery of the Jews.

Upon the head of Joab—that is, upon the leaders and priests of that people, and upon all the house of his father, namely, the synagogue of Satan and the assembly of the wicked—will come the iniquity of the impious, so that all the righteous blood poured out upon the earth may be required from them, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah (Matthew 23).

Nor will there cease from the house of this Joab one who suffers a discharge of semen—that is, one flowing away through various desires, because such people place their whole hope in the pleasures of this life. Nor will there be lacking lepers holding a staff—that is, people stained by various errors, following the instability of heresies and worldly luxury. According to the desires of their hearts, they will heap up teachers for themselves, having itching ears and turning their hearing away from the truth.

“There also will not be lacking one who falls by the sword or lacks bread”: although they continually lack the bread that descended from heaven and do not deserve to be refreshed by it, they will not escape the sword of future vengeance (the supplied citation is corrupt).

**CHAPTER IV**

“The sons of Remmon the Beerothite, Rechab and Baanah, came and entered the house of Ishbosheth during the heat of the day, while he was sleeping upon his bed at noon. They entered the house, and the woman guarding the door of the house, cleaning wheat, fell asleep. Taking wheat ears, they entered secretly and struck him in the groin,” and what follows.

These two men were commanders over the expeditions of Ishbosheth. After Abner’s death, as the Hebrews relate, they conspired with Mephibosheth to kill Ishbosheth together, to establish that same Mephibosheth as king. Mephibosheth himself became the informer of the plot, and for this reason the same Mephibosheth is introduced here in the narrative.

“Jonathan, son of Saul, had a son who was weak in his feet; for he was five years old when the messenger came from Jezreel with news of Saul and Jonathan,” and so forth.

When Baanah and Rechab saw that their plot had been betrayed by Mephibosheth, they were terrified and fled to Gittaim, where they remained as fugitives until that time. “That time” is to be understood as the time when, returning from there, they entered the house of Ishbosheth during the heat of the day, took wheat ears, and struck him in the groin. They carried wheat ears as though they were bringing the firstfruits, so that they might appear to be paying honor to the king and their treachery might not be detected.

Mystically, however, the woman guarding the door, cleaning wheat, signifies the mind’s guardian, separating virtues from vices through discernment. If she should fall asleep, she will admit murderers to the death of her own master, because, when the solicitations of demons…

### [Scan page 177]

**343 — Angelomus of Luxeuil, Monk: Commentary on the Books**

If he has sharpened his mind for murder, he opens a path for evil spirits. They enter and remove the ears of grain, because they immediately take away the shoots of good thoughts. And they strike him in the groin, because carnal pleasures kill the virtue of the heart. To strike in the groin is to pierce the life of the mind with carnal pleasure.

But this Ish-bosheth would certainly not have fallen by an unexpected death if he had not assigned a woman—that is, a lax guard—to the entrance of the house, meaning the access to the mind. A strong and watchful understanding must be placed at the gates of the heart, one that is overcome neither by the sleep of negligence nor deceived by the error of ignorance. Hence Ish-bosheth is rightly so called: he is stripped by hostile swords while a woman guards the doorway. For Ish-bosheth means “man of confusion.” A man of confusion is one who is not fortified by a strong guard of the mind, because, while he thinks he is practicing virtues, vices entering secretly kill him unawares.

Therefore the entrance to the mind must be fortified with every strength, lest lurking enemies penetrate it through an opening made by neglected thought. Hence Solomon says: “Guard your heart with all vigilance, for from it life proceeds” (Prov. 4). It is therefore fitting that we weigh the virtues we practice with the greatest care from the source of our intention, lest even the good things they display arise from an evil origin.

### Chapter V

“And all the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron, saying: Behold, we are your bone and your flesh,” and so forth. What does this gathering of the tribes of Israel to David signify except the gathering of all nations to Christ? They say to him, as if with flattering words, “Behold, we are your bone and your flesh,” since in him they love and venerate the incarnation that he assumed from our nature in the Virgin’s womb, and desire to subject themselves to his rule and to serve him at all times.

Hence the Psalmist says: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord. And all the families of the nations shall worship before him, for the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he shall rule the nations” (Ps. 21). The elders of Israel also came to the king at Hebron: together, with one faith and equal devotion, they hasten to our Mediator. Of them it is written: “The princes of the peoples gather together with the God of Abraham” (Ps. 46). And elsewhere: “He shall be glorified in the sight of his elders” (Isa. 24).

“David was thirty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years.” In Hebron he reigned over Judah for seven years and six months; in Jerusalem he reigned thirty-three years over all Israel and Judah. Why, then, are forty years and six months not counted as the total? The Hebrews resolve this in two ways. They say that David fled from his son Absalom for six months; consequently, those same six months are rightly excluded from the total of his reign. They also say that, during six months of his reign in Hebron, David suffered from a bodily illness, and for this reason those six months were not counted in his reign.

They say that he reigned in Hebron from the time when, after defeating the Amalekites, he sent gifts from their spoils to the elders of Judah—to those in Hebron, those in Bethel, and the rest who were in the places where David himself and his men had dwelt.

Mystically, the fact that David began to reign at thirty years of age foreshadowed that our Lord, at thirty years of age, came to baptism and began to preach the gospel of the kingdom, whose kingdom is everlasting and whose authority shall not be taken from him. The number forty, which consists of four tens, signifies the fullness of times and the perfection of things.

“And they anointed David king over all Israel,” and so forth. David is said to have been anointed twice; likewise, the Lord Jesus Christ first assumed rule among the Jewish people and afterward among the Gentile people. When David was thirty years old, he obtained the kingdom; at the same age, the Lord Jesus Christ was baptized by John in the river Jordan and began to gather disciples.

“And the king and all the men who were with him went to Jerusalem, to the Jebusite inhabitant of the land. And it was said to David by them: You shall not enter here unless you take away the blind and the lame, who say: David shall not enter here. But David captured the stronghold of Zion, which is the city of David. For David had promised a reward on that day to whoever struck the Jebusite and touched the water-pipe, and the lame and the blind who hated David’s life. Therefore it is said in the proverb: The blind and the lame shall not enter the temple. David dwelt in the stronghold and called it the city of David. And he built around it, from the Millo inward,” and so forth.

For he says: “You shall not enter here unless you take away the blind and the lame,” and so on. It is as though they said to him: “David shall not enter here until he removes us from here, whom he regards as unarmed and weak, like the blind and the lame, and whom he thinks he will conquer in battle as though we were blind and lame.”

“Therefore it is said in the proverb: The blind and the lame shall not enter the temple”; that is, no one shall enter the house of the lame and the blind so long as the blind and the lame remain within.

“For David had promised a reward on that day to whoever struck the Jebusite and touched the water-pipe, and the blind and the lame who hated David’s life.” In the Hebrew text it is written: “And David said on that day: Whoever strikes the Jebusite and touches the water-pipe shall be chief.” And in Chronicles: “Whoever strikes the Jebusite first shall be prince and leader”; that is, whoever is so bold and strong that he reaches the city wall and touches with his spear the water-pipe that is in the wall shall himself be prince.

Joab, son of Zeruiah, therefore went up first and became prince. Josephus describes this clearly. He says: “David rose with all his men and came to Jerusalem, while the Jebusites inhabited the city”—for they were descended from the Canaanites—“and, having shut the gates, they placed blind men, lame men, and all the lepers, as a mockery of the king, on the wall, saying that they would prevent him from entering the city.”

### [Scan page 178]

**345 — Commentary on the Books**

They did these things because they despised him and regarded them as the greatest protection of the walls. The king grew angry and began to besiege Jerusalem, striving with great zeal and labor to capture it, so that at the very beginning of his rule he might display his strength. He therefore threatened them and any others who might perhaps attempt to resist him, and with great valor captured the lower city.

Since he still could not seize the stronghold, he began, by promising honors and gifts, to encourage his fellow soldiers to undertake the work of war, so that whoever climbed up through the underground passages into the stronghold and captured it would possess the command of the entire army. While everyone hastened to climb and no one delayed because of the reward, Joab, son of Zeruiah, went before them all. Climbing to the summit, he shouted to the king and claimed the military command.

The king then drove the Jebusites from the top of the stronghold and, rebuilding the city, called it Jerusalem; he dwelt there throughout the entire period of his reign.

But since in this book Jerusalem is here first read as the city of the Jebusites—and since in Genesis it is called Salem, as the Hebrews relate, while in the Book of Judges it is called Jebus, and in many writings, especially in the New Testament, it is called Jerusalem—we must inquire why it is read as “Jerusalem.” Let us say what we find in the writings of the teachers.

The Jews, they say, assert that Shem, son of Noah, whom they identify with Melchizedek, first inhabited the city. It was called Salem at that time; afterward the Jebusites possessed it, and from them it received the name Jebus. Thus, by joining the two names Jebus and Salem, it was called Jerusalem. Later Solomon called it Hierosolyma, as though it were “Hierosolomon,” that is, “the temple of Solomon.” Poets, by a corrupt form, call it Solyma. Hence, through the figure that grammarians call *tmesis*, the poet places the word separately in a poem: “Hiero, whom David’s offspring begot in Solymis,” that is, “in Jerusalem.” Later it was called Aelia by the emperor Hadrian.

But it seems to us that it was called by two names, as certain cities are, as is shown in the Book of Judges, where we read: “He who was going toward the mountain of Ephraim came,” says Scripture, “opposite Jebus, which by another name was called Jerusalem.” We discussed its name more fully in the little book that we recently published on Genesis.

With these preliminary remarks, let us turn our style toward the allegorical meaning. David captured the stronghold of Zion, first removing the blind and the lame who hated David’s life. In the same way, the Lord Jesus Christ, after rejecting the scribes and Pharisees—who were called blind and lame because they hated the life of the same Lord Jesus Christ, that is, because they attempted to take it away—obtained the rule of the Church that he acquired from the Gentiles.

There is no doubt that the water-pipes signified the false knowledge of this world or the doctrines of heretics. The Lord Jesus Christ, through his preachers, struck and destroyed all these things as through Joab, and he does not cease to destroy them in his Church.

The Jebusite, whose name is interpreted as “trampling,” signifies the people of the Gentiles, who, before they believed, trampled upon the divine commands by holding them of little account.

Let us give another interpretation. In the fact that David expelled the Jebusite, inhabitant of the land, from Jerusalem and made it his own city, it was signified that the true David, the Lord, would come and expel contrary powers from the hearts of the faithful, thus establishing his dwelling in them. Hence he says through the prophet: “I will inhabit and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people” (Lev. 26; 2 Cor. 6).

According to this understanding, Jebusite may rightly be interpreted as “the trampled one.” For David also appointed Joab, who captured the stronghold, as prince and leader, because our Lord and Redeemer not only destroyed every principality of the devil through the mystery of the cross and won for himself the glory of victory, but also granted his faithful power over all the authority of the devil, as he himself says to his disciples in the Gospel: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy” (Luke 10).

It was therefore rightly said that David, after expelling the blind and the lame who hated David’s life, captured the stronghold of Zion and called it his own city. Our Savior, having expelled evil spirits together with their throng of vices from any soul and having claimed it for himself through the illumination of wisdom, causes it rightly to be called the stronghold of Zion, that is, “watchtower” and “vision of peace.”

Concerning it the Psalmist rightly says: “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel. His place has been made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion. There he broke the horns, the bow, the shield, the sword, and the war” (Ps. 75).

### [Scan page 178]

**346 — Commentary on the Books**

“And Hiram, king of Tyre, sent messengers to David, together with cedar wood, carpenters, and workers in stone for the walls; and they built a house for David.”

Hiram, whose name is interpreted as “living and exalted,” prefigured the preachers from the Gentile people, who built for David—that is, the Lord and our Redeemer—from cedar trees, namely incorrupt and strong minds, and from stones, that is, holy and perfected people, made square through the four virtues—prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance—not only through themselves but also through the skill of their disciples, as through their craftsmen, a house, that is, the holy Church. To them it is said: “You yourselves, as living stones, are built up into a spiritual house” (1 Pet. 2).

Then David—that is, the Lord—knew that God the Father had established him as king over Israel and had exalted his kingdom over his people Israel, that is, over all who believe and see God in their minds—not only Jews, but especially also the Gentiles, concerning whom the Father had promised him, saying: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 2).

Therefore it rightly follows: “David took still more concubines and wives from Jerusalem.” But someone may ask: If David bore the image of Christ, how is he said to have had many wives and concubines, since Christ both abhors and condemns these things?

### [Scan page 179]

**347 — Commentary on the Books**

It was a figure. The fact that David is said to have had many wives unquestionably prefigured that Christ Jesus would unite himself, through faith in the Church, to peoples from many nations under the number seven. His concubines signify assemblies of Jews or of heretics, who generate offspring into slavery and not into freedom, as Scripture says.

They are called not wives but concubines because they pursue Christ for carnal gain and, under the name of Christ, claim to abide in him. Indeed, if kings now had several wives or concubines, they would be considered guilty, since the figures for which forgiveness was granted in the case of wives or concubines have already passed away. Now that the figure has passed, no forgiveness is granted.

“And sons were born to David, and other sons and daughters; and these are the names of those born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon, and Ibhar, and Elishua, and Nepheg, and Japhia, and Elishama, and Eliphelet.”

Since we have placed these names together, we shall set down the interpretations of the Jews, so that they may correspond to the higher understanding and to spiritual interpretations, according to the judgment of the prudent reader. For if the historical account had not wished to suggest something spiritual, it would never have taken care to add which sons had been born to David in Jerusalem. Since David signifies the Savior, his sons therefore rightly signify believers from both Churches, namely, from the Jews and from the nations.

In the Book of Chronicles four sons are said to have been born from Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon. These represent the Church of the Gentiles, as we shall discuss more fully in what follows under Christ’s leadership.

Shammua is interpreted as “boldness”; Shobab, “turning back”; Ibhar, “he chooses”; Elishua, “the salvation of my God”; Nepheg, “bringing forth”; Japhia, “he illuminates” or “he manifests”; Elishama, “my God hears”; Eliada, “my God knows”; Eliphelet, “my God saves.” These interpretations, as we said, suitably apply to the faithful, who gladly hear the divine commands and turn to the practice of faith. Having touched upon these matters, let us turn our discourse to the subjects that follow.

“Again the Philistines came up to fight against David. David consulted the Lord, who answered: ‘Do not go up; rather, go around behind them, and come upon them opposite the pear trees,’” and so forth.

Although some, as I read in a certain volume, maintain that the Hebrew text does not have “opposite the pear trees,” but “opposite the weeping ones”—that is, as they relate, opposite their idols, where the idols in which they trusted were situated. These are called “the weeping ones” because they are worthy of weeping and lead those who worship them to the weeping of miseries. Hence they add: “And when you hear the sound of one walking in the tops of the weeping ones.” That is, as they explain it: “When you hear, through angelic powers, that their idols, in which all their strength lies, are being broken and trampled underfoot, then you shall begin battle, because then the Lord will go out before you,” and so forth.

Since I believe our interpretation to be true, just as our translator, skilled in three languages, sets forth an armed example in his preface, we understand the flight of the Philistines simply in connection with trees. But since, with the teacher’s agreement, we have expounded the history, let us now briefly undertake to indicate what it signifies allegorically.

In the words, “When you hear the sound of steps in the tops of the pear trees,” and so forth, the coming of the Lord is signified: he passes over the heights of the prophets and apostles by the power of his divinity, as it is written in the Song of Songs: “Behold, he will come leaping upon the mountains, passing over the hills” (Song 2). The tops of the pear trees signify the highest parts of trees. What are trees but exalted fathers? When a sound is heard in their tops—that is, when the sound of preaching thundered forth in the sublimity of their lives through the breathing of the Holy Spirit—our David, by the power of his divinity, through which he surpasses the height of the saints, overcame the Philistines, that is, the unclean spirits.

### Chapter VI

“David again gathered all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand, to bring up the ark of God,” and so forth, until it says: “The Lord was angry,” because Uzzah stretched out his hand to the ark and held it, since the oxen were kicking, “and he struck him, and he died.”

In this account, the blessed kings and prophets, who are said to have brought up the Lord’s ark, show humility approved, pride condemned, and rashness punished. David himself, who was not ashamed to dance humbly before the Lord’s ark, immediately deserved to receive the promise that the Son of God would be born from his line; but his wife, who despised his humility, did not deserve to bear him offspring and paid the penalty of perpetual barrenness.

The priest who touched the ark with inconsiderate rashness likewise cleansed the guilt of his presumption by an untimely death. Here one must consider how greatly the person who approaches the body of the Lord in a guilty state sins, since that priest, who touched the ark—the figure of the Lord’s body—with less reverence than he should have shown, was punished by death.

According to the allegory, David signifies Christ, and the ark signifies the Church or the sacred Scriptures. David wished to bring the ark into his city, but because an opposing circumstance intervened, it temporarily turned aside elsewhere. Thus he afterward explained what had greatly troubled him.

When the Lord appeared in the flesh, he preached the gospel to the sons of Israel, that is, to his own people; but blindness occurred in part in Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles entered (Rom. 11). To make this clearer, let us examine each detail.

David gathered all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand, because the Lord established the primitive Church from Israel—not from all Israel, but from those whom he chose for himself. Not all who are from Israel are counted as Israelites; rather, the children of promise are appointed to salvation. These are represented by thirty thousand: perfected in works of faith and in steadfastness of hope.

Three, because of the confession of the holy Trinity, pertains to faith; ten, because of the Decalogue of the law, pertains to works; and a thousand, because of perfection, pertains to the hope of eternal life, since nothing higher exists, just as no number is greater than a thousand. Even if one says “thousands,” “thirty thousand,” or “a thousand thousand,” one does not go beyond the number one thousand itself, but multiplies it by repeating it either by itself or through smaller numbers.

Multiply three by ten, therefore, so that faith may not be dead without works. Again multiply thirty thousand by a thousand, so that the faith that works through love may hope for its reward nowhere but in heaven. Thus the chosen from Israel rightly indicate a people believing, working, and hoping.

The men of Judah who were with David signify the apostles and teachers, who clung familiarly to Christ’s side. Surrounded by this twofold army, the Lord rejoices to bring up the ark—that is, to extend the Church and implant faith in the hearts of those who did not believe.

The ark is placed upon a new cart, so that the grace of the New Testament, renewed in baptism, may be poured into the Gentiles; and it is entrusted, as something new, to be preserved by new powers. The ark had previously been in the house of Abinadab, who was in Gibeah, because the faith of the Church now preached had flourished even before the time of the Lord’s incarnation among those who followed the devotion of the patriarchs and prophets.

Abinadab, whose name is interpreted as “my spontaneous father,” signifies either Abraham, the father of faith, or Moses, the lawgiver. Both, in Gibeah, guarded the ark, which by the example of their lofty virtue fortified the hearts of believers. Hence Gibeah is interpreted as “hill”; it is a place in the city of Kiriath-jearim.

When the ark had gone forth, David and all Israel danced before the Lord with various kinds of musical instruments.

“For as soon as the new grace began, the Lord invited everyone to offer praises to God the Father in humility, saying: ‘Whoever serves me, let him follow me’” (John 12). “To one is given the word of wisdom through the Spirit; to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another kinds of tongues; to another the grace of healings” (1 Cor. 12), and so forth.

With these and similar kinds of spiritual gifts, as the ark advanced—that is, as the primitive Church grew—they came to the threshing floor of Nacon, that is, to the threshing floor prepared for the Gentiles, namely, the Church consecrated to the truth of the faith. Concerning it John says: “He will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor” (Matt. 3).

There the priest who touched the ark with a hand as though correcting it immediately fell, struck by the Lord, because the Jewish people, envying the Gentiles, deprive themselves of the gift of salvation. While they mingle the legal rites with the gospel, they take away from themselves the grace belonging to both.

### [Scan page 180]

**349 — Commentary on the Books**

“And he touched the ark, for the oxen were kicking.” The oxen kicking signifies the preachers of the gospel acting freely in the faith and refusing to proceed according to the custom of the law. They interpret spiritually the Sabbaths, new moons, circumcision, and sacrifices. Those who descended from Judea tried to correct them as though they were wandering, teaching the brothers: “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved” (Acts 15). James also says to Paul: “You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews who have believed, and they are all zealous for the law” (Acts 21).

“Because of the priest’s death, David did not wish to divert the Lord’s ark to himself, into the city of David; instead, they carried it into the house of Obed-edom the Gittite.” Because the Jews rejected the word, lest preaching heard but not received should cause further harm, the apostles were taken away from them and sent to instruct the Gentiles with the gospel.

The place of the threshing floor of Nacon, which shows the threshing floor prepared for the faith of the Gentiles by the grace of the Lord, is called the striking of Uzzah, namely because their offense becomes salvation for the Gentiles.

Obed-edom is interpreted as “serving man.” He is certainly the one of whom the Lord says to the Father: “You will make me head of the nations; a people whom I did not know has served me” (Ps. 17). There, anticipating the action of the Jews as though it were Uzzah’s death, he says: “You will rescue me from the contradictions of the people” (ibid.).

The name of the city also agrees with this. Gath is interpreted as “winepress,” signifying the cross, in which Christ deigned to be trodden and pressed as the true vine. The whole people of the Gentiles may rightly be called Gittite, since it is said: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6).

The three months during which the ark remained there signify faith, hope, and charity. Just as a month is completed in days, so each virtue reaches perfection through its own stages. The months continue to run until the fullness of the Gentiles enters.

Then David returns and brings the ark into the city. The Lord, through the preaching of Enoch and Elijah, will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, offering oxen and rams—that is, those who thresh the Lord’s floor and lead his sheep—and crowning them with the blood of the martyrs. He himself also openly reveals to the Jews the example of his incarnation and passion, which they had not believed until then. This is signified by the fact that David himself was girded with a linen ephod. For linen, produced from the earth and brought to the whiteness of cloth through manifold labor, displays the truth of human flesh triumphing amid sufferings.

While everyone rejoices and hymns resound as the entrance to the heavenly stronghold approaches, Michal, daughter of Saul, is absent from those bringing up the ark; indeed, she despises David as he is humbled by the spectacle. In the same way, among the Jews who believe only in name, there will be some who follow Christ in profession alone but follow the Antichrist in their works. For them it is rightly fitting that Michal, who represents the instability of carnal people, from whom every iniquity proceeds, is called not David’s wife, as custom would suggest, but Saul’s daughter. Those who serve Christ only in name will not be crowned with him, but will be condemned to the anathema of his persecutors, whom they imitated.

### [Scan page 181]

**350–351 — Commentary on the Books**

Although the wicked are enraged and despise the humility of the Church, the ark of the Lord nevertheless enters its place. It is placed in the middle of the tabernacle that David had pitched for it; that is, the faith preached by the Church advances and is implanted in the hearts of all whom the Lord had predestined for eternal life.

David offers burnt offerings and peace offerings before the Lord, and Christ commends the faith and devotion of the Church to the Father, who is at the right hand of God and also intercedes for us. By this example he nourishes the faithful and humble with the food of saving mystery.

“He distributed to each one a round loaf of bread,” namely, the one who came down from heaven and gives life to the world; “and one portion of roast beef,” namely, that of the fattened calf slaughtered for the younger son returning to his father and roasted in the fire of passion. It says: “My strength has dried up like a potsherd” (Ps. 21).

“And one cake fried in oil,” namely, flesh completely clean from the stain of sin, but, for the sake of human salvation, abundantly cooked in the frying pan of the delights of the cross. One round loaf of bread and one portion of meat are rightly given, because “there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all” (Eph. 4).

In another sense, the faithful receive these gifts: because “we, though many, are one bread and one body in Christ,” each of them chastises the wantonness of his flesh, subjects it to service, and cooks it in the fire of the Holy Spirit. They also make the fruits of good works, made extremely rich by the oil of mercy, boil with compassion for their neighbor.

But the daughter of Saul, having entered the king’s chamber in vain, bears no fruit of seed conceived, because those who receive the word of God only with their ears, without the offspring of good works, await the day of perpetual death.

Blessed Pope Gregory, when discussing morally the audacity of subjects against their rulers, speaks as follows:

“Often, because they do not wish to understand, inferior people are displeased by the deeds or words of better men; but they should not rashly criticize them, because they cannot truly grasp them. Often something is done by those of higher rank in a way that conceals its purpose, and is considered an error by those of lower rank. Often many things are said by the strong, which the weak judge because they do not understand them. The ark of the covenant, inclined while the oxen were kicking, represented this well. The Levite, believing that it was about to fall, tried to raise it and immediately received the sentence of death.

“For what is the mind of the just person except the ark of the covenant? It is carried by oxen that are kicking and is inclined, because sometimes even one who rules well, shaken by the confusion of subject peoples, is moved by love alone to a condescension of administrative accommodation. But what is done as an act of dispensation is considered by the ignorant to be an inclination of strength and a fall.

“Therefore some subjects raise against this hand the hand of criticism, but by their very rashness they immediately fall away from life. The Levite therefore extended his hand as though to help, but by his offense lost his life, because when the weak criticize the deeds of the strong, those who thought themselves strong in the Lord judge the deeds or words of their betters as weak.”

“Uzzah” is rightly called a Levite, for it is interpreted as “strong of the Lord.” He perished through the presumption of his boldness, because by rashly undertaking to correct the ark he lost his life.

“Then the ark of the Lord dwelt in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite for three months, and the Lord blessed Obed-edom and all his household.”

Obed-edom is called a Gittite because his father had dwelt in Gath. As for the statement that follows—“The Lord blessed him and all his household”—some wish it to be understood in this way: that all his wives and concubines, daughters-in-law, and maidservants bore male children, and that his cattle and four-footed animals likewise produced twin offspring.

Then follows the account of how David and all the house of Israel brought the Lord’s ark back to Jerusalem. When he danced before the Lord’s ark, Michal, daughter of Saul, despised him, and so forth.

When David transferred the Lord’s ark to Jerusalem and danced before it, he was mocked with hostile derision by Michal, daughter of Saul, his wife. In the same way, when the Lord Jesus Christ wished to transfer God’s Testament into his Church—that is, the evangelical commandments from the Old Testament, as though he were founding something new—he was seized by the Jewish people and suspended on the cross, becoming an object of mockery to them.

On that cross he appeared to them as though naked, concealing from them the power of his divinity and showing only the weakness of his flesh. The maidservants of David’s servants, whom Michal reproached him for, undoubtedly represented the saints. Concerning them the true David—that is, the strong-handed Lord—became more glorious among the Gentiles after his ascension into heaven through evangelical preaching, miracles of virtue, and finally the triumph of martyrdom, than he had appeared to the Jews in his passion.

“Michal had no child.” Michal remained barren as a type of the Synagogue. Thus much for the allegorical interpretation.

Next, let us consider morally how many gifts of virtue David had received, and how he perhaps preserved himself in humility amid all of them. Who would not be exalted by breaking the jaws of lions, tearing apart the limbs of bears, being chosen over his older brothers, being anointed to rule after the rejected king, striking down Goliath—feared by all—with one stone, bringing back numerous foreskins after destroying the Philistines whom the king had designated, receiving at last the promised kingdom, and ruling all Israel—?

[The supplied text ends here.]
the Jewish people without any contradiction? And yet, when he brought the ark of God back to Jerusalem, as though he had forgotten that he was set above the others, he mingled with all the people and danced before the ark. And because dancing before the ark was, as is believed, the custom of the common people, the king turned himself about in the dance as an act of divine service. Behold: the one whom the Lord had singularly preferred above all others submitted himself to the Lord; by making himself equal to the lowliest and displaying himself in a despised manner, he was held in contempt. He did not call to mind the power of his kingdom, nor fear that, by dancing, he might become base in the eyes of his subjects; he did not recognize that he was preferred in honor above the others before the ark of the one who desires honor. Before God he performed lowly, even extreme, acts, so that by this humility he might strengthen the brave deeds he had done before men.

What others thought of his actions I do not know; for my part, I am more amazed at David dancing than at David fighting. By fighting he subjected his enemies, but by dancing he subjected himself before the Lord. Michal, daughter of Saul, still irrational through fear of her royal lineage, looked with contempt upon him in his humiliation and said:

> “How glorious was the king of Israel today, uncovering himself before the maidservants of his servants, and stripping himself as one of the buffoons might strip.”

Immediately he heard:

> “Before the Lord, who chose me rather than your father.”

A little later he said:

> “I will play, and I will become even more contemptible than I have been, and I will be humble in my own eyes.”

It is as though he openly said: “I desire to become contemptible before human beings, because through humility I seek to preserve my understanding before God.” There are indeed some who think humbly of themselves: placed in positions of honor, they consider themselves to be nothing but dust and ashes. Yet they shrink from appearing contemptible before human beings and, contrary to what they inwardly think about themselves, cover themselves outwardly with a kind of rigid dignity. There are also some who desire to appear contemptible to human beings and, by displaying themselves as cast down, despise everything they are; yet inwardly, as though swollen by the very merit of the contempt they display, they become proud within, and are more exalted in heart the more vigorously they suppress outward signs of exaltation.

David detected and overcame both these struggles of a single pride with great discernment and remarkable virtue. For while inwardly thinking humbly of himself, he did not seek outward honor, as he indicates by saying:

> “I will play, and I will become more contemptible.”

And because, by first making himself contemptible outwardly, he did not swell inwardly, he adds:

> “And I will be humble in my own eyes.”

It is as though he said: “Whatever I display outwardly by despising myself, I also regard myself as being inwardly.” What, then, should those do whom doctrine elevates? If David knew the Redeemer who would come from his own flesh, and by prophesying announced his joys, yet forcefully crushed the neck of his heart with the heel of discernment, saying, “I will be humble in my own eyes”—

## Chapter VII

> “And it came to pass, when the king sat in his house and the Lord had given him rest, that he said to Nathan the prophet: ‘Do you see that I dwell in a house of cedar, while the ark of God is placed in the midst of a tent?’ And Nathan said to the king: ‘Go, do all that is in your heart, because the Lord is with you,’” and so forth.

Nathan said this from himself, not from the Lord’s word; and therefore he erred by presuming upon his own judgment. He ought first to have consulted God.

Here, then, it is shown that the spirit of prophecy does not always illumine the minds of the prophets, because, as it is written of the Holy Spirit, “He breathes where he wills” [John 3:8]. Hence also, when Elisha saw a weeping woman but did not know the reason, he said to the servant who wished to restrain her:

> “Let her alone, for her soul is in bitterness; and the Lord has hidden it from me and has not told me” [2 Kings 4:27].

Almighty God arranges this by a great dispensation of mercy: when he sometimes gives and sometimes withdraws the spirit of prophecy, he both raises the minds of the prophets to sublime heights and preserves them in humility. Thus, when they receive the spirit, they discover what they are through God; and when they do not possess the spirit of prophecy, they recognize what they are in themselves.

Therefore the prophet believed that what he had spoken from himself had been spoken through the spirit, because of the customary operation of prophecy. For this reason, what follows he spoke from the Lord’s word:

> “Will you build me a house?” and the rest.

It is as though he said: “You will not be able to build me a house, because you are a man of blood and have shed much blood.” Hence he says that he dwelt in a tent and tabernacle, because neither Moses nor Joshua could build a house, since they were men of blood. Therefore he also says later:

> “Have I ever spoken a word to any of the judges of Israel’s tribes, whom I commanded to shepherd my people Israel, saying: ‘Why have you not built me a house of cedar?’”

He commanded none of the judges to build him a house of cedar because all had fought against enemies, and all had been shedders of blood. Yet your son, against whom the wars of enemies will not arise, and who will not be a man of blood, will build me a house.

As for what follows—

> “through all the places where I have gone with all the sons of Israel”—

these are understood to be Shiloh, Gilgal, Nob, and the other places where the tabernacle and the ark were located.

Moreover, what he says above—

> “Will you build me a house in which I may dwell?”—

may also be understood in a higher sense. Almighty God, who is an unbounded spirit, does not dwell in houses made by human hands. Hence he says:

> “For I have not dwelt in a house from the day when I brought the sons of Israel out of the land of Egypt, but I have walked in a tabernacle and in a tent.”

Tabernacles or tents figuratively express the hearts of the saints, in which the Lord deigns to dwell.

But why, when David wished to build a temple, was he forbidden by the Lord?
