This is shown by Scripture’s prefiguring: the man of blood—that is, the one who still devotes himself to carnal actions—ought not, through the ministry of preaching, to build a temple for God, namely, the holy Church. Or it may be suggested morally that the person who wishes to correct the vices of others must himself be pure within. He must not be occupied with earthly things, lest he submit to low desires, so that he may foresee more clearly what others must avoid, insofar as he himself more truly shuns such things through knowledge and life.

An eye burdened by dust cannot clearly see a stain on a limb, nor can a hand unable to wipe away the dirt spread over it cleanly remove the filth that holds the mud. Thus David, who had struggled in external wars, is told:

> “You shall not build me a house, because you are a man of blood.”

He builds the temple of God who devotes himself to correcting the minds of his neighbors through disciplined instruction. But the man of blood is forbidden to build the temple of God, because one who still clings to carnal actions must necessarily be ashamed to instruct the minds of his neighbors spiritually.

> “And I made your name great.”

That is, so that he might be called the God of David, just as he is called the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. As I did for Moses and Joshua, whose names are most famous throughout the earth, so I have done for you.

> “And I will appoint a place for my people Israel.”

The place which the Lord promised that he would prepare for his people is understood not as a territorial site or any earthly place, but as the heavenly Jerusalem, although it may appear to refer to the temple and to the time of Solomon. For then the sons of Israel would in some manner rest under peace; and if Solomon should commit any fault, he would be corrected “with the rod of men and with the blows of the sons of men”—that is, not by the sword of enemies or by bodily afflictions.

We read that this was fulfilled later in the heavenly Jerusalem, where, after the day of judgment, all the elect, transferred there, will remain under the Lord without any disturbance forever.

> “And the Lord announces to you that the Lord will make you a house,”

and so forth.

The house of David is the Church of Christ. It is absurd to apply this to Solomon: he began to reign while his father was still alive. Here, however, he says:

> “When your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your seed after you.”

It is pious to understand and believe this of Christ the Lord, who deigned to be born according to the flesh from the seed of David. His kingdom endures continually forever; his house, that is, the catholic Church, remains faithful before him forever.

> “If he commits any iniquity,”

and so forth.

This must not be understood of the Lord Jesus Christ, who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found [Isaiah 53:9], but of his elect, who are his members and among whom no one could be found without sin.

> “And your house will be faithful.”

Everyone who knows the sacred Scriptures is aware that Solomon’s house was filled with foreign women. The faithful house, therefore, is understood as the holy Church, which remains before the Lord forever.

We too will build this house by living well, and God will build it by assisting us so that we may live well, because:

> “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” [Psalm 126:1].

When the final dedication of this house comes, then what God spoke here through Nathan will take place:

> “And I will appoint a place for my people Israel, and I will plant him, and he will dwell apart, and he will no longer be disturbed; nor will the son of iniquity again humble him as at the beginning, from the days when I appointed judges over my people Israel.”

Whoever hopes for this great good in this age and on this earthly sphere reasons foolishly; so does anyone who thinks that it was fulfilled in Solomon’s peace or in the kingdom of any other person. For during the periods of the judges, the son of iniquity—that is, the people’s oppressor—rose up at intervals, and periods of peace are found that lasted longer than Solomon’s, although he reigned for forty years. Under the judge called Ehud, for example, there were eighty years of peace.

Therefore, far be it from us to believe that these times were promised to Solomon in this promise. The place that is promised, a habitation so peaceful and secure, is eternal and belongs to eternal beings, in the free mother Jerusalem. There the people of Israel will truly be, and there they will dwell forever with God and in their God; and God will be with his people and within his people, so that God will be the fullness of his people, the people full of their God, and God will be all in all. He grants the reward in peace who is the strength in war.

> “Then King David went in and sat before the Lord,”

and so forth.

To sit before the Lord is to confess his benefits with humility of heart.

> “For this is the law of Adam, O Lord God.” That is: “This is the law of man, O Lord God: that he should serve you with simplicity of heart and parity (*parilitas*), and that you should show your mercy, as you have deigned to do for your servant.”

> “For you know your servant, O Lord God.”

> “Because of your word and according to your heart you have done all these great things, so that you might make them known to your servant.”

It is as though he said: “Because of your word, which you promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, you have done all these things for me, your servant.” But the only-begotten Son of the Father is also the Word, who is blessed forever. Many things were done in David because of the mystery of his incarnation and of his descent from David. When he says “according to your heart,” this means, “according to your mercy.”

> “For there is none like you, nor is there any God besides you, in all that we have heard with our ears.”

“There is no God,” he says, “like you, who has done these great things that we have heard with our ears,” and so forth, until he says:

> “For you, Lord of hosts, God of Israel, have revealed this to the ear of your servant, saying: ‘I will build you a house.’”

He revealed it to his ear because, through the prophet, it was foretold that the Lord would build him a house.

> “For what other nation on earth is like your people Israel?”

What other nation is there on earth besides the chosen people, for whose sake God the Son deigned to come into this world as into Egypt, so that, having assumed the form of a servant and by the exchange of his blood, he might redeem for himself a people devoted to good works?

The God of this chosen people must be understood as the Lordly man, whom he assumed from Egypt—that is, from this world—through the womb of the Virgin.

> “And the house of your servant David will be established before the Lord.”

The house of David is undoubtedly the Church of Christ; enough has already been said about this above.

> “Therefore your servant has found his heart, so that he might pray to you.”

When thought is restrained by the guardianship of discernment, the heart that was accustomed to flee is found. Nothing in us is more fugitive than the heart, which departs from us whenever it flows away through corrupt thoughts. But David says that he has found his heart—that is, he has found boldness in his heart to pray to the Lord with this prayer.

## Chapter VIII

> “And it came to pass after this that David struck the Philistines and humbled them; and David took the bridle of tribute from the hand of the Philistines. And he struck Moab and measured them with a line, making them equal with the ground. He measured two lines: one for killing and one for giving life,”

and so forth.

The bridle of tribute refers to the five cities of the Philistines, which frequently made Israel tributary to themselves. David took these from them, humbled them, and made them tributary to himself. Hence it is also read in Chronicles:

> “He humbled them, and took Gath and its villages from their hand, and struck Moab and measured them with a line, making them equal with the ground” [1 Chronicles 18:1–2].

What is written of David—that he struck Moab and measured them with a line, making them equal with the ground—must be understood hyperbolically. It could not happen that human beings living on the earth would be humbled to such an extent that, with a line stretched across the surface of the earth, they would appear equal to the earth itself. Rather, Scripture wished by this expression to magnify the immense humiliation of the captured and oppressed nation: they were made equal to the ground because they were despised and rejected, so that no human beings living on earth could any longer be compared with them in anything.

There are many examples of this kind of expression in the Scriptures, such as the Gospel passage:

> “There are also many other things that Jesus did, which, if they were written down one by one, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would have to be written” [John 21:25].

How could the world not contain books that could have been written in the world? Scripture used this expression to suggest the greatness and multitude of the Lord’s works.

The same appears in David’s lament over Saul and Jonathan:

> “Swifter than eagles, stronger than lions.”

A similar expression is found even in secular literature:

> “They surpassed snow in whiteness and the winds in speed.”

When it says that he measured them with a line, the line is allegorically understood as a lot, since the extent of fields is customarily measured with a line. Hence it is written:

> “And by lot he divided the land among them, by the line of distribution” [Psalm 77:55].

This signifies that David divided the regions of the Moabites among whatever heirs he wished, with as free a disposition as any owner separates his own fields according to his will by drawing a line here and there.

> “He measured two lines, one for killing and one for giving life.”

This too is said allegorically, signifying that he had such power, with no one resisting him, that he could kill some of them as rebellious and spare others as submissive.

What is said—

> “David struck the Philistines and humbled them, and took the bridle of tribute,”

may be understood allegorically. David struck the Philistines because Christ the Lord, triumphing over the powers of the air, broke the bridle of error that had been imposed upon the human race.

What is said—

> “He struck Moab and measured two lines, one for killing and one for giving life”—

signifies the hidden dispensation of our Lord Jesus Christ. From the unbelieving people, he predestined some to eternal freedom, giving them life by gratuitous mercy; others, however, he abandoned in their impiety by a hidden judgment and condemned to perpetual death.

The fact that David subdued Moab, whose name is interpreted as “from the father,” as well as Damascus and Syria and other regions, making them tributary, mystically signifies that Christ, holding all nations under his dominion, makes them render him the due of servitude. Each nation, united in the confession of his name, pays him the tribute of good works with devotion.

Damascus is a noble city of Phoenicia, with the same name by which the son of Abraham’s maidservant, Meseth, is also called. Damascus is interpreted as “exalted” or “moistened.” And rightly: the one that formerly, moistened with lust and proud in spirit, thirsted insatiably for human blood now, commanded by the baptism of Christ and exalted by progress in virtue, desires to receive the cup of his blood.

What does it signify that David sanctified to the Lord the golden, silver, and bronze vessels that he had taken from all the nations, except that Christ sanctifies to the Lord all whom he calls to faith from all the nations? Some are like gold—that is, distinguished by spiritual understanding; others like silver—that is, shining with the brilliance of eloquence; and others he sanctifies to the Lord through the preaching of divine honor, so that, serving faithfully in his tabernacle, they may most suitably fulfill his ministry forever.

> “David also made a name for himself when he returned from striking down eighteen thousand in the Valley of Salt.”

He is said to have made a name for himself because, after eighteen thousand had been struck down in the Valley of Salt, he erected a triumphal arch for himself. He is also said to have made a name for himself because, after defeating Syria of Damascus and Syria of Zobah, he is said to have erected another triumphal arch.

If anyone is troubled that many Latin codices read that David struck down not eighteen thousand in the Valley of Salt but twelve thousand, let him know that this error was introduced by scribes into those codices. In truth, David struck down eighteen thousand in that valley, while Joab struck down twelve thousand, as is written in the title of Psalm 58.

Allegorically, what is signified by the multitude struck down by David in the Valley of Salt except that our Redeemer, by the judgment of his severity, extinguishes the folly of immoderate taste in those who think wrongly about him? Hence it is said through a certain wise man:

> “The hard of heart will fare badly at the end, and whoever loves danger will perish in it.”

## Chapter IX

> “And David said: ‘Is there perhaps anyone left of the house of Saul, that I may show him the mercy of the Lord?’ And Ziba said to the king: ‘There remains a son of Jonathan, lame in his feet.’”

David had not forgotten the covenant he had made with Jonathan long before, but he took care to fulfill the mercy he had promised him. He sought out his son and showed him mercy. David did not belong to the company of those about whom it is written elsewhere:

> “Whoever removes mercy from his friend abandons the fear of the Lord.”

This action both demonstrated faithfulness in the man according to the historical sense and revealed a sacramental meaning according to the allegory.

It has often been said that David represents the person of Christ; and above it was also mentioned that Jonathan, whose name is interpreted as “the gift of a dove,” bears the type of the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Jonathan therefore had a little son named Mephibosheth, lame in both feet, as Scripture testifies. David ordered him to be summoned. When God’s predestination and foreknowledge see someone whom the world regards as weak in speech and action for the conduct of worldly affairs, yet whom God chooses for divine service, they do so because the one whom the world despises through the arrogance of pride, God acquires because of his devotion to humility.

Mephibosheth is interpreted as “the beauty of disgrace.” Thus the one whose speech and foreknowledge the pride of the world despises will, by God’s gift, appear useful for spiritual service in the Church.

What else does it mean that David, seeking Ziba, Saul’s servant, from the family of Saul, found Mephibosheth when Ziba revealed his existence, except that our Redeemer, examining the number of the elect among those who have left the world in contempt, brings them to himself?

Ziba, having gone out, came at the proper time. When the king questioned him, Ziba replied that Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, was in the house of Machir son of Ammiel, in Lo-debar.

This accords well with the present interpretation. Machir is interpreted as “selling” or “from weakness”; Ammiel means “his people”; Lo-debar itself means “word.” Thus our David, choosing the contemptible things of this world and the things that are not, in order to destroy the things that are, found them saleable to the world and established in weakness, and enrolled them as worthy of his people through the word of preaching. He granted them royal honor among his sons.

Therefore David, giving Saul’s fields to Mephibosheth as a possession, ordered Mephibosheth himself to be his guest at his table together with his sons. This signifies the grace of our Mediator, which, according to Mary’s words,

> “He has cast down the mighty from their seats and exalted the humble” [Luke 1:52],

and according to the prophecy of Hannah,

> “Raising the needy from the dust and lifting the poor from the dungheap, to seat him with princes and give him the throne of glory” [1 Samuel 2:8].

By taking contemptible persons away from the world, he makes them possessors of virtues, and daily refreshes them with spiritual knowledge at the table of the holy Scriptures.

It follows that such people beget offspring called Micha. Micha in Latin sounds like “Who is he?” [or “Who?”]. For such people frequently come to the admiration of the people: recently taken away from the contempt of the world, they will appear glorious in the Church through God’s gift.

## Chapter X

> “And it came to pass after this that the king of the sons of Ammon died, and Hanun his son reigned in his place. And David said: ‘I will show mercy to Hanun son of Nahash, as his father showed mercy to me,’”

and so forth.

When David fled from Achish, king of Gath, he went to Nahash, king of Ammon, who showed him mercy by bestowing many benefits upon him. From the house of Nahash he therefore came to the cave of Adullam, where his father, mother, and all his household came to him. From there he went to Moab, left his father and mother and all his household with the king, and returned to Achish.

When he saw him, Achish the king of Gath said:

> “Is this man to enter my house?”

David then departed from there and fled to the cave of Adullam. “He departed from there,” that is, from the house of Nahash, and fled to the same cave.

If it is asked, in view of what is read much earlier, why David returned to Achish, before whose presence he had fled, it must be understood that this Achish was the son of that earlier Achish. Hence the Achish with whom David went into battle against Saul is said to have been the son of Maoch. He did not take this patronymic name from his father, but from his mother, who was called Maacah. The reason he did not take it from his father was that David had rejected him. Having clarified these matters, let us turn to the spiritual interpretation.

He says:

> “And David said: ‘I will show mercy to Hanun,’”

until he says:

> “Hanun therefore took David’s servants, shaved off half of their beards,”

and the rest.

Hanun, whose name is interpreted as “their sorrow,” whom can he better signify than the devil, who appears to be the ruler of the spiritual Ammonites, that is, of the wicked spirits? He is also the prince of this world, namely, of the people of sorrow, who are always placed in distress and desire to oppress or constrict human beings.

Just as Hanun, king of Moab, disfigured David’s servants sent to him, shamefully abused them, and sent them back to David, so the devil, the prince of this world, is accustomed to disfigure the conduct of many religious people and preachers of the Word of God through creeping vices.

When he exposes their hidden evils as open crimes and perpetrated lust, he leaves them, as though their garments had been cut away to their buttocks, naked of the dignity of chastity, and reveals before the eyes of human beings the shameful acts he himself had persuaded them to commit. And when he removes their former strength, he is like one shaving off their beard.

Yet the true David, the Lord and Savior, does not exclude them from forgiveness. In his merciful regard, through repentance, he commands them to remain in Jericho—that is, under the ban of repentance and the reproach of their betters—until they recover, through satisfaction, the spiritual mysteries and strength of mind that they had lost by sinning, and can finally stand in his presence.

Certainly, we must not believe that our David allows his soldiers to remain unavenged. He advances against his enemies with an assembled army and avenges the injuries done to his own. Not only does he now confound his adversaries through the victory of the saints, but at the final judgment he will also hand them over, by a just sentence, to be tormented in everlasting fires.

## Chapter XI

> “And it came to pass, when the year had turned, at the time when kings usually go out to war, that David sent Joab and his servants with him,”

and so forth.

In the Hebrew text it is read:

> “At the time when kings go out to war, David sent Joab,”

and so forth.

These are called “kings” who went out to fight against David, namely the king of Rehob, Ish-tob, Zobah, and Maacah. They were kings of Syria and wished to fight against David, having been hired by the king of Moab; they are recorded as having been defeated by him.

> “And Joab said to Abishai his brother: ‘If the Syrians prevail against me, you shall be my help; but if the sons of Ammon prevail against you, I will help you.’”

This is what Solomon says in Proverbs:

> “A brother helped by a brother is like a fortified city, and judgments are like the bars of cities” [Proverbs 18:19].

> “And it happened one day that David rose from his bed after midday and walked about on the roof of the royal house. And he saw a woman opposite him washing herself on her roof.”

A little later it adds:

> “And David sent messengers and took her. When she had entered to him, he slept with her,”

and the rest.

In explaining this passage, we do not put forward anything of our own; rather, we attempt to insert the statements of the holy teachers. Very often, a matter is virtue in its historical sense and guilt in its signification. Sometimes an event is a cause of condemnation in fact but a prophecy of virtue in writing.

We can show this more readily to be true by presenting this testimony of sacred Scripture to establish both points. For who, on hearing it—not only among the faithful but also among unbelievers—would not immediately condemn David, who, walking on the roof, desired Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah? Yet he urges Uriah, returning from battle, to go to his house and wash his feet. Uriah immediately replies:

> “The ark of the Lord is under coverings, and I should rest in my own house?”

David then receives him at his own table and gives him letters by which he is to be put to death.

But whose type does David represent when he walks upon the roof, except the one of whom it is written:

> “He has set his tabernacle in the sun” [Psalm 18:5]?

And what does it mean to bring Bathsheba to himself except to join the law according to the letter, joined to the carnal people, with spiritual understanding belonging to himself?

Bathsheba is called “the seventh well,” because through knowledge of the law the infusion of grace and perfect wisdom is supplied to us.

Whom does Uriah signify except the Jewish people, whose name is interpreted as “the Lord is my light”? The Jewish people, because they are exalted by the knowledge of the law they have received, glory as though in the light of God.

But David took Uriah’s wife away from him and joined her to himself, because the one called David—“strong of hand”—appearing in the flesh as the Redeemer, made it known that the law spoke spiritually about him. Because the law was held according to the letter, he showed it to be foreign to the Jewish people and made it his spouse, since he declared that it had always been preaching him.

Yet David urges Uriah to go to his house and wash his feet. For the incarnate Lord, coming among the Jewish people, commanded them to return to conscience and cleanse the filth of their works with tears, so that they might understand the commandments of the law spiritually. After the great hardness of the commandments, finding the font of baptism, they were to return to the water after their labor.

But Uriah remembered that the ark of the Lord was under coverings and replied that he could not enter his house, as though the Jewish people were saying: “I shall see the commandments of God in carnal sacrifices, but I do not seek to return to conscience through spiritual understanding.”

For one who understands the commandments of God only as the performance of carnal sacrifice is, as it were, saying that the ark is under coverings.

Yet even when he refuses to return to his house, David calls him to his table. For although the Jewish people despise returning to conscience, the Redeemer, when he comes, nevertheless preaches spiritual commandments to them, saying:

> “If you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe me also, for he wrote about me” [John 5:46].

The Jewish people therefore possess the law, which speaks of the divinity, yet that same people disdain believing in him.

Hence Uriah and Joab are sent with the letters by which Uriah is to be killed. The Jewish people themselves carry the law by which they will be condemned. While retaining the commandments of the law and resisting their fulfillment, they themselves bring forward the judgment by which they will be condemned.

What, then, could be more wicked than David in this deed? What could be called purer than Uriah? Yet, again, through the mystery, what is found holier than David and more unbelieving than Uriah? The former, through the guilt of his life, signifies innocence in prophecy; the latter, through the innocence of his life, expresses guilt in prophecy.

The power of sacred speech narrates past events in such a way as to express future things; it approves the deed-doer in such a way as to contradict him in the mystery; and it condemns actions in such a way that, by their mystical performance, it commends them.

In another sense, David is interpreted as “strong of hand” or “desirable.” As a figure of Christ, David walked on the roof after midday, saw a woman washing herself, and desired her.

Thus the Lord, when the world was already declining, as though walking upon the roof, set the body he had deigned to assume in the sun, because he made it manifest to all. He saw the woman—that is, the Church from the nations—upon the roof, namely, on the height of contemplation, washing herself from the stains of the age through the bath of regeneration, transcending and trampling upon the earthly house through spiritual contemplation. He looked upon her; and, after the devil had been killed, he joined her to himself by faith in an indissoluble marriage.

Bathshe—
## [scan page 187]

### ANGELOMUS, MONK OF LUXEUIL

For Beersheba is interpreted as “well of seven,” or “well of satiety,” prefiguring, that is, the holy Church, in which the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit is present, and by whose gift all the elect are satisfied. Uriah, however, is called “my light is the Lord.” Hittite is interpreted as “the severed one,” expressing in himself the figure of the devil: although he is dark and severed from the land of the living, he transforms himself into an angel of light and pretends to be what he is not, daring to say of God, “my light,” as though it were his own. Let us therefore hate the sin, but not extinguish the prophecy. Let us love that David insofar as he must be loved, who by mercy freed us from the devil. Let us also love this penitent David, who healed in himself so grievous a wound of iniquity through repentance and humble confession.

For this reason the sins of such men in Holy Scripture—namely, David and Peter—are disclosed, so that the fall of the great may be a warning to the lesser. For this reason, too, the repentance and forgiveness of both are immediately made known, so that the recovery of the lost may be the hope of those who are perishing. When David falls from his position, let no one become proud; when David rises again after his fall, let no one despair.

But perhaps someone may say: if David bore the figure of Christ, how is it written that he had many wives and concubines, when Christ rejects and condemns such things? This occurred figuratively. David’s many wives signified the image of many peoples and nations, who were to be joined through faith to the fellowship of Christ. His concubines, however, signify the churches of heretics, which boast that they remain under the title of Christ’s name; but because they follow Christ for carnal gain, they are called not wives but concubines. Finally, even if kings have several wives or concubines, this is not a crime, because the figures have now passed away for which permission concerning wives or concubines was granted; but now, since the figures have passed away, no permission is granted.

### CHAPTER XII

> “Therefore the Lord sent Nathan to David, and when he had come to him, he said: ‘There were two men in one city,’” and so forth.

It must be understood that the prophet Nathan was not sent by the Lord to King David immediately when David himself sinned with Bathsheba, but after he had brought that same woman into his house and a son had been born from her, so that the obstinacy of the sin would have no opportunity for defense.

When powerful men are reproved by the rulers of the Church of this age, they should first be questioned through certain parables, as though concerning another person’s affair. When they have themselves pronounced the right judgment against another, they should then, in appropriate ways, be struck with regard to their own guilt. Thus minds swollen with temporal power may not rise up against the one who corrects them, since by their own judgment they have bound themselves with the words of their own mouths.

> “Therefore the sword shall not depart from your house forever.”

Note how from David’s house—that is, from the Jewish people—the sword of vengeance shall not depart forever.

> “And David said to Nathan: ‘I have sinned against the Lord.’ And Nathan said to David: ‘The Lord also has taken away your sin; you shall not die. Nevertheless, because by this deed you have caused the enemies of the Lord to blaspheme, the son who has been born to you shall surely die.’”

Here we can consider how much a person’s true repentance avails before God, if it proceeds from the heart. For after the prophet had rebuked him and he had recognized his sin, David said nothing except one word, confessing: “I have sinned against the Lord”; and immediately he obtained forgiveness, as the prophet himself testifies when he says: “The Lord also has taken away your sin; you shall not die.”

This is what is written: “If, having confessed, you groan, you shall be saved.” And this: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live” [Ezek. 18]. Again it is written: “On whatever day the sinner turns, all his sins shall be forgotten before me” [Ezek. 33].

Thus Peter, when the Lord looked upon him, wept, and by weeping wiped away the sin of his denial. Thus the thief, at the very extremity of life, by entrusting himself to God and acknowledging his sin, saying, “We are receiving what we deserve for our deeds” [John 13], earned paradise.

But because the circumstances required that David be brought forward in the order of the history, and we have recalled so great a crime, the reader’s mind may perhaps be disturbed: why does almighty God not preserve from bodily vices those whom he has chosen forever and whom he also raises to the summit of spiritual honor?

Since we believe that an answer can be given quickly, we reply briefly. Some people, through the virtues they have received and the abundant grace of good works, fall into the vice of pride, yet do not recognize the place from which they have fallen. Therefore the ancient enemy, who already rules within them, is permitted to rage against them outwardly as well, so that those who have become exalted in thought may be cast down through the lust of the flesh.

We must understand that it is sometimes a lesser evil to fall into bodily corruption than to sin through silent, deliberate pride. But since pride is considered less disgraceful, it is avoided less; whereas people are more ashamed of lust, because everyone recognizes it as disgraceful. Thus it often happens that some, after falling from pride into lust, become ashamed of their hidden fault because of their manifest fall, and then correct greater faults when, having been overthrown in lesser ones, they are more deeply confounded. They see themselves as guilty who had considered themselves free amid greater offenses.

By the merciful dispensation of the Lord, therefore, the loosened are sometimes led by the malignant spirit from one fault to another; and while he strikes more severely, he thereby loses the one whom he had captured. Thus he is seen to have conquered where he is in fact overcome.

It is useful to contemplate the shelter of grace, when God in his merciful favor holds us fast. Behold, the one who exalted himself because of virtue returns to humility through vice. The one who is lifted up by the virtues he has received is wounded not with a sword but, so to speak, with a medicine. For what is virtue except a medicine? And what is vice except a wound? Since, therefore, he makes a wound for us from a medicine, he makes medicine from the wound, so that we who perish through virtue may be healed through vice.

Yet it must be understood that many people who fall in numerous ways are bound more tightly. When the ancient enemy strikes them through one vice, they fall into another as well, so that they may rise only with difficulty. Consequently, a person engaged in warfare with the adversary, if he realizes that he has sinned in some matter, should fear that he may be drawn from sin into sin, and should diligently avoid the wounds by which he is frequently injured.

For our enemy very rarely serves the salvation of the elect even through their wounds.

The Lord, as we have said, often subjects his elect to temptation, as after the gates of paradise and after the secrets of the third heaven, lest Paul should become exalted by the greatness of his revelations, the angel of Satan was given to him [2 Cor. 12]. Yet, as we have already stated, temptation itself is arranged so that those who might have perished through exaltation may be saved through humiliation.

By a hidden order of providence, therefore, from the place where the devil’s iniquity is permitted to rage, God’s goodness is also piously accomplished. Our adversary obeys the commands of heavenly grace precisely where he exercises the anger of his most wicked will.

It should be noted that for this reason the sins of such men in Holy Scripture—namely, David and Peter—are set down, so that the ruin of the great may be a warning to the lesser. For this reason, too, the repentance and forgiveness of both are immediately made known, so that the recovery of the lost may be the hope of those who are perishing. When David falls, let no one become proud of his own state; when David rises after his fall, let no one despair.

## [scan page 188]

### COMMENTARY ON THE BOOKS OF KINGS — BOOK II

> “And David persisted in fasting, and, entering separately, lay upon the ground,” and so forth.

David, lying for seven days because of his crime until the child died, displayed perfect repentance, leaving a model of repentance for all sinners. Thus, whenever any one of us falls into some crime, he ought to persist in weeping until the desire for sin has been completely wiped out from our will.

The seven days undoubtedly signify the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, without whose gift no penitent can obtain the indulgence of sins. For, as we have said, the Lord subjects his elect to temptation, just as after the gates of paradise, and after the secrets of the third heaven, the angel of Satan was given to Paul. Yet, as we have already stated, temptation itself is arranged so that those who might have perished through exaltation may be saved through humiliation.

Therefore the ancient enemy is permitted to rage where the mercy of God is piously perfected. Our adversary obeys the commands of heavenly grace precisely where he exercises the anger of his wicked will.

It should be noted that for this reason the sins of such men in Holy Scripture—David and Peter—are set down, so that the ruin of the great may be a warning to the lesser. For this reason, too, the repentance and forgiveness of both are immediately made known, so that the recovery of the lost may be the hope of those who are perishing. When David falls, let no one become proud; when David rises after his fall, let no one despair.

Behold how wonderfully Holy Scripture presses down the proud with the same word by which it raises the humble. It recounts one and the same event, yet in different ways recalls the proud to the strength of humility and the humble to confidence in hope. O immeasurable medicine of the new creation, which, placed in one and the same order, dries up what is swollen by pressing it down and pours moisture into what is parched by raising it up! It terrifies us by the fall of the great, but strengthens us through their restoration. Thus divine mercy always restrains the proud and supports us lest we fall into despair.

But it must be asked: if the Lord took away David’s sin, which was so detestable, what does it mean that he later endured everything that had been said to him by the Lord through the prophet because of that same sin?

Without doubt, the Lord removes the sin, but he does not leave it without punishment. Either the person himself punishes it through repentance, or God strikes him by taking vengeance together with him. The sin, therefore, is never spared if it is released without punishment. Thus David deserved to hear after his conversion: “The Lord has taken away your sin”; yet, afflicted afterward by many torments, he fled and paid the debt of the guilt he had committed.

By the retribution that brings salvation we are released from the guilt of our first parent, but even after being absolved, while cleansing away the debt of that same fault, we still die bodily. For God cuts away our sins, whether through us or through himself, even when he forgives them. From his elect he strives to wipe away by temporal affliction the stains of iniquity that he does not wish to see in them forever.

> “The Lord loved him. And he sent him by the hand of Nathan the prophet, and called his name Amabilis Domino, ‘beloved of the Lord,’ because he loved him,” and so forth.

In Hebrew it is written: “And he called his name Dida,” that is, “beloved of the Lord.” He is called beloved because of the Lord, that is, because of the Lord’s gratuitous mercy, by which he graciously chose to love him, although he was unworthy of that love and mercy, since it was evident that he was illegitimate.

> “Therefore Joab fought against Rabbah of the sons of Ammon,” and so forth.

It should be noted that in Hebrew, when the name is written with the addition of a noun, it is written Rabbah, as here. But when it occurs without the addition of a noun, it is written Rabba.

> “David therefore gathered all the people, and went against Rabbah. And when he had fought against it, he captured it and took the king’s crown from his head, weighing a talent of gold,” and so forth.

In the book of Chronicles it is written: “David took the crown of Melchom from his head, and found in it a talent’s weight of gold and precious gems, and made a crown from it.”

Melchom is not the proper name of the king, but was an idol; and it is interpreted as “their king.” David is said, according to the law, to have melted and purified the gold and gems of this crown and to have made himself a crown, which is said here to have been placed upon his head.

> “He also carried away a very great amount of spoil from the city. He brought out its people, and put them under saws and harrows and iron carts. He divided them with knives and passed them through the pattern of bricks.”

That is, he sawed the bodies of the people with iron carts and divided them with iron knives, as bricks are usually divided—bricks made from straw and clay.

What does this victory of David over the Ammonites signify? His commander began the battle, but the king himself completed it. It signifies the victory of our King over all the nations. David the commander wages war against the enemies when the order of holy preachers opposes the shield of faith to the powerful of this world. But the end of the struggle and the triumph of the war are attributed solely to Christ the King, because all power and royal authority are ascribed to him.

For according to the Apostle, “It is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish,” and he himself always triumphs for us in Christ Jesus.

## [scan page 189]

### ANGELOMUS

David therefore took the crown of the hostile king’s people from his head and made a diadem for himself from it, when our Redeemer, taking the kingdom from the opposing power, prepared for himself a crown of glory.

What crown of David can be understood better than the gathering of the Catholic people? With believing hearts it nobly surrounds our Head, namely Christ the King, and by living worthily crowns him fittingly. For all the labor, struggle, and victory of the saints is referred to the honor of the heavenly King, because he is the one before whom every knee bends—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue confesses that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father [Phil. 2].

Rabbah, therefore, is a city of the kingdom of Ammon, now called Philadelphia, which the prophet Jeremiah also mentions [Jer. 49]. Rabbah is interpreted as “many”; and the Savior says in the Gospel: “Many will come from the east and the west, and will recline with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” [Mark 9].

According to the historical account, however, the Book of Chronicles relates the matter as follows:

> “He also took a very great amount of spoil from the city. He brought out the people who were in it, and put them under harrows, drags, and iron carts, so that they were cut apart and crushed.”

Thus David acted toward all the cities of the sons of Ammon, and he returned with all the people to Jerusalem.

I have therefore added these details so that I might present the history more clearly.

### CHAPTER XIII

Next follows the account of how Amnon hated his sister Tamar after the sin, with exceedingly great hatred, and so forth.

Amnon violated his sister Tamar, thereby offending his father David. This was the beginning of the scandal in his house. But the fact that he is read to have hated her after committing the crime expressed the figure of those who, after committing some offense, hate it more than they loved it before committing it; and for this reason they obtain forgiveness more quickly than those who both commit and love their sins—provided that they do not offend again in another sin.

Thus it was with Amnon, who, after committing the outrage against his sister, did not escape death because he failed to avoid drunkenness, which is the fuel of lust.

Morally, however, we are warned by this event always to act cautiously and prudently, lest vices and the prince of sin gain dominion over us. He promises a false peace to those in danger, finds us unprepared and unsuspecting, and then slaughters us—just as Absalom killed his brother Amnon, who was careless after violating Tamar.

Absalom is interpreted as “father of peace” or “the peace of the father.” Amnon means “one who gives,” and Tamar means “bitterness.” Whoever gives his members over to lust has handed himself over to serve iniquity for iniquity and falls into the bitterness of sin, although the enemy may display himself as a father of peace and falsely promise prosperity as the result of such deeds.

It is necessary that after a crime we return quickly to repentance, lest the devil, if we continue to serve drunkenness and dissolve into the luxury of the world, conspire against our destruction through the evil spirits who obey him and deliver us to eternal death.

> “But Absalom, fleeing, went to Talmai, son of Ammihud, king of Geshur,” and so forth, up to the passage: “And King David ceased pursuing Absalom, because he was consoled concerning the death of Amnon.”

The Hebrews report—as I have learned from certain sources—that Talmai was the father of Maacah, Absalom’s mother. David captured her in battle and, as they say, took her as his wife after cutting off her nails according to the law; from her he fathered Tamar and Absalom. They therefore say that Absalom fled to him.

For what follows—“David ceased pursuing Absalom”—is read in Hebrew, according to the same Hebrew authorities, as: “The king ceased going out,” that is, David himself ceased wishing to go out in order to bring Absalom back. Reflecting in his heart that whenever he saw him, the death of Amnon would be brought back to his memory, he is therefore said to have ceased going out after Absalom, the implied purpose being to recall him to his own place.

They likewise wish the statement “David was consoled concerning the death of Amnon” to be understood in this way: after he no longer went out after Absalom to bring him back and see him, he began to be consoled concerning Amnon’s death. For as long as Absalom was thought to be brought back and seen by David, the death of his son Amnon continually came before his mind. Or, as seems to us, he was consoled concerning his death because he knew him to be disgraceful and worthy of death, and to have perished deservedly.

## CHAPTERS XIV AND XV

> “When Joab, son of Zeruiah, understood that the king’s heart was turned toward Absalom, he sent to Tekoa and brought from there a wise woman, and said to her: ‘Pretend to be mourning, put on mourning garments, and do not anoint yourself with oil, so that you may be like a woman who has long been mourning for the dead.’”

Joab is said to have seen that the king’s heart was turned toward Absalom because he saw him sighing for Absalom; from this he understood that his heart had turned toward him.

> “He sent to Tekoa and brought from there a wise woman.”

Tekoa is the city from which the prophet Amos came. It is thought that this widow was the grandmother of that same prophet Amos.

She replied:

> “Alas, I am a widow. My husband is dead, and your servant had two sons who quarreled with each other in the field, and there was no one who could restrain them. One struck the other and killed him. And behold, the whole family has risen against your servant, saying: ‘Hand over the one who struck his brother.’”

In truth, as the Hebrews report, this woman could have been a widow who had two sons who quarreled in the field over their father’s inheritance, and one was killed by the other. Yet this same widow placed herself in the role of David and her two sons in the roles of Amnon and Absalom. The family that rose against her son represented David’s other sons.

## [scan page 190]

### COMMENTARY ON THE BOOKS OF KINGS

The woman said:

> “Let the iniquity be upon me, my lord the king, and upon my father’s house, but let the king and his house be innocent.”

As though she were saying: because one son rose against the other, let the iniquity be upon me, since you are without guilt in the matter in which those two brothers fought among themselves. And just as I am without guilt because my two sons rose against each other and one was killed by the other, so you are also without guilt because Absalom killed Amnon, who deserved death.

> “She said: ‘Let the king remember the Lord his God, so that the avengers of blood may not multiply to take vengeance and utterly destroy my son.’”

“Remember” is here put for an oath, as though it were openly said: let the king remember the promise—or rather the oath—which he made to me by the Lord his God, that the avengers of blood would not multiply to take vengeance.

> “And the woman said: ‘Why have you devised such a thing against the people of God, and in speaking this word the king has become guilty, because he does not bring back his banished one?’”

From this passage it is demonstrated that what was said above—“King David ceased going out after Absalom”—means that he ceased so that no one would go out and bring Absalom back.

The woman therefore said: “In speaking this word the king has become guilty, because he does not bring back his banished one.”

When she says, “Why have you devised such a thing against the people of God?” she calls Absalom himself, or those who were with him, the people of God. They were like captives and outcasts, and because they were not brought back to the inheritance of God, they might perhaps be compelled to serve foreign gods in a foreign land.

> “God does not desire the destruction of a soul, but, while considering, he turns back, lest the one who has been cast away perish utterly.”

As though she were saying: God calls sinners, who are held captive by the devil, so that they may turn back to him; and you, who ought to imitate him, why do you not act in the same way?

> “And whenever he cut his hair—for it was cut once a year.”

In Hebrew it is read as follows: “And whenever the hair of his head was cut, it was cut at the appointed time,” and so forth. For it was not cut once a year, as the Latin books have it, but at the appointed time, that is, every thirty days.

But setting aside the opinion of some, we have decided to read the passage simply as it is found among us—“whenever he cut the hair of his head; now he cut it once a year”—because we believe that this translation was drawn from the Hebrew source.

It is also said:

> “For in all Israel there was no man as handsome as Absalom, exceedingly beautiful. From the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him. He later made for himself chariots and horsemen, and, standing at the gate, criticized his father’s judgment.”

Absalom himself, the son of David—his name is interpreted as “the peace of the father,” and we shall speak of this interpretation below—can figuratively be understood to have represented the Jewish people. He is rightly said to have been beautiful, insofar as this refers figuratively to that people, because of the kingdom, the priesthood, and the other gifts once bestowed upon it by God.

Yet he did not wish to have peace with our David, that is, with the Lord and Savior. For Absalom himself said:

> “Who will appoint me judge over the land?”

and so forth.

Absalom displays feigned humility. For nothing is worse than magnifying false virtues through hypocrisy and, through pride of heart, defaming the acts and strength of one’s superiors by criticizing them. Thus Absalom did not fear rashly to criticize his father’s just judgments before the whole people.

> “After forty years Absalom said to the king: ‘I will go and fulfill my vows which I vowed to the Lord in Hebron.’”

The fortieth year was reckoned from the time when Saul killed the city of Nob, together with eighty-five priests, because of David. This fortieth year is therefore inserted to show that divine vengeance was stirred up against David because he had deceived Abimelech the priest and because the slaughter of the priests had occurred on his account.

Beware, reader, of the many corrupt books in which it is written “after four years,” not “after forty years.” In the older books, however, and in the Hebrew truth, the years are written not as four but as forty.

If someone obstinately wishes to assert that the period was four years, he will plainly find himself in error if he investigates carefully. From the time when Absalom killed his brother Amnon until the time when he said to his father, “I will go and fulfill my vows which I vowed to the Lord in Hebron,” the chronology does not allow it. After Amnon was killed, Absalom remained three years with King Talmai; afterward, when he had been recalled to Jerusalem, he remained two years without seeing his father; in the sixth year he saw his father’s face and prepared rebellion against him.

He falsely said that he had vowed a vow, namely that he would pray in the place where Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob rest.

> “Zadok also came, and all the Levites with him, carrying the ark of the covenant of the Lord; and they set down the ark of God. And Abiathar went up until all the people who had gone out from the city were completed.”

They are said to have set down the ark of God so that the Lord might be consulted through Abiathar the priest regarding where David ought to go. Abiathar is said to have gone up—that is, to have prayed—and because no divine oracle was given to him, David later ordered that the ark of God be carried back into the city.

## CHAPTER XVI

> “David came as far as Bahurim. And behold, a man from the family of Saul came out from there, named Shimei, son of Gera, and cursed David. Abishai said: ‘I will go and cut off his head,’” and so forth, up to the passage: “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Let him curse.”

The Hebrew does not have “Let him curse,” but only “Curse.” Abishai alone had said, “I will go and cut off his head”; and David answered Abishai and Joab, saying: “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah?”

As though he were saying: Do you wish to kill this man as you killed Abner? For the Lord commanded him to curse David. And who is there who may say, “Why has he done this?”

The implied sense is: why has he done this—not the Lord, but Shimei?

Shimei who cursed David is, according to the Hebrews, Nebat, the father of Jeroboam, who is called the son of Jemini; and in his zeal for the house of Saul he cursed David. His grandfather’s name, however, was Shimei, and this Shimei belonged to the tribe of Ephraim, the son of Joseph. Hence that same Shimei said to David:

> “Today I am the first to come from the whole tribe of Joseph.”

> “When Hushai the Archite, David’s friend, had come to Absalom, he said to him: ‘Hail, king! Hail, king!’ Absalom said to him: ‘Is this your loyalty to your friend?’”

In Hebrew it is read: “Is this,” he said, “mercy toward your friend?” This must be pronounced not as an affirmation but as a denial. The sense is: Is it mercy—or should it be called mercy—that you have abandoned David, your friend, and have not gone with him?

## CHAPTER XVII

> “Then Ahithophel said to Absalom: ‘Let me choose twelve thousand men, and I will arise and pursue David tonight. I will fall upon him, for he is weary and his hands are weakened, and I will strike him. When everyone who is with him has fled, I will strike the king when he is alone and bring back all the people, just as everyone usually returns.’”

That is, just as those who return after losing their king in battle usually return, so the whole people of Israel will return to you.

> “And when anyone has fallen at the beginning, whoever hears it will say: ‘A slaughter has taken place among the people who followed Absalom.’ And every brave man, whose heart is like a lion’s, will melt with fear.”

In Hebrew it is read: “Will even the bravest man, whose heart is like the heart of a lion, melt with fear?” This must be pronounced not affirmatively but negatively. “The bravest man” is to be understood as David, as the following words also make clear.

> “For all Israel knows that your father is a mighty man, and all who are with him are strong.”

But what this Ahithophel signifies, we shall explain later.

> “Jonathan and Ahimaaz were standing beside the spring of Rogel. A maidservant went and told them, and they went away.”

This maidservant had gone to the spring with clothes, supposedly for washing, so that the matter might not be detected at all. The boy who reported the affair to Absalom is said to have been the little son of this same maidservant.

We have decided to touch upon this briefly while continuing the history, so that later we may set forth what follows in its mystical meaning. But since the history of Absalom goes beyond the present point, it is worth considering allegorically what is signified by the fact that the parricidal son pursues his father.

First, his father flees, withdrawing from the face of his son who is waging war against him, secure in victory, because he knew that the impious man would perish. Yet he also mourned him greatly and lamented the parricide’s end. For it is written that David fled from the face of his son who was fighting against him.

Elsewhere it is written concerning the people of Jerusalem, with the Lord saying:

> “I have nourished and exalted sons, but they themselves have despised me” [Isa. 1].

His impious son can therefore be understood figuratively as the Jewish people, who betrayed him.

As has already been said, Absalom is interpreted as “the peace of the father.” It seems astonishing in the historical account how “the peace of the father” can be understood as one who pursued his father in war. But those who attend carefully to the allegory recognize that Absalom is Jerusalem, which is itself also interpreted as “vision of peace.”

Christ flees from its face into Galilee—that is, he leaves it through his suffering and withdraws among the Gentiles through faith.

Others understand Absalom as Judas the betrayer, whom Christ endured as though he were good, with such goodness and wondrous patience, although he did not fail to know his thoughts. He admitted him to the banquet at which he commended and handed over to the disciples the figure of his body and blood; finally, at the very betrayal, he also received a kiss from him.

It is rightly understood that Christ displayed peace toward his betrayer, although Judas was being ravaged inwardly by the war of his wicked thoughts. Absalom is therefore called “the peace of the father,” because the father possessed a peace which Absalom did not possess.

We have offered this latter interpretation not as our own invention, but have drawn it from the sayings of blessed Augustine, specifically from the title of the third psalm, in which he explains the matter in argument as though it were resounding like a very clear trumpet.

Ahithophel, therefore, who abandoned David and migrated to Absalom, signifies heretics, who depart from the path of truth, join themselves to the ancient enemy, and follow error. His name is interpreted as “my brother has fallen”; Gilonite means “migration.”

Against such people the prophet rebukes, saying:

> “In the Lord I trust; how can you say to my soul, ‘Migrate to the mountain like a sparrow’?” [Ps. 10].

And deservedly such people bring their own lives to an end by the noose of the devil and their own wickedness, since they strive to corrupt another’s life through depraved persuasion. Thus he perished by hanging in his own house, the man who plotted against another’s life—that is, against David’s.

Hence it is written:

> “Whoever digs a pit will fall into it” [Prov. 26; Eccles. 10].

But what else he signifies, we shall explain later.

> “Zadok also came, and all the Levites with him, carrying the ark of the covenant of God; and they set down the ark of God. Abiathar went up until all the people who had gone out from the city were completed. And the king said to Zadok: ‘Carry the ark of God back into the city. If I find favor in the eyes of the Lord, he will bring me back and show me it and his tabernacle. But if he should say, “You do not please me,”’” and so forth.

We have already emphasized what these things signify according to the history. But as far as the higher understanding is concerned, Zadok the priest—whose name is interpreted as “just”—who carried the ark of the Lord back into the city, represented the saints, namely those who, at the time of the Lord’s Passion, departed from him bodily for a short time but were not at all separated from him in faith and love.

> “David said to Hushai the Archite: ‘If you come with me, you will be a burden to me,’” and so forth.

For this Hushai too was David’s friend. His name is interpreted as “my haste” [the printed form is uncertain]. and, returning from him to Jerusalem, [the counsel of Ahithophel—sentence fragment].

## [Scan page 192]

### Commentary on the Books of Kings — Book II

[Continuation:] “...phel dispersed,” he represented those among the Jewish people who were secretly disciples of the Lord, such as Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea, or others of this kind. It may also be understood to signify believers from the Gentiles, who, although they were at one time seen to have been with Absalom, did not participate in his wicked deeds, nor ever consent to Ahithophel’s evil counsels, but remained faithfully with David.

“Chusai” is interpreted as “Ethiopian,” and “Arachite” as “my length.” Hence also it is written in the prophet: “Can an Ethiopian change his skin?” (Jer. 13); and: “Ethiopia shall hasten to stretch out her hands to God.” For after the Gentile people had stripped themselves of the blackness of sins, they never withdrew from the Lord; and the one who had been far away was brought near through the blood of Christ.

Then follows the account of how Siba, the servant of Mephibosheth, met David with two laden asses, lied about his master, and therefore David said to him: “Yours shall be all that belonged to Mephibosheth.” Here it is shown that the spirit of prophecy—as we said above—is not always present to the prophets, nor are they continually touched by it. For David did not understand that Siba, Mephibosheth’s servant, was lying against his master, and therefore granted him everything belonging to his master. Had the spirit of prophecy been present to him, he would have detected the liar.

He had likewise not been touched by it in the immediate context when earlier he had promised Amasa, saying: “May God do this to me and add this, if you will not be commander of the army before me forever in place of Joab,” without knowing what would follow. For Amasa not only would not assume the command of the army in place of Joab, but would also shortly afterward end his life after Joab.

When he wished to build a temple for God, he likewise did not know what would follow immediately and sought another prophet.

A note in our copy once again places here **CHAPTER XVI**, since the exposition given above is repeated.

“Then King David came to Bahurim. And behold, a man from the family of the house of Saul came out, named Shimei, son of Gera, and he cursed David,” and so forth, up to the point where he says: “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Why should you become Satan to me today? Let him alone.”

That is perfect patience: willingly to endure one whom anyone could easily repay in kind. Thus it was displayed in David, who took greater care patiently to endure Shimei’s blasphemy than to avenge it. Although Shimei pressed him with every kind of insult and the armed nobles were eager to take revenge, David said: “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Leave him, that he may curse, according to the Lord’s command, if perhaps the Lord will look upon my affliction and repay me good for this day’s cursing.”

By these words he clearly indicates that, because of the crime committed with Bathsheba, when he fled from the son rising against him, he brought back to mind the evil he had committed; he endured calmly what he heard and regarded the insulting words not so much as reproaches as aids, through which he indicated that he might be cleansed and receive mercy. We tolerate insults well when, in the secret of our mind, we recall the evil we have committed. For it will seem lighter that we suffer injury while we see that what we deserve is worse. Thus insults are to be answered with gratitude rather than anger, since it is hoped that, through their intervention, a more severe punishment may be averted before God the judge.

“And David said: Why are you becoming Satan to me today?” The apostle Peter provides a similar example, although he spoke from weakness of understanding, not from the pride of heart shown by Abishai. After hearing of the Lord’s future passion, he is read in the Gospel as having answered: “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall not happen” (Mark 8). But why did the Lord respond in the opposite way, rebuking him, just as David answered Abishai: “Get behind me, Satan, because you do not understand the things that are of God, but those that are of men” (ibid.)?

“And Ahithophel said to Absalom: Go in to your father’s concubines,” and so forth. There is no doubt that David’s concubines, whom his son Absalom wickedly violated, prefigured the Jewish people. The teachers of error—namely, the scribes and Pharisees—corrupted that people through their empty superstitions and perverse teaching and alienated it from the Lord Jesus Christ, just as heretics also frequently do. Likewise, the apostate Angel, by seducing through heretical perversity certain men who appear to rule over and guard the people of God, deceives them by means of those whom he treats as David’s concubines.

Yet David no longer goes in to them; rather, he provides food for them while they are kept in confinement. They live in widowhood and remain shut up until the day of their death. For while those deceived by heretics wander away from the truth, they pretend that they are unwilling to return to it; they are not worthy of dwelling with Christ, but remain shut up—that is, separated and alienated from his fellowship. Yet that merciful one who makes his sun rise over the good and the wicked does not cease in this world to provide such people with nourishment through his gifts, so that by means of the benefits bestowed he may offer them an opportunity for conversion.

“Then Ahithophel said to Absalom: Let me choose twelve thousand men, and I will rise and pursue David this night.” Ahithophel, who gave wicked counsel against David, represented Judas the betrayer, who gave the Jews counsel against Christ concerning his betrayal. Ahithophel is interpreted as “the ruin of a brother,” which certainly suits Judas the betrayer, because he became the ruin of the one who deigned to say: “I will declare your name to my brothers” (Ps. 21).

After putting his household in order, Ahithophel afterward died by hanging. Judas likewise is read in the Gospel to have done the same as Ahithophel.

Here follows the account of how Jonathan and Ahimaaz were left to investigate Absalom’s counsel and report it to David. Fleeing, they turned aside into the house of a certain man at Bahurim, who had a well in his courtyard, and they descended into it. The woman took a covering, spread it over the mouth of the well as though she were drying peas, and thus concealed them.

These two young men—Jonathan, whose name is interpreted as “the dove of the Lord,” and Ahimaaz, “my brother”—signify those who, reborn through the grace of the Holy Spirit, are enrolled among the number of the brethren. They withdraw from Absalom when they seek to escape the evil spirits.

They stood beside the spring of Rogel, a name interpreted as “sad” or “going downward,” because they desire to have sadness and contempt in this world for the sake of their longing for the heavenly kingdom. Thus, fleeing, they quickly turn aside into the house of a certain man at Bahurim, a place whose name is interpreted as “chosen” or “young,” because they recall the time of adolescence.

They descend into the well that was in the courtyard when they humbly submit themselves with patience to what is necessary for all, before the end of the present life. The woman spreads a covering over the mouth of the well when the Church strives, through continual prayer, to conceal the sins of the youth and ignorance of her children, as though drying peas, while she restrains the wantonness of the flesh through the severity of self-control.

Thus the transgression of human life remains hidden: through continual prayer amid compunction and tears, and through bodily discipline, all sins are concealed and human beings are protected and freed from the persecution of the ancient enemy.

A further note in this copy once again places **CHAPTER XVII** here.

## [Scan page 193]

### Angelomus, Monk of Luxeuil

Jonathan, whose name is interpreted as “the dove of the Lord,” and Ahimaaz, “my brother,” signify those who, reborn through the grace of the Holy Spirit, are enrolled among the brethren. They flee from Absalom when they seek to escape the evil spirits.

They stood beside the spring of Rogel, which is interpreted as “sad” or “downward,” because they desire to experience sadness and contempt in this world for the sake of their longing for the heavenly kingdom. They therefore flee swiftly into the house of a certain man at Bahurim, a place interpreted as “chosen” or “young,” because it brings the time of youth back to memory.

They descend into the well that was in the courtyard when they humbly submit themselves with patience to what is necessary for all, before the end of the present life. The woman spreads a covering over the mouth of the well when the Church, through the constancy of prayer, strives to hide the sins of the youth and ignorance of her children, as though drying peas, while she restrains the wantonness of the flesh through the severity of self-control.

Thus the transgression of human life remains hidden. Through continual prayer in the compunction of tears and through bodily chastisement, all sins are concealed, and human beings are protected and liberated from the persecution of the ancient enemy.

“And when David had come to Mahanaim, Shobi son of Nahash from Rabbah of the Ammonites, and Machir son of Ammiel from Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite from Rogelim, brought him beds and carpets,” and so forth.

The camp to which David came is called *Mahanaim* in Hebrew, as we indicated above. This is the place where the angels of God met Jacob, as it is read in Genesis. Hence it is written: “Jacob called the name of that place Mahanaim” (Gen. 32), that is, “camps.”

Shobi rested there with the gifts he brought to David. He was the son of Nahash the king, with whom Saul had fought. After Nahash’s death, David said: “I will show kindness to the Ammonites, as his father Nahash showed kindness to me.” After David had killed Ammon, who had wronged him by shaving his servants, he appointed Shobi in the place of his brother.

Spiritually, however, the service offered by him and by the other Galileans to David represented the faith of the Gentile peoples in the Lord Jesus Christ. Just as David, fleeing from the persecution of his son, withdrew from Jerusalem and was kindly received by the Galileans, so the Lord Jesus Christ, abandoning the Jews because of their impiety, was received by the Gentile people, who offered the Lord many believers adorned with a variety of virtues and teachings.

### CHAPTER XVIII

“And the king commanded Joab, Abishai, and Ittai, saying: Preserve the boy Absalom.”

When his father David calls Absalom a “boy,” he does not speak of the age of his flesh but of the smallness of his understanding—that is, of his folly—not of the size of his body.

“There was a battle there spread over the face of the whole land, and many more of the people were those whom the forest devoured than those whom the sword consumed in the battle.”

The forest is said to have consumed more than the sword devoured because of the exceedingly savage beasts that were in the forest, by which more were consumed than were swallowed up by the sword.

“It happened that Absalom encountered the servants of David while riding on a mule,” and so forth. As the mule on which Absalom was riding passed beneath the oak, he himself, clinging to the oak, was suspended between heaven and earth.

In the same way, the scribes and Pharisees, the leaders of the Jews, were condemned by a hidden judgment on the same wood on which they had hung the Lord Jesus Christ on the cross. As they passed over into the dispersion of the Gentiles, they lost both the leadership and the people of the Jews whom they had appeared to govern as an irrational mule, subject to carnal understanding.

Let us state the matter more explicitly. Absalom, fleeing on a mule, was suspended from an oak by the hair of his head. This signified that the Jews, sunk in the folly of carnal understanding, would corrupt the law through Pharisaic superstition and, through the very law they had received for the correction of life, would incur the occasion of death.

Hence the Savior said to them in the Gospel: “Do not think that I shall accuse you before my Father. Moses, in whom you trust, is the one who accuses you” (John 5).

Joab thrust three spears into Absalom’s heart when the ancient enemy implanted pride, avarice, and envy—or treachery—in the heart of the Jewish people. These were especially the causes of their destruction.

They were proud when, in contempt of God, they fashioned idols. They were greedy when they preferred transient pleasures to the delights of virtue. They were treacherous and envious when they not only opposed the words of the law and the prophets but also despised the presence of the Savior himself and proved ungrateful for his benefits.

Hence, in his passion, they said to Pilate with blasphemous voice: “We have no king but Caesar.” They showed themselves ungrateful when they said: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend” (John 19).

After his death Absalom was cast into a pit and covered with a great heap of stones, just as every wicked person after the death of the flesh is plunged into the pit of hell. A heap of stones is piled over him when the hardness of his mind is reproached.

David indeed mourned the dead man, just as the Lord mourned the destruction of the Jewish people, as it is read in the Gospel: “When he saw the city of Jerusalem, he wept over it” (Luke 9). He had such compassion for its misery that he remained, even unto the death of the cross, in teaching and care for its salvation.

“Then Ahimaaz ran by the shorter road and passed Chushai.” Ahimaaz, son of Zadok, who began later but himself ran ahead first, undoubtedly prefigured the eagerness of certain saints. Although they are the last in conversion, many of them surpass those who seemed to precede them in faith, love, and spiritual fervor.

### CHAPTER XIX

“And all the people came before the king,” namely, those who had remained with David. But when it says, “Israel fled to his tents,” these are to be understood as those who had been rebels and had joined Absalom’s revolt.

## [Scan page 194]

### Commentary on the Books of Kings — Book II

“Mephibosheth, son of Jonathan, also came down to meet the king on unwashed feet.” In Hebrew it is not read “on unwashed,” but “with prepared” or “made” feet. For, as the Hebrews report, he had made wooden feet for himself, which he used as though they were natural ones, as the lame commonly do; and he was lame in this way.

“But the king said to Mephibosheth: Why do you speak further? What I have said is fixed. You and Siba shall divide the possessions.” In Hebrew, “the field” is read.

In this passage David was forgetful of friendship and covenant, indeed of the oath he had made with Jonathan, and he gave this cruel judgment: “You and Siba shall divide the field.” For this reason, they say, Rehoboam and Jeroboam divided his kingdom.

In the Book of Samuel, Mephibosheth is read as *Miphiboseth*. The name is interpreted as “one who contends with the Most High.” He is said to have contended with the Most High—that is, with God—because he had brought David back in peace.

Therefore, when he says to the king: “Let him take everything, since my lord the king has returned peacefully to his house,” this is not thought to have been said in a spirit of congratulations, but of insult, as though he were murmuring against God because the Lord had brought David back in peace.

“And Barzillai said to the king: There is your servant Chimham; let him go up with you.” *Chimham* is interpreted as “sighing.” For as long as he remained with his father, he was called “sighing.” But after he passed into David’s teaching, he was called not *Chamaam* but *Chama*, which means “faithful.”

### CHAPTER XX

“It happened that there was there a man of Belial, named Sheba, son of Bichri, a man of Jemini,” and so forth.

Sheba, the man of Belial who attempted to divide the Israelite people from the house of David, represented the heretics. They seek to divide the people of God, but are first condemned by the Church in their own wicked intention and die before they can accomplish what they have begun.

We shall speak more fully about him later.

“Joab therefore said to Amasa: Hail, my brother. And he took Amasa’s chin with his right hand as though to kiss him. But Amasa did not notice the sword that Joab had, and he struck him in the side and poured out his entrails upon the ground.”

What does it mean that Joab held Amasa’s chin with his right hand, while secretly moving his left hand to the sword and spilling his entrails, unless this is plainly understood? To hold the chin with the right hand is, as it were, to flatter someone with apparent kindness. But he moves his left hand to the sword who secretly strikes out of malice. Thus Joab spoke smoothly and kindly, but killed through deceit and malice.

“And a wise woman cried out from the city to Joab, saying: A saying, she said, was spoken in an ancient proverb: Let them ask Abel, and so they would prosper. Am I not the one who answers truth in Israel? And you seek to destroy a city?” and so forth.

She says: “A saying, she said, was spoken in an ancient proverb: Let them ask,” and so forth. It is as though she were saying openly: This city has been a city of counsel, and those who sought any counsel asked here. Do you seek to destroy so great a city and overthrow the mother of counsel in Israel?

Let us give a more fitting interpretation. It says: “A saying is spoken in an ancient proverb,” and so forth. In Hebrew the word “proverb” is not present. This saying is a saying of the law, in which the Lord commanded through Moses that, when the Israelites were about to enter the land of Canaan and destroy the nations, they should first offer peace. If peace were accepted by them, those who accepted peace were to become their tributaries; if they did not accept peace, then they were to be destroyed by the Israelites.

For this reason the wise woman from the city is said to have cried out: “Am I not the one who answers truth in Israel, and do you seek to destroy the city? Why do you cast down the inheritance of the Lord?” It is as though she were saying: Why do you wish to destroy this city before offering peace by asking for it, as the law commands? Why do you not also keep among us Israelites the law that was once observed toward foreigners?

“Joab was over all Israel.” The return of the Israelite people to David after the killing of Absalom signified the return of the former people to Christ after the destruction of the wicked teachers.

Sheba, son of Bichri, who by seducing the people turned them away from David, signifies the error that long held power in the synagogue of the Jews and turned the people away from hearing the truth.

*Sheba* is interpreted as “sect,” from “cutting off,” not from “following.” *Bichri* is interpreted as “my firstborn.” Thus Israel, of whom it is written, “Israel is my firstborn son, whom I brought out of Egypt” (Mic. 6), by following Sheba—that is, error—separated itself from the house of David and severed itself from the Church, rejecting its assembly.

After, through the suggestion of the wise woman and the instruction of spiritual teaching, they had cut off Sheba’s head—that is, had cast the devil out of their heart—they immediately return to David when, with believing hearts, they honor Christ, the Son of God.

### CHAPTER XXI
