Here follows the account of how a famine occurred in David’s days for three years. When he consulted the Lord, the answer was given: “It is because of Saul and his house and the bloodshed, because he killed the Gibeonites,” and so forth.

The sons of Saul who, together with Doeg the Edomite, while they were still boys, killed the priests and the Gibeonites at Nob were Armoni and Mephibosheth, whom Rizpah, daughter of Aiah, bore to him, and the five sons of Michal, daughter of Saul, whom she bore to Adriel son of Barzillai, who was of the house of Laish.

It is asked why they are called the sons of Michal, when it was not Michal but her sister Merab, the wife of Adriel son of Barzillai, who was their mother. The matter is resolved in this way: Merab naturally bore them, while Michal, David’s wife, who is also called Eglah, raised them in the place of sons and adopted them as her own sons; therefore they are called her sons.

“For the children of Israel,” as Scripture reports, “had sworn to the Gibeonites, but Saul sought to strike them in his zeal for the children of Israel and Judah,” because Joshua had once allowed those same people to live by a kind of gratuitous favor and had unjustly taken their spoil from the children of Israel.

Because of this vengeance against the Gibeonites, Abimelech the priest arose, and therefore the famine occurred.

This famine signifies the barrenness of good works among the peoples, caused by the negligence of teachers who serve earthly desires and do not take care to provide the nourishment of preaching.

The Gibeonites are killed when the practice of upright conduct and the restoration of repentance are withdrawn from the careless after a fall, through heretics or evil spirits. *Gibeon* is interpreted as “hill of mourning.” It is fitting that the Gibeonites are said to have been killed when the sluggish, after committing crimes, are deceived by the devil through a vain hope of security. They say: “Let us do evil, so that good may come to us” (Rom. 3); their condemnation is near.

But Rizpah, which is interpreted as “course” or “running,” daughter of Aiah, which is interpreted as “brother who takes up sackcloth,” spread sackcloth beneath herself upon the rock and remained until water dripped upon them from heaven. She did not allow the birds to tear them by day or the beasts by night.

This signifies the pious concern of the saints, who come to the aid of such people and apply themselves to the severity of fasting and the constancy of prayers until they obtain God’s mercy for them from heaven. In this way they restrain wicked people and evil spirits from further corrupting their life through evil suggestions.

“And there was again a battle of the Philistines against Israel,” and so forth, up to the point where it says: “There was a third battle at Gob against the Philistines, in which Adeodatus, son of the forest, a worker in patterned textiles, a Bethlehemite, struck Goliath the Gittite.” Many people therefore ask who this Adeodatus was, son of the forest, poly-militarist, and Bethlehemite.

The Hebrew scholar mentioned frequently above explains it in this way. Adeodatus, he says, is David himself. He is called *Adeodatus* because he was chosen by God for kingship. He is called “son of the forest” because he was brought out from the forest where he pastured sheep.

He is called a “worker in patterned textiles” because his mother was of the family of Bezalel; and “Bethlehemite” because he came from the city of Bethlehem. For Naomi and Ruth, in the time of abundance, from whom David descended, returned to Bethlehem.

Since the matter concerning Ruth and Boaz is well known, that place was called “house of bread.” Hence the one against whom he fought, as that same Hebrew scholar translated it, is interpreted as “one who rushes headlong.” The reason is that, just as a lion leaps and rushes headlong, so David boldly opposed Goliath in battle.

That this is the meaning understood of Adeodatus David is also demonstrated by what follows, where, after the battles have been completed, it is added:

“These four were born of Rapha in Gath, and they fell into the hand of David and his servants.”

The Jews also believe that this Rapha, the mother of giants, was Orpah, Naomi’s daughter-in-law. We too found this written in a certain volume.

Josephus agrees with the Book of Kings concerning two battles. Concerning the third battle he says that a mighty man appeared, when David sent out an army under the command of a relative of his named Ephani. But whether he called Adeodatus himself Ephani, or designated someone else by that name, is uncertain.

“The fourth battle was at Gath,” and so forth, up to the point where it says: “These four were born of Rapha in Gath, and they fell into the hand of David and his servants.”

These four battles against the Philistines signify Christ’s battle, which throughout the whole time of this life he wages unceasingly in his members against all the faithless of this age and against spiritual wickedness.

Although worldly pride, or the malice of evil spirits, rises against the Church of Christ, all the power of the adversaries is overcome when the true David—namely, Christ the King—reigns and directs the battles of his servants. Hence the Psalmist confidently says in the person of the Church: “In God we shall do valiantly,” and so forth.

### CHAPTER XXII

“David spoke to the Lord the words of this song on the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul. And he said: The Lord is my rock,” and so forth.

It is asked why only the seventeenth psalm is found written in the Book of Kings. The psalm is found alone in the Books of Kings for good reason, because it signifies that kingdom in which we shall have no adversary. This is what is written in the title of the psalm: “On the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul.”

“And he said: The Lord is my rock and my refuge.” For who is represented in David except the one who came according to the flesh from David’s seed? In his body, which is the Church, he still suffers enemies. This body is not delivered from the hand of enemies until “the last enemy, death, is destroyed” (1 Cor. 15), so that we may reach the kingdom of God.

This psalm, however, cannot apply to only one person; rather, it is subject to four divisions. First, the prophet speaks, giving thanks because divine mercy has deemed him worthy of deliverance from grave dangers. Second, the Church speaks, because through many calamities Christ gathered the Christian people from the whole world to baptism. Third, the voice of the Savior is heard, where his power and authority are described through beautiful allusions. Fourth, the words of the Church are again spoken, and the gifts granted by Christ are praised.

“And he will hear from his holy temple.” The temple of God is the Son of God.

“And the earth trembled.” The earth signifies sin.

“The foundations of the mountains.” These signify the hopes of the proud.

“Because he was angry with them.” This means that they recognized God’s anger.

“Smoke.” This signifies the compunction of penitents.

“Coals were kindled by him.” These are the hearts of human beings inflamed by the Holy Spirit.

“He inclined the heavens.” He inclined those of whom it is written, “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18). He sent his messengers and descended, assuming human form.

“Cherubim.” These signify the fullness of knowledge.

“The wings of the winds.” These signify the knowledge of the saints.

“The Lord thundered from heaven,” that is, from the apostles.

“He sent out his arrows.” The arrows are the evangelists.

“Lightning.” This signifies the miracles of the saints.

“The foundations of the earth.” These are the faith of the Church made manifest.

“He sent from heaven and took me up.” That is, the Father sent his Son and took up his Church.

“He delivered me from my most powerful enemy,” that is, from the devil.

“And he led me out into a broad place,” that is, into charity.

“He will repay me according to my righteousness.” That is, according to the innocence of faith, good works, and deeds.

“With the holy one you will be holy.” This is said of the Lord, who is holy with the holy one.

“With the chosen one you will be chosen, and with the perverse you will be made perverse.” He appears to be perverse because he does not favor them, since “he resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4).

“In my God I shall leap over a wall.” The wall is that which sins had raised between God and the human race.

“He makes my feet equal to those of a stag.” He calls spiritual men stags because of the eagerness of their swift course.

“Thorns and briers.” These are the entanglements of this world, which they leap over.

“I shall pursue my enemies and crush them, and I shall not turn back until I have consumed them.” Christ consumes the Jews and all unbelievers; likewise, the elect soul completes the destruction of its vices through the growth of virtues.

“You have given me the backs of my enemies.” This is what is written elsewhere: “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool” (Ps. 110).

“You will save me from those who contradict my people.” This is the voice of Christ, saved from the contradiction of the Jews through the power of his Father and established as head of the nations.

“The sons of strangers will resist me.” The sons of strangers are the Jews, to whom it was said: “You are of your father the devil” (John 8).

“God, who gives me vengeance.” This refers to the future judgment, when he begins to repay them what they deserve.

“You will deliver me from the wicked man.” This means that he will rescue his Church from the power of the devil.

“And showing mercy to his Christ, to David.” David signifies Christ; his seed signifies all the elect.

### CHAPTER XXIII

“These are the last words of David, son of Jesse.”

He does not call David’s final words words that are to be ended, but words that are to be perfected—not words that are to be consumed, but words that confer the fullness of perfection upon all the faithful. Therefore they signify the final confession of praise, which the saints will sing to God forever after the enemy has been overcome and the victory over death accomplished.

“The man to whom it was appointed concerning the Christ of the God of Jacob, the excellent psalmist of Israel.”

That is, the noble psalmist, a man and prophet who, in splendid and most manifest speech, prophesied concerning Christ, the Son of the God of Jacob, and concerning his incarnation and the redemption of the human race.

“The Spirit of the Lord spoke through me, and his word was upon my tongue. The God of Israel spoke to me; the strong one of Israel, the ruler of men, the just one.”

The Spirit of the Lord is the Holy Spirit, and the word of the Lord is the Son of God. The prophet was granted, through his grace, to proclaim truthfully what he had prophesied.

“For the Spirit of the God of Jacob rules in the fear of the Lord, like the light of dawn when the sun rises, shining in the morning without clouds.”

The dawn is the Church. When the sun—Christ—rises after his resurrection from the dead, the Church shines without clouds, that is, it gleams without the darkness of unbelief in miracles.

The rain signifies evangelical preaching; the grass signifies the believing people; the earth signifies the Church.

It may more suitably be understood morally. Whoever exercises dominion over his subjects in the fear of the Lord produces works of light illuminated by the sun of righteousness. Nothing dark will remain in them; watered by the rain of heavenly grace, they bear the shoots of virtues while living in the flesh and produce fruit.

“My house is not so great with God that he would make an everlasting covenant with me, firm and secure in every respect. For all my salvation and all my desire: there is nothing in it that does not germinate.”

Hence the same prophet says in the Psalms that the blessed man who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night is like a tree planted beside streams of water, which gives its fruit in its season; its leaf does not wither, and everything he does prospers (Ps. 1).

“But transgressors shall all be plucked up like thorns, which are not taken up by hand. If anyone wishes to touch them, he arms himself with iron and the shaft of a spear, and they shall be burned with fire and consumed utterly.”

This may be understood, in accordance with the preceding interpretation, specifically of the Jews and heretics. They are like thorns plucked from the Church, which is the land of the living, and handed over to eternal fire.

It may also be understood more generally of all the reprobate, according to what is said in the Gospel: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down” (Matt. 3), and so forth. Again: “The Son of Man,” he says, “will send his angels, and they will gather from his kingdom all scandals and those who practice iniquity, and they will cast them into the furnace of fire; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 13).

That person, as though touching thorns, will be armed with iron and a spear-shaft. By sharing in the sins of others because of the hardness of his heart, he is weighed down by the burden of iniquities and pierced by the darts of sins. His works, deserving of the eternal fires of Gehenna, will be reduced to nothing.

“These are the names of David’s mighty men, sitting in the chair of the most wise, chief among the three: he is like ...”

### [Scan page 197]

**ANGEL0MI**

> “the very tender woodworm, who killed eight hundred at a single charge.”

This is said of David’s most wise commander of mighty men, whose name is omitted in the Book of Kings, but who is called Jashobeam in the Book of Chronicles.

“He is like the very tender woodworm.” In this man military valor and modest civility are simultaneously portrayed: for, just as the woodworm appears tender and fragile throughout its body, and also very small, yet nevertheless eats through the strongest substance of the wood, consuming it and making it rough and rotten—for it is from wearing away wood that the woodworm receives its name—so that man appeared approachable to everyone at home, quiet and humble, but in public combat he showed himself strong and unbearable to his enemies.

But this commander, the Hebrew suspects, was David himself. We have touched upon the history; let us briefly investigate what it signifies spiritually. For he says:

> “He is like the very tender woodworm.”

David is said to have been a woodworm, which certainly applies especially to the Lord’s man; concerning his person the Psalmist sang:

> “But I am a worm and not a man” (Psalm 21).

For just as wood produces a worm from itself, so also the blessed Virgin Mary—namely, from the root of Jesse—without marital intercourse brought forth the Lord and Savior as a flower. He is said to have killed eight hundred at a single charge because, as the Evangelist declares concerning one man who bore the type of all nations, “at a single charge,” that is, by the command of his word, he expelled a legion of demons.

> “After him was Shammah, son of Age, the Hararite. And the Philistines gathered themselves together at a station,” and so forth.

Shammah means “hearing,” Age means “meditating” or “speaking,” and Ararite means “mountain-dweller.” Shammah, son of Age, represented the person of our Lord and Savior, or of his holy preachers: standing in the field of the Church, he protects its weak members from hostile powers like barley; or, certainly, in those who practice continence he defends the modesty of chastity against lust, as though with the sword of his mouth he were defending lentils.

> “And three of the chiefs among the thirty had gone down beforehand and came at harvest-time to David in the cave of Adullam.”

These three were Abishai, son of Zeruiah, and under him Hushathite, and Jonathan, son of Shammah, David’s brother.

> “These three also broke through the camp of the Philistines and drew water from the cistern of Bethlehem. And of these three Abishai also, Joab’s brother, son of Zeruiah, was chief. He was the most renowned among the three named, among those three, and was their commander. David therefore desired it and said: ‘If only someone would give me a drink from the cistern that is in Bethlehem beside the gate!’ So the three mighty men broke through the camp of the Philistines and drew water. But he was unwilling to drink it, and poured it out to the Lord.”

We have already emphasized above who these three very mighty men were. Spiritually, however, whom did David himself prefigure in this desire, if not all the holy Fathers who lived before the Law or under the Law, awaiting the coming of the Savior, but unable to reach his presence? They thirsted for that fountain in which there is forgiveness of sins—not a fountain to be sought through the dangers of others, but one that would erase the dangers brought by others.

Morally, we must think very carefully about this deed, so that one who remembers having committed unlawful acts may strive to abstain even from certain lawful ones, in order by this means to make satisfaction to his Creator. One who has committed what is forbidden ought to cut himself off even from what is permitted, and should rebuke himself in small matters who remembers that he sinned in great ones.

What I say is excessive if I do not confirm it from the testimony of sacred speech. Certainly the Law of the Old Testament forbids coveting another man’s wife; but it does not likewise forbid a king to command brave deeds of his soldiers, or to desire water. We all know that David, pierced by the sword of desire, desired and took another man’s wife, and that worthy blows followed his guilt; he corrected the evil he had committed through the lamentations of repentance.

Later, when he was sitting opposite the gate, he desired to drink water from their cistern. His chosen soldiers, bursting through the midst of the hostile ranks, brought back unharmed the water that the king desired. But the man instructed by scourges immediately rebuked himself for having desired water at the risk of his soldiers; pouring it out to the Lord, he offered it as a libation, just as it is written:

> “He poured it out to the Lord.”

The water poured out as a sacrifice to the Lord was accepted because by the rebuke of his repentance he had slain the fault of his desire. Thus he who once had not feared to desire another man’s wife afterward feared because he had desired it. Since he remembered having committed what was unlawful, he was now strict with himself and abstained even from what was lawful.

Let us therefore do penance in such a way that we perfectly mourn the things we have committed. Historically, however, by refusing to drink the water that had been brought to him and instead pouring it out to the Lord, he gave his soldiers an example of courage and steadfastness. He conquered nature, so that although he was thirsty he did not drink, and by his example taught the whole army to endure thirst.

> “Abishai also, Joab’s brother, son of Zeruiah, was chief among the three. He raised his spear against three hundred, whom he killed; he was renowned among the three, and was more illustrious than the three, and was their commander, but he did not reach the first three.”

It should be known that who those first three were—those whom Abishai, who was the most illustrious and commander among the three, is said not to have equaled—is recorded neither in this volume nor in the Book of Chronicles. Even though, with burning eagerness, we searched through the books of Josephus’s *Antiquities*, we could not find them, unless perhaps they are understood to be those whom we named above, as the Hebrews relate; or those whom Josephus says brought David water from the cistern of Bethlehem: he calls them Jashobeam son of Hachamoni, whom Eusebius elsewhere calls son of Achim; Eleazar son of Dodo, whom he says is son of Dodai; and Shammah son of Age, whom elsewhere he calls son of Heli. Sacred Scripture says nothing about them.

Therefore some—not only Hebrews but also Latins—wish the first three to be understood figuratively as three virtues of David: wisdom, humility, and courage, as is said in the preceding passage:

> “Sitting in the chair of the most wise”—behold, wisdom.
>
> “He is like the very tender woodworm”—behold, humility.
>
> “Who killed eight hundred at a single charge”—behold, courage.

No one among David’s mighty men reached these three virtues; therefore he himself is the commander of his mighty men. If anyone should discover another interpretation, let him make it known, and we shall gladly render him our service, for we have not been able to find another.

Having completed this, let us indicate what it signifies spiritually. This Abishai, who raised his hand against three hundred, plainly prefigured the Savior or his holy preachers: by the banner of the cross and the spear of preaching they convict and overthrow the enemies of the faith like three hundred men.

**LUXOVIENSIS MONACHI**

### [Scan page 198]

**ENARRATIONS ON THE BOOKS OF KINGS**

> “And Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, a very mighty man of great deeds from Kabzeel, struck down two lions of Moab. He also descended and struck down a lion in the middle of a cistern on a snowy day. He also killed an Egyptian, a man worthy of spectacle, who had a spear in his hand. When he had gone down to him with a staff, he tore the spear from the Egyptian’s hand and killed him with his own spear.”

It should be noted that the Hebrew does not have “a man of great deeds,” as it is found in a certain volume, but “a master of deeds.” Kabzeel is interpreted as “assembly of God.” He was therefore master of the assembly and legion of God, that is, of the Cherethites and Pelethites, which are interpreted as “cutters off” and “life-givers.”

He struck down two lions of Moab. Some wish these to be understood as two powerful and very mighty men in the kingdom of Moab. A certain learned man in the Scriptures, skilled in the love of wisdom, who was accustomed to instruct me in sacred letters, appears to agree with this interpretation. Chronicles calls them “two Ariels of Moab.” Hence Ariel is interpreted either as “powerful men of Moab” or as “lions,” for Ariel means “lion of God.” When Benaiah was challenged by them, he overcame and killed them.

When David attacked those same Moabites in war and made three measuring lines, two for putting to death and one for keeping alive, these powerful Moabites were ruling them.

As for the statement concerning Benaiah:

> “He descended and struck the lion in the middle of the cistern on a snowy day,”

Josephus explains more clearly how this happened. The cistern was exceedingly deep; in winter, when everything was full of snow, it too had been leveled by a great heap of snow. When a lion, unaware of the danger, fell into it and, trapped there, cried out with a great roar, people ran to see what had happened. While Benaiah was coming with others to view the spectacle, he immediately leaped into the cistern, attacked the lion amid the snow, struck it, and killed it.

Spiritually, Benaiah, whose name is interpreted as “the Lord’s builder,” expressed in himself the person of the Savior, concerning whom the Prophet had foretold that through him the Church would be built, saying:

> “The Lord, building Jerusalem” (Psalm 147).

And again:

> “The Lord will build Zion” (Psalm 101).

Seeing her being built, Paul said:

> “You are God’s building” (1 Corinthians 3).

He descended from heaven into the pit of this age. He refreshed the hot waters—that is, the minds of human beings burning with malice—with the snow and cold of unbelief, through the water of his preaching or the stream of baptism. “And he killed the lion,” that is, the devil, with the sword of his word.

For he is David’s confidant, namely, of God the Father, to whom the true divinity imparted all knowledge and understanding.

> “Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, did these things, and he was named among the three most valiant men who were among the thirty more illustrious. Yet he did not reach the three.”

This is understood to mean that he was worthy to be named among the mighty, namely Abishai, Shobachai, and Jonathan, since he could equal them in strength; they too were among the thirty.

It should be noted that certain Hebrews wish the lion whom Benaiah killed to be understood as Joab, who was killed in the middle of the cistern—that is, in the house of the Lord—where he held the horns of the altar. They suppose that the altar is signified by the cistern, since, as they say, just as a cistern’s water brings cleanliness, so the Lord’s sanctuary expiated sins.

“On a snowy day,” because he expiated sin through death, according to the Psalmist’s words:

> “You shall wash me,”

which was fulfilled “in the middle of the cistern”; and:

> “I shall be whiter than snow” (Psalm 51),

which was fulfilled in the phrase “on a snowy day.”

Concerning what follows:

> “He also killed an Egyptian, a man worthy of spectacle,”

they suppose that this Egyptian was Shimei, son of Gera, who cursed David. It should be known that this same Shimei was from Bahurim and was therefore called an Egyptian, because he imitated the deeds of that Egyptian who blasphemed God and whom Moses, at the Lord’s command, killed in the wilderness.

That man blasphemed God; this one cursed the prophet and king.

> “A man worthy of spectacle.”

He was being watched so that if he went out of Jerusalem he would be killed.

> “Having a spear in his hand,”

that is, the Law of God, which, if he had meditated upon it by remaining in Jerusalem, would not have destroyed him. Since he disregarded the king’s command by going outside Jerusalem, Benaiah descended upon him “with a staff,” that is, with the uprightness of justice; and the spear, which he no longer held uprightly, was forcibly torn from him.

We do not reject this interpretation, but leave it to the diligent reader. For the catalog of the mighty men is described in part as a figure of the saints: although they may advance in the exaltation of virtues, they can never attain to the excellence of the divine Trinity. Hence it is written there concerning Joab:

> “He did not reach the three.”

For who can equal the Lord, or who can be like one among the sons of God? Thus the interpretation we gave above concerning the first three very mighty men—namely, the three virtues of David—can indeed be true: no mighty man could reach them. Therefore the divine word figuratively brought this forth as a figure of the Savior, saying:

> “Yet he did not reach the first three.”

> “Asahel, Joab’s brother, among the thirty. Elhanan, son of his uncle, of Bethlehem. Shammah of Arari. Elika of Harod. Helez of Phalti. Hira, son of Acces, of Tekoa. Abiezer of Anathoth. Mobonnai of Hushath. Selmon the Ahohite. Macharai the Netophathite. Heleb, son of Baana, likewise a Netophathite. Itai, son of Ribai, of Gibeah of the sons of Benjamin. Benaiah the Pharathonite. Hedai from the torrent of Gaash. Abialbon the Arbathite. Azmaveth of Berhomi. Elihaba of Saalbon. Pihi Jasen. Jonathan. Shammah of Herod. Ahiam, son of Saar the Ararite. Eliphalet, son of Ahasbai. The sons of Maachath. Eliaam, son of Achitophel the Gilonite. Hesrai of Carmel. Pharai of Arbi. Igaal, son of Nathan of Soba. Bonni the Gadite. Selec the Ammonite. Naharai the Berothite, armor-bearer of Joab, son of Sarviah. Hira the Jethrite,” and so forth, until it says, “all thirty-seven.”

It should be noted that, together with these thirty, seven stronger men, named in this reckoning, are also included: David, who was called Adeodatus; Abishai; Shobachai; Jonathan; Eleazar; Shammah; and Benaiah—behold, seven.

These are the thirty: Asahel, Elcanan, Shammah of Arari, Elika, Helez, Hira, Abiezer, Mobonnai, Selmon, Macharai, Heleb, Itai, Benaiah the Pharathonite, Hebai, Abialbon, Azmaveth, Elihaba, Shammah of Rorodi, Aiam, Eliphelech, Etiam, Hesrai, Pharai, Igaal, Konni, Selech, Naharat, Hira, Gareb, and Uriah the Hittite.

Uriah the Hittite is therefore placed last because of what follows afterward.

> “And the anger of the Lord continued to be kindled against Israel.”

Vengeance had already been inflicted upon David and his house. But among the people who had not resisted David when Uriah was destroyed, divine vengeance had not yet been exacted. He is therefore placed last so that the vengeance for his great sin might be shown.

In this number, moreover, the perfection of the saints is signified. The number ten belongs to the Decalogue of the Law; the number three to faith in the holy Trinity; and the number seven to the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. Three times ten makes thirty.

### Chapter 24

> “And again the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and he moved David against them, saying: ‘Go, number Israel and Judah.’ And the king said to Joab, the commander of his army: ‘Go through all the tribes of Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, and number the people,’” and so forth.

Struck by the pride of arrogance and inflated by a sudden swelling of exaltation, David was compelled by a hidden judgment of God, against the Lord’s will, to number the same people, because of the guilt of the people—especially because he had not rebuked them in Uriah’s betrayal. His own guilt had been punished, but the people’s sin, as has been said, remained unpunished.

> “So Joab gave the number of the census of the people to the king; and there were found in Israel eight hundred thousand valiant men who could draw the sword, and in Judah five hundred thousand fighting men.”

It should be noted that in Chronicles the number is read as one million one hundred thousand from Israel, and from Judah four hundred and seventy thousand.

### [Scan page 200]

**ENARRATIONS ON THE BOOKS OF KINGS—BOOK II**

It should be noted, however, that in Chronicles there are read one million one hundred thousand from Israel, and four hundred and seventy thousand from Judah; Joab counted these, but David did not wish to know their total. Moreover, in the Book of Exodus the Lord commanded Moses:

> “When you take the census of the sons of Israel according to their number, each shall give the Lord a ransom for his life, and there shall be no plague among them when they are counted” (Exodus 30).

Everyone who passes into the census shall give half a shekel according to the measure of the sanctuary. The shekel contains twenty obols. Half a shekel shall be offered to the Lord. The rich shall not add to the half-shekel, and the poor shall not diminish it. You shall receive the money that has been offered by the children of Israel and devote it to the service of the tabernacle of testimony, so that it may be a memorial of them before the Lord and may make atonement for their souls.

David forgot to do this; therefore he offended God, and for this reason the plague came upon Israel.

> “And when Gad came to David, he announced it to him, saying: ‘Either seven years of famine will come to you in your land,’” and so forth.

This may be understood mystically as seven years of famine, if anyone wishes. For seven years unbelieving Jews have suffered famine, because the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit does not feed them with the bread of God’s word. For three months they flee before their enemies pursuing them, because they have not been renewed in the name of the holy Trinity through the washing of regeneration; unable to resist their enemies—that is, unclean spirits—they turn their backs.

Finally, the angel strikes them, as though scourging them for three days, because, denying the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, through faith in whom they could have lived, they die in their unbelief.

> “And God sent a pestilence upon Israel from morning until the appointed time; and seventy thousand men of the people died, from Dan to Beersheba.”

Josephus reports at length how this happened, saying:

When the prophets declared to David that God was angry with him, he began to supplicate and beg that God be merciful and grant pardon for his sin. Then God sent the prophet Gad to him, bearing three conditions of punishment, so that David might choose whichever he preferred: whether he wished famine to arise in the land for seven years; or to be conquered by his enemies in battle for three months; or for disease and sickness to fall upon the Hebrews for three days.

Since he was anxious and greatly troubled in mind, and the prophet said that the matter was pressing in every way and urgently demanded an answer so that he could report to God which condition David had chosen, the king reasoned that if he chose famine, it would seem that he was doing this against others: since he himself possessed much grain, he would not suffer want, while the others would be in distress. Likewise, if he chose three months of flight before his enemies, he himself, having many very brave men and guards, would fear nothing, while his army would be subjected to danger. Among these alternatives, therefore, he chose the common suffering of both rulers and subjects, in which fear would be equal for all, saying:

> “It is better for me to fall into the hands of God than into the hands of enemies.”

Hearing this, the prophet reported it to God, who sent disease and death upon the army of the Hebrews. For they died—as the same historian says—not in one way, so that the sickness could easily be recognized: they perished readily, one falling upon another. Some died upon those whom they were burying. Thus they died from various diseases, as Josephus relates.

When the deadly sickness began to strike them from the morning hour until the hour of the midday meal, seventy thousand were consumed.

Here we can say nothing other than what Pope Gregory, an outstanding interpreter, brought forth morally concerning this deed of David. He says:

The actions of rulers are arranged according to the qualities of their subjects, so that often, because of a bad flock, even the life of a genuinely good shepherd may go astray.

David is praised with God as his witness; that David, the prophet conscious of heavenly mysteries, sinned by numbering the people after being lifted up by the pride of sudden exaltation. Yet, while David sinned, the people received God’s vengeance.

Why? Because, according to the merit of the peoples, the hearts of rulers are arranged. The just Judge corrected the ruler’s fault through the punishment inflicted upon those because of whom he had sinned. But because David was not free from guilt through his own will, he was not free from the vengeance of guilt: he also received the punishment.

For the anger that struck their bodies also overthrew the ruler of the people by the inward grief of his heart. It is certain that the merits of rulers and peoples are joined to one another, so that often through the guilt of shepherds the life of the people becomes worse, and often through the merit of the people the life of shepherds is changed.

But since subjects have their own judge, it is a matter of great caution for them not rashly to judge the lives of their rulers. For the Lord did not, by another, overturn the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those selling doves, but did so himself (Luke 19), plainly signifying that he judges the lives of the people through their teachers, but examines the deeds of teachers himself.

Even the faults of subjects which are now either overlooked by their teachers or cannot be judged are undoubtedly reserved for his judgment.

Therefore, while the matter is conducted with the faith preserved, there is merit in virtue if whatever belongs to one’s superior is patiently endured. Only it should be humbly suggested, if perhaps what is displeasing may be corrected. But one must take the greatest care that an unregulated defense of justice does not pass into pride. For while uprightness is loved without caution, the humility that teaches uprightness itself is lost, lest someone despise the one set over him because he happens to find fault with him in some action.

Against this swelling of the subjects’ pride, the mind is disciplined for the preservation of humility if its own weakness is constantly considered. We neglect to examine our own powers truthfully, and because we believe ourselves stronger, we strictly judge those placed over us.

The less we recognize ourselves, the more we see those whom we attempt to rebuke. These are evils often committed by subjects against superiors and often by superiors against subjects: those who rule scarcely consider all their subjects wise, while those who are subject judge the actions of their rulers and, if they themselves happened to hold authority, think they would act better.

Hence rulers often see less prudently what ought to be done, because the mist of exaltation itself darkens their eyes. And sometimes the subject, once he has become a superior, does what he had previously criticized as a subject; and because he perpetrates the things he had judged, he is at least ashamed of what he once condemned.

Therefore, just as superiors must take care that the higher position of singular wisdom does not inflate their hearts, so subjects must take care that the deeds of their rulers do not displease them. If the life of a teacher is rightly reproached, subjects ought nevertheless to honor the teacher even when they are displeased.

But one must also observe carefully that you do not despise venerating someone whom you disdain to imitate. A subtle path of uprightness and humility must be maintained, so that the reprehensible deeds of teachers may displease subjects without the mind of the subjects departing from the reverence owed to the teaching office.

> “Now the angel of the Lord was beside the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite. And David said to the Lord, when he saw the angel striking the people: ‘Behold, I have sinned; I have acted wickedly. These, who are like sheep, what have they done? Let your hand, I beg you, be turned against me,’” and so forth.

In Chronicles it is written:

> “The angel of the Lord was standing beside the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. David lifted up his eyes and saw the angel of the Lord standing between heaven and earth, with a drawn sword in his hand, turned against Jerusalem,” and so forth (1 Chronicles 21).

The threshing floor of Araunah, or the threshing floor of Ornan, is Jerusalem itself.

> “Then Gad came to David and said to him: ‘Go up and establish an altar to the Lord on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.’ And David went up according to the word of Gad, as the Lord had commanded him. When Araunah looked out, he saw the king and his servants crossing over toward him; he went out and bowed before the king with his face to the ground. And Araunah said: ‘Why has my lord the king come to his servant?’ David said to him: ‘To buy the threshing floor from you and to build an altar to the Lord, so that the slaughter which is raging among the people may cease.’ And Araunah said to David,” and so forth.

Araunah is interpreted as “ark,” while Ornan in Latin sounds like *lumen nobis*, “light for us.” Properly, therefore, when he wished to appease God for the offense through which he had sinned, he was commanded to build an altar in the ark of Araunah or Ornan, so that everyone might understand from this that divinity cannot otherwise be appeased by a human being except when, in the ark of his heart, through the light of right faith and true love, he establishes an altar of devoted humility, on which he offers God the acceptable sacrifice of faithful confession and praise.

### [Scan page 201]

**ANGELOMI**

This is rightly made clear by the same prophet in the Psalms, where he speaks in the person of the Lord:

> “The sacrifice of praise will honor me” (Psalm 50).

And again:

> “The sacrifice for God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Psalm 51).

> “So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver.”

In Chronicles it is read as follows:

> “Therefore David gave Ornan six hundred shekels of gold of the finest weight for the place.”

It must therefore be understood that he bought the oxen for fifty shekels of silver, but the threshing floor for six hundred gold pieces.

> “And David built there an altar to the Lord, and offered holocausts and peace offerings. And the Lord was reconciled to the land, and the plague was restrained from Israel.”

The Book of Chronicles likewise relates:

> “The tabernacle of the Lord which Moses had made in the wilderness, and the altar of holocausts, were at that time on the high place at Gibeon, and David could not go to the altar to beseech the Lord, for he had been terrified by the sight of the sword of the angel of the Lord. And David said: ‘This is the house of the Lord God, and this is the altar for the holocaust of Israel.’”

And he commanded that all the proselytes from the land of Israel be gathered, and appointed them as stonecutters to cut and polish stones, so that the house of the Lord might be built.

According to the Hebrews, it was at that place that Abraham had once offered his son Isaac. When he was already prepared to kill his son and present him as a holocaust, a ram suddenly appeared and stood beside the altar; Abraham sacrificed it instead of his son.

The threshing floor of Araunah, where David built the altar, can also be understood in a higher sense. What does the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite signify except the Church gathered from the Gentiles? After the true David, that is, our Savior, erected the altar of faith in this Church, the death of unbelief, which had been raging among God’s people, immediately ceased.

David bought this threshing floor for fifty shekels of silver, because the Lord Jesus Christ also bought his Church with his precious blood and, through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, purified it from all its sins and sanctified it as an everlasting dwelling for himself.

## Book III

### Preface

Having completed the two little books of the volume of the Kings, with the divine clemency assisting our unworthiness, we have drawn two small portions, so to speak, from the treasuries of the rich—that is, from the holy teachers—and, as we were able, have placed them in the treasury of the Lord. We did this lest we should seem ungrateful to the Lord because of the poverty of our own talent, and lest the very talent entrusted to us in frugality should be found hidden, buried in the ground, and we should be punished with the harshest sentence of condemnation.

Here we have crossed a very wide sea, with the help of the Almighty, who commands the winds not to harm the ship. Now, although fearful, we shall attempt to undertake the third book. In it we shall especially need the breath of the divine Spirit, lest our vessel finally be broken upon the rocks, or, striking the sandbank, remain submerged in the surging depths.

But if he himself breathes upon us and graciously gives his assistance, may it joyfully reach the harbor of peace, so that the Lord’s commerce may in some way remain unharmed, and from so great a depth of the book and treasury of the divine storehouse we may at least be able to bring gifts to the Lord with the Magi: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.

For if we need the help of the Holy Spirit in all things, we now need divine assistance especially in this sacred book, because it appears to be hidden beneath many obscurities in its allegorical meanings, particularly in the mysteries of the temple buildings and of the prophets. With his help—he who gave Solomon the greatest wisdom—may we be able to complete the work we have begun with discernment.

Therefore, trusting now in his aid, let us turn our attention to describing it.

**LUXOVIENSIS MONACHI**

### Book III, Chapter 1

> “King David was old, advanced in years,” and so forth.

David’s old age prefigured the Old Testament of the human race. In it, because faith had failed as though in David, love of God had grown cold. There is no doubt that his garments, with which he was covered but could not be warmed, typified the Jewish people. Before the Savior’s coming, through knowledge of the Law, they clung to the Lord like garments.

But because that people, as the Apostle says, “had a spirit of slavery and not of freedom” (2 Corinthians 3), it did not possess the warmth of divine love.

The beautiful virgin who was sought throughout all the borders of Israel and brought to him by David’s servants, who slept in his bosom, warmed him, and remained a virgin, plainly bore the figure of the holy Church. She came to Christ from all the nations through the apostles, and she burned with such ardor of faith in his love that for the love of the Son she willingly exposed herself to various dangers and, at last, did not refuse to die for his name. We shall speak more fully about her below.

> “Now Adonijah, son of Haggith, exalted himself, saying: ‘I will reign,’” and so forth.

This Adonijah, who was lifted up by pride and wished to reign gratuitously, and who was killed by Solomon, represented the pride of the Jews. Because they wished to possess an earthly kingdom rather than the kingdom of Solomon—that is, Christ—they lost the kingdom and forfeited their life.

We foretold this concerning him in passing, but we shall investigate it more fully in what follows.

> “Now the king was very old, and Abishag the Shunammite ministered to him.”

The question therefore arises what, in this matter,
## Exposition of the Books of Kings — Book III

what this may signify: that David, a warlike man who had lived seventy years, could not be warmed because his old age had grown cold. Therefore this beautiful girl is sought, who would sleep with the king, warm his aged body, and minister to the king. For if we follow the literal sense, it seems almost a farcical invention: an old man, cold despite being wrapped in clothing, does not grow warm except through the embrace of a young woman. Bathsheba was still alive, as was Abigail, along with his other wives and concubines, all of whom Scripture seems to reject as cold; yet this aged man is warmed by the embrace of one young girl alone. Abraham was much older than David, yet while Sarah lived he sought no other wife. Isaac lived twice as many years as David, and, even when Rebecca was old, never grew cold toward her. I say nothing of the men who lived before the Flood, who, after five hundred years—not merely with aged limbs but with joints already almost decayed—did not seek the embraces of girls. Certainly Moses, leader of the people of Israel, was one hundred and twenty years old and did not change Zipporah.

Who, then, is this Shunammite, both wife and virgin, so ardent that she warmed the cold, and so holy that she did not provoke the warm man to lust? Surely she is wisdom, which, as blessed Jerome says, usually burns in the old, although, as we indicated above, she also bore the person of the holy Church. Let the most wise Solomon explain her: let him recount the delights of his father and the embraces of the peaceful warrior:

> “Possess wisdom; possess understanding. Do not forget her, and do not turn away from her. Do not forsake her, and she will take hold of you; love her, and she will preserve you. The beginning of wisdom is: possess wisdom; and in all your possessions acquire understanding” (Prov. iv).

And so forth.

This wisdom, although the limbs grow cold, is nevertheless embraced by the old man with ardent love and the highest devotion of charity, and she also ministers spiritual delights. Almost all the virtues of the body are diminished in old age; as wisdom alone increases, the rest decline: fasts, vigils, almsgiving, journeys here and there, receiving pilgrims, defending the poor, earnestness in prayer, perseverance, visiting the sick, and the labor of the hands by which alms may be provided. To avoid extending the discourse, all the deeds performed through the body become lesser in an aged body. Wisdom alone—not only in the young but also in the old, who meditate on the law of the Lord day and night—remains, and reaps the sweetest fruits of study.

Hence Abishag is rightly interpreted as “the joy of my father,” or “the roar of my father.” In the present passage this signifies a virtue that is greater and overflowing in the old: abundant wisdom. It becomes almost a roar, like the sound of the sea’s waves; or, so to speak, a noise coming from the deep is heard. This shows that, in the old, the thunder of divine speech dwells in abundance, beyond the power of human expression. *Sunamitis*, however, in our language sounds like “red” or “scarlet,” signifying that she is skilled in wisdom and burns with divine reading. Although this may indicate the sacrament of the Lord’s blood, it also shows the ardor of wisdom.

Hence our Lord says in the Gospel:

> “I have come,” he says, “to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke xii).

He kindled the hearts of the disciples and compelled them to say:

> “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke xxiv).

We ought, therefore, to embrace and love this girl, who signifies the greater wisdom of the old—not childish declamations, nor the little flowers of dialectical sophists, nor the seductive charms of words, nor other things of this kind drawn from human wisdom and the inventions of poets; nor the cares of this age or the honors of this world. Rather, wisdom, like Abishag with David, should rest in our bosom and never grow old. For she is undefiled in perpetual virginity and, like Mary, is incorruptible: although she gives birth every day and is always in labor, she remains uncorrupted.

If Cato, the most eloquent of the Roman race, as one of the teachers has reported, when he was already a hundred years old and an old man, did not blush to learn Greek letters or despair of learning them; and if, as they say, Homer reports that from the tongue of Nestor, already very old and almost decrepit, “speech flowed sweeter than honey”; and if a certain wise Greek, when he had completed one hundred and seven years and saw that he was about to die, is said to have declared that he grieved to leave life just when he had begun to become wise; and if Plato died while writing in his eightieth year; and if Socrates completed seventy-nine years in the labor of teaching and writing—then, when the vigor of bodily youth is at its greatest, amid the battles of the body and the incentives to vice, we ought to learn wisdom, so that, even when our limbs grow cold in old age, she may rest in the bosom of our mind, warm us, and sleep with us—or rather, minister to us the nourishment of spiritual understanding.

This woman may also bear the figure of the contemplative life, which all the perfect embrace with incredible love and in whose devotion they burn.

> “Adonijah, son of Haggith, exalted himself, saying, ‘I shall reign.’ He made for himself chariots and horsemen and fifty men to run before him. His father never rebuked him, saying, ‘Why have you done this?’”

And so forth.

What does it signify that Adonijah, David’s elder son, wished to succeed his father in the kingdom through the arrogance of pride and not through the virtue of discipline? What else does it signify except that the Jewish people, which seems to be the elder son because it received the law first, despised the gentile people, who were called later through God’s grace, and thought that it alone would reign with the Lord? Hence the name Adonijah—interpreted as “dominating lord”—aptly expressed the type: he thought that he alone would dominate with the Lord. But the people of the Church are appointed to the kingdom with the true Solomon, that is, with our Peaceful One, whose body he is, by divine ordinance. Because of his faithlessness, the elder son—that is, the earlier people—was deservedly cast down.

This Adonijah, with Bathsheba intervening—for Bathsheba is interpreted as “daughter of satiety”—desired to violate Abishag the Shunammite. For the Jewish people, through its observance of the ceremonies of the law, because it was sated and completely full, wished to violate the true wisdom of spiritual understanding joined to our David, but did not obtain the companionship of the one whose immaculate throne it sought to violate.

What David commanded his son Solomon concerning the just recompense of those who had helped him or unjustly harmed him, although David himself had endured them with the greatest patience while reigning—what could this signify more clearly than the future retribution of the coming judgment, in which the wicked will receive everlasting punishment as their reward, while the just will receive eternal blessedness? Even in the present time God’s patience often permits the good to be afflicted and distressed, while, conversely, he allows the reprobate to enjoy temporal pleasures and earthly prosperity. Yet to both groups the Judge of the living and the dead will certainly restore their due reward in the future, when he will say to those who are at his right hand:

> “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. xxv).

But to those who will be at his left he will say:

> “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels”; and “they will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (ibid.).

> “Bathsheba bowed and worshiped the king.”

Bathsheba, whose name is rendered in Latin as “daughter of the oath,” represented here the image of the ancient Church, which had been established with the holy fathers under the law, and from whose stock the true Solomon—that is, our Peaceful One—was promised to be born.

> “And they announced to the king, saying, ‘Nathan the prophet is here.’”

Nathan, whose name is interpreted as “gift,” clearly bore the figure of the ancient prophecy.

> “And King David said, ‘Call Zadok the priest to me.’”

Zadok is interpreted as “just,” bearing in himself the figure of our Lord and Savior, who is the

> “true priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. cix).

> “And put my son Solomon upon my mule.”

Some have said that David’s mule signifies the Church; others have said that it signifies the Synagogue because of its barrenness.

## Chapter II

> “David said to Solomon: ‘You also know what Joab son of Zeruiah did to me, what he did to the two commanders, Abner son of Ner and Amasa son of Jether,’” and so forth.

David, who commanded Joab to kill Shimei, bore the figure of the ancient prophecy, which judged and commanded what ought in the future to happen to the enemies of Christ and of his saints—namely, the scribes and Pharisees, as well as heretics. This is represented by the fact that David commanded concerning Joab and Shimei, while Solomon fulfilled the command.

> “Solomon sat upon the throne of Israel.”

Solomon, who succeeded his father David, unquestionably bore the figure of Christ: first, in that he built a temple, just as Christ built the Church; and also in that he administered the kingdom in peace and possessed peace according to his name. Thus the Lord too is called the King of Peace, and Solomon’s name most truly corresponds to him through whom, having received remission of sins, we are reconciled to God from being enemies:

> “When we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son” (Eph. ii).

He himself is the Peaceful One who made the two one, breaking down in his flesh the middle wall of partition, abolishing the law of commandments expressed in decrees, so that he might create the two in himself as one new man, making peace for those who were far away and peace for those who were near. In the Gospel he himself says:

> “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John xiv).

By these and many other testimonies the Lord Jesus is shown to be the Peaceful One. There is no doubt that in wisdom, riches, and glory also he bore the figure of the Lord Savior.

> “Adonijah said to Bathsheba: ‘I ask you to say to King Solomon that he should give me Abishag the Shunammite as my wife.’”

When Adonijah, in the type of the Jews, wished to violate the Church of Christ, which is a virgin incorrupt, he met by a just judgment the death he deserved.

> “Bathsheba therefore went to King Solomon to speak for Adonijah.”

Bathsheba, who wished to intervene with Solomon on behalf of Adonijah, yet accomplished nothing, undoubtedly presented here the figure of the law, which the Jews think is their helper before God.

> “The king also said to Abiathar the priest: ‘Go to your field at Anathoth.’”

Abiathar, who was expelled from the priesthood but was not killed, signifies the Jewish people. Although their priesthood has been taken away, they have not been completely destroyed, because some from among them will believe.

> “Joab therefore fled to the tabernacle of the Lord and grasped the horns of the altar. It was reported to King Solomon that Joab had fled to the tabernacle of the Lord and was beside the altar. Solomon sent Benaiah son of Jehoiada, saying: ‘Go, kill him,’” and so forth.

Joab, who fled to the altar and was killed there at Solomon’s command, signifies the scribes and Pharisees, or the heretical teachers of perverse doctrine. Because they kill their neighbors—that is, ecclesiastical men—by ambush, just as Joab is said to have done to Abner and Amasa, they will be expelled from the altar of faith and punished by perpetual death.

> “But for David, his offspring, his house, and his throne, let there be peace forever from the Lord.”

That is: when the Jews have been abolished, the heretics rooted out, and all the enemies of Christ destroyed, the throne of David—that is, the Church—will remain forever, enjoying eternal peace.

> “Solomon said to Shimei: ‘Did I not testify to you by the Lord and forewarn you that on whatever day you go out and depart from this place, know that you will certainly die?’”

We are commanded by the true Solomon, just as Shimei was commanded by King Solomon, to dwell in Jerusalem and never leave it. If our enemy flees from us—the one who had previously been subjected to us—and goes to the Philistines, we must not leave the walls of our city or follow the tracks of fugitives, lest, while wishing to save those who flee, we ourselves perish. Rather, let us leave

[scan page 204]

the dead to bury their dead (Matt. viii), and, while it is permitted, let us tear out and cut away from ourselves the eye, hand, or foot that causes scandal (Mark ix).

## Chapter III

> “Solomon took Pharaoh king of Egypt’s daughter.”

There is no doubt that the daughter of Pharaoh whom Solomon took in marriage prefigured the Church from the gentiles.

> “The Lord appeared to Solomon in a dream by night, saying, ‘Ask what you wish me to give you.’ And Solomon said: ‘You have shown great mercy to your servant David my father,’” and so forth.

The grace of God seeks the free choice of the human being.

> “And the Lord said to Solomon: ‘Because you asked for this, and did not ask for long life, nor riches, nor the lives of your enemies, but asked for wisdom to discern judgment’...”

Whoever wishes his prayer not to be frustrated before God should ask him for what Solomon sought—that is, wisdom, knowledge, and understanding. To seek riches and temporal glory, the lives of one’s enemies, or the greatest possible number of days in the present life belongs to the reprobate, not to the elect.

> “But if you walk in my ways and keep my commandments, I will lengthen your days.”

Here it is especially clear that even the reprobate may possess wisdom and riches or temporal glory in the present life; but no one can attain long days—that is, eternal blessedness—without observing God’s commandments.

> “Then two women who were prostitutes came to King Solomon and stood before him. One of them said: ‘I beg you, my lord, I and this woman dwell in one house,’” and so forth.

There is no doubt that the two women between whom Solomon first exercised his judgment—one of whom burned with love, while the other was overcome by deceit—prefigured the Church and heretical depravity. Between them the Lord Jesus Christ, by the breath of his mouth, restores to each what is due while determining what is just.

It is well said that through this woman the impiety of the heretics, or of the Synagogue, is also generated: by wickedly nourishing their own, they destroy them, while by enticing and persuading outsiders they lead them to ruin. But since vices often arise after virtues, so that human hearts may be tested by temptation, lest the mind, standing at the summit of virtues like Solomon in his kingdom, glory in itself, this too is permitted by God, who deigns to illuminate it by the brightness of his light. Thus, by the approach of grace, a person is raised to receive gifts of steadfastness; by its withdrawal, what he is of himself is tested, so that he may humbly recognize his weakness.

This is demonstrated in Solomon himself. He received wisdom from God, yet after receiving that same wisdom he was tested by the dispute of the two prostitutes. For often, when the light of intimate generosity illuminates our minds with the virtues granted to us, slippery thoughts immediately disturb them, so that the mind which exults because it has been raised up by an immense gift may discover through temptation what it is.

For this reason we have decided to unfold more fully what these two prostitutes signify—having touched on them briefly according to what we have found in the statements of the teachers. The sacred historical narrative says:

> “Then two women who were prostitutes came to King Solomon and stood before him,” and so forth.

In Solomon’s judgment, therefore, he was a figure of Christ. The wicked woman—namely, the people of the Synagogue or of the heretics—desired the true mother’s son, that is, the Church’s son. She desired him not in order to preserve him but truly in order to kill him. But just as, when Solomon’s sword divided the child, the true child was recognized by the lament of his own mother, so also, when the Spirit of Jesus Christ teaches, those who have been deceived and captured by their mother’s error—by the error of heretics—sometimes deserve, by groaning for themselves, to recognize the Church as their mother.

Thus it appears sufficiently and appropriately that this woman signified the impiety of the Synagogue or of the heretics: she kills her own by wickedly nourishing them and persuades outsiders by enticing them until she destroys them.

In another way, as far as the simple historical sense is concerned, it is clear that a boy of twelve years, contrary to the measure of his age, judged from the deepest feeling of human nature. Hence all Israel rightly marveled at him and feared him, because manifest things did not escape him and he detected hidden matters so wisely.

As for the typological meaning, the Apostle says:

> “All these things happened to them in a figure. They were written for us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. x).

Some of the Greeks think that the passage should be understood of the Synagogue and the Church, and that everything should be referred to the time when, after the cross and resurrection, the true Solomon—that is, the Peaceful One—began to reign both in Israel and among the gentile peoples.

There is no doubt that the Synagogue and the Church are called adulterous women and prostitutes in Scripture, although at first sight this seems blasphemous. But if we turn to the prophets—especially Hosea (ch. i), who took a promiscuous woman as his wife and fathered promiscuous children, and afterward an adulterous woman; and Ezekiel (ch. xvi), who rebuked Jerusalem as a prostitute because she had followed her lovers, spread her feet to every passerby, and built a brothel in a prominent place—we understand the matter more clearly.

We perceive that Christ came for this reason: to endow prostitutes with marriage and to make the two flocks one sheepfold. By destroying the middle wall, he gathered into the same enclosures the sheep that had previously been diseased. These are the staffs that are joined together in Ezekiel, and concerning whom the Lord speaks through Zechariah:

> “I took for myself two staffs; I called one Beauty and the other I called Cord, and I shepherded the flock” (Zech. xi).

That prostitute in the Gospel who washed Jesus’ feet with her tears, wiped them with her hair, and to whom all sins were forgiven plainly signifies the Church gathered from the gentiles.

For this reason I have repeated the point at the outset, lest anyone should think it incongruous that the women should be called prostitutes, one of whom was granted possession of the child by Solomon’s judgment.

Let the prudent listener ask how a prostitute can signify the Church, which has neither spot nor wrinkle. We do not say that the Church remained a prostitute, but that she had been one. The Savior is also recorded as having entered the house of Simon the leper—not because Simon was a leper at the time when he had the Savior as his guest, but because he had previously been a leper. Matthew too is called a publican in the list of the apostles, not because he remained a publican after attaining apostolic dignity, but because he had previously been a publican:

> “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. vi).

At the same time, consider what the Church says against the Synagogue that slanders her:

> “I and this woman lived in one house.”

After the resurrection of the Lord and Savior, one people was gathered from both peoples. How elegantly the Church says:

> “I gave birth in her, in the chamber.”

For the Church from the gentiles, which previously did not possess the law and the prophets, gave birth in the house of the Synagogue. She did not leave the chamber but entered it. Hence it is said in the Song of Songs:

> “The king brought me into his chamber” (Song of Songs iii).

And again:

> “Taking you without despising you, I will bring you into the house of my mother and into her chamber who conceived me” (Song of Songs viii).

> “On the third day after I had given birth, this woman also gave birth.”

If you consider Pilate washing his hands and saying:

> “I am innocent of the blood of this just man” (Matt. xxvii),

and the centurion confessing before the cross:

> “Truly this was the Son of God” (Matt. xxvii);

and if you consider those who, before the Passion, desired to see the Lord through Philip, you will not doubt that the Church gave birth first and that afterward the Jewish people was born, for whom the Lord prayed:

> “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”

On a single day three thousand believed, and later another five thousand:

> “The multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul” (Acts iv).

> “We were together, and no one else was in the house with us except the two of us.”

There were no blaspheming Jews, nor gentiles serving idols.

> “For the son of this woman died during the night.”

While she follows the observance of the law and joins the grace of the Gospel to the yoke of Mosaic teaching, she is covered by the error of darkness.

> “Her mother lay upon him as he slept.”

She could not say:

> “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song of Songs v).

At midnight she arose, took the son from the bosom of the Church as she slept, and placed him in her own bosom. Read the entire Epistle of the Apostle to the Galatians, and you will observe how the Synagogue hastens to make the Church’s children its own. The Apostle says:

> “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. iv).

> “She took him while he was alive.”

She did not take him to possess him but to kill him. She did this not out of love for the child but out of jealous hatred, and placed her own dead child—through the ceremonies of the law—in the bosom of the Church.

It would take too long to go through each point: how, through the apostle Paul and other ecclesiastical men, the Church understood that the child held under the law was not hers, and recognized in the light the one whom she had not seen in the darkness. Hence, in the presence of the king, a quarrel arose, with one woman saying:

> “Your son is dead, but my son is alive.”

The other replied:

> “You are lying; my son is alive, and your son is dead.”

In this way they contended before the king. Then King Solomon—who is plainly understood as the Savior according to Psalm lxxi, whose title is addressed to Solomon, where there is no doubt that everything said applies not to the dead Solomon but to the majesty of Christ—pretends ignorance and, according to the dispensation of the flesh, feigns human emotions.

So too in another passage he says:

> “Where have you laid Lazarus?”

And to the woman with the flow of blood:

> “Who touched me?”

He asks for the sword about which he had said:

> “Do not think that I have come to bring peace upon the earth. I have not come to bring peace but a sword” (Matt. x).

For he came to divide a man against his father, a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man’s enemies would be those of his own household. The Lord tests nature against nature and wishes, according to the will of both women, to divide the living child between the law and grace—not because he approves this division, but in order to expose it and to show that the living child can be freed only through baptism.

She willingly wished the child to be divided, not in order to possess him but in order to kill him. The Church, knowing that he is hers, willingly concedes him to her rival, provided that he at least remains alive with the adversary, lest, divided between law and the grace of the Savior, he be struck by the sword.

Hence the Apostle also says:

> “Behold, I, Paul, say to you that if you observe the law, Christ will be of no benefit to you” (Gal. v).

In another way: what is signified in this judgment by the names of the nursing mothers except the order of teachers? And what is signified by their sons except the persons of the disciples? Teachers who are awake in knowledge but asleep in life, while nourishing their hearers through the vigils of preaching, kill them through the sleep of temporal negligence when they fail to do what they say, and through negligence crush those whom they seemed to feed with the milk of words.

Hence, because they themselves often live reprehensibly and cannot have disciples whose lives are praiseworthy, they try to draw others’ disciples to themselves. By showing that they have good followers, they seek to excuse before human judgment the evil things they do, and, as it were, to cover their deadly negligence with the life of their subordinates. Thus the woman who had killed her own son sought another’s.

But Solomon’s sword found the true mother, for the final judgment of the strict Judge reveals whose fruit will live and whose will perish. There too we must carefully observe that the living son is first commanded to be divided, so that afterward he may be restored to his sole mother. In this life the disciple’s life is permitted, as it were, to be divided, since one person may sometimes obtain merit before God and another praise before human beings.

But the false mother does not fear killing the one whom she did not beget, because

[scan page 206]

arrogant teachers, ignorant of charity, if they cannot obtain the fullest reputation for praise through others’ disciples, cruelly persecute their lives. Inflamed by the torches of envy, they do not want others to live in what they see themselves unable to possess. Hence the perverse woman also cries:

> “Let him be neither mine nor hers.”

As we have said, those whom they do not see obeying them, for the sake of temporal glory, they begrudge others their living according to the truth.

But the true mother strives that her son may at least live with a stranger. For faithful teachers permit some of their disciples to gain the praise of teaching, provided that those same disciples do not lose the integrity of their lives. By these compassionate feelings this same woman is recognized altogether as the true mother, because her teaching is approved in the judgment of charity, and she alone deserves to receive the whole because she appeared to surrender the whole.

For faithful superiors do not merely refrain from begrudging others the praise arising from their good disciples; they also pray that others may benefit from their progress. They themselves receive their children whole and alive when, in the final judgment, they obtain the joys of a perfect recompense from their lives.

## Chapter IV

After the princes of Solomon have been enumerated—those who had been assigned various offices in his kingdom or presided over different provinces—the Scripture continues:

> “Solomon was in authority over all the kingdoms from the River to the land of the Philistines, as far as the boundary of Egypt; they brought him tribute and served him all the days of his life.”

Who is better signified here than our Peaceful One, whom that same Solomon prefigured? He holds all the kingdoms of the earth in his authority, from the rising of the sun to its setting, and, as Scripture testifies, he rules:

> “from sea to sea and from the River to the ends of the earth” (Ecclus. xlix).

All peoples, tribes, and languages serve him, offering him gifts—namely, of right faith and good works.

> “The kings of Tarshish and of the islands will offer gifts; the kings of Arabia and Sheba will bring presents. And all the kings of the earth will worship him; all nations will serve him” (Ps. lxxi).

What is added—“all the days of his life”—means “forever and ever,” because he will remain always, his kingdom will have no end, and his power is eternal; his years will not fail.

> “Solomon’s provision for each day was thirty *chor* of fine flour and sixty *chor* of meal, ten fat oxen, twenty oxen from the pastures, and one hundred rams, besides deer, gazelles, buffaloes, and fattened birds. For he held the whole region beyond the River, from Tiphsah to...” 

What, then, does this provision of Solomon signify except the nourishment of our King, Jesus Christ? He is fed, as it were, by right faith and good works, which are offered to him daily by the Catholic Church.

The thirty *chor* of fine flour can signify faith in the Holy Trinity, according to what is written in the law of the Lord. The sixty *chor* of meal can signify the perfection of good works. The ten fat oxen signify teachers of the Decalogue. The twenty oxen from the pastures signify preachers of the New Testament, who possess within themselves, as it were, a doubled Decalogue, since they preach the New and Old Testaments equally, full of love of God and neighbor.

What do the hundred rams better signify than those who rule well in the Lord’s flock and hasten, together with their subjects, to attain the glory of eternal blessedness? The hunting of various animals may also appropriately be understood as the acquisition of human beings, who are captured each day from different nations in the nets of the Gospel by spiritual hunters and brought into the pasture of our Savior.

> “Solomon had peace on every side round about. Judah and Israel dwelt without any fear, each under his own vine and under his own fig tree, from Dan to Beersheba, all the days of Solomon.”

Isaiah also says this about our Redeemer:

> “His dominion will be multiplied, and there will be no end of peace” (Isa. ix).

Under his protection the true Judah and the true Israel dwell without any fear. With their hearts raised toward the Lord, they despise all earthly things and do not fear the threats of enemies; instead, they persevere continually in the praises of God, delighting in God’s grace and in the sweetness of the charity they unfailingly possess toward the Lord and toward their neighbor.

> “Solomon had forty thousand stalls for chariot horses and twelve thousand horsemen, and the prefects of the aforesaid king provided them with food.”

What else is signified by the number forty except the times of the ancient law? Moses fasted for forty days when he was about to receive it, and the people of Israel, who were instructed through it, remained in the wilderness for forty years.

The number twelve signifies the present time, in which apostolic teaching nourishes the people of the New Testament. The stalls of Solomon’s horses are appropriately counted by the number forty or twelve, because in both peoples—the legal people and the evangelical people—those who were less understanding are invited to the stalls of the Holy Scriptures, so that they may receive there the nourishment of sacred teaching and become fit for the cavalry of the supreme King.

> “And the prefects of the aforesaid king provided them with food.”

Each of the teachers strives, through the word of faith and the example of good works, to provide them with salutary nourishment. Hence the following Scripture says of them:

> “They also brought the provisions for King Solomon’s table, with great care at its appointed time. They brought barley and straw for the horses and beasts to the place where the king was, each according to his assignment.”

So that nothing may be lacking to those who remain in the king’s house, the entire order of holy preachers labors by writing and speaking, so that the Lord’s table may abound in the wealth of books and that each of the faithful may receive suitable nourishment from it.

> “God also gave Solomon wisdom, and...”

## [Scan page 207]

### ANGELÓMI

“...very great wisdom and breadth of heart, like the sand that is on the seashore. And Solomon’s wisdom surpassed the wisdom of all the Easterners and Egyptians, and he was wiser than all human beings—wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, Heman, Chalcol, and Darda, sons of Mahol.”

Therefore God gave our Solomon wisdom and prudence beyond all human beings and every rational creature. Of him John says: “For the one whom God sent speaks the words of God; for God does not give the Spirit by measure. The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand” (John 3). Elsewhere Truth itself says: “For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself; and he has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John 5).

Hence the Apostle Paul says of the Lord Christ:

“He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation; for in him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers. All things were created through him and in him, and he is before all things, and all things hold together in him. He is the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he might hold first place in everything. For in him all the fullness of divinity was pleased to dwell bodily, and in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 1–2).

Thus the wisdom of the true Solomon surpasses that of all others, because there is a great difference between those who are wise through participation in wisdom and the one who is himself the source of wisdom and the origin of virtues.

Hence what follows:

“And he was renowned among all the nations round about.”
