For his name is proclaimed throughout the whole world: “There is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts 4).

“Solomon also spoke three thousand proverbs, and his songs were five thousand.”

For what is signified by the three thousand proverbs except the fullness of faith handed down by Christ in the Law and in the Gospels? Since the whole of it is expounded in manifold ways through allegorical meanings under the mystery of the Trinity, it is, as it were, called three thousand proverbs. His five thousand songs, however, are understood through the five bodily senses. Whoever governs these senses well through various virtues is blessed, and through them sings to the Lord, as it were, five thousand songs.

“Solomon also discoursed about the cedar, down to the hyssop.”

By the cedar is understood the loftiness of glory in the elect. Hence the Prophet testifies, saying: “The righteous will flourish like the palm tree and will multiply like the cedar of Lebanon” (Psalm 41 [source citation; the quotation is Psalm 92]). Hyssop, however, is a lowly plant clinging to rock, by which Christ’s humility is signified. For our Redeemer discoursed from the cedar down to the hyssop because, descending from the lofty excellence of heavenly glory, he reached the humility of the flesh.

Indeed, by the cedar the proud exaltation of the wicked is also signified. As it is said through David: “The voice of the Lord breaking the cedars” (Psalm 28 [29]). Thus Christ discourses from the cedar down to the hyssop because he himself judges the hearts of the proud and the humble.

He discoursed about wood when he hung upon the cross. Then he judged the arrogance of the world, signified by the cedar. He also brought it down to the humility of hyssop—that is, to the foolishness of the cross and to the contemptible proclamation of faith. Hence Paul says:

“For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God” (1 Corinthians 1).

For it is written: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the prudence of the prudent I will reject” (Isaiah 29). And shortly afterward: “Since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the folly of preaching to save those who believe” (1 Corinthians 1).

“Solomon discoursed about animals and birds, reptiles and fish.”

Our Solomon discoursed about every species of animal, because all things are naked and open before his eyes, and no creature is invisible in his sight. He knows all human thoughts. He counts the multitudes of the stars; the abyss lies open before him, and hell is not hidden from him.

It is as though he discourses when he sets before us the account of each thing, and in his Scriptures makes manifest the mysteries that had been hidden from ages and generations, so that we may consider the blessedness of the angels, the usefulness of human beings, and the cunning of evil spirits. Thus, rejecting what is evil, we may choose what is good and always pursue it toward one another and toward all.

“And people came from all nations to hear Solomon’s wisdom, and from all the kings of the earth who had heard of his wisdom.”

The prophet Isaiah says this:

“It shall come to pass in the last days that the mountain of the house of the Lord will be prepared on the top of the mountains, and it will be exalted above the hills. All nations will flow to it, and many peoples will go and say: ‘Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will teach us his ways, and we will walk in his paths; for the law will go forth from Zion and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem’” (Isaiah 2).

## CHAPTER V

“He built the house of the Lord.”

The house of the Lord that King Solomon built in Jerusalem was made as a figure of the holy universal Church. From the first elect person to the last who will be born at the end of the world, it is daily built by the grace of the peaceful King, namely, its Redeemer. Part of it is still a pilgrim on earth; part, having escaped the hardships of pilgrimage, already reigns with him in heaven. After the final judgment has been completed, the whole Church will reign with him.

The elect angels also belong to this house; their likeness is promised to us in the future life, when the Lord says:

“Those who are deemed worthy to attain that age and the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage; for they cannot die anymore, because they are equal to the angels and are children of God, being children of the resurrection” (Luke 20).

The mediator of God and human beings himself also belongs to it, the man Christ Jesus, as he testifies when he says: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2). Explaining this, the Evangelist added: “But he was speaking about the temple of his body.”

The Apostle says of us: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3).

If, then, he became God’s temple through the humanity he assumed, and we become God’s temple through his Spirit dwelling in us, it is clear that that material temple bore the figure of all of us—of the Lord himself, that is, and of his members, who are us. Yet he was chosen and established uniquely as the cornerstone, precious and laid as the foundation; we, however, are like living stones built above, upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets—that is, upon the Lord himself.

The tabernacle once made by Moses in the wilderness also represents this same spiritual house of God. Yet that house was built during the journey toward the promised land, whereas this one was built in the promised land itself and in the city of Jerusalem. The former was carried repeatedly from place to place through the ministry of the Levites, until at last it was brought into the land of the promised inheritance; the latter, built immediately in the homeland itself and in the royal city, was to stand forever upon an unshaken foundation, until the heavenly gift destined for it was fulfilled.

In the former may be figured the toil and exile of the present Church, and in the latter its future rest and blessedness. Or, certainly, because the former was made only for the children of Israel, while the latter was made also from proselytes and the nations, the fathers and that ancient people of God may principally be expressed figuratively in the former, and the Church gathered from the nations in the latter.

Nevertheless, the structure of both houses, when examined more closely in a spiritual sense, is shown in many ways to signify the daily wandering and labors of the present Church, the eternal rewards and joys of the heavenly kingdom in the future, the election of the first Church from Israel, and the salvation of all nations in Christ.

The historical account says that, when Solomon was about to build the house of the Lord, he sought help from Hiram, king of Tyre, who had always been David’s friend. After Solomon had obtained the kingdom, Hiram had also begun to maintain peace with him and soon proved ready to help him in everything. He supplied craftsmen, timber, and gold, as the work required. In return for this service, Solomon gave him every year many kors of wheat and oil as food for his household.

There is no doubt that Solomon, whose name means “peaceful,” signifies both by his name and by the most peaceful condition of his reign the one of whom Isaiah said: “His government will be multiplied, and there will be no end of peace.” Hiram, whose name in Latin means “living on high,” figuratively expresses believers converted from the nations, glorious in life together with faith.

Nor does anything prevent Hiram—who was a king and who assisted Solomon in the building of the house of the Lord with royal power—from typologically declaring those rulers of earthly affairs who have been converted to the faith. Through their efforts the Church is often known to have been assisted and nobly enlarged, and against heretics, schismatics, and pagans to have been raised up by the decrees of rulers.

“Therefore Solomon sought the assistance of Hiram for the work of the temple.”

When the Lord came in the flesh and planned to build the house he loved, namely, the Church, he chose helpers not only from the Jews but also from the nations. For he appointed ministers of the word from both peoples.

“Hiram sent Solomon prepared cedar and fir wood from Lebanon, to be placed in the house of the Lord.”

The converted Gentile world sent to the Lord certain men who had been distinguished according to the world, but who had already been cast down and humbled from the mountain of their pride by the axe of the Lord’s rebuke. Trained according to the norm of evangelical truth, each was placed in the building of the Church according to his merit and in his proper time.

“He also sent craftsmen.”

The Gentile world offered the Lord philosophers converted to true wisdom, who, because of their gift of learning, were rightly set over peoples also for their governance. Such were, in the time of the apostles, Dionysius the Areopagite, and afterward the most gentle teacher and most courageous martyr Cyprian, together with many others.

It also sent gold, which is understood in nearly the same sense: it denotes men distinguished by wisdom and intellect. For all these offerings the Gentile world awaits heavenly gifts of grace from the Lord.

It is fitting for the affairs of the Church that, when asking Hiram for assistance in the holy work, Solomon says:

“Command, therefore, that they cut cedars for me from Lebanon, and let my servants be with your servants. I will give you whatever payment you request for your servants. For you know that there is no man among my people who knows how to cut timber as do the Sidonians.”

“When Hiram heard Solomon’s words, he rejoiced greatly and said: ‘Blessed be the Lord God today, who has given David a very wise son over this great people.’ And Hiram sent to Solomon, saying: ‘I have heard everything that you commanded me. I will do all your will concerning cedar and fir wood. My servants will bring the timber down from Lebanon to the sea; I will assemble it into rafts on the sea as far as the place that you indicate to me, bring it there, and you will take it. You will provide what is necessary for my household’s food.’ Thus Hiram gave Solomon cedar wood and fir wood according to all his wishes. Solomon gave Hiram twenty thousand kors of wheat as food for his household and twenty kors of the purest oil. Solomon gave this to Hiram every year. The Lord also gave wisdom to Solomon, as he had said to him; and there was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and they made a covenant between themselves.”

Hiram’s servants who cut cedars for Solomon from Lebanon are the chosen teachers from the nations. Their duty is to correct and crush those whom worldly wealth and glory had inflated with pride, transferring their desires to the service of their Redeemer.

With these servants of Hiram were also Solomon’s servants, and together they devoted themselves to the work. For the first teachers from the nations needed the apostles, who had learned from the Lord and had been instructed in the word of faith. If they had begun to teach without masters, they would have become teachers of error. Therefore Solomon wished Hiram to cut the timber from Lebanon, because Hiram’s servants were more skilled than Solomon’s servants at cutting it.

Yet he also wanted his own servants to be present, so that they could show those who were cutting what measure the timber should have. The figure of this is readily apparent: the apostles knew with certainty the word of the Gospel that they had heard from the Lord, but the Gentiles, converted from error and transferred to the truth of the Gospel, knew the errors of the nations better. The more certainly they knew them, the more skillfully they learned to defeat and abolish them.

“The king Solomon chose laborers from all Israel, and the levy amounted to thirty thousand men. He sent ten thousand to Lebanon each month in rotation, so that they were two months in their homes.”

Here it should first be noted that Solomon did not choose workers from all Israel without reason, nor was there any portion of the people from which men worthy of so great a work were not taken. For it is not now priests from one lineage, that of Aaron, who are to be chosen; rather, from the whole Church those who are sufficient to build the house of the Lord by their example or their speech must be sought. Wherever such men are found, they should immediately be promoted to the office of teachers, without respect of persons.

When such men are appointed to instruct unbelievers and call them into the fellowship of the Church, they are sent, like strong and chosen men, to cut the materials for the temple in Lebanon. The number of thirty thousand, by which the cutters of timber were counted, can suitably be referred to the figure of those who are perfected in faith in the Holy Trinity, a quality especially fitting for teachers.

But since the thirty thousand were arranged so that ten thousand served the work each month, we should consider more closely the mystery of the number ten. Ten thousand men from Israel are sent to cut timber for the work of the house of the Lord because all who are to be appointed teachers and instructors of the ignorant must themselves observe the ten commandments of the Law in all things and show them to their hearers for observance. They must also always hope for the future rewards in heaven, which are commonly represented by the denarius, and continually proclaim that their hearers should hope for them as well.

The three months, between which the cutters of timber were divided, figuratively announce the perfection of the three evangelical virtues: almsgiving, prayer, and fasting.

By almsgiving we understand everything by which we benevolently fulfill love of neighbor: laboring by teaching, correcting, spending temporal goods, and displaying examples of life. The other two months, during which they were permitted to remain in their homes and attend to their own needs, are prayer and fasting. Through these, in addition to the works we perform outwardly for the needs of our brethren, we turn inward toward the Lord and care for our own salvation in mind.

And since those who humbly submit themselves to divine grace rightly care perfectly for their own salvation and that of their brethren, it follows:

“Adoniram was over such a levy.”

Adoniram, whose name in Latin means “my exalted Lord,” signifies none other than the Lord and Savior himself, whom the name imitates and indicates. Adoniram is placed over the workers of the temple so that, by his provision, he may properly arrange in which months each should go out to work and in which they should return again to care for their own house.

This happens when our Lord and Savior, by his more intimate illumination, instructs the minds of holy teachers to discern when it is necessary to begin the work of building the Church—by preaching or by carrying out other works of piety—and when it is fitting to return again to examine their own conscience, as though returning to inspect their own house, and by prayers and fasts to make it worthy of the heavenly overseer and visitor.

“And Solomon had seventy thousand carriers and eighty thousand stonecutters in the mountain, apart from the overseers who were in charge of the individual works, numbering three thousand three hundred, who directed the people and those who carried out the work.”

Stonecutters are cutters of stones. These stonecutters, like the cutters of timber, figuratively signify the holy preachers, who work upon the minds of the ignorant with the axe of the word of God. They strive to transform them from the crookedness and deformity in which they were born, and to render them, regularly instructed in the unity of the faithful, suitable for the building—that is, the house of God.

The fact that both timber and stones were cut on the mountain, and that both kinds of prepared material were transferred to the mountain of the house of the Lord, makes the meaning clear: we were all born on the mountain of pride, but all who by the grace of God are predestined to life are cut away from the mountain of pride through catechesis and reception of the sacraments of faith and are transferred to the mountain of the house of the Lord. For, rescued from the power of darkness, we reach the stronghold of virtues that exists in the unity of the holy Church.

It should also be noted that these workers were distributed in such a way that some cut stones on the mountain while others carried burdens. The gifts of the Spirit are diverse. Some possess greater firmness in speaking and rebuking the obstinate; others are gentler, suited to console the fainthearted and support the weak; others are endowed with both virtues and serve the work of the house of the Lord. The Apostle wished those to whom he speaks to become such men, saying: “Admonish the disorderly, encourage the fainthearted, support the weak, be patient with everyone” (1 Thessalonians 5).

The overseers who were in charge of the individual works are the sacred authors of Scripture. Under their instruction we learn in all things how it is fitting to teach the ignorant and correct the contemptuous, and how to bear one another’s burdens (Galatians 6), so that we may fulfill the law of Christ.

The workers are rightly said to number seventy thousand and eighty thousand. Seventy thousand signifies the sabbatical rest of souls, since the seventh day was consecrated as the Sabbath, that is, as rest. Eighty thousand signifies the hope of the resurrection, which took place for the Lord on the eighth day, that is, after the Sabbath, and which we also hope for on the eighth day and in the future eighth age.

The overseers numbered three thousand three hundred, on account of the faith in the Holy Trinity that they proclaim to us through the sacred words.

The fact that, instead of three thousand three hundred overseers, the Book of Chronicles records three thousand six hundred (2 Chronicles 2) refers entirely to the same perfection of holy works. Since the Lord completed the adornment of the world in the number six, good works are rightly represented as perfected in that number. And because Holy Scripture teaches works of righteousness to be performed together with faith in the Truth, the overseers of the temple works are rightly said to have numbered three thousand six hundred.

Nor should it be passed over that these seventy thousand burden-bearers and eighty thousand stonecutters, together with their overseers, were not from Israel but from the proselytes—that is, from resident foreigners living among them. For it is written in Chronicles:

“Solomon counted all the proselyte men who were in the land of Israel, after the census that David his father had taken, and they were found to number one hundred fifty-three thousand six hundred. From them he made seventy thousand carriers of burdens on their shoulders, eighty thousand stonecutters in the mountains, and three thousand six hundred overseers of the people’s work,” and so forth.

Proselytes were called, in Greek, those who were descended from other nations and had passed over into the faith and fellowship of the people of God after accepting circumcision.

Thus the workers of the house of the Lord came from the children of Israel, from proselytes, and from the nations. From the children of Israel came the thirty thousand sent to cut cedars from Lebanon. From the proselytes came the stonecutters of whom we have just spoken. From the nations came Hiram himself and his servants, who cut timber from Lebanon together with Solomon’s servants.

Therefore every kind of human being through whom the Church was to be built preceded its construction in the building of the temple. Jews, proselytes, and Gentiles converted to the truth of the Gospel build one and the same Church of Christ, whether by living rightly or by teaching.

## [Scan page 210]

“And the king commanded them to bring great stones and precious stones for the foundation of the temple, and to square them.”

Mystically, no other foundation of the temple is to be understood than the one the Apostle points out when he says: “For no one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 3). He can rightly be called the foundation of the house of the Lord because, as Peter says, “there is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts 4).

Great and precious stones are brought to this foundation when men distinguished by their works and holiness adhere to their Creator with the familiar devotion of their minds. The more firmly they place their hope in him, the more strongly they are able to direct the lives of others—which is to carry the breadth of the wall.

The stones placed in the foundation to support the whole building are properly the prophets and apostles, who received the word and sacraments of the truth from the Wisdom of God itself, whether visibly or invisibly.

They are rightly ordered to be squared first and then placed in the foundation. Everything square, in whatever direction it is turned, normally remains fixed and stable. To this figure the hearts of the elect are compared, for they have learned to stand so firmly in the faith that no adversity of circumstances, not even death itself, can make them deviate from the rectitude of their state.

“Solomon’s masons and Hiram’s masons dressed them.”

The precious stones are dressed when each of the elect, through the instruction and diligence of the saints who preceded them, abandons whatever harmful or useless thing he has within him and displays before the sight of his Creator only the rule of justice implanted in him, like the stable form of a square.

These stones were dressed not only by Solomon’s masons but also by Hiram’s masons, because teachers of the holy Church came from both peoples.

“Moreover, the men of Gebal prepared timber and stones for building the house.”

Gebal is a city of Phoenicia, mentioned by Ezekiel when he says: “Your wise men, Tyre, became your pilots, the elders of Gebal and its wise men” (Ezekiel 27), and so forth.

In Hebrew it is called Gebel or Jabal, which means “defining” or “separating.” This name aptly suits those who prepare human hearts for the spiritual building constructed from the virtues of the soul.

For they are able to teach their hearers faith and works of righteousness only when they themselves have first been carefully instructed in the sacred pages about the faith that must be held and about the path of virtues into which they must enter by a firm definition of the truth. The person who does not know the distinction of the catholic faith uselessly assumes the office of teacher.

Those who attempt to teach others a rule they themselves have not learned build not a sanctuary for the Lord but a ruin for themselves.

Therefore, in building the house of God, the first things to be cut are timber and stones from the mountain. For those whom we seek to instruct in the faith of the truth must first be taught to renounce the devil and be rescued, through rebirth, from the share in the first transgression in which they were born.

Finally, great and precious stones are to be sought and placed in the foundation of the temple, so that, with their former way of life rejected, we may inspect their life and conduct in all things and set before our hearers for imitation those whom we know to adhere especially to the Lord through the virtue of humility.

The wall of holy works must then be raised upward. As though stones were placed one upon another in successive courses, we must walk and advance from virtue to virtue.

Or certainly, the large, precious, and squared stones of the foundation are, as we said above, the teachers of the Churches, who heard the word of salvation from the Lord himself. The stones placed above them in successive courses, whether of stone or timber, are the priests and teachers who follow at each period, through whose preaching and ministry the Church is built or ordered in virtues.

What colors the stones used for the temple possessed is clearly declared in the Book of Chronicles, where David says to Solomon, when he showed him the expenses he had prepared for the temple: “I have prepared in abundance every precious stone and Parian marble” (1 Chronicles 29).

Parian marble is called white marble, such as the same island habitually produces. Hence the poet wrote of it:

“Paros, white as snow, scatters its shores across the sea,  
and we read of the frequent straits stirred by the Cyclades.”

Paros is therefore called snowy because it sends forth marble of the brightest kind. It is one of the Cyclades. Josephus also indicates that the temple was built with this stone, saying: “He raised the temple as far as the roof, constructed from white stone. Its height was sixty cubits,” and so forth.

The spiritual meaning is not hidden. It is clear to everyone that the white marble from which the house of the Lord was constructed signifies the pure action of the elect, together with a conscience cleansed from every stain of corruption.

The wise architect wanted those whom he placed as precious stones upon the foundation of Christ to be redeemed with gold and silver. He says: “Beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God” (2 Corinthians 7).

## CHAPTER VI

“It came to pass in the four hundred and eightieth year after the departure of the children of Israel from the land of Egypt, in the fourth year, in the month of Ziv—which is the second month of the reign of Solomon over Israel—that he began to build the house of the Lord.”

What is said here—“in the fourth year, in the month of Ziv, which is the second month of the reign of Solomon over Israel”—has this order of meaning: in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign over Israel, in the month of Ziv, which is the second month.

He calls the second month May. For April, in which Passover was celebrated, was the beginning of the months and was the first month of the year among the Hebrews. From this it is plainly evident that, immediately after Passover had been completed, he began to build the house of the Lord, and that the people, consecrated by the mystical solemnity, set their hands to the mystical work.

The departure from Egypt is recalled when the tabernacle began to be built, so that the reader may be reminded that a period of years passed between the construction of the two houses and may recognize that this total span of time also contains a spiritual mystery.

Four times one hundred, and twenty, make four hundred and eighty. Four suitably signifies the perfection of the Gospel, on account of the number of Evangelists; one hundred and twenty signifies the teaching of the Law, because there were that many years of the Lawgiver. In this same number the primitive Church received the grace of the Holy Spirit, clearly showing that those who use the Law lawfully—that is, those who recognize and embrace the grace of Christ in it—are rightly filled with the grace of his Spirit, because they burn more fully in his charity.

We said that the tabernacle made by Moses and the children of Israel in the wilderness can signify the Synagogue, while the temple that Solomon and the children of Israel built with the assistance of proselytes and Gentiles can signify the Church of the Gentiles.

The worship and religion of the tabernacle continued for four hundred and eighty years, and then the temple began to be built. That the house of the Lord began to be built in the fourth year of King Solomon can be mystically referred to the fact that, after the dispensation of the Lord’s incarnation had been completed—the dispensation written in the four books of the Gospel—and after the Holy Spirit had been sent from heaven, the structure of the Church began.

That it began in the second month can refer to the election of the nations, who, after Israel, received in themselves the building of their Creator in the second place. Hence the second month was also permitted in the Law for the celebration of Passover, because those who were unclean in soul or far away on the journey and therefore unable to celebrate Passover in the first month could do so then.

Here we are most plainly signified: unclean because of the death of our soul and still far from the people of God, we could not celebrate the first Passover, which was accomplished in the flesh and blood of the Lamb. But today we celebrate the second Passover, which was accomplished in the body and blood of our Redeemer, by whom we were sought out and cleansed.

The place where the temple was built is shown more clearly in the Book of Chronicles, where it is written:

“Solomon began to build the house of the Lord in Jerusalem, on Mount Moriah, which had been shown to David his father, in the place that David had prepared on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite” (2 Chronicles 3).

Therefore the house of the Lord is built in Jerusalem—that is, in the vision of peace—which, having been extended throughout the whole world...

## Commentary on the Books of Kings

### [Scan page 212]

The Church consists in one and the same faith and in the catholic fellowship of truth. For “God is not in the division of minds; rather, ‘his place has been made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion’ (Psalm 75).”

It is built upon a mountain—namely, upon the Lord and Savior himself, of whom Isaiah says: “And it shall be in the last days that the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the summit of the mountains” (Isaiah 2). And he himself says of himself in the Gospel: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matthew 5). For it is itself the mountain of mountains, which indeed arose from the earth through its origin, but by the singular height of its dignity surpasses the power and holiness of all earthly beings. On this mountain, surely, the city—or house—of the Lord has been built, because unless Zion fixes its root in him, our hope and faith are nothing.

It is rightly called Mount Moriah, that is, “of vision,” because he deigns, during this present life, to see and assist his elect, whom he preserves for the vision of his eternal glory, while they labor here. It “had been shown to David his father.” For the Lord who was to come in the flesh had been shown to David, just as to the other prophets.

The same place was fittingly the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, because the Church too is customarily designated by the word “threshing floor,” as John says of the Lord: “Whose winnowing fan is in his hand, and he will cleanse his threshing floor” (Matthew 3). Ornan, which is interpreted as “illuminated,” was by nation a Jebusite; by “nation,” he signifies the Gentiles. He shows that these people, who were to be enlightened by the Lord and changed into sons of light, are those to whom the Apostle rightly says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5).

Jebus is the same city as Jerusalem. Jebus is interpreted as “trampled,” while Jerusalem means “vision of peace.” As long as Ornan the Gentile reigned in it, it was called Jebus, even when David had already purchased the place of the holocaust there. But when Solomon built a temple for the Lord in it, it was no longer called Jebus but Jerusalem. For while the Gentiles persisted in ignorance of divine worship, they were trampled upon and mocked by unclean spirits and were led toward mute idols, following them. But when the grace of their Creator looked upon them, they immediately found both peace and a dwelling within themselves, and the name that expressed these things.

> “The house that King Solomon built for the Lord was sixty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high.”

The length of the house signifies the long-suffering of the Church, which patiently endures every adversity in the exile of this pilgrimage until it reaches the homeland that it awaits.

The breadth signifies charity, by which the enlarged bosom of the mind rejoices in loving not only friends in God but also enemies for God’s sake—until the time comes when, whether they have been converted to its peace or all its enemies have been utterly destroyed, it rejoices with its friends alone in God.

The height proclaims the hope of future reward. With its gaze fixed upon this reward, it willingly despises all lowly things, whether those that delight or those that oppose it, until, having passed beyond both, it merits to see only the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.

Here it should be noted that the thirty cubits of height reached not to the roof of the temple but to the lower upper chamber. For it is plainly written in the Book of Chronicles that the height was one hundred and twenty cubits; we shall speak about this later.

> “There was a portico in front of the temple, twenty cubits long, corresponding to the breadth of the temple, and it had a breadth of ten cubits in front of the façade of the temple.”

The temple faced east, as did the tabernacle. Its portico had an entrance from the east, opposite the entrance of the temple, as the historian Josephus of the Jews teaches very plainly. Thus, at the equinox, the rising sun could pour its rays in a straight line through the entrances of the three structures—namely, the portico, the temple, and the inner sanctuary—and reach the ark of the covenant.

Since the temple signifies the holy Church, what could be clearer than that the portico, which stood before the temple and customarily received the light of the sun more directly, symbolically proclaims that part of the Church which preceded the times of the Lord’s incarnation? In it are the patriarchs and prophets, who were the first to receive the Sun of justice rising upon this world and who bore witness to the Lord born in the flesh—by living, preaching, being born, and even dying.

The door of the temple is the Lord, because “no one comes to the Father except through him” (John 14). And elsewhere he says: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John 10).

The door of the portico is the prophetic word, which led those entering by a straight path onward to the door of the temple, because it openly proclaimed the grace of the Lord Savior, by whom the world was to be redeemed. Thus the entire portico signifies the faithful of that time. The door in the portico represents the teachers who opened to others the gate of life and the entrance to the Lord.

It is fitting that there was one door, because all the saints share a harmonious faith and love of the truth.

This portico, corresponding to the breadth of the temple, was twenty cubits long, because the ancient righteous, through the long-suffering of their devoted minds, desired to come to the expansion of the Church in the charity that is in Christ our Lord.

> “He made windows with sloping frames in the temple.”

The windows of the temple are the holy teachers and all spiritual people in the Church, to whom, when they rise above ordinary understanding, it is granted to see more deeply than others the hidden secrets of heavenly things. When they publicly disclose to the faithful what they see in secret, they are like windows receiving the sun’s light and filling the inner chambers of the temple.

Therefore these windows are fittingly said to be sloping—that is, wider on the inside—because whoever has received, even for a moment, the radiance of heavenly contemplation must immediately enlarge the bosom of the heart through discipline and prepare himself by diligent practice to undertake greater things.

> “He built an encircling structure against the wall of the temple, around the walls of the house and the inner sanctuary, and he made side chambers all around.”

### [Scan page 213]

> “The lowest structure was five cubits wide, the middle structure six cubits wide, and the third structure seven cubits wide.”

These structures are called the pinnacles of the temple in the Gospel, where the Lord is tempted by the devil. We also read that James, the brother of the Lord and apostle, was raised onto the pinnacle of the temple so that he might preach to the people.

Whether it was customary for teachers to sit in these structures and address the crowd standing below, we nowhere find written. The sacramental meaning, however, is clear: these three structures signify three corresponding grades of the faithful—married people, the continent, and virgins. They are distinct in the height of their profession, but all belong, through the fellowship of the same faith and truth, to the house of the Lord and cling to it with fixed minds.

It is beautifully stated that the lowest structure was five cubits wide, the middle six, and the third seven. The upper structure was therefore narrower than the others; the middle was wider than the upper but narrower than the lowest. For the higher profession of virtue ought to maintain a narrower manner of life.

Each structure had sides around it—that is, small enclosing walls—so that someone standing or sitting on those structures could not easily fall to the lower levels. We read that this happened to King Ahaziah in Samaria. These sides aptly signify the daily safeguards of divine protection. Concerning them the Psalmist says: “The Lord will send his angel around those who fear him, and he will deliver them” (Psalm 33).

King Ahaziah of Samaria ascended to the upper chamber, having separated himself from the house of David, but he fell through the lattice. Likewise, even if heretics or schismatics seem to climb some height of good action, because they do not possess the structure of ecclesiastical unity, they continually fall back to the depths of vice, as though the protection of the enclosing walls were open and not firmly joined. They perish through divine judgment because of the arrogance of their obstinacy.

By what means these structures were fastened to the walls of the temple is explained when the text continues:

> “He placed beams around the house on the outside, so that they would not be fastened into the walls of the temple.”

The beams that strengthened and adorned the house on the inside were so long that their ends projected outward: in the lowest row they were seven cubits long, in the middle six, and in the uppermost five. The structures were assembled upon these projecting ends, not inserted into the walls of the temple, but laid beside the walls upon beams extending from them.

What, then, are the beams of the house that carried the structures symbolically except the holy preachers? While they themselves occupy a high and honorable place in the Church of God, they lift the weaker and more fragile through their preaching away from the desires of weakness and suspend them toward the desire and hope of heavenly things. Through their intercessions also they help them persevere in what they have begun.

We read in the Book of Chronicles that the beams of the temple, like its other interior furnishings, were covered with gold. This was undoubtedly done so that those portions of the beams which were inside the temple would be covered with golden plates. But those portions that appeared outside were only lightly gilded, so that they displayed to everyone the appearance and form of the cedar, while nevertheless carrying the structures placed upon them.

What therefore projected outward from the beams signifies the life of the saints insofar as it could become known to us on earth. What shone inside the temple, covered with gold, symbolically proclaims that glory by which they rejoice in the heavenly homeland in the sight of their Creator.

> “The house was built of dressed and finished stones, and neither hammer, axe, nor any iron tool was heard in the house while it was being built.”

These words properly concern that part of the Church which, after the labors and struggles of this age, has merited to be brought into eternal rewards. For there only the perfect and those made spotless and cleansed from every stain of iniquity enter.

Nothing defiled enters that city, nor anyone who practices abomination and falsehood, as John wrote in the Apocalypse: “There neither hammer, nor axe, nor any iron tool is heard” (Revelation 21). Here we are struck by adversities and trained by the discipline of truth, so that there we may be assigned to places appropriate to our merits; and when chastisement has ceased, we may be filled with one spirit and permeated solely by the bond of love by which we are joined to one another.

> “The entrance to the middle side-chamber was in the right-hand wall of the house, and by winding stairs they ascended to the middle chamber, and from the middle to the third.”

Some who misunderstand this passage think that the entrance of the temple was on the south side, failing to observe that if Scripture had intended to signify this, it would not have said, “The entrance of the middle side-chamber was on the right-hand side of the house,” but would instead have said simply, “The house had an entrance toward the south.”

The passage now signifies something quite different. The right-hand part of the house refers to the southern side of the temple. In its eastern portion there was an entrance, made at ground level in the very corner. Those entering immediately ascended step by step to higher levels, following a route of ascent through the interior of the wall itself, until they reached the middle chamber and from the middle arrived at the third.

There is no doubt that, although Scripture does not say so, those ascending in this way had numerous windows on the southern side, through whose light they could travel everywhere without hindrance. This place properly refers to the body of the Lord, which he took from the Virgin.

The entrance of the middle side-chamber was in the right-hand part of the house because, when the Lord died on the cross, one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance. It was fittingly in the right-hand part of the house because the holy Church believes that his side was opened by a soldier on his right.

The Evangelist also used an apt word (John 19), saying not “he struck his side” or “he wounded it,” but “he opened it”—as though it were the door of the middle side-chamber, through which the way to heavenly things was opened for us. Finally, he adds:

> “And immediately blood and water came out”—

water, namely, by which we are washed in baptism, and blood by which we are consecrated in the holy chalice. Through this door we ascend to the middle chamber and from the middle to the third, because through faith and the mysteries of our Redeemer we ascend from our present life in the Church to the rest of souls after death, and again from the rest of souls, when the day of judgment arrives, to the immortality of the bodies. Thus, as though entering the third chamber through a more exalted progress, we shall live forever in the great blessedness of both body and soul.

This journey is undertaken invisibly, so that only those who have entered know it, although even those outside can see the door itself. For the deeds performed in this age and the celebrations of the sacraments can also be observed by the reprobate, but no one recognizes the true and hidden grace of inward faith and love unless, with the Lord as guide, he ascends to heavenly things. “For whoever says that he knows God but does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John 2).

It should certainly be noted that the thirty cubits of height mentioned above extended as far as the middle chamber, where the portico surrounding the temple reached its roof on the south, north, and west sides, as we learn from Josephus. Above this, sixty more cubits were counted up to the highest roof of the temple, and thus the total height of the house, according to the Book of Chronicles (2 Chronicles 3), amounted to one hundred and twenty cubits.

The portico in front of the eastern façade of the temple likewise had the same height, according to the testimony of the aforementioned book. That book calls the porticoes around the temple, which we have mentioned, storerooms and chambers:

> “David gave Solomon his son the plan of the portico of the temple, the storerooms, the upper chambers, the inner chambers, and the house of the mercy seat” (1 Chronicles 28).

There he also mentioned the outer buildings that stood outside the priests’ court around the temple, immediately adding:

> “And also the plan of all the courts and chambers around, the treasuries of the house of God and the treasuries of the holy things.”

The fact that the entire temple was one hundred and twenty cubits high refers to the same mystery. After the Lord’s passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, the primitive Church at Jerusalem received the grace of the Holy Spirit in this number of men.

The number fifteen, which consists of seven and eight, is sometimes used to signify the life now lived by the souls of the faithful in holy baptism; this life will be perfected at the end of the age through the resurrection of immortal bodies. Fifteen multiplied triangularly—that is, with all its parts added together—produces one hundred and twenty. Therefore, appropriately, by the number consisting of one hundred and twenty, the great blessedness of the elect in the future life is signified.

It is also fitting that the third chamber of the Lord’s house is completed in this number, because after the present labors of the faithful and after the future rest received by souls, the full happiness of the entire Church will be completed in the glory of the resurrection.

> “He built the house and completed it. He also covered the house with cedar panels.”

What are the ceiling panels? They are structures composed and adorned with great beauty, fastened to the beams from below. Because the house of the Lord was made with three levels of height, it likewise had three ceilings.

What more suitably can the ceilings signify than the more exalted righteous in the holy Church? Their deeds and teaching are set before everyone as an example, projecting as though farther above; through their intercessions and exhortations they protect the minds of the weak so that they do not fail in temptations.

These ceilings are rightly described as made of cedar. Cedar is a tree of entirely imperishable nature, pleasant in fragrance and bright in appearance; by its burning scent it is said to drive away and kill serpents. All these qualities suit the perfect, whose patience is unconquerable, whose reputation for virtue is outstanding, whose presence is most welcome to all, and whose authority in good things is most steadfast in refuting and confuting those who resist the truth. Both in this life and in the future, they shine with a distinction surpassing that of the other saints.

> “He built the upper structure over the whole house, five cubits high” (Deuteronomy 22).

This signifies the parapets that were made around the highest roof of the house, so that no one who reached the higher places might suddenly slip and fall to the depths. Moses commanded that such a parapet be made on every house that anyone built:

> “When you build a new house, you shall make a wall around your roof, lest blood be shed in your house and you become liable when someone falls from it and plunges headlong” (Deuteronomy 22:8).

These structures, or parapets, are what were earlier called the enclosing sides. When it had been said:

> “He built structures around the wall of the temple, around the walls of the house and the inner sanctuary,”

it was immediately added:

> “And he made sides all around.”

In these sides, therefore, we understand divine protections to be signified. While we still labor in this age and strive upward according to our capacity, they help us daily not to fail.

It is fittingly recorded that this upper structure on the roof of the Lord’s house was five cubits high, because in that homeland the brightness of the divine presence so fills us that our sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch have no guide except to love the Lord our God with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength, and to love our neighbor as ourselves (Matthew 22; Deuteronomy 6).

> “He covered the house with cedar wood.”

This is said of the highest roof of the house, that is, of the structure placed upon the uppermost beams. For the temple did not have a ridge at the top, any more than the tabernacle did, but was level, as is customary among all who build houses in Palestine and Egypt.

This same structure with which the house was covered, and which also signifies the ceilings—that is, the most eminent among the righteous—

### [Scan page 215]

—in the glory of the resurrection, those who by singular holiness attain the very summit of virtue. Concerning one of them it is said: “Among those born of women, no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist” (Matthew 11). If you wish to know who is comparable to him in greatness, hear what the angel says about his father: “He will go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1).

> “He built the walls of the house within with cedar panels, from the floor of the house to the top of the walls; and up to the ceilings he covered it within with cedar wood.”

Inside, the house was clothed with cedar, for outside the stone itself, from which it had been built, shone with such brilliance as though it were covered with white marble.

In the mystical sense, the walls of the temple are the peoples of the faithful, from whom the universal holy Church consists. Their expansion throughout the world is signified by the breadth of the walls; their hope and every intention raised toward heavenly things are signified by their length.

Or, certainly, the height of the wall, which consists of courses of stones placed one upon another, signifies the present state of the Church. The elect, all built upon Christ the foundation, succeed one another in order through the passage of time and, bearing one another, fulfill the law of Christ, which is charity.

Those who are now instructed by teachers who preceded them themselves in turn instruct others, like successive courses of living stones placed one upon another in the house of God. They are carried by others with firm constancy, so that they themselves may be sufficient to carry others, even to the last righteous who will be born at the end of the world. These, placed as though at the summit of the house of God, are taught and carried by others, but have no one whom they must teach or whose weakness they must bear.

The walls are covered within with cedar panels when the hearts of the faithful overflow with the love of virtues. Just as the nature of cedar, as we explained above, symbolically indicates perfected people, so in suitable places it also signifies the height of the virtues by which that same perfection is reached.

Everything is covered with wood from the floor of the house to the top of the walls and to the ceilings when the elect, from the first rudiments of faith through the perfection of good action and to their entrance into the heavenly homeland, do not cease to devote themselves earnestly to good works. From the first righteous to the last at the consummation of the age, all strive after the virtues, by whose merit they may truly declare: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place” (2 Corinthians 2).

> “He covered the floor of the house with fir boards” (2 Chronicles 3).

How this was done is explained more fully in the Book of Chronicles, where it is written:

> “He also laid the floor of the temple with very precious marble, with great beauty” (2 Chronicles 3:6).

It is therefore clear that he did not place the fir boards with which he covered the floor directly upon the ground. First he covered it with marble, then placed the boards upon the marble, and finally added a third covering of gold over both, as is read below.

Just as the breadth of the wall, rising upward and reaching to the ceilings, signifies either the progress of the virtues by which the elect reach the heavenly kingdom, or the choirs of the elect themselves succeeding one another through successive ages, so the levelness of the floor fittingly demonstrates their common humility. While they are still placed in temporal life, they live together in mutual charity, as charity dictates.

This floor was laid with very precious marble and great beauty. The same marble was covered with fir boards because the life of the righteous must first be fortified in the heart by firmness of faith and then adorned in action with the breadth of spiritual virtues. Otherwise, what value would the beauty of the most precious marble have if it were covered with wooden boards, unless it silently signified something mystical? It taught that the abundance of good works must be supported by the strength of unwavering faith.

Because of its height and its long-lasting strength, the fir fittingly represents the mind of the elect, which despises every lowly desire, remains always intent upon the contemplation of heavenly things, and excels uniquely in the virtue of patience.

The sheets of gold placed over the marble and the fir boards signify the breadth of charity arising from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith (1 Timothy 1). Just as gold is more precious than other metals, so charity shines in the temple of God with a light surpassing the other virtues.

> “He also built twenty cubits at the rear of the temple with cedar panels, from the floor to the upper parts, and made the inner house—the inner sanctuary—the Holy of Holies.”

By the rear part of the temple he means the western part. The temple had its entrance from the east, where the sun rises, while from the west one entered the inner house, that is, the Holy of Holies.

The panels that separated the inner house from the outer one are said to have been built from the floor to the upper parts—not up to the ceilings, which were suspended thirty cubits above the floor, as was said earlier, but only to a height of twenty cubits, as is made clear below. The remaining space above these panels was open and empty up to the ceilings: ten cubits high and twenty cubits long, corresponding to the breadth of the house. Through this opening the smoke of the incense customarily rose from the altar of incense into the Holy of Holies and penetrated toward the ark of the Lord.

In this division of the Lord’s house the figure of the mystery is evident, and, as the Apostle explains it (Hebrews 9), it is clearer than light. The first house, into which the priests continually entered to complete the duties of the sacrifices, is the present Church, where, devoted daily to good works, we offer sacrifices of praise to the Lord.

The inner house, which was made at the rear of the temple, is the life promised to us in heaven. The outer house is our present condition in exile; the inner house is the condition in the presence of the supreme King, where the perpetual solemn celebration of the blessed, both angels and human beings, takes place. Hence the servant is rightly told: “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew 25). But this latter house is later in time, because after the labors of this age we are brought to its entrance.

The panels that divide the two houses from one another are the very barriers of heaven, for whose opening we sigh daily; and, so far as the Lord grants, we knock with devout persistence until they are opened and we may enter. Even if we are not yet permitted to enter before the dissolution of our bodies, we nevertheless have open the door of divine mercy, through which we may send beforehand the incense of our prayers, alms, fasts, and other good works.

This is why the inner house, built with cedar walls, has an opening above extending throughout, by which the smoke of the incense might enter: because the eyes of the Lord are open over his house night and day, and his ears attentive to the prayers of his servants, and this throughout the breadth of the Church spread over the world.

The altar of incense in the outer house, though standing near the entrance of the inner house, was a type of the perfect: though still retained in the flesh in the world, they are raised to heavenly things in all their desire. Like burning incense, they send up smoke into the Holy of Holies, because, aflame with love for things above, they assail the ears of their Creator with frequent words of prayer. The door is opened wide, and the smoke of the incense rises above, because the purer persons are on earth and, as it were, the nearer they dwell to the heavenly homeland, the more quickly they receive all that they ask.

The inner house was rightly made twenty cubits long, on account, of course, of the mystery of the twofold love, of which we have spoken above. In this present life it chiefly enlightens the minds of the elect; but in that homeland, when the works of the other virtues have ceased, it alone reigns forever.

> “The temple itself before the doors of the inner sanctuary was forty cubits long.”

We have said that the temple itself before the doors of the inner sanctuary bore the type of the present Church. It was therefore rightly forty cubits long, since this number is often used to signify the present labor of the faithful, just as fifty signifies future rest and peace. The commandments, by whose observance life is attained, are contained in the number ten. The same number ten also signifies the everlasting life which we desire and for which we labor. The world, in which we contend to acquire that life, is four-square. Hence the Psalmist, foreseeing that the Church would be gathered from the nations, said: “He gathered them from the regions, from the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea” (Psalm 106:3).

> “And the whole house within was lined with cedar, having its carvings, skillfully wrought joints, and projecting carved work.”

We have said that cedar signifies the unconquerable beauty of the virtues. The whole house of the Lord was lined within with this wood when the hearts of the righteous shine solely with love for good works. The house has its carvings and skillfully wrought joints in its cedar panels when those same elect are bound to one another by the most beautiful bond of charity, so that, though the multitude of the faithful is innumerable, they are rightly said, through their fellowship in a common faith and love, to have one heart and soul. For the carvings placed at the joints of the panels, so that one structure might be made from all of them, are the offices of charity by which holy brotherhood is joined together and formed into the one house of Christ throughout the whole world.

This house also has projecting carved work when the saints do not cover up their virtuous deeds in secrecy, but publicly display what they themselves are and do, as an example of how to live, for all to see.

> “Everything was lined with cedar panels; no stone at all could be seen in the wall.”

The stones of the wall or floor, the panels, and the gold all signify the life of the saints in the Church. Yet, when they are set together, they do so with this distinction: the living stones are the saints, united to one another in one and the same rule by the strength of faith; cedar or fir panels are the saints joined to one another in one and the same faith by the holiness of diverse virtues according to the gifts of the Holy Spirit; the sheets of gold are the saints who possess the charity surpassing knowledge and rejoice together in its most gracious splendor.

The blessed Apostle comprehended these three in one statement, saying: “For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love” (Galatians 5). Stone represents invincible faith; cedar, fragrant action; gold, love surpassing all things. A stone wall is lined with cedar panels when the profession of faith is adorned with good works, lest it be judged idle or dead.

But because the law was written on stone, while the true teaching of the Gospel was confirmed by the wood of the Lord’s passion, that people was circumcised in the flesh with stone, whereas we are consecrated on the forehead with the sign of the cross. The stone walls of the temple, or the floor laid with most precious marble, may fittingly signify those who lived faithfully and perfectly under the law; whereas the cedar or fir panels signify the righteous of the New Testament, who, wishing to come after the Lord, deny themselves and, taking up their cross daily, follow him.

Since the common glory of heavenly recompense awaits the righteous of both times, a third kind—the sheets of gold—is joined to the stones and precious woods. Nor should it seem contradictory that above we said that the portico before the temple prefigured the ancient faithful, the temple itself those who came into the world after the time of the Lord’s incarnation, and the inner house the joys of the heavenly kingdom given to the righteous of both groups. Now, however, we say that the stone walls signify the ancient people of God, the cedar structures the new people, and the golden sheets the rewards of both in heaven, since the same walls of the temple—in the portico, in the temple itself, and in the Holy of Holies—were alike constructed of stone, wood, and gold. For the same figures recur in different things in many ways. But this too must be said: for—
## [Scan page 217]

### ARGELOMI, 413

For there were also, both under the Law and before the Law was written, very many who served the Lord according to the Law: not killing, not committing fornication, not stealing, not bearing false witness against their neighbor, honoring father and mother, and loving their neighbors as themselves. These belonged to the stone walls of the portico.

There were others who, with greater perfection, abandoned the affairs of the world and, taking up their cross, followed the Lord. The Apostle writes of them:

> “They endured mockeries and scourging, and moreover chains and prisons. They were stoned, they were cut in pieces, they were tested; they died by the sword. They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, afflicted, tormented—of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb. 11).

Those who led an evangelical life before the times of the Gospel had been revealed shone, as it were, in the cedar paneling of the portico before the entrance to the temple. Since the heavenly kingdom receives both groups together—although in distinct dwelling places—the portico of the temple, after the stones and cedar, is covered within with gold.

At the present time there are many who, content with the precepts of the Law—which we have mentioned above—believe that it is enough for them merely to deserve to enter into life. There are others who, not sluggish in pursuing perfection, sell everything they possess and follow the Lord, mindful of his promise that such people would receive in the resurrection not only life but also a special honor:

> “Amen, I say to you, that you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19).

The former figuratively belong to the cedar paneling; the latter to the wall of the temple made of white stone. Both await from the Lord the rewards of perpetual light, like sheets of gold with which they may be adorned. In the inner chambers there are precious stones; there are panels of aromatic wood; both are covered with gold, because both those who had walked blamelessly in the Law of the Lord and those who had perfectly received the grace of the Gospel alike enjoy eternal life.

> “He had made the oracle in the middle of the house, in the inner part, to place there the ark of the covenant of the Lord.”

This was explained earlier by anticipation: namely, that the inner house signified the secret place of the heavenly homeland; the ark of the covenant signified the Lord the Savior, in whom alone we have a covenant of peace with the Father. After his resurrection he ascended into heaven and placed at the Father’s right hand the flesh that he had taken from the Virgin.

> “The oracle was twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high.”

The statement that it was twenty cubits high signifies the cedar wall that separated the oracle—that is, the Holy of Holies—from the outer house, as we also said above. The oracle, where the ark was, was twenty cubits in length, width, and height—that is, square—because in that heavenly homeland, where the eyes of the saints behold the King in his beauty, only divine and fraternal love shines everywhere. This is further established by the words that follow:

> “And he overlaid it and covered it with pure gold.”

This is plainly to say that he filled the heavenly walls of the city with the grace of charity.

> “He also covered the altar with cedar.”

He calls this the altar of incense, which stood before the oracle. A little later it is added:

> “He also covered the whole altar of the oracle with gold.”

From this it is understood that the same altar was made of stone, clothed with cedar, and then covered with gold. Figuratively, it signifies the perfect lives of the righteous, who have been placed, as it were, near the oracle because, having abandoned inferior pleasures, they devote all their care to the entrance into the heavenly kingdom. Hence on this altar not the flesh of victims but only incense was burned, because such people still have to sacrifice within themselves the sins of the flesh and the allurements of their thoughts; but they offer before their Creator only the fragrances of spiritual prayers and heavenly desires through the fire of inward love.

> “He also covered the house before the oracle with pure gold and fastened sheets of gold with golden nails.”

We have said that the house before the oracle represents the present Church, where we burn with love for our Redeemer, although we are not yet able to see him face to face. Thus this house was appropriately covered with pure gold, but it was separated from the oracle by an intervening wall. The place is called an oracle when either a divine or an angelic utterance is granted to human beings together with the revelation of hidden things. Therefore the oracle was rightly made in the inner chambers, that is, in the inner house, because the heavenly homeland, the sight and speech of the angels, and God’s own presence will be revealed there.

The house before the oracle, then, is covered with gold because, in this life—where they cannot yet hear openly from the Father, that is, cannot yet see the Father openly—the perfect and righteous adorn the faith and work of justice with divine love, through which they may deserve to attain full knowledge of God. The sheets of gold with which the house is covered are the manifold works of piety that pure love displays in the service either of its Creator or of fraternal need. The golden nails with which the sheets were fastened are the commandments of charity themselves, by which, through the grace of Christ, we are held firm in the exercise and practice of the virtues so that we do not fail.

Concerning these same nails it is appropriately written in the Book of Chronicles:

> “He also made golden nails, so that each nail weighed fifty shekels” (2 Chron. 3).

The number fifty commonly signifies in Scripture the remission of sins, the grace of the Holy Spirit, and eternal rest. Each nail weighed fifty shekels, and with these the sheets of gold were fastened to the walls of the Lord’s house. For the heavenly words, by which we advance and are preserved in the love of good works, promise us forgiveness of sins, the grace of the Holy Spirit, and the eternal Sabbath in the future.

These, then, are the nails of love. There are also other nails, those of fear, with which beginners and those who have not yet reached perfection mortify the allurements of vices and carnal pleasures. These are the words of truth whose instruction teaches us to crucify our flesh with its vices and desires. The Prophet desired to possess them when he said:

> “Pierce my flesh with the nails of your fear, for I have feared your judgments” (Ps. 118).

When he had again reached more perfect things, he said concerning the nails of love:

> “But it is good for me to adhere to God” (Ps. 72).

### LUXOVIENSIS MONACHI, 424

## [Scan page 218]

### ENARRATIONES IN LIBROS REGUM

> “There was nothing in the temple that was not covered with gold. He also covered the whole altar of the oracle with gold.”

The portico before the temple was gilded because the Fathers of the Old Testament pleased God through charity. The temple itself was gilded because that same “charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5). The inner house was gilded because in the heavenly homeland charity alone reigns. There it reigns all the more truly and securely because God himself, who is charity, is seen. There the mediator of God and human beings, who alone is conscious of the Father’s secrets, is always seen, as it were, as the ark of the covenant.

The fact that the upper chambers too were covered with gold refers to the same meaning. Just as the inner house, the Holy of Holies, where the ark was, signified the inward life of the saints in the sight of their Creator and Redeemer, according to the Psalmist:

> “You will hide them in the hiding-place of your face, from the disturbance of men” (Ps. 30),

so the upper chamber signifies that same life as being in heaven and not in this world, as the Apostle says:

> “Seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are upon the earth” (Col. 3).

> “And in the oracle he made two cherubim of olive wood, ten cubits high.”

Cherubim, as the prophet Ezekiel clearly declares, is the name of an angelic rank; in the singular it is called cherub, in the plural cherubim. Thus, in the figurative sense, the cherubim made in the oracle can be understood as the angelic ministries that always stand before their Creator in heaven. They are rightly said to have been made of olive wood, because the angelic virtues have been anointed with the grace of the Holy Spirit so that they may never grow dry in the love of God.

They are ten cubits high because they are built upon the number ten of eternal life, possessing within themselves the inviolate image of their Creator, and preserving the perpetual holiness that they received from justice and truth at their first creation. The number ten consists of ten obols and commonly contains within itself the name and image of the king. It therefore most appropriately suits the figure of the heavenly kingdom, where the holy angels always remain according to the image of their Creator, in whose likeness they were made, and where the elect receive again the image that they had lost through sin.

> “Five cubits was the wing of one cherub, and five cubits the wing of the other cherub: that is, they had ten cubits from the tip of one wing to the tip of the other.”

When wings are placed in the figure of the saints, they signify the virtues by which they continually fly toward heavenly things and delight to have their conversation there. When they are used to signify angels, what could they more suitably indicate than the grace of the perpetual and unfailing happiness of those who always remain in heavenly service to their Creator? Or perhaps they signify that they are endowed with the lightness of a spiritual nature, so that wherever they wish they arrive immediately, as if flying. Angels are represented with wings here, and prophets too have appeared with wings.

It is rightly said that the wing of one cherub was five cubits and the wing of the other cherub five cubits, because the angelic virtues guard the law of God, which is written in five books, with tireless devotion: loving the Lord their God with all their strength and their neighbors as themselves. “The fullness of the law is charity” (Rom. 13). Their neighbors—and likewise one another—are the angelic spirits and the elect human beings who are their fellow citizens.

One cherub and both his wings are said to have been of the same measure because, with the same devotion by which they love one another in God, they also desire our fellowship as we ascend to them. Thus the wings together make ten cubits when the angels rejoice in the presence of their Creator through the expression of the twofold charity.

> “The second cherub was also ten cubits, of equal measure, and the work was one in the two cherubim: one cherub was ten cubits high, and likewise the second cherub.”

Two cherubim were made to signify the fellowship of the same charity of which we are speaking, because charity cannot exist with fewer than two. Hence the Savior took care to send his disciples two by two to preach, silently teaching that those who preach the word of faith must hold the virtue of love above all.

The two cherubim were of one measure and one workmanship because in the heavenly homeland there is no disparity of wills or thoughts, where all are enlightened by one and the same vision and glory of the God who is present.

> “And he placed the cherubim in the middle of the inner temple. The cherubim extended their wings, and one wing touched one wall, and the wing of the second cherub touched the other wall; their other wings touched one another in the middle of the temple.”

From what has been said above it is clear why the cherubim were placed in the middle of the inner temple: their dwelling is always in heaven. The cherubim extended their wings as if for flight because the angelic spirits always have their readiness prepared for the service of the divine will.

The fact that one wing touched one wall and the wing of the second cherub touched the other wall refers to the administration of charity that the angels provide for us. The fact that their other wings touched one another in the middle of the temple expresses the grace of love by which they embrace one another.

The text appropriately continues:

> “He also covered the cherubim with gold, and he carved all the walls of the temple round about with various engravings and with the chisel.”

## [Scan page 219]

### ANGELOMI LUXOVIENSIS MONACHI, 428

> “And he made in them cherubim, palm trees, and various figures, as if projecting from the wall and emerging. He also covered the floor of the house with gold, within and without. At the entrance of the oracle he made doors of olive wood, with five-cornered posts, and two doors of olive wood. He carved upon them figures of cherubim and palm trees and very prominent reliefs; he covered them with gold and overlaid with gold both the cherubim and the palm trees and the rest. At the entrance of the temple he made quadrangular posts of olive wood, and two doors of fir wood on either side; each door was double and, joined to the other, opened. And he carved cherubim, palm trees, and very prominent reliefs, and covered everything with sheets of gold, laid squarely according to the rule.”

And so forth. “He covered the cherubim with gold,” because their Creator exalted their nature with immortal brightness and filled their minds with true love and humility. It should be noted that, when Moses made the tabernacle, he also made two cherubim of beaten gold, which he placed on the mercy seat above the ark. Solomon, however, added two others, much larger, to place in the temple, so that he might set the ark in the middle beneath their wings, together with the mercy seat and the earlier cherubim. Thus there were two cherubim in the tabernacle, but four in the temple; yet both sets pertain to one and the same signification. This was repeated in order to teach figuratively that, after the Lord’s incarnation, when the Church had been multiplied, a broader multitude of citizens of heaven would be gathered from the nations. They praise their Creator with the devoted service due to him, and rejoice that, through our deliverance, we too are brought into the same blessedness.

For they stretch their wings toward one another above the ark when they refer to the praise of the Lord and Savior every good thing they have received. They stretch their other wings toward the walls of the oracle when they rejoice to see holy human beings with them, and touch, with the tips of their wings wherever they will, those whom they rejoice to have been companions and imitators of their purity in this life. They touch with their wings the two equal walls because they have with them, as possessors of the heavenly court, believers of both peoples, namely Jews and Gentiles—not because there is a local distinction between the two peoples in that homeland, but because the festival of inward blessedness is greater through the fellowship of brotherhood united in God. The cherubim therefore stretch their wings toward both walls of the oracle because, rejoicing in the heavenly homeland, they also stir up the righteous of both peoples, by the sight of their glory, to praise their Creator.

The heavenly hosts rejoice not only in the blessedness of those righteous human beings whom they have with them within; they also care for us who are still outside, crying to the Lord from the depths. Hence it is rightly written of these same cherubim in the Book of Chronicles: “They stood with their feet erect, and their faces were turned toward the outer house.” Because we are far from their fellowship and desire to attain it, they stand with their feet erect and stretch their gold-covered wings toward the walls of the oracle, yet have their faces turned toward the outer house: just as they preserve their own innocence perpetually, so they rejoice in the heavenly blessedness of holy souls, and do not cease to help those elect whom they see still wandering on earth, until they bring them too into the heavenly homeland. For all are ministering spirits, sent to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation.

The two cherubim can also signify the two Testaments. These cherubim were made in the oracle because, in the counsel of divine providence—indeed inaccessible and incomprehensible to us—it was disposed before the ages when, how, and through what authors the sacred Scriptures should be written. They are made of olive wood because they bestow on us the light of knowledge, with the aid of the flame of God’s love, which is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit. They are ten cubits high because they proclaim that God must be served by observing the Decalogue of the Law, and show that those who serve God faithfully are to be rewarded with the number ten, the eternity of the kingdom. They have double wings because they show their hearers that the Testaments of their Creator must be followed with tireless spirit through adversity as well as prosperity.

One wing of a cherub is five cubits, and the other wing of a cherub is five cubits, because amid every variety of changing things the saints extend all the senses of their body in the service of their Creator.
