The work in the two cherubim was one because the writers of both Testaments served the Lord with one and the same chastity of conduct and devotion of love, and preach with one harmonious voice and faith of the Lord. Thus the inner wings of the cherubim are joined together above the ark because the Testaments agree in equal testimony concerning the Lord. Again, with their outer wings one touched one wall and the other the other wall, because the Old Testament was properly written for God’s ancient people, whereas the New was written for us, who have come to faith after the Lord’s incarnation. We are rightly compared with the second wall, that is, the northern one, because after the cold and darkness of idolatry it was granted to us to know the light of truth. The cherubim have their faces turned toward the outer house because the divine books were composed for the sake of us who still stand outside and have been saved not in actuality but in hope: their writers, now reigning with God and praising him in heaven, care for our salvation and intercede with his mercy for our errors.

“And he carved all the walls of the temple round about with various engravings and with the chisel.” All the walls of the temple round about are all the peoples of the holy Church, which, founded upon Christ, has filled the whole circuit of the world and does not cease daily to enlarge the begun building of faith through a new generation of its members, as though by the addition of precious stones. These walls are carved with various engravings when to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing in the one Spirit, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the discernment of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, and to another the interpretation of utterances (1 Cor. 12). And, to come to the virtues that all of us can have: “charity, joy, peace, long-suffering, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, modesty, self-control” (Gal. 5), and the other fruits of the Spirit—what are they but engravings upon the walls of the temple? For they are the adornment of the minds of God’s people.

The same walls are also carved for endurance, and promise everything, saying sincerely in every circumstance that occurs: “I shall bless the Lord at all times” (Ps. 33); and, “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I shall sing and make melody to the Lord in my glory” (Ps. 107). They are carved with the chisel when they devote themselves so earnestly to virtues that no adversities of surrounding circumstances and no blandishments can turn them from this path. For, because the chisel surpasses other arts in speed and itself preserves the rule by which it completes its work without error, it aptly signifies the devout life of the saints, which is always ready for the service of the divine will and has learned, through long practice in virtues, to perform it without wandering into error.

“And he made in them cherubim, palm trees, and various figures, as if projecting from the wall and emerging.” He carved cherubim in the walls of the temple because the Lord grants his elect to direct their lives according to the rule of the holy Scriptures, in which there is a multitude of knowledge. He makes cherubim when, in this world, he teaches them, according to their measure, to imitate the angelic manner of life—a manner carried out especially through vigils and divine praises, and through sincere love of the Creator and of one’s neighbor.

He makes palm trees when he impresses the memory of eternal reward upon their minds, so that they may be less able to slip from the ark of justice the more they keep the reward of justice before their eyes. He makes various figures, as if projecting from the wall and emerging, when he grants the faithful manifold works of virtue—for example, compassion, kindness, humility, patience, and modesty.

> “He also covered the floor of the house with gold, within and without.”

“Within and without,” that is, in the oracle and in the temple itself. Solomon therefore covered the floor of the house with gold within and without because our peaceful King has separated the angels and the souls of the righteous in heaven from the sight of the other mortals through the perfect and complete gift of love.

> “At the entrance of the oracle he made doors of olive wood, with five-sided posts, and two doors of olive wood.”

What he had first said—“he made doors of olive wood”—he seems to have wished to explain more clearly when he added, “and two doors of olive wood.” There was one entrance to the oracle, but that same entrance was closed by two doors. When they were opened again, the entrance was opened, just as the temple too was opened. The portico before the temple likewise had only one entrance.

This was certainly for a definite reason connected with the mystery, because the entrance of the oracle stood opposite it. The doors of this entrance can be understood figuratively in many ways. They most appropriately signify the angelic spirits through whose ministry we are brought into the dwelling of the heavenly homeland. They also represent the apostles and apostolic men, to whom the keys of the kingdom of heaven have been given. Having received from the Lord the power of binding and loosing, they admit those who are worthy within the gate of the kingdom, while they exclude the stubborn, impure, and proud from entry into eternal life by excommunication or anathema.

The works of justice, by whose merit the heavenly kingdom is reached, can also rightly be signified figuratively by the doors through which the high priest entered the Holy of Holies, according to what is written in the Book of Wisdom:

> “The keeping of the laws is the completion of incorruption; and incorruption makes one near to God. Therefore the desire for wisdom leads to the everlasting kingdom” (Wis. 6).

All these interpretations agree appropriately with the fact that the same doors were made of olive wood. For both angels and perfect human beings present themselves gloriously in the house of God through the fruit of mercy and works of light; indeed, all the elect open the way for themselves into the heavenly homeland through the arms of light and piety.

There are two doors, either because angels and all the saints love God and their neighbors, and no one can enter the gate of life except through this twofold love, or because the same gate of life is opened to the faithful of both peoples, namely Jews and Gentiles.

The five-sided posts of the angels signify that the heavenly court receives not only the souls of the elect but also opens its doors at the judgment to bodies endowed with immortal glory.

> “He carved in them figures of cherubim and palm trees, and very prominent reliefs, and covered them with gold; he overlaid both the cherubim and the palm trees and everything else with gold.”

*Anaglypha* is the Greek term for what are called in Latin *caelaturae*, “engravings” or “reliefs.” Through the works of virtue—which the Church throughout the whole world exercises in its holy and perfect members—those to whom the care of the faithful and the keys of the kingdom of heaven have been entrusted ought especially to devote themselves to the works by which they may excel others in merit to the same degree that they excel them in rank.

They have the figure of cherubim sculpted in them when they imitate an angelic life on earth, as far as is possible for mortals, both in mind and in deed. They have figures of palm trees when, with fixed attention, they continually contemplate the gift of heavenly reward. The palm is the ornament of a victorious hand. They have very prominent reliefs when they display to all who look upon them the most certain evidence of good works, which no one can interpret in a sinister sense.

All these things are covered with sheets of gold when—as has often been said and must always be said—the radiance of love shines more conspicuously in the great members of the Church than all the other flowers of virtue.

The Books of Chronicles report that a veil was also added to these doors:

> “He also made a veil, he says, of hyacinth, purple, scarlet, and fine linen, and embroidered cherubim upon it” (2 Chron. 3).

This was made for the sake of beauty, so that even among the gilded walls the silk would shine. But it was also hung before the ark and the entrance of the oracle with a fitting significance belonging to the same mystery as the doors, so that, just as the doors were opened at appropriate times, the veil too might be drawn aside whenever those times arrived at which one had to enter the Holy of Holies.

The diligent unveiling of this veil signifies, according to the Law, the opening of the heavenly kingdom, which was granted to us through the incarnation of our Lord and Savior. Hence, when he was baptized, the heavens were opened, to show that through the baptism he himself consecrated for us we were to enter the gate of the heavenly homeland.

When he died on the cross, the same veil was torn in two from top to bottom, so that it might be plainly shown that the figures of the Law had then passed over to faith, and that the truth of the Gospel, the heavenly mysteries, and the very entrance into heaven were no longer to be prophesied and signified figuratively, but were already about to be opened to all who, from the beginning of the world until that time, had passed from the world in the faith of truth.

The same veil, under which one entered the oracle, is rightly said to have been made of hyacinth, purple, scarlet, and fine linen, and to have had cherubim woven into it.

Hyacinth, which imitates the color of heaven, is appropriately compared with the desires for heavenly things. Purple, which is made from the blood of shellfish and bears a blood-red appearance, not improperly signifies the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion, which we must contemplate while carrying our cross. Scarlet, which glows with a red, fiery color, fittingly expresses the virtue of love. Concerning it the disciples who had walked with the Lord said in wonder:

> “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24).

Fine linen, which grows from the green earth and, through the long labor of craftsmen, loses its natural green color and is brought to a bright whiteness, fittingly signifies the chastisement of our flesh. The Apostle commands its great moisture, as it were, to be dried up, saying:

> “Put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and greed, which is the service of idols” (Col. 3).

He shows elsewhere to what brightness he wishes this to be brought, saying:

> “I appeal to you, brothers, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, your rational worship” (Rom. 12).

Cherubim are woven into it because, when all that we do piously is protected by the angelic guardianship granted by the Lord from the poisonous darts of demons, it is fashioned from four outstanding colors. Cherubim are woven into it when, in the good things we do, we continually employ the multitude of knowledge, always looking to the divine words; and lest we stray from the path of virtue, we continually guide our footsteps by their example.

> “At the entrance of the temple he made posts of olive wood, quadrangular, and two doors of fir wood on either side; each door was double, and they opened by holding one another.”

Just as the entrance of the oracle, by which one reached the hidden things of God and the cherubim, signifies the heavenly kingdom, into which we hope and desire to be introduced for the vision of our Creator and the heavenly citizens, so the entrance into the temple figuratively represents the beginnings of our formation in conversion to God, when we enter the present Church.

The former entrance designates our entry into faith; the latter, our entry into vision. Therefore the posts of this entrance were appropriately made quadrangular, either because of the four books of the holy Gospel, by whose teaching we are instructed in the faith of truth, or because of the four principal virtues—prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice—upon whose firmest foundation the whole structure of good actions rests.

Prudence is the virtue by which we learn what we ought to do and how we ought to live. Fortitude is the virtue through which we accomplish what we decide must be done. The Prophet briefly embraces these virtues in one verse when he says:

> “The Lord is my illumination and my salvation” (Ps. 26).

Illumination teaches us what we ought to do; salvation strengthens us to carry it out. Temperance is the virtue by which we discern lest we be found to devote either more or less than is just to prudence or fortitude. Whoever uses prudence with respect to fortitude in a temperate manner will be proved just without any distortion.

The fourth virtue, after prudence, fortitude, and temperance, is justice.

The two doors made at this entrance are the love of God and of one’s neighbor. They are rightly said to have been made on either side because they face one another, so that one cannot exist without the other.

> “Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God. And everyone who loves him who begot him loves him also who has been begotten by him” (1 John 5).

And again:

> “He who does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 4).

Thus the outer door is rightly understood as fraternal love, while the inner door is divine love, because the former comes earlier in time and the latter is higher in divinity. Through the former one enters into the latter, because it is in love of one’s neighbor that one is taught how the Creator ought to be loved.

It should certainly be noted that at the entrance of the oracle two doors are said to have existed, but they are not said to have been double. At the entrance of the temple—that is, of the earlier house—there were two doors, each of which was double. For in the present Church it is necessary for us to enter and lead such a life…

## COMMENTARY ON THE BOOKS  
433

…in which we preserve love of God and neighbor through faith and works, through patience and kindness. But in the life to come, where we shall see God and our neighbors in the light of eternal blessedness, we shall assuredly enjoy that same twofold love without any labor whatever—indeed, amid a great abundance of divine sweetness. Hence the entrance of the inner house appropriately had two doors; but these were single.

For faith is not necessary there, where we shall see in manifest light all that we now believe and hope for. Labor in works is not necessary, where we shall be granted the everlasting reward for the things in which we labor here. Patience is not necessary, where no one inflicts any adversity. Generous kindness is not needed where no one is in want. This, following in the footsteps of the Fathers, we have said concerning the figure of the doors according to our measure.

But according to the structure of the work itself, provision was made for beauty that there should be two doors in one and the same entrance of the temple. For it was necessary that the walls of the house, which were one hundred and twenty cubits high, should also have several cubits of thickness. At the outer edge of that thickness the doors were fixed, so that each door lay against the same wall; whether a person stood inside or outside the temple and looked at the door, one continuous wall would appear to him throughout.

Likewise, the cedar wall, being twenty cubits in length and height, itself had to have no small thickness. Therefore two doors were made at its entrance, so that on either side—that is, both within and without—a door equal to the wall might stand open; and, by means of the same pictures of the doors that the wall also bore, one wall might truly appear throughout to extend continuously: presenting one feature for beauty’s sake, while prefiguring another, an arrangement for service.

What follows concerning the carved doors of the temple—“And he carved cherubim and palms and very projecting carvings, and covered everything with plates of gold, worked squarely to the rule”—means that the same mysteries of faith, hope, and charity which the lofty and perfect understand in a lofty manner, and which all the elect fully perceive in the divine vision, are also handed down to unlearned catechumens, each according to his capacity, to be learned and confessed; so that, initiated into the sacred mysteries, they may one day attain to grasping what they have piously believed.

> “King Solomon built the inner court with three courses of hewn stones and one course of cedar beams.”

He speaks briefly of the inner court and seems to say nothing at all about the outer court. But both are mentioned in the Book of Chronicles, where it is written:

> “He also made the court of the priests and the great basilica, and doors in the basilica, which he overlaid with bronze” (2 Chronicles 4).

The inner court, called that of the priests because priests and Levites ministered in it, surrounded the temple on every side. But on the eastern side of the same temple its entrance was set much farther from the temple than on the other three sides, because on that side—that is, in front of the temple—the services of the saints were performed: there stood the bronze altar for offering victims to the Lord; there the ten lavers for washing those victims; there the bronze sea for washing the priests’ hands and feet.

This court was three hundred cubits high, as Josephus relates, so that it might exclude others from the entrance of the temple and signify that this was permitted only to priests. It had a gate on the eastern side, as far as which the people brought their victims and sacrifices, to be received by the priests and carried to the altar.

Of the outer court, which the Book of Chronicles calls the great basilica, Josephus writes:

> “Outside this temple he built another court, made in a quadrangular form, erecting very large and broad porticoes, and containing lofty and wide gates in it on the four sides of the world; each of these faced one of the four winds, where he set golden doors.”

And a little later:

> “Into this sanctuary, therefore, entered all peoples who had purification and observance of the legal requirements.”

Cassiodorus the Senator, in the picture of the temple which he placed in the *Pandects*, as he himself recalls in his exposition of the Psalms, arranged these porticoes in three orders. He placed the first order outside the priests’ court, squarely on every side; the second likewise outside the inner porticoes, all around; and the last similarly around the preceding porticoes on every side. Thus the temple was fortified on every side by a threefold defense of buildings. There was an open-air pavement between the several buildings, of marble; and the inner walls of the houses—that is, those facing the temple—were made in columns, while the outer walls were solid. Thus the entire structure of the temple was rationally distinguished by a variety of levels.

For the high priest entered the Holy of Holies; purified priests entered the temple itself; purified and unpurified priests, together with Levites and singers, entered the priests’ court; purified Jewish men entered the inner court of the greater basilica, standing and praying in the open air if the weather was fair, but withdrawing into the nearer porticoes if there was a storm; purified widowed women entered the outer court; and Gentiles and Jews recently converted from the Gentiles, until the sixth day of purification, entered the outermost court. We have briefly noted these matters as we found them distinguished in Cassiodorus’s picture, judging that he had learned them from the ancient Jews and that so learned a man would not have wished to offer an example for reading unless he had first recognized it as true.

These are the places mentioned by the last of the gradual psalms, which begins:

> “Behold now, bless the Lord, all you servants of the Lord, who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God” (Psalm 133).

In these porticoes Jeremiah and the other prophets, the Lord and the apostles, preached the word to the people. In one of them the Lord sat teaching when that adulterous woman was brought before him for judgment by the Pharisees who were testing him (John 8). In them he found persons selling and buying sheep, oxen, and doves, and expelled them from the temple together with their merchandise (Matthew 21). And in them—

## ANGELOMI  
435

Peter and John healed the lame man whom they found and brought him with them inside to worship (Acts 3). In these porticoes the whole multitude of the people prayed when the angel appeared at the altar of incense to Zechariah as he was offering incense, and instructed him concerning the birth of the Lord’s precursor (Luke 1).

Yet these courts, together with their porticoes, could not conceal from those looking from a distance the sight of the temple, because the place where the temple stood was much higher than the place where the porticoes were founded. For, as Josephus writes, the outermost structures of the courts, although erected at a height of four hundred cubits, reached only to the summit of the mountain on which the temple had been built.

We have thought it useful, studious reader, to make these observations about the structure of the temple. In whatever matters Holy Scripture has chosen to report them, however, let us seek the figures of its mysteries; in the other matters, let us use them simply for historical knowledge.

The building of the temple within the priests’ court therefore expresses the life of the perfect and exalted men in the holy Church: namely, those who both draw near to the Lord through the excellence of their virtues and customarily show others the way of salvation by word and deed.

For the Latin name *sacerdos*—“priest”—is derived from the fact that he ought to offer what is sacred as a dedication to his inferiors. In the mystical sense of Scripture, this name refers not only to the ministers of the altar, bishops and presbyters, but also to all who excel in the height of upright conduct and salutary teaching, benefiting not only themselves but many others. By presenting their bodies as a living, holy, and acceptable sacrifice to God (Romans 12), they truly perform the ministry of a priest spiritually.

The apostle Peter was speaking not only to bishops and presbyters but to the whole Church when he said:

> “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for acquisition.”

The ancient people of God were likewise marked with this honor of dignity, when God said to Moses (Exodus 19):

> “Thus you shall say to the house of Jacob and declare to the children of Israel.”

And shortly afterward:

> “You shall be for me a priestly kingdom and a holy nation.”

The great basilica, which stood outside the priests’ court and in which the whole multitude of the people customarily gathered either to worship or to hear the word, figuratively conveys the life and conduct of ordinary people in the holy Church. To such people the Apostle says:

> “And I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal—as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Corinthians 3).

They are appropriately represented by the great basilica, because there is without doubt a much greater number of such people in the holy Church than of the perfect. But in proportion as they surpass them in number, so they fall short in merit. Hence the basilica is rightly called great: although it contains very many, it does not admit them into the inner parts of the temple, gilded with gold; nor to the service of the altar; nor even into the priests’ court. For all who are still carnal and weak in the Church, although on account of the merit of their pure faith and devotion they belong to the company of the elect devoted to the Lord, are nevertheless far from being equal to those who speak with confidence:

> “I will not dare to speak of anything except what Christ accomplishes through me for the obedience of the Gentiles, by word and deed” (Romans 15).

And again:

> “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. From now on the crown of justice is laid up for me” (2 Timothy 4).

The common people did indeed approach as far as the priests’ court, carrying their sacrifices to its door. Once the priests had received them and offered them on the altar, the people followed them with their eyes. Even when the temple was opened, they directed their gaze toward it from a distance, but they did not have permission to enter the priests’ court.

Nevertheless, from below they cried out to the Lord, because the simplicity of the carnal in the Church is not despised by the Lord when they faithfully offer to him, with a devout intention, what they are able to offer. They direct their eyes from afar toward the temple of God when they rejoice earnestly in learning about and admiring the life of the exalted. Those whom they cannot follow by imitating their virtues, they embrace with the affection of pious veneration. They see the priests’ sacrifices consumed on the altar by sacred fire, because they recognize that the works of the great are graciously accepted by the Lord through the Holy Spirit.

They also bring their own sacrifices to be offered to the Lord in the priests’ court on behalf of those people. When they do the good works of which they are capable, they commend themselves to the Lord through the exhortation and intercession of their elders and teachers. They also offer their sacrifices to the priests for commendation to the Lord when, seeking the highest reward, they give to the holy poor whatever necessities of this world they possess in abundance, as the Lord admonishes and says:

> “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16).

It is rightly remembered that the priests’ court was built with three courses of hewn stones and one course of cedar wood. The three courses of hewn stones are faith, hope, and charity. They are rightly called hewn, because a certain necessary skill in expression is required, by which each person may understand how he ought to believe, what he ought to hope for, and what he ought to love. The single course of cedar wood is good works themselves, presented without the corruption of pretense. Without the addition of good works, faith, hope, and charity cannot be genuine.

It has often been said that cedar wood, on account of its fragrance and the incorruptible strength of its nature, signifies the endurance and good reputation of a pious action. All the elect who desire to please God by faith, hope, love, and works ascend to this court. The perfect rise above it by the grace of their merits when they advance to such a summit of virtues that they can say to their hearers:

> “Be imitators of us, as we are of Christ” (1 Corinthians 4);

and they glory and say:

> “Do you not know that we shall judge angels, how much more matters of this life?” (1 Corinthians 6).

## COMMENTARY ON THE BOOKS  
437

> “In the fourth year the house of the Lord was founded, in the third month; and in the eleventh year, in the month of Bul—which is the eighth month—the house was completed in all its work and in all its furnishings; and he built it over seven years.”

The allegorical meaning is clear: why is the house of the Lord said to have been built in seven years? Because the holy Church is constituted from elect souls throughout the whole period of this age, which proceeds through the cycle of seven days, and at the end of the age brings its own growth to completion.

Or certainly it is built in seven years because of the significance of spiritual grace, through which the Church receives the power to be the Church. Isaiah enumerates seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, without which no one can become faithful, preserve the faith, or, by the merit of faith, reach the crown of justice.

But when it is said that in the eighth year and in its eighth month the house was completed in all its work and in all its furnishings, this refers to the future age and the day of judgment. Then the holy Church will attain such perfection that nothing more can be found to add to it. For it will then possess what that pious suppliant desired and asked of the Lord:

> “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John 14).

Yet a question arises that should not be dismissed: how is it said that the dedication of the house of the Lord was completed in the seventh month, while in the eighth month it was completed in all its work and in all its furnishings, when the following passage says otherwise?

It is not believable that Solomon built the temple in seven years, completed it in the eighth month of the eighth year, but then deliberately postponed its dedication until the seventh month of the next year. It therefore seems more likely that the house was built in seven years and seven months, so that the solemnity of the dedication was celebrated in that seventh month and Solomon dismissed the people to their tents on the twenty-third day of that month, as the Book of Chronicles relates. Thus, after one week had passed and the eighth month had arrived, the house of the Lord was found to be complete—both in all its works and in the dedication itself, which had already been completed.

Unless, perhaps, we should think that some furnishing for the service of the temple was still added to the temple mentioned above, and that the king, hastening so that the temple might be dedicated entirely in the seventh month—which was wholly solemn—brought it to completion only at the beginning of the eighth month. In this way both statements would prove true: the temple was completed in its work and furnishings in the eighth month, and it was dedicated in the seventh month.

### CHAPTER VII

> “King Solomon also sent for and brought Hiram from Tyre, the son of a widow from the tribe of Naphtali, whose father was a Tyrian, a craftsman in bronze, full of wisdom, understanding, and skill, to perform every work in bronze. When he came to King Solomon, he made all his work.”

This too was done for the sake of mystery. The Tyrian craftsman whom Solomon took as his assistant in the work signifies the ministers of the word chosen from the Gentiles. He is appropriately called a craftsman because he was the son of an Israelite widow. In that woman the Church of the present time is often represented: her husband, Christ, having tasted death, rose again and, reigning in heaven, left her behind on earth to continue her pilgrimage.

There is no need to labor over explaining how the sons of this widow are holy preachers, since all the elect confess themselves to be sons of the Church; and since the prophet specifically promises these preachers of the New Testament:

> “Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them princes over all the earth” (Psalm 44).

> “Hiram made all Solomon’s work.”

For holy teachers, while faithfully devoting themselves to the ministry of the word, perform the work of God. By speaking, they open outwardly the way of truth for those whom God himself has predestined inwardly, by illumination, for the eternal way.

> “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Corinthians 3).

> “He made this work from bronze,”

because the diligent teacher seeks to entrust the word to those who desire piously to receive it and preserve it perseveringly, and who also desire to proclaim more broadly to others what they themselves have learned. Bronze is known to be extremely durable and wholly sonorous.

> “And he cast two bronze columns, each column eighteen cubits high.”

These are the columns of which Paul says:

> “James, Cephas, and John, who were reputed to be pillars, gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, so that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcision” (Galatians 2).

By these words he seems almost to explain the mystery of the material columns: what they represented and why two were made. For they signify the apostles and all spiritual teachers, strong in faith and works and raised up in contemplation toward heavenly things.

There are two columns so that, by preaching, they may bring both the Gentiles and the circumcision into the Church. They stood in the vestibule before the doors of the temple and wonderfully adorned its entrance on either side by their dignity and beauty.

The door of the temple is the Lord, because no one comes to the Father except through him (John 14). As it is said elsewhere:

> “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John 10).

The columns stand on either side before this door when ministers of the word show both peoples the entrance to the kingdom of heaven. Whether someone comes to the faith of the Gospel from the light of the knowledge of the Law or from the severity of paganism, they have ministers prepared to show them the way by word and example.

Or certainly, because of these same columns it is written in the Book of Chronicles:

> “He also placed the columns in the vestibule of the temple, one on the right and the other on the left” (2 Chronicles 3).

The two columns were therefore made and arranged in such a way that they might teach us to keep the entrance to our heavenly homeland before the eyes of the mind both in prosperity and in adversity.

It should be noted in this sentence from the Book of Chronicles that I have quoted that the portico of the temple was also called the vestibule of the temple; and where we read in the prophets that the priests prayed between the vestibule of the temple and the altar, “between the portico and the altar” should be understood.

It is rightly remembered that each column had a height of eighteen cubits. For three and six make eighteen. Three pertains to faith because of the Holy Trinity; six to works, because the world was made in six days. Three is multiplied by six when the righteous person lives by faith and increases the knowledge of pious belief by the performance of good works.

A column eighteen cubits high stands before the temple doors when each outstanding preacher openly impresses upon everyone that only through faith and works of righteousness can we attain the heavenly joys of life. The prophet Isaiah explains this more fully when, speaking of the Lord who was to be born in the flesh, he says:

> “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isaiah 11).

There were therefore seven cord-meshes in each capital, because the elect fathers of both Testaments received knowledge through the grace of one and the same sevenfold Spirit.

> “And a line twelve cubits long encircled each column.”

The line of twelve cubits is the rule of apostolic teaching. It encircles both columns when every teacher, whether preaching to Jews or Gentiles, takes care to do and teach only what the Church received and learned through the apostles. If someone wishes to live or preach otherwise—rejecting apostolic decrees or preferring to establish whatever new things he pleases—he is not a column suitable for the temple of God. For by despising the apostolic statutes, he shows himself either too narrow because of his sluggishness or too inflated because of his pride to fit the thickness of a twelve-cubit line.

> “He also made two capitals, cast to be placed upon the tops of the columns: one capital was five cubits high, and the other capital was five cubits high.”

The heads of the columns—that is, their upper parts—are the hearts of faithful teachers. Just as the head directs the members, so all their works and words are directed by thoughts devoted to God.

The two capitals placed upon these heads are the two Testaments, to whose meditation and observance holy teachers submit themselves with their whole mind and body. Each capital was rightly five cubits high, because the Mosaic Law is contained in five books, and the entire series of the Old Testament encompasses five ages of the world. The New Testament proclaims nothing other than what Moses had foretold would be proclaimed through it, together with the prophets.

> “And fashioned like a net and chains woven together with wondrous workmanship. Each capital of the columns was cast.”

In the Book of Chronicles this is written:

> “And also chainwork in the sanctuary, and he placed it upon the tops of the columns” (2 Chronicles 3).

The appearance of chains and the likeness of a net in the capitals signify the variety of spiritual virtues in the saints, concerning which the Lord is praised in the Psalms:

> “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in gold, surrounded with variety” (Psalm 44);

that is, clothed in the shining garment of love and surrounded with the variety of different spiritual gifts.

Or certainly, the manifold interweaving of chains and the spreading of a net signify the many kinds of persons among the elect. By faithfully listening to and obeying the words of holy preachers, they adhere to them; like a net and little chains placed upon the capitals of the columns, they display to all who behold them the marvel of their own connection.

> “And he completed the columns and two rows of networks around each, to cover the capitals.”

There were indeed two rows of networks around the capital, but each row ran in sevenfold fashion, until, having gone around the capital, it returned to itself like a circle.

The sacramental meaning of this figure is not hidden. There are two rows of networks because the virtue of love has a twofold distinction: namely, we are commanded to love the Lord with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength, and our neighbor as ourselves. But each of those rows has seven networks of cords, because neither God nor neighbor can be loved without the grace of the Holy Spirit.

These networks were made to cover the capitals, that is, to surround them on every side in a circle, because every page of Holy Scripture, when rightly understood, proclaims throughout the grace of love and peace. The capitals are the volumes of the divine utterances; the networks are the bonds of mutual love. The capitals are covered with networks when the sacred utterances are, so to speak, shown on every side to be clothed with the gift of charity. For charity lies hidden both in those things that we do not understand in Scripture and in those that we do understand.

It is rightly added concerning these same networks or capitals:

> “which were above the top of the pomegranates.”

Pomegranates, whose nature is to surround many seeds within a single outer rind, are appropriately placed as a figure of the holy Church. By the protection of one catholic faith, it habitually encloses innumerable hosts of the elect.

The pomegranate can also signify the life and conduct of each just person. Like one rind enclosing many seeds, he takes care to fortify, lest they flow away, the many signs of spiritual thoughts and virtues with the firm guard of faith and humility and with every pious ministry.

The tops of the columns were surrounded on every side with pomegranates, because holy teachers must recall the life of the faithful who came before them and always strengthen their actions and words on every side by their examples. Otherwise, if they live or teach in any way contrary to the rule of those predecessors, they will fall into error.

## COMMENTARY ON THE BOOKS  
444

When it is said of the networks that they covered the capitals, which were above the top of the pomegranates, it appears, according to the order of the work itself, that the pomegranates were made around the capitals on the lower side, and that from those same pomegranates the networks arose, by which the capitals were partly covered.

The meaning of the mystery is clear: the networks were attached above the top of the pomegranates, since both belong to nearly the same significance, whether of persons or of spiritual virtues. For we know that virtues arise from virtues, and that the saints proceed from virtue to virtue until the God of gods is seen in Zion—a virtue than which none greater can be named. Hence the Apostle says:

> “Knowing that tribulation produces patience, patience produces testing, and testing produces hope” (Romans 5).

> “The capitals that were upon the tops of the columns were made like the work of a lily, in the portico, four cubits.”

What else is signified by lilies but the pleasantness of paradise, fragrant with the flowers of the brightness of the heavenly homeland and immortality? What else by four but the Gospel message, which promises us entrance into that eternal blessedness and shows the way by which we may reach it?

When holy teachers show us the promised thresholds of the heavenly kingdom in the four books of the Gospel, they display, as it were, upon the heads of the columns a work of lilies four cubits in extent.

Here one should note literally that, when the work of the lily in the capitals is said to be four cubits, and neither its breadth nor its height is added, it is left to the reader’s judgment whether this should be understood as referring to height or breadth. It is certain, without any doubt, that the column which the twelve-cubit cord encircled had a thickness of four cubits. Every circle has in its circumference three times the space that it has in its diameter. Thus the bronze sea, whose diameter was ten cubits, as is read below, consequently had thirty cubits in circumference.

But because the work of the lily is said to have been four cubits, whether this indicates its breadth or its height, the meaning of the figure is nevertheless clear. For only through the Gospel does that most desirable voice resound throughout the world:

> “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew 3).

What follows is:

> “And again there were other capitals at the top of the columns above, according to the measure of the columns,”

that is, they were as broad as the column itself, although the height of the column is not reported.

These capitals, whatever their form and whatever their size—for Scripture does not openly specify their dimensions—appear to have been placed in the mouths of the lilies. If one wishes to inquire into their mystical meaning, they may not incongruously signify the sublimity of the everlasting kingdom,

> “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2).

Since that same heavenly fellowship of citizens is granted to the faithful of both peoples, it is rightly added:

> “There were two hundred rows of pomegranates around the second capital.”

For, as we have said, pomegranates represent either the whole holy Church or each of the faithful individually. The number one hundred, which is the first number to reach the right hand, is often accustomed to be placed as a figure of eternal blessedness. This number of pomegranates is doubled around the second capital, to signify mystically that the people of both Testaments are to be united in Christ and brought into the crown of eternal life.

> “And he set up two columns in the portico of the temple. When he had set up the right-hand column, he called its name Jachin,”

which is interpreted as “firmness.”

> “Likewise he raised up the second column and called its name Boaz,”

that is, “in strength.”

The right-hand column, as we said above, represents those teachers who established the primitive Church in Jerusalem. The second represents those who were sent to preach to the Gentiles.

Or certainly the right-hand column signifies those who foretold by prophecy that the Lord would come in the flesh; the second signifies those who testify that he has already come and redeemed the world by his blood.

Both columns were appropriately designated by similar names: one was called “firmness,” the other “in strength,” to show that the strength of faith and works ought to be present in all teachers, and to expose the inertia of our own time. Some teachers, priests, and columns of the house of God wish to be seen and called such, although they possess no firmness of faith within themselves, no strength to despise the pomps of the world and desire invisible goods, no vigor for correcting the errors of those placed under their authority, and not even diligence for understanding them.

> “He also made the cast bronze sea, ten cubits from rim to rim, circular all around.”

This cast sea was made in the form of the saving font in which we are cleansed for the remission of sins. For the priests washed in it, as the Book of Chronicles clearly attests. In Scripture, priests are understood typologically to signify all the elect, because they are members of our high priest, the Lord Jesus Christ.

Scripture rightly gave this vessel the name “sea,” evidently in memory of the Red Sea, in which, through the drowning of the Egyptians and the liberation of God’s people, the pattern of baptism first took place. The Apostle explains this, saying:

> “Our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Corinthians 10).

The sacrament of baptism seeks purity of life for us in this age and promises us the glory of eternal life in the age to come. Both are signified in one statement by this bronze sea when it is said to be ten cubits from rim to rim.

For the Lord expressed in the ten commandments all that we ought to do. He also signified the reward of good works by the denarius when he foretold that it would be given to those laboring in the vineyard.

The sea was therefore “ten cubits from rim to rim,” because from the first person baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, up to
