[scan page 227]

# Angelomus, Monk of Luxeuil

…to the last, who at the end of the age will be believed and baptized, the entire chorus of the faithful must enter by one and the same way and hope from the Lord for the common crown of justice.

“It was round all around,” so that the whole world, in its circular expanse, might be shown as cleansed from the filth of sins by the laver of life. Of this it is rightly added: “Its height was five cubits,” because whatever we sin by sight, hearing, smell, taste, or touch, all this the grace of God releases for us through the washing of the life-giving font.

But forgiveness of past sins is not enough if thereafter each person does not strive to persist in good works. Otherwise the devil who had departed from the man, if he sees him empty of good things, returns with others, and “the last state of that man becomes worse than the first” (Matt. 12). Hence it is appropriately added:

“And a cord of thirty cubits surrounded it all around.” By the cord may fittingly be signified the discipline of heavenly commandments, by which we are driven away from our pleasures. Scripture says: “A threefold cord is not easily broken,” because observance of God’s commandments, which is made firm in the hearts of the elect by faith, hope, and love of heavenly reward, cannot be dissolved by any temporal obstacle.

“And sculptured work was beneath its rim all around, encircling it; ten cubits embraced the sea. There were two rows of sculptured work in relief, cast.” Since it was stated above that a cord of thirty cubits surrounded the sea, and it is now added that the sculptured work placed beneath the rim encircled it for ten cubits, it is clear from both statements that the vessel was made in the likeness of a broad and expanded bowl, whose circumference at the rim—thirty cubits—was narrowed to ten cubits below. The sculptured work was in relief, imitating certain stories of events. Hence, appropriately, through the reliefs by which the sea was surrounded, examples of earlier times were signified, which we must diligently contemplate, so that we may see by what works the saints pleased God from the beginning, through what obstinacy the wicked persisted in crimes, and with what misery they perished because of their sins.

“And it stood upon twelve oxen. Three looked toward the north, three toward the west, three toward the south, and three toward the east.” The twelve oxen are therefore the twelve apostles, and all who have received the governance of the holy Church in Christ through their teaching. These oxen bear the sea placed upon them when the apostles and their successors strive with ready devotion to fulfill the evangelizing office entrusted to them. Three look toward the north, three toward the west, three toward the south, and three toward the east when they preach the faith of the holy Trinity to the parts of the universal square of the world.

“Their hindquarters were all hidden within.” For the reward with which holy preachers are to be endowed forever has been determined in the judgment of the eternal Judge; but for us, who are still outside, it remains entirely hidden. Nevertheless, it cannot be wholly hidden from those who receive the laver of baptism for salvation and must possess true faith, hope, and charity; without these three virtues no one can accomplish anything, nor can anyone enter into life. Hence it is rightly added:

“The thickness of the laver was three handbreadths.” The thickness of the laver—that is, of the sea—is the firmness of virtue in baptism. Its thickness is three handbreadths when the reception of baptism is fortified by the strength of faith, hope, and love. It is shown not to be profitable to those who receive it unless the firm certainty of these virtues, together with the works of the recipients, confirms the mind.

“And its rim was like the rim of a cup, and its edge spread out like a lily.” By the rim of the cup the taste of the Lord’s Passion is expressed; by the edge spread out like a lily, the revealed splendor of his resurrection is signified.

“It held two thousand baths.” The number one thousand is customarily used in Scripture as a sign of perfection. For the number ten, multiplied by itself, makes one hundred. This figure is already squared, but is not yet complete. To make it rise in height and become solid, multiply one hundred by ten, and it becomes one thousand. By this number the stable, unconquerable, and, as it were, squared conscience of the righteous is signified. However one turns a square, it stands. So the mind, too, does not know how to be bent from the state of its uprightness by any assault of temptations.

The bath is a Hebrew measure, which they themselves call *bath*. It contains four *modii* and an *ephah*, which they call *epha*. The *ephah* is a measure for various dry crops—wheat, barley, and legumes. The bath, however, is used for liquids, wine, oil, and water. Thus the bath, because it is a fixed standard of measure, signifies the works of equity and justice by which those who are baptized for the remission of sins must necessarily be trained.

The sea held two thousand baths when, washing the people of the Jews with the water of baptism, it conveyed them to the heavenly kingdom. It also held another thousand when it made the crowds of the nations, reborn in the same font and confirmed by works of justice, sharers in that kingdom forever.

“And he made ten bases of bronze, each base four cubits long, four cubits wide, and three cubits high; and the construction of the bases was interlaced, and so forth.” In many ways and by many means, the one and same mysteries of our salvation are prefigured. For the same apostles and apostolic men who are signified by the oxen bearing the sea are also signified by the bases prepared for carrying the lavers, just as the lavers themselves represented the same spiritual washing that the sea also represented.

For the Books of Chronicles relate that everything offered for holocausts was washed in them. The holocaust, however, may generally be understood as the whole multitude of the elect, which, in accordance with the voice of the Forerunner, was baptized by him in the Holy Spirit and fire. Thus, just as the priests who washed in the sea…

[scan page 228]

# Commentary on the Books of Kings — Book III

…represented those who are made fellow heirs of the supreme Priest, the Lord Jesus Christ, through baptism, so too the holocausts most aptly represent the same people after baptism, when they are filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit. The victim is washed in the laver when one of the faithful is drenched with the water of baptism. It is carried to the holocaust when, through the laying on of the bishop’s hands, they receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.

That ten bases were made for carrying the lavers may be interpreted mystically: the ministers of the life-giving laver dedicate those whom they instruct to the eternal joys of blessedness, which are customarily represented by the number ten. But since it is written more distinctly about these same lavers in what follows, namely, that five of them were placed on the right side of the temple and five on the left, the mysteries contained in the number five are to be observed especially in them. Bases for the lavers were placed on both sides of the temple so that they might signify that the grace of the sacred font was to be opened to both peoples of God. And there were five on each side so that, as we have already said in the exposition of the sea, which was five cubits high, it might be shown typologically that all the sins committed by the faithful through the five bodily senses are forgiven through the laver of baptism.

Thus, just as in the one sea, borne upon twelve oxen, the unity of baptism was expressed, which was to be preached throughout the world by the apostles, so also through the two rows of lavers it is mystically shown that the Gentiles were to be gathered together with the Jews into one fellowship of faith. That each base was four cubits long, four cubits wide, and three cubits high is easily understood. Length pertains to the patience of long-suffering; width to the breadth of love; height to hope of heavenly reward.

There are four principal virtues, upon which the structure of the other virtues rests: prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice. Therefore the bases were four cubits in length and width, because the holy preachers, whether they bear outwardly the adversities of the world and the length of their present labors, or enlarge their heart inwardly through love of their Creator and their neighbors, always strive to devote themselves to the virtues: prudently discerning between good and evil, bravely enduring adversity, tempering the heart from the desire for pleasures, and maintaining justice in action.

The bases were three cubits high when, through the exercise of the virtues by which they practice patience in adversity and love of what is good, they strive with constant attention to attain the vision of the holy Trinity.

“And the construction of the bases was interlaced, and there were panels between the joints.” He seems to call “joints” those places where the boards of the lavers were joined to one another, so that one base was made from four or five boards. Whatever carvings the bases had between the joints, that is, on their own sides, are explained below.

“And between the little crowns and the interlaced work were lions, oxen, and cherubim, and likewise above upon the joints.” Thus no side of the bases had a flat surface; rather, they were engraved on every side with mystical figures, because the minds of the saints—indeed, their whole manner of life—display the grace of virtues in all things. No hour passes for them empty and idle, in which they cease from devout works, words, or thoughts. They have little crowns sculptured upon them when, amid the desire for the heavenly country that is above, they never dissolve the bonds of fraternal fellowship that is near at hand. They have lions among the little crowns and interlaced work when, as they raise their minds to hope for heavenly things, so they also expand themselves in love for their neighbors, and do not delay to exercise the fervor of stern rebuke against sinners entrusted to them. They have oxen with the lions when they exercise that same rebuke in correcting others while displaying a spirit of gentleness; when, in their zeal for rebuke, they never cease to possess the cloven hoof of discerning conduct and speech, nor to turn over in their mouths, as it were by chewing the cud, the words of divine reading.

“And beneath the lions and oxen there hung down, as it were, straps of bronze,” when holy teachers, both in the strictness of truth by which they judge sinners and in the gentleness of mildness by which they forgive the penitent, fear the judgment of their Creator, lest perhaps in binding or loosing anyone they should deserve to act unjustly or incur the judgment of him who cannot err.

“And four wheels belonged to each base, with axles of bronze; and at the four corners there were supports beneath the laver, cast facing one another.” The four wheels are the four books of the Gospels, which are most appropriately compared to wheels. For just as the turning of a wheel runs with swift course wherever it is led, so the evangelical word, at the Lord’s command, quickly filled all the regions of the world through the apostles.

Just as the whole earth, placed upon a vehicle, is lifted by it and, once lifted, is carried wherever the driver directs, so evangelical preaching lifts the minds of the elect from earthly desires to heavenly longings, and, once lifted, guides them toward progress in good action or toward the ministry of preaching wherever the grace of the Spirit wills to lead them. For he says below: “The wheels were made like the wheels of a chariot.”

We read of the saints: “The chariots of God are ten thousand, many thousands rejoicing” (Ps. 68). If, therefore, the bases of the lavers are holy teachers who minister to us the laver of life, and the wheels of the bases are the four books of the Gospels, what are the axles of the wheels that carry the bases except the very hearts of those teachers? While they earnestly apply themselves to the commandments of the Gospel, they loosen them from the desire for lower things, like axles inserted into wheels, and lift the base higher from the earth.

The supports placed before the wheels, so that they could not slip from the axles, are the prophets, through whom the evangelical and apostolic Scripture is confirmed, lest any reader should perhaps fall into doubt.

It is rightly said that the supports placed beneath the laver on its four sides faced one another, because all the prophecy of Scripture agrees with itself, having been composed by one Spirit of God. There were four supports for each base, corresponding to the number of wheels—not because there are only four prophetic books, but because in all that the prophets and Moses spoke, they provided testimony to the words of the four Evangelists. Thus, through the agreement of both Testaments, one faith and love of Christ might strengthen the hearts of us all.

[scan page 229]

# Angelomus

“And the opening of the laver was within, at the top of the head; and what appeared outside was one cubit in all, round, and it also had a cubit and a half.” The opening of the laver was one cubit, because of the unity of confession and faith: we are all baptized in confession of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, as the Apostle says: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all” (Eph. 4). The opening was at the top of the head to teach that through baptism a way has been opened for us to the heavenly kingdom.

The laver itself was one and a half cubits in breadth, signifying the perfection of action and the beginning of contemplation. The whole cubit in the laver signifies the perfection of good action, which that man possessed without any doubt concerning whom the Lord said to the tempter: “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth—a simple and upright man, fearing God and turning away from evil?” (Job 1).

The other half cubit is the vision of God, which is customarily granted in part even in this life to the faithful who remain here. Thus the same Job, after conquering the adversary, says to the Lord: “I have heard you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you” (Job 42).

For it is written below:

“One wheel was one cubit and a half high.”

And shortly afterward:

“At the top of the base there was a rounded surface of one and a half cubits, so fashioned that the laver could be placed upon it.”

The lavers measured one and a half cubits, because we are washed in the font of life with such faith that through works of justice we may enter into life, although, while we live here, we cannot be without sin. We can taste in part and love the sweetness of heavenly life during the present life, but we cannot fully see it by any means.

The wheel, too, was measured at one and a half cubits, because the reading of evangelical Scripture shows how those who wish to be perfect ought to live and demonstrates to us in the present the hope of eternal reward; it promises that the nature of that reward will be revealed and given to us in the future.

The bases themselves also had a breadth of one and a half cubits at their top, where they received the lavers, because those supreme teachers and ministers of salvation shone forth as perfect in their works in this life, but enjoyed the light of contemplation only in part. Hence they say: “We know in part and we prophesy in part. But when perfection has come, what is in part will be abolished” (1 Cor. 13).

“In this manner he made ten bases, cast alike, with the same measurement and similar sculptured work. He also made ten bronze lavers.”

Why ten bases were made, and as many lavers placed upon them, has already been explained. But the fact that all the bases or lavers had one casting, one measurement, and similar sculptured work was not done to signify that the merits of all teachers could be equal; rather, it signified that there is one faith of the Gospel by which they are instructed, one sacrament of baptism by which they are washed, and one and the same Spirit by whom all the elect are consecrated, although they have different gifts in that Spirit, who distributes to each as he wills (1 Cor. 12).

“One laver held forty baths.” The number forty generally represents great perfection, since four times ten makes forty. Ten are the commandments by which all our action is prescribed in the divine law. There are also four books of the Gospels, in which, through the dispensation of the Lord’s incarnation, the entrance to our heavenly homeland has been opened to us. Since all who belong to the mystery of baptism must, with faith and the sacraments of the Gospel, display the fruit of right action, the individual lavers in which the holocausts were washed appropriately held forty baths.

What follows—“And it was four cubits”—whether this refers to height or breadth, is readily understood as a mystery. One laver was four cubits either because of the books of the holy Gospel, in which the form of baptism has been set before us, or because of the four cardinal virtues by which every faithful person, if faithful not in vain, must be instructed, or because of the four regions of the world in which the laver of salvation is administered, as the Psalmist says: “Those whom he redeemed he gathered from the regions, from the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea” (Ps. 107).

When he said above that it also had one cubit, without adding whether he meant height or breadth, he seems to have wished it understood that the bottom of the laver had a breadth of one cubit. The measurement of the base on which each laver was placed may very easily be inferred from the following description:

“At the top of the base there was a rounded surface of one and a half cubits, so fashioned that the laver could be placed upon it, having its own panels and various sculptures. On those panels, which were of bronze and copper, he also carved cherubim, lions, and palm trees, as though in the likeness of a standing man, so that they appeared not carved but applied around it. In this manner he made ten bases, with one casting, the same measurement, and similar sculptured work. He also made ten bronze lavers. One laver held forty baths; it was…”

[scan page 230]

# Commentary on the Books of Kings

“…four cubits,” and so forth. The breadth of the bottom of the lavers was therefore one and a half cubits, while the capacity of the lavers was four cubits. But whether he speaks of height, breadth, or both, who can know?

“And he placed ten bases, five on the right side of the temple and five on the left.”

By the right and left side of the temple he does not mean inside the temple itself, but before the temple, toward the eastern region, in the court called specifically the priests’ court.

He placed them on the right side of the temple because of the Jews, who in ancient times were accustomed to use justice through the teaching of the Law. And he placed five on the left because of us, who for a long time had clung in blind hearts to the servitude of him who says: “I will set my throne in the north.” This openly means: “I desire to rest in those hearts which I perceive to be alienated from the light of truth and the flame of divine love.”

“And he placed the sea on the right side of the temple, opposite the east, toward the south.” This too was placed in the same court, toward the east. What he calls the right side of the temple he repeats by saying “toward the south.” For those entering the court from the east had first to turn toward the south, where the sea stood in the very corner, prepared for the washing of the priests. Then, as they proceeded farther, the lavers placed on both sides appeared before them for the washing of the victims.

Among these was a bronze base, five cubits long, five cubits wide, and three cubits high, on which Solomon stood and dedicated the temple. As they proceeded farther, the altar of holocausts appeared opposite the middle of the court; beyond it was the portico of the temple, or vestibule, in which bronze columns stood around the entrance to the temple.

That he placed the sea on the right side of the temple signifies that through the laver of baptism we must reach the heavenly kingdom, which is rightly represented by the term “right.” “For whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark 16).

Where both right and left are taken in a good sense, they signify either Judea and the Gentiles—as we said above in the exposition of the bases—or the present life and the future life of the Church, or joyful and sorrowful things, or something of this kind. But where the right is placed absolutely in a good sense, it most often demonstrates eternal joys.

That he placed the sea opposite the east looks to the same meaning: through the washing of the sacred font, the splendor of inward brightness is disclosed to us. That he placed it on the southern side of the court signifies that through receiving the Holy Spirit the faithful are accustomed to be kindled for the burning love of charity. In Scripture the heat of the southern sun commonly signifies both the ardor of love and the illumination of the Holy Spirit, through whom that same love is poured into the hearts of the elect.

“All the vessels that Hiram made for King Solomon in the house of the Lord were of bronze. In the plain of the Jordan the king cast them in clayey ground.”

The vessels of the house of the Lord were appropriately cast in the region of the Jordan, in the river in which our Lord deigned to be baptized and, having been immersed in its waters, transformed the element into an instrument for the washing away of sins. Since every baptism of the faithful, by which they are consecrated to the Lord, is celebrated as an imitation of that baptism by which he himself sanctified the waters, the vessels of the Lord were rightly made in the region of the Jordan.

For we cannot otherwise become vessels of election and mercy unless, looking to the baptism which he underwent in that river, we too strive to be washed in the life-giving river. It should be noted, however, that these vessels are said to have been made not only in the region of the Jordan but in its plain, signifying the future multiplication of the faithful, which was to occur not only in Judea but in the breadth of all nations, fulfilling the prophecy: “The plains and all that is in them will rejoice” (Ps. 96).

What better can be understood by the clayey ground from which the molds for casting the vessels of the Lord were made than Holy Scripture, from which we receive the rule of good living? Just as clay hardened by fires presents the form of the vessel of the Lord and shows how great and of what kind the vessels ought to be, so Holy Scripture shows us the rule of justice that we are to follow and sets before us the examples of the saints who persevered invincible through the fire of tribulations, to be followed in all things.

Yet we see that the vessels in the house of the Lord are chosen and precious, and that the bronze, melted by fire, enters the clay molds so that the vessel may be made suitable for heavenly ministries. This occurs when we, profitably humbled and softened by the flame either of divine brightness or of human adversity, enter by good works upon the way of our fathers, so that by living well we may reach the rewards of our fathers.

“And Solomon made all the vessels in the house of the Lord: the golden altar and the golden table on which the bread of the Presence was to be placed.”

The golden altar signifies the hearts of the perfect righteous, shining with the light of inward love and purity. The place of that altar is also appropriate for signifying their sublimity. It stood before the entrance of the Holy of Holies, as we plainly read in the construction of the tabernacle.

On that altar neither the blood of victims nor libations were burned, but only incense. Its smoke ascended above, covered the ark, and filled the oracle with the fragrance of sweetness. In this was represented the figure of the saints, who, neglecting the desires of temporal things and seeking heavenly things with their whole attention, are placed near the oracle and are not far removed from the veil that separates the temple and the Holy of Holies. Although in body they inhabit the earth, according to the inner person they have their whole manner of life in heaven.

The smoke of incense rises from such an altar into the Holy of Holies, where the ark is hidden, when the prayers of the saints, kindled by the flame of charity, reach heaven itself, where Christ sits at the right hand of God. For on this altar the blood of victims is not burned, but only incense, because such men do not possess works of flesh and blood which they might sacrifice and slay for the Lord upon the altar of their hearts, but only tears and…

[scan page 231]

# Angelomus, Monk of Luxeuil

…prayers and vows, offered for the desire of the heavenly kingdom, as the Psalmist says: “You have prepared a table before me in the sight of those who trouble me” (Ps. 23).

Lest our adversaries, by troubling us, bend us toward error, our Redeemer has prepared for us the table of heavenly knowledge, through which we may be strengthened in the faith of truth.

The bread of the Presence signifies the holy teachers, whose works or saving words are always set before us as an example of life. Hence these same loaves were rightly and fittingly commanded in Exodus to be made twelve in number, namely on account of the twelve apostles, through whose ministry the Scripture of the New Testament was composed for us and, by the Lord’s gift, the mysteries of the Old Instrument were revealed. By their number are signified not only the apostles themselves, but all those who, by preaching the word, minister the food of life to the faithful; for all follow the form of doctrine that the apostles received from the Lord.

As to the size of this altar, Scripture does not state how great an altar Solomon made, but it nevertheless says that he made a golden altar. It is clear, however, that it was made no larger than the altar of holocausts, since if it had been twenty cubits in length and breadth, it would have occupied the entire width of the temple.

Therefore, the more exterior the altar of holocausts was than the altar of incense, and the more inferior it was in the kind of offering and in the baseness of its metal, the more it excelled in the magnitude of its measurements and in the frequency of its victims. For there are many to whom it is said: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matt. 19). But there are many fewer whom it pleases to hear: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor.”

Nevertheless, the measurement of this altar is not without mystical meaning. It had twenty cubits in length, the same in breadth, and ten cubits in height. We spoke above, in the exposition of the temple and its vestibule, about this number. But it must now be said briefly that, if the altar of holocausts holds the type of those in the Church who seek to consecrate body and soul to the Lord through the fire of his love, their perseverance in good action is represented by the length of the altar, breadth by love of God and neighbor, and height by hope in the contemplation of divine vision.

The fact that the altar’s length and breadth were twenty cubits clearly signifies the great perfection of the same tireless long-suffering and sincere love, which is granted to us through observance of both Testaments. For four times five makes twenty. The five books of the Mosaic Law are joined to the four books of evangelical freedom. When, with the grace of the Gospel enlightening us, we attain spiritual understanding and observance of the Law, we complete this twenty as a number of perfection.

The same number is found in the length and breadth of the altar when the hearts of the elect, instructed by both Testaments and assisted by the one author of both Testaments, preserve perseverance in good works even under persecution, in the joy of love, and display it even toward those who persecute them.

The number ten generally signifies hope of heavenly rewards, as when the Lord assures us that those who labor in the vineyard of the great householder are rewarded with a denarius. The same altar, made as a figure of the elect to signify their perpetual life, was ten cubits high.

Because it was said that Solomon made a golden altar, it is immediately added that he made a golden table on which the bread of the Presence was placed. The golden table is Holy Scripture of spiritual understanding, shining with brightness, concerning which the Psalmist says to the Lord: “You have prepared before me a table in the presence of my enemies.”

For just as the altar of incense signifies the holy doctors, who offer the sacrifice of prayers to God, so the golden table signifies those same doctors, who, by preaching, provide the food of life to the faithful, because all follow the form of doctrine that they received from the Lord through the apostles.

What we read in the Books of Chronicles (2 Chron. 4)—that Solomon made ten tables and placed them in the temple, five on the right and five on the left, and also one hundred golden bowls—we may understand mystically in several ways. These tables were probably made not so much for the bread of the Presence as for carrying the vessels of the Lord: the bowls, that is, which Scripture reports were made together with the incense vessels and the other objects mentioned below.

When, shortly afterward, in the same book, it says: “Solomon made all the vessels of the house of the Lord God, and the altar of bronze, and the tables, and upon them the bread of the Presence,” it may either use the plural number for the singular, in the very common manner of Scripture—as in Joshua: “The children of Israel transgressed the commandment and took from the devoted thing” (Josh. 7), although Achan alone, and not several of the children of Israel, did this—or it may be because the bread of the Presence was customarily baked before the Sabbath so that it could immediately be placed upon the table of the Presence on the Sabbath.

It could have happened that newly baked loaves were placed upon those tables, and there kept covered during that night, until at first light, after the vessels had been removed, they were placed warm upon the table of the Presence.

These ten tables do not differ in figure from the one table of the Presence. Just as one table laden with twelve loaves signifies the unanimous harmony of all Scripture, fortified by apostolic authority, so the ten golden tables figuratively signify the divine words of the Law and the Prophets, which either offer us refreshment through the word of God, like the bread of the Presence, or set before us the examples of the faithful, like vessels of the Lord placed upon them, together with their brightness and miracles.

There are rightly five tables on each side, not only because the Lawgiver wrote five books, but also because the whole sequence of the Old Testament encompasses five ages of the world. The number of the tables is doubled: five are placed on the right and five on the left, when, after the Lord’s incarnation, the same Scripture is handed on to both peoples of God, namely Jews and Gentiles, and the access to evangelical preaching is opened [final words materially uncertain because of OCR].

[scan page 232]

**COMMENTARY ON THE BOOKS OF THE KINGS — BOOK III**

**453**

which was once thought to be understood only according to the letter by the ancient people of God.

> “He also made the basins, the forks, the bowls, and the mortars of purest gold.”

For the basins signify the hearts of the saints, filled with the water of wisdom and the wine of compunction. The forks, likewise, with which meats are prepared, prefigure the same preachers, whose words are like goads and like nails driven deep: they administer to their hearers the food of spiritual understanding. Their office, moreover, is to distribute the body and blood of the Lord to believers and to deny them to unbelievers; more will be said concerning them below. The bowls signify the apostles and teachers, full of life-giving waters. The mortars signify the labor and patient endurance of holy penitents, by which they put to death the members of their bodies that are upon the earth. The censers signify the virtues of works, or certainly the prayers of the saints, by which the fragrance of sweetness rises to God from a pure conscience and an unfeigned faith.

> “And he made five golden lampstands on the right and five on the left, opposite the oracle, of pure gold, with something like lily-blossoms, and golden lamps above them.”

For just as tables are rightly understood as figures of Holy Scripture—since they provide the hungry with the bread of the word of God, and since the vessels were ministers of heaven, that is, they present to us the examples of the righteous—so also the same divine utterances are most appropriately signified by the lampstands, because they bring the light of wisdom to those who wander. Hence the Psalmist says:

> “Your word is a lamp to my feet, O Lord, and a light to my paths” (Psalm 118 [119]).

Solomon likewise says:

> “For the commandment is a lamp, and the law is light” (Proverbs 6).

Why, however, five lampstands were placed on the right and five on the left is readily apparent from what we have discussed concerning the tables. When he had said, “five on the right and five on the left,” he suitably added, “opposite the oracle.” For the oracle, where the ark was, as has often been said, signifies the entrance to the heavenly homeland, where Christ sits at the right hand of God, the eternal knower of mysteries. The golden lampstands of the temple were placed opposite the oracle because the divine utterances always look toward the dwelling of the heavenly city, so that they may kindle in our hearts the knowledge and desire of it, and may set those who have an eternal origin in the flesh aflame with the desire to seek and obtain an everlasting dwelling in heaven.

But if you ask what typological distinction there is between the lampstands and their lamps, we can rightly understand the lamps to be the holy men who, infused by the Holy Spirit, themselves burn in their hearts with the fire of love and bring the light of knowledge to their neighbors by their speech. The lampstands, however, which hold these lamps aloft so that they may be seen far and wide, are the sacred Scriptures in the Church, which by their reading display to us the virtues and teaching of the saints.

The Lord’s saying, in which it is spoken of John, confirms this interpretation:

> “He was a burning and shining lamp” (John 5).

It is also fittingly said that the divine utterances are lamps, in accordance with the Psalmist’s words cited above:

> “Your word is a lamp to my feet, O Lord, and a light to my paths.”

The golden lampstands of these lamps are all the saints, who submissively place their hearts and bodies beneath the commandments of the Lord. Whoever does not seek to follow his own will in anything, but strives to fulfill everything that Holy Scripture commands, to subject himself to its precepts, and to listen eagerly to its promises, bears, as it were, as a golden lampstand of the house of God, its golden lamps—namely, the chaste members of his body and the chaste thoughts of his mind—and strives to subject them to doing what God commands, with an intention as steadfast as the lampstand. For it is necessary that the lampstand, raised firmly toward heavenly things, preserve the lamps entrusted to it not only without damage but also without any movement of its position.

When he had said, “five golden lampstands on the right and five on the left, opposite the oracle, of pure gold,” he added, “with something like lily-blossoms and golden lamps above them.” According to the literal sense, this seems to mean that the upper part of the lampstands was fashioned in the form of an open lily, as we read that this was done in the lampstand of the tabernacle. Its central shaft and the branches proceeding from it are said to have had many cups and knobs in the shape of lilies.

These lilies, as has often been said, signify the eternity of the ever-flourishing land of the living. Concerning them blessed Peter says that we have been regenerated by the Lord into a living hope, into an incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading inheritance, kept in heaven (1 Peter 1). The golden lily-blossoms on the lampstands are therefore rightly understood as the works of the Lord’s servants, because divine Scripture, scorning temporal joys, habitually urges us to desire the goods of the heavenly homeland. And just as an upright lampstand has golden lily-blossoms and lamps at its summit, so all the elect contained in that same sacred Scripture are shown, with their minds raised toward heavenly things, to have sought and obtained heavenly goods from the Lord.

> “And the hinges of the doors of the inner temple, the Holy of Holies, and of the doors of the temple sanctuary were of gold.”

The doors of the inner house, the Holy of Holies, signify the angelic ministries, which unlock for us, when we have departed from the body, the entrance to heavenly life. The doors of the temple house signify the holy teachers and priests, who, by teaching, baptizing, and communicating the mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood, open for the sons of the present Church the first gates of salvation.

What are the hinges of both sets of doors except the understanding and hearts of those same angels or holy men? They cling immovably to the contemplation and love of their Creator, so that they may rightly fulfill the divine ministry assigned to them, never turning their eyes away from the will of the one whom they serve. The doors are opened and closed at an appropriate time, but the hinges never leave their place at any time, because angels and all saints, whether in this life of faith or in that life of hope, receive the faithful and elect and hold fast [the concluding object is uncertain in the damaged text].

[scan page 233]

**ANGELomus OF LUXEUIL**

**455**

Hence the same hinges are rightly said to have been made of gold, either because of the merit of their own radiance or because of the love that they possess for God.

> “And Solomon completed all the work that King Solomon was doing in the house of the Lord.”

Our peaceful king Solomon completed the work that he was doing in the house of the Lord when, on the last day, he glorifies all the elect with the immortality of the resurrection. Otherwise, as long as the condition of this age continues, Solomon has indeed done the work of the house of the Lord, but has not yet completed it, because the Lord inspires and assists the hearts of the elect so that they may do good. Yet he does not grant anyone who remains in this life to be without sin, for he reserves this gift for the blessedness of the future life.

He completes every work of his temple and makes it suitable for dedication when he brings his elect, transferred from this life, into the eternal kingdom. This is also well signified by the fact that the temple was built in four years but completed and dedicated in the eighth, for the whole of this period is encompassed by seven days. The eighth is the day of judgment and the future resurrection; the sixth and eleventh Psalms were entitled with reference to it.

To this time the following is appropriately related:

> “And he brought in what David his father had sanctified, silver, gold, and vessels, and placed them in the treasuries of the house of the Lord.”

Silver signifies the radiance of eloquence, gold the splendor of wisdom, and vessels generally signify rational creatures. David, Solomon’s father, sanctifies the silver when God strengthens eloquent men by the grace of his Spirit to speak the word of the Gospel. He sanctifies the gold when, filling those who have been ruined by natural ingenuity with his Spirit, he enlightens them to contemplate his wonders in the law. He also sanctifies the vessels when he bestows upon all the children of the Church generally the grace of the same Spirit, which inflames them to love and desire the gifts of perpetual salvation.

Solomon brings this silver, this gold, and these sanctified vessels into the temple when our Lord, after the universal judgment, introduces all the elect—the company both of teachers and of the other faithful—into the joy of the heavenly kingdom. He places vessels of different kinds, whether silver or gold, in the treasuries of the house of the Lord when he hides those who have deserved to enjoy the abundance of his sweetness in the secret place of his face, away from the disturbance of human beings.

There are appropriately many treasuries in which the vessels of election are stored, but only one house of the Lord in which these treasuries are made, because there is one Church in which all the elect are contained, however much they differ in merits. There is likewise one, not several, heavenly homeland promised to all the elect, although, just as star differs from star in glory, so also is the resurrection of the dead.

The Judge and distributor of rewards himself demonstrated this in a single saying when he said:

> “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John 14).

### CHAPTER VIII

> “And the priests brought the ark of the covenant of the Lord into its place, into the oracle of the temple, into the Holy of Holies, beneath the wings of the cherubim. For the cherubim spread their wings over the place of the ark and covered the ark and its poles from above. And when the poles projected and their ends appeared outside before the oracle, they were no longer visible externally, because they remained there to the present day. There was nothing in the ark except the two stone tablets that Moses had placed in it at Horeb, when the Lord made a covenant with the children of Israel as they went out from the land of Egypt,” and so forth.

The statement that the ark was brought into the Holy of Holies, and that when the poles projected and their ends appeared outside the sanctuary they were no longer visible externally, is expressed more clearly in the book of Chronicles (2 Chronicles 5):

> “The ends of the poles by which they carried the ark, because they were somewhat longer, were visible before the oracle.”

If someone had been standing a little way outside, however, he could not have seen them. It should be noted that although the ends of the poles were visible before the oracle to those who approached more closely and looked more carefully, they did not project outward. For it was necessary that, when the oracle was closed and the veil was hung before its doors, the poles too, together with the ark and the cherubim, should be drawn inside. This could not have happened if the projecting poles had extended outward and prevented room from being made for the doors to close.

Scripture took such care to explain the placement of the poles not without reason, but rather with close attention to its sacramental meaning. It is clear that the outer house of the temple signifies the Church journeying on earth, while the Holy of Holies signifies the interior blessedness of the heavenly homeland. The ark brought into the Holy of Holies signifies the humility assumed by Christ and brought within the veil of the heavenly kingdom.

The poles by which the same ark was carried typologically signify the preachers of the word, through whom he himself was made known to the world. In the ark there was a golden urn containing manna, because in the man Christ dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily. There was Aaron’s rod, which, though cut off, blossomed again, because all power of judgment belongs to him whose judgment seemed to have been taken away in the humility of his passion. There were the tablets of the covenant, because in him “are hidden all the treasures of wisdom” (Colossians 2).

The poles by which it was carried clung to it because the teachers who once labored in the word of Christ now rejoice together in the glory of Christ through present vision. What one of them said of himself—

> “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Philippians 1)—

he left to be understood of all his fellow workers.

The ends of the poles appeared outside before the oracle, not always, but when the doors of that oracle happened to be opened. Nor were they visible to everyone, but only to those who approached more closely and more attentively sought to look at what was inside. The ark itself, and the manner in which it was placed, could be seen only by those who had entered the oracle. For no saint still situated in this life, even if he raises himself to the heights of contemplation, can fully behold the glory of his Redeemer there; only the citizens of that homeland behold it completely.

The poles were also hidden with the ark in the oracle, because the perfected elect who have gone forth from the world are now hidden in the secret place of God’s face, away from the disturbance of human beings. Yet the ends of their poles are visible to those who approach when the oracle is opened, whenever divine grace grants those who purify the eye of their heart with complete attention a glimpse of the joy of the heavenly citizens. Contemplation is not granted to those who have withdrawn too far away: the more they remain outside with wandering minds, the less they see what the inward joys are.

**COMMENTARY ON THE BOOKS**

**457**

> “And when the priests had come out of the sanctuary, a cloud filled the house of the Lord, and the priests could not stand and minister because of the cloud. For the glory of the Lord had filled the house of the Lord,” and so forth.

The statement that a cloud filled the house of the Lord, and that the priests could not stand and minister because of the cloud, indicates proud high priests and teachers who, while they disdain to investigate the mysteries of Christ’s birth, lost the ministry owed to God through the cloud of error. The darkness of unbelief filled their minds so completely that, as their own merits demanded, they did not recognize the worship of faith.

The cloud therefore filled the Synagogue, that is, the house of the Lord, and the priests could not minister because of the cloud, because, while they disdained to investigate the mystical meanings of the letter of the Old Testament, covered by a veil amid the dark obscurities of allegories, they lost the ministry of the faith owed to God on account of the cloud.

To them, even then, the Lord uttered his voice in the cloud of their teaching, when he spoke openly about himself. For what is more open than:

> “I and the Father are one” (John 10)?

What is clearer than:

> “Before Abraham was, I am” (John 8)?

But because the minds of the hearers were filled with the darkness of unbelief, the intervening cloud concealed the ray of the sun, as though it had been emitted.

> “And the king and the children of Israel dedicated the temple of the Lord.”

The temple of the Lord is the holy Church, as was shown above. Christ the King dedicated it when he cleansed it with his blood, sanctified it by the grace of the Holy Spirit, and multiplied it with various gifts of virtue. The children of Israel also dedicate it with him when each of the faithful, according to the gift bestowed upon him by God, strives by the word of preaching and by works of virtue to turn all his neighbors whom he can toward better and more perfect things.

For the Apostle says:

> “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Corinthians 3).

But the king and the people, the head and the members, do not complete this sanctification equally, because John says concerning Christ:

> “Of his fullness we have all received, and grace for grace” (John 1).

Hence Paul says:

> “So neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3).

But how much the dedication performed by human beings is worth, the same Apostle explains subsequently when he says:

> “He who plants and he who waters are one. Each will receive his own reward according to his labor. For we are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s field, God’s building” (ibid.),

and so forth.

Therefore he himself sanctifies his temple as God and Lord by dwelling in us, while we preserve ourselves as worthy of his dwelling.

The text continues:

> “On that day the king sanctified the middle of the court that was before the house of the Lord. For there he offered a burnt offering and a sacrifice and the fat of peace offerings, because the bronze altar that was before the Lord was too small and could not contain the burnt offering and the sacrifice and the fat of the peace offerings.”

What does it mean that Solomon sanctified the middle of the court, offering a burnt offering and a sacrifice there, because the bronze altar placed before the doors of the temple according to the ordinance of the law could not contain everything, except that Christ now fully accomplishes in the Catholic Church those things that could not be perfected in the law because of its weakness?

For he himself is the court of the house of the Lord; through him the entrance into the house of the Lord, namely the heavenly Jerusalem, stands open. Since, therefore, all burnt offerings and sacrifices could not be offered on the typological altar of the Old Testament because everything there was done figuratively, our king and priest raised the altar of faith in the Catholic Church. On it, rich burnt offerings and acceptable sacrifices are offered to God daily in a spiritual manner.

Hence the Lord, rejecting the old sacrifice, says through the Prophet:

> “I did not desire burnt offerings and the blood of sacrifices” (Psalm 39 [40]; Hebrews 10).

And again in the Psalms:

> “The sacrifice of praise will honor me; and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God” (Psalm 49 [50]).

> “Solomon therefore held a solemn festival at that time, and all Israel with him, a very great multitude, from the entrance of Hamath to the Brook of Egypt, before the Lord our God.”

The statement that Solomon held a solemn festival, and that all Israel with him, a great multitude, were before the Lord from the entrance of Hamath to the Brook of Egypt, designates by the entrance of Hamath the northern region of the promised land, and by the brook or torrent of Egypt the southern region, as the Book of Chronicles calls them. I think it will please the reader if I set down at greater length some passages from the words of Saint Jerome.

It is written in the Book of Numbers (Numbers 34), in which the whole promised land is divided in brief language according to its four regions:

> “The southern region shall begin from the wilderness of Zin, which is beside Edom, and shall have boundaries toward the east at the Salt Sea, which surrounds the southern region by the ascent of the Scorpion, so that they pass into Zin and extend southward as far as Kadesh-barnea. From there the boundaries shall go out to the village called Adar and extend as far as Azmon. The boundary shall turn from Azmon to the Brook of Egypt and end at the shore of the Great Sea.”

In the final vision of the prophet Ezekiel it is accordingly said:

> “The southern region shall be from Tamar as far as the waters of Meriboth” (Ezekiel 48).

The waters of Meriboth mean “of contradiction.” Kadesh also, together with the torrents as far as the Great Sea—which signifies the broadest wilderness—is beside Edom.

[scan page 235]

**ANGELomus**

**458**

The boundary surrounds the Red Sea and proceeds by the ascent of the Scorpion, through Zin and Kadesh-barnea and the court or village of Adar; from Azmon it reaches the Brook of Egypt, which flows into the sea beside the city of Rhinocorura.

This boundary of the southern region begins at Tamar, a city in the wilderness, which Solomon also built with marvelous works and which today is called Palmyra. In Hebrew Tamar means what in our language is “palm.” It extends to the waters of contradiction, Kadesh, which undoubtedly lies in the desert, and to the torrent entering the Great Sea, the sea that stretches along the shores of Egypt and Palestine.

The Book of Numbers continues:

> “The western region begins at the Great Sea, and its end is there.”

That is, it extends from sea to sea: from the torrent of Rhinocorura, which flows into the sea, as far as the place where the city of Hamath in Syria is located. Its name is also placed in this region in Ezekiel:

> “The region shall be the Great Sea, from the boundary straight onward until you come to Hamath.”

This city is now called Epiphany, its name having been changed from that of the most cruel tyrant Antiochus, who bore the title Epiphanes.

> “On the northern side,”

he says,

> “the boundaries shall begin from the Great Sea and proceed as far as the highest mountain. From there, going toward Hamath, they shall extend to the boundaries; then the boundaries shall go as far as Zephron and the village of Enan. These shall be the boundaries on the northern side.”

The Hebrews say that the northern region begins at the Great Sea, which extends along the shores of Palestine, Phoenicia, Syria—which is called Coele Syria—and Cilicia, and stretches through Egypt toward Libya.

As for the statement that the boundaries proceed as far as the highest mountain, the Hebrews think that the mountain of Tel Imatim is meant, or Taurus; the latter seems more likely to us. “The boundaries,” he says, “shall go as far as Zephron,” which the Hebrews today call Zephuim, a town of Cilicia.

As for what follows, “and the village of Enan,” the Hebrew has Aser-enan, which means “the court of the fountain”; this is the boundary of Damascus. Hence it is said in Ezekiel:

> “The boundary shall be from the sea as far as the court of Enan,”

or Aser. Enan is the boundary of Damascus.

From the north, the northern region extends from the village of Enan to Sephama, and from Sephama the boundaries descend to Riblah opposite the spring. From there it reaches eastward to the Sea of Galilee, then extends to the Jordan, and finally closes at the very salty sea.

Thus, from the end of the northern region—that is, from the court of Enan—the boundaries extend as far as Sephama, which the Hebrews call Apamea. From Apamea the boundaries descend to Riblah, which is now called Antioch in Syria. To make clear that Riblah signifies this city, which is now the most distinguished city in Coele Syria, the text continues:

> “Opposite the spring,”

which properly signifies Daphne. From this spring the city mentioned above enjoys an abundance of water.

“From there,” it says,

> “the boundaries shall reach eastward to the Sea of Chinnereth,”

that is, the Lake of Tiberias. It is called a sea although it has fresh water, in accordance with the language of divine Scripture, which calls gatherings of waters “seas.” “They shall extend,” it says, “to the Jordan, and finally they shall be closed by the sea,” either the Dead Sea or, as some think, the tongue of the Red Sea, on whose shore Abila is situated.

The Book of Kings next relates that the aforesaid festival was celebrated by Solomon and the children of Israel for seven days and seven days—that is, fourteen days—and that on the eighth day he dismissed the people. It should be considered how the same matter is written in the Book of Chronicles:

> “Solomon held a festival at that time for seven days, and all Israel with him, a very great assembly, from the entrance of Hamath to the Brook of Egypt. On the eighth day he held a closing assembly, because he had dedicated the altar for seven days and celebrated the solemnity for seven days.”

Therefore, on the twenty-third day of the seventh month he dismissed the people to their tents. But I think that this means nothing other than that, when the seven days of the temple’s dedication had been completed, the days of the Feast of Booths followed. According to the law, these began on the fifteenth day of the seventh month and ended on the twenty-second day. Thus, when both festivals had been duly completed and the eighth day of the Feast of Booths had ended, King Solomon dismissed the people to their homes,

> “rejoicing and glad because of all the good that the Lord had done for David, Solomon, and Israel his people.”

Josephus appears to support this interpretation when he says:

> “Solomon therefore dismissed the assembly after he had offered sacrifices for himself and for all the Hebrews—namely, twenty-two calves and twelve thousand sheep. At that time sacrifices were first celebrated in the temple, and all the Hebrews feasted there with their wives and children. In addition, he held before the temple, with great splendor and magnificence, for fourteen days, the festival called the Feast of Booths; and the king feasted together with all his people. When these things had been sufficiently accomplished and nothing was lacking in the worship of divine piety, each person, dismissed by the king, returned to his own home, giving thanks to the king for the providence he had shown and for the works he had performed, and asking God to grant them Solomon as king for a long time. They returned with joy and exaltation, singing hymns with delight, so that in this happiness they went back to their homes without weariness.”

Mystically, however, Solomon’s celebration of a solemn festival after completing the work of the temple, as some understand it, together with all Israel and a very great multitude before the Lord God from the entrance of Hamath to the Brook of Egypt, signifies the inward joy that the saints possess perpetually with their king, Christ, the true peacemaker.

The very places by which the boundaries of the land of Israel are described do not contradict this meaning: Hamath means “the Lord is truth,” and by the Brook or Torrent of Egypt we can understand nothing more suitably than temporal death, since no one can escape it while dwelling in Egypt—that is, in the darkness of this world. The Prophet bears witness to this when he says:

> “Who is the man who lives and will not see death?” (Psalm 88 [89]).

Hence concerning the Mediator himself between God and human beings it is written in the Psalm:

> “He shall drink from the brook by the way; therefore he shall lift up his head” (Psalm 109 [110]).

The torrent was the violent persecution of the Jews, which the Lord Christ drank on the way, that is, in this life, when he endured it. But when it is said “on the way,” the labor is indicated, and the swift passage by which travelers are accustomed to proceed from one place to another is signified. For because of the glorious merit of his passion,

> “God bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth” (Philippians 2).

Thus all Israel, from the Brook of Egypt to Hamath, celebrate a solemn feast with Solomon when, after the end of the present life, the saints truly enjoy eternal joys with the Lord Christ.

The fact that they celebrated the same festival for seven days and seven days can signify that the elect, enlightened by the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, now rejoice in hope in this life, which runs its course according to the number seven of the days, and then, in the true Sabbath—that is, in the future rest of souls—will rejoice in the perception of truth itself.

The statement that on the eighth day Solomon dismissed the people, who departed blessing the king, each to his own tent, rejoicing with glad hearts over all the good things that the Lord had done for David his servant and for his people Israel, can signify the end of this life. This will come after the Sabbath of the holy souls, in which they now rest before the day of judgment. In the eighth age, that is, on the day of resurrection, the saints will receive immortal bodies and will be placed in heavenly dwellings according to the quality of their merits. There they will always rejoice with glad hearts, rejoicing and praising God for all the good things that the almighty Father has bestowed in the Lord Christ upon the whole Christian people.

### CHAPTER IX

> “King Solomon gave Hiram twenty cities in the land of Galilee. Hiram went out from Tyre to see the cities that Solomon had given him, and they did not please him. He said, ‘Are these the cities that you have given me, brother?’ And he called them the land of Cabul to this day.”

Josephus relates the following about this:

> “The king of Tyre contributed much gold and silver to the building, and in addition cedar and cypress wood, for which Solomon repaid him with great gifts, sending him each year wheat, wine, and oil, commodities that he especially needed because, as we have said, he lived on an island. In addition, he assigned to him twenty cities of the Galilean region, situated not far from Tyre. When Hiram had gone around them and inspected them, and the gift had displeased him, he sent to Solomon and said that he had no need of the cities. From that time they were called the land of Gabalon. For in the Phoenician language Gabal means ‘to displease.’”

But if Gabal is interpreted as “germ,” as we find in the Book of Hebrew Names, how does this name signify two things? We find no explanation unless perhaps it was said ironically, as though the land would not produce an abundance of fruits like a germ.

> “Solomon therefore built Gezer, Lower Beth-horon, and Baalath, and Tamar in the land of the wilderness. He fortified all the villages that belonged to him and that were without a wall,”

and so forth.

The cities that Solomon is said to have built—Millo, the wall of Jerusalem, Hazor, Megiddo, Gezer, Beth-horon, Baalath, and Tamar—signify the beauty of the holy Church, which the true Solomon prepared for himself in the joy of his kingdom, for praise and everlasting gladness. Millo is interpreted as “fulfillment”; Hezer as “one who separates,” or perhaps “[a] grassy [place]” [the second reading is materially uncertain]; Megiddo as “his dining room”; Gezer as “precipitation” or “division”; Beth-horon as “house of mountains”; and Baalath as “ascending.”

The holy Church is itself the city of the living God, in which the will of God is fulfilled daily. Having overcome every error of unbelief, it has been sanctified in faith and good works. In it there is refreshment of virtues; it distinguishes the clean from the unclean and virtues from vices. It is the house of the mountain, that is, the dwelling of the saints. The fruit of righteousness, like a palm tree in flower, “ascends from strength to strength, until the God of gods is seen in Zion” (Psalm 83 [84]).

> “Solomon fortified the villages that belonged to him and that were without a wall,”

because Christ fortified the dwellings of his faithful by the protection of his grace, so that they might always remain unconquerable by spiritual enemies.

> “All the people that remained from the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, who were not of the children of Israel—their descendants who remained in the land, whom the children of Israel could not exterminate—Solomon made tributary to this day. But Solomon did not make any of the children of Israel serve as slaves; they were men of war, his ministers, princes, commanders, and overseers of chariots,”

and so forth.

Our peaceful king made all the people who were not of the children of Israel tributary, since he keeps under his power those who are not numbered among the children but are placed in the condition of servants, and he uses each of them for his own service. Whether Jews, gentiles, or heretics, they remain under his dominion, because he is the ruler of all and uses them for his own purposes, in whose will all things have been placed, and no one can resist his will. Although such people oppose him in many ways, they frequently serve the needs of the Church, since in the present time they provide necessities and offer support from their possessions.

But concerning the children of Israel—that is, those who are not children of a slave woman but of a free woman, whom the Son of God has liberated by his blood—our Solomon did not appoint anyone to serve as a slave. He compels no one to live according to pagan custom, nor does he compel anyone to observe the ceremonies of the old law in the times of the New Testament. Rather, he makes them men of war, who fight against spiritual wickedness with the shield of faith and the sword of the Spirit, and makes them his ministers—that is, spiritual service in good works to him …
...to be subject; and princes and commanders, namely, so that they may rule themselves well in the virtues and subdue the wantonness of the flesh, or so that they may govern their subjects well, they also serve the way of justice. What follows:

> “There were five hundred and fifty officials over all the works of Solomon, who had the subject people under them and commanded them in their appointed tasks.”

What does this signify except that those who deserve to possess the grace of the Holy Spirit, who are learned in the law of the Lord, can govern both themselves and others well? On the fiftieth day after Passover, the Law was given on Mount Sinai in the Old Testament; and in the New, the Paraclete Spirit came upon the apostles and those who were with them.

## Chapter X

> “King Solomon also offered three times each year burnt offerings and peace offerings upon the altar which he had built for the Lord, and he burned incense before the Lord.”

Our Peacemaker also offers burnt offerings to the Lord three times each year in his members, when through faith in the Holy Trinity he presents an acceptable sacrifice to God. Each believer offers a burnt offering to the Lord when, by chastising his body, he mortifies it and hastens to consume all the desires of the flesh in the fire of the Holy Spirit. He offers peace offerings when he presents the gift of good works. He offers sacrifices when he spends the vows of his lips in the praise of the Lord.

All these things must be offered upon the altar which he built for the Lord. Whoever labors in abstinence, in good works, and in thanksgiving upon the altar of the heart—where the divine fire ought always to burn, that is, where the flame of charity ought always to glow—must offer everything to God with the sweetness of the Holy Spirit. Thus he will burn incense before the Lord when he prepares pure prayer for God in the secret place of his heart and asks for things worthy and pleasing to God. But whoever seeks transitory things and those belonging to the luxury of the world is not said to burn incense before the Lord, since he is shown not to pray with a pure conscience.

> “King Solomon also made a fleet at Ezion-geber, which is beside Elath on the shore of the Red Sea in the land of Edom. Hiram sent his servants in the fleet—sailors and men knowledgeable about the sea—together with Solomon’s servants. When they came to Ophir, they brought from there to King Solomon four hundred and twenty talents of gold.”

Ezion-geber is said to have been an island not far from Elath in the Red Sea, where Jehoshaphat’s fleet was shattered by the violence of a storm. Ophir, however, is the name of a province, named after Ophir, one of the descendants of Eber. They are said to have come from his lineage and to have lived from the river Cophene as far as the region of India called Hieria, as Josephus relates.

The fleet, therefore, which Solomon made at Ezion-geber—*Ezion-geber* being interpreted as “hastening,” or “strong,” or “manfully”—I consider to signify nothing other than the Church of the faithful. Situated upon the sea of this world, she devotes herself to acquiring the treasures of wisdom and knowledge and the riches of virtue, where there are the seafaring men of Hiram, sailors and men skilled in the sea, together with Solomon’s servants. The gentiles, instructed in manifold wisdom, are joined in the unity of faith with those who are learned in the law of Moses.

Our Solomon therefore sends them to Ophir, which is interpreted as “strengthening” or “confirming,” so that they may bring him from there the gold acquired, when they seek the precious meaning in the usefulness of the letter. Thus, having received the sum of four hundred and twenty talents of gold, they bring it to the king, when they expound the precious sense of history allegorically and tropologically, find anagogy in the two Testaments, and attribute it to divine wisdom and counsel.

## Chapter X

> “But the queen of Sheba, having heard the report of Solomon, came to test him with riddles. She entered Jerusalem with a very large retinue and with riches, with camels carrying spices, an exceedingly great quantity of gold, and precious stones. She came to Solomon and spoke to him about everything that was in her heart.”

The queen of the South, who, rising from the ends of the earth, came to hear Solomon’s wisdom, already prefigured the Church from the gentiles, which desired Christ. According to the Prophet, she was clothed in a richly embroidered golden garment (Psalm 44), and, forgetting her people and her father’s house, hastened—not barbarian in spirit, though she had been a stranger in outward place, but desiring to become a citizen in the cultivated place of the saints.

For this reason she is considered worthy not only of the heavenly reward of resurrection but also of apostolic authority to judge the adulterous Jews, because, marveling at Christ in Solomon, the Church had fulfilled in a mystical image the true affection of the heavenly Queen.

When the queen of Sheba saw Solomon and his glory, she was astonished at his wisdom and said:

> “The word is true which I heard in my land concerning your words and your wisdom. I did not believe those who told me until I came myself and saw with my own eyes and proved that scarcely half had been told me. Your wisdom and your works are greater than the report which I heard.”

This fittingly applies to the holy Church, which, having heard of Christ’s miracles, was moved to seek him. But after she reached him through baptism and faith, and, considering the testimonies of Holy Scripture, recognized the power of his divinity, everything previously told her about him seemed little in comparison with the grace she had received. Therefore, in wonder, she broke forth into his praise, saying:

> “Blessed are your men, and blessed are your servants who stand before you continually and hear your wisdom! Blessed be the Lord your God, who was pleased with you and set you upon the throne of Israel, because the Lord loved Israel forever and appointed you king, to execute judgment and justice.”

The Psalmist, likewise burning with desire for the kingdom of heaven, spoke similar words in their person:

> “How lovely are your tabernacles, Lord of hosts! My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord. My heart and my flesh have exulted in the living God” (Psalm 83).

And shortly afterward:

> “Blessed,” he says, “are those who dwell in your house; forever and ever they will praise you” (ibid.).

Those are blessed whose king is Christ. Because they deserve to enjoy the eternal vision of him, to behold the glory which he has with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and perpetually to receive the wisdom by which he deigns to reveal himself to the pure in heart, they rejoice. Thus they will prove true what is written:

> “What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2).

> “King Solomon gave the queen everything she desired and requested, apart from what she herself had brought him as a royal gift.”

That is, our Peacemaker will give his true queen, the Church, everything she asks, apart from what he had voluntarily offered her as a royal gift. Of him it is written:

> “You have granted him the desire of his heart, and you have not withheld from him the request of his lips” (Psalm 20).

And in the Gospel he himself says:

> “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you” (John 14).

He gives not only what we ask, but also, as a gratuitous gift, those things which human frailty either does not know or does not dare to ask.

> “The king made supports for the house of the Lord, the royal house, and harps and lyres for the singers from thyine wood. No such thyine wood has been brought or seen to the present day.”

Josephus relates the matter as follows:

> “At the same time, precious stones and thyine wood were brought to the king from the land called Golden. He used them for strengthening the Temple and the royal houses, and for musical instruments; he made harps and nablas so that the Levites might sing a hymn to God. Of all the things ever brought to the king, those which were brought then surpassed the others in size and beauty. No one should therefore suppose that the thyine wood now so called because of the price at which merchants sell it was similar to that wood. Those trees are round in appearance, almost like pine trees, but much whiter and exceedingly bright.”

I have said this so that no one may be ignorant of the nature of the true wood. For, as I read in the volume of a certain writer, they are imperishable and thorny, resembling white thorn, and are unknown to the Jews even to this day.

It is rightly said that King Solomon made supports for the house of the Lord and the royal house, and harps and lyres for the singers, from exceedingly precious wood. Our Creator likewise places precious wood—that is, teachers of the saints, whose vigor in faith never diminishes and whose leaves of speech never fall, but who produce the fruit of good works in their seasons—for the defense of the house of God and of the royal house, that is, for the strengthening of his Church. Surrounded on every side by their teachings and examples, she does not experience the ruin caused by sins.

Such men are rightly said to have been fashioned as harps and lyres for praising the Lord, since whatever they do prospers, and they do not cease to proclaim the Lord’s praise, in adversity and prosperity alike, with heart, mouth, and action. Whatever they do in word or deed, they do entirely for the glory of God. Of such men the Lord says through the prophet:

> “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have appointed watchmen; all day and all night they shall not be silent in praising the name of the Lord” (Isaiah 62).

> “Solomon also made two hundred shields of pure gold. Six hundred gold shekels were used for the plates of one shield, and three hundred shields were made of tested gold. Three hundred minas of gold were used for one shield. The king placed them in the house of the forest of Lebanon.”

In the Books of Chronicles it is likewise written:

> “King Solomon made two hundred golden spears, using six hundred pieces of gold for each spear. He also made three hundred golden shields, using three hundred pieces of gold for each shield. The king placed them in the armory which stood in the wooded enclosure.”

The golden shields and spears which they used—those who, as is shown below, were commanders keeping watch before the entrance of the king’s house—what do they signify except the spiritual armor possessed by holy preachers? They guard the house of the Lord and keep watch at its entrances, preventing crafty plotters from gaining access lest they deceive the innocent. Of them it is written in the Song of Songs:

> “Sixty mighty men surround Solomon’s bed, chosen from the strongest of Israel, all holding swords and most skilled in war” (Song of Songs 3).

Holy preachers defend the Church’s present rest and peace against the attacks of heretics, while the more perfect among them also watch with fixed attention over the inward rest of the heavenly homeland.

It is rightly added: “Chosen from the strongest of Israel.” *Israel* is interpreted as “a man seeing God.” All who strive toward the joys of the divine vision are rightly called Israel. But among them, he says, there are the strongest: those who are either raised up to contemplate the heavenly dwelling or undertake the ministry of preaching in due order.

They are appropriately designated by the number sixty, since such men await the tenfold reward of eternal recompense for the perfection of their good works:

> “All holding swords and most skilled in war.”

They hold the swords of which the Apostle says:

> “Take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6).

They are most skilled in those battles concerning which the same Apostle warns:

> “Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil; for our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against rulers and authorities,” and so forth (ibid.).

They are rightly called most skilled, because those who are enclosed in flesh, placed upon the earth, and fighting against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places require great skill in warfare. Indeed, they need great skill—and even greater grace from God—when the frailty of the flesh fights against an archangel trained through so many thousands of years for battle.

Thus it is rightly said that two hundred spears were made from a total of six hundred shekels, because we are recognized as perfected through the teaching and practice of both Testaments when we confirm by good examples whatever we teach in speech. Likewise, the two hundred shields, each of which was covered with three hundred pieces of gold, signify the perfect faith which they possessed in the confession of the Holy Trinity.

## Page 239

It is rightly said that the guards of God’s house carry golden spears and shields at the gate, because holy preachers, who are the guardians of the holy Church, shine with the splendor of heavenly wisdom. With the darts of their words they pierce their enemies, and with the shield of holy faith they repel and extinguish the fiery arrows of the wicked one.

What is added—

> “The king placed them in the house of the forest of Lebanon”—

fits this mystery appropriately. What, then, does the forest of Lebanon signify except the Church of the gentiles, which, cut down from the pride of its arrogance, is suitably fitted into the construction of God’s house? Hence the Psalmist says:

> “Behold, we heard of it in Ephratha; we found it in the fields of the forest” (Psalm 131), and so forth.

> “King Solomon therefore made a great throne of ivory and overlaid it with very pure gold. The throne had six steps. The top of the throne was rounded at the back, and there were arms on either side of the seat, with two lions standing beside each arm; twelve young lions stood on the six steps, on either side.”

The throne which King Solomon made is rightly understood as the holy Church, in which our Peacemaker is recognized as reigning and carrying out his judgments, since “the soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.”

It is also rightly remembered as having been made of ivory.
