We should understand that it was fitted not merely for wealth, but also because the elephant, whose bones ivory are, is said to be distinguished among quadrupeds by great chastity. It mates temperately with the female and does not use a second partner. This is suitably applied to chaste souls, since those who follow the commandments of Christ the Lord through chastity are recognized as having become ivory.

He covered it with exceedingly pure gold because he caused the splendor of his glory to shine within it, displaying the power of his majesty through signs and miracles.

This throne had six steps. What is signified by the number six except the perfection of good works?

> “In six days he completed the adornment of the world, and on the seventh he rested from his works” (Genesis 2).

Six is also the first number recognized as perfect through its parts. Its half is three, its third is two, and its sixth is one; and one, two, and three make six. Since the world also consists of six ages, in which anyone who desires to reach the heavenly homeland may labor, let him hasten to ascend by good works, for no one reaches that place except by good deeds.

> “The top of the throne was rounded at the back.”

What does the roundness of the throne at the rear signify except the eternal rest which is destined for the saints after this life? Whoever labors well here will receive the reward of his work and enjoy perpetual rest.

This same throne is mentioned under another figure in the Song of Songs:

> “King Solomon made himself a litter from the wood of Lebanon; he made its pillars of silver, its backrest of gold, its seat of purple, its interior lined with love, for the daughters of Jerusalem” (Song of Songs 3).

A litter is so called because it either carries the bodies of those reclining and feasting at a banquet or is carried from place to place as circumstances require. The holy Church is rightly compared with it, for she carries believers toward the nourishment of eternal life through the ministry of her preachers.

The litter of our king, therefore, is the holy Church, constructed from strong preachers as from imperishable cedar wood. She is rightly called a litter because each day she carries souls to the eternal banquet of their Creator.

Its pillars were made of silver: these are holy preachers, shining with the brightness of eloquence. A golden backrest was placed upon the silver pillars, because through what is spoken clearly by holy preachers, the minds of their hearers are kindled by the radiance of charity, in which they are to be renewed.

He also made a backrest for the litter when he promised the faithful the rest of perpetual peace:

> “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11).

He made this backrest golden because he prepared for his servants eternal rest in the glory of his vision.

The ascent to the litter was purple, because no one enters the Church unless he has been imbued with the sacraments of the Lord’s Passion. Hence he himself says:

> “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day” (John 6).

He lined its interior with love for the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, with the very love by which he suffered for us. No one has greater love than to lay down his life for his friends. He added “for the daughters of Jerusalem,” that is, for souls aflame with heavenly desire. The more greatly God commended his love for us by suffering for us, the more people he kindled to love him in return and to suffer for him.

> “There were two arms on either side holding the seat.”

What do the two arms holding Solomon’s seat signify except the supports of divine grace, which carry the Church to the heavenly kingdom? They are suitably described by the number two, because this is preached and especially commended in both Testaments: nothing good can be accomplished except through divine assistance. Hence the Truth himself says:

> “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15).

> “Two lions stood beside each arm.”

What are signified by the lions except the Fathers of both Testaments, who through strength of spirit learned to be of benefit both to themselves and to others? Two lions therefore stood beside the arms because in the Law and in the Gospel the holy Fathers attributed whatever good they did not to themselves but to God. Hence the Psalmist says:

> “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory, because of your mercy and your truth” (Psalm 113),

and the Apostle:

> “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Corinthians 15).

Again:

> “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (2 Corinthians 10).

> “Twelve young lions stood upon the six steps, on either side.”

What are signified by the twelve young lions except the order of preachers who follow apostolic teaching? They stand on either side above the six steps because they strive, through their teaching and examples, to strengthen the steps of good works on every side, so that the labor of those who have begun well may not weaken in their practice but may preserve uprightness in the progress of virtue.

Hence it is written:

> “Strength and dignity are her clothing, and she will laugh at the last day. Her sons rose up and proclaimed her most blessed; her husband praised her. Many daughters have gathered riches; you have surpassed them all” (Proverbs 31).

The text continues:

> “All the vessels from which King Solomon drank were of gold, and all the furnishings of the house of the forest of Lebanon were of purest gold. There was no silver, nor was it considered of any value in the days of Solomon.”

All the vessels which serve the ministry of our Peacemaker become golden, because all the souls of the saints, which are God’s vessels, shine with the splendor of wisdom and love in serving the divine will. They contain the drink which is life, and in them there is a fountain of water springing up to eternal life.

Silver was not considered to be of any value in the days of Solomon, because, according to the Apostle:

> “The word of God is not in speech but in power” (1 Corinthians 4).

And:

> “The preaching of the Gospel does not consist in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in the demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that our faith might not rest in human wisdom but in the power of God” (1 Corinthians 2).

Hence the Truth himself says:

> “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 7), and so forth.

Again:

> “Whoever loosens one of these least commandments and teaches people to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5).

> “They brought Solomon gold from Tharshish, silver, ivory tusks, apes, and peacocks.”

What gold or silver signifies is known. Ivory tusks may signify teachers who are strong because of the brilliance of wisdom. Of them it is said to the Bride:

> “Your neck is like an ivory tower.”

By apes, which appear to imitate human actions but live like beasts, are signified those who come to the faith from the gentiles and seem to hold the faith while denying it by their works.

Peacocks, whose flesh, if dried, is said to remain incorruptible, may signify those who are clothed in the beauty of virtues and are refined by the fire of tribulations, so that they are adorned with varied virtues and retain the incorruptibility of faith and mind. Although, if they are to be referred to virgins, we may understand them accordingly; the following printed words, *de Tharsis fortiter conservet*, are corrupt or uncertain.

What follows is also appropriate:

> “Such work had never been made in all the kingdoms.”

This suitably applies to the holy Church, of which it is written that such things are brought to our Solomon from the salty and bitter waves of this world. Tharshish is interpreted as “exploration of joy.”

> “King Solomon was greater than all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom, and the whole earth desired to see Solomon’s face, to hear his wisdom which God had put into his heart. Each one brought him gifts, silver and gold vessels, garments, and weapons of war,” and so forth.

It is rightly said that “King Solomon was greater than all the kings of the earth,” because our Peacemaker is exalted above every height of the saints, who are truly called kings, and no one can be compared with him. For:

> “Who among the clouds can be compared with the Lord, or who is like God among the sons of God? God is glorified in the council of the saints; he is great and fearful above all who surround him.”

Again:

> “Great is our Lord and great is his power, and of his wisdom there is no number.”

Hence John says:

> “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1).

The whole earth desires to see the face of our king, because the entire Church of the saints desires only this: to reach the sight of his glory. Through the prophet it is said:

> “My heart has said to you: I have sought your face; your face, Lord, I will seek.”

And elsewhere:

> “As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God” (Psalm 41).

Each person brings him gifts when, according to the strength granted him, he strives to offer service to God in word or deed.

## Chapters XI and XII

> “King Solomon loved many foreign women, including Pharaoh’s daughter, Moabite and Ammonite women, Edomite, Sidonian, and Hittite women from the nations concerning which the Lord had said to the children of Israel: ‘You shall not enter into relations with them, nor shall they enter into relations with you,’” and so forth.

What shall I say now about Solomon’s remaining works? Holy Scripture vehemently censures and condemns him, and says nothing at all about his repentance or about God’s pardon. Nothing readily presents itself here for the salvation of the allegorical meaning; rather, this is clearly a lamentable abyss of destruction.

Unless perhaps someone says that the foreign women whose love inflamed him signify the churches chosen from the gentiles. This interpretation could perhaps be understood without absurdity if, because of Solomon, they had abandoned their gods and worshiped his God. But when he offended his God because of them and worshiped their gods, no good meaning can be inferred from the matter.

Nevertheless, I do not think that the episode signifies nothing; rather, it signifies evil, as we said concerning Lot’s wife and daughters. In Solomon’s person there appears both marvelous excellence and marvelous ruin. Whatever therefore existed in him at different times—good first and evil afterward—is displayed in the Church at one and the same time in this present age. His good things, I think, signify the good members of the Church; his evil things, the wicked members of the Church, as though within his one body.

Just as in one human being there are good people as grains and wicked people as chaff, or in the unity of one harvest there are good people as wheat and wicked people as weeds.

## Chapter XI

> “It happened at that time that Jeroboam went out from Jerusalem, and the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite met him on the road, covered with a new cloak. They were alone in the field. Ahijah seized the new cloak with which he was covered, tore it into twelve pieces, and said to Jeroboam: ‘Take ten pieces for yourself. For thus says the Lord God of Israel: Behold, I will tear the kingdom from the hand of Solomon and will give you ten tribes. One tribe shall remain to him for the sake of my servant David and Jerusalem, the city which I chose from all the tribes of Israel,’” and so forth.

The fact that, after Solomon’s death, ten tribes were separated from the house of David and from the Temple, while two remained, sufficiently indicates what the Apostle says about that whole people:

> “The remnants, saved according to the election of grace, have come to be” (Romans 11).

Jeroboam, who separated the ten tribes from the house of David and from the Temple of God and led them into idolatry, signifies heretics. They love division, tear apart the unity of the catholic faith by their heresies, and, following the worship of evil spirits, hand people over to them.

Jeroboam is interpreted as “judging the people.” Heretics also seem to judge the people when they make them followers of their error. To this matter the words of the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite, who was sent to Jeroboam, aptly apply:

> “Take ten pieces for yourself. For thus says the Lord God of Israel: Behold, I will tear the kingdom from Solomon and will give you ten tribes. One shall remain to him for the sake of my servant David and Jerusalem, the city which I chose from all the tribes of Israel.”

Jeroboam received ten pieces when he seized upon the commandments of the Law in order to violate them. The two tribes remained with David’s offspring when the portion of the elect, according to the Apostle’s teaching, remained within the rule of the catholic faith:

> “One Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Ephesians 4).

Finally, Rehoboam, Solomon’s son (1 Kings 14), abandoned the counsel of the elders and followed the counsel of the young men. Although he belonged to the house of David, he did not walk in his way. For, as Scripture testifies, Judah did evil before the Lord in those days and provoked him beyond all that their fathers had done in their sins. They too built for themselves altars, pillars, and sacred groves upon every high hill and beneath every leafy tree. There were also male prostitutes in the land, and they committed all the abominations of the nations which the Lord had destroyed before the face of the children of Israel.

He therefore signifies wicked rulers in the Church, who, devoted to earthly desires, neglect to care for their subjects. They take pleasure in the multitude of those who obey them, yet do not show worthy concern for those entrusted to them.

Rehoboam is interpreted as “the breadth of the people.” Those may rightly be called the breadth of the people who, walking on the broad and spacious road by which many go to death, refuse to enter the narrow way which belongs to the few and leads to eternal life (Matthew 7). They abandon the counsel of the holy Fathers, whose doctrine and examples tend toward the height of perfection, and choose to obey the commands of the young—that is, of those enslaved to youthful desires, who burden them with wicked praise and flattery.

Thus in them is fulfilled what the prophet says:

> “As is the people, so is the priest. From the least to the greatest, all are devoted to greed, and, becoming blind guides of the blind, they fall together into the pit of destruction” (Jeremiah 6; Matthew 15).

The Wisdom of God threatens them, saying:

> “Woe to you, land whose king is a child and whose princes eat in the morning” (Ecclesiastes 10).

Conversely, concerning the holy people and their king, Christ, Scripture continues in praise:

> “Blessed is the land whose king is noble and whose princes eat at the proper time,” because whatever they do prospers.

## Chapter XIII

> “Behold, a man of God came from Judah by the word of the Lord to Bethel, while Jeroboam stood beside the altar and was burning incense. He cried out against the altar by the word of the Lord and said: ‘Altar, altar, thus says the Lord: Behold, a son shall be born to the house of David, Josiah by name, and he shall sacrifice upon you the priests of the high places who now burn incense upon you, and human bones shall be burned upon you,’” and so forth.

The prophet who had been sent by God to Bethel to rebuke Jeroboam for the idolatry he had committed was deceived by a false prophet, ate and drank there contrary to the Lord’s command, and was therefore killed by a lion on the road. What does this signify except one who becomes proud in prosperity, so that he despises the Lord’s commandments? Such a person is torn by the tooth of the wicked one’s persuasion and killed through consent to sin by “the lion who prowls around, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Peter 5).

It is therefore necessary always to seek the help of almighty God and to hope with one’s whole heart in his mercy and protection. For what is a human being, whatever his merit, if he is abandoned by the protection of his Creator?

Protection is considered less necessary when it is always possessed; but it is often withdrawn usefully, so that a person may be shown what he is like when he knows nothing without it. The hand of God sometimes makes us aware of ourselves through adversity, even though, without our knowing it, he carries us in prosperity. For when we are deprived of support and begin to fall, yet are held back by assistance, our trembling in the fall becomes instruction, and our remaining upright becomes evidence of his guardianship.

Let no one therefore consider himself to possess any virtue, even when he is able to do something bravely. If divine protection abandons him, he is suddenly overwhelmed in weakness precisely where he boasts that he stands firmly.

What else does it mean that the man of God, sent to prophesy against the altar at Bethel, exercised the authority of a free voice in the presence of the king, and wonderfully paralyzed the king’s outstretched arm, yet soon mercifully restored it to health; that, when invited into the king’s house, he refused to eat because he had obeyed the Lord’s command not to eat on the road; and yet, on that same road, he was deceived, ate, and died after being fed?

What do we gather from this upon careful reflection, what do we suspect was intended to be formed in us, unless perhaps it is that, within himself...

[scan page 242]  
**COMMENTARY ON THE BOOKS OF KINGS**

**Book III**

…boasting silently that he had despised the king for the Lord’s commands, he was soon shaken in his inward strength, and from the same source from which glory had crept into his heart, guilt also stole into his deed? Thus the false prophet’s words taught him that it had never been by his own strength that he had resisted the king.

It was fitting, moreover, that he received the sentence of death from the mouth of the man by whose deception he had departed from the commandments of life, so that he might truly suffer punishment from the source through which he had negligently incurred guilt. Here it is plainly shown that the sin of disobedience was released in death itself: for the same lion that had presumed to kill him while alive did not dare to touch him once he was dead. He who had possessed power to kill him did not receive permission to eat the corpse of the slain man. For the one whose guilt had been punished during life was already just through death.

This event shows that no one ought to consider himself possessed of any virtue, even when—as has been said—he may be able to act bravely. This man, because he had gloried in despising the king at the Lord’s command, fell, so that, deceived by the false prophet’s words, he might learn that it had not been through his own strength that he had resisted the king.

### CHAPTER XIV

> “In the fifth year of the reign of Rehoboam, Shishak, king of Egypt, went up against Jerusalem and took away the treasures of the house of the Lord, and the royal treasures, and carried everything off. He also took the golden shields that Solomon had made. In their place Rehoboam made bronze shields and handed them over to the commanders of the shield-bearers and to those who kept watch before the entrance of the king’s house. Whenever the king entered the house of the Lord, those whose duty it was to go before him carried them; afterward they returned them to the armory of the shield-bearers,”

and so forth.

Concerning this king, a fuller account is given in the book of Chronicles, where we read as follows (2 Chronicles 12):

> “In the fifth year of King Rehoboam, Shishak king of Egypt went up against Jerusalem, because they had sinned against the Lord, with twelve hundred chariots and sixty thousand horsemen. The people who came with him from Egypt were without number—Libyans, Troglodytes, and Ethiopians. He captured the strongly fortified cities in Judah and came as far as Jerusalem. The prophet Shemaiah entered before Rehoboam and the princes of Judah, who had gathered in Jerusalem while fleeing from Shishak, and said to them: ‘Thus says the Lord: You have abandoned me, and I have abandoned you into the hand of Shishak.’ The princes of Israel and the king were humbled and said: ‘The Lord is just.’ When the Lord saw that they had humbled themselves, the word of the Lord came to Shemaiah, saying: ‘Because they have humbled themselves, I will not destroy them. I will grant them a little assistance, and my wrath will not be poured out upon Jerusalem by the hand of Shishak. Nevertheless, they shall serve him, so that they may know the difference between serving me and serving the kingdoms of the earth.’ Then Shishak king of Egypt withdrew from Jerusalem, carrying away the treasures of the house of the Lord and of the king’s house; he took everything with him, as well as the golden shields that Solomon had made, in place of which the king made bronze ones and handed them over to the commanders of the shield-bearers who guarded the vestibule of the palace.”

What, then, does it signify figuratively that, because of Rehoboam’s sin, Shishak king of Egypt carried away the treasures from the house of the Lord and the royal treasures, except that negligent rulers, on account of their negligence, figuratively provoke the king of Egypt—that is, the prince of darkness—against Jerusalem, namely, against the Church entrusted to them? For he seems to rule over it for a time, and carries away the treasures of the house of the Lord and the royal treasures when he withdraws from the careless and negligent both the knowledge of the holy Scriptures and the practice of virtue.

Thus Shishak is interpreted as “byssus of sackcloth” or “joy of sackcloth.” Since byssus signifies subtlety, while sackcloth, which is made from goats’ hair, signifies sins, what can “byssus of sackcloth” more suitably mean than the cunning of the devil’s deceit in persuading people to sin?

Shishak carries away Jerusalem’s riches when the devil, who deceives craftily and rejoices in a multitude of sins, plunders ecclesiastical people of spiritual knowledge and the practice of virtue, and drags those who seemed to be an adornment in the Church, stripped of their possessions, down with him into the abyss of his own destruction.

The same meaning is also indicated by the fact that this king took away the golden shields made by King Solomon, in place of which King Rehoboam made bronze shields and handed them over to the commanders of the shield-bearers. Solomon stored golden shields and gave them to the keepers of his house when our Redeemer entrusted spiritual knowledge, through the two Testaments, to the teachers of the Church for the protection of his people.

The ancient enemy takes this knowledge away through the carelessness of rulers. For when they are occupied with earthly matters and show less concern for heavenly things, he leaves them stripped of their former office and knowledge, as though their own house had been plundered of its riches. Finally, when such men see themselves deprived of spiritual understanding, they seek an abundance of verbal eloquence, so that by the sonority of their speech they may set up a defense against their enemies for those subject to them, as though by the strength of bronze shields.

But just as bronze is an inferior metal to gold, so empty eloquence is inferior to the fruit of true eloquence. Hence a wise man says of eloquence:

> “Where there are many words, there is often poverty” (Proverbs 13).

And in the Psalms we read:

> “The man of a ready tongue shall not be established upon the earth” (Psalm 140).

But of wisdom it is written:

> “Wisdom is more precious than all riches, and all desirable things cannot be compared with her. Length of days is in her right hand, and in her left are riches and glory” (Proverbs 8).

Whoever wishes to provide the Church with suitable defense against heretics and against all enemies of wisdom ought certainly to accomplish this with wisdom’s assistance. Eloquence contributes nothing to this without wisdom; indeed, it does great harm.

As for what is read later, that there was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam, and between King Asa of Judah and King Baasha of Israel, throughout all their days, I think it signifies nothing other than that the holy Church, which persists in the unity of faith, is always at war with heretics and schismatics, and with all who attempt to violate the Catholic faith.

> “All who wish to live piously in Christ,” as the Apostle says, “will suffer persecution” (2 Timothy 3),

because the ancient dragon persecutes the woman, lying in wait for her heel, while she crushes his head.

Asa is interpreted as “lifting” or “one who lifts up,” and Baasha as “confusion” or “dryness.” It is fitting, therefore, that the people of the Church are called “lifting” or “one who lifts up”: they raise their minds toward heavenly desires and despise the confusion of earthly passions, together with the devil who suggests them, treating them as though they were dry and useless things.

### CHAPTER XVI

> “The word of the Lord came to Jehu son of Hanani against Baasha, saying: ‘Because I exalted you from the dust and appointed you leader over my people Israel, but you walked in the way of Jeroboam and caused my people Israel to sin, so that you provoked me to anger through their sins, behold, I will cut off the posterity of Baasha and the posterity of his house, and I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat. Whoever dies of Baasha in the city, the dogs shall eat; and whoever dies of him in the countryside, the birds of the air shall eat.’”

These words were spoken prophetically against all sinners, heretics, and pagans. For those who add new sins continually to their former sins become worse than those whose viscera are corrupted, because they imitate their examples.

> “I will cut off,” he says, “the posterity of Baasha and the posterity of his house, and I will make his house like the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat.”

The Lord cuts off Baasha’s posterity when he punishes the sins of the wicked after their life; he cuts off the posterity of his house when he condemns their imitators to eternal torments.

> “And I will make the house of Baasha as I made the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat,”

when sinners who persist in their wickedness are delivered together with the devil and his angels to the torments of hell.

Baasha, as we have said, is interpreted as “confusion” or “dryness.” Jeroboam means “judging the people,” and Nebat signifies “spontaneous.” Whoever, therefore, follows the confusions of errors and sins, neglects to possess the spiritual grace of virtues, and perseveres in the aridity of sins until the end of life, has his posterity cut off like that of the devil, who, by proudly exalting himself through his own will, brought death upon himself. And he seems to judge the people of the lost when he does not exercise a judgment of equity but is recognized as carrying out judgment of condemnation against them.

Then the posterity of sinners and of all the wicked will be cut off, together with their head, the devil, when the Judge of the living and the dead says at the end of the world to those standing at his left:

> “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his associates.”

And:

> “These shall go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matthew 25).

> “Whoever dies,” he says, “of Baasha in the city, the dogs shall eat; and whoever dies of him in the countryside, the birds of the air shall eat.”

What does it mean to die in the city except for someone who perseveres in the faith within the Church yet becomes liable to capital crimes? He dies in the city who practices wickedness within the Church of God.

He is torn apart by the mouths of dogs when he is reproved, convicted, and condemned by the judgments of the holy teachers. Of these dogs it is written in the Psalm:

> “They shall go around the city like dogs” (Psalm 59).

Dogs are so called from barking. It is the nature of dogs to defend those places in which they know they find food. The city that these dogs go around is Jerusalem, spread universally throughout the world.

That Paul went around this city is attested by the Letters of salutary teaching, which resounded like sacred divine trumpets among all nations. O blessed dog, who pursues unbelieving peoples, drives away thieves, and guards the sacred sheepfold, whose barking resounded throughout the whole world like a deep-toned trumpet!

> “Whoever dies,” he says, “of Baasha in the countryside, the birds of the air shall eat.”

Those who are of Baasha—that is, of the body of the devil, full of confusion—and die in the countryside are those who, separated from the Church, serve idolatry or heresies by their impious speech and conduct. The birds of the air eat them: those birds, namely, of which the Lord speaks in the Gospel’s parable of the sower, when the seed scattered beside the road was eaten by the birds of the air (Matthew 13). These birds eat them when, having been burdened with sins, they carry them away with themselves into eternal destruction.

> “In the thirty-first year of Asa king of Judah, Omri reigned over Israel for twelve years. He reigned for six years at Tirzah. He bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver, built upon it, and called the city that he had built by the name of Shemer, after the name of the lord of the mountain of Samaria.”

How this happened is made clear by Josephus’s account, which reads as follows:

> “In the thirtieth year of King Asa, Omri received the kingdom and held it for twelve years. For six of these years he ruled at Tirzah; for the remaining years, in the city called Mare, but by the Greeks Samaria. He named it Samareton after a certain Samaros, who had sold him the mountain on which he established the city. In nothing did he differ from the earlier kings, except that he was worse.”

> “And Ahab continued in his works to provoke the Lord God of Israel to anger above all the kings of Israel who had been before him. In his days Hiel of Bethel built Jericho,”

and so forth.

Of the time of Ahab’s reign it is written:

> “In his days Hiel of Bethel built Jericho. In Abiram, his firstborn, he laid its foundation, and in Segub, his youngest, he set up its gates.”

The meaning is clear. When the aforementioned builder of the city began to lay its foundations, his firstborn, named Abiram, died. When he attempted to fortify the gates after the city had been built, Segub, the youngest of his sons, perished.

Joshua foretold that this would happen when he destroyed the city and consigned it to the ban, cursing it:

> “Cursed before the Lord be the man who rises up and rebuilds this city, Jericho. In his firstborn shall he lay its foundations, and in his youngest shall he set up its gates” (Joshua 6).

Hiel of Bethel restored the walls of Jericho, which had been destroyed and anathematized by Joshua, when someone who had assumed the religious habit in the Church returns to the crimes that the Lord had forbidden him on the day of baptism and again pursues, by luxurious living, the pomp of the devil that he himself had anathematized. When he revives the dogmas of error or the fables of the pagans, he raises up the ruins of Jericho as though departing from Bethel, in opposition to the ecclesiastical truth with which he had been instructed.

Such a person is rightly accursed before the Lord. He loses both the foundations of faith, from which good works ought to begin, and the fortifications of good conduct by which they ought to have been completed: he loses them through the wicked foundation laid in his firstborn and through the placement of his gates in his youngest.

### CHAPTER XVII

> “And Elijah the Tishbite, from the inhabitants of Gilead, said to Ahab: ‘As the Lord God of Israel lives, in whose sight I stand, there shall be neither dew nor rain during these years except according to the word of my mouth.’ And the word of the Lord came to him, saying: ‘Depart from here and go toward the east, and hide yourself by the brook Cherith, which is opposite the Jordan. There you shall drink from the brook, and I have commanded the ravens to feed you there.’ So he went and acted according to the word of the Lord. When he had gone, he sat by the brook Cherith, which is opposite the Jordan. The ravens also brought him bread and meat in the morning, and likewise bread and meat in the evening, and he drank from the brook. After some days the brook dried up, for no rain had fallen upon the earth.”

Before discussing allegorically what these things signify, let us inquire according to the moral sense what is meant by the words:

> “As the Lord lives, in whose sight I stand.”

It should be understood that we come into the presence of the Lord in two ways: when, at the final judgment, we stand before his tribunal; and whenever we bring the power of our Creator back into our awareness, we stand in his presence. Hence it is rightly said here through the man of God Elijah:

> “As the Lord God of Israel lives, in whose presence I stand.”

Here he stands in the Lord’s presence and lives faithfully; there he receives the crown of life truly.

Tishbe, from which Elijah is called the Tishbite, is a city of the region of the Gileadites. Spiritually, however, the name is more suitably understood of the Son of God, to whom both its meaning and its title properly belong. For Elijah is interpreted as “the Lord God,” or “God is strong”—a name that belongs substantially to the Son of God, whose authority naturally consists in doing whatever he wills. Of him the Psalmist says:

> “The Lord is strong, mighty in battle” (Psalm 24).

Tishbite is interpreted as “captivating” or “converting,” as it is also written of the Lord:

> “Turn again, O Lord, our captivity” (Psalm 126).

Just as the origin of Melchizedek is not stated in Scripture—although he certainly bore the type of the Savior—so too Elijah’s genealogy is not narrated. He is introduced suddenly, and it is not disclosed from what tribe or family he arose.

The brook Kishon, which is also called Cherith, is interpreted as “knowledge,” or “cutting off,” or “division,” and this most certainly corresponds to the Jewish people.

The bread and meat by which Elijah was fed, with the ravens ministering to him, undoubtedly prefigured the work of piety and service that the faithful among the Jewish people offered to the same Lord. The drying up of the brook signifies the abolition of the Law, which, with the coming of the Savior, is understood to have failed in its carnal observances.

Some wish to understand the passage differently; this interpretation seems to us at variance with the other. They say:

> “Our Elijah was hidden in the brook Cherith, which is interpreted as ‘Calvary,’ and there he drank from the brook, when, on the place of Calvary, where the power of his glory was hidden, the Lord tasted from the stream of our mortality.”

The ravens fed Elijah, bringing him bread and meat morning and evening, when the Gentile world, coming from the blackness of sins, offered to Christ the Lord, who hungered for our salvation, the bread of faith and the hope of resurrection, having been illumined by his grace—namely, in the morning of evangelical preaching.

Likewise, they brought bread and meat in the evening, when they preserved the same faith undefiled until the end of the world and presented it to the Judge who was coming with the resurrection of the flesh.

After some days, however, “the brook dried up,” because, when the course of the present life has been completed,

> “death will be swallowed up in victory” (1 Corinthians 15),

and:

> “There shall be no more death, nor mourning, nor crying, nor pain, for the former things have passed away” (Revelation 21).

I leave this interpretation to the judgment of the prudent reader, if he wishes to form it for himself, because the interpretation seems to conflict with our understanding of the ravens.

Then the word of the Lord came to him, saying:

> “Arise, go to Zarephath of Sidon, and remain there. For I have commanded a widow there to feed you.”

Elijah is sent to be fed by a foreign widow. This widow, therefore, represents the Church of the Gentiles. After being abandoned by her Creator for a long time, she, like a poor and needy woman, nourished the people who lacked true faith and knowledge of right truth, teaching them, as it were, the fruit of the word in part, until the prophetic word came and fed her there.

That prophetic word was endangered in Judea because Israel’s dew had dried up, as though heaven had been closed. It both received nourishment and supplied it: it was received by believers and itself refreshed those who believed.

Hence this same widow is rightly said to have lived in Zarephath of Sidon. Sidon is interpreted as “useless hunting”; Zarephath as “burning” or “the distress of bread,” because:

> “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5).

Where concern was devoted to acquiring useless things, as though to occupying oneself with them; where the fierce burning of thirst and the distress of spiritual hunger had previously been present—there the flour and oil are blessed through the prophetic word.

> “She intended to gather two sticks before she died.”

The mention here is not only of wood but also of the plural “woods”; the sign of the cross is expressed, by which the bread of life has been prepared for us eternally.

Her flour and oil are blessed: this means the grace of the Lord’s body and the anointing of chrism, or the fruit and gladness of charity. When these are expended, they are said not to fail:

> “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9).

This widow, whom the Lord fed not with bread made from grain but with the bread of the word, is the same one of whom it is said in the Psalms:

> “Blessing, I will bless her widow” (Psalm 132),

and so forth.

She is the one of whom Paul also says (Romans 7):

> “When her husband has died, she is free to marry whom she wishes,”

because, when the letter of the Law has ceased—whose end is Christ—she passes into the freedom of grace: namely, the Church, like a widow of the Law, passes over to Christ.

Now the oil of grace in her vessels and the flour of blessing do not fail, although famine persists among almost all the nations. Their hunger for the food of life and their lack of faith in the Trinity were fittingly prefigured by that former famine of three years.

> “After these things the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, became ill. His illness was extremely severe, so that no breath remained in him. Therefore she said to Elijah: ‘What have I to do with you, man of God? You have come to me so that my iniquities may be remembered and my son may be put to death?’ And he said to her: ‘Give me your son.’ He took him from her bosom and carried him up to the upper room where he lived, and laid him on his bed,”

and so forth.

This deed of Elijah, in raising the widow’s dead son in the house where he was staying, and whose flour and oil he had blessed, clearly expresses the deed of our Redeemer in the resurrection of the people converted to faith.

For what widow can better be understood here than the synagogue of the Jews, which, widowed after the manner of Moses, nourished a little son—that is, the carnal people of the Jews?

At Elijah’s entrance—that is, at the entrance of our Savior—the child became ill, because, by not believing in him but rejecting him, he fell sick with the severe fever of unbelief. Hence the mother herself, lamenting the child’s illness, says to the prophet:

> “What have I to do with you, man of God? You have come to me so that my iniquities may be remembered and my son may be put to death?”

When the synagogue of the Jews complains about the Savior’s coming, it is as though the Savior himself were the cause of the Jewish people’s death.

This is why Caiaphas, conspiring over Christ’s death, said to the crowd:

> “It is better for you that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish. If we let him go on in this way, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and our nation” (John 11).

But just as God’s prophet was not provoked by the widow’s words but rather took pity on her and said:

> “Give me your son,”

and took him from her bosom, carried him to the upper room where he lived, laid him on his bed, stretched himself over the child, measured himself over him three times, and cried to the Lord:

> “Lord my God, I pray you, let the soul of this child return into his inward parts,”

so our Redeemer was not provoked by the malice of the Jews. Rather, taking pity on the believing people, he took the child from his mother’s bosom when he took him away from the carnal observance of the Law.

> “And he laid him on his bed,”

that is, he showed him that life is present in his death.

> “He stretched himself over him three times and measured himself over the child,”

when he taught and demonstrated to him the faith of the Trinity.

And crying out to the Father, he said:

> “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23).

And again:

> “Father,” he said, “glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you, just as you gave him authority over all flesh, so that he might give eternal life to all whom you have given him. And this is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17).

> “Elijah was heard, and the child’s soul returned within him, and he revived. Elijah took him and returned him to his mother.”

So too our Lord, when saving the people who believed and displaying signs and miracles, showed the unbelieving that they might recognize that whoever believes in his name truly lives.

And it will happen that the words of the woman marveling at the child who had been raised will be repeated by the Jewish people, overcome by the truth, when they proclaim to Christ:

> “Now by this I know that you are a man of God, and that the word of the Lord in your mouth is true.”

### CHAPTER XVIII

> “After many days the word of the Lord came to Elijah in the third year, saying: ‘Go, show yourself to Ahab, and I will send rain upon the face of the earth.’”

The three years of famine prefigured the fact that knowledge of the Holy Trinity was lacking among the Jewish people, or throughout the whole world. The six months pertain to the work of good, which had entirely ceased among them, of whom the prophet says:

> “There is none who does good, not even one.”

Obadiah, the steward of the house of Israel, whose name is interpreted as “servant of the Lord,” prefigured in a certain way those among the princes of the Jews who had believed and were secret disciples of the Lord, such as Nicodemus and others.

When he says to the people:

> “How long will you limp between two sides?”

this can be understood in the following way: those limp with both feet who wish to serve God and the devil alike.

> “So Elijah went to show himself to Ahab. Now there was a severe famine in Samaria. Ahab called Obadiah, the steward of his house,”

and so forth.

When Elijah gathered all Israel and disputed against the prophets of Baal, and when they struggled in vain, he repaired the altar of the Lord that had been destroyed. He took twelve stones according to the number of the tribes of the sons of Jacob, to whom the word of the Lord had come, saying:

> “Israel shall be your name.”

And he built an altar of stones in the name of the Lord.

> “He made a trench around the altar, large enough for two measures of seed, arranged the wood, divided the ox into pieces, laid it upon the wood, and said: ‘Fill four jars with water and pour it over the burnt offering and over the wood.’ Again he said: ‘Do it a second time.’ When they had done it a second time, he said: ‘Do the same thing a third time.’ They did so a third time, and the water ran around the altar, and the trench was filled with water,”

and so forth.

What could be represented more suitably than our Redeemer, contending against and overcoming the prince of this world and his satellites, cleansing the hearts of his faithful from every stain of iniquity, and dedicating to God the altar of the Lord that had been destroyed?

This altar is said to have been constructed from twelve stones because from those who follow the prophetic and apostolic faith and teaching an altar most pleasing to God is built, on which the sacrifice of praise is offered daily as a fragrance of sweetness.

He made a trench around the altar, large enough for two measures of seed, from a contrite heart and humbled spirit, bringing forth streams of tears through fear of hell and desire for eternal life. There too he arranged the wood, because he established the words and deeds of the saints as an example for believers.

He divided the ox into pieces and placed it upon the wood when he taught the faithful to shape all their actions according to the example of the holy fathers.

He commanded water to be poured over the burnt offering and the wood once, again, and a third time, because at all times it is necessary for us to cleanse our words, thoughts, and deeds through pure prayer and compunction expressed in tears. We must not cease until the trenches are filled with water—that is, until the future joy that follows present sorrow has been perfectly completed.

Thus the passage that follows will be fulfilled:

> “Fire fell from heaven at Elijah’s invocation and consumed the burnt offering, the wood, and the stones and dust; it also licked up the water that was in the trench. When all the people saw this, they fell on their faces and said: ‘The Lord himself is God; the Lord himself is God.’”

When the judgment of the heavenly Judge examines our words and deeds and our whole life perfectly, and makes us approved as silver is tested by fire, he will place us, made immortal and blessed, in an everlasting dwelling. Then, like the Israelites, we will sing forever in rejoicing:

> “The Lord himself is God; he made us, and not we ourselves. We are his people and the sheep of his pasture” (Psalm 100).

After the Lord’s altar had been cleansed and the burnt offerings consumed, Elijah the prophet of God said to the people:

> “Seize all the prophets of Baal; let not one of them escape.”

When they had seized them, Elijah led them to the brook Kishon, which is interpreted as “their hardness,” and killed them there.

In the same way, when the day of judgment comes, our Redeemer will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all stumbling blocks and those who practice iniquity. They will cast them into the lake of fire and sulfur, where the beast and the false prophets are, and where the devil who led them astray has been cast; there they will be tormented according to the hardness and impenitent character of their hearts, day and night, forever and ever.

> “After this Elijah went up to the summit of Carmel and immediately placed his face upon the ground between his knees. He said to his servant: ‘Look toward the sea and go up.’ When he had gone up and looked, he said: ‘There is nothing.’ Again he said to him: ‘Return seven times.’ On the seventh occasion, behold, a small cloud, like a man’s footprint, was rising from the sea,”

and so forth.

What is signified by this except that, when Christ the Son of God rose among human beings and took upon himself the tenderness of our flesh, after tasting death and ascending victoriously from the world to heaven, he sent from above to the earth the rain of divine grace through the sevenfold Spirit. This rain cleansed us from sin and enabled us to produce spiritual fruits.

### CHAPTER XIX

> “Elijah was afraid, and he rose and went wherever his desire led him. He came to Beersheba of Judah, dismissed his servant there, and went on into the wilderness a day’s journey. When he had come and sat beneath a juniper tree, he asked that his soul might die, and said: ‘It is enough, Lord; take my soul, for I am no better than my fathers.’ He threw himself down and fell asleep under the shade of the juniper,”

and so forth.

Holy men who, when the Spirit raises them up, are carried toward the highest things are restrained by certain temptations as long as they remain in this life, lest they become proud through exaltation and so be unable to advance as far as they wish.

They are prevented from being lifted up by pride, even when a certain measure of virtues is present in them. This is why Elijah, although he had advanced to great heights through so many virtues, was held back to a certain measure when he fled from Jezebel, who, though a queen, was nevertheless only a woman.

I consider this man of extraordinary virtue drawing fire from heaven, suddenly burning up two companies of fifty men with all their members by a sudden command, closing the heavens against rain by his word, opening the heavens to rain by his word, raising the dead, and foreseeing all future things. Then again I recall with what fear he fled before one little woman.

I consider a man struck with fear asking death from the hand of God but not receiving it, while fleeing death from the hand of a woman and thereby avoiding it. He sought to escape death, saying:

> “It is enough; take my soul, for I am no better than my fathers,”

and he fell asleep under the shade of the juniper.

How, then, was he so powerful that he could perform so many virtues? How was he so weak that he feared a woman in this way? It is because the dispensations of the heavenly will are weighed according to the measure of a hidden balance, so that the holy men themselves may be very powerful through God’s power and yet, by a certain measure, be restrained through their own weakness.

In those virtues Elijah showed what he had received from God; in those weaknesses he recognized what he was capable of on his own. That power was the virtue; this weakness was the guardian of virtue. In those virtues he displayed what he had received; in these weaknesses he guarded what he had received. Elijah was revealed in the miracles; he was preserved in the weaknesses.

> “And behold, an angel touched him and said to him: ‘Arise…’”

[Scan page 247]

### [Heading partly illegible in the scan]

“Eat.” He rose and found at his head a hearth-baked loaf and a jar of water; he ate and drank, and fell asleep again. The angel of the Lord returned a second time, touched him, and said to him: “Rise, eat, for a great journey remains to you.” When he had risen, he ate and drank, and walked in the strength of that food for forty days and forty nights, as far as the mountain of God, Horeb.

When the mind is raised by the sublimity of contemplation, whatever it is able perfectly to discern is God. But when it discerns something subtle, it hears what is said concerning the incomprehensible substance of eternity. For we perceive something like a whisper of a gentle breeze when, in sudden contemplation, we subtly taste the savor of inmost truth; then we also perceive that we cannot know anything of God.

What, then, did Elijah receive from the angel in these things, if not the weakness of nature? Those for whom simple nourishment is insufficient require a double nourishment, so that we may be able to ascend to heavenly things. Just as the body cannot subsist without bodily nourishment, so the soul cannot live without the word of God. For the angel who fed Elijah—whom does he more fittingly signify than the angel of the supreme counsel, by whose help we subsist both in bodily and in spiritual nature? After he had risen from sleep, Elijah walked, ate, and drank, in the strength of that food for forty days and forty nights, as far as the mountain of God, Horeb.

So also, while we carry out the journey of our earthly life with the aid of divine consolation, we must hasten with the greatest diligence to continue throughout the whole time of the present life in the work of good deeds, and to ascend to the mountain of God and to his holy place, so that there we may find eternal rest.

“And when he had come there, he stayed in a cave. And behold, the word of the Lord came to him, and said to him: ‘What are you doing here, Elijah?’ But he answered: ‘With great zeal I have been zealous for the Lord God of hosts, because the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant; they have torn down your altars and killed your prophets with the sword. I alone have been left, and they seek my life in order to take it away.’ And he said to him: ‘Go out, and stand on the mountain before the Lord.’ And behold, the Lord passed by, and a great and powerful wind overturned the mountains and shattered the rocks before the Lord. The Lord was not in the wind. And after the wind, an earthquake. The Lord was not in the earthquake. And after the earthquake, a fire. The Lord was not in the fire. And after the fire, the sound of a gentle breeze. When Elijah heard it, he covered his face with his cloak, and, going out, stood at the entrance of the cave. And behold, a voice came to him, saying: ‘What are you doing here, Elijah?’ And he answered: ‘With great zeal I have been zealous for the Lord God of hosts, because they have forsaken your covenant, the children of Israel. They have torn down your altars and killed your prophets with the sword; I alone have been left, and they seek my life in order to take it away.’ And the Lord said to him: ‘Go, and return on your way through the wilderness to Damascus. When you arrive there, you shall anoint Hazael as king over Syria, and Jehu son of Nimshi as king over Israel; and you shall anoint Elisha son of Shaphat, who is from Abel-meholah, as prophet in your place.’ And whatever follows.”

The Spirit of the Lord overturns mountains and shatters rocks, because the fear that arises at his coming casts down the height of our heart and melts its hardness. Yet when it is said that the Lord is not in the wind, the earthquake, or the fire, his presence in these things is not denied, for immense truth is thereby disclosed in proportion to the ignorance with which the human being is veiled.

For the covering of the face signifies that the higher mind, which desires to seek, must veil this contemplation by considering its own weakness. It must by no means hurl the eyes of its understanding rashly beyond itself; rather, toward what it cannot grasp, it must close itself with reverent restraint.

While doing this, Elijah is described as standing at the entrance of the cave. For what is our cave except this dwelling of corruption in which we are still held by our ancient condition? But when we begin to perceive something concerning the knowledge of divinity, we already stand, as it were, at the entrance of our cave.

Although we cannot advance farther, yet, longing for the knowledge of truth, we already begin to breathe something of the air of freedom. To stand at the entrance of the cave, therefore, is to begin to go out toward knowledge of the truth while the obstacle of our corruption is held in check.

For this reason, when the cloud descended upon the tabernacle, the Israelites are said to have watched from a distance and to have stood at the entrances of their tents, because, to some extent, they beheld the coming of the Divinity, as though they were already going out from their dwellings.

“And behold, a voice came to Elijah, saying: ‘What are you doing here, Elijah?’ And he answered: ‘With great zeal I have been zealous for the Lord God of hosts, because they have forsaken your covenant, the children of Israel. They have torn down your altars and killed your prophets with the sword; I alone have been left, and they seek my life in order to take it away.’ And he said: ‘Go out, and stand on the mountain before the Lord.’ And behold, the Lord passed by, and a great and powerful wind overturned the mountains and shattered the rocks before the Lord. The Lord was not in the wind. And after the wind, an earthquake. The Lord was not in the earthquake. And after the earthquake, a fire. The Lord was not in the fire. And after the fire, the sound of a gentle breeze. When Elijah heard it, he covered his face with his cloak,” and so forth.

It is certain that the one who neglects to consider the merits of those who are better than himself, while he acts rightly, extinguishes the eye of his heart in the darkness of pride. By contrast, the one who carefully weighs the good deeds of others illuminates himself with the ray of great humility. When he sees and recognizes in others the good deeds that he himself has performed, he suppresses the swelling of pride that strives to burst forth from his inward uniqueness.

Hence, by the voice of God, Elijah, who thought that he alone remained, is told: “I have left myself seven thousand men who have not bent their knees before Baal” (Romans 11). This was said so that he might recognize that he had not been left alone, and that he might bow down the glory of pride that arose in him from his supposed uniqueness.

[Scan page 248]

### *Exposition on the Books of Kings*

The prophet was, indeed, and had often known heavenly mysteries. What difficulty, then, would there have been in recognizing that faithful servants of God remained in this world? But here we must carefully observe how wickedly pride closes the eye of the heart, since the man who, in humility, had known hidden things belonging to God did not know things that were manifest.

“And the Lord said to Elijah: ‘Go, and return on your way through the wilderness to Damascus. When you arrive there, you shall anoint Hazael as king over Syria, and Jehu son of Nimshi as king over Israel. But Elisha son of Shaphat, who is from Abel-meholah, you shall anoint as prophet in your place. And whoever escapes the sword of Hazael, Jehu shall kill; and whoever escapes the sword of Jehu, Elisha shall kill,’” and so forth.

This must not be understood as though Elisha, the prophet of God, would be a murderer and a tyrant. It must rather be understood spiritually: divine justice, which repays each person according to his deeds, punishes human sins sometimes by manifest vengeance and sometimes by hidden judgment.

It takes vengeance through kings and rulers; it takes vengeance through prophets and priests, when it causes some wrongdoers to be punished by the sword and strikes others through the sword of the tongue. Thus David, Solomon, and the other kings inflicted the punishment of the sword when they ordered people to be killed. Elsewhere it is written concerning the punishment of the proud and disobedient: “I cut them down,” he says, “through the prophets, and I killed them by the words of my mouth” (Hosea 6).

“Therefore Elijah departed from there and found Elisha son of Shaphat, plowing with twelve yoke of oxen, and he himself was one of the twelve plowmen. When Elijah came to him, he threw his cloak over him,” and so forth.

Thus Elijah departed and found Elisha son of Shaphat plowing with twelve yoke of oxen. When our Redeemer descended from heaven, by divine judgment he acquired a people still intent upon earthly works, among whom he accomplished salvation when he converted them to the faith.

As we have already said, Elijah is interpreted as “the Lord God”; Shaphat, as “of the one who judges”; and Elisha as “the salvation of my God.” How wonderfully, therefore, did the prophet throw his cloak over him, when the Lord clothed him with the Catholic faith! “All of you,” says the Apostle, “who have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians 3).

“And immediately, leaving the oxen, he ran after Elijah and said: ‘Let me kiss, I beg you, my father and my mother, and then I will follow you.’” As soon as the chorus of the elect heard the Lord speaking through the Gospel: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14), it immediately ceased to desire earthly gain and to serve worldly desires.

He devoted himself entirely to the service of Christ, yet he did not cease to preach the word of life to others. For to kiss one’s father means to correct by speech anyone whom one is able to correct, whether from the Jews or from the Gentiles.

“Therefore Elisha took a pair of oxen, slaughtered them, cooked their flesh with the plow of the oxen, and gave it to the people, and they ate.”

When the Christian people slaughter carnal desires and devote their entire strength to the work of evangelization, they are able to provide a very sufficient nourishment for their hearers. Elisha himself follows our Elijah and ministers to him; that is, by following his footsteps and faithfully observing his commands, he strives to render him a worthy ministry of good works.

### Chapter 20

“Now Ben-hadad, king of Syria, gathered all his army, and thirty-two kings with him, together with horses and chariots. He went up and fought against Samaria and besieged it,” and so forth.

When Ben-hadad, king of Syria, began to besiege and attack Samaria, he said:

“May the gods do this to me, and may they add this, if the dust of Samaria shall be enough for handfuls for all the people who follow me.”

This has the following meaning. Samaria, according to the custom of cities, necessarily had earth inside the walls, so that the walls themselves might have an equal support and not, standing without the assistance of the surrounding earth, be easily thrown down by the repeated blows of hostile hands and battering rams.

On the outside, however, the height of the towers rose far above the surface of the earth, especially since, as Scripture reports, the city itself had been situated on the summit of a mountain. Thus the arrogant king, terrifying the besieged city, said that he had such a multitude of troops with him that, even if each of his soldiers brought only one stone, clod of earth, or stake for constructing a mound against the city, the mound would rise until it appeared equal to the surface of the city that lay within the walls. In this way, those fighting against the city from the mound would be able to cast weapons and torches into it.

Checking his rash arrogance with a restrained reply, the king of Israel said:

“Tell him: Let not the one who girds himself boast as though he were already ungirded.”

For one person is girded, another ungirded, and another not yet girded. The girded person is one who walks about encircled with a belt. The ungirded person is one who has recently removed his belt—for example, someone about to enter a bath, climb into bed, or perhaps put on a tunic for lying down on the ground. The person not yet girded is one who, although clothed in a tunic, has not yet strengthened himself by fastening a belt around it.

Thus, in a military expedition, the man who has taken his place properly girded is called girded, that is, armed. The man who returns home victorious after the battle is rightly called ungirded, because, having laid down his arms, he enjoys the leisure of desired peace. But the man who has not yet begun either to fight or to prepare himself for battle is rightly said to be not yet girded.

Therefore the king of Israel said to the king of Syria, who was boasting as though he had already captured Samaria, which he had only begun to besiege: “Let not the one who girds himself boast as though he were already ungirded.” It was as though he openly said: “Do not boast as though you were already the victor in the danger of battle, when you are still stationed in the battle-line and do not know whether victory will follow you.”

He was speaking truly. For as soon as the battle was joined, Ben-hadad did not triumph over his defeated enemies, but returned home in flight with his whole army.

Mystically, Ben-hadad, the enemy of Israel, signifies the devil, the enemy of all good people, who draws the various armies of wicked spirits into battle against the people of God. Yet he is conquered through the sons of the leaders of Israel, that is, through good hearers of holy teachers, who strive to fulfill in deeds whatever they hear with their ears.

He is said to have had two hundred thousand and thirty-two men, because those who possess the knowledge of both Testaments perfectly and preserve the faith of the Trinity together with the twofold love of God and neighbor are shown to be fit in every way for the army of the supreme King.

“Ben-hadad, king of Syria, also fled on horseback with the horsemen. Then the king of Israel went out and struck the horses and chariots, and inflicted a great defeat on Syria.”

Why is Ben-hadad, king of Syria, described as fleeing on horseback with his horsemen, unless because the devil, the prince of all the wicked, has lofty eyes? Syria is interpreted as “lofty.” He sits upon the horse of his pride with his horsemen—that is, with all the proud—for he is the head of all the sons of pride. He is put to flight by the army of Christ, namely, by the humble who fear God.

The king of Israel strikes the horses and chariots because it is written of the King of kings that he drowned Pharaoh and his army, horse and rider, in the Red Sea (Exodus 15), when he overwhelmed the spiritual wickednesses with the true Pharaoh, namely the ancient enemy, in the water of baptism, wiping away the sins of the human race.

“Then the prophet came to the king of Israel and said to him: ‘Go, strengthen yourself, and know and see what you are doing. For at the turn of the year the king of Syria will come up against you.’ The servants of the king of Syria said to him: ‘Their gods are gods of the mountains; therefore they overcame us,’” and so forth.

That Ben-hadad, king of Syria, after being defeated once, renews the battle against Israel signifies that the devil never ceases from his malicious purpose. Although he is frequently defeated by holy men, he nevertheless renews the battle against them. When he is conquered in one way, he immediately attempts to conquer in another.

Hence the servants of the king of Syria said to him: “Their gods are gods of the mountains; therefore they overcame us. But it is better that we fight against them in the plains, and we shall overcome them.”

For the wicked, always thinking deceitfully, strive to prepare a bodily battle if they are defeated in spiritual things. The devil and his entire army are especially intent upon this: to cast human souls down from heavenly things to earthly ones, so that they may conquer them more easily.

If they see people desiring heavenly things, they thrust earthly and perishable things before them for their love. If they see them giving thanks to God amid prosperity, they strive to break them through adversity.

But just as the words of the king of Syria and his servants did not agree with their actions—for where they trusted that they could prevail, there they were defeated—so the prince of evil is often conquered with his army precisely where he thinks he can prevail: “God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong, and the things that are not, to destroy the things that are” (1 Corinthians 1).

Thus the ancient enemy tested blessed Job. While he asked the Lord that Job’s possessions and children be handed over to him, so that through this he might overthrow his soul, he nevertheless did not prevail to the end, so as to be given power over Job himself. Having been granted this, he wounded Job’s flesh with a severe ulcer, as though he were at once the victor. And Paul the Apostle also was given a thorn in his flesh, an angel of Satan, to strike him, so that strength might be perfected in weakness (2 Corinthians 12).

“Then a certain man, one of the sons of the prophets, said to his companion in the word of the Lord: ‘Strike me.’ But he refused to strike him. And he said to him: ‘Because you would not listen to the voice of the Lord, behold, when you depart from me, a lion will strike you.’ And when he had gone a little way from him, a lion found him and struck him. He then met another man and said to him: ‘Strike me.’ He struck him and wounded him. The prophet went away and met the king on the road. He changed his appearance by putting dust over his eyes. When the king had passed, he cried out to the king and said: ‘Your servant went out to battle,’” and so forth.

Josephus reports the matter in the following way. Meanwhile the prophet Micaiah approached one of the Israelites and asked him to strike him on the head according to the will of the Lord. When the man refused, he foretold to him that, because he had disobeyed God and his command, a lion would meet him and kill him. When this had happened to that man, the prophet again approached another and commanded him to do the same.

When the man had struck him and bloodied his head, the prophet approached the king with his head bound up and said that, while he had been stationed in the army, he had received a captive from a certain tribune to guard, and that the tribune had told him that if the captive escaped, he himself would die. When the captive escaped, the man who had entrusted him to his keeping threatened to put him to death. When Ahab replied that his death was entirely just, the prophet loosened the cloth from his head, and the king recognized that he was Micaiah.

He used this parable because of the words he was about to speak to the king. He said that God had granted him the punishment of his enemy, yet he himself had dismissed Ben-hadad, his enemy who had blasphemed God. For this reason God had decreed that Ahab himself should be killed by him, while his people should be destroyed by the invasion of the army.

In anger, Ahab ordered that the prophet be kept in confinement. Confounded by Micaiah’s words, he returned to his own house.

According to the laws of allegorical interpretation, the servants of God must take the greatest care not to flatter themselves with harmful security, after the example of Ahab, king of Israel. While the enemy is still alive, they must not imagine themselves perpetual victors, lest, through the devil’s deceit in promising peace, they be overthrown all the sooner.

For just as the prophet then announced to the king a swift and just vengeance because of his ill-considered mercy, so prophetic speech now announces that, if we make a pact with the devil, an eternal punishment awaits us on account of it.

### Chapter 21

“After these events, Naboth the Jezreelite had a vineyard in Jezreel, beside the palace of Ahab, king of Samaria. Ahab therefore spoke to Naboth, saying: ‘Give me your vineyard, so that I may make it into a garden of vegetables, because it is near and close to my house. I will give you a better vineyard in exchange for it; or, if you prefer, I will give you its price in silver, as much as it is worth.’ Naboth answered him: ‘The Lord be gracious to me, and do not let me give you the inheritance of my fathers.’ Ahab therefore came into his house, angry and gnashing his teeth because of the words that Naboth the Jezreelite had spoken to him, saying: ‘I will not give you the inheritance of my fathers,’” and so forth.

Scripture relates that Ahab, king of Israel, coveted the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, which was in Jezreel beside the king’s palace, in order to make a vegetable garden there. When Naboth refused to give it to him, the same Naboth was stoned and killed through the counsel of his most wicked wife, namely Queen Jezebel, after false witnesses had been secretly brought in. His vineyard was then seized and taken into the possession of the king.

Let us therefore consider who this Naboth the Jezreelite was and what his vineyard signifies. Naboth is interpreted as “conspicuous” or “possession”; Jezreel as “the honor of God” or “the seed of God.” Whom can we more appropriately call the holiness or seed of God than the Son of God, who is the splendor of his glory and the figure of his substance, whom God appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages?

To him the Psalmist, praying, says: “You who sit upon the cherubim, appear before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh. Stir up your power and come, that you may save us” (Psalm 79).

This Naboth had a vineyard of which Isaiah speaks at greatest length in a song, concluding: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel.” And in the Psalm: “You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it” (ibid.).

He surrounded it with a hedge, as we read in the Gospel—that is, either with the wall of the city or with the assistance of the angels. He dug a winepress in it, either an altar or those winepresses whose titles stand at the head of three Psalms, namely the eighth and the eighty-sixth Psalms. He built a tower, plainly the temple, of which Micah says: “And you, tower of the mist, daughter of Zion” (Micah 4).

He leased it to tenants, whom elsewhere he called the workers or cultivators of the vineyard.

Ahab, whose name is interpreted as “brother of the father,” coveted this vineyard. He signifies the Jewish people, from whom Christ deigned to take flesh, so that he might make a vegetable garden in it—that is, where the tender shoot of spiritual grace ought to have flourished, transplant all sorts of frail doctrines through Pharisaic superstition.

But when Naboth refused to give him the vineyard—that is, when Christ did not consent to the superstitions of the Pharisees—the impious wife Jezebel plotted against him. Her name is interpreted as “dweller with” or “empty flow,” which aptly corresponds to the Synagogue. It appeared to dwell in the house of the Lord, but was flowing away through various desires of vanity.

“Therefore Jezebel sent letters to the elders and nobles who were in the city, ordering them, after false witnesses had been secretly introduced, to bring false testimony against Naboth, claiming that he had blessed God and the king, and then to lead him out of the city and stone him to death.”

When the Synagogue, through the chief priests, scribes, and Pharisees, plotted the death of Christ, of which it is written in the Gospel:

“The chief priests and the whole council were seeking false testimony against Jesus, so that they might hand him over to death; and they did not find any, although many false witnesses came forward. Finally two false witnesses came and said: ‘This man said: I can destroy the temple of God and rebuild it after three days’” (Matthew 26).

Thus two false witnesses gave false testimony against Naboth, saying that he had blessed God and the king. The Jews likewise brought forward two false witnesses against Christ, alleging that he ascribed to himself divine power and nature.

Hence, when Pilate said to the Jews: “Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no charge in him,” the Jews answered him: “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.”

“Therefore Naboth was stoned outside the city, at the instigation of Jezebel, so that, after he was dead, Ahab might possess his vineyard.”

So also the Savior suffered outside the gate, crucified in the place of Calvary, when the Synagogue, inflamed by zeal, stirred up the people to demand Christ’s death, so that, once he had been killed, they might live more securely.

Hence, as though consulting their own interests, they said: “Behold, the whole world has gone after him. If we let him go on in this way, everyone will believe in him” (John 12).

The inheritance of Christ is therefore the Church, which was given to him from the Gentiles joined to him. His Father did not leave it to him when he died; rather, he wondrously acquired it through his own death, because by rising again he took possession of it.

After Christ had been killed, the evil tenants tried to claim this inheritance for themselves. The Jews who crucified him attempted to extinguish the faith that exists through him, to place above it their own righteousness derived from the Law, and to implant that righteousness among the Gentiles whom they sought to instruct.

The heir of the vineyard is killed outside the vineyard (Matthew 21), because Jesus suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his blood.

It is fitting for this mystery that, in the place where the dogs licked Naboth’s blood, they should also, according to the prophet’s sentence, lick the blood of Ahab. In the field of Jezreel the dogs also ate the flesh of Jezebel.

For when those dogs of whom it is written, “Many dogs have surrounded me” (Psalm 22), sought the blood of our Redeemer with a poisonous tongue, they themselves were handed over to those dogs of whom Scripture likewise says: “It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs” (Matthew 15). Thus the most wicked plunderers and criminal possessors of the Lord’s vineyard were slaughtered in the same place where the Lord suffered, and their flesh was given to beasts and birds to be eaten.

And so that impious people, who during the Lord’s passion cried out with profane voices, “His blood be upon us and upon our children,” deserved to have their most foul blood poured out in the very place where they demanded that their Savior be killed.

Josephus reports that from all Judea, on the solemn day of Passover, the people gathered at Jerusalem as though compelled by some deadly force. He says that three million persons were present. It was by the just judgment of God that this time was chosen for vengeance, so that the whole multitude who, during the days of Passover, had violated their Savior and the saving Christ of the Lord with bloodstained hands and sacrilegious voices might, as though enclosed together in a single prison, undergo the destruction of the deadly punishment they deserved.

[Scan page 251]

### Chapter 22

“Therefore the king of Israel summoned a certain eunuch and said to him: ‘Hurry and bring Micaiah son of Imlah.’ The king of Israel and Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, were sitting, each on his throne, clothed in royal attire,” and so forth.

When Micaiah was summoned before the king of Israel, he said:

“I saw the Lord sitting upon his throne, and all the army of heaven standing beside him on his right and on his left. And it was said: ‘Who will deceive Ahab, so that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?’ One answered one way, and another another way. Then a spirit came forward and said: ‘I will deceive him.’ And it was said: ‘By what means will you deceive him?’ He answered: ‘I will go out and become a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.’”

What should we understand by the throne of the Lord except the angelic powers? God presides over their minds at a higher level and disposes all things at a lower one. And what is meant by the army of heaven except the ministering angels?

What does it mean, then, that the army of heaven is said to stand on his right and on his left? God is within all things in such a way that he is confined neither by right nor by left. But the right side of God signifies the part of the angels that has been chosen; the left side of God signifies the part of the angels that has been rejected.

For God has not only good beings who assist him, but also evil ones who burden those unwilling to return. Nor does the phrase “the army of heaven” prevent us from understanding the rejected part as angels.
