We call the birds that we know to be suspended in the air “birds of heaven.” Paul likewise spoke of these spirits: “Against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6), and, naming their ruler, he said: “According to the prince of the power of the air.”

The army of angels therefore stands at the right and at the left, because the will of the elect spirits agrees with divine mercy, while the mind of the reprobate, serving its own wickedness, obeys the judgment of God’s severity.

Hence a lying spirit is immediately described as coming forward into the midst, through whom King Ahab might be deceived according to his deserts. For it is not permissible to believe that a good spirit wished to serve deceit when he said: “I will go out and become a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.”

But because King Ahab, on account of his preceding sins, was worthy to be condemned by such a deception, so that the man who had often fallen willingly into guilt might at last be captured willingly for punishment, hidden justice grants permission to wicked spirits, so that they may strangle in the snare of sin those who sin willingly and drag them, even unwilling, into the punishment of sin.

Finally, the man who does not change his wicked life and does not turn his mind away from the commission of sins, when he consults a prophet, hears, by God’s arrangement, what he deserves to hear as one who is to be condemned.

For, to mention one or two examples among many, the house of Israel had withdrawn from the worship of almighty God under the slavery of idols, yet it often came, seeking prosperity, to the prophets by whom it was accustomed to be deceived. Since it acted perversely, it deserved to hear prosperity from the mouths of its prophets.

What else were the heavenly judgments accomplishing except that the sinful people might be caught in their own heart? The people had abandoned the truth by following faithlessness, and so they were deceived by the flattering words of their prophets that they no longer feared having sinned. Thus, the more securely they lived in guilt, the more harshly they would afterward be dragged to punishment.

But now, by the generosity of almighty God, a very large part of the human race has been moved away from the worship of idols. It publicly professes the true faith and refuses to submit in worship to wood, stones, or any creature.

Anyone who stands in the faith may now safely consult a prophet, because he will hear what it is fitting for a believer to hear. I say confidently that, if he had withdrawn from all impurity and wicked deeds, he would withdraw from them again.

For when the outstanding preacher Paul cries out, “Flee avarice, in which there is the worship of idols” (Colossians 3), whoever remains subject to avarice is not free from the worship of idols.

If someone who burns with the fires of avarice appears to stand in the faith, but seeks to receive what belongs to another, desires to grasp the honors of the world, longs to possess temporal glory, and consults a prophet about that same glory, it is entirely just that, according to the merit of his guilt, he should hear prosperity from the prophet’s mouth.

In this way, the man who refused to hear the words of God in sacred Scripture, so that he might despise earthly things and seek heavenly ones, hears by God’s judgment from the mouth of his prophet the very thing through which he falls under a greater obligation: delighted by the hope of earthly glory, he feeds his own desires and is always led downward.

For that spirit was not good which desired to be a liar in the mouth of the prophets. Hence it was previously stated that the army of heaven stood at the Lord’s right and left.

God is unbounded truth in that eternal blessedness which is called his right hand; he has no left hand, because there is nothing that can displease him. But because he sees all things together and observes everything simultaneously, he is described as having the army of heaven at his right and left, so that by the right we understand the elect angels, and by the left the reprobate spirits.

Nor should it trouble us that the rejected angels are also called the army of heaven. Although they have been expelled from the ethereal heaven, they nevertheless still remain in the aerial heaven, as Paul says: “Against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6).

## Commentary on the Books of Kings

### Book Four

#### Preface

At last, with the Lord’s help, we have, as it were, reached the fourth book by sailing, where our hand—which steers the oars obliquely across the seas of the teachers—may at some time find rest. We have crossed a vast sea, as it were, by the favorable breezes of the zephyrs that aided the preceding little book; and, with the Lord blowing, we have, so to speak—as someone says—sailed past the Sirens’ songs with deafened ears. Our sailors, or rather our pilots, skilled in the sea, have frequently traversed the deep of this journey with the Holy Spirit filling their sails.

But now we may see the harbor from afar, as it were: we consider what we have crossed and also toward what we are approaching; we rejoice, and, as though turning our eyes behind us after having passed through, we contemplate how bravely, sailing through the straits, we have compressed the billowing sea. What remains to be crossed toward the shore now seems more certain. Yet although the stretch of sea we must cover may appear small, it is nevertheless necessary for us that, with the north wind descending gently and the south wind breathing favorably, the latter should drive the raised sails forward, so that the ship may prosper.

For it often happens that, while some rashly desire to cross the blue waters of the sea without the breath of the supreme Spirit, they strike rocks, dash against a mountain, and find not a harbor but rather lamentation. Therefore we must guide the stern carefully, so that it may move gently and safely over the open sea, until the harbor receives it and it can finally emerge from the whirlpool and rest, fixed upon the shore, rejoicing. Thus, at least, it may convey whatever small cargoes it has gathered from the teachers, since, although the mysteries of Christ and the Church were disclosed by the preceding book, this one above all demonstrates the Savior’s passion, or rather his ascension.

For this reason the books of Kings rightly prefigured the four books of the Gospels, in which what was enacted figuratively in those books has evidently been fulfilled in reality. Therefore I wish to return to this work in triumph, lest the hidden mystical gifts remain concealed any longer. From the books of the teachers whose words have been cited, I have decided to gather many passages and, with the Lord’s favor, to bring our work to a close in the form of a little book, in a concise and brief style, lest I seem to exceed the proper measure of a small work.

Sacred history says:

### Chapter One

> “Now Moab rebelled against Israel after Ahab had died. And Ahaziah fell through the lattice of his upper room which he had in Samaria, and he became ill. He sent messengers, saying to them: ‘Go, consult Beelzebub, the god of Ekron, whether I may recover from this illness.’
>
> “But the angel of the Lord spoke to Elijah the Tishbite, saying: ‘Rise and go up to meet the messengers of the king of Samaria, and say to them: “Is there no God in Israel, that you are going to consult Beelzebub, the god of Ekron?” Therefore thus says the Lord: “You shall not come down from the bed on which you have gone up, but you shall surely die,”’” and the rest.

After the most impious king Ahab had died, an impious heir succeeded him—his son Ahaziah. Scripture relates that he did evil in the sight of the Lord, walked in the way of his father and his mother, and in the way of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin. He also served Baal and worshiped him, provoking the Lord God of Israel, according to everything his father had done.

But he did not prosper for long, because he fell through the lattice of the upper room that he had in Samaria and became ill. “He sent messengers to Beelzebub, the god of Ekron, to consult him whether he could recover from this illness.” When Elijah met the messengers and announced that death was near, the king sent a commander of fifty with his soldiers to bring him in. But when these were consumed by heavenly fire, he sent another commander of fifty, who was likewise burned with his men. He sent a third, who was spared.

Thus this king signifies the Jewish people, and especially their rulers, who, devoted to sins and vices, rejected the truth from themselves, indeed persecuted it. Hence we read in the Gospel: “The chief priests and Pharisees sent officers to seize Jesus” (John 7). Again: “So they sought to seize him, but no one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come; and he went away to the mountain alone to pray” (John 8). And again: “They took counsel to kill him” (John 11).

“Jesus therefore no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went away into the region near the desert, to a city called Ephraim.” The house of Ahaziah, therefore, is the Synagogue of the Jews, enclosed on every side by the commandments of the law as by the latticework of an upper room. But just as Ahaziah, falling through the lattice by which he ought to have been protected, suffered a grievous illness, so the Jewish people, exceeding the limits of the law’s observance, fell into the incurable sickness of sins.

Because it had abandoned divine protection, it did not deserve to find remedies for its salvation. For, like the impious king, it fled to the protection of false gods, by whom it was harmed rather than helped. Therefore it is rebuked by the prophetic mouth, and its approaching death is foretold. Hence Isaiah says:

> “When they say to you, ‘Consult the mediums and the diviners who chirp and mutter in their incantations’” (Isaiah 8), “should not a people inquire of its God on behalf of the living and the dead? To the law rather and to the testimony!”

But if they do not speak according to this word, there will be no morning light for them. Whoever passes through it will fall and hunger; and when he is hungry, he will become angry and curse his king. They will look upward and gaze upon the earth. Behold: distress and darkness, dissolution, anguish, and pursuing gloom; and they will not be able to flee from their distress.

The impious king sends two commanders of fifty with the soldiers subject to them to bring Elijah, but they are consumed by divine fire; the third, however, is saved. The number fifty signifies the confession of repentance, by which the forgiveness of sins is declared. The Jews, therefore, unwilling to acknowledge Christ as perfect God and the prince of repentance, say to him: “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?” In the future they are burned and consumed by divine fire. But the third commander of fifty, because he turned to faith in the Trinity and recognized the sacrament of repentance, obtained pardon.

### Chapter Two

> “And it came to pass, when the Lord was about to take Elijah up into heaven by a whirlwind, that Elijah and Elisha were going from Gilgal. And Elijah said to Elisha: ‘Stay here, because the Lord has sent me as far as Bethel.’ Elisha said to him: ‘As the Lord lives and as your soul lives, I will not leave you,’” and the rest.

What does it mean that Elijah is said to have been taken up into heaven? Do we believe that, while he was still placed in this corruptible flesh, he was brought to that heaven of supreme rest before the Lord’s resurrection and ascension? But one heaven is the aerial heaven, another the ethereal. The aerial heaven is nearest to the earth; hence we speak of “the birds of heaven” (Matthew 6), because we see them flying in the air.

Elijah, therefore, was lifted into the aerial heaven, so that he might suddenly be brought to a hidden region of the earth, where he might live in great rest of body and spirit until he returns at the end of the world and pays the debt of death. In being lifted up, Elijah signified the Lord’s ascension. He postponed death but did not escape it; our Redeemer, however, because he did not postpone death, overcame it and destroyed it by rising again, and he revealed the glory of his resurrection by ascending.

It should also be noted that Elijah is said to have ascended in a chariot, so that it might plainly be shown that a mere human being required assistance from another. For these aids were accomplished and displayed through angels, since even to the aerial heaven he could not ascend by himself, burdened as he was by the weakness of his nature.

Our Redeemer, however, is not said to have been lifted up by a chariot or by angels, because he who had made all things was carried above all things by his own power. He was returning there where he was, and from there he was returning while remaining here: for when he ascended into heaven through his humanity, through his divinity he continued to contain earth and heaven alike.

Just as Joseph, sold by his brothers, foreshadowed the selling of our Redeemer, so Enoch, translated, and Elijah, lifted into the aerial heaven, signified the Lord’s ascension (Genesis 37). The Lord had two heralds and witnesses of his ascension: one before the law, the other under the law, so that he might eventually come who would truly be able to penetrate the heavens.

The order of their two elevations is likewise distinguished by certain stages of progress. Enoch is remembered as having been translated, while Elijah was carried up into heaven, so that afterward there might come one who, neither translated nor carried, would penetrate the ethereal heaven by his own power. To us who believe in him he would grant purity of flesh, and under him the virtue of chastity would increase through the progression of time.

In their very translation—both of those servants who signified the Lord’s ascension and of the Lord himself, who ascended into heaven—he displayed a distinction. Enoch had wives and children, whereas Elijah is read to have had neither wife nor children. Consider, therefore, how the purity of chastity grew through successive stages, plainly shown both by the translated servants and by the person of the ascending Lord.

Enoch was translated, having been begotten through intercourse and begetting through intercourse. The Lord, however, was taken up, neither begetting through intercourse nor begotten through intercourse.

It is asked how Elisha, when his teacher Elijah offered him the opportunity to make a request, could have asked for a double spirit of Elijah, when the Lord says in the Gospel: “A disciple is not above his teacher; but everyone who is perfect will be like his teacher” (Matthew 10). When the mystery of this request is considered, it is judged to be not an importunate but a necessary petition.

> “Then Elijah said to Elisha: ‘Ask what you wish me to do for you before I am taken away from you.’ And Elisha said: ‘I ask that your spirit may be doubled in me.’ He replied: ‘You have asked for a difficult thing. Nevertheless, if you see me when I am taken away from you, it will be granted to you; but if you do not see me, it will not be granted.’”

Whom does Elijah signify here except our head, namely the Lord our Redeemer? And whom does Elisha signify except his body, which is the Church? Our Elijah gives the opportunity to ask when he says in the Gospel: “Ask, and it will be given to you” (Matthew 7). And again: “Ask,” he says, “and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete” (John 16).

Having received this confidence from the Lord, Elisha—that is, the Christian people—asks that the spirit of Christ may be doubled in them: namely, the twofold grace of the Holy Spirit, for the forgiveness of sins and for the bestowal of virtues.

Our Redeemer, therefore, who “committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2), did not need the forgiveness of sins, since he had no sin. But he performed works of virtue in the Holy Spirit, as he himself says to the Jews in the Gospel: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Matthew 12).

The works of the Holy Trinity—that is, of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—are therefore inseparable, as the Truth testifies when it says: “Whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise” (John 5). And the Apostle says: “All these things are accomplished by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each one individually as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12).

The Church rightly asks to receive the doubled spirit of Christ: she needs the forgiveness of sins, which Christ did not need, and the gift of virtues, which Christ, in the fullness of his own Spirit, grants through the Holy Spirit. He “ascended on high, led captivity captive, and gave gifts to human beings” (Ephesians 4)—namely, to those who firmly place their hope in him.

This is why Elijah says to Elisha:

> “If you see me when I am taken away from you, it will be granted to you; but if you do not see me, it will not be granted.”

For unless someone rightly fixes the eyes of faith upon him and faithfully believes in his passion, resurrection, and ascension to the Father, he will not receive the fruit of his petition. The following account makes this clear.

> “As Elijah, accompanied by Elisha, came to the bank of the Jordan, he took his mantle, wrapped it up, and struck the waters, which were divided in two directions, and both crossed over on dry ground. When Elijah had been taken up, Elisha lifted Elijah’s mantle, which had fallen from him. He returned and stood upon the bank of the Jordan; and with Elijah’s mantle, which had fallen from him, he struck the waters, but they were not divided. He said: ‘Where is the God of Elijah, even now?’ He struck the waters, and they were divided this way and that,” and so forth.

What does Elijah’s mantle signify except the Lord’s Incarnation, by which our Redeemer cleaves the river of death and prepares for us a passage to life? Elisha therefore retained this mantle after Elijah’s departure, because after Christ’s ascension into heaven the Church preserved faith in Christ’s Incarnation, through which she strives to cross the waves of the present life.

But just as Elisha, striking the river with the mantle, did not divide the waters before saying, “Where is the God of Elijah, even now?” and then struck the waters and they were divided, so the Church can perform no virtues except through invocation of the Lord’s name. For as he himself said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15). Human effort is nothing unless divine assistance is present.

Hence the Apostle says: “It is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish according to his good pleasure” (Philippians 2). And the prophet says to the Lord: “In you we will toss our enemies with the horn, and in your name we will trample those who rise up against us” (Psalm 43), and so forth.

> “The men of the city said to Elisha: ‘Behold, the situation of this city is good, as you yourself, Lord, see; but the waters are bad and the land is barren.’ He said: ‘Bring me a new vessel and put salt in it.’”

The people asked Elisha to heal the evil and barren waters of Jericho. He took a new earthen vessel, threw salt into it, and cast it into the river; immediately the river’s waters were healed. By this the prophet foretold that the Word would become flesh and dwell among us.

Thus, in the likeness of the Word, he placed salt—that is, wisdom—in an earthen vessel, namely the human body, and cast it into the water. This signified that all peoples, represented by the waters throughout the world, who were barren, would receive fruitfulness and blessing through Christ’s Incarnation.

> “From there he went up to Bethel. As he was going up by the way, little boys came out of the city and mocked him, saying: ‘Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead.’ When he looked behind him and saw them, he cursed them in the name of the Lord. And two bears came out of the forest and mauled forty-two of the boys.”

As we have often said, the prophet Elisha bore the figure of Christ. Indeed, his name means “salvation of God.” And who is the salvation of God except his Son, who is everywhere called the Savior?

Those little boys who mocked the salvation of God—that is, Elisha—represented the Jews who jeered at the Lord the Savior at the cross, saying: “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead,” because Christ was to ascend the cross at the place called Calvary.

When Elisha turned and cursed them, and two bears came out of the forest and killed the forty-two boys who were blaspheming, this signified that Christ, after his passion and resurrection from the dead, after he had ascended into heaven—as Elisha ascended to Bethel, that is, to the house of God—turned and cursed the Jews. In the forty-second year after his ascension, he sent two bears from the forests of the nations, namely Vespasian and Titus, who struck them down in a cruel slaughter.

### Chapter Three

> “Now Mesha, king of Moab, kept many sheep and paid the king of Israel one hundred thousand lambs and one hundred thousand rams with their wool. But when Ahab died, he broke the treaty that he had with the king of Israel,” and the rest.

After this, war was waged by three kings—that is, the king of Israel, the king of Judah, and the king of Edom—against Moab. The prophet Elisha was consulted by them, and after other words he added:

> “Make this valley full of trenches and pits. For thus says the Lord: ‘You shall not see wind, and you shall not see rain, but this valley shall be filled with water; and you shall drink, you and your families and your animals. And this is a small thing in the sight of the Lord: he will also deliver Moab into your hands, and you shall strike every fortified city, every choice city, cut down every fruit-bearing tree, stop up all the springs of water, and cover every excellent field with stones.’”

What do these three kings waging war against Moab signify except the rulers of the faithful, who, through faith in the Holy Trinity, fight against the prince of this world and against his people—that is, philosophers, heretics, schismatics, and all the wicked—with the shield of faith and spiritual weapons?

Moab, who was born from incest and whose name means “from the father,” aptly represents those to whom the Lord said: “You are from your father the devil, and you wish to do your father’s desires” (John 8).

These people oppose the Church, partly by threats, partly by persecutions, and partly by deceit and false inventions. But through the power of Christ, who is the head of the Christian people, they are overcome and driven away.

The Lord’s prophet says to them:

> “Make this valley full of trenches and pits. You shall not see wind or rain, but this valley shall be filled with water, and you shall drink, you and your families,”

and the rest.

Behold, the Lord’s prophet, through a miracle performed by the Lord, gives counsel to a people exhausted by thirst. In the same way, the words of the prophets give the faithful counsel about how they may quench their spiritual thirst and refresh their souls.

He commands that trenches be made in the valley of the torrent, and in this way he foretells an abundance of water without wind or rain. What is making trenches in the valley of the torrent except seeking deep mysteries in the sacred Scriptures with good purpose? They are filled with water without rain or wind because divine power often grants wisdom to those who investigate it without human assistance.

Hence the apostle John says:

> “You have no need for anyone to teach you, but his anointing teaches you about everything” (1 John 2).

“From these, human beings and animals drink”—that is, both the gifted and the simple receive teaching. For as suitable the soul of the recipient is, so much instruction for salvation will it find there.

The text continues:

> “And this is a small thing in the sight of the Lord; he will also deliver Moab into your hands,”

and so forth.

It is not enough for God’s servants to know hidden mysteries; they must also preach them to others and refute those who contradict them. A certain victory over the enemy has been promised to them, so that they may “strike every fortified city and every choice city,” and so forth.

By “fortified cities” and “choice cities” we may understand secular wisdom, in which philosophers and heretics place their greatest confidence. These are overthrown by the preachers of the holy Gospel.

Hence the Apostle says:

> “The weapons of our warfare are not carnal but powerful through God for the destruction of strongholds, destroying arguments and every height that rises against the knowledge of God, and taking every thought captive into obedience to Christ, while we stand ready to punish every disobedience” (2 Corinthians 10).

“All the fruit-bearing trees are cut down”—not those trees that produce good fruit, but those that generate deadly food, which, cut down at their roots by the axe of examination, will become fuel for eternal fire.

“All the springs of water are stopped up” when the founders of heresies, together with their followers, are condemned by catholic teachers.

“And all the excellent fields are covered with stones” when the beauty of heretical and philosophical speech is overwhelmed beneath the weight of anathema.

> “Nothing will remain in the land of Moab except earthen walls.”

These are the false arguments of fragile doctrines, which are surrounded by the slingers—that is, by the holy preachers of the Church—and are for the most part refuted and reduced to nothing.

When the Moabites, at sunrise, saw the water opposite them red like blood, they thought it was blood, saying that the three kings who had come against one another to battle had killed each other; thus they were deceived.

In the same way, philosophers, thinking the word of Christ’s cross foolishness, deride the Passion and regard the Church’s martyrdom as madness. But according to the Apostle:

> “What is foolish in God is wiser than human beings, and what is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (1 Corinthians 1),

because “the wisdom of the flesh is death, but the wisdom of the Spirit is life and peace” (Romans 8).

To demonstrate that in this passage Moab is understood as the pride of philosophers—concerning whom it is said, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the understanding of the intelligent” (1 Corinthians 1)—a few examples from the prophets may be added.

Amos says:

> “Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Moab, and for four, I will not revoke his punishment, because he burned the bones of the king of Edom to ashes.”

Indeed, whatever in this age belongs to perverse doctrines, whatever belongs to earthly wisdom, is thought to be robust. This dialectical strength is overthrown and dissolved, like a fire, into ashes and dust, so that what was thought most powerful may be proved to be nothing.

Isaiah also rebukes Moab’s pride, saying:

> “We have heard of Moab’s insolence; he is exceedingly insolent. I have taken away his pride” (Isaiah 16).

Jeremiah too, prophesying against all the nations, speaks specifically to Moab (Jeremiah 48): “Trusting in your strongholds,” and shortly afterward, “having confidence in your glory.” Again: “How do you say, ‘We are strong’?” Then: “The day of Moab is near, when his calamity will come, and his evil is very great.” More explicitly he says: “How the glorious staff is broken, the rod of magnificence!” And again: “The horn of Moab is broken.”

These things are said under the name of Moab so that the pride of the world’s foolishness, whose wickedness continually raises itself toward heaven, may be crushed.

### Chapter Four

> “A certain woman among the wives of the prophets cried out to Elisha, saying: ‘Your servant, my husband, is dead, and you know that your servant was one who feared the Lord. And behold, the creditor has come to take my two sons to serve him.’
>
> “Elisha said to her: ‘What shall I do for you? Tell me, what do you have in your house?’ She replied: ‘Your handmaid has nothing in the house except a little oil with which I may anoint myself.’
>
> “He said to her: ‘Go, ask empty vessels from all your neighbors—not just a few. Then go in and shut the door behind you and your sons, and pour into all those vessels; and when they are full, take them away.’ The woman went,” and the rest.

Whom does this woman signify except the holy Church? She is the mother of two peoples—the Jewish and the Gentile peoples—as though of two sons. Formerly, by a perverse deed, consenting to the persuasion of the cunning spirit, she had received, as it were, a coin of sin from a creditor and feared losing the two sons whom she had begotten in faith.

But obeying the prophet’s words—that is, the precepts of sacred Scripture—she pours what little oil she has into empty vessels. While many empty minds receive from the mouth of one teacher a small amount of love for divinity, they are filled to the brim by the overflowing grace of divine love’s ointments.

Even now the hearts of many, which had previously been empty vessels, are full of the ointment of the Spirit. They seemed to be filled only from a small quantity of oil. As this oil is given to one person after another and faith is received by the hearers, the woman—namely, the holy Church—is freed and is no longer held under the debt of her creditor.

> “Afterward, on a certain day, Elisha passed through Shunem. There was a prominent woman there who pressed him to eat bread. And whenever he passed by, he turned aside to her house to eat bread. She said to her husband:
>
> “‘I know that this is a holy man of God who passes by us continually. Let us make a small upper room for him and put there a bed, a table, a chair, and a lampstand, so that whenever he comes to us, he may stay there.’ On a certain day,” and so forth.

This woman who received the prophet as a guest may aptly suggest the origin of the Israelite people, which was among the patriarchs. Just as she deserved to receive the prophet Elisha as a guest, so Israel deserved to receive the Lord of the prophets.

For Abraham and Sarah deserved to receive and feed three men near the valley of Mamre.

Since this woman had no son, the prophet promised her, saying:

> “At this time, and at this same hour, if life accompanies you, you shall have a son in your womb.”

She replied:

> “No, I beg you, my lord, man of God; do not lie to your handmaid.”

The woman conceived and gave birth to a son at the appointed time, at the very hour when Elisha had spoken.

The boy grew. One day, when he had gone out to his father among the reapers, he said to his father: “My head, my head hurts.” His father said to the boy: “Carry him and take him away,” and so forth.

The Lord likewise said to Abraham:

> “I will return to you at this time, life accompanying you, and Sarah your wife shall have a son.”

When Sarah heard this, she laughed behind the door of the tent, secretly saying:

> “After I have grown old, and my lord is elderly, shall I give myself to pleasure?” (Genesis 18)

The Lord visited Sarah as he had promised and fulfilled what he had said. She conceived and bore a son in her old age, at the time God had foretold.

After the boy had grown, he was struck by an immense pain in the head and died around midday. In the same way, after the Israelite people had grown in Egypt and had been led out into the desert by Moses, after hearing the voice of the Lord in fire and cloud, when it ought to have been illumined by the light of knowledge, it immediately returned in spirit to idolatry and died.

> “Elisha said to Gehazi, his servant: ‘Gird your loins, take my staff in your hand, and go. If you meet anyone, do not greet him; and if anyone greets you, do not answer him. Place my staff upon the boy’s face.’
>
> “But the boy’s mother said: ‘As the Lord lives and as your soul lives, I will not leave you.’ So he arose and followed her. Gehazi had gone ahead of them,” and the rest.

What does it signify that the servant sent by Elisha with the staff does not raise the dead boy, whereas Elisha himself comes, stretches himself over the dead boy, conforms himself to his limbs, walks back and forth, and breathes seven times into the dead boy’s mouth, immediately bringing him back to life through the ministry of compassion?

It signifies that God, the author of the human race, mourned, as it were, the dead boy when, in compassion, he looked upon us extinguished by the sting of iniquity. Since through Moses he set forth the terror of the law, he sent the staff through the servant, as it were. For God held the rod through the law when he said: “If anyone does this or that, let him die.”

The law could not raise us from the death of sins, but, by breathing the grace of gentleness, it raised us to the state of life. The boy, however, could not raise the dead with the staff, because, as Paul testifies, “the law brought nothing to perfection.”

But Elisha himself, coming in person, humbly stretching himself over the corpse, and conforming himself to the dead man’s limbs, signified Christ, who, “though he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being” (Philippians 2).

“He walked back and forth,” because he calls both the Jews nearby and the nations far away.

“He breathed seven times upon the dead man,” because, through the opening of the divine gift, he breathes the grace of the sevenfold Spirit into those lying in the death of sin.

“Immediately the living boy rises,” because the one whom the rod of fear could not raise is restored to life through the spirit of love.

> “There was a famine in the land, and the sons of the prophets lived before him. He said to one of his servants: ‘Put on the large pot and cook a stew for the sons of the prophets.’”

“There was,” he says, “a famine in the land”—not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of the Lord.

“And the sons of the prophets lived before Elisha.” The sons of the preachers who walked in the law of the Lord and sought him by searching his testimonies with all their heart always live in the presence of the Lord and Savior.

> “A boy went out into the field to gather wild herbs, in order to cook a stew from them. He found what seemed to be a wild vine, gathered from it wild gourds, and, cutting them up, put them into the pot and made a stew.”

When someone, devoted to the letter of the law or assiduous in philosophical disciplines, seeks nourishment from the word and, finding either bitterness in the letter of the law or something deadly in the books of philosophers, mixes it with evangelical truth and cooks it in the pot of his heart, he prepares such a stew—that is, such instruction—for the refreshment of his hearers.

The Apostle says:

> “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (1 Corinthians 3).

And again:

> “The wisdom of the flesh is death, but the wisdom of the Spirit is life and peace” (Romans 8).

Perceiving this, the faithful people cry out that there is death in the pot, detesting false teaching as a deception of souls and shouting aloud.

But at Elisha’s command, flour is put into the pot when spiritual knowledge is introduced into such instruction, so that, with all the bitterness of depravity removed, nourishing food may be prepared for the faithful.

> “A man came from Baal-shalisha, bringing the man of God bread from the firstfruits, twenty barley loaves, and new grain in his sack. He said: ‘Give it to the people, so that they may eat.’ His servant replied: ‘What is this, that I should set it before one hundred men?’ Again he said: ‘Give it to the people, so that they may eat,’” and the rest.

[scan page 257]

[fragmentary: …]salisa is described as coming, bringing the man of God the firstfruits, twenty barley loaves, and new grain in his sack. Whom, however, can we better understand this man to signify than the company of the holy fathers, who excel in strength of spirit and good works? He is rightly said to have come from Baalsalisa. For *Baalsalisa* is interpreted as “having a third” [or “possessing the third”]. Thus the man is rightly from Baalsalisa who preserves the number three in belief and confession of the Holy Trinity.

He therefore offers the man of God loaves of the firstfruits when, inspired by his grace, he offers our Redeemer books composed concerning the origin of creatures. He offers twenty barley loaves, that is, the Decalogue of the Law contained in the writings of Moses and the prophets. He offers new grain in his sack when, after the coming of our Mediator, he brings forth the New Testament in the writings of the holy Gospel and the apostles (Matthew 13).

Our Elisha therefore commands his servants—namely, the holy preachers—to distribute this offering to the faithful people, so that, according to that saying of the Gospel (Matthew 14), like a learned scribe in the kingdom of heaven they may bring forth from their treasury things new and old, and thus be refreshed with the nourishment of the divine word.

We read this mystery repeated in the Gospel (Matthew 15), when, at the breaking of the five loaves, five thousand men are said to have been fed, and, after the crowds had eaten their fill, twelve baskets—or seven baskets—of fragments were gathered. For no one can comprehend all the sacraments of divine Scripture without something remaining for him after he has been satisfied, according to the word of the Lord.

### Chapter V

> “Naaman, commander of the army of the king of Syria, was a great man with his lord and held in honor.  
> For through him the Lord had given salvation to Syria.  
> He was a mighty and wealthy man, but he was a leper.”

This Naaman, who is described as commander of the army of the king of Syria, whom could he more fittingly signify than the gentile people? Throughout the three-cornered world it held supremacy through the strength of its wars and enjoyed the splendor of possessions, as is expressed in the interpretation of his name. *Naaman* is interpreted as “beauty” or “their agitation.” Yet although this man is remembered as mighty and wealthy, he is nevertheless said to be a leper, because, although through the power of the kingdom and abundance of possessions he appeared to rule, through the wickedness of error and the leprosy of idolatry he was shown to be foul.

> “Now raiders had gone out from Syria and had taken captive from the land of Israel a little girl, who was in the service of Naaman’s wife.  
> She said to her mistress: ‘Would that my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria! Surely he would cure him of the leprosy that he has.’”

The raiders from Syria—which is interpreted as “loftiness”—went forth when, driven by desire and entangled in various occupations, and placing their hope in the uncertainty of riches, the gentiles wandered throughout the whole earth. Coming thence to the land of Israel, they carried away a captive girl who, although placed in captivity, bore witness concerning the prophet in Israel. For the fame of Israel, conveyed by the merchants of the gentiles throughout the city and arousing human curiosity—which Naaman’s wife signifies—revealed that the true prophet and Savior of all remained in Judea.

> “Naaman therefore went in to his lord and reported to him, saying: ‘Thus and thus spoke the girl from the land of Israel.’  
> The king of Syria said to him: ‘Go, and I will send a letter to the king of Israel.’  
> When he had departed, he took with him ten talents of silver, six thousand gold pieces, and ten changes of garments, and delivered the letter to the king of Israel, containing these words: ‘When you receive this letter, know that I have sent to you Naaman my servant, so that you may cure him of his leprosy.’”

When knowledge of the word of God reaches those who are set over them, they suggest to them the greatness of spiritual knowledge. The king of Syria sends a letter to the king of Israel for the healing of his servant. When the leaders of the gentiles hear that God is in Israel—for “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Psalm 75)—and foresee the salvation of their people, they send an embassy to Judea so that through apostolic teaching they may receive faith in the Savior. Thus Cornelius the centurion sent from Caesarea to Joppa for Peter (Acts 10). Likewise, in a vision a Macedonian man appeared to Paul (Acts 17), exhorting him to come and help those who were in Macedonia, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles.

> “When the king of Israel had read the letter, he tore his garments and said: ‘Am I God, that I can kill and give life? For this man has sent to me to cure a man of his leprosy. Consider and see that he is seeking an occasion against me.’  
> When Elisha the man of God heard this—namely, that the king of Israel had torn his garments—he sent to him, saying: ‘Why have you torn your garments?’”

What does this king of Israel signify, when he is said to have feared, except the priests, scribes, Pharisees, and rulers of the Jews? When they saw that crowds were coming from everywhere to our Redeemer for the sake of their salvation, they tore their garments as though they regarded it as blasphemy, just as we read in the Gospel (Matthew 26) that the chief priest did this after hearing Christ’s preaching.

Although the king of Israel trembles at such a report, the prophet of God persuaded those whom he knew had come over to him to come to himself, saying:

> “Let him come to me, and he shall know that there is a prophet in Israel.”

And our Lord says:

> “Those whom he foreknew, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified” (Romans 8).

> “Naaman therefore came with horses and chariots and stood at the door of Elisha’s house. Elisha sent a messenger to him, saying: ‘Go and wash seven times in the Jordan, and your flesh shall be restored to you, and you shall be clean.’  
> Naaman became angry and departed, saying: ‘I thought that he would come out to me, stand, call upon the name of the Lord his God, touch the place of the leprosy with his hand, and cure me. Are not Abana and Pharphar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel, so that I might wash in them and be clean?’”

[scan page 258]

The gentile people, coming to the house of our Elisha—namely, the holy Church—received from him the promised message that they should wash seven times in the Jordan and thus receive health and be cleansed. For through the evangelical preachers the Lord says:

> “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3).

And again:

> “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16).

The waters of the Jordan therefore signify holy Baptism, because in them our Savior consecrated baptism for us. But Naaman’s indignation at such an answer and his contempt for washing in the Jordan’s water signify the simplicity of the uneducated, who could not understand its spiritual efficacy:

> “The natural person does not receive the things that belong to the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 2).

> “When he had turned away and was departing in anger, his servants approached him and spoke to him: ‘Father, if the prophet had told you to do some great thing, surely you ought to have done it. How much more, since he has now said to you, “Wash, and you shall be clean”?’  
> He went down and washed seven times in the Jordan, according to the word of the man of God, and his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was cleansed.”

Naaman’s servants therefore rightly persuaded him, with better counsel, to fulfill the prophetic command, because often the Lord reveals what is better to the younger (Matthew 11). And according to Peter’s testimony:

> “God is not a respecter of persons” (Romans 2),  
> “but in every nation whoever fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts 10).

He went away and washed seven times according to the word of the man of God, and his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child. Thus, cleansed by the waters of Baptism through the invocation of the sevenfold Spirit, each person receives true health, so that he may be restored to the innocence of childhood and become worthy to receive entry into eternal life. Hence Truth itself says to his disciples:

> “Unless you turn and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 18).

> “Finally, Naaman returned to the man of God with his entire company. He came and stood before him and said: ‘Truly I know that there is no other God in the whole earth except in Israel.’”

This is the catholic confession: that “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob is not the God of the dead but of the living” (Mark 12); and, “All the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens” (Psalm 95).

And so that all the sacraments of Baptism might be prefigured here—Baptism in which we are commanded to renounce Satan and confess faith in the Lord—Naaman denies that he will henceforth sacrifice to foreign gods and declares that he will serve the Lord alone in all things. He is also glad to take a portion of the holy land with him, because those who have been baptized ought also to be strengthened by participation in the Lord’s body.

> “Gehazi, the servant of the man of God, said: ‘My lord has spared this Syrian Naaman, in not receiving from him what he brought. As the Lord lives, I will run after him and take something from him,’” and the rest.

After this Scripture relates that Gehazi, the servant of the man of God, coveted the money that the Syrian mentioned above had brought to the man of God. Since his master refused to accept anything, Gehazi acquired through a shameful lie what his master had refused to accept in faith.

*Gehazi* is also interpreted as “one who sees the precipice” or “valley of vision,” and he signifies the Jewish people, who were at one time called the servant of the man of God, as the prophet Hosea says:

> “When Israel was a child, I loved him” (Hosea 11).

But after rejecting the Gospel and crucifying the Son of God, casting itself headlong into the pit of avarice through such a fall from divine dignity, it pursued earthly desire, which those reborn through Baptism as sons of God rejected. Through the judgment of the just Judge, it brought upon itself the leprosy of error that believers had cast off.

Likewise, all who, after Baptism and amendment of life, return to their former vices become entangled again in the filth from which they had hoped to be freed. Hence it is written:

> “The dog returns to its vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mire: so is a fool who repeats his folly” (Proverbs 26).

### Chapter VI

> “The sons of the prophets said to Elisha: ‘Behold, the place in which we dwell before you is too small for us. Let us go as far as the Jordan, and let each of us take from the forest one piece of timber, so that we may build ourselves a dwelling there.’  
> He said: ‘Go.’  
> One of them said: ‘Come, then, you also, with your servants.’  
> He answered: ‘I will come.’  
> And he went with them. When they had come to the Jordan, they were cutting wood. It happened that, when one had cut down a piece of timber, the iron of the axe fell into the water.  
> He cried out and said: ‘Alas, alas, alas, my lord! And I had borrowed this very thing.’  
> The man of God said: ‘Where did it fall?’  
> He showed him the place. He then cut a piece of wood and threw it there. The iron floated, and he said: ‘Take it.’ He stretched out his hand and took it.”

This action is fittingly applicable to our Redeemer by way of signification. When wood was being cut with axes, the iron, slipping from the handle, sank into the depth of the river; then, after a piece of wood had been thrown over it by Elisha, it returned to the surface.

So also, when Christ’s bodily presence was working among the impious Jews and cutting them down like fruitless trees—for John had said of them, “Behold, the axe is laid to the root of the trees” (Matthew 3)—during the intervening Passion the body itself departed from them and descended into the depths. Once placed in the tomb, it rose again when the spirit returned, as though returning to its handle.

Alternatively: the iron in the handle is the gift of understanding in the heart. To cut wood with it is to rebuke those who act wickedly. But sometimes, when this is done negligently, when the fall of vainglory is not avoided in the knowledge that has been received, the iron is lost in the water, because through dissolute conduct understanding becomes dull.

We know that this understanding is given precisely so that it may be restored before the eyes of the giver through good action. Thus the one who had lost the iron rightly cried out:

> “Alas, alas, alas, my lord! And I had borrowed this very thing.”

For the elect have this characteristic: whenever the fault of vainglory furtively creeps into their knowledge, they quickly return to their hearts. Whatever they find in themselves to be blameworthy before the eyes of the strict Judge, they pursue with tears. In their weeping they carefully examine not only the evils they have committed, but also the good things that, having received the gift, they ought to have rendered. They feel themselves all the more sinners because, through the good things they neglected though they could have done them, they remain debtors.

Therefore the one who lost the iron rightly cries:

> “Alas, alas, alas, and I had borrowed this very thing.”

As if he were saying: “Through negligent carelessness I lost what I had received from the creditor’s grace in order to return it through good works.”

Yet God never abandons the mind that truly recognizes itself in sins. Hence Elisha came and sent the wood downward, and brought the iron to the surface. Our Redeemer, looking mercifully upon us, humbles the sinner’s heart and restores the understanding that he had lost. He raises the wood and brings the iron to the surface, because our Redeemer both restores knowledge and humbles the heart that has been lifted up in thought.

Hence another translation rightly says:

> “He broke the wood and threw it in, and thus raised the iron.”

To break the wood is to crush the heart’s pride. To throw the wood down to the depths is to humble the heart raised up in the knowledge of its own weakness, as we have said. Immediately the iron returns to the surface, because the mind returns to the former exercise of understanding.

Since, therefore, the gift of understanding that is received is scarcely guarded amid so many difficulties, great care must be taken that it does not grow sluggish through idleness and that, through the stimulus of action, it does not vanish by the fault of pride. Holy men do not exult when they recognize what they are doing. But when they do what they have recognized, they rejoice greatly through understanding in the gift of the giver, while nevertheless grieving as they consider the debt of action: that they may repay through action what has been entrusted to them in understanding.

For a debtor is foolish if he gladly accepts borrowed money but does not consider the time when he must repay it. The joy of receiving is moderated when prudent foresight also considers the appointed time for repayment.

> “The king of Syria was warring against Israel. He took counsel with his servants, saying: ‘In such and such a place let us set an ambush.’  
> The man of God sent to the king of Israel, saying: ‘Beware of passing through that place, for the Syrians are lying in ambush there.’  
> The king of Israel sent to the place that the man of God had told him about, and he took precautions there,” and the rest.

Whom, then, can this king of Syria more suitably signify here than earthly power? Often, arrogantly raging, it persecutes the people of God—that is, the children of light—but through the teaching of the true Elisha, namely, our Lord, they are taught to anticipate the ambushes of their enemies. Thus it is said:

> “Be wise as serpents and innocent as doves.”

And again:

> “Beware of men” (Matthew 10).

And elsewhere:

> “Beware of false prophets” (Matthew 7).

Recognizing this, worldly power resolves to kill the prophet himself, when it hastens to extinguish Christ in the hearts of the elect.

> “The king of Syria therefore sent horses, chariots, and a strong army there. When they had arrived by night, they surrounded the city.”

Everyone who trusts in the weapons of iniquity prepares ambushes for Christ’s servants and, blinded by the night of treachery, wages war against the Church.

> “When the servant of the man of God arose at dawn and went out, he saw an army surrounding the city, with horses and chariots. He reported this, saying: ‘Alas, alas, my lord! What shall we do?’”

This statement denotes those who, because of faintness of heart, fear bodily punishments. The prophet answered them:

> “Do not be afraid, for there are more with us than with them” (2 Chronicles 32).

And the Savior says to his disciples:

> “In the world you will have tribulation, but take courage, because I have overcome the world” (John 16).

And again:

> “Do not fear those who kill the body and after that have nothing more that they can do to you; rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matthew 10).

And to Peter, during his Passion, the Lord said:

> “Do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he would provide me with more than twelve legions of angels?”

> “When Elisha had prayed, he said: ‘Lord, open this man’s eyes so that he may see.’ The Lord opened the eyes of the servant, and he saw: and behold, the mountain was full of fiery horses and chariots around Elisha.”

It is therefore greatly necessary that our Elisha open the eyes of our hearts, so that we may consider and recognize that all who trust in him will not be put to shame (Psalm 24).

> “Elisha prayed to the Lord, saying: ‘Strike, I beg you, this nation with blindness.’ And the Lord struck them, so that they could not see, according to the word of Elisha.”

It is good for those whose eye causes them to stumble that it be torn out and cast away from them (Matthew 5), so that their perception of malice and pride may be closed and the eye of sound faith and simplicity opened. Hence the Apostle says:

> “If anyone among you thinks that he is wise, let him become a fool, so that he may become wise” (1 Corinthians 3).

> “When the king of Israel saw them, he said to Elisha: ‘Shall I strike them, my father?’  
> He answered: ‘You shall not strike them. For you did not capture them with your sword or bow, so as to strike them. But set bread and water before them, so that they may eat and drink and go to their lord’s house,’” and the rest.

After Elisha had brought the enemies to Samaria, he did not permit them to be killed. Instead, preparing a great feast of food for them, he dismissed them in peace.

Likewise, the Lord first blinded Saul, who had long been kicking against the goad; then he filled him magnificently with spiritual knowledge and sent him to preach his Gospel among the gentiles (Acts 2). He commands us in this way:

> “Love your enemies and do good to those who hate you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5).

[scan page 260]

> “After this, Ben-hadad king of Syria gathered his whole army and went up and besieged Samaria. And there was a great famine in Samaria,” and the rest.

Scripture relates that Ben-hadad, king of Syria, besieged Samaria. When famine occurred, the people were afflicted, but, through the mercy of the Lord, the word of the Lord was revealed to Elisha, and he announced it to the people, saying:

> “Thus says the Lord.”

### Chapter VII

> “At this time tomorrow, a measure of fine flour will be sold for one shekel, and two measures of barley for one shekel at the gate of Samaria.”

When one of the officers, on whose hand the king leaned, did not believe this, he said to the man of God:

> “Even if the Lord made floodgates in heaven, could what you say happen?”

He answered:

> “You shall see it with your eyes, but you shall not eat of it.”

At this point Ben-hadad and his army may mystically be understood as the devil, because he stirs the hearts of the wicked through envy to wage war against the Church. Under this king are the false Jews of whom it is written in the Apocalypse (Revelation 2) that they say they are Jews and are not, but are a synagogue of Satan. Under this king are the pagans, and also the heretics.

When persecution is therefore carried out by the ancient enemy, the people of God—placed in Samaria, that is, under the guardianship of the divine Law—are afflicted through such people. A severe famine arises when teachers are not permitted to preach the word of God freely. But when this is revealed by the Son, that is, by our Redeemer, who indicates it through the Gospel, it is recognized that salvation, which is far from sinners, is near to those who fear God.

For our Lord says to his servants:

> “At this time tomorrow, a measure of fine flour will be sold for one shekel, and two measures of barley for one shekel at the gate of Samaria,” and the rest.

As if he had said: “When the storm of persecution that is happening today has ceased, tomorrow—that is, in the future—God will give peace and tranquility, so that the preaching of the Gospel may be perfectly fulfilled among believers.”

At the time of the Lord’s Passion there was, as it were, a famine of the word of God, when the apostles all fled after abandoning him and shut themselves indoors through fear of the Jews. It is written again that no one dared to speak openly about him. But when the light of the Resurrection dawned, the time had arrived when Christ’s companions, seeing that he was alive and afterward seeing him ascend into heaven, received the grace of the Holy Spirit and freely preached the word of God, both to the Jews and to the gentiles.

For Isaiah’s prophecy was fulfilled:

> “For waters burst forth in the desert and torrents in the wilderness; he made the dry land into a pool and the thirsty land into springs of water” (Isaiah 41).

Hence the Lord himself speaks through the prophet:

> “All who thirst, come to the waters; and you who have no money, hurry, buy, and eat. Come, buy without money and without price wine and milk. Why do you spend money for what is not bread, and your labor for what does not satisfy? Listen, listen to me, and eat what is good, and your soul shall delight in abundance. Incline your ear and come to me; listen, and your soul shall live” (Isaiah 55).

With the enemies thrown into confusion and put to flight, Scripture adds that four lepers went into the Syrian camp. Finding no one there, they ate and drank, carried away gold, silver, and clothing and hid them; afterward, moved to repentance, they announced this to the city and provided signs of the salvation that had occurred.

Who, then, are these lepers except those devoted to various vices or entangled in diverse errors, who, bringing forth the foulness of an inward disease, display it on their skin? When the Lord often converts such people to the faith and cleanses them from error and vice, he makes them messengers of true salvation.

> “The lepers entered the camp of the Syrians, ate and drank, and carried away gold and silver from there.”

When people despised by this world devote themselves to the study of philosophy, they acquire subtlety of intellect and elegance of expression, so that, well equipped, they may serve the uses of the Church. The Lord often grants such people both sharpness of mind and the gift of true wisdom.

They are rightly remembered as four, because, instructed in the learning of the four Gospels, they proclaim the truth of the faith in the four parts of the world.

We read in the Gospel (Matthew 9; John 12; Luke 7) that when the Lord ate with publicans and sinners, and when the woman who was known in the city as a sinner washed his feet with her tears, wiped them with her hair, and anointed them with ointment, he made Matthew, a publican, an apostle and evangelist. After his resurrection he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons; she went and announced this to those who had been with him, mourning and weeping (Matthew 28).

> “The officer on whose hand the king had leaned, who had disbelieved the words of the prophet, was stationed at the gate. The crowd trampled him at the entrance, and he died, according to what the man of God had said.”

This officer represents the scribes and Pharisees, who possessed the key of knowledge but neither entered the Catholic Church through faith themselves nor allowed those who wished to enter to do so. Truth itself says to them:

> “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who shut the kingdom of heaven before men; for you yourselves do not enter, nor do you allow those who are entering to enter” (Matthew 23).

“He was trampled by the crowd at the gate” because he stood uselessly before the door of faith and impeded the steps of those entering. Therefore he was rightly trampled—that is, condemned by the examination of the just Judge—and will be sent into everlasting darkness. For the Lord also says in the Gospel:

> “If salt has lost its taste, it is no longer good for anything except to be thrown outside and trampled by men” (Matthew 5).

[scan page 261]

### Chapter IX

> “Elisha the prophet called one of the sons of the prophets and said to him: ‘Gird your loins, take this flask of oil in your hand, and go to Ramoth-gilead. When you arrive there, you will see Jehu son of Jehoshaphat, son of Nimshi. Enter, raise him up from the midst of his brothers, lead him into an inner chamber, and, taking the flask of oil, pour it over his head and say: “Thus says the Lord: I have anointed you king over Israel,”’” and the rest.

The history in this Book of Kings then relates how the Lord appointed Jehu to eradicate the house of Ahab and kill the priests of Baal. He struck Joram, king of Israel, and Ahaziah, king of Judah, and caused Jezebel, the most wicked queen, to be thrown from the palace in Jezreel.

Typologically, Jehu can signify the dominion of the gentiles, which the Lord and our Redeemer appointed to exercise judgment in the sacrilegious city that killed the prophets and the Lord of the prophets himself and persecuted his apostles. He appointed it to destroy that city by a just vengeance, to overthrow the empty priesthood that it had vainly retained after Christ’s coming, to overturn its temple, and to cast down from the height of royal power the impious synagogue that had always thirsted for the blood of the saints, killing its rulers.

### Chapter XI

> “Athaliah, the mother of Ahaziah, seeing that her son was dead, arose and killed all the royal offspring. But Jehosheba, the daughter of King Joram and sister of Ahaziah, took Joash the son of Ahaziah, stole him from among the king’s sons who were being killed, and hid him from Athaliah so that he would not be killed. He remained with her, hidden in the house of the Lord, for six years, because Jehosheba was the wife of Jehoiada the high priest.”

Athaliah, who sought to extinguish David’s offspring and destroy the royal line, rightly expresses the impiety of the Synagogue. Through wickedness of mind it lay in wait for David’s offspring—that is, Christ—and always carried hatred against him in its heart. It once appeared to reign when it observed the ceremonies of the Law temporarily.

*Athaliah* is interpreted as “the temporality of the Lord.” But Joash—whose name is interpreted as “memory of the Lord,” namely Christ, in whom there is remembrance of the Lord’s name—was preserved through the diligence of Jehosheba, whose name means “the abundance of the Lord,” that is, the Church, in which true delights are found. He was preserved so that he would not be killed by the cruelty of the raging enemy, but might be nourished in the house of Jehoiada the high priest, whose name means “beloved of the Lord.” Of him the Father’s voice says:

> “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3).

His house is the holy Church. Remaining there in holy faith among the elect, he daily brings about the increase of his body until, at the time of judgment, he raises the scepter and power of his kingdom against those who intended to crush him and consigns the murderess of the saints to eternal punishments.

> “In the seventh year Jehoiada sent for the centurions and soldiers, brought them to himself in the temple of the Lord, and made a covenant with them. He bound them by oath in the house of the Lord, showed them the king’s son, and commanded them, saying: ‘This is the word that you must do. Let one third of you enter on the Sabbath and keep watch over the king’s house. Let another third be at the gate of Sur, and the third part at the gate behind the quarters of the shield-bearers; and you shall guard the watch of the house of Messa.  
> “The other two divisions among you, all who go out on the Sabbath, shall guard the watches of the house of the Lord around the king, surrounding him while holding weapons in your hands. If anyone enters the precincts of the temple, let him be killed. You shall be with the king as he enters and as he leaves.”  
> The centurions did everything that Jehoiada the priest had commanded them. Each took his men, those who entered on the Sabbath together with those who went out on the Sabbath, and they came to Jehoiada the priest. He gave them the spears and weapons of King David that were in the house of the Lord. Each man stood with his weapon in his hand, from the right side of the temple to the left side of the altar and the building, around the king.”

If anyone carefully recalls what was said above concerning the courts of the house of the Lord, he can understand how these things were done and in what places. But, so as not to weary our readers, let us pass over what has already been explained and turn to what was said about the division of the crowd.

The explanation is as follows. There were twenty-four divisions of priests, Levites, and gatekeepers, which succeeded one another in order through an equal number of weeks. On the Sabbath a new group entered for service, while after the Sabbath the group that had ministered during the preceding week returned home.

But on this occasion the high priest, because of the necessity of acting on behalf of the new king, received those whose turn it was to enter for the week and retained those who had already completed their week of service, so that they would not depart. He had also summoned other Levites from all the cities of Judah, together with the heads of the families of Israel, and gathered them in Jerusalem through the centurions.

He divided them in this manner in order to bring out the king’s son: all who had completed their Sabbath duty and were about to leave were divided into two groups and, armed, surrounded the king in the inner parts of the court. The rest of the multitude—that is, those who were not of the tribe of Levi—guarded the outer doors of the courts against any royal violence, in case anything adverse should be attempted.

Those who had come for the Sabbath—the priests, Levites, and gatekeepers—were divided into three groups and guarded the king’s house, that is, the palace, lest the queen, having gathered an army, defend it against the king. They also guarded the gate of the quarters of the shield-bearers, through which one descended from the temple to the palace, as is stated below.

They led—
king from the house of the Lord, and they came by way of the gate of the guards’ quarters into the palace, and he sat upon the throne of the kings—where the gate of Seir, the house of Messa, and the gate of the guards’ quarters appear also to be mentioned. He calls the guards the king’s protectors, as the Book of Chronicles testifies. After mentioning that Rehoboam had bronze shields instead of golden ones, it adds: “And he handed them over to the commanders of the guards, who kept watch over the entrance of the palace.” In that book, indeed, all these matters are set out more distinctly:

> “A third of you who come on the Sabbath, of the priests, Levites, and gatekeepers, shall be at the gates. Another third shall be at the king’s house, and a third at the gate called the Foundation. Let all the rest of the people remain in the courts of the house of the Lord, and let no one else enter the house of the Lord except the priests and those Levites who minister. Let them alone enter, because they are consecrated; and let all the rest of the people keep the watches of the Lord. Let the Levites surround the king, each with his weapons,” and so forth.

The same account continues:

> “Then he brought out the king’s son and placed upon his head the diadem and the testimony.”

By the diadem, the royal insignia of the head is meant; by the testimony, he designates the decrees of God’s law, by which the king must be instructed what to do and how to live. Finally, the Book of Chronicles says more plainly:

> “They placed the diadem upon him and the testimony, gave him the law to hold in his hand, and made him king” (2 Chron. xxiii).

Great indeed and saving was the prudence by which, after the death of the tyrannical and impious queen, the legitimate king’s son, succeeding to the kingdom, was entrusted with both the royal dignity and the observance of God’s law; so that he who saw himself set over the people for their governance might remember that he himself ought to be subject to divine laws for his governance.

## CHAPTER XII

> “And Joash said to the priests: Let all the money of the holy things that is brought into the temple of the Lord by passers-by, the money offered for the valuation of a life, and whatever anyone voluntarily and according to the inclination of his heart brings into the temple of the Lord, be received by the priests according to their order, and let them repair the damaged places of the house wherever they see anything necessary for its restoration.”

Our king commands his teachers to receive all the money that is offered by passers-by in the temple of the Lord, both as the price of a life and as the offering of the heart. Whatever, therefore, is contributed by passers-by to the treasury of the Lord in spiritual knowledge or in examples of good conduct is, through the offices of the priests—that is, of preachers—to be applied to the restoration of the spiritual temple. Thus whatever they find torn there through error or vice, they may restore, lest through the negligence of teachers the multitude of their hearers should perish.

But what follows—

> “Nevertheless, until the twenty-third year of King Joash, the priests did not repair the damaged places of the temple”—

signifies that, before the coming of the Savior, although the teaching of the Law existed among the Jewish people, it was nevertheless corrupted in many respects through the negligence of teachers, until he came who had given the Law and taught that, through faith in the Holy Trinity, the Decalogue of the Law was to be observed spiritually in the writings of Moses and the prophets.

> “Then King Joash summoned Jehoiada the high priest and the priests and said to them: Why are you not repairing the damaged places of the temple? Therefore, do not continue to receive money according to your order, but return it for the restoration of the temple,”

and so forth.

So also our Lord, commanding the teachers of the Gospel, says:

> “Lift up your eyes and see the regions, for they are already white for the harvest” (John iv).

> “Ask the Lord of the harvest to send workers into his harvest” (Matt. ix).

And again:

> “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark xvi).

> “Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons; you have received without payment, give without payment” (Matt. x).

> “And Jehoiada the high priest took one treasury, opened an opening above it, and placed it beside the altar, on the right side of those entering the house of the Lord.”

The altar, evidently, is the body of the Lord. The treasury is placed beside it when the Church joined to Christ is on the right side of those entering the house of the Lord, because this is the intention of the elect who enter the Church through faith: that they may reach eternal blessedness, which is signified by the right hand.

The priests who guard the doors of the temple therefore place this treasury there to receive all the money brought to the temple of the Lord. In the same way, holy preachers who guard the entrance of faith present the vows of the faithful in words and deeds, and commend them properly to God in the Church through prayers.

> “The king’s scribe and the high priest came up, and they poured out and counted the money that was found in the house of the Lord. They gave it, according to its number and measure, into the hands of those who supervised the carpenters and builders of the house of the Lord. They spent it on the woodworkers and builders who worked on the house of the Lord,”

and so forth.

He calls the king’s scribe and the high priest the supreme teachers. They assigned the money that had been collected according to number and measure to those who supervised the carpenters and builders—that is, to the dispensers of the divine word. These distributed the measure of the Gospel wheat to their fellow servants, those who work in the house of the Lord and construct works of virtue in the divine building.

What else, then, did the apostles do, whom divine election established as leaders in the Church, when through disciples subject to them they scattered the seeds of the divine word throughout the whole world, so that they might appoint among their hearers suitable workers for the will of God? Some were carpenters, since they strove to prepare themselves and those obedient to them as fruitful timbers in the house of the Lord. Others repaired the damaged places of the temple, rebuilding what had been broken by heresy and schism. Others cut stones, when they strongly reproved the hard-hearted and unbelieving, so that the restoration of the house of the Lord might be completed in all that required expenditure for the maintenance of the house of the Lord, according to what the Apostle says:

> “To each of us grace was given according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Eph. iv).

A little later he says:

> “And he himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists, and others as teachers and pastors, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ” (ibid.).

But what follows—

> “Nevertheless, water jars of the temple of the Lord, forks, censers, trumpets, and every vessel of gold and silver were not made from the same money. The money brought into the temple of the Lord”—

signifies that one method must be used for forming vessels for the ministry of the Lord, and another for preparing timbers and stones for the building of the house. The instruction by which beginners are imbued with faith must differ from that by which those already mature are trained toward the fullness of knowledge.

The vessels of the house of the Lord may rightly be understood as those already suited to receive divine gifts and made capable of God’s ministry. The water jars may signify those who contain within themselves the water of divine wisdom. The forks may signify spiritual teachers, whose duty is to distribute the body and blood of the Lord to believers, to withhold them from unbelievers, and also to distribute the spiritual nourishment of the word to each person as is appropriate.

There are, indeed, certain things in the words of God that he has deigned to reveal to our humility and grant for the nourishment of our banquets. There are also other things of such great depth that they are disclosed only to the knowledge of the Holy Spirit, while they altogether exceed the measure of our capacity.

The censers figuratively signify those who offer God pure prayer from a clean conscience and sincere faith, and who can say with the prophet:

> “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Ps. cxl).

And what else are the trumpets than holy preachers who send forth throughout the whole world the voice of evangelical proclamation? Of them it is said through the prophet:

> “Cry out; do not cease. Raise your voice like a trumpet, and announce to my people their crimes and to the house of Jacob their sins” (Isa. lviii).

And the Psalmist says:

> “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. xix).

It continues:

> “No account was required from those men who received the money to distribute it to the craftsmen, but they dealt with it faithfully.”

This demonstrates the devotion of those of whom the passage speaks. They were so diligent in religion that no one doubted that they handled the Lord’s money without any suspicion of fraud. Having taken it from the treasury, they faithfully offered it to the craftsmen for the repair of the house, according to the needs of each.

Therefore those who receive the spiritual money of the word of God in order to distribute it to their fellow servants—that is, to the divine workers—must consider with what faith and discretion they must act, since they must render an account of that same money. They should strive to be found no less faithful in spiritual matters than these men were found in material matters.

> “But the money for a transgression and the money for sins they did not bring into the temple of the Lord, because it belonged to the priests.”

This statement shows that no one ought lightly to presume to believe according to his own judgment, but should rather understand that the confession of sins and penance must be carried out according to the judgment of the priests. They possess the knowledge to distinguish between clean and unclean, to judge the stain of leprosy, and either to condemn or to declare clean.

## CHAPTER XIII

> “Now Elisha was ill with the illness from which he also died. King Joash of Israel went down to him and wept before him, saying: My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its charioteer. And Elisha said to him: Bring a bow and arrows. When he had brought him a bow and arrows, he said to the king of Israel: Place your hand upon the bow. When he had placed his hand upon it, Elisha laid his hands upon the king’s hands and said: Open the eastern window. When he had opened it, Elisha said: Shoot an arrow. And he shot. And Elisha said: The arrow of the Lord’s salvation and the arrow of salvation against Syria. You shall strike Syria at Aphek until you consume it,”

and so forth.

What does it mean that the prophet commands the king of Israel to bring a bow and arrow, except that our Redeemer commands the rulers of the Church to arm themselves with spiritual weapons and fight against the ancient enemy?

The bow is sometimes used in sacred language for sacred Scripture itself, which consists, as it were, of a horn and a string from both Testaments.
