The Old Testament is represented by the horn because of its hardness. The New Testament, signified by the Lord’s incarnation, is represented by the string. When the string is drawn, the horn is bent, because when the New Testament is examined, the hardness of the letter of the Old is inclined and bent toward spiritual understanding; it is no longer held by the rigor of that hardness.

The arrows are the very words that teachers utter. Hence it is also appropriately said through the prophet of holy teachers entering the nations:

> “With sharp arrows and a bow they shall enter there” (Isa. vii).

When we weigh the sayings of sacred Scripture, we draw the bow; when we give words of instruction, we shoot arrows.

Elisha places his hands upon the hands of the king when the Lord, through his own examples, directs and strengthens the actions of teachers. He commands the eastern window to be opened and the arrow to be shot because he urges his own people first to be illumined by the light of knowledge and true doctrine, and then to send forth words like arrows.

> “And Elisha said: The arrow of the Lord’s salvation and the arrow of salvation against Syria; you shall strike Syria at Aphek until you consume it.”

The Lord’s arrow of salvation is therefore holy preaching when it is properly presented, and it is the sure destruction of spiritual enemies when it is carried out perseveringly. It is not permitted that the dispenser of the word of God should ever grow sluggish or torpid, since he has been commanded to care for the Lord’s flock. It does great harm to devoted hearers when inertia prevails among teachers.

The prophet says:

> “Cry out; do not cease” (Isa. lviii).

And the Apostle says to Timothy:

> “I testify before God and Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead, and by his appearing and his kingdom: preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season; reprove, entreat, rebuke with all patience and doctrine” (2 Tim. iv).

Therefore a teacher ought not, because of greed, to neglect the care of souls, but should rather, through piety, strive toward eternal rest. This is signified by Aphek, for it is interpreted as “he will contain” or “he will apprehend.”

Hence the same Apostle, after listing the vices that accompany greed, says to the disciple mentioned above:

> “But you, man of God, flee these things; pursue righteousness, piety, faith, charity, patience, gentleness. Fight the good fight; fight the fight of faith; apprehend eternal life, to which you were called” (1 Tim. vi).

> “And Elisha said to the king: Take the arrows. When he had taken them, he said to him again: Strike the ground with an arrow. When he had struck it three times and stopped, the man of God became angry with him and said: If you had struck it five or six or seven times, you would have struck Syria until its destruction. But now you shall strike it three times.”

See how the prophet commands King Joash to strike the ground, and when he strikes it three times and stops, he becomes angry with him because he did not strike the ground more often. So teachers too are commanded to strike the ground—that is, the carnal—with the arrow of preaching. Those who do this with insufficient zeal are rightly reproved by divine correction.

What does it mean to strike the ground three times with an arrow except to insinuate the faith of the Trinity to carnal people through instruction? But once the teacher has done this sufficiently and brought people to faith, he must still persist in the word until he teaches them to control the five senses of the body, to devote themselves to good works—which are expressed by the number six—and also to meditate diligently upon spiritual knowledge, which the grace of the sevenfold Spirit has established in the sacred Scriptures and brought forth for the salvation of the human race through the two Testaments.

Those who believe that faith alone, without good works and meditation upon God’s law, is sufficient for salvation are rightly reproved by the prophet, according to the judgment of the apostle James:

> “Just as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead” (Jas. ii).

And elsewhere it is written:

> “Whoever is ignorant will be ignored” (1 Cor. xiv).

> “So Elisha died, and they buried him. Bands of Moabites also entered the land in that year. Some men were burying a man, but when they saw the raiders, they threw the corpse into the tomb of Elisha. As soon as it touched the bones of Elisha, the man came back to life and stood upon his feet.”

What does this resurrection of a dead man through contact with the bones of Elisha signify except the life of the faithful, which is truly established in the death of Christ? Whoever, therefore, touches the death of Christ with firm faith and truly places his hope in him will undoubtedly share in his resurrection.

The Truth himself says:

> “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live; and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die forever” (John xi).

And elsewhere:

> “Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life” (Num. xxi; John iii).

## CHAPTER XIV

> “What is said concerning Amaziah, king of Judah: He struck Edom in the Valley of Salt, ten thousand men, and captured the Rock in battle; and he called its name Joktheel to the present day.”

The Valley of Salt was the place where salt was made, either from a salty substance, cut in many places, dried, and burned; or from salty well-water, heated and boiled until it reached the solidity of salt; or by some other process by which salt is customarily made. It was also in this place, as we read, that Joab struck twelve thousand Edomites.

Nor should it be overlooked that, in place of “Valley of Salt,” the old edition gives, as though it were the name of a region, “Gemela.”

The Rock is a famous city of Arabia in that same land of Edom. In the Book of Numbers it is called Rekem (Num. xxxi), and by the Syrians today it is called by a similar name. Joktheel, however, the name Amaziah the victor gave it, is interpreted as “the assembly of God” or “the help of God.” He gave it this name so that posterity might faithfully preserve the memory that he had captured either an assembly of God’s people or a place with God’s help.

## CHAPTER XV

> “In the twenty-seventh year of Jeroboam, king of Israel, Azariah son of Amaziah, king of Judah, began to reign. He was sixteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem,”

and so forth.

Azariah is the same person as Uzziah. Because of his contempt for the Lord, when he wished to offer sacrifice in the temple contrary to the law of Moses, he was struck with leprosy by the Lord while standing beside the altar and attempting to offer burnt offerings.

King Uzziah, the leper, can signify the devil, whose leprosy is the incurable disease of iniquity. When he refused to recognize his proper measure and attempted to seek greater things, he became marked by the foulness of the worst leprosy, was expelled from the house, and remained a leper until the end, separated from the people of God.

While this king was reigning, and, so far as he could, dissipating the priesthood, the prophet Isaiah could not see that magnificent vision in which he had seen the Lord seated upon a lofty throne. As long as Uzziah held the kingdom in Judah, the prophet did not lift his eyes to heaven; the heavenly things were not opened to him; the Lord of hosts did not appear; and the holy name was not heard faithfully in its mystery.

When Uzziah died, all that the following account relates revealed itself in open light. Something similar is written in Exodus: while Pharaoh lived, the people of Israel, occupied with work in clay, bricks, and straw, did not sigh toward the Lord. While he reigned, no one sought the God of the father Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. But when he died, the children of Israel sighed, as Scripture says, and their cry ascended to the Lord—although, according to the historical sense, they ought rather to have rejoiced and sighed before his death, while he was still alive.

When Ezekiel was prophesying, Phaltias son of Benaiah also died; after the death of that wicked leader, the prophet says:

> “I fell upon my face and cried out with a loud voice, and I said: Alas, Lord God! Are you making a complete end of the remnant of Israel?” (Ezek. xi).

If, therefore, you understand Uzziah, Pharaoh, Phaltias, and the others of this kind as contrary powers, you will see how, while they live, none of your people sees or sighs, and how they fall into repentance:

> “Let not sin reign,” says the Apostle, “in your mortal body” (Rom. vi).

While sin reigns, we build cities for the Egyptians in ashes and live amid filth. In place of grain, we have straw; in place of solid stone, works of clay.

But what is said concerning Jeroboam, king of Israel, is that he restored the boundaries of Israel from the entrance of Hamath to the Sea of the Arabah. Hamath, now called Epiphaneia, was the northern boundary of Israel. The Sea of the Arabah, which in Hebrew is called the Arabah, signifies the Dead Sea. In width it extends for eighty stadia as far as Zoaras of Arabia, and in length for one hundred and fifty stadia toward the vicinity of Sodom.

Josephus mentions this place in the following words:

> “In the fifteenth year of the reign of Amaziah, Joash’s son Jeroboam reigned in Israel, in Samaria, for forty years. This king was exceedingly impious and unjust toward God, worshiping idols and committing many inappropriate and foreign deeds. Yet he became the occasion of many good things for the people of Israel. Jonah prophesied to him that he would have to conquer the Syrians in battle and enlarge his own kingdom: in the northern regions as far as the city of Etham, and in the south as far as Asphaltus. For these were anciently the boundaries of the Canaanites, as the leader Joshua determined those places. Jeroboam therefore encamped against the Syrians and devastated their entire province, just as Jonah had prophesied.”

## CHAPTER XVI

> “In the seventeenth year of Pekah son of Remaliah, Ahaz son of Jotham, king of Judah, began to reign. Ahaz was twenty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. He did not do what was pleasing in the sight of the Lord his God, as David his father had done, but walked in the way of the kings of Israel. Moreover, he consecrated his son, making him pass through the fire, according to the abominations of the nations, which the Lord had destroyed before the children of Israel.”

Josephus gives the following account:

> “Jotham ended his life after living forty-one years, of which he reigned twelve. He was buried in the royal tombs, and the kingdom came to his son Ahaz. Since Ahaz was impious toward God and a transgressor of his father’s law, he imitated the kings of the Israelites, established altars of idols in Jerusalem, and sacrificed upon them. Among other things, he offered his own son as a burnt offering according to the custom of the Canaanites, and committed many other crimes.”

He also turned the Musach of the Sabbath, which he had built in the temple, and the outer entrance of the king, into a temple of the Lord, on account of the king of Assyria.

I have read in a certain book that the Musach of the Sabbath is understood to be a particular place or building situated in the vestibule of the temple of the Lord, where kings, when they went to the temple on the Sabbath for prayer, deposited money for almsgiving. Thus the Musach of the Sabbath was the treasury of the kings, just as the Corban was that of the priests.

It appears that Ahaz did not turn that building and the outer entrance of the king into the temple of the Lord because divine worship was to be performed there, but so that it might be profaned together with the temple. He was striving to please the king of Assyria more than the God of his fathers and the Lord.

The Book of Chronicles appears to support this interpretation, where it is written:

> “Therefore Ahaz plundered the house of the Lord, the house of the kings and the princes, and gave gifts to the king of Assyria, but it did not profit him. Moreover, in the time of his distress he increased his contempt for the Lord. King Ahaz himself sacrificed to the gods of Damascus, who had struck him, and said: Since the gods of the kings of Syria help them, I will placate them with sacrifices, and they will help me—whereas they became his ruin and the ruin of all Israel. After Ahaz had stripped all the vessels of the house of the Lord and broken them, he closed the doors of the temple of the Lord and made altars for himself in every corner of Jerusalem. In all the cities of Judah he also built altars for burning incense and provoked the Lord, the God of his fathers, to anger” (2 Chron. xxviii).

Since we found these things written in this form, we judged that they ought to be placed here, ready to listen to the opinion of anyone who may have expressed something more certain about them.

> “Then Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, went up to fight against Jerusalem. When they besieged Ahaz, they were unable to overcome him. At that time Rezin king of Syria restored Elath to Syria and expelled the Jews from Elath. The Edomites came to Elath,”

and so forth.

The impious king who had abandoned the Lord, the God of his fathers, and followed the idols of the nations was justly abandoned by the Lord’s help. Rezin king of Syria—that is, of Aram—and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel in Samaria, rose up against him and came to Jerusalem to attack it.

We read in the Book of Chronicles that King Rezin of Damascus, after defeating Ahaz, transferred many from Judah to Damascus; and that Pekah son of Remaliah, king of the ten tribes called Israel, who reigned in Samaria, struck down one hundred and twenty thousand armed men of Judah in a single day and led an innumerable spoil captive into Samaria.

Again they came into Judah and wished to conquer Jerusalem, but they could not, because the Lord helped it, so that, under the occasion of the mercy by which he delivered the besieged people, he might announce that his Son would be born from a virgin, as the book of the prophet Isaiah records (Isa. vii). To this man, not because of his own merit but by displaying the grace of the Lord, Isaiah went out to meet him on the road to the Fullers’ Field and said to him:

> “See that you keep silent. Do not be afraid, and let your heart not grow faint because of these two tails of smoking firebrands, at the wrath of the fury of Rezin king of Syria and the son of Remaliah, because Syria, Ephraim, and the son of Remaliah have plotted an evil plan against you, saying: Let us go up against Judah, rouse it, tear it away from us, and set the son of Tabeel as king in its midst. Thus says the Lord God: It shall not stand, and it shall not be. For the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin. And yet sixty-five years, and Ephraim shall cease to be a people.”

He calls Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah king of Samaria “two tails of smoking firebrands,” because in them the kingdom of Syria—that is, Damascus—and the kingdom of Samaria—that is, the ten tribes otherwise called Ephraim—were destined to end.

The sixty-five years are counted not from the time of Ahaz but from the time of Uzziah. The Hebrews explain the passage as follows. Amos, who began to prophesy under Uzziah, when Isaiah also began his prophetic ministry, was the first to prophesy against Israel, saying:

> “Israel shall surely be led captive from its land.”

The title of his prophecy is also directed against Samaria, and he began to prophesy in the days of Uzziah king of Judah, two years before the earthquake. They wish this earthquake to have occurred at the time when Uzziah entered the temple of God and claimed the priesthood for himself; the earth was struck, the ashes of the altar were scattered, and the king himself was struck with leprosy.

They maintain that this occurred in the twenty-fifth year of Uzziah, when twenty-seven years of his reign remained. In all, he reigned fifty-two years. After him his son Jotham reigned for sixteen years, and Jotham’s son Ahaz for another sixteen. After Ahaz, Hezekiah reigned; in the sixth year of his reign Samaria was captured, and thus the total becomes sixty-five years.

For it is written that Tiglath-pileser, king of the Assyrians, went up against Damascus under King Ahaz, devastated it, transferred its inhabitants to Cyrene, and killed Rezin. It is also written that Hoshea son of Elah plotted against Pekah son of Remaliah, struck and killed him, and reigned in his place over Israel for nine years; and that Shalmaneser, king of Assyria, came and besieged Samaria, now called Sebaste, for three years, and in the ninth year of Hoshea’s reign captured it, sent Hoshea bound into prison, and transferred Israel to Assyria, placing them in Halah and Habor beside the river Gozan, in cities—or, as the Septuagint translated it, in the mountains—of the Medes.

According to the allegorical interpretation, the meaning is readily understood. When Ahaz, the impious king, reigned, the king of Aram, whose name is interpreted as “lofty” or “exalted,” represents the arrogance of worldly wisdom. Pekah son of Remaliah, who, according to the prophet Hosea, is also associated with Israel and with the tribe of Ephraim—from which Jeroboam son of Nebat had established golden calves at Bethel and Dan and separated the people of God from the house of David—refers to the heretics who agree among themselves in order to attack the Church.

The heretics and the pagans fight against the house of David with the weapons of argument and dialectical art. Although they disagree among themselves, they agree in attacking the Church, according to the example of Herod and Pilate, who, though they had been at odds with one another, were joined in friendship in the Lord’s passion (John xii).

In Isaiah, the prophet is commanded to go out from his place to meet the impious king, at the Fullers’ Field, where impurities were cleansed. Although Ahaz reigned over Judah, because he was impious he remained at the outermost boundaries of the upper pool. God therefore shows mercy not so much to the king, whom he judged unworthy of salvation, as to his people.

As we have said, he calls the two tails of smoking firebrands worldly wisdom and the discourse of the heretics, whose end is burning. They plotted in vain to go up against Judah, to seize it as though it were negligent and asleep, join it to their errors, and set over it the king, the son of Tabeel—that is, the good God.

Each adversary considers that he possesses severity and that his own doctrine is best. Thus Marcion the heretic believes that Christ is the son of the good God—that is, of another god—and not of the just [God], whose prophets [lacuna] are; he calls him a bloodthirsty and cruel judge.

While they say these things, the Lord and ruler declares that their plan will not stand, but that, so long as this present world stands, the things of the world will remain within their boundaries and their cities. When the time of consummation arrives—that is, the sixty-five years—both the affairs of the world, which were made in six days, and all things pertaining to the five senses will come to an end. Then everything will be dissolved, though the pagans and heretics do not believe that this will happen; and because of their unbelief they do not understand what is being said.

## CHAPTER XVII

> “The Lord was exceedingly angry with Israel and removed them from his sight, and none remained except the tribe of Judah alone. But Judah itself did not keep the commandments of the Lord its God, but walked in the errors of Israel that it had committed. And the Lord rejected all the seed of Israel, afflicted them, and delivered them into the hand of plunderers, until he had cast them from his presence.”

What does the overthrow of the Israelites, carried out by the kings of Assyria, signify except the pitiable and deeply lamentable ruin of the ecclesiastical people? The Assyrian king—that is, the devil—brings this about daily by devastating and besieging them with his army. Because of the sins they have committed, he removes them from their own dwellings and carries them into a foreign land, where he takes greater pleasure in making them mourn than in producing songs of joy.

Hence the Psalmist also, in mystical language, speaks of this same matter…

### Angelomus, Monk of Luxeuil

[Scan page 267]

He recalls this when he says:

> “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept when we remembered you, O Zion. Upon the willows in its midst we hung up our instruments. For there those who had taken us captive asked us for the words of songs; and those who had carried us away said, ‘Sing us one of the hymns of Zion.’ How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land?” [Psalm 136]

This is said concerning those who were brought into Samaria by the king of the Assyrians from among the nations.

> “Each nation made its own god. They placed them in the shrines on the high places that the Samaritans, nation by nation, had made in their cities, in which they lived. The men of Babylon made Succoth-benoth; the men of Cuth made Nergal; the men of Hamath made Ashima. The Avvites made Nibhaz and Tartak.”

In the *Book of Places* it is written that Benoth and Nergal were cities which the Samaritans who had crossed over from Babylonia built in the region of Judaea. They also built the town of Ashima, those who came to it from Hamath. Nibhaz and Tartak are cities which the Avvites founded in the same land of Judaea.

Yet, according to the sequence of the passage and the idols which these peoples had formerly served in their own land, these names may also be understood here as names of idols. For when it had been said, “Each nation made its own god,” the statement “The men of Babylon made Succoth-benoth” seems to have been added to complete the thought. And, if I am not mistaken, the translator would have done better to render *Sochoth* into Latin as *tabernacula* (“tabernacles”) and to leave the name of the idol *Benoth* untranslated, just as is clearly done in what follows.

> “Those who were from Sepharvaim burned their sons in the fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim.”

This shows that Adrammelech and Anammelech were idols of the city of Sepharvaim. It therefore appears to follow that Nergal was the idol of the Cuthaeans, Ashima that of the Hamathites, and Nibhaz and Tartak those of the Avvites.

After this, Scripture tells concerning the Samaritans themselves that, although they feared the Lord, they also served their own gods according to the customs of the nations from which they had been transferred to Samaria. A little later it adds:

> “Thus these nations feared the Lord, but nevertheless served their idols. Their sons and their grandsons also do as their fathers did, to this day.”

Since heretics are represented by the person of the Samaritans, their wickedness is appropriately expressed in the statement just quoted. Heretics possess certain sacraments in common with the holy Church, and they correctly understand certain teachings of the holy Scriptures; nevertheless, they do not cease to serve the idols of unclean spirits.

They seem to themselves to preserve the fear of God properly, since they think that, according to their own understanding, they favor the truth. But because they reject unity with the catholic faith, they plainly show themselves obedient to the will of evil spirits. It is not only the first inventors of error, signified by the fathers of the Samaritans, who act in this way; their followers also act similarly, and these we may rightly understand to be represented by the names of sons and grandsons.

### Chapter XVIII

> “In the third year of Hoshea son of Elah, king of Israel, Hezekiah son of Ahaz, king of Judah, began to reign. He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Abi, daughter of Zechariah. He did what was good in the sight of the Lord, according to all that David his father had done. He destroyed the high places, smashed the statues, cut down the sacred groves, and broke in pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made. For until that time the children of Israel had burned incense to it. They called it Nehushtan. He trusted in the Lord God of Israel.”

*Nehushtan* is interpreted as “their bronze,” so that those who worshiped it as a divinity might recognize from its name that it was bronze and not a god.

Because Hezekiah destroyed the high places, smashed the statues, cut down the groves, and also demolished all the images, he bears the type of the Savior. For Hezekiah is interpreted as “one who grasps the Lord” or “the strength of the Lord.”

In the very act of smashing the bronze serpent that Moses had made, he appropriately bears the figure of the Redeemer. For our Lord and Redeemer, of whom the Prophet says, “The Lord is strong, the Lord is mighty in battle” [Psalm 23], not only crushed the idols of the nations and destroyed all their images, so that they might know the omnipotent God and be rightly devoted to his worship; he also shattered the very letter of the Mosaic law, which that legal people continually recited and regarded as of great importance, and taught them to understand its spiritual meaning.

> “In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of the Assyrians came up against all the fortified cities of Judah and captured them. Then Hezekiah king of Judah sent messengers to the king of Assyria at Lachish, saying: ‘I have sinned; withdraw from me, and whatever you impose upon me I shall bear.’ So the king of Assyria imposed upon Hezekiah king of Judah three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold. Hezekiah gave him all the silver that was found in the house of the Lord and in the treasuries of the king,” and so forth.

The history is clear, for it is described in the Books of Kings, in Chronicles, and in the prophecy of Isaiah in essentially the same way.

Hezekiah was twenty-five years old when he began to reign; he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem, rebelled against the king of Assyria, and did not serve him. Then Sennacherib entered Judaea and besieged its fortified cities. While he was besieging Lachish, Hezekiah sent him three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold, breaking open the doors of the temple and removing their plates, as though he himself had torn them off.

[Scan page 268]

> “The king of Assyria sent Tartan, Rabsaris, and Rabshakeh with a powerful army to Jerusalem. Eliakim son of Hilkiah, the steward of the palace, went out to them,” together with Shebna the scribe and Joah son of Asaph the recorder, and so forth.

This is the Eliakim of whom Isaiah said in his vision of the Valley of Zion:

> “I will summon my servant Eliakim son of Hilkiah” [Isaiah 22],

and what follows. He was appointed after Shebna as steward of the palace. The Hebrews maintain that Rabshakeh, who had been a commander of the armies, led the Assyrian forces, conquered Jerusalem, and captured the whole of Judaea except the fortress of Zion and the temple. Some think that, for this reason, Eliakim himself went out to Rabshakeh.

Rabshakeh, who spoke in Hebrew, was, according to the opinion of some, the son of Isaiah the prophet, because he himself was a renegade. They say that he had another name, Jaub, which in Latin means “one who cries out.” Others think that he was a Samaritan and therefore knew the Hebrew language, and that he blasphemed God so boldly and impiously.

For, like a certain contrary power, he imitated in his arrogance the prophets who said, “Thus says the Lord,” by saying, “Thus says the great king, the king of the Assyrians.” First, his assertion, “You trust in Egypt,” is false; for no history reports that Hezekiah had asked Pharaoh for assistance.

As for the statement, “If you say to me, ‘We trust in the Lord our God,’” this is true. But he adds another lie to the truth:

> “Hezekiah has removed his high places and his altars.”

He did not do this against God, but for God: by destroying idolatry and every remaining error, he taught the people to worship God in Jerusalem, where his temple was.

When he says that he will give two thousand horses, which Hezekiah does not possess, he does not point to the weakness of the people, as though they were ignorant of horsemanship, but to their observance of God’s commandments. For God commanded Moses that the king of Israel should not multiply horses or wives for himself.

“If,” he says, “you cannot withstand even one of the least of my master’s servants, how will you endure his immense power?”

To the statement, “If you say to me, ‘We trust in the Lord our God,’” he cleverly replied that he had come not by his own will but at the Lord’s command:

> “The Lord said to me: ‘Go up against this land and destroy it.’”

This, he argued, was the proof. “Certainly I could not have come here without the Lord’s will. Since I have come, captured many cities, and part of Jerusalem still remains untouched, it is clear that I have come by his will.”

> “Eliakim son of Hilkiah, Shebna, and Joah said to Rabshakeh: ‘Please speak to your servants in Aramaic, for we understand that language; do not speak to us in Judean in the hearing of the people who are on the wall.’ Rabshakeh replied to them: ‘Has my master sent me to your master and to you to speak these words? Has he not sent me to the men sitting on the wall, who must eat their own dung and drink their own urine with you?’” and so forth.

Rabshakeh’s accusation is a testimony to Hezekiah. After capturing the cities of Judah, he trusted in the Lord and encouraged the people to hope in the Lord. Therefore Rabshakeh wishes to destroy what Hezekiah had built, and he says to the people:

> “Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, and do not let him make you trust in the Lord your God.”

The fact that Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah humbly beg Rabshakeh to speak in Aramaic has this meaning: the people must be shaken by terrifying threats, and he must boast of his strength. “Speak the language which the people do not understand, for we too have knowledge of your language.”

But when he arrogantly says, “Has my master sent me to the Lord and to you?” and continues until he says, “and drink their own urine with you,” he shows that he considers them fools and idiots. At the same time, he softens fear by means of enticement, so that those whom he has conquered through terror may be deceived by persuasion.

He speaks in the person of the king:

> “Make peace with me”—that is, do what will benefit you. Make peace with the Assyrian king and acknowledge him as lord, so that you may receive rewards. Until I return from Egypt, or until I come back after capturing Lachish, remain in your city and enjoy your possessions. Afterwards I shall lead you into a land like your own land.”

He did not name it “your land,” because he could not find one similar to it, but he named it by comparison. Each person desires whatever resembles the place in which he was born.

Some think that he promised them a land which, like Judaea, resembled it in both location and produce. When Rabshakeh, among his other blasphemies against God, shouted against Jerusalem:

> “Where is the god of Hamath and Arpad? Where is the god of Sepharvaim, Ana, and Ava? Have they delivered Samaria from my hand?”

he showed that the gods of all these cities—or nations—had been subject to Samaria, and that they were not gods but idols; their worshipers, devotees of vanity, had rightly been overthrown.

Hamath is a city of Coelesyria, which is called Epiphaneia and lies near Emesa. Arpad is a city of Damascus, which was conquered by the king of Assyria. Jeremiah mentions Sepharvaim, whose name in Hebrew is expressed in the plural. These were places whose inhabitants the Assyrians transferred to Samaria, as is recorded in the *Book of Places*.

In Isaiah, however, this word appears as the name of a city, where it is plainly said:

> “Where is the king of the city of Sepharvaim?” [Isaiah 37]

The form is nevertheless plural, like *Thebae* and *Athenae*. The old edition reads *Ana et Ava*, as though it were making *Ana* the name of one city. In Hebrew it is written similarly.

Since the fifth Hebrew syllable is marked with a conjunction, and since the conjunction has the same force among them, the passage can also be divided so that it reads “Hena and Ivvah,” as Aquila translated it, or “Ana and Ava,” as the other translator rendered it.

But if five tribes, with their gods, could be so easily destroyed, how much more should we see Jerusalem as protected by one God alone? Truly the righteous Hezekiah prohibited everyone from answering him, so that he would not provoke him to greater blasphemies.

> “Eliakim son of Hilkiah, the steward of the palace, Shebna the scribe, and Joah son of Asaph the recorder came to Hezekiah with torn garments and reported to him the words of Rabshakeh.”

### Chapter XIX

[Scan page 269]

When Hezekiah heard this, he tore his garments, covered himself with sackcloth, entered the house of the Lord, and sent Eliakim the steward of the palace, Shebna the scribe, and the elders of the priests, covered with sackcloth, to Isaiah the prophet, son of Amoz. They said to him:

> “Thus says Hezekiah: ‘This day is a day of tribulation, rebuke, and blasphemy. The children have come to the point of birth, but she who is giving birth has no strength,’”

and so forth. They tear their garments because they hear Rabshakeh blaspheming. He also tears his garment because he believed that Rabshakeh had gone as far as the gate of Jerusalem and had spoken such things against the Lord. Wonderful humility and prudence in the king: leaving royal attire behind, wrapped in sackcloth, he goes from the palace to the temple; he sends the chief priests to Isaiah, covered not in robes but in haircloth, and says: “This is a day of our tribulation, God’s correction, and the enemies’ blasphemy.” He offers the comparison of a woman in labor and pain, who has reached the point of birth but cannot give birth.

> “Perhaps the Lord your God will hear. Therefore lift up our prostrate prayer for the remnant of the people that is besieged.”

Isaiah anticipated them, because by the Spirit through which he knew the future he also heard what was said in his absence. “Say these things,” he says, “to your master: Thus says the Lord: ‘Do not fear the words by which I—not you—have been blasphemed. Nor do I say all that I shall do to the king of Assyria, lest I seem to boast of my power. But a spirit, not of God but of the adversary, shall be given to him; on hearing a report, he shall return to his own land and fall by the sword there.’” Thus Hezekiah was to hear at once the two things he desired: that he would be freed from the siege and that his enemy would die in his own land.

Rabshakeh therefore returned and found the king of Assyria attacking Libnah, for he had heard that he had withdrawn from Lachish. When he heard people saying of Tirhakah king of Ethiopia, “Behold, he has come out to fight against you,” he went against him and sent messengers to Hezekiah, saying: “Say this to Hezekiah king of Judah: ‘Do not let your God, in whom you trust, deceive you, nor say: Jerusalem shall not be delivered into the hand of the king of Assyria.’” In accordance with God’s will Rabshakeh abandoned the siege of Jerusalem and went to his master, whom he found attacking Libnah after Lachish had either been captured or abandoned. Sennacherib, however, while advancing to meet the Ethiopian king, sent messengers and letters to Hezekiah, in order to terrify by words those whom he had not taken by force. Herodotus relates that Sennacherib fought against the Egyptians and besieged Pelusium, and that, when siege mounds had been built and the city was about to be captured, Tirhakah king of Ethiopia came to their aid.

When Hezekiah received the letter from the hand of the messengers and had read it, he went up into the house of the Lord, spread it out before the Lord, and prayed in his presence, saying:

> “Lord God of Israel, who are enthroned above the cherubim, you are God alone over all the kingdoms of the earth. You made heaven and earth. Incline your ear, Lord, and hear; open your eyes, Lord, and see; hear all the words of Sennacherib, which he has sent to reproach the living God,”

and so forth.

Previously, terrified by fear of the Lord, Hezekiah had not dared to pray in the temple or to pour out free petitions. Then he heard Isaiah say:

> “Do not be afraid because of the words which you have heard” [Isaiah 37].

He returned to Jerusalem and boldly prayed to the Lord against the one who had spoken such things.

> “Isaiah son of Amoz sent word to Hezekiah, saying: ‘Thus says the Lord God of Israel: I have heard what you have prayed to me concerning Sennacherib king of Assyria. This is the word which the Lord has spoken concerning him: “The virgin daughter of Zion has despised you and mocked you; behind your back the daughter of Jerusalem has shaken her head. Whom have you reproached and blasphemed? Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes on high? Against the Holy One of Israel,”’”

and so forth.

At last Hezekiah boldly prays to the Lord. He did not send for Isaiah as he had done before; the prophet himself did not go to him, but he sent messengers to convey God’s answer:

> “The virgin of Zion and the daughter of Jerusalem.”

She is called both virgin and daughter because, among all the nations, she alone preserves her chastity for the religion of God and the worship of the one divinity, while those who worship the images of dead things have abandoned it. And so that she would not provoke him to greater blasphemy, she did not answer him while he was present, but “after he had departed, she shook her head,” confident of vengeance and secure regarding his punishment.

> “You have blasphemed the Lord through the hand of your servants—not by yourself, but through your servants, which makes your arrogance greater.”

The height of the mountains and the lofty peaks of Lebanon, its cedars and firs, may metaphorically be understood of all the nations and their rulers, or of Jerusalem, which is the cedar of Lebanon, with its firs, the powerful and the nobles.

The height of the summit and the thickets of Carmel signify the temple. When he adds:

> “I dug wells and drank water; I dried up with the sole of my foot all the streams of the fortified places,”

he may have said this because, on account of the multitude of his army, he dried up all the flowing waters and was compelled to dig wells for himself; or because he devastated by his army all the peoples signified by the waters.

> “Have you not heard what I did long ago? From ancient days I fashioned it, and now I have brought it about; it has come to pass for the destruction of warring hills and fortified cities. Their inhabitants, weakened in hand, trembled and were crushed; they became like the grass of the field, the herbage of the pasture, and the grass of the roofs, which withered before it ripened. I know your dwelling, your going out and your coming in, and your rage against me. Because you raged against me, your arrogance rose to my ears. I shall therefore put a ring in your nose and a bridle on your lips, and lead you back by the way by which you came.”

These words are to be understood as spoken by God against the Assyrian’s claims. The Lord answers his blasphemy:

“Do you not know that the things you have done were done by my will, and that I foretold them and openly commanded that they should happen? What I decreed long ago has now been fulfilled: the hills—that is, the rulers who had previously fought among themselves—and the most heavily fortified cities have been uprooted because I withheld my hand and did not provide my customary assistance. They trembled and perished.

“They are compared not with olive trees, vineyards, and fruit-bearing trees, but with hay, grass, and the herbs of doctrines that hinder true understanding and wither before reaching maturity. I knew your resting, your going out, and your coming in, and I spoke through the prophets of the madness with which you were going to rage against me. Through them I knew that you would one day say, ‘I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will set my throne; I will be like the Most High.’

“Your fury and arrogance therefore reached my ears, and I will no longer tolerate you, so that you may understand that what you were able to do was not accomplished by your own strength but by my decision. The impious nations and unfruitful trees deserved to be cut down and fall through you, as through my axe and saw. I shall therefore put a ring—or hook—in your nose, to restrain your blaspheming mouth, so that you will no longer dare to speak such things; and I shall place a bridle on your lips, which will subdue your ferocity and lead you back into Assyria.”

> “This shall be the sign for you, Hezekiah: this year you shall eat what grows of itself; in the second year, what springs up spontaneously; but in the third year sow and reap,”

and so forth.

It should be noted that in the Book of Isaiah, where the prophet’s words to King Hezekiah are recorded, they are related as follows:

> “This year eat what grows of itself, and in the second year eat the fruit of what is left. In the third year sow and reap, plant vineyards and eat their fruit. The remnant that escapes from the house of Judah shall again take root below and bear fruit above, because a remnant shall go out from Jerusalem and survivors from Mount Zion. The zeal of the Lord of hosts shall do this” [Isaiah 37].

Now he speaks directly to Hezekiah: “This,” he says, “shall be the sign of the things I announce as future: this year you shall eat what grows of itself, or, according to the Septuagint, ‘what you previously sowed.’ In the second year, according to Symmachus, you shall eat fruit, or, according to the same translators, what has sprung up from the former crops and from seed fallen upon the ground. In the third year, once the Assyrian has been driven away and the siege has been relaxed, sow and reap, plant vineyards, and eat their fruit.

“For the small remnant of this city, which is now surrounded by the enemy army and does not believe that it will escape, will receive such abundance and prosperity in everything that, like a tree firmly rooted below, it will be filled with the densest fruit.”

[Scan page 270]

For from Jerusalem and from Mount Zion a remnant will go forth and fill the land of Judaea, not through its own merit but through God’s mercy, indeed through the zeal with which he has shown zeal for his people against the wicked.

> “Thus says the Lord concerning the king of Assyria: ‘He shall not enter this city and shall not shoot an arrow there; he shall not seize it with a shield and shall not build a siege ramp around it. By the way he came, by that same way he shall return, and he shall not enter this city,’ says the Lord. ‘I will protect this city and save it for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant.’”

By the hope of future things he dispels present fear. He says that they will be preserved not because of their own merit but through God’s mercy, indeed for the sake of the memory of their father David. In this they are warned both of their own negligence and of his faith and righteousness, since God loves righteousness so greatly that he protects the descendants of virtuous ancestors.

> “That night the angel of the Lord went out and struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand in the camp of the Assyrians. When they arose at dawn, they saw all the bodies of the dead, and they withdrew and departed.”

One hundred and eighty-five thousand very strong men were slain by one angel in a single night. Without visible wounds, savage death moved through them, separating their souls from their bodies by the will of the Lord.

Concerning this, Chronicles says:

> “The Lord sent his angel, and he struck every mighty man, warrior, and commander of the army of the king of Assyria. He returned with shame to his own land” [2 Chronicles 32].

He was spared for this reason: that he might recognize God’s power, restrain his blaspheming mouth, and become a witness to the majesty of the one whom he had shortly before despised.

> “Sennacherib king of Assyria returned and dwelt in Nineveh. While he was worshiping in the temple of Nesroch, his god, Adrammelech and Sharezer, his sons, struck him with the sword and fled into the land of Armenia; and Esarhaddon his son reigned in his place.”

Pharaoh was preserved through the ten plagues of Egypt so that he might perish at the end; this man suffered something similar. When he returned to Nineveh, the first city of his kingdom, and worshiped in the temple of his god Nesroch as though he had returned victorious from his enemies, he entered the shrine of his idol in triumph and rejoicing, despising the man of God. There, in the sanctuary of a god bearing a false name, he was slaughtered.

Nor did he perish by an angel’s sword, which would have been common to many, but by the parricide of his sons. After they fled into the land of Ararat, which is understood to be Armenia, Esarhaddon succeeded to his father’s place. Scripture records that he sent inhabitants to Samaria so that the land would not remain uncultivated.

Ararat is a region of Armenia in level country, through which the Araxes flows. It is extraordinarily fertile and lies at the foot of Mount Taurus, which extends as far as that region. Thus the ark in which Noah was saved with his children, after the flood had ceased, was not carried merely to the mountains of Armenia in general, but to the lofty mountains of Taurus, which overlook the plains of Ararat.

### Chapter XX

[Scan page 271]

> “In those days Hezekiah became sick unto death, and Isaiah son of Amoz the prophet came to him and said: ‘Thus says the Lord: Set your house in order, for you shall die and not live.’”

So that Hezekiah would not become exalted after his remarkable triumphs and victory over captivity, he was visited by bodily weakness and heard that he was going to die, so that, turning back to the Lord, he might bend God’s sentence.

We read the same thing in the prophet Jonah and in the threats made against David: future events are announced, yet they do not happen—not because God changes his decision, but because he calls the human race to knowledge of himself.

The Lord “repents concerning evil,” because punishments are threatened to human beings in this world, though by the hidden counsel of the omnipotent God he does not truly repent. For God decreed before the ages all things that would come to pass and how they would be arranged throughout the ages.

A fixed order has already been established for human beings: how much prosperity in this world each person will experience, how much adversity will strike him, and that neither excessive prosperity should make his elect arrogant nor excessive adversity crush them.

It has also been determined how long each person will live in this mortal life. Although the omnipotent God added fifteen years to Hezekiah’s life, he already knew, when he allowed him to die, that he would die at that time.

A question therefore arises: how could the prophet say to him, “Set your house in order, for you shall die and not live,” when, once the sentence of death had been pronounced, life was immediately added to him through his tears?

The Lord said through the prophet at what time he deserved to die; the divine arrangements were not overturned. The years of life that would be increased through God’s generosity had also been fixed before the ages, and the additional span of life that unexpectedly appeared externally had already been established internally as an increase to the present life.

> “He turned his face to the wall and prayed to the Lord, saying.”

Hezekiah turned his face to the wall because he could not go to the temple. He turned toward the wall of the temple, beside which Solomon had built the palace; or simply toward the wall, so that he would not seem to display his tears to those sitting nearby.

Or, certainly, in accordance with Jeremiah, he turned toward his heart—for this reason Scripture calls the heart a “wall,” because he prayed to the Lord with his entire mind.

> “I beseech you, Lord, remember how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done what is pleasing in your sight.”

Blessed is the conscience that, in a time of affliction, recalls its good works.

> “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” [Matthew 5].

And as it is written elsewhere:

> “Who can say, ‘I have made my heart clean’?” [Proverbs 20]

This is resolved by saying that “perfection of heart” is used here to mean that Hezekiah had destroyed the idols, opened the temple doors, crushed the bronze serpent, and done the other things that Scripture records.

Often the just, compelled by pressing needs, must acknowledge their own works; but when the unjust hear them, they think that these statements were made out of pride rather than truth. They judge words about virtue from their own hearts and do not think that good things can be said humbly.

Just as it is a serious fault for a person arrogantly to claim what he does not possess, so it is often no fault at all for someone humbly to state the good that he does possess. Hence it frequently happens that the just and the unjust use similar words, while their hearts remain utterly different; and in the same statements by which the Lord is offended when they are spoken by the unjust, he is pleased when they are spoken by the just.

For the Pharisee, entering the temple, said:

> “I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I possess,”

yet the tax collector went away more justified than he [Luke 18].

When King Hezekiah, afflicted by bodily distress, had reached the point of death, he said in his prayer with compunction:

> “I beseech you, Lord, remember how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart.”

The Lord neither despised nor rejected this confession of his perfection; rather, he soon heard him in his prayers.

Behold, the Pharisee justified himself in his works; Hezekiah asserted that he was righteous even in his thoughts. The one pleased the Lord by the very thing in which the other displayed himself. Why was this, unless because the omnipotent God weighs the words and thoughts of each person, and in his ears the words spoken by a proud heart are not the same as those spoken by a humble heart?

> “Hezekiah wept with great weeping. Before Isaiah had gone out from the middle of the court, the word of the Lord came to him, saying: ‘Return and say to Hezekiah, ruler of my people: Thus says the Lord God of your father David: I have heard your prayer and seen your tears. Behold, I have healed you. On the third day you shall go up to the temple of the Lord, and I shall add fifteen years to your days. I shall also deliver you and this city from the hand of the king of Assyria, and I shall protect this city for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant.’”

He wept with great weeping because of the Lord’s promise to David, which he saw would perish with his own death. At that time Hezekiah had no sons; after his death Manasseh began to reign in Judah when he was twelve years old. It is therefore clear that Manasseh was conceived after the third year had been added to Hezekiah’s life.

Thus all this weeping was because he feared that Christ would not be born from his line.

Others, however, maintain that holy men are not terrified by uncertainty regarding judgment or by ignorance of God’s sentence, nor do they know what dwelling-place they will receive. At the same time, the question is resolved by the bonds of necessity and causation: the day of death is not fixed for each person in such a way that he must die on that particular day, but a person may live or die according to God’s will and causes unknown to mortals.

This is especially so since the necessity of death may now be delayed, and we read that many who had died were later raised again.

The Lord’s prophet returns to the king at God’s command, so that the one who had struck him might heal him. Hezekiah is called “ruler of my people” and “son of David,” whose works he imitated. For he had done what was right according to all that David his father had done, and his prayer is heard and his tears are seen because he had walked before the Lord in truth and with a perfect heart.

He had wept with great weeping and had done what was pleasing in the Lord’s eyes. Fifteen years were added to his life—[the supplied text breaks off: “which he had not been able to …”].

## Exposition of the Books of Kings — Book IV

…and, while he was still alive, the king’s security be restored [by] the rising of the sun, as both the histories of former times and men of our own age who come from those regions report most abundantly. Those, however, who inhabit the innermost parts of the south never see the sun return from the west to the east through the southern regions. But if, as some suppose, to live in the body is condemnation, in accordance with the saying, “Return, my soul, to your rest,” and elsewhere, “Bring my soul out of prison,” death is to be desired, so that we may be released from prison. How, then, does he now grant as a benefit that one who was to be set free should still live fifteen years in prison?

“And Isaiah said: Bring a mass of figs. When they had brought it and laid it upon his ulcer, he was healed.” The Hebrews say that the word *schehin*, which the Septuagint leave untranslated, denotes an ulcer, not a wound. Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translate it *helkos*, by which they wish the royal disease to be understood. Things that are either taken as food or applied to the body, whatever is sweet, seem contrary to this. Therefore, that God’s power might be shown, health was restored by three harmful and contrary things.

Guides to the holy places in this province commonly show, within the temple precincts, the steps of Hezekiah’s or Ahaz’s house down which the sun descended. But I can never believe—not to speak of Ahaz, an impious king, but of any just king—that a king’s house was within God’s temple. Solomon, indeed, is said among other things to have offended God because he built Millo on high, from which, while walking on the tower of his palace, he was accustomed to look down upon the temple court. Some transfer these ten steps or lines to the mystery of Christ, interpreting the shadows of the figures as Christ’s descent.

Others suppose that *schehin* means not an ulcer but an abscess, when the swollen body is filled with redness and putrefying pus, and, according to the physicians’ art, every discharge is driven by pains and bruises to the surface of the skin. Consequently medicine should not be despised, since its usefulness is established by practice and experience.

Hezekiah had said to Isaiah: “What will be the sign that the Lord has healed me and that I shall go up on the third day to the temple of the Lord?” Isaiah replied: “This shall be the sign from the Lord, that the Lord will do what he has spoken: Do you want the shadow to advance ten lines, or to return ten lines?”

A sign is given, then, that the sun should return ten steps, which we have rendered, following Symmachus, as “lines,” in accordance with the Hebrew expression. He understood the steps as lines in order to make the meaning clearer to readers. Alternatively, the steps may have been constructed by mechanical art in such a way that the descending shadow marked the intervals of the hours. It was the tenth hour of the day when the prophet was speaking to the king.

“Do you want,” he said, “the shadow to ascend ten lines as the sun advances over the earth toward the northern regions and then to the east—something it would accomplish beneath the earth according to the daily custom of its course—or do you want the shadow to return the same number of steps, with the sun’s face turned backward and itself returning through the southern region toward the east?”

The king said: “It is easy for the shadow to increase by ten lines. I do not want that, but rather that it return backward by ten steps.” For he saw that the greater miracle would be for the sun to reverse the customary course of its motion than for it to proceed along its accustomed path—although much higher, that is, raised above the earth toward the east—and, as if making the morning of a second day without any intervening night, to fly onward. Indeed, those who live on the island of Thule, which lies beyond Britain, or in the remotest regions of the Scythians, see something of this occur for several days every summer. For while the sun is elsewhere beneath the earth and set in the west, it nevertheless appears above the earth to them throughout the night, and its low return from the west toward the east can plainly be observed until the proper time comes for the whole world to receive the return of daylight.

The first step of descent, then, was from God into the angel, because he was “the messenger of the great counsel” [Isaiah 9]. Jacob likewise speaks to him thus: “And the angel of the Lord said: I am the God to whom you set up a pillar and vowed a vow” [Genesis 31], so that he might show himself to be both angel and God.

The second step of descent was from the angel into the patriarchs, because, as the Apostle says, “he himself wrought [it] in all things” [1 Corinthians 12] …

The third was into the giving of the Law, because he himself spoke in the Law.

The fourth was in Joshua, son of Nun, through whom he led the people into the promised land.

The fifth was in the judges, because through them he himself governed the same people.

The sixth was in the kings of Judah, because he himself reigned in them.

The seventh was in the prophets, because through them he was announced beforehand.

The eighth was in the priests, because he is the supreme priest of the Father.

The ninth was in humanity.

The tenth was in the Passion.

Through these ten steps, as through the shadow of the ancient Law, Christ descended; and after his resurrection Christ, the Sun of righteousness, ascended through the same steps into heaven. He illuminated the whole shadow of the Law of truth with his rays, revealing what was obscure, opening what was closed, and laying bare everything that had been covered.

> At that time Berodach-Baladan, son of Baladan, king of the Babylonians, sent letters and gifts to Hezekiah, for he had heard that Hezekiah was ill. Hezekiah rejoiced at their arrival and showed them his house of spices, gold and silver, various perfumes, ointments, the house of his vessels, and everything that he possessed in his treasuries. There was nothing that Hezekiah did not show them in his house, in all his power.

We read above [2 Kings 18] that in the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, came up against all the fortified cities of Judah and captured them. Afterwards he besieged Lachish, passed on to Libnah, and sent part of his army against Jerusalem. One hundred and eighty-five thousand of his troops were killed by an angel, and he himself fled to Nineveh. There he was killed by his sons, and his son Esarhaddon reigned in his place.

Hezekiah became ill, and at the prophet’s message he received the sign that the sun returned to its rising, so that nearly two days were made into one. Now we read that at that time—that is, in the same year in which these events occurred—Berodach-Baladan, son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent books and gifts to Hezekiah. It was not Esarhaddon, who had succeeded his father Sennacherib among the Syrians, and concerning whose death or life Scripture is silent. It is therefore perfectly clear that there was then one kingdom of Assyria and another of Babylon.

The Assyrians had already captured Samaria, that is, the ten tribes; later, as we read, the Chaldeans captured Judah and Jerusalem, whose king was Nebuchadnezzar. Since the Babylonians were skilled in observing the stars and had learned the courses of the heavenly bodies through long practice and experience—a fact also demonstrated at the Lord’s birth—they understood that the sun had turned back and that the day had been doubled. They served the one whom they thought to be the only god, namely the sun.

When they investigated the cause and explanation of this miracle, its fame having spread among all nations, they learned that, because of King Hezekiah’s illness, even the course of the most renowned sign had been altered. That this is not merely my opinion but the testimony of Holy Scripture is shown by the words of Chronicles [2 Chronicles 32], which say after other matters:

> He is the Hezekiah who stopped the upper spring of the waters of Gihon and turned them underground toward the west of the city of David. In all his works he prospered and accomplished whatever he wished.

Yet during the embassy of the princes of Babylon, who had been sent to him to inquire about the portent that had occurred over the earth, God abandoned him so that he might be tested and so that everything in his heart might become known. He was left to this testing because, after such a great victory, the return of the sun, and the congratulations of the most powerful kingdom, his heart had been lifted up.

The same book accordingly records:

> Many brought sacrifices and offerings to the Lord in Jerusalem, and gifts to Hezekiah king of Judah, who was exalted before all the nations. In those days Hezekiah became ill unto death and prayed to the Lord. He heard him and gave him a sign, but not according to the benefits he had received, for his heart had been lifted up. Therefore wrath came against him, and against Judah and Jerusalem. Yet Scripture again says that the elevation of his heart was softened by repentance, adding: “Afterward he humbled himself, because his heart had been lifted up, both he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem; therefore the wrath of the Lord did not come upon them in the days of Hezekiah.”

Hezekiah therefore rejoiced at the arrival of Berodach—whom the Hebrews maintain was Nebuchadnezzar’s father—and at the presentation of the gifts. In celebration of his recovery he showed them what the Septuagint call his “house of vessels,” whereas Symmachus translates “his house of spices,” together with the treasures of gold and silver, spices, the finest ointment—written in Hebrew as *shemen ṭov*, “good oil”—and all the treasures of his vessels. *Gaza* is the Persian word for riches; it is not Hebrew but barbarian.

“There was no word,” he says—that is, according to Hebrew usage, no thing that he did not show them in his house and in all his power. Hence God’s anger was most just, because he showed them not only his treasures and palace but also the temple, which certainly lay within the authority of the man who had previously removed the bronze plates from the doors of its court.

Isaiah the prophet entered King Hezekiah’s presence and said to him:

> What did these men say, and from where did they come to you?

Hezekiah replied:

> From a distant land they came to me, from Babylon.

And Isaiah said:

> What did they see in your house?

Hezekiah answered:

> Everything that is in my house they saw. There was no word or thing that I did not show them in my treasuries.

Isaiah said to Hezekiah:

> Hear the word of the Lord of hosts: Behold, days will come when everything that is in your house and that your fathers have stored up until this day will be carried away to Babylon. Nothing will be left, says the Lord. And some of your sons who will come forth from you, whom you will beget, will be taken away, and they will be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.

Hezekiah said to Isaiah:

> The word of the Lord that he has spoken is good.

And he added:

> Let there at least be peace and truth in my days.

The rest of the deeds of Hezekiah, all his strength, and how he made the pool and the aqueduct and brought water into the city—are these not written in the book of the annals of the kings of Judah?

The Hebrews report that Hezekiah became ill because, after his unprecedented victory and the destruction of the Assyrian king, he had not sung praises to the Lord as Moses did after Pharaoh was drowned, Deborah after Sisera was killed, and Hannah after Samuel was born. He was therefore reminded of his frailty. Then, after the restoration of his bodily health and the greatness of the sign, an opportunity for pride was removed—an opportunity that he, as a prudent worshiper of God, ought to have avoided. He should not have displayed to foreigners the riches he possessed by God’s gift.

From this, according to the principles of allegorical interpretation, we also learn that one must not “cast pearls before swine, nor give what is holy to dogs” [Matthew 7]. Whoever is faithful in spirit conceals his affairs; for anyone who fails to do this, all his virtue is weakened, his posterity perishes, and, having lost his manly strength, he is reduced to womanly softness.

Isaiah therefore enters the king’s presence and, as though he did not know, asks: “What did these men say, and from where did they come?” He asks two questions: what they had said and from where they had come. He answered only one and passed over the other. His reply must be read with emphasis and pride:

> From a distant land they came to me, from Babylon.

The more distant the land from which they had come, the more glorious he considered himself to be, because of whom they had come. “They came to me,” he says, when he ought to have said, “They came to glorify God, on account of the greatness of his name, from Babylon,” a city most powerful throughout the world.

Isaiah asks again: “What did they see in your house?” He answered partly truthfully: they had seen everything in his house, and there was nothing that he had not shown them in his treasuries. But he was silent about the point that he feared would provoke offense: he had shown them everything that he possessed within his authority, undoubtedly including the temple furnishings. Therefore Isaiah, speaking God’s sentence, says:

> Hear the word of the Lord of hosts: The time will come when all these things that are in your house, acquired not by your labor but by the labor of your fathers, will be carried away to Babylon, and some of your descendants will become eunuchs in the royal court [Isaiah 39].

For this reason the Hebrews believe that Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah—who were of royal descent—were eunuchs; there is no doubt that they served in Nebuchadnezzar’s court.

Hezekiah said: “The word of the Lord that he has spoken is good.” The Hebrews criticize him for this, asking why he did not imitate Moses’ goodness, when Moses said to the Lord:

> Either forgive them this offense, or, if you will not, blot me from the book that you have written [Exodus 32].

The Apostle likewise wished to be accursed from Christ for the sake of his brothers, who are Israelites [Romans 9].

This sentence of the prophet against Hezekiah can also be understood mystically as spoken against hypocrites. After great virtues they decline because they neglect to guard against the snares of evil spirits and refuse to hide those same virtues. By displaying their good works, they make enemies of them; and, acting without prudence, they suddenly lose whatever they had achieved through long devotion.

Hence the Psalmist says:

> He delivered their strength into captivity, and their beauty into the hands of the enemy [Psalm 78].

The strength and beauty of the proud are handed over to the enemy’s power, because every good that is displayed through the desire for praise is surrendered to the hidden adversary’s control. Those who expose their riches to the knowledge of their enemies invite their enemies to plunder them. For as long as we are separated from the security of the eternal Father, we walk along a road beset by lurking thieves. Whoever fears being robbed on the road must hide the good things he carries.

Wretched are those who, desiring human praise, dissipate within themselves the fruits of their labors. When they wish to display themselves to the eyes of others, they condemn what they do; for evil spirits provoke them to boast, and, as we have said, their enemies strip their works bare.

For this reason Truth says through the Gospel:

> Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing, so that your almsgiving may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you [Matthew 6].

For this reason it is said of the Church of the elect through the Psalmist:

> All the glory of the king’s daughter is within [Psalm 45].

Paul likewise says:

> This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience.

The Church is the daughter of kings, generated through the preaching of spiritual sons by good works. She possesses glory within, because what she does contains no boastful display. The Apostle calls the testimony of his conscience his glory, because he does not seek the favor of another’s speech and does not know how to place the joys of his life outside himself.

What we do must therefore be hidden, lest, carrying these things carelessly along the road of this life, we lose them through the assault of plundering spirits.

## Chapters XXI and XXII

> Hezekiah slept with his fathers, and Manasseh his son reigned in his place. Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem, and so forth.

After Hezekiah’s death, Scripture relates that his son Manasseh reigned in Jerusalem. He turned to the worship of idols and the practice of abominations, abandoning the God of his fathers and the good examples that he had observed in his father Hezekiah. The Lord spoke to him and to his people, but they would not pay attention. Therefore he brought upon them the commanders of the army of the king of Assyria. They captured Manasseh, bound him with chains and fetters, and brought him to Babylon.

When he was afflicted, he prayed to the Lord his God and repented greatly before the Lord God of his fathers. He entreated him and pleaded earnestly, and God heard his prayer, brought him back to Jerusalem and restored him to his kingdom. Then Manasseh knew that the Lord alone was God.

Manasseh’s repentance is an example that, after committing crimes, no one should despair of God’s mercy. Rather, through suitable repentance, one should maintain hope of forgiveness, provided that one completes it properly.

After him his son Amon reigned, an idolater. After Amon, his son Josiah reigned as a most righteous king. He cleansed away all the filth of the idols that his fathers had manufactured and devoted himself energetically to the worship of God. This was deserved, since the prophet had foretold him long before.

Josiah is interpreted as “whose sacrifice belongs to the Lord,” or “the salvation of the Lord,” or “the strength of the Lord.”

When the account continues that, after hearing the book of the Lord’s Law—which Hilkiah the priest found in the house of the Lord—Josiah tore his garments and sent Hilkiah the priest and the others who are subsequently listed to the prophet Huldah, the wife of Shallum, who lived in Jerusalem “in the second,” the meaning of this phrase is explained in the Book of Chronicles.

Concerning the aforementioned king Hezekiah it is written [2 Chronicles 32]:

> He also built up the entire wall that had been broken down, raised towers upon it, and constructed another wall outside.

Zephaniah also mentions this place, saying:

> The sound of a cry from the Fish Gate and a wailing from the second [Zephaniah 1].

The old edition translated this as though *Masena* were a proper name. *Masena* means “second.” Therefore, when it is said that the prophetess lived “in the second,” understand that she lived in the second section of the wall.

Concerning King Josiah it is said:

> He also defiled Topheth, which is in the valley of the son of Hinnom, so that no one could dedicate his son or daughter through fire to Molech.

This place is frequently mentioned in Scripture, especially in the Book of Kings and by the prophet Jeremiah. The valley of Hinnom, or of the son of Hinnom, lies beside the wall of Jerusalem toward the east, where a beautiful grove is watered by the springs of Siloam.

Topheth, or Tophet—for both forms are written—was a place in the same valley beside the washer’s pool, which Scripture mentions, and near the field of the potter. It can still be pointed out on the southern side of Mount Zion.

At Topheth, because it was a most pleasant place and even today offers the delights of gardens, people used to place an altar and sacrifice to demons. They consecrated their children to the impious fire or offered them as burnt sacrifices. Thus it is written in the Book of the Annals of the Days concerning King Ahaz [2 Chronicles 28]:

> He is the one who burned incense in the valley of Ben-Hinnom and passed his sons through the fire.

*Ben-Hinnom* signifies “the son of Hinnom.” The valley of Hinnom is called in Hebrew *Ben-Hinnom*; from its name the punishment of the underworld is called *Gehenna* in the New Testament.

For just as those who served idols were in the valley of Hinnom, so sinners, as the prophets testify, will be punished in Gehenna with eternal condemnation for the sins they committed.

When Jeremiah reported that the Lord had commanded him, saying [Jeremiah 19]:

> Go out to the valley of the son of Hinnom, which is beside the entrance of the Potsherd Gate,

he shortly afterward added:

> This place shall no longer be called Topheth or the valley of the son of Hinnom, but the valley of slaughter. I will destroy the counsel of Judah and Jerusalem in this place, and I will overthrow them by the sword.

Isaiah also most clearly calls Topheth hell. Describing the eternal destruction of the devil under the name of Assyria, he says [Isaiah 30]:

> At the voice of the Lord Assyria will be terrified; he will be struck with the rod. The passage of the rod will be firmly established, which the Lord will cause to rest upon him.

Immediately afterward he explains how and where Assyria will perish:

> For Topheth has been prepared from yesterday, prepared by the king, deep and wide.

He rightly says “wide,” because *Topheth* signifies “breadth.” He continues:

> Its fuel is fire and abundant wood; the breath of the Lord, like a stream of sulfur, sets it ablaze.

Josiah defiled Topheth either by scattering the bones of the dead there, as he is later said to have done in other places of idolatry, or by dispersing various unclean things throughout it, so that the place would appear more suited to abomination than to pleasure to everyone who saw it.

The account then continues concerning the same King Josiah.

## Chapter XXIII

> He also removed the horses that the kings of Judah had given to the sun, at the entrance of the temple of the Lord.

And shortly afterward:

> He burned the chariots of the sun with fire.

This shows that at that time the Jews had become subject to the superstition of all idolatrous nations. They believed that the sun was a god, after the manner of the Gentiles, and therefore dedicated to its worship the image they had made, together with chariots and horses, placing them in the courts of the temple of the Lord.

The Gentiles commonly paint or make an image of the sun by placing a beardless boy in a chariot and attaching horses to him as though they were carrying him through the heavens. They give the sun the form of a boy because, being born every day in a new rising, it never declines into old age.

That they also assigned a chariot and horses to it was taken from the miracle of Elijah the prophet, who was carried up into heaven by a fiery chariot and fiery horses, as John, bishop of Constantinople, believes.

Since the sun is called *Hēlios* in Greek, Sedulius likewise, when singing of Elijah’s ascent, composed these lines:

> How fittingly the shining path of heaven  
> corresponded to Elijah, glorious in merit and name.  
> He was worthy of this gift, because, with one letter  
> changed in the speech of the Greeks, “Elijah” means “sun.”

The Greeks had heard from the Israelites, who were reputed to possess divine writings, that Elijah had been carried into the heavens in a fiery chariot and with fiery horses. Or perhaps, seeing this very event depicted among other scenes on a wall, they believed—misled by the similarity of the name of the sun—that a passage through the heavens had been represented there. They turned a miracle divinely performed into an argument for error, through human folly and invention.

The Jews themselves imitated them, striving not to appear less foolish in any respect than the most foolish of the Gentiles.

Concerning the same king it is said shortly afterward:

> He also defiled the high places that were in Jerusalem, on the right side of the mount of Offense, which Solomon king of Israel had built for Ashtoreth, the idol of the Sidonians, and Chemosh, the offense of Moab, and Milcom, the abomination of the sons of Ammon; and the king demolished the statues.

It is as clear as daylight that Scripture commonly calls “high places” locations situated on wooded hills, where people either sacrificed to demons or, attracted by the pleasantness of the sites, offered victims to the Lord contrary to the prohibition, abandoning the altar that was in the temple. Hence, throughout this book, kings who were not perfectly righteous are nevertheless said not to have removed the high places.

It calls the mount of Offense the mountain of the idol, because Scripture commonly names idols “offenses”: either God is offended by them, or they bring offense and ruin upon their worshipers.

This is made clear in the same passage, which continues:

> These were the places that Solomon king of Israel had built for Ashtoreth, the idol of the Sidonians, and for Chemosh, the offense of Moab, and for Milcom, the abomination of the sons of Ammon; and the king defiled them.

Here, unless I am mistaken, it is also openly shown—though otherwise it would not be evident—that Solomon never fully repented of the sin of idolatry that he had committed. For if he had produced worthy fruits of repentance, he would have made every effort above all to remove from the holy city the idols that he himself had erected, rather than leave them as a scandal to the foolish, as though the things he had done wrongly, despite being the wisest of men, had been wisely and properly done.

Scripture also mentioned this place earlier, saying:

> Then Solomon built a shrine for Chemosh, the idol of Moab, on the mountain opposite Jerusalem, and for Milcom, the idol of the sons of Ammon [1 Kings 11].

It should not seem contradictory that the mountain on which these idols were made is here said to be in Jerusalem, although earlier it was said to be opposite Jerusalem. It was located so near the city that it belonged to it and appeared to defile the city itself with the filth that was gathered there.
