> Josiah turned and saw the tombs that were there on the mountain. He sent for the bones from the tombs, burned them upon the altar, and defiled it.

Why did Josiah order the bones of the dead to be burned upon the altar, unless to show that their sacrifices had been profane? They had not only offered sacrifices of animals to demons but had also delivered themselves through the fire of idolatry into the power of demons. Therefore, by the just judgment of God, they were to be destroyed together with the altar that they had built for idols.

Mystically, these things signify all who, enslaved to the service of the devil, have temporarily committed sacrilege and are to be consumed by eternal punishments, with the devil himself repaying them according to the proper merits of their works.

Josiah returned to Jerusalem and commanded the whole people:

> Keep the Passover to the Lord your God, according to what is written in the book of this covenant.

The account says that after this king had removed idols from the land, together with the diviners, the augurs, and every unclean and abominable thing, he celebrated a most solemn Passover for the Lord in the eighteenth year of his reign.

Morally, this teaches us first to cleanse the land of our heart from every vice and to purify our actions from every defilement of sin and from dead works, so that we may serve the living God and thus celebrate an acceptable Passover to the Lord—not “with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” [1 Corinthians 5].

According to the allegory, this Josiah represents the Lord and Savior, who is rightly called the salvation and strength of the Lord. Scripture says of him:

> The Lord is strong; the Lord is mighty in battle [Psalm 24].

And elsewhere:

> He himself will save his people from their sins [Matthew 1].

He alone, as God, cleanses the land of Judah and Jerusalem from every uncleanness and abomination. Through the prophet he says:

> The zeal of your house has consumed me [Psalm 69].

John also speaks of him:

> His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will cleanse his threshing floor [Matthew 3].

Malachi says of him:

> Behold, he comes, says the Lord of hosts. Who can endure the day of his coming, and who will stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s fire and like fuller’s soap. He will sit refining and cleansing silver; he will purify the sons of Levi. He will refine them like gold and silver, and they will offer sacrifices to the Lord in righteousness. Then the sacrifice of Judah and Jerusalem will please God, as in former days and as in ancient years. I will draw near to you in judgment, and I will be a swift witness against sorcerers, adulterers, and perjurers; against those who defraud the hired laborer of his wages, oppress widows and orphans, and drive away the stranger, and do not fear me, says the Lord of hosts [Malachi 3].

Our Josiah therefore celebrates the true Passover in the eighteenth year of his reign, when, at the eighth age, the general resurrection has occurred. Having cast out every scandal from his kingdom, he leads his saints to the perfection of their works and brings them to receive the reward of eternal blessedness.

The prophet foretold this, saying:

> Behold, the day comes, burning like a furnace, and all the arrogant and all who commit wickedness will be stubble. The coming day will set them ablaze, says the Lord of hosts, and will leave them neither root nor branch. But for you who fear my name the sun of righteousness will rise, and healing will be in his wings. You will go out and leap like calves from the herd, and you will trample the wicked, for they will be ashes beneath the soles of your feet [Malachi 4].

It is rightly said that “no Passover like that had been celebrated from the days of the judges who judged Israel, nor throughout all the days of the kings of Israel and the kings of Judah, as in the eighteenth year of King Josiah in Jerusalem.” For, when the figures have been removed, the saints will truly pass on the day of judgment from death to life and from corruption to glory.

Thus they will rejoice forever in the sight of their Creator in the heavenly Jerusalem, because “the God of gods will be seen in Zion.” That city will need neither sun nor moon to shine upon it, for the glory of God will illuminate it, and its lamp will be the Lamb. The nations will walk by its light, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory and honor into it. Its gates will not be shut by day, for night will not exist there. They will bring into it the glory and honor of the nations. Nothing unclean will enter it, nor anyone who practices abomination or falsehood, but only those who are written in the Lamb’s book of life [Revelation 21].

From that day the name of the city will be “The Lord is there.” “Blessed is the Lord, for he has made his mercy wonderful in a fortified city” [Psalm 31].

> After King Josiah was killed at Megiddo, the people of the land took Jehoahaz, son of Josiah, anointed him, and made him king in place of his father. Pharaoh Neco bound him at Riblah and took him to Egypt. He imposed a tribute on the land of one hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold. He made Eliakim, son of Josiah, king in place of Josiah his father, and changed his name to Jehoiakim.

What else does the death of Josiah, who was killed by Pharaoh Neco at Megiddo, signify except the persecution of the ancient enemy against holy preachers? Out of envy the enemy strives to deliver them to death and remove them from the earth of the Church, so that he may more easily scatter and attack the whole people.

*Pharaoh* is interpreted as “the one who scatters,” *Neco* as “striking,” and *Megiddo* as “temptation.” When the devil is permitted to rise up against the saints, this is all that he seeks and attempts with all his strength: by striking the Lord’s flock through temptation, to scatter it and first remove those whose support would have enabled the rest to fight against the enemy.

> The people of the land took Jehoahaz, son of Josiah, anointed him, and made him king in place of his father.

Jehoahaz, whose name means “the one held back,” signifies evil teachers. The people of the land—namely, carnal people devoted to earthly desire—according to their customs …

[scan page 277]

# Angelomus of Luxeuil, Monk

“They choose persons who consent to their vices. ‘Whom Pharaoh bound at Riblah and led into Egypt’: when the devil weakens and deceives the hearts of rulers through a multitude of flatterers. For Riblah is interpreted as ‘multitude,’ and thus, bound by the chains of sins, he plunges them into the dark abyss of spiritual Egypt.

Moreover, when Pharaoh Necho made Joakim king, he imposed upon the land a fine of one hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold. When the evil spirit demands the allotted burden of its servitude from the aforesaid people, it requires that they be ready for obedience to it in every respect, both in understanding and speech. Hence Joakim, in accordance with Pharaoh’s command, exacted from each according to his means, that he might give both silver and gold to Pharaoh. For through men devoted to him the devil demands from each person, according to his strength, payment of the reckoning of sin; and thus, through wicked rulers, he daily prepares destruction for their subjects.

## Chapter XXIV

“In those days Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came up, and Joakim became his servant for three years; then he again rebelled against him,” and so forth.

Whenever someone enslaves himself to any vice, he will be subject not to one master but to many. Thus Joakim, whom Pharaoh had previously compelled to pay him tribute, is now compelled by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, to serve him for three years. But whom do we understand by Nebuchadnezzar, except the very one whom we have said is Pharaoh: namely, the prince of confusion and ruler of this darkness? Therefore, when the ancient enemy persuades someone to pay him the tribute of sin, he immediately urges him to yield himself wholly to his lord and render complete service. What else is it to be a servant of the king of Babylon for three years than to be subjected to the ancient enemy by persuasion, delight, and consent, wholly given over to vices and, as it were, freely possessed by him?

Yet it often happens that such persons, prompted by God’s mercy, plan to rebel against the wicked spirit; hence what follows: “He again rebelled against him.” Nevertheless, it is not enough to rebel if one does not persevere in the struggle. Whoever desires to free himself from the power of the ancient enemy must fight bravely against him and implore help from the supreme Power with continual prayers, so that, aided by divine grace, he may overcome the most powerful enemy and escape the harshest yoke.

“After Joakim, his son Joachin reigned in his place. And he did evil before the Lord, according to everything that his father had done. At that time the servants of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came up against Jerusalem, and the city was surrounded by fortifications. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came against the city with his servants to besiege it. Joachin, king of Judah, went out to the king of Babylon—he himself, his mother, his servants, his princes, and his eunuchs—and the king of Babylon received him in the eighth year of his reign.

“And he broke up all the golden vessels which Solomon, king of Israel, had made in the temple of the Lord, according to the word of the Lord. And he carried away all Jerusalem, all the princes, and all the mighty men of war—ten thousand captives—and every craftsman and clusor; nothing was left except the poor of the people of the land. He also carried Joachin away to Babylon, together with the king’s mother, the king’s wives, his eunuchs, and the judges of the land; from Jerusalem to Babylon he led into captivity all the strong men, seven thousand, and craftsmen and clusors, one thousand—all men strong and trained for war; the king of Babylon led them captive to Babylon.”

Scripture adds: “and every craftsman and clusor.” This is what is related above concerning what the Philistines did when they ruled over Israel, where it says (1 Kings 13): “Now there was no smith to be found throughout all the land of Israel. For the Philistines had taken precautions lest the Hebrews make themselves a sword or a spear.”

For just as at that time they took care that the Hebrews, having smiths, would not make weapons with which to resist, so now the Chaldeans, after destroying Jerusalem and laying waste the whole land of promise, take pains that no craftsman and no clusor should remain in it, either to restore the ruined walls of the city or to repair what had been destroyed. Rather, whatever skill they had found among the exterminated nation, they transfer entirely to Babylon, so that it may either be useless thereafter or serve the interests of that city.

Although this belongs to a lamentable history, because it corresponds closely to the great negligence of our own time, I do not think the allegory should be passed over in silence. It is clear that Jerusalem and the land of Israel signify the city of Christ, that is, the holy Church. Babylon, the Chaldeans, and the Philistines signify the city of the devil, that is, the whole multitude of the wicked, whether human beings or angels.

Israel serves the Philistines or Chaldeans when the faithful, remaining in the Church in name only, deceived by unclean spirits or by wicked people, submit the necks of their minds to avarice, lust, or any other sin.

Nebuchadnezzar carries away the king of Jerusalem, all the princes, and ten thousand strong troops into captivity when he causes the teachers of the peoples and those who seemed, with unconquerable courage, to serve the Lord and faithfully preserve the Decalogue of the Law in love of God and neighbor, suddenly—overcome either by the allurements of the world or by adversities—to defile themselves with greater crimes, or, by turning aside into heresy, openly to incur the mark of apostasy.

The weapons with which, resisting the devil, we defend the freedom given us by God—what else are they but the words of Scripture? In them we learn, with the clearest light, by the examples of the Lord himself and of his saints, in what order the battles against vices must be overcome.

But the Philistines deprive the sons of Israel of the smiths who make weapons when evil spirits hinder the minds of the faithful from meditating on sacred reading by inserting worldly concerns, lest they themselves gain confidence through the exercise of resistance, or approach others who do not know how to read by exhorting or correcting them to resist vices.

They remove the makers of weapons when they overwhelm those who know the sacred words with such crimes that they are utterly ashamed to speak the good things they had learned.

[scan page 278]

# Commentary on the Books of Kings

They transfer every craftsman and clusor from Jerusalem to Babylon when they turn aside from their purpose those who were accustomed, through the manifold works of the virtues, to benefit many and fortify the city of God against the corruptions of temptations. They compel the intelligence that ought to have been devoted to the protection of the holy Church to be expended instead according to the will of the king of vices.

If in this passage we wish to understand the clusor not as a worker on doors or walls, but rather as a worker in gold and gems, the spiritual interpretation nevertheless looks toward one and the same end. It has been said concerning wisdom that gold and a multitude of gems cannot be compared with it; and therefore we can understand no one more suitably by “makers of these things” than teachers. As long as they live and teach rightly, they employ the resources of holy skill for the adornment of the holy city. But if they should happen to go astray, what are they except captives carried away by the king of the Chaldeans to Babylon?

Since the transfer of a craftsman and clusor from Jerusalem to Babylon signifies that the talent of the word received from heaven is buried in the earth—that is, that spiritual knowledge is turned toward the works of sinners—we must understand also that all the strong men and warriors were led into captivity together. These are those who seemed to be strong men and warriors but were deceived by the cunning of evil spirits and taken captive into the prison of spiritual Babylon.

We must therefore work so that we may escape the power of the most savage king. Let us watch and be sober; let us keep the fear of God always before our eyes and flee entirely from forgetfulness of his commandments. Let us build for ourselves the land of good works and ascend into it by progress in virtue, “clothed with the breastplate of righteousness and the helmet of salvation, carrying the shield of faith and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6).

Let us guard the gates of our senses, lest death enter through the windows. With every care let us guard our heart, because from it life proceeds. Above all, let us place our hope in the goodness of the heavenly King, asking that by his grace we may be freed from every evil. Thus we shall always remain unharmed by spiritual enemies, because “the Lord is the strength of his people and the protector of the salvation of his Christ” (Psalm 26), who saves all who hope in him.

“After Joachin had been taken captive, Nebuchadnezzar appointed Mathaniah, his uncle, in his place, and gave him the name Zedekiah. Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. He did evil before the Lord, according to everything that Joakim had done.”

What else can we understand by Zedekiah except what we previously indicated concerning Joakim: namely, wicked rulers in the Church who abuse their office and divine gift and falsely appropriate for themselves the name of righteousness? Mathaniah means “gift” or “present,” while Zedekiah means “righteous of the Lord.” He is said to have reigned eleven years, signifying that he was a transgressor of the Law. For the number eleven, which exceeds ten, signifies transgression of the Decalogue. Nor can someone rightly be called a king who is unwilling to rule himself and his subjects according to the Lord’s commandments.

## Chapter XXV

“It happened in the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, himself and all his army, came against Jerusalem. They surrounded it and built fortifications around it. The city was enclosed and blockaded until the eleventh year of King Zedekiah, on the ninth day of the month. Famine prevailed in the city, and there was no bread for the people of the land.”

The number nine, because it lacks one from ten, signifies the imperfection of the Law, just as eleven signifies transgression. It is rightly said that Nebuchadnezzar besieged the city in the ninth year of Zedekiah’s reign, in the tenth month and on the tenth day of the month, because wicked shepherds, although they possess knowledge of the commandments of the Decalogue, neglect to fulfill them in conduct and teaching.

The ancient enemy must therefore surround the people entrusted to them with his army and, having built a fortification of error and vices, close the city by blockading it. Thus famine prevails in the city: the famine, that is, of the word of God, because the bread of teaching is not freely distributed to the people of the land.

“And the city was breached, and all the men of war fled by night.” The guardianship of the peoples is breached through the various depredations of evil spirits. Those who ought to have defended the city with weapons flee, enclosed by the night of ignorance and the darkness of sins, because, according to the word of Truth: “The hireling, and he who is not the shepherd, sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees; and the wolf snatches and scatters the sheep” (John 10). The Apostle likewise says: “Those who sleep, sleep by night, and those who are drunk are drunk by night” (1 Thessalonians 5).

What follows—that they fled by the road of the gate situated between the two walls toward the king’s garden—quietly exposes the inertia of teachers. Positioned between the two walls of the two Testaments, they seek not to fight but to flee, and they prefer to luxuriate in pleasures, which the garden signifies, rather than resist their enemies with the shield of faith.

“Now the Chaldeans were surrounding the city. Therefore Zedekiah fled by the road that leads to the plains of the wilderness. The army of the Chaldeans pursued the king and overtook him in the plain of Jericho. All the warriors who were with him were scattered and abandoned him,” and so forth.

When evil spirits surround the people, the ruler flees—not to the mountains, of which it is written, “The mountains surround it, and the Lord surrounds his people” (Psalm 125), but to the plains of solitude…

# Angelomus

## Chapter XIX

“When Hezekiah heard this, he tore his garments, covered himself with sackcloth, entered the house of the Lord, and sent Eliakim, master of the household, Shebna the scribe, and the elders of the priests, clothed in sackcloth, to Isaiah the prophet, son of Amoz. They said to him: ‘Thus says Hezekiah: This is a day of tribulation, reproach, and blasphemy. The children have come to the point of birth, but the woman in labor has no strength,’” and so forth.

They tear their garments because they hear Rabshakeh blaspheming. The king also tears his garment because he believed that Rabshakeh had come to the gate of Jerusalem and spoken such things against the Lord on account of the sins of the people and his own. What marvelous humility and prudence in the king! Having put aside royal adornment, he goes from the palace to the temple wrapped in sackcloth. He sends the chief priests—not in stoles but covered with haircloth—to Isaiah and says: “This is the day of our tribulation, of God’s correction, and of the enemies’ blasphemy.” He compares their situation to that of a woman in labor who has reached the moment of giving birth but cannot bring forth.

“If somehow the Lord your God will hear.” We do not dare to call him the Lord of all of us, since we are suffering such things because he is angry; instead we call him your Lord. Yet we have this confidence of vengeance: the living God is being blasphemed by one who worships idols, which are dead.

“Raise, therefore, our prayer for the remnant of the people who are under siege.”

Isaiah anticipated them (Isaiah 37), because by the same Spirit through whom he knew future events he had also heard what was being said in his absence. “Say this,” he says, “to your lord:

“‘Thus says the Lord: Do not fear the words by which not you but I have been blasphemed. Nor do I recount everything that I will do to the king of Assyria, lest I seem to boast of my power. But because a spirit not of God, but of the adversary, will be given to him, when he hears the report and returns to his own land, he will fall by the sword. Thus two things that Hezekiah wished to hear will occur together: that he would be delivered from the siege and that his enemy would die in his own land.’”

Rabshakeh therefore returned and found the king of Assyria attacking Libnah. He had heard that he had withdrawn from Lachish. When they told him concerning Tirhakah, king of Ethiopia, “Behold, he has set out to fight against you,” and he went out against him, he sent messengers to Hezekiah, saying:

“‘Thus you shall speak to Hezekiah, king of Judah: Do not let your God, in whom you trust, deceive you, and do not say, “Jerusalem will not be delivered into the hand of the king of Assyria.”’”

According to God’s will, Rabshakeh abandoned the siege of Jerusalem and went to his lord, whom he found attacking Libnah, whether he had captured Lachish or abandoned it. Sennacherib, however, encountering the king of the Ethiopians, sent messengers and letters to Hezekiah in order to terrify by his words those whom he had not conquered by force.

Herodotus relates that Sennacherib fought against the Egyptians and besieged Pelusium; when the city was already about to be captured, with the embankments built, Tirhakah, king of the Ethiopians, came to its aid.

# Angelomus of Luxeuil, Monk

“Then Hezekiah received the letters from the hand of the messengers and read them. He went up to the house of the Lord, spread them out before the Lord, and prayed in his presence, saying: ‘Lord God of Israel, who sit upon the cherubim, you alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth; you made heaven and earth. Incline your ear, Lord, and hear; open your eyes, Lord, and see; hear all the words of Sennacherib, which he has sent to reproach the living God,’” and so forth.

Earlier, terrified by fear of the Lord, Hezekiah did not dare to pray in the temple or pour out free prayers. Now, however, because he hears Isaiah saying, “Do not be afraid of the words that you have heard” (Isaiah 37), and so forth, he confidently entreats the Lord.

“Isaiah, son of Amoz, sent to Hezekiah, saying: ‘Thus says the Lord God of Israel: I have heard what you have prayed to me concerning Sennacherib, king of Assyria. This is the word that the Lord has spoken concerning him:

“‘The virgin daughter of Zion has despised you and mocked you. The daughter of Jerusalem has shaken her head behind you. Whom have you reproached and blasphemed? Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes on high? Against the Holy One of Israel,’” and so forth.

At last Hezekiah confidently entreats the Lord. He does not go to Isaiah as he did previously; the prophet himself does not come to him, but sends messengers to convey God’s response:

“Virgin daughter of Zion and daughter of Jerusalem.”

She is called virgin and daughter because, while all the nations worship images of the dead, she alone preserves the chastity of the worship of God and the veneration of the one divine nature. So that she might not provoke a greater blasphemy, she did not answer at once but, “after he had departed, shook her head,” confident of vengeance and secure of punishment.

“You have blasphemed the Lord in the hand of your servants,” not by yourself but through your servants; for your arrogance is all the greater. “The height of the mountains and the peaks of Lebanon, its lofty cedars and firs,” may be understood metaphorically of all nations and their princes, or of Jerusalem, which is the cedar of Lebanon, and its powerful and distinguished men. “The height of its summit and the forest of Carmel” signifies the temple.

When he adds, “I dug and drank water, and I dried up with the sole of my foot all the streams of the embankments,” he may have said this because, on account of the multitude of his army, he dried up every stream and was compelled to dig wells for himself; or because he laid waste with his army all the peoples signified by the waters.

[scan page 280]

# Commentary on the Books of Kings

“Have you not heard what I did long ago? From ancient days I fashioned it, and now I have brought it about, and it has become the destruction of fortified hills and fortified cities. Their inhabitants, with their hands weakened, trembled and were crushed, like the grass of the field, the pasture-grass, and the grass of the rooftops, which withers before it comes to maturity. I know your dwelling, your going out, and your entering, and your madness against me. Because you raged against me, your pride has risen into my ears. Therefore I will put a ring in your nostrils and a bridle on your lips, and I will lead you back by the way by which you came.”

These words must be understood as spoken by God against the Assyrian’s words. The Lord responds to his blasphemy: “Do you not know that what you have done you have done by my will, and that I foretold these future events and openly commanded them to be done?”

Therefore what I decreed long ago will now be fulfilled: the hills—that is, princes who previously fought among themselves—and the very strongly fortified cities will be destroyed when I draw back my hand and no longer offer my customary help. They will tremble and perish. They will be compared not with olive trees, vineyards, and fruit-bearing trees, but with hay, grass, and the plants of doctrines that hinder the fruits and wither before reaching maturity.

I therefore know your sitting, your going out, and your entering, and I have spoken through the prophets of the madness with which you were about to rage against me. Through them I knew long ago that you would say: “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will set my throne; I will be like the Most High.” Thus your rage and pride have reached my ears, and I will no longer tolerate you, so that you may understand that what you were able to do was not accomplished by your own strength but by my decision.

The impious nations and barren trees deserved to be cut down and fall through you, as though through my axe and saw. Therefore I will put a ring—or hook—in your nostrils, to restrain your blaspheming mouth, so that you will no longer dare to speak such things. I will put a bridle on your lips to tame your ferocity and lead you back to Assyria.

“But for you, Hezekiah, this shall be the sign: Eat this year what you find; in the second year, what grows of its own accord; but in the third year sow and reap,” and so forth.

It should be noted that in the book of Isaiah, where the words of the prophet himself to King Hezekiah are recorded, they are related in this way:

“Eat this year what grows of its own accord, and in the second year feed on fruits. In the third year sow and reap, plant vineyards and eat their fruit. And what has been saved of the house of Judah, what remains, will send its root downward and produce fruit upward, because a remnant will go forth from Jerusalem and salvation from Mount Zion. The zeal of the Lord of hosts will do this” (Isaiah 37).

Now he speaks to Hezekiah himself: “This,” he says, “will be the sign of what I foretell will happen: this year you shall eat what grows of its own accord,” or, according to the Septuagint, “what you previously sowed.” In the second year, according to Symmachus, “feed on fruits”; or, according to the same translators, eat what has sprouted from the previous crops and from seed scattered upon the ground.

In the third year, once the Assyrian has been driven away and the siege has been lifted, “sow and reap, plant vineyards, and eat their fruit.” For the small remnant of this city, which is now surrounded by the enemy army and does not believe that it will escape, will receive such abundance and prosperity in all things that, like a tree firmly established by a deep root, it will be filled with a dense crop of fruit.

From Jerusalem and Mount Zion the remnant will go forth and fill the land of Judah—not through its own merit but through God’s mercy, indeed through the zeal with which he has been zealous for his people against the impious.

“Thus says the Lord concerning the king of Assyria:

“‘He shall not enter this city and shall not shoot an arrow there. He shall not occupy it with a shield and shall not cast up an embankment around it. By the way he came, by that way he shall return, and he shall not enter this city, says the Lord. I will protect this city and save it for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant.’”

By the hope of future things he drives away present fear. He says that they will be preserved not through their own merit but through God’s mercy, indeed through the memory of their father David. In this they are warned both of their own negligence and of his faith and righteousness, because God loves righteousness so greatly that he protects the descendants of the righteous through the virtue of their ancestors.

“It happened, therefore, that on that night the angel of the Lord came and struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand men in the camp of the Assyrians. When he arose at dawn, he saw all the bodies of the dead and departed.”

One hundred and eighty-five thousand very strong men are killed in a single night by one angel. Without wounds, savage death runs through them, separating their souls from their bodies by the will of the Lord.

Concerning this it is written in Chronicles: “The Lord sent his angel, who struck every strong man, warrior, and prince of the army of the king of Assyria. He returned with disgrace to his own land” (2 Chronicles 32). He was preserved for this reason: so that he might know God’s power, restrain his blaspheming mouth, and become a witness to the majesty of the one whom he had shortly before despised.

“Sennacherib, king of Assyria, returned and remained in Nineveh. While he was worshiping in the temple of Nesroch, his god, Adrammelech and Sharezer, his sons, struck him with the sword and fled into the land of Armenia; and Esarhaddon his son reigned in his place.”

Pharaoh too was preserved through the ten plagues of Egypt so that he might perish at the end; this man suffered the same fate. When he had returned to Nineveh, the chief city of his kingdom, and worshiped in the temple of Nesroch his god, as though he had won a victory over his enemies, he proceeded from the shrine of his idol in triumph and rejoicing, as one who had scorned the man of God. But he was slaughtered in the temple of a god bearing a false name. He did not perish by the sword of an angel, which was common to many, but by the parricidal swords of his sons.

When they had fled into the land of Ararat, which is understood as Armenia, Esarhaddon succeeded his father. Scripture testifies that he sent inhabitants to Samaria, lest the land remain uncultivated.

Ararat is a region in Armenia, in the plains through which the Araxes flows, of astonishing fertility, at the foot of Mount Taurus, which extends as far as that place. Thus the ark in which Noah was delivered with his children, when the flood had ceased, was not carried merely to the mountains of Armenia in general, but to the highest mountains of Taurus, which overlook the plains of Ararat.

## Chapter XX

“In those days Hezekiah became sick unto death, and Isaiah the prophet, son of Amoz, came to him and said: ‘Thus says the Lord God: Set your house in order, for you shall die and shall not live.’”

So that Hezekiah would not become proud after his extraordinary triumphs and victory from the midst of captivity, he is visited by bodily illness and hears that he is going to die, so that, turning back to the Lord, he might bend his sentence.

We read the same thing in the prophet Jonah and in the threats against David: future events are announced but do not occur—not because God changes his decision, but because he provokes the human race to recognize its own condition. “The Lord repented concerning the evil,” it says. Nothing happens to human beings in this world apart from the hidden counsel of almighty God.

For God decreed before the ages everything that would follow, and how all things would be arranged throughout the ages. It was already established how much prosperity of this world each person would experience and how much severity of adversity would strike, so that neither excessive prosperity might lift up his elect nor excessive adversity weigh them down.

It was also established how long each person would live temporally in this mortal life. For although almighty God added fifteen years to the life of the king who was already dying, when he allowed him to die, he had foreknown him as mortal. Here a question arises: how could the prophet say to him, “Set your house in order, for you shall die and shall not live,” when, after the sentence of death had been pronounced, life was immediately added to him in response to his tears?

Yet through the prophet the Lord said that he deserved to die at that time, and the divine ordinances were not overturned. Rather, the years of life that increased through God’s generosity had also been foreknown before the ages, and the extension of life that unexpectedly appeared had been established in that present increase.

“He turned his face toward the wall and prayed to the Lord, saying…”

Hezekiah turned his face toward the wall because he could not go to the temple. He may have turned toward the wall of the temple, according to the tradition that Solomon had built the palace next to it; or simply toward the wall, so that he would not appear to display his tears to those standing nearby. Or, according to Jeremiah, he turned toward his heart. For this reason Jeremiah calls the heart a wall: so that with his whole mind he might entreat the Lord.

“I beg you, Lord, remember how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done what is pleasing in your sight.”

Happy is the conscience that, in a time of affliction, recalls its good works: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5). But how is this reconciled with what is written elsewhere: “Who can boast that he has a pure heart?” (Proverbs 20)?

The answer is that perfection of heart is here said to exist in the sense that he had destroyed the idols, opened the gates of the temple, crushed the bronze serpent, and done the other things that Scripture records.

Often the needs of the righteous compel them, when afflicted, to confess their works. But when the wicked hear such statements, they think that these words have been spoken through pride rather than truth. They judge the words of the righteous from their own hearts and do not believe that it is possible to speak true good things humbly.

Just as it is a grave fault to arrogate to oneself what one does not possess, so it is often no fault at all to speak humbly of the good that one does possess. Hence it frequently happens that the righteous and the unrighteous have similar words, while their hearts remain utterly different; and in the very statements by which the Lord is offended when spoken by the wicked, he is pleased when they are spoken by the righteous.

When the Pharisee entered the temple, he said: “I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I possess,” but the tax collector went out more justified than he (Luke 18). Hezekiah, too, when afflicted by bodily distress and brought to the point of death, said in a contrite prayer: “I beg you, Lord, remember how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart.”

The Lord did not despise or reject this confession of his perfection; rather, he immediately heard him in his prayers. The Pharisee declared himself righteous in his works; Hezekiah asserted himself righteous even in his thoughts. From the very thing by which the Pharisee offended, Hezekiah pleased the Lord.

Why is this? Because almighty God weighs the words and thoughts of each person; in his ears, words uttered by the humble in heart are not proud.

“Hezekiah wept with a great weeping. Before Isaiah had gone out from the middle of the court, the word of the Lord came to him, saying: ‘Return and say to Hezekiah, leader of my people: Thus says the Lord God of your father David: I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears; and behold, I have healed you. On the third day you shall go up to the temple of the Lord, and I will add fifteen years to your days. I will also deliver you and this city from the hand of the king of Assyria, and I will protect this city for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant.’”

He wept with a great weeping because of the Lord’s promise to David, which he saw would perish with his own death. At that time Hezekiah had no sons, for after his death Manasseh began to reign in Judah when he was twelve years old. From this it is clear that Manasseh was born after the third year of the life granted to Hezekiah.

Thus all this weeping arose from his fear that Christ would not be born from his offspring. Others, however, assert that holy men are not terrified because of uncertainty concerning the judgment or ignorance of God’s sentence, that is, of the place where they will dwell; and at the same time the question concerning necessity and causes is resolved. The day of death is not individually predetermined, but according to God’s will and causes unknown to mortals, a person either lives or dies.

This is especially so when the appointed necessity of death is deferred, and we read that many were raised after death. The prophet returned to the king at the Lord’s command, so that he himself might heal the one whom he had struck. Hezekiah is called “the leader of my people” and “the son of David,” whose works he followed. For he had done what was right according to everything that David his father had done. His prayer was heard, and his tears were seen, because he had walked before the Lord in truth and with a perfect heart. He had wept with a great weeping and had done what was pleasing in the Lord’s eyes.

Fifteen years were added to his life, which he did not…

[scan page 282]

## Commentary on the Books of Kings — Book IV, 534

had stolen, and while he still survived, the security of the kingdom was promised to him. But if—as some think—there is a condemnation to live in the body, and according to the saying, “Return, my soul, to your rest,” and elsewhere, “Bring my soul out of prison,” it is to be desired that we should be freed from prison: how does he now grant as a favor that the one who was to be released should still live fifteen years in prison?

“Isaiah said: Bring a cake of figs.” When they had brought it and placed it upon his ulcer, he recovered. The Hebrews say that the word *schehin*—which the Septuagint rendered *ulcer*—means an ulcer, not a boil. For Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated it as *ἄνθραξ* (*ánthrax*), by which they wish a royal disease to be understood. The things contrary to this are thought to be whatever sweet substances are either taken in food or applied to the body.

Therefore, in order that God’s power might be displayed, health was restored through three noxious and adverse things. Others suspect that *schehin* means not an ulcer but an abscess, when the swollen body is filled with red matter and decaying pus, and when, according to medical practice, all the discharge is brought out onto the surface of the skin by drier and crushed substances. Accordingly, medicine should not be despised when its use is established by experience and God has made it effective.

Isaiah had said to Hezekiah: “What shall be the sign that the Lord has healed me and that I shall go up on the third day to the temple of the Lord?” Isaiah replied: “This shall be the sign from the Lord that the Lord will do what he has spoken: shall the shadow advance ten lines, or return ten lines?” The sign is given that the sun should return ten degrees, which we have rendered, following Symmachus, as “lines,” so that the sense might be clearer to readers; or perhaps the steps had actually been constructed in such a way, by mechanical art, that the descending shadow marked the intervals of the hours.

It was the tenth hour of the day when the prophet was speaking to the king. “Do you wish,” he said, “that the shadow should ascend ten lines, while the sun proceeds above the earth through the northern regions toward the east, as it would do beneath the earth according to the daily custom of its course; or that the shadow should return the same number of degrees, with the face of the sun turned backward and with it returning through the southern region toward the east?”

The king replied: “It is easy for the shadow to grow ten lines, and I do not want this to happen; rather, let it return backward ten degrees.” He saw that it could be a greater miracle if the sun followed a course contrary to its customary movement than if, proceeding along its accustomed path, though carried much higher—that is, above the earth—it flew toward the east as though toward the morning of a second day, with no intervening night.

For those who live on the island of Thule, which lies beyond Britain, or at the furthest boundaries of Scythia, see something of this kind happen every summer for several days: while the sun is set for the rest of the world and lies beneath the earth, it nevertheless appears above the earth to them throughout the whole night. It can clearly be seen how, from the western region, it returns low toward the east, until at the appropriate time it restores day to the whole world. Both ancient histories and men of our own age who come from those regions report this most abundantly; but those who inhabit the interior of the south never report seeing the sun return eastward from the west through the meridian regions.

But I do not believe that this was the house of Ahaz—I do not mean Ahaz, who was an impious king, but the house of any just king—nor that it was situated in the temple of God. For Solomon is said to have offended God precisely because he built Millo on high, from which, while walking in the palace tower, he was accustomed to look toward the temple courtyard.

Some wish to transfer these ten steps to the mystery of Christ, so that they may interpret them as figures of Christ’s descent, through whom the Sun of righteousness, Christ, after his resurrection, ascended again. The first step of descent, from God into an angel, was made because he was “the messenger of great counsel” (Isaiah 9); and finally Jacob is addressed as follows: “And he said,” the angel of the Lord said, “I am the God to whom you made a vow and offered a vow” (Genesis 31), thereby showing both the angel and God.

The second step of descent, from the angel into the patriarchs, took place because, as the Apostle says, “he himself worked in all things” (1 Corinthians 12). The third was in the giving of the Law, since he himself spoke in the Law. The fourth step was in Jesus son of Nave, through whom he led the people into the promised land. The fifth was in the Judges, because through them he himself ruled the same people. The sixth was in the kings of Judah, because he himself reigned in them. The seventh was in the prophets, because he was announced through them. The eighth was in the high priests, because he is the Father’s supreme priest. The ninth was in the human being. The tenth was in the Passion.

Through these ten steps, as though through the shadow of the Law, Christ descended; and again, after his resurrection, Christ, the Sun of righteousness, ascended through the same steps into heaven. He illuminated every shadow of the Law with the rays of truth, revealing what was obscure, opening what was closed, and laying bare everything that had been covered.

“At that time Berodach-Baladan, son of Baladan, king of the Babylonians, sent letters and gifts to Hezekiah. For he had heard that Hezekiah had been ill. Hezekiah rejoiced at their arrival and showed them the house of his spices, gold, silver, various perfumes, ointments, and the house of his vessels, and everything that he had in his treasuries. There was nothing that Hezekiah did not show them in his house, in all his power.”

Above we read (2 Kings 18) that in the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, came against all the fortified cities of Judah, captured them, and afterward besieged Lachish. He crossed over to Libnah, sent part of his army against Jerusalem, and, having slain one hundred and eighty-five thousand of his army through an angel, fled to Nineveh. There he was killed by his sons, and his son Esarhaddon reigned in his place.

Hezekiah fell ill and received through the prophet’s message an extraordinary sign: the sun returned to its rising, so that almost two days were made into one. Now we read that at that time—that is, in the same year in which all these events occurred—Berodach-Baladan, son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent books and gifts to Hezekiah; not Esarhaddon, who succeeded his father Sennacherib among the Syrians, concerning whose death or life Scripture is silent. From this it is clear that the kingdom of the Assyrians was then one thing and that of the Babylonians another.

Finally, we read that the Assyrians captured Samaria, that is, the ten tribes, while later the Chaldeans captured Judah and Jerusalem; their king was Nebuchadnezzar. Since among them the observation of the stars and the courses of the heavenly bodies were known through long practice and training—and this is also demonstrated at the Lord’s birth—they understood that the sun had returned and that the periods of the day had been doubled. They served the one whom they thought to be the only god, namely the sun.

When they sought the reason and explanation of this miracle, while the report flew through all nations, they learned that, because of King Hezekiah’s illness, the course of this most illustrious sign had also been changed. That this is not my personal opinion but the testimony of Holy Scripture is demonstrated by the words of the Book of Chronicles (2 Chronicles 32), which say afterward:

“He is the Hezekiah who stopped the upper spring of the waters of Gihon and diverted them underground toward the west of the city of David. In all his works he prospered in whatever he wished.”

Nevertheless, during the embassy of the princes of Babylon, who had been sent to him to inquire about the portent that had occurred over the earth, God abandoned him so that he might be tested and so that everything in his heart might become known. He was left to the test because, after such a great victory, the return of the sun, and the congratulations of the most powerful kingdom, his heart had been lifted up.

The same book accordingly says:

“Many brought sacrifices and offerings to the Lord in Jerusalem, and gifts to Hezekiah king of Judah, who was exalted thereafter before all the nations. In those days Hezekiah became ill, even to the point of death, and he prayed to the Lord. He heard him and gave him a sign; but he did not repay him according to the benefits he had received, because his heart was lifted up. Therefore wrath came against him, Judah, and Jerusalem.”

Holy Scripture also says that the elevation of his heart was softened by repentance, adding:

“And afterward he humbled himself, because his heart had been lifted up, both he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem; therefore the wrath of the Lord did not come upon them in the days of Hezekiah.”

Hezekiah therefore rejoiced at the arrival of Berodach, whom the Hebrews think was the father of Nebuchadnezzar, at the presentation of gifts, and at the congratulations over his recovery. He showed them, according to the Septuagint, his house of vessels, for which Symmachus translated “his house of spices,” together with his treasures of gold and silver, perfumes and the finest ointment, which in Hebrew is written *oiei boni*, “good ointment,” and all the treasures of his vessels. *Gaza*, as the Persians call it, means “riches”; it is not a Hebrew word but a foreign one.

“There was no word”—which, according to Hebrew usage, frequently means “no matter”—“that he did not show them in his house and in all his power.” Hence God’s most just anger, because he showed not only his treasures and palace but also the temple, whose doors he had certainly already stripped of their plates.

Isaiah the prophet entered King Hezekiah and said to him: “What did these men say, and from where did they come to you?” Hezekiah replied: “From a distant land they came to me, from Babylon.”

And Isaiah said: “What did they see in your house?” Hezekiah replied: “Everything that is in my house they saw. There was no word—or thing—that I did not show them in my treasuries.” Isaiah said to Hezekiah: “Hear the word of the Lord of hosts: Behold, days will come when everything that is in your house, and what your fathers have stored up to this day, will be carried away to Babylon. Nothing will be left, says the Lord. And some of your sons who will come forth from you, whom you will beget, they will take away; and they will be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon. Hezekiah said to Isaiah: ‘Good is the word of the Lord that he has spoken.’ And he said: ‘Let there at least be peace and truth in my days.’”

“The rest of the words of Hezekiah, and all his strength, and how he made the pool and the aqueduct and brought water into the city—are these not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?” and so forth.

The Hebrews transmit that Hezekiah became ill because, after his unheard-of victory and the destruction of the Assyrian king, he did not sing praises to the Lord as Moses did when Pharaoh was drowned, Deborah when Sisera was killed, and Hannah when Samuel was born. He was therefore reminded of his weakness. Again, after the restoration of his bodily health and the greatness of the sign, an occasion for pride ought to have been removed—an occasion which, as a prudent worshiper of God, he ought to have avoided—and he ought not to have displayed his riches to foreigners, riches that he possessed through God’s gift.

From this, according to the rules of allegorical interpretation, we also learn not to “cast pearls before swine or give what is holy to dogs” (Matthew 7). Whoever is faithful in spirit keeps secrets hidden; and whoever does not do this loses the strength of all his virtue, his posterity perishes, and, deprived of manly strength, he is reduced to womanly softness.

Isaiah therefore enters the king and, as though unaware, asks: “What did these men say, and from where did they come?” He asks two things: what they said and from where they came. He answered one and omitted the other, which must be read with emphasis and hauteur: “From a distant land they came to me, from Babylon.” The farther away the land from which they came, the more glorious he considered himself because they had come for his sake. “They came to me,” he says, when he ought to have said, “They came to glorify God because of the greatness of the sign, from Babylon, which is the most powerful city in the whole world.”

[scan page 283]

## Angelo of Lucca, Monk

Again Isaiah asks: “What did they see in your house?” He answered partly truthfully: they saw everything in his house, and there was nothing that he did not show them in his treasuries. But he suppresses the other matter for which he feared offense: that he had shown them everything he possessed in his power, unquestionably including the temple vessels. For this reason Isaiah, speaking God’s word, delivers the sentence:

“Hear the word of the Lord of hosts: The time will come when everything that is in your house—not acquired by your labor but by the labor of your fathers—will be transferred to Babylon, and those descended from you will become eunuchs in the royal court” (Isaiah 39).

From this the Hebrews wish Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah—who were of royal descent—to have been eunuchs; there is no doubt that they served in Nebuchadnezzar’s household.

“Hezekiah said: ‘Good is the word of the Lord that he has spoken.’” In this he is reproached by the Hebrews: why did he not imitate the goodness of Moses, who said to the Lord: “Either forgive them this sin, or, if you do not, blot me out of your book that you have written” (Exodus 32)? Hence the Apostle also wishes to be accursed from Christ for the sake of his brothers, who are Israelites (Romans 9).

This sentence of the prophet to Hezekiah can also be understood mystically as spoken against hypocrites. After great virtues they decline because they neglect to guard against the snares of evil spirits and do not wish to conceal their virtues. By displaying their good deeds, they make them weapons for their enemies; and, acting imprudently, they suddenly lose whatever they have achieved through long and careful effort.

Hence the Psalmist says: “He gave their strength into captivity, and their beauty into the hand of the enemy” (Psalm 78). The strength and beauty of the arrogant are handed over to the enemy, because every good that is displayed through the desire for praise is subjected to the power of the hidden adversary.

They provoke enemies to plunder when they expose their riches to their knowledge. For as long as we are separated from the security of our eternal homeland, we walk along the road among lurking robbers. Whoever fears being robbed on the road must hide the good things that he carries.

Unhappy are those who, seeking human praise, dissipate within themselves the fruits of their labors. When they desire to display themselves to other eyes, they condemn what they are doing. For evil spirits, when they incite them to boasting, as we have said, expose their works to enemies.

Hence Truth says through the Gospel: “Let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing, so that your almsgiving may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matthew 6).

Hence it is said of the Church of the elect through the Psalmist: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Psalm 45). Paul says: “Our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience.”

The Church is indeed the daughter of kings, generated by the preaching of spiritual sons through good works. She has her glory within, because what she does contains no boastful display. The Apostle calls his glory the testimony of his conscience, because he does not seek the favor of another; he does not know how to place the joys of his life outside himself.

What we do must therefore be concealed, lest, carrying these things carelessly along the road of this life, we lose them through the attack of plundering spirits.

## Chapters 21 and 22

“Ezekiah slept with his fathers, and Manasseh his son reigned in his place. Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem,” and so forth.

After Hezekiah’s death, Scripture relates that his son Manasseh reigned in Jerusalem. He turned to the worship of idols and to the practice of abominations, abandoning the God of his fathers and the good examples he had observed in his father Hezekiah. The Lord spoke to him and to his people, but they would not listen.

Therefore he brought upon them the commanders of the army of the king of Assyria. They captured Manasseh, bound him with chains and fetters, and led him to Babylon. After he had been brought into distress, he prayed to the Lord his God and repented greatly before the Lord God of his fathers. He entreated him and prayed earnestly, and God heard his prayer. He brought him back to Jerusalem and restored him to his kingdom. Then Manasseh knew that the Lord himself was God.

Manasseh’s repentance is an example: after committing crimes, no one should despair of God’s mercy, but should rather hope to obtain it through appropriate repentance, if he performs it properly.

After him his son Amon reigned, an idolater. After Amon, his son Josiah, a most righteous king, reigned. He cleansed all the filth of the idols that his fathers had made and devoted himself vigorously to the worship of God. This was fitting, because long before it had been foretold of him by the prophet.

Josiah is interpreted as “whose sacrifice is the Lord,” or “the salvation of the Lord,” or “the strength of the Lord.” Concerning this same king it follows that, when he heard the book of the Law, which the priest Hilkiah had found in the house of the Lord, he tore his garments and sent Hilkiah the priest and the others who are subsequently listed to the prophet Huldah, the wife of Shallum, who lived in Jerusalem “in the second quarter.”

What “in the second quarter” signifies is explained in the Book of Chronicles, where it is written concerning the aforementioned King Hezekiah (2 Chronicles 32):

“He built up with great diligence the whole wall that had been destroyed; he raised towers upon it, and constructed another wall outside.”

Zephaniah also mentions this place, saying: “A cry from the Fish Gate and a wailing from the second quarter” (Zephaniah 1). The old edition translated this almost as a proper name, *Masena*. *Masena* means “second.”

When, therefore, the prophetess is said to have lived “in the second quarter,” understand this as the section of the second wall.

Concerning King Josiah it is said:

“He also defiled Topheth, which is in the valley of the son of Hinnom, so that no one might consecrate his son or daughter through fire to Molech.”

This place is frequently mentioned in Scripture, especially in the Book of Kings and by the prophet Jeremiah. The valley of Hinnom, or of the son of Hinnom, lies beside the wall of Jerusalem, toward the east. In it there is a most beautiful grove watered by the springs of Siloam.

Topheth—or *Tophet*, for both forms are written—was a place in the same valley, beside the fuller’s pool, which Scripture mentions, and near the field of Akeldama, still shown today to the south of Mount Zion.

At Topheth—for it was a most pleasant place, which is why it now offers the delights of gardens—people used to sacrifice upon an altar to demons and to consecrate their children through an abominable fire, or to offer them as burnt offerings. Thus it is written in the Book of the Chronicles concerning King Ahaz (2 Chronicles 28):

“He is the one who burned incense in the valley of Ben-Hinnom and passed his sons through the fire.”

*Benennon* indeed signifies *Ennon*; the valley of Ennon is called *Benennon* in Hebrew. From this name, in the New Testament the punishment of hell is called *Gehenna*. For, just as those who served idols in the valley of Hinnom were punished there, so, according to the testimony of the prophets, sinners will be punished there with eternal damnation for the things they have committed.

Finally, when Jeremiah reported that the Lord had commanded him and said (Jeremiah 19): “Go out to the valley of the son of Hinnom, which is beside the entrance of the Potsherd Gate,” he shortly afterward added:

“This place shall no longer be called Topheth or the valley of the son of Hinnom, but the valley of slaughter. And I shall destroy the counsel of Judah and Jerusalem in this place, and I shall overthrow them by the sword.”

Isaiah also most clearly calls Topheth hell. When he described the everlasting destruction of the devil under the name Assyria, saying (Isaiah 30):

“At the voice of the Lord Assyria shall fear, struck by the rod; and the passage of the rod shall be firmly established, which the Lord will cause to rest upon him,”

he immediately added how and where he would perish:

“For Topheth has been prepared from yesterday, prepared by the king, deep and broad.”

He rightly says “broad,” because *Topheth* means “breadth.” “Its fuel,” he says, “is fire and much wood; the breath of the Lord, like a stream of sulphur, sets it ablaze.”

Josiah defiled Topheth either by burning there the bones of the dead, as we read that he did in the case of other places of idolatry, or by scattering other kinds of impurity, so that the place might appear to all who saw it to be suited rather to abomination than to delight.

What follows concerns the same King Josiah.

[scan page 284]

## Commentary on the Books of Kings — Book IV, 537

## Chapter 23

“He also removed the horses that the kings of Judah had given to the sun, at the entrance of the temple of the Lord.” A little later:

“He burned the chariots of the sun with fire.”

This shows that at that time the Jews were enslaved to the superstition of all idolatrous nations. They believed the sun to be a god and therefore had subjected to its image, which they had made, horses and chariots, even in the courts of the temple of the Lord.

For this is how pagans commonly paint or fashion the image of the sun: they place a beardless boy in a chariot and attach horses to him as though they were striving toward heaven in their course. They give it the form of a boy because the sun, as though born anew each day at its rising, never falls into old age.

That they also attributed a chariot and horses to the sun was taken from the miracle of the prophet Elijah, who was carried into heaven by a fiery chariot and fiery horses, as John, bishop of Constantinople, thinks.

Since the sun is called *Ἥλιος* (*Hēlios*) in Greek, Sedulius likewise, when singing of Elijah’s ascent, indicated this when he said:

> How well the shining path of heaven  
> suits Elijah, who gleams in both deed and name.  
> He was worthy of this, because in the speech of Achaia,  
> with one letter changed, his name means “sun.”

When the Greeks heard from the Israelites—of whom it was reported that they possessed divine writings—that Elijah had been transferred to the heavenly regions in a fiery chariot and with fiery horses, or when they saw this very event depicted among other scenes on a wall, they believed, deceived by the similarity of the name *sun*, that this passage through the heavens represented the divinely accomplished miracle. Human folly turned it into an argument for error.

The Jews themselves imitated them, taking pains not to appear less foolish than the gentiles in any respect.

Concerning the same king it is said a little later:

“He also destroyed the high places that were in Jerusalem, on the right side of the Mount of Offense, which Solomon king of Israel had built for the idol Ashtoreth of the Sidonians, for Chemosh, the offense of Moab, and for Milcom, the abomination of the Ammonites; and the king defiled them and crushed the statues.”

It is clearer than daylight what Scripture usually calls “high places”: places situated on wooded hills, where people either sacrificed to demons or, attracted by the pleasantness of the location, offered victims to the Lord contrary to the prohibition, having abandoned the altar that was in the temple.

Therefore, throughout this book, it is often said of kings who were not perfectly righteous, though they were nevertheless righteous, that they did not remove the high places.

The Mount of Offense is called the mountain of idols, since it is customary in Scripture to call idols “offenses,” either because God is offended by them or because they bring offense and ruin upon their worshipers.

This is indicated in the very sentence that follows, where it says:

“Those that Solomon king of Israel had built for Ashtoreth, the idol of the Sidonians, and for Chemosh, the offense of Moab, and for Milcom, the abomination of the Ammonites, the king defiled.”

Here, unless I am mistaken, it is also openly shown—though I wish it had not been shown—that Solomon never fully repented of the crime of idolatry that he had committed. For if he had produced worthy fruits of repentance, he would have taken care above all that the idols he had built be removed from the holy city, rather than leaving them as a scandal to the foolish, as though he wisely and rightly left in place what he himself had made in error despite having been the wisest of men.

Scripture mentioned this place above as well, saying:

“Then Solomon built a shrine for Chemosh, the idol of Moab, on the mountain that is opposite Jerusalem, and for Milcom, the idol of the Ammonites” (1 Kings 11).

It should not seem contradictory that there the mountain on which these idols were made is said to be opposite Jerusalem, while here it is asserted to be in Jerusalem. The city was so extensive that the mountain was regarded as belonging to it, and it seemed to defile even the city itself through the abominations gathered upon it.

[scan page 285]

## Angelo of Lucca, Monk

“And Josiah turned and saw the tombs that were on the mountain; he sent and took the bones from the tombs and burned them upon the altar, and defiled it.”

Why did Josiah order the bones of the dead to be burned upon the altar, unless to show that their sacrifices had been profane? They had not only offered animal victims to demons, but through the error of idolatry had also handed themselves over to the power of demons. By God’s just judgment, they were to be destroyed together with the altar that they had built for idols.

Mystically, this signifies all those who, enslaved to the service of the devil, have ended their temporal life in sacrilege and are consumed by eternal torments, receiving from him according to the merits of their works.

Josiah then returned to Jerusalem “and commanded the people, saying: Keep the Passover to the Lord your God, according to what is written in this Book of the Covenant,” and so forth.

The fact that this king, after removing the idols from the land, as well as the soothsayers, diviners, and every impurity and abomination, celebrated a most solemn Passover to the Lord in the eighteenth year of his reign teaches us spiritually that we must first cleanse the land of our heart from every vice, purify our acts from every defilement of sin and from dead works, and thus serve the living God and celebrate the Passover with grace—not in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Corinthians 5).

According to allegory, this Josiah represents the Lord Savior, who is rightly called the salvation and strength of the Lord, because he is the one of whom Scripture says:

“The Lord is strong; the Lord is mighty in battle” (Psalm 24),

and elsewhere:

“He himself will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1).

He alone cleanses the land of Judah and Jerusalem from every impurity and abomination. Through the prophet he said:

“Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Psalm 69);

and John says of him:

“His winnowing fan is in his hand, and he will cleanse his threshing floor” (Matthew 3).

Malachi also says of him:

“Behold, he comes, says the Lord of hosts; and who can contemplate the day of his coming, and who can stand to see him? For he is like a refiner’s fire and like fullers’ herb. He will sit refining and purifying silver; he will cleanse the sons of Levi. He will refine them like gold and silver, and they will offer sacrifices to the Lord in righteousness. Then the sacrifice of Judah and Jerusalem will please God, as in the days of old and as in former years.

“I shall draw near to you for judgment, and I shall be a swift witness against sorcerers, adulterers, perjurers, those who defraud the laborer of his wages, oppress widows and orphans, and turn away the foreigner, and who do not fear me, says the Lord of hosts” (Malachi 3).

Our Josiah, therefore, celebrates a new Passover in the eighteenth year of his reign, when, after the general resurrection has taken place in the eighth age, he leads his saints, perfected in good works, to receive the denarius of eternal blessedness, after all scandals have first been expelled from his kingdom.

Of this the aforementioned prophet says:

“For behold, the day comes, burning like a furnace, and all the arrogant and all who commit wickedness will be stubble. The coming day will burn them, says the Lord of hosts, leaving them neither root nor branch. But for you who fear my name, the Sun of righteousness will rise, and healing will be in his wings. You will go out and leap like calves from the herd, and you will trample the wicked when they are ashes beneath the soles of your feet” (Malachi 4).

Rightly, therefore, it is said that “a Passover such as this had not been kept from the days of the Judges who judged Israel, nor throughout all the days of the kings of Israel and the kings of Judah, as in the eighteenth year of King Josiah in Jerusalem.” For, when the figures have been removed, on the day of judgment the saints will truly pass from death to life and from corruption to glory.

Thus, in the sight of their Creator, they will rejoice forever in the heavenly Jerusalem, because “the God of gods will be seen in Zion”:

“That city has no need of the sun or the moon to shine upon it, for the glory of God illumines it, and its lamp is the Lamb. The nations will walk by its light, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory and honor into it. Its gates shall not be shut by day, for night shall not be there. They will bring the glory and honor of the nations into it. Nothing unclean shall enter it, nor anyone who practices abomination and falsehood, but only those who are written in the Lamb’s book of life” (Revelation 21).

“And the name of the city from that day shall be: The Lord is there.” “Blessed is the Lord, for he has magnified his mercy in a fortified city” (Psalm 31).

“After King Josiah was killed at Megiddo, the people of the land took Jehoahaz, the son of Josiah, anointed him, and made him king in place of his father. Pharaoh Neco bound him at Riblah and took him to Egypt. He imposed a fine upon the land of one hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold. He made Eliakim, the son of Josiah, king in place of Josiah his father, and changed his name to Jehoiakim.”

What does the killing of Josiah signify—he was killed by Pharaoh Neco at Megiddo—except the persecution of the ancient enemy against holy preachers? Through envy he strives to deliver them to death and remove them from the earth of the Church, so that he may more easily scatter and attack the whole people.

Pharaoh is interpreted as “the one who scatters,” Neco as “striking,” and Megiddo as “temptation.” The devil is permitted to rise against the saints for this one purpose: he exerts all his strength so that, by striking the Lord’s flock through temptation, he may scatter it and first remove those whose support would have helped the others to fight against the enemy.

“The people of the land took Jehoahaz, the son of Josiah, anointed him, and made him king in place of his father.”

Jehoahaz, whose name is interpreted as “one who is seized” or “one who is held,” signifies evil teachers, whom the people of the land—that is, carnal people devoted to earthly desire—according to their customs…
do: “Behold the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1). And the Father himself from the cloud: “This is my beloved Son,” he says, “in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3). Understand John, one of the many friends of the bridegroom, preparing the bride, whose presence enabled the Church of Christ to receive holy kisses, he himself bearing witness concerning Christ: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom. But the friend of the bridegroom rejoices greatly at the bridegroom’s voice” (John 3). John marvels, therefore, when he sees him coming to baptism for the sanctification of the waters, and says: “I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me?” (Matthew 3). But he rejoices with joy when he hears him say: “Let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (ibid.). Here the prayers of the Church, long before promised to God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, are fulfilled: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” But while the holy Church still desires the bridegroom who is to become incarnate and is absent, suddenly she sees him present. For our Redeemer’s grace has this effect: when we speak while seeking him, we enjoy his presence, as is written in the Gospel of two disciples, Cleopas and another. Hence it adds: “For your breasts are better than wine,” and “the fragrance of your ointments surpasses all spices” (Song 1).

Wine was the knowledge of the Law, the knowledge of the prophets. But when the Lord came, because he wished his wisdom to be proclaimed through the flesh, he made it, as it were, become milk in the breasts of the flesh. And what we could in no way comprehend in his divinity, we came to recognize through his incarnation. Therefore his breasts are rightly praised, because through his preaching his condescension accomplished in our hearts what the teaching of the Law could in no way accomplish. The preaching of the incarnation nourished us more than the teaching of the Law.

“And the fragrance of your ointments surpasses all spices.” The Lord’s ointments are his virtues. The Lord’s ointment was the Holy Spirit, of whom it is said to him through the prophet: “God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44 [45]). He was anointed with this oil when he became incarnate. For he did not first come into being as a human being and afterward receive the Holy Spirit; rather, because he was incarnate through the agency of the Holy Spirit, he was anointed with this same oil when he was created as a human being.

The fragrance of his ointments, then, is the savor of the Holy Spirit, who, proceeding from him, remained in him. The fragrance of his ointments is the savor of the virtues that he performed. This Church possessed spices because she possessed many gifts of the Spirit, and in the house of God—that is, in the congregation of the saints—she gave off the fragrance of a good reputation. But “the fragrance of your ointments surpasses all spices,” because the savor of the Bridegroom’s virtues, which came about through his incarnation, surpassed the proclamations of the Law, which had previously been bestowed by the bridegroom as earnest pledges. Those spices of the Law were administered through angels; this ointment was given through the presence of the Bridegroom. The Church believes with that much greater understanding with which she has been deemed worthy to be enlightened by a greater grace of vision.

What we have said generally about the Church, let us now understand specifically of each soul. Let us set before our eyes a soul devoted to the study of gifts, receiving understanding from another’s preaching, yet desiring by divine grace to be enlightened itself, so that one day it may understand by itself. It considers that it understands nothing except through the words of preachers, and says: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” As though it were saying: “Let him himself touch me inwardly, so that I may know understanding—not now by the voices of preachers, but by enjoying the touch of his inner grace.”

The Lord, as it were, kissed Moses with the kiss of his mouth when he offered him understanding through the confidence of familiar grace. Hence it is written: “If there is a prophet among you, I speak with him in a vision, and not as with my servant Moses. For mouth to mouth I speak with him” (Numbers 12). To speak mouth to mouth is, as it were, to kiss, and to touch the mind with inner understanding.

It follows: “Your breasts are better than wine.” The breasts of God are, as we said earlier, his very humble preaching of the incarnation; but the wisdom of the world is, as it were, a kind of wine. It intoxicates the mind because it makes it alien to an understanding of humility. Philosophers are intoxicated, as it were, with such wine when, through worldly wisdom, they go beyond the common way of the people.

The holy Church despises this wisdom and desires the very humble preaching of the Lord’s incarnation. Let that which nourishes her through the weakness of his flesh taste sweeter to her than that by which this world is exalted through the arrogance of false prudence. Let her say: “For your breasts are better than wine,” that is, “The preaching of your very humble incarnation surpasses the world’s exalted wisdom.” Hence it is written: “What is weak in God is stronger than human beings, and what is foolish in God is wiser than human beings” (1 Corinthians 1).

But because the wise men of this age sometimes seem to devote themselves to certain virtues, we see that many possess charity, preserve gentleness, and practice outward propriety in all things. Yet they display these virtues not in order to please God, but in order to please human beings. For this reason they are not virtues, because they do not seek to please God. Nevertheless, they smell sweet to human nostrils when they produce a good reputation in human judgment.

But let these be compared with the true fragrance of our Redeemer; let them be compared with true virtues, and let it be said: “And the fragrance of your ointments surpasses all spices”—that is, “The savor of your virtues surpasses every appearance of the virtues and wisdom of the world,” because it transcends their false images through the truth.

Since we said that, in a second sense, what was said may be understood of each soul, let us, with God’s help, pursue the same meaning more subtly. Every soul that fears God is already under his yoke. Yet it is still far away, because it fears. For each person comes near to God only when he abandons the fear of punishment and receives love for him as grace.

Let us set before our eyes the soul of any elect person, continually inflamed by desire for the love and vision of the Bridegroom. Because it cannot fully perceive in this life what it contemplates, it gazes upon his majesty and is transformed by love for him. The very compunction that arises through eagerness, because it is kindled by desire, is a kind of kiss. For the soul kisses God as often as it is pierced by love for him.

There are many who already fear God and already receive him in good works, but do not yet kiss him because they are not at all pierced by love for him. This was well signified at the banquet of the Pharisee. When he had received the Lord and inwardly disparaged the woman who was kissing his feet, he heard: “I entered your house; you did not give me a kiss. But she, from the moment she entered, has not ceased kissing my feet” (Luke 7).

Everyone who already gives alms and applies himself to good works receives Christ, as it were, at a banquet; he feeds Christ, because he does not cease to support him in his members. But if he is not yet pierced by love, he does not yet kiss his footprints.
