It is well said: “She has not ceased kissing his feet” (ibid.). For it is not enough to be pierced by love of God once and then rest; compunction must also increase and become more frequent. Thus the woman is praised because she did not cease kissing, nor did she cease to be pierced by compunction.

Hence it is also said through the Prophet: “Establish the solemn day amid frequent gatherings, even to the horn of the altar” (Psalm 117 [118]). The solemn day for the Lord is the compunction of our heart. But the solemn day is established amid frequent gatherings when the heart is continually moved to tears through love of the Lord.

Why, if we were to ask how long we must do these things, as long as we are afflicted by tribulations, did he immediately add the endpoint, saying: “Even to the horn of the altar”? The horn of the altar is the exaltation of the inward sacrifice. When we have reached it, there is no longer any need for us to make a solemn day for the Lord out of our lamentation.

Let the soul, then, which already desires to be pierced by love and longs to contemplate the vision of its Bridegroom, say: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” Or certainly, the kiss of his mouth is the very perfection of inner peace. When we have reached it, nothing further will remain for us to seek. Hence it fittingly continues:

“For your breasts are better than wine.” Wine is the knowledge of God that we receive while placed in this life. We embrace the Bridegroom’s breasts when, already in our heavenly homeland, we contemplate his presence by embracing him. Let the soul say: “Your breasts are better than wine.” As though it were saying: “Great indeed is the knowledge that you have bestowed on me concerning yourself in this life; great is the wine of your knowledge with which you intoxicate me. But your breasts are better than wine, because then, through the manifestation and sublimity of contemplation, whatever is now known about you through faith is surpassed.”

“And the fragrance of your ointments surpasses all spices.” The holy Church possesses spices when she abounds in the virtue of knowledge, the virtue of chastity, the virtue of mercy, the virtue of humility, and the virtue of charity. If the life of the saints did not give off the fragrance of spices through virtues, Paul would not say: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place” (2 Corinthians 2).

But far more excellent is that anointing of the contemplation of God to which we shall one day be led; far more excellent is the fragrance of God’s ointments than the spices of our virtues. And although what we have received is already great, what we shall receive from contemplation of our Creator is nevertheless far better.

Therefore let the soul pant and say: “The fragrance of your ointments surpasses all spices”—that is, “Those good things that you prepare through contemplation surpass all the gifts of virtues that you have bestowed in this life.”

Let us say this of the Church; let us say it also of the soul that loves and burns with love for its Bridegroom, and ask from where it has received its desire and from where it has grasped knowledge of his divinity. But behold, it expresses this itself and says:

“Your name is ointment poured out.” The ointment poured out is the divinity made incarnate. If ointment remains in a vessel, it gives off less fragrance outwardly; but if it is poured out, the fragrance of the poured ointment spreads abroad. The name of God, then, is ointment poured out, because from the immensity of his divinity he poured himself outwardly into our nature and made himself visible from being invisible.

If he had not poured himself out, he would in no way have become known to us. The ointment poured itself out when he both preserved himself as Lord and displayed himself as a human being. Concerning this outpouring Paul says: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2). What Paul called “emptied himself,” Solomon called “poured out.”

Since, then, the Lord became known to the human race through the humility of his incarnation, let it be said to him: “Your name is ointment poured out.”

But because the Hebrew text has something differently, we are compelled to turn back to what precedes and insert certain matters differently. When it had said: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth,” it added: “For your breasts are better than wine,” where the immense joy of love is shown to be completed through the touching of the breasts. Immediately afterward, according to the Hebrew, it added: “Fragrant with the best ointments.” Although these words have been more elegantly expounded above by the supreme interpreter, we can nevertheless repeat them here according to the opinions of some.

They say that wine was the word announced and conveyed through the angels who spoke to the prophets or in the prophets, as the prophet Zechariah says: “And he said to the angel who was speaking in me” (chapter 2). This gladdened the heart of the Church when she heard of the coming of the one whom she desired.

But when she touched his body and blood with mouth and hands, she recognized breasts that were better: those flowing with the milk of apostolic and evangelical teaching. In them is all the divine perfection now ministered, surpassing the wine of the Old Testament and of the Law, which, according to the Apostle, brought no one to perfection.

Although the perfect apostolic men, the teachers prescribed for the Christian people, may be understood as the breasts of Christ, and Christ nourishes them as little children, nevertheless it will not be inappropriate to understand specifically the two breasts of Christ as John the Baptist and John the Evangelist, the two Johns. After the kiss of the sacrament mentioned above, they offered the Church words in fullest measure: one showed the Church him alone who takes away the sin of the world, as the Lamb, while the other demonstrated him remaining in the beginning as the Word, God with God the Father.

## [Scan page 289]

Through their immaculate life they clung to his love like breasts to the chest; one showed the true human being to the still small and nursing Church under the name of the immaculate Lamb. The one, by demonstrating the effect of the creation of all things, showed him in the beginning as the Word, God, the maker through whom all things were created.

Until that time, therefore, no such taste of sweetness had reached the Church that, through the gentleness of the Lamb, the terrifying troops of wolves—the demons—might be driven away. His presence strikes terror into all earthly and heavenly powers. He clothes some with the protection of the Holy Spirit and himself has no need of anything from another; through the assumption of flesh he raises the Church from earthly things and leads her into fellowship with the Father. With him she has been made one in mind and matter; he sits at the right hand of the Father, with whom the Word, God, was in the beginning.

The Bridegroom’s breasts mentioned above, flowing with this teaching that bestows eternal life, belong to Christ our Lord. From his milk-white breast the eternal life that Adam lost was poured into the apostles through the brightness of teaching. The Church received it in believers through the breasts, and through the interpretation of the word she daily offers it to her descendants, as though butter made from milk.

For milk first contains the sacrament by its nature, namely, a pure liquid; and when the liquid has been worked by art, it produces butter. So too the milk of apostolic teaching, when it encounters a teacher, reveals that it contains within itself the undivided Trinity. Unless the soul continually uses these foods, it cannot live forever.

The Church received this food from the breasts mentioned above in the sacrament of baptism. There, through the threefold confession of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, she recognizes the fragrance of knowledge, since it is often said to her that the milk of teaching has bestowed the threefold marrow of redemption: namely, the purest liquid of baptism, the sweet juice of Christ’s body, and the richest butter, the oil of sacred chrism, through which the Holy Spirit is poured in.

Concerning this richness, the Church prays in another prophet that the marrow of her soul may be filled, saying: “As with marrow and fatness my soul shall be filled” (Psalm 62 [63]). Its fragrance revives souls wounded by sins. Through the power of this richness, the hidden savor in the breasts mentioned above is praised, which, after the kisses have been received, the following verse teaches us to praise, saying: “Fragrant with the best ointments.”

There was indeed an ointment of good fragrance—that is, of merit—composed under God, the teacher, in the Old Testament; kings, prophets, and priests were anointed with it. But as far as a living human being differs from a painting covered with artificial colors, so far does what the Church receives by being reborn in the Spirit differ from what the Synagogue received bodily. The things associated with the latter were so great that God granted supremacy through it scarcely to one nation, Judea, and to only a few.

But the Church bears within herself an ointment possessing such power, both fragrant and medicinal, that it makes all believers most holy and establishes them as kings and priests, and its fragrance of knowledge fills the whole world from sunrise to sunset. What other fragrance can she be understood to contain within herself except the name of Christ? Hence it follows: “Your name is ointment poured out.”

Just as people shut up among a multitude of rotting corpses are endangered by disease, so it had happened to the inhabitants of this world through Adam, when the devil, speaking through the mouth of the serpent, introduced the plurality of gods, saying: “You shall be like gods” (Genesis 3). But when the name of the one true God was introduced and hidden in the body as in a vessel through the mystery of the incarnation, once the vessel was broken by the blows of nails and the spear, the fragrance of knowledge of him wiped away from the whole world all the stench of the devil’s teaching.

That great name, which among the people of Israel alone had been known through the anointing of chrism, now, as though the vessel of ointment had been poured out, fills the whole house with fragrance. Likewise, from the time of the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, the whole world has demonstrably been filled with knowledge of the one true God through the name of Christ. Among all the nations of the Gentiles, the fragrance of his virtues continually spreads like the scent of ointment: “the dead rise when his name is invoked, the blind see, the lame walk, the mute speak”; demons are driven away, every disease falls, and infirmity is expelled through the power of this invoked name.

Behold by what fragrances the affection and love of Christ raise the souls of the young women, concerning whom it now says: “Therefore the young women have loved you.”

With these matters first set forth, let us return to the higher and most pleasing sense of the teacher. For it follows: “Therefore the young women have loved you.” Whom do we understand here by the young women except the souls of the elect renewed through baptism? The life of the sinner belongs to the old human being; the life of the righteous to the new.

Therefore, because the ointment poured itself outward, it made the young women burn with love for him, displaying renewed souls aflame with desire for him. Childhood is not yet suited to love. A child is one who has not yet begun to devote himself to a burning life. An old person is one who began but has ceased. Therefore neither those who have not yet begun burn in the Lord, nor those who have already begun in faith but have grown cold. Setting aside the childish and senile life, the young women are said to run—that is, those souls who are aflame in the very fervor of love.

Yet we can understand this in another way as well. Youth may be referred to weakness. The youthful ages are the orders of angels, which have been conquered by no weakness and overcome by no infirmity. Let it therefore be said: “Your name is ointment poured out; therefore the young women have loved you”—that is, “Through your incarnation you poured out knowledge of yourself outwardly; for that reason weak souls are able to love human nature.”

Those supreme powers, as though they were youthful ages, love you even where you have not been poured out, because they see you there also, where you remain in the state of your divinity. You, who are seen by those supreme orders as though by youthful ages even without being poured out, are poured out outwardly for human beings so that you may also be loved by the young women—that is, by weak minds.

It follows:

## [Scan page 290]

“Draw me.” Everyone who is drawn is led out either unwillingly or without willing it; he is brought out against his will. But the person who says, “Draw me,” has something that is effective and something that is not effective. Human nature wishes to follow the Lord, but, overcome by the habit of weakness, it cannot follow as it ought. It therefore sees that there is one thing in itself toward which it strives and another thing in itself that it cannot accomplish, and rightly says: “Draw me.”

Paul saw himself as willing but unable when he said: “With my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin” (Romans 7); and: “I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind” (ibid.).

Because, then, there is something that urges us and something else that weighs us down, let us say: “Draw me; we shall run after you in the fragrance of your ointments.” We run in the fragrance of God’s ointments when, breathed upon by his spiritual gifts, we pant for love of his vision.

We must know that, when human beings follow God, they sometimes walk, sometimes run, and sometimes run strongly, as though after God. The person who follows sluggishly walks. The person who follows fervently runs. The person who follows perseveringly runs perfectly.

The human heart was immobile in following God and unwilling to walk after him when the Lord’s coming appeared in the world and moved human minds from their senseless standing still. Hence it is written: “His feet stood, and the earth was moved” (Psalm 76 [77]). To these people, however, not movement but running is attributed, because it is not enough to follow unless we also run with desire.

But because it is not enough to run unless one also runs perfectly, Paul says: “Run so as to obtain” (1 Corinthians 9). Yet some, while running too much, fall into indiscretion. They are wiser than is necessary and set aside the judgments of the one whom they were following.

Hence, when it was said “we shall run,” it was rightly prefaced by “after you.” Those run after God who consider his judgments, prefer his will to their own, and strive to reach him through worthy action with discernment.

For this reason the Prophet, considering and following God’s will, says: “My soul has clung to you” (Psalm 62 [63]). Here Peter is told, when he gives counsel: “Get behind me, Satan. For you do not understand the things of God, but those of human beings” (Matthew 16).

Because perfect souls observe God’s judgments with the greatest caution and presume neither to get ahead through sluggishness nor through indiscriminate fervor, it is rightly said: “We shall run after you in the fragrance of your ointments.” We run after God when we follow him lovingly and, through fear, do not presume to get ahead of the divine judgments.

It follows:

“The king has brought me into his chamber; we shall exult and rejoice in you.”

The Church of God is like a royal house, and this house has a gate, an ascent, a dining hall, and chambers. Everyone who possesses faith within the Church has entered the gate of this house, because, just as a gate opens the rest of a house, so faith is the entrance to the other virtues.

Everyone who possesses hope within the Church has already come to the ascent of the house. Hope raises the heart so that it desires lofty things and abandons the lowly. Everyone who possesses charity in this house walks, as it were, in the dining halls. For charity is broad, extending even to the love of enemies. Everyone who, placed in the Church, already investigates lofty secrets and considers hidden judgments enters the chamber, as it were.

Concerning the gate of this house someone said: “Open to me the gates of righteousness; entering through them I shall confess to the Lord” (Psalm 117 [118]). Concerning the ascent of hope he said: “He has arranged ascents in his heart” (Psalm 83 [84]). Concerning the broad dining halls of this house it is said: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Psalm 118 [119]). In the broad commandment, charity is specifically signified.

Concerning the king’s chamber he said: “My secret is for myself” (Isaiah 24). And elsewhere: “I heard secret words that it is not permitted for a human being to speak” (2 Corinthians 12).

The first entrance of this house, then, is the gate of faith; the second stage is the ascent of hope; the third is the breadth of charity; the fourth is the perfection of charity for the knowledge of God’s secrets.

Because the holy Church, in her perfect members, in her holy teachers, and in those who are already full and rooted in the mysteries of God, reaches lofty secrets and, while still placed in this life, already penetrates them, she says: “The king has brought me into his chamber.”

Through the prophets, apostles, and teachers who, while placed in this life, already penetrated the lofty secrets of that life, the Church had entered the chamber of that king.

We must carefully observe that she does not say “into the chamber of the bridegroom,” but “into the chamber of the king.” By naming the king, she wishes to show reverence for the secrets. For when a chamber is open, the greater the reverence that must be shown toward those things into which one enters. Thus, lest someone, while learning God’s secrets, investigating hidden judgments, and being raised to the heights of contemplation, become elated and fall into pride, he is said to enter the king’s chamber.

The greater the extent to which the soul is led to know his secrets, the greater the reverence that must be shown toward him. Thus everyone who makes progress, who has already been exalted by grace and reached lofty secrets, should attend to himself and humble himself more deeply because of that very progress.

Hence Ezekiel, whenever he is led to contemplate lofty things, is called “son of man.” It is as though he were told: “Pay attention to what you are, and do not become exalted because of the things to which you are raised.”

Yet few in this Church investigate and comprehend the lofty and hidden judgments of God. Nevertheless, when we see strong men able to reach such wisdom that they contemplate God’s secrets in their hearts, we little ones may have confidence that one day we shall come to forgiveness and, one day, to his grace.

Hence it is added from the words of the young women: “We shall exult and rejoice in you.” While the Church, in those who are perfect, enters the king’s chamber, the young women promise themselves the hope of exultation. For when the strong reach the contemplation of lofty things, the weak gain hope of the forgiveness of sins. Therefore she says: “The king has brought me into his chamber; we shall exult and rejoice in you.”

“Let us remember your breasts more than wine. The upright love you.”

This bridegroom has breasts, and because he is also called a king, they are mentioned with reverence. The breasts are fixed close to the chest, and draw nourishment from within for those whom they nourish outwardly. Thus holy men are the Bridegroom’s breasts, because they draw from inward things and nourish outwardly.

His breasts are the apostles and all the preachers of the Church. As we said above, wine was found among the prophets; wine was found in the Law. But because greater commandments were given through the apostles than had been given through the prophets, it says: “Let us remember your breasts more than wine.” Those who are able to fulfill the commandments given in the New Testament undoubtedly surpass the knowledge of the Law.

We can also understand this in another way: “Let us remember your breasts more than wine.” There are many who possess the wine of wisdom but do not possess knowledge of humility. This knowledge puffs up, because charity does not build up.

There are, however, many who possess the wine of knowledge in such a way that they know how to consider the gifts of teaching. The gifts of spiritual grace are like breasts in the chest, which subtly minister through hidden spiritual channels and nourish those who receive them.

Therefore it says: “Let us remember your breasts more than wine.” Those who know how to remember the gifts of your grace, so that they do not attribute to themselves what they understand and do not become exalted because of the wisdom they have received, surpass those who are exalted and carried away by their own wisdom. It is greater to be wise humbly than to be wise arrogantly.

For not to be wise humbly is not truly to be wise. Therefore it says: “Let us remember your breasts more than wine.” Those who know how to consider the gifts of spiritual grace surpass those who possess knowledge but do not keep the remembrance of the gifts in mind.

It is plainly said: “Let us remember your breasts more than wine,” because humility is stronger than knowledge. Wine is knowledge, which intoxicates the memory of the breasts and intoxicates the person whom it raises to knowledge of the gifts. Let the soul say: “Let us remember your breasts more than wine,” because humility conquers the abundance of knowledge.

“The upright love you.” No one, he says, loves you except the upright; and no one is upright except the one who loves you. For everyone who does good works out of fear, even if he is perfect in his action, is not upright in his desire. He would wish there were nothing for him to fear, so that he might not do good works.

But the one who does good works out of love is upright both in action and in desire. Yet the sweetness of love is hidden from those who fear. Hence it is written: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you, and perfected for those who hope in you” (Psalm 30 [31]).

The sweetness of God is unknown to those who fear him; it becomes known to those who love him. Whoever strives to be upright through love has love perfected in him, so that he does not fear the Judge when he comes and does not dread whatever he hears concerning eternal punishments.

Thus Paul, while awaiting the Judge’s coming and seeking the rewards of eternal life, said: “Which God has prepared not only for me but for all who love his appearing” (2 Timothy 4). Eternal rewards are prepared for those who love him, because everyone who knows that he has committed evil deeds fears the coming Judge. But the one who presumes upon his works seeks the Judge’s coming.

Rewards, then, are prepared for those who await God’s coming and love his appearing, because no one loves the Judge’s coming unless he presumes upon his own case. Every certainty of uprightness consists in love; therefore it is rightly said: “The upright love you.”

It follows:

“I am black but beautiful, daughter of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon. Do not look at me because I am dark,” and so forth.

We know that in the beginnings of the Church, when the grace of our Redeemer was preached, some believed from Judea and others did not believe. But those who believed were despised by the unbelievers and suffered persecution, as though they had been judged to have departed into the way of the Gentiles.

Therefore the Church speaks in these same people against those who have not been converted: “I am black but beautiful, daughter of Jerusalem.” Black indeed according to true judgment, but beautiful through the illumination of grace.

How is she black? “Like the tents of Kedar.” Kedar was the second son of Ishmael, and Kedar’s tents belonged to Esau. How, then, is she black? “Like the tents of Kedar,” because in your sight I have been judged to resemble the Gentiles—that is, to resemble sinners.

How, then, is she beautiful? “Like the curtains of Solomon.” It is said that when Solomon built the Temple, he covered all the Temple vessels with curtains. But surely Solomon’s curtains could have been beautiful, since they were suitable for the tabernacle. Since they were in his tabernacle, they could have been nothing but beautiful, in service to the king.

But because Solomon is interpreted as “peaceful,” we understand the true Solomon himself: all souls clinging to God are Solomon’s curtains, mortifying themselves and bringing themselves into the service of the king of peace.

“I am, in your judgment, like the tents of Kedar,” because I am judged to have departed, as it were, into the way of the Gentiles; “but according to the truth I am like the curtains of Solomon,” because I cling to the king in his service.

“Do not look at me because I am dark, for the sun has discolored me.”

The part that had believed in Christ was being regarded as sinful by the part that had not believed. But let this part say: “Do not look at me because I am dark, for the sun has discolored me.”

The sun itself, the Lord himself, coming, discolored me. Through his commandments he showed that I was not beautiful in the commandments of the Law. The sun discolors the one it touches most closely; so too the coming Lord discolored the one whom he touched more closely through his grace, because the more we approach grace, the more we recognize ourselves to be sinners.

Let us look at Paul, coming from the Jews and discolored in the sun. “If, seeking to be justified in Christ, we ourselves were found to be sinners.” Whoever finds himself a sinner in Christ is found discolored in the sun.

But behold, the part that believed from Judea suffered persecution from the unbelieving Jews; it was afflicted by many tribulations and oppressed. Hence it follows:

“The sons of my mother fought against me.”

Because those who remained in the synagogue in unbelief waged the battle of persecution against me—
[scan page 292]

## Commentary

Thus the faithful part from Judea, while undergoing persecution, departed to preach to the Gentiles. Hence it follows:

> “They made me keeper of the vineyards. I did not keep my own vineyard.”

For while those in Judea persecute me, they have made me a keeper in the churches.

> “I did not keep my own vineyard,”

because I abandoned Judea. Hence Paul also says:

> “The word of God was sent to you, but since you judged yourselves unworthy, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13).

It is as though she said: “We wished to keep our own vineyard, but because you yourselves rejected us, you send us to tend other vineyards.”

What we have said about the Synagogue converted to the faith, let us now say about the Church called to the faith from the Gentiles:

> “I am black, but beautiful, O daughters of Jerusalem.”

The Church coming from the Gentiles considers the souls of the faithful whom she finds, and calls them “daughters of Jerusalem.” Jerusalem, of course, means “vision of peace.” She considers what she was; she considers what she has become; and she confesses her former faults, so that she may not become proud. She confesses her present life, so that she may not be ungrateful, and says:

> “I am black, but beautiful.”

Black through merit, beautiful through grace; black through her former life, beautiful through the conduct that follows.

How is she black?

> “Like the tents of Kedar.”

Kedar’s tents were tents of the Gentiles; they were tents of darkness for the Gentiles. It is said:

> “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5).

How is she beautiful?

> “Like Solomon’s skins.”

We have been worn down through penitence and, through penitence, put to death, as a skin is brought into the service of the king. All who afflict themselves through penitence make themselves members of Christ. The members of Christ, therefore, afflicted through penitence, are Solomon’s skins, because they become mortified flesh.

But there were faithful people in Judea who disdained to come to the faith of the Gentiles. Hence they also rebuked Peter because he had received Cornelius. Therefore the Church of the Gentiles adds:

> “Do not consider me that I am dark.”

Do not despise my Gentile character because of my unbelief; do not despise my former sins; do not attend to what I was. Why?

> “Because the sun has discolored me.”

For the sun discolors that person upon whom it presses more closely and intensely. When God exercises strict judgment, when he displays his discernment more fully and discolors, he does so while shining more intensely, because, while he exercises his severity more subtly, he judges more strictly. The sun seems to suspend its rays when it mercifully desires our works; it seems to display its power strictly when it weighs our works strictly.

Let the Church therefore say: “I am dark here, sinful here, because the sun has discolored me; because, when my Creator abandoned me, I fell through sorrow.” But you, afflicted woman, so abandoned—what have you deserved? What have you obtained as a gift?

> “The sons of my mother fought against me.”

The sons of the mother are the apostles. The mother of human beings is the Jerusalem above. They fought against the Church when, in their preaching, they pierced her unbelief as with spears. Hence Paul says, like a combatant:

> “Destroying counsels and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God” (2 Thessalonians 2).

He who destroys a height is certainly a combatant. These combatants, therefore, these sons of the mother Jerusalem, fought the Church away from her error, so that they might establish her in righteousness:

> “The sons of my mother fought against me.”

And what did those who fought do?

> “They made me keeper in the vineyards.”

The vineyards of the Church are the virtues that bear fruit, because, while they fight against the vices in me, they conquer my evils within me. They gave me the fruitfulness and pursuits of virtue; they made me keeper in the vineyards, so that I might bring forth fruit.

After the particular struggle she says:

> “I did not keep my own vineyard.”

The ancient vineyard of the Church is her former custom of error. When she is appointed as keeper over virtues, she abandons the vineyard—that ancient custom of her error.

We have spoken about the Gentile woman converted; let us now speak generally about the whole Church, and specifically about what should be understood concerning each soul.

Bad hearers do not consider their teachers as they are, but as they were. Good teachers, however, both confess what they were and proclaim what they are, so that they neither conceal that they are sinners nor, as ungrateful people, deny their gifts.

Let the Church therefore say to such people:

> “I am black, but beautiful.”

Black through my merit, beautiful through the gift; black because of the past, beautiful because I have been made so in what follows.

How is she black? How beautiful?

> “Black like the tents of Kedar, beautiful like Solomon’s skins.”

It is not right for anyone to be judged from his former life, with attention paid not rather to what he was, but to what he is. Hence she adds:

> “Do not consider me that I am dark, because the sun has discolored me.”

Sometimes in Sacred Scripture the sun signifies an excessive passion for earthly desires. How then is she dark?

> “Because the sun has discolored me.”

The meaning is: “Do not consider that I was black through former unbelief, because Christ is the sun, of whom it is written:

> ‘But for you who fear my name the sun of righteousness shall rise’ (Malachi 4).”

He has discolored me through faith.

> “The sons of my mother fought against me.”

In every creature there are two rational creatures: the human and the angelic. The angel fell and persuaded the human being. The mother of every creature is the goodness and power of God. Therefore we and the angels, since we were created rational, have a kind of fellowship of brotherhood, because the angels were created by the same power by which we were created.

Yet because the fallen angels wage war against us daily, she says:

> “The sons of my mother fought against me.”

Behold: while these rational spirits fight, these spirits—the sons of the mother—make the soul devote itself to earthly matters, occupy itself with worldly affairs, and seek transitory things. Hence she adds:

> “They made me keeper in the vineyards; I did not keep my own vineyard.”

For the vineyards are earthly activities. It is as though she said: “They made me keeper in earthly activities.” And what then?

“I neglected to keep my vineyard,” that is, my soul, my life, my mind, because, while I was externally entangled in the activity of earthly things, I fell away from interior watchfulness. Most people consider themselves by what is beside them, not by what they are.

[scan page 293]

For beside them are dignities; beside them are interior ministries. While they guard what they have beside them, they neglect to guard themselves.

Let her therefore say:

> “They made me keeper in the vineyards; I did not keep my own vineyard,”

that is, while I served external guardianship in secular activities, I lost the concern for interior guardianship.

But behold, the soul has been brought back to the grace of its Creator. Now it loves; now it seeks where it may find its Redeemer. Hence it follows:

> “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at midday.”

At midday the sun is hotter; everyone who burns with faith burns with love. This bridegroom, who below is called a young fawn, feeds in their hearts upon the greenness of virtues. She says:

> “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at midday.”

Why she seeks where he pastures and where he lies down, she explains by giving the reason for her inquiry:

> “Lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.”

God’s companions are his friends and intimates, such as all who live well. But many appear to be companions and are not. Many teachers, while persuading people with perverse doctrine, seemed indeed to be companions but proved to be enemies. When Arius, Sabellius, and Montanus were teachers, they appeared to be companions; but when they were examined strictly, they appeared to be enemies.

Let her therefore say:

> “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at midday, lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.”

It is as though she said: “Tell me in whose hearts you truly rest, lest I begin to wander after the flocks of those who appear to be your companions, that is, who are believed to be your intimates but are not.”

All priests and all teachers are companions in appearance; in life, however, many are not companions but adversaries. Many little ones within the Church, the faithful, desire to live well and wish to maintain a life of righteousness. They observe the life of the priests placed over them, and when those priests do not live well, their followers fall into error.

Hence the Church, as though speaking in those same little ones and faithful people, says:

> “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at midday,”

that is, “Show me the life of those who truly serve you, so that I may know where you pasture in the greenness of virtues; so that I may know where you lie down at midday, that is, where you rest in the fervor of charity. Otherwise, while I look upon the flocks of your companions, I may myself begin to wander, not knowing whose words I should believe or whose instruction I should follow.”

Behold, the bridegroom’s words are returned to the bride:

> “If you do not know yourself, O fairest among women, go out and follow the footsteps of your flocks, and pasture your kids beside the shepherds’ tents.”

Every soul ought to care about nothing so much as knowing itself. For whoever knows himself recognizes that he was made in the image of God. If he was made in the image of God, he ought not to follow the likeness of animals, whether by falling into lust or by yielding to present appetite.

Concerning this ignorance it is said elsewhere:

> “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Psalm 48).

The footsteps of the flocks are the actions of peoples. The more numerous they are, the more confused and perverse they are.

Let it therefore be said to the Church:

> “If you do not know yourself, O fairest among women, go out and follow the footsteps of the flocks, and pasture your kids beside the shepherds’ tents.”

O you who were ugly through ignorance, you have become beautiful through faith among the souls of others. This is clearly said to the Church of the elect.

“If you do not know yourself,” that is, if you do not know that you were made in my image, “go out”—come outside. If you do not recognize what you have become, go out and follow the footsteps of the flocks. Follow not my examples but the examples of peoples.

> “And pasture your kids beside the shepherds’ tents.”

Our kids are the movements of the flesh; the kids are our illicit temptations.

> “Go after the footsteps of the flocks,”

that is, depart after the examples of peoples.

> “And pasture your kids,”

that is, nourish your carnal impulses, not spiritual perceptions but carnal movements.

Go beside the shepherds’ tents either to pasture lambs, that is, in the teachings of the teachers, in the teachings of the apostles, and in the teachings of the prophets; or, if you pasture kids beside the shepherds’ tents, pasture them so that you may be called Christian by faith and not by works—because you appear to be within through faith, and not within through works.

Behold, you have rebuked her; behold, you have reproved her. What have you not said? What have you done kindly in her? Say it plainly. For it follows:

> “I have compared you, my beloved, to my cavalry in Pharaoh’s chariots.”

All who serve lust, pride, avarice, envy, and deceit are still beneath Pharaoh’s chariot, that is, beneath the rule of the devil; they are, as it were, beneath Pharaoh’s chariot.

But everyone who burns with humility, chastity, learning, and charity has already become a horse of our Creator; he has already been placed in God’s chariot; he already has God as his rider. Hence it is said to one over whom the Lord presided:

> “It is hard for you to kick against the goad” (Acts 9).

It is as though he said: “You are my horse; you can no longer hurl your heels against me; I now preside over you.”

Concerning these horses it is said elsewhere:

> “You sent your horses into the sea, troubling many waters” (Habakkuk 3).

God therefore has a chariot, because he presides over holy souls and travels everywhere through holy souls. Hence it is written:

> “The chariot of God is ten thousandfold” (Psalm 67),

and so forth.

Pharaoh also has a chariot, but that chariot was submerged in the Red Sea.

The bridegroom therefore says:

> “I have compared you to my cavalry in Pharaoh’s chariots.”

“While you were still serving demonic works, I compared you to my cavalry, because I considered what I would do in you through predestination, and I compared you to my horses.”

Here God’s hidden judgments must be considered: many appear through preaching, wisdom, chastity, generosity, and patience to be God’s horses, yet by God’s hidden judgment they are compared with Pharaoh’s horses. And many appear through avarice, pride, envy, and lust to be Pharaoh’s horses, yet by God’s hidden judgment they are compared with God’s horses, because he sees the former being turned from good to evil and the latter being brought back from evil to good.

[scan page 294]

For just as, through predestination, many who appear to be God’s horses are Pharaoh’s horses because of the reprobate life that follows them, so through piety many who appear to be Pharaoh’s horses are compared with God’s horses because of the holy life they will preserve at their end.

Hence he caresses her and says:

> “I have compared you, my beloved, to my cavalry in Pharaoh’s chariots,”

that is: “You were still serving vices in Pharaoh’s chariots; you were running beneath vices; but I considered what I would do with you through predestination. I compared you to my cavalry, that is, I regarded you as like my elect.”

At last, magnificent Caesar, you perceive how, in the preface, we stated that nothing historical is found in this volume, but that everything is fragrant with allegorical allusions, ablaze with the courses of dramatic action, and rich with the sweetness of moral meanings.

Therefore I desire—indeed, though perhaps rashly, I venture to suggest—to your exalted eminence that, since you have acquired great wisdom and prudence and have obtained the defense and protection of the holy Church, you should persist not only as one stationed in the battle line, surrounded by the ranks of nobles and pressed by troops of soldiers, protecting her from the incursions of foreign enemies through the support of arms, but also as a devoted and diligent student of sacred doctrine and of the understanding of the divine Scriptures.

Thus, armed with the Gospels, girded with the swords of the divine Scriptures, and adorned with the darts of their meanings, you may defend that same holy Church against the servants of the inner evil spirits, who always seek to destroy not bodies but the souls of the faithful.

Hence Peter exhorts us, saying:

> “Be watchful, because your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour; resist him, strong in faith” (1 Peter 5).

And so that your nobility may wisely be able to avoid the snares of the ancient enemy and preach to others, you should earnestly devote yourself, after arranging the affairs of the empire, to studying the expositions of this volume and of other books. Thus you may deservedly rejoice and say what is read here:

> “The king brought me into the wine cellar; he ordered charity within me.”

And also:

> “Tell me where you pasture, where you lie down at midday, lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.”

May the bridegroom himself—the Lord, of course, who below is called the young fawn—deign, through your vigilance and understanding and through that of others, to pasture in you, as it were, by the greenness of virtues, and to lie down in the fervor of charity, through the guardianship of the sacred Scriptures.

It follows:

> “Beautiful are your cheeks, like those of a turtledove.”

After the holy kisses have been received; after all the joy previously recounted; after the battle with the aforementioned sons of the mother; after self-knowledge; after concern with how and by whom she was created; after the virtue compared with the Lord’s cavalry—the voice of Christ speaks to the Church.

Now we are taught to recognize the beginnings of beauty before the other members in her cheeks. These are compared with the great turtledove, so that through its enigmas he might show that she is to remain amid the tumultuous disturbances of this age.

This beauty of the cheeks, adorned with the blush of chastity and the whiteness of modesty and situated on the face of the body, is nothing strange if the persons who adorn the face of the Church are compared with them. Thus the ancient Fathers are in the cheeks of the Church: they stand first in the very face of her honor and blush with the beauty of martyrdom.

The Church is compared with a turtledove because of the variety of her different goods, or because of the chastity of her virtues. This bird, alone among birds, withdrawn from the crowds of human beings, loves to inhabit secluded places. There it builds its nest and raises its young, where its enemy either never or scarcely has access.

So indeed the holy Fathers, and so the holy and faithful soul, which is called a beloved by the Word of God, by fleeing and rejecting the companionship of the wicked, send to heaven the heavenly offspring which they produce in this way: begotten by the word of their teaching and nourished by the example of their life.

For, as we briefly mentioned in the preface, those who have described the natures of birds report that the turtledove is of such great chastity that it knows no mate except one spouse. If the other should die by chance, the survivor never joins itself to another, but throughout its life seeks its lost mate in longing.

Because of this beauty of chastity and modesty, the Church is fittingly compared in her cheeks. For he says:

> “Beautiful are your cheeks like those of a turtledove.”

It is as though Christ said: “I have adorned you with such a variety of virtues that the chastity of the faith you promised me would not be corrupted by the seduction of wicked teachers.”

These things have been said according to the historical order. But according to the opinion of some, a more exalted meaning is said to lie hidden in this comparison. For some think that the cheeks of the Church are compared with the beauty of that turtledove of which it is said in the Psalm:

> “Indeed, the sparrow has found a house for itself, and the turtledove a nest for itself, where it may place its young” (Psalm 83).

No wise person will fail to recognize that the figure of the Holy Spirit is named in the sparrow, and that of the immaculate flesh assumed in the turtledove.

The Church is then praised as beautiful by both the good and the wicked in her cheeks, which are visible to all, when she has drawn even a little of the assumed humanity of Christ into her likeness through the supreme good of chastity.

Then the whole body of the Church is seen as most beautiful, when the impious admire the modest appearance of her cheeks through the glory of purity. For chastity is then proved to possess great virtue before her enemies, when those who attack it cannot conquer it.

Just as the members that are on the head, if they are beautiful, excuse the ugliness of the other members hidden by clothing, so those who are known to be members of the head of the Church through priestly honor adorn by their chastity the ugliness of the people’s negligence.

Conversely, nothing in the body of the Church is so deformed or so abject as when a most shameful life or reputation is seen in those aforementioned members. And because the holy Church, in her prelates and teachers, imitates the turtledove—that is, the image of Christ—in chastity and in the variety of virtues, she is necessarily praised by him, who says:

> “How beautiful are your cheeks like those of a turtledove.”

[scan page 295]

It follows:

> “Your neck is like necklaces. We shall make you golden pendants, studded with silver.”

Those who instruct others toward salvation through the word of edification seem to be praised in the neck: those who transmit spiritual food by their discourse to the members of Christ, whose only support is faith, wherever they interpret it; those who are displayed in the neck of the Church through golden doctrine and the jewel of a life exemplary.

A necklace is recognized by its adornment of gems. But, for their appearance to be more beautiful, such ornaments require the material of gold, by which the gems are joined and held in their proper place.

Our nature too—formed in the likeness of a gem, as though cut from a stony heart—requires the radiant assistance of the Holy Spirit. Through him the words of the New and Old Testament, which the divine Scriptures proclaimed or displayed when they announced that the Savior of the world had come, become as it were a single chain of truth. Passing through gemlike minds and joined by harmony of faith and unanimity of understanding, they adorn the neck of the Church.

And because the holy teachers, who are designated by the neck, administer the word of preaching adorned with other virtues, and perform in works what they teach in words, their works are expressed by the necklaces. The Scripture of both Testaments is designated by the golden pendants, because inwardly it shines with the gold of spiritual meanings, while outwardly it gleams with the silver of heavenly eloquence.

The Church is rightly praised in them when it is said:

> “Your neck is like necklaces. We shall make you golden pendants, studded with silver,”

because the holy teachers cannot possess the gifts mentioned above unless they receive them from him in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

It follows:

> “While the king was at his banquet, my nard gave its fragrance.”

Nard is an aromatic shrub, they say, with a strong and thick but short root, black, fragile, and, although rich, fragrant like cypress; it has a harsh taste and a small, dense leaf. Its tops spread into spikes, and therefore perfumers celebrate the spikes and leaves of nard for their double excellence.

This is what Mark says:

> “An ointment of precious spikenard” (Mark 14).

You see that the ointment Mary brought to the Lord was made not only from the root of nard but also, to make it more precious, from the addition of its spikes and leaves; thus the grace of its fragrance and power was increased.

Physiologists also report that nard is a principal ingredient of ointment, and therefore the anointing offered to the Lord’s head and feet was fittingly made from it. There are indeed many kinds of it, but all are herbs except the Indian variety, which is more precious.

Mystically, this devotion of Mary serving the Lord signifies the faith and piety of the holy Church, which speaks here in the Song of Love, saying:

> “While the king was at his banquet, my nard gave its fragrance.”

Mary fulfilled these words once, literally, with her hands; and the Church does not cease to fulfill them spiritually every day in all her members. Spread throughout the whole world, she glories and says:

> “But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph everywhere, because we are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (2 Corinthians 2).

When the Church confesses, praises, and proclaims with worthy reverence the power of his divine virtue, which he possesses together with the Father, she certainly pours precious ointment upon his head.

But when she receives with equally worthy reverence the mysteries of the humanity he assumed, she pours faithful and true nard ointment upon the Lord’s feet. She does this because she commends by preaching and venerates with devout service that nature of his by which he touched the earth—that is, by which he deigned to live among human beings.

Hence Christ’s reclining is understood as his burial, although at that time he had reclined in the house of Simon the leper. The nard also signifies those women who came to the tomb at first light with spices, so that they might anoint Christ and proclaim the fame of his resurrection to believers. Therefore it was said to them:

> “Go, tell my brothers that he is going before you into Galilee; there you will see him” (Matthew 28).

Alternatively, the king’s banquet is the blessedness of heavenly secrecy. He says:

> “While the king was at his banquet, my nard gave its fragrance,”

because, while Christ the king rests in the blessedness of heavenly secrecy, nard gives its fragrance—that is, the virtues of the saints in the Church minister to us a great grace of sweetness.

Or the king’s banquet may be understood as the holy Church of the elect. In it Christ finds rest for himself, as he himself says through the Prophet:

> “This is my rest forever and ever” (Psalm 131).

The Church is called nard because of the fragrance of her virtues. Hence the Apostle says:

> “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God everywhere” (2 Corinthians 2).

When the devil sees this Church enriched and adorned with innumerable necklaces of spiritual gifts, despising all the sweet allurements of the present life and hastening toward the one sweetness of eternal rest, he continually inflicts innumerable attacks of bitterness, both through himself and through his agents.

But because God the Redeemer is always in her midst, she is not moved from the path of truth, nor is she disturbed by the attacks of the impious rushing upon her, because Christ is everything and in everything. For if bitter things are endured for the love of Christ, they are sweetened by the dew of future hope and everlasting joy.

Therefore it follows:

> “My beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me; he will dwell between my breasts.”

The holy Church, or the faithful soul, perseveres in the praise of her Creator, whom she understands to have suffered in the bitterness of his passion. Therefore, always keeping in the memory of her heart how close he is to her breasts and how he suffered for her for the glory of her redemption, she says:

> “My beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me; he will dwell between my breasts.”

It is as though she said: “The death of my beloved, which he endured for my salvation, will always dwell in my memory, for imitation and for the glory of praise.”

And because she rejoices that he suffered and glories that he rose again from the dead, she rightly adds:

[scan page 296]

> “My beloved is a cluster of cyprus to me, in the vineyards of Engaddi.”

She rightly says:

> “My beloved is a cluster of cyprus to me,”

as though she openly exclaimed: “He who was a bundle of myrrh in the bitterness and sadness of the passion is himself the cluster of cyprus in the sweetness of the resurrection.”

Myrrh signifies sadness; wine signifies joy. Christ, born according to the flesh from the Jews and suspended by them on the wood of the cross like a cluster, showed the joy of the resurrection to his disciples on the third day after the press of death.

And he appropriately says, “in the vineyards of Engaddi,” because of the gifts of spiritual graces that he bestowed after the resurrection on those who participated in baptism.

For Engaddi is called “the fountain of the kid,” or “the eye of the kid,” signifying baptism, where kids become lambs. The interpretation “eye of the kid” also points to Christ himself, who is the light of all sinners who come to him.

For the sake of brevity these things have been said briefly, so that they may more quickly impress themselves upon the reader’s mind. But because the holy Church desires to imitate the mystery of Christ’s passion in her members, so that she may reach the glory of the resurrection with Christ and deserve to be separated not with the kids on the left but with the sheep on the right, let us speak more fully.

After saying:

> “My beloved is a bundle of myrrh,”

she added “to me.” She understood that he suffered for her salvation and rose from the dead for her glory. For she says:

> “My beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me; he will dwell between my breasts.”

Myrrh is interpreted as bitter; it signifies within itself the salutary discipline that the Church received in Christ. By enduring, for his name, various bitter torments in her different members, she becomes a bundle of myrrh—and Christ becomes so in her.

The myrrh tree, from which a sap useful for many bodily illnesses is produced, is said by those who have described the natures of trees to resemble the willow, and to put forth branches with very fine, twisted twigs in the form of bundles.

When the Church, or any holy soul, has received at the bridegroom’s coming the sweetness of the taste of eternal life, she no longer feels the many kinds of bitter sufferings inflicted upon her: prisons, exiles, confiscation of present possessions, hunger, thirst, chains, unjust executions, insults, dangers, shipwrecks, showers of stones, being hurled into the depths, the stings of various punishments, and many other things.

When she has endured these things for the death of her Redeemer, she says with great joy:

> “My beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me.”

When she has patiently endured many corrections inflicted by God in order to heal many illnesses, or has joyfully endured the various sufferings inflicted for his name, as was said above, Christ becomes her bundle of myrrh, driving all the diseases of the vices from her breast.

Then, cleansed and prepared with prayers, she becomes a divine lodging, so that with great confidence she may invite Christ to enter her heart, as though she were saying within her breasts, as in the Gospel:

> “I and the Father will come, and we will make our dwelling with him” (John 14).

She also invites him to dwell in the breasts of the Church, unquestionably among those men who, according to their age or ability, nourish spiritual little ones with the milk of their teaching. Concerning them the Lord himself says:

> “If two or three agree on earth, whatever they ask in my name will be done for them.”

And:

> “Where two or three have gathered in my name, there I am in their midst” (Matthew 18).

One of them said to his hearers from his own breasts:

> “I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Corinthians 3).

If anyone wishes, the two breasts of the Church may also be understood as Moses and Elijah. In their midst Jesus was transfigured on the mountain; the beloved of the Church is shown to have dwelt in the future glory of that same Church. One of them displayed the promise, while the other proclaimed that he had already come, signifying the two Testaments.

Hence it is said:

> “You will be known in the midst of two living creatures.”

These two Testaments are the breasts of the Church; Christ dwells in their midst.

And because the lawgiver Moses and Elijah, the chief of the prophets, spoke about the departure of his passion, it follows:

> “My beloved is a cluster of cyprus to me, in the vineyards of Engaddi.”

It is said that the island of Cyprus, among all lands, produces clusters of grapes of extraordinary size. Such was the size of the cluster that two young men are read to have carried from the Promised Land into the desert. It signified in every way the figure of the assumed humanity of Christ our Redeemer, which, according to place, time, or circumstance, became the food and drink of the Church through the sacrament of his body and blood.

Cyprus is interpreted as “fruitfulness” or “sorrow.” Engaddi, as has been said, is the fountain of the kid.

The cluster of Cyprus is therefore the beloved of his Church when he sows sadness, or the sorrow of penitence, in the minds of sinners, so that he may raise them to that blessedness of which he himself said in the Gospel:

> “Blessed are those who mourn now, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew 5).

Like the cluster mentioned above, he was raised to the gallows of the cross by two peoples: namely, the persecuting Jews and the ruling Roman soldier. To this day he has begotten, in those who after innumerable heaps of crimes are gathered into the bosom of the Church, sadness and grief that confer eternal life, as was said above.

The aforementioned cluster supplies spiritual food and drink daily to those who believe in it, but only to those who are gathered in the vineyards of Engaddi, that is, at the fountain of the kid. This is the font of sacred baptism, where the kids descend—those who were destined to be placed on the left before the tribunal of the Judge and handed over to eternal fire—and where the immaculate lambs ascend, those who will be gathered on the Judge’s right and given the eternal kingdom.

It is therefore certain that, just as the one nation of the Jews is called the Lord’s vineyard through its knowledge of the divine law, so the various nations brought to the faith of Christ through the cultivation of the apostles and the teaching of teachers are called many vineyards, in the midst of which, as has been said, ...

## [Scan page 297]

### ANGELOMI

The fountain of holy baptism is water, to which the goats come so that they may become lambs. These vineyards of Engaddi do not produce wine but balsam. Engaddi is a very large village in the land of Judea, beside the Dead Sea. That land represents the land of the living, where there are vineyards of balsam. Within its boundaries there were once only twenty *jugera*. After the Romans acquired that region, the plant was propagated even across the broadest hills. Its stem resembles that of a vine, its leaves those of rue, but they are whiter and evergreen.

The tree is called balsam; its wood, *chirobalsamum*, that is, its little branch; its fruit or seed, *carpobalsamum*; and its sap, *opobalsamum*. It is given this name with the prefix because, when the bark of the wood has been struck with iron claws, it distils a drop of fragrant sap through the fissures. For “fissure” is called *opē* in Greek. Its drops are adulterated by mixing in Cyprian oil or honey. But if the balsams are pure, they possess such power that, when the sun has grown hot, they cannot be held in the hand.

Many kings transplanted shoots of the balsam tree from these vineyards into other places and lands; the Romans are also said to have done this, but the plants were unable either to take root fully or to survive. Hence, as we indicated above, great care was taken in that same place or within those same boundaries by kings who planted vineyards producing balsam. It is worthwhile to understand why vineyards flourish on no other soil except that of Engaddi.

I think, as one of the learned has said, that the sap of these vineyards represents the confession of one faith, in which the hope of the faithful is established, and in which each medicinally fragrant odor of Christ is shown to germinate, restoring life to dead souls. Whatever nation or soul is torn away and transplanted from this confession by wicked cultivators or heretics withers. This is proved to have happened to many souls: after they had torn themselves away from the one true confession of faith mentioned above, they dried up and offered themselves as food for Gehenna.

For just as a body cannot subsist without food and drink, so the voice of the Church declares that, without the cluster which is Christ—eternal life descending from heaven—one cannot live. He is found by those who hunger and thirst for righteousness in no other promised land and in no other vineyard except the vineyards of Engaddi; that is, he is found in no gathering of heretics, in no philosophical sect, and in no flattery of schismatics. If someone, deceived by the reputation of his own perversity, is transplanted there, he perishes, dried up.

Understanding this, the Church says:

> “My cluster of henna (*cyprus*) is my beloved to me, in the vineyards of Engaddi.”

It follows:

> “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved; behold, you are beautiful:  
> your eyes are like those of doves.”

After praising the beauty of the cheeks and neck in the person of the bride, he now praises the beauty of her eyes, in the simplicity of her teachers, and with a repeated commendation of what is hidden. The beauty and radiance of the whole body are compared with the eyes of doves. They are compared with that creature which is found superior to all winged animals in gentleness, fertility, keenness of sight, and speed of wing.

The eyes are therefore proved to be the guides of the whole body. Without them the body either cannot move forward or proceeds with difficulty, stumbling. By them the holy teachers are understood: with spiritual sight they contemplate heavenly things, and because of their simplicity and innocence they are compared with the dove.

Priests may also rightly be understood here, to whom the holy mysteries have been entrusted, in whose faith the Church is adorned, and in whose spotless life she is exalted by frequent praises. She is beautiful when she offers God the purest knowledge; she is beautiful when she displays an irreproachable manner of life to enemies and to those alienated from the faith of Christ.

A third praise of beauty is also introduced in connection with the keenness of the eyes. For, in addition to what we have said, the nature of doves is known to possess this particular quality: they watch from afar for the approach of an enemy behind them, and before them they keep watch in the water. That is, when a hawk approaches, they observe it so that it cannot seize their young.

In the same way, the holy teachers, endowed with simplicity and innocence, and the priests of the Church, by the keenness of their contemplation, contemplate heavenly things. They sit meditating over the streams of Scripture, and strive, by the admonition of their words, to warn their hearers to beware of the snares of the devil, who hastens to seize the souls of believers. For this reason the beauty of the Church is praised in such persons by the bridegroom.

Thus he repeats “beautiful” twice, because he saw her to be praiseworthy in them both in preaching and in action.

It follows:

> “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and comely;  
> our couch is flowering.”

The voice of the Church speaks to Christ, as though saying: “You alone are beautiful; I am beautiful through you.” Because she understands that she was not justified by her own merits and that she received from him the beauty of the virtues, she is inflamed with love for him and praises his beauty.

No one can praise the beauty of someone whom he does not greatly love, nor can anyone love a person whose character does not agree with his own, as the Apostle teaches when he says:

> “No one speaking in the Spirit of God says, ‘Anathema to Jesus’; and no one says, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit”  
> *(1 Corinthians 12).*

Therefore the beauty and appearance of the beloved Son of God can both be seen and exalted in praise by the person who has retained his spirit in his own mind through holy works.

For this reason, in the present passage, the Church, full of the spirit of truth—as the bridegroom himself previously showed when he said, “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved”—recognizes him who descended from heaven upon the assumed human being in the likeness of a dove in the Jordan. Recognizing the beauty of his sinless body and the comeliness of his true soul, without falsehood or deceit, she offers a reciprocal and repeated praise, saying:

> “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and comely;  
> our couch is flowering.”  
> *(Song of Songs 1:15–16; the printed “Ephesians 5” refers to Paul’s one-flesh interpretation in the sentence that follows.)*

Although a beautiful face or costly garment reveals a precious bridegroom standing at a distance, it does not know the beauty of the remaining limbs until the union of the couch has taken place. But when the lawful union has been celebrated and the two have become one flesh, according to the sentence of the first human being—and the teacher Paul asserted that this sacrament is fulfilled in Christ and in the Church—so also the aforesaid beloved, until the day of burial, loved him by desiring his coming and praised him when she saw and kissed him. Yet all his love and every aspect of his beauty are shown to have reached their fulfillment, from the time of the resurrection until the appointed end, in the shedding of blood for his name.

## [Scan page 298]

### ENARR. IN

The flowering couch, that is, the couch strewn with flowers, in which the Church recognized his beauty and comeliness in all his members, is understood through an enigma as the Lord’s tomb. There, it is proved, the Word of the Father rested in the body he had assumed.

The couch is rightly called flowering because spices or aloes—compounded by the art of the perfumer from the juices or flowers of many kinds of herbs—were brought in with Christ’s body, and with them the tomb was sprinkled when he rose.

Through the teaching associated with this, the Church—that is, the multitude of the faithful—found freedom: life in death, silence in burial, and rest amid harsh labors, the labors she had daily completed under the lashes of demons. There the true human being is recognized as having lived under the sign of the impious through the assumption of the body, and the true God is shown to have risen and departed from the designated tomb.

There, under the name of the couch, the union of the Son of God and the Church was celebrated. With him the Church deserved to find the delightful sleep of the Passion and the joy of eternal wakefulness, while the Apostle cries out to his members:

> “If you have died with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is at the right hand of God the Father”  
> *(Colossians 3).*

In view of his resurrection, both human minds are daily prepared as dwellings for the Holy Spirit and the roofs of believing congregations are prepared; moreover, visibly, countless houses of God and of the Church are enlarged without ceasing at all times. What materials they are constructed from, by what kinds of materials, how durable or beautiful they are—this he taught by saying:

> “The beams of our houses are cedars;  
> our panelled ceilings are cypress.”

It should be known, however, that some teachers understand the flowering couch as the peace of the holy Church, in which she rests in Christ, secure from the tumult of vices and the domination of evil spirits; she flourishes with holy virtues and increases through spiritual fruit.

But let us continue, as we began, to expound the former meaning. We understand the Lord’s tomb as the couch, where his flesh rested through the sleep of death as though on a couch, and which truly flowered through the glory of the resurrection. For the divine word says:

> “The beams of our houses are cedars;  
> our panelled ceilings are cypress.”

The beams and panelled ceilings are perhaps teachers and hearers, or the hearts of the learned, because of their protection and beauty. He calls them cedar and cypress because of their outstanding virtues, the fragrance of a good life, and incorruptibility; in them Christ rests as beneath a roof.

To make this clearer, let us give an example. Cedars are said always to continue growing and never to be allowed to grow old, according to the Psalmist:

> “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree,  
> and shall multiply like a cedar of Lebanon”  
> *(Psalm 91).*

According to the opinions of physicians, the sap of these trees possesses such power that it heals various bodily members, kills the worms of ulcers, and protects bodies rubbed with it from the bites of flies. With the wood of this tree, together with living water and a bundle of hyssop tied with scarlet in an earthen vessel, the cleansing of sins by sprinkling was celebrated in the Old Testament.

Now this is taught to be celebrated in truth through the priest, through baptism, and through the blood of Christ. The blood, embracing the multitudes of one faith as though in a bundle, protects them from the attacks of the devil and celebrates the remission of sins both eternal and temporal.

The houses of the Son of God and of the Church—the meeting places of the Christian people where the redemption of souls mentioned above is celebrated—are known to exist throughout the whole world. These houses are shown to be built from teachers, or rather by teachers, furnished with the tools of their doctrine; and in their minds the Lord deigns to dwell.

The cedar beams themselves are understood as the imperishable timbers of the preachers’ houses. They do not decay in their strength of holiness through the suggestions of foolish and wicked thoughts; always forgetting what has passed and reaching toward the things that lie ahead through good works, they grow daily like cedars—that is, they multiply through the fruits of the saints for the assistance and profit of holy souls.

The sap of their speech or consolation protects souls from the stings of demons, heals the wounds once inflicted by the habits of filthy deeds, and kills the worms of most wicked thoughts.

For the delight of those who dwell in them, cypress panelled ceilings properly hang from the faithful houses. Cypress wood, when shaped by the hand of the craftsman, gives a beautiful appearance and produces a most pleasant fragrance; it is also proved to contain medicinal power against many bodily ailments.

These panelled ceilings are understood to express the chastity, purity, obedience, humility, charity, and mercy that form the hearers, and the honor they show to the priests they revere. The hearers depend continually upon the teachers’ word and, like a vaulted ceiling, console the teachers for their just labors in the present time. Thus the panelled ceilings, fastened to the beams, adorn the houses and cover their nakedness.

The glory of the teachers is the people, and likewise the glory of the people is the firm stability of the teachers. When the teachers impart spiritual gifts to the people and the people offer them bodily gifts, glorious houses are prepared for Christ. The Lord himself bestows upon those houses flowers of heavenly wisdom and lilies of integrity, produced through their repentance, to their great joy and honor.

Hence it follows.

## CHAPTER II

> “I am the flower of the field  
> and the lily of the valleys.”

As though it were plainly said: “I am the adornment of the world and the glory of the humble.”

The underworld may also be understood here as an additional meaning: the place to which Christ deigned to descend in order to free the patriarchs, as some understand it. But, having mentioned this in advance so that we would not be accused of being ignorant of someone’s interpretation, let us set forth more fully the words of blessed Ambrose.

“Before his incarnation,” he says, “the Savior spoke to the patriarchs and prophets in the person of an angel. He alone had no equal among the angels, thrones, or—

## [Scan page 299]

“—dominions; among them all he was admirable, singular and alone, shining throughout the whole field of heaven. Through the prophets and the power of signs he imparted knowledge that had to be understood: through the waters of the flood, for example, or through the fire that struck the Sodomites, so that the foolish might understand wisdom and fools might at last learn not to exalt themselves in pride. Above the other orders he remained the judge who exacted just vengeance.

“But when, through the mystery of the incarnation, he descended into this valley of tears, he showed himself to be a lily among thorns. In this valley, what else is meant except the most filthy religion of idolatry, envy, rage, murder, and the ruin of souls, or the disgrace of divination and magic arts, which flourished among the thorns? In their midst the teaching of the Gospel and the example of Christ’s purity daily free the multitude of believers.”

Thus, before the mystery of the incarnation, the Son of God spoke to the fathers “in many and various ways,” according to the Apostle:

> “In many parts and in many ways God spoke formerly to the fathers through the prophets”  
> *(Hebrews 1).*

After the aforesaid mystery he brought many good things, in different ways and by different means, to human nature in this valley of the world: the abolition of sin, the wiping away of falsehood, the tempering of the fires of our birth, from which the love that preserves virginity arises.

Whoever of either sex keeps away from such things is kindled by the examples of the glorious humanity he assumed and of the blessed Virgin Mary.

This mystery was accomplished to liberate his people: the different members of his body were to heal our different ailments, and his teaching was to heal wounds inflicted by demons’ fiery darts of fornication. The sharp points of wickedness that had wounded the beloved in the prophets and teachers were to be changed into the delight of lilies produced from the feet of the four evangelists. Reborn from them, the Church shines again even while she is pierced by the bitterest goads, as she says in what follows:

> “As a lily among thorns,  
> so is my beloved among the daughters.”

The daughters among whom the Church exists as a lily among thorns are not specified. Yet, from the fact that they are compared with thorns, we can infer that they are begotten not by God but by the devil through an exceedingly wicked teaching.

Amid so many poisonous thorns the Church lives: that is, amid the world of the Gentiles or of heretics, who attack her. She is permitted to be attacked so that she may not grow torpid in idleness, but may arm herself and contend against her enemies, so that her strength may appear after the battle.

The Lord says concerning these matters:

> “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees”  
> *(Matthew 16),*

which means the teaching of heretics. The Apostle says:

> “What fellowship has light with darkness?  
> What agreement does Christ have with Belial?  
> What communion has the temple of God with idols?”  
> *(2 Corinthians 6).*

And Isaiah says in nearly the same way:

> “Come out from their midst, and those who carry the vessels of the Lord must be cleansed”  
> *(Isaiah 52).*

When he says, “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters,” he does not condemn the righteous, who are members of the Church, but praises them. He teaches how exceedingly praiseworthy it is to live devoutly among the impious, to endure patiently the sharpness and stings of their malice, and not to be drawn into the thorny conduct of the perverse. Among them the righteous person shines in darkness like a light and continually admonishes them by teaching.

It is as though he said to the Church: “You seek rest, but remember the praise of the couch: the thorns of tribulation will make you whiter, and you will gain greater fruits of preaching than of repose.” Thus, just as a lily among thorns retains its own fragrance and whiteness, so the chosen Church among wicked Christians and heretics, if it does not yield to them, burns with virtues.

The nature of the lily contains three things delightful and pleasing to the eyes: whiteness, fragrance, and medicine when it is burned. These three are compared in a wonderful likeness with different persons and things, according to time, place, or cause. Christ is called the mountain of God, according to David the prophet (Psalm 67), because the fullness of divinity was to dwell in him. He is the young bullock putting forth horns through the two Testaments and hooves through the eight beatitudes; through the immaculate assumption of his body he is the flower of the field and lily of the valleys. As the Lamb taking away the sin of the world, he possesses the perfection of meekness; by imparting the Holy Spirit he clothes others yet always remains abundant.

The beloved is also “a bundle of myrrh” and “a cluster of henna (*cyprus*) in the vineyards of Engaddi.” The Church likewise calls him an apple tree or pomegranate tree because he is the tree of life, offering himself to different persons with different flavors. Without doubt this apple or pomegranate tree shelters and defends beneath the shade of his protection souls afflicted by hunger and bound beneath the burning sun of justice; by the fruit of the lips—that is, by teaching—he refreshes those who hunger and thirst with his sweetness.
