From the expulsion from paradise until the birth of the Virgin, the human race suffered many labors and intolerable attacks from demons. Here it is called the beloved in the person of the Church, until the coming of the one who said:

> “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened,  
> and I will give you rest”  
> *(Matthew 11).*

Believing in the one God, she says that she rests beneath the shade of his protection:

> “I sat beneath the shade of him whom I desired.”

Although the sweetness of the kingdom of heaven may be understood as the present protection and may also designate the rest of the blessed, she rejoices while tasting his body and blood, which confer eternal life, and says:

> “And his fruit is sweet to my taste.”

This may also be understood as the sweetness of the divine Scriptures, spoken by the holy preachers, who are called the throat of the Lord. Concerning this sweetness the Prophet says:

> “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet.”

## [Scan page 300]

### ANGELOMI LUXOVIENSIS MONACHI

> “Blessed is the man who trusts in him”  
> *(continuation of Psalm 33).*

And again:

> “How sweet are your words to my palate,  
> more than honey to my mouth”  
> *(Psalm 118).*

At his coming the multitude of believers, languishing as though in the wound of despairing weakness, was revived by the fruit of this tree, the juice of the pomegranate. This fruit is shown to be poured daily into the throat of the Church through those who act in Christ’s place. Thus she is led through each stage of progress into the hidden understanding of the divine law, so that she may recognize everything done in the Old Testament.

For he says:

> “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest,  
> so is my beloved among the sons.”

As though he were saying: “Just as the apple tree, through its appearance, fragrance, and fruit, surpasses all the wild trees, so Christ surpasses all the saints who are called the sons of God.”

Concerning them it is said:

> “Then all the trees of the forest will exult before the face of the Lord, for he has come”  
> *(Psalm 95).*

Therefore the sons are not called sons of evil, just as the daughters are compared with thorns. There is indeed great exultation among the forest trees when they see such a tree rise in their midst, a tree whose fruit has adorned the whole forest, removed all the sicknesses of souls, and transformed all the fruits of bitterness.

Under whose shade, after every heat of sadness and every burden of sin had been cast aside, the Church tells of the rest she had long desired and the joys she obtained, nourished by the sweetest fruit, to the souls of the young:

> “I sat beneath the shade that I desired,  
> and his fruit was sweet to my taste.”

As though she were saying: “With him who has always been my desire protecting me, I remain quiet and secure. By his grace he has made me a participant in heavenly sweetness.” Thus she testifies that she is led in due order toward the understanding of higher mysteries, saying:

> “The king led me into the wine chamber;  
> he ordered charity in me.”

The wine chamber should be understood as the Church, as some believe, in whose unity the Holy Spirit alone is accustomed to be given and received. His grace is designated here by the name of wine. When the apostles had received the Holy Spirit, the Jews said:

> “These men are full of new wine”  
> *(Acts 2).*

In this chamber charity is ordered, so that each person may love God with all his heart, more than himself, and his neighbor as himself.

The wine chamber may also, as an additional meaning, be understood as the mystery of Christ’s Passion, into which the Church was introduced when she deserved to participate by faith in his sacraments.

But since she testifies that she was introduced into mysteries that are to be understood in due order by youthful souls, the wine chamber must necessarily be understood as the knowledge and sweetness of the divine law. To this sweetness he invites the young women and urges them to hasten by praising it, as Christ teaches when he says:

> “Work for the food that does not perish,  
> but endures unto eternal life”  
> *(John 6).*

With this work placed before him, the Prophet pronounces a blessing:

> “Blessed are those who search his testimonies;  
> they seek him with their whole heart”  
> *(Psalm 118).*

For in the Old Testament there are the testimonies of the law, which prove that Christ, the Redeemer of the human race, was to come, has come, and will come again in glory.

Let us therefore suppose that the law is a wine chamber prepared in the fullness of joy, in which Christ, the Word of the almighty Father, dwells. Into it the souls of believers are introduced for eternal service, and she says that she has been introduced into the same understanding of the law in order to contemplate the wonders that God worked through each patriarch and prophet up to the birth of the Virgin. This understanding he now calls, figuratively, a wine chamber, into which she was introduced and in which she received the order of charity.

What, then, must first be instilled through this order of charity except that one must first believe and recognize that the Father must be named first, in whom the Son always is, as the Word invokes him; second, the Son, in whom the Father always is; and third, the Holy Spirit, who truly proceeds from the Father through the Son, as is proved by the voice and Word of the Father?

The first order is that by which the one God must be loved by all creation. The second follows the commandment of the Decalogue:

> “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart.”

The second order is:

> “with all your soul.”

The third order is:

> “with all your strength”  
> *(Exodus 20).*

Then, in the individual commandments of the laws, charity orders how and with what affection one’s neighbor should be loved, or how each person in the Church should be treated.

For love must be measured according to another order toward God, who, according to the Apostle, loved first and is proved to have bestowed upon us the whole sum of charity through Christ *(1 John 4)*; according to another order toward a faithful friend; according to another toward a beloved son; according to another toward parents, through whom we came into being although we did not previously exist; according to another toward a brother; according to another toward a stranger; according to another toward someone known to us; according to another toward a priest; and according to another toward relatives and neighbors.

To give what is necessary to a needy or sick person, or to a traveler, not for the display of human praise but for the sake of eternal recompense, is a judgment of ordered charity. To console the needy, visit those oppressed by an unjust judgment, and visit the sick or those confined in prison demonstrates ordered charity.

In no matter to respect a human person for the sake of truth, mercifully admonish the foolish, and rebuke the proud with the utmost truthfulness—this is the order of charity.

But whoever loves a father, mother, wife, children, brothers, or the riches of the present age more than God certainly possesses charity, but it is not ordered. For we must love him above all things, and our neighbor as ourselves. This is the order of charity.

Therefore the Son of God ordered charity in his Church, so that each son of the Church might know in what order he should offer the service of charity to each person. He says in the Gospel:

> “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s,  
> and to God the things that are God’s”  
> *(Matthew 22).*

And through the Apostle he says:

> “Pay everyone what is owed: honor to the one to whom honor is owed; fear to the one to whom fear is owed; tribute to the one to whom tribute is owed; tax to the one to whom tax is owed”  
> *(Romans 13).*

Not all who are called by the Christian name are introduced through this order of charity into the aforesaid understanding, which he called the wine chamber, but only those who, however little, have imitated Paul, who said:

> “I have labored more than all—

## [Scan page 301]

> —in vigils, in fastings, and in other things,”

and:

> “I have regarded everything as refuse, so that I might gain Christ”  
> *(Philippians 3).*

At the beginning of this song, the Church, introduced into the king’s chamber or storeroom, praises him. Having entered, she says:

> “We shall exult and rejoice in you,”

recognizing his bodily presence—he who is in the wisdom of the Father and who, as though in the inner chamber of the prophets, lay hidden in their proclamations. In him are all exultations, joys, and treasures.

Here, however, she says that she has been introduced in order to understand the divine law and to learn the order of charity. She does not say that she rejoices and exults, but that she languishes, because, according to Solomon:

> “He who adds knowledge adds pain”  
> *(Ecclesiastes 1).*

And the more closely anyone begins to approach wisdom by pursuing it, the more he scarcely perceives it, as though it were receding.

From this pain the blessed love of Christ is born, and from love comes the more glorious health of the soul: a languor that withdraws all its strength from sinning. Although she has attained the secret mysteries of God’s manifold wisdom, and although she holds the summit of perfection, she nevertheless does not believe that the whole of the aforesaid sentence or understanding is sufficient for her unless she is accompanied and supported by various flowers.

Therefore she immediately adds:

> “Sustain me with flowers, cover me with apples,  
> for I am sick with love.”

She seeks the bodily presence of the wisdom of God the Father, that is, Christ, in the chamber of the knowledge of the law. But because she is not yet permitted to see him whom she desires to see as he is, she asks for the examples of others, by which she may meanwhile temper her languor.

For she says:

> “Sustain me with flowers, cover me with apples,”

that is, “Console me with examples, whether of those beginning a good work or of those who have completed one. For while I remain weary in the fatigue of pilgrimage, I languish from desire for the heavenly vision.”

Therefore, not without reason, by flowers are understood souls beginning a good work and fragrant with heavenly desire; by apples, souls already perfected in good works, who have reached the fruit of their labor from the beginning of their holy purpose.

She who therefore languishes from love seeks to be sustained with flowers and covered with apples, because she is not yet permitted to see the one whom she desires. It is a great consolation if she rejoices in the progress of others, so that the soul—which cannot yet contemplate the face of God—may rest in the good work of her neighbor.

Let us see what sort of mind Paul possessed. He said:

> “For me to live is Christ and to die is gain”  
> *(Philippians 1).*

For this reason he says again:

> “I desire to depart and to be with Christ, which is much better”  
> *(ibid.).*

But let us see what it is that you desire to depart from, and with what love you languish. Since you see that, for the time being, your departure is delayed, why, I ask, do you not seek to be sustained with flowers?

You certainly do seek this, for it follows:

> “But to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake”  
> *(ibid.).*

And to his disciples who were making progress he says:

> “For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of glory? Is it not you before our Lord Jesus Christ?”  
> *(1 Thessalonians 2).*

The soul, therefore, joined to the Word of God and introduced into the understanding of the law, proceeds through every detail of Scripture, as has often been said, tasting the flavors of the individual vessels of the divine books in the wine chamber. As though intoxicated by the wine of the joy of future blessedness, although she does not see the bridegroom in the present, she says that she languishes from love because he is slow to come to her.

He is undoubtedly the one of whom the Prophet says:

> “My soul thirsted for the living God.  
> When shall I come and appear before the face of the Lord?”  
> *(Psalm 41).*

Through this love of knowledge, love of eternal life is germinated, and from love of eternal life comes endurance of persecution.

Having tasted this love, and as though placed upon a couch, she begs to be embraced by the left hand of promise and the right hand of Christ’s assistance, saying:

> “His left hand is beneath my head,  
> and his right hand embraces me.”

What else is signified by the left hand except the present life or the temporal gifts of almighty God? And what else by the right hand except everlasting life?

The left hand of God, that is, the Church, has placed the prosperity of the present life and temporal gifts beneath her head, pressing them down with the intention of supreme love. The right hand of God embraces her, because she is held with complete devotion beneath his eternal blessedness. Here, through hope, the bridegroom strengthens the mind; there, through recompense, he glorifies it.

Alternatively, the Old Testament is indicated by the left hand and the New Testament by the right. This may be understood as follows: Christ’s left hand sustains the soul on the left, so that she may not be caught by the hooks of the incentives of vice. Rather, constantly held before her, she is raised by hidden compunctions toward the kingdom.

And lest, lifted up in pride, she fall into the right hand—the fall by which the devil fell—he permits tribulations and restraints of many kinds, and, when she is wearied, his right hand helps and embraces her.

The passage may also be understood in an additional sense: the left hand beneath the head is the shield of faith, which the combatant holds in his left hand; the right-hand embrace is the sword of prayer. Armed always with the right hand, he repels the adversary with one kind of weapon and strikes him down with the other.

It follows:

> “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem,  
> by the gazelles and the stags of the fields,  
> that you do not rouse or awaken my beloved  
> until she herself wills it.”

After the Church’s many labors and wanderings, through which she is worn out with anxiety inside the holy wine chamber and brought into sleep, the daughters of Jerusalem are adjured not to awaken her too quickly from sleep and return her to her former labors. By this they are adjured to love her with firm charity.

The gazelles and stags of the fields signify souls of no small merit or labor, through whom the daughters of Jerusalem are adjured. For in the Christian people souls are compared with different animals according to the quality of their merits.

Our Lord Jesus Christ therefore possesses a palace which is understood to contain within itself many storerooms, a wine chamber, and expanses of fields. Entering this palace, blessed Paul praises its flowers in wonder:

> “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!”  
> *(Romans 11).*

Within this palace, amid many riches, that is, amid the multitude of the saints, he is understood also to possess souls of various kinds: [the supplied source ends at this colon].

[scan page 302]  
**Commentary on the Song of Songs**

Angelomus of Luxeuil, monk

As in a great house, according to the Apostle (2 Thess. ii), there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also of clay and wood, so not without reason are the daughters of Jerusalem understood as the souls of the elect, contemplating the vision of the heavenly fatherland of peace. By “does” or “hinds” he calls the spiritual fathers of the Old and New Testaments, for whom the multitude of the sacred Scriptures is pasture.

Alternatively, some wish the does to be understood as souls accustomed, through the sharpness of dialectic and the intellectual discernment acquired through philosophy, to range through both reason and mind. Now, enclosed within the palace mentioned above by the hunters’ art, caught by the hand of the apostles and the other teachers, and converted to a better religion, they range through the fields of the divine Scriptures, interpreting whatever is most wise, lofty, and obscure; and the cultivation of the gods is daily turned into praise of the Creator. In faith they display the speed of their course, and with the sharpness of their understanding, like does, they perceive the adversaries’ ambushes from afar.

The nature of does is to have the forepart of the body higher and the hind part lower. For this reason, always ascending upward as they run toward the mountain, they are found to be faster, since along that route the adversary has less opportunity to pursue them. The stags, however, seem to be understood as those who, in the very speed of their philosophical inquiry, confessed not many gods but one invisible, immeasurable, ineffable God, Creator of all, filling the whole world and present everywhere. They too were caught by the holy teachers in the net of preaching and brought into the bosom of the Church.

They dwell in the high places of life; like stags, they seek springs of water, kill serpents, and, like clean animals, ruminate. These, therefore, are without doubt the stags of the fields and the does: namely, the souls of faithful philosophers converted from the unbelief of superstitions. Through them the Bridegroom adjures the daughters of Jerusalem to allow the bride to rest for a little while in the sleep of repose. They rejoice that the Church runs together with them in those works by which they themselves have been raised to heavenly glory, so that, having laid aside the bodily burden, they may feast with them in heaven.

The Lord Christ commands her bodily rest for the strengthening or consolation of other souls, until she herself wills it—until the Bridegroom himself, looking to her advantage, recognizes her strength, since without him she can do nothing.

According to the earlier interpretation, however, in which we said that the does and stags signify the fathers of the Old and New Testaments, the passage may be understood thus: “I adjure the peaceful souls of the faithful, signified by the clean and ruminating animals through their several virtues, not to impede by any importunity the pious efforts of the brethren, but for each to rejoice in the progress of his neighbors as though it were his own.”

Alternatively, Christ admonishes that none of the teachers should frighten believers by gifts or threats, but should proclaim only what is holy and lead those who believe or are converted to religion voluntarily, either to the end or to religion itself. They should not disturb them in their tranquility until, driven by divine inspiration, they gird themselves for the practices of a higher life.

But the perfect soul of the elect—and, so to speak, the holy Church—always hears him in the very sleep of repose, fearing him always, and always sees him by loving him. Hence he now says; that is, this is the voice I heard adjuring the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken me while I rested in his embrace. Or it is his evangelical preaching. What this voice of the Beloved says to the Church he himself declares in the Gospel:

> “See that you are not led astray by false prophets. For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am the Christ,’ and they will lead many astray and perform signs, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led into error” (Matt. xxiv).

And:

> “See that your hearts are not weighed down with gluttony or drunkenness” (Luke xxi).

And:

> “Be like servants waiting for their lord, when he returns from the wedding” (Luke xii).

This is so that the Church, resting in the Bridegroom’s embraces, may not be deceived under the guise of teachers. And lest she grow sluggish in idleness after her labors or be dissolved by pleasures, she is admonished in the Gospel in this way. But in the repose of this security she should always be diligent in applying the ear of her heart to Christ’s voice—that is, in the divine Scriptures—and should devote herself continually to prayer.

Through these words, therefore, those who preside over the Christian people are admonished to announce without interruption what this voice of the Church’s Beloved commands: namely, how he came from the bosom of the Father into human fellowship, so that the Word might become flesh; how, according to the prophet Habakkuk (chap. iii), by humbling the pride of demons he broke the mountains of violence and melted the everlasting hills, trampling Satan beneath the feet of believers as he crossed the mountains mentioned above.

Considering this, the Church says:

> “Behold, he comes leaping upon the mountains, bounding over the hills.”

Do you wish to hear what leaps he made? These, I say, are the leaps of my Beloved: from heaven he came into the womb; from the womb into the manger; from the manger to the cross; from the cross to the tomb; from the tomb he returned to heaven. He is the one who was also exalted above all mountains and hills—that is, above the fathers of the New and Old Testaments, who surpass the others in the merit of their virtues and the height of their faith.

The Lord is said not merely to dwell in them but to leap over them, because he appeared incomparable not only in divinity but also in humanity. Or, through the apostles, as we began to say above, he melted all the pride of worldly wisdom that lifted itself against the Creator, and, reduced to nothing, it was humbled. In them shone not rhetorical arguments but the power of the Holy Spirit; and, with the host of demons prostrated beneath the feet of believers, the Church was shown that he had come into the world, leaping upon the mountains and bounding over the hills, and had lived among human beings.

Hence it immediately follows:

> “My Beloved is like a doe and a fawn of the stags.”

We understand Christ to have been compared to a doe not through any diminution of his divinity—for he is always the same—but through the mystery of the Incarnation: namely, because he appeared in the likeness of sinful flesh, through which the nature of flesh, received into heaven, attained increase.

[scan page 303]

Some also think that the doe is so called because the illumination of our salvation, removing the darkness of the heart, showed itself in the latter part of the age by coming in the flesh—the same illumination that he had shown to Moses when he asked on Mount Sinai. Concerning this mystery David says:

> “The feathers of the dove are silvered, and its hind parts with the pallor of gold” (Ps. lxvii).

Just as the hind part of the doe displays whiteness, so many—not only from the Jews but also from the philosophers of the nations—believed through the humility of his Incarnation. These are understood as the souls once more wild, but purer than the others mentioned above, who through his teaching were gathered into the fellowship of the one true Israel.

According to the opinion of some, he is therefore proclaimed by the voice of the Church to be like such souls because of the innocence and multitude of believers, and is compared to a fawn of the stags. He is called a fawn of the stags because he was born from the stock of the patriarchs, who are designated by the name of stags; or a fawn of the stags because of the form of his humility, not yet exalted by the horns of power with which, at the second coming, he will judge the world. Concerning these it is said in the Psalm:

> “Then the horns of the righteous will be exalted” (Ps. lxxiv).

A fawn of the stags, being without horns, displays in itself rather the attraction of beauty than terror, as our Lord Christ is recognized to have done at his first coming. Concerning this first coming it immediately follows:

> “Behold, he himself stands behind our wall, looking through the windows, gazing through the lattices.”

Clothed in the wall of our mortality, he concealed the substance of his divinity. Yet he gazed upon us through lattices and windows when he performed miracles, so that through the miracles it might become apparent who was concealed by the sufferings.

For when he displayed to human eyes what he had assumed from mortal nature, and in himself, who remained invisible, showed himself openly to those seeking to see him, he stood, as it were, behind a wall, because he did not offer himself to be seen in manifest majesty. He stood, as it were, behind a wall: he displayed the nature of humanity that he had assumed and concealed the nature of divinity from human eyes. Whoever looks through windows or lattices is neither seen wholly nor wholly unseen.

Our Redeemer, therefore, because he performed divine deeds and endured human sufferings, came to human beings as God through lattices and windows: he appeared through his miracles, as has been said, and remained hidden through his sufferings; and through his sufferings he was seen as man. Rightly it is said:

> “Behold, he himself stands behind our wall,”

and what follows.

It may also be understood thus, if anyone wishes: Behold, he who was crucified, who by the right hand of his divinity embraced the weakened—that is, grieving—Church in the apostles with the consolation of his embrace, and was buried with that flesh, now stands with it, rising again behind the wall of our unbelief, which we had built with works of clay by sinning. Concerning this he says through the prophet Isaiah:

> “Is my hand too weak to save? But your sins made a wall between you and God” (Isa. l).

Standing behind this wall, the Lord Christ waits to be invoked by the impious and calls the sinful soul to repentance; he waits to be believed by unbelievers. Behind this wall he stands until the time of baptism or repentance.

Although we are not worthy to see him, nevertheless, by renouncing idolatry we make windows in the wall mentioned above, through which Christ looks upon us while defending us from unclean spirits. We also make lattices by bending the knees of our bodies, through which he looks upon us as we turn to him in remorse.

When, however, we have come to true conversion through the baptism or repentance mentioned above, he removes from our midst the wall of sins that had been granted to our wickedness, and he speaks to us, saying:

> “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. xi).

And:

> “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. xxv).

As the teacher of the nations, Paul, eloquently declared, this was accomplished at his coming:

> “He is our peace, who made both one and broke down the dividing wall, and reconciled us to God the Father through his blood” (Eph. ii).

When the Church was enclosed, as it were, within the wall of idolatry and confined by its barriers because of persecution, after his resurrection—when the apostles, terrified by his death, were still overcome by fear—he entered through closed doors and brought great confidence and great joy, saying:

> “Peace be with you. It is I; do not be afraid” (Luke xxiv).

Then what follows was fulfilled:

> “My Beloved speaks to me: ‘Arise, hasten, my beloved, my dove, my beautiful one, and come.’”

He speaks to her, calling her to perfection of life, telling her no longer to fear the author of death, the devil, or to remain within the prison of unbelief and sluggishness.

> “‘Hasten,’ he says, ‘and come,’”

because by dying I restored the life that had been lost. Now do not fear death, whose dominion I have destroyed.

He stood behind our wall because he was concealed from us by the shadow that obstructed the Sun of Justice, concerning whom the prophet had promised:

> “For you who fear God the Sun of Justice will rise, and healing will be in his wings” (Mal. iv).

He speaks to the Church in the apostles when, rising from the dead, he consoles them, saying:

> “Take courage, for I have conquered the world” (John xvi).

And:

> “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. xxviii).

And:

> “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. x).

Through this saying she is summoned to the duty of preaching, as it says:

> “My Beloved speaks to me,”

that is, he urges me to preach, saying:

> “‘Arise, hasten, my beloved, and come,’”

that is, arise from the bed of repose in which you seek to care only for yourself; hasten and come to fulfill also the concern for the salvation of your neighbor, devoting yourself diligently to the ministry of preaching.

He also gives her confidence through affectionate words when he adds:

> “For now the winter has passed, the rain has gone and departed. The flowers have appeared in our land; the time of pruning has come.”

He teaches her no longer to fear at all the violence of wicked people or to dread the terrors of demons, because he has reconciled God the Father to the Church through the offering of the assumed flesh and has subdued the army of demons through the cross.

[scan page 304]

He drove away the winter cold and harshness, and then he showed the faithful what the time of his coming would be, and that we shall see him as he is (1 Cor. xiii). Then it became apparent how great and what sort of joys were prepared for her through the flowers on the earth. For when he would display his presence in the blessedness of the age to come, he narrated that the beginnings of a certain life of blessedness had already appeared.

Hence it is also said to her:

> “Arise, my soul; you have begun, as it were, already to smell the flowers. Hasten, my beloved, my beautiful one, and come.”

She goes forth, so that after she has gone forth she may have fruit more abundantly; hence the following is added:

> “The time of pruning has come.”

For in pruning, branches are cut back so that those which are stronger may bear fruit more abundantly. One becomes beloved by knowing God, beautiful by preserving Christ’s humility, and a dove by seeking nothing from earthly desires except the most meagre food and clothing for the body, by always keeping the dove’s simplicity, and by joining oneself to the Holy Spirit.

Alternatively, she is called beloved through love, beautiful and comely through the adornment of virtues and the washing of regeneration, and a dove through the infusion of the Holy Spirit. The time of our pruning will come when we leave behind the unfruitful and harmful flesh of corruption; the fruit then most abundant for us will be the vision of the one God. Thus the time of pruning is the calling of a soul from the world to heavenly things.

It follows:

> “The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.”

Let us mention the opinions of various interpreters, lest we appear to have been ignorant. Some wish the turtledove to signify blessed Mary, whose voice was first heard in our land when she said to the angel:

> “How shall this happen, since I do not know a man?” (Luke i).

And:

> “Behold, the handmaid of the Lord; let it happen to me according to your word” (ibid.).

And:

> “From now on all generations will call me blessed” (ibid.).

To her the angel replied:

> “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.”

And:

> “The holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God.”

Truly she is worthy: all generations call her alone blessed, and not only the nations of diverse peoples but even the powers of heaven admiringly praise her as glorious among all women. For through the entry of Life we rejoice that death has been put to flight and the world reconciled.

Just as, when spring arrives—the forerunner of summer that drives winter away—all creation rejoices at returning to life: animals of every kind prepare for offspring and build their gravid dwellings, birds make nests and call one another with distinct cries and movements, the earth prepares food for creeping things so that winged creatures may not lack nourishment, the melodious voice of birds sweetly resounds and chirps, and the wing-armed bee goes forth to plunder flowers; so our Lord Jesus Christ, after the harsh winter of idolatry and philosophical teaching, brought on spring through his passion, which is our Passover, the passage from death to life. He adorned the face of the world with the flowers of faith in believers—or rather, with every holy work—and, by his example, calls the Church from the bed of repose to the duty of preaching, indeed from the valley of human weakness to the mountain of God’s paradise. When he had said:

> “Arise, hasten, my beloved, my beautiful one, and come,”

he immediately added:

> “For now the winter has passed,”

that is, the power of darkness, which made the world sorrowful, passed from this world to Tartarus when Christ, the Sun of Justice, came. The cold of unbelief and the rain of iniquity, which had covered the whole world until the time of the Lord’s Incarnation and resurrection, have withdrawn.

> “The flowers have appeared in our land,”

that is, the beginnings of faith and justice have blossomed in the world as the growing Church. 

> “The time of pruning has come,”

that is, after the useless shoots of empty religion have been cut away, human hearts are prepared for the future faith. For the summer season has come, when those of one bodily stock are separated from evils, lest the good perish through proximity to the wicked and lest believers be endangered by the faithlessness of unbelievers.

This is the time of pruning that was foretold as coming, concerning which the Lord said in the Gospel:

> “For I have come to separate a son from his father, and a daughter-in-law from her mother-in-law, and a daughter from her mother” (Matt. x),

and so forth.

Alternatively, “the winter has passed” because the tribulation of the present life has departed. The rain has also gone, because when we are led to contemplate almighty God in his substance, the necessary drops of words will no longer be needed, as though the rain of preaching had to be poured upon us. For what one can scarcely hear here, one will see there:

> “For now we see through a mirror, in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Cor. xiii).

Some, rejoicing and praising together, understand this as the entry into life, the expulsion of death, and the reconciliation of the world.

Others assert that the blessed John the Baptist is meant, whose voice was heard saying:

> “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, ‘Prepare the way of the Lord’” (Matt. iii).

And:

> “Produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke iii).

For as long as the winter of transgression—sorrowful and shut off from every good sprout—had covered the face of the world, and the devil held the earth under his power, this most sweet voice of the turtledove, whether through blessed Mary or through John, had not been heard in our land.

But when that great Sun of Justice arose for us, bringing the abundance of summer through indulgence, the voice of the turtledove began to be heard in our land, through the desire to preserve chastity. Rightly, then, virginity is compared to the most chaste bird, the turtledove, which holds primacy in John or Mary.

Once joined to the Word of God or to the Holy Spirit, it never thinks of another partner and desires no other union of its love except with the one to whom it is known to have been once attached—like the turtledove that loves the dwelling of its beloved in the desert, calls its mate, and makes a sweet sound. When it has lost him, it seeks no other, but always sends forth to him the voice of its promise and of its heart, to whom it promised to preserve the affection of love.

When he has died, it is said never to join itself to another, but throughout all the days of its life it seeks in longing the one to whom it had once been joined.

It must nevertheless be understood that, although this is the voice of the turtledove heard in our land, it is also the voice of the Lord Savior, who says in the Gospel:

> “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matt. iii).

Or, very properly, the holy Church is understood by the turtledove, adorned with the variety of virtues as with feathers.

[scan page 305]

> “The fig tree has put forth its unripe figs.”

As the summer of human redemption and the glorious Redeemer’s coming drew near, the fig tree—namely, the Synagogue—constricted by the winter and cold of iniquity, is understood to have possessed nothing in itself except the bitter sap of teaching, which it falsely claimed to be food for souls.

But at the Lord’s coming, after the turtledove’s voice had been heard saying, “Repent,” and so forth, the fig tree put forth its unripe figs: that is, the precepts of the Law fell away, and through the apostles it itself produced its unripe figs, who, begotten from it, became the sweetest food of teaching for souls.

But because it refused to believe in them, it withered in eternal sterility, and, stripped of every beauty, was preserved within itself as nothing but food for eternal fire. Once the people had been freed from the shadow of its perverse oppression, after the evil Pharisaic teachers had been removed, they began to flourish by believing in Christ and, by their example, to summon the nations of other peoples to the flowering of faith.

Concerning these it is said in the following verse:

> “The flowering vines have given forth their fragrance.”

For by believing in one almighty God, the vines flourished—that is, the evangelical people. Or, the flowering vines are holy ways of life, which gave forth their fragrance far and wide throughout the world.

Just as vines in winter are without beauty, lacking leaves and flowers, so it is certainly shown that the nations throughout the world, which he now called vines, had been without the beauty of justice and the adornment of holiness.

It follows:

> “Arise, hasten, my beloved, my beautiful one, and come, my dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall.”

The Church therefore lay in a very low and hidden place, called from far away; now she is shown to reign throughout the whole world, having been disturbed or oppressed by the storm of demons. But when the mysteries of Christ’s passion had been celebrated through the teaching of the apostles, in whom Christ speaks, she is summoned to rise and come, to walk with the Bridegroom through the vineyards, to rejoice with him, and to bring forth the fruit of justice among the nations mentioned above.

It is as though he says to her: O bride and beloved, to whom I have offered such great blessings and for whom I have endured so much, arise and come; gird yourself for the contest, so that you may receive eternal rest:

> “In the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall.”

The Apostle explains what the rock is:

> “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. x).

Whoever therefore desires to be snatched from the enemies of the aerial power and to escape unharmed should always enter into the clefts of this rock by preserving the faith. That is, he should contemplate the wounds of the nails and the lance that the Bridegroom received for the salvation of the bride, and enter into the hollow of the wall—that is, the custody of the heavenly virtues.

This rock has many clefts, namely entrances, through which believers enter into the kingdom of the Father, who prepares it for them. These are gentleness, humility, patience, contempt of riches, impartiality, perseverance in prayer, the ministry of mercy, steadfast chastity, the pattern of kindness, the unique mirror, and the indivisible recognition of the Trinity, in which our redemption lies.

These are without doubt the clefts in which the soul is taught to come to the joys of the kingdom of heaven.

The cleft of the rock may also be understood as the protection of the same Lord Jesus Christ, to which the Church flees like a dove to the cleft of the rock. Hence Isaiah says:

> “Enter into the rock; hide yourself in the pit of the earth” (Isa. ii).

The hollow of the wall may signify the defense of the Holy Spirit or the congregation of the faithful. Yet the clefts of the rock may also be understood as the assertions of the four Gospels, which testify that the body of the same rock was pierced by the blows mentioned above. The hollow, however, may signify the teaching of the apostles, concerning whom it is shown that God built, as it were, a very firm wall for the vineyard of the believing people against the attacks of evil spirits.

For just as they recognize the divine mysteries through Christ, so we recognize them through the apostles and remain within the sight of the faith that they confessed. And because “faith without works is idle” (Jas. ii), it rightly follows:

> “Show me your face. Let your voice sound in my ears. For your voice is sweet, and your face is beautiful.”

As though he openly said: Show me your face; I beg you, come forth into the public sphere of action. Do not remain at rest under the sluggishness of repose, but show your faith through works. Let your voice sound—that is, the voice of preaching, praise, and confession—in my ears.

For the voice of that person is sweet to God who knows how to proclaim the Lord’s words sweetly and pleasantly to his neighbors from the sweetness of the kingdom, and to resound with praises to the Lord himself. And that faith is beautiful which adorns itself with works and does not fear to endure adversity.

It follows:

> “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards, for our vineyard has blossomed.”

When the storm of demons mentioned above—the “winter”—had passed, the bride, now joined to the king’s body through the sacrament of baptism, is invited into the vineyard, that is, into the people of believers gathered from the nations, and he finds it producing flowers through the goodness of nature and prepared to trust in God and heaven.

But because it was ready to be destroyed and devoured through the cunning and ambushes of foxes waiting for the ripeness of the fruit, which are the most biting doctrines of heretical souls, Jesus says to his teachers:

> “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards,”

that is, refute heretics and schismatics who are perverse in faith, and those who are crafty in speech. By the tooth of perverse doctrine they are accustomed to tear the inexperienced minds of the faithful.

> “For our vineyard has blossomed,”

that is, the holy souls of the elect are germinating the fruit of faith and good works far and wide.

What he says—“our”—is understood in two ways: either he calls it his own and the Father’s, or he calls the Church joined to himself a participant in it. Seeing that this Church was bringing forth flowers both from the Jews and, in the greatest measure, from the nations, he first prepared hunters or guardians to catch the foxes before the flowers produced ripe fruit.

One of their number is the person who said:

> “We refute every person and bring into captivity every knowledge that exalts itself against the knowledge of God.”

Whether demons are understood as the foxes, or heretics and perverse teachers through whom the demons speak blasphemies, it is clear that both interpretations fit: through them the minds of human beings, in which the right faith of the Church dwells, are destroyed.

[scan page 306]

We must diligently avoid their destruction and hidden ambushes, and love God with all our heart, so that we may deserve to be loved by him. Therefore the Church most rightly adds:

> “My Beloved is mine, and I am his.”

Thus the Church, joined to Christ, or the soul joined to the Word of God, is filled by him with more abundant joy in every respect. He shows in what things he himself rejoices and what delights him in her, and she is taught what she ought to reply for such great benefits. The Bridegroom desires in her a beautiful face, as he indicated above: one unstained by the blackness of sin, not hidden by shameful words and deceit, nor made harsh by the hoarseness of blasphemies, but returning an echo that resounds with sweetness in her praises.

The same Church says:

> “My Beloved is mine, and I am his.”

Christ and the Church—head and body—are like one person; and just as the members follow the head, she follows him by loving him, and therefore speaks in this way. For no one is the Beloved and helper of the Church except Christ, and no one is Christ’s beloved except the Church: no one else rightly loves Christ except the one Church, and no one else is loved by him except her.

> “He who feeds among the lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows incline.”

That is, he who feeds upon the purity of faith and the brightness of virtues until the true day of the coming age and of his judgment arrives, and the light rises; and until the shadows—that is, the errors of the present age that impede us—pass away and incline, with their lovers, into the chaos of hell beneath the sun of justice.

> “Return. Be like, my Beloved, a doe and a fawn of the stags upon the mountains of Bethel.”

This is the voice of the Church mentioned above to Christ:

> “I beg you, my Beloved, return to me more often through the coming of your visitation. For, rising from the dead, you have ascended above all the heavenly mountains in the flesh that you took from the origin of the patriarchs, so that by the contemplation of eternity you might relieve the labor of my pilgrimage.”

Here, as we briefly explained above, the doe signifies Christ’s flesh because of the likeness of sinful flesh. He himself is called a fawn of the stags because he was born from the stock of the patriarchs and, returning to heaven after his resurrection, was exalted above the mountains of Bethel, which is interpreted as “the house of God”: that is, the heavenly fatherland of the angels.

Hence the Psalmist, speaking to him, says:

> “Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth! How exalted is your majesty above the heavens!” (Ps. viii).

A moral sense should certainly not be excluded. Each believer makes himself either a mountain of God through holy conduct or a mountain of the devil by living perversely. Bethel, as we have said, is interpreted as “the house of God.” Whoever therefore orders his life in such a way that the Holy Spirit delights to dwell in him becomes a mountain of God, which is the Church of God.

If, then, he has at times been offended by the sins of the people and prolonged his absence, he returns, becoming like a doe and a fawn of the stags in course or habit. Their nature is, when their cry has echoed before them in the mountains and is sent behind them while they suppose it is coming to meet them, to return with a swifter course to the place from which they had departed. This is also why, when irritated by enemies, they do not wish to abandon their accustomed dwelling.

So too Christ our Lord, although provoked and angered by human sins, recalled by fasts and prayers, returns to his accustomed dwelling of mercy. And if he sometimes seems to be provoked so that our diligence in seeking him may be increased, no one should despair or cease searching for him.

## Chapter III

> “On my bed, by night, I sought him whom my soul loves. I sought him and did not find him.”

In some manuscripts the following is added:

> “I came, and I called him, and he did not answer me.”

Although these words may seem to have been announced and fulfilled in the Lord’s burial, when the women kept vigil at the Lord’s tomb while the apostles mourned intolerably, one should look more closely at what follows. It is as though the Church, or any holy soul, says more openly:

“I have long sought him with great effort, but because I was still subject to the allurements of my flesh and blinded by the darkness of profound ignorance, I did not find the light of truth—that is, the Lord.”

Alternatively, the Church or holy soul seeks her Beloved on her bed when, tranquil and at rest in her heart, she thinks upon her Lord, free from every disturbance of the world. She who seeks him does not find him for this reason: that, set aflame by love of him, more ardently seeking…

We seek him by night because, even if the mind is already awake in him, the eye is still dim.

> “I called him, and he did not answer me.”

Whoever believes Christ to be merely human will not find him. Whoever does not believe in Christ’s divinity will not find him. Whoever does not believe in Christ’s divinity does indeed call the Son of God “Lord” during the nights of his perverse perceptions, but he does not answer him—just as God did not answer King Saul, from whom he had departed.

He labors in vain, therefore, seeking him who has not confessed both natures: God, equal to human beings in everything except sin and coeternal with the Father, who redeemed; and man, through whom God redeemed the lost. Concerning him the Psalmist says:

> “A brother cannot redeem; a man will redeem” (Ps. xlviii).

> “I will rise and go around the city; through the streets and squares I will seek him whom my soul loves. I sought him and did not find him.”

I resolved in my mind to rise from the bed of carnal pleasures, travel through lands and seas, and approach the mysteries of the philosophers, but even so I did not find him.

The passage may also be understood differently. Here “the city” signifies the holy Church of the elect, or the divine Scripture. By “streets” and “squares” he calls the books of the Law and the Prophets, in which the Church or the elect soul finds her Beloved—that is, Christ—when she seeks him ardently, though she does not find him in the books of the philosophers.

> “The watchmen who guard the city found me. ‘Have you seen him whom my soul loves?’” (Ps. cxxxvi).

The watchmen who guard the city—that is, the Church…

## [Scan page 307]

### Angelomus

“Whether apostles or other teachers, they are those who, by anxious zeal, have sought and found the truth. Concerning them it is said: ‘Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it keep watch in vain’ (Psalm cxxvi).”

“After I had passed on a little, I found him whom my soul loves.” That is, when I had entrusted myself to their teaching, I found the light of truth that I had sought.

Alternatively: while we are seeking, the watchmen who guard the city find us, because the holy Fathers who guard the condition of the Church come to meet our good studies, so that by word or writing they may teach us. When we have passed them by a little, we find him whom we love, because although our Redeemer was a human being among human beings in humility, he was nevertheless above human beings in divinity. For no one can find him unless, by the steps of faith and with a pure mind, he has passed beyond all the saints and believed Christ to be more excellent than all the saints.

“I held him and would not let him go until I brought him into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her who bore me.”

I hold him with firm faith until, at the end of the age, by the ministry of preaching, I introduce him into the house and chamber of the Synagogue, which bore me in the Lord; and there will be “one flock and one shepherd” (John 10).

It follows:

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and the does of the fields, that you do not awaken or rouse my beloved until she herself wills it.”

Therefore, wherever similar words are found in this song, the persons of believers from different times and of different peoples are introduced. Here the person of that people seems to be introduced which, wearied after Christ’s ascension by longing and seeking him whom its soul loved—that is, the Church from the nations—desired to rest for a little while, fortified by the peace of tranquillity, in the sleep of security. For this reason the bridegroom repeats this verse, lest one should think that he had less concern for the Church gathered from the nations than for the Jews, but so that there might be one bride from both peoples, and that she might be most beloved. We have already expounded this verse above.

The daughters of Jerusalem are the souls of the elect, who contemplate from above the vision of Jerusalem, namely, peace. The gazelles or does signify the Fathers of the New and Old Testaments, whose pasture is in the height of contemplation.

“What is this that comes up through the wilderness?”

I think that this is the nation ascending through the wilderness, which Paul, the teacher of the nations, gathered from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum, anointed with the perfumes of doctrine and sprinkled with the spices of the sacraments of the mysteries, and led to the couch of the peaceful King, concerning which we read in what follows.

Hence the Synagogue wonders how the people of the nations, cleansed by no mystery of circumcision and instructed by no admonition of the prophets, could suddenly ascend from the lowest pleasures, through the wilderness of paganism and idolatry, to the heights of virtues and the embraces of the bridegroom. Truly it was a wilderness where the name of Christ had not been proclaimed.

“Like a column of smoke, from myrrh and frankincense, and from every powder of the perfumer.”

That is, either the smoke of burning love, or one who strives toward heavenly things with every exertion of virtue.

By myrrh is signified the mortification of bodily pleasures; by frankincense, the purity of prayers; and by the various powders of the perfumer, the fragrance of all virtues.

Morally, the holy Church of the elect, when she rises from this world in holy prayers with ardent love, ascends through the wilderness that she has abandoned. Smoke rises from incense. Through the Psalmist it is said: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight, O Lord” (Psalm 140).

Smoke from spices is therefore the compunction of prayer conceived from the virtues of love. Yet this prayer is called a slender column of smoke, because, while it seeks only heavenly things, it advances so directly that it does not turn back to desire earthly or temporal things. It should also be noted that it is called not a column but a slender column, because at times the power of love in the ardor of compunction is of such subtle force that even the person who has deserved to possess it cannot comprehend it.

It is rightly said to be of myrrh and frankincense. Frankincense is burned in sacrifice according to the law of the Lord. With myrrh, dead bodies are embalmed so that they may not be corrupted by worms. Those, therefore, offer the sacrifice of myrrh and frankincense who both afflict the flesh so that the vices of corruption may not dominate them and kindle before the Lord the fragrant offering of their love, presenting themselves to God in holy virtues.

Hence it is added:

“And every powder of the perfumer.”

The powder of the perfumer signifies the virtue of good works. It should be noted that the virtues of those who act well are called not spices but powders. When we perform any good deeds, we offer spices. But when we also scrutinize the good things we have done and, by a judgment of retraction, consider whether anything sinister is present in them, we make powder from the spices, as it were, so that we may kindle our prayer to the Lord more subtly through discernment and love.

“Behold Solomon’s litter: sixty of the mightiest men of Israel surround it.”

“A litter King Solomon made for himself from the wood of Lebanon.”

Solomon, whose name is interpreted as “peaceful,” designates the Lord Jesus Christ. Solomon’s litter is the quiet mind of the saints, in which he rests as in a litter. The sixty strong men are holy preachers and very strong warriors, who are worthy to see God with a pure heart.

The number six is perfect because of the six days in which God made the world and the six ages of the world. The number ten pertains to the Decalogue of the law. Multiplied by six, it makes sixty: six times ten is sixty.

“All holding swords and most skilled in war, each man’s sword upon his thigh, because of terrors by night.”

They hold the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God; what they teach with their mouths, they complete by their works. The sword is also vigilant guardianship, restraining the desires of the heart lest the word of preaching stain itself with the impurity of life. The terrors of night are the ambushes of the devil and hidden temptations.

[The sentence breaks off at the page boundary.]

## [Scan page 308]

### Commentary on the Song of Songs

[The opening line is materially damaged in the scan.] The abundance of riches signifies the virtues which, among the saints—preachers and martyrs—establish a way to the heavenly realms through the precepts of charity. For those who rise in virtues, if they do not neglect the good things they are able to do through charity, are not alienated from God’s building. Everyone who possesses love of God and of his neighbor approaches this rest and these banquets joyfully, because Christ has provided all the ornaments of the Church, constructed as it were from strong souls, through the immense charity with which he loved us and gave himself for us.

“Come out and see, daughters of Jerusalem, King Solomon.”

For this joy and for contemplating the secrets of this mystery, perfect souls are summoned—not the negligent—but those who are called into rest in the kingdom of infinite glory, in which the souls of the elect understand that King Solomon rules. They are told:

“Solomon’s litter is made of wood from Lebanon.”

Solomon’s litter is the holy Church, which gathers those hastening toward eternal blessedness to the banquet. Christ has furnished all the Church’s ornaments, constructed as it were from strong souls like the woods of Lebanon.

“Its columns he made of silver.”

The silver columns signify teachers shining with the light of eloquence: “Its backrest is of gold.” The golden backrest is the rest of perpetual peace promised to the faithful, or the eternal rest in which the souls of the elect recline. It is called a golden backrest supported by silver columns because, through the light that shines from holy preachers, the minds of their hearers discover the splendor of the glory in which they will recline. Through what they hear clearly and openly, they rest in that which shines in the heart.

The silver columns and golden backrest therefore signify that, through the light of speech, the brightness of rest is found within the mind. The person whose interior is illuminated already shines, so that through intention he may rest there, where the grace of preaching is no longer sought.

But he adds what kind of ascent is involved when, immediately concerning the same litter, he says:

“Its ascent is purple.”

What is the purple ascent except the blood of the martyrs and the passion of our Redeemer? One does not ascend to the banquets of life except through the mystery of Christ’s passion. The purple ascent is rightly added, for true purple is dyed with blood and therefore rightly appears in the color of blood. Since a great multitude of the faithful at the beginning of the nascent Church reached the kingdom through the blood of martyrdom, our King made a purple ascent in the litter, because one reaches the brightness perceived within through the tribulation of blood.

What, then, shall we wretches do, deprived of every strength? Behold, we cannot be columns in this litter, because in us there is neither the strength of works nor the light of preaching. We do not possess the backrest, because we do not yet behold, as we ought, the rest of eternal charity through spiritual understanding. We are not the purple ascent, because we are unable to pour out our blood for our Redeemer.

What, then, must we do? What hope will there be if no one reaches the kingdom except one endowed with the highest virtues? Yet our consolation is also present. Let us love God as much as we can, let us love our neighbor, and together let us approach God’s litter. For, as it is written:

“He made it with love for the daughters of Jerusalem.”

It says “daughters,” not “sons,” that is, the weak. Through the daughters of Jerusalem the weak are understood, because charity, which is said to have constructed it, has them. Charity undoubtedly goes before them wherever the silver column is raised and the purple ascent is held. Since this is said on account of our weakness, it is plainly shown when it is added:

“Come out and see, daughters of Jerusalem, King Solomon, in the diadem with which his mother crowned him, on the day of his betrothal and on the day of the joy of his heart.”

Come out in mind and action from the turbulent conduct of the world, so that you may be able to see the king.

See the Lord Christ in his humanity, which he assumed from his virgin mother and placed at the right hand of the Father’s majesty.

“On the day of his betrothal.”

That is, in the time of his incarnation, when he came forth from a virginal womb to join the Church to himself as his bride.

“And on the day of the joy of his heart.”

That is, of the Redeemer of the human race, for whom that day was the day of his passion.

Alternatively: it admonishes them always to keep before the eyes of their hearts the holy soul’s King Solomon, our peaceful one, who is Christ, in the diadem—that is, in the crown of thorns—with which his mother crowned him, namely the Synagogue of the Jews, from which he was born according to the flesh, on the day of his betrothal, when he betrothed the Church to himself. What greater joy could Christ have had than when, through his passion, the redemption of the human race was accomplished?

## Chapter IV

“How beautiful you are, my beloved, how beautiful you are!”

Having stripped away every habit of the vices of the flesh and turned from the worship of many shameful gods to the one true God, he praises the Church’s twofold beauty. He called the Church beautiful and repeats that she is beautiful because he saw her to be praiseworthy both in preaching and in action.

“Your eyes are like those of doves.”

Your senses, he says, are excellent and modest in the contemplation of spiritual things. Or the eyes may signify the holy teachers, the glory of the people.

“Without what lies hidden within.”

The glory of an open work is indeed great, but the reward of the future age, which cannot yet be seen, is far more desirable.

“Your hair is like flocks of goats that have come up from Mount Gilead.”

The faithful people may be understood by the hair, since by their multitude they provide the Church with its greatest adornment. Gilead is interpreted as “a heap of testimony,” which aptly suits the gathered multitude of the saints.

The hair may also specifically designate those who believed from the circumcision. They came up from Mount Gilead because they came to the faith through the testimonies of the sacred Scriptures.

“Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing.”

By the hair, the weaker are designated; by the teeth, those who are more perfect, including the interpreters of the sacred Scriptures, who are suited to govern the Church. They do not need the milk of instruction; by eating solid food, they give it to others. They have come up from the washing—that is, from the font of sacred baptism—and they are both shorn and washed: stripped of possessions through renunciation of the world and cleansed by the washing of life.

“All of them bear twins.”

That is, they are fruitful in the twin virtues of charity, or in faith and works.

“And there is no barren one among them.”

There is no one who does not produce the offspring of good works.

“Your lips are like a scarlet thread, and your speech is sweet.”

Scarlet is the color of blood. The scarlet thread—also called “myrrh”—signifies the blood of the blessed martyrs. Or the scarlet thread signifies the doctrine of truth.

The lips of the bride, that is, of the Church, are likened to scarlet because she never ceases to preach the price of the Lord’s blood, by which she was redeemed; and in preaching she burns with the ardor of holy charity and makes her hearers burn with love of God.

“As a piece of a pomegranate, so are your cheeks, apart from what lies hidden within.”

In the cheeks, modesty is expressed; in the pomegranate, Christ’s passion. The bride therefore has the redness of a pomegranate in her cheeks when she confesses the mystery of the Lord’s cross in words and proves it by deeds.

Alternatively: those adorn the face of the Church who, accompanied by modesty, preserve chastity. Or certainly the cheeks of the Church are the holy martyrs, who, imitating Christ’s passion, are suffused with the rosy beauty of their blood, like a piece of pomegranate.

“Your neck is like the tower of David, built with its battlements.”

The tower of David is the holy Church, or the perfection or teaching of the saints, which is not from itself but from Christ. Its neck is the preachers, through whose steadfastness the same city is made firm and everywhere impregnable. Its battlements are the defenses of the sacred Scriptures, or the examples of the Fathers who have gone before.

“A thousand shields hang upon it.”

Because however many commandments there are in the divine books, so many are the defenses of our breast, by which we are protected against every ambush.

“All the armor of the strong.”

This is every equipment, whether of action or of heavenly teaching, by which we not only escape but also overcome.

Let us speak as Pope Gregory, in his customary remarkable thunder. In the neck, the throat is the voice within the throat. What is designated by the neck of the holy Church except sacred speech? Upon it a thousand shields are said to hang. Through this perfect number, the whole number is indicated, because all our defense is contained in sacred speech. There are God’s commandments there; there are the examples of the righteous.

If the soul grows sluggish in its desire for its Creator, let it hear what is said: “You shall love the Lord your God” (Exodus 20), and so forth. If it falls into hatred of its neighbor, let it hear what is said: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 22). If it covets another’s property, let it hear what is written there: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (Exodus 20). If the mind is inflamed to anger by an injury inflicted by a neighbor’s word or deed, let it hear what is said: “You shall not seek revenge, nor remember the injury done by your fellow citizens” (Leviticus 19).

When the mind, wounded by carnal desire, is inflamed so that the eye may not follow the mind, let it hear what was said: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5). If someone prepares to release his hostility against an enemy in hatred, let him hear what is written there: “Love your enemies” (Matthew 5), and so forth.

But one who no longer seizes another’s possessions may nevertheless retain them in an improper manner; let him hear what is said there: “Sell what you possess and give alms” (Luke 12). The weakened soul that desires to enjoy both God and the world should hear what is written there: “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6).

Another person retains his possessions not from the necessity of support but from the will of desire; let him hear what is said there: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14).

On the neck of the Church—that is, in the preaching of sacred speech, which on account of its defense and height is compared with the tower of David—a thousand shields hang, because as many commandments as are there, so many are the defenses of our breast. As it is said: in order to preserve innocence, even when injured by a neighbor, we hasten to persevere in humility. Let Abel come before our eyes: he is said to have been killed by his brother, and he is not read to have resisted. The same should be understood of the other examples of the saints.

Therefore, whenever we seek the defenses of virtue in the voice of sacred speech, we find them. “A thousand shields hang upon it, all the armor of the strong.” For if we hasten to become strong against the aerial powers, we find in this tower the armor of our mind, so that from it we may take the Creator’s commandments and from it the examples of the Fathers who went before, by which we may arm ourselves impregnably against our adversaries.

It should be noted that it is said to be “built with its battlements.” The battlements perform here the function of shields, because both protect the combatant. But there is this difference between them: we move shields wherever we wish for our defense, whereas we can be defended by a battlement but cannot move it. A shield is in the hand; a battlement is not held.

What, then, is the difference between battlements and shields except that in sacred speech we read of the miracles of the Fathers who went before, which we are unable to perform, and of the virtues of good works, by practicing which we are able to be defended?

“Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle, which feed among the lilies until the day breathes and the shadows incline.”

The two breasts of the Church are the two Testaments. The two fawns are the two peoples coming from circumcision and from the nations, because they are nourished by them. They understand themselves to be little through humility and sinners, and, running with charity, they pass through all the obstacles of the world.

They feed among the lilies, that is, among the most radiant examples or teachings of the saints. We read above that these were discussed as the armor of the strong.

“Until the day breathes and the shadows pass away”—that is, until the shadows of the present life pass away. We have already discussed this above.

## [Scan page 310]

“‘I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense.’ By myrrh the mortification of the flesh is expressed; by frankincense, devotion in prayer.”

As though he were saying: “I will frequent those whom I find to be exalted in virtues, and I will glorify them through the kindness of my visitation, either through passions or through prayers.”

Alternatively: this is the voice of the imperfect, who, when they ascend to the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense, desire to become imitators of those who have pleased God through the mortification of the flesh and the purest prayers.

The bridegroom continually repays the Church in turn, just as the Church praised him above. Therefore he says:

“You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride,” and so forth.

“How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride.”

By the name of breasts, the holy teachers are signified, because they express support for the weak and the little ones. The sweetness of grace is more pleasing than the austerity of the law.

“And the fragrance of your perfumes is above all spices.”

The most delightful fame of faith, spread throughout the whole world, extends more widely than that of the old law and of the Fathers within it, which is confined to Judaea alone. By the spices are meant the gifts of the Old Testament, compared with the fragrance of the Church—that is, with the grace of the Holy Spirit—or with its most beautiful virtues.

“Your lips drop honeycomb, my bride.”

What is meant by wax except the letter, and by honey except the spiritual meaning? Honey is in wax: the spiritual meaning of divine sayings is in the letter. Honey drips from wax because almost every individual sentence gives birth to many meanings. The lips of the bride are the teachers, who disclose that many different meanings are present in the sacred writings.

“Milk and honey are under your tongue.”

In milk is signified the instruction of the little ones; in honey, the stronger doctrine of the perfect. Under the tongue—that is, in the meditation of the heart.

It is not necessary to add what the Apostle Paul says about this:

“And the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of frankincense.”

The garments of the Church are her good works, which are compared with the fragrance of frankincense, because everything holy that the Church does for the Lord gives forth the fragrance of prayers for one another. The garments of the Church may also be understood as her preachers, who send pure and clean prayers to the Lord.

“A garden enclosed, my sister, my bride; an enclosed garden, a sealed spring.”

We decided above, in the preface, to discuss this briefly. The enclosed garden is the Church: enclosed because, fortified by the Lord’s protection, she remains in holy faith; a garden because she produces shoots of spiritual works of many kinds, or because she is called a garden on account of her spiritual children through baptism. She is a spring because she overflows with saving doctrine. She is called sealed by the word of faith.

“Your plants are a paradise of pomegranates with fruits of orchard trees.”

Through the irrigation of sacred baptism, the holy Church sends forth from herself a paradise, because she desires to direct to the heavenly paradise the people whom she generates through holy baptism. The pomegranates are called the saints, namely the martyrs; the fruits of orchard trees signify the sweetness of good works.

Since not only the command but also the coming is at hand, from this point we have decided to gather the book’s meanings more hastily than we had begun to extend them above, lest we seem to exceed the limits of the little book, as we acknowledged.

“Cyprus with nard, nard with saffron, reed and cinnamon.”

Cyprus is an aromatic tree signifying the blessing of heavenly grace. Nard represents the type of the Lord’s passion. Saffron expresses the fervor of charity. Cyprus is joined to nard when divine grace strengthens us to suffer with Christ. Likewise, nard is joined to saffron when, through charity, we willingly embrace Christ’s death.

Reed, which is called “cassia,” is an aromatic tree, but a small one, and therefore signifies a humble spirit.

Likewise cinnamon, which deceives serpents, signifies [a tree] that is itself short but fragrant and sweet. Thus humility has great praise and sweetness before him.

“With every tree of Lebanon.”

Just as reed and cinnamon signify the humble thoughts of the saints, so the trees of Lebanon signify their exalted actions, because “a good tree cannot bear evil fruit” (Matthew 7).

“Myrrh and aloe with all the finest perfumes.”

Myrrh and aloe are aromatic trees that express mortification of vices and penitence of the flesh. “With all the finest perfumes” means with the more excellent gifts of the virtues. The joining of these trees with the perfumes is beautiful, because when we restrain the flesh from lust, it follows that we receive greater gifts from the Spirit.

“A spring of gardens, a well of living waters flowing with force from Lebanon.”

The Church is both a garden and a spring of gardens, because she produces spiritual fruits; and she is a well of living waters because of the hidden mysteries which are disclosed only to the saints through the revelation of the Holy Spirit. They are called living waters because of the divine sayings which proceed from the invisible treasuries of divine grace. They flow with force from Lebanon—that is, from the Church herself, which is both bright through the purity of faith and lofty through the glory of virtues.

Alternatively: by the spring of gardens Christ is understood, watering his Church. The well of waters signifies the Holy Spirit, from whom different gifts are said to proceed. They are called living waters because those whom they fill they make living. They flow from Lebanon because the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son.

The spring that flows openly may signify Christ according to his humanity; the well, which has hidden and extremely deep water, may signify the same Christ according to his divinity. From him rivers often flow, as he himself testifies in the Gospel:

“Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7).

“Rise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and let its spices flow.”

This is the voice of the bridegroom. In the north, adversities of the world are designated; in the south, consolations, because the Church is proved by a twofold struggle.

“Rise” is a word of permission, not of command. In the spices, the wondrous fragrances of living consciences are understood.

Alternatively: by the north wind, which is said to be cold and to freeze the earth so that it does not bear fruit, the devil is understood. He is ordered to withdraw from the garden, that is, from the Church. By the south wind, which is warm and is said to release the earth from cold, the Holy Spirit is understood. By blowing—that is, by infusing the Church with holy illumination—he causes her to abound in various fruits of virtue.

“Rise, north wind, and come, south wind,” and the rest.

For when the two spirits have filled the holy Church broadly with the virtues of their gifts, [the text continues at the page boundary].

## [Scan page 311]

### Angelomus of Luxeuil, monk

### Chapter V

“Let my beloved come into his garden and eat the fruit of his trees.”

That is, let Christ come into his Church, preserve her everywhere undefiled, make her fruitful in the fruit of faith, and gladly look upon and graciously receive the works of his saints.

“I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride.”

This voice is not commanding but indicating a past action. It is as though he were saying: “I have very often come into my Church, and I come to correct, help, and strengthen her, as you have asked.”

“I have gathered my myrrh with my spices.”

By myrrh, passion or mortification is expressed; by spices, all the virtues are expressed. He gathers myrrh with spices because he brings martyrs, together with the other elect, to the maturity of their rewards.

“I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey, I have drunk my wine with my milk.”

In the honeycomb and wine, the preachers are understood; in the honey and milk, the hearers. The inner judge of both is the one who tests and rewards.

“Eat, friends, and drink; drink deeply, beloved.”

This is Christ’s voice to the Church, as though he were saying openly: “Friends,” by doing what I command; “beloved,” by embracing it with complete charity. Therefore, by the deeds of the saints as by the choicest banquets, fill your hearts.

The Church replies:

“I sleep, but my heart is awake.”

That is: by the grace of God granted to me, I honor him in the peace of the present life; and the more peacefully I am free from inward assaults, the more deeply I see how good God is.

Morally, one sleeps with an awake heart when, by advancing inwardly through contemplation, one rests from outward disturbance in action.

Yet it must be understood that, as long as one lives in this mortal flesh, no one progresses so far in the virtue of contemplation that he can fix the eyes of his mind upon the unbounded ray of light itself. For the almighty God is not yet seen in his own clarity; rather, the soul contemplates something beneath that clarity, by which it is refreshed and progresses, until afterward it reaches the glory of his vision.

This voice may also be understood as addressed to the apostles:

“Eat and drink.”

As though he were saying: “Let there be joy or refreshment for us from the conversion of the peoples who pass into your fellowship.”

“The voice of my beloved knocking: ‘Open to me, my sister, my beloved, my dove, my undefiled one.’”

The Lord knocks when he teaches what is good through holy doctrine. He knocks at the door of our heart when he stirs us toward the fruit of virtues. The Church opens when she makes the innermost parts of her heart accessible to him.
