She is called “sister” because she is co-heir through Christ’s blood; “beloved” because she is privy to his mysteries, or because of her love, since she keeps what is commanded; “dove” because she is illumined by the gift of the Holy Spirit; “undefiled” because she alone is worthy of the sight of God.

“For my head is full of dew, and the locks of my head with drops of the night.”

The head of Christ is God. The locks are the gatherings of the faithful. In the dew and drops of the night, the cooling of charity in many is shown, although they ought to possess charity toward God and neighbor. Therefore the Lord necessarily stirs each of the faithful toward preaching [the text breaks off at the page boundary].

[Heading partly illegible: *Commentary on the Song of Songs*]

[Scan page 312]

… that they may stir them to work, the Church replies:

> “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on again?”

As though she plainly said: “I have abandoned secular affairs for your sake; how shall I take them up again?”

> “I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them again?”

That is: “I have already washed the thoughts of earthly things with the tears of secret compunction; how shall I again defile myself with filth?” For the office of preaching cannot exist without secular occupation. Another interpretation: The priests in the Church, who within the congregation of the faithful administer visible sacraments, are represented as certain curls in an ornament. But because they are often obscured either by the vanity of this mortal life or by works of darkness, or seem, weighed down by the drops of night, almost to cling to Christ, yet do not sincerely acknowledge the same Christ, therefore the bride, grieving over such persons, continues:

> “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on again? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them again?”

That is: “When I came to the faith, I put off the old man according to my former way of life and put on the new. And if, while I was walking upon the earth, any contamination clung to my feet, it has been washed away by Christ. Yet now I see ministers of the sacraments, through whom I am adorned, infected with carnal vices. Shall I allow myself to be defiled again by their bad example, living according to the former evils?”

> “My beloved put his hand through the opening.”

He sends his beloved hand through the opening when, through a hidden and invisible compunction, the Lord kindles us to works of virtue, teaches us to pass through the narrow and difficult way to the kingdom of heaven, and recalls to our memory how and how greatly he suffered for us, descending from the bosom of the Father.  

> “And my belly trembled at his touch.”

The bride, reflecting upon this within her conscience, wholly terrified, hastens to the labor of preaching, accusing herself of the sluggishness of repose. Morally: He sends his hand through the opening when our Lord, by his power, strikes our inner chamber through subtle understanding. And her belly trembled at his touch because our weakness, when it delights in the understanding of heavenly joy, is troubled by that very exaltation; fear arises in the mind because it already senses something of heavenly joy, yet still fears that it may fail to attain what it barely perceives. What, then, remains except what follows?

> “I rose to open to my beloved; my hands dripped with myrrh, and my fingers were full of the finest myrrh.”

This is the voice of the bride. To rise is to awaken to a vigilant heart. To open is to preach the word of God or to utter a sincere confession. In the hands are signified works; in the fingers, discernment or martyrs. In the myrrh is the mortification of the flesh or sufferings. These are then most precious when they arise solely from love of God and neighbor, whether as continence or as suffering.

> “I opened the bolt of my door to my beloved.”

The Church opens the bolt to her bridegroom because she makes the temple of her breast worthy of divine visitation and indwelling.

> “But he had turned aside and gone away.”

Because no one in this life possesses the fullness of the vision of God, as it will be granted in the future, he is said to have gone away, since in the future he will reveal himself more fully to be seen and enjoyed.  

> “My soul melted when my beloved spoke.”

The Church perseveres in wonder and astonishment at herself. “The more sweetly,” she says, “I received the voice and nearness of my beloved, the more sublimely whatever coldness was in me was kindled by love, and whatever was rigid melted.”

> “I sought him and did not find him.”

For the gift of compunction and inward sweetness is not at the disposal of the one who wishes it, but depends upon the mercy of the giver. Therefore they do not always possess it equally, because God offers himself differently to those who labor in exile and to those who reign in their homeland.

> “The watchmen who patrol the city found me; they struck me and wounded me; the watchmen of the walls took away my veil.”

The watchmen of the city—that is, of the Church—are the holy teachers, who by diligent preaching surround the hearts of individuals. They wound them with the darts of heavenly love, so that they may burn more ardently with divine love; and, as it were, they remove from them the veil of their former way of life.

The watchmen of the city may also be understood as the powers of this age, who are known to govern the commonwealth as though it were a city. For, seizing the chosen Church at its beginnings, when it believed in Christ, they devastated it with blows and torments, killing its priests and ministers, and, as it were, taking away a veil from its adornment.

> “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem: if you find my beloved, tell him that I am faint with love.”

Who are the daughters of Jerusalem? Here Jerusalem, as has often been said, signifies the faith; and the bride rightly languishes when, struck by the sword of God’s word, she removes the earthly garment of her actions. She adjures the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, souls worthy of God—to report to God the greatness of her love and to ask heavenly assistance for herself, that she may see his glory.

> “What is your beloved more than another beloved, O most beautiful among women? What is your beloved more than another beloved, that you have so adjured us?”

This is the voice of the holy preachers questioning the bride and seeking to learn the faith of the Church from her answer. They say, in effect: “I beg you, since you have so adjured me, show me the love with which you say that you languish for me, and reveal what kind of beloved he is above another beloved—that is, the Son from the Father, God from God—and in what way he may be loved rather than feared; for ‘perfect love casts out fear.’”

> “My beloved is white and ruddy, distinguished above thousands.”

The beloved of the Church, Christ, is white because he is without sin. Alternatively, he is called white according to the saying, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” He is ruddy because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” Alternatively, white in virginity, ruddy in the blood of his passion. Distinguished above thousands because he alone is the mediator between God and human beings.

[Scan page 313]

> “His head is the finest gold.”

The head of Christ is God. As nothing among metals is better than gold, so nothing among creatures can be compared with the Creator, because he alone is good and supremely good.

> “His locks are like clusters of palms, black as a raven.”

The locks of Christ are the multitudes of saints who cling to God in faithful service. They are like clusters of palms according to the Apostle’s saying:

> “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3).

They are black because of contempt among human beings, or because they acknowledge themselves to be sinners. They may also be called raised up because of victory and black because of affliction. The bridegroom praised the beauty of the bride; therefore the bride returns the favor and praises him.

> “His eyes are like doves beside streams of water.”

That is, they are the holy teachers through whom the Church sees what is right. They are rightly compared with doves because of their simplicity and innocence, and with streams of water because of the divine gifts.

> “Washed in milk and resting beside abundant waters.”

He says “washed in milk,” that is, cleansed by the sweetest grace, or purified through baptism. The abundant waters are the overflowing abundance of all spiritual gifts. The streams may signify instruction from the Old Law, and the abundant waters the perfection of evangelical teaching, because the holy preachers bring forth from their treasures things new and old (Matthew 13).

> “His cheeks are like beds of spices, planted by perfumers.”

In the cheeks of our Savior are expressed both his gentle piety and his severity. The beds of spices signify his virtues, sweetness, and fame of glory. “Planted by perfumers” means that the prophets and apostles, narrating the future mysteries of his incarnation and his deeds, planted them.

Alternatively: As the apostles are understood in the eyes, so in his cheeks the Church is understood: those who believed at the beginning through the apostles and, by their holy way of life, produced from themselves virtues like beds of spices, planted—that is, instructed—by pious preachers.

> “His lips are lilies, distilling the finest myrrh.”

His lips are the words of teaching. They are called lips because they promise the heavenly kingdom with radiant clarity. They distill the finest myrrh because they preach that one must reach it through contempt for present pleasures.

Alternatively: The lips of Christ are his teachers, virgins in mind and even in body. They preach his passion and death, so that for him who died for us we may not refuse to undergo death.

> “His hands are golden, wrought on the lathe,” and so forth.

His hands are his works, because what he taught in words he fulfilled in deeds. They are turned gold because they contain in themselves the whole rule of righteousness, as he himself says:

> “For thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matthew 3).

They are called golden because everything he did as a human being was filled with the glory of his divinity. They are full of hyacinths, because he awakens in us hope of heavenly things and love for them, since hyacinth is a gem of an ethereal color.

Christ’s hands may also signify those appointed to perform good works: they do not cease to perform good works, but persevere continually for the hope of the kingdom of heaven and are ready to complete what they undertake.

[Running heading: Angelomus, monk of Luxeuil]

[Heading: *Exposition on the Song of Songs*]

> “His belly is ivory, adorned with sapphires.”

The belly of the beloved signifies the frailty of his humanity. Ivory signifies the beauty of chastity; sapphire, the sublimity of heavenly virtues. It is adorned with sapphires because in it are understood partly the frailty of humanity—hunger, temptation, weariness, and death—and partly the loftiness of divinity—miracles, resurrection, and the glory of the ascension.

By the belly may also be understood those who, believing in Christ, bring forth a good work within the body of Christ. The ivory belly may be the fountain of holy baptism, or ivory may signify perseverance in chastity: from it all believers are born into the faith and persevere in the chastity of faith and mind.

> “His legs are marble columns founded upon golden bases.”

By the word “legs” are suggested the paths of Christ’s incarnation, which are compared with marble columns because of their firmness and uprightness. They are founded upon golden bases because whatever was done through him or concerning him had been arranged, according to the counsel of the divine promise, before the ages.

Alternatively: The legs, which carry the whole body, are those who uphold the house of the Church like columns. In both the tabernacle and the Temple, silver columns were fashioned as a sign of the teachers who support the structure of the Church. They are founded upon golden bases—that is, upon the preaching of the fathers who came before, and strengthened by the books of the Law and the Gospel.

> “His appearance is like Lebanon.”

As Lebanon surpasses other mountains in the height and beauty of its trees, so the Lord Christ surpasses all the saints in the height of their merits and the beauty of their virtues.

> “He is chosen like a cedar.”

As the cedar surpasses in dignity the other trees born on Lebanon, so Christ surpasses in glory all those who are born into life in the Church.

> “His throat is most sweet, and he is altogether desirable.”

In the throat, the inward sweetness of his words is recalled; whoever has tasted it does not hunger. His throat may also signify those who expound the mysteries of Christ and meditate daily upon his law, bringing forth the word of preaching from their mouths.

And he is altogether desirable. O human being, what more do you seek? He is altogether desirable because he is wholly God and wholly human, the one upon whom the angels desire to look. God in the majesty of the Father, human in the virginity of his mother: in the former, Creator; in the latter, Savior.

> “Such is my beloved, and he is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem.”

The Church speaks with exultant joy over the reconciliation and over the mysteries of her bridegroom, now known to her, as though she were rejoicing and had become more familiar, saying: “The more devotedly anyone loves God, the more familiarly he possesses him as a friend. And,” she says, “you must understand him in this way if you wish to have him as your friend.”

[Scan page 314]

> “Where has your beloved gone, O most beautiful among women? Where has your beloved turned? We will seek him with you.”

This is the voice of the young women speaking to the bride. For the sake of the beauty of the poem, the persons speaking are varied; nevertheless, this most beautiful woman among women signifies the Church of Christ, expressed under the name of the bride. Each of the holy churches is beautiful, but the whole of the holy Church throughout the world is the most beautiful.

Alternatively: The holy Church is rightly called the most beautiful among women because she is a virgin and undefiled. To her the Apostle says:

> “For I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11).

The women, then, are the peoples of the heretics, Jews, and hypocrites, corrupted in faith and conduct. The Church alone is most beautiful, not only through the font of baptism and the variety of virtues, but in faith and conduct, having neither stain nor wrinkle.

The young women say: “Where has your beloved turned? We will seek him with you”—that is, “He who once lived upon earth in bodily form, tell us where he has turned, so that we may follow him with you.”

### Chapter VI

> “My beloved has gone down into his garden, to the beds of spices,”

and the rest. As though he had said: “He has ascended to the place from which he descended.” He goes into the garden—that is, into his Church—to irrigate it with the fountain of his grace, so that it may germinate with the flowers of virtues.

Alternatively: The beloved of the Church, Christ, went down into his garden when he visited his former people. He calls the holy virgin Mary, from whom he was born according to the flesh, a bed of spices:

> “To pasture in the gardens and gather lilies.”

That is, he reigns among the nations, or delights in the Churches, so that from them he may take up virgins and saints. Alternatively:

> “To pasture in the gardens and gather lilies.”

He pastures in the gardens when he delights in the labors of the pious saints. He gathers lilies when he leads to the heavenly kingdoms those who attain the whiteness of perfect merits.

> “I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine, who pastures among the lilies.”

The Church speaks this out of the confidence of her love. “For my beloved I prepare within me a place of habitation, and he prepares one for me with himself. I am his kingdom, and he is my king. I am his body, and he is my head. He always pastures—that is, delights—in the holy desires of chaste minds or bodies.”

Up to this point it is the voice of the holy Church seeking and praising; now what the one sought answers is added:

> “You are beautiful, my friend, sweet and fair like Jerusalem, terrible as an army drawn up in battle array.”

You are beautiful, holy Church, through righteousness; friend because you are always peaceful—for Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace,” and by that name the heavenly homeland is expressed.

The holy Church is called sweet and fair like Jerusalem because her life and desire are compared with the inward vision of peace. In loving her Creator and desiring to see his appearance, of whom it is written, “Into whom angels desire to look” (1 Peter 1), she is said to be like the angels through the desires of her love.

The more pleasing she becomes to God, the more she acts so as to become terrifying to evil spirits. How she is terrifying is shown by the comparison that follows: an army drawn up in battle array is terrifying to its enemies when it has been so compacted and massed that it appears broken at no point. For if it is arranged so that an empty place is left through which the enemy may enter, it is plainly no longer terrifying to its foes.

Therefore, when we set the line of spiritual battle against evil spirits, we must take the greatest care to be always joined and built together through love, and never found broken by discord. For what good works can exist among us if love is absent? Through the evil of discord a place is opened in the line, through which the enemy may enter and strike us.

The ancient enemy does not fear chastity in us if it is without love, because he is not weighed down by the flesh and cannot be dissolved into its lust. He does not fear abstinence, because he does not use food and is not pressed by bodily necessity. He does not fear the distribution of earthly goods if works of love are lacking in them, because he himself has no need of the resources of riches. What he greatly fears in us is true love—that is, the humble love we show to one another. He greatly envies our concord because we hold on earth what he, unwilling to preserve it, lost in heaven.

Therefore it is rightly said, “Terrible,” and so forth: evil spirits fear the multitude of the elect insofar as they see them united and gathered together against them through the concord of love.

> “Turn your eyes away from me, for they have made me fly away.”

That is: Do not seek to know me perfectly with the eyes of your mind along the road of your pilgrimage, for this cannot happen. The more earnestly you seek to know me, the more certainly you understand that I am incomprehensible. Nor should you seek on the way the reward that is reserved for you in your homeland.

Alternatively, it may be understood as though he said: “Why do you continually seek to behold bodily the one whom you always see better through faith? For this reason I ascended into heaven, so that I might always appear to you as one localized in a place.””

> “Your hair is like flocks of goats that have come up from Mount Gilead.”

These verses were explained earlier, but repetition is an indication of firmness. In the hair are understood the peoples, in the teeth the teachers, and in the twin clusters the precepts of love.

> “Your cheeks are like the rind of a pomegranate, without your eyes.”

The spiritual fathers of the Church are her cheeks, as we said above. They are wondrous in virtues and venerable in conduct, and are not ashamed to glory in the cross of Christ. These things seen in her are very great, but those not seen and reserved for the future are much greater. Hence the Prophet says:

> “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Psalm 44).

> “There are sixty queens, eighty concubines, and young women without number.”

The queens are those who, out of love for the bridegroom and in view of the heavenly reward, by preaching the truth and faith and by the font of sacred baptism, beget spiritual offspring for the eternal King.

The number six pertains to the perfection of the present life, because of the six days in which it is permitted to perform good works. The concubines signify the simple within the Church, who, having received the seed of the word, understand it not spiritually but carnally; or those who teach Christ in some carnal fashion, merely preaching or baptizing.

The young women are souls newly reborn in Christ, whose number, because of the multitude of the heavenly citizens, transcends enumeration. In the young women may also be understood those who always desire to hear what is holy, but do not take care to fulfill in their works what they have heard.

> “One is my dove, my perfect one; one is she to her mother, the chosen one of her who bore her.”

The universal holy Church throughout the whole world is one. Her mother is the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the mother of us all; from her the grace of the Holy Spirit descends upon us, through which we are reborn to God.

She is called one because, after all the reprobate have been expelled, she alone will be joined to Christ.

> “The daughters of Zion saw her and called her most blessed; the queens and concubines praised her.”

Those whom he previously called young women he now calls daughters. The queens and concubines are the same as before, all of whom praise the catholic Church.

> “Who is this who rises like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army drawn up in battle array?”

This is the voice of the Synagogue, admiring the beauty of the Church from among the nations, because, without the judgments of the Law and the instruction of the prophets, she so suddenly grew to such perfection of virtues at the preaching of the Gospel, just as it had already admired above.

For it says: “Who is this who rises like the dawn,” and so forth. The Church advances like the dawn because, after the darkness of long ignorance, the true light is already shown to have risen in her, or because, leaving behind the works of darkness, she lives chastely and soberly and moves toward the perfect day.

> “Beautiful as the moon,”

because, illumined by the sun of righteousness, she illuminates the night of the world.

> “Chosen as the sun,”

because she bears the image of her Creator in all justice, holiness, and truth.

Alternatively: “Beautiful as the moon” refers to virtue and beauty in the present age; “chosen as the sun” to future blessedness. Or “beautiful as the moon” refers to married people, and “chosen as the sun” to virgins. She is terrible to the powers of the air through the power of binding and loosing, ordered in the unity of faith, hope, and love, and in the arrangement of the mysteries.

> “I went down into the garden of nuts, to see the fruits of the valleys.”

The garden of nuts is the present Church, where we do not yet clearly see one another’s consciences; but when the shell of the flesh or body is broken by temptation, the taste of inward sweetness will appear.

The fruits of the valleys are fruits of humility. For the holy Church descends through holy teachers to see who are advancing toward the fruits of good works and who still require the watering of instruction.

The garden of nuts may also designate the canon of the New and Old Testament, in which, beneath the covering of the letter, as beneath a shell, the spiritual meaning lies hidden.

> “To see whether the vines had blossomed,”

that is, whether the faithful people had blossomed in the pursuit of virtues,

> “and whether the pomegranates had budded.”

That is, whether they had prepared themselves, after the example of the Lord’s passion, to shed their own blood.

> “I did not know; my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Amminadab.”

This is the voice of the Synagogue: “I did not know that the gift of spiritual grace was in you, O bride; but my soul troubled me because of the chariots of the New Testament and the Gospel.”

For Amminadab is interpreted as “my people is spontaneous,” that is, Christ, who is carried throughout the whole world.

The Church immediately replies to console her:

> “Return, return, O Shulammite; return, return, that we may look upon you.”

That is: “Do not remain troubled, but return to the knowledge of your Redeemer, who was promised to you beforehand in the prophets and the Law. Return in purity of faith; return in perfection of works. O Shulammite”—that is, captive—“return now from the bonds of unbelief to your Redeemer, that you may be saved.”

### Chapter VII

> “What will you see in the Shulammite, except the chorus of armies?”

That is: “You who grieve over the hardened Synagogue will soon see in her the choirs of those who fight against evil spirits and praise God.”

It may also be understood otherwise: “My soul troubled me because of the chariots of Amminadab.” What did Christ not know except sin? He did not know even those to whom he will say at the judgment:

> “Truly I tell you, I do not know you” (Matthew 25).

By the chariots of Amminadab he means the evangelists. For Amminadab is interpreted as “my people is spontaneous,” that is, the faithful people of the Church.

This Shulammite signifies the Church, whose figure was represented by that Shulammite in the Book of Kings. Because she is adorned with Christ’s blood—*coccinea* means “scarlet” in Latin—she is frequently told by the holy preachers:

> “Return,”

so that even if she has sinned amid adversity, she may not fall into despair, but may recover from her habit of sinning with hope of pardon.

> “How beautiful are your steps in sandals, O daughter of the prince!”

Now the praises of the Church are spoken by the bridegroom himself. First, the constancy of her works and the mortification of pleasures are praised in her; and he calls her the daughter of the prince—that is, of Christ—because of the grace of baptism and the nobility of her virtues.

> “The joints of your thighs are like necklaces fashioned by the hand of an artist.”

The concord of two peoples, made fruitful by a special offspring, is signified by the joining of the thighs. They are like necklaces fashioned by the hand of an artist—that is, by the ineffable generosity of our Creator. Good works are expressed in the necklaces.

> “Your navel is like a turned bowl, never lacking mixed wine.”

Your navel is the frailty of our weakness. The bowl becomes turned when, mindful of our mortality, we strive with ready minds to offer the cup of the saving word.

The navel may also signify those who dwell not at the extremity but in the middle of the body of the Church. In them useful things are stored. It is turned because they are always ready to obey and to perform every good work. It never lacks mixed wine because they are filled completely with the grace of the Holy Spirit.

[Scan page 316]

> “Your belly is like a heap of wheat, enclosed with lilies.”

Those who always receive the nourishment of the holy Scriptures, gather within themselves what is wholesome, and, distributing their teaching to others like wheat, do not cease to preach, are represented by the belly.

A heap of wheat enclosed with lilies exists when an abundance of good works is gathered solely through the hope of perpetual light. In the belly is expressed memory; in the wheat, the multiplication of good works; in the lilies, the chastity of hope.

> “Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle.”

This verse was discussed above, but repetition is an indication of firmness. The two breasts are the teachers of the two peoples. They are twin fawns because of their single concord.

The two breasts of the Church are also the two Testaments, fitted to the two peoples who come from the stock of sin. For they are reborn in Christ like fawns and suck the milk of wisdom from these two Testaments.

> “Your neck is like an ivory tower.”

The teachers are signified by the neck; they are compared with an ivory tower because of their firmness and beauty, since they provide strength and adornment to the city of God.

The neck may also signify knowledge of the holy Scriptures, which is called an ivory tower because those who devote themselves to the word of God advance through daily progress in righteousness to higher things.

> “Your eyes are like pools in Heshbon, beside the gate of the daughter of the multitude.”

The eyes of the Church are the teachers, because of their foresight, just as the neck is so called because of nourishment. They are rightly compared with pools because they never cease to provide their hearers with streams of teaching.

Heshbon is interpreted as “belt of sorrow,” because the saints, rejecting the empty joy of the flesh, are bound with the belt of abstinence. And rightly are they said to be beside the gates of the daughter of the multitude, because of the abundance of peoples entering the Church through the gate of faith. Christ himself may also be understood by the gate.

> “Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon.”

By the nose are designated the ministers of the word of God, because of their discernment. Perceiving the fragrance of righteousness that is in Christ, they offer it to their hearers; and through intellectual discernment they distinguish from above between the fragrance of virtues and the stench of vices.

They are compared with a tower because through wisdom they hold the highest place in the Church. It looks toward Damascus—that is, toward the bloodthirsty and impious—for Damascus is interpreted as “drinking blood” and signifies the carnal and cruel. Against these the holy teachers, in the tower of Lebanon—that is, in the firmness of the Church—keep continual watch.

> “Your head is like Carmel, and the locks of your head like purple bound in channels.”

In the head, faith is signified; in the locks, thoughts. And just as the head governs the members, so thoughts are governed by the mind, so that they may be occupied in Carmel—that is, in the sublimity of virtues—and in the passion of Christ, expressed under the name of purple.

The channels are the inner hearts of the saints, in which such thoughts are bound.

Alternatively: The head of the Church is Christ, above whom nothing is higher. The locks of the head are the more eminent of the saints, namely the blessed martyrs, joined like purple to royal ornaments and salutary doctrines.

> “How beautiful and fair you are, my dearest, in delights!”

The Church is called beautiful in faith and conduct, fair in the ornaments of virtues, and dearest through love; “in delights,” that is, in spiritual virtues.

> “Your stature is like a palm tree, and your breasts like clusters of grapes.”

That is, the uprightness of good works always tends toward victory. The breasts are compared with the teachers of the Church because of the milk of their first instruction, and with grape clusters because of the sweet mysteries of eternity.

> “I said, ‘I will climb the palm tree; I will take hold of its fruit.’”

The most victorious cross is compared with a palm tree, and Christ, climbing upon it, took hold of its fruit. Those climb the palm tree who advance through the cross of Christ. Concerning this the Apostle says:

> “Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires” (Galatians 5).

> “And your breasts will be like clusters of the vine.”

That is, they are the gifts which he bestowed upon the holy Church, which from that time caused clusters of the vine to sprout—that is, holy teachers who, after the Savior’s cross and resurrection, abounded in greater wisdom and grace.

The breasts may also be understood as the preachers of the Church, who nourish those being reborn in the faith.

> “And the fragrance of your breath will be like the fragrance of apples. Your throat will be like the finest wine to drink.”

In the throat the doctrine of the present is signified; in the fragrance, the hope of what is absent. The throat is compared with wine because of the ardor of virtues; the fragrance with apples because of the sweetness of absent things.

> “Worthy for my beloved.”

The bride takes up the word from the mouth of the bridegroom, because he compared her with the finest wine and subjected it to her. “Worthy for my beloved”—that is, the sublimity of evangelical preaching is so great that my beloved, appearing first through the incarnation, opened the heavenly way to the world.

The throat may also signify those who, through evangelical preaching, stir the hearts of their hearers to love; hence Christ is said to drink from it, when from the Christians who are his members he is satisfied with incomparable sweetness.

> “For drinking, worthy of my beloved, passing over his lips and teeth for chewing.”

That is, the apostles and preachers, whom he especially appointed for meditation.

> “I am my beloved’s,”

and not another’s, to whom I devote all the care of service and love.

> “And his turning is toward me.”

That is, he loves me alone and helps me, so that I may not fail along the way. To this beloved, and truly to the Church, the Psalmist says:

> “My soul clings to you; your right hand upholds me” (Psalm 62).

> “Come, my beloved; let us go out into the field, let us stay in the villages. Let us rise early for the vineyards; let us see whether the vine has blossomed, whether the flowers have produced fruit, whether the pomegranates have blossomed.”

For the Church must in every way either go forth to advance toward the performance of good, or persist in the exercise of good works …

[scan page 317]

**614 — ANGELOMI LUXOVIENSIS MONACHI — 623**

“...or at least to linger in the intention of doing good. It is enough to rise up toward the purpose of good action, or to discern how much his hearers have progressed, unless aided by the grace of God, who said: ‘Behold, I am with you all days, until the end of the age’ (Matthew 28:20).”

Christ goes out with the Church into the field when, through holy teachers, he visits the world. He dwells in the villages, that is, by faith among believing peoples from the nations, scattered everywhere. In the morning he rises toward the vineyards, so that the souls which have already deserved to be gathered through faith may recognize in the morning that Christ has risen and no longer doubt the resurrection of his body.

“Let us see whether the vineyard has flowered, whether the Church flowers and brings forth fruit, whether the flowers bring forth fruit”—that is, whether the holy faithful proclaim with their mouths what they have believed in their hearts. “Whether the pomegranates have flowered”: whether those who have believed in Christ advance in such great love that they even take delight in being killed for him. For each of these things the bride seeks [the reading is uncertain] from her beloved.

“There I will give you my breasts,” that is, the instructors of my little ones. Because holy teachers advance in all these matters, in this holy confession my teachers will be joined to you. And because they are prepared to suffer for you, they will reign with you.

“The mandrakes have given forth their fragrance at our gates.” There are two kinds of mandrake, male and female. The female is red, the male white; both possess the same medicinal power. They are called mandrakes because they have sweet-smelling fruits, as large as an apple; hence the Latin name *malum terrae*, “earth-apple.” The poets call it *anthropomorphon* (ἀνθρωπόμορφον, “human-shaped”), because its root resembles the shape of a human being. It is given to drink in wine; the body of the person to whom it is administered must be cut, so that, having been put to sleep, he may not feel the pain.

Because of their many kinds of medicinal properties, mandrakes are compared with the virtues of the saints. Like physicians, these virtues are shown to heal souls from the sicknesses of vices for their salvation. The gates of the Church are the holy teachers; at such gates the mandrakes give forth their fragrance when spiritual persons scatter the palm of virtue far and wide from themselves.

“All fruits, new and old, my beloved, I have kept for you.” The new and old fruits are the commandments or promises of the New and Old Testament, all of which the Church refers to his grace. Alternatively, the Fathers of the New and Old Testament may be understood, because there is one and the same Church.

**CHAPTER VIII**

“Who will give me my brother, sucking the breasts of my mother?” This is the voice of the ancient righteous, longing for the coming of Christ in the flesh and for his being born and nourished in the Synagogue according to the condition of human nature.

“That I may find you outside and kiss you.” The beloved was within when “in the beginning was the Word”; outside when “the Word became flesh.”

“And I will kiss you”: I will speak face to face and mouth to mouth. I believe enough has been said about this kiss at the beginning of the book.

“And now no one will despise me.” Before Christ’s coming, the Church was confined within the narrow boundaries of Judaea; after the Ascension, it was expanded throughout the whole world and made venerable. Earlier it had been said: “God is known in Judaea”; now it is said: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory above all the earth.”

It may also be understood in another way. Christ sucks his mother’s breasts when the Christian people are nourished by the histories of the ancient Law. The Synagogue is called the mother of the Church, that is, of the body of Christ. To her the divine utterances were entrusted at the beginning; what was concealed under figures in the Old Testament is found through the Gospel in the New in its truth.

“I will take hold of you,” that is, I will receive you when you come with ready and faithful devotion.

“And I will lead you into the house of my mother.” When the dispensation of the flesh has been completed, I will lead you, returning with joyful lights, into the house of my mother, that is, the heavenly Jerusalem, which is our mother.

“There you will teach me,” that is, you will make me hope for better gifts than I had possessed under the Law.

“And I will give you a cup of spiced wine,” that is, fervent love fragrant or adorned with various spices of virtue.

“And the new wine of my pomegranates,” that is, the triumph of the glorious holy martyrs, who do not hesitate to pass over to you through iron and flames with the most fervent love.

Alternatively: the Church leads Christ into the house of the heavenly mother, Jerusalem, when she herself deserves to be led there together with all the good things she has obtained through his grace. There she is taught “to see no longer in a riddle through mirrors, but face to face,” when she has produced the best and sweetest fruits of martyrdom, like the new wine of pomegranates.

“His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me.” In the left hand are expressed the gifts of Christ’s incarnation; in the right, the future joys of the saints with Christ. Or, in the left hand is the present life, which the saints place beneath the head of their understanding because they despise it; in the right is blessedness, which the saints will embrace because of their immense desire. This verse has been discussed above at greater length and in sufficient detail.

“Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, overflowing with delights?” We have also discussed this passage earlier, but because repetition of verses—as we have often said—is an indication of firmness, let us now touch upon it briefly.

This is the voice of the Synagogue or of the prophet, wondering how the Church had suddenly come up from the wilderness of the nations into the embrace of the bridegroom. To her it is said through the prophet: “Because you were forsaken and hated” (Isaiah 60), and so forth. And in the Psalm: “They wandered in the wilderness, in a waterless place” (Psalm 106).

“Overflowing with delights,” that is, with the beauty of all gifts.

“Leaning upon my beloved.” She refers everything she possesses to his grace, established in him through faith, hope, and charity, whom they believed should be entrusted to me alone.

“I awakened you beneath the apple tree.” The bride responds on behalf of the Synagogue. “I delivered you from perpetual death beneath the tree of the cross,” says the bridegroom, “so that you might be the apostles and the other elect from Judaea.”

“There your mother was corrupted; there your mother gave birth in pain”—that is, the greater part of the people, by denying Christ and choosing Barabbas, corrupted itself at the cross.

[scan page 318]

**ENARRATION ON THE SONG OF SONGS**

“Set me as a seal upon your heart, and as a seal upon your arm.” We bind a seal upon the arm or finger for the remembrance of any matter. By “heart,” thought is signified; by “arm,” action. That is: if you wish to have me as your bridegroom, let there be within you charity with sincere faith, and outwardly devoted action. Regard my faith in such a way that you preserve it undefiled.

And because through my cross you have received a seal, do not fear that the treasure of righteousness which I have bestowed upon you may be stolen by any thief. In both thought and action, return to that sign. Just as I loved you so greatly that I was willing to die for you, so, conversely, let your saints not refuse death for me.

“For love is strong as death, jealousy hard as hell.” My love for you, O Synagogue, is strong even unto death; but your jealousy against me was hard as hell. Turn your jealousy into love, and you will be to me bride, sister, and friend.

“Her lamps are lamps of fire and flame.” The lamps of love are the hearts of the faithful, in which charity dwells. They are always radiant and pure with the brightness of charity, burning with the fire of the Holy Spirit and shining with the flame of good works.

“Many waters could not extinguish love, nor will rivers overwhelm it.” By “many waters” and “rivers” he means the assaults of temptations, which visibly or invisibly attack the souls of the faithful, but to which charity does not yield.

“If a man were to give all the substance of his house for love, they would despise it as nothing.” Those who give the riches of their entire substance because of the greatness of Christ’s love despise the world as nothing.

The meaning may also depend upon what precedes. After he had said that “many waters” or rivers could not extinguish charity, he added: “If a man were to give all the substance of his house,” and so forth. This is to be understood in the sense of what the Apostle says: “If I distribute all my possessions to feed the poor, and if I deliver my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:3).

“My little sister is small and has no breasts. What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be addressed?” This designates the first period of the Church born from the nations, when she was still small in number and less capable of preaching the Word, as the Apostle says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as little ones in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Corinthians 3:1–2).

It is as though the bridegroom or the apostles had said of her to the Synagogue: “What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be addressed?” As if he said openly: The Church of the nations is indeed small and not yet sufficient to undertake the mystery of God’s word. What, then, do you think should be done about our sister, O Synagogue, when she is to be addressed—that is, when through the mystery of the word she is to be led into faith?

While the Synagogue remains silent, the bridegroom himself, or the apostles, answered what ought to be done.

“If she is a wall, let us build upon her silver battlements.” As if he said: If she has within her people strong in faith, distinguished in intellect, or trained in philosophy, let us add to them silver battlements—that is, knowledge of the divine Scriptures—so that they may more easily protect the weak and the unlearned.

“If she is a door, let us panel her with cedar boards.” That is: if they are simple, but eager in their desire to be taught, and understand, like a door that opens and closes, “a time to keep silence and a time to speak,” let us set before them the examples of the righteous who came before, so that they may fulfill the office of teaching with greater certainty and effectiveness.

The cedars signify the virtues of the saints, and the boards signify the breadth of charity. Thus they may be able to say with the Apostle: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14).

To this the Church herself responded:

“I am a wall, and my breasts are like towers; from that time I became in his presence as one finding peace.” I am built from living stones and joined by the cement of charity; I am established upon an immovable foundation; and my teachers are very strong, like towers. They know how to nourish the little ones and drive out every evil thing. From the time when Christ reconciled me, it happened that I found peace through him.

“A vineyard belonged to the peaceful one, in which the people dwelt; he entrusted it to keepers.” Of this the Apostle says: “He is our peace, who made both one” (Ephesians 2:14). And the prophet says of him: “His dominion will be multiplied, and there will be no end of peace” (Isaiah 9:7).

The vineyard—that is, the Catholic Church—was rich in the fruit of faith. It belonged to the peaceful one, that is, to Christ, who made peace among all things in heaven and on earth. It was in that congregation which possesses many peoples from the whole world, not in Judaea alone. He entrusted it to keepers, to prophets, apostles, those instructed in the Gospel, and angelic powers.

“A man brings a thousand silver pieces for its fruit.” That is, Christ offers the kingdom of heaven in return for the holy labors or almsgiving of his people.

It may also be understood otherwise: “A man brings a thousand silver pieces for its fruit,” that is, as an eternal reward. The man of this vineyard brings a thousand silver pieces for its acquisition of the heavenly kingdom, which is the fruit of the vine, after he has left everything behind for the sake of purity. The number one thousand is taken for the perfection of the person who has abandoned everything. Hence “silver pieces” are understood as all money.

“My vineyard is before me.” This is the voice of the bridegroom, because after the resurrection all the saints will always be with the Lord, as he himself says: “Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24).

Alternatively, it is as though the bridegroom said: Although I entrust you to other keepers, I nevertheless always keep you in my presence, seeing and rewarding the devotion of your labor in all things.

“A thousand are yours, O peaceful one.” “A thousand of yours” means, implicitly, silver pieces. It is as though he said: Let the person who leaves all his possessions for love of me know that they are kept for him in peace. This signifies the simpler members of the Church, who for the love of God abandon every possession marked by the number one thousand.

“And two hundred for those who keep its fruit.”

[scan page 319]

**ANGELOMI LUXOVIENSIS MONACHI ENARRATIO IN CANTICA CANTICORUM**

“...its fruit.” That is, silver pieces for those who keep its fruit: the holy teachers, who abandon all the world’s things and do not cease laboring in the word of preaching. These receive from me a double reward, represented by the number one hundred.

It may also be understood in another way: twelve multiplied by one hundred makes one thousand two hundred. This number appropriately belongs to the apostles or apostolic men. They are called “peaceful ones,” that is, disciples of Christ, and rightly so, because the holy Church is governed by them:

“You who dwell in the gardens, friends listen to you; let me hear your voice.” The Church dwells in gardens, for she has already been filled with the greenness of hope and good works. As if he openly said: Since the authority of the Scriptures must be brought to completion by constant meditation, always remain at the gates of the virtues. Know that friends—that is, angelic spirits and the souls of the saints—are devoted to you and rejoice in your progress.

“Friends also listen,” for all the elect, in order to live again in the heavenly homeland, desire to hear the words of life.

“Let me hear your voice,” that is, the word of preaching and the voice of praise, which, as much as you are able, is always heard by me.

To this the bride responded:

“Flee, my beloved, and be like the gazelle and the fawn of the deer upon the mountains of spices.” As if she openly said: Since, appearing in the flesh, you brought me the commandments and gifts of life, now, these things having been accomplished, return to the bosom of the Father.

“O my beloved, be like the gazelle and the fawn of the deer upon the mountains of spices.” Let this also be a consolation for me: since I cannot see you continually, remember to console me at least by frequent visitation.

Christ is like a gazelle because of the likeness of sinful flesh, for he was born outwardly from the patriarchal stock. He is called a fawn because of the variety of his virtues; with the flesh in which he ascended into heaven, he lived among us on earth.

The mountains of spices signify the angels, above whom the assumed man was exalted, as the Psalmist says: “God has ascended with jubilation, and the Lord with the sound of the trumpet” (Psalm 47:5).

Hence he truly says: “Christ, ascending on high, led captivity captive and gave gifts to men” (Ephesians 4:8). Luke likewise says: “And the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God” (Mark 16:19).

At last, with God’s favor, this book now asks for its conclusion. With his assistance, I believe that I have pursued it to the end by a straight investigation and, according to the examples of the teachers and the weakness of our understanding, in truthful fashion. I have attempted this work, though fearfully and humbly, under your imperial decrees and Augustal authority, O Caesar Augustus.

I humbly and repeatedly beseech the excellence of your eminence not to disdain examining it with subtle investigation, and to read through with your own skill the little works of the holy teachers with the greatest diligence.

For if the emperor Theodosius, born and raised in imperial power, was of such extraordinary excellence that he possessed the singular sovereignty of the whole world, and took care to copy out with his delicate fingers the book of Priscian the grammarian, the distinguished ornament of Roman eloquence, and was accustomed always to live from its price and trading proceeds, despising imperial banquets; and if he flourished with such zeal that by continual meditation and his own transcription he set forth the Roman law, corrected the distorted customs of the Romans with the sword, as it were, of the law’s standard of rectitude, and restrained their harshness—so that, after other matters had been completed, the angelic trumpet sounded from heaven in a nocturnal vision, and through the dream he joyfully raised his voice, saying: “Let not the book of the law depart from your mouth; meditate upon it day and night”—how much more, O most gentle prince, should you sanctify yourself through your own studies, diligently meditating upon the authority of the Scriptures.

Thus you may be instructed in spiritual teaching, advance yourself wisely to the higher things of virtue, and call others to the path of righteousness.

You will not be able to penetrate this more fully, or in a certain sense ascend the mountain of divine Scripture, except through diligent study, purity of heart, and chastity of body. For sacred Scripture, as the commentator mentioned above often says, is a mountain from which the Lord comes into our hearts.

Of this the prophet says: “God will come from Lebanon, and the Holy One from the shadowed and dense mountain.” This mountain is dense because of its meanings and shadowed because of its allegories.

But it must be understood that when a voice sounds upon the mountain, we are commanded to wash our garments and cleanse ourselves from every defilement of the flesh if we hasten to approach the mountain. For it is written: “If a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned” (Hebrews 12:20).

A beast touches the mountain when someone devoted to lust or irrational impulses approaches the height of sacred Scripture and does not understand it as he ought, but bends it irrationally toward the interpretation of his own pleasure. Such an absurd or foolish person, if he is seen near this mountain, is killed by the most terrible judgments, as though by stones.

This mountain burns, because sacred Scripture, which fills the person spiritually, sets him ablaze with the fire of love. Hence it is said through Moses: “At his right hand was a fiery law” (Deuteronomy 33:2). For in the minds of the elect, who are to be placed at the Judge’s right hand, the divine commandments burn and are kindled by the heat of charity.

Therefore, O Augustal majesty and glory of the Frankish people, strive with rational understanding and bodily chastity to ascend this mountain, and, set aflame by the fervor of charity, penetrate it by reading. Thus, according to the merit of your understanding and of the others whom your discerning wisdom will strive to correct, you may at last, with the Lord’s favor, reach the mountains of spices—that is, the heights of the angels—and through the support of their prayers deserve to be placed at the Judge’s right hand with the holy emperors and consuls. May you likewise hear from the Lord:

“Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew 25:21).

Amen.

**ANNO DOMINI DCCLV. — LEO IV — HISTORICAL NOTICE**

*(In the most ample collection of the Councils, volume [corrupted in the scan], page 853.)*

**Leo IV**—of Roman origin, son of Radoald [Pseudoradolphus]—sat for eight years, three months, and five days. He was a very Catholic and apostolic man, of great patience and great humility, generous, devout, innocent, and kind; a most fervent lover of justice and piety, a most excellent governor, and an unceasing student of the divine Scriptures. Always devoted to vigils and prayers, in his most blessed breast, according to what is read in the holy Gospel (Matthew 10:16), there dwelt both the wisdom of the serpent and the simplicity of the dove.

He was filled with the beauty of every holiness, a lover of religious men who continually served God in all things, a nourisher of the poor, and a despiser of himself.

At first, for the study of letters, he willingly entered the monastery of Saint Martin the Confessor of Christ, situated outside the walls of this city of Rome near the church of the blessed apostle Peter, and remained there until he had learned the sacred writings more fully. There he learned not only letters, but also, in the pursuit of holy conduct, remained not as a boy—as he had entered—but as a perfect monk.

By the example of his devout conduct, others living under the same monastic discipline served almighty God with pious devotion, and he lived among them as one of them.

Since “a city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matthew 5:14), the reputation of this most holy man likewise could not long remain concealed. His fame, or the report of his holiness, spread brightly here and there, and through the reports of many faithful people soon reached the ears of the most blessed Father and Pope Gregory. When the latter heard of such great purity and worthy conduct, he immediately ordered him to leave the monastery where he lived devoutly, brought him to the bosom of holy Mother Church, and commanded him to remain familiarly in his service at the Lateran patriarchate.

**He became a subdeacon and afterward a presbyter.**

He also made him a subdeacon because of the fame of his praiseworthy life. Although Leo held the office or rank, he nevertheless bound his life and conduct even more strictly than before to the service of our supreme Creator, and multiplied his good works.

After Gregory, pope of this most sacred see, had died, Sergius, then archpriest of the holy Roman Church, having been made its bishop, consecrated this man—Leo, the most blessed pope, concerning whom we have related some matters above—as a priest, and granted him the title of the Four Holy Crowned Martyrs.

While he was endowed with good morals and ministered there to those in need, he cared for pilgrims and the poor and restored those who had little not only with words, but also with bodily nourishment.

At that time Sergius, bishop of the Roman see, was taken from the present life. During his pontificate the churches of the most blessed princes, Peter and Paul, were also completely plundered by the Saracens.

Because, through this calamity and misery, the strength of all the Romans had been weakened and crushed, the entire assembly of Romans, fearing two dangers—namely, the sudden death of the pontiff and the devastation which had taken place in the holy churches and throughout the territory of the Romans—confessed that it could in no way escape the danger of death.

While all the Roman leaders were considering the future pontiff with equal devotion and common counsel, asking whether there might be someone able to govern and rule such a holy and inviolable office of almighty God in the fear of God, the fame and virtues of the most blessed prelate were immediately revealed by everyone and spread throughout the whole city. The pontiff had not yet been carried to his due burial.

**He was chosen pope by the unanimous decision of all.**

And behold, all, from the last to the first, with one voice and in complete agreement, demanded that Leo, the venerable presbyter, become their future pontiff. They declared, through many oaths and acclamations, that they wished to have no other prelate over them but this man.

We believe that the hearts of all of them were inflamed and united in seeking him by nothing other than divine love and the clemency of divine virtue.

**He was compelled to accept the papacy. The ancient custom of kissing the pope’s feet. The Romans do not dare elect a pope without the emperor’s permission.**

Then all, as noted above, proceeded with joy and great eagerness to the church in which he lived, that of the blessed Four Crowned Martyrs. Forcing and dragging him away against his will, they led him from there with hymns, praises, and distinguished celebrations to the Lateran patriarchate.

He then enclosed the basilica of Saint Peter with a wall, so that it would not remain continually exposed, as before, to the incursions of the Saracens. He consecrated the completed and perfected city with solemn rites and permitted it to be called Leonine after his own name.

Charles, the son of Louis, terrified by a new invasion of the Northmen and lacking counsel, took those same men as partners in the kingdom, granting them the part of the kingdom which, from their name, is called Normandy (the *Annals of Pithoeus*).

**p. [uncertain]. This is entirely false, as will be shown elsewhere.**

**Note (a).** Leo succeeded Pope Sergius II on the day before the Ides of April, in the year of the Lord 847; he was Pope Leo IV, and indeed succeeded on the same day on which Sergius died. At the beginning of his pontificate he miraculously drove from the city a pestilential serpent, a basilisk, and extinguished by the sign of the cross, in a marvelous manner, an immense fire in the city. After the Saracens had stripped the sacred buildings of all their ornament and treasure, he spent great sums on restoring, rebuilding, and adorning them.

When he was entering the second year of his pontificate, he built a new city at God’s command and began to enclose it with walls. [The supplied text breaks off here.]

[scan page 321]

**LEO IV**

The Romans, observing the ancient custom, all kissed his feet. No one can briefly relate how great the agreement and unanimity were in his election to the pontificate.

As for what divine power accomplished against those Saracens, through the prayers of the apostles and their holy intercession, at the time of Leo’s election—those who had committed such a wicked crime—it is not inappropriate or blameworthy to record it in the present writing, whether from fear of what might happen in the future or in remembrance of what had happened.

For when all of them wished to return to the African region from which they had come, after perpetrating the crime of iniquity and plunder, they were, as we learned from a reliable report, drowned by the violence of the sea, through winds and storms, God permitting it.

Thus the prayer of the apostles newly obtained that ancient miracle of the Egyptians.

The Romans, as we have said, rejoiced in the election of the new pontiff, but soon began again to grieve greatly because they did not dare, without imperial authority, to consecrate the future pontiff, and they were especially afraid of danger to the city of Rome, lest it should again be besieged by other enemies, as formerly.

Terrified by this fear and by the danger that might follow, they consecrated him as prelate without the prince’s permission, preserving his faith and honor after God in all things.

**Gifts offered by Leo to the churches of Saint Peter, the Four Crowned Martyrs, Saint Andrew, and Saint Anastasius**

Since human judgment is not sufficient to assess, nor the mouth able to recount, how great was the goodness and piety of this most blessed pontiff, let us return to what he offered to the churches of the saints, trusting in the love of God, and let us recount these gifts from the beginning of his pontificate.

This distinguished and renowned prelate, burning with heavenly love, offered in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter one crown of the purest silver, weighing twenty-four pounds; two engraved *gabathae*, weighing two pounds; and seven curtains, two of *fundatum* fabric, two of *stauracium*, and three of *spaniscum*.

In the same place, for the splendor and glory of that venerable basilica, he offered one Alexandrian curtain of marvelous beauty, bearing a scene of peacocks carrying men above them, and another scene of eagles, wheels, and birds among trees.

That distinguished and prudent pope offered in the basilica of the Four Holy Crowned Martyrs, where he had most diligently exercised his priestly office, three baskets of the purest silver, weighing [an amount omitted].

Likewise, an *aquamanile* of the purest silver, together with a *cantharus* and a censer, weighing [an amount omitted]. Twelve *fundatum* curtains, which appear to hang in the arch of the church for its splendor; thirty-four white silk curtains.

In the same basilica, for the splendor of the sacred altar, he made a silk vestment bearing a border of *chrysoclavus*. He also made a white vestment with roses, having seven roundels and, in the middle, a small panel of *chrysoclavus* with the image of a man wearing five green gems on his head.

Likewise, a white vestment of *chrysoclavus* with six roundels. In the aforementioned basilica, for the honor and glory of the sacred altar, he made thirty-three curtains bearing crosses and *hammadiae* of *chrysoclavus*, gems, and golden bosses.

He also made one embroidered hanging bearing the image of a man seated upon a peacock; three curtains bearing a scene of the holy Mother of God; fourteen other *fundatum* curtains; and two others together with a garment of *blatta*.

That eminent and most blessed pope made in the basilica of the holy Mother of God, situated in the street called the Street of the Sardians, a *fundatum* vestment bearing a scene of the holy Mother of God in *chrysoclavus*, together with prophets.

This beloved and prudent pope also constructed marble seats at the entrance to the patriarchate, which no pontiff had believed he could complete. The gallery which Pope Leo III of blessed memory had built, when it was seen overturned and ruined because its beams had broken through excessive age, he restored anew, more beautifully and in improved form.

This distinguished and devout prelate, relying upon heavenly love, established in the basilica of the blessed apostle Paul, for the evening of his feast, public psalmody and praises by the entire clergy and the choir.

During the time of this blessed prelate, an earthquake occurred in the city of Rome in the tenth indiction, so that all the elements appeared shaken to everyone.

This often-mentioned and most diligent pontiff, in accordance with ancient custom and by canonical authority, decreed and established that, while the solemn rites of Mass were being celebrated in the church, no layperson should presume to stand, sit, or enter in the presbytery, except the sacred people who appeared to be appointed to the administration of the sacred office.

After the slaughter and plunder committed by the savage people of the Hagarenes in the churches of the holy apostles, this most blessed pontiff continually directed his attention to their restoration, so that he might repair everything that had been taken away by impious hands, hoping for the reward of an eternal recompense.

Therefore he offered in the basilica [text breaks off].

**Note (a).** “They did not dare to consecrate the future pontiff.”

That right of confirming elected pontiffs, which had been wrongly promised to the emperors by the Roman people through fear, or most unjustly usurped by the emperors themselves, Pope Leo annulled with great courage and entirely abolished with the consent of those emperors. This can be seen in chapter 31, distinction 63, where a canon is cited from a letter to Lothair and Louis. It reads:

“Between us and you it has been established and confirmed by formal agreement that the election and consecration of the future pontiff must take place only justly and canonically.”

Conversely, Pope Leo promised them that he would preserve the imperial rights inviolate, together with those things which had been established by their Roman predecessors, the pontiffs.

“Regarding the capitularies,” he says (Distinction 10, chapter 9), “or the imperial commands of your authority, and those of our pontiffs and predecessors, which must be preserved and maintained without resistance, we profess that, as far as we have been and are able, with Christ’s favor, we shall preserve them in every way, both now and forever. And if anyone should say, or should have said, anything else to you, know for certain that he is a liar.”

By “capitularies” he means the capitularies of the Frankish kings, which Benedict the Levite collected and published, and which various pontiffs confirmed. Pope Nicholas explains in his letter to Michael what imperial rights these were and in what manner the pontiff promises here to observe them: “That the pontiffs should employ imperial laws only for the worship of temporal things.”

The father of heretics and schismatics declares that these were impostures rather than imperial laws—those laws which, for the vindication of imperial majesty and the confirmation of the elected pontiff, are found to have been issued elsewhere in the name of Lothair and his son Louis.

For it is established in Distinction 10, chapter 13, that Pope Leo demanded from both of them that the Romans be permitted to use their ancient laws.

That Lothair agreed to this request is shown by his rescript preserved among the laws of the Lombards, book 11, title 57. In the same place, book 3, he professes that he had given the peoples or churches no other laws than those collected by Charles the Great and by his father Louis.

Although Louis’s desire to rule Rome and its Church and clergy continued from that time until the age of Pope Nicholas, nevertheless, through divine mercy, he eventually came to his senses and showed himself most obedient to the same Roman pontiffs, so that it is plainly evident from this that whatever that most Christian emperor did at some time was done more through the persuasion of wicked men than of his own accord.

[The text begins mid-sentence:] of blessed Peter the apostle, a basin of the purest silver with seven silver bowls, skillfully worked in chains. Twenty-five curtains of gold-threaded fabric, more beautiful ones, hang around the sacred altar. And forty-six other curtains of gold-threaded fabric gleam between the venerable basilica itself and the choir. There were also eighteen other curtains of gold-threaded fabric, which that beneficent pope arranged to hang in various places of the same basilica. There were also four curtains hanging before the doors of the sacred basilica.

This distinguished and prudent prelate, relying upon heavenly love, made in the basilica of the holy martyrs the Four Crowned Ones a vestment of gold-threaded fabric bearing a representation of the Resurrection of the Lord Jesus Christ and images of the aforesaid martyrs. The spirit of that beneficent prelate himself shone so greatly with divine love that, since innumerable possessions had previously been carried away from the church of the apostle Peter by impious hands, he especially wished, in his own time, gladly and wholeheartedly to restore them all anew.

Therefore, for the adornment and honor of the aforesaid church, he made two crowns of the purest silver, wonderfully fashioned, hanging on silver chains with gems and gilded bosses. One weighed 132 pounds and the other 130; together they had thirty-seven small silver pendants hanging beneath them. He made another in the same manner, having forty.

And because he was always richly adorned by a divine gift and devoted himself happily to the worthy care and solicitude of all things, he made in the oratory of the apostle Andrew at Saint Peter’s two larger curtains of gold-threaded fabric and five other smaller ones, ornamented around the edge with purple silk.

Protected by God, that venerable and illustrious pontiff made in the monastery of Saint Anastasius, for the eternal redemption of his soul, one silk vestment of gold-threaded fabric bearing a representation of eagles. Likewise, two curtains of gold-threaded fabric, trimmed around the edge with purple silk. In the same way he made one vestment of gold-threaded fabric in the monastery of Saint Praxedis.

This aforesaid prelate also, from the day on which, relying upon divine power, he ascended the sacred seat of the apostle Peter with every kindness, immediately strove eagerly and willingly to restore to the memory of his sanctity all the ancient or former usages and ordinances of the sacred palace that had existed under the pontificates of his predecessors but had been abolished by various custom, or to arrange everything in a better condition than it had recently been.

For the dining hall that Pope Leo III, of blessed memory, had built from its foundations, together with all the furnishings he had prepared there, had been brought down through excessive age and the neglect of his pontifical predecessors. On the day of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh, neither Lord Gregory nor Lord Sergius of holy memory had dined there at all. But that same most blessed and supreme prelate, Leo IV, with joy and the greatest affection, repaired anew all the furnishings and provisions that had been removed from there, and magnificently restored them to their former use.

### The cross offered by Charlemagne

He also restored to its former use and splendidly adorned for the holy Church of God and Mother of God, the Roman Church, a cross of the purest gold decorated with gems. Charles, emperor of the Franks and Romans, of pious memory, had offered it in the basilica of our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior, which is called the Constantinian Basilica, during the time of Lord Leo III, of holy memory. It was customary for this cross to precede the most sacred pontiff during the litanies, and so it remained until the time of Lord Paschal, pope of holy memory. Then, through diabolical suggestion, it was extorted by wicked men and secretly stolen by thieves during the night.

None of the pontifical predecessors thereafter—Lord Paschal, Lord Eugenius, Lord Valentine, Lord Gregory, or Lord Sergius—remembered to restore it and repair it for the use of the holy Church of God at Rome. But this same aforesaid and magnificent prelate had one made of the purest gold, skillfully adorned with pearls of extraordinary size and with hyacinth-colored and green gems, and wonderfully beautified it for its former use in the holy Roman Church of the Mother of God.

This foremost and distinguished prelate was highly esteemed as a preacher, learned and accomplished in the knowledge and study of the divine Scriptures. He became so renowned for the fame of his blessedness and sanctity that, in the sight of all the people of this Church founded in Christ, he performed miracles.

In the first year of his pontificate, near the basilica of blessed Lucia the martyr, which is situated in Orfea [Ortea], a serpent of terrible kind arose in certain hidden lands and caverns. In Greek it is called *basiliskos*—that is, “basilisk”—and in Latin *regulus*, “little king.” By its breath and its sight it quickly killed all who approached those same caverns and exposed them to the danger of death. Thus astonishment and fear seized everyone as they marveled at the serpent’s powers and the destruction it caused.

### Pope Leo drives away the basilisk

When that most blessed and illustrious pontiff heard of this slaughter and destruction of the people, he turned to prayer and did not cease to beseech the Lord with fasts, asking that he might free everyone from such a danger. While these things were taking place, the splendid and celebrated day arrived on which the Assumption of blessed Mary, the Mother of God and ever-virgin, is celebrated.

Then the aforesaid universal pope went from the patriarchium with hymns, songs, and spiritual chants, a holy icon preceding him, to the basilica of Saint Adrian the martyr, as is customary, proceeding on foot with all the clergy. Returning from there with the entire gathering of the faithful, he proceeded amid the praises of God and accompanied by a great crowd of people to the basilica of the blessed Mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is called “at the Manger.”

When he had reached the place where, as we said above, that most savage basilisk lay in dark caverns, he ordered all the clergy and people to stand still. He then advanced to those caverns and stood fearlessly over the opening from which the serpent’s deadly breath issued. He raised his eyes and hands equally toward heaven and prayed with abundant tears to Christ, who is God over all, asking that by his power he drive that dreadful serpent’s kind from the place.

After giving a prayer over the people, he proceeded to the basilica mentioned above to offer praises to God. From that very day the pestilential basilisk was driven away and expelled from those caverns, so that thereafter no trace of its harm appeared in those places.

That beneficent pope also performed another miracle, which we shall begin briefly to recount.

### Again, he extinguishes a fire by prayer and the sign of the cross

At the very beginning of his pontificate, mentioned above, a powerful fire seized the Saxon quarter. By the force of its flames it began to consume everything with great violence. Large groups of people gathered there, wishing to extinguish the flames of the fire; but, driven by the blasts of the winds, the fire rose higher into the air, consuming and destroying everything, until it advanced near the basilica of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, burning and ravaging the houses of the Saxons and Lombards and the portico.

When he heard this, the most blessed pontiff hurried there anxiously. He came face-to-face with the advance of the fire and prayed to the Lord to extinguish the flames of that fire. Making the sign of the cross with the fingers of his right hand, he prevented the flames from spreading farther; unable to withstand the power of the pontiff, the fire died down and the flames were reduced to ashes.

## POPE LEO

### Gifts in the church of Saint Peter, of the Four Crowned Ones, and elsewhere

That beloved and prudent pope, protected by God, made in the basilica of the apostle Peter 445 curtains of gold-threaded fabric, trimmed around the edge with purple silk.

That same distinguished pontiff made in the monastery of Saint Martin, which adjoins the basilica of blessed Peter, a very beautiful and spacious vestment for the praise and glory of blessed Martin. It bore the previously mentioned image of the saint lying on a bed, together with an image of our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior. It also bore an image of the holy martyr Agatha, with an image of that beneficent pontiff himself at her feet, and seventeen hyacinth-colored gems. In the same oratory he made four curtains, one of them having three roundels of gold-threaded fabric.

He likewise made in the basilica of the Four Holy Brothers one vestment of gold-threaded fabric bearing a representation of those holy martyrs and an image of that beneficent prelate, with twelve gems. Likewise, four curtains of gold-threaded fabric.

This venerable and illustrious pontiff made in the basilica of the apostle Peter, his patron, a pierced silver basket of the purest silver, weighing [lacuna] pounds. In the place mentioned above he offered crowns of pure silver, weighing [lacuna] pounds.

This most blessed and illustrious pope, relying upon heavenly love, offered to the apostle Peter, for the splendor and glory of his most holy basilica, a two-wicked lamp of the purest silver, weighing forty-five pounds.

The same most blessed prelate made in the church of the confessor and pontiff blessed Silvester, which is located on Mount Soracte, one vestment of gold-threaded fabric having four corners, two of Tyrian purple and two of gold-threaded fabric.

The same most holy and blessed prelate also made in the church of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, ten curtains hanging in the arch of the presbytery, woven of gold and bearing a representation of blessed Peter the apostle.

He also made in the oratory of the confessor and pontiff blessed Leo, situated within the aforesaid church, one vestment of gold-threaded fabric bearing a representation of eagles. In the place mentioned above he offered one silver crown weighing [lacuna] pounds. He also made there twenty curtains of gold-threaded fabric, ornamented on both sides with purple silk.

He also offered to the apostle Peter sixteen silver chalices, which stand around the circumference of the altar, weighing [lacuna] pounds. There was also a hanging chalice with chains and dolphins, weighing [lacuna] pounds.

Likewise, after the Saracens had ravaged this church, the most holy and angelic prelate mentioned above made over the body of the apostle blessed Peter three silver images altogether.
