One, placed in the middle, bore an image of our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior, with gems on his head, ornamented by a cross of hyacinth-colored and green gems. Another was placed on the Savior’s right and bore the faces of the apostle blessed Peter and of blessed Petronilla. Another was placed on the left and depicted the face of the apostle blessed Andrew, together with the face of the aforesaid supreme prelate. They weighed [lacuna] pounds and four ounces.

In the place mentioned above he made twelve bronze beacons, which stand before the vestibule of the sacred altar.

### He restored monasteries and preached to the people. He ordered the octave of the Blessed Virgin to be celebrated

This most blessed pope always greatly desired to rebuild all the places of the saints that had been constructed. For the monastery of Corsarum, situated near the basilica of blessed Felix the confessor and pontiff, had been destroyed through the work of certain wicked men and reduced to secular habitation. For the salvation and future reward of his soul he restored it most completely. There too he established a congregation of handmaids of God to offer the praises of almighty God daily; he increased it with gifts, adorned it with wealth, restored all the sacred furnishings that had been taken away from it, and confirmed them with his own holy fingers.

This often-mentioned and most blessed pope, through the address of his preaching, led many to knowledge of the truth and daily demonstrated salutary actions.

He ordered that the octave day of the Assumption of the blessed Mother of God—which had not previously been celebrated at Rome—should be observed with sacred vigils, spending the night in the basilica of that same ever-virgin, our Lady, with the entire clergy, in hymns and matins. The basilica is situated outside the walls, near the basilica of blessed Lawrence the martyr.

A great multitude of people had also gathered there, eager to celebrate the solemnity of the new feast. When that magnanimous pontiff saw them, he distributed gifts generously among all who were present for this celebration.

That same most blessed man made one vestment of gold-threaded fabric in the church of that same Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary. He also made forty-five curtains there. And within that church, in the oratory called that of blessed Barbara, he offered one vestment of gold-threaded fabric.

### Gifts offered to churches

That foremost prelate, protected by God, made one vestment of gold-threaded fabric in the oratory of Saint Eugenia.

This diligent, most holy, and in every respect distinguished and foremost pontiff, with great generosity and pure intention, offered one vestment of gold-threaded fabric in the church of the blessed protomartyr Stephen, situated outside the walls near the church of blessed Lawrence the martyr.

Within the enclosure of this church, in the oratory of blessed Leo the martyr, he made one vestment of gold-threaded fabric. And this gentle pontiff, discerning in all good things, offered in the church of the blessed Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, our Lady, situated within the aforesaid monastery called Corsarum, one vestment of gold-threaded fabric. In the place mentioned above he offered one vestment of gold-threaded fabric in the oratory of Saint Caesarius.

This most benevolent man also newly made a golden cross. As was customary from ancient times, this cross was carried by subdeacons before the horse of the pontiffs’ predecessors. With God’s help he renewed it more splendidly in gold, silver, and gems.

He offered one vestment of gold-threaded fabric in the church of the blessed martyr Nympha, which is said to be situated in the city of Portus. Similarly, he made one vestment of gold-threaded fabric in the church of the blessed martyrs Cosmas and Damian, which is said to be in Silva Candida. In the place mentioned above he also offered three curtains of gold-threaded fabric ornamented around the edge with purple silk.

This most blessed pope visited the tombs of the most sacred martyrs continually, with devoted mind and burning heart; through sacred vigils and prayers he interceded for the entire people of the orthodox faith.

### He built a monastery

One day, when he had reached the tomb of the blessed martyr Lawrence and was carrying out his prayer in the usual manner, he began to inquire more carefully, saying: “How many monks here daily render praises to almighty God?”

Then all who were present told the blessed pontiff that two monasteries had once been constructed there by certain pontiffs, but through great poverty and extreme want they had been reduced to desolation.

Immediately, moved by a heavenly prompting, that beneficent pontiff restored the monastery that is now called that of Saints Stephen and Cassian, and adorned the place most fully with gifts and riches. In it he also established several monks of Greek origin, of holy conduct, to offer praises day and night to almighty God and to the blessed martyr.

[scan page 324]

## NOTICE

That same man, protected by God and a venerable prelate, constructed within the basilica of the apostle blessed Peter an oratory of extraordinary beauty and supreme elegance. He surrounded and splendidly adorned it with beautiful marble, and decorated its apse with a gold-covered mosaic. In it he deposited the venerable body of blessed Leo, confessor and pontiff; above it he constructed a sacred altar and, relying upon this love, completed a ciborium with a gilded cross, for the praise and glory of the name of Christ, so that he might gain for himself a fitting place in heaven.

### Gifts offered to churches

After all these works had been completed and finished, whose names have already been written or mentioned individually above, that same excellent shepherd and father—although he exercised a worthy care and solicitude over all the churches of God and was above all devoted to every good work—drew long sighs from the depths of his heart.

For every day he saw the most sacred altar of the most blessed prince of the apostles, Peter, violated and reduced to such disgrace and degradation by the perfidious Saracens, hostile to God. He also saw—and we say this with grief and mourning—that Christian people from every quarter were still being sent to the threshold of that blessed prince for the sake of prayer and devotion, and that for this reason he was unable fully to accomplish his vows, as he had formerly desired.

Therefore, relying upon the help of almighty God and strengthened by counsel and power, he adorned not only the confession but also the front of the aforesaid altar, with gold and silver panels, in a sufficiently seemly and honorable manner, as the work itself, dedicated there in every respect, makes clearer than daylight.

Accordingly, he newly adorned the principal front of the venerable altar with panels of the finest gold and surrounded it entirely with very many excellent and precious gems, restoring it to a better condition and beauty than before.

On these golden panels, as has been said, not only does the image of our Redeemer shine forth, but also his venerable Resurrection and the judgment of the sacred and saving cross.

The faces of Peter and Paul likewise shine and gleam on the aforesaid panels, as does that of Andrew. Among them were depicted, for everlasting remembrance or reward, the persons dear to God of the most holy prelate Leo IV and of his special son, Lord Emperor Lothair.

Finally, he made an enamel panel, a work weighing 216 pounds of refined gold.

He likewise restored the confession of the frequently mentioned altar, with panels prepared from the purest silver, to its ancient splendor and condition, with equal devotion of spirit. On these panels we see the Savior seated on a throne, bearing precious gems on his head; on his right are cherubim, and on his left the faces of the apostles and others are depicted.

He also made the grating of the sacred confession from silver, bearing the faces of the most blessed Peter and Paul and weighing 208 pounds.

This beloved and prudent pontiff, protected by God, made in the basilica of the apostle blessed Peter eleven curtains woven of gold, hanging in the arches and ornamented around the edge with purple silk.

He also made in the oratory of Saint Leo the pontiff, within the church of the apostle blessed Peter, one white silk vestment embroidered with *gammadia* and *periclysis* of purple silk. Likewise, two larger white curtains and eight smaller ones.

In the monastery of Saint Caesarius, situated in the palace, he made one vestment of gold-threaded fabric and eight curtains.

That venerable pontiff, protected by God, made, for the recompense and reward of his soul, one vestment of gold-threaded fabric and eight curtains in the cemetery of the blessed martyr Agatha, which is situated outside the gate of Saint Pancras.

Who could say, or sufficiently narrate, how many gifts that pope, protected by God and most diligent, offered with devoted mind to the holy places?

In the oratory called that of Saint Paul he offered one vestment of extraordinary beauty bearing a representation of eagles and a history, with a cross of gold-threaded fabric and *gammadia*.

He made in the oratory of Saints Processus and Martinianus one vestment of considerable brilliance, with roundels, human figures, and a history with a cross, likewise of gold-threaded fabric and *gammadia*.

He made another vestment of shining appearance in the basilica of Saint Petronilla, bearing roundels and an eagle, with a cross of gold-threaded fabric and *gammadia*.

In the oratory of the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin, our Lady Mary, which is situated in Mediana, he likewise offered one vestment with roundels, eagles, and a cross of gold-threaded fabric with *gammadia*.

He made in the oratory of Saint Adrian one vestment with roundels and human figures, likewise with a cross of gold-threaded fabric and *gammadia*.

This often-mentioned and most blessed pope offered in the basilica of the holy martyr Sebastian, which is situated at Frascata, one vestment of the most precious brilliance, with a cross of gold-threaded fabric and *gammadia*.

### He repaired the walls of the city

That supreme and foremost prelate made in the basilica of the apostle blessed Peter one large silk curtain, with many scenes of immense brilliance, for the adornment and glory of that most sacred basilica.

When this and the works that have been written above had been completed, and when that most blessed man and prelate had offered them more fully to the Lord, in gratitude for his love and devotion, through various holy places, he then began to consider the condition and restoration of the walls of the city of Rome. They had already been weakened by long age and excessive antiquity and appeared entirely broken and ruined.

He consulted with the Lord Jesus Christ, lest, if they remained for a long time in such neglect or forgetfulness, they might, with the Lord permitting it, more easily be captured or perhaps stormed by enemies.

Therefore, lest this evil occur in the future, during the twelfth indiction he took every care to renew all the aforesaid walls of the city of Rome and restore them to their former order and beauty.

He not only ordered the walls mentioned above to be repaired with rapid diligence, but also hastened to command that the gates, by which the city is often closed, be rebuilt with new ornamentation and very strong timber, because of fear and terror of the enemies.

Finally, so that all these works might be completed quickly and brought to proper effect and beauty, the aforesaid apostolic man was constantly present—not only seated on horseback, but also running on foot himself along the walls and gates with his faithful people—so that no delay or postponement might arise in their restoration.

Therefore, as has already been said, while the venerable pontiff exercised the greatest care for the city of Rome, he brought everything everywhere into a better and newer condition. He ordered fifteen towers, which he found completely ruined around the circuit of the city, to be restored with new construction.

Of these, he arranged for two to be built near the Porta Portuensis, so wisely and prudently, at the very bank of the Tiber—that is, beside the river’s shore—that no one previously could have imagined or considered it possible.

Since through this place not only ships but also people had formerly entered easily, whereas now scarcely any small boats could pass through it, he did this for the future danger posed by the Saracen enemies and for the safety of the city of Rome.

He therefore had these towers secured not only with stones but also with iron chains, so that, unless necessity required it, no ship could pass through that same place.

This newly constructed work provides for the defense of the city of Rome and, to those who see it, is not a small but a great miracle, because it was accomplished with great wisdom, subtle prudence, and propriety.

[scan page 325]

## POPE LEO

### He brought the bodies of saints into the city. He built a church. Gifts bestowed upon churches

That man, protected by God, and the most blessed pope gathered many bodies of saints, which had long lain hidden, within the walls of this noble city, with the greatest care and devotion of heart, for the honor of almighty God.

With diligent care he also sought out and found the bodies of the Four Crowned Ones. Because of his desire for these precious relics, he rebuilt from its foundations, through the merciful assent of heavenly power, the basilica consecrated in the name of those saints. When he had been raised to the summit of the pontificate, he had governed it with the wisest moderation; but, shaken by the ravages of age, worn down by the passage of time, and almost broken into ruins, it appeared to have been devastated by long antiquity. He rebuilt it in a more splendid and beautiful condition.

For the praise of almighty God he placed beneath the sacred altar their most holy bodies: Claudius, Nicostratus, Symphorianus, Castorius, and Simplicius; also Severus, Severianus, Carpophorus, and Victorinus, the four brothers; likewise Marius, Audifax, and Abacuc, with their attendants [or servants], eighteen in number; Aquilinus, Aquila, and Prisca; Narcissus and Marcellinus; Felix and Symmetrius; Candidus and Paulinus; Anastasius and Felix; Diogenes and Liberalis; Festus and Marcellus; Exuperantius; Pudentiana and Benedictus; Felix and Venantius; as well as the head of Saint Protus and of Saint Cecilia, of Saint Alexander, of Saint Sixtus, and of Saint Sebastian, and likewise of the most sacred virgin Praxedis. He placed there many others whose names are known to God.

Above them he also made, with marvelous workmanship and extraordinary beauty, a ciborium of the purest silver covered with gold, with green and hyacinth-colored gems, weighing 313½ pounds.

Moreover, in the same church he offered four red curtains hanging around the altar.

That same most holy prelate made in the oratory of the aforesaid blessed Barbara, which had been constructed within the church of the Four Crowned Ones, a silver crown weighing twelve pounds.

In the same oratory he also offered ten silver bowls weighing [lacuna] pounds.

In the oratory mentioned above he made three vestments of gold-threaded fabric, having crosses with *gammadia* in the middle, and twelve curtains.

The aforesaid venerable pontiff also made in the basilica of blessed Stephen the pontiff, on the Via Latina at the third milestone, one vestment of gold-threaded fabric with a cross in the middle and six curtains.

There he offered a paten and a small sacred chalice of silver, weighing one and a half pounds.

The most blessed prelate also offered in the church of the blessed prince of the apostles a thurible of gilded silver, bearing the apostolic inscription of the name of Lord Leo IV, pope, weighing four pounds.

There, in the oratory of blessed Gregory, confessor and pontiff, he made one vestment of gold-threaded fabric with *gammadia* and one cross of woven silver.

Likewise, in the oratory of blessed Pastor the martyr, he made one vestment in the same manner.

In the oratory of the blessed Mother of God, which is situated by the ambo, he likewise made one vestment in the same manner; and in the oratory of the exalted holy cross he made one vestment in the same way.

In the oratory situated by the font he likewise made one vestment and curtains of quadruple fabric.

That venerable and illustrious pontiff made in the church of the Four Crowned Ones, over the high altar, one vestment of gold-threaded fabric with a cross in the middle, *gammadia*, and a surrounding border of gold-threaded fabric.

In the place mentioned above, in the oratory of Saint Barbara, he likewise made one vestment of gold-threaded fabric.

In the oratory of Saint Sixtus he made one vestment in the same way.

In the oratory of Saint Nicholas he likewise made one vestment with an eagle.

He also made in the same church one linen curtain with a cross in the middle and, around the edge, a border of gold-threaded fabric of extraordinary size.

Adorned with these pious customs and sacred works, the pope offered in the aforesaid church, which he had founded through his love, a paten of the purest silver covered with gold, decorated with a trophy of the cross, an image of the Savior, and beautiful representations of the holy Mother of God and of the holy apostles. It weighed seven pounds.

Likewise, he offered a sacred chalice covered with gold, bearing an image of the evangelists and a cross, weighing four pounds.

He also offered a gilded pitcher of the purest silver, on which a depressed sign of the cross can be seen around the circumference, together with images of the prophets and an icon of the most blessed Stephen, the first martyr.

There was also one apostolic thurible of the purest silver.

Four gilded bowls, for the splendor of that venerable basilica, weighing two and a half pounds.

After all these things had been done, he adorned the confession with silver panels weighing ninety-three pounds and embellished it with images of the saints.

Above it he also offered a crown of the purest silver with the most precious gems, having a cross in the middle, which can still be seen hanging over the same altar.

There too he offered forty-three curtains of gold-threaded fabric.

### Gifts bestowed upon monasteries

That often-mentioned and illustrious prelate, inflamed by heavenly love, offered in the monastery of Saint Silvester, Saint Benedict, and Saint Scholastica, which is called “Sub lacu,” three vestments of gold-threaded fabric and likewise seven curtains of gold-threaded fabric.

After the Saracens’ ravaging, the most blessed prelate also had a crucifix of extraordinary size constructed in the church of the apostle blessed Peter, made of the purest gilded silver and adorned with hyacinth-colored gems. It weighed seventy pounds and had seven other white gems, one of them larger.

We shall also recount, not without usefulness, the things that were miraculously done or accomplished during the twelfth indiction through the constant prayers and tears of the most holy prelate, if we strive to insert them more clearly into this work for lasting memory, so that present and future generations may more easily learn how great a degree of sanctity this man possessed in this troubled life.

### The Saracens’ attack

Finally, after the impious and mournful devastation of the Saracens, full of every misery, which they had carried out through the devil’s prompting against the first of all churches, namely the holy Roman Church, those sons of Satan wished once again to inflict similar injuries upon the Roman territories and the Church of the most blessed apostle Peter, as before, and then to return victorious to the places from which they had departed.

But, because of the care and vigilance of the supreme shepherd, they were utterly unable to accomplish this. Nevertheless, so that the faithful may rightly become still more faithful in the Lord and may not doubt that his signs and venerable miracles have newly proceeded from ancient examples, what divine mercy miraculously did to them at that time, and through what miseries and calamities that pestilent people was deservedly crushed and scattered, must be recounted from the beginning.

Accordingly, remembering their former profit, or the booty they had taken, they cruelly resolved, with a multiplied force of wicked men and many ships, to come to attack the city of Rome while the twelfth indiction was in progress.

They also remained for many days in a place called Tozarum, near the island of Sardinia. From there they departed and attempted to come to the Roman port, but God did not assist them.

## Account

### The Neapolitans and others join battle against the Saracens

Their wicked and abominable arrival greatly terrified the Romans. But because almighty God has always kept his Church inviolate, and does not cease to preserve it, he then stirred the hearts of the Neapolitans, Amalfitans, and Gaetans, among all the others, so that they might rise up together with the Romans and fight bravely against them.

For immediately they left their own places, came before the Saracens, and joined them with their ships [that is, they arrived with them]. They announced their sudden arrival to the most blessed Pope Leo IV and declared that they had come for no other reason than that, with the Lord’s help, they might emerge victorious over the pagans. Then the venerable pope ordered some of them to come to him first at Rome, wishing specifically to learn from them whether their arrival was peaceful or not; and so it was done.

### The pope celebrates Mass at Ostia

Among them came Caesar, the son of Sergius, master of the soldiers, who had been appointed over the army. The pope received them kindly in the Lateran palace and asked the reason for their arrival. They testified that they had come for no other purpose than that which has been written above.

The pious apostolic prelate, believing their words, immediately proceeded with a great armed retinue to the city of Ostia and received all the Neapolitans with great and extraordinary devotion. When they saw the supreme prelate, they prostrated themselves reverently at his feet, kissed them, and gave thanks to the almighty Most High, who had chosen to send them such a bishop to strengthen them.

Wishing to emerge victorious over the sons of Belial, they earnestly begged that they might be worthy to receive the Lord’s Body from his sacred hands. With his own mouth he sang Mass for them in the Church of Saint Aurea, and all received communion from his hands, as has been said. Before this took place, he went together with the Neapolitans to the aforesaid church, with hymns, litanies, and distinguished songs, Christ assisting them. There too, kneeling, he prayed to the Most High that by his prayers he might deign to deliver the enemies of the Christians into the hands of those resisting them.

### A prayer composed against the Saracens

With many tears he also offered this prayer over them, saying:

> God, whose right hand raised the blessed apostle Peter, walking upon the waves lest he be drowned, and delivered his fellow apostle Paul from the depths of the sea when he suffered shipwreck for the third time, mercifully hear us. Grant that, through the merits of both, the arms of these your faithful ones, fighting against the enemies of your holy Church, may be strengthened by your almighty right hand and may prevail, so that, after victory has been won, your holy name may appear glorious among all nations. Through our Lord, etc.

### The Saracen fleet is scattered by the wind

The Saracens were miserably scattered and perished.

On the following day, after the venerable prelate had returned from the city just mentioned, those accomplices—or participants—in crime appeared beside the Ostian shore with many ships. The Neapolitans wished to attack them and fight bravely; they even wounded some of them. They would then have won a triumph if a sudden obstacle had not intervened. For while they were fighting one another with great attention, a wind arose suddenly, so violent and powerful that no one in those times could remember its equal. It immediately separated the two fleets.

At first the Saracen ships advanced as far as the seashore; then, as the wind blew and the sea rose in storms, they were scattered, and after their strength had been somewhat broken they turned back again.

For almighty God, as we firmly believe, had brought forth from his treasury the wind that prevented them from going out to inflict harm. Concerning these new and mysterious miracles—which the divine power has deigned to reveal and demonstrate in our times, although we are not worthy of them—the mercy of our true God must always be glorified and praised. He allowed them to see the place they desired, yet by the power of his strength drove them far away, so that they could not seize it. Afterward, not only through the intercessions and merits of the most blessed princes Peter and Paul, but also through the depths of the sea, hunger, and the sword, he continually destroyed many of them.

### Some Saracens are left among the ruins

Of these, many, suffering from hunger on certain of our islands, were killed by our people. The others, whom they captured alive for the sake of truth and testimony, they brought to Rome. The Roman nobles ordered many of them to be hanged on a wooden structure near our Roman harbor, lest their number appear to have increased.

We also ordered some whom we had bound in chains to be kept alive, solely so that they might recognize, as clearly as possible, the hope that we have in God, his ineffable compassion, and also our own tyranny. Afterward, so that they might not live idly or without hardship among us, at one time we ordered them to carry loads for the various works of craftsmen at the wall that we had begun to build around the church of the most blessed apostle Peter; at another time, we ordered them to carry whatever seemed necessary.

## Gifts offered to the churches

For these benefits, as has already been related, the blessed pontiff offered in the basilica of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, after the plundering of the Agarene people, thirteen arches of the purest silver. Of these, he placed two, one on the right and one on the left, in the presbytery; they weighed [a number of] pounds of remarkable size [the weight is incomplete in the source].

The same most blessed prelate also made in the church of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, one gold-woven vestment bearing a depiction of how blessed Peter preached to the holy Roman Church, with seven white gems—that is, pearls—eleven green gems, and twenty-seven hyacinth-colored gems.

In the church of the blessed apostle Andrew he made a marble ciborium over the altar, as well as a silver chalice with twelve hanging crowns in the same ciborium, weighing [an incomplete amount] of pounds. He also made there the bell-tower and placed a bell with a bronze hammer and a gilded cross. In addition, in the Church of the blessed apostle Peter he offered a thurible of the purest gold, decorated with various gems.

In the church of the blessed and ever-virgin Mother of God, our lady Mary, which stands at Saint Lawrence Outside-the-Walls, he made one vestment bearing a depiction of the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ and an image of the aforementioned gracious prelate.

In the church of the four holy Crowned Martyrs he made eleven silver baskets, weighing twenty-four pounds. He also offered in the church of the blessed apostle Peter a cross of the purest gold, decorated with hyacinth-colored and white gems and emeralds, of remarkable size, which stands on the right beside the main altar.

There too he newly repaired the staff and silver-plated it—the staff in which the aforesaid cross is contained. It weighed eleven and a half pounds of silver and bore the inscription of the name of Pope Leo IV.

He offered in the church of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr a gold-woven vestment with four hyacinth-colored gems.

The same aforementioned gracious and supreme prelate, moved by great love and devoted to good morals, made in the Church of the blessed martyr Lawrence, situated outside the walls of the city of Rome, a pure-silk vestment with eagles. It had three gold-woven panels on each side, bearing a depiction of the martyrdom of the aforesaid martyr and an image of the aforesaid prelate.

### Further gifts to the church of the four Crowned Martyrs

In the church of the four holy Crowned Martyrs he also made three gilded silver images: one bearing the face of the Savior, and the other two bearing the faces of the saints Claudius and Nicostratus. They weighed fifty-two and a half pounds.

In the same church he offered a crown of linen, weighing twenty-five pounds. At the entrance of that church, which is before the main altar, he hung a silver lily with crystal balls and a censer. In the same place he also made seven silver baskets, weighing nineteen pounds.

The most gracious pontiff made these things in the monastery that he had arranged to be built at his own house, from the foundations, and which seemed to have come to him by right of his parents: a monastery of the handmaids of God in honor of the saints Simitrius and Caesarius. He also gave there a paten and a chalice of gilded silver, decorated with various gems, weighing [an amount omitted in the source].

In the same place he offered a silver dish with a cup, weighing [an amount omitted in the source]. He also offered in the monastery three baskets of the purest silver and six stone cups, weighing altogether twelve and a half pounds.

There he made, for the redemption and reward of his soul, three gold-woven vestments bearing one embroidered panel with an interwoven design. He also made there a crown of the purest gold with green and hyacinth-colored gems, which hung above the altar and weighed [an amount omitted in the source].

## Additional church furnishings

The pope, protected by God and venerable, offered in the basilica of the holy and ever-virgin Mother of God, our lady Mary, which stands beside the walls of this city of Rome near Saint Lawrence, one gold-woven vestment bearing in the middle a gilded panel with an image of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ and an image of the gracious pontiff himself.

In the church of the martyr Lawrence he made a silver thurible, with its cover gilded and decorated all around with chains and bosses; it weighed six pounds.

The aforesaid prelate restored the church of the blessed and ever-virgin Mother of God, our lady Mary, across the Tiber, which was threatening to collapse because of its great age.

In the church of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, for the honor and protection of that church, he made a silver throne of the purest silver, hanging in the presbytery before the main altar; it weighed 149 pounds.

Likewise, in the church of the blessed martyr Sebastian, which stands at Frascati, he made a basket of the purest silver, weighing two pounds, bearing the name of the gracious prelate and of Saint Sebastian.

## The great ciborium of Saint Peter

After these things had been suitably completed and brought to an end, and after the shameful and wicked plundering of the Saracens, the catholic and wholly praiseworthy prelate made, for the honor and praise of the church of the prince of the apostles, Saint Peter, a ciborium of remarkable size and beauty over its venerable altar, with columns and gilded lilies of the purest silver, weighing 1,606 pounds.

Over the ciborium he offered four crowns and sixteen chalices of the purest gold, weighing [an amount omitted in the source]. He also made for the honor and glory of the same ciborium, from silver as above, forty-six chalices and crowns, weighing twenty-two pounds and seven ounces.

Moreover, for greater beauty, he made upon the columns of the ciborium four silver baskets of the purest silver, weighing forty-two pounds. He also made there, around the altar, fourteen white silk hangings stamped with seals, having gold-woven borders.

He also offered fourteen other linen cloths with silk-white borders, stamped with seals. He also offered there a basket of the purest silver, weighing fifty pounds.

In the oratory of Saint Sylvester within the Lateran palace he made one gold-woven vestment, having in the middle a small panel of gold-and-purple brocade, and four gold-woven hangings.

He also made in the church of Jerusalem one gold-woven vestment and likewise four gold-woven hangings.

He also made in the deaconry of the holy virgin Mary, which is situated in the [place-name is unclear in the OCR], a silver crown surrounded within by golden bells.

In the church of the holy and ever-virgin Mother of God, our lady Mary, which stands at Frascati, he offered one gold-woven vestment with a small gilded panel enclosed in the middle, and four gold-woven hangings.

Likewise he offered in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, which stands at Maruli, one gold-woven vestment with a small gilded panel enclosed in the middle, and four gold-woven hangings.

The pope, protected by God and venerable, offered in the basilica of the blessed and ever-virgin Mother of God, our lady Mary, which stands at Saint Lawrence Outside-the-Walls, one linen curtain with a gold-woven border around it and, in the middle, a cross likewise made of gold-woven material.

In the church of Saints Cosmas and Damian, which appears to be in Silva Candida, he offered one red vestment with a silver border around it and an embroidered cross in the middle, and four hangings with eagles.

He also offered in the church of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, a silver crown encircled on the outside by bison [the reading is uncertain], gilded, weighing seven pounds.

The pope, protected by God and most blessed, moved by heavenly love, offered in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, before the confession of the sacred altar, on the right and on the left, for the adornment of the basilica, six angels of pure silver weighing sixty-four pounds.

Over the ciborium he made hangings that hung around the altar, bearing four gilded panels and four gammadia.

In the same place he made four silver arches standing in the presbytery; they weighed one hundred pounds.

The most blessed prelate offered to the monastery of Saints Cosmas and Damian, situated at a place called Subiaco, approximately forty miles from the city of Rome, one gold-woven vestment and three gold-woven hangings.

The same prelate also made in the church of the blessed martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, situated within the city called Fundi, one gold-woven vestment with a cross of woven gold in the middle, and one gold-woven hanging.

He also offered in the church of the blessed martyr Caesarius, situated within the city called Terracina, one gold-woven vestment with a cross bearing gammadia in the middle and a purple border, bearing the inscription of the name of Pope Leo IV, and likewise five gold-woven hangings.

He also offered in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter four vessels of the purest silver, weighing eighty-four pounds.

In the basilica of the blessed martyr Rufina at Silva Candida he made a gold-woven vestment with a cross of purple border in the middle and a purple border around it, bearing the name of Pope Leo IV.

The same most blessed prelate also made in the church of the blessed martyr and bishop Clement six bowls of the purest silver: three bore a large image of Christ, two likewise bore palm branches, and one was inlaid and made of stone. Together they weighed four pounds.

The most blessed and distinguished pontiff made in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter three silver arches with columns and lilies, weighing together 102 pounds.

The same venerable pontiff made in the basilica of Saint Caesarius, which stands at Terracina, a gold-woven vestment decorated around the edges with purple, having in the middle a cross of gold-and-purple brocade and bearing the name of Pope Leo IV.

In the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter he also made three silver arches with columns and lilies, weighing sixty pounds.

## The church at Portus and other gifts

In the church of the holy Mother of God Mary, which is situated in the city of Portus, he made a silk vestment decorated around the edges with gold-woven material and having a silver cross in the middle. Likewise, three silk hangings decorated around the edges with gold-woven material.

He also made four gilded silver panels in the church before the confession of the blessed apostle Peter, and two lambs, weighing together forty-four pounds.

In the same place he offered extraordinarily large porphyry crowns, decorated with pure gold and twelve dolphins, bearing the name of the gracious prelate; they weighed three and a half pounds of gold.

He also made ten arches of the purest silver, weighing together 181 pounds. There were forty-eight linen hangings, hanging from the arches in the same place and decorated around the edges with gold-woven material.

## The completion of the Leonine City

Now, after everything written above, I wish to state in the present record, for eternal memory, what the most powerful and venerable prelate, with careful and diligent effort, sought and accomplished within a very short time for the defense of the universal mother, the Church, inspired by divine zeal.

### Emperor Lothar is asked to complete the city begun by Pope Leo

When all the Roman nobility were living in extreme fear because of the wicked and malicious Saracens, who had long ago brought the abominable plundering, lest they be able to perpetrate worse things in the future—unless the church of the blessed apostle Peter were quickly fortified on every side—the gracious pontiff began to suffer great anxiety on behalf of all the Romans. He anxiously considered how and by what means he might remove such resentment or fear from their hearts.

While he was laboring over these matters for a long time, the Lord revealed the following plan to him. He immediately decided that he should make this known more clearly to his beloved and special son, the lord Emperor Lothar Augustus, so that, with the Lord’s consent and through his assistance and counsel, he might bring to completion the city which his predecessor, Pope Leo III, had begun to build for the Church of the eminent apostle, and for which he had already laid foundations in several places.

Although after his death certain men had removed them, so that not even a trace could be seen of where the aforesaid wall had first been begun, the pope hoped that, if life permitted, he could bring the desired work to completion with Christ’s help.

When the most pious and serene emperor recognized this, he was immediately filled with great joy and exultation. He urgently begged and pressed his spiritual father in every respect to bring the undertaking to completion through constant labor.

For this purpose he sent him, together with his brothers, a considerable amount of silver, so that, as has been said, this useful work might not remain unfinished through delay. At this desired message the prelate was especially filled with joy.

From that time onward he devoted himself intensely to the undertaking. He summoned all the faithful of the holy Church of God and asked their counsel as to how the construction of such great walls could be completed quickly. It then seemed good to everyone that workers should be brought in turn from every city, from all the public estates, and from the monasteries; and this was done.

### The new city is completed in the fourth year and called Leoniana

In the fourth year the new city, called Leoniana, was completed. The pope, barefoot with all the clergy, circled the walls.

Therefore, in the second year of his pontificate, he began to think seriously about building it. In the sixth year, the famous city was completely founded and finished.

After the many labors and struggles of the most blessed prelate had been completed, and the entire work of the walls had been finished and brought to the desired conclusion, he began to give manifold and countless thanks to almighty God, who had deigned to hear and fulfill his daily prayers for the building of the walls.

No human tongue can briefly describe how much care, effort, and concern this pious and praiseworthy shepherd devoted, day and night, until the work was completed. After performing the required duties of the sacred rites, he did nothing except what has been written above. Neither cold, nor wind, nor rain, nor great or moderate disturbance of the weather could make him slacken from day to day.

Sometimes here, sometimes there, he moved about alertly and anxiously among the various building works, so that our almighty Redeemer might prosperously fulfill his good purpose and desire through the pious intercession of the apostles Peter and Paul. Then, as we have frequently related, all the works of the new city were completed and perfected.

The most blessed pope, always praiseworthy in all things, wishing that the aforesaid city—called Leoniana after its founder—might remain permanently firm and strengthened, ordered with great devotion and joy of heart that all the bishops and priests with him, the inhabitants of the city, and all the orders of clergy of the holy catholic and apostolic Roman Church should, after the litany and psalmody had been sung, circle the entire circuit of the walls barefoot, carrying ashes on their heads, with hymns and spiritual songs.

Among other things, he ordered the cardinal bishops to bless water, so that during the prayers they might cross over the wall and diligently sprinkle that water everywhere for the sake of sanctification. They humbly carried out what he had ordered.

### Three prayers over the gates

The venerable pontiff himself, with his own mouth, offered three prayers over the same wall, with many tears and sighs. He asked that the aforesaid city might be preserved forever by the aid of Christ and remain secure and undaunted from every attack of enemies through the protection of all the saints and angels.

He made the first prayer over the gate facing Saint Peregrinus. Its opening and beginning are:

> God, who entrusted to your apostle Peter, after giving him the keys of the heavenly kingdom, the authority to bind and loose, grant that through his intercession we may be freed from the bonds of our sins. Make this city, which we have newly founded with your help, remain forever secure from your wrath, and grant it new and manifold triumphs over the enemies on whose account it was built. Through our Lord, etc.

The same pious pope also offered the second prayer over the postern where a very high fortress stands, which is called Saint Angel.

The text of that prayer is:

> God, who from the very beginning of Christianity have deigned to guard and preserve this holy catholic and apostolic Roman Church from its enemies, mercifully wipe away the record of our iniquities. Permit this city, which we have newly dedicated to your holy name through the intercession of your apostles Peter and Paul, to remain always secure and undaunted from every attack of enemies. Through our Lord, etc.

He made the third prayer over another postern, which faces the School of the Saxons and is called, after them, the Saxon Postern. This third prayer specifically contains the following:

> Grant, we ask, almighty and merciful God, that, as we call upon you with our whole heart, through the intercession of the blessed apostle Peter, we may be preserved by your mercy, and that this city, which I, Leo, bishop, have built as a new work with your help and named Leoniana after my own name, may remain secure and free from enemies and from the sons of Satan in all future times; command that it may always remain unharmed and continually endure in safety before the clemency of your majesty. Through our Lord, etc.

In this city, in accordance with the promise of his desire which he had vowed to God, he distributed a great gift to the Romans and to various nations on the solemn day.

## The pope enriches Rome with many gifts

Afterward, as has been said, proceeding with the priests and all the Roman nobles to the church of the blessed apostle Peter, he solemnly celebrated Mass with prayers and divine praises for the salvation of the people, the safety of the city, and its perpetual stability.

After these sacred rites had been completed, he honored and enriched all the nobles of Rome with many gifts—not only with gold and silver, but also with silk and precious fabrics. That day was filled with great joy for everyone, namely the twenty-seventh day of June, on the eve of the feast of Saint Leo the pope and the vigil of the holy apostles Peter and Paul.

Indeed, before the vigil of the most blessed Peter and Paul, countless joys and innumerable celebrations of exultation took place throughout the whole city of Rome.

It is therefore more worthy and fitting that for so great a prelate and so great a shepherd we should continually beseech almighty God with all our heart and a pure soul in our prayers. Through him, with the power of Christ assisting, we know that this admirable and most honorable work was quickly accomplished and completed for the salvation of all Christians. We should pray that the pope may flourish here for a very long time and, there, may deserve to possess everlasting and eternal rewards with all the saints for his innumerable struggles and labors.

## Gifts given to the churches

The most blessed pope made in the church of Saint Bibiana one gold-woven vestment with panels of gold-and-purple brocade in the middle, bearing an image of the Savior with three green gems on his head, and images of Saint Sinzigus and the most blessed prelate, together with four gold-woven hangings.

In the church of the four holy Crowned Martyrs he made two candle-holders of the purest silver, weighing five pounds and six ounces, and four silver cups, weighing [an amount omitted in the source].

In the church of the holy Mother of God Mary, which stands at Saint Lawrence Outside-the-Walls, the aforesaid prelate made twenty-seven gold-woven hangings.

He also made in the church of the blessed martyr and bishop Clement a crown hanging over the main altar, sculpted from the purest gold without gems, with a gold cross in the middle bearing gems fixed in the same crown.

He offered in the church of the blessed martyr Hippolytus, situated on the island of Portus called Arsis, one gold-woven vestment with a silver-woven gammadion and four gold-woven hangings.

He also offered in the church of the blessed and ever-virgin Mother of God, our lady Mary, situated in the city called Anagni, one gold-woven vestment with gold-woven gammadia and four gold-woven hangings.

## The pope considers fortifying Portus; Corsican exiles take refuge with him

So that we may not pass over in silence the things written above—which have been clarified and recorded by truthful testimony and reliable evidence, although silence is wholly inappropriate—I shall set out more clearly the other works of the most blessed pope, accomplished through the powerful mercy of Jesus Christ, although they were very numerous.

While the mind and spirit of the supreme bishop labored tirelessly in good and God-worthy works, he began to be greatly concerned about the city of Portus, so that in some way or order it might be inhabited both by his own people and by others.

The Corsicans, who had been terrified by fear of the Saracens and were living as exiles from their own lands, wandering here and there without a home, came to the Roman see as a place of refuge and salvation as quickly as possible, just as indeed they did.

When they arrived at the most sacred threshold of the prince of the apostles, they were immediately brought before our most blessed lord Pope Leo IV.

After he had prudently questioned them and their nobles about the danger that then threatened them and the reason for their arrival, they explained their needs, disasters, and distress in order.

They openly declared before the aforesaid pope that they wished to live there for all their days in obedience and service to him and to his successors.

Recognizing this, the benevolent prelate was immediately lifted into great exultation and joy. He gave thanks to God, who had sent him such men, who could live permanently in the city mentioned above.

After hearing their many promises, the aforesaid pope replied to them and to his leading men in a clear voice:

> If you take care to fulfill what you have told us in words, we have very good places where you will be able to live, provided that you remain good and faithful to us and to our successors, the pontiffs. The city that we shall give you is very strong and well fortified. With the protection of our Redeemer, we have restored it to its former condition by means of new gates and structures in places where these were necessary for its use.
>
> If, as we have said, you wish to remain there, we shall grant you vineyards, lands, and meadows, so that you may suffer no want. We shall also give you, so that by your labor you may provide fully for yourselves, your wives, and your children: [lacuna] oxen, horses, and other animals, as we have said, if you do everything in good faith.

When the Corsican people heard these promises, they became happier. They immediately asked for messengers from the pious pontiff who could show them the city and its lands in detail; and this was done.

Everything pleased them, and they all unanimously promised that, if our pope and lord would deign to grant them all the lands around which they had traveled, they would hasten with their entire families and possessions, with complete eagerness, into the service of Saint Peter and his successors.

After the city and all its possessions had been inspected, they returned with the messengers to the venerable pontiff. He summoned everyone so that they too might unanimously testify in accordance with the messengers’ report.

Then, in accordance with his promise, and for the sake of the reward and perpetual memory of our most serene emperors Lothar and Louis, as well as his own, he sent them a papal charter in the following terms, with this condition attached: it would remain firm and stable only so long as they remained obedient and faithful in every respect to the authorities of the holy see and to the Roman people.

If, God forbid, they failed to observe the entire content of the charter without violation, it was decreed in the same document that it should be void and null.

The places given to them and assigned by the papal messengers—whether belonging by ecclesiastical right to the Church, to venerable monasteries, or even to individual neighboring proprietors—are specifically recorded in the papal privilege granted to them.

Such was the abundant mercy of the often-mentioned prelate, who loved his Roman nobles not only for the defense of the city...

## Historical Notice

### Other Gifts

…but wherever he was able to gather people, he invited them to their aid and consolation; he valued the defense of the churches more than temporal and fleeting gains, for the sake of which we often recall that many lost both life and possessions in which they had delighted.

Moreover, in the church of the holy Mother of God, situated in the quarter of the Sardinians at the thirtieth mile from the city of Rome, he offered four Catholic books: one of the Gospels, another of Kings, a Psalter, and sermons. In the church of Saint Martin, confessor and pontiff, outside the gate of the blessed apostle Peter, he made one silver chalice with chains, weighing four pounds and two ounces. In the church of the Four Holy Crowned Saints he made two thuribles of the purest silver, weighing two pounds and one ounce. Likewise, in the church of blessed Petronilla he made three embroidered vestments and twelve curtains: four embroidered, three of Spanish cloth, and five of linen.

### Leo Repairs Certain Cities

After all that has been briefly set forth above, the bishop, who was very diligent and worthy of praise, undertook works of a similar kind. For the cities of Hortana and Ameria—very ancient cities whose walls and gates, through excessive age, had fallen to the ground and remained utterly ruined—were easily entered, sometimes by thieves and sometimes by robbers, through their open approaches, with no guard resisting them. He himself, recognizing the negligence of the citizens of the aforesaid cities, restored those cities by his exhortation and diligence to their former condition, with new walls and gates not unlike the earlier ones, strengthened by divine grace.

In these cities, now set forth, the inhabitants dwell more securely, protected from the ambushes of enemies. Once the walls and gates had been closed, thieves and robbers could thereafter inflict no damage or theft, either by night or by day.

### Gifts Presented to the Churches

When these matters had been carefully completed, as has been said, he made many other gifts in the hall of blessed Peter the apostle and prince of the apostles. In the church of the Four Holy Coronati he made one crown of the purest silver with four small silver chains, containing forty-two dolphins and weighing altogether twenty-three pounds.

This pontiff also, always relying upon Christ’s help and divinely inspired, made around the altar of the blessed apostle Peter four green silk curtains, with panels of gold embroidery bearing images of the Savior, the apostles Peter and Paul, and the beneficent pontiff himself; in their midst were crosses and *gammadiae* of gold embroidery with roundels containing images of the apostles, wonderfully beautiful and adorned. They are hung there on feast days for ornament.

Likewise, in the same place he made other white rose-patterned silk curtains, wonderfully adorned with latticework, to shade the sacred mysteries at Easter. He also offered there another, smaller crown with four chains and ten dolphins, having a lily and a hook, weighing two pounds.

In the basilica of the holy Mother of God, Mary, our Lady, situated in the quarter of the Sardinians, he offered a gilded silver chalice and paten bearing the name of Pope Leo IV, weighing together four pounds and five ounces.

This distinguished and pre-eminent bishop, after completing innumerable works of the highest beauty in the basilica of blessed Peter, keeper of the keys of heaven, restored the doors which the Saracen nation had destroyed and plated with silver. He adorned them with many silver panels carved with luminous and life-giving histories, and restored them in a more beautiful form than they had formerly possessed, so that all who enter that basilica may render praise to almighty God and to His holy bishop, and may pray that the life of the one who adorned it with so great a work of splendor and so great a weight of beauty may be prolonged through many years. He decorated it with silver weighing seventy pounds.

This supreme and God-beloved pope, at the beginning of his pontificate, when the portico on the left side of the basilica of blessed Peter had collapsed through excessive age, promptly and more splendidly renewed it.

For he also repaired the roof of that principal church with great beams, raised with skill and craftsmanship, and restored it brightly. Moreover, when the portico adjoining the church of Saint Andrew appeared likely to collapse, he newly restored it in better form. He also renewed and adorned the chamber visible before the silver doors of the aforesaid hall, relying upon an immeasurable love.

He performed many pious works of the same kind in the churches; if we wished to commit them all to writing, our tongue would not suffice to recount them, nor would the pens of writers be able to bear the burden. While he was completing many distinguished works throughout the various churches of God, the most blessed pontiff also renewed more splendidly and beautifully the portico standing before the basilica of the holy Mother of God, situated near the basilica of Saint Lawrence outside the walls.

In the church of the holy Mother of God, which he had newly built from its foundations beside the school of the Saxons, he offered three embroidered vestments and likewise four embroidered curtains.

He also made in the basilica of blessed Peter the apostle silver candlesticks standing in the presbytery, twenty-seven in number, weighing together forty-two pounds. He also clothed the entrance and middle of the presbytery with the purest silver, weighing sixty-seven pounds and three ounces.

When he was inflamed by heavenly zeal for his country and was adorning Christ’s beautiful churches in order with metals and ornaments, he afterward made many other objects in the hall of blessed Peter the apostle, prince of the apostles: one crown of the purest silver with four silver chains, having forty-two dolphins and weighing twenty-three pounds; and one crown of pure gold, hanging above the high altar, likewise with golden chains, bearing in its center a cross decorated with fourteen gems, five of them fixed in the cross itself and the others hanging there.

He made six white and three hyacinth-colored curtains in the same place, weighing together one pound and half an ounce. In the basilica of the holy Mother of God, Mary, our Lady, situated in the quarter of the Sardians, he offered one silver chalice and paten, gilded, weighing together four pounds and five ounces.

This most blessed bishop also offered in the church of the Four Holy Coronati two curtains of white silk, beautifully decorated with rose-colored borders and latticework, shading the sacred vessels at Easter. He also offered there another, smaller crown with four chains and ten dolphins, having a lily and a hook, weighing two pounds.

The mind of this most blessed bishop, always devoted to God, continually strove, out of immense love and for the salvation of eternal life, to adorn the churches of Jesus Christ with precious ornaments. What none of his pontifical predecessors had thought to do, he, undoubtedly burning with and compelled by the Holy Spirit, ordered to be made: two crowns of the purest gold, shining with the illustrious faces of Christ and the saints, hanging to the right and left in the church of Peter, prince of the apostles, beside the altar beneath which his most sacred body rests. They were decorated with golden chains, bosses, and green gems, contained sixty dolphins together, and weighed twenty pounds.

He also made in the same church a silver crucifix painted with marvelous workmanship. It was placed on the left side of the entrance between the great columns, shining with splendid beauty, and weighed sixty-two and a half pounds.

This most blessed pontiff also made in the oratory of the blessed apostle Andrew, adjoining the church of Saint Peter, one silk vestment bearing a scene of eagles, and in the middle a panel with gold embroidery, in which images of Christ and His disciples shine on the right and left, together with the image of the beneficent pontiff himself.

After the completion of the whole work, he likewise made in the church of the Four Holy Coronati a vestment of the same silk, with a panel of gold embroidery, bearing the scene or miracle in which the Lord Christ, from five loaves and two fish, abundantly fed five thousand men.

## Synod of Sixty-Seven Bishops Convened at Rome

Among the matters written above, the frequently mentioned most holy bishop began to exercise special care and concern for the individual rulers of the churches—namely, bishops, priests, deacons, and the whole Christian militia.

Desiring, therefore, with Christ’s help, to establish a new rule from ancient authorities, concerning how each of them should lead a chaste and sober life and please God, whom we ought always to serve irreproachably in all things, he then, with the grace of the Holy Spirit revealing it, and with the unanimous agreement of the most serene emperors Lothair and Louis, in the thirty-fifth year of their reign and the seventh of the pontificate of the aforesaid bishop, in December, on the eighth day, in the second indiction, convened a holy and venerable synod in the church of the blessed apostle Peter.

At it sat both that Catholic and apostolic man himself and sixty-seven other bishops with him. Among them were four bishops sent by the emperors: Joseph of Ivrea, Notingus of Brescia, Peter of Spoleto, and another Peter of Arezzo. Among them also sat Paul, deacon of the holy church of Ravenna, representing his archbishop John, without the priests, deacons, and clergy of the holy mother church.

Then, in the presence of all, he ordered forty-two chapters—plainly known to pertain to the salvation and profit of all Christian people—to be read by the deacons of the holy and universal apostolic see. He also ordered these chapters to be written into the sacred canons after the other decrees, so that they might be preserved inviolate by all in the future, and so that all bishops might have before their eyes an example of this authority, enabling them better to instruct and educate their subjects.

### Cardinal Anastasius Deposed

Finally, at this synod, after the other proceedings, Anastasius, priest and cardinal of the title of Saint Marcellus, was canonically deposed by all, because he had abandoned his parish for five years contrary to the statutes of the canons and had continued to reside in foreign lands up to that time.

Since he was unwilling to come either to the two councils convened on his behalf, or in response to apostolic letters, or when summoned by three bishops—namely Nicholas, Petronacius, and John—the holy synod rightly deposed him by unanimous agreement, according to what the sacred canons provide concerning such men, and deprived him of priestly honor, in the year, month, day, and indiction noted above.

### Gifts Presented to the Churches

After the principal decision of this council, the mind of that most blessed bishop, always kindled by the heavenly fire of love, again began to devote immense effort to restoring the ornaments and vessels of all God’s churches.

In the church of blessed Peter, keeper of the kingdom of heaven, he made one lamp of the purest silver, weighing sixteen and a half pounds. Likewise, in the monastery of Saint Martin, which adjoins the church of the prince of the apostles, he made another cast-silver lamp, weighing twenty-seven and a half pounds.

Similarly, in the monastery of Saints John and Paul he made another silver lamp like the preceding ones, weighing twenty-two and a half pounds. On Sundays and feast days it stood near the reading stand while the sacred lessons were read, shining with a great brilliance of light.

The same most holy pope made silver screens with small chains at the entrance of the presbytery, before the confession of blessed Peter the apostle, his beloved, shining with beautiful splendor and presenting a spectacle of admiration to human minds. Two of them weighed 642 pounds, while the other two weighed 580 pounds.

In the church of Saint Vincent, situated at Frascati, he offered one embroidered vestment.

Since, as we have often said, the mind of this most serene bishop was filled above all with love for the most blessed prince of the apostles, and since he always desired to complete many ornaments for the principal church of that apostle, whose throne he governed by divine dispensation, he made upon his holy altar a vestment of gold embroidery. It bore in the middle a scene of the Savior shining among angelic faces and handing the apostle Peter the keys of the kingdom of heaven; on the right and left shone the glorious passion of Peter and Paul.

Among these figures the bishop himself was depicted offering the city which he had ordered to be built, with Peter intervening, together with a cross shining with gold and gems. Around and above the altar he placed silk cloths woven with a precious scene of eagles, two of which were visible as curtains.

In the same place he offered four curtains with gold embroidery, in which the bishop himself was depicted offering the city which he had completely prepared to the image of the Savior shining among angelic faces.

Since we have now, though briefly, described the ornaments which the aforesaid pontiff offered to the church of blessed Peter, we shall now make known, in summary and for eternal remembrance, what he accomplished in the church of the most blessed apostle Paul, teacher of the nations, after the impious devastation of the Agarenes.

Over his most sacred body he made a ciborium of marvelous beauty, skillfully fashioned and adorned with silver columns, weighing 946 pounds.

Since the benevolent mind of that pontiff, both before and after the general works undertaken for all the churches, always sought to offer something excellent and more precious to blessed Peter, according to the desire of his ingenuity, he offered him three remarkable silk hangings, woven and painted in color, which on feast days were hung around the high altar.

He also made in the church of Saint Marcian, situated in Domuscella, which is called Balnearola, one embroidered vestment and two Spanish curtains.

Likewise, in the church of blessed Lawrence, martyr and levite of Christ, he offered embroidered curtains, which hang in the arches beneath the larger columns, twenty-four in number.

He also made in the church of blessed Clement, martyr and pontiff, one pair of silver hand basins, bearing a carved likeness of a human head with a vine, together with another scene, weighing three pounds.

The same most blessed and beneficent bishop also offered in the church of the holy Mother of God, Mary, in the locality called by the Aurelia road, one embroidered vestment.

Similarly, in the church of Saint Stephen, in the place mentioned above, he offered another embroidered vestment.

That illustrious and beneficent bishop, protected by heavenly power and persevering with a sincere spirit in the service of God, after many good works, also richly adorned with many beautiful columns and paintings the church of Saints Sylvester and Martin, which his predecessor, Pope Sergius, had newly built from its foundations. Its beauty continues to inspire great admiration in human eyes to this day.

He also covered and adorned its venerable and sacred altar with the purest silver, weighing 116 pounds.

## The Rebuilding of the City of Centumcellae

For this reason, after the beautiful and praiseworthy works in various churches which the generous bishop accomplished with complete devotion of heart, he ensured that the Christian people would no longer be destroyed by enemies in the fortress of Centumcellae, as often used to happen.

For forty years that city had remained with its walls destroyed and without its own inhabitants. Like beasts, the people who had been left there, abandoning their proper dwellings out of fear of the Saracens, wandered through the dark forests and unknown mountains, making homes for themselves wherever they could. Because of fear of the enemy, they could have neither sleep for their eyes by day or night nor even the slightest measure of rest according to human custom.

When that pious and praiseworthy bishop daily grieved beyond measure over their burden and intolerable distress—more than can be believed—he continually entreated the Lord, creator of all things, with many tears and countless prayers, asking that He might graciously reveal to him, as a gift of grace, the place to which the city of Centumcellae could be transferred for the safety and liberation of the frequently mentioned Christian people.

He himself then went to those places, which were connected with him by proximity, and examined and surveyed them with diligent care and effort.

But when a place seemed suitable for building a city, it suffered from a shortage and scarcity of water, which is always sufficiently necessary for human beings.

After he had examined all the places, as we have said, he finally came, by divine mercy, to an excellent and very well-fortified location. His mind was greatly encouraged by it, because it supplied an abundance of water to strengthen the people, as well as other human necessities and fully adequate watermills.

It is nevertheless worthy of being recalled how and by what order divine clemency revealed this to him, in praise of the venerable pontiff, so that all people may truly believe and recognize that the work, long sought, was completed by divine counsel and design.

One night, when the illustrious bishop was lying in his own bed according to custom and was thinking about his usual works of charity, he was led in a dream to the place already foreseen and appointed, situated twelve miles from the city of Centumcellae. In that revelation, a certain Peter, master of the soldiers, appeared as though he were physically present and was to lay out and construct each location in order with his assistance.

Since, because of the narrowness of the site, only two gates were to be built there, he marked them with his own fingers in that secret revelation.

When morning came, the vision he had seen became the cause of great activity. He immediately ordered the aforesaid Peter to come into his presence, told him everything he had seen in the dream, and gave him many silver coins, so that he might act as builder for the people of the city of Centumcellae and complete the city with them as quickly as possible.

With God as its guide, everything now shines there, built just as the praiseworthy pope had marked out with his own hand. He gave it the name Leopolis, from his own name.

After construction had begun, he went affectionately with a multitude of his faithful to see and inspect the building. When he saw the gates and churches in the very places he had indicated, and saw that his desire had been fulfilled under Christ’s protection, he gave endless thanks to almighty God, who had deigned to show him such a place—one in which the people could be safe, an abundance of water could be supplied, and stones and sand were also available, so that the newly constructed building could grow without difficulty for the workers.

### The Pope Consecrates and Blesses the New City

Rejoicing in all these things, the aforesaid pontiff went around the city of Leopolis on foot, with hymns and prayers, and consecrated it perpetually with three prayers in the name of the Trinity. He duly celebrated the Mass, as was his custom, and ordered holy water to be sprinkled over the walls.

With his own hands he distributed a considerable gift to the whole people, commending to almighty God both the people and the city divinely revealed, so that it might never be captured or invaded by enemies.

When all this had been accomplished, he returned to his own see with immense joy and eagerness, in the eighth month, with Christ assisting him. On the fifteenth day of the aforesaid month, the circuit of all the walls was completed and finished, in the eighth year of his pontificate and the second indiction.

### Gifts Given in the Church of Saint Peter at Leopolis

He also offered many gifts in the churches which he built there.

In the church of Saint Peter he gave seven large and small cast-silver bowls, weighing together sixteen pounds and one ounce; one gilded basin; three gilded cups; five large and small brooches; one cross of gilded silver with a single gem; another cross of gold with a central *monocassis*; and another silver cross bearing forty gems.

He gave one gilded silver censer, one stone vessel, twelve golden crowns, one basin, and two ostrich eggs.

In the same church of the aforesaid city he made two silk vestments. One had in the middle a panel of gold embroidery; the other had in the middle a cross and four small circles with *gammadia*. He also gave eighteen embroidered curtains.

He made a crucifix of the purest silver weighing seven pounds.

In the church of Saint Leo, in the place mentioned above, he offered one gilded paten, one silver chalice, and two vestments: one embroidered, ornamented around the edge with *oloverum*, having in the middle a wheel of gold embroidery and *gammadia*; and the other of Spanish cloth.

Likewise, he gave seven Catholic books: Histories, Solomon, an antiphoner, a psalter, a sacramentary, a book of deeds together with sermons, and a Gospel book with silver covers.

He also adorned the most sacred altar of God, beneath which the most holy body of the blessed apostle Peter rests, with gilded silver plates on the right and left of the prince of the apostles, bearing his miracles. They shone with immense splendor like the stars of heaven. Together they weighed eighty-four pounds and five ounces.

After these marks of an immense undertaking and these divine works, with the eternal mercy of God inspiring him, and after what this most holy pope had accomplished in various places for the salvation of Christians, he continued each day to adorn with the most precious ornament of all metals the church founded by the Lord’s word upon the firm rock and shining gloriously under the holy name of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

There he also completed a silver reading stand, fashioned with distinguished workmanship and standing on four feet. At its summit the head of a lion shone; it weighed thirty-one pounds and eleven ounces.

He also made four silver *cerostata*, which for a long time had been erected in the middle of the presbytery on feast days by the supreme pontiffs. With prudent judgment he covered these with the purest silver and decreed that they should remain standing there perpetually—something none of his predecessors had thought to do. Together they weighed fifty-five pounds.

In the same place he made one pair of larger silver *cerostata*, weighing forty-eight pounds and ten ounces, on which stood lamps of the purest silver, shining beside the high altar, weighing together forty-nine pounds.

He also made seven other silver-plated *cerostata*, weighing twenty-five pounds and three ounces.

In the same manner he made another seven iron *cerostata*, plated with silver above, weighing twenty-one pounds and three ounces.

Upon the altar itself he placed a vestment woven with gold, shining throughout with white pearls, and having on the right and left gem-studded panels with golden circles around them, on which the illustrious name of the pontiff himself is inscribed.

### The Pope Restores the Monastery of Saint Martin

He also restored with remarkable buildings the monastery of Saint Martin, which through great age was about to collapse, and adorned it throughout to a greater honor than it had previously possessed. There he offered a rose-patterned *subam* [an uncertain textile term] vestment with roses, depicting the Savior with the apostles and the Virgin, and bearing the name of Pope Leo IV. Likewise, he gave five white rose-patterned curtains, one of which had thirteen *gammadiae* and three almond-shaped ornaments of gilded silver. In the church of the Four Holy Crowned Saints he made one embroidered vestment.

Furthermore, the same supreme and orthodox pontiff, moved by divine inspiration, made in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter chalices of the purest silver, hanging above the principal arch and likewise beneath the great columns on the right and left, eighty-three in number and weighing altogether 441 pounds. He also made before the threshold of the sacred altar a beam of marvelous beauty, which, after the impious plundering by the cruel nation, he adorned with the purest silver; upon it are represented sacred and venerable images of God, weighing sixty pounds.

He also offered in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, situated in the city of Leopolis, one gilded silver censer.

Likewise, in the church of the holy Mother of God, Mary, situated in the quarter of the Sardinians, he made gilded silver bowls with a basket. Similarly, in the venerable monastery of Jerusalem, which stands beside the church of the blessed apostle Peter, he made an embroidered vestment adorned around its edge with roundels and with a band of gold embroidery, together with two curtains of purple cloth and three embroidered ones.

That venerable and illustrious pontiff, protected by God, also made the *propitiatorium* [altar covering] of the sacred altar of Peter, prince of the apostles, where his most holy body rests, of *spanoclistum* [uncertain textile/material], containing seventy-two pounds of silver and eighty pounds of gold.

### Gratian, Master of Soldiers, Is Falsely Accused before the Emperor; Emperor Louis Comes to Rome

In his time a certain Daniel, master of soldiers, blinded by the weight of wickedness and folly, hastened to the feet of the most serene lord Emperor Louis. He did not hesitate to speak to him many false and worthless words, which could by no means be believed, against Gratian, the most eminent master of soldiers and distinguished superintendent and counsellor of the Roman palace. Persisting in his false accusation out of envy, he said to the emperor: “Gratian, superintendent of the Roman city, whom you believe to be faithful toward you, said secretly to me alone in his house, murmuring greatly against the Franks: ‘The Franks do us no good and provide no assistance; rather, they violently take what is ours. Why then do we not summon the Greeks, make a treaty of peace with them, and expel the king and people of the Franks from our kingdom and dominion?’”

On hearing this, the aforesaid emperor was immediately inflamed with immense anger and hastened to come swiftly to Rome, without even sending letters to the Roman pontiff and senate. Yet Pope Leo received him honorably, as was customary, seated upon the great steps of the blessed apostle Peter, and began to pacify him with honeyed words of preaching.

### A Hearing Is Held concerning the Accusation; the Accuser Is Handed over to Gratian, Who Releases Him; the Pope Dies

One day, when the emperor and the most holy pontiff Leo, all the Roman nobles, and the best of the Franks were seated together in the house which Pope Leo III of blessed memory had built beside the church of the blessed apostle Peter, a hearing was held concerning the aforesaid accusation. Then Daniel, armed with shamelessness and filled with false intent, said before them all: “This Gratian took counsel with me to remove this Roman land from your power and hand it over to the Greeks.” Immediately not only Gratian but also all the Romans said before the emperor: “You lie; what you say is in no way true.”

The emperor and all the Roman and Frankish nobility, recognizing that the aforesaid Daniel had brought such a charge against Gratian through falsehood and envy, immediately decreed—this most merciful emperor not wishing to act against the institutions of the ancient Roman Augusti—that they should be judged according to Roman law. At this judgment Daniel, reproved by many speeches, confessed with his own mouth that he had borne false witness against him. Therefore he was handed over before all to the aforesaid Gratian, that he might have power to do whatever he wished with him.

But when the emperor earnestly and humbly begged Gratian for the now-delivered Daniel, Gratian consented; the emperor at once gladly received him back into his full favor, and thus he was delivered from the danger of death.
