When these things had been done, the emperor departed; and not many days later the most holy lord Pope Leo IV fell asleep in the Lord, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August. He was buried in the church of the blessed apostle Peter.

He held two ordinations, one in December and the other in March. He created nineteen priests, eight deacons, and sixty-three bishops in various places.

## Letters and Decrees of Pope Leo IV

### I. To the Army of the Franks

“Having laid aside all fear and terror, strive to act manfully against the enemies of the holy faith and the adversaries of all lands.”

Likewise: “Up to this time, whenever your fathers have set the public army in motion, they have always been victorious, and no multitude of peoples has been able to overcome them. For we have not heard that they ever returned without the fame of victory.”

Likewise: “We wish all your charity to know that …”

*Ivo, chapter 87.*
[scan page 334]

## Letters and Decrees

**Whoever (which we say without wishing it) has died faithfully in this battle will by no means be denied the heavenly kingdom.** For the Almighty knows that, if any one of you dies, he has died for the truth of the faith, for the salvation of the fatherland, and for the defense of the Christian name; therefore he will receive the reward appointed for him by God.

### II. To Lothair Augustus

#### Why I do not grant the pallium to Alto, bishop of Auxerre

You commanded us to grant a privilege and the pallium to Alto, bishop of Auxerre. We therefore ask that Your Highness not be displeased with us on this account, since we do not at all remember that what was done by the most holy Pope Gregory up to our own time was ever done, and we have not been able to do it, nor to alter the bounds fixed by the Fathers.

Likewise: What custom does not prescribe that we imitate with justice and diligence, from that we ought to guard ourselves as from a great precipice.

### III. To Lothair Augustus

#### Concerning those three men already publicly condemned and rejected—George, Hadrian, and Peter—as Your Highness commanded us

*Ivo, chapter 88.*

We were altogether astonished that they were still required to confess before another tribunal. For, when your envoys had been sent to us, a sentence had already been fixed and promulgated against them according to Roman law. And unless the festival of Easter had intervened—for the law forbids the pronouncement of a sentence of death during it—their wickedness and unjust presumption would not have allowed them to live. For this reason alone, therefore, the sentence against both parties has been suspended until that time.

*(Fragment of Ivo, Decretum X, chapter 88.)*

#### “Concerning those three”

### IV. To Louis [Lothair], King

*Ibid., part X, chapter 73.*

We shall never receive Peter and Hadrian to live with us. And if—which we scarcely believe—you have regarded as worthless either the requests that we sent you for their retention, or the honors of the Roman pontiff, and have loved us less than Hadrian and Peter, we declare to Your Highness what we have already determined for the future.

Certainly, when the prelates of the Roman See formerly went around to each church with its clergy, either for the performance of Mass or, as usual, for arranging ecclesiastical affairs, they and their clergy carried nothing except priestly vestments. This is what we too have done until now. But we must by no means do more than this if you decide to send men whom we have never sought and do not wish to have.

We make this finally known for certain: whenever we depart for any church or other place subject to us by right, so that no one may triumph because of the peril of our death. For whereas, on account of divine worship or fear of God, we ought to carry only the stole and the chasuble, we shall order that a lance, shield, and sword be carried.

### V. Judgment of Pope Leo IV and the Emperor Louis II

#### In the Roman Council, on behalf of the bishop of Siena against the bishop of Arezzo, concerning a dispute over various churches or parishes, in the year 853

*In Mansi, Concilia, vol. XV.*

“In the name of the Lord, amen. While we, Leo, supreme pontiff and universal pope, the fourth of that name, seated in the chair of the blessed apostle Peter, together with the most pious and most glorious Louis, son of Lothair, Augustus emperor, and many archbishops, bishops, and abbots, were holding a synodal council assembled at Rome—namely, in the church of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles—the bishop of the church of Siena, named Cantius, came into the presence of the holy council and reported how he had often petitioned the aforesaid Lothair, especially by letters written by Pope Hadrian, so that the dispute between the church of Siena and Peter, bishop of the church of Arezzo, concerning the churches, baptisteries, and monasteries situated within the county of Siena, together with their appurtenances—a dispute already prolonged through many occasions—might receive a definitive sentence according to canonical authority.

“Then we, Leo, supreme pontiff, spoke as follows: ‘Since we perform the priestly office—which, although unwillingly, we nevertheless exercise—it is necessary for us to cut through to the root with the spiritual sword disputes of this kind, carried on by the savage cunning of the ancient serpent, and to uproot their roots, lest discord perhaps prevail where the blessings of long-established peace ought to remain.’

“The entire council together said: ‘The just, true, Catholic, and apostolic chair has issued its decision.’

“Then the bishop, holding in his hands the decretal and judicial documents in which the definitive sentence for Siena was recorded, and relying on the authority of Hadrian, supreme pontiff and universal pope, and of Constantine, said in complaint: ‘Brother and our fellow bishop Peter has invaded, by a perverse procedure and against the canonical rule, the parishes and diocese of the church of Siena, and is holding them by force.’

“Then we and the emperor Louis ordered the decretal documents displayed by Bishop Cantius to be read aloud in the presence of the great council. When they had been read, we, Leo, supreme pontiff, began to address the universal assembly as follows:

“‘The greater the dignity of the order of dignities, and the more exalted the dispensation of souls entrusted to us from above, the more we are compelled to render an account to everyone who asks. It is one thing for each person to conduct his own affairs; it is another to hold the governance of the Lord’s Church. Therefore, following canonical doctrine, it belongs to us to oppose the dissensions and disagreements of priests by apostolic censure, following the commands of our Redeemer, who says: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John 14).

“‘For by this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another (John 13). “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim good things” (Matthew 11). “By the grace of the Holy Spirit,” he says. Whenever an excessive dispute has arisen, it must be cut away with the spiritual sword, lest it grow and shake Christ’s people, and lest the faithful sin on account of discord. Obeying the apostolic admonitions of holy Peter, they must cast away all filth, so that pure grain may remain in the Lord’s granary.

“‘Thus, when the Lombard people, over a period of several years, seized territories and laid waste to the places they invaded, it happened that one bishop invaded another’s dioceses and, with reckless audacity, held them without measure; and they have remained in great error down to the present. Ignorant of the definitions of the canons, and eager to seize one another’s parishes, they incur the guilt of perjury. Moreover, fighting among themselves with crafty deceit, they prepare worse disasters; through such error they fall into evil and into the crime of sacrilege, while they cast far from them the censure of the canons and transgress the decrees of our most holy predecessors, the pontiffs, which are supported by canonical authorities.

“‘Therefore, prohibiting such things, by apostolic ordinance, together with the most glorious and most pious Louis and the holy bishops seated in the crown of this sacred council, and promulgating this decree by the privilege of an apostolic constitution, we decree that, just as the canons establish in their decrees according to the territories or appurtenances of cities, so we judge that bishops should hold parishes and dioceses for administration, observing the canonical censure which says:

“‘“A bishop may not invade another’s parish beyond his own boundaries” [F.: “outside his own boundaries”].

“‘And again:

“‘“A bishop may not invade another city that is not subject to him, nor approach any possession belonging to another, nor appoint priests or deacons subject to another bishop, unless perhaps with the consent and will of the bishop of that region. But if anyone should do or attempt such a thing, his ordination shall be invalid, and he shall be restrained by the synod.”

“‘And just as the decrees of our predecessor, the blessed Pope Celestine, state:

“‘“Let each bishop be content with the people granted to his own city; let no one presume anything in another’s province”—

“‘so we too, taking as our authority the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, whose place, although unworthy, we occupy by God’s kindness, decree that, as has been established, each bishop shall possess without disturbance the parishes or dioceses belonging to the boundaries assigned to his city, under the solemn appeal to divine judgment and with the imposition of anathema.’”

While we, Leo, supreme pontiff, were therefore concluding this speech of holy exhortation, the decretal documents named above having been displayed and read again in order, Peter, bishop of the church of Arezzo, said to Bishop Cantius:

“Your decretal and judicial documents, which you have displayed here, cannot cause any loss or disadvantage to my church. For we and our predecessors have possessed for more than forty years the monasteries and baptisteries within the boundaries of the county of Siena, together with their chapels, appurtenances, and adjacent properties, over which you, brother and fellow bishop, are bringing a complaint against my church.”

Then Bishop Cantius replied:

“Always, he said, the monasteries and baptisteries situated within the boundaries of the territory of Siena were and are parishes of our church. We administered chrism there and performed consecrations. I and my predecessors ordained the priests and deacons there and consecrated the churches. But you, brother, have craftily and fraudulently usurped the aforesaid monasteries and baptisteries against the ordinances of the sacred canons.”

When Bishop Peter of the city of Arezzo heard this, he said:

“Truly, these monasteries and baptisteries situated within the boundaries of your territory, concerning which you bring a complaint against us, came to the church of Saint Donatus from the time of the Lombards. For I possess a judgment according to which, in the time of Liutprand, king of the Lombards, they were joined by your predecessors to the advantage of my church. I also possess a royal charter which King Charles confirmed in the church of Saint Donatus. But I do not now have it in my hands, since we did not think that we would have a dispute here on this matter. I ask the sacred council for a delay and a period of time, until I can hasten to Arezzo and bring my judgment and charter in support of my claim—as I have promised—in the presence of our lord, the supreme pontiff, the most pious emperor, the entire council, and your parties.”

They granted a delay of twelve days, so that each of them might bring within that period whatever proof he possessed through the sanctions of charters or the provisions of decrees, and so that each might also bring suitable witnesses from the aforesaid church to assist in the investigation of the truth.

When the twelve days had elapsed, Peter, bishop of the church of Arezzo, and Cantius, bishop of Siena, came in person in the presence of us and of the most pious Augustus, Emperor Louis. They appeared before the bishops whose names are appended below: John, archbishop of the city of Ravenna; Ambrose, bishop of the church of Lucca; Oschesis, bishop of Pistoia; Donatus, bishop of the city of Fiesole; John, bishop of Pisa; Andrew, bishop of the city of Volterra; Taceprandus, bishop of the city of Chiusi; Otto, bishop of Roselle; Tanimundus, bishop of Sovana; Peter, bishop of the city of Orvieto; John, bishop of Tuscania; John, bishop of Centumcellae; Peter, bishop of Spoleto; and many others.

In the presence of these men, therefore, both bishops—that is, Cantius, bishop of Siena, and Peter of the church of Arezzo—with the sanctions of the charters and provisions of the decrees, and with suitable witnesses summoned from both sides as had been requested, again took their places with us in the council. The crown of the holy council was seated in the same church of the blessed prince of the apostles, where it had earlier assembled, and we all wished to weigh the dispute of so great a litigation with the straightest balance and conclude it after weighing it on the scales of equity.

Then the decretal documents of Peter of the church of Arezzo, together with the charters, which he had promised to produce and was holding in his hands, were brought forth by order of us and of the most pious Augustus Louis, and handed to Joseph, archchaplain, to be read.

---

[scan page 335]

## Leo

When they had been read in the presence of the great council, the emperor Louis addressed the whole church as follows:

“Since the possession of every matter ought to be such that the beginning of the possession contains no defect, we can clearly conclude that, although it is established that the church of Arezzo held these parishes only from the time of the Lombards, its opposition based on possession is not sufficient. For before the sword of the Lombards devastated Italy by laying it waste, while the Roman emperors ruled the world in the happiness of tranquil peace, the church of Siena governed and held these same parishes, as ancient custom had established.”

Then the entire council proclaimed that the emperor had spoken truly, plausibly, and most worthy of praise.

Bishop Peter of Arezzo replied:

“Since the imperial majesty and the apostolic dignity have ordered that not only written documents but also witnesses be brought forward in this matter, let them order the priests who live in these same parishes to give the truth of their testimony—priests who, through the accounts of ancient men transmitted through their ancestral lines, are conspicuously connected with the truth.”

Then we, Leo, universal pontiff, and the emperor Louis ordered priests and other faithful men to be brought forward. They were immediately summoned into the presence of the great council.

First came Gisulpherianus, from the parish of Saint Quiricus at Ausimora; Aterpalianus, priest and monk, from the parish of Saint Stephen at Cinnano; Gesilarus, archpriest of Saint Mary at Pava; Malperianus, priest from the parish of Saint Mary at Soleta; Lanfrancus, priest from the parish of Saint Mary at Cusona; Benedictus, archpriest from the parish of Saint Vitus at Vitaliano; Agiprandus, archpriest from the parish of Saint Andrew at Malcino; Leucarius, priest from the parish of Saint Mary at Sexta; and Aliperus, archpriest from the parish of Saint Donatus at Ziliano.

“These are my archpriests from the aforesaid parishes,” said Peter, bishop of Arezzo.

Then we, Pope Leo, ordered the Book of the Gospels to be placed in the middle of the council, and the standard of the holy cross to be placed there as well. Through these objects we questioned them as follows:

“Listen, priests, to whom the holy council has granted the opportunity to give testimony. In virtue of obedience and under the solemn appeal to divine judgment, we command you to tell us the truth about this matter immediately.”

First of all Gesolfrandus, the aforesaid archpriest, said:

“Since it is impious to remain silent when one is swearing under such a solemn appeal, I consider it sacrilege to give false testimony in the presence of this sacred council. Therefore, what I learned from my parents, and what I myself remember, although I am nearly ninety years old, I shall recount without any appearance of falsehood.

“I know that, according to the report of my parents, the church of Siena held the aforesaid parishes firmly and without any dispute until the time of the Lombards. But the wicked sword of that people, plundering everything and reducing lands filled with inhabitants to solitude, brought about this result. Finally, as a consequence of the devastation of that time, one bishop, by a crafty invasion, began to reside in another’s parish through a wicked act of presumption, and held the parish he had invaded with all his strength.

“Thus we know that this happened to the church of Siena at the hands of the church of Arezzo. Although Bishop Peter of Arezzo brought us here in support of his own cause, we nevertheless believe that it would be impious to conceal the truth. Thus, with the matter placed in great ambiguity, both churches have to yield to the other—one from necessity, the other from choice. We remember the aforesaid parishes: to the church of Siena by choice, to the church of Arezzo by necessity.

“It is established that, to this day, we have rendered churches and the established service to the church of Siena, that we received chrism from that same church, and that we have until now received the consecration of deacons and priests from it. We do not deny that, shaken by the force of arms, we have rendered service under compulsion to the church of Arezzo. Therefore let the apostolic dignity and the imperial majesty rescue us and our parishes from such danger, and establish by the decrees of this sacred council the church to which we ought henceforth to render service freely and without disturbance.”

Nevertheless, each of them was questioned individually, one after another, and each affirmed that the testimony of Gesolfrandus was entirely true.

Aripaldus, priest and monk from the parish of Saint Stephen at Anciano, reported the same as Gesolfrandus. Gelsahus, archpriest of the saltus, likewise confessed. Benedictus, archpriest of Saint Vitus, spoke likewise. Aliprandus, from the parish of Saint Donatus, spoke likewise. Aliprandus, from the parish of Saint Andrew, likewise. Laufridus, archpriest of Saint Mary at Osona, likewise. Laucarius, archpriest from the parish of Saint Mary at Sexta, likewise.

All of them, as though with one voice, firmly and consistently asserted that the aforesaid parishes belonged by the most direct right to the church of Siena.

When Peter heard this, and saw the aforesaid priests giving their testimony, he accused them of having incurred the guilt of perjury. Then, at our command, and at the command of the most pious emperor and the entire council, all the aforesaid priests swore that what they had recounted under examination as testimony was sufficiently true and credible, and that the truth was as they had said.

Then we, Leo, supreme pontiff, spoke as follows to Bishop Peter and the entire council:

“Brothers, it is likewise necessary for us to weigh this matter on the balance of equity. For although our brother Peter hoped through the testimony given above to obtain justice for his church, the church of Siena has won the triumph of its contest.”

At this the entire assembly said:

“It is plainly evident that the aforementioned parishes belong to the church of Siena, since it has been clearly proved that they belong within the boundaries of the same county; the assertion of the most truthful witnesses proclaims it; and the writings of the most holy pontiffs confirm it. Therefore let Your Holiness and the imperial majesty order that what formerly belonged to the church of Siena be restored to it, so that discord may be removed from their midst, and each of them may govern the parishes subject to him, as has been established in every matter.”

## Letters

Afterward the decretal documents and charters of Peter of the church of Arezzo, just as he had promised, were held in his hands and, by order of us and of the most pious Augustus Louis, brought forth for reading by Joseph, archchaplain.

When they had been read in the presence of the great council, the emperor Louis addressed the whole church as follows:

“Since possession of every matter ought to be such that the beginning of the possession contains no defect, we can clearly conclude that, although it is established that the church of Arezzo held these parishes only from the time of the Lombards, its opposition based on possession is not sufficient. For before the Lombard sword invaded Italy and devastated it, while the Roman emperors ruled the world in the happiness of tranquil peace, the church of Siena, as ancient custom established, governed and held these same parishes.”

Then the entire council acclaimed that the emperor had spoken truly, plausibly, and most worthily of praise.

To this Bishop Peter of Arezzo replied:

“Since the imperial majesty and the apostolic dignity have ordered that not only documents but also witnesses be brought forward in this matter, let them order the priests to state the truth of their testimony—those who, living in these same parishes, are connected with uncorrupted truth through the reports of ancient men transmitted through their ancestral lines.”

Then we, Leo, universal pontiff, and the emperor Louis ordered priests and other faithful men to be produced. They were immediately summoned before the great council.

“Since it is impious to remain silent when one swears under such a solemn appeal, I consider it sacrilege to give false testimony in the presence of this sacred council. Therefore, what I learned from my parents, and what I myself remember, although I am nearly ninety years old, I shall recount without any taint of falsehood.

But the wicked sword of that people, plundering everything and reducing lands filled with inhabitants to solitude, brought about this result. Finally, as a consequence of the devastation of that time, one bishop, by a crafty invasion, began to dwell in another’s parish through a wicked act of presumption, and held the parish he had invaded with all his strength.

“Thus we know that this happened to the church of Siena at the hands of the church of Arezzo. Although Bishop Peter of Arezzo brought us here in support of his own cause, we nevertheless believe that it would be impious to conceal the truth. Thus, with the matter placed in great ambiguity, both churches must yield to the other—one from necessity, the other by choice. We remember the aforesaid parishes: to the church of Siena by choice, to the church of Arezzo by necessity.

“It is established that, to this day, we have rendered churches and the established service to the church of Siena, that we received chrism from that same church, and that we have hitherto received from it the consecration of deacons and priests. Nevertheless, this was done one by one: each was questioned individually, and each confirmed that the testimony of Gesolfrandus was entirely true.

Aripaldus, priest and monk from the parish of Saint Stephen at Anciano, reported the same as Gesolfrandus. Gelsahus, archpriest of Saint Vitus, likewise confessed. Benedictus, archpriest of Saint Vitus, likewise spoke. Aliprandus from the parish of Saint Donatus likewise spoke. Aliprandus from the parish of Saint Andrew likewise spoke. Laufridus, archpriest of Saint Mary at Osona, likewise spoke. Laucarius, archpriest from the parish of Saint Mary at Sexta, likewise spoke.

Thus all of them, as though with one voice, firmly asserted that the aforesaid parishes belonged to the church of Siena by the most direct right.

When Peter heard this, and heard the aforesaid priests giving their testimony, he accused them of having incurred the guilt of perjury. Then, at our command, and at the command of the most pious emperor and the entire council, all the aforesaid priests swore that, when summoned to testify, they had related what was sufficiently true and credible, and that the truth was as they had said.

Then we, Leo, supreme pontiff, spoke as follows to Bishop Peter and the entire council:

“Brothers, it is likewise necessary for us to weigh this matter on the balance of equity. For although our brother Peter hoped through the foregoing testimony to obtain justice for his church, the church of Siena has won the triumph of its contest.”

At this the entire assembly said:

“It is plainly evident that the aforementioned parishes belong to the church of Siena, since it has been clearly proved that they belong within the boundaries of the same county; the assertion of the most truthful witnesses proclaims it; and the writings of the most holy pontiffs confirm it. Therefore let Your Holiness and the imperial majesty order that what belonged to the church of Siena be restored to it, so that discord may be removed from their midst and each may govern the parishes subject to him, as has been established in every matter.”

[scan page 337]

## Leo

“Let each govern the parishes subject to him, and let no one presume in any way to approach the neighboring diocese of his brother.”

Then Bishop Comeranus said to everyone:

“I still have suitable witnesses whom I have brought here from my city. The uncertainty of the dispute before us is clear to them, for through the ancient account of noble parents they know everything concerning it with particular distinction. If they are brought in, they will in no way conceal the truth.”

Then Willeradus, son of the good-memory Merempridus; Gunteramus, son of the late Sicheradus Ginnonus; who were the king’s soldiers; and Lamfredus, a soldier of the aforesaid Bishop Peter of Arezzo, entered.

Willeradus, questioned by us under the solemn appeal to the divine name, said:

“We know, therefore, that the aforesaid parishes and monasteries belonged to the church of Siena, according to the report of my ancient parents. We have seen the bishop of the church of Siena perform the confirmations, the consecrations of rectors, and the ordinations of priests there. It is a manifest fact that no dispute existed there except from the time when the Lombard people entered Italy. For the church of Siena had held the aforesaid parishes firmly until their time.”

All the others, after being questioned individually, declared that Willeradus had given truthful testimony. Then, giving testimony with one voice, they touched the holy Gospels, which had been placed in the midst, and swore that the aforesaid parishes belonged properly to the church of Siena and did not rightly belong to the church of Arezzo.

When this oath had been completed, we, Leo, supreme pontiff, said to Bishop Peter:

“Brother Peter, you must now be content with your own parishes alone and desist from unlawful presumption. Bring this unusual dispute to an end, or, if you have anything useful to oppose, produce it. For this sacred council accepts nothing vain, superfluous, or alien to the truth.”

Bishop Peter replied:

“According to your holy examination, the dispute has been weighed rightly, and I do not place in doubt what has been defined here by you. Nor am I now able to produce the presence of other men whom you might trust more, or any other written decrees besides those which I have displayed here.”

The emperor then said:

“It is therefore clearly established that Bishop Peter has been defeated, since the church of Siena has won the victory through the testimony of those by whom he thought himself able to be saved. It is just, he said, that he remain silent on this matter and presume no longer to enter into dispute over it. It is superfluous for him, while retaining the parishes subject to his own city, to cross with reckless audacity into the diocese of another bishop. Therefore we wish this sacred and venerable council to enclose and define the dispute of this litigation with so equitable an end that it may not be renewed between them in the future through any scruple.”

Then the emperor, leaving with us his envoys for the purpose of bringing this matter to an end—namely Joseph, archchaplain; Angelbert, archbishop; Notingus, bishop; and Adelchesi, count—departed from the council.

Cantius remained with twelve suitable priests, whose oath had not yet been taken. Then Cantius and the twelve priests swore that the truth had been presented without any deceit in the oaths of the witnesses mentioned above.

Then the entire council cried out together:

“Let the holiness of the apostolic summit, by decree of the entire council, order Bishop Peter to make a formal renunciation of the aforesaid parishes to the church of Siena, which he rashly invaded, and thereafter to remain entirely silent concerning this matter.”

Then, at the command of the Apostolic See, the emperor’s legates, and the entire council, Bishop Peter completely abandoned and renounced to the church of Siena the aforesaid parishes, which he had unlawfully and wickedly invaded.

When these matters had been completed, we, Leo, supreme pontiff, defined the matter as follows:

“It is therefore appropriate that we apply our authority to the definition of this litigation and, by imposing anathema, put an end on every side to a dispute concluded by the most equitable reasoning, lest at some future time anyone filled with wickedness dare to violate what has now been defined by us justly and canonically.

“We decree that whatever has been discovered through the investigation of witnesses to belong to the church of Siena shall remain firm and stable for that church. Therefore, if anyone at any time should attempt to violate this decree of our privilege—whether cleric or layman, whether endowed with rank or decorated with honors, or any person, great or small—let him know that, by the authority of our lord Peter, prince of the apostles, he is deprived of every honor, bound by the chains of the anathema *maranatha*, and condemned to everlasting punishment with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, and with Ananias and Sapphira.

“And since we have gathered in the name of God, it is believed that the Lord is truly among us, and that by his help whatever we do or define is strengthened. Therefore whoever attempts to violate whatever has been decreed by us, with God’s help, binds himself to the aforesaid curse.”

Leo, by the grace of God bishop of the Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church, confirmed this decree of judgment with my own hand.

Joseph, archchaplain of the lord emperor, subscribed.

John, archbishop of Ravenna, subscribed.

## Letters and Decrees

Peter, bishop of Spoleto, subscribed.

### VI. Confirmation of the Privileges of a Certain Church

We ordered Stephanus, notary of our see, to write this in the month of September, on the fifth day, in the fourteenth indiction. Given on the day before the Kalends of September [31 August], through the hand of Tiberius, first secretary of the Holy Apostolic See, in the reign of our most pious and perpetual Augustus, our lord Lothair, crowned by God, great emperor, in the thirty-third year, and after his consulship in the thirty-third year; and likewise in the year … of Louis, his son, the noble emperor.

### VII. Excommunication of Anastasius the Priest

Under the rule of our lords Lothair and Louis, Augusti, on the sixteenth day of December, in the forty-fourth indiction.

#### 1

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

Anastasius, a priest of our cardinal clergy, whom we ordained at the title of the blessed Marcellus, withdrew from that title and departed to other parishes without our pontifical knowledge. We summoned him through messengers and letters, and, concerning him, we petitioned the lord emperors through our messengers that they order him to return to his own parish. He has now spent two years hiding here and there during this departure. He did not come when summoned to two of our councils, nor could he be found; for, as we have said, like a wandering sheep, at the devil’s urging, he was secretly inhabiting foreign regions.

Therefore, according to the canonical ordinances, by the authority of almighty God, the blessed apostle Peter, and our own apostolic authority together, from this day let him be deprived of communion until he has been brought before my special presence for canonical judgment; and if he does not come, let him never communicate again.

#### 2

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all bishops, priests, deacons, subdeacons, all clergy, and the entire Christian people.

You know, beloved brothers, that we are in a good and complete relationship with you. Now, for the sake of caution and for the memory of future times, we wish your charity to know again how Anastasius, a priest of our cardinal clergy whom we ordained at the title of the blessed Marcellus, instigated and persuaded by the devil, abandoned his province and church contrary to the statutes of the Fathers.

Behold, for five years now he has wandered through foreign parishes like a wandering sheep. Supported by canonical authority, we summoned him through apostolic letters a third and a fourth time. But when he delayed returning, we assembled two councils of bishops on his behalf. Since, when they met, we could neither see him nor obtain his personal presence, we deprived him of holy communion by common decree, wishing through the censure of this excommunication to bring him back as a person to the bosom of the holy mother Church from which he had departed.

But, disregarding the apostolic admonitions and those of the holy council, ensnared in the darkness of error, he absolutely refused to return. Therefore, just as we promulgated concerning him at Ravenna, while we were staying there, in the church of the blessed martyr Vitalis, on 29 May, in the first indiction, by our own mouth, so now we have promulgated it again in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, on 19 June, in the indiction noted above:

“Let him be anathema from the holy Fathers and from us. And let all who wish to provide him assistance or any kind of comfort, whether in his expulsion—which may God forbid—or in the honor of the pontificate, likewise be subject to anathema.”

#### 3

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

Here begins the holy and venerable synod, which was assembled by the grace of the Lord and by his divine counsel in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, namely in the seventh year of the pontificate of the most holy, fellow-evangelist, and universal Pope Leo IV, and in the forty-second year of the imperial reign of the most invincible emperors Lothair and Louis, in the month of December, on the eighth day, in the second indiction.

At this holy and venerable synod, nobly celebrated with the assistance of the Lord’s grace, after various pious and salutary admonitions and exhortations had been given to bishops, priests, clergy, and all Christians, Anastasius, priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, was deposed justly and canonically. He had abandoned his own parish contrary to canonical authority for five years and had remained in another parish down to the present day. Although summoned, excommunicated, and finally anathematized, as the truthful account concerning him in this synod demonstrates, he refused to come to the two councils of bishops assembled on his behalf.

Therefore, both by the supreme pontiff and by all the bishops then presiding at the synod—sixty-seven in number—because of his …

The foolish audacity, as we said above, was rightly punished: he was deposed and deprived of priestly honor, in the year, month, day, and indiction stated above.

## I. To whom the ecclesiastical order belongs

It was stated in the first chapter to whom the ecclesiastical order belongs: there is no doubt that it belongs to bishops and ordained clergy. We do not believe that you are ignorant of this; you know it from the apostolic men themselves. Since the rules promulgated by bishops in sacred councils have been promulgated and received, who besides bishops could have issued canonical judgments?

## II. Each parish is to be governed under a bishop’s supervision

Each parish is to be governed under the provision and protection of the bishop—“Each parish is to be governed” (*Causa* XI, question 1, “Each parish is to be governed”)—by priests or other clerics whom the bishop himself, with the fear of God, judges to be properly assigned to it; and he is to visit it whenever ecclesiastical necessity requires.

## III. A priest is not to be compelled to bring eulogies to sacred councils

Concerning bringing eulogies to sacred councils (*Distinction* 18, “Concerning eulogies”), we find nothing determined by the ancients, but only what each priest may wish. For if it were established that blessings should be brought at that time, they might come to synods less willingly and be more reluctant to attend. Such things, in my opinion, are neither reasonably to be demanded nor to be rejected when offered voluntarily.

## IV. Lot-casting is nothing other than divination and sorcery

You ask about the practice of divinations or sorceries, concerning those who do not fear selling doves in the Lord’s temple for the sake of the most shameful profit and joining their wicked deeds to the heresy of Simon (*Causa* I, question 2, “You ask about these”), whether they may perform penance while remaining within the clerical order, or only outside the order and after being removed from the priestly rank.

As for those whom we know to have been convicted of committing this detestable wickedness, already condemned by many councils, we cannot assist them through penance and thereby oppose so many spiritual fathers; rather, let it be certain that we agree with the judgment of those fathers. Nevertheless, everything in councils must belong to the bishops. For we hold that no condemnation of bishops is ever valid (*Causa* I, question 7, “No condemnation”), unless it is issued either before the legitimate number of bishops—twelve bishops—or by a proven sentence supported by seventy-two suitable witnesses, such as are able to accuse and who first swear before the four sacred Gospels of Christ that they will utter nothing false, as blessed Sylvester handed down to us and as the holy Roman Church appears to hold.

And if among those whom men have declared condemned there is a bishop who has asked that his case be heard in the presence of the bishop of the Roman See, no one may presume to give a final sentence against him; rather, we decree that he must in every respect be heard.

As for the rest, your letters have made clear to us what and how we ought to answer concerning the chapters about which you inquire. We have therefore endeavored to comply with your requests and to show, one by one, what must be done, whether established by the holy Fathers or handed down by ancient custom.

The sacred canons state the following concerning the practice of divinations or sorceries, using the very words of the Council of Ancyra:

“Those who seek divinations and follow the custom of the pagans, or introduce such people into their houses to inquire into something by magical art or for the purpose of expiation, shall lie under the rule of five years.”

Accordingly, the lots by which you distinguish all matters in your judgments (*Causa* XXVI, question 5, “The lots by which”), are nothing other than what those Fathers condemned; we decree them to be divinations and sorceries. Therefore we wish them to be utterly condemned, and we do not wish them even to be named among Christians; we command that they be cut off under the prohibition of anathema (*Ivo*, part IX, chapter 11).

## V. No one is to marry within his own kinship

As the Fathers have defined, no one may dare to take a spouse from his own kinship; otherwise let him be anathema (*Distinction* 20, “From the books”). Hence the decrees of blessed Gregory the Younger must be especially retained.

## VI. By which decrees bishops are to judge

No one should judge according to *The Little Book* and the commentaries of others while abandoning the canons of the holy councils or the rules of the decretals—that is, those rules which are held among us together with the canons and which we use in all ecclesiastical judgments. These are the rules of the Apostles; of Nicaea, Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra, Antioch, Laodicea, Chalcedon, Sardica, Carthage, and the African councils; together with the rules of the Roman pontiffs Sylvester, Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Celestine, Leo, Gelasius, Hilary, Symmachus, and Simmas.

These are the authorities by which bishops judge and by which bishops and clergy together are judged. For if an unusual matter should arise or occur that could in no way be settled by these authorities, then, if writings of those whom you remember—Jerome, Augustine, Isidore, or other similar holy teachers—are found, they should be retained and promulgated with magnanimity, or the matter should be referred to the apostolic See.

For this reason I do not fear to pronounce more clearly and loudly that whoever—whether bishop, cleric, or layman—does not accept without distinction the statutes of the holy Fathers that we have mentioned, which among us are called canons, proves himself neither to hold the Catholic and apostolic faith nor to preserve and effectively carry out the four holy and true Gospels of Christ.

*Note:* These words are absent from the Roman edition and in the Vatican manuscript, as Lucas Holstenius observed.

## VIII. To the bishops of Britain

He teaches that simoniacal bishops are to be judged in a council; he then answers the rest of their questions.

Leo to all the most reverend fellow bishops of the British people.

Your letters addressed to us reveal with what zeal and diligence you feed the flock entrusted to you by the Lord and nourish it with divine food. Therefore I congratulate you with no slight rejoicing; and, delighted by the investigation of so many ambiguities, I have been raised, as it were, from a serious illness and, though deprived of complete health, have risen in spirit more safely than before from the fear of negligence that oppressed me in the lowest depths because of that region. For when I learned that certain laymen had been placed over ecclesiastical affairs, and was compelled by eager concern to respond to their vigilance, I could think of nothing else than that you, who have entered upon divine and ecclesiastical responsibilities, had fallen asleep. Now, however, by divine grace, these fellow bishops of ours—men of this kind and such rulers of churches—have been brought to us and made known, and I am safer now than before.

Finally, having presented to us the joint embassy of all the most reverend bishops, you ask concerning the matters stated above.

## IX. To the Emperor Lothair Augustus

From the *Register of Leo IV*:

“Since reports often arrived from the Saracen side that certain men were even planning to come secretly and by force into the Roman Port, we ordered our people to assemble at the Port and resolved to descend to the seashore; and we went out from Rome.”

## X. To the Emperor Louis

“You ought to know that we never allow our men to be oppressed by anyone; but if necessity should befall them, we avenge them in person, because we must be avengers and chief helpers of our flock in all things.”

## XI. To John the Archbishop

“Know for certain that we never permit our men and subjects to be torn apart or oppressed by you. But if—which we do not expect—you neglect the words of this admonition and inflict further oppressions on the aforementioned or other men of ours, we shall avenge them in person and shall arrange to seize everything belonging to you, with furious and cruel boldness.”

## XII. To the Emperors Lothair and Louis

Leo asks the emperors Lothair and Louis to grant the deacon Colonna the church of Reate, saying:

“If we obtain your permission, may we consecrate a bishop there; but if you do not wish a bishop to be appointed in the aforesaid church, may your Serenity deign to grant him the church of Tusculum.”

## XIII. To Anastasius, an excommunicated priest

### Decrees

Leo, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to Anastasius, an excommunicated priest.

We know that you were begotten for us from our spiritual entrails, and we daily lament your deception: although you have emerged from the bosom of your mother, you do not hesitate, entangled in the darkness of error, to remain in foreign parishes or regions, contrary to the precepts of the Fathers and the sanction of the canons.

Return, therefore, and take the greatest care to walk the path of salvation, lest empty hope deceive you and fleeting flatteries overthrow you. Raise your mind above earthly concerns and remember to yearn with unceasing contemplation for the things that remain above and are infinite. For we always desire to see the salvation of your soul and body, and we continually implore the mercy of almighty God lest the snares of the devil entrap you.

Furthermore, by apostolic letter we command you: for five years you have been hiding here and there and running about like a serpent. You must present yourself, without allowing any excuse to intervene, at the council that we shall gather on the fifteenth day of November, in the expected second month of the indiction [in manuscript F: “of the month” is omitted; “of the second indiction”]. Thus we may examine your case with careful attention in the venerable assembly of the holy congregation and treat your conversion more humanely.

But if you neglect what we command, we bind you with a greater bond. For we have often reproved you and judge you reprehensible because you delayed coming to the two councils convened on your behalf. The venerable bishops Nicholas, Petronacius, and John, who are present and through whom we have now ordered you to be summoned by canonical authority, will state this with their own mouths.

If, at the appointed time, you neglect to come to the aforesaid council, we decree that you shall remain under excommunication and anathema in every respect.

*References:* *Ivo*, chapter 83; *Ivo*, chapter 84; *Ivo*, chapter 85; Gratian’s *Decree* I.63.16, “Of the blessed Church”; “In many ways”: it is read in chapter 46 of book XI of Cardinal Deusdedit.

## XIV. To the bishops of Britain

Priests are not to be compelled to bring eulogies to sacred councils.

Concerning bringing eulogies to sacred councils, we find nothing determined by the ancients, but only what each priest may wish. For if it were established that blessings should be brought at that time, they might perhaps come to synods less willingly and be more reluctant to attend. Such things, in my opinion, are neither reasonably to be demanded nor to be rejected when offered voluntarily.

## XV. To Lothair Augustus

### Fragment

“You have no small reward with God if, although disregarding the doctrines of the ancient law, you chastise and correct them with your imperial authority to the best of your ability. Likewise, we implore your Clemency that, just as Roman law has hitherto flourished without every kind of disturbance and has not been corrupted for the sake of any person, so now it may retain its own strength and proper vigor.”

*Notes:* Pithou: “Concerning eulogies.” See Paulinus, *To Severus*, and Centuriator, vol. IX, p. 407. This letter is found in a Roman manuscript. *Ivo*, part IV, chapter 181; this is also cited in *Distinction* II, chapter “Your Clemency.”

## XVI. To Lothair Augustus

### Fragment

“Concerning your imperial chapters and precepts, and those of your pontifical predecessors, which must be irrefragably observed and preserved: as much as we have been and are able, with Christ’s favor, we openly profess that we shall preserve them in every way, both now and forever. And if anyone has said or should say something different to you, know for certain that he is a liar.”

## XVII. To Charles the Bald

### Fragment

“If perhaps—which we do not believe—we are judged useless by you, nevertheless the Church over which we preside is not useless; rather, it is rightly called by everyone the beginning and source of all things.”

## XVIII. To Charles the Bald

### Fragment

“It appears to be contrary to the censures of the holy Fathers if a secular person or layman attempts to expel priests from the churches in which they were named or installed at the time of their ordination” [manuscript AL: “appears to strive”].

## XIX. To Count Guido

### Fragment

“It is greatly unworthy, and even contrary to future generations, that so glorious a law, which many emperors in the past observed, should now lose its force and be unjustly condemned.”

## XX. To Colerod, Archbishop, and Bertus

“Therefore, by God’s permission, we have been made shepherds of men, so that we must in no way overstep what our Fathers established either in the holy canons or in secular laws. For we act against their most salutary institutions if we do not preserve untouched what they established by divine council.”

## XXI. To Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

### That the monastery built by Adremarus should be consecrated

Leo, bishop and servant of the servants of God, sends greetings to the most reverend and holy Prudentius, bishop of the See of Troyes.

Let the prudence of Your Holiness know that this religious monk, named Adremarus, together with his monks, desires with the greatest devotion to consecrate a monastery in praise and glory of the holy Trinity, and for the remedy of his own soul and those of all his people, in honor of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of Saint Leo, pope and vicar of that same apostle.

He desires to establish and found the site and structure of this holy monastery upon the properties belonging by right to the blessed apostle Peter, which truly belong to him and which have been granted to the most glorious Count Guido by pontifical charter.

For this reason we command and exhort Your Holiness that, whenever you are humbly asked by the aforesaid monk, you should go there; and, at the place he indicates to you, you should deposit and consecrate the relics of the saints named above, which he received from us, under this condition and arrangement: that the aforesaid monastery should always and perpetually remain under the jurisdiction and power of our holy Roman Church.

May almighty God preserve Your Holiness in safety, brother. Farewell.

*References:* Gratian’s *Decree*, Distinction 10, chapter 9; Ivo’s *Decree*, Distinction 5, chapter 11; Gratian’s *Decree*, Causa XVI, question 6, chapter “If perhaps”; *Ivo*, same work, chapter 182.

## XXII. To Hincmar, Archbishop

### Why he delays confirming the Council of Soissons

We shall explain to Your Charity the reasons why we have suspended this matter until now.

The first is that, just as the synod mentioned above was usefully examined or settled by the bishops, so you ought to have sent the statutes of your synod through several of them, so that every doubt might be completely removed.

Another reason, contrary to your desired expectation, prevented us from completing the matter: the legates of the apostolic See were not present there, nor was an imperial letter presented to us of such a kind that it could have specifically indicated what you sent us to request.

The fourth reason is that those whom Your Charity affirms to have been deposed by the authority of the synod have appealed to the apostolic See by their own letters and wish to be heard again in our apostolic presence; and, if they are found guilty, they do not refuse to submit to canonical censure.

## XXIII. To the same Hincmar

### He writes that two legates were assigned concerning the same synod

To carry out and obtain what you request, we have instructed Peter, the venerable and most beloved bishop of Spoleto, as executor in our place by our own spoken word. We have also notified by letter another Peter, a venerable and equally beloved bishop of Arezzo, and likewise other faithful men of yours and ours; and so forth.

## XXIV. To Nomenoius, Duke of Brittany

### That he should cease defending Gislardus, the usurper of the See of Nantes

“We perceive Gislardus to be a thief and robber (*Causa* VII, question 1, ‘A thief’), who did not fear to usurp the place of a living man, which he was not permitted to do. You must no longer defend him for the sake of any gifts or payment.”

*Note:* Gratian incorrectly gives “Vemoni” in the title of the chapter in Causa VII, question 1, instead of “Nomenoius,” reading: “Likewise Leo IV to Vemoni, duke of Brittany.”

## XXV. To Ebruin and Adelfred, Bishops

### Fragment

Since the teaching of our episcopate—which you know well—must be concerned not only with the usefulness of priests but also with that of secular persons, we wish Your Fraternity to know that this present priest has come to the apostolic See and has reported to us, in due order, the violence and excommunication inflicted upon him. He also stated that his church had been taken from him without a proper legal process, and that another priest, driven by envy after giving a payment, had presumed to usurp it.

Consequently, his relatives, compelled by great grief, immediately seized the priest who held his church and tore out his eyes. Nevertheless, the aforementioned priest says that this was done without his consent and without his counsel.

If this is so, as he testified to us with his own mouth, you must take the greatest care that, if he was not canonically excommunicated, canonical remission be made on his behalf.

*References:* Gratian’s *Decree*, Causa II, question 4, chapter 1; *Ivo*, part IV, chapter 196; same work, chapter 86; Gratian’s *Decree*, Causa XXI, question 1, chapter 3, “Those who are more numerous”; Gratian’s *Decree*, Distinction III, chapter 11, “Concerning the flesh of rams.”

## XXVI. To the Judge of Sardinia

“Neither the custom nor the newly introduced practice of our Church and of our predecessors has been to presume anything new or unusual against the holy canons. Therefore, although we desire more devotedly to receive your petitions, the censure of the holy Fathers would have to assist us in these matters. But since the synodal pages do not appear to support this, we cannot presume such a great novelty or deviate from that most upright path.”

## XXVII. To the Judge of Sardinia

“We deem it necessary to beseech Your Highness that you deign to send us as many armed men as Your Magnificence may foresee—whether boys, adults, or young men with their weapons—who may carry out our daily commands.”

## XXVIII. Concerning one who holds several churches

### Fragment

Whoever holds several churches must retain one as a titular church and another under commendation.

## XXIX. Concerning the eating of meat

### Fragment

The fast is to extend from the end of the supper held at the beginning of the night of the fourth feria—which becomes Wednesday—until dawn of the fifth feria, and likewise from the supper of the night of the sixth feria—which becomes Friday—until the light of Saturday.

## XXX. To the Emperor Louis

### Fragment

“If we have done anything improperly, and have not preserved the path of just law toward our subjects, we wish to correct everything according to the judgment of Your Majesty and your envoys. Therefore we implore you to send to these regions men who will investigate the matters we have mentioned, men who fear God in all things and who will diligently examine everything as though Your Imperial Glory were personally present.

Let them not investigate only the matters mentioned above, but, whether the affairs judged against us are lesser or greater, let everything be brought to a proper conclusion by a precise legal examination, so that nothing arising from them may thereafter remain unexamined or undecided.”

## XXXI. To the Emperors Lothair and Louis

### Fragment

“It has been established and confirmed by treaty between us and you that the election and consecration of the future Roman pontiff must take place only justly and canonically.”

## XXXII

All voluntary violators of the canons have been anathematized in all authoritative councils.

## XXXIII

From the register of Pope Leo IV:

“Concerning tithes, it has seemed right not only to us but also to our predecessors that they should be given only to the parishes where the sacred baptisms are administered.”

I, p. 908; cited from Leo IV by Gerhoh in the *Dialogue*, vernacular edition, in Pez’s *Anecdota*, vol. II, p. 482.

# Homily of Pope Leo IV

## The collector’s preface

A letter of Pope Leo to be read at the synod.

I think I shall render an ecclesiastical service if I present the homily of Pope Leo in three forms, since the text is found in manuscripts in different colors and does not always agree with itself in the printed editions.

One form is that of the Labbe edition; another is taken from Martène, *Veterum Monumentorum*, vol. VII, p. 1, where it is found among important manuscripts, although Leo’s name is not written there; finally, the third is from a twelfth-century manuscript of the library of the cathedral at Lucca.

The reason for the interpolation seems to have been that this homily was commonly read at synods for the instruction of the clergy, and that, because the discipline of places or dioceses varied according to the customs of the province to which it was delivered, the text was adapted accordingly.

Martène has added the variant readings from a manuscript of the library of Saint Victor. I transfer them here, together with the variants from the synodal sermon which Labbe, in volume XI of the Venetian edition, p. 1075, took from Mark Welser, without expressly giving the name of Pope Leo, although in reality it is Leo’s homily interpolated into the text.

The Lucca manuscript contains:

### Manuscript of Lucca

#### Instruction of each bishop to the priests subject to him

Brothers, priests of the Lord, you are fellow workers of our order; and we, although unworthy, hold the place of Aaron, while you hold the place of Eleazar and Ithamar. We act in the place of the twelve apostles; you, in that of the seventy-two disciples. We are your shepherds; you are the shepherds of the people entrusted to you. We shall render an account of you to the supreme Shepherd, our Lord Jesus Christ; you shall render an account of the people entrusted to you. Therefore, dearest ones, consider your danger.

We admonish and beseech Your Fraternity to commit to memory what we suggest to you and to strive to put it into practice.

### I

First of all, we admonish you that your life and conduct be irreproachable, namely, that your cell be beside the church and that you have no women in your house.

### II

Every night rise for vigils; recite your office at the appointed hours.

### III

Perform the solemn celebrations of Mass devoutly; receive the body and blood of the Lord with fear and reverence; wash and wipe the sacred vessels with your own hands.

### IV

Let no one sing unless fasting; let no one sing who does not communicate.

### V

Let no one sing without an amice, alb, stole, fanon, and chasuble. These vestments are to be clean and are not to be used for any other purposes.

[In Martène’s text, unlike Labbe’s, no light is specified here.]

*References:* From the *Collectanea* of Saint Anselm of Lucca, in *Antiqua Lectio Canonum*, vol. III, part 1, p. 394. Augustine, “Concerning the common observance,” as in the Labbe edition.

## Homily of Pope Leo IV

### Labbe’s edition

**A letter of Leo to be read at the synod.**

Brothers, priests, priests of the Lord, you are fellow workers of our order. We, although unworthy, hold the place of Aaron; you, the place of Eleazar and Ithamar. We act in the place of the twelve apostles; you correspond to the seventy-two disciples. We are your shepherds; you are the shepherds of the souls entrusted to you. We shall render an account of you to our Shepherd, our Lord Jesus Christ; you, of the peoples entrusted to you.

Therefore, dearest ones, consider your danger. We admonish and beseech Your Fraternity, as it is written elsewhere, to listen more attentively while reflecting upon your common salvation, and to commit to memory what we suggest to you and strive to put it into practice.

### I

First of all, we firmly admonish and command that your life and conduct be irreproachable: your cell and dwelling are to be beside the church, and you are not to have women in it.

### II

Every night rise for the hours; recite your office.

### III

Celebrate the solemnities and celebrations of Mass devoutly; receive the body and blood of the Lord with fear and reverence. Wash and wipe the sacred vessels with your own hands.

### IV

No one is to sing Mass alone. No one is to sing before sunrise, except at the Nativity of the Lord. No one is to sing Mass unless fasting. No one is to sing if he does not communicate.

### V

No one is to sing without a light, an amice, an alb, a stole, a fanon, and a chasuble. These vestments are to be clean and are not to be used for any other purpose.

*References:* Augustine or Victor: “to sing”; Augustine adds “Mass”; “No one is to sing Mass alone” is absent from Augustine and Victorinus; Augustine and Victor: “or perhaps the four”; Augustine adds “with the body of the Lord for the sick”; Augustine and Victorinus: “so that the churchyard may often be kept clean”; Augustine: “after and before Communion”; Augustine: “a scholar”; Augustine: “let it often be kept clean”; Augustine and Victorinus: “or perhaps the four”; Augustine: “no one is to sing Mass”; Augustine: “let none quarrel.” The text agrees throughout this chapter with the Lucca manuscript.

### VI

No one is to presume to celebrate Mass in an alb that he uses for ordinary purposes. No one is to dare to celebrate Mass with a wooden, leaden, or glass chalice.

### VII

No woman is to approach the altar of the Lord or touch the Lord’s chalice.

### VIII

The corporal is to be completely clean. The altar is to be covered with clean linen cloths. Nothing is to be placed upon the altar except reliquaries containing relics of the saints, or perhaps the four holy Gospels of God, or a pyx with the body of the Lord for viaticum for the sick; everything else is to be stored in a clean place.

### IX

Each church is to have a complete missal, a lectionary, an antiphonary, and the entire book of forty homilies.

### X

A place is to be prepared in the sacristy or beside the altar where water may be poured when the sacred vessels are washed. There a clean vessel containing water is to hang, and the priest is to wash his hands after Communion.

### XI

Churches are to be well roofed and vaulted; the churchyard is always to be kept clean.

### XII

No one is to sing Mass outside the church, in houses, or in unconsecrated places without the permission of his bishop.

### XIII

Every priest is to have a cleric or scholar who can read the Epistle or lesson, respond to him at Mass, and sing psalms with him. No one is to sing Mass wearing spurs or carrying knives, since this is indecent and contrary to the rules of the Church.

Sign the chalice and the offering with the proper cross—that is, not in a circle or by varying the fingers, as many do, but with two extended fingers and the thumb enclosed within. Through these the Trinity is signified. Strive to make this sign correctly, for otherwise you cannot bless anything.

### XIV

Visit the sick and reconcile them to God. Anoint them with holy oil according to the Apostle and administer Communion with your own hand. No one is to presume to give Communion to a layman or woman to carry to the sick.

### XV

No one is to sell holy chrism. No one is to demand a payment or gift for baptizing infants, for the body of the Lord, for reconciliation, for burial, or for consecrating churches. See to it that through your negligence no infant dies without baptism.

### XVI

Let none of you be drunk, and let none be quarrelsome, since it is not fitting for a servant of God to quarrel. Let none of you carry weapons.

#### Martenii edition

**XVII.** Let no one be quarrelsome; let no one carry weapons during a riot; let no one serve the games of dogs or birds. Let no one drink in taverns.

**XVIII.** Let each of you, according to his understanding, announce to his people from the Gospel, the Epistle, or some other divine Scripture on Sundays or feast days.

**XIX.** Let him care for the poor, pilgrims, and orphans, and invite them to dinner, so that others may receive from you and from such examples a pattern of conduct.

**XX.** Every Sunday before Mass, make holy water, with which the people and the places of the faithful may be sprinkled.

**XXI.** Let sacred vessels and priestly vestments not be given as security to a merchant or any layman.

**XXII.** Let none of you bring a penitent to reconciliation unworthily, for any matter whatsoever, and let him bear for him testimony of reconciliation.

**XXIII.** Let none of you exact interest, and let him not become the collector of a usurer. Know that the property and possessions which you acquire after the day of your ordination belong to the church which you serve.

**XXIV.** Let no one acquire a church without our knowledge and consent. Let no one obtain a church through secular power. Let no one abandon the church to which he has been appointed and migrate to another for the sake of gain.

**XXV.** Let no one hold several churches without the assistance of other priests; under no circumstances should one church be divided among several persons.

**XXVI.** Let no one receive another’s parishioner for Mass, except while traveling or if it should please him. Let no one sing Mass in another’s parish without that priest’s permission.

**XXVII.** Let no one receive a tithe belonging to another.

**XXVIII.** Let no one invite a penitent to eat meat or drink wine unless he has given alms for him at that time.

**XXIX.** Let no one presume to baptize except at the vigils of Easter and Pentecost, unless there is danger of death.

Let no cleric or layperson dare to speak in church unless praying, especially during the divine office. On Holy Saturday, after the old fire has been extinguished, let a new fire be blessed and distributed among the people; likewise, let holy water be blessed.

#### Historical notice concerning Benedict III

*(In Mansi, Enlarged Collection of Councils, vol. XV, p. 101.)*

**Benedict’s virtues; made subdeacon by Gregory IV; made priest by Leo.**

**In the year of the Lord 858. Benedict III, Roman Pontiff.**

Benedict, the third of that name, a Roman by nation, son of Peter, sat for two years, six months, and ten days.

This blessed man, most beloved and born from a noble stock, was powerful in faith, rich in virtues, and grew swiftly in divine studies. By his father’s decision he was entrusted for instruction in the study of divine learning. Like a sponge quickly absorbs water, so he learned the reading of the sacred books. Thus he became acquainted with the rudiments of sacred conversation, received them, and by the foundation of his mind extended them with invisible roots.

Pope Gregory, observing that he was learned and useful in doctrine, appointed him subdeacon of the holy Roman Church. In that rank he displayed many proofs of holy conduct: he overcame the flesh, despised the world and all its snares, and defeated every one of its contrivances. Gregory subsequently, in the consulship of Ursus, departed from this world to the Lord.

Sergius then assumed the governance of the Roman Church; after his death Pope Leo succeeded to the apostolic see. Moved by the heavenly impulse and loving him for his most excellent deeds, Leo solemnly consecrated him priest with a distinguished ecclesiastical title. His blessedness shone and flourished so widely that all declared him blessed in word and deed. He was wise in speech, eminent in learning, sober in conduct, peaceable in conversation, compliant and compassionate toward all, and most kind.

After Pope Leo’s death, Benedict III was appointed by the consent of all. Through the faction of certain wicked men, aided by the emperor’s legates, the schismatic Anastasius was intruded; but the clergy and people of Rome resisted, the schismatic was expelled, and Benedict was restored to his see. This is the brief notice summarized from Anastasius.

In Benedict’s time Emperor Lothair, having renounced the world, assumed the monastic habit in the fifteenth year of his reign, A.D. 855.

#### Editorial note

(a) Benedict. After Leo’s death Benedict was immediately chosen, with the consent of all, to succeed him in the Roman Church. But, the Roman clergy and people resisting, the schismatic Anastasius was expelled and Benedict restored to his see. Through the faction of certain wicked men who, with the aid of the emperor’s legates, combined for this crime, Anastasius, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellus—whom, as stated above, the Roman synod held under Leo IV had excommunicated—had been intruded schismatically into the apostolic see. This is summarized from Anastasius. In Benedict’s time Emperor Lothair, having renounced the world, assumed the monastic habit in the fifteenth year of his reign, A.D. 855. See Baronius.

### [Scan page 348]

#### Historical notice

He was known to abide in divine wisdom, because he cherished all with lavish and pure affection, adorned them with gifts of grace, rejected the delights of the perishable and passing world, and distributed whatever he possessed to the needy and the poor. He remained steadfast in fasts, constant in prayer, and vigilant, continually praising God every day.

When this pontiff was taken from the light, the entire clergy, the protectors of the Roman Church, all the nobles, the whole senate, and the people gathered, entreating the clemency of the Lord to grant them a pastor who could rule the apostolic office peacefully.

Therefore, divinely inflamed by heavenly light, with one accord and one mind they chose Benedict as pontiff for the many sacred works in which he excelled.

Benedict noticed that he was being sought for the papacy. But the whole people and the assembly of the clergy hurried to him with joyful devotion. They found him pouring out prayer to almighty God, as was his custom. Rising, he recognized the densely gathered crowds and understood what had happened. Then, bending his knees with many tears, he earnestly begged them in a sorrowful voice, saying:

“Do not lead me from my church, I beg you, because I am not capable of bearing or carrying the burden of such a high office.”

He was compelled to accept the papacy.

#### By fraud they attempt to make Anastasius pope after his deposition

Certain people attempted, through fraud, to make the deposed Anastasius pope. But the others did not consent in any way. They drew Benedict from the same title-church with hymns and spiritual songs, in great exultation and ineffable joy, and led him to the Lateran patriarchate. There, according to the custom and established practice of pontiffs, they placed him on the pontifical throne and consecrated him.

The city rejoiced, the Church exulted, the old men praised God, the virgins sang divine praises, the poor were enriched, the rich were made more generous, the afflicted were consoled, the weak were strengthened, and those who had been saddened by grief contemplated the restoration of peace.

After these things had been accomplished, the clergy and all the nobles drew up a decree, confirmed it with their own hands, and sent it to the emperors Lothair and Louis.

Nicholas, bishop of Anagni, and Mercurius, master of the soldiers, who had brought the decree concerning the election of the most gracious Benedict to the emperor, left Rome with certain others and, under the influence of Arsenius, bishop of Eugubium, joined the presbyter Anastasius—already deposed, excommunicated, and bound by anathema in the holy synod presided over by Pope Leo. They were plainly intent on confounding God’s commands and raising this expelled and anathematized Anastasius to the apostolic summit, contrary to the tradition and sanctions of all the holy pontiffs.

They presented the decree to the most gracious Emperor Louis, while concealing this double intention in their hearts, then returned to Rome and announced the arrival of the imperial envoys, producing letters containing the emperors’ replies. They said to all the clergy and civic officials that they must go out to meet the imperial envoys, in obedience to the emperors’ commands.

#### The legates sent to Rome defect to the false pope; several conspire against Benedict; the false pope invades Saint Peter’s and smashes the images

After several days the envoys whose arrival had been announced hastened to Orte, forty Roman miles from Rome. There Adelbert and Bernard, counts, at the urging of Bishop Arsenius, joined the condemned presbyter Anastasius. They despised the oath which they had made to the gracious Benedict, forgot the elected pope, allied themselves with the deposed presbyter, and departed from the city, devising the counsel of which the prophet said that they could not make it stand firm (Ps. 20 [Vulgate 19]).

At Orte, near the basilica of the blessed martyr Leucius, they boasted in their strength. With them were Raduald, bishop of Porto, and Agatho, bishop of Todi, who had secretly left Rome and joined themselves to this anathematized man, their minds darkened.

Hearing this, Benedict, God’s elect servant, resolved to send “G. G. and Major” (the personal names are damaged in the supplied OCR), venerable and prudent bishops full of wisdom, to the imperial Caesars with letters. At Orte those emissaries were seized, bound together with the anathematized presbyter, and handed over to guards—a deed which, the text says, even pagan barbarians are not heard to have committed against envoys.

Afterward the frequently mentioned Benedict, Christ’s elect minister, sent Adrian, distinguished *secundicerius* of the Holy Apostolic See, and Duke Gregory to meet them. On the following day, as the mission approached, the senate and the whole people were summoned and ordered to go beyond the Milvian Bridge to meet the imperial legates, so that they might obey the emperors’ commands.

They then came to Rome. The imperial envoys met the bishops and nobles with crosses and imperial banners; Adrian, the distinguished *secundicerius*, was led bound under guard, while Gratian, *sacellarius* of the sacred palace, and Theodore, a nobleman, were dragged away with drawn swords and fettered, because they had not obeyed the emperors’ command. The unhappy presumption of the deposed presbyter drove the latter, together with the emperor’s own envoys, suddenly to invade the basilica of the Prince of the Apostles. Disregarding the judgment which he ought to have respected, he committed there evils which not even a Saracen had presumed or thought to commit.

He smashed the images and burned them with fire. He destroyed the synod which Pope Leo had ordered to be held above the sacred doors of the church of the blessed Pope Leo. He cast down with a battle-axe the icon of our Lord Jesus Christ and of the ever-Virgin Mother of God, which he ought not to have touched. Because of this detestable deed, all the orthodox worshipers of the faith shed tears, groaned, and were filled with sadness and grief.
