#### Benedict III, Roman Pontiff

#### The usurper occupies the pontifical throne and removes Benedict

After these events, the deposed presbyter himself entered Rome by hostile force and quickly proceeded to the Lateran with his wicked followers and secular power. Opening its doors with many kinds of weapons, the tyrant entered the patriarchate like a bloodstained man, sat upon the throne—which he ought not even to have touched—and ordered a bishop of Balneoregium, named Romanus, who was so overshadowed by bestial thoughts that he could not see the deed’s enormity, to expel the most blessed Benedict from the pontifical throne on which he was seated. Benedict had been elected by the entire Roman people, as we have said above.

Romanus seized and stripped him of the pontifical vestments with which he was clothed, like a barbarian, and inflicted many insults and blows upon him.

#### The whole people and clergy mourn; they refuse to consent to the false pope

Then the deposed Anastasius attempted, by human rather than divine power, to hand the same most gracious elect Benedict over to guards who would bind him more tightly—namely John and Adrian, formerly priests, who had been condemned and deposed from every priestly office by Pope Leo because of their crimes.

Soon the whole city was filled with wailing and abundant tears and was shaken by a grave murmur. All the bishops, the clergy, and the people of God immediately entered the Holy of Holies, beat their breasts, poured forth tears, and lay prostrate on the ground before the vestibule and altar, praying the majesty of God to free them with his victorious right hand from the darkness of so great an error. The course of the seventh feria was then being celebrated.

On the following day, the aforesaid bishops, with the entire clergy and people, assembled at the title-church of Saint Emilianus. The frequently mentioned envoys of the emperors also arrived there, raging and swollen with great pride. They made an assault upon the apse where the bishops were chanting the psalms with the clergy, climbed it like ferocious lions, and, raising their spears, attempted to strike them and punish them with swords, saying:

“Consent, and by your agreement let Anastasius be installed on the pontifical throne.”

But the bishops, filled with the Holy Spirit, replied:

“We shall never consent to a deposed and anathematized man, condemned by the holy pontiff and the blessed synod; rather, in every way we reject him and separate him from the assemblies of God.”

The envoys then declared in furious words, with threats and torture, that they wished to punish them. But the most blessed bishop of God Almighty and those who were present with him disregarded their terrors and threats and stood firm.

When the aforementioned Franks saw their constancy, they withdrew from them filled with anger and entered a certain chamber of the basilica. There they devised various plans. They also forcibly brought in the bishops of Ostia and Alba, whom they tried to win over by gentle speech and flattering entreaties; afterward they surrounded them with harsh threats, saying in a loud voice:

“You cannot possess your lives in any way; you will be subject to capital punishment unless you grant Anastasius the favor of consecration.”

But the bishops declared that they would hand themselves over to death and allow themselves to be torn limb from limb before giving the blessing of consecration to one who had been deposed and condemned by anathema.

They argued against the envoys and set before them every written authority of the sacred reply, showing that they could by no means establish the deposed man in the rank he sought. Yet, while they conferred secretly, the fury that had swollen within them abated and seemed to be expelled from their minds.

#### The whole people in the church demand Benedict; the emperor’s envoys finally consent to Benedict’s election

At dawn on the third feria, all the bishops, with the clergy and people, assembled in the basilica of the Savior called Constantiniana. There the entire crowd of clergy and people cried out in a loud voice:

“We want the most blessed Benedict as pope; we desire him.”

The envoys, hearing this, were astonished. Seeing that the unity of Christ and holy concord could not be swayed toward Anastasius by any means, they summoned the bishops to a chamber of the patriarchate, together with other priests and the clergy.

They attempted to engage them in a lengthy dispute, but the bishops overcame the envoys’ audacity with arguments and teachings so convincing that the envoys’ disastrous intention appeared crushed and confounded.

Seeing this, the envoys said to the venerable bishops:

“Take your elected man and lead him to whatever basilica you wish. We are now expelling Anastasius, whom you call deposed, from this patriarchate. Let us celebrate a three-day fast with prayers; afterward, whatever the heavenly clemency reveals shall be carried out.”

But the noble bishops cried out:

“Let the invader and deposed Anastasius be expelled from our presence and driven from this patriarchate; then we shall do what you urge.”

#### Anastasius is expelled

Immediately the aforesaid Anastasius was expelled and driven from the patriarchate with great disgrace, so that all the orthodox worshipers of the faith might give thanks to our Lord Jesus Christ.

#### Benedict is led to the Lateran church; his adversaries kiss his feet

The bishops, with the entire clergy and people, took the most blessed Benedict, brought him out of the basilica where the clergy were staying—for Anastasius had placed him there under the guard of the most savage men—and led him with great eagerness and rejoicing into the basilica of the Savior called Constantiniana.

When they came out, they placed him, amid the rejoicing of the people, upon the horse on which Pope Leo had been accustomed to sit. With a great crowd of people preceding him, they led him to the basilica of the Mother of God, called the basilica of the Crib. There they devoted themselves for three days and nights to fasting and prayers, entreating the supreme majesty of the Lord with many tears.

When the fast had been completed, all those who had joined themselves to the anathematized and deposed man, moved by divine compunction and inflamed by God’s favor, assembled unanimously in the aforementioned basilica in which the most blessed Benedict was present, as we have said. They approached and began to kiss his feet, saying:

“We have erred and departed from you with an unsteady foot; but, as a most holy shepherd, receive the flocks of us wandering sheep, gather your little lambs into your weary bosom, and shelter us beneath your wings.”

At once Benedict, protected by God, stretched out his arms and, with pure minds and a kindly heart, longed to embrace them all and adorned them with kisses. He also said to them:

“Rejoice,” he said, “dearest ones, and rejoice even more, because Christ the Son of God has deigned by his power to unite the Church which had been divided.”

As he said these and similar things, the imperial envoys also came there. They spoke privately with the elected pope in salutary and gentle words.

#### He is placed upon the pontifical throne and consecrated pontiff

Then all the bishops, the entire clergy, and the countless multitude of the Roman people led him from that basilica with hymns and spiritual songs into the Lateran patriarchate. They placed him upon the pontifical throne from which he had been expelled.

At last the whole Church rejoiced together, and the entire people rang out with loud cries.

## Letters

### 690

Moreover, at dawn on the Lord’s Day he was led into the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter by the bishops, clergy, and nobles. In the sight of all, while the imperial envoys looked on, he was consecrated and ordained pontiff in the apostolic see, as custom and ancient tradition prescribe. The bishop of Porto, however, was barred from the church and performed no ordination over him, as he ought to have done, because he had joined himself to the anathema and had fallen—and remained—in the abyss of perjury.

After the sacred solemnity of Mass had been celebrated, the newly ordained pontiff returned to the Lateran patriarchate. For he was exceedingly gentle, adorned with every sacred work, handsome in appearance, distinguished in mind, sweet in speech, and benevolent in teaching.

### Michael, son of Theophilus, Eastern emperor, sends gifts to Rome

At this time Michael, son of Theophilus, emperor of the East, sent gifts to Rome to the blessed apostle Peter through the hand of Lazarus, a learned monk, a Chazar by race: namely, a Gospel-book of the purest gold, with various precious stones.

Likewise, a chalice of gold surrounded with jewels, with a hanging net decorated with white precious gems of extraordinary beauty; two veils of *olosericum* (all-silk fabric), with a cross of the same fabric; likewise a gold-striped band (*chrysoclavus*); and small coverings for the chalice, as is the custom of the Greeks.

Likewise, a clean garment of imperial purple for the high altar, decorated on every side with an embroidered scene and latticework, and with roses of great beauty in gold-striped cloth; also one veil of *stauracinum*, with a cross of gold-striped cloth and Greek letters in gold.

### The Saxon king comes to Rome for religious reasons

At this time the king of the Saxons, named …, came to Rome for the sake of prayer. Leaving behind all his possessions, he abandoned his own kingdom and proceeded to Rome to the thresholds of the apostles Peter and Paul with a multitude of people. He offered the blessed apostle Peter a crown of the purest gold weighing four pounds, and two *bancas* of the purest gold weighing [number illegible].

[Variant A: “a sword, bound with the purest gold, weighing [number illegible] pounds.”]

Likewise, two smaller images of the purest gold; four silver basins gilded with gold; one *saraca* of all-silk fabric with gold-striped cloth; white, stamped silk shirts with gold-striped cloth; and two larger cloths of *fundatum*.

And the king of the Saxons himself, when the most holy lord Pope Benedict asked him to make a public offering in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, gave gold—measured by the pound—to the bishops, priests, deacons, the entire clergy, and the Roman nobility, and small silver coins to the people.

Afterward, when his purpose of prayer had been fulfilled, he returned to his own kingdom. A few days later he ended his life and departed to the Lord.

Finally, that same prelate, who showed great care for the holy churches of God and always rejoiced, with pious affection and zeal, in their restoration, made and renewed beside the lectern, with marvelous workmanship, in the basilica of his patron, the key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven, a four-[materially corrupt object] formerly carried off by the Saracens, on which lamps and candles were placed at that basilica on feast days and Sundays; it weighed [number illegible] pounds.

For he was always intent upon the love of divine worship, a lover of peace, and a cultivator of every heavenly work through chaste conduct.

### The pope customarily attends the burial of clergy

He established that whenever a bishop, priest, or deacon died, the pontiff, together with all the bishops and priests, the deacons, and the remaining clergy, should assemble to bury his body and commend his soul. Likewise, they were to do the same when the pontiff departed this life. He not only taught this but also practiced it.

Following his example, his successor, in this matter of piety as in other matters, imitated him as a most devoted heir. In the month of December he carried out one ordination: five priests, one deacon, and sixty-six bishops in various places.

He was buried before the doors of the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter.

# First Letter of Benedict III

[Source: Mansi, ibid.]

## To Hincmar, Archbishop of Rheims

### He confirms the synod of Soissons together with the privileges of the Church and of the archbishop of Rheims

Benedict, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and holy brother Hincmar, archbishop of the holy Church of Rheims.

The definitions of worthy and sacred proceedings delight the minds of those who hear them and make them joyful; they fill mortal hearts with such gladness that they overflow with praises of the Creator of all things. By an easy contemplation they confirm the useful intentions and actions of those proceedings, and with a strong and unshakable foundation they strive earnestly to extend them.

The letters of your benevolence, sweet in sound, have made the heart of us, the pontiff, joyful and glad. As we read them with diligent investigation, we recognize inwardly that you are joined to our affection and effective in divine blessings. Examining the text of the synod attentively, and the actions that your Beatitude took care to celebrate at the city of Soissons with the bishops of your diocese and the venerable archbishops—namely Wenilo of Sens, Amalric of Tours, and the other bishops—we know that you set them forth in writing and endeavored to explain them with subtle demonstration.

We find that the measures enacted there by pious authorities for the advancement of the holy Church were especially worthy of approval. Above all, we saw you as comparable to those men who were not pleased with earthly affairs and passing observances, but, inflamed with boundless zeal for God, promulgated ecclesiastical statutes and orders.

Having considered these things, we do not hesitate to incline ourselves wholly toward what you desire, since we wish to fulfill the affection of your veneration. And because, as a devoted and faithful son in all things, you are always seen returning to this see for instruction or confirmation concerning ecclesiastical acts and rules, we hereby promulgate, by apostolic authority, the definitions of your fraternity and of the other bishops, which you confirmed with your own fingers at the aforesaid synod by apostolic and canonical authorities, if matters are as you reported to our pontificate in writing and demonstrated in the record of the proceedings.

We establish that these definitions shall always remain fixed, so that no question may ever arise concerning them, and so that those who improperly aspire to them may be completely and permanently restrained. Thus the Church of God may no longer be troubled by the hostility of contradictors, but, freed from all errors of savage treatment, may remain forever united in Christ.

Among these matters we also decree that no one subject to the ecclesiastical rules of your diocese, despising you, may dare or be able to seek or expect judgments elsewhere with impunity, as has been established by the traditions of the holy Fathers and by the promulgations of the canons. In all things, however, the right of our apostolic see remains intact, as has been ordained by it, by Christ, and by the sacred canons.

Let all, whether in the precedence due to you or in the obedience owed to you, observe the order handed down by ecclesiastical rules and strive to obey more diligently.

We also promulgate and establish that you, who are recognized as the primate of that province, may never be stripped by anyone, through any attack contrary to the canonical and apostolic decrees, either of the ecclesiastical judgments entrusted to you or of your authority or power; nor may anyone condemn you before the hearing of the Roman pontiff.

If, when accused, you wish to appeal to this holy see, we order that the matter be reserved for the judgment of the apostolic pope, by our authority—or rather, by the authority of blessed Peter. You are not to be subjected to anyone’s jurisdiction or judgment whatsoever, except that of the Roman pontiffs.

We also wish that no one from the province and diocese of your metropolitan see, subject to you, should in any way, through contempt, tear away the right owed according to ecclesiastical constitutions to the primacy of your Church and to you, or presume stubbornly to inflict any violence upon you or your Church contrary to these canonical constitutions and the decrees of the Roman pontiffs. We prohibit this under threat of our apostolic anathema and by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

We desire that your fraternity may now and always prosper in Christ.

[References: Ivo, part IV, chapter 156; Hincmar, Letter 100, chapter 21.]

# Letter II

## To the bishops established in the kingdom of Charles

### Against the cleric Hubert: that he should come to Rome within thirty days to answer the charges brought against him

Benedict, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and holy archbishops and to all the bishops residing in the kingdom of the glorious King Charles.

We are always renewed by hearing good things, and we rejoice in the actions of those who love God and possess heavenly strength of mind—those whom blessedness exalts and whom divine fellowship raises to the heights of heaven.

But we lament the cruelties and deeds of evil men, whose crimes surround them and whose conduct remains full of wickedness. In all things their course is detestable, their persistence savage, and their reputation unhappy.

We have learned through reports that Hubert the cleric, formerly the son of Buson, is like such men. Entangled in such filth and not raising his mind toward heavenly things, he appears unwilling to be a participant in eternal life.

Through the loud cries of many grieving people and through the horrifying assertions of witnesses, our legates have learned of many evils and dreadful crimes committed by his unhappy audacity.

Once he was numbered among the clergy, so that, when the divine mysteries were celebrated, he would ascend the ambo in the manner of subdeacons and proclaim the sacred readings to the people. But now—as we report with tears—he has joined himself to the company of the most wicked and unrighteous men, united to an infamous way of life and filled with many offenses and crimes. Through an unjust struggle he hastens toward the peril of his soul, which he ought not to endanger, and persists in bloody tyranny.

Many have also reported that he does not hesitate to live every day with theatrical women, who destroy souls, wound bodies, and drag people down to the depths.

And because, through an association joined to him by a multitude of harmful men, he has inflicted many evils upon the people of the Lord—whom Christ redeemed by his precious Passion from the jaws of the “most just” lion [probably an OCR-corrupt reading]—he does not cease to commit murders, countless adulteries, shameful fornications, and unlawful and intolerable acts of plunder.

They have learned not only these things but also, from the testimony of many others, that he seized the monastery of the holy and glorious martyr Maurice with such ferocity—although it was protected by apostolic privileges—that no order of the ancient religious life is now observed there.

What had previously been supplied from its resources to those serving God there is now, by his order, distributed to prostitutes, dogs, birds, and other wicked people. Aimoinus, the bishop who appeared to preside over it, does not hesitate to detach that monastery from the Church and indecently possess it, violating the sanctions of the sacred canons and the Fathers.

He also invaded, like an enemy, the monastery established at Luxovium in memory of the blessed apostle Peter, whose cloistered entrance had never been open to women; and he did not fear to remain there for several days with illicit women.

He also took a certain woman who, for the sake of chastity, had separated from her own husband, vowed herself to God, and promised to dedicate herself to him. Later, pierced and struck by the dart of the devil, she fled from the monastery, joined herself to an adulterer, and placed herself under his protection. Finally, when she was sought by the assembly of the archbishops and bishops, she was not presented to them. Together with her defenders, they expelled her from ecclesiastical communion; yet to this day he does not cease to retain her under his protection, without fearing divine judgment.

He also does not hesitate—as we have heard—to disturb, through his most miserable greed, the peace between Louis, the emperor, ever Augustus, and his glorious brothers, bringing about the death and danger of many Christians.

Hearing these and many similar things about him, we grieve with abundant tears, lest such an end of his frailty come upon him and he be delivered to the abyss of Gehenna.

Therefore we wish, and by apostolic authority earnestly command you, that, setting aside every excuse and acting with promptness, after thirty days have elapsed from the time this letter is presented to him, he should not delay beginning his journey but hasten with all speed to Rome.

We wish to see him in person and learn whether the things reported against him truly exist, so that we may wash him through spiritual discipline and restore his wounded members with the healing ointment of heaven.

For we desire that he be freed from such crimes and, through the sacred admonitions of the heavenly homeland, become a citizen of it.

But if he neglects to come and refuses, according to our command, to proceed to our apostolic see, we wish you to know that we shall immediately expel him from ecclesiastical communion, so that he may have no fellowship of faith with you or with any other worshipers of Christianity, and we shall make him alien from the body and blood of the Lord.

We wish your Blessedness to prosper in Christ.

[References: Ibid., chapter 24; Ibid., chapter 26.]

# Letter III

## To the bishops of Gaul

### In confirmation of the privileges of Corbie

Benedict, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to all the bishops of Gaul.

[Reference: Acheri, *Spicilegium*, vol. VI, p. 307.]

Since it is established that the pontiff of the Roman see is the head and prince of all the Churches of Christ, acting as the representative of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to whom Christ entrusted the primacy of the whole Church, saying, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 16:18), no doubt remains for any of the faithful that we ought to exercise solicitude for all the churches and provide for the salvation, peace, and tranquility of all who believe in Christ.

Thus we must correct what is wrong, strengthen what is established, restore what has been corrupted, and preserve what remains sound.

Although we must guard this care for the universal body of the Church spread throughout the breadth of the whole world, a special prerogative nevertheless requires us to show particular concern for the churches of Gaul after those of Rome and Italy, as it is clear that our predecessors did.

The present condition of the commonwealth itself testifies that this ought now to be done with still greater appropriateness: the scepter of one empire governs both provinces without division, and the dignity of the Roman Church, together with the earthly principate, administers the kingdom of both provinces by a common right. Thus the rulers of earthly affairs fortify their decrees with the sanctions of the Roman Church, while ecclesiastical rights are supported by the statutes of the princes.

The governors of the earthly commonwealth consider that they rule happily when apostolic authority is joined to their sanctions. When they receive and venerate that authority in us, they rejoice that they receive the one who says to his disciples: “Whoever receives you receives me” (Matthew 10:40). Conversely, he says of those who despise them: “Whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16).

Therefore, since, as has been said, the administration of the universal Church has been entrusted to apostolic solicitude, and since it is fitting that our constant care should keep watch over the condition of all the faithful, we must nevertheless take the greatest care of those churches whose special protection the responsibility we have undertaken teaches us to provide. We must ensure not only that what has remained undefiled in its proper condition is preserved, but also that what has fallen is restored to the dignity of its former form.

Therefore let the reverend fraternity of all the holy prelates residing throughout Gaul know that the venerable Odo, abbot of the monastery of Corbie in the province of Gaul—built in the district of Amiens on the river Somme—came to us through the venerable Abbot Anselm. He asked us to grant the aforesaid monastery of Corbie a privilege of our authority concerning its own right of election and the free possession and administration of its goods.

He also showed us privileges issued by bishops: one by the bishop of Amiens, to whose diocese that place belongs, made and confirmed with his fellow bishops in ancient times; and another written by Hincmar, archbishop of the Church of Rheims, together with the universal council of the bishops of Gaul a few years later and confirmed by their own subscriptions. They asked that, whenever these privileges reached any person—whether bishop or abbot—he should not hesitate to subscribe to them.

In these privileges it was decreed that the aforesaid monastery of Corbie should have free dominion over its property and should always have the power to choose its abbot from among its own members. Those who contradicted or resisted this sanction were to be condemned by perpetual anathema.

In addition, the magnificent emperors Lothair, Louis, and Charles sent a mandate and petition requesting the same thing: that the privileges of the bishops should also be confirmed by our authority.

Since we saw that this was a religious request, and that we ought not to disregard what the holy pontiffs had piously decreed for the peace of the servants of God, what the magnificent princes had devoutly requested, and what the abbot of the congregation himself necessarily sought, we judged that, when asked, we should grant what our pastoral solicitude ought willingly to have offered.

We also learned, from the report of the venerable Abbot Anselm, that the monastery in question had been nobly built by the most excellent queen of the Franks, Balthild, and had flourished from the beginning of its foundation in the nobility of holy men and the observance of religious monastic discipline, as well as through the special favor and protective patronage of the Frankish princes.

[Reference: *Spicilegium*, vol. VI, p. 887.]

For this reason it came about that everyone granted it immunities for its property and the privilege of choosing its abbot, decreeing that these grants should remain forever. They placed the documents confirming their concessions in the monastery’s archives, to be preserved for the memory of future generations.

Having learned all these things, we judged that it would be wrong not to follow the devotion of religious princes and the examples of holy prelates by granting our authority of concession to the monastery of Corbie. We did not wish to be found later than those who had come first because of the primacy of the apostolic see in the ordering of ecclesiastical affairs. We are commanded by our example to provide the light of authority to the rest for securing the peace of God’s servants; the Lord says, “You are the light of the world” (Matthew 5:14). We must not, through the tepidity of negligence, fail to offer others the radiance of good work.

Therefore let all the Church of Gaul and the entire assembly of bishops presiding over that Church know that we confirm by the present decree of our authority the privileges of the holy prelates—whether those enacted in ancient days or those enacted in recent times—for the monastery of Corbie, built in the district of Amiens on the river Somme in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and of the holy protomartyr Stephen.

That is, the property of the monastery, and whatever may be offered by the faithful to God and to the congregation of the brothers serving Christ there, shall remain under the administration of the abbot and the brothers.

Neither the bishop of Amiens, to whose diocese that monastery belongs, nor any other bishop in whose parish the monastery’s property or churches are known to lie, may presume to take anything from it. Nor may any bishop, steward, archpriest, archdeacon, or any of their ministers, officials, or assemblies do anything on its farms, estates, properties, or in any of the places belonging to their jurisdiction or dominion; they may not hold banquets there, prepare entertainments, claim any right of authority for themselves, or demand anything that they might otherwise claim.

Let all bishops whose parishes are known to contain property belonging to the monastery of Corbie understand that they are bound by this same condition.

Let no one claim that what we decree is new or unusual. It is known that this was formerly granted to this monastery, and we see the same privilege still granted to many others, not only in Gaul or Italy but throughout the whole world—not only to monasteries of monks but also to monasteries of canons. Each church ought to remain content with its own privileges; one church must not invade or usurp what is recognized as belonging to another’s jurisdiction (*alia* in the printed text; corrected *alio*).

Since the churches of Gaul are known to have been enriched by the offerings of the faithful, so that scarcely any bishop exists whose resources are not sufficient, or more than sufficient, for the expenses of his church, with what conscience would they presume to divert to their own expenses what has been contributed for the needs of Christ’s servants?

If clerics who abound in revenues of their own are forbidden access to what is contributed to the church, much less should those who abound in resources of their own receive it while the poverty of those who have nothing is not relieved.

With what conscience, then, would a bishop whose own resources are sufficient for the expenses of his church presume to touch what has been contributed for the use of God’s servants?

Does he not fear what the Lord reproaches the priests through the prophet, saying: “You have plundered the poor in your houses” (Isaiah 3:14)?

Who does not know that Christ’s poor are those who, despising the substance of the world and following the footsteps of our Savior—who, though he was rich, became poor for us (2 Corinthians 8:9)—consider the title of their holy profession their riches?

Therefore, whoever presumes to take any of what has been contributed for their needs and apply it to his own advantages gathers the plunder of the poor into his house.

Everything offered or assigned to churches is certainly intended for the needs of the poor, orphans, and widows. Therefore whoever demands any of it for his own use retains in his house the plunder of the poor.

The apostle also says: “The rapacious shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6:10).

Accordingly, from everything belonging to the monastery of Corbie—whether offered to it or possessed by any legitimate right, in money, lands, estates, houses, cells, or churches—neither the bishop nor any of his ministers may presume to take anything. Otherwise, acting against our authority and that of our predecessors, and despising the decrees of kings established for the peace of Christ’s servants, he will make himself liable to the holy council and to perpetual condemnation.

Since monks ought to have the peace of tranquility and the leisure of security, so that, free for God, they may observe the rule of their profession, neither the bishop nor his archdeacon may approach the aforesaid monastery or presume to disturb the peace of God’s servants—unless perhaps the abbot or the brothers should invite him for some useful purpose.

Otherwise he shall have no authority over the abbot or any of the brothers, nor may he inflict anything upon them through episcopal arrogance. Rather, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict (chapter 65), the abbot shall have free authority over his own monastery, and the monks shall look only to his governance as to that of their shepherd. The episcopal ministry shall exercise no dominion over them (ibid., chapter 2).

Since the abbot is believed to act in the monastery in the place of Christ and is recognized as exercising the office of shepherd over the sheep entrusted to him, he must not be subjected to the disturbing authority of anyone if he is to carry out the ministry of his administration worthily. He must be free from all episcopal domination and acknowledge Christ alone as judge, since Christ will demand an account from him concerning the sheep entrusted to him.

Therefore we establish in every way that, when the bishop arrives, his presence must not disturb the peace of the monastery. He may not presume to do anything there by episcopal authority, nor inflict any annoyance or disturbance upon the brothers or the abbot.

If he presumes to violate this, let him understand that he is exercising not the office of a shepherd but the tyranny of an overthrower and disturber of the Lord’s flock. Accordingly, he must not be received as a shepherd but removed from Christ’s fold as a wolf; struck by the sword of anathema, he shall suffer the penalties of his condemnation.

If the abbot requests it for the sake of Christ, the bishop may consecrate and bless the altars or churches in the monastery. He shall also provide chrism, or consecrated oil, each year.

If the abbot asks that one of the monks or canons be consecrated to some ecclesiastical rank, the bishop shall in no way object—unless the person requested is shown by the testimony of truth to be unworthy of such an honor. For just as it is not fitting to bestow the sacrament of divine blessing as a favor upon one who is unworthy, so it ought freely to be granted to those who are worthy, as the Savior says: “You have received freely; give freely” (Matthew 10:8).

We decree that the brothers of the same monastery shall have the privilege of election: that is, they shall have the power, according to regular authority, to elect from among themselves anyone who belongs to the monastic profession and is nevertheless worthy of pastoral precedence.

Concerning this matter we admonish and beseech our glorious sons, Lothair, Louis, and Charles Augustus [“Augusti,” according to the manuscripts of Labbe], that, just as their memorable august father and grandfather and the earlier kings of the Franks granted this monastery the right to elect an abbot from among its own members, and themselves confirmed the same thing by their decrees, so they too may graciously preserve it during their reigns and establish by laws of perpetual duration that it be preserved forever.

Thus, by granting the servants of Christ the freedom of election and striving to preserve what they have granted, they may deserve to receive from the Lord both the kingdom of the present life and the glory of eternal blessedness.

Whatever has been offered to that monastery, whether through royal generosity or through the devotion of the faithful, to God and to his servants, they themselves must neither offer away nor permit others to take away.

For it is clearly most just and religious that those who have deserved to receive from the Lord the honor of royal power should preserve for God what has been given to him through the pious devotion of believers. Those who have been elevated above others by Christ through royal magnificence should not deprive Christ’s servants of the freedom to choose their own shepherd.

For who does not know that what has been given to God through the hands of the faithful is entrusted to the divine possession, transferred from human right to divine right, and cannot be transferred to human dominion once it is known to have been claimed for the possession of the divinity?

Therefore, whoever attempts to attach such things to the dominion of his own right is certainly an invader of another’s right—that is, God’s right.

If someone attempts by violence to usurp the possession of another human being, he becomes liable under public law and is subject to legal punishment as a robber and invader of another’s inheritance. How much more, then, is anyone who transfers things consecrated to God into his own possession liable not only under human law but also under divine law! He shall be condemned as guilty not only of robbery and invasion but also of sacrilege, and shall be punished by heavenly judgment.

Therefore let the magnificent princes consider how great a crime they bind themselves with before the sight of the divine majesty when they do not fear to invade things handed over to God and convert them from ecclesiastical uses to their own advantage.

If they unjustly invade and violently take away the possessions even of private though free-born men, they are called and regarded not as kings—that is, just and moderate men—but as tyrants, that is, cruel and unjust men. By what name and with what honor, then, should those be judged who unjustly invade the divine inheritance—that is, the possession of the Church of Christ—and violently take it away?

Therefore, considering these matters, let our most religious sons, the princes, guard the property of the monastery of Corbie inviolate and untouched, as sacred things belonging to the divinity. Let them neither take it themselves nor permit it to be taken by others, so that before the sight of the heavenly King they may rightly be regarded as kings in name as well as in reality. While they preserve for God what is his, may God preserve for them both the principate of their earthly kingdom and the crown of eternal blessedness.

Accordingly, we admonish and exhort them, while preserving unimpaired both their own concessions and those of earlier princes, and in no way violating the decrees of the pontiffs or of ourselves, to preserve for the monastery named above the privilege of election both in their own times and in the times of their heirs, and to decree by a perpetual sanction that it be preserved.

For the voice of Truth teaches us that if anyone enters the fold of Christ not through the door but climbs in by another way, “he is a thief and a robber” (John 10:1). Such a person seeks not the salvation of the Lord’s flock but his own profits; he enters not to save but to destroy.

No prudent person doubts that the holy community of monks is Christ’s fold. Someone enters this fold through the door when, according to the order of election and the regular constitution, he receives the pastoral ministry. But whoever, supported by royal authority and not by the grace of election, seizes primacy over the Lord’s flock is recognized as not a shepherd—that is, not Christ’s vicar—but a thief and robber. He is found to have entered not to guard the Lord’s flock but to destroy and scatter it.

Therefore whoever grants him this dominion of power will be judged guilty on the day of judgment for the death of so many souls, as many as he caused to perish through examples of wickedness.

For this reason, glorious princes, grant this monastery the prerogative of election. Do not install over it any layperson or canon—something contrary to the whole ecclesiastical order—or even a monk from another monastery, or someone not elected according to the rule, by royal power. Otherwise the house of God, which ought to be a house of prayer, will through you become a den of thieves.

You surely do not fail to understand that such appointees, and the authors of such appointments, are by divine judgment to be expelled from the house of eternity and consigned to the punishments of perpetual vengeance … [source breaks off].

[scan page 355]

**BENEDICT III**

...to be carried away. What sentence of condemnation, then, ought to be pronounced by us against such men, except that which the Holy Spirit uttered through the prophetic mouth, saying:

> “All their princes who said, ‘Let us possess the sanctuary of God as an inheritance’—my God, make them like a wheel, and like stubble before the face of the wind; as fire that burns the forest and as a flame that sets the mountains ablaze, so pursue them in your storm and trouble them in your anger” (Psalm 82).

For who are those said to possess the sanctuary of God as an inheritance, except those who, through secular power and domination, seek to obtain the things dedicated to God and granted for the use of the poor and his servants, rather than through the grace of election? Their princes are those who, by giving them their votes or handing over ecclesiastical possessions to them, consent to this.

The divine punishment inflicted upon both groups is described by the sentence quoted above. It shows that they are to be cast out from the stability of the heavenly homeland, whirled about in the instability of temporal things like the revolution of a wheel; and, after the end of the present life, to be snatched away by the storm of divine judgment, like the lightest bit of dry stubble; while their barrenness and pride, like the sterile growth of a forest, and their swelling arrogance against God, are to be consumed by devouring fire and flame.

Therefore, in order that they may not undergo this severity of divine vengeance, let the most Christian princes take care to preserve the rights of election for Christ’s churches, and let them not take away from the monastery of Corbie what is owed to the whole Church. Thus, when they have granted it the right of election for the honor of God and have preserved the monastery’s possessions uncontaminated, so that they may not serve the ambitions of violent men, may they themselves obtain a share in the heavenly kingdom with Christ.

Nor should they ever permit it to fall into secular hands or under canonical domination; this would mean the utter destruction of its inhabitants and the complete condemnation of both the giver and the recipient. For what else is it than to establish the abomination of desolation in the temple of God, to place a secular person in the Church of God in the position of a shepherd? Whoever does this is found to resemble Pilate, who set up images of Caesar in the Lord’s temple to be venerated.

And when the Apostle speaks to the faithful, saying, “Do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed in the renewal of your mind” (Romans 12), whoever places a secular person over monks drives them, so far as concerns the form of the spirit, from the form of the spirit toward the form of the age, and from the image of Christ toward the image of an earthly king; for every subject ought to imitate his superior by following his image.

Therefore, he should consider himself involved in no small offense who places over Christ’s Church men in whose manner the servants of Christ will always behold and learn not Christ’s humility but the world’s pride, not desire for the heavenly homeland but the world’s craving.

Since you see, most excellent princes, that this is a most wicked act, always drive this impious sacrilege away from the monastery of Corbie; and never place, or permit to be placed, over it a person belonging to the canonical order. Remember that Nadab and Abihu, because they offered strange fire to the Lord as incense, were consumed by divine fire (Leviticus 10). Indeed, he offers strange fire as incense to the Lord who promotes someone belonging to the canonical profession over a monastic religious house so that he may exercise the shepherd’s office.

But because such men are struck by punishment, their death marks out what their imitators deserve: consumed at once by the penalty of the present life, they have shown posterity, by the example of their condemnation, what fate awaits those who imitate them.

Likewise, all men—even if they belong to the monastic profession—who have been appointed rulers of the monastery in question not by regular election, and who are known to have been admitted through gifts, that is, through money, favor, or service, are condemned by us, by the authority of Peter, prince of the apostles, together with Simon, whose imitators they are, with an anathema.

And so that religious princes may remain free from this sentence of condemnation, let them strive in every way always to preserve inviolate the privilege of election concerning the monastery mentioned above. For, in accordance with the promulgation long ago defined by the holy Fathers, we anathematize both the person who gives and the person who accepts the leadership of the church of Corbie otherwise than through the legitimate election of the monks serving Christ in that monastery, and contrary to regular and canonical authority. They cannot have a share in the heavenly Jerusalem who attempt to divide it while it is journeying on earth.

It is certain that all who do this—those who are not afraid to establish over it not shepherds but thieves, not vicars of Christ but followers of Antichrist, so that the house of God may become not a house of prayer but a den of thieves, and so that not the image of Christ but the abomination of desolation may dominate there—...

[Editorial note:] On that frequent abuse in Gaul at that time, involving ecclesiastical goods possessed by secular men [the intervening OCR is uncertain], see the separate work in which Joannes Filesacus learnedly collected much material concerning such sacrileges committed against princes.

[Editorial note:] Aeberitti reads *nobilitate lapsos*, “fallen through nobility.”

[scan page 356]

...if the secular rulers, despisers of the divine commandments and of the bishops, and contemners of our authority decreeing on this matter, should place over the congregation not the man whom regular election has chosen but the man whom their domination has desired, let the bishop of the place, in whose diocese the monastery lies, entreat them either personally or together with them to report the matter to the archbishop of Reims, and let them also approach the prince together and warn him of the danger of his transgression.

But if the bishop of that diocese, whether through fear of the prince, favor toward him, imprudence, or negligence in pastoral care, should either refuse or disdain to offer assistance, let the brothers themselves go to the aforesaid archbishop and the neighboring bishops, disclose to them the cause of their distress, and beg them to bring them aid.

The archbishop, either alone or together with the other bishops, should approach the princes concerning these sacrileges and should not cease, by persuasive words and entreating prayers, to admonish and beseech them to correct their offense. But if he refuses to heed them and is unwilling to correct the fault of his sin, let him receive the sentence of apostolic excommunication.

If the bishop in whose parish the monastery lies, or the archbishop, or the other suffragan bishops should prove negligent in this matter, or despise it, or regard it as insignificant, they should know that they will be held liable to the sentence of condemnation.

For the prophet says: “If you do not announce to the wicked his wickedness, I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezekiel 3). Therefore, let them know that they will be bound by the same anathema if they neglect to provide the Lord’s flock with the solicitude of pastoral care.

**EPISTLE IV**

**TO LOUIS, ABBOT OF SAINT-DENIS**

*He confirms the privileges of the monastery of Saint-Denis in France.*

Benedict, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to Louis, abbot of the venerable monastery of the holy martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, where their sacred bodies rest, and to the whole congregation of faithful monks that is with him: peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

You have complained, my dearest sons, that in the lands which you appear to possess among the Anglo-Saxons, many men are troublesome to you through their insolence, especially when kings, who hold the highest lot, die and others succeed in the kingdom. Therefore you have asked that we confirm, by the page of our authority, those donations made by kings, princes, or anyone else who, out of love for the supreme God and reverence for the aforementioned martyrs, or for the sake of his own salvation, has bestowed anything in that land upon your monastery.

Considering, therefore, that what is usefully requested of us is just, by the authority of God the almighty Father, with the Son and the Holy Spirit, and of blessed Peter, prince of the holy apostles, whose unworthy vicars we are, with the invocation of the heavenly powers, we decree and strengthen by confirmation that whatever possession throughout the land of Britain—or anywhere else—whether on land or on water, of whatever kind, has been given to the monastery of the holy martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius by kings, princes, or any other person, shall remain forever, without invasion or violence by anyone, under the authority of the abbot and the administration of the monks of that monastery.

If anyone should attempt to violate this decree, or should wish to do so through another, let him know that he is condemned by an unbreakable anathema by the privilege of our authority, alienated from the kingdom of Christ, and assigned to eternal fires with the impious, unless he repents and comes to make suitable satisfaction.

But whoever preserves, increases, or assists these possessions, may he receive a blessing from our Lord Jesus Christ forever and ever. Amen. Farewell.

Written by the hand of Theodore, regional notary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of May, in the seventh indiction. Given by the hand of Megistus, bishop and librarian of the holy apostolic see, on the fifth day before the Ides of May, while the most pious and perpetual lord Augustus, Louis, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor, was reigning, in the eighth year of his consulship, in the seventh indiction [fifth].

[Editorial note:] Since Louis received the empire and consulship on one and the same day in December of the year 850, as was customary, and Benedict III died in the following year before May, this letter could not have been issued later than the current year, marked by the fifth indiction and the seventh consulship of Louis II Augustus. Pagi, under the year of Christ 857, no. 8.

**DIPLOMA III**

**BY WHICH IT RECEIVES THE MONASTERY OF FULDA UNDER APOSTOLIC PROTECTION AND CONFIRMS ITS RIGHTS AND IMMUNITIES**

(*Fulda, p. 134.*)

Benedict, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to Theodot, religious abbot of the venerable monastery of the Lord Savior, and through you to the abbots who will succeed you in that venerable monastery, forever.

Since things that accord with reasonable desires ought always to be granted, the authority of the pious founder of a holy institution ought not to be denied when privileges are being bestowed. Therefore, since you have asked us that the monastery of the Savior, constructed by the archbishop Saint Boniface in the place called Bochonia, on the bank of the river Fulda, should be adorned with the support of the privilege of the apostolic see, we make effective, in favor of your pious requests, what has been asked for by this authority of ours.

Accordingly, we bring it about that the monastery, established under the jurisdiction of our holy Church, which by God’s ordering we serve, shall be subject to the jurisdiction of no other see. Therefore, favoring your pious desires, by this authority of ours we bring what is requested into effect. We exclude every priest of any church from having any jurisdiction or authority whatsoever in the aforesaid monastery except the apostolic see; thus, unless invited by the abbot of the monastery, no one at all may presume to celebrate there the solemnity of Mass. Therefore, in accordance with what is established by the firm privilege of the apostolic see, it shall remain undisturbed and endowed with the places and property which it now holds or possesses, as well as those which divine mercy may wish in future to add to the right of that monastery from the gifts, offerings, and tithes of the faithful, without opposition from any person, and it shall endure with perpetual stability.

We also establish by the page of this decree of ours that whoever, whatever his person or dignity, belonging to any church under the jurisdiction of the holy see, should attempt to violate this charter of our privilege, which we confirm by the authority of the prince of the apostles, shall be anathema, incur the wrath of God, be expelled from the company of all the saints, and—nevertheless—let the dignity of the aforesaid monastery, granted by us, remain forever inviolate, supported by apostolic authority.

Written by the hand of Zacharias, notary and scriniary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of October, in the fifth indiction.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of November, by the hand of Theophylact, secundicerius of the holy apostolic see, while the most pious and perpetual Augustus Louis, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor, was reigning, in the fifth indiction.

**ACTS OF SAINT EULOGIUS, ARCHBISHOP OF TOLEDO**

(According to the edition of Francisco de Lorenzana, *Works of the Holy Bishops of Toledo*)

**NOTICE TO THE READER**

The writings of D. Eulogius rightly follow those of the holy bishops, for he was already designated as their successor in the see of Toledo when, as a priest of Córdoba, he died after obtaining the palm of martyrdom. He was a man whom everyone should receive with the greatest veneration, as a singular ornament of Córdoba, his homeland; the perpetual glory of Toledo; and the light of all Spain—not less on account of his praise for virtue than for his learning. His holy life, crowned by a glorious death, sufficiently bears witness to the former; his writings, committed to letters and left behind, to the latter.

Indeed, if anyone compared Eulogius with that great African teacher and illustrious martyr of Christ, Cyprian, he would not thereby be considered an unfair judge of men. Except for a certain roughness of expression—for those times scarcely admitted a more polished and refined style—I would readily place Eulogius on a level with Cyprian in other respects: in fertility of intellect, sacred learning, education, the powerful and ardent zeal of faith, strength of spirit, and finally the supreme ardor of charity. Whether he attempts to describe the glorious contests of Christ’s athletes, undertakes their defense against detractors of the holy martyrs, encourages the weak and feeble, or endeavors to strengthen the wavering, almost all of Eulogius’s writings are praised in this respect.

At that time he produced the admirable *Martyrial Document*, addressed to the holy virgins Flora and Maria, who were being held in chains for confessing the faith, while he himself was also bound in the Lord and confined in a dark prison. Anyone who claims not to be moved by reading it confesses himself wholly alien to every sense of piety and faith. That work seems to have been composed not so much by human ingenuity as under the inspiration of the divine Spirit. Thus the great father of ecclesiastical annals, Baronius, expressed himself excellently when he said that Eulogius, while writing the *Martyrial Document*, seemed to have dipped his pen into the inkstand of the Holy Spirit.

All Eulogius’s works, as we have said, deal with matters of this kind: either narrating the contests of the martyrs of Córdoba in his own time, or defending their prudence and righteous zeal in offering themselves. They include the *Memorial of the Martyrs*, divided into three books; the *Martyrial Document*; the *Apology of the Martyrs*; and several letters.

We undertake to publish all these works here, together with the life of Saint Eulogius by Alvarus of Córdoba, written with the greatest familiarity and care. In it everything relating to Eulogius is pursued fully and minutely.

It is fortunate that the learned Ambrosius Morales preceded us long ago in this undertaking. We owe him much gratitude, since in the sixteenth century he undertook to publish Eulogius with the greatest care and illuminated him with excellent observations. Accordingly, almost our entire work after his has consisted in purifying Morales’s edition of the typographical errors with which it was stained, using the edition prepared at Frankfurt by Andreas Schottus. Although that edition too is full of errors, it carefully corrected passages that had been corrupted in Morales’s edition.

With the assistance of many other manuscript codices, therefore, when we accurately compared the two editions with each other, the result was that ours appeared more complete and sounder than either. We have also occasionally increased Ambrosius Morales’s notes: sometimes to illuminate the author’s text more fully, sometimes to explain or confirm the opinions of the annotator himself, and sometimes even to correct them. In this matter we took care to leave each man his own, so that we would not deprive the most learned scholar of his due praise.

[Editorial note:] The works of the bishops of Toledo discussed here—namely Eugenius, Ildefonsus, and Julian—are printed in the *Patrologia*, volumes LXXXVII and XCVI.

[scan page 358]

Since Morales’s observations are sometimes longer and nearly burdensome for the reader’s convenience, we adopted the following method: we placed the shorter notes at the foot of the text, and relegated the rest to the end—not of each individual book, but of the entire work. In this we follow the example of distinguished editors.

As far as permitted, we assigned the writings to the period in which each work appears to have been composed. This was not always possible. It would not have been appropriate to divide the three books of the *Memorial of the Saints* from one another, although they were not written at the same time.

Moreover, we removed the account of the holy virgins Flora and Maria—which had previously formed chapter 8 of book II of the *Memorial of the Saints*—from its place, so to speak, and thought it suitable to publish it separately together with the *Martyrial Document* prefixed to it. We did this both because that portion of the history is not so closely joined to the rest of the narrative that it could not be separated from it, and especially because the *Document* immediately adjoining it shows more clearly how great a flame of divine love and contempt for this perishing life Eulogius’s fiery words kindled in the breasts of the virgins.

The *Apology*, the last of all Eulogius’s works, is preceded by a letter to Wilesindus, bishop of Pamplona. That its authenticity was doubted without sufficient reason by Petti­zer, marquis of Mondéjar, and by Maiansius is clearly demonstrated, by every kind of argument, by the often-praised Father Flórez, volume X of *Sacred Spain*, treatise 33, chapter 12, section 10 and following.

We have placed the remaining letters, which Morales published together, before the treatises that occasioned their composition; and in the *Acts of the Martyrs* we have added several notes from the Bollandists, so that nothing might be lacking from our edition.

**NOTICE TO THE COMPLUTENSE EDITION**

We had two copies of this life of the holy Eulogius. One was joined at the end to his works in the very ancient codex of Oviedo. The other was kindly lent to me by Michael Ruiz Azagra, secretary to the most serene princes Ernest and Rudolf of Bohemia, a young man highly distinguished in talent and letters and singularly diligent and careful in investigating every kind of antiquity.

This codex too was written in Gothic letters on parchment and, as many indications showed, was likewise very ancient. It contains several poems: namely, two books by Dracontius on the six days of creation, with supplements by Saint Eugenius, third archbishop of Toledo; three books by the African grammarian Coryppus addressed to the emperor Justinian; epigrams by the same Saint Eugenius; and some other works. At the end this life of Saint Eulogius had been attached.

The Oviedo codex had no title prefixed to this work. The other had the title which we have adopted. But the date was marked variously in the margin, with the number erased, so that it appeared that another year had been written above it. The year of the Lord’s incarnation was correctly recorded. Therefore, using both our astronomical method of calculation—which Alvarus enabled us to apply at the end of the work, as will appear there—we correctly established and supplied the dates in both copies.

The king’s name was also incorrectly written in the title. It read “Abd al-Rahman”; but since that king had died, it must have been Muhammad, his son, who, as is clear from Eulogius’s third book, crowned the saint with martyrdom. Alvarus also calls that king Muhammad.

Alvarus himself appears to have been of a very noble and illustrious family, since the most serene Eulogius does not address him merely by his name. He even calls him his teacher, which is certainly an expression of humility, since—as will immediately become clear to the reader—they were fellow students. Moreover, Alvarus is called a doctor by a kind of abuse of the term: he was a layman and, so far as one may infer, married, and such a title could scarcely have applied to him at that time.

**LIFE OF SAINT EULOGIUS, ARCHBISHOP OF TOLEDO AND MARTYR**

**LIFE OR PASSION OF SAINT EULOGIUS, ARCHBISHOP OF TOLEDO AND MARTYR**

(*From the Toledo manuscript of Azagra; the edition of Morales; Schottus; Flórez, volume X of* Sacred Spain; *and volume IV of* Hispania Illustrata, *Antwerp, at 11 March.*)

He suffered in the Spanish era 897, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 859, under King Muhammad, on the fifth day before the Ides of March.

**PREFACE**

1. Preparing to write the passion of the most blessed martyr and doctor Eulogius, I first thought that I should set out his life in an orderly fashion before describing the struggle of his end, so that the reader might know beforehand what kind of man he was and how great he was, and so that, from then on, the palm of victory which he obtained through merit might shine forth by the clearest indications.

[Editorial note:] The numerical notes interspersed in the text refer to the scholia of Ambrosius Morales, reprinted after the Life of Eulogius.

In the beginning of this work, relying upon the mercy of our Lord and Redeemer, I profess that I shall relate not things heard and doubtful but things seen and proved by me. For, with the grace of God cooperating, from the first flower of youth we were joined by one bond of concord in the sweetness of charity and the love of the Scriptures, and, although not in equal order, we bore the yoke of this life with equal affection in all its questions.

But he, adorned with the office of priesthood and lifted on the wings of virtue into the heights, flew higher; while I, overcome by the mud of luxury and pleasure, crawl close to the ground, scarcely able to stand upright. For that reason I have resolved to narrate not matters uncertain or established by the reasoning of any people whatsoever, but events that occurred with me and that I myself came to know.

Just as I acknowledge that it would be dangerous rashly to pronounce upon uncertain matters, so I do not think it free from danger to suppress matters that ought to be known once they are known. Truth, when it is praiseworthily proclaimed as an example to all, is also to be commended; and the falsehood composed by rhetoricians is no less to be detested.

For it is better to say nothing about many distinguished deeds than to spread many lies from a few small truths. It is better to pass over everything that happened than to invent something that did not happen. He errs more mildly who, not through a desire for evil but through the arrogance of indolence, suppresses the truth than he who openly fabricates falsehood.

For truth, when spoken out of a love of truth and not from the ostentation of empty glory, builds up the house; but falsehood, if uttered by someone, destroys the one who utters it. Therefore, just as I rejoice that I ought to be rewarded if I speak the truth, so I do not deny that I ought to be condemned if I speak falsely.

For what reasons, then, should I rush to weave falsehood, when I have no reward for doing so, and have learned that truth, in every respect without deceit, is not unrewarded?

**CHAPTER I**

**Eulogius’s noble birth, education, ordination as priest and deacon, his teaching, and his friendship with Alvarus, the author of the Life**

2. The blessed martyr Eulogius was born of noble stock, descended from the senators of the patrician city of Córdoba. He was devoted to the ministry of the Church, serving the holy and most blessed Zoilus, and leading his life in the college of that church’s clergy. He flourished in many distinguished virtues and was vigorous in great and praiseworthy works.

From his earliest beginnings he clung to ecclesiastical letters, and every day grew through the study of good works. He attained perfection, surpassing all his contemporaries in knowledge of doctrine and shining with the light of learning; he became a teacher of teachers.

For, carrying an aged mind in a very small body, he surpassed all—not certainly in age, but in knowledge. He was an exceedingly diligent student of the Scriptures and an intensely committed investigator of their meaning, so that he preferred nothing to sacred Scripture and chose nothing more readily than to meditate day and night on the law of the Lord.

Nor was he content with the instruction of his own teachers. If he happened to hear of others, he sought them out even from a distance; and, so as not to offend his own teachers, he secretly withdrew from them at whatever hours he could. He often visited the abbot Sperandeus, a man of blessed memory, remarkable and renowned for his learning, and depended, like a listener in an auditorium, upon the eloquence of his most articulate speech.

At that time he was sweetening the whole region of Baetica with streams of wisdom. There I first had the privilege of seeing him; there I became attached to his friendship by its sweet bond; there I was joined to him by an indivisible sweetness.

I was already one of the aforesaid illustrious man’s hearers. As I more frequently wore out the threshold of his dwelling and cultivated my uncultivated intellect, at last, through divine providence, I was joined to the companionship of so great a man.

I was not merely bound to him in an unbreakable chain, but united to him. We became hearers of that man and lovers of one another, so much so that that unlearned age did not regard itself as wholly without an educated pursuit.

We engaged with one another in the delightful play of the Scriptures and, not knowing how to steer a boat on a lake, thought ourselves carried along amid the roar of the great sea. In youthful contests over the teachings by which we were divided, we exchanged letters with one another—not bitterly but delightfully—and praised one another in rhythmic verses.

This was an exercise sweeter than honey, more pleasant than flowers, more delightful than anything else. Stretching ourselves every day toward these things, our immature childish ability compelled us to attempt many things not fit to be heard in Scripture. We even composed volumes which, when afterward we had reached more mature age, we destroyed so that they would not remain for posterity.

3. When Eulogius was approaching the years of youth, he undertook the ministry of the diaconate and, soon afterward, having deservedly advanced upward, was elevated to the rank of the presbyterate. At once he was joined to the teachers in order and manner of life.

What humility, what goodness, what charity dwelled in him! His love for everyone revealed it. From then on he began to bind himself with a stricter austerity of life and to adorn all his actions with the laws of moderation: to devote himself to the divine Scriptures; to chastise his body with vigils and fasts; to frequent monasteries; to visit monastic communities; and to establish the rules of the brothers.

Here and there he attended to everything in such a way that, if it had been possible, he would have been present in both places. Thus he conducted his own clerical estate without abandoning the regular order of another: thus ...

[Editorial notes:]

- Schottus has in the margin, “they ought not to be known,” as in the manuscript.
- The manuscript reads *falle*.
- Schottus has in the margin *fuerint*, as does the manuscript.
- The printed editions read *mancipatur*.
- Schottus says that *opinatabilem* is a Hispanic usage meaning “of great repute”; below, in the Passion, he similarly calls Eulogius *opinatissimus*, “most renowned.”
- The manuscript and Schottus read *insolubilis*, in place of Morales’s *inconcussus*. Flórez rightly notes that Alvarus uses *inadibilis* in two senses: first, “not to be undertaken,” as in “to attempt many things not fit to be heard from the Scriptures”; secondly, “stable, firm, immutable,” as when he says that this *inadibilis* man never wavered. In this latter sense it may stand in the phrase *adeo inadibilis*, without moving the word, as Morales proposed.
- Schottus reads *ex Scripturis ... egit*, as does the manuscript.
- The manuscript reads *mutua*; Morales, *multum*; Schottus, *muco*; the Antwerp editions, *multa*. The manuscript’s reading is preferable: it subsequently has *abolenda* (“to be destroyed”), rather than *abtuenda*.
- Schottus reads *cum annos*; the manuscript, *dum*, and does not have *Eulogius* or *jam*.
