## LIFE OR PASSION

…adhering to monasticism, so that he might be approved as a cleric; thus living among the clergy so as to appear a monk, suited to both conditions and readily applying himself to each profession, sufficiently fulfilling them both in one person. He frequently hastened to the most sacred flocks of the monasteries; but, lest he seem to despise his own order, he returned again to the clergy. When he had remained there for some time, lest the strength of his spirit be weakened by secular cares, he likewise returned to the monasteries. Here adorning the Church with the teaching of his speech, there embellishing it by displaying his own life, endowed with every virtue, he went his sorrowful and anxious way through the world. Daily longing to fly to heaven, he was weighed down by his bodily burden. So greatly that he planned to go to Rome, in order to subdue—or rather, once subdued, to destroy—the blemishes of youth by tears and the journey of pilgrimage. But behold, we all press upon him from every side and hold him back more in body than in mind.

## CHAPTER II

### Saint Eulogius’ captivity; his instruction of the martyrs; the constancy born from contemplating their deeds

**4.** Truly, while these and other matters were being related, at last Bishop Reccafred, like a violent whirlwind, fell upon the churches and clergy; and he bound in prison every priest whom he could. Among them Eulogius was led away like an expelled ram, and was bound together with his bishop or with the other priests. In that confinement he devoted himself more to prayers and readings than to his chains.

There he composed, in a single book, that *Martyrial Document* for the holy virgins Flora and Maria, who had been arrested for the faith. In it he strengthened them for martyrdom with the strongest cords, and taught them to despise death, both personally through his words and through letters. He entrusted himself and his companions to be released from their bonds through their intercession; and he soon deserved to obtain this, six days after their passion. For they completed their martyrdom on the eighth day before the Kalends of December, while the priests of the Lord obtained their release on the third day before those same Kalends.

There exists on this subject a letter composed in a more polished style and sent to me in these days, containing both the passion of those virgins and the liberation of the priests through the merits of the same virgins.

From there he also sent me an epistle dictated in return for books; the intervening description, concerning his defense or adornment of the martyrs, is materially corrupt in the supplied scan.

While all those who were with him were enjoying leisure and quiet, he ceased neither by night nor by day from reading, repeating nights and days alike, tasting the honey of the Scriptures with his mouth and spiritually chewing it over in his heart.

**5.** Yet I think it worthwhile, proceeding a little farther back, to insert how he proved himself during the persecution. For while the bishops, priests, clergy, and learned men of Córdoba were walking along a devious path in the martyrdom that had recently arisen, and, driven by fear, were almost denying the faith of Christ—not in words, perhaps, but at least by a sign—this steadfast man was never seen to waver, even at the faintest whisper.

But as all were going forth to the contest, he met them, reverencing the spirits and the bones of all and setting them in order; and he burned with such ardor for martyrdom that in those days he himself seemed to be the instigator of the martyrs. For this zeal for righteousness he was subjected to many insults and wearied by great terrors.

One of the nobles attacked him and provoked him with threats. By the just judgment of God he was turned into a reprobate mind: he attacked the faith that he had unknowingly been holding, and soon, wretched and foolish, lost it. The blessed man has already discussed him more fully in the third book of the *Memorial of the Saints*. In those books he explained the passions of the martyrs one by one in a clear stream of speech and, with adequate continuation, made known to succeeding generations whatever had been done among the martyrs of God and whatever was to follow.

How great, and how excellent, his learning was, his little works reveal more brightly than light. He composed them with Attic salt and prose charm—or rather, by divine inspiration.

**6.** But we must return to the time of Bishop Reccafred and explain by what art he withdrew from the sacrifice, so that he would not be joined to Reccafred’s error. For in those days all who were subject to him by force and authority, and subordinated by royal command, seemed to be attached to an unjust enemy. Those who had opposed him and stood upright against him, driven by fear, clung to him like relatives—not in mind, but in body; not from affection of heart, but under compulsion of terror—and so that he would have no further opportunity to harm them.

Thus the king, raging against us, had imposed necessity through laws, interfering with free choice and subjecting everyone, savage as he was, to the enemy. The truth of this history will be discussed more clearly in another work.

**7.** [The opening words of this section are badly damaged in the supplied scan; the following renders the recoverable syntax.] Now, however, it remains to say only so much about this admirable man: when, with the grave impulse of grief, he saw everywhere the bishop’s treacherous disposition growing more violent and perceived that those communicating with him had no opportunity to resist or any license to remove themselves, he began to wear himself down with a heavy groaning and, as we have said, to be inwardly slaughtered by great pain.

[The two source columns are interleaved at this transition; their separate sequence is retained here.] But by God’s providence it happened that one day, in the presence of Bishop Reccafred, a letter of blessed Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, addressed to John, bishop of Jerusalem, was read—the reading of it I had ordered a certain deacon to undertake. In it that most blessed pontiff, refuting Origen’s errors, clarified the case concerning the ordination of a certain presbyter assigned by himself to a monastery, defending the legitimacy of the ordination and interweaving with his praise of the continence of the most blessed priests Jerome and Vincent the argument that priests should abstain from sacrifice.

When the aforementioned Eulogius seized this account with an eager mind rather than merely receiving it, and recognized the opportunity given him by God, he seemed struck by a great wound. Drawing sighs from the depths of his heart, he turned to the bishop and said:

> “If the lamps of the Church and the pillars of our faith have done this, what ought we to do, whom the burdens of our loved ones weigh down and oppress so heavily? Let your paternity therefore know that I have forbidden myself the freedom to sacrifice.”

Thus, by such a device, during Reccafred’s time he bound himself by his own choice. Although he undertook the order of this profession in this way and enjoyed its pleasing practice, he afterward did not wish to resume the rejected status. But his own bishop compelled him so forcefully to return to the admitted office of sacrificing that he did not fear to strike him with anathema unless he promised to return at once.

## CHAPTER III

### Saint Eulogius’ learning and virtue; his journey; his election as archbishop of Toledo

**8.** That man was pre-eminently and not moderately adorned in every profession, serving all equally; and although he surpassed everyone in learning, he nevertheless appeared humbler even than the lowliest.

He was distinguished in countenance, eminent in honor, radiant in eloquence, and luminous in the works of his life: an encourager and praiser of martyrs, a most skilled expositor and writer. Who could describe, with whatever stream of eloquence prudence might command, his natural ardor, the beauty of his eloquence, the brilliance of his learning, or the customary graciousness of his service?

What volumes were not open to him? What kinds of learning could the minds of Catholics, philosophers, heretics, and even pagans conceal from him? Where were there metric works, where prose works, where histories, that escaped his inquiry? Where were the verses whose musical quality he did not know? What hymns or foreign little works did his most beautiful eye not survey?

Every day, as though digging treasures out of ruins and pits, he brought forth something new and wonderfully admirable. How great was the teachability of so precious an intellect, and how inexhaustible his diligence—no learned person could comprehend it.

He corrected what was corrupted, strengthened what was broken, restored what was unusual, renewed what was ancient, revived what had been neglected; and whatever deeds he could discover among the men of old, he strove to fulfill in his own works. He displayed within himself, variously combined, the severity of Jerome, the modesty of Augustine, the gentleness of Ambrose, and Gregory’s patience in correcting errors, supporting the weak, soothing the great, and enduring terrors.

**9.** Nor was it enough for him to visit the monasteries of his own country. Rather, on account of his brothers, who in those days were exiles in the regions of France, he took up the arduous road. Advancing of his own accord into the territories of the people of Pamplona, he entered the monastery of Saint Zacharias; and, traveling through the other coenobia of those regions with an ever-growing desire, he was sweetened by the friendship of many Fathers.

He set out their conversation by name and place in the letter that he gave to the bishop of Pamplona while he was in prison. In those places he discovered many volumes of books, obscure and almost removed from the reach of many; returning here, he brought them back to us.

There he enjoyed the conversation of blessed Odoarius, under whom one hundred and fifty regular monks served. From there he brought with him the book *The City of God* by the most blessed Augustine; Virgil’s *Aeneid*; likewise the metrical books of Juvenal; the satirical poems of Flaccus; the ornate works of Porphyry; the epigrammatic works of Adelhelm; and also the fables of Avienus—metrical works, and the splendid songs of the Catholic hymns, together with many very small matters gathered from holy questions through the ingenuity of many men. He brought these not privately for himself, but for the common use of the most diligent investigators.

Moreover, he continually displayed to all present and to those who would follow the brilliance of his work and the flashing of his intellect through shining paths, always making them evident by specific signs and leading them along luminous tracks. Everywhere he walked radiant, everywhere he returned brilliant; clear, sweet, nectar-like, and crowned by Christ, he shone forth as a servant to all.

**10.** I think that this also must not be omitted from this work: after the death of Wistremirus, bishop of the see of Toledo, he was elected to that same see by all the provincial and neighboring bishops, deemed worthy, and approved according to the report of all.

But the divine disposition, which was reserving him for martyrdom, placed certain barriers in the way. When the common election was already acclaiming him for consecration to the episcopate, those prevented by the adversity of circumstances forbade themselves to elect another while he was alive. Although he was cleverly thwarted from the office, he was not deprived of the dignity of that order. For he obtained the heavenly episcopate when, through the glory of martyrdom, he was joined to Christ.

For all holy bishops are indeed saints, though not all bishops are holy. He, however, having found sanctity through the shedding of his blood, fulfills the office of the episcopate, since, received into heaven, he is rewarded with eternal promises.

**11.** Since he was distinguished by these virtues and teachings, and since he shone out above all like a lamp placed on a lampstand and like a city situated high upon a mountain’s summit, and since, as a learned scribe, he brought forth new and old things from the treasure of his Lord for all the household, he was first among priests, highest among confessors, and, when seated among judges, not the least.

At last, having attained the fulfillment of his desire, by the divine clemency cooperating with him, he was raised to the heights by an unexpected judgment but deliberate purpose. What he had requested from the martyrs in tears, and had scattered throughout all his little works in the manner of prayers, he deserved to obtain through works of holiness. He who takes care to read his distinguished works will be able to know this more truly.

And since it seemed useful and fitting to us for the benefit of readers and for the annual return of his feast, to explain his passion briefly, we have therefore set apart, purely and sincerely, the most beautiful conclusion of his contest.

## CHAPTER IV

### A new persecution of the Christians under King Muhammad. Saint Leocritia instructed and assisted by Eulogius and his sister

**12.** At the time when the savage rule of Arab cunning was miserably devastating every region of Spain, when King Muhammad, with incredible rage and unrestrained resolve, was planning to destroy the Christian race utterly, many who feared the terror of that bloodiest king, and who tried to moderate his madness, attempted, through the cruel exercise of an iniquitous will, to attack Christ’s flock by various carefully contrived opportunities.

Most of them plunged themselves into ruin by denying Christ; others, driven by harsh tortures, were shaken; still others flourished in virtue and stood firm. In his time, as we have said, the martyrdom of the faithful shone brightly, while the error of the deniers wavered.

For some who retained the faith of Christ only in their minds, moved by God’s prompting, brought into the light and openly declared what they had concealed. They sprang forward to martyrdom without hesitation and seized a crown from their torturers.

Among these was the blessed Christopher, an Arab by race, whose passion we intend to set out elsewhere. From their number also came the blessed Aurelius and the holy Felix, who, after many long hiding places, came forth with their wives to the glory of martyrdom.

Among them too was Flora, a blessed virgin flourishing in virtues. Despising the fleeting pomp of this world, she deserved an eternal crown without end. Our most holy teacher set out the contest of these people individually and explained their deeds and lives in brilliant speech.

**13.** At that time there was a certain girl named Leocritia, noble by birth but nobler in mind, born from the filth of the pagans and brought forth from the entrails of wolves. Some time earlier, through a certain relative close to her by birth, a woman named Litiosa who was dedicated to Christ, she had been washed in saving waters, had secretly put on the faith of Christ, and had spread the nectar-like fragrance of her knowledge among all.

For when, in the years of childhood, she used to visit that religious woman according to the custom of kinship, and the woman instructed her daily with whatever words she could, Leocritia at last received the faith of Christ in her mind through heavenly regard and preserved in her heart, with ardent love, what she had received.

When she reached the years of wisdom and touched the lights of knowledge, she nourished that faith—which she had secretly learned through the tenderest instruction—by daily spiritual encouragement, increasing and growing ever greater: at first secretly, afterward openly and publicly.

Her parents admonished her assiduously, accomplishing nothing at all. They tried to attack her with lashes and blows, so that, since they could not turn her away by persuasion, they might restrain her by terror. But that fire which Christ sent into the hearts of the faithful knows no weakening through threats.

In this conflict, while she was being beaten day and night and saw herself exposed to the fiercest punishments and bound with harsh chains, though she had not publicly declared her faith, she was burned with the branding-iron of perfidy. Through intermediaries she made her case known to the most blessed Eulogius, a man already most richly endowed with many such works, and to his sister Anulo, a virgin dedicated to God. She explained that she wished to go to safer places where she could proclaim her faith without fear.

At once the blessed Eulogius recognized his accustomed duty; as he was a supporter of the most fervent martyrs, he arranged for those messengers to bring her out secretly. She quickly devised a plan: pretending to agree with her parents, attacking our faith in words, and deliberately putting on all the ornaments she had chosen, she presented herself in their manner as though she were pleased and about to marry the world. She attempted to bend their minds and [the corrupt phrase *et sibi exosos … comere gressus* is not securely recoverable from the supplied scan].

When she judged that everything was now safe, she went in an elegant procession, as the occasion required, to the wedding of certain relatives of hers, which was being celebrated in those days. She disguised herself for the purpose, and, hastening her course, presented herself to the blessed Eulogius and his sister Anulo for protection.

They immediately received her with grateful affection and entrusted her concealment to their most trusted friends. When her father and mother, waiting for their daughter, did not see her, they lamented that they had been deceived and, maddened by unheard-of rage and tormented by an unbearable grief, disturbed everything and polluted all things. They ran among strangers and acquaintances alike, and, with the authority and order of the governor, burdened with prisons and chains whomever they thought ought to be seized.

They afflicted men and women, confessors, priests, and devout persons with lashes and imprisonment, if by these and still greater means they could somehow recover their daughter.

But that holy man remained unmoved and changed her hiding places, taking every precaution lest the sheep be handed over to wolves. She, meanwhile, persevering in fasts and vigils, covering her limbs with sackcloth or sleeping on dust, severely disciplined her bodily members.

The most blessed man Eulogius, whose name must be mentioned with reverence, also sought out the night watches. Prostrate on the ground in the basilica of Saint Zoilus, he spent sleepless nights in prayer, imploring the Lord’s help and strength for the virgin and consecrating himself to the Lord through these exercises.

**14.** In the midst of these events the most serene virgin wished to see the sister of blessed Eulogius, whom she loved with ardent longing. Moved by a revelation from the Lord and led by her desire for consolation, she came by night to their dwelling, intending to remain with them for one day only and then return to her accustomed hiding places.

In answer to those who asked her, she recounted that once, while praying, her mouth had been filled with honey, which she had not spat out through rashness but swallowed; it presented the wondrous appearance of a thick element. The holy man explained this as a sign of the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom, which she was to enjoy.

## CHAPTER V

### The martyrdom of Saint Eulogius and Leocritia; the burial of their bodies

**15.** When the virgin intended to return on another day, it happened that her companion did not come at the customary hour but at daybreak. She could not find a way out, since she was accustomed to move by night to avoid ambushes.

It was therefore arranged that she should remain in the same place until the sun had completed its course, and that, when night’s darkness had supplied the desired quiet, the virgin of God should remain where she was staying.

This happened by human planning, but she was retained by divine judgment, so that she might receive her own crown and place a diadem of glory upon blessed Eulogius. For on that day—I do not know by whose prompting or through whose treachery—the location of the hiding place was disclosed, and the entire dwelling was suddenly surrounded by soldiers sent for this purpose.

It came about that the chosen and predestined martyr was present. In his presence they brought out the virgin, seized him together with her, beat them, afflicted them with many insults, and presented them to the unjust governor and wicked judge.

The judge immediately intended to kill him with lashes. Inflamed by violent fury, with a savage face and impatient mind, he questioned him in furious words and demanded, with threats, why he had kept the virgin in his house.

With the splendid manner of speech customary to him, the saint gladly and patiently set forth the truth of the matter in this order:

> “Governor, the order of preaching has been entrusted to us, and it accords with our faith that we offer the light of faith to those who inquire of us and deny nothing holy to anyone hastening along the road of life. This is proper to priests; true religion demands it; Christ our Lord also taught us this: whoever thirsts and wishes to draw from the rivers of faith should find drink in double measure, rather than merely what he sought.
>
> “And since this virgin seemed to be seeking from us the rule of holy faith, it was necessary for me to apply my intention to her all the more willingly, so that her affection might be kindled more greatly. It was not fitting to reject one who desired such things, especially one who has been chosen by Christ for this very service.
>
> “Therefore, insofar as I was able, I enlightened and instructed her, and explained that the faith of Christ is the way to the heavenly kingdom. I would gladly do the same for you, if you had thought it right to question me.”

Then the governor, with a troubled face, ordered rods to be brought in, threatening to kill him with lashes.

The saint said to him:

> “Why do you wish to use those rods?—‘I want,’ he replied, ‘to draw out your soul through them.’
>
> “Sharpen and prepare a sword, and by it return the soul, freed from the bond of the body, to him who gave it. Do not suppose that you will cut my limbs apart with whips.”

Immediately, with a clear invective and forceful eloquence, reproaching the falsity of the prophet and of his law and repeatedly proclaiming the word of preaching, he was led with all speed to the palace and dragged before the king’s counselors.

There one of them, well known to him, sprang forward in compassion:

> “If fools and idiots have rushed into this deadly madness, while you are girded with the dignity of wisdom and made illustrious by the morals of your life, what madness has compelled you to commit yourself to this death-bringing case, your natural love of life having been obliterated? Listen to me, I beg you, and I ask you not to fall through a headlong misfortune. Say only one word in this hour of necessity, and afterward use your faith wherever you can. We promise that you will nowhere be questioned.”

The most blessed martyr smiled and said:

> “O, if you could know how great the things preserved for the worshipers of our faith are! And if I could entrust to your heart what I retain in mine, you would no longer try to call me back from my purpose; rather, you would more willingly consider removing yourself from this worldly honor.”

He began to offer them the eternal word of the Gospel and to pour the preaching of the kingdom into them with steadfast freedom.

Since they immediately refused to listen to him, they ordered him to be struck with the sword. As he was being led away, one of the king’s eunuchs struck him on the cheek.

The saint presented the other cheek and said:

> “I beg you to strike this one also, so that by striking it again you may complete what you began.”

When he struck him a second time, the patient and gentle man again offered the first cheek.

Then he was led by the soldiers to the place of execution. Bending his knees in prayer, extending his hands toward heaven, fortifying himself entirely with the sign of the cross, and praying inwardly in a few words, he presented his neck to the sword and, despising the world at a single blow, found life immortal.

He completed his martyrdom on the fifth day before the Ides of March, on a Saturday, at the ninth hour.

O happy and admirable man for our age! He presided over many through the fruit of his work and left in the virgin a pattern to be followed. With her he raised the victorious standard in his hands, offering to the Lord the labor of his own life as a sacrifice, presenting a pure oblation and peaceful offerings, and displaying in himself to Christ, the Lord of all, what he had taught others.

As soon as the corpse had been thrown from a higher place into the channel of the river, a dove, growing white as snow, was seen by all to cut through the air with its wings and settle upon the martyr’s body. Although everyone tried to drive it away from every side by throwing stones, and although they could not repel it even while it remained there, they attempted to frighten it away at close range.

But it did not fly around the body. Rather, leaping, it settled nearer on a tower rising above the body and remained close to the body of the most blessed man.

Nor should it be passed over in silence what Christ performed above the martyr’s body for the praise of his name. A palace official in the city, while he was carrying out the service of the royal residence among the other palace officials and was spending the night there in his vigils, rose up, desiring no sleep, and went to the channel of the river that flows past those places.

There he saw above the body lying below priests shining with marvelous whiteness, holding glittering lamps and reciting psalms with the solemnity of those who chant.

Terrified by the vision, he returned to the place of residence, fleeing rather than walking. After recounting everything to his companion, he wished to return with him to the place; but, when he looked again a second time, he was no longer able to see it.

The curiosity of the Christians redeemed the body of the most blessed man on the following day, while on the third day they gathered his remains and buried them beneath the protection of the most blessed martyr.

**16.** The most blessed virgin Leocritia, softened by many flatteries and pressed by many promises, was at last strengthened by divine grace in the constancy of her faith. On the fourth day after his martyrdom, she was taken out and thrown into the river *Bastis* [the place-name is uncertain in the corrupt text].

But she could neither be submerged nor hidden. Her body, raised upright and moving onward, presented a sight marvelous to all.

Thus, brought out by the Christians, she was buried in the basilica of the holy martyr Genesius, which is situated near the place called Tertios [another reading: Terzos].

This was the end of the most blessed doctor Eulogius; this was his admirable departure; this was the conclusion of his passage through life, accomplished in such a work.

## CHAPTER VI

### Alvar’s affectionate devotion toward Saint Eulogius; an invocation

**17.** Now, at the end of the volume, it remains to give thanks to the King of the ages, who, from the beginning of his faith, adorns the Church with martyrs, gives strength to the weary, and leads the things concerning himself to everlasting glory. To our God himself be glory and dominion through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

**18.** But now, since we have completed in pedestrian speech the account of the contest of our teacher and martyr, it remains for us to turn our discourse toward that same most beloved patron, as though he were listening and present at our prayers, and to report to him our request.

Certainly he is able to hear those who pray, and his patronage, joined to many intercessions, will assist our merits, if our devotion should not be obstructed by hardship, if affection should demand this from us.

Therefore, exalted martyr of God, sweet Eulogius, turn your attention to your Alvar: regard as your servant the one whom you knew to be your own through the love of his soul. I invoke you not for others, but for your own [the damaged Latin *Non aliorum quam tuis…* is retained here with its uncertainty].

Certainly I am the one whom you used to say was united with you…

[The supplied source ends incompletely here.]

**[Page 360, a]** The edition omits *iterum* (“again”).

**[Page 360, b]** The same edition reads *praehibuerit* (“may have furnished or displayed beforehand”).

**[Page 360, c]** The surviving note begins *Ita ms.; sed edit.* (“Thus the manuscript; but the edition …”); its cited reading is illegible in the supplied scan. No further wording is supplied securely.

**[Page 360, d]** *Hoc modo* (“in this manner”) is absent from the manuscript; the source note states that the following portion is also wanting or defective in the manuscript.

**[Page 360, e]** The edition reads *etiam* (“also”).

**[Page 360, f]** The manuscript reads *dederunt*. The editor remarks that this reading, if it were to be approved, would provide sufficient evidence for attributing to Alvar a writing in defense of the martyrs.

**[Page 360, g]** The edition omits *exstat* (“there exists”) in the present passage.

**[Page 360, i]** The manuscript reads *qualis* (“what sort of” or “how great”).

**[Page 360, 1]** The numbered cross-reference is printed after “while these and other matters were being related”; the discussion to which it refers is outside this supplied chunk.

**[Page 360, 2]** The martyrs completed their passion on the eighth day before the Kalends of December; the priests obtained their release on the third day before the same Kalends.

**[Page 361, e]** From this passage the Antwerp editors infer that Alvar held some ecclesiastical dignity, since he ordered a deacon to read the letter. Morales, Nicolás Antonio, and Enrique Flórez, however, believe that he was bound by marriage; on this matter the editor remains doubtful. He judges their arguments insufficiently firm, while the circumstances as understood by the Antwerp editors also do not make the matter entirely clear.

**[Page 361, i]** Morales’s cited reading appears as *animati* in the supplied OCR [the form is uncertain]; the Antwerp edition omits the word at this locus.

**[Page 361, j]** At “who could describe,” the manuscript has *elicere* or *edicere* (“draw out” or “declare”) for printed *dicere* (“say/describe”).

**[Page 361, k]** At the image of digging treasures “from ruins and pits,” the manuscript reads *jugeribus* (“acres/plots”) for printed *ruderibus* (“ruins”).

**[Page 361, l]** In the question about how much teachability was present in his precious soul, Schott follows the manuscript with *inerat* (“was present”).

**[Page 361, m]** At the deeds of ancient men that he strove to fulfill, Schott and Antwerp follow the manuscript with *competere* (“to attain, belong, or be fitting”) for printed *petere* (“seek”).

**[Page 361, n]** Schott reads *sorores* (“sisters”); the manuscript may permit that reading, though the associated phrase itself appears corrupt as *in sufferendos orores*. The printed main text has *in sufferendo horrores* (“in enduring terrors”).

**[Page 361, o]** The manuscript omits *varium* (“varied”) and the pronouns *se* and *ei*, as well as the preposition *in* before *Francia* and *Pampilonensium*.

**[Page 361, p]** Unless the other Ovetan manuscript used by Morales—and mentioned in his notice to the reader—read this passage differently, Morales indulged his own interpretation too freely. The Azagra manuscript reads: “Returning here, he placed them for us in his most sacred heart.”

**[Page 361, q]** At the list of books, medieval writers very frequently used *sive*, *seu*, or *aut* (“or”) for *et* (“and”); the editor therefore judges the printed substitution of *et* at this locus erroneous.

**[Page 361, r]** In *Flacci saturata poemata*, the manuscript and the editions of Morales and Antwerp read *saturata* (“filled/saturated”); see the scholion explaining the reference to Horatian satires.

**[Page 362, a]** Morales reads *sequentibus* (“those following”) here less correctly.

**[Page 362, b]** From this sole testimony of Alvar—that Eulogius was elected bishop of Toledo—everyone can see how mistaken Fabricius was in volume II of the *Bibliotheca Latina medii et infimae aetatis*, Padua edition, 1754, page 123, note (c), where he wrote: “That some make Eulogius archbishop of Toledo is by no means established by suitable arguments.” For what argument could be more suitable than Alvar’s testimony? Fabricius could hardly have been unaware that Alvar wrote the *Life of Eulogius*, as is evident from volume I of the same *Bibliotheca*, page 75.

## Saint Eulogius, Archbishop of Toledo

### 719–720

…abbot, to whom and for whom you spoke in this manner: (2)

“So that,” you say, “there may not be one Alvarus other than Eulogius, nor anywhere else than in the innermost heart of Alvarus may all Eulogius’ love be placed.” May this sweet and faithful affection between the two of you prosper, O Christ the Lord. May it prosper at the everlasting summit of holiness, and, like a shining light, advance and increase until the perfect day.

Behold, Lord, I hold in my hands your testimony, painted in letters of gold and gems of meaning; but I desire the completion of your patronage. For what you prayed unceasingly for while you were still on earth, that it might be effective, now that you have been transferred to heaven you can obtain for me by your intercession. True love, as you yourself said, faithfully preserves affection for one who is absent, and offers the beloved what it could offer to itself.

Therefore, outstanding martyr and dearest friend, while it is still permitted and the time of mercy still endures, extend to your friend the gift of intercession, so that an amendment of my conduct may be granted me; let gifts of tears be frequent; let love of virtues be brought to my unstable mind; let heartfelt compunction be constant; let a pure desire for repentance be present; let a desirable place be rightly granted; let access be opened, not to be broken by any obstacle.

Let the bonds of every perplexity be loosed; let the burdens of every impediment spring back, and the barriers of every restraint; by the transformation wrought by the right hand of the Most High, let aids be changed into obedient assistance. Let the doors of the heart be opened to receive the kingdom of the Most High God; let the proud neck bend, and let the shoulders be subjected to bear Christ’s most gentle yoke.

I would still ask for greater things, but I fear incurring the charge of presumption. Yet you, O exalted servant of God, who are satisfied by the Lord’s countenance and rejoice in his perpetual gift, obtain for this wretch, through worthy intercessions, that which you know cleanses a thousand sins. I also desire eternal life and thirst for the rest of the heavenly kingdom. Therefore, whatever torment or scourging is necessary, care to bring relief to your servant, and desire to purify your beloved with that fire of ardor by which here on earth you seemed to be bound with us, so that that love may now shine forth in clearer light, since it shines with a fuller radiance and is able by a more powerful intercession to obtain the things sought.

### 19. (3)

As for me, my sweet Eulogius, I have illuminated the memory of your name as far as I could; I have arranged your life, expressed your teaching, and explained your most glorious struggle. And so that the delightful memory of your name may always flower in the world, and that your remembrance may shine here with everlasting brilliance as your life does in heaven, I have dedicated it, if not in the most fully polished language, nevertheless with the clearest efforts of which I was capable.

For I have constructed a monument to your glory more enduring than bronze, which neither stormy rainstorm nor stone-laden hail can destroy, nor a pyre melt with any fire.[^c0072-1] I have fixed a memorial of your name in refined gold and precious stones of every kind, which no tyrant, however violent, will be able to overthrow in the manner of a plunderer. I have fashioned the structure of your summit and raised high the tower of your dwelling, so that you may be a beautiful beacon shining from here and there for all travelers.

I have adorned the inscription of your beauty with pearls gleaming with wondrous whiteness and with radiant topaz, so that it may sparkle throughout all the regions of the earth. I have strewn the holy ashes with nectar-like little flowers, which neither fade in any heat nor yield to an applied fire.[^c0072-2] I have anointed your precious body with costly genuine nard, mixing in various kinds of incense, amomum, balsam, and *bisamum*, so that the sweetest fragrance of your holiness, diffused and filled throughout all ages, may remain warm without end.

I have completed the bond of friendship and have not wished to send your name naked into the world, so that, just as you shine in heaven through life and works, you may also shine in the world through speech and name. Thus the next generation may find you praised and look to you for imitation, and may recognize, through our slight talent, how great you were in teaching. Nor will the age to come marvel at you as being merely packed with bodily honors, outward forms, and flowers of the ancient writers, which customarily perish through the age’s decay; rather, it will venerate you as adorned with spiritual gifts and exalted by immortal titles.

### 20.

You, therefore, venerable Lord, repay us with a reward equal to our service, so that, because your relics are honored and your funeral rites adorned by our service, we may henceforth be enlightened by a happy regard and visited by a heavenly gift. May I—who until now, along steep and precipitous paths, failing to flow clearly, have fallen away through my iniquity; who, wasting away until now in my evils, have withdrawn from the face of my God and clung to the malignant enemy—be enlightened by prevenient grace and, completed by gratuitous mercy at whatever end of life, deemed worthy to possess with you the uninterrupted joys of heaven, just as here, worn down by equal weeping and groaning and earthly distress, I have endured long and prolonged sighs.

And even if I have not been granted an equal share in glory, at least let forgiveness of my sins be brought to me, so that I may not grieve, submerged in the punitive abyss, but, forgiven to you or to my other lords who are your companions, may rejoice in heavenly rest. Amen.

## Hymn for the Day of Saint Eulogius, 11 March

Now the fruitful festivals return,
of our renowned martyr Eulogius.
Let us sing songs to the Lord, the sovereign,
with a chorus of faith, a heavenly gift.

We praise in varied musical song
things that are not endowed with the Lord’s light:
here now the sacred matter is more suitably revealed,
when metrical strings resound Christ.

Here now the mind is eager to ponder great things;
it breathes splendidly toward brilliant balsams,
growing and striving freely toward excellent things,
so that sweet music may resound in its breath.

A warrior of the Lord, more powerful in word,
and likewise more celebrated for his teaching,
is thus surrounded by Christ’s glory,
so that he may flourish and thrive here and in heaven.

While the learned ruler was restoring the peoples,

[The following four verses are severely corrupt in both copies and are translated only approximately from the editor’s conjectural reconstruction.]

When he spoke of gypsum: “Come forth from the fragment”;
he leads forward a crowd crowned with many-branched laurel,
shining with a heavenly host.[^c0072-3]

Thus burned with the Lord’s zeal,
turning the fluid morals of the rebellious,
and enriching them with noble bounty,
he raises those drawn away from the abyss to the lofty heavens.

But when almighty Christ wished to repay him with rewards worthy of his merits, he soon raised up the pleasing virgin Leocritia, so that she might restore his illustrious servant to heaven.

Then the exalted one, offering his customary consolation and a peaceful, fitting remedy, also instills the teaching of faith, while a just rebellion opposes the peoples. Immediately the exceedingly anxious herald, the plunderer, troubles the fatherland; by order of the populace the command of the enraged prince is carried far through every street.

The illustrious mind of the heavenly servant, endowed by God, rejects the swollen ruler. At last, seized by a notable, precipitous arrest, he soon spoke freely, saying:

“O nobles, reject the impious one;
believe Christ, the heavenly prince;
properly drive away the shameless prophet,
who has consigned so many peoples to the fire.”

Rejoicing, he proclaims these things boldly from on high and speaks other brave words in lament; then they command that his head be struck with the sword, lest the holy throng be able to receive him.

The warrior stands present, fearless and assenting. They strike him with slaps; but he offers his face to the cruel man, asking that the other cheek too be given over to alternating blows from both hands.

Then the little servant arms his breast with the golden sign of faith in God, his milk-white neck supplied with rose-colored blood. He bends before the Lord and persists in pleading.

Thus, by the stroke of the sword, he is hidden among the stars;
thus, by the word of faith, he is carried clearly onward.

Be present to the wretched, we beg you, at once;
hasten to release the perplexed through prayers.
Stand beside those stirred by groans, we ask,
now bending the gracious hearing of your divine power
toward your servants, so that it may more serenely
refresh the mind through holy prayers.

May the ruler destroy savage kingdoms;
may he, strong, trample impious doctrines;
may the radiance of adorned faith shine forth,
by which it may open the gleaming heights of heaven.

May heresy, writhing, recoil far away;
may the worship of the Lord shine more brightly.
May the rulers of the fatherland breathe forth like flowers;
may they freely scatter hostile wedges.

May there be life for the peoples;
may religion also be provident for the saints through all ages;
may constant glory be given to the Triune Lord,
who gloriously reigns through eternal ages. Amen.

## Translation of the Body of Saint Eulogius

After the foregoing, the following was continued in another copy.

The translation of Saint Eulogius, martyr and teacher, took place in the basilica of Saint Zoilus, at the principal title, on the Kalends of June, in the era 897. His birthday, however, is celebrated on the aforementioned seventh day, because his solemnity always falls during the days of Lent.[^c0072-4]

## Epitaph of Saint Eulogius

Here lies the graceful martyr and resplendent teacher,
Eulogius, a light, a sweet name through the ages.

He, glowing with zeal for the faith and foremost in ancient virtue,
kindled the spirits of men with great radiance.

Here, celebrated, he is praised in books and hymns,
vigorous in life and flashing without the sun.

Scorning what flows away, he climbed to heaven’s brightness.
He did not perish through death, but lives in an everlasting seat.

Believe me, I beg you: he lives; through the ages he lives,
whoever rejoices in the heavenly glory of the kingdom.

## Alvarus’ Prayer

Now I ask you, holy one, to remember the name of your friend,
whom your sweet friendship held firmly here.

May your prayer bring back to life’s pastures this fallen Alvarus, polluted by the ruin of guilt and proceeding, infected with vice, through the world’s byways; that, as is customary, he may be bound with holy love, by which, joined to you, he remained dear through the ages.

Grant this, God of gods, reigning through everlasting ages. Amen.

# Ambrosius Morales’ Life of Eulogius

## Scholion on the Life

### In the Preface

**(1) “And teacher.”** In the Council of Caesaraugusta, chapter 7, a decree was written in these words: “Let no one assume the name of teacher for himself except those persons to whom it has been granted, according to what has been written.” Hence Saint Eulogius was regarded and called a teacher in the Church of Cordoba. A little later Alvarus notes that Eulogius was counted among the teachers even at the time when he was made a priest.

Eulogius himself, addressing the president, testifies to this more than once concerning himself. I have mentioned the first Council of Caesaraugusta because three councils celebrated in that city are found in very ancient copies preserved in the Royal Monastery of Saint Lawrence.

**(2) “I, a man of luxury.”** He speaks humbly of himself, although he wishes to indicate that he had taken a wife.

### In Chapter I

**(1) “Cordoba.”** In both copies, not *Corduba* but *Cordoba* was written here and everywhere, in keeping with that old corruption of the true name common in those times, which, as we shall say in its place, had already become established. It was also written everywhere *eglesia*, not *ecclesia*, so that here too one may recognize the Spanish pronunciation of this name gradually creeping in, which we now retain.

**(2) “Of senatorial descent.”** As we have shown at length in our *History*, after the Goths and other foreign peoples invaded Hispania, three classes of people inhabited the entire province: the ancient Hispanians; the Romans, who had mingled with them several centuries earlier; and the Goths, together with the Alans and Suebi and the others, who were later called by the single name “Goths.”

Although this is clear from many testimonies, it is especially evident from the Gothic laws contained in what they call the Book of Judges. For the later Gothic kings, addressing the peoples of Hispania collectively in their laws, separately name the distinctions among these three groups. They are also mentioned by Paulus Orosius.

When nobles of Roman descent are intended, the writers of those times call them senators. Paulus, the deacon of Mérida, who wrote about the bishops of that city; Samson, abbot of Cordoba; and our own Alvarus Eulogius all use the term in this way.

Accordingly, I believe that “patrician” here signifies a man of Roman stock. If anyone thinks that, by catachresis, Eulogius is called noble merely in the sense of distinguished, and not of Roman origin, I will not dispute the point. Eulogius’ mother was called Elisabeth, as he himself writes in the letter to the bishop of Pamplona. His grandfather was likewise named Eulogius, as he says in the *Apologeticus*.

**(3) “At Saint Zoilus.”** This church is mentioned in several places in the works of Saint Eulogius. A few years later Samson, the abbot, presided over it; more will have to be said about him below. Saint Eulogius and that same Samson state that the body of the martyr was preserved in this church at their time. I shall discuss Samson the abbot in Book II; at the beginning of Book III I shall speak of Paulus, the deacon of Mérida.

**(4) “Speraindeus, a man of this name.”** Eulogius mentions him in Books I and II. His name is written variously in the copies: *Speraindeus* and *Sperandeus*.

### In Chapter II

**(1) “At last Reccafredus.”** Since Saint Eulogius often mentions this calamity of his and his being thrown into prison, it is strange that he never mentions Reccafredus, nor clearly explains what this disturbance was. From what follows, and from Eulogius’ statements, we may conjecture that Reccafredus was a metropolitan bishop, through whose agency King ʿAbd al-Raḥmān wished to restrain the Christians. Either driven by perverse zeal or compelled by unfaithful fear, he grievously afflicted the Church of Cordoba and others: he threw into chains the bishop of Cordoba, whose name is nowhere disclosed, and other ministers of the churches. Yet the sources do not say why they were later released, and we cannot infer it from elsewhere.

**Source note:** Reccafredus is now known not only to have been metropolitan of all Baetica in Hispania from about 850 to 862, but also earlier to have governed the Church of Cordoba, over which he presided in 839. On the ninth day before the Kalends of March that year, a council was assembled there against certain Acephalous heretics; see the beginning of volume XV of the *Hispania Sacra*, and volume IX, treatise 29, chapter 7, no. 29 and following. The unnamed bishop of Cordoba was Saul, who governed before 850 until 861; see *Hispania Sacra* X, chapter 8, treatise 23.

**(2) “There exists a letter concerning this.”** That letter still exists. Everything is described there at greater length. Likewise, the other letter which Alvarus immediately mentions also survives. Morales edited both letters; the present editors state that they will publish them again.

**(3) “There he wrote in metrical feet.”** Saint Eulogius implies that, while imprisoned, he composed hymns in those kinds of verse that were unknown to the Hispani of that time. For, as will soon appear, he had recently discovered the works of the poet Horace and, attracted by their variety of poetic forms, had undertaken to attempt similar compositions.

### In Chapter II (continued)

**(4) “For in those very days.”** Here, then, you see that Reccafredus afflicted the Church by royal command. Yet although Saint Eulogius and the other true Christians wished openly to resist him, they delayed because of a pious reason which Alvarus did not conceal. For Saint Eulogius, considering him deservedly excommunicated and estranged from the Church, resolved to abstain from sacred rites throughout that time, lest he himself be bespattered by the stain of the man with whom he seemed outwardly to agree. Yet he showed clearly enough how greatly he disagreed, since he conducted himself in this way. Nevertheless, he could not avoid Reccafredus altogether, because he would thereby harm the guarantors whom he had provided.

**(5) “The truth of this history.”** When Alvarus had written the book he mentions, in which he had set out all these matters more fully, he was content merely to allude to it here, with the result that this slight and obscure piece of information alone has reached us.

**(6) “Since guarantors had been given.”** It appears that Reccafredus had taken precautions by means of a pledge or security, so that Eulogius could not be separated from him after he had been released from his chains.

**(7) “Of blessed Epiphanius.”** This letter survives, translated into Latin by Saint Jerome and printed among his works.

### In Chapter III

**(1) “But rather on the occasion of his brothers.”** All these matters are narrated more fully in the letter which Alvarus mentions immediately afterward. The sequence of events must be carefully observed. On his return from this journey, Eulogius was thrown into prison by Reccafredus. After being brought out, he took part with other metropolitan bishops in the Council of Cordoba, although he did not at all agree with their opinion. He himself mentions this in Book II, chapter 15. The council was celebrated in 852, after 16 September.

Time therefore proceeded and continued in such a way that Reccafredus’ name would have contributed much to understanding what Eulogius relates; yet Eulogius himself never added it, through genuinely Christian modesty, as I interpret it. Consequently, all these matters must be understood from this passage.

**(2) “From there.”** One should observe with what desire and diligence the holy man pursued the discovery of ancient books. It will also become sufficiently clear how ardently literary studies flourished at Cordoba even in that rough and wholly miserable age for Christians.

**(3) “Poems saturated with Flaccus.”** He alluded to a verse of Juvenal. Horace calls them *saturae* when he says, “etc.” Morales reads *saturata*; the editors follow Schott in that reading because, with the Antwerp editors, they believe Alvarus is speaking of Horatian satires.

**(4) “Works adorned by Porphyry.”** Porphyry was a Tyrian philosopher, a pupil of Plotinus and teacher of Iamblichus. His earlier name was Malchus or Basil; afterward he was called Porphyry because of the purple clothing he always wore on account of his noble birth. He was an exceptionally fierce enemy of the Christians and was defeated by the distinguished leaders of the Church Methodius, Eusebius, and Apollinarius, who fought against him. Suidas says much about him. By Porphyry’s “adorned works,” mentioned by Alvarus, I believe those works concerning eloquence which Suidas lists are intended.

**(5) “Or the works of Aldhelm’s epigrams.”** He plainly means Aldhelm, bishop of the West Saxons, renowned in sacred letters and, in his own time, exceptionally distinguished in humane studies and poetry. He flourished under Justinian the Younger, more than two hundred years before Saint Eulogius. Abbot Trithemius drew up a catalogue of his works, among which is a book written in verse on the virginity of the saints, which I believe is chiefly meant here.

**(6) “And the metrical fables of Avienus.”** Rufus Festus Avienus, or Avienus, was a poet whom some consider a Spaniard. Among other works, he described Virgilian fables in iambic verses; many also affirm that the fables of Aesop circulating in elegiac verse are his. We may understand either of these works or both. Anyone who wishes to know more about this author and other matters should read Lilius Giraldus’ dialogue *On the Poets*.

**(7) “After the memory of Wissemirus.”** Returning from Gaul to Cordoba, Eulogius, as he himself relates in his letter to the bishop of Pamplona, spent some time at Toledo with this most holy bishop. This doubtless explains why the Mozarabes of Toledo, and especially the ministers of the holy Church, who through this association had thoroughly perceived the man’s holiness and learning, wished to have him as their bishop and elected him.

**Source note:** Although Saint Eulogius, in his letter to the bishop of Pamplona, praises this prelate as a most holy old man, a torch of the Holy Spirit, and with other remarkable commendations, and Alvarus here calls him a man of divine memory, it is nevertheless not established that he was enrolled among the saints at Toledo or elsewhere, whatever Tamayo Salazar says in the *Martyrologium Hispanum* under 31 December, along with the unreliable followers whom he cites.

The other copy has *Toletana* here, certainly through a scribal error. Toledo is a most celebrated city of Hispania, mentioned more than once by Livy and also counted by Pliny and Ptolemy among the other cities. Regarding it, as Sallust wrote of Carthage, it would be sufficient to say little, especially since the magnificence and excellence of this lofty city in our own time are known to everyone.

**(8) “At the annual return of his festival.”** Observe that the festival of Saint Eulogius and of the other Cordoban martyrs had already been instituted and celebrated each year. The translation of Saint Eulogius was likewise celebrated with solemn observance, as will appear shortly.

### In Chapter IV

**(1) “King Muḥammad.”** ʿAbd al-Raḥmān was the father of this man, as is clear from the beginning of the third book.

**(2) “The blessed Christopher, of Arab origin.”** After Saint Eulogius had briefly treated his martyrdom in Book II, Alvarus intended to describe it more fully.

**(3) “From the dregs of the Gentiles.”** Eulogius always calls the Arabs of the Muhammadan religion “Gentiles.” This too seems to arise from that fondness for Roman expressions by which consuls, fasces, and other such terms are frequently repeated.

**(4) “Dedicated to Christ.”** In the Spanish councils our religious women are called by various names: *devotae*, “devoted women”; *religiosae*, “religious women”; *Deo dicatae*, “dedicated to God”; *sacrae virgines*, “sacred virgins”; and *Christo dicatae*, “dedicated to Christ.” Saint Eulogius and Alvarus use these same names in different ways.

**(5) “Named Litiosa.”** The other copy reads *Litiosa*; here we have followed the reading that agreed with Saint Eulogius’ works.

**(6) “Or his sister Anulona.”** In addition to this sister, Saint Eulogius had another named Niola. He also had three brothers: Alvarus, Isidore, and the youngest, Joseph.

**(7) “To adorn their steps.”** This reading occurred in both copies. Nevertheless, the meaning is perfectly clear, with all its subtlety.

**(8) “To be named with reverence.”** In these two copies, and in other very ancient books written in Mozarabic Christian script that I have so far had the opportunity to see, *f* is consistently written for *v*, and *v* for *f*. Thus *referentia*, not *reverentia*, was written here; likewise always *juroyanus*, not *profanus*, and conversely. I do not know whether this has something to do with the Aeolic digamma, of which Quintilian speaks.


## Scholion

### In Chapter V

**(1) “To whom the most blessed martyr …”** Saint Eulogius portrayed and truly fulfilled, in vivid form, the example of the holy old man Eleazar. Since that example is itself exceptionally illustrious and was written with great eloquence under the dictation of the divine Spirit, it is most worthy of reading.

**(2) “He completed his martyrdom.”** The day of the month is specified, namely 11 March; it is also said to have been a Saturday, while Alvarus did not state the era or year. Nevertheless, although it could not be established from any other source, it is conclusively proved that Saint Eulogius suffered martyrdom in the year of the Lord 859, which we have placed in the title.

For in that year 11 March fell on a Saturday; it had not fallen on that day of the week during several preceding years, nor would it fall on a Saturday during several succeeding years. Nor could Eulogius have suffered outside this limited span of years. For three or four years before this he was still alive, as is clear from his own books.

Our method of calculation, when the day of the week is given, is not only correct but entirely irrefutable, being based on the canonical conversion of the solar cycle and on the observed relation of years and months. The holy Church of Christ used this method from the beginning; afterward, as most writers relate, the teaching and diligence of Abbot Dionysius arranged and established it in a clearer and more reliable form.

We explained at length in our history, when we reached the period of the Goths, how this method provides the firmest possible means of calculating and arranging historical years whenever the day of the week is mentioned. Peter Appianus in his *Caesarean Astronomy*, and Father Onuphrius Panvinius in one or two places in the *Fasti*, had earlier supplied us with the occasion for this observation. Now we see that Gerardus Mercator’s *Chronicle*, published last year, also retains an astronomical method of calculation—different from ours, to be sure—by means of recording eclipses found in historical writers.

Since it is customary to record the day of the week on which Saint Eulogius and other martyrs were killed, and since we have often demonstrated the year’s assertion and certainty from this fact, it was necessary to discuss our entire discovery somewhat more fully here.

**(3) “The service of the lunar watch.”** This signifies monthly watches, which were kept in the fortress when, at the completion of the month, new watchmen succeeded the former ones. Saint Eulogius also occasionally uses this adverbial expression, formed in the usage of those times, especially in the passage where he laments the tribute imposed on Christians every month.

**(4) “And to the projecting channel of the aqueduct.”** The body of Saint Eulogius certainly lay near the fortress, on the bank of the river, close to the tower now called the Tower of the Arches, since the watchman would not have dared to withdraw farther. And close to the fortress there was undoubtedly either a spring or an aqueduct for which he was making. Otherwise he could very quickly have descended to the river that washed the foundations of the fortress to obtain water.

He is speaking of the fortress that still remains at Cordoba. It had already been built, as is clearly established by the *Chronicle of Rasis* and by the special history of Arab affairs by Rodrigo, bishop of Toledo, which had not yet been printed. Morales notes that the history commonly circulated under Rasis's name is, according to Michael Casiri, entirely unworthy of him—a compilation from Arabic and Latin monuments and plainly spurious; see *Bibliotheca Arabico-Hispana Escurialensis* II, p. 329 and following. Rodrigo's history was subsequently published in *Hispania Illustrata* II (Frankfurt, 1603), and again at Leiden in 1625. It should also be noted that there is a great precipice from the fortress’ square down to the riverbed, so that the descent is down a slope at its side.

**(5) “In the basilica of Saint Genesius.”** This church and place will be mentioned more than once in the books of Saint Eulogius.

### In Chapter VI

**(1) “Sweet in the name Eulogius.”** He alludes to the Greek origin of the name. For *Eulogius* means “good speech” or “well-spoken.” Otherwise, Alvarus may also have spoken in this way from tenderness of affection.

**(2) “So that there may not be, you say.”** Eulogius had undoubtedly written these words in a letter to Alvarus. That letter has been lost.

**(3) “But I, my sweet Eulogius.”** He now offers this work of his to Saint Eulogius. While striving to elevate his speech, repeating and accumulating many expressions, he could not avoid affected imitation and produced something more swollen than sublime. The fertility of Cordoba’s soil evidently always produced this abundance in its minds as well.

**(4) “For I have constructed a monument more enduring than bronze.”** He merely dissolves a verse of Horace and tries to sprinkle something from a recently read work into his own. Horace’s verse is in the third book of the *Odes*:

“I have completed a monument more lasting than bronze,” etc.

**(5) “Mixing in *bisamum*.”** In one copy it is *bisamo*; in another it was written *visamo*. I have found no explanation of what either word means.

**Later source note:** Even after Du Cange's *Glossary*, what *bisamo* means here remained uncertain. Since Abbot Samson uses the same word in *Apologeticus* II.25, however, Flórez correctly explains it as a kind of exceptionally fragrant ointment (*Hispania Sacra* XI, p. 498).

**(6) “Nor will the ancient writers …”** The passage is exceedingly corrupt in both copies and has deprived us of the means of conjecturing its meaning.

**Later source note:** The later editor instead judges this passage so plain and open that he cannot cease wondering how it escaped Morales's perspicacity.

## On the Hymn and Epitaph

**(1) “Hymn for the day.”** We have preserved the titles found in the ancient manuscripts. This hymn, like the epitaphs, was, in my opinion, composed by Alvarus. It is a poem like “Illustrious joys of the merits of the saints.”

**(2) “We praise in varied song.”** The meaning is: “We customarily celebrate in songs various things that do not pertain to God’s glory. How much more rightly are songs now devoted to divine praises.”

**(3) “While the ruler was restoring the peoples.”** The next four verses were exceedingly corrupt in both copies; we have emended them as best we could by conjecture and ingenuity.

**(4) “Gypsum.”** In the ancient books it was read as follows: “When he taught gypsum, to reveal it from the fragment.” We substituted: “When he spoke of gypsum, come forth from the fragment.” Thus the verse is metrically sound, and some meaning can be extracted from it, namely this allegory: Eulogius was crying out, “Look deeply into Muḥammad’s law; it will expose and reveal itself together with its most evil shame.” Like an earthen or clay vessel that has been broken, it will show how fragile it is.

**(5) “Thus burned with the Lord’s zeal.”** He says this because Eulogius strengthened in the faith certain martyrs whose constancy was wavering and almost failing. Eulogius himself attests to this elsewhere.

**(6) “The translation of the body.”** The copy joined to Saint Eulogius’ works contained nothing about his translation, having only the epitaph. The same text appeared in another copy belonging to Michael of Azagra. Since he was first buried in this same church, as is stated in his life, I understand the present passage to mean that a solemn elevation of the body took place.

For the words “at the principal title” do not, as far as I can understand, indicate a different church but some object or feature within the same one.

## Editorial and Textual Notes

[^c0072-1]: The edition reads *liquefiat* (“may be melted”) in place of the printed *liquescat* (“may melt”).

[^c0072-2]: At “applied fire,” the manuscript reads *indicio* (“by a sign/judgment”) for the printed *indito* (“applied”).

[^c0072-3]: Textual readings in this hymn are as follows. For *Hic nunc*, another copy has *A nunc hic*. Morales and Antwerp read *dulcis* (“sweet”), while the printed text has the less satisfactory *roboet* (“may resound”). Morales and Antwerp read *licet in*. Schott follows the manuscript with *doceret* (“was teaching”), while the editions read *perdere* (“to destroy”). Morales has *praestant* (“they offer”), Schott *praestat* (“he offers”). Schott retains the manuscript's *mox* (“soon”); another reading is *optans* (“desiring”). One copy has *quaestuus*, the manuscript *quaestuve*. Another reading has *purpura* (“purple”), while the manuscript has *lactinea* (“milk-white”). Morales and Antwerp read *atque* (“and”). The four lines beginning “When he spoke of gypsum” remain a conjectural reconstruction of severely corrupt text in both copies.

[^c0072-4]: The date is correctly era 897, not 898, as printed by Morales and those who followed him, including Schott, Baronius, and Antwerp. Schott noted in the margin that *vui* should be read as *vii* in the manuscript. Because “VII” immediately followed *dies*, the Antwerp editors joined the words and read “the seventh day of his birthday,” supposing that Eulogius's festival continued through the octave. They then wrongly replaced *coto* with *loco*; here *cotus* means a day, not a place. Schott, followed by Antwerp, also proposed *piorum* (“of the pious”), without justification.

Additional readings belonging to the prose are preserved here in their source order:

- At “through worthy intercessions,” the manuscript wrongly reads *intervenientibus* for printed *interventibus*.
- In *Quocunque ergo tormento*, the manuscript likewise wrongly has *ego* for *ergo*; *termino* (“limit/end”) in place of *tormento* (“torment”) would not be an unsuitable reading.
- At “I have illuminated,” Morales and Antwerp read *lustravi* (“I have surveyed”) for printed *illustravi* (“I have illuminated”).
- At the “beacon … for all travelers,” Morales and Antwerp read *virtutibus* (“virtues”) for printed *viantibus* (“travelers”).
- For “diffused and filled throughout all ages,” Schott follows the manuscript with *tota reficiens* (“restoring all things”).
- At “shine in the world,” the manuscript and Schott read *elucescas* (“shine forth”) for the printed reading. The printed edition omits *solite* (“customarily”); Morales reads *qui* (“who”) for *quae* (“which”) and *Domini* (“of the Lord”) through a mistaken interpretation of the manuscript.
- In the opening of the hymn, the manuscript has *revehit festa* (“brings back the festivals”) where the printed text has *redeunt festa* (“the festivals return”).
- In Alvarus's prayer, Morales and Antwerp read *teneat* (“may hold”) for printed *revehat* (“may bring back”).
- In the epitaph, Morales and Antwerp read *rigidus* (“unyielding”) for printed *vigidus* (rendered “vigorous”).

From these and other copies of the Councils of Caesaraugusta, García de Loaysa, archbishop of Toledo, first published the councils after Morales's death; Cardinal Aguirre and many others followed his edition. Schott explains *patricius* as “of the senatorial rank or family” and notes that Alvarus uses it in that sense, as Eulogius does in *Memorial of the Saints* III.17.1. The editors also discuss Samson below and mention him at *Memorial* I.7. The account of Alvarus's otherwise unknown work follows Flórez, *Hispania Sacra* XI, treatise 34, chapter 2, section 63; others deny, with substantial arguments, that this second book, the *Index of Luminosus*, is missing. The linguistic note cites Quintilian, *Institutio Oratoria* I.4, and Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights* XV.8 and XIX.13.
