…[The preceding text is incomplete.] They signify that it was at some time founded by a king. This is the sense in which it is written in our councils.

**(7) *Cotum*.** This is a word used by our Spaniards, corrupted from the Latin *cautum*, as the most ancient royal diplomas and the stones on which one reads “the king made a *cotum*” and “made a *cautum*” demonstrate; the two forms are used indifferently. There are many examples of this kind.

It will be worthwhile to observe and examine the following point. Since Saint Eulogius was put to death on 11 March and translated on 1 June, why is his feast placed on 20 September in Usuard’s *Martyrology* and in the Roman *Martyrology* recently printed and enlarged? Indeed, the Breviary of Córdoba also has it on that day.

I should think that the reason was this: on that very day, namely 20 September, the death of Saint Eulogius the priest—he who was distinguished among the earliest inhabitants of the desert—had been recorded in the book entitled *Lives of the Fathers*, attributed to Saint Jerome, and in the Roman *Martyrology*.^1 Some people, ignorant of the truth but believing that this Eulogius and our Cordoban Eulogius were one and the same, assigned to our Eulogius the feast belonging to the other; and in the Roman *Martyrology* the feast of both is indeed recorded on the same day.

It must also be observed that Usuard could not have written the passions of Saint Eulogius and the other Cordoban martyrs of the same age, whom he frequently mentions in his *Martyrology*. For although he dedicated his *Martyrology* to Charles the Great,^2 and although he may have written to an emperor who was very old while he himself was young, it is scarcely credible that he survived Saint Eulogius. It remains that someone later added these native martyrs to his work; and that person certainly drew from Saint Eulogius not only the facts but sometimes his very words.

The Roman *Martyrology*, however, if it is attributed to Saint Jerome, could not have remembered Saint Eulogius and the martyrs of his generation. Everything read there concerning these saints is an addition, as is appropriate for a work open to new insertions and additions.^3 The same must be said of Bede’s *Martyrology*, who preceded Saint Eulogius by two hundred years and nevertheless inserted Lupus and the Cordoban martyrs in his *Martyrology*; the few things he records about them are plainly drawn from elsewhere. His history extends to the twentieth year after Saint Eulogius’s martyrdom.

^1 Which Roman *Martyrology* Morales has in mind escaped the Antwerp hagiographers, unless it was the one published by Maurolycus, in which both Eulogii are commemorated. Besides Usuard, Bellinus, Canisius, Ferrarius, and Galesinius inserted Eulogius on 20 September [the final digit is damaged in the supplied reading]; but Baronius, more correctly following Alvarus, judged that our Eulogius should be transferred to 11 March, whatever Solerius, the editor of Usuard, may say.

^2 Morales, like many others, is mistaken in believing that Usuard flourished under Charles the Great and dedicated his *Martyrology* to him. It has long been established, as Adrianus, Valesius, Mabillon, and, after the other Antwerp scholars, Sollerius have shown, that he lived under Charles surnamed the Bald and dedicated his work to him around the year 875, and therefore sixteen years after Eulogius’s death.

^3 The time at which these saints lived is uncertain. Bede does not mention them; rather, according to the Barberini manuscript, the material seems to have been taken from the *Supplement of Florus*, as may be seen at the beginning of volume II for March among the Bollandists. Nor is it sufficiently established that Lupus and Aurelius suffered martyrdom at Córdoba. On this matter consult Henricus Florez, volume X of the *Hispania Sacra*, treatise 33, chapter 9, number 99 and following.

^4 That is, in the year 1305, on the Nones of January; there is no need to correct, with the same Morales, *Chronicle*, book XV, chapter 10, the reading “the year 1300, on the fifth of the Ides of January.” For here no mention is made of the translation of the holy martyrs from Córdoba to Oviedo on 9 January 884, commemorated by the Church of Oviedo on that very day, but of another translation performed much later, in 1305, from the chapel of Saint Leocadia to the Holy Chamber, as it is called, within the walls of that same holy Church of Oviedo.

## The Life of Eulogius

In our own time, the body of Saint Eulogius, together with that of Leocritia, is most honorably preserved at Oviedo in the celebrated treasury of the bodies and relics of many saints, which they call the Holy Chamber.

They are kept in a very large reliquary, covered everywhere with silver and beautifully adorned with figures. On its summit these letters are read, engraved in silver:

> IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1305, ON THE NONES OF JANUARY [note 4], THE LORD FERNANDO ALVAREZ, BISHOP OF OVIEDO, TRANSLATED [LACUNA OF THREE WORDS; note 5] OF EULOGIUS AND LUCRITIA INTO THIS SILVER CHEST.

^5 Three words are missing here. Nevertheless, there can be no doubt that, where the removal of the silver produced a gap, the text was written approximately as follows: “the bodies of the holy martyrs.”

I myself, though unworthy—for I gladly recall this as a supreme benefit mercifully granted me by God Almighty—have contemplated this silver chest with the holy bodies, not so much with eyes dimmed by age as dazzled by the sanctity of the spectacle. With these wretched hands and these undeserving arms I reverently lifted it in that very year of the Lord 1572, when Philip II, the most powerful king and truly Catholic both in name and in his zeal for piety and religion, sent me on an embassy sacred and especially worthy of such a religious prince [note 6]: to visit reverently the bodies and relics of the saints throughout León, Galicia, and Asturias, and to investigate carefully and report whether their custody, worship, and veneration were worthy of their dignity.

To summarize briefly the whole of that sacred embassy, and to report the king’s most provident and grateful care and concern for his ancestors, I had also been instructed to inspect the tombs of the ancient kings of Spain and to observe whether their bodies had been buried worthily and honorably; to learn how fully and accurately memorial observances were made for them on the appointed days, both on solemn anniversaries and daily. I was further instructed to examine all public libraries carefully, draw up a catalogue of all ancient copies, and advise that they be preserved under diligent custody. But I return to the bodies of the saints.

The holy Church of Oviedo also celebrates the feast of the translation of the bodies of these two saints. In its matins lessons is written the manner in which they were brought to Oviedo:

> “King Alfonso”—which Alfonso he was they do not state [note 7]—“sent a certain envoy named Dulcidius to Muhammad, king of Córdoba.

^6 The history of this most worthy embassy, later written by Ambrosius, was published by the often-praised Henricus Florez. Madrid, 1765, folio.

^7 Morales subsequently indicates that this Alfonso was the third of that name, surnamed the Great, but he added nothing about the embassy or the envoy. From the Chronicle of Albelda, in Florez’s edition, volume XIII of the *Hispania Sacra*, we offer the following excerpts. Abū Ḥafṣ, the Saracen commander, sent by King Muhammad of Córdoba to overthrow the Christians, when he was in the territory of León, “directed many words of peace to our king Alfonso”—you are hearing the author of the chronicle himself. For this reason the king also sent an envoy named Dulcidius, a priest of the city of Toledo, with letters to the king of Córdoba. He says that he departed in the month of September, “and to this day he has not returned,” while November was passing. Thus writes the author in the month of the year 883 in which he was composing this.

Afterward Dulcidius, having obtained the bodies of the blessed martyrs, entered Oviedo with them on 9 January 884; on that day the bodies were received with solemn ceremony by the king, the bishop, and the clergy. The king, undoubtedly grateful for the excellent services of the envoy, advanced him to the see of Salamanca, which he already held on the day before the Nones of May in the year 899, when the church of Compostela was consecrated. For the rest concerning this bishop, see Florez, volume XIV of the *Hispania Sacra*, pages 281 and following. It should be known that there, as often elsewhere, he multiplied the bishops named Dulcidius because of the confused chronology of that consecration, to which he adhered from the second volume all the way to the seventeenth, from which he began to establish the day of that feast as the sixth of May, as we have said.

[Scan page 371]

## Saint Eulogius

Assisted by a certain Samuel—who testifies that he himself wrote this history of the translation—he obtained the holy bodies and finally brought them to Oviedo.

The king, together with Hermenegild, then archbishop of Oviedo, reverently placed the blessed bodies, enclosed in a cypress chest, in the stone tomb excavated beneath the altar in the chapel of Saint Leocadia. That tomb can still be seen empty. Soon afterward a miracle occurred: a paralytic was healed.

Much later, Rudericus Guterrius, archdeacon of Oviedo, suddenly became mute, with his mouth distorted. Through the intervention of these holy martyrs, whose patronage he had implored with fervent prayers, he was healed. On the occasion of this miracle it happened that the bodies were removed from the tomb, placed again in a silver chest, and elevated into the Holy Chamber, as we have related.” Thus far the lesson.

From the mention of Archbishop Hermenegild and King Muhammad we understand that the King Alfonso to whom the holy bodies were brought from Córdoba was Alfonso III, surnamed the Great.

Nor will I hesitate to append the verses sung at that feast in place of antiphons and responsories, although they are somewhat rough and unpolished, since in their poems the Spaniards of that period preserve a vivid image of the antiquity of their language:

> The worship of Eulogius grows through many ages;  
> The festivals of Leocritia likewise follow.  
> Nor does Oviedo fear that sudden death will come,  
> For he who ordered the joyful feast commanded fear to depart.

### Prayer

O God, who adorned the Church of Oviedo through your most blessed martyrs Eulogius and Lucritia, grant us, your servants, forgiveness of our sins, so that, strengthened by their patronage, we may return to you the thanks due for your benefits. Through the Lord, etc.

At Oviedo, Lucritia is everywhere written, not Leocritia. We have preferred to follow the older manuscripts.

Alvarus also wrote a book entitled *Scintillae*. We saw it in the royal monastery already mentioned, the monastery of the holy Facundus and Primitivus, in a manuscript on parchment bearing this title:

> In the name of Christ begins the book of *Scintillae* of Alvarus of Córdoba, collected from the sayings of the holy Fathers.

At the end it is stated that the manuscript was copied more than four hundred years ago. We also saw the same work, written in much older Gothic letters but mutilated and lacking both its beginning and its end, in the celebrated Cistercian monastery near Valladolid called El Espina. The church of Mondoñedo in Galicia also possesses it in its library.

The subject of this work was exceedingly useful at a time when books were scarce, nor is it now to be despised. For it contains, arranged under commonplaces concerning virtues and vices, many things found in sacred Scripture and many things said by the holy Doctors. A mutilated copy, without the author’s name, is also circulated as having been printed at Basel.

Furthermore, as the Bishop of Plasencia believed,^8 the same Alvarus wrote an excellent work entitled *Indiculus Luminosus*. It remains written in Gothic letters on parchment in Córdoba, in the library of the principal church, but without the author’s name. The author himself records only that the work was written in Córdoba in the year of the Lord 854, at which time, as will frequently appear, Alvarus was both flourishing and writing. Its style is either wholly Alvarus’s or very similar to his.

That work contains much relating to the very matters contained in these works of Saint Eulogius. For it mentions some of the martyrs whose lives and sufferings Eulogius records, so that the work also appears to be Alvarus’s. There is only one point that wholly persuades me not to believe it Alvarus’s work: namely, that Saint Eulogius is nowhere mentioned in it. Nor do I think that Alvarus could have restrained himself in such affection from mentioning Eulogius, who was writing the same things. More on this will be said again in the scholia to the first book, at the end.

^8 The illustrious bishop quite correctly believed—whatever Ambrosius may have thought otherwise, both here and in the scholia to book I, numbers 1 and 23—that Alvarus had written the *Indiculus Luminosus*. The same Florez discusses this argument very thoroughly in volume X of the *Hispania Sacra*, pages 41 and following, and he also published the *Indiculus* in that volume.

## Memorial Book of the Saints

### Letter of Saint Eulogius, Archbishop of Toledo, to Alvarus of Córdoba

**Argument.**—He sends Alvarus the work called *Memorial of the Martyrs*, records when it was begun, interrupted, and finally completed, and requests his correction and revision. Only the first book of the work is now sent; from this and from Alvarus’s reply it appears that Saint Eulogius wrote to Alvarus while he was imprisoned.

> To my dearest brother in the Lord Jesus Christ, Alvarus: Eulogius.

O my brother, while I was strengthened by domestic tranquility and my household cares were at peace, everything was proceeding more favorably for me. But when suddenly we were all thrown into turmoil by the martyrdom of blessed Isaac, and the whole city was astonished at the novelty of so great an event, everyone—both clergy and laity—began courageously to honor what had been done and to extol with the highest praise the steadfastness of so great a preacher.

But when the growing divine ardor had inflamed many and driven crowds of believers down into the forum, so that, after making a confession of the faith previously professed, they might curse the enemy of the Church, suddenly, terrified by the wrath of the raging tyrant, they all change their judgments with unheard-of fickleness: they withdraw, curse, and denounce as authors of a great crime both those who do such things and those who support them. There were very few—only those who had kept themselves apart from such sacrilege—who did not alter their first judgment concerning the reverence due to the saints.

For this reason I have undertaken to persevere in this work and, according to the measure of my strength, with the Lord’s help, to compose this modest little book in concise form, so that, by bearing witness concerning us to future generations, it might receive from them either the infamy of falsehood or the title of praise.^9 Yet we hope no less to receive from the Lord, through the intercession of him who defended justice, the reward that is due.

When the work was now almost completed, and a raging official of the governor’s court had sent me to the dreadful prisons, my whole household having been thrown into confusion by the sudden incursion of the guards, I supposed that the work, which had been arranged on various sheets and tablets, had been scattered in different places. But the Lord preserved it there; and now, amid the straits of imprisonment, with his help, I have not only been able to complete it but also to have it copied elsewhere. It has chosen to become known first to no one other than you.^10

For it dares not—or rather does not wish—to be published to others, lest its uncultivated material give adversaries an opportunity to disparage it, or its unpolished speech expose it to the ridicule of those who hate it. Therefore, dearest brother, I have first taken care to send the work itself to you, still arranged on humble parchment, as the most just judge of my learning, so that, if you approve it after refining it by fraternal judgment, it may be made public; but if you reject it, it may remain silent.

Then, once it has been made ready, let it cut through the ranks of whisperers with an unimpeded stride and armed right hand,^11 and approach its faithful followers in triumph, so that, while imbuing the Catholic flock with simple exhortation, whatever glory it has earned may be admitted to your praises, and its entire blessing may be applied to your side.

But if, wrapped in its own storms, you decide to put it to sleep in everlasting silence, let no one mock it for being mute, and let no one be able to brand it with infamy for being silent. Therefore I ask your serenity, out of the charity by which we are both inseparably joined, to revise this work called the *Memorial of the Saints* by reading it according to the freedom of your judgment; to correct it, review it, and strengthen it with your testimony, if it deserves it; and, if it does not, to reject it.

Thus you will rejoice that the memory of your name has been inscribed in the heavenly page together with those very saints of whom we speak, while for me, even in the remotest corner of paradise, their intercession will obtain a place of rest. Amen. Farewell in the Lord Jesus Christ, most serene brother.

^9 “Either the infamy of falsehood.” He speaks somewhat obscurely out of confidence in the truth. — Morales.

^10 “Although we hope to receive [the reward] through his intercession.” Here too he does not speak very clearly, although these words are nevertheless spoken with confidence in the zeal for faith and truth. — The same.

^11 *Pitacium.* Tablets; in Greek, *pittakia*. The ancients called everything on which writing was placed “tablets,” even when it was parchment or paper. — The same.

^12 “Through various [places].” Something seems to be missing: perhaps “intervals” or “locations.” — The same.

^13 “For it dares not.” In wishing to express something subtle, he could not avoid obscurity. “Although,” he says, “he is indignant that the work should be suppressed, he nevertheless dreads its appearing before the public. He both desires and fears its publication.” He seems in a few words to have wished to express what Horace, addressing his book, develops in many verses. — The same.

^14 “With an unimpeded stride.” That is, with a firm step, from which comes *labescere*, “to falter.” — The same.

[Scan page 372]

## Alvarus’s Reply to Eulogius

**Argument.**—In reply to the preceding letter, Alvarus greatly praises both the importance of the events and the gravity of the style, and urges Eulogius to publish the work. But, aiming at elevation of diction, he falls through affectedness into bad taste.

> To the most reverend Father Eulogius, Alvarus.

> You have restored, my lord, the benefits of former times; you have reopened to all the faithful the earlier, now almost obliterated Catholic splendour—or the fountain of eternal life, stopped up but flowing full from the streams that spring from Jesus’ breast. For he who has pitied the error of our age, disclosed the hidden contest of his athletes, and inspired their great teacher above all others, has also girded you as their most truthful eulogist.
>
> Clothed in heavenly, not fleeting worldly, strength, and adorned alike with divine and human eloquence, you are foremost in exhorting to martyrdom; before other soldiers you labour in the everlasting wrestling-ground in defence of the Church, wage the Lord’s wars, and rise above all. That true Spirit touched the hearts of your wisdom which, once sent to the apostles, adorned the Church with diverse gifts. He who armed the heroes of whom we speak for battle, fitted them for glory, and brought them to an enduring crown, has sharpened beyond his custom the constancy of your faith, the eloquence of your fluent tongue, and the teaching of your wisdom overflowing with divine learning; in matters pleasing to him he has imbued you with that gift by which alone he knows how to be pleased.
>
> Although your philosophical diction and the speech flowing from Tully’s spring retain, through an innate natural caution, the threefold manner of speaking, yet what has been arranged in apostolic fashion deserves greater praise. In one small volume, as it seems, you set forth the inexpressible light of heaven and display no slight beauty of human speech: you scatter the rhetorical flower of the orators and offer readers divine food. Beneath you flows Livy’s milky stream; Cato’s sweet secular tongue, Demosthenes’ fervent genius, Cicero’s once-rich eloquence, and flowering Quintilian will yield to you. All learning long celebrated in writings on vain and transient matters, carried away by the flight of a fleeting age and cultivated in a thousand kinds, compared with your most brilliant work is obsolete and defiled. For earthly brightness cannot in any respect be compared with heavenly, and immortal genius is exalted by immortal praise. What has been bestowed by a heavenly gift does not know how to end with the age.
>
> You have adorned, most holy one, the last times of our age and supplied an unfading fragrance to generations to come, so that our age may be praised from generation to generation and your name may be fragrant throughout all the ends of the earth. Divine vigour does not need human proclamation; what is praiseworthy in itself leaves no doubt what is first glorious in appearance. For what is beautiful is loved as soon as it is seen, even though seen from afar; and the fire-haired traveller of the centre, as soon as it rises, is recognized as the eye of heaven, and needs no laborious gaze, since by rising it offers itself to the sight even of those who do not see.
>
> As for your submitting to humility what you have set forth by a divine oracle, although you disavow your own words for our edification and, I think, would rather divert truth from the course of its path, overflowing in a sweet evenness: take care, nevertheless, lest, while serving humility too much, you weaken the judgment of truth; lest you set the low style—which you have often censured—over so great a subject, and not merely fail to separate the precious from the vile, but, what is more to be feared, wrap it in mire and mud. But because you command us—though we have no right—to decide whether this should be suppressed or published, patiently accept our judgment. Let this very book, radiant with heavenly splendour, shine in writing for ever, for the solid benefit of many, if it is lawful to say so.
>
> You have composed, most blessed Father, a resounding song by which the fear of death may flee, the numbness of the soul hardened by ancient ice may be warmed, and cold may be driven away; so that the warmth of life and that divine fire which Christ came to send may burn, and extinguished coals—or dead bodies—may live when the Spirit blows from the four quarters of the world, and may recover the light extinguished by Arabic deceit. Hail in virtue; hail, ever worthy of glory: you have not only performed the office of your tongue in the praises of the confessors, but through the grace of your speech you in some measure undergo the reward, namely the suffering, of a confessor; and amid savage prisons and close custody, sowing the word of the kingdom, you possess a happier victory. You are to be proclaimed through all ages: even amid punishments you do not restrain your tongue, and alone you are not silent for all. Shine, and become more resplendent in the ampler light by which you shine, for rewards are laid up, a hundredfold crown awaits you, and protect us by your intercession, by which you have always cherished us.

^15 “Livy’s milky stream.” Quintilian calls Titus Livy’s abundant and harmonious eloquence “milky,” and Jerome likewise says that he flows from a milky fountain of eloquence.

^16 “The secular tongue of Cato.” I do not see why he calls it the secular tongue of Cato, unless perhaps the name *Cato* is a scribal error, or unless *singular* should be read in the epithet.

^17 “And long ago proclaimed.” Although this author ought to have been named above all others, he left him unnamed, and it is impossible to guess whom he intends. Moreover, the conjunction was absent from the copy, and an extremely ancient Mozarabic hand had added it. It is entirely clear that Alvarus inserted the conjunction; for what follows cannot be attributed to Quintilian. — The same.

^18 “But also for the grace of speech.” This is subtle and obscure, besides the fact that I do not know how the words themselves should be disentangled. The sense is: “You not only perform the proper duty of your tongue by praising the confessors, but you also receive the reward of this praiseworthy service, as well as many other rewards. Through the martyrs whom you have praised, God bestows this office upon you, so that you almost become a martyr yourself.” — The same.

^19 *Victoriando.* A newly coined word at that time, as is also *inconvulsibiliter* shortly afterward; many such expressions occur, which require no annotation because we have already supplied a catalogue of them at the beginning of the work. — The same.

^20 “The fiery traveler of the center.” This is plainly a tragic epithet, though it is also poetic, as is the expression “the eye of heaven.” Ovid calls it “the eye of the world” in *Metamorphoses* 4. — The same.

^21 “Your words you deny.” That is: “Immerse what you say in this color, and use this as your pretext.” — The same.

## The *Memorial of the Saints*—Preface

### 1

I had indeed planned this volume, which I call the *Memorial of the Saints*, only for those monastic communities from which that first band of monks had come forward to resist the most lying prophet. But after I learned that men and women were rushing eagerly to this contest from cities, villages, small towns, and castles, and found that no one feared the governor’s tribunal, but saw all unhesitatingly choose death for the testament and laws of our God, I dedicated it to all the churches founded upon that most solid rock. Thus all might receive from their triumph an example of consolation, glory, and joy, in proportion as they had come from different places and undergone the perils of suffering as an example to the whole Church.

### 2

But I think that among them blessed Isaac the monk unquestionably holds the first place. He was the first to come down from the Tabennesian monastery to the forum, approach the judge, and address him in these words:

> “I should wish, judge,” he said, “to become a vigorous worshipper of the faith, if you would not delay in explaining to me its order and reason.”

[Scan page 373]

## The *Memorial of the Saints*—Preface

### 2

When the judge willingly began to explain it—as though to a young recruit already prepared to believe the faith, with puffed cheeks, swollen throat, and deceptive tongue uttering the crackling words of his instruction within the hollow of his palate—he declared that the founder of this sect was Muhammad, who, enlightened by the instruction of the angel Gabriel, had received from the Most High the prophetic word to transmit to the nations; that he had established a law, described paradise, and taught that the kingdom of heaven was full of banquets and sexual pleasures.

He added many other things which would take too long to set out here, following the rite according to his empty will.

At once that venerable young monk, who was thoroughly trained in Arabic letters, answered him in Arabic:

> “He has lied to you”—and may he waste away under divine curses—“who, entangled in so great a crime, attacked such armies of the damned and handed them over with himself to the abyss of hell. For, full of the demon and favoring demonic deceits, he offers a deadly cup to the sick and will pay the punishment of eternal destruction. Why, then, do you, endowed with knowledge, not withdraw from such dangers? Why, renouncing the ulcer of pestilential doctrine, do you not desire the everlasting evangelical health of the Christian faith?”

### 3

When blessed Isaac had spoken these and similar words with the utmost reverence, boldness, strength, and piercing speech, the judge is said to have been greatly disturbed by astonishment and, as though driven out of his mind, to have shed abundant tears. Seized by a certain dullness of mind, he is said scarcely to have been able to answer the monk who reproached him.

When the judge had stretched out his hand and struck the monk’s face, the monk immediately said:

> “Do you dare to strike a face made in the likeness of God? See what account you will have to render for this.”

For this reason, the learned men sitting with the judge detected and reproved him: forgetting the dignity of a censor, he had lightly taken it upon himself to strike the martyr, especially since, according to the judgment of their own laws, a person worthy of death for a crime should scarcely be wounded by anyone’s insults.

Then the judge turned to Saint Isaac and said:

> “Perhaps you are drunk with wine or seized by madness and therefore cannot easily understand what you are saying. For the judgment of our prophet, whom you rashly attack with insults, remains irrefragable: punishment must be inflicted on those who are not afraid to make such statements about him.”

The venerable Isaac answered him fearlessly:

> “I, judge, am neither drunk with wine nor afflicted by any illness. Burning with zeal for justice, of which I have found your prophet and you to be destitute, I have set the truth before you. If for this a furious death should come upon me, I shall gladly receive it and willingly undergo it; I shall not turn my neck away from its blows. For I know that the Lord said: ‘Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven’ (Matthew 5:10).”

Then the judge handed him over to prison and immediately informed the king of the case. Terrified by the outcome of so serious an accusation, the king at once issued a savage decree with still more savage intent, declaring that such a man, who had offered an insult to the author of their faith, must in every way be condemned to death.

Thus the servant of God was condemned to death and struck on the head. Then he was raised upon a stake, hung head downward, and placed beyond the river as a spectacle for the city on the third day before the Nones of June, Wednesday, in the Spanish era 889.^22 After several days his body was burned with those who had been killed in imitation of him, reduced to ashes, and then thrown into the river.

^23 Here he calls the censor the person whom earlier and shortly afterward he calls the judge; see also below, book III, chapter 16.

**Scholion.** We shall speak about this in Morales’s scholia below.

### 4

But it is necessary to explain by what indications or prodigies this blessed Isaac was marked out in infancy, so that from them we may believe that he was divinely chosen for the martyr’s crown. From the time he was in his mother’s womb he caused his parents terrible astonishment.

For on one day, shortly before he was born, he was seen to speak three times. Terrified by the novelty of this event, the woman almost died and could not understand the meaning of the words at all.

At another time, when he was still seven years old, a certain virgin saw in a vision a globe of light descend from heaven. While the whole crowd of those waiting looked on, he alone stretched out his arms, received the light in his hands, and drank in all its brightness through his mouth. They called him then happy and truly blessed, worthy of such a gift.

These are the prodigies and signs of his infancy, which long beforehand foretold that he would be worthy of martyrdom.

### 5

For a certain priest from the Tabennesian monastery, from which this same blessed man had gone forth to the contest, had completed the solemnities of Mass on a Sunday—namely, on the seventh day before the Ides of June, which fell on the fifth day after his martyrdom. As he was lying on a little bed among the brothers, he began to fall briefly asleep.

Suddenly, in a dream, he saw a boy of exceptionally beautiful appearance come from the eastern regions and stand before him, holding in his hands a tablet of marvelous beauty. Having received it from him, he began to read its writing. It was written in these words:

> “Just as our father Abraham offered Isaac his son to God as a sacrifice, so now blessed Isaac has been sacrificed before the Lord for his brothers.”

Immediately certain people came from the city and said that blessed Jeremiah had been crowned with martyrdom together with the others, through our Lord Jesus Christ, by whose example some others had also been put to death publicly under the same profession.

### 6

But long before them there was the priest Perfectus, of blessed memory. He suffered on account of the same profession as these men, although he did not fall in the same manner as they did. For that priest, forcibly dragged to his passion, completed the course of the holy contest courageously.

These men, however, came voluntarily and resisted the enemy fiercely; by a kind of violence, through the shedding of blood, [the] kingdom—

### 8. Eulogius, Archbishop of Toledo

…are absent. In what order the venerable presbyter Perfectus completed the course of his passion, my readers will more easily understand from the beginning of the second book; and thereafter he will relate the names, ages, origins, times, and sufferings of the others. I have therefore placed this preface at the head of the volume, so that, as I range through the praises and reproaches of the saints and sometimes encounter the profane author, my readers may understand more easily, make expiation through prayers, and assist by their prayers; and so that, with their favor, both they and I may render our own judgment now and before the Lord.

### BOOK ONE

#### 1.

It should always be the prudent concern of highly learned men not to make light of the interests of the Catholic Church, nor to desist from pursuing its perfection; and, if through anyone’s dullness inventions adulterating pious religion intrude, not to allow them through culpably negligent silence to increase to greater harm. It therefore pleased me, according to the measure of my slight ability, to devote myself to such matters and, though in my rustic speech, to instruct those whom the author calls *parvipendulos* (a Hispanism for the thoughtless or mockers), oppose rivals, and extol the deeds of the saints to heaven.

**Editorial note:** A Hispanism: “those whom we commonly call *poco considerados* [thoughtless] and *burladores* [mockers].” He frequently uses the same word and, in the same sense, *parvipendens*, below in the prayer at the end of Book II and in *Apologeticum*, no. 4. Schottus.

For, in proportion as the holy Church is raised upward by the merits of distinguished conduct and the stages of holy doctrine, elevated to sublimity, and enlarged everywhere by the increase of faith, so also—or even more—is she cast down by the negligence of the careless, miserably shaken by their assaults, and hurled to the depths by the slothfulness of some. Hence her increased strength is always weakened to the detriment of the faithful, and the loss is magnified for the little flock to which it pleased the Father to give the kingdom (Luke 12:32). This occurs when, at times, all things are held in sluggish silence, or when, through a more grievous final fall, they are plunged into the abyss of vice, with no one present to redeem or save them (Psalm 7:3).

The Prophet says: “You have not gone up into the breaches, nor built a wall for the house of Israel, to stand in battle on the day of the Lord” (Ezekiel 13:5). I am especially afraid of that prophecy in which the Lord rebukes the negligence of useless shepherds: “You ate the milk and clothed yourselves with the wool; but wolves attacked my sheep” (the same, 34:3, 5); and while you do not provide healthy pastures, poisonous grasses have been supplied to them by their enemies.

#### 2.

Therefore, lest I be called by the Lord a dumb dog, unable to bark (Isaiah 46:10, as printed), and so that I might escape the future judgment of the negligent, I have attempted to draw something from the very poor treasury of our knowledge and, from the dishes of others—though prepared with Catholic zeal—to satisfy the hunger of the faithful. I mean those who retain the truth of the Christian faith with sound belief, as they received it from the holy Fathers, lest, when the nourishing food of our care ceased, they should take deadly food from their enemies.

Thus, urged by the spur of divine charity and concerned for the Catholic people, whom I knew to be wavering amid the struggles of Christ’s soldiers, I have endeavored to come to meet them, though girded with the word of God. I wished not only to receive them among the martyrs, but also—after the printed fragment breaks off at *redi-*—[lacuna/uncertain continuation].

#### 3.

But I do not know toward what end my evil mind might turn, since the authority of Scripture confronts me in the Lord’s words:

> “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my justice and take up my covenant in your mouth?” (Psalm 49:16).

For this reason I had resolved to remain silent; indeed, I had judged it better to withdraw from such an undertaking, since I had thought it sacrilegious for a mouth not supported by any holiness rashly to compose accounts of the saints. I also considered that my weak intellect might succumb to the majesty of the subject. For just as a divine matter surpasses human effort, so a tongue occupied with earthly things cannot speak heavenly mysteries. Just as one who is too entangled in sins does not know how to preach freely, so the doctrine of one whose life is stained should be rejected. But will a mind that delights in such studies lose its reward before the Lord, or be deprived of the grace of eternal gifts? Whoever does what is pleasing to God, even if he does not bring it to completion, at least possesses a pious intention.

Or will it not be recompensed before the Lord that those who, armed with zeal for God, have waged open war against the public and manifest enemy, may raise us thereby into the ineffable joy of gladness? For just as I know that I myself am implicated in sins and entangled in crimes, so I am by no means distrustful of the mercy of my Redeemer. Though he excludes sinners from the office of preaching—since it is not lawful to give what is holy to dogs (Matthew 7:6)—he does not reject the beneficial intention of sinners toward that which pleases him.

In short, the works of the reprobate are to be abhorred, but the commendable intentions of sinners are not to be despised. For just as an evil deed utterly casts us down, so the Lord does not disdain a pious intention within us. Therefore my dejected mind is at once raised up, and, recalling Christ who teaches and promises, is encouraged by a certain hope of possibility. He says: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Psalm 80:11). And elsewhere:

**Editorial note:** We have restored this passage thus, since we believe it corrupt both in the edition of Ambrosius Morales and in that of Andreas Schottus. Where we place *sicut* in both clauses, Morales placed it in the first and Schottus in the second.

## [Scan page 376]

> “The Lord will give the word to those who evangelize with many powers” (Psalm 67:12).

Having obtained the fulfillment of my wishes, I believe that the same true Teacher will deign to grant us a praiseworthy word for the honorable instruction of Catholics, most worthy praise of the saints, and most effective overthrow of their adversaries—the one who enabled an irrational animal to speak in the manner of human beings (Numbers 13:28 and following, as printed).

And just as I confess myself unworthy of so great a work, so I trust that, through his perfection, I shall not only be freed from guilt but also drawn away from punishment, and that, through his intervention with the Lord, I may find a more excellent grace:

> “This work, perhaps, will one day rescue me from the fire.”

#### 4.

Since, then, I am about to say something concerning the memories of the martyrs, let the beginning of our speech be directed toward you, O holy brothers of ours and blessed sisters in Christ, from whose communities a sacrifice has been offered to the most holy God. I shall not fear the shame of uncultivated speech, nor strive after the beauty and charm of liberal learning, since I have not received instruction from the teaching of any master. Especially in matters of this kind, I know that simple truth must be observed rather than the swollen pomp of the thundering Muses.

I shall also speak to you, O assembly of the universal holy Church, so that, embracing with the peaceful arms of your minds the word of truth that is proclaimed by our mouth, you may in no way wish to exclude from our preaching the instruction which, on the authority of the Apostle, is freely offered for the instruction of all. For it kindles hearers of one faith, distinguished by varied talent, with the diverse utterance of its precepts; and there it soothes the sharper virtue of patience in spirit where it has armed the gentle with the living command of the one who orders.

To one it says:

> “Reprove, entreat, rebuke, with all patience and doctrine” (2 Timothy 4:2);

but to another it gives this command:

> “Reprove with all authority. Let no one despise you” (Titus 2:15).

Therefore:

> “Be ready always to give an answer to everyone who asks you for a reason concerning the hope that is in you” (1 Peter 3:15),

lest—God forbid—you reject the doctrines of sound teaching with dull hearing and be judged subject to that sentence of apostolic condemnation which says:

> “For there will be a time when they will not endure sound doctrine, but, according to their own desires, they will heap up teachers for themselves, having itching ears; and they will indeed turn their hearing away from the truth, but they will turn to fables” (2 Timothy 4:3–4).

For just as the duty of preaching is imposed upon us, so the necessity of hearing is imposed upon you. Nor, because we live disorderly lives and are cast down by shameful conduct, should the teaching of God’s word be rejected: for we often know that, in a great household, servants with deplorable lives nevertheless serve the household of the master without ambiguity, and through their ministry the needs of the household are sometimes attended to.

Water is brought to worldly emperors through leaden channels; and among the sacred vessels of the Lord, fashioned from gold and silver and adorned with the ornaments of precious stones, earthen vessels too are not to be rejected.

For the sinner is often compelled by the Spirit of God to say daily into the ears of the people:

> “Thus says the Lord: Cry aloud; rebuke my people concerning their transgressions against God’s commandments; speak of the severity of judgment, which is owed to the excesses of sins; admonish them concerning the return of pardon and the hope of deserving mercy.”

Yet that same man neither sets a limit to his own crimes nor fears the terror of the future judgment, and by his conduct himself attacks what he preaches to others. Nevertheless, some who attend to his word abstain from unlawful things and cling to what is more perfect.

Of such men it is said in the Gospel:

> “Observe and do everything they tell you; but do not act according to their works, for they say and do not do. They bind heavy and unbearable burdens and lay them on people’s shoulders, but they themselves do not wish to move them with their finger” (Matthew 23:3–4).

Accordingly, when the Church possesses a ruler of life who is cast down by his morals, she should not consider his preaching contemptible, even though he himself attacks it by his evil deeds. The duty of the common people, therefore, is to attend to the preacher and hear him who speaks, to carry out the teacher’s preaching in their deeds, and not to pass judgment upon the merits of their superiors, whom the Lord has reserved for his own examination and judgment. He says:

> “For prophet and priest are polluted, and in my house I have found their wickedness, says the Lord. Therefore their way shall be to them like a slippery path in darkness; they shall be driven on and fall upon it. I will bring evils upon them in the year of their visitation” (Jeremiah 23:11–12).

And again:

> “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord” (Deuteronomy 32:35).

Although the authority that I have discussed at such length may seek the defense of my merit and show by what means I cannot evade the just law, it nevertheless strives more earnestly to kindle the simple congregation of religious people, so that they may not reject the holy of holies, even when it is brought forth by an unworthy mouth.

**Editorial note:** “Without doubt,” or “certainly.” Schottus.

#### 5.

In the struggles of these confessors, therefore, we should rejoice with spirits all the more eager, and with such freedom of heart and voice should we celebrate the glorious completion of their victorious course, in proportion as the divine voice offers them the true consolation of salvation through a most generous promise, saying:

> “He who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10:22).

For we have learned that the reward is owed not to those who begin but to those who persevere. So greatly did that original renunciation of worldly things and contempt for the world burn within them, urged on by their foremost desires and more ardent zeal, that they longed to behold God swiftly and to enjoy the companionship of the blessed. They even eagerly desired the end of their fleeting life, judging it better to endure for the space of a single moment the sentence of men—which would carry them to heaven without any intervening delay—than to suffer, through varied and prolonged trials of time, the grievous harassment of demons.

The Lord, moreover, instructing his disciple in the duty of preaching the truth, commands us with fearless courage to be content, saying:

> “Go throughout the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Matthew 23; Mark 16, as printed).

And again:

> “Do not fear those who kill the body, because they have nothing more that they can do; but rather fear him who can destroy both body and soul and cast them into Gehenna” (Matthew 10:28).

> “You are the light of the world. A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden; nor do they light a lamp and place it under a bushel” (Matthew 5:14–15).

> “What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops” (Matthew 10:27).

What you have learned in mystery, explain more openly; what you have been taught in secret, speak publicly; what I have instructed you in a small and hidden place, proclaim boldly in all cities and throughout the whole world.

He teaches confidence in preaching, so that the apostles may not hide through fear and become like lamps beneath a bushel. Those who have received from God the freedom to speak the word among the peoples should in no way withdraw from preaching the truth, even when dangers threaten, so that they may appear not as lamps beneath a bushel but as lamps set upon a candlestick.

#### 6.

Although the fearful have been granted the ability to avoid the fury of persecution, this must not be observed everywhere by the perfect, who, already marked out and enrolled by the foreknowledge of the Redeemer’s power, have been chosen, as it were, from immense legions for the exercise of God’s battles.

If a cruel death should confront them for the sake of truth, they must not care about the loss of their limbs, when without doubt the consolation of eternal life for their souls is acquired. The Lord says:

> “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me. For whoever loses his soul for my sake will find it unto eternal life” (Matthew 16:24–25).

Thus the holy men, receiving the evangelical truth with peaceful ears, strive with all their strength to fulfill it, believing that the virtue of this proclamation consists solely in the way of holy confession. Immediately leaving the cities and the things that cling to worldly desires, burning with an eager desire to seize the kingdom of God, they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, afflicted, and tormented—men of whom the world was not worthy—in deserts, mountains, caves, and caverns of the earth (Hebrews 11:37–38), awaiting the Lord, who would save them from faint-heartedness and storm (Psalm 54:9).

But counting these things as nothing, indeed daily engaging in doubtful combat against the enemy of spiritual wickedness, they are kindled by God’s command toward the sudden mortification of temporal life. According to the Apostle, they desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ (Philippians 1:23), seeking a shortcut by which, freed from this body of death, they might quickly reach the heavenly homeland and seize the kingdom of God by holy violence.

Thus armed with the breastplate of righteousness, they leap into the forum, preaching the Gospel of God to the rulers and nations of the world.

**Editorial note:** The author’s wording is almost the same as that of the *Indiculi Luminosi*: “Let the weak and infirm rest; let the strong, girded with courage and honorable purpose, fight. If you are weak, feeble, empty, timid, rest. … If you are capable, strong, bold, steadfast, … hurl your weapons against these enemies vigorously, and not like a coward against your own.” Volume XI of *Hispania Sacra*, pp. 223, 238.

### Eulogius

Raised by contemplation of mind above the mountain that is Christ, the blessed confessors learned from the Psalmist’s oracle that the justice of the Lord must be proclaimed in the great Church (Psalm 39:10). Therefore, with perfect hatred, they rise against the adversaries attacking the Church. They rebuke the impious for the false doctrine of the wicked prophet, full of magic arts, sacrileges, and the vanities of the world. They also detest him and attack the author of such great perversity with curses, condemning with perpetual anathema the same group that serves such practices.

Thus they raise the standard against the public enemy, the manifest adversary of truth, undauntedly—as though before the gates of the governor’s palace, and at the very entrance to the court—bearing witness against the leader of perdition, confusion, and disgrace. They do not fear that they might suffer punishment and torture for the same truth, or through what dangers of this life they might meet their end. An immense longing to depart to heaven was driving them, as they hastened to see the face of him whom they had served.

The impious crowd is stirred by zeal for vengeance, and punishment swiftly arises against those who criticize its sect. They do not understand that the confessors, in order to receive this premature death, freely resisted the enemy of justice and adversary of the Church of God with unrestrained voices. They spoke of the testimonies of the Lord in the presence of kings (Psalm 118:46), fearing nothing, because they regarded their death as nothing other than eternal life. They willingly desired the destruction of the flesh, offering their souls as a voluntary sacrifice to God.

To them the prophetic voice rightly sings:

> “You who freely offered your souls to danger in Israel, bless the Lord” (Judges 5:2).

For this reason they seem to me to be true imitators of the Apostle Paul, who says:

> “If anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1:9).

Instructed by the utterances of this testimony, they rush against the angel of Satan and the forerunner of Antichrist, openly confessing the holy things which now the whole Church of Spain also proclaims, though clandestinely, as one oppressed.

**Editorial note:** Schottus reads *numerosis* (“numerous”) in place of *omnis* (“whole”).

#### 7.

For the author of the same perverse doctrine, the destructive overthrower of many souls, alone among the founders of heresies after the Lord’s Ascension, established a sect of a new superstition at the devil’s prompting and separated himself far from the unity of the Catholic Church.

Rejecting the prophecies of the prophets, defaming the teachings of the apostles, trampling upon the truth of the holy Gospel, and abolishing the doctrines of pious teachers, he introduced through his sect something more ridiculous than an account of necessary matters. He taught that Christ was the Word of God and indeed a great prophet, but not supported by any power of divinity; that he was like other human beings, though not equal to God the Father.

He also proposed feasts in paradise and pleasures of the flesh. When the most eloquent man, a great light of the Church in our times, the abbot Speraindeus, took up the style of this wicked teaching against him and attempted in a single little work to refute some of its ravings, he introduced, in the sixth chapter of that work, an objection as though spoken by its followers and then set forth his own answer. He argued as follows:

> “In the age to come,” they say, “we shall all be carried rejoicing into paradise. There God will grant us beautiful women, exceedingly lovely beyond human nature, and prepared for our pleasure.”

**Response:** Then your people will by no means possess a state of blessedness in paradise, if both sexes devote themselves to the practice of lust. That will not be paradise but a brothel, and a most obscene place. When the Pharisees asked the Lord which woman would be the wife in the resurrection of the woman who had married seven brothers according to the law of Moses in order to raise up the offspring of her nearest relative, he answered:

> “You are mistaken, not knowing the Scriptures or the power of God” (Matthew 22:29).

> “The children of this age marry and are given in marriage; but in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but will be like the angels of God in heaven” (Luke 20:34–35).

I shall say nothing of that sacrilege—an atrocious deed that must be rejected by the entire hearing of Catholics—which an impure dog dared to utter concerning the most blessed Virgin, the Queen of the world, the holy and venerable mother of our Lord and Savior, Mary. He even declared—and I speak with due reverence for so great a Virgin—that her virginity would be violated by him in the world to come.

O head empty of brains, with its inner parts occupied by Satan’s “privilege”! O vessel of perdition and dwelling-place of unclean spirits! O tongue that ought immediately to be cut off with a sharp sword! O organ of demons and harmony of the devil! What madness or insanity compelled you to defile yourself with such blasphemies? Who deprived you, O sewer of filth, snare of perdition, whirlpool of iniquity, and cesspool of every vice, of human understanding, so that it was not enough for you to bring destruction upon so many nations, to which you recommended your magical teaching, and to serve with all your strength the obscenities of lust both now and in the future, but you also dared to commit a crime against the Creator?

You, impious and presumptuous man, assert that the heavenly dwelling and undefiled, unpolluted, pure, holy, and clean receptacle of the Holy Spirit is to be contaminated in the future age by the uncleanness of your sacrileges.

She who, by a supreme nod, received the Word of the Godhead in her womb and clothed the Creator in her flesh, and, with her modesty unharmed, brought forth the Word himself, to redeem by his death the fallen creature. Entirely untouched by, and unacquainted with, a man, she was alarmed by the angelic greeting; and although she knew that no woman could conceive without a man, nevertheless, trusting in the heavenly divinity and knowing, through God’s revelation, that she had been chosen for so unprecedented a conception, she consented and said:

> “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke 1:38).

Of her glorious birth-giving the Lord once deigned to prophesy through Ezekiel, saying:

> “I turned toward the way of the gate of the sanctuary that looked toward the east, and it was closed. And the Lord said to me: This gate that you see closed shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it, because the Lord God of Israel has entered through it, and it shall remain closed” (Ezekiel 44:1–2).

**Editorial note:** This man, whom Alvarus mentions at the beginning of the *Life of Saint Eulogius*, and whom Eulogius here and in the *Life of the holy virgins Flora and Maria* both call their teacher, was their instructor. Of his work against Muhammad we possess nothing more than this fragment translated by Eulogius. He also wrote the acts of the martyrs Adulphus and John of Seville, which Eulogius likewise praises in the aforementioned *Life*; but these have entirely perished. He composed another doctrinal work against certain heretics who undermined the mysteries of the Trinity and the Incarnation; this work, having remained hidden until now, will be brought to light in volume CXV of the *Patrologia*.

**Editorial note:** Schottus takes *privilegium* here in the sense of “authority” or “power.” But, considering that Eulogius, Speraindeus, and other medieval writers use this word not for every kind of authority but for tyrannical power, as can be seen in *Memorialis*, Book II, chapter 1, and in our *Collection*, p. 11, we have no doubt that *privilegium Satanae* in this passage means Satan’s tyranny.

#### 8.

Finally, the same wicked man, at the prompting of the evil spirit by whom he was possessed, fashioned himself into the angel of light, Gabriel, and built many other temples in which his most evil doctrine might be worshiped. Several of our philosophers, armed with zeal for God, set forth the madness of this error, the ravings of its preaching, and the impious commands of its novelty in commentaries and books, and struck against him with the battering rams of justice.

But the blessed confessors, unable to bear his filth lightly, attacked him and his sect more powerfully in open contests of argument. For they knew that, because of the very truth that they proclaimed concerning that blind leader, they would immediately fall beneath the avenging sword.

#### 9.

Although the holy presbyter Perfectus first provided everyone with an example of hatred for the enemy of detestable faith and, by the strength of his confession, excluded fear of dying for the truth from many—concerning him we promise, with God’s favor, to speak more fully in the second book—the praiseworthy constancy of that unconquered John must not be undervalued. He endured savage and terrible blows with a courageous spirit and encouraged many to martyrdom by his example.

The enemies of the living God brought false testimony against him before the judge and laid this charge against him:

> “Judge, we know that this man is always intent upon mocking our teacher and attacking him irreverently with insulting words. Thus, whenever he wishes to conduct his commercial business in the markets, this most subtle mocker cannot attract buyers unless he sets forth our sacrament in contemptuous words. We are witnesses of this, and in truth confess that he deserves death.”

But because their accusation was supported by insufficient testimony, and because their testimony could not inflict death upon him, the servant of God was condemned to harsher scourging and, torn by cruel beating, was compelled to deny Christ. He not only confessed that he was not guilty of such charges but also loudly declared that he would never, even unto death, abandon the religion of the Crucified One.

The judge, provoked to violent fury by his steadfastness, handed him over to be tormented with five hundred lashes and more, ordering the beating to continue until he fell lifeless among the hands of his executioners. Then, scarcely alive and barely breathing, he had him placed backward upon a donkey and led throughout the whole city and marketplace, preceded by the voice of a sacrilegious herald proclaiming:

> “This is what the reviler of our prophet and the mocker of our worship deserves to suffer.”

After they had carried out such things in vengeance for their teacher, they finally assigned him to prison, weighed down by a very heavy iron burden. We found him still chained there, while the wounds on his back were still fresh, and admitted him to our fellowship during the same period in which we had been confined.

For the most blessed presbyter Perfectus, whom we mentioned above, and whom John succeeded in bonds and beatings, had been violently dragged to his passion. After he entered the prison, however, he was divinely enlightened and armed for battle. Turning necessity into willingness, and considering that violence, in a certain heavenly perspective, as the means by which he might be deemed worthy of martyrdom, he was wholly lifted toward heavenly things, estranged from the present, and awaited the rewards of the future. Free from every worldly affection, he was prepared, as a future martyr, for the things promised to those who love God.

Thus, dead to the world and living for God, he later freely confessed before the judge what at first he had denied saying. He preferred to die for the truth, using the opportunity to proclaim God’s justice to the Gentiles and condemn the adversary’s faith, rather than deny the truth and deprive himself of so great a reward.

## [Scan page 379]

#### 10.

The course of these two men toward their passion—one voluntary and the other forced—compelled the others to come forward of their own accord in a single and common agreement to fight. Those who knew that men dragged to martyrdom by force had received the crown of the eternal kingdom were not uncertain of the crown themselves.

Therefore, following the order arranged in the preface to this volume, the entire crowd of saints runs to the arena of combat and rejects the adversary of God and enemy of justice. All praise Christ with one voice. Sustained by his great power, they shone in the struggle, fearing no earthly punishment at all, for, enlightened by the grace of the supreme Redeemer, they knew that eternal torment was the greater thing to fear.

I explained this at the beginning of the book so that later generations would not lack knowledge of what brought death upon our confessors, and of the hatred for which the Gentiles were aroused to a most grievous rage, turning the whole fury of their savagery toward the destruction of those who professed such things. From this prudent readers will also easily perceive how deservedly this little work labors in the praises of the blessed, setting up barriers against those who, through hesitation and doubt, refuse to allow them the place of martyrs.

#### 11.

As for the bodies of those same saints who were killed in the first encounter, the Gentiles fastened them to torture-racks with their feet turned backward and, on the sixth day after their killing—that is, on the day before the Ides of June—by an unexpected crime of cruelty consigned them, already wholly dissolved by putrefaction, to savage fires. Moreover, lest they should provide any benefit of their virtues to Christians, the disfigured ashes that could be gathered from the furnace were cast into the final abyss of a threatening riverbed.

#### 12.

The whole body of the pagans also persisted in mocking and rebuking the worship of piety, because, in avenging its own people, it had given the adversaries no cause for reproach.

They rejoiced that, in vengeance for their teacher, it had cast down the bodies of so many despised men, with no new prodigy intervening that might inspire horror in the wicked. They said:

> “If God truly exists, in whose name you submit yourselves to such calamity, and if you believe this to be true martyrdom—or if our prophet has not been endowed with any truth of prophecy [the printed text marks this passage]—he was, as he himself taught, permitted, under the instruction of the angel Gabriel, to preach God’s word to the nations and to the whole world; and the law upon which his worshippers meditate was promulgated by the teaching of that same angel.
>
> “While the unformed first-created man, Adam, still inhabited paradise, he is said to have contemplated that name, inscribed in heaven and set in a sphere of glittering brightness, and to have asked the Creator what was that light shining more brightly than the rest in its center and illuminating the Lord. The Creator answered: ‘This is the true prophet who will be in the world, who, arising from your seed, will be called Makomad by the very name at whose radiance you marvel; and by his merits you, though created, have deserved to subsist.’
>
> “Why, then, do you not strike his followers with terror by some prodigies, or shine with signs before any assembled crowd? For, while you are appointed to an unforeseen death on account of some superfluous assertion, you excel in no miraculous power capable of overturning the sentence pronounced by us for your destruction; you give no help at all to your own party and inflict no loss upon our community.”

#### 13.

For this very reason many among our own people, treating the matter lightly, thought that it was not truly martyrdom, because it displayed no miracle either to confound unbelievers or to strengthen the faithful.

They did not know that, at the end of the age, as Saint Gregory relates in Book XXXIV of the *Moralia* (no. 7), signs of power would be absent from the Church:

> “By a terrible order of hidden disposition, before Leviathan appears in that condemned man whom he will assume, signs of power will be withdrawn from the holy Church. Prophecy will be concealed, the grace of healings will be taken away, the virtue of prolonged abstinence will be diminished, the words of doctrine will fall silent, and the marvels of miracles will disappear.”

This heavenly dispensation does not utterly withdraw these things, but they do not occur in the same manner as in former times…

[scan page 380]

## Memorial of the Saints — Book I

### 13

This is openly and in many ways demonstrated. Yet this is brought about by a wondrous dispensation, so that through one and the same divine act both piety and justice may be fulfilled. For when the holy Church appears somewhat humbled by the withdrawal of the gifts of miraculous signs, the reward of the good increases—those who venerate her for the hope of heavenly things and not because of present signs—and the disposition of the wicked against her is more quickly revealed: they neglect to follow the invisible things she promises because they are not held by visible signs.”

For signs of miraculous powers are neither given to everyone nor to be performed indiscriminately at every time. Indeed, even those who have received this gift from God cannot bestow it unless they have been proved in hope and faith, as the Evangelist relates: “And he could do no mighty work among them because of their unbelief” (Matt. 13:58). Truth itself also says: “There were many lepers in Israel in the time of Elisha the prophet; and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian” (Luke 4:27). For when the faith of those who ask ceases, the generosity of those who give is weakened. Although the Lord very often comes as a comforter to the ardent prayers of many, saying, “Go in peace; your faith has saved you,” nevertheless, when faith is lacking, power accomplishes nothing. At times, when the faith of the sick demands it, even wicked and corrupt-minded men confer such benefits.

Thus we read in the Gospel of those who will one day stand before the Lord’s doors asking: “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name? And in your name cast out demons? And in your name perform many mighty works?” (Matt. 7:22–23). To them the Lord will certainly say: “I do not know you; depart from me, workers of iniquity” (ibid.). And again: “False Christs and false prophets will arise and give great signs and wonders, so that, if possible, they will lead astray even the elect” (Matt. 24:24). And in Exodus: “The magicians also did this by their enchantments, just as Moses did” (Exod. 7 and 8).

### 14

In former times the Lord therefore granted signs of miracles through his servants to the world at a suitable moment, because, in his foreknowledge, he knew that those who awaited them would nevertheless profit from them, and he knew that the workers of miracles would not labor in vain. At least, those who rejected the saving precepts of the sacred Law might yield to the novelty of prodigies.

In those times it was entirely appropriate for God’s martyrs to shine with miraculous signs, since they endeavored to make Christianity, which had been widely diffused in an uncultivated state, firm with deep roots in the hearts of believing peoples—sometimes by instruction in words, sometimes by exhortation from the Scriptures, sometimes by the display of signs, and sometimes even by the illustrious examples of their sufferings.

For since the exercise of signs is not appropriate at every time, as was stated above, and since not everyone is worthy of contemplating heavenly powers, this can easily be understood by comparison with what was done by the Apostles. When they wished to preach the good news to the Asians, they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit (Acts 16:6–7). He who had earlier commanded that the Gospel be proclaimed to every creature (Mark 16:15), knowing by the foreknowledge of his divinity that in Asia there was no one worthy to receive evangelical truth, withheld the disciples from bringing them salvation. For they were about to reject the word of life in an arrogant spirit, and would not listen because they despised it.

### 15

Finally, when God’s providence works miracles either for the faith of believers or for the future belief of those standing by, we ought not so much to marvel at the miracles themselves as to examine with provident judgment whether the performers of those signs excel in moral integrity after their vices have been expelled; whether, dead to the world, they live for God; whether, because of that true charity which surpasses all the gifts of grace, they regard all worldly attachments as nothing; whether they refer the virtue they have received not to their own glory but to the benefit of the giver; whether, having listened attentively with the ears of their hearts to the admonition of the true teacher, they rejoice not because demons are subject to them (Luke 10:17–20), but because their names are written in heaven.

Therefore this enumeration of virtues in the authors of those prodigies is more worthy of admiration than the signs themselves. It is a greater proof of the way to be sought toward the kingdom, rather than something that publicly displays us as conspicuous and remarkable. For holiness, the fear of the Lord, and devotion to the heavenly kingdom proceed only from those who are suitable and perfect. But both saints and reprobates perform signs and wonders. These sometimes bring nothing more than a vain reputation among human beings. Hence it happens that one who is known to people, unless he is just, reaches eternal punishments and is condemned. But the person who, illumined by heavenly grace, has lived under the knowledge of his Creator will be counted among the future joys of the saints, even if he is unknown to mortals.

### 16

Nor, by pursuing this argument, do we altogether reject the marks of miracles, which have been bestowed on certain persons as a heavenly gift and ordered by God’s dispensation for an appropriate time. Rather, we confront the barking of rabid dogs who attempt to destroy the purpose of our martyrs while hoping to rebuke them on account of their miracles.

We have shown, on the authority of the divine books and the sayings of the holy Fathers, what ought generally to be followed. We do not—God forbid—eradicate altogether the gifts of heavenly graces.

### 17

The root, therefore, and foundation of every virtue, and the sign of victory, is faith. Through it the righteous live (Hab. 2:4); through it all the saints conquered kingdoms, practiced righteousness, obtained the promises, stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, recovered strength from weakness, and became mighty in war (Heb. 11:33–34).

Truly following in their footsteps, these saints, by their fearless confession, professing God and the Lord Jesus Christ before the council of rulers, also reject and curse every prophecy that evangelical authority does not accept, detesting it as the prophecy of thieves and robbers.

For this reason the raging crowd of pagans, boiling with unheard-of savagery, sends them all to heaven under the blow of the sword: priests, deacons, confessors, and blessed virgins.

[Editorial note: “An interpretation may be added to Cangius’s Glossary.”]

[scan page 381]

## Saint Eulogius, Archbishop of Toledo

### 18

Nor are they content to understand the Scriptures in a sound sense. Instead, interpreting them as they please, whenever they find on the surface of the letter testimonies seemingly consonant with their madness, they neither employ them simply in the Christian manner nor investigate the force of their meaning with the more learned; rather, as heralds of some unheard-of matter and pretentious connoisseurs of novelty, they parade these same sayings through forum, streets, crowds, and marketplaces, boldly proclaiming, rehearsing, and singing them at the top of their voices.

And so that they might more easily be recognized as defenders of their party, through the subtle devices of their own intelligence they abandon the truth of Scripture and, by their own arbitrary judgment, distort the line of sound doctrine. Thus, what the prophet declares with the greatest indignation comes upon them for the destruction of their souls:

“Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness light and light darkness, who make bitter sweet and sweet bitter” (Isa. 5:20).

That is, they interpolate the clarity of the sacred Law through perverse error and, by wrongly interpreting its sweetness, turn it into the bitterness of falsehood. What is good and pious they infect with malicious interpretations, imagining that we lack the understanding of those testimonies by which the intention of the most victorious holy martyrs is diminished—namely, that we should believe ourselves to share in their sufferings because, on account of their profession, we endured their cause, their prisons, their chains, and even the loss of our property, and finally, by the grace of their intercession, escaped through God’s mercy.

### 19

Uttering these and similar things with their poisonous mouths against God’s soldiers, they corrupt the hearts of many. For the words of heretics creep like a cancer into the minds of the humble (2 Tim. 2:17), and, as a little leaven more easily corrupts a great mass of bread (1 Cor. 5:6), so the deadly assertion of error quickly drives out the children of God.

Of such people the blessed Apostle says: “For some, having missed the mark, have turned aside to empty talk, wishing to be teachers of the Law, though they understand neither what they say nor the things about which they make assertions” (1 Tim. 1:6–7). And again: “They have taught their tongue to speak lies; they have labored to act unjustly” (Jer. 9:5), not fearing to detract from the glory of the strong, who now undoubtedly raise before their King the standard of their victory.

Nor are they content to understand the Scriptures in a sound sense. Rather, interpreting them according to their own pleasure, they have found, on the surface of the words, as if in agreement with their madness, evidence for mocking the prophet and despising his worship. Soon, when their necks had been cut off, they fell. And as though they possessed some trace of human feeling, they ordered certain persons whom they had forced, under the testimony of truth, to pass beyond the threshold of this life by the avenging sword, to be left unburied before the gates of the palace; they even ordered them to be exposed to dogs, with guards placed at the same time so that no Catholic, moved by pity, might bury the bodies after they had been stripped of their flesh.

They seemed to believe that the punishment of the persecutor could harm the souls of those whose spirits were enjoying the rest of paradise—or that the punishments inflicted on their bodies could in any way injure souls reigning in heaven. Yet these men who truly understood knew that, just as an impious burial would be of no benefit, so a burial prepared with increased solemnity and honor could in no way harm the blessed saints by its poverty or lack of ceremony.

It was also possible to make a fitting jest about these poets:

> “He is covered by the sky who has no tomb.”

### 18

There are, however, many of the faithful—and, alas, even priests—who do not fear to rashly deprive these confessors of their glory. They command that they not be admitted to the catalogue of the saints, considering it unusual and profane that such people should be martyrs. They assert that they were killed by their own will, since no violence compelled them to offer themselves to danger, but that, out of pride—which, as they say, is the beginning of every sin (Ecclus. 10:15)—they voluntarily exposed themselves to death and became murderers of their own souls.

They believe that these martyrs ought also to be accused by the evangelical precepts that say:

“Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:44–45).

And again:

“Do not extort anything from anyone, and do not falsely accuse anyone” (Luke 3:14).

And:

“When the Lord was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but entrusted himself to the one who judges justly” (1 Pet. 2:23).

They also bring forward the Apostle’s statement:

“Nor will the revilers possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:10).

### 20

We believe that we now share more evidently in the sufferings of these saints, since, on account of their confession, we too have endured prisons, chains, and even loss of property, and finally, through their intercession and by God’s propitious grace, have escaped.

The saints themselves, who undertook this slaughter of the body for the sake of truth, did not in any respect turn aside from the custody of the commandments mentioned above. Because of God they loved their enemies, and, being deeply concerned for their salvation lest they remain longer in the labyrinth of impiety, they did not cease to rebuke them.
