They did good to those who hated Christ and seemed better to instruct their madness through the shedding of blood than through words of doctrine, so that, abandoning the vanity of superstition, they might strive not only to believe in Christ but also to fight for him even unto death.

Without doubt, they also obtained from the Lord, through prayers and supplications, the salvation of those who often and continually slander the members of the Church.

Thus, educated in the example of the true teacher, when they were led to suffering they did not revile in return when reviled, nor murmur when scourged, and they observed silence when threatened. They reproached only this: that the man insulted God and attacked his awesome majesty. They reproached the sacrilegious prophecy of that most vain and lost little man, who, armed with a demonic spirit, was not afraid to insert himself among the prophets and to add himself to the holy preachers as though he were a divine evangelist, though he was a Lucanian.

[Note: The poem is cited by Isidore without the author’s name.]

[Note: This passage occurs in Lucan, Book 7. Schott.]

For, when evangelical truth already prevailed through almost the whole world, the light of the Christian faith was not absent from the knowledge of the nations—“for its sound has gone out through all the earth” (Ps. 18:5). The house of David was now open, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem were dwelling amid streams of purification, for the washing away of sinners and the menstruous woman (Zech. 13:1). This was especially so in the East, where the mystery of Christ’s incarnation had in a certain special way been accomplished, and where also this most wicked and perverse prophet had arisen and been nourished.

I do not know by what madness he was seized that he did not fear to plunge himself into so great a snare of destruction when lights had already begun to shine throughout the world, nor did he shrink from becoming the irreverent murderer of so many souls, since it is written: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11).

The prophet Zechariah once spoke about him, saying:

“On that day, says the Lord of hosts, I will destroy the names of the idols from the land, and they shall no longer be remembered. I will also remove the false prophets and the unclean spirit from the land. And if anyone prophesies thereafter, his father and mother who begot him will say to him, ‘You shall not live, because you have spoken lies in the name of the Lord.’ And his father and mother, who begot him, will pierce him through when he prophesies” (Zech. 13:2–3).

To resist this lost and most filthy prophet is the strength of a victorious crown; to overthrow the worship of such a great mocker is a fitting triumph. If our age had found him still alive, Christians would certainly not have shrunk from destroying him. How much more is it fitting today to break his poisonous doctrine, curse his sect, and detest his teaching, since it brings about the destruction of so great a multitude and has devoted them to the eternal abyss?

As I think, it would then have been better to bear the repentance of killing one wretched little man than to suffer the ruin of so many nations, since we would rightly judge that the whole flock should be protected when one diseased sheep was being torn away from its midst.

For just as it is not without guilt to curse the righteous, persecute the pious, or prepare adversity for the elect, so I believe it is a matter of great merit to overthrow the impious, oppose the enemies of the Church, prepare war against unbelievers, and cut down the adversaries of the faith with the sword of God’s word. Thus, according to the Psalmist (Ps. 138:22), we should rise up armed with perfect hatred against those who envy God, without concern for the hostility of those whose friendship is impiety.

Nor does the teaching of the Fathers permit, without guilt, those who grow numb through wicked silence toward the doctrines of heretics and do not confront the enemies of the faith, or who do not exercise the Creator’s vengeance against heretics out of zeal for him.

Arnobius the rhetorician, interpreting Psalm 139, expressed this well when he said:

> “Whoever spares the heresiarchs or preachers of falsehood, and does not slaughter them with the sword of his faith, who can doubt that what happened to Saul will happen to him? Or whoever thinks that he is showing mercy by extending it to those who remain in heresy—who can deny that he will likewise be excluded from the kingdom of God, just as Saul is shown to have been excluded from the human kingdom?”

Saul, sparing the Amalekites through empty compassion, suddenly lamented that he had been deprived of God’s blessing and the scepter of the kingdom.

And if this is promised to those who do not resist the contradictors of truth, what kind or degree of vengeance will await those who disparage the elect? For they not only refuse to overthrow the heretics but also rush against those who do overthrow them, armed with the weapons of curses.

[Note: No one is unaware that Muhammad was born in Felix Arabia. Morales.]

[Note: This Arnobius is different from the one who flourished in the time of Diocletian. Sixtus of Siena correctly observed this, and learned men today follow him, against Trithemius and Erasmus, who are supported by Laurence de la Barre. They hold that the Arnobius who commented on the Psalms is the one mentioned by Jerome in his book On Ecclesiastical Writers.]

### 21

Moreover, they say that those should not be martyrs, or be regarded as martyrs, who were not forcibly dragged to martyrdom but came voluntarily and insulted those who had done them no harm. They think that the destruction of basilicas, insults against priests, and the tribute—which we pay under compulsion and with deep grief—are no form of harm, so that it would be easier for us to choose the shortcut of death than the burdensome hardship of a most wretched life.

If it is hateful to God to curse the devil and his minister, then the Church uses exorcisms against every demonic attack in vain. Since it is forbidden to curse those within the household of the faith, and no weak person ought to scandalize a member of the Church, does it therefore follow that it is unnecessary to curse the devil’s guest and Satan’s dwelling?

Where then is what is written:

“Cursed are all who despise you, Jerusalem, and all who blaspheme you; cursed are all who hate you and all who have spoken a harsh word against you” (Tob. 13:16 and following)?

No one doubts that this was said concerning the Church.

And among all the persecutors of the faithful, who has pursued the Church more bloodily than this unspeakable man? Who has brought such calamity upon the overthrow of Catholics as this unfortunate one? For, so to speak, none of us can enter among them safely, none passes through undisturbed, and no one crosses their enclosure without being dishonored.

Whenever the necessity of some household matter has compelled us to go out in public, and domestic need has required us to rush from the corner of our hut into the marketplace, as soon as they notice upon us the marks of the sacred order, they attack us with shouts of mockery as madmen and fools. In addition to the daily insults of children, they are not satisfied merely to heap verbal abuse upon us and exaggerate shameful jests; they also persist in pelting our backs with stones.

What should I say of the insult they utter against the venerable sign? When the proper time for chanting happens to come and the sign is given to the faithful, and when the accustomed summons to prayer is made to the people, as soon as the deceived crowd, misled by false superstition, hears the ringing sound of the metal, it does not delay to turn its tongue toward every curse and obscenity.

Therefore those who shape their fellow creatures into such hatred against God’s people are not cursed without reason. We are frequently and continually slandered by them, and everywhere endure their savagery on account of our religion. So far does this go that many of them judge us unworthy even of the touch of their garments and curse themselves for approaching us, considering it a great pollution if we become involved in any of their affairs.

Yet the soldiers of God confessed the truth before them more than they uttered curses, observing the commands of the true teacher by whom he formerly instructed his disciples:

“Whoever confesses me and my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man will also confess him when he comes in the glory of his Father and of the holy angels” (Mark 8:38).

Who is so foolish as to detract from the praises of blessed men who confront the worshipers of impiety in defense of justice?

They had rightly been told:

“Behold, I send you as sheep among wolves; therefore be wise as serpents and innocent as doves” (Matt. 10:16).

I believe the meaning of this command to be that the host of the faithful, sent among the nations, was compelled to endure the savagery of wolves while possessing the innocence of sheep. And lest those devoted to sluggishness should more easily succumb to the cleverness of their enemies, they are suitably admonished by God to be supported always by appropriate caution against the adversaries of the faith, and everywhere alert and prudent against the tricks of their enemies. Otherwise, ensnared by the words of false doctrines, their minds would be corrupted immediately and they would depart from righteousness.

Moreover, Christians are admonished:

“Show yourselves to your brothers and members of the household of faith as God’s ministers, in much patience, in long-suffering, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in sincere love, in the word of truth, in the power of God; through the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left; through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute; as deceivers and yet truthful, as unknown and yet known, as dying—and behold, we live” (2 Cor. 6:4 and following).

And again:

“Be kind and compassionate toward one another, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you” (Eph. 4:32).

Thus, following the simplicity of doves, seek your neighbors’ salvation with the same concern with which you seek your own.

Of their constancy, simplicity, fortitude, discernment, and prudence, Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, writing his Ecclesiastical History, says: “Christ’s martyrs, then, were humble among their brethren, exalted among persecutors, gentle toward their own, terrible to their adversaries, subject to Christ, and steadfast against the devil.”

Arnobius also, of whom we have spoken above, says something similar in the same Psalm: “Act, then, and fight alongside those who fight; and if you have sought help from the King, show yourself resistant. The tongues which heretics sharpen like serpents fight against you; be you also a prudent serpent toward them, and show yourself a dove, simple toward your fellow citizens—that is, toward Catholics alone. But toward heretics and all who come against the truth, be more shrewd than the serpents themselves. Do not be afraid: your Lord has commanded you. Shrewdness against malice is as good as kindly simplicity toward righteousness. Kill heretics, and with your Lord’s spiritual sword slay his enemies.”

[Note: We believe that Eulogius quoted the Gospel text according to Mark, although we have not yet read any biblical version that does not have *confusus* (“confounded”), *confundetur* (“he will be confounded”), *pro confessus* (“for having confessed”), and *confitebitur* (“he will confess”), as in Saints Matthew and Luke. Nevertheless, if anyone should assert that the Gospel passage was compiled from two or three Evangelists, we will not object. See *Documentum Martyriale*, no. 14, note 3.]

[Note: We have corrected this from Arnobius, since previously *cæteris* was read.]

[Note: The words marked here are those which Morales says are found in the Toledan Codex of Eulogius.]

[Note: These words are taken from the same account of Emetherius and Celedonius, first edited by Juan Tamayo de Salazar in the *Martyrologium* under 3 March, later on the same day by the Antwerp editors, and finally by Manuel Risco, vol. 33 of *Hispania Sacra*, Appendix 2. In all these places the words “Let confession, brandished as missiles, strike the enemy everywhere, and let us seek out the hidden enemy of faith wherever he may be” appear to belong to one of the two martyrs—according to several manuscripts, to Emetherius—and the remainder to the other, namely Celedonius.]

[Note: From this passage the lacuna in the ancient version preserved by Peter Sabatier may be filled.]

### 22

Thus the blessed martyrs Emeterius and Celedonius, when they longed to surrender their souls to the Lord, encouraged one another as they stood ready for suffering with these words:

> “Let confession, brandished as missiles, strike the enemy everywhere, and let us seek out the hidden enemy of faith wherever he may be.”

Unparalleled is the greatness, admirable the courage, and worthy of praise and imitation the strength of the saints! Even if the enemy is sluggish and allows the Church of God to be persecuted, we are nevertheless commanded to break into his hiding place and stir him to battle, so that the vigorous trainer of the contest may rouse the sluggish enemy, bring him forth from hiding, and raise him up for the conflict.

And although, with his limbs drenched in blood, he falls exhausted, he will nevertheless carry to the Father’s throne a triumph captured from the enemy, while his warrior spirit receives the laurel of victory. For the excellence of the soldier is proved by this: that, without being summoned, he voluntarily offers himself to the arena of martyrdom, as Holy Scripture bears witness:

“Because you offered yourselves willingly to danger, bless the Lord” (Judg. 5:2).

If someone, zealous in charity, should faithfully confront our adversaries, take up arms, rage with swords, and strive to lay down his life, we would certainly not allow him to remain without a worthy reward; we would judge that his freedom should be enriched with a generous benefit. How much greater an honor of glory, then, should be borne by those who, in order to obtain the grace of the eternal King, strengthened by the vigor of justice, resisted their enemies even unto death and were killed by a cruel death?

### 23

The precursor and messenger of truth and of the justice of the Redeemer, John the Baptist, when he rebuked the wicked king concerning Herodias’s adultery and forbade him to violate his brother’s marriage-bed through incest, was thrown into prison because of his profession of the truth, and there was beheaded without any persecution of the faith (Mark 6:17). He did not refuse to suffer such a loss, for he undoubtedly knew, through the revelation of the divine Spirit, that to die for justice was equal to being struck down for confession of the faith.

Therefore the Lord, imparting the vital precepts of doctrine to his disciples, addressed them from the mountain:

“Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:10).

And what else is the fulfillment of all blessedness than the kingdom of heaven, which is to be acquired?

Our enemies also slander their voluntary advance toward death, although the king’s liberality had allowed them everywhere freely to practise Christianity.

But I think that this example was already set in those seven brothers whose deeds are related in the account of the blessed Julian. Because they were distinguished by the nobility of their ancestry, they openly practiced the worship of the Catholic religion by decree of the rulers. Yet when they saw the blessed Julian sweating in the contest, they immediately rushed into battle and, out of love for martyrdom, sought a voluntary death.

We also read of the Lord in the Gospels:

“He set his face firmly to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51).

The holy Jerome explains this as follows (in his *Questions to Algasia*):

> “Firmness and courage are necessary for one who hastens voluntarily toward suffering. Thus also, to Ezekiel, to whom God had said, ‘Son of man, you dwell among scorpions; do not fear,’ he says, ‘Make your face firm. And I have made your face like adamant and your forehead like iron’ (Ezek. 2–3), so that, if perhaps the hammer of the whole earth should rise against him, he might resist like the hardest anvil and crush the hammer. Concerning this it is written: ‘How the hammer of the whole earth has been broken and crushed!’ (Jer. 50:23).”

The same teacher, explaining a Gospel saying in the work mentioned above, says:

> “Confession before God is not delicate and secure: whoever believes in me must pour out his blood. For whoever loses his soul in the present will gain it in the future.”

Finally, when the prophet Agabus came to the Apostles, he took Paul’s belt, bound his own feet and hands with it, and said:

> “Thus says the Holy Spirit: The man to whom this belt belongs will be bound in Jerusalem by the Jews and handed over into the hands of the Gentiles” (Acts 21:10 and following).

When the Apostles and those who were there heard this, they pleaded with him in tears not to go up to Jerusalem. Then Paul replied:

> “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.”

And when they could not persuade him, they fell silent, saying:

> “Let the Lord’s will be done.”

[Note: *Publice*, “publicly, openly,” Schott; but less correctly.]

[scan page 384]

## Memorial of the Saints — Book I

### 24

In this way also the most blessed Felix, when he learned from a faithful report of the persecution of the Catholics that was taking place at Gerunda, a Spanish city bordering Gaul, and when he learned that the Church of God there was being cruelly harassed by pagans, immediately abandoned the studies of liberal learning that he was pursuing at Caesarea in Mauretania. He crossed the sea by a rapid voyage, went to the aforementioned town, and there, as a devoted soldier of Christ, triumphantly completed the martyrdom that his homeland lacked.

Thus Saint Sebastian, thus the most blessed Thyrsus, thus the chosen Adrian, thus Justus and Pastor, thus Eulalia, the virgin of Barcelona, thus Bishop Babylas, and many others voluntarily offered themselves and were crowned.

Therefore, as one of the wise men recalls:

> “Among the foremost dignities of the heavenly kingdoms must be placed those who came to suffering without being sought; and it is an excellent vow to leap into torments where it is no crime to have remained hidden.”

### 25

But in truth it must be acknowledged that hiding is a crime if it is an act of exceptional merit to come forward voluntarily, whenever confession of our faith demands preaching and testimony calls for witness.

For if, after hearing the word of truth, an unbeliever does not give his faith to it and instead reproaches the evangelist rather than believing, although he was guiltless before the truth was known, afterward he becomes liable to the holy preaching. He will not be able to excuse himself on the ground of ignorance when the truth has been made clear, as the Lord and teacher testifies:

> “Remember the word that I spoke to you: ‘A servant is not greater than his master.’ If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you. If they kept my word, they will keep yours also. But they will do all these things to you because of my name, because they do not know the one who sent me. If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” (John 15:20).

Our adversaries also object to the corruption of their bodies. But let them answer, I ask, what harm this does to those already crowned with a heavenly reward—as though they had sought the honor of the flesh—when they truly knew the law once imposed upon mortals, for it was said to Adam:

> “You are dust, and into dust you will return” (Gen. 3:19).

Or what harm can the body suffer when, through the tortures of tyrants to whom power was given to kill the body, it eventually comes to an end? For “all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field” (Isa. 40:6).

When Scripture says “all,” it leaves out no flesh born from human seed. And, if I may say so boldly, this includes not only patriarchs, prophets, Apostles, and martyrs.

Let those who dream such things read the Acts of the Apostles. There they will find that, according to Peter’s testimony, David—the one chosen by God and his most faithful servant, a man after God’s own heart—suffered the corruption of the grave, as the Apostle declares:

> “Men and brothers, I may boldly speak to you concerning the patriarch David: he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day; and his flesh [lacuna].”

[scan page 385]  
**S. EULOGIUS, ARCHBISHOP OF TOLEDO**

…saw corruption (Acts 2:29). [Continuation from the preceding source page.] Let us consider the patriarch Job, teeming with worms (Job 2:7–8), and Lazarus of the Gospel, ulcerated and begging before the doors of the rich man clothed in purple (Luke 16:20). Let them survey the shining deeds of the other saints, radiant with diverse victories like the stars of heaven; and let the sacrilegious man, if he dares, mock their decayed limbs, consumed by the pains of torments and punishments.

Yet this temporal corruption of bodies causes no harm whatever to the souls of the saints; while the intact substance of the flesh will be unable to benefit the wicked in the future. For why should those who truly knew that all temporal well-being perishes with the world itself be distracted by vain anxiety over the integrity of bodies? They knew that the sentence of death pronounced upon Adam, the first-formed man, applies generally to all mortals: “You are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. 3:19).

For the saints, who are not exempt from that law, know and believe that, in their own land—that is, the heavenly Jerusalem—they will receive a double reward. They do not greatly weigh the bodily loss which, in the universal resurrection of humanity, they know will be restored and reconstituted in an instant, whatever the dismemberment, place, cavern, or cave in which the scattered corpses may have perished, or whatever the most hidden recess of the other elements may have concealed them, by the authority of the law. Thus the saints, rejoicing in a double reward, will overwhelm the impious and sinners with a double confusion.

**27.** Therefore I beseech you, our holy brothers and blessed sisters in Christ, do not let yourselves be disturbed by the assertions of fools, nor, through the conjectures of ignorant people, be moved even slightly—God forbid—against the soldiers of God. For these are people who are not pierced by the ardor of pious religion; and therefore they can neither favor the truth nor defend the holy faith which they lightly and without a deep foundation of belief carry in their hearts. They show greater displeasure if someone voluntarily dies for that faith than sorrow if many abandon it and fall into the snare of transgression.

Hence they easily slide into the sacrilege of impiety, since they do not fear condemning what has been justified by God. They are an undisciplined populace, of whom it is written: “And the impious will act impiously, and none of the impious will understand” (Dan. 12:10). Like salt that has lost its savor, they are to be cast outside from the assembly of Catholics, trampled upon by all, cut down with the Gospel axe like an unfruitful grove, and consigned to everlasting fire.

**28.** Brothers, let it be considered what loss will overtake the person who does not fear disgracing the glory of so great a victory, who goes out to meet the triumphs of so many men. Those men, certainly not forgetful of the apostolic preaching, did not blush to bring forward publicly, to the confusion of the impious teacher and all his followers, the testimony of our Lord Jesus Christ and the truth of the holy Gospel.

They had recognized him as one of the great false prophets whom the Lord's mouth had formerly indicated through the Gospel, when he commanded the apostles to remain intent and circumspect, saying: “See that no one leads you astray; for many false prophets will come in my name and lead many astray” (Matt. 24:4–5). Yet we, through fear of losing temporal honor, declare those whom we do not honor as martyrs to be heretics. Woe to those who follow such things! Woe to those who, taking good for evil and turning light into darkness (Isa. 5:20), pursue with secret insults what they have rejected with open blasphemies! “Let them not be counted among the martyrs, nor let the reverence due to them be shown: approaching the enemy of the faith with blasphemous mouth in a spirit of stubbornness, they were consumed by deserved vengeance” (49). And lest others enter this arena, orders are given for them to be condemned in various places by written decrees of anathema.

If, then, the Lord withholds a reward from these men because they waged open and voluntary war against the enemy of religion, how much farther will those be from the fellowship of the eternal King who act daily in secret murmuring, weighed down by fear of the flesh? Is this preaching absent from our mouths? Is the Catholic profession empty of such a proclamation?

**29.** Therefore we must resist the adversaries of justice completely, and in no way postpone bodily death in defense of the truth. For this is rightly practiced by those who, strengthened by increased virtue and divinely enlightened through magnanimity, reckon the fruit of combat more valuable than the advantage of a safe confession. Yet the weaker members of the Church are not thereby to be entirely despised, for it is written: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. 26:41) (20).

Nor are those who have not been pierced by zeal to be dragged violently into this struggle; for it is written: “Let the one who is able to receive it receive it” (Matt. 19:12). And again: “They will be purified, and many will be whitened and tested by fire” (Dan. 12:10)—not all.

Therefore let each person be content with the limits of the gifts which he recognizes himself to possess by God’s dispensation; and let no one rashly attempt to extend himself beyond the measure of the gift bestowed. Accordingly, when someone knows that he lacks the strength to fight, and, judging by his own capacity, considers that he is unable to set his battle line against the enemy, let him not resist those who willingly prepare themselves for the confrontation.

Thus, although he is not equipped for combat and his fear makes him timid in warfare, let him not encounter the just punishment of detraction. For it is written: “Every idle word that people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matt. 12:36). If every idle talker will come under condemnation at the judgment, with what sentence will the slanderer of the saints be punished?

Whoever is not ignorant of himself does not undertake great things; let him not oppose those advancing toward higher things. Let him cling to lowly and level ground, since he cannot contemplate lofty matters. As it is written in Solomon: “Do not investigate things higher than yourself, and do not seek out things deeper than yourself” (Ecclus. 3:22).

And consequently (21) the philosopher Cato adds:

> Attempt the work that you can; lest labor, weighed down by its burden,  
> collapse, and you abandon what you have attempted in vain.

[scan page 386]

**30.** Certainly, if hell holds those who openly profess what is holy, much more do the prison-houses of hell possess those who secretly preach the truth. For if the struggle in the arena harms the defenders of justice, surely it will do no good to those who confess the truth in secret.

What religious mind could believe this madness: that the truth should come into disgrace because it rejects evil, simply because we are not violently dragged into pagan evil? And therefore that justice itself should receive no reward for martyrdom, although it openly brings accusation against the author of wickedness?

On this account, we are willingly allowed by the worshippers of that same prophet to carry the banner of the Christian faith among the privileges of their kingdom. As though it were to be attributed to their patience that we live among them without harassment of our faith, rather than to divine dispensation, by which God preserved His patriarchs, prophets, and apostles amid the savagery of the nations, raised them to honor, and exalted them in dignity.

He also consoles His disciples with the pious promise, saying: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

Therefore the Church deserves to be guarded not by the favor of this impious nation, under whose rule—because of our own crime—the scepter of Spain was transferred after the destruction and uprooting of the kingdom of the Goths (a land which formerly flourished through the most blessed cultivation of the Christian faith, bloomed with the dignity of venerable priests, and shone with the admirable construction of basilicas), but by the grace of its Redeemer and by His continual companionship, who said:

> “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters”  
> (Song of Songs 2:2).

And again:

> “Among a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine as lights in the world”  
> (Phil. 2:15).

**31.** But let those who, with obstinate minds, hold these opinions about the martyrs of God, and who do not fear mutilating the glory of the saints with impure tongues, know that they will plead their case with those same saints at the future judgment, and that, unless fruitful satisfaction has preceded it, they will render an account before the tribunal of the Lord.

With what face will such a person then look upon their countenance, glorified by the glory of passion, in the company of the eternal King, in view of the steadfastness of those whom here he attacked with such blasphemies, tore apart with such reproaches, and afflicted with such injuries?

Then, certainly, when the just stand with great confidence against those who oppressed them, who did not honor the glory of their martyrdom, and who robbed them of their labors, they will be shaken by terrible fear and will be amazed at the unexpectedness of their salvation. They will say among themselves, repenting and groaning in anguish of spirit:

> “These are the ones whom we once held for mockery and made into an object of reproach. We fools considered their life madness and their end without honor.  
> Behold how they have been counted among the sons of God, and how their lot has been found among the saints”  
> (Wis. 5:1 and following).

**32.** I should like the mockers of Christ’s soldiers to answer me whether love of death led them to death, or whether it was rather delight in paradise that compelled them to go to punishment, so that they might escape the fires of eternal death. As I judge it, no one would answer that the saints sought death because they desired dying, but rather that they might avoid the fires of everlasting death through temporal destruction.

Therefore the same reward will undoubtedly follow them, determined by the cause for which they died, not by the will to die which they possessed. Let each person among them believe, say, or think what he wishes. For my part, I firmly defend that side which venerates their worship with the highest reverence and exalts their honor. There I give faithful assent under the testimony of our Lord Jesus Christ, where their triumph is exalted by its outstanding titles.

Therefore I have decided that this treatise should remain for the knowledge of those who come after us, so that both the people of our age and those of the future may know what judgment I rendered concerning the struggle of my lords.

**33.** But you, brothers, believe with me—or rather, believe with all who piously and religiously venerate the contests of the blessed—that the martyrs who accomplished such things are blessed, and that the souls who die under their testimony are more blessed still.

Arm your breasts with the belief of faith; release your mouths to divine praises; exalt the benefits of the supreme Redeemer; proclaim and say:

> “Let our souls die the death of these men,  
> and let our last things be like theirs”  
> (Num. 23:10).

May He who gives strength to the weary, and who, with His powerful right hand, strengthens in combat those who have no strength, grant me to fight for Him until death with a braver spirit, together with those who burn with perfect desire for His love.

For an intention exerted for the truth will not go unrewarded before the Lord; nor is a death inflicted for justice in any way to be rejected. In such a conflict Christ is praised, the wicked enemy remains detested, and under the same confession the brave soldier receives a furious death.

**34.** Therefore not only those who fell beneath the sword while confessing such things are to be celebrated with worthy praise, but those also are to be extolled with fitting commendation who take delight in praising such men.

For when the glory acquired by the sufferings of the martyrs is recalled, and the contests of the blessed that have been recorded are brought to light, due honor is rendered to the martyrs, and pious minds are armed with the incentives of their examples.

Even if they cannot attain martyrdom, they will nevertheless deserve to be advanced to a share in the rewards bestowed upon those who are honored. Since by the consent of their will they desire to be inscribed among their triumphs, they will receive an equal reward for their devotion.

For if accommodating one’s mind to the worst deeds is perversity, how can sharing in the best deeds not be virtue? And since Almighty God shows Himself to be the judge not only of deeds but also of vows, why should the most pious intention directed toward the martyrs not gain the joys of the blessed?

As holy David approves:

> “But to me, O God, your friends are exceedingly honorable”  
> (Ps. 138:17).

And again:

> “Whoever loves you loves me, and whoever receives you receives me”  
> (Luke and Matthew 10).

**35.** Finally, the saints, offering their bodies to the swords, obtained everlasting safety for their souls; and, gaining for themselves a chosen fellowship in the kingdom of Christ, they nevertheless left to their persecutors the fire of eternal punishment.

For although it is written:

> “They gave the corpses of your servants as food to the birds of heaven,  
> the flesh of your saints to the beasts of the earth.  
> They poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem,  
> and there was no one to bury them”  
> (Ps. 79:2–3),

nevertheless those who committed such acts will meet them in order that their savagery may be punished. This will not diminish the virtues of those who endured such things; rather, that very cruelty will increase the heap of perdition for the executioners, while obtaining for the holy martyrs the reward of everlasting blessedness.

For although these things may appear dreadful and harsh to human eyes, nevertheless “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 116:15).

*Why Morales and Schottus called this passage utterly corrupt escapes us; its sense is perfectly plain if it is read: “Yet they will come to punish the savagery of those who did these things.” It is as though he said: Whatever persecutors inflict upon the bodies of the holy martyrs will not diminish their virtues, but will result in the punishment of the persecutors. For this purpose they will come at the day of judgment: “the just stand in great confidence against those who afflicted them.”*

**36.** But you, brothers and holy sisters in the Lord Jesus Christ, rejoice and exult, because you have already sent the sheaves of your harvest to be stored in the granary of the Lord.

Already that blessed city, Zion, possesses the fruit of your seed. That heavenly Jerusalem, the vision of peace, has received your own kin into peace. Go forward securely; proceed rejoicing. No adversary will be able to oppose your journey, and no opponent will stand against you.

When you reach your homeland, not only will that band of saints who have recently been crowned come out to meet you, but also the entire multitude of the elect, in whose fellowship these newly made martyrs have been numbered.

**37.** Therefore, brothers, I am pleased to speak with you for a little while in the manner of one who rejoices; and, for the sake of charity, bear with one who is wordy, since you see me engaged out of love for Christ in praising the saints.

To escape the debt owed for my own merits and to obtain the assistance of the intercession of the blessed, I have dedicated this work to the victories of the martyrs and decided to call it the *Memorial of the Saints*, so that, since we sympathize with those in chains and venerate the friends of God, we may at least be helped by their patronage.

For it is said in the Psalm:

> “To me, O God, your friends are honorable,  
> for their principality has been greatly strengthened”  
> (Ps. 138:17).

Therefore, dearest brothers and blessed sisters, command that I be admitted to your rejoicing—I whom the confession of this work does not allow to remain absent from such joys. Do not, through jealous possessiveness, claim for yourselves alone the patronage of the holy martyrs whom you know to have undergone the dangers of suffering for the members of the whole Church.

But why should I linger longer over these joys, as though it were for you to satisfy our desire? Surely, so that the witnesses of God whom we have sought in tribulation may be present with us, at least not without your consent—for they are concerned for the Catholic flock before the Father and His angels.

Therefore they belong both to you and to us. They came forth from you according to the flesh, but with us they were reborn from one baptismal font. There is nothing in their glory which you may claim privately for yourselves, because in Christ we are all one.

Indeed, we encouraged some of them to battle; and, although we ourselves ceased fighting, we nevertheless supplied the weapons with which they were to serve. We sent certain of our blood-relations among the martyrs to heaven: I speak of Paul, the outstanding Levite, related to us by flesh, and of Sanctus, one of our hearers, who after the blessed Isaac went to Christ in a second conflict ^.

Will we alone, then, glory in their perfection, because we see that those whom we instructed and whom we held as brothers have conquered? Let the joy be common to all; let the blessed memorials of these men be enjoyed without distinction by everyone.

Let us mingle our vows, and with equal devotion offer libations of praise to God, by whose gift the happy ages of this troubled time have been restored to us. In former times, amid the most violent storms of persecution, the Christian Church fittingly joined stones together into the structure of that heavenly Jerusalem, to the glory of God. By His gift the saints fight and conquer; they meet death and live. By His grace the steadfastness of the martyrs is strengthened; by His power they advance with manly courage through whatever the savagery of the impious has produced.

For “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the glory that is to be revealed in them” (Rom. 8:18). Nor do they care by what kind of death they lose this life, since through this deficiency of the flesh they await the blessedness of the kingdom.

**38.** But because moderation is always praiseworthy, and because joined brevity more easily delights the reader than wearisome prolixity, the book must therefore be closed at its final boundary, lest, besides the one great absurdity of my own unpolished work, prolonged verbosity give birth to another labor for those who reflect upon it.

Therefore, now that the end of the volume is at hand, I myself, Eulogius, though unworthy to be your praiser, ask you, O crown of saints, to make this work approved by yourselves, to accept and sanctify it, and to offer it as something sanctified to God. Do not weigh the disordered sequence of its narrative; consider rather my willingness than my ability, and reward the vow of my intention, not the deficiency caused by my inability.

For this reason I took care to offer you, before all the philosophers of our homeland, the first-fruits of this commentary (24), so that through its presentation I might have your patronage, and through your intervention might be free from every fault—so that I might deserve to find the Lord, who is offended against me on account of my sins, favorable to me both now and forever.

Although my conscience reproaches me because my uncultivated barbarity of speech has rashly introduced matters that ought to have been arranged for the knowledge of posterity in a praiseworthy style, and thus makes me liable to a more serious fault, nevertheless I hope to obtain a remedy for so great an offense from the fact that the whole force of my intellect has been expended in your praise.

At the same time, by confronting the whisperings of slanderers, I have overthrown the ranks of the treacherous, subverted their foundations, and broken their strength. Like dogs who, burning with the most ardent zeal for their masters, never cease barking, and who become all the more provoked in their importunate barking when they have perhaps been wounded by the blows of an attacker, so we, although confined by the distress of a most difficult time and overwhelmed by impending dangers, have nevertheless in no way withdrawn our tongue from your praises or ceased attacking the wicked.

These things compel us, in a certain hope, to remain joyful and confident in the mercy of our good Father. Therefore neither this unpolished speech nor this lowly offering, made in hope of the Redeemer’s grace, will cause me to despair; for I know that before Him a devoted affection has more power than a sluggish abundance of gifts.

Therefore, with repeated supplication, I beseech you, soldiers of God, noble warriors, worthy witnesses, martyrs of Christ and companions in the everlasting kingdom: join me here to God in faithful service, and remove from me the sentence of retribution due for my sins at the future judgment. May this book, which we have called the *Memorial of the Saints* and which proclaims the glorious memory of your deeds, by the favor of your acceptance enroll my memory before the tribunal of the future Judge among the lot of the sheep.

Thus, transferred from the left to the right hand, may I deserve to enjoy without shame the sight of the gracious Redeemer, and, impeded by no guilt, to be rewarded with that company to which the same Redeemer will say in a loving voice: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34).

^ He writes about these men in Book II, chapters 3 and 6. Morales.

* Schottus correctly notes here that Eulogius does not mention Louis, Paul’s brother, because, while he was writing this commentary, Louis had not yet suffered martyrdom. For he was killed on the day before the Kalends of May in the year 855, as is clear in Book III, chapter 13; and Eulogius wrote the first book in the year 851, as we have already said.

*For “crime.” Schottus.*

[scan page 388]

**MEMORIAL OF THE SAINTS**

## BOOK II

### PREFACE

The brevity of this second work, which sets forth only the deeds of the blessed martyrs, will present their names, ages, origins, and days of their struggles in a faithful account. Thus the prudent reader, compensating for the somewhat extended sequence of the preceding little book, will more easily be able to infer whom the author raised up in his praise and, conversely, whom, armed with zeal for God, he attacked.

For what the former work arranges obscurely amid the varied circuit of its disputation, this one discusses clearly and concisely in a brief account. We have arranged it by chapters so that the beginnings of each martyr’s struggle might be displayed more freely to those who meditate upon them.

### CHAPTER ONE

**On Perfectus, a presbyter of Córdoba and martyr**

In the name of the Lord. Our Lord Jesus Christ reigning forever, in the eight-hundred-and-fiftieth year of His incarnation, the eight-hundred-and-eighty-eighth year of the era, (1) and in the twenty-[ninth?] year of the consulship (2) of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān [the supplied ordinal after *vicesimo* is corrupt: *fiiono*, plausibly *nono*]—during whose time the Arab people increased in power and dignity in Spain and occupied almost the whole of Iberia under a cruel authority (3)—he raised Córdoba, once called Patricia ^ and now called the royal city because of the seat of its ruler, to the highest pinnacle, exalted it with honors, enlarged it with glory, enriched it with wealth, and increased it with an abundance of every delight in the world, beyond what is lawful either to believe or to say.

Thus, in every secular pomp, it surpassed, exceeded, and conquered the kings who had preceded it in its lineage. While under its most oppressive yoke the Church of the orthodox groaned and languished almost to destruction, Perfectus, the presbyter of venerable memory, born at Córdoba and reared in distinguished learning under the teachers of the basilica of Saint Acisclus, was thoroughly imbued with ecclesiastical disciplines and captivated by a vigorous literary education (4). He also possessed some knowledge of the Arabic language and spent almost all his youth (5) in the aforementioned monastery.

^ See the note in Book I, no. 7.

^ We have already said much about both names of the city, and likewise about the seat of the Arab kingdom established there. Morales.

**2.** One day, while traveling because of a necessity concerning his household affairs, and entering the city to attend to domestic business, he was questioned by certain pagans about the Catholic faith and was ordered to give testimony before them concerning Christ and the prophet Muḥammad.

Immediately, with open expression, he proclaimed the power of Christ’s divinity and declared that He is God, blessed above all forever. He said:

> “I do not dare to explain how your prophet is regarded among Catholics, because I do not doubt that you would be wounded by this with serious distress. But if an amicable agreement were made and you granted a peaceful compact concerning the faith, I would say by what testimony of the Gospel he is identified and with what veneration he is honored by Christians.”

They deceitfully promise faithfulness, and, casting off every fear, compel him to relate everything that is held about Muḥammad among religious people.

Then the prudent priest, addressing them in Arabic, brought forward from the Gospel the account of that false prophet and most false teacher, saying that he had led many astray:

> “Many false prophets will come in my name, and they will lead many astray; and they will perform great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect”  
> (Matt. 24:24).

> “Among the others, this prophet of yours, seized by the tricks of the ancient enemy, enticed by demonic fabrications, and devoted to the sacrileges of magical practices, has corrupted the hearts of many who think little of such matters with deadly poison and handed them over to the snares of eternal perdition. Without any spiritual prudence or discernment, he pledges their faith to the prince, Satan, with whom he himself will pay the harshest torments of hell; and he has destined you also, as his followers, to burn with him in the fires of an unquenchable furnace.
>
> “For how can he be reckoned among the prophets, or why should he not be punished by heavenly malediction, when, blinded by the beauty of Zaynab, the wife of his own servant Zayd, he took her away by barbarous law, and, like a horse or mule in which there is no understanding (Ps. 32:9), joined her to himself in an adulterous union, declaring that he had done this at the command of an angel? (6)”

Then blessed Perfectus added many other statements about the foulnesses and lusts commanded by the law of Muḥammad, and finally concluded with these words:

> “Thus, as a patron of uncleanness and a servant of the pleasure of lust, he has consecrated all of you to the impurities of everlasting wantonness.”

After explaining before everyone many other matters concerning his most abominable teaching, insofar as he knew them, and denouncing much that was hateful to hear, they did not attack him then with an arrogant eye; nevertheless, they stored in their hearts a fury of vengeance, inflamed for his destruction.

[scan page 389]

**3.** The servant of God thus accomplished the necessary purpose of his journey; and, when his journey was completed, he returned to his own quiet cell and remained secure there for some time.

After not a long interval, however, when an occasion arising from a household necessity compelled him to go somewhere, he happened by chance to pass among the same people with whom he had earlier engaged in dispute.

When his enemies saw him approaching from a distance, they brought into open flame the ancient wound they had kept concealed in their breasts against him, and urged the assembled crowd to avenge their prophet in the following manner:

> “Behold the man who, driven earlier by rash madness, uttered before us such words of malediction against the prophet—may God bless him and save him—that none of you could endure hearing them.”

They always use this form of blessing in his honor: *Zalla, Aliah, Halla, Anabi. V. A. Zallen*. In Latin: *Psallat Deus super prophetam, et salvet eum*—“May God bless the prophet and save him.”

Thus, like a whole swarm of bees provoked by stings, that entire company of perdition rose furiously against him. They seized him and, with all speed, presented him to the judge, his feet scarcely touching the ground. They gave the judge the following testimony against him:

> “This man, whom we have dragged before your most reverend tribunal, judge, we have discovered to have cursed our prophet and reproached his worshippers. What sentence should restrain such audacity and blunt such fury, your prudence knows better how to determine.”

Then the unjust judge handed over the future martyr of God to the prison, constrained him in iron bonds of unbearable weight, and postponed his execution until the day on which the festive joy of Passover is celebrated among them according to profane rites.

The soldier of Christ went with a joyful spirit to the hidden prison. He entered that gloomy cave of the condemned as though invited to a feast. There, endowed with the greatest reverence for fear and holiness, he devoted himself to vigils, prayers, and fasts. It is said that he confirmed with a stronger mind, in the power of the Holy Spirit, the sentence which earlier, before the judge, he had denied through fear of death.

Before he was led out to be punished in the forum, they report that he had been strengthened by a prophetic spirit and had said concerning a certain eunuch named Nazar, a chamberlain and governor (who at that time administered the whole state in Spain):

> “This man, whom pride in his authority today raises above all the leading men of Iberia, and whose glorious power has exalted him to the heavens in this western region, when the course of the coming year has revolved, will not himself reach the day which he will decree for my execution.”

Divine power did not delay fulfilling what it had revealed to its confessor, already purified through the squalor of prison.

^ This passage was cut out from the text by Ambrosio Morales; hence the place is somewhat obscure. Schottus. See the Scholion in Book I, no. 7.

**4.** Therefore, after not many months had passed in prison, and after the thirty days of their fasts had been completed, during which—as has been set out in the first book—they devote themselves more zealously than usual to the gluttony of the stomach and the impurity of lust, the martyr’s day dawns, more glorious than all other days: namely, the day which they celebrate as dedicated to their god with solemn veneration and the greatest rejoicing, according to the rite of their vain law.

On that day, thinking that they would render a great service to their god, they led him out from the cave and slaughtered him with an avenging sword. He confessed Christ, who remains in the glory of His divinity, and freely reproached the enemy of the Church, saying:

> “I both cursed and curse your prophet: a great man of demons, an adulterer, and a liar. As I have confessed, so I confess. I declare that the inventions of your sect’s profanations are the fabrications of the devil. I also declare that you, together with the prince of darkness, will suffer eternal torments.”

The crowd of pagans, which, out of regard for the magnitude of that festival (8), had gone out onto the broad plain beyond the bridge of the river, on the southern side of the city, to pray, joyfully turned aside on its swift return to watch the martyr’s execution.

When it saw him already prostrate before the doors of the governor’s residence and rolling in his own blood, with the traces of the blood of the slain priest also upon the ground, its joy increased. Having achieved the fulfillment of its sacrilegious vow, it returned, confident that it would more easily obtain what it desired as it walked with measured steps through the blood of so great an enemy.

**5.** But let us return to the subject and relate what divine piety accomplished for the glory of its martyr on the very day on which he fell, as we have learned from the faithful report of many. For the swift vengeance of his…

^ Perhaps *daemoniosum*, “demoniacal,” as in the *Apologeticus*, no. 12, and in the *Documentum*, no. 15. Either form expresses the common Spanish idiom *hombre endiablado*, “a devil-possessed man,” or *hombre de los diablos*, “a man of the devils.” Schottus.

[scan page 390]

## Memorial of the Saints — Book II

### 5.

…pouring out his vengeance upon them, he drowned some of that wicked band in the river’s whirlpool. As they returned, the faithful execution of the persecutors first visibly exacted what had been deserved; and what he had persuaded them to undertake by a hotly contrived stratagem—namely, to avenge themselves by sacrilegious rites at the place of prayer—afterward led many of them to ruin. Most of them, embarking upon ships and willingly exposing themselves to such danger, were carried home upon the scaly backs of the river-creatures by a swift voyage, after the boats’ keels had been split. Indeed, the whole multitude of pagans was shaken with such tremendous terror that, when one boat was overturned by a single surge of the waves, the vessel carrying eight men was swallowed amid the billows and hidden in the bosom of the inner abyss. Only six escaped by swimming; two perished in the shipwreck.

Thus the Scripture would not prove empty, for it says:

> “I, the Lord, will give the wicked for your burial, and the rich for your death” (Isaiah 53:9).

For the cruelty of the persecutor sent one of them ahead into the grave, and the savage storm of the river consigned two others to death. The body of the holy martyr, however, through the pious offices of the religious and the worthy service of the bishop and priests, was buried in the basilica of blessed Acisclus, in that shrine where his blessed limbs rest. And the prophecy which he had uttered by divine inspiration concerning the eunuch and executioner Nazar, the proconsul, was fulfilled, by God’s dispensation, just as he had foretold while still bound in prison.

For before, in the following year, the paschal joy of the profaned solemnity could reach those destined to perish, the same eunuch died many days beforehand. An inward fiery fever burned his entrails, and—as some report—he was corrupted by a poisonous draught. Before his death, while bodily necessity compelled him to seek a secluded chamber to relieve his bowels, his entrails poured out and he died.

As a Christian poet, describing the end of Arius, sported heroically in verse, saying:

> “His intestines, emptied of all their contents, remained void …”

Thus the Lord, glorifying his soldier by both miracles, strengthened the hopes and prayers of the faithful with the consolations of great expectation, and drove the sacrilegious vanity of the impious into profound astonishment. Let it suffice that we have said these few things from the deeds of the blessed Martyr. We learned them to be true from Catholic men who, from the beginning, had remained with him in bonds; but we also learned them from the testimony of the pagans themselves, since, at the time of our own imprisonment, we found scarcely a few of all those with whom that future Martyr had lived still at liberty.

The man of God completed the course of his contest in peace, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, a Friday, in the era noted above.

### 6.

The reality of so great a crime committed against a priest compelled many who were enjoying, in the leisure of a secure confession, the contemplation of God amid mountain wastes and solitary woods, to rise spontaneously and publicly to detest and curse the wicked prophet, and it furnished a greater fuel for the ardor of dying for justice. Thus, from the one man whose faithful execution first exacted vengeance, and from what he had brought about by a hotly contrived stratagem, many others were afterwards moved.

And so, as the preface of this volume relates, let us faithfully pursue in writing the ages, origins, times, and deaths of our combatants, so that the plain sequence of this little book may make known to future ages what has been granted us by divine gift and joined to our own times—namely, to behold with our own eyes the contest of the saints. Let a future generation also share in our joy when, with believing minds, it does not refuse to accept as true what it reads that the diligence of Catholics has committed to writing.

## Chapter II

### On Isaac, the monk and martyr

Blessed Isaac, born of noble and wealthy parents among the citizens of Córdoba, was entering the earliest years of adolescence and was living tenderly amid his parents’ wealth and possessions. He was so skilled and learned in the Arabic language that he held the office of interpreter for the public administration. Suddenly inflamed with spiritual ardor and desiring the life of monks, he went to Tábanos, a village situated to the north, seven miles from the city, amid steep mountains and dense forests. It was celebrated by the most favorable reports of men and women of God who practiced the monastic life there.

In that same monastery he had as his paternal uncle Jeremiah, a man endowed with the highest reverence and fear of God. Jeremiah was also illustrious in wealth and abundant in possessions; his venerable wife Elizabeth, his children, and almost the whole family had earlier gone there, laying the foundations of the monastery at their own expense and devoting themselves permanently to obedience to the divine laws.

There blessed Isaac served in the holy purpose for three years under regular discipline, under the most reverend abbot Martin, brother of the woman mentioned above. Then, immediately enlightened by God, he went to the forum, sought the judge, and—according to the order which I set out in the preface of the book—died a blessed death, in the presence of our Lord Jesus Christ, in that royal city, on the third day before the Nones of June, a Wednesday, in the 889th year of the era.

His body, suspended upon a hook, was after several days, together with the others who had been beheaded in imitation of him, committed to a most ravenous fire and reduced to the last ash; thereafter it was thrown into the river to be carried away.

This man, so great and so distinguished, together with the blessed old man Jeremiah—of whom we spoke above, and who also, among the other servants of God, died after being afflicted with harsher scourgings—died. These six most courageous and illustrious men, together to overcome the wicked enemy, all cried out as though with one voice:

> “We too remain under the same profession, under the same judge, in the same royal city, in which our brothers, the most holy Isaac and Sanctius, fell. Carry out your sentence, heighten your cruelty, and burn with every fury to avenge your prophet. For we confess that Christ is truly God, and that your prophet is the forerunner of Antichrist and the author of a profane dogma. We declare that you are infected with his deadly poison and corrupted by his venomous preaching; knowing that you have been offered the draught of Zabuli and will afterwards suffer eternal torments, we grieve over your bereavement and lament your ignorance.”

Having made this profession with courageous spirit, they were immediately ordered to be beheaded. The pious old man Jeremiah, however, was severely beaten with whips—perhaps because of some assertion—and, as they report, died amid the blows. Still scarcely able to walk, he was dragged outside. As the martyrs went to the place of slaughter, they invited one another to the banquet, as it were. First the most reverend ministers of God, Peter and Walabonsus, fell; the others were then slaughtered under the same yoke at the same moment, namely on the seventh day before the Ides of June, a Sunday, in the era stated above. Their bodies were fastened to stakes and consumed in a huge fire after several days; their ashes were scattered upon the river.

*He calls river vessels “rain-bearing ships” by a certain abuse of language. — Morales.*

*Sedulius, Book I of the Paschal Work, near the end.*

*Usuard, in his Martyrology, says that the holy Isaac died on 3 June, in the twenty-seventh year of his age; although Henschenius did not know where he obtained this information, we believe with Enrique Flórez that Usuard could readily have investigated the matter at Córdoba, since he remained there for nearly two months in the year 858. In that city he transported to Paris the bodies of the saints George the monk, Aurelius, and Nathalia. See vol. X of Sacred Spain, pp. 369, 387 ff.*

*Morales and Schott printed “days” here; but with Henschenius we restore “dies” chiefly because Eulogius uses the same expression in the preface to Memorial I, no. 1.*

[scan page 391]

## Chapter III

### On Sanctius the martyr

The holy Sanctius, our hearer, a layman and adolescent, was captured from the town of Albi in Gaul, but was later enrolled among the military pages of the king and supported by royal provisions. He was impaled in the same royal city under the same profession on the Nones of June, in the era stated above, on a Friday.

The manner of his prostration and affliction indicates that form of punishment. Papebrochius says under 5 June that, even today, among the Turks and Hungarians, traitors of the sort Sanctius was considered to be are stretched out upon a rack, their bodies transfixed with a stake, which is then raised aloft, prolonging their death and making them a spectacle. They call this impalement.

## Chapter IV

### On Peter, Walabonsus, Sabinianus, Wistremundus, Habentius, and Jeremiah, martyrs

Let us now come to that most sacred company of six martyrs who, on one day and at one hour, were killed by the stroke of the savage sword for bearing witness to the truth.

Among them Peter, a priest, was born in the city of Écija, while Saint Walabonsus, a deacon, came from the city of Elepla. Both, contemporaries of the earlier martyrs, went to Córdoba to pursue study and were instructed in the liberal disciplines. With God’s favor, possessing knowledge and learning in the Scriptures, they were formed under Frugellus, abbot of the monastery of the holy and glorious Virgin Mary. This monastery shines in the distinguished purpose of the servants of God at the village of Cuteclara, not far from the city on the western side.

The holy Sabinianus, born in the village of Froniano in the mountains of Córdoba, was already a monk in the full vigor of youth. Wistremundus, an adolescent from Écija, had given himself to the monastery of Saint Zoilus at Armilata, where they had long ago placed themselves under the rule and abbot. Sabinianus had served for a long time in the camp of the Lord; Wistremundus, having recently entered the same monastery, both hastened toward martyrdom.

That place lies nearly thirty or more miles north of Córdoba and is surrounded by a vast solitude among mountain wastes. At the foot of the hill on which it stands, the river Armilata flows and refreshes the monks’ fasting with the great comfort of its little fish. From this the monastery is also called Armilatense.

The blessed Habentius, already mature in manhood, was a citizen of Córdoba. Desiring the monastic life, he lived in the monastery of Saint Christopher, situated as a spectacle of the city on the southern side above the farther bank of the Baetis. There he died to the world, living under an exceedingly strict rule: he had surrendered himself to a voluntary prison, enclosed within high walls and hedges and bound inside with iron plates against his flesh; through windows he showed himself to those who came to visit him.

*On the mysteries of the number six, John Tamayo de Salazar says much in his Martyrology of Spain under 7 June. We have thought it worthwhile to transcribe it in the Notes, since Papebrochius refers us there.*

*“To apply oneself to letters.” Eulogius uses “meditatio” for study here and below, chapter 10. — Schott.*

*We add “was” from Papebrochius himself under the same day, since otherwise the sense remains incomplete.*

*Supply an interval here, as Papebrochius did; or read “days,” as we noted above.*

## Chapter V

### On Sisenandus, the Levite and martyr

Finally, the most holy Levite Sisenandus, born in the town of Badajoz, came to Córdoba for the sake of study. There, at the basilica of the blessed Acisclus, where the body of that martyr rests, he was suitably nourished, as he himself told his friends. When the blessed Peter and Walabonsus, already placed among the martyrs in heaven, invited him, he too undertook martyrdom.

While he remained bound in prison, they relate that, enlightened by a prophetic spirit, he foretold and announced the hour of his own punishment. One day, when he was preparing a reply to a certain friend who had questioned him and was writing him a return letter, after three or four verses had already been arranged, he was suddenly overcome by immense joy and invigorated, as it were, by heavenly gladness. Rising from his seat, he said to the boy standing nearby who was carrying the letter—which the soldier of Christ intended to answer:

> “Move away for a while, son, lest you be crushed by the rush of the soldiers; for now the power of darkness, ordering them to drag me from my bonds, will present me to itself for beheading.”

After this prophecy he remained fixed in the same place, unable to move his feet. At that very moment the executioners arrived shouting, and with precipitous fury dragged him to the place where he was to complete his martyrdom, beating him with fists and slaps.

The servant of God went on with a joyful spirit, certain of the crown of victory, having been invited by the saints to the heavenly banquet. Presented before the judge, he continued with the same steadfastness as before in his holy confession. The delicate youth was killed by a glorious death and left unburied before the palace gates, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August, a Thursday, in the era stated above. After many days, by God’s gift, some women found his bones among the pebbles of the riverbank; they were carried to the hall of the aforesaid martyr Acisclus and buried there.

## Chapter VI

### The martyrdom of Paul, deacon of Córdoba, and Theodemirus, monk

The holy Paul, our fellow citizen and a most worthy Levite, was born among the citizens of Córdoba. While he was still in the first flower of adolescence, he was extremely simple, obedient, and humane, always extending the compassion of his wealth to prisoners. He was nourished in spiritual disciplines at the basilica glorified by the presence of the body of the blessed martyr Zoilus.

Following the example and instruction of the most holy Sisenandus, he did not fear to appear before princes and magistrates. He reproved them for the vanity of their worship and the madness of the wicked prophet, and, confessing Christ as true God, he was put to death.

It is nevertheless reported that, while he was still detained in prison, Tiberinus, a priest from Badajoz, appealed to him, saying:

> “Obtain my release before the Lord, blessed minister, and by your worthy intervention, when you come crowned to Christ, remove from me this prolonged squalor of imprisonment.”

For that priest had been confined in a prison for nearly twenty years, accused by his enemies before the king—I do not know for what crime. Though he had formerly excelled in the full vigor of youth and possessed manly beauty, he had been assigned to an underground cavern and was brought out almost decrepit and exhausted by old age; finally he was committed to the public prisons.

In these prisons the martyrs of Christ lived until the hour of death. There the wicked audacity and accursed insolence of parricides, murderers, robbers, and fornicators, together with criminals of many kinds, were confined under the strictest guard. In that place the priest mentioned above entrusted the cause of his imprisonment to blessed Paul.

The holy martyr, confident of the crown of victory, promised to satisfy his request. Not many days after his own martyrdom, he faithfully kept his pledge: by God’s favor he secured the priest’s release from prison and restored him to his native city.

*Perhaps the reading is “wish” (*optationi*), if we trust the Bollandists, under 10 July.*

The servant of God completed his martyrdom in peace on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, a Monday, in the era stated above. His unburied body was left before the palace gates; after several days some of the faithful secretly took it away and, together with the body of blessed Theodemirus, a monk from Carmona, buried it at the shrine of the aforesaid martyr Zoilus.

Theodemirus himself died six days after Paul’s fall, namely on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, a Saturday, in the era stated above, while our Lord Jesus Christ reigned, who helped his saints and crowned them in peace forever and ever. Amen.

*He was related by blood or kinship, since in Book I he says that he was connected with him by family; and in the same manner he later calls his brother Ludovicus a fellow citizen, in Book III, chapter 13. The same is clear from chapter 17 of that Book III, where Saint Aurea is visited by her relatives as fellow citizens. — Schott.*

## Chapter VII

### Nunilo and Alodia, virgins and martyrs

Until this point I had decided to bring Book II to an end; until this point I had thought that the procession of saints running toward such a contest had reached its limit. I did not suppose that anyone, after so many dangers to the Churches and our imprisonment, would undertake such struggles.

But since foreknowing divinity was still arranging for the number of saints to be increased by such a profession, it afterward inflamed the minds of certain people with a manifold ardor and destined more to the same contest. Instilling the rest with a similar vow and courage, it armed men, women, and children for the exercise of their battles. No one enrolled for such a great and demanding service could withdraw from the contest.

The heavenly book retained, recorded from the beginning of the age, the name of each person enrolled for such a contest, and saw his strength grow for this arena through divine enterprises. Their names, ages, and deeds of battle must be set out in their proper place and time.

First, however, those trophies of the saints must be elaborated which the order and course of the months bring forward as they occurred, even if their deeds took place in other regions.

*Up to this point Eulogius wrote before the end of November 851. Everything that follows is later than 853 and earlier than 857. — Enrique Flórez, vol. 10 of* Sacred Spain*, p. 439.* But since there is one confession which crowned both groups, and the same time sent both into heaven through savage impiety, I think it is not absurd that the order of our annotation has inserted them among the ranks of the saints and united them to the assembly of the blessed: so that those whom one record has entered among the heavenly company might be raised by us on earth with equal magnificence of praise.

For this reason it has happened that the concise brevity promised by this little work has exceeded the measure of its intended compactness. The book, which had hoped to speak more sparingly, has been unexpectedly drawn into a long series of writing by the growth of additional events.

### 2.

Accordingly, when the most holy and venerable man Venerius, bishop of Complutum, reported to me that, in the city of Huesca, near the town of Barbitanum, there were two virgin sisters—one called Nunilo and the other Alodia—born of a pagan father and a Christian mother, I decided to write about them.

After the death of their impious father, their mother, following the custom of her people, entered another marriage. The girls, however, could not freely maintain the faith of Christ because of their stubborn and victorious paganism; for their minds had already been irrigated by the pious spring of Christ. Rejecting their mother’s bed, they were secretly nourished by the faithful instruction of their maternal aunt, and they began to adhere faithfully to Christ the Lord in their holy childhood. Forgetting their father’s rites, they preserved the religion of the Crucified One with tender and sanctified minds.

Although they were still very young, their purpose could not remain hidden from the city, since the conduct of their holy faith gave off a fragrance and shone brightly. They had already reached the first flower of adolescence, and the rumor of their holiness had filled almost the whole province. Everyone was astonished that the twin beauty of roses had sprung from thorns.

Then the jealous ancient enemy, grieving over the loss of his members, trusted that those already marked for the bridal chamber could be changed by the terror of the authorities according to his envious will. By hastening the promised reward through harsh deaths, he brought the holy virgins to their end. He therefore disclosed their case to the city prefect through the efforts of his agents, and the prefect immediately ordered them to appear before him.

Attempting to entice them with empty promises of rewards, he urged them to abandon their devotion to Christ. If they did so, he said, they would be restored to their families, enriched with abundant possessions, and joined in marriage to the most distinguished young men. But if, with a more stubborn spirit, they trampled upon the prefect’s advice, they would be condemned to the torture of punishments on the final day and eventually perish by the avenging sword.

The blessed virgins, animated by the Holy Spirit, replied with one confession, steadfast and undaunted:

> “How do you order us, prefect, to turn away from the piety of God, when holy piety, examining us with its light, has made us understand that nothing is richer than Christ and nothing happier than the Christian faith, by which the just live and by which the saints conquered kingdoms? Without him there is no life; without him eternal death flourishes. To remain with him and live in him is true consolation; to depart from him is eternal destruction. From his fellowship we shall never depart in this life, because, entrusting our purity to him, we hope one day to be admitted to his bridal chambers.

> “We count as nothing the advantages of passing things with which you think to entice us, because we scorn them in the sight of him, having learned that all things beneath the sun are vanity. Nor are we disturbed by your threats of punishments, which we know to last only briefly. Indeed, we desire the very death which you propose as your final terror with the greatest longing, because we believe that through it we shall immediately ascend to heaven, approach Christ, and cling inseparably to his embraces.”

The two sisters, therefore, having displayed the steadfastness of their faith and the excellence of their confession, were handed over to the sword and beheaded on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November, in the era stated above.

Their bodies were left where they had fallen and guarded with the greatest vigilance by soldiers, lest Christians secretly carry them away for the benefit of their intercession and bury them. Nevertheless, it is said that those virginal corpses, in the place where the pagans buried them in deep pits—more properly concealed than buried—shine with signs and miracles and display to both the faithful and the pagans, through the efficacy of the virtues they have won, the glory of their consolation.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one God, forever and ever. Amen.

*Schott reads “gentile.”*

*Schott reads “fall.”*

## Chapter VIII

### The life and passion of the holy virgins Flora and Maria

We deliberately omit this chapter for the present, intending to publish it later together with the martyrological document of the holy Doctor; we have explained the reason for this decision above in our notice.

## Chapter IX

### Gumesindus of Toledo and Servus Dei, martyred at Córdoba

The holy priest Gumesindus, from the town of Toledo, came to Córdoba long ago with both parents while he was still a small child. Through the devotional affection of his parents he was enrolled in the heavenly service through the sacred clerical order. At the basilica of the three saints—Faustus, Januarius, and Martialis—whose bodies rest there in the ashes of their relics, he grew in the fear of God under worthy teachers.

After some time he was ordained to the holy ministry of the diaconate and eventually, as a young man, appointed priest of a certain church of the Córdoba Campania. From there he went down to the city with the blessed monk Servus Dei, who at that time, still a young man, remained shut up with the priest Paul in the aforesaid shrine. Both appeared before the princes and judges and died under the same confession on the Ides of January, in the 890th year of the era.

Their bodies were secretly taken away by Christians and now lie buried with religious honor in the basilica of the martyr Saint Christopher, beyond the river on the southern side.

*The text means the church of the three saints, Faustus and his companions.*

## Chapter X

### On the holy martyrs Aurelius, Felix, George, Sabigotho, and Liliosa

### 1.

There was also a certain young man named Aurelius, distinguished by birth and abundant possessions. His mother was a Christian, but his father was a pagan. During childhood he was entrusted to the faithful guardianship of his aunt, who protected and instructed him until adolescence and taught him to believe truly that Christ is God.
