He absorbed this instruction so thoroughly that, although his relatives compelled him to be educated in Arabic literature, they were nevertheless unable to alter the knowledge of the holy faith that had been divinely fixed in his mind by any empty fabrications. Rather, the more he applied himself to reading the letters intended to perish, merely for the sake of derision, the more fiercely he burned with love for the Christian faith, since, by recognizing the subtle deception of that demonic falsehood, he more clearly exposed the ravings of the perverse doctrine.

Because he could not publicly profess the worship of the faith, he nevertheless commended himself everywhere to the priests of God and asked that they pray more effectively on his behalf.

### 2.

Meanwhile the vigorous youth advanced in years, and his manly face was adorned with the beauty of flourishing cheeks. His relatives therefore urged him to seek a marriage suitable to his nobility. Each of them, according to what he knew, declared that this or that girl was of the finest lineage. But he, meditating inwardly, entrusted the matter of his marriage to Christ, repeatedly entreating the divine power in prayer that, in accordance with his earnest desires, a wife might be granted him who would strive to advance his secret faith and would support in mind and body the worshipper who lived hidden.

At length, helped by this favor, he found a virgin of honorable lineage, distinguished in possessions, adorned in character, and most beautiful in appearance. Although she was outwardly decorated with an exceptional grace of beauty, she shone inwardly with a still more excellent spiritual beauty. For “all the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Psalm 44:14), that is, in the inner chambers of the mind. There, clothed in holiness, in golden fringes and the variety of virtues, she offered Christ the King a pleasing service.

### 3.

This girl, born of pagan parents, was orphaned of her father while still lying in the cradle. Her mother took another husband, who secretly retained the faith of Christ. He uprooted his wife from the error of impiety and strove to assign his stepdaughter to Christ, causing her to be called Sabigotho through the sacrament of baptism.

Though they were publicly mixed with pagans, both carried the religion of piety in a firm heart. The venerable young man took this girl as his wife and, after completing the formalities of betrothal and exchanging the pledge of the dowry, they were at last joined according to the custom of the priests. Thus, by a mutual arrangement, they secretly practiced the faith of Christ for some time, revealing the secret of their faith to no one. Their bodily weakness did not lessen their vow.

The blessed Aurelius also had a certain kinsman named Felix, likewise closely attached to him by holy affection. Felix, wavering in the faith through an opportunity afforded by the devil, afterwards deeply lamented his fall into apostasy; he could no longer practise Christ’s religion openly. He too took as wife the daughter of secret Christians, named Liliosa, and worshipped Christ more secretly in hidden places.

Accordingly, clinging unshakably to one another, they always maintained one fellowship and the same affection, never separating in prosperity or adversity. Such was the obligation of piety in both brethren that it brought the perfection of charity: neither life nor death divided those whom a common occasion of religion had united. Of them it is fittingly said: “Holy, lovely, and beautiful: as they loved one another in their life, so in death they were not divided” (2 Samuel 1:23).

After not many years had passed, it happened that the venerable Aurelius went to the forum on the day when John—whom we mentioned in the previous book, no. 9—was being publicly paraded. Because of his hatred of the name of Christ, John had been beaten bloody almost to death, carried backward upon a donkey, and weighed down with enormous chains. A layer of straw had been placed beneath the part of the animal from which his legs hung. Led around the whole city by the attendants of the soldiers for the spectacle of the crowd, he was accompanied by heralds who mocked him.

When voices of reproach rang out on every side, people said that he had by no means yet paid a punishment worthy of his crime. They claimed that he, who had not feared to attack with mockery a prophet held in such reverence, deserved to be punished by the most disgraceful death, so that he might serve as an example.

Aurelius, pierced by the example and inflamed by the battle of martyrdom, was inspired by a heavenly breath and believed that this spectacle had been shown to him for his own instruction: that he should not fear those who kill the body, since they can inflict no distress upon souls …

*“Study,” as above, chapter 1. — Schott.*

*The excellent Enrique Flórez notes that this probably refers to Muhammad, and that among medieval writers “demonic” was used in the sense of “devilish.” On this matter, see, if desired, Du Cange’s Glossary and Schott’s note above, chapter 1, no. 4.*

*“This one or that one” is a Hispanicism. — Morales.*

*Marriage between a man and a woman of another religion, as above, chapter 7, no. 2. — Schott.*

*Sabigothonem. Others, such as Usuard, Surius, Baronius, and the writers of the Fathers, always call her Natalia.*

*Many external authors correctly suspect that the names were two names belonging to the same woman. Enrique Flórez, vol. X of Sacred Spain, believes that she bore the name Natalia from birth and Sabigotho from baptism, as Eulogius indicates here. To the Bollandist Sollerius, however, Sabigotho seemed somewhat unlikely as a Christian name. Anyone who reads our history attentively will easily notice that women such as Baridona, Liubigotho, and Baldegotho retained their Gothic names even after baptism, without any offense.*

## Saint Eulogius

779

…to inflict, but rather to fear him who can destroy both body and soul and cast them into Gehenna (Luke 12:4).

### 6

Admiring the steadfastness of his faith, he said:

“Truly, this man’s dwelling of faith is founded upon the angelic rock; so great a force of torments has not shaken it, nor has the breeze of fleeting punishments disturbed it. If one who bears the banner of Christ openly before the eyes endured so many grievous tortures through zeal for the Redeemer, although he could have escaped the ruin of that punishment by apostasy, and, judging the loss of his flesh better than the destruction of his soul, did not allow himself to be drawn away from the religion of Christ by a single word—by what reproaches ought I to consider myself worthy of being instructed, or to what punishment ought I to deliver myself for correction, so that I may acquire the strength of that condemned man whom I have today seen and may be fortified by steadfastness?”

### 7

While he was pondering these things in his mind, as the sighs of the heavenly calling were already growing more frequent, he returned home and reported to his devout companion everything that he had seen. Then, moved by the same spirit, he added:

“You, my sweetest wife, when I was living for myself and dead to God, constantly urged me toward confession; every day you pressed me to tear myself away from the pleasures of the world. You preferred the happiness of the eternal kingdom to the dark affections of the world. You persuaded me to abandon all transient things and everything that is confined by an end. You praised monks who renounced the world; delighting in the conduct of religious people, you often sighed for the life of the saints.

“But I, not yet cleansed by the compunction of heavenly grace, could not at all yield to your saving exhortations. Or perhaps, because I was not yet attending to the correction appointed for me by God the Father, I delayed carrying out in deeds what I had meditated in my mind, however faintly.

“Behold, now the acceptable time has come; the days of salvation are at hand, in which, recoiling from things past and external, let us stretch ourselves toward what lies ahead. And first of all, applying ourselves more perfectly to purity and continence, let us devote ourselves to prayer, so that we may more easily hasten toward the task of holiness.

“Let her who was a wife now become a sister; let the bed of our union pass into the affection of siblinghood; let offspring of souls advance and a spiritual generation increase; and, despising the filthy union of bodies, let the mind know that it is more excellent—once fleshly delight has been taken away—to bring forth the seeds of everlasting incorruptibility, so that by meditating upon such labours we may in some way be judged worthy of the fitting reward of martyrdom.”

[Note: “Hispanism,” for *nullo strangulo* or *velie strato*. Schott.]

[Note: “Separately, one from the other.” Id.]

[Note: In Surius we read much inserted here, which is absent from all printed editions and from our manuscript. We do not know on whose authority this codex relies; nevertheless, we thought that we should present it to readers.]

Thus Surius continues the narrative:

“The separation of the holy pair’s purpose was adorned by the following divine miracle. One night, when he had entrusted his limbs to rest on such a bed, in the middle of the night the venerable woman suddenly saw a company of candidates entering her house through the open doors. When the heavenly throng had entered, a radiance brighter than the sun appeared, shining from linen garments with snow-white brilliance.

“Then, after a short while, a young man followed, crowned with incomparable splendour, whom no one could look upon with human eyes without great trembling. He approached the bed of the noble Aurelius, fortified him on every side with the sign of the cross, and spoke certain solemn words there, which she confessed that, because of her excessive fear, she could not understand.

“Afterward, approaching Natalia’s bed, he performed the same rite and departed with the same splendour. We leave it to the reader’s judgment who the young man, attended by so great a retinue, was. Yet it is not unreasonable to understand that he who promises in his holy Gospel, ‘Where two or three are gathered in his name, there he will be in their midst’ (Matthew 18:20), visited his soldiers destined for so great a contest.

“But if anyone—which we scarcely believe—should call this fictitious, let him know that the Creator and Judge of all is witness that I received it from persons who said that they had often heard her herself relate these same things.

“The same chosen woman of Christ also testified that she had recently seen that same house entered by a crowd of monks saying, ‘Behold, the Lady comes; behold, the Lady comes.’ As they spoke, there immediately followed a certain virgin, of inestimable appearance and most lovely dress. At once she approached her husband, smiled upon him, and withdrew.

“Sabigotho confessed that this was the Mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, who always goes about helping, cherishing, and gently embracing all followers of this grace through her love of chastity. Therefore, the more these events inflamed them, the less were they moved by the spur of pride; rather, they burned ever more fervently in God’s service. They fasted, and so forth.”

### 8

The venerable woman received the counsel of her husband with joyful spirits; rejoicing in many ways at the sudden and unexpected salvation, she said:

“This is the transformation of the right hand of the Most High; these are now the beginnings of our calling; these are what I have always desired—the commerce of the eternal King: that, dying in the flesh, we may live in the spirit, so that we may more easily be united with him of whom it is written: ‘God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth’ (John 4:24).

“Therefore, my lord, since this has not been revealed to you by human means, but the heavenly Father, who long ago destined you for eternal military service, now wishes you to hasten with swift steps, let us be freed from every bond, let us shake off the dust, and let us rise through desire for perpetual life.”

### 9

Thus the common consent of both was established in the service of God. They separated in their sleeping quarters but were united in their vows. Their beds gleamed with the variety of coloured coverings by which they concealed their way of life from the public. In the inner corners of the chamber, however, they lay on a bed raised over raw brick and furnished only with rough haircloths, unlike the others.

They often fasted; they prayed without interruption; and whatever psalms they had vowed, they meditated upon at night. Through the labour of their vigils they overcame the darkness and chaos of night, and by such practices they defeated every deception of the demons. They ministered to the needy and devoted themselves entirely to caring for the poor.

Since the aforesaid John was still held in prison, and we too, brought out of the cave, were detained in these chains, while both virgins—Mary and Flora—were then living in women’s hiding-places for the sake of the faith, their visits to those in chains were frequent: to the blessed monk Isaac and the other saints, who, endowed with a tongue for proclaiming truth, had stood before princes and judges to confess what was true and had died for that same truth. By their enduring constancy the strength of these saints increased with manifold vigour of virtues. He sought out the men, while she sought out the women kept in their cloisters.

[Note: “I would prefer *latibula*, ‘hiding places.’” Sollerius.]

### 10

There I recognized him; there I renewed his friendship, and there he begged me to advise him what should be done concerning both the property and the two children that he had received by God’s gift: whether, if it were permissible to leave them destitute, he should do so, since he grieved deeply that after his death they would be handed over to profane rites; or whether it was more fitting to leave them the abundance of his wealth immediately gathered into the treasury.

I considered that he ought to abandon his possessions for the sake of the heavenly kingdom and for the purpose of eternal reward—not merely to leave them, but even to distribute them. I judged that the interests of souls should be preferred to those of children, for Christ, the Father and protector, claimed them for himself.

I taught him that nothing temporal ought in any way to be preferred to the desire for the Redeemer or to the enjoyment of the fellowship of the saints. I immediately added:

“If prudent opportunity permits, by which all these matters can be arranged through a teacher’s intercession and discretion, we judge it best that the offspring first be transferred to a safer place, where they may be assigned more freely to Christ; and that, after selling your possessions according to the Lord’s command and distributing them to the poor, the way may be opened for you to enter more freely after Christ.

“Thus the holy Truth asked the young man how he might possess eternal life: ‘If you wish to be perfect,’ he said, ‘go, sell everything you possess and give to the poor; then come, follow me, and you will have treasure in heaven’ (Matthew 19:21).

“Yet if some portion is left for the support of the children, this cannot be blameworthy, as many teachings of the Fathers make clear. Therefore, if you can accomplish this arrangement, it is an excellent thing and a more perfect work. Freed from all business, it will compel you to go more securely into the heavenly military service.

“But if this arrangement is frustrated by the barking of certain difficulties, and no freedom is available by which these things may be completed with indulgence—especially since you fear that disturbances may arise from some quarter and obstruct your purpose—then you must not hesitate to despise the patrimony, which is found much better and more abundantly in heaven, where you are longing to depart.

“The affection of children is not to be preferred to the fellowship of the saints. God can nourish them in this world, since he fashioned them in the womb; for he has provident care of all things. Not all little ones are sustained by the diligence of their parents, nor are all children raised by their parents’ labour. A human being is born and deprived of a parent’s consolation in the cradle, but is not deprived of the Creator’s governance, for he is the father of orphans and the judge of widows.

“O how many little ones, through the care of nurses, are brought from dreadful poverty into great abundance, and, having been more delicately reared, fall into worse conditions?

“Many born of Christians, when a falling-away intervenes, are deprived of membership in the Church; and many pagans, by the prevenient grace of the Lord, have recourse to the redemption of saving faith. Nor does their parents’ sacrilege harm the latter, nor does their ancestors’ piety benefit the former: for those who depart from the faith are estranged from God, while those who believe in Christ—through whom the righteous live—are rescued from the devil and cleave eternally to God.

“The Lord himself bears witness to this, saying in the Gospel as he rebukes the stubborn vanity of the Jews:

“‘Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath? Therefore produce worthy fruits of repentance, and do not wish to say among yourselves, “We have Abraham as our father.” For I tell you that God is able to raise up children for Abraham from these stones’ (Matthew 3:7–9).

“And again:

“‘Many will come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven; but the children of the kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth’ (Matthew 8:11–12).”

[Note: “For daily sustenance.” Sollerius.]

[Note: Sollerius says that he means that he would learn to contend through experience, which also recurs below.]

[Note: “Or would it not be better to resist?” Id.]

### 11

Thus instructed how he should meditate upon the course of the martyrial contest, the venerable young man, imploring consolation from the prayers of those in chains, departed in happier spirit.

While those dreadful prison enclosures held them, we did not cease to visit them; but the most prudent Sabigotho more frequently visited by night, as though herself one of the prisoners, that women’s hiding-place in which the most sacred virgins Flora and Mary were confined. She did so either to console those who were striving or to commend herself to the affection of the strivers; indeed, rather, that she might be trained in the practices of fighting for Christ the King and acquire the habit of enduring.

She persisted in prayers and laboured in entreaties that they should remember her after attaining the fellowship of the Bridegroom in triumph, so that she too might deserve to enter heaven by shedding her blood. The holy virgins immediately gave assurance that they would grant this favour. They knew that after their victory their prayers would be denied in nothing, nor could they refuse anything to those whose petitions they did not doubt would be heard.

### 12

While, therefore, the handmaid of the Lord, Sabigotho, was fulfilling without suspicion her service to Christ within the domestic walls, immediately after the martyrdom of the virgins, and, caring for her weary body after the exertion of vigils, had rested for a little while, they say that both virgins—Mary and Flora—appeared to her in a dream.

They were clothed in snow-white *cyclades*, carrying in their hands bundles of various privets, and were accompanied by a choir of saints bearing bowls and palms—I suppose, in order to bring before the Lord the prayers of those who had come to be trained for battle. They all shone with the brightness of the heavenly luminaries.

When she saw them, as she supposed, seated, and herself reclining humbly upon a seat of privet, she desired, in an earnest supplication, to address them. Terrified by the majesty of heaven, she scarcely managed to speak in a faint voice, saying:

[Note: The same editor says: “Here *sedilis* is above *ligustrium*, below *deflorata*, to be understood as *exponenti*; and there are several such expressions that must be reconciled with the language of this age.”]

“With what confidence do you now command me, most sacred virgins, to have recourse to the appeal that I made earlier? And if I am to obtain the fulfilment of my vows, answer me graciously, lest we run in vain and fall into emptiness; lest the strength of our efforts be completed in fruitless labour, while one purpose seeks one thing and merits seek another.

“For although God favours merits more than prayers, he nevertheless knows how to reject the repetition of petitions, which the dignity of merits does not assist.

“Therefore, my ladies, spouses of Christ, if until now your hope of receiving the reward of your promise has remained with us, command us to tell you what it is, so that we may hasten more readily toward heavenly things and be strengthened more firmly in the contest.”

### 13

Then the holy virgins, soothing her with the distinguished utterances of heavenly grace, said:

“The rewards of your labour have been stored up for you in the heavens; at the appointed time you will receive and reap them. The reward prescribed for the contest will not fail, the reward that compels invincible athletes to go to the kingdom. Your martyrdom was divinely fixed and predestined from the foundation of the world. Since you will fulfil it shortly, it is fitting that you devote yourselves to the practices of holiness with greater zeal than usual.

“Therefore, add the offerings of priests to your labours; implore the intercession of the saints; everywhere entrust yourselves through the prayers of those who serve Christ; visit the venerable sanctuaries of God in devout pilgrimages; and seek the prayers of all religious people.

“For although the rewards prescribed for you will one day certainly be yours, nevertheless, by this diligence, relying as though upon certain steps, you can truly reach the citadel of such goodness.

“Our statement is confirmed by this sign: as your contest approaches, we will send into your company a monk who has been ordained from heaven to obtain with you the palm of martyrdom.”

### 14

After this vision had disappeared from her watchful eyes, the blessed Sabigotho was driven all the more vigorously by the miracle to complete the battles of the Lord. Soon rising more joyful from sleep, she increased her works of holiness, raised her fragile sex to battle, and strengthened her power for the contest by a heavenly gift.

From that point, encouraging her husband with firmer hope, she taught him to strip himself entirely of earthly things, since from the beginning of the world they had been dedicated to heavenly military service and, immediately after victory, would be admitted among the inhabitants of heaven.

### 15

From then on they burned more and more with an ardent desire to enjoy the Redeemer and to join their holy companions. Setting aside affection for their children, they despised whatever the world’s perishing appearance contains. They sold everything; leaving some portion of the price to the little children, they devoted all the rest to the support of the needy.

They visited the monasteries of men and women, especially the monastery of Tabanos, about which we shall speak more fully, because it shone with the strict rules of monastic discipline and the whole of honourable conduct. From there our strongest athletes drew their instruction; from there they learned their practices; there they drank deeply from the cup of eternal life. There the most holy Sabigotho often stayed with the handmaids of God; there they placed the two children under the protection of the blessed women.

### 16

O wondrous renunciation of the world, and admirable divine ardour: the love of children is rejected, abundance of wealth is resisted, the sweetness of relatives is refused, death is chosen instead of life, and all passing things are despised. With the eyes fixed upon eternal happiness, bonds, chains, crosses, prisons, blows, and tortures are regarded as the highest delights!

One of the daughters was eight years old; the other was five. After the death of their parents, I found the younger one barely able to express words with her tender mouth. She urged me with childish speech to write down and publish the deeds of her parents and to labour over their trophies.

When I asked her what favour I might expect from her in return, she replied—and I shall relate something marvellous, namely, that such an age could perceive such things, unless we should believe that she had been instructed inwardly by him who perfects praise from the mouth of infants and nursing children (Psalm 8:3):

“I shall obtain paradise for you, father, from the Lord.”

[Note: Morales and Schott printed this reading; Sollerius, however, reads *instantissime*. Paulinus of Nola, in a letter [21], calls a very young child *infantium infantissimus*; Prudentius calls himself *infantissimum* in the hymn of the Roman martyr. The word here seems to mean “most inarticulate,” following the usage of the age.]

[Note: The divine ardour by which affection for children is rejected, abundance of wealth resisted, the sweetness of relatives refused, death chosen instead of life, and all passing things despised; by which, with the gaze fixed upon eternal happiness, bonds, chains, crosses, prisons, blows, and tortures are regarded as the highest delights.]

### 17

But because, on a suitable occasion, in order to discuss the little girls, we have departed somewhat from the direct order so that we might insert the event that occurred nine months after their martyrdom, we have now incorporated it into the history, which still suffers under worldly troubles.

For this reason, fraternal criticism ought not to defame us, since we do not fear being convicted of fault by the Lord. Nor does it matter whether the truth is discussed at the end, at the beginning, or in the middle, since the defender of truth is in no way deprived of blessing.

Therefore, retracing our steps, let us hasten more diligently to report the remaining deeds of the blessed.

### 18

While they were intent upon heavenly things and constantly occupied with vigils, prayers, almsgiving, and fasts—although they were often sprinkled by a heavenly star in the chamber where they meditated upon these things, so that the radiance of the heavenly light, falling upon it and eclipsing the appearance of every present luminary, compelled one to declare the surrounding darkness horrible by comparison—they were frequently raised up by divine revelations and enjoyed conversations with angels; united in mind and spirit with the joy of the inhabitants of heaven, they bore the burden of the body not without grievous distress.

[Note: The word is discussed in the Glossary. Neither Paulinus nor Eulogius, if he wrote it thus, seems to provide this sense; nevertheless, this appears to be the meaning. For that reason the Glossary of Du Cange should have assigned another sense to the word, immediately explaining Paulinus’s expression.]

[scan page 398]

## Memorial of the Saints — Book II

785

One day, when I had asked to meet our most renowned teacher Aivarus—praised throughout the West for his knowledge of all Scripture—in order to exchange views and instruct my mind through alternating questions concerning difficult passages of Scripture, I found with him the soldier of Christ, Aurelius. He was seeking advice about his contest and asking how he might undertake the beginning of martyrdom.

That distinguished teacher, the fountain of wisdom of our age, instructed him through the examples of the Fathers. He ordered him first to weigh the strength of his constancy, to examine his secret intention, to consider the hidden purpose, and to determine whether he knew better how to endure the punishments that threatened him than to avoid them. Finally, he was to be prepared to receive the sword upon his delicate neck.

He was to consider whether he sought rather to attain the merits of martyrs than to be called a martyr; whether, remaining unknown on earth, he preferred to have himself entered in the catalogue of the elect because of his flourishing merits in heaven, rather than to crave the famous name of temporal martyrdom with a diminished heavenly reward.

[Note: I cannot be sufficiently surprised that Sollerius slipped here so far as to add “Tovar” after “Aivarus,” conjecturing that this was a second name or surname of Aivarus. The cause of the error is very clear. In the Frankfurt edition of the *Hispania Illustrata*, page 272 ends in the first syllable of *Aivari*, while the remaining syllables continue on the following page, which begins: “vari toto in Scripturarum scientia…” The syllable *A-* had beneath it the ordinary typographical mark which we call a catchword, namely the beginning of the following page, intended to prevent mistakes in setting the pages. Sollerius read that catchword as part of the text and consequently printed “Alvari Tovari.”]

[Note: The editor further observes that the scholia of our Morales on the Acts of these martyrs were wrongly attributed to André Schott; it is correctly noted that Morales’s subsequent explanation of *collatio* as “conversation” or “association” is superfluous, since the word is not obscure.]

### 19

Then he promised that he would fight to the death and declared that no force of tortures could overcome his purpose.

“For me,” he said, “for me Christ is the greatest gain of life, and death is gain. To one for whom earthly life is the darkness of a most dreadful night, the memory of the world’s passing breathes the fragrance of perpetual light.”

Thereafter a common joy arose because of my arrival; we rejoiced greatly at seeing one another. We believed that the Word of the Most High Father was present in our consultation, since he testified that he enters every gathering dedicated to his name, saying: “Wherever two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matthew 18:20).

When we had related further matters appropriate to his contest, and he had received our instruction with the greatest gratitude, he was, as I believe, sufficiently strengthened by our conversation. Immediately undertaking the battles of the Lord, he returned to his own place.

### 20

A few days before her passion, the blessed Sabigotho was sitting alone in the house and was imploring Christ, through whatever petitions she could offer, for the perfection of her martyrdom. Suddenly she saw a virgin of marvellous beauty standing before her, endowed with angelic grace and, as she thought, displaying the first flower of adolescence.

She said to her:

“Who are you, daughter? And if you come from nearby, explain the reason for your arrival.”

At once the splendid virgin replied:

“I am the daughter of your friend Montesisa, whom you know to have been removed long ago from worldly troubles, and whom, at the very hour when she was suffering her last agonies, before you came nearer, you found lifeless.

“Although, when you had almost been removed from the world, I did not know you, nevertheless, at the very moment of my death, when the Lord revealed to me who you were, I recognized you.

“Now, sent by him, I have come beforehand as the messenger of your palm. For the time of winning victory is already pressing upon you; the days are at hand for publicly confessing the Catholic faith and repelling the most foul enemy. When these conflicts have been settled, the inner chambers of heaven will receive you to be crowned and thereafter established in perpetual peace.”

### 21

The venerable woman therefore searched her heart and pondered the words of the one who stood before her. Immediately, as her memory returned, she recognized the event that had occurred. Before she could give thanks to the girl who had brought her this Gospel, the virginal figure, messenger from heaven and herald of her martyrdom, slipped from her sight.

She rejoiced at such a proclamation; she was encouraged by the heavenly oracle; and she was stirred to battle with a hope all the firmer because she saw herself instructed by the truth of an event that had already taken place.

### 22

But so that they might direct themselves ever more closely toward the goal of their predestination and might be certain of the reward laid up for them—and so that the decree of the holy virgins might be fulfilled—the confessor promised long before was admitted into their company eight days before their arrest. Bound to them, as it were, in an unshakable union, he was crowned together with them in a blessed martyrdom at one and the same moment.

For this reason we judged it appropriate to explain the account of that monk, since the opportunity arose, and to entrust to later generations something worthy of being read because of the intense admiration with which his case shook our age. Thus the piety of Catholics may be increased in faith by seeing fulfilled, in a special manner, the oracle of their Redeemer.

For our teacher and Lord had foretold that many would come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 8:11). We behold this testimony perfectly fulfilled in the monk and levite George.

### 23

He was born in Bethlehem, and foreign shores provided him with a heavenly homeland. This man, born beyond the seas, had delighted in the service of God from adolescence. For twenty-seven years he lived under regular discipline with five hundred brothers in the monastery of Saint Sabas, which lies eight miles from Jerusalem on its southern side.

As he himself told us, the venerable abbot David, then administrator of that monastery, sent him to Africa to obtain the monks’ support. George did not in any way shrink from undertaking the dangers imposed by the great distances of land and sea, through which he knew that he could promptly merit the highest reward of virtue through obedience.

But when he found the Church of God there suffering harshly from the assaults of tyrants, he also approached Spain, in accordance with the purpose of those by whom he had been sent. For, as we established with absolute certainty concerning him, he was a man of the greatest humility and of great abstinence.

In all his speech, words, and replies, the fear of the Lord resounded. Always drawing charity quickly from a pure fountain of the heart, he brought forth the honeycomb of love. He preached that the compunction of heavenly desire must be sought. He commanded them to mortify their limbs together with their vices and desires, so that, when the Lord came, they might appear more glorious with the renewed strength of virtues.

Although endowed with sober holiness, he utterly refused to appear or even to be called righteous. He was exceedingly pleasant, cheerful, modest, and abstinent, using the world as though he did not use it.

If, sometimes, fraternal love compelled him to take food, he ate sparingly and drank temperately, so that you would judge him more abstinent than a diner. He diluted wine with water until its colour was spoiled and its taste disappeared. For, as he said, that tasteless drink permits neither excessive drinking nor drunkenness at a banquet.

He frequently hurried to pray, kept more attentive vigils, and more often meditated upon the divine song in his heart. He used to say:

“I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise will always be in my mouth” (Psalm 33:2).

Although he was skilled in various languages—Greek, Latin, and Arabic—he did not seek any kind of glory on account of them. From the day on which he entered the monastery and joined the company of monks until the crown of his martyrdom, as he privately related to certain people, he neither washed with water nor used baths.

During the entire time he lived among us, he revealed his order to no one, except when he was already being held in prison.

### 24

He composed for his brothers, his relatives, and all his fellow countrymen a brief account of his martyrdom, which he sent to me so that I might polish it, lest its unrefined language deprive the events described of credibility. At the beginning of his account he testified that he was a monk and a levite.

But why prolong the narrative? Does not the martyr’s blood itself show the highest reverence for the life of the man of God, especially when it indicates how great and what kind of person he was?

His martyr’s blood, poured out for the justice of God, proclaims that, a stranger to the world, he did not refuse a foreign burial and wholly rejected every attachment to his native soil and relatives.

Or who could praise the soldier of Christ more fittingly than the one who gave death for the Lord, his soul for life, and blood for the Crucified One? Thus the redemption of the servant was itself the victory of the Crucified One.

[Note: Sollerius correctly understands this to refer to alms for the support of the monks, which are here called their *stipendium*, or provision.]

[Note: That he crossed from Africa to Spain by sea.]

### 25

But how the blessed minister was joined to the company of the saints, we believe can best be made known through the words of Saint George himself. In this way, either the sequence of our writing may be seasoned, as it were, with the salt of blessing from above through the insertion of the martyr’s speech, or we may learn more fully, from his own account, the character of his association with the other saints.

For during the very days in which he lived with the saints, he set down in a sufficiently brief style the deeds of himself and the aforementioned martyrs and finally sent the account to us for approval. We have therefore taken care to insert his words into this work, since we foresaw that they would sufficiently indicate their union.

The other matters that follow after the servant of God’s own words we investigated according to the purpose with which we began. He speaks as follows:

“In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. To the whole Catholic Church: from me, the unworthy and sinful George, a monk and also a deacon, brother and companion of the servants of God, the sons of Saint Sabas, five hundred men: perfect salvation in the Lord Jesus Christ.

“Know, dearest brothers, that my entry into Spain had no other purpose than the grace of seeking your support. You live under the strictest rule and under the governance of the holy father David in Jerusalem. Sent by you to Africa, I later migrated to Spain.

“But when I found this very island exceedingly afflicted, I began to be troubled by various thoughts, considering whether I should revisit my native land or seek the kingdoms of the Christians, that is, France. When I consulted my nearest and dearest friends about this matter, some ordered me to travel onward, while most urged me to return to my monastery.

“Thus, uncertain and hindered by conflicting advice, I did not know which thought I should follow first. As I was travelling from Córdoba to the monastery of Tabanos, so that the blessing of the brothers and sisters might accompany my journey, that abbot, Martin, and his sister, the lady Elisabeth, said to me:

“‘Come, brother, and receive the blessing of the handmaid of God, Sabigotho.’

“As soon as she saw me, she said:

“‘This monk will be the companion and colleague promised for our contest.’”

### 26

“When I had understood her cause and learned the circumstances, I immediately fell at her feet and asked her to pray to the Lord for me, so that, perhaps enlightened by the regard of the Holy Spirit, I might be deemed worthy to attain what she was expecting.

“And she said:

“‘How is this fitting for us, father, that you should go with sinners?’

“When I had remained there that night, the venerable woman Sabigotho appeared to me in a vision of the night, and …”

[Note: The expression is a *catacrisis* of the language of those times, of which there are many elsewhere. Morales.]

[Note: *Minis*—Sollerius.]

[The supplied source ends here.]

## Memorial

### Chapter X

#### 26

I do not know what sort of fragrance, prepared from the most precious wood, he was bearing. A richer treasure than this is mine. When morning came, we both descended into the city to her husband Aurelius. I fell at his feet, asking him to pray for me, since I wished to be his companion in martyrdom. He immediately gave his assent, and through their prayers a heavenly fire blazed within me; I became one of them. From that time I was not separated from them, but all of us gathered together in the house of Saint Aurelius joyfully rendered to the Lord the vows of our praise.

There I found blessed Felix with his most holy wife Liliosa. They too had already sold all their possessions and distributed them among holy places or the poor, ready to endure every kind of torture for the Son of God and to receive it out of love for him.

At that very hour I went away from them and, with all haste, arranged the matters that had hindered me. Thus, finally greatly strengthened, I returned to them. They, delighted and exultant at our return, gave thanks to God, saying: “We know, dearest brother, that the Lord has sent you to us.”

#### 27

“After this, we all began together to consider how we might reach the desired crown. By the Lord’s arrangement, it seemed best to us that our sisters should go to the church with their faces unveiled, in case an opportunity might be given for us to be arrested. And so it happened.

For when the women were returning from the church, a certain official came to meet them. Recognizing in the women the cause of their religious observance, he immediately asked the men what this return of women from the sanctuaries of the Christians meant.

They answered: ‘It is the custom of the faithful to visit the churches and to seek the shrines of the venerable Martyrs with pious devotion. Since we are Christians, we therefore profess that we bear the banner of that faith.’

Immediately an informer approached the judge and, with deceitful words, laid our whole case before him. After this, Lord Aurelius went to visit his daughters. Having blessed them with the kiss of peace, and armed with heavenly power, he hastened to the battle.”

But here Saint Eulogius restrains his pen and asks us to continue with what remains.

#### 28

On the very day when blessed Aurelius learned that he had been arrested, before the first breath of dawn, he revisited our house to bid us farewell. He begged us to pray to the Lord for him and requested our fraternal charity as an aid to his contest.

There we commended him to God. We asked and obtained from him, by kissing his hands, that he make himself our patron and the patron of the whole Church. After exchanging kisses, we separated in peace.

#### 29

When the judge brought forward the charge against the saints of God, and knew that Aurelius was the author of this affair, he was deeply wounded inwardly by it and ordered them to be brought before him as quickly as possible.

Then the soldiers, rushing swiftly, occupied the house of blessed Aurelius, where all the saints were gathered. Standing at the doors, they began to shout:

“Get out, wretched men; come forth, you who are going to die, for whom this present life is a burden and death is counted as glory. Behold, the judge is calling you; he is intent on pouring out the decree of vengeance. He wishes to crush those who have turned away from the worship and is prepared to sever the necks of rebels. Go now and pay the debt of death, and endure the sentence due for your transgression.”

#### 30

The men then came forth with their wives as though invited to a banquet. They went rejoicing and sprang forward happily. You would have thought that they were already going to find gifts before the judge, although they could expect nothing but torments.

When Saint Georgius saw that the soldiers were not holding him, he immediately took courage and turned to reproach the executioners:

“Why,” he said, “do you inflict this privilege upon the faithful and violently compel those whom holy faith has hitherto protected to worship a worthless deity? Why do you seek to heap upon your own destruction those who are alien to the true God and predestined to life? Will you be unable to enter the gates of hell unless you have us as companions? Will eternal torments not burn you without us?

“Go away; proceed thither to perish, so that together with your leader you may enjoy the delights of the underworld. For what have we to do with Tartarus, which Christ our God entered, stripped, and conquered, so that it no longer dared to hand over the faithful, although formerly it had been accustomed, by its privilege, to plunder the saints?”

#### 31

He had scarcely finished speaking when the right hand of the raging attendants began to assail the monk. They tore him with various goads, threw him to the ground, and beat him fiercely with kicks and fists.

When Saint Sabigotho thought him already dead, she cried: “Rise, brother; let us go!” He, as though he had suffered no harm, replied: “All these things, sister, are beneficial to our merits and increase the crown.”

They lifted him, half-dead, from the ground and, in the same escort as the saints, brought him to stand before the judge.

When they had been presented, the judge first addressed them gently, asking for what reason they had withdrawn from his worship, refused to live, and tried to destroy the advantage of temporal prosperity, which blossomed with many delights. He reminded them that afterward they would be awaited not only by the marvelous pleasure of women, but also by the allurements of honors and the abundance of banquets.

Immediately, as though with one voice, they replied:

“No abundance of the present age, O judge, can be compared with the eternal rewards for whose sake we despise this life through the faith of Jesus Christ, by which every worker of holiness is justified. In the future we trust that we shall possess the blessed rest promised to the saints.

“But every worship that disagrees with the divinity of Christ, that does not confess the essence of the Holy Trinity, rejects baptism, dishonors Christians, and diminishes the priesthood, we judge altogether reprobate. We count as nothing the things that pass away and do not long endure.

“What Christ has promised to those who love him is ineffable, yet it endures forever with unwearied constancy. It is neither contemplated by the eyes, nor grasped by the ears, nor weighed by the heart.”

But, as I believe, while the saints were asserting something still more religious with open speech before the judge and vigorously attacking the sect of the impious, the judge was provoked to the utmost fury. He ordered them to be taken rapidly to prison and burdened with unbearable chains.

#### 32

Immediately, with exultant hearts, the blessed martyrs entered the prison. They rejoiced at the beginning of their passion, despised the punishment, resounded with hymns, uttered praises, recited psalms, and persevered in prayer, by which, with the Lord’s favor, they might prevail in attaining victory.

They were visited by angels and made illustrious by miracles. Their chains burst apart and did not dare to restrain those whom Christ had released. There also, God revealing what portion they would have in heaven, they came to know their destiny.

Remaining secure in the palm of victory and eagerly longing to see Christ, whom they had faithfully served, they prolonged their death until the fifth day. They considered themselves too long separated from the sweetness of the kingdom of heaven, which they had already almost seen through frequent bodily experiences.

#### 33

When they were being led out to be thrown down in the forum, the venerable Sabigotho began to arm her husband with holy exhortations. She encouraged, instructed, and strengthened him.

They were brought into the palace and stood before the magistrates. Wealth was offered, and the official insignia were displayed, promising that they might enjoy these things if they believed. But because they remained steadfast in their profession, the magistrates instructed the executioners to kill them.

They decided that Saint Georgius should be allowed to depart unharmed, because those same nobles and leading men of the palace had heard him utter no insult against their prophet. But that excellent servant, as soon as he realized that he was being abandoned and would not be killed by the same sword-stroke as his companions, said:

“Why, O princes, do you hesitate over my profession, which I have not stated before you, or suppose that I can think anything favorable about Satan’s disciple? For, so that you may recognize the truth more clearly, I believe that the angel who appeared to that teacher of yours, transforming himself into an angel of light, was a demon. I judge him lower than all men, as one credulous of the devil, a minister of Antichrist, and a labyrinth of every vice.

“He has not only plunged himself into the abyss of the pit, but has also devoted you, his followers, to eternal fires through his empty institutions.”

#### 34

Then the nobles, driven into madness, ordered that he be killed together with the others, by one and the same sentence.

Thus they first slaughtered blessed Felix, then Saint Georgius, and afterward the venerable Liliosa. Finally they killed the distinguished champions Aurelius and Sabigotho, on the sixth day before the Kalends of August, in the year 890 of the era.

Our Christians secretly carried away their bodies and concealed them in various places. Georgius and Saint Aurelius are preserved in the monastery of Pilemelaria. Blessed Felix guards the church of Saint Christopher, which lies beyond the river. Saint Sabigotho has been joined to the ashes of the three saints. Venerable Liliosa rests with the martyr Genesius. The heads of Georgius and Sabigotho reside [the location is absent from the supplied text].

#### 35

These are those who, fighting to the death for the testimony of God and the faith of Jesus Christ, preferred nothing to his love: neither sons, nor parents, nor relatives, nor neighbors, nor friends, nor possessions, nor villages, nor estates, nor farms.

Casting everything behind them and putting their bodies to death together with their vices and desires, they were led forth to eternal immortality.

Our Lord Jesus Christ reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## Chapter XI

### Christophorus and Leovigildus, monk-martyrs

#### 1

Next came Christophorus, our fellow citizen, a young man born at Córdoba and, from childhood, our disciple. After our instruction, he entered the monastery of Saint Martin, situated in the Cordoban mountains at a place called Aojana, and offered a great example of holiness to those who wished to live a pious life.

When he learned of the death of the preceding saints, he descended rapidly into the city and did not fear to meet the judge. Giving testimony before him to the truth, he proclaimed the Gospel, preached the holy things of the Lord, exhorted the populace devoted to profanations, and warned those who believed wrongly that, together with their false author, they would suffer eternal fire.

The judge, immediately stirred by savage anger, assigned him to prison and handed him over to be tormented in tighter chains.

#### 2

At that time Leovigildus, a monk and the firstborn of Eliber, also came forward. He was in the fullness of youth, a holy, just, and God-fearing man from the monastery of Saints Justus and Pastor, situated in the inner Cordoban mountains, at a place called Fraga, amid the mountains and dense forests, near the boundary of the district of Lejulense. It lies five miles from Córdoba.

He had recently withdrawn there to remain for a time, but came in order to obtain martyrdom. Before entering the forum, he sought us out so that we might instruct him. He begged and earnestly requested that we assist his efforts with our prayers and give him our blessing for the completion of his contest, promising that he would care for us before the Lord.

When he had departed from us in peace, strengthened by our blessing, he soon stood before the judge to make his profession. There he gave testimony to the faith with the same steadfastness as the others. He was struck with blows and insults and was immediately handed over to the savage prison to be bound.

There the servants of God encouraged one another with everlasting counsel and were strengthened in mutual support. When the hour of slaughter was approaching, Saint Christophorus wished, out of respect for age, that blessed Leovigildus should go before him; afterward he himself would fall.

And so, in this order, both died, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the same year as above. Their bodies were placed beneath fires, but before they were completely burned, the care of the faithful rescued them and buried them beside the basilica of Saint Zoilus.

*The date agrees in Usuard, Ado, Equilinus, and the breviary of Córdoba.*

*Perhaps: “learning” or “being instructed.”*

*Morales says that the village is now unknown; but almost everyone knows it. On this subject Henricus Florez should be consulted, volume XII of Hispania Sacra, treatise 37, chapter 6, number 247. Parapanda is a Greek word which, according to the same author, means “to all things” in Latin.*

## Chapter XII

### Emila and Jeremias, martyrs

After a short interval, two distinguished young men from among the citizens of Córdoba, born of noble families, came forward together for the arena of martyrdom: Emila and Jeremias.

From childhood they had been taught letters at the basilica of Saint Cyprian. One had been ordained to the ministry of the deaconate; the other lived simply in the lay habit.

Since both were exceptionally proficient in the Arabic language, it is said that Emila, through the fluency of that language, heaped such outstanding insults upon their prophet that the reproaches of the preceding martyrs were forgotten. They saw that these men’s attacks against their dogmatist were more forceful.

For this reason they began to devise not merely the deaths of those who resisted them, but also the destruction of the whole Church. The pagan population had been shaken by the immense terror caused by so many people coming forward for martyrdom, and they thought that the destruction of their kingdom was imminent when they saw even young men girded with such courage.

After tormenting them in prison, they finally killed them with the avenging sword.

The whole day had been bright with clear weather. Suddenly, at the very hour when they were beheaded, a violent crash of thunder rose up and struck the world. The sky scattered flashes as bright as lamps; one might have thought that the upper regions were being torn apart. The sky was armed with a cloud of hail; the day grew dark, and the air was disfigured by whirlwinds. The elements themselves confessed that pious champions had fallen.

They suspended their bodies on racks and set them beyond the river, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October, in the same year as above.

## Chapter XIII

### On the martyrs Rogelius and Servus Dei

#### 1

While the aforementioned martyrs were still being held in prison, two others arrived. They held the same profession as the others and, with the same resolve, attacked the enemy of the faith.

One of them, Rogelius, was born of Eliber, from a village called Parapanda. He was a monk and a eunuch, already advanced in age.

The other, called Servus Dei, was still a young eunuch. A few years earlier he had come as a foreigner from the regions of the East, across the seas, to live in the aforementioned city.

These two bound themselves together by an equal covenant and undertook the resolve of fighting to the death for the justice of God, never to withdraw from one another until they had purchased heavenly things with their blood.

Therefore they went to that temple of the sacrilegious people, where the common crowd was accustomed to gather and perform its detestable rites. They crossed the threshold, mingled with the crowds, preached the Gospel, mocked and reproved the sect of impiety, and announced that the kingdom of heaven had drawn near for the faithful, while destruction in Gehenna awaited unbelievers—a fate they themselves would certainly incur unless they returned to life.

#### 2

They were still exhorting the people with these and similar words when the speech had scarcely left their mouths. Then, behold: like a fire crackling among thorns, a band of evildoers blazed against the servants of God. They cut, struck, beat, overwhelmed, and tried to kill the saints who had dared to enter their sanctuary, an act which they too regarded as a great crime.

Unless the judge had been present and, by a certain privilege of his authority, restrained the uproar of the maddened crowd, they would then have deprived them of the breath of life.

The judge rescued them from the hands of the attackers, assigned them to prison, ordered them to be bound with heavier iron, and placed them among thieves.

There they continued to preach and prophesy. They announced that death was approaching for the tyrant, praised religion, and refuted vanity. Even when their bodily strength had completely failed and they could no longer endure punishment, their tongues did not cease, until death, to proclaim the oracle of truth.

Because they had entered the temple while preaching the Gospel, the tyrant and the magistrates decreed that they should first have their hands and feet cut off and then be beheaded.

The servants of Christ rejoiced at this decree and were exceedingly glad to receive such a sentence of death. The most savage executioner approached. He shouted, raged, wondered, and ordered the chosen men to hasten toward punishment. He saw that they had a greater desire to depart than he had to inflict death.

Who could describe, dearest brothers, the cruelty of that hour? Who could recount the disasters? Who could announce the crosses? Who could finally narrate the marvelous steadfastness of the saints? Even the pagan population, stunned by such a spectacle, was beginning to think more favorably of Christianity.

#### 3

When the holy martyrs had been stationed at the place of execution, before the executioner gave the signal, they stretched out their palms and prepared their arms. They received the sword placed against their necks between their arms and extended their hands in opposite directions.

Then, after their legs had been cut off, they fell without any sorrowful complaint when their necks too had been severed.

They fastened their mutilated corpses to crosses and joined them to the crosses of the others beyond the river, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the same year as above.

*That is, a magistrate.*

*That is, a sword or axe.*

## Chapter XIV

### The council for destroying the Christians, which the king held with the nobles

Moreover, the pagans were thrown into confusion because of the martyrs, and the king himself was driven into a frenzy of rage. He considered various plans by which he might suppress the determination of the saints.

He consulted the wise, questioned the philosophers, and asked the magistrates of his kingdom about the matter. All of them, conspiring unanimously for the destruction of the faithful, decreed that the Christians should be arrested and bound in the strictest prisons.

From then on, the task of killing them was certainly made easier, if no rash reprover of the prophet appeared again.

When we unfortunate men learned of this plan, we fled, departed, wandered about, and hid ourselves. With fearful movements and changed clothing, we made our way through the silence of night. As the leaves fell, we were driven from place to place; we frequently changed our lodgings, sought safer locations, and scattered trembling in every direction, fearing to die by the sword, although destined to die at some point by the debt we owed.

We therefore perhaps avoided martyrdom, not because we fear death, which will come in due course, but because we are unworthy of martyrdom, which is granted to some and not to all.

For those who are now being martyred, and those who are to be martyred, were marked out from the beginning of the world. As the Apostle says:

“Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Romans 8:29–30).

## Chapter XV

### The disturbance among the Christians and their various opinions at the council of bishops assembled at Córdoba

#### 1

Many, therefore, useless for the Lord’s granary and cast outside the apostolic net, deserved to be stored not as good vessels but rather, like straw, to be consigned to an extinguishable fire. They refused either to flee with us, to suffer with us, or even to hide themselves.

They abandoned piety, betrayed the faith, renounced religion, and detested the Crucified One. Alas, surrendering themselves to impiety, they bowed their necks to demons, blasphemed, slandered, and subverted the Christians.

Many others, both priests and laymen, who formerly with sound judgment proclaimed the victories of the martyrs with us, praised their steadfastness, extolled their triumphs, and magnified their contest, changed their opinions. They now thought and judged differently and declared indiscreet those whom they had previously affirmed to be most blessed.

They did this because the saints, unwilling to show compassion to the weaker, had preferred the advantage of their own tranquility and peace, which they believed they could purchase in heaven with blood, to the safety of the Church amid the reefs of the faithless. They tried to strengthen their change of speech and their shifting tongue with certain little maxims drawn from the Law.

They did not consider that no one marked out for such a great military service and enrolled among the heavenly host could, when the hour of his calling came, be held back by mortal bonds. For every day in the sacred Scriptures they read with us that neither life, nor savage dangers, nor even death itself can ever prevail to separate the saints from the love of our Lord Jesus Christ (Romans 8:35 and following).

#### 2

But those who from the beginning had never ceased to defame the saints, and who tried through foul whispering to overturn their purpose, turned against us with cruelty the war that they had been unable to wage against the glorious soldiers.

They asserted that we were the authors of this affair and accused us of having caused everything to be carried out at our instigation.

Among them was a certain public official of that period, powerful in vices and riches, known only by the name of Christian but unknown in his works to God and his angels. From the beginning he had been hostile to the contests of the blessed: a detractor, a disparager, and a defamer of them; unjust, arrogant, haughty, proud, and shameless.

One day, in the presence of the assembled council of bishops, he moved his tongue and heaped many insults upon me. He decreed that those who thought such things should be anathematized, ordered them to be cursed, and demanded that the chosen be persecuted—this most wretched of men, fearing that he might suffer any loss of honor.

He not only made no effort to show reverence to the saints, but also ordered that what they were doing among the people should be proclaimed wrong.

#### 3

Although, driven by fear—or by the judgment of the metropolitan bishops, who had then been gathered from various provinces by the king—we might have composed something that would reach the ears of that tyrant and the people, the letters themselves announced that martyrdom had been prohibited and that no one was henceforth permitted to enter the arena of profession, a pontifical decree having first been issued.

The same document, while in no way attacking the contest of those who had died, was understood to praise future soldiers commendably. Nevertheless, since it had been published allegorically, its meaning could not be perceived except by the prudent.

We do not, however, think that this was blameless advice disguised in this way, since, saying one thing while carrying another, it seemed to restrain the people from the martyrial course. Indeed, we confess that it must by no means be forgiven, even for the sake of the people, unless due satisfaction is made.

## Chapter XVI

### King ʿAbd al-Raḥmān suddenly dies; his son Muḥammad succeeds him in the kingdom

#### 1

Finally, when destruction threatened the Christians from every side, and the ruler’s threat, driven by monstrous fury, compelled many of the chosen to go astray, many reproached us with that Israelite complaint which they made when they saw themselves being oppressed more severely:

“May the Lord see and judge, for you have made our sweat offensive before this tyrant and his servants, and you have handed them the sword so that they might kill us.”

As the number of martyrs increased, so too did the ruler’s anger increase, and the disturbance among the faithful grew. Our situation almost seemed comparable to the ancient persecutions of Pharaoh against Israel.

Just as the Egyptians, because of Moses’ intervention with Pharaoh on behalf of God’s people, raged more fiercely and oppressed their subjects with the unbearable calamity of the heaviest labors, so we too, from the time when the saints went forth to battle in order to speak in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ before the king, magistrates, and judges, to profess the evangelical truth and expose the falsehood of the wicked prophet, have been overthrown more harshly than usual and pursued to utter destruction by the ministers of demons.

#### 2

When we groaned repeatedly under such great distress, while we ourselves were hiding and wandering about, and when the pontiff was again handed over to the dreadful pit of the prisons, no noble layman dared to approach the doors, fearing that on the following day he too would be imprisoned, the king began to climb to the upper part of his residence.

He ascended the high rooftop in order to survey the city. Immediately he saw, opposite him, the bodies of the saints hanging from stakes.

At once he ordered them to be burned beneath fires. Their ashes, by God’s favor, were placed in holy sites.

O admirable power of the Savior, and wondrous strength of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is always present in tribulation when sought, opens when struck, and hears when invoked!

For that mouth which had ordered the saints of God to be burned was suddenly closed by divine power at that very hour. His tongue, struck by an angel, was restrained and clung to his palate; he could speak no further.

Thus, carried back in the hands of those bearing him and laid upon a bed, he gave up his spirit at some hour of that very night, before the fire consuming the bodies of the saints had gone out. He too was removed from this life and consigned to eternal punishment.

He left as successor to the empire his firstborn Muḥammad, an enemy of God’s Church and a hostile persecutor of Christians. Driven by an inborn hatred, he often brought charges against the faithful and proved himself in merit no inferior to the man whose name he bore.

On the very day when he obtained the royal scepter, he ordered the Christians expelled from the palace, deprived them of dignity, and stripped them of honor. He planned to inflict many further evils upon us if he attained prosperity and favorable success in his kingdom.

But as the end of this little work approaches, let us place the hope of our safety in the Lord and not fear what man can do to us. We believe that we are saved everywhere through the intercession of our advocate, our Lord Jesus Christ, who said:

“Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

Amen.

## Supplication to the Lord Jesus Christ by the same Eulogius, as a completion of the little book, or concerning every fault committed in this work

Behold, O Lord my God, Alpha and Omega, beginning and end, our true Emmanuel, the beginning of my life, the fullness of my soul, and the perfection of my salvation.

Set aflame by your zeal, compelled by love for your saints, constrained by affection for the brethren, moved by compassion for those who take little account of themselves, and stirred by hatred of your enemies, I—so small in knowledge, so limited in talent, so weak in understanding, yet magnanimous in contemplating your goodness and mercy, relying on your piety and strengthened by your clemency—with your assistance have undertaken, completed, and brought to an end this work, as I was able, not as I ought, but rather as you granted me the ability.

I opened my mouth, O Lord, and spoke because you commanded. Whatever you willed, you fulfilled, and you compelled a heart cast down by iniquity to recount the most righteous deeds of your righteous ones.

You armed a tongue impeded by crimes to proclaim your praises. You opened my mouth, which the bolt of vices had long closed, suddenly endowing it with a certain ardor to labor over your faithful testimonies.

I feared my works, O Lord my God, and remained anxious about my own crime. Although I postponed the remedy of correction, I nevertheless reflected upon my iniquities, having often tested the testimony against myself. I weighed the judgment and considered the vengeance owed for my guilt.

When my terrified mind recognized that the knowledge of its deed remained with you, burdened by offenses, it scarcely dared to raise its eyes to heaven.

Yet you deign to impel my tongue, as though suited to your ministries, to set in order the heavenly mysteries.

For although I attempted, with my scant merits, to construct the material of so great a merit; although, being unclean, I discussed what is clean; and although, being sordid, I arranged the holy of holies, I did this not supported by the swelling of pride, but in humility and lowliness, in the hope of acquiring rewards and obtaining the patronage of the saints.

Or at least I did it so that I would not be ungrateful before you for the talent entrusted to me, and so that matters worthy of heaven might not, without anyone to support them, be handed over to everlasting oblivion.

You, O Lord my God, knew my affection, penetrated my intention, understood my vow, and were not ignorant of the reason why I undertook such reflections.

You gave inspiration to one so small, assisted a most wretched effort, raised the weak to great things, and made the feeble courageous.

For I never supposed, O Lord my God, that I had been chosen for such great things, so that I would finally become the author of the deeds of the saints, when I had been a serious perpetrator of sins.

If I lie, are you not my witness? If I assert what is false, do you not see it? If I affirm something otherwise than it happened, can you be unaware of it? If I do not speak the truth, it cannot be hidden from you, who know all things.

Certainly you consider everything, penetrate all things, understand what is secret, see the depths, and every mystery lies open before you. And all things, past and future, remain present to you, wholly in your [reading incomplete in the supplied text].

*Editorial notes:* At §26, Sollerius notes that *reddidimus* is undoubtedly to be read in place of the printed reading. At §29, the persons meant are certainly Aurelius and Felix, who had proceeded with their wives (Morales). At §32, the “frequent bodily experiences” are, as Morales explains, something like repeated trials or experiences.

At §34, Sollerius proposes that *Pilemelariensi* should be written, as Eulogius himself gives it in Book III, chapter 11. Schott reads *aulam* (“hall” or “church”) in the phrase concerning Saint Christopher. The reading concerning Sabigotho is correct: she was deposited in the basilica of Saints Faustus, Januarius, and Martialis. The bodies of Saints Georgius and Aurelius, together with the head of Pelagia, or Sabigotho, were translated from Córdoba to Paris in 858 by the Gallic monks Usuard and Odilard. Morales did not know of this translation; Mabillon published it from the monk Aimoin in the fourth century of the *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*, part 2, and it was thought fitting to transcribe it in an Appendix so that it should not be lacking from this edition.

For Chapter XI, the date agrees in Usuard, Ado, Equilinus, and the breviary of Córdoba (Morales). At “letters,” the editor suggests *addiscentes* (“learning”) rather than the printed *edocentes*. Morales says that Parapanda is now an unknown village, though almost everyone knows it; consult Henricus Florez, *Hispania Sacra*, vol. XII, treatise 37, chapter 6, no. 247. According to the same author, *Parapanda* is a Greek word which in Latin means “for all things.”

At the close of Chapter XIII, Morales notes that these martyrs were killed on the day after Emila and Jeremias and that no breviary commemorates them. At Chapter XIV, Morales explains that this was a concession permitted by the indulgence of divine law for the weaker persons and for those unequal to so dreadful a martyrdom. Against these people Eulogius argues more fully both in the first book and in the *Apologeticus*. At Chapter XVI, Morales explains that the noble Christians were staying at home and did not dare to set foot outside.

The heading of this supplication appears in this form in the exemplar, as does that of the following preface (Morales).

## [Scan page 405]

### Saint Eulogius, 799

…will be entered in the book. Whatever your inspiration prompted my mind to ponder, whatever the power of heavenly grace brought forth, whatever the spur of vain praise sought amid compunction, and whatever I involuntarily incurred there through a slip of the tongue—all these things remain stored up with you, and everything is written in the books of your examinations.

Therefore, returning to you, Lord my God, corrupted by varied wrongdoing, multiplied in crime, overflowing with iniquity, I beg, ask, and implore you: from that blessed seat of your unspeakable mercies, hear me as I plead; look upon me, stricken with terror; stand by me as I entreat, so that, first cleansing the hidden places of my heart, you may establish me always free in confessing you.

Then purify the finished work of this little book, if the subtle ambush of the tempter has, without my willing it, sprinkled it with any tares of perverse meaning; if, through my ignorance, it has sown any weeds of misguided exposition. Whatever error breathes there by chance, whatever sounds unpolished, whatever is alien to you, whatever is opposed to you and refutes your will, whatever does not know piety—teach all these things, my almighty God; wash everything clean, and sanctify the whole through purification, so that this work may be as acceptable to the Lord my God as it is most pleasing to your holy angels.

May it obtain your grace for me, draw the blessing of the saints, and secure peace for the Churches. May it present before you the condition of this age, recount before you the calamities of your people, and, turning your merciful regard upon the tablet on which I have written these things, wipe away every crime to which the tempter’s cunning, as before, enticed me when weakness yielded.

May it be the guardian of my crown, the protector of my life, and my guide to eternal rewards, so that, sanctified by you, it may be called the *Memorial of the Saints*, and that through its intercession you may inscribe me among the memories of your elect.

Through you, our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit are one God, eternal and immortal, for ever and ever. Amen.

### Book Three

Since the succession of the preceding volumes has abundantly set forth the cruelty of the impious, which for a long time strove to wear down the steadfastness of invincible men, and since it has traversed, in the true course of its account, the origins, ages, and warlike deeds of the saints, I think that this third book will reveal something even greater: the savagery committed against us, and not without immense injury.

Nor should anyone suppose that I am taking this opportunity to arrogate anything to myself because I have supplied so small—and, so to speak, so worthless—a support for so great a subject; or perhaps condemn us for not having worked out true events, since we constructed the structure of this work with the understanding that all things will one day be judged by the equity of the strict Judge, whom neither the hidden things of thoughts nor the quality of deeds can deceive.

For I know that each person lies subject to his own burden before the Lord. Why, then, would I wish to weigh down my own frail substance with the heavy external burden of such a task? Or what advantage could I hope to gain from a carefully composed falsehood, when I shall later have to render an account of every word?

Yet my slender knowledge is troubled by this: it attempts to irrigate a subject requiring the abundance not merely of a great river but even of an immeasurable sea, although it scarcely produces, sprinkling it with the sweat of a few drops, something like forced and extorted droplets of liquid.

Nor shall I hesitate to use the comparison of a weary traveler. Exhausted in bodily strength, he often sits down on the road and grows more fatigued the more frequently he is delayed in various places. So we, lacking every abundance of knowledge, sit as though with faltering speech and, proceeding with sluggish steps, scarcely touch the limit of our little works; everywhere we long to bring our discourse to an end.

Then the weakened traveler is shaken still more when, already rejoicing and hoping that the journey is nearly over, he suddenly sees an unforeseen stretch still remaining for him to complete. Thus we too, who believed that we had already finished our little work, and who were rejoicing as though we had crossed a stormy sea by rowing through a shipwreck and were safely enjoying the quiet of the desired harbor, now see that something else has fortuitously arisen which it is worthwhile to add to the preceding works.

We proceed, therefore—constrained by the poverty of our eloquence, occupied by the dangers of impending persecutions; and, as though a contrary wind had arisen, we are ashamed to find ourselves at last cast into the open sea.

Yet we trust that we shall prosper through the unfailing help of the goodness of him who judged us worthy to see and befriend those whose sweetness we enjoyed, so that we might also be instructed by their triumphs.

### Chapter One  
### The Beginning of the Reign of King Muhammad

As was noted at the end of the second work, once Muhammad had obtained his father’s empire, he immediately burst forth into open hatred against us. On the very day when, crowned with the emblems of office, he ascended the throne to reign alone, he dismissed all Christians from the palace and proclaimed them unworthy of the principal courtly service.
