After a short interval he again imposed upon them the status of tributaries, depriving many of the royal rewards with which they had previously been sustained from military provisions. And concerning the *scrinobilli*, the king’s Saracen recruits, it has already been said …

### [Editorial note]

In the account of the martyr Sanctio, concerning these Christians.

### Moral

## [Scan page 406]

### Moral

It is written: “As is the judge of the people, so also are his ministers” (*Ecclesiasticus* 10:2). At the same time he entrusted the government of the city to satraps of darkness who, seized by a similar zeal against God’s people, labored everywhere to afflict, overturn, and oppress them, so that they would not only presume in any way to disgrace their prophet but, compelled by fear, would also profess an abominable worship.

In the same way, an unbearable sorrow and savage persecution met us everywhere, and cast many into the snare of apostasy.

### Chapter Two  
### The Apostasy of That Exceptor Who Had Previously Compelled the Saints to Be Anathematized

Many, of their own accord turning away from Christ, joined the wicked and cherished the devil’s sect with the greatest affection. So did that illegitimate man, unworthy of the blessing of the saints, whom we mentioned in the second book and whose conduct we now relate.

He placed the pomp of worldly honor above heavenly things and, with unheard-of lust, revered office instead of God. Twelve months after he had decreed that the saints should be anathematized and had assailed us with filthy insults, he was stripped of his honor.

Because of the distinction of his command of the Arabic language—for he was exceptionally gifted in it—he alone among the Christians was retained by the consuls in the office of *exceptor*. After several months, however, he was dismissed both from the palace and from his ministry.

He did not bear this event lightly. Seeing himself deposed and sighing deeply because he had been deprived of so great a dignity, he preferred to die for God rather than live without the world’s esteem. He immediately spurned the faith of the Holy Trinity, yielded to the sect of perversity, and no longer wished to appear a Christian.

Thus turning toward worse things—he who had never meditated on anything straightforward—he became an exile from the Christians and joined the pagans. Frequently wandering about, he repeatedly entered that shrine of impiety, as though he were one of the devil’s ministers. He had been expelled from the temple of the Lord, which, while he was still faithful, he had inhabited through tardy and sluggish attendance.

For it is written: “He who practices arrogance shall not dwell in the midst of my house; and he who speaks unjustly has not been directed in the sight of my eyes” (*Psalm* 100:7).

After his denial, however, he was restored to his former honor and reinstated in the palace. He became a snare and a hook by which others there might be enticed, a cause of scandal in apostasy—he for whom temporal glory had itself become a trap.

### Chapter Three  
### The Destruction of the Basilicas

Meanwhile, as the savage conspiracy of the prince against God’s host increasingly grew and afflicted Christ’s people everywhere, and as not all had yet fallen away into his rite as he hoped, he ordered the destruction of the churches recently built. Whatever shone with new ornament in the ancient basilicas, and whatever had been added during the period of Arab rule in rough workmanship, he ordered to be demolished.

On this occasion, the satraps of darkness also seized and overthrew the roofs of those temples, which had been erected more than three hundred years after the city’s foundation.

### Chapter Four  
### The Revolt of the Provinces

Because rebellions were rising everywhere and great wars were causing him distress—for he had freely exercised dominion in all the cities of Spain, which his father had subdued and occupied through the strength of his power, the excellence of his intelligence, and the lavish distribution of rewards—especially when he saw his army defeated and put to flight in certain places, and everywhere feared that matters were turning for the worse, he delayed for the future the destruction long meditated against us and worked slowly and sluggishly at the ruin of the churches.

For I believe that he would have tolerated no Christians remaining with him, unless these obstacles of circumstance stood in the way. Indeed, as has already been stated elsewhere, if he had possessed a convenient freedom to reign, he would have compelled even the Jews to be driven from him. He would have deserved to be surrounded solely by the company of his own people and to rule only over those with whom he would suffer the punishments of the eternal abyss, without the unity of his damnable worship being divided by the diversity of another religion.

When, however, God called many away and pierced them through the shining mysteries of the holy faith, they withdrew and clung to piety, accepting death for Christ with firmer hope. He groaned over this, except for those who, impeded by excessive fear of the flesh, still serve Christ the King beneath the cloak of a difficult contrition of heart.

### Chapter Five  
### The Hatred of His Own People toward the King, His Avarice, and the Tributes Imposed upon the Christians

While he wasted away, inwardly consumed by the thought of burning the Church of God with the flames of envy, and while he desired peace among his own people and planned to exercise such measures against us, human insolence could nevertheless in no way prevail over or alter the divine dispensation.

God’s arrangement made him hateful to all, detested by everyone, and accursed in the eyes of all; even members of his household—and, as they say, his concubines—attacked him with hatred or cursing.

But, as it is written, “A just king raises up the land, but a greedy man destroys it” (*Proverbs* 29:4), so this man, burning with unheard-of bundles of desires, cut down the provisions of the soldiers, restricted the gifts of the tribunes, and reduced the monthly distribution of rewards.

When he saw that the taxes returned to him from the neighboring places were extremely low and almost insignificant [the parenthetical explanation is corrupt in the supplied text; the accompanying Moral supplies: “Although, by God’s dispensation, he was raised to the sceptre through the people’s fault, nevertheless, because of the wickedness of his merits, the cities and nations, driven to rebellion, did not pay him in full the provincial tributes together with the soldiers”], he therefore turned against us the weapons of his severity.

And, through the favoring wickedness of certain Christians, in order that he might trample the mud of the streets in lamentation—though they should be called Christians no more than they should be called workers of iniquity—he granted them the privilege of exacting written bonds. By pledge or culpable service, they bargained with the king for the lot of the Lord and the assembly of the faithful, and, having obtained the privilege of exacting written bonds, they burdened the necks of the wretched with an unbearable tax, daily oppressing the Lord’s people.

Without doubt, they will be punished in the future by the sentence that condemns such excesses and says: “Those who oppress your people will find destruction” (*Ecclesiasticus* 36:11).

According to the decree of truth, it would have been better for such men to be drowned in the depths of the sea with millstones hung around their necks than to disturb the weak with so great a scandal (*Matthew* 18:6), or to inflict such violence upon the little flock to which it pleased the Father to give the kingdom (*Luke* 12:32).

God is not before their eyes, and the judgments of God have been removed from their sight. They are always envious, always unjust, everywhere malicious; angry toward one another, peaceful when others are overthrown; treacherous in alliances, agitated in conspiracies, crafty in circumventing others; most adept at preparing harm, separated when acting for themselves but united to destroy others; eager to deceive, slow to show mercy; arrogant in their bearing, proud in their assertions, doubtful in promises, miserly in giving, sparing in generosity, greedy in receiving.

They promise what cannot be given and bestow what it is not permitted to enjoy. They do not sleep unless they have done evil (*Proverbs* 4:16), and they hasten to rise up for wrongdoing. They rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things (*ibid.* 2:14).

Although they declare themselves Christians, they crucify Christ daily in his members, following the example of Judas the traitor. By selling his teacher for money and handing him over to be crucified, Judas dug for himself a noose of destruction but brought the world the liberty it owed.

These men, however, incorporating themselves into Christ, injure the redeemed through cruel accusation and—something I say not without a grave wound in my heart—compel him to deny those whom they ought to protect, since we are members of Christ one another (*Ephesians* 4:25).

### Chapter Six  
### The Insulting of the Nobles against the Martyrs

While these evils threatened and the Church was being beaten by such sufferings, they say that the king, overcome by immense gladness, promised to inflict still greater scandals upon the faithful. As was noted elsewhere, if he obtained lasting success in his reign, he would crush us with savage assault and affliction.

Thus several nobles, mocking the steadfastness of the martyrs who had died in former times, said to us:

“Where now is the courage of your champions? Where has their greatness of spirit fled? Where is the boldness that has been swallowed up and lies hidden? Where has their enervated strength withdrawn?

Those who, not long ago, rushed forward with impetuous steps to attack our teaching were killed in due vengeance. Let them appear now; let them come; let them hurry, if they preserve that contest in truth under divine inspiration.”

### Chapter Seven  
### The Martyr Fandila

While they were mocking us with such insults and, by this mockery, were nearly exhausting our wretchedness to complete ruin, a certain young man named Fandila—a handsome youth in appearance, commendable in the uprightness of his life, a holy and devout priest—first opened the way and the entrance to the exercise of martyrdom amid these massacres and savage dangers, under the privilege of this tyrant.

He was born in the city of Accitunum and came to Córdoba for the sake of study. There he spent nearly all his adolescence under the instruction of a tutor. As soon as he entered manhood, attracted by monastic life, he immediately joined the monks in order to serve God continually.

After traveling through several places and finally leaving them, because his fervent and devoted mind could not rest in them, he ultimately betook himself to the monastery of Tabanos. There he remained for some time under regular discipline and under the governance of Abbot Martin, and he shone more perfectly in the fear of the Lord.

#### 2

Because he possessed the greatest humility and immense obedience, and because the grace of holiness with which he shone from heaven was so evident, the monks of the monastery of Saint Saviour repeatedly begged and implored him to accept the priestly office. The monastery stood not far from the city of Córdoba, on its northern side, at the foot of the peak of Mellaria.

Although chosen unwillingly—and, so to speak, compelled by the insistence or authority of his abbot—to undertake the holy ministry, he nevertheless increased his labors in fasting, vigils, and prayers beyond his accustomed practice. He advanced from virtue to virtue, intending to see the Lord in Zion, raised up by the ladder of merits.

His venerable life and conduct, necessarily imitable by all, are related at length with a fitting proclamation of praise by those brothers and sisters over whom he presided. Yet they are declared all the more magnificently because, passing beyond his flourishing youth with a stronger spirit, he did not hesitate to submit himself to the sword of martyrdom.

#### 3

When the perfection of the fear of the Lord accompanied him, and he despised all earthly things, suspending his mind in heaven, he desired to be dissolved and remain with Christ rather than cling to passing things.

One day, standing before the judge with a resolute face, he proclaimed the Gospel, reproached the shameful prophet, and declared that the assembly united in a wicked worship would suffer the fires of avenging punishments unless it repented and embraced the faith of piety.

He was then thrown into prison, bound in chains, and confined in the lodgings of thieves, to be beheaded afterward by the sentence of the prince.

Above, chapter 4.

### [Scan page 408]

## Memorial of the Saints

When the judge heard that this had been done, he was inflamed with the boundless fire of anger and, stunned by a kind of horror, wondered in his stupidity what victorious boldness this was that had not been terrified by such glory, and that had opposed such endeavors to the king—whose head was raised by so lofty a vanity and pride and who believed himself superior to everything.

Therefore, at that very moment, he ordered the bishop to be seized in a terrible voice; but the bishop himself was saved because flight anticipated the order. For they say that the king had already decided to punish him without any intervening delay.

He had also ordered all Christians to be destroyed by a general sentence and the women to be dispersed through public sale, except those who, rejecting their religion, would turn to his worship.

Had this decree not been overthrown by the counsel of the satraps—for they argued that since no wise man, no civilized person, and no Christian noble had committed such an act, the king ought not to kill everyone whom no personal leader had led into battle—I believe that from then on he would have utterly extinguished our Christianity, partly by the sword and partly by apostasy.

After killing the strongest athlete by the sword, he ordered him to be suspended on a gibbet beyond the river.

### Chapter Eight  
### The Deeds of the Martyrs Anastasius, Felix, and Digna

#### 1

On the following day Anastasius the priest followed him. From early childhood Anastasius had been educated in learning and letters at the basilica of Saint Acisclus of Córdoba. Until full youth he had served there in the office of deacon; afterward, having embraced monastic life—which he had long desired after rejecting his former ministry—he spent time among the elders and was finally admitted to the priesthood.

Proceeding swiftly, he went to the palace and stood before the consuls. Striking the enemy of the faith with the goads of truthful assertions, he was immediately beheaded with the sword and hanged.

With him, Felix the monk also suffered. Born in the town of Complutum, a Gaetulian by nation, he had been carried by some circumstance into Asturias, where he learned both the Catholic faith and the monastic life. On the same day he was killed for this profession.

#### [Editorial notes]

We follow Henschenius in assigning this to 15 June, although Morales and Schott published it otherwise, and hence this reading.

Following Henschenius under 14 June, we restore this passage thus, since Morales and Schott read it corruptly: “After the monastic life … he had spent [it] in …” See Schott. [The surviving printed restoration is itself corrupt.]

#### 2

As that day completed the greater part of its course and was already nearly passing into the ninth hour, a certain young virgin named Digna, both in merit and in name, from the community of the venerable Elisabeth, whose story the second book has related, came forward to receive the palm.

A little before her martyrdom, she saw in a dream a girl of angelic appearance and beautifully adorned, carrying roses and lilies in her hands. When Digna asked her name and the reason for her coming, she replied:

“I am Agatha. Once I was crushed by terrible torments for Christ, and now I have come to give you a share of this purple gift. Gladly accept the offering and act courageously in the Lord. For the remainder of the roses and lilies that I am holding in my hands I shall give, after you, to those who will depart from this place.”

At last, enlightened by this vision and gift, the most holy virgin received a rose from the right hand of the speaker. Then, mingled with heavenly things, the girl was lifted from the sight of the observer.

#### 3

Although this girl, because of her profound humility and obedience, considered herself the least among the virgins and was an incomparable servant in her conduct, she never allowed herself to be called Digna. She used to say with tears:

“Do not call me Digna—‘Worthy’—but rather Indigna—‘Unworthy’; for I am of such merit that I ought to be marked even by the name.”

From the day of her revelation, she began, with a heart pierced by longing for martyrdom, silently to consider by what signs she might aspire to it. She often pondered the matter and, when she was fully informed of the martyrdom of these men, became exceedingly joyful, as though she would follow these predecessors with a firmer step to the crown.

Therefore, after quietly opening the monastery’s gates, when she learned that the blessed martyrs had been hanged, she hurried to the judge and asked with fearless assertion why he had slaughtered his brothers, the heralds of justice:

“Is it because we are worshipers of God and faithfully honor the holy Trinity—confessing the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be one true God—and because we not only deny but also detest, curse, and condemn everything that differs from this belief? Is that why we are pierced through?”

#### 4

While the girl was speaking such things and others like them with a holy and immaculate mouth, the judge did not hesitate to commit her to the lictors for beheading, and they immediately brought the sword to her delicate neck.

Without delay, as her stricken limbs collapsed, she was suspended upside down on the *equuleus* and joined the others beyond the river.

In this order, these three—Anastasius the priest, Felix the monk, and Digna the blessed virgin—fell in different ways on the same day, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the year 853.

### Chapter Nine  
### Benildis the Married Woman and Martyr

Finally, Benildis, a woman already advanced in age and, as they say, not lacking in fear of God, followed these and fell under the profession of the others on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July, in the same year.

After several days their bodies were burned in a great fire and finally thrown into the river and scattered.

### Chapter Ten  
### Saint Columba the Martyr

#### 1

We are compelled, either by the number of the combatants or by the obligation of our promised vows, to extend our style through a long series of discourse.

This is why the work, enlarged beyond what we expected into a great book of material, has nearly exceeded the bounds of moderation. For after so many deaths and the dangers of unbearable sufferings, we had thought that no one at all would undertake such a task.

Nevertheless, we shall in no way fall silent concerning what we have begun, so that, as we promised, we may recount the accounts of all.

#### 2

Meanwhile there was a certain noble and beautiful virgin named Columba, born in the town of Córdoba. She was the sister of the aforementioned Abbot Martin and Elisabeth, whom we mentioned in the preceding books.

While she was still very young and living tenderly among her parents’ possessions, she recognized the purpose of her sister Elisabeth, who, together with her husband Jeremiah, had embraced it while still living publicly among the people. Long before they went to the monastery, they had consecrated themselves to Christ through many religious observances in the midst of the crowds.

Columba often left the company of her parents and visited her sister’s house more frequently. She desired to dedicate herself to such vows and longed eagerly to become the handmaid of this way of life.

Accordingly, she immediately desired to despise all earthly things. But her mother opposed the girl’s intention and resisted it. Stirred by shameful outbursts of anger against Elisabeth, her daughter, and her husband, she bitterly complained that they were seducing the girl’s mind; that, just as they had destroyed themselves, so they would destroy her; and that, dissolving their marriage and leaving behind the world while it flourished in their youthful bloom, they wished to gather her into the consolation of strangers.

#### 3

During this conflict, as is customary among ordinary people, the girl was sought in marriage. They repeatedly tried to envelop in worldly affairs one who had been divinely appointed for the marriage of the heavenly chamber.

When the girl would not consent and her mother would not desist from arranging her marriage, the mother herself—by God’s providence—was suddenly seized by the affliction of illness and, called away swiftly, departed from the world.

The servant of God remained, grieving less over her mother’s death than rejoicing that, without anyone’s injury, the grace of her devotion could now be fulfilled.

#### 4

After the two sisters had spent some time in holy religious life in the city, the monastery of Tabanos having then been completed at their own expense, as we have said, the men and women went there to serve Christ.

There the holy virgin stripped herself of earthly things and clung to heavenly ones. Turning her mind to the study of Scripture, she became exceedingly learned in investigating and explaining obscure meanings.

The blessed virgin’s holiness increased, and the monastery’s fame spread widely, attracting visitors even from distant cities, where they might be instructed by examples of such people.

This virgin, remaining under the governance of her brother Martin and Elisabeth, surpassed all in merit and led all in the grace of propriety: praiseworthy in conduct, exalted in humility, perfect in chastity, firm in charity, attentive in prayer, ready to obey, gentle in correcting, easy to forgive, eloquent in preaching, and prompt in instruction.

Shining in these virtues, she drew everyone’s affection to herself, becoming for all a rule and mirror of holiness.

Because she was frequently attacked by the temptations of the adversary, she sacrificed herself before the Lord with increasingly frequent tears, fearing that the accumulated labor of the most worthless servant might perish through the enemy’s assault.

For this reason she was raised to greater vigilance in holiness, and, driven by fear of the enemy, she strove more diligently toward the summit of the virtues through a stricter life.

#### 5

The tempter often tormented her with bitterness, sent weariness upon her, assumed the appearance of men, held out a long life, and exhausted her with various fantasies.

Driven by these things through terrible fear, she mourned inconsolably, lest through the fall of death she be separated from the company of the Bridegroom. She declared that inwardly she was so aflame with the ardor of charity for him that, as though her flesh had been cut away and her mind left wounded by a scar through desire for him, she could in no way be healed except by seeing him alone in heaven.

She never harmed any sinner by her speech, however burdened by grave sin; she judged no one’s actions; she despaired of no one’s salvation; and she despised no one, even if defiled by shameful rumors.

“I know,” she would say, “the devices of demons; I know the insolence of human beings, who sometimes attack with mockery and cursing one whom the Almighty has judged worthy through more excellent merits.

“For many things are condemned by human judgment that are approved and sanctified by divine counsel. Often people transgress divine judgment through their own opinions because they do not know what merit each person retains before God; yet, as though they were prophets of hidden things, they either proclaim someone worthy or denounce him as rejected.

“If they would return to themselves and judge how free from blame they were, and if each person would consider what burden he bears or what debt he owes, they would not blamefully discuss things unknown.

“Yet some do these things so that the divine reproach once spoken against us may be confirmed. It says: ‘Pay attention and listen. No one speaks what is good; there is no one who does penance for his sin, saying: What have I done?’” (*Jeremiah* 8:6).

They neglect the beam of their own crime and remain concerned with the splinters of others. Whatever they have caught with a light whisper in the ear, they nevertheless assert to be true and entirely beyond doubt.

#### 6

The most gentle virgin never became angry without cause, unless perhaps she saw a child or one of the sisters being negligent; then she would humbly rebuke the person with a mere glance of her eyes.

She never burst into an insult against anyone. Her mouth was never occupied with idle chatter, and she never allowed vain and empty stories to enter her ears.

Meditating frequently on Christ in her heart and on Christ with her mouth, she often sang with complete devotion the antiphon … [The supplied text ends mid-sentence.]

### Editorial notes

- In the *Life of the Martyr Sanctio*, concerning these Christians.
- The stipend is understood as the amount paid each month. Glossarium of Du Cange.
- That is, they were placed in charge of collecting the tribute through written bonds.
- Above, chapter 4.
- The office of deacon, whose principal function in the Church is to minister, as the word itself sounds in Greek.
- From this point some have written that this Felix, both by name and in fact, was a martyr who suffered in Asturias.
- We do not here follow Henschenius, who corrected the text to: “the impact struck the throat of the neck.”
- In book II, chapter 4, we clearly showed that this was the same Jeremiah who is written about as a martyr in chapter [uncertain].
- That is: she desired, after leaving her parents, to move into Jeremiah’s monastery and become, as a handmaid, attached to him. [The supplied sentence ends here.]
- Correctly, Constantinus Stiltingus, under 11 September: instead of *perhibebat*, read *perhiberet*, so that the following *sanari* should replace *sanare*.

# Memorial of the Saints

For the hymn which the blessed Fathers composed in sweet chant in praise of the saints: “Open for me, Lord, the gate of paradise, that I may return to that homeland where there is no death and sweet joy endures.”

She delighted in conversing with those whose minds were girded with spiritual virtue and whose limbs were mortified together with their vices and desires; nor did she grant anyone access to see her, except perhaps spiritual men—and even that very rarely and only after a considerable interval. The women’s enclosure was separated from the monks’ cells by substantial intervening walls. Although all were governed under the direction of one father, they nevertheless shut themselves away in their separate little rooms and gave absolutely no one the opportunity of looking upon them. But if at times a suitable necessity pressed upon the brothers, or the charitable courtesy of guests required it, the venerable Elisabeth alone displayed herself at a window to be seen; she was the superior and true mother of the entire monastery.

## 7. The Solitude Requested by Columba

At a certain time, therefore, Columba asked her fellow sisters that a little cell be given to her in some corner within the enclosure, where she might remain alone and, free from the noise of the others, become more recollected. The holy sisters consented to her request and, by their agreement, offered assistance toward increasing the virgin’s holiness, hoping thereby to receive some reward as well. For just as the devotion of holy conduct is worthy of reward, so too is religious affection toward those who live piously. Nor is a good agreement different from good deeds when it is not broken by lack of goodwill but only by weakness of strength: if the body happens not to possess the vigor to perform such things, the intention of the mind may nevertheless take delight in similar acts.

For the works of holiness are common exchanges, and they become all the more pleasing to Christ when, with simple and perfect charity, we refer to our own advantage the devotion of our fellow sisters’ holiness.

### Editorial Notes

* Suysken suggests *imperaret* (“might require”).
* A woven bedding of esparto grass or reed; hence Ovid’s *Fasti* has “a mat of rushes.” — Morales.
* This is a Greek term, as though one said “contemplation” (*theōria*). — Idem.

## 8. Columba’s Prayer and Tears

Finally, having obtained the sisters’ blessing and freed from every concern relating to the common life of the monastery, the venerable virgin remained for a long time in contemplation of God and meditation on the Scriptures. After frequent sighs and immense weeping—through which, by a special gift, she shone above very many, by divine grace—she returned to the community to instruct the minds of her fellow virgins with divine nourishment.

They say that she often remained lying in prayer for three or four hours, and even until midday. Although no sighs sounded and no sob shook her limbs, she nevertheless poured forth tears in profound silence, so that beneath the mat on which she prayed with her body prostrate, the pavement could be seen wet with tears. She also spent the greatest part of her time standing in supplication, and was suddenly carried into such contemplation that a double stream of tears, descending from both eyes to her chin, became a single channel and flowed drop by drop, as though from a roof onto the ground.

## 9. Columba During the Persecution

Meanwhile, when the fury of persecution—which raged for the destruction of the churches—approached this community of women, they withdrew to a small estate which they had long before built for themselves at the boundary of the basilica of Saint Cyprian. Once established there, the most blessed virgin wept incomparably and mourned abundantly, both over the peace she had enjoyed in the mountains and over the tumults into which she had fallen in the city. Yet she always cried out in heart and tongue:

> “You know, Lord, that I have not desired the day of man upon the earth” (Jeremiah 17:16).

She always preached, always prayed, always sang psalms, and the praise and blessing of the Lord continually sounded from her mouth.

Because the virgins’ dwelling adjoined the walls of the aforesaid sanctuary, and was separated from the entrance of the altar only by the obstruction of a wall, if she happened to hear, on the festivals of the martyrs, some song resounding in praise of the saints from the clerics who were singing psalms, she would immediately be pierced by a certain joy of heavenly desires and burst into tears. You would have thought that inwardly she was proclaiming no less than this:

> “My soul thirsts for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God? My tears have been my bread day and night, while they say to me every day: ‘Where is your God?’” (Psalm 41:3–4).

For by those bonds of the body by which the mind of every saint is held during this pilgrimage, she was joined to that ineffable brightness of the saints, consumed by a great thirst for heavenly desires. It was as though the barriers of the walls prevented her from reaching with swift steps the city of the living, wherever she wished to go; she seemed to believe that the burden of her limbs resisted her, and she wept and said:

> “My tears have been my bread day and night, while they say to me every day: ‘Where is your God?’”

She desired to be with him with whom the Apostle, longing to remain after mortality had been dissolved, said:

> “To depart and to be with Christ is better” (Philippians 1:23).

## 10. Columba’s Desire for Martyrdom

As holy Columba persevered unceasingly in these prayers, she inflicted upon herself, as I believe, even more than the raging executioner would have imposed, by continuing the labors of vigils, fasts, and prayers. As though all these things were small, and as though the torments she voluntarily imposed upon herself were of little account, she did not trust even in her own merits, however much greater her exertions might be.

Fearing that she might find the hundredfold fruit of her virginity lacking in value before the Father, she aspired to the unmistakable gain of martyrdom, which sends even sinners by a direct path into the kingdom of heaven, as the Gospel says:

> “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matthew 11:12).

Hence, already inflamed more ardently with love of Christ, she hastened toward him whom she had faithfully served, panting to reach him with rapid steps. She was frequently urged toward this by certain revelations. One day, breaking out of her hiding place and quietly opening the doors, she went out into the marketplace. Although she was unfamiliar with the city’s streets, by careful inquiry she learned where the judge was staying.

When she had arrived there and stood before him, she professed the Catholic faith, proclaimed the truth of the Gospel, refuted the impious doctrine, and, condemning the author of so great a crime for presuming such things, gently urged the judge himself to consider why he was involving himself in such sacrileges.

Amazed by her appearance and words, he immediately led her into the palace and presented her to the governor. There she continued to profess, preach, and admonish everyone that they ought rather to attend to their salvation than persist in the empty deceptions by which they were attempting to convert her.

She also said:

> “Christ does not have such a bride as could be overcome and changed from her former covenant with him. For who is richer than he, that you should believe me enticed by the abundance of your possessions? Who is more beautiful than he, whose appearance and form shine before the sons of men, that you should suppose me pleased by an earthly marriage? What discipline or sect is holier than the truth of the evangelical faith, which, proclaimed throughout the whole world by the voices of the apostles and promising the reward of eternal hope to believers, plainly declares every prophecy that dissents from it to be anathema in truth? Therefore, abandoning vanity, seek the true guide of the Gospel, so that you may more rightly be called sons of light than offspring of darkness and death. For he said: ‘Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness’; and: ‘Everyone who lives and believes in me will never die’ (John 8:12; 11:26).”

### Editorial Notes

* “Judges” here is used for magistrates or leading men of the people. Thus, in Book II, chapter 1, the year of the consulship of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān is used for the year of that kingdom. — Suysken. See also the note there in Morales.
* “Throat” here means a sword or axe, by which the throat is usually cut. — Idem.
* “This basilica was inside the city.” — Idem.
* That is, “he would have inflicted.” — Suysken.
* For “ignorant.” — Idem.

## 11. The Death of Saint Columba

When all the governors perceived the virgin’s exceedingly steadfast constancy, and saw that she could not be changed, having been instructed by such oracles, nor could they withstand her exhortation and declaration, they immediately ordered her to be killed before the palace gates.

They placed her in the forum with the greatest reverence. The most sacred virgin did not allow herself to be beheaded until she had honored the executioner with a reward. Then, willingly inclining her neck, she laid her delicate body low as her throat was cut.

There was no delay. Since she was clothed in linen, the princes ordered her corpse to be put into a basket and thrown into the river, and did not, as with the corpses of the other slain, either leave it before the gates or suspend it from a gibbet. This took place on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the era 891.

Six days later, through the diligence of certain monks, her body was divinely brought to us unharmed and intact. It deserved an honorable burial in the basilica of the holy virgin and martyr Eulalia, which stands in the district of Fragellas.

This is what has been reported to us about her in accordance with the faith.

## 12. Prayer to Saint Columba

But you, most sacred virgin, who benefited the Catholic Church both by the example of your life and, in death, by the lofty patronage of your merits, remember your worshiper. Rescue me from the snares of the world, draw me away from the disturbances of the age, and grant me, after death, the rest of paradise.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one and immortal God, throughout endless ages of ages. Amen.

# The Martyrdom of Saint Pomposa

## 1. Pomposa’s Calling

When, on that very day, news of the completed martyrdom of the aforesaid virgin reached the knowledge of many, and spread not only throughout the whole city but also through the neighboring regions, a venerable virgin named Pomposa, from the monastery of the Holy Savior situated at the foot of Peña Mellaria, was a member of that community.

Long before, she had gone there with her parents, brothers, and relatives in order to serve Christ. From that place the most blessed Fandila, once priest of the same monastery, had also descended.

As soon as she learned from those who reported it of that martyrdom, she hastened there the next day. This blessed virgin, seeing the holy way of life that her parents and relatives had led in Córdoba, from which they had originated, immediately, with eager mind, dedicated herself to such a vow. At the same time she despised the world, abandoned transitory things, promised integrity, and strove with all her strength to seek what would endure forever.

## 2. Pomposa’s Life at Peña Mellaria

Accordingly, her parents, having sold their property, built the aforesaid monastery in the place which, because our ancestors had long ago seen honeycombs gathered there through the industry of bees on that lofty cliff—and which remain there to this day—was called Peña Mellaria.

Having settled there for the practice of monastic life, they handed over this blessed virgin to their community. She flourished among them, more beautiful through the grace of holiness. Although she held the lowest place by age, she was raised above the others by the more excellent height of innocence and simplicity.

She remained so devoted to meditation on the Scriptures that, if it had been possible, she would have given neither days nor nights to anything but reading, unless the storms of certain pressing tempests prevented her. If she happened to sense that some wrong had been done to her, she—who excelled through the grace of humility—endured everything with a patient spirit.

She devoted herself to vigils, and applied herself frequently to fasts and prayers, by which, with the Lord’s favor, she might inviolably preserve the vow she had promised.

## 3. Pomposa’s Desire for Martyrdom

We learned many things about her holiness from Felices, a servant of Christ and abbot of the same monastery, but, to avoid weariness, we shall pass over them and hurry to the matter that undoubtedly sent her to heaven.

For while she was pursuing the highest holiness and serving God faithfully, as soon as she learned of the martyrdom of the blessed Columba, she was immediately set ablaze inwardly by the fire of martyrdom and became exceedingly joyful, refreshed by such news. She pondered silently, with singular desire, by what steps she might attain it.

O wonderful calling of the Lord, and opening made by heavenly disposition: no one who was predestined to martyrdom was defrauded of the glory of martyrdom; no one inscribed among the company of the saints could be held captive by human entanglement!

For they say that this virgin had long before hastened toward martyrdom, had she not been restrained by certain barriers imposed by her own people, who, because of the raging persecutions, kept her under strict guard.

### Editorial Notes

* The word *martyrio* is absent from Schottus’s text, though it is found here. For this reason, on 19 September Constantine Suysken added the following note: “Not merely anyone predestined, but anyone predestined for martyrdom, is not deprived of its glory.” The observation is unnecessary in the text edited by Morales.
* “And through a difficult road, broken by slopes and stones.” — Morales.
* See again: the marketplace stood directly before the citadel. — Idem.
* Suysken rightly reads: “It was believed by some that she was dragged to martyrdom through the plotting or deceit of certain pagans. But that servant of God, seeing herself being prepared from heaven by a certain calling for the true sacrifice, approached willingly what she was being led to unwillingly and with a grateful spirit.”
* Hence we clearly understand that when Eulogius names another day—as in chapter 9—he must mean the following day. — Morales.
* Felices uses this word again in this sense. — Idem.

## 4. Pomposa’s Escape and Death

But what can the wretched condition of a guard accomplish when, as it is written, “Unless the Lord keeps watch, those who suppose that they are keeping anything watch in vain” (Psalm 127:1)? What can human beings believe they are capable of guarding?

That very night, after the nocturnal vigil had been completed with the praises of God, one of her brothers, while the others were returning to their beds for the sake of sleep, seemed to be divinely warned—and certainly not without the Lord’s providence. He took up the key, opened the monastery gate, though this was not his custom, and closed it again after placing only the smallest bolt across it.

She approached it silently, opened the door secretly, and went through the darkness of night, illuminated by heavenly light. She crossed the entire road—which was terrifying in its vast solitude—before dawn’s first brightness. When morning grew light, she entered the city and did not delay in presenting herself before the judge.

Proposing to him the account of the holy faith and confounding the impious prophet through simple exhortation, she was immediately condemned by him to be killed with the sword. Thus, after being placed before the palace gates, she was beheaded on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the era 891.

Those who threw her corpse into the river, through the agency of certain mercenaries, had it buried in a pit and covered with a great quantity of earth. Yet, by Christ’s favor, after almost twenty days certain monks’ diligence removed it from there and carried it to the aforesaid sanctuary of the blessed virgin Eulalia. There, through the worthy ministry of priests and religious, it was buried at the feet of Saint Columba.

We believe that this, too, was accomplished by divine providence, so that those who had loved one another with such charity in life might remain united even in death and burial, while the Lord Jesus Christ reigns throughout the ages of ages.

# Chapter XII

## Abundius, Priest and Martyr

From this time, after ten months had passed, a certain priest named Abundius arose from the village of Ananelos, which lies in the mountains of Córdoba, and carried out his priesthood there.

It is reported that, although certain people had brought him to martyrdom through the plotting of some pagans, or through their deceit, this servant of God, perceiving himself being prepared by a heavenly calling for the true sacrifice, approached willingly what he was being led to unwillingly and with a grateful spirit.

When questioned by the judge, he set forth the reason for his faith in an unshaken reply and finally reproached the impious teacher and his followers with truthful arguments. Therefore, in a swift outburst of indignation, he was killed and exposed to be devoured by dogs and beasts, on the fifth day before the Ides of July, in the era 892.

# Chapter XIII

## The Martyrdom of Saints Amator, Peter, and Ludovicus

At a later time, a certain young priest named Amator, who had once come to Córdoba from the town of Tucci with his father and brothers for the sake of study; Peter, a monk; and Ludovicus, our fellow townsman and brother of Paul the deacon, whose martyrdom is described in Book II, arose from among the citizens of Córdoba.

Joining themselves together in one fellowship, they prepared themselves to proclaim the truth of the Gospel. Therefore they were quickly killed under the profession of the aforesaid faith, on the second day before the Kalends of May, in the era 893.

Their bodies, immersed in the river’s swirling waters, were cast upon the shore after several days by God’s favor. Although the holy priest gave no further indication of the place of his rest, the other saints nevertheless remained honorably deposited in known places. The blessed Peter was buried in the monastery of Peña Mellaria; Ludovicus rests honorably in the village of the province of Italica called Palma, which stands beside the river Singilis.

# Chapter XIV

## On Witesindus the Martyr

At that time a certain man named Witesindus, already advanced in age, from the province of Egabrum, who, I do not know through what persecution, had earlier fallen away from the holy faith, was being urged to practice the worship he had recently undertaken. He denied that he remained infected with such sacrilege, whether he had suddenly contracted it through weakness of the flesh or through the devil’s deception.

As soon as he made such a confession, he was killed in a swift outburst of indignation, at the same date as above.

# Chapter XV

## The Martyrdom of Helias the Priest and Paul and Isidore, Monks

Moreover, Helias, an already elderly priest from the province of Lusitania, together with Paul and Isidore, monks still flourishing in the vigor of youth, were killed under the profession of the faith on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the era 894.

Their bodies, raised upon gibbets, were buried in the Baetican gulf after many days.

[Note: Suysken rightly judges that those mercenaries were Christians, or had been hired by Christians, so that they might remove the venerable body from the river and commit it to the earth.]

### Editorial Notes

* Perhaps “having been gathered together.” — Suysken.
* The following year is now indicated; it was 854. — Morales.
* I shall inquire in vain what can be said about this little word. — Idem.
* This should be emended into more correct Latin, or one should read: “it is reported that he was dragged away.” — Schott.
* This town has already been mentioned above. — Morales.
* See the Scholion on Book II, chapter 8.

# Chapter XVI

## On Argimirus, Monk and Martyr

After this, a certain Argimirus, a confessor, a noble man already advanced in age, traced his family from the town of Egabrum. At one time, in Córdoba, he had been appointed censor of Patricia by the king.

When he had been removed from the administration of judgment and was living quietly in the leisure of the monastery, he was accused before the judge through the deceit or hatred of certain pagans. He was charged with mocking his prophet, reproached for professing the divinity of the Son of God, for confessing that there was no one more powerful than he, and for asserting that he was the author of vanity and leader of the lost.

The servant of God was immediately thrown into the great and most savage rage of the judge and was forced into harsher imprisonment. After several days the judge ordered him to be brought before him and attempted, through his exhortations and enticements, to make him submit some of his words to the pagan rite. When he could not prevail, he placed the soldier of Christ, steadfast in his holy purpose, alive upon the rack and killed him by piercing him with a sword, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, in the era 894.

After many days, when his body was removed from the gibbet at the judge’s command, the diligence of a religious man carried it to the basilica of Saint Acisclus, where, through the worthy ministry of priests, it was buried near the tomb of the aforesaid martyr and Saint Perfectus.

### Editorial Notes

* “Or through some enticement, or through certain enticements, or through the enticements of someone’s words.” Schott rightly emends the passage.
* She was therefore Artemia, whose daughter is mentioned in Book II, chapter 8. — Morales. “This chapter contains the life of Saints Flora and Maria, which we publish after the account of their martyrdom.”
* Perhaps “to accuse.” — Guillelmus; Cuperus, under 10 July.

# Chapter XVII

## On Aurea, Virgin and Martyr

### 1. Aurea’s First Denial

At that time there was a certain noble virgin named Aurea, sister of the holy martyrs Adulphus and John, whom we mentioned earlier. Since the time of their conflict, she had devoted herself to religious observance. She lived in the monastery of Cuteclara, which had long ago been dedicated to the name of the holy and glorious virgin Mary, openly displaying the practices of sacred religion for nearly thirty years and more.

She gave everyone knowledge of her faith and, daunted by no fears, conducted her Christian way of life in public confrontation. Because she was girded by noble lineage and adorned with the great pride of an Arabic ancestry, no outsider dared to attack the virgin’s faith.

At last, however, certain members of her own people from the province of Seville, from which she derived her family, were divinely—or so I believe—stirred up so that the crown of martyrdom already owed to the virgin before the foundation of the world might be prepared for her, and so that she might rejoice more splendidly in heaven at the completion of her triumph.

They came under the pretext of investigating the truth of the report brought to them about her and her purpose, and cunningly pretended that they were visiting their kinswoman in order to lodge with her. When they saw that she was not only a Christian but also marked with the insignia of sacred devotion, they immediately reported the matter concerning her to the judge. He too was attached by right of birth to the same noble family.

### 2. The Judge’s Threat

Stimulated by this report, he ordered her to stand before him and, with a very mild exhortation, demanded why she had degraded such a noble station by serving the Christian faith and polluted the dignity of so exalted a lineage with such a base purpose.

> “But,” he said, “you can very quickly be freed from all your stains and recover the proper brightness of your interrupted lineage, if, taking thought for yourself, you choose to admit our faith’s worship into your innermost desires; if, obeying us with the deepest affection, you follow what we follow and strive to go where we are being led.
>
> “But if you despise both us and what we worship, and decide, out of regard for the faith, to follow those whom you have hitherto imitated, then, after various tortures of cruel torment and after the immense punishments of multiple sufferings—which you will pay as one guilty of so great a crime—you will finally incur the penalty of a most shameful death.”

They report that at that very moment the virgin yielded under the judge’s rebuke and promised that she would willingly carry out everything commanded of her.

Since it is better to remain silent about matters not known by experience than arrogantly to discuss what is unknown, I do not dare to testify what caused this denial itself, by which she was to become a martyr—whether fear of the flesh or an intention to arrange her family affairs. Unless, perhaps, from the events that followed, in which she later persevered obstinately in her profession and earned the deserved crown, one may infer that, as human conjecture judges, she did not yield through bodily weakness.

### 3. Aurea Returns to the Faith

After the judge had heard the profession of her lips, by which she had promised to live according to every rite of his law, he immediately granted her freedom to depart wherever she wished. She returned straightaway to her home, and, as before, serving Christ, did not in any way abandon the purpose of the holy faith.

Nor did she allow herself to be separated from the company of the faithful. Rather, she frequently joined their assemblies, mourning with fitting tears and inward feeling the lapse of her tongue. She bound the true confidence of her hope to the Redeemer’s indulgence, if he should not reject a servant made liable by the guilt of transgression—he who rescued the adulterous woman from the danger of stoning (John 8:11), received Peter as he sank amid the waves of the sea and restored him to apostolic primacy (Matthew 14:31), and admitted the thief stained by parricide into his company while cleansing him for paradise (Luke 23:43).

She did not believe that a momentary crime committed by an unprofitable servant could harm the Lord’s abundant and incomparable mercy, before which manifold compassion and plentiful redemption anticipate the unworthy with the gift of grace and, in deliberate kindness, justify those to whom no wages of vigorous labor are supplied.

The holy virgin increased her contrition, multiplied her devotion to lamentation, doubled her vows, and, pressing her mind with redoubled grief and feeling, strove with happy prayers lest, at the final judgment, she should either be condemned for her crime and handed over to eternal punishment or be driven away from the fellowship of her brothers, the blessed martyrs Adulphus and John, by the appropriate barriers of their merits.

### 4. The Devil’s Frustration

Then, in clear and fearless progress, she frequently went to church. Already strengthened by the power of the Lord, withdrawn from earthly contamination, and panting to be enrolled among the heavenly citizens, she lived in readiness in case, through some renewed challenge, she should again be brought before the court.

But the cunning veteran did not endure this lightly. He understood that she had escaped him through a more faithful alliance and now served her Creator more than before; he saw that the trickery of his deception had gained nothing at all. Then, having cast some stupefaction over her through I know not what dullness, he noticed that the virgin’s tongue had been turned aside from a profession of the truth only lightly and superficially, and that it had been removed from her mouth but not from her heart.

Undoubtedly he complained to his demons about the weakening of his campaign, saying:

> “This unmarried woman, who recently honored me accidentally with her lips, now has her heart fortified by heavenly virtue and is separated from my seductions by a great barrier.”

For this reason he stirred up a certain person again against the blessed virgin and compelled him to seek out the novice of her faith.

### 5. Aurea’s Second Trial

Meanwhile, certain pagans investigating her way of life found her nevertheless living as a servant of Christ according to her former custom. They immediately lodged a complaint about her before the judge, asserted that she was guilty, and alleged deception. They argued with perverse tongues that a punishment should be imposed by legal authority to avenge so great an abuse and strike down such presumption.

The judge, immediately moved by vehement anger, ordered her to be dragged before him by the savage service of brutal attendants. When she had been brought before him, he rebuked her for her contempt of the appearance she had recently adopted, threatened her for neglecting her promised purpose, and asked with terrible shouting whether she did not fear the decree of the law.

Then the virgin, who knew that she had been divinely chosen for such a contest, replied to the judge with eloquence worthy of her wisdom, already enlightened by holy regard:

> “I have never been separated from Christ my God; I have never departed from the religion of his piety; I have never even for a moment clung to your profanations, although earlier, before you, my tongue yielded through a certain lapse in speech.
>
> “My heart, however, had confidence in the Lord, who raised me inwardly by the support of his promises, saying: ‘Whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live’ (John 11:25). Therefore, although in words I fell into the snare of transgression, my heart was nevertheless fortified by the living constancy of holy belief.
>
> “For immediately after I departed from you, I practiced in tears, both in desire and affection, the worship I had learned from my infancy; I kept the faith and maintained my purpose.
>
> “It remains now that, according to the rite of your profanation, I should either be punished by the avenging sword, or, if an act of this kind can be allowed to pass unpunished, that thereafter you leave me entirely free to cling to Christ the Lord.”

### 6. Aurea’s Martyrdom

Then the most savage judge, inflamed by the virgin’s declaration, intending to report the matter concerning her to the king, committed her to prison and burdened her with an enormous weight of chains.

On the following day, by the prince’s decree, he killed her with the sword. He immediately ordered her lifeless body to be suspended head downward from the gibbet of a certain murderer who had been hanged only a few days earlier. Her blessed corpse, together with the limbs of the other thieves who had then been killed for their crime, was thrown into the whirlpools of the Baetis and has given no sign of reappearing to this day.

But Christ, our God and Lord, who is the helper of those who fight and the crowned of martyrs, who gives strength to the weary, and who, revealing his own desire to be sought, grants the intention of knocking at the door of his mercy, received his servant in peace. Through the many effects of events, according to his will and his foreknown dispensation—predestined before the foundation of the world for the crown of martyrdom—he brought her to himself.

To him are honor and glory, might and power throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

This virgin was crowned on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the era stated above.

### Editorial Notes

* Schottus, and with him Cuperus, read “to lodge”; the reading “to greet” is preferable.
* Cuperus rightly observes that the “dignity” is metaphorically called a *fillet* or *headband*, that is, a shameful dignity, as the sense makes clear.
* In the old edition, only “in matters experienced” appeared; this was evidently the copyist’s fault, since it plainly contradicted the sense. We have therefore added the negation. — Morales.
* See the Scholion on the *Apologeticus*, no. 1.
* Perhaps “of the judge.” — Morales.

# Document of the Martyrdom

## Letter of Eulogius to Alvarus

Eulogius sends to Alvarus the account of the martyrdom which he had written for the virgins Flora and Maria before giving it to them to read, moved, as appears at the end, by Christian modesty and notable circumspection.

### Eulogius to His Most Beloved Brother Alvarus

Always pierced with remorse by the recollection of my sins, I do not cease from daily mourning, because through frequent practice the inclination to sin is never absent from me.

In addition to these things, I am overcome by the intense sorrow of imprisonment, and an unexpected weariness has confronted me no less since the day on which your Serenity warned me not to cease glorifying the soldiers of Christ and not to invalidate my first judgment concerning them.

Because those men courageously resisted the enemy of justice, the cruelty of the tyrant has delivered us over to prison hardships, attributing to our exhortations what had been divinely inspired in them. It would be as though this were to become for us an occasion—God forbid—of easily disparaging those whom I had formerly praised and elevated as worthy of praise in word and writing.

For this reason I have been compelled to undertake the labor of this little work. Perhaps it will provide future generations with a testimony of our faith in their victory, and offer support for the hope of contending to these virgins, who, because of their profession of the truth, are bound together with us.

I have decided, according to my own judgment, that it should be called the *Document of the Martyrdom*. It is yours, dearest brother, to grant authority to this volume, because I wished to submit it to your judgment before it reached the eyes of those same virgins, lest through an error of ignorance it should disagree in any respect with Catholic doctrine.

Hail in the Lord Jesus Christ, dearest brother.

## Alvarus to Eulogius

He praises the work sent to him and declines to pass judgment upon it, both out of modesty and because of the work’s excellence.

I have read through the luminous *Document* of your work, elegantly gathered from those “eastern” fruits of which it is written that they are very good, and carefully composed from the vital juices and the fourfold fountain of virtues, in accordance with my inborn devotion to literary studies.

I traversed the text of the entire praiseworthy work not by examining it critically but by admiring it. What was brought forth from the treasure of divine wisdom by a learned scribe, from the new and the old, I examined throughout, deeply and profoundly, and I found nothing in the poor and very narrow breast of your servant worthy of being offered in return for so great a work.

Truly, like that Joseph, you distribute stored-up grain in a time of need; you give nourishment to those suffering from hunger for truth, and you make dry hearts rich with spiritual fatness. Whatever anyone could ever draw from the fountains of the holy Scriptures, you have taken up, examined, and arranged.

Indeed, silence is now imposed upon all of us who wish to say something of value. For the whole work has been arranged eloquently and splendidly in the manner of orators—or rather with scholastic learning—and perfected with both human and divine instruction. It does not require examination so much as it seeks to be praised.

Nor does it submit itself to be dissected by those laboring under poverty of knowledge. Rather, like a flower worthy of proclamation and adorned with the praise of virtues, it pours itself into the hearts of the unlearned and invites itself to be exalted.

But that you entrust so great a brilliance to my judgment—although you assign this, as is evident, to your innate humility—requires care, lest the brightness of the subject and the splendor of the author be stained by the dark horror of my inadequacy.

Light dispels darkness, and thick gloom is always driven away by splendor, when the golden ray makes dense clouds clear. It is not known, in the contrary manner, for darkness to dispel light or dense air to subject the sun to its judgment.

But I, my lord, would not dare to submit to human judgment a work worthy of the Church of God and consecrated at its beginning to Christ, its maker and the crowner of martyrs, by a votive offering of the heart. I know with certainty that it was brought forth by divine inspiration from the secret chamber of your heart.

Therefore, just as the Holy Spirit spoke through you, so also the name which that same author of good, by your agreement—or rather by your choice—imposed upon it should remain forever attached to it, and should live in perpetual memory. as the lowliness which you consult sees fit.

I read the little work rapidly and in haste, but I hesitated to retain it for copying, lest I should somehow prove guilty toward your affection. I ask, however, that it be written for those sisters in another quire, in a clearer hand, and that this copy be returned to me so that I may copy it anew.

### Editorial Notes

* He alludes to the description of the earthly paradise found in Genesis, chapter 2. — Morales.
* “Lofty and exalted.” He speaks in the manner of the poets, using a metaphor taken from the elevated buskins that were raised on high. — Idem.

[scan page 416]

# The Martyrdom Document

## In the Name of the Lord Begins the Book of the Martyrdom of Eulogius the Priest

Which I address to the virgins of Christ, Flora and Maria, confined in prison.

## Prologue

Those who abound in resources and in manifold financial gain easily obtain whatever they seek in earthly affairs. But it is far otherwise with those troubled by want and hunger, who can scarcely procure their daily food by laborious sweat. The rich man conceived and acted; the poor man failed in conceiving. But I, far inferior to those endowed with learning, and the very last among those supported by even a scant provision of letters, have called this work, arranged in a style and sense sufficiently humble, a *Document of Martyrdom*: because I wished, as though with a goad, to instruct the spirits of certain virgins confined as criminals, so that they might complete the course of their contest; or because I believed that such matters would be useful to others seeking them.

I have therefore undertaken the matter of this book not with the brilliance of eloquence, which is altogether lacking in me, nor have I aimed at the charm of elegant speech in its composition; rather, I have considered how through the virtue of this instrument I might make God propitious and free myself from my guilt. For it is written: “He who causes a sinner to be converted saves his soul and covers a multitude of sins” (James 5:20). And again: “Those who instruct many unto righteousness shall shine like stars for everlasting eternities” (Daniel 12:3). Thus this prologue offers a humble prayer to present and future readers: that they may strive to read with a simple mind what simple speech sets forth and simple intention dictated.

And if perhaps in some matters they find my judgment opposed to sound doctrine, let them ascribe this to ignorance, not to voluntary error; and let them graciously correct me rather than spend their time on disparagement through reproaches. For before the Lord no crime will be imputed to me as a ground of guilt if it was not committed by a deliberate lapse.

## Eulogius, Servant of Christ, to the Sacred Virgins Flora and Maria, Confined in Prison: Greetings

### 1

I have thought it worthwhile to compose this small work for your instruction, most holy sisters in the Lord Jesus Christ. With God’s favor it will be useful to you and will stand as testimony for me both now and at the future judgment: either because, through his gift and the illumination of the Holy Spirit, I trust that I have found the instrument of my tongue fitted for the proclamation of truth; or because I hope that he will both complete and sanctify the labor of this volume once begun; or because I have judged that you have done great and praiseworthy deeds, which I admire in thought and extol in writing. Whatever men have achieved in earthly matters, I acknowledge that you have surpassed men and surpassed clerics.

Your outstanding virtue has surpassed the glorious memorials of men, and the standard of your labor, raised on high, gives all a devout lesson in prayer: urging the idle to triumph, arming the weak for battle, strengthening the feeble for war, encouraging the hesitant with hope of victory to make a renewed return to the camp of the fighters, and showing yourselves as standard-bearers of the whole Church by offering an example of dying for the truth.

Therefore your praise shall not depart from the mouths of men forever. For though the victory of men is celebrated and males are commonly extolled in the triumph of their victories, more excellent still is the palm borne by women; and it is to be cherished with the praise of greater admiration when women have done a man’s deed. Forgetting the frailty of their sex, they do not fear to seek lofty virtues, at which the vigor even of the strong sometimes fails. Thus in former times the women of the Law, Esther and Judith, were sustained by this virtue of magnanimity, when for the salvation of God’s people they exposed themselves to the dangers posed by enemies. Did not one persuade the king that Haman, wickedly plotting Israel’s ruin, should be crucified (Esther 7ff.)? The other killed Holofernes while he lay sunk in the quiet of vice, preserving her chastity (Judith 13:4ff.); and so, cleaving the battle-lines of the warriors by her outstanding victory, she returned to see her people, having attained her wish.

[Editorial note:] Written around the end of October in the year 851.

[Editorial note:] We have retained all the headings that were present in the exemplar. — Moral.

### 2

Therefore, I beg you, my sisters, girded with their example, raise up a courageous spirit for the destruction of God’s adversary, and rescue both yourselves and the company of the faithful from the snares of the river of perdition. Strive to complete the path you have begun, for this road will lead you more easily and swiftly to the bridal chamber of your bridegroom. It is indeed a narrow and strait path, but by its shortness it will bring you, within the space of a single hour, to the joy of your bridegroom.

Let not the first ardor for battle be lacking from the sanctuary of your breast; rather, let it be increased daily in the recesses of your minds, solemnly ringing out, as though you both cried with one voice: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14).

### 3

Do not let the allurements of the world deceive you, my sisters, since with apostolic authority you have heard Christ the Lord say:

“Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. For everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life, which is not from the Father but from the world. And the world will pass away, and its desire” (1 John 2:15ff.).

Let the abundance of possessions not entice you, since it is written: “Do not hope in iniquities or in robberies; do not desire riches. If they abound, do not set your heart upon them” (Psalm 61:11). And again: “Do not hope in the uncertainty of riches” (1 Timothy 6:17).

Let not the filthy horror of the prison turn you aside, since you know truly that prophets, apostles, and blessed martyrs reached the heavenly homeland through prison bonds, and that many hidden mysteries were revealed to those placed in caves.

Let not companionship with prostitutes disturb you, since it is written: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters” (Song of Songs 2:2). And the Lord was “reckoned among the wicked” (Mark 15:28), and was crucified between the two thieves.

Let not the terror of the raging judgment frighten you, since not even a hair of your head will be plucked out without the command of your Father.

Let not abusive insults deter you, since it is written: “Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not be afraid of their blasphemies. For as a garment, so the worm will consume them; and as wool, so the moth will devour them” (Isaiah 51:7–8).

Let not the punishments inflicted upon you make you wither; let not the enormity of your sufferings overcome you; let not the strength of your faith yield to the wounds of torture, since it is written: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot harm the soul in anything; rather, fear him who can destroy both body and soul and cast them into Gehenna” (Matthew 10:28).

Your Lord and teacher commands this, my sisters, and these words have come from his divine mouth: “There is no longer anything for you to fear, little flock, because it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12:32).

Let human weakness be strengthened with all vigor, and with an outstretched hand let it practice battle in the contest for its God. He himself will give help; he himself will confer the reward of victory, who has imposed this command upon his hearers: “Behold, I am with you all the days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

The enemy certainly threatens that you will be sold publicly, placed on the market, handed over to the obscene practices of the common people, and cruelly distributed for execution in the manner of merchandise. But do not, I beg you, be calmed by such raging threats: “For the Lord will not leave the rod of sinners over the lot of the just, lest the just stretch out their hands to iniquity” (Psalm 124:3).

For he who searches your secrets with foresight and grants you strength will not allow the vexations of temptations to drive you away. Through these he hopes that your spirit may be tested, not overcome.

But if—which God forbid—the wicked pleasure of the persecutor should intervene and, inflicting violence upon your bodies, should lustfully violate against your will the members dedicated to God, let only the pernicious consent of the mind be far from the appetite; for another’s corruption will not defile a mind which its own pleasure does not defile.

[Editorial note:] This passage was sadly torn and corrupted in the exemplar; it had no sense whatever. We have corrected and supplemented it as best we could. — Moral.

### 5

Therefore, amid the danger of these temptations, in whose severe conflict human weakness is tormented by battles rising on every side, a woman who fears losing the integrity of her body, or grieves that what has been lost has perished, may nevertheless, even before the Lord, merit the rewards of her integrity.

Nor is it a crime that, having suffered violence among human beings, she is ashamed that her flesh has received the disgraceful mark of infamy. Rather, one must look to and pursue by every means what renders us blameless before God, and not fear the judgment that the common crowd will pronounce concerning us.

For the mind will not be deprived of the reward of incorruption, provided that, even when bodily integrity has been taken away, the inner person’s chastity remains undefiled under the testimony of its creator.

### 6

For however much the weakness of the flesh may yield to adversaries who have been granted power to slaughter bodies, afflict them with torments, defile them with sexual violence, and subject them to various punishments, they can nevertheless harm in no way the souls that preserve their resolve for holiness.

For, as blessed Jerome says: “The body of holy women is not defiled by violence but by pleasure.”

And again, most holy Augustine says: “The body does not lose its holiness while the holiness of the soul remains, even when the body is oppressed; just as the body’s holiness is lost when the holiness of the soul has been violated, even when the body remains untouched.”

Thus Joseph, Jeremiah, Daniel, and the three boys, together with many Hebrews who faithfully worshiped God, were sold in that period; yet they did not depart from the word of God. For they never reached a condition in which they did not find their God—the very one whose passion they bore in mind and intention. While they were beaten, cut apart, stoned, and sold, they thought upon Christ’s passion, who, many centuries later, was to be sold through the commerce of a treacherous disciple.

### 7

Finally, the prophet Jonah, cast from the ship by God’s command (Jonah 1–2), seized by bestial jaws, is suddenly confined in a dreadful prison. Yet that monster, wholly devoid of reason, rationally obeyed its Creator and mystically understood that the prophet entrusted to it was to be preserved; accordingly, it placed the venerable prey, not to be ruinously destroyed, in the caverns of its belly.

Thus what had been the prophet’s cause of danger might afterward become a sacramental sign of the mystery for nations that would believe; and, enclosed in its entrails, he remained whole and unharmed—the very event by which he foreshadowed the Lord’s burial for the space of three days.

[Editorial note:] His life was admirably written by Saint Jerome, says Baronius in his note on the *Martyrology*, on 21 October. The monk mentioned here is different from the one whom Sozomen calls Malchion, although they resemble one another in many respects; that Malchion lived in the same period and is discussed in book 6, chapter 32.

[Editorial note:] This is drawn from the subtlety of ancient philosophers, as appears from Cicero’s third *Tusculan Disputation*. There is something similar in Seneca: “Pain falls away when it has no place in which to grow.” — Moral.

[Editorial heading:] Moral.

[scan page 418]

## The Document

Thus he preferred to sail to Tarsus, abandoning obedience to the commands of his God, which foretold the burial of the Lord.

So Malchus the monk, in captivity, guarded his chastity with his victorious right hand and was freed from the yoke of cruel masters. In his place, with chastity intervening, an armed hoof served, crushing the impious master with savage ferocity—the master who had left the chaste Malchus unharmed in his cave.

Thus Paulinus, bishop of Nola, a man of outstanding holiness and incomparable merit, voluntarily undertook slavery for the sake of an only son of a widow, moved by the example of the true teacher. Although he enjoyed with the Father and the Holy Spirit the free and coeternal authority to dispose of all things, and although the Father’s power did not precede the majesty of the coeternal Son—for the nature of the Godhead remained indivisible, while the distinction of persons remained without confusion, since the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit possessed one and the same substance—he “did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; he humbled himself even to death, and death on a cross” (Philippians 2:6–8).

[Editorial note:] The life of Malchus was written by Saint Jerome. The author distinguishes him from the Malchion mentioned by Sozomen.

[Editorial note:] Concerning this distinguished example of charity, first commemorated by Saint Gregory the Great, learned men have disputed sharply on both sides. See the seventh dissertation of Jean-Baptiste Le Brun at the end of the Paris edition of the works of Blessed Paulinus, 1685; also Daniel Papebrochius, in the appendix on 22 June, *On the Three Paulinuses*, section II, and the others whom we mention in volume 1 of our Collection, chapter 17, in the work of Saint Isidore, *On Illustrious Men*.

### 8

Therefore, my sisters, setting this likeness of the Lord’s passion before the eyes of your hearts and following his footprints through constant meditation, consider every temporal punishment as nothing. Although it is harsh and bitter, it is nevertheless brief and close to its end; and within the space of a single moment either the one who inflicts it perishes or the one who endures it gives way.

For if punishments are more severe, they quickly impose the limit of endurance; if they are lighter, they are more easily tolerated. In either case, the triumph of glory always remains yours; in either case, your progress toward blessedness is continually increased. Through manifold torture, like gold tested by fire, your souls are rendered purer as the dross of vices falls away.
