And when punishment advances more fiercely, it brings you, who are destined to be crowned, to a mature death, while at the same time it sends you without hesitation toward the true consolation of which the prophet says: “I will give them true consolation, peace upon peace” (Jeremiah 14:13).

[Editorial note:] If the punishments are more severe, they soon produce the failure of endurance; if lighter, they are more easily borne. — Moral.

### 9

In the corruption of this present life, however much each of us may enjoy tranquility, be strengthened by comforts, or be carried along by prosperity, nevertheless, because we are pilgrims away from the Lord, we must acknowledge that there is more desolation than peace in truth.

For everything that clings to temporal affairs and is illuminated by the world’s changing light nevertheless falls under vanity and corruption, and easily slips from its condition, as Solomon says: “All is vanity under the sun” (Ecclesiastes 1:14).

### 10

For this reason we must pray to God with all the greater devotion and frequently devote ourselves to holy pursuits. Like a lamp shining in a dark place, the commands of the divine Scriptures and the authoritative words of the saints must be contemplated and observed amid the darkness of our pilgrimage, by which we are separated from the Lord and from the company of the blessed, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in our hearts (2 Peter 1:19).

Therefore, if we long to behold God with an unobstructed gaze, our hearts must first be purified by faith, consecrated by works, and fortified on every side by the ramparts of charity. By these means we shall undoubtedly be made worthy of the promise of the sacred Gospel, which says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).

Therefore, blessed virgins, I beg you, do not lose the crown prepared for you, and do not let the attraction of any worldly thing separate you from the charity of Christ. Rather, with a steadfast heart proclaim with the Apostle:

“For who will separate us from the love of God? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? As it is written: ‘For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter.’ But in all these things we conquer through him who loved us.

“For I am certain that neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present nor things to come, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:35ff.).

Indeed, all these things must be sought and endured for the sake of eternal recompense with more joyful hearts and more ardent desires. For a crown for one’s labor remains stored up with the Lord for each person, and he will repay the fruit of reward according to the quality of the contest.

### 11

Indeed, we do not believe that we have been made outcasts from divine favor, nor do we hope to be deprived of or ungrateful for the heavenly gift. For although unwillingly, we are bound to him for his name and tied by the deep chain of the prisons.

The inner chambers of the prison are filled with troops of clerics; the Church has been deprived of the sacred ministry of bishops and priests. The divine tabernacles are horrified by a filthy solitude; a spider has woven over the temple; everything is held in silence.

The priests and ministers of the altar are confounded, because “the stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street” (Lamentations 4:1). And when hymns and songs of heavenly praise cease in the assembly, the hidden places of the prison resound with the holy murmur of psalms.

The cantor does not proclaim the divine song in public; the voice of the psalmist does not sound in the choir; the lector does not preach from the pulpit; the Levite does not proclaim the Gospel among the people; the priest does not bring incense to the altars.

For when the shepherd has been struck, dispersion has overtaken the flock.

[Editorial note:] The author laments the wretched times of Bishop Reccafredus, of which Alvarus writes in the *Life of Saint Eulogius*.

### 12

How much more distinguished a glory and more excellent a crown awaits you, my holy sisters, who have voluntarily renounced the world and its transitory things and, armed with zeal for God, have advanced with fearless steps against the enemy of the faith!

You have proceeded forth with a free advance, worthy indeed of the divine gift, and in accordance with the prophetic oracle, which says: “You who willingly offered your lives from Israel to danger, bless the Lord” (Judges 5:2).

As witnesses to the truth against the author of wickedness and the originator of a perverse doctrine, take up victorious weapons against him: fasting, vigils, prayers, and cries, persisting day and night.

I ask you, holy sisters, do not abandon what you have undertaken; do not cease from what you have begun; do not retreat from the opening of the battles. For the reward is given not to those who begin, but to those who persevere.

Do not look back. Do not make your first faith void. Do not, while holding your hand upon the plough, turn aside from the royal road into a byway. Hasten to gird yourselves for the reward of your labor; strive to ascend to the summit of perfection.

For after victory the vigorous soldier is crowned, and when the labor has been completed, wages are distributed to the hired workers. “The one who competes in the contest is not crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Timothy 2:5).

To compete lawfully is to exclude from the heart all affection for passing things and to undertake the contest with a view to obtaining the heavenly kingdom; it is either to live justly unto death or not to fear death for the sake of justice.

For although the just person continually endures the revived assault of demons until death, and although temptations do not abandon him until the end, he is to receive in the future a reward according to the quality of his contest. However outstanding his holiness may be, he does not proceed securely or go to God without fear.

But the one who pursues justice and chooses to die for justice brings a swift end to the wars pressing upon him and ascends without uncertainty to the eternal kingdom.

Whatever his condition, and from whatever snares of vices or filth of sins he may have come—even if he hastens to martyrdom unwashed by baptism—nevertheless he is crowned.

[Editorial note:] “Whatever he wishes to be, and from whatever vices or sins he has come.” — Moral.

[Editorial note:] The theologians call this “the baptism of desire” (*baptismum flaminis*).

### 13

Do not be terrified, sisters, by the rage of your persecutors, nor fear their faces. For the Lord will not allow you to fear their appearance.

He is with you who armed you; the one who encouraged you is himself fighting on your behalf. Nor will he cease to help who chose you to complete this contest, so that, once the goads of adversity have been overcome, he may make you reign with him by perpetual right through endless ages.

### 14

But let us come to those who have thought that you should be prevented from this resolve and have ordered you to violate and deny that first confession which, Christ urging you on, you freely uttered before their judge. We, however, forbid you to do such things, because God must be obeyed rather than men.

For our master, the founder of the Church, instructing our apostles for the preaching of the Gospel, gave them this command: “Whoever confesses me and my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, him the Son of Man also will confess when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels” (Mark 8:38).

It is not fitting, my sisters, to render your vow void, for it is written: “If you have vowed anything to God, do not delay in paying it; for an unfaithful and foolish promise displeases him. Whatever you have vowed, pay it. It is much better not to vow than, after a vow, to deny what was promised” (Ecclesiasticus 5:3–4).

God will not leave it unpunished if, after confessing the truth, you again repudiate it, and pollute with falsehood the mouth which was divinely consecrated by uttering the testimony of truth. For those who order you to do this urge nothing but lying; and those who strive to incline your minds to it compel nothing but the denial of truth.

There is therefore no difference between a liar and one who denies the truth, since it seems to me that the one who abolishes the truth is bound by the same guilt as the one who utters falsehood. The liar tries to insert a fabricated falsehood in place of the truth; but the person who conceals the truth strengthens falsehood by his silence.

Thus it happens that hidden truth does not appear, while falsehood, supported by it, prevails. Yet the two are one, and for this reason they will not go unpunished. For it is written: “A false witness will not be unpunished” (Proverbs 19:5). And again: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wisdom 1:11).

Why, then, holy sisters, are you not afraid of killing yourselves and becoming murderers of your own souls? For the one who kills himself does nothing other than kill a human being, and the executioner of souls is judged liable to heavier crimes than the executioner of bodies. The flesh, once struck down, will at some time rise again and reign in glory with the soul according to its merits; but when the soul has been killed by vices, it drags the flesh along with it into Gehenna.

### 15

Have you lied in what you openly asserted against the adversary of the Catholic faith? Is every insult that you directed against that precursor of Antichrist not true and certain? That he is a demoniac man, a minister of Satan, full of falsehood, and a son of perpetual death and perdition?

Does not the entire Catholic Church repeatedly offer to God the same testimony as you?

### 16

Certainly, the destroyers of your holy purpose set before you the desolation of the churches, the fetters of the priests, and the dispersion of the ministers. They say that at this time we have neither sacrifice nor holocaust nor offering nor incense, because the sacrilegious hand has laid everything waste and disturbed it with tyrannical violence, as in Daniel 3:38ff.

But the answer must be made to them that “an acceptable sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit” (Psalm 50:19), and that a soul which is contrite and humble in spirit is received by the Lord in this way, as though it were among the holocausts of rams and bulls and among thousands of lambs. For there is no confusion for those who confess him (Daniel, at the passage cited).

You, therefore, blessed sisters, have already been caught in that net of the Lord which, at the command of the master, was cast on the right side of the boat, filled with great fish, and brought to shore (John 21:6). You have been reserved for this purpose: that, after the evil faces have been cast away through the apostles’ scrutiny, you may be joined forever to the catalogues of the elect.

But if, when questioned by the judge, you deny that you have cursed the net, you will be cursed; and if you deny that you detested what the Lord detested, you will be liable to a double sin.

One sin will be lying, by denying the truth that you have already confessed; the other will be withholding before the enemy of justice the word of confession. Certainly, what we do not curse we bless by contrast; and whoever we do not detest we admit into our fellowship as though by favoring him.

### 17

Therefore, my sisters, you must persist so that, with divine help, you may complete the battles you have begun in the peace of your souls and protect us from heaven through your more powerful intercession.

For if the merciful Lord does not fail to hear you in this way, he will more easily grant whatever you ask of him when you remain joined to his companions.

Thus immaculate virginity follows the Lord with unhindered steps; thus pure chastity is not separated from the companionship of its Redeemer; thus, sprinkled with the purple blood of martyrdom, the victorious woman follows him clothed in wreaths and diadems.

For God will defend his Church from the distress of the destroyer. He will also, as he wills, rescue us from these bonds by invincible power, guard us, and in his mercy restore us to our proper seats.

You, sisters, must persevere until the death of the flesh, so that you may not only escape the danger to your souls but also preserve them for eternal life, as the Lord says: “Whoever loses his soul for my sake will preserve it for eternal life” (Matthew 10:39).

### 18

But how could you be blameless if, together with our Church, you used silence in this matter—not publicly testifying against the one whom you frequently attack in secret?

Would the Lord not charge you with guilt because you brought him before the tribunal only by meditation of the heart and not by confession of the mouth, while you imitate the pretext of our Church, which at this time attacks that unjust prophet through clandestine accusations?

Because of the crime that has intervened, the Gothic commonwealth, once enlarged in Spain through the prosperity of the churches and possessing the highest dignity of priests who governed it, has, by the hidden and just judgment of God, been transferred into the privilege of this impious cult.

For whatever the Lord has brought upon us, he has brought in true judgment, and all these things have come upon us because of our sins. As it is written:

“Our inheritance has been turned over to foreigners, our houses to strangers. We drink our water for money, and we purchase our wood at a price. Servants rule over us, and there is no one who rescues us from their hands.”

They press the necks of the faithful with a most grievous yoke and, as you see, strive to exclude the Christian people from all the boundaries of their kingdom. Now they allow us to practice Christianity only according to their own pleasure; now, in the manner of Pharaoh’s rite, they force us through dreadful slavery to sweat out our labor; now they intolerably extort from us a written tax obligation; now they place a public census upon the necks of the wretched; now they strip us of our possessions and cruelly crush us through the loss of our goods.

And so, wearying the orthodox community by various forms of oppression and afflicting the Lord’s flock through different attacks of persecution, they believe that they render pleasing service to their god through our losses.

How much greater glory would then be granted us by the Lord if, rejecting our sloth, stirred up by your example, we hastened to undertake such things and did not allow ourselves to labor under the divine goad of this people!

But we wretched people, delighted by their crimes, are aptly marked by the Psalmist’s oracle, which says:

“They were mingled among the nations, and they learned their works; they served their carved images, and it became a scandal to them” (Psalm 105:35–36).

Alas, what grief! We count it a pleasure to live under the nations and do not resist bearing the yoke with unbelievers. Hence, through daily familiarity, we often use their sacrileges and desire their companionship more than we desire, following the example of the patriarch Lot, to leave the land of Sodom and be saved upon the mountain.

### 19

But you, blessed virgins, after you bravely advanced as female warriors into the public contest and, before the kings and rulers of the world, rejected the enemy of justice through your fearless confession, must fight unto death.

For this kind of contest is glorified in death, and the soldier receives the prize when he dies. He becomes certain of the crown of victory precisely by throwing himself into the burning battle as one who is going to die.

Thus, putting off bodily death, you will purchase the eternal condition of everlasting life, devoted to perpetual light. And while acquiring heavenly things in exchange for earthly, and distributing what is passing away, you will receive what remains forever.

Through the outstanding examples of your merits you instruct the Catholic Church, so that, renouncing worldly things, she may attend to heavenly matters.

Therefore, my sisters, the benefit of victory remains with you on both sides; on both sides there remains the gain of unending rewards. And on this account the prophecy of the Psalmist fittingly stands prepared for your righteous labors:

“Glory and riches are in his house, and his righteousness remains forever and ever” (Psalm 111:3).

### 20

But now that I have been placed in the harbor of silence, before the volume reaches its end and ceases to furnish weapons for battle, weapons produced by holy inspiration, I wish to speak with you for a little while, most holy sister Flora, flourishing in the merits of your virtues. Receive with a peaceful hearing the words of our familiarity, admit them to be stored in the chamber of your heart, and place our counsel in your sanctified mind as the instruction of a loving father.

Listen, then, daughter, and see; incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house.

## S. Eulogius, Archbishop of Toledo

### [Page 421]

...of your father, because the king desires your beauty. Your calling, therefore, is not like that of the others. For you, begotten from a wolfish union and born of a ewe for a mother, blossom like a rose from the senses. Although no pagan seed opposed you, having been conceived by divine providence and born in a Christian birth, you honored the Lord Jesus Christ with such believing devotion that, after being cut by severe scourges for his name, you in no way rejected your former confession. For you knew that your Bridegroom had said:

> “They will hand you over to councils and synagogues, and they will scourge you; and you will be led before governors and kings because of me, as a testimony to them and to the nations. But whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10:17 ff.).

### 21

From this point onward, with God as your guide, the glory of martyrdom began to accompany you. From this point the magnificence of your name began to be spread throughout the whole world; from this point reports of your struggle, traveling through peoples and nations, began to become known to many. Finally, during the time of your persecution, I saw the skin of your venerable head torn away by the blows of scourges, and the wound through which your beautiful hair had flowed down. You graciously showed it to me as to a close father, in the purity of your reverence. When I touched it with a gentle hand—for I did not think that the wounds themselves should be soothed by kisses—after I had departed from you, I sighed for a long time, reflecting deeply within myself.

When, however, the abundant grace poured down from heaven through your lips recounted to me your immense sufferings, the dangers that had pressed upon you, and how, once the guarded enclosure in which you had been confined had been divinely opened, the silence of the night had provided you with an opportunity to escape, I judged that in these events you were comparable to the sufferings of the Apostle Peter, which you had displayed to everyone in the same way.

For you, once divinely released, after six years, from city to city and from town to town, through many and varied exiles, had been content with the remedy of flight, taking refuge in hiding places. And you who previously had crossed enormous obstacles in order to escape now, as though your Bridegroom Christ were warning you and saying:

> “Where do you pasture, where do you lie at noon, my sister?” (Song of Songs 1:7)

and again saying to you, “I am coming again to be crucified,” returned with renewed eagerness for battle. You went to the forum, sought the public place, and, fearless, confessing Christ and detesting the adversary of the faith, offered yourself to the judge. Resisting him bravely, praising Christ, the author of your salvation, you extolled the religion of piety; then, denouncing the shameless prophet, you declared that he had been unable to preach anything true and that he was full of falsehood.

For this reason you appropriately sang David’s song:

> “I spoke of your testimonies, O Lord, before kings, and I was not put to shame” (Psalm 118:46).

And again:

> “I proclaimed your righteousness in the great assembly. Behold, I will not restrain my lips, O Lord; you know it. I have not hidden your righteousness in my heart; I have declared your truth and your salvation. I have not concealed your mercy and your truth from the great assembly” (Psalm 39:10–11).

As though you were openly saying:

> “Until now, O Lord, I have concealed the testimony of your truth through fear of the flesh; now, armed with your strength, I will reveal it, because one devoted to God does not know how to fear in this way, nor does a mind enriched by your gift know how to tremble.”

*What follows Eulogius recounts more fully in the Passion of these two virgins; there too he wrote at length concerning the martyrs whom he names here. —Moral.*

### 22

For this reason, servant of Christ, my lady and sister Flora, I have set these things before you: recalling the benefits of such great virtues, do not think that the gifts bestowed upon you from heaven are to be lost, and do not trample them underfoot. Hasten to the prize; run toward the reward, while the especially favorable time for receiving it is at hand.

For your Bridegroom, the Lord Jesus Christ, is ready to bestow upon you the title of perfection, if you do not cease to fight even unto death; if you strive to die for him, as you chose from the beginning, until the very end; and if, delighting in heavenly joys, you count as nothing this painful struggle endured for his sake. For:

> “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to come, which will be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18).

Fight the good fight, my sister, blessed virgin; and if you are wounded more severely, do not yield. For these wounds are the beginnings of eternal happiness, and they bring an end to everlasting pains. Everything remains unharmed. This death gives life, gathers you into the company of the saints, and grants the state of eternity to those who persevere faithfully and courageously in the struggle.

But because this book had long hoped already to be brought to a close, when the beginnings of your martyrdom formerly compelled me to address you separately, sister Flora, I now return to both of you. Still speaking with you together for a little while, I shall explain the reward you have deserved, and then bring this extended discourse to its conclusion.

### 23

Your rewards, my sisters, are unspeakable; exceedingly splendid gifts have been prepared for you. For you will receive from the Lord the hundredfold fruit of virginity and the indescribable benefit of glorious martyrdom.

The holy and venerable Queen of the world, the Virgin Mary, adorned with the most flourishing choirs of virgins, will come to meet you. The very brave soldiers of God, your fellow confessors, will also be present: Perfectus, Isaac, Sancius, Petrus, Walabonsus, Sabinianus, Wistremundus, Habentius, Jeremias, Sisenandus, Paulus, and Theodemirus. They went before you bearing the sign of faith, won victory over the enemy, opened the door for you to reach the kingdom, and prepared a worthy welcome for your journey. They will say:

> “Come, holiest sisters; enter the bridal chamber of your Bridegroom, whom you loved so greatly that you did not fear to die for him. For winter has already passed, the rain has gone away and departed” (Song of Songs 2:11), since the tribulation of time, overcome by you, has withdrawn.
>
> “Hasten, holy sisters; hurry joyfully to behold the face of him whom you served in truth and for whom you did not refuse to die, so that you may live forever. Receive the reward of your labor and take up the crown of your glorious contest.”

*See the Scholion on the Passion of Flora, no. 6.*

*The martyrdoms of all these preceded those of these two holy virgins, as is established in Book II of the* Memorial of the Martyrs.

### 24

Who, then, could imagine the extent of your joy, sister Maria? Who could measure, by human conjecture or words, the joy poured out from heaven into your most blessed minds? Who could explain the rejoicing of both of you, now established in the divine embrace, when, placed amid the overflowing riches of paradise, you receive without delay the gifts of his recompense?

> “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart what God has prepared for those who love him” (Isaiah 64:4).

### 25

Therefore I beseech you, holiest sisters, most prudent virgins, who, always overflowing with the oil of chastity, shall shine with the most splendid radiance of heavenly lamps when you enter the tabernacles of the Lord: remember me, so that, when you enter the bridal chamber of your Bridegroom and deserve to enjoy his unceasing embrace, you may keep me in mind. Protect me by your prayers; defend me by your merits.

May this little book, composed in brief form and produced with burning love for you and concern for your salvation, benefit me, a sinner. I wrote it to instruct you; I used it to encourage you to complete the battles of the Lord; I armed you with the sword of preaching so that you would not fail in the struggle; I showed you the allurements that you ought to flee; I set forth the rewards you deserved; and, as far as I was able, I turned them to your praise.

You know what I asked of you and what, out of regard for charity, I enjoined upon you. May I, through your worthy intercession, be free from every fault and stripped of my sins, and may I know no further offense. Thus, joined to my almighty God by faithful service, may I, after my passing, enjoy the company both of you and of my lords, in whose defense and praise I composed this work, the *Memorial of the Saints*. The violence of the persecutor compelled me to leave it unfinished; nevertheless, with Christ’s favor, it will at some time be completed.

At the end of the volume I have added a very brief supplication. I composed it in simple words and judged it necessary for your purpose. Bind it to your memories through frequent meditation, and offer it to the Lord both for yourselves—who already hold in your hearts a path toward the lights of the heavenly court—and for the benefit of the whole Catholic Church. At the end, mention me as the wording of the prayer requests.

Thus may the God of peace sanctify you completely, so that your souls and bodies may be preserved blameless at the coming of the Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

*An epilogue artfully inserted, with greater elaboration through the device of style. —Editor.*

*At the time when Eulogius was sent into prison by Bishop Reccafredus, he had not yet finished the second book; afterward, as he relates there, he completed it. —Editor.*

### Likewise, a Prayer of the Same Eulogius for the Aforesaid Virgins

*Thus it is read in all editions; however, it seems to us that this prayer should receive another title, namely: “A formula of prayer composed by Eulogius, by which the holy virgins may implore God both for the whole Church and for himself.”*

“Lord God almighty, who are true consolation to those who hope in you, an unfailing remedy to those who fear you, and everlasting joy to those who love you: kindle our heart with the fire of love, and consume the recess of our breast with the flame of your charity, so that we may complete the martyrdom we have undertaken. So that, while the fire of your love flourishes within us, the incentives to sin may fall away from us and the evil-persuading enticements of vices may flee far off. So that, enlightened by the gift of grace, we may be able to despise all the world’s delights, and always love, fear, desire, and cherish you with pure minds and simple vows. Give us help, Lord, in tribulation, for human salvation is vain. Give us strength to fight in this contest, and look upon us from Zion to deliver us, so that, following in your footsteps, we may drink the cup of suffering with joyful mouth. For you, Lord, not only freed your Israelites of old, groaning under the harsh Egyptian yoke, by your mighty right hand, but also utterly crushed Pharaoh and his army, drowned in the midst of the sea, to the glory and honor of your name. Give our weakness in this encounter an unconquered defense against the enemy. Amid the battle-lines of demons and men rising against us, grant the impregnable aid of your right hand. Set the shield of your divinity in our defense, and grant us support, so that by the pouring out of our blood we may fulfill the obligation of our vow of suffering. Just as you yourself deigned to die for us, so make us also die for you by a worthy martyr’s death; so that, escaping the torments of eternal punishment through the temporal sword, and laying aside the burden of the flesh, we may deserve to come happily to you. May your most merciful power also be present without hindrance to your Catholic people, defending your Church from the affliction of the destroyer; and may you, with the crown of holiness and chastity supporting all your priests, command them, after an unstained ministry of sacred duty, to approach the heavenly homeland. Among them, make your servant Eulogius, whose teaching instructs us after the gift you bestowed, whose writings educate us, whose consolations strengthen us, and whose preaching encourages us, faithful to your service, cleansed from every sin and washed free of every crime, and perpetually devoted to your obedience. May he, having rendered you service pleasing to you in this mortal life, worthy of your future gifts of grace, obtain at least the final resting place in the land of the living. Through Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with you forever and ever. Amen.”*

*Doubtless taken from the devout prayer used at the sixth hour in the office of the most holy Virgin Mary: “Grant, merciful God, to our weakness,” and so forth.*

## St. Eulogius, Archbishop of Toledo and Martyr

### On the Life and Passion of the Holy Virgins Flora and Maria

### Author’s Preface

### 1

Although the worship offered to martyrs belongs to the praise of Christ, whatever is devoutly performed in the festivals of the blessed nevertheless provides the faithful with a remedy for their souls, especially since through this worship and through the patronage of the martyrs and of the supreme Redeemer a reward is obtained in whose honor the virtues of the saints are recalled.

Therefore, when we set out to arrange the glorious deeds of our virgins Flora and Maria, let us not serve the charm of eloquence or the resounding harmonies of words. Let us observe only what may simply convey to the faithful the truth of what happened. We believe that pure truth, arranged with simplicity, is sufficient for us, rather than falsehood dressed in empty ornament. It is enough for us faithfully to report what was; for it is not fitting to adorn with verbal beauty something that did not occur.

For unalloyed truth, however it is expressed, stands upon a firmer footing, while an elaborately fabricated falsehood endures only briefly. Nor does Christ permit an advocate of justice to be deprived of the reward of blessing when the speaker of falsehood is nevertheless held bound by the guilt of homicide.

### 2

It is therefore necessary to set out individually the calling of these virgins, born of one native soil and united to the heavenly realms by the same occasion of death, and, with God’s help, to describe in at least a modest style the ways in which each attained the summit of sanctification to which she had been predestined.

Flora’s parents and homeland: she was born in Córdoba and, after her father’s death, was piously raised by her mother.

*The remarkable abstinence of Flora.*

### 3

First, then, the most holy virgin Flora flourished exceedingly in physical beauty and loveliness, but flourished still more in her inner character. She had a Christian mother, from the village of Ausinianos, eight miles west of Córdoba, descended, as I might say, from pure and noble stock; but her father was a pagan from the town of Seville. For some reason, they were exiled from their native places and came to Córdoba in order to live there.

From their last child they begot this little girl. After her father was taken away by death, she was raised as Christ’s bride under the protection of her most faithful mother. Her devout mother, instructing her in the laws of sacred religion, taught her to worship Christ God with faithful belief: he came to us in the final age through the womb of the Virgin Mary, drawing near to human beings through the humanity he assumed, yet through his ineffable divinity he remained always invisible, incomprehensible, and beyond estimation.

The venerable girl, drinking in the devotion of faith in her tenderest years, began to build within the recesses of her mind a holy altar, upon which she would always offer to Christ the holocausts of good works. From the very beginnings of childhood she deprived herself of all the vanities of the world, and trampled underfoot, already touched by heavenly dew, everything to which that age—being without the fullness of understanding—was childishly inclined.

At one time, when I visited her mother to learn the beginning of the girl’s way of life, her mother said:

> “I speak to you truthfully: from her earliest years, when my daughter had hidden the love of Christ in her heart, she rejected every form of worldly pleasure and always sought to meditate in her heart upon the things of God. She never ceased to perform holy works.
>
> “Thus, during the days of Lent, either to accommodate her smallness or so that her still-developing age might grow stronger, I would offer her food at the appropriate hour of the midday meal. But, keeping her heart fixed upon the strength of the Lord, she would distribute it to the needy and secretly practice blessed fasting.
>
> “As she did this each day, almost the whole period of abstinence had passed before the child’s hidden devotion was scarcely revealed by certain indications. I resisted such wishes, lest her tender body should be weakened by the wasting effects of abstinence before it had matured, and I tried to persuade her to take a daily meal. Yet I could not induce her to eat except late in the day and after constant threats. Nevertheless, Christ’s chosen bride accomplished her vow.”

### 4

From that time onward, the mother, by watchful care, took responsibility for her daughter’s conduct. Seeing that the girl had been assigned to Christ in all things, she no longer dared to oppose her pious inclinations.

The venerable girl, seeking to please God alone, attentively followed the Gospel, listening to Christ’s warning and saying:

> “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23).

Thus, preparing within herself a most pure dwelling through the fulfillment of the heavenly commandment, she nevertheless deserved to enjoy daily the coming of the holy and undivided Trinity.

*A pure Hispanism. —Moral. See the scholia on Book I of the* Memorial, *no. 18.*

### 5

But while, through the practice of holiness, that which she meditated upon secretly was advancing more fruitfully into the love of Christ, and while she was striving to be more firmly joined to Christ through the same religion, she still did not dare to attend the gatherings of the faithful openly, because she had a brother who was an adherent of a deadly and perfidious doctrine and who constantly watched her conduct.

Since she was naturally prudent and keen of mind, she learned from wise people that hidden belief achieved nothing, nor did a concealed confession of the Trinity, especially since it is written:

> “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10).

And again in the Gospel:

> “Everyone who confesses me before men, I also will confess him before my Father who is in heaven; but whoever denies me before men, I also will deny him before my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 10:32–33).

*She abandons her father’s house, to which she later returns.*

### 6

Having therefore been usefully instructed in how she ought to conduct herself in confessing Christ’s name, and knowing that there was a serious difference between secretly believing in Christ and publicly appearing marked with Satan’s ensign, she left the house without consulting her mother and secretly fled with her sister.

She settled in safer places among Christians, while her brother—whom we mentioned above—was savagely persecuting the Church of God on account of them. He delivered some clerics to prison and pursued religious women everywhere. When they recognized the persecution that was raging against the Lord’s flock, and judged that they ought not to remain safe while the Church of God was being beaten, holy Flora, knowing that she had been divinely chosen for such a battle, returned openly to the house and said:

> “Behold, I whom you seek am here in your midst. It is on my account that you persecute God’s flock. I stand here fearless, believing in Christ, supporting the Catholic religion, bearing the marks of the cross, and desiring everything that expresses the worship of piety.
>
> “Now, if you can, weaken this confession. Strive, with crueler tortures, to overcome my faith and attempt—something I very much doubt can happen—to separate me from Christ. For love of him, I have resolved to endure with the greatest joy whatever the savage judge may inflict as my punishment.
>
> “I believe you will prove that, amid torments, I possess a more unyielding perseverance in confessing Christ Jesus than I now display at the first encounter.”

*This is a hemistich of Virgil, inserted knowingly and deliberately by Eulogius, as are other such passages. —Moral.*

### 7

Her brother tortures her and accuses her of being a Christian, but she bravely confesses Christ; for this reason she is scourged severely.

Her perverse brother, hearing these things, sometimes tried to turn her back through blows and threats, sometimes through flattering words. But when he saw that all his efforts accomplished nothing and that he himself was being worn out by fruitless labor, he brought her before the judge, saying:

> “This is my sister, whom my mother’s final childbirth brought forth for me. She had always reverently observed the ceremonies of the law with me and faithfully fulfilled the obligations owed to the worship of our faith. But Christians, repeatedly pressuring her, made her deny our prophet and detest our rite; and through a certain seduction they persuaded her to believe that Christ is God.”

The judge asked whether the brother’s accusation was true. At once she denied her impious brother and testified that she had never known the worship of Muhammad. She added:

> “I have known Christ from my infancy. I have been instructed by his teachings. I have resolved to possess him as God, and I promised him the integrity of my body, to be delighted one day in his bridal chamber.”

When the most holy virgin had said this, the judge’s sacrilegious heart was immediately shaken by monstrous fury. Turning his anger against the martyr’s death, he ordered her to be stretched out by the hands between two attendants. He covered her head with savage blows and continued to scourge her until, the skin and hair of her head having been torn away, the bare bone of her skull was exposed.

Nevertheless, the young martyr and virgin persisted in her confession. Then the judge handed her over, half dead and nearly lifeless, to her wicked brother, ordering that, after she had been restored with medicines and instructed in the words of the law, she should finally be brought before him again unless she converted.

She is confined at home by her brother, but escapes and remains hidden until the time of her martyrdom.

### 8

The enemy of Christ had brought the virgin into his house. Yet that wicked brother did not entrust her to the household women to be comforted by care and words; instead, he shut her in the wild interior of the house with great chains. Since the entire estate was surrounded and fortified by a massive wall, he believed that no one would have any concern about escape.

Therefore, after a few days, when the courageous Flora had been purified by her wounds and felt herself restored, one night she climbed, with the Lord’s assistance, over a high wall through a small hut adjoining the courtyard of the house, and from there threw herself out onto the public street.

*A chain sometimes serves as a door-bolt. —Moral.*

Unmoved by any pain, she began to make her way through the darkness of night, guided by an angel, wherever the Lord might lead. After being refreshed by the hospitality of a certain faithful person amid that nocturnal confusion, and remaining there for some time, she then sought out, for the sake of hiding, a celebrated little settlement of the city of Tucci called Ossaria. There she remained concealed with her sister until the time when she completed her martyrdom.

*Although this town is called celebrated, it has left behind no memory of itself. —Editor.*

And I—I, that sinner; I, rich in iniquities—who from the beginning of her martyrdom enjoyed her friendship, touched with my joined hands the scars of that most reverend and delicate head after the virgin’s hair had fallen away beneath the blows of the scourges.

*The holy virgin and martyr Maria. She is entrusted for education in the monastery of Cuteclara.*

### 9

But since, with God’s help, the beginning of blessed Flora’s manner of life and martyrdom has been recorded, I think it worthwhile likewise to explain the course of the holy virgin and martyr Maria’s birth and the beginnings of her religious life. Thus, since their agreement in battle and their shared consent to die for justice were equal, the intention of my pen may also be similar in recounting the calling of this virgin.

Her father, said to have come from the town of Elepha, was not of lowly lineage and was nevertheless a Christian. Taking a wife from the Arab people, he cleansed her of every error of impiety and dedicated her to the faith of Christ. Therefore, unable to remain in his own fields with that wife, he was driven as an exile through various places until, under divine guidance, he reached the town of Froniano, which lies in the mountains of Córdoba, twelve miles west of the city.

He was accompanied by both children whom he had received from her, namely Walabonsus and Maria. There they supported their life as best they could. There that woman, rescued from the jaws of wolves and persevering in the faith of Christ, after some time rested in the Lord. There her surviving husband, having attained the rank of a confessor, entered the very narrow path of everlasting life, to be delighted by heavenly joys.

But he entrusted the boy to the priest Salvator, of blessed memory, to be educated according to ecclesiastical regulations and admitted to the Lord’s flock. At that time Salvator governed, with splendid discipline, the monastery of Saint Felix founded in that place.

This holy virgin, however, he dedicated to God and entrusted to the monastery of Cuteclara, where the glorious memory of the ever-virgin holy Mary, the Mother of the Lord, shone. He placed her under a woman of supreme holiness named Artemia, who herself had once sent two sons before her to heaven through martyrdom, namely Adulfus and John.

*Without doubt Baldegothona, to whom Eulogius himself addressed a letter after Flora’s martyrdom. —Scholion [continues beyond the supplied text].* They triumphed bravely over the enemy at the beginning of the reign of the present ruler.

Their deeds, shining like stars in the sky for the benefit of the holy Church and as an example to the weak, were composed in a more expansive style by our old man and teacher, the most illustrious doctor, the abbot Speraindeo of blessed memory, whom we mentioned in the first book (*Memorial*, no. 7).

*How she was piously educated.*

### 10

Artemia, therefore, by the grace of her holiness and the advancement of her age, or because of the martyrdom of her sons, surpassed the other women living in the same monastery. Through her authority, the entire virginal community of the monastery was placed under her direction.

She taught the girl, as she herself had learned, to serve God in all humility, chastity, and obedience, exercising her mind in the fear of the Lord. Not long afterward, when the priest Salvator had departed from the world, the father brought the boy back to himself to raise him.

The two future martyrs made great progress in the fear of God through the grace of the Holy Spirit. At length, as the young Walabonsus grew through the ecclesiastical grades, he assumed the office of deacon, while continuing to excel in every form of uprightness.

Because the religious maiden loved him with excessive affection, and because they obeyed one another in every spiritual love with the sweetness of sibling affection, their relationship was marked by complete devotion. Since the most holy virgin was older than her young brother, he honored her in the place of a mother, and she transformed fraternal affection into the love of a daughter.

*After her brother is killed for Christ, the saint leaves the monastery; Flora meets her, and both offer themselves to the judge.*

### 11

While these things were continually taking place between them, God arranging it, the most worthy Levite Walabonsus, together with the blessed priest Peter and the other confessors—as was related above (*Memorial*, Book II, chapter 4)—was the first by his election to martyrdom.

At last the servant of Christ Maria was left deprived of the bodily consolation of her brother. She had been predestined for martyrdom before the foundation of the world and had always been sustained inwardly and outwardly by the intercession of her brother.

But, as is the condition of human frailty, when she longed more and more often for the sight of her brother, whose company she would soon enjoy, the holy martyr in a dream admonished a certain religious woman that sister Maria should cease weeping for him, since she would shortly come to him in heaven.

From that day the virgin’s heart was consumed by love of martyrdom. She who had impatiently mourned her brother’s death, suddenly enlightened by God, yearned for martyrdom with an impatient ardor.

### 12

One day, then, I believe at Christ’s invitation, she left the monastery and descended toward the forum, so that, like the other martyrs who were already delighting in their heavenly reward, this virgin too might obtain the crown of martyrdom by confessing Christ and repelling the adversary of the holy faith.

While she entered the church of the blessed martyr Acisclus, which still stood along the route, in order to beseech the Lord, by God’s will she found holy Flora there, invoking the martyrs in prayer for her support. Flora herself, burning with renewed eagerness for battle because Christ had said to her, “I am coming again to be crucified,” had come down from her hiding place, eager to recover the palm of the martyrdom she had once begun.

Then they greeted one another with kisses and, by mutual consultation, examined each other’s purpose. When their mutual confession revealed that they shared one and the same vow, Christ having fulfilled the words he had spoken:

> “Wherever two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matthew 18:20),

they were immediately bound together by an indissoluble bond of charity. No circumstance was to separate them from one another, no fortune was to make them break away, and no danger, however savage, which might be raised against their destruction for the confession of truth, was to divide them from each other—until one of them should approach Christ and the other her brother Walabonsus in heaven.

And so, advancing in the very force of their resolve before the judges, holy Flora, with an even firmer exhortation than before, as I believe, first addressed them, saying:

43. “Behold, I am she who, because I was born of Gentile stock and adhered to Christ, was long ago torn by you with cruel lashes so that I might deny him. Until now, wandering here and there in flight and hiding because of the weakness of the flesh,[a] I now, supported by the strength of my God, do not fear to stand before your tribunals; with the same constancy as at first I profess Christ God in truth, and declare that your criminal teacher is a false prophet, an adulterer, and a great evildoer.”

Then the venerable virgin Maria, her mouth sanctified by an outpouring of heavenly graces, spoke: “And I too, judge, had a brother among those illustrious confessors who died after reviling your prophet with no slight mockery; with like boldness I affirm that Christ is truly God, and I declare that your rite and the ceremonies of your law are fabrications of demons.”

Immediately the most savage judge, stirred by mad rage, gnashing beneath that terrible utterance, tried to frighten their virgin resolve by a most harsh roar; he assailed them with reproaches and shouts, adding the filth of prison and the company of prostitutes. They are committed to prison, where Saint Eulogius comforts them.

14. At last he receives into his care the hidden members of Christ’s brides in prison, to be guarded rather than destroyed: they who, always adorned with chaste comeliness and eminent in the practice of holiness from their very cradles, had shone forth with the especial grace of virtues. While the holy virgins remained there for some time, they persisted in fasting, devoted themselves to prayer, and dispelled all the horrors of that prison-house by heavenly meditation upon hymns. Then we too, brought out of the cave[b] when they were assigned to this prison, composed, by God’s favor, the book *Document of Martyrdom* for their instruction; and, as they were now almost slipping from their resolve under the persuasion of certain persons, we dedicated it to them as a consolation for contemplating and completing the contest they had begun, joining a prayer appropriate to their struggle and to the whole Church at the end of the work.

They are then led out and killed.

15. Remaining therefore in the praises of God and of the most holy Virgin, after a third admonition to prostrate themselves they were brought out into the forum. I shall pass over the judge’s repeated questioning of them, whether jointly or separately of the most blessed Flora, as I have already set it forth elsewhere; and, for the sake of brevity, say nothing further, lest a prolonged discourse weary readers. The precious death of the virgins brings my pen to its fitting end. They were then hurried to the place of execution and made the sacred signs upon their faces. Thus, with necks extended, holy Maria was laid low after blessed Flora. Leaving their bodies there to be devoured by dogs and torn apart by birds, the next day they cast them into the river. Of these bodies, that of the holy virgin and martyr Maria was, by God’s gift, placed in the monastery of Cuteclara, from which she had come down to martyrdom; but in what place the Lord has laid the body of the most blessed virgin and martyr Flora is wholly unknown. Their heads, however, are deposited in the basilica of Saint Acisclus the martyr, who protects the Christian people there by the favor of his bodily presence.

16. Finally, we are concerned to indicate only this in the history: before the blessed virgins were killed, they promised certain sister-companions that, on the very occasion when they stood before Christ their crowner, they would ask their Spouse, through the grace they had obtained, to free us from our bonds; and this was accomplished with God’s aid. For they completed their martyrdom on the eighth day before the Kalends of December, and on the third day before those same Kalends drew us, released from our fetters, out of the filth of prison, in the era stated above. Through Christ our Lord, who lives with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

[a] For a full six-year period from the time of her flight, as is clear from the *Document*, no. 21. — Schottus.

[b] We have already spoken of the difference between the two prisons of Córdoba (scholium on chapter 6, book II of the *Memorial*). — Morales.

## Letters

### Letter I of Saint Eulogius to Alvarus

Celebrating the martyrdom of the two virgins Flora and Maria.

**Eulogius to his most beloved brother Alvarus, in the Lord Jesus Christ.**

1. The Lord has magnified his mercy toward us, my brother, and we have rejoiced [Psalm 125:3]. For those to whom we once entrusted the word of life amid tears, we now see reaping the fruit of victory with joy. We see our virgins, having conquered the prince of darkness and trampled the attractions of worldly desires, their lamps kindled with the fragrance of good works, going forth to meet the Bridegroom and King of heaven.

Because they had always prepared themselves as a living and holy sacrifice, pleasing to God, they entered the halls of the heavenly court. Christ invited them to the wedding feast, and they sang a new song, saying:

> “Worthy are you, Lord our God, to receive glory and honor, because you redeemed us from the power of darkness, made us worthy to share in the lot of your saints, and transferred us into your eternal kingdom” (Revelation 5:9–10).

And although the universal Church rejoices in their victories, I am especially lifted up by a particular joy, because I see that the *Document of Martyrdom*, which I presented to them when certain people were almost falling away from their purpose through reproach, was not given in vain.[^c0084-1]

Although both their calling and their sanctification had proceeded from God the Father from the beginning of the world, our intention in instructing them nevertheless has its own reward stored up with the Lord, who promised to repay in his name a gift given to the thirsty (Mark 9:40).

Now, ten or more days before they were led to martyrdom, the wicked judge summoned my lady Flora alone to a hearing. After she had made her invincible profession—by which, calling the judge himself an enemy of the faith, she struck him down by her fearless answer—he ordered her to return to prison.

I approached the enclosure in which they were being held and humbly asked my lady what the judge had asked her and what answer she had given him. She, adorned as she was with angelic beauty and shining with the grace of heavenly chastity, replied to me with a cheerful face and modest lips, as though already nourished by the joy of the heavenly homeland:

> “Today, when I was brought before the judge, with my brother standing not far away opposite me—that enemy of our faith whose persecution has brought me to this prison—I recognized him. I declared that he was my blood brother, and the judge said: ‘Why does this man, who is so distinguished as a guardian of our faith, remain firm while you profess Christ?’  
> 
> “I replied: ‘Eight years ago, judge, I too was occupied by the darkness of ignorance. Serving the laws of my fathers, I was enslaved to pagan error. But when the author of mercy enlightened me, I chose the faith of the Christians, for which I have resolved to contend until death.’  
> 
> “The judge then said: ‘What is your judgment today concerning what you professed before me some time ago?’  
> 
> “He thereby reproached the prophet whom he worshiped, and repeated the question by which I had once openly condemned that sect’s author, when, casting aside fear, I had detested him and then, returning from my hiding-place to suffer, had come before the tribunal and faced the judge.  
> 
> “I answered again: ‘Judge, I say what you heard me say at first; and if you question me further, I shall tell you even greater things against him than before.’  
> 
> “Then, puffing out his cheeks and hissing threats of death through his swollen throat, he ordered me to return to the prison.”

3. After my lady had related these things to me in the honeyed sweetness of her speech, I commended her to the Lord in whatever words I could. Then, commending myself to her prayers and happy merits, and refreshed by that most reverent conversation, I returned to the hiding-place of my prison.

Therefore, I ask your fraternity, most beloved brother, to arrange for posterity a brief account of their passion, so that you may always deserve to be protected by their intercession. On the very day when, under confession of Christ’s name, they were reported to us to have died, we all hastened to the weapons of prayer and spent the ninth hour in praise of God. Thereafter, with solemn rejoicing, we celebrated in honor of our virgins the evening office, the morning office, and the sacrificial Mass; and we commended ourselves to their patronage, to be protected and favored by them.

Because the hope of all has been placed in the merits of these women, Christ, who favors their victories and glorious intercessions, released us from our chains on the sixth day after they had been crowned and brought us out of the closed prison. Before they suffered, they had also promised certain familiar sisters that, as soon as they stood before Christ their crowned Lord, they would intercede for our liberation. Thus, on the eighth day before the Kalends of December, they completed their martyrdom, and on the third day before those same Kalends we were released in daylight, magnifying and blessing the name of our God, who strengthened his holy virgins Flora and Maria in the contest and gave them the victory, and who, through their worthy merits, liberated us in peace. He is blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

*Concerning the difference between the two prisons at Córdoba.*

[^c0084-1]: This is what we explained earlier in the work concerning these virgins (Scholium, no. 2).

[^c0084-2]: Since everything has already been discussed and related in the second book—that is, the *Memorial*, chapter 38—in which I warned Flora about the hope of obtaining the crown and urged her to adore the angelic gaze with bowed neck, I commend myself to your prayers and to her happy merits, refreshed by the reverence of that conversation, and return to my prison’s hiding-place.

[^c0084-3]: What follows concerns the calamities of our Church and the martyrdoms of the saints; they are read earlier in Books I and II, where we have added whatever seemed necessary. Here Saint Eulogius repeats certain things in the same words as in his *Document of Martyrdom*.

---

### Letter II to Bildegoth

It relates the martyrdom of Flora, Bildegoth’s sister, and sends her belt.

**Eulogius, servant of Christ, to his most beloved sister Bildegoth, greeting in the Lord Jesus Christ.**

Let it be known to you, my lady and sister, that your sister Flora, our lady and most holy patron, completed her martyrdom in peace on the eighth day before the Kalends of December, a Tuesday, at the ninth hour, together with her companion, the blessed Maria, a religious woman of Cuteclara—who, among those earlier martyrs, was led into heaven with her brother Walabonsus the deacon—persevering in her holy profession unto death.

Therefore, dearest sister, remain supported by as great a consolation as we unquestionably believe them to possess, now placed among the citizens of heaven and the choirs of blessed virgins, holding the palms of victory and singing every day before the Lamb’s throne a new song:

> “Worthy are you, Lord our God, to receive glory and honor, because you redeemed us from the power of darkness and transferred us through the glorious trophy of martyrdom into your kingdom” (Revelation 5:9–10).

You, beloved sister, should strive to adorn your life with worthy and God-pleasing conduct, so that you may reign with Christ eternally and be joined to the company of the blessed virgins.

Moreover, we have sent you, as a memorial of your venerable sister Flora, the belt which she used in prison. Farewell in the Lord, dearest sister, and pray for us.

---

### Letter III to Wiliesindus, Bishop of Pamplona

When Saint Eulogius was traveling into Gaul, he stayed with this bishop, who had asked him for relics of the blessed martyr Zoilus of Córdoba. Here he recounts the story of his journey and also sends relics of Zoilus and Acisclus, describing the disasters suffered by the Church of Córdoba and listing the martyrdoms of many.

**Eulogius the presbyter to the most reverend and holy minister of God, my lord and father Wiliesindus, bishop of the see of Pamplona, greeting.**

1. Formerly, most blessed father, when the dreadful misfortune of the age removed my brothers Alvarus and Isidore from their native land and compelled them to live in exile near the farther regions of Gaul, around King Louis of Bavaria, it also forced me, because of them, to visit various regions and undertake unfamiliar and difficult journeys.

The road was crowded with brigands, and all Gothia had once been thrown into confusion by the violent invasion of William, who, rebelling against Charles, king of the Franks, and relying at that time on the assistance of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, king of the Arabs, acted as a tyrant and made every route impassable and inaccessible.

As I traveled toward the region of Pamplona, I thought that I would soon depart from there. But the very people who hold the road between Pamplona and the Gascon territories, raising their rebellious necks against the destruction of the aforesaid Charles through the factions of Count Sancho Sanchez and acting against the law of that prince, blockaded the entire route and brought enormous danger upon travelers.

At that time Your Beatitude offered me great consolation during my pilgrimage. Truly representing the supreme Teacher and obeying his commands in truth, you did not delay to refresh with hospitality the man whom the true charity of Jesus Christ had commended to you, when he said: “I was a stranger and you welcomed me” (Matthew 25:35).

Thus you strive to store treasures of merit with the Father in heaven: you provide what is necessary to the needy, encourage everyone, and protect all. Consequently, during my exile I could draw breath nowhere except in the affectionate presence of my pilgrim brothers and my destitute household. I often grieved, but you, father, constantly consoled me in my sorrow; I wept greatly, but you lifted me up with pious compassion. For, according to the Apostle, you were weak with me, you were sad with me, and you wept with me (Romans 12:15; 2 Corinthians 11:29).

Since many sorrows did not permit me to remain in one place, I wished to visit the places of the saints, so that I might soothe my spirit, cast down by the deepest grief.

2. Above all I desired to visit the monastery of the blessed Zacharias,[^c0084-4] situated at the foot of the Pyrenees, in the aforesaid territories of Gaul, where the river Aragus rises and, flowing swiftly, waters Seburia and Pamplona before emptying into the Cantabrian Sea. The monastery, adorned by its famous devotion to the exercise of regular discipline, shone throughout the West.

But you, father, assisted my longing, instructed me with salutary counsel as I departed, and supported me with the pious companionship of brothers on my journey. Before I reached that place, I spent several days at the monastery of Leyre and learned especially that men devoted to the fear of God remained there.

Afterward, wandering through various places, I finally reached, by divine favor, the monastery I had so often desired to visit. At that time Odoarius was its abbot, a man of supreme holiness and great learning. He received us with more kindness than can be expressed and showed us every form of humanity.

3. The community of that blessed congregation numbered nearly a hundred men. Some were already citizens of heaven; others, in different ways, were advancing through diverse virtues toward that goal.

In some, perfect charity toward Christ prevailed, casting out fear. In many others shone a profound humility, by which each one considered himself the least and lowest, and they strove to imitate the commandments of God. Many, although weak in body, were strengthened by the virtue of great courage and undertook demanding acts of obedience with minds that rose above their physical condition.

In certain others, obedience—teacher of every virtue—so vindicated their authority that it did not permit those under them to degenerate; rather, it compelled them to perform great deeds beyond their strength, so that each might be distinguished by his own office.

All worked eagerly, each striving to surpass the other. Their ardor to please God and the brothers increased through mutual example, and each exercised the ingenuity of his own skill for the common benefit.

Some devoted themselves most diligently to the care of pilgrims and guests. As though Christ himself were turning aside to their hospitality, they served every newcomer with complete attention.

Although they were so numerous, no one was boastful or arrogant. They practiced silence, and throughout the night, devoting themselves to fervent prayers, they overcame the nocturnal hours by vigilant meditation. They surrounded themselves with great watchfulness, lest they be condemned by the words of the Psalmist:

> “They slept their sleep, and found nothing” (Psalm 75:6).

4. But what mortal can adequately recount the virtues of saints who, while placed on earth, live like angels, and who, although they live among human beings, truly pursue a heavenly way of life? When I wished to learn from them, they all fell prostrate and asked me to pray for them.

After I had returned to my home, I found everything safe: my mother, my two sisters, Nicole and Anullon, and the last of all our relatives in age, my younger brother Joseph. The venerable abbot Odoarius and John the provost spent the entire day, until evening, in conversation with us about the divine Scriptures. After we exchanged kisses and departed from one another, we retraced our steps to you, apostle of God. Through your recommendation we deserved to be received by those fathers with such honor and reverence.

5. When affection for my own land, my dear mother Elizabeth, my two sisters Nicole and Anullon, and my younger brother Joseph urged me to return, you compelled me to remain longer and did not allow me to depart in sorrow. But you could no longer heal my heart, wounded by both afflictions: the exile of my brothers and the desolation of those at home brought me daily lamentation.

Thus, embarrassed by our affection, you asked me, when I returned to Córdoba, to send you the relics of the holy martyr Zoilus and to illuminate the people of Pamplona with this gift.[^c0084-5] I immediately replied that I would fulfill your request and truthfully promised that I was your debtor in this matter.

6. When I departed from you, I hurried to Zaragoza because of my brothers, whom popular rumor claimed had joined the companies of merchants recently descending there from the farther parts of France. As I approached the city, I indeed found merchants, but from their report I learned that my pilgrim brothers had gone into exile at Mainz, the most distinguished city of Bavaria.

In due course, when our brothers returned from inner Gaul by God’s favor, we learned that this report of the merchants had been true.

7. After remaining for some time with the Senior Pontiff, who then governed that city with upright conduct, I later descended to Complutum, passing rapidly through the city of Segontia, where the prudent Sise-mundus was then bishop.

When I was kindly received by Venerius, bishop of Complutum, I returned to Toledo on the fifth day. There I found our most holy old man, Wistremirus, bishop and lamp of the Holy Spirit and light of all Spain. His holiness of life illumined the whole world, and by the nobility of his character and the greatness of his merits he continued to nourish the Catholic flock.

We spent many days with him and enjoyed his angelic companionship.

8. When I returned home, I found everything unharmed: my mother, my two sisters, and our youngest brother Joseph, who had been deposed from his position by the tyrant’s savage anger at that time. His abandoned household received its pilgrim with joy, as though someone raised from the grave, and rejoiced to see its lord again after so long a time.

For my part, in all my conversations I exalted you as a father; in every conversation with my family I recalled your kindness; and, carrying the affection of your charity in my heart, I embrace you in the arms of my mind.

9. Since the long course of earthly time separates us by great distances, and another immense chaos also stands in the way—while I remain in Córdoba under the impious rule of the Arabs, you, settled at Pamplona, enjoy the protection of a Christian prince who continually fights against them in a grave conflict and denies travelers free passage—it has happened either that we have not rendered the service owed to your goodness, or that we have not fulfilled your pious desire by sending the relics, or that we did not think it right to entrust such great treasures to just anyone.

Now, however, because, by God’s providence, Lord Galindo, son of Enneco, is returning to his homeland and desires to revisit his own lands, we have sent you through him the relics of the aforementioned martyr.

We have also sent those of Saint Acisclus, although you did not request them, so that, happily fulfilling your promise to build a basilica in honor of their blessed memory, their patronage may, by God’s favor, come to us because of this obedience. May Christ repay and grant you everything that you have done for us and everything that you have shown toward us. Your former service to us is not hidden from him, and he is able to repay it to you with pious increase, a hundredfold. For he said:

> “Whoever receives you receives me; and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me. Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward; and whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward” (Matthew 10:40–41).

Everything has been stored up for you before the Lord. All that is owed to you for your pious labors remains safe and unharmed with him, to be received at the appointed time, when the just Judge comes to render to each person, according to the quality of his labors, either reward or punishment.

10. Finally, most blessed father, we do not wish you to remain unaware of the tribulation which, through our present fault,[^c0084-6] we have been suffering during these days. Defend us more earnestly than usual with the shield of your prayers, so that, through the unassailable merit of your intercession—which we trust has great power with the Lord—we may deserve to be rescued from the deep labyrinth of our sorrows.

For in the present year, which is the era 889, a savage tyrannical fury has blazed up against the Church of God. It has overturned everything, devastated all things, and scattered the whole community. It has thrust bishops, presbyters, abbots, deacons, and the entire clergy into prison, binding in iron all whom it was able to seize at that time and burying them, as though dead, in the underground caverns of the age.

Among them I, your beloved sinner, am bound, and together with all the others I endure the dreadful squalor of the prisons. The Church has been deprived of its sacred ministry, deprived of its prophetic voice, and stripped of its office. At this time we have no offering, sacrifice, incense, or place for firstfruits by which we can appease our God.[^c0084-7] Instead, with contrite soul and humble spirit, we offer Christ vows of praise, so that when the assembly’s psalmody ends, the inner parts of the prison resound with the holy murmur of hymns.

The lord Galindo will be able to recount all these matters to you carefully. We, partly weighed down by sorrow and partly avoiding the weariness of unpolished speech, have confined this little sheet within its proper limits, lest its brevity as a letter pass over into the form of a commentary.

11. To illuminate the ages of future generations, and so that they may not remain ignorant of our troubles and tears, let us at least touch briefly upon a few matters.

Certain presbyters, deacons, monks, virgins, and laymen, suddenly armed with zeal for divine things, descended into the public square and drove back the enemy of the faith. They detested and cursed the impious and criminal prophet of the Muslims, Muhammad, and, raising their courageous spirit against him, offered this testimony:

> “We have discovered that this man, whom you honor with the highest veneration and whose deceptive sect, produced by the inspiration of demons, you receive with such honor, is a magician, an adulterer, and a liar; and we confess that those who believe him must be handed over to the snares of eternal destruction. Why, then, since you are most prudent men, do you share in such sacrileges instead of attending to evangelical truth?”

12. Confessing these and similar things, as the Spirit granted them utterance, in the presence of kings and princes, they were all killed by the avenging sword.

Their decapitated bodies were hung on stakes and, after several days, burned in the fire. Their ashes were scattered into the waters of the rivers, while many bodies were left unburied before the palace doors and exposed to birds and dogs. Soldiers were assigned to guard them, so that no Christian, moved by human compassion, might bury the corpses stripped of their flesh, as it is written:

> “They have given the dead bodies of your servants as food to the birds of heaven, the flesh of your saints to the beasts of the earth. They have poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them” (Psalm 78:2–3).

We shall list their names and the days of their deaths at the end of the letter.

For this reason we remain bound and are held in chains: we attribute their deeds to our own prompting and ascribe to our instruction whatever they accomplished after being divinely enlightened.

Therefore, we ask you to employ the support of your prayers in our defense, to make our imprisonment known throughout all your monasteries, and to order them to remain vigilant in earnest prayer for us. Then, after the struggle is complete, may you rejoice in the eternal reward of the world to come.

13. We now render with bowed mind the offices of greeting which we formerly omitted while setting forth other matters,[^c0084-8] and pray that you may flourish through a happier course of times. We ask that, without prejudice to the reverence due to your honor, you do not disdain to greet for us our beloved and most dear fathers: Fortunius, abbot of the monastery of Leyre, with his whole community; Athilius, abbot of the monastery of Cella, with his whole community; Odoarius …

[^c0084-4]: This work was separately published under the title *Life and Passion of Saints Flora and Maria, with the Added Letter*; in both places whatever seemed necessary was annotated. Here only what required scholia remained.

[^c0084-5]: He calls him his spiritual son—the one whom, as Saint Paul says, he had begotten in Christ—educating him, instructing him, and advancing him to that degree of dignity in the Church.

[^c0084-6]: Perhaps “through our offense.”

[^c0084-7]: The monastery was founded under the name and protection of Saint Zacharias. The other name, Serasian, by which it is now known, belonged either to the place or to the region.

[^c0084-8]: It appears that Eulogius had earlier written another letter to this same Wiliesindus without greetings. The editor believes this is what he means here and has retained the words as they stood in the exemplar.

[^c0084-9]: The text here and in the other letters follows the order found in the old manuscript, *Fuldensis*.

[^c0084-10]: The upper part of Gaul which was joined to Italy was called *Togata* because its inhabitants wore the toga.

[^c0084-11]: We have already discussed this word in the scholium to the Preface of Book I of the *Memorial*.

[^c0084-12]: The monastery stood under the name and patronage of Saint Zacharias. Its second name, Serasian, was the name of the place or district.

[^c0084-13]: Some say that they saw certain short works of this abbot. Certainly Trithemius does not mention him among his ecclesiastical writers.

[^c0084-14]: The Benedictine and Cistercian monasteries of our own time, in addition to an abbot, also have a prior, as their ancient institution requires. Saint Eulogius calls this officer the *provost*.

[^c0084-15]: Bavaria, or Bavaria proper, is correctly called “farther France,” since at that time the kingdom and name of the Franks extended as far as the outermost parts of Germany. Mainz is a very famous city in Upper Germany.

[^c0084-16]: Morales rightly reads *domnus*, without needing to correct it to *dominus* with Schottus. No one is unaware that *domnus* or *domnus* was frequently used in place of *dominus*. Strictly speaking, however, *Dominus* is applied only to God, while *domnus* is applied to saints and illustrious men and women, as well as to abbots and monks, as may be seen in the Glossary of Du Cange.

[^c0084-17]: Schottus reads “cultivating.”

[^c0084-18]: Baronius incorrectly reads *Wistremonius* in the *Annals* under the year 844, no. 22.

[^c0084-19]: The editor follows Morales in reading *domnus Galindo*, since *domnus* is appropriate for a distinguished man.

[scan page 431]

...the monastery, with his entire company; Scemenus, abbot of the monastery of Gal, with his entire college; Dadilanus, abbot of the monastery of Hurdaspal, with his entire college. We also greet the other fathers whom we had as guides and consolers during our pilgrimage, and the entire school of the Lord, with a holy kiss.

In the name of the Lord, while the Lord Jesus Christ reigns forever, in the year 850 of his Incarnation, in the era 888, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, the priest Perfectus died.

But in the following year, which is the present one, in the era 889, on the third day before the Nones of June, the monk Isaac fell; after him, on the Nones of June, in this same era, Sancio the layman, from the town of Alba, triumphed in a martyr’s death.

Then the priest Peter, the deacon Walabonsus, Sabinianus, Wistremundus, Habentius, and Jeremiah, monks, were killed on the same day and at the same hour, on the seventh day before the Ides of June, in the aforesaid era.

The deacon Sisenandus was struck down on the tenth day before the Kalends of August, in the same era.

The deacon Paul was killed on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the same era.

The monk Theodemirus was killed on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, in the same era.

These are those who surrendered their bodies to death for the testimony of the truth, so that they might live forever. For two virgins of Christ, Flora and Maria, have likewise been thrown with us into prison on account of the same profession, and they are threatened with death every day.
