On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December, through Galindus, an illustrious man, son of Enneco, in the era 889.

[Editorial note:] I do not doubt that he means the monastery which we now call Urgell. It lies beyond the Pyrenees toward Gaul, not very far from the city of Bayonne. And since in Eulogius’s time the Order of Saint Benedict was present there, it is now Premonstratensian.

[Editorial note:] Thus it stood in the exemplar. The same.

[Editorial heading:] Moral.

## Saint Eulogius, Archbishop of Toledo

# The Apologetic Book of the Martyrs

## Argument of the Work

[Editorial note:] Written in 867.

The blessed Eulogius had counted on writing in this work only the life and martyrdom of the saints Rudericus and Salomon. He already indicates this at the beginning, and it becomes apparent at the end of the work. But since certain fainthearted Christians were still pressing forward—people moved by a kind of zeal, though not according to knowledge, who disparaged martyrs freely offering themselves as judges of their own passion—he rises against them once again in this work, as though he had not fought vigorously enough against them in the first book. He treats certain passages from those to which he had already replied and refutes other arguments anew.

The exemplar was miserably corrupt, since the copyist was evidently already exhausted and was taking down everything with insufficient care. Hence in this part one had to labor much more earnestly in correcting the text. Nevertheless, we have not allowed ourselves to add, alter, or transpose more than one or two words. We have already said that the author of the *Brief Catalogue of Luminosus* wrote this work in defense of the martyrs, supported by the same arguments.

## Author’s Prologue

While, in my eagerness to make known the deeds of the martyrs, I was attempting to construct the brevity of this work and to apply my feeble style to the investigation of the saints’ struggles, I immediately recalled the opinions of the foolish, barking men who, passing judgment on the matter according to the measure of their own intelligence, assert that the same reverence ought not to be shown to these martyrs as to those who came before them. I therefore tried, at the beginning of the work, to answer them.

This resulted in the material passing beyond the limits of an account of deeds and into the vigor of an *Apologetic*. Although the final section of the commentary on the martyrs explains the struggle of the athletes of God and how the soldiers of God shone through their trophies of victory, I nevertheless decided to call the work an *Apologetic of the Saints*, rather than simply *The Deeds of the Martyrs*, because at the beginning I had confronted the accusations of the slanderers. By designating the whole by a part, I wished immediately to make clear the intended scope of the volume, lest, by naming a part as the whole, the prudent reader should stumble upon something other than what he expected, and lest hostile people should easily find an opportunity for disparagement when one title announced one thing but the volume presented another.

Let my readers therefore pass simply through what our faithful devotion has dedicated to the pious Redeemer in defense of the martyrs; let them not mock our labor with malicious intent in the manner of the heathen, since it is written: “Every slanderer shall be rooted out.” Although our work may deserve criticism, judgment of us belongs to God, not to the envious; for with him the will to pardon is available, and the power to carry it out immediately follows.

## Here Begins the Text of the Little Work

### 1

The outstanding struggles of the blessed, and the splendid memorials of fortunate men who, with God’s favor, left to mortals an example of how to fight, although the more prudent and reverent may find it unsuitable to investigate their fellowship, and although it may rightly be held, by a certain privilege, that the holiness of the justified should be expounded by the justified, nevertheless the true voice of sinners who speak forth the truth must not be rejected.

For not only is the counsel of foreigners, such as Jethro and Hiram, considered useful—Moses preserved from one the form of judgment he had been shown, and from the other Solomon received skill for the construction of the Temple—but even an irrational animal is permitted to exercise human eloquence [Exodus 18:13 ff.; 3 Kings 5:2 ff.; Numbers 22:28 ff.]. Why, then, should someone who presumes to speak in this way be judged blameworthy, when he is in truth worthy of the reward of blessing for recounting the truth?

And if holiness rewards the righteous and makes him worthy to proclaim the Holy of Holies, why should a sinner not be regarded as acting piously when he magnifies the righteous, provided that he strives to reveal the victories of the blessed for the benefit of the foolish? If those victories were blotted out by silence, they could offer the faithful no example of pious perseverance, so that the trophies of the elect, worked out through reflection, might rouse the sluggish to battle and teach those who struggle to aim at the goal of perfection.

Although all the saints have no need of earthly praise, since they already abound in heavenly gifts and rewards, nevertheless whatever goodness their example works in mortals is necessarily attributed to their merits.

### 2

I shall therefore recount the victorious deeds of my lords and spend my efforts on such matters insofar as the ability granted to me permits. I do not doubt the mercy of the Redeemer: through such labors we hope not only for a remedy for our faults, but also confidently expect to obtain fellowship with those whom we celebrate with our devoted pen. The Lord says:

“Whoever loves me loves me; and whoever receives me receives me. Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward; and whoever receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man will receive a righteous man’s reward” (Matthew 10:40–41).

And again in the Psalms: “But your friends, O God, have been greatly honored” (Psalm 138:17).

### 3

But before I set forth their distinguished trophies, I thought it worthwhile to resist the ignorant, who, with blasphemous mouths disparaging the martyrs of these times, maintain that they are not comparable to the earlier martyrs.

They say, in short, that paganism, once devoted to the worship of idols and occupied with various sacrileges committed against images, was subdued by the thousandfold portent of idols; and, because the variety of worldly things delighted it, it established for itself so many forms of gods, thinking that temporal prosperity could not otherwise be obtained—prosperity for which it expended its miserable efforts with all its strength—unless it maintained a carefully ordered worship of the divinities.

Deceived by this error, the credulous persecution harassed the Christian army that resisted and opposed it with insults, torments, whips, racks, fires, wild beasts, drowning, and various kinds of torture. It hoped that souls already thoroughly trained by spiritual conflict could be recalled from the worship of religion by punishments, even though it knew that they could very easily overcome the material battles of their tormentors.

Thus, while dull in mind, it both admired the invincible courage of the strongest soldiers and, astonished by the immense miracles displayed, mocked them, attributing to demonic magic what, with its blind mind, it could not perceive to have been accomplished through the work of piety. And, as we read in many exemplars, the very miracles of the signs were occasions for the blessed to turn people to Christ.

For those recruits, the confessors of our own times, received death only from the blow of the sword and suffered none of the bitter tortures of the executioners; they did not sweat beneath prolonged goading. Especially since they were killed by men who worshiped God and acknowledged the heavenly laws, their death was brief. Thus they have enough if they have obtained remission from their former crimes, because they did not hear the clanking of chains, bear the weight of fetters, endure the filth of prison, or suffer the varied punishments of their persecutors.

### 4

Therefore this empty invention of those who make light of these things must necessarily be beaten back by the authority of the laws and, insofar as the Lord grants his help, driven away by the force of truthful assertions. Thus the mind of religious people, nourished by the most sacred utterances, may learn from the truth to venerate recent patrons in the same way as ancient ones, whom it sees, through a glorious death, proceeding to heaven with universal devotion.

### 5

For what harm does a swift death do to holy soldiers, by which they quickly reached the place to which the catalogue of the blessed once came through various harsh tortures? Or what difference does it make by what kind of death one departs from this life of death, when, as it is written, “Whatever death overtakes the righteous, his soul will be at rest” (Wisdom 4:1)? Or what does it matter whether he falls through prolonged torments or by a sudden death, when one and the same thing crowns both: zeal for God and love of the everlasting kingdom?

Are those not to be considered perfect fulfillers of Christ’s commands who, inflamed by sudden mortification, despised the pleasures of the world and, for a moment of time, denied even the affections of parents, children, spouses, brothers, and all their relatives? And what is more cruel than death among all punishments? What is more terrifying than to see a flashing sword before one’s eyes, about to fall immediately upon the necks of the confessors?

Or what else is sought through the long struggles of the holy martyrs except death—the death of which the Psalmist sings and says: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Psalm 115:13)? The crown is promised not to the one who merely suffers for a long time, but to the one who conquers. And the blessed man, awaiting the end of his holy struggle with more fortunate perseverance, is in a certain way encouraged still more by hope of eternal salvation, as the Lord says: “He who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10:22).

Whether, through delays, or through the accidental circumstances of their passion, a swift or a late death comes to the brave soldiers fighting for Christ, this alone must be considered: whether they receive their sufferings for the cause of faith, whether for Christ they desire to lose their souls so that they may be saved forever, as it is written: “If anyone wishes to save his soul, he will lose it; but whoever loses it for my sake will preserve it for eternal life” (ibid., 39).

Even if they remain liable for sins and come to martyrdom infected by whatever stain of vice, nothing prevents them from attaining Christ’s crown, since all such things are wiped away by the martyr’s trophy. To surrender one’s soul in death in the name of the Crucified through many torments and to fall for him in a single blow are the same, according to the one who said: “Whoever loses his soul for my sake will find it for eternal life.”

Although it is written that “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom” (Acts 14:21), when such tribulations are available they must indeed be endured until death. But if the sudden attack of the persecutor brings an expedited death to Christ’s confessors, their glory is in no way diminished by this, because they persevered to the end.

### 6

The noble soldier, inflamed by zeal for God, would therefore hasten toward the prize in vain and expend his strength in the first exercise with fruitless effort if he were deprived by the emperor of the triumphs of his hard-won victory merely because he obtained the palm from the tyrant while standing in battle formation and at the very opening of the war, without seeking it through prolonged and laborious conflict or attaining it through a lengthy course of struggle.

Those laborious afflictions, rather than the crown of an easy victory, would properly be owed if the length of the battle were valued more highly than the hastened trophy. Thus it is the quality, not the quantity, of the intention of the one hastening toward the reward that must be considered, since the desired result is achieved by whatever means.

There is nevertheless one and the same eternal King, for whose love all the saints submit themselves to temporal sufferings. What prevented the evangelical thief, who mounted the cross with hands stained by fraternal blood? What miracles did he perform amid the very dangers of death—the man who, so to speak, had spent the whole course of his life in theft, robbery, and plunder?

Yet at the confession of a single moment, he was not only rescued from so great a crime but was also regarded as worthy of the Redeemer’s company and as the first possessor of paradise, when the Lord said: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

And if “no one has greater love than the one who lays down his soul for his friends” (John 15:13), with how much greater charity must the one be regarded who fights for his God until death?

For the head of a household, when he distributes an equal wage to laborers sent into the vineyard at different hours, does not greatly concern himself with the difference in time; in the work of labor he compensates the work of the last workers, who were not without the intention of the first. “Many who are last will be first, and the first last” (Matthew 19:30); and “many will come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (ibid., 8:11).

### 7

The signs of miracles were once displayed by God’s power amid the sufferings of these same athletes of God for this reason: either to mitigate by the power of wonders the madness of the furious persecutors that wearied the steadfastness of the blessed, or to turn from the error of unbelief the unbelieving race that, with hardened hearts, rejected the authority of the heavenly Scriptures.

At that time it was much more necessary for God’s witnesses to shine through signs of power, because they were attempting to establish Christianity, which had been spread through the ages in an unformed state, firmly in the hearts of believing peoples: now by instruction in words, now by the exercise of the Scriptures, now by the display of signs, and now also by the famous trophies of their sufferings.

As it is written:

“Go throughout the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned. These signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will take up serpents; and if they drink anything deadly, it will not harm them. They will lay hands on the sick, and they will be well.”

And after they had gone forth, they preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word by the signs that followed (Mark 16:15 ff.).

And again:

“Go and preach, saying: ‘The kingdom of heaven has drawn near.’ Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons. You have received without payment; give without payment” (Matthew 10:7–8).

These were the first beginnings of our faith. Through the exercise of these powers, like the first efforts of nursing infants, its tender growth was both strengthened and nourished, so that through the ministry of signs either the number of believers might increase or the faith of those who believed might be strengthened.

They were, as it were, instruments and tools by which ornaments of gold and silver—necklaces, pendants, and royal diadems—could be fashioned, fitted together, and joined.

### 8

Thus, for the confirmation of the catholic faith, we see that at its beginning signs and miracles were displayed more abundantly, with Christ cooperating. Therefore miracles do not precede faith, nor does faith yield to miracles, since their accomplishment is reached only through faith.

Thus the holy lawgiver Moses, worthy of converse with God, became great through faith. Thus Abraham, believing in God, deserved to be justified, as Scripture says: “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness, and he was called the friend of God” (Genesis 15:6; James 2:23).

Thus “the righteous live by faith,” and all the saints “through faith conquered kingdoms, worked righteousness, obtained promises, shut the mouths of lions, quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, recovered from weakness, and became strong in war” (Hebrews 11:33–34).

### 9

Do you see, whoever you are who rise up against this, that all these things are instruments of faith and, as a servant is subject to a pious religion, are subordinate to it? You ought therefore now to believe in truth that the martyrs became excellent not through signs and wonders but through the integrity of their faith and the steadfastness of their profession.

The only thing to be admired in them is that with stronger courage they accepted death for Christ, who said: “Whoever loses his soul for my sake will find it for eternal life” (Matthew 10:39).

Faith is, in truth, the root and foundation of all virtues. It helps those who struggle, crowns those who conquer, and by a heavenly gift compensates some for the absence of signs. Nothing is denied to sincere faith, because God demands nothing else from us but faith. He loves it, seeks it, and promises and grants everything to it.

“Your faith,” he says, “has saved you.” And again: “Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life” (Revelation 2:10). Faith therefore lacks nothing; it declares that nothing is impossible for it.

### 10

Nor should one place much confidence in the splendor of miracles, which are often performed by unbelievers, as it is written in Exodus: “The magicians also did this by their enchantments, just as Moses did” (Exodus 7:11–12; 8:7, 15).

I think this question was discussed sufficiently in the work called the *Memorial of the Saints*. Whether God’s witnesses shine through miracles or complete their blessed struggle without wonders makes no difference, since the heavenly author asks only this of them: that, without abandoning the steadfastness of their hope, they should bravely complete the contest to the end, so that, joined forever to the catalogue of the saints, they may rejoice in the perpetuity of salvation, as the Lord says: “He who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10:22).

### 11

Our original plan had been simple: by recounting the victories of the victorious, we intended to devote ourselves to concise brevity. But, obstructed by the barriers of insolent people, I have tried to offer this *Apologetic* against uncertain accusers, and therefore perhaps I have exceeded the proper measure of history.

It is still necessary to confront their depravity for a little while, so that the faithful assembly may learn to love with more ardent desire what it believes, when from the authority of sacred law it has discovered both the truth of religion and the error of impious novelty.

### 12

For they say that these men suffered at the hands of people who worship God and the law, and that they were killed not for the sacrileges of idols but after being invited to the worship of the true God. Therefore, they say, the martyrdoms of these men are not to be venerated like those of the earlier martyrs.

Are these worshipers of vanity to be believed to possess God and the law in any sense, when they not only fail to believe the life-giving commandments of the Gospel’s teaching, spread throughout the whole world, but also, with every zeal of perversity, inflict great danger upon those who confess them? Do they not think it hateful and unjust to believe that Christ is true God and true man?

Thus, with wicked mockery, they daily disgrace God’s portion and everywhere assault, ridicule, and curse the practice of sacred religion, placing the hope of their belief and faith in the divinations of some pestilential and demonic little man. Possessed by an unclean spirit, he established, as a true forerunner of Antichrist, some law of novelty according to his own pleasure and the prompting of demons, for the ruin of the foolish multitude.

Concerning their impiety, the blessed apostle Paul, through open prophetic revelations inspired by the Holy Spirit, says to the Thessalonians:

“Because they did not receive the love of the truth so that they might be saved, therefore God sends them a spirit of error, so that they may believe a lie and all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity in every deception” (2 Thessalonians 2:10–11).

He likewise says to the Romans:

“For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of those who hold the truth in unrighteousness, because what may be known of God is manifest in them.”

And:

“Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools. They exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served vanity rather than the Creator, who is God, blessed forever. Therefore he gave them over to a depraved mind, to do what is unfitting: filled with every kind of wickedness, malice, fornication, greed, and evil; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, and malignity; whisperers, slanderers, hateful to God, insolent, proud, boastful, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents, senseless, disorderly, without affection, without treaty, without mercy. Although they knew God’s justice, they did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death; and they not only do them but also approve those who do them” (Romans 1:18 ff.).

For the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles and the firmest foundation of the catholic Church—for the Redeemer himself said to him, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16:18)—says in his Epistles:

“Brothers, we possess the prophetic word made more certain, and you do well to attend to it as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts. Understand this first: that no prophecy of Scripture comes from private interpretation. For prophecy was never brought forth by human will, but holy men of God spoke as they were inspired by the Holy Spirit.

“There were also false prophets among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you, who will secretly introduce destructive sects, denying the master who bought them and bringing upon themselves swift destruction. Many will follow their debaucheries, and because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed. In their greed they will exploit you with fabricated words. Their judgment from ancient times is not idle, and their destruction does not sleep” (2 Peter 1:19–21; 2:1–3).

[Editorial note:] By “living faith,” blessed Eulogius evidently means a faith vigorous and full of works, such as he attributes to the martyrs; you will find none more vigorous, since it operates through immense charity. For Christ declared that charity to be greater when someone lays down his soul for his friends. Moral.

[Editorial heading:] Martyrs.

### 13

All these things, as this blessed proclamation of the apostles contains, many very learned men understand to apply not only to that false prophet but also to those who receive him reverently; nor do they fail to see that we have not assembled so many passages from the holy Scriptures against him and his followers in vain.

[Editorial note:] Moral.

[Editorial note:] Book 1, section 13 ff.

[scan page 435]

## Saint Eulogius, Archbishop of Toledo

For they now see him proclaimed by the preaching of the sacred law and denounced by the oracle of the true teacher: “Many false prophets will arise, and they will lead many astray” (Matthew 24:11). Certainly they could find no fault with our reproach of him, when they saw him assailed by the authority of so many Fathers.

### 14

Therefore I do not think it absurd at this point to present the earlier testimony of learned men concerning him, so that those who now, with unsound judgment, maintain that he introduced that law or worshiped God in truth may better recognize from their statements how the ecclesiastical men of that time judged him, how they condemned him in faith and profession, and how great and of what kind he was among our people.

### 15

When I was once staying in the town of Pamplona and lodging at the monastery of Leire, I was leafing through all the books that were there, investigating matters unknown to me. Suddenly, in a certain part of a little work, I found the following short history of that impious prophet, without the author’s name:

### 16

“For Muhammad arose, a heresiarch, in the time of the emperor Heraclius, in the seventh year of his reign, in the era 656. At that time Isidore, bishop of Seville, shone in catholic doctrine, and Sisebut held the royal throne at Toledo. The church of the blessed Euphrasius was built at the city of Iliturgi over his tomb. At Toledo also, by order of the aforesaid prince, the hall of the blessed Leocadia was extended upward with a lofty roof of wondrous workmanship.

“That impious prophet Muhammad held power for ten years; when they were completed, he died and was buried in hell. His beginnings were as follows.

“When he was a small boy, he became subject to a certain widow. As he traveled about greedily in business as a usurer, he began to attend Christian gatherings regularly. Being, as he was, a clever son of darkness, he began to commit certain Christian discussions to memory and to be wiser than all his brutish Arabs.

“Inflamed by the fuel of his lust, he entered into a union with his patroness according to barbarian custom. Then the spirit of error appeared to him in the form of a vulture, showed him a golden mouth, declared that it was the angel Gabriel, and obtained for him the appearance of a prophet.

“When he was filled with the swelling of pride, he began to preach unheard-of things to brutish animals. As though by some kind of reasoning, he urged them to abandon the worship of idols and adore the incorporeal God in heaven. He ordered those who believed him to take up arms and, as though moved by a new zeal for the faith, established that they should slaughter their opponents with the sword.

“By a hidden judgment of God—for God had once said through the prophet, ‘Behold, I am raising up the Chaldeans against you, a bitter and swift nation, marching across the breadth of the earth to possess dwellings not their own, whose horses are swifter than evening wolves and whose faces are like a burning wind, to rebuke the faithful and reduce the land to a desert’ [Habakkuk 1:6, 8]—God permitted him to harm them.

“For first they killed the brother of the emperor, who held dominion over that land, and, exulting in their triumph, became famous through victory; at Damascus in Syria they founded the beginning of their kingdom.

“Finally, that false prophet composed psalms in the mouth of senseless animals, making particular mention of a red calf. He also composed a story about a spider’s web for catching flies. In addition, he composed songs for a hoopoe and frogs, so that the stench of one might belch from his mouth while the chatter of the other would not cease upon his lips.

“He also digressed in his writing, as a seasoning for his error, in honor of Joseph, Zechariah, and even the Lady Mary.

“While he continued in the error of such a prophecy, he desired the wife of his neighbor, a man named Zayd, and subjected her to his lust. When her husband perceived the crime, he recoiled from it and gave her over to her prophet, whom he was unable to oppose. He then, as though speaking with the voice of the Lord, inserted this in his law, saying:

‘When that woman displeased Zayd in his eyes and he repudiated her, we joined her in marriage to our prophet, so that it might serve as an example to the rest and to later believers who wish to do such things, and might not be counted as sin.’

“After the commission of so great a crime, the end of his soul and body together drew near. But when he sensed that his end was approaching—for he knew no way by his own virtue to rise again—he predicted, through the angel Gabriel, who, as he claimed, was accustomed to appear to him in the form of a vulture, that he would be resurrected on the third day.

“When he had surrendered his soul to the underworld, those anxious about the miracle he had promised them ordered that his corpse be guarded by a strict watch. When on the third day they saw it stinking and could in no way see it rising, they said that the angels were not present because they were terrified by the presence of their own people.

“Having therefore found what they thought was a sound solution, they left his corpse without a guard. At once, in the manner of angels, dogs entered because of its stench and devoured his side. When they discovered what had happened, they committed the remains of his corpse to the fire.

“And to avenge the injury done to him, they decided to kill dogs every year, so that those who deserved to undergo martyrdom for him might rightly have a share with him there.

“It was fitting that it should happen to him that so great and so notable a prophet should fill the belly of dogs, since he had delivered not only his own soul but also the souls of many others to the underworld. He committed many other crimes as well, which are not written in this book. This alone has been written so that readers may recognize what kind of man he was.”

### 17

Behold the kind of sorcery to which the foolish multitude is devoted, and the leader of such great impiety whom many do not fear to honor under the name of pious religion.

They assert that these recruits, the soldiers of our own times, were killed by people who worship God and possess the law, without carefully discerning—even to the extent of noticing through prudent reflection—that if such a cult or law...

### *The Apologetic Book of the Martyrs*

[...], it must be said, certainly the vigor of the Christian religion will be weakened.

**18.** Although—as must truthfully be acknowledged—the knowledge of the holy faith has penetrated the crossroads of the whole world, traversing all the nations of the earth, we trust that no part of the globe will now remain deprived of its light. Especially since “their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:5), we confess that every other gospel, apart from that which the apostles handed down to the nations, is rather an anathema than a word of salvation, as the Apostle says: “If anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be accursed” (Gal. 1:9).

And the Truth itself warns the disciples with these words: “Many false prophets will arise and lead many astray; and they will give great signs and wonders, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led astray” (Matt. 24:11). And again: “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are from God” (1 John 4:1).

By what reasoning, then, should one believe a demon-possessed and mendacious man to speak the truth? Should one accept a law wrapped in deceit? Should a corrupt tree produce good fruit? Meanwhile that impious man, bringing forth evil from the evil treasure of his heart and supplying the foolish populace with a guide to impiety, will fall into the eternal abyss, where both of them will pay the penalty.

Concerning him and others like him the Lord speaks through Hosea: “They have made kings, but not by me; they have appointed princes, and I did not know them” (Hos. 8:4).

**19.** Finally, among the other authors of heresies after the Lord’s Ascension, this unfortunate man alone, prompted by the devil, established a new sect of superstition. Cut off from the assembly of the holy Church, he dishonored the authority of the ancient Law, rejected the prophets’ predictions, trampled upon the truth of the holy Gospel, and despised the teaching of the apostles (6).

By insinuating through his sect causes that were ridiculous rather than necessary matters, he taught with blasphemous mouth that Christ was the Word of God, his Spirit, and indeed a great prophet, but endowed with no divine power; like Adam, not equal to God the Father. He claimed that, because of the merit of his holiness, Christ was filled with the Spirit, that through God’s power he shone forth in miracles and excelled in signs and wonders, but that he possessed no superiority from his own majesty or divinity. Rather, as a just man devoted to God in pious service, he supposedly deserved through humble prayers to obtain many things from the Almighty.

But he also proclaimed other unheard-of crimes of vanity. Through the contrivance of the crafty one who possessed him—who had transformed himself into an angel of light—he constructed shrines in which his wicked doctrine was to be worshiped. At the highest point of idolatry he set up a tower, rising above the other buildings on a lofty pinnacle, from which he might proclaim to the people, enticed by the poison of his wickedness, the decree of sacrilegious madness that the priests of his impiety, instructed by him, observe to this day.

Thus, in the manner of an ass, with jaws gaping and impure lips open, they do not emit their dreadful proclamation until they have stopped up both ears with their fingers, as though they were announcing to others something to be carried out, like an edict of crime; for that same prophet does not allow them to hear it.

When my grandfather Eulogius, now divinely remembered, heard this voice of impiety being proclaimed, they say that he immediately fortified his forehead with the sign of the cross and, groaning, was accustomed to sing this Psalm:

“God, who is like you? Do not be silent, nor be still, O God, for behold, your enemies have sounded forth, and those who hate you have lifted up their heads” (Ps. 82:2–3).

But as soon as we hear the voice of the deceptive herald, we immediately pray:

“Save us, O Lord, from evil hearing, and now and forever.”

And again:

“Let all those who worship carved images be put to shame, those who boast in their idols” (Ps. 96:7).

**20.** Whoever wishes to learn the madness of this error, the delirious claims of its preaching, and the impious prescriptions of its novelty will perceive them more clearly by investigating the worshipers of that same sect. For, imagining that they possess and believe something sacred, they proclaim the doctrines of their prophet not only privately but openly and aloud.

Much will also be found among certain of our own writers, who, armed with zeal for God, have risen against that shameless prophet with a discerning pen. We too, in the little work entitled *Memorial of the Saints*, have arranged, refuted, and condemned some of the errors of this sect.

**21.** Now that the apologias of the blessed have been completed, it remains for us to reveal something of their victories, for the emulation of the Catholic people (7).

The blessed Rudericus, a priest, was born of a certain village in the territory of Egabrum. In that same city he attained instruction in the teaching of the holy Law and the priestly rank. He had two brothers. Of these, one held the faith of Christ rightly; the other, corrupted by pagan error, rejected the Catholic religion.

Just as he remained divided from the holy faith, so he was always involved in discordant quarrels with his Catholic brother on various occasions. One night, for some reason, when they had become embroiled in a tumultuous dispute and were violently attacking one another with shameful savagery, the holy priest intervened in order to settle the quarrel between them.

But when all, already inflamed with excessive rage, seized the priest in blind indignation, they—more from ignorance than from intention—tormented him even to the point of death. After this assault had left him greatly bruised, and when, deprived of all strength, he was being laid on a small bed with his limbs broken, that profane brother placed him on a bier and had him carried on men’s shoulders through the streets and surrounding districts and brought back again.

Like a true imitator of the devil, he then contrived a deceitful scheme over the lifeless priest and said:

“This brother of mine, the priest, moved by God’s visitation, has chosen the worship of our faith; and, as you see, now at the point of death, he did not wish to depart from the world before this became known to you.”

As he traveled with him through various places, he related these and similar things about him in criminal words, while the priest himself knew absolutely nothing—indeed, did not even perceive—what that wicked man was preparing against him.

By God’s providence, after several days, when the priest had recovered somewhat from the suffering of his illness and his strength had begun to return, he learned through a servant of the household of his brother’s machinations.

Following the example of the Lord, who withdrew from Herod’s ambush in order to instruct us (Matt. 2:13), or as a not-deaf hearer of the holy Gospel, by which we are commanded to conceal ourselves from city to city in order to avoid persecution (ibid., 2:13), he left his own countryside and went elsewhere, intending to serve Christ freely.

It was as though he could escape temporal punishment, although martyrdom had been divinely prepared for him from the foundation of the world; or as though, by hiding himself for a time and deceiving his profane persecutor, he could also be absent from the eyes of his pious Redeemer and from those of the one who had called him to the kingdom.

**22.** At that same time a severe madness of the authorities was raging against us, so that in Cordoba—formerly Patricia, but now a most flourishing city of the Arab kingdom—it overthrew the towers of certain basilicas, demolished the strongholds of the churches, and cast down the lofty pinnacles (8), which bore the signs that daily signaled to Christ’s people the canonical assembly.

Finally, when the wicked offspring recognized the desire of their father, namely, that the Church should be harassed by every possible means and strength, that offspring of darkness exercised every effort of cruelty against the children of light with ever greater zeal.

[Note: Morales understands the father and son as the kings ʿAbd al-Raḥmān and his son Muḥammad.] It considered that it had gained too little unless it had burned with the utmost fury against the overthrow of the faithful.

For the holy Truth had foretold this to its hearers, saying:

“They will expel you from the synagogues; and the hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God.”

And again:

“I have said these things to you so that in me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation” (John 16:2, 33).

**23.** Therefore, when necessity concerning his household affairs had caused him to descend from the interior Cordoban mountains—where the blessed priest had previously gone in order to remain concealed—to the marketplace, where goods were being bought and sold, his wicked brother recognized him.

When he saw him bearing the marks of the pious religion, he subjected him to no small injuries (9) and, in return for the reward sought, brought him before the judge.

[Note: Bollandus correctly reads *non modicis* (“not inconsiderable”); Morales and Schott incorrectly have *non mediis*.] There, before the magistrate, he lodged against him an accusation of apostasy from the sect of Muhammad, which he claimed that the priest had formerly confessed he would truly worship.

But the soldier of God, already illumined by a heavenly gift, did not, as formerly, expose his back to his adversary. Rather, endowed with great courage, he declared before the judge that he had never been separated from Christ and had never at any time consented to the perverse doctrine. He confessed that he was not merely a Christian, but also a minister of Christ.

At first the judge thought to recall him with flattering words:

“You can be honored by an abundance of possessions and the trappings of rank, and you can escape the sentence of death that threatens you, if, restoring yourself to your former vows with renewed fervor, you believe that our prophet was sent by the Almighty in truth and testify that Christ is not God.”

The blessed priest replied:

“Judge, propose such observances to those who, devoted to your laws and immersed in profane rites, seek temporal advantage and honor rather than eternal honor.

“But we—for ‘to live is Christ, and to die is gain’ (Phil. 1:21)—follow him to whom that holy keeper of the keys of the future kingdom said: ‘Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life’ (John 6:68), and who warned his disciple in prison, saying: ‘Blessed is the one who is not scandalized because of me’ (Matt. 11:6).

“How, then, shall we abandon the cup of the everlasting fountain in order to drink a whirlpool made turbid by the filth of the mire of falsehood and vices? Or by what vengeance should the arrogance of children be punished, who, scorning the pious rights of their parents, seek an unjust union with the victorious?”

At these words the judge was stirred to violent fury. He ordered the martyr to be taken to the prisons and said to the lictors:

“Take him away to the custody of the condemned. Let the dreadful caves of the prisons receive him to be tormented; let him enjoy the comfort of parricides and thieves. Deprived altogether of every consolation, let his obstinacy be crushed even in this way.”

**24.** The servant of God entered that den of criminals with a joyful face and exultant spirit. He truly knew that the author of his salvation, invoked everywhere, was present there and could not be absent from any place, since his dominion penetrates every location.

The Lord had once also given his followers this faithful promise through the command of his divine power:

“Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

“These, devil, are the threatening laws of your savage power; these are your carefully devised terrors. But it has been said to us:

“‘Do not fear those who kill the body, since they have nothing more that they can do; rather, fear him who can destroy both body and soul and cast them into Gehenna’ (ibid., 10:28).

“And again:

“‘They will hand you over to councils, and in their synagogues they will scourge you; you will be led before governors and kings for my sake, as a testimony to them and to the nations. But whoever perseveres to the end will be saved’ (ibid., 10:17–18).

“If you can, then, fight against the soul and overcome the spirit in its steadfast confession. You will see me advance all the more through torments; and the more fiercely you rage, the more completely you will fail and the happier you will make me as I attain glory.”

**25.** In prison Rudericus found the blessed Salomon, whom the cruelty of his persecutors had confined there earlier because of his confession of Christ’s name.

For he too was attacked on a similar charge: because he had rejected the worship of the holy religion, he had for some time adhered to the Muhammadan sect.

Immediately they bound themselves together by an indivisible vow. Providing one another with the support of consolation, they armed each other to complete the contest. They jointly established that, trampling upon worldly desires, they would daily cling to God in pious service.

Their mutual assent was harmonized in the fear of God. Their limbs were disciplined by fasts, wearied by vigils, abraded by haircloth, pierced by meditations, and refreshed by prayers. Thus, kindled by a certain ardor for the heavenly homeland, they longed to be dissolved and to be with Christ, hastening to see his face, whom they had served and for whose love they did not fear the loss of this life as though it were something of no account.

[Editorial note: “Morales: one temptation is that of riches; another, that of honors.”]

**26.** While the saints therefore remained engaged in exercises of heavenly sacrifice and daily rendered hymns of praise to the Redeemer, they regarded that cave as their greatest delight.

Accordingly, the unjust judge, driven by the most wicked zeal, rebuked the prison guards and ordered them to be separated from one another, forbidding anyone to illuminate them with a visit for the sake of consolation. He commanded that they be left to all the fury of his madness.

But you do not help yourself, devil, when through this separation you think that the constancy of the saints can be wearied, for they retain one and the same indissoluble vow to die for Christ.

Thus these blessed confessors—different in rank and nation, but not unequal in charity—although they entered the field of combat at different times, were nevertheless inflamed by one and the same ardor of faith and set before the world an outstanding example of blessed suffering.

**27.** Meanwhile, after not many days, the judge ordered them to be brought before him. At once he invited them to adopt his rite and attempted to persuade them with offers of material abundance and the honor of rank—although holy divinity had written them down as chosen and predestined before the foundation of the world for adoption as sons of God.

When he saw their persistence in confessing God, after exhorting them a second and a third time, he decreed that they should be punished according to the king’s command.

Before they went out into public, however, they fell at the feet of their fellow prisoners and begged to be aided by continual prayers, lest, seized by human temptation, they should look back and be disturbed in their contemplation of the banner of victory that they were about to receive.

Thus reconciled by a kiss of peace—although they had never been separated by quarrel—they all wept for joy and implored the saints to protect them by their prayers. Then, as the attendants urged them on, they sprang forward with complete eagerness, hastening more quickly to the place where they would complete their passion.

**28.** When the hour of execution was already at hand, they were again more gently exhorted by the judge, with the promise of riches and exalted honors, which they would certainly enjoy if they returned to the former faith.

The saints rejected the judge’s proposal just as they had at the beginning. The most holy Rudericus, strengthened by a certain vigor of spirit and already illumined by a heavenly gift, boldly answered:

“How do you compel us, instructed in the sacraments of the holy faith, to abandon piety and turn aside into error, when we firmly lament your ignorance and see you infected with so great an error?

“We judge this despicable sect so detestable that we would not permit even our dogs to inhabit it, much less submit ourselves to its most deceitful inventions.

“Or why should we take pleasure in an abundance of possessions or the dignity of passing honors, when, at the very moment of the proposed exchange, we shall suddenly lose everything through death? We know that with Christ our crown-bearer there remain ineffable things, which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the human heart, promised to those who love him.

“Therefore, hasten to exercise your cruel vengeance against us, whom you see in no way shrinking from the confession of Christ until death, so that what is owed to the enemies of God may increase for you, and the reward long delayed for us may quickly arrive.”

**29.** At this the criminal judge, gnashing his teeth more fiercely, brought forth the final sentence of his cruelty and said to the lictors:

“Hurry to cut off the necks of these traitors and repay the punishment owed to their heads. Turn your vengeance upon them more swiftly.”

Thus, standing upon the bank of the basin, they fortified themselves with the sign of the cross and were again struck down by the sword.

The first to fall, the priest of God, entered heaven as the triumphant forerunner. The judge had ordered this to happen first in case the sight of the blessed Salomon’s severed corpse should bend his spirit. But when he proved him steadfast and most courageous after various enticements of deception, he ordered him to be butchered by the avenging sword.

Nevertheless, he ordered that the sword not sever his neck completely at one stroke, because he inflicted a quicker death upon the blessed Rudericus than upon this Salomon.

**30.** But since the cunning serpent cannot prevent souls from entering the kingdom of heaven, it still raises war against lifeless bodies, as though it could conquer dead corpses, when there was no longer any spirit that might feel the torments rather than mock them; or as though it were thought some title of victory to wage war against the dead.

Therefore, so that the martyrs might share in the sufferings of Christ, the governor, armed by the devil’s ferocity—under whose dreadful cruelty the entire dignity of Cordoba was then being grievously afflicted—ordered the bodies, drenched in the blood of martyrdom, to be fastened with their feet reversed and then hidden in the abyss of the river.

That same night, tied down with a great weight of stones, they were separately plunged into the vast whirlpool. The wretched man hoped to command the elements of the waves, which knew better how to obey the command of their Creator, so that the riches entrusted to them by the martyrs might not only be preserved from beasts but that, freed from the weight of the stones, the limbs might be carried by the gentle movement of the waves to a place of rest.

**31.** Meanwhile I, the sinner Eulogius, who had long ago resolved to work out the deeds of the blessed with my pen, when news of the completion of their passion was spreading everywhere, went to visit their bodies, strengthened by a certain boldness after the completion of the solemn Masses. I did not fear to approach more closely than the rest of the crowd of onlookers (14).

My Redeemer, who will examine this account, is witness that I do not lie: those severed corpses shone with such beauty of appearance that, if one had questioned them, one would have thought that they would immediately begin to speak.

**32.** Some also came from the crowd of pagans. They took stones from the river, which had been spattered with the martyrs’ blood, washed them in the water, and threw them into the sea (15), believing that this would benefit Christians through the relics.

They did not know that nothing could be taken away from those to whom the Lord had determined to grant the whole of the passion. For, entrusted to the hiding places of the seaweed and committed to the deep hollows of the abyss—where they had been received both to be concealed and to serve as food for the fish—the limbs were immediately recalled by divine power to the heights.

They could not be held back. Rather, through the gentler breath and returning motion of the waves, the alternating movement of the waters brought them safely to the shore, where they had been scattered.

The blessed priest’s head was not attached to his shoulders, because the executioner had severed it with a single stroke. Thus the head was found in one place and the body, thrown elsewhere, in another. The body had been covered with sand at a certain place by the inhabitants of the village where it had been cast up by the rushing waves.

**33.** Meanwhile, although nearly twenty days had passed since the report of the place of their rest, and no indication of their appearance had been given, the matter was unexpectedly revealed through the report of certain pagans.

They reported that the body of a certain priest (16) had appeared near the village of Tertios, in the district of Comares, where the monastery of Saint Genesius was founded.

When he heard this news, the same priest rose and went to bring the blessed corpse to the Church. As he returned, a great crowd of the faithful met him, eager to pay the honor owed to the supreme victor, who had endured such things for his God as an example to the Catholic people.

Because the sun had failed, a thick darkness spread over the earth, and night changed the entire appearance of the world. Through the service of the people coming to meet them, the horror of the darkness was driven away by the many flames of lamps. The immense brilliance illuminated everything so greatly that the returning night seemed to display the emergence of day.

All rejoiced; joy was mingled with the sound of dancing; no sadness contracted their faces; and pious lamentation poured forth from their lips.

**34.** The venerable bishop also arrived, accompanied by a troop of clergy. They hastened with ardent prayers to take part in such a funeral. As soon as they approached the holy relics (18), the illustrious pope uncovered the head and kissed the sacred limbs.

The hidden chambers of the room into which the blessed priest’s body had first been carried filled with a marvelous fragrance. All the floors of the cell, even after the dust had been swept away, seemed for some time to breathe the sweetest odor.

Everyone was astonished that the unburied body had suffered no decay, that no wound had damaged it, that no corruption had spoiled it, that no ravenous hunger of beasts or birds had torn it apart, and that the quality of its own skin had not changed after so many intervening days.

Thus the clergy of priests and religious carried the holy body of the priest into the church to be buried, and all raised an immense heavenly cry. The mouths of the faithful resounded with harmonious songs; everyone made a joyful sound in the melody of divine chant; the courts of the Lord were filled with the holy murmur of psalms; and, as though with one mouth, all performed odes of blessed praise.

As everything resounded with sweet harmony, and the abundant flame of lamps penetrated every part of the entire hall, they signaled that Christ the King, accompanied by the heavenly host, was present at the spectacle of the saints’ funeral.

**35.** When the funeral rites of the most holy Rudericus had been completed, everyone’s desire to seek out the little body of the blessed Salomon became more ardent. Many reported that it had been carried out to sea by the force of the river.

This belief restrained the prudent courage of the Christians more than the furious conspiracy of the governor, who had promised to punish the discoverer of the relics with harsher laws.

For, since there was no indication of where the hidden body lay, and since everyone was moved by hope in God’s beneficence—who is accustomed to reveal hidden things and to conceal what is manifest—the power of divinity, which orders, arranges, and accomplishes in heaven, on earth, in the sea, and in the abysses everything that it wills, suddenly gave the priest a sign by which he might know where the martyr’s body was concealed.

When the priest asked the one giving the warning to indicate the place of its hiding and sought to learn what sign he should use in searching, the other said:

“On that bank of the river which adjoins the village of Nymphianus, there, among passers-by and thrown beneath the tamarisk branches, I lie in a poor tomb covered with muddy turf.”

That priest proceeded confidently to the place divinely shown to him and found it exactly as it had been revealed.

He immediately adorned it with the highest reverence and service, carried it to the village of Colubris, and had it honorably buried in the basilica of the holy priests Cosmas and Damian through the ministry of the venerable priests of God.

The blessed martyrs completed their contest on the third Ides of March, in the year 895 of the Spanish Era, while our Lord Jesus Christ reigns throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

Behold my most revered patrons, soldiers of Christ, trustworthy witnesses, excellent warriors, mighty conquerors, guardians of the Catholic flock. I have come forward against your detractors and resisted them with all the strength of my ability; I have also arranged the deeds of your victories as an example for the faithful, so that this work might benefit those wishing to go to the kingdom and serve as an expiation for my crimes.

I believe that what I have truthfully set down concerning you will not displease you; rather, I have believed that everything I have published in this work will be pleasing to you and worthy of Christ through your intercession.

Therefore I, the sinner Eulogius—poor in merits, deficient in holiness, and manifold in guilt—beseech you: may your worthy intercession provide protection for me amid the scandals of the world that press upon me and amid the punishments of the underworld, which I dread on account of my merits. May it sanctify me and make this work, which I have sullied in my uncleanness, pleasing and worthy.

And if perhaps an error contrary to the faith has appeared in any part of this little book, may the Lord’s indulgence, through your intercession, pardon me.

[Editorial note: “Thus it is found in the printed copies of Morales.”]

---

## Ambrose Morales’s Scholia on All the Saints Mentioned in the Preface to Book II of Eulogius’s *Memorial of the Saints*

**(1)** “I indeed...” He gives an account of the purpose of his work, so that, in the preface itself, he may provide, as far as can be believed, a foretaste of the work to come. He recalls the life and death of this martyr.

**(2)** *Ascesis*—a Greek word, from which the name is derived—means the exercise or training of the mind in contemplation of divine things. Hence *asceteria* are called monasteries. The word was used by the emperor Justinian in [the relevant law concerning] bishops and clergy. Eulogius himself also uses it in *Epistle III to the Cordoban bishops*, and Saint Basil, Book IX, and Gregory Nazianzen use it frequently.

**(3)** Those who are said to have preceded [him] were undoubtedly the martyrs Adulphus and John, as will appear in Book II, chapter 2. Here he is speaking only of those who were crowned with martyrdom during these three or four years. Although the priest Perfectus had also preceded them, Eulogius himself would nevertheless shortly give an account of him, since he mentions him as having been earlier.

**(4)** No mention of the monastery of Tábanos occurs elsewhere in this work. Saint Isaac had especially received his education there, because he had an uncle, Jeremiah, who had founded that monastery for him. He himself also became a monk there and lived there, as will appear in the proper place.

**(5)** Twenty-seven years had passed when Eulogius recalls this martyrdom. In Book II he says that he encountered it while he was still a boy and had only just entered adolescence, and that the martyrdom had occurred almost thirty years earlier.

**(6)** This expression of imprecation is more common among our Spaniards than among the ancients in ordinary speech. Virgil has:

“Gods, avert such a pest from the earth” (*Aeneid* III.620).

And likewise:

“May the gods first turn that omen upon himself” (*Aeneid* II.189).

**(7)** The heading is absent in the copy: it is, however, the *Life and Passion of the holy martyrs Flora and Maria*, which we have added after the *Martyrial Document*. This is not because the third day of June, on which the feast is noted, was the first day on which they suffered: that day in that year fell on a Wednesday, the dominical letter being D. On that same day Usuard’s martyrology records their passion; the Roman Martyrology, recently enlarged, and Vettelius’s edition seem to have derived it from there. The Church of Córdoba celebrates that day as dedicated to the same holy martyrs.

**(8)** The *Hieremia* of the martyrs. On these, see Book II, chapter 3; likewise on the priest Perfectus, chapter 1. He introduced mention of the latter here in order to show on what ground he had referred to Isaac at that point.

**(9)** The most pious men of the holy Church—which was, and always will be, as our Lord Jesus Christ foretold, filled with good and evil people indiscriminately—has never ceased to contain certain wicked persons among Christians who disturb it importunately and, driven by various unprofitable motives, harass it.

This also occurred in the time of the holy Eulogius, when the Spanish Church was held captive under harsh and bloody servitude and suffered shameful evils under the most inhuman tyrants.

One notable consolation that Christians could have amid so many calamities was that there were still those who, animated by holy zeal, contended boldly for Christ and, by their steadfastness, encouraged others to sustain the Church of God. Yet someone sought wickedly and foolishly to deprive them of this very consolation.

They were called martyrs, although their accusers judged them unworthy of the name, and they were summoned rather to the assembly of the Spanish Church than to profess Christ. Eulogius wished to respond to this in Book II, so that he might commend the martyrs whose deeds he would relate below, defend them against their accusers, and establish the truth of the matter.

[The supplied text of this scholium breaks off after the opening of the following reference: “See …”]

## [Scan page 441]

### SCHOLIA

He composed that entire work in defense of those same martyrs, so that it could rightly be called an *Apology*. Nor were there detractors of the martyrs only in the age of St. Eulogius, but also in the early periods of the Church. For the First Council of Carthage, under Sylvester I, severely restrained such disparagers of the martyrs in its second canon.^1

(2) But I do not know toward what end this tends. Everywhere St. Eulogius displays remarkable modesty; indeed, it is all the more conspicuous because, although he was, as those times required, highly learned, he shows no confidence in his talent or literary ability, and no confidence—most assuredly—in his virtue.

(3) “The Church of Spain.” By this period many words, especially proper names, had already been corrupted, so that they gradually transformed themselves into the Spanish language that we now possess. Hence they pronounced *Spaniam*, not *Hispaniam*; *Cordobam*, not *Cordubam*; *Eglesiam*, not *Ecclesiam*. Nor was this corruption recent, arising after the Arabs entered Spain; rather, it was inherited from the time of the Goths, as we have already demonstrated from coins in St. Eulogius’s *Life*. They wrote as they pronounced. Thus, in ancient writing, it was always *Eglesiae*, not *Ecclesiae*. Nevertheless, in printing we have retained the propriety of the Latin language, writing *Hispaniae* and *Ecclesiae*, just as we have retained *Cordubae* in the name of Corduba.

(4) “Carousals” [*Comessationes*]. In this passage St. Eulogius was setting forth what Muhammad had taught most wickedly about Christ the Savior and his most sacred mother, as found in the abominable Qur’an. We have, however, removed several lines for sound reasons.^2 For what was necessary at that time in order to expose the disgracefulness of the abominable sect might now offend pious ears. Moreover, the most provident decrees of the holy Inquisition have taken care that the impious teachings of the Qur’an should not be read indiscriminately. Yet we did not wish, merely at our own discretion, to remove anything from the work of the holy martyr, which we undertake with due dignity and approach reverently; rather, we did this on the advice of the wisest men. We wished to record these matters here so that, if anyone should come upon a copy of St. Eulogius, he may understand what these few omissions are. And, as I judge, the words of Abbot Speraindeus continue up to “and they are enclosed.” For here the force of the speech becomes more vehement, and he undertakes something different from the rest of the work, worthy of a more eloquent craftsman.

(5) “Some of our philosophers.” He calls Christians who excelled in learning, and who were teachers in the Church, philosophers. The usage is not without some justification by resemblance.

(6) “That most unconquered John, author of the *Indiculi luminosi*.” He described John’s punishment at length. Since the book has not yet been printed,^3 it may be worthwhile to set down here John’s own words. After the martyrdom of the presbyter Perfectus, he says:

> “Let us proceed to set forth a second case. After a year had passed, or somewhat more, that eye of envy did not cease, but—as is customary among them, to mock Christianity and insult all of us Christians—they attempted to exaggerate the trading and commercial dealings of this John, whom they had kept confined for a long time in prison,^4 and to harass him. Burned with envy because of his commerce, they brought many reproaches against him,^5 saying: ‘You despise our prophet; you continually repeat his name in mockery; and by oaths, as you see fit, you often affirm to the ears of ignorant Christians that your falsehood is the religion of our people.’ To them he replied confidently, suspecting no deceit against himself. Wishing to show that he was free from the charges they were bringing against him, he answered that the raging fury and headlong anger of those men, repeating and reiterating the same accusation, had often threatened him with it. Then, unable to endure such a cloud of generations [or: such a mob], and becoming indignant, he armed himself with a sufficiently urbane wit and replied with elegant confidence: ‘May he be cursed by God who wishes to name your prophet.’ Immediately a great uproar arose, and a compact crowd of wretches gathered—an assembly hating the disease [or: the hated infirmity], like bees collected into one ruinous heap, sprinkled with the conspiracy of a single mass of malice—and they dragged him, half-dead, before the judge. After producing witnesses of little reliability, emerging from that very mass of criminals, they brought forward stronger and weightier accusations against him on their own testimony. He denied all of them and openly exposed their envious pretense against him. But the unjust judge had him beaten with four hundred blows of the whip and ordered a herald’s proclamation to pass through all the seats of the saints, declaring that one who derogated from God’s prophet deserved to suffer such things. Then he confined him in prison under strict guard, threatening to inflict still greater punishments upon him.”  

On this John St. Eulogius also writes again in Book II, chapter 10. In an old manuscript of Michael Ruiz de Azagra there were also epigrams by Cyprian, archpresbyter of the Church of Corduba; among them was this distich, under the title:

> **Likewise, upon the tomb of Saint John the Confessor**
>
> John endured prisons and dreadful iron chains  
> for love of Christ. Having fulfilled these things, he rests in peace in the royal hall.

I believe this is the same John whom St. Eulogius mentions, although the epitaph has reported fewer details than it could and should have done. But such were the times that merely closing a verse in any fashion was considered a great achievement. This Cyprian lived and wrote, as is evident from his other epigrams, forty years or somewhat more after the death of St. Eulogius.

(7) “As he himself also taught.” The parenthesis is exceedingly long, and, because of the transposition—which Fabius also condemns—it is more than sluggish. Yet we did not dare alter anything here.

(8) “And all whom confession …” From this point it must be observed that Christians throughout Spain, and especially at Corduba, had been left and tolerated under the condition, as we explained at the beginning, that they should not disparage the sect of Muhammad. On this very matter we read in the *Indiculi luminosus* as follows:

> “Behold, the public law hangs over them, and legal commands run throughout their whole kingdom, so that whoever blasphemes is flogged, and whoever strikes another is killed. And behold, every day, by day and by night, in their towers and mist-covered mountains, they curse the Lord, while with one voice they exalt an impudent, perjured, frenzied, and unjust prophet together with the Lord of testimony.”

As for the other things that Christians suffered from the Saracens, which Eulogius records here, that author writes in this manner:

> “Every day they overwhelm us with insults and with a thousand bundles of abuse; yet we say that we do not have persecution. For, to say nothing of other matters, when they see the bodies of the dead being carried by priests for burial, as ecclesiastical custom requires, do they not say aloud, with the most impure groans: ‘God, do not have mercy on them’? And when they attack the priests of the Lord with stones, marking the people of the Lord with shameful words, and passing through the Christians, they bespatter them with the foulness of filth and unspeakable stench, gnashing their teeth while threatening worse things?”

And shortly afterward:

> “Likewise, whenever the priests of God happen by chance to meet anyone on the road, they heap stones before them, roll the driest potsherds before their feet, and, insulting them with a disgraceful and infamous name, mock them with a vulgar proverb and an indecent song; they mutilate the sign of the faith with a reproachful expression. But when they hear the signal of the basilica—that is, the sound of ringing bronze struck at all the canonical hours to summon the Church to assembly—they gape in derision and contempt, shake their heads, repeat unspeakable words, and attack and ridicule every sex, every age, and the whole flock of Christ the Lord, not with a single mockery but with a thousandfold infamy. Are these not the people who curse Jerusalem, destroy the walls of holy Zion, and set them on fire? Of them it is said: ‘Cursed are all who despise you, and all who blaspheme you; cursed are all who destroy your walls, all who overthrow your towers, and all who set your dwellings on fire’ (Tobit 13:16).”

And although all these things were carried out by them, as we have said, through contempt, mockery, or hatred, they were nevertheless also perpetrated literally against the dwellings of the Lord and the buildings of the sanctuary, while the churches of God were destroyed and temples, strengthened by ancient solidity, were leveled to the ground.

(9) “Stripped of their flesh.” Here it is necessary to pause briefly, in order to understand better what is being established by this passage of the law. The learned Marquis del Risco, who investigated the origin of this bull in his *Legal History of the Bull*, found no older monument of its antiquity than the *Roman Ceremonial* of St. Gregory X, published by Jean Mabillon in volume II of the *Musaeum Italicum*. But since Alvarus plainly speaks of a custom maintained at least by the Church of Spain, namely, publicly cursing enemies every year, we discover in such a rite—whether of our own or another particular church—a foundation for that bull that is neither obscure nor slight; from such a source the Roman Church may have received the discipline. For although this Church is the mother and teacher of all, she does not disdain to embrace the customs of other churches when they seem not unreasonable. As Gregory the Great says admirably in Letter 12 of Book IX: “If another Church has anything good … I am prepared to imitate it, and my inferiors with me, in what is good.”

Nor should some ignorant person dare reproach us for asserting that it is good for enemies to be cursed by the Church. For, as that same most gentle pontiff says excellently in Book IV of the *Moralia*, no. 2, a curse is pronounced in one way by the judgment of justice, and in another by the bitterness of vengeance: “When holy men pronounce a sentence of cursing, it bursts forth not from a desire for vengeance but from an examination of justice,” and so forth—passages worthy of reading.

Neither Eulogius nor Alvarus, nor anyone else, tells us on what day in Spain these curses were pronounced. The Greeks, as Martène reports from the words of Leo Allatius in chapter 19 of Book IV of *De antiquis Ecclesiae ritibus*, read the *Synodicon* on the first Sunday of Lent, in which nearly all heretics are anathematized. The Latins, however, as is clear from the aforementioned *Ceremonial of Gregory X*, publicly pronounced those excommunications on the days of the Lord’s Supper and the Ascension, and on the feast of the Dedication of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. Therefore, if anyone should conjecture that such a rite was customarily celebrated among us on one of these days, except the feast of the dedication, we would not object.

### Notes

1. Whoever desires a longer discussion of this matter should consult Benedict XIV’s learned work, full of every kind of erudition, *On the Beatification of the Servants of God and the Canonization of the Blessed*, Book III, chapter 16, no. 7 and following. There, in his usual manner, he considers and discusses the question: “May a martyr offer himself for martyrdom, and does a voluntary offering of himself for it impede his merit?” It will not weary one to read the examples gathered there from all ecclesiastical antiquity; among them occurs this case of the martyrs of Corduba, with praise of their eminent apologist and defender, our Eulogius. Benedict repeatedly transcribes Eulogius’s words from this very first book of the *Memoriale*, evidently judging that their voluntarily offering themselves to martyrdom had an appropriate, and perhaps necessary, cause: namely, the cause which, Eulogius testifies, moved them—when the faith was endangered by silence and its suppression would have followed unless, in their confession of the truth of their faith, they had forced it upon unwilling enemies and had even challenged those enemies by their noble confession.

2. For this reason the highly learned Thomas Malvenda censured Morales in his work *De Antichristo*. It is worth reproducing here his words, transcribed by Fabricius from the Lyons edition of 1647, volume II of the *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae aetatis*, p. 124, Padua edition of 1754: “St. Eulogius had reviewed many things concerning the abominable and most disgraceful works and doctrines of Muhammad, most of which Morales removed … which certainly does not seem to us to have been done by him on sufficiently sound grounds,” however much he excuses himself. For the works of the Fathers ought not to be handled or mutilated in this manner; neither were the most foul and filthy examples of the Gnostics erased from the books of St. Epiphanius, and among other Fathers and ancient writers such detestable and dreadful heresies are found described. It was of no small importance to know them, and they were not related without a strong and vigorous refutation. But St. Eulogius always inveighed with the utmost sharpness, as befitted so great a man, against Muhammad’s perverse errors.”

3. “Since the *Indiculi luminosus* has now been published by Henry Flórez in volume XI of *España Sagrada*, p. 219, as we stated in the note to the *Scholia* on Alvarus’s Hymn and Epitaphs concerning Eulogius, no. 5, we shall append here what he noted there.”

4. Flórez reads *claustra* more appropriately in keeping with Alvarus’s meaning, and rightly observes that *claustra*, feminine singular, was used by writers of Late Latin.

5. Flórez: *negotiationum mercimonia* (“commercial dealings”).

6. In Flórez, *ipsum* (“himself”) is absent.

7. The same editor notes that one should perhaps read *ingessere* (“they brought forward” / “they thrust upon him”).

8. The same: *ignorantibus* (“to the ignorant”).

9. The same: *cum fidenter … suspicans se immunem* (“confidently … suspecting that he was free [of the charges]”).

10. We have adopted *exosae* (“hating” / “hated”) from Flórez, since Morales read corruptly *ex ore* (“from the mouth”).

11. Flórez has *conspersione* (“sprinkling”), and notes that this should be retained, or *consparsione*, since the ancients used *consparsum* for *aspersum* (“sprinkled”).

12. Flórez, p. 228, reads *legalis jussa*; he notes that *jussa*, feminine singular, is used like *claustra*, or that one should read *legali jussione* (“by legal command”).

Since, however, no such mark is indicated in the manuscript, and since the words may have been spoken from the minds of the adversaries, we have allowed ourselves no alteration. I wished to retain the mark with Morales.”

16. The same: *genis* (“cheeks”); he observes that this is not an implausible reading, since the same author later uses the word in this sense.

17. Flórez: “*casu quo quem obviant, perviantes lapides testaque aridissima ante vestigia*, etc.” He notes that Morales embroidered from his own invention what he read, although he restored *testas aridissimas* (“very dry potsherds”) better than the manuscript’s *testa arissima*.

18. Flórez says that Morales wrongly printed *detruncant* (“they cut off”) instead of *decolorant* (“they disfigure”).

19. We have already stated, under no. 21 of Book I, that these words are from Tobit and are sought in vain in the Vulgate, although they are presented in the Mozarabic Breviary. We now add, from Alvarus, the passage that Morales uses here: this curse of the Church against its enemies is not proclaimed secretly but openly and luminously. The traces of this discipline—namely, that the enemies of the Church were overwhelmed with curses every year—were preserved by the Roman Church down to our own times in the annual publication of the famous bull commonly called *In Coena Domini*. In it, heretics, apostates, schismatics, and the other enemies of the Church were first excommunicated, as they had been for three or more centuries. But Pope Clement XIV, in 1770, was the first to abstain from publishing it; his successor, our Most Holy Lord Pope Pius VI, happily reigning, followed his example.
