### SCHOLIA AMBROSII

“He threatened to inflict greater punishments upon him.” Concerning this John, St. Eulogius again writes in Book II, chapter 10. In an old manuscript of Michael Ruiz de Azagra there were also epigrams by Cyprian, archpresbyter of the Church of Corduba, and among them this distich under the title:

> **Likewise, upon the tomb of Saint John the Confessor**
>
> John endured prisons and dreadful iron chains  
> for love of Christ. Having fulfilled these things, he rests in peace in the royal hall.

I believe this is the same John whom St. Eulogius mentions, although the epitaph has reported fewer details than it could and should have done. But such were the times that merely closing a verse in any fashion was considered a great achievement. This Cyprian lived and wrote, as is evident from his other epigrams, forty years or somewhat more after the death of St. Eulogius.

(7) “As he himself also taught.” The parenthesis is exceedingly long, and, because of the transposition—which Fabius also condemns—it is more than sluggish. Yet we did not dare alter anything here.

(8) “And all whom confession …” From this point it must be observed that Christians throughout Spain, and especially at Corduba, had been left and tolerated under the condition, as we explained at the beginning, that they should not disparage the sect of Muhammad. On this very matter we read in the *Indiculi luminosus* as follows:

> “Behold, the public law hangs over them, and legal commands run throughout their whole kingdom, so that whoever blasphemes is flogged, and whoever strikes another is killed. And behold, every day, by day and by night, in their towers and mist-covered mountains, they curse the Lord, while with one voice they exalt an impudent, perjured, frenzied, and unjust prophet together with the Lord of testimony.”

As for the other things that Christians suffered from the Saracens, which Eulogius records here, that author writes in this manner:

> “Every day they overwhelm us with insults and with a thousand bundles of abuse; yet we say that we do not have persecution. For, to say nothing of other matters, when they see the bodies of the dead being carried by priests for burial, as ecclesiastical custom requires, do they not say aloud, with the most impure groans: ‘God, do not have mercy on them’? And when they attack the priests of the Lord with stones, marking the people of the Lord with shameful words, and passing through the Christians, they bespatter them with the foulness of filth and unspeakable stench, gnashing their teeth while threatening worse things?”

And shortly afterward:

> “Likewise, whenever the priests of God happen by chance to meet anyone on the road, they heap stones before them, roll the driest potsherds before their feet, and, insulting them with a disgraceful and infamous name, mock them with a vulgar proverb and an indecent song; they mutilate the sign of the faith with a reproachful expression. But when they hear the signal of the basilica—that is, the sound of ringing bronze struck at all the canonical hours to summon the Church to assembly—they gape in derision and contempt, shake their heads, repeat unspeakable words, and attack and ridicule every sex, every age, and the whole flock of Christ the Lord, not with a single mockery but with a thousandfold infamy. Are these not the people who curse Jerusalem, destroy the walls of holy Zion, and set them on fire? ## [Scan page 443]

### IN BOOK I OF THE *MEMORIALIS*

Let us understand the holy martyr. At this very time there lived in Corduba a presbyter named Samson, later abbot of the monastery of St. Zoilus, a learned man of subtle intellect, versed in the study of philosophy and sacred letters. His *Apology*, which he wrote in three books against Hostegesis, bishop of Málaga, makes this clear; Hostegesis had called him a heretic with insults at the Council of Corduba, as Samson himself recounts at length in the preface to his second book. There he shows that he had become abbot of the Church of St. Zoilus the martyr in the year 901 of the Spanish Era—that is, in the year 863 of the Lord. This was the third or fourth year after Eulogius’s martyrdom.

When I was still a young man, in the mountains of Corduba, ten miles from the city and not far from the town called Trassierra, in the district known as the County of Espiel, peasants cleaning out an old well drew out a small bronze bell nearly a foot high. It is still preserved in the monastery of St. Jerome. Its form differs greatly from those we now use. It bears the following letters, not cast in relief but hollowed out with a chisel in a circular pattern, and linked together by so many interlacements, with one letter enclosed within another, that their appearance cannot be represented in type:

> “Samson, abbot, offers this gift to the house of St. Sebastian, martyr of Christ, in the Era 913.”

This is the year of the Lord 875. Samson himself died later, in the year 890. This is established by his epitaph, composed by Cyprian the archpresbyter and found among the rest of his epigrams in that same manuscript of Azagra, under the title:

> **Epitaph which the same man published in the tomb of Lord Samson, in heroic meter**
>
> Who and how great was Samson, the illustrious abbot,  
> whose sacred limbs rest in this urn beneath this hall?  
> All Hesperia resounds with his fame.  
> Bend God by your prayers, reader; now, I beseech you, bend him,  
> so that he may be able to ascend the heavens, cleansed of his sins.  
> He departed, widely known and full of days,  
> on the twenty-first day of the month of Sextilis,  
> namely, on the first-and-twentieth sun of the month of Sextilis.  
> Era 926.

The Era was written in this manner. His *Apology* is preserved in Toledo, in the library of the holy Church, written in Gothic letters in a very ancient manuscript. All these facts sufficiently indicate that this Samson flourished in the time of St. Eulogius. We wished to establish this more precisely because, in the preface to his second book, concerning the Christian count Servandus, a wicked man who threatened the burial of the holy martyrs, he writes as follows. After recounting the many evils he had inflicted on living Christians, he continues:

> “Then, not content with the deaths of the living, nor with those at rest—whose souls’ repose he could not impede—so that he might not seem to spare even them, that notorious gravedigger dragged their bodies from their tombs, where they had been laid beneath the altars of God, and showed them to the royal faithful, as they had been mutilated by the two-edged sword, in order by this act to stir up royal minds to the destruction of our people, so that before him those who had dared to bury men struck down by his dagger might be proved liable to the death they deserved.”

Thus far Samson.^5 I believe that no one can doubt that he is speaking of the holy martyrs killed in earlier years.

### Notes

1. Flórez lacks *requiem* (“rest”).

2. The same: more correctly, *aris* (“altars”).

3. The same: *vespillo* (“grave-digger” / “corpse-bearer”).

4. The same: *penes* (“in the possession of”).

5. We discussed Abbot Samson in our note to the *Antikimenon* and the two Orations of St. Julian.

6. Flórez has written the life of this presbyter sufficiently accurately in chapter 4 of volume X of *España Sagrada*, near the end.

### SANCTORUM

(10) “For we who now …” Eulogius is speaking of himself. As Alvarus wrote, he himself had later been sent to prison, more than once. Through the prayers of the holy virgins and martyrs Flora and Maria—as they themselves had testified before their martyrdom—he was released together with the other Christians. This is what he implies. Observe that St. Eulogius wrote this book after that release of his.

(11) “We pay monthly.” *Lunariter*, like *lunatim*, is an adverb newly coined in those times. They mean “each month.” Leovigild, a presbyter of Corduba who lived in this same century and wrote a little work on the clerical habit, also mentions this monthly tribute. Explaining the reasons why he wrote, he says:

> “So that if one of us, prevented by bodily weakness, is unable to return to the remaining teachers, or if inquiry, census, or the tax which we are compelled to pay every lunar month for Christ’s name has detained him, at least during the night, amid ecclesiastical duties, he may read what is necessary.”

Abbot Samson mentions this Leovigild. It is exceedingly bitter and worthy of tears to recall the misery of Christians who endured so many and such great insults and losses.

(12) “Marks upon us.” He understands this as the sacred tonsure. The word *stigma*, which otherwise belonged especially to slaves, was made venerable even among Christians because St. Paul used it.

(13) “Emeterius and Chelidonius.” The poet Prudentius sufficiently indicates in the hymn of these saints that they voluntarily desired to seek death, when he introduces them speaking as follows:

> Let it be enough that, once captured,  
> life, under its bond,  
> has paid every debt;  
> having fulfilled its duties to Caesar,  
> it is time to repay to God  
> whatever belongs to God.  
> Go, masters of the standards,  
> and you, Tribunes, stand back:  
> take away the golden collars,  
> rewards of the wounded;  
> henceforth the shining wages  
> of the angels already call us.  
> Christ presides there  
> over cohorts of the chosen;  
> reigning from his throne on high,  
> he condemns the shameful gods,  
> and you who, for our mockery,  
> fashion monsters into deities.

The holy Church of Toledo also possesses a very ancient manuscript containing the lives of our martyrs. In the history of Emeterius and Chelidonius it contains these very words, which Eulogius cites shortly afterward. They are the words spoken by Chelidonius in response to Emeterius, who was exhorting him to proceed before the judge. In former times the holy Church of Toledo evidently used to read this very history at Matins, and some churches in Spain still read portions of it today. It must be carefully noted how ancient this history is, since it had already been written in the time of Eulogius.

(14) “Among those seven brothers.” We read these same words in the published history of the saints Julian and Basilissa, in the passage concerning Bishop Equitius, in the most ancient sanctorals, and wherever the account is given in full. For nearly all the churches, eager for brevity at Matins, used to derive many things from it. We regret that the same thing has happened in almost all the histories of the saints.

From this one may understand how much authority there is in many histories of the saints, and how much veneration their antiquity ought to command. Who would believe that these histories of Julian and Basilissa, and of Emeterius and Chelidonius, had been written more than eight hundred years earlier, unless he saw them cited here by St. Eulogius? Yet we routinely despise many such works and disdain them as though they were newly invented.

(15) “Felix the Most Fortunate.” All this concerning this martyr, who was the brother of St. Cucufas, is read at Matins in nearly all the churches of Spain. Gerunda lies at the farthest limits of Spain, where Spain is joined to Narbonese Gaul by the Pyrenees, and is situated in the territory of the Ausetani. Without entirely erasing its name, we now commonly call it Girona. Prudentius called it a small city when he also mentioned Felix in his hymn of the martyrs of Caesaraugusta. It is generally thought to be the same as Caesarea in Mauretania, whose enormous ruins still remain together with its name.

(16) “And likewise Saint Sebastian.” These are examples of holy martyrs who surrendered themselves voluntarily to martyrdom, without being sought out. It would be tedious to pursue each case individually. The deeds of all these saints are sufficiently well known that anyone can understand what Eulogius implies, or can read their histories.

(17) “Thus Eulalia, the virgin of Barcelona.” From this it can easily be understood that Eulalia of Mérida did not proceed of her own accord to confess the Christian faith, but was brought forward by the command of the judge. Otherwise Eulogius would also have presented her example. Some, however, report the matter differently. Those who wish the two Eulalias to be one and the same are refuted from this point onward by the testimony of St. Eulogius. The fame of the city of Barcelona is so great that it is unnecessary to say more about it here.

(18) “But in truth.” He weighs very skillfully the testimony he had brought forward and demonstrates how it should be understood. This is something frequently outstanding in St. Eulogius, and an excellent indication of his intellect and judgment. The same Hispanic expression has been preserved down to our own time. When asserting something strongly, we often begin: *en verdad* (“in truth”).

(19) “Not outsiders.” The foolish zeal of certain bishops had advanced this far. He later shows in the *Apology* that bishops too had been stirred in this manner.

(20) “Nor does it move …” The holy martyr treats everything with the greatest prudence and immense circumspection. Therefore, what he had established in common he restrains, as though curbing it, by applying the necessary qualification.

(21) “Cato the philosopher.” Amid the great calamity and miserable servitude of the Church of Spain, even Christian teachers suffered from a scarcity of books. Hence Eulogius is compelled to insert verses by an author who was not especially distinguished, although otherwise serious and full of true precepts of wisdom.

(22) “Their lot has been found.” Although in the old manuscript a blank section of parchment had been left here, large enough to contain eight or ten lines, nevertheless nothing at all was missing. For the entire leaf, written quite loosely and divided into far fewer lines than the others, clearly reveals the anxiety of the copyist, who was trying to occupy the whole leaf. Since he could not accomplish this fully, and since what follows had a new beginning and seemed suitable for the opening of a leaf, he was content to cover one page and begin the next, continuing for several lines.

(23) “Before all the philosophers of our country.” He calls learned men philosophers, using the same *catachresis* [transferred usage] explained above. When he wrote in the year of the Lord 851, three years before the author of the *Indiculi luminosus*, he was writing before that author. This may serve as an argument that Alvarus was not the author of that work, since he certainly would not have written it after Eulogius.

(24) “And although it does not …” Eulogius again returns to his customary modesty. His humility does not allow him to forget himself for long. While he celebrates the praises of the holy martyrs and inwardly exhilarates himself and all the pious with the holiest joys, the thought of humility suddenly intrudes, comes back to his memory, interrupts him as he enjoys heavenly gladness, and recalls him, as though unworthy of that rejoicing. Everything in him breathes a heart truly devoted to God; everything already gives off the fragrance of the future martyr.

## INTO BOOK II

### CHAPTER ONE

(1) “Consulate.” This too belongs to that license of the Latin language about which we spoke above. He calls the kingdom the “consulate,” the highest magistrates of the kingdom “consuls,” and even offices and dignities “fasces.” Abbot Samson of Corduba, whom we mentioned earlier, does the same.

(2) “In the twenty-ninth year of Abd al-Rahman.” The historical books of our people always write *Abderramen*, wherever this and other kings bearing the same name are mentioned. I believe, however, that the form found in both manuscripts gives the true pronunciation of the name. It has a distinctly Arabic sound, whereas the other form seems softened to suit the sweetness of the Spanish language. This Abd al-Rahman is the third of that name, as is clear from Rasis the Moor and from the particular history of Arab affairs by Rodrigo, archbishop of Toledo.

Moreover, besides the many and most sacred benefits of these books of St. Eulogius, which they provide by commemorating the deeds of the holy martyrs, they also furnish a not insignificant store of learning and usefulness because a clear and almost indisputable chronology of the years in Spanish history—from the time of King Pelagius to Ordoño I, son of Ramiro I—is established with complete certainty from this passage and from the beginning of Book III. It is not the place here to explain how this is done. Only those who have exerted themselves to some degree in this matter can know how important it is, for the reckoning of years and for all chronology, to have found something certain and fixed, like a hinge around which everything else turns. We discussed this at length at the beginning of our Gothic history, in our *Chronicon*.

(3) “But Corduba.” Rasis does not write that Corduba alone, but that all Spain was ennobled by the illustrious works of this king. “He,” he says, “brought water from the mountains into the cities, built temples, and established throughout Spain workshops for cloth of greater value, woven with gold.” The Toledan historian relates that the streets of Corduba were paved with stone by this king; likewise, that water was brought from the neighboring mountains—

### Notes

1. The Church of our city solemnly celebrated the feast of these saints, as is clear from the Missal and Gothic Breviary for 9 January, on which we have in the Breviary three hymns celebrating their martyrdom. Of the prose Acts published by Bollandus for the same day, Papebrochius says in volume I of the May collection, p. 8, column 1, that although they present themselves as the work of a contemporary eyewitness, we now judge them to have been fabricated, for reasons whose traces can easily be recognized by later generations.

2. These saints’ feast is solemnly celebrated by our Church, as is evident from the ecclesiastical books for 1 August. If you wish, consult Jean-Baptiste Sollier for that day.

3. In the same books, under 20 January, you will find the Acts of Sebastian, and in the new edition of the Gothic Breviary another hymn, whose author is lavish in praising Sebastian, p. 94. Blessed Ambrose also mentions this saint in his exposition of Psalm 118, sermon 20, no. 44, where he says that Sebastian had discovered at Milan that there was no contest or conflict, and therefore had gone to Rome, so that he might be found where persecution was raging because of devotion to the faith.

4. Morales slips in this conjecture, since it is clear from Prudentius and from the Gothic Missal and Breviary for 10 December that Eulalia of Mérida voluntarily advanced to martyrdom. See Flórez, volume XIII, treatise 41, chapter 18, throughout.

5. See our note to the *Scholia* on the Hymn and Epitaphs.

6. We have already spoken of these two histories in our note to the *Scholia* on the *Life of St. Eulogius*.

**SCHOLIA ON BOOK II OF THE MEMORIAL OF THE SAINTS**

879

…carried through lead pipes into the temple, the citadel, and the city’s other more celebrated places. Water still flows into these places, though not in great quantity. Hence it is clear that this aqueduct, by which water is now brought here, differed from that other wondrous structure, which is seen interrupted in many places. Through it a far greater volume of water flowed into the city, conveyed from nearly the tenth milestone. It is not enough that very great mountains were pierced throughout this route and deep valleys spanned by aqueduct-bridges: the incredible mass of the mountains themselves is supported, lest it press down the subterranean work, by frequent towers rising from the vast channel itself like little forts and projecting high above the mountains. Although this aqueduct could reach the citadel and temple by a direct and short route, it bends in a long circuit through the district named from the croaking of frogs, so that water might also be supplied to the upper parts of the city. I have always believed this to be the work of this king; for no other builder is recorded. And the water at the citadel and temple which remains now is scanty, whereas that earlier supply was certainly immense and marked by such celebrated testimony of writers. I shall set down his words, so that it may appear how closely they agree with what I shall relate about the holy Eulogius:

> “And first, let us behold the priest Perfectus, slain by the zeal of the gentiles in this very place, now adorned with the constancy of his wonderful faith, endowed with martyrial glory, and truly enrolled among the number of the elect. Let us sincerely recount how he came to his death. As he was going elsewhere, attending to secular business, and considering nothing of what had occurred, he was assailed by incursions of demon-worshippers. Against them he cautiously and circumspectly—as they thought, but, in my view, timidly—sought assurance; and, lest he be impeded by his own answers, he prayed, saying: ‘I had many things by which I could most abundantly refute your errors or destroy the old wives’ tales of your stories, if I did not fear to incur, in every direction, the judgments of your vengeance with its avenging sword.’ When they had granted him this, and, having first exacted an oath, required him to say what he thought, he boldly accepted permission to speak; taking their falsehoods for a true oath, after many varied contests of argument he reproached, as best he could, the voluptuous wantonness of their prophet and the luxury of his seduction, and proved it by an eloquent speech. But when, in a dispute of words, he had made some mocking remark about his prostitution or the adulterous collusion of married persons, they gnashed their teeth, raged with doglike jaws, hissed with viperous mouths, and roared with leonine ferocity; yet because of the oath just given they let him depart unharmed. After some time, however, continually retaining poison in their hearts and reckoning that the earlier harsh compact imposed on him had been erased by lapse of time, they ensnared him by deceit, seized him, and brought him before the judge; greedily intent on falsehood, they impiously alleged that he was destroying the rite of their faith, and, on the testimony of utterly worthless men, affirmed that he had cursed their prophet. Terrified by this unforeseen event and bewildered by an unfamiliar entrapment, ignorant of the fraudulent scheme which their deceitful contrivance had prepared against him, he disclosed, with a rather weak defence, that he had not said this at all. But once he had been thrown into prison and come to himself, he began, with bold resolve and manly courage, to assail their whole law; and he began not only to repeat what he had said the previous day—which the ignorant faction alleged against him—but also to add weightier matters, and to expect the glory of death rather than death itself. They then led him out on the very day of his dreadful Passover, when they customarily enjoy fleshly food and abundantly supply sustenance to belly and lust, and killed him with the avenging sword. As though they had gained victory over enemies, they went in exaltation to their assembly for prayer, believing that they had rendered service to God; stained with innocent blood, they came, as was their annual custom, to complete their rite once again.”  

(4) **Also known through a knowledge of the Arabic language.** This is plainly a Hispanicism. It does not mean that blessed Perfectus was moderately skilled in Arabic. Rather, in a Spanish idiom, it means that his outstanding command of Arabic caused him to be known to and esteemed by the Moors. Thus we often say: *Por parte de su virtud era muy bien querido* [“On account of his virtue he was greatly beloved”]. We have already noted several other Hispanicisms of this kind.

(5) **He spent his time in the aforesaid monastery.** The building which he had previously called a basilica he now calls a monastery. For at that time churches and monasteries alike were almost indiscriminately both called and were monasteries. This usage had remained from the time of the Goths, as we especially learn from the councils and from the history of Paul of Mérida. Every notable church had its own abbots, who presided over a body of deacons and others established in the lesser grades of the Church, who ministered there day and night. This had to be said once, lest it repeatedly confuse anyone who encounters it. This Paul, a deacon of Mérida, whom we mention elsewhere, wrote the history of the Church of Mérida and its bishops, and also added certain matters concerning other holy men. His *Catholic Confession* also survives. Both works are preserved in fairly ancient manuscripts in the library of the holy Church of Toledo. We have seen much older copies in several other libraries.

(6) **He had said beforehand that he had done it.** For the same reason that in the first book we removed certain passages concerning the obscenities of the Muhammadan law, we have here also omitted a few matters, almost in the same words repeated. Saint Eulogius himself professes here that he passes over certain things which might cause horror to pious ears.

(7) **May God grant better things.** Concerning our imprecations, we give an account in the preface to the first book. Conversely, wishes for prosperity and honour also occur in the same fashion. Such is the phrase in comedies, *Dii meliora* [“May the gods grant better things”], and similar expressions. But we Spaniards use blessings in this manner more frequently and more openly in the middle of conversation.

(8) **Into the plain beyond the bridge.** That plain is now called the Field of Truth.

Whoever [the author was] also wrote about this martyr Perfectus.

*The work of Paul the Deacon entitled* On the Life and Miracles of the Fathers of Mérida *first appeared at Madrid in 1633, and subsequently at Antwerp in 1638. Cardinal Aguirre reprinted that edition in volume II of his* Councils of Spain; *finally Enrique Flórez edited the work much more accurately in volume XXIII of* Sacred Spain.

*See what we note under no. 4 of the Scholia on Book I.*

Flórez reads *imprecarent* [“they might invoke curses”].

Flórez reads *passivam luxuriam* [“passive lust”]; *melius post aliqua* [“better, after ‘some’”]; and, after *adulterii* [“of adultery”], adds *factionis* [“of faction”]. Flórez reads *dimiserunt* [“they dismissed”], *circumvectione* [“circumvention”], and *delati* [“carried away / brought forward”].

As we have already said in the note to the Scholia in the Life of Saint Eulogius, this bishop is Saul.

(9) **And worthy of the bishop.** Although the holy Eulogius mentions a certain bishop of Córdoba who governed the Church in his own time, he nowhere leaves his name written. I cannot understand why he did this.

(10) **In the title in which…** From this we may suspect that at that time there was not merely one temple of the holy Acisclus in Córdoba. Even now two ancient shrines are visible: one a small sanctuary in which the holy martyr was brought up with his sister Victoria; the other, at the river, in the vestibule of a very ancient structure, where they are believed to have been buried together. Hence that temple is held in great veneration; a few years ago it was granted to the friars of the Order of Saint Dominic, who established a monastery there.

**SCHOLIA OF AMBROSE**

(11) **On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May.** This is the eighteenth day of April, which in that year fell on a Friday. For that year was the nineteenth of the thirty-one-year solar cycle, and the second after the leap year. It therefore evidently had the Sunday letter E. Everything consequently agrees correctly.

(12) **And the king’s terror from heaven.** I have treated more fully of this king’s terror in Book I and elsewhere frequently. That other terror is different, namely the one at the end of this second book, as is clear from the beginning of chapter 7 of this book. Meanwhile, let us reverently contemplate the power of God, the strength of Christian truth, and the force of evangelical law. The impious tyrant consumes, destroys, and slaughters Christians; but the little flock, to which it pleased the Father to give the kingdom, though scattered and butchered, rises up stronger and casts a great terror upon royal power. This is surely the fire that Christ came to cast upon the earth, desiring nothing more than that it burn: if you try to extinguish it, a greater flame bursts forth. The grains of wheat, dying as they fall into the earth, have always produced abundant fruit in the Church.

**CHAPTER II**

(1) **Of the secretary of the commonwealth.** Budaeus taught in his earlier annotations on the *Pandects* that public scribes ought to be understood by this name.

Flórez, in volume X of *Sacred Spain*, treatise 33, chapter 7, no. 55, believes that *exceptor* here means not scribes but tax-farmers; but we agree with Budaeus, whom Morales follows. For although *exceptor* elsewhere signifies a tax-farmer—which we do not deny—blessed Isaac, unless we are wholly mistaken, held the office of a scribe, not of a tax-farmer. See Du Cange’s *Glossary*.

(2) **Tabanos the town.** No trace of this town remains, nor is there any basis from which we can conjecture its site. It was later destroyed by the Moors as a monastery, and the monks took refuge within the city, as Eulogius writes in chapter 11 of Book III. Saint Columba, as is related there, was connected with the holy martyr Isaac by the same degree of kinship as Martin and Elizabeth. The rest of this martyr’s deeds he had narrated more fully in the preface to Book I.

(3) **In the royal city.** This title was formerly given to Constantinople after Constantine, as is clear from the authorities of that period. Hence, after the Goths established the seat and, so to speak, the capital of their kingdom there, they appear to have given the same title to the city of Toledo. In precisely the same way Córdoba, the capital of the Arab kingdom in Spain, was also called “the royal city” by a similar antonomasia in the time of Eulogius. The holy martyr himself related this very thing at the beginning of this second book.

(4) **On the third day before the Nones of June, Wednesday.** A year and more had passed between the martyrdom of Perfectus and that of Isaac. The third day of June in the year 851 is here indicated. It is correctly said to have been a Wednesday. That year had the twentieth solar cycle and the Sunday letter D. All this is established from the calculation of the preceding chapter. It is also confirmed in Book I, where it is stated that the fifth day after this martyrdom was a Sunday. The reckoning is inclusive at both ends.

But concerning the martyr Isaac, the *Bright Calendar* says:

> “Let us hasten to our spontaneous martyrs. Isaac, religious in his zeal for God, moved not by human instigation but by divine impulse, walking not along the customary path of our times but along one long forgotten, unable to endure the ancient smoke of persecution, went to the judge. What that other, tormented by a dreadful scourge, denied, and what the weak pretender loudly claimed he had not said amid the blows, the strong athlete, the warrior soldier, confirmed with a fuller defense, undertook with a more powerful contest, and began with a noble mind; with a noble death he completed, consummated, and fulfilled it. Thus he showed men that he had been moved by the zeal of faith, not driven on by fear of necessity; so that the Church, fighting with steadfast confidence, might openly and plainly bring forth the battles which certain men had tried to establish against the one apprehended. The Lord also brought forth to the world the victory of his athletes and proclaimed the steadfastness of his soldiers to a crude age; and he showed that even in the last times he would have victors who would fight the Lord’s battles with the same impulse with which they had first undertaken them.”

Flórez reads *ille* [“that man”]. Álvarus seems to allude to Saint Perfectus, discussed above in the Scholia on chapter 1, no. 8, where he says that Perfectus denied having cursed Muhammad and his sect.

**CHAPTER III**

(1) **From the town of Alaba.** I read *Alabensi* more willingly from Pliny and Strabo, since *Alabense* was found in the exemplar.

(2) **Among the military youths.** The author of the *Life and Martyrdom of Saint Pelagius* calls these boys noble recruits. That little work will be inserted in its proper place.

> “And Joseph, the youngest by birth of the brothers of the holy Eulogius, as I believe, served the king among these palace recruits.”

This will become clear later.

(3) **On the Nones of June.** Sanctius suffered only two days after Isaac, on the fifth day of June. It is therefore correctly stated to have been Friday. Eulogius says nothing about his holy corpse or burial, since it was burned with the martyrs who followed.

**CHAPTER IV**

(1) **On the mysteries of the number six.** Morales says nothing about the sixfold number, which Eulogius called the most holy company of martyrs—perhaps because its common symbols were known to him but unknown to others. We shall add some hidden matters, so that the reader may not leave our scholia starved of nourishment concerning so mystical a number, commended as it was by the holy martyr.

Whether one examines the sacred books or consults the books of the philosophers, the number six offers a rich harvest of mystical meanings. The number six is more perfect than all others because God, the supreme craftsman, completed all his works in it. Nor is the sacred and perfect character of six asserted only because the various kinds of created things were fashioned in that number of days, as William Hamerus thought when he followed Saint Gregory the Great, *Moralia*, book XXXV, chapter 20. God also completed his works in six days because six is perfect and most holy. Thus, even if these things did not exist, the number would still be perfect; but unless it itself were perfect, these things would not have been made perfect according to it.

Hugh of Saint Victor seems to have understood this when writing *On the Sacraments*:

> “Six, because it consists of its parts, is a sign of perfection; and therefore God wished to complete his works in six days, so that he might show that in the things he had made he had placed nothing superfluous and left nothing imperfect.”

Saint Augustine confirms this axiom in *On the Trinity*, book IV, and in *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book IV:

> “The perfection of six is commended to us by the sacred Scriptures chiefly in this: that God completed his works in six days and on the sixth day made man in his own image and likeness.”

Just as nothing is lacking from what is perfect, so nothing can be added to the order of things, as though it were deficient, or taken away, as though it were excessive—not by an externally imposed limit, but because the very sequence of things prescribes its own boundaries. It was as though Scripture had said that, by that sixfold number, no better order or arrangement of created things could be assigned or exist. Hence, on the sixth day, the prophetic word adds:

> “God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good; and there was evening and morning, the sixth day.”

Therefore, when you hear that the world was constructed in six days, understand not merely the number of days but the perfection of the universe, which is signified by the perfect number six. Thus, when God’s work had reached this complete number, the scribe of the divine word said:

> “The heavens and the earth were finished, and all their array.”

And so, writes Petrus Bungus in *On the Mysteries of Numbers*, folio 269:

> “Orpheus, prince of the Mystae, commands hymns to be brought to an end in the sixth generation,”

when he says:

> “In the sixth age, make an end of your song.”

Nothing further can be sung concerning created things, since their perfection is wholly completed there.

Having recognized the perfection of this number, let us turn to sacred mysteries. The tabernacle was six cubits on each side. For six days the glory of the Lord descended upon Mount Sinai, covering it with a cloud; this signifies the time of the present life. The six wings of the cherubim demonstrate the time of the age. The sixth month was that in which the word of the Lord came by the hand of the prophet Haggai. The six tribulations in Job signify the sufferings of this life. For six years the Hebrew servant served his master. For six years the land was to be sown. For six days it was lawful to work. For six days manna was to be gathered, and on the sixth day twice as much. There are many other examples devised by Bungus. So much for this number.

(2) **In the city of Astigi.** A colony in the time of the Romans, called Julia Firma after the time of Julius Caesar, Astigi had a judicial assembly. Its ancient name, Astigi, which is by no means Roman in sound, establishes its great antiquity. It is watered by the Singilis River, which after the Baetis is the larger river of all Baetica. The city and river retain their ancient names, though somewhat altered: they are now called Écija and Genil. The territory of the city, though otherwise not large, enriches its inhabitants greatly through its fertility. It is distinguished by the abundance of its oil. Gardens, overflowing with every kind of fruit, make the whole district useful and exceedingly pleasant. It formerly had a bishop, as is evident from the councils of Toledo and Hispania. It is thirty-two miles from Córdoba and somewhat more from Seville. Pliny, Pomponius Mela, and Ptolemy, among others, mention it.

(3) **And Saint Walabonsus.** He was the brother of the martyr Mary, who suffered together with Flora, as will appear in chapter 8.

(4) **And of Ilipa.** Although *Ilipa* or *Ilipula*—for the authorities vary—is the true name of the city, from which *Ilipensis* and *Ilipulensis* are derived, I nevertheless saw a very ancient coin on which the inscription *mun. elepla* appeared. There were two towns called Ilipula, as is clear from Pliny, Strabo, and Livy: one in Lusitania and the other in Baetica. I believe that the latter is meant here. We have proved at length, in the antiquities of Hispania appended to our chronicle, that it was situated where we now see the fairly modest town called Peñaflor, approximately midway between Córdoba and Seville. Whoever wishes may consult that work; this place requires no more here.

(5) **In the village of Cuteclara.** This small town and the monastery in it are described more fully in chapter 8.[^c0088-3]

(6) **From the village of Froniano.** This village too will be mentioned later, in chapter 8, with fuller explanation.

(7) **Of Saint Zoilus.** A separate occasion for speaking about this saint will arise in the letter of the holy Eulogius to the bishop of Pamplona.

(8) **The Armilata River.** With its name altered, it is now called the Almodóvar; with the Arabic word *Guad*, meaning “river,” added at the beginning according to the custom of the Saracens, its full name becomes Guadalquivir—[OCR uncertain]. This river, descending from the mountains, enters the Baetis about twelve miles above Córdoba. The thirty or more miles that the holy Eulogius mentions plainly show that this monastery was situated not far above the notable Franciscan monastery that we now see and venerate, which bears the name of Saint Francis of Monte. It is located more than twenty-four miles from our city, on an elevated site toward the north, beside the bank of this river.

(9) **Of Saint Christopher.** Almost opposite the city, an extremely ancient church of Saint Julian can now be seen. It may have changed its name. Certainly no traces of any other church appear.

(10) **Of whom we spoke above.** It is perfectly clear from this that the Jeremiah mentioned here is the same one who was said above, in chapter 2, to have founded the monastery of Tabanos. He is also mentioned in Book I and in Book III, chapter 11.

(11) **Namely, on the seventh day before the Ides.** It is clear how fervently the saints of Córdoba then burned with love of martyrdom, since they suffered so frequently. Only two days—a Saturday and a Sunday—intervened between Sanctius and these six martyrs. Here the eighth day of June is indicated. But in Book I it is reported that their bodies were burned on the day before the Ides of June, the sixth day after their martyrdom, and that their ashes were thrown into the river. The martyrdom of these six saints is found in Usuard, but it is placed on the preceding day. It is also found in the eleventh book, final chapter, of Equilinus.

**CHAPTER V**

(1) **From the town of Pax.** The colony of Pax Julia in Lusitania, which according to Pliny was also distinguished by a judicial assembly, was reduced by the devastation of the Arabs who occupied Spain to the form of the small town we now see. It belongs to the kingdom of Portugal and is now called Beja. Andreas Resende, writing to Vasæus, as he is always accustomed to do, has discussed its name, location, and antiquity with great distinction. Rasis describes the destruction of the city.

(2) **On the seventeenth day before the Kalends.** This is the sixteenth day of July, which in that year fell on a Thursday, as anyone may already determine from what precedes. More than forty days had passed without a martyrdom.

**CHAPTER VI**

(1) **Which belonged to the body.** The matter of the basilica of Saint Zoilus will be discussed when we write about the martyr himself in the letter to the bishop of Pamplona.

(2) **In that underground cave.** It was the custom of the Moors to have underground caves excavated in the form of a rather spacious well, as prison cells for confining servants at night and keeping criminals in custody. Such places are seen throughout Baetica, especially in fortresses. We still call them *mazmorras*, the proper word of that people. In the courtyard of Córdoba’s principal temple, two such wells are still shown today, and everyone asserts that they were constructed by the Moors for use as prisons of this kind. I, however, would judge that they were made to contain and preserve for a longer time the water of the river. For since the Arabs were superstitious worshipers of their temples, they would certainly have believed that prisoners, captives, and their filth and stench would contaminate them. I believe that this underground prison was in the fortress, or somewhere nearby.

The practice came from the Greeks and Romans, who had underground prisons of this kind and called them by the customary term *putealia*. We have already spoken in its proper place of the *puteal* that the Romans had at Córdoba. The holy Eulogius also mentions elsewhere the difference between the two kinds of prison.[^c0088-4]

## In Book II of the *Memorial*

There are other traces of ancient remembrance, and there they are honored as natives and indigenous inhabitants with the highest veneration of the whole region. I can affirm this as wholly established and beyond doubt. Those names—*Fiebetanum* or *Urbevetanum*, and *Castro Bigeti*—which are read in our breviaries seem to have arisen through corruption from *Castro veteri* (“the old castle”). What town Bosca was, I cannot explain. In an old exemplar it was *Osca*, not *Bosca*; I restored the more customary name. For I do not believe that the holy virgins were transferred to the very distant Osca in Aragon.

> That this was so in the old exemplar fully persuaded us to put *Osca*, not *Bosca*, in the text—a correction Morales made rather unsuccessfully. For, besides the ancient exemplar of Eulogius which, by Morales’s own admission, reports that these virgins suffered at Osca, all the martyrologists who mention them, with Usuard leading the way and Baronius bringing up the rear, confirm the same. As to where this Osca was situated, authors differ, and the dispute remains undecided. Francisco Diego de Aínsa y Iriarte argues in his history, Book II, chapters 34 and 35, for the well-known Osca of Aragon; the very learned Emmanuel Risco rather cautiously supports him (*Hispania Sacra*, vol. XXXIII, treatise 69, chapter 19, no. 7). The RR. Fr. Mohedani, *Historia Literaria*, vol. V, Book IX, §2, no. 16, note 1, do not hesitate to maintain that the Osca mentioned by Pliny was near the city of Tucci (now Martos) in the kingdom of Jaén; they leave others to examine whether this was Eulogius’s Osca. In so doubtful a matter, we reject Morales’s opinion that assigns the holy virgins to the Rucones, but do not dare decide the controversy between the Baetican and Aragonese locations.

### (4) Nunilo and Alodia

The old text had *Elodia*. We substituted *Alodia*, following the widespread custom of the many churches throughout Spain that celebrate the feast of these holy martyrs and read their history at Matins.

### (5) Brought up by their aunt

The lessons read at Matins throughout Spain, and the manuscripts called sanctoralia, give a very different account. They say that a certain close relative, himself an orphan, undertook their care; and since he was held in the error of Islam and could not turn the holy virgins away from the faith of Christ, they were betrayed by him and brought before the governor.

### (6) They fell beneath the sword

The lessons in the breviaries recount in detail many further matters, all of them exceedingly devout, concerning the slaughter and burial of the holy women. They are presented at greater length especially in the manuscripts called sanctoralia. We shall therefore append them, since they are most worthy of knowing and confirm the history of these virgins, which had not fully come down to Saint Eulogius.

> Then the king ordered the executioner, saying: “Strike with the sword and cut off their heads.” The executioner asked the king a third time whether he should strike. When he had heard for the third time that he should strike, he said to the elder: “Stretch out your neck.”
>
> Then Saint Nunilo said to her younger sister: “See, sister, that you do not act otherwise than I am about to act.” Saint Alodia replied to her: “Do not doubt, sister, that I shall do otherwise.”
>
> Immediately Saint Nunilo, advancing with a joyful spirit, seized her hair, bound it around her head, and said to the executioner: “Strike quickly.” He raised the sword high and brought it down upon her—not upon the middle of her neck, but upon her jaw. Thus he did not completely sever her head. When her body fell to the ground, a little of her thigh was exposed. Seeing this, her sister hurriedly covered it by drawing down her garment.
>
> When this had been done, the multitude marveled. The faithful rejoiced; the unbelievers wasted away. The wicked king said to the executioner: “Leave her for now; do not strike her.” Then he said to Saint Alodia: “What benefit will it be to you if you die? Consent to us, and you will live among us with great honor.”
>
> The martyr replied: “I will not consent. Hurry; strike me, so that I may not go alone.” And, raising her eyes, she saw her sister’s soul in the form of a dove, surrounded by angels, and said: “Wait for me, sister; wait for me a little.”
>
> O wondrous power of the Most High! The girl who could not avoid the sword flashing not far away did not fear when it descended upon her own neck. Instead, seizing the linen cloth in which she was dressed, she tied it around herself in the form of a cross, and with her hair wiped her face. Then, kneeling upon her sister’s body, she offered herself to the executioner, who severed her head with a single blow.
>
> Thus, on the same day and at the same hour, the martyrs completed their martyrdom in peace, on Thursday, the twelfth day before the Kalends of November.

We transcribed this from a very ancient sanctorale codex, written in Gothic letters on parchment more than six hundred years ago. It belonged to the renowned Benedictine monastery of Saint Peter of Cardeña and is now preserved in the royal monastery of Saint Lawrence of the Hieronymites.

Its title stated that the holy virgins had suffered under the prefect Zumahil, but neither an era nor a year was given. Since the twenty-first day of October is marked there, and it is additionally stated that in that year it fell on a Thursday, our customary astronomical computation establishes that in the year of the Lord 840 the holy virgins were crowned in confession of Christ. For that year was the ninth after thirty complete revolutions of the solar cycle, in the thirty-first cycle. It was a leap year and had the dominical letters D C; and, since the reckoning began in October, the twenty-first day fell on a Thursday.

### (7) The eleventh day before the Kalends

Since Saint Eulogius, as we have shown, was mistaken about the year, the day also cannot be correctly assigned on that basis. In Usuard’s martyrology, the feast of these holy virgins occupies the twenty-second day of October, and this is also preserved in our breviaries; but royal diplomas, as will soon appear, establish the twenty-first day. Nearly all the churches of Spain celebrate the feast of these virgins together. Such was the excellence and illustrious renown of their martyrdom.

### (8) Whose bodies

Their bodies were later taken from this place and transferred to the monastery of Saint Savior at Leire, which, as we said, is not very far away. Although the transfer is sufficiently attested by that one diploma of King Íñigo Arista which we cited above, I wish to add two others that we obtained, among many more, copied from the same monastery of Leire. One of them will establish that the holy virgins died on 21 October, not on the 22nd.

> In the year 1060, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, Sancho, the great king of Navarre, Castile, and Aragon, makes a donation, for the strengthening of the Order of Saint Benedict, to his lord and master Sancho the bishop and to the monastery of Leire, founded in honor of Saint Savior, which contains the bodies of the virgins and martyrs of Christ, Nunilo and Alodia, together with innumerable relics of the saints.
>
> For, considering that he had always triumphed over his enemies and had subjected all those around him to himself; and seeing also that, after the invasion of the Moors, laymen and secular persons had possessed the churches throughout Spain, he resolved to hand them over to ecclesiastical men. And hearing that the teaching of blessed Benedict was shining everywhere, he considered how he might transplant it into his own regions. He therefore sent to the monastery of Cluny and summoned from there Abbot Paternus together with a band of monks, whom he established in the monastery of Saint John the Baptist.
>
> Now the aforesaid King Sancho commends and grants, with devout mind, to the aforesaid lord and master, Sancho the bishop, the aforesaid monastery of Leire, together with the possessions that earlier kings had given it, and others, insofar as he may establish there an order of monks where the bodies of the king’s parents may rest.

The charter was executed as above in the presence of many who had come to worship God and celebrate the feast of the holy martyrs in the aforesaid monastery, while the most illustrious king Sancho reigned in Castile, Pamplona, Álava, Aragon, Sobrarbe, Ribagorza, all Gascony, and Leire. Witnesses:

> “Queen Eximena, mother of the king;
>
> “Queen Doña Munia Mayor García;
>
> “Ramiro Gundissalvus;
>
> “Bernard Mattus, bishop of Aragon;
>
> “Sancho, abbot of Leire and bishop of Pamplona;
>
> “Paternus, abbot of Saint John;
>
> “Eneco, abbot of Oña;
>
> “Lord Exemeno Garcés;
>
> “Lord García López; Fortunio Sanz; Acenar Fortunionis; Fortunio Ossuaz; García Fortunionis; and Lope Sanz.”

In the year 1032 the same king granted a diploma of this kind to the same monastery.

> We print “Era 1070, the seventh day before the Kalends of January, Tuesday,” correcting an error of the Complutensian printer, whose edition reads “Era 1077,” etc.; the error passed from there into the Frankfurt edition. Nor was it difficult to detect, since immediately beforehand Morales himself wrote that this diploma was granted in 1032, which he also noted in the margin. Had Gabriel Gossart noticed this, he would doubtless have refrained from criticizing Ambrosius. In his notes on the Council of Pano, held at the monastery of Saint John of the Rock in Aragon, Gossart considers Ambrosius mistaken and conjectures that the reading should be era 1047, or the year 1029, when Sancho the Great was still reigning in Aragon. Yet this attempt fails: in the year designated by Morales, 1032, Sancho was reigning and 26 December, the date assigned, fell on a Tuesday. Where Manctius, bishop of Aragon, is to be read, whereas the privilege has Martinus, we gladly agree with him and correct the text accordingly. For, adducing the weightiest evidence, he proves that at that time there was no bishop of Aragon named Martinus, nor one named Sanctus, although both names are read in certain copies of this privilege.

> “In the year 1070, on the seventh day before the Kalends of January, on Tuesday. I, Sancho, by the grace of God king, give to you, lord and most holy prelate, Lord Sancho, and to the entire college of monks of the monastery of Leire, under the church of Saint Savior, where are the bodies of the most blessed virgins and martyrs Nunilo and Alodia, as well as the relics of the apostles and martyrs that are deposited there:
>
> “I give you, I say, in the valley of Oteiza, near the village called Portiella, the monastery called Saint John, with its boundaries; and in Pamplona the parish of Saint Cecilia; and in the valley of Garonio the monastery called Zeyazahassa.
>
> “I, King Sancho, most serene, reigning in Pamplona and Aragon, in Sobrarbe, Ribagorza, all Gascony, and the whole of Castile and León, or Astorga, confirm.
>
> “Munia Mayor, queen, confirm. Ramiro, the king’s son, confirm. García, his brother, confirm. Gundissalvus, his brother, confirms. Fernando, his brother, confirms.
>
> “Manctius, bishop of Aragon, confirms. Sancho, bishop of Pamplona. Arnolfus, bishop of Ribagorza. Munio, bishop of Álava. Julian, bishop of Castile. Pontius, bishop of Oviedo.
>
> “Fortunio Sancii, governor of Caparroso. Fortunio Sancii, governor of Falces. Acenarius Fortunionis, governor of Ugarte. García Fortunionis, governor of Funes. Lope Eneconis, governor of Arruesta. Fortunio Uxuaz, of Cantabria. Don Pedro, governing Nájera under the authority of the king.
>
> “I, Valassius Fenestella, wrote this out from the king’s palace, and I received as payment for this writing five *modii* of wheat.
>
> “I, Queen Eximena Vetula, servant of God, residing at Reperus, confirm.”

A few years after the martyrdom of these holy virgins, a queen of Spain was named Nunilo. Since this is not recorded in our histories, I see it attested at Oviedo in the Holy Chamber, of which we have already spoken. There, among the ancient gifts of our kings, is a chest two feet long, assembled and fashioned from precious panels of agate stone, enclosed with gold, and rich with gems on every side.

On its silver bottom it bears the following inscription, which I myself copied with the utmost fidelity:

> “Peacefully received, this remains in honor of God,  
> which the servants of Christ Fruela and Nunilo offer,  
> surnamed Scemena.  
>
> This work was completed and granted to the Savior  
> at Oviedo.  
>
> Whoever should presume to remove these gifts of ours,  
> may he himself perish by divine thunderbolt.  
>
> It was made in the era 949.”

There can be no doubt that this gift belonged to King Fruela II. Apart from its wealth, which is plainly royal, many other things clearly demonstrate this.

Vasseus wrote that the bodies of these holy virgins were later transferred from here to Bologna. But no one now doubts that they are still preserved in the same monastery of Saint Savior at Leire.

### Chapter IX

#### (1) Qua Faustus

We have already spoken of the illustrious city of Toledo.[^c0089-1] The memory of these three sacred martyrs of Córdoba has been consecrated throughout all the churches of Spain by a most solemn feast, and their abundant history is repeated in the lessons at Matins. All the martyrologies, and every writer who has written about the saints, make notable mention of them; but the feast day varies in some places. In some it is marked as 28 September; elsewhere as 13 October. Everywhere they are said to have been burned. It must be carefully noted that the ashes of these holy martyrs were preserved at Córdoba down to the time of Saint Eulogius.

#### (2) The Campania of Córdoba

The name *Campania* was formerly applied by the Romans in particular to that region of Italy which contained Naples, Capua, and other neighboring cities; because it was entirely open country and level, it was so called. Otherwise, *Campania* may be used in the same way for any similar region. We Spaniards have certainly transferred the name to every level plain. Thus the plain among the Vaccaei, which stretches over a long expanse and is now called *Campos*, was formerly called *Campi Crothorum*, as Rodrigo of Toledo reports. I find it called *Campania* in the Compostellan History, written four hundred years ago.[^c0089-2] Yet it seems more likely that the plain of Córdoba was called *Campania* in particular, since Strabo so highly praised its fertility. The name survives, somewhat altered, in our use of *Campiña*.

#### (3) In the era 890

In this place, in an ancient codex, a certain sign and an unusual combination of letters were used to indicate the number ninety. They were wholly unknown to us Spaniards, so that it was evident that they were Gothic. The sign was as follows: a larger X.

The ordinary sign of the number fifty was then placed beside it. An X was added, but a small second stroke was attached above it to the upper part of the apex, so that the ordinary sign for forty, XL, was completed; from the signs for fifty and forty together, the full number ninety was formed.

I had previously observed this sign, joined in that manner, in four ancient codices of the sacred councils preserved by the Holy Church of Toledo and by the royal monastery of Saint Lawrence of the Order of Saint Jerome, near the town called the Escorial, and I had clearly determined what it was. All this had to be demonstrated here point by point, so that if anyone came upon an ancient codex of Saint Eulogius, he would not be confused or uncertain, but would immediately recognize the manifest truth and see all that follows properly arranged.[^c0089-3]

### Chapter X

#### (1) Furthermore, there was

From a sufficiently humble beginning, Saint Eulogius later rises to a more elevated style of speech, in order, in accordance with Horace’s precept, to bring splendor out of smoke. He wished to continue the history of these martyrs more fully in a grander style and to express in words the ardor of a truly Christian spirit yearning for martyrdom. Pious readers will notice this in many places, not without a devout stirring of the soul.

It appears that Brother Laurentius Surius, the Carthusian, came upon a fragment of Saint Eulogius. For in the fourth volume of his *Approved Histories of the Saints* he inserted this entire chapter with the author’s name. There Natalia is always named, not Sabigotho, as the wife of Aurelius. Surius, however, in his customary manner, also polished the diction here and the style of the holy martyr.

This should be noted so that no one will be surprised that the thread of that discourse differs so greatly from what we have preserved here with the utmost scrupulousness, changing nothing at all, exactly as it stood in the exemplar. Wherever different readings are reported in Surius, we have noted them here in their proper places.[^c0089-4]

#### (2) So that the straw formed part of the burden

He obscurely indicates that the weight of the chains had overturned and thrown down the donkey’s panniers, so that they hung down toward its tail; for the legs of the man riding the donkey seem to have been inclined backward.

In Laurentius Surius, this is reported quite differently, and shortly afterward heavenly visions in a dream are appended.[^c0089-5] I see nothing missing from our exemplar that would lead me to think these additions were once made by someone else. Later, the names of Aurelius’s wife are also given as Felicitas and Maria. What Eulogius deliberately continues concerning Alvaro is missing, although more is related in the punishment of Sabigotho.

#### (3) Most serene teacher

We have explained with what modesty Eulogius calls Alvaro, who had been his fellow student, his teacher; and we have demonstrated that the title “most serene” was also added in order to establish Alvaro’s nobility.

#### (4) The monastery of Saint Sabbas

This monastery is celebrated in books concerning the Lives of the Holy Fathers; and Saint Sabbas himself is famous wherever the holy inhabitants of the desert are discussed.

#### (5) A brief account of his martyrdom

By using this expression, Pliny and Suetonius teach that any work, and especially a historical work, written summarily and in abbreviated form was customarily called a *breviarium*.

#### (6) With their faces uncovered

It is certainly apparent that, according to the teaching of the Apostle Paul, it was then a Christian custom for women to veil their heads not only in church but also while traveling to church. Christian women could also have walked with covered heads for the sake of modesty and so that they would not be assaulted by the Saracens during that wretched period of captivity.

#### (7) Having kissed his hands

Although he was not a priest, Eulogius nevertheless sought, from the future martyr, as it were a priestly blessing, out of reverence. Unless one believes that the modern custom had already begun by which we Spaniards set about kissing hands, both in word and deed.

#### (8) The sixth day before the Kalends

It is evident in many places that Ado, the archbishop, had read these books of Saint Eulogius, especially in his account of these martyrs. Although in abbreviated form, he nevertheless reported all the more important details that Eulogius records here. Bishop Equilinus, however, names Natalia in this place, not Sabigotho.

Neither Ado nor Surius’s fragment correctly recorded the day or month, since they assigned 27 August to these martyrs.

#### (9) At the monastery of Pilemelaria

Since a fuller mention of this monastery will occur again, we shall then discuss its location and whatever else ought to be said about it. That will be in the eleventh chapter of Book III. In Surius, Aurelius is said to have reported that he was to be buried there.[^c0089-6]

#### (10) At the martyr Genesius

This is a metonymy, like that of Horace:

> “Whatever writings Apollo has received in the Palatine.”

Christians frequently use many expressions of this kind.

#### (11) They occupy Sabigotho

This passage was mutilated in the old codex, and a complete line and a half were left blank so that it might perhaps be supplied at some time. In Surius there is not even a mention of the chapters.

### Chapter XI

#### (1) Our fellow tribesman

Both here and above, Eulogius uses this expression to indicate plainly only proximity of residence.[^c0089-7]

#### (2) Rajona

Although I have investigated it, I find nothing to say here. I shall likewise pass over in silence the place called Fraga and the village of Lejulense, which are mentioned shortly afterward.

#### (3) Égert

The Gothic period had corrupted the name of this city, whereas the Romans had used *Iliberi*.

[^c0089-1]: *Scholia on the Life of Eulogius*, no. 20.

[^c0089-2]: Book I, chapters 10, 20, and 30, and Book II, chapter 33, in *Hispania Sacra*, vol. XX.

[^c0089-3]: We are indeed astonished that Morales, who in this very place finally admits that he understood the force of this sign X, which occurs so frequently in Gothic manuscripts, did not notice that in his editions of the *Chronicles* this information could easily have corrected many later errors that he otherwise left in great confusion. For when he took this sign, wherever it occurred, as ten rather than forty, as it should have been taken, he inadvertently and unknowingly fell into various chronological errors, which it would be too lengthy to indicate here.

[^c0089-4]: The celestial-vision narrative mentioned by Morales may be seen below the text in our note. We too believe that it is an addition. But since we have never been able to persuade ourselves that Surius invented it according to his own practice, and instead think that he found it in some codex, we decided to transcribe it.

[^c0089-5]: Since we are equally convinced that this other addition in Surius is not his own fabrication, but rather that he obtained it from some codex, we set it before you: “The same martyr of Christ, Aurelius, had foretold that after his death he would be carried to that place and buried there. For, having come there for the sake of prayer about three days before he was arrested, he said to one of the women consecrated to God who were enclosed there: ‘Lord Aurelius, behold, you must now proceed to martyrdom. What, then, will you give me?’ And he said: ‘I have nothing that I can give you now; nevertheless, afterward I shall give you myself, if the Lord permits.’ And it came to pass that, having died to the world, he fulfilled what he had promised, now living with Christ, through the favor of him who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God for ages of ages. Amen.”

[^c0089-6]: Correctly, Petrus Dolmans assigns the date 20 August. Since the same expression in chapter 6 of this book signifies blood relationship, I do not see why it should be transferred here to another meaning. See Schott’s annotation in that chapter.

[^c0089-7]: Rather “the eleventh,” as in Eulogius; this agrees with Thursday and with the letter D of the year 851.
