## Scholia of Ambrosius Morales

… the times, when the Romans had brought forth Iliberis. From that corruption the Arabs later introduced a greater alteration, calling it *Elbtriam*, from which we eventually pronounce it *Elvira*. This city was not far from the illustrious city of Granada, on the hill now called Mount Elvira; the city gate leading there is also called the Gate of Elvira.

It is worth noting that it seems very probable that in the ancient language of the Spaniards *Iliberri* signified a town. Hence so many towns, especially in Baetica, retained names beginning with that element: *Ilurgi, Iliberri, Ilipula, Ilipa*, and others of this kind. We shall discuss this in our *Antiquities of Spain*.

### Chapter XII

#### (1) The seventeenth day before the Kalends

This is 15 September, which is clearly marked in the old exemplar. Usuard, the breviary of Córdoba, Ado, and Equilinus differ by a few days. In Ado and Equilinus one reads *Emilianus*, not *Emila*. Eulogius correctly wrote that these two martyrs were crowned not long after Christopher and Leovigild.

### Chapter XIII

#### (1) While he was still …

Here too he indicates a short interval of time; indeed, not a single day intervened.

#### (2) That shrine

He means this Cordoban temple of Arabic construction, which still survives today and holds the dignity of the greater church. Its size, the multitude of its columns, the excellence of its marble, the delicacy of its workmanship, and many other features offer spectators both admiration and, indeed, astonishment. It had already been built by King Abd al-Rahman II and his son Hisham. The authorities are Rasis and Rodrigo of Toledo, historians of the Arabs.

### Chapter XIV

#### (1) Then, undoubtedly, from that time onward

This either means that thereafter no one, whether Christian or Saracen, dared fail to report to the judges anything he heard from a false prophet cursing Muhammad; or that previously the Saracens had permitted anyone who heard a Christian uttering such a curse to kill him immediately and with impunity, without waiting for a public condemnation.

#### (2) What to some

Sacred theologians teach in this manner that martyrdom is a gift of God, granted by God particularly to some persons. It must be observed, however, that this persecution of the churches in Spain was different from the persecution at Córdoba in which Saint Eulogius was arrested. The chronology makes this entirely clear. We examined the matter more carefully in the first chapter of Book I.

### Chapter XV

#### (1) We too are witnesses

Saint Eulogius brought forward this most serious accusation as a kind of prelude to his future martyrdom: he was not to be killed merely by a sudden stroke of the sword, but his executioners were to be Christians themselves, his own brothers, who would lacerate him daily with abuse.

#### (2) At the present council of the bishops

In such a great calamity and under such a terrible persecution of the Church, the prelates had assembled to consider, if they could, some remedy by which they might provide assistance. The king too, as soon becomes clear, had ordered the metropolitans to assemble from every direction.

This was therefore what is called a national council—unless one prefers to call it a council assembled by such an authority a mere assembly.

We shall speak of this matter later, in Book III, chapter 4.

#### (3) That martyrdom had been prohibited

What follows to the end of the period contains the decree issued by the council, though in somewhat obscure form. The bishops’ plan at the council was to issue and prescribe what might appear acceptable to the king and the nobles at a superficial glance, so that they might in this way assist the Church, which was suffering and endangered.

But because they feared asserting anything that might offend the majesty of the supreme God or the Christian religion, they adjusted the wording of the decree and deliberately fashioned it so that, if anyone examined it closely, it would assert nothing impious. This is what Saint Eulogius continues to explain.

Everything in the exemplar was much more obscure, and the passages were clarified only with great labor, using also the judgment and refinement of the wisest men. They were rendered somewhat clearer by the addition of one or two words.

#### (4) Blameless

That is, “entirely without guilt.” Saint Eulogius already states his own judgment here. He also seems to be referring to this very decree, which had been circulated in booklets and written sheets, near the end of Book I.

Nevertheless, it is clear that at the beginning of this book, in chapter 1, he writes about another and different disturbance among the Saracens, as the words of the saint himself plainly declare both there and here, as well as at the beginning of chapter 7.

#### (5) Or rather, unless by legitimate satisfaction

He says this: it was certainly necessary to satisfy the weak, so that they would not be scandalized by the decree if they happened to understand it to mean only what the council intended the Saracens to understand. It was therefore necessary to satisfy them—those weak and insignificant persons, I mean—both by applying a legitimate interpretation to them and for their sake, and by explaining the reasons that had compelled the decree to be framed in that manner.

### Chapter XVI

#### (1) The bishop again

I understand him to mean the bishop of Córdoba, whom he nowhere identifies by his proper name. It appears, however, that this same prelate had previously been thrown into chains during the revolt of Reccared, as I suppose.

#### (2) Hanging from the stakes

It is necessary to understand the four martyrs Emilas and Hieremias, Rogellus and Servus Dei, who suffered last. For the others, as is clear from what precedes, were no longer alive: some had been burned and others buried. It was appropriate to note this here in preparation for the investigation of the subsequent period.

#### (3) But we

It is evident from this that Saint Eulogius wrote this second book at the very time when Muhammad began to reign. For the events that he pursued in the third book had not yet occurred. The additional explanation supplied here demonstrates this even more fully; he says that he was still concealed when he wrote.

### In the Oration

It was a custom inherited from the time of the Goths that Spanish writers should begin or end their works with a prayer poured out to God. This is evident in Saint Ildefonsus’s work *On the Praise of the Most Holy Virgin Mary’s Virginity* and in the books of Saint Julian, archbishop of Toledo.

## In Book III

### Chapter IV

#### (1) And because, from every side …

Rasis writes that Omar, son of Hacan, rebelled against this Muhammad, the king, and that he himself was killed in battle by the king’s army. Thereafter, according to the same authority, he lived peacefully in the kingdom.

Rodrigo writes in his history of the Arabs that the people of Toledo rose up against the king. The Toledans were defeated and destroyed in a great slaughter together with King Ordonio, who had come to their aid. I would suppose that Omar was the leader of the Toledans.

#### (2) Defeated and put to flight

I would be more inclined to believe Saint Eulogius than Rasis, who reports that everything everywhere happened peacefully and prosperously for him. Yet although his army may have been routed in the first battle, he could afterward have prevailed himself and subdued the rebels.

### Chapter VII

#### (1) From the city of Acci

This city is now called Guadix in the kingdom of Granada. It is not the place here to set out the reasons and evidence for this, which are discussed in the *Antiquities of Spain*.

## IN BOOK III OF THE *MEMORIAL*

…we assembled [these materials] in order to prove that it is the same city as Guadix and the Accitana, formerly a Roman colony.

**(2) “At Tabanense.”** There has already been frequent mention above of this monastery and likewise of the other monastery of Saint Saviour. He also referred earlier to Pinna Mellaria; but there will still be an occasion to speak of it in chapter eleven.

**(3) “The most valiant athlete.”** Here Eulogius omitted the day and the year. From Usuard, Ado, and Equilinus, it was the Ides of June—that is, the thirteenth of that month. Since Anastasius suffered on the following day, as is written in the next chapter, it is also clear from Eulogius that Saint Fandila was put to death on 13 June.

### CHAPTER VIII

**(1) “Whom he followed on the next day.”** That “the next day” means the following day, with no intervening day—that is, the day after—appears from the day of Saint Fandila’s execution.

**(2) “He had acted in the *cenibus*.”** The passage, as far as I can understand it, is corrupt; for I find no Latin word *cenibus* that conveys any meaning, nor does any way of emending it occur to me. Yet this is plainly how it was written in the old manuscript, unless perhaps one should read *scenibus*, with *s*, and understand “tents”; from these the Arabs’ *Scenitae* are also named.

**(3) “By nation a Getulian.”** Getulia is a region of Africa. Hence arose the opinion that this saint was born from the stock of the Saracens. He could certainly have been born of Christian parents. For there were Christians in Africa, although it had been occupied by the Saracens, just as there were Mozarabs in Spain.

**(4) “At the ninth hour.”** This is the Roman reckoning, also used in the sacred Gospels. Several churches of Spain celebrate the feast of this holy martyr, and in their readings they relate the whole account of the virgin Digna’s dream in almost the same words.

From this it is clear that whoever arranged a history for that feast had read the books of Saint Eulogius. We too wrote something in the book concerning the holy martyrs Justus and Pastor, though at that time we had not yet seen the writings of Saint Eulogius.

**“Do not call me Digna.”** True humility, cast down through knowledge of oneself, is nevertheless lifted up to heaven through the knowledge of God. There are many things capable of giving us a perfect knowledge of ourselves. Yet there is one thing that often leads me precisely to that knowledge. I never offer myself for complete self-knowledge; I cannot endure looking within myself on every side and from every perspective. When, miserably deceiving myself, I almost rejoice at having left something undiscovered, this finally shows me what sort of person I am. This wretched shame at looking upon myself makes me fully visible to myself.

Long ago, while lamenting our misery, we expressed this in an epigram:

> Whenever I wish to search myself with inward light  
> and, examining my soul, to behold it clearly,  
> my conscious mind fears what sort of self it will reveal  
> and conceals from me a part of myself.  
>   
> Yet when it thought it had hidden me from myself by deception—  
> miserable that I am!—then I see myself more fully.

For the common purpose of stirring the mind to self-reflection, we also once composed a tetrastich, based on the Bridegroom’s exhortation in the *Song of Songs*: “Unless you know yourself, O fairest among women, go out after the footsteps of your flocks; feed your young goats” (*Song* 1).

> Unless you know yourself, O fairest of the things  
> which God created beautiful throughout the whole world,  
> the desire that lifts you toward the stars  
> will be troubled by the shameful love of earthly things.

No one can fail to see how superfluous all that Morales inserts here concerning self-knowledge is for the purpose of illuminating Eulogius.

The author himself candidly corrected this passage in *Chronicle*, book XIV, chapter 23: “Although in the scholia on Saint Eulogius I said that the holy body which was at Carrión was that of Saint Felix of Alcalá, it is instead the body of this other Saint Felix, companion of the others”—that is, of Felix, who was the companion of Aurelius.

### CHAPTER IX

**(1) “Their corpses.”** In the monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict at Saint Zoylus, near the noble town of Carrión, the body of Saint Felix of Complutum is preserved in a silver reliquary and venerated with great devotion. It was transferred there together with the body of Saint Zoylus, as is related in the ancient records of the monastery, which I read there myself.

Yet from these records we see that his corpse was scattered through fire and water. Pious Christian diligence, however, may have drawn from the river bones that had not been entirely consumed by the fire. This would certainly have been easy, since, dried by the fire, they would have floated.

### CHAPTER X

**(1) “With the greatest reverence.”** Understand that the holy martyr, with the utmost dignity and composed firmness of countenance, went toward martyrdom and drew after her the attendants and executioners. But what reverence could there have been in them?

**(2) “Setting them up in the forum.”** It is evident from this that the forum stood before the gates of the palace, so that the open space extended before the fortress, enclosed by the walls of the citadel, yet spread out with a view toward the river before one entered the citadel itself.

Alternatively, perhaps the forum was the vacant ground lying between the tower called the Tower of the Lions and the episcopal house. But the former explanation is closer to the truth.

**(3) “Not before herself.”** Since she understood that it was the greatest benefit to die for the faith of Christ, she wished to show favor even to the executioner, although he did not deserve it, by giving him something. Eulogius hints at this, but does not explain what she gave him.

**(4) “Of Saint Eulalia.”** Spain formerly had two martyrs of this name: one at Emerita and the other at Barcelona. We must not listen to those who wished to make one saint out of the two. We argued this matter at length in our history. Yet Eulogius did not indicate which of the two possessed the basilica; nor do I have anything to say about the little town of Fragellas.

On the two Eulalias, consult Alexander Lesleus, pp. 481 and 566, in the notes to the *Mozarabic Missal*, Rome, 1755; the distinguished Francis Pérez Bayer, in the *Historical Dissertation for Saints Lawrence and Damasus*, pp. 96, 110, 136 and following; and the frequently cited Henry Flórez, volume XIII, treatise 41, chapter 12, and volume XXIX, chapter 8.

**(5) “But you, most sacred one.”** Just as Saint Eulogius had written the life and death of this holy martyr more fully and also more eloquently, so here I wished to address her at the end with a devout prayer.

In both respects she was a most worthy virgin. For, since her life was full of outstanding examples of holiness and her steadfastness in death was admirable—things that deserved a fuller historical account and the splendor of a more excellent style—so, too, having attained great dignity in heaven, she could bring a more efficacious and greater patronage to her own people before God, and therefore ought eagerly to be entreated.

Indeed, this distinction of hers in life and death, and this worthy invocation of her, for which Eulogius had already laid the foundation, make us believe that this was our Cordoban Columba, not the other Columba of Sens, whom all Spain celebrates everywhere with such distinguished devotion.

There are also several other reasons that move me, while none exists that can persuade us to the contrary. For what reason, I ask, could have led us to venerate with such devotion a Gallican martyr from Sens—that is, from the most distant region of Gaul in relation to Spain—who was merely heard of among us? I think it was the fame of her martyrdom, of which the martyrologies make scarcely a single-word mention and of which Equilinus wrote only a few things, whereas our breviaries agree neither in their readings nor on the day of her feast.

The Columba of Sens was certainly a most holy virgin and a vigorous martyr; but, now dwelling in heaven and kindly hearing us from there, she wishes us to discover and uphold the truth, and to claim for the Spanish saint the legitimate worship owed to her by Spaniards. That worship is so great, so conspicuously distinguished, and nearly unique, that it ought to seem due not to a foreigner but to a native daughter.

Very many sanctuaries in the Spanish countryside are dedicated to Saint Columba and are solemnly frequented on fixed days with extraordinary veneration by the people. Parents, moved by devotion to this saint, give her name to their daughters. The Church of Burgos has, among its dignities, an abbess of Saint Columba. The Church of Sigüenza likewise has a priest of the chief dignity bearing the same name and honour. There is also a chapel of this saint in the principal church there, distinguished in its worship and remarkably rich in revenues, although in both places, now under a corrupted name, she is called Saint Coloma rather than Columba.

Why should so great a veneration, so varied a form of religious observance, devotion attested by the signs of so many persons, declared by so many testimonies, and continually increased by so devout an inclination of minds, be assigned to an outsider rather than a native, to a stranger rather than a fellow citizen, to a foreign rather than a domestic—and almost tutelary—saint? Did we have a native and seek a foreigner? Was our own at hand and did we invoke another? Certainly we worship our own saint, venerate a Spanish martyr, and in her rightly seek, by legitimate devotion, a patronage in some sense owed to us by our shared native land.

“But,” you say, “the day on which Saint Columba’s feast is celebrated in Spain—the last day of December—is the birthday feast of the Columba of Sens, not of the Cordoban Columba, whose feast, if she were worshipped, should have occupied 17 September.” I shall say what I think. First, the breviaries differ here: that of Sigüenza has Saint Columba on 8 January and that of Coria on 3 April. But I believe that, when some of our people wished to celebrate Saint Columba of Córdoba, did not know the day on which she suffered martyrdom, and saw Columba honoured on the last day of December, they supposed her to be the Cordoban saint and assigned that day to her indiscriminately.

The readings recount the martyrdom of the saint of Sens. Of course, just as the birthday feast of our saint was unknown, so too were her life and passion, which were not commonly read in the books of Saint Eulogius. They therefore seized on what was at hand, and the identity of the name gave it, as it were, a proprietary claim.

We see the same thing happen in the case of our Saint Marina—that is, the Galician saint. There was nothing distinctive for them to read; they adapted to her in part the history of Saint Margaret. This is what I had to say about the worship of this our Saint Columba, while leaving free judgement meanwhile to those who prefer to think otherwise.

See also Flórez, volume X, treatise 33, chapter 2, numbers 88 and following.

**Editorial note.** Whatever Morales may say here, and whatever he may have assembled elsewhere in the *Chronicle* to prove that the Columba once so greatly celebrated by the Spanish Church was Cordoban rather than of Sens, he will certainly never persuade us of it. For, even if what he writes concerning the present-day solemnity is true after he himself had published Eulogius, we must admit that Spaniards honoured, two or three centuries and more before the ninth century, a Columba who without doubt could not have been this Cordoban saint.

The Office which the Breviary and Gothic Missal possess for this martyr is earlier than the seventh century, as all who know the discipline of our rite are aware. Since that Office exists not only in the most ancient Spanish codices but is also contained, in hymn and prayers of the Breviary, in the Veronese manuscript published by Blanchini—which even Cajetan Cenni did not dare deny belongs to the seventh century—it clearly appears that the Goths celebrated the Gallican Columba.

This argument is excellently discussed by Father Emmanuel Risco, volume XXXIII of *Hispania Sacra*, treatise 69, chapter 19, no. 114 and following; we most willingly subscribe to his opinion.

### CHAPTER XI

**(1) “For this sacred virgin.”** All these words, down to “her studies and meditation upon the sacred Scriptures,” were so corrupted in the old copy that scarcely any sense could be extracted. We restored them as best we could, adding one or two words.

**(2) “Which remain there today.”** They still remain even at the time at which we write. Nor is there any doubt that Saint Eulogius meant the place which, on a higher hill and rock, rises above the summits of the neighbouring mountains at the fourth milestone from the city, above the noble estate called *el A… Sazum* [reading uncertain], the very rock of Saint Miranda.

There bees make honey every year in holes in the rock. At the foot of its summit a perpetual spring flows forth, watering nearby gardens planted with citron trees of every sort. The site is very suitable for a monastery, and in more than one place the remains of buildings are visible amid the ruins. It should be remembered that, in chapter seven, Saint Eulogius placed this monastery not far from the city. We must therefore believe that he meant this very rock.

Otherwise one might understand the famous place on the banks of the river Guadiato, which we were able to identify from the multitude of bees making honey through the rocks and which is popularly called *Apiaria*, “Bee-farms.” But that place is about twenty miles from Córdoba.

**(3) “Era 897.”** It was written thus plainly in the old codex, but it is clearly an error of the copyist. For Saint Columba’s martyrdom stirred up Pomposa on that same day; and the writer’s slip is plainly refuted in the following chapter as well.

### CHAPTER XII

**(1) “The fifth Ides of July.”** This is the eleventh day of that month. The feast of this martyr is celebrated the day after tomorrow, because the preceding days were occupied by the feasts of other saints. Usuard’s Martyrology differs, placing it on 8 June.

### CHAPTER XIII

**(1) “Leontius” (*Λεόντιος*).** This name always had an aspiration in the exemplar. Onuphrius Panvinius likewise always writes it so from the diplomas of the emperors who bore this name, in his *Caesars*.

**(2) “Of the province of Italica.”** It would take too long to report the arguments by which it may be proved that the city of Italica formerly stood on the very site now called Old Seville, where there are great ruins, almost directly opposite that city across the river. In our *Antiquities of Spain* we assembled everything that we could discover on the subject.

**(3) “Palma.”** The town, which is the head of a county and a very celebrated market town, retains this very name. It also has the noteworthy distinction of singular pleasantness that it lies between rivers: the Singilis enters the Baetis on the other side of the town. It is thirty-two miles from Córdoba.

Understand “Palma of the province of Italica,” that is, of the diocese; for it had a bishop at that time, just as it had in earlier centuries. Thus in the following chapter he calls the Egabran diocese a province.

### CHAPTER XIV

**(1) “Of Egabra.”** *Aigas* (*αἶγας*) is Greek for “goat.” The Latins formerly retained the Greek name of this city. For where Pliny, in book III, chapter 1, lists the towns nearest Córdoba, the more correct manuscripts, aided by ancient copies, read *Aegabro* rather than *Eburo*.

We Spaniards render the earlier Greek term as *Cabra*, and now call the town by that name. In the aforesaid work on the *Antiquities of Spain*, we showed by almost manifest evidence that ancient Aegabrum was the very town which is now Cabra.

It is thirty-six miles from Córdoba. It is a notable town, giving its name and title to a county, surpassing in the pleasantness of its location, and having nearby that celebrated chasm which we call the Sima, opening amid wilderness and rocks and popularly believed to have no bottom. Hence it has become proverbial. Rasis greatly celebrates the mountains near this town for their flowers and fragrance, and that most delightful scent is still perceived in springtime. It formerly had a bishop.

### CHAPTER XV

**(1) “The fifteenth Kalends.”** This is 17 April. Usuard mentions them on the same day, although in his text one reads Felix, not Elias. Ado’s Martyrology has them on the same day; so also does the Roman Martyrology, recently enlarged by Maurolico. Equilinus too mentions them in the final chapter of book XI.

### CHAPTER XVI

**(1) “A noble confessor.”** It appears that Argimir publicly professed the Christian faith and the falsity of Muhammad the false prophet at some time before his martyrdom, and therefore had already received the name and glory of confessor. For, as is known, from the earliest times of the rising Church, “confessors” were called those who so conducted themselves before judges that they did not suffer death, although they had been subjected to severe punishments.

**(2) “Censor.”** We do not know what magistracy this was among the Arabs. It perhaps retained at least some shadow of the Roman censorship, derived from the census of citizens; and Saint Eulogius may therefore have applied this name to him.

John Tamaius is correct in his *Hispanic Martyrology* under 29 June: “I marvel at the error of our Ambrosius in saying this, since those who collected the census among the Romans were called not *censores* but *censitores*.”

For further discussion of the censorship and its office, see book XIII of the *Theodosian Code*, title 10, *On Censors*, and title 11, *On Census-Takers*; Rosinus, *Roman Antiquities*, book VII, chapter 10; Laurentius Polymathes, book III, *Syn.* 4, §4, and elsewhere. The editors of Saint Ambrose of the Benedictines make the same point in book II on Luke, §38. Schottus added: “It appears that he was a judge from the same chapter, since Argimir is said to have been removed from the administration of justice.” See also the preface to book I.

### CHAPTER XVII

**(1) “For almost thirty years.”** Everything agrees well. For he had related that Adulfus and John suffered at the beginning of the reign of Abd al-Rahman, and now recalls that Aurea dedicated herself to God in a monastery after their martyrdom.

**(2) “Marked with the stigma.”** We have already spoken of the metaphor of the stigma in scholion 12 of book I. As we have also said elsewhere, the badge of sacred virgins was a veil for the head, either black or red, as appears from the Councils of Toledo. They now wear black, signifying sorrow for the death of our Lord Jesus Christ. The red colour may have referred to the memory of his most precious blood, by which we have been redeemed.

**(3) “The fourteenth Kalends of August.”** This is 19 July of the year 856, to which day Saint Eulogius carried his history. He seems subsequently to have continued it when, in the *Apologeticus*, he added the holy martyrs Solomon and Rudericus, who suffered in March of the following year, 857. I would therefore suppose that during the whole two years in which Saint Eulogius survived, there was no martyr; for he would not have omitted to write of them.

## SCHOLIA OF AMBROSIUS MORALES

### IN THE DOCUMENT

**(1) “To the sacred virgins Flora and Maria.”** We have already said that in the Gothic period consecrated women were called by various names, as the Councils of Toledo show. Among other names, they were called “sacred virgins.” Saint Eulogius does not call these two women sacred virgins because both were nuns, since only one of them was a nun; rather, because, already destined for martyrdom, they deserved the name much more appropriately as sacred victims.

**(2) “With the triumph of *adoreae*.”** Verrius Flaccus, or Festus Pompeius, says that *adora* means “praise,” because they thought someone glorious who possessed abundant grain. Later the word especially signified glory acquired through military achievements. Hence emperors, after a successful campaign, were customarily presented with a kind of grain called *adora*.

Pliny, book XVIII, chapter 3, says that glory itself was called *adorea* from the honour of grain. In chapter 8 of the same book he mentions public gifts made of grain. Saint Eulogius often favours such unusual words, as we have also noted elsewhere.

Saint Ambrose uses the same word in book *On Widows*, chapter 4. The Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maurus note there what Morales notes here: that *adora* was a military reward consisting of a type of grain, and that the Romans lived on it in the year 300 from the foundation of the City. Hence, by a trope, *adora* came to mean praise and honour, especially military honour.

Horace also uses the word in book IV of the *Odes*, ode 4; Plautus in *Amphitryon*, act I; and Apuleius in book III. All of these, in addition to those whom Morales cites, show that Eulogius used the word entirely correctly.

### SCHOLIA ON THE LIFE AND PASSION OF THE HOLY VIRGINS FLORA AND MARIA

**(1) “From the village of Ausinianos.”** He mentions this town elsewhere too, but nowhere more fully. We have absolutely nothing more that we can say about it. He does, however, separately relate much concerning the martyrdom of Flora in the second letter to Alvarus.

**(2) “Within the court.”** This Latin term, known to reputable authors, is frequently used in the older diplomas of our kings. It means an open space within a house, farther removed from the dwelling, enclosed for raising chickens and for similar purposes.

**(3) “Of the city of Tucci.”** Numerous Roman monuments and inscribed stones clearly show that there was formerly a colony of Tucci in the town which we now call Martos in Baetica, not far from the city commonly called Jaén. We have demonstrated this fully in our *Antiquities of Spain*.

**(4) “Named Artemia.”** Besides these two sons, Artemia also had a daughter named Aurea, herself likewise a martyr; she will be treated at the end of book III.

The martyrdom of Adulfus and John, however, is celebrated in many ways. Many churches throughout Spain celebrate their feast day on 27 September. Usuard’s Martyrology records that they suffered at Córdoba on that day. From there the notice seems to have been transferred into the Roman Martyrology recently enlarged by the abbot Maurolico. Ado of Vienne, a bishop in Gaul, also placed them on the same day in his martyrology, from which Bishop Equilinus included them in his catalogue.

It is clear from Saint Eulogius here that all these martyrs preceded the beginning of this king’s reign by twenty years or more, since he says that they suffered at the beginning of the reign.

### IN THE LETTER TO ALVARUS

**(1) “As your serenity warned me.”** This form of address, *your serenity*, which the author uses more than once in writing to Alvarus, makes me believe that he was a very noble man. We shall discuss this expression later in the diploma of King Vermundus.

The diploma of which Morales speaks was published by Morales himself at the end of Eulogius’s works, since it is the sole document on which he bases the history of the *Life of Dominic the Saracen and his Companions*. In scholion 13 there, concerning the address *your serenity*, he writes: “This honourable form of address, like also ‘Our Glory,’ ‘Your Sublimity,’ and ‘Your Nobility,’ was plainly taken from the Goths, as is evident from the Councils of Toledo and the laws of the Goths. Kings called themselves by these titles, and others used them for kings as a mark of honour.”

**(2) “Because of this.”** In the preceding letter he had stated that this same cause was responsible for the bonds of imprisonment. In his *Life*, Alvarus says that Eulogius was sent to prison by Bishop Reccafredus. In any case, both accounts come down to the same thing.

The letter mentioned by Morales is the one that he wrote to the bishop of Pamplona and that we publish afterward, addressed to Baldegoth.

### IN THE LETTER OF ALVARUS

**(1) “Worthy of the praises of the mitre.”** As far as I can understand, he means that the work ought to have been entrusted to bishops, or rather to learned men worthy of the highest priestly offices. For Alvarus himself, being a layman—as we Christians customarily say—could not have possessed the authority to judge sacred works such as this work of Saint Eulogius.

The following words in this passage were terribly corrupted in the old manuscript. We restored them as best we could.

### IN THE DOCUMENT

**(1) “To the sacred virgins Flora and Maria.”** We have already said that in the Gothic period consecrated women were called by various names, as the Councils of Toledo show. Among other names, they were called “sacred virgins.” Saint Eulogius does not call these two women sacred virgins because both were nuns, since only one of them was a nun; rather, because, already destined for martyrdom, they deserved the name much more appropriately as sacred victims.

**(2) “With the triumph of *adoreae*.”** Verrius Flaccus, or Festus Pompeius, says that *adora* means “praise,” because they thought someone glorious who possessed abundant grain. Later the word especially signified glory acquired through military achievements. Hence emperors, after a successful campaign, were customarily presented with a kind of grain called *adora*.

Pliny, book XVIII, chapter 3, says that glory itself was called *adorea* from the honour of grain. In chapter 8 of the same book he mentions public gifts made of grain. Saint Eulogius often favours such unusual words, as we have also noted elsewhere.

**(3) “The reader does not preach from the pulpit.”** He calls *concionari* the act of reading something in church, either from Sacred Scripture or from the holy teachers and councils, for the instruction of the faithful. This was the proper function of readers. During the solemn celebration of Mass, the subdeacon read the Epistle and the deacon the Gospel, as is still done today.

To deliver homilies—that is, sacred addresses to the people—belonged only to bishops and teachers.

**(4) “But let us come to them.”** He plainly means those against whom he fought in the first book and separately in the *Apologeticus for the Martyrs*: men who wished, by arguments that were hardly sound, to draw Christians back from public confession.

He wrote that these two virgins had wavered at the insane advice of such men, as though slipping with uncertain steps, both in their Passion and in the letter to Alvarus. For that reason he thought they needed to be confirmed more strongly and drawn more firmly out of this error.

## THE HOLY VIRGINS FLORA AND MARIA

**(5) “Again I come to be crucified.”** These are Christ’s words to the apostle Peter as he came to Rome, where he suffered the punishment of the cross, as the history of his martyrdom relates. From this we now understand that that history is extremely ancient. A chapel is still visited at Rome on the very spot where Christ is said to have appeared to Saint Peter.

The history of the martyrdom of the blessed Peter is certainly very ancient, since it was written under the name of Linus in the second century of the Church; nevertheless, scholars have rejected it as apocryphal. In the third century Origen cites from it the words quoted here by Eulogius in volume XXI on John, p. 239, Paris edition of 1604; in the fourth century Ambrose cites them in *Sermon against Auxentius, On the Delivering of the Basilica*, no. 13, col. 867, volume II, Paris edition of 1690; later the pseudo-Hegesippus cites them in *History of the Destruction of Jerusalem*, book II, chapter 2, volume V of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Lyons edition of 1677; in the sixth century Gregory the Great cites them in his commentary on the fifth Psalm, and elsewhere.

The Acts of the saints Processus and Martinianus are also found in the Bollandists, volume I of July, under 2 July; in volume V of June one may read that history attributed to Saint Linus. It is better treated there than in the other editions of it, if one wishes to consult the learned Vincent Alexander Constantius, chapter 12 of the appendix to the monuments of Cardinal Cortesius, *On the Roman Journey and the Deeds of the Prince of the Apostles*, Rome, 1770.

**(6) “As elsewhere already.”** In the letter to Alvarus, which will be supplied in its proper place, all these matters are described more fully. There he also says that they were killed on 24 September. The year can readily be established from the letter to the bishop of Pamplona.

The Church of Córdoba celebrates the feast of these holy women on the same day. Usuard’s Martyrology, the enlarged Roman Martyrology, Ado’s Martyrology, and the catalogue of Bishop Equilinus all mention them.

Eulogius is lacking here only in naming the day of the week, from which a definite chronological certainty could have been applied to what follows. But it is enough for the credibility and truth of the history that the holy martyr reported these things.

## LETTERS OF EULOGIUS

Although these pious commemorations, which Saint Eulogius frequently employs, glow with zeal for the martyrs, they nevertheless sufficiently show what fire of divine love burned in the breast of this holy man. He indeed burns intensely in these…[the supplied source ends here]

## In the Epistles

### [Scan page 457]

**903**

A devout mind is indeed refreshed by reading these things, but when it sees itself kindled by the martyr’s flame, it plainly feels that a greater fire is being supplied to it from a torch of words such as these; so that the author seems, from his own fire, to make fire rise up in the hearts of his readers. For suppose that someone else, without this fervor of devotion, were to recall the very same matter in a lukewarm manner: although the subject would be the same, they would scarcely kindle a spark in the readers’ hearts.

**(2) “The morning and the Mass sacrifice.”** It is not easy to understand how Christians shut up in prison could celebrate Mass, or how they could have a suitable place and equipment, or how they could have been permitted to do so by their impious guards. They could certainly have sung the canonical hours in the solemn manner, in a subdued voice. Indeed, the good and almighty God did not fail the pious devotion of his people; in his kindness he provided the means by which they could console and arm themselves through receiving the divine sacrament.^a For in the *Document of the Martyrdom* he plainly says that Christians, ministers of the Church confined in prison, were accustomed to chant the canonical hours.

## In the Epistle to the Bishop of Pamplona

**(1) “To the bishop of the see of Pamplona.”** The true name of the city is *Pompelo*, as it appears in Strabo, Pliny, and Ptolemy. It was gradually corrupted into *Pampilona*; we Spaniards pronounce it still more corruptly as *Pamplona*. It is a very well-known city among the Spanish Vascones, the capital of the kingdom of Navarre and a most strongly fortified citadel. Although Strabo did not write the matter out fully, he nevertheless clearly says that it was founded by Pompey, since he teaches that it was called *Pompelon*, as though *Pompeiopolis*, that is, “the city of Pompey.” The city’s very name therefore plainly recalls its founder.

**(2) “Long ago, most blessed pope.”** From what Saint Eulogius mentions shortly afterward it can be inferred that this journey of his took place at the beginning of the reign of Charles the Bald, king of the Franks. After the death of his father, the emperor Louis, this Charles began to reign in the year of the Lord 840, as is recorded in the ancient annals of Anno. This letter, then, was written ten years or somewhat fewer afterward, as is noted in the text and as we investigated in *Nunilo and Alodia*. Hence he was justified in saying here “formerly,” and shortly afterward he will also say “once.” We have already spoken above about the pope’s name.

**(3) “King Louis.”** In the copy, the name was written with an initial aspiration in this form. F. Onuphrius Panvinius everywhere follows this reading from the ancient records.

This Louis must necessarily be identified here as the son of Louis the Pious, emperor, and brother of Charles the Bald, king of the Franks. When their father died, he left Germany to him as his hereditary possession, and afterward it was also confirmed to him in the division arranged between the brothers after the war. The authorities are Rhegino of Prüm and the annalist Anno. From them Paulus Aemilius and Robert Gaguin drew their material. Wolfgang Lazius, moreover, in Book VII of his work on the migrations of peoples, also adduces charters of this King Louis, granted during these years, in which he calls himself king of Bavaria. For this reason Saint Eulogius calls him king of Bavaria. *Bajoaria* is a corrupted form used by Paul the Deacon and the other writers who follow him. The correct name is *Bojoaria*, from the Boii, a people who lived near Noricum in Germany, whom Caesar mentions in Books I and VII, and Pliny in Book III, chapter 24, and elsewhere. Paul the Deacon describes the country as enclosed on every side by its boundaries in Book III of his *History of the Lombards*, chapter 29.

**(4) “And once, at the time of the expedition of William.”** Nothing is more important in this letter than attending to the sequence of events and the chronology. In this way nothing discordant will appear in the history of Gaul that might otherwise disturb the attentive reader. It will also become clear that Saint Eulogius is consistent with himself and has related nothing contradictory, although, unless the times are clarified in relation to the events, the holy martyr may seem to report something different and incompatible.

We shall draw the sequence of times and events chiefly from those annals of the Franks that were printed some time ago at Cologne together with the life of Charlemagne. Their author did not disclose his name; it is sufficiently clear, however, that he composed the history of his own age, and therefore his testimony and authority deserve considerable weight. He says, then, that in the year 827 Louis, the emperor, sent the priest and abbot Elysachar, together with Hildebrand and Donatus, as counts, to settle the disturbances of the Spanish March.

Before their arrival, Aizo, relying on the aid of the Saracens, inflicted much harm on the guards of that frontier and harassed them so greatly by continual incursions that some of them abandoned the castles they were supposed to defend. Wiliemund, the son of Bero, went over to him, as did many others eager for revolutionary change with the fickleness characteristic of their people. Joining the Saracens, they daily ravaged and burned Cerretania and Vallensis.

While Abbot Elysachar, with the others sent by the emperor, was prudently laboring to calm and pacify the minds of the Goths and Spaniards living in those regions, using both his own considerable diligence and the counsel of his companions, Bernard, count of Barcelona, also resisted with the greatest determination the plots of Aizo and the cunning and fraudulent schemes of those who had defected to him, rendering their rash attempts ineffective. An army sent by the Saracen king Abd al-Rahman to aid Aizo was approaching from Caesaraugusta.^b

In this connection Eulogius, thoroughly versed in every aspect of ecclesiastical discipline, celebrated, as he says, the Mass sacrifice in prison in honor and glory of the holy virgins Flora and Maria, after the evening and morning offices had been completed—that is, as we understand it, after the most holy doctor had performed Vespers and Matins; consequently he celebrated the sacred rite early in the morning in honor of the virgins. Saint Gregory of Tours mentions this Mass, which was called “the morning Mass,” among others in Book *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 65, where he reports that a certain woman attended a morning Mass and received the divine Eucharist there.

^a “Since confessors detained in prisons,” says Martène correctly in *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, Book I, chapter 3, article 5, “could not participate in the divine mysteries together with the other faithful of Christ, it was the concern of the pontiffs to send priests to them. These priests, after offering the sacrifice of our salvation in the prisons themselves, refreshed them with the heavenly banquet. When, however, the confessors themselves were priests or bishops, they celebrated for themselves and for the others thrown into chains with them.” Martène then adds the example of Saint Lucian, priest of Antioch and martyr, who is said to have performed the sacred mysteries in prison on the feast of Epiphany, with his chest serving as an altar because no altar was available; he was lying on his back and so battered by wounds that he could scarcely move. Since neither Eusebius of Caesarea nor the holy Fathers Jerome and Chrysostom mention this event when speaking of the holy martyr—and especially since Chrysostom celebrated his praises in an outstanding encomium—Tillemont and Ceillier rightly called it into question. In any event, what Martène establishes concerning priests and bishops thrown into chains and celebrating there is certain.

^b Pagi inserts here: “At the monastery of Saint Maximin near Trier.” In his notes on Baronius, year 827, no. 12, Pagius again discusses this revolt of Aizo under year 844, no. 11. Under year 826, no. 7, he says: “It is uncertain who this Aizo was, except that we learn from the Annals of Fulda that he was a Goth; and from the events themselves it is evident that he had connections with the Ausonian peoples, by whom, although deceived through his veteran cunning, he was readily received.”

## Scholia on Ambrose

**905**

…having been sent, he is reported to have come from Caesaraugusta. Over him, Abumarban, a relative of the king, was appointed leader and, persuaded by Aizo, promised himself a certain victory. Against him the emperor sent his son Pepin, king of Aquitaine, with a very large Frankish force, and ordered him to defend the boundaries of his kingdom. This would have been accomplished had the commanders whom he had placed over the Frankish army not arrived at the March later than the needs of the situation required.

The delay was so harmful that Abumarban, after laying waste to the fields of the people of Barcelona and Gerona, burning the villages, and plundering everything he found outside the cities, withdrew with his army intact to Caesaraugusta before our army could even see him. Since these disturbances of William had begun so many years earlier, Saint Eulogius therefore said “once.” I understand him to mean that the war then begun had grown, one development springing from another, into the time of King Charles the Bald.

Eulogius’s brothers had also gone to Gaul during the time of Louis and had remained there until Charles the Bald, his son. While this Charles was already reigning, Eulogius was at Pamplona. The chronology cannot otherwise be made consistent with what Eulogius himself suggests more than explicitly states. It is clear that Eulogius is speaking of Charles the Bald, who ruled the Frankish kingdom from the year of the Lord 840 until 878. By “Gothia” he means that part of Gaul around Narbonne which, because it had always been subject to the Goths, was called Gothic Gaul.

**(5) “But the same people who again possess Pamplona.”** As appears here and shortly afterward, these were the Seburic people, located in the Pyrenees and to be counted among the Vascones. They took their name from the city of Seburis, as we shall soon see. The ancient geographers make no mention of them. They are entirely different from the Sebusii or Sebusiani, whom Caesar mentions and Cicero in his speech for Quintius. The former lived near Narbonne, the latter far to the west; the former belonged to Gaul, the latter to Spain.

Understand “Comata Gaul” as joined to the Seburic people in such a way that, at the borders of Spain, the Seburici were the furthest inhabitants. For the river Aragus belongs entirely to Spain. Eulogius immediately afterward states that the city of Seburis stood on the Aragus.

**(6) “Through the factions of Count Sancho Sancion.”** This count’s name appears to be Spanish and to belong precisely to the period when, among the Navarrese and neighboring Celtiberians, sons were already retaining their fathers’ names. Hence, in ancient times, surnames of this customary form—Fernández, Rodríguez, González, and many similar names—were very common, being derived from father to son. But who this Sancho was, or for what reason he rebelled against Charles the Bald, is nowhere recorded in the ancient annals of the Franks, in ours, or in those of Aragon. I have no information from elsewhere that would enable me to say anything about it.^c

**(7) “For which the river Aragus…”** With a slight alteration of the name, it is now called the Arga. It rises not far from the city of Bayonne in Gaul, near the town of Azpeleta. Thus Saint Eulogius correctly says that it rises at the entrance to Gaul. From there, flowing toward Pamplona, it enters the river Ega below the town of Lérida. It is therefore clear, according to this argument, that the Ega is the river which Saint Eulogius here calls the Cantabrian.^d

The city of Seburis certainly stood on the bank of the Arga and before Pamplona, as appears from this passage. Its name, however, no longer survives, nor can its location be determined.

**(8) “The monastery of Leger.”** Eulogius also mentions this monastery in his *Apologeticus of the Martyrs*. It is now called San Salvador de Leyre; it lies eight miles from the city of Estella and twenty-four miles from Pamplona. I have seen there many monuments of the ancient kings of Navarre and Aragon granted to the monastery, and preserved there, in which the monastery is always called Legerense.

It had already been built by King Íñigo Arista. This is recorded in the history of the prince of Navarre and in the annals of Aragon. Among other things, the charter of Sancho the Great, previously appended in *Nunilo and Alodia*, mentions the towns and estates with which earlier kings had enriched the same monastery.

**(9) “Relics there.”** We have already noted elsewhere that the bodies of the holy martyrs Zoilus and Acisclus of Córdoba survived intact down to this time. This is also established by the present passage and by the end of the letter. The people of Pamplona could not have been enlightened except by receiving some distinguished portion of the relics, nor would a basilica have been requested for construction in the manner that follows if this were otherwise. Nor could Eulogius have enriched the bishop with a full gift unless almost the entire bodies of these martyrs were still preserved at Córdoba.

Saint Zoilus suffered martyrdom at Córdoba during the time of the Roman emperors. A well is now held in religious veneration; it is said that part of his entrails was thrown into it. His body was revealed to Agapius, bishop of Córdoba, during the time of the Gothic kings. Hence the feast of its translation is also celebrated. Many years after Eulogius, as we stated in the case of Felix of Complutum, it was finally translated.

**(10) “I reached Caesaraugusta.”** This city is now very celebrated, and Pliny, Ptolemy, Antoninus, and others mention it. Formerly it was called Salduba by its ancient Spanish name; after Augustus Caesar made it a colony, it received its present name. Hieronymus Zurita, himself a native of the city, traces this matter, together with all its other antiquities, most excellently in his *Annals of Aragon*. In doing so he does not so much honor his homeland as show that he can boast of so distinguished a son.

His exceptionally pleasant intellect, rare judgment in literary matters, remarkable knowledge of Latin and Greek, outstanding mastery of the whole of antiquity, excellent reputation in writing the history of his people, and prudence long tested in important affairs made him fully worthy for King Philip the Catholic to honor him with the high office of secretary, as it is called, in the Supreme Council of the Holy Inquisition. This occurred after he had already received from his fellow Aragonese, by public decree of the entire kingdom, the office of public historian.

I too have every right to boast that for many years I have enjoyed both his good will and his friendship, and that the royal council assigned him to me as a critic of my history and, in part, of this present labor. Thus what I have written may rightly be thought not to be displeasing, since it has pleased so great a man.

^c This Sancho was the first duke of Spanish Vasconia and the full brother of Aznar, or Asenarius, duke of Gallic Vasconia. He succeeded him in that lordship from the year 836, when Asenarius died a terrible death, according to the *Annals of Saint-Bertin*, under the year 864. See Manuel Risco, *Hispania Sacra*, vol. XXXII, tract 68, chapter 4, §7, no. 3; §8, no. 13; and chapter 18, no. 3 and following.

^d The same author notes in vol. XXXI, tract 67, no. 11, that this is not the Ega, but the Ebro, which Eulogius calls the Cantabrian river.

^e After Baronius, Marca, and Pagi, the often-cited Enrique Flórez rightly observes that Morales confused this William, or Wilihelm as Eulogius calls him—the son of Bernard, count of Barcelona—with Wiliemund, son of Count Bero. The annalist Eginhard, whose name Morales did not know, speaks of Wiliemund’s defection to Aizo’s party; Eulogius, however, speaks of William’s rebellion against King Charles, which arose after 844, the year in which Charles killed his father Bernard. Finally, William was captured at Ampurias and Barcelona and killed in 850. Therefore, when Eulogius wrote to the bishop of Pamplona about the end of the following year, 851, saying that all Gothia had been disturbed by William’s fatal incursion, he was plainly speaking of the year 848, when he made his journey and William’s revolt was in full ferment.

## In the Epistles

**907**

**(11) “I descended to Complutum.”** On the direct route from Caesaraugusta to Córdoba, one first passes through Segontia, then Complutum, and finally Toledo. The name Segontia is read more than once in Livy. Strabo and Pliny also mention the city. With its name slightly altered, it is now called Sigüenza, whose own bishop presides over it. Its cathedral church is especially distinguished by the fact that it is enriched by the body of Saint Liberata and a most magnificent tomb.

There was another Segontia in Baetica, toward the strait, mentioned by Pliny. Its ruins are seen not far from the bank of the Lethe River, and the place is still called Guisgonza. We have established with many weighty testimonies, in the work which we published some years ago on the holy martyrs Justus and Pastor, that Complutum is precisely the town now called Alcalá de Henares, where we are writing these comments.

Since this town still had a bishop in the time of Saint Eulogius, this strongly confirms what we also argued there: that the famous basilica in which the bodies of Saints Justus and Pastor had once been buried had always remained in Christian hands and had not been taken from them by the Moors. Since Saint Urbicius had by that time carried those bodies away to Huesca through a pious theft, Saint Eulogius does not mention them here.^f Without doubt, if they had been present, he would not have passed them over; he would have reverently honored those holy bodies and would have made Wilesindus a participant in his own devotion.

**(12) “I returned to Toledo after the fifth day.”** He says “returned” because, when he first left Córdoba, he had also made that journey. He may mean the fifth day from the day on which he departed from Segontia, or from the day on which he entered Complutum. Otherwise, the journey from Complutum to Toledo takes only two days.

Toledo is a most celebrated city of Spain. Livy mentions it more than once, and Pliny and Ptolemy also record it. Concerning it, as Sallust did concerning Carthage, it will be preferable here to say nothing more than a few words, especially since we shall discuss much about it in its proper place, namely in our work on the antiquities of Spain.

**(13) “Bishop Wistremirus.”** It was surely a source of immense glory for the Christian Mozarabs of Toledo to have possessed such a great man as bishop at this time. But much distinguished praise also accrues from this to my fellow Cordobans, since Saint Eulogius was their contemporary, and was judged worthy—by the suffrage of many bishops and the devout efforts of the people of Toledo—to succeed Wistremirus, such a bishop, good God!

This was plainly done with careful judgment and mature deliberation. By his residence among them, the Mozarabic Church of Toledo had learned through a noble experiment what sort of man it required through worthy endeavor and the people’s approval. The holy Church of Toledo owes Saint Eulogius a great debt for preserving here the memory of so holy a predecessor. It owes a similar debt to Alvarus of Córdoba, who transmitted to our own age the information concerning the elected bishop who would eventually deserve to become a martyr.^g

Yet since Eulogius says up to this point that Wistremirus was still alive, it is clear that he means that he was still archbishop in the very year in which this letter was written. We therefore plainly discover that Saint Eulogius was elected archbishop of Toledo in the years that followed—that is, nearer to his martyrdom.^h

**(14) “Whom the tyrant’s savage indignation…”** As we saw in the first book, King Abd al-Rahman ordered that all Mozarab Christians who held public offices or served him in any capacity at the palace—of whom there was no small number—should be deprived of their offices, expelled from the palace, and deprived of their royal allowances.

It appears that Joseph, the brother of Saint Eulogius, had also been punished among them. This is surely what Eulogius calls “being cast down from authority,” alluding to Saint Joseph, who once held the position of administrator of Egypt. What other authority could he have had in mind amid the wretched servitude of the Mozarab Christians?

**(15) “You protect the Christians under the dominion of the prince.”** The emperor Charlemagne, grandfather of Charles the Bald, who was then reigning, had taken Pamplona away from the Moors long before. He and his son Louis the Pious had also restored it several times when it rebelled.

The annals of that unnamed author say the following concerning this matter:

> “In the year 778, the emperor Charlemagne attacked Pamplona, a town of the Navarrese, and received its surrender.” Shortly afterward: “He returned to Pamplona.” He destroyed its wall to the ground so that it could not rebel again. Then, in the year 806: “In Spain, the Navarrese and the people of Pamplona, who in earlier years had defected to the Saracens, were received back into allegiance.” And in the year 824, under Louis, the son of Charlemagne, emperor and king of Gaul: “The counts Aeblus and Asinarius were sent with forces of Vascones against Pamplona; when they had completed the task assigned to them, they were returning,” and so forth.

Here it is plainly evident that Pamplona was recovered by this expedition, if it had indeed defected; or, if not, that it was pacified amid whatever disturbance had arisen.

**(16) “Galindo Enneconis.”** This Galindo Íñiguez, to use ordinary names, was either Navarrese or Aragonese. In the ancient annals of both peoples the name Galindo, and the surname derived from it, is frequently found among the nobles. The annals of Hieronymus Zurita, Book I, attest this more than once. The name Galindo is also found among the other nobles in the ancient charters of the earliest kings.

From these records I have reached the following conclusion. In the era 819—that is, in the year of the Lord 881—on 22 April, King Ordoño II, together with his wife Elvira, granted to the Church of Compostela, where the body of Saint James is buried, numerous gifts of gold and silver, as well as villages and other properties. Galindo subscribed and confirmed the document among the other nobles.

Likewise Queen Elvira, wife of King Vermudo II, who, according to her own statement, was the mother of Alfonso V, granted many gifts to the same church on 18 August of the era 1055—that is, in the year of the Lord 1017. Galindo the abbot subscribed and confirmed the document among the other prelates.

Still more extensive is a charter of King Alfonso IV, father of Froila, dated 25 October in the era 950—that is, in the year of the Lord 912—and granted to the same church. In it Galindo also confirms the grant among the other nobles. These three charters are preserved in the archive of that holy church.

I have wished to collect these materials here in order to establish by reliable testimony the antiquity among us of this noble family, whose surname is Galindo or Galíndez. Since in both this passage and shortly afterward the copy had written *Galindo* in the nominative, at the end it once again has *Galindum* in the accusative.

**(17) “For building the basilica in their blessed memory…”**

^f This pious theft by Saint Urbicius is described at length by Morales in the work on the holy martyrs Justus and Pastor which he published at Complutum in 1568. It is rightly challenged by Enrique Flórez in *Hispania Sacra*, vol. VII, tract 13, chapter 5.

^g It is believed—as we shall say elsewhere—that Wistremirus lived until the end of the year 858. At the close of that year, or at the beginning of the next, Eulogius was elected, but, as Alvarus says, was prevented by the adversity of circumstances from being consecrated. Since he was beheaded for Christ on 11 March 859, he certainly died before his consecration.

^h Everyone can see that the reading “era 819,” which is said to be the year 881, must contain a serious error. Morales corrected it in his catalogue of errors, assigning era 919, which corresponds to that year. But the statement that Ordoño was already married to Elvira at that time presents more difficulty than Ambrosius seems to have believed. Whatever year is assigned, it is impossible that he married in 881, since his parents’ marriage must have occurred later than 867, and Ordoño cannot have been born before 870, being their second son. Although the charter of Ordoño printed by Sandoval and Yepes is regarded as unquestionably genuine—which may rightly be doubted—it records five sons already born to Ordoño in the year 898, on 27 April: Sandoval, in his account of the monastery of San Pedro de Montes, fol. 21; Yepes, vol. II, *Chronicon*, charter 14. No one who has considered this matter will deny that the king’s marriage must have taken place later than the year 800. I believe that in Ordoño’s charter the era number was *DCCCCXXXIX* (939), and that Morales, through his frequent error, failed to notice the value of this numeral.
