## Scholia on the Book

**(1) “Because of fraternal blood.”** Observe that it was the accepted opinion of those times that the holy robber had killed his brother. Saint Eulogius suggests this very thing in other passages as well.^a

**(2) “And at the monastery of Leger.”** He also mentions this monastery in the letter to the bishop of Pamplona, where we said several things about it and about the city. It still survives there intact.

**(3) “For Muhammad arose.”** The seventh year of the emperor Heraclius was the 617th year of Jesus Christ our Lord. The year noted here adds one year to that figure. Yet there is no contradiction. The difference of one year may have arisen because one writer counted the incomplete years of Heraclius, as they say, while another counted the complete years. It is not the place to investigate this matter more precisely.

What Eulogius reports from the codex of the monastery of Leger concerning the beginnings, progress, and death of Muhammad is read in the same words in a small and very ancient codex, written in Gothic letters on parchment, which is in the library of our Complutensian academy, although a missing leaf has carried away several lines at the beginning. An exemplar of the councils, written six hundred years ago and brought from the monastery of San Millán de la Cogolla to the royal monastery of San Lorenzo at El Escorial, contains this same history.

**(4) “The church of Saint Euphrasius.”** Saint Euphrasius was one of the seven bishops whom Peter and Paul, the apostles of Rome, sent first into Spain. Many say that they were disciples of Saint James the son of Zebedee. I have found nothing established on this point from reliable authorities. I investigated whatever I could in our history. Everyone affirms, and nearly all the churches of Spain read it at Matins, that Saint Euphrasius both preached at Iliturgi and died there.

Iliturgi was a town on the river Baetis above Córdoba, mentioned by Livy, Polybius, Strabo, Pliny, and Ptolemy. Pliny reports that it was situated in such a place that it can rightly be believed to have occupied the same site, or one not far distant, as the city now called Andújar. We have discussed this more fully in our work on the antiquities of Spain.

Here it was worth noting that even in the time of the Goths the blessed body of this saint remained there together with the temple dedicated to him. Now not even the slightest memory of him survives in that city. Beside that wealthy monastery of Saint Benedict called Samos, of whose antiquities we shall say more in our work on Córdoba, the body of this saint is said to be in the small town called Met… [the place-name is materially uncertain]. We saw his tomb venerated with great devotion by the inhabitants.

^a Schottus correctly notes here, in no. 3 of chapter 17 of the *Memorial of the Saints*, that the man was not a fratricide but a patricide.

## Apologeticus

…at the usual time at which Saint Augustine used the term, and several others as well, “memorial of the martyrs” denoted a place where martyrs were assembled. Here the term is used with a somewhat different meaning, namely “a cemetery of martyrs,” in ordinary usage. It seems that Saint Eulogius took this statement from a decree of the African, or Carthaginian, council. Its words are:

> “It was also decided that altars which are set up throughout the fields or along the roads as memorials of martyrs, where no body or relics of martyrs are proved to have been buried, should, if possible, be overthrown by the bishops who preside over those places.”

And shortly afterward:

> “No memorial of martyrs is to be accepted as genuine unless either a body or certain relics are present there, or a trustworthy origin is handed down concerning some habitation, possession, or passion.”

**V. APOLOGETICUS**

…the monastery of Saint Benedict, called Samos, concerning whose antiquity we shall speak in the *History of Córdoba*. The body of this saint is said to be in a small town called …, and we saw the tomb being venerated there with great devotion by the inhabitants.

**(5) “Also at Toledo.”** Fridegisius of Toledo, Lucas of Tuy, and other historians of our affairs celebrate the construction of this church as having been begun by this king and completed with marvelous workmanship. We find that councils were held in that temple in subsequent times, and never before that.

It is believed that this is the church of Saint Leocadia, which still survives outside the city, not far from the river Tagus. Two churches dedicated to the holy virgin can be seen within the city.

**(6) “Which was rather ridiculous.”** Saint Eulogius had used the same words in the first book. Concerning the cry of the Saracens from the towers, which Saint Eulogius mentions shortly afterward, the author of the *Illustrious Book* also made reference.

**(7) “Then blessed Rudericus.”** *Rudericus* is the correct form of the name, which we Spaniards have corrupted into *Rodericus*. I have seen a gold coin of Ruderic, the last king of the Goths, which, together with his portrait, bore these letters arranged in a circle:

> “In the name of God, Ruderic, king.”

On the reverse, around a cross, were the words:

> “Agitania, the Pious.”

In the oldest manuscript books the name is always written *Rudericus*. We have seen several autograph subscriptions of Ruderic, archbishop of Toledo, in public archives throughout the present metropolitan jurisdiction of Toledo. There he calls himself Rudericus, not Rodericus.

**(8) “What were the supports of the images.”** It is astonishing that bronze bells of this sort were permitted in Christian churches before this plundering, while they forbade other things much more tolerable to their impiety, as we see in this author. I suppose that this object had previously been redeemed at a price and spared on payment of tribute; but now impiety, contending with avarice, prevailed. We have discussed elsewhere the bell of that period which still survives.^b

**(9) “As a substitute for an exquisite gift.”** I cannot discover by conjecture what sense these words may have, nor can I think of a way in which they might be emended.

**(10) “Who sent a disciple to the prison.”** He says this because Saint John the Baptist, when he had already been imprisoned, sent his disciples to the Lord Jesus. Eulogius calls the holy robber a disciple.

^b Scholia on Book I of the *Memorial*, no. 9.

## EPISTLES

### [Scan page 461]

These very words are said to have been ordered to be announced to the same man whom he here calls “the disciple.”

**(11) “These are the things, devil.”** The words seem to be Ruderic’s taunt directed at the demon. Something, however, seems to be missing by which it would be indicated that these words were spoken by him. Otherwise, “bursting in suddenly” cannot be made to fit.

**(12) “Different in rank and nation.”** I do not doubt that something is also missing concerning Solomon’s homeland and way of life. For how could Eulogius now report these matters unless he were confident that he had already related what was necessary for them to be understood?

**(13) “And upon the rim of the riverbed.”** From this it is plainly understood that the forum stood on the bank of the Baetis. For when these two martyrs had been led into the forum to be killed, they were beheaded on the riverbank. The body of Saint Eulogius was thrown into the riverbed and lay not far from the fortress, as we noted in his Life. There was doubtless a forum and tribunal in the square before the fortress, as was said there.

**(14) “And nearer than the rest of the crowd.”** This was the holy audacity of Saint Eulogius, this the magnanimity worthy of a future martyr. While the other Christians, mingled among the unbelievers, held themselves back lest they incur the danger of death by approaching nearer to look upon the bodies of the martyrs, he alone, despising the fear of death and intending to praise God in his saints, separated himself from the crowd and advanced almost to the very place of execution. It is sufficiently clear how great a danger those courageous steps of his encountered, since the Arabs were standing there, so fiercely hostile to the Christian name and to the martyrs’ glory that, as follows, they even became angry at the smallest drops of their blood.

**(15) “In the open water.”** Thus it stood in the old copy. Although I believe that it signifies some kind of river water, I will not conceal that the part of the Baetis extending from the Sun Gate, or a little above it, to the bridge, or a little below it—that is, toward the fortress and the walls of the ancient city—was called, as we shall say in its proper place, *pelagus*. Since this name was given—or rather adapted—from the circumstance itself, because throughout that stretch the river evidently spread more broadly and extended in the form of an open sea, it is easy to believe that it was already called this at that time and that Saint Eulogius himself used the established name.

**(16) “At the hamlet of Tertius.”** Alvarus mentions both the hamlet and the monastery in the Life of Saint Eulogius; Saint Eulogius himself does so elsewhere more than once. There are, however, two saints named Genesius, both highly celebrated martyrs in the Church of God: one Roman, the other Arelatensis. The martyrdom of both is commemorated on the same day, namely 25 August.

**(17) “And because of the failure of the sun.”** At this point the sentence attempts to rise, and the heart of Saint Eulogius, filled with God and ardently desirous of the glory of the saints, bursts forth under the impulse of inward devotion. Nor is natural force of eloquence lacking; but it is deprived of what belonged to the age, and it lacks what belonged to the region.

**(18) “And the renowned pope.”** Several centuries earlier the title *pope*, which signifies “father,” had also become common among bishops. Prudentius, writing to Bishop Valerian in the Passion of the martyr Hippolytus, says: “I saw the tips of the rocks weeping, excellent pope.” Many letters of Sidonius Apollinaris written to bishops likewise bear this title. Later usage established that, by a kind of antonomasia, this name should be attributed exclusively to the Roman Supreme Pontiff, the head of the entire Christian Church.

**(19) “The era 895.”** In the old copy it was eighty-five, but certainly incorrectly. The era should have been recorded as ninety-five, since, as he had said above, these two martyrs were killed during the reign of King Muhammad; they appear to have been the last of all those who suffered at that time before Eulogius, in the year of the Lord 857.

## DEDICATION TO THE AMBROSIAN EDITION

To Philip II, Catholic king, greatest and most powerful of all kings, Peter Pontius of León, of Córdoba, Bishop of Plasencia, chief inquisitor of the Christian faith throughout his kingdoms and dominions, sends greetings and true happiness.

Among the many distinguished virtues, worthy of a Christian prince, by which you rightly retain and perpetually uphold the title “Catholic,” Philip the Great, your Spanish subjects regard and always recall with immense delight and truly heavenly joy this one above all: that amid the most serious cares of governing so many kingdoms and the varying anxieties of war and peace, you have always devoted yourself to the glory and veneration of our native saints, and, inspired by devotion to them, have continually labored on their behalf with remarkable foresight and great expense.

It would take too long to celebrate all the testimonies of your religion and devotion toward the Spanish saints. I shall pass briefly over a few. By the most magnificent transfer of their bodies; by ensuring that they are everywhere buried with the honor due to them and that their worship flourishes with proper veneration; by sending a most pious embassy for this very purpose to investigate and learn; and by seeking from the Supreme Pontiff a public declaration of their sainthood, you have abundantly demonstrated this aspect of your piety.

There is, moreover, one further matter of this kind which I especially admire and which, for the sake of public benefit, I gladly consider. You desire and command that the writings of the Spanish saints, diligently sought out and rescued from miserable oblivion, should be published for the people intact, corrected, enriched with annotations, and restored to their proper brilliance. Nor do you merely wish this and command it: you have already entrusted the task to the most learned men. Yet Your Majesty meanwhile spares neither foresight nor generosity. Your exceptional devotion and most pious provident purpose at so lofty a station delight me all the more and compel me to return immense thanks to God Almighty, because I myself long ago burned with the same desire, gathered many writings of our saints from ancient libraries, and at last prepared this work, which I humbly offer here, as wholly worthy of that sacred zeal and holy inclination of Your Majesty.

For we offer you the works, now for the first time brought to light, of Saint Eulogius of Córdoba—martyr, teacher, and Archbishop of Toledo—you who are the prince most devoted to the Spanish saints, and especially devoted to them in this respect. I do not doubt that they will be most welcome to you. For I know how pleasing and venerable to Your Majesty the mere hearing of a martyr’s name will be.

What if you should be pleased briefly to recall the martyr’s ardor, wonderfully expressed in these writings of his? What if you should think that he himself, restored to life, is coming to you, speaking, teaching, and exhorting? What if you should reflect that these works of the martyr lay hidden for more than nine hundred years, and that almost all hope of finding them again had been taken away?

Moreover, the contents of the writings of this most holy martyr are such that, had they been written by anyone at all, they would certainly be held in the highest value and regarded as the discovery of some great treasure. For he has clearly written and fully transmitted nearly fifty lives and passions of our martyrs, of whom we had previously known almost nothing but their names, as a Spaniard who was himself present at nearly all of them. How highly it is fitting that they should be valued among Spaniards! Furthermore, a martyr wrote of martyrs; an eyewitness and teacher of martyrdom wrote of disciples who were martyrs—matters that no one can adequately value. Thus we plainly understand that you, a truly Catholic and truly most august prince, devoted to this very study and religious care, will receive and venerate them, as is fitting, with grateful mind.

The reader will indeed understand that Saint Eulogius’s other works, apart from his history of the martyrs, are of such a kind that—to pass over the fact that they are very great aids to history—he will see the martyr’s most ardent heart breathing everywhere through them and, as it were, presenting a living image of him.

This treasure seems to me to have been shown by divine goodness for this purpose: that I, a citizen of Córdoba, might discover a martyr of Córdoba and, having offered him to Your Majesty, more happily share him with my city and with the Christian world under your name. We obtained from the library of the holy Church of Oviedo a codex of these works, written in Gothic characters on parchment, of remarkable antiquity and, as may be believed, contemporary with the holy martyr. It had been brought there from Córdoba, together with the holy martyr’s body, not long after he received his crown. For this Spain owes much to that holy Church, since it preserved so rich a treasure for more than six hundred years and now, at an opportune time, graciously communicated it to me and, through me, to all.

But so that we Cordobans might render every service to our own most holy citizen, Ambrosius Morales of Córdoba, your historian, most powerful king, was opportunely at hand to elucidate throughout the works of Saint Eulogius and enrich them with quite necessary annotations. He also added certain new accounts, now discovered for the first time, concerning other martyrs of Córdoba who were killed shortly afterward for Christ’s faith.

Receive, therefore, Philip, greatest of kings, Saint Eulogius, truly yours: born and educated in your Spain, there a teacher and encourager of martyrs, and finally himself a martyr.

## DEDICATION TO THE AMBROSIAN EDITION

### II

The same Peter Pontius sends greetings in the Lord to the Church and city of Córdoba, wishing them to fare well, to receive worthily the glory of their martyrs, and, as those who invoke their patronage, worthily to enjoy it.

Although all our studies and the long labors we have spent on letters might rightly claim us continually for the dignity to which God’s kindness, despite our unworthiness, has raised us, and for the duties entrusted to us, nevertheless, being strongly inclined to investigate and illuminate the writings of the Spanish saints, we have always willingly devoted some portion of our studies, care, and diligence to that task.

Since I considered the monasteries of Saint Benedict throughout Spain to be especially rich in such resources because of their remarkable antiquity, I likewise always believed that the holy Church of Oviedo was particularly rich in them. For I remembered that, during the miserable devastation of our Spain in the time of the Goths, when our people fled and sought safer places, very many books were brought there together with the relics of the saints.

Accordingly, in both places we sought, with the greatest industry and diligence, for several years to discover the ancient codices of our authors and, above all, of our saints. Nor was our undertaking without a most fortunate result. God graciously assisted and advanced our pious diligence. For, besides finding many things in the sacred councils of our country that were extremely worthy of knowledge but had never previously been seen, we also obtained some excellent commentaries on the sacred books.

Yet the discovery of Saint Eulogius alone would have amply compensated for all our labor, even had it been much greater. Who, after all, would even have dared hope to be blessed with so great a treasure? I had indeed heard the name of this saint and had read it somewhere, and I had retained only a faint memory of what he had written. But I could not even conceive in my wishes that I would one day obtain any of his writings. And although I would have preferred no other gift, I was thinking of none less than this.

### [Scan page 464]

Having at last become possessor of so great a treasure, I first gave thanks to God Almighty, who had suddenly presented me—a man of Córdoba—with the sacred writings of a saint of Córdoba, including the triumphs of so many martyrs of Córdoba, although I had never hoped for them and had scarcely considered the possibility.

Although the writings themselves were worthy on their own account of being highly valued for many reasons, what moved me most was that I saw them astonishingly increasing the already outstanding glory of our city. I rejoiced greatly that I possessed a gift which I could worthily offer to the city and which it would gladly receive.

For besides being born and educated at Córdoba, and instructed in the first rudiments of letters and in the knowledge of the Latin language, I recognize that I owe to it as much as anyone could ever owe to his most illustrious homeland. I also entirely express my paternal stock: I descend from the conqueror of the city in the time of the Moors. I do not know by what impulse of even greater affection and most eager love I am always drawn toward it, and I am wonderfully refreshed by its glory.

I then paid whatever thanks I could to the holy Church of Oviedo, which had preserved these treasures for so many centuries and had now willingly shared them with me. But because the praise and glory of our Córdoba concerned me with such urgency, I did not wish to allow it to remain any longer without this increase. Eager to publish the works, I arranged for the exemplar that the people of Oviedo had kindly lent me to be copied as soon as possible.

This cost us and our household great labor. Since it had been written in Gothic letters, many passages could not be read without long practice. Add to this the incredible antiquity of the codex. When it was compared with others known to have been written nearly six hundred years earlier, those others seemed to have been written only a few years ago. So great was the antiquity, and so manifest the difference in the ancient characters, the parchment, and even the binding, that, while this gave the codex much authority and evidentiary weight, it also brought enormous difficulty to the task of copying it.

Accordingly, when our household assistants, to whom we had entrusted the care and labor, were at times losing hope, we ourselves came to their aid in this arduous work and copied with our own hand several passages at which they had become stuck. And just as we willingly undertook this labor ourselves, so too we would not have avoided the much greater task of correcting and annotating the work, had not pastoral care and the various affairs of our Church of Plasencia—over which the Lord willed that we should preside, although unworthy—occupied and hindered us, and had not our fellow citizen Ambrosius Morales of Córdoba, a worthy son of that city and royal historian of our lord Philip II, supplied his assistance in this matter.

With the zeal and diligence that he brings to illuminating the lives and deeds of the Spanish saints, he undertook this labor in a manner worthy of it; and with the affection he bears our Córdoba, he embraced it eagerly. Thus he eagerly embraced the undertaking so that this whole work—indeed, a very great increase in Córdoba’s dignity and glory—might be attributed to no others than the people of Córdoba.

Saint Eulogius himself first provided the outstanding contribution: through his nobility, learning, truly Christian labor, written books, preservation of the memory of our martyrs, and finally his own martyrdom. We have rescued his writings from the darkness of perpetual oblivion and now bring them to light. We devoutly believe that this has come to us by God’s gift, and we rejoice greatly.

Our Ambrosius, as the entire book will everywhere make clear, refused no labor so that the works of the holy martyr might be published more accurately, more richly, and more clearly. It will be your task, most reverend priests and most devoted fathers of our commonwealth, to receive this gift of ours, prepared for the true glory of Córdoba, our common homeland, with a kindly and joyful spirit; to recall with the greatest pleasure the almost restored glory of your native holy martyrs; and always to turn toward it with continual veneration—to praise the Lord constantly in them, to follow their examples, to invoke and merit their patronage, and always to magnify this exceptional glory of our city, this genuinely heavenly distinction, with worthy worship and Christian service.

Thus at last it will come about that you will gain from this a great fruit of religion and a benefit of piety, while we shall acknowledge that, through this gift of ours—worthy in itself, yet, by God’s good favor, contributing something still greater—we have given something to you.

Farewell, most distinguished men, most worthy citizens of the illustrious city.

### III

To the most illustrious and reverend lord Peter Pontius León of Córdoba, Bishop of Plasencia, chief inquisitor of the Christian faith throughout the kingdoms and dominions of Philip II, Catholic king, most learned in divine law and the sacred canons, and most devoted to humane studies, Ambrosius Morales of Córdoba, royal historian, respectfully offers the fullest greetings.

Our Córdoba has always acknowledged that it owes you much, most illustrious prelate, and for many reasons. For although its glory, extolled by the birth of so many distinguished men, greatly surpasses the renown and singular celebrity of cities famous for their citizens, and although it has always stood forth splendid and exalted, your greatness has completed it through your own radiance, holiness of character, learning, and the achievements of your lofty virtues, so that in our time it is especially renowned.

You have made yourself a citizen capable of being an exceptional honor and ornament to your most illustrious homeland and to a city fertile in great men. To pass over your nobility and the distinction of your lineage—although almost all that is distinguished in the two most magnificent cities, Córdoba and Hispalis, which elsewhere shines separately, has been united and has blazed forth in your ancestors—let us consider what is truly your own, which has been evident to me as a witness from almost your earliest childhood.

Educated from almost your earliest years in a most holy manner under Don Peter Pontius, your father, a primicerius and canon of the Church of Córdoba—whose excellent virtues and most approved examples our city will never cease to recall with a kind of sacred admiration—and already imbued with knowledge of the Latin language... Then, already imbued with that knowledge, you were sent to Salamanca at your father’s care and expense to be trained in higher studies.

There you happily learned the institutions of the sacred canons and the counsels of the holy Fathers at so early an age that, when you publicly offered the results and, as it were, specimens of your studies according to the custom of that university, your skill amazed everyone, even though your age had not yet fully matured. The same happened soon afterward in the great—but for your age still premature—honors, offices, and dignities bestowed upon you.

For when you were elected by the Emperor Charles V to the most august and supreme office, as it is called, of senator of the Holy Inquisition, people congratulated you on the honor as one who most deserved it, yet expressed amazement that it had come to a very young man. Advancing with equal speed in virtue, learning, and merit, you were soon created Bishop of Ciudad Rodrigo.

When, in that dignity, you conducted yourself most prudently at the Council of Trent, in the censure of the Valladolid assembly, and in other most serious affairs of the Spanish commonwealth, King Philip II, the Catholic king, raised you to the bishopric of Plasencia, a greater reward and a more spacious office in the Church of God.

And so that the fullness of your greatness and excellence might finally be increased by a worthy addition, you were recently chosen by the most Catholic king to be Supreme Inquisitor of the faith. Nothing in our Spain is more holy, more august, or more venerable than the dignity of this office. May this dignity, most distinguished prelate, grow through your great labor, and may it bring our Córdoba, which rightly glories in such an honor, an even greater abundance of renown.

How much true glory it adds to our homeland that, at the summit of this higher dignity, at this most illustrious height of fortune and splendor, you retain your former love of good letters with such zeal and frequent them with such assiduity that, if this praise alone had fallen to a humble and ordinary man, it would rightly seem to have earned him very great commendation!

An even more distinguished quality, deserving of still greater praise, shines in your love of good letters: your excellence does not wish your studies to serve your own interests or pleasure alone, but seeks to benefit everyone in common.

Therefore, since you have always devoted great care, diligence, and even expense to collecting and searching everywhere for the books of the Spanish saints, who does not see that you have labored in this field with such dedication for the sake of public benefit? You gather these treasures most eagerly, but soon intend to make them available for everyone’s use.

Many things will soon testify to this; for the present, Saint Eulogius alone, discovered through your efforts and restored, as it were, from the grave to life, makes it abundantly clear. Although, by offering and publishing the works of this holy martyr, you have destined this distinguished gift to our Córdoba and have, as it were, assigned it exclusively to that city, pious men and lovers of higher studies, enriched by so great a treasure of Christian wealth and rejoicing in the magnitude of so great a benefit, will later proclaim more clearly how much advantage all Spain, and indeed foreign nations, will derive from it.

When, moreover, your greatness wished me to undertake a portion of this distinguished labor and ordered me to supervise the correction, annotation, and ultimate publication of the works of Saint Eulogius, I give you immense thanks for that reason. I regard it as the greatest benefit to be able to serve the holiest martyr with whatever work I can offer and to be, in some measure, a craftsman of the glory of Córdoba.

Although neither task could be completed without immense labor, I accepted both with the greatest pleasure. For who would not rejoice in offering to the holiest martyr, and to the herald of so many martyrs, the service of his intelligence, learning, and industry—services which I know to be very small, but which, whatever their quality, I would nevertheless be delighted to provide?

And would I not take pleasure in increasing the glory of our Córdoba, enriching, polishing, and to some extent illuminating the distinguished gift you were preparing for it for that very purpose? Although this work has been especially delightful to me because of our Córdoba, whose glory was thereby so greatly increased, I am also pleased that the dignity and holy splendor of the Church of Toledo—whose majesty, elevated by the primacy of all Spain and honored for many other reasons, rightly commands the highest veneration—has thereby been augmented by an increase previously unknown and now restored.

For from the same works of Saint Eulogius it will be understood that the holy martyr himself was its bishop and that he succeeded the most holy Archbishop Wistremirus, celebrated throughout all Spain. The Church will greatly rejoice that it has now learned about these two prelates of such outstanding glory, of whom previously it had possessed no knowledge.

For my part, I willingly devoted whatever I had and contributed whatever I could, for both purposes, first calling upon God, whom I had entreated in humble prayer for this very task. What that contribution has been, our work itself will show, so that there is no need to recount it here.

I dedicate the whole of it first to God Almighty; I assign it to Saint Eulogius and to the martyrs celebrated by him; I offer it to the glory of Córdoba, thereby increased by heavenly benefits; and I present the labor, undertaken under your auspices and by your benefaction, most celebrated prelate, enriched as far as I have been able.

Farewell, most illustrious prelate, and may you long enjoy this great blessing of yours.

Alcalá, in the year of the Lord 1672, in the month of November.

## EXCERPTS FROM THE WORKS OF SAINT EULOGIUS

### [Scan page 464]

## ON INVENTED AND NEWLY COINED WORDS

How great Saint Eulogius’s intellect was, and how great the learning with which it was cultivated, his works will sufficiently and fully teach. Moreover, although one can detect in the holy martyr, through many indications, a notable knowledge of sacred literature, his skill in explaining and formally expounding the testimonies that he adduces will especially reveal it.

His style, although always pious and often graceful, is far inferior to the greatness of his intellect and even of his natural eloquence; and one often feels that he lacks the assistance of that eloquence. Evidently, the excellence and purity of the Latin language had already declined everywhere, and many impurities had obscured its clarity; our own disasters had buried it still more deeply among us.

Indeed, considering the dreadful captivity and misery that we endured for nearly one hundred and fifty years in the time of Saint Eulogius, it is more worthy of praise what the holy man was able to accomplish in this field than blameworthy what he failed to attain.

Those times had also long since fashioned for themselves a distinctive and particular style, in which it was considered a matter of praise and glory to excel. They did not permit wit, subtlety, a measure of force, or a certain elevated impulse in great matters to remain absent. Yet one must regret that excellent efforts were blunted and obscured by neglect of words and of the language as a whole.

Moved by a kind of reverent scruple, we did not wish to correct anything. We have merely thought it necessary to append here a catalogue of the invented and newly coined words and phrases.

“Once and again”; “I tell you in truth”; *Hispanis D[ii]*; “delighting the life of the monks,” instead of “delighting in the life of the monks”; *in ante*, “before”; *in amplius*, “further.”

[The following lexical forms are retained with their English meanings:]

- *gerens* for *consulens* or *prospiciens*: “conducting” for “taking counsel” or “providing for.” The sequence of the book will make the grounds clear, so that it is an active form.
- *praeconabile*: “worthy of proclamation.”
- *praeconari*: “to proclaim.”
- *parvipendulus*: “of little account.”
- *gloriositer*: “gloriously.”
- *deicola*: “worshipper of God.”
- *decisus*: “killed” or “cut down.”
- *itus*: “a journey” or “a road.” The neuter *itum*, meaning “a going” or “a course,” is also found in Nonius Marcellus.
- *prophetismus*: “prophetic utterance,” on the model of *Christianismus*.
- *incultio*: “roughness” or “barbarity of speech.”
- *adepsit*: “he has attained,” for *adeptus est*.
- *medie*: “moderately.”
- *epistolatim*: “by letters” or “in letters.”
- *lunatim*: “each month” or “month by month.”
- *metabulum*: “a period” or “interval.”
- *victoriare*: “to triumph.”
- *pausare*: “to rest”; for *pausa*, “rest,” was used by the ancients.
- *eremititas*: “a desert” or “solitude.”
- *officiositas*: “a service” or “office.”
- *oramen*: “a prayer.”
- *victimare*: “to offer as a victim.”
- *sospitare*: “to save” or “greet.”
- *deliquium*: “sin.”
- *optio*: “occasion,” and also “petition.”
- *vindicium*: “vengeance,” for *vindicta*.
- *grassedo*: “thickness.”
- *sol* for *sole*; the distinction is one of Latin inflection.
- *multiplicus*: “multiple.”
- *versibilitas*: “changeability” and “inconstancy.”
- *inconvulsibiliter*: “in an unshakable manner.”
- *combinatus* for *imbutus*: “imbued” or “steeped.”
- *jugitas*: “perpetuity.”
- *dibellio*: “rebellion.”
- *potestative*: “by power.”
- *praesentiatiter*: “with present awareness.”
- *dulcoratus*: “sweetened.”
- *repriorans* [sense uncertain].
- *anticeps* [sense uncertain].
- *fulcimen*: “support.”
- *noxietas*: “harmfulness.”
- *taxatum*: “related” or “narrated.”
- *compactare*: “to form,” as if to fashion something.
- *pusillitas*: “smallness.”
- *mundiatis* [sense uncertain].
- *disertitudo*: “eloquence.”

And certain other expressions of this kind.

The confused genders, corrupted cases, and neglected numbers in nouns and verbs—indeed, the entire resulting disordered structure of the Latin language—were plainly the fault of the copyists, not of the author. For that reason we have not corrected all such matters, since in the rest we have allowed ourselves no such liberty.

## WHAT THE CONDITION OF THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION WAS IN CÓRDOBA UNDER ARAB RULE IN THE TIME OF SAINT EULOGIUS

### [Scan page 464]

When Spain had been occupied by the Saracens, the barbarian conquerors spared the Christians for many reasons. What moved them above all was that they themselves could not fill the broad and widely extended provinces of Spain with inhabitants.

Accordingly, so that there would be people to cultivate the fields, carry on the customary commerce, and pay tribute to the ruler, they preserved as many Christians as they could in Spain. The practice of their religion was left to them; in many places the churches remained untouched; and they were freely permitted to attend them according to the Christian rite.

At Córdoba, however, a larger number of Christians remained, and they retained an even greater degree of religious practice. For, in general, that city had already been distinguished by the Moors in many ways. The seat of the whole kingdom, which had stood at Seville for a few years—as reported by Rasis and by Ruderic, Bishop of Toledo, in his history of the Arabs, which has not yet been published—was transferred there by Abdalazim, the successor of Muza in the administration of Spain.

There they erected a fortress; there they built a temple, now still admired by the whole world amid so many immense buildings; and there they established schools of philosophy and public academies of learning. As is related in the history of King Alfonso, called the General History, they wished the city to possess these institutions and, once established as the capital of the kingdom, raised it everywhere to lofty grandeur and majesty.

It would take too long to review everything that was contributed at that time to the greatness and majesty of the city of Córdoba. Yet although the barbarians, competing with one another, brought whatever splendor they could to our city at that time, God Almighty nevertheless wished to make it illustrious with a far greater radiance, causing the Christian Church there—though captive, oppressed, and afflicted by many evils—to excel in religious observance and in love of the Catholic faith.

That Church, whose noble shoots of the Christian faith had already long before been watered by the blood of martyrs and had produced abundant fruits, now, more fully drenched by overflowing streams of sacred blood, gained for itself in heaven a more distinguished crown of glory and prepared for its citizens, for all time, a firm and certain pledge of God’s protection in still greater abundance.

The nature and magnitude of this divine gift of generosity will be explained more fully and abundantly in the books of Saint Eulogius.

And since Córdoba, together with the Arab empire, had been...

[scan page 465]

## Excerpts from Ambrosius Morales

With the council and see established there, they transferred thither all the highest rights of Spain, both sacred and secular; whatever dignity and authority the Christian religion possessed also moved there from the entire province. This does not mean that the Church of Toledo, as it was formerly—and still is—the primatial church of all Spain, ceased at that time to be regarded among us as the head of the Christian religion; nor that the Church of Córdoba failed to acknowledge its own metropolitan, the Church of Seville. Rather, because the tyrants could do everything and referred everything to themselves, they compelled the other bishops to assemble there for council, and wished there to deliberate and decide whatever matters they pleased. Two councils assembled at Córdoba during that period bear witness to this. One, which Saint Eulogius mentions,[^c0093-1] was celebrated by all the metropolitans of Spain together with their subject bishops; the other is mentioned in the *Apologeticus* of Samson, abbot of Córdoba, of whom we shall speak in his proper place.[^c0093-2]

And since the Church of Córdoba appeared to possess this greater authority—which, I say, arose from a truly miserable cause—many more churches, basilicas, and monasteries of men and women both remained there and were newly built, as the writings of Saint Eulogius testify. It will be worthwhile, for the glory of almighty God, to set down here a catalogue of the sacred places that existed at Córdoba, drawing especially on the books of Saint Eulogius. The following are said to have been within the city.

- The basilica of Saint Acisclus, martyr of Córdoba, where his holy body rested.
- The basilica of Saint Zoilus, martyr of Córdoba, in which his holy body had been buried.
- The basilica of the three martyrs of Córdoba, Faustus, Januarius, and Martial, where their ashes were preserved. This church is also mentioned in the ancient Annals that the Compostelan book contained at the beginning; we shall discuss that book in connection with Dominicus, martyr of the Saracens.[^c0093-3] There it reads:

> “In the year 1033, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, Count García Fernández of the Saracens was captured and lanced between Alcocer and Langa, on the bank of the Duero. He died on the fifth day, was taken to Córdoba, and buried at the Three Saints; from there he was taken to Cardeña.”

- The basilica of Saint Cyprian.
- The basilica of Saint Genesius, martyr.
- The basilica of Saint Eulalia, virgin and martyr.[^c0093-4]

### Outside the City

- The monastery of Saint Christopher, situated beyond the nearby river.[^c0093-5]
- The monastery of Cuteclara, in the mountains near the city, dedicated to the Virgin Saint Mary.
- The monastery of Tábanos, a cenobium built in those same mountains during the lifetime of Saint Eulogius.[^c0093-7]
- The monastery of Pinnamellariense,[^c0093-6] of the Holy Savior, likewise founded at that time in those mountains; its ruins can still be seen today.
- The cenobium of Armilat, on the bank of the Armilata River in the mountains, dedicated to Saint Zoilus.
- The monastery of Saint Felix, martyr, in the town of Froniano, among those same mountains.
- The monastery of Saint Martin in the mountains, near the town of Boiana.
- The cenobium of the holy martyrs Justus and Pastor in the mountains, near the village of Leiulense.

Palma, the town of Annanellos, and certain other small towns that are named also had their own churches. Among them, the village called Colubris had a church of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian. There was also, near Córdoba, a church of Saint Sebastian.

In these and many other churches, which Saint Eulogius could not name, the custom of teaching and educating very many people continued, in addition to the performance of sacred rites. Saint Eulogius teaches this in many passages, as does Alvarus in his *Life* of him. It also appears there that this was not an ordinary cultivation of learning, but one that surpassed the circumstances of the captivity and misery in which the faithful lived.

The churches themselves within the city also possessed their towers and bronze bells, by which they continually summoned God’s people. One small bell, preserved from those times, still survives at Córdoba, as we shall relate in its proper place.[^c0093-8] Priests, monks, and holy virgins, clothed in distinctive dress and lawful religious habit, and even tonsured, were publicly visible. All this is clear from Saint Eulogius and two other writers of the same age.[^c0093-9]

Yet these privileges were not granted without payment and continual new exactions, as the same holy martyr and others relate. Christians were forbidden, under threat of death, only one thing: they were not to assail their false prophet Muhammad with curses or disparage their law with reproach. If the faithful of Christ abstained from this, did not enter the Arabs’ temples, and paid their taxes, they could remain secure and almost free.

The dignity of counts also continued at Córdoba among the Mozarabs. This is established by Samson the abbot and by Cyprian of Córdoba, in writings composed during this very period. Saint Eulogius records that Christians held the public office of official secretaries and, among the royal attendants—of whom we shall speak in its proper place—were fed from the royal provisions, to use the holy martyr’s own words. When Samson the abbot begins his account of Count Servandus in the second book, he openly calls him “the count of Córdoba.”

We must therefore understand that, following the custom of the Goths, a count of Córdoba was assigned to the Christian Mozarabs, to preside over them, administer justice among them, and decide lesser disputes that did not belong to the public majesty of the king or to the royal treasury. In the Gothic period, as is shown especially by their laws, this was the particular and distinctive function of the count: to govern cities, whereas military duties were chiefly performed by commanders.

Among the clergy, in addition to the abbots who, as we have said, presided over the churches, the offices and dignity of archdeacons and archpriests also continued. Cyprian calls himself “archpriest of the see of Córdoba” in the titles of his epigrams. We shall shortly cite a mention of the archdeacon by the same author.

It is also worth knowing that our people had public libraries in the churches of Córdoba, so that anyone may easily understand how ardently our people pursued learning. Cyprian the archpriest celebrated in a long epigram one especially notable collection of books that Count Adulfus had placed in the church of Saint Acisclus. He also mentions another, which he largely composed at the request of Saturninus the archdeacon.[^c0093-10]

Yet, although these things were so, the Saracens, according to Saint Eulogius, entirely avoided contact with Christians as though it were a contamination; and their children publicly inflicted many unworthy indignities upon our people. The same holy martyr laments that the taxes were extremely heavy, especially the payments made every month. The Christian Mozarabs were also burdened with new taxes, to such an extent that they were compelled, under a newly devised impost, to pay a portion of the offerings of all the churches.

Samson laments this in the following words, speaking of Servandus, count of the Christians of Córdoba, but a wicked man:

> “From that time he made all the basilicas of the aforesaid city tributary, and the impious enemy sought to enlarge the treasures of the treasury from the purest offerings of the faithful, which had been contributed for the uses of the Lord’s temple: so that, by stripping Christ’s table and enriching the palaces of the treasury, he seemed to take water away from the thirsty and pour it into the vast bosom of the sea. Thus it came about that the basilicas themselves, enduring a venal priesthood, could not, according to their accustomed practice, admit the worthy and reject the unworthy priests.”

And what follows.

These things, however, were done six or eight years after Saint Eulogius’s martyrdom, as we shall show more fully in its proper place when treating Samson.

Moreover, although, as I was saying, the Christian congregation at Córdoba in Saint Eulogius’s time was relieved in its cruel captivity by the many and great consolations of churches, monasteries, learning, and the examples of most holy men, so that it could not seem altogether captive or deserted, it nevertheless possessed this true and solid consolation from divine goodness, and through that greater benefit experienced God’s great mercy: many martyrs then came forth from it, who confirmed the true faith among the living by their death and, once dead, rendered God’s mercy favorable to the living through their patronage. Saint Eulogius’s books, together with what we have added to them, will show more fully who and how many they were.

## The Chronological Account from the Works of Saint Eulogius

Before the year 850 of the Lord’s Nativity, from which we may conveniently begin our chronology, Adulfus and John, both of Hispalian origin, were crowned with martyrdom at Córdoba. (*From Book II, chapter 8.*) We cannot assign the year, except that they clearly seem to have been killed before the year 830.

Before that year Saint Eulogius also travelled to Gaul, visited the bishop of Pamplona and very many abbots of Navarre, and, on his return, stayed with and came to know the bishops of Zaragoza, Sigüenza, Complutum, and Toledo. (*From his letter to the bishop of Pamplona.*) In what year he made this journey is not sufficiently clear. We reasoned about it in its proper place, insofar as the evidence permitted.[^c0093-11]

### Year of the Lord 850

This is the first year that Saint Eulogius records at the beginning of the second book. It came after thirty complete revolutions of the solar cycle and was the nineteenth year in the thirty-first cycle; it was the second year following a leap year, and the Sunday letter was E. All these matters had to be noted here especially, since Saint Eulogius sometimes names the days of the week as well. From them we constructed the chronology of the period and confirmed it by manifest evidence.

This was the fourth year of Leo IV, supreme pontiff, who survived for another five years. (*From Onuphrius Panvinius.*)

Lothair, emperor of the Romans, was still alive and continued for five more years. (*From the same source and many others.*)

Michael Porphyrogenitus, successor of Theophilus and emperor of Constantinople, reached the year 867; this was his ninth year. (*From the same sources.*)

At the beginning of this year Ranimir, first of that name, ruled in Oviedo and León, succeeding King Alfonso the Chaste. He died on the first day of February and left the kingdom to his son Ordoño I. This is clearly established by his tomb, which we saw in Oviedo in the royal church called that of Alfonso the Chaste, bearing this epitaph:

> **RANIMIR, KING, DIED IN BLESSED MEMORY  
> ON THE KALENDS OF FEBRUARY, IN THE ERA 888.  
> I BESEECH YOU ALL WHO READ THIS,  
> THAT YOU DO NOT CEASE TO PRAY FOR HIS REST.**

Sampiro, bishop of Astorga, and Lucas, bishop of Tuy, likewise recorded this year as the year of Ranimir’s death. The very ancient tomb also shows that the epitaph was carved not long after the king’s death.

Íñigo Jiménez, surnamed Arista, held the kingdom of Navarre and the mountains of Aragon, as may be gathered from the more plausible reckoning of those times, although amid the great diversity of authorities nothing certain and indisputable can be affirmed here.

### Year of the Lord 850

Charles, surnamed the Bald, son of the emperor Louis and grandson of the emperor Charlemagne, ruled in Gaul. (*All the historians of Gaul.*) This was the eleventh year of his reign. The same Charles retained whatever his father and grandfather had taken from the Saracens in Catalonia, the mountains of Aragon, and Navarre. (*The Annals of Aragon; the historians of Gaul.*)

Habdarragman, the third Saracen of that name, ruled over a wide extent of Spain, with Córdoba established as the seat of his kingdom. This was the twenty-ninth year of his reign. (*From Saint Eulogius at the beginning of the second book, and from the history of the Moorish Rasis; likewise from the unpublished history of Roderic, bishop of Toledo, concerning the Arabs.*)

In this same year, on 18 April, which fell on a Friday, Perfectus, a priest of Córdoba, was crowned with martyrdom. (*Book II, chapter 1.*)

After him John was beaten almost to death for the faith of Christ, and, as the cause of the public spectacle, was carried through the city on an ass; he thereby attained the glory of a confessor. (*Book I.*) The time cannot be determined except that the event appears to have taken place in this year rather than the next.

### Year of the Lord 851

The letter marking Sunday in this year was D. On 3 June, which fell on a Wednesday, Saint Isaac, a monk of Córdoba, was beheaded. (*Book II, chapter 2.*)

Sanctius, a layman of Gallic nationality, was crowned with martyrdom two days later, namely on the following Friday, 5 June. (*Book II, chapter 3.*)

Only two days intervening, on the eighth day of the same month and on the first day of the following week, six holy martyrs were likewise slaughtered: Peter, a priest of Astigi; Walabonsus, a deacon of Niebla; Sabinianus, a monk born in the village of Froniano near Córdoba; Wistremundus, an Astigitanian monk; Habentius, a monk of Córdoba; and Jeremiah, likewise a monk of Córdoba. (*Chapter 4 of the same book.*)

On 16 July, which fell on a Thursday, Saint Sisenandus, a deacon of Pax Julia in Lusitania, completed his martyrdom by being beheaded. (*Chapter 5.*)

With only Friday, Saturday, and the following Sunday intervening, on Monday, which fell on 20 July, Paul of Córdoba gained the palm of martyrdom by decapitation. (*Chapter 6.*)

On the following Saturday, 25 July, Theodemirus, a monk from Carmona, was crowned with martyrdom. (*The same chapter.*)

Meanwhile Reccafredus, bishop, by order of the tyrant, grievously disturbed the Church of God at Córdoba and cast Saint Eulogius into prison. (*From the Life written by Alvarus, from the letter to the bishop of Pamplona, and from many passages of the second book, where we noted this very point.*) We cannot determine exactly when Saint Eulogius was captured. It can only be gathered from other indications that it occurred during these months, as we shall see in its proper place. He himself gives the reason for his imprisonment in the *Martyrdom Document* and in his letters: namely, that he encouraged the martyrs and incited them to martyrdom.

In this year Saint Eulogius recorded the martyrdom of the holy virgins Nunilo and Alodia, who did not suffer at Córdoba. We shall investigate the date in its proper place.

Flora of Córdoba and Maria of Niebla, Arab virgins, the latter being the sister of the martyr Walabonsus, were crowned together with martyrdom on 25 November. (*The following chapter.*)

[^c0093-14]: Elsewhere we discuss the history of Rasis the Moor and Roderic of Toledo, mentioned here.

### Year of the Lord 852

Six days later Saint Eulogius was brought out of prison. (*The same source and the letter to Alvarus.*)

Gumesindus, a priest of Toledo, and Servus-Dei, a monk, suffered death for the name of Christ on 13 January. (*Chapter 9.*)

The holy martyrs Aurelius and Felix of Córdoba, with their wives Sabigotho and Liliosa, accompanied by George, a monk from Syria, were killed on 27 July. (*The following chapter.*)

Christopher of Córdoba and Leovigildus of Niebla, monks, were beheaded on 20 August for confessing the Christian faith. (*Chapter 11.*)

Emilia and Jeremiah of Córdoba were crowned with martyrdom on 15 September. (*The following chapter.*)

Rogellus, a monk of Niebla, and Servus-Dei, a monk from Syria, were cruelly mutilated and beheaded on the following day, 16 September.

King Habdarragman, terrified by the steadfastness of so many martyrs, contemplated preventing martyrdom and ordered a council of bishops, including metropolitans, to assemble at Córdoba. (*From the following chapters.*) This disturbance of the king and persecution of the Church is entirely different from that which we related above. This is clear from the sequence of events itself in Saint Eulogius and from his words.

### Year of the Lord 853

At the beginning of this year King Habdarragman suddenly died. His son Muhammad succeeded him in the kingdom. (*Chapter 16 of Book II.*)

At the beginning of his reign Muhammad persecuted the Christians with extreme severity and destroyed the churches. (*The first four chapters of Book III.*) This is now the third persecution of the Church of Córdoba; I believe it is mentioned in the history of Saints Roderic and Solomon. (*From the years noted there in the *Apologeticus*.*)

Several Arab princes in Spain rebelled against King Muhammad. He burdened the Christians with taxes and aroused the hatred of his own people against himself. (*The following two chapters.*)

Fandila, a priest and monk of Guadix, was crowned with martyrdom on 13 June. (*Chapter 8.*)

On the following day, 14 June, Anastasius, a priest and monk; Felix, a monk of Complutum; and Digna, a virgin dedicated to God, received the crown of martyrdom. (*The following chapter.*)

Benildis, a married woman, was beheaded for the faith of Christ on the fifteenth of the same month. (*Chapter 10.*)

Saint Columba of Córdoba, a virgin dedicated to God, was beheaded and crowned with martyrdom on 17 September. (*The following chapter.*)

Pomposa, a virgin and martyr of Córdoba, died by the sword of the Saracens on 16 October. (*Chapter 12.*)

### Year of the Lord 854

Abundius, a priest from the village of Annanellos near Córdoba, suffered martyrdom on 11 July. (*Book III, chapter 13.*)

### Year of the Lord 855

Amator of Tucci, a young man; Peter, a monk of Córdoba; and Ludovicus, likewise of Córdoba, were all crowned with martyrdom together on the last day of April. (*Chapter 14.*)

Witesindus, an old man of Egabrum, was made a martyr in the same year. Saint Eulogius does not mention the day. (*Chapter 15.*) Morales and Schott are mistaken here in assigning it to the first day of May.

### Year of the Lord 856

Helias, an elderly priest from Lusitania, and Paul and Isidore, monks of Córdoba, suffered on 17 April. (*Book III, chapter 16.*)

Argimirus of Egabrum, a monk, was killed in confession of Christ on 28 June. (*The following chapter.*)

Aurea, a virgin dedicated to God and sister of the martyrs Adulfus and John, received the palm of martyrdom on 19 July. (*The final chapter.*)

### Year of the Lord 857

Roderic of Egabrum and Solomon suffered martyrdom on 13 March. (*From the *Apologeticus* of the saints.*)

### Year of the Lord 858

This year had no martyr, nor is there any mention of it in Saint Eulogius.

### Year of the Lord 859

Saint Eulogius of Córdoba, priest and teacher, and elected archbishop of Toledo, also became a martyr this year, on 11 March, which in that year fell on a Saturday. (*Alvarus, in his *Life* of him.*)

Leocritia, a virgin of Córdoba, on whose account and especially for the sake of the Christian faith Saint Eulogius had suffered death, followed her teacher four days later, that is, on 15 March, crowned with martyrdom. (*From the same source.*)

### Year of the Lord 860

On 1 June of this year the body of Saint Eulogius was transferred from the basilica of Saint Genesius to the basilica of Saint Zoilus, martyr. (*From another copy in which only the Life of Saint Eulogius was found.*)

These ten years alone are enumerated by the works of Saint Eulogius.

He added Pelagius, Eugenia, and Dominicus the Saracen, whom we have already said belong to the tenth century; and we have judged that their Acts should deliberately be omitted, since they contribute nothing to the elucidation of Eulogius.

## IV. On the Origin, Situation, and Antiquity of the City of Córdoba

Saint Eulogius inserted so much about our Córdoba in his works, and so frequently mentioned its districts, towns, fields, rivers, and similar matters, that it became necessary to set down here a good deal concerning its situation and antiquity. In the work that we added to our history of the antiquities of Spain, we treated more fully the origin and situation of Córdoba, its changes, and whatever else could contribute to investigating its antiquity. From there we shall transfer some material here.

Córdoba lies almost in the very center of the province of Baetica, among those peoples whom Ptolemy, Pliny, and Strabo call the Turduli. On the east that region extends as far as the Bastuli or Bastetani; on the west, touching the Turdetani, it ends in the territory of Seville. To the south it has broad open plains extending toward the Mediterranean Sea and the Strait of Hercules. On the northern side toward which Córdoba looks, it is situated at the very foot of the Marian Mountains, which the Spaniards now call, with the ancient name corrupted, *Sierra Morena*, that is, the Dark Mountains.

The part of these mountains overlooking Córdoba is either a portion of the Castulonian forest or joins it toward the east. In these mountains, according to Pliny, the region of Baeturia—taking its name from the river Baetis—is divided into two districts and stretches as far as the river Anas.

The Baetis itself, which flows past Córdoba and was formerly called Certis and also Tartessus, as in Pliny, Livy, and Strabo, has always enjoyed such renown that it gave its name to the entire province. It is moreover so large that, swallowing up immense rivers, it received its present name from the Moors. For *Guadalquivir*, the name now given to this river by them, means “great river” in their language.

From east to west, touching Córdoba’s southern side, it separates the mountains from the plain in such a way that nature seems deliberately to have intended this arrangement, in order to divide the most dissimilar kinds of soil and separate them as though by a boundary.

Hence the mountains, which almost touch the suburbs themselves, rise in lofty hills, are broken by hard and precipitous rocks, and are planted with gardens, vineyards, olive trees, and trees of every kind. Beyond the river lies a level plain, bare and crumbly with gravel and mud, suitable only for growing grain.

The fertility of this tract is sufficiently shown by the granaries of our distinguished city, which supply all Spain with grain. But the beauty of the other soil, which rises toward the mountains and is joined to remarkable fertility, scarcely anyone could explain with sufficient dignity. The very crags and cliffs themselves, wherever there is even a little level ground—for it is not truly soil, but a mass of stones—produce in abundance wild lotus and vetch, while cultivated land produces olives, vines, figs, cherries, pomegranates, peaches, and, most remarkably, citrons of every kind.

This is largely due to the abundant springs of the purest, sweetest, and healthiest water for drinking. Bursting forth almost everywhere from the earth, they irrigate all the surrounding country.

Hence the valleys nearer the city received their names from beauty, paradisal gardens, royal gardens, and the abundance of roses.[^c0093-15] Hence there is such a supply of wine and oil at Córdoba, and such an abundance of fruit of every kind, that this one feature could greatly ennoble any city, however famous.

Citrons of every kind abound so greatly in the city that they frequently amaze visitors and foreigners—not merely the heaps seen for sale in the streets at a low price, but also those that, when the new fruit arrives, are thrown into the fields and onto the dung-heaps. The trees are shaken at no small expense to remove the fruits, lest their excessive weight impede the flowers.

There is such abundance of flowers on these trees everywhere within the city and in the neighboring suburbs, and such fragrance in springtime, that what Virgil said of those same flowers is no longer sufficient:

> “May they soothe the souls and fragrant mouths of the citizens,  
> and heal their panting senses”;

rather, the whole city and the fields of the Ticinus are drenched with the sweetest scent, and at night people roam awake to catch that fragrance.

Yet we should not linger longer in celebrating the pleasantness and fertility of Córdoba. One testimony of the highest authority will suffice. It is that of Muza, commander of the Arabs, conqueror of the whole of Spain, who had travelled throughout it and knew every part of it thoroughly. Rasis the Moor, in his history of the Arabs, faithfully renders his words into Latin:

> “Abibus, son of Aluydus, a man who would never lie in any matter, wrote as follows: When Muza departed from Córdoba to sail to Africa, accompanied on his journey by the foremost men of Spain, and came to a hill from which a view of the entire city opened out, the mule on which he was riding turned backward.” He halted for a little while and silently contemplated the city; at last he burst forth with a groan in these words: ‘Alas, Córdoba, how remarkable you are! What and how great are your delights! How much good God has wished to bestow upon you!’ Having spoken these words, he continued his journey in grief.”

Thus far Rasis. No one can fail to judge this man a proper evaluator, when he sees that the excellence of the native soil itself compelled from him such groans, such words, and such praise.

The metals of Córdoba are also celebrated among authors. Poets call Córdoba “gold-bearing,” as will soon appear; and Pliny especially praises Marian copper, that is, the copper extracted in the mountains near the city, while today we see in that region extremely rich mines of quicksilver and antimony.

The city had two names, as we read in Pliny. For it was called Córdoba, and likewise Colonia Patricia. The name Córdoba was ancient and of very old origin; when the other name was given to it, we shall say in its proper place.

That Córdoba is the true and correct form of the name is attested by Silius Italicus, Martial, Prudentius, and other poets. The law of verse preserves names in a purer and less corrupted form.

The truth of this name could more faithfully be established from coins and stones. Some claim to have seen coins. But I, who have investigated such matters carefully and am especially devoted to the antiquities of my homeland, have not yet seen a Roman coin bearing the name Córdoba inscribed upon it, although I have seen the name Colonia Patricia on very many coins of Augustus, Tiberius, and Germanicus, some of which I possess myself.

I shall set down five stones on which both names, or one of them separately, occur. I myself saw and copied the first four; the last I learned from the report of highly learned men.

At the town of Linares, a black marble base, brought from the ruins of the very nearby city of Castulo, bears the following letters:

*[The inscription is materially illegible in the supplied scan.]*

> **CAES. P. LICINI GALLIENI**  
> **PII. FEL. ET. INVICTI. AVG.**

At Lorca, a town situated approximately halfway along the road from Córdoba to Seville, there is a marble base before the church:
