# Excerpts from Ambrosius Morales

## [Scan page 470]

At Hispalis (Seville), in a street called “the Serpent,” a stone bearing this epitaph is seen:

> Q. FABIUS, SON OF Q. FABIUS,  
> OF THE QUIRINA TRIBE,  
> FABIANUS ILURCONENSIS,  
> ALSO A PATRICIAN,  
> AGED FORTY-FOUR.  
> JUST AMONG HIS OWN.  
> HERE HE LIES.  
> MAY THE EARTH LIE LIGHT UPON HIM.

The name “Patrician,” however, came more freely into use during the time of the Roman emperors, as a more honorific and illustrious designation, as we shall see later, and was bestowed upon Corduba. I believe that the name Corduba remained uncorrupted together with the Roman empire and language down to the time of the Goths. Only then did it begin to change, so that it was called Cordova, as the Spaniards now pronounce it; yet this did not happen suddenly, but gradually, through the introduction of corruption.

Two Gothic gold coins that I possess, struck with sufficiently different types, bear witness to this. They belong to Reccesvinth, king of the Goths. On one side, together with the king’s own face, they bear the inscription:

> RECCESVINTHUS REX

On the reverse is written in a circle:

> CORDOBI

On the other side:

> PATRICIA,

so that the *u* had already been changed into *o*, while the *b* had not yet been changed into *v*. In the same manner, both in the old copy of the blessed Eulogius and in all the books written in Gothic letters that I have seen—very many of them—the form *Corduba* is always found.

So much concerning the names of our city. Now its antiquity must be discussed.

I am led to believe that Corduba was a very ancient and venerable city, whose origin, because of its extreme antiquity, has no beginning preserved in human memory, chiefly for two reasons.

First, it is established that all the cities in Spain which in ancient times, during the Roman period, were called by two names possessed one Spanish name—ancient, of the most remote origin, and, as it were, the vernacular name of their own language—and another name impressed upon them as a mark of Roman rule and empire, or certainly expressed through the flattery of their rulers.

Such were, in Celtiberia, *Illurcis*, called *Graccuris* by Tiberius Gracchus after its name had been changed, as Verrius Flaccus records; and *Salduba* in the same region, later called *Caesaraugusta*, according to Pliny. According to the same author, and also attested by ancient stones, *Obulco* received the title *Municipium Pontificense*. *Attubi* was called *Claritas Julia*; *Astigi*, *Julia Firma*; *Tucci*, *Augusta Gemella*; *Iliturgi*, *Novum Julium*; and *Hispalis*, *Colonia Romulensis*.

There are many examples of this kind in that author, and in ancient marbles and coins there are numerous duplications of names belonging to cities. In all these cases one cannot deny that the earlier name was vernacular and Spanish, and that it shared the antiquity of the city’s origin.

Such was Corduba, later surnamed *Colonia Patricia*. As a witness to its antiquity it possesses its ancient name, given to it long ago, as it were, at its birth.

A further consideration can establish the extreme antiquity of our city. Since Strabo reports that the Turduli were the most ancient and wisest of all the peoples in Baetica, and since the site of Corduba surpasses all others in fertility and beauty, it is reasonable to believe that a settlement was founded there many centuries ago, and that the inhabitants of that region did not neglect so excellent a place for habitation.

Therefore, just as nothing certain can be brought forward concerning Corduba’s origin, so it is rightly believed that the city itself was of the greatest antiquity.

Some assert that Corduba was founded by the Persians, whom Pliny, following Varro, also says came to Spain. The name of the city itself, I think, drew them into this opinion, for they believed that there was also a city called Corduba in Persia. But the conjecture is slight, and so entirely unsupported by any foundation in truth that, when the opportunity arises in our history, it will be easy for us to overthrow it.

Among authors one finds no earlier mention of Corduba than that which occurs in Silius Italicus. In his catalogue of the cities of Spain that sent soldiers to Hannibal when he crossed into Italy, he also included Corduba in these verses:

> Nor did Corduba cease to be the glory of its gold-bearing land.

Nor can it be established with sufficient certainty in which place Corduba was first founded, since two sites of the same city now appear. One is occupied by the city itself; the other, which lies at the fourth mile west of the city near the famous monastery of the blessed Jerome, is seen abandoned under the ancient name of Corduba.

Nevertheless, I am led by no slight conjectures to believe that the ancient city stood on the same site as this younger city now occupies. We shall demonstrate this when we have dealt with what must necessarily be set forth beforehand.

The next particularly notable and celebrated mention of Corduba after that of Silius Italicus is found in Strabo. He reports that Corduba was, as it were, founded by Marcus Marcellus and shortly afterward greatly enlarged. In the third book of his work are these words:

> “Corduba, a foundation of Marcellus, grew to such a size that it enjoys renown and power.”

[The Greek wording in the supplied scan is illegible.]

I see that these words have moved not a few learned men to believe that this was the original foundation of our city and that Marcellus himself was its true founder. It will therefore be necessary to investigate the whole matter carefully and examine it more precisely.

It is established from Livy and Appian of Alexandria that Marcus Marcellus—the son, grandson, or great-grandson of that Marcus Marcellus who taught that Hannibal could be defeated—received all Spain as his province during his praetorship in the very year in which Quintus Marcius Philippus for the second time and Gnaeus Servilius Caepio were consuls. That year was 167 before the birth of Jesus Christ our Lord.

Marcellus assumed the government of the whole of Spain in that year because the two provinces had been formed into one only two years earlier. He also undoubtedly built Corduba in that same year. Since it is clear that the city was built at this time—for from then onward it is mentioned increasingly often and appears at once in Roman history—and since Strabo calls it Marcellus’s work, while no other Marcellus, either in earlier years or for many succeeding years, came to Spain with magistrate’s authority, it is plain that the construction of the city must be attributed to him.

Without doubt Marcellus completed whatever work there was in that year, not fifteen years later, when he returned to Spain during his third consulship. At that time Spain was again divided into two provinces, and he governed only Hispania Citerior, which had been disturbed by great wars and required a consular commander and army. In that same year Hispania Ulterior—that is, Baetica together with Lusitania—had its own separate praetor, Marcus Acilius, as Appian records.

But what, finally, was it that Marcellus did, so that he is said either to have founded or to have built Corduba? I shall say what I think, and what the evidence almost plainly indicates.

## [Scan page 471]

[…he] broke out into these words with a groan: “Alas, Corduba, how illustrious you are! How many and how great are your blessings! How many good things God has wished to confer upon you!” Having said this, he continued his journey in sorrow. Thus far Rasis. No one can fail to judge him a fitting appraiser, when he sees that the truth of the matter itself and the excellence of its native soil drew from him such groans, such an utterance, and such high praise.

The mines of Corduba are also most celebrated among writers. Poets, as will shortly appear, call Corduba gold-bearing; and Pliny especially commends the Marian bronze (*aes Marianum*), that is, what is dug in the mountains near that city. Even today we see in its district very rich mines of quicksilver and antimony.

That city had two names, as we read in Pliny. For it was called Corduba and likewise Colonia Patricia. But the name Corduba was ancient and of very remote origin; in its proper place we shall say when the other name was bestowed upon it. Silius Italicus, Martial, Prudentius, and other poets attest that *Corduba* is the true and correct form, for the metrical law preserves more uncorrupted and uncontaminated words.

The authenticity of this name could indeed be established more reliably from coins and inscriptions. Some affirm that they have seen coins; but I, who have investigated these matters with care and have been especially devoted to the antiquities of my native country, have so far seen no Roman coin inscribed with the name Corduba, although I have seen the name Colonia Patricia on very many coins of Augustus, Tiberius, and even Germanicus, some of which I possess. I shall set down five inscriptions in which both names, or one of them separately, occur. I myself saw and copied the first four; I possess the last on the report of very learned men.

At the town of Linares there is a black marble base, brought from the ruins of the very nearby city of Cástulo, inscribed as follows:

> [Fragmentary inscription; several readings are materially uncertain in the supplied scan.] To Valeria … Patina, of Sacitanum; of the colony of Corduba; priestess of the divine Augusta; of Tucci Augusta Gemella; priestess … or priestess of the municipium … Tulonense.

In former years at Corduba a marble base, with the head and fragments of the limbs of a statue, was dug up, bearing this dedication:

> To the Divine Manes. To Cornelia Salonina Augusta, wife of our lord the imperator Caesar P. Licinius Gallienus, pious, fortunate, and unconquered Augustus, conqueror of the Dacians and greatest conqueror of the Germans, holder of tribunician power for the fourth time, consul for the second time, acclaimed imperator for the third time, father of his country, and proconsul: the Colony Patricia of the Cordubans, devoted to his divine power and majesty.

At Corduba, in the church of Blessed Saint Mary, there is a stele whose surviving inscription is too damaged in the supplied scan for a reliable transcription.

He built a new city on the site that is now called the Old City and raised it entirely from its foundations. Since there had previously been a settlement there that was not especially large, he decided to move it elsewhere and enlarge it on another site. Re-establishing the city in a new form—Roman, certainly—he completed it as a city founded and named after himself.

He therefore built the city that is now called Old Corduba. This is demonstrated by the form of the city and by its entire structure, which the ruins still display and which clearly declare that it was wholly constructed as Roman work according to Roman planning.

The whole site is square in form, so that it appears plainly to have been laid out and marked off at the beginning with a straight line. Its entire circuit is twice as long as it is wide. I measured it carefully with a cord: having found 2,400 feet along the front, I discovered exactly 4,800 along the side.

By “feet” I mean one-third of the Spanish ell, by which we measure linen and silk cloth; this corresponds closely to the measure of the ancient Spanish foot.

Such precise care in squaring and doubling the dimensions belonged entirely to the Romans, not to our Spanish people, who have only in our own time begun to learn the form of more refined construction.

Moreover, in the middle of the square city there projects a level area, also square in form—whether it contained a citadel or a forum—which clearly appears to have been laid out according to a perpendicular. It is equally distant from both fronts; on the upper side—for the entire city was placed upon sloping ground—it joins the wall for a short distance.

Who does not see that such care and such subtle attention to form and symmetry belong to the Romans rather than to the ancient Spaniards?

There are also the foundations of four great towers, clear testimony of the same Roman industry and architectural purpose, since they were attached to the four corners of the walls.

An indication of the same Roman symmetry is a road paved with square stones. It leads from the lower side of the city, joined—as one may believe—to a gate, toward a nearby hill where the remains of some large building still survive. One may reasonably conjecture that an important temple once stood there, to which the noble paving and the greater convenience of the road were owed. The place, separated from the city and only slightly elevated on level ground, does not invite the supposition that it was a fortress.

All these features belong to a man building with the greatest care, as though he had been sitting at leisure over the construction.

The peace of Spain, which Livy and Appian describe, shows that Marcellus had almost the entire year available for this work.

It would take too long to continue recounting how many Roman remains have been unearthed in the site of this city during earlier periods and even in our own age. They plainly establish that the city was Roman and that Marcellus, himself a Roman man, was its founder.

Since it is already sufficiently clear from what has been said above that, before Marcellus’s construction, an ancient settlement called Corduba existed in those places, we cannot clearly determine whether Marcellus incorporated the old site into his work or selected a new one. The following facts will indicate that, having disregarded the old settlement, he transferred it entirely to a site he himself had chosen.

After the city had been rebuilt in this manner and magnificently enlarged, Roman history mentions it much more frequently. The settlement, previously not especially famous, had grown, and it now began to be ennobled by the Romans as a thoroughly Roman city.

Soon afterward praetors recalled their armies there for winter quarters, and the people assembled there to seek justice. We discuss all these matters at length in our history, collecting them from Roman and Greek writers.

From there Metellus Pius, after defeating Sertorius, brought to Rome a group of poets who were citizens of the city. If, as Cicero said of them, they sounded somewhat coarse and foreign, that was a fault of the age, not of their talents. Rome itself did not then possess more cultivated poets.

The praetor Piso also furnished that celebrated example of strict restraint and extreme frugality, as Cicero records. Since the words of the greatest orator themselves are worth presenting, I shall set them down:

> “I shall bring forward nothing excessively ancient. There are many of you, gentlemen, who knew Lucius Piso, the father of this Lucius Piso who was praetor. When he was praetor in Spain—the province in which he was killed—while he was engaged in military operations, his gold ring, which he was wearing, was somehow broken and shattered. Wishing to have a ring made for himself, he ordered a goldsmith to be summoned in the forum, to his seat at Corduba, and publicly weighed out gold for him. He ordered the man to set up his seat in the forum and make the ring in the presence of everyone.

> “Someone may perhaps say that this man was excessively careful. Let anyone criticize him thus, if he wishes; let him say nothing further. Yet this much must be granted him: he was the son of that Lucius Piso who first carried the law concerning extortion.

> “It is ridiculous for me now to speak of Verres after having praised the frugal Piso. Yet observe how great the difference is. When Verres was making gold vessels for certain friends, he took care that not only in Sicily but even at Rome, during the trial, he should make the whole of Spain know that a half-ounce of gold had been used to make a ring for the praetor. Thus, just as he established his name, so he also established his nickname.”

[See *In Verrem*, book IV, no. 25.]

Not long afterward came the period of the civil wars between Caesar and Pompey, during which Corduba is called by Aulus Hirtius—or perhaps Oppius—the capital of the entire province of Baetica. Many indications clearly show that all those events took place in the Corduba built by Marcellus, which is the city under discussion here. Most notably, after the bridge had been crossed, battle was repeatedly joined between Caesar and the city itself. But this is not the place to treat those events.

A little later, in the time of Caesar Augustus, when Strabo both lived and wrote, that author could rightly assert with distinguished praise that Corduba had grown to such a size that it possessed power through its renown and fame.

For it had shortly before been made a colony; and it had not been granted the dignity of an ordinary colony, but one distinguished in name and majesty, so that it was and was called *Colonia Patricia*.

The same author, while still speaking of Corduba, wrote these words:

> “At the beginning it was inhabited by selected men, both Romans and natives.”

For this was the first colony sent to these places by the Roman people.

Behold, then, Corduba as the first colony in Spain—or at least in Baetica—and one distinguished by great dignity and, as it were, by precedence. Both facts are remarkable and singularly contribute to Corduba’s fame and glory.

Nor is there space here to explain at length how great this distinction was. I shall pass over only this point: Corduba obtained such dignity—that only men of patrician rank, both Romans and Spaniards, were selected to immigrate into the colony and make it the most illustrious home of both kinds of nobility—chiefly because of the extraordinary loyalty and steadfastness with which it always supported the cause of Julius Caesar in that war and often protected and preserved Roman citizens.

The coins of that city, from the time when it first became a colony, bear witness to this. They all have *Colonia Patricia* inscribed on the reverse, and they display the same designation enclosed within a civic crown.

Who does not know that among the Romans the civic crown was both the reward and the distinction of one who had saved a citizen? I therefore believe that Julius Caesar granted Corduba this reward when he made it a colony.

Certainly Seneca the Elder, when speaking of the civil wars, already calls it Corduba the colony; and on coins of the colony of Corduba we see the face and name of Caesar Augustus.

I fully understand from Livy that Carteia was a somewhat older colony in Baetica. Yet the saying of Strabo presents no obstacle to this, as anyone will readily understand who observes from what class of people—namely, the Parthenii and freedmen—that colony was settled.

## [Scan page 472]

[Fragmentary inscription; its surviving letters in the supplied scan do not permit a reliable translation.]

Aristotle, moreover, in the *Politics* (book III, chapter 16), teaches that only great cities were accustomed to possess a *puteal*, that is, an underground prison excavated in the likeness of a well.

We read in Horace, in more than one passage, of the *Puteal of Libo* at Rome; we also see it depicted and inscribed on silver coins. No one has ever doubted that all these objects, together with many other inscribed Roman stones visible in various places throughout the city, were brought here at different times from ancient ruins.

In that city of Marcellus, then, were born the two Senecas, father and son; Lucan; Porcius Latro; and other distinguished Cordubans whom Seneca the Elder mentions.

The same city also produced the famous and brave citizen Aemilius Regulus, who, together with others who followed him as their leader, conspired against the life of the emperor Caligula. “While private hatreds,” says Josephus (*Jewish Antiquities*, book XIX, chapter 1), “were stirring the others, only public wrongs moved him.”

How long that old city founded by Marcellus endured, and at what time it was transferred, through the relocation of the settlement, to the site it now occupies, I cannot explain with certainty, though I would very much like to do so. I shall bring forward what I can establish by conjecture.

In the time of the emperors Tiberius and Caligula, the old city of Marcellus not only still stood but remained highly renowned and flourishing. This is indicated by ancient coins found there bearing the face and name of Germanicus; on their reverse they have *Colonia Patricia* inscribed within a civic crown.

Nor have many such coins ever been found together, as though they had been deliberately deposited; rather, one or another appears to have fallen accidentally and been lost. Yet no one has ever said that he found there coins of the emperors who followed.

Moreover, the city’s renown at that time was too great to have suddenly collapsed, when the Romans ruled us in complete peace and tranquillity. It must have required mature deliberation over many years and a long period of preparation before the inhabitants could entirely move away from it.

A new city also had to be founded, and many things had to be procured with great effort. The migration—

## [Scan page 473]

The fact itself testifies that there was a migration and a change of settlement, and I shall show this shortly afterward.

We may therefore believe that the city stood for more than sixty years after Caligula and endured down to Trajan. Then nearly two hundred years passed, up to the reign of Diocletian, during which we find no mention of Corduba in the authors.

There remained only the marble base of which we have already spoken. It was found, together with fragments of a female statue, in the house of García Méndez de Sotomayor, bearing an inscription to Cornelia Salonina, wife of the emperor Gallienus.

But in the time of Diocletian there can be no doubt that the old city had already perished and that the new city, which exists today, had become extremely famous.

The surviving monuments of the holy martyrs crowned at Corduba in that period bear witness to this. There is the house of the holy Acisclus and Victoria, in which they were brought up; there is the tomb which, according to their Passion, stood at the river gate; there is the well into which part of the entrails of the holy martyr Zoilus was thrown; and every one of these places is venerated throughout the whole city with great devotion.

Thus no devout person could now endure the claim that these holy martyrs suffered in the old city.

The same must be established concerning the three holy martyrs Faustus, Januarius, and Martialis. Since it is certain that the Goths held this new city, and since during the reign of King Sisebut Agapius, bishop of Corduba, found there the body of Zoilus—who revealed it to him in a dream, the same body that had been missing since the time of his martyrdom—it must certainly have been in this city that he had been tortured and killed.

For we read that the pagans concealed his body among the graves of strangers so that it would not be recognized by Christians. The same martyr, as the history of his discovery relates, indicated both to Bishop Agapius the place where he had suffered and the place where his concealed body lay.

All these facts can clearly prove that this new city was founded during the time of Diocletian and his fellow emperors—that is, around three hundred years after the birth of our Lord—and after the old city had been destroyed.

That marble stone, therefore, excavated near the church of Saint Nicholas, as it is called, within the city, and inserted into its wall—for its inscription indicates that it was the base of a statue of the Caesar Constantius—once served as the base of a statue. It appears to have been dedicated in this new city, rather than brought from the old one.

Someone might also suppose the same concerning the statue and base of Salonina.

Among the citizens, the generally accepted explanation for this change and for the occasion of Corduba’s rebirth is a shortage of water from which the old city of Marcellus supposedly suffered, since it was nearly four miles distant from the river.

I, however, see that nothing could have been less responsible for the change. Within the city’s own site, springs emerge in more than one place. Near the walls, toward the east, there is also a very large spring, which received its name from the abundance of watercress: *Fuente de los Berros* (“Spring of the Watercresses”).

The gardens of the friars of Saint Jerome, near this spring, likewise received their name from the abundance of springs: *Los Hontanares* (“The Springs”).

Furthermore, a larger channel, from which the same monastery of Saint Jerome now draws its water, ran into the city through the valley itself and along the projecting ridge. A portion of its aqueduct, built of square stone, still remains at the very source of the spring. The remainder was consumed by the structure of the monastery itself, which used similar stones.

Even if wells were dug, especially in the lower parts of the city, they would certainly have supplied an abundance of water most convenient for every use.

Since this is so, we must believe that the unhealthiness of the site, together with its inconvenience for habitation, were the chief reasons for transferring the city.

Marcellus had selected a site that was unsuitable in many ways for establishing a city. First, he placed it so far from the river, although at that time the river offered very great advantages for navigation. The city could be fortified neither by its position nor by its construction.

For the city was lowered through that slope onto level ground, while the mountain ridges tower above it in such a way that the walls could be overwhelmed and demolished merely by rolling down stones and rocks, even ones not especially large, of which there is an abundant supply in the heights.

But the unhealthiness of the site is especially noteworthy. The same lofty mountains protect the northern side of the city so completely that it cannot in any way receive the northern winds, which are considered the healthier winds.

Since the entire site extends lengthwise from east to west, while its breadth stretches downhill from north to south onto the plain, the whole city lay exposed to the sun’s heat, which is particularly intense in that region.

The lower buildings could not shield the higher ones on the slope or prevent the heat from joining their effects, while the steep mountain summits blocked whatever relief might have been provided by the cold north winds.

This is why the entire site of the old city still abounds in scorpions: the fertility of the place in producing poisonous creatures reveals the defect of its unhealthy character.

This in particular makes me believe that ancient Corduba, which existed before Marcellus, stood on the site now occupied by the city, and that Marcellus later returned to that same place because of its remembered and proven healthfulness.

## [Scan page 474]

Once the new city had been restored, or founded anew, it retained, as far as I can conjecture, its square form.

Two sides of the walls, laid out with exactness, survive together with the ancient work and, indeed, the traces of Rome itself: from the citadel to the gate called del Sol, following the southern side beside the river; and from there to the gate called de los Ángeles, on the eastern side.

The foundations of the two other sides have been confused, I believe, by the Moors, who removed, added, and altered them in many ways.

Apart from the fact that this square form and the square stones indicate Roman construction, the spacing of the gates on the eastern side is itself wholly Roman. When they opened five gates, they placed one in the middle—the gate called Ferrea, now destroyed, though its name remains—and then added two at equal intervals on either side.

Four of these still remain: Sol and Ángel at the corners; and the two middle gates, now called *portulillas* through a slight alteration of the word, one situated at the quarter of the Emporio and the other at the Fuente Seca. Each received its name from its location.

Our Corduban people do not doubt that all the ornaments of public and private buildings were transferred from the old city of Marcellus into this new one. Hence there are in the city many statues of Roman workmanship, many inscribed stones, and many marble columns and other objects of this kind, visible everywhere.

Nevertheless, we proved above that some of these belonged originally to the new city itself.

It is now clear how greatly the common people of our city are mistaken when they claim that the house now joined on the south to the public senate-house and facing almost opposite the church of Saint Benedict was Seneca’s house.

Long ago the most illustrious Pedro de Córdoba, first Marquis of Priego, purchased it, moved by this belief, and gave it as a gift to my father, the excellent physician Doctor Antonio Morales, saying that the house of the wisest Corduban ought to be possessed only by the wisest Corduban.

I was born in that house. But who cannot now see that it never belonged to Seneca? We have discussed this matter at greater length in our history and in our account of the antiquities of Spain.

When I mention Seneca, I always mean Seneca the Elder, the father of Seneca the philosopher. For the latter, Nero’s tutor, was never in Corduba except perhaps as a very young child; he was taken from there to Rome by his father when he was almost an infant.

Still, it would not be right to pass over in silence the fact that, although no mention of Seneca himself survives in the ancient monuments of Corduba, his family name is found on a very ancient base.

Recently Hieronymus Morales, my paternal cousin, a young man highly distinguished for talent and learning and most devoted to antiquity, arranged to transfer it to the house of his father, my brother, Doctor Augustinus Oliva, himself also an excellent physician.

It bears the following inscription:

[scan page 476]

“To Fabia [?] Prisca, daughter of Gnaeus, of Asido: Fabius Seneca and …eria Prisca, daughter of Quintus.” [The first name is damaged and the second dedicator’s name has a lacuna.]

This new city too had its own magnificence in Roman times, since it possessed a teacher of Greek letters who could maintain the title of grammarian—at that time the mark of the most distinguished learning—and who, besides, had this quite singular distinction: he lived for more than a hundred years. His jasper monument still exists in the house of that same brother of mine, Doctor Augustinus Oliva, with this inscription:

[Inscription, partly uncertain in the scan]

D. M. S.  
DOMITIUS . ISQUI-  
LINUS . MAGIS-  
TER . GRAMM.  
GRAECUS . ANNOR.  
[uncertain]

“To the spirits of the departed. Domitius Isquilinus, Greek master of grammar, [aged] [uncertain] years. He lies here. May the earth be light upon him.”

This inscription, however, belongs to a later and more barbarous period, as both the already-debased characters and the words themselves, together with the neglected orthography, show. I therefore gave this stone to the new city.

This new city, then, once itself distinguished and famous, but thereafter much more famous because it had been consecrated by divine favor through the blood of illustrious martyrs, passed from the Romans to the Vandals and from them finally to the Goths, among whom it was always held in high esteem. It was able by itself to undertake war against King Agila and to put him to flight after inflicting a great defeat.

The same city joined Ermenegild, the son of King Leovigild, then a prince and later a renowned martyr, when he rebelled against his father, and embraced the cause of the Catholic faith in a pious war. John, abbot of Biclarum, who lived at that very time, left it written in his *Chronicle* that the holy prince, after the war had been concluded, was captured by his father at Córdoba; for he had fled to the friendly city that supported his cause.

I also possess a gold coin of that prince, and I venerate it as an excellent memorial of the most holy martyr, since it is clear that it was struck during that sacred war. I hope I shall give the readers great pleasure if I describe it here.

On one side it bears the youthful face of the prince himself, with the letters **ERMENEGILDI**. On the other it displays a winged Victory, so that, by its appearance, under God’s leadership and aid, it might instill in the hearts of his followers a firm hope of attaining victory. The inscription surrounding the Victory, since it is wholly heavenly and remarkable, makes it quite plausible that the holy prince used the same words in that war as a military password. They are:

**RE6EM DEVITA** [apparently **REGEM DEVITA**, “Avoid the king”].

Anyone even slightly versed in the sacred writings immediately sees that this was taken from Saint Paul’s words to Titus: “Avoid a heretical person after the first and second admonition” (Titus 3:10).

Everything was so subtly, prudently, and piously conceived and adapted that it may be believed to have been devised by Leander or Isidore—most holy men, outstanding in learning and talent, and also the uncles of Saint Ermenegild—and handed over to the prince, who was piously in rebellion, as a symbol and password.

This coin was found near Córdoba, at the third milestone, in the field called *Casa Blanca*, that is, “White House.” We may also suppose that it was struck at Córdoba. Both the city’s immense renown and those coins of King Reccesvinth, about which we spoke earlier, show that there was a mint there. For no other reason could the name of Córdoba have been placed upon those coins in that manner, except that they had been cast and struck there.

But all this, together with the other fortunes of our city, we pursue at length in our *History of the Affairs of Spain*.

**Thus far Morales.**

## Notice to the Following Appendix

When all the material that Ambrosius Morales commented upon in his several works concerning Saint Eulogius had been reviewed, together with what he wrote about the antiquities of Córdoba, we thought that, for the better understanding of those works and for the readers’ benefit and pleasure, we should append the following two monuments. One concerns the holy martyrs Georgius, Aurelius, and Natalia; the other concerns Abbot Speraindeus; all are frequently mentioned in the writings of Saint Eulogius.

The first contains the history of the translation of the relics of the aforesaid holy martyrs from Córdoba to Paris. Saint Eulogius described their glorious contest in chapter 9 of Book II of the *Memorial of the Saints*. This history was written by Aimoin, a monk, and first published by Jean Mabillon; we reproduce it here because it most fully illuminates the glory of those martyrs.

The second work is a brief treatise, or refutation, of certain heretics who denied the Trinity of persons in the unity of substance and the divinity of Christ. It was written by Abbot Speraindeus, who was the teacher of Saint Eulogius and Alvarus. They never mention him without great praise for his virtue and learning, as will be clear to anyone reading Eulogius, *Memorial of the Saints*, Book I, no. 7, where he inserts a fragment of another work by that same teacher, and in the *Life of Saints Flora and Maria*, and anyone reading Alvar in the *Life of Saint Eulogius*, chapter 1, no. 2; no one will wonder that this work, previously unknown but now newly discovered, should first come to light together with the works of his most distinguished pupil.

Father Flórez had indeed already published, in vol. X of *España Sagrada*, p. 441, the two letters preceding this little work: the first from Alvar to Abbot Speraindeus, the second Speraindeus’ reply to Alvar. He lamented, however, that this dogmatic treatise, which Alvar had requested from him, could nowhere be found. We have been permitted to see it through the efforts and generosity of the Reverend Father Master Paul Rodríguez, who arranged for a copy to be sent to us from his royal monastery of Saint Benedict at Sahagún.

[scan page 477; continuation of the notice]

We name this man with honor: his abundant learning acquired by constant reading and his exceptional, profound knowledge of Spanish history, both ecclesiastical and civil, have been at our disposal in the present edition of the holy Fathers of Toledo. This most diligent investigator and highly expert judge of such remains obtained his copy of this little work from Don Carlos Espinos, canon of the holy Church of León. Espinos, thoroughly skilled in diplomatics and in the whole of our history, and tireless in examining and elucidating ancient documents, himself transcribed it from a very ancient codex of that holy Church.

## Translation of the Holy Martyrs Georgius the Monk, Aurelius, and Natalia from Córdoba to Paris

By Aimoin, monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, from the very ancient manuscript of Saint Germanus at Paris, no. 653.

### Mabillon’s Preliminary Observations

1. Aimoin, a monk of the monastery of Saint Germanus at Paris, whose books concerning the miracles of Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, we have elsewhere published, committed to writing in one book the history of the translation of the holy martyrs Georgius, deacon and monk of Bethlehem, Aurelius, and his wife Natalia. To this he added two books concerning the miracles performed during their translation.

Jacobus Brolius, a monk of the same monastery, published these books mutilated in many places. Here we have thought it appropriate to reproduce them complete from an ancient codex written in the author’s own age.

2. Saint Eulogius, priest of Córdoba, described the acts of these martyrs in *Memorial*, Book II, chapter 10, where he calls Natalia “Sabigotho.”

She distributed her possessions among the poor together with Aurelius, her husband. Both of them regularly visited monasteries of men and women, but especially the monastery of Tábanos, which was considered the most famous in those regions and was suitable for both sexes.

Natalia often withdrew there. She gave her two daughters, Felicitas and Maria, to God in that place.

Later, at Maria’s request, Eulogius recounted the passion of Aurelius and Natalia, her parents. Aimoin, as I believe, abridged it under Eulogius’s name, in the form in which it appears in our manuscript.

Georgius, a monk from Bethlehem, joined these two—that is, Aurelius and Natalia. From his adolescence he embraced the service of God and spent twenty-seven years at the monastery of Saint Sabbas, eight miles south of Jerusalem, living under regular discipline with five hundred brothers.

He was sent by the venerable David, abbot of that monastery, to Africa to procure provisions for the monks. Finding there the Church of God harassed by the tyranny of persecutors, he travelled to Spain on the advice of the bishop of Carthage. Arriving at Córdoba, he later proceeded to the monastery of Tábanos so that, on his return—for he was preparing to return to his homeland—he might be strengthened by the blessing of the brothers and holy sisters living there.

There the abbot of that place, named Martinus, and his sister Elisabeth, dedicated to God, presented him to Natalia. He returned to Córdoba with her the following day.

At last, he was arrested with them, with Felix, and also with Liliosa, and was killed by the sword together with them in the year 852. Their bodies were buried in various places, and those of Georgius and Aurelius in the monastery of Pinnamellaria, from which place this translation took place.

Aimoin learned the course of the translation from Usuardus and Odilardus, monks of Saint Germanus, who were his authorities; Usuardus himself was the author of the *Martyrology*. Aimoin saw with his own eyes the miracles performed at Acmantum—which is a village in the diocese of Sens, subject to the monastery of Saint Germanus, where the monks of Saint Germanus had then taken refuge with the body of Saint Germanus out of fear of the Northmen—as is related in Book III, chapters 46 and 49.

The *Bertinian Annals* mention this translation under the year 858 in these words:

> “A certain monk returning from the monastery of Saint Vincent the Martyr, or of Saint Germanus the Confessor, from the city of Córdoba in Spain, brought with him the bodies of the blessed martyrs Georgius the deacon and Aurelius, and the head of Natalia, and placed them in reliquaries at the villa of Arcmantum to be preserved.”

These relics are preserved among us to this day in the monastery of Saint Germanus.

## Preface to the Translation of the Cordoban Martyrs Georgius and Aurelius

If it is impossible to explain in words all the miracles that God and Lord of all has granted to his faithful, then it is certainly often thought excessive to set them down in writing. The Apostle and Evangelist John testifies that Jesus performed many other signs

[scan page 478]

in the presence of his disciples which are not written in the book of the Gospel.

But since it is said that those signs which concern faith and eternal life have been inserted there, it is considered a fault if all the works of the saints, flourishing with miracles, are concealed in silence, as though the mirrors of divine instruction were obscured by a cloud of miserly reticence.

Therefore, in order to explain the events surrounding the translation of the holy martyrs Georgius and Aurelius, although unworthy, I have nevertheless approached this task as one laboring in the household, summoned by a suitable request, so that I might at least lay branches in the road before those domestic animals who carry Christ by faith.

I have not been driven by presumption or sophistical recklessness, but rather by the example of the canonical writers, which calls for imitation, and by the venerable Fathers’ admonitions and most gentle commands. Careful consideration showed me that persisting in resistance to these was wrong.

The divine majesty, which cooperates with us, is raised up while the divine flock resounds and, with the Psalmist, says: “Wonderful is God in his saints, and holy in all his works.” If those deeds are recounted by which the holy friends of God are shown to have radiated with admirable virtue even after their triumphant departure from the flesh—he who rewards them after the momentary battles of their passion, as though they had labored in the camps of the heavenly army, with the everlasting rewards of consolation—then he grants that, crowned with the prize of victory, they may rejoice eternally in the place where he himself is delighted in everlasting blessedness.

## Book I: Translation of the Same Holy Martyrs, Celebrated on [unclear numeral] before the Kalends of November

### Hilduin being abbot and the king in power, men are sent to seek Saint Vincent’s body from Spain, but in vain

1. In the year 858 of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, and in the [ordinal uncertain: supplied *auodHvigesimo*] year of the reign of Charles, son of the glorious Emperor Louis, the bodies of the holy martyrs Georgius and Aurelius were brought out of Córdoba and conveyed into Gaul in a memorable manner.

At the monastery of the Holy Cross and of the blessed martyr Vincent, where the precious confessor of God, Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, shines in the honor of his miracles, it was widely reported that the body of that same holy martyr and deacon could readily be obtained from Valencia, the city in which he suffered, because that city had been grievously devastated by Saracens or Moors. Therefore the brothers of our monastery, with the support and approval of Lord Hilduin the Second, their abbot, and with royal authorization, arranged to send men there, longing, by Christ’s gift, to bring this so great and long-desired pledge back to themselves.

2. Having set out, the brothers who had been sent came to Hunfrid, margrave of Gothia (Languedoc), then ruler in those regions, in order to proceed in this pious undertaking with his assistance. When he had received them at Beaune in the manner befitting nobles, mindful of his promise, he immediately summoned his men and began carefully to deliberate about the reason for their arrival and how the matter ought to be carried out.

Some of them maintained that the places on that route were everywhere beset with dangers, so that no one, even protected by a large escort, could safely undertake the journey. Our men, on the contrary, persevered, citing the Apostle: “If God is for us, who is against us?” and likewise: “For we walk by faith, not by sight.” They then entered with him the district of Uzès, where they learned from the religious bishop Walefrid—as they had already heard at Viviers—that the body of the blessed martyr Vincent had been transferred from Valencia to Benevento. This, however, was otherwise.

For a monk in Aquitaine, warned by a divine revelation, as he himself told us, hastened to Valencia and carried it away with him. The bishop of Zaragoza, called Senior, seized it from him by force; at Zaragoza it was kept beneath the veneration due to a certain martyr Marinus and shone with no small miracles. This was the name which the monk professed; nor could the bishop, even by torturing him, force from him Vincent’s true name. The monk knew that Vincent had been archdeacon of that city; he therefore feared that Vincent would be dearer to the bishop, and irrecoverably lost to himself. Consequently both the bishop and our men were entirely unaware that the saint’s body was present there. Marinus was believed among them to be a martyr of illustrious merit. Yet they learned certainly that it was no longer at Valencia. How this happened, and how, years later, the monks of Saint Benedict’s monastery at Albi recovered it and transferred it to that same place, may be seen in our sufficiently full account of the translation of that holy deacon and martyr.

### They deliberate concerning another holy body

3. Our men grieved and wept anxiously that, after so much labor over so long a journey, they would return empty-handed. While they stayed at the fortress of Barcelona, lingering there, to use their own words, as though worn down by a prolonged illness through this sickness of grief, and could neither decide nor deliberate what course would be more prudent, they finally approached a man familiar to them, named Sunifridus, of the same [source breaks off mid-sentence].

[Continuation repeated in the supplied scan:] where he inserts a fragment of another work by that same teacher, and in the *Life of Saints Flora and Maria*, and anyone reading Alvar in the *Life of Saint Eulogius*, chapter 1, no. 2; no one will wonder that this work, previously unknown but now newly discovered, should first come to light together with the works of his most distinguished pupil.

Father Flórez had indeed already published, in vol. X of *España Sagrada*, p. 441, the two letters preceding this little work: the first from Alvar to Abbot Speraindeus, the second Speraindeus’ reply to Alvar. He lamented, however, that this dogmatic treatise, which Alvar had requested from him, could nowhere be found. We have been permitted to see it through the efforts and generosity of the Reverend Father Master Paul Rodríguez, who arranged for a copy to be sent to us from his royal monastery of Saint Benedict at Sahagún.

We name this man with honor: his abundant learning acquired by constant reading and his exceptional, profound knowledge of Spanish history, both ecclesiastical and civil, have been at our disposal in the present edition of the holy Fathers of Toledo. This most diligent investigator and highly expert judge of such remains obtained his copy of this little work from Don Carlos Espinos, canon of the holy Church of León. Espinos, thoroughly skilled in diplomatics and in the whole of our history, and tireless in examining and elucidating ancient documents, himself transcribed it from a very ancient codex of that holy Church.

## Translation of the Holy Martyrs Georgius the Monk, Aurelius, and Natalia from Córdoba to Paris

By Aimoin, monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, from the very ancient manuscript of Saint Germanus at Paris, no. 653.

### Mabillon’s Preliminary Observations

1. Aimoin, a monk of the monastery of Saint Germanus at Paris, whose books concerning the miracles of Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, we have elsewhere published, committed to writing in one book the history of the translation of the holy martyrs Georgius, deacon and monk of Bethlehem, Aurelius, and his wife Natalia. To this he added two books concerning the miracles performed during their translation.

Jacobus Brolius, a monk of the same monastery, published these books mutilated in many places. Here we have thought it appropriate to reproduce them complete from an ancient codex written in the author’s own age.

2. Saint Eulogius, priest of Córdoba, described the acts of these martyrs in *Memorial*, Book II, chapter 10, where he calls Natalia “Sabigotho.”

She distributed her possessions among the poor together with Aurelius, her husband. Both of them regularly visited monasteries of men and women, but especially the monastery of Tábanos, which was considered the most famous in those regions and was suitable for both sexes.

Natalia often withdrew there. She gave her two daughters, Felicitas and Maria, to God in that place.

Later, at Maria’s request, Eulogius recounted the passion of Aurelius and Natalia, her parents. Aimoin, as I believe, abridged it under Eulogius’s name, in the form in which it appears in our manuscript.

Georgius, a monk from Bethlehem, joined these two—that is, Aurelius and Natalia. From his adolescence he embraced the service of God and spent twenty-seven years at the monastery of Saint Sabbas, eight miles south of Jerusalem, living under regular discipline with five hundred brothers.

He was sent by the venerable David, abbot of that monastery, to Africa to procure provisions for the monks. Finding there the Church of God harassed by the tyranny of persecutors, he travelled to Spain on the advice of the bishop of Carthage. Arriving at Córdoba, he later proceeded to the monastery of Tábanos so that, on his return—for he was preparing to return to his homeland—he might be strengthened by the blessing of the brothers and holy sisters living there.

There the abbot of that place, named Martinus, and his sister Elisabeth, dedicated to God, presented him to Natalia. He returned to Córdoba with her the following day.

At last, he was arrested with them, with Felix, and also with Liliosa, and was killed by the sword together with them in the year 852. Their bodies were buried in various places, and those of Georgius and Aurelius in the monastery of Pinnamellaria, from which place this translation took place.

Aimoin learned the course of the translation from Usuardus and Odilardus, monks of Saint Germanus, who were his authorities; Usuardus himself was the author of the *Martyrology*. Aimoin saw with his own eyes the miracles performed at Acmantum—which is a village in the diocese of Sens, subject to the monastery of Saint Germanus, where the monks of Saint Germanus had then taken refuge with the body of Saint Germanus out of fear of the Northmen—as is related in Book III, chapters 46 and 49.

The *Bertinian Annals* mention this translation under the year 858 in these words:

> “A certain monk returning from the monastery of Saint Vincent the Martyr, or of Saint Germanus the Confessor, from the city of Córdoba in Spain, brought with him the bodies of the blessed martyrs Georgius the deacon and Aurelius, and the head of Natalia, and placed them in reliquaries at the villa of Arcmantum to be preserved.”

These relics are preserved among us to this day in the monastery of Saint Germanus.

## Preface to the Translation of the Cordoban Martyrs Georgius and Aurelius

If it is impossible to explain in words all the miracles which God, the Lord of all, has granted his faithful to perform, it is certainly often considered excessively laborious to embrace them in writing and to wish to cover all these things, as the Apostle and Evangelist John bears witness, who says that Jesus performed many other signs… [The supplied page ends here. The next supplied page resumes later in Book I.]

[scan page 480]

## Translation of Saints Georgius, Aurelius, and Natalia

[Continuation of Book I; the intervening source is absent at this scan boundary.]

Eulogius, who himself later received the crown of glorious martyrdom and, as a perfected soldier, sought Christ the King, committed the account to writing in a truthful narrative, omitting many things—as he himself reported to our men.

9. While these matters were being considered, it happened by divine providence—for this must undoubtedly be acknowledged—that the aforesaid priest Samson was appointed abbot of the place called Pennamellan, where the bodies of the holy martyrs lay buried, about five miles distant from the city.

At once, as though the opportunity had been secured, summoned by Leovigildus they unanimously decided that, since the time had come and the place was open, the desired undertaking should be brought to completion, with Christ’s favor.

After they had deliberated for a very long time, sometimes joined by brothers from other places, they discovered that the others were so opposed to their efforts that they sadly judged the matter could in no way be permitted.

Nevertheless, they continued to press the point, repeatedly insisting that their purpose was to ensure that the bodies of the blessed martyrs would be honored with a more celebrated cult. Finally, by common deliberation, everyone agreed that it should be done, provided only that the consent of the proper bishop be obtained, as was fitting and as was done.

When the time came for the return, the bodies of the saints remained buried in that same place under this concession. I therefore think that I should explain what difficulty arose for them when they were leaving the city, from which they dared depart only with great relief.

## War of Muhammad. Saul, Bishop of Córdoba, Favors the Monks

10. The king of Córdoba, Muhammad, ruler of that foremost and distinguished Saracen city, hastening to war against the tyrant of Toledo, who had rebelled against his decrees, ordered everyone to be present.

By public edicts he commanded that no citizen or foreigner, except those assigned to the guard, should remain in the city without accompanying him.

Meanwhile, when our aforesaid brothers began to speak to the monks of the above-mentioned place, Pennamellan, about the bodies of the martyrs that had been granted to them—for the opportunity to leave the city was now open—the monks once more categorically refused to do anything of the sort, especially in the absence of their venerable abbot Samson; for it happened that he was away.

Accordingly, becoming very sad, they sent certain faithful men to the bishop of that city, a modest man named Saul. They asked him to obtain, by his own arrival, from the inhabitants of that place the holy bodies that had been granted to them through the kindness of Abbot Samson and of the bishop himself.

The messengers accepted this request and immediately hastened away. They conveyed the bishop’s command and earnestly begged that he come to the aid of the foreigners and assist those who had been left desolate.

They therefore said to the bishop:

> “Father, we humbly beseech your piety by our earnest prayer that the bodies of the blessed martyrs Georgius and Aurelius be given to the Gallic monks, just as you formerly arranged with Abbot Samson. Why, then, should those exhausted by the hardship of their journey be unjustly harassed by delay over the pledge that has been granted to them? It is not right that this should come to the knowledge of your religious community, which could be defamed by such a charge.”

There was no delay. They hastened to the place. After a lengthy dispute, and after the bishop had struggled greatly with petitions, consent was granted—indeed, reluctantly, as from men unconquered, and only with difficulty was agreement obtained.

The sacred remains were then raised, though not the body of Saint Aurelius nor the head of Saint Natalia.

11. At that time our petitioners, summoned and proceeding eagerly, approached together with the others. No less energetically, they began to excavate the bodies of the saints after removing the altar above them.

When they came to open the tomb, the other persons were dismissed, and only the priests designated by the bishop remained. With the bishop himself receiving them, they lifted the sacred members from the tombs amid hymns and litanies.

Wrapping them continually in clean linen cloths, they also placed them in suitable vessels for carrying them away. With divine assistance, the secret undertaking was honorably completed.

To ensure that their integrity would not be violated by anyone who might seek them for any reason before they reached their appointed destination, they asked the bishop to seal them with his own seal under the authority of King Charles.

After he had done this, the relics, to be carried and venerated with many attestations, were entrusted to them, though secretly because of the pagans. For the Saracens do not permit the veneration of those whom they make martyrs.

Rejoicing at the reward of so great a gift, they took up the relics and, accompanied by several brothers, hurried back to the city, eager to travel as far as Toledo with certain others who were going there.

12. Moreover, I do not doubt that it would be wicked to pass over in silence the admirable way in which provision was made for this matter.

When the ministers of the devil had struck down those bodies, strong in the contest of the heavenly battle, by a death inflicted with the sword, Christians, whenever they could, stirred by the solitary duty of love, came by night. Secretly taking the bodies for themselves, they divided them.

They carried away and buried the body of Saint Georgius intact, but that of Aurelius without its head, in the church beneath an altar, as we have said.

But while the body of Saint Natalia, having been separated from the others, was carried away elsewhere, her head was buried in the same church where her husband’s body lay.

Thus it happened that, when they were exhumed, the head of the blessed athlete Aurelius was not found with his body, and it was unknown where the sacred body of Natalia had been buried.

But so that the saying might also be fulfilled in them after death—“the two shall be one flesh”—the head of Natalia, his wife, was substituted for the head of blessed Aurelius and placed with his body. It was given to those who sought it with immense wonder, and we believe that no one who hears of this divine deed can remain unaware of it.

Since they had lived as companions in a single marriage and had likewise been companions in equal martyrdom, so in death they were to share the same honor of veneration on earth, just as they share the one happiness in heaven.

And since, through the mystery of the sacrament, we have digressed a little from our undertaking by speaking, as it were, in an excursus (*oikonomikōs*, “by way of arrangement”), it is fitting to return to the matter itself.

## From Córdoba They Travel to Toledo, Then to Complutum and Zaragoza, Afterwards to Barcelona, Then Gerona and Narbonne, and Finally Béziers

13. When the day was already pouring its rosy light over all the earth with the full force of the chariots of dawn on the vigil of Christ’s Ascension, they prepared to leave the city of the aforementioned King Muhammad, whose army was setting out.

A considerable company of Catholic brothers gathered to bid them farewell. No one could adequately describe the affection with which, during the fifty-six days they had lived together, they had treated them.

Their present devotion, however, or rather their tearful conduct, revealed how great it was; anyone could see that they did not wish ever to be separated from them by any event.

Thus they left Córdoba, the most renowned of the Iberian cities, rich both in citizens and in material resources. For a time they were entrusted to the protection of certain faithful men who were going with the king to war, and then they cheerfully resumed their journey.

Several days later, Leovigildus met them among the armies. He was a man worthy of frequent remembrance, who, because he had been occupied with royal business when they left the city, had not been present.

Embracing them with the sweetest affection of his heart, he thereafter did not permit himself to be absent from their company all the way to Toledo, which is renowned because of the confession of the blessed virgin Leocadia.

His sister Babilla, a virgin consecrated to God, had generously prepared, according to her means, whatever they might need during the journey, including two cloaks with which the bodies of the saints could be covered in turn.

14. Finally, when the king of Córdoba was hastening his military forces against the tyrant of Toledo, the reason for his expedition, many ambushers from that same city returned to it, hastening to fortify themselves as quickly as possible with the protection of its fortresses. When peace had been restored— [sentence continues beyond the supplied fragment]

[scan page 481]

## APPENDIX TO THE WORKS OF ST. EULOGIUS

… the roads are rendered secure, and the travelers’ progress is safe wherever they go.

Then our men, with great kindness and affection, abandoning their military preparations, separated from the aforementioned Leovigild and set out for Complutum, a town distinguished by the trophies of the glorious martyr-brothers Justus and Pastor. From there they proceeded to Caesaraugusta, a most noble city crowned with the triumph of the saints, and especially of its eighteen martyrs. They approached the citadel, where they were again received humanely by the bishop mentioned above and, for as long as they wished, were granted excellent hospitality by him. Nor even then were they able either to learn anything more certain or to hear anything concerning blessed Vincent, whom that same bishop, as we related above, retained under the name of the martyr Marinus. For, after the monk Audaldus, who had carried out the translation, had been driven away, there was no one to disclose the knowledge of this affair.

They were also presented to Abdilvar, the previously mentioned governor of that same city, giving thanks because they had been assisted by his support both on their outward journey and on their return. On departing from him they received greetings for Hunfridus and letters for the guardians of the castles, so that they might pass through the fortified places under his authority without any impediment or examination. For, lest an embassy of deceitful persons should unexpectedly be sent against them, or, more certainly, a hostile attack should descend upon them, they continually strive to block access to all the roads with guards, especially those places which they call excluded from the imperial route.

> That is, “vice-count.” See below, Book I, 1, *On Miracles*.

# HERE BEGINS THE FIRST BOOK OF THE MIRACLES OF THE HOLY MARTYRS, THE SECOND BOOK OF THE TRANSLATION

## Chapter I

We are therefore compelled, by the worthy order of events, to set down for the remembrance of future generations the things that we learned had been accomplished in the same city of Béziers and by them on the journey that followed, under the governance of supreme mercy.

While they were staying for a time with the aforementioned Gerinus, who was keeping them there for the sake of rest, a certain man named Brictius lay for almost half a year ulcerated throughout his shins and upper genital parts by an elephantine and incurable disease. He appeared not only mutilated in body by this weakness, but also deprived of the comfort of life, since such affliction had laid hold upon him.

For one night he was allowed to lie in the church where the bodies of the holy martyrs were located. Through their intervention and divine mercy he was so completely cured that, restored to health immediately on the following day, he stood before everyone’s astonished eyes and resumed his customary work. For he was a favorite servant of his master, that same Gerinus, and served as his cupbearer.

## Chapter II

What has been said, and what is still to be said, we learned from those very men who, being present while these events took place, saw them with their own eyes. Moreover, he already seemed to be preparing the sacred miracles that the Lord was to bestow upon the people through them.

That same night, this further miracle is known to have shone forth amid a twofold proclamation of the holy martyrs. A certain young man named Guisandus had suffered painfully from a form of fever for three months and could suspect nothing about himself except the approach of death. For he was afflicted hour after hour by the sharpest alternations of cold and heat, now tormented by one, now by the other.

He was allowed to keep vigil during the night at the aforementioned bodies of the saints, with a similar confidence in their power to heal; and by no different miracle his fever was driven away and he was cured. Giving thanks, and himself restored to no small degree of health, he returned home.

## Chapter III

Although we have already heard that others there were cured of various illnesses through the merits of the saints, we have hastened to relate one further miracle that shone forth there with even greater distinction, so that it would not be left unmentioned.

The aforementioned Gerinus, vice-count of the same city, was suddenly afflicted throughout his body by an exceedingly severe torment of pain. Taking two candles of his own height, and one valuable pallium—still preserved as testimony—he ordered himself to be carried, since he had little hope of remaining alive, into the presence of the martyrs. Lying there and rolling upon the ground, he publicly confessed with humbled spirit what he had committed against them and the reason for his suffering.

At the first sleep of the night, through the saving visitation of blessed George, he was suddenly relieved and, having obtained a cure, awoke in that same church. For he said that the same holy martyr had appeared before him in the monastic habit that he had formerly worn, holding a golden pyx in his hand. From it he poured an ointment white as snow and gently anointed his head, eyes, and hands, as he himself perceived.

Exactly as he later declared, while he was still gathering peaceful sleep upon his eyes, health spread through his limbs. Revived in his whole body, Gerinus returned home rejoicing, no longer doubting that they were martyrs—indeed, proclaiming them the most powerful of martyrs.

## Chapter IV

After about two months had passed, when they had recovered their strength and prepared what was necessary for the journey, our men, the aforementioned brothers, departed from that city and reached the district of Viviers (*le Vivarat*), not without miracles, since Gerinus himself accompanied them.

When they heard that the body of the holy martyr Fructuosus, a disciple of the great Polycarp—who is known to have been a hearer of blessed John the apostle and evangelist—was not far from the place, they devoted themselves zealously to venerating it. After receiving relics of his own body, they returned to complete the journey that remained, and from there …

[scan page 482]

# TRANSLATION OF SAINTS GEORGE, AURELIUS, AND NATHALIA — BOOK III

After receiving relics of his body, they returned to complete the journey that remained; and from there, after four days, safe and sound, they were received by Reimundus,* from whom, in a village called Apaliacus, they were gladly welcomed by Hunfridus. They explained to him, since he was very eager to hear it, what had happened to them on the journey and what they had obtained through the gift of divine generosity. When he had learned these things, the count himself gave thanks with amazement, ordered the necessities to be supplied, and dismissed them with gifts.

> *From the district of Belna, so called from Belna, a town in the diocese of Chalon; Aimon likewise dealt with this above.*

## Chapter V

But because the Lord had determined to magnify his servants, proven by faith and confession, through their virtues, and to show by signs what merit each possessed before him, it is worthy to report the miracle that occurred in the same district of Viviers and in the village itself of Argilly.

A certain widow named Theothildis lost a horse through the unjust violence of a certain plunderer, whose spirit was swollen with pride. Mournful, she tortured herself with weeping and languished in despairing grief. When she had concluded that no ingenuity and no human consolation could restore the animal to her sorrow, she went to await the assistance of the same holy martyrs, with complete confidence in the hope of recovering it.

There she remained for a long time, weeping and persevering in prayer to God, who administers judgment to the injured, until on the third day the plunderer, struck by an inspiration of heavenly fear, was compelled to satisfy the widow and voluntarily return what he had apparently taken away.

Thus faith obtains its reward, and divine fear produces its effect.

## Chapter VI

As we hasten onward and wish to reach the end of this little book, let us recall and relate what happened in a certain village called Cora (*Core*), in the district of Auxerre.

When the holy relics had been brought into the church of that place and reverently displayed upon the altar, a certain young man entered secretly while the custodian was absent for a short time and suddenly stole the pallium with which their sacred relics were covered. But the most equitable action of supreme righteousness did not permit him either to escape unpunished for long or to inflict injustice upon the holy martyrs.

In the place where he had hidden it, he was immediately struck by a malignant pustule. On returning, he secretly threw the pallium at the church door; then, seeking an impunity he did not deserve, he fled and concealed himself. But as the discomfort caused by the ulcer grew more severe, he was compelled by fear, by the despair of life, and by the pain of the torment to confess his crime.

When it had been disclosed and laid bare before all who heard it, he obtained, although long afflicted, the aid of complete health through the benefits of the saints, by the grace of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns, almighty, throughout infinite ages of ages. Amen.

> In Book I, no. 3. In that district there is a village called Argilly, of which mention is made immediately below.

# HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE OF THE SECOND BOOK OF MIRACLES, THE THIRD BOOK OF THE TRANSLATION

We have related, in part, the order of the translation of the holy martyrs George and Aurelius and the miracles that, by God’s gracious favor, they performed on the journey through the assistance of their merits. Now let what remains be set forth; and although the writer is unskilled, let the account nevertheless be faithful. It seemed fitting to divide these matters into two books, so that neither the eager readers would find them superfluous nor the devout hearers be burdened by what is to be related at length.

For the very fact that, while one volume ends and another begins, some relief is provided by the length of the narrative; and because the preceding little book was adorned—not by human, but, I confess, merely by a predetermined arrangement—with twice three titles of miracles, the numerical structure of the series itself shows how fully it indicates the consummation of the same holy martyrs.

# SECOND BOOK OF MIRACLES OF THE THIRD TRANSLATION

I think it laborious to relate in full how they adorned the journey with such manifest miracles, but pleasing if it is recounted in part.

## Chapter II

When they had turned aside to a village in the same district called Puteoli (*Puteaux*) for the celebration of the solemn Masses, a very young boy came among the others seeking benefits, for he was ill.

Some of those present encouraged the child and advised him to approach the patronage of the martyrs as best he could, in order to obtain the remedy of health. When he had done this, he crept forward and threw himself prostrate before their relics rather than walking. Immediately, in the sight of everyone present, he obtained the medicine of complete health.

He departed upright, I say, so that he might accompany them from there, although he had arrived lame through the weakness of both feet.

## Chapter III

Nor should it be unpleasant to hear what Christ, the co-worker of goodness, was pleased to accomplish for the merits of his soldiers. If it pleases him, we make another person’s good our own.

There was therefore a certain old woman named Tedelgrima, who, from childhood—as many of her neighbors knew—had lain equally deaf and mute. She was being supported out of mercy in the house of a religious man named Bovo, to which, perhaps, the same holy bodies had also turned aside to remain.

She considered that the alms given on earth to the poor are received in heaven by Christ, as Martin’s half-cloak bears witness. Carefully reflecting with herself upon the remedy of the health she desired, she climbed to the place where the bodies of the blessed martyrs were being venerated.

But as soon as she had poured out her prayer, she was granted the grace of healing. Thus, through a miracle renewed in the same hour as the Gospel miracle, she deserved to speak and hear at once; and she went out rejoicing, bringing joy to the entire household.

## Chapter IV

What Bovo himself said, with the faithfulness of an oath, had happened to him at the arrival of those martyrs must not be passed over, since it is a matter worthy of a miracle.

When the monks who were carrying the holy relics had been received that night, nearly thirty of them together with their companions, the hospitable man distributed the necessities to them with a cheerful spirit, himself not being a deaf hearer of the apostles’ teaching.

But so that the overflowing work of such great and abundant charity might be rewarded, the vessels of his wine cellar were found in the morning as though nothing had been drunk from them the previous evening. For wine had been poured so abundantly for everyone—for his entire household, its servants, and those who had arrived because of the holy martyrs—that all, filled to satiety with wine in suitable sobriety, rejoiced.

The wine cellar was situated beneath the granary, which drew blessing from above; that was where the bodies of the blessed martyrs had been admitted to rest that night.

## Chapter V

The same Bovo often related, with wonder, another event not unlike this one.

After the bodies of the saints had been carried out of his house, it happened on the fourth day that men from the army of Hludwig, king of the Bavarians, entered it and, remaining there for several days, ravaged it inhumanely.

Although Hludwig had gone forth, deceived in this hope, at the invitation of certain nobles, intending to invade and usurp the kingdom of his brother, lord Charles, who was at that time fighting the Danes with a naval fleet on the Seine, he nevertheless seemed, alas, to have already placed victory within his grasp, and to have squandered it through such an unfortunate tyranny.

For, when the king had been left with only a few men on the ship, without being greeted, all who had treacherously adhered to him departed. Having cut the ropes of that ship, so that the king would not be aided by any protection, they approached the same Hludwig and made him their king; this became, to their disgrace, a fitting insult.

The king, therefore, divinely delivered, immediately gathered the small army that faithfulness had preserved for him and nobly expelled his brother from the kingdom. Although he could have captured him alive, he mercifully granted him a place of departure. He also received his fleeing followers, although he could have taken royal vengeance upon them, welcoming them back to himself with his customary compassion after he had regained the scepter and the kingdom.

Thus the aforementioned enemies, exterminating beyond measure the property of the house they had entered, carried away from Bovo’s wine—so it was thought—not less than sixty *modii*. But when they had departed, the entire quantity was found restored through the merits of the saints, as Bovo testified.

There was no need to hesitate before believing that the wine had increased through charity, which, poured into the man’s heart, flourished with a double goodness.

## Chapter VI

In Villeneuve-l’Archevêque, in the same district of Sens, there was a certain girl named Arochild. She had been deprived of the light of both eyes by eight years of blindness. When she was brought to the blessed martyrs, renowned for the light of their virtues—and of whose benefits we are speaking—she dedicated herself to them by a vow of perpetual service. She was suddenly cured, so that all who were present were astonished at the event.

Afterward, wishing to fulfill the service she had vowed, she was severely rebuked by her father as though she had presumed upon a rash undertaking. She was compelled to change the decision of her promise, although she knew that it had been made for the sake of her salvation.

As soon as she began, favoring her father’s words, to return home, she incurred again the former calamity of blindness and, in addition, a severe fever. Her father and the rest of her relatives became mournful, and she herself lay in a most pitiable state. They hurried back to seek the pious assistance of the martyrs.

When her father had compelled her in every way to swear that she would never again fail to keep what she had promised, she recovered the full health that she had previously obtained. She remained there and afterward joyfully paid the appointed service at fixed times in the worship of the church.

## Chapter VII

As they approached the village of Acmantum (*Bmant*), a possession of ours—where at that time the greater part of the brothers were living because of the grievous persecution of the pagans*—they were received by the inhabitants with great expressions of thanks and abundant praise, in a manner sufficiently worthy.

The Lord wished to adorn their reception with such flowers of virtue that no one could doubt that precious testimonies, rather than anything ordinary or uncertain, had been brought to them.

A certain nun named Leutgardis was mingled with the crowd of people who had come out to meet them. She too carried a lighted candle in honor of the saints, when suddenly she was deprived of the honor of its light. Ashamed that it had failed, she hid it secretly for the time being in a folded garment.

But what Christ accomplished thereafter to display his martyrs must by no means be concealed. While she walked along in this way, waiting for the time when she might relight it, the candle was suddenly kindled in the very place where it had been hidden, and it caught the part of the garment covering it.

When the woman saw this, she was terrified. Raising her voice as loudly as she could in praise of so great a miracle, she caused the event to be made known.
