Even though the woman remained silent, the scorched portion of the garment declared the event plainly and greatly astonished those who saw it.

> *See the Annals of Bertin for the year 858, when these events occurred; there the translation of the holy martyrs is mentioned. Brolius mutilated this entire passage, together with several others.*

## Chapter VIII

Then Boso of the village of Alise lay so paralyzed from the waist downward that he was deprived not only of the ability to walk but even of the ability to sit. It was painful to behold his condition.

When he heard of the signs of such great gifts, he was carried among many others by the hands of his relatives. He approached the relics of the holy martyrs, so near to his illnesses, and was immediately flooded with remedies of the health he requested. He did not leave them but, by his own efforts and steps, followed them all the way to the church into which they were to be carried.

After a few days he was made entirely whole and returned home with a joyful spirit. His neighbors congratulated him and marveled that health had come to him so quickly.

## Chapter IX

That same day a woman from a village called Rethica, named Regina after the place, was also brought there. For twelve years she had lain crippled in her loins—not, like the Syrophoenician woman, suffering from a flow of blood—and seemed already deprived of the vital support of life. She was oppressed by extreme poverty and hunger, as well as by the idleness imposed upon her hands.

When she was presented among the rest of the crowd to be healed through the patronage of the blessed martyrs, she recovered before the assembled crowds the use of her former happy condition. Walking and joyfully giving thanks to her healers, she restored herself, with the aid of others’ hands, to the journey by which she had come, now proceeding with the step of a healthy person.

## Chapter X

Adalbert of the village of Talsiniac, greatly fearing an enemy attack, vowed to the lights of the holy martyrs one vessel full of bees, for the protection of others.

Suddenly, some men from the army of the aforementioned Hludwig, king of the Bavarians, broke into his house. Being greedy for the honey, they first tried to carry away that hive, because it was larger and better than the others. But, despite their astonishingly futile efforts, it remained immovable, as though it had been fixed firmly into the ground in the place where it stood.

The enemies, disturbed and greatly astonished by this, eventually learned that it had been dedicated to the holy martyrs for the preservation of others. Consequently, they not only refrained from touching that hive but did not dare thereafter to show disrespect toward the saints anywhere in the same house, having perceived that divine protection was present there through their merits.

## Chapter XI

Because the venerable praises of miracles grow together, let the number of pages increase along with the glory.

For many years Ingalbert of the village of Vimpopuli had been deprived of the gift of light in both eyes. When he learned of the many and very wondrous virtues of the saints, he ordered himself to be taken there as quickly as possible.

With the assistance of his wife and accompanied by much confidence, he set out and reached the place. Entering the church, he remained for a long time prostrate on the ground, persevering in prayer and groaning, imploring in mournful words that the holy martyrs would have mercy on him, unworthy though he was.

Then, when the fountain of heavenly mercy flowed into him through their intercession, he immediately deserved to be healed. Magnifying God and the saints, he returned from there able to walk and see, no longer needing the support of his wife’s hand.

## Chapter XII

Two blind men from a village called Simportus were also brought to seek the splendid mercy of the blessed martyrs. Their whole devotion obtained no small share of divine mercy, and goodness that gives sight to the blind.

When they entered the house where the sacred relics of the martyrs were honorably venerated and devoted themselves to prayer, the darkness that had covered their eyes soon fled. They deserved to recover the ability to see. Rising from the pavement, they dismissed their guides and ran about here and there, seeing clearly.

Thus praising the provident kindness of God and of the holy martyrs toward them, they departed rejoicing, like those once illuminated in the Gospel by the Savior, the Son of David.

## Chapter XIII

When the fame of these miracles had spread widely through the districts, many people flocked together, hastening to surpass one another in arriving.

Among them was a certain young man named Acleulfus, from a village called Laudrado, who had been seized by madness. He had frequently raved for a year and was moreover violently insane, in the condition commonly called “lunatic.” Although bound in chains, he was brought by the faith of his parents to the often-mentioned bodies of the holy martyrs.

His parents did not possess the words, “Lord, if you can do anything, help us and have mercy on us,” but nevertheless they asked that the sick man be healed for their sake. After he had been detained there for a short time for the remedy of his health, he deserved to obtain fully, through their devout merits, what had been sought through the devotion of another’s faith.

Having recovered the strength of his former senses, he departed in high spirits and thereafter remained, as he had formerly been, possessed of a sound mind.

## Chapter XIV

From the same village came a bold girl named Teutberga. On an occasion when she was quarrelling with her mother, as she was accustomed to do, she was not afraid to attest her insolence by the sacred pledges of the holy martyrs, namely George and Aurelius.

When certain people rebuked her, asking why she behaved in such a way toward her parent and why she so rashly swore by the names of the saints, she did not cease. As an immediate punishment, the hand that she had raised in swearing was contracted.

Thereafter, she was compelled earnestly to seek the saints whom she had wickedly presumed to invoke in perjury through the stubbornness of her tongue, and to demand from them the cause of her remedy as though it were a due gift.

When, repentant of what she had done, she most devoutly approached their threshold, her weakened palm was healed and extended more quickly than words can tell. The woman, now made sound, returned to her mother to serve her for the rest of her life.

## Chapter XV

There was also a woman from a village called Casella, named Amaluvara, who had remained in the darkness of blindness for one hundred and forty-four months. No human medicinal hand had helped her, for divine power had reserved her healing for these saints.

In the middle of the night, as it seemed to her, she was warned by a most beautiful woman that, in order to obtain the use of light, she should diligently sweep the pavement of the church where the bodies of those same holy martyrs rested, until the saints looked upon her with mercy.

When she had been brought there and had completed this task once, she recovered so much sharpness of vision that it has been sufficient for her to the present day. She became a religious woman and no longer needs the guide on whom she had previously depended.


## Chapter XVI

We think it should not be neglected to relate what was revealed to this same woman one night while she was keeping vigil in the church with the others.

While the others were sleeping, she alone, as she was certain and later told us, sat as though awake. She looked toward the window behind the altar of that church and saw it shining as though with a great ray of sunlight. Through the ray she saw a boy covered with an immeasurable light descend as far as the foot of the altar.

Stretching out his hand, he approached the place where the bodies of the saints rested. After slightly raising the pallium by which they were covered, he began to look carefully inside. Then a dove appeared, of wondrous brightness, at the right-hand horn of the altar. It flew over them and remained there, gazing intently at the boy, as though contemplating something divine in him and considering what he intended to do.

Terrified by the vision and overcome, as though worn out by anguish, she fell into a deeper sleep. In an ecstasy of mind she saw two venerable men adorning the church itself with certain costly and very precious ornaments. They said to her:

> “Go quickly to the custodians of this holy house, and tell them to adorn it with greater care, because those who are around the saints will now come here through the grace of these martyrs. Indeed, we too have come from the regions of Spain, from which they were recently brought, and have hastened to visit them, to see how they are here.”

When these words had been spoken to her, the vision was removed and the woman awoke. Repeating the matter to herself, she remained greatly perplexed, since she did not know what the boy or the dove signified.

But the prudent reader—or, we believe, the discerning hearer—will understand the boy to be Christ and the dove to be the Holy Spirit, consort of the Father and the Son, breathing around the relics of the holy martyrs.

## Chapter XVII

Teuthildis, from the girls’ monastery of Dedentium, since it was Sunday and she was free from work, went to the threshold of those same holy martyrs, prompted by the girlish curiosity of seeing them.

Others also went forward devoutly. Although they differed in spirit, they reached the church together in a common procession and devoted themselves together to prayer before the altar. Then, as they rose and hurried to join the station of those who had arrived earlier, while the others departed, the aforementioned Teuthildis remained in the place where she had been standing.

She remained so immovable upon the pavement that she raised everyone to no small amazement by this new miracle. There, for so long …

[scan page 485]  
**APPENDIX AD**  
**955**

With all looking on, she was rendered motionless in both feet until she confessed the guilt of her misconduct: namely, that she had approached with insufficient reverence, delighting in frivolous amusements, and that she had pleaded less earnestly than was fitting for her offenses. Thus, while the brothers who were present prayed for her and recited litanies, she deserved to be absolved through the ineffable intercessions of the holy martyrs.

### Chapter XVIII

Likewise, a certain man named Altearius, from the village of Scau, lay for a very long time in great sorrow, crippled in the loins. Hearing that many sick people were being cured through the merits of the saints, and acquiring a firm hope of obtaining healing—as he himself later reported—he entrusted himself to the care of parents or friends and set out to seek their mercy. When he attempted, as best he could, to rise and sit, so that he might fashion with his own hands a candle which he was carrying with him for the saints’ lights, he suddenly recovered the health he had desired in his own house. Raising himself, and finding himself unexpectedly sound, he completed—now made whole by God’s mercy—the task which, previously weak, he had been attempting.

He therefore hastened to the holy martyrs with an offering of light, rejoicing, and with joyful expression explained to everyone what had happened to him.

### Chapter XIX

This too deserves to be set down, since it brings both wonder and terror. For one person is corrected by another’s misfortune, in accordance with the prophecy of David, who says:

> “The righteous man will rejoice when he sees vengeance;  
> he will wash his hands in the blood of the sinner”  
> (Psalm 57 [Vulgate 56]:11).

There was therefore a certain servant from the same village of Acmanto, named Isardus, who was himself a gardener of the brothers. Having received the grain allotted to him, he went to the mill of that village to have it ground. There, in his pride, he attempted to seize a poor woman’s place and stubbornly sought to throw his own grain onto the grain that was already being milled.

When she resisted with all the strength she possessed, but, being weaker, could not overcome the stronger man, she raised her hands toward the church and said, weeping:

> “I adjure you by these holy martyrs of God, George and Aurelius: do not do me violence.”

The wretched man disregarded this appeal. As he began to leave the place, he was immediately struck down and understood that, because of such contempt, a danger was threatening him. With difficulty he gasped for breath and, in the faint voice of which he was capable, begged the mill’s overseer to remove quickly the grain that had been thrown on top.

After saying this—which is both astonishing and terrifying—he fell, became speechless, and visibly expired, granted a present death. Many people came running—for it was Sunday—and they were utterly astonished at such a spectacle. Yet we should believe that it came about not as the occasion of future damnation, but rather for the correction of such rashness, as we have already indicated, through the just though hidden judgment of God. For, to use the words of blessed Gregory, the death of the wicked is a help to the good, but to the wicked it is a testimony that they should beware.

### Chapter XX

Afterward, a certain woman from the village called Civiacus, named Godohis, was afflicted by so severe and terrifying a disease of transparent swelling that, deprived of the use of all her limbs, she appeared wretched and desolate. Within her she also suffered from another evil, namely a cardiac illness, which continually suffocated and greatly exhausted her. As, moment by moment, she seemed to be brought near death by this twofold calamity, she was finally placed by the hands of her relatives on a cart and thus brought to the merciful aid of the saints.

She was so oppressed by the harshness of her suffering that, lying before the church doors, she could scarcely be perceived to have any breath at all. After three days, however, her stomach having been relieved, she was so wondrously and completely healed that thereafter, on her own feet and with the cart removed, she deserved to return home rejoicing.

**OMRA 6. BULOGH.**

### Chapter XXI

We also know of a certain man named Jerome, from the neighboring village of Wastinensis, who was cured by a similar power of the saints. For nearly half a year he had been overwhelmed throughout his body by the anguish of weakness. Through the piety of his parents he was carried to the consolation of the blessed martyrs; his illness was more unknown to physicians than cured by them.

When they had scarcely found a way to place him, because none of his limbs was sound, in a wine-vessel of the sort called a *tonna*, upon a wagon, they did so and reached the sacred presence of the martyrs. There, while many who still survive looked on, he was strengthened by such a restoration of his former health that, made well, he rose and, once God’s mercy had been shown him as he had hoped, returned home giving thanks.

### Chapter XXII

Likewise, a certain woman, lamenting that she had been deprived of the consolation of children, took with her a son who was both mute and deaf and led him to the relics of the saints, radiant with miracles. After she had prayed and had stood some distance from the altar, she signaled to her son, as though he were deaf, to come nearer, and to offer at the altar to the saints the candle of a vow which she was holding in her hand.

Suddenly the child’s mouth, which had been closed from birth, opened, and, uttering his first voice, he asked his mother to whom he should hand the candle. When his mother replied that he should carry it to the altar, he demonstrated clearly, by carrying out the task, that he could also hear. When this became known, those who had known him until then as both mute and deaf proclaimed with amazement that, through the merits of the saints, the Gospel miracles had come to life again.

Nor is this surprising, since the Savior not only promised what great things he would do, but also promised greater things to his disciples when they were about to depart.

### Chapter XXIII

We do not therefore believe that it is displeasing if something useful and honorable is narrated. Faith is nourished, growing through the works of faith. One Sunday, when some women were keeping vigil at the entrance of that church—some for the sake of their salvation, others out of devotion to the holy martyrs—a wondrous and astonishing vision was shown to them, not as once to the shepherds who were instructed about Christ’s birth, but to devout women through a power worthy of proclamation.

During the first watch of the night they looked through a crack in the door of that church and saw a great brilliance of light proceeding from within toward them. Then one of them approached more closely and attempted to examine carefully what it was. She saw the whole church shining with such an unbelievable splendor that, by that very light, it partially illuminated the portico outside where they were sitting.

And behold, they heard within various voices and a hymn of extraordinary sweetness, as though a multitude were rejoicing together, singing hymns and chanting praises to God with jubilation. They declared that they heard it softly and in turn until the brothers awoke at the signal for the nocturnal office.

If we consider the causes of the miracles, arranged by an orderly providence, this vision is judged to complete the earlier vision, in which we showed that, through the grace of these martyrs, the saints who were in the surrounding area would come there, joyful in the company of angels alone.

### Chapter XXIV

From the parish of Parisiacus, and from a village called Theodasius [perhaps *Théodais*], a certain young man had, it was said, groaned for about five years in the continual darkness of blindness. He therefore implored the aid of so many and such great holy martyrs, asking that he might be led to their merciful help.

For he had already begun, as though catechized by the light of faith, to see that he would receive this gift; and when it occurred, he deserved quickly to obtain what he had sought through their gracious intervention. Indeed, after not much time had passed, when he had completed his tearful prayers at the life-giving threshold of those same holy martyrs, the darkness was driven away from his eyes, and heavenly power immediately restored to him the light of day.

He returned seeing, glorifying God and giving thanks: a renewed man, reporting a new miracle to his neighbors.

[scan page 486]  
**TRANSLATION OF SS. GEORGE,**  
**957**

### Chapter XXV

There was therefore a certain man from the parish of Angers, named Adalsadus, whose bodily structure had been impaired for nearly five years, so weak that his heels were held most tightly attached to the backs of his legs. Having learned of the power of so many miracles—for they were being proclaimed by very many people—he transferred himself, as best he could, to the grace of those martyrs on a certain Sunday.

When the time of the nocturnal office arrived, and the brothers were celebrating the same office with angelic worship, his limbs began to loosen their bonds—as commonly happens in such cases—and he emitted such cries that, lamenting, he completely broke through the voices of those singing psalms. Meanwhile, having soon recovered some remedy of health, after a few days he was restored to his former soundness. Raised up by their prayers, he rose so completely that he walked upright on his own and returned home on healthy feet.

### Chapter XXVI

Finally, Ramnoldus, from a village commonly called Fontanas, who for a full year had been lame from the feet up to the loins, came in his misery to the flourishing mercy of those martyrs. I say that he came—not by his own steps, but conveyed by an external contrivance—in such a wretched condition and so emaciated by the weakness of his whole body that, with illnesses multiplied within him, he was thought more likely to die than to be cured.

Nevertheless, he approached in faith and was laid out before the ashes of the holy martyrs by those who carried him. Immediately, looked upon from above with the gift of healing, and restored by their devout intercessions, he was healed whole: the affliction of his kidneys, shins, feet, and every weakness being driven away, as his continuing vigor still testifies.

He was restored to such health that, thereafter suffering nothing from the same illness, he is said to have remained continually in that place serving God.

### Chapter XXVII

Since it commonly happens—as blessed Gregory writes in his sacred *Dialogue*—that greater miracles sometimes occur where a smaller portion of the saints’ relics is preserved, we think it pleasing that what was done through their relics should also be inserted here.

### Chapter XXVIII

How greatly the glorious king Charles rejoiced when, after reading the accounts of their passion, he learned of the arrival of these martyrs, it is not for us to explain. He rejoiced that, in the time of his kingdom, Gaul had deserved such flowers. So that he might possess the whole through a part of them, after receiving their relics he also showed by this religious example what should be done by the faithful.

Nor did he neglect to send Mancio of Córdoba to investigate the truth of this matter at its source. When Mancio returned, he also learned from the acts of the martyrs the following mutilated account, which is considered worthy of remembrance and inscription.

After the bodies of the holy martyrs had been slain and laid out in the streets, the tyrant Abdirama had ordered them to remain unburied, so that dogs and birds of the sky might eat them. Thus, indeed, we see fulfilled in them the psalmody of David, who sings:

> “You gave the dead bodies of your servants as food to the birds of the sky,  
> the flesh of your saints to the beasts of the earth”  
> (Psalm 79 [Vulgate 78]:2).

But so that their dignity and the greatness of their merit might be made clear, they were guarded from all the rapacious animals by divine power, just as Daniel was once guarded from the lions. For during the three days in which they lay there in this manner, neither a bird nor even a fly’s appetite touched them.

Mancio also testified that he had heard this very truth from the faithful citizens of Córdoba. Likewise, he reported that he had seen two noble girls, sisters by birth, completing their martyrdom for Christ in his presence. When the elder saw the younger drinking the cup of suffering before her, she said:

> “No, sister, it is not fitting that it should be so. I will follow you, my guide, to the prize just as I followed you to the spectacle. Do not be afraid; I will not abandon you. I shall show in dying the faith and love that I used to show while living.”

Thus, when the heads of both had been severed, their souls, borne away with the consolation of angels, departed to God, destined to live forever.

**AURELIUS AND NATHALIA — BOOK III**  
**958**

### Chapter XXIX

But, to return to Count Eddo—as it is time for us to do—when a portion of the relics of the holy martyrs that had been requested was being carried to him, it happened on the way that a certain priest, asking that he be allowed to pray there for a longer time, entered the room of the house in which the relics were being kept and presumed to steal them, with no one attending.

Taking whatever first came to his hand—namely, a portion of the hair of blessed Nathalia—he hastened through the darkness of that very night, delighted with his theft, to return to his dwelling. But before he was permitted to go any farther, he suddenly fell senseless in the middle of the streets, deprived of every power of perception.

Then, as though recalled to himself after an hour, and repentant of his offense, he rose and, returning as though he had gone out for some ordinary necessity, placed the relics of the holy martyr back in their place, again invoking them in prayer and longing.

Although he had thus offered them back properly, because he had not acted rightly by committing fraud against those to whom they belonged, he suddenly collapsed again before all who were present and was tormented as he rolled about on the ground. Everyone rose, struck with terrible fear, and placed fetters on him to restrain him. They saw that he was insane and thought that he was about to die immediately. Yet, so that the significance of the miracle might not be concealed, once his mind had been restored he was compelled to confess his crime.

Thus, after the mercy of the saints had first been invoked by the priest Usufridus, his guilt was forgiven, and the priest, restored to life, returned more cheerful.

### Chapter XXX

Therefore, omitting very many things, let the end of writing now be set down, after admitting this account, through which it may become clear that the blessed bishop Germanus rejoices not only in the eternal, but also in the present, companionship of the saints.

A certain Teutgaudus, in the new town situated on the River Loire, had lain ill with an adverse sickness. In addition, this calamity befell him: from the thighs downward he was so contracted that, bound by this constriction and denied entirely the use of walking for nearly two years, he remained unable to move.

Then, when rumor informed him that he could be helped by the merits of these venerable martyrs, he begged that he be carried there on the hands of friends or relatives. This was done and hastened. When he had arrived and remained there for some time in prayer, he awaited the appointed day of his healing.

As the festival of the translation of our most blessed patron, Lord Germanus, was now approaching, he came earlier, soon to find what he had sought in devotion. Placed before the altar of that great prelate, where the bodies of those same holy martyrs were kept above it, he stood, so that—as we believe through the simultaneous intercession of the saints—the sick man might obtain swift health.

Once he had been restored, as we saw, he went away resounding with great thanksgiving. While everyone acclaimed the greatness of the power of almighty God, holy Germanus, and the martyrs, he remained there until death, forgetting his homeland, his parents, and the friends who had carried him.

And rightly was blessed Germanus a participant in their miracle accomplished on earth, in whose fellowship he rejoices in heaven, exulting—in that desired homeland, in that splendid joy, in that truly honey-flowing region, in that land of the living, humanity’s portion, in that heavenly Jerusalem, our mother, and in those most delightful pastures of eternity.

[scan page 487]  
**APPENDIX AD**  
**999**

For there those who always live and gaze toward him with longing stand before God; the spirits applaud, and, in one and the same glory, rejoice together with the saints who have already been joined to them from this mortality. They also rejoice together with those who, although still pilgrims on earth, they know and understand will soon be associated with them by him who knows and understands all things.

**SPERAINDEO**

**Against Certain Heretics Who Deny the Trinity of Persons in the Unity of Substance, and the Divinity in Christ**

### LETTER OF ALVARUS  
**ADDRESSED TO ABBOT SPERAINDEO**

[Editorial note: Flórez wrongly prints *Alvari* (“of Alvarus”) in place of *abbati* (“to the abbot”).]

To my most beloved lord and father in Christ, Sperain­deo, abbot, Alvarus, his servant.

The foreknowing and omnipotent God, seeing the times into which we have come and the great hunger for the word of God which we suffer, has set you before us as a strong *aestina*—a supporting prop—so that you might nourish our famine and feed our hearts with the dishes of instruction.

[Editorial note: St Isidore uses this word in *Sentences* III.40; García Loaysa explains that an *aestina* is a prop placed beneath a crumbling wall so that it does not fall. The African poet Corippus likewise uses it in *On the Praises of Justin the Younger*, as do Arnobius, book II, and St Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, in his *Life of St Isidore*. See Juan Bautista Pérez, note to chapter 47 of *De viris illustribus* of this saint, p. 281, vol. I of our collection; and Flórez, *España sagrada*, XI, p. 106.] But because I now know that you are devoted to tribulations and oppressed by bitterness, I ask you to take as a word of consolation the saying of the Apostle.

For he says, speaking of the dangers of tribulations which he endured:

> “In dangers in the city, in dangers in the wilderness, in dangers among false brothers”  
> (2 Corinthians 11:26).

And afterward, in another place, he said:

> “We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces patience, patience produces testing, and testing produces hope; but hope does not disappoint us”  
> (Romans 5:3–5).

Therefore, venerable Father, excellent priest of all priests, do not keep silent about what has been requested because of the dangers of tribulations. Instead, grant what your servant has sought, because a gift is increased by being given and diminished by being withheld.

For Moses the lawgiver instructed me when his word resounded:

> “Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will announce it to you”  
> (Deuteronomy 32:7).

And because I recognize you as a spiritual father, I therefore seek spiritual help from you.

That heresy which my negligence long ago brought to your attention is tearing apart the Church of God and, through its deadly assertion, dragging a band of people after it to destruction. For, according to the Apostle’s saying:

> “The word of heretics spreads like cancer”  
> (2 Timothy 2:17),

especially among the hearts of the humble, because “the poison of asps is under their lips” (Psalm 14 [Vulgate 13]:3).

For this reason we ask your help and assistance, so that their dark and unspeakable heresy may perish through heavenly power and the most glorious doctrine of Christ’s bride may shine forth resplendently through you. Their objections are those which I have already communicated to you.

The chief point of those most wicked men, which must be cut away by the sickle of truth, is this: they do not believe that the Trinity is in unity and unity in the Trinity. They reject the sayings of the prophets and repudiate the doctrine of the teachers. They say that they accept the Gospel, but they misunderstand what is written:

> “I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God”  
> (John 20:17).

They assert that Christ our God and Lord was merely a man, because of what they read about him in the Gospel:

> “But of that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven nor the Son, but the Father alone”  
> (Matthew 24:36).

Yet I ask with all my efforts that you refute these old-wives’ questions of the pagans, since they generate deadly consequences for their hearers, especially those who are inexperienced and do not examine the texts of Holy Scripture.

Adorn these two responses with the flowers of Scripture, as you are accustomed to do in other matters, and publish an appropriate answer to each of the assertions which we have brought before you. Thus may you receive from the Lord a radiant dwelling among the saints in the heavenly kingdoms. Amen.

### RESPONSE OF ABBOT SPERAINDEO  
**ADDRESSED TO ALVARUS**

To my most illustrious lord, venerable Alvarus, renowned and embraced with every affection in Christ’s charity, Sperain­deo.

While I was exceedingly occupied with the most severe tribulations, while my mind seethed and my spirit was ensnared by the darts and pierced by the arrows of my rivals, sitting wounded by the injuries of vexations, and while my spirit, surrounded by bitterness, tossed like a ship amid the whirlpools of the sea, suddenly your messenger came in to me and brought me the gift of your letter.

I read the written letter itself quickly and recognized at once the words of your serenity. They shone back more brightly than light to one who was already almost dead, and immediately that inner man was raised up. I began, astonished, to consider who I was, or who he might be through whom I had deserved to be raised up in such a condition, and to be questioned about such difficult matters from the Holy Scriptures.

At a time when many do not attend to this, they prefer to linger over vulgar speech, not considering the Lord’s saying:

> “Every idle word that people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment”  
> (Matthew 12:36).

Or they want to extend their tongue in detraction of their companions, not remembering that sacred Gospel:

> “You see the speck in your brother’s eye, but you do not consider the beam in your own heart”  
> (Matthew 7:3).

Some immediately believe things that are harmful and that enemies invent for the injury of a brother, and they do not recall the Psalmist’s words:

> “The words of the enemy are iniquity and deceit”  
> (Psalm 36 [Vulgate 35]:4).

The hearers themselves then broadcast the inventions of their enemies and expose them again to others in detraction, insulting them and casting behind their backs the words of the holy Apostle:

> “The one who detracts from his brother and judges his brother detracts from the law and judges the law”  
> (James 4:11).

We must prudently withdraw from such occasions, lest the Lord’s voice ring clearly against us through the prophet Jeremiah:

> “I attended and listened, says the Lord: no one speaks what is good; there is no one who does penance for his sin”  
> (Jeremiah 8:6).

Therefore, contemplating our sin at every moment and awaiting the end of our former life, we ought, with the deepest compassion, to offer a lamenting groan for the fall of a brother and to fulfill and proclaim the apostolic saying:

> “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?”  
> (2 Corinthians 11:29).

We must not therefore readily believe when someone’s words of accusation strike our ears, unless they have first been usefully examined and faithfully recognized. We have the example of what the Lord said:

> “The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied, and their sin has become exceedingly grave. I will go down and see whether they have acted according to the outcry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, so that I may know”  
> (Genesis 18:20–21).

Why does the omnipotent Lord, who knows all things, appear to doubt before investigation, unless to give us an example of seriousness, so that we do not presume to believe people’s evils before testing them? Thus he says:

> “I will go down and see whether they have acted according to the outcry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, so that I may know.”

But I shall omit all these things that I have spoken in the contrition of my heart and return to what your excellence requests. Who would dare say anything about so ineffable a matter, when blessed Jerome says:

> “The mysteries of the Lord’s incarnation and the sacrament of his birth are ineffable”?

And therefore we do not attempt to declare what that birth itself is, but only what we are able to express in words. In truth, what that birth itself is, we cannot explain—not even the holy Evangelists were able to state it fully. If the holy Evangelists, inspired by the Holy Spirit, could not state it fully, it is better to remain silent than to assert, and rightly to believe what was said than, by searching beyond it, to commit something to writing, according to the true judgment of the teacher, which is expressed thus:

> “We believe the Father with his offspring, and the life-giving Spirit proceeding, three in persons; we believe one in divinity.”

How the Virgin’s childbirth proceeded without violation, or how the one born wished to suffer, no one may discuss; one must simply believe. If discussion of this is forbidden, who would dare to write anything about it with a pen or utter it with the tongue?

Since you seek testimonies from the books of the Gospels and the Apostles against the points noted in your letter, in order to destroy their contrivances and to confirm the doubtful with the greatest force, your kindness is nevertheless more able to accomplish this than any tribulation or worldly adversity has ever wearied. Your understanding and judgment therefore retain the highest integrity, because the bitterness of this age has already crushed me almost in every way.

But since, as I think, you are fully sufficient for this task, you seek it for no other reason than to learn the text of my belief. I shall therefore humbly present what I believe and simply explain what I think concerning the questions you have asked. Whatever our lord and your father may there perceive to be contrary to the rule of truth, let the speed of the scribe immediately correct it, and let him secretly instruct me again, as he once instructed others, for the sake of your honor. Let your skill conceal from the outside world the heart of one who is ignorant and uninstructed, so that no one may perceive the error; for this has been entrusted to your certainty, whether to amend, remove, or add.

As your excellence commanded, I have performed, insofar as I could, the service of a humble servant. I shall introduce the objections noted in your letter under the name of the one making the assertion, produce testimonies from the Holy Scriptures in your text, and join them with the sayings of the teachers, so that I may compose the answers in accordance with the truth.

[Editorial note: Read “together with the sayings of the teachers and with the truth,” Flórez.]

[Editorial note: Thus in the manuscript.]

[Editorial note: *Sapientia*—“wisdom.”]

**AGAINST CERTAIN HERETICS**  
**962**

**He responds to the first part of Alvarus’s question: that is, he refutes the error of those heretics who did not believe in one God who is threefold in unity and one in the Trinity.**

The faith of the one substance of the Trinity—that is, of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—without beginning in time, is beyond understanding and speech: one power, one God, three names. When I name God, I name one light in light from the three. They are three according to the distinctiveness of their essence, but one according to substance, or according to the reality of divinity, so to speak, indivisibly. There is one divinity in the three, and there are three in whom the divinity exists.

Let us leave aside anything greater or lesser, so that there may be neither confusion in the Trinity nor division in the unity.

The Word was born from the Virgin Mary, taking an animate body. But what is said of the mind sending forth its word? The Word was not enclosed by flesh, but was in flesh and above flesh. Thus he is called the foreknowledge of God, the power of God, the truth of God. He suffered human things, but the Word of God is incapable of suffering. In the Passion the human being died so that he might give life to the first-formed man, who had fallen through disobedience.

O human being! Do you inquire about the divinity? I rebuke you. If you believe, you do well; but if you say, “How is he the Father?” you have fallen away from the light. And if you say, “How is he the Son?” you have likewise fallen away from the light. For no one knows the Father except the Son, nor does anyone know the Son except the Father (Matthew 11:27).

Whoever introduces three powers confesses three gods. We believe in three persons, but one power and one divinity. When you name the Father, you glorify the Son; and when you name the Son, you adore the Father.

If we again say that there is one person of the Trinity, “we become Jews,” because the Jews speak of one person and confess one God. If we say that there are three gods, we become like the pagans. But we confess the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father together with the Holy Spirit. The divinity is not separated or divided: God from God, power from power, light from light, truth from truth.

There is no witness—not heaven, not earth, not the sea, not light, not darkness, not angels, not archangels, not cherubim, not seraphim—but from the beginning the Son was with the Father. No one knows the one who is unborn except the one who was born; he certainly knows from whom he was born. Nor does anyone know anything about the one who can be born except the one who begot him: the Father knows what he generated. The one begotten is like the Father, his begetter.

Counsel and wisdom: one power and one divinity. Do you ask about the birth of the Son of God? You have his proper birth from the Virgin Mary; but the birth of the Son of God was from the beginning with the Father.

For I confess one unborn and one born. I confess the almighty Father, without beginning and without end, who holds all things and is held by none, governs all things and is governed by none, sees all things and is himself invisible.

I also confess Jesus Christ, the Son of God, with all the counsel and power of the Father’s divinity. Whatever power the Father has, the Son has also. The one begotten is not diminished by the one who is unborn; for there is one power and one divinity of the unborn and the born.

The Holy Spirit, however, was neither born nor unborn; he was not made or created. If I say that he was born, I establish two sons from one Father, and not one from one, or alone from alone. Where then is “one God the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (1 Corinthians 8:6)?

If I say that he is unborn, there is no longer one almighty and unborn Father, but I establish two almighty beings. If I say that he is made, I speak like a pagan; for pagans worship the work of human hands and not the maker of heaven and earth.

What, then, am I to say? A phantom? Far from it. For the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven (Matthew 12:31–32). How—
## APPENDIX AD

### 969

Therefore I say: when two pieces of wood joined together are thrown into a furnace of fire, and from the two pieces an inseparable flame proceeds, so from the power of the Father and the Son proceeds the Holy Spirit, possessing that same power and divinity, just as the most blessed apostle Paul stated, saying:

> For there is one God, one Mediator of God and humanity, the human being Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2:5);

not “God of God” as Mediator. For there is one even unto the Trinity; but, receiving a body from the Virgin Mary and putting on the old human being who had fallen through disobedience, he became Mediator in the flesh through the power of the Father—that is, Jesus Christ.

When, moreover, he takes the apostles with him, as the Gospels testify (Matt. 17:1 ff.), and ascends a high mountain, he changed the power of his divinity; and behold, a bright cloud covered him. The splendid cloud, however, displayed the power of the Father in him. As certain people teach through vain talk: “How are there three persons in one substance?” They, however, say that there are three powers; we believe in three persons in one power: three names, but one God in three names, in the one name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Again, by dividing the power and divinity of the Trinity, they say: “Like a perfect emperor and a count.” Away with it! I do not transmit this doctrine, or this exposition, or this faith; rather, I anathematize it. For it is written in the divine commands:

> For the visible things of this world are compared with the invisible (Rom. 1:20).

An earthly emperor consists of three things, but there is one empire. If he removes the diadem from his head, he is Caesar, but not a perfect emperor. Thus those who blaspheme the Holy Spirit are not Christians. And if he removes the purple garment, he is a solitary man. Just as the Jews worship one person, so we confess the heavenly emperor in the same manner as the earthly emperor. The man is in the purple, and the purple is in the man; but the crown of the head, containing the purple and the man, displays one empire. Thus the Father is in the Son, and the Son in the Father; while the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son: the power of the divinity and the unity of the Trinity.

## II

He responds to the second part of Alvar’s question—that is, he refutes the impiety of those who, through a perverse explanation of the Gospel, confessed Jesus Christ to be merely human.

**The Assertor said:** “If he is truly God, why did he begin by saying to the disciples: ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God’ (John 20:17)?”

**Response:** In one person, the one true and proper Son of God consists of two natures, namely divinity and humanity. Therefore, in the Gospel he foretold to his disciples that he would endure all these things only in the body of his humanity:

> Behold, we are ascending to Jerusalem, and everything that has been written through the prophets about the Son of Man will be accomplished: for he will be handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, scourged, and spat upon; and after they have scourged him, they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise again (Luke 18:31 ff.).

All this was spoken of Christ according to the human being, not with respect to the substance of his divinity, but with respect to the nature of the flesh. For even during his passion, rebuking the betrayer, he said:

> With a kiss are you betraying the Son of Man? (Luke 22:48)

Whom does he question as betrayer, if not the human being whom they also seized—not the divinity, which, blinded by their treachery, they were unable even to recognize? Likewise, the fact that he reasoned, that he was hungry, thirsty, slept, wept, was sorrowful when near his passion, assumed the condition of death after the passion, and ascended into heaven according to what he said—“I am ascending to my God and your God”—all this belongs not to the incomprehensible substance of the divinity, of which he said, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), but to the weakness of his humanity, in which he asserts himself to be lesser than the Father, saying:

> The Father is greater than I (John 14:28).

And therefore he says, “I am ascending to my God and your God,” so that he might raise to the throne of heaven the human being whom, coming from heaven, he had assumed from the Virgin, from which throne he had never departed through his divinity.

The Lord himself also says:

> No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven (John 3:13).

He did not say, “who was in heaven.” Therefore, while he was on earth, he was in heaven, just as he said, “the Son of Man who is in heaven,” although he was speaking on earth; but on earth he was human and God.

For if God was not on earth, how did the angels minister to him, as it is written:

> Then the tempter left him, and behold, angels approached and ministered to him (Matt. 4:11)?

The apostle Paul again said:

> The one who descended is himself the one who ascended above all the heavens, in order to fulfill all things (Eph. 4:10).

For by descending he emptied himself and took the form of a servant. Here his voice is heard in the Psalm when he says:

> From my mother’s womb you are my God (Ps. 21:11).

Indeed, because of what he assumed from his mother’s womb, he said:

> I am ascending to my God and your God.

By saying “my” and “your,” as though he did not say “my” commonly, but speaking distinctly and separately, he indicates that he possesses the same Father and God differently from us. For when he says, “I am ascending to my Father,” namely, by his proper generation, the Father’s voice concerning him is:

> From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you (Ps. 109:3).

And again:

> My heart has uttered a good word (Ps. 44:2).

And in the Gospel:

> In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God (John 1:1).

And as we believers profess in the Creed: the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father before all ages, God from God, light from light, true God from true God.

For this reason he said, “I am ascending to my Father,” namely, by nature, “and to your Father,” by grace—that is, by voluntary adoption; or because, having abandoned idols, we are sons through the grace of faith and baptism, according to the Gospel:

> But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name (ibid., 12).

And when he said, “I am ascending to my God,” it is because I descended and assumed flesh; “and to your God,” because you ascend through faith. Since I am also human, God is my God; since he frees you from error, God is your God. “To my God,” by the unity of the mystery; “to your God,” indeed by heavenly power. Thus, distinctly and separately, the Father is my Father and God, because the one who begot him as God before the ages created the human being together with me at the end of the ages.

**The Assertor said:** “While raising this question from the sayings of Scripture, I shall introduce another passage in which, as I think, nothing remains for you to bring forward. It is this:

> But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven nor the Son, except the Father alone (Matt. 24:36).

Since he declared that he did not know, what can you now produce?”

**Response:** I am able, in fact, to produce many testimonies, and more magnificent ones, by which you will perceive that he certainly knew the day and hour. For when the Lord was asked by the apostles, “Tell us what will be the sign of your coming and of the consummation of this age,” he replied:

> See that no one deceives you. For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom, and there will be pestilences, famines, and earthquakes in various places. Then they will hand you over to tribulation and kill you, and you will be hated by all nations because of my name. Then many will be scandalized, and they will betray one another and hate one another. Many false prophets will arise and deceive many. And because iniquity has abounded, the charity of many will grow cold … For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world and will not be … For just as lightning comes out from the east and appears as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. Immediately after the tribulation of those days, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of heaven will be shaken. And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven (ibid., 3 ff.).

The one who narrated all these things knew the day itself and the hour, because his coming and the day of judgment will occur when the sign he foretold appears in heaven.

It continues:

> And then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty; and he will send his angels with a trumpet and a loud voice, and his elect will be gathered from the four winds, from the highest parts of the heavens to their farthest boundaries (ibid., 30 ff.).

The one who sends his angels and gathers his elect from the highest parts of the heavens to their farthest boundaries certainly knows the day itself on which he will do these things. And the one who foretells that he will come with great power and majesty cannot be ignorant of the day on which he will come. Or how could he be ignorant of that day when he foretold that the Father knew it and chose to declare himself one with the Father?

> I and the Father are one (John 10:30).

And again:

> Whoever sees me sees my Father.

And:

> I am in the Father, and the Father is in me (John 14:9–10).

Since, therefore, he brought forward all these things and foretold that he was one with the Father in the nature of divinity, he certainly knew the day, but did not wish to tell it to the apostles, in accordance with what he said to them after his resurrection when they asked him:

> It is not yours to know the times or moments which the Father has placed in his own power (Acts 1:7).

When he says, “It is not yours to know,” he shows that he himself knows, but that it is not expedient for the apostles to know, so that, always uncertain about the Judge’s coming, they may live each day as though they were to be judged on that day.

If, however, you persist in your obstinate opinion that the Lord does not know that day, then, according to your objection, the Lord himself did not know where Adam had hidden himself in paradise when he said to him:

> Adam, Adam, where are you? (Gen. 3:9)

And he said to Cain:

> Where is Abel, your brother? (Gen. 4:9)

And he said to Abraham:

> Where is Sarah, your wife? (Gen. 18:9)

The one who narrated all these things as though he were ignorant also asked, as it is written in the Gospel, Lazarus, whom he was coming to raise:

> Where have you laid him? (John 11:34)

The one who had already made the death known to the disciples while he was far away inquired about the place of the tomb as though he did not know. But according to your assertion, the Lord likewise did not know that Abraham feared the Lord; rather, after he had offered his son in sacrifice, he then perceived that Abraham feared him, and therefore said to him:

> Do not stretch out your hand against the boy, and do nothing to him; now I know that you fear the Lord and have not spared your only-begotten son for my sake (Gen. 22:12).

Consider all these things, and do not be ashamed to ask how they are to be understood: for the one who foretold these various things of the world—as though he did not know them—truly knew everything, and he himself fashioned and created all visible and invisible things.

*Perhaps “some [people]” (*quidam*).*

*Perhaps “the purple garment” (*purpuram*).*

## DCCLXI. PRUDENTIUS, BISHOP: ON SAINT PRUDENTIUS

*(Bibliotheca vetus Hispana)*

## SAINT PRUDENTIUS, BISHOP OF TROYES

### 966

[Continuation of the preceding argument, translated above.]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

*(In Antonius, *Bibliotheca vetus Hispana*)*

During the reign of Alfonso the Great and while Charles the Fat ruled Gaul, Prudentius, a Spaniard by birth, obtained the church of Troyes among that people. The *Annals of Bertin* call him “Galindus, or Galindo, surnamed Prudentius” (a), in the year 861; this further confirms that he was Spanish by nation. That this was a Spanish name is immediately clear from Galindo, count of Aragon II, son of Aznar, from the ancient records of that kingdom (b), and this leaves us no reason to doubt it. What, indeed, prevents our Prudentius from having belonged to the same family as Galindo? They also lived at approximately the same time; the death of Count Galindo is said to have occurred after the year 800, which clearly establishes the point.

Galindo, son of Eneco, was likewise a man of this region, mentioned by Eulogius the martyr in his letter to Wilesindus, bishop of Pamplona. Ambrosius Morales, in his annotations to three ancient documents of the Church of Compostela, says that he himself saw the name of Galindo attached to them.

The author of the *Deeds of Frodoard*, whom Bartholomew cites in *Adversaria*, book 18, chapter 11, is uncertain about Prudentius’s homeland:

> At that same time, he says, there was a bishop of the aforesaid see named Prudentius, a Spaniard by nation, very distinguished in the manner of his episcopal life, and not moderately learned in divine matters from every source.

Prudentius himself also says in a poem prefixed to a Gospel manuscript that he was born in Spain and brought down among the Celts, where he grew to maturity. The same anonymous Bertinian author calls him an exceptionally learned man. Lupus of Ferrières also praises him greatly.

Among more recent writers, Bartholomew calls him the foremost scholar of his age in *Adversaria*, book 44, chapter 19, where he adds:

> His contemporaries unanimously proclaim him a most learned bishop, and imitation of the best authors was exceedingly rare in his age.

And in book 18, chapter 11, he calls him “a thoughtful man and knowledgeable about antiquity.”

He is said to have taken part as a bishop in several synods of Gaul: at Paris in 846; at the fourth Council of Tours—or, according to Philippe Labbe’s observation (a), at Paris—in 849; and at the second Council of Soissons in 858. We possess a letter of Pope Leo IV addressed to him in the editions of the councils (b), and Baronius mentions him in more than one place (c).

There is also another letter addressed by several bishops, among whom Prudentius, bishop of Troyes, was numbered, to Nominoë, as he is called, count of the Breton people. Among other letters edited by Servatus Lupus, it was finally published by Baluzius. It is the synodal letter of the Council of Tours or Paris mentioned above.

We also possess another letter of the same Lupus to Prudentius (d), from which we learn that Charles appointed both of them to visit and reform the monasteries of his kingdom. This is a particularly notable indication of the high regard in which both men, and their dignity, were held by the king.

The same Prudentius also wrote, together with the other bishops of the province of Sens, letter 99 among the letters of Lupus already mentioned, to the clergy and monks of the Church of Paris concerning the election of Æneas as bishop by those men.

A record of the customary relationship between our bishop and Hincmar, bishop of Reims—the most celebrated churchman of the age—survives in book 3, chapter 21 of Flodoard’s *History of Reims*.

As for Prudentius’s writings, the already-mentioned author of the *Annals of Bertin* judged them calumniously and unjustly. He says:

> Galindo, surnamed Prudentius, bishop of the city of Troyes, a Spaniard by nation and exceptionally learned in letters, who some years earlier had resisted Gottschalk the Predestinarian, was later stirred by bitterness against certain bishops who resisted him as a heretic, and became a most ardent defender of that heresy. From that point he composed writings differing among themselves and contrary to the faith, and died. Thus, although he had been worn out by prolonged labor, he gave proof of his faith both in living and in writing (e).

These statements about his doctrine and writings must be weighed. They were, as we have said, uttered calumniously and unjustly against Prudentius; Gilbert Maguinus, to be praised below, and the truth itself, which will now be explained, sufficiently refute them.

Gottschalk, certainly, a monk of the monastery of Orbais in the diocese of Soissons, put forward at this time certain articles of doctrine concerning God’s predestination and Christ’s redemption, and had many followers until he was heard and condemned at the Council of Mainz, presided over by Rabanus, bishop of that city (g). The bishops of Belgic Gaul summoned him again for judgment at a gathering at Quierzy in 849, and he was condemned once more. He was then sent to Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, to be held in custody, as is clear from a letter of that same Hincmar to Pope Nicholas I, which is preserved in Flodoard (h).

Hincmar is said to have claimed that Gottschalk had revived a certain heresy of the Predestinarians, formerly condemned in Africa or Gaul—that is, a branch of Pelagianism. Hincmar discusses it extensively in his work on God’s predestination and free will, addressed to Charles the Bald.

According to Hincmar, these were the principal doctrines of the Predestinarian sect, which Gottschalk was believed to defend:

1. That God predestined some to life and likewise others to eternal death.

2. That God does not will all human beings to be saved, but only those whom he predestined to life.

3. That Christ did not die for all, but only for those who are saved.

These three propositions belong to one class and order. He added a fourth: that the divinity is threefold.

Against these heresies Hincmar sharpened his pen in two published works. The first, in defense of the articles of the Council of Quierzy against Gottschalk, which the bishops of Lyon had attacked in their writings, was preserved by Flodoard in the form of an encyclical letter, book 3, chapter 15.

The second work survives in full among Hincmar’s writings; Flodoard also recalls it in the following chapter. In it Hincmar attacks our Prudentius because, in a certain letter to Wenilo, bishop of Sens, and the bishops of that province concerning the ordination of Æneas as bishop of Paris, he held opinions consistent with the Gottschalkian articles on predestination. Hincmar published this letter in the preface to his own commentary *On God’s Predestination* and repeatedly attacked it throughout the work.

But Prudentius’s opinions are genuinely Catholic and unworthy of Hincmar’s censure. He says:

> 1. Some were gratuitously predestined by God to life, while others were predestined by inscrutable justice to punishment.

But he immediately explains this:

> That is, whether he predestined the saved or the damned, he predestined them to what he had foreknown that he would judge and accomplish,

as the Prophet says:

> He who made the things that are to come.

Consult Suárez, book 1 *On Predestination*, chapter 5; Macedo, in the *Comparison of the Doctrine of Saint Thomas and Scotus*, collation 11, dissertation 3, sections 1–2.

> 2. The blood of Christ was shed for all believers, but not for those who never believed, do not believe today, and will never believe.

See Lupus of Ferrières, in the *Collectanea*, question 3, *On the Blood of Christ*, published by Maguinus together with other authors on predestination. Maguinus should also be consulted in his *Historical Dissertation*, chapter 29.

> 3. Almighty God saves all whom he wishes to save; no one can be saved except one whom he himself has saved; and those who are not saved are not such that it is God’s will that they be saved.

Regarding antecedent and consequent will, see Saint Thomas, *On the Sentences*, book 1, distinction 40, article 6, response to objection 1; Scotus, book 1, part 1, distinction 46, single question, section “to the first”; and Macedo, in the work just mentioned, collation 12, dissertation 2, section 1. All these statements have a correct and Catholic sense (i).

Thus, among the bishops of Gaul and other eminent theologians, this inquiry concerning God’s predestination was vigorously disputed in the ninth century, with the cause and confessions of Gottschalk dividing some against others, provinces against provinces, and men against men.

On one side stood Rabanus of Mainz, Hincmar of Reims, Pardulus, bishop of Laon, and—called upon by the last two to give a written judgment—Amalarius and John Scotus, surnamed Eriugena, who flourished through the favor of King Charles.

On the other stood our Prudentius, bishop of Troyes; Lupus, abbot of Ferrières—there were in fact two men of that name, not one, as Baluzius believed (j); Ratramnus, monk of Corbie; Saints Amolo and Remigius, his successor, archbishops of Lyon; Florus the teacher, together with the entire Church of Lyon. Their opinion was confirmed by the Council of Valence in 855 (a) and by the Council of Langres, held shortly thereafter (b).

### 967

All the writers on this controversy, however many there are, and the defenders of both sides—with the exception of Hincmar, whose works had already become known through those edited by Jacques Sirmond—were gathered under the title *Ancient Authors Who Wrote on Predestination in the Ninth Century* by Gilbert Maguinus, counselor to the king of France and president of the supreme mint. He published them in two volumes in 1650. He gave the second volume the following title:

> *Vindication of Predestination and Grace, containing a historical and chronological synopsis, with two dissertations and the peaceful crown of the work.*

Maguinus and other learned men of Gaul had regretted that Jacques Sirmond, attached to Hincmar’s side, had published in 1643, as though by an author who had lived 1,200 years earlier, a refutation of the heresy of the Predestined or Predestinarians and of the books falsely attributed to Saint Augustine. In this work he had seemed to support the doctrine of the later society concerning grace and its aids, or concerning predestination. Two years later he published Hincmar’s work *On Predestination*, and in 1647 he added the *History of the Predestinarians* and similar materials.

Those responding to Sirmond—among them Auvray, a doctor of theology at the Sorbonne, who wrote in French the *Censure of Sirmond’s Predestinarian*, later translated into Latin and published in 1648 together with the *Predestined* itself, and the aforementioned Maguinus, who wrote a historical and chronological controversy against Gottschalk—argued in extended works that this Predestinarian heresy was a mere fiction and an invention of the Semi-Pelagians. In the dissertation we have mentioned, Maguinus argues at length and learnedly that Gottschalk was free from every charge of heresy; he asserts that the Predestinarian heresy was an invention of Hincmar (d), accuses Hincmar of obstinacy, calumny, and cruelty (e), and records in many places the holiness of Prudentius and, no less, his praise of Catholic doctrine in the works he composed on this controversy (f).

Prudentius’s writings would still have lain in darkness without the aforementioned Maguinus. Thus neither the immense industry of Gerardus Johannes Vossius, who claimed to have gathered all the materials and monuments concerning the Gottschalkian controversy as appendices to his *History of Pelagianism*, obtained any notice of an important work by Prudentius on this matter (g); nor did any of the celebrated ecclesiastical writers, ancient or recent, remember this man.

Nor—to say nothing of the Magdeburg Centuriators, among whom there is complete silence about our subject—did Bœclerus, who devoted a special commentary to illuminating the ninth and tenth centuries, assign Prudentius a place among the distinguished men of that age, whether in literature or in reputation. Indeed, Nicholas Faber, or Andreas Duval, confuses the bishop of Troyes with Florus the teacher (h).

Plainly, to set aside the disparagement and censure laid upon the doctrine of Prudentius by the *Annals of Bertin* and by all the other writers who have written about an obscure matter long disputed throughout Gaul, according to their ability or their partisan zeal, it will be sufficient to cite as abundant witnesses to the common reputation for holiness enjoyed by Bishop Prudentius Demochares, Camuzat, Ferrarius, Bollandus, Saussay, and the church of Troyes itself. In its catalogues of bishops, that church calls him a saint and honors him with worship and liturgical office as one who obtains miraculous works from God (i).

We add Hincmar himself, his adversary, who, even before Prudentius had begun writing the later commentary on *Predestination* that survives, nevertheless frequently calls Lord Prudentius an honored man in praise, although he intended to disparage his doctrine.

But the anonymous author of the *Annals of Bertin*, having lent his support to Hincmar, his metropolitan, treats not only this Prudentius but also Rothad, bishop of Soissons, and Nicholas I himself, the most holy pontiff—all of whom Hincmar had as opponents—with the greatest indignity and injustice (j).

Nor is it true that Prudentius ever opposed Gottschalk or wrote anything different from or contrary to the faith, as those calumnious *Annals* claim. This is enough, lest we merely repeat Maguinus.

Prudentius therefore wrote on this subject the works that we set out below.

### I

A short work addressed to Hincmar, bishop of Reims, and Pardulus, bishop of Laon, written in 849. Jacques Sirmond copied it in his own hand from a manuscript of Saint Arnulf of Metz, but did not publish it, contenting himself with granting the aforementioned Maguinus permission to transcribe it from that copy, together with the preface that he himself published (a).

It begins: *The Lord will proclaim …* Rabanus mentions this short work in a letter to Hincmar (b), and Prudentius himself, its author, mentions it in the work praised immediately below; Hincmar also mentions it in chapter 34 of *On Predestination*. Maguinus discusses it in the first part of the *Vindications*, chapter 13.

After John Scotus, or Eriugena, had been prompted by Hincmar to write against Gottschalk—and Maguinus was the first to bring John’s book *On Divine Predestination* to light—our Prudentius responded to it (m).

### II

*On Predestination against John Scotus, surnamed Eriugena*; or, *John Scotus’s Book Corrected by Prudentius, or by the Other Fathers, namely Gregory, Jerome, Fulgentius, and Augustine*—for this is how the title is worded—addressed to Wenilo, or Venilo, archbishop of Sens.

It begins: *Your blasphemies, John…* Maguinus published these two writings of John and Prudentius from a very ancient and complete manuscript of the library of Corbie. Bartholomew had desired them, as can be seen in *Adversaria*, book 18, chapter 11.

Prudentius wrote his work in 852; see Maguinus, first part of the *Vindications*, chapter 19 (n).

### III

A *Tractoria* letter which he sent through his representative Arnaldus to the Synod of Sens concerning the ordination of Æneas as bishop of Paris.

It begins: *As regards the merit of sinners…*

Æneas was ordained bishop by the Fathers. Before his ordination, Prudentius apparently required him to profess and subscribe to four propositions; Hincmar had arranged for contrary propositions to be subscribed by King Charles and certain bishops at the palace of Quierzy. Hincmar himself mentions this in chapter 5 of *On Predestination*.

It is worthwhile to consult Maguinus, chapter 34, concerning the history of this matter; he [lacuna].

31

*The work ends with this sentence: “On Predestination. 56. Predestination is twofold, whether of the elect to rest or of the reprobate to death. Both …”*

## Saint Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

### Works attributed to Prudentius

…preserved, excerpted for public use and benefit. Maguinus published the treatise in the second part of his *Vindiciae* (a).

On the designation “tractoria epistle,” see, after Franciscus Ferrandus and Philippus Pithoeus’s dissertation *On Canonical Letters*, with its appendix on tractoriae and synodal letters, the place where he discusses this work of Prudentius (b). Maguinus repeatedly cites a witness in the Petavian Library in the first part of his *Vindiciae*, chapter 44; the name is uncertain in the scan.

VI. Poems and other verses, which Nicolas Camusat published from a manuscript Gospel-book of the Church of Troyes in his catalogue of the bishops of Troyes (d), while discussing this Prudentius. One of these poems, written in the aforesaid Gospel codex, is illustrated by Gaspar Barthius in book XVIII, chapter 11 of his *Adversaria*. Barthius urges Camusat, hoping that whatever further writings of this Prudentius he possesses may no longer be withheld from the public good.

IV. *Annals*, or *Annals of the Kings of France*, as Hincmar testifies in his letter 24 to Egilo, bishop of Sens. Hincmar says: “A certain Lord Prudentius, in the *Annals of the Deeds of Our Kings*, which he composed to confirm his own opinion, inserted, under the events of the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 859, the statement: ‘Nicholas, pope and Roman pontiff, by the grace of God and free choice, fully confirms and decrees as Catholic the truth of the twofold predestination and of the Blood of Christ, as it had been set forth by all believers before.’ This,” Hincmar says, “we have not heard through another source, nor have we read it elsewhere. The king himself has the *Annals* of which I speak; it is the book which, in the church where he entrusted you to us, I returned to him after he had lent it to me before you.” The work has nevertheless perished or still lies hidden. Barthius saw it and supplied emendations and several explanations in book LXIV, chapter 19 of his *Adversaria*. Vossius praises Prudentius in book III, part IV, chapter 4 of his *History of Latin Literature*, on this account, not on account of the *Annals*, of which he had not heard.

A manuscript in the library of the king of France preserves a certain Prudentius’s *Collectanea from the Psalms*, a subject not alien to the manner of our Prudentius (e). Prudentius died, as we learn from the *Annals of Bertin*, in the sixty-first year of this century.

V. Under the name of Prudentius, the *Penitential Canon* and many other works that have not come down to us are cited in Fabrisius’ *Bibliotheca medii et infimi aevi*, volume VI, page 19: a treatise *On the Edifice*, or *Description of the House of God*, proposed in the Apocalypse; or a commentary on the poem which Prudentius—and, I do not know, some later writer—had prefixed to the book in the library of Saint Martin of Séez [or Sagium]. Likewise, *Flowers from the Psalter by Prudentius of Troyes*; Cellerius says that these were appended to the *Flowers of the Psalter* of Cardinal Thomasius, published at Rome in 1741, volume II, part II, page 464. He is also said to have composed an *Instruction for Those Being Promoted to Holy Orders*. Among the manuscripts of Quedlinburg there is also a book by Eckhart entitled *On the Seven Deadly Sins and the Seven Opposing Virtues*; however, Eckhart considers its author to have been the later Prudentius.

### Saint Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes  
### Epistle to Hincmar and Pardulus

*(From the Library of the Fathers, ninth-century section, part II.)*

### Author’s Preface

To the most praiseworthy lords, pre-eminent in learning and holiness, and worthy to be named with honor, the bishops Hincmar and Pardulus: Prudentius, their most devoted lover and faithful supporter, eternal salvation in the Lord.

Rabbanus Maurus, in his letter to Hincmar, says the following about the work that follows:

“For Prudentius, bishop of the city of Troyes, writing to you and to Pardulus, collected in his quires many testimonies of the Fathers who had gone before. In some places he agrees with our understanding: namely, where he says that God is not the author of sin and compels no one to sin; that he mercifully grants an immense reward to the just, but justly repays the wicked with a punishment corresponding to their evil deeds, because ‘the Lord is just in all his ways and holy in all his works’ (Psalm 144). But when he says that, just as God by his predestination brings the elect to eternal reward, so by his predestination he compels sinners to go to destruction, I would think that, in collecting his testimonies, he intends us to believe and confess, according to the teaching of Gottschalk, and of you, bishops, that there is a twofold predestination: namely, that just as God, foreknowing and predestining the elect, leads them to life, so, foreknowing and predestining the reprobate, he leads them to punishment.

“But because I have nowhere found this stated in such a combined form in the sacred Scriptures, I do not consent to his teaching. My bodily weakness and the infirmity of old age do not allow me to answer each of his propositions individually, point by point, or to set against the opinions that he gathered from many books the contrary opinions.”

This criticism of Prudentius by Rabbanus seems somewhat too severe. For nowhere does Prudentius assert, in Gottschalk’s sense, that just as God brings the elect to eternal reward by his predestination, so by his predestination he compels sinners to go to destruction.

For what Prudentius says in chapter 3 is: “He predestined”—that is, he foreordained—not that they should sin, but that because of sin they should perish by everlasting punishments. He predestined—that is, he foreordained—not to guilt but to punishment. This must be understood in such a way that the reprobate are not punished by a predestination to punishment, but on account of sin, foreseen from eternity and later freely committed by them in time.

Thus Prudentius favors neither Gottschalk nor Calvin nor the doctrine of Jansenius, which was condemned by the supreme pontiffs Innocent X and Alexander VII. His statement that Christ died for the elect alone can likewise be explained suitably. For he is not speaking of the sufficiency of Christ’s death for all, but of its efficacy for the elect alone.

Similarly, when he says that God does not will all human beings to be saved, he is plainly speaking of the absolute and consequent will, not of the conditional and antecedent will, as is evident from the passages of the holy Fathers Augustine, Prosper, Gregory, and others, many of which he collected here.
