## Epistle to Hincmar and Pardulus

To Hincmar and Pardulus, Prudentius, their most devoted lover and faithful supporter, eternal salvation in the Lord.

I had indeed wished, most venerable Fathers, and greatly beloved in God and in our Lord Jesus Christ, to discuss with you in secret and friendly conversation the questions that had been proposed, and diligently to seek whatever, after every obstinacy in disputation had been entirely removed and each person’s private inclination put aside, might appear sounder and more salutary through the gift of heavenly grace.

But when matters were turned in another direction, I found such resistance that I was not even granted the opportunity to set forth my intention. Therefore, since the freedom of conversation has been denied so completely, I have been compelled, in the most sincere affection of charity that I specially owe to your unanimity, to offer whatever literary service I can, however small it may be, and to make known in writing what I have conceived in my mind.

### Chapter I  
### On the doctrine of Saint Augustine and the Roman pontiffs who confirmed it

First and above all I admonish and ask your sincerity not to allow the doctrine of the most blessed Father Augustine—without any doubt the most learned of all men, and in every respect most harmonious with the authority of the sacred Scriptures—to be attacked during your pontificate by anyone under any pretext. No teacher has probed the hidden matters of Scripture more scrupulously, sought them more diligently, found them more truly, explained them more faithfully, retained them more firmly, defended them more vigorously, or spread them more abundantly.

That doctrine has been endowed with so great a gift of heavenly grace that it cannot in any way be torn away by anyone’s effort, since both the dignity of the Apostolic See and the unity of the whole Catholic Church have approved and strengthened it with thoroughly concordant authority. No one can oppose it in isolation without also opposing the universal Catholic Church, with it and in it.

For if he had perceived anything contrary to orthodox faith in it, the venerable Innocent, bishop of the Roman Church, would never have embraced it together with the bishops of the whole world; nor would he have honored that memorable Father with the services of his letters, both publicly and privately. Nor would his successor Zosimus have followed the same path. Nor would Boniface, prelate of the same Apostolic See, have sent him the letters of the Pelagians that had been brought to him for reply; nor would he have received his reply, published in four books, with such approval and honor.

Coelestine also, bishop of that celebrated city, declared through the authority of the Apostolic See what he thought about Augustine and his doctrine against the madness of the Gauls. The decrees state as follows:

“Nor can we be surprised if they now dare to attempt such things against the living who strive even to destroy the memory of their brothers who have fallen asleep. We have always held Augustine, a man of holy remembrance, in our communion on account of his life and merits, and never has even a rumor of sinister suspicion touched him. We remember that he was once a man of such great learning that even my predecessors counted him among the best teachers. All therefore held the same good opinion of him, since everywhere he was both loved and honored.”

Nor should we doubt that Pope Leo the Blessed held the same view of him. When condemning the madness of Eutyches and establishing orthodox faith by gathering the opinions of Catholic teachers, Leo did not hesitate to insert the opinions of blessed Augustine.

How highly the most blessed Pope Gregory regarded him is shown by Gregory’s letter to Bishop Innocent, in which these are his words:

“As for the fact that you wished the book of the exposition of holy Job to be transmitted to you, we rejoice greatly in your zeal, since we see that you apply your Eminence to this matter, which does not allow you to go entirely outside yourselves and gathers you back again to the heart from cares scattered among worldly affairs. But if you desire to be nourished with a rich pasture, read the little works of blessed Augustine, your father; and, in comparison with that meal of wheat, do not reject our bran.”

### Chapter II  
### Those who defended the doctrine of Saint Augustine

Saint Fulgentius, a bishop of extraordinary learning, would certainly not have written to Monimus, who was asking about the destruction of the lost, a book in defense of the opinion of so great a Father, if he had known or believed that Augustine had thought or written anything contrary to the Catholic faith.

The title of chapter 3, however, should not trouble the reader, although on its surface it seems to approach condemned doctrine. Perhaps Prudentius used these words because he feared—as the Church of Lyons and the Council of Valence feared at the same time—that Hincmar might favor the Origenist heresy. The Origenists were called “merciful,” because they believed that God’s will to save absolutely all human beings had been effective and that Christ had effectively died for absolutely all human beings, so that, descending to hell, he had freed from it all those formerly condemned, while intending to free the others in the age to come. Hence it is not surprising if Prudentius inclines toward the opposite side, as did the Church of Lyons and the Council of Valence.

[scan page 495]

## Saint Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

None of the Gauls—although someone said of them that their decisions were always sudden (*Caesar, Gallic War*, III)—rejected the predestination of the lost; rather, they preferred by a new conspiracy to detract from the predestination of the saints. Against their insane presumption, that same memorable and outstanding teacher Augustine, responding orthodoxly at the request of Prosper and Hilary, composed two books with the greatest completeness and fidelity: one *On the Predestination of the Saints*, the other *On the Gift of Perseverance*. In them he discussed very little about those predestined to destruction, but much more, and with complete truth, about those predestined to glory.

Prosper, the foremost teacher of the province of Gaul, a consistent follower and defender of Augustine’s salutary statements and writings, after that memorable Father had unquestionably departed to the heavenly realms, confronted the raging Gauls—his own people—with a Catholic response. He asserted beyond doubt both that Augustine’s doctrine was orthodox and that Augustine had neither thought nor written anything at all contrary to the rule of truth.

I would consider this response of Saint Prosper sufficient for the questions proposed, if the obstinacy of certain people who think otherwise did not summon me to other matters.

At that time the entire controversy against the predestination of the saints was conducted by certain fabricated inventions, to which the Fathers of venerable memory had already given a sufficient and abundant answer. Now, however, different efforts are being made, and the predestination of the lost is entirely abolished by some—as though either the incomprehensible and therefore irreproachable justice of the omnipotent Judge could be emptied of meaning, or as though it could not be supported by the authority of the sacred Scriptures.

Yet to those who read devoutly and attentively, it is by no means kept silent. Even if the same word is not used, it is expressed through other terms and through sentences bearing the same meaning, as the following passages will demonstrate with the greatest clarity, by Christ’s favor.

Are we so foolish as to think that blessed Jerome, the most faithful and learned interpreter of both Testaments, could have spared that same Father if he had known him to deviate in any respect—especially since Jerome rebuked him in one of his letters, accepted him immediately after he had been corrected, and thereafter very often extolled him with many praises and always held him in love and honor?

With these points established, let us finally carry out, with the Lord’s favor, what we have begun.

### Chapter III  
### He introduces three questions for discussion: the predestination of the reprobate; Christ’s death for the elect alone; and God’s will not to call and save all human beings

Following, then, the most salutary doctrine of so great a Father, we say—to omit other matters—that God, supremely and unchangeably good and just, created the human being from the abundance of his goodness, endowed him with a rational soul, and most fittingly adorned him with freedom of choice. Thus, if the human being used that freedom well and generously, with the assisting grace of the Creator, he could live; but if he used it stubbornly and wrongly, he could most justly be condemned to death by his own choice.

The human race, having miserably swollen with pride, first experienced the gratuitous goodness and liberality of God, and then, having been most rightly bound by his perfectly just equity, experienced its consequences. The mass of the whole human race, condemned on account of the guilt of disobedience in its first parents, God both foreknew and predestined—that is, by his omnipotence he foreordained—to lead those whom, through the grace and blood of his own Son, God and our Lord Jesus Christ, he mercifully separated from that same mass of perdition back to life, glory, and an everlasting kingdom.

He likewise foreknew and predestined—that is, foreordained—that whomever the grace and blood of that same Son, God and our Lord Jesus Christ, did not separate from the aforesaid miserable mass, he would justly punish with everlasting penalties.

He predestined, I say—that is, he foreordained—not that they should sin, but that because of sin they should perish in everlasting punishments. He predestined—that is, foreordained—not to guilt but to punishment; not that he should commit or admit some evil, but that, because of the evil which he would willingly commit, he should justly condemn him to everlasting punishment.

But those whom the blood of his own Son, God and our Lord Jesus Christ, mercifully liberated: was it poured out for all human beings whatsoever, or for certain people—that is, for the elect, predestined by an undeserved election? Let the all-powerful Truth itself, which mercifully assumed him into the unity of its own person and poured out his blood, teach us after due inquiry.

For when, as the holy Evangelists—most truthful witnesses and writers of his words and deeds—testify, Christ was declaring during the supper the mysteries of his death, which he underwent by his own will, a wholly undeserved death and the redemption of us, he indicated for whom he would suffer.

Matthew says:

“And taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them, saying: Drink from this, all of you; for this is my blood of the New Testament, which will be poured out for many for the remission of sins” (Matthew 26).

Mark says:

“And taking the cup, giving thanks, he gave it to them, and they all drank from it. And he said to them: This is my blood of the New Testament, which will be poured out for many” (Mark 14).

Luke says:

“And taking bread, he gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them, saying: This is my body, which will be given for you; do this in remembrance of me. Likewise also the cup after supper, saying: This cup is the New Testament in my blood, which will be poured out for you” (Luke 22).

In these words of incorruptible Truth, all the obscurities and controversies of the dispute, as far as my weakness allows, are brought to an end. They shine with such clarity that if anyone attempts to understand them otherwise and to assert the contrary, he will be defeated by the inescapable—so to speak—clarity of Truth itself.

For behold, Truth says not “for all,” but “for many”; not “for others,” but “for you.” And does anyone dare to mutter in any way against such majesty, otherwise than did the outstanding preacher, the teacher of the Gentiles, who immovably follows him in faith and truth? Concerning God, Paul cries out:

“Who wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2).

Those whom Truth calls “many,” the preacher of Truth now calls “all”; those whom that same Truth calls “few” and “elect”…

[The sentence continues on the following page.]

## Epistle to Hincmar and Pardulus

…[the preacher of Truth calls] “all.” In what way, then, can “many” or “few” be understood by the word “all”? You are not to be instructed by the little stream of my arid understanding, since you have grasped everything effectively.

Yet, as you recall, the memorable Augustine says that God wills all to be saved—but whom does he save? Either all from every class of human beings, or he wills all to be saved because he does not make all human beings willing to be saved. Otherwise, if “all” is to be understood generally and not specifically, where is that omnipotence by which he made everything whatsoever that he willed in heaven and on earth—not merely some things, but everything generally? (Psalm 134).

Of this it is most truly sung:

“All that the Lord willed, he made in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the depths.”

And it is said to him:

“In your will, or under your rule, Lord, all things have been placed; and there is no one who can resist your will” (Esther 13).

And where will be that which we faithfully profess in our daily and nightly confessions, when we say that we believe in God the almighty Father? If he wills something and does not do it—and may that thought be far from the hearts of all who are to be saved—then the one proclaimed omnipotent is accused of impotence. Let your prudence consider how great a folly that would be.

[Ratramnus, book I, *On Predestination*.]

### Chapter IV  
### The third principal proposition is proved by the authorities of sacred Scripture

Having therefore weighed the pages of the sacred Scriptures more carefully, consider what blessed Job says:

“And his soul does whatever he wills” (Job 23).

What is it that Moses sings in the Song of Deuteronomy?

“He established the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the sons of Israel or of the angels of God; but the Lord’s portion is his people; Jacob is the cord of his inheritance” (Deuteronomy 32).

And in the Book of Esther, when he cast two lots, he received one for the people of God and the other for all the nations (Esther 3).

And Solomon says:

“Consider all the works of God: no one can save the one whom he has destroyed or rejected” (Ecclesiasticus 7).

And in the Psalm:

“He declares his word to Jacob, his ordinances and judgments to Israel. He has not dealt so with every nation, and he has not revealed his judgments to them” (Psalm 147).

And again:

“Do not have mercy on all who work iniquity” (Psalm 58).

And in the Book of Ecclesiasticus:

“On two things my heart was saddened, and at the third anger came upon me: a warrior failing through poverty, and a prudent man despised; and one who passes from justice to sin. God has prepared him for the sword” (Ecclesiasticus 26).

In the same book:

“All human beings are from the ground, and from the earth from which Adam was created. In the abundance of his discipline the Lord separated them and changed their ways. From them he blessed and exalted; from them he sanctified and drew them to himself; from them he cursed and humbled, and turned them away to their separation, like clay in the hand of the potter: to shape it and dispose it according to his judgment. All his ways are according to his disposition. As a human being is in the hand of the one who made him, so he will repay him according to his judgment” (Ecclesiasticus 33).

And in Job:

“When he goes out to seek bread, he knows that a day of darkness has been prepared for him in his hand” (Job 15).

And Isaiah:

“For Topheth has been prepared from yesterday; it has been prepared and made wide” (Isaiah 30).

In the same prophet:

“Where their worm will not die and their fire will not be extinguished” (Isaiah 66), a statement which the Lord confirms in the Gospel according to Mark in the same words (Mark 9).

Consider, I beg you, why God gives grace to one person and does not give it to another. Why, after so many thousands of years, did the Savior come for the redemption of the human race, while, apart from the Jewish people, the entire world remained in error without God’s grace through so many ages? Why did he call Abraham alone, and not the whole world, to knowledge of his mercy? Why did the dew of divine grace remain for so many years only on the fleece of the Jewish people, and why did the threshing floor of the whole world not deserve to be watered by God’s mercy? Or why did the single fleece afterward—the Jewish people—dry up from God’s grace, while the threshing floor of all the nations was drenched by the dew of divine mercy?

And when our Lord and Savior said in the Gospel:

“If the miracles that were performed in you, Chorazin and Bethsaida, had been performed in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have done penance in sackcloth and ashes” (Matthew 11; Luke 10),

why did he perform miracles where people would not only fail to believe in him but where he would even suffer, and not perform them where people would have repented and believed?

He himself also says:

“Not all receive this word, but those to whom it has been given” (Matthew 19);

“Let anyone who has ears to hear, hear” (Matthew 13).

And again:

“To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the others in parables, so that those not seeing may see and those seeing may become blind” (Luke 8).

And:

“They could not believe, because Isaiah said: ‘Blind the heart of this people, and make their ears heavy, lest they see with their eyes, understand with their heart, and be converted, and I heal them’” (Isaiah 6).

And again:

“I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me” (John 17).

And:

“No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6).

And:

“No one can come to me unless it has been given to him by my Father” (the same passage).

And:

“No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14).

And:

“No one knows the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Matthew 11).

And:

“I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Luke 10).

And when two wished to follow him, he admitted one and rejected the other.

And:

“As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills” (John 5).

If, therefore, he wills all human beings to be saved, why does he not give life to all, since he gives life to those whom he wills? Why does the Holy Spirit breathe wherever he wills (the same passage), but not in everyone? And why does he distribute to each person, not to all, as he wills (1 Corinthians 12)?

It is also read in the Acts of the Apostles that in past generations he allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways, and chose only one nation, the Jewish nation (Acts 14).

And when the apostles preached, only those who had been ordained to eternal life believed (Acts 13).

---

[scan page 497]

## Saint Prudentius

When Paul and Barnabas wished to preach in Asia, the Spirit of Jesus prevented them (Acts 16).

And while Paul was teaching, God opened the heart of Lydia, the seller of purple, and not the hearts of the other hearers, so that she believed the things that were spoken by Paul (the same passage).

And the Apostle Paul proclaims that the remnant has been saved according to the election of grace.

And:

“God has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills” (Romans 9).

And, shaken by such great depths, he himself exclaims—so that you may not be ashamed to cry out with him:

“O human being, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’ Or does the potter not have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (the same passage).

And:

“O depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and how unsearchable his ways!” and so forth (Romans 11).

Consider, I beg you, which people are meant by the statement in the Gospel:

“He himself will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1).

And in the Psalm:

“He sent redemption to his people” (Psalm 110).

And again:

“Let those redeemed by the Lord say so, whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy and gathered from the lands” (Psalm 106).

And:

“Save us, Lord our God, and gather us from among the nations” (Psalm 105).

If, therefore, he has done everything whatsoever he willed, and wills all human beings to be saved, then what he did not do he did not will, and those whom he does not save he does not will to save—by a most hidden, lofty, incomprehensible, and irreproachable judgment, but nevertheless an entirely just one.

### Chapter V  
### The collection from the Fathers begins, by which the first proposition concerning the twofold predestination is proved

Having considered these matters carefully and diligently, let us finally append the opinions of Catholic teachers and show how they agree with them—not explanations of everything stated above, but passages containing their thoughts in words or meanings corresponding to those propositions.

Pope Innocent, in the letter addressed to Bishop Laurence, chapter 49 (*Letters*, XII):

“But lest they should have any further opportunity to rage and drag the souls of the simple and uncultivated into Gehenna, to which they have been destined…”

Ambrose, in his exposition of the Apostle Paul’s Letter to the Romans, at Romans 9:

“He chose one by foreknowledge and rejected the other. In the one whom he chose, God’s purpose remains, because nothing else can happen than what he knew and purposed concerning him, so that he might be worthy of salvation. In the one whom he rejected, likewise the purpose remains which he formed concerning him, because he will be unworthy.

“This is as though it were predestination, not respect of persons: for he condemns no one before he sins, and crowns no one before he conquers.

“This concerns the case of the Jews, who defend their prerogative on the ground that they are children of Abraham. The Apostle consoles himself because, having said that he had continual sorrow of heart on account of their unbelief—for they possessed adoption as sons, the covenant, and the law, and from them came Christ the Savior, as he himself says, ‘salvation is from the Jews’ (John 4)—he goes on to say that not all who are in Israel will believe, nor are all who are called children of Abraham to be called Abraham’s children, as I mentioned above.

“He lessens his own sorrow when he finds that it had formerly been foretold that not all would believe, so that he may grieve only for those who through envy labor in unbelief. Yet the unbelievers mentioned need not be greatly mourned, because they were not predestined to life; for God’s foreknowledge long ago decreed that they would not be saved.”

The same author, in the same place:

“Foreknowledge is that by which God has determined what the future will of each person will be, in which he will remain, and by which he will either be condemned or crowned. Thus those whom he knows will remain good are often previously evil, and those whom he knows will remain evil were sometimes previously good.

“Therefore let the complaint cease, since God is not a respecter of persons” (Acts 10). Saul and Judas were good beforehand, as Scripture says of Saul: ‘He was a good man, and there was no one better than he among the children of Israel’ (1 Samuel 9). And concerning Judas Iscariot the Apostle Peter says: ‘He obtained a share in this ministry’ (Acts 1), that is, in the apostleship.

“How, then, could he obtain a share in a saving ministry unless he had been good? For in the allotment of God’s judgment, he was considered worthy at the time when he was chosen.”

Again, in the same work:

“It is clear that some vessels are made for honor, because they are needed for honorable uses, while others are made for dishonor, because they are intended for base purposes; yet they are of one substance and differ by the will of the craftsman, some for honor.

“So also God, although we all possess one and the same substance and are all sinners, has mercy on some and rejects another, not without justice. In the potter there is only will; but in God there is will together with justice, for he knows on whom he ought to have mercy, as I have mentioned above.

“And if, wishing to show his wrath and make known his power, he endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, and to show the riches of his glory on vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory” (Romans 9), the meaning is that, by God’s will and long-suffering—which is patience—the unbelievers are prepared for punishment.”

### Chapter VI  
### From Saint Augustine, in his Letter to Sixtus

Augustine, from his letter to the presbyter Sixtus (*Letter* 105):

“Hence elsewhere it is said: ‘Peace to the brothers, and charity with faith,’ and, lest they should attribute this to themselves, he immediately added: ‘from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ’ (Ephesians 6).

“For faith does not belong to all who hear the word, but only to those to whom God apportions the measure of faith. Just as not everything that is planted and watered grows, but only what God gives growth to.

“But why does one person believe and another not believe, when both hear the same thing and the same miracle occurs before their eyes, so that both see the same thing? It is the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God, whose judgments are unsearchable, and with whom there is no injustice, since he has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills” (Romans 9).

They are not therefore unjust because they are hidden.

In the same work: “And lest anyone suppose that believers belong to his foreknowledge in the same manner as unbelievers—that is, that faith itself is not given them from above, but only their will is foreknown—he immediately adds: “For this reason I told you that no one can come to me unless it has been given him by my Father” [John 6]. This is why, of those who heard him speaking of his flesh and blood, some withdrew in offense while others remained in faith: no one can come to him unless it has been given him by the Father, and consequently also by the Son himself and by the Holy Spirit. For the gifts and works of the inseparable Trinity are not separate. But in thus honoring the Father, the Son supplies no evidence of any inequality, but provides a great example of humility.

Here again these defenders of free choice—indeed deceivers because they are puffed up, and puffed up because presumptuous—when they speak not against us but against the Gospel, say nothing other than what the Apostle set before himself as though it were being said by such people: “You will say to me, then, ‘Why does he still find fault? For who resists his will?’” [Rom. 9]. He set this objection before himself as though from the voice of those unwilling to accept what he had said above: “He has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills.” To such people, therefore, let us say with the Apostle—for we cannot find anything better to say than he did—‘O man, who are you to answer back to God?’ [Rom. 9].”

“We seek the desert of hardening, and find it. For by the desert of sin the whole mass was condemned, since all sinned; and God does not harden by imparting wickedness, but by not imparting mercy. Those to whom it is not imparted are neither worthy nor deserving of it; indeed, they are worthy and deserving precisely that it not be imparted to them. But when we seek the desert of mercy, we find none, lest grace be nullified if it is not given freely but paid out according to merits.”

In the same work: “But if they are vessels of wrath, made ready for destruction, which is repaid to them as their due, let them blame themselves, because they were made from that mass which God justly and deservedly condemned on account of the sin of the one in whom all sinned. If, however, they are vessels of mercy, to whom, though made from the same mass, he did not wish to repay the punishment they deserved, let them not be puffed up, but glorify him who grants them undeserved mercy.”

In the same work: “If this is a just excuse, then the grace by which they are freed is no longer free grace, but they are freed because of the justice of this excuse [or: ‘it is no longer free grace, but they are freed because of the justice of this excuse’]. But if it is grace by which they are freed, then this excuse is certainly not just. For grace is truly grace when a person is freed without being repaid according to the debt of justice.”

* Hincmar, Book 1, *On Predestination*, chapter 9.  
† *Sentences*, distinction 40, chapter “Whoever…”

“Therefore, when they say, ‘Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?’—what is accomplished except what is read in Solomon’s book: ‘The folly of a man perverts his ways, but he blames God in his heart’” [Prov. 19 according to the LXX]?

“Although God makes vessels of wrath for destruction, in order to display wrath and demonstrate his power, he nevertheless makes good use of evils; and in order to make known the riches of his glory in vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory, he made them for honor—not a gift owed to the condemnable mass, but one bestowed by the generosity of his grace. Yet in those same vessels of wrath, made for dishonor by the desert of the mass—that is, human beings created good according to nature but destined for punishment because of their vices—he came to condemn the iniquity which Truth most rightly disapproves, not to create it. For just as the human creature is ascribed to God’s will, which no one doubts should be praised, so guilt is ascribed to the human will, which no one refuses to condemn.”

In the same work: “But, to leave this aside for the moment, let me say only this about infants: they too, terrified by evangelical authority—or rather, crushed by the unanimous agreement of Christian peoples’ faith—admit without any excuse that no infant enters the kingdom of heaven unless reborn of water and the Spirit. What explanation will they give for the fact that one child is governed in such a way that, baptized, he departs this life, while another, delivered into the hands of unbelievers or even of the faithful, dies before being brought by them to baptism? Will they say that this is the result of fate or chance? I do not think they would dare to break out into such madness, however much they might wish to uphold the Christian name.

“Why, then, does no infant enter the kingdom of heaven without receiving the washing of regeneration? Did he himself choose unbelieving or negligent parents from whom to be born? [The supplied readings are *Nunquid non ita sibi parentes* and, as a variant, *Nunquidnam ipse sibi parentes*: the first asks “Did he not thus choose parents for himself?”, the second “Did he himself choose parents for himself?”] What shall I say of the innumerable unexpected and sudden deaths by which even the infants of devout Christians are often overtaken and deprived of baptism, while, conversely, the infants of sacrilegious persons and enemies of Christ, somehow coming into Christian hands, depart this world not without the sacrament of regeneration? What will those say here who maintain that certain human merits must precede in order that grace may be given, lest God be an acceptor of persons? What merits, finally, preceded here? If you consider the infants themselves, they have no merits of their own: the mass is common to both. If you consider the parents, those whose children perished through sudden deaths without Christ’s baptism are good, whereas those whose children came, through some Christian agency, to the sacraments of the Church are evil.

“Why does God’s providence—by whom our hairs are numbered, without whose will no sparrow falls to the ground, who is constrained by no fate, hindered by no accidental occurrences, and corrupted by no injustice—not provide for all the infant children of his own people to be reborn for the heavenly inheritance, while providing even for some infants of the impious? This infant, born of believing spouses and received with his parents’ joy, is suffocated through the drowsiness of mother or nurse and becomes deprived and bereft of his family’s faith; that infant is born of sacrilegious sexual violation, exposed through his mother’s cruel fear, gathered up by the merciful compassion of strangers, baptized through their Christian care, and becomes a sharer and participant in the eternal kingdom. Let them ponder and consider these things; here let them dare to call God either an acceptor of persons in his grace or a rewarder of preceding merits.”

* Hincmar, Book 1, *On Predestination*, chapter 7.

## Saint Prudentius

### 983

In the same work: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!” [Rom. 11]. Let them not, therefore, oppose the free mercy of God with obstinate madness. Let them know [*sciant*; variant *sinant*, “let them allow”] that the Son of Man seeks and saves in every age what had perished; and let them not dare to judge his inscrutable judgments—why, in one and the same matter, his mercy comes upon one person while his wrath remains upon another.

For who are these people who answer God, when he spoke concerning Rebecca, who had twins by one act of intercourse with Isaac our father? Before they had been born and had done anything good or evil, so that his purpose according to election might remain—namely, the election of grace, not of debt, the election by which he himself makes people chosen rather than finding them so; not from works but from him who calls—he said that “the elder would serve the younger.” In this connection the blessed Apostle also took up the testimony of a much later prophet: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” [Mal. 1], so that what was later made explicit through the prophet might be understood to have existed by grace in God’s predestination before they were born.

For what did he love in Jacob before Jacob had been born and had done anything good, except the free gift of his mercy? And what did he hate in Esau before he had done anything evil, except original sin? For he could not have loved justice in Jacob, since Jacob had done none; nor could he have hated nature in Esau, since he himself had made it good.

In the same work: “But if it is grace, then it is not from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace” [Rom. 11]. Accordingly, taking up the prophetic testimony in keeping with this grace, he says: “As it is written: Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” And immediately: “What shall we say, then? Is there injustice with God? By no means. But why, by no means? On account of the works which he foresaw would be performed by both? Certainly not. For Moses says: ‘I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show mercy to whom I show mercy.’ Therefore it depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy” [Rom. 9].

* “And so that the vessels made from the same mass for honor may recognize, in the vessels made ready for destruction, whose punishment is owed to the condemned mass, what divine mercy has bestowed on them, he says what Scripture says to Pharaoh: ‘For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my patience in you and that my name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth’” [Exod. 9]. Finally, he concludes concerning both: “Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills.” He with whom there is no injustice does this. He has mercy by a free gift, but he hardens by a most just desert.

## Bishop of Troyes

### CHAPTER VII

## From various books of the same Saint Augustine

Augustine, *Against the Pelagians*, Book 2 [*Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, Book 2, chapter 7]:

“In the case of these two twins, who undoubtedly had one common cause, the difficulty of the question—why one died in one way and the other in another—seems as though the Apostle had not resolved it. Yet when he himself had proposed something of this kind concerning two twins, because it was said not from works, since they had not yet done anything good or evil, but from him who calls, ‘The elder shall serve the younger,’ and, ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated’ [Rom. 9], and had carried the terror of this profound mystery to the point of saying, ‘Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills,’ he immediately perceived what this statement might provoke and set against himself the words of one who contradicted him. For he says: ‘You will say to me, then: Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?’ And he responds to the one who says this: ‘O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, “Why have you made me thus?” Does the potter not have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?’ [Rom. 9].”

“Then he disclosed as much of so great and hidden a secret as he judged ought to be revealed to human beings, saying: ‘But if God, wishing to show wrath and to demonstrate his power, endured with great patience the vessels of wrath made ready for destruction, and in order to make known the riches of his glory in the vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory’ [ibid.]. This is both an aid of God’s grace and a demonstration: an aid in the vessels of mercy, but a demonstration in the vessels of wrath. For in them he shows wrath and demonstrates his power, because his goodness is so powerful that he makes good use even of evil things, and in them he makes known the riches of his glory in the vessels of mercy. For what justice as punishment exacts from the vessels of wrath, the grace that delivers remits in the vessels of mercy; and the benefit freely granted to some would not be apparent unless God showed, by a just judgment, what was owed to both groups by condemning others, equally guilty, from the same mass.”

Augustine, *Against the Pelagians*, Book 4 [*Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, Book 4, chapter 6]:

“But why does he make these people sheep and not those, with whom there is no partiality? This is the very question which the blessed Apostle, when it was proposed with excessive curiosity and beyond one’s capacity, answered: ‘O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, “Why have you made me thus?”’ [Rom. 9]. This is the very question that belongs to that height which the same Apostle, wishing to contemplate, was in a manner terrified by and exclaimed: ‘O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, so that he might be repaid? For from him and through him and in him are all things; to him be glory forever and ever’ [Rom. 11].”

### 985

“Let them not, therefore, dare to investigate this inscrutable question—those who defend merit before grace, and therefore already defend something against grace, wishing to give God something first so that it may be repaid to them: wishing, of course, to give first something from free will, so that grace may be repaid as a reward. Let them understand wisely, or believe faithfully, that even what they think they first gave was received from him from whom all things exist, through whom all things exist, and in whom all things exist.

“But why one person should receive and another not receive, when neither deserves to receive and whoever receives receives undeservedly, let them measure their own powers and not investigate matters stronger than themselves. Let it be enough for them to know that there is no injustice with God.

“For when the Apostle had found no merits by which Jacob might precede his twin brother before God, what does he say? ‘Is there injustice with God? By no means. For he says to Moses: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show mercy to whom I show mercy.” Therefore it depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy’ [Rom. 9]. Let his free mercy therefore be pleasing to us, even if this profound question remains unresolved. Yet it is resolved to the extent that the same Apostle resolves it when he says: ‘But if God, wishing to show wrath and to demonstrate his power, endured with great patience the vessels of wrath made ready for destruction, and in order to make known the riches of his glory in the vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory’ [ibid.]. Wrath is not repaid unless it is owed, lest there be injustice with God; but mercy, even when it is granted undeservedly, is not injustice with God. From this the vessels of mercy understand how freely mercy is granted to them: the vessels of wrath, with whom they share a common ground for perdition and a common mass, receive the wrath that is owed and are justly punished.”

This is enough against those who wish by free choice to destroy the generosity of grace [or: “the giver of grace”].

“Behold what was said according to the Gospel: ‘The enemies are for your sake’ [Rom. 11]. For God’s hand and plan predestined as much to be done by the hostile Jews as was necessary for the sake of the Gospel, which exists for us.”

Augustine, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, to Prosper and Hilary, chapter 6: “For nothing happens except what he himself either does or permits to happen.”

In the same work, chapter 14:

“Accordingly, as the Apostle says: ‘It depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy.’ He also comes to the aid of infants whom he wills, even when they do not will or run, whom he chose in Christ before the foundation of the world; and he gives them grace freely, that is, with none of their merits of faith or works preceding it. He also comes to the aid of adults, even of those whom he foresaw would believe through his miracles if they had been performed before them. Those whom he does not wish to aid, he does not aid; concerning them he has judged secretly, but justly, according to his predestination. For there is no injustice with God, but his judgments are inscrutable and his ways unsearchable; for all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” [Ps. 24].

Augustine, excerpt from the *Retractations*, concerning *The Book of Eighty-Three Questions*, question 21 [Book 1, final chapter]:

“Whether God is not the author of evil.” There it must be seen that what I said—“He is not the author of evil, because he is the author of everything he made, and insofar as things exist, they are good”—must not be misunderstood. Nor should it therefore be supposed that the punishment of the wicked, which certainly is evil for those who are punished, does not come from him. But I said this in the same manner in which it is said: “God did not make death” [Wis. 1], although elsewhere it is written: “Death and life are from the Lord God” [Sir. 11]. The punishment of the wicked, therefore, which comes from God, is indeed evil for the wicked, but it belongs among God’s good works, because it is just that the wicked should be punished, and whatever is just is certainly good.

Augustine, in his exposition of Psalm 7 [after the middle]:

“He fashioned his arrows for those who burn.”

I would gladly understand this bow as the holy Scriptures, in which the hardness of the Old Testament has been bent and subdued by the strength of the New Testament, as though by a kind of bowstring. From it the apostles are sent out like arrows, or divine proclamations are launched.

“He fashioned his arrows for those who burn”—that is, arrows by which those who are struck might burn with divine love. For what other arrow wounded the one who says: “Bring me into the house of wine, set me among perfumes, press me among honey [*mella*; suggested correction *mala*, “apples”], for I am wounded by love” [Song 2]?

By what other arrows is the person set aflame who, desiring to return to God and turning back from this pilgrimage, seeks help against deceitful tongues and says [or, according to another reading: “and is told”]: “What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, against a deceitful tongue? The sharp arrows of the mighty one, with devastating coals” [Ps. 119]. That is, when struck and inflamed by them, may you burn with such love for the kingdom of heaven that you despise the tongues of all who resist and try to draw you away from your purpose, and laugh at their persecutions, saying: “Who will separate me from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? For I am certain,” he says, “that neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” [Rom. 8].

Thus “he fashioned his arrows for those who burn.” For in the Greek manuscripts it is found in this form: “He fashioned his arrows for those who burn”; but most Latin copies have *ardentes*, “burning arrows,” instead of *ardentibus*, “for those who burn.” Whether the arrows themselves burn or cause others to burn—which they could not do unless they themselves also burned—the sense is complete.

But since it says that the Lord prepared not only arrows but also vessels of death in the bow, one may ask what the vessels of death are. Perhaps heretics? For they too spring from the same bow, that is, from the same Scriptures, leaping upon souls not to inflame them with love but to kill them with poisons—something that does not occur except through their own merits. Therefore this arrangement too must be attributed to divine providence: not because providence makes them sinners [*faciat*, subjunctive; variant *facit*, indicative “makes”], but because it orders them after they have sinned. Ensnared by sin through an evil choice, they are compelled to understand badly, so that this itself becomes the punishment of sin. Yet through their death the sons of the Catholic Church, as though by certain thorns, are stirred up from sleep so that they may advance toward an understanding of the divine Scriptures.

“For there must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” [1 Cor. 11]—that is, among human beings, although they are manifest to God. Or perhaps he arranged the same arrows and vessels of death for the punishment of unbelievers, while he fashioned the arrows burning, or for those who burn, for the exercise of the faithful? For what the Apostle says is not unreasonable: “We are the aroma of life for some unto life, and the aroma of death for others unto death. And who is sufficient for these things?” [2 Cor. 2].

It is therefore no wonder if the same apostles are vessels of death to those among whom they suffered persecution, and fiery arrows for inflaming the hearts of believers. After this just dispensation, judgment will come. He speaks of it in such a way that we understand each person to receive punishment from his own sin, and that his iniquity is turned into punishment. Let us not suppose that God’s tranquility and ineffable light itself produces something from which sins are punished; rather, it orders sins themselves so that, because they were pleasures to the sinful person, they become instruments for the Lord who punishes.

Augustine, in his exposition of Psalm 9: “Of the hidden things of the Son.”

What, then, are the hidden things of the Son? In this expression we must first understand that there are certain manifest things of the Son, from which these called “hidden” are distinguished.

Since we believe that the Lord has two comings—one in the past, which the Jews did not understand, and another in the future, which both groups await—and since the coming which the Jews did not understand benefited the Gentiles, it is not unfittingly understood that this title, “of the hidden things of the Son,” refers to that coming, when partial blindness happened to Israel so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter [Rom. 11].

Scripture indicates two judgments, if one pays attention: one hidden and the other manifest. The hidden judgment is now taking place, concerning which the Apostle Peter says: “It is time for judgment to begin from the house of God” [1 Pet. 4]. The hidden judgment is therefore the punishment by which each person is now either exercised for purification, warned toward conversion, or, if he has despised God’s calling and discipline, blinded for condemnation.

The manifest judgment is that in which the Lord will come to judge the living and the dead, with everyone confessing that he is the one from whom rewards are given to the good and punishments to the wicked. But then that confession will serve not as a remedy for the wicked but as an increase of their condemnation.

Concerning these two judgments, one hidden and the other manifest, it seems to me that the Lord spoke when he said: “Whoever believes in me passes from death to life and does not come into judgment” [John 5]—that is, the manifest judgment. For the passage from death to life through some affliction, by which the Lord chastises every son whom he receives, is the hidden judgment.

“But whoever does not believe,” he says, “has already been judged” [John 3]—that is, by the hidden judgment he has already been prepared for the manifest one. We also read of these two judgments in the Book of Wisdom, where it is written: “For this reason, as though to senseless children, you gave them a judgment for mockery; but those who were not corrected by this judgment will experience a judgment worthy of God” [Wis. 12]. Therefore those who are not corrected by that hidden judgment will be punished most deservedly by the manifest one.

Accordingly, in this psalm the hidden things of the Son are to be observed: both his humble coming, which benefited the Gentiles amid the blindness of the Jews, and the punishment now taking place secretly—not yet by the condemnation of sinners, but either the exercise of those who have turned back, or a warning that they may turn back, or blindness preparing for condemnation those who do not wish to turn back [or: “who did not wish to be converted”].

Augustine, in Book 2 of *On the Baptism of Infants*, writing to Marcellinus [*On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, Book 2, chapter 7], said among other things:

“Ignorance and weakness are therefore vices that hinder the will from moving toward the performance of a good work or from abstaining from an evil work. But for what was hidden to become known, and for what was not pleasing to become sweet, there is the grace of God, which orders [or: ‘assists’] human wills. If they are not assisted, the cause lies in themselves and not in God—whether those predestined for condemnation are so because of the wickedness of pride, or whether, if they are children of mercy, they are judged and instructed against that very pride.”

Augustine, from Book 15 of *The City of God*, chapter 1:

“I think that we have now dealt sufficiently with the great and difficult questions concerning the beginning and end of the world, or of the soul, or of the human race itself, which we divide into two classes: one consisting of those who live according to man, the other of those who live according to God. We also call these, mystically, two cities—that is, two societies of human beings, one of which is predestined to reign eternally with God, and the other to undergo eternal punishment with the devil.”

Augustine, *On the Perfection of Man*, to Eutropius and Paul:

“God looked down from heaven upon the sons of men, to see whether there was anyone understanding or seeking God” [Ps. 13]. This good, therefore, which is to seek God, there was no one who did—not even one—except in that human race which is predestined to eternal life. Upon them, therefore, God’s foreknowledge looked and issued its judgment.

“Therefore, just as through one transgression condemnation came upon all human beings—though from this condemnation infants are to be delivered through the sacrament of baptism—so through one justification justification comes upon all human beings” [Rom. 5].

In the same work:
