“Temporal death of the body, however, is left for the time being even to those who are redeemed by the death of Christ, for the exercise of faith and the contest of the present struggle [or: ‘strife’], in which the martyrs too contended. It too will be taken away in the renewal of the body promised by the resurrection. For there death will be completely swallowed up in victory; meanwhile the grace of Christ deprives it of its reign, lest it drag souls with it into the punishments of Tartarus.”

Augustine, from the *Enchiridion*, chapter 100:

“These are the great works of the Lord, sought out according to all his will, and so wisely sought out that, when the angelic and human creature sinned—that is, when it did not do what he wished but what it itself willed—he nevertheless fulfilled through that same creature’s will, by which what the Creator did not will came to pass, what he himself willed. He makes good use even of evil things, as supremely good, for the condemnation of those whom he predestined to punishment and for the salvation of those whom he mercifully predestined to glory.”

## CHAPTER VIII

### From Saint Fulgentius, *On Predestination*, to Monimus

Fulgentius, from *On Predestination to Monimus*, Book 1, chapter 5:

“Therefore, insofar as the truth itself—which is the true light—has granted me the ability to understand while illuminating the darkness in the investigation of this question, I think nothing else should be understood in that statement of Saint Augustine by which he affirms that certain people are predestined to destruction except destruction through punishment, not through sin; not to the evil which the unjust commit, but to the punishment which they most justly suffer; not to the sin by which they either fail to receive or lose the benefit of the first resurrection, but to the torment which their own iniquity wickedly produces for them and divine justice rightly repays.

“Nor is it to be understood as referring to the first death of the soul, in which infants are born or into which sinners fall when, as blessed James says, they are drawn away and enticed by their own desire; rather, it refers to the second death, which they must suffer under the judgment of the most just Judge—whether those who depart this world before receiving the grace of baptism, or those who receive God’s grace in vain after baptism and, until the end of their present life, prefer to remain slaves of sin and refuse, while the acceptable time and day of salvation last, to turn from their evil way so that they may live.

“They do not know that God’s kindness leads them to repentance; instead, according to their hardness and impenitent heart, they store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s just judgment.”

In the same work, chapter 7:

“Therefore the wicked are not predestined to do the evil things into which they are drawn and enticed by their own desire, but to suffer justly against their will. For by the name ‘predestination’ no coercive [or: ‘constraining’] necessity of the human will is expressed; rather, the eternal disposition of God’s merciful and just future work is proclaimed.

“The Church sings of God’s mercy and judgment. His work in a human being is that, by the hidden counsel of his will, though not by an unjust plan, he either grants gratuitous mercy to the wretched or repays due justice to the unjust; indeed, he either mercifully gives the debtor what he could justly exact if he wished, or justly exacts with interest what belongs to him and repays the wicked debtor what is owed to his iniquities.”

In the same work, chapter 11:

“In both groups, therefore—that is, in the just and the unjust—I think three things must be considered: the beginning of the will, the progress of the work, and the end of the repayment. Thus, whatever we see that is just and good, we should attribute to the just and good God; but we should recognize as unworthy of God those things in which we find neither goodness nor justice.

“Having considered the quality of the works, let us believe that those works are predestined by God which are found worthy and appropriate to divine mercy or justice. For the Lord is merciful, compassionate, and just. And first we must confess that the beginning of every good will comes from that eternal Trinity, which alone is the one and true God; we must confess that it is predestined and given by him.

“For what he prepared to bestow in eternal predestination, he bestows upon a human being through free justification.”

In the same work, chapter 17:

“And therefore, in order that the sequence of the little book may be properly ordered, we must also consider the will, action, and repayment of the wicked, so that we may determine whether the just God also predestined the wicked to do what he would punish as having been done by them.

“Or did he predestine the wicked justly to punishment because, although he foresaw their evil works as future [or: ‘although he foreknew them’], he did not himself predestine that they should be future, because he did not himself make them happen?”

## St. Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

### [Scan page 503]

Likewise, in the same work (chapter 49):

“God did not predestine man to an evil will, because he himself was not going to give it to man. For how could God predestine to an evil will the man whom he made in his own image, when he himself did not make that will?

“Likewise, in the same work (chapter 21):

“Moreover, since we cannot deny that the good God made man good, if we say that he was predestined by God to some evil work, we ascribe to the merciful and just God—God forbid!—such a work as cannot be found either merciful or just in him. For if, when man was made by God, he was good in God’s present work in such a way that in his predestination he was evil, then without doubt he was going to be made evil by God’s work, since he was predestined by him to sin. Immediately there follows the absurdity that God—of whom the Prophet says, ‘who made the things that shall be’—had within himself, God forbid, the origin of iniquity, if he himself had predestined the man made by him to be a sinner. For his predestination is the preparation of his works. And just as it belongs to the good God to be the cause of every good work, so it is incongruous that he should be thought the cause of any evil work.

“Furthermore, let us consider that no reason is given why man should be believed to have been predestined to sin by God. For if, among those whom God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ blessed with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, ‘just as he chose them in love, predestining them for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ in himself’ [Ephesians 1:3–5], the cause of predestination is sought, no other cause is found there, but only the gratuitous mercy of God.

“Likewise, in the same work (chapter 22):

“But when the cause of that predestination is sought in those who are thought to have been predestined, not to undergo punishments but to commit sins, I do not see what answer anyone who attempts to assert this can give. For can we rightly say that the saints were predestined for this purpose: that, with God mercifully working in them, the evil might become good and the impious just? When we say this, we say it to God’s glory. Shall we therefore be able to say, with equal correctness, that the wicked were predestined for this purpose: that, with God working in them—not mercifully, but at least justly—the good might become evil or the just impious? Far be this from us and from all Christians: that anyone should dare to assign the cause of any sin to divine equity, since it cannot be the cause of anyone’s wickedness or impiety.

“Likewise, in the same work (chapter 23):

“Who, then, would think that a man was predestined by the good and gentle God either to the wickedness of a will by which he would abandon the good God, or to the bitterness of obstinacy by which he would not fear the gentle Lord? Accordingly, it is fitting for the faithful to believe and confess that the good and just God certainly foreknew that human beings would sin, since nothing future could be hidden from him—for things would not even be future if they had not been present in his foreknowledge—but that he did not predestine any man to sin. For if God predestined a man to some sin, he would not punish him for his sins. By God’s predestination, either the merciful remission of sins or the just punishment of sins has been prepared.

“God, therefore, could never have predestined a man to that which he himself had purposed both to forbid by commandment, to cleanse by mercy, and to punish by justice. Accordingly, God foreknew that the wicked would end this life in sin, and predestined them to be punished with endless punishment. Just as the foreknowledge of human iniquity is not blameworthy, so the predestination of vengeance is worthy of praise, so that it may be recognized that the man whom he predestined to be punished for the merit of sin was not predestined by him to any kind of sin.

“Likewise, in the same work (chapter 24):

“And although it was not in his predestination that he should give wickedness to the human will, it was nevertheless in his predestination what he would repay the wickedness of the human will. Therefore, as the Psalmist testifies, ‘The Lord is merciful and just’ [Psalm 111:4], he predestined the just to glory and the wicked to punishment. To those who were to be justified and glorified, therefore, he both foretold and promised the work of his mercy; but to the wicked he foretold the work of his justice only; he did not promise it (chapter 25).

“If someone asks why God foretold that all things were predestined, but did not promise all things predestined, we answer that a promise cannot be said to exist unless something is foretold as going to be done for the purpose that, once accomplished, it may benefit the one to whom it is promised. A promise always concerns a gift, but not always a judgment; for the generosity of a promise always brings blessedness, whereas the severity of judgment sometimes brings grief.

“Fearing this, the Prophet pours out this prayer to God: ‘Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight’ [Psalm 143:2]. For he knew that all would be held equally under the bond of punishment unless God, in those whom he wished, should exalt mercy above judgment. Justification and glorification, therefore—which do not come to man from man but from God—were foretold and promised because they would greatly benefit the saints. Punishment, however, which would harm the impious eternally, was foretold only, not promised.

“This is also more readily demonstrated by divine testimonies. In that passage of the Prophet, both matters are found expressed together, where God, through Isaiah, reproves those who do not serve him in these words: ‘Behold, those who serve me shall eat, but you shall be hungry; behold, those who serve me shall drink, but you shall thirst; behold, those who serve me shall rejoice, but you shall cry out because of the grief of your heart, and you shall howl because of the contrition of your spirit’ [Isaiah 65:13–14]. In all these statements, whatever pertains to the persons of the wicked is merely foretold, not promised. For what severity threatens to inflict on the merit of iniquity must not be said to have been promised through the generosity of goodness. Whatever pertains to the persons of those who serve God, however, is both foretold and promised.

“Something similar appears in the saying of our Savior, when he says: ‘Then they will go away into eternal fire, but the righteous into eternal life’ [Matthew 25:46]. He both foretold and promised the reward that the righteous would enjoy; but he did not promise, only foretold, the punishment by which the wicked would be punished. Just as he predestined the saints to be summoned to receive justice, so he predestined the impious to lose that same justice, because the Lord is merciful and just. He could freely deliver from depravity those whom he wished, but he was never the author of depravity; rather, depravity’s author was the one who departed from God. Nor did God predestine the departure, although in his divine foreknowledge he knew that the creature would depart (chapter 26).

“God, therefore, is not the author of evil thoughts, although he is the disposer of evil wills; and from the evil work of anyone he never ceases to bring about good. Nor does he destroy the just order of their works in the very acts of an unjust will, since even this belongs to the order: that he justly abandons an evil will. Yet he abandons it as it departs from him in its evil works in such a way that the good operation of the permitting God is not absent there. He himself fulfills justice in the sinner’s unjust will, and from the evil by which he judges the sinner he bestows a benefit on those whom he wishes.”

Likewise, in the same work (chapter 26):

“He predestined such people to destruction because he prepared for such people the punishment of just retribution. The Lord himself plainly taught this in his discourse, in which he showed that not only the kingdom where the good rejoice had been prepared, but also the eternal fire where the wicked are tormented. For to the good he will say: ‘Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world’ [Matthew 25:34]. But to the wicked he will say: ‘Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels’ [Matthew 25:41].

“Behold to what the Lord predestined the wicked and impious: to just punishment, not to any unjust work; to penalty, not to guilt; to punishment, not to transgression; to the destruction that the anger of the just Judge repays to sinners, not to the destruction by which the iniquity of sinners provoked God’s anger against itself. The preaching of the blessed Apostle makes this clear: he calls those whom God is going to condemn eternally ‘vessels of wrath,’ not ‘of guilt.’

“Likewise, in the same work:

“The wicked, therefore, were not predestined to the first death of the soul, but they were predestined to the second death—that is, to the lake of fire and sulfur.”

### Chapter IX

### From St. Pope Gregory’s *Moralia*

Gregory the pope, *On Job*, book IX (chapter 12, on Job 9):

“In that whirlwind, therefore, the just man is by no means crushed. For, while still placed on the road of the present life, he considers how strict the exactor of works will appear in judging human acts: he condemns some who are bound by the guilt of original sin even without works. Hence the holy man rightly adds at once, speaking in the voice of the human race: ‘He multiplies my wounds even without cause.’

“For some are taken away from the present light before they reach the point of producing good or evil according to the merit of active life. For those whom the sacraments of salvation do not free from original guilt, and who have done nothing here by any action of their own, nonetheless arrive there at torments. One evil is theirs: to be born corruptibly; another: to die corruptibly. But because eternal death also follows after death by a hidden and just judgment, their wounds are multiplied even without cause: for they undergo perpetual torments although they have sinned by no act of their own will. Hence it is written: “No one is clean in his sight, not even an infant of one day upon the earth.” Hence Truth himself says: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” [John 3:5]. Hence Paul says: “We were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” [Ephesians 2:3]. If an infant is put to death solely because of original guilt, what, in that final examination, can he be said to be—so far as human judgment is concerned—except wounded without cause? Yet under the strictness of divine judgment it is just that the mortal offspring, like a fruitless tree, should preserve in its branches the bitterness it drew from its root. Thus he says: ‘In the whirlwind he will crush me and multiply my wounds without cause.’ It is as though, plainly considering the losses of the human race, he said:

“‘The strict Judge who kills with punishment those whom the guilt of their own actions condemns—if he also strikes eternally those whom the guilt of their will does not bind, then, in human estimation, he wounds them without cause.’”

Gregory the pope, *On Job*, book XI (chapter 2, on Job 12):

“The tents of robbers abound, and they boldly provoke God, although he has given everything into their hands.”

It is easy for a person to despise riches when he has them; but it is difficult for one who does not have them to consider them worthless. Hence it is clearly shown how great was the contempt for earthly things in blessed Job’s thought: he says that nothing belongs to the wicked who prosper only when he has lost everything. He says, therefore: “The tents of robbers abound, and they boldly provoke God.”

For they often grow more proud against God precisely in proportion as they are enriched by his generosity and contrary to their deserts; and those who ought to have been stirred by gifts toward better things become worse through the gifts.

But we must understand how they are called “robbers,” when it is immediately added: “although he has given everything into their hands.” If they are robbers, they have taken things away by violence; and there is no doubt that God is not the helper of violent men. How, then, does he himself give what these robbers wickedly take?

We must understand that one thing is what almighty God mercifully bestows, and another what, in anger, he allows someone to possess. What robbers do wickedly, the most just Dispenser permits to happen only justly: he allows the one permitted to rob to increase his guilt through blindness of mind, and the one who suffers the robbery to be struck, in the loss caused by that same robbery, for another fault previously committed.

For behold, someone stationed in a mountain pass lies in wait for travelers. But perhaps the traveler has at some time committed some injustice; and almighty God, repaying his evil in the present life and handing him over to the robber’s hands, permits him either to be despoiled of his goods or even to perish.

What the robber does unjustly, therefore, the just Judge permits to be done, so that the one might receive what he had unjustly done, and the other might at some time be struck more severely, since through his most wicked will almighty God justly avenged guilt in another. The oppressed is thereby purified; in the oppressor guilt is increased, so that he may either return from the depths of justice to repentance or, if he does not turn back, be struck by eternal condemnation all the more severely the longer he has persisted in his iniquity.

With the one, therefore, God deals mercifully, so that he may cease from sin; with the other, strictly, so that he may multiply sin unless he has recourse to repentance. In the former, evils are purged while he endures violence; in the latter, they accumulate while he commits them.

Almighty God, therefore, justly allows what he forbids to be done, so that from the very thing he now tolerates in those who do not turn back, he may at some time strike them more severely.

It is rightly said, then: “The tents of robbers abound, and they boldly provoke God, although he has given everything into their hands.” Whatever the wicked take away, he himself gives them this, since he could resist their robbery if he had wished to show them mercy.

From the same book (chapter 8):

“If he shuts a man in, there is no one who can open.”

By what he does wickedly, a man makes for himself nothing other than a prison of conscience, so that the guilt of his mind weighs him down and he cannot escape outwardly. When, by God’s judgment, he is left in the blindness of his wickedness, he is enclosed, as it were, within himself and finds no way of escape. He wishes to emerge from his evil deeds, but because the weight of his former conduct presses upon him, he cannot leave himself; he is shut up in the prison of evil habit.

Some, desiring to punish their own sins, turn what they rightly think they should do into more serious sins. In a remarkable way, what they think is an exit becomes for them an enclosure. Thus the reprobate Judas, when he brought death upon himself in opposition to sin, reached the punishment of eternal death; and he repented of his sin more wickedly than he had committed it.

Let it therefore be said: “If he shuts a man in, there is no one who can open.” For just as no one resists the generosity of the One who calls, so no one opposes the justice of the One who abandons.

God’s shutting a man in, therefore, is his not opening what has been closed. Hence it is said to Moses concerning Pharaoh: “I will harden his heart.” God is said to harden through justice when he does not soften a reprobate heart by grace. He therefore encloses the man whom he leaves in the darkness of his works.

From the same book (chapter 8):

“He loosens the belt of kings.”

He loosens the belt of kings when, because of the guilt of pride, he destroys the restraint of chastity in those who seemed to govern their own members well. But what is signified by a rope, if not sin? As Solomon says: “Iniquities seize the wicked, and he is bound by the cords of his sins” [Proverbs 5:22].

Gregory the pope, *On Job*, book XII (chapter 2, on Job 4):

“You have set his bounds, which cannot be passed.”

Nothing that happens to human beings in this world comes without the hidden counsel of almighty God. For God, foreknowing all future things, decreed before the ages how they would be arranged through the sequence of times. It has already been determined how much prosperity in this world should follow a person, and how much adversity should strike him, lest either excessive prosperity exalt his elect or excessive adversity crush them. It has also been determined how long each person should live temporarily in this mortal life.

Gregory the pope, *On Job*, book XIV (chapter 18, on Job 9):

“They surrounded my tent on every side.”

They surround a tent when they encircle the mind on every side with their temptations. By their evil suggestion they persuade it now to mourn over temporal things, now to despair of eternal things, now to fall into impatience, and to hurl words of blasphemy against God.

As we have already said, these words also fit blessed Job according to the historical sense. When he gathered before his eyes the evils he had suffered, he indicated that he had been struck not as a son to be corrected but as an enemy. Through him also the robbers made a way for themselves, and through them the evil spirits received permission to strike him. They surrounded his tent on every side: after his possessions and children had been taken away, they also covered his entire body with wounds.

It is very remarkable, however, that when he spoke of robbers he added “of God,” thereby showing that those same robbers were God’s. If the will and power of the evil spirits are distinguished in this matter, it becomes clear why they are called both robbers and God’s.

For evil spirits continually pant to harm us; but although they possess an evil will from themselves, they do not possess the power to harm unless the supreme Will permits it. They themselves desire to injure us unjustly, but they are permitted to injure any particular person only justly by God. Since their will is unjust but their power is justly granted, they are called both robbers and God’s: from themselves comes what they unjustly desire to inflict as evil, and from God comes what they justly accomplish from that desire.

From the same book (chapter 22):

“And I prayed for the sons of my womb.”

In God, who is not circumscribed by bodily form, bodily members—hands, eyes, and womb—are named so that the effect of his power may be designated through the vocabulary of bodily members. He is said to have eyes because he sees all things; he is described as having hands because he works all things; and in a womb offspring is conceived, which is brought forth into this life.

What, then, should we understand as God’s womb except his counsel, in which we were conceived before the ages through predestination, so that, created through the ages, we might be brought forth? God, therefore, who remains before the ages, prayed for the sons of his womb because, having created them powerfully through his divinity, he came in the flesh and humbly prayed for them.

Gregory the pope, *On Job*, book XVI (chapter 21, on Job 21):

“And in a moment they descend to hell.”

This may also be understood in the sense that those who have long been tolerated in iniquity are often carried away by sudden death, so that they are not even permitted to mourn before death for the sins they have committed. But since the life of the just is also sometimes ended by a sudden death, we understand the passage better if we take it as referring to their temporal life: whatever can pass away passes suddenly.

### [Scan page 506]

Job, who for this reason was believed by them to be unjust because they saw him scourged, rightly showed through the voice of that same holy man, concerning the flourishing and destruction of the wicked, that prosperity in the present life is not proof of innocence: many return to eternal life through scourges, and many are led to endless judgments without suffering a scourge.

From the same book (chapter 13):

“And as the whirlwind scatters a cinder.”

Before the eyes of the Almighty, the life of the wicked is a cinder. For although it appears green for a moment, it is nevertheless already seen as consumed by his judgment, because it has been appointed for eternal destruction. The whirlwind scatters this cinder because God will come manifestly: “Our God will come, and he will not be silent. Fire will burn before him, and a mighty tempest around him” [Psalm 50:3].

In the same book (chapter 32):

“But behold, when we hear these things” [variant: “when we hear”], “a question arises in our heart: why did the omnipotent and merciful God permit the reasoning of the human mind to fall into such blindness?” Lest anyone presume to investigate God’s hidden judgments beyond what is proper, it is rightly added:

“‘Will anyone teach God knowledge, who judges those on high?’”

When we are uncertain about what is done concerning us, we ought to contemplate other things that are certain to us and quiet the complaint of thought that arises from our uncertainty. For behold, he calls the elect back to life through scourges, while the reprobate are not corrected by scourges from their evil deeds. The judgments of almighty God concerning them are exceedingly hidden, but they are not unjust.

If we turn the eye of the mind toward higher things, however, we see there that we have no just cause for complaint against God. For almighty God, discerning the merits of the angels, established some to remain in eternal light without falling; others, who fell of their own accord from their high station, he cast down into the retribution of eternal damnation.

The Creator, therefore, does nothing unjustly when he has judged a more subtle nature than ours justly. Let him say:

“‘Will anyone teach God knowledge, who judges those on high?’”

For he who performs wondrous things above us clearly disposes all things concerning us with knowledge. After these matters have been set forth, there follows the passage where the human mind is wearied by questioning:

“This one dies strong and healthy, rich and happy; his entrails are full of fat, and his bones are moistened with marrow. Another dies in bitterness of soul, without any works.””

Since these things are so, who can investigate the secrets of almighty God, asking why he permits them to be so? The lives of the elect and the reprobate are indeed different, but the corruption of the flesh in death is not different.

From the same book (chapter 17, on Job 10):

“Fire devoured him which is not kindled.”

In a truly remarkable way, the fire of Gehenna is expressed in a few words. Bodily fire, in order to be fire, requires bodily fuel. Since it must be preserved, it is undoubtedly nourished by accumulated wood; it cannot exist unless kindled and unless replenished.

By contrast, the fire of Gehenna, although incorporeal, burns the reprobate cast into it bodily. It is not kindled by human effort, nor nourished by wood; rather, created once for all, it remains unquenchable, requires no kindling, and does not lack heat.

It is rightly said of this wicked man: “Fire will devour him which is not kindled.” For the justice of the Almighty, foreseeing future things from the very origin of the world, created the fire of Gehenna so that it would begin to exist as punishment for the reprobate, but would never cease its burning even without wood.

[Footnote: Hincmar cites this entire passage in support of his own case in his book *On Predestination*, chapter 16.]

From the same book (book XVI, chapters 16–17, on Job 12):

“For he alone is, and no one can turn aside his thought” [Wisdom 12:13].

Are there not angels and human beings, heaven and earth, air and sea, all winged creatures, quadrupeds, and reptiles? Certainly it is written that he created all things so that they might exist. Since there are so many things in the nature of things, why is it now said by the voice of the blessed man: “He alone is”?

To exist is one thing; to exist principally is another. To exist changeably is one thing; to exist immutably is another. All these things exist, but they do not exist principally, because they do not subsist in themselves at all. Unless they are held by the hand of the One who governs them, they cannot exist.

Everything subsists in him by whom it was created. Those that live do not give life to themselves, nor are those that move—and do not live—brought to movement by their own wills. Rather, he moves all things: he gives life to some, while preserving others without life, ordering their final essence in a wondrous way.

All things were made from nothing, and their essence would return toward nothing unless the author of all things held it by the hand of his governance. Therefore, none of the things that have been created can subsist or move by itself; they subsist only insofar as they have received existence, and they move only insofar as they are disposed by a hidden impulse.

Thus, when the sinner is to be scourged, the earth withers in his labors, the sea is shaken in his shipwrecks, the air burns in his sweat, heaven grows dark against him through floods, human beings burn in their oppression of him, and angelic powers are moved in his adversity.

Are the lifeless things or the living things we have mentioned moved by their own impulses, and not rather by divine commands? Whatever rages outwardly is intended to point to the One who inwardly disposes it.

In every cause, therefore, we must look only to him [variant: “fear only him”] who exists principally, who also says to Moses: “I am who I am. Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” [Exodus 3:14].

When we are scourged through the things we see, we ought carefully to fear the One whom we do not see. The holy man should therefore despise whatever terrifies outwardly, whatever, by its own essence, would tend toward nothing if it were not governed; and, suppressing all else with the eye of the mind, he should contemplate the One in comparison with whose essence our existence is nonexistence, and say: “He alone is.”

Of his immutability it is immediately and appropriately added: “And no one can turn aside his thought.” For just as his nature is immutable, so is his thought immutable. No one turns aside his thought, because no one prevails against his hidden judgments.

### [Scan page 507]

For although there have been some who seemed to turn aside his thought by their prayers, his inward thought was such that they could turn aside his sentence by praying and receive from him what they were to do before him.

Let him therefore say: “And no one can turn aside his thought,” because once established, his judgments can in no way be changed. Hence it is written: “He issued a command, and it will not pass away” [Psalm 148:6]. And again: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” [Luke 21:33]. And again: “My thoughts are not like your thoughts, nor are my ways like your ways” [Isaiah 55:8].

When the sentence appears to be changed outwardly, the inward counsel is not changed, because what is outwardly done changeably is inwardly established immutably in each matter.

It follows:

“And his soul does whatever he wishes.”

Although God is exterior to all bodies and interior to all minds, the very power by which he penetrates all things and disposes all things is called his soul. Nothing that appears to happen against his will resists his will. Sometimes he permits even what he does not command to happen so that, through it, what he commands may be fulfilled more certainly.

The will of the apostate angels is perverse, but it is nevertheless wonderfully ordered by God, so that even their snares serve the benefit of the good, whom they purify while tempting them. Thus his soul does whatever he wishes, because he fulfills his will even through that by which his will appears to be opposed.

### Chapter X

### From Saints Isidore and Jerome

Isidore, from book I of the *Sentences*, “On Grace and Predestination” (chapter 22):

“Just as a human being does not know the boundary between light and darkness, or what the end of either may be, so he does not fully know who is overtaken by the light of justice before his end; or who is darkened by the darkness of sins until his end; or who, after falling into darkness, is converted and rises again to the light. All these things are open to God but hidden from human beings.”

Jerome, *Commentary on Isaiah*, book XI (chapter 6, on chapter 5):

“How those who are occupied with the pleasures of the world, not looking upon the works of God, are led captive into sin and do not possess the knowledge of God; and therefore they perish from hunger and thirst for good works and virtues. They will be dragged down into Gehenna, and there, condemned to eternal torments, they will see power and pride changed by misery and humiliation.”

Jerome, *Commentary on Isaiah*, book III (on the first part of chapter 9):

“For just as a garment stained with human blood cannot be healed but, defiled with blood, is burned with fire, so that the stains of foul blood may perish together with the garment, so the violent plunder of the devil, and the tumult and confusion by which he subjected the human race to himself, have been assigned to the fires of Gehenna.”

In book XII (on chapter 25):

“So that all his works may be brought into public view, and his inhabitants scattered into different places, assigned [variant: destined] to rewards or punishments.”

### [Scan page 508]

From book X (on chapter 30):

“For from yesterday and from former time Tophet has been prepared by the King, the Lord—that is, Gehenna, broad and spacious—which burns them with eternal fires.”

Jerome the presbyter, *Commentary on Ezekiel*, book IV (on chapter 14):

“Son of man, these men who sit before you have placed their abominations in their hearts, namely, their thoughts; and, according to Symmachus and Theodotion, idols and stumbling-blocks. Should I answer such men, who come to me with their former thoughts, not even at this time abandoning the crimes of their impiety?

“Since they have come to you with a perverse heart, answer them not from your own person but at my command, and say to them: ‘Thus says the Lord.’

“The meaning of the entire passage is this: ‘Man, man’—not members of other nations, whose error may perhaps be forgiven, but the house of Israel, which comes to inquire of the Prophet while retaining the former vices about which we spoke above. I will answer according to their heart and their uncleannesses, so that, according to what each wishes and believes, so also he may hear.

“For he does not deserve correction who asks not with the desire to learn but with the intention of testing. He must be caught by his own heart, according to the example of the scribes and Pharisees who, when they questioned the Lord—or rather, tested him—heard: ‘Why do you test me?’ [Matthew 22:18]; and again: ‘Nor will I tell you by what authority I do these things’ [Matthew 21:27].”

In the same work:

“What follows appears to pose a question: ‘When a prophet has gone astray and spoken a word, I, the Lord, have deceived that prophet.’ Let us not think that this is said of a true prophet, but of a false prophet, who is called a “false prophet” (ψευδοπροφήτης).

“This passage of Scripture can also be explained by the case of Ahab, king of Israel. Going to battle, he would not listen to Micaiah the prophet but accepted the counsel of the false prophets. Micaiah says that he saw the Lord sitting on his throne and a spirit of error voluntarily offering himself in order to deceive the king [1 Kings 22:19–22].

“The devil also, in the book of Job, is said to range through the earth and stand in the presence of God, and to receive from the Lord power first over Job’s possessions and then over his body [Job 1:7–12].

“Balaam the diviner, too, is sent by the Lord to deceive Balak the son of Beor [Numbers 22].

“All this is said so that the fact that the people are deceived and prefer to hear falsehood rather than lend their ears to the truth may not be attributed to the strength of the false prophets. Rather, it is said because it is an act of God’s anger that a perverse and unbelieving people should listen to false prophets rather than to the prophets.

“Finally, he stretches out his hand over him—that is, over the prophet—and he is removed from the midst of his people, so that he may bear his iniquity, because the terror and the punishment are alike: both the one who inquires and the one who is inquired of bear their iniquity.

“Thus the house of Israel, those who are willing to hear the words of God, is not mocked by perverse predictions; rather, it becomes God’s people and is deemed worthy to have the Lord himself.

“In the statement, ‘I, the Lord, have deceived him,’ Solomon’s words agree, for, speaking about God, he says: ‘He mocks the mockers’ [Proverbs 3:34].”

## Chapter XI

### Prosper’s Replies to the Gallican Objections

Prosper’s fourteenth objection is set out as follows (from Fulgentius, *To Monimus*, chapters 30 and the final chapter):

> “That those who do not believe the preaching of the Gospel do not believe by God’s predestination; and that God so determined that whoever does not believe does not believe by his own constitution.”

To this depravity—which was brought against the statements of blessed Augustine not from truth but from malice—Prosper replied in these words:

> “The unbelief of those who do not believe the Gospel is in no way generated by God’s predestination. For God is the author of good things, not of evil things. Therefore God’s predestination is always concerned with what is good, whether it pertains to the retribution of justice or to the gift of grace; for ‘all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.’ Accordingly, the unbelief of those who do not believe must be referred not to God’s constitution but to his foreknowledge. His foreknowledge did not thereby impose the necessity of not believing, because it could not be deceived concerning the unbelief that was going to occur.”

The fifteenth objection is likewise inserted in these words (the same work, chapters 15–16):

> “That foreknowledge is the same thing as predestination.”

Prosper replied to this:

> “He who distinguishes God’s foreknowledge in no respect from his predestination attempts to attribute to God regarding evil what must be attributed to him regarding good. But since good things are to be referred to God as their giver and co-worker, whereas evil things are to be referred to the voluntary wickedness of rational creatures, there is no doubt that, without any temporal difference, God both foreknew and predestined those things which were to be done with him as their author, or which were to be repaid to evil merits by a just judgment; but he merely foreknew, and did not also predestine, those things which were not going to have their cause in him.”

[Thus far is from Fulgentius.]

From the same work of Prosper, chapter 9:

> “There is absolutely no one among all human beings whose nature was not assumed in Christ our Lord, although he was born in the likeness of sinful flesh, whereas every human being is born in sinful flesh. Therefore God the Son, having become a participant in human mortality without sin, bestowed this upon sinners and mortals: that those who had become sharers in his birth might escape the bondage of sin and death.
>
> “Just as, therefore, for the renewal of human beings it is not enough that the man Jesus Christ was born unless they are reborn in the same Spirit from which he himself was born, so for the redemption of human beings it is not enough that the Lord Christ was crucified unless they die with him and are buried with him in baptism. Otherwise, since the Savior was born in the substance of our flesh and crucified for all of us, it would not have been necessary for us to be reborn and to be grafted into the likeness of his death.
>
> “But since without this sacrament no one attains eternal life, he has not been saved by Christ’s cross who has not been crucified in Christ; and he has not been crucified in Christ who is not a member of Christ’s body, who has not put on Christ through water and the Holy Spirit. For this reason he shared in our weakness and death, so that we might share in the power of his resurrection.
>
> “Although it is therefore rightly said that the Savior was crucified for the redemption of the whole world, because he truly assumed human nature and because of the common ruin of all in the first man, it can nevertheless be said that he was crucified only for those whom his death benefited. For the Evangelist says: ‘Jesus was going to die for the nation, and not only for the nation, but also to gather into one the scattered children of God’ (*John* 11).
>
> “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him; but to as many as received him he gave the power to become children of God, who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God (*John* 1). Their lot, therefore, is different from that of those who are counted among them concerning whom it is said: ‘The world did not know him.’ Accordingly it can be said: ‘The Redeemer of the world gave his blood for the world, and the world did not wish to be redeemed,’ because darkness did not receive the light—those to whom the Apostle says: ‘You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord’ (*Ephesians* 5).
>
> “The Lord Jesus himself, who said that he had come to seek and save what had perished, says: ‘I was not sent except to the sheep that had perished of the house of Israel’ (*Matthew* 15). Nor are all who are Abraham’s seed his children, but ‘in Isaac your seed shall be called’; that is, ‘not those who are children of the flesh are children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as seed’ (*Romans* 9).
>
> “Among these, therefore, are those of whom we recalled above that it was said: ‘Jesus was going to die for the nation, and not only for the nation, but also to gather the scattered children of God into one’ (*John* 11). For not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles, through him who calls things that are not as though they were and who gathers the scattered Israel, the children of promise are gathered into one Church, so that what was promised to Abraham might be fulfilled, when it was said to him that in his seed all the tribes of the earth would be blessed (*Genesis* 17).”

## Chapter XII

### From Cassiodorus on the Psalms, and from Bede

Cassiodorus, in his exposition of Psalm 9:

> “The Lord will be known as one who executes judgments; the sinner has been caught in the works of his hands”—a very true and unqualified sentence. For the Lord will then plainly be known to execute judgments when sinners are subjected to eternal torment. Since their crimes are now free, they are perhaps thought to remain unpunished; but when that day of manifestation arrives and the Lord sits upon his throne of majesty, then it will universally be recognized that he exercises his judgments, when the human race has been separated at his discretion, whether to the left or to the right. This is indeed the judgment by which the merits of each person are distinguished, without any confusion.”

The following is an open explanation of this sentence. For he says where it is known that the Lord truly executes judgments: namely, when the sinner is bound by the chains of his deeds and receives retribution according to the quality of his actions.

That interpretation must be avoided altogether which supposes that the sinner is tortured merely by recollection of his sins. For if that alone were sufficient, why would it be said, “Go into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (*Matthew* 25)? And likewise: “Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be extinguished” (*Isaiah* 66). This does not here deny that places of torment are given to sinners, but says that they are to be tormented according to the qualities of their deeds.

Let us therefore understand that a place of punishment has been prepared for sinners; let us understand inwardly the punitive evil by which the wicked perish. This is the meaning he expressed above, when he said that they were destined for eternal punishment, separated by certain boundaries from the blessed.

Cassiodorus on Psalm 2:

> “God most beneficially destroys in this life those whom he has decided to destroy again. But in the end, the one who is destroyed is assigned to eternal punishments.”

Cassiodorus on Psalm 54:

> “He does not allow such persons to complete their days, when, although they promise themselves a long life, they find the end of death very quickly. For the days of all are known to have been fixed in predestination.”

Cassiodorus on Psalm 65:

> “You placed human beings over our heads.” He says “you placed” so that it might be clear that all things were done by his will, just as the Lord says to Pilate: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (*John* 19).

Cassiodorus in his exposition of Psalm 87:

> “‘He sent upon them the wrath of his indignation: indignation, wrath, and tribulation, and the sending of evil angels.’ The order of vengeance is narrated with the truest description. First, the Lord is angry at our sins when we do not turn back with any repentance. Then he abandons human wickedness to his indignation, wrath, and tribulation, so that those who scorn obedience to divine commands may be afflicted by adversities of their own.
>
> “As it is written: ‘Therefore God gave them over to the desires of their heart, to impurity, so that they might do what is improper,’ and so forth (*Romans* 1). In the wicked person, indignation belongs to swollen pride, wrath to criminal boldness, and tribulation to confused despair.
>
> “Then, through evil angels, they are driven into illicit acts, and, as if stripped of divine protection, they fall into the snares of demons. This is what is meant by the beasts of the forest, that is, demons, and the lion cubs whom the devil’s corrupted will has begotten, seeking someone whom they might devour. They went out to find some persons as food for their malice, although the Lord permitted it. For nothing can be done by anyone except what he has permitted, by a secret judgment, either for testing or for vengeance.”

Cassiodorus on Psalm 81:

> “It is a great thing indeed, lest, by fleeing the saving remedy, you prepare eternal destruction for yourselves.”

Cassiodorus on Psalm 83:

> “‘And let them fear and perish.’ This is the meaning he stated above: because there, through fearing, they do not improve, but perish—those destined for eternal punishment.”

Cassiodorus on Psalm 88:

> “Divinity often cleanses those whom it scourges, so that it may receive one purified whom it had rejected as defiled by sins; but those whom it removes from cleansing—that is, withdraws from it—it has already resolved to condemn.”

Cassiodorus on Psalm 92:

> “‘Your throne is prepared, O God.’ ‘Prepared’ signifies predestination, because whatever may happen in the governance of the world wholly subsists in that truth.”

Cassiodorus in his exposition of Psalm 101:

> “He turned their heart to hate his people and to deal deceitfully with his servants.”

He has come to the fourth division, where he recalls that the Egyptians most savagely envied the Hebrews and subjected them to extremely harsh labor. By granting prosperity to the people of Israel, the Lord turned the Egyptians’ hearts toward hatred and deceit—not because he himself is the author of evil, but because, by granting benefits to others, he aroused hidden resentments. For it is necessary that wicked people swell with pride at the prosperity of others, since they know that they cannot deserve similar things.

The same occurred in the sacrifices of Cain and Abel, when he rejected the sacrifice of one and gladly accepted that of the other (*Genesis* 4).

Bede the presbyter, in his book on the *Hexaemeron* on Genesis:

> “‘And behold, the men stretched out their hand and brought them inside,’ and so forth (*Genesis* 19). That they are prepared for eternal burning is not improperly suggested.”

An exposition of this passage is found in Bede. Therefore, since only a few words suffice for the conclusion, we are compelled to be content with them.

## Chapter XIII

### On Grace and Free Choice, from Various Sources

These are the words of the venerable Pope Innocent on free choice, addressed to the Council of Carthage (*Innocent, Letter 29*):

> “For free choice, which that man formerly possessed, while he used his own goods without sufficient care, fell and was plunged into the depths of transgression. Since he found no way by which he could rise from there, and since he had been deceived in his freedom forever, he would have remained crushed beneath this ruin unless the coming of Christ later raised him up through his grace. Through the purification of new birth, Christ cleansed every former vice by the washing of baptism.”

From the letter of the African bishops to Pope Zosimus:

> “The sound meaning is found most clearly: that free choice does not exist,” and so forth, “and that one should work according to a good will.”

From Augustine’s letter to the presbyter Sixtus:

> “For those who think that free choice is taken away from them if they admit that a human being cannot possess even a good will without God’s help do not understand that they are not strengthening free choice but driving it onward to be carried through empty places, rather than being established in the Lord as upon a firm rock. ‘The will is prepared by the Lord’ (*Proverbs* 16, according to the Septuagint; the Vulgate reads: ‘He will obtain salvation from the Lord’).
>
> “When they think that they would believe God to be a respecter of persons if they believed that, without any preceding merits, he has mercy on whom he wills, calls those whom he deigns to call, and makes religious whom he wills, they pay little attention to the fact that a deserved punishment is given to the condemned, while undeserved grace is given to the liberated. Thus the one cannot complain that he is unworthy, nor can the other boast that he is worthy.
>
> “Rather, there is no respect of persons precisely where one and the same mass, a mass of condemnation—and indeed of offense—envelops all, so that the person who has been liberated may learn from the person who has not been liberated that the same punishment would also have suited him unless grace had come to his aid. And if it is grace, it is certainly not repaid for merits, but given by gratuitous goodness.
>
> “But they say: ‘It is unjust that, in one and the same evil condition, this person should be liberated and that one punished.’ Surely, then, it is just that both should be punished. Who could deny this? Let us therefore give thanks to the Savior, since we do not see returned to us what we recognize would also have been due to us in the damnation of those like us.
>
> “For if every human being were liberated, it would remain hidden what is owed to sin by justice; if no one were liberated, what grace bestows would remain hidden. Therefore, to use the Apostle’s words in this most difficult question: ‘God, wishing to show wrath and to make his power known, endured with much patience vessels of wrath made for destruction; and, in order to make known the riches of his glory in vessels of mercy’—to which the creature cannot say, ‘Why have you made me thus?’—‘having power from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor’ (*Romans* 9).
>
> “Since this entire mass has been justly condemned, justice returns the dishonor that is owed, while grace grants the undeserved honor—not by a privilege of merit, not by the necessity of fate, not by the recklessness of fortune, but by the depth of the riches of God’s wisdom and knowledge. The Apostle does not disclose these riches but marvels at them while they remain hidden, crying out: ‘O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, so that it might be repaid to him? For from him and through him and in him are all things; to him be glory forever and ever. Amen’ (*Romans* 11).”

Augustine, *Against Pelagius*, book 1 (*Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book 1, chapter 2):

> “They call Catholics Manichaeans—those with whom we have just now had no fellowship, that is, all those with whom we disagree—because they say that by the sin of the first man, that is, of Adam, free choice perished, and that no one now has the power to live well, but that all are compelled into sin by the necessity of their flesh.”

He calls Catholics Manichaeans in the manner of Jovinian, who a few years earlier had become a new heretic, destroying the virginity of holy Mary and equating the marriage of the faithful with sacred virginity. He made this accusation against Catholics for no other reason than that he wished them to appear to be accusers or condemnors of marriage.

> “In defending free choice, they rush headlong into making people rely upon it for doing justice rather than upon the Lord’s help, and into making each person glory in himself rather than in the Lord.
>
> “But who among us says that free choice perished from the human race through the sin of the first man? Freedom certainly perished through sin, but it was the freedom that existed in paradise: the power to possess complete righteousness together with immortality. For this reason human nature needs divine grace, as the Lord says: ‘If the Son makes you free, then you will truly be free’ (*John* 8)—free, that is, to live well and justly.
>
> “For free choice did not perish in the sinner to such a degree that all who sin with pleasure and love of sin do not sin by it. They take pleasure in what they desire because it pleases them. Hence the Apostle says: ‘When you were slaves of sin, you were free with respect to righteousness’ (*Romans* 6). Behold, it is shown that they could serve sin only through another kind of freedom.
>
> “They are therefore free from righteousness only by the choice of the will; but they are not free from sin except through the grace of the Savior. For this reason the admirable teacher carefully distinguished the very words:
>
> “‘When you were slaves of sin,’ he says, ‘you were free with respect to righteousness. What fruit did you then have in those things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death. But now, having been freed from sin and made slaves of God, you have your fruit in sanctification, and the end is eternal life.’
>
> “He called them free with respect to righteousness, not freed from righteousness; but he did not call them free from sin, lest they attribute this to themselves. Instead, he was most vigilant to say ‘freed,’ referring it to the Lord’s statement: ‘If the Son makes you free, then you will truly be free’ (*John* 8).
>
> “Since human beings do not live well unless they have been made children of God, what is this man doing when he wishes to attribute to free choice the power of living well, when this power is given only by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord? The Gospel says: ‘But to as many as received him, he gave the power to become children of God’ (*John* 1).”

>

>
> “For he would not have said ‘with me’ if, together with prevenient grace, subsequent free choice did not also exist. >

Gennadius, bishop of Marseille, *Definitions of Ecclesiastical Dogma*:

> “From the very first creation of the world, human beings were entrusted to the freedom of their own choice, so that, provided they maintained watchfulness of mind and also persevered in observance of the commandment, they might, if they wished, remain in what they had been created.”

[Variant:] “From the beginning of creation, so that, by watchfulness of mind alone and perseverance in observance of the commandment, they might remain, if they wished, in what they had been created.”

After he fell through the serpent’s seduction by Eve, however, he lost both the good of nature and the vigor of choice, but not choice itself, lest what he avoided should not be his own, and lest forgiveness be deserved for what he had not cleansed by choice [variant: amended sin]. Thus freedom of choice remains for seeking salvation—that is, the rational will—when God first admonishes and invites it to salvation, so that it may choose, follow, or act upon the opportunity for salvation, that is, God’s inspiration. But that it may attain what it chooses, follows, or does upon that opportunity, we freely confess to be God’s work.

> “Therefore, through God’s mercy we have the beginning of our salvation; to acquiesce in saving inspiration belongs to our own power; to obtain what, by acquiescing in the admonition, we desire, belongs to the divine gift; not to fall away from the gift of salvation once obtained [variant: unobtained] belongs both to our care and to heavenly help; to fall away belongs to our own power and sloth.”

[Editorial note:] The apograph appends these few words to Gennadius’s testimony; since they are not Gennadius’s own, they appear to be attributable to Prudentius and plainly have the character of the letter’s conclusion.

# Saint Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

## On Predestination

### Against John Scotus, or the Book of John Scotus, called Erigena, attacked by Prudentius, or Jerome, or Fulgentius

### Preface

To the most reverend Father and most blessed pontiff, illustrious among the shepherds of Christ for the excellence of his life and doctrine, Gueilo, Prudentius sends eternal greetings in the Lord.

Burning, as is fitting and necessary, with zeal for the Catholic faith and affection for true charity, most blessed Father, you sent me a certain memorandum containing nineteen chapters selected from a book by a certain Scotus. You said that these chapters diverged in some way from our understanding, and you asked and urged me to refute, with authorities from evangelical books and from Catholic teachers, whatever I found in them to depart from the truth.

[Manuscript note:]

> On the first page of the manuscript codex of this work, preserved in the monastery of Hautvillers, the following observation is found:
>
> “This book, which seems to speak in defense of the faith against unbelief and to produce testimonies from Scripture and the names of Catholics, must be read cautiously. In reading it, one should follow the Apostle’s statement: ‘Test everything; hold fast what is good’ (*1 Thessalonians* 5). For its author, Prudentius, did not think catholically about certain ecclesiastical doctrines, as other writings of his demonstrate.”

[Editorial note:]

> This judgment should not diminish the holiness and sound doctrine of so great a man. It may perhaps have arisen from someone whose doctrinal capacity was not sufficient to read through and understand the works of Prudentius, which are filled with mysteries drawn from the most hidden chambers and inner sanctuaries of divine wisdom. This will become clearly evident when the aforementioned book has emerged from darkness into the light.
>
> —Nicolaus Camusat, *Promptuarium of the Antiquities of the Diocese of Troyes*, folio 463.

# Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

## On Predestination

### Against John Scotus, surnamed Erigena, and against errors condemned by the ancient Fathers, namely Gregory and Augustine

## Against John Scotus

After you had sent me a certain memorandum containing nineteen chapters selected from a book by a certain Scotus, chapters which, as you say, diverged in some way from our understanding, you asked and urged me to refute, with authorities from the evangelical books and from Catholic teachers, whatever I found in them to depart from the truth.

[The supplied text ends here.]

## [Scan page 513]

### Saint Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

—from the deviant chapter, to draw forth fitting replies in abundance. Having gone through them and examined them carefully, I found in them the poisons of Pelagian perfidy, and on several occasions the madness of Origen and the frenzy of the Collyridian heretics—men whom the strongest cultivators and defenders of the Catholic faith rightly refuted and whose most justly severe judgment condemned long before our own times.

I trembled, I confess, and was terrified that so many errors, once lulled to rest together with their authors, should in our own age again begin to sprout, and that certain fading fumes should burst forth once more through a new ignition, making the eyes of many grow dim with their harm. When I prepared myself to refute them, as you had ordered, I was frightened by the difficulty of the labor and was considering abandoning it altogether. But when I weighed the authority of the one who commanded me, I said that it was better, with the fruit of obedience—even if not fully—to stumble somewhat than, through the timid fear of filial reverence, to oppose it in foolish obstinacy.

Thus encouraged by the merits of the one who asked, and by the most insistent purity of the one who wrote, I decided to seek out that same book with diligent curiosity, if perhaps something could be found by whose sequence I might more easily observe the tortuous paths of so many errors. Having, by the grace of God, without whom I am and can do nothing, attained what I had hoped, I discovered—as far as I could be divinely inspired—that John, namely Scotus, was in every respect a follower of Pelagius, Caelestius, and their fiercest associate and defender, Julian, barking against orthodox faith and the Catholic Fathers with such impudence that one spirit seems to have instructed Julian and John. It is as though one and the same spirit had been in them and, not a different spirit, had spewed through their tongues so many and such great nauseating blasphemies.

For they equally attack the gratuitous grace of God, similarly deny the justice of God, and with indistinguishable babbling dissuade people from believing in original sin—which we contract when we are born and from which we are released only by heavenly grace through the mystery of baptism. They lose themselves in an equally empty display of dialectical arguments. They also pervert the most correct understanding of the holy Scriptures and the soundest judgment of the Catholic Fathers with such polished perversity that one would think nothing had ever been done against their errors.

Since the Fathers, and especially the most blessed Augustine, have answered them most suitably and abundantly, I did not presume—

### It begins

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit: Prudentius, servant of Christ and member of his household.

### Chapter One

#### The fourfold way of the whole philosophy for resolving every question

I did not suppose that I should be judged by pious readers if, gladly obeying at the prompting of your holiness, I offered, in my humble measure, among the offerings of the tabernacle of my Lord what I could, leaving to those more capable and learned what they might better be able and willing to offer. Nor, as Saint Jerome says, should one person’s resources be sullied by another’s poverty.

Therefore, trusting in his grace, by which we are moved beforehand to will what is good and are then enabled to follow through lest we will in vain, I carefully gathered, by turning through the harmonious pages of the Fathers, whatever antidote each of them had prepared against these same poisons. I prefixed the name of each teacher and likewise identified the book.

I also inserted John’s own words in several places exactly as he arranged them, placing his name before them together with the preceding note called in Greek *sēmeion* [“sign”], which some customarily place before the principal propositions to be condemned. For in many places I have not inserted his words, which through excessive loquacity produce weariness in readers; rather, according to the capacity of my small mind, I have faithfully addressed their meaning. Wherever the insertion of my own speech required a necessary place, lest I claim for myself anything good that heavenly grace might speak through the instrument of my tongue, I made it my practice to place above it the sign called by the scribes a *chrisimon*, because it appears in a certain way like a monogram representing the name of Christ. In this way I wished to show that everything of his kindness which I had absorbed came through his abundant and undeserved gifts.

I also thought it necessary to warn you that your blessedness’s discernment should attend carefully and attentively to the many contradictions with which this same John attacks himself: what he now affirms he later denies, and what he presently rejects with loquacious vanity he subsequently confesses with loquacity. So completely that either he did not see what he had said, or he supposed that no one had ever seen it.

I therefore ask you, as you pass through everything with watchful diligence, to attribute whatever you judge to have been faithfully said to the author, giving thanks to the Lord. If, however—God forbid—you find anything otherwise, do not delay to correct it, showing compassion toward my weakness. In this way you will obtain a doubled fruit of pious devotion, if both what has been piously spoken answers the wishes of one who piously commands, and whatever has gone astray is directed back to its proper path.

May almighty God’s power preserve your most holy Fatherhood vigorous and safe, while you pray for me, burdened by many infirmities of mind and body.

### Book

John, having gone through your book of perversity, which you cast forth under the name of a certain Gottschalk against all Catholics, I received your blasphemies and shameless attacks—by which you insolently assail God’s gratuitous grace and inflexible justice—with all the more distress because I had embraced you more familiarly and loved you more particularly, since you have burst into such madness that you dared to twist the most weighty authority of the holy Scriptures by your depraved interpretations and to teach the meanings of the Catholic Fathers by reversing them into perverse meanings.

You impose upon us a certain fourfold way of understanding the Scriptures, which our Fathers—namely, all the Catholic interpreters, shining with divine and human wisdom—completely ignored, although they left behind many things learned and eloquent, explaining them and opening up various rules of understanding and modes of expression. They are shown never to have mentioned your fourfold way. Instead, they set before us much better, holier, and more learned paths. Supported by their help, we can avoid the filth of your tricks and draw and offer the purity of the simplest faith from the clearest and sweetest fountains, in the name and with the assistance—indeed, the prevenient assistance—of God’s grace.

## [Scan page 514]

### John Scotus  
*(Chapter 1, number 1, section 1)*

It follows from this that true philosophy is true religion, and conversely that true religion is true philosophy. Although it is divided in many ways and by diverse methods, it is nevertheless recognized as having four principal parts, necessary for resolving every question, which the Greeks have chosen to call *diairetike*, *horistike*, *apodeiktike*, and *analytike*. In Latin we may call them divisive, definitive, demonstrative, and resolutive.

The first separates one thing into many by division; the second gathers one thing from many by defining; the third reveals hidden things by demonstrating them through what is manifest; and the fourth resolves composites by separating them into simples. We have shown examples of these in the course of this work, insofar as the very light that illuminates the heart of those who seek has opened for us an entrance into the matters we are attempting to enter.

For by means of this fourfold way, like a useful and honorable fourfold road of human reasoning, one reaches the very discipline of disputation, through which every learned person is undoubtedly brought to the truth.

### Correction

† How much our greater predecessors accomplished against various heresies is testified by the councils gathered from the Fathers of the whole world through the Holy Spirit; it is testified by the synodal acts; it is also attested by the truthful writings of approved teachers. By their irresistible authority, the simplicity and solidity of the faith concerning these matters were defended and invincibly approved, and are recognized as not being entangled or more deeply involved in the tricks of your fourfold way.

For, as we are faithfully instructed by the order of the acts and by the writings of the Fathers, when at Nicaea, Chalcedon, Ephesus, Constantinople, Antioch, Mesopotamia, Africa, Rome, and very many other places, they acted unanimously against the opponents of the Catholic faith—indeed in different ways, but with the same sincerity of faith—and when, in the conflict, the opposing party relied on dialectical, or rather sophistical, conclusions, the holy Fathers, without doubt by the inspiration of the Spirit, took care that the defenders and champions of the simple faith should not be carried away by sophistical illusions, but should be armed with the clearest testimonies of the holy Scriptures.

Since these testimonies are many and so well known that it would be judged lengthy and superfluous to insert them all in this work, we have decided to set down the judgment of only one Father, without in any way diminishing the credibility of the others by this support for the faith.

#### Leo, Bishop, to Leo Augustus  
*(Letter 164)*

“I rejoice that many and most manifest proofs have shown me how greatly you consult the universal Church through your devotion. As soon as it was permitted, I did not delay to obey the commands of your piety, sending Donatianus and Geminianus, my brothers and fellow bishops, who, carrying out the requests of my solicitude in your presence, might plead with you for the peace of evangelical doctrine and obtain the freedom of the faith in which, according to the teaching of the Holy Spirit, you yourself especially excel.

Let the enemies of Christ be driven far away. Even if they had wished to conceal their fury, they could not remain hidden, because the holy simplicity of the Lord’s flock is one thing, and the simulation of beasts hiding beneath the clothing of sheep is another. Those whom such manifest madness has exposed can no longer creep in through hypocrisy.

Recognize, therefore, venerable Emperor, to what extent divine providence has prepared you as the protection of the whole world, and understand what you owe to your mother, the Church, which especially glories in you as her son. Let the struggles that have been extinguished not be allowed to rise again against the triumphs of the omnipotent right hand, especially since this is forbidden to the long-condemned assaults of the heretics. This fruit is owed to pious labors, so that the fullness of the whole Church may remain secure in the solidity of her unity and nothing at all may be reconsidered of what has been rightly established.

For after lawful and divinely inspired constitutions, to wish to enter into conflict is not the disposition of a peaceful mind but of a rebel, as the Apostle says: ‘Do not contend over words; it is useful for nothing except the subversion of those who hear’ (2 Timothy 2:14). For if it is always free to dispute through human persuasion, there will never be a lack of those who dare to resist the truth and trust in the loquacity of worldly wisdom.

Christian faith learns from the institution of our Lord Jesus Christ himself how much it must avoid this most harmful vanity. When he was about to call all nations to the illumination of faith, he did not choose philosophers or orators to serve the preaching of the Gospel, but humble men and fishermen, through whom he manifested himself, lest the heavenly teaching, which was full of virtues, appear to require the assistance of words.

Hence the Apostle protests and says: ‘Christ did not send me to baptize, but to evangelize—not in the wisdom of speech, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power. For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to those who are being saved it is the power of God. For it is written: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the prudence of the prudent. Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the investigator of this age? Has God not made the wisdom of this world foolish?’ (1 Corinthians 1:17–20).

For rhetorical arguments and the clever disputational devices established by human beings chiefly glory in this: that, amid uncertain matters and confused variety of opinions, each person chooses for assertion what he has defended with greater eloquence, and thus whatever is defended with greater eloquence is judged more true. But the Gospel of Christ has no need of this art, since the doctrine of truth is made manifest by its own light; nor is it asked what pleases the ears, where for true faith it suffices to know who teaches.”

† Leo continues in the same letter:

“May Your Clemency, I beseech you, make use of the petitions of my aforesaid brothers, whom—as I said in my previous letter—I have sent to you not to dispute with the condemned but to supplicate you for the stability of the Catholic faith alone.”

† The same Leo again *(Letter 162)*:

“We must therefore detest and persistently avoid what heretical fraud attempts to obtain, and matters that have been piously and fully defined must not be recalled for debate, lest, at the whim of the condemned, we ourselves appear to doubt matters that plainly agree in every respect with prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic authorities.

Therefore, if there are any who dissent from what has been established from heaven, let them be left to their opinions and depart from the unity of the Church with the perversity they have chosen. For it is in no way possible that those who dare to contradict the divine mysteries should be joined with us in any communion.

Let them boast in the vanity of their eloquence and glory in the cleverness of their arguments, which is hostile to faith. We prefer to obey the Apostle’s command: ‘See that no one deceive you through philosophy and empty seduction of men’ (Colossians 2:8).”

† Since these statements have been brought forward beyond doubt by authority and reasoning, it is certain that all who support the Catholic faith have judged that one must proceed more through the clear explanations of the holy Scriptures and the Fathers than through the empty and inflated games of learning, by which Christian simplicity is offended and the conceit of human vainglory increased.

### John Scotus  
*(Chapter 4, number 2, section 2)*

“We are necessarily commanded to use the rules of this discipline when we are compelled to answer a certain *saphrophilus* named Gottescalchus, both the inventor and advocate of his heresy, and its supporters—if indeed there are any, and would that there were not. We are compelled to do this by the most vigilant Fathers of the Catholic Church, in whose fold such poison attempts to creep. Especially does the orthodox prince, the venerable lord Charles, assent to it, whose greatest concern is to think piously and rightly about God, to refute the perverse doctrines of heretics by true arguments and the authority of the holy Fathers, and finally to uproot them completely.

Therefore, lest we appear to make the defenders of truth fight unarmed against the advocates of falsehood, we shall not inappropriately use the rules of the disputational art.”

### Correction

† Gregory, in the Paschal Homily *(Homily 22, on Holy Saturday, near the end)*:

“‘You shall not eat any of it raw, nor cooked in water’ (Exodus 12:9).

“Behold, the very words of the historical account now drive us more boldly from a merely historical understanding. What, dearest brothers, does that Israelite people, established in Egypt and accustomed to eating the lamb raw, signify, except that the law says to it: ‘You shall not eat anything of it raw,’ adding: ‘nor cooked in water’?

“What is the raw lamb’s flesh if not an inconsiderate and irreverent thought concerning Christ’s humanity? Everything that we think about subtly, we cook, as it were, by meditation. But the lamb’s flesh must be eaten neither raw nor cooked in water, because our Redeemer neither ought to be considered a mere man nor should it be pondered through human wisdom how God could have become incarnate.

“Whoever believes our Redeemer to be merely human—what else does he do than eat the lamb’s flesh raw, since he does not wish to cook it through an understanding of his divinity? Whoever attempts to examine the mysteries of his incarnation according to human wisdom wishes to cook the lamb’s flesh in water; that is, through dissolute learning he wishes to penetrate the mystery of his dispensation.

“Whoever therefore desires to celebrate the solemnity of Paschal joy should cook the lamb neither in water nor eat it raw, so that he does not seek to penetrate the depth of its incarnation through human wisdom; rather, he should eat the flesh roasted in fire, so that he may know that all things are administered through the power of the Holy Spirit.”
