† Although we do not fail to recognize that, by the Lord’s command, gold and silver vessels, garments, and the varied beauty of gems borrowed from the Egyptians were offered for his tabernacle (Exodus 3:22), and that they were to be offered with devotion (Exodus 12:35), nevertheless, whenever the greatest necessity compelled action against those who, puffed up by such things, gloried in their vanities and regarded the simplicity of our faith as foolishness, the Fathers did not forbid this to be done at the appropriate time but used it faithfully and prudently.

But you, writing more impudently against the faithful concerning faith, who rely on no sophistries, why have you turned to sophistical ravings? Clearly eager for vainglory, and wishing to appear not a philosopher but a lover of ingenious constructions, you chose to thrust upon us things which you had believed no one among us could understand, detect, or certainly refute.

While you strive to please people whom you knew to cherish such things—if indeed there are any, which eternal Truth avert—you neither took care nor feared to displease him concerning whom the Prophet solemnly foretells in such matters: “Because God has scattered the bones of those who please men; they have been confounded, because God has despised them” (Psalm 52:6).

Nor did you fear, like Achan, to bring a golden bar from the anathema of Jericho into the Lord’s camp, contrary to the prohibition (Joshua 7:24), and now, unless you quickly repent with humble penitence, you will deservedly undergo with him the sentence of divine punishment:

## [Scan page 516]

For all who have diligently searched the prophetic or apostolic writings have understood them vividly and explained them skillfully: opening what was obscure, expanding what was plain, disentangling what was most knotted, and uncovering what was allegorical. Above all, they took care to use that manner of speaking by which even simpler people could grasp without serious difficulty what they either heard or read.

Since this has been wisely observed by all, it shines forth especially in the works of the most blessed and most learned Father Augustine, of venerable memory, particularly in the works he composed on Christian Doctrine. In them he most learnedly and humbly established and taught that the monstrous inventions of you and those like you must be avoided and fled. The same is true of those works which he wished to be designated under the title *Questions or Expressions of the Heptateuch*, a marvelous exposition.

The most blessed Jerome, incomparably learned in the literature of so many languages and books, repeatedly emphasizes in all his explanations, both prophetic and apostolic, that he made it his greatest concern that the sayings of the holy Scriptures should be understood in themselves rather than made to serve the disputes of rhetoricians.

He had been instructed, as it were, by the blow of the dreadful judge. Because he had read Cicero too excessively, he was harshly beaten and finally released through the prayers of those standing around him. He swore that he would never again meditate on or read Cicero’s books. In his preface to the Epistle to the Galatians he expressed his contempt for this kind of disputation as follows.

### Jerome  
*(Preface to Book 3 of the Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians)*

“Here we compose [alternative reading: *cudimus*, ‘forge’] the third volume on the Galatians, O Paula and Eustochium, not unaware of our weakness and conscious that the stream of our small talent runs with a very slight murmuring sound.

“For now these matters are also asked about in the churches. The simplicity of the apostles and the purity of their words having been abandoned, people gather as though to Athens and its lecture halls, to arouse the applause of those standing around, so that an oration adorned with the falsehood of rhetorical art may proceed into public like some little prostitute, seeking not so much to educate the people as to win the people’s favor, and, like a psaltery and sweetly singing lyre, to caress the minds of its hearers.

“Thus that word of the prophet Ezekiel can truly be applied to our times, when the Lord says to him: ‘You have become to them like the sound of a sweetly singing lyre, well composed. They hear your words, but they do not do them’ (Ezekiel 33:32, section 62).

“But what shall I do? Shall I remain silent? Yet it is written: ‘You shall not appear empty before your God’ (Exodus 23:15). Isaiah also—as it is found in the Hebrew volumes—groans: ‘Woe is me, miserable that I am, because I was silent’ (Isaiah 6:5).

“Shall I speak? But the harshness of Hebrew reading has sullied all the elegance of speech and the beauty of Latin eloquence [alternative reading: ‘the elegance of every speech’]. You yourselves know that it is more than fifteen years since Tullius, Maro, or any author of pagan literature has come into my hands. If anything from them perhaps slips in while we speak, we remember it as though from an ancient dream through a mist.

“What progress I have made through tireless study of that language I leave to the judgment of others. I know what I have lost within myself [alternative reading: ‘what I have lost in my own work’].

“Moreover, because of the weakness of my eyes and of my entire little body, I do not write with my own hand, nor can I compensate for the slowness of my eloquence through labor and diligence. They say the same of Virgil: that he shaped his books by licking them into form like bear cubs [alternative reading: ‘by smoothing them’].

“But when I summon a secretary, I either immediately dictate whatever comes into my mouth, or, if I wish to think for a little while before bringing forth something better, the silent man reproaches me, draws back his hand, wrinkles his forehead, and by the whole gesture of his body declares that he is present in vain.

“Although an oration may proceed from a well-disposed talent, be arranged through invention, and adorned with a flower of words, unless it has been fashioned and polished by the hand of its author, it is not refined and does not possess gravity mingled with beauty. Rather, like the possessions of wealthy rustics, it is exposed more by its wealth than adorned by it.

“Why these remarks? Obviously, so that there may be an answer both to you and to others who may perhaps wish to read: I am not writing a panegyric or a controversy but a commentary. That is, I have set myself this aim—not that my words should be praised, but that what has been well said by another should be understood as it was said.

“It is my task to discuss obscure matters, to touch briefly upon what is clear, and to linger over doubtful points. Hence the work of commentaries is also called by many an explanation.

“If anyone seeks eloquence or delights in declamations, he has Demosthenes and Tullius in both languages, Polemon and Quintilian. The Church of Christ was gathered not from the Academy and the Lyceum [alternative reading: ‘the Lyceum’], but from a lowly crowd. Hence the Apostle says: ‘Consider your calling, brothers: not many are wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble; but God chose the foolish things of this world to confound the wise; and God chose the weak things of this world to confound the strong; and God chose the base and despised things of this world, and things that are not, to destroy things that are’ (1 Corinthians 1:26–28).

“Because the world had not known God through wisdom from the order, variety, and harmony of created things, it pleased God to save believers through the foolishness of preaching—not in the wisdom of speech, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power. Where is the scribe? Where is the grammarian? Where are the investigators of natural causes?

“Not in persuasive words of wisdom, but in the demonstration of power and of the Spirit, so that the faith of believers might not rest in human wisdom but in the power of God.

“For this reason the Apostle himself spoke to the same Corinthians: ‘And I, when I came to you, brothers, came not with sublimity [alternative reading: “subtlety”] of speech or wisdom, announcing to you the testimony of the Lord. For I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified’ (1 Corinthians 2:1–2).

“And lest anyone perhaps think that, by saying this, he was declaring himself an unintelligent preacher, he overturned in advance, with prophetic insight, what could be raised against him. ‘But we speak,’ he says, ‘the wisdom of God in a mystery, which has been hidden; which none of the rulers of this age has known’ (1 Corinthians 2:7–8).”

## [Scan page 517]

How many people now read Aristotle? How many know even the name or books of Plato? Hardly a few idle old men recall them in corners. But the whole world speaks of our rustics and fishermen; the entire world resounds with them.

Therefore their simple words must be set forth in simple speech [alternative reading: “must be opened up”]. I say: their words, not their meanings. Otherwise, if through your prayers I can possess in explaining their Epistles the spirit which they possessed when dictating them, then you will see how great a majesty and breadth of true wisdom existed in them, compared with the arrogance and vanity of the learned men of this age.

Briefly I confess to you the secret of my mind: whoever is going to understand the Apostle through me, I do not want him to understand my writings with difficulty and, in order to know the interpreter, to seek another interpreter.”

† Cassiodorus likewise, in the remarkable work which he composed on the exposition of the Psalms, although he inserted many figures belonging to those same arts, did not explain the Psalms through them. Rather, he demonstrated that those figures were present in the sacred writings, so that he might plainly show that their author was the Lord, who is proclaimed in those divine utterances, and not those who claimed to have invented such things while knowing him either not at all or only in part.

Concerning him it is said: “All wisdom is from the Lord God, and it was always with him and is before him” (Ecclesiasticus 1:1). The word “every” is necessarily added to show that whatever is rightly and usefully known in the good arts and talents is given and distributed to all by him as its author.

Of him it is written: “Distributing to each as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12:11). He alone is essentially, immutably, and eternally wise—or rather, he is truly believed and faithfully proclaimed to be Wisdom itself.

When, in the preface to that same admirable work, he discussed the eloquence of the whole divine law, he spoke as follows.

### Cassiodorus  
*(Preface to the Psalms, chapter 15)*

“Here is the greatest proof: the divine law is known to have been received throughout all parts of the world. It exercises many kinds of its own expression; it is concise in definitions, adorned with figures, marked by the propriety of words, made clear by the combinations of syllogisms, and enriched by disciplines. Yet it does not receive an alien beauty from them; rather, it confers upon them their own dignity.

“For when these things shine in the divine Scriptures, they are certain and most pure. But when they come into human opinions and most empty questions, they are tossed about by the ambiguous waves of disputes, so that what is always most firmly true here is frequently made uncertain elsewhere.

“Thus, when our tongue sings psalmody, it is adorned by the nobility of truth; when it turns to foolish stories and blasphemous words, it is excluded from the honor of uprightness.

“As the Apostle James says: ‘With it we bless God and the Father, and with it we curse human beings, who were made in the image and likeness of God’ (James 3:9).

“Thus the arts of the world—which plainly came much later than the beginning of the divine writings—were transferred to collections of arguments, which the Greeks call *topoi*, and to the arts of dialectic and rhetoric. It is therefore evident that what the Gentiles later thought suitable for human wisdom had first been given to upright minds for expressing the truth.

“These arts shine in the sacred readings like brilliant stars, and they fittingly illuminate the meanings of things with highly useful brevity. We shall briefly call them to attention in suitable places, since the matters themselves will most conveniently bring them forward, through which the conceived meanings will shine more clearly.

“For Father Augustine also, in Book 3 of *On Christian Doctrine* (chapter 29), declared: ‘Let the educated know that our authors used all the modes of expression which grammarians call by the Greek name *tropes*.’ A little later he adds: ‘Those who know these tropes—that is, the modes of expression—recognize them in the sacred writings, and their knowledge helps them to some extent in understanding them.’

“He made the clearest mention of this matter in other books as well. In the books which he entitled *On the Modes of Expression*, he proved that various figures of secular literature are found in the sacred writings, while he declared that there are other proper modes in the divine utterances which grammarians and rhetoricians have not touched at all.

“Other most learned Fathers among us said this as well, namely Jerome, Ambrose, and Hilary, so that we may not appear presumptuous in this matter but rather followers.

“But someone may say: ‘Are neither the parts of syllogisms themselves, nor the names of figures, nor the terms of the disciplines, nor anything of this sort found in the Psalms?’ They are plainly found there in the force of their meanings, not in the utterance of their words. Thus we contemplate wine in the vine, the marrow in the seed, the leaves in the roots, and the fruits in the branches of trees; we contemplate the nuts themselves in their shells.

“Indeed, a delicious fish is caught from the deepest abyss, yet before its capture [alternative reading: ‘before its conception’] it is not seen by human eyes. Therefore we rightly say that things are present when we perceive them to be present in their power.

“For the Apostle forbids us to be led astray by the empty wisdom of the world (1 Corinthians 3:18); but he does not deny that these things exist in the divine writings.”

† Therefore, whenever necessity compels us to use such things, as we have said, it is certainly not disapproved that we act piously and humbly against those who mock the sincerity of our faith and, puffed up by these matters, swell with pride—especially since we read that Moses, the outstanding prophet, was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians (Acts 7:22), and that Daniel and his companions surpassed all the magicians and diviners of the Chaldeans tenfold in their knowledge (Daniel 1:20).

Now, in the name of God and with his assistance, we are about to enter the labyrinth of your heresies. Let us invoke the grace of him without whom we are and can do nothing, so that, with him as our guide, we may penetrate your inextricable tangles and escape from them with unhindered steps, relying not at all upon the entanglements and distortions of your fourfold way but upon authority and truth.

Therefore, through the copious preface of your disputation—
[scan page 518]

**ON PREDESTINATION AGAINST JOHN SCOTUS**

…in which you truly establish that true philosophy is true religion, but falsely assert that it must be discovered through the learning of secular disciplines, although true religion is attained and approved by faith and the grace of God, not by human inventions. You set forth Gottschalk’s opinion, by which he attempts to affirm that, by the necessity of predestination, both the good are inevitably impelled toward good things and the wicked toward evil things. Let him himself see whether, or why, he said this. We neither believe nor confess that anyone is impelled by the necessity of God’s determination toward anything, or—as many say—compelled by fate; but we have no doubt that everything is ordered, arranged, administered, determined, ruled, and governed by His eternal providence and omnipotent foreknowledge, in ways fitting for each thing. Scripture truthfully says of Him: “She reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wisdom 8:1). In these words all God’s wisdom is briefly and immutably defined as preceding, reaching, and ordering everything; for it would never reach and order anything unless it preceded it, nor would it precede anything unless it existed essentially, eternally, and omnipotently.

It is therefore established that nothing exists except the Creator and the creature: the Creator from no one, the creature from the Creator. The Creator is without beginning, change, or end; the creature has a beginning and change, and in part also an end. For rational creatures—angels and human beings—began, but do not cease; other things, made and assigned for human use, partly cease and partly endure. Yet by that endurance they do not attain the eternity of their Author; it is not now the time to discuss these matters at length.

Since it is established that nothing else exists besides the Creator and the creature, and that the creature received the beginning of its existence not from itself but from the Creator, it nevertheless belonged to the Creator to arrange, order, determine, and predestine what He had made, as it is said: “She reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly”—that is, from the end of the invisible and incorporeal creature to the end of the visible and corporeal creature; from what is highest among all creatures to what is lowest among all creatures. If this is denied, God is asserted to be either envious—which God forbid—or impotent. For if He did not order, arrange, administer, determine, or predestine what He made, it follows that He had no care for His own work.

Yet He did care for the creatures He made, because truthful Scripture confesses this when it says: “To whom there is care concerning all things” (Wisdom 12:13). The Prophet also speaks to Him: “By Your ordinance the day continues, for all things serve You” (Psalm 118:91). In our prayers we say to Him: “O God, whose providence is not deceived in its ordering.” In the Gospel He says: “Are not two sparrows sold for an assarius? And not one of them falls to the ground without your Father” (Matthew 10:29). Again: “If, then, God so clothes the grass which is today in the field and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will He clothe you, you of little faith?” (Matthew 6:30). There are countless other passages with which the divine writings abound and which no one is unaware of.

From this it follows that God cared for, ordered, arranged, administered, determined, or predestined everything just as He created it—whether what He has made or what He is going to make—in accordance with the statement: “He who made the things that are to be” (Isaiah 45:11, according to the Septuagint). For He who is believed to have established all creatures in the beginning: what was He going to make, except the governance, multiplication, and ordering of the things He had made?

Hence Truth itself speaks in the Gospel, saying: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17), because in His foreknowledge, which cannot be deceived or changed, He predestined what work He would accomplish externally and toward what end the work He performed would be brought. And what is this work except His ordering?

What has been said amounts to this and is rightly understood in no other way than as follows: determination and predestination are divided in two ways, namely into the good and the evil. The good exist only through the author who is good and supreme, that is, God. The evil do not exist through God as their author, but through the will of the rational creature, which turned away from its Author and, thereby becoming worse, culpably departed from Him.

Accordingly, God is the author of all good things. But of evil things—that is, vices and sins—God is not the author; rather, He is the most provident foreknower, the wisest examiner, and the most powerful and just judge. Of those evil things which are tribulations, afflictions, infirmities, or punishments of any kind, which in this intervening life He inflicts in mixture upon both the just and the unjust, God is called the author; but in the world to come, that is, in Gehenna, divine equity justly and deservedly repays them to the impious alone.

The Prophet says: “Is there evil in the city which the Lord has not made?” (Amos 3:6). Again, the Lord Himself is introduced through Isaiah as saying: “Making good and creating evil, forming light and creating darkness: I am the Lord, making all these things” (Isaiah 45:7). Likewise, the Gospel testifies that He will say the same to the impious at the judgment: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41).

What does “prepared” mean except “created and determined”? And by whom was it created, except by Him who through the Prophet said that He had created evil and darkness? By Him, unquestionably, it is also said to have been determined for the impious, as the Prophet Isaiah testifies: “For Topheth has been prepared from yesterday, prepared and made deep” (Isaiah 30:33). Here he plainly indicates that the creation and determination of the fire of Gehenna were made and ordered by God. For “Topheth” means Gehenna; “from yesterday” means from the beginning; and “by the king” is understood to mean by almighty God, as Saint Jerome explains.

Since, then, God is without contradiction called the author, orderer, and arranger of these evils, what, I ask you, prevents Him from also being called their determiner and predeterminer? For to determine and predetermine means nothing other than to order and pre-order, to arrange or arrange beforehand, or something similar, as sound minds understand.

Hence Augustine, in Book One of *On Free Will*:

**Augustine, *On Free Will*, Book I, at the beginning:** “Tell me, I beg you, whether God is not the author of evil.”

“I will tell you, if you make clear which evil you are asking about; for we commonly call something evil in two ways: first, when we say that someone has done evil; second, when we say that someone has suffered some evil. I want to know about both. But if you know or believe that God is good—for it is not lawful to think otherwise—He does not do evil. Again, if we confess that God is just—for it is sacrilegious to deny this—then, just as He gives rewards to the good, so He gives punishments to the evil. These punishments are certainly evils to those who suffer them. Therefore, if no one suffers punishment unjustly—which we must believe, since we believe that this whole universe is governed by divine providence—God is in no way the author of evils of the first kind, but He is the author of those of the second kind.”

That “to order” or “to pre-order” may be used for “to determine” or “to predetermine” is indicated by the Book of the Acts of the Apostles, where the blessed evangelist and writer Luke says: “And as many as had been preordained to eternal life believed” (Acts 13:48). This is more correctly understood as meaning “predestined to eternal life.” That determination or predestination ought to be understood as God’s ordering, Saint Fulgentius declares in his book *On Predestination to Monimus*.

**Fulgentius, *On Predestination*, chapter 2:** “Will the Lord, then, complete in the saints what He graciously gave them in order that they might be good, and what He foreknew He would give, He predestined in the eternal ordering of His goodness? For this is the predestination of God: the eternal ordering of God’s future work.”

This most certain, most knowing, and omnipotent pre-ordering, ordering, determination, or predestination of God drives no one to sin, incites no one, and compels no one. Rather, He justly punishes and justly condemns those who fall into crimes by their own will and obstinately persist in them. He would not preserve justice if He did not assign deserved punishments to those who turn away and depart from Him by their own will and do not return to Him by any conversion.

Because He is just, He preserves justice. For a long time, through the patience of His inexhaustible goodness, He tolerates the wicked, gives them gifts, and invites them with rewards. Yet they are not softened by so great a remedy of kindness. Instead, through irrevocable hardness and dreadful ingratitude, they persist in their voluntary iniquities. It therefore wholly and most deservedly accords with His equity that those whom unconquerable goodness has in no way recalled from crime should be punished by eternal justice in torments.

The most just and therefore irreprehensible condemnation of wicked people has been faithfully stated and truthfully proclaimed by the holy Fathers as both foreknown and predestined by God. We both say and confess this.

Hence Augustine, in Book Three of *On Free Will*, chapter 22:

**Augustine, *On Free Will*, Book III, chapter 22:** “But now, since this is so, if he is not good and does not have it within his power to be good—either because he does not see what he ought to be, or because, although he sees it, he is unable to be what he sees he ought to be—who would doubt that this is a punishment? Every punishment, if it is just, is the punishment of sin and is called a penalty. But if the punishment is unjust, since no one doubts that it is a punishment, it has been imposed upon a man by some unjust ruler.

“Since it is madness to doubt God’s omnipotence and justice, this punishment is just and is paid for some sin. For no unjust ruler could have seized a human being, with God unaware, or extorted him against God’s will as from one weaker—whether by frightening or coercing him—in order to torture the man with an unjust punishment. It remains, therefore, that this just punishment arises from the condemnation of man.

“Nor is it surprising that, either through ignorance, he lacks the free choice of the will to choose what he ought rightly to do, or, because of the resistance of carnal habit—which, through the violence of mortal succession, has in a certain way naturally grown strong—he sees what ought rightly to be done and wishes to do it, but is unable to accomplish it. For this is the most just punishment of sin: that each person lose what he did not wish to use well, although he could have done so without difficulty if he had wished. That is, whoever knowingly does not do what is right loses the knowledge of what is right; and whoever, when he could do what is right, did not wish to do so, loses the ability to do it when he wishes.

“For these two things are truly punishments for every sinful soul: ignorance and difficulty. From ignorance comes the disgrace of error; from difficulty, affliction through suffering. But to approve false things as true, so that one errs unwillingly, and, while the bonds of the flesh resist and torment him through pain, to be unable to restrain oneself from lustful works—this is not the nature with which man was established, but the punishment of the condemned.”

## CHAPTER 2

**From the argument of necessity it is inferred that there cannot be two predestinations**

But you, impudently opposing so great an authority, attempt, with the second exhalation of your foul productions, to overwhelm truth with your arguments and to obscure statements clearer than daylight with clouded conclusions.

For, in arguing against Gottschalk, if I may put it so, you deny that there are two predestinations, which the Fathers reduce to a single expression when they speak of “the predestination of the good” and “the predestination of the evil.” For Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, says:

**Isidore of Seville, *Sentences*, chapter 26:** “Predestination is twofold.”

You overturn this on the occasion of the question of necessity, although no orthodox person has believed or proclaimed that anyone is compelled toward anything good or evil by the necessity of predestination. For this reason you affirm that predestination is neither twofold nor two predestinations. Then, by introducing an unnecessary argument, you discuss the divine essence at greater length than necessary, and you carry the intention of your discussion to the point of asserting:

> Predestination in God must be understood in the same way as essence; in God it makes no difference whether it is called essence, wisdom, justice, power, truth, eternity, will, operation, or predestination.

You then infer:

**John Scotus, chapter 2, no. 1, section 6:** “If it is impious to teach two essences in God, or two wisdoms, knowledges, virtues, and all the other things said of God, doubled, tripled, or accumulated in any multiplied form, whoever is convicted of asserting two predestinations in God is bound by the guilt of impiety. For there is one divine predestination, just as there is one divine operation, one divine wisdom, one divine substance, and one divine will.”

### CORRECTION

In these words of your discussion you have shown, with shameless pride and proud shamelessness, that you have branded as impious all Catholics and orthodox Christians who have written or believed that some are predestined to destruction.

Then an intolerable blasphemy is revealed when you assert that God’s predestination is nothing other than His substance, nature, and will. You preferred to support this with your feeble little arguments, so to speak, rather than to establish it by the authority on which the truth of our faith is strengthened and defended. Your perversity has so blinded you with the darkness of error that you neither saw nor consulted the truth.

You deny that these things can be doubled, tripled, or accumulated in any multiplied form, and therefore that predestinations may be spoken of in the plural, just as essences, wisdoms, knowledges, virtues, wills, and operations may be so spoken of. You say:

> “There is one predestination, just as there is one divine operation, one divine wisdom, one divine substance, and one divine will.”

You then continue:

**John Scotus, chapter 2, no. 2, section 6:** “For Scripture cries out: ‘Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all His wills’” (Psalm 110:2).

And below:

**John Scotus, chapter 2, no. 3, section 6:** “He did not say ‘according to all His necessities,’ but ‘according to all His wills.’”

### CORRECTION

Now raise the eye of your mind—if indeed you possess one—to contemplate the truth. If you do not possess it, humble yourself faithfully, asking the truth to deign either to cleanse it for you, illuminate it, or at least restore it to you.

You said that God’s will, like His essence, cannot be doubled or multiplied, that is, that it lacks plurality. Yet this is refuted by the very prophetic statement which you yourself added. When it says, “according to all His wills,” behold, God’s wills are expressed multiply and therefore in the plural. You yourself produced the passage, and yet you said that it is impious for anyone to express God’s will, which is in God, in a multiplied—that is, plural—way.

Indeed, like the Pharisee whom the Gospel narrative rebukes for boasting of his merits (Luke 18:11–12), you opened your most clouded eye as arrogantly as you could to display your bloated little knowledge, and, refusing to humble yourself truthfully with the publican, you turned your understanding away from the sight of truth.

If you say that God’s will is one thing and God’s wills another, the authority of Scripture exposes how impiously you have raved in this matter. For although we know and confess that in God there is nothing other than willing to be, and nothing other than being to will—for His will is His essence, and His essence is His will—He Himself, who is His essence and His will, speaks through the Prophet:

> “For the saints who are in his land, he has made all my wills wondrous in them” (Psalm 15:3).

He is not one thing and His wills another, because if they were something else, they would be outside Him; and if they were outside Him, He would no longer be His own will. But He is His own will; therefore His wills are within Him.

It is therefore false that you said that will in God is not multiplied, that is, that it is not spoken of in the plural, since whatever is multiplied must necessarily be expressed in the plural.

Although God’s essence is unquestionably simple, and is neither doubled, tripled, nor multiplied in any way, there are nevertheless certain things which are predicated essentially in God or of God and which are found expressed in the plural without contradiction in the divine writings. God’s will is called His essence, and His wills are also called His wills in the plural. Yet His essence is not expressed in the plural. Rather, while His essence remains immutable and far removed from every capacity for multiplicity, His will is expressed in the plural—not because the essence itself is multiplied, but because the effects of His will are declared multiple in accordance with the appropriateness and diversity of its distributions.

Holy Scripture cries out against you. In the Book of Wisdom, concerning the Spirit of God, who is certainly God, among the praises of His power it says:

> “For in her is a spirit of understanding: holy, unique, manifold, subtle” (Wisdom 7:22).

How, then, can He be called both unique and manifold? Do not chatter against the truth.

You likewise said that the term “predestination,” which is God’s substance, cannot in any way be multiplied. Yet the most blessed Gregory, bishop of the apostolic see and—as you truthfully asserted—the most truthful interpreter of the Scriptures, paying no regard to the arguments of your conclusions, or rather condemning them before reading them, did not fear to speak in the plural.

For in Book 29 of his remarkable and admirable work, composed with most eloquent sweetness in explanation of the Book of Job, Gregory says among other things:

**Gregory, Book 29 on Job, final chapter:** “To know the order of heaven is to see the hidden predestinations of the heavenly arrangements.”

He then taught at length which predestinations he meant. With the abundance of his sweetness, he discussed the gratuitous election of the good and the most just rejection of the evil. To make this shine more clearly, we shall set forth the whole context of that passage.

**Gregory, Book 30, chapter 32:** “The Father, in His own time, brought forth Lucifer, because, as it is written, ‘When the fullness of time had come, God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law’ (Galatians 4:4–5). He, born of a virgin, appeared like Lucifer amid the darkness of our night; for, driving away the obscurity of sin, He announced to us the eternal morning.

“He made Himself known as Lucifer because He rose from death at dawn and by the radiance of His light crushed the foul darkness of our mortality. To Him John rightly says: ‘The bright and morning star’ (Revelation 22:16).

“For by appearing alive [variant: appearing] after death, He became for us the morning star, because, while He displayed in Himself the example of resurrection, He indicated what light would follow. The Lord makes evening rise over the sons of earth (Job 38:32), because He permits Antichrist to rule in the hearts of the faithless Jews, their deserts demanding it. They are therefore justly subjected by the Lord to this evening, because they themselves willingly wished to be sons of earth. Seeking earthly rather than heavenly things, they were blinded from seeing the brightness of our Lucifer; and while they desire evening to rule over them, they are plunged into the eternal night of the condemnation that follows.

“From this it is also said in the Gospel by the Lord: ‘I have come in the name of My Father, and you did not receive Me. Another will come in his own name; him you will receive’ (John 5:43). Hence Paul says: ‘Because they did not receive the love of the truth so that they might be saved, therefore God will send them an operation of error, so that they may believe a lie, so that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity’ (2 Thessalonians 2:10–11).

“Therefore evening would not rise over them if they had wished to be sons of the light. But while they desire visible things, having lost the light of the heart, they grow dark under the guide of night.

“Yet if we examine this morally, we find that it happens every day. For Lucifer rises for the elect, while evening, by God’s permission, rules over the reprobate. The word of God is one and the same in the mouth of the preacher. While some hear it with joy, others hear it with envy; they turn the brightness of Lucifer into the darkness of evening for themselves.

“When the former humbly receive the holy voice of preaching, they open the eyes of their hearts to the light of the star. But when the latter envy what is proclaimed and seek not the cause of salvation but the glory of exaltation, their iniquity breaks forth, and they close their eyes in the evening of death.

“Thus, by a hidden judgment, he who is Lucifer for the elect becomes evening for the reprobate hearer. Through the holy exhortation by which the good return to life, the wicked die more deeply in their guilt. Hence Paul rightly says: ‘We are the good fragrance of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing: to some, indeed, an odor of death unto death, but to others an odor of life unto life’ (2 Corinthians 2:15–16).

“He therefore saw that His word is both Lucifer and evening for its hearers: through it He saw some raised from iniquity and, conversely, others lulled to sleep in iniquity. Because this occurs through God’s hidden judgments, which cannot be grasped by human beings in this life, he rightly added there: ‘And who is sufficient for these things?’ (ibid., verse 16). It is as if he said: We are indeed sufficient to observe that these things happen, but we are not sufficient to investigate why they happen.

“Here too the Lord, because He had said that Lucifer rises for some and evening rises for others, immediately adds, lest a human being dare to scrutinize God’s hidden judgments:

> ‘Do you know the order of heaven, and can you establish its reasoning upon the earth?’”

To know the order of heaven is to see the hidden predestinations of the heavenly arrangements. To place its reasoning upon the earth is to reveal to human hearts the causes of such secrets.

To place the reasoning of heaven upon earth is either, by considering, to discuss the mysteries of the heavenly judgments, or, by speaking, to make them manifest. No one who is placed in this life can accomplish this. For, to proceed from small things to greater, who can understand how great the subtlety [variant: refinement] of the secrets of the heavenly judgment is?

Who can understand why a just man often comes away from judgment not merely unavenged but even punished, while his unjust adversary departs not merely unpunished but even victorious? Who can understand why one person lives while plotting the deaths of his neighbors, whereas another dies who would have benefited the lives of many? One person desires to be free from affairs yet becomes entangled in countless business matters; another desires to be entangled in business but is forced into idleness. One, beginning badly [variant: while beginning badly], prolongs worse things to the end of his life; another, beginning well, advances through the length of time toward an increase of merits.

Conversely [variant: but conversely], one who lives badly is preserved for a long time so that he may be corrected [variant: correct himself]; another who seems to live well continues in this life until he breaks out into perverse conduct. One fails in error; another, born in the uprightness of the Catholic faith, is brought to completion in the uprightness of the Catholic faith. Conversely, another, born from the womb of a Catholic mother, is devoured near the end of life by the abyss of error. Yet another completes his life in Catholic devotion, although, born in unbelief, he had imbibed the poison of error with his mother’s milk.

One desires, wishes, and is able to aspire to the height of a good life; another neither wishes nor is able; another wishes but is unable; another is able but does not wish. Who, then, could investigate these secrets of the heavenly judgments? Who could understand the secretly balanced scales of hidden equity? No one ascends to know the depths of these secret judgments.

Let it therefore be said to a human being that he should recognize that he does not know; let him recognize that he does not know and fear. Let him fear so that he may be humbled; let him be humbled so that he may not presume upon himself; let him not presume upon himself so that he may seek the help of his Creator. The one who, trusting in himself, has died may live again by seeking the aid of his Author.

Let the just man therefore hear—now knowing himself, but still not knowing what is above him:

> “Do you know the order of heaven, and can you establish its reasons upon the earth?” (Job 38:33)

That is: Do you comprehend the hidden orders of the heavenly judgments, or are you capable of opening them to human ears?

Job’s guilt is therefore examined in relation to the investigation of judgments that cannot be comprehended. It is as though he were told plainly: You ought to bear all that you suffer with greater patience precisely because, ignorant of heavenly secrets, you do not know why you suffer this [variant: these things].

Following him in faith, understanding, and words, Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, inserted almost the same statement into his own writings. Whoever wishes to compare the two will find that they spoke with one spirit and one voice, so that there can be no doubt that the same Holy Spirit was present with both and spoke unanimously through both.

[scan page 522]

**Isidore, *Sentences*, Book II, chapter 6:** “Predestination is twofold: either of the elect to rest, or of the reprobate to death. Both are brought about by divine judgment, so that He always makes the elect follow heavenly and interior things, and always permits the reprobate, by abandoning them, to delight in low and exterior things.

“Just as man does not know the boundary between light and darkness, or what the end of either may be, so he does not fully know who will be overtaken by the light of justice before his end, who will be darkened by the darkness of sins until his end, or who, after falling into darkness, will turn and rise again to the light. All these things are open to God but hidden from man.

“Although the conduct of the just in this life may be praiseworthy, it nevertheless remains uncertain to human beings toward what end they have been predestined; all things are reserved for future examination. What a wondrous ordering of the heavenly distribution is this, by which the just person here becomes more justified and the impious more defiled!

“A wicked person is sometimes converted to good, and a good person sometimes turns back toward evil. One wishes to be good but is unable; another wishes to be evil but is not permitted to enter into it. It is given to one who wishes to be good; another neither wishes nor is it given to him to be good.

“This one is born in error and dies in it; that one perseveres to the end in the good with which he began. This one stands until he falls; that one, living badly for a long time, is saved at the end and, being regarded with mercy, is converted. The just person wishes to be useful in good but does not prevail; the wicked wishes to harm and succeeds.

“This one wishes to be free for God but is hindered by the world; that one desires to become involved in worldly affairs but does not accomplish it. The wicked rules over the good; the good is condemned in place of the wicked; the impious is honored in place of the just. In such great darkness man cannot scrutinize the divine ordering or assess the hidden order of predestination.”

What blessed Gregory called “predestinations” in the plural, Saint Isidore called “twofold predestination,” because, as the statements of both testify, he understood that Gregory, together with the other Catholic interpreters, held that some are predestined to glory and others to dishonor; some to the kingdom and others to torment; some to the blessedness of the heavenly realms and others to the punishment of hell.

Consider now whom you contradict and whom you have marked with the guilt of impiety—those who spoke these things before your ravings were uttered, before you were born. Let us therefore set you beside blessed Gregory: he expressed predestinations in the plural, while you judge plural expression to be impious.

Who will listen to you now? Who will not shudder on seeing that you have advanced so far in madness that you are not ashamed to say that such authoritative men were impious and, even more blasphemously, that they wrote these things? Who will listen to you denying the plurality of predestination when he has read or heard so many Fathers expressing it in the plural? Who will lend an ear to your little arguments, by which you detract from the faithfulness of so many Fathers’ true words and writings? And who will credit you with truth and assign falsehood to them?

Will you take on whatever forms of the fabled Prometheus, or whatever colors of the chameleon you please? You will certainly never escape, nor will you find a place of evasion. For either what you denied is true and what Gregory and Isidore said is false—which is impious for anyone to believe or even think—or, if what Gregory and Isidore put forward and committed to venerable writings is true, then what you, in utter blindness, affirmed is false.

Since in this matter you are not merely caught but also convicted, with the Lord’s help it will now be easy to proceed against the other things which you vomited from your diseased mouth in similar madness. For once the mark of falsehood has been stamped upon you in the earlier matters, faith is entirely removed from you in what follows.

You likewise deny that operation in God is expressed in the plural, that is, multiplied or doubled, or anything of that kind. But what is the meaning of all the Scriptures’ celebration of God’s operations or works?

The chosen vessel, the teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth, cries out:

> “There are divisions of graces, but the same Spirit; there are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are divisions of operations, but the same God” (1 Corinthians 12:4–6).

And lest you cry out something else in the manner of madmen, he adds:

> “Who works all things in all” (ibid., verse 6).

After listing the distributions of these same operations, he says:

> “But all these things one and the same Spirit works, distributing to each as He wills” (ibid., verse 11).

If you contend that God’s operation is one thing and His works another, see how you can oppose such weighty authority—namely, the divine writings and their most faithful interpreters, whose books are known to be filled with the plural forms of these same terms.

For the moment, while I leave the other matters aside, I ask you this: what accords more closely with God’s essence, power or operation? It seems to me that no one can operate without power; for how can someone be said to operate if he is unable to do so? You will not deny that power is the greater. Therefore power accords more closely with God’s essence than operation does, since operation is the effect of power.

Yet although God’s essence rejects plurality, we read of His powers expressed in the plural. The Prophet says:

> “Who will speak of the powers of the Lord? Who will make all His praises heard?” (Psalm 105:2).

If, then, God’s power is not excluded from plurality or multiplicity, why should operation—which is unquestionably its consequence—be judged excluded from multiplicity?

If some distinction is to be made between God’s operation and His works, for the moment nothing else occurs to me, until the matter is examined more carefully, than that operation is what occurs while something is being done, whereas the work is what is done. If this is so, who would doubt that both belong to God?

**Augustine:** “When the operation of the Father is mentioned, it must not be understood as operating without the Son and the Holy Spirit; and when the generation of the Son is mentioned, it must not be understood as occurring without the Father and the Holy Spirit; and when the operation of the Holy Spirit is mentioned, it must not be understood as occurring without the Father and the Son. This is sufficiently known to those who believe rightly, or even to those who understand as they are able.

“And it was said of the Father that ‘He Himself does the works’ (John 14:10) because the origin even of the works is from Him, from whom comes the existence of the persons who cooperate. For the Son is from Him…”

[scan page 523]

## SAINT PRUDENTIUS, BISHOP OF TROYES  
1034

[continued from previous page] …was born from him, and the Holy Spirit proceeds principally from him, from whom the Son was born and with whom that same Spirit is common. And when the Lord says, “If I had not done among them the works that no one else has done” (John 15:24), he did not refer this to the Father or the Spirit, as though they had not cooperated with him in those works, but to human beings, of whom many miracles are read to have been performed, and yet by none of them were the things done that the Son did.

And when the Apostle says of the Holy Spirit, “But all these things one and the same Spirit works” (1 Corinthians 12:11), this was not said because the Father and the Son do not cooperate with him, but because in these works there are not many Spirits, but one Spirit, and in all his operations he is not different from himself.

Yet it is not said vainly, but reasonably and truly, that the Father—not the Son or the Holy Spirit—said, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 17:5). Nevertheless, although we acknowledge that this miracle of the audible word from heaven pertained solely to the person of the Father, we do not deny that the Son and the Holy Spirit cooperated in it. For because the Son was then carrying flesh and dwelling among human beings on earth, he was not therefore absent from the bosom of the Father as the only-begotten Word when that voice came from the cloud. Nor can it be believed wisely and spiritually that God the Father separated the operation of his spoken words, sounding and passing away, from the cooperation of his Wisdom and his Spirit.

In the same way, although we rightly say that not the Father, nor the Holy Spirit, but the Son walked upon the sea (Matthew 14:25–26)—for that was his human flesh, and his feet rested upon the waves—who would deny that the Father and the Holy Spirit cooperated in the work of so great a miracle?

Thus, too, we say most truly that the Son alone assumed flesh—not the Father or the Holy Spirit—yet whoever denies that the Father or the Spirit cooperated in this incarnation, which pertained to the Son alone, does not think correctly.

Likewise, we say that neither the Father nor the Son, but only the Holy Spirit, appeared in the form of a dove and in tongues as if of fire, and sat upon those to whom he had come, proclaiming the mighty works of God in many different languages (Acts 2:2–3). Yet we cannot separate from that miracle, which pertained to the Holy Spirit alone, the cooperation of the Father and the only-begotten Word.

Thus the Trinity performs the works of each individual person in the Trinity: the two others cooperate with each one who acts, and the three act in concord, not with efficacy failing in one of them. Since this is so, the Lord Jesus cast out demons in the Holy Spirit (Matthew 12:28). He was not unable to accomplish this alone and therefore took that assistance as though it were insufficient for the work; rather, the divided spirit was fittingly expelled by that Spirit whom the Father and the Son, undivided in themselves, possess together. Likewise, since sins are not forgiven outside the Church, they had to be forgiven in that Spirit in whom the Church is gathered into unity.]

† Now, if according to you operation is in God in the same way as his essence and will, it necessarily follows that the other things which are undoubtedly said to proceed from the will of God should also be predicated as the essence of God: for example, thought, sight, foreknowledge, creation, disposition, administration, determination, decree, arrangement, preparation, judgment, affliction, correction, weakening, killing, slaughter, destruction, annihilation, confinement, hardening, making obstinate, abandonment, desertion, unwillingness, seduction, leading into error, deception, diseases, famine, pestilences, storms, shipwrecks, ambushes, and many other things which are set forth in the divine writings and are most familiar in the works of the Fathers, so that no prudent person is unaware of them.

Whoever denies that these things, being done by the will of God, are always good and just, wickedly contradicts the justice and judgment of the Creator. But because it would be lengthy to establish these matters by examples, let them be deferred for now, so that if the hydra should again raise its head or the viper attempt to hiss, they may, by the Lord’s favor, be brought forth at greater length and more conveniently. For the present, however, it will suffice to insert one testimony from the holy Augustine’s statements concerning the will of God. In his book *Enchiridion* he discusses it in the following words.

### Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 100

“These are the great works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills” (Psalm 111:2), and they are sought out so wisely that, although the angelic and human creature had sinned—that is, had done not what he, but what it itself, willed—even through that same creature’s will, by which what the Creator did not will had been done, he himself fulfilled what he willed. He makes good use of evil things, as supremely good, both for the condemnation of those whom he justly predestined to punishment and for the salvation of those whom he graciously predestined to grace.

For insofar as those creatures themselves are concerned, they did what God did not will; but insofar as the omnipotence of God is concerned, they were in no way able to thwart him. Indeed, by the very fact that they acted against God’s will, his will was accomplished through them. Therefore the great works of the Lord are sought out according to all his wills, so that in a wondrous and ineffable manner what occurs even against his will does not happen apart from his will. For it would not happen if he did not permit it; and certainly he permits it not unwillingly but willingly. Nor would the good God permit evil to occur unless he were omnipotent enough to make good come even from evil.”

### Chapter 101

Sometimes, however, a human being wills something with a good will that God does not will, even with a will that is by far and much more certainly good [variant: “he himself”]; for God’s will can never be evil. It is as though a good son wished his father to live, while God, with a good will, wished him to die.

Again, it can happen that a person wills with an evil will what God wills with a good one: for example, if an evil son wished his father to die, and God also willed this. The former wills what God does not will, whereas the latter wills what God also wills; and yet the piety of the former, although he wills something different, accords more with God’s good will than does the impiety of the latter, who wills the same thing.

How much difference there is between what it is fitting for a human being to will and what it is fitting for God to will, and toward what end each directs his will, determines whether that will is approved or condemned. For God fulfills certain of his own wills, which are entirely good, through the evil wills of human beings, just as through the evil wills of the Jews Christ was killed for us by the good will of the Father. So great was the good accomplished that when the Apostle Peter did not want it to happen, he was called “Satan” by the one who had come to be killed (Matthew 16:23).

How good appeared the wills of the pious faithful who did not want the Apostle Paul to go to Jerusalem, lest he suffer there the evils which the prophet Agabus had foretold (Acts 21:12)! Yet God willed him to suffer these things for the proclamation of the faith of Christ, making him a martyr of Christ.

Nor did he fulfill this good will of his through the good wills of the Christians, but through the evil wills of the Jews. It belonged more to those who did not will what he willed than to those through whom, willingly, what he willed was accomplished; for both groups did the same thing, but he did it through the former with a good will, whereas they did it with an evil will.

### Chapter 102

However great the wills of angels or human beings may be—whether good or evil—and whether they will what God wills or something other than what God wills, the will of almighty God is always unconquered. It can never be evil; even when it inflicts evil, it is just, and certainly it is not evil because it is just [variant: “which is just”].

Therefore almighty God, whether through his mercy, by which he wills to have mercy, or through his judgment, by which he hardens whom he wills, does nothing unjustly and does nothing except willingly; and he does whatever he wills.

Accordingly, when we hear and read in the sacred writings that he wills all human beings to be saved, although it is certain to us that not all human beings are saved, we must not thereby detract anything from the will of the most omnipotent God. Rather, we should understand what is written—“who wills all human beings to be saved”—as though it said: no human being is saved unless he himself wills that human being to be saved; not that no human being is saved except one whom he wills to save, but that no one will be saved [variant: “but that no one is saved”] except one whom he wills to save. For this reason he must be asked to will it, because it must happen if he wills it.

The Apostle was speaking about praying to God when he said this. In the same way we understand what is written in the Gospel: “He enlightens every human being” (John 1:9). This does not mean that there is no human being who is not enlightened, but that no one is enlightened except by him.

Or certainly it was said in this sense: “he wills all human beings to be saved”—not as though there were no human being whom he did not wish [variant: “would not wish”] to save, since he refused to perform miracles among those who, he says, would have repented if he had performed them; rather, we should understand “all human beings” as every kind of human being, distributed according to every distinction: kings, commoners, nobles, ignoble persons, lofty and humble, learned and unlearned, sound in body and weak, intelligent and slow-witted, foolish, rich, poor, those of middling status, males, females, infants, children, adolescents, young men, older men, old men; in every language, every manner of life, every art, every profession; established in innumerable varieties of wills and consciences; and whatever other distinctions there are among human beings.

For what is there among them from which God does not will human beings to be saved through his only-begotten Son, our Lord, among all nations—and therefore does so, because the omnipotent God cannot vainly will whatever he wills?

For the Apostle had commanded that prayers be offered “for all human beings” [variant: “for each individual human being”], and had specifically added, “for kings and for all who are in high positions” (1 Timothy 2:1–2), who might be thought, through worldly arrogance and pride, to recoil from the humility of the Christian faith.

Therefore, when he said, “For this is good in the sight of God our Savior” (ibid., verse 4)—that is, that prayer should also be offered for such people—he immediately added, in order to remove despair, “who wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (ibid.). For God judged this good: that he should deign to grant the salvation of the exalted through the prayers of the humble. We already see this accomplished.

The Lord also used this manner of expression in the Gospel when he said to the Pharisees, “You tithe mint and rue and every herb” (Luke 11:42). For the Pharisees did not tithe every herb belonging to foreigners and to all foreign peoples throughout all lands. Therefore, just as “every herb” means every kind of herb, so there we may understand “all human beings” as every kind of human being. The expression may also be understood in any other way, provided that we are not compelled to believe that almighty God willed something to happen which did not happen. For, without any ambiguity, as Truth sings, “in heaven and on earth he has done whatever he willed” (Psalm 113:11); therefore he certainly did not will whatever he did not do.

### Chapter 104

For this reason, God would also have wished to preserve the first human being in the salvation in which he had been created, and, at the appropriate time, after children had been born, to bring him without the intervention of death to better things, where he would then be able not only not to commit sin but not even to possess the will to sin, if he had foreknown that he would have a perpetual will to remain without sin, as he had been made.

But because he foreknew that he would use free will badly—that is, that he would sin—he prepared his will for this instead: that he himself would do good even from one who acted badly. Thus the evil will of the human being would not be made void, but the good will of the omnipotent God would nevertheless be fulfilled.

### Chapter 105

For it was necessary that the human being first be made in such a way that he could will either good or evil: not without reward if he willed well, and not without punishment if he willed evil. But afterward he will be such that he cannot will evil; and yet for that reason he will not lack free will.

Indeed, the will will be much freer when it cannot serve sin at all. For a will by which we wish to be blessed in such a way that we not only do not wish to be miserable but are altogether unable to wish to be miserable is not to be blamed, nor is it not a will, nor is it to be called unfree.

Therefore, just as even now our soul possesses an aversion to unhappiness, so it will always possess an aversion to iniquity. Yet the order was not to be omitted in which God wished to show how good it is for a rational soul [variant: “rational animal”] to be capable even of sinning, although it is better that it cannot sin. It was likewise a lesser immortality, yet it was still immortality in which it could also die [variant: “could not die”], though a greater immortality was to be that in which it could not die.

### Chapter 106

For human nature lost through free will what it would have received through grace, which it would have received through merit if it had not sinned—although without grace there could then have been no merit either.

Although sin consisted solely in free will, free will was nevertheless not sufficient to retain righteousness unless divine assistance were supplied through participation in the immutable good. For just as death is within human power when one wishes it—there is no one who cannot kill himself, to say nothing else, simply by refusing to eat—so, for retaining life, the will is not sufficient if assistance is lacking, whether in the form of food or of any other protection.

Thus, in paradise, the human being was capable, according to his will [variant: “through his will,” or “by his will”], of killing himself by abandoning righteousness; but in order that he might retain the life of righteousness, it was not enough for him to will it unless the one who had made him assisted him.

After that fall, however, God’s mercy is greater, since free will itself has been liberated from the slavery over which sin rules through death. It is not liberated by itself, but solely through the grace of God, which is placed in faith in Christ, so that the will itself, as it is written, may be prepared by the Lord (Proverbs 8:35, according to the Septuagint), and through it the other gifts of God may be received, by which one comes to the eternal gift.

† After reading this passage, you ought rather to have imposed silence upon your mouth than to make such a shameless din or mutter anything at all. For just as God’s essence is one and always the same, yet his wills are expressed in many ways, so that you can neither resist nor ought to resist them, in the same way you ought to have understood something different concerning predestination. For he predestined nothing other than what he willed to be done by himself—namely, mercy and judgment. And just as his wills are expressed in many ways, so sound reason teaches that his predestinations are expressed in many ways.

Thus it was rightly said: “he predestined to punishment,” “he predestined to grace,” because in the one he preserved justice, while in the other he displayed mercy.

It is read in the Book of Chronicles that Rehoboam came to Jerusalem and summoned the entire house of Judah and Benjamin, numbering one hundred and eighty thousand chosen and fighting men, in order to wage war against Israel and bring the kingdom back to himself. “Speak to Rehoboam, son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to all Israel who are in Judah and Benjamin: Thus says the Lord: You shall not go up, nor shall you fight against your brothers. Let each man return to his house, for this thing has been done by my will” (2 Chronicles 11:1–4).

And just as his wills are spoken of in the plural, so his predestinations are expressed in the plural. You must not contradict this.

Yet, having set aside the true instruments of relative predication, you suddenly turned to establishing an essential predication. You have likewise joined relative predicates to the essential nature and, without inserting any distinction between them, asserted one and the same thing in a long-winded argument. [scan page 526]

1035 — ON PREDESTINATION

## CORRECTION

† Here you assert, without any cloud of doubt, that relative predicates are essential, contrary to the opinions of all who have treated such matters acutely and prudently.

Since it is established that there are ten categories, the first of them substance and the remaining nine accidents—that is, things which occur in a substance—and that relation is certainly predicated according to accident, I do not see how you make an accident into a substance.

For anyone with even a little training in the subject plainly knows that “to determine,” “to predestine,” “to make,” “to create,” “to dispose,” “to administer,” “to order,” “to govern,” “to judge,” and other similar terms are expressed relatively. For what is predestined necessarily has something else that is predestined; one thing is the predestiner, another the predestined.

Thus “to predestine” is not said substantially in the same way as “to be” is said. “To be” signifies substance, whereas “to predestine” signifies an accident—that is, a relation. Therefore, when “human being” is said, substance is asserted; but when “predestiner” is said, an accident, namely a relation, is predicated of him. The former demonstrates one thing essentially, whereas the latter includes several things.

For by saying “human being,” I pronounce nothing other than “human being”; but when I say “predestiner,” I announce both a human being and his accident at the same time. For a predestiner must predestine something, whereas “human being,” considered simply, indicates substance related to nothing else.

It is therefore clear that predestination is said accidentally, not essentially, since it is predicated not of the subject but in the subject. For if substance is so called because every thing subsists in itself, then a body, since it subsists, is a substance. Accidents, however, which exist in something subsisting and in a subject, are not substances, because they do not subsist but change.

A human being, a horse, or a stone must remain the same; but “good,” “bad,” “wise,” “foolish,” “beautiful,” and “deformed” are not always said of the same thing, since they are shown to be changeable whenever and however they occur. Therefore, although a human being can always exist, it does not follow that he is always a predestiner. For example, when he has nothing that he predestines, he is not rightly called a predestiner; yet he is called a human being even if he predestines nothing.

If this is rightly said of rational creatures, it is said very differently of God, to whom nothing happens as an accident. Whatever is said of God by a human being must necessarily be said either according to substance or according to relation, either properly or metaphorically.

“God” is great, good, omnipotent, wise, just, and eternal—these are said essentially. “Creator,” “founder,” “maker,” “operator,” “disposer,” “predestiner,” “ordainer,” “governor,” and “judge” are expressed relatively. Yet this relation in God is directed partly toward himself and partly toward creatures.

For the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are certainly related to one another: the Father is the Father of the Son; the Son is the Son of the Father; the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Father and of the Son. “Lord,” however, is the lord of a servant; the Creator, operator, and predestiner is without doubt the creator, operator, and predestiner of a creature.

Therefore it is in no way to be granted that predestination is predicated essentially of God. Although he has always existed essentially, he was never called “Lord” before he made that over which he was to be called Lord.

Similarly, although from eternity he always possessed in the counsel of his will what, when, how, and where he would make, he was not called “maker,” “predestiner,” or “disposer” before he predestined and disposed to make it.

Therefore, when he is said to make, operate, predestine, and dispose, this in no way demonstrates his substance; rather, it demonstrates the effect of his almighty will, in which reason always existed. Whatever he had willed, he, subject to neither temporality nor change, would predestine, operate, and make—temporal and changeable things temporally and changeably, without labor or fatigue, in the deepest tranquility.

But Augustine’s definition, which you wished to introduce, does not say that God’s predestination is his substance, but that it is “the preparation and disposition of all the things he was going to do.”

Moreover, who does not know that wisdom and knowledge are predicated essentially of God? They are not said relatively. The Father is wise, the Son is wise, and the Holy Spirit is wise; the Father knows, the Son knows, and the Holy Spirit knows. Indeed, the Father is wisdom, the Son is wisdom, and the Holy Spirit is wisdom; the Father is knowledge, the Son is knowledge, and the Holy Spirit is knowledge, just as the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God.

Yet there are not three wise beings, three knowing beings, three wisdoms, or three knowledges, any more than there are three gods. There is one wise being, one knowing being, one wisdom, and one knowledge, just as there is one God.

For “to be wise” and “to know” are essential to him as “to be” is; neither is related to anything. But since “to predestine” and “to dispose” are related to something, they are in no way predicated essentially of him.

Since it is therefore established that predestination is expressed metaphorically or by transference when it is spoken of God, it is certainly not expressed essentially but relatively. For if God were said to predestine essentially, as he is said to be, to be wise, and to know, it would follow that his predestination was related to nothing, just as neither his essence, greatness, goodness, power, wisdom, knowledge, nor justice is related to anything.

When greatness, goodness, power, wisdom, knowledge, and justice are said of God, he himself is judged to be these things essentially. Predestination, however, declares not what he is, but what he wills, disposes, and performs.

The substance of God is never expressed in the plural. We show that his predestinations, like his dispositions, administrations, ordinations, operations, and distributions, are expressed in the plural, and, when it is appropriate, we shall demonstrate this more fully with the Lord’s favor.

But because, later in this work, with Augustine’s support, I have treated these matters either more fully, or perhaps more tediously, or certainly more falsely, when we reach that point in the work, you will be refuted by the testimony of Augustine himself, with the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ consenting.
