## SAINT PRUDENTIUS, BISHOP OF TROYES  
1039

## CHAPTER III  
### On the fact that reason does not permit there to be two predestinations

Next, your argument is so full of the frivolity of your errors—repeating unnecessary matters with such a profusion of superfluities for the third time—that every honorable person would be ashamed to hear, much less read, it. For while you labor in prolixity, you have been wholly unable to escape what is said: “You will not escape sin through many words” (Proverbs 10:19).

You say, and repeat at length, that from the will and essence of God, and likewise from predestination, all necessity is absent. Who does not know this? Who does not know that God is subject to no harmful necessity?

Accordingly, although it is necessary that everything whatever God willed, disposed, and predestined should happen in precisely that way and not otherwise, we have already said—and we acknowledge—that no violence can be imposed upon anyone by either of his predestinations.

Thus, since I have neither read nor heard of anyone who favors this assertion, I cannot see why you have argued so long about the necessity of predestination, unless, having nothing true to say, you sought a point over which to rave, in order to abolish completely the predestination of the impious, which is so often inculcated by the Fathers.

For after many such arguments:

## JOHN SCOTUS

### Chapter 3, number 1, section 3

“You say, therefore, that that is not predestination which compels life, justice, and blessedness by inevitable necessity, nor that which compels their opposites, namely death, sin, and misery.

“This, you say, is concluded by the argument of an enthymeme, which is always drawn from an opposite. Its proposition is as follows: ‘If God is not the highest essence and is not the cause only of those things which are from him, and if God is the highest essence, then he is the cause only of those things which are from him.’

“Sin, death, and misery are not from God; therefore God is not their cause.

“The same syllogism may also be put together in this way: ‘If God is the cause of things that are, and is not the cause of things that are nothing, and God is the cause of things that are, then he is not the cause of things that are not.’

“Sin and its effect—namely, death, which certainly clings to it—and misery are not beings; therefore neither God nor his predestination, which is what he is, can be their cause.”

## CORRECTION

† I cannot sufficiently marvel at your presumption in saying what no author or interpreter of the divine writings has ever said.

You say that predestination is God. The prophetic and apostolic Scripture never said this; nor do its interpreters, as far as I have found, ever say it. With what audacity have you dared to invent what you cannot affirm by the authority of Scripture?

Now, as for your statement that God’s predestination contains no force by which anyone is compelled to anything, we say this too, and we prove it. Likewise, your addition that God and his predestination are not the cause of things that do not exist—namely, sin, death, and misery—we also entirely approve. God is no more the author of sin than he is its cause.

But he is not the cause of death, which, as you say, is the effect of sin, nor of misery; he is nevertheless their most just author and inflictor.

For God is neither the cause nor the author of that death which occurs when the soul abandons true and supreme eternal life and turns lustfully toward things low and perishable. Concerning this death it is said that “God did not make death” (Wisdom 1:13), because the Creator did not establish it; rather, the malice of an angel or the pride of a human being devised it and, through pride, brought it upon itself.

But the death which occurs when the soul departs from the body is from God, as Scripture testifies. God said to the first human beings of our race, threatening them:

“Eat from every tree that is in paradise, but you shall not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; for on whatever day you eat from it, you shall surely die” (Genesis 2:16–17).

In these words he foretold only the death of the soul; he did not yet inflict it. Therefore he is not thereby shown to be either its cause or its author.

Then, after the eating of the forbidden tree, the Lord—after that most merciful and immeasurable rebuke and patience by which he mercifully invited them to repentance, while they obstinately rejected it and, with the greatest pride and stubbornness, attributed the cause of their own fall to God—pronounced the sentence of condemnation by an inevitable judgment, saying to Adam:

“Because you have done this and have listened to the voice of your wife more than to me: cursed is the earth in your work. When you work it, it shall not give you its fruits, but it shall produce thorns and thistles for you. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread all the days of your life, until you return”;

and to Eve:

“I will multiply your sorrows and your conceptions. In sorrow you shall bear children; you shall be under the power of your husband, and he shall rule over you” (Genesis 3:16 and following).

Although God is not the cause of this death and misery, he is nevertheless most certainly believed to be their author—that is, their most just inflictor—as the preceding words make clear. Whoever wishes to oppose this, I think, will be convicted of impiety even if I remain silent.

The death of the body is the soul’s departure from the body. God is therefore called its author because, when he punishes and wills it, the soul is withdrawn from the body, until, when he himself wills and judges it, all rise again, each to receive back his own body either for evil according to his merits or for good.

For it is just that, by the authority of the one by whom the body is created, given, and joined to the soul, it should, because of its deserts, be withdrawn by that same authority; and that what was first bestowed by his kindness should afterward be taken away by his justice, so that what goodness bestowed, equity may remove.

When the soul is joined to the body, it gives life; when it is taken away, it removes life. This very taking away, removal, or withdrawal is called by the name “death.” Since it occurs only under God’s judgment, who would dare deny that God is the author of this death?

The same must be understood concerning misery: since it is called a lack of blessedness, it is not attributed to God as author [sentence incomplete in the supplied source].

## On Predestination

1041

…but is attributed to the rational creature, which is undoubtedly understood to have brought misery upon itself through a voluntary turning away from the highest good of true blessedness and through a damnable adherence to the lowest good. But when the penal misery of this present life’s condition, or the subsequent retribution in Gehenna, is spoken of, who does not know that God is its author, by whose judgment all things are administered? For if, as Scripture says, “Nothing happens on earth without cause” (Job 5:6), it is plainly evident that, just as good things exist with God as their author, so evils and miseries—whether inflicted here or hereafter as punishment for the testing of the godly or the condemnation of the ungodly—must likewise be believed to proceed from no other author than God, the supremely just.

When we consider whatever things are inflicted as punishment, we find scarcely any punishments or miseries apart from God’s creatures. And since, as blessed Gregory teaches, every judgment upon human beings is carried out through angels, it is entirely clear that whatever is inflicted upon human beings as punishment under God’s judgment is effected through his creatures. For example, through corrupted air, or disturbances of the winds, or excessive heat of the sun, or destructive downpours of rain, or through whatever other forms of heavenly retribution, concerning which the Prophet testifies:

> “He sent,” he says—without doubt meaning God—“against them the anger of his indignation, indignation and anger and tribulation, a sending through evil angels,” and so forth (Psalm 77:49).

Although he says that the sending was dispatched through evil angels, we nevertheless read that, under God as avenger, it is also repeatedly carried out through good angels. Thus the true history relates that at Sodom and the neighboring cities the Lord rained down fire from heaven (Genesis 19:24); and no one who reads that history faithfully is unaware that those angels were blessed.

Since, therefore, it is well known that in this age or in the fire of Gehenna the punishments due to sinners are inflicted through God’s creatures, who would dare deny that God, supremely just, is their author? If you ask their cause, sinners immediately present themselves: by their evil deeds they have provoked the supremely good and just God to repay these things to them deservedly.

Nevertheless, when inquiry is necessarily made concerning the soul and the apostate angels, and concerning the punishments by which they are afflicted—whatever they are, that is, punishments or torments, however they may more conveniently be named—they are not for that reason called evil because they are truly, that is, naturally, evil, since they are God’s creatures. For “God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Genesis 1:31). Rather, because they are undoubtedly contrary to those who suffer them, they are designated by the term “evil” from the standpoint of those who experience them.

Accordingly, blessed Augustine, while revising his books, when he came to the revision of the book whose title he wished to be *On Eighty-Three Questions*, says (*Retractations* I.26):

> “Whether God is not the author of evil. Here one must take care that what I said—‘He is not the author of evil’—not be misunderstood. He is the author of all things that exist, because insofar as they exist, they are good. Nor should it consequently be supposed that the punishment of the wicked does not come from him, although it is certainly evil for those who are punished by it. I said this in the same sense in which it is said, ‘God did not make death’ (Wisdom 1:13), although elsewhere it is written, ‘Death and life are from the Lord God’ (Wisdom 16:13). The punishment of the wicked, therefore, which comes from God, is indeed evil for the wicked, but it belongs among God’s good works, since it is just that the wicked be punished, and whatever is just is certainly good.”

### Correction

1042

Among the holy writers, Jerome too, in his *Commentaries on the Prophets*—which are especially full of this kind of expression, since he walked in the same footsteps because he was guided by the same Spirit—says, in explaining the prophet Jonah (chapter 1):

> “Here we must understand ‘evil’ as affliction and calamity, in accordance with the saying, ‘Sufficient for the day is its own evil’ (Matthew 6:34); and in the prophet Amos: ‘If there is evil in a city which the Lord has not done’ (Amos 3:6); and in Isaiah: ‘I am the Lord, who make peace and create evil’ (Isaiah 45:7). In another passage, however, ‘evil’ is understood as contrary to virtue, according to what we read above in this same prophet: ‘The cry of its evil has risen up to me’ (Jonah 1:2).”

All these statements plainly indicate that God is neither the author nor the cause of sin; but that he is faithfully proclaimed the author of evils—that is, of every kind of punishment and affliction—is beyond doubt. Their cause, however, is the sinners and their sins.

You proceed from there to other matters and, as though you had emerged victorious from the first encounter with your opponent, advance boastfully and furiously to refute other points. You attack your opponent with many insults and assail him with curses; if he read them and had the opportunity, perhaps he would answer more gently or more appropriately. We have passed these things over, since we undertook to examine and, insofar as we can with divine assistance, refute only those matters in which you dissent from Catholic truth. We therefore directed our style solely toward examining and considering those points.

You say that charity is one, although it has two commandments; we say the same, following blessed Gregory, because just as charity is one and its commandments are two, so there is one Spirit and two gifts.

You say that charity is God, and we agree, instructed by the one who reclined upon the most blessed breast of the Lord and said, “God is charity” (1 John 4:8). But we reject your use of all this to destroy a twofold predestination. Scripture says, “God is charity”; it never says, “God is predestination.” What more is needed? Even if nothing else were available to us for refuting your perversity, this alone would suffice: no prophetic, evangelical, or apostolic Scripture testifies to it. I read of the Lord’s charity; I do not read of the Lord’s predestination. The prophets did not foretell this, the evangelists did not announce it, and the apostles did not preach it. No venerable Father is found to have said it—those Fathers through whom the prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic Scriptures have been faithfully and beneficially explained for us in different places and times.

We therefore do not admit what we do not find in the sacred writings, especially when you fabricate it through your own argumentative devices against the testimony of the divine utterances.

[scan page 529]

### Saint Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

1043

And because nothing outside is admitted, whatever you say outside is deservedly rejected. [A damaged passage, introduced as a citation, reads in substance: “Rightly, among/in Samaria … the well … that he might establish them in charity; therefore, when something good is signified by this binary number, twofold charity is especially commended.”] Although, as was shown above, the authority of the holy Fathers and the truth of the twofold predestination are commended, your—that is, solitary—predestination is condemned as false. For who would listen to or follow you, a barbarian marked by no ecclesiastical dignity, when you oppose the bishop of the Roman city and apostolic see, Gregory, and his associate in teaching, dignity, and office, the blessed bishop Isidore?

Indeed, if someone were to despise the authority of blessed Isidore alone, who would listen to you or follow you, unless he were mentally deranged? His doctrine appears to all Catholics to be consistent with the faith and appropriate to the circumstances, especially since even today Leo, the venerable bishop of the apostolic see, in a letter of reply sent three years ago to the bishops of Britain who inhabit the lower parts of Gaul concerning certain questions, judged that whenever something came into doubt and could not be found in the sacred canons, one should have recourse to the writings of the Catholic Fathers, and that whatever was ambiguous in them should be sought and followed. When he expressly named them, he noted blessed Isidore among the others with equal honor and dignity.

Since Isidore’s doctrine in a matter of faith is seen to have been approved by the apostolic see, whatever you have attempted against it is refuted and must not thereafter be supported by any force.

Nevertheless, when you deny a twofold charity just as you deny a twofold predestination, and condemn its proponents as heretics, consider what you yourself have done. The orthodox Fathers are sometimes found to have set forth twofold charity or love in their writings. The same author, in book IV of *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, says:

> “Him who is always the Son of God, for us made the Son of Man, so that his eternal power and divinity, accommodated to our weakness and mortality, might make for us in himself and unto himself a way from ourselves; so that he may faithfully hold fast with the great joy of hope that, lest he sin, he is ruled by Christ the king; if perhaps he sins, he is cleansed by that same priest; and thus, nourished in the practice of good conduct and life by the wings of twofold love, as though borne up from earth on two strong wings, he is enlightened by that very Christ the Word.”

The same author, in the book *Annotations on Job*, adds a passage whose opening is materially corrupt in the scan: “Rightly, among/in Samaria … the well, that he might establish them in charity; therefore, when something good is signified by this binary number, twofold charity is especially commended.”

The venerable presbyter Bede, in his *Exposition of the Tabernacle* (book II, chapter 11), where it is read that Moses, at the Lord’s command, set up [the relevant object], says:

> “With a fork—that is, with a two-pronged implement—the priests tend the fire of the altar, when, in all that the holy preachers teach, they instill in us the power of twofold charity and, by its grace, command us at once to burn and to give light.”

Again, the same Bede, in the same work (book III, chapter 4):

> “There was not gold in one part of the breastplate, hyacinth in another, and still other colors elsewhere. Rather, all the colors were woven throughout together with the gold itself, because, plainly, in priestly action no one of the great virtues, or of those appropriate to human beings, ought ever to be interrupted. The priest or teacher of the faithful must always be radiant with the gold of wisdom, always raised by the hyacinth of hope toward heavenly things, always courageously clothed in the purple of the heavenly kingdom against the battles of vices, always flaming with the twice-dyed scarlet of twofold love, and always bright with the twisted linen of chastity of the flesh.””

Augustine, in his sermon on the thirty-eight years of the sick man (*Tractates on John*):

> “With wings spread out, immobile, and facing south, with the virtues of twofold love unfolded and freed from every worldly impediment, remaining unshaken in faith, yet not presuming upon himself in this very matter, but hoping in God and recalling no one into temptation [another reading: ‘directing his attention toward him’]. From him the tree of charity itself is inspired, so that he may preserve his strength for him, saying: ‘Is not my soul subject to God? From him comes my salvation. For he is my God and my savior, my protector; I shall not be moved again’” (Psalm 62:1–2).

Leo, in his sermon on the fast of the seventh month:

> “And since it is said, ‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and you shall love your neighbor as yourself’ (Matthew 22:37), with Christ the Lord saying, ‘We know that on these two commandments the whole Law and the Prophets depend’ (ibid., verse 40), so great is the union of this twofold commandment of charity that, without the connection of these virtues, no king is found to be justified, nor is grace.”

And again in the same work:

> “Love of neighbor is love of God, who brought the fullness of the Law and the Prophets to completion in the unity of this twofold charity, so that no one might doubt that whatever he had bestowed upon a human being he had offered to God, since the Lord and Savior says, speaking of feeding and assisting the poor: ‘Whatever you did for one of the least of these, you did for me’ (Matthew 25:40).”

Certainly I do not see what is contrary to reason and truth if charity is called twofold, although God is called charity, since many things are found in the sacred writings that are said of God and expressed in the plural. Who does not know that God is said to possess mercy, mercies, justice, justification, knowledge, goodness, praise, praises, truth, and many other things, and yet that anyone who attentively observes can easily find these expressed in the plural?

The Prophet says: “My God, my mercy” (Psalm 59:18); and again: “I shall sing the mercies of the Lord forever” (Psalm 89:3). Again: “Remember your mercies, O Lord” (Psalm 25:6). Again: “The justice of the Lord is upright” (Psalm 19:9). Again: “I shall meditate on your justifications” (Psalm 119:16). Elsewhere: “For the Lord is a God of knowledge” (1 Samuel 2:3). Again: “For you are my strength and my praise, O Lord God” (Psalm 118:14).

[scan page 530]

## On Predestination against J. Scotus

1044

Again: “The Lord is my strength and my praise” (Psalm 118:14). Again: “That I may proclaim all your praises” (Psalm 30:24). Again: “For the Lord seeks truths, and the truths of the children of human beings have been diminished” (Psalm 12:2).

These passages plainly show that such things can indeed be said of God and yet are not prevented by their being expressed in the plural. No one is unaware that our Lord is truthfully and properly called Savior, Salvation-bringer, and Christ; yet no one therefore proclaims that saviors, salvation-bringers, and Christs are to be expressed in the plural. Whoever has absorbed knowledge of the divine utterances through use and memory knows such examples without difficulty.

Nor should one pass over the fact that you say predestination belongs to God’s nature because it exists before every creature, just as God does. Then say that God’s election also belongs to his nature, since, as the Apostle teaches, “he chose us in Christ Jesus our Lord before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4). Say also that God’s promise is his substance, since the same Apostle testifies that “the God who does not lie promised before eternal times” (Titus 1:2), and that he decreed that whatever he wills according to the eternal counsel of his will—whose beginning no times initiate and whose duration no times shorten, which neither past things make pass away nor future things replace—should begin, proceed, and be completed for us through times and places.

Since it is therefore established that whatever things naturally exist, however they exist, exist only by his will, it follows that whatever occurs by his will should be said to belong to his essence, since his doing, working, foreknowing, predestining, administering, governing, judging, condemning, and all other such things are nothing other than his willing. For he is not wearied by labor or disturbed by work; his will is his work.

Therefore, since God’s willing is his being, it can only be said impiously that whatever is known to proceed from his will belongs to his nature. God judges; does it follow that his judgment will therefore be his nature? The same must be understood of all the other things that are said of him relationally.

## Chapter IV

### On the one true and only predestination

You proceed to other matters and, in the fourth jest of your lies, assert that a third heresy has been made out of the two. You indicate one of the two by naming its author, while presenting the other without naming it. For you say:

## John Scotus

*(Chapter IV, number 1, section 1.)*

> “This heresy, therefore, of Gottschalk—if it may be called by that name—is situated between two other heresies opposed to one another, as though in the middle between them: between the one plainly called Pelagian, and the one that contradicts it. One of these abolishes divine grace; the other condemns free will. The Pelagian sect, by praising the freedom of the rational soul, commends it as sufficient, by the gift of nature, for attaining the Lord’s righteousness without the assistance of grace. The contrary sect confounds grace with the gift of nature, so that it alone, in all who are under its influence, and without any effort of free will, brings about the entire righteousness of the faithful. One, then, as has been said, despises the gift of grace; the other, the gift of free will. Both are equally impious, though the sects are distinct. The one now under discussion lies in the middle between the two foregoing extremes, which are opposed to one another, joining itself partly to each and partly contradicting each, while claiming as its own precisely what it contends that they do not possess. For when it attempts to establish as necessary and inevitable causes, within divine predestinations as it imagines them, all the virtues by which blessedness is attained and all the vices by which misery is incurred, what else does it seem to advocate than the destruction of God’s gifts—namely, free will and the aid of grace? By these two, the righteousness of a human being is both begun and perfected.”

### Correction

We have set down the words of your statements thus far, not to expand our own discussion at greater length, but to reveal plainly what your poison consists of.

We know and condemn the Pelagian position, because it exalted free will and strove by its own powers, without the aid of God’s grace, to attain righteousness.

We neither defend nor maintain the second heresy, which you assert to be compounded from two heresies—namely, one established by the necessity of predestination for all good and evil things, which you now call by the new name “Gottschalkian.”

Nor have we read or heard of the third position, which you assert to be contrary to Pelagianism and which is said to preach the gift of grace in such a way that free will is entirely removed. For, having carefully examined blessed Augustine’s book *On Heresies*, we have found no such position in it.

You ought therefore to have explained more clearly by what author this position was maintained, so that it might be answered more easily—or rather, more suitably. But after thinking about it for a long time, and wavering excessively between conflicting judgments, I have found nothing else expressed by you in it except that, under this name—as also under the name of twofold predestination—you wished indirectly to detract from all Catholics who either already labor in the Lord or, still weighed down by the weakness of the flesh, sigh until they reach the goal of their salvation through the gift of grace. All Catholics, with one and wholly harmonious agreement, preach the gift of grace in such a way that they affirm that without it the freedom of the will is powerless for any effort toward the good.

Since so much has been sufficiently and abundantly written by the Fathers and by us, as well as by other most learned Catholic men, concerning grace and free will, it should suffice for me to bring forward only the judgment of the blessed Father Augustine, who, in the book he composed *On the Rebuke and Grace* for Valentinus and his monks, says among other things (chapter 1):

> “And by this very fact, to desire the aid of grace is the beginning of grace. Concerning this it is written: ‘A person’s steps are directed by the Lord’” (Psalm 37:23).

### [Continuation of Augustine’s quotation]

“Free will, therefore, whether for doing good or for doing evil, is not taken away from the human being. But in doing evil everyone is free from righteousness and a slave of sin; in doing good no one can be free unless he has been freed by the one who said: ‘If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free’ (John 8:36).

Nor is it the case that, once someone has been freed from the domination [another reading: condemnation] of sin, he no longer needs the help of his liberator. Rather, when he hears from him, ‘Without me you can do nothing’ (John 15:5), he should himself say to him: ‘Be my helper; do not abandon me’ (Psalm 27:9).”

A little later (chapter 2):

> “For there is the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, by which alone human beings are freed from evil, and without which they do absolutely no good—whether in thought, willing and loving, or action—not merely so that, when it shows them what ought to be done, they may know it, but also so that, when it supplies the power, they may do with love what they know.

> “The Apostle sought this inspiration of good will and action for those to whom he said: ‘We pray to the Lord that you may do no evil—not so that we may appear approved, but so that you may do what is good’ (2 Corinthians 13:7).”

And so forth, which he explains at greater length in the same work.

Since this is the true and complete agreement of the Catholic faith, I do not know by what description you wished to mark it as your third heresy, unless you intended to mark the statements of blessed Augustine that we have cited above—or rather, those of all Catholics—whose faithful and truthful followers we are.

Your statement concerning this supposed third heresy is therefore wholly superfluous and irrelevant.

## John Scotus

*(Chapter 4, number 2, section 3.)*

> “If you cannot believe in free will, you do not believe that there will be a judgment of the world.”

And below:

*(Number 3.)*

> “It is therefore impious not to believe that free will was given to human beings by God.”

### Correction

Who, unless entirely alien to the faith and the Christian name, would ever deny either that free will was given to human beings by the Creator or that a future judgment will take place? We therefore believe and confess, without any hesitation, that free will was given to human beings. But it was so corrupted and weakened by sin that, unless God’s grace precedes it, it cannot rise toward any good by its own will and power.

For what strength could one sold under sin possess, by himself or from himself, for accomplishing any good? The one who had the freedom to sell himself and submit to a tyrant’s domination was, without doubt, already handed over to slavery; he had no freedom to release himself or be absolved from tyrannical servitude unless he were freed by the unmerited grace of the one whose word we have learned: “If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free” (John 8:36).

We read that the Lord himself said this to the Jews who boasted of the nobility of their lineage, falsely denied the mark of servitude, and said, “We are free and have never been slaves to anyone”: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:33, 36).

## Saint Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

1048

Who does not know that they first served the Egyptians, then various nations in the promised land, and, after obtaining royal power, the Assyrians, Chaldeans, Medes, Persians, Greeks, and finally the Romans, under a miserable yoke? Even when they spoke these words against the Lord, the Gospel history shows that they were subject to the Romans and paid them tribute.

What, then, does the Lord mean when he says, “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free”? Did he intend to subjugate the Romans, subject the world to his earthly empire, and come to reign among earthly beings with those whom he had freed, so that he would say, “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free,” when, in response to those deceitfully asking whether it was lawful to pay tribute to Caesar, he answered, “Give to Caesar what belongs to Caesar” (Matthew 22:17)?

Far be this from the hearts of the faithful. They read and believe that, for the sake of our liberation, he approached death and willingly submitted to the tribunals of earthly power, answering the governor: “My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my ministers would certainly fight, so that I would not be handed over to the Jews; but now my kingdom is not from here” (John 18:36).

Why, then, does he declare that, if they are freed by the Son, they will be rescued and become free, when they were subject to every sin—and especially when they not only failed to believe in the Son of God but also handed him over to death? Who could doubt this? Who could be unaware of it?

It remains, therefore, that we understand the Lord to have spoken of the slavery of sin by which they were inevitably bound and of the dominion of the devil to which they were attached: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free.”

And where is that liberty by which those who were freed from Egyptian slavery, through the mystery of circumcision as a type of the shedding of the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, are undoubtedly understood to have been absolved from the bond of original guilt? What baptism now accomplishes among us in faith in that same blood already shed, circumcision accomplished among the ancients in faith in that blood still to be shed; no orthodox person doubts this. How, then, are those considered in need of liberation who are known already to have been liberated?

Unless it is because, according to the Apostle who says, “For in hope we were saved” (Romans 8:24), we still await true—that is, perfect—liberty. For if we have already been liberated and saved only in hope, why do we pray to be delivered from evil? Why do we cry out to the Lord, saying, “Arise, help us, and deliver us for the sake of your name” (Psalm 44:26)? Who could doubt that this is the voice of the liberated and redeemed?

Yet, as we said earlier, we are instructed by the apostolic teaching: “For in hope we were saved. Now hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Romans 8:24 and following).

And again:

> “The whole creation groans and labors in birth, awaiting the revelation of the children of God. For creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it in hope. For creation itself will be set free from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (ibid.).

[scan page 532]

## On Predestination against J. Scotus

1049

1050

The apostolic authority therefore teaches us that we have been liberated, but are still to be liberated: liberated from the bond of the first transgression, to be liberated from every vice of corruption; liberated in hope, to be liberated in reality; liberated so that we may fight against the enemy, to be liberated so that we may never fear the enemy.

There will be true freedom where there is certain security; secure freedom where no iniquity attacks; true liberation where no corruption remains; freedom will truly be possessed where no captivity presses upon us.

But here, where the adversary resists without ceasing, where an intense and continuous struggle against vices is constantly at hand, where freedom is often compelled to serve even against its will, we must humble ourselves and continually ask for the aid of liberating grace. Thus, humbled with the Apostle and presuming nothing upon the powers of our own freedom, we should say:

> “I delight in the law of God according to the inner person; but I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin, which is in my members” (Romans 7:22–23).

Struck by this humility and salutary shame, let us cry out with the same Apostle:

> “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (ibid., verse 24).

And, in no way despairing of mercy, let us add:

> “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (ibid., verse 25).

Behold the enemy attacking; behold the captivity dragging us away; behold the rebellious law; behold the body of death. And where is freedom? But hear where there is the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Free will therefore exists in a human being, but it is so sluggish, so weak, and so infirm with respect to the good that, unless grace goes before it, it can neither will nor do good.

Hence blessed Augustine, in the book *On the Gift of Perseverance* (chapter 7), says:

> “This does not belong at all to the powers of free will as they now exist; it did belong to them in the human being before the fall. How powerful that freedom of the will was in the excellence of its first condition became evident in the angels, who, when the devil and his companions fell, stood in the truth and merited to attain perpetual security from falling—the condition in which we are entirely certain they now exist.

> “After the human being’s fall, however, God willed that it should belong solely to his grace that a human being approach him; and he likewise willed that it should belong solely to his grace that a human being not depart from him. He placed this grace in the one in whom we have obtained our portion, predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things.”

The same blessed Augustine expresses this all the more clearly because more briefly in the book *Enchiridion* (chapter 30), where he says:

> “By using free will badly, the human being both lost himself and lost free will itself.”

In these brief, truthful, and faithful words, blessed Augustine plainly made known the weakness of free will [another reading: “presented it as known”], saying that the human being, by using free will badly, both lost himself and lost free will itself—that is, free will.

How the same free will was lost is explained by what has already been said. He lost himself because he subjected himself to death; he lost free will because he sold himself to the enemy. He lost it, I say, for willing or doing good. For toward evil a servile freedom, if I may call it that, always remained available to him. Thus, in order that he may now will or be able to do good, this belongs solely to the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Let him therefore be healed so that he may be liberated; let his bleary eye be anointed with the medicine by which the eyes of one blind from birth were healed. For the one who says, “I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” (Psalm 41:5), needs healing.

And again:

> “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak; heal me, Lord, for my bones are troubled, and my soul is greatly troubled. But you, Lord—how long? Turn, Lord; rescue my soul; save me for the sake of your mercy” (Psalm 6:3–5).

Those of whom the Lord said in the Gospel, “The healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are ill. For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Matthew 9:12–13), needed this healing and freedom.

And again:

> “The Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost” (Luke 19:10).

That is: the Son of Man came to seek the fugitive and liberate the captive. If he was free, how had he perished? Clearly, he had perished because, having turned away from the true light, he served as a slave to vices and demons.

But in order that he might be liberated, the one in whom the ruler of the world had nothing came (John 14:30), and who alone among the dead was free (Psalm 88:5). If we desire to attain his true and perfect freedom, let us humbly and submissively place ourselves under his prevenient and assisting grace—he who came to seek and save what was lost (Luke 19:10).

You then add:

## John Scotus

*(Chapter 4, number 4, section 5.)*

> “Rational life ought not to have been made otherwise than voluntary, since it was created by that will which is the cause of all things, in its image and likeness. Or how, you ask, could the divine will—the supreme reason of the universe, which is constrained by no necessity, since it possesses its most free power—make an image of itself like itself if it did not create its substance as a free, rational will?”

### Correction

In this statement, you say that the substance of the image of God—that is, the human being’s will—is free and rational. This sounds new and previously unheard by our ears, since you assert that the human will is its substance, and explain it at greater length by adding:

## John Scotus

*(Chapter 4, number 5, section 6.)*

> “This is proved most clearly by an argument drawn from the sin of the first human being. Although, you say, by sinning he lost the blessed life, he did not lose his substance.”

And you add what that substance itself would be:

*(Number 6.)*

> “What is it? To be, to will, and to know. For he both is and wills and knows; he wills himself to be and to know; he knows himself to be and to will.”

[scan page 533]

## Saint Prudentius

### Correction

You establish that the will and knowledge of man are his essence—something which, although you support it with your inventions and arguments, you do not support with authority. For who does not know that the rational soul exists, and that willing and knowing are present in it? But existence is its nature and substance; willing and knowing are not its substance and nature, but adornments of the substance, bestowed by the gift of the Creator. For, in making it, the Creator conferred existence upon it; he freely granted it willing and knowing.

For the human soul was made in the image of its Creator not in willing and knowing, but in the rational mind. This is firmly proved by the Apostle’s authority, when he says: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind and put on the new man, who according to God was created in justice and holiness of truth” (Ephesians 4:23). By these words the Apostle, calling the image of God the spirit of the mind together with justice and holiness of truth, did not call its will and knowledge its substance.

What else is free will than the free will of the soul? This, as I think, may rightly be defined as follows: free will is the will of the soul, which of its own accord and by its own power is moved either toward good or toward evil.

Willing is natural to us, just as understanding and remembering are. These three—intellect, memory, and will—are so naturally present in the human soul that they are nevertheless not said to be the soul itself, but to be in the soul. Therefore, just as these natural affections of the soul are not the soul itself, so they can be varied in many ways while the same soul remains.

Thus willing belongs to nature; but willing good or evil is not nature, but a certain movement and function of nature. For if it were natural for us to will good or to will evil, it would not be possible for one of the two alternatives to be otherwise. In that case the very nature of the soul could not be otherwise, and it would be as natural for us to will well or ill as it is natural for us simply to will. In this way, willing well or ill would not be virtue or vice in us, but nature. Nor could we in any way be anything except either wholly good or wholly evil; nor would reward rightly be owed to us for good, or punishment for evil, since we could not be otherwise and there would be no merit of our own, whether good or evil, but only of the Creator—or, which may it never be, of the guilt of one who had established such a nature unchangeably in either direction.

Therefore, from the beginning, willing itself was natural to man; but the movement of his will was given to him as good in such a way that, if he were moved of his own accord toward good, he could also of his own accord incline toward evil. Thus, according to the choice of his own will, he would possess merit, good or evil, and consequently a just reward or punishment.

When man therefore fell into sin, he did not lose existence, which belongs to nature; he did not lose willing, which is natural to him. But he lost willing well and fell into willing evil. Thus the movement or function of nature was changed in him, or even lost; nature itself was changed for the worse, but it was changed, not destroyed.

Man therefore lost free will by sinning—the free will by which he previously possessed strength for good. He lost the movement and function of good will, but he did not lose himself; he did not lose the nature of the soul, but the health of the soul; he lost the vigor of good will. Both of these—the nature changed for the worse and the will corrupted toward evil—are restored through Christ’s grace.

A good will is therefore the health of free will; an evil will is the sickness of free will. Man lost this health and incurred this sickness by abandoning God and acting against his will. Thus, when a sick man becomes ill, he loses the strength of his former health but does not lose himself; when he is cured, health is restored in him and his nature is invigorated—nature which had not been destroyed, but corrupted by sickness.

[Editorial note: The words that follow this section and the next are not in the text, but may perhaps have been added in the margin.]

Since it is established that everything created was made by God as its author, it is plainly evident that everything which the supremely good author created is good, as Scripture testifies: “God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Genesis 1:31). It is therefore clear that every creature of God, as the Apostle says, is good: “There is no creature of God that is not good” (1 Timothy 4:4).

But not every will of man is good, for some will is evil. Therefore the will of man is not a creature of God, since no creature of God is evil, whereas some human will is evil. Hence it is clearer than daylight that the will and knowledge of man are not his substance, but gifts of God implanted in human substance—that is, in the rational soul. If it uses them well, it preserves and adorns in itself the image and likeness of God; but if it abuses them wantonly, as it does the other gifts of God, it wickedly deforms and disgraces that image.

For what are virtues except dispositions and adornments of the rational soul bestowed by divine gift? And what are vices except the nakedness and disgrace of the rational soul, turned away from the true and supreme Good?

If willing is the substance of man, why does the Apostle say: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish, for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13)? Those to whom the Apostle said this had already been made by God; they had already received the substance of existence according to soul and body. If, then, as you say, the will of man is his essence—which they already possessed—what need was there for God to work in them the substance that had already been made? Especially since, by using the present tense, he shows that he was speaking not of the past and of a creature already made, but of the gift of gratuitous grace, which the Lord must continually work in us.

Hence the Prophet also prays, saying: “Create a clean heart in me, O God.” Although he already had a created heart, he shows why he asks that it be created when he adds: “And renew a right spirit within me” (Psalm 50:12). Here he declares that he has used “creation” for renewal, which every holy person needs as long as he bears a body which is corrupted and weighs down the soul, and as long as an earthly dwelling presses down the mind occupied with many thoughts (Wisdom 9:15).

[scan page 534]

## On Predestination

If, I say, the knowledge of man is his essence, why does the Apostle James exhort that it be requested from the Lord? For he says: “If anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask it of the Lord, who gives to all generously and does not reproach, and it will be given to him” (James 1:5). And the Psalmist prays: “Teach me goodness and discipline and knowledge” (Psalm 119:66). It is foolish to ask to receive something which one already possesses. If, then, knowledge is your nature, why do you ask that your nature be taught?

### Augustine, *Confessions*, Book XIII, chapter 11

“Who understands the omnipotent Trinity? And who does not speak of it, though scarcely any soul, when it speaks of it, knows what it is speaking about? Yet they contend and dispute, and no one sees this vision without peace.

I wanted men to consider these three things in themselves. These three are very different from that Trinity; but I say where they may exercise themselves, test themselves, and perceive how far they are from it. I mean these three: being, knowing, and willing. For I am, and I know, and I will: I am knowing and willing; and I know that I am, and that I will; and I will to be and to know.

In these three, let whoever can see how inseparable are one life, one mind, and one essence, and finally how inseparable yet distinct is the distinction. Let whoever can see this look before himself, attend to himself, and see, and tell me. But when he has found something in these things and said it, let him not think that he has found that which is above them—the immutable, which is immutable in being, immutable in knowing, and immutable in willing.

And whether the Trinity is there because of these three, or whether these three are in each individual, so that each individual has three—or threefold things—or whether both alternatives are true in marvelous ways, simply and multiply; whether, within its infinite unity, it is sufficient to itself, known to itself, and sufficient for itself, unchangeably the same, in the abundant greatness of its unity—who can easily think this? Who can express it in any way? Who would rashly pronounce upon it in any manner?”

### The same Augustine, in the sermon *On the Words of the Apostle*

“When we were in the flesh, the passions of sins, which are through the law, worked in our members to bear fruit for death” (Romans 7:5). He therefore came to you not because you had come to him; he came and freed you where he found you—sold under sin, lying in the death of the first man, bearing the sin of the first man, bearing guilt before you could possess free choice.

See where he found you: when he found you as a little child. But you passed beyond childhood in age; behold, you grew up; in addition to the first sin you committed many others. You received the Law and became a transgressor. But do not be anxious: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded” [variant: “superabounded”] (Romans 5:20).

### The same Augustine, in the Gospel of Blessed John, sermon 19

“In the beginning was the Word.” He is in the same way, he is as he is, and he is always thus; he cannot be changed. This is God, of whom he said to his servant Moses: “I am who I am,” and, “He who is has sent me” (Exodus 3:14).

Who can comprehend this? When you see all mortal things subject to change; when you see the world itself changing through time, through the conditions of being born, growing, declining, and dying; when you see human beings able to acquire wisdom if they draw near to its light and warmth, and able to lose wisdom if they withdraw from it with an evil disposition—when, therefore, you see all these things to be changeable, what is that which is, except what transcends all things which exist in such a way that they are on the point of not existing?”

But you proceed to confirm what you had said with many arguments, and you say:

## John Scotus

### Chapter 4, number 7, section 1

“What, then, did the first man have before sin which he lost after sin? For he did not yet possess the blessed life which would have been bestowed upon him if he had kept the commandment. If we say that he lost free will, he therefore lost his nature. But if reason teaches that no nature can perish, we are forbidden to say that he lost free will, which is undoubtedly substantial. For God did not create captive will in man, but free will, and this freedom remained after sin.”

### A little later

#### Number 8

“Or perhaps he lost through sin the strength and power of free will by which alone he could have kept the commandment, if he had wished; and thus the strength and power of free choice did not derive their existence in the first man from substance, but from the grace of the Creator? He lost this great gift by using the freedom of his will badly. For he did not wish to do what he could do—that is, to keep the commandment—which after sinning he cannot do even if he wishes, unless grace assists him.”

### Correction

By this you attribute to grace what is owed to nature, as is sufficiently clear. For when you say that, if he lost free will, he lost his nature, this is false, because the will is not nature but something implanted by the author of nature.

What you add—that no nature can perish—is also false. For the opinion of the teachers of the Church, or almost all of them, agrees on this point: every creature of God, made from nothing, was partly so established by the hand of the Creator that it could never perish; but part of it was destined for destruction. That is, some things remain as they were made, some await transformation into better things, and some entirely perish so as no longer to exist.

It would therefore be much better and more credible for you to say that it is certain that no rational creature can perish, as Saint Jerome says in his exposition of the blessed Apostle Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, chapter 6:

“Whoever loves someone always rejoices in that person’s happiness; and if he sees him deceived by some error and fallen into the mire of sins, he will indeed grieve and hasten to rescue him. But he will not be able to turn his mind from grief, knowing that no rational creature can perish forever before God.”

### Jerome, in his commentary on Matthew, chapter 6

“Consider the birds of the sky, for they do not sow, nor do they reap, nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them” (Matthew 6:26). This must therefore be understood simply: if birds, without care and anxiety, are fed by God’s providence—birds which exist today and will not exist tomorrow, whose soul is mortal, and which, once they have ceased to exist, will never exist again—how much more are human beings, to whom eternity is promised, governed by God’s will.”

### Fulgentius, in his book to Peter on the faith

“God created certain spirits in such a way that they would exist forever, but others in such a way that at some time they would cease to exist.”

And later:

“The remaining spirits of all animals, which lack understanding, derive their origin, some from the earth and some from the waters. Reptiles and birds are from the waters; from the earth arose some creatures which crawl and others which walk. They are spirits as long as they live in bodies.

For the soul which has not been divinely made capable of reason begins and ceases to live together with its flesh, because when it no longer gives life to the body, it too does not live. Thus, although the soul is in a marvelous way the cause of life for all flesh, an irrational spirit lives only as long as it can remain in the flesh; when it is separated from its flesh, it is weakened [variant: extinguished].

Thus, although it is itself the life of its flesh, it cannot live when it ceases to supply life to the flesh. And if there is no flesh to which it can give life, it too will immediately no longer possess life. Therefore neither eternity has been given to irrational spirits, nor is any judgment prepared for them in which blessedness for good works or condemnation for evil works might be repaid to them.

No distinction of works is required in them because they received no faculty of understanding from God. Their bodies will therefore not rise again, because their souls possessed neither righteousness nor unrighteousness for which eternal blessedness or punishment might be assigned to them.”

### Bede, on Genesis

“All the days of the earth, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, night and day shall not cease” (Genesis 8:22). When he had said “all the days,” he immediately added “of the earth,” so that you might understand that, for all the days during which the earth is to possess its present condition, human beings are to be secure from the force of a universal flood.

Yet there will be a time when, with this alternation of fleeting things—which takes place annually throughout the whole world—ceasing, the world together with its living creatures will be destroyed by fire.”

### Bede, in the same work

“For this reason God requires the souls of men from beasts, and men from those by whom they had been driven out of the body, because he made man in his own image (Genesis 1:26), inasmuch as he willed that man should remain for eternity and not perish with the death of the body like the animals.”

### Gregory, *Dialogues*, Book IV, chapter 3

“Almighty God created three living spirits: one which is not clothed with flesh; another which is clothed with flesh but does not die with the flesh; and a third which is clothed with flesh and dies with the flesh.

The spirit which is not clothed with flesh belongs to the angels; the spirit which is clothed with flesh but does not die with the flesh belongs to human beings; and the spirit which is clothed with flesh and dies with the flesh belongs to cattle and all brute animals.”

## Saint Prudentius

As for what you add—“We are forbidden to say that free will was lost”—this too is shown to be false by blessed Augustine, as we cited above, when he says: “By using free will badly, man lost both himself and free will itself.” The phrase “and itself” is to be understood as referring to free will. He therefore lost free will—that is, freedom of will for choosing good—but he did not lose freedom of will for choosing and carrying out evil. For the person who voluntarily subjected himself to sin no longer remained in his own power, but in the gift of grace, so that through its inspiration he might will and be able to do good.

Augustine teaches this very thing in his letter to Vitalis, saying:

“The grace of God is not in the nature of free choice, nor in law and teaching, as Pelagian perversity foolishly supposes; rather, it is given for individual acts by the will of him concerning whom it is written: ‘You set apart a voluntary rain, O God, for your inheritance’ (Psalm 68:10; Romans 7:12).

For by the greatness of the first sin we lost free will for loving God; and although the law and teaching of God are holy, just, and good, they kill if the Spirit does not give life (2 Corinthians 3:6). Through the Spirit it comes about that we are held not merely by hearing but by obeying, and not by reading but by loving [variant: ‘that it may be held’].

Therefore, that we may believe in God and live piously, it is ‘not of him who wills or of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy’ (Romans 9:16)—not because we ought not to will and run, but because he himself works in us both willing and running (Philippians 2:13).”

Saint Isidore supports this, explaining the distinction in his work *On the Gifts of God and Free Will* (*On Differences*, Book II, chapter 32):

“Between the infusion of divine grace and the will of human choice there is this difference: choice is the will of free power, which of itself and spontaneously can desire either good or evil. Grace, however, is divine; it is the gratuitous gift of divine mercy, through which we merit both the beginning of good will and the accomplishment of the work.

For divine grace is what precedes a man so that he may be good; human choice does not precede the grace of God. Rather, God’s grace itself precedes the unwilling man, so that he may also will what is good. For, under the burden of the flesh, man is so driven that he is weak toward sinning, readily inclined to transgression, and slow to repentance [variant: ‘readily inclined to transgress, slow to repent,’ and so forth].

He has within himself the source of his fall, but he has no source of rising again except the grace of the Creator, so that he may be raised up and may stretch out his hand to those who lie fallen.

Finally, through the grace of God, free will is restored to man, which the first man had lost. For the first man possessed free will to begin the good, although that good would be perfected by God’s assistance. We, however, receive both the beginning and the perfection of free choice from God’s grace. For we have both the beginning and the perfection of good from him, from whom the gift of grace has been given and in whom free will has been restored to us.

The gift of God, therefore, is what we do because of preceding and following grace; what is ours is what we do because of the obedient will of free choice. For if it is not God’s, why do we give thanks to him? And if it is not ours, why do we expect repayment for good works?

Accordingly, in that we are preceded by grace, it is God’s; but in that, by doing good, we follow the preceding grace [variant: ‘in that we are for the purpose of doing good’], it is ours.

No one precedes God by merits, so as to be able to hold him as though he were a debtor. Yet the Creator, in a marvelous manner just toward all, chose some beforehand by predestining them, while by a just judgment he left others in their wicked ways.

Hence the true gift of grace is not obtained from human virtue or the merit of choice, but is bestowed solely by the goodness of divine mercy. Some are saved by the free gift of his preceding mercy, having been made vessels of mercy; others, regarded as reprobate and predestined to punishment, are condemned, having been made vessels of wrath.

This is understood from the example of Esau and Jacob, who, although not yet born, were conceived and born from one conception and birth and bound by the same bond of original sin; nevertheless, the preceding goodness of divine mercy gratuitously drew one of them to itself, while the other, regarded with hatred by the severity of justice, was left in the mass of perdition and condemned [variant: ‘drew the other by preceding mercy; the other, by a certain…’].

Thus God himself speaks through the Prophet: ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated’ (Romans 9:13). It follows that grace is not conferred on the basis of preceding merits, but solely by divine calling; and no one is saved or condemned, chosen or rejected, except according to the purpose of the predestining God, who is just in the rejected and merciful in the elect.

‘All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth’ (Psalm 25:10).”

What you infer—that the will, that is, the will of man, is undoubtedly substantial—is false according to what has been established above. You endeavor to assert that the will is substance; but in another sense the will is rightly called substantial and natural. It is substantially and naturally implanted in the same substance and nature as a gift of the first creation.

We absolutely do not say that the will itself is substance. For if it were substance, it would not be evil; yet there is no doubt that will exists abundantly both in apostate angels and in perverse human beings. Every creature of God is good, but not every human will is good.

From different appearances comes a different appetite of souls; from different appetites come different outcomes; from different outcomes comes different habit; and from different habit comes a different will. The order of things produces different appearances—an order hidden, indeed, but nevertheless certain under divine providence.

One must not therefore think that the natures of souls are different because their wills are different. Indeed, the will of one and the same soul varies with the passage of time. At one time it wishes to be rich; at another, having despised riches, it desires to be wise. Even among temporal desires, at one time business pleases a man, at another military service, and so with many similar things.

[scan page 536]

## On Predestination

What you add—“For God did not create captive will in man, but free will, and this freedom remained after sin”—is also false.

God created the soul free and implanted in it a free will, not a captive one. Yet, by turning toward what was worse, the soul itself made that will captive. For, although with the help of grace it could have kept it free if it had wished freely to obey the command of the Creator, it preferred, through a damnable turning away and disobedience, to sell it to the devil, by whom it was thereafter held captive.

Thus the soul itself made itself captive; it was the soul that sold itself, not the Creator who had made it free. It therefore lost not substance, but the freedom he had created—not freedom altogether, but in part: it could not will good without grace, while by nature it could will evil. Nature itself it had not lost, but had changed for the worse.

Therefore after sin there remained in it the freedom to will and do evil; but there did not remain the freedom by itself to withdraw from evil and turn toward good. For what it possessed from itself so as to fall, it did not possess from itself so as to rise again.

Thus, constrained by the clearest words of the most blessed Father Augustine—words which you had read, namely, that man had lost free will itself—lest you should appear to contradict his most truthful statements and lest any Catholic should follow your madness, you turn your head here and there like a serpent, searching for a way to escape the blow that strikes you. At last you say that man lost the strength and power of free will.

In this you do not differ greatly from us. For if he lost the strength and power of freedom, freedom itself plainly did not remain. How can there be freedom if it lacks strength and power? How is that free which lacks strength and power?

If, therefore, he lost strength and power, he undoubtedly also lost freedom; for there is no freedom if it lacks strength and power. Who is free when strength and power are absent? Thus, while you try to loosen what is bound, you bind it more tightly; while you deceitfully labor to untie the knots, you fasten them more firmly.

This, then, is the whole of what we say: by sinning, man lost freedom, strength, and power of choice, because he who could fall by himself was in no way able to rise by himself.

And when you say that by this alone—that is, by its power—he could have kept the commandment if he wished, you depart far from piety. However great the excellence with which the rational creature of free choice was distinguished by the gift of the Creator, it nevertheless always needed grace, whether to support it, strengthen it, or restore it.

This is evident in the transgressing angels: if they had possessed grace supporting or strengthening them, they would certainly never have fallen so gravely. Because that grace was divinely bestowed upon the holy angels, they deserved to receive from it both certainty of perseverance and security from ever falling.

It is therefore mercifully bestowed for the restoration of sinful man, because he fell not so much through his own transgression as through the persuasion of his deceiver.

[scan page 537]

## Saint Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

Although God bestowed upon the rational creature so great a gift—namely, freedom of choice—he nevertheless did not wish to make it equal to himself in every respect, so that it would always need his grace, by whose goodness it had received the very fact of existing and of being free.

But when you apply a corrupting interpretation to words that are clear and evident, you plainly endeavor to introduce a cloud of error over the truth. Why did you suppress the preceding and following words of the same passage? If they are carefully considered, your interpretation is altogether convicted of distortion and error.

To make this clearer, let us set forth the entire sentence of that blessed Father, as it was published by him:

### Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 30

“But can this portion of the human race, to which God promises liberation [variant: ‘liberty’] and an eternal kingdom [variant: ‘promised’], be restored by the merits of its works? Far be it.

For what good can the lost person do [variant: ‘what good can he perform’], unless he has been restored from perdition? And this also is far from being possible [variant readings: ‘liberated’; ‘Can it be by free choice? This too is far from being possible,’ and so forth].

For, by using free will badly, man lost both himself and free will itself. Just as a person who kills himself kills himself while living, but, having killed himself, does not live and cannot resurrect himself after he has killed himself, so, when free choice sinned, free choice itself was lost through the victory of sin. For ‘by whatever anyone is overcome, to that he is enslaved’ (2 Peter 2:19).

This is certainly the Apostle Peter’s sentence. Since it is true, what kind of freedom, I ask, can belong to an enslaved servant, except when it delights him to sin? For he serves freely who willingly does the will of his master. Thus he is free for sinning who is the slave of sin.

Therefore he will not be free for doing justice unless, liberated from sin, he becomes a servant of righteousness. That is the true freedom, for the sake of the justice of right action, and at the same time the pious servitude required by obedience to the commandments [variant: ‘the license of right action together with obedience to the commandment’].

But from where will this freedom for doing good come to a man who is enslaved and sold, unless he is redeemed by the one whose voice says: ‘If the Son makes you free, then you will truly be free’ (John 8:36)?

Before this begins to take place in a man, how can anyone glory in a work of free choice for the good, unless he is puffed up and lifted up by empty pride? The Apostle restrains this pride when he says: ‘By grace you have been saved through faith’ (Ephesians 2:8).

And lest people arrogate faith itself to themselves, so that they would not understand that it too had been divinely given, the same Apostle says elsewhere that he obtained mercy so that he might be faithful (1 Corinthians 7:25). Here also he adds: ‘And this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God—not from works, lest anyone should boast.’

And lest it be thought that good works would be lacking in the faithful, he adds again: ‘For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand so that we should walk in them’ (Ephesians 2:8–10).

Hence we become truly free when God forms us—that is, shapes and creates us—not as human beings, which he has already done, but as good human beings, which he now accomplishes by grace, so that we may be a new creation in Christ Jesus (Galatians 6:15), according to what has been said: ‘Create a clean heart in me, O God’ (Psalm 51:12).

For, insofar as the nature of a human heart is concerned, God had not failed already to create his heart.

Again, lest anyone should glory, even if not in works, in free choice itself, as though merit began from him and free freedom itself were owed a reward for good action, let him hear the same herald of grace saying: ‘For it is God who works in us both to will and to work for his good pleasure’ (Philippians 2:13). And again: ‘It is not of him who wills or of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy’ (Romans 9:16).”

You further add, to confirm your error by which you assert that willing in man is his substance, the testimony of the Lord speaking in the Gospel to his disciples: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5), and you add an explanation—or rather a corruption—of it.

## John Scotus

### Chapter 4, number 15, section 8

“He did not say, ‘You can will nothing.’”

### Correction

Your most perverse understanding must necessarily be condemned by truth and authority. For you wish the Lord to be understood as having said, “Without me you can do nothing,” as though without him we could will some good thing; and you contradict the Apostle, who says: “For it is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish, for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13).

If, then, according to the Apostle, it is God who works in us to will, it is plainly evident that you falsely assert that we can will anything good without him. As though the will of man did not itself belong to action, when Scripture cries out that God will judge human beings not only for their deeds but also for their thoughts, which ordinarily arise from the will.

Hence the same Lord speaks through the Prophet Isaiah: “I am coming to gather all their works and their thoughts, together with all nations and tongues” (Isaiah 66:18). Saint Jerome explains this as follows:

### Jerome, on Isaiah 66:18

“God therefore comes to gather the works and thoughts of each individual. From this we learn that not only works but also thoughts are to be judged on the day of judgment. For whoever looks upon a woman in order to lust has already committed adultery with her in his heart (Matthew 5:28).

Of these thoughts it is said: ‘Now their thoughts have surrounded them’ (Hosea 7:3), when the Lord will judge the hidden things of men according to the Gospel of Jesus Christ (Luke 8:17), so that what the Apostle writes may be confirmed by the truth of judgment: ‘Their thoughts accusing or even defending them, on the day when God will judge the hidden things of men’ (Romans 2:15–16).

Thus all our thoughts, gathered together at one time, prove the just Judge, while our conscience either accuses us or makes satisfaction for the offense; whether sins or good works are more numerous, and whether they are old or new; whether …”

…joyful repentance, or repentance renewed by new crimes, when the Lord says:

To this also corresponds the statement:
