and elsewhere:

> “But Jesus, knowing their malice” (Matt. 22:18).

And lest the heretics who slander the Word of God have any opportunity for doubt, as though he did not know everything, the Epistle written to the Hebrews says at greater length:

> “For the word of God is living and effective and sharper than every two-edged sword, piercing as far as the division of soul and spirit, of joints also and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart. No creature is invisible in his sight; but everything is naked and exposed to his eyes, of whom we speak” (Heb. 4:12–13).

When all thoughts have been gathered together into one place, accusing or defending us, then all nations and languages, together with their thoughts, will likewise be brought into the midst. According to the Apostle Paul, we read of languages not only of human beings but also of angels (1 Cor. 13:1).

From this it is understood that all creatures will be judged by the Lord—not only those upon the earth, but also those in the sea [or, in the air] and in the heavenly places—according to what he himself had said above:

> “My sword is drunk in heaven, and it will descend upon the earth” (Isa. 34:5).

Indeed, the Prophet makes clear that thoughts conceived by the will alone belong to action when he says:

> “For in the heart you work iniquities; upon the earth your hands prepare injustices” (Ps. 58:3).

For what reason is anyone judged concerning thoughts, unless it is because they are such that they are reckoned as deeds, and are either crowned according to their merit or condemned? The Lord also declares this when he says:

> “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28).

This statement plainly indicates that will and thought belong to action, when someone thinks, wills, and looks with such an inclination that the only thing lacking is the ability to carry the act out.

# Against John Scotus

### 1062

I cannot sufficiently wonder that you have said that we can do nothing without God, but can will without him. For if, according to you, “to will” is essentially “to be,” and without doubt we cannot exist without God, how can we will without him? For if we can will without God, because, as you assert, willing is being for us, then we can exist without God. But we cannot exist without God; therefore it follows that we cannot will anything good without God. For in what way could anyone will without God who cannot exist without God?

Even if someone thinks that in the Lord’s saying only action is to be understood, let him hear what the Apostle says:

> “We have such confidence toward God, not because we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as though from ourselves; rather, our sufficiency is from God” (2 Cor. 3:4–5).

Here he shows that the beginning of conceiving and thinking a good will is not from us or out of ourselves, but from God. Thus your falsehood is refuted, when you had said that we can will without God.

Who could doubt that faith is the gift of God, when the Apostle says:

> “For to you it has been given by God not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Phil. 1:29)?

It is evident that no one believes except by the will. What, then, has been given to believers so that they may believe in him and suffer for him, except a will given divinely, by which they believe in him and suffer for him? If, therefore, the will to believe in him and to suffer for him is given by God, it plainly follows that without him we can will nothing good.

Accordingly, the words of the Lord,

> “Without me you can do nothing,”

must be understood more soundly and correctly as referring to both kinds of doing: to the deed of the mind and to the deed of the body. Scripture calls both of them “work,” because something is done not only by action but also by being conceived through the will.

Let us now consider the denial of the blessed apostle Peter, and we shall clearly recognize that willing comes to us from God, not from ourselves. For he who denied by his own will did not repent by his own will at all, until the divine regard returned him to himself. He had been briefly abandoned, so to speak, and had departed from himself—from that self, I mean, which he had been when, while following the Lord even from a distance, he had entered the courtyard of the high priest.

The Evangelist says:

> “When the rooster had crowed for the third time, and the Lord looked at Peter, Peter remembered the word of the Lord, in which he had said: ‘Before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times.’ And he went out and wept bitterly” (Matt. 26:74–75).

Have you become so dull that you do not hear, “The Lord looked, and Peter remembered”? For Peter did not remember first and the Lord look afterward; rather, the Lord looked first, and afterward Peter remembered. First grace looked upon him, and afterward repentance remembered. First mercy looked upon him, and afterward misery wept.

Whose, I ask, is this willing now: that of the one who looked, or that of the one who remembered after being looked upon? Certainly, when he denied, he did not have the will to confess the Lord; but the divine regard bestowed the will—not only to confess but also to feel shame.

Hence the Evangelist says:

> “And Peter remembered the word of the Lord, in which he had said: ‘Before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times.’ And he went out and wept bitterly.”

He remembered because he had presumed too much upon himself when he said:

> “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (Matt. 26:35).

He confessed, and rightly so, because he had damnably denied at the voice of a maidservant. Therefore he went out and wept bitterly. The fact that he did not remember until after he had been looked upon clearly indicates that the will had not been his own possession by itself, but that he received it from the one by whom he was looked upon.

Where, then, is your interpretation, according to which, when the Lord said, “Without me you can do nothing,” he did not say “will”? Do you not see that Peter could not remember unless the Lord had first looked upon him—that is, unless he had mercifully infused the will to remember and weep?

## [scan page 539]

# Saint Prudentius

### 1063

Let us also examine his fellow apostle Matthew, to see whether he too followed the Lord after being preceded by grace or through his own will. He himself writes in his Gospel:

> “Jesus saw a tax collector named Matthew sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him: ‘Follow me.’ And he rose and followed him” (Matt. 9:9–10).

What he says, “Jesus saw,” should be understood not so much as the sight of a human being, but as the gaze of grace looking upon him. He saw because he had mercy; he saw because he infused the will to see him; he saw because he made himself visible.

The tax collector was sitting at the tax booth, intent upon profits and greedily occupied with earthly business. The eye of his mind, together with the eyes of his body, was lowered toward public and private gain; he gave no thought at all to heavenly things. Should he be said to have possessed willing until he was seen? He was seen, and immediately he willed, because that vision flowed from the dew of grace.

The fact that he calls him a tax collector sufficiently indicates that, moistened and softened by the dew of heavenly regard, he was converted—not by his own will, which he had not yet possessed. Here the force and power of the grace that sees is greatly to be admired: as soon as it sees, it accomplishes its work. Its seeing requires no intervening delay. It penetrated the tax collector’s mind with such power that he immediately followed the grace calling him.

The omnipotence of God certainly accomplishes this in human hearts by a hidden impulse, whether through gentleness or through an incomprehensible fear, by causes concealed from our knowledge, so that, every delay driven away, they humbly and devoutly follow the regard of his freely given grace.

Let us also contemplate that most ardent champion, most truthful defender, and most faithful preacher of freely given grace. We shall clearly see that he was what he was by grace, not by his own will. His most truthful companion in his deeds and inseparable companion of his pilgrimage, the holy evangelist Luke, writes of him:

> “Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, went to the chief priests. He asked them for letters, so that wherever he found men or women belonging to this way, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem” (Acts 9:1–2).

You hear a ravening wolf—where is the will? You hear a persecutor armed for slaughter attacking the sheep—where is the will? Certainly, there was in him a will, but it was evil, and he was devoted to it and pursued it with such zeal.

Let us hear what follows:

> “And it happened, as he was going to Damascus, that a light from heaven suddenly shone around him. Falling to the ground, he heard a voice from heaven saying to him: ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’ He said: ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And the Lord said to him: ‘I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting. It is hard for you to kick against the goad’” (Acts 9:3–5).

Thanks be to God. We had heard the wolf roaring; let us hear the lamb growing gentle. “Who are you, Lord?” he says. Previously he did not even deign to recognize a human being, and suddenly, trembling, he confesses the Lord.

How is it that in one and the same moment both wolf and lamb are revealed? The wolf is thrown down before he is prostrated, and he is made a lamb. The fiercest persecutor is cast down, and the gentlest preacher is raised up. He raged and was blinded; he is blinded and enlightened.

From where, I ask you? From his own will? Far from it; from the dew of grace. We heard the will of the raging man before he was prostrated:

> “Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter.”

Let us hear and rejoice at the bleating of the lamb growing gentle:

> “Who are you, Lord?”

Certainly this was not from the will he possessed by himself, but from the will he received through grace, which inspired him in that same radiance. He received it, I say, because he did not have it before.

Hear what he himself testifies concerning himself:

> “When it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace, to reveal his Son in me” (Gal. 1:15–16).

For he who testifies that he was set apart by God from his mother’s womb plainly declares that this was not the work of his own will, but of the grace that predestined and called him. Did he have, while still in his mother’s womb, the will to be set apart, before he was born, when, after being brought forth from the womb and grown to maturity, he had the will to oppose with such determination the knowledge of the one who had set him apart? Certainly not.

Therefore, when surrounded by heavenly light, he received this sudden will: to preach afterward with the greatest obedience what he had previously opposed with the greatest iniquity.

Let us see whether he confirms this same point:

> “For what do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

If, according to your interpretation, Paul possessed willing essentially, then what he says, “What do you have that you did not receive?” is false. He acknowledged that he received, in that radiance, what he knew he had not possessed from birth. He rejoiced that he had received as a heavenly gift what he denied having possessed by nature.

Again, you misuse another testimony of the same Apostle, and it is certain that you have entirely failed to understand it and have consequently distorted it through false interpretations. For you say as follows:

# John Scotus

*(Chapter 4, no. 16, section 8.)* “And the Apostle says: ‘To will is present with me, but to accomplish is not’” (Rom. 7:18).

# Correction

You appear to have understood this as though he had said that willing was his by nature, but accomplishing was possible only by grace. Although the same Apostle refutes your perversity according to the points already set forth,

nevertheless, so that the meaning of his words may become clearer—and lest you proudly reject our interpretation—we have thought it appropriate to insert what the blessed Augustine thought about these matters in Book Six [chapter 23] against the Pelagian bishop Julian.

> “As for the words of the Apostle where he says, ‘I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh,’ and so forth, up to where he says, ‘Wretched man that I am! In doing so, you give me far too much credit: for I was neither the only nor the first person to understand this passage in a way that overturns your heresy, and in accordance with how it ought to be understood. > “It did not seem possible to me that the Apostle could say of himself, ‘But I am carnal’ (Rom. 7:14), since he was spiritual, or that he could say that he was led captive under the law of sin which was in his members (Rom. 7:23). I thought that these things could be said only of those whom the lust of the flesh had so subjected that they did whatever it compelled them to do. It is foolish to believe this of the Apostle, since an innumerable multitude of saints, so as not to fulfill the desires of the flesh, lust against the flesh in the spirit.

> “But afterward I yielded to better and more discerning interpreters—or rather, to the truth itself, as must be acknowledged—in order to see that in those words of the Apostle there is the groaning of the saints who are fighting against carnal desires. Although they are spiritual in mind, they are nevertheless still rightly understood to be carnal in that they possess this corruptible body, which weighs down the soul; for they will be spiritual also in body when the natural body has been sown and the spiritual body rises again.

> “They are also rightly understood to be subject to the law of sin in that part which is subject to the movements of desires to which they do not consent. Hence I came to understand these things in the same way as Hilary, Gregory, Ambrose, and the other holy and renowned teachers of the Church: they judged that the Apostle had strenuously fought against the carnal desires that he did not wish to have but nevertheless had, and that he had borne witness to this very conflict in those words of his.

> “You yourself have confessed that the saints exercise glorious contests against these movements, which must first be conquered so that they do not dominate, and afterward healed so that they may be completely extinguished. Let us therefore recognize together the words of those who are fighting, if we are fighting. For in this way we do not live by ourselves, but Christ lives in us, if we trust in him both to wage the battle against desires and to obtain victory unto the final defeat of those same enemies, rather than trusting in ourselves.

> “He himself has become for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, sanctification, and redemption, so that, as it is written, ‘Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord’ (1 Cor. 1:30–31).

> “It is not therefore contradictory, as you think, that the one who says, ‘I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me’ (Gal. 2:20), should also say, ‘I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh’ (Rom. 7:18). For to the degree that Christ lives in him, to that degree he fights against and overcomes the fact that good does not dwell in his flesh, but evil does.

> “Nor would anyone’s spirit rightly desire against its flesh unless the Spirit of Christ dwelled in him. Far be it from us, therefore, to say that the Apostle spoke these words as though he wished to be understood as resisting while being led by some pestilential hand of lust into a brothel, when he says, ‘It is no longer I who do it’ (Rom. 7:20). He thereby shows that the desires of the flesh produce only the impulse of lust, without the consent of sin.

> “Why do you vainly attempt to transfer these words to the pride of the Jews, as though the Apostle were transforming into himself those who despised Christ’s gifts as unnecessary for them? This is what you imagine; would that you at least understood Christ’s gifts so well as to believe that they have some power to conquer desire.

> “But you say that the gifts were despised by the Jews because he offered forgiveness for sins which they had avoided through the admonition of the Law. As though remission of sins accomplished this for a human being: that the flesh should not desire against the spirit. Hence those words arose: ‘I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh,’ and similar statements.

> “But you do not depart from your doctrine, by which you suppose that the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord operates only in the remission of sins, and does not assist in avoiding sins and conquering carnal desires by pouring charity into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5).

> “Nor do you consider the one who says, ‘I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind,’ and who declares that he is freed from this evil only through the grace of God by Jesus Christ our Lord (Rom. 7:23–25). > “You say that the Apostle intensifies the force of habit. Answer, then: does the baptized person not fight against this force? If you deny it, you contradict the understanding of all Christians. > “By the good law, you say, and by the holy commandment, the violent impulses of the soul were aroused [or, had become violent], since no instruction could inspire virtue without one’s own will.

> “O sharp interpreter! O distinguished expositor of divine utterances! What will you do with the words of the one who says: ‘I do not do the good that I will’; ‘To will is present with me’; ‘The evil that I do not will, that I do’; and ‘I delight in the law of God according to the inner person’?

> “You hear these statements and say that, because the will was lacking, virtue was lacking. What if not only the will but also the virtue was present, so that he would not consent to the desire of the flesh, which by its own depraved movements served the law of sin? He did not yield to these movements or offer his members as weapons of iniquity to sin, yet he felt in his flesh the desire against the spirit for what he did not will, and in turn desired against it in the spirit. With the truest voice of chastity he said: ‘Therefore, I myself with my mind serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin.’”

# Saint Prudentius

### 1067

### Augustine, Book Four, chapter 3

> “You call human nature good because it deserves the assistance of such grace. I would gladly hear this if you said it because human nature is rational. For the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord is not bestowed upon stones, wood, or cattle.

> “But because the human being is the image of God, he deserves this grace—not, however, so that his good will can precede grace. Otherwise the will itself would first give something for which a return might be made, and grace would no longer be grace (Rom. 11:35), since it would not be given freely but repaid as a debt.

> “What, then, is the meaning of your claim that, according to your position, I have called the effect of the human will a heavenly gift? Is it as though the human will were moved toward the good without God’s grace, so that God would repay its effect as something owed?

> “Had you so completely forgotten that we say against you with Scripture, ‘The will is prepared by the Lord’ (Prov. 8:35, according to the Septuagint), or that ‘God works in us both willing and acting’ (Phil. 2:13)?

> “O enemies of God’s grace, enemies of Christ’s grace, Christians in name alone! Does the Church not pray for its enemies? What, I ask, does it pray for? If it prays that the price of their will may be repaid to them, what does it pray for them except a great punishment, which is already directed against them and not offered for them?

> “But it prays for them. Therefore it does not pray because they possess a good will, but so that their evil will may be converted into a good one. For the will is prepared by the Lord, and God is the one, as the Apostle says, who works in you both willing and acting.”

By these explanations of the blessed Augustine, which must be preferred, we are taught with the clearest light that those apostolic words describe a person established under grace, fighting with a pure mind against the desire of his flesh, not someone alienated from that same grace.

Accordingly, the person established under grace says:

> “To will is present with me” (Rom. 7:18),

that is, by the gift of grace I possess the will to be chaste and to live chastely; “but to accomplish is not,” since the desire of the flesh resists. I cannot extinguish entirely its goads and provocations, while the corruptible body weighs down the soul. Nor is he alienated from grace, although he had not yet received this will as a gift of grace.

For when he says, “With my mind I serve the law of God,” he says the same as, “To will is present with me.” And when he says, “With my flesh I serve the law of sin,” this is the same as saying, “But to accomplish is not.”

Therefore, if willing is natural to us—that is, if it is our essence, as you maintain—who does not know that all human beings possess it? Yet who does not know that all human beings, except those illumined by the regard of grace, do not possess the will to live chastely and to fight against the desires of the flesh, but rather submit to them with the greatest obstinacy and fervor?

If, then, according to you, all human beings possess the essence of willing, but not all possess the will to resist—in fact, they possess the will to obey—the desires of the flesh, it is clear that they do not all attain this from the good of nature. Rather, it comes from the generosity of grace, bestowed only upon those predestined as children of God, so that through that same grace they may be conformed to the proper and only Son of God (Rom. 8:29).

You add:

# John Scotus

*(Chapter 4, no. 17, section 8.)* “Likewise, when the same Apostle says, ‘It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy’ (Rom. 9:16), this is not understood otherwise than while he is willing and running. For these two things are naturally implanted in a human being. He wills, and therefore is willing; and he desires blessedness, and therefore is running. It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs to begin, perform, or complete good works; for this is the gift of the merciful God.”

# Correction

It is sufficiently apparent that, to strengthen the perverse meaning of your interpretation, you exaggerate these matters and twist the Apostle’s words into something other than what he said.

When you say that “not of the one who wills or of the one who runs” cannot be understood except while he is willing and running—that is, while he naturally possesses willing and running—you are wrong. The Apostle was not speaking of the will and running of nature, but of a person who, already illumined by grace, had received will and running—that is, the performance of good work—lest, after the grace that illumined him, he should trust in his own strength with the Pelagians and presume that he could accomplish anything without the assistance of grace.

When you say, “For these two things are naturally implanted in a human being,” you would speak correctly if the context did not show that you understand the matter otherwise. For to say that willing and running are naturally implanted in a human being—that is, that they are gifts granted to nature by its Creator—is something that the Catholic Church confesses elsewhere as one of the gifts of divine generosity. But it does not accept the claim that the will itself is nature.

On the contrary, you diminish grace so greatly while arrogating to nature more than truth permits that, with astonishing blindness, you shamelessly oppose such manifest truth and repeat the same point more often than necessary.

Therefore you add:

# John Scotus

*(Chapter 4, no. 18, section 8.)* “Nevertheless, it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs to begin, perform, or complete good works; for this is the gift of the merciful God.”

# Correction

You say this in order to show that the will and the desire—which you call “running”—are not the gift of God who precedes, but the gift of God who shows mercy, that is, who repays and assists.

But where is what the same Apostle proclaims?

> “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

And again:

> “Who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, so that he might be repaid? For from him and through him and in him are all things; to him be glory for ever and ever. Amen” (Rom. 11:34, 36).

If, then, you possess the will and desire for good from yourself—that is, from nature—it follows that beginning, performing, or completing good works is not the gift of the merciful God but the gift of one who repays. And what the Apostle says will be false:

> “Who has first given to him, so that he might be repaid?”

If, I say, you possessed by nature the will and desire for good, it plainly follows that you gave your will to God first, before he gave you the gift of beginning, performing, or completing the work. Thus what is repaid to you is the justice of one who returns a debt, not the generosity of one who gives freely.

Because, with all ambiguity removed, it is true that the Apostle says, “Or who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid to him?” it is plainly evident that the will and desire for good are a gift of prevenient grace, not of nature existing by its own force. “For what do you have that you did not receive?” If you have a good will, you have undoubtedly received it; and you received it not from the gift of nature that is blind, but from the gift of grace that shows mercy. For “from him and through him and in him are all things”; undoubtedly, then, the generosity of the good will is from him. To him be glory for ever and ever. Amen (Rom. 11:36).

> “We read the Apostle saying: ‘I received mercy so that I might be faithful,’ not ‘because I was faithful.’ Therefore mercy is indeed given to the faithful, but it is given so that they may become faithful.

> “And so, in another place in the same book, I said very rightly: ‘Since we are called not from works but through the mercy of God, and those who believe are granted that they may do good works, this mercy is not to be begrudged, although I treated there more carefully the calling that occurs according to God’s purpose.’

> “If, then, no Christian would dare say that it is not of the merciful God but of the willing human being, lest he openly contradict the Apostle, it remains that the statement ‘It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy’ should rightly be understood in such a way that everything is attributed to God, who both prepares the human being’s good will to be assisted and assists it once prepared.

> “A good will precedes many gifts of God, but not all of them; and among those gifts which it does not precede, it is itself included. For both statements are read in the holy Scriptures:

> “‘His mercy will precede me’ (Ps. 59:10);

> “and:

> “‘His mercy will follow me’ (Ps. 23:6).

> “He precedes the unwilling so that they may will; he follows the willing so that they may not will in vain.

> “For why are we admonished to pray for our enemies, who surely do not wish to live piously, unless that God may work in them…”

[The supplied source ends mid-sentence.]

[scan page 543]

**S. Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes**  
1071

“...may help [us] to will [according to another reading: ‘that they may will’]?” Likewise, why are we instructed to ask that we may receive, unless it is so that what we will may be brought about by him from whom it has come that we will? We therefore pray for our enemies, that God’s mercy may go before them, just as it went before us; but we pray for ourselves that his mercy may follow us.”

To this assertion of yours (*Against John Scotus*, chapter 4, no. 19, section 8), you apply the example of a man placed in the densest darkness, possessing the faculty of sight but seeing nothing, because he cannot see anything until light comes from outside. This light he can perceive even with his eyes closed; but with them open he can see both the light itself and everything surrounding him in it. You explain by this analogy that, so long as the shadow of original sin and of personal sins covers the human will, it is hindered by the darkness itself; but when the light of divine mercy has shone upon it, it not only destroys the night of all sins and their guilt, but also opens the sight of the weakened will by healing it and makes it fit, through purification by good works, to contemplate the divine light itself.

But I ask you: the will of what sort of person do you say is hindered by the darkness itself so long as the shadow of original sin and of personal sins covers it? Do you mean the baptized, or those who have not yet received the grace of baptism? If you intend those not yet baptized, it is certain that each one is so darkened by the darkness both of original and of personal sin that, apart from the regard of divine grace, he can neither know nor will what is good. But once he has received the heavenly dew of mercy, has been cleansed from the stain of original and personal sins, and has been renewed through the mystery of baptism, there is no doubt that, with the passage of time, the growth of faith, good works accompanying them, he may attain both the will and desire for good, the progress and perfection of good action, and the capacity for divine contemplation.

But if you think that this must be understood of a person already initiated into the mysteries of Christian faith, it is astonishing that you say he is hindered by the darkness of original sin, when the Catholic Church truthfully confesses and proclaims that this sin has already been remitted for him in baptism. How alien this is from the Catholic faith is clearer than daylight.

And when you say that the light of divine mercy opens the sight of the weakened will by healing it and makes it fit to contemplate the divine light by purifying it through good works, how is it free if it is weakened? For someone who is weakened is clearly unable to possess the freedom and capacity to do what he wishes. Or how does one who does not see perceive light, when he is entirely ignorant of light? Consider how many there are who have never seen the light, or who, having lost their sight, can never see it. How, then, can someone be said to perceive light without seeing it, when it is proved that he possesses no capacity for living?

Therefore withdraw from the disease of your inherited nature, and seek more diligently the medicine of grace that heals, so that, having obtained the gift of prevenient grace, you may also be able, with the help of him who assists you, to attain the completion of perfection and glory.

What of the countless little children who, amid the very sacred mysteries of baptism, are scarcely brought from the waters of the life-giving font by the hands of the laboring priests before they expire, and are led on to the heavenly kingdoms? What will of nature is in them? What freedom raises them to such blessedness? None of their own, unquestionably. What, then? Surely, the gratuitous grace of the merciful God, not a recompense owed to a willing substance. For how is it grace if it is not given freely? If your will precedes, it is no longer to be called grace but recompense, since it is not given freely but repaid for the preceding merit of the will. Thus the Apostle’s statement is nullified: “Or who has first given to him, so that he may be repaid?” (Romans 11:35).

Since, once every ambiguity has been removed, what the Apostle says is true, it follows that what you have not feared to assert mendaciously and shamelessly is false. Let the Catholic Church therefore freely and faithfully confess that God’s grace is given freely—that is, without any merits of nature, will, or desire preceding it—and let her never cease to give thanks to the giver of so great a gift, since it is true that no one has first given to him so that he might be repaid. “For from him and through him and in him are all things; to him be glory forever and ever. Amen.”

The prophet cries out against you: “My God, his mercy will go before me” (Psalm 58:11). It will go before him by inspiring a good will, not by finding one already present; for if it found it, it would in no way go before it. Since, therefore, it goes before, it certainly does not find it. Hence also, through the prophet, the Lord promises: “I will take away from you the heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 11:19). What is meant here by “heart” except the will? By “stone” except hardness? By “flesh” except softness? “I will therefore take away from you the hardened will by which you stubbornly resist my commandments and will, and I will give you a pliant will”—that is, one that does not resist, but is teachable and readily obedient to my disciplines—“by which you will follow my commandments and my will with the greatest goodwill.”

But if you say that God’s mercy goes before only in order to begin, and not also in order to will, consider how many and how great Catholic teachers you oppose. They understood and proclaimed with complete orthodoxy and faithfulness that this applies not only to the beginning of a good work but also to the inspiration of a good will.

Fulgentius, in his book *On Faith to Peter the Deacon*:

> “The merciful and just God, just as he established the other angels in the eternity of his love while the devil and his angels fell by their own will, so also did not permit the entire human race to perish forever. Rather, those whom his gratuitous goodness chose, he predestined to be brought back to the light from the darkness in which all human birth is enveloped by the condemnation of original sin. In this he especially demonstrated that he would release these people from the bonds of original sin by the undeserved grace of the liberator, while he left others—and especially infants, in whom no good or evil can belong properly to the matter of their will—under the insoluble bond of eternal damnation. God also clearly shows that the beginning of a good will and thought does not arise in a human being from himself, but is both prepared and bestowed divinely, since neither the devil nor any of his angels, from the time when by the merit of their fall they were thrust into that lower darkness, has been able or will be able to recover a good will. For if this were possible, human nature, after turning away from God and losing the goodness of its will, could much more readily have recovered it from itself; and angelic nature would have possessed this capacity all the more, since, being less burdened by the weight of an earthly body, it would have been endowed with it to a greater degree. But God shows from where good will is given to human beings: the angels had it and lost it, and thereafter cannot possess it again.”

**On Predestination Against John Scotus**

Fulgentius says the same thing later:

> “For he who, by predestining them, prepared them to be worthy of the kingdom, prepared them to be called according to his purpose, so that they might obey; he prepared them to be justified, so that, having received grace, they might believe rightly and live well; he also prepared them to be glorified, so that, made co-heirs with Christ, they might possess the kingdom of heaven without end. To that kingdom, through the sacraments that Christ instituted for the faith of his incarnation, they came at different times—those whom God saved freely, without any preceding merit of good will or good work.”

Blessed Innocent, chief bishop of the Apostolic See, writing against Pelagius to the African bishops (*Epistle 61*):

> “For free will, while using its own goods too heedlessly, fell into the depths of transgression and found no way by which it might thereafter rise; and, deceived in its freedom forever, it would have lain crushed beneath this ruin, had not Christ’s coming afterward raised it up by his grace.”

The 214 bishops of the African province, in a letter to blessed Zosimus, bishop of the Roman See (in Prosper, *Against the Collations*, chapter 10):

> “We have established that the judgment pronounced against Pelagius and Coelestius through the venerable bishop Innocent from the see of blessed Peter shall remain in force until they confess with the clearest acknowledgment that, through Jesus Christ our Lord, we are assisted by grace not only to know but also to do justice in each individual act, so that without it we are able to possess, think, say, or do nothing belonging to true and righteous piety [alternate reading: ‘holy piety’].”

Saint Pope Zosimus, writing against the Pelagians to the whole world:

> “Nevertheless, at God’s prompting—for all good things must be referred to their author, from whom they arise—we have referred everything to the conscience of our brothers and fellow bishops.”

The African bishops, approving his true statement as completely true, replied to him:

> “We understood what you placed in your letter, which you arranged to be sent to all the provinces, when you said: ‘Nevertheless, at God’s prompting—for all good things must be referred to their author, from whom they arise—we have referred everything to the conscience of our brothers and fellow bishops.’ You seemed to cut down, with the sword of truth, as though in passing, those who exalt human free will against God’s assistance. For what have you left so free to the will as to refer everything to the conscience of our humility? Yet you faithfully, wisely, truthfully, and boldly declared that this was done at God’s prompting. Certainly this is because ‘the will is prepared by the Lord’ (Proverbs 8, according to the Septuagint), and because, in order that they may do something good, he himself touches the hearts of his children with paternal inspirations: ‘For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God’ (Romans 8:14). Thus we do not feel that our free will is absent, and yet we do not doubt that his assistance is more powerful in each movement of human will toward good.”

Prosper, a most eloquent and learned man, writing against you under the name of Cassian, the defender of the Pelagian heresy, said among other things (*Against the Collations*, chapter 11):

> “Why do you strive to gather together broken weapons from the fragments of your arguments? Why, by reviving the ashes of an extinguished doctrine, do you try to raise the stench of dying smoke into a renewed flame? There is no danger to free will from the grace of God, nor is the will taken away when the willing of good is generated within it. For if, merely because it is formed, governed, ordered, and instructed, it is not to be regarded as ours, then the children of God who are led by the Spirit of God (Romans 8:14) are robbed of their freedom; their rational mind loses its strength, and those to whom the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, counsel and fortitude, knowledge and piety, and fear of the Lord is given (1 Corinthians 12) are deprived of every praise for voluntary devotion. Those who think that they do not need these transformations have passed from the habit of an old disease into madness; they reject [alternate reading: ‘rejecting’] the remedy, cry out, rage, and resist. But if they are children of the promise, they will rest and be healed.”

The same author, in the same work:

> “According to this definition, then, you previously said falsely that not only the beginning of actions but also the beginning of good thoughts is from God, who both begins what is good and carries it out and completes it in us. But this cannot in any respect be false: ‘because’ [alternate reading: ‘to whom’] no contrary conclusion ought to be drawn from what you rightly professed: that we begin from grace, and then subsequently claim to possess it through the goodness of nature and through free will.
>
> “The blessed Apostle indeed says: ‘For to will is present with me, but to perform the good I do not find’ (Romans 7:18). But he also says: ‘Not that we are competent to think anything from ourselves, as though from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God’ (2 Corinthians 3:5). And again he says: ‘For it is God who works in us both to will and to work according to his good pleasure’ (Philippians 2:13).
>
> “The Apostle is therefore not contradicting himself. But when the good will has been given to us, we do not immediately find the ability to do what is good, unless we ask, seek, and knock, so that the one who gave the desire may also grant its fulfillment. For the voice of the one who says, ‘To will is present with me, but to perform the good I do not find,’ belongs even to one who has been placed under grace. He delights in the law of God according to the inner person, but he sees another law in his members resisting the law of his mind and taking him captive in the law of sin (Romans 7:23). Although he has received the knowledge of willing rightly, he nevertheless does not find within himself the power to do what he desires, until, for the good will that he has received, he deserves to find the capacity for virtue that he seeks [alternate reading: ‘until he deserves to find one who may do it’].”

**S. Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes**  
1075–1076

Saint Fulgentius, a man beyond all hesitation most learned and most faithful, in his book *On Faith to Peter the Deacon* (column 360):

> “Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in any way, that no human being can perform repentance unless God has enlightened him and converted him by his gratuitous mercy. For the Apostle says: ‘Lest perhaps God may give them repentance for the acknowledgment of the truth, and they may recover from the snares of the devil’ (2 Timothy 2:25).
>
> “Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in any way, that a person whom neither ignorance of letters nor any weakness or adversity prevents from reading the words of the holy Law and Gospel, or from hearing them from the mouth of some preacher, nevertheless cannot obey the divine commandments unless God’s grace has gone before him. Thus, what he hears with the body he may also receive with the mind of the heart; and, having received from God a good will and power, he may both will and be able to perform God’s commandments. ‘Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase’ (1 Corinthians 3:7); and he also works in us ‘both to will and to work [according to another reading: to complete] according to his good pleasure’ (Philippians 2:13).”

The venerable presbyter Bede, in a homily on the Gospel for the Lord’s advent, when explaining, “We have all received from his fullness, and grace upon grace” (John 1:16), added:

> “Since, then, we have all received whatever good we possess from the fullness of our Creator—not some of us, but all—one must take the greatest care that no one, through negligence, exalt himself because of a good action or thought. Otherwise, remaining ungrateful to the giver, he will lose the good he received and rightly be struck by the apostolic rebuke: ‘What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?’ (1 Corinthians 4:7).
>
> “Therefore the Apostle himself, because we would be unable either to think or to perform anything worthy unless we received it from Christ’s fullness, openly testifies elsewhere, saying: ‘Not that we are sufficient to think anything from ourselves, as though from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God’ (2 Corinthians 3:5). And elsewhere: ‘His grace in me was not empty, but I labored more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God with me’ (1 Corinthians 15:10).
>
> “He diligently impresses this same truth upon his hearers as something to be pondered humbly. Hence the saying: ‘Work out your salvation with fear and trembling; for it is God who works in you both to will and to complete according to his good pleasure’ (Philippians 2:12–13).
>
> “When the Evangelist had said that we had all received from Christ’s fullness, he immediately added, ‘grace upon grace.’ He thus testifies that we have received a twofold grace: one in the present and another in the future. >
> “Faith that works through love is the grace of God, because we receive from him—without any preceding merits of our own—the ability to believe, to love, and to do the good that we know. He crowns us with mercy and compassion when, because of the good works that he mercifully granted us the ability to perform, he repays us with the rewards of heavenly blessedness.
>
> “This is what is meant by receiving ‘grace upon grace’: for, in return for the grace of a good life which he has given, and which he himself preserves and helps so that it cannot fail, he will give the grace of blessed recompense, in which we shall sing his mercies forever.
>
