This is not because eternal life is not justly given by the just Judge for good merits, but because the merits for which it is given were themselves first freely bestowed by the merciful Savior.”

Gregory, in the *Moralia*, book 22, chapter 5:

> “Holy men know that, after the fall of our first parents, they were formed from a corruptible stock, and that they were changed toward better desires or works not by their own virtue but by heavenly grace going before them. Whatever evil they recognize in themselves, they attribute to the merit of mortal descent; whatever good they see in themselves, they recognize as the gift of immortal grace. For the gift they have received makes them debtors to him who, going before them, gave them the good will that they had not wanted, and, following them, granted them the ability to do the good that they will.”

Through the agreement of so many and such great teachers, the truth confirmed by the Holy Spirit in them, and the most truthful concord of the whole holy Catholic Church, is no less established by the humble, faithful, and continual petition with which she never ceases to beseech the Lord in her prayers, saying:

> “O God, who have made all those reborn in Christ a royal and priestly race, grant us both the will and the ability to do what you command, so that among the people called to eternity there may be one faith of hearts and one devotion in action.”

And again:

> “Graciously grant us, Lord, we ask, always the spirit of thinking what is right and of doing it, so that, since we cannot exist without you, we may be able to live according to you.”

Again:

> “O God, who on this day, through your Only-Begotten Son, opened for us the entrance to eternity after conquering death, carry forward by your help the desires that you inspire by going before us.”

Hence Saint Innocent, writing to the African bishops in condemnation of the Pelagian error, says that the prayers of the Roman Church resound with the grace of God.

Rise up now, monstrous Lernaean beast, and with your fourfold stream overturn the faith and humility of the whole world, so that, with you forbidding it, no one may dare to believe what he asks, or humbly ask what he truly believes. Inflate the bladder of your own free will, so that you may empty the grace of Christ, whom you attack and persecute and whose grace you strive to overthrow—yes, the grace of him who, while Saul was still puffed up, rebuked him with a heavenly thunderbolt, saying: “I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you persecute. It is hard for you to kick against the goad” (Acts 9:5).

At the beginning of this venomous outpouring of your poison (chapter 4, no. 29, section 1), you had fabricated three different heresies. You had called the first Pelagian, the second Gottschalkian, and inserted a third without author or name, which throughout your work you have persisted in attacking most obstinately. We assert and approve that this is not a heresy at all, but the Catholic faith: namely, that we truthfully and steadfastly confess that the will for good is divinely given to us freely—that is, to those who do not deserve it and in no way possess it—and is likewise assisted, so that what we rightly will through its inspiration we may rightly perform and rightly complete through its help. We do not possess this will through the goodness of our corrupted nature, but receive it as the gift of undeserved grace.

For God’s grace goes before us so that we may will well, and follows us so that our willing may not be in vain. We sing to the Lord with the Psalmist: “My God, his mercy will go before me” (Psalm 58:11), and, “Your mercy shall follow me all the days of my life” (Psalm 22:6).

Unless perhaps you alone, abolishing the authority of the Apostolic See and wickedly scattering the concord of the whole world, as the most powerful censor will decree that all the books of the sacraments be erased or destroyed, and, speaking with the Antichrist against the God of gods, attempt to sit in the temple of God as though you were God (2 Thessalonians 2:4). For what do you leave to God when you falsely claim that willing comes from yourself?

But you, a marvelous conqueror of heretics, refute the Pelagians in such a way that you yourself are proved to be a Pelagian. You detest one part of the Pelagians while in every way demonstrating that you confirm the other. For by saying that we can in no way begin, perform, or complete anything good without God’s grace, you refute and crush the Pelagians with us. But by saying that willing is part of our essence, you unquestionably favor the Pelagians, who were so inflated by the goodness of nature that they attributed both willing and being able to themselves and to their own power, and did not affirm that they obtained these things from the free gift of grace. No one who reads faithfully and intelligently what has been set out above can fail to recognize that you obstinately agree with them.

But because we think that enough has been said about these matters, let us proceed, with the Lord’s help, to examine other portents of no lesser shamelessness.

## Chapter V

### That no one is compelled by God’s foreknowledge or predestination to do either good or evil

After this, in the fifth book of your blasphemies, you repeat what you have already repeated and do not cease to repeat it again with still greater tedium, following the example, so to speak, of Elihu, who does not himself deserve to be rebuked by the Lord, but of whom it is said to blessed Job: “Who is this that wraps up arguments in ignorant words?” (Job 38:2).

Although you ought necessarily to have taken care to avoid this, you preferred to dwell arrogantly on verbosity rather than cling more firmly to the purest truth. For you argue that, just as God’s foreknowledge does not make the sins that he foreknew happen, so God’s predestination does not make the sins that he never predestined happen.

**John Scotus**  
(chapter 5, no. 1, section 1):

> “If foreknowledge does not make everything that it foreknew happen, how can predestination make everything that it did not predestine happen? God is believed, through his foreknowledge, not to have predestined the future evil deeds of human beings; how, then, is he thought to make them happen?”

**Correction**

And the rest, which also confirms the judgment of blessed Augustine: “Who, after you, has dared to presume either to have read or to have understood the books of the memorable Augustine?” You then conclude and say:

**John Scotus**  
(chapter 5, no. 2, section 3):

> “Therefore it must be most firmly confessed that the foreknowledge of God, by which he foreknew the sins that he permits in his creature, is not their cause; but that his predestination, by which he did not predestine them, is their cause.”

We say this too. You then add:

**John Scotus**  
(no. 3):

> “Whatever is concluded concerning sin, whether generally or specifically, must necessarily also be understood concerning its punishment.”

**Correction**

If you say this in the sense that God’s foreknowledge and predestination, just as they are not the cause of sin, are likewise not the cause of sin’s punishment, you do not err. But if you mean that God’s foreknowledge and predestination did not arrange and inflict punishment deservedly for sins, you err greatly. You immediately add:

**John Scotus**  
(no. 4):

> “The punishment of sin is death. Therefore whatever is said concerning sin must necessarily be said concerning death.”

**Correction**

If by this you say that God’s foreknowledge and predestination are not the cause of death, we agree with you. But if you deny that he is the predestiner, disposer, inflicter, and repayer of these things, you err vehemently.

For Scripture says in the book of Ecclesiasticus:

> “Do not say: ‘What is this? Why is that?’ For everything will be sought in its own time. His blessing will overflow like a river. As a flood overtakes dry land, so his wrath will inherit the nations that have not sought him. As he turned waters into dryness and the earth became dry, and his ways were made straight, so offenses will be for sinners in his wrath.
>
> “Good things were created good from the beginning, and likewise good and evil things for the wicked. The beginning of the necessary things of human life is water, fire, iron, milk, bread made from fine flour, honey, the cluster of grapes, oil, and clothing. All these things are good for the holy [alternate reading: ‘are thus good for the holy’]; so they will be turned to evil for the impious and sinners.
>
> “There are spirits created for vengeance, and in their fury they have strengthened their torments. At the time of consummation they will pour out the power and wrath of him who made them, and will confound [alternate reading: ‘will appease’]. Fire, hail, famine, and death—all these were created for vengeance. The teeth of wild beasts, scorpions, snakes, and the sword avenge the impious to their destruction. They will rejoice in his commandments; on earth they will be prepared in necessity, and in their appointed times they will not transgress the word” (Ecclesiasticus 39:26–37).

And again:

> “For these things also—death, bloodshed, strife, the sword, oppressions, famine, affliction, and scourges—were created against the wicked; all these things were made for them, and because of them the flood came” (Ecclesiasticus 40:9).

You then explain what death you meant.

**John Scotus**  
(chapter 5, no. 5, section 3):

> “I do not speak of every kind of death, but only of that which follows sin. For we say, ‘We die to sin,’ that is, we die because of the merit of sin. Again, we say, ‘We die to sin’ when, having been freed from sin, we live for righteousness. Therefore, if the cause of every sin has been established neither in God’s foreknowledge nor in his predestination, it is most certain that there is likewise no cause of every death which follows sin in God’s foreknowledge, nor in the same way in his predestination.”

**Correction**

By these words you try to assert that bodily death, which certainly follows sin, is not from God as its author—that is, as its judge. You direct the intention of your mind toward this end, as the following statements will demonstrate: to establish that predestination differs in no respect from foreknowledge.

And what you say is:

**John Scotus**  
(chapter 5, no. 6, section 3):

> “Therefore, if the cause of every sin has been established neither in God’s foreknowledge nor in his predestination, it is most certain that there is likewise no cause of every death which follows sin in God’s foreknowledge, nor in the same way in his predestination.”

**Correction**

I cannot sufficiently wonder why you have suddenly wished to change the order of the argument. Earlier you said that God’s foreknowledge and predestination are not the cause of sin, or of its punishment, or of death; afterward you said that in God’s foreknowledge and predestination there is no cause of the death that follows sin.

But one thing appears to be meant by saying that God’s foreknowledge and predestination are not the cause of sin, punishment, or death, and another by saying that in God’s foreknowledge and predestination there is no cause of sin, punishment, or death.

God’s foreknowledge and predestination are not the cause of sin, punishment, or death because they do not compel or command anyone to sin, so that, having sinned, he may suffer punishment and undergo death. They are not the author of sin but its judge, avenger, and punisher.

It is said that there is no cause of sin in God’s foreknowledge because in it he foresaw that the will of a rational soul would be evil in the future: turned away from the true and highest good, it would fall willingly toward inferior goods—that is, it would sin. No one doubts that this turning away of the will is the cause of sin. Through it alone a person sins culpably and damnably, yet no one is driven to sin by that foreknowledge.

Likewise, predestination is in no respect said to be the cause of sin, because God predestined, commanded, or compelled no one to sin. But in his predestination, just as in his foreknowledge, the recompense of punishment and death is established, because he arranged and judged that those whom he had certainly foreseen would sin and persevere in sins should justly be punished with deserved penalties.

Because you had undertaken to deny this, yet could not deny it altogether, you add:

**John Scotus**  
(chapter 5, no. 7, section 3):

> “Although holy authors are accustomed, in a certain abusive manner of speaking, to say that people are predestined to death, destruction, or punishment, we shall speak about this later, as the Lord may reveal.”

**Correction**

Since you postpone the demonstration of your fiction, let us for the moment also postpone our reply of truth. With these matters deferred, you return to what you had asserted beyond all justice: that the will is your nature, not a gift. For you say:

**John Scotus**  
(chapter 5, no. 8, section 4):

> “For the time being we must consider whether, just as God compels no one to sin through either his foreknowledge or his predestination, so he compels no one to live piously. Here it must be understood that true freedom belongs to no will if some cause has compelled it. Therefore, if some cause precedes the human will and forcibly draws it unwillingly toward good or evil, or toward thinking or doing something, it follows not only that it is not truly free, but that it does not exist at all. For where there is a cause that compels, there is no nature that wills. But human nature is not only will; it is also free. Nor is its freedom false, but true.”

**Correction**

Although these matters have been sufficiently dealt with above both by authority and by the agreement of the Fathers, nevertheless it is not out of place ...

[The supplied source ends here incomplete.]

## On Predestination

### Against John Scotus

### St Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

It seems worthwhile, then, to indulge in a little folly with you and repeat the same points unnecessarily. When you say, therefore, “There is no true freedom of the will if some cause has compelled it,” you are trying to establish that the human will is not preceded by any gift of divine inspiration, because you do not wish it to be compelled unwillingly toward some good. After you have spent time on vain arguments concerning this matter, it would have been worthwhile for you to consult the truth and declare whatever authority should recommend.

What, I ask you, is the meaning of the Prophet’s prayer: “Convert us, Lord, and we shall be converted to you” (Lamentations 5:21)? For how does he convert us unless, by grace going before us, he mercifully instills the will to be converted? He himself converts first, because he inspires the will to turn to him; and we are converted to him because, with him helping, we humbly follow the grace of him who calls.

Should we say that those people had no hearts to whom the Second Book of Maccabees, while they were praying, says through their brothers: “May he give you all a heart, so that you may worship him and do his will” (2 Maccabees 1:3)? If there is no doubt that they possessed a heart, why was it necessary to ask that what they had be given to them, unless by “heart” they wished a good will to be understood—namely, the will to worship God and do his will? Therefore, by saying, “May he give you all a heart, so that you may worship him and do his will,” the meaning must be nothing other than: “May he give you the will to worship him and do his will.”

But if no one is compelled to love and fear God, what does the Lord say through the Prophet: “I will cause you to walk in my commandments and to keep my judgments” (Ezekiel 11:20)? What is the meaning of all those threats by which heavenly mercy toward sinners is so often read in the prophetic writings, threats by which it would convert them from error? Read the Prophets and their most truthful interpreter, Jerome, and there you will plainly find that God has used—and has not ceased to use—many kinds of terrors by which he converts sinners to repentance, that is, to a good will. They would in no way be converted unless they had first turned away.

When they are converted by God, however, they do not cease humbly to prostrate themselves and ask for what they read that the man requested who, defiled by adultery and stained by murder, was finally reproved by the Prophet at the Lord’s command. After pronouncing upon himself a sentence of death of this kind, when he heard that he himself was subject to that sentence, he said—fearing the death that was immediately to follow—“I have sinned” (2 Samuel 12:1 ff.). Afterwards, amid groans and tears, he earnestly prayed, saying: “Create in me a clean heart, O God,” and so forth (Psalm 50:12). He certainly had a heart, but it was unclean; and he humbly asked the Lord to create in him what he knew with absolute certainty could neither exist nor be made by himself.

Likewise another prophet, confessing to the Lord, said: “I know, Lord, that a man’s way is not his own, nor is it in a man to walk and direct and correct his steps. Correct me, Lord, but with judgment and not in your anger, lest perhaps you reduce me to nothing” (Jeremiah 10:23–24). By asking to be corrected, he clearly shows that his correction consists not in his own will but in the most salutary correction of the merciful God.

Elsewhere, too, instructing a son with fatherly affection, he says: “My son, do not reject the discipline of the Lord, nor grow weary when he reproves you; for the Lord disciplines the one whom he loves, and scourges every son whom he receives” (Proverbs 3:11–12; Hebrews 12:5–6). Again he admonishes the father: “Strike your son’s sides while he is an infant” (Sirach 30:12). “Do not withdraw discipline from a child; for if you strike him with the rod, he will not die. You strike him with the rod, and you deliver his soul from hell” (Proverbs 23:13–14).

The Apostle likewise says: “All discipline at the present time seems not to be joy but sorrow; afterwards, however, it yields the most peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it” (Hebrews 12:11). Again: “Persevere in discipline. God offers himself to you as to sons; for what son is there whom his father does not correct? But if you are without discipline, you are illegitimate and not sons” (ibid., 7–8). Again: “Correct the disorderly” (1 Thessalonians 5:14). And once more: “Reprove sinners before everyone, so that the others may also have fear” (1 Timothy 5:20). Likewise: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke, with all authority” (2 Timothy 4:2).

God also, as it is said in the Gospel (John 2:15), having made something like a whip from cords, drove everyone out of the temple. He also says in the Apocalypse: “Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline” (Revelation 3:19).

Why did the Prophet also rejoice and say: “You chastised me, Lord, and I was instructed like an untamed young bull. Convert me, and I shall be converted, for you are the Lord my God. After you converted me, I did penance; and after you showed me, I struck my thigh. I was ashamed and confounded, because I bore the reproach of my youth” (Jeremiah 31:18–19)? Another boasts, saying: “The Lord chastising has chastised me, but he has not handed me over to death” (Psalm 117:18). There are many other passages, but it would be lengthy and unnecessary to pursue them, since they lie openly before readers.

Since, however, in this assertion of your perversity (chapter 5, number 10, section 5) you frequently mention your “compelling cause,” we must ask for the grace of eternal Wisdom, so that it may deign to disclose to us how that word is used in the sacred writings, and thereby suppress your dead boastfulness.

The holy evangelist Luke, when describing the parable of a man who made a great supper and invited many people, reports that the master said to his servant: “Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel them to enter, so that my house may be filled” (Luke 14:23). Therefore blessed Gregory, in his homily on this reading (Homily 36 on the Gospels), says:

> “It should be noted that in this third invitation it is not said, ‘Invite,’ but ‘Compel them to enter.’ Some are invited and disdain to come; others are invited and come; of others it is not said at all that they are invited, but that they are compelled to enter.
>
> “Those are invited and disdain to come who receive the gift of understanding but do not follow that understanding in their actions. Those are invited and come who perfect the grace of understanding they have received by putting it into practice. Some, however, are invited in such a way that they are also compelled.
>
> “There are some who understand that they ought to do good, but cease to do it; they see what they ought to do, but do not follow it out of desire. As we said above, it generally happens to such people that the adversity of this world strikes them amid their fleshly desires. They try to grasp temporal glory but cannot; and while they propose to sail across the deep sea, as it were, toward greater concerns of this age, they are continually driven back by contrary winds to the shore of their own downfall.
>
> “When they see themselves broken in their desires by the world’s opposition, they are reminded of what they owe their Creator, so that, ashamed, they return to him whom they had proudly abandoned for love of the world. Often, indeed, some who wish to advance toward temporal glory waste away through prolonged illness, collapse under injuries, or are afflicted by severe losses. In the world’s distress they see that they ought to have placed no confidence in its pleasures; and, reproaching themselves for their desires, they turn their hearts to God.
>
> “Concerning such people the Lord says through the Prophet: ‘Behold, I will hedge in your way with thorns; I will wall it in, and she shall not find her paths. She will pursue her lovers and will not overtake them; she will seek them and will not find them. Then she will say: I shall go and return to my first husband, because it was better for me then than now’” (Hosea 2:6–7).
>
> “The husband of every faithful soul is God, because the soul is joined to him through faith. But the soul that had been joined to God follows its lovers when the mind, although it has already believed through faith, nevertheless submits itself in its actions to unclean spirits, seeks the glory of the world, feeds on fleshly pleasure, and is nourished by refined delights.
>
> “But almighty God often looks mercifully upon such a soul and mingles bitterness with its pleasures. Hence he says: ‘Behold, I will hedge in your ways with thorns.’ Our ways are hedged with thorns when, in what we wickedly desire, we encounter the prickings of sorrow. ‘I will wall it in, and she shall not find her paths’: our ways are walled in when harsh obstacles in this world resist our desires. We cannot find our paths because we are prevented from obtaining what we wickedly seek.
>
> “‘She will pursue her lovers and will not overtake them; she will seek them and will not find them’: the soul cannot attain the fulfillment of its desires from the evil spirits to whom it has subjected itself through those desires.
>
> “But to show what benefit arises from this salutary adversity, he adds: ‘And she will say: I shall go and return to my first husband, because it was better for me then than now.’ After she finds her ways hedged with thorns, after she is unable to overtake her lovers, she returns to the love of her first husband. For often, after we cannot obtain in this world what we want, after we are wearied by the impossibility of earthly desires, then we bring God back to mind; then the one who had been displeasing begins to please, and he whose commandments had been bitter to us suddenly becomes sweet in our memory.
>
> “Who, then, are those who, broken by the adversities of this world, return to the love of God and are corrected by the desires of the present life, if not those who are compelled to enter?”

### Correction

Behold, the Truth says, “Compel them to enter,” while you say that no compelling cause precedes the human will toward good. The preacher of truth—whom you also acknowledge to be entirely truthful—now explains by what means human souls are compelled, so to speak, to will good. You, on the contrary, whisper that the will is not only not truly free but does not exist at all.

You say: “Where there is a cause that compels, there is no nature that wills.” Let us see what the holy Jerome also thinks in his exposition of the prophecy of Hosea (on chapter 2, verse 6). When he had presented the history according to both editions, he added in his explanation:

> “The harlot had said: ‘I shall go after my lovers, who provided me with abundance of all things.’ The Lord replied: ‘I will hedge in your way with thorns, or stakes, so that you cannot go where you desire; and I will place a wall, or a rampart, between you and your paths, which your feet had frequently worn down [variant: which her foot had worn down]. You will not find them, so that you may not overtake those whom you pursued with such eagerness; and, compelled by genuine necessity, you may return to your husband and say what is said in the Gospel: “How many hired servants in my father’s house abound in bread, while I am perishing here from hunger! I shall arise and go to my father and say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you, and now I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants”’” (Luke 15:17–19).
>
> “From this we understand that, by God’s providence, evils often befall us so that we do not have what we desire, and that through the various calamities and miseries of this age we may be compelled to return to the service of God.
>
> “Historically, let us understand the lovers of Jerusalem and the Jewish nation as the Assyrians, Chaldeans, Egyptians, and other nations of that period, with whose idols she fornicated, and from whom, in time of war and when evils pressed upon her, she vainly hoped for help.
>
> “According to the spiritual interpretation, these lovers are heretics, whom Israel often abandons and from whom it returns to the bosom of Mother Church under the weight of greater troubles. Israel is instructed through every scourge and torment.”

Let us consider whether the prodigal son returned under compulsion or voluntarily. He had squandered his share of his property in riotous living and had gone away to a distant country. There he attached himself to one of the citizens of that region. While serving that man’s pigs, he began to be in want and desired to fill himself with the pods that the pigs ate, but no one gave him any. At last, coming to himself, he said: “How many hired servants of my father abound in bread, while I am perishing here from hunger!”

He had gone far away from his father’s house when he sinned; and if he had not been hungry, he would never have returned to himself. After he became needy in earthly things, he then began to consider what he had lost in spiritual things.

The Book of Chronicles also reports that Manasseh had raised himself against God through many impieties. God humbled him, handed him over to the Babylonians, and bound him in chains in prison. There he remembered the Lord God and did penance while still imprisoned; thus he deserved both release from his chains and restoration to his former kingdom (2 Chronicles 33:11–13).

What should I say about the wicked king Antiochus? To pass over the other things reported about him, he raged so fiercely against God’s people, worship, and temple, forbidding circumcision, abolishing his laws, and setting up in the temple of Jerusalem a statue of himself and of Olympian Jupiter. Finally, struck from heaven by an incurable disease, so that his army could not endure his stench, he confessed in an unproductive repentance that the God whom he had previously opposed was the true God. Compelled, clearly, by overwhelming pain, he declared that he would become a Jew, serve God, and do many other things, though his promises were fruitless (2 Maccabees 9:7–17).

Even if examples were lacking, the daily outcome of events could teach us that many people are compelled to evil. We see some driven by hunger, others by disease, and many by threats and terrors, so that they burst into such monstrous crimes that one might refuse to believe those who report them, were not the immediate evidence of manifest deeds to convey certainty.

How many, alas, placed in martyrdom, who from early youth had commended the integrity of their faith by the uprightness of their conduct, have finally been compelled by tortures and the most elaborate forms of punishment to deny what they had hitherto steadfastly been seen to proclaim! Hence it is also read in the Book of Maccabees that, by order of King Antiochus, the Jews were compelled to eat swine’s flesh and to do many other things contrary to the laws divinely promulgated (2 Maccabees 6:18; 7:1).

The Apostle also repeatedly speaks of himself and of those groaning under the same condition when he says: “I do not do the good that I want, but I do the evil that I do not want” (Romans 7:15). Again: “I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin that is in my members. Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (ibid., 23–25). He develops this and other matters pertaining to the same meaning at greater length.

The prophetic and apostolic Scriptures plainly indicate how much the Antichrist will inflict upon the faithful and others, partly by persuasion, partly by gifts, and sometimes by signs and sometimes by terrors, in order to be believed as God. Above all, the Lord himself indicates this when he foretells his coming’s deceptions and intolerable effects: “For then there will be such tribulation as has not been from the beginning of the world, nor shall be, so that, if it were possible, even the elect would be led into error” (Matthew 24:23).

Behold, the judge of all testifies that even the elect will be led into error by terrible violence, if that were possible; and you dare object that no one can be compelled either toward good or toward evil when no compelling cause precedes? But because it is impossible for the elect to be completely led into that error, it is understood that those who are not elect will be led into it completely.

You hear that there will be a tribulation such as has not been from the beginning of the world, by which they will be led into error, and you dare chatter that no compelling cause precedes.

Although these things are so, the freedom of the will is in no way removed. Rather, by such methods, wills, and counsels of eternal Wisdom, a person is either compelled so that from being servile he becomes free, and thereafter, freed from servitude, freely serves his liberator; or, having been abandoned according to his merits, he clings more tenaciously and more pleasurably to servile freedom, so that both of the things terrifyingly spoken in the Apocalypse may be fulfilled: “Let the holy be sanctified still, and let the just be justified still, and let the one who is in filth remain filthy still” (Revelation 22:11). Thus, in both cases, each acts gladly according to his own will, though moved by different impulses; and the just Judge rightly repays each according to what he deserves.

Therefore no one who considers the matter even slightly can remain uncertain that what you said is false: “Where there is a cause that compels, there is no nature that wills.” What, then? Is the human being not a nature who, according to the preceding authority, is compelled now toward good and now toward evil, as the one who judges all things wills—one person in this way, another in that?

It is certain, however, that the apostate angels never wished, nor wish, our Lord Jesus Christ to be proclaimed by anyone; yet the Gospel history relates that they confessed the Son of God. For they say: “What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come here before the time to torment us?” (Matthew 8:29). By these words they plainly indicate that their testimony was in no way one of love and praise but of fear; not voluntary but unwilling; not the spontaneous discharge of an honorable duty, but a confession unwillingly extorted amid torments and blows.

Since this cannot be denied, who would say that they lost their nature when they had long before irrecoverably lost their good will? That good will will never be liberated or healed by our Lord Jesus Christ. Who, then, cannot see that your definition is false, when you say: “Where there is a cause that compels, there is no nature that wills”?

That demons are compelled to confess God is attested by their own words, in which they say: “You have come before the time to torment us.” It is clear that those who were tormented confessed unwillingly. Since you cannot deny the nature of the angels who apostatized, you will never be able to find in them a good will after the ruin of their first turning away. Their heart has been hardened by such obstinacy that their stubbornness will never be softened toward good.

Concerning their head, the Lord also says to blessed Job: “His heart will be hardened like an anvil of a smith”; and again: “He was made so that he would fear no one” (Job 41:15, 24). For the one who fears no one—not even God himself—has plainly lost a good will, not his nature.

Who, however, does not know that his nature is good? “God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Genesis 1:31). Hence in the holy Scriptures he is often called “the Spirit of the Lord,” but with an addition such as “evil,” “wicked,” or something else, lest anyone suppose that the goodness of his will remained—since, once he had lost it, he is believed never to recover it and never again to possess it.

Unless perhaps, with Origen, you promise him repentance and, after many cycles of ages, pledge to him the restoration of the lost state, its full splendor and dignity, and the honor he received at his creation. But the Lord testifies that at the judgment he will say to the ungodly: “Go into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41). He said “eternal,” not finite or temporal; elsewhere he calls it “unquenchable,” so that it is understood that its end will never come.

If you wish to deny this, we are prepared, with the Lord’s assistance, to answer according to our ability. But if you reply that you said this not of angelic nature but of human nature, your meaning will be restrained by what you have repeatedly asserted above: that rational creatures—namely, angels and human beings—possess this freedom of the will.

There is, therefore, to return to the human being, a nature that is compelled to will the good that it did not want, indeed that it fled from and opposed. It is compelled to will freely, once it has received from heaven the will for the good; thereafter it remains free by divine grace and is upheld by it, lest it will in vain.

You then continue and say:

### John Scotus

**(Chapter 5, number 13, section 4.)** “The human will is not merely will, but also free; and its freedom is not false but true,” although after sin freedom itself has been so corrupted that its punishment prevents it either from wishing to live rightly or, if it wishes, from being able to do so. From this misery it is liberated, as the Apostle says, by the grace of God through Jesus Christ (Romans 7:25), while natural freedom nevertheless remains—the appetite for blessedness, which has been naturally implanted in it.”

### Correction

How, then, do you affirm that the will is free when you assert that after sin it has been so corrupted that its punishment prevents it either from wishing to live rightly or, if it wishes, from being able to do so? How is the will called free when it does not wish to live rightly? How is it proclaimed free when, if it wishes to live rightly, it cannot?

Who is called free if he does not exercise his own freedom according to his will? What blind person can see light if he wishes? What lame or weak person can act or walk if he wishes? There may be a will in such a person; but is there freedom? It is not free for the blind person to see, for the lame person to walk, for the mute to speak, for the deaf to hear, or for the mentally incapacitated to understand.

These examples have nevertheless been introduced to establish that freedom is lacking from the will [variant: freedom], not to confirm the introduction or removal of a good or evil will. It is exceedingly strange to call the will free when it either does not wish what ought to be willed or, if it does wish it, is entirely unable to do so. Even if you establish this by petty legal disputations, you will never be able to prove it by authority.

For you labor with all your strength to abolish entirely the grace of the Liberator, without which—as sound, orthodox, and catholic doctrine holds—no one has been able, or will be able, even to conceive the beginning of a good will.

When you say, “From this misery he is liberated, as the Apostle says, by the grace of God through Jesus Christ, while natural freedom nevertheless remains,” it is astonishing that you do not also assert freedom to be nature, just as you assert the will to be nature, when truth proclaims and defends that nature as divinely granted and bestowed.

We shall see later, if the Lord wills.

But when you think that no compelling cause—whether good or evil—may precede the will of a human being or of another rational nature, lest the merit of its freedom be taken away from it, whether good if it has lived well with the cooperation of divine grace, or evil if it has lived badly through its own irrational and perverse motion, it is sufficiently clear that you are confirming the most perverse dogma of the Pelagians. After refuting them on one side, you defend them on the other.

When, however, the gift of orthodox grace is proclaimed in good actions as something that compels, the merit of freedom is not taken away; rather, grace is granted and assisted so that freedom may exist. When a compelling necessity is spoken of in evil actions, even there the merit of freedom is not removed; instead, as evils increase and what was previously good is converted into evil, the person is judged and condemned more severely.

### John Scotus

**(Chapter 5, number 15, section 5.)** “Therefore, in those matters in which no cause constrains a human being to live either well or badly—”

### Correction

And indeed, the Apostle commands that the man who had unlawfully joined himself to his father’s wife be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord (1 Corinthians 5:5). What, then, is the meaning of the canonical authority’s command, and of the Church’s customary practice, by which vices are restrained through beatings, prisons, fetters, excommunications, and many other kinds of discipline that serve as remedies?

Hence blessed Augustine, in the *Enchiridion*, when discussing the forgiveness of sins (chapter 72), said among other things:

> “The one who corrects by a beating someone over whom he has authority, or restrains him by some discipline, and yet forgives from the heart the sin of the person who has wearied or offended him, or prays that it may be forgiven him, performs almsgiving not only in forgiving or praying but also in correcting and inflicting some corrective punishment. For he gives alms because he shows mercy.
>
> “Many good things are done for the unjust when their welfare, rather than their will, is consulted, since they are found to be enemies to themselves; while those whom they regard as enemies are in fact more truly their friends. In their error they return evil for good, although a Christian ought not to return evil, not even for evil.”

Hence blessed Gregory, in his exposition of blessed Job (book 6, chapter 13), says:

> “He will save the needy from the sword of their mouth and the poor from the hand of the violent” (Job 5:15).
>
> “The poor is everyone who is not proud in himself. Hence the Truth says through the Gospel: ‘Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven’” (Matthew 5:3).
>
> “A person is drawn into guilt in two ways: either he is led by pleasure or overcome by terror. The sword of the mouth is the wickedness of persuasion; the hand of the violent is the adversity of power.
>
> “But because the truly humble person, who is here called poor, desires none of this world’s prosperity, he also boldly despises adversity. Thus it is rightly said: ‘He will save the needy from their sword and the poor from the hand of the violent.’ It is as though he openly said: God so strengthens the minds of the humble that neither the flatteries of persuasion draw them into committing wickedness nor the pains of punishment break them.”

You add that God is not the necessary but the voluntary cause of all good things, wishing by that argument to show that the perverse motion of a rational substance is not a necessary but a voluntary cause. You ought to have paid attention to the sentence of blessed Augustine, which you yourself previously wished to insert from the book he wisely and faithfully composed on the gift of perseverance. There he says (chapter 7):

> “If there were no other proofs, this prayer of the Lord alone would suffice for the cause of grace that we defend, because it has left us nothing in which we may glory as in our own possession. For, when it shows that we must ask God that we may not depart from him, it shows that this can be given only by God; for the one who is not led into temptation does not depart from God.
>
> “This is not at all within the power of free will as it now exists; it was so in the human being before the fall. How powerful that freedom of the will was in the excellence of that first condition was shown in the angels: when the devil and his followers fell, they stood in the truth and deserved to attain the perpetual security from falling in which we are now certain that they remain.
>
> “After the fall of the human being, however, God willed that it belong only to his grace that a person should approach him; and he likewise willed that it belong only to his grace that a person should not depart from him. He placed this grace in him in whom we have obtained our lot, predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things” (Ephesians 1:11).

You hear that he left us nothing; you hear that this is not at all within the power of free will as it now exists, though it was so in the human being before the fall. You hear that after the fall of humanity God willed that a person approach him only by his grace, and yet you dare, with shameless presumption, to claim free will for yourself.

It certainly existed in the human being before the fall, but did it exist without grace? Certainly not. After the fall of humanity, it belongs only to the grace of God that a person approach him—that is, only through the grace of God does he receive the will to wish to approach God through Jesus Christ our Lord. As he himself said: “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44).

You hear of one who draws, and where is freedom? You hear of one who is drawn, and where is free will? Whoever is drawn is certainly drawn unwillingly; and if he is drawn unwillingly, without doubt he is led against his will.

But so that the unwilling person may become willing, hear what follows: “It is written in the Prophets: ‘They shall all be taught by God’” (ibid., verse 45). If, then, all who are drawn by the Father to the Son are to be taught by God, it is plainly clear that they do not possess from themselves the will to come to the Son; rather, from the Father who draws them they receive the will and knowledge by which they both wish and know how to come to the one to whom they are drawn.

Concerning this gratuitous grace, which you so vehemently attack by denying it, blessed Augustine says in the *Enchiridion*, when speaking of the twofold substance of the Son of God (chapter 36):

> “Here, above all, the grace of God is greatly and clearly commended. For what did human nature merit in the man Christ, that it should be assumed uniquely into the unity of the person of the only Son of God? What good will, what zeal for a good purpose, what good works preceded this man, by which he might merit to become [variant: by which he might become] one person with God? Was he previously a human being, and was this singular benefit then bestowed upon him so that he might singularly merit God?
>
> “Certainly, from the moment he began to be a human being, he began to be nothing other than the Son of God—and this Son was the only one. On account of the Word of God, who assumed him and was made flesh, he was God. Thus, just as every human being is one person, namely a rational soul and flesh, so Christ is one person, the Word and the human being.
>
> “Whence did such glory belong to human nature, without any preceding merits and unquestionably as a free gift, unless those who faithfully and soberly consider the matter see plainly here the great and sole grace of God? Through this same grace human beings understand that they are justified from sins—the grace by which it came about that the man Christ could have no sin.
>
> “Thus the angel also greeted his mother when he announced to her the birth that was to come: ‘Hail,’ he said, ‘full of grace.’ A little later he says: ‘You have found grace with God’ (Luke 1:28, 30). She is called full of grace and is said to have found grace with God so that she might be the mother of her Lord, indeed of the Lord of all.
>
> “Concerning Christ himself, the evangelist John, after saying, ‘The Word became flesh and dwelt among us,’ adds: ‘And we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth’ (John 1:14–15).
>

The Prophet speaks of this to God: “For you went before him with blessings of sweetness” (Psalm 20:3). How was he preceded by blessings of sweetness except because, solely through God’s gratuitous grace, it came about that he neither acquired a defect by being born nor committed one by living?

### Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

[Opening fragment uncertain], having become man, the Son of God alone suffered no compulsion and no necessity toward either good or evil. All other human beings, after the first transgression had been committed, are held bound by such great necessities that, even when willing, they are compelled to do what they neither ought nor wish to do. From these necessities the Prophet asked to be delivered when he said:

> The troubles of my heart are multiplied; deliver me from my necessities.  
> (Psalm 24:17)

For whoever has voluntarily fallen into sin must, as a consequence of that same voluntary fall, become entangled in many difficulties. From these he must be delivered, not by his own will or freedom, but by the grace of God.

The blessed Augustine speaks in this way in the *Enchiridion*:

> It must be understood that in our times so many evils—although not such evils—have already entered openly into customary practice that, on account of them, we do not dare either to excommunicate a layman or even to degrade a cleric. Thus, when several years ago I was expounding the Epistle to the Galatians, at the very passage where the Apostle says, “I fear that perhaps I have labored among you in vain” (Galatians 4:11), I was compelled to cry out: “Woe to the sins of human beings, which we shudder at only when they are unusual! But those customary sins, for the cleansing of which the blood of the Son of God was poured out—although they are so great that they altogether close the kingdom of God against those who commit them—we are often compelled to tolerate, seeing everything; and, by tolerating certain things, often even to commit them ourselves! Would that, O Lord, we might do everything that we are unable to prevent. But let us see whether excessive grief has compelled me to say anything rashly. I shall now say what I have often said elsewhere in my little works: We sin for two reasons—either because we do not yet see what we ought to do, or because we do not do what we already see ought to be done. Of these two, the former is the evil of ignorance, the latter of weakness. We ought indeed to fight against this [another reading: these]; but we are completely overcome unless we are helped by God, so that we may not only see what must be done, but also, when health has been added, the delight of righteousness may overcome in us the delights of those things which, whether by desiring to possess them or by fearing to lose them, we knowingly and consciously pursue in sin. Then we are not merely sinners—as we were even when we sinned through ignorance—but also transgressors of the law, since we do not do what we now know ought to be done, or do what we know ought not to be done.”

These are the necessities by which human weakness is so tightly bound that, once it has voluntarily rushed into any sin, unless it quickly repents through the regard of heavenly grace, it necessarily falls into one or more worse things. Thus it is rightly said:

> When the wicked comes into the depth of evils, he despises.  
> (Proverbs 18:3)

The Prophet gloried that he had been saved from these necessities when he said:

> But I will hope in the Lord; I will exult and rejoice in your mercy, for you have regarded my humiliation; you have saved my soul from necessities, and you have not shut me up in the hands of the enemy.  
> (Psalm 31:8, 10)

### Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

The movement of the rational soul, therefore, had been as free as it was voluntary before sin. After sin, however, it was subjected to the servitude of the harshest necessity, so that it is compelled to serve its Lord even against its will.

For this reason the Lord—most penetrating observer of human minds, most vigilant examiner, and most just judge—when he commanded that the distinctions among sinners be corrected by the differing kinds of offerings, distinguished the unwilling from the willing, determining that one should be punished or purified in one way and the other in another.

He likewise ordained that cities of refuge be set apart, to which one who had shed blood unwillingly could flee and escape the avenger’s sword. For it is written in the Book of Numbers:

> The Lord said to Moses: “Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: When you have crossed the Jordan into the land of Canaan, determine which cities are to be places of refuge for those who have shed blood unwillingly.”  
> (Numbers 35:9–11)

And below:

> He shall flee to one of these cities who has shed blood unwillingly.  
> (Ibid., verse 15)

In the same book:

> The priest shall intercede for the whole congregation of the children of Israel, and it shall be forgiven them, because they did not sin voluntarily.  
> (Numbers 15:25)

Following this authority, the venerable Fathers who established the sacred canons, distinguishing involuntary homicide from voluntary homicide, judged that one should be healed by one kind of penitential satisfaction and the other by another.

The blessed Pope Gregory, examining with exceptional acuteness these inextricable alternations of necessities in the twenty-fourth book of the *Moralia*, speaks as follows:

> It must be understood above all that every wicked person is crushed in the night in two ways: either when he is struck by the tribulation of an external judgment, or when he is inwardly blinded by a hidden sentence. Then he is compelled to be cast into the outer darkness because now he is voluntarily blinded in his inner darkness.
>

>

>

### On Predestination

Paul rightly perceived this as a kind of seed of error in unbelievers and those given to lust when he said: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts” (Romans 1:21). Thus the pit of subsequent sins is covered over by the merit of the preceding sin, so that one who knowingly commits evil may afterward justly fall into other evils unknowingly.

> This is done so that fault may be punished by fault, and so that the very increase of vices may become the punishment of sinners. Hence David says: “Add iniquity upon their iniquity, and let them not enter into your righteousness” (Psalm 69:28). Again, the same Psalmist says of the Lord: “He sent among them the sending of evil angels; he made a path for his anger” (Psalm 78:49–50).

Hence it is said that he made a path for his anger—or, according to another reading, that the Lord made a way from his path of anger. For a way is wider than a path: to make a way from the path of his anger is to extend, by a strict judgment, the causes of anger. Thus those who, once enlightened, were unwilling to act rightly may, after being justly blinded, continue to do things by which they deserve greater punishment.

>

They already have grounds for deserving to be struck; nevertheless, their sin is still allowed to grow, so that a more atrocious punishment may torment them. The sin already deserves punishment and is the cause of sin, but it is still awaited that sin which is also the punishment of sin may furnish an increase of punishment.

>
> This adultery, placed between gluttony and homicide—arising from the former and generating the latter—is sin, punishment, and the cause of sin. >
