To have brought on night [another reading: “to have blinded in the night”] is therefore to have refused to free them from the darkness into which they have been plunged.

You then respond to those who, unwilling—[the OCR reading *uno spernente* is uncertain]—to correct their sins, complain about God’s action and ask why God gave free choice, by which alone they are convicted of sinning. In this response, what you say—that God gave the occasion of sins—is false: he did not give an occasion, but freedom.

If, as you add, free choice is not the cause of sins because it is a gift, it follows that it is not the occasion of sins either. If, according to you, freedom and human will are nature, I do not see how nature can be called the occasion of sins.

If, I say, free choice is not the cause of sin, but its perverse movement and blameworthy inclination toward what is lowest and forbidden, how can it be called the occasion of sin? The commandment could indeed be called the occasion of sin, just as the Apostle says:

> “Sin, taking an occasion through the commandment, deceived me through it and killed me” (Romans 7:11).

He did not say “through free choice,” which is a gift of God, nor “through nature,” which is God’s work, but “through the commandment,” which may be called the test by which the rational creature’s voluntary desire is tested to see what it

## [Scan page 555]

chooses to follow.

### John Scotus

> But what you say—which nevertheless is nothing, if it is acquired by a coerced will or possessed without freedom—  
> (John Scotus, chapter 5, number 10, section 7)

### Correction

If it is nothing, how can it be acquired in any manner? If it is nothing, how can it be possessed even without freedom? For what altogether does not exist can neither be acquired nor possessed. We must therefore admit that blessed life exists, and that here it is inspired in us by divine grace, desired through subsequent moral uprightness, acquired with the assistance of grace through honorable conduct, and afterward possessed in the fullest freedom by the recompense of the just Judge.

But if you call miserable life “hell,” it is certain that no one voluntarily submits to it. Nevertheless, all voluntarily bring it upon themselves, although they are compelled to undergo it. On the other hand, they pursue blessed life with such great desire and ardor that they never wish to be separated from it. Yet many are so delightfully fixed in the mire of a damnable life that they do not even aspire to it, nor wish to hear, think, or entertain any notion of it. If they happen to hear of it, they immediately turn away, become indignant, flee, and persecute it.

The Prophet speaks of such people:

> “He refused to understand, so as to act well; he meditated iniquity upon his bed. He stood upon every way that was not good; but he did not hate wickedness.”  
> (Psalm 36:4–5)

For how can a pagan desire what he does not know, or a false Christian, under a false name, desire what he attacks? Of the former it is said:

> “The one who is ignorant shall be ignored.”  
> (1 Corinthians 14:38)

Of the latter:

> “Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?’ And then I will declare to them: ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, workers of iniquity.’”  
> (Matthew 7:22–23)

But in order to confirm your error, by which you strive to empty God’s grace of its operation of every good will in us, asserting that your willing is from yourself—or rather, that you yourself are your own willing—and that you do not receive it as a gift of heavenly inspiration, you maintain that every human being naturally possesses a desire for blessedness, that is, a desire to live well, and that no one desires a miserable life, that is, a shameful and criminal one.

Yet the opposite is demonstrated with equal certainty by daily—or rather continual—multitudes. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel:

> “Strive to enter through the narrow gate, because narrow is the gate and constricted the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it.”  
> (Matthew 7:13–14)

These are the people in whom the desire for blessedness is divinely inspired; it is not the swelling pride of nature.

He also says:

> “How broad is the gate and spacious the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter through it.”  
> (Ibid., verse 13)

None of these people desires to live blessedly, either because they do not know what blessed life is or because they do not wish to follow what they know.

The blessed Augustine clearly expounded this distinction among sins in the statement cited somewhat earlier. We, however, freely confess and humbly ask that both the desire to live well and the desire and ability to escape and avoid misery are given to us by the free gift of grace.

But if you call blessed life eternal life, then, according to the hidden and inscrutable judgments of the divine dispensation, many are driven and compelled toward it, so that neither free choice is taken away nor grace is entirely denied.

> Indeed, in accordance with the fact that human freedom has become degraded and remains enslaved, the desire for blessedness is left to a person as testimony to his condemnation. When he hears that word, he is enticed by its sweetness and desires blessedness, but he does not wish to reach it by living well, rightly, and piously. And because such desire proceeds from the testimony, so to speak, of enslaved freedom, and not from the gift of grace, when left to itself it is weakened, withers, and immediately vanishes.

[Marginal addition.]

Now it has been demonstrated sufficiently and more than sufficiently what free choice was before sin and what it was after sin.

But when you write that God has now created and established free choice and will in man, and has now given it to man, it is astonishing unless, following your Pelagian fathers, you call human nature itself grace, so that whatever is afterward given from heaven is not the gift of free grace but the recompense of merit.

Although they placed grace in the condition of nature, they are nowhere read to have said that the will and freedom either of man or of any other rational creature is a substance. It is therefore plainly evident that you are worse than your Pelagian fathers, insofar as you presume to add to their assertions of error things that neither they nor anyone before you is found anywhere to have said.

What the errors of the Pelagians were can indeed be learned from the synodal acts by which they were condemned, but they are especially and most easily detected from the books of blessed Augustine, which he wrote either against them or on the eighty-nine heresies. Having examined these, I have nowhere been able to find what you have exhaled from the stench of your monstrous inventions.

### John Scotus

> Anyone who derogates from free choice, either by diminishing it, taking it away altogether, or blaspheming it, is without doubt an enemy of the entire Christian discipline.  
> (John Scotus, chapter 6, number 2, section 9)

### Correction

Who diminishes it except one who sins? Who takes it away entirely except one who is ignorant? Who blasphemes except one who departs from piety?

The person who voluntarily sins diminishes free choice for himself, because he has subjected himself to slavery. Thereafter he cannot be freed from the dominion of slavery except through the grace of God and of the Lord, the Mediator.

No one takes it away except one ignorant of authority and devoid of reason, unable to contemplate with the eyes of his mind either the goodness or the justice of God.

Anyone who departs from piety and is shamefully stained by his own impieties blasphemes when he prefers to complain most unjustly about the judgments of God rather than to be accused, corrected, or certainly judged for his own crimes. Such people are unquestionably strangers not only to discipline but also to the fellowship of the Catholic Church.

Whoever denies that sin is voluntary has paid no careful attention to the manner of the first transgression. Afterward, although all except the one Mediator of God and human beings are constrained by the necessity arising from that transgression, and are consequently compelled to many things that they previously neither wished nor intended, it must nevertheless be admitted that the things for which a just retribution of punishment is appropriate are committed not without the will.

Thus some are compelled unwillingly to perpetrate them, yet the will—although already captive and enslaved—is not absent; and it is this will that is deservedly punished.

## Chapter VI

### That all sin arises solely from the free choice of one’s own will

Since, in the sixth article of your superfluous disputations (chapter 6, number 1, section 1), you tediously and unnecessarily reply that all sin arises solely from the free choice of one’s own will—a matter about which no sound mind can doubt—you employ an argument drawn from comparison, saying:

### John Scotus

> If the human will exists according to nature—and it would be exceedingly foolish to doubt this—there is no doubt that it is not the highest of all wills, especially for this reason: it is mutable. For if it were the highest of all, how could it be mutable? Therefore it is not the highest. But since we see that it participates in supreme reason, we cannot doubt that it is itself a rational substance.

### Correction

You add the statement of blessed Augustine (number 3, section 2), which, although in certain respects it confirms your own—or rather, Catholic—position, in no way agrees with or supports you in asserting that the human will is a rational substance, since it is never proved that his words contain this.

## Chapter VII

### That free choice of the will must be numbered among the goods that God bestows upon man, although he uses it badly; and that it is the cause of sin and is itself sin

In the seventh installment of your nauseating arguments (chapter 7, number 1, section 1), you judge that free choice of the will must be numbered among the goods bestowed upon man by divine generosity. In this we both agree and rejoice.

But we are astonished that you say it was created previously by God, since creating is one thing and giving another. We do not deny that, in creation itself, many good things were divinely given to man: for example, to say nothing of the rest, the soul given to the body that was formed, the will given to the soul that was formed, knowledge, and other things belonging to its nature, by which the image of God is fittingly preserved and adorned in it.

We do not assert that there was some interval, whether of place or of time, between creation and gift; rather, we do not doubt that what was given was given through creation.

For who does not know that will, knowledge, and the other gifts of God in a rational creature can increase or diminish? The Prophet says of the saints and those worthy of God’s tabernacle:

> “They shall go from strength to strength.”  
> (Psalm 84:7)

For what is it to go from strength to strength except to advance through increases of pious will and sound knowledge until the God of gods is seen in Zion?

The Evangelist also shows that wisdom grows in a rational soul when, narrating the infancy of the Lord and Savior, he says:

> “Jesus advanced in wisdom, and in age, and in grace with God and men.”  
> (Luke 2:52)

Wisdom pertains to the soul, age to the body, and grace to both. Therefore, when someone is said to advance—that is, to grow and increase—in wisdom, he is not enlarged by the passage of ages, but is elevated by increases of virtues.

Whoever is said to advance in knowledge and wisdom must be understood not to increase in substance but to be exalted in virtues. Conversely, whoever is polluted by the effects of vices decreases in virtues in proportion to how deeply and delightfully he clings to them.

From this it follows that the will, knowledge, and the other gifts of God given and implanted in a rational soul are not its substance. For if they were natures, incorporeal natures would necessarily grow by increases and diminish by losses in the manner of corporeal natures. No one is unaware that this is wholly foreign to an incorporeal creature.

The daily—or rather constant—alternation of human wills teaches that wills grow, that is, increase or diminish, as do thoughts, which proceed only from the will. It is certain that the substance of a rational creature does not grow or diminish through any increases belonging to its nature.

There is no doubt that knowledge and wisdom in rational creatures increase or diminish. Therefore, whoever affirms that human will and knowledge are the human being’s nature must necessarily assert that an incorporeal creature is subject to corporeal increases. No one except one devoid of reason is unaware how alien this is to reason.

The Apostle indicates that the gifts of God, whether great, moderate, or small, are distributed to the rational soul according to the will of the giver. After enumerating certain gifts of God, he concludes:

> “All these things one and the same Spirit works, distributing them to each one as he wills.”  
> (1 Corinthians 12:11)

Therefore, whoever asserts that knowledge is nature in man contradicts the Apostle, who, counting it among God’s gifts, said:

> “To one is given through the Spirit a discourse of wisdom, to another a discourse of knowledge, in the same Spirit,” and so forth.  
> (Ibid., verse 8)

He said “is given,” not “is established” or “is created.” Therefore what is given is a gift, not nature. What is given is given according to the will of the giver, not according to the power of the nature that receives it.

For the one who gives bestows according to his will; the one who receives does not receive through the power or desire of his own will, but according to the decision of the giver, who has established all things in measure, weight, and number.

Free choice—that is, the election of the human will—is therefore not the creature itself, but must be numbered among the intermediate goods of God’s gifts. Hence it could easily be turned away from the highest good and bent toward lower things; and for this reason it is deservedly punished and pays deservedly severe penalties for its voluntary turning away.

## Chapter VIII

### On the difference between human nature and his free choice

In the eighth order of your disputation (chapter 8, number 1, section 1), you attempt to establish a distinction between the free will of man, which, as you say, is from nature, and his free choice, which is plainly and unquestionably a gift of the Creator.

After laboring long and hard over this, you define free will as the human substance, but free choice as the movement of free will.

Since you have fabricated this from your own invention, I am amazed that you have been so dulled by blindness that you could not see how impudently you were chattering against the sound judgment of all Catholics, and how you deceitfully considered your loquacity—which everyone ridicules—the height of wisdom.

When you brought forward the statement of blessed Augustine in support of your definitions, and recognized that in that statement, as everywhere else, he called nothing other than free will “free choice,” you feared that his authority would overturn your trivial arguments. Therefore you added this monstrous explanation:

### John Scotus

> In these words we must take care lest anyone confuse substance and movement when he hears “free will,” which is unquestionably substantial. In this manner of speaking, therefore, Saint Father Augustine used “free will” for what is the movement of free will, or free choice, just as we customarily use terms for their effects through substantial causes. Hence “the circuit of true reason” is used for “the circuit of true reasoning.”

### Correction

Your statement must immediately be rejected as not an explanation but a corruption of the words of blessed Augustine. Defining free will as the free movement of the soul, he spoke in the book he published against the Manichaeans on the two souls as follows:

> “Will is a movement of the soul, constrained by no one, toward accepting or not accepting something, or toward attaining it.”  
> (chapter 10)

[Marked +:] These words directly cut away your error, by which you defined the human will as its essence. And lest this opinion appear to support your Pelagian fathers, Augustine thus revised it in his *Retractions*:

> “This was said so that by this definition one who wills might be distinguished from one who does not will, and so that the intention might be referred to those who were the first origin of evil for the human race in paradise: they sinned under no compulsion, that is, they sinned by free will, because they knowingly acted against the commandment, and the tempter persuaded them to do this but did not compel them.
>
> “For even one who sins unknowingly may appropriately be called to have sinned unwillingly, although he nevertheless voluntarily did what he did unknowingly. Thus even his sin could not exist without will. That will, as it has been defined, was a movement of the soul, compelled by no one, toward accepting or not accepting something, or toward attaining it.
>
> “For if he had not wished to do what he did, he would not have done it; he was not compelled to do it. Therefore he did it because he willed it, even though he did not sin because he willed it, since he did not know that what he did was sin. Thus such sin too could not exist without will: it was the will of the act, not the will of sin, although the act was nevertheless sin. For what was done was something that ought not to have been done.
>
> “But whoever knowingly sins, if he is able to resist the one compelling him to sin without sinning and nevertheless does not do so, sins willingly, because one who can resist is not compelled to yield.
>
> “Whoever cannot resist a compelling desire with a good will, and therefore acts against the precepts of justice, is guilty of sin in such a way that it is also the punishment of sin.”

Behold, the most truthful teacher strongly contradicts both your errors.

When he defined will as a movement of the soul, he undoubtedly understood and committed to writing that it was nothing other than free will, that is, free choice. It is therefore false that you fabricated this distinction between free will and free choice, teaching that free will should be referred to nature but free choice to the movement of free will.

He makes this unmistakably clear in the same book of his *Retractions*, when he says:

> “But when I said, ‘Whatever these souls do, if they do it by nature and not by will, that is, if they lack a free movement of the soul for doing or not doing, and if, finally, no power of abstaining from their action is granted to them, we cannot hold them guilty of sin,’ I said this because the question concerning little ones is not disturbing: we are held by the origin of the one who sinned by will, when he lacked no free movement of the soul for doing and not doing, and when he possessed the fullest power of abstaining from the evil deed.”  
> [Another reading: “not for doing.”]

Here again he distinguishes will from nature and does not call it anything other than a free movement of the soul. He also vigorously contradicts your error when he fully teaches that one may be compelled to sin, whereas you assert that no one is compelled to do either good or evil.

For what this compulsion is, and for what reason it occurs, is held with complete certainty in the same *Retractions*, where he goes on to add:

> “Likewise, I defined sin when I said: ‘Sin is the will to retain or acquire what justice forbids, and from which one is free to abstain,’

### [scan page 558]

## Against John Scotus on Predestination

For this reason the statement is truly correct, because it defines what is understood to be sin, which is not also the punishment of sin. For I spoke elsewhere in the same discussion about such a punishment, as was necessary.

Again, in the *Retractions* of the book *On True Religion* (*Retractions*, chapter 13):

> “And elsewhere I said: ‘Sin is so entirely a voluntary evil that in no way is it sin if it is not voluntary.’ This definition may seem false; but if it is carefully examined, it will be found to be entirely true. For that is to be understood as sin which is only sin, not also the punishment of sin, as I showed above when I recalled certain passages from book III of *On Free Choice of the Will*. Although those acts which are called involuntary sins are not committed without the will—for they are perpetrated either by those who are ignorant or by those who are compelled—they nevertheless cannot be committed altogether without the will. For the one who sins in ignorance sins voluntarily [variant: ‘acts voluntarily’], because, although he ought not to do what he does, he thinks that it ought to be done. And the one whose flesh desires against the spirit and who does not do what he wills, desires indeed unwillingly and therefore [variant: ‘in this respect’] does not do what he wills; but if he is overcome, he willingly consents to desire, and thereby does only what he wills—free, indeed, from righteousness and a slave of sin. Therefore, by the grace of God not only is the guilt of all past sins forgiven in all who are baptized in Christ, through the Spirit of regeneration; but in those who make progress in good works the will itself is healed and prepared by the Lord (Proverbs VIII, according to the Septuagint), which takes place through the spirit of faith and charity.”

Augustine also retracted the following (*ibid.*):

> “Again, what I said: ‘Nowhere, certainly, is sin except in the will,’ the Pelagians may think was said with reference to infants, whom they deny to have sin, because they are baptized unwillingly and therefore do not use the choice of the will. But the sin which we say that they derive originally from Adam—that is, that they are implicated in its guilt and held liable to this punishment—could never have been in the will by which it was committed, when the transgression of the divine command took place.”

This statement, in which we say that sin is nowhere except in the will, may also be thought false, because the Apostle said:

> “But if I do what I do not will, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me” (Romans VII, 16–17).

For this sin is called sin precisely because it was produced by sin, and it is the punishment of sin, since this is said about the desire of the flesh, as he explains in what follows:

> “I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. For to will is present with me, but to accomplish the good is not” (ibid., 18).

The perfection of the good is that even the desire of sin should not exist in a human being. For when one lives rightly, the will does not consent; nevertheless, it does not accomplish the good, because desire still remains, and the will resists it. The guilt of this desire is released in baptism, but its weakness remains; until it is healed, every believer who makes progress in the good struggles against it with the greatest diligence.

The sin which is nowhere except in the will is to be understood especially as that which has incurred just condemnation. For:

> “Through one man sin entered the world” (Romans V, 12).

Nevertheless, even the sin by which one consents to the sin of desire is committed only by the will.

Augustine said the same when retracting the acts against Fortunatus the Manichaean (*Retractions*, book I, chapter 16):

> “Again, elsewhere I said: ‘I declare that sin is nothing if it is not voluntary.’ Elsewhere, in what I said about the Lord Jesus Christ—‘He did nothing by force, but everything by persuasion and admonition’—it had not occurred to me that he drove the sellers and buyers from the temple by scourging them (Matthew XXI, 12). But what is this, or how much does it amount to? Even demons, unwilling to leave human beings, were driven out not by the word of persuasion but by force of authority.”

Since you have previously set forth many passages from Augustine’s books *On Free Choice of the Will* by which you particularly fortified your errors, it is not inappropriate to bring together what he wrote in the retraction of those same books, so that it may easily become clear to anyone that he condemned your errors before they were even born.

He began the retraction of them in this way (*Retractions*, book I, chapter 9):

> “In these books many things were discussed, so that certain questions arose which I either could not resolve or which required a lengthy treatment at the time. They were therefore postponed in such a way that, whether from both sides or from all sides of the questions, where it was not apparent what was more consistent with the truth, our reasoning nevertheless concluded that, whichever of the alternatives was true, God should be believed, or even shown, to be worthy of praise. For that discussion was undertaken on behalf of those who deny that the origin of evil derives from the free choice of the will and maintain that, if this is so, God, as creator of all natures, must be blamed. In this way they wished, in accordance with the error of their impiety—for they are Manichaeans—to introduce a certain immutable and coeternal nature of evil. Nothing was discussed in these books about the grace of God by which he so predestined his chosen that, in those who already use free choice, he himself also prepares their wills, because of the question proposed [variant: ‘because this question had been proposed’]. Whenever the subject arose so that this grace had to be mentioned, it was mentioned only in passing, not as though the laborious reasoning of the discussion had been directed toward defending it. For it is one thing to ask where evil comes from, and another to ask from where one returns to the original good or advances to a greater good.”

Therefore, let the new heretics, the Pelagians, not exalt themselves as though I had pleaded their cause, because they assert free choice of the will in such a way that they leave no place for God’s grace, claiming that grace is given according to our merits. In these books I said many things in favor of free choice, because the purpose of that discussion required them.

In the first book I said that evil deeds are punished by God’s justice, and I added:

> “They would not be justly punished unless they were committed voluntarily.”

Again, when I showed that the good will itself is so great a good that it is rightly preferred to all bodily and external goods, I said:

> “You see, then, as I think, that it has been established in our will whether we enjoy or lack so great and true a good; for what is so much in our power as the will itself?”

Elsewhere I said:

> “What reason, then,” I asked, “could we have for thinking it doubtful that, even if we had never previously been wise, we might by our will merit and live a praiseworthy and blessed life, and by our will merit and live a shameful and wretched one?”

Again, elsewhere:

> “From this it follows,” I said, “that whoever rightly and honorably wishes to live, if he wishes this in preference to fleeting things, attains so great a matter with such happiness that he has nothing other than the very act of willing in order to possess what he willed.”

Again, elsewhere I said:

> “For that eternal law, to whose consideration it is now time to return, established with unchangeable firmness that merit lies in the will, while in blessedness and misery there are reward and punishment.”

Elsewhere:

> “It is clear that what each person should pursue and embrace has been placed in the will.”

And in book II:

> “Humanity itself,” I said, “insofar as it is human, is some good, because when it wishes to live rightly, it can do so.”

Elsewhere I said:

> “One cannot act rightly except by that same free choice of the will.”

And in book III:

> “Why need we ask,” I said, “from where that movement arises by which the will is turned away from the immutable good toward a mutable good, when we acknowledge that it is nothing other than a movement of the soul, voluntary, and therefore blameworthy? Every useful instruction concerning this matter serves the purpose that, by rejecting and restraining that movement, we may turn our will from the fall into temporal things toward enjoyment of the eternal good.”

Elsewhere:

> “Truth cries out to you most clearly,” I said. “You cannot think that anything else is in our power except what we do when we will it. Therefore nothing is so completely in our power as the will itself. For it is immediately present, without any interval, as soon as we will.”

Again:

> “If you are praised,” I said, “because you see what you ought to do, although you do not see it except in the one who is immutable truth, how much more should he be praised who both commanded willing and granted the ability, and did not permit unwillingness to go unpunished?”

Then I added:

> “If each person ought to possess what he has received, and if a human being was made in such a way that he necessarily sins, then he ought to sin. When he sins, he does what he ought to do. But if it is wicked to say this, then no one is compelled by nature to sin.”

And again:

> “What, finally, could be the cause of the will before the will? Either it too is the will, and we do not move back from this root of the will; or it is not the will, and there is no sin. Therefore either the will is the first cause of sinning, or no one is the first cause of sinning. Sin cannot rightly be imputed to anyone except the one who sins. It cannot rightly be imputed to anyone except the will [variant: ‘the one willing’].”

A little later:

> “Who sins in what cannot in any way be avoided? Yet sin is committed; therefore it can be avoided.”

Pelagius used this testimony of mine in one of his books. When I answered that book, I wanted my own book to bear the title *On Nature and Grace*.

Because God’s grace was not mentioned in these and similar statements of mine—for at that time it was not under discussion—the Pelagians think, or may think, that we held their position. But they think this in vain. We were discussing the will by which one sins and lives rightly.

The will itself, therefore, unless it is freed by God’s grace from the slavery into which it was made a slave of sin, and unless it is helped to overcome its vices, cannot live rightly and piously among mortals. Unless this divine benefit by which it is freed anticipated it, it would be given according to its merits and would not be grace, which is given freely.

We dealt with this sufficiently in our other works, refuting these new heretics, enemies of grace. Although these books *On Free Choice of the Will* were written not against them—for they did not yet exist—but against the Manichaeans, we nevertheless did not altogether remain silent about this grace of God, which they attempt to remove with unspeakable impiety.

For in book II we said that not only great goods but also the smallest goods cannot exist except from the one from whom all good things come, that is, God. A little later:

> “The virtues by which one lives rightly,” I said, “are great goods. The forms of any bodies, without which one can live rightly, are the smallest goods. The powers of the soul, without which one cannot live rightly, are intermediate goods. No one uses virtues badly; but with the other goods—that is, the intermediate and smallest goods—each person can use them not only well but also badly. Virtue is never used badly because the work of virtue is the good use of those things which we can also use badly; and no one uses something badly by using it well. Therefore the abundance and greatness of God’s goodness has supplied not only great goods but also intermediate and smallest goods. His goodness is more worthy of praise in great goods than in intermediate ones, and more in intermediate than in the smallest; but it is more worthy of praise in all of them than if he had not bestowed all things [variant: ‘on everyone’].”

Elsewhere:

> “Hold fast to piety,” I said, “with such unwavering firmness that no good comes before you—whether you sense, understand, or think about it in any way—which is not from God.”

Again, elsewhere I said:

> “But since humanity cannot rise of its own accord in the same way that it fell of its own accord, let us hold with firm faith the hand of God stretched down to us from above, that is, our Lord Jesus Christ [variant: ‘the Lord Jesus Christ’].”

And in book III, after I had said the words which I mentioned Pelagius had used from my works—“Who sins in what cannot in any way be avoided? Yet sin is committed; therefore it can be avoided”—I immediately continued:

> “Nevertheless, certain acts committed through ignorance are also condemned and judged in need of correction, as we read in the divine authorities. The Apostle says: ‘I obtained mercy because I acted in ignorance’ (1 Timothy I, 13); and the Prophet says: ‘Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorance’ (Psalm XXV, 7). There are also acts committed under compulsion which must be condemned, when a person wishes to act rightly but cannot. From where, then, come the words: ‘For I do not do the good that I will, but the evil that I hate, that I do’ (Romans VII, 15); and: ‘To will is present with me, but to accomplish the good is not’ (ibid., 18); and: ‘The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. For these are opposed to one another, so that you do not do what you wish’ (Galatians V, 17).”

But all these conditions belong to human beings who come from the condemnation of death. For if this is not the punishment of humanity but its nature, then these are not sins. If humanity has not departed from the condition in which it was naturally made, so that it could not be better, then it does what it ought to do when it acts in this way. If it were good, it would be otherwise. But now, because it is as it is, it is not good, nor does it have the power to be good, whether because it does not live as it ought to be, or because, while living, it lacks the power to be what it sees it ought to be.

Who could doubt that this is a punishment? Every punishment, if it is just, is the punishment of sin and is called a penalty. If the punishment is unjust, then, since no one doubts that it is a punishment, it has been imposed on an innocent person by some unjust ruler. But since it is insane to doubt God’s omnipotence and justice, this punishment is just and is paid for some sin.

No unjust ruler could have imposed it on a human being by deception, as though God were ignorant, or by extorting it from one unwilling, as though God were weaker, or by frightening or troubling him, so that he would torment a human being with an unjust punishment. It remains, therefore, that this just punishment comes from the condemnation of humanity.

Elsewhere:

> “To approve falsehoods as truths, so that one errs unwillingly, and, while the pain of the bodily bond resists and tortures him, to be unable to abstain from lustful acts, is not the nature with which humanity was instituted but the punishment of one condemned. When we speak of the will to do what is right, we are speaking of the will in which humanity was made.”

Thus, long before the Pelagian heresy arose, we argued as though we were already arguing against them. For while all goods were said to come from God—great, intermediate, and smallest—free choice of the will is found among the intermediate goods.

### [scan page 559]

For we can use it badly; nevertheless it is such that we cannot live rightly without it. Its good use is already virtue, which is found among the great goods, with which no one can use badly. Since all goods, as has been said, great, intermediate, and smallest, come from God, it follows that the good use of free choice is also from God, since this good use is virtue and is numbered among the great goods.

It was then said that God’s grace frees us from the misery justly inflicted upon sinners, because humanity could fall voluntarily—that is, by free choice—but cannot rise in the same way. To this misery of just condemnation belong ignorance and the difficulty suffered by every human being from the beginning of birth. No one is freed from this evil except by God’s grace.

The Pelagians do not wish this misery to descend from a just condemnation, since they deny original sin. Yet even if ignorance and difficulty were natural beginnings of humanity, God would still not be blamed but praised, as we argued in the same third book.

You see, distinguished teacher, with what force he crushes your perverse interpretations. By repeatedly naming free choice of the will, and by defining it as nothing other than the movement of the soul, he is so surrounded by truth against your distinctions that he confirms them to be entirely nothing.

You yourself are also so thoroughly opposed to yourself that either you did not notice, or thought that others would not notice, that you had defended free choice of the will to the extent of defining free will as the choice of free will, and of saying that humanity would have lost its nature if it had lost free choice of the will. Now, however, either having forgotten yourself or attempting to deceive your readers, you try to separate the movement of the soul from the will, as though anything other than willing could constitute the movement of the soul.

The soul is moved by willing, just as that memorable Father defined it, to such an extent that its movement is nothing other than the will. Scripture and the agreement of so many Fathers clearly and immutably teach, proclaim, and indeed confirm that this will is also prepared by the Lord.

Yet because you have denied this until now, and, so to speak, disowned it, you have dared, by a new invention, to say that your movement is prepared by the Lord, not your will. Since this has been shown to be both contrary to the truth and opposed to authority, with the Lord’s help let us pass on to see how great are the other poisons of your slanders.

You say (chapter 8, no. 5, section 1):

> “With Saint Augustine repeatedly impressing this upon us, it is most clearly to be believed that the substantial trinity of the inner human being is contained in these three things: essence, will, and knowledge.”

And shortly afterward (chapter 8, no. 6, section 2):

> “These three, therefore, are one and one nature; moreover, the whole nature of the soul is will,” and so forth.

How clouded these words of yours are by the mist of lies is made clear by the words of that same most holy Father Augustine. In book XV of *On the Trinity*, chapter 3, inviting us to know it truthfully insofar as this is granted to mortals, he teaches by inviting and invites by teaching:

> “Through the truth which is understood, and through the supreme good from which every good comes, and through the justice for whose sake the just soul is loved even by a soul that is not yet just, I admonished that the nature not only incorporeal but also immutable—which is God—should be understood insofar as this can take place. And through charity, which is called God in the Holy Scriptures (1 John IV, 8), by which the Trinity began in some way to appear to those who understand, as lover, what is loved, and love.”

In book IX the discussion reaches the image of God, which the human being according to the mind attains. In it a certain trinity is found: mind, the knowledge by which it knows itself, and the love by which it loves both itself and its knowledge. These three are shown to be equal to one another and of one essence.

In book X the same matter is treated more carefully and subtly, until a clearer trinity is found in the mind—namely, memory, understanding, and will.

But since it was also discovered that the mind could never exist in such a way that it did not remember itself, understand itself, and love itself, although it did not always think of itself; and since, when it thought of itself, it did not distinguish itself in that same thought from bodily things, the discussion of the Trinity, whose image this is, was postponed so that a trinity might also be found in bodily visions themselves, and the reader’s attention might be exercised more distinctly in it.

Therefore, in book XI, the sense of sight was selected, so that what was discovered in it could also be recognized, even without being stated, in the other four bodily senses. Thus the trinity of the outer human being first appeared in what is perceived externally: the body that is seen, the form impressed by it upon the eye of the observer, and the intention of the will joining the two.

But these three were shown neither to be equal to one another nor to belong to one substance.

Then, in the soul itself, as though brought inward from the things perceived externally, another trinity was found, in which the same three appeared to belong to one substance: the image of the body, which is in memory; the formation of it when the eye of the thinker turns toward it [variant: “is turned toward it”]; and the intention of the will joining the two.

This trinity was found to belong to the outer human being because it was introduced from bodies that are perceived externally.

In book XII, wisdom had to be distinguished from knowledge [variant: “knowledge from wisdom”]. In what is properly called knowledge, because it is inferior, a certain trinity of its own kind had first to be sought. Although this already belongs to the inner human being, it should not yet be called or considered the image of God.

This is carried forward in book XIII through the commendation of Christian faith.

In book XIV the discussion concerns the true wisdom of humanity, that is, the gift of God bestowed through participation in God himself, which is distinct from knowledge. The discussion reaches the point at which a trinity appears in the image of God, which is the human being according to the mind. This mind is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of the one who created humanity in his own image, and thus attains wisdom, where there is contemplation of eternal things.

After this distinguished and subtle treatment of so many trinities, carried out with such depth of discovery that they are clear only to those endowed with the capacity of a heavenly gift, nowhere does he call the soul essence, nor does he call it the essence of the soul. Rather, he discusses and carefully treats the matter as follows: whatever trinities are discovered in it exist as one essence, whatever that essence itself may be.

He says that there is an essence in the soul, not that the essence of the soul is this; and the extensive discussion of so many books clearly teaches this, while reason in no way contradicts it.

To make this still clearer to the less learned, let us set forth the statement of the same memorable and worthy-of-remembrance Augustine from book XV of the same work, in which he truthfully and subtly distinguishes those trinities from the essence of the soul (*On the Trinity*, book XV, chapters 6–7):

> “Behold, then, the trinity: wisdom, knowledge of itself, and love of itself. For thus also in humanity we find a trinity: mind, knowledge by which it knows itself, and love by which it loves itself. But these three are in a human being in such a way that they are not themselves the human being. For a human being is, as the ancients defined him, a rational mortal animal.
>
> “Those three, therefore, are superior in humanity, but they are not themselves the human being; and one person—that is, each individual human being—possesses those three in the mind. Even if we define a human being by saying, ‘A human being is a rational substance consisting of soul and body,’ there is no doubt that a human being has a soul which is not body, and a body which is not soul. Thus those three are not the human being, but they belong to the human being or are in the human being.
>
> “If the body is removed and the soul alone is considered, something belonging to it is called mind, as though its head, eye, or face—but these terms must not be conceived in the bodily sense. Therefore it is not the soul but what is superior in the soul that is called mind.
>
> “Can we say that the Trinity is in God in such a way that something belongs to God but is not itself God? Therefore each individual human being, who is called the image of God not according to everything belonging to his nature but according to the mind alone, is one person and is the image of the Trinity in the mind. But that Trinity whose image it is is wholly nothing other than God; it is wholly nothing other than the Trinity. Nor does anything belong to God’s nature which does not belong to that Trinity; and the three persons are of one essence, unlike each individual human being, who is one person.
>
> “There is also this great difference: whether we call the mind the human being [variant: ‘in the human being’] and its knowledge and love, or memory, understanding, and will, we remember nothing of the mind except through memory, understand nothing except through understanding, and love nothing except through will. But in that Trinity, who would dare to say that the Father understands neither himself, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit except through the Son, or loves except through the Holy Spirit, while by himself he merely remembers himself, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit?”

And there are many other passages in which that most subtle and truthful interpreter discussed the incomprehensibility of such great majesty at length and with great skill. Because of their length, we refrain from inserting them into this work.

### [scan page 562]

Again, after much discussion, when he was speaking about the knowledge of God (*ibid.*, chapter 13):

> “It is written,” he says, “in the book of Ecclesiasticus: ‘All things were known to him before they were created, and likewise after they had been completed’ (Ecclesiasticus XIV, 29). Thus,” he says, “they are known to him in the same way both before they were created and after they were completed. Therefore our knowledge is very different from this knowledge.
>
> “Whatever God’s knowledge is, that is also his wisdom; and whatever his wisdom is, that is his essence or substance. For in the marvelous simplicity of that nature, to know wisely is not one thing and to be another; rather, what it is to know wisely is also what it is to be, just as we have often said in the earlier books.
>
> “Our knowledge, however, is both liable to be lost and capable of being acquired in very many matters because, for us, being is not the same as knowing or being wise. We can exist even if we do not know or understand wisely what we have learned from elsewhere.
>
> “Therefore, just as our knowledge differs from God’s knowledge, so our word, which is born from our knowledge, differs from God’s Word, which was born from the Father’s essence. It is as though I were speaking of the Father’s knowledge, of the Father’s wisdom; or, more explicitly, of knowledge from the Father and wisdom from the Father.”

Again, in the same work, chapter 20:

> “Therefore the dialectic of Eunomius, from whom the heretics called Eunomians arose, is to be ridiculed. He was unable to understand, and unwilling to believe, that the only-begotten Word of God, through whom all things were made, is the Son of God by nature—that is, begotten from the substance of the Father. He therefore said that the Son was not of the Father’s nature, substance, or essence, but the Son of God’s will, wishing thereby to assert that the will by which God begot the Son was something accidental to God.
>
> “He reasoned, plainly, from the fact that we sometimes will something which we previously did not will, as though our nature were not understood to be changeable on this account—something which, God forbid, we should believe to exist in God.
>
> “For it was not written for any other reason: ‘There are many thoughts in a man’s heart, but the counsel of the Lord remains forever’ (Proverbs XIX, 21), except so that we may understand or believe that, just as God is eternal, so his counsel is eternal, and therefore immutable, just as he himself is. What is said about thoughts can most truly also be said about wills: ‘There are many wills in a man’s heart, but the will of the Lord remains forever.’”

And shortly afterward (*ibid.*):

> “With respect also to the creature which God made, we admonished, as far as we were able, those who ask for an explanation of such matters, so that they might behold, insofar as they could, his invisible qualities understood through the things that have been made, and especially through the rational or intellectual creature which was made in the image of God. Through it, as through a mirror, they might see, insofar as they could and if they could, the Trinity.
>
> “God the Trinity is reflected in our memory, understanding, and will. Whoever vividly perceives these three, divinely established naturally in his mind, and recognizes how great a thing there is in the mind from which the eternal and immutable nature can also be recollected, contemplated, and desired, remembers it through memory, beholds it through understanding, and embraces it through love, undoubtedly discovers the image of that supreme Trinity.
>
> “But in remembering, seeing, and loving that supreme Trinity, in order to remember it, contemplate it, and delight in it, one must refer everything by which one lives to it.
>
> “Yet one must not compare this image, made by that same Trinity and changed for the worse by its own fault, with the Trinity in such a way as to suppose it entirely like it. Rather, in whatever likeness it possesses, one should also perceive a great unlikeness. I have said as much as seemed sufficient.”

[The printed page marks the following passage with an uncertain or damaged paragraph marker.]

There are many other passages in which that most subtle teacher prudently pursues the same matters. Because of their length, we refrain from inserting them into this work.

What are you doing, dialectician? You slander the most blessed Augustine by claiming that he repeatedly said what he is nowhere found to have said, although you fabricate it in your own manner.

You say that the essence of the soul is will and knowledge. Blessed Augustine says that will and knowledge are not its essence. For when God, the creator and founder of the universe, created the rational soul, he granted it the ability to remember, understand, will, know, be wise, love, act, and distinguish, along with many other capacities which his eternal goodness judged should be granted to it.

Therefore your assertion is unquestionably proved false. In favoring the Pelagians and stubbornly nourishing their errors, you have presumed to attribute so much to the human will that neither the Pelagians themselves nor anyone else is found to have attributed as much.

Is this the prayer of yours by which, at the beginning of this section (chapter 8, no. 7, section 1), you said that God’s mercy should be sought so that it might lead you into the labyrinth of such great errors?

The apostolic protest has plainly been fulfilled:

> “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly” (James IV, 3).

For the Lord, seeing with his all-powerful gaze and knowing that:

> “The thoughts of human beings are vanity” (Psalm XCIII, 11),

saw that the intention of your soul served vanity rather than truth. Therefore he turned the hearing of his mercy away from a foolish prayer, because, having abandoned will and truth, you fell into such impiety.

## Saint Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

**1112**

[Continuation:] “It is in him, just as in a human being, whose being is one thing and whose understanding is another.”

Let us see how another falsehood of yours works: how the fleshly limbs of Behemoth adhere to one another and one scale is joined to another. For you say:

### John Scotus

*(Chapter 8, no. 8, section 5.)*

“Therefore the human body was first animal before sin, because what had to be added to it for the observance of the commandment was still lacking—that is, the spiritual element. Thus, because something was lacking from the perfection of nature, it was animal; because nothing was lacking to it, it would have been spiritual. Hence,” he says, “it is understood that the first will of man was naturally created free, although something would have been added to it if it wished to keep God’s commandment. Thus, just as the animal body could die because it was not yet perfect, so the free will was still animal in merit, because it could sin as mortal, since it was not yet perfect. This perfection of freedom would be completed after the commandment had been kept, when the will to sin would be entirely removed from it.”

### Correction

You appear to follow the opinion of the first progenitors of our race, who, after sinning by their own will, insolently turned the blame back upon God. For, when questioned, the woman answered: “The serpent deceived me, and I ate” [Gen. 3:13]. But the man said: “The woman whom you gave me as a companion gave me, and I ate” [ibid., 3:12]. They extended the insolence of their answers to the point of attributing the guilt of their transgression not to their own will but to the Creator’s ordering—because he had either admitted the serpent into paradise or given the woman as a companion to the man—as though every creature, rather than the author of nature and of the commandment alone, were to be heard and followed without question. Yet the cause of their transgression was nothing other than the spontaneous turning of free will toward lower things.

You, on the contrary, because you say that death came upon body and soul on account of their imperfection, assign the cause of death to God, who made man imperfect. For if, according to you, he was created imperfect, it follows that his fall, arising from imperfection, is to be attributed not to him but to God. No one who is sound in judgment can doubt how impious and alien to the truth this is.

The Catholic faith, however, firmly holds and proclaims that human nature was created upright and perfect by the supremely and uniquely good Creator, and that it was endowed with all the goods which he judged necessary for it to subsist according to both substances. For, according to the body, nothing honorable was lacking to it, and according to the soul, nothing of beauty was absent from it. Thus, if he had obediently kept the commandment, he would always have possessed, through the gift of an utterly free will, the freedom to cling to the Creator.

Accordingly, he sinned not through any necessity but through the freedom of his own will—a freedom by which he could in no way avoid sin, because, according to you, he was created imperfect. That imperfection itself therefore compelled him to sin: for whoever is forced by imperfection to transgress the commandment of his Creator must be said to have fallen not through freedom of will but through the necessity of imperfection.

It is therefore evident that whatever sin is committed through the necessity of imperfection must be attributed to the author of imperfection. Since this is most absurd, indeed impious, to believe, it remains for us to confess that man was created perfect and transgressed the commandment by the freedom of his will.

For if an imperfect freedom of will was given, it should not be called free at all. Every free being is either perfectly free or, if not perfect, certainly not free. For how is one free who is imperfect in some part of himself? We must not, then, doubt that the first man was created perfect and was not yet subject to any death—a death that was justly imposed upon him in return for the admission of sin.

Even those who have already been committed to death are, in a certain manner, called perfect, as we read: “Noah was a righteous and perfect man” (Gen. 6:9); and the Lord teaches in the Gospel: “Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matt. 5:48); and the Apostle says: “Let us therefore, as many as are perfect, hold this conviction” (Phil. 3:15), and so forth.

It is clear from the earlier, ill-fated portions of your argument that you have labored to establish that free will—that is, free choice, as you understand it—was divinely created for rational creatures, namely angels and human beings. Yet the Catholic faith declares that this gift of God’s undeserved generosity was bestowed upon intellectual creatures, both angelic and human; and yet you plainly stamp the angelic creature too with the mark of imperfection.

For if both—the angel, that is, and the human being—received free choice through the generosity of the Creator, you must either assert that both were imperfect or that they were not endowed equally with freedom of choice. I do not think you would dare the latter, since you have so often asserted that both rational creatures possess free will, even more fully than necessity would require.

If, then, it is established that both were endowed with freedom, it is established that both were created not imperfectly, as you imagine, but perfectly, as the truth requires.

The prophet testifies that the perfect angel was created in the beginning. Rebuking his voluntary fall, he says: “You were the seal of the likeness of God, perfect in beauty, in the delights of the paradise of God” (Ezek. 28:12). And the Lord says to Job: “He is the beginning of the ways of God” [Job 40:14], the explanation of which blessed Gregory gives in his *Book of Morals* XXXII (ch. 48), as follows:

> “It is as though he plainly said: ‘He is sufficient for so many great things with such strength because, when creating the substance of the things of nature, the Creator made him first.’
>
> “For what are the ways of the Lord except his actions, concerning which he says through the prophet: ‘My ways are not like your ways’ (Isa. 55:8)? Behemoth is called the beginning of the ways of God because, when creating all things, he made him first and made him more eminent than the other angels.
>
> “The prophet perceives the eminence of his primacy when he says: ‘The cedars were not higher than he in the paradise of God; the fir trees did not equal his summit; the plane trees were not equal to his branches. No tree of the paradise of God was compared with him in beauty, because he was made beautiful with many thick branches’ (Ezek. 31:8–9). What can the cedars, fir trees, and plane trees signify except those lofty ranks of the heavenly virtues, planted in the everlasting verdure of joy? Although they were created lofty, they were neither placed above nor made equal to him.
>
> “He is said to have been made beautiful with many thick branches because, being set over the other legions, his appearance was made more beautiful in proportion to the multitude [quanto; variant: quanta, “how great”] of angels placed beneath him. This tree in the paradise of God had, as it were, as many thick branches as it had legions of heavenly spirits beneath it.
>
> “He was therefore condemned without pardon when he sinned because he had been created incomparably great. Again, through the same prophet, it is said to him: ‘You were the seal of the likeness of God, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God’ (Ezek. 28:12).
>
> “Since he was about to speak of his greatness at length, the prophet first summed everything up in a single expression. For what good did he not possess if he was the seal of the likeness of God? For from a ring’s signet (signaculum; variant: sigillum, “seal”), a likeness is figuratively expressed such as is possessed essentially in that same seal. Although man too was created in the likeness of God, the angel is credited with something greater: he is said not merely to have been created in the likeness of God but to have been the seal of God’s likeness. Thus, the more subtle he is in nature, the more fully [variant: entirely] the likeness of God is believed to have been expressed in him.
>
> “The same prophet, further indicating the power of his primacy, adds: ‘Every precious stone was your covering: sardius, topaz, and jasper; chrysolite, onyx, and beryl; sapphire, carbuncle, and emerald’ (ibid., 28:13). He named nine kinds of stones because there are nine orders of angels. For when Scripture expressly mentions angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, virtues, principalities, powers, cherubim, and seraphim, it shows how many distinctions there are among the heavenly citizens.
>
> “This Behemoth is described as having been covered with them because he possessed them as his clothing and adornment; and because he surpassed their radiance, he was more brilliant by comparison with them.
>
> “The prophet continues his description: ‘The workmanship of your adornment was gold, and your openings were restored [variant: prepared] on the day when you were created’ (ibid.). The gold was the workmanship of his adornment because he shone with the brightness of wisdom, which he had received when created good.
>
> “Openings are made in stones so that, when bound with gold, they may be joined together in the composition of an ornament and may not fall apart from one another, as though molten gold, filling the openings, fastened them together. The openings of this stone were prepared on the day of its creation because it was created capable of charity.
>
> “If he had wished to be filled with it, he could have remained attached to the standing angels, like stones set in a royal ornament. For if he had made himself penetrable to the gold of charity, he would have been joined to the holy angels and would have remained, as we have said, a royal stone fixed in the ornament.
>
> “This stone therefore had openings, but through the vice of pride they were not filled with the gold of charity. Since stones are bound with gold so that they may not fall, he fell because, although pierced by the craftsman’s hand, he scorned being bound by the bonds of love.
>
> “The other stones, however, which had been pierced in the same way, were bound by charity penetrating one another; and when this one fell, they obtained this as a gift: that they would no longer be separated by falling from the royal ornament.
>
> “The same prophet, still contemplating the height of his primacy, adds: ‘You were a cherub, extended and protecting, on the holy mountain of God; you walked perfect in the midst of fiery stones’ (Ezek. 28:14). The cherub signifies the fullness of knowledge; and he is called this cherub because there is no doubt that he surpassed all in knowledge. He walked perfect in the midst of fiery stones because he stood resplendent in the glory of his creation among the hearts of angels inflamed with the fire of charity.
>
> “He is rightly called extended and protecting. For whatever we protect by extending ourselves over it, we overshadow. Since he is believed to have overshadowed the radiance of the others by comparison with his own brightness, he is said to have been extended and protecting. By overshadowing them, he covered the others, surpassing their greatness by a greater excellence.
>
> “What is there called beautiful with many branches, and here called protecting, is here called by the Lord’s voice Behemoth, the beginning of the ways of God.
>
> “The Lord indicates both the great things in which he was created and the things he lost, so that he may show frightened man what he himself will suffer from the guilt of his pride if he becomes arrogant, since he did not spare in striking the one whom, by creating him, he had raised to such great glory and splendor.
>
> “Let man therefore consider what he deserves when he becomes proud on earth, if even an angel who was set above others is cast down in heaven.
>
> “Hence the prophet rightly says: ‘My sword has become drunk in heaven’ (Isa. 34:5). It is as though he plainly said: ‘Consider with what anger I shall strike the proud of earth, if I did not spare even those whom I created beside me in heaven, striking them because of the vice of presumption.’”

These authorities, worthy of the highest regard and wholly venerable, make it clearer than the sun that both angel and man were created perfect, and that their ruin occurred not through an imperfection of nature but through an abuse of free will.

If the human body could die because it was imperfect, and the soul could sin because it was made imperfect, then the cause of its death would no longer be the sinner’s will but—God forbid—the injustice of the Creator, who made it imperfect for the very purpose that it should necessarily sin and likewise die.

And where is the Apostle’s statement: “Is there injustice with God?” (Rom. 9:14), followed by his answer, “Certainly not”? If, then, as the truth requires, there is no injustice with God, it is clear that, in creating the intellectual creature, he imposed no necessities by which it would be forced, against its will and as a captive, to surrender itself to sin.

If you assign this imperfection to mortality, you do not in any way withdraw from the same impiety. For even if man was originally made in such a way that he could not die if he did not sin, but could die if he did sin, he should not for that reason be called imperfect merely because he could sin. He did what he wished, not compelled by imperfection but attracted by his will. Nor did he die because he acted as an imperfect being, since death occurred because of sin, and sin occurred because of the sinner’s spontaneous turning away through free will.

You are altogether favorable to the Pelagians. Therefore say with them that Adam, whether he sinned or did not sin, was made mortal and would die—an opinion wholly condemned by the Catholic Church (Council of Africa, ch. 1).

He who was created in such a way that he could not die if he did not sin is thereby shown not to have been created imperfect but perfect. For nothing would have been lacking to his perfection if he had not sinned. Without any contamination of death or disease, nourished healthfully by the food of the tree of life, united in blessedness with the society of angels, he would have rejoiced forever.

If you attribute this imperfection to human nature, you must subject our Lord Jesus Christ to the same imperfection. But who would dare to say that his nature was imperfect, of whom we faithfully sing that he is “perfect God, perfect man, subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh”?

Nor should we heed Apollinaris, who denies that Christ had a soul, saying that whatever activity belonged to the soul was performed in him by his divinity; nor the Manichaeans, who deliriously claim that he assumed a phantom body. Rather, with the fullest faith and the most firmly established authority, we must confess that he truly had and has a body and truly had a soul, and that nothing was in any way lacking to him of what he himself, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, had bestowed in the beginning upon human perfection through his omnipotent goodness.

The prophet Isaiah testifies truthfully that he assumed both, when he says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel; he shall eat butter and honey, so that he may know to reject evil and choose good” (Isa. 7:14–15).

For the woman, who is human, could conceive or bear nothing other than what she was—that is, a human being. Nor could Emmanuel, that is, “God with us,” be called anything other than a true human being who was also God. Nor could he eat butter and honey, by which all foods necessary for the human body are comprehended, unless he had a body. Nor could an inanimate corpse know, desire, or touch food except through a soul animating itself. Concerning this the same prophet says: “Cease from the man whose breath is in his nostrils” (Isa. 2:22). No one doubts that both constituents of human nature are included here.

Of him the divine promise to Abraham speaks, saying: “In your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18). And Moses says to the children of Israel: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall hear him” (Deut. 18:18). For what is “like me” except a human being such as I am?

To David the Lord himself says: “I will set the fruit of your womb upon your throne” (Ps. 131:11). The Apostle agrees with this when he says: “Who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. 1:3).

Gabriel also agrees with this when, announcing to the blessed Virgin Mary, he says: “And the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father” (Luke 1:32).

The Lord himself, asking the Pharisees whose son they said the Christ was, and their replying, “David’s,” immediately added: “If therefore he is his son, how does he call him Lord?” (Matt. 22:42–45). While agreeing with their answer and not denying that he was David’s son—that is, a human being from a human being—he nevertheless exalted the eminence of his divinity, proving himself to be Lord of his father, that is, of David. For how could he be the seed of Abraham and the son of David unless he were a true and perfect human being from true and perfect human beings?

Hence the Apostle also says: “For he did not take hold of angels, but he took hold of the seed of Abraham. Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in all things, tempted in all things without sin” (Heb. 2:16–17; 4:15).

Since, therefore, he underwent every human temptation without sin, he plainly declared himself to be a complete and perfect human being.

The Catholic faith holds that our Lord Jesus Christ assumed from the undefiled womb of the virgin, into the unity of his own person—that is, the person of the Son of God—a human being of the condition in which he himself had created the first man.

But if you assert that the first man died through imperfection, it follows that you must also assert that the second man, Christ, died through the same imperfection. Yet he testifies that he died not through imperfection but through power and his own will, when he says: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of myself, and I take it up again” (John 10:18).

The Evangelist says of him: “And he bowed his head and gave up his spirit” (John 19:30). Therefore, since he testifies that he is able to lay down his life and afterward take it up again, he plainly demonstrates that he underwent death not through the necessity of imperfection but through the power of his own will.

Accordingly, if you thought it necessary to show the distinction between the animal and the spiritual human being, you used an outrageously inappropriate term when you called him “imperfect” instead of “not yet spiritual.” If he had kept the commandment, completed the course of his life in the greatest purity by God’s will, and tasted the tree of life, he would have been joined to angelic blessedness and glory.

Having therefore rejected the necessity of imperfection, we confess that he sinned by the freedom of his will and received the punishment of death deservedly because of sin, not through the necessity of imperfection.

But when you assert, “The body was able to die because it had not yet been made spiritual,” you contradict the truth, which the eminent preacher loudly proclaims: “The body indeed is dead because of sin” (Rom. 8:10); and again: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7:24).

The Catholic Church has always held and taught this; against the Pelagians she has defended it with the greatest strength, vindicated it with complete truth, and established it with unconquerable firmness.

Human nature was not compelled to die in its first progenitors by the unavoidable necessity of innate weakness. Rather, on account of its spontaneous crime, it was deservedly handed over to a judgment that was justly imposed.
