## Against John Scotus on Predestination

**1117–1118**

Since you remove the necessity of nature from created beings, it is astonishing that you do not see that, while asserting that human nature can sin through its own imperfection and therefore can die, you subject it to an unavoidable yoke of necessity. Thus it could avoid neither sin nor its punishment—that is, death—because the imperfection of its condition had subjected it to such an inextricable necessity.

You therefore commit an intolerable injury against the Creator of the universe in two respects, namely, against his goodness and his justice. For, while you attribute sin and death to human imperfection, you contradict the goodness of the Creator, who—God forbid—would not have wished to create man perfect, although he would have condemned him after he had been created. Again, while you attribute man’s punishment, that is, death, to the necessity of imperfection, you reject the justice of the Judge; or else, loosening the reins with the pagans, you attribute everything to fate or fortune and utterly destroy divine providence. No one who understands the holy Scriptures even slightly, yet faithfully, is ignorant how contrary all this is to the Catholic faith.

Now, when you assert that you are asking extraordinarily about man’s will before sin (chapter 8, nos. 9–10, section 7), who does not see how absurdly you entangle your arguments? After discussing free will after sin for so long, you suddenly fly back to the question of what that will was like before sin. Since no one doubts this or thinks it needs to be asked, you have most insolently shown that you are devoted to verbosity and self-display.

But we give thanks to God, who has at last deigned to make you confess that the movement of the soul—which we do not doubt is its will, although you directed your intention elsewhere—is brought about by him, that is, by God. Hence Scripture cries out: “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Prov. 8, according to the Septuagint); and the Apostle says: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work according to his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:13).

All Catholic writers agree in this, and the orthodox faith of the holy Church neither keeps silent nor will ever in any way keep silent.

Finally, when you exaggerate the madness of those who, as you say, falsely invent unavoidable and coercive causes of sins within divine predestination, and most impudently assert that they thereby condemn themselves and those who agree with them to everlasting destruction on account of their error, I wonder why you did not first consider yourself. For you, a recent advocate of the necessities of imperfection, have introduced them in such a way that, without the protection of authority, you proclaim that the first man both died and sinned through them.

That all human beings, with the singular exception of the one in whom the prince of this world found nothing, became voluntary slaves of sin—not through the necessity of predestination but through the just and therefore unavoidable judgment of God after the most just condemnation of the first transgression—and that they are even compelled to sin, has already been sufficiently established above and is made clear by the Apostle, who says:

> “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts, and their senseless heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, and four-footed animals, and reptiles.
>
> “Therefore God handed them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they might dishonor their bodies among themselves. They exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. Amen.
>
> “For this reason God handed them over to shameful passions. Their women exchanged natural use for that which is against nature; and likewise the men, abandoning the natural use of the woman, burned in their desire for one another, men committing shameful acts with men, and receiving in themselves the recompense which they ought to have received for their error.
>
> “And since they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge, God handed them over to a disapproved mind, to do things that are not fitting: filled with every kind of injustice, wickedness, fornication, greed, evil; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, malice; whisperers, slanderers, hateful to God, insolent, proud, boastful, inventors of evils, disobedient to parents, senseless, disorderly, without affection, faithless, without mercy.
>
> “Although they knew God’s justice, they did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death—not only those who do them but also those who approve of those who do them” (Rom. 1:21–32).

And the prophet says: “Confusion was poured out upon their princes, and he caused them to wander in a trackless place, and not in the way” (Ps. 106:40).

The Lord himself says through the prophet: “When that prophet has gone astray, I, the Lord, have deceived him” (Ezek. 14:9).

And concerning the deception of Ahab, who listened to his fanatical prophets rather than obeying the prophet of the Lord, and went and fell at Ramoth-gilead, hear how the spirit of error was sought by the Lord, who asked who would go to deceive him. The spirit said: “I shall be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.” And the Lord said: “You shall deceive him and prevail; go out and do so” (1 Kings 22:20, 22).

Again the Apostle says: “He has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens” (Rom. 9:18).

The Lord himself says: “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart” (Exod. 10:27); and again: “For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my strength in you” (Rom. 9:17).

A devout mind attributes all these things not to the fault of God, who causes death, but to the justice of God, who punishes most justly.

### Chapter IX

**That foreknowledge and predestination are spoken of God not properly but by analogy with temporal things**

In the ninth article of your arguments you try to show that foreknowledge and predestination are predicated of God not properly but by analogy with temporal things. In this connection you say:

### John Scotus

*(Chapter 9, no. 2, section 1.)*

“Nothing worthy can be said of God.”

### Correction

It is indeed true that that ineffable, incorporeal, and immutable nature, which is the Trinity, the one true God, cannot be expressed by any signs or words drawn from bodily things. Nevertheless, insofar as the author of the universe himself grants and permits it, and distributes the capacity for receiving according to the gift he has given to those to whom he granted human nature, he willed and ordained that what belongs to him should be worthily proclaimed through the meanings of words.

But when you say (no. 3) that God uses these expressions because of the laborious poverty of human reasoning after the first man’s sin, would it not have been more faithful and truthful to speak of the authority of the divine utterances? For what human reasoning has ever fully known God, or asserted that it did so?

Although certain philosophers have competently said some things about God, insofar as they were touched by him, they were never able, before the promulgation of the divine law, to perceive the sublimity of so great a matter or discover it through their own reasoning. This should rather be attributed to the goodness of God, who, wishing to have himself announced faithfully and truthfully by his own people, did not deprive even those who were alien to the worship of his name of some knowledge—however slight—of his majesty.

Yet, according to the Apostle, “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their desires; claiming to be wise, they became fools” (Rom. 1:21–22).

Since they are said to have known God and to have reasoned about God, can they be said to have known or grasped God—that is, the holy Trinity—through their own disputations? Who is so impoverished in mind and so foolish as to affirm that they apprehended this? It is more credible, therefore, that they first received this knowledge from true preachers and, touched to some extent by the gift of heavenly generosity concerning so great a matter, directed the eye of their mind toward its consideration.

For, as the Apostle says, God revealed himself to them (Phil. 3:15), but because they did not glorify God or give thanks, they became futile in their desires. They had thought that they could grasp him by their own reasoning rather than through piety and divine authority; abandoned to this presumption, they were shown what they could not accomplish by their own powers.

This has rightly happened to you also. While you do not fear subjecting God to their reasonings, deprived of the truth and weighed down by the burden of your own weakness, you rightly succumb.

Having abandoned the rules of the Catholic Fathers, which they prudently and appropriately established on the basis of their examination of the divine utterances, you invent new ones and fail so completely in the matter itself that you find nothing by which you may approve them.

Indeed, in discussing those things that are taken as matters of contrariety, some of which are said absolutely and others conjointly, you testified that no example of an absolute form could be found in God. What benefit, then, was there in establishing a rule for speaking of God whose example cannot be found? I would rather say that you ought to have kept silent than brought forward rules that could be supported by no example.

But what you added (chapter 9, no. 4, section 4)—that it is not easy to affirm of the things that apply only to the man Christ and not also to his divinity, although after the union the inseparable unity of God and man is truthfully proclaimed, and although the things of man are customarily attributed to God and the things of God to man—is wholly contrary to reason. For one thing is divine and another human.

It would therefore have been much better to adhere to the rules of the Fathers than to vanish into your own inventions.

Blessed Augustine, when he discussed this same matter most acutely and, in his customary manner, most magnificently, spoke as follows in Book V of *On the Holy Trinity* (chapters 8, 9, 13, 16):

> “Let us therefore hold this above all: whatever is said of that most excellent and divine Trinity in relation to itself [variant: ‘sublimity’] is said substantially; but whatever is said in relation to something else is said not substantially but relatively.
>
> “So great is the force of the same substance in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit that whatever is said of each in relation to themselves is understood not plurally in the totality but individually.
>
> “For just as the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God—something no one doubts is said according to substance—we nevertheless do not say that there are three gods but one God, the same most excellent Trinity.
>
> “Thus the Father is great, the Son is great, and the Holy Spirit is great; yet we do not say that there are three great beings but one great being. For it was not said of the Father alone, as heretics perversely think, but of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: ‘You alone are the great God’ (Ps. 74:10).
>
> “The Father is good, the Son is good, and the Holy Spirit is good; yet there are not three good beings but one good being, concerning whom it is said: ‘No one is good except one, God’ (Mark 10:18).
>
> “Indeed, so that the Lord Jesus would not be understood merely as a human being when the one who said to him, ‘Good Teacher’ (Luke 18:19), addressed him as a man, he did not say, ‘No one is good except the Father alone,’ but: ‘No one is good except one, God.’ For in the name ‘Father’ the Father himself is pronounced personally; in the name ‘God,’ however, both the Son and the Holy Spirit are included, because the Trinity is one God.
>
> “Position, appearance, places, and times are spoken of God not properly but metaphorically and by analogy. For he is said to sit upon the cherubim (Ps. 79:2), which refers to position; and: ‘Clothed with the abyss as with a garment’ (Ps. 103:6), which refers to appearance; and: ‘Your years will not fail’ (Ps. 102:28), which refers to time; and: ‘If I ascend into heaven, you are there’ (Ps. 138:8), which refers to place.
>
> “As for doing, perhaps it is said most truly of God alone. For God alone acts, and he is not made or subject to suffering, insofar as this concerns his substance, according to which he is God.
>
> “Thus the Father is omnipotent, the Son is omnipotent, and the Holy Spirit is omnipotent; yet there are not three omnipotent beings but one Omnipotent, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, and in whom are all things; to him be glory (Rom. 11:36).
>
> “Whatever, then, is said of God in relation to himself is said similarly [variant: ‘individually’] of each person—that is, of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and at the same time of the Trinity itself, not plurally but individually.
>
> “For it is not one thing for God to be and another for him to be great; rather, his being is the same as his being great, since what he is is also his greatness.”

## On Predestination

Therefore, just as we do not say “three essences” but “one essence,” so we do not say “three magnitudes” but “one magnitude.” By “essence” I mean what is called *οὐσία* in Greek, which we more commonly call “substance.”

Therefore, just as we do not say “three essences,” so we do not say “three magnitudes,” nor “three great ones.” For in things that are great by participation in a great magnitude—things in which being is one thing and being great another, such as a great house, a great mountain, and a great soul—magnitude is one thing and what is made great by that magnitude another. Indeed, magnitude is not the same thing as a great house. Rather, true magnitude is that by which not only the house that is great is great, and by which the mountain is great, whoever is great, but also by which anything else called great is great: so that magnitude itself is one thing, and those things that are called great by it another.

This magnitude is itself originally great, and much more excellent than those things that are great by participation in it. But God is not great by a magnitude that is other than what he himself is, as though God, when great, were a participant in it; otherwise that magnitude would be greater than God, and nothing is greater than God. He is therefore great by the magnitude that he himself is, since he himself is that magnitude. Thus, just as we do not say “three essences,” so neither do we say “three magnitudes”; for in God being is the same as being great.

For the same reason we do not say “three great ones,” but “one great one”: God is not great by participation in magnitude, but is great by himself, who is great, because he himself is his own magnitude. Let this be said also of God’s goodness, eternity, omnipotence, and of all the other categories that can be predicated of God: whatever is said of him in relation to himself is said properly, not metaphorically or by way of likeness—if, indeed, anything can be properly said of him by a human mouth.

But whatever [al., which things] is properly said of the individual persons within the same Trinity is said in no way in relation to themselves, but in relation either to one another or to creation; and therefore it is clear that such terms are said relatively, not substantially.

For just as the Trinity is called one God, great, good, eternal, and omnipotent, and may likewise be called its own deity, its own magnitude, its own goodness, its own eternity, and its own omnipotence, so the Trinity cannot be called “Father” in this manner.

“Father” is therefore said relatively; likewise, “principle” is said relatively, and perhaps something else as well. But “Father” is said in relation to the Son, whereas “principle” is said in relation to all things that are from him.

Likewise, “Son” is said relatively, and “Word” and “image” are also said relatively; in all these names he is referred to the Father, while none of these terms is used of the Father. The Son is also called “principle.” For when he was asked, “Who are you?” he answered: “The beginning, who am also speaking to you” (John 8:25).

But is he the Father’s principle? He wished to show that he was the Creator when he said that he was the beginning, just as the Father is also the principle of creation, since all things are from him. For “Creator” is likewise said relatively to creation, just as “lord” is said relatively to servant.

And therefore, when we call both the Father “principle” and the Son “principle,” we are not speaking of two principles of creation, because the Father and the Son together are one principle of creation, just as they are one Creator and one God.

If whatever acts within itself and generates or produces something is the principle of what it generates or produces, we cannot deny that the Holy Spirit is also rightly called “principle,” since we do not separate him from the designation “Creator.” It is written of him that he works; and certainly he works while remaining within himself, for he is not changed or transformed into any of the things he works.

Consider what he works:

> To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good. To one is given through the Spirit the utterance of wisdom, to another the utterance of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another gifts of healings in the one Spirit, to another workings of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the discernment of spirits, to another various kinds of tongues. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each individually as he wills (1 Corinthians 12:7–11).

He works, certainly, as God does. For who could work such things except God? It is the same God who works all things in all (ibid., 6).

And if we are asked separately about the Holy Spirit, we answer most truly that he is God, and that together with the Father and the Son he is one God. God is therefore called one principle in relation to creation, not two or three principles.

How, then, shall we maintain that nothing is said of God accidentally, except by recognizing that nothing happens to God’s nature by which it is changed, whereas relative accidents arise together with some change in the things of which they are predicated?

For example, “friend” is said relatively; one does not begin to be a friend except when one begins to love. A change of will therefore occurs so that someone may be called a friend.

A coin, however, is called “price” relatively, yet it is not changed when it begins to be a price, nor when it is called a pledge, nor in any similar case.

If, therefore, a coin can be called relatively by many names without any change in itself—so that neither when it begins to be called something nor when it ceases to be called something does any change occur in its nature or form, by which it is a coin—how much more ought we to understand that something may be said relatively of that immutable substance of God in relation to creation in such a way that, although it begins to be said temporally, nothing is understood to have been added to God’s substance itself, but only to the creature to which the term is applied?

“Lord,” he says, “you have become our refuge” (Psalm 89:1). God is therefore called our refuge relatively, for he is referred to us; and he becomes our refuge when we flee to him. But does something then come to be in his nature that was not there before we fled to him? A change therefore occurs in us: before we fled to him we were worse, and by fleeing to him we are made better. In him, however, there is no change.

Likewise, he begins to be our Father when we are regenerated by his grace, because he gave us power to become children of God (John 1:12). Our substance is therefore changed for the better when we become his children; at the same time he begins to be our Father, but without any change in his substance.

What therefore begins to be said of the Lord [al., God] temporally, although previously it was not said, is clearly said relatively. Yet this is not by an accident of God, as though something happened to him, but plainly by an accident of the thing to which he is related: God begins to be called “Lord” relatively [al., “God begins to be called something”].

And when a righteous person begins to be a friend of God, that person is changed; but far be it from us to suppose that God begins to love someone temporally, as though he acquired a new love—something not previously in him [al., which was not previously in him]—since with him neither past things have passed away nor future things have not already been accomplished.]

Thus he loved all his saints before the foundation of the world, just as he predestined them. But when they are converted and find him, they are said to begin to be loved by him, so that what is said may be understood in a way accessible to human feeling.

Likewise, when he is said to be angry with the wicked and peaceful toward the good, they are changed, not he—just as light is harsh to weak eyes and gentle to sound ones, by a change in the eyes themselves, not in the light.]

These rules concerning God the blessed Augustine, inspired by God, has left us with the greatest acuteness and truth, in answer to the subtle arguments of the Arians, who proclaimed with dialectical arguments, in mouth and in their pestilential hearts, the inequality of the holy Trinity.

But you, as the warmth of true charity has grown cold in you, have chosen neither to contend sophistically against the dialectician nor to consult for the simpler brethren. Indeed, while you add what is superfluous, you obscure even what is clear.

Therefore, who does not know that what you wished to place among the catalogue of substantive names as “predestination” (chapter 9, no. 5, section 2) is false? For such terms never signify a relative substance; there is no doubt that they belong to something else. “To destine,” however, is said relatively, just as “to create,” “to make,” “to work,” “to arrange,” “to administer,” and “to judge” are said relatively. These terms certainly do not indicate substance, but are spoken in relation to something: one who destines or predestines destines or predestines something.

Therefore, when we say “to destine,” we are not saying “to be,” but “to arrange something,” just as with “to create,” “to make,” and “to work.” “Destination” is therefore not spoken substantively but relatively. Relative terms do not demonstrate substance. This is proclaimed not only by divine but also by human writings; and the ordinary manner of speech among even the most learned people repeatedly uses “to destine” in the sense of “to order” and “to arrange.”

Predestination is therefore not God’s substance, nor a substantive term for him, but rather a relative term signifying that before the ages he arranged whatever he himself was going to do in time or after time.

Accordingly, although these terms are relative and may properly be predicated of God or concerning God, “predestination” belongs more fittingly to no nature than to that nature which, by the sole power of its omnipotence, was itself to make all things and was able to know and foresee all things beforehand; which, being the Trinity, is one and true God, and works, according to the Apostle, all things “according to the counsel of his will” (Ephesians 1:11).

Although human beings may also be called creators, founders, makers, workers, arrangers, administrators, destiners, and predestinators, he nevertheless is to be called, in a special sense—even though relatively—Creator, Founder, Maker, Worker, Arranger, Administrator, Destiner, and Predestinator, who alone was able to foresee all things before he made them. For he alone did whatever he willed in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the depths: “from him are all things, through him are all things, and in him are all things; to him be glory forever and ever. Amen” (Psalm 113:3; Romans 11:36).

Who, moreover, would not be astonished at your folly? Earlier you asserted that God’s foreknowledge and predestination were his substance; now you insist that, by a metaphorical usage among Latins, terms that never indicate substance are said of him, although it is clear to anyone of even modest intelligence that these terms are relative and in no way substantive.

Nevertheless, I would not deny that God may also be called predestination, not substantially but relatively, just as he may be called refuge, praise, or laudation, although the divine writings in no way commend this usage. Otherwise, just as “creation,” “work,” and “founding” are not substantially God, neither should “destination” or “predestination” be pronounced or acknowledged as substantially God by any Catholic, lest one be convicted of shamelessly—or rather faithlessly—contradicting the clearest authority of reason, the authority of Scripture, and the most truthful arguments of Father Augustine.

## Chapter 10

### On what must be understood in the contrary sense when God is said to know beforehand or predestine the sins, death, or punishments of human beings or angels

The tenth title of your blasphemies is this:

**John Scotus, chapter 10, no. 1, section 1:** “On what must be understood in the contrary sense when God is said to know beforehand or predestine the sins, death, or punishments of human beings or angels.”

### Correction

In this matter, while you serve dialectical and rhetorical arguments, you are altogether deserted by the truth. You divide foreknowledge and predestination, as well as preparation and foreseeing, and assert that they are transferred to God with two different meanings. When they are taken metaphorically, you say that they signify nothing other than what the Creator himself was going to do, either in establishing the substance of the universe and its natural qualities, or in its administration—but only in those whom he foresaw and predestined to be, according to the purpose of his grace, conformed to the image of his Son (Romans 8:28–29).

But when they are understood according to the contrary sense, you say that nothing is to be understood by them except what God permits to occur in the creature he himself made, through the proper and free motion of a rational nature perversely using the natural goods it received through the generosity of its Creator. You say that this is the whole meaning of what is called evil and its varied and manifold punishment.

To put it more briefly for people like me, I will explain. You wish to understand God as foreknowing and predestining only what is good, while he neither foreknows nor predestines what is evil. No one before you is found to have presumed such a perversity, since all the pages of the divine books repeatedly insist that almighty and most just God knows and foreknows not only the deeds but also the thoughts and words of human beings.

For what of this? Is God to be said not to have known beforehand that the first ancestors of our race would sin? Why, then, did he first forbid them the evil of disobedience and later justly condemn them? He certainly prohibited them from sinning, and he foresaw and foreknew what evil the human being would commit through disobedience and what he would receive according to justice.

If he neither foresaw nor foreknew the sins of the human beings who were to perish in the flood, why did he command an ark to be built over a hundred years, so that, after the others had been destroyed because of their sins, Noah alone with his household might be saved?

Why, when announcing Israel’s liberation to Moses, did he say that Pharaoh and the Egyptians would harden their hearts obstinately amid so many and such great plagues? (Genesis 6:1ff.; 7:1ff.; Exodus 4:21.)

If he neither foresaw nor foreknew the crimes and many sins of that same people of Israel, why did he explicitly command them to abstain from every sin? When he deigned to address them with divine majesty and authority amid fire, darkness, thunder, and flashing lightning, he began thus:

> I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. You shall have no other gods before me. You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor any likeness that is in heaven above, or on the earth below, or in the waters under the earth. You shall not worship them or serve them. You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain. Remember to keep the sabbath day holy. Honor your father and your mother, so that you may live long upon the land that the Lord your God will give you. You shall not kill. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor. You shall not covet your neighbor’s house, nor desire his wife, nor his servant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his donkey, nor anything that belongs to him (Deuteronomy 5:6ff.).

And there are the other things contained in the sequence of the divine law.

How can God be believed to have prohibited all these things if he neither foresaw nor foreknew that human beings would do them? Why did he so often, with such insistence and, so to speak, such importunity—but importunity that was timely—foretell through so many prophets the future sins of human beings and their punishments, if he neither foresaw nor foreknew them?

But why is it necessary to repeat at greater length what is as familiar to everyone as it is common in their reading? God is therefore said to have foreseen and foreknown sins—not, as you wrongly think, in the contrary sense, but truthfully: he prohibited them from being committed, foretold that they would be punished, and condemned them once committed.

**John Scotus, chapter 10, no. 2, section 1:** “Therefore, when we hear that God foreknew, predestined, or prepared sins, or death, or the punishments of those whom he justly abandoned,”

Who has said this, or even conceived it in thought? God is said to have foreknown sins, death, or punishments; but I have never found or read that God predestined or prepared sins before you. On the other hand, prophetic and apostolic writings proclaim that he predestined or prepared death or punishments for sinners. But because you confuse foreknowledge and predestination, treating them as one, you say that God predestined and prepared sins—something no Catholic has ever thought or said. We have already discussed the difference between foreknowledge and predestination above, and we will not hesitate to discuss it again when appropriate.

Therefore, when God is said to have foreknown sins, death, and punishments, we should not understand this in the contrary sense, by the figure called antiphrasis, as you deliriously do. We should understand it according to the rule established for us by all orthodox interpreters: in accordance with the authority of the holy Scriptures, God is described not only as having foreknown these things, but also as having punished them and as going to punish them.

And when you add:

**John Scotus, chapter 10, no. 3, section 2:** “That class of evils which, although naturally good, is called evil by the same rule of contrariety, such as that eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41).

### Correction

The exposition of the Catholic teachers proves this to be false. They repeatedly teach that these things are called evils not in the contrary sense, as you foolishly suppose, but from the perspective of those who suffer them, who regard them as evils.

Among these teachers is Saint Jerome. Explaining what the prophet said—“If there is evil in a city which the Lord has not done” (Amos 3:6)—Jerome writes:

> “The evil that the Lord has done in the city is not contrary to virtue, but is affliction and suffering, concerning which we read: ‘Sufficient for the day is its trouble’ (Matthew 6:34), that is, tribulation and distress. And in the prophet we read: ‘I am God, who made light and darkness, who make peace and create evils’ (Isaiah 45:7). For just as darkness is contrary to light and day, so war is contrary to peace; yet war is not evil in itself, but appears evil to those who endure it.”

And so that we may know that in the holy Scriptures “evil” is sometimes understood not as contrary to virtue but as affliction, punishment, and distress, let us take one more example from Jonah:

> “God saw their works, that they had turned from their very evil ways, and God relented concerning the evil that he had said he would do to them” (Jonah 3:10).

The evil there is certainly the overthrow [al., destruction] of the Ninevites, which God had threatened through the prophet. It is not contrary to virtue, which pertains to sin, for which he threatens [al., will threaten] punishment to sinners.

This same point he develops in nearly all his books. That God foreknew sins and punishments he also stated in his *Exposition of the Prophet Malachi*, as follows (on Malachi 1:2):

> “Israel—that is, Judah, to whom the word and vision of the Lord used to come—must bear the burden of the gravest punishments because of its deeds, so that it may lay aside its more serious sins and experience through sufferings what it did not experience through benefits.”

And lest punishment toward his own people seem unjust, the Lord adds:

> “For whom the Lord loves, he disciplines [al., chastises], and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:6).

And by saying “I have loved,” he reveals the present by confessing the past. They respond to him with the boldness with which they sin, having forgotten his benefits: “In what way have you loved us?” (Malachi 1:2).

To this the Lord replies, leaving aside the rest:

> “Since you have recently returned from the captivity of Babylon, I will discuss your origins. Before you were born—indeed, before Rebecca brought forth Esau and Jacob from her womb—I loved you in Jacob and hated the Edomites in Esau” (Genesis 25:23).

The Apostle Paul, expounding this passage mystically, joins together two testimonies, one from Genesis and one from Malachi, in his letter to the Romans:

> “And Rebecca also had conceived by one man, our father Isaac. For when the children had not yet been born and had done nothing either good or evil, so that God’s purpose according to election might stand, not because of works but because of him who calls, it was said to her: ‘The elder shall serve the younger.’ As it is written: ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated’” (Romans 9:10–13).

The phrase “as it is written” refers both to the book of Genesis (Genesis 25:23) and to the prophet Malachi (Malachi 1:2). He does not merely say, “I loved Jacob before he was born, and I hated Esau before he was brought forth from his mother’s womb”; he also preserved his love and hatred toward their descendants.

He preserved hatred toward Esau, whose mountains, called Seir, he reduced to a wilderness, whose cities he made desolate and caused to be inhabited by serpents and wild beasts (Malachi 1:3). But if Edom—that is, Esau—should say, “We have been destroyed by God’s anger, but we will rebuild the cities [al., city],” understand from the Lord’s declaration that when they build, he will destroy; and their perpetual desolation will demonstrate his anger (ibid., 4).

Hatred toward Esau was therefore shown in events, while love toward you—that is, toward Jacob—is demonstrated in what follows, when they have been destroyed and reduced to solitude:

> “Your eyes shall see, and you shall say: ‘The Lord is magnified beyond the borders of Israel’” (ibid., 5).

From comparison with the evils suffered by your brother, you will recognize God’s benefits toward you, and so forth.

Moreover, God’s love and hatred arise either from foreknowledge of future things or from works.

The same point appears in his exposition of Amos (3:12):

> “I know your many crimes and your strong sins” (Amos 5:12).

This “knowledge” is not to be understood according to what we read elsewhere—“The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2:19)—but in the sense that nothing escapes God, and that he recognizes all the thoughts of sinners.

“I have known,” he says, “many impieties, which are not only many but also strong, oppressing or trampling down the just person, or justice itself, or the one who is just” (Amos 5:12).

Behold this teacher, renowned throughout the world for the glory of sacred learning: he clarifies the prophetic words everywhere, not in the contrary sense, as you dream, but according to the rule we have mentioned, a rule commonly used by all interpreters.

If God did not foresee evils, what is the meaning of his saying to Abraham, under the forms of a heifer, a goat, a ram, a dove, and a turtledove, that the condition of peoples would arise from him—including the spiritual peoples who would belong to the seed in which all nations were to be blessed, that is, our Lord Jesus Christ? There would also be future carnal peoples who would be deprived of the same seed. He speaks as follows:

> “Know in advance that your seed shall be a stranger, and they shall afflict them for four hundred years in a land that is not theirs. But I will judge the nation whom they will serve” (Genesis 15:13).

So many years beforehand, the Lord commands Abraham to know and foreknow, and foretells, the evils of the Egyptians, by which they were to rage against God’s people and for which they were to receive the most just retribution. And you deny that God foreknew evils?

**John Scotus, chapter 10, no. 4, section 3:** “Whatever he declares that human beings know by foreknowing, he shows that he himself knows and foreknows.”

The Prophet confirms this, saying:

> “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are futile” (Psalm 94:11).

And again:

> “O God, you know my foolishness, and my sins are not hidden from you” (Psalm 69:6).

And again:

> “You foresaw all my ways, for there is no word on my tongue that you, Lord, did not know. Behold, you know all things, the last and the first” (Psalm 139:3–5).

And likewise:

> “You alone know the hearts of human beings” (Proverbs 15:11).

And Solomon says:

> “You see what is in the human heart, Lord; in your book all things are written. Human beings look upon the face, but the Lord looks upon the heart” (Psalm 139:16; 1 Samuel 16:7).

And again:

> “For he searches every heart and understands every thought of the mind” (1 Chronicles 28:9).

And the Apostle:

> “The word of God is living and effective, sharper than any two-edged sword, penetrating to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions. No creature is invisible in his sight; everything is naked and exposed to his eyes” (Hebrews 4:12).

He is called “the discerner of thoughts,” and this proves that he knows and judges both good and evil thoughts.

The blessed Job also humbly confesses to him:

> “I know that you can do all things, and that no thought is hidden from you” (Job 42:2).

If no thought is hidden from him, it follows that evil thoughts are not hidden either. Thus the Lord is frequently described in the Gospels as seeing the thoughts of the wicked. When he said to the paralytic, “Your sins are forgiven,” the scribes and Pharisees began to say within themselves—that is, in their thoughts—“This man blasphemes. Who can forgive sins except God alone?”

When the Lord saw their thoughts, he said:

> “What kind of thoughts are these? Why are you thinking evil things in your hearts?” (Matthew 9:2–4).

Without doubt, he showed that he saw and reproved their evil thoughts. But how could he see or rebuke their evil thoughts if he did not know them?

The same is said to have happened with a Pharisee to whose meal he had been invited. While he mercifully received the repentance of the sinful woman, who testified to it with her tears and her hair, he both saw and restrained the Pharisee’s thoughts:

> “The Pharisee said within himself: ‘If this man were a prophet, he would certainly know who and what sort of woman this is who touches him, that she is a sinner’” (Luke 7:39).

The Lord undoubtedly confronted the Pharisee’s corrupt and most evil thoughts with power, while mercifully absolving the repentant woman.

Again, when the Lord was attacked by the Pharisees because his disciples ate without washing their hands (Matthew 15:2), he answered:

> “Eating with unwashed hands does not defile a person, but what comes out of the heart defiles a person. For from the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, envies, blasphemies; these are what defile a person” (ibid., 17–20).

I therefore ask whether he knew these things or did not know them. If he did not know them, how did he explain them? It is therefore evident that the Lord knows the sins that he reproves, forbids people to commit, and does not allow to pass unpunished once committed.

Was he ignorant of the evil of Judas the betrayer and of the Jews who persecuted him, when he foretold it so long beforehand? He says:

> “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that has been written concerning the Son of Man will be accomplished. For he will be handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, scourged, spat upon, and crucified” (Matthew 20:18–19).

And during the meal:

> “One of you will betray me” (Matthew 26:21).

And to the betrayer himself:

> “What you are going to do, do quickly” (John 13:27).

And to the apostles:

> “You will all be scandalized because of me on this night” (Matthew 26:31).

And specifically to the blessed Peter, his most faithful confessor:

> “Amen, amen, I say to you: on this night, before the cock crows twice, you will deny me three times” (Mark 14:30).

And in the Apocalypse:

> “To the angel of the church of Laodicea write: ‘These things says the Amen, the faithful and true witness, the beginning of God’s creation: I know your works, that you are neither cold nor hot. Would that you were cold or hot! But because you are lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I am beginning to vomit you out of my mouth. Because you say, “I am rich, I have grown wealthy, and I need nothing,” and you do not know that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked’” (Revelation 3:14–17).

If, I say, God neither foresaw evils nor prepared punishments, why did he foretell so long beforehand that the children of Israel would be captured by the Assyrians and Babylonians; likewise, that the Assyrians and many other nations would be captured by the Babylonians; that the Babylonians themselves would be captured by the Medes and Persians; that these in turn would be captured by the Greeks; that the Greeks would be captured by the Romans; and that the Romans themselves would finally be destroyed?

All the prophetic pages resound with the declaration that they were handed over because of their crimes and impiety toward God, and that their persecutors were raised up for this purpose, although those very persecutors are sometimes also found to have been false.

For example, Rabshakeh [al., Necho], who said that the Lord had commanded him to come against Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 35:21).

It is also read in Genesis that the Lord said to Cain:

> “What have you done? Cursed are you upon the earth, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your hand. You shall be a fugitive and a wanderer—or trembling—upon the earth” (Genesis 4:11–12).

Here his sin is reproved and punishment inflicted by the Lord.

If the Lord neither foresaw death nor punishment, who brought the waters of the flood by which, apart from those in the ark, all flesh was destroyed? It was he himself who said to Noah:

> “The end of all flesh has come before me. The earth is filled with iniquity because of them, and I will destroy them together with the earth. Behold, I will bring the waters of the flood upon the earth, to destroy all flesh in which there is the breath of life under heaven; everything that is on the earth shall perish” (Genesis 6:13, 17).

If he neither foresaw the death and punishments of the impious, who burned the Pentapolis with heavenly fire? Yet truthful Scripture testifies that the Lord rained fire and sulfur from the Lord upon Sodom and the neighboring cities (Genesis 19:24). Who is “the Lord from the Lord” except the Son from the Father?

If the Lord did not prepare punishments for sinners, who, taking vengeance upon Pharaoh and his servants for their hardness, struck them with so many plagues? Scripture certainly cries out that the Lord did and inflicted all these things. Thus the Lord himself speaks to Pharaoh through Moses:

> “For this very purpose I have raised you up, to show my strength in you, and so that my name may be proclaimed throughout all the earth” (Romans 9:17).

Finally, who brought the waters of the Red Sea upon them with such powerful destruction that, surrounded by waters flowing from both sides, they were all overwhelmed and none of them escaped?

If you wish to say that God divided the sea but that someone else—I do not know who—brought it back together, who would not laugh at your folly? Scripture says:

> “For Pharaoh’s horse went in with his chariots and horsemen into the sea, and the Lord brought the waters of the sea back over them.”

And again:

> “Your right hand, Lord, is glorious in strength; your right hand, Lord, struck down the enemy, and in the greatness of your glory you overthrew my adversaries” (Exodus 15:19, 6), and so forth.

If the Lord neither predestined nor prepared death and punishments, who decreed that human beings who transgressed his commandments should be stoned or killed by other forms of death? Scripture most clearly declares that God commanded and did all these things. It also repeatedly affirms that, after the death of Joshua, God raised up adversaries against the children of Israel because of their sins.

The history of Kings likewise tells of Solomon: after he had offended God, God raised up adversaries against him, including Hadad the Edomite and others.

If all these matters are understood in the contrary sense, according to your perversity, every truth would be entirely removed from them.

The blessed Augustine himself makes it perfectly clear—especially in the fourteen books that he composed on the Pentateuch with marvelous learning, as in nearly all his other works—that they are not to be understood as you invent.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Amos:

> “I struck you with scorching wind and mildew. Your gardens and vineyards, your olive trees and fig trees, the locust devoured; yet you did not return to me, says the Lord. I sent among you death on the way to Egypt. I struck your young men with the sword …”

## S. PRUDENTIUS

### 4131

“...and into the captivity of your horses; and I caused the decay of your camps to rise into your nostrils, and you did not return to me, says the Lord.”

Therefore Saint Jerome spoke as follows (*In Amos* II):

> “[Israel is instructed through every scourge and torment. Hence, at the time when they were seeking help from the Egyptians, death is sent against them; their young men are struck down with the sword, and the captivity of the horses which they multiplied for themselves against God’s command—[variant: had multiplied]—shuts them up cruelly, so that the decay of the camps and the stench of the dying army fill the nostrils of the survivors. Even after he had done these things, in order to rebuke the delinquents and correct those who had gone astray, they still did not return to him, says the Lord.]”

And in the prophet Jonah we read:

> “And God prepared a worm at the rising of dawn, and it struck the gourd, and it withered. And when the sun had risen, God commanded a hot and scorching wind, and the sun struck Jonah’s head, and he fainted” (Jonah 4:7).

Behold, God is said to have prepared a worm which, as punishment for the disobedient prophet, ate the *kikaion*—a gourd which had sprung up in a single night by God’s wondrous power and suddenly afforded the shelter of green shade. When the sun had risen, the Lord commanded a hot, scorching wind, which struck the prophet so severely that, overcome by the heat, he asked that his soul might die.

The same teacher, explaining the prophet Micah, Jerome (*In Mic. III, 4*):

> “[And they will suffer all these things, he says, because they acted most wickedly in their pursuits and pleasures. They were not kings but tyrants, nor governors but lions, nor masters of disciples but wolves of sheep. They gorged themselves on flesh and grew fat, and, like the fattest sacrificial victim, they were prepared for slaughter [variant: for the slaughter] and for the Lord’s punishments.]”

Likewise, in his exposition of the prophet Habakkuk, explaining the prophetic words, “Lord, I heard your report, and I was afraid,” Jerome (*Habakkuk III, 1*) says:

> “[I heard, he says, the punishments which you prepared for Nebuchadnezzar and the devil.]”

Likewise, in his exposition of the prophet Zechariah (*Zech. XI, 7*):

> “[When, however, we read according to the Septuagint, ‘And I will pasture the sheep of slaughter in the land of Canaan,’ we can understand it as meaning that the Lord pastures and nourishes the Jewish people, who have been destined for death, scattered throughout the whole world—that is, in the land of Canaan and among the nations—in order to be sacrificed.”

In the same work (*ibid., discourse XI, 11*):

> “The Jewish people, to whom it is said, ‘Seed of Canaan,’ and not ‘of Judah,’ who is now guarded by my rites”—or because they interpret *Canaan* as “humiliation”—“will recognize that they were formerly prepared to be humbled by the Lord.”

Likewise, in his exposition of the prophet Habakkuk, explaining the words of the Lord:

> “Behold, I am raising up the Chaldeans, a bitter and swift nation, marching over the breadth of the earth in order to possess dwelling-places not its own; it is horrible and terrible” (Habakkuk 1:6),

and so forth, after the historical interpretation he adapted an allegorical interpretation as follows (*In Habac. I, 6*):

> “[God is aroused against the despisers and calumniators of his providence. He says that he will raise up the Chaldeans, who are interpreted as signifying demons or the worst angels, who minister to his fury, wrath, and the tribulation which he inflicts upon sinners, or through whom he torments the souls of wicked men. The Chaldean nation is bitter and swift; it spares no one and quickly accomplishes whatever it has been commanded. It walks over the breadth of the earth, for broad and spacious is the way that leads to death” (Matthew 7:13).”

Likewise, in the prophet Obadiah (*Obadiah 16*):

> “For how did you rejoice in their destruction and celebrate a feast on my holy mountain”—that is, you drank in the Church, not my cup but the devil’s? Concerning this it is said in Habakkuk: “Woe to him who gives his neighbor drink from a turbid overturning” (Habakkuk 2:15).

Thus either all nations assigned to punishments, or all opposing powers, will drink and consume your blood.

But now, because you accuse us more sharply of having been designated by the epithet of heresy, and of possessing no light by which we can see that evil arises from the perverse movement of free will, we, on the contrary, knowingly and through the grace of God, understanding the source of evil and sufficiently and abundantly instructed in it, say and wish: would that you possessed humbly from heaven the light which you most arrogantly deny us, and did not stumble into so great, so wicked, and so perverse an error. You would then see how falsely you have said:

> “Those whom he justly abandoned”—that is, “he permitted to be punished by their own perversity.”

For you wish it to be understood that the punishment and chastisement of the sinner is nothing other than his own perversity, so that you entirely remove both death and the punishments inflicted upon sinners by God’s just judgment, and pretend that only their own conscience is a punishment. Because Origen falsely taught this, he incurred the sentence of just condemnation.

When you say, “Every evil, therefore, is either sin or the punishment of sin,” it is astonishing that you did not consider that nothing can in any way be punished by nothing. If, then, sin is nothing, and its punishment likewise nothing, I do not see how nothing can be punished by nothing. Indeed, I affirm that the whole of this is nothing; but I confess with the Catholic Church that sin is punished by God as judge, whose prohibition and condemnation of it are most certainly demonstrated.

Whenever someone is said to be condemned by his own iniquity, this should rather be understood to mean that, because of his own deserts, the sinner is justly condemned by him who judges all things. Likewise, whenever sin is called the iniquity, crime, or impiety of its perpetrators and is said to be repaid to them, sound understanding perceives that a punishment fully worthy of their deserts is most justly repaid to them—not sins in place of sins, or crimes in place of crimes.

So, too, when sins are said to be “visited,” it is believed that not the sins themselves, which are not substances, but their authors and lovers receive the sentence of retribution. And what you add:

### JOHN SCOTUS

(*Chapter 40, number 6, Ecclesiastical...*)

> “If no true argument permits one to say that God foreknows these two things, how much less that he predestines them—who would dare say this except contrariwise?”

## DE PREDESTINATIONE

### 1132

“How much more, then, does he predestine?” Who would dare say this except by contradiction?

### CORRECTION

We have already said that God truly foreknows sins alone, and does not also predestine them; but we freely confess that he both foreknows and predestines their punishment. Yet I cannot explain sufficiently how astonished I am at your blindness: although you have hitherto asserted that foreknowledge and predestination are one and the same, to the point of insisting that they differ in nothing, now you have placed them with a certain distinction, saying:

> “If no true reason permits God to foreknow these two,”

and adding:

> “How much more does he predestine them.”

You do not permit these words to be understood without some distinction between them. You confirm this very point in what follows, saying:

### JOHN SCOTUS

(*Chapter 10, number 7, section 3*)

> “Likewise, if predestination is nothing other than the preparation of those things which God foresaw would be done, how can the predestination of those things which God neither did nor prepared to be done be called predestination?”

### CORRECTION

In confirming, therefore, that predestination is nothing other than the preparation of those things which God foresaw would be done, you are plainly shown to separate it from foreknowledge. For no preparation can in any way be spoken of without foreknowledge, whereas foreknowledge is very frequently found without preparation. We foreknow many things that are to be done by our servants or by others, although we ourselves do not prepare them.

It is therefore clear that predestination differs greatly from foreknowledge, since you define it as nothing other than the preparation of those things which God foresaw would be done. For we say that God, the creator of all things that exist insofar as they exist, foreknows all things, whether they are from him or are not from him.

All creatures are from him: foreknowing them, he predestined and created them, just as he ordered and arranged them. Sins are not from him. He neither created them nor wished them to occur; indeed, he prohibited them. They are therefore called “nothing” because they are not created substances, but the depraved wills and perverse movements of rational substances created by God, culpably and damnably distorted toward evil.

No faithful person may doubt that it is impious and alien to truth and piety to say that God neither sees, nor knows, nor judges any movements of the creatures he himself made. He sees whenever, however, and wherever his creatures move, and likewise judges them. Therefore he should not be said merely to see and judge them as though they had previously been unknown to him, but as things which, before they came to be, he foreknew, foresaw, and judged.

While they are occurring, he knows, sees, and judges them; once they have occurred, he does not judge them by some new judgment previously unknown to him, but by the judgment through which he predestined them before the ages according to that foreknowledge which neither errs nor changes. As the most just retributor, he punishes and condemns.

It is therefore true that the predestination of those things which God neither made nor prepared to be done does not exist; but the predestination of those things which God either made or prepared to be done does exist—that is, their disposition and preordination. The authority of the divine utterances and the unanimous agreement of orthodox teachers teach this most harmoniously.

Accordingly, we have often said and confess that the evil which is sin—whether it is called corruption or defect of the good—is not God, was not created by him, and was not pleasing to him. But its consequences, that is, punishments, occur with no other author and judge than God. We proclaim this with complete freedom, because the prophet says:

> “The Lord loves righteousness; his countenance has seen equity” (Psalm 11:8).

We know without doubt that it belongs to his justice to punish the transgressor who prohibited transgression and not to leave unpunished the violator whom he kindly warned not to transgress.

If you paid attention to the true light and humbly sought to be illuminated by it, you would see how contradictory are the claims you yourself make when you say:

> “These things”—that is, sin, death, and misery—“having abandoned the one principle of all things, return downward into nothingness and cause the goods which they corrupt to perish” (*Chapter 10, number 8, section 4*),

although above you said that no nature perishes. For who does not know that what returns into nothingness perishes?

Argue as much as you wish, therefore, and deny that sins, death, and punishments are either foreknown or predestined by God because they are nothing; and whenever anything of this sort is read in Scripture, understand it contrariwise.

But the Catholic faith, following the rules carefully set down by the Fathers, will faithfully teach that God both knows and foreknows sins, and predestines and prepares death and punishments for them. For God, eternal and true wisdom and justice, prohibits not nothing but something, and punishes not nothing but something.

That he prohibits sins—that is, the perverse movements of an evil will and the wicked uses of the bodily members—and justly inflicts suitable punishments upon them is proclaimed throughout the divine Scriptures, as we have already touched upon briefly.

Your blindness, therefore, is remarkable—or rather lamentable: by a portent unheard of among all people before you, you attempt to overturn, through a most perverse interpretation, the whole unshaken truth of the holy Scriptures, teaching that things truly said—and also our statements, so often and maliciously imputed to us by you—must be understood falsely. Yet, with the Lord illuminating our darkness insofar as he deigns to grant and aid us, we assert and hold that same truth unshakably.

If that truth had shone upon you even somewhat, you would certainly never have said:

> “Predestination and foreknowledge are the nature of God” (*Chapter 10, number 9, section 5*).

For, as the preceding arguments abundantly confirm, relative terms do not designate natures and substances. No one doubts that these are relative terms. It is therefore false that foreknowledge and predestination are the nature of God. The one who foreknows foreknows something else, and the one who predestines predestines something else.

If, I say, foreknowledge and predestination are the nature of God, it will follow that he foreknew and predestined himself as future. But this could not happen unless his foreknowledge and predestination were absurdly said to have existed before him, and unless he were impiously divided into two things. Everyone sees how impious and blasphemous this is. For God is not one thing in being and another in knowing; rather, for him, knowing is being.

For this knowledge is not an accidental good for him, as it is for us, who may happen not to know many things. Not-being does not befall him; rather, knowledge, like wisdom, is truly predicated of his nature and substance.

As Augustine says, his knowledge is in no way altered so that he does one thing in it concerning things that do not yet exist, another concerning things that already exist, and another concerning things that have existed. He does not, in our manner, look ahead at what will be, look at what is present, or look back at what has passed. Rather, in a certain other manner, far different from the habit of our thoughts, he sees all things.

His thought does not change from this to that. He sees everything altogether and immutably, so that things which occur temporally are future before they are, present when they are, and past when they are no longer; but he comprehends all of them in a stable and eternal present. He does not see one way with his eyes and another with his mind, for he is not composed of soul and body, nor is he one way now, another previously, and another afterward.

His knowledge, unlike ours, is not changed by the variation of the three times—present, past, and future—for with him there is no change and no shadow of turning. His attention does not pass from thought to thought; in his incorporeal vision all that he knows is present simultaneously. He moves temporal things without undergoing temporal movements of his own.

There, therefore, he saw that what he made was good, where he saw that it was good to make it. When he saw that it had been made, he did not double his knowledge or increase it in any respect, as though his knowledge had previously been less perfect. He could not have worked so perfectly unless his knowledge had been equally perfect, with nothing added to it by his works.

Nor does God repent of any work of his as a human being does. His judgment concerning all things is as fixed as his foreknowledge is certain.

“How, then, can the Lord repent of anything?” (Augustine, *To Simplicianus*, book II, question 2, throughout.)

We, however, when we add this concerning God in the divine Scriptures, judge it unworthy to think of him in that manner; yet something must be said by which this may in some way be demonstrated. Since his eternal power and divinity wonderfully and unquestionably exceed all the words by which human conversations are conducted, whatever is said of him in human terms—even what would appear contemptible among human beings—reminds human weakness that the expressions which it considers appropriately used in the holy Scriptures concerning God are more suited to human capacity than to divine sublimity.

Accordingly, even this language itself must be transcended by sounder understanding [variant: by a sounder understanding], just as these partial analogies have been transcended. For what human being would not recognize that repentance is impossible in God, who foreknows all things? Yet Scripture certainly contains the two words “repentance” and “foreknowledge,” of which, because we have believed that one is fitting for God—namely, foreknowledge—we deny repentance in him.

But when another person, examining these matters more clearly, asks how foreknowledge itself is fitting for God, and discovers that even the meaning of this word is surpassed far and wide by his ineffable divinity, he does not wonder that both terms can be used of God for the sake of human beings, although neither can properly be used of him for his own sake.

For what is foreknowledge except knowledge of future things? But what is future for God, since he transcends all times? If God’s knowledge possesses the things themselves, they are not future for him but present. Consequently, it should no longer be called foreknowledge but simply knowledge.

If, however, as happens among temporal creatures, future things do not yet exist for him, but he anticipates them by knowing them, then he experiences them twice: first according to foreknowledge of future things, and afterward according to knowledge of things present. Thus something temporal would be added to God’s knowledge, which is most absurd and false. For he could not know in their arrival the things he foreknew were coming unless they became known to him twice—first by foreknowing them before they existed, and then by knowing them when they already existed.

Thus, contrary to the truth, something temporal would be added to God’s knowledge, since temporal things which are foreknown are also perceived as present, though they were not perceived before they came to be, but only foreknown [variant: foreseen]. If, when the things foreknown as coming [variant: as future] arrive, nothing new occurs in God’s knowledge, but that foreknowledge remains as it was even before the things arrived, how can it then be called foreknowledge, when the things are no longer future?

They are now present—the things which he saw as future—and shortly afterward they will be past. But the foreknowledge of past things, just as of present things, cannot in any way be called foreknowledge.

We are therefore brought back to the position that, once things are present, knowledge arises concerning them which had been foreknowledge when those same things were future. If what was previously foreknowledge afterward becomes knowledge in God, this admits change and makes it temporal, although God truly and supremely is, is not changeable in any respect, and does not know through any new temporal movement.

It is therefore preferable not to speak of God’s foreknowledge but only of his knowledge. Let us ask how this is possible. For among ourselves we do not ordinarily speak of knowledge except when we retain in memory things sensed and understood—that is, when we remember that we sensed or understood something, so that we may recall whatever we wish.

If this is so in God, so that he can properly be said to understand and to have understood, to sense and to have sensed, then he is subject to time, and that changeability which must be removed far from God’s substance is nevertheless introduced.

Yet God both knows and foreknows in an ineffable manner. In this way he also repents in an ineffable manner.

Although God’s knowledge is so far removed from human knowledge that comparison between them is laughable, both are nevertheless called knowledge. Human knowledge is such that the Apostle says of it:

> “Knowledge will be destroyed” (1 Corinthians 13:9).

This cannot rightly be said of God’s knowledge.

Human anger is likewise turbulent and not without anguish of soul. But God’s anger is described in the Gospel:

> “The wrath of God remains upon him” (John 3:36),

and the Apostle says:

> “For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness” (Romans 1:18).

God exercises vengeance in wondrous equity while that tranquility continually remains in the creature subject to him.

Human mercy also contains a certain misery of the heart, which is why it received its name in Latin. Hence the Apostle exhorts us not only to rejoice with those who rejoice but also to weep with those who weep (Romans 12:15). Yet who in his right mind would say that God is touched by any misery, whom Scripture everywhere bears witness to be merciful [variant: of great mercy]?

We understand human anger and jealousy as inseparable from the plague of envy. But God’s jealousy—mentioned in Exodus 20:5 and 34:14—is not like this: the word is the same, but not the manner.

It would take too long to go through the other examples, and they are innumerable. They show that many divine attributes are called by the same names as human attributes, although they are separated from them by an incomparable difference.

The same names are not, however, given to both things without reason. Things known to us, which occur in daily life and become familiar through ordinary experience, provide some path toward understanding those sublime realities.

When I remove from human knowledge its mutability and its transitions from one thought to another—when we recall something in order to behold mentally what was not present in our vision a little earlier, and thus leap repeatedly from one part to another through recollection, which is why the Apostle says that our knowledge is partial—when I remove all these features and retain only the lively force of a firm and unshaken truth, illuminating everything in a single eternal contemplation—or rather, I do not retain it, since human knowledge does not possess this, but conceive of it according to my ability—then the knowledge of God is in some way suggested to me.

The name “knowledge” could be common to both because, through knowing something, a person is not ignorant of it, although even among human beings knowledge is usually distinguished from wisdom. Thus the Apostle says:

> “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:8).

In God, however, these are plainly not two things but one. Among human beings they are reasonably distinguished in this way: wisdom pertains to the understanding of eternal things, while knowledge pertains to things experienced through the bodily senses.

Although someone else may propose another distinction, unless the terms were different the Apostle would not have distinguished them in this way. If the term “knowledge” must be assigned to things which we experience through bodily sensation [variant: has been assigned], then God possesses no knowledge at all; for God does not consist of body and soul in himself, as a human being does.

It is better to say that God’s knowledge is of another kind, not of the same genus as the knowledge called human. Likewise, the very thing called “God” is something entirely different from what is meant when it is said that he “stood in the assembly of the gods”; nevertheless, in both cases the shared word has some connection with not being hidden.

So, too, from human anger I remove turbulent movement, leaving the force of vengeance; in this way I rise, as best I can, toward knowledge of what is called God’s anger.

From mercy I remove compassion, since compassion shares in the misery of the one for whom one feels pity, and I leave the tranquil goodness of giving help and delivering from misery. Thus some kind of knowledge of divine mercy is suggested to me.

Nor should we reject or disdain God’s jealousy when we find it written of him. Rather, let us remove from human jealousy the pallid wasting of grief and the morbid disturbance of the mind; let only that remain by which corruption is not permitted to go unpunished, and we rise toward beginning, in some manner, to grasp God’s jealousy.

Therefore, when we also read God saying, “It repents me” (1 Samuel 15:11), we consider what the act of repenting ordinarily is among human beings. It plainly involves a will to change, but in a human being it is accompanied by sorrow of mind, since he reproaches himself for having acted rashly.

Let us remove, then, those features which arise from human weakness and ignorance, and let only the willing remain that something should not be as it was. In this way we can somewhat suggest to our minds the rule by which we are to understand God’s repentance.

When God is said to repent, he wills that something which he had made to exist should not remain as it was; yet, while it was so, it ought to have been so, and when it is no longer permitted to remain so, it ought no longer to be so. This occurs according to a perpetual and tranquil judgment of equity, by which God disposes all changeable things with unchangeable will.

Since, however, we ordinarily speak with praise of foreknowledge and knowledge in human beings, and since the human race is accustomed to fear anger itself in persons of great power rather than criticize it, we think that such terms are appropriately used of God.

But the one who is jealous, and the one who repents of something, is ordinarily either blamed or corrects a fault in himself; therefore these terms are used of human beings with criticism. For this reason it is disturbing when we read that something of this kind exists in God.

Yet Scripture, consulting the needs of all, includes these expressions precisely so that the more agreeable attributes may not be understood in God in the manner in which they are customarily understood among human beings. Through the things which displease us, since we do not dare to understand them in God exactly as they are found in human beings, we learn also to seek those things which we had thought suitable and fitting in a different way.

For if something may not be said of God because it is displeasing in human beings, then we should not call God unchangeable, since Scripture says reproachfully of human beings:

> “There is no change in them” (Psalm 55:20).

Likewise, some things are praiseworthy in human beings but cannot exist in God, such as modesty, which is a great ornament of vigorous youth, and the fear of God. For the latter is not praised only in the ancient books [variant: was not praised only in the ancient books]; the Apostle also says:

> “Bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God” (2 Corinthians 7:1).

There is certainly no fear of this kind in God.

If, therefore, certain things praiseworthy in human beings are not rightly said of God, then certain things blameworthy in human beings are rightly understood of God—not in the same way as in human beings, but under merely common names and with a wholly different reason and manner.

For shortly afterward the same Samuel, to whom the Lord had said, “It repents me that I made Saul king,” says to Saul concerning God:

> “For he is not like a human being, that he should repent” (1 Samuel 15:11, 29).

Here he clearly shows that even when God says, “It repents me,” the expression is not to be understood in the human manner, as we have already discussed as far as we have been able.

Hear also how that same most subtle disputant distinguishes God’s foreknowledge from his nature, in his sermon on the words of the Apostle:

> “For if a law had been given which could give life, righteousness would truly have been from the law” (Galatians 3:21).

Augustine (*On the Apostle’s Words*, sermon 11):

> “[Those who do not exist are chosen; the one who chooses does not err, nor does he choose in vain. Yet he chooses and possesses the chosen, whom he is going to create and who are to be chosen; he possesses them in himself, not in his nature, but in his foreknowledge.]”

The same author (*City of God*, book XI, chapter 13):

> “But because God foreknew all things, and therefore could not be ignorant that the human being would sin, we ought to assert the holy city according to what he foreknew and arranged, not according to what could not come within our thought [variant: knowledge], because it was not part of God’s dispensation [variant: arrangement]. For human sin could not disturb the divine plan, as though it had compelled God to change what he had established, since by foreknowledge God had anticipated both things: both the human being whom he himself created good, and how evil he would become, and what good he himself would subsequently bring about through him.

“For although God is said to change his decrees—whence Scripture, by a figurative expression, also says that God repented (1 Samuel 15:11)—this is said with reference to what the human being expected or what the order of natural causes required, not with reference to what the Almighty had foreknown that he would do.

“God therefore made the human being upright, as it is written (Ecclesiastes 7:30), and consequently with a good will; for he would not have been upright if he had not possessed a good will. A good will, therefore, is the work of God, since by it the human being was made by him.

“But the first evil will, since all evil works preceded it in the human being, was rather a certain defect from God’s work toward the human being’s own works than any work itself. Its works were therefore evil because they were according to the human being, not according to God, so that the will itself, like the fruit of evil works, was as an evil tree, or the human being insofar as he possessed an evil will.

“Although an evil will is not according to nature but contrary to nature, because it is a defect, it nevertheless belongs to the nature whose defect it is. It cannot exist except in a nature, and that nature was created from nothing by God, not generated by the Creator from himself and in himself [variant: from himself].

“Thus he generated the Word through whom all things were made. Although God formed the human being from the dust of the earth, that same earthly material—indeed, all earthly matter—is entirely from nothing. He also gave the soul, made from nothing, to the body when the human being was made.

“Evil things are so overcome by good things that, although they are permitted to exist to demonstrate how the most provident justice of the Creator can make good use even of them [variant: how he himself can make good use of them through the most provident justice of the Creator], good things can exist without evil—such as God himself, true and supreme, and every heavenly, invisible, and visible creature above this dark earth.

“Evil things, however, cannot exist without good things, because the natures in which they exist, insofar as they are natures, are certainly good. When evil is removed, no nature which had been added is taken away, nor is any part of a nature removed; rather, the nature which had been corrupted and depraved is healed and corrected.

“The freedom of the will is therefore truly free when it does not serve vices and sins. Such freedom was given by God; once lost through its own fault, it cannot be restored except by the one who was able to give it.

“Hence Truth says:

> ‘If the Son makes you free, then you will truly be free’ (John 8:36).

“This is equivalent to saying:

> ‘If the Son saves you, then you will truly be saved.’

“For he liberates from the same source from which he saves.”

But because you attempt, together with Cicero and the Stoics, to overthrow God’s foreknowledge, hear what Saint Augustine discussed concerning it, or against Cicero, when arguing against the astrologers in the fifth book of *The City of God* according to Christian truth (*City of God*, book V, chapter 9):

> “[Cicero, he says, tries to refute them in such a way that he does not think he can accomplish anything against them unless he removes divination. He attempts to remove it by denying that there is knowledge of future things, and insists with all his strength that there is no such knowledge at all, either in human beings or in God, and that there is no prediction of events.
>
