> “Thus he denies God’s foreknowledge and attempts to overthrow every prophecy, clearer than light, through empty arguments, setting against it certain oracles which can easily be refuted, although he himself does not refute them. In refuting the conjectures of the astrologers, his argument prevails, because they are truly such as to destroy and refute themselves.
>
> “Those who assign fate to the stars are much more tolerable than this man, who removes foreknowledge of future things. For it is the clearest insanity both to confess that God exists and to deny that he foreknows the future.
>
> “When he saw this himself, he also attempted to assert what is written:

> ‘The fool says in his heart, “There is no God”’ (Psalm 14:1).

> “But he did not assert it in his own person, for he saw how hateful and troublesome that would be. Therefore, in the books *On the Nature of the Gods*, he made Cotta argue this matter against the Stoics, and, in the case of Lucilius Balbus, to whom he assigned the defense of the Stoic position, he preferred to allow the Stoic view to be stated rather than the view of Cotta, who maintained that no divine nature exists.
>
> “But in the books *On Divination* he openly attacks foreknowledge of future things in his own person. He seems to do all this so that he will not have to admit fate and lose free will. For he thinks that, once knowledge of future things is conceded, fate follows necessarily, and that this cannot be denied at all. But however he...”

[scan page 578]

## On Predestination

…may be brought about by the vain arguments and disputes of philosophers; but we, while confessing the supreme and true God, likewise confess his supreme will, supreme power, and foreknowledge. Nor do we fear that we shall not do something voluntarily because he foreknew that we would do it voluntarily—he whose foreknowledge cannot be mistaken. Cicero feared this and therefore attacked foreknowledge; the Stoics feared it so that they might not say that everything happens by necessity, although they maintained that everything happens by fate.

What, then, did Cicero fear in the foreknowledge of future events, so that he attempted to undermine it with such detestable argument? Clearly, he feared that, if all future events are foreknown, they will occur in the order in which they are foreknown to occur; and if they occur in that order, the order of things is fixed for God, who foreknows them. If the order of things is fixed, the order of causes is fixed as well, since nothing can happen without some efficient cause preceding it. But if the order of causes is fixed, everything that happens happens by fate, he says; and if that is so, nothing lies within our power, and there is no freedom of will. If we concede this, he says, all human life is overturned: laws are enacted in vain; reprimands, praise, blame, and exhortations are employed in vain; and no justice has established rewards for the good and punishments for the wicked.

To prevent these consequences—unworthy, absurd, and destructive to human affairs—Cicero refuses to admit foreknowledge of future events. Thus he constrains the religious mind to choose one of two alternatives: either something lies within our will, or there is foreknowledge of future events. Since he thinks that both cannot exist, but that if one is affirmed the other is removed, choosing foreknowledge removes freedom of will, while choosing freedom of will removes foreknowledge.

Accordingly, Cicero, as a great and learned man, and one deeply concerned for the welfare of human life, chooses between these two the freedom of the will and, in order to establish it, denies foreknowledge of future events. In wishing to make men free, he thereby makes them sacrilegious. But the religious mind chooses both, confesses both, and confirms both by the faith of piety.

“How,” he asks, “can this be? For if there is foreknowledge of future events, all those consequences connected with it will follow, until one arrives at the conclusion that nothing lies within our will. On the other hand, if something lies within our will, by retracing the same steps one arrives at the conclusion that there is no foreknowledge of future events.” For the argument proceeds in this way: if there is freedom of will, not everything happens by fate; if not everything happens by fate, the order of causes is not fixed; if the order of causes is not fixed, the order of those things that cannot happen except through preceding and efficient causes is not fixed for God’s foreknowledge. If the order of things is not fixed for God’s foreknowledge, not everything occurs as he foreknew it would occur. But if not everything occurs as he foreknew it would occur, then, he says, God does not possess foreknowledge of all future events.

Against these sacrilegious and impious men, we assert both that God knows all things before they happen and that we act voluntarily, since nothing done by us is done except voluntarily. We do not say that everything happens by fate; rather, we say that nothing happens by fate, since when speakers commonly use that term they mean the configuration of the stars by which each person is conceived or born. We show that this notion is empty and worthless.

We neither deny the order of causes, in which God’s will has supreme power, nor call it by the name of fate. Unless, perhaps, we understand *fatum* as derived from *fari*, “to speak”—from *loquendo*, “from speaking.” For we cannot deny that it is written in the Holy Scriptures: “God has spoken once; these two things I have heard: that power belongs to God, and that to you, Lord, belongs mercy; for [variant: because] you will repay each person according to his works” (Ps. 61:12–13 [Vulgate numbering]).

The statement “He has spoken once” is understood to mean that he has spoken immutably—that is, unchangeably—just as he immutably knows all that will happen and all that he himself will do. In this sense, we could call the order of causes “fate,” were that name not already accustomed to being understood in another sense, one toward which we do not wish human hearts to incline.

Nor does it follow that, because the entire order of causes is certain to God, nothing lies within the freedom of our will. For our wills themselves have a significant place in the order of causes, which is certain to God and contained within his foreknowledge, since human wills are also the causes of human actions. Thus, he who foreknew all the causes of things could not have been ignorant among those causes of our wills, which he foreknew to be the causes of our actions.

The point that Cicero himself concedes—that nothing happens unless an efficient cause precedes it—is sufficient to refute him in this question. What advantage does he gain by saying that nothing happens without a cause, but that not every cause is fatal, since a cause may be accidental, natural, or voluntary? It is enough that he admits that everything that happens occurs only when a preceding cause exists.

We, however, say that the causes called accidental—from which the name “fortune” itself derives—are not nonexistent but hidden. We attribute them either to the will of the true God or to that of various spirits; and we in no way separate natural causes from the will of the one who is the author and creator of all nature.

Voluntary causes belong either to God, to angels, to human beings, or to whatever animals may properly be said to possess wills—if the movements of souls [variant: animals] lacking reason, by which they do things according to their nature when they seek or avoid something good or bad, are to be called wills.

By angels I mean either the good angels, whom we call God’s angels, or the evil ones, whom we call the angels of the devil or demons; and likewise, I mean the wills of human beings, both good and evil.

From this it follows that the efficient causes of everything that happens are voluntary causes, belonging to that nature which is spirit and gives life. For this air or wind is also called “spirit,” but because it is a body it is not a life-giving spirit. The life-giving Spirit who gives life to all things (Esdras, III; the printed reference is uncertain), who is the creator of every body and of every created spirit, is God himself, the uncreated Spirit.

## Against J. Scotus

[scan page 579]

### S. Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

His supreme power, which [variant: who] assists the good wills of created spirits, judges the evil, orders them all, and grants power to some while withholding it from others, is exercised through his will. For just as he is the creator of all natures, so he is the giver of all powers, but not of all wills. Evil wills do not come from him, since they are contrary to the nature that comes from him.

Bodies, therefore, are subject principally to wills—some to our wills, that is, to the wills of all mortal animals, and more especially to those of human beings than of beasts; some to the wills of angels. But all things are subject above all to God’s will, and all wills are subject to it, since they possess no power except what he grants.

The cause of things, which makes but is not made, is God. Other causes both make and are made, as do all created spirits, especially rational ones. Bodily causes, however, which are more acted upon than acting, are not to be counted among efficient causes, since they can do only what the wills of spirits accomplish through them.

How, then, does the order of causes, which is certain to God’s foreknowledge, result in nothing lying within our will, when our wills themselves occupy such an important place within that order of causes? Let Cicero contend with those who call this order of causes fatal—or rather, who call it “fate,” a term from which we chiefly recoil because it is not customarily understood in accordance with the truth.

But when he denies that the order of all causes is absolutely certain and fully known to God’s foreknowledge, we detest this more than the Stoics do. For either he denies that God exists—which, indeed, he tried to do by adopting another person’s voice in his books *On the Nature of the Gods*—or, if he confesses that God exists while denying that God foreknows future events, he says nothing other than this: “The fool has said in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Ps. 13:1). For one who does not foreknow all future events is certainly not God.

Therefore our wills have as much power as God wished and foreknew that they would have. Whatever power they possess, they possess with absolute certainty; and what they are going to do, they themselves will entirely do, because he foreknew that they would possess this power and would do these things—he whose foreknowledge cannot be mistaken.

Accordingly, if I wished to apply the name “fate” to anything, I would rather say that fate is the will of the weaker in the power of the stronger who holds him in his power, than that the freedom of our will is removed by that order of causes which the Stoics, using the term in their own unusual way, call fate.

*(The same, chapter 10.)* Thus we need not fear that necessity which so troubled the Stoics that they attempted to distinguish causes of things in such a way that they removed some from necessity and subjected others to it. Among those things that they did not wish to be subject to necessity, they placed our wills as well, lest, if subjected to necessity, they should no longer be free.

For if we call that necessity which is not within our power, but which accomplishes what it can even against our will—such as the necessity of death—it is clear that our wills, by which we live rightly or wrongly, are not subject to such necessity. We do many things that we would certainly not do if we did not wish to do them; and this applies first of all to willing itself. For if we will, we will; and if we do not will, we do not. We would not will if we did not wish to will.

But if necessity is defined as that according to which we say that something must be or must happen in a certain way, I do not know why we should fear that it will take away the freedom of our will. For we do not place either God’s life or God’s foreknowledge under necessity when we say that God must always live and must foreknow all things, just as his power is not diminished when we say that he cannot die or be deceived. Indeed, he cannot do these things in such a way that, if he could do them, he would necessarily possess less power. Properly speaking, he is called omnipotent because he does whatever he wills, not because he suffers what he does not will; if the latter happened to him, he would in no way be omnipotent.

Thus he cannot do certain things precisely because he is omnipotent. Likewise, when we say that, whenever we will, we must will by a free choice, we speak the truth without subjecting free will to the necessity by which we remove freedom [another reading: “which removes freedom”].

Our wills, therefore, exist, and they themselves accomplish whatever we do by willing—something that would not happen if we did not will it. Whatever a person suffers unwillingly through the will of another, even in that case the will has power—not, perhaps, the will of that other person alone [another reading: “only”], but the power of God.

For if it were merely a will and could not do what it willed, it would be hindered by a stronger will. Yet even then it would still be a will, and it would belong not to someone else but to the one who willed, even if he could not accomplish what he wished.

Accordingly, whatever a person suffers against his will, he ought not to attribute [variant: attribute back] to the wills of human beings, angels, or any created spirit, but rather to the one who grants power to those who will. It is not therefore the case that nothing lies within our will because God foreknew what would lie within our will. The one who foreknew this did not foreknow nothing. Moreover, if the one who foreknew what would lie within our will foreknew not nothing but something, then, with him foreknowing it, something certainly does lie within our will.

We are therefore compelled in no way either to remove freedom of will while retaining God’s foreknowledge or, while retaining freedom of will, to deny—an impious act—that God foreknows the future. We embrace both; we confess both faithfully and truthfully: the one so that we may believe rightly, the other so that we may live rightly. For one lives wrongly unless one believes rightly about God.

Far be it from us, then, to deny his foreknowledge in order that we may be free, since by his help we are—or shall be—free. Accordingly, laws, reprimands, exhortations, praise, and blame are not given in vain, because he foreknew that these too would occur, and they have the greatest efficacy to the extent that he foreknew they would have efficacy. Prayers also have power to obtain what he foreknew he would grant to those who pray; and just rewards have been established for good deeds, and punishments for sins.

A person does not sin because God foreknew that he would sin. Rather, he undoubtedly sins because the one whose foreknowledge cannot be mistaken foreknew that he himself would sin—not fate, not fortune, not anything else, but the sin itself. If he does not wish to sin, he certainly does not sin [another reading: “does not sin at all”]; but if he does not wish to sin, God also foreknew this.

[scan page 580]

## On Predestination

*(The same, chapter 11.)* The supreme and true God, together with his Word and the Holy Spirit—three who are one, one omnipotent God, creator and maker of every soul and every body, through participation in whom all who are happy are happy in truth and not in vanity; who made the human being a rational animal consisting of soul and body; who neither permitted the sinner to remain unpunished nor abandoned him without mercy; who gave both good and evil beings existence, as he gave it even to stones; vegetative life, as he gave it to trees; sensory life, as he gave it to animals; and intellectual life only to angels; from whom come all measure, form, and order; from whom come number, weight, and whatever exists naturally, whatever its kind or whatever its value; from whom come the seeds of forms, the forms of seeds, and the movements of seeds and forms; who gave flesh its origin, beauty, health, fertility for reproduction, the arrangement of its members, preservation, and harmony; who gave irrational souls memory, sensation, and appetite, and to rational souls, in addition, mind, understanding, and will; who left neither heaven and earth, nor angel and human being, nor even the entrails of a tiny and despised animal, the feather of a bird, the little flower of a plant, or the leaf of a tree without the fitting harmony of their parts and a kind of peace among them—this God must in no way be thought to have wished human kingdoms, and all their dominations and servitudes, to lie outside the laws of his providence.

*(The same, in Homily 53 on the Gospel of John.)* “Although he had performed so many signs before them, they did not believe in him, so that the word of the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled, which he spoke: ‘Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?’” (John 12:37; Isa. 53:1). Here he sufficiently shows that “the arm of the Lord” is the name given to the Son of God, and so forth.

Some people therefore mutter among themselves, and whenever they can they cry out and contend in turbulent dispute, saying: “What did the Jews do, or what was their fault, if it was necessary for the word of the prophet Isaiah to be fulfilled?”

We answer them that God, who foreknows future events, foretold through the prophet the unbelief of the Jews. He foretold it; he did not cause it. God does not compel anyone to sin merely because he already knows the future sins of human beings. The Jews therefore committed the sin; he did not compel them to commit it. He does not approve of sin, but foretold that they would commit it, since nothing is hidden from him.

If they had wished to do good rather than evil, they would not have been prevented; and they would have been foreseen as going to do this by the one who knows what each person will do and what he will repay that person for his deed.

After these most lucid statements of the blessed Father, nearly all the stench of your arguments has been exhausted above. Nevertheless, we have thought it not inappropriate to bring forward additional sayings of the same Father, so that it may be clear what he thought about punishments inflicted and to be inflicted by God—namely, from his book *Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets*.

*(Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets, book 1, chapter 15.)* “But whoever is displeased that the sinner was forbidden access to the tree of life—what does he want except to live wickedly with impunity? It would not have been difficult for God, or for anyone else, to take life away from the human being whom he did not wish to live. But because rational souls live from wisdom, whose death is folly, the tree of life was placed in paradise so that, by means of its fruit, it might signify this matter and prevent the human being from dying in body.

“What was therefore signified by his being separated from it and handed over to death, to be consumed by age (Gen. 3:22–23)—something that would not have happened if he had always enjoyed that food—was that his soul had first been excluded from the tree of spiritual life because of sin and had thus already died a kind of inner death. For it is written concerning wisdom: ‘She is a tree of life to those who embrace her’ (Prov. 3:18).

“Not understanding this, he says: ‘How, then, could the immortal human being have lived forever before the curse, when he had not yet eaten from that tree?’ It is as though someone had told him, or he had read somewhere in that book, that Adam had not yet eaten from the fruit of the tree of life. Rather, the passage should be understood to mean that, from that tree, perpetual bodily life was supplied to him so that he would not be consumed by the decay of age.

“He was then forbidden access to it so that, as a punishment for sin, the necessity of death might already be imposed upon him. ‘How,’ he asks, ‘did he begin to die through God’s curse, when life itself had never begun from him?’—as though God had wished him dead, as one human being may wish another dead, and as though the words of God referred to the anger of one who curses, rather than to the sentence of one who punishes.

“To punish the body with bodily death was to separate him from the tree of life, since he had already died spiritually, his soul having been separated from the nourishment of wisdom. God therefore wished to signify what had happened to him in his soul by separating him from the tree of life, by which wisdom was signified.

“But to whom,” he says, “was this tree, which bore the fruit of life in paradise, useful? To whom except those first human beings, the male and the female, who had first been placed in paradise? After these had been expelled from paradise in proportion to the merit of their iniquity, the tree remained as a memorial signifying the spiritual tree of life—which, as we have said, is wisdom itself, the unchangeable food of blessed souls.

“Whether anyone now feeds upon that food, except perhaps Enoch and Elijah, I do not presume to assert rashly. Yet unless the blessed souls were nourished by that tree of life which is in the spiritual paradise, we would not read that paradise was granted by the same gift of God to the soul of the thief who believed in Christ: ‘Amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise’ (Luke 23:43). To be there with Christ is to be with the tree of life. For he himself is the wisdom of which, as was said above, it is written: ‘She is a tree of life to those who embrace her’” (Prov. 3:18).

[scan page 581]

### S. Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

*(Chapter 16.)* Must this also be refuted—that he derides, as though cleverly, what seems to him to be the case: first, that God did not foreknow what happened; second, that he was unable to fulfill what he had earnestly intended; and third, that, having been defeated, he resorted to a curse?

How does he know that God did not foreknow what happened? Or did it happen because God did not foreknow it? On the contrary, if it had not happened, he could in no way have foreknown it as future, because it would not have been future.

Or, if he thinks that God did not foreknow it because, had he foreknown it, he would have taken measures to prevent it [another reading: “would have foreseen it”], he can say the same thing of Christ, who gave a talent to a man who would acquire nothing. Christ had certainly given it so that his money might increase, whatever that money signifies (Matt. 25:24 and following).

Therefore, because it happened that the man acquired nothing through his own laziness, did the one who gave it not foreknow this? He can also say that Christ failed to fulfill what he had earnestly intended concerning this profit.

He can even make the third accusation: that, having been defeated, Christ resorted to a curse, since he said: “Bind his hands and feet and cast him into the outer darkness” (Matt. 22:13), just as it was said concerning Adam that, after being separated from the tree of life (Gen. 3:22–23), he would also be punished by bodily death.

To this forsaken man, the command of one who fails seems to be the curse of one who is powerless [alternate reading: “of one who defines”]. Let him therefore call Christ powerless, because he was unable to accomplish what he wished concerning the acquisition of spiritual wealth. Let him call him envious and malicious because he begrudged his servant light and salvation and ordered him cast into the darkness, where there would be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matt. 22:13).

But if he would not speak this way about Christ—and let him judge himself not to be a Christian if he did—why does he dare to say it about the creator of humanity and the one who condemns sin according to its merit, when he does not dare to say it about humanity’s redeemer?

And if he despises his commands, let him be punished with the punishment of eternal death by that same one, namely Christ. For against whom else, without knowing it, does this man hurl his curses? Christ himself says: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also, for he wrote about me” (John 5:46). For what did the Father ever do, or do now, without the Son?

If, therefore, Holy Scripture commends not only God’s goodness but also his severity for our salvation—for God is beneficially loved and feared, and the Apostle mentions both in the same passage, saying, “See therefore the goodness and severity of God” (Rom. 11:22)—what is one to make of this mad and reckless man, who boasts that he is a Christian yet reproaches in the God of the prophets what he finds in the God of the apostles? The God of the former and of the latter is one and the same.

As for the man whom I mentioned, whom he sent, because of his laziness, into the outer darkness (Matt. 25:24), this is God’s severity. God is not there called improvident concerning the future, since he entrusted his money to such a man; nor powerless, since the one whom he did not himself guide so as to act well, he himself corrected; nor envious or malicious, since he sent him from the light into darkness.

A faithful reader ought to observe the same principle concerning all the punishments of human beings that are read to have been inflicted upon sinners in the books of the Prophets. This applies also to the Flood. The Lord Jesus announced that something of this kind would occur at his coming when he said: “As in the days of Noah they were eating and drinking, planting new vines, building, marrying, and taking wives; the flood came and destroyed them all. So also will be the coming of the Son of Man” (Luke 17:26).

The same applies to the hardening of Pharaoh’s heart. The writings of the New Testament likewise say of certain people: “God handed them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is not fitting” (Rom. 1:18).

The same applies to the lying spirit whom God, who makes good use even of evil things, sent by a most righteous judgment to deceive the impious king (1 Kings 22:20). The prophet Micaiah testifies that this was shown to him in a prophetic vision.

The Apostle Paul did not hesitate to say something similar, knowing that he was speaking most truly, when he said: “God will send them an operation of error, so that they may believe a lie, and that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity” (2 Thess. 2:10).

The same applies to what was done through Moses, to whom God said: “Take all the leaders of the people and offer them to the Lord against the sun”—that is, openly, in the daytime (Num. 25:4). Moses avenged the making of the idol in such a way that no one spared even his neighbor but slew the impious with the sword (Exod. 32:27–28).

Nor did the Lord Jesus fail to say: “But those enemies of mine who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and slay them before me” (Luke 19:27). Since this certainly signifies the death of souls, it is more dreadful and fearsome to the faithful than the death of bodies.

Hence the same Lord says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matt. 10:28).

If anyone considers with a faithful mind, as is fitting, these deaths by which souls are sent into Gehenna, he will judge them incomparably more terrible than any enormous slaughter, rivers of human blood, or deaths of mortal bodies—however and whenever those bodies may die.

This man exaggerates such massacres and describes them with scholastic vanity in order to blaspheme God, who chastised with such deaths those for whom that kind of terror had been useful. He frightens mortal senses and thinks that he is acting like one who throws something against a goad, so that, while he accuses God’s providence over the death of the flesh, in the death of the heart he enters Gehenna [variant: may be sent into Gehenna].

What human being of either sex would not rather be cut down by the sword—even in the manner in which Phinehas the priest struck down the fornicators in the very embrace of their wicked pleasure, setting up a terrifying example of vengeance against execrable lusts, an act that was especially pleasing to God (Num. 25:7–8, 11)? Who, I ask, would not prefer to be killed by such a death?

Who would not finally prefer to be consumed by fire, or torn apart by the bites of wild beasts through the very private parts, rather than be sent into the fire of eternal Gehenna?

Why, then, does the God of the Christians punish sinners with such deaths, so that after the transitory destruction of the body there follows punishment in Gehenna without end, unless [another reading: “namely”] because he is both just and merciful?

[scan page 582]

## On Predestination

For the Jews could say, against this man’s impiety, however much he may exaggerate wars, massacres, wounds, funerals, and blood, that they have a God incomparably more merciful than our God—plainly, one who punishes far more mildly with transitory bodily deaths [another reading: “transient deaths”] than with the perpetual flames of Gehenna.

Yet this man thinks that the God of the Law and the Prophets—who is one and the true God—must be accused of the crime of cruelty because, for very slight or even laughable reasons, he inflicted the punishment of death, even bodily death: because David numbered the people; because infants, as this man says, the sons of the priest Eli, had tasted something prepared for God from the pots or vessels.

I do not discuss how great and how pernicious a vice of pride it was that had crept even into so holy a man, making him wish to number God’s people, and how he was scourged by the deaths—not eternal, but destined to come according to the human condition and soon to pass away—of those whose multitude had made him proud (2 Sam. 24:1 and following).

Nor do I say that the sons of Eli were not infants, as this man claims, ignorant of what he is saying; rather, they were of an age at which they could and ought to have been restrained by a fitting punishment for the sacrilegious boldness with which they placed themselves before the Lord God in the sacrifices (1 Sam. 2:12 and following).

God avenged this neglect not for his own advantage but for the sake of the people, whom religion and piety would have benefited. He also avenged it through war, in which those who were to survive could increase their fear of God through the deaths of those who had been—and who, if they did not know themselves, would die after no long interval of time.

For we read that, through bodily deaths, some have died not because of their own sins but because of the sins of others (1 Sam. 4:10). In such cases, the wound is more truly a wound of the heart in the living than a punishment of those dying in the dissolution of the flesh. Souls departing from bodies have their own causes, whether good or evil; they are not made guilty merely because they have been stripped of the body. In the death of souls, however, no one is punished in place of another.

But let us consider how serious this man thinks the sin was. A man was found at the wedding banquet without a wedding garment. If we measure the matter by human judgment, I think it ought to have been enough for him to feel some shame, and, at most, for the host’s indignation to extend to compelling him to change his garment. Yet it was said: “Bind his hands and feet and cast him into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 22:13).

But what is said [another reading: “but he says”] does not signify a slight fault in failing to possess a wedding garment, since these small things are signs of great realities. Likewise, the visible sacrifices, though slight in earthly matters, are signs of great, because [variant: and] divine, realities, among which the sons of the priest were placing themselves before God, whose honor is observed in the sacrifices.

The guest did not place himself before the bridegroom; he merely failed to be appropriately dressed because he did not have the tunic of the wedding [variant: the wedding tunic]. Nevertheless, among the punishments by which both men were punished, the one who distinguishes them perceives how different they are and how incomparably one exceeds the other—provided that he places spiritual and eternal things above bodily and temporal things.

But why should we labor over the mystical meanings of the sacrifices and the wedding garment, attempting to press them upon carnal senses? Let us bring forward something more obvious.

The Lord compares the Gospel with the old Law and declares that the Gospel is more perfect—not the evil that people had previously learned, but what he himself was teaching. “You have heard,” he says, “that it was said: ‘You shall not kill; and whoever kills will be liable to judgment.’ But I say to you: Everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment; whoever says ‘Raca’ will be liable to the council; and whoever says ‘Fool’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. 5:21–22).

What is as small among sins as saying “Fool” to one’s brother? What is as great among punishments as the fire of Gehenna? If this man had found in the Law or the Prophets that someone had been ordered by divine command to be stoned because he had said “Fool” to his brother, how greatly would he accuse God of cruelty?

Who would not prefer—not merely to be stoned, but to be torn apart and consumed alive and conscious, limb by limb, indeed fragment by fragment, gradually and bit by bit—rather than be condemned to the fires of Gehenna?

Yet far be it from anyone to call the God of the Gospel more cruel than the God of the Law, when he understands that the God of both is one and the same: in the Law terrifying people with bodily punishments, in the Gospel with spiritual punishments, and faithful both there and here, cruel nowhere.

What if he were to find a tongue alien to Christ and blasphemous against him, and were to rage against it with impious chatter of the sort found in this man? Would he be more bitterly and harshly provoked than by the punishment, bodily and temporal, which this man indignantly claims was inflicted for the sacrilege of tasting sacrificial food?

The Lord threatens that he will come and say to those placed on the left: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41–42).

I ask the cause of this great punishment. “I was hungry,” he says, “and you did not give me food.” Behold: for food that was not withheld but simply not given, an eternal and dreadful punishment is threatened—and rightly, if you consult the truth. For what is given in alms is very little; but when it is given piously, eternal merit is thereby acquired. Therefore, precisely because what is given is little, it is not given through great impiety.

It is no wonder, then, that the punishment of eternal fire is prepared for such great barrenness, as for trees without fruit. But if you consult human judgment and ask a person to answer for himself, when “every human being is a liar,” he diminishes the guilt and exaggerates the punishment. He does not see the former with a carnal mind, but recoils from the latter with mortal flesh.

Such is this man’s attitude toward all human beings who are punished or corrected in the Old Testament by bodily punishments far milder than those read of in the Gospel. For what comparison can be made between the Flood and the eternal fires? What comparison between massacres, wounds, and deaths of bodies and everlasting torments?

He inflates himself over the twenty-four thousand who fell (Num. 25:9) with such noisy boasting that one would think innumerable thousands did not die every day throughout the world, but that this was some transitory death of the body [another reading: “of bodies”]. Yet who could estimate how many thousands from all nations will stand at the left hand, who eternally … [source breaks off]

[scan page 583]

## Saint Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

[Fragment] ... must be condemned to such fires? Let him go and cry out with open mouth and closed eyes, as though he had confessed God’s cruelty, because he says through the prophet:

> “I will sharpen my sword like lightning; I will intoxicate my arrows with blood, and my sword shall devour flesh from the blood of the slain” (Deut. 32:41–42).

On the basis of these words he accuses God as though God were always hungering for human blood—as though he had said: “I will intoxicate myself with blood, and I will eat flesh from the blood of the wounded.” But however much this salutary threat of God may be abhorred by that empty-headed and mad man as though it were greedy for crime and, as he says, boasting only in sheer cruelty, what force or weight does it have when compared with the words of the one who says:

> “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41).

There the arrows will not be intoxicated with blood, but the flames will not be satisfied even with all their limbs. Nor will the sword eat flesh, quickly removing the sensation of pain from the dead rather than inflicting it upon the wounded; instead, no one will be withdrawn from the torments even by dying, lest the punishment itself should die at the same time as the one who dies.

Why does he not say here whether this one should be worshiped, or rather execrated and fled from? Is he afraid to say such things about Christ, lest he himself fail to escape the eternal punishment of that fire into which Christ prepares to send the impious? Miserable man: he does not understand that, in saying these things about the God of the prophets, he is speaking of the very one whose dreadful severity in the Gospel he fears to offend.

He also criticizes the fact that God says the punishments of the impious—signified by the grape of gall, the cluster of bitterness, and the fury of dragons and asps—are stored up with him and sealed in his treasuries, to be repaid when their foot slips (Deut. 32:32–34). He is ignorant that “treasuries” here means the hidden dispositions of God, who has determined to repay each person according to his works (ibid., v. 35).

Therefore the Apostle says:

> “But according to your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God, who will repay each person according to his works” (Rom. 2:5–6).

With whom, indeed, does the impenitent heart store up wrath for itself, if not with the one who will judge the living and the dead?

Those ancient books also know the “desirable treasure” (Prov. 21:20), of which it is written there that it rests in the mouth of the wise. And in Proverbs we read that God “stores up salvation for those who love him.” The prophet Isaiah likewise says:

> “In the treasuries is our salvation; there are wisdom and discipline and piety toward the Lord” (Isa. 33:6).

These are the treasuries of righteousness. But those empty talkers and seducers of minds who oppose the sacred writings because they do not wish to understand them choose from those writings the harsh passages, which are there to commend God’s severity, and from the Gospel and apostolic writings the mild passages, which are there to commend God’s goodness. Among the ignorant they create horror on one side and seek favor on the other—as though it would be difficult for someone equally blasphemous and impious to oppose the New Testament in the same way as this man opposes the Old, selecting from the Old what commends God’s goodness and, conversely, from the New what commends God’s severity.

Let such a malicious and poisonous person cry:

> “Behold the God whom one ought to worship: merciful and compassionate, long-suffering and abundant in mercy; he will not be angry forever, nor will he be indignant eternally. He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities; but as far as the east is from the west, so far does he put [alternate reading: has put] our sins from us. As a father has compassion on his children, so he has had compassion on those who fear him” (Ps. 102:8–13).

He is the one who says:

> “I do not desire the death of the impious [alternate reading: sinner], except that he may return [alternate reading: but that he may be converted] and live” (Ezek. 18:23).

Not the one who, because of his greed for profit, is about to throw into the outer darkness—with hands and feet bound—the servant who did not lose the talent he had received, but merely did not acquire more, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matt. 22:12); and who removes from his banquet the man who does not have a wedding garment and punishes him with the same punishment, likewise bound; and who answers those who come to him, knock, and say, “Lord, open to us,” with the words, “I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12), merely because they did not bring oil with them to pour into their lamps; and who sends a person to Gehenna for a single insulting word; and who, for food that was not received, condemns him to eternal fire (Matt. 5:22 and elsewhere).

If anyone, with a deranged and sacrilegious mind, gathers from one side what is mild and from the other what is harsh, and attempts by this means to turn unlearned people away from Christ as though he were savage and cruel and to convert them instead to the merciful and gentle God of the prophets, would not this very man who does such a thing appear impure and impious in relation to the Old Testament, just as a similarly sacrilegious person could do so in relation to the New?

But the person who rightly worships God recognizes that the God of both Testaments is one, loves the goodness of that one God in both, and fears his severity in both—in the former understanding Christ as promised, and in the latter receiving Christ as given.

Was it not first read in those ancient books that evil should not be repaid with evil, where it is commanded that, if anyone finds his enemy’s animal wandering, he should bring it back to its owner, and if it has fallen on the road, he should not pass by but lift it up with him? (Exod. 23:5.) Was it not first written there what the Apostle cites:

> “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink” (Rom. 12:20; Prov. 25:21)?

Was it not first there that the man of God says to his God what he certainly knows is pleasing to him?

> “Lord my God, if I have done this, if there is iniquity in my hands, if I have repaid evil to those who repaid me evil” (Ps. 7:4).

Was it not first there that the prophet Jeremiah describes the patience of the holy person who offers his cheek to the one striking him? (Lam. 3:30.) Was it not first there, through another prophet, that each person is commanded not to remember the wrongs of his brother? (Lev. 19:18.)

What, then, is this blasphemer doing when he gathers from the New Testament such things as though they were contrary to the Old Testament—either not knowing both bodies of Scripture, or pretending not to know them in order to deceive the unlearned?

[scan page 584]

## Concerning Predestination

Yet if he is asked whether the one who sends a person into eternal fire for food that was not received repays evil with evil (Matt. 25:42), he will certainly be disturbed and reminded that it is incomparably milder to take an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth from a person, where the measure of vengeance does not exceed the measure of the injury (Exod. 21:24; Lev. 24:19–20), than to inflict [alternate reading: repay] such great severity on account of kindness shown—where the fault is temporary but the punishment has no end.

Thus, if he is not obstinate, he will learn that in both Testaments of the one God goodness must be loved and severity feared.

Although in the Old Testament, because of the promise of temporal goods and the threat of evils, temporal Jerusalem bears servants as children, and although in the New Testament, where faith commands charity through which the law can be fulfilled, eternal Jerusalem bears free children not so much through fear of punishment as through delight in righteousness—or [reading: “love”]—nevertheless there were also spiritual righteous people in those earlier times, whom the letter commanding did not kill, but whom the Spirit, assisting them, made alive.

Hence the faith of the coming Christ certainly dwelt in the prophets who announced that Christ would come. And now there are many carnal people who either produce heresies because they do not understand the Scriptures or, within the Catholic Church itself, are still nourished as little children on milk, or remain like persistent chaff prepared for future fires.

Just as the one true God is the creator of good things, both temporal and eternal, so he himself is the author of both Testaments, because the New is prefigured in the Old and the Old is revealed in the New.

The merciful gentleness of forgiveness, on account of which it was said that one must forgive a brother’s sins not only seven times but even seventy-seven times (Matt. 18:22), does not mean that iniquity should go unpunished or that discipline should grow sluggish and fall asleep—something which would do more harm than diligent and watchful vengeance.

Christ gave the keys of the kingdom of heaven to the Church in such a way that he not only said:

> “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16:19),

where the Church most clearly repays good rather than evil with evil, but also added:

> “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven,”

because the justice of punishment is good.

For what he says—

> “If he does not listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector” (Matt. 18:17)—

is more severe than if he were struck with a sword, consumed by flames, or exposed to wild beasts. For there too he adds:

> “Amen I say to you: whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven.”

This was so that it might be understood how much more severely punished is the person who, as though abandoned, has been left unpunished.

Let this man say, if he pleases: “Do we accept the Savior’s commands in this way, when he orders us: ‘Repay evil to no one with evil’; and, ‘If someone strikes you on one cheek, offer him the other also’; and, ‘Forgive the injuries done by your brothers’?”

Behold: the person who does not repay evil with evil is bound by the Church’s keys more bitterly and more miserably than by any exceedingly heavy and hard iron or adamantine chains.

## Chapter 11

### That it can be proved by divine and human authority that there is no predestination of God except concerning those who have been prepared for eternal happiness

In the eleventh monster among your prodigies you say:

### John Scotus  
*(Chapter 11, no. 1, section 1.)*

That it can be proved by divine and human authority that there is no predestination of God except concerning those who have been prepared for eternal happiness.

### Correction

In replying to these statements you reveal your madness, for you say:

### John Scotus  
*(No. 2.)*

“And how would it depart from the truth if, just as it is said by analogy that God foreknew everything he would do, it is said conversely that he foreknew what he would not do, instead of ‘he did not foreknow’? The same must be understood concerning predestination: by analogy, God predestined those whom he prepared to receive his gratuitous gift; conversely, he predestined the impious to destruction or eternal punishment, although he did not predestine them.”

### Correction

O intellect infected with poisons! O understanding incomparably darkened by the shadows of error! Never before you did any heretic admit this impious interpretation; no Catholic even conceived it in his mind: namely, that “to know” should mean “not to know,” and “to predestine” should mean “not to predestine,” or that anyone should understand or urge these meanings.

All the most faithful and learned interpreters of the sacred Scriptures have never taught that, by opposition, God knows or predestines any evils. Rather, as the truth of the reading stands, so it sounds; and, with every cloud of obscurity removed, they have proclaimed that it must be understood truthfully.

Therefore, if, according to such perversity—which God forbid—“to know” is taken to mean “not to know,” and “to predestine” to mean “not to predestine,” I do not see what could be said that is more absurd, indeed more perverse. For everything similar that is expressed either in divine writings or in the writings of the Fathers would be subjected to the same madness.

Thus, whenever one reads that God “does,” “creates,” “knows,” “foreknows,” “appoints,” “predestines,” “orders,” “preordains,” “disposes,” “assigns,” “delegates,” “decrees,” “establishes,” “constitutes,” “hands over,” “punishes,” “rouses,” “raises up,” “converts,” “damns,” “condemns,” “judges,” “destroys,” “scatters,” “leads,” “induces,” “hardens,” “kills,” “prepares,” or “makes ready,” all these expressions would have to be understood conversely:

“does not do, does not create, does not know, does not foreknow, does not appoint, does not predestine, does not order, does not preordain, does not dispose, does not assign, does not delegate, does not decree, does not establish, does not constitute, does not hand over, does not punish, does not rouse, does not raise up, does not convert, does not damn, does not condemn, does not judge, does not destroy, does not scatter, does not lead, does not induce, does not harden, does not kill, does not prepare, does not make ready.”

If this is admitted, then the entire truth of God’s judgments is abolished.

For if what we have said, and many other things wherever they are said about God, are understood by adding a negative particle, it follows that one must confess that God in no way cares for mortal affairs. God’s judgment would then be removed, although the Scriptures cry out that it was established precisely so that the righteous and sinners might be judged in it. Once the impious have been separated from the fellowship of the righteous, both groups will receive the reward they deserve, so that, according to the Lord’s statement:

> “These will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25:46).

Therefore, if God does not know sinners and their sins, he should not be believed to be going to judge them.

Whatever he is now believed to do in particular concerning sinners, or to do at the end in general, Scripture openly proclaims that he does and will do it in true judgment.

Moreover, when such things concerning God are reported either in the divine utterances or in the writings of the Fathers, we find that they have been understood and expounded by everyone exactly as they sound. Who would not recoil from this madness of your perversity, by which you claim that orthodox interpreters of the sacred pages—whose entire concern was to open what was hidden, unlock what was closed, explain what was figurative, and clarify what was obscure—either did not understand these matters or deliberately suppressed them out of envy?

No one among them can be found who, according to your perversity, understood, treated, or taught these things. For how could they be believed to have understood such statements in the opposite sense, when, wherever it was necessary, they were completely silent about those supposed opposites? And how could they have used figurative modes of speech in their writings and explanations when they had undertaken those very explanations in order to unfold all figurative expressions in plain language?

O horrifying monster! O tongue that ought to be cut out! Who would dare attribute either ignorance or envy to such great teachers, so that those who had undertaken to reveal obscure matters would be believed to have entangled them in still more obscure statements? This is especially absurd concerning sermons to the people, which were delivered or dictated with the greatest clarity and which ought to instruct their hearers through plain speech, not obstruct them with figurative expressions.

The books of the most blessed Father Augustine bear witness to this. He published them on Christian Doctrine, filled with true charity, and in them he persuaded every preacher to speak in such a way that, setting aside every desire for applause and driving away the artificial coloring of embellished speech, he would serve the ears of his hearers so as to benefit their minds in every respect.

Nor, in the fourteen books of Questions and Expressions—which we have often mentioned—is there any trace of his having made mention of this perversity of yours. On the contrary, just as in almost all his books and sermons, so in these too he is found to have used the terms “predestine” and “assign.”

For in the seventh book of Questions, when he was explaining the story of Jephthah, he placed both terms—“predestine” and “assign”—under one and the same meaning, teaching that they differed in no respect (Augustine, *Questions on the Heptateuch*, book 7, chapter 49):

> “Certainly, when he says ‘they are appointed for eternal punishment,’ those enemies are signified who, persisting in unbelief from that very people, were previously mentioned ...”

[The supplied text breaks off here.]

[scan page 585]

For if, according to the statement we have made, and many other similar statements wherever they are made about God, a negative particle is added, it follows that one must confess that God has no concern whatsoever for mortal affairs. God’s judgment would be removed, although the Scriptures proclaim that it was established so that the righteous and sinners might be judged in it. Once the impious have been separated from the fellowship of the righteous, both groups will receive the reward they deserve, according to the Lord’s saying:

> “These will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25:46).

Therefore, if God does not know sinners and their sins, he should not be believed to be going to judge them. Whatever he is now believed to do in particular concerning sinners, or to do at the end in general, Scripture testifies that he does and will do it in true judgment.

Nor, in the fourteen books of Questions and Expressions—which we have often mentioned—is there any trace of his having made mention of this perversity of yours. On the contrary, just as in almost all his books and sermons, so in these too he is found to have used the terms “predestine” and “assign.”

For in the seventh book of Questions, when he was explaining the story of Jephthah, he placed both terms—“predestine” and “assign”—under one and the same meaning, teaching that they differed in no respect (Augustine, *Questions on the Heptateuch*, book 7, chapter 49).

[The supplied quotation resumes:]

> “Certainly, when he says ‘they are appointed for eternal punishment,’ those enemies are signified who, persisting in unbelief from that very people, were previously mentioned. They are all predestined to eternal punishment, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matt. 22:30), like a people of mourning. Yet the devil and his angels may also suitably be understood as the people of mourning, either because they acquire eternal misery for those whom they deceive, or because they themselves have been assigned to eternal misery.”

The holy bishop Fulgentius is also a witness to this matter. When Monimus asked him about this question, he published a most complete and lucid volume in reply, in which he followed none of your fabrications, but taught and proved by Catholic truth, in clear language, that God predestined the impious to destruction.

Therefore either what you assert is true and what so great a teacher faithfully wrote is false, or, since it is impious to believe this of such a great and eminent teacher, what you have written deceitfully is entirely false, and what so great a teacher faithfully and truthfully declared is unquestionably true.

Certainly, even if no other authority or argument were supplied to us, that one man could suffice for us in understanding this question. His teaching and knowledge acquired such honor and esteem in the Catholic Church that no one has ever doubted or disparaged his writings. He is found to be splendidly learned in the liberal disciplines, exceptionally distinguished in the teaching of the sacred Scriptures, and no less skilled in Greek than in Latin eloquence.

The holy Prosper is also a witness, a man most learned and eloquent in every branch of literary knowledge. He opposed the impudence of the Gauls and of the other followers of Pelagius both through books faithfully published and through the decree of the Roman pontiff, which he obtained through his own persistent efforts; in this he proved himself a most courageous and faithful defender.

You are therefore shown to be more impudent than the rest of your kind, since, after reading the venerable writings of these men, you dared to mutter something contrary to them.

Even if you had never read their writings, they ought to have instructed you sufficiently concerning all these matters. Two years ago, from their books, I had excerpts selected and sent—with the consent of a synod—to certain brothers. If you could not otherwise know that these had reached you, your most wretched book, to which, with the Lord’s help, we are replying, could probably have informed you adequately. In it we have found many of those same excerpts inserted and violently distorted and bent to serve your perverse opinions.

Far be it—far be it—from the hearts of Catholics to attribute ignorance in any way to God.

Nevertheless, as far as my memory serves, God is said in the divine utterances to “not know” in three figurative ways: either by not experiencing, by rejecting, or by causing not to know.

The Lord himself says through the prophet:

> “What I did not know, they asked me about” (Ps. 34:21),

because they were demanding from him a sin which he had never known—that is, which he had never experienced or committed. As the blessed Apostle Peter says:

> “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:22),

and the blessed Apostle Paul says:

> “He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us” (2 Cor. 5:21),

that is, he had neither experienced nor committed it.

God therefore knows sin in the sense that it does not escape his knowledge; but he does not know it through experience, since he could never be corrupted by it.

[scan page 586]

Again, in the Gospel he says that at the judgment he will say to certain people:

> “I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12),

meaning, “I do not approve you in the practice of my discipline, which you have always opposed through your wicked works.”

Again he says to the disciples:

> “But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son, but the Father alone” (Matt. 24:36).

For how could the Son not know the day which, by his inescapable power, he is believed to have established even before temporal days existed? Therefore “not to know the day” must be understood to mean “to cause the apostles not to know it,” since it was not useful for them to know it.

Accordingly he later says to them:

> “It is not yours to know the times or moments which the Father has placed in his own authority” (Acts 1:7).

When God is said in these figurative expressions not to know or to be ignorant, nothing at all could he have been, can he be, or will he be ignorant of according to the proper nature of his majesty, essence, and knowledge.

The prophet had contemplated this knowledge of God when he addressed God humbly:

> “Your eyes are pure, so that they cannot see evil” (Hab. 1:13),

that is, so that they do not approve or experience it.

Another prophet says:

> “For behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon the sinful kingdom, to destroy it” (Amos 9:8).

And again:

> “In every place the eyes of the Lord behold the good and the evil” (Prov. 15:3).

And again:

> “The face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth” (Ps. 33:17).

All Catholic interpreters have firmly established that these statements must not be understood conversely, but must be accepted according to the straightforward truth of their words.

Go, then, and be the most detestable of all heretics, since, contrary to the opinion of everyone, you have most shamelessly presumed to attribute ignorance to God.

Now, concerning what you add about the impious being predestined to destruction:

### John Scotus  
*(Chapter 11, no. 3, section 1.)*

“If they are predestined, they will necessarily perish and suffer unavoidable punishments. But if this is so, how will the world be judged justly, when the necessity of predestination compels it to perish?”

### Correction

Although this matter has already been treated sufficiently and at length, I am not reluctant truthfully to repeat what you were not ashamed to assert deceitfully.

The predestination of God, just like his foreknowledge, imposes no force upon future events and introduces no coercion of necessity. Although whatever God foreknows and predestines must necessarily happen in such a way and cannot happen otherwise, it does not happen because it was foreknown or predestined. Rather, because it was known immutably as future, it is understood to have been most powerfully foreknown and predestined.

Something does not happen because God foreknew it; rather, God foreknew it because he knew that it would happen.

Therefore, if someone perishes, the fault does not belong to the God who foreknows and predestines, but to the rational creature who, by living badly through a corruptible body and abusing the gifts of God’s goodness, brought this upon himself.

God therefore predestined the sinner to eternal punishment, because he knew that he would live wickedly and persevere most obstinately in wicked works. The fault is consequently his who was foreknown to become such, not God’s, who, foreknowing such a person, justly predestined him to punishment.

Could you not, with the same freedom to slander, say:

“If those who are not predestined to life will necessarily perish and suffer unavoidable punishments, how will the world be judged justly, when the necessity of predestination compels it to perish because it has not been predestined to life?”

Likewise, if some have been mercifully elected while others have justly been abandoned, they will necessarily perish and suffer unavoidable punishments. If this is so, how will the world be judged justly, when the necessity of election or abandonment compels it to perish because they have not been elected but abandoned?

This appetite for slander extends so widely that it can be directed obliquely against everything that is faithfully proclaimed concerning God’s supreme mercy and justice. Therefore this damnable assertion of perversity must be utterly rejected, and we must confess that this world will be judged justly by the Lord.

Those who sin do not sin because they will be judged; rather, because they sin, they will necessarily be judged. It is therefore not the necessity of judgment that compels sinners to perish, but the necessity of sinning—which they have deliberately and inseparably brought upon themselves—that compels them inevitably to perish.

Just as the necessity of judgment compels no one to perish, so the necessity of predestination imposes upon no one the force of perishing.

Yet if you examine everything carefully—or nearly everything—that belongs to God’s judgment, you will find the same things in predestination.

God established a future judgment in which he will repay each person according to his works (Matt. 16:27): rewards to the elect and eternal punishments to the impious. This is the whole matter that is faithfully and beneficially affirmed concerning predestination: that the Judge of all will repay the elect with blessedness through mercy, and those left behind with punishments and torments through justice.

We read:

> “The one who does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18),

that is, condemned.

Let the shameless sycophant now rise and complain:

“If the one who does not believe has already been judged, he will necessarily perish and suffer unavoidable punishments. But if this is so, how will the world be judged justly, when the necessity of judgment—that is, of condemnation—compels it to perish?”

The evangelist John also says concerning the Jews who did not believe in the Lord:

> “For this reason they could not believe, because Isaiah the prophet said: ‘He has blinded the heart of this people and made their ears heavy, lest they see with their eyes and understand with their heart and turn and I heal them’” (John 12:39–40).

If they could not believe because Isaiah had foretold this, then they did not believe necessarily and will suffer unavoidable punishments. But if this is so, how will the world be judged justly, when the necessity imposed by the prophecy compelled it not to believe?

The Lord himself says:

> “For this reason you do not hear, because you are not of God” (John 8:47),

and again:

> “For this reason you do not believe, because you are not of my sheep” (John 10:26);

and again:

> “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44);

and:

> “No one can come to me unless it has been granted to him by my Father” (John 6:65).

Everything that the prophetic and apostolic pages affirm about the hidden judgments of God will likewise be subjected to these same slanders.

Let every coercive necessity be driven away from these matters, then, and let the depth of God’s judgments be contemplated with humility. Let us say with the Apostle:

> “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Rom. 11:33).

Now, with the Lord’s favor, let us proceed to examine what remains.

Finally, wishing to prove that the authority of sacred Scripture places foreknowledge and predestination together—or predestination alone, absolutely—only among those whom God has chosen to possess eternal blessedness, you set out the apostolic testimonies from the Epistle to the Romans:

> “We know,” it says, “that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called according to his purpose. For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. 8:28–30).

Likewise, from the Epistle to the Ephesians:

> “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, so that we might be holy and without blemish in his sight in love, predestining us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will, to the praise of the glory of his grace, with which he has graced us in his beloved Son. In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace, which he has lavished upon us in all wisdom and prudence, making known to us the mystery of his will according to his good pleasure, which he purposed in him, for the dispensation of the fullness of times, to restore all things in Christ, those in heaven and those on earth. In him, in whom we have also been called by lot, we were predestined according to the purpose of God, who works all things according to the counsel of his will” (Eph. 1:3–14).

Having set these passages out, you add:

[scan page 587]

### John Scotus  
*(Chapter 11, no. 4, section 3.)*

“Against so clear a trumpet of truth, what person of sober and watchful faith would admit human voices? What mind would not hear that predestination belongs entirely to the saints and cannot in any way belong to the reprobate?”

### Correction

O how necessary sobriety and vigilance in true faith would have been for you, so that you might see what the apostolic trumpet was saying and not invent something which the harmony of so great a trumpet had not sounded at all!

In the examples you have presented, the Apostle, the preacher of truth, directed his entire intention toward commending the predestination and glorification of God’s elect. He did not undertake to record either the predestination or the condemnation of the reprobate, since he remembered that he had already dealt sufficiently with that matter in the preceding sections of the same Epistle to the Romans.

Your madness therefore gains nothing from the apostolic words. He did not say either that only the elect were predestined or that the reprobate were not predestined. Yet, whenever it was appropriate, he did not hesitate to commend both points in turn.

For, when he was treating subtly and truthfully in the same Epistle the election of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jews, he says:

> “But if God, wishing to show his wrath and to make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath, according to Ambrose prepared, according to Augustine and all the Africans perfected, and according to the usage of our manuscripts fitted or made fit for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy which he prepared for glory—those whom he also called, not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles” (Rom. 9:22–24), and so on in what follows.

If, according to what you attempted to establish above, God’s predestination is nothing other than the preparation of works, then the Apostle plainly proclaims that the vessels of wrath were prepared, perfected, fitted, or made fit for destruction. I do not presume to judge the variety of interpreters; but, as far as my own simplicity is concerned, I accept and approve all these readings.

If, I say, according to Ambrose, the vessels of wrath were prepared for destruction, and according to your definitions “to predestine” means nothing other than “to prepare,” then it is perfectly clear that, when the Apostle speaks of vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, he means nothing other than “predestined.” For the entire context of the same apostolic argument contains this very meaning, so that no person of sober mind can be found who has understood or taught this apostolic proclamation otherwise.

Although the authority of such great bishops—Ambrose and Augustine—is sufficient for me in asserting this matter, nevertheless, lest anyone be displeased by the variety of interpretations, the same Apostle, writing to the Corinthians, says:

> “I think that God has displayed us apostles as the last, like men sentenced to death” (1 Cor. 4:9).

Lest you distort this in a way especially favorable to your perversity, hear how Saint Ambrose explains it.

### Ambrose, on 1 Corinthians 4:9

> “For this reason he assigns this to his own person: he was always in necessity, suffering persecutions and afflictions beyond the others, just as Enoch and Elijah will suffer, who are to be apostles at the end of time. For they will be sent before Christ to prepare the people of God and fortify all the churches to resist Antichrist. The reading of the Apocalypse testifies that they will suffer persecutions and be killed. The Apostle therefore compared their time with his own time when he said, ‘like men sentenced to death,’ for they will come for this purpose: to be killed.”

The book of Ecclesiasticus also says:

> “God prepared him for the sword” (Sir. 26:27).

And the Lord himself says to Job, when he sets before him the most malicious and, apart from God, unconquerable weapons and arguments of the devil:

> “Which I have prepared for the day of battle and war” (Job 38:23).

These passages plainly destroy the structure of your falsehoods, by which foreknowledge ...

## On Predestination against John Scotus

You have strenuously endeavored to confirm that God’s foreknowledge, predestination, or preparation concerns the elect alone unto life, and not the reprobate unto punishments as well—although we have dealt sufficiently with all these matters above, insofar as seemed appropriate. Therefore either criticize Ambrose and Augustine and accuse them of falsehood, indeed of heresy; or, since this cannot in any way be done, bow to the most salutary judgments of such great Fathers and admit what is true: that God’s foreknowledge, predestination, and preparation pertain in two ways—that is, both to the elect and to the reprobate.

Since these apostolic statements, insofar as they concern God’s foreknowledge and predestination, are entirely clear and have no bearing on what you attempted to assert, and since you have consequently been deprived of the truth, you pass to those testimonies which Gotteschalk extracted from the writings of blessed Augustine and, as you say, twisted to his own error. While you assert that these have not been understood according to the Apostle—“to some we are the fragrance of life unto life, to others the fragrance of death unto death” (2 Cor. 2:16)—would that you yourself, with sound judgment, approached their examination simply, so that you might not belch forth such nauseating torrents of vomit concerning them. For such clarity shines in the statements of these men to pious minds that no devout person can hesitate concerning interpretations worthy of faith and authority. To you, therefore, unless you soon recover your senses, they have become “the fragrance of death unto death”; and you have not been ashamed deceitfully to interpret them, not as words spoken by him, but as interpolated by your own depravity.

This practice is recognized as having belonged to all heretics: whatever prophetic, apostolic, or orthodox patristic statements opposed their fabrications, they either erased from their books, declared those books unauthoritative, or at least corrupted them by perverse interpretations and attempted by any collusion to attach them to the confirmation of their errors. No one who has read your work is unaware that you have served this vice beyond all others. Therefore, having set forth the testimonies of the aforesaid Father, in which he very frequently said that the impious were predestined or prepared for destruction, since you could not deny it in any way, you strive to corrupt them, so as to lie that he spoke figuratively—that is, by contraries—which neither he nor any of the Catholic teachers can be shown to have done. Thus you say:

### John Scotus

*(Chapter 11, number 5, section 6.)* “For who among those ignorant of the modes of expression customarily used by the holy Fathers could not easily be led astray on hearing that some are predestined and prepared for eternal fire unto the wrath of God, predestined to everlasting death, predestined to destruction and punishment, and the like, so that without any hesitation he would grant either that there are two predestinations—one plainly belonging to the saints and the other to the impious, entirely opposed to each other—or that there is one and the same divine predestination embracing both the saints and the impious, and that it can simultaneously contain contraries, which reason denies?”

### Correction

We have already stated that neither Augustine nor the other holy Fathers—and especially not in treatises and sermons addressed to the people—used figurative expressions of this kind concerning contraries. Yet holy Fulgentius, in the volume published precisely for this purpose, keeps such language far from the term “divine predestination”; Prosper and many others teach the same clearly and without ambiguity. We have also shown, from the statements of Pope Gregory and Bishop Isidore, that predestinations are expressed in the plural.

But, as far as the matter itself is concerned, I ask whether you consider God’s judgments to be two, or however many, or one alone. For predestination and God’s judgment appear to me to correspond so closely that one cannot exist without the other. Just as predestination does, so God’s judgment leads some to the kingdom and condemns others to Tartarus: the former through mercy, the latter through justice.

Since all Scripture testifies that both the good and the wicked are judged, we believe that one testimony from the Lord’s Gospel is sufficient for the present discussion. He says:

“When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then he will sit upon the throne of his majesty; and all nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them from one another, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. He will set the sheep at his right hand, but the goats at his left. Then the King will say to those who are at his right hand: ‘Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you welcomed me; naked, and you clothed me; sick, and you visited me; I was in prison, and you came to me.’

“Then the righteous will answer him, saying: ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you drink? And when did we see you a stranger and welcome you, or naked and clothe you? Or when did we see you sick or in prison and come to you?’ And the King, answering, will say to them: ‘Amen I say to you, insofar as you did it for one of the least of these my brothers, you did it for me.’

“Then he will also say to those who are at his left hand: ‘Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink; I was a stranger, and you did not welcome me; naked, and you did not clothe me; sick and in prison, and you did not visit me.’ Then they too will answer, saying: ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry, or thirsty, or a stranger, or naked, or sick, or in prison, and did not minister to you?’ Then he will answer them, saying: ‘Amen I say to you, insofar as you did not do it for one of these least ones, neither did you do it for me.’ And these will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25:31–46).

Behold, the Lord himself, King of kings, almighty and eternal, who established before the ages the future day of judgment, himself foretold that at the end of time he would carry out that judgment. Without any veil of figurative expression, he testified that a kingdom had been prepared for the righteous and an eternal fire for the devil and his angels. No faithful preacher or teacher has ever taught—or even thought—otherwise; yet you alone among all men have not at all feared to invent that the kingdom prepared for the good is not figurative, whereas the punishment prepared for the impious is figurative—that is, not prepared—contrary to every divine and human truth, which proclaims that God has prepared both kingdom and punishment for the respective parties. As blessed Gregory expounds in the *Morals*, judgment is to be exercised either in twofold or in fourfold fashion.
