On the side of the elect, however, some are judged and reign: they wipe away their sins with the tears of their life, redeeming their preceding evil deeds by those that follow, and covering whatever unlawful acts they have committed from the Judge’s eyes by the giving of alms. When the Judge comes, he says to those standing at his right hand: “I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you welcomed me; naked, and you clothed me; sick, and you visited me; I was in prison, and you came to me.” To them he says in advance: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34–35).

There are also those who are not judged and reign. These have surpassed the precepts of the law through the perfection of their virtues. They were not content merely to fulfill what the law commands to all, but, moved by a more outstanding devotion, desired to offer more than they were able to hear in the general commandments. To them the divine voice [variant: the Lord’s voice] says:

“You who have left everything of yours and followed me, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28).

And concerning them the prophet says: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people” (Isa. 3:14). Solomon, speaking of the bridegroom [variant: bride] of holy Church, likewise says: “Her husband is noble in the gates, when he sits with the senators of the land” (Prov. 31:23).

Therefore, at the final judgment, they are not judged but reign, because they come as judges with their author. For, leaving everything, they carried out with ready devotion more than they had generally heard commanded. By a special command given to a few more perfect persons, and not generally to everyone, this was said to the rich young man: “Go, sell what you have [variant: all that you have], and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21).

If a general command under this dispensation bound everyone, it would certainly be sinful for any of us to possess something in accordance with this command. But one thing is what holy Scripture commands generally to all, and another what it enjoins specially upon the more perfect. These people, therefore, are rightly not held under the general judgment, because by living they surpassed the general precepts. For just as those are not judged but perish who, persuaded by unbelief, scorn being held by the law, so those are not judged but reign who, persuaded by devotion, advance even beyond the general precepts of divine law.

Hence Paul, also surpassing the special precepts, displayed more in action than he had received by the institution [variant: permission] of the promise. Although he had received this: “The one who preaches the Gospel should live by the Gospel,” and although he conveyed the Gospel to those who heard it, he nevertheless refused to be supported by the Gospel’s provisions. Why, then, is he judged so that he may reign, when he received a lesser command to observe but discovered a greater rule of life?

It is rightly said: “He has given judgment to the poor” (1 Thess. 2:9), because the more greatly they despised this world with humility, the more exalted seats they will then receive, as the greatness of their merits increases. To the latter, because of their preceding evils, he will justly repay punishment. Of them the Apostle proclaims: “For on whom he has mercy, he has mercy; and whom he wills, he hardens” (Rom. 9:18). Surely God shows mercy without any injustice on his part, since there is no injustice with God (Rom. 9:14); and he who inflicts wrath either hardens one who deserves it or exacts vengeance upon one who unquestionably deserves it.

There are two divisions of the elect and the reprobate, but within each of these divisions there are two orders:

- Some are judged and perish.
- Some are not judged and perish.
- Some are judged and reign.
- Some are not judged and reign.

Those who are judged and perish are addressed by the Lord’s voice in condemnation:

“I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink; I was a stranger, and you did not welcome me; naked, and you did not clothe me; I was sick and in prison, and you did not visit me.”

To them he says: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:42–43).

But those who are not judged and perish are not judged at the final judgment. Concerning them the Lord says through the prophet [variant: the prophet says]: “The impious will not rise in judgment” [variant: “will not rise”] (Ps. 1:5); and the Lord says concerning them: “He who does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18). Paul likewise says concerning them: “Those who have sinned without the law will perish without the law” (Rom. 2:12).

All unbelievers do indeed rise, but for torments, not for judgment. Their case will not then be examined, because they descend [variant: approach] into the sight of the strict Judge already bearing the condemnation of their unbelief. Those who retained the profession of true faith but did not possess the works of that profession are convicted so that they may perish. Those who never held the sacraments of faith do not hear the rebuke of the Judge in the final examination, because their unbelief has already prejudged them. They do not deserve to be convicted by a rebuke from the one whose authority they had despised.

At least those hear the words of the Judge because they held to his faith through words alone [variant: at least held to his words]. These, in their eternal condemnation, do not perceive the words of the eternal Judge, because they were unwilling to preserve even verbally the reverence due to him [variant: preferred not to preserve it].

The former perish according to the law, because they sinned while placed under the law. In the destruction of the latter, nothing is said about the law, because they made no effort to possess anything of the law. A terrestrial ruler governing a commonwealth punishes a citizen who commits an internal offense differently from an external enemy who rebels. In the former, he considers his own laws and, with words of appropriate rebuke, condemns him; against the enemy, however, he wages war, employs instruments of destruction, and repays his wickedness with suitable penalties. [The surrounding text is damaged in the scan.]

### On the judgment of the poor

“But he does not save the impious, and he gives judgment to the poor” (Job 36:6)—that is, he destroys the proud and sets the humble free through judgment; or certainly, he has given judgment to the poor, because those who are now unjustly oppressed will then come as judges over their oppressors.

Those who are not judged but reign are also those who surpass the commandments of the law through the perfection of their virtues. To them the Lord says:

“You who have left all your possessions and followed me, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28).

These, therefore, are not judged but reign, because they come as judges with their author. For, leaving everything, they carried out with more ready devotion what they had heard commanded generally. This was said by a special command to a few more perfect persons, not generally to all: “Go, sell what you have [variant: all that you have], and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21).

If a general command under this dispensation bound everyone, it would certainly be sinful for any of us to possess something. But one thing is what holy Scripture commands generally to all, and another what it commands specially to the more perfect. These people, therefore, are rightly not held under the general judgment, because by living they surpassed the general precepts. For just as those who, persuaded by unbelief, scorn being held by the law are not judged but perish, so those who, persuaded by devotion, advance beyond the general precepts of divine law are not judged but reign.

Hence Paul, surpassing even the special precepts, displayed more in action than he had received by the institution [variant: permission] of the promise. For although he had received the Gospel’s command that the one who preaches the Gospel should live by the Gospel, and although he imparted the Gospel to those who heard it, he nevertheless refused to be supported by the Gospel’s provisions. Why, then, is he judged so that he may reign, when he received less than he preserved but found greater what he lived?

Let it rightly be said: “He has given judgment to the poor” (1 Thess. 2:9), because the more greatly they despised this world with humility, the more exalted seats they will then receive, as the greatness of their merits increases.

### On God’s justice and judgment

Whatever you have written concerning the inevitable and fearsome judgment of almighty God, or whatever his preachers have committed to writing in pious and truthful letters, we agree with humility and truth. We think nothing else concerning his predestination: we confess that neither predestination exists without judgment, nor judgment without predestination. For what he foreknew he would judge, that same thing he undoubtedly predestined to do. These are the words:

“Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills” (Ps. 110:2)—namely, mercy and justice, by which he renders to each according to his works (Matt. 16:27). He predestined himself to do these things because he foreknew and foresaw that he would judge and repay them. This is that judgment of God capable of contraries which displeases you, which, although your reason denies it, the truth proves: judgment, certainly, of the wicked and of the good. Even if you wish to deny it, you can never destroy it, so evident is it that no one may doubt it.

If you deny that predestination possesses this capacity for contraries, it must exist in judgment, since, as we have said, what God foresaw that he would judge, he predestined himself to do. In every respect this agrees with the definition of predestination given by the most blessed Father Augustine, which you strive to distort and utterly overthrow. For, as you set it down, he says in the book to Prosper and Hilary, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 10:

“Predestination is that which cannot exist without foreknowledge; foreknowledge, however, can exist without predestination. For by predestination God foreknew those things which he himself was going to do; hence it is said: ‘He made the things that are to be’ (Isa. 45:11, according to the Septuagint). But he can also foreknow things which he himself does not do, such as all sins.”

We say and acknowledge this ourselves, and in no way depart from this definition. If you had regarded it in the light of truth, you would never have confused foreknowledge and predestination in such a way as to affirm that they are one and the same and entirely indistinguishable.

God foreknew everything: both what he himself was going to do, namely, all good things, and what he himself was not going to do, namely, all sins. But he predestined nothing other than what he himself was going to do—that is, mercy and judgment, or justice, or truth; all these amount to the same thing. The Prophet speaks of these two:

“God has spoken once; these two things I have heard: that power belongs to God, and to you, Lord, mercy; for you will render to each according to his works” (Ps. 61:12–13).

These are the great works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills (Ps. 110:2). These, clearly, are the works, and no others, which he predestined himself to do: to show mercy freely and to condemn justly. He shows mercy to those who have not deserved it; he condemns them, without doubt, because they have deserved it—to the former freely, that is, by grace; to the latter justly, because of preceding merits.

If you take away predestination, take away judgment; once judgment is removed, consequently remove justice; and once justice is removed, deny God himself, who is not accidentally but essentially, and therefore immutably, eternal justice. How, then, will he render to each according to his works? Will he render only the reward of good works and none of evil works? Let everyone sin as much as he wishes, since, once judgment and justice have been removed, he may sin with impunity. And say to those who have set their mouths against heaven and whose tongue has traversed the earth: “How does God know? And is there knowledge in the Most High?” (Ps. 72:9–11).

That both the good and the wicked will be judged is declared by the Lord’s sentence, and the Apostle testifies, saying:

“We know that the judgment of God is according to truth against those who do such things. But do you suppose, O man, who judge those who do such things and yourself do them, that you will escape the judgment of God? Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering? Do you not know that the goodness of God leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and your impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the just judgment of God, who will render to each according to his works: to those who, according to their patience in good works, seek glory, honor, and incorruption, eternal life; but to those who are contentious and do not obey the truth but believe iniquity, wrath and indignation, tribulation and distress upon every soul of man who works evil, of the Jew first and also of the Greek. But glory, honor, and peace to everyone who works good, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. For there is no partiality with God” (Rom. 2:2–11).

Since, therefore, God’s justice and judgment cannot in any way be denied, it follows that his predestination and preparation cannot be denied either, at least in those matters in which his justice and judgment are proclaimed. For these are what blessed Augustine said in his definition of predestination:

“That which God foresaw or foreknew he would do.”

Since this definition strongly conflicts with your assertions, you attempt to invert it and fabricate something which neither Augustine said nor believed. For you say:

### John Scotus

*(Chapter 14, number 6, section 7.)* “There is therefore this difference between predestination and foreknowledge: all predestination is foreknowledge, but not all foreknowledge is predestination. For that foreknowledge by which God foreknew those things which he himself was going to do is properly and specially called predestination. But that foreknowledge by which he foreknew those things which he does not do—that is, their sins and punishments—has pleased him to be called simply foreknowledge, so that only that foreknowledge which is called predestination is always understood as concerning the good; foreknowledge alone, without predestination, belongs entirely to the evil things which God does not do.”

### Correction

We give thanks to God, who, perhaps against your will and without your realizing it, has caused you to confess something of the truth. For, whereas until now you had asserted that foreknowledge and predestination are one, you now confess—although deceitfully—that they differ. By saying that all predestination is foreknowledge but not all foreknowledge is predestination, you clearly demonstrate that they differ in some way.

Yet, when you call foreknowledge predestination, you depart from the truth. For foreknowledge is not predestination, nor is predestination foreknowledge, although foreknowledge is sometimes used in place of predestination—as when the Apostle says, “elect according to the foreknowledge of God” (1 Pet. 1:2), where he is understood to have used “foreknowledge” for “predestination.” Predestination, however, is nowhere found used for foreknowledge.

Therefore, it should have been said, as the memorable Father Augustine said (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 10): “Predestination cannot exist without foreknowledge, but foreknowledge can exist without predestination.” Why do you obscure the clarity of these words? Why do you muddy the purest waters with filthy disputations? Why do you lead us away from drinking the purest water of the living fountain to cisterns unable to contain water (Jer. 2:13)?

When one thing is put in place of another, it is necessarily the case that the thing put in place is one thing and the thing for which it is put is another. When it is said that predestination cannot exist without foreknowledge, but foreknowledge can exist without predestination, it is plainly declared that foreknowledge is one thing and predestination another.

Predestination cannot exist without foreknowledge because no one predestines except by foreknowing; no one predestines by not knowing. Foreknowledge, however, can exist without predestination because many things can be known and foreknown which are in no way predestined.

This is contained in the definition of the most blessed Augustine, and all Catholic interpreters of the divine words follow it. Prosper, arguing against the Pelagians, your ancestors, speaks as follows (*Against the Conferences of Gaul*, chapter 15):

“He who distinguishes foreknowledge of God in no way from his predestination attempts to ascribe to God concerning evil also what must be attributed to him concerning good. But since good things are to be referred to God as their giver and co-worker, whereas evil things are to be referred to the voluntary wickedness of rational creatures, there is no doubt that God, without any temporal difference, both foreknew and predestined those things which were to be done with him as their author, or which were to be assigned by a just judgment to evil merits; but he merely foreknew, without predestining, those things which were not to have their cause of action from him.”

Fulgentius, at the beginning of the second book of his responses to Monimus, begins as follows:

“Enough, as I think, dearest Monimus, has been treated and resolved in the preceding discourse concerning the difference between the predestination of the righteous and that of the wicked—that is, between those whom God’s prevenient and gratuitous mercy converts so that they may be justified and glorifies once converted, and those whom God’s just severity leaves in their sins and punishes once condemned—insofar as the Lord has deigned to assist our weakness. Thus, although many are accustomed to be not slightly disturbed by this question, they can easily be instructed by the testimonies of the divine books, and informed by the books of Augustine and by the responses of the most learned man Prosper. From these they may recognize that God’s predestination is nothing other than the preparation of his works, which, in his eternal disposition, he foreknew that he would accomplish either mercifully or justly.

“And because neither mercy nor justice is found in sins, the whole evil will of the wicked by which they sin was foreknown by God but was not predestined by God. They would not have that evil will in any other way than by departing from the Lord. God did not predestine man’s departure from himself, since the cause of that departure was solely the sinner’s voluntary turning away. Because God was not ignorant that this would occur, the sinner found in God’s eternal foreknowledge the punishment prepared for him by just retribution.”

These definitions of the holy Fathers make clear that foreknowledge is one thing and predestination another.

But when you say, “Foreknowledge alone, without predestination, belongs entirely to the evil things which God does not do,” this is true only if by “evil things” you mean sins, and not also their punishments, which no Catholic denies are repaid by God as judge.

Furthermore, when you speak of the foreknowledge of evil things, why did you earlier deny, even for a time, the foreknowledge of evil things? Or whether in those words of yours you once again intend “by contraries” to be understood is not clear. If this is admitted, your statement is shown to be altogether meaningless.

But lest you continue to complain about a capacity for contraries, it must be confessed with unshaken faith that neither predestination nor God’s judgment is rightly said, in a certain sense, to be capable of contraries, since there is nothing at all contrary within them. For it is certain that nothing belongs to God’s predestination and judgment except mercy and justice, whatever other names they may be called. These cannot in any way be called contrary to each other, since both mercy and justice are unquestionably good, through the author who is supremely, truly, and eternally good, and from whom everything good proceeds.

Therefore, if anyone denies that God’s mercy and justice are good, he is undoubtedly proved an enemy of the Catholic faith. Let predestination and God’s judgment, then, in no way be capable of contraries, because things that exist through a good author—namely God—cannot in any way be contrary to one another.

Prosper says (*Against the Conferences of Gaul*, chapter 6):

“Predestination of God, whether to good or to evil in human beings, is most ineptly said to operate, as though some necessity compelled human beings toward either one or the other; for in good things the will is to be understood as proceeding from grace, while in evil things the will is to be understood without grace.”

The same Prosper says:

“God’s predestination, therefore, is always directed toward the good: either it pertains to the repayment of justice or to the granting of grace.”

And again:

“God’s predestination is also always directed toward the good, for it knows that sin, committed solely by the human will, is either to be forgiven with the praise of mercy or punished with the praise of justice.”

You add and say:

### John Scotus

*(Chapter 11, number 8, section 7.)* “And lest anyone should doubt this, he added: ‘Therefore, the predestination of God, which is directed toward the good, is the preparation of grace, while grace is the effect of that very predestination.’”

In the book *On the Gift of Perseverance* he makes the same point entirely clear, saying:

“Therefore, whatever gifts God gives to anyone, he undoubtedly foreknew that he would give them and prepared them in his foreknowledge. Those whom he predestined, he also called” (Rom. 8:30), with that calling of which it is said: “The gifts and calling of God are without repentance.” For in his foreknowledge, which cannot be deceived or changed, he arranged his future works; and this is precisely, and nothing else, what it is to predestine.”

Who would dare to dissent from this clearest trumpet and most open proclamation of the Christian armies, which never ceases to resound with the clearest voice? To predestine is precisely, and nothing else, for God to arrange in his foreknowledge those works which he himself was going to do.

### Correction

You undoubtedly dared to dissent from this clearest trumpet, since, contrary to Augustine’s definition, you wished, insofar as you could, by the force of argument to establish that God’s predestination should be understood as nothing other than his foreknowledge, and that the punishments which he justly prepared for sinners should in no way be counted among his works.

While attempting to establish this by the reasoning of the definition itself, you pass to those conjoined and customary little arguments of yours by which you contrive to break down the defenses of truth. You begin them from another starting point of your disputation.

## Chapter XII

### On the definition of predestination

The title of the twelfth of your disputations is therefore:

### John Scotus

*(Number 1, section 1.)* “On the definition of predestination. Let the conversion of this definition be made as follows,” you say: “If it is true that foreknowledge, which cannot be deceived or changed, arranges future works, then to predestine is precisely, and nothing else, than to arrange one’s future works in foreknowledge, which cannot be deceived or changed.”

### Correction

Because this conversion of the definition is true and conflicts with you in every respect, you devise another conversion that is entirely contrary to it, when at the end of the preceding passage you set down, from Augustine’s words:

“A definition contains neither less nor more than what has been undertaken for explanation; otherwise it is altogether faulty.”

From this it is inferred that your other conversion is false. It is as follows:

### John Scotus

*(Chapter 12, number 2, section 1.)* “If all foreknowledge by which God arranged his future works is divine predestination, then all predestination by which God arranged his future works is divine foreknowledge.”

### Correction

This is not contained in Augustine’s definition. For he did not say that all foreknowledge by which God arranged his future works is divine predestination. Rather, he said that to arrange his future works in his foreknowledge—which cannot be deceived or changed—is precisely, and nothing else, what it is to predestine.

Nor did he say, “Foreknowledge is the arrangement of God’s future works”; instead, he placed the arrangement—that is, predestination—in foreknowledge. Foreknowledge, therefore, is one thing, in which God’s future works are arranged, that is, predestined; arrangement—that is, the predestination of his future works—is another thing, established in his foreknowledge.

Foreknowledge arranged, that is, predestined, his future works; it did not, by predestination, foreknow his future works. Foreknowledge precedes predestination in order, because predestination proceeds from foreknowledge, not foreknowledge from predestination. And just as it is correctly said, “By foreknowing he predestines; by predestining he foreknows,” so it is not generally correct to say, “By foreknowledge he predestines; by predestination he foreknows.”

That is, although it is correctly said that foreknowledge predestines, it is not equally broadly correct to say that predestination foreknows. For foreknowledge does not arise from predestination; rather, predestination is derived from foreknowledge.

Therefore many things can be foreknown without predestination—that is, they can be merely foreknown and not predestined—but nothing can be predestined unless it is foreknown. Certainly, nowhere do we find Augustine or the other Fathers saying that all foreknowledge is predestination or that all predestination is foreknowledge. Rather, they say that foreknowledge can exist without predestination, whereas predestination can never exist without foreknowledge.

Your conversion is therefore proved false. It exceeds the boundaries of the definition and fabricates what the truth of the definition does not contain. Nor is it surprising that you call this a “conversion,” since, departing from the truth, it attempts to introduce falsehood; for the word “conversion” is ambiguous and can signify either a turning from evil to good, which is praiseworthy, or a turning from good to evil, which is blameworthy.

It should not, therefore, be said: “All foreknowledge by which God arranged his future works is divine predestination.”

[scan page 593]

**SAINT PRUDENTIUS**

…and every predestination by which God disposed his future works is divine foreknowledge; but in God’s foreknowledge, by which he disposed his future works, there is divine predestination, and every predestination of his by which he disposed his future works is contained in divine foreknowledge.

What you conclude, therefore, is true when you say:

**JOHN SCOTUS**  
*(Chapter 10, no. 3, section 1.)* “It is therefore acknowledged that God’s predestination exists only in his works, since its definition contains neither less nor more than the disposition of divine works.”

**CORRECTION**

You show that you have brought this forward deceitfully when you immediately add:

**JOHN SCOTUS**  
*(Chapter 11, no. 4, section 2.)* “But to this, you will say, it belongs to God’s works to predestine those who are rightly to be damned to punishment, just as it belongs to his works to predestine those who are to be saved by grace to blessedness. And you will try to confirm this with the testimony of the same blessed Augustine, which, in the order in which you have placed it, we have also placed, so that in them we may see not what you, but what he, intended; for if one of them is rightly expounded, it will suffice for understanding the others. Let us therefore put forward this passage [Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 100]:

‘Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills’ (Ps. 110:2). And he sought them out so wisely that, when the angelic and human creature sinned—that is, when it did not do what he intended but what it itself willed—he nevertheless fulfilled through that same creature’s will what the Creator did not will. He used evil things well, as supremely good, both for the damnation of those whom he justly predestined to punishment and for the salvation of those whom he mercifully predestined to grace.’

Behold: in one and the same sentence he says, ‘he predestined to punishment, he predestined to grace.’ Where, we ask, does this answer the question we are putting: whether predestining the wicked to punishment belongs to God’s justice or to his grace? You will answer, I believe, ‘to his justice,’ for he says, ‘whom he justly predestined to punishment,’ and not ‘to grace.’ Therefore, if predestination to punishment is not God’s gift but the judgment of sin, it necessarily follows either that what Augustine himself said is false—‘God’s predestination, insofar as it is in the good, is the preparation of grace’—or that predestination to punishment must be understood in the opposite sense. Yet what he said is true and immutable: ‘God’s predestination, insofar as it is in the good, is the preparation of grace.’ Therefore, by contrast, he intended what he stated—‘he predestined to punishment.’”

**CORRECTION**

Anyone illumined by the light of truth plainly sees how falsely you have made this statement, claiming that blessed Augustine presented the predestination of the wicked in a contrary sense. We have already refuted the absurdity of this interpretation by the authority of Scripture and by examples from venerable Fathers. Omitting the others, Saint Fulgentius of Ruspe alone is more than sufficient for this purpose,

**PRUDENTIUS, BISHOP OF TROYES** [scan page 594]

who, setting aside—or rather, not even considering—your perversity, confirms that blessed Augustine understood and stated the predestined-to-punishment not contrarily but rightly, not by negation but in truth.

Accordingly, since predestination to punishment is not God’s gift but the judgment of sin—that is, the recompense of justice—it does not necessarily follow that what Augustine himself said is false: “God’s predestination, insofar as it is in the good, is the preparation of grace”; nor must predestination to punishment be understood in the opposite sense. For he does not say absolutely, “God’s predestination is the preparation of grace,” or “all God’s predestination is the preparation of grace,” or “God’s predestination is nothing other than the preparation of grace.” Rather, by adding “insofar as it is in the good,” he clearly indicates that he defined only that predestination which pertains to the elect, not that which justly punishes the reprobate. And in the same sentence, just as he truthfully said “predestined to grace,” so he truthfully added “predestined to punishment.” Since this displeases you, and since you appear to think that the matter is hidden from others, anyone prudent could oppose you with what we have now briefly set forth.

You continue by adding:

**JOHN SCOTUS**  
*(Chapter 11, no. 5, section 3.)* “But lest perhaps you object that he did not say, ‘God’s predestination is the preparation of grace,’ but, ‘God’s predestination, insofar as it is in the good, is the preparation of grace,’ it seems to you that room is left for another predestination, which is somehow in evil; or, if there is one and the same predestination, it is not denied that it can exist in good and evil. First observe that one definition cannot contain two predestinations at all. Next, if no other definition of predestination can be found more true or more suitable than the one given above, and if it comprehends nothing except divine works—which no pious believer doubts are good—what compels us, when we hear ‘God’s predestination, insofar as it is in the good,’ to understand anything else except that it is always both good and in the good?”

**CORRECTION**

O offspring emerging from the root of the serpent, of whom it is sung: “O crooked serpent, who through a thousand winding passages and deceitful turns agitate tranquil hearts,” and likewise, you who possess a thousand arts of causing harm—why do you oppose the truth with such obstinacy? Why do you strive to infect the clarity of truth with the tunnels of falsehood?

If Fulgentius had known that Augustine thought and spoke in the way you claim, he would never have spoken of a diversity of predestination; Gregory would never have referred to predestinations in the plural; Isidore would never have called predestination twofold; nor would all the other Catholic teachers so often have stated in their writings that people were destined, predestined, prepared, made ready, assigned, or appointed for punishment or destruction. Therefore we too unhesitatingly confess that God’s predestination is always good and is in the good, just as his judgment is; for since God’s predestination and judgment contain nothing other than mercy and justice, his predestination and judgment can in no way be evil or be in evil, since they contain nothing other than good things—namely, mercy and justice. Yet although, as we have said, it is always good and in the good, blessed Augustine considered something else in his definition, saying *(On the Predestination of the Saints, chapter 10)*:

“God’s predestination, insofar as it is in the good, is the preparation of grace.”

“Insofar as it is in the good,” he says—that is, insofar as it pertains to the good of the election of the saints—so that another predestination may be understood to be in evil, though it is not itself wholly evil, because it pertains to God’s justice; nevertheless, it justly punishes the reprobate, because justice is certainly good, since nothing opposes it.

That he understood it in this way he himself makes clear in other statements in his books. In the *Enchiridion* (chapter 52) he says:

“For sometimes God’s judgment is spoken of as being in evil; hence the statement: ‘Those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment’ (John 5:29). Sometimes it is spoken of as being in good, according to the words: ‘Save me, O God, by your name, and judge me by your strength’ (Ps. 53:3). For by God’s judgment the separation of the good and the evil itself takes place, so that the good, who are to be delivered from evil and not destroyed with the wicked, may be separated at the right hand. Therefore he cries out: ‘Judge me, O God.’ And as though explaining what he had said, he adds: ‘And distinguish my cause’ (Ps. 42:1).”

Thus, just as he willed God’s judgment to be spoken of and understood as being either in evil or in good, so without hesitation he willed predestination to be spoken of and understood as being either in evil or in good, since it in no way differs from God’s judgment. Meanwhile you continue:

**JOHN SCOTUS**  
*(Chapter 12, no. 6, section 3.)* “But if you say, ‘It is good to predestine the wicked to punishment, and therefore this must be reckoned among God’s works,’ we answer: It is good because it is just. But since it is not God’s gift, because it is his judgment, while all God’s predestination is wholly the preparation of grace, and every grace is a gift, it necessarily follows that all divine predestination is the preparation of his gifts. Punishment will undoubtedly torture the wicked justly; it is not a gift. Otherwise, if it were a gift, it would not torture but would certainly liberate. Therefore it is not predestination to punishment; for if it were, it would not be punishment but grace. But it is punishment; therefore it is not its predestination.”

**CORRECTION**

Anyone who reads attentively will easily see how far you depart from the truth and fall like Balaam with his eyes open. When you say that it is good to predestine the wicked to punishment because it is just, you plainly see the truth with open eyes. But when you add:

“But since it is not God’s gift, because it is his judgment, it is therefore not predestination to punishment; for if it were, it would not be punishment but grace,”

you either wholly deny God’s justice and judgment or affirm that they are entirely evil. For if nothing else belongs to God’s goodness except freely bestowing gifts, it remains that his justice and judgment, by which the reprobate are punished, are either evil or do not exist at all. Yet all Scripture proclaims God both just and judge. If these things are not good because they are not gifts, what remains except that you deny God to be the one who is both just and judge?

You have separated his judgment from everything else as though you wished the judgment to be understood as evil. Such, indeed, are your words: “But since it is not God’s gift, because it is his judgment”—as though nothing else could be good except God’s gift. Yet it is judgment, and it is justice, and it is wholly good. Therefore, if justice and judgment are unquestionably good, it necessarily follows that predestining the wicked to punishment is good, since it is God’s justice and judgment. Whoever denies this to be good is undoubtedly convicted of irreligion.

Likewise, what you say *(chapter 11, no. 7, section 3)*—“All God’s predestination is wholly the preparation of grace”—is false according to the definition of blessed Augustine, which is found nowhere in the form you give it. For he nowhere says simply, “All God’s predestination is the preparation of grace”; rather, because he speaks truly, he says: “God’s predestination, insofar as it is in the good, is the preparation of grace.” Therefore, just as God’s justice and judgment distribute good to the good and evil to the evil, so predestination has disposed good things for the good and evil things for the evil.

Then you insert *(chapter 12, no. 8, section 4)*:

“Punishment will undoubtedly torture the wicked justly; it is not a gift. Otherwise, if it were a gift, it would not torture but would certainly liberate. Therefore it is not predestination to punishment.”

But do you not consider that punishment belongs to God’s justice precisely because it is just? Since you admit that the wicked are tortured justly, you must necessarily admit that this is good, because everything just is good. Therefore, if it is good because it is just, and if it is established that the wicked are tortured by punishment, it is false that there is no predestination to punishment. For just as it was just to recompense them, so it was likewise just—and therefore good—to have predestined this recompense. For if there were no justice, there would be no predestination; nor would there be a future judgment. Yet there is a judgment by which each person is recompensed according to his works. Therefore it is the predestination of that judgment, that is, the preparation and disposition in God’s foreknowledge of future works. There is also punishment, by which the wicked are recompensed; and there is recompense, by which the pious are rewarded. If this is the whole of what it means for God to have predestined what, with himself as its author, was going to occur—namely, mercy and judgment—then I plainly marvel at your blindness: you deny at one moment and affirm at another.

For while you had everywhere denied punishments due to sins, now you confess them when you say: “Punishment will undoubtedly torture the wicked justly.” And again: “It is punishment.” Since you already acknowledge punishment, it is plainly madness to deny its predestination, since it is just. Everything just is good; therefore predestination to punishment is good, just as judgment is, because it is undoubtedly just. Nothing unjust is good; everything just is good; therefore predestination to punishment is good, because it is certainly just.

For this reason your frivolous argument is deservedly condemned, since you are attempting to overthrow what both authority and reason clearly establish. But the testimony of Augustine which you adduce in confirmation of predestination, when rightly understood, in no way supports your assertion. For when he says *(Augustine, On the Gift of Perseverance, chapter 17, at the end)*:

“These gifts of God, if there is no predestination such as we defend, are not foreknown by God; but they are foreknown. This, then, is the predestination which we defend,”

and goes on:

“Thus this same predestination is sometimes signified also by the name of foreknowledge, as the Apostle says: ‘God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew’ (Rom. 11:2). What he says, ‘he foreknew,’ cannot rightly be understood except as ‘he predestined,’”

he clearly shows by what follows that he was speaking only of the predestination pertaining to the saints. He adds, namely, “which we defend,” since he had undertaken to defend that predestination; for it was already being attacked by your, so to speak, champions. The letter of Prosper and Hilary to him, his reply, the title of the book, and the whole proceeding make this sufficiently and plainly evident. For the predestination of the wicked had not yet begun to be denied; indeed, we frequently find it stated in the books of the Pelagians and even of Origen. We have therefore not thought it necessary to produce their testimonies, since, by the Lord’s favor, we rejoice that we possess a more abundant store of Catholic defenses. From this Augustine’s statement, inserted from his book *On the Gift of Perseverance* and judged by you, although wholly ineptly, to be included in your own arguments, you derive your customary error: while discussing the predestination of the saints, he taught that foreknowledge is sometimes used in its place.

**JOHN SCOTUS**  
*(Chapter 10, no. 10, section 5.)* “All foreknowledge pertaining to the elect is predestination; there is no predestination except of the elect; therefore no foreknowledge pertaining to the elect is not predestination. No one is chosen for punishment; how, then, is punishment predestined, since it belongs properly to the reprobate?”

**CORRECTION**

This argument is shown to be false by what has preceded. When you say *(no. 11)*, “There is no predestination except of the elect,” you are lying, because the authority of Holy Scripture and the unanimity of the holy Fathers plainly and consistently indicate that people are destined, predestined, prepared, made ready, assigned, or appointed for punishment or destruction.

And when you infer: “No one is chosen for punishment; how, then, is punishment predestined, since it belongs properly to the reprobate?” you seem to understand election and predestination as one and the same, although everyone knows that they differ greatly. For who does not know that choosing is one thing and predestining another? Just as choosing is one thing and disposing another, so choosing is one thing and designating another; for it has already been shown above that to designate or predestine means nothing other than to dispose, prepare, or whatever else expresses the same meaning.

Moreover, Scripture rarely testifies that anyone is chosen for punishment or destruction; but all the Scripture of the Old and New Testaments testifies that people are predestined to punishments.

But when you say *(no. 12)* that punishment is peculiar to the reprobate, it is astonishing why you call it peculiar to the reprobate, since the truth of the Christian faith holds that, apart from God and our Lord Jesus Christ, no one born from sinful descent is born except as a sinner, and therefore deserves punishment by God’s just judgment. Accordingly, just as we hold without hesitation that all are sinners through the transmission of nature, so all are liable to punishment; and just as no one is freed from sin except by free grace, so no one is freed from punishment except by the same mercy.

Punishment, therefore, is proper to all sinners, just as, after the first transgression, sinful nature is common to all. Thus punishment is common to all, just as guilt is common to all, as the Apostle says: “Just as through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death” (Rom. 5:12); and again: “In whom all sinned” (ibid.).

Certainly, by the tradition of our forebears we believe and confess that the first man, although he sinned so gravely that he subjected the whole human race, which was to be born from his descent through the intercourse of man and woman, to sin and death, was saved by God’s grace and joined to the company of the saints. Just as he was the first of all human beings to sin with his wife, so he was the first to receive the punishment of condemnation.

Let us ask, then, whether his punishment was proper to him or foreign to him. No one doubts that his sin was his own; it was therefore just that he should receive his own punishment—although unwillingly—for he had committed his own sin willingly and not unwillingly. Punishment, therefore, should be called proper to all sinners, not merely to the reprobate, because the guilt by which they deserved punishment is common to all, not merely to the reprobate.

And this is what is faithfully meant when we say that God predestined, prepared, disposed, assigned, or appointed for sinners the punishments which he had foreseen he would justly render to them as sinners. For if he did not predestine punishments, what does it mean that, when giving the command of obedience to the first human beings, he said: “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall surely die” (Gen. 2:17)? And again, if he did not render deserved punishments to them, what does it mean that he said to those same sinners: “Until you return to the earth from which you were taken, for dust you are and to dust you shall return” (Gen. 3:19)?

If, I say, he neither foreknew nor predestined this punishment, how did he foretell it before the sin as something future and then inflict it after the sin? Therefore, just as I might perhaps not improperly call his guilt his own, so I might call his punishment his own, as I might say of every sinner, since, according to the Apostle, “all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. 3:23), and, “Scripture has confined all things under sin, so that he might have mercy on all” (Gal. 3:22).

But because you twist the word “election” toward the perversity of contradiction which is so congenial to you, and because, by bringing forward a statement of blessed Augustine, you try to prove that the reprobate are called elect although they are not elect, you very clearly show that you have not yet fully understood what he meant. Augustine says *(Augustine, On Rebuke and Grace, chapter 7, §9)*:

[scan page 596]

“Those who are elect are elected to reign with Christ, not in the same way that Judas was elected for the work suited to him. For he was elected by the one who knows how to use even evil things well, so that through his damnable work the work for which Christ himself had come might be accomplished. Therefore, when we hear, ‘Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?’ (John 6:71), we ought to understand that they were chosen through mercy, but he through judgment. He chose them to obtain his kingdom, but him to shed his blood.

“Yet God’s firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: ‘The Lord knows those who are his’ (2 Tim. 2:19). Their faith, which works through love (Gal. 5:6), certainly either does not fail at all, or, if there are some whose faith fails, it is restored before this life ends; and their perseverance to the end is reckoned to them after the iniquity into which they had fallen has been blotted out.

“But those who will not persevere, and who will fall away from the Christian faith and way of life so that the end of this life finds them in that condition, are certainly not to be counted among the number of these even at the time when they live well and piously. For by God’s foreknowledge and predestination they have not been separated from that mass of perdition. Therefore they were not called according to the purpose, and consequently they were not elect, but belong among those of whom it is said, ‘Many are called,’ and not among those of whom it is said, ‘but few are elect’ (Matt. 22:14).

“And yet who would deny that they are elect when they believe, are baptized, and live according to God? They are plainly called elect by those who do not know what they will become, but not by the one who knows that they do not possess the perseverance which brings the elect to blessed life, and who knows that they stand only in the way he foreknew [variant: “foreknew”] that they would fall.”

Nor should it disturb us that God does not give this perseverance to certain of his children. Far be it from being so if they were among those predestined and called according to the purpose. But those who are not children of promise—[variant: “who truly are children of promise; for these…”]—are called children of God by us while they live piously; but because they will live impiously and will die in that same impiety, God’s foreknowledge does not call them children of God.

For there are children of God who are not yet so to us but are already so to God. Of these the evangelist John says: “Jesus was about to die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the scattered children of God” (John 11:51–52). They were to become such by believing through the preaching of the Gospel; nevertheless, before this occurred, they were already children of God, inscribed in the unshaken permanence of their Father’s eternal memory.

There are again certain children who, because they have temporarily received grace, are called by us children, but are not so to God. Of these the same John says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2:19).

Therefore, when those who did not possess perseverance are called children of God, it is said of them: “They went out from us, but they were not of us.” And it is added [variant: “and they add”]: “For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us.” What else is meant than that they were not children even when they were in the profession and name of children?”

**CORRECTION**

Because you defer the evidence of this statement to another passage, we too shall defer our response to it for the time being.

## CHAPTER XIII

**What can be gathered from the foregoing statement of Saint Augustine**

The thirteenth chapter is therefore introduced under this heading:

**JOHN SCOTUS**  
*(Chapter 13, no. 2, section 1.)* “What can be gathered from the foregoing statement of Saint Augustine?”

**CORRECTION**

In this passage, while you try to gather from the words of Saint Augustine *(Augustine, same work)* support for what you are attempting to persuade us to prove, you depart very far from Augustine’s meaning. For when he introduced the testimony of the Lord, “Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?” (John 6:71), he added:

“We ought to understand them as chosen through mercy, but him through judgment; them to obtain his kingdom, but him to shed his blood.”

These words, considered carefully and weighed soberly, express something quite different from what you infer. He said that the eleven were chosen through mercy and that Judas the betrayer was chosen through judgment.

We must therefore gather from his other books and sermons, or nearly all of them, everything he treated in various ways—but not with a different faith—concerning Judas’s election, so that it may clearly be weighed whether he ever taught, as you imagine, that the passage should be understood in the opposite sense, or whether the manifest truth of his statements is what all orthodox teachers have unanimously recognized without disagreement.

On this matter the same venerable teacher spoke in his book *Questions on Genesis* *(book 11, question 47)*. Explaining the passage of Scripture which says, “These are the sons of Israel who were born to him in Mesopotamia, and they are counted as twelve” (Gen. 35:26), although Benjamin was born much later, he says:

“There is no easier solution to this question than to understand it by synecdoche. For where the greater or more important part is present, what does not properly belong to that name is also usually included under it. Thus, among the twelve apostles, Judas no longer belonged to the number when the Lord rose from the dead—and indeed he was already dead—yet the Apostle retained the name of the number twelve in his Epistle, where he says that Christ appeared to the twelve (1 Cor. 15). The Greek copies have the article, so that ‘any twelve’ cannot be understood, but rather those distinguished by that number. In the same manner, I think the Lord’s statement, ‘Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?’ (John 6:71), was spoken so that Judas himself should not appear to belong to the election. For the name of the elect is not easily found in an evil sense, except when the wicked are chosen by the wicked.

“Yet if we suppose that he too was chosen so that through his betrayal the Lord’s passion might be fulfilled—that is, that his evil was chosen for some purpose, since God makes good use even of evil—let us attend to the Lord’s statement: ‘I am not speaking of all of you; I know whom I have chosen’ (John 13:18). There he declares that election pertains only to the good. Therefore the statement, ‘I chose you twelve,’ was spoken by synecdoche, so that in the name of the greater and better part what does not properly belong to that name might also be included.”

**CORRECTION**

This statement frustrates your delirious argument, by which you impose upon us interpretations of contradiction; for through the rhetorical figure of synecdoche the passage is instead opened up to understanding. Once these objections have been removed, it must be understood that the word “election” is always used by God in a good sense: either, according to the statements just cited, for the receiving of the eternal kingdom, or, according to other orthodox interpreters of the Church, for some good that is to be bestowed temporarily by God’s will and command.

Thus Scripture reports concerning Saul, when Samuel said to the people: “Surely you see whom the Lord has chosen, for there is none like him among all the people” (1 Sam. 10:24). Here the word “election” by no means signifies the obtaining of an eternal kingdom, but the administration of a temporary office.

The same prophet, describing his father’s genealogy more carefully, sets it out as follows:

“There was a man of Benjamin named Kish, son of Abiel, son of Zeror, son of Bechorath, son of Aphiah, son of a man of Benjamin, mighty in strength. And he had a son named Saul, chosen and good; and there was no man among the sons of Israel better than he” (1 Sam. 9:1).

If you had perhaps been uncertain about the meaning of “chosen,” the words “good” and “better” have dispelled every cloud of hesitation. In the same way Judas was chosen by the Lord for the temporary office of apostleship, though not for the eternal reward of apostleship.

The Gospel indicates that he received from the Lord, together with the others, the power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy (Luke 10:19), and that, after performing miracles through the power he had received, he returned with the others to the Lord (Mark 6:13). These examples teach that they were chosen by the Lord neither falsely nor deceitfully nor hypocritically, but altogether truly, though not to attain eternal blessedness, but to administer some temporary dispensation.

And lest you think that Saul’s election should be taken in the opposite sense or twisted toward evil, truthful Scripture plainly testifies that he was good and that there was none better than he among the sons of Israel. This was not said or imagined by those who were ignorant of the matter, but by the prophet, whose knowledge of his goodness was illumined by the Lord.

Augustine, in Homily 27 on the Gospel of John:

“The Lord Jesus says: ‘Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?’ (John 6:71). Therefore this man too was chosen, so that, though unwilling and ignorant, a great good might come from him. This is characteristic of God, the opposite of what belongs to the wicked.

“For just as the wicked make bad use of God’s good works, so, conversely, God makes good use of the wicked works of wicked people. Wicked people, I say, listen and understand: just as the wicked make bad use of God’s good works, so, conversely, God makes good use of the wicked works of the wicked.

“How good it is that the members of the body are arranged in a way that could not occur except by the art of the Lord! Yet how badly the eyes are used by the covetous! How badly the tongue is used by the deceiver! Does not a false witness first slaughter his own tongue and soul, and then, after destroying himself, try to injure another? He uses his tongue badly, but the tongue is not therefore evil; the tongue is God’s work, but that wickedness makes bad use of God’s good work.

“How do those who run toward crimes use their feet? How do murderers use their hands, and the good creatures of God that are attached to them externally? How badly do the wicked use gold, when they corrupt judgments and oppress the innocent! The wicked use light badly: by living badly, they even usurp the light which they see for the service of their crimes. When an evil man goes to do something evil, he wants light for himself so that he may not stumble, though he has already stumbled inwardly and fallen. Whatever befalls him in the body has already occurred in the heart.

“To avoid going through each instance individually, the wicked person makes bad use of all God’s good things. Conversely, the good God makes good use of the evil works of evil people. And what is as good as the good God? For the Lord himself said: ‘No one is good except God alone’ (Mark 10:18). Therefore, the better he is, the better he makes use even of our evils.

“What was worse than Judas? Among all those who clung to the Master, he was entrusted with the purse of the twelve, and the distribution of aid to the poor. Ungrateful for so great a benefit and so great an honor, he accepted money, lost justice, and betrayed life, though dead. He followed Christ as a disciple and persecuted him as an enemy. All this was Judas’s evil, but the Lord made good use of his evil. He allowed himself to be betrayed in order to redeem us. Behold, Judas’s evil has been turned into good.

“How many martyrs did Satan persecute? If Satan had ceased to persecute, we would not today celebrate so glorious a crown as that of Saint Lawrence. If, then, God makes good use of the evil works of the devil himself, what the wicked man does by using them badly harms him; it does not contradict God’s goodness. The craftsman makes use of him—and a great craftsman. If he could not make use of him, he would not even permit him to exist.

“Therefore, ‘one of you is a devil,’ he says, although ‘I chose you twelve’ (John 6:71).”

The same author, in Homily 7, *On the Lord’s Supper*:

“One of you will betray me” (John 13:21)—one of you in number, not in merit; in outward appearance, not in virtue; in bodily association, not in spiritual bond; in physical proximity, not in unity of heart. Therefore he is not one who is truly of you, but one who will go out from you.

“For how will what Jesus declared be true when he said, ‘One of you,’ if what he himself says in his Epistle—the Epistle whose Gospel this is—is true: ‘They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us’ (1 John 2:19)?
