**1182**

**ON PREDESTINATION AGAINST JOHN SCOTUS**

… is it written: “I chose to be cast down in the house of my God rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners” (Psalm LXXXIII, 11)? Surely not. What, then, were we except wicked and lost? For we had not yet believed in him, so that he might choose us. For if he chose us as already believing, the chosen one chose him. Therefore, when he said, “You did not choose me,” what else did he say except that his mercy preceded us (Psalm LVIII, 11)—universally, certainly, not personally, so that divine justice might remain consistent toward all? Here indeed the empty reasoning of those who defend God’s foreknowledge against God’s grace is refuted. They say that we were chosen before the foundation of the world because God foreknew that we would become good, not because he himself would make us good.

That is not what he says. What does he say? “You did not choose me”; for if he had chosen us because he foreknew that we would become good, he would likewise have foreknown that we would first choose him. He therefore chose by grace, just as he also chose Judas; but it is necessary that human obedience and diligence respond to divine election.

*Behold how often that holy man has spoken prudently and faithfully about one and the same matter, and nowhere is he found to have taught the word “election” in an opposite sense. Moreover, as an assertion of the contrary you add (chapter 12, number 3, section 2) that “the friend who had always been an enemy”—I wonder with what authority you have ventured to say this, since nowhere is it believed or read that he had an inimical disposition at the time of his choosing, until, after so many benefits and gifts, he prepared his mind for betrayal.*

*For at the very moment of his calling he could not yet have contemplated the Lord’s destruction: he knew that the Jews were not, I will not say persecuting him, but not even recognizing him as Prophet or Lord. Nor is it credible that he was chosen as an enemy by the Lord, although the Lord did not fail to know that this would happen in the future; rather, in the course of time he changed from goodness to wickedness. Thus both the angel and the human being were undoubtedly created good by the supremely good Creator, and thereafter became evil through their own voluntary turning away.*

*The evangelist, when he related the breaking of the flask of ointment at the Lord’s feet, says that Judas murmured: “Why this waste of ointment? For it could have been sold for much and given to the poor.” But he said this because he was a thief, and, having charge of the money-box, he used to carry away what was put into it (Matthew XXVI, 8). It must be believed that he conceived the evil of betrayal from the time when he himself received from the Lord the office of administering the funds and learned that the fury of the Jews was being stirred up against him.*

*Blessed Gregory repeatedly taught this very thing, and, leaving it for us to believe in the writings of his venerable authority, said in his homily on the Gospel concerning those invited to the wedding, when he was discussing the man who had dishonored the wedding celebration by wearing a garment unsuitable for the wedding and had been rebuked by the king under the name of “friend” (Gregory, Homily 38 on the Gospels):*

> “It is exceedingly astonishing, dearest brothers, that he both calls him ‘friend’ and rejects him—as though he were saying more openly: ‘Friend, and not friend; friend by faith, but not friend by works.’”

*Jerome says:*

> “He calls him ‘friend’ because he had been invited to the wedding, but ‘son of shamelessness’ because, having come in a filthy garment, he had defiled the wedding festivities.”

*He also repeatedly taught that this should be understood in Judas’s greeting. Likewise Gregory (*Moralia*, book III, chapter 14):*

> “But heretics, because they desire to teach the holy Church their doctrines, approach it as though to console it. Nor is it surprising that those who represent the form of adversaries are called friends, since even to the betrayer it is said: ‘Friend, for what have you come?’ (Matthew XXVI, 50). And the rich man who is consumed in the fire of hell is called a son of Abraham (Luke XVI, 25), because, although the wicked neglect to be corrected by us, it is nevertheless right that they should be called friends by us—not because of their wickedness, but because of our kindness.”

*The same author (*Moralia*, book X, section VI, chapter 11):*

> “Accordingly, the following is rightly said by the prophet under the figure of Babylon to the reprobate mind: ‘Come down, sit in the dust, virgin daughter of Babylon; sit on the ground; there is no throne, daughter of the Chaldeans’ (Isaiah XLVII, 1). In this passage the human mind is called a virgin not, as I think, because it is undefiled, but because it is unfruitful. And because ‘Babylon’ means ‘confusion,’ the unfruitful mind is rightly called the daughter of Babylon: since, in that it produces no good works and is ordered by no discipline of upright life, it is as though it were born from a mother who is confusion. But if ‘virgin’ is understood not as unfruitful but as undefiled, then, after it has lost the state of salvation, it is called by the name of what it was, to increase its confusion.”

*Jerome (*Against Jovinianus*, book I):*

> “‘A bad tree does not produce good fruit, nor a good tree bad fruit’ (Matthew VII, 17). If this is so, answer me: how did Paul, when he was a bad tree persecuting the Church of Christ, afterward produce good fruits; and how did Judas, when he was a good tree performing signs with the apostles, afterward, having turned into a betrayer, produce bad fruits? Therefore, for as long as they persevere either in their goodness or in their wickedness, neither does the good tree produce bad fruits, nor the bad tree good fruits.”

*The same author, on what you say.*

**JOHN SCOTUS**

*(Chapter 12, number 4, section 1.)* 8. “And just as they are not sons if they are not heirs, so they are not chosen if they are not loved. How, then, unless it were said in the opposite sense, could Judas be called chosen when he was not loved?”

**CORRECTION**

*You ought to have investigated more carefully the words “love” and “election” in the Holy Scriptures, on whose authority you rely when you mutter things contrary to them. For in the Books of Kings and the Books of Chronicles we read that Solomon was called Jedidiah—that is, “beloved of the Lord”—and that “the Lord loved him.” This was not said by some ignorant person, but certainly by a prophet who knew the Lord’s will (II Samuel XII, 24–25).*

*Likewise, when the evangelist described the rich young man, possessing great wealth, who came to the Lord and professed that he had observed the commandments, he continued: “And Jesus, looking at him, loved him” (Mark X, 21)—plainly because of his observance of God’s commandments. Yet because he had many possessions, he went away sorrowful.*

[scan page 599]

**1183**

Behold: the prophet and the evangelist declare that those whom they perhaps did not doubt were not sons of promise were nevertheless loved by the Lord. For Saint Gregory shows that a good action can also please God in the wicked, when in his exposition of the prophet Ezekiel he says (*Book I, Homily 10*):

> “Thus, when Ahab, the wicked king, was rebuked by the prophet and heard the divine sentence against him, he was afraid and was weighed down by great sorrow, so that the Lord said to his prophet: ‘Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before me? Because he has humbled himself for my sake, I will not bring the evil upon him in his days’ (III Kings XXI, 29). In these words of the Lord we must consider how sorrowful bitterness pleases him in his elect, who fear losing the Lord, if repentance pleased him even in the reprobate who feared losing the present age; or how voluntary affliction for sins is pleasing to him in those who please him, if it pleased him temporarily in one who displeased him [another reading: and in those who displeased him].”

*He ought therefore to have observed from the Fathers that the words “love” and “election” were not understood and used in an opposite sense, but were assigned, according to the variety of circumstances, either to eternal blessedness or to a temporal arrangement.*

*And although I have brought forward the preceding statements concerning election according to Augustine’s understanding, the word “election” is nevertheless also found used in an evil sense by the prophet Ezekiel, who says:*

> “I will bring you into the wilderness of the peoples, and there I will enter into judgment with you face to face. Just as I entered into judgment with your fathers in the wilderness of the land of Egypt, so I will enter into judgment with you, says the Lord. I will subject you to my rod and bring you into the bonds of the covenant. I will choose from among you the transgressors and the wicked, and I will bring them out of the land of their sojourning, but they shall not enter the land of Israel; and you shall know that I am the Lord” (Ezekiel XX, 35–38).

*Jerome explains this as follows (*On Ezekiel*, chapter XX, 35):*

> “He says: ‘I will do to you who are in Babylon and now serve idols what I did to your fathers in Egypt: I will bring you into the wilderness of the peoples, and there I will enter into judgment with you face to face, just as I contended with them in judgment when they came out of Egypt. After I have judged you, I will subject you to my rod and rule, make a covenant with you, and bring you into your land in the bonds of charity, so that, bound by love for me, you cannot depart from me. But from among you I will choose transgressors and wicked persons who persist through hardness of heart in evil deeds, not in order to possess them, but to cast them away. I shall indeed bring them out of the land of their sojourning, so that, once brought out, they may not enter the land of Israel, but perish in different regions; and by the distinction between good and evil you may know that I am [another reading: that I am] the Lord, who does all things in judgment.”*

*It is therefore clear, in accordance with the prophet’s confirmation and the Lord’s threat, that God’s election is also used in an evil sense. But that it also signifies a temporal dispensation is attested by outstanding interpreters of the divine utterances, who taught that this occurs most often not through your contrariety, but through a certain temporal dispensation of God. Hence the Lord says through Ezekiel: “On the day when I chose Israel and lifted up my hand for the offspring of the house of Jacob,” and so forth (Ezekiel XX, 5). Jerome, in the same place (chapter XX, 5), says:*

> “Literally, no one can doubt that the land of Judea is renowned and more fertile than all other lands, if he considers the whole territory from Rhinocorura to Mount Taurus and the Euphrates River, as well as the power of its cities and the beauty of its regions—Palestine, Phoenicia, Arabia, Syria, Coele-Syria, Cilicia, and the other regions that the Lord promised to Israel if it kept God’s commandments. Since Israel did not receive them, this was the fault of its unbelief; for even in Palestine and the province of Judea many nations remained that were not expelled. Nor is the promisor guilty if the one to whom the promise is made makes himself unworthy of the promise, especially since the choice of the one making the promise is proposed: ‘If you are willing and obey me, you shall eat the good things of the land; but if you are unwilling, the sword shall devour you’ (Isaiah I, 19–20). Therefore they are chosen by foreknowledge [another reading: by presence]; but the one who is chosen is not thereby immediately incapable of being tested or of perishing, since both Saul, chosen as king, and Judas, chosen as an apostle, afterward fell through their own fault.”

*The same author in the same work (*On Ezekiel*, chapter I, verses 13–14):*

> “As the heavens therefore flash with frequent fires, and in the blink of an eye and a moment the lightning darts forth and returns, without losing its matrix and, so to speak, the source and material of the fire, so these living creatures, proceeding with unhindered step, hasten toward what lies before them. But if they see something opposed to their effort [another reading: obstructing it], they do not so much turn back as contract themselves while extending upward [another reading: extending backward], and they provide the light that they had hidden for a little while, so that they may give the servants their food at the proper time, neither giving what is holy to dogs nor casting pearls before swine. Hence Paul says: ‘I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able to receive it’ (I Corinthians III, 2). The election of Judas and the anointing of Saul therefore do not prove that God was ignorant of future things, but show that he is the judge of present things.”

*Ambrose, in his Letter to the Romans IX, 11:*

> “God’s foreknowledge is required in these matters, in which nothing other than what God knows will happen can occur; for, knowing what each of them would be, he said: ‘The one who will be lesser shall be worthy, and the one who will be greater shall be unworthy’ (Genesis XXV, 23); he chose one by foreknowledge and rejected the other (Malachi I, 2). In the one whom he chose, God’s purpose remains, because nothing other than what he knows and has purposed in him can come about, so that he may be worthy of salvation. In the one whom he rejected [another reading: rejected], the purpose he formed concerning him likewise remains, because he will be unworthy. This is how he is foreknowing and not a respecter of persons (Romans IX, 13), for he condemns no one before he sins and crowns no one before he conquers (II Timothy II, 9). This pertains to the case of the Jews, who defend their privilege by claiming that they are children of Abraham (John VIII, 39). But the Apostle consoles himself: because he loved them, he says that he has sorrow in his heart, and immediately discusses the cause of their unbelief, although they had the adoption as sons, the giving of the law, and from them Christ the Savior, as he himself says: ‘Salvation is from the Jews.’ Examining the law, he found that not all who are from Israel would believe, nor should all who are called Abraham’s children be called Abraham’s children, as I mentioned above. Thus he lessened his sorrow when he found that it had long before been foretold that not all would believe (John IV), so that only those who labor in unbelief through envy would grieve. Yet it is possible to believe what he explains in what follows: that one should not greatly grieve over those unbelievers already mentioned, because they were not predestined to life; for God’s foreknowledge had long ago decreed that they would not be saved. Who would grieve for one who is regarded as already dead? But when the nations, formerly without God (Ephesians II, 3), entered in and received the salvation that those others had lost, the sorrow is relieved; and again, because they themselves are the cause of their destruction, it is quieted.

> “God therefore, foreknowing that they would be of evil will, did not number them among the good. Yet the Savior says to those seventy-two disciples whom he had chosen in a secondary rank, and who afterward withdrew from that company: ‘Your names are written in heaven’ (Luke X, 20). But this was said according to justice, because it is just that each person should receive according to merit. Since they were good, they were chosen for ministry, and their names were written in heaven, according to justice, as I have said; but according to foreknowledge they were numbered among the wicked.

> “For God judges according to justice, not according to foreknowledge. Hence he also says to Moses: ‘If anyone has sinned against me, I will blot him out of my book’ (Exodus XXXII, 32–33), so that according to the justice of the Judge he may then appear to be blotted out when he sins, while according to foreknowledge he had never been in the book of life.

> “Hence the apostle John says concerning such people: ‘They went out from us, but they were not from us; for if they had been from us, they would certainly have remained with us’ (I John II, 19). There is no respect of persons in God’s foreknowledge (Colossians III, 25). Foreknowledge is that by which God has determined what the future will of each person will be, in which he will remain, and by which he will either be condemned or crowned.

> “Finally, those whom he knows will remain in goodness are often previously evil, and those whom he knows will remain wicked are sometimes previously good. Therefore let complaint cease, because God is not a respecter of persons. Saul and Judas Iscariot too were at first good. Scripture says of Saul: ‘There was a good man, and there was no better man among the sons of Israel’ (I Samuel IX, 2). And the apostle Peter says of Judas Iscariot: ‘He obtained a share in this ministry, in the performance of signs and wonders’ (Acts I, 17). How, then, would he have obtained a saving ministry unless he had been good? In the casting of lots there was God’s judgment: he judged him worthy at the time when he was chosen, just as with the seventy-two whom I mentioned above (John VI, 67).

> “Hence, after Judas had committed every evil crime, he was moved by repentance and ended his life by hanging himself (Matthew XXVII, 5). For all goodness cannot be entirely obliterated in anyone, since nature cannot be changed, but the will can—though not in every respect, because something remains in nature that bears witness to the Creator.”

*All these points clearly show that the holy Fathers did not follow your method of contrariety in explaining the Holy Scriptures. Wherever necessity required, they spoke by the figure of antiphrasis in order to clarify what needed clarification; but reason altogether contradicts the claim that they ever used this way of speaking in their own assertions. For those who undertook to explain the obscurities of the divine utterances in order to open their mysteries to their hearers could not reasonably have labored over figurative expressions by which they would fail to instruct their hearers and instead obscure matters further.*

*Accordingly, the expression cannot be considered identical when the predestined are said to be destined for punishment or destruction and Judas is said to be chosen. The name “election” is found to have been used by Holy Scripture and its most faithful interpreters rarely except in what is good, whether eternal or temporal. But they preferred to use the meaning of “predestination” in two ways, publicly and privately, in sermons to the people and in treatises not delivered to the multitude, with such frequency that no student may doubt it unless obstinately and faithlessly.*

*Thus he says:*

**JOHN SCOTUS**

*(Chapter 13, number 5, section 2.)* 6. “If, then, the Lord did not blush to call his betrayer chosen, why would his imitator, Saint Augustine, blush to call that same betrayer predestined, and likewise to call the Jewish people, filled with the treachery of envy, the betrayer and consequently the slayer of our Lord Jesus Christ? Why would he hesitate to call them predestined for destruction?”

**CORRECTION**

*He understood one thing by the name “predestination” and another by the word “election.” He was unwilling to accept God’s election except in what is good; but he declared the meaning of predestination, like that of his justice and judgment, to be twofold. Therefore he was not ashamed to say that some were predestined for punishment or destruction, because he knew that this agreed in every respect with the truth and justice of God’s judgments.*

*It is one thing to be called “the elect” or “sons of God” through eternal mercy, and another to be called so through creation or through some temporal arrangement—which is nevertheless in no way false or fictitious. For when one comes to the mystery of sacred regeneration, people are not falsely or deceitfully absolved from all sins, even if afterward, through the pollution of their own iniquity, they are deprived of the benefit of that same holy absolution and anointing.*

*Therefore, if the absolution of holy baptism was true in the removal of sins, it is necessary that the sonship produced by regenerating grace was true. Thus, just as evil sons according to earthly generation are rightly disinherited if they depart from the morals of their fathers, although they cannot in any way have ceased to be sons, so those whom grace regenerates are truthfully called elect or sons, although by wickedly departing from their parent they may make themselves so unworthy of the inheritance that they do not obtain it.*

*For the Lord says: “I have begotten and exalted sons, but they have despised me” (Isaiah I, 2). Who would be so foolish as even to suppose that the Lord did not truly say this, but said “I have begotten” contrary to the truth for “I have not begotten”? Surely, if you say “I have begotten sons” in the sense of “I have not begotten sons,” or “I have not begotten sons,” you will not be able to explain what is meant in the words that follow. For if they were not sons, and if they were not begotten, how could they be said to have despised the one who fathered and begot them? How could those who were neither sons nor begotten have despised their father and begetter?*

*Indeed, in the Holy Scriptures people are called “sons” in many ways, of which the more common are nature, adoption, imitation, and teaching.*

*By nature: Isaac and Ishmael were sons of Abraham; likewise Jacob and Esau were sons of Isaac. Although Ishmael and Esau did not receive, through the promise, the cords of their father’s inheritance, they nevertheless did not cease to be sons.*

*By adoption: this occurs through the affections of human custom, as is usual, and, much more excellently, when by undeserved grace we are adopted so as to be sons of God. Hence the Apostle says: “You have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you have received the spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’ Therefore you are no longer slaves but sons; and if sons, then heirs—heirs, indeed, of God, and fellow-heirs with Christ” (Romans VIII, 15 ff.).*

*By imitation, as the same Apostle admonishes: “Be imitators of God, as beloved sons” (Ephesians V, 1). And when the Jews appealed to their natural descent from Abraham and thereby exalted themselves proudly, the Lord said to them: “You are from your father the devil” (John VIII, 44). He reveals the sense in which he said this when he adds: “And you wish to do the desires of your father.” The Jews were sons of the devil by imitation, not by nature. Although by nature they were sons of Abraham, they had departed far from imitating his character. Hence the Lord also reproached them: “If you were sons of Abraham, you would do the works of Abraham” (John VIII, 39). He did not deny their nature, but rebuked their dissimilarity in imitation.*

*He also rebuked their teaching, as the Apostle says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians IV, 19); and again: “In Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel” (I Corinthians IV, 15).*

*They are also called “sons of the kingdom” (Matthew VIII, 12), “sons of light” (John XII, 36), and “sons of the resurrection” (Luke XX, 36); and, conversely, “sons of darkness,” “sons of destruction,” and “sons of Gehenna”—not because they were begotten by it, but because they were destined for it.*

*Someone is also called a “son of iniquity” (Matthew XXIII, 15), not because he was begotten by iniquity, but because he is inseparably joined to it. When we have received all these expressions with the authority of Holy Scripture and the tradition of the Fathers, we have nowhere adopted your method of contrariety.*

[scan page 600]

**1185**

*Therefore, when blessed Augustine says in the preceding statement (*On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 8):*

> “Sons of God are called so according to foreknowledge of what they will be, not by him who knows that they lack the perseverance which leads the elect to blessed life, but [the transmitted wording is corrupt here: ‘equally, that they will stand, as he foreknew that they would fall’]. Do not let it trouble you that God does not give this perseverance to some of his sons. Far be it that this should be so if they were predestined and called according to his purpose. But those who are not sons of promise, when they live piously, are called sons of God; yet, because they will live wickedly and die in that same wickedness, God’s foreknowledge does not call them sons of God.”*

*Augustine must by no means be understood to have wished to add another kind of sonship to the foregoing kinds, which he knew that both he himself and the other equally Catholic Fathers had carefully embraced.*

[scan page 601]

**SAINT PRUDENTIUS, BISHOP OF TROYES**

**1187**

*Augustine must by no means be understood to have wished to add another kind of sonship to the foregoing kinds, which he knew that both he himself and the other equally Catholic Fathers had carefully embraced. Rather, he wished to show how far human weakness—and therefore ignorance—is removed from divine knowledge, whose counsels and judgments human minds do not behold.*

*Let them therefore be called by us sons of God, and yet not deceitfully, because of the temporal grace by which they are generated not deceitfully but truly, although they have not yet been chosen to receive the inheritance together with the sons of promise.*

*They are therefore sons temporally; they are not sons eternally. For if they are truly generated, they are truly sons, although they do not remain in that generation and will not reach the inheritance of those who remain. They are sons of regeneration temporally, but not sons of promise eternally.*

*“They went out from us” (I John II, 19) through the communion of faith, which they shared with us for a time; “but they were not from us” through the election of grace, which grants perseverance. They went out from us through participation in the mystery that they had received, but they were not from us through adoption into the kingdom, since by wicked living they had made themselves unworthy of it.*

*They were therefore sons temporarily through regeneration, but they were not sons eternally through the promise of the inheritance.*

*Accordingly, when you say (chapter 13, number 5, section 3): “There are no sons of God except the elect, nor are there elect except those predestined by him; and conversely, there are no predestined except the elect, nor elect except sons,” this is true if it is understood only of those who are predestined to the kingdom.*

*For, as we said, God speaks not deceitfully or contrary to the truth, but truly: “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exodus IV, 22), when he said this about the people serving the Egyptians; and: “I have begotten and exalted sons, but they have despised me” (Isaiah I, 2). Again: “Is he not your father, who possessed you, made you, and created you?” (Deuteronomy XXXII, 6 ff.). “You abandoned the God who begot you and forgot the Lord your Creator. The Lord saw this and was moved to anger, because his sons and daughters provoked him; for it is a perverse generation, unfaithful sons” (Deuteronomy XXXII, 18–20, etc.).*

*Since all human beings are called sons of God even by creation alone, would they therefore have to be called “sons of God” in an opposite sense merely because not all will receive the inheritance? If, I say, God is called the Father of all by creation, and not in an opposite sense, it follows that they are also called his sons by creation, not in an opposite sense.*

[scan page 602]

**1189**

**ON PREDESTINATION AGAINST JOHN SCOTUS**

If you understand “sons” and “father” in an opposite sense, it follows that you must also understand “creation” and “making” in an opposite sense and deny that God is the Creator of human beings. For if, as they think, God is called the father of human beings, or they are called sons of God, in an opposite sense, then consequently “creator” and “maker” are also said in an opposite sense.

The Lord himself says in the Gospel: “The sons of the kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness” (Matthew VIII, 12). Will you say here too that they are called sons of the kingdom in an opposite sense? Since that is absurd, indeed impious, we must confess that even those who will not receive the lot of his saints are not called sons of God in an opposite sense.

But, lest you suppose that we are judging this by our own conjecture, hear what Augustine himself also brought forward in defense of the truth, writing against the adversary of the law and the prophets (*Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets*, book I, chapter 22):

> “He also slanders and blasphemes the testimony of the prophet Isaiah, because he said: ‘I have begotten and exalted sons, but they have despised me’ (Isaiah I, 2, 4). Shortly afterward he called those same people ‘a wicked seed,’ as though he were presenting himself as the begetter [another reading: generator] of evils, whose sons are a wicked seed. He did not know that they are called a wicked seed because, by sinning, they degenerated from the grace of God by which they had been made sons, and became sons of those whom they chose to imitate.

> “Hence elsewhere it is said to them: ‘Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite’ (Ezekiel XVI, 3)—whose impiety and wickedness they followed, although they did not derive their fleshly origin from them. But he resolved the Gospel question in which the Lord says: ‘If you, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him?’ (Luke XI, 13).

> “Let him explain how God is good, the father of the wicked; for the truth said both things. Were those to whom he said, ‘If you, although you are evil,’ not evil? Did they not have God as a good father, to whom he said, ‘How much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him’?

> “Moreover, if they were called evil because of sins, without which the life of any of the just in this mortal weakness is not found, how much more fittingly would that seed be called ‘a wicked seed’ which was born from an impious will and sprang up in detestable conduct?”

*Jerome, in the first book of his commentary on the prophet Isaiah.*

*Jerome (*On Isaiah*, chapter 18):*

> “Nor is it surprising that Zion is called a daughter, since Babylon too is very often called a daughter. For all are naturally sons of God [another reading: we are], but through our fault they become strangers [another reading: we become strangers].”

*The same author, in the sixteenth book on Isaiah (Isaiah LVII, 5):*

> “Are you not wicked sons, a deceitful seed, or, according to the Septuagint, ‘sons of destruction, a seed of iniquity’ (John XVII, 12)? You have done these things, you wicked ones, which the preceding discourse recounted. The Catholic Church surpasses [them], pursuing the footsteps of her Redeemer with pure faith and perfect in her charge.

[f] Will you deny that anyone who has strayed from a good purpose was either good or in the good? Indeed, the Lord proclaims something very different through the prophet: “If the righteous man turns away from his righteousness, none of his righteousnesses will be remembered” (Ezek. 18:24).

And in the Apocalypse of John: “I know your works and labor and patience, and that you cannot tolerate the wicked; you have tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and have found them liars” (Rev. 2:2). “You have patience and have endured for my name and have not grown weary; but I have this against you, that you have abandoned your first charity. The Apostle Peter likewise says: “There will also be among you false teachers, who will introduce destructive sects, even denying the Lord who bought them” (2 Pet. 2:1). And below (verse 20): “For if, having risen again [variant: having fled] from the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, their latter state has become worse than the former. For it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them” (verse 21). “For what happened to them accords with the truth of the proverb: ‘The dog has returned to its vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mud’” (verse 22).

Paul likewise says: “For it is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, who have become participants in the Holy Spirit, who have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the coming age, and then have fallen away, to be renewed again to repentance, crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and holding him up to contempt” (Heb. 6:4–6).

“If we sin voluntarily after receiving knowledge of the truth, no sacrifice for sins remains; but a certain fearful expectation of judgment and the fury of a fire that will consume the adversaries. Anyone who disregards the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by one who has trampled upon the Son of God, regarded the blood of the covenant as polluted, by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace? For we know him who said: ‘Vengeance is mine; I will repay,’ says the Lord” (Heb. 10:26–29). And again: “For the Lord will judge his people. It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (verses 30–31).

Therefore, either deny these and similar statements and perversely twist them according to your manner of contradiction; or, if that is impious, allow that the holy, chaste, temperate, humble, merciful, just, filial, elect, sanctified, enlightened, and redeemed are named in the divine utterances not fantastically, superficially, or deceptively, but truly—even though, by straying and living most wickedly, they have made themselves unworthy of such gifts and deprived themselves of them.

### TRECENSIS EPISCOPI

### 1492

Accordingly, whatever you contrive in your conclusions and distinctions is true if, as we have said, you are speaking only about those who are predestined, elected, and adopted for the kingdom. But if you are laboring—as appears—to deny the predestination of the impious and the punishments due to them, it is wholly false.

Thus anyone who knows how to weigh God’s justice both by reason and by authority can very easily discover that the perfidious Jews, to whom the Savior says, “You are of your father the devil” (John 8:44), were predestined by God to destruction. For because he foreknew that they would perish eternally in the mass of perdition, he predestined them—that is, prepared, assigned, and appointed them—to be punished by his just judgment.

Attend, I ask, to the Apostle’s words: “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called according to his purpose, who are saints. For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers; and those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. 8:28–30).

And to Timothy: “Do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me, his prisoner, but share in the gospel according to the power of God, who saved us and called us with a holy calling.” Do you hear “according to his purpose”? (2 Tim. 1:8–9). Do you hear that “those whom he predestined, he also called, and those whom he called, he also justified”? Do you hear that he “saved us and called us with his holy calling”?

Hear what the Lord says: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20:16). What, I ask, is the explanation of such great diversity in one and the same word?

The faithful servant says: “Those called according to his purpose are saints”; “those whom he predestined, he called”; “those whom he called, he justified”; and again, “called with a holy calling.” But the Lord cries out: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 22:14). Should we suppose that the most faithful servant preached something contrary to his Lord? Or could he have sown in the ministry entrusted to him anything other than what he had received from his heavenly teacher? Far from it.

Indeed, he himself testifies with the freest assertion that he was chosen neither by human beings nor through a human being who had chosen or instructed him, but by God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ (Gal. 1:1). Since a faithful steward could distribute nothing except what he had received from his creditor, we must admit that he nowhere either thought or taught anything contrary to his Lord.

Accordingly, one calling must be understood as that which the Lord proclaimed, and another as that which the servant taught. For those who receive the eternal inheritance are called according to God’s purpose in one way; those who receive eternal punishment are called otherwise, not according to that purpose.

Therefore, just as the calling of the elect is one thing and that of the reprobate another, so the foreknowledge and predestination of the righteous are one thing and those of the impious another. For just as the elect are said to be called with a holy calling, so many who are not elect are also said to be called.

The Apostle certainly would not have said “called saints according to his purpose” (2 Tim. 1:9), and “with a holy calling,” unless, for the sake of distinction, he intended to separate this calling from that by which many who are not elect are called.

Therefore, just as the diversity of calling cannot be denied, so in no way should the diversity of foreknowledge, justice, judgment, election, and predestination be rejected. Either deny the diversity of calling, or, if that is blasphemous, admit the variety of predestination. Either deny the diversity of calling, or, if that is blasphemous, admit the variety of predestination.

Accordingly, as you shamelessly command, the most faithful integrity and purest charity of orthodox believers will not be silent, but will truly preach God’s predestination, just as they preach the most just judgment of the lost. Nor will they, as you foolishly do, accept “predestined” as the opposite of “not predestined”; rather, they will believe that God’s unbending justice will punish them irrevocably.

## CHAPTER XIV

### Testimonies of Saint Augustine collected together, by which it is clearly established that there is only one predestination, and that it belongs solely to the saints

The fourteenth section of your fantasies has this:

### JOHN SCOTUS

*(No. 1, in book T, chapter 44, no. 2, section 1.)* Testimonies of Saint Augustine collected together, by which it is clearly established that there is only one predestination, and that it belongs solely to the saints.

And lest anyone perhaps think that we have said such things merely from our own judgment, unsupported by the weight of any authority, we have decided to collect together the testimonies of the holy Father Augustine, so that every prudent person may recognize that he in no way taught two predestinations, nor divided one into two, nor taught a double predestination as Gottschalk teaches. He taught that the one divine predestination belongs only to the saints, and that the impious can in no way possess it.

In the book *On Rebuke and Grace* (chapter 12): “[To the saints, he says,] predestined by God’s grace for the kingdom of God, the gift of perseverance is given—not merely so that they cannot persevere without this gift, but also so that through this gift they can be nothing other than persevering [variant: not merely is such assistance for perseverance given, but it is given in such a way that perseverance itself is bestowed upon them].”

And shortly afterward: “Therefore, he makes those persevere in the good whom he made good [variant: he makes them persevere]; but those who fall and perish were not among the number of the predestined.”

Observe how absolutely he said: “Those who fall and perish were not among the number of the predestined.” How could he have said this if he wished either to assert two predestinations, or one divided into two parts, or a double predestination, one assigned to the saints and the other to the impious?

### CORRECTION

O most subtle disputant! When you said these things, you were neither dipping your pen in your mind together with Aristotle, nor drinking the streams of saving doctrine while reclining on the breast of the Lord, from true wisdom. Surely we see fulfilled in you what the Apostle says: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and reject the understanding of the prudent” (1 Cor. 1:19).

## AGAINST SCOTUS

### 1194

Either you failed to see with your inward sight what ought to have been seen, or you pretended not to see it; and so you rushed headlong into such slanders that you might fabricate Saint Augustine as saying what he had never even imagined, mocking your readers as though they were incapable of understanding it.

Ireland sent you alone, the sharpest-minded of all Gaul, so that through your learning you might obtain what no one could know without you. But let not Celtic eloquence, intoxicated by such mighty floods of rivers, admit your clouded obscurities—although the height of Christian humility does not forbid one person to supply the other in turn with the service of charity; indeed, let each, wherever he thinks it useful, judge that what is right should be presented alternately.

Therefore, bring purity of mind to the matter, and show the simplicity of charity through the kindness of your understanding, so that, under its guidance, you may understand piously what has been said piously, and, in the abundance of piety, as a cultivator of piety, offer it to the instruction of the devout.

If you had wished to do this when you wrote these things, you would certainly have seen that Saint Augustine did not, as you dream, either assert or confirm absolutely that the predestination of the elect alone exists. Rather, he defended only that predestination which he had undertaken to discuss and strove to fortify it with Catholic truth against the crafty devices of heretics.

He was acting against the new heretics of his time, namely the Pelagians, who utterly denied the predestination of the saints. They said that God would be a respecter of persons if he predestined some people, and not all humanity generally, to eternal life. The most blessed teacher, hastening to oppose their folly, equipped with the weapons of orthodox faith, always brought forward the predestination of the saints, as anyone who attends soberly to his words understands.

For he frequently says that he is speaking about the predestination which “we defend,” or which “we have undertaken to defend,” or which “we assert.” It would have been foolish, while neglecting the matter being opposed and attacked, to pass over to another matter against which no one had yet risen to deny or attack it.

For it is clearly established by the evidence that, in the times of the Fathers, no question had been raised about those predestined to punishment. No one wrote for or against it, except Monimus, who, far from reproving it, piously sought its true interpretation and thereby moved Saint Fulgentius to explain, in a volume magnificently produced for this sole purpose, how it had been understood or expressed by blessed Augustine—a man worthy of every respect.

Blessed Augustine himself clearly shows from the sentence mentioned above what he meant. He begins it in this way:

“[To the saints, he says,] predestined by God’s grace for the kingdom of God” (Augustine, *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 12). And below: “He therefore makes those persevere in the good whom he made good; but those who fall and perish were not among the number of the predestined.”

What could be clearer or more explicit? He had begun by speaking of the saints predestined by God’s grace for the kingdom of God, and then added concerning those same people that he makes them persevere in the good whom he made good.

### 38

## S. PRUDENTIUS

### 1195

Unless, perhaps, you are preparing to lead us into new rhetorical flourishes, so that the matter under discussion may never be indicated except by frequent—even continuous—repetition of itself, and so that what would be sufficiently stated once, or as often as occasion required, may weary its hearers through repeated iteration.

I say without hesitation that if he had thought either you or anyone else—whether a dull or a plainly slanderous interpreter of his writings—would later treat this matter in such a way, he would have written with such complete clarity that he would have anticipated and more appropriately disposed of everything suited to slanderers.

Prosper and Hilary likewise indicate this clearly. Writing to him zealously concerning those who attacked him, they asked for a response to the questions raised solely about the predestination of the saints. Satisfying their requests, he produced fitting answers to what had been asked. The principal question concerned the predestination of the saints, and the most gentle and truthful teacher devoted as much effort as he thought sufficient to explaining it; nevertheless, he did not suppress the other matter so completely that, wherever he judged it appropriate, he would not commend that as well.

Can such a manner of expression be found in the sacred Scriptures, both ancient and new? The Psalmist says: “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. 77:25), where “angels” must be understood as holy angels. For since angels are said to be both good and evil, they are often accompanied by an added expression of their proper distinction, as in: “He will command his angels concerning you” (Ps. 91:11); and “Bless the Lord, his angels, mighty in strength, who do his word, obeying the voice of his words. Bless the Lord, all his powers, his ministers, who do his will” (Ps. 103:20–21); and “He makes his angels spirits and his ministers a burning fire” (Ps. 104:4); and “Praise him, his angels; praise him, all his powers” (Ps. 148:2).

In the Gospel, the Lord says: “The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will separate the wicked from the midst of the righteous, and cast them into the furnace of fire” (Matt. 13:41). Of the wicked: “A cruel angel will be sent against him” (Prov. 17:11); and “He sent among them an invasion through evil angels” (Ps. 78:49); and “The evil spirit of the Lord.”

But without an addition concerning the good, he says: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him” (Matt. 25:31); and again: “The reapers are angels” (Matt. 13:39); and again: “You who sit upon the cherubim”; and again: “To which of the angels did he ever say, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’?” (Heb. 1:5); and again: “But of the angels he says” (ibid.); and again: “Some, by receiving guests, unknowingly welcomed angels” (Heb. 13:2).

Of the wicked, however: “In the outspread and protecting cherub, on God’s holy mountain” [reading uncertain] (Ezek. 28:14); and “Do you not know that we will judge angels, how much more worldly matters?” (1 Cor. 6:3); and “Release the four angels who were prepared for the hour, day, month, and year, to kill a third of humanity” (Rev. 9:15).

Does it follow that whenever such terms are placed without an addition, anyone may, according to his own inclination, take “wicked” for “good” or “good” for “wicked”? Far from it. Under the Lord’s guidance, this is reserved for devout understanding, so that, after faithfully and truthfully weighing the context of the passage and the matter itself, one may investigate what is to be understood and in what manner.

The Lord spoke in this way in the Gospel when he said: “Whatever you wish that people would do to you, do likewise to them” (Matt. 7:12). Would the perverse desires of evil people say here that the Lord commanded them, while entangled in lusts and other crimes, to do to others whatever wicked deeds they want others to do to them? Far from it!

Pious benevolence understands that the Lord spoke this in a particular sense: whatever good and honorable things, in accordance with God’s will and with sincere charity, we wish to have done to us, we should do the same to others. There are many other matters which we judge necessary to carry out.

What you say is as follows:

### JOHN SCOTUS

*(Chapter 14, no. 3, section 1.)* Every human being is either good or evil; the same applies to an angel.

### CORRECTION

[f] Holding the same definition, and following the authority of Scripture and the concordant teaching of the venerable Fathers, we say that the good are predestined to life and the wicked to punishment. For these things are written:

“Great are the works of the Lord, sought out in all his wills”—namely, mercy and judgment (Ps. 111:2).

“We must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. 5:10). If, therefore, we shall all be manifested before Christ’s tribunal, we shall all be judged; and concerning all, it has been predestined how we shall be judged.

This is what the Apostle says: “So that each may receive according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil.” The judgment will not be accidental, nor will it concern something that no one had foreknown or predetermined.

God alone foreknew and predetermined, arranged, or predestined and preordained his judgment; an angel and a human being foreknew it, but did not predestine or arrange it. Since the future judgment of the good and the wicked cannot be denied, neither can its predestination—that is, God’s arrangement—be denied in any faithful manner.

For it belongs to God’s foreknowledge that he arrange and predestine within it what he was going to do. He will therefore have a judgment in which he will judge the good and the wicked, and he predestined this—that is, arranged it—in that foreknowledge which can neither be deceived nor changed.

If the wicked were not predestined to what they deserve, consequently they would not be judged. But they will be judged; therefore they are predestined to be judged. There is therefore a predestination of the wicked.

For he will repay each according to his work; he will judge everyone, and the Father has given him all judgment.

## AGAINST J. SCOTUS

### 1196

Moreover, as for your quibble (chapter 44, no. 4, section 2) that Saint Augustine did not say, “They were not in the number of those predestined to life,” but simply, “They were not in the number of the predestined”: it should suffice devout minds that I said he began with the saints and good people predestined by God’s grace for the kingdom of God, and pursued a most salutary discourse concerning them. Nor was it necessary that what had once been impressed on sound minds should be repeated again and again—more laboriously and tediously.

Anyone who reads this piously easily notices that the same book was published for this reason: when the predestination of the saints began to be preached, certain people, especially the Pelagians, arose and began to overturn the whole discipline and correction of the Church, saying: “There can be no need for rebuke where everything is accomplished by God’s grace”; and that, while each person acted with impunity as he wished, grace worked in them so that they might be good.

The most eloquent teacher answered their inquiry with Catholic truth and explained how correction and ecclesiastical discipline, through God’s grace, benefit the saints predestined for the kingdom. Therefore, whenever mention had to be made of the predestined, it would have been superfluous to repeat what had already been impressed upon devout minds and was sufficient for everything that had to be said about the same matter.

This is clearly shown in the sentences you judged should be included, where it is said: “[This is the predestination of the saints, and nothing else: namely, the foreknowledge and preparation of God’s benefits by which those who are delivered are most certainly delivered” (Augustine, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 14).]

Throughout the whole course of that book, the teacher’s speech is composed with such moderation concerning the predestination of those whom he discusses at such length that this becomes even clearer.

Nevertheless, astonishing—or rather horrifying and detestable—is the cunning of your trickery. Suppressing everything that he said about the predestination of the wicked, although he mentioned it rarely, you have extracted only what he said about the predestination of the saints, as though he had said nothing about the former (chapter 14, no. 6, section 2).

Listen, then, to what he also pursued on that subject in the same book (Augustine, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 11):

“Therefore, as the Apostle says, ‘It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy’ (Rom. 9:16), who also comes to the aid of those whom he wishes—even when they do not will or run—whom he chose in Christ before the foundation of the world, intending to give them grace freely, that is, without any preceding merits of their faith or works; and even to greater ones than these, whom he foresaw would believe in him if his miracles had been performed among them. To those whom he does not wish to assist, he does not assist, and concerning them he secretly but justly judged something else in his predestination.

“For there is no injustice with God” (Rom. 9:14), “but his judgments are inscrutable and his ways unsearchable” (Rom. 11:33). “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 25:10). Unsearchable, therefore, is the mercy by which he wills to have mercy on whom he wills, without any preceding merits of his own; and unsearchable is the truth, because he hardens whom he wills, indeed on account of that person’s preceding merits. Yet when, of two twins, one is taken and one left, their merits are equal, God’s great goodness so delivers one that the other is condemned through no injustice of his. Is there injustice with God? Far from it; but his judgments are unsearchable (Rom. 9:14).”

Behold: in one and the same book the most truthful teacher teaches the predestination of the righteous and of the impious. For it is clear what he says: “even to greater ones than these, whom he foresaw would believe in him if his miracles had been performed among them; to those whom he does not wish to assist, he does not assist, and concerning them he secretly but justly judged something else in his predestination.” What could have been said more plainly?

Certainly, without any obscurity, he indicates that he predestined those whom he does not wish to assist, so that they might be punished.

The same author says in the same work (*On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 16):

“But they say,” he writes, “that the knowledge of predestination makes the incentives of correction useless, as is said in the hearing of many assembled in the Church. This is the defined judgment of God’s will concerning predestination: that some of you, having received the will to obey after their unbelief, may come to faith, or, having received perseverance, remain in the faith; but that others, who linger in the delight of sins, have not yet risen because the assistance of the merciful grace has not yet raised them.

“Nevertheless, if there are among them some who have not yet been called, whom grace has predestined to be chosen, they will receive that same grace by which they may will to be and may be chosen. And if there are some who obey but are predestined to be rejected, the power of obedience will be withdrawn from them, so that they will cease to obey.

“When these things are said, they should not deter us from confessing the true grace of God—that is, grace which is not given according to our merits—or from confessing the predestination of the saints according to that grace [variant: according to this predestination]. We are not deterred from confessing God’s foreknowledge if someone speaks of it to the people in such a way as to say: ‘Whether you now live rightly or not, you will afterward be such as God foreknew you would be—good, if good; evil, if evil.’

“For if, on hearing this, some are driven into laziness and sloth, and turn away from labor toward lust and follow their desires, should what has been said about God’s foreknowledge therefore be considered false? If God foreknew that they would be good, they will be good, however much wickedness they may now practice; but if he foreknew that they would be evil, they will be evil, however much goodness they may now perform.

“There was a certain man in our monastery who, when the brothers rebuked him for doing things that ought not to be done and failing to do things that ought to be done, replied: ‘Whatever I am now, I shall be such as God foreknew I would be.’ He was certainly speaking the truth, but this truth did not advance him toward the good. Rather, it advanced him so far toward evil that, abandoning the fellowship of the monastery, he became ‘a dog returning to its vomit’ (2 Pet. 2:22). Yet even now it is uncertain what he will be in the future.

“Should what is truly said about God’s foreknowledge therefore be denied or kept silent on account of souls of this kind, especially when, if it is not said, others fall into error?”

### 1197

[f] Likewise, after much else (Augustine, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 22):

“Although the defined judgment of God’s will concerning predestination is such that some, having received the will to obey after unbelief, are converted to the faith or persevere in the faith, while others who linger in the pleasure of damnable sins—if they too are predestined—have not yet risen because the assistance of merciful grace has not yet raised them; nevertheless, if some have not yet been called, whom grace has predestined to be chosen, they will receive that same grace by which they may will to be and may be chosen.
