And so on concerning the manner in which predestination should be preached.

Again, in what you say he placed near the end of the same book (chapter 44, no. 6, section 3):

“There is no more illustrious example of predestination than the Mediator himself. Whoever wishes to understand it rightly should attend to him, and in him he will find himself” (Augustine, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, final chapter).

Whatever he said either long before this brief statement or afterward, up to the end of the book, was plainly spoken only about the predestination of the saints. Anyone who approaches it with a devout understanding recognizes this without hesitation.

Accordingly, it is evident that none of this provides support for your assertion—as though he had approved the predestination of the saints alone and denied that of the wicked. With the matter standing thus, you turn to open falsehoods and attribute to Augustine a sentence intended to show that God predestined no one to punishment, but prepared punishment—that is, predestined it—for those deserving condemnation.

First, I observe how much the contradiction between your own statements exposes you to ridicule before your hearers. Earlier you denied that punishments had been foreknown, predestined, or prepared by God; now you undertake to fortify and confirm your assertions with testimonies from the Fathers.

Next, the sentence by which you attempted to support this position (chapter 14, no. 7, section 4) is not Augustine’s. It is not excerpted from any of his books, letters, or sermons. While I had long been uncertain where it could be found among his writings, a certain pseudonymous booklet suddenly came to mind, falsely entitled Augustine’s *Hypomnesticon*.

There are many proofs that it is not the work of the most blessed Augustine: it was not revised by him together with his other books; it is not found in the catalogue of his sermons, books, and letters compiled by Saint Possidius, his disciple and bishop; and it is very easily shown to be inconsistent with his other statements.

Anyone who continually feeds and nourishes himself on the writings of so great a Father through meditation and delight can easily judge from its very manner of expression that it belongs to someone else. Although Augustine, as he himself confesses, wrote progressively and was so richly endowed with the grace of God that he revised most of his books, correcting what had been wrongly said, he would never have been so opposed on one and the same matter—repeatedly treated in so many books and sermons—by a single little work that would obscure the greatness of so many books and sermons through its contradiction.

Indeed, while revising his writings, he would certainly not have passed over it, but with censorial severity and Christian humility he would both have marked and corrected it.

For in the book of *Questions*, in the volume which we call *Questions on Judges*, when he was also explaining figurative or obscure matters, he spoke of this same predestination just as we quoted above, while treating the history and deed of Jephthah the judge.

Augustine, *Questions on the Heptateuch*, book VII, question 49:

“As for what was asked concerning Jephthah, who led an army against the sons of Ammon (Judg. 11:8), by whose defeat those who wished to fight against them under his leadership would be delivered: since ‘Ammon’ is interpreted as ‘son of my people,’ or ‘people of sorrow,’ the enemies who are foretold as persevering in unbelief from that people are certainly signified; or, altogether, all who are predestined to Gehenna [variant: to punishments]. For there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth for them (Matt. 25:30), as for a people of sorrow.

“Moreover, the people of sorrow may also appropriately be understood as the devil and his angels, either because they acquire eternal misery for those whom they deceive, or because they themselves have been assigned to eternal misery.”

[f] You see that he teaches that both human beings and the devil with his angels were predestined and assigned to Gehenna and eternal misery. Yet you bring forward a contradiction of his, something he never said and never wrote.

This too must be noted: if, according to your invention, the passage were to be understood figuratively, he would certainly not have chosen to speak figuratively in an exposition of questions and figures, where he would not have dissolved what was obscure but would have made even what was clear obscure.

Therefore, both authority and reason persuade us that God predestined—that is, arranged and judged—sinners for punishments and punishments for sinners, because “the just Lord loves justice; his countenance beholds equity.”

He plainly shows that he did not use the same word in the opposite sense when, explaining the Lord’s words, “Now the prince of this world has been judged,” he added that the word “judged” should be understood as follows (Augustine, *Tractates on the Gospel of John*, homily 95):

“Certainly he has been judged, because by the judgment of eternal fire he has been irrevocably assigned.”

And likewise …

## On Predestination

### Chapter XIV

“Those whom you gave me I have guarded, and none of them perished except the son of perdition.” The “son of perdition” is called Christ’s betrayer, predestined to perdition.

If this passage, as you foolishly claim, were intended to be understood in the opposite sense, it would certainly not disclose what is obscure to the people, but would bind what is clear with great obscurities. It is also very strange that, on the basis of Father Augustine’s statements, you say that God in no way predestined sinners to punishment, but that punishments deserving of their merits were predestined for them by Him. Although you repeat this frequently, in order to abolish the truth of predestination you turn it into something else, now thinking one way and now another, so that you later attempt to deny what you had earlier constructed, as the following passages will sufficiently show.

As for what you seek to establish by an analogy with human laws—namely, that men are not destined for punishments, but that penalties are defined for those who will sin—if you were not blind, you would certainly have seen that men are judged and condemned under the laws so that each may perish by punishments proportionate to him. What else is accomplished in so many councils of senators and judges except that, after the sinner has been examined and convicted, he is assigned and condemned, by the judgment of all, to the punishment he deserves? He is first judged and assigned to punishment on account of his merit, and afterward punished. Thus, indeed, you speak.

### John Scotus

*(Chapter 14, number 9, section 5)*

“For no temporal laws define a man as destined to sin.”

### Correction

As though anyone could be so dulled by folly as to say that God had predetermined any angel or human being to sin. Since this matter seems to have been sufficiently treated above, let us examine the remainder.

Among these matters I cannot cease to marvel that a man of such keen intellect, whom no page of human laws or histories escaped, could have allowed this knowledge or memory to pass him by. When the condition of the state had once been weakened by many—indeed continual—incursions of war, the Roman senate established the proletarians by a senatorial decree, so that, through their use, the State’s warlike and many-sided youthful population might continually beget offspring by any women whatever.

*This is fabulous.*

Saint Augustine also recalls this, among other matters, in the third book of *The City of God* (chapter 21):

“For then,” he says—that is, between the second and the final war against Carthage—“the Voconian law was also enacted, so that no one might make a woman his heir, not even an only daughter. I do not know what could be said or imagined more unjust than this law.”

It is also worth mentioning, to pass over other examples, that after the Lord’s Passion the senate decreed that no one should be enrolled among the gods except by its own decision; and likewise that, so many times, the laws of emperors and consuls were enacted for the persecution of Christians and the abolition of the faith and name of Christ.

Semiramis, too, is reported to have been the first of all to decree that sons should be joined in marriage with their mothers, although she herself was already polluted by the same abomination. What of Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Babylonians? Did he not decree by royal edicts that the statue of gold which he had made should be worshiped, imposing the punishment of a burning furnace upon the disobedient? (Dan. 3:5.) Darius, compelled by the leaders of the Medes and Persians, is likewise reported to have enacted the same thing; and therefore the prophet Daniel, through the plot of malicious men, was cast to the lions, but was miraculously delivered by the power of the true God (Dan. 6:16, 22).

Aelius Hadrian was so inflamed by shameful devotion to his Antinous that, after Antinous’s death, he established by law a temple, priests, and sacred rites for him.

What of Antiochus? In order to abolish the worship and laws of the true God, did he not issue decrees and also inflict disasters, persecutions, and deaths upon the worshipers of God? (2 Macc. 6 and following.)

Every censure of the divine law cuts off interest, prohibits it, and condemns those who desire it (Deut. 23:19–20); whereas Roman law decreed that profits from interest should be exacted according to fixed rates.

Valentinian, a Christian emperor, overcome by lust, brought another woman over his former wife and established a law permitting any man to use two wives simultaneously, according to his pleasure (Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History* 4.26).

Since these examples are so numerous and so evident that it would either be superfluous or unnecessary for me to rehearse them, let us set aside what you said—“For the state has never decreed that men should sin”—and, under the guidance of the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, turn our attention to what follows.

Meanwhile, it must by no means be passed over negligently that, favoring the wickedness of certain people, you said that the terror of human laws is applied to those who will sin so that, frightened by the atrocity of punishments, they may be restrained; and that, by this means, human transgressors are treated more as an act of mercy than of vengeance. Since the Catholic faith long ago condemned this perversity with the severity of its judgment, and the venerable gray hairs of the Fathers cut it down, we must not linger over its destruction.

For we can gather the contrary from this: if it is false that punishments are repaid to sinners, it will also be false that rewards are repaid to the righteous. But if it is true that blessedness is bestowed upon the saints, it is true that deserved penalties and punishments are repaid to the impious.

He who said, “These will go away into eternal punishment,” also said, “but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25:46). He also truthfully declared that he would say to the impious: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid., 41). But to the righteous: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom which has been prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (ibid., 34).

Therefore, just as the righteous will truly attain blessedness, so the impious will truly be condemned to their deserved punishments.

It is therefore false that, by analogy with worldly laws, you said that nothing else is sought through the severity of punishments than that those inclined to sin should be restrained by fear of the atrocity of punishments, and that transgressors are thereby treated no less mercifully than vindictively. For not only worldly laws but also divine laws decree that many, even in this temporal life, should be punished by death and by various kinds of penalties, and no corrective remedy can now avail them.

## Page 609

Should divine reproof of Antiochus and Herod (2 Macc. 9:11) be called a medicinal correction, rather than an increase of eternal punishment? What began temporally here would be suffered eternally there.

We must therefore acknowledge that divine and human laws impose punishments upon sinners so that, warned by fear of them, they may cease from sinning. Yet if, in their obstinacy, they choose rather to resist these punishments than humbly to obey, they will not obtain the mercy which they stubbornly rejected; instead, they will deservedly suffer the inextricable punishment which they brought upon themselves by their own iniquity.

### Chapter XV

#### The kind of language by which God is said to foreknow sins, although they are nothing, or to predestine their punishments, which likewise are nothing

The fifteenth (number 1) of your phantoms is branded with the horror of this entire heading:

### John Scotus

“By what kind of language is God said to foreknow sins, although they are nothing, or to predestine their punishments, which likewise are nothing?”

### Correction

There is no need to dwell longer here on refuting you, since what must be known is always sufficiently evident from what has preceded, from your repeated statements, and from the authority already cited.

For, as you have insinuated—more tediously than in the earlier parts of your sickening work—you wish the opposite meaning to be understood whenever God is said to have foreknown sins or to have predestined their punishments: namely, that He did not know them and did not predestine them at all. This is contrary to the understanding of all Catholics, or at least to the opinion of all men, among whom you will be unable to find any author whose doctrine you can prove yourself to follow.

No one has ever recorded that foreknowledge and predestination should be understood in this manner. No one has in any way denied His knowledge and disposition concerning sins and their punishments. I would now refrain from speaking about these matters, were it not that I must restrain your boastfulness, lest falsehood should invent something for which truth would have no answer.

Therefore, among the testimonies you distort, you say this about Judas the betrayer:

### John Scotus

*(Chapter 15, number 2, section 2)*

“Elsewhere, he had improperly been heard as though he were a sharer in divine love, gathered among the true predestined, elect, and friends: ‘I do not call you servants but friends’ (John 15:14).”

### Correction

The truth of the Gospel clearly teaches that this is false. Anyone who observes that the Lord spoke these words after the morsel had been handed to the betrayer and shamelessly taken by him, after the Lord’s admonition—“What you are doing, do quickly” (ibid., 27)—and after Judas’s departure, will understand the matter. From this it is evident that you prefer to rely on sophistries rather than devote yourself to meditation on the Scriptures.

You immediately add the following:

### Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

### John Scotus

*(Chapter 15, number 3, section 3)*

“In like manner, the Lord, as though speaking to one cast out from all ecclesiastical fellowship, as to a son among sons, said: ‘Do not call anyone your father on earth, for one is your Father, who is in heaven’ (Matt. 23:9); as though the gift of understanding had been granted to the wise among the wise, when he says to the apostles: ‘To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom’ (Mark 4:11).”

### Correction

+ For this reason it seems to have been inserted irrelevantly: the Gospel records that he preached the mystery of the kingdom of God together with the other apostles. He would certainly never have preached it if he were ignorant of it. For by knowing it he preached, and by preaching he demonstrated his knowledge.

Unless, perhaps, following certain heretics, you maintain that prophets and apostles raved in madness, so that, as the poet plays,

> “He produces sound without a mind,”

and that they did not know what they had prophesied or preached. Since this is rejected both by truth and by reason, we must acknowledge that he truly grasped the mysteries of the kingdom of God, but that, through the magnitude of his avarice and the impiety of his betrayal, he was deprived of so great a gift and condemned by the just judgment of God.

The Lord must certainly not be believed to have denied him, among the other gifts granted according to the present dispensation, an understanding of the heavenly secrets that He foresaw to be appropriate to that dispensation. He makes His sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust (Matt. 5:45), so that, by the gifts granted to the betrayer, He might both restrain his rage and judge his ingratitude more justly.

To pass over other matters, after the Lord had been condemned and handed over to the tribunals of either the priests or the governor, as the Evangelist says:

> “Moved to repentance, he returned the thirty pieces of silver, saying: ‘I have sinned by betraying innocent blood’” (Matt. 27:3).

He could not have considered Him just unless he knew Him to be just; and he could in no way have known Him to be just unless he had in some measure drawn from the mystery of the heavenly kingdom. Nor would he have plunged irrecoverably into the deadly precipice of despair unless he had recognized the enormity of his intolerable crime.

Without that exception, he heard the words of the divine oracle together with the others, and he too was sent to preach the kingdom of God. I cannot see by what reasoning he could have preached it if he were ignorant of its mysteries. Thus you should believe that nothing was gained by your assertion that the words “To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God” were said to him in the opposite sense (Mark 4:11). It was certainly given to him also, although by his ingratitude he made himself unworthy of so great a gift.

For, as blessed Gregory says, simple Truth does nothing through duplicity: it is the nature of truth that, if it acts deceitfully in some matter, it is no longer truth. Simple Truth therefore truly granted him knowledge of the mystery of the kingdom of God to the extent that it judged this to accord with the present dispensation according to its hidden counsel. It certainly foreknew that he would in no way remain among the gifts of that kingdom, so that he might be recalled from the enormity of his impiety by the greater sweetness of the gifts and might be condemned more justly because he despised and rejected them.

Accordingly, your assertion that Augustine, the keenest investigator and defender of truth, deliberately left us examples of such expressions in his works so that we might not hesitate to understand the same meaning in divine predestination and foreknowledge is false. For nowhere is Saint Augustine found to have said that foreknowledge and predestination are one and the same, although he truly taught that foreknowledge is sometimes used in place of predestination.

You add:

### John Scotus

*(Chapter 15, number 6, section 4)*

“Accordingly, we ought to think with the most salutary and truthful understanding what he himself says, as though admonishing us: ‘Every predestination is foreknowledge, but not every foreknowledge is predestination’” (Augustine, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 10).

“As though he had said openly: Although foreknowledge does not transcend the boundaries of predestination—for they are one and the same, namely, the divine nature, in which there is no more or less of one thing than another—where there is the simplicity of nature there is no diversity, since in it all things are one; therefore foreknowledge has as much force in God as predestination, precisely because they are one.”

### Correction

If you understood with the “most salutary and truthful understanding” what Augustine says—“Every predestination is foreknowledge, but not every foreknowledge is predestination”—you would never turn to such impostures as to fabricate in his words what he neither thought nor said.

Foreknowledge does transcend the boundaries of predestination, because things are foreknown either by God Himself or by rational creatures even when they are not done by those who know them. But only those things are predestined which are either done by them or arranged to be done by them.

Nor are foreknowledge and predestination, as you foolishly claim, one and the same divine nature. No authority of God calls the divine nature itself foreknowledge or predestination, especially since these are relative terms, whose substances cannot be demonstrated. Nor does foreknowledge have the same force in God as predestination, because they are not one. God foreknows every sin, although He does not commit it; but He predestines only what He Himself does—whether benevolently, mercifully, or justly.

### John Scotus

*(Chapter 15, number 7, section 5)*

“If God’s foreknowledge is God, it is necessarily truth; I would say the same of predestination: if it too is God, it is undoubtedly truth.”

### Correction

If you had perceived with the pure and simple eye of the mind, you would certainly have seen that both authority and reason show truth to be God’s substance. For He said, “I am truth” (John 14:6); but nowhere did He say, “I am foreknowledge” or “I am predestination.” Truth is not a relative term, any more than wisdom, knowledge, justice, or goodness is; therefore, whenever it is said of God, it is predicated essentially. Foreknowledge and predestination, however, refer to something else. God neither foreknew nor predestined Himself: therefore He foreknew and predestined something other than Himself—that is, something which He is not. Foreknowledge and predestination, then, are not God as truth is, because truth is said essentially, but foreknowledge and predestination relatively.

You further argue that sin does not come from truth, but is nothing, and consequently comes neither from God’s foreknowledge nor from His predestination. Who, except a madman, could think this?

Both authority and reason teach that sins are foreknown by Him. Authority and reason likewise teach that the just retributions for them—namely, penalties, torments, and punishments—are foreknown and predestined by Him.

You also say that Augustine, by his authority, previously declared that no one is prepared for torments by divine predestination. It is not surprising that, in constructing a deceitful falsehood, you have introduced falsehood into it, since it is established that the book from which you extracted this statement was never written by Augustine. He was exceedingly opposed to such a way of speaking in many of his sermons and books.

When that most blessed man was revising his shorter works and reached the place in the work of revision concerning the book entitled *Eighty-Three Questions* (book 1, chapter 68), he spoke as follows:

> “Whether God is the author of evil. Here, he says, we must be careful lest what I said be understood wrongly: ‘He is not the author of evil,’ because He is the author of all things that exist, and because, insofar as they exist, they are good. Nor should it be thought from this that the punishment of the wicked is not from Him, although it is evil for those who are punished. I said this in the same way as it is said, ‘God did not make death’ (Wis. 1:13), although elsewhere it is written: ‘Death and life are from the Lord God’ (Sir. 11:14). The punishment of the wicked, therefore, which comes from God, is evil for the wicked, but it is among God’s good works, because it is just that the wicked should be punished, and whatever is just is certainly good.”

The same author says in the book *Questions on Judges* (question 13):

> “What is meant by the fact that the angel of the Lord, among the other divine threats, says: ‘I will not drive out the people whom I said I would drive out; I will not remove them from your sight, and they will be snares for you, and their gods will be a stumbling-block to you’ [cf. Exod. 23:29–33]? Should we understand that some sins also come from the wrath of God? For, just as the nations among whom the Israelites wished to dwell were not exterminated, so that they might become a stumbling-block to them—that is, so that they might cause them to stumble against the Lord their God and live in opposition to Him—God, in anger, threatened this. It is certainly clear that this is a great sin.”

The same author says in *Questions on Deuteronomy* (question 2):

> “Sihon, king of Heshbon, was unwilling to let us pass through his territory, because the Lord our God had hardened his spirit and made his heart strong, so that he might be delivered into your hands, as is the case today” (Deut. 2:30).

In saying this, Moses, when addressing the people, recalls something like what is said in Exodus: “I have hardened Pharaoh’s heart” (Exod. 10:1); and what is read in the Psalms: “He turned their heart to hate His people” (Ps. 105:25).

The reason for this hardening is not left unmentioned when it says, “so that he might be delivered into your hands,” that is, so that he might be defeated by you—which would not happen unless he resisted, and he would not resist unless his heart were hardened.

If we seek the justice of this, “the judgments of God are unsearchable” (Rom. 11:33); “there is no injustice with God” (Rom. 9:14). It should certainly be noted that a strengthened heart may also be spoken of in an evil sense.

The same author says in *Questions on Exodus* (question 143):

> “‘And the Lord relented from the evil which He had said He would do to His people’ (Exod. 32:14). Here he wished “evil” to be understood as punishment, as in: ‘Their departure was regarded as evil’ (Wis. 3:2). In this sense good and evil are said to come from God, not in the sense of the evil by which wicked men are evil. God is not evil, but He inflicts evils upon the wicked because He is just.”

In the same work (question 148):

> “It is rightly asked: since Aaron was said above to have scattered the people, why did no vengeance proceed against him, either when Moses ordered every person who encountered the Levites as they went to and returned from the gate with weapons to be killed, or when what Scripture later says took place: ‘The Lord struck the people because of the making of the calf which Aaron made’—especially since this is emphasized here by repetition? For it does not say, ‘The Lord struck the people because of the making of the calf which they made,’ but ‘which Aaron made’; and yet Aaron was not struck. Indeed, what God had commanded concerning his priesthood before his sin was fulfilled. He commanded that both Aaron and his sons be washed, and thus they were ordained to the priesthood.

> “He therefore knows whom to spare until a change for the better, whom to spare for a time although He foreknew that he would not change for the better, whom not to spare so that he might be changed for the better, and whom not to spare while awaiting a change in his life. All this pertains to what the Apostle says when he exclaims: ‘How unsearchable are His judgments and how inscrutable His ways!’ (Rom. 11:33).”

### John Scotus

*(Chapter 15, number 10, section 6)*

“Either predestination is used for foreknowledge by way of similarity, or by that figure which is called *hypallage*, which we may call substitution, and so forth.”

### Correction

If it were necessary to understand “destined” or “predestined to punishment” in the opposite sense—that is, through the figure called *antiphrasis*, or through the figure called *hypallage*—would so many other passages bearing on the same matter, found throughout the holy Scriptures and among Catholic teachers, have to be twisted so that they too might be made to support such madness?

Since neither reason nor authority permits this, we must acknowledge that both the divine words and orthodox interpreters understood these passages as they sound: that God, without any cloud of someone’s interpretation, assigned them by His most just judgments.

*Here an entire leaf, cut out, is missing from the manuscript codex; in its place have been supplied the remainder of a sentence of Saint Augustine and a passage of John Scotus corrected in what follows.*

The fact that sins are not from God is disputed by no one. Both authority and reason establish that punishments for sinners are either made by God or inflicted by Him. Accordingly, as we have already cited above from the words of blessed Augustine, all punishments of sinners are good because they are just. For everything just is good, and nothing just is not good. Therefore whatever comes from the supremely good and supremely just One is good.

It is just that sinners should receive what they deserve, just as the good receive what they deserve. Augustine himself makes it sufficiently clear that he did not understand or state the contrary, repeatedly expressing the same point in other words while avoiding the term “predestination.”

What, I ask you, do you consider greater: to predestine or to make? Almost always, or nearly always, inserting the Apostle’s words concerning “vessels of wrath prepared or fitted for destruction” (Rom. 9:22), he uses the term “prepared” or “made,” indicating that he never understood or expressed the meaning of predestination in the opposite sense.

Thus, in the fifteenth book of *The City of God*, Augustine speaks as follows (chapter 1):

> “For in one man we experience what the Apostle said: that the spiritual does not come first, but the animal, and afterward the spiritual (1 Cor. 15:46). Hence, because each person arises from a condemned lineage, he must first be evil and carnal through Adam; but if he progresses by being reborn in Christ, `poterit esse` means “he can be” [al. `postea erit`, “he will afterward be”] good and spiritual.

> “So also, in the whole human race, when these two cities first began to proceed through birth and death, the citizen of this world was born first, and later (`posterius`; al. `posterior`, “the later one”) the pilgrim in this world, who belongs to the city of God—predestined by grace, chosen by grace, a pilgrim below by grace, a citizen above by grace.

> “For, insofar as he himself is concerned, he arose from the same mass, which in its origin is wholly condemned. But nevertheless (`sed tamen`; al. `tanquam`, “as”), God, like a potter—for the Apostle introduces this comparison prudently, not rashly—made from the same mass one vessel for honor and another for dishonor (Rom. 9:21). The vessel for dishonor was made first, but afterward the other for honor. For in that one man also, as I have already said, the reprobate comes first, from whom we must necessarily begin, but in whom we must not remain. The approved comes afterward, toward whom we progress and in whom, once we arrive, we remain.”

The same author says in *On Marriage and Concupiscence* (book 2, chapters 28–29):

> “What, then, does he mean when he says: If nature is God’s work, it is not permitted that the devil’s work should pass through God’s work? Did not the devil’s work, when it first arose in the angel who became the devil, arise within God’s work? Therefore, if evil, which previously existed nowhere, could arise in God’s work, why could evil, which already existed somewhere, not pass through God’s work—especially since the Apostle uses precisely this expression when he says: ‘And so it passed into all human beings’ (Rom. 5:12)?

> “Are not human beings God’s work? Sin therefore passed through human beings—that is, the devil’s work passed through God’s work. To put the same thing another way, since the devil’s work, namely sin, arose through the devil himself, who is God’s creation or work, and passed through another work of God, namely man, it is the work of God’s work passing through God’s work.

> “Therefore God alone is unchangeable and of supremely powerful goodness. Before any evil existed, He made all things good; and from the evils which arose in the good things He made, He works good throughout.”

“In one man,” he says, “intention is rightly blamed and origin praised, because these two things are assigned to opposite causes. In an infant there is only one thing, namely nature, because there is no will. That one thing, therefore, is attributed either to God or to the devil. If nature is from God, he says, original evil can exist in it. If it is from the devil, there will be nothing by which man can be claimed for God’s work.”

He is therefore (`itaque`; al. `autem`, “however”) a complete Manichaean who defends original evil. Let him instead hear what is true against these claims.

In one man intention is rightly blamed and nature praised, because these two things are assigned to opposite causes. But in an infant there is not only one thing, namely nature, in which man was created by the good God; there is also the fault which passed through one man into all human beings (Rom. 5:12), as the Apostle teaches—not as Pelagius, Celestius, or any of their disciples foolishly teach.

Of these two things which we have said are present in the infant, one is attributed to God and the other to the devil. Both are subjected to the power of the devil because of one of them, namely the fault; this is not incongruous, because it does not happen by the devil’s power but by God’s.

Nature is subjected to the fault of nature, since both are present in the devil; and [al. `ut`, “when”] when the beloved and elect are rescued from the power of darkness, to which they are justly subject, it becomes evident what is granted by the good God to those justified as good, as He works good from evils.

As for what this man seemed to say with religious seriousness—“If nature is from God, original evil cannot exist in it”—would not another person seem equally religious if he said, “If nature is from God, no evil at all can arise in it”? Yet this is false. The Manichaeans wanted to assert this, and they attempted to fill not a creature made by God from nothing but God’s own nature with every evil.

Evil arose only in something good, though not in the supreme and immutable good, which is God’s nature, but in something made from nothing through God’s wisdom. Thus there is a means by which man may be claimed for God’s work, since man would not exist unless he were created by God’s work.

Natural evil (`malum naturae`; printed `malum natura`; al. `autem, id est natura`, “however, that is, nature”) would not exist in infants unless the first man had sinned by his will and original sin had been drawn from a corrupted origin.”

The same author says in the third book of *On the Agreement of the Evangelists* (chapter 13):

> “Let, then, the judgment of the person who thinks this passage ought to be placed here yield to the judgment of Mark the Evangelist, who judged that it should be placed at the point where it was suggested by divine inspiration. For their memories were governed by the hand of Him who governs the water, as it is written (Luke 8:24–25), according to His good pleasure.

> “Human memory flows through various thoughts, and it is not in anyone’s power to determine what comes to mind and when. When, therefore, these men—namely truthful men [al. `sancti et veraces`, “holy and truthful”]—as though by chance entrusted the memories of their recollections, according to the order of their narrative, to the hidden power of God, for whom nothing is accidental, no one ought to say that any of them was far cast away from God’s sight or wandering far from Him.

> “This is the place where it ought to be put, although he is greatly ignorant of why God wished it to be put there. For even if our Gospel is veiled, as the Apostle says, it is veiled among those who are perishing (2 Cor. 4:3). And when he had said, ‘To some we are the fragrance of life unto life, and to others the fragrance of death unto death’ (2 Cor. 2:16), he immediately added, ‘And who is sufficient for these things?’ (ibid.). That is, who is sufficient to understand how this is done justly?

> “The Lord says the same thing: ‘I have come so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind’ (John 9:39). This is the depth of the riches of God’s knowledge and wisdom, by which from the same mass one vessel is made for honor and another for dishonor (Rom. 9:33 [reference as printed]). And it is said to flesh and blood: ‘O man, who are you to answer back to God?’ (Rom. 9:20).

> “Who, then, in this matter knows the mind of the Lord, or who has been His counselor (Rom. 11:34), when He so governed the hearts of the Evangelists in their recollections and raised them to such a summit of authority in the Church that, through the very things which may appear contradictory in them, some might be blinded—handed over deservedly to the desires of their hearts and to a reprobate mind (Rom. 1:28)—while many others might be exercised in refining a pious understanding according to the hidden justice of the Almighty?

> “For the Prophet says to the Lord: ‘Your thoughts are exceedingly profound; the foolish man does not know them, and the fool does not understand them’ (Ps. 91:6).

> “I ask and admonish those who read these things, which have been worked out with the Lord’s help by means of us, to remember this discourse, which I have judged should be inserted here, whenever they encounter a similar difficulty of questions, so that the same matters may not have to be repeated frequently.”

The same author says in his letter to Sixtus (*Letter* 105):

> “Although God makes vessels of wrath for destruction, in order to display His wrath and make His power known, showing how well He makes use even of evil things, and in order to make known the riches of His glory in vessels of mercy (Rom. 9:22–23), which He made for honor—not as something owed to a condemned mass, but as a gift bestowed by His grace—nevertheless, in those same vessels of wrath, made for dishonor because of the merit of the mass, that is, in human beings created good with respect to nature but destined to punishment because of their faults, He knows how to condemn the iniquity which truth most rightly condemns; He does not make it.

> “For just as human nature, which no one doubts should be praised, is attributed to His will, so guilt is attributed to the human will, which no one refuses to condemn.”

Since these things are unquestionably good and just, they are not contrary to Him from whom they come, even though to those who suffer them, or to those who do not suffer them—
## Saint Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

“They seem to be contraries.”

### John Scotus

*(Chapter 15, number 11, section 8.)*

> But to whom is it not easy to see that things contrary to one another cannot arise from one origin? Certainly, where good is, evil will not be; where humility is, pride will not be. Iniquity never flows from the fountain of justice; death never proceeds from the source of life; blessedness is not the cause of misery. Finally, the highest essence in no way produces things that are not: sin, death, and punishment are deficiencies of justice, life, and blessedness. Therefore they are not from him who is; and, if they are not from him, who would dare say that they have any being?

Augustine, in Book VIII, chapter 5, of the *Confessions*:

> For lust is made from a perverse will; and while lust is served, habit is made; and when habit is not resisted, necessity is made. These were like links joined together—whence I called it a chain—which held me fast in a harsh slavery. But a new will, which had begun to arise in me so that I might worship you freely and enjoy you, O God, the only certain joy, was not yet strong enough to overcome the earlier will, strengthened by long age. Thus my two wills—the old and the new, the carnal and the spiritual—were in conflict with one another, and by their disagreement they tore my soul apart. So I understood in myself what I had read: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Galatians 5:17). I was indeed present in both, but more fully in that which I approved in myself than in that which I disapproved. For there I was already less truly myself, since for the most part I endured unwillingly what I was doing willingly.

### Correction

In the same Augustine (chapters 9–10):

> And therefore there are two wills, because neither of them is whole, and what is present in one is absent from the other. May they perish from before you, O God, as perish idle talkers and deceivers of minds, who, when they have observed two wills in deliberation, maintain that they are two natures of two minds, one good and the other evil.

And below, Augustine (chapter 10):

> I was the one who wanted; I was the one who did not want. I myself, I myself was; yet I neither wanted completely nor refused completely. Thus I was in conflict with myself and was scattered within myself. This scattering indeed happened against my will, yet it did not show that the nature of my mind was alien, but rather that it was my punishment. Therefore it was no longer I who was carrying it out, but sin dwelling in me (Romans 7:14), the punishment of the freedom of sin, because I was a son of Adam. For if there are as many contrary natures as there are wills resisting one another, there will no longer be two, but more.

Augustine, *Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets*, Book I, chapter 22:

> “But the Lord Christ,” he says, “called him a good tree bearing evil fruits” (Matthew 7:17). Rather, this blasphemous statement itself, belonging to one who thinks such things, is an evil fruit, like that of an evil tree. For the Lord sufficiently and clearly testifies that when he called the evil man an evil tree whose fruits were evil—that is, evil works—and the good man a good tree whose fruits were good—that is, good works—he was speaking of the very wills of human beings, whether the evil will of an evil man or the good will of a good man, as different trees bearing different fruits. He says:

> “The good man brings good things out of the good treasure of his heart, and the evil man brings evil things out of the evil treasure of his heart” (Matthew 12:35).

> But how could he say either, “Make the tree good and its fruit good,” or, “Make the tree evil and its fruit evil,” unless a human being could, now in one direction and now in another, turn through a change of will?

Although, as I judge, what we have set forth above has sufficiently refuted your position, nevertheless, since you strive to establish it from contraries, I marvel that you, most subtle of dialecticians, have not at all perceived the nature of the soul: that it is capable of both good and evil, and that from the will proceeding from it either evil or good may be conceived, spoken, or accomplished; indeed, that good and evil may be conceived at one and the same moment and continue for a considerable time in alternation.

Let us take one testimony to this from the book of blessed Augustine called the *Enchiridion*:

> “What,” he says (chapters 13–15), “is an evil man except an evil nature, since a man is a nature? Moreover, if a man is some good because he is a nature, what is an evil man except an evil good? Yet when we distinguish these two, we find that he is not evil because he is a man, nor good because he is unrighteous, but good because he is a man and evil because he is unrighteous. Therefore whoever says, ‘It is evil to be a man,’ or, ‘It is good to be unrighteous,’ falls into that prophetic sentence: ‘Woe to those who call evil good and good evil’ (Isaiah 5:20). For he blames the work of God, which is man, and praises the vice of man, which is unrighteousness. Thus every nature, even if it is vicious, is good insofar as it is a nature, and evil insofar as it is vicious.
>
> “Accordingly, in these opposites called good and evil, the rule of the dialecticians fails—the rule by which they say that two opposites cannot simultaneously inhere in one thing. No air is simultaneously dark and bright; no food or drink is simultaneously sweet and bitter; no body is simultaneously white where it is black; nothing is simultaneously deformed where it is beautiful. This is found in many, indeed almost all, opposites, so that they cannot simultaneously exist in one thing. But although no one doubts that good and evil are opposites, they can not only exist together, but evils cannot exist at all except with goods and in goods, although goods can exist without evils. A man or an angel can be without unrighteousness, but an unrighteous being can exist only as a man or an angel: the good is that he is a man or an angel; the evil is that he is unrighteous. These two opposites are present together in such a way that, if there were not good in which the evil existed, the evil could not exist at all. It would have neither a place in which to subsist nor a source from which corruption could arise, unless there were something for it to corrupt.”

## On Predestination

### [Scan page 614]

For corruption is nothing other than the destruction of the good. Evils, therefore, arose from goods, and they do not exist except in certain goods; nor was there any other source from which any nature of evil could arise. For if it existed insofar as it was a nature, it would certainly be good; either an incorruptible nature would be a great good, or even a corruptible nature could in no way exist unless it were some good which corruption could injure by corrupting it.

But when we say that evils arose from goods, this does not conflict with the Lord’s saying:

> “A good tree cannot bear evil fruits, nor can an evil tree bear good fruits.”

For, as the Truth says, one cannot gather grapes from thorns (Matthew 7:16, 18), because grapes cannot grow from thorns; yet we see that both vines and thorns can grow from good soil. Thus [alternate reading: “and in the same way”], an evil will, like an evil tree, cannot produce good fruits—that is, good works—but from the good nature of a human being both a good will and an evil will can arise. There was no source from which an evil will could first arise except the good nature of an angel or a man. The Lord himself also makes this perfectly clear in the same passage, where he was speaking of the tree and its fruits. He says:

> “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree evil and its fruit evil” (Matthew 12:33).

This sufficiently warns us that good fruits cannot arise from an evil tree, nor evil fruits from a good tree, while also showing that both trees can arise from the same soil to which he was speaking.

Do you see how your entire argumentative structure has been overturned, by which you were attempting to establish that things opposed to one another cannot arise from a good origin? The most eloquent man has shown that opposites proceed from one origin, namely the nature either of an angel or of a man.

From the same source, then, come humility and pride—that is, from the good nature of an angel or a man, from which either a good or an evil will arises. Humility is therefore called a good will, and pride an evil will. Yet although this good will was originally implanted in rational nature by the gift of the Creator, once corrupted by its own perversion it cannot in any way exist as good from itself or through itself until it is healed, restored, and infused by him who is always, supremely and essentially, the good will.

No one is ignorant that iniquity never flows from the fountain of justice—that is, from God—for “there is no iniquity with God” (Romans 9:14). Nevertheless, he justly repays sinners with the punishments they deserve. “For you will repay,” he says, “each one according to his works.” From the source of life—that is, from God—death is inflicted upon sinners, since Scripture testifies: “From him come life and death” (Ecclesiasticus 11:14).

Blessedness is not the cause of misery, because God is not the cause of any sin or punishment. Yet he is the irrigator and inflictor of misery, death, and punishment. Since these are justly repaid by God’s authority, through the testimony of sacred utterance, either in the present or afterward eternally, they are rightly judged to have been foreknown and predestined by him, by whose judgment they are inflicted.

With what impudence, then, are sinners and the ungodly denied to have been foreknown by God or appointed to their deserved punishments, when both reason and authority openly declare that both occur under God’s judgment?

### Against John Scotus

As for the punishments inflicted by God even temporally upon sinners and the ungodly, it is sufficient to bring forward one testimony from the prophets. In the passage where the prophet Joel says:

> “I will restore to you the years which the locust, the caterpillar, the rust, and the creeping locust consumed: my great army which I sent among you” (Joel 2:24).

Saint Jerome, explaining the same passage, says after some introductory remarks:

> We ask why the caterpillar has been called the strength or power of the Lord, and not merely power, but great power. Just as the power of God was displayed in the plagues of Egypt through tiny animals, especially gnats (Exodus 8:16–17), which are so small that they can scarcely be seen by the eyes, so now also God’s power and human frailty are demonstrated in a small and sluggish worm which can scarcely move and is crushed by a light touch.
>
> This is not because God, according to his will and the majesty of his power, is unable to overturn the earth, cover everything with a flood, or consume it with lightning; rather, through small things, or, so to speak, through points of bodily matter, he displays human frailty. Hence we customarily give this answer to Marcion and the other heretics who tear apart the Old Testament: God made fleas, gnats, bugs, and creatures of this kind in order to display the fragility and weakness of our flesh, which is so insignificant that it is wounded by things that are small.
>
> But if the locust and the little worm are stronger than man, why does earth and ashes boast (Ecclesiasticus 10:9), and, lifted up in pride—since man is made from earth, from which he is called man—despise human beings? 
>
> Some interpret this passage as follows. In the Scriptures we read of powers and strengths of God on the right and on the left, which the Greeks call *dynameis* (δυνάμεις), “powers.” On the right are the seraphim, cherubim, and all the angelic powers; on the left are opposing powers, concerning which it is written: “He sent among them the fury of his indignation, wrath, anger, and tribulation, an envoy of evil angels” (Psalm 77:49).
>
> Of these also Micaiah speaks in the Book of Kings: “I saw the Lord God of Israel sitting upon his throne, and all the army of heaven standing beside him on his right and on his left” (1 Kings 22:19). I think that the spirit who went out and stood before the Lord was on the left, and said: “I will deceive Ahab, and I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets” (1 Kings 22:22).
>
> To this left-hand and opposing power, which had been prepared for deception, trained for ruin, and had previously deceived many, God says: “You shall deceive and prevail; go out and do so.” The spirit that was strangling Saul, of which his servants said to him, “Behold, an evil spirit from God makes you tremble” (1 Samuel 16:14–15), was also from the left-hand side. These spirits were sent by the Lord—or, according to another reading, “who minister to the Lord”—to punish those who deserved to be tormented because of their sins.
>
> For not only are human beings ministers and avengers of his anger against those who do evil, and do not carry the sword without cause; opposing powers also exist, which are called the fury and anger of God, and of whom the Prophet, turning away from them, says:
>
> “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger” (Psalm 6:1).
>
> The Apostle handed over a sinner of this kind, so to speak, to such interrogators and torturers, for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit might be saved (1 Corinthians 5:5). Satan also belongs to these, and to him he handed others over so that they might learn not to blaspheme (1 Timothy 1:20). This is what may be said about the caterpillar and why it was called the power of God.

Then you continue:

### John Scotus

*(Chapter 15, number 12, section 9.)*

> Sin, if I am not mistaken, and sins and punishments are neither made by God nor foreknown or predestined by him. For who understands delicts? (Psalm 18:13).

### Correction

We have often said that sins are in no way made by God, but we have proved by authority that they are foreknown, since blessed Job says:

> “He knows both the deceiver and the one who is deceived; he brings counsellors to a foolish end and judges into stupor” (Job 12:16).

Gregory, *Moralia on Job*, Book XI, chapter 7:

> Since everyone who attempts to deceive his neighbor is wicked, and the Truth says to the wicked, “I never knew you; depart from me, all you who work iniquity” (Matthew 7:23), how can it be said here that the Lord knows the deceiver?
>
> But because God’s knowing is sometimes said to mean recognizing and sometimes approving, he knows the unrighteous person because, by knowing him, he judges him—for he would not judge anyone as unrighteous if he did not know him—and yet he does not know the unrighteous person because he does not approve his deeds.
>
> Thus he knows him because he detects him, and he does not know him because he does not acknowledge him as belonging to the form of his wisdom. In the same way, it is said of any truthful man that he does not know falsehood—not because he does not recognize it when he or others speak falsely, but because he knows that very deceit in judgment and does not know it in love, so that he himself does not do what he condemns when done by others.
>
> It often happens that certain people, occupied with ambushes, spread the snares of their perversity over another person’s life. When someone is seen to be caught unknowingly in those snares, people perhaps wonder whether these things are seen by divine providence; they are astonished and ask: If God sees this, why does he permit it to happen? Yet he himself knows both the deceiver and the one who is deceived.
>
> He knows the deceiver because he often sees his earlier evils and, in a just judgment, permits him to fall into other sins as well. He knows the deceiver because, abandoning him to the hand of his own deeds, he allows him to rush into worse things, as it is written: “Let the unrighteous person continue to do wrong, and let the filthy person continue to be filthy” (Revelation 22:11).
>
> He also knows the one who is deceived, because people often commit evils of which they are aware, and for this reason they are permitted to be deceived, so that they may fall into evils of which they are unaware. Yet what happens to the deceived is sometimes for purification and sometimes for the beginning of punishment.

That he foreknew and predestined punishments is proved by both authority and reason, since this belongs to the judgment of his justice.

The prophetic testimony that you brought forward is entirely irrelevant to the matter under discussion. Properly understood and treated by the Fathers, it completely overturns your perversity.

Jerome, in his *Commentary on Ephesians*, chapter 2, verse 1:

> Sin is plainly called the death of the soul in the words: “And you, when you were dead in your trespasses and sins,” in accordance with what is also written in Ezekiel: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezekiel 18:20).
>
> Since “delicts,” called *paraptōmata* (παραπτώματα) in Greek, is properly a Scriptural term according to that language’s etymology—although *plēmmeleiai* (πλημμέλειαι) is a more exact rendering of “delicts”—let us ask what they signify and how they differ from sins; that is, what is the difference between *paraptōmata* and *hamartiai* (ἁμαρτίαι)?
>
> They say that *paraptōmata* are, as it were, the beginnings of sins, when a silent thought creeps in and, with our partial consent—or, according to another reading, while we merely connive—we are not yet driven into ruin. Hence in the eighteenth Psalm it is written: “Who understands delicts?” (that is, *paraptōmata*), because it is difficult to understand the roots and beginnings of sins. Sin, however, occurs when something has been completed in action and reaches its end.

Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XI, chapter 21:

> There is this difference between crimes and delicts: a crime goes beyond the weight of sin, whereas a delict does not go beyond the weight of sin, because when the law commands a sacrifice to be offered, it commands it equally for sin and for delict. Sometimes a crime consists in an act, whereas a delict is often found only in thought.
>
> Hence the Psalmist says: “Who understands delicts?” (Psalm 18:13). Sins of action are recognized more quickly because they are seen outwardly; sins of thought are more difficult to understand because they are committed invisibly.

Cassiodorus, on Psalm 18, verse 45:

> We must nevertheless observe that there are many sins which we are completely unaware of, whose origins and stealthy beginnings we are unable to recognize. Therefore “all delicts” should be understood: “Who understands all delicts?”
>
> For when he was going to say in Psalm 50: “My delict is always before me,” and elsewhere, “I have made my delict known to you” (Psalm 31:5), how can it not be understood that the sinner is compelled to confess? But if you add the word “all,” then the question is excluded.

Augustine, in his *Questions on Leviticus*, question 20:

> After speaking of a ram offered for a delict and explaining the law of sacrifice, he says: “As that which is for sin, so also that which is for delict; there is one law for them” (Leviticus 7:7). The question is what difference there is between sin and delict. For if there were none, it would not at all be said: “As that which is for sin, so also that which is for delict.”
>
> Although the law and its sacrifice do not differ, because there is one law for them, nevertheless the two things themselves—one of which is sacrifice for sin and delict—would not differ from each other if the two were merely different names for one thing. Scripture would not so carefully emphasize that their sacrifice is one.

Perhaps, therefore, sin is the commission of evil, while delict is the abandonment of good: just as in a praiseworthy life it is one thing to turn away from evil and another to do good, as Scripture admonishes us: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 36:27), so in a condemnable life it is one thing to turn away from good and another to do evil; the former is delict and the latter sin.

For if the word itself is examined, what does *delictum* mean except “something abandoned”? And what did the person who *delinquit* abandon except the good? [Alternate reading: “what does the person who *delinquit* abandon?”]

The Greeks also assigned two customary names to this matter. Among them, delict is called both *paraptōma* (παράπτωμα) and *plēmmeleia* (πλημμέλεια). In this very passage of Leviticus the Greek has *plēmmeleia*. But when the Apostle says, “If a man is overtaken in any delict” (Galatians 6:1), the Greek has *paraptōmati* (παραπτώματι). If the origin of these names is examined, in *paraptōma* the person who commits a delict is understood as falling. Hence the word *ptōma* (πτῶμα), which the Latins call a “corpse” from falling, comes in Greek from *piptein* (πίπτειν), that is, from the verb meaning “to fall.” Therefore the one who does evil by sinning first falls from the good by committing a delict.

Likewise, *plēmmeleia* is a name resembling negligence. For in Greek negligence is called *ameleia* (ἀμέλεια), because what is neglected is not cared for. Thus a Greek says: “I do not care,” *ou melei moi* (οὐ μέλει μοι). The particle added to make *plēmmeleia*, namely *plēn* (πλήν), means “besides” or “beyond,” so that *ameleia*, which is called negligence, seems to signify “without care,” while *plēmmeleia* signifies “beyond care,” which is almost the same thing. Hence some of our writers wished—or, according to another reading, preferred—to interpret *plēmmeleia* not as “delict” but as “negligence.”

In Latin, however, what is neglected except what is not read—that is, not chosen? Hence Latin authorities are also said to have called the law *lex*, from *legere*, “to read,” that is, “to choose.”

Following these traces, it is gathered, in a manner of speaking, that the one who commits a delict abandons the good, and by abandoning it falls from the good, because he neglects it—that is, does not choose it.

But I do not at present find in either language the origin of the word *peccatum*, which in Greek is called *hamartia* (ἁμαρτία).

It may also be thought that the term “delict” refers to what is done imprudently—that is, ignorantly—whereas “sin” refers to what is committed knowingly. The following divine testimonies seem to agree with this distinction:

> “Who understands delicts?” (Psalm 18:13)

And:

> “For you know my imprudence”; immediately he adds, “and my delicts are not hidden from you” (Psalm 68:6),

as though he were repeating the same statement in another form.

Nor does the Apostle’s statement cited shortly before disagree with this reasoning:

> “If a man is overtaken in any delict” (Galatians 6:1).

For by saying “overtaken,” he indicates that the man has fallen unwittingly—or, according to another reading, has fallen “unwittingly.”

But that sin belongs to one who acts knowingly, the Apostle James states almost as a definition:

> “Therefore, whoever knows how to do good and does not do it, for him it is sin” (James 4:17).

### Against John Scotus

After this you bring forward several examples (chapter 15, number 14, section 9) by which you deny the reality of punishments and penalties—namely darkness, silence, pain, sadness, labor, and stupidity—which, you say, cannot be known except through ignorance, since when light, sound, health, joy, rest, or wisdom is said to be absent, their absence or deficiency is designated by such terms.

Holy Scripture plainly proclaims that fire has been prepared by God in Gehenna for the devil, his angels, and sinners. The Lord himself says:

> “Go into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41).

And the prophet Isaiah says:

> “For Topheth has been prepared from yesterday, prepared and widened” (Isaiah 30:33).

If you say that this fire is nothing, you make God a liar, since both by himself and through his prophet he says that it has been prepared by him. Nothing is prepared; rather, whatever is prepared must be something.

If, on the contrary, you assert that it means “not prepared,” let us see by what authorities you can persuade anyone of this; for the children of truth will not listen to it at all.

Are you going to claim in the same madness that cold is nothing, or heat, food and drink, harmful humors, winds, demons, and many other things that are called punishments or penalties?

You assert something still more extraordinary about the philosopher Dionysius. At first he maintained that pain was not an evil; afterward, when oppressed by misfortunes and tormented by pain, he began to affirm that pain was the greatest of all evils.

And because, with Epicurus, you say, “Death itself is nothing,” you could also say with him, “After death there is nothing,” and with certain sinners:

> “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die” (1 Corinthians 15:32).

If, then, God does not inflict punishment upon those who deserve it, what is the meaning of the prophet Isaiah’s statement?

> “The princes of Zoan have become fools; the princes of Memphis have withered away; they have deceived Egypt, the cornerstone of its peoples. The Lord has mingled within it a spirit of vertigo” (Isaiah 19:13–14).

Saint Jerome speaks as follows on this passage:

> This signifies that the kingdom of secular wisdom is shown to be foolish, and that the leaders of its various teachings—who are interpreted as its tribes—are accused of having foolish teachers. For the Lord mingled in them a spirit of vertigo, or error, in accordance with what is written: “Since they did not approve of having God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind” (Romans 1:28).
>
> Just as the one who is holy can say with Isaiah, “We will bring the spirit of your salvation upon the earth” (Isaiah 26:18), so the sinner drinks—or, according to another reading, “makes”—the spirit of error, that is, the spirit of wickedness, in accordance with what we also read in Jeremiah: “Your apostasy will rebuke you, and your wickedness will correct you” (Jeremiah 2:19).
>
> But if the heretic is scandalized that the Lord is said to mingle a spirit of error or vertigo, let him hear what is written by the Apostle, that is, in the New Testament: “God gave them over to the desires of their heart, to impurity” (Romans 1:24). And again: “Therefore God gave them over to dishonorable passions.” And once more: “God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do things that are not fitting.”
>
> They are given over to the desires of their hearts because they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, four-footed animals, and reptiles.

We read this not only in the Epistle to the Romans but also in the Epistle to the Thessalonians concerning the Antichrist:

> “Because they did not receive—or, according to another reading, ‘accept’—the love of truth so that they might be saved, God will send them an operation of error, so that they may believe a lie and all may be judged who did not believe the truth but took pleasure—or, according to another reading, ‘were pleased’—in the lie” (2 Thessalonians 2:10–11).

You hear of a handing-over, a sending, a mingling—God’s mingling among the ungodly—and you dare to deny that punishments are foreknown and predestined by God?

If, on the contrary, you wish these things to be understood otherwise, what will you do with those passages in which interpreters of the word of God repeatedly confess, under the same term, that people are appointed or predestined to punishment or glory?

For Saint Jerome, in his exposition of the prophet Isaiah, speaks as follows:

> “And he will reveal his face, so that the dead may come forth from their tombs; or he will uncover it, so that all his works may be brought into public view, and his inhabitants may be dispersed into different places, appointed for rewards or punishments” (Isaiah 34:1).

Augustine, in Book XV, chapter 1, of *The City of God*:

> These two societies we rightly call two cities, that is, two communities of human beings, one of which is predestined to reign eternally with God, and the other to undergo eternal punishment with the devil.

It is said without any exception that all are appointed to rewards or punishments, and the opposite must be understood in the same way. If those appointed to punishments are understood as “not appointed,” then those appointed to rewards must likewise, without doubt, be understood as “not appointed.” Since it is absurd even to think this, it must be confessed without hesitation that people are appointed both to rewards and to punishments. With God as the most just judge, this must be confessed freely and with unshaken faith, without any contradiction.

Therefore, in whatever manner or sense you wish to understand either sins or punishments, whether God knows or predestines rational creatures, we shall confess, on the authority of divine utterances and with the agreement of all orthodox believers, that God foreknew and knows sins, judges and condemns them, and established, made, created, foreknew, and predestined their punishments; that he inflicted, imposed, sent, willed, decreed, prepared, arranged, and provided them—either before the ages, in foreknowledge and predestination; in the ages, through suitable places and times; or afterward, in eternity.

### John Scotus

*(Chapter 15, number 15, section 10.)*

> For the Creator does not punish what he made, nor does he take away from them their natural gifts.

### Correction

How contrary this is to the truth is perfectly clear. If God does not punish what he made, then God himself is mistaken when he says:

> “I will destroy man, whom I created, from the face of the earth, from man to animals, from creeping things to the birds of the air, for I am sorry that I made them” (Genesis 6:7).

And again:

If God does not punish what he made, who will judge the living and the dead? Who will say to the ungodly, “Go into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41)?

If God does not take away from what he made its natural gifts, what shall I say of the rest, when we see so many people blind, deaf, mute, weak, lame, infirm, sluggish, and dull, to the point that they seem to possess no understanding at all—those whom people commonly call fools?

Why does he himself say in the Gospel concerning the keeper of his money:
