Thus he says:

## John Scotus

*(Chapter 15, number 16, section 10.)*

> Therefore, what does the one who suffers know except that health is absent? In suffering, then, he recognizes not the suffering itself but health itself—which he certainly would not know if he did not possess some conception of it. The memory of health remains in the senses, but health itself resides in that substance which God created. For the Creator does not punish what he made, nor does he take away from it its natural gifts. If health were in no way present in the nature of the one who suffers, he would be utterly unaware of it; nor would the memory of its absence be formed from the hidden knowledge of it in the mind of the sufferer, nor would he be tormented by love of its presence.

## Correction

You are attempting to deprive God of all power and truth in judging, although sinners are very often deprived of God’s gifts because of their own impiety; even bodily health is frequently taken away not only from sinners but also from the just, for reasons hidden from us but unquestionably manifest to God.

Whenever someone falls ill or is afflicted by any ailment, is health present in him? If you had ever fallen ill, you would have been able to recognize that health was absent from you, saying with the Prophet in salutary repentance:

> “There is no health in my flesh because of your anger; there is no peace in my bones because of my sins” (Psalm 37:4, 8).

And shortly afterward:

> “For my loins are filled with delusions, and there is no health in my flesh” (ibid., verse 8).

And the Lord says through the prophet:

> “The whole head is sick, and the whole heart is mourning; from the sole of the foot even to the crown there is no health in it” (Isaiah 1:6).

Although, when we are sick, the memory of health—which we desire and seek—is present in our memory, we nevertheless recognize that health is absent from us and grieve deeply. Therefore health is not then in our nature, even though we remember it; it is not the substance of our soul, but a gift of divine generosity bestowed upon our substance.

Accordingly, Augustine says in Book Fourteen of *The City of God* (chapter 15):

> In short, to state it briefly: in the punishment of that sin, what was there except disobedience repaid with disobedience? For what other misery belongs to humanity than its own disobedience against itself, so that the human being, who was able to do what he wished, should now wish what he cannot do? In Paradise, even though before sin he could not do everything, whatever he could not do he did not wish to do; and therefore he could do everything he wished. But now, as we know in his offspring and as divine Scripture testifies, the human being has become like vanity (Psalm 143:4). Who could enumerate how many things he wishes to do but cannot, when he himself—that is, his own mind—and the flesh subordinate to him do not obey him? Against his will, his mind is often disturbed, his flesh suffers, grows old, and dies; and we endure whatever else we would not endure unwillingly if our nature obeyed our will in every respect and from every side. Yet the flesh suffers something by which it is not permitted to serve. What difference does it make from where this comes, provided that, through the justice of the God who rules—for whose justice we refused to serve—our flesh, which had been subject to us, becomes troublesome to us by not serving us, although by not serving God we were able to become troublesome to ourselves, not to him? For he does not need the service of the body as we do; and therefore what we receive is our punishment, not his punishment for what we did.  
>   
> The pains called pains of the flesh belong to the soul in the flesh and arise from the flesh. For what does flesh by itself, without the soul, either suffer or desire? When the flesh is said to desire or to suffer, either the human being himself is meant, as we have explained, or something belonging to the soul which affects the flesh: something harsh, so that it produces pain, or something gentle, so that it produces pleasure. But bodily pain is merely an offense against the soul arising from the flesh, and a certain disagreement of the soul with its affection; just as the soul’s pain, which is called sadness, is disagreement with things that have happened against our will. Sadness is often preceded by fear, which is itself in the soul, not in the flesh. Bodily pain, however, is not preceded by anything like fear of the flesh, felt in the flesh before the pain. Pleasure is preceded by a certain appetite, which is felt in the flesh as its desire, such as hunger and thirst, and that which is more commonly called lust in the sexual organs, although this is a general term for every desire.

Then he adds:

## John Scotus

*(Chapter 15, number 17, section 10.)*

> For no rational nature exists that does not wish to flee misery and attain blessedness, or that, having tasted blessedness, would wish to depart from it and become miserable.

## Correction

Do you not consider that the devil and his angels voluntarily departed from the blessedness they had tasted, became miserable, and never wish to depart from misery or attain blessedness—especially since the Lord says to Job:

> “He was made so as to fear no one” (Job 41:24).

Accordingly, blessed Gregory says in the *Moralia*, Book Thirty-four (chapter 17):

> “He was made so as to fear no one.” No one, clearly, because he fears neither God nor what he is going to suffer. It would plainly have been happier for him to avoid punishments by fearing them than to endure them by not fearing them. Thus his desire for exaltation was turned into hardness of mind, so that, already condemned once for his hardness, he does not perceive that he is damned, although he sought to rule in glory. Since he did not obtain the authority he sought, he found, as it were, a remedy for his pride in the madness of insensibility; and because he could not surpass everything by advancement, he prepared himself against everything by contempt.

Gregory says in the same work:

> “His heart will be hardened like a stone”; for the heart of the ancient enemy will be hardened like a stone because no repentance of conversion will ever soften it.

Since you pursue this matter at length in what follows, let us meanwhile, with the Lord’s favor, take a breath.

## Chapter XVI

### That no nature punishes another nature, and that the punishments of sinners are nothing other than their sins

The sixteenth horror of your fantasies is entirely alien to the truth and to the authority of the Old and New Testaments. For this is how the poison of your faithlessness is forged.

## John Scotus

*(Number 1, in the text.)*

### That no nature punishes another nature, and that the punishments of sinners are nothing other than their sins

## Correction

That God punishes sinners is testified by every page of the divine writings. You therefore deny that God is the nature which punishes, as well as the apostate angels and the transgressing human beings whom he punishes.

For concerning the devil it is said to God through the prophet:

> “Have you not struck down the proud one and wounded the dragon?” (Isaiah 51:9).

And again:

> “You humbled the proud one as one wounded; with the arm of your power you scattered your enemies” (Psalm 88:11).

And again:

> “You crushed the heads of the dragon; you gave him as food to the peoples of Ethiopia” (Psalm 74:14).

To the sinful human being God said:

> “Cursed is the earth in your work” (Genesis 3:17).  
> “When you work it, it will not give you its fruits” (Genesis 4:12).  
> “It will produce thorns and thistles for you. In the sweat of your face you will eat your bread all the days of your life, until you return to the earth from which you were taken, for you are dust and to dust you will return” (Genesis 3:18–19).

Do you hear God punishing and the human being punished? And not only the human being, but also the earth punished as his penalty? Yet you deny that nature is punished by nature!

Likewise the Lord God said to the serpent:

> “Because you have done this, you are cursed among all cattle and beasts of the earth. Upon your breast you shall crawl, and you shall eat earth all the days of your life. I will place enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and hers. She shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel” (Genesis 3:11).

To the woman also he said:

> “I will multiply your hardships and your conceptions. In pain you shall bear children; you shall be under your husband’s power, and he shall rule over you” (Genesis 3:16).

You hear an angel punished, and likewise a woman, yet you deny that nature is punished by nature!

### [scan page 619]

Was Cain not a nature, the first of all mortals to kill his brother, inflamed by the torches of envy? Hear how he himself was punished:

> “The Lord said to him: ‘What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth. Now therefore you shall be cursed upon the earth, which has opened its mouth and received your brother’s blood from your hand. When you work it, it will not yield its fruits; you shall be a wanderer and a fugitive upon the earth.’ Cain said to the Lord: ‘My iniquity is greater than that I should obtain pardon. Behold, today you cast me away from the face of the earth, and I shall be hidden from your face; I shall be a wanderer and a fugitive on the earth. Therefore whoever finds me will kill me.’ The Lord said to him: ‘By no means shall this happen; rather, whoever kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold.’ And the Lord placed a sign upon Cain, so that no one who found him would kill him” (Genesis 4:10–15).

Likewise:

> “Lamech said to his wives Adah and Zillah: ‘Hear my voice, wives of Lamech; listen to my speech. For I have killed a man for my wound, and a young man for my bruise. Sevenfold vengeance shall be taken for Cain, but for Lamech seventy-sevenfold’” (Genesis 4:23–24).

You hear those who punish; you hear those who are punished; yet you dare to babble that nature is not punished by nature?

Either, then, what truthful Scripture testifies is false, and what deceitful fiction invents is true; or, if reason in no way allows the Scripture of Truth to lie, it follows in every respect that what your falsehood has devised is false.

Is it not nature that says:

> “I will destroy the human being whom I created from the face of the earth, from human being to beast, from creeping thing to the birds of heaven, for I repent that I made them.”

And below:

> “The end of all flesh has come before me; the earth is filled with iniquity because of them, and I will destroy them together with the earth.”

And again:

> “Behold, I will bring the waters of the flood upon the earth, to destroy all flesh in which there is the breath of life under heaven. Everything that is on the earth shall perish” (Genesis 6:7, 13, 17).

And again:

> “When seven days had passed, the waters of the flood covered the earth. All the fountains of the great deep were broken open, and the cataracts of heaven were opened; and rain fell upon the earth forty days and forty nights” (Genesis 7:10–12).

And below:

> “The water rose fifteen cubits above the mountains that it had covered. All flesh that moved upon the earth perished: birds, cattle, beasts, and every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth, all human beings, and everything on earth that had the breath of life died. He destroyed every substance that was upon the earth, from human being to beast, both creeping things and birds of heaven; and they were destroyed from the earth” (Genesis 7:20–23).

What could be sought that is clearer or more certain?

God is indeed an incorporeal, immutable, omnipotent, eternal nature, the creator of all other natures, corporeal and incorporeal, mutable and changing. Behold, truthful Scripture proclaims that God destroyed the creatures—human beings, birds, beasts, and creeping things. Since Scripture can never lie, it most certainly teaches us to believe and freely confess that nature punishes nature.

### [scan page 620]

This punishment, however, produces complete destruction in some cases and temporary destruction in others. Reason and authority indicate that irrational animals are entirely consumed; rational creatures, however, are not destroyed altogether, so that they no longer exist, but are ordered and judged justly and suitably according to their respective conditions. They indeed exist in substance, but do not exist in the mercy which, placed in the punishments they deserve, they will never be worthy to attain.

Indeed, the Lord rained fire and sulfur from the Lord, and consumed the people and everything that had been in the Pentapolis (Genesis 19:24). In all the plagues inflicted by the Lord upon the Egyptians, the Lord is always presented as acting, and creatures as carrying out the Lord’s will.

Were not the waters of the Red Sea natures that killed Pharaoh and his army (Exodus 14:28)? Were not the serpents in the wilderness and the destroyer natures of fire, which killed so many thousands of human beings (Numbers 21:6–7 and following)?

But why is it necessary to heap up so many passages from Scripture, when daily events teach us that nature is never punished except by nature? Either the Creator himself, by his most omnipotent command, punishes rational natures that rebel against him and disobey him, or he commands or permits created natures to be punished by created natures—sometimes through a manifest judgment, sometimes through a hidden one, but never through an unjust judgment.

Does not a human being kill a human being, a beast a beast, a bird a bird, fire wood, or iron something else? Are not all living things natures that punish and are punished?

We have both heard and grieved that many are killed by poison, mushrooms, excessive consumption of any kind of food, and excessive drinking. There has never been any disagreement about this among Catholic commentators.

As for your further assertion that the punishments of sinners are nothing other than their sins: how can you now declare sins to be the punishments of sinners, when up to this point you have labored to establish that they are nothing? How can sins, which are nothing, be punishments, which according to you are likewise nothing?

But because you want punishments to be understood as nothing other than the consciousness of sins, following Origen, or, according to your own view, merely the absence of blessedness—and because in what follows you develop this at greater length, or rather more deceitfully—we shall, with Christ’s favor, examine each point in its proper place.

You continue, then, and say:

## John Scotus

*(Chapter 46, number 2, section 1.)*

> In the great heat of the eternal fire, therefore, the misery of the condemned is nothing other than the absence of blessed happiness.

## Correction

The orthodox commentators hold, on the authority of Sacred Scripture, that Gehenna involves not merely one punishment but a twofold punishment. In the words of blessed Job:

> “Let them pass from the waters of snow to excessive heat” (Job 24:19).

Saint Jerome, in his exposition of the Gospel according to Matthew (chapter 11, verse 28), explains this as follows:

> We read with complete clarity in Job that Gehenna has a twofold character, of excessive fire and cold.

Bede, in his exposition of Solomon’s *Proverbs* (Book 3, chapter 31, in the middle), says:

> “She will not fear the cold of snow for her household.” The cold of snow can also be understood as the eternal punishments, which we read are mingled with fire and cold. When it is said, “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 8:12), weeping is produced by the eyes, fire and smoke; but cold commonly produces the gnashing of teeth. Hence blessed Job, speaking of the punishments of the reprobate as eternal, says: “Let them pass from the waters of snow to excessive heat” (Job 24:19).

If, however, this same twofold punishment is thought to refer not to two substances, water and fire, but rather to one—namely, fire—it may also be understood according to Philip the presbyter, commentator on blessed Job, who spoke in this way concerning the words of blessed Job (in *Job*, Book 2, chapter 24, near the end):

> Blessed Job seems to speak of two Gehennas, of fire and of cold, through which the devil, the heretic, and the impious human being will be changed, although in the Gospel we do not possess an authoritative statement concerning two punishments of this kind that differ from one another. It is certain that cold produces burning no less than fire; but if Gehenna is fire alone, perhaps the experience of torments there will nevertheless be such that those who are tortured in it will at one time feel burning fire and at another the burning of excessive cold. The change of punishment may be regarded as a passage from one state to another, with them at one time feeling cold and at another heat.  
>   
> Perhaps this is why the Lord says in the Gospel: “Cast him into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 22:13), so that the gnashing of teeth may arise from the severity of the cold. Here too we can find some analogy in our bodies. When there is an excess of yellow bile—which is extremely hot in local diseases—an intolerable chill precedes the feverish heat that follows. Physicians say that these two contrary conditions arise from one and the same bodily humor.

Blessed Gregory says in his *Exposition of Job*, Book 12:

> “Fire will devour the tents of those who gladly accept bribes” (Job 15:34). If we should understand their tents as the bodies in which their souls dwell, then the fire devours their tents, because those who burn here in the mind with the fire of greed will there also be burned in the flesh by the fires of Gehenna.

The same author says in Book 16 (chapter 26):

> “Is not their uprising cut down, and will fire devour their remains?” (Job 22:20). Here the wicked are raised up because they are lifted up in evil actions: they act perversely and yet are not immediately struck for their perverse deeds. They sin and flourish; they increase their sins and multiply their earthly goods. But their uprising will then be cut down when they are either dragged from the present life to destruction or brought from the presence of the eternal Judge to the eternal fire of Gehenna.  
>   
> Although here they leave behind their dead flesh, they will receive that same flesh again in the resurrection, so that they may burn with the flesh in which they sinned. Just as their guilt was in mind and body, so their punishment will likewise be in soul and body. Since, therefore, what they leave here dead will not be free from torment, it is rightly said: “Fire will devour their remains.”

The same author says in Book 15 (chapter 30):

> “Like ash which the whirlwind scatters before the eyes of almighty God” (Job 21:18). The life of the wicked is ash. Although it appears green for a moment, it is already seen as consumed by his judgment, because it has been assigned to eternal destruction. The whirlwind scatters this ash because God will come openly, our God, and will not be silent: “Fire will burn before him, and a mighty storm around him” (Psalm 49:3–4).  
>   
> By the whirlwind of this storm the wicked are snatched away from the eternal sight of the Judge. Those who here solidified their minds in perverse desire will there appear as chaff and ashes, because the whirlwind, snatching them away, carries them off to eternal punishments.

The same author says in Book 4 (chapter 17):

> “Fire will devour him that is not kindled” [variant: “that will not be kindled”] (Job 20:26). In a remarkable way the fire of Gehenna is expressed in a few words. Bodily fire, in order to be fire, requires bodily fuel; when it must be maintained, it is undoubtedly nourished by heaped-up wood, and it cannot exist except when kindled and fed.  
>   
> By contrast, since the fire of Gehenna is incorporeal and nevertheless burns corporeally those who are cast into it, it is neither kindled by human labor nor nourished by wood. Once created, it endures unquenchably; it needs no kindling and does not lack heat.  
>   
> Therefore it is rightly said of this wicked person: “Fire will devour him that is not kindled” (Job 20:26). For the justice of the Omnipotent, foreknowing future things, created the fire of Gehenna from the very beginning of the world, so that it would begin to exist once for the punishment of the reprobate; yet its heat would never end, even without wood.  
>   
> It must be understood that all the reprobate, because they sinned together in soul and flesh, will there be tormented together in soul and flesh. Hence the Psalmist says: “You shall place them like a furnace of fire at the time of your presence; the Lord in his anger will trouble them, and fire will devour them” (Psalm 20:10). A furnace burns inwardly, whereas what is devoured by fire begins to burn from the outside. Thus, to show that the sacred writings represent the reprobate as burning both externally and internally, they testify that they are devoured by fire and placed like a furnace, so that they may be tormented in body by fire and burn in mind through pain.  
>   
> Hence, when it is said of this wicked person, “Fire will devour him that is not kindled,” the following is immediately added concerning his spirit:

> “He will be afflicted, left in his tent” [variant: “he will be afflicted in his tent”].

For the flesh is the tent of the wicked (Job 18:13), since the wicked person gladly inhabits it and, if possible, desires never to leave it. The just, however, place their joy in hope of heavenly things, and their citizenship is in heaven (Philippians 3:20). While they are still in the flesh, they are as though they were no longer in the flesh, because they are nourished by no bodily pleasure. Hence it is said to some:

> “You are not in the flesh but in the spirit” (Romans 8:9).

They were not literally outside the flesh, since they were receiving the words of exhortation through the apostle’s letters; rather, to be “not in the flesh” means to have no attachment to carnal desires.

But this wicked person, because he placed all his joy in carnal life, dwelt in the tent of the flesh. When he receives that flesh again in the resurrection, he will burn with it after being handed over to the fires of Gehenna. Then he will wish to be taken out of it; then he will seek, if he can, to escape its torments; then he will begin to wish to avoid what he loved. But because he preferred that flesh to God, by God’s judgment he will be compelled to suffer more intensely in the fire through it.

Here he does not wish to leave it, yet he will be dragged away from it. There he will wish to leave it, yet it will be preserved for him because of his punishments. Thus, to increase his torment, here he is taken unwillingly from the body, and there he is held unwillingly in the body. Since his spirit will wish to escape in torment from the flesh which he wrongly preferred through his love for it, but will be unable to do so, it is rightly said:

> “He will be afflicted, left in his tent.”

The same author says in Book 9 (chapter 38):

> “Before I go—and do not return—to the land that is dark and covered with the gloom of death” (Job 10:21). What is signified by the name “dark land” except the recesses of Tartarus, which are covered by the gloom of eternal death? For it separates the condemned forever from the life of light. Hell is rightly called a land, because whoever is held captive by it is kept there immovably.  
>   
> It is written: “One generation passes away, and another generation comes, but the earth remains forever.” The dark recesses of hell are therefore rightly called a land, because those whom they receive for punishment are not tormented by a transitory punishment or by some fantastic imagination; rather, they preserve them in the solid retribution of eternal damnation.  
>   
> They are sometimes also designated by the name of a place, as the prophet testifies when he says: “They bore their disgrace with those who descend into the pit” (Ezekiel 26:20). Hell is therefore also called a land, because it holds those whom it has received securely; and it is called a pit, because those whom it has once seized it continually swallows, surrounded by fluctuating and fearful torments.  
>   
> The holy man, whether speaking in his own voice or in that of the human race, asks to be released before he goes—not because the one who is destined to repent of his guilt goes to the dark land, but because without doubt the one who has neglected to mourn goes there. It is like a creditor saying to his debtor: “Pay the debt before you are imprisoned because of it”; yet the debtor is not imprisoned if he does not delay in paying what he owes.  
>   
> It is rightly added: “I shall not return,” because the mercy of the one who spares cannot free those whom the justice of the Judge has once condemned in places of punishment. These places are then described more subtly. When it says “a land of misery and darkness,” misery refers to pain and darkness to blindness. The land of misery and darkness is therefore said to hold those expelled from the sight of the strict Judge, because outside, pain torments those whom blindness, separated from the true light, obscures within. The land of misery and darkness may nevertheless be understood in another way as well.

### [scan page 622]

For this earth in which we are born is indeed a land of misery, but it is not a land of darkness. Here we suffer many evils arising from our corruption, yet, while still in it, we return to the light through the grace of conversion, as Truth urges when it says:

> “Walk while you have the light, lest the darkness overtake you” (John 12:35).

That other land, however, is at once a land of misery and darkness, because whoever descends into it to endure its evils does not thereafter return to the light.

In its further description it adds:

> “Where there is the shadow of death and no order” (Job 10:22).

Just as outward death separates the soul from the body, so lower death separates the soul from God. The shadow of death is therefore the obscurity of vision [variant: division], because every condemned person, while being burned by eternal fire, is deprived of inward light.

The nature of fire is to provide both light from itself and burning. But that avenging flame of the transgressions of the wicked possesses burning and does not possess light. Hence Truth says to the reprobate:

> “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41).

And, again, signifying all of them in the person of one individual, he says:

> “Bind his hands and feet and cast him into the outer darkness” (Matthew 22:13).

If the fire that torments the reprobate could possess light, the one who is rejected would not be said to be cast into darkness.

Hence the Psalmist also says:

> “Fire fell upon them, and they did not see the sun” (Psalm 57:9).

For fire falls upon the wicked, and when the fire falls the sun is not seen. The flame of Gehenna devours them in such a way that it blinds them to the vision of the true light, so that the pain of burning torments them externally while the punishment of blindness obscures them internally.

Thus those who sinned against their Creator in body and heart are punished in body and heart together, and those who, while living here, served their perverse pleasures with both are made to feel punishments in both.

Hence it is rightly said through the prophet:

> “They descended into hell with their weapons” (Ezekiel 32:27).

The weapons of sinners are the members of the body by which they carry out the perverse desires that they conceive. Hence Paul rightly says:

> “Do not present your members as weapons of iniquity to sin” (Romans 6:13).

To descend into hell with one’s weapons, therefore, is to endure the torments of the eternal Judge together with those very members by which one has satisfied the desires of pleasure, so that pain may absorb from every side those who are now subjected to their pleasures and fight everywhere against the justice of the just Judge.

It is also very remarkable that it says:

> “Where there is no order” (Job 10:22).

For almighty God, who punishes evil well, is in no way disorderly; nor does he permit punishments to be without order. The punishments themselves, which proceed from the balance of justice, cannot be inflicted without order. For how could there be no order in punishments, when retribution follows each condemned person according to the measure of his crime?

Hence it is written:

> “The mighty shall suffer mighty torments, and stronger punishment awaits the stronger” (Wisdom 6:7, 9).

In the condemnation of Babylon it is said:

> “As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so much give her torment and mourning” (Revelation 18:7).

If punishment is distinguished according to the measure of guilt, it is plainly established that order is preserved in punishments. And unless the sum of the torments were distinguished according to the merits of the condemned, the Judge who was to come would never be said to declare to the reapers:

> “Gather the weeds first and bind them into bundles to burn them” (Matthew 13:30).

For if no order were preserved in punishments, why would the weeds be bound into bundles for burning? To bind bundles for burning plainly means to join together those who are to be handed over to eternal fire with their equals, so that those stained by similar guilt may be bound by an equal punishment, and those who are not polluted by unequal wickedness may not be tormented by unequal suffering.

Thus the same condemnation crushes those whom the same pride had exalted; an equal affliction constrains those whom ambition had similarly inflated; and an equal flame of punishment torments those whom an equal flame of luxury had inflamed.

For just as there are many mansions in the house of the Father (John 14:2), so the diversity of virtue and the disparity of crimes subject the condemned to diverse punishments in the fires of Gehenna. Gehenna is one for all, yet it does not burn all with one and the same quality.

Just as one sun touches everyone, but not everyone is warmed by it in the same way, since the strength of the heat is felt according to the condition of each body, so there is one Gehenna which afflicts the condemned, but it does not burn all with the same intensity. What differing bodily health does here is performed there by the differing causes of merit.

How, then, can it be said that there is no order in punishments, when each person is certainly tormented according to the measure of his guilt?

After the holy man has described the shadow of death, he adds how great the confusion is in the minds of the condemned:

> “And where there is no order.”

The punishments themselves, although ordered, are certainly not ordered in the hearts of those who are dying. As we said shortly above, while each condemned person is burned externally by the flames, he is inwardly devoured by the fire of blindness. Placed in pain, he is confused both externally and internally, so that he is tortured by his own utter confusion.

There will therefore be no order in the punishment of the reprobate, because in their minds the confusion itself rages more cruelly, although the justice of the Judge, by a wondrous power, orders it so that the punishment confuses the soul as though without order [variant: disorderly].

It may also be said that there is no order in the punishments because, although various things rise up to punish them, their proper qualities are not preserved. Hence it is immediately added:

> “And an everlasting horror inhabits it” [variant: “will inhabit it”] (Job 10:22).

In the torments of this life, fear possesses pain, but pain does not possess fear. Fear no longer torments the mind when it has begun to suffer what it feared. But there both darkness and the shadow of death endure, and everlasting horror inhabits them, because those handed over to its fires feel the pain of punishments while, with anguish pressing upon them through fear, they are continually shaken by dread; and they endure what they fear, and again …

## [Scan page 623]

### Saint Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

...they should fear without cessation. For concerning these it is written: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished” (Isaiah 66:24). On one side, the flame that kindles gives light; on the other, as we learned above from the words of the Psalmist (Psalm 37:9), the fire that tortures brings darkness. Here fear is lost once what was feared has begun to be endured; there both pain burns and terror constricts. In a dreadful manner, therefore, the reprobate will then have pain together with dread, flame together with darkness. Thus, plainly, the weight of supreme justice ought to be felt by the condemned: because, while they lived, they did not fear to depart from the will of the Creator, eventually, in their destruction, the very torments will also be at variance with their own properties, so that, by attacking them in different ways, they may increase their sufferings and, as they arise variously, be felt in manifold ways.

Yet these punishments torture the condemned diversely and beyond their strength; and, extinguishing in them the support of life, they preserve them [al., by extinguishing it], so that the end may punish life in such a way that it lives forever without an end to its torment. For it hastens toward its end through torments, yet endures in perpetual decline without an end. Thus, for the wretched there is death without death, an end without end, decay without decay: death lives, the end always begins, and decay does not know how to cease.

Since death destroys but does not extinguish, pain tortures but in no way drives away terror, and flame burns but utterly fails to dispel the darkness, it follows—as far as can be gathered from the knowledge afforded by the present life—that punishments which do not retain their proper character in every respect have no order. Nevertheless, there the fire neither shines for consolation nor fails to shine in some degree so as to torture more intensely. For the reprobate will see their own followers with them in the torment, illuminated by the flame, those for whose love they sinned. Thus, those who had carnally loved the lives of these persons contrary to the Creator’s commandments will also be afflicted by their destruction, to increase their own damnation.

We gather this, surely, from the testimony of the Gospel. Truth itself announces that the rich man who descended to the torments of eternal fire is described as remembering his five brothers (Luke 16:27–28). He asked Abraham to send someone to instruct them, lest, when they came there, they should be tortured by an equal punishment. If, then, to increase his own pain he remembered absent relatives, there is no doubt that shortly afterward he could also see them present as an additional argument for his punishment. What is surprising, then, if he sees the reprobate burning with him, since, to increase his pain, he saw Lazarus—whom he had despised—in Abraham’s bosom? If the elect man appeared to him in order that his punishment might increase, why should it not be believed that he can also see in the torment those whom he loved contrary to God? From this it follows that those whom the reprobate now love in a disordered manner they will then see with themselves in torment, by a remarkable order of judgment, so that the carnal kinship placed before the Creator may intensify their proper punishment, condemned before their eyes by an equal vengeance.

The fire, therefore, which torments in darkness must be believed to retain light for the sake of torment. If we cannot establish this by testimonies explicitly expressing it, we must teach it by another means. Three boys of the Hebrew people were thrown, by the command of the Chaldean king, into a furnace whose fires had been kindled, with their hands and feet bound. Yet when the same king, moved by pity, inspected them in the furnace’s blaze, he saw them walking about unharmed in their garments (Daniel 3:22, 24, 50ff., 92). From this it is plainly gathered that, by the wondrous dispensation [al., arrangement] of the Creator, the nature of the fire was moderated with differing effects: it did not touch the garments, yet it burned the bonds; for the holy men the flame was cool for inflicting torment, yet burned for the service of releasing them.

Just as, then, fire knows how to burn for the consolation of the elect but does not know how to burn for their punishment, so conversely the flame of Gehenna neither shines for the reprobate as a grace of consolation nor fails to shine for their punishment. Thus, in the eyes of the condemned, the fire of punishment will glow without any brightness, yet, to increase their pain, it will show them how those whom they loved are being tortured.

What is surprising if we believe that the fire of Gehenna contains the punishment both of darkness and of light, when experience teaches us that even the flame of torches shines obscurely? Then the devouring flame will burn those whom carnal pleasure now pollutes; then the immeasurably deep abyss of hell will swallow those whom empty pride now exalts; and those who here, through whatever vice, fulfilled the will of the crafty persuader will then arrive with their leader, the reprobate, at the torments.

Although the nature of angels and human beings is very dissimilar, one punishment nevertheless entangles those whom one guilt binds in crime. The prophet indicates this well and briefly when he says: “There is Asshur, and all his multitude, and around him are his graves” (Ezekiel 32:22).

For whom does “Asshur,” under the name of a proud king, signify except the ancient enemy, who fell through pride and, because he draws many into guilt, descends with all his multitude into the chambers of hell? Graves cover the dead. And who endured death more grievously than he who, despising his own condition, abandoned life? Human hearts receive him as one dead and therefore become his graves. “Around him are his graves,” because those in whose minds he now buries himself through desires he afterward joins to himself through torments. And because the reprobate now receive evil spirits into themselves by committing unlawful acts, their graves will then burn with the dead.

† But why should it be incredible that the wretched, once condemned there, will remain forever, when in this life—while they still live under the hope of repentance—they are liable to be entangled in many miseries? Concerning these blessed Gregory says in Book XX of the *Moralia* (chapter 15):

“Those who gnawed in the wilderness, wasted by calamity and misery” (Job 30:3). For if the flesh is neglected when it ought carefully to be cared for, the squalor laid upon it from above makes the illness worse; and, while the misery of negligence is added to the calamity of sickness, a heavier distress is endured when squalor has arisen. Human nature, therefore, created good but fallen through the fault of its own will into infirmity, entered into calamity, because, oppressed by countless necessities, it found in this life nothing except that by which it might be afflicted. But when, in relation to these same necessities of our nature, we often serve beyond what is fitting and neglect the care of the mind, we add to the misery of infirmity the squalor of negligence.

For natural necessities are often very dangerous, because it is scarcely discerned in them what is undertaken from a concern for usefulness and what is done through the vice of pleasure. Frequently, when an opportunity for seduction is found, while we render what is owed to necessity, we serve the vice of pleasure; and, under the cloak of infirmity, our excuse disguises itself before the eyes of discernment, concealing itself as though under the protection of necessity while pleasure is being fulfilled. To relax the infirmity of our nature through negligence is nothing other than to add misery to calamity and, through that misery, multiply the squalor of vice.

Hence holy men distinguish with the greatest care whatever they do, lest the infirmity of their nature demand more from them than is owed to it, and lest vice of pleasure grow up under the cover of necessity. They endure one thing from infirmity and another from the suggestion of temptation; and, placed—as it were—as very upright judges between necessity and pleasure, they relieve the one by consulting it and restrain the other by suppressing it. Thus they both endure the calamity proper to infirmity and do not descend through negligence into the squalor of misery.

For this itself is to be in calamity: to endure the necessities of nature through the weakness of still-corruptible flesh. The Psalmist wished to escape these necessities when he said: “Deliver me from my necessities” (Psalm 25:17). For he knew that the sins of pleasure often burst forth from the occasion of necessities; and, so as not willingly to admit anything unlawful, he labored to remove the very thing that he unwillingly endured from the root.

But the wicked rejoice in these necessities of our corrupt condition, because they turn them toward the use of pleasure. When they serve nature by nourishing their bodies with food, they stretch themselves out in the indulgence of gluttony through the pleasure of the throat. When they seek clothing for covering their limbs, they want not only what will cover them but also what will delight through softness; not only what will caress the touch by its softness but also what will seduce the eyes by its color [al., “but they also seek things that exalt them, and against the numbness of cold they seek not only things that protect by their thickness”].

To turn the cause of necessity toward the use of pleasure: what else is this than to join the squalor of misery to the calamity proper to oneself?

When the Church is pressed by the time of adversity, therefore, let her remember those through whose merit she suffers such things, and let her say: “They gnawed in the wilderness, squalid through calamity and misery” (Job 30:3). They would not be squalid through calamity if, in these innate necessities, they did not add the misery of pleasure; necessities which, plainly, we deserved through the fault of our first parent.”

† After this you add blasphemies and heap worse things upon worse, when, contrary to everyone’s judgment, you attribute happiness to those condemned in hell and take misery away from the wretched. For you say:

## [Scan page 624]
### *On Predestination Against John Scotus*

### John Scotus  
(*On the Division of Nature*, Book V, chapter 16, no. 3, section 1)

“In whom there is no one who does not naturally possess within himself a notion of the absence of blessedness and its desire, so that he is tortured all the more intensely the more ardently he desires what the just judgment of God does not allow him to comprehend. This desire would certainly not exist in the wretched if he did not possess at all what he desires.

“In the deepest and most genuine manner, therefore, the condemned will have happiness in the depths of their punishments, and will not have it. They will indeed have a certain notion of it for the purpose of remembering it, but they will not have its appearance in the fruit of contemplation. For, as we have said, the wretched would not have a notion of happiness in their memory if some knowledge of it did not occur in their nature. Just as no one outside the truth possesses a notion of truth, so neither does anyone outside happiness possess knowledge of it. No one, therefore, will possess outside his own nature either the notion or the knowledge of happiness. In the nature of the wretched, then, there will be truth, and therefore there will be happiness. But how will that nature be wretched if happiness—which is truth—is present in it? What if no nature is punished? Will it be wretched? I do not see how. For what reason will any nature be wretched unless it is punished? Therefore, if no nature can be punished, no nature will be wretched.

“Who, moreover, will not believe that every nature is either God or exists from God? It is utterly foolish to suppose that created nature is capable of misery. But I cannot see by what justice the creative nature is punished, since it punishes the natures it itself created. No nature, then, will be punished; and what is not punished will not be wretched.”

### Response

What an utterly vain argument! What a pestilential dogma! What vanity smeared with deadly poisons! A little earlier you had said that, in the great heat of the fire of Gehenna, penal misery was nothing other than the absence of happiness. Now, however, your argument has been extended so far that you remove the misery you had previously attributed and grant the happiness you had previously taken away.

You entangle yourself in such contradictions that, having entered a labyrinth, you find no way to escape because you do not seek the thread of guiding grace. What, then? Will a blind man for that reason not lack eyes because he still retains in his memory the notion of eyes he once possessed? Will a lame man for that reason have sound feet because he either remembers that he was once upright, or desires to be so, or sees others walking upright? Will a paralytic, deprived of the use of all his limbs, for that reason be healthy and strong because the desire and knowledge of health remain in his memory? And, not to repeat many examples, will any sinner for that reason not be a sinner or impious because he recalls in his memory a notion of justice and piety? Or, conversely, will a just and pious person for that reason not be just and pious because he remembers the injustice and impiety by which others are afflicted, whether by seeing them or by forbidding others to commit them?

That the knowledge of blessedness is absent from the condemned there is testified by Solomon, who says: “Whatever your hand is able to do, do it diligently, because there is neither work, nor reasoning, nor knowledge, nor wisdom in the underworld to which you hasten” (Ecclesiastes 9:10). Since this is altogether contrary to truth and reason, it must be confessed, on the authority of the divine utterances, that those placed in punishment are both miserable and given over to eternal misery—especially since, as we stated above, blessed Job, describing the places and punishments of Gehenna, said:

“Before I go to the land that is dark and covered with the gloom of death, a land of misery and darkness, where there is no order, but everlasting horror inhabits” [al., “inhabits”] (Job 10:21).

You hear “a land of misery and darkness,” yet you dare to deny the misery of the condemned. You hear of the place where everlasting horror dwells, yet you promise happiness to the miserable.

Will that rich man buried in hell, vainly asking that Lazarus, resting in peace, refresh his tongue, therefore be blessed because he revolved the blessedness of Abraham’s bosom not only in his mind but also saw it with his eyes? (Luke 16:19ff.) Yet Abraham’s reply indicates something quite different, for he said:

“Son, remember that you received good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted, while you are tormented” (Luke 16:25).

Here is torment: where is happiness? Just as Abraham and Lazarus are not to be called miserable merely because they both saw and knew the rich man’s misery, so neither was the rich man happy or blessed because he saw from afar and remembered the blessedness of those placed in rest. Scripture says:

“For in death no one remembers you; and in hell, who will confess to you?” (Psalm 6:6).

And again:

“Will anyone in the grave declare your mercy, or your truth in destruction? Will your wonders be known in darkness, and your justice in the land of forgetfulness?” (Psalm 88:12–13).

### Cassiodorus on Psalm 55

“‘But you, O God, will lead them down into the pit of destruction’ (Psalm 55:24). Having spoken of the just, he now speaks of the impious, who are to be plunged into the depths of Gehenna. A pit is a wide opening excavated in the earth’s interior and containing waters assigned for human use. But lest you understand this pit merely as such, he added ‘the pit of destruction,’ which is read elsewhere: ‘Nor let the pit close its mouth over me’ (Psalm 69:15)—a mortal pit, a dreadful sinking, where no space is granted and no breathing-room of misery is provided, but a dark obscurity surrounds it and removes the sight of pleasant light. By the likeness of a pit, therefore, it warns us to fear the torments of Gehenna.”

† Augustine on Psalm 6:

“That rich man confessed in hell of whom the Lord said that he saw Lazarus in rest while he himself was suffering in torments (Luke 16:23). He confessed so completely that he even wished his brothers to be moved, so that they might be restrained from their sins on account of the punishments believed to exist in hell. Although he confessed in vain, he nevertheless acknowledged by his confession that those torments had befallen him, when he wished others too to be taught not to fall into them. What, then, is meant by ‘In hell, who will confess to you?’ (Psalm 6:6)? Is hell to be understood as the place into which the impious will be cast after the judgment, where, because of the deeper darkness, they will see no light to which they may confess?”

† If happiness is present among them and misery absent, then, without doubt, the memory and confession of God are present among them. But it is certain that there is no blessedness apart from God. If, therefore, the impious are removed by the sentence of a strict judgment so that they do not see the glory of God, there will assuredly be no blessedness or happiness for those from whom the opportunity of seeing God is taken away.

Moreover, it is certain that those who are still living in this present life are called miserable, as is testified by the penitent prophet, who healthfully lamented his misery:

“I have become miserable and bowed down to the end; all day long I went about mourning” (Psalm 38:7);

and by the Apostle:

“Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?” (Romans 7:24).

The Apostle James also agrees with these words, saying: “Be miserable and mourn” (James 4:9).

If, I say, those of whom there is no despair while they live here, since through salutary repentance they may attain the joys of blessedness, are called miserable, who can doubt that those who are irrecoverably miserable—whose destruction is as certain as the sentence of strict judgment fixed against them—are miserable?

We read, in the Lord’s words:

“I have been reckoned among those who descend into the pit; I have become like a man without help, free among the dead” (Psalm 88:5–6).

Only he could truly say this who, by the same rule of truth, could alone say:

“The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14:30).

It is plainly evident that those who retain nothing of freedom have been handed over to eternal misery. But what happiness exists without freedom? Happiness without freedom is rightly judged rather to be unhappiness.

Thus Solomon’s proverbs predicted long beforehand concerning the Antichrist, the son of iniquity, that he would proceed happily. Yet happiness will never come to him, nor to all his members who possess and rejoice in a transitory prosperity, nor will true and everlasting blessedness ever be theirs, although his earthly happiness will continue until he has exalted himself above everything called God or worshiped as God (Proverbs 30:29; 2 Thessalonians 2:4).

Of him it is written:

“The Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of his mouth and destroy him by the brightness of his coming” (2 Thessalonians 2:8).

You hear that he is killed; you hear that he is destroyed; yet you attribute happiness to one who is killed and destroyed. Surely, whoever is killed and destroyed is punished as one deprived of freedom and happiness. No one is ignorant that he is a created nature, since he is a human being, even though filled with the devil. Nature, therefore, is punished when the man of sin is killed. Concerning his members the prophet cries out:

“Transgressors will be punished, and the seed of the wicked will perish” (Psalm 37:28).

And the Lord says concerning Cain:

“Everyone who kills Cain will be punished sevenfold.”

He will be condemned to the vengeance of every deserved punishment. Since, therefore, it is not doubted that natures are punished, there must be no doubt that sinful natures—and sin itself—can afterward become punishment and misery.

## [Scan page 626]  
### *On Predestination*

Therefore, when you say that you cannot find by what justice created nature is punished by the nature that created it (Book V, chapter 16, section 1), have you not read that the supremely just God punished the first ancestors of our race for disobedience? (Genesis 3:16–17.)

From the words with which the Lord rebuked them, while in his most benevolent patience he sought their repentance, it is shown by what justice they were punished. “And the Lord God called Adam,” Scripture says, “and said to him: ‘Where are you?’ Adam replied: ‘I heard your voice in Paradise, and I was afraid because I was naked, and I hid myself’” (Genesis 3:10).

Augustine says in Book XI of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis* (chapter 34):

“It is sufficiently probable that God was accustomed to appear to those first human beings in human form through a creature suited to such an action; yet he never allowed them to notice their nakedness, lifting their attention toward higher things, until, after the sin, they had felt the shameful movement in their members under the law of punishment affecting the members. Thus they were affected as human beings are accustomed to be affected under the eyes of other human beings. This very affect was part of the punishment of sin: they wished to hide from one whom nothing can escape and to conceal their flesh from the one who examines the heart.

“But what is surprising if, wishing in their pride to be like gods, they became empty in their thoughts and their foolish heart was darkened? (Romans 1:21.) For they declared themselves wise in their abundance, and when he turned his face away they became fools (Romans 1:22). What they were already ashamed of in relation to themselves, for which they had made coverings, they appeared much more ashamed to be seen by him who, as though through a familiar mode of dealing, offered himself to be seen by them through a visible creature as if by human eyes.

“For if he appeared in this way so that they might speak with God as with a human being, just as Abraham did at the oak of Mamre (Genesis 18:1), that very likeness of friendship which before the sin had given them confidence burdened them with shame after the sin. They no longer dared to display to such eyes the nakedness that displeased even their own.”

The Lord, therefore, wishing to punish the sinners—now questioned according to the manner of justice—more severely than was implied in the punishment about which they had already been forced to blush, said:

“Who told you that you were naked, unless you ate from the tree from which I commanded you not to eat?” (Genesis 3:11).

For from this arose the death conceived through the sentence of God, by which the concupiscence of the members was noticed, when it was said that their eyes were opened. What followed was shame:

“Adam said: ‘The woman whom you gave to be with me—she gave me from the tree, and I ate’” (Genesis 3:12).

Did pride say, “I have sinned”? Pride has the deformity of shame but does not possess the humility of confession. These things were written because the questions themselves were plainly made so that they might be written both truthfully and profitably; for if they had been written falsely, they would not have been profitable.

We should observe the disease of pride from which people suffer today: they habitually attribute to a creature whatever evil they have done, while they wish whatever good they have done to be attributed to themselves:

“The woman whom you gave to be with me”—that is, whom you gave so that she might be with me—“she gave me from the tree, and I ate” (Genesis 3:12).

It is as though she had been given for this purpose, rather than so that she herself might obey the man and both might obey God.

“And the Lord God said to the woman: ‘What have you done?’ And the woman said: ‘The serpent deceived me, and I ate’” (Genesis 3:13).

She does not confess her sin, but refers it to another—though of a different sex, she displays the same arrogance.

From these two, nevertheless, was born the one who did not imitate them, although he was exercised by many evils [al., “was tested by many evils”], who said—and continues to say to the end of the age:

“I said: ‘Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you’” (Psalm 41:5).

How much better would it have been if these two had spoken thus! But the Lord had not yet broken the necks of sinners (Psalm 125:3). There remained labors, pains, deaths [al., “death”], and every sorrow of the age, as well as the grace of God, which [al., “because it”] comes to the aid of human beings at the appropriate time, teaching afflicted people not to presume upon themselves.

“The serpent deceived me, and I ate,” she said—as though any persuasion ought to have been preferred to God’s command.

“And the Lord God said to the serpent: ‘Because you have done this, you are cursed above all cattle and above all the beasts that are upon the earth. Upon your breast and upon your belly you shall walk, and you shall eat earth all the days of your life’” [al., “all the days”] (Genesis 3:14).

“And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. She shall guard your head, and you shall guard her heel” (Genesis 3:15).

This entire sentence is figurative, and the faithfulness of the writer and the truth of the narrative owe it nothing other than that we not doubt that it was spoken. For the words “And the Lord God said to the serpent” are solely the words of the writer; these must be understood literally. That it was said to the serpent is therefore true (Genesis 3:14). The words of God that follow are left to the reader’s free understanding, whether they should be taken literally or figuratively, as we stated at the beginning of this work.

Therefore, since the serpent was not asked why it had done this, it may be understood that it did not itself act in its own nature and will, but that the devil had worked through it, by it, and in it, since the devil had already been destined to the eternal fire because of the sin of his impiety and pride. What is now said to the serpent, therefore, and what certainly refers also to the one who worked through the serpent, is figurative. For in these words the tempter is described as he was to be toward the human race—the human race beginning to be propagated at the time when this sentence was pronounced against the devil as against the serpent, and so forth.

“And to the woman he said: ‘Multiplying, I will multiply your sorrows and your conception; in sorrows you shall bear children, and your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you’” (Genesis 3:16).

These words of God to the woman are better understood figuratively and prophetically. Nevertheless, since the woman had not yet given birth, and the pain and groaning of childbirth could arise only from the body of death into which she had been conceived when she transgressed the commandment—

## [Scan page 627]  
### Saint Prudentius of Troyes, Bishop

—with animal members indeed even then, yet, had she sinned in some other way, she would not have died and would have lived in some happier state until, after a life well conducted, she deserved to be changed into something better, as we have indicated above in several places.

This punishment is also referred to the literal meaning. Unless, perhaps, what is said—“Your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you”—must be considered as to how it can literally be understood. For it is not right to believe that, even before the sin, the woman had been made otherwise than so that the man would rule over her and she would turn toward him by serving him. Yet it can rightly be understood that a form of servitude is signified here which belongs more to a condition of subjection than to love. Thus the very servitude by which human beings afterward began to be servants of other human beings is also found to have arisen from the punishment of sin.

The Apostle said: “Serve one another through charity” (Galatians 5:13), but he would certainly not say, “Rule over one another.” Husband and wife can therefore serve each other through charity, but the Apostle does not permit a woman to rule over a man (1 Timothy 2:12). This sentence of God assigned such rule rather to the man, and the woman earned a husband as her master not by nature but by guilt. Nevertheless, unless this is observed, nature will be further corrupted and guilt will increase.

He also said to the man:

“Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree concerning which I commanded you that you alone should not eat from it, cursed is the earth in your works. In sorrows you shall eat of it all the days of your life. Thorns and thistles it shall produce for you [al., “it shall sprout”], and you shall eat the grass of the field. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Genesis 3:17–19).

“Who is unaware that this means the labors of the human race upon the earth? And since they would not exist if the happiness that had been in Paradise had been retained, there is no doubt that these words should also initially be accepted literally.”

† This is unquestionably the justice by which nature, supremely and eternally good, punishes nature that has become proud and obstinately transgressed the command of its Maker. This punishment is divided in two ways: first, now, at the separation of the soul from its body, according to the merit of that first transgression, which has been transmitted from its very root into, and made innate in, the whole race of its descendants; and afterward in Gehenna, acquired through the multiplicity both of this and of other crimes contracted through lustful perversity, as Solomon says:

“God will bring everything that is done into judgment, for every error, whether it be good or evil” (Eccli. 12:14).

And again:

“Rejoice, therefore, young man, in your youth, and let your heart be in good things in the days of your youth; walk in the ways of your heart and in the sight of your eyes, and know that for all these things the Lord will bring you into judgment” (Eccli. 11:9).

If no nature is punished, why, I ask, will there be a judgment? For if the impious are not to be punished in it, I utterly fail to see for what reason judgment should be held. Is it only for the sake of the just, so that they may receive the rewards they deserve? Who but a madman would say this?

All the pages of the divine utterances proclaim that a day of judgment has been appointed, so that on it each person—both the just and the unjust—may receive according to what he has done, whether good or evil (2 Corinthians 5:10). And this is the catholic faith, because it is true and sincere. Since, therefore, it is certain that judgment will come and that in it each person, both pious and impious, will receive what he deserves, it is equally certain that, just as the good receive rewards, so the wicked are handed over to torments.

They will be tortured, handed over to endless punishments; they will therefore be punished, since to punish is nothing other than to afflict with either temporal or eternal punishments. It is just, then, that creative nature punish transgressing nature, which placed its most perverse will before the supremely righteous will of its Maker.

If this is certain beyond all ambiguity, it follows with equal certainty that all who will be punished are miserable and subject to eternal misery, never to escape either the torments of mind or those of body.

This, I say, is the inflexible justice of the terrifying Judge, which you now pretend not to find but will shortly experience once it has been found.

Now, as for the sentence of Saint Augustine that you cite from Book XI of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis* (chapter 21), in which he says:

“It is true and evident that it is contrary to justice that, without any preceding merit, God should condemn in anyone the very thing that he himself created in that person,”

it is clear to anyone, even to the simplest reader, how much this agrees with catholic truth. For no one should be believed to be condemned by God unless evil merits have preceded, since this is his justice’s unfailing retribution upon those alone whom the most equitable Judge hands over to avenging punishments to be tortured without remedy.

Concerning the devil, however—that it is in no way the nature created by God, but his own evil will, that is punished by the penalty of eternal fire, and that his nature is not signified when it is said, “This is the beginning of the Lord’s creation, made so that his angels might mock it” (Psalm 104:26)—Augustine has discussed many matters with subtle reasoning in this and the following, twelfth, book.

He explains that the phrase may refer either to an aerial body, which God fitted to such a will, or to the very arrangement in which he made the devil useful to the good even against his will, or to the fact that, foreknowing that he would become evil, God nevertheless did not withhold his goodness in granting life and substance to a will that would later become harmful, while at the same time foreseeing how many good things he would bring about through that devil by his wondrous goodness and power.

These matters, discussed in the same book and in the following twelfth book, were expounded and resolved differently by other equally catholic men, who offer a more suitable understanding to those piously and rightly seeking the authority of the divine teaching. Every devout investigator gladly and steadfastly assents to their salutary interpretations. Yet Augustine retracted some of his statements; concerning others he himself testifies that more questions were raised than answered, that fewer of the things discovered were firmly established, and that the remaining matters were set down as though they still required investigation.

By these words the most humble teacher gave other interpreters of the Holy Scriptures an opportunity concerning the matters that had been more scrupulously treated and more clearly elucidated with respect to divine authority, con-
## On Predestination

They might disclose in their little works to the learned both of the present age and of posterity what they have written. But he himself, in his work *The City of God*, discussed the same matters much more fully and more orthodoxly, refining them and explaining what he had discussed; these passages will be inserted in their proper place later, if the Lord permits.

It is also clear that in your earlier letter you did enough to show that the will is nature. But if this were true, it is surprising how you now seek to assert from the words of blessed Augustine that it is not nature but the will that ought to be punished. For if the will is nature, and the will, although perverse, is punished, then nature is certainly punished. For although all natures were established good by the good Creator, rational natures are not irrationally called evil through their own fault. Therefore, if the perverse will is punished and the will is nature, it necessarily follows that nature is said to be punished.

Yet the will is separated from nature so far that the orthodox Fathers often appear to distinguish them with the utmost clarity. Their memorable witness, Augustine, speaks as follows in the eleventh book of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis* (chapter 9):

> “But,” he says, “if God had willed it, these too would have been good. How much better did God will that they should be what they willed to be? Yet they would not be good fruitlessly, nor evil with impunity, and even in this they would be useful to others. But he foreknew that their future will would be evil—indeed, he foreknew it; and because his foreknowledge cannot be deceived, the evil will is not his but theirs. Why, then, did he create those whom he foreknew would be such? Because, just as he foresaw what evil things they would do, so also he foresaw what good he himself would bring about from their evil deeds. For he made them in such a way that he left them something by which they too might act, so that, whatever they chose culpably, they would find him working laudably through them. They have the evil will from themselves, but from him they have good nature and, according to the punishment due to them, a place; [variant: a place due to them as a just punishment], while for others they are an aid to discipline and an example of fear.”

“But,” they say, “could he not also convert their will to the good, since he is omnipotent?”

“Certainly he could. Why, then, did he not do so?”

“Because he did not wish to. Why he did not wish to is in his own power.”

The same author says in Book VIII (chapter 19):

> “A great and unmissable subject is set before us, so that, as far as we can, we may contemplate how greatly the work of divine providence is divided between nature and will.”

Accordingly, while discussing many matters usefully and truthfully, Augustine says among other things (chapter 23):

> “Creating natures in goodness, ordering wills in power: so that among natures there may be many things that are not from him, while among wills there may be no good will that does not benefit from him, and no evil will that he cannot use well.”

Augustine likewise says:

> “He never punishes an evil will in such a way as to destroy the dignity of nature.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Therefore God’s providence, ruling and administering the whole creation, both natures and wills—natures so that they may exist, but wills so that neither the good may be fruitless [variant: unfruitful] nor the evil go unpunished.”

The same author says in the same work:

> “God, therefore, who is above all and created all things, creates all natures good and justly orders all wills.”

Jerome, in his *Commentary on the Prophet Isaiah*, Book VI (chapter 14, verse 21), says:

> “For God made all things good, but from those who are most evil by their own will evil arose [variant: seed arose], which comes about through will, not through nature.”

The same author, in Book XIII (chapter 47, at the end), says:

> “From this it is evident that they become good by nature and evil by will. Finally it is added: man went astray in himself, not by nature but by the judgment of his mind.”

The same author, in Book XV (chapter 54, section 16), says:

> “For I am he through whom you will have proselytes, I who created the smith blowing upon the fire of coals” (Isaiah 54:16)—that is, the devil, the craftsman of all evils—not by necessity of nature but by the judgment of the mind. He will stir up fires and bring forth against you weapons, such as Simon and Elymas the magicians, who resisted the apostles Peter and Paul. I created the slayer of those who will be unbelievers—not because I am the cause of their destruction, but because an adversary has been created for battle, and defeat is the cause of destruction for the defeated and of rewards for the victors. All who have been fashioned against you by the smith who blows upon the fire will not be guided; rather, they will feel both present punishments and future ones.”

The same author, in Book XVI (chapter 19, section 8), says:

> “Their ways are perverse (Acts 8:13), not by nature but by their own will.”

Since it is therefore clear that the will is not nature, I do not at all understand how what is not nature can be punished. But whenever perverse wills—that is, sins—are said to be punished, I think this should rather be understood metonymically: the effect is put for the agent, that is, the will for the one who wills, and the sin for the sinner. For I consider it most just that the one who wills perversely—that is, the one who sins—should himself receive what he deserves. For it is certain that the body acts according to the willing mind: the mind performs some things by itself through thought, and others through the body subject to it; thus, when the mind wills, the body carries out the act. It is therefore fitting that, just as they do not differ in acting, so they should not differ in suffering.

For what is it that is worn down by so many diseases, dissolved by death, stinks to the worms, rots, decays, is reduced to dust, and a thousand times brought almost to nothing, if not nature? Let us question the corpses of so many buried people, the remains of so many animals, birds, reptiles, and schools of fish, and the things born from the earth, falling away through annual, monthly, or daily changes: in the very ruin and unavoidable process of their corruption we shall see natures punished, natures corrupted, natures dissolved, and almost driven to nothing.

Hence Augustine, in Homily 39 on the Gospel of John (Treatise 42), says:

> “For this reason you do not hear, because you are not from God” (John 8:47). Again, do not pay attention to nature but to vice. These people are from God and are not from God: from God by nature, not from God by vice. For nature is good, since it is from God; it sinned by believing through the will what the devil persuaded, and it was corrupted. Therefore it seeks a mediator, because it is not sound. Thus, when the Lord says, ‘Whoever is from God hears God’s words; for this reason you do not hear, because you are not from God’ (John 8:47), he did not distinguish the merits of natures, nor did he find in human beings, besides their soul and flesh, some other nature that had not been corrupted by sin.”
