## John Scotus  
*(Chapter 46, number 8, section 2)*

> “For nothing is justly punished except what is proved to have sinned.”

## Correction

This is true; and for that reason soul and body are justly punished, because both are known to have sinned. But when this is said concerning sinners, it does not exceed the rule of truth. Nevertheless, we see and read that many are punished in cases where your opinion is entirely frustrated.

Let us begin with Abel, the first martyr, and we shall find that no iniquity was punished in him, but that he was killed by reason of his righteousness; both the Book of Genesis and the Lord himself commend his righteousness (Genesis 4; Matthew 23:35).

The First Book of the Prophet Samuel tells us that Achimelech and the other priests were killed through Saul’s iniquity because they had compassionately assisted David (1 Samuel 22). And, not to recount many examples from ancient times, the Second Book of the Maccabees reports that seven brothers were killed for the laws of God, which they refused to abandon under any threats, and with such tortures that they inspired horror in those who inflicted and witnessed them (2 Maccabees 7).

Blessed John the Baptist was sanctified in his mother’s womb (Luke 1:15), and among those born of women no greater than he arose (Luke 7:28); nevertheless, the reward for a young girl’s wanton dance is set forth, and the beheading of his head defiles the banquet of the ill-fated king (Matthew 14).

The Son of God, our God and Lord Jesus Christ, who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found (1 Peter 2:22), after suffering such insults finally died suspended from the gibbet of the cross, fastened with nails. Nor did the fury of his persecutors cease; his most pure side was opened by a spear.

Peter, the universal shepherd of his holy Church, condemned Nero’s madness by being hung upon a cross. Paul, the teacher of the nations, stained Nero’s sword with blood. So too did the other apostles and their companions, all the martyrs of our Lord Jesus Christ throughout the ages. Is it believed that they were punished for their own iniquity, or that any iniquity in them was punished or is to be punished? But if you wish to deny that the Son of God was punished, all the pages of the divine writings rise up against your words and voluntarily confront them. Among them, as we call it, let us obey the Book of Wisdom, addressing God the Father:

> “You also condemn him who ought not to be punished” (Wisdom 12:15).

Blessed Gregory explains this as referring to Christ himself in the books of his *Moralia*. And the Psalmist says:

> “They will lie in wait for the soul of the righteous and condemn innocent blood” (Psalm 94:21).

You hear so many hosts of saints suffering for the confession of truth and justice, and you dare to say that the human substance is not punished?

Again, you add:

## John Scotus  
*(Chapter 16, number 9, section 2)*

> “No human being’s iniquity is found except the culpable perversity of his own will, which most truly is not nature, because it was not created in any substance by God, the Creator of all; therefore it is justly punished and made wretched.”

[Scan page 632]

## On Predestination

## Correction

If it is neither nature nor a created substance, how is it punished, or how does it become wretched? That which absolutely does not exist—how can it be punished or become wretched? Or how can what never possessed blessedness be subjected to misery?

Accordingly, what you append in order to confirm your opinion from the words of blessed Augustine—who says that he will restore in many things what he himself made and punish in many things what he himself did not make—does not at all support your perversity. For the punishment of vices must rather be understood according to the rule we discussed above: the lover and perpetrator of vices is punished on account of his vices. It is not what absolutely does not exist that feels punishment, but what exists in some manner.

What, I ask, was punished in the transgressors of the ancient law by the various kinds of temporal punishments divinely imposed, if not nature? Hence Augustine, in his *Epistle to the Galatians* (chapter 3, verse 12), says:

> “The Law is not from faith, but ‘the one who does these things will live by them.’ He does not say, ‘The one who does it will live in it,’ so that you may understand that in this passage ‘the Law’ stands for the works themselves. Those who lived by these works certainly feared that, if they did not perform them, they would suffer stoning, crucifixion, or punishments of that kind. Therefore, ‘the one who does these things,’ he says, ‘will live by them’—that is, he will have a reward, so that he may not be punished by this death.”

The same author, in Book XXI of *The City of God* (chapter 24), says:

> “For the Ninevites repented in this life (Jonah 3), and therefore their repentance was fruitful, as though they were sowing in this field in which God willed that what would afterward be reaped with joy should be sown with tears.
>
> “Yet who will deny that what the Lord foretold was fulfilled in them, unless he pays little attention to the manner in which God overthrows sinners, not only in anger but also in mercy? Sinners are overthrown in two ways: either as the Sodomites were (Genesis 19:24), so that the people themselves are punished for their sins; or as the Ninevites were (Jonah 3:5), so that the sins of the people themselves are destroyed through repentance.”

You then continue:

## John Scotus  
*(Chapter 16, number 10, section 3)*

> “Since, therefore, God created the whole nature of all human beings in the first man, what was naturally created in that nature could in no way transgress the Creator’s natural law. Therefore it did not sin in him, because God created it in him.”

## Correction

The soul and body of man were created by God, and both sinned together: the soul by willing and desiring the fruit of the forbidden tree, and the body by eating in the utmost disobedience. Just as God made both, so both sinned—the mind willing and the body most wickedly obeying. For just as willing belongs to the mind, so acting belongs to the body.

For if the will is not itself a nature, it must be the will of some nature. There is therefore the willing of the mind, and by its will—that is, by its movement—it moves either itself or its body toward this or that. From this it follows that the sin belongs to the one to whom the willing belonged. For the will is never found except in a nature and from a nature, which God, the supreme and immutable will, created.

On this subject we have already set forth the opinion of blessed Augustine from his *Enchiridion* (chapter 15), where he says:

> “From the good nature of man the will can arise both good and evil; nor was there any source from which the evil will could first arise except the good nature of angel and man.”

He also continues in the same work (chapter 25):

> “But these are common evils of human beings and angels, who are condemned by God’s justice for their wickedness. Yet man has a punishment peculiar to himself, by which he was also punished with bodily death. For God had threatened him with the punishment of death if he sinned. Thus, while granting him free choice, he nevertheless ruled him by command, terrified him by destruction, and placed him in the happiness of paradise, as in the shade of life, from which, if he preserved justice, he might ascend to better things.
>
> “After sin, therefore, he was made an exile and also bound his offspring—which, by sinning in him as in its root, he had corrupted—with the punishment of death and damnation. Thus whatever offspring was born from him, and from the wife who had been condemned together with him, through carnal desire, in which a similar punishment for disobedience was repaid, drew original sin. Through various errors and sufferings this sin would be dragged to that final state where it would endure endless punishment with the deserter angels, its corrupters, possessors, and companions.
>
> “Just as through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned (Romans 5:12)—for in that passage the Apostle called the whole human race ‘the world’—so matters stood: the condemned mass of the whole human race lay in evils, or was even rolled about in them, and was hurled from evils into evils. Joined to the company of the angels who had sinned, it paid the punishments most deserved by impious desertion.
>
> “For whatever evil people do willingly through blind and untamed desire, and whatever they suffer unwillingly through manifest and evident punishments, belongs to God’s just anger.”

You then add and say:

## John Scotus  
*(Chapter 16, number 11, section 3)*

> “In whom, nevertheless, all sinned, and for this reason all die in him, and consequently all are punished—therefore this is rightly believed. Just as God wished to create in that one man the general substance of the human race, so in him he also established the proper will of all human beings.
>
> “If in one man the fullness of the common human nature, both bodily and spiritual, was constituted for all, then the individual will of each person necessarily existed in him. Therefore it was not the universality of nature that sinned in him, but the individual will of each person.”

## Correction

The flesh is certainly nature; no one doubts that the soul is a nature. It has been demonstrated sufficiently, both by reason and by authority, that the will is not nature. Therefore the will of children is not generated from the will of their parents, just as no one doubts that the flesh of offspring comes from the flesh of their parents. Therefore, it was not by the will in Adam that all later generations sinned, which they did not derive naturally from him …

[scan page 633]

**B. [heading illegible]**

[The opening is materially damaged in the supplied scan.]

…yet nature, corrupted by the will of that same first parent—which is not itself vice but, once corrupted, could produce nothing whatever from itself except what was corrupted—brought forth whatever it propagated by natural generation. Hence the Apostle says: “Death passed through all by the will of one man”—and I say, into all wills—“and so all sinned”; but rather: “Through one man death passed into all men, in whom all sinned” [Romans 5:12].

Since he sinned not under any necessity of nature but by his will, he so corrupted himself—that is, his nature, namely soul and body—by sinning that nothing could proceed from natural generation except what was corrupted. This was shown in the shameful movement of the genital members after the disobedience of the first parents: they are said never previously to have been ashamed of their nakedness or to have made themselves aprons [Genesis 3:7]. Nature, therefore, in the pleasurable and lustful mingling of the sexes, is wholly—although not without the will—convicted of sin, since it is plainly shown to serve such an extremely improper movement.

Listen. Now at last you certainly reveal yourself as a Pelagian, a Caelestian, indeed—if one may put it so—as a Julian, since, after their heresy was once condemned by the common judgment of the whole world, you emerge as a new awakener, so to speak, of slumbering ashes. You reject natural and original sin in the human race in order to remove gratuitous grace. For they uttered the same madness: that Adam’s sin passed into his descendants by imitation, not by nature, just as the truth declares in the Apostles and through the Apostle. You are shown to be their most devoted follower, repeatedly asserting that it passes by the will, not by nature.

Since it is evident—and even today, while the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ shines everywhere among the nations—that scarcely any children of more advanced age, but almost all infants of tender age, are carried to the sacraments of baptism, what sin of their own will is washed away in them, when they have not yet been able to possess one through the development of age? Catholic faith therefore holds this doctrine without wavering: they are not cleansed from a private sin of their own, but from original, natural, ancestral sin. This sin was committed by the will of the first parents, not by the personal will of each one being born; yet it so corrupted them and all the posterity proceeding from them through desire that they remain bound under eternal condemnation unless they are freed by the mercy of assisting grace.

It would not be called natural sin if it did not also belong to nature—already corrupted—not merely to the will, which is not nature; this has already been demonstrated even with your own agreement. Therefore either deny with the Pelagians that there is natural sin, and so overwhelm the Apostle who says, “We were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” [Ephesians 2:3], as well as all Catholics; or, as we desire, receive the truth of natural and consequently original sin, and join yourself to the sincerity of Christian faith.

**JOHN SCOTUS**

(Chapter 16, number 12, section 2.) “If anything in nature transgresses, and since nature is one, it certainly perishes as a whole; but it did not perish, since the medicine of the wound—that is, the substance of the Redeemer—remained wholly incorrupt, apart from which all sinned together in one man. For they did not sin in themselves, but all in him; just as he had his own will, so he had his own sin. And just as each person in him could commit his own offense, no one is justly punished for another’s sin; therefore nature is in no respect punished, because it is from God and does not sin. But a voluntary nature, using the good of nature lustfully, is punished because it transgresses the law of nature, which it would certainly not transgress if it had been created substantially by God.”

From this it is plainly inferred that the wicked do not suffer punishment for what God made, but for what they wickedly devised through pride. Lust is tortured by a perverse will, since it is not permitted to possess what it wrongly or unworthily desires.

**CORRECTION**

Although your depravity has been sufficiently answered by these arguments, one point must nevertheless continually be pressed upon you: you appear to separate will from substance, although in the first parts of your work you most stubbornly affirmed that it was substance. But if nature is not substance, I do not see how you can say that it was constituted by God in man. For if nature is not substance, how did it pass, as nature, to all? No one doubts that the nature of the body was present in that one man as the nature of all human beings, for flesh is born from flesh; but whether the soul is likewise born from the soul is a great question, long and extensively discussed by the Fathers, yet left without a certain definition.

Therefore whatever you assert concerning the will—which plainly is not nature in itself, but belongs to nature, that is, the soul’s spontaneous movement—is judged wholly frivolous and contrary to truth. For just as the will cannot exist by itself, so it cannot by itself will—that is, move—and whatever is done by the will is undoubtedly attributed to the one who wills. The soul does will, however; and when it wills perversely, it is justly punished for the merit of its perversity.

If nature does not sin, you accuse the Apostle of falsehood when he says of God the Father that he sent his Son “in the likeness of sinful flesh” [Romans 8:3]—a flesh that he never had, if nature, which is man, that is, soul and body, does not sin. You therefore detect the Apostle lying in two ways: both in saying that the Son of God had the likeness of sinful flesh—that is, true flesh—and in saying that there is no sinful flesh, namely our flesh, which originally and naturally bears sin.

Nor do you notice—or perhaps you pretend not to notice—how great an absurdity, indeed impiety, follows from this. For if nature does not sin, man does not sin; and if man does not sin, our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, did not differ from other men except by the singularity of his generation and birth. If this secret exception makes him in no respect different from other mortals, then what the Prophet says is false: “Who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord? Who shall be like the Lord among the sons of God?” [Psalm 88:7].

[scan page 634]

**ON PREDESTINATION**

For if nature, that is, man, does not sin, the true Son of God and his adopted sons are equal. Since this surpasses almost every blasphemy, we must confess, on the testimony of the truthful Apostle, that our flesh is sinful flesh—that is, generated, conceived, and brought forth with sin. In the likeness of this flesh—that is, in the reality of flesh neither generated, conceived, nor brought forth with sin—God the Father sent his Son.

And lest, according to your customary perversity, you twist the apostolic words toward another meaning, listen to what follows: “that, through sin, he might condemn sin in the flesh”—that is, from his own flesh, which he had appointed to be an offering for sin, he condemned the sin implanted in our flesh. Apart from Christ alone, no flesh of ours has ever been free from it, nor has any been free from it since the disobedience of the first parents and the just punishment of the dreadful Judge; nor can any flesh be born free from it.

Therefore, if it must be confessed without hesitation that the flesh of the Son of God was the likeness of sinful flesh—that is, it was not sown, conceived, or brought forth with sin, without which sinful flesh, namely ours, cannot be sown, conceived, or brought forth—it follows that nature, which is sinful flesh, namely our flesh, is proved to sin. “Who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord? Who shall be like the Lord among the sons of God?” [Psalm 88:7].

For Catholic faith holds and proclaims without wavering that the Son of God, except for the eminence of his divinity, is distinguished from other human beings by this: he was conceived neither through desire nor through sexual union, but solely through the operation of the Holy Spirit, and could not be corrupted by any taint of original sin. Therefore, in conception, birth, and the whole course of life, he alone, free from every sin, could be “free among the dead” [Psalm 88:6], through whose natural purity all our natural and affective impurities might be cleansed.

Nature as a whole therefore sinned in the first man: that is, the soul desiring what was unlawful, and the body obeying the desires of its soul. For we cannot rightly say that will is born from will or transmitted by hereditary propagation, since it is not nature; whereas we rightly say that man is born from man, because man is nature.

Thus nature as a whole perished because it sinned as a whole; and because it wholly perished, it was wholly assumed, truly and mercifully, by the Son of God. It was wholly assumed so that it might be wholly liberated; and it was wholly liberated because it wholly suffered in the Son of God. The whole of it endured torment in him, although undeservedly: the body was worn down by sufferings and committed to burial, while the soul, having left the body for a time, entered the underworld in complete freedom. It was likewise wholly freed, because through the glory of the swift resurrection it passed from corruption to incorruption, from death to life, and from mortality to immortality.

It was therefore not the will in the Son of God that was punished—for it was never subject to any perversity—but nature, which, lost in Adam, he wondrously restored and liberated in himself. For, as we stated shortly before, in him and in certain of his members it was not iniquity that was punished, but nature. Nature was punished because nature had perished, as he himself says: “The Son of Man came to seek and to save what had perished” [Matthew 18:11]. For if it was not nature that had perished but an evil will, it would have been necessary for the Son of God to assume nature, but only that which had perished—namely, the will.

The soul had perished, exiled and banished for a very long time from blessedness; the body also had perished, decaying into the dust from which it had been taken. Both, however, were restored: the soul to blessedness and the body to incorruption, through the ineffable humility of the Mediator.

Ambrose, explaining the Apostle’s words in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, “proclaiming the Lord’s death until he comes” [1 Corinthians 11:26]:

“Since we have been liberated by the Lord’s death, in eating and drinking we commemorate this event and signify the flesh and blood that were offered for us. Having received the New Testament in these things, which is the new law that delivers those obedient to it to the heavenly kingdoms. For Moses too, having taken the blood of a calf in a basin, sprinkled the children of Israel, saying: ‘This is the Testament which God has established for you’ [Exodus 24:6–8]. This was a figure of the Testament which the Lord, through the Prophet, called New, so that what Moses delivered might be Old.

“The Testament was therefore established in blood, because blood is the witness of divine beneficence. In its likeness we receive the mystical cup of blood for the protection of our body and soul, because the Lord’s blood redeemed our blood—that is, it saved the whole human being. The Savior’s flesh was for the salvation of the body, but his blood was shed for our soul, as had previously been prefigured by Moses [Hebrews 9]. For he says: ‘The flesh is offered for your body, but the blood for your soul’ [Leviticus 17:11]; therefore blood is not to be eaten.

“If, then, among the ancients there was an image of the truth that has now appeared and been manifested in the Savior’s advent, how can the Old Testament seem contrary to the New to heretics, when the two bear witness to one another?”

Bede, in his *Exposition of Genesis*:

“They had indeed made themselves aprons from fig leaves with which to cover their nakedness [Genesis 3:7]; but God made them tunics of skins with which to clothe their entire bodies. They, having lost through transgression the glory of innocence, attempted to set before themselves a veil of excuses by which they might transfer their guilt to the Creator; but the Creator himself, through the sentence of just judgment, deprived them of their former state of unchanging life and punished them with mortality in soul and body alike.”

Remember what blessed Augustine said [*Enchiridion*, chapter 30]:

“What good can the lost person do—or, according to another reading, what good can he be able to do—unless he has been restored from perdition—or, according to another reading, liberated from it? Is it by free choice of the will? Far from it. For by using free choice badly, man both lost himself and lost free choice itself.”

The same author, in his letter to Vitalis:

[The quotation begins mid-sentence.] “…to his vessels, whatever he predestined to rescue, he committed free choice, so that, with him assisting, they may believe in him by free will. Therefore this is the work of grace, not of nature—the grace, I say, which the second Adam brought us, not the nature which the first Adam lost in himself. There is therefore one torment of a perverse will: when, freeing it from the power of those things which it desires wrongly or unworthily, he does not permit it to have that which it nevertheless wills to its torment. There is another when soul and body, either here or hereafter, are afflicted by manifest and evident torments. Let us consider the seed of any male sowing in a female. You will never deny that it is nature, proceeding from the nature—that is, the flesh—of the sower.”

[scan page 635]

**ST. PRUDENTIUS, BISHOP OF TROYES**

He indeed lost himself—that is, his nature, which is soul and body. Therefore this had perished, because it had itself sinned; and because this whole had sinned, it had consequently corrupted the entire mass, so that nothing born from that natural union of male and female was other than corrupt and, accordingly, subject to death. For that reason another’s sin—that of the first man—is justly punished in another, namely his offspring, which is the whole human race, because the entire progeny naturally drew the corruption of its paternal root from its stock. Certainly you cannot maintain in infants any individual distinctness of will or action; yet all who die outside the grace of baptism are condemned to eternal punishment, not for their own sin but for that of the first parent.

Hence Augustine in the *Enchiridion* [chapter 46]:

“Infants are not implausibly said to be bound by the sins of their parents, not only of the first human beings but also of those from whom they themselves were born. For that divine sentence, ‘I will repay the sins of the fathers upon the children’ [Deuteronomy 5:9], holds them until they begin through regeneration to belong to the New Testament. This Testament was prophesied when Ezekiel said that children would not receive the sins of their fathers and that this proverb would no longer exist in Israel: ‘The fathers ate a sour grape, and the children’s teeth were set on edge’ [Ezekiel 18:20]. For each is born again in order that whatever sin is in him with which he is born may be loosed; sins committed later by evil conduct can also be healed by repentance, as we see happening even after baptism. Therefore regeneration was instituted for no other reason than that generation is defective—so much so that even one begotten in lawful marriage says, ‘I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother nourished me in the womb’ [Psalm 51:5]. He did not say ‘in iniquity’ or ‘in sin,’ though that too could rightly have been said; rather, he preferred to say ‘iniquities’ and ‘sins.’ For in that one sin which passed into all human beings, and which was so great that human nature was changed and turned toward the necessity of death, there are, as I explained above, several sins and other sins of parents which, although they cannot alter nature in the same way, nevertheless bind their children by guilt unless gratuitous grace and divine mercy come to their aid.”

You hear that infants are bound by their parents’ sins, and you say that another’s sin is justly punished in no one. You hear that nature is punished by death, and you say that nature is punished in no one. Thus it is very truly said that the wicked suffer punishments in that which God made—that is, in the whole human substance—but deservedly because of sin, which the whole substance committed.

Certainly no one denies that male seed is lifeless when it is emitted. Where, then, is will in the seed? Who does not know that will belongs to a soul? Since, therefore, in the begetting of offspring only lifeless seed is sown, and after intervals of time it is by the Creator of all things first congealed in the womb, then delineated in its proper members, delineated and formed, formed and solidified, and solidified and animated by the breath of life, it is plainly established that will cannot be present in it before it receives the soul by the Creator’s gift, to which willing properly belongs.

Yet the Prophet cries out in lamentation and says: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” [Psalm 51:5]. No one is unaware that the seed is conceived, and that, without contradiction, it is good because every creature of God is good, and everything good is pure, while nothing impure is good. We must therefore ask why he laments that he was conceived in iniquities.

He does not mean his own iniquities, since through his own will they did not yet exist, but undoubtedly the iniquity of our propagator, from whom, being born with the human substance, we inherit a condemned iniquity, which we can escape in no way except by being born again.

Blessed Job likewise did not hesitate to call this very seed impure, saying: “Who can make clean what has been conceived from unclean seed? Is it not you alone?” [Job 14:4]. Why, I ask, is it unclean, when the Lord says to the Church’s shepherd: “What God has cleansed, do not call common” [Acts 11:9], and in the Gospel: “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the heart; that is what defiles a person” [Matthew 15:11]?

Who does not know that in the seed which is sown there is no personal capacity or knowledge of willing? How, then, is it unclean? Is it because it is a creature of God? Far from it. It remains, therefore, that we must confess it unclean through the transmission of the primordial iniquity, although the Catholic Church holds and proves that it was made clean by the dignity of the first creation.

It is therefore evident that, through the guilt of the father’s transgression, what was made clean by the purity of the first creation is sown, conceived, and born unclean. No one who is free from the truth is unaware of this or denies it.

Gregory, in the eleventh book of the *Moralia*, at the end:

“He who alone is clean in himself can cleanse the unclean. For a human being living in corruptible flesh bears within himself the uncleanness of temptations, because he plainly drew them from his origin. His very conception is unclean through the pleasure of the flesh; hence the Psalmist says: ‘Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me’ [Psalm 51:5]. Hence it is that he is often tempted even against his will; hence it is that he suffers certain impurities in his mind, although his judgment resists them. For, being conceived from uncleanness and striving toward cleanness, he endeavors to overcome what he is.”

Whoever overcomes the movements of hidden temptation and the uncleanness of thought should not attribute his purity to himself, because no one can make clean what has been conceived from unclean seed except the one who alone is clean in himself [Job 14:4]. Therefore, whoever has already reached the place of purity in mind should look back upon the path of his conception by which he came, and from this understand that he does not possess purity of life through his own virtue, since he was made from uncleanness.”

And what you further infer is:

**JOHN SCOTUS**

(Chapter 6, number 13, section 4.) “If reason has persuaded us that no nature is punished, it will necessarily advise that no nature punish. For neither does a creature punish a creature, since no substance can be contrary to another substance.”

**CORRECTION**

The utterance of Truth is sufficient to dissolve this fancy: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who has power to destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” [Matthew 10:28]; and likewise: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” [Matthew 25:41]. He will certainly say this to human beings—that is, to natures—not to wills existing by themselves, which cannot exist by themselves because they are not natures.

As to the condemnation of original sin, through whose desert the most just sentence of God made the whole human race subject to death, it is evident how greatly you have favored your Pelagian fathers. We refrain from saying more, because we know that the Fathers have treated and settled the matter more than sufficiently. There are many examples of substances contrary to substances. To omit the rest: water is plainly contrary to fire; fire to water, wood, and other earthly materials; poison to a human being; the saliva of a person long fasting to a serpent; one human being to another; the devil to a human being; and so forth.

God, however, is not contrary to the natures he created insofar as they were created by him. But insofar as they depart from him in pride, he is shown, by the equity of justice, to be so contrary not only to rational but even to irrational creatures that he rightly punishes the former for transgressing through prevarication, and either destroys the latter on their account or changes them for the worse—as we read happened in the Flood, at Sodom, and in many other regions of the world, and as we believe and expect will happen at the judgment. The Apostle also says: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. These are opposed to one another, so that you do not do the things that you wish” [Galatians 5:17]; and again: “I see another law in my members resisting the law of my mind and making me captive under the law of sin which is in my members” [Romans 7:23].

**JOHN SCOTUS**

(Chapter 16, number 14, section 4.) “For what reason, you ask, is it proved above all that the authorship of no sin is to be referred to God, unless most foolishly and impiously? For if sin were from nature, and nature from God, it would plainly follow that sin was from God.”

For our crimes are not justly ascribed to God, although it is beyond doubt that we are from him—that is, that our nature is from him. God certainly bestowed freedom of choice upon man, and by that freedom of choice man sinned. Is vice therefore to be attributed to God because he is the giver of free will, since he is most certainly believed to be the giver of free will?

Every nature, then, is from God; vice, however, is from nature, and nature is punished because of it. The same doctrine was once asserted by Caelestius, a disciple of Pelagius, who attributed so much to nature, in agreement with you, that he declared it untouched by every vice after sin, and had no fear of attributing whatever evil occurred solely to the will. Yet the Fathers answered him:

“Sin is not a vice of nature in the first man as God created it—as though it had been created in and with nature—but as nature was corrupted and tainted by its own will. How, then, can sin be said to belong to the will alone, when the will is not substance in itself? If nature does not exist in itself, it follows that, just as it cannot subsist by itself, so it cannot by itself will or perform anything good or evil.”

The will belongs to some nature; nature therefore wills either the good that comes from God or the evil that comes from itself. Sin is therefore the sin of a corrupted and depraved nature, which wills what the Creator forbade or what reason and uprightness discouraged. Nature is therefore rightly punished, since everything that is committed by its own will belongs to it.

Hence the Apostle admonishes us: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires. Nor present your members to sin as weapons of iniquity, but present yourselves to God as those alive from the dead, and your members as weapons of righteousness for God” [Romans 6:12–13].

And again: “We must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil” [2 Corinthians 5:10].

And again: “Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I therefore take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Far be it. Or do you not know that the one who joins himself to a prostitute becomes one body with her? For, he says, ‘the two will be one flesh’” [1 Corinthians 6:15–16].

And the Lord says through the Prophet: “The soul that sins shall itself die” [Ezekiel 18:4].

By this reasoning your syllogism is not very true but extremely false; not pious but impious; not full of charity and Catholic faith but entirely empty. It is therefore destroyed. You proposed it as follows:

**JOHN SCOTUS**

(Chapter 16, number 15, section 4.) “Every good is either God or has been made by God. Everything made by God makes no good defective. Therefore no good can make any good defective. And conversely: no defect of the good is from the good.

“Every sin, because it is evil, is a defect of the good. No defect of the good is from the good. Therefore every sin, because it is evil, cannot be from the good.

“Every rational creature is a great good. Evil is from no good. Therefore sin is from no rational creature.”

Long before this we placed the words of blessed Augustine by which your deceitful syllogism is exposed. He says [Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 13]:

“What is an evil human being except an evil nature, since man is nature? Moreover, if man is something good because he is nature, what is an evil man except an evil good? Yet when we distinguish these two, we find that he is not evil because he is man, nor good because he is unrighteous, but good because he is man and evil because he is unrighteous.”

And below [chapter 14]:

“These two opposites exist together in such a way that, if there were no good in which evil existed, evil could not exist at all. For it would have not only no place in which to subsist, but also no source from which corruption could arise, unless there were something to be corrupted; and unless that were good, it could not be corrupted, since corruption is nothing other than the destruction of good.

“Evil therefore arose from good, and unless it existed in some goods it would not exist; nor would there otherwise be anything from which any evil nature could arise. For if it existed, insofar as it was nature it would certainly be good. Either an incorruptible nature would be a great good, or a corruptible nature would not exist at all unless it were some good which corruption could injure by corrupting it” [chapter 15].

“But when we say that evils arose from goods, this must not be thought contrary to the Lord’s statement that ‘a good tree cannot bear evil fruits,’ and the rest. For, as the Truth says, ‘grapes cannot be gathered from thorns’ [Matthew 7:16, 18], because grapes cannot be born from thorns; but we see that vines and thorns can arise from good earth.

“In this way [variant: ‘And in the same way’], an evil will cannot produce good fruits—that is, good works—as a bad tree; but from the good nature of man a will can arise that is either good or evil. Nor could an evil will have arisen originally from anywhere except from the good nature of an angel and a human being.”

This judgment likewise nullifies what you had brought forward to prove your syllogism, saying:

**JOHN SCOTUS**

(Chapter 16, number 16, section 5.) “Hence the Truth itself says: ‘The good man brings good things out of the good treasure of his heart; the evil man brings evil things out of the evil treasure of his heart’ [Matthew 12:35]. It is as though he said:

“Everything good that the good man brings forth from his thought is bestowed from a good treasure—that is, from the one in whom ‘all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden’ [Colossians 2:3]. Everything evil that the evil man brings forth from his evil thought is from an evil treasure, namely pride, which is the beginning of every sin [Ecclesiasticus 10:13].”

**CORRECTION**

That heretics have always made a practice of twisting the upright meaning of Holy Scripture toward their own errors is abundantly demonstrated by all Catholic teachers, and especially by blessed Gregory in the books of the *Moralia*. You are convicted of having done this in the present case, not by exposition but by corruption.

For Christ did not say “from his thought,” but “from the treasure of his heart,” by which he intended to signify an abundant store of good thoughts and pious wills. Nor did he say “is given by God,” although this treasure receives from him alone whatever it can possess, but “brings forth.” The persons and the actions differ greatly from one another: to bring forth one thing is not the same as to bestow another thing.

Likewise, the treasure of the evil man is not comprised in a single thought, but in the tumult of many depraved thoughts. Nor is it stirred and brought forth from pride alone, but from the forces of many other vices.

Bede, in a homily on the Gospel:

“The treasure of the heart is the intention of the thought, from which the inner Judge assesses the outcome of the work. Hence it often happens that persons who perform lesser good works receive a greater reward of heavenly grace, because of the intention of the heart by which they wished to accomplish greater good works if they had been able; while others, displaying greater works of virtue, receive smaller rewards from the Lord because of the injury caused by a lukewarm heart.

“Finally, the work of the widow who gave two coins into the temple is preferred by the examiner of hearts to the innumerable gifts of the rich. For ‘the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart’ [Matthew 12:34]. Human judgment often fails, because it knows the heart of one’s neighbor only by weighing what comes from the mouth and the work; but God considers our very works and words from the root of the heart. Therefore the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart in the case of the person whose words it knows proceed from what intention.”

Leo, in Sermon 7 on the Fast of the Seventh Month:

“For what the Lord says is utterly true: ‘Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also’ [Matthew 6:21]. What, then, is a person’s treasure except a certain collection of his fruits and gathering of his labors? For whatever one sows, that one will also reap; and whatever one’s work is, such is one’s reward. Where the delight of enjoyment is established, there the concern of the heart is bound.

[“For the evil things which do not subsist by any nature of their own are not created by the Lord; but the Lord indicates that he creates evil when he reshapes things well created into a scourge for us who act badly. Thus the same things are evil for the guilty through the pain by which they strike, and good through the nature by which they exist. Hence poison is indeed death to a human being, yet it is life to a serpent.

“We withdrew from the love of our Creator through love of present things; and the perverse mind, while submitting itself to the pleasure of the creature, separated itself from the fellowship of the Creator. Therefore those things which the erring human being had placed above the Creator had to be struck by the Creator, so that from the very source by which the proud person did not fear to incur guilt, he might find punishment by which he would be corrected; and so that he might recover more quickly what he had lost, when he saw himself filled with the pain which he had sought.

Through guilt we became estranged from God; it is therefore fitting that through scourges we should return to his peace, so that, when each thing well created is turned for us into pain, the corrected mind may be humbly restored to peace with its Creator.

“Blessed Job therefore calls these scourges evil, because he considers the good of salvation and tranquility by the disturbance with which they strike.”]

f Concerning, however, the difficulties and sins which are called not only sins but also the punishments of sins, which occur especially in this intervening life, and concerning the fact that other punishments, whether present or future, are in no way excluded by these, there are extensive treatments by orthodox writers.

# SAINT PRUDENTIUS

Among them Saint Augustine, in Book V, chapter 3, *Against Julian the Heretical Pelagian*, spoke as follows:

[“You insert other words from my book, as I said: ‘the disobedience of the flesh was most justly repaid to the disobedient man, because it was unjust that his servant—that is, his body—should obey one who had not obeyed his own Lord.’ And you try to show that this disobedience of the flesh is rather worthy of praise if it is the punishment of the sinner. You adorn it with the pomp of speech as though it were some person who knowingly afflicts the sinner, as though it were an avenger of crime and, in this respect, a minister of God, as though that were some great good.

“You do not consider that in this way you could praise the wicked angels, who are nothing but transgressors and ungodly, yet through whom Holy Scripture testifies that God inflicts deserved punishments upon sinners, saying: ‘He sent upon them the wrath of his indignation, indignation and wrath and tribulation, the sending of evil angels’ (Psalm 77:49). Praise these also; praise their prince, Satan, because he too was an avenger of sin when the Apostle handed a man over to him for the destruction of the flesh (1 Corinthians 5:5).

“You are very well equipped against the grace of Christ, and fit to deliver a panegyric for Satan and his angels, through whom God is both judge and avenger of many sinners, repaying them according to their works, making those very worst and most damnable spirits the instruments of punishment for the condemned—he who uses both good and evil things well and justly.

“Therefore praise the most wicked powers, because through them evil things are repaid to the wicked; and for that reason praise the desire of the flesh, because disobedience was repaid to the sinner’s disobedience. Praise the wicked king Saul, because he too was the punishment of sinners, as the Lord says: ‘I gave you a king in my anger’ (Hosea 13:11). Praise the demon whom that king suffered, because this too was the punishment of a sinner.

“Praise the blindness of heart which happened in part to Israel; nor is Israel’s blindness passed over in silence, since it is said: ‘until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter’—unless perhaps you deny that this too was a punishment. If you loved the light of truth, you would proclaim it not merely some punishment but a very great punishment. For this blindness was to the Jews a great evil of unbelief [al. *at ista caecitas*, “but that blindness”] and a great cause of sin, so that they killed Christ.

“If you deny that this blindness was a punishment, you will judge that you too suffer a similar blindness by failing to acknowledge it. But if you maintain that it was indeed a punishment, though not the punishment of sin, you admit, for the moment, that one and the same thing can be both sin and punishment. If this is not so [al. *haec*, ‘this’], then the punishment is certainly unjust, and you make God unjust, at whose command or permission—or weak, because he did not avert it—it is inflicted upon an innocent person [al. *nocenti*, ‘a guilty person’].

“But if you also concede that it is the punishment of sin—lest, by refusing to concede this, you appear blind in heart yourself—see now what you did not wish to see: that the question you thought you had resolved has been settled. For, just as the devil and his angels, and wicked kings, are not only themselves sinners but, through God’s justice, also become the punishments of sinners, so they are not on that account worthy of praise, because a punishment is justly inflicted upon those who deserve it.

“Thus the law of the members, resisting the law of the mind (Romans 7:23), does not therefore act justly because the punishment of the one who acts unjustly is just. Likewise the blindness of heart, which God alone, the illuminator, removes, is both a sin, by which God is not believed; a punishment of sin, by which a proud heart is punished with deserved correction; and a cause of sin, because something is committed through the error of a blind heart [al. *cum mali aliquid*, ‘when some evil is committed’].

“In the same way, the desire of the flesh, against which the good spirit desires, is both a sin, because disobedience against the dominion of the mind exists in it; a punishment of sin, because it has been repaid to the merits of the disobedient; and a cause of sin, through the defection of one who consents or through the contagion of one who is born.

“Accordingly, whatever you said in support of this blind and inconsiderate opinion of yours—by which you thought that the desire of the flesh, precisely because we said it was the punishment of sin, was not only not to be blamed but even to be praised—however long you lingered over it in discussion has most certainly vanished.

“For when you said: ‘If lust is the punishment of sin, chastity must be rejected, lest chastity, as rebellion against God, be said to weaken the sentence imposed by him,’ the other arguments of this kind which you weave as consequences of, and connected with, this vanity are equally affected. The same thing can be said, in a similar manner [al. *simillimo*, “in a most similar manner”], about blindness of heart: ‘If blindness of heart is the punishment of sin, doctrine must be rejected, lest you rebel against God if the illumination of the mind is said to have been given by him.’

“But if it is utterly absurd to say this—although blindness of heart is the punishment of sin—then, in the same manner, it is utterly absurd to say what you yourself said, although lust—that is, the disobedience of the flesh—is the punishment of sin. For knowledge resists blindness, and continence resists lust. The punishment which is neither error nor lust must be endured with patience.

“Therefore, when by God’s gift one lives from true faith, God himself is present to illuminate the mind, overcome desire, and endure hardships. All this is rightly done when it is done for his sake—that is, when he himself is loved freely.

“Such love cannot exist in us except from him. Otherwise, when a person is greatly pleased with himself and trusts in his own virtue, if he is handed over to the desires of pride, this evil increases all the more as other desires yield to it and he suppresses them, as though they were praiseworthy, by indulging this one desire.

“Therefore, what you say you have read in my other works, and what you tried in vain to refute, namely, that there are some sins which are also punishments of sins, lay aside your desire to conquer and attend carefully; you will find it to be completely true, in accordance with what has been discussed concerning blindness of heart.

“For what have you accomplished, I ask, by recalling the apostolic testimony by which I proved what you read in another of my discussions? The Apostle wrote concerning certain people: ‘God handed them over to a reprobate mind, to do things that are not fitting’ (Romans 1:28). You wanted this to appear to be a hyperbolic statement—that is, one in which, in order to move the emotions, the speaker exceeds the truth of the matter. Show, then, where the Apostle did this.

[scan page 640]

# ON PREDESTINATION AGAINST JOHN SCOTUS

“When he was attacking,” you say, “the crimes of the ungodly, he aggravated them with the names of punishments, showing how much their shamefulness horrified his breast, the dwelling place of every virtue; he says that they seemed to him not so much guilty as condemned.”

On the contrary: just as he himself speaks—not as you make him speak—he showed them both condemned and guilty; not merely guilty because of past acts for which they were condemned, but also guilty in that for which [al. *unde etiam*, “whence also”] they were condemned. For he shows them guilty when he says: “They worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. Amen” (Romans 1:25). Then he shows them condemned because of this guilt, for he continues: “For this reason God handed them over to passions of dishonor” (ibid. 1:26).

You have heard the words “for this reason,” and you ask vainly how God’s handing them over is to be understood, laboring greatly to show that he handed them over by abandoning them. However he hands them over, it was “for this reason” that he handed them over; “for this reason” he abandoned them. And you see what followed from his handing them over, however and in whatever manner you understand it. The Apostle took care to say how great a punishment it is to be handed over by God to passions of dishonor, whether by abandonment or in some other way, explicable or inexplicable, by which the supremely good and ineffably just God does this.

“For their women,” he says, “exchanged the natural use for that use which is against nature; and likewise the men, abandoning the natural use of the woman, burned with desire for one another, men committing disgraceful acts with men and receiving in themselves the due recompense for their error” (ibid. 1:26–27). What could be more evident, more open, more explicit than this? He says that they received a mutual recompense—that is, that they were condemned—to do such evil things; and yet this condemnation is also a guilt by which they become more deeply entangled.

Thus these things are both sins and punishments of preceding sins. And what is more astonishing, he says that they had to receive this mutual recompense. The Apostle’s preceding words have the same force, the words you yourself quoted: “They exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, and four-footed animals, and serpents. Therefore God handed them over to the desires of their heart, to impurity,” and the other things that follow. Here too you see the cause for which they were handed over displayed without any ambiguity. He said what evil they had previously done and added: “For this reason God handed them over to the desires of their heart.”

Therefore this is a punishment of preceding sin, and yet it is itself also sin, as he explains in the words that follow. But in arguing against this, you think that you have resolved the question because the Apostle said that they were handed over to their desires. “They were already burning,” you say, “with the wicked desires of shameful acts” [al. *inquis*, “you say”]; and you add: “How, then, are they to be considered to have fallen into such acts through the power of the one handing them over?”

What more, I ask you, was done? Or what would he have said by saying, “God handed them over to the desires of their heart,” if they were already, in some manner, possessed by the evil desires of their heart?

Is it necessarily the case that, if someone has evil desires of the heart, he already consents to committing the corresponding evils? Therefore, having evil desires of the heart is one thing, and being handed over to them another. A person is handed over to them so that, by consenting, he may be possessed by them; this happens when he is handed over to them by divine judgment.

Otherwise the saying would be pointless: “Do not go after your desires” (Sirach 18:30), if everyone were already guilty merely because he feels desires that are in turmoil and strive to draw him toward evil, yet does not follow them because he has not been handed over to them, waging glorious battles against them if he lives in grace.

What do you think of the person who observes what is written: “If you give your soul over to its desires” —and what else are these than its evil desires?—“it will make you a joy to your enemies and to those who envy you” (ibid. 18:31). Is this person already guilty merely because he has such desires of the soul, to which he ought not to give himself lest he become a joy to the devil and his angels, who are our enemies and our envious adversaries?

Therefore, when a person is said to be handed over to his desires, he becomes guilty because, abandoned by God, he yields to them, consents to them, is conquered, captured, and possessed by them. “For by whatever anyone is overcome, to that he is enslaved” (2 Peter 2:19). Thus the consequent sin is the punishment of the preceding sin.

Is it not both sin and the punishment of sin where it is written: “The Lord mixed into them a spirit of error, and they led Egypt astray in all its works, as a drunkard is led astray” (Isaiah 19:14)? Is it not both sin and the punishment of sin where the prophet says to God: “Why have you made us err, Lord, from your ways? You have hardened our hearts, so that we would not fear you” (Isaiah 63:17)?

Is it not both sin and the punishment of sin where it is again said to God: “Behold, you were angry, and we sinned; therefore we went astray and became all like the unclean” (Isaiah 64:5–6)?

Is it not both sin and the punishment of sin where it is written concerning the nations whom Jesus son of Naveh defeated: “For it was done by the Lord that their hearts were strengthened, so that they might go out to battle against Israel, in order that they might be destroyed” (Joshua 11:20)?

Is it not both sin and the punishment of sin that King Rehoboam did not listen to the people who gave him good counsel? For, as Scripture says: “The turning was from the Lord, so that he might establish his word which he had spoken through Ahijah the prophet” (1 Kings 12:15).

Is it not both sin and the punishment of sin in the case of Amaziah, king of Judah, who refused to listen to Joash, king of Israel, when he gave him good counsel not to go out to battle? For it is written: “Amaziah did not listen, because it was from God that he should be handed over into the hands of the enemies, since they had sought the gods of Edom” (2 Chronicles 25:20).

We can recall many other examples in which it plainly appears that, by God’s hidden judgment, perversity of heart occurs, so that what is true is not heard; sin then follows, and the sin itself becomes also the punishment of a preceding sin.

To believe a lie and not to believe the truth is certainly sin; yet it comes from that blindness of heart which, by God’s hidden but just judgment, is also shown to be the punishment of sin. Consider also what the Apostle writes to the Thessalonians: “Because they did not receive the love of the truth, so that they might be saved, therefore God will send them an operation of error, so that they may believe the lie” (2 Thessalonians 2:10–11).

[scan page 641]

# SAINT PRUDENTIUS

Here the punishment of sin is plainly sin itself. Both points are clear; the statement is brief and explicit; and it was spoken by the one whose other words you have attempted in vain to twist to your position.

But what do you mean when you say that, when people are said to be handed over to their desires, they are to be understood as abandoned by divine power, not compelled into sins by power—as though the same Apostle had not placed [al. *posuerit*, “had placed”] both patience and power together when he says: “What if God, wishing to show his wrath and make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction” (Romans 9:22)?

Which of these do you say applies to what is written: “And if a prophet should err and speak a word, I, the Lord, have deceived that prophet, and I will stretch out my hand against him and destroy him from the midst of my people Israel”? Is this patience or power? Say whichever you prefer, or confess both. You nevertheless see that the prophet’s sin is falsehood and that it is also the punishment of sin.

Or will you say that the words, “I, the Lord, have deceived that prophet,” are to be understood as “I abandoned him,” so that he was deceived and erred according to his merits [al. *ejus*, “his merits”]? Have it as you wish; nevertheless, in that very manner he was punished for his sin, so that by prophesying falsely he sinned.

But consider what the prophet Micaiah saw: the Lord sitting upon his throne, while all the army of heaven stood around him, on his right and on his left. And the Lord said: “Who will deceive Ahab, king of Israel, so that he may go up and fall [al. *ascendet et cadet*, “he will go up and fall”] at Ramoth-gilead?” One said one thing and another another. Then a spirit came forth, stood before the Lord, and said: “I will deceive him.” And the Lord said to him: “How?” He replied: “I will go forth and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.” And he said: “You shall deceive him, and you shall prevail; go forth and do so” (1 Kings 22:20–22).

What will you say to this? Certainly the king himself sinned by believing the false prophets. Yet this very thing was also the punishment of sin: God indicated it and sent the evil angel, so that we might understand more clearly how the Psalm says that he sent “the wrath of his indignation through evil angels” (Psalm 77:49).

But was he mistaken? Did he judge or act unjustly or rashly in anything? Far from it. It was not said to him without reason: “Your judgments are like a great abyss” (Psalm 35:7). Nor did the Apostle say without reason: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and inscrutable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, so that it might be repaid to him?” (Romans 11:33–35).

He chose no one who was worthy; rather, by choosing, he made the chosen person worthy. Yet he punishes no one unworthily [al. *indignum*, “no unworthy person”].

“You say,” you object, “the Apostle says: ‘The goodness of God leads you to repentance’ (Romans 2:4).” That is certainly true; but he leads the one whom he predestined, although that person himself, “according to the hardness and impenitence of his heart” (so far as he himself is concerned), stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s just judgment, “who will repay each according to his works” (ibid. 2:5–6). However much patience he may show [*quantumlibet*; al. *quantamlibet*, “however much”], unless he himself gives repentance, who has it [*habet*; al. *agit*, “acts”]?

Have you forgotten that the same teacher says: “Perhaps God may give them repentance for the recognition of the truth, and they may recover from the snare of the devil” (2 Timothy 2:25–26)? Yet his judgments are a great abyss (Psalm 35:7).

Certainly, if we allow people over whom we have authority to perpetrate crimes before our eyes, we shall be guilty along with them. But how innumerable are the things he permits to occur before his eyes—things which, if he did not wish them, he would in no way permit—and yet he is just and good. By showing patience, he gives a place for repentance, “not wishing anyone to perish” (2 Peter 3:9). “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2:19).

“And he works all things together for good” [*cooperatur*; al. *cooperantur*, “all things work together”] “for those who are called according to his purpose” (Romans 8:28). For not all who are called are called according to his purpose. “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 22:14). Those, therefore, who are chosen are called according to his purpose.

Hence elsewhere he says: “According to the power of God who saves us, and calls us with his holy calling, not according to our works but according to his purpose and the grace which was given to us in Christ Jesus before eternal ages” (2 Timothy 1:8–9).

Finally, after saying, “All things work together for good for those who are called according to his purpose,” he immediately adds: “For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Romans 8:28–30). These are the ones called according to his purpose (Ephesians 1:11); they are the chosen, chosen before the foundation of the world by him who calls things that are not as though they were (Romans 4:17).

They are chosen through the election of grace. Hence the same teacher says concerning Israel: “The remnant has been saved through the election of grace” (Romans 11:5). And lest they be thought to have been chosen before the foundation of the world on the basis of foreknown works, he continued and added: “But if it is by grace, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace” (ibid. 11:6).

From this number of the elect and predestined, even those who have led the worst lives are brought by God’s kindness to repentance. Through his patience they have not been removed from this life while perpetrating their crimes, so that it may be shown both to them and to their fellow heirs from how deep an evil God’s grace can liberate. None of these perishes, at whatever age he dies [*moriantur*; al. *moriatur*, “he may die”].

Far be it from us to suppose that one predestined to life is permitted to end this life without the sacrament of the Mediator. For their sake the Lord says: “This is the will of the Father who sent me: that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me” (John 6:39).

But the mortals who are not from this number are from the same mass from which these also come, yet they have been made “vessels of wrath” (Romans 9:22–23), and are born for the benefit of the others. God does not create any of them rashly or by chance, nor is he ignorant of what good he works through them, since he also works this very good: that he creates human nature in them and adorns the order of the present age through them.

[scan page 642]

# ON PREDESTINATION AGAINST JOHN SCOTUS

He brings none of these to salutary and spiritual repentance, by which a person is reconciled to God in Christ, whether he grants them greater patience or no less patience. Although all, from the same mass of perdition and condemnation, “according to the hardness of their heart and impenitent heart” (so far as they themselves are concerned) “store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath, when he will repay each according to his works” (Romans 2:5–6), God nevertheless brings some of them to repentance through merciful goodness, while by just judgment he does not bring others. For he has the power to lead and draw, as the Lord himself says: “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44).

Did he bring Ahab, the sacrilegious and ungodly king, to repentance? Or did he at least grant patience and long-suffering through the lying spirit to one who had already been deceived and led astray? (1 Kings 22:20.) Was not the matter for which he had been deceived immediately completed in him when death carried him away? (ibid. 22:34.)

Who would say that he did not sin by believing the lying spirit? Who would say that this sin was not the punishment of a sin, proceeding from the judgment of God, by which he either sent or permitted the lying spirit? Whoever says any one of these things does so only because he says what he wants and does not want to hear what is true.

Who, being of sound mind, would be so foolish as to hear what is sung in the Psalm—“Do not hand me over, Lord, to the desire of my sinner” (Psalm 140:9)—and say that a person asks this lest God be patient toward him, if God does not hand him over so that evils may be done unless he shows patience and goodness when they are done?

What else do we say daily when we pray, “Do not lead us into temptation” (Matthew 6:13), except that we may not be handed over to our desires? “Each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire” (James 1:14).

Or do we perhaps ask God by this prayer not to show us his patient goodness? Then we are not invoking his mercy but rather provoking his anger. Who could understand such a thing while sane? Indeed, who, even if mad, could say it?

God therefore hands people over to passions of dishonor, so that they do what is not fitting (Romans 1:26). But he hands them over fittingly; and the same acts become both sins, punishments for past sins, and merits of future punishments.

Thus he handed Ahab over to the falsehood of the false prophets (1 Kings 22:20). Thus he handed Rehoboam over to false counsel (1 Kings 12:15). He does these things in marvelous and ineffable ways—he who knows how to operate his just judgments not only in human bodies but also in human hearts. He does not make evil wills, but uses them as he wills, since he cannot will anything unjust.

[“What God graciously grants in accordance with human wishes, or refuses in anger; and again, what he grants in anger, or does not grant graciously; and again, what he graciously does contrary to human wishes, and what he does not do in anger: in all these things he remains good and just.”]

He hears graciously, and does not hear in anger; again, he does not hear graciously, and hears in anger; he spares graciously, and does not spare in anger; again, he does not spare graciously, and spares in anger. In all these things he remains good and just.

*This was omitted by the Louvain editors, as though it did not belong in the text.*

“But who is sufficient for these things?” (2 Corinthians 2:16)—who, that is, is sufficient to examine and investigate these judgments of his? “Who is sufficient to investigate them?” (Wisdom 9:13), when the corruptible body weighs him down, even if he already possesses the pledge of the Holy Spirit?

Yet you, an intelligent and sharp-minded person, say that lust is just and should be proclaimed with praise, because by refusing to obey him it punished the man who did not obey God. If you were wise here in a prudent manner, you would certainly see that there is an injustice by which the lower part of a person resists the higher and better part—and yet that this unjust thing is justly punished by the injustice of the flesh, just as the unjust king was punished by the injustice of the evil spirit.

Do you intend to praise the evil spirit himself as well? Why do you delay? It is fitting that you, an enemy of the goodness of God’s grace, should be a praiser of the lying spirit. Nor will you have difficulty finding what to say: you have your praises ready.

If you transfer to him the very words that you set down in praise of lust, as though they followed from my statement—“For it was unjust that his servant, that is, his body, should obey one who had not obeyed his Lord”—then, by denying this and ridiculing it as false, you seemed to wish to show what absurdity would follow, as though, if this is so, you were praising lust as the avenger of sin [al. “praising lust”].

Certainly you do not deny that this lying spirit was an avenger of iniquity, since by deceiving the ungodly king as he deserved, he drew him to death (1 Kings 22:21).

Here too I say: “For it was unjust that one who had not believed in the true God should not be deceived by the false one.” Praise, therefore, the justice of this falsehood also, and say—as you said in praise of lust—that nothing can be judged more praiseworthy if, through great iniquity [al. “many iniquities”], it avenged an injury against God.

And since it did not share in sin in such a way that it assumed the office of avenger, all these things are correctly said according to your most acute reasoning, and in praise of that unclean spirit. Therefore, in a similar case, either give the panegyric of your praise to the lying spirit or take it away from rebellious lust.

Why do you flee to that most obscure question concerning the soul in paradise? Elevation began in the mind, and from there came consent to transgress the commandment, because the serpent said: “You shall be like gods” (Genesis 3:5). But the whole human being committed that sin; then the flesh became the flesh of sin, whose vices are healed only through the likeness of sinful flesh.

Therefore, if both soul and flesh are to be punished equally on both sides—unless what is born is corrected by being reborn—then either both are drawn in a corrupted state from the human being, or one is corrupted in the other as in a corrupted vessel, under the hidden justice of the divine law.

Which of these is true I prefer to learn rather than to state, lest I dare to teach what I do not know. This, however, I know: one of these alternatives is true in such a way that the ancient and true Catholic faith—which believes and asserts original sin—has not proved it false.

This faith must not be denied; and this matter concerning the soul … [text ends here].
