### S. PRUDENTIUS, BISHOP OF TROYES

…or—as with many other things in this life—it is unknown without injury to salvation. For it is more important to consider, whether in children or in adults, by what aid the soul may be healed than by what merit it has been corrupted; yet if its corruption is denied, it will not be healed.

I could not devise why you said this concerning what you recalled the Apostle to have said: “Their foolish heart was darkened” [variant: “was filled with darkness”] (Romans 1:21). For you added that it should be noted that he calls foolishness the cause of all evils. It is not sufficiently certain that the Apostle said this, but I do not argue the point. Rather, I ask why you said it. Is it perhaps because children are not properly called foolish, since they cannot yet share in wisdom? Therefore you want it believed that no evil is present in them, which you consider to follow if foolishness is the cause of all evils.

But if the question of whether the first human beings were made proud by foolishness or foolish by pride requires the most subtle and polished discussion, then, as regards what is now at issue between us, who does not know that all human beings who become wise become so from foolishness—unless perhaps some, through the heralds of the Mediator, by his great and altogether extraordinary grace, have been able to pass to wisdom not from foolishness but from infancy?

If you contend that this can happen by nature without faith in the Mediator, you reveal the hidden poison of your heresy. For it is clear that you are doing nothing else by such a vigorous defense and praise of nature than making Christ’s death gratuitous (Galatians 2:21). We say that faith in him, which works through love (Galatians 5:6), also comes to the aid of those who are foolish by nature.

There are indeed some who are born with such dullness of heart that they seem more like cattle than human beings. You cannot call the great stupidity that naturally appears in them any merit, since you deny the existence of original sin. Who, moreover, does not prove daily—human affairs themselves bearing witness—that a child at first knows nothing, then, as it grows, knows worthless things, and afterward, if it belongs to the company of the wise, knows what is right, and thus passes from infancy to wisdom by way of an intermediate foolishness?

Therefore human nature, which lies in infants, is something from which you envy the Savior his praise, as though it were sound. You see that it first produces the fruit of foolishness rather than of wisdom, yet you do not wish to see the defect of its root—or, worse, you see it and deny it.]

If your obstinacy has not closed the ears of your understanding and truth, you can clearly see that you have undertaken a most futile labor, worn yourself out to no purpose, and sweated in vain in order to say that God arranged, for the exercise of our understanding, both in his Scriptures and in their interpreters, that when we hear such modes of expression our attention should be awakened to understand what mystery lies hidden in them, not what the simple surface of the words displays. In other words, we are supposedly to understand “God foreknew” and “God predestined” as “God did not foreknow” and “God did not predestine.”

Behold, the outstanding teacher, acting against you under the name of Julian, once every trick of such expressions had been removed, has taught what the simple surface of the words displays, and has asserted that it is not some mystical fiction that is being stated.

For he has made it abundantly clear that, for those living in this mortal life and voluntarily defiling themselves with sin, the just judgment of God repays the penalty of another sin—whether one sin or several—and that, blinded by these sins, they are rightly led into the abyss owed to them. Yet this does not exclude the penalties by which both soul and body are punished, either temporally here or eternally there.

Accordingly, the judgment of Saint Augustine from Psalm 7, which you employ as a support for your error, as you suppose, favors the truth rather than agreeing with falsehood. For he says (Augustine, on Psalm 7, near the end):

> “Let us understand that each person is punished because of his own sin, and that his iniquity is turned into punishment. Let us not suppose that God’s tranquility and ineffable light bring forth from themselves that by which sins are punished; rather, let us understand that he orders the sins themselves in such a way that what had been pleasures to the sinful human being become instruments to the Lord when he punishes.”

### JOHN SCOTUS  
*(Chapter 16, number 18, section 6)*

Beautifully and excellently defining that there are no other instruments for torturing impiety besides that very impiety…

### CORRECTION

Yet by saying this you endeavor to exclude even the punishment of eternal fire. If no one will burn in it, I confess that I utterly do not know why it was prepared for the devil and his angels (Matthew 25:41), or why impious human beings will be sent into it.

But lest you flatter yourself with the foregoing sentence of Augustine—which by itself would have been sufficient—let us set beside it another of his statements that refutes your impiety. For in his book *On Faith and Works* (chapter 15) he says:

> “Nor will this avail here [variant: ‘nor can this be said here’], as some deceive themselves by saying: ‘Eternal fire’ is spoken of, not ‘eternal punishment’ [variant: ‘burning’]. For they suppose that those to whom salvation is promised through dead faith will pass through the fire, which will be eternal, while their burning—that is, the effect of the fire—will not be eternal in them. But the Lord, foreseeing this as Lord, concluded his sentence in this way: ‘Thus they will go into eternal burning, but the righteous into eternal life’ (Matthew 25:46). Therefore the burning will be eternal, just as the fire is, and Truth says that those will go into it whose faith, not their good works, he declared to have been absent.”

Compare the statements of this Father, and either show that he is free of contradiction, if he did not say things contrary to himself, or accuse him of falsehood if you establish that he spoke otherwise. Therefore, lest anyone deceitfully pretend that he set mutually contradictory statements beside one another, let us say that each person is punished because of his own sin and that his iniquity is turned into punishment. For, according to what we have set out more fully above from his words, the sinner is handed over, because of preceding sins, to worse ones, by whose merit he is brought to destruction; or, after this life, he is confined by the merit of his perverse acts in perpetual torments.

## [scan page 644]

### On Predestination

### 1273

Let this be what it means for his iniquity to be turned into punishment: he is assigned punishments by the merit of his iniquity. Let the sins be called instruments of the Lord when he punishes, because by their means he repays just punishments to the one who has deserved them. Or certainly, because perpetual punishments are inflicted equally upon souls and bodies, let the sins themselves also be the punishments of souls, so that they may be tormented by the continual memory and fruitless repentance of them, while the eternal fire and burning are in no way removed from the bodies.

For it is not at all necessary that God’s tranquility and ineffable light produce from themselves—that is, from their own substance—a sword, fire, water, or anything of that sort by which sins may be punished. Rather, through the sins themselves he orders punishments in such a way that by them—as we have said—he punishes the obstinate.

Thus, when you had discoursed at excessive length and finally concluded:

### JOHN SCOTUS  
*(Chapter 16, number 19, section 7)*

> “Meritedly,” he says, “the pernicious sweetness of lust here will there be turned into the bitterness of vengeance. For because here he had wickedly wished to turn into uses of shameful pleasure the gift of divine generosity—that is, free choice of the will, which is the gift of natural understanding, namely the mind’s acuity, which the Creator generally bestowed upon all for seeking, loving, and enjoying him—there he will most justly lose the ability to enjoy the dignity of truth at all. He will not escape, either inexorably or as punishment, the darkness of eternal ignorance in that prison of his own iniquity into which he had here shut himself.”

### CORRECTION

I am astonished that, forgetting yourself, you do not see what you said at the beginning of this passage: that the concept, knowledge, and truth of happiness exist there among the wretched, and consequently that misery is absent from them, so that, since nature would not be punished, unpunished misery would not exist.

For how will happiness, and knowledge and awareness of it, exist in them if they have lost the acuity of their minds and have not escaped, inexorably and as punishment, the darkness of eternal ignorance?

Either happiness and knowledge of it will be lacking there, and what you said will stand—that they lose the acuity of their minds and do not escape, inexorably and as punishment, the darkness of eternal ignorance—or, if happiness and knowledge of it are present in them, they will neither lose the acuity of their minds nor suffer, inexorably and as punishment, the darkness of eternal ignorance.

But because every happiness will be taken away from the unhappy, it is true that they will endure, inexorably and as punishment, the darkness of eternal ignorance—yet in such a way that they will not escape the bodily burning of eternal fire.

As for the statements of the Fathers Augustine and Gregory that you introduced in support of your heresy, in which they truly taught the blindness of the heart and the imprisonment of sin, in order to exclude by them the punishments of retribution: anyone who attends carefully will see, in light of their earlier statements, that they by no means removed the torments physically inflicted upon bodies, but faithfully indicated the punishments that, by God’s just judgment, are meanwhile ordinarily imposed here upon blinded minds.

### Against John Scotus

### 1274

Augustine, in his book *On True Religion*—not as you maliciously presented it, but as it is found most sincerely in that book—is recognized to have treated this matter.

Finally, by abstaining from those things without which this life can be conducted, they also experience bodily rest.
>

>

Complete health, no deprivation, and no weariness will be present in the body, because this corruptible body will at its proper time and in its proper order, when the resurrection of the flesh takes place, put on incorruption (1 Corinthians 15:53).
>
> “It is not surprising that this will be given to those who love only truth in their knowledge, only peace in their actions, and only health in their bodies. For what will be perfected in them after this life is what they love more greatly in this life.”

Those, therefore, who misuse so great a good of the mind by desiring visible things outside it more than they desire the intelligible things for which they ought to have been reminded, will be given outer darkness. For the beginning of this darkness is the wisdom of the flesh and the weakness of the bodily senses. Those who delight in conflicts will be separated from peace and entangled in the greatest difficulties, for war and contention are the beginning of the greatest difficulty.

I think this is signified by the fact that their hands and feet are bound (Matthew 22:13): that is, every facility for action is taken away. Those who wish to thirst and hunger, burn with lust, and grow weary so that they may gladly eat, drink, have intercourse, and sleep love deprivation, which is the beginning of the greatest pains.

Therefore what they love will be brought to perfection, so that there will be “weeping and gnashing of teeth” for them (Matthew 13:50). For there are many who love all these vices together, whose life consists in watching, contending, eating, drinking, having intercourse, sleeping, and embracing in their thoughts nothing except the phantasms they gather from such a life. From their deceit they establish rules of superstition or impiety by which they are deceived and to which they cling, even if they try to abstain from the enticements of the flesh.

For they do not use well the talent entrusted to them—that is, the acuity of the mind by which all those who are called learned, cultured, or witty seem to excel. Rather, they have it bound in a napkin [variant: tied up] or buried in the earth—that is, wrapped up and weighed down by delicate and superfluous things or by earthly desires.

“Therefore their hands and feet will be bound, and they will be cast into outer darkness. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 22:13), not because they loved these things—for who would love that?—but because the things they loved are the beginnings of these punishments and necessarily lead those who love them to them.

For those who love going more than returning or arriving must be sent farther away, because they are flesh, “a wandering spirit and not returning” (Psalm 77:39).

But those who use even the five bodily senses well, for believing and proclaiming God’s works and nourishing love of him through action and knowledge, for pacifying their nature and knowing God, enter into the joy of their Lord.

Therefore the talent that is taken away from the one who uses it badly is given to the one who used five talents well (Matthew 25:29). This does not mean that the acuity of understanding can be transferred; rather, it signifies that those who are negligent and impious, though ingenious, can lose it, while those who love to reach it and are pious, though slower in intellect, can possess it.

For that talent was not given to the one who had received two—for he too possesses it, since he already lives well in action and knowledge—but to the one who had received five. The one who believes only in visible things, that is, temporal things, does not yet possess an acuity of mind suitable for contemplating eternal things. He may possess it if he praises God, the maker of all these sensible things, and commends him by faith, beholds him in hope, and seeks him in love.

Gregory, in Book 11 of the *Moralia*, chapter 5:

The blessed Gregory most clearly explained, by the statement prefixed above, that this imprisonment, by which sinners are usually blinded in this life, does not signify the punishment of Gehenna. The circumstances of that statement unmistakably demonstrate this. I have therefore decided to add its conclusion, so that it may be evident what he understood in the preceding statement.

## [scan page 647]

### S. PRUDENTIUS

### 1279

The theft that proceeded from covetousness and produced perjury therefore became sin and the punishment of sin: it was punishment for the preceding sin and the cause of the subsequent sin, because it was born from the former and gave birth to the latter.

The Apostle Paul aptly indicates this concerning certain people who understood God but did not honor him, saying:

> “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their reasoning” (Romans 1:21).

Here there is sin and the cause of sin. He adds what followed from that cause:

> “And their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools. And they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, and four-footed animals, and reptiles” (Romans 1:21–23).

Here there is sin and the punishment of sin. But it would be merely sin and the punishment of sin if another sin did not also follow from it. For after their unbelief he adds:

> “Therefore God handed them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they dishonored their bodies among themselves” (Romans 1:24).

Since, therefore, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God (Romans 1:21), from that sin—which was also the cause of sin—they were led on to fall into the worship of serpents and birds. But because through this blindness they also fell into impurity and the dishonor of the flesh, the blindness of their unbelief is both sin and the punishment of sin in relation to their earlier understanding; in relation to the subsequent impurity, it became sin and the cause of sin.

But because these matters have been treated at length in the *Moral Works*, we need not linger over them any longer now.

We must consider with trembling how the just and omnipotent God, when he is angry at preceding sins, permits the blinded mind to fall into others. Hence Moses says: “The sins of the Amorites have not yet been completed” (Genesis 15:16). David also says:

> “Add iniquity upon their iniquity, so that they may not enter into your righteousness” (Psalm 69:28).

The prophet likewise says:

> “Cursing, lying, murder, theft, and adultery have overflowed, and blood has touched blood” (Hosea 4:2).

Blood touches blood when sin is added to sin, so that, as iniquities are joined together, the soul is stained before God’s eyes.

The Apostle Paul says:

> “So that they may always fill up their sins” (1 Thessalonians 2:16).

It is also said to John through the angel:

> “Let the one who does harm continue to do harm, and let the one who is filthy continue to be filthy” (Revelation 22:11).

Hence the Lord also says:

> “If the righteous person turns from his righteousness and commits iniquity, I will place a stumbling block before him” (Ezekiel 3:20).

It is as though he openly said: Because he was unwilling, through repentance, to see where he had already stumbled, I will justly abandon him and place before him something over which he will stumble elsewhere as well.

Yet for the Lord to place this does not mean that he presses anyone toward sin, but that he is unwilling to free him from sin, just as it is said concerning Pharaoh: “I will harden his heart” (Exodus 4:21). For the Lord does not harden the heart of the sinner; he is said to harden it when he does not free it from hardness.

In his mercy God grants us time for repentance. But when we turn the patience of his grace into an increase of guilt, he turns that very time, which he mercifully ordained for sparing us, into a stricter occasion for punishment. Thus, when someone is unwilling to return even after receiving a period of time, he increases his guilt through the very means by which he could have wiped it away, had he wished to turn back.

Hence it is written:

> “Do you not know that the kindness of God leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the just judgment of God” (Romans 2:4–5).

The reprobate therefore stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath from the kindness of almighty God, because, while time is granted for repentance, it is used for sinning, and he turns the very remedy of grace into an increase of guilt.

Thus almighty God, seeing that the remedies bestowed are drawn into an increase of guilt, turns the very kindness he bestowed into the strictness of judgment, so that he may strike more severely by that very means [variant: afterward] by which he now waits more patiently. And because the human being does not wish to abandon evil in order to live, he increases the means by which he will die.

But whether the righteous person falls into guilt or the sinner into death, the watchman must fear lest the guilt of sinners involve him also because of his silence.]

If, with the affection of true piety, you eagerly devote yourself to Christian humility, then, with no difficulty standing in the way, you can see most plainly that the imprisonment explained by blessed Gregory from the words of blessed Job does not signify the punishment of Gehenna, but the punishment by which the reprobate, fatally favoring their pleasures in this mortal life, are struck by the just judgment of God.

Nevertheless, as a Christian, I admonish you not to cling so tenaciously to the words of blessed Augustine—which in his many little works he appears to have understood in different ways concerning the punishments of the impious—that you contradict the truth so greatly.

That holy and learned man wrote many things in the earlier periods of his conversion that he later judged necessarily needed to be retracted. By a special gift granted from heaven, he retracted many things, and in later works he examined and discussed certain matters more truthfully. Death prevented him from retracting many others, leaving them behind.

Therefore any intelligent and pious person will judge most soundly that whatever he either retracted or later investigated and wrote with greater refinement and consequently greater truth is to be followed and revered and held with pious love.

Yet he never so affirmed the punishments of the heart as to deny those of the body. As he thought appropriate, he treated both together or each separately, as in Book 3 of *On Free Choice of the Will*, chapter 20, where he briefly and clearly says:

> “But in order that we may be born from that first union both in ignorance and in difficulty, and in mortality…”

**Against John Scotus**

**CONTRA J. SCOTUM**  
**Against John Scotus**

It is little for us to say, “God makes these things; God gives these things”; but he alone makes them, he alone gives them. What then? Does God make these things, but does someone who is not God also make them? He makes these things, and he alone makes them; and it is without reason that these things are sought either from human beings or from demons. Whatever good the enemies of God receive, they receive from him; and when they seek and receive them from others, they receive them from him without knowing it. In the same way, when they are punished and think that they are being punished by others, they are punished by him without knowing it. So too when they are strengthened, filled, saved, or liberated. And if, without knowing this, they attribute it either to human beings, demons, or angels, they have it from none but him in whose power all things are.

### Chapter XVII

**Why God is said to have predestined punishments, although he neither makes nor predestines them**

The seventeenth of your propositions has the title:

**John Scotus**  
*(Chapter 17, no. 1.)*

Why God is said to have predestined punishments, although he neither makes nor predestines them: by the reasoning and authority through which the matter is firmly established, it must be held most certainly that God is in no way the author, in no way the maker, and in no way the predestiner of the punishments by which proud impiety will be tortured with eternal suffering.

### Correction

It has been sufficiently demonstrated, both by the authority of sacred Scripture and by the agreement of the teachers, that God is the author and predestiner of punishments, whether temporal or eternal. But because you whisper that the punishments of sinners are nothing other than sins, we certainly do not call God the author of sins. Nevertheless, whenever sins are converted here or hereafter into punishment for their authors, we proclaim that this occurs only through God’s vengeance, in accordance with what the preceding discussion has abundantly explained.

**John Scotus**  
*(Chapter 17.)*

Yet, you say, he is called their author, maker, and predestiner in the same sense in which he is most truly believed to be the author and governor of the whole universe. For, before creating his entire creation, he predestined its future state of beauty in such a way that the ugliness of evils—which he did not predestine, since he would not make it—would not be ugly in the universe; the wickedness of those who harm would not harm; the error of those who err would not err; and the misery of those who are tormented would not disturb the happiness of the elect. For no ugliness, wickedness, error, or misery is permitted to dishonor the natural order predestined before the ages.

### Correction

If God is called the maker and predestiner of punishments in the sense in which he is most truly believed to be the maker and governor of the whole universe, then he must truly be called the maker and predestiner of those punishments, since he is truly regarded as the maker and governor of the universe. But because you maintain that punishments are nothing other than sins, there is no need for us to linger here any longer, since the preceding discussions clearly show that the matter has been thoroughly treated. And you add:

**John Scotus**  
*(Chapter 17, no. 3, section 2.)*

When, therefore, we hear that “God predestined them either to destruction, punishment, penalties, or torture”—whatever name may be given to the misery by which iniquity is tormented by itself, in itself, and through itself—we are commanded to understand nothing other than that before the ages he foresaw and predestined the order in which those persons would exist who, by his most hidden yet most just judgment, he permitted to feel the bitterness of their sins, because he left them in their damnable origin.

### Correction

Although you put forward statements that are different and opposed to one another—having asserted the predestined as though they were not predestined—you nevertheless bring much that belongs to the truth of predestination into agreement with yourself, apart from those things which you insert contrary to the truth. For the truth itself proclaims that God ordained the order in which those would exist who, by his most just judgment, would feel the bitterness of their sins—not, as you falsely say, by “permitting” it, but, as is true, by judging it, and by judging it compelling them. Nor is the only punishment inflicted upon them that he left them in a damnable origin, as you say; the punishment of eternal fire has also been assigned to them, so that they may be tormented against their will.

**John Scotus**  
*(Chapter 17, no. 4, section 2.)*

You assert that there is a very well-known difference between foreknowledge and predestination: although predestination extends as widely as foreknowledge—for both signify one and the same divine substance—predestination applies only to things that are good, whereas foreknowledge applies to both good and evil. Yet this difference does not arise from nature but from the use of the expressions. Just as it is said of God, “He is present everywhere,” but he does not dwell everywhere by the grace of habitation, so it may be said of him: “He is everywhere by foreknowledge, but not everywhere by predestination.” Yet the truth most clearly proclaims of God: wherever God is present, there he is certainly by habitation; likewise, wherever there is foreknowledge, there necessarily is predestination.

### Correction

Without doubt, what you say is false, as we have abundantly shown above. First, God’s predestination and foreknowledge are not his substance, since they are relational terms, which do not disclose his essence. Furthermore, foreknowledge and predestination differ from one another to such an extent that God’s foreknowledge is also spoken of with respect to those things which he did not make, such as sins; whereas predestination concerns only those things which he was going to make, whether in the constitution and ordering of things, in the election of grace, or in the condemnation of an inflexible—yet never unjust—judgment.

Accordingly, just as it is rightly said of God, “He is everywhere present by his power, but he is not everywhere by the grace of habitation,” so it may rightly be said of him: “He is everywhere by foreknowledge, but not everywhere by predestination.” For he who foresaw all things, both good and evil—that is, sins—predestined only good things: mercy and judgment, in which there are also punishments that are called evil by those who experience them, although they occur with no author whatsoever except him.

Finally, when you say that the truth proclaims of God that wherever there is foreknowledge there is habitation, and therefore that wherever there is foreknowledge there is necessarily predestination, you so transgress the rule of truth and piety that you do not hesitate to contradict the clearest testimonies of the divine oracles. The Truth itself says:

“If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23).

And again:

“I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, so that he may remain with you forever: the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it does not see him or know him. But you will know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you” [John 16:17].

Hence the Book of Wisdom also says:

“For wisdom will not enter into a malevolent soul, nor will it dwell in a body subjected to sins” (Wisdom 1:4).

And the Apostle:

“You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit—if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. And if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. 8:9, 11).

And again:

“Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership has righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what share has a believer with an unbeliever? And what agreement has the temple of God with idols? For you are the temple of the living God, as God said: ‘I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be my people’” (2 Cor. 6:14–16).

And again:

“Do you not know that your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God?” (1 Cor. 6:19).

From all these passages it is clear that God inhabits none but his temple, and that his temple is nothing other than the members of Christ, as the same Apostle says:

“Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?” [ibid., 15].

This is what the truth proclaims; this is what piety teaches: that God dwells only in his temple, and that his temple is none but his saints. Hence Augustine, in the book addressed to Dardanus, *On the Presence of God* [Epistle 57 to Dardanus, before the middle]:

[It is truly much more wonderful that God is wholly everywhere, yet does not dwell in everyone. For it cannot be said of everyone what the Apostle says—or what has already been said: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” Hence, conversely, he says of certain people: “Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Rom. 8:9). Who, then, would dare to suppose—unless he is entirely ignorant of that inseparable Trinity—that the Father and the Son can dwell in someone in whom the Holy Spirit does not dwell, or that the Holy Spirit can dwell in someone in whom the Father and the Son do not dwell? Therefore it must be confessed that God is everywhere through the presence of his divinity, but not everywhere through the grace of habitation. Because of this habitation, in which the grace of his love is undoubtedly recognized, we do not say, “Our Father, who are everywhere” (although this too is true), but “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matt. 6:9), so that in prayer we may rather name his temple, which we ourselves ought to be; and insofar as we are such a temple, we belong to his fellowship and to the household of adoption.

For if the people of God, who have not yet been made equal to his angels, are called his temple while still on this pilgrimage (1 Cor. 3:16), how much more is his temple in heaven, where the people of the angels are, to whom we shall be joined and made equal when, our pilgrimage ended, we receive what was promised? Since, therefore, he who is everywhere does not dwell in everyone, even in those in whom he dwells he does not dwell equally.]

**The same, in the same place, shortly afterward:**

[Just as he is not absent from the one in whom he does not dwell, and is wholly present although that person does not possess him, so he is wholly present in the one in whom he dwells, although that person does not comprehend him wholly.]

**The same, in the same place, near the middle:**

[Since, therefore, he increasingly justifies those who are making progress, in whom mortality dwells, while they are renewed from day to day; hears those who pray; and cleanses those who confess, so that he may present to himself an immaculate temple forever. He is rightly said not to dwell in those who, although they knew God, did not glorify him as God or give thanks to him (Rom. 1:21); for by worshiping and serving the creature rather than the Creator, they did not wish to be the temple of the one true God.]

**The same, in the same place, near the middle:**

[Therefore God, who is present everywhere and wholly present everywhere, does not dwell in everyone, but only in those whom he makes his most blessed temple or temples, rescuing them from the power of darkness and transferring them into the kingdom of the Son of his love, which begins with regeneration (Col. 1:13).]

**The same, in the same place, near the end:**

[God, therefore, is present everywhere, and wholly present everywhere, but does not dwell everywhere—only in his temple, toward which he is gracious and favorable through grace.]

Therefore the difference between foreknowledge and predestination is not derived from the use of the expressions but from their nature; for by nature it is one thing to foreknow and another to predestine, just as it is one thing to be present and another to dwell. For many things are foreknown that are not predestined, just as many things are present that are not inhabited. Often we are present in places and with persons in which and with whom we do not dwell. For one is said to dwell only in a house, whereas one may be present even outside a house. In the same way God is said to be everywhere through the omnipotence of his majesty, yet he is said to be present by the grace of habitation only in his temple and in his house.

**John Scotus**  
*(Chapter 18, no. 6, section 3.)*

Therefore, just as God’s presence and habitation are found only in those things which have been made by him, so his foreknowledge and predestination must be believed to concern only those things which he was going to make. Accordingly, just as, conversely, his presence and habitation are said to be in those things which are neither from him nor made by him, although they are not in them, so his foreknowledge and predestination are conversely proclaimed with respect to those things which he did not make or give, because they are nothing.

### Correction

God’s presence is proclaimed everywhere in sacred Scripture, but his habitation is found only in his temple. Nowhere will you find God said to dwell everywhere, as you find him said to be everywhere, except in your writings and those of your like. For the Lord himself says:

“I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23:24).

And the Prophet says to him:

“Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present. If I take the wings of the dawn and dwell at the ends of the sea, even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me. And I said: Perhaps darkness will trample me, and night will be my light in my pleasures. But darkness will not be dark to you, and night will be illuminated like day; its darkness is like its light” (Ps. 138:7–12).

God is therefore not said to be present everywhere in the opposite sense, as you foolishly and senselessly imagine, since the passages we have cited, whether from God himself or from his prophets, are not statements made in opposition. The same Prophet was speaking truthfully when he said:

“I said to the wicked: ‘Do not act wickedly,’ and to sinners: ‘Do not lift up your horn; do not lift up your horn on high; do not speak iniquity against God.’ For neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the desert mountains”—it is understood, “the way of escape lies open”—and he adds the reason: “for God is judge” (Ps. 74:5–8).

Thus, although God is frequently found to be present everywhere by the power of his majesty, nowhere except in his house is he found to have a dwelling place. Therefore, just as what you attempted to assert about God’s presence and habitation is false, so without doubt what you attempted to prove about his foreknowledge and predestination is false. It is consequently very surprising that you say this.

**John Scotus**  
*(Chapter 17, no. 6, section 3.)*

They are not unreasonably considered to be in those things which have arisen through the defect of creation, since he not only orders creation itself wisely, but also does not permit its defect to exceed his laws.

### Correction

How can they reasonably be considered to be in those things—that is, in sins which have arisen through the defect of creation—when sins are nothing? Or how can you say that they arose through the defect of creation, when above you repeatedly asserted, with deceptive falsehood, that creation did not sin and that sin did not arise from creation but from the will? It is therefore evident that what you say is not true. For truth is never contrary to itself, nor does it ever attack itself; yet we have often detected you doing and continuing to do precisely this, Christ being merciful. We are prepared to demonstrate it.

### [scan page 649]

**Against John Scotus**

Now the likeness of any father of a large household, whose house is most spacious and magnificently arranged, ordering his children in one way and his servants in another, the healthy in one way and those tormented—as you say—by the lack of evil desires which they have incurred through the intemperance of their lust, gnashing their teeth, swarming with worms, and suffering under various kinds of everlasting sadness: by this likeness you endeavor to establish that one who is praised as a most just governor cannot rightly be considered an exceedingly harsh punisher. Nevertheless, it does not altogether conflict with the truth of the judge, nor does it in any way weaken the rigor of his justice, if the truth is carved down to the innermost marrow.

For what else can the Founder, Governor, and Judge of the universe rightly be said to do in the beauty of this universe than gather his children through grace, and condemn the wicked through justice, either by abandoning them or by judging them? Could not the one whom you introduced by analogy as the father of a large household have come to the aid of the wretched established in his house, if he had wished, and freed them from misery? Since he did not do so, what else are we to understand him to have intended than that, because they had been assigned a misery they deserved, they should never be granted dignity? Therefore, since he who could have freed them from misery did not wish to do so, he himself plainly condemned them, judging that they would never be liberated from misery.

But why need we linger any longer over these matters, when both reason and authority, from what has been discussed and examined in the preceding arguments, have abundantly persuaded us that God is the avenger and punisher of all evils? For, as blessed Augustine says—and you yourself have cited it in opposition—:

**Augustine, *On True Religion*, chapter 23:**

[The soul’s defect is not its nature but something contrary to its nature; and it is nothing other than sin and the punishment of sin. Hence it is understood that no nature—or, better expressed, no substance or essence—is evil. Nor do the sins and punishments of the soul cause the universe to be disfigured by any deformity, because rational substance, cleansed from every sin and subject to God, rules over the other things subject to it. But the soul that has sinned has been ordered where it is fitting for such things to be, so that, with God as the Founder and Governor of the universe, all things may be beautiful. And the beauty of the whole creation consists in these three things, all of them blameless: the condemnation of sinners, the discipline of the righteous, and the perfection of the blessed.]

Observe what he says: although sinful souls are punished, the universe is nevertheless in no way disfigured by their punishment. For justice introduces no deformity; rather, it is proved to be most beautiful. Thus all the order and justice of God are beautiful. Consequently, wherever and in whatever things they exist, they produce not ugliness but beauty. Hence the same teacher says in the same book, chapter 41:

[“By its own defect,” he says, “it is hurled into corruptible beauties,” that is, into the order of punishments. “Nor should we be surprised that I still call them beauties, for nothing is ordered that is not beautiful,” and so forth.

What wonder, then, if the soul of a human being—which, wherever it may be and whatever it may be, is better than every body—is beautifully ordered, and other beauties are made from its punishments, since, when it is wretched, it is not where the blessed ought to be, but is where the wretched ought to be?]

Observe that he says that the sinful soul is hurled into the order of punishments, and that it is there where it is fitting for such a soul to be—plainly, in the place of punishments, that is, in Tartarus. Do not therefore say, “The wicked man is punished in no part of the universe, but by his own wickedness, in himself,” as the statements of the holy Fathers cited above testify. When these statements are examined and discussed truthfully, they are found to affirm what belongs to truth, not what falsehood introduces.

For they had read that it was said of the Lord:

“Fire burns before him, and it will inflame his enemies round about” (Ps. 49:3).

And again, he himself says:

“A fire has been kindled in my wrath, and it will burn to the depths of hell; it will devour the earth with its produce, and burn the foundations of the mountains. I will gather evils against them, and I will exhaust my arrows against them” (Deut. 32:22–23).

Likewise:

“I will raise my hand to heaven and say: ‘I live forever. If I sharpen my flashing sword, and my hand takes hold of judgment, I will repay vengeance to my enemies, and I will requite those who hate me. I will intoxicate my arrows with blood, and my sword will devour flesh’” (ibid. 40–42).

Meanwhile [alternative reading: “Suspend”], I beg you to moderate the sharpness of your exceedingly vigorous disputation, so that you may deign to consider what you have set forth from the words of so great a Father. You say: “The soul that has sinned has been ordered where it is fitting for such things to be.” In this passage [*On True Religion*, chapter 23] he has made two statements contrary to you: he has stated that a substance sinned, which you deny; and he has said that the substance that sinned was ordered where it is fitting for such things to be.

Nothing is ever ordered without predestination, nor is anything predestined without order. Whatever, therefore, is said about predestination is most truly proclaimed in the same way about order, as the Apostle says: “Those things which are from God have been ordered” (Rom. 13:1); as though he were saying in other words: “Those things have been destined and arranged by God.” Only the distinction we established above from Augustine’s words must be preserved: the ordering of the thing itself is regarded as its effect, whereas its destination is regarded as the prior disposition of that thing in the counsels; and preordination is held to be nothing other than predestination.

You therefore by no means deny the predestination of the wicked, whom you read to have been ordered—that is, placed and situated—where it is fitting for the wretched to be, and whom you nowhere deny to have been ordered there. Yet they could not have been ordered there unless they had been predestined to be ordered there.

From all this it is gathered that your argument is utterly vain, by which you endeavor to show that no punishment is inflicted upon the wicked except the consciousness of their own wickedness. You proceed:

**John Scotus**  
*(Chapter 17, no. 8, section 7.)*

### [scan page 650]

**On Predestination**

For just as God did not make the sun so that the sight of eyes looking at it in an orderly manner might be refracted by its rays and strike them in darkness—for this is caused not by God himself but by disordered vision itself—nor did he make it to torment a person suffering from an extremely serious affection of the eyes, since in their suffering nothing harms them so greatly as the sun’s brightness, while the suffering itself does not affect the nature of things externally but torments the sufferer internally through some corruption of bodily health; so, evidently, that eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels (Matt. 25:41) was in no way created for this purpose. Rather, if it is believed, as is more probable, to be the fourth element of the world, it was created for the integrity of the universe which God foresaw he would make, not to burn the apostate, whose own pride would have been sufficient to torment him.

### Correction

However the burning of the eternal fire may relate to the devil and his angels, who were certainly created by God as spirits by nature, the clear testimonies of sacred Scripture nevertheless do not permit us to deny that it was prepared for them and plainly declare that they are to be tortured and tormented in it. The Lord testifies in the name of their head that they are to be cast into it, saying to Job: “And before all see it, he will be hurled down” (Job 40:28).

Yet we are not unaware that Origen once said something similar, and that for this and other damnable opinions of his heresies he was condemned and cast out. Nevertheless, what you add is as follows:

**John Scotus**  
*(Chapter 17, no. 9, section 7.)*

To this reasoning, you say, it is added that, since the ethereal body was first created by God, in which it could suffer nothing, after it had swollen with pride its ethereal body was cast down from the heavenly, that is, ethereal, seats into this air, thick with moisture, dark with gloom, and subject to disturbances, so that from there a body corresponding to its deserts might be joined to it against its will; and thus it might be tormented in that body by its iniquity.

### Correction

These matters are so difficult to explain that no proof for them can be found. No page of the prophetic or apostolic writings reports that the Creator made either an ethereal or an aerial body; it reports only that a spirit was made and, after the swelling of its most proud impiety, was driven from the heavenly realms. According to the statement of blessed Peter the Apostle, it is being kept in the prison of this air for punishment with that fire on the day of judgment, together with all the companions of its defiance (2 Pet. 2:4; 3:7).

Among other things, two points seem to me especially astonishing. If an ethereal body was first made for him, and “ether” is called either fire or at least the seat of fire, why could he not suffer punishment in an igneous body rather than in an aerial one? According to your opinion, that fire is the fourth element of the world, and there would have been no need for him to be driven down to lower regions to be tormented by that fire, since, established in it and possessing a body from it, he could have been tormented there more fittingly than by being transported from it to another place to be tormented by it or in it.

And as for the aerial body which you say was joined to him so that he would no longer be burned by fire but tormented by his iniquity: if he sinned with an ethereal body when he grew proud against the Creator, what reason was there, once that body had been taken away, for another to be added to him in which he could be tormented? For it would seem far more consistent with reason and justice that he should be tormented in the very body in which he had sinned, and that no other body, which had in no way shared in his iniquity, should be joined to him for punishment.

I therefore do not see by what justice a body free from his impiety was added to him for punishment, since, as you say, by the very condition of his nature he already had a body with which and in which he was believed to have grown proud. Since this matter seems to me exceedingly obscure, intricate, and very difficult to resolve, let us proceed to the remaining points in the name and with the help of the Lord.

Nor should we pass over the fact that we read that the human body was made from earth and the soul divinely breathed into it. As for the angels—whether they are called the beings of the first heaven or of the primordial light—we must accept from the Scripture of Genesis, by faith, or in whatever other way their condition may be explained more suitably and clearly, that they were made in the higher heavens at the creation of the universe. All the opinions of the Fathers agree on this, and we hold it with complete certainty.

They were not established in ether, as you maintain, but in the heavens—that is, above this visible firmament adorned with stars—continually occupied with the praises of their Creator and serving his commands with unshakable obedience. Although they are always spirits, when they are sent to appear to human beings they are certainly believed to assume bodies, either from ether or from this denser air, with which they can speak and eat with earthly beings.

Hence Augustine, in Book 8, chapter 22 of *The City of God*:

[Since, therefore, none of these four elements should be selected, lest one should think so badly of the gods in any one of them, it remains that we should in no way believe what Apuleius, and whatever other philosophers hold the same opinion, endeavor to persuade us of: that there are middle demons between gods and human beings, serving as messengers and interpreters, who carry our petitions from here and bring back the gods’ assistance from there. Rather, they are spirits exceedingly desirous of doing harm, utterly alien to justice, swollen with pride, livid with envy, and cunning in deceit. They dwell in this air because, having been cast down from the heights of the higher heaven, they have, by the merit of an irreparable transgression, been condemned beforehand to this air as to a prison suited to them.]

**Philip, in his *Exposition of Blessed Job*, chapter 24, near the middle:**

Not without reason does blessed Job say of them in this passage: “As in the day they agreed among themselves” (Job 24:16), when, with the archangel persuading the others—of whom it is said, “He dragged with him a third of the stars against God”—a conspiracy of rebellion was formed in heaven (Rev. 12:4).

I judge that their conference was a certain movement of the will and a mutual agreement rather than audible conversation, since they are spirits and not bodies composed of limbs. It is therefore possible that, through the subtlety of their nature, they perceived similar movements in one another, and that this was called a conference. For nothing of their affections [survives only as an incomplete fragment: “from one another—”].

### Correction

Your first proposition is shown to be false by the fact that you falsely claim that Augustine calls that fire corporeal and Gregory incorporeal; for both, without contradiction, affirm that it is corporeal. And since you yourself are more deeply mistaken concerning Augustine, we judged it unnecessary to set out his opinion. But, concerning Gregory’s judgment, so that no one may doubt it, although a little above we have already quoted his opinion about this same fire from his *Moral Expositions*, in which he declares it corporeal, it nevertheless seems useful to draw out a similar passage from another of his works.

For, as the book entitled *Dialogues*, written by Peter the Deacon, reports, when Peter was asking Gregory about the aforesaid fire, he began as follows:

“And since it must be believed on rational grounds that corporeal fire can hold an incorporeal being—”

### Gregory

“If the incorporeal spirit of a living human being is held within a body, why should it not, after death, when it is still an incorporeal spirit, also be held by corporeal fire?”

### Peter

“In a living person, an incorporeal spirit is held in the body for this reason: because it gives life to the body.”

### Gregory

“If an incorporeal spirit, Peter, can be held here in what it gives life to, why should it not also be held there in what mortifies it? We say that the spirit is held by fire, since in the burning fire it is punished by seeing and feeling [another reading: ‘so that it is punished in the torment of fire by seeing and feeling’]. For it suffers that fire precisely in seeing it; and because it sees itself being burned, it is burned. Thus it happens that a corporeal thing burns an incorporeal thing, while invisible burning and pain are drawn from visible fire.

“Yet from the sayings of the Gospels we may infer that the soul suffers this burning not only by seeing but also by experiencing it. For, by the voice of Truth, the rich man is said to have died and been buried in hell; and that his soul is held in fire is indicated by the rich man’s own voice, as he begs Abraham: ‘Send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame’ (Luke 16:24). Since, therefore, Truth declares that the sinful rich man is condemned to fire, what wise person would deny that the souls of the reprobate are held in fires?”

### Peter

“How can an incorporeal thing be held and afflicted by a corporeal thing [another reading: ‘how can a corporeal thing hold and afflict an incorporeal thing’], I do not know.”

### Gregory

“Tell me, I ask you: do you suppose that the apostate spirits who were brought down [another reading: ‘cast out’] from heavenly glory are corporeal or incorporeal?”

### Peter

“What sane person would say that spirits are corporeal?”

### Gregory

“Do you admit that the fire of Gehenna is incorporeal or corporeal?”

### Peter

“I do not doubt that the fire of Gehenna is corporeal, in which it is certain that bodies are tormented.”

### Gregory

“Certainly Truth declares at the end to the reprobate: ‘Go into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels’ (Matthew 25:41). If, therefore, the devil and his angels, although incorporeal, are to be tormented by corporeal fire, what is surprising if souls, even before they receive their bodies again, can feel corporeal torments?”

### Peter

“The argument is clear, and the mind ought not to doubt this further question.”

While we set forth these certain testimonies concerning that corporeal fire, a truthful response was thereby supplied to almost everything that you had set down in your aforementioned proposition. For, by the authority of so great a teacher, not only is that fire asserted to be corporeal, but it is also credibly taught that human souls and apostate spirits are sensibly tormented in it. Nor is that other point any less clearly established for us, concerning which our weakness had hesitated to some extent—namely, concerning the bodies of unclean spirits.

For this most learned and holy teacher does not say that corporeal bodies are added to them, nor that they suffer in some bodies, but that they undergo torments in the very things of which incorporeal spirits consist. Therefore it is not called destined or prepared for the devil merely because he was to be placed in it, but because in it he was to be tormented either by seeing, or by experiencing, or in both ways. Nor is it called evil because evil beings are most orderly disposed in it, but because every punishment is judged evil by those who suffer it. It is most appropriately called the punishment of those who are to be tormented because in it not only their souls but also their bodies will be sensibly tormented.

That fire is therefore a punishment, prepared, made, and predestined for this purpose: that in it all the wicked may be consumed not only in conscience but also through sensation and experience—not that it should be the dwelling-place of the impious, but that it should be the punishment, torment, and condemnation of the reprobate.

### Correction

O unheard-of insanity! O detestable folly! O horrifying stupidity! O subtlety harder than every dullness! O venom that must be eradicated more than every abomination! What is it, O most arrogant of mortals, that you have dared to proclaim with such shamelessness?

You attribute to the wretched no less than to the blessed the fire which Truth says was prepared from the beginning for the devil and his angels. Certainly, at the judgment the Judge of all declares that he will say to the reprobate: “Go into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41). But to the just he says: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34). To the latter he says that the kingdom—not punishment, but glory—has been prepared. To the former, the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels—not glory, but punishment.

Hence it is also said there: “And these will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matthew 25:46).

What does this mean, O most wretched of all those formed from earthly dust? Truth distinguishes the places of both parties according to their merits, and you dogmatically assign one and the same fire as a dwelling-place to the just and the unjust.

Clearly, what you intend is being revealed: although you have not stated it openly, it nevertheless becomes clear what you have conceived in your mind, or what you have wished to persuade people of by such words, even if perversely. I remember hearing you say—something which rumor has now spread widely—that beyond this visible heaven, which Scripture calls the firmament and which the Apostle interprets as the veil of the tabernacle (Hebrews 9:3), which was situated before the sanctuary, there is nothing; and that likewise beneath the earth there is nothing. Rather, in this structure, as though in a single house, the entire circuit of heaven and earth is contained; and that what we call hell extends from the earth to the moon, while paradise, or the kingdom of the saints, extends from the moon to the firmament. There, you say, both the holy angels, the souls of the saints, and our Lord Jesus Christ himself dwell bodily.

Yet Truth and the authority of the catholic faith proclaim something else; nor can any ecclesiastical writer be found—or even be believed capable of being found—who supports or agrees with such madness. On the contrary, you are shown to have drawn and vomited forth deadly poison from that very reading on which you rely with all your strength.

For, apart from other influences, your Capella is believed above all to have led you into this labyrinth, since you have directed your mind more toward his speculation than toward evangelical truth. Moreover, when you were reading the books of blessed Augustine, which he composed with remarkable abundance in *The City of God* against the most deceptive and false opinions of the pagans, you found that he had quoted and refuted certain passages from Varro’s books. Because these seemed to agree with your Capella, you chose to assent to them rather than to put faith in the statements of truthful Augustine.

For Augustine sets out the following from Varro’s words:

### Varro, quoted by Augustine

*(Augustine, *The City of God*, book 7, chapter 6.)*

“Varro, then, introducing his discussion of natural theology, says that he considers God to be the soul of the world, which the Greeks call *kosmos* (κόσμος), and that this world itself is God. But just as a wise human being, although composed of body and soul, is called wise because of the soul, so the world is called God because of its soul, although it is composed of soul and body.

“Here he seems in some manner to confess one God. But, in order to introduce more gods as well, he adds that the world is divided into two parts: heaven and earth. Heaven is divided in two, into ether and air; earth into water and land. Of these, ether is the highest, air the second, water the third, and land the lowest.

“He says that all four parts are full of souls: the ether and air with immortal souls, water and land with mortal souls. From the highest circuit of heaven to the circle of the moon, the ether contains the stars, and these celestial gods are understood not merely to exist but also to be seen. Between the circle of the moon and the region of clouds and winds, the air contains souls; but these are perceived by the mind, not by the eyes. They are called heroes, household gods, and spirits.”

How contrary this is to the truth and to the authority of the divine Scriptures and of the venerable Fathers, we shall, with the Lord’s help, demonstrate as far as our ability and strength permit.

First, it must be observed where our Lord and Savior dwells: in the body which he assumed from the inviolate Virgin and conducted without sin. For he himself testifies in the Gospel that all the saints will be gathered there, saying: “There will be two in one bed: one will be taken and the other will be left; two in the field: one will be taken and the other will be left.” They answered him, “Where, Lord?” He said to them: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered” (Luke 17:34–37). Without doubt, all catholic and orthodox teachers understand this to mean above the starry heaven.

Saint Ambrose also understands this as the place to which blessed Paul was caught up, saying in his exposition of the Second Epistle to the Corinthians:

### Ambrose

*(On the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 12.)*

“He is understood to have been caught up beyond all the stars of the world, and therefore what he relates is magnificent and marvelous. For he signifies that he was caught up above the firmament, in the third heaven, into the spiritual heavens.”
