“That hell has a lower region is demonstrated by the Gospel passage which says that, when the impious rich man was being tormented by avenging flame, he lifted up his eyes and saw Lazarus in Abraham’s bosom (Luke 16:23). From this it appears that both were in hell, since they were able to see one another, and that the rich man lifted his eyes from the lower place to the higher.

“Although both thus seemed to be in hell, Augustine judges that, according to their merits, by a distinction of justice, the higher place should be assigned to the saints and the lower to sinners. Hence the faithful people, giving thanks, say that God has delivered their soul from the lower hell—that is, from punitive hell.”

If you think that Varro’s opinion should be preferred, because Augustine discussed the matter differently in the twelfth book of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, listen to what Augustine himself brought forth when he reconsidered the same matter:

### Augustine

*(Retractions, book 1, chapter 11.)*

“In the twelfth book, concerning hell, it seemed to me that I ought rather to have taught that hell is beneath the earth than to give an account of the reason why it is believed or said to be beneath the earth.”

By these truthful discussions of so many Fathers all your subtleties, and all your deceptive, inappropriate, and unsuitable comparisons, have been crushed and thrown down, so that they are judged to be entirely worthless. To these matters is also joined what you add in conclusion:

### John Scotus

*(Chapter 47, number 12, section 9.)*

“Therefore,” he says, “if there is no blessedness except eternal life, and eternal life is the knowledge of truth, there is no blessedness except the knowledge of truth.

“But so that this conclusion may in no way waver in our minds, let us hear Truth itself openly proclaiming: ‘Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him’ (John 14:21). And elsewhere: ‘This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent’ (John 17:3).

“Whatever, then, is believed concerning blessedness, the opposite must be believed concerning its absence—that is, concerning misery. Therefore, if there is no misery except eternal death, and eternal death is ignorance of the truth, there is no misery except ignorance of the truth.

“Where truth is unknown, there is no life; and where there is no life, continual death must necessarily be present. If these things are so, who would dare to say that God is the predestiner of punishment, unless he also dares to assert that he is the author of ignorance, although all understanding comes from him?

“Each person is therefore punished by his own obstinacy, which in no way comes from God; and consequently he must in no way be considered its author.”

### Correction

Unless your iniquity had blinded you, you would never have uttered propositions so completely contrary to one another.

For in the sixteenth section you said that the wretched possess the conception and knowledge of blessedness:

“Blessedness,” you say, “is truth. Therefore no one outside his own nature will possess either the conception or the knowledge of blessedness. In the nature of the wretched, therefore, there will be truth; consequently there will be blessedness. But how will that nature be wretched if it possesses blessedness, which is truth? Finally, you concluded: ‘No nature will thereafter be punished; and what is not punished will not be wretched.’”

But now you say:

“If there is no misery except eternal death, and eternal death is ignorance of the truth, there is no misery except ignorance of the truth. Where truth is unknown, there is no life; and where there is no life, continual death must necessarily be present.”

What is this? Now you grant the wretched knowledge of truth and remove their misery; now you attribute to them ignorance of truth and death—
and misery. For if it is true that they possess knowledge of the truth, it is false that they have ignorance of it. Again, if it is true that they have ignorance of the truth, it is false that they possess knowledge of the truth. Likewise, what you say is false: “There is no misery except eternal death.” For many sinners and righteous people in this life are afflicted by miseries and calamities, from which they are sometimes rescued by God’s grace and sometimes, by that same justice, are not delivered. For if blessedness is said to consist in attaining—and lacking nothing—that which you may reasonably desire, when you are deprived of so great a good you are rightly called miserable. And since we very often see the pious subjected to so many temporal miseries, we certainly do not believe that they are hastening toward eternal death; nor, because we see someone afflicted temporarily by frequent misfortunes, is ignorance of the truth thereby imposed upon them.

Therefore, if this were said only of those delivered to hell, it would in no way depart from the truth. But since it is said generally that there is no misery except eternal death, and that eternal death is ignorance of the truth, the very constant experience of seeing and testing these things proves it utterly false. May blessed Job pierce this perversity of yours with the sword [or perhaps “with the blade”] of truth; for he laments human miseries in these words: “Man, born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries” (Job 14:1).

Agreeing with him in his explanation, St Gregory [Moralia, book XI, at the end] declares what miseries we ought to understand:

“What strength can one possess who is born from weakness, who lives for a short time, and is filled with many miseries? Behold, the whole condition of human life is briefly expressed in the words of the holy man: it is both narrowed toward life and widened toward misery. For, if what is signified here is considered carefully, it is punishment and misery. To be subject to the corruption of the flesh for the sake of necessities and permitted things is misery: clothing is required against the cold, food against hunger, coolness against heat; the body’s health is guarded with great care, yet even when guarded it is lost, and when lost is restored only with great labor—and nevertheless, once restored, it is always in doubt. What else is this than the misery of mortal life?

“We love our friends and fear that they may be offended; we fear our enemies and are not secure concerning those whom we fear. Often we speak to enemies as boldly as though they were friends, and sometimes we receive the sincere words of our neighbors, who perhaps love us greatly, as though they were the words of enemies. Though we never wish to deceive, through our own caution we nevertheless make more serious mistakes. What, then, is this if not the misery of human life?

“Man, expelled from his heavenly homeland, languishes in exile, is weighed down by cares, and yet pretends not to consider how burdensome his condition is, because many other things occupy his thoughts. Deprived of the inner light, he nevertheless wishes to endure his blindness in this life. What else is this than misery born from our punishment? Yet although he might long to remain here for a long time, the course of mortal life presses upon him so that he may depart.”

[Scan page 658]

**St Prudentius**

And in the same way, what he says elsewhere [chapter 17, number 2, section 5]: “Where there is no truth, there is no life” (John 14:6), is no less thoroughly refuted. For truth can neither be unknown nor known except by some living being. The condemned person in Gehenna will therefore possess life and the existence of the body, although without the true life of him who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” I say that they will have life, but a miserable one, since the soul will always live in order always to be tormented, and the body, consumed and worn down by punishments and burning, will never fail, never dissolve into dust, and never be so utterly destroyed that it ceases to exist; rather, it will endure forever amid eternal tortures.

We confess with every fear and dread that God, the most just judge, is the inflictor of all these punishments, and therefore also their author, since Scripture bears witness: “Death and life are from the Lord God” (Wisdom 16:13); and the Psalmist says: “He has bent his bow and prepared it.” Cassiodorus [on Psalm 7:13]:

“By the bow of Scripture we rightly understand the New and Old Testament, which, through two flexures bent in a certain manner, embraces the necks of the faithful. Here a gentle yoke is shown to the faithful; to the rebellious, terrifying weapons are revealed. ‘He has bent it’ is added so that his patience might not be thought lax; finally he adds, ‘he prepared it,’ so that the very practice of archers might be fully represented: after they have bent the bow toward the target, they place their hand upon it, preparing their arms for the work of shooting.

“But let us see what arrows the prepared bow has sent forth: ‘And in it he prepared the vessels of death; he made his arrows burning’ (Psalm 7:14). Here the distribution of divine majesty is displayed: through the bow—that is, through the Old and New Testament, as has already been said—the effect of death arrives, and through his arrows life is bestowed. From this bow came forth arrows, namely the apostles, who, with burning—that is, desirous—souls, sent salutary commands in the manner of arrows. Thus the impious would be wounded, and effective healing would arise for the faithful. ‘He made’ means ‘he brought about.’”

Who, then, will bring the ignorance of truth upon the condemned, unless it is the terrifying and most just judge, who knows what to take away from each person and what to grant? But enough has been said about these matters. Now, in the name and with the help of the Lord, let us turn to what remains.

## Chapter XVIII

**That the error of those who think differently from the holy Fathers concerning predestination arises from ignorance of the liberal disciplines**

The eighteenth chapter of the work on the obstinacy of the Irishman is introduced as follows:

**John Scotus.**

*(Chapter 18, number 1, section 1.)* “That the error of those who think differently from the holy Fathers concerning predestination arises from ignorance of the liberal disciplines.

“Thus, the exceedingly savage error of those who oppose the opinions of the most venerable Fathers, especially St Augustine, and who, as a result, leave behind the path of the most prudent truth, is shown to arise from ignorance of the liberal disciplines, which eternal Wisdom wished to have as her companions and investigators.”

[Scan page 659]

**St Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes**

**Correction.**

“It seems to me that this utterance echoes the saying of him who is recorded as the first to have said: ‘I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will set my throne; I will sit upon the mount of the Testament, on the sides of the north; I will be like the Most High’ (Isaiah 14:13). Of him the Lord says to blessed Job: ‘He sees every lofty thing; he himself is king over all the children of pride’ (Job 41:25). Nor are they to be separated from his members, of whom the Prophet declares: ‘They have set their mouth in heaven [another reading: “unto heaven”], and their tongue has passed through the earth’ (Psalm 73:9).

“Yet the children of humility and truth are never so moved by such injuries as to return insults for insults and reproaches for reproaches. Rather, being made humbler, they strive with all their strength to refer to the glory and honor of the giver whatever they know has been freely given them by humility and truth, their teacher. If you had sought either to be taught by, or to employ, that teacher’s instruction, you would never have burst forth into such blasphemies and shamelessness.

The ignorance of these disciplines is branded upon our forehead. Why should this move our humility, when we see that all our orthodox Fathers have been subjected to the same insult and branded with the same disgrace? All of them shone with so much learning in the liberal disciplines that no one whom the world regards as an especially accomplished philosopher could be compared with them. For they were so instructed in every true wisdom that, the more closely they adhered to true wisdom, the more clearly they knew what in these disciplines ought to be avoided and what ought to be sought.

But because the truth did not forbid them to know these things in their own time, did it therefore command them to lie or to become blind? Yet anyone who reads what you have written, illuminated by that same truth, plainly recognizes in how many minds you dwell. And so, as we shall show with the Lord’s help, you have not only distorted the words of the Lord but also the opinions of the Fathers with such corruption through your errors that the reader must have both diligent practice and the most immediate knowledge of the truth.

Therefore it is evident that you have strayed so far from the truth because, relying upon inflated learning, you abandoned what was true through deliberate—and consequently most arrogant—aversion.

Did the holy Fulgentius, a man learned beyond all hesitation, lie through ignorance of these disciplines when he explained Augustine’s view of predestination and completed, with marvelous eloquence and knowledge of the truth, a book filled with that explanation? We know him to have lived so near to Augustine’s own time that he could have learned the integrity of Augustine’s teaching either from Augustine himself or from his hearers.

Did the holy Prosper also err through ignorance of these matters? He consulted Augustine in his own letters and, instructed by Augustine’s Catholic replies, was so strengthened in his defense of the truth that he defended, and endeavored to have defended, the teaching of so great a Father both by writings of his own learning and by the decrees of the Apostolic See.

Did the blessed bishops Gregory and Isidore err through ignorance of these disciplines, when we certainly know that they possessed the greatest knowledge of them? Cease, then, to heap this insult upon Catholic and highly learned men, whom Truth, their teacher, taught all truth through the Holy Spirit.

Indeed, when I see holy companies from so many cities and monasteries gathering flowers from the aforementioned arts, bearing fruit, and composing the sweetest honey, I would never attribute wisdom to you alone, as though it had been assigned uniquely to you. “He is rich toward all who call upon him” (Romans 10:12), and he is known to distribute it everywhere with such abundant generosity.

Nor should the following be passed over in silence: you dared to say that the liberal disciplines are companions and investigators of eternal Wisdom, although it is clear that they were discovered through human invention and found by men separated from and lacking the one Wisdom who is God. For if they are believed to be companions and investigators of eternal Wisdom, it follows that their inventors, the men through whom they are said to have been discovered as her companions and investigators, are made equal to eternal Wisdom herself. But no creature ought to be made equal to eternal Wisdom, nor can it in any way be so. It is therefore false that these disciplines—that is, human inventions—and their discoverers are companions and investigators of the true and eternal Wisdom, as the Prophet says: “Who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord? Who shall be like God among the sons of God?” (Psalm 88:7), much less among the sons of the devil?

Next you attach another charge of ignorance, which is likewise proved irrelevant to the matter.

**John Scotus.**

*(Chapter 18, number 3, section 1.)* “Moreover,” he says, “ignorance of the Greek language, in which the interpretation of predestination generates no obscurity of ambiguity, provided that it is attended to more carefully by investigators of truth rather than by defenders of falsehood, would plainly reveal to the pious and understanding how often, whether concerning good things in the proper sense or concerning evil things in an improper sense, predestination has opened the principal parts of its face—parts well known to the wise but most obscure to those puffed up with pride. For the Greek word is ὁρῶ (*horō*), which is expressed in Latin by three words: for ὁρῶ is interpreted as ‘I see,’ ‘I define,’ and ‘I destine.’ Likewise, its compound προορώ (*proorō*) means ‘I foresee,’ ‘I predefine,’ and ‘I predestine.’”

**Correction.**

“O most perceptive man, who, finding Latin deficient, drags us back to Greek and fabricates Greek origins in Roman speech! What, I ask, have the Latin words *video* (‘I see’), *definio* (‘I define’), and *destino* (‘I destine’) to do with the Greek word ὁρῶ (*horō*)? Are they derived from it or formed from its name? Does even the mere surface of these letters represent anything similar? Yet because you brand us with this ignorance, will you also make the same accusation against the holy Fathers, who shone with Greek learning no less than with Latin? Omitting the others, I call Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Gregory, Isidore, Fulgentius, and Cassiodorus as witnesses to the truth. No one who knows nothing can be unaware that they knew both the Greek language and its learning. All of them pursue the meaning of this word in another sense.

“For St Ambrose, in the passage where the Apostle says to the Ephesians, ‘predestining us to adoption as sons through Jesus Christ unto himself’ (Ephesians 1:5), explains it as follows:

“‘This means that God decreed that those who believe in Christ should be adopted as sons by God, so that Christ, the true Son of God, might be their head.’

“And below:

This is what he means: the administration of preaching was decreed by God for those from the Jews who believed in Christ. Hence no one from the Gentiles was chosen as an apostle; for it was fitting that those should be chosen as preachers who had previously hoped for the salvation promised to them in Christ.’”

In those whom he has deigned to gather, he has drawn the cord of the hidden measure; from those whom he has judged should be abandoned, what else has he done but withdraw the cord? [Scan page 662]

**On Predestination against John Scotus**

What does it mean that the holy apostles are called to go where perhaps they were not thinking of going, while they are forbidden to go where they desired to go? It means that the cord and the measuring reed of hidden judgment are held in the hand: some hear the words of life, while others do not deserve to hear them at all. The cord is therefore a measure, drawn toward one person and withdrawn from another. We have also learned from the witness of the holy Gospel [another reading: “with the Gospel bearing witness”] that iniquity, when it falls from above, strikes violently as it descends; then it explains powerfully how the wicked are tormented. For when their own sins descend upon them, they are destined by their own evils and crimes for due punishments.

I have inserted this statement of blessed Gregory so that it may be understood from it what he understood, and wished others to understand, concerning predestination. For, since he explained the same meaning more fully in the *Moralia*, and used the plural “predestinations” there while in Ezekiel he used “dispensation” likewise in the plural, he plainly taught that by the term “predestination” God’s dispositions, dispensations, and ordinances are to be understood. It is clear that these and many other terms are used in one and the same sense, both in the sacred utterances and in expositions by commentators.

Fulgentius, in his work addressed to Monimus (book I, chapters 20 and 21):

“‘For his predestination is nothing other than the eternal preparation of his future works. In it no cause of evil can be found, because the origin of sin has never proceeded from the will of God. For the Lord is merciful and just; and elsewhere it is written of him: “The Lord God loves mercy and truth” (Psalm 84:12). Therefore in all his works either just truth is maintained or merciful compassion is bestowed.’”

And below (ibid., chapter 21):

“‘For his predestination is the preparation of his works.’”

And again (ibid., chapter 23):

“‘By God’s predestination either the merciful remission of sins is prepared, or the just punishment of sins. God could therefore never predestine a human being to that which he had determined both to forbid by commandment, to wash away by mercy, and to punish by justice. Thus God predestined the wicked, whom he foreknew would end this life in sin, to be punished by unending punishment.’”

This teacher and bishop, unquestionably most faithful and learned, knew the Greek expression extremely well. He knew how the expression “the predestination of the wicked,” used by blessed Augustine, was to be understood—namely, not as foreknowledge but as preparation and disposition. If you either do not know or deny that he possessed knowledge of Attic Greek, read his books entitled *Mythologies, or the Content of Virgil*, and you will find that he possessed very great mastery of that language, by which he could most readily know what ought to be understood under the utterance of this term.

Cassiodorus (on Psalm 7, near the end):

“‘The first is the one who came and said: “Master, I will follow you wherever you go.” He was answered: “Foxes have dens and birds have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.” Another came and said: “Master, allow me first to go and bury my father.” He is told: “Let the dead bury their dead; but you, follow me and proclaim the kingdom of God” (Matthew 8:19–20, 21–22). Why is it that the one promises to go and is left behind, while this one wishes to return home and yet is commanded to follow? The former is not received; the latter is not released from service even for an hour. Therefore, in the hidden judgment, the cord and measuring reed of hidden judgment are drawn: this one is drawn and that one is left behind, so that the heavenly structure may be built not without a merciful and just examination.’”

“God causes to prosper in this life those whom he has decreed to build up again; but at the end, whoever is to be destroyed is assigned to eternal punishments.”

The same author, on Psalm 55:

“For all the days of human beings are known to have been determined in predestination.”

The same author, on Psalm 82:

“‘Let them be confounded and troubled forever and ever who are to be condemned to eternal punishment. It follows: ‘And let them fear and perish’ (Psalm 82:18).’ The meaning is the same as that which he stated above: for by fearing they do not advance but perish, those who are destined for eternal punishment.”

The same author, on Psalm 87:

Primasius too, the most learned bishop of the African Church, is found to have thought the same in his explanation of the Apocalypse of blessed John, when he says:

“‘For the dispensation of Christ the Lord is assigned to the past time as to an earlier period; as it is read as having been foretold by the prophets, so it is taught as already completed. Boniface, bishop and martyr of Germany:

“‘For what benefit is it to a parent if he has a son assigned to perpetual torments?’”

I considered it necessary to gather this collection of statements from the volumes of the Fathers so that, through the variety of their vocabulary and the unity of their meanings, one might most easily discern what they intended by the designation “predestination.” For when it was necessary to explain the same matter repeatedly, they preferred, to avoid weariness, to express the same thing through different meanings rather than serve tediously one and the same word, as though suffering from poverty of speech. Therefore you ought not to have invited us from Latin words to Greek origins, since it is not established that they received from Greek either their derivation or their designation. Between—

## S. PRUDENTIUS, BISHOP OF TROYES

1311

This, perhaps, I have rightly judged worth noting: that the orator, by a beautiful composition, seems to have discovered for our ignorance the word *praedefinio* (“I predetermine”), when he could have said much more conveniently and correctly *praefinio* (“I predetermine”), as we also inserted above from Saint Jerome. All these considerations clearly refute what you foolishly asserted: that *destinare* or *praedestinare* can mean “to see” or “to foresee,” since none of these authors can anywhere be found to have used it in that sense.

Nor should it be passed over that you asserted that the disciplines mentioned were companions and investigators of eternal Wisdom (chapter 18, no. 4, section 1), contrary, surely, to the authority of the prophetic and apostolic writings. For if Wisdom had companions, it follows as a great absurdity that she is proclaimed to need something which belongs to another. Yet she is proved never to have needed or to need anyone, since by her sole eternity and omnipotence she disposed all things, “reaching from end to end mightily” (Wisdom 8:1), and could never have been weakened by any impotence. I do not understand at all why she summoned your “companions” as necessary—why she would have needed their support and, as it were, their assistance either to investigate herself or for some other purpose—when Scripture testifies that she enters holy souls and inserts herself into thoughts that are without deceit (Wisdom 1:4), so that whoever receives her becomes wise, according to the gift of the one who enlightens and the capacity of the one who receives.

Thus, having traversed all the pages of both Testaments, I nowhere find that God is commanded to be investigated through these disciplines. Rather, I have been taught that he must be sought faithfully and truly found through faith “which works through love,” purity of heart, and obedience and observance of God’s commandments. For what? Are all the prophets to be said to have investigated and found God through these disciplines? Certainly, to pass over the others, Amos, taken suddenly from pastoral work to prophesy by inspiration (Amos 1:1), cannot be believed ever to have acquired their learning. What of blessed Peter and the other Apostles, fishermen and uneducated men (Mark 1:16)? Did they, instructed by study of these disciplines, investigate and attain eternal Wisdom?

Truth proclaims something entirely different when it says: “When he, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will teach you all truth” (John 16:13); and again: “When the Paraclete Spirit comes, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance everything that I have said to you” (John 14:26); and again: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matthew 11:27). Again: “Jesus, rejoicing in the Holy Spirit, said: ‘I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to infants. Yes, Father, for such was your gracious will before you’” (Matthew 11:25). And to blessed Peter: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 16:17). The Apostle also says: “Since the world through its wisdom did not know God, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe” (1 Corinthians 1:21); “but God has revealed it through his Spirit” (1 Corinthians 2:10).

The philosophers of the world neither possessed nor found the Holy Spirit. How, then, however clever and acute they might be, could they investigate the Lord through the instruction of those same disciplines, when he is neither truly investigated nor found except through the Holy Spirit? It follows, therefore, that those disciplines were not companions of the Wisdom of God, which is one, identical, and always alone; nor can she be investigated through them, but is revealed through his Spirit.

Was blessed Father Augustine, instructed thoroughly in all these matters, able either to investigate or to find God through the acumen of those disciplines? Although he devoted many years to their study, and was hindered by many errors, especially by the madness of the Manichaeans, he could never know the truth until, through the persistence, prayers, and tears of his holy mother, through the attention of God’s heavenly inspiration, and through the preaching of blessed Ambrose, he deserved both to recognize God and to receive the grace of faith.

Therefore the most blessed Augustine himself, in Book Eight of *The City of God*, says (chapter 11):

> “In the *Timaeus*, however, Plato, who wrote a book about the constitution of the world, says that in that work God first joined earth and fire. It is evident that he assigns the place of heaven to fire and the earth itself to earth. This statement, therefore, has a certain resemblance to that saying: ‘In the beginning God made heaven and earth’ (Genesis 1:1).
>
> “Then, as the two intermediate things by which these extremities would be joined to one another, he names water and air. Hence he is thought to have understood in this way what is written: ‘The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters’ (Genesis 1:2), paying too little attention to the manner in which that Scripture usually calls the Spirit of God, since air too is called *spirit*. He thought that the four elements might be seen as mentioned in that passage.
>
> “Again, when Plato says that the philosopher is a lover of God, nothing in those sacred writings burns with such force; and especially the following passage—which strongly moves me, so that I almost agree that Plato was not ignorant of those books. When the words of God are conveyed through an angel to holy Moses, and Moses asks the name of the one who commands him to go to the Hebrew people to liberate them from Egypt, the answer is: ‘I am who I am.’ And you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’ (Exodus 3:14)—as though, in comparison with the one who truly is, because he is immutable, the things that have been made and are mutable did not exist. Plato held this very firmly and commended it with the greatest care. I do not know whether this is found anywhere in the books of those who lived before Plato, except where it is said: ‘I am who I am. And you shall say to them: He who is has sent me to you.’
>
> “But whoever said these things—whether he found them in books of the ancients who preceded him, or rather, as the Apostle says, because ‘what can be known about God is manifest among them; for God has manifested it to them. For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are understood and perceived through the things that have been made, as are his eternal power and divinity’ (Romans 1:19–20)—I have not unreasonably chosen the Platonic philosophers with whom to deal, since this is what is at issue in the question we have now undertaken.”

Therefore blessed Paul the Apostle says: “See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of this world, and not according to Christ, because in him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2:8–9).

Ambrose, on Colossians, chapter 2:8:

> “He calls it earthly philosophy, by which those who desire to be considered wise in the world are usually led astray. It is composed of arguments and the subtlety of certain trifles, as though it had investigated physical causes (Wisdom 13:14), with certain things mixed into it that serve as exhortations to a good life or as teachings—sometimes arranged according to measures, sometimes according to numbers, sometimes according to the qualities and quantities of the elements. Whoever falls into its discussions scarcely, or rarely [variant: never], escapes. For he is held by plausible causes and invented notions, considering nothing so true as what is seen and understood in the elements (Wisdom 15).
>
> “And because the things that exist and are seen at present appear pleasant and attractive to the eye, they lead some astray—those who think that spiritual reasoning must be despised and rejected because they despair of the future (Wisdom 2), assigning all power to the stars (Wisdom 12). Subject to carnal reasoning, they refuse to believe that weighty things can be lifted into heaven, or light things come down to earth, or anything bodily be generated without a mixture of substances, resisting the power and providence of God. For they know that in the ancient divine books of the Hebrews many things are recorded as having been done through Moses which human reason cannot grasp (Deuteronomy 4). In the same way, in the new books, the carnal mind forbids belief in things done by the Lord or through the Apostles (Acts 13).
>
> “He therefore calls this tradition a deceitful and empty philosophy (1 Corinthians 2), because it was not ordered by the power of God, but by the weakness of human reasoning, which confines God’s power within its own knowledge, so that he is not believed capable of acting otherwise than carnal reason allows. They assign divinity to the individual elements in a diversity [variant: the diversity] of worship, in order to bind the minds of the ignorant and prevent them from reaching out to the true God.
>
> “For this reason he warns that this tradition must be avoided, because it is a worshipper of the world (Wisdom 13), not of the one God; and it draws one away from Christ rather than toward Christ, in whom the perfection of divinity exists.”

But, to return to the subject: since you import Attic origins into Latin words for us, although so many teachers of the Churches were thoroughly acquainted with Greek, we have never read *praedestinatio* used for *praevisio* (“foreknowledge”), because they knew that the two differ in every respect. For although nothing can be predestined without foreknowledge, as we have already gathered many examples concerning the distinction between foreknowledge and predestination, if the word *predestination* is subject to this interpretation, what do you think should be made of the other terms which are very frequently used in the same sense—such as *deputatus* (“assigned”), *delegatus* (“delegated”), *paratus* (“prepared”), *praeparatus* (“made ready”), *decretus* (“decreed”), *judicatus* (“judged”), *damnatus* (“condemned”), *addictus* (“handed over”), *dispositus* (“disposed”), *dispensatus* (“administered”), *ordinatus* (“ordered”), *statutus* (“established”), *constitutus* (“constituted”), *praefixus* (“fixed beforehand”), *definitus* (“defined”), *praefinitus* (“predetermined”), and so forth?

These terms, converging on the same meaning, are found throughout the divine pages and the writings of the venerable Fathers. Yet who does not know that “he foresaw” is not the same as “he predetermined”? Since *praefinire* (“to predetermine”) and *praedestinare* (“to predestine”) agree with one another, it is clear to every sober person that *praevidere* (“to foresee”) differs greatly from them, because, as has often been noted, many things are foreseen which are in no way predetermined.

Meanwhile, I see that the astonishing interpreter deserves to be treated with what honor: while inventing new lines of interpretation for us, he could not perceive that not all Latin words used to translate a single Greek, Hebrew, or other-language word must always signify one and the same thing. Rather, according to the character of the passages, they indicate now one thing and now another. Saint Jerome demonstrates this especially clearly among others, as with *bar*—which in our language signifies “son,” “pure grain,” “a bundle of ears,” and “chosen.” Are all those Roman words therefore said to signify one and the same thing merely because they are used to render one Hebrew or Syriac word according to different senses?

Accordingly, what you keep repeating with tiresome verbosity—more babbling than eloquence—about predestination, foreknowledge, and predetermination, death, punishments, and torments, has already been sufficiently and abundantly refuted and demolished above. To avoid unnecessarily repeating the same things after your example, we have prudently thought it best to pass over them.

Nevertheless, I think this must be noted: although you denied that death is from God (chapter 18, no. 5, section 5), you said that the death of death is eternal life, that is, our Lord Jesus Christ, who himself foretold this through the prophet: “I shall be your death, O Death; I shall be your bite, O Hell” (Hosea 13:14). If he himself declares that he is the death of death, how dare you deny that death is from God?

Likewise, you say that being abandoned by God means being deprived of existence (chapter 18, no. 6, section 5), and that what he himself made in them is neither left nor abandoned; otherwise, their nature would return to nothing if the supreme Essence were not in them. But you say that what he did not make in them—that is, pride and contempt—is abandoned (chapter 18, no. 7, section 6). You plainly resist the truth, which proclaims that God, the most just and irreproachable judge, rightly punishes what he made—namely, apostate angels and impious human beings—for the wickedness of their iniquity.

You also falsely assert that God always dwells in that nature which he created for himself, although Scripture teaches that his dwelling occurs only through grace. Accordingly, when, in your praise of blessed Augustine, you insist that he did not intend the statement “those whom he justly predestined to punishment” to be understood in the same way as “those whom he mercifully predestined to grace,” the arguments already given refute you abundantly. There is no need to keep repeating, as though they were fearful, matters that have already been sufficiently avoided.

Why do you trample so violently upon God’s providence and impiously oppose his dispositions? Certainly, although those who lived without knowledge of God’s power and dispensation possessed whatever force of intellect they may have had, and tried to persuade people that human life was governed by fate and fortune, they nevertheless did not declare that it occurred without providence, since they attributed it to gods and goddesses whom they called by those very names—namely, Fate and Fortune. They also assigned a threefold distribution of fate to the names Megaera, Alecto, and Tisiphone, attributing to their arrangements the beginning, progress, and end of human life. Thus they did not assert in any way that either happiness or unhappiness, good fortune or misfortune, could occur without the ordering of their gods and goddesses.

You, by contrast, contradicting both truth and fictions alike, remove the providence, disposition, and judgment of the true—in fact, the only—God, although the prophet Isaiah plainly proclaims concerning the one true God, as Saint Jerome explains in Book Five on Isaiah:

> “This is the counsel that I have devised over all the earth, and this is the hand extended over all the nations; for the Lord of hosts has decreed, and who can invalidate it? His hand is extended, and who can turn it away?” (Isaiah 14:26–27).

In this passage some think that a general prophecy against the whole world is intended, and that the devastation of Babylon and the city of Assyria is a type of the consummation of the world. We do not contradict this, while knowing that here the whole land of the Assyrians is properly signified, and that all the nations allied with the king of Assyria are indicated. Whatever the Lord has decreed is prevented by no power; no one can restrain his extended hand, prepared to strike.

The same author, in the same work:

> “This word which the Lord spoke concerning Moab from that time” (Isaiah 16:13)—from what time do you think? Clearly, from the time when Moab was created. And the Lord says: “The Moabites and Ammonites shall not enter the assembly of God” (Deuteronomy 23:3). Or, if we understand ‘from that time’ as referring to ancient time, it means that this divine sentence was decreed long ago—not that God’s foreknowledge caused the devastation, but that the future devastation was foreknown by God’s majesty.”

The same author, in the same work:

> “The Lord of hosts devised that he should remove the pride of all glory and bring all the illustrious of the earth to dishonor” (Isaiah 23:9), because above, in the manner of one asking a question, he had said: “Who devised this against Tyre, once crowned?” (Isaiah 23:8). Now he himself answers: it was not that the threads of fate, as fools suppose, were spun in this way; nor did the wheel of fortune run. Rather, it was accomplished by God’s judgment and will—by him who ‘resists the proud and gives grace to the humble’ (James 4:6)—and he admonishes the arrogant concerning their condition, so that they may learn his power through misery, since they were unwilling to experience his mercy through benefits.”

It is certain, by the authority of divine Scripture and the harmony of faithful commentators, that the all-powerful judge judges no one by beginnings but by the end. Scripture says: “He himself considers the end of all things” (Job 28:3). Why, I ask, does he consider the end of all things? Is it so that he may learn something new which he had previously not known? Far from it. Rather, he who establishes the limits of human beings, limits which they cannot pass, considers the end of all things in order to judge each person by it—namely, to reward each person with good according to a good end, and to repay evil with evil according to a bad end.

What, then, contrary either to faith or to God’s justice, is dared if it is most faithfully proclaimed that God predestined what truthful Scripture does not conceal that he either decreed, established, or considered? He established, that is, predestined and disposed, the limits of human beings: “He himself considers the end of all things,” so that he may render to each according to what he deserves. Without doubt he predestined this—that is, disposed it before the ages—because he certainly foreknew and foresaw it. Therefore, what is established by the clearest authority and reasoning of truth must not be denied or attacked with such obstinacy.

Hence Gregory, in the *Moralia* (Book 18, chapter 47), says:

> “‘He set a time for the darkness, and he himself considers the end of all things’ (Job 28:3). He set a time for the darkness, clearly the limit at which the wicked cease to be wicked. Therefore the Apostle says to them: ‘You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord’ (Ephesians 5:8).
>
> “As this same outstanding teacher says elsewhere to his disciples: ‘The night has passed, but the day has drawn near. Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light; let us walk honorably as in the day’ (Homily 13, 42). Therefore, when the Church comes, it is said to her in the *Song of Songs*: ‘Who is this that comes forth like the dawn, rising up?’ (Song of Songs 6:9).
>
> “The Church is plainly described by comparison with the dawn: through the knowledge of faith she is changed from the darkness of her sins into clear light. Thus, ‘he set a time for the darkness, and he himself considers the end of all things’ (Job 28:3). Under the name ‘all things’ he intended both the elect and the reprobate.
>
> “For God, who does and orders good things, does not himself do evil, but evil comes from the wicked; nevertheless, he disposes it so that it does not occur disorderly. He considers the end of all things and patiently tolerates everything. He also observes the end of the elect: that they may be changed from evil to good. He observes the end of the reprobate: that they may be withdrawn from evil deeds and brought to deserved punishment.
>
> “He saw the end of the persecuting Saul, who, struck down, would say: ‘Lord, what do you command me to do?’ (Acts 9:6). He saw the end of the apparently obedient disciple, who, for the crime he had committed, would tighten a noose around his throat (Matthew 27:5), both punishing himself as a sinner and, by punishing himself more severely, deceiving himself. He saw the sinning Ninevites (Jonah 1:2), but considered the end of the sinners: the repentance of those who were corrected (Jonah 3:10). He also saw Sodom sinning (Genesis 18:20), but considered the end of the burning of lust: the fire of Gehenna (Genesis 19:24). He saw the end of the Gentiles: possessing the darkness of iniquities, they would eventually shine with the light of faith. He also saw the end of Judea: that, blinded by the hardened faithlessness and darkness, she would turn away from the light of faith which she had held.”

## AGAINST JOHN SCOTUS

1318

If, I say, predestination is nothing other than preparation, it follows that, just as those who were prepared—that is, permitted to prepare themselves—for punishment, so certainly those who were predestined—that is, permitted to predestine themselves—to punishment must be understood in the same way.

But it is evil, and, so to speak, the worst of all evils, for anyone to prepare or predestine himself for punishment, to which no one is prepared or predestined by himself except by committing evil, that is, by sinning.

And what will you do with your much-vaunted exposition, in which you have undertaken so obstinately to assert that God’s predestination, preparation, and foreknowledge are placed only in the elect? A little earlier you had said:

## JOHN SCOTUS

(Chapter 18, no. 15, section 8)

> “The number, therefore, of all whom God created was predestined. But since the Creator foresaw that this number would generally perish in the first man, except for the remedy of the wound, which is Christ, he predestined—that is, defined before they existed—the number of those whom he would free by his grace and the number of those whom he would leave to his justice: in the former he would bestow the gifts of his mercy; in the latter he would complete the number of nature, by which the whole would be perfected.”

### Correction

You placed “he foresaw” in relation to evil with such clarity that you can deny it only with complete shamelessness. For who would not say that perishing is evil? If, then, God foresaw that the human race as a whole would perish in the first man, he certainly foresaw evil. And if, as you insist—or rather, perjure yourself—predestining is nothing other than foreseeing and preparing, it follows, according to the constructions of your obstinacy, that just as God foresaw the number of the human race that would perish, so also he predestined and prepared it.

Your statements therefore cannot stand—those by which you have hitherto tried so obstinately to establish that God neither foresaw nor predestined nor prepared evil, sin, punishments, and torments. For anyone’s perishing through his own fault is evil; likewise, for each person to acquire punishment for himself through evil deeds is evil. If, therefore, God foresaw these things and permitted sinners to prepare themselves for them, he certainly foresaw, predestined, and prepared evil.

And what you add is:

## JOHN SCOTUS

(Chapter 18, no. 18, section 9)
