## S. PRUDENTIUS, BISHOP OF TROYES

1319–1320

### Correction

However this punitive condemnation may stand, you plainly assert that it was predestined by God, by whom the wickedness of those who perish is restrained and held back so that it does not reach the courses they desire. You therefore say:

## JOHN SCOTUS

(Chapter 19, no. 12, section 1)

> “Concerning the eternal fire, however, about which the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Go into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels’ (Matthew 25:41), there is no doubt that it should be understood as corporeal, although on account of the subtlety of its nature it is called incorporeal—just as I would not believe that the spirit of the ether is corporeal, since the fourth part of creation is bodily. Nor do I believe that another fire was prepared to punish the devil with all his members, apart from this very one, which is the fourth element of the world.”

What, then? Is it surprising if those bodies of the impious—which are certainly composed from these four bodily elements and, at the time predetermined for them, must be dissolved into those same elements, only to be restored from them again at the moment of the resurrection—suffer the eternal torments of their impiety in that fire in which all bodies will be resurrected and which will be most substantial?

### Correction

All orthodox Christians agree that the flame and visible fire of Gehenna is corporeal, mixed with darkness. Whether it is the same fire that is called the fourth element of the world is a considerable question. Yet it appears, both from the words of Saint Gregory which we quoted above and from the Lord’s statement, to be another fire, since he says: “Go into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41).

For what need would there have been to say specifically that it was prepared for the torment of sinners if it were the same fire known to have been provided for all mortal needs and uses? Moreover, when Scripture says: “A fire will devour him that is not kindled” (Job 20:26), something else must be understood. For this fire, which is supplied for our daily needs, cannot subsist without fuel of wood or some other material; but it is clear that the fire of Gehenna needs no such fuel. Hence in the Gospels it is called “unquenchable” (Mark 9:42, 44).

Its quality also differs greatly from that of this fire. This fire consumes whatever it touches without distinction; that one, although it will burn souls and bodies, does not act so that they cease entirely to exist. Nor does it burn everything equally. Rather, according to the variety or enormity of their crimes, it is said to torment one less and another more. Thus, just as in the kingdom of heaven the diversity of dwelling places arises from the unequal merits of the inhabitants, so in the abyss of hell the unequal wickedness of deeds produces a variety of torments for those plunged into it.

From this passage Gregory’s dialogue partner Peter addressed blessed Gregory as follows (*Dialogues*, Book 4, chapter 43):

> **Peter:** “I ask you: should one fire of Gehenna be believed to exist? Or, according to however great the diversity of sins has been, should we also suppose that as many fires have been prepared?”
>
> **Gregory:** “There is indeed one fire of Gehenna, but it does not torment all sinners in one way. For each person—”

[scan page 668]

## On Predestination

Thus, each person will feel punishment there in proportion to the measure of his guilt [or: “there is felt punishment in such measure”]. For just as in this world many stand beneath one sun, yet do not all feel the heat of the same sun equally, since one is hotter and another less so, so there the mode of burning is not one and the same in the one fire. For what the diversity of bodies does here, the diversity of sins does there: they possess a fire that is not different, yet it burns each of them differently.

**Peter** [same work, chapter 44]: “I ask you, then: are we to say that those who have once been plunged into that place will burn forever?”

**Gregory:** “It is altogether certain [or: unquestionably so] and indisputably true that, just as there will be no end to the joy of the good, so there will be no end to the torment of the wicked. For since Truth says, ‘The wicked will go into everlasting punishment, but the righteous into everlasting life’ (Matthew 25:46), because what he promised is true, there is no doubt that what God threatened was not false.”

**Peter:** “What if someone says that he threatened sinners with everlasting punishment for this reason: that he might restrain them from committing sins [or: ‘might have restrained them’]?”

**Gregory:** “If what he threatened was false, so that he might correct them from injustice, then what he promised was also false, so that he might summon them to righteousness. But who would dare to say this, unless he were insane? And if he threatened what was not going to be fulfilled, while we wish to call him merciful, we are compelled to proclaim him deceitful—which it is impious to say.”

**Peter:** “I should like to know how it is just that a fault committed with an end should be punished without end.”

**Gregory:** “This would rightly be said if the strict judge considered not the hearts of human beings but their deeds. The wicked transgressed with an end because they lived with an end; for, if they could have lived without end, they would certainly have wished to live so that they might sin without end. They show that they desire to live forever in sin, since while they live they never cease to sin. It therefore belongs to the great justice of the judge that those should never lack punishment who in this life never wished to lack sin.”

**Peter:** “But no righteous person feeds on cruelty, and a delinquent servant is ordered by his own [or: ‘just’] master to be beaten for this reason: that he may be corrected from his wickedness. He is therefore beaten so that he may be reformed. But if the wicked, handed over to the fires of Gehenna, do not attain correction, for what end will they burn forever?”

**Gregory:** “Almighty God, because he is merciful, does not feed upon the suffering of the wretched; but because he is just, he is not forever sated with vengeance upon the wicked. All the wicked, however, assigned to everlasting punishment, are indeed punished for their own wickedness, yet they will burn for a purpose: namely, so that all the righteous may see in God the joys that they receive and may behold in them the punishments that they escaped. Thus they may recognize all the more that they are eternally debtors to divine grace, the more they see eternally punished the evils which they had overcome by his help.”

**Peter:** “And where is the holiness of the saints, if they do not pray for their enemies when they see them burning then, although it was certainly said to them, ‘Pray for your enemies’ (Luke 6:28)?”

**Gregory:** “They pray for their enemies at the time when they are able to turn their hearts toward fruitful repentance and to save them through that conversion. For what else is it to pray for one’s enemies than what the Apostle says: ‘That God may grant them repentance for the knowledge of the truth, and that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive for his will’ (2 Timothy 2:25–26)?”

**Peter:** “I accept what you say. And how will prayer then be offered for those who can no longer in any way be changed from wickedness to works of righteousness [or: ‘how will they pray’]?”

**Gregory:** “The same reason, therefore, explains why prayer is not then offered for human beings condemned to everlasting fire. It is also the reason why prayer is not now offered for the devil and his angels, assigned to everlasting punishment; and it is likewise the reason why holy people do not now pray for unbelieving and wicked persons who have died: namely, because they refuse to have the merit of their prayer annulled before the presence of the just Judge on behalf of those whom they already know to have been assigned to everlasting punishment. If even now the righteous who are alive do not greatly pity the unjust who are dead and condemned, although they themselves know that some judgment concerning their own case is still to be endured, how much more strictly will they then regard the torments of the wicked, when, stripped of every corruption of vice, they will themselves already cling more closely and firmly to righteousness? For their minds will be so absorbed by the force of strict judgment, because they cling to the most just Judge, that they will not at all delight in whatever they see to be at variance with the subtle rule of that eternal law [or: ‘whatever is at variance with it’; with *viderint* omitted in one reading].”

Since all this certainly cannot be accomplished by the fire provided for our temporal needs in this world, it is inferred that another fire must be understood—the one said to have been prepared for the devil and his angels (Matthew 25:41). Thus it may perhaps, without improbability, be said that another fire was created for tormenting the ungodly by God: a fire capable of burning their bodies without fuel from material substances, and their souls without diminution either of itself or of them. It is manifest that this present fire is wholly incapable of doing so without bodily fuel.

Since I presume to affirm nothing rashly about these matters, I hold this as certain concerning that fire: the fourth element, as it is called, will in no way substantially persist in the bodies of the saints. For those whose glory and incorruption will be true will certainly need neither air nor water; reason also indicates that fire will not be necessary to them. It is promised to all the saints that in the glory of that blessed resurrection they will be equal to the angels of God (Luke 20:36). Just as the holy angels do not possess the glory of their blessedness in this fire—for they are believed not to have been composed from the elements but to have been made from nothing—so the saints, although they possess the same bodies that had been dissolved through death, will be changed by everlasting glorification; nevertheless, they will receive the reward of blessedness in no way in fire, but always in the contemplation of the living God, who is bounded by no intervals of the elements or of any created things. Rather, by his almighty power he fills, governs, completes, and contains all things.

Since, as we have already proved, our Lord Jesus Christ truly and faithfully is believed and proclaimed to have ascended bodily above all creatures, we believe that all the saints will be there, rejoicing in eternal exultation in the company of blessed spirits, for he himself says: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered” (Matthew 24:28)—not within the four elements of the world, which faith holds and affirms that they will no longer need.

For if it is utterly absurd to suppose that the holy angels have received the reward of their blessedness within the elements of the world, how could holy human beings, who are said to be equal to their blessedness, be placed anywhere other than where they are most certainly believed to abide and to whom they are equal? I see that this agrees neither with reason nor with authority. Concerning this you continue by adding:

## John Scotus

(*On the Division of Nature*, book XIX, number 3, section 2)

“Where it is not incongruously to be believed that the bodies of the saints will be changed into an ethereal quality, which cannot be consumed by another quality, although it can change into itself the qualities of inferior bodies; but the bodies of the impious will pass into an airy quality, so that they may suffer from the superior fire.”

## Correction

I pronounce this wholly contrary to the Catholic faith, since blessed Job says: “And again I shall be surrounded by my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God; I myself shall see him whom I shall see, and my eyes shall behold, and not another” (Job 19:26–27). For the ether is not flesh: it is not surrounded by skin, nor is it joined together by bones and nerves. The Lord himself shows that he possessed these things after he had been glorified in the resurrection, when he said: “See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself; touch and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39). Likewise he said to the apostle Thomas: “Put your finger here, and see my hands; bring your hand, and put it into my side; and do not be unbelieving but believing” (John 20:27). For Thomas had said: “Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and put my finger into the place of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.” After touching these places, Thomas answered and said: “My Lord and my God” (ibid., 25, 28). No orthodox person has ever asserted or taught that these things could occur in an ethereal body.

You, however, grant the opinions of Origen, who, discussing the resurrection in many ways, repeatedly emphasizes the resurrection and glorification of bodies, but either entirely denies the flesh or craftily conceals it under the word “body.”

Therefore it seems necessary first to ask what the ether is, so that the remaining matters may be treated more appropriately in sequence. Ether, as Isidore says (*Etymologies*, book XIII, chapters 5 and 7), is a place in which the stars are, and it signifies fire, which is borne upward from a place in the world. Properly speaking, ether is the element itself; *aither* is the brilliance of the ether; and it is called *aithēr* by the Greeks. Air has much in common with the emptiness of space, whereas the other elements are more substantial. This [air] is partly close to the earth and partly close to the heavens. The subtler air, in which windy and stormy movements cannot exist, belongs to the heavenly region. The other, more turbulent air, which takes shape from moist exhalations, is assigned to the earth and produces many forms from itself: when in motion, it makes winds; when stirred more violently, fires and thunder; when gathered together, clouds; when thickened, rain; when the clouds freeze, snow; when they freeze more violently, hail; and when it is dispersed, clear weather results. For dense air is evidently a cloud, while a rarefied cloud is loose air.”

Bede, in *On Genesis* (*Hexaemeron*, book I, column 22):

“For after the stars had been made, it [light] was added to the increase of the primordial light, so that even luminous night might arise, whether from the brightness of the moon or of the stars, or from whatever else was irradiated—which until then had known nothing beyond its ancient darkness. For although night very often appears dark and blind to us, because the air that is nearest the earth has been obscured by cloudy vapors, nevertheless those higher spaces, which are called by the name of ether and extend from this turbulent air as far as the stars’ heaven, always return a shining brilliance from the surrounding stars.”

Since these things are so, if the bodies of the saints are changed into an ethereal quality, either they will be fire and will lose the reality of an earthly body, or they will be heaven and stars, and will nevertheless be flesh, bones, and nerves. No serious student is unaware of how far this is from the sincerity of the Christian faith. For when the Apostle says, “We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:51 and following), let him himself teach us what kind of change is to be believed:

“It is sown in corruption, it rises in incorruption; it is sown in dishonor, it rises in glory; it is sown in weakness, it rises in power; it is sown an animal body, it rises a spiritual body.” And again: “We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed. For this corruptible thing must put on incorruption, and this mortal thing must put on immortality.”

Behold: the Apostle proclaims the change of the saints, not the loss of their substance, but their glorification—namely, that the body which is buried in corruption, dishonor, and weakness may rise in that blessedness of resurrection incorruptible, strong, and glorious. Thus it will continue to exist in the truth of its substance as tangible, touchable, and visible, so that glory will be added according to its merits, and its nature will not be changed into some other nature by an invention.

Hence Saint Jerome, in his *Letter to the Galatians*, says:

“For when, he says, the holy trumpet has sounded, there will be neither circumcision nor uncircumcision, neither Jew nor Gentile, but a new creation, into which the body of our humiliation is transformed in conformity with the body of Christ’s glory. For the former things have passed away; behold, all things have become new. And just as one star differs from another star in glory, so also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Corinthians 15:41–42).

[scan page 670]

Daniel agrees with this in a clear voice, saying: “Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will rise, some to everlasting life, and others to everlasting shame and everlasting disgrace; but the intelligent will shine like the splendor of the firmament, and many of the righteous like the stars forever and ever” (Daniel 12:2–3). For in the sun and moon, the firmament, and the stars, neither circumcision nor uncircumcision avails anything; rather, there is a new condition without those parts of bodies that can be cut off. Thus we would deny that Peter and the Lord possessed true bodies, since they walked upon the waters (Matthew 14:25 and 29), which is contrary to nature. In the resurrection of the dead they will neither marry nor be given in marriage, but will be like the angels (Luke 20:35–36); and afterward others will be in heaven, while virgins will begin to be on earth with the likeness of angels. This is the difference between them according to substance and according to glory.

“We know him according to the flesh.” Certainly, in the resurrection the substance of bodies will be the same as that which we now have, although their glory will be greater. For after his descent into the underworld, the Savior had that same body in which he had been crucified: he showed his hands pierced by nails and displayed the wound in his side (John 20:20 and 27). Moreover, he entered when the doors were shut (ibid., 19 and 26), something which human bodily nature does not permit. Therefore we shall deny that Peter and the Lord had true bodies and walked upon the waters (Matthew 14:25, 29), which is contrary to nature.

We shall have what “neither eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart” (1 Corinthians 2:9), when, having been transformed from the body of our humiliation, we shall be conformed to the body of the glory of the Lord Jesus Christ. We shall have a body into which neither a Jew can intrude with circumcision, nor a Gentile with uncircumcision, nor anything else [or: “not anything else”] that differs according to substance but according to glory.

Jerome, likewise, in his exposition of the prophet Jonah:

“And you will raise my life from corruption, Lord my God” (Jonah 2:7). The Septuagint has: “And my life will ascend from corruption, Lord my God.” He therefore said “you will raise” or “will ascend from the corruption of my life,” because he had descended into corruption and into the underworld. This is what the apostles interpret as having been prophesied in the fifteenth Psalm concerning the person of the Lord: “For you will not abandon my soul in the underworld, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption.” This plainly refers to David, since he died and was buried; but the flesh of the Savior did not see [or: “will not see”] corruption.

Others, however, interpret it as meaning that, in comparison with the blessedness of God’s eternity and Word, the human body is corruption: it is sown in corruption, and this is signified in the hundred and second Psalm concerning the person of the righteous: “He heals all your infirmities; he redeems your life from destruction.” Hence the Apostle also says: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from the body of this death?” (Romans 7:24), and it is called “the body of death” or “the body of humiliation.”

The heretics use this as an occasion to fabricate the Antichrist under the person of Christ, to possess the churches so that they may fatten their bellies, and, living according to the flesh, argue against the flesh. But we know that Christ took a body from the incorrupt virgin: it was not Christ’s corruption but a temple.

If we are drawn into the meaning of the Apostle in the First Letter to the Corinthians (15:44), where the body is called spiritual, then, lest we seem contentious, we shall say that the very same body and the same flesh will rise which was buried and placed in the earth, but that it will change its nature. For “this corruptible thing must put on incorruption, and this mortal thing must put on immortality.” When the body is said to rise, it is, in a certain manner, grasped between two fingers: this body in which we are born, this in which we die; this which the womb receives, this which breasts nourish; this which virginity awaits as a reward, and which adultery fears as punishment.

Jerome, likewise, in book I *Against Jovinianus*:

“We who believe in Christ follow Christ’s example. We know that there is one condition according to the flesh, but another is promised according to the spirit. Among the angels there is no difference of sex. Either we shall be without sex, as the angels are, or—what the evident proof of the resurrection clearly confirms—we shall rise in our proper sex, but sex will not perform its function.”

Augustine, in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 88:

“For the earthly matter from which the flesh of mortals is created does not perish from God. Whether it is dissolved into whatever dust or ash, dispersed into whatever breezes and airs, changed into the substance of whatever other bodies or into the elements themselves, or becomes food for any animals, even for human beings, and is changed into flesh, it returns in an instant of time to that human soul which originally animated it, so that a human being might be made, grow, and live.”

And later in the same work (chapter 91):

“The bodies of the saints will therefore rise without any defect, without any deformity, without any corruption, burden, or difficulty, with as much ease as there will be blessedness. For this reason they are also called spiritual, although they will unquestionably be bodies, not spirits. Just as what is now called an animal body is nevertheless a body and not an animal soul, so then it will be a spiritual body: nevertheless a body, not a spirit.

Therefore, insofar as concerns the corruption that now weighs down the soul (Wisdom 9:15), and the vices by which the flesh lusts against the spirit (Galatians 5:17), then it will not be flesh but body—for heavenly bodies are also so called. Hence it is said, ‘Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God’; and, explaining what he meant, he adds: ‘Nor will corruption possess incorruption’ (1 Corinthians 15:50, 53). What he first called ‘flesh and blood,’ he later called ‘corruption’; and what he first called ‘the kingdom of God,’ he later called ‘incorruption.’

But insofar as concerns substance, even then it will be flesh. For after the resurrection Christ’s body was also called flesh (Luke 24:39). The Apostle therefore says, ‘It is sown an animal body, it will rise a spiritual body’ [or: ‘it will rise’], because then there will be such harmony between flesh and spirit that the spirit will vivify without conflict and will have the flesh subject to it without any resistant need [or: ‘without any contentious necessity’; variant: ‘without any contentious need’], so that we may not have an enemy within us, but may suffer such an enemy outside us.”

Gregory, in *Moralia*, book XIV, chapter 29:

[scan page 671]

“I hear of the resurrection, but I seek to know its effect. For I believe that I shall rise, but I wish to hear what kind of body I shall have. It is necessary for me to know whether I shall rise in some other body, perhaps ethereal or airy, or in the body in which I shall die. For if I rise in an airy body, then I shall not be the one who rises; for how can there be a true resurrection if the flesh cannot truly exist? Reason plainly suggests that, if there is no true flesh, there will certainly be no true resurrection, for resurrection cannot rightly be called resurrection where what fell does not rise.

But blessed Job, remove from us these clouds of doubt; and, since through the grace of the Holy Spirit you have received you have begun to speak openly to us concerning the hope of our resurrection, judge clearly whether our flesh truly rises. It follows: ‘And again I shall be surrounded by my skin’ (Job 19:26). When skin is plainly mentioned, every doubt about the true resurrection is removed. For it is not as Eutychius, bishop of Constantinople, wrote: that our body will possess another glory of resurrection, impalpable and subtler than wind and air. In that glory of resurrection our body will indeed be subtle through the effect of spiritual power, but palpable through the truth of its nature.

Hence our Redeemer, when his disciples doubted his resurrection, showed his hands and side and offered bones and flesh to be touched, saying: ‘Touch and see, for a spirit does not have bones and flesh, as you see that I have’ (Luke 24:38–39). When, therefore, he had brought this testimony of the Gospel [or: ‘of Gospel truth’] against Eutychius, who was placed in Constantinople, he said: ‘The Lord did this for this reason: to remove from the hearts of the disciples their doubt about his resurrection.’

To him, I say, what you assert is exceedingly strange: that doubt should arise for us from the very thing by which the hearts of the disciples were healed of doubt. For what worse thing could be said than that this should make us doubt the reality of his flesh, by which his disciples were restored to complete freedom from doubt? If it is asserted that he did not possess what he showed, then from the very thing by which the faith of his disciples was confirmed our faith is destroyed.”

He also added:

“He possessed a palpable body, which he showed. But after he had confirmed the hearts of those who touched him, everything in the Lord that could be touched was reduced to some subtle state.”

To this he himself replied:

“It is written: ‘Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death will no longer rule over him’ (Romans 6:9). Therefore, if anything in his body could have been changed after the resurrection, then, contrary to Paul’s truthful statement, after the Lord’s resurrection he would have returned to death. Who would dare to say this, unless he were foolish, except one who denies the true resurrection of his flesh?”

Then he objected to me:

“When it is written, ‘Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God’ (1 Corinthians 15:50), on what grounds should we believe that flesh truly rises?”

I replied that in sacred Scripture “flesh” is spoken of in one way according to nature and in another according to guilt or corruption. Flesh according to nature is meant where it is written: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Genesis 2:23), and: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). Flesh according to guilt is meant where God says: “My Spirit will not remain in these human beings forever, because they are flesh” (Genesis 6:3), and where the Psalmist says: “He remembered that they were flesh, a spirit that goes away and does not return” (Psalm 77:39). Hence the disciples of Paul were not “in the flesh” (Romans 8:9), although they were not without flesh; rather, because they had overcome the passions of fleshly desires through the power of the spirit, they were not in the flesh.

When the Apostle says that flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God, he wishes “flesh” to be understood according to guilt, not according to nature. He shows this immediately when he says: “Nor will corruption possess incorruption.” In that glory of the heavenly kingdom, therefore, there will be flesh according to nature, but not according to the desires of passion [or: “passions”], because, having conquered the sting of death, it will reign in everlasting incorruption.

After these words, Eutychius immediately replied that he agreed. Nevertheless, he still denied that a palpable body could rise. In the little book he had written on the resurrection, he had also inserted the testimony of the Apostle Paul:

“You fool, what you sow is not made alive unless it dies first; and what you sow is not the body that will be, but a bare grain” (1 Corinthians 15:36–37).

By this he was hastening to demonstrate that the flesh would either be impalpable or would not exist at all, since the holy Apostle, speaking of the glory of the resurrection, had said: “You do not sow the body that will be.” But he must be answered at once. When the Apostle Paul says, “You do not sow the body that will be, but a bare grain,” the grain signifies what we see: the grain is born with stalk and leaves, but it is sown without stalk and leaves.

In the increase of the glory of the resurrection, therefore, he did not say that what existed in the seed was lacking, but that what did not exist was added. This man, however, while denying that the true body will rise, does not say that what was lacking will be added, but that what existed will be lacking.

When the dispute over this matter had thus been prolonged in a lengthy controversy, we began to resist together by the most serious reasoning. When the emperor Tiberius Constantine, of pious memory, received both him and me privately and learned what disagreement existed between us, he weighed the arguments of both parties and, destroying with his own arguments the same book which Eutychius had written on the resurrection, decided that it ought to be burned in the flames.

After we had left him, a severe illness immediately followed me, while Eutychius was followed by sickness and death. After his death, since there was scarcely anyone who would follow his opinions, I refrained from pursuing what I had begun, lest I seem to be hurling words into ashes [or: “little tales”].

Nevertheless, while he was still alive and I was suffering from very serious fevers, as I learned from the reports of those who visited him to greet him, he held the skin of his hand before their eyes and said: “I confess that we shall all rise in this flesh.” As they themselves acknowledged, he had previously been accustomed wholly to deny this.

[scan page 672]

But setting these matters aside, let us examine carefully the words of blessed Job to determine whether the resurrection will be a true resurrection of the true body. We cannot doubt the hope of the resurrection when he says: “And on the last day I shall rise from the earth” (Job 19:25–26). He also removed doubt concerning the restoration of the true body when he said: “And again I shall be surrounded by my skin.” To remove any remaining ambiguity from our thought, he adds: “And in my flesh I shall see God.”

Behold: he openly confesses resurrection, skin, and flesh. What, then, remains from which our mind could doubt? If this holy man believed, before the effect of the Lord’s resurrection, that the flesh would be restored in its complete state, what ground for our doubt remains if the true resurrection of the flesh is not believed even after the example of the Redeemer?

For if the body will not be palpable after the resurrection, then plainly something other than what dies rises—and it is impious to believe that I die and another rises. Therefore, blessed Job, I ask you, add what you feel and remove from us the scruple of this question. It follows:

“Whom I myself shall see, and my eyes shall behold, and not another” (ibid., 27).

For if, as certain erroneous followers believe, the body will not be palpable after the resurrection, but the subtlety of an invisible body will be called flesh, although it is not the substance of flesh, then plainly one person dies and another rises. But blessed Job destroys this opinion with a truthful voice when he says: “Whom I myself shall see, and not another, and my eyes shall behold.”

Following the faith of blessed Job, and truly believing in the palpable body of our Redeemer after the resurrection, we confess that our flesh will exist after the resurrection and will be both the same and different: the same by nature, different by glory; the same in reality, different in power. It will therefore be subtle [or: “spiritual”], because it will be incorruptible; it will be palpable, because it will not lose the essential truth of its nature [or: “the truth of its nature turns”].”

The truth of flesh and bones, however greatly they are to be glorified in the glory of that resurrection, is unanimously proclaimed by all, and no one teaches a change into an ethereal quality.

But lest you think that we should be prejudiced against Augustine by his words—for in the book of the *Eighty-Three Questions* he is said to have stated that the angelic bodies we hope to have must be believed to be exceedingly luminous and ethereal—listen to what he himself later retracted concerning this statement.

Augustine, *Retractations*, book I, chapter 26:

“If this is understood as meaning that there will be no members such as we now have and no substance of flesh, although incorruptible, the view is mistaken. The question is treated much better in the work *The City of God*.”

The same author, retracting his book *On the Christian Contest* (*ibid.*, book II, chapter 3):

“In that work the following was written: ‘Nor should we listen to those who deny that there will be a resurrection of the flesh and recall what the Apostle Paul says: “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 15:50), without understanding that the same Apostle says: “This corruptible thing must put on incorruption, and this mortal thing must put on immortality” (ibid., 53–54). For when this has happened, it will no longer be flesh and blood but a heavenly body.’

This should not be understood as though the substance of flesh will not exist in the future, but rather that the Apostle called the corruption of flesh and blood by the name “flesh and blood”; that corruption will certainly not exist in that kingdom where flesh will be incorruptible. It may also be understood in another way: that the Apostle called the works of flesh and blood “flesh and blood,” and that those who persistently loved such things will not possess the kingdom of God.”

Likewise, in his retraction of the book *On Faith and the Creed*:

“In this book, when the resurrection of the flesh was being discussed, I said: ‘The body will rise according to the Christian faith, which cannot deceive. Whoever thinks this incredible considers what flesh is now, but does not consider what it will be then, because at the time of that angelic transformation it will no longer be flesh and blood but only body.’ I also discussed there the change of earthly bodies into heavenly bodies, because the Apostle said, when speaking of this: ‘Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God’ (1 Corinthians 15:50).

But anyone who understands this as though the earthly body, such as we now have, is changed in the resurrection into a heavenly body in such a way that these members will not remain and that there will be no future substance of flesh must unquestionably be corrected by being reminded of the Lord’s body. After the resurrection he appeared with those same members, not only to be seen by the eyes but also to be touched by the hands, and he confirmed in speech that he possessed flesh, saying: ‘Touch and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have’ (Luke 24:39).

It is therefore clear that the Apostle did not deny that the substance of flesh will exist in the kingdom of God, but either called those who live according to the flesh by the name ‘flesh and blood,’ or called the corruption of flesh by that name—corruption which will certainly not then exist.”

Augustine, in book XXII of *The City of God*, chapter 24:

“What, then, will those things be, if all these things are so great and of such a kind? What will he give to those whom he predestined to life, who gave these things even to those whom he predestined to death? What good things will that blessed life make them receive, for whose sake in this miserable life he wished his only-begotten Son to endure such great evils even unto death?

Hence the Apostle, speaking of those predestined to that kingdom, says: ‘He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how will he not also, together with him, graciously give us all things?’ (Romans 8:32).

When this promise is fulfilled, what shall we be, and what kind of beings shall we be? What good things shall we receive in that kingdom? For we have already received such a pledge in Christ’s dying for us. What will the spirit of a human being be like when it has no defect whatsoever—nothing beneath which it lies, nothing to which it yields, nothing against which it must even laudably struggle—but is perfected in completely peaceful virtue?

Of all the things there—”

## [Scan page 673]

### S. Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

[They will have] every thing, however great, however splendid, however secure in knowledge, without any error or labor, when the wisdom of God is drunk from its own source with the highest happiness and without any difficulty. What will the body be like, wholly subject to its spirit and sufficiently [al.: in a fitting manner] nourished by it, so that it will need no food? For it will be spiritual, not animal, possessing indeed the substance of flesh, but without any carnal corruption.]

*The same author, in his Paschal Homily* (Sermon 18):

[Listen, ignorant man; deaf to the daily readings, listen to how it returns indeed to the body, but not to this death—not because it will be another body, but because “this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality” (I Cor. 15:52). My brothers, when the Apostle said “this corruptible, this mortal,” he was in a certain manner touching his own flesh with the word; therefore it will not be another. “I do not,” he says, “lay aside an earthly body and receive an airy body, or receive an ethereal body; I receive this very body, but no longer subject to this death, because this corruptible must put on incorruption—not another, but this one—and this mortal—not another, but this one—must put on immortality.”]

The unanimous judgment, therefore, of all orthodox Christians concerning the resurrection of human bodies is that they will rise in the very same flesh in which they were dissolved and reduced to corruption and dust—sharing the same bones, the same limbs, and the same organs—with immortality added to all, but perpetual glorification to the saints alone; while to the impious the immortality of nature will be preserved only for punishment.

For whatever could falsely be asserted or deceitfully imagined concerning the bodies of those who rise has been dispelled by the truth of the flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ when he rose again. By offering it as tangible, visible to mortal eyes, and even recognizable by its scars, he showed what ought to be believed concerning his limbs: namely, that he would rise not in an ethereal or airy body, but in that body in which he could have been dissolved, although glorified in every way.

Nor is the following consideration any less persuasive in support of this assertion: since all sinners also will see the Lord and Savior at the Judgment, they are believed to see him not in an ethereal body, but in flesh, although immortal, because “they will look upon him whom they pierced.” There are no scars, nor can there be any, in an ethereal body. It remains, therefore, that he will be seen in the earthly substance which, although thereafter heavenly, incorruptible, indeed ineffably glorified, will nevertheless be a body in which the impious will see the scars of the wounds which they inflicted most cruelly and unjustly, and which they despised and mocked most stubbornly and proudly.

Unless, perhaps, you intend to say with Marcion and his associates that our Lord Jesus Christ, when ascending into heaven, laid aside his tabernacle—that is, his body—and either remains in heaven without a body, or has resumed another body, whether ethereal or whatever you may prefer. The ecclesiastical piety of old condemned that impiety together with its authors.

It is therefore certain that none of the bodies of the saints will be changed into an ethereal quality, nor any of the bodies of the reprobate into an airy quality; rather, the same bodies that had died in time will rise again, so that in them they may receive what they deserve.

Your impudence is especially exposed by the fact that you attribute to the damned the transformation which the Apostle assigns to the saints alone, saying: “We shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed” (I Cor. 15:51). And again: “The dead shall rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed” (ibid., 52).

Nor is it surprising that you impudently oppose the clear teaching of the Apostle and the faith, since you have dared to bark against apostolic sublimity. Nor will the bodies of the impious, as you deliriously claim, suffer a consuming fire above; rather, they will burn unchangeably in that fire “which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41).

Hence Augustine, in the twenty-first book of *The City of God* (chapter 4):

[What further examples are required from us, by which we may teach that it is not incredible that the bodies of human beings punished with everlasting torment may neither lose life in the fire nor burn without destruction, and may suffer without perishing? For this flesh will then possess a quality bestowed on it by him who has bestowed such marvelous and varied qualities on so many things that we see, so that we do not marvel at them merely because they are numerous.]

In the same work (book 21, chapter 9):

[Whatever God said through his prophet would happen to those condemned to everlasting punishment will happen completely: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished” (Isa. 66:24).

For the purpose of impressing this more forcefully, the Lord Jesus also, speaking of the limbs which cause a person to stumble, ordered them to be cut off for the sake of all those whom each person loves as his own members with his right hand. “It is good for you,” he says, “to enter into eternal life maimed, rather than, having two hands, to be cast into the gehenna of unquenchable fire, where their worm shall not die and their fire shall not be extinguished” (Mark 9:43).

Likewise concerning the foot: “It is good for you,” he says, “to enter into eternal life lame, rather than, having two feet, to be cast into the gehenna of unquenchable fire, where their worm shall not die and the fire shall not be extinguished” (ibid.).

He says the same concerning the eye: “It is good for you, with one eye, to enter into the kingdom of God, rather than, having two eyes, to be cast into the gehenna of unquenchable fire, where their worm shall not die and the fire shall not be extinguished” (ibid., 47).

He was not troubled to say the same words three times in one place. Who would not be terrified by this repetition and by the forceful declaration [al.: threat] of that punishment from the divine mouth?

Some say that both of these—the fire, namely, and the worm—which they wish to refer to the punishments of souls [al.: of the soul], not of the body, mean that those who have been separated from the kingdom of God will be burned by the pain of their spirit [al.: soul], repenting too late and fruitlessly; and they contend that the fire burning for this pain could appropriately be understood in this way.

Hence the Apostle’s statement: “Who is made to stumble, and I am not on fire?” (II Cor. 11:29). They think that the same thing should be understood by the worm. For, they say, it is written: “As the moth consumes a garment and the worm wood, so sorrow tortures the heart of a man” (Prov. 15:21).

Those, however, who do not doubt that punishments of both soul and body will occur, yet maintain that the body is burned by fire while the soul is in some manner gnawed by the worm of sorrow. If this seems more credible to them because it is surely absurd to give life to fires, they contend that incorporeal souls can be afflicted by corporeal fires. But, as I have said, it is wholly marvelous and beyond human understanding that spirits adhere to bodies and become living beings—and that the human being himself is such. I nevertheless find it easier to say that both fire and worm pertain to the body than that neither does.

Accordingly, the soul’s pain is left unstated in those words of divine Scripture, because it is understood as a consequence even if not said: as the body is afflicted by pain, so the soul too is afflicted by fruitless repentance. For even in the ancient Scriptures it is written: “The vengeance of the flesh of the impious is fire and worm” (Ecclus. 7:19). It could have been said more briefly, “The vengeance of the impious”; why, then, is it called that of the flesh unless both—that is, both fire and worm—are the vengeance of the flesh? Or, if he wished to speak of the vengeance of the flesh because what a person did according to the flesh will be avenged in him—for on that account he will come to the second death, as the Apostle signified when he said, “For if you live according to the flesh, you shall die” (Rom. 8:13)—let each person attach to whichever he prefers: either fire to the body and the worm to the soul, the former literally and the latter figuratively [al.: literally, the former, and not the latter]; or both literally to the body.

I have already argued sufficiently above that even living things may exist in fire without being consumed, by a miracle of the omnipotent Creator: in pain without death.]

A little later, in the same work:

[Let each person, therefore, attach either the fire or the worm to whichever he prefers, and decide whether the worm properly belongs to the body or to the soul, the word having been transferred from bodily things to incorporeal ones, and so forth.

Yet in no way should we believe that those bodies will be such that they cannot be affected by any pain from the fire (chapter 10).

Here the question arises: if the fire is not incorporeal, like the pain of the soul, but corporeal and harmful by touch, so that bodies can be tormented by it, how will it also be the punishment of malignant spirits? For the same fire will be the punishment assigned to human beings and demons, as Christ says: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41).

Unless, since demons too possess certain bodies of their own, as learned men have thought, they are made of that dark and moist air whose pressure is felt by the wind. If this kind of element could suffer nothing from fire, it would not burn when heated in baths. For as the substance that burns first is burned, so also it burns what it touches.

But if anyone asserts that demons have no bodies at all, there is no need either to laboriously investigate this matter or to contend over it in disputation. For why should we not say that, although in marvelous ways, incorporeal spirits too can be afflicted by corporeal fire as a punishment, since the spirits of human beings, although they too are certainly incorporeal, have nevertheless been able to be enclosed in corporeal limbs and will then be able to be bound inseparably by the bonds of their bodies?

Therefore, if they have no bodies, the spirits of demons—or rather, demons who are spirits—will adhere to corporeal fires, although incorporeal, in order to be afflicted by them; not so that the fires to which they adhere become living beings for them, as this human being becomes a living being when spirit adheres to body, but, as I have said, in marvelous yet true ways.

Thus both that flame by which the rich man was tormented and that drop which he requested were incorporeal, as are even the visions of sleepers or of those who see things in ecstasy: incorporeal realities, yet possessing a likeness to bodies. For a person himself, when his spirit is without the body, nevertheless sees himself in dreams in such a way that he cannot distinguish everything from his body.

But that gehenna, which is also called “the lake of fire and brimstone” (Rev. 21:8), will be a corporeal fire and will torment the bodies of the damned—either the bodies of human beings and demons, human bodies being solid and demonic bodies airy; or only human bodies together with their spirits, while demons, as spirits without bodies, will cling to it and receive their punishment without imparting life to corporeal fires.

For there will be one fire for both, just as the Truth said:]

The same author, in the book *Enchiridion* (chapter 112):

[All those who are not freed from that mass of perdition which came about through the first human being by the one Mediator between God and human beings will indeed rise, each with his own flesh (I Tim. 2:5), but in order to be punished with the devil and his angels.

Whether they rise with the vices and deformities of their bodies—whatever [al.: whichever] diseased and deformed members they bore in them—why should we labor to investigate? We ought not to be troubled by the uncertain condition or beauty of those whose eternal and certain damnation will be assured.

Nor should it move us to ask how their body will be incorruptible if it can suffer pain, or how corruptible if it cannot die. There is no true life except where one lives happily, and no true incorruption except where what is sound is corrupted by no pain.

But where the unhappy person is not allowed to die—so that, in a manner of speaking, death itself does not die—where perpetual pain does not destroy but afflicts, corruption itself does not end. This is called the second death in Holy Scripture.

Nor would the first death, by which the soul is compelled to leave its body, nor the second, by which the soul is not permitted to leave its punished body, have happened to a human being if no one had sinned.]

It has been shown clearly enough, and with the authority and agreement of the Fathers, that at the time of the resurrection human bodies will be neither ethereal nor airy, but fleshly; and that this flesh, endowed with eternal immortality, will receive according to its merits either glory or disgrace.

### On Predestination, against John Scotus

The rest that follows, since it has already been refuted and reduced to nothing by what precedes, seems to be included only so that the nausea of your vomit may become more easily apparent to anyone.

### John Scotus

(Cap. 19, no. 4, section 2.) Hence, you say, after the devil had fallen from the ethereal region, an airy body was joined to him against his will, in which the punishment of his pride is endured, in a marvelous and ineffable manner of nature; yet by a hidden and just judgment, so that what the elements of the world, united among themselves as though by a natural bond of love, seek in an inseparable and most orderly movement, is turned into punishment for those who hate the truth.

For the fiery quality, by a superior natural power, continually seeks to transfer into itself the qualities of the lower elements, as though by a natural movement it were seeking a kind of nourishment for itself. When, therefore, as we have said, the highest of all bodily qualities—the ethereal—both surrounds and confines within itself the lower qualities and does not cease to move them within itself, insofar as the law of nature permits, it produces within natures a marvelous joy, but within perverse wills an ineffable torment.

Accordingly, the bodies of all the impious—namely, of angels and human beings who have become perverse—will suffer the punishments of eternal fire in such a way that the integrity of their substance will in no way be destroyed, their beauty in no way diminished, and their natural soundness preserved; moreover, all the goods of nature will shine forth in marvelous order for the adornment of the universe, except for the blessedness of which they will be deprived, since that does not come from nature but from grace.

While the quality of the higher corporeal fire contends with the bodies of the lower air by a natural force, the intention of the unhappy souls will suffer eternal distress in their bodies, so that the very same fire will become glory to all bodies, while to the souls condemned within them by their own wickedness it will be changed externally into punishment.

### Correction

I have judged it not inappropriate, in abundance of caution, to give a brief answer to these exhalations of such perversity, and sufficiently to show by the statements of the Fathers what they thought concerning the airy bodies of demons. In their view, it is rather by their own substance than in bodies gathered and compounded from elsewhere that they will pay the punishments due to their merits.

The blessed Fulgentius also confirms this to Peter when he says:

[God created certain spirits so that they would always exist, but others so that they would at some time cease to be spirits. Those, therefore, who were destined to cease to be spirits he produced—some from water, and others, because the Almighty willed it so, from earth; but he made the higher spirits share no natural fellowship with corporeal elements.]

If, therefore, we accept the authority of so great a teacher, we grant neither ethereal nor airy bodies to angelic spirits.

As for the fables you extract from the friendship of the elements—as though the lower elements, by some bond of love, yielded to the higher, that is, to fire, so that they did not refuse to become its nourishment—it is remarkable if the higher fire needs the lower elements and can subsist only by being fed with them. You ought, by the same reasoning, to treat the other elements likewise, so that each of them would need the others in order to subsist.

For the nature of our fire is such that, apart from miracles, whatever it touches it consumes. Why, then, does that fire not consume the other elements, if they are its nourishment? And since we read and hold with complete certainty that, in the sight of the trembling Judge, a fire will be kindled through which heaven and earth—that is, the cloudy air and the surface of earthly matter—will pass, I do not know why it would be necessary for it to be kindled with such manifest power and terror for the renewal of these things, if, as you say, they could be consumed by its ethereal nourishment.

It is therefore false that everything is confined by being surrounded within this ethereal fire, and that within it a marvelous joy of natures and an ineffable torment of perverse wills are produced. For how can joy and torment be compatible? No one who is being tortured rejoices, except those who willingly undergo torments, as is especially clear in all the saints.

But when you remove all punishments from the bodies, and in addition bestow joy, beauty, radiance, and glory on all the impious, both angels and human beings, while claiming that only their wills suffer torment, I cannot see what distress the intention of the unhappy souls is to suffer in their bodies.

For if they will rejoice, if their bodies will possess every beauty, if they will shine, if glory will belong to all their bodies, and if they are condemned only inwardly by their own wickedness, what punishment will be heaped upon them externally? If their bodies will neither suffer pain nor feel punishment, what punishment will be heaped upon their souls externally?

If that fire will never become glory to all bodies, it follows that no punishment will be heaped externally upon the souls. Or by what reason do you exclude blessedness from those from whom you do not remove joy, beauty, radiance, and glory?

How frivolous this is, both reason and authority plainly indicate. Anyone of sound judgment can easily overturn the absurdity of your talk concerning the struggle of the higher fire with airy bodies.

But I can scarcely understand how you can add that the bodies will burn forever, when with such obstinacy and impudence you have maintained that they suffer nothing. For how will that burn which suffers nothing and is adorned with every beauty, radiance, and glory?

You say:

### John Scotus

(Cap. 19, no. 5, section 4.) But if it seems incredible to anyone that the bodies will burn forever and that nothing of their nature will perish, let him consider the stone which is born in Arcadia beneath Mount Erimanthus. Although it is iron-hard, it is ignited by touch; once kindled by fire, it cannot be extinguished. The Greeks call it *asbestos*, that is, “inextinguishable,” and say that it both takes on a fiery color and loses nothing of its substance. Let him also consider the salamander, which lives in fire.
