## [Scan page 675]

### Correction

Although you have borrowed these things from the books of blessed Augustine—or rather, compiled them—you have presented them with a meaning entirely different from that in which he set them forth.

He proposed the likeness of asbestos, the salamander, and the mountains of Etna for this purpose: to answer the objections of the pagans by examples from temporal things and from many realities that were not unknown to them. They denied that it could happen that bodies burned in fire could nevertheless not be consumed at all.

These and other examples were therefore used to answer their unbelief, so that it might be taught that the bodies of the impious would suffer pain in that fire forever, but would never be consumed or perish. Thus the faithful teacher established through these examples that the integrity of their substance would always remain; yet he did not remove from them perpetual torments and pains, as you plainly do when you bring the conclusion of this perversity to such an end.

### John Scotus

(Cap. 19, no. 6, section 4.) Hence, he says, it can be inferred that not the substance, nor its qualities, will be tormented by the flame of gehenna, but that the senses and the resisting spirit will patiently endure eternal misery.

### Correction

Here again, with your customary contradiction, you declare eternal misery for those to whom shortly before you had attributed joy, beauty, radiance, and glory.

But concerning the patient spirit, hear the judgment of Saint Jerome—brief in words, but lofty in meaning and in the truth of the faith. In his letter to the Ephesians he is read as remembering and explaining this matter in the following way, when he expounds what the Apostle says: “Let no one deceive you with empty words; for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience” (Eph. 5:6):

[The words that deceive and overthrow are empty and void; but those that build up their hearers are full, rich, and substantial.

Since, therefore, there are many who say that there will be no punishments in the future for sins, and that no torments will be externally imposed, but that sin itself and the consciousness of guilt will be the punishment—since the worm does not die in the heart and the fire is kindled in the soul—in the likeness of a fever which does not torture the sick person externally but, seizing the very body, punishes what it possesses without the imposition of outward torments: such beliefs and fraudulent snares he called empty and void words.

They seem to possess a kind of flourishing eloquence and to flatter sinners, but, while they give them confidence, they lead them all the more toward eternal punishments, because God is angry at nothing as he is when a sinner becomes proud and, standing upright and rigid, is not bent into tears or asks mercy for his offense.]

Cassiodorus, on Psalm 20, verse 10:

[“You will set them as a furnace of fire.” A furnace is a vessel for baking bread, drawn out into a rounded shape from baked clay; it burns inwardly beneath consuming flames. In this likeness, sinners are placed, because at the future Judgment they will be tormented both by sorrow of mind and by punitive torture, since they lived with obstinate minds contrary to the Lord’s commands.

The Lord in his anger will trouble them and fire will devour them. The order of the Judgment is described in a most beautiful account. He says that those sinners who torment themselves on account of the wickedness of their deeds will be troubled by the Lord’s anger when they hear: “Go into the eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41); and this sentence will follow, that they will be devoured by perpetual flame.

For no delay follows the Lord’s command; as soon as he decrees it, it is fulfilled. Yet this fire consumes in such a way that it preserves, and preserves in such a way that it torments. To the wretched will be given a mortal life and a punishment that preserves.]

The same author, on Psalm 48:

[Sinners placed in hell are consumed by eternal death. For just as sheep continue forever without losing their wool, so in that place punishment always finds something in them to torment without diminishing their substance. “It consumes” is taken from the treatment of animals, which do not pull up grasses by the roots but rather cut off their upper parts.]

We believe that it must not be omitted that, although in other matters you have chosen to hold views equal to those of Origen, in the matter of punishments you have departed far from him.

For he both understood and taught that the fire and worms of the impious were the consciousness of their own crimes; while you, dogmatizing that this fire is the fourth element, assert that, except for the blessedness of which they will be deprived, no punishment whatever is inflicted upon them, either in soul or in body.

Hence Saint Jerome, writing against Rufinus, a follower and interpreter of Origen, speaks as follows (see Jerome, *Against Rufinus*, book 2, at the beginning):

[When you invoke eternal fires with the devil against the brothers—that is, against those who accuse you—you seem not so much to be pressing your brothers as to be raising up the devil, since he is to be punished by the same fires as Christian human beings.

As for the eternal fires which Origen habitually understands, I think it cannot have escaped you that he means the consciousness of sins and the inward repentance that burns the heart. Isaiah also speaks of this: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished” (Isa. 66:24).

And it is written concerning Babylon: “You have coals of fire; you shall sit upon them; they will be your help” (Isa. 47:14).

And in the Psalms the repentant person hears: “What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, against a deceitful tongue? The sharp arrows of the mighty, with desolating coals” (Ps. 119:3–4). These are the arrows of the commands of God, concerning which the Prophet says elsewhere: “I was afflicted while the thorn was driven into me” (Ps. 31:4): that they may wound and pierce, and make a desert of sins within it.

The testimony also in which the Lord says, “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and how I wish that it were kindled!” (Luke 12:49) is interpreted in this way: “I desire all to repent and to purge away vices and sins by the Holy Spirit.” For I am he concerning whom it is written: “God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4:24).

It is therefore no great thing to ascribe this to the devil, since it has also been prepared for human beings. You ought rather to have said, as a warning concerning the devil’s ruin: “You have become a perdition, and you shall no longer exist forever” (Jer. 27 [reading uncertain]).

And from the person of the Lord speaking to Job concerning the devil: “Behold, his hope shall be frustrated, and at the sight of all he shall be cast down” (Job 40:28). This is not as though the Lord were cruelly raising him up, for who can resist my face? Who has given to me, that I should repay him? Everything beneath heaven is mine. I will not spare him, with powerful words and words composed for entreaty (Job 41:1–2).]

### Cassiodorus on Psalm 9

[“The Lord shall be known as he executes judgments; the sinner has been caught in the works of his hands.” A truly profound and unequivocal sentence, because then the Lord will plainly be known to execute judgments, when he gives sinners over to be tormented by eternal sufferings.

Here, because their crimes are free, they are perhaps thought to remain unpunished. But when that day of revelation has come and the Lord Savior has sat upon his throne of majesty, then it will generally be recognized that he is carrying out his judgments, when the human race has been separated by his decision, whether to his left or to his right.

This is truly to execute judgments: to distinguish the merits of each person without any confusion. The following sentence openly declares this.

For it says from what it is known that the Lord truly executes judgments—namely, when the sinner is bound by the chains of his wicked works and receives a worthy punishment according to the quality of his deeds.

That interpretation must be entirely avoided which supposes that the sinner is tormented only by the recollection of his offenses. For if that alone were sufficient, why would it be said: “Go into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41)? And: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished” (Isa. 66:24)?

He does not deny here that places of torment are given to sinners; rather, he says that they are tormented according to the qualities of their works.

Let us therefore understand that a place has been prepared for the punishments of sinners, and let us recognize the external penal evil which, as we read, threatens the wicked. For, if we wish truly to understand that blessedness is separated from damnation by certain boundaries, let us recall that the rich man raised his eyes, that the poor Lazarus was seen in Abraham’s bosom, and that he himself was assigned to avenging flames.

This order of truth would in no way be stated if sinners were tormented only by the recollection of their evils. These are the hidden things that the title of the psalm has foretold.]

Isidore, *Sentences*, book 1, chapter 28:

[The punishment of the damned in gehenna is twofold: sorrow burns their mind, and flame burns their body, in a reciprocal correspondence, so that those who conceived in their mind what they accomplished in their body may be punished together in soul and body.

The fire of gehenna has light for one purpose and does not have it for another: it has light for condemnation, so that the impious may see the source of their sorrow; it does not have light for consolation, so that they may not see the source of their joy.

The furnace of the three youths (Dan. 3:23 and following) provides an apt comparison for the fire of gehenna. Just as that fire did not burn the three youths for their punishment, but did burn the bonds of their servants, so the fire of gehenna will shine upon the wretched to increase their punishments, so that they may see the source of their sorrow, but it will not shine for consolation, so that they may not see the source of their joy.

There is a great distinction between the present life and the misery of future unhappiness. Here there is misery because of the pain of torments, and darkness because of the turning away from light; one of these exists in this life—that is, misery—but the other does not. In hell, however, both exist.]

Ambrose, in the First Letter to the Corinthians (15:22):

[“For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive.” He says this because, just as Adam, by sinning, found death, and all descended from his origin so that they might be dissolved, so Christ, without sin and therefore conquering death—for whoever does not sin conquers death, since death comes from sin—acquired life, that is, resurrection, for all who are from his body.

Although, therefore, he granted a general resurrection, so that just as all—whether righteous or unrighteous—die in Adam, so in Christ all—both believers and unbelievers—may rise (Rom. 5:9, 18, and elsewhere), although unbelievers rise to punishment, nevertheless they appear to be made alive, because they will receive their bodies, no longer to die but to suffer punishment without end for what they refused to believe.]

The same Ambrose, in the same work (15:37):

[“What you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare grain, such as wheat or some other kind of seed. But God gives it a body as he wills [al.: as he wishes], and to each seed its own body.”

If, therefore, a bare grain is sown and, by God’s will, is clothed, in a manner of speaking, through the ministry of the elements and rises [al.: may rise] bearing with it many increases useful to human life, why should it not be credible that by God’s power what has died can rise again, its substance merely improved, not multiplied in number? (John 12:24.)

What, then, does the unbeliever require concerning the body in which the dead will rise, when examples have preceded that proclaim this improved resurrection to faith [al.: proclaim the faith of the resurrection], without the substance having been lost? Each person will receive his own body, in which Adam was created.

The examples cited above are appropriate. “Not all flesh is the same flesh”: there is one flesh of human beings, another of cattle, another of birds, and another of fish (I Cor. 15:39).

Since all flesh comes from the same mass, whence and how does such great diversity exist among these things, so that one substance produces different kinds? Let the sophists of the world and the investigators of the stars now speak, if they are able to comprehend what lies outside themselves, when they do not know what lies within themselves.

Finally, all the philosophers of the world, who refused to humble their minds before the law of God in order to receive its faith, asserting things always diverse and contradictory, confused one another in their most empty disputations, because in none of them was the mark of attested truth recognized, which, set forth beforehand, commends doctrine by words, just as God also ordained for our instruction—a doctrine proved not by words but by power, to which no one can…]

These are the words [of the Apostle]. How, then, just as the flesh of living creatures, though one, is diverse, so also persons of one flesh will be different in dignity in the resurrection, so that each may appear such as he was in merit.

And shortly afterward Ambrose [XV, 46]:

> The resurrection of the faithless is like the gloomy stars, the very last of all; for, having followed error, they are to be compared with stars that lead into error. As the apostle Jude says in his Epistle (Jude 13): “Faithlessness cannot have a clear resurrection; for just as a coal, covered with its own ashes, is darkened, so they too, surrounded by the darkness of their faithlessness, will be deprived of light.”

## EPILOGUE

### On divine predestination

Your epilogue, finally concluded in the number twenty, containing your confession of faith, is excluded from nearly all Catholic sincerity and purity. For you say:

### John Scotus

*(Book I, section 1)*

> Since these things are so, behold: I worship one God.

### Correction

You demonstrate clearly enough that you worship God in no other way than by assailing him with so many and such great falsehoods—indeed, blasphemies—from which he is known to be wholly alien. Consequently, you are not shown to worship him truthfully, since you do not fear to accuse him of so many fantasies.

And when you add that you confess yourself to worship one God:

### John Scotus

*(Epilogue, no. 2, section 1)*

> One, he says, [I profess] as the principle of all things, and wisdom by which whatever soul is wise is wise, and the very gift by which whatever things are blessed are blessed.

### Correction

We utterly execrate this as detestable, because his relative attribute can never be his substance. For “to predestine” is one thing, and “to be” another: the latter is said substantively, the former relatively.

Again, you say:

### John Scotus

*(Epilogue II, 4, section 1)*

> Just as he predestined no one to wickedness, because he is good, so he predestined no one to destruction, because he is life; and conversely: just as he predestined wickedness to no evil person, since it is destruction, so he predestined destruction to no evil person, since it is wickedness. For no Catholic may believe that supreme goodness, from which every good proceeds, predestined wickedness to anyone, or that supreme life, from which, in which, and through which all things live, predestined destruction or punishment to anyone—since he does not even permit that which destroys itself to perish.

### Correction

You spew forth the purulence of your poisons, with which, most shamelessly, you do not blush to obstruct the truth and authority both of the sacred Scriptures and of their faithful interpreters.

We therefore say that God, supreme goodness and supreme life, predestined no one to wickedness—that is, to sin. Nor did he compel anyone, whether by foreknowing, foreseeing, or predestining, nor did he in any way impose necessity upon anyone. But he predestined punishment for sinners—the punishment that you designate by the terms “destruction” and “wickedness”—because he is just; and he predestined sinners to deserved punishments because he is just.

Although any punishment, whether temporal or eternal, inflicted upon the deserving by the equity of the almighty Judge may seem evil or wickedness to the one who suffers it, nevertheless, since it proceeds from the supreme good and the supremely just one, it is plainly both just and good.

Moreover, you add:

### John Scotus

*(Epilogue II, 8, section 1)*

> Accordingly, when I hear your preachers, O most blessed Truth, the common life of all, saying that you predestined the impious to destruction, or destruction to the impious, I immediately understand that you predestined them—that is, before the ages you defined within your immutable laws the certain number of those who would perish in their impiety, which you never predestined at any time or place. You predestined, Lord, in your foreknowledge, which can neither be deceived nor changed, the number of those who would prepare for themselves impiety, punishment, and destruction—not so that you might punish in them what you had made, but so that you might leave them to be punished for what you had not made.

### Correction

This is judged no less impious than foolish. For the preachers of truth do not say what you make them say; rather, they say truthfully and faithfully that God has destined sinners to punishment, just as he has destined punishment for sinners. For it unquestionably belongs to his justice, and truthful Scripture also proclaims it:

> “For you will repay each one according to his works” (Matthew 16:27).

It does not say, “You will permit each one to be repaid,” or, “You will leave them to be punished by themselves”; it says, “You will repay each one according to his works.”

Therefore he will punish—the one who repays—not the one who merely receives. He also testifies that he will say to the impious at the judgment:

> “Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41).

He does not say, “I shall leave you to suffer from yourselves what you have prepared,” but, with judicial severity and irrevocable power:

> “Go into the eternal fire.”

Nor does he say, “which the devil and his angels prepared or prepare for themselves,” but:

> “which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.”

If you ask by whom it was prepared, hear the prophet Isaiah thundering terribly:

> “For Tophet has been prepared from long ago; it has also been prepared and made spacious” (Isaiah 30:33).

Saint Jerome, with no one objecting, rightly explains that Tophet signifies Gehenna and that the king signifies God, designated by these prophetic words.

Although it is rightly customary to say that each sinner prepares death or punishment for himself, which he has acquired by sinning, nevertheless, one who never wished to die or suffer torments cannot rightly be said to have made or inflicted these things upon himself, since he is led and dragged to them unwillingly. Thus the Prophet says to God:

> “But you, O God, will lead them down into the pit of destruction” (Psalm 55:24).

Unless, perhaps, in the same foolish manner you will also say here that “you will lead down” means “you will permit to be led down”—a claim that the strict Judge immediately overturns when he foretells that he will say to his reapers at the time of harvest:

> “Go, gather the weeds and bind them in bundles to burn them, and throw them into the furnace of fire; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 13:30, etc.).

For the holy angels will have this duty: after receiving the Judge’s sentence, they will separate and assemble all the impious according to the character of their crimes and cast them into devouring flames—both human beings and the devil and his angels. Concerning the devil, the Lord says to Job:

> “Before all eyes he will be hurled down” (Job 40:28).

By whom, I ask, except by the command of the strict Judge and the obedience of angelic service? And where, except into the eternal fire prepared for him from the beginning of the world?

For just as the kingdom was prepared for the just, so fire was prepared for the unjust and impious from the beginning of the world. Since they are gathered, bound, and thrown into the furnace of fire, how can they be said to be left to punish themselves, when they are dragged to all these things by others, unwilling and reluctant?

We therefore say, in accordance with the Scriptures, that God creates evils—that is, punishments and penalties—lest we be condemned with the heretics called Colatians, who, saying that God does not create evils contrary to what is written, “I am the Lord, creating evils” (Isaiah 45:7), were condemned and expelled by the Church.

Again, in accordance with the Scriptures, we say that evils—that is, sins or evil natures—are not from God, lest we be driven from the unity of the Church together with the heretics called Florimanians. They, on the contrary, said that God created evils, contrary to what is written:

> “God made all things good” (Genesis 1:31).

God therefore punishes what he made—that is, the angelic and human nature that sinned. He does not leave to be punished in them what he did not make, namely, the evil will alone, which, just as it is not a nature, cannot by itself experience punishment. Rather, the nature that willed and acted perversely will deservedly experience punishment.

Let the Doctor of the Gentiles, in faith and truth, come forward and cut short these absurdities of your perversity by apostolic authority. When he was arguing most forcefully about this most difficult—indeed, insoluble—question, he added:

> “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Will the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why have you made me like this?’ Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Romans 9:20–21, etc.).

What does the Apostle intend by the image of the potter making from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor, except to demonstrate thereby the goodness and justice of God, who makes some, by gratuitous mercy, for glory, and others, by inflexible justice, for everlasting disgrace?

Lest we be distracted hither and thither in the manner of the frenzied and fashion into his words something other than what he himself said, he does not say “to leave” or “to permit,” but “to make,” having driven away the whole cloud of ambiguity.

Let his fellow apostle Peter also come forward and, with an equal sentence, disturb your madness. When he said:

> “The Lord knows how to rescue the godly from temptation,”

he added:

> “But to reserve the impious for punishment in the day of judgment” (2 Peter 2:9).

Behold this most powerful champion and most faithful victor: he did not say, “He knows how to leave the impious to be tortured by eternal fire in the judgment,” but “to reserve them.”

Let blessed Jude the apostle also hasten forward and bring against you the same sentence as against his fellow apostles. In his Epistle he speaks of you and those like you as follows:

> “I found it necessary to write to you, exhorting you to contend for the faith once delivered to the saints. For certain men have secretly slipped in, men long ago designated for this judgment, impious persons who pervert the grace of our God into licentiousness and deny the only ruler and our God, Jesus Christ.
>
> “I wish to remind you, though you know all things once for all, that Jesus, after saving a people from the land of Egypt, later destroyed those who did not believe; and that he has kept the angels who did not preserve their own principality but abandoned their dwelling under guard in everlasting bonds, in darkness, for the judgment of the great God.
>
> “Likewise, Sodom and Gomorrah and the neighboring cities, which in the same manner committed fornication and pursued other flesh, have been set forth as an example, undergoing the punishment of eternal fire” (Jude 3–7).

You hear that they were designated beforehand, yet you deny that they were predestined. You hear that the Sodomites were made an example of eternal fire, yet you say that they were left to punish themselves.

For the Sodomites did not punish themselves, nor were they left to be punished by themselves. Rather, by living wickedly, they deserved to be burned by showers of flame and sulfur pouring down from heaven. Thus, when they have been thrust into Tartarus, they will unquestionably be burned by a fire made and prepared for this purpose.

Let us also see how great a contradiction you yourself, by your own assertions, bring against your own position. For you yourself had said much earlier that the fire is called predestined or prepared for the devil because he was to be punished in it together with all his companions in wickedness. And just as the same fire is certainly good because it was made by the good God, and is called evil for no other reason than that evil beings are most orderly disposed within it, so punishment is not improperly so called because the same evil beings are tormented in it—painfully and miserably—for the sins they have committed lustfully.

Either, then, it is false that God made that fire which is the punishment of the reprobate, and what you say will be true: that God neither predestined nor prepared punishment; or, if it is true that it was made by God, and was also, as you yourself maintain, prepared, then it will unquestionably be false that God did not destine or prepare punishment.

For its Creator and Inflictor himself plainly foretold long beforehand that he would say:

> “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41).

He who, according to his apostles, can

> “make from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor” (Romans 9:21),

and who knows how to rescue the godly from temptation but to reserve the impious for punishment by fire (2 Peter 2:9)—he, by his irrevocable sentence, condemned beforehand and judged, in his unutterable foreknowledge, the reprobate—who were to be tormented with punishments made, predestined, prepared, preordained, and disposed by him—even before he created them.

He alone could foresee what each person would become and by what end each would bring his earthly life to its conclusion. For concerning some of them he said:

> “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18).

He did not say “will be judged,” although we most certainly believe that this will happen in the future. In the sense noted above, he said, “has already been judged.” When, I ask, except before he was made?

If, then, the one who does not believe has already been judged—that is, condemned—why should it not most truly be said, according to the same rule of divine equity, that he was predestined or prepared for punishment? For he who could judge and condemn him so long beforehand in his foreknowledge could certainly predestine him to that condemnation and prepare him for it.

Moreover, if we set forth the statement of God:

> “I make evils and create darkness” (Isaiah 45:7),

while you deny—or rather reject—it, anyone of sound mind will offer humble assent of belief to God rather than to you, especially since orthodox faith judges that nothing different should be understood concerning God’s predestinations than concerning his most just and equally unavoidable judgments.

If, then, according to you and your accomplices, God is to be blamed because he predestined the impious to punishments and punishments to the impious, it follows that he must also be blamed because he has already judged and already condemned those who do not believe. Since that is blasphemous and impious, it remains that the sincerity of Catholic faith, humbly and faithfully prostrate before the inscrutable abyss of such judgments, should in no way complain about heavenly dispositions, but should cry out with the Apostle:

> “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, that he should be repaid? For from him and through him and in him are all things. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen” (Romans 11:33–36).

Let it also hear him threatening terribly:

> “Do not be wise in your own estimation, but fear” (Romans 11:20);

and the Prophet giving salutary warning:

> “Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not investigate what is deeper than you” (Ecclesiastes 3:22).

Hence the Psalmist also testifies:

> “Terrible in his counsels above the children of men” (Psalm 65:5);

and again:

> “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Psalm 36:7).

Therefore, as blessed Gregory says, it is necessary for each person to humble himself all the more because he does not know whether he is elect, even if he is elect.

What help, in truth, does your explanation contribute to your assertions, when you say *(Epilogue, no. 6, section 2)* that God predestined—that is, before the ages defined—the certain number of those who would perish in their impiety? I see no way in which this contradicts them; rather, I know that it supports them.

For what is “to predestine,” that is, “to define the number of those who will perish,” except to predestine those who will perish—that is, to define them? If, then, he predestined—that is, defined—the number of those who would perish, he certainly foreknew that they would perish.

What worse or more destructive thing can be said of rational creatures than that they perish? Therefore, he who foreknew that they would perish certainly foreknew an evil, for to perish is an evil, and worse than every evil.

If, I say, he predestined—that is, defined—how many would perish, then, without anyone resisting, he predestined the evil and those who were evil—that is, he defined them. Where, then, is your claim, by which you so strenuously tried to affirm that God neither foreknew nor predestined the evil that is punishment and penalty?

For he could never predestine—that is, define—the certain number of those who would perish unless he had foreknown that they would perish. Therefore he foreknew an evil, since to perish is unquestionably an evil.

And when you add *(Epilogue, no. 7, section 2)* that it may be expressed in another way—namely, that God predestined the number of those who would prepare for themselves the punishment and destruction of their impiety, not so that he might punish in them what he had made, but so that he might leave them to be punished for what he had not made—this is indeed true: the impious prepare punishment and destruction for themselves by sinning, that is, by living impiously.

But it is no less true that God most justly prepared the same punishment for them. For what they prepare for themselves by living wickedly, God prepares for them by judging most justly and repaying most justly. For it is written:

> “For you will repay each one according to his works” (Romans 2:6).

But nowhere is it written: “He will repay each one according to his works,” in the sense that he merely permits the repayment.

It is likewise written:

> “We must all appear before the tribunal of God, so that each may receive according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (2 Corinthians 5:10).

But nowhere is it written that God will allow each person to receive his own body according to what he has done, whether good or evil. For whoever receives undoubtedly receives from another what he does not possess from himself.

And what worse thing can be said than to be abandoned by God? Hence the Psalmist himself says:

> “He gave them over to the desires of their hearts; they went according to their own devices” (Psalm 81:12–13).

For this reason every devout person also prays with the Psalmist to God:

> “Do not abandon me, Lord my God; do not depart from me” (Psalm 38:21).

If, therefore, God’s abandoning someone is an evil, then according to you God altogether predestined evil when he decided to abandon those whom he would leave to perish. Your definition can no longer stand: that God predestined evils.

For what worse thing can be said than that a person is left by God? Who would in any way wish to punish himself, unless he were fleeing the unavoidable necessity of the one who punishes, if he were able?

Indeed, no one wishes to punish himself even with temporal death, much less with the torments of eternal Gehenna. Although we read that some have inflicted death upon themselves by the sword, the noose, fire, poison, a precipice, or drowning, and that many philosophers are also known to have desired it—so much so that the letters of the famous Seneca are known to have argued most eloquently in praise of it—nevertheless, the Christian faith and religion regard it as the height of impiety if anyone violently lays hands upon himself.

On the other hand, it considers it a great glory for the holy martyrs to have gladly endured death inflicted upon them for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, rather than to have voluntarily brought it upon themselves. Hence they had received his command, saying:

> “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matthew 10:23).

Nor did the Lord Jesus himself punish or kill himself, since he committed no sin and no deceit was found in his mouth (1 Peter 2:22). Nevertheless, he willingly submitted and endured the passion inflicted upon him by his enemies.

Should the great multitude of blessed martyrs be said to have punished themselves, when, although their persecutors inflicted upon them so many kinds of torture, they not only did not resist, but preferred to succumb fearlessly through faith?

If it is certain that this would be utterly absurd in this life, how much less should we believe that anyone punishes himself where no opportunity for escape is granted?

We must therefore admit that God does not leave anyone there to be punished by himself. Rather, by his own inescapable justice, he repays each person what he deserves. He said:

> “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matthew 10:28).

He did not say “who leaves the person to destroy himself,” but “who can destroy both soul and body.” He also said:

> “I kill,”

not “I permit them to be killed by themselves”;

> “and I make alive,”

not “I leave them to live by themselves”;

> “I strike,”

not “I leave them to be struck by themselves”;

> “and I heal,”

not “I leave them to heal themselves.”

And why is this so? Hear why:

> “There is no one who can deliver from my hand” (Deuteronomy 32:39).

And again:

> “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay in due time” (Deuteronomy 32:35).

And again:

> “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord” (Romans 12:19).

Now, what you say *(Epilogue, no. 8, section 2)*—that God will not punish in them what he made, but will leave them to be punished for what he did not make—is shown in every respect to be false.

For he himself made both body and soul. When he said that the body can be killed by human beings, but not the soul, and judged that both—that is, body and soul—are to be destroyed by himself in Gehenna, he declared clearly enough that he himself will destroy, that is, punish, what he made in them.

See at least now what your devious disputation has accomplished thus far.

You then add:

### John Scotus

*(Epilogue, no. 9, section 2)*

> This, O eternal light of minds, is my faith concerning your predestination: that you are it.

### Correction

On the contrary, this is your faithlessness concerning God’s predestination, for predestination is not God himself. Many things are predicated relatively of God which it is certain God does, although he himself is not those things.

For it is written:

> “God tested Abraham” (Genesis 22:1);

and again:

> “The Lord your God will test you.”

The Lord himself says:

> “I, the Lord, have deceived that prophet” (Ezekiel 14:9).

The Psalmist says concerning him:

> “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Psalm 5:6).

Again:

> “He turned their heart to hate his people, to deal craftily with his servants” (Psalm 105:25).

Again:

> “He made them wander in the wilderness and not on the way” (Psalm 107:40).

And the Prophet says to him:

> “Make the heart of this people dull, and make their ears heavy” (Isaiah 6:10).

The Apostle says:

> “God handed them over to a reprobate mind,”

and:

> “God handed them over to dishonorable passions” (Romans 1:28, etc.).

There are many other passages of this kind, which it is both lengthy and unnecessary to pursue now.

Will all these things that we have cited, and others like them concerning God, be of the same substance as God, so that God may be said to be testing, seducing, destroying, turning toward evil, leading astray, blinding, hardening, handing over, killing, and many other things that are truthfully and faithfully proclaimed throughout the divine utterances concerning God’s justice?

No one except one deranged in mind fails to understand that none of these things demonstrates his substance.

It is therefore false that God’s substance is his predestination. Rather, predestination is predicated of him relatively, in the same way as creation, operation, deed, ordination, disposition, administration, governance, and many similar things by which his omnipotence, goodness, equity, or judgments are made known.

Finally, as though victorious through the contributions of his arguments, you exultantly exhale the strength of your pestilential breath, saying:

### John Scotus

*(Epilogue, no. 10, section 3)*

> By this, orthodox faith is condemned by anathema, because orthodox believers say that there are two predestinations, or one twofold predestination, either bipartite or double. For if there are two, it is not one divine substance; if twin, it is not indivisible; if bipartite, it is not simple but composed of parts; if double, it is composite. And if we are forbidden to call divine unity threefold, with what madness does the heretic dare to call it twofold? Therefore, once this monstrous, poisonous, and deadly doctrine has been rooted out from our hearts, let us believe that there is one eternal predestination, that it is God, and that it pertains only to things that are, and in no way to things that are not.

### Correction

> “Who will grant water to my head, and a fountain of tears to my eyes, so that I may weep for the wounded children of my people?” (Jeremiah 9:1).

And the Lord himself, seeing the impious city that was about to perish and weeping over it, said concerning it:

> “If only you had known—even you…” (Luke 19:42),

with “you would have wept” understood.

These two testimonies would fit your case, if you would consider them with a devout mind and lament, since I have neither sufficient ability to defend your misery nor do you possess a cautious means of escaping the precipice of the destruction that is closing in upon you.

Since it was not enough for you to rush into such great blasphemies against God, you did not fear to open your mouth with the most shameless and obstinate impudence against his elect, whom you declare must be anathematized and who, together with him, rejoice in eternal blessedness—or rather, with the beast that is written to ascend from the abyss, you opened your mouth with the most shameless and persistent impudence against God himself, the Lord of all, uttering the greatest blasphemy.

But so that the rest may be more easily exposed to all, let the first and most insane falsehood be marked out. It is therefore beyond doubt utterly false that you anathematize together with yourself all orthodox believers.

For no orthodox believer grants your opinion; no one of the orthodox indulges your impieties; no one acquiesces in your insanities.

It is exceedingly astonishing, moreover, that a man who was himself anathematized before he was born should presume to pronounce an anathema against anyone. You demonstrate that you belong to the number of those “who set their mouth against heaven, while their tongue traverses the earth” (Psalm 73:9).

It must therefore be carefully considered against whom you have pronounced an anathema with such impiety: namely, against Popes Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, Sixtus, Leo, Celestine, and Gregory; against all the pontiffs of the city of Rome, as well as the ranks and peoples of the orders that followed them; against the bishop Ambrose together with all the Italians; against Augustine, Primasius, and Fulgentius, bishops, together with all the Africans; against the presbyter Jerome together with all the Easterners and Greeks; against Prosper and Hilary together with all the Gauls; against Isidore together with all the faithful in Spain; against Cassiodorus also together with all his associates; against the presbyter Bede together with all the English and Britons; against Bishop Boniface together with all the Germans; against the apostles and prophets themselves; and, greater than all these, against God himself, the God of gods.

Saint Augustine frequently used this expression, saying that God predestined his judgments toward the good and the reprobate, in an unchangeable disposition, at the appointed time. Rather, whatever he had foreseen for us either through the ages or at the end of the ages, he established before he created it, and judged and determined it outside time.

For whatever the prophets and the successors of the apostles have proclaimed by voice or committed to writing concerning God’s judgments, they spoke only under his inspiration, instruction, and command. Consequently, whatever anathema is directed against them undoubtedly redounds as an injury against the one who spoke through them.

Since they agreed in their understanding of God’s predestination and unanimously proclaimed it—and since we have already demonstrated sufficiently and more than sufficiently how this is so—we refrain from repeating it here.

With all these, we do not fear to call predestination twofold, nor do we fear to state it in the plural; and we approve your argument when you say: “If there are two, it is not one divine substance.” This is true: divine predestination is not God’s substance, but his disposition, ordination, and judgments.

Likewise, you say: “If it is twin, it is not indivisible; if bipartite, it is not simple; if double, it is composite. And if we are forbidden to call divine unity threefold, with what madness does the heretic dare to call it twofold?”

Although predestination does not signify his substance—for it shows not that he is, but that he disposes—nevertheless, “to dispose,” like “to predestine,” is said relatively of his creatures, as was stated, by the Lord’s favor, in the first parts of this work.

Many things are predicated essentially of God, and their being expressed in the plural does not prejudice the unity of his essence. Omitting these, so that they may not be repeated out of weariness, we shall offer you one example from the Gospel that does not obstruct the confirmation of the others.

The Lord, creator and disposer of the universe, says:

> “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25).

Yet although he proclaimed the resurrection with such clarity, elsewhere in the same Gospel he says:

> “Do not marvel at this, for the hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and will come forth: those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; and those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5:28–29).

In accordance with these testimonies of the Lord, the Fathers explain, and the truth teaches, that there are two resurrections: one of the saints and the other of the impious. The Lord named them the resurrection of life and the resurrection of judgment; and the Fathers understand “judgment” in this passage as “condemnation.”

Just as there is also a resurrection of the soul, by which a person, abandoning vices through the grace of God, begins to live by virtues—concerning which the same Lord says:

> “Amen, amen, I say to you: the hour is coming, and is now, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live” (John 5:25),

where “they will hear” means “they will obey and comply”—so also there is a resurrection of bodies, of which he likewise speaks in the passage cited above:

> “The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and will come forth: those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; but those who …”

*Epistle 95 to Innocent, On Grace, chapter 6.*
## [Scan page 683]

### Saint Prudentius

…into the resurrection of judgment. Thus there is one resurrection by which the just will receive everlasting blessedness, and another by which the unjust will be sent into everlasting punishment—not because they occur at different times, but because they are stirred by different impulses. The angel, likewise announcing this distinction of resurrections to the prophet Daniel, commends it in these words:

> “And many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life and others to reproach, so that they may see it forever” (Dan. 12:2).

What word in the Christian religion can be spoken that is more sacred, sweeter, or more desirable than “resurrection”? Yet it is uttered with such a distinction that only madness could doubt it. He, therefore, who designated himself by the name of resurrection, and who, being destined to live forever, first displayed himself as the victor over death by rising through his own power, predestined—that is, ordained—before the ages that he would do this. In the truth and distinction of the resurrection, he both foresaw what he would do and afterward brought it to pass. For, since he is himself the author and judge, those who have done good will rise “to the resurrection of life,” while those who have done evil will rise “to the resurrection of judgment.”

He predestined himself to do this who foreknew that he would do it: namely, to exercise mercy and judgment, in which the entire ordering of every rational creature is comprehended, and outside which nothing can be found.

And just as God’s dispositions, ordinations, dispensations, governances, and administrations—since they emphatically denote not his essence but his effect—are expressed in the plural, so unquestionably his predestinations are reckoned by a most free plurality. As you say that they are predestinations of those things which are, so we also say that they concern what exists: mercy and judgment, glory and disgrace—that is, eternal life and eternal fire—of whose existence from God no Catholic doubts. But who except one who does not exist himself would judge that God’s predestinations belong to things that do not exist? For what does not exist is neither predestined nor ordained. Eternal life exists, and eternal fire exists: the former for glory, the latter for punishment; the former for a kingdom, the latter for torment.

We say that God’s predestinations concern these things because we have no doubt whatsoever that they exist. God therefore predestined eternal life for the good; he predestined eternal fire for the wicked; he predestined eternal life for the godly; he predestined the punishment of eternal fire for the ungodly. Hence he also foretold that at the final judgment he would say to the latter:

> “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels”;

and to the former:

> “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34, 41).

He spoke of a prepared kingdom and likewise did not conceal the prepared fire. By whom, I ask, was it prepared, except by himself? By that judge the kingdom is awarded to the former and the punishment of fiery torment to the latter.

This is our faith, because this is the true prophetic, apostolic, orthodox, and catholic faith. I could indeed have pronounced an anathema against you myself, if I were not waiting for, preferring, and desiring your correction rather than your destruction. Therefore I do not yet hurl against you the severity of an anathema, because I exhort, warn, and ask with the whole affection of my heart that, with regard for heavenly grace, you come to your senses and at last awaken from so deadly a lethargy; that you inquire benevolently into what Christian equality of judgment holds, grasp it humbly, accept it gently, follow it meekly, hold it devotedly, and carry it out faithfully in every respect.

Abandon the quadrivium of vanity, by following which you have become an exile from the way of truth. How much better and more salutary it would be for you to rely upon the one everlasting way and ride in its humble chariot, rather than, swollen with the pride of your quadrivium, rush headlong in different directions! The chariot of this way is the four Gospels, flowing from one fountain of paradise, by which a saving path is opened to us.

The chariot of this way is also the four virtues—prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice—with which all moral goodness is adorned. The chariot of this way is the four kinds of the divine utterances: historical, ethical, allegorical, and anagogical, by which, with his grace illuminating us, we are led to the whole understanding of the sacred Scriptures. If you had humbly and faithfully endeavored to follow these, you would never have fallen into so great a precipice of errors and abominations—or rather, blasphemies.

But while you clung with such obstinacy to your tortuous quadrivium, you were wholly unable to escape the saying of the book of Ecclesiasticus:

> “Whoever speaks sophistically is detestable; by everything he is defrauded. For grace has not been given to him by the Lord; for he has been deprived of all wisdom” (Ecclus. 37:23).

And also:

> “In much speaking you will not escape sin” (Prov. 10:19).

If you desire to be freed from these things, prostrate yourself suppliantly in the deepest humility before the Crucified One, so that with the Apostle you may be able to say:

> “I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. 2:2).

And again:

> “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14).

In his name and with God’s help, according to the capacity and strength of my smallness, written more devotedly than learnedly, for the sake also of your correction, brother John, I am pleased to set out each point in chapters, as briefly and concisely as possible, so that what the reader or hearer has read or heard may be more firmly commended to his tenacious memory.

### Summary of the Whole Work

**Definition I, chapter 1 and section 1**

You say: “The quadrivium of the four rules solves every question of the whole of philosophy.”

[Note: See Cellotium, *On Gottschalk*, p. 133.]

We answer: Neither that quadrivium nor any branch of worldly wisdom is sufficient to resolve every question without the grace of God and the faith which …

## [Scan page 684]

### On Predestination against John Scotus

**Definition II, chapter 2, sections 2 and 6, and chapter 3, section 1**

You say: “Predestination and foreknowledge in God are one and the same as his will, wisdom, and truth.”

We answer: Wisdom, truth, and will are predicated essentially of God, whereas predestination and foreknowledge are predicated relatively; therefore they are not God’s substance.

**Definition III, chapter 2, section 2, and chapter 3, section 4**

You say: “Foreknowledge and predestination are one and the same.”

We answer: They differ greatly, since many things are foreknown that are not predestined; but nothing is predestined unless it has first been foreknown.

You say: “God cannot impose the grace of his will upon free choice unless free choice, through labor, study, and cooperation, contributes to the same labor, study, and cooperation.”

We answer: No one can contribute even the aspiration of labor or study unless the preceding grace of God comes first.

**Definition V, chapter 2, section 9**

You say: “Predestination is in God according to his substance and cannot be relative.”

We answer: It is very easy to show that predestination in God is always relative, but it is never said according to substance, since it is referred to something else. For one never predestines except …

**Definition VI, chapter 2, section 6**

You say: “Just as it is impious to double, triple, or multiply the essence and all the other things said of God, so it is impious to assert two predestinations and incur the charge of impiety.”

We answer: God’s essence is in no way doubled, divided, or multiplied. Nevertheless, many things that are predicated of him substantially are expressed in the plural; nor is his essence thereby doubled, divided, or multiplied, since by such plurality it is no longer his essence but his effects that are being indicated. Accordingly, one who asserts predestinations in the plural is not bound by the charge of impiety, because the term expresses not his essence but his effects.

**Definition VII, chapter 2, section 2; chapter 3, section 1**

You say: “God’s predestination is one, just as the divine operation, wisdom, substance, and will are one.”

We answer: Predestination and the divine operation are spoken of relatively in relation to many things; wisdom, substance, and will, however, are spoken of according to the simple nature alone, although the wills of God are very frequently read of as his effects.

### Summary

**Definition VIII, chapter 2, section 2; chapter 3, sections 1 and 2**

You say: “Whatever is understood from the divine will must be understood from God’s predestination.”

We answer: Although someone may will something, nevertheless to will is one thing and to predestine another. “To will” is said with reference to oneself alone, whereas “to predestine” is referred to other things; and therefore they are not one and the same.

**Definition IX, chapter 3, section 5**

You say: “Predestination, like charity, is not twofold, doubled, or multiple, and has no plurality.”

We answer: The Fathers frequently speak of predestination and charity as both twofold and divided into two parts; and they speak of predestinations in the plural.

**Definition X, chapter 4, section 1**

You say: “There are three heresies: that of the Pelagians, who commend free choice without grace; the second, of those who commend grace alone; and the third, that of Gottschalk, who imposes necessity and coercion through predestinations.”

We answer: We detest the Pelagians, who assert that something good can be done through free choice without the help of grace; and we also detest those—although we have never heard of any such people—who commend grace alone in such a way that they remove free choice. Rather, free choice is wounded and weakened by the transgression of the original sin of the human race, so that by itself it is wholly unable to attain anything good unless it is preceded by an aspiring grace and followed by assistance.

We likewise reject those who imagine that necessity and coercion are imposed upon creatures through God’s predestinations. For although God, with supreme foreknowledge, has predestined his will concerning all creatures, nevertheless, just as he predestined all things by his foreknowledge, he does not compel any creature by that same foreknowledge to act.

**Definition XI, chapter 5, section 1**

You say: “The substance of a human being consists of three things, namely being, willing, and knowing; and he did not lose these by sin.”

We answer: Willing and knowing are not the substance of a human being, since although a human being always has being, he does not always have willing and knowing. For by sin he lost both good willing and good knowing, and he cannot recover them by himself except through the preceding grace of God.

**Definition XII, chapter 6, section 6**

You say: “No nature can perish.”

We answer: Rational creatures cannot perish entirely, whereas irrational creatures can.

You say: “Human beings did not lose free will, that is, their nature.”

We answer: Human nature is not free will, although it always possessed free will toward evil; toward good, however, it lost it in such a way that without the preceding grace there is none.

**Definition XIV, chapter 7, section 5**

You say: “Human freedom remained after sin, but its strength and power were lost.”

We answer: There is no freedom if it lacks strength and power. Freedom therefore remained in human beings only toward evil.

**Definition XV, chapter 4, section 8**

You say: “A human being can will by nature; but to begin, to be able, and to complete a good work is possible only through grace.”

We answer: Human beings can neither will, begin, be able to do, nor complete anything good unless God’s grace precedes and follows them.

**Definition XVI, chapter 5, sections 4 and 5**

You say: “Just as God compels no one to sin, so he does not compel anyone to live well.”

We answer: God drives no one to sin, but he invites—or rather compels—many to live well by various exhortations, saying himself:

> “I will cause you to walk in my commandments” (Ezek. 11:20).

And again:

> “Compel them to enter” (Luke 14:23).

**Definition XVII, chapter 5, section 4**

You say: “If some cause precedes the will—that is, nature—in order to make it think or do good or evil, it is not nature.”

We answer: The will is not nature. Nevertheless, it is preceded toward good by various causes of the merciful and compassionate God; toward evil, it is preceded by none except the merits of its own perversity, which demand it.

**Definition XVIII, chapter 6, section 1**

You say: “No sin and no punishment can arise from anywhere except from the human will itself, freely making bad use of its choice.”

We answer: Sin arises from the human will itself; punishment, however, is inflicted by God as just judge.

**Definition XIX, chapter 8, section 5**

You say: “Just as an animal body could die because it was not yet perfect—that is, spiritual—so free will, while still animal because mortal, could sin, since it was not yet perfect.”

We answer: A human being did not sin because he was not yet spiritual, but because, having been created from nothing and not brought forth from the substance of the Maker, he turned himself away from the highest good by his own will, and by turning away he fell.

The devil likewise did not sin because he was not yet spiritual, since his whole nature was spiritual—indeed, he had been created a spirit—but because he too was made from nothing and willed what he ought not to have willed. The will was not able to sin because it was not yet perfect, but because it voluntarily turned away from the true liberator and savior—the author of the will, whom you most foolishly call a mortal nature.

**Definition XX, chapter 8, section 9**

You say: “There is such a difference between human free choice and human substance that nature is in rational willing, whereas free choice is in its freedom, whether it is called the movement of naturally willing freedom or the gift of intelligence.”

We answer: Such a distinction is utterly false, since human will is not its nature; rather, free choice is nothing other than the will of freedom—that is, the choice of good or evil.

**Definition XXI, chapter 10, section 1**

You say: “God’s foreknowing or predestining sins, death, or punishments of human beings or angels must be understood in the opposite sense.”

We answer: God both foreknew sins and foreknew and predestined death and punishments. It must in no way be understood in the opposite sense.

**Definition XXII, chapter 10, section 3**

You say: “Every evil is both sin and its punishment, and these things are nothing.”

We answer: Sin is nothing, but its punishment is something; that is, the creatures of God which are made punitive for sinners—except for those sins that are called the punishments of preceding sins.

**Definition XXIII, chapter 10, section 5**

You say: “Death and the misery of eternal punishments are altogether nothing; and therefore they are neither foreknown nor predestined.”

We answer: Death in itself is not a nature; nevertheless, the separation of soul and body, and the punishments of infernal torments, occur only by God’s judgment. Therefore they are both foreknown and predestined by him.

**Definition XXIV, chapter 11 and section 1**

You say: “God’s predestination concerns only those who have been prepared for eternal blessedness.”

We answer: If that is so, then God’s judgment also concerns only those who have been prepared for eternal blessedness, for every predestination of God belongs to his most just judgment.

**Definition XXV, chapter 11, section 1**

You say: “It is an improper transfer of language to say that God foreknows and predestines.”

We answer: That is true, but by this improper and transferred usage the terms properly and principally apply to no one except him.

**Definition XXVI, chapter 11, section 2**

You say: “Whenever God is said to have foreknown and predestined the ungodly to destruction or eternal punishment, this means that he did not foreknow and did not predestine them.”

We answer: None of the holy Fathers admitted this perverse madness. Rather, they all thought as did Saint Fulgentius in his exposition, as the catholic Church still thinks today: just as it is truthfully said that he judged the good to glory and the wicked to punishment, so it is truthfully said that he predestined the good to the kingdom and the wicked to torment.

**Definition XXVII, chapter 11, section 1**

You say: “If they have been predestined, they will necessarily perish and suffer unavoidable punishments. But if this is so, how will the world be judged justly, since the necessity of predestination compels them to perish?”

We answer: I would certainly have endured the same argument from the saints. For if those who have been predestined will necessarily be saved and will receive the kingdom unavoidably, how will the world be judged justly, when the necessity of predestination compels them to be saved? Where necessity is imposed, force of a kind is applied, not grace bestowed.

---

## [Scan page 685]

**Definition XXVIII, chapter 11, section 3**

You say: “The holy Scriptures place foreknowledge and predestination only among the saints.”

We answer: We ought to believe God rather than you. For he himself speaks in the Fourth Book of Kings through the prophet Isaiah against Sennacherib, among other things:

> “I have foreknown your dwelling, your going out, your entering, and your way, and your fury against me. You raged against me, and your pride has risen into my ears” (2 Kings 19:27).

Likewise through Jeremiah:

> “We have heard of the pride of Moab: he is exceedingly proud. I know his loftiness, his arrogance, his pride, and the haughtiness of his heart, says the Lord, and his boasting, and that his strength is not according to it, nor has he attempted to do as much as he was able” (Jer. 48:29–30).

And the Apostle says:

> “God has chosen us as the last of the apostles, as though sentenced to death” (1 Cor. 4:9).

**Definition XXIX, chapter 11, section 2, and chapter 12, section 2**

You say: “Augustine sometimes placed predestination concerning the reprobate in the opposite sense.”

We answer: We agree with Saint Fulgentius’s most truthful exposition, not with your most false corruption of it.

**Definition XXX, chapter 12, section 5, and chapter 15, section 4**

You say: “All of God’s foreknowledge is predestination, and all predestination is foreknowledge.”

We answer: This is false, since God foreknows sins that he does not predestine.

**Definition XXXI, chapter 12, sections 1 and 4**

You say: “All of God’s predestination is altogether a preparation of grace.”

We answer: This too is false, because God predestined punishments for sinners, which belong not to his grace but to his justice.

**Definition XXXII, chapter 12, sections 5 and 6**

You say: “The elect are spoken of for the non-elect, and the children of God for those who are not children.”

We answer: The Fathers never understood it in this way.

**Definition XXXIII, chapter 13, sections 1 and 2; and chapter 15, section 2**

You say: “The chosen Judas is to be understood as the non-elect Judas, and ‘friend,’ although he had never not been an enemy, is to be understood in the opposite sense.”

We answer: Judas was chosen for the office of apostleship and for the work appropriate to it, although not for the eternal kingdom. Similarly, the one who was first chosen, although afterward made an enemy by the weight of avarice, may rightly be called a friend, in accordance with God’s saying through the Psalmist:

> “If an enemy had cursed me, I would certainly have endured it; and if one who hated me had spoken great things against me, I would perhaps have hidden myself from him. But you, my one in heart, my leader and my intimate friend, who together with me used to enjoy sweet companionship; we walked in the house of God with agreement” (Ps. 54:13–15).

And again:

> “For even the man of my peace, in whom I hoped, who ate my bread, magnified his treachery against me” (Ps. 40:10).

**Definition XXXIV, chapter 13, section 4**

You say: “Sinners are left to eternal fire, not predestined.”

We answer: They are not merely left, but are also predestined, judged, and handed over to be punished by eternal fire.

**Definition XXXV, chapter 14, section 1**

You say: “Augustine’s words prove that ‘predestined’ is said only of the just.”

We answer: Augustine never thought this and never said it.

**Definition XXXVI, chapter 14, section 4**

You say: “Contrary to yourself, punishment is predestined for sinners, whereas the sinners themselves are only foreknown, not predestined.”

We answer: Although you bring forward this contradiction against yourself, nevertheless you have said that punishment is predestined for sinners, and that the sinners themselves are not merely foreknown but also predestined.

**Definition XXXVII, chapter 15, section 8**

You say: “Punishments are evil and therefore do not come from God, since no evil comes from him.”

We answer: God said through the prophet:

> “I am the Lord, forming light and creating darkness, making peace and creating evils. I am the Lord, doing all these things” (Isa. 45:7).

**Definition XXXVIII, chapter 15, section 8**

You say: “God does not punish what he has made.”

We answer: God punishes—that is, subjects to punishment—nothing other than what he has made, but he does so because of the merit of sin, which he himself did not make. For in blessed Job no sin was being punished, but only the flesh that God had made; and, what is greater than all, in our Lord Jesus Christ nothing was punished except what he himself had made, namely, his flesh.

**Definition XXXIX, chapter 15, section 8**

You say: “God does not take away from those whom he has made the natural gifts.”

We answer: God makes people blind, deaf, mute, lame, sterile, and so forth.

**Definition XL, chapter 16, section 1**

You say: “No nature punishes another nature.”

We answer: No nature is punished except by another nature—namely, a created nature by the creating nature—so that he who is the maker of created natures is himself their judge and punisher; or created natures are punished by created natures.

## [Scan page 686]

### On Predestination against John Scotus — Summary

**Definition XLI, chapter 16, section 1**

You say: “In the first human being it was not the generality of nature that sinned, but the individual will of each person.”

We answer: In him the generality of nature sinned, which Scripture calls the mass of damnation; and therefore the whole of it was condemned by the just Judge—not the will alone, nor something that could be restored except through the humility of the Mediator.

**Definition XLII, chapter 16, section 3**

You say: “If the whole of nature sinned, since it is one, the whole would certainly perish.”

We answer: The whole nature sinned and therefore in a certain sense the whole perished. Nevertheless, we read in many cases that punishments for crimes are deservedly inflicted upon bodies through illnesses. For the apostles, thinking that the man born blind had been punished for his sins, asked the Lord:

> “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he should be born blind?” (John 9:2).

He himself answered:

> “Neither did this man sin nor his parents, but that the works of God might be manifested in him” (John 9:3).

Likewise, concerning Lazarus, who was ill:

> “This illness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it” (John 11:4).

Yet we also read in many places that bodily illnesses are deservedly inflicted as punishments for crimes, as the Lord said to the paralytic after healing him:

> “Go, and sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5:14).

**Definition XLII, chapter 16, section 1**

You say: “In eternal fire there is no other punishment than the absence of blessedness.”

We answer: This absence is indeed a punishment, but so are the excessive burning of the fire and the consumption by worms.

**Definition XLIII, chapter 16, section 4**

You say: “In that fire there is no one who does not possess within himself, by nature, a conception of the blessedness that is absent, together with a desire for it.”

We answer: We ought rather to believe the prophet, who says:

> “Will your wonders be known in darkness, and your justice in the land of forgetfulness?” (Ps. 87:13).

**Definition XLIV, chapter 16, section 1**

You say: “The wretched will have no conception, knowledge, or desire of blessedness and happiness, and therefore they will not be wretched or punished.”

We answer: The prophet said:

> “He will enter to the generation of his fathers; forever he will not see light” (Ps. 48:20).

Therefore they are wretched, because they will never rise to blessedness, and punished, because their punishment will never end.

**Definition XLV, chapter 16, sections 2 and 7**

You say: “In devils and ungodly human beings there is no punishment except the perversity of their own will.”

We answer: Their nature, corrupted and vitiated by their own will, is punished.

**Definition XLVI, chapter 16, section 2**

You say: “It was not nature that sinned, but the will.”

We answer: Nature did indeed sin, but not the defect of nature as it was created by the good God; rather, it sinned as it was corrupted through its own will. The sin itself therefore belongs not only to the will, which is not nature, but also to the nature whose will it is; and therefore the nature bears the punishment of sin. Nature—that is, Eve—admitted the serpent’s persuasion, and through nature—that is, through her body—she ate the fruit of the forbidden tree.

Hence she needs a liberator. For in infants it is not the will of sin, which is absent, but the nature of a condemned origin that is punished.

**Definition XLIX, chapter 16, section 3**

You say: “Nature cannot be punished at all, because it is from God and does not sin; rather, the perverse will is tormented when it is not permitted to possess what it shamefully desires.”

We answer: This too is a punishment, both in the present life and until the day of judgment; afterward there will be another punishment, including the memory of sins and the unquenchable fire of Gehenna.

The Apostle, however, cries out to the contrary:

> “We were by nature children of wrath” (Eph. 2:3).

And again:

> “Just as you presented your members as slaves to uncleanness and iniquity for iniquity, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness for sanctification” (Rom. 6:19).

And again:

> “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin which is in my members” (Rom. 7:23).

The members of the body are indeed natural; and although they were made by God, they do not have from God the fact that they sin, but from themselves, through their own will. Therefore they are deservedly punished.

**Definition L, chapter 16, section 2**

You say: “Evil does not come from any good.”

We answer: No evil exists except from a good.

**Definition LI, chapter 16, section 7**

You say: “The person who changes free choice of the will—which is the gift of natural intelligence, that is, the clarity of the mind—to shameful uses, so that he may no longer enjoy the honesty of truth at all, is most justly destroyed and cannot avoid the darkness of eternal ignorance.”

We answer: This is indeed true, but it is against yourself, since shortly before you had granted them a conception, knowledge, and desire of blessedness, happiness, and truth. Nevertheless, they do not escape the punishments of eternal fire by this truth.

**Definition LII, chapter 17, section 3**

You say: “Wherever God’s presence is, there he is also by habitation.”

We answer: Scripture says: “Wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul, nor dwell in a body enslaved to sins” (Wis. 1:4).
