## [Scan page 687]

### Saint Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

**Definition LIII, chapter 17, section 4**

You say: “God’s presence and habitation in those things which are not from him and which he did not make must be understood in the opposite sense, since he is not in them.”

We answer: In the divine utterances God’s habitation is nowhere said to be in things that do not exist; but his foreknowledge is not absent even from our wickedness and sins.

**Definition LIV, chapter 17, section 5**

You say: “By comparison with a certain householder’s house, heaven and earth are this house, the wicked are placed in the air, and the good in heaven.”

We answer: The wicked are confined beneath the earth in perpetual infernal fire, while the good are glorified in everlasting blessedness above all this visible heaven, which sacred Scripture calls the firmament.

**Definition LV, chapter 17, section 7**

You say: “The eternal fire was made to burn the devil and his angels, not human beings.”

We answer: God said:

> “If your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and cast it from you. It is better for you to enter life eternal with one eye than, having two eyes, to be sent into the unquenchable fire, where their worm does not die and the fire is not extinguished” (Mark 9:46–47).

He says the same concerning the hand and the foot.

**Definition LVI, chapter 17, section 7**

You say: “After the devil was thrust down from the ether, where, in his ethereal body, he could not feel punishments, an aerial body was added to him in which he could feel fire.”

We answer: This cannot in any way be proved by the authority of prophetic or apostolic Scripture.

**Definition LVII, chapter 17, section 8**

You say: “That fire is neither a punishment nor prepared or predestined for punishment.”

We answer: The Lord said, after he had pronounced the parable of the good and evil fish:

> “The angels will go out and separate the wicked from among the just, and they will cast them into the furnace of fire; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 13:49–50).

It is plainly shown that you have spoken against yourself, since earlier you said that this same fire was made to burn the devil and his angels. For I do not see how anyone can be burned except by way of punishment.

**Definition LVIII, chapter 17, section 8**

You say: “The same fire was made as the dwelling place of the wicked, in which the blessed dwell no less than the miserable.”

We answer: It is not, as you foolishly suppose, a dwelling place of sweetness and dignity for the wicked, but an eternal torment. Nor will the blessed dwell in it, since the Lord says:

> “These will go into eternal punishment, but the just into eternal life” (Matt. 25:46).

Nowhere in sacred Scripture is that fire called eternal life.

**Definition LIX, chapter 17, section 9**

You say: “There is no misery except eternal death; no eternal death except ignorance of the truth; and no misery except ignorance of the truth. Where the truth is unknown, there is no life.”

We answer: In this life the repentant sinner salutarily says:

> “I have become miserable, and I am bowed down to the end” (Ps. 37:7),

and the Apostle says:

> “Wretched man that I am!” (Rom. 7:24).

Another says:

> “Be miserable and mourn” (Jas. 4:9).

We freely confess that these people have been rescued from eternal death by God’s grace and are not darkened by ignorance of the truth. But whoever does not notice that your opinions and statements contradict one another lacks understanding. For above you said that they possess a conception, knowledge, and desire of blessedness, happiness, and truth. You also said that where the truth is unknown there is no life. If the ungodly are merely to have a dwelling place in that fire, and are not also to suffer punishment, how will they have no life? But the Truth cries out that the ungodly will have life there—but a punitive life.

**Definition LX, chapter 18, heading and section 1**

You say: “The error concerning predestination arose from ignorance of the liberal arts and lack of knowledge of Greek literature.”

We answer: It is not an error but the truth of the twofold predestination, approved and proclaimed so greatly by the Fathers; and we have no doubt that they possessed perfect knowledge of those arts. Rather, you have swollen beyond your strength with your tiny scrap of learning and have impiously burst forth into such great blasphemies.

**Definition LXI, chapter 18, section 1**

You say: “God wished his wisdom to be accompanied and investigated by them.”

We answer: God’s wisdom needed no companion, nor was it investigated through them. Rather, it was made known through his Spirit, concerning whom he himself promises:

> “When the Spirit of truth has come, he will teach you all truth” (John 16:13).

This is proved without contradiction in prophets who were shepherds and in apostles who were fishermen, ignorant of letters. The Apostle says:

> “Since the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe” (1 Cor. 1:21).

And the Evangelist says:

> “He was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1:9).

And again the Apostle says:

> “The Gospel preached by me is not according to man; for I neither received it from man nor learned it, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ” (Gal. 1:11–12).

**Definition LXII, chapter 18, section 3**

You say: “Predestination and predefinition are nothing other than foresight.”

We answer: This is false, since many things are foreseen that are neither predestined nor predefined.

**Definition LXIII, chapter 18, section 4**

You say: “God neither foresaw nor predestined death and punishments, because they are nothing.”

We answer: God both foresaw and predestined death and punishments, because …

[scan page 689]

## Saint Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

**Definition LXVIII, chapter 18, section 1.**

He foresaw him and forbade him to sin, and foretold that, if he sinned, he would die.

**Definition LXIV, chapter 18, section 7.**

**You say:** This eternal fire is that same fourth element of the world.

**We answer:** It seems rather to be another, since its quality and nature are also different.

**Definition LXIX, chapter 19, section 1.**

**You say:** In that body the saints will pass over into an ethereal quality, while the bodies of the wicked will pass over into an aerial quality.

**We answer:** The bodies of the saints will by no means undergo any change into an ethereal quality, even in that fire; rather, they will remain in the truth of their own flesh and members, however glorified, and will live for ever. The bodies of the wicked, however, will undergo no change whatever, except immortality, by which they can never again be corrupted through death or fail away.

**Definition LXIV, chapter 18, section 7.**

**You say:** God’s wisdom predestined, in its laws, limits beyond which the wickedness of the wicked cannot proceed, nor can anyone’s wickedness be extended to infinity as far as it wishes, since the divine laws impose a limit upon its advance.

**We answer:** This is true, as blessed Job says: “You have appointed his bounds, which he cannot pass” (Job 14:5). But this statement acts more against you than with you; for you maintain that this is a punishment for sinners, when they are not permitted to sin as much as they wish. If, therefore, this is their punishment, from whom does it come except from him whose laws restrain it? Admit, then, that this penal restraint was imposed upon them by God, and consequently, without contradiction, that it is a punishment from him.

**Definition LXV, chapter 18, section 7.**

**You say:** All the wicked, and the devil’s wickedness, desire nothing except to withdraw from him who is the supreme essence, so that, if the divine law permitted it, their nature would return to nothing.

**We answer:** We are astonished at so acute a disputant: earlier you said that the desire for blessedness is implanted naturally in everyone, and that all desire it; now, on the contrary, you assert that they desire nothing except to withdraw from him who is the supreme essence, although the supreme essence itself is unquestionably eternal blessedness. Likewise, earlier you said that no nature perishes; now you assert that nature would return to nothing if the divine law permitted it.

**Definition LXVI, chapter 18, section 8.**

**You say:** The wicked serve God unwillingly—not the nature that he made in them, and which he does not punish in them, but the evil will, which he did not make in them and which he punishes in them. Insofar as they serve him unwillingly, they are punished in their own punishments.

**We answer:** Both—the nature, namely, and the will of the wicked—serve God unwillingly and are justly punished, not by themselves as their own punishment, but by him whose power is just. Yet by these words you are very greatly refuting yourself, since earlier you had asserted that no one is compelled either to good or to evil.

**Definition LXVII, chapter 18, section 8.**

**You say:** Those whom he does not justly free from punishment, he in a certain manner prepares for it, permitting them to prepare themselves for it.

**We answer:** The Fathers never intended this to be expressed in such a way. On the contrary, they said that they prepare themselves for punishment by living wickedly and persevering in wickedness, while God either prepares or predestines them by judging them most justly.

**Definition LXX, chapter 19, section 3.**

**You say:** In the same fire there is a marvelous fulfillment of joy for the natures, but an ineffable torment for the will of the wicked.

**We answer:** There is no joy there for the natures, since, as the Lord testifies, “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” You are thereby most forcefully contradicting yourself, since earlier you had said that there is no misery except eternal death, and that eternal death is ignorance of the truth; and where the truth is unknown, there is no life. What joy, I ask, do you assign to those whom you had taught to be subject to eternal death, misery, ignorance of the truth, and no life?

**Definition LXXI, chapter 19, section 3.**

**You say:** The bodies of the wicked angels and of human beings will possess beauty and natural soundness and will shine.

**We answer:** Scripture says: “Where no order exists, and everlasting horror dwells” (Job 10:22).

**Definition LXXII, chapter 19, section 3.**

**You say:** Except for the blessedness of which they will be deprived, they will have no punishment.

**We answer:** They will suffer eternal torments both in soul and in body.

**Definition LXXIII, chapter 19, section 3.**

**You say:** The intention of the unhappy souls will eternally suffer anguish because of their bodies.

**We answer:** We see no reason why the human beings whom you previously made happy should be unhappy, or what anguish they could suffer because of their bodies, to which you granted integrity, beauty, soundness, and radiance.

**Definition LXXIV, chapter 19, section 3.**

**You say:** That same fire will become glory for all bodies.

**We answer:** It will become no glory at all, but truly unending torment.

**Definition LXXV, epilogue, section 2.**

**You say:** God predestined the wicked to destruction.

**We answer:** We embrace and confess this, once your evasion—by which you mean something other than what you say—has been rejected.

[scan page 690]

## Venilo

See the discussion of this Definition in the Epilogue, no. 6. The final Definition in Hincmar’s *On Predestination* is found at chapter 31, p. 232; hence it has been placed here.

**Definition LXXVII and final, epilogue, section 3.**

**You say:** You anathematize those who speak of a twofold predestination, or who express the word “predestination” in the plural.

**We answer:** This accusation suits you better, since you have attacked the impartiality of God’s judgments; denied the faith of truthful statements; utterly distorted the meaning of the venerable Fathers; and, in addition, proclaimed as inventions certain falsehoods that no one is found ever to have said or written before you.

**Definition LXXVI, epilogue, section 2.**

**You say:** God is not punishing in them what he had made, but what he had not made; he will leave them to be punished.

[What remains—namely, the response to this Definition together with the final Definition—is missing from the manuscript of the library of Jacques-Auguste de Thou, from which this text was copied.]

## Saint Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

### A Letter of Exhortation to Venilo

Which he sent through a representative to the ordination of Aeneas of Paris, since he himself could not be present.

To the venerable Father and to the other Fathers and brothers, most sincerely beloved, and to his reverend fellow bishops, Prudentius sends eternal salvation in the Lord.

### On free will

So far as the deserts of my sins are concerned, I am, by God’s most just judgment, prevented from being present at your holy and most desirable assembly, being burdened by almost every infirmity known to men; but, so far as his unfailing and inexhaustible mercies are concerned, I offer through this letter, and through Arnold, the priest and representative of our church, my assent to the ordination, provided that the man to be ordained is willing, in confession, to subscribe—and, in subscribing, to confess—the ordinances of the apostolic see and the writings and sayings of the blessed Fathers: Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, Sixtus, Leo, Gelasius, Celestine, Gregory, Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, Isidore, Primasius, Fulgentius, Gregory, Jerome, Cassiodorus, Bede, and other Catholic and orthodox men, especially concerning the four chapters by which the whole Catholic Church fought against and conquered Pelagius and the adherents of his heresy, and committed them to writing, most full of authority and truth, for the remembrance of posterity. Otherwise, I neither assent at all nor advise Christ’s faithful to assent. Although I do not doubt that your prudence knows the sequence of the four aforesaid chapters much more vividly than my own insignificance, I have nevertheless judged it necessary to append it briefly, so that your kindness may more easily recognize what I think and to what truth I assent.

First. Let him confess that free will, deservedly lost in Adam through disobedience, has been restored and liberated for us through our Lord Jesus Christ: for the present in hope, but afterwards in reality, as the Apostle says: “For in hope we were saved” (Romans 8:24). Yet let us know that in every good work we always need the grace of almighty God—whether to think it, begin it, carry it out, or persevere in bringing it to completion—and that without that grace we can in no way think, will, or perform anything good.

### On the twofold predestination

Second. Let him believe and confess, according to the most profound secret counsel of almighty God, that some have by God’s gratuitous mercy been predestined before all ages to life, and others by his inscrutable justice predestined to punishment; namely, that whether in saving or in condemning, he predestined what he foreknew that he himself would do in judging, as the prophet says: “He made the things that are to come” (Isaiah 45:11, according to the Septuagint).

### On the death of Christ

Third. Let him believe and confess, with all Catholics, that the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ was poured out for all human beings throughout the whole world who believe in him; but not for those who never believed in him, do not believe today, and will never believe, as the Lord himself says: “For the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matthew 20:28).

[scan page 691]

### On the will of God

Fourth. Let him believe and confess that almighty God saves whomever he wills, and that no one can in any way be saved except the one whom he himself saves: “He saves all those whom he wishes to save.” Therefore, whoever is not saved is altogether not one whom he willed to be saved, as the prophet says: “The Lord does whatever he wills, in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses” (Psalm 134:6).

Let him also agree with the universal Church, which, in its effort against certain persons condemned with Pelagius and his accomplices, has been rescued, vindicated, and defended from their snares through the apostolic see, at the insistence of the most blessed Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, and Augustine, together with other Catholic bishops; and which has been published throughout the world in many letters and books, and which even today rejoices in, confesses, preaches, holds, and will hold this teaching. May heavenly grace preserve your fatherhood, worthy of all praise, and your fraternity, wholly consonant with these things, unconquered and most strong, and make it steadfast for ever by its gift.

## The Same: Letter to a Certain Bishop

(Mabillon, *Veterum Analecta*.)

To his lord, reverend in the Lord who is Lord of lords, distinguished by the dignity of the priesthood and the rank of fatherhood, Prudentius, the most humble servant of Christ’s servants, sends eternal salvation in the Savior of all.

How greatly, dearest brother, the sweetness of the text of your letter—so desired by me—has refreshed my thirst and burning, long accumulated and insatiable; and how much most delightful pleasure it has brought, I cannot adequately express. For, tossed miserably amid so many and such great waves of troubles, I had almost been shipwrecked beyond recovery, and could not, as the saying is, draw even a little from anything by which I might learn whether you had already happened to return to the Lord. But when, at last released from the Palatine watches in which I had been taught to serve cruelly, I met the bearer of your most desirable letter … [the intervening words are corrupt], whom your grace, not any abundance of my merits, had deigned to visit; immediately, with joy overcoming my fears, I recovered breath in my other self, whom I had feared extinguished, from sleep—or rather from despair, not forgetfulness—that had seized me. Giving thanks to the heavenly goodness, which is accustomed to preserve its own amid adversity and prosperity, I clung to the insatiable and repeatedly renewed reading of the letter, and at last found in it my brother in spirit, indeed my other self, whom I had been seeking. I rejoice exceedingly because he who seemed dead to me by report suddenly appeared alive, and I do not doubt that he whom I thought gone away has returned.

Accordingly, giving thanks to the author of all good things, I am unceasingly and inexpressibly gladdened by this one good: that I hear not merely that you live, but that you live well. Hearing, I rejoice; rejoicing, I desire; desiring, I ask; and I hope through your holy prayers and merits to deserve to live with you, and to be steadfastly relieved from all that tirelessly assails the purpose and vow of Christian warfare which I have undertaken. Therefore, sweetest of brothers, do not cease, by the grace of him who orders all things and makes all things serene, to support me and those entrusted to my charge by the aid of your most holy and most urgent intercession. May the power of the almighty arm deign always to preserve you well in the Lord, and to carry us—who, while repeatedly visiting by gifts of your own composition, whether bound or unbound, command that they be sent to needy persons who long for them—to the harbor of the desired shore by the nail of importunate prayers.

## Saint Prudentius of Troyes

### Sermon on the Life and Death of the Blessed Virgin Maura

(From the *Promptuarium* of Garnier, …)

Although I have often, suitably or unsuitably, at the proper time or at an inconvenient one, spoken to you on solemn days about the glorious life and precious death of our sister Maura, I shall not merely say something … [the opening is fragmentary in the supplied scan].

## Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

### Life of the Glorious Virgin Maura

(From the ancient church of Troyes)

Yet I shall leave a written account for those who come after, so that it may benefit them. For her brother Eutropius, your provost, who was more closely related to her in spiritual affection than in bodily kinship, and Leo, our fellow priest, who catechized her and regenerated her from water and the Holy Spirit, frequently urged me on behalf of the holy monks.

I rejoice in the Lord over the abundant handfuls of your devotion. It is not enough for you to have seen God’s virtues in her with your own eyes; you also drink them in repeatedly with your own ears. At the repeated hearing of them you run more fervently after the fragrance of her ointments; and, stirred by the example within your own household, you again embrace the labor and await the fruit and honor that the prudent virgin has already obtained. Having received oil and prepared her lamp, she entered with the Bridegroom into the everlasting wedding feast. Of that feast let us now sing in our own fashion, while we remain travelers, until we are able to recline among those who have reached their destination, where the righteous, received there, feast and exult in the sight of God.

Sedulia, the widow devoted to the service of Christ and the Church, the blessed girl’s mother, and her aforementioned brother Eutropius assert that she had not yet completed her twenty-third year when, rejecting carnal marriage, she was admitted to the heavenly wedding feast.

Her father Marianus, who is buried in the church of the Apostles, departed from this age shortly before her. His daughter, physically begotten by him in the world, earnestly labored to beget him specially for God through many seeds of tears. Though rich, powerful, and noble, he had already entered the broad roads of the age; but, led by God’s grace onto the narrow road that leads to life, he turned back. He was in truth an approachable man, willing to listen to advice, and he believed nothing that could in any way diminish his fatherly affection for the salvation of his son Eutropius; nor did he refuse to believe in his own salvation through the virgin Maura.

A woman brought a man to me, a young woman brought an old man, a daughter brought her father, a little sheep brought a lion. Causing him to fall at my feet, she taught him, with admirable prudence, both to repent from the depths of his heart of his sins and to confess them fully. Then, on my advice and that of his daughter, whom I had found to be an excellent helper, he renounced temporal possessions, appointed the church of the Apostles his heir, and finally ordered, out of great devotion of heart, that his own body be buried there.

I give you thanks, Lord God, who were pleased to grant us such a fellow worker in your service. Like a fire that consumes the forest and a flame that burns up mountains, she first set fire to whatever was nearest—as is evident in her father and her father’s household—and afterward to what was more remote, with the fire that you came to cast upon the earth and willed to burn.

When her brother Eutropius converted, he brought nothing from his father’s possessions, leaving everything to his only sister Maura, with the intention that, through those possessions, she might enter more noble marriage chambers and celebrate a more solemn marriage.

A marvelous thing! Eutropius, if I may speak without offending him, when bidding farewell to the world was thinking about worldly matters; but Maura, remaining in the world, was thinking with herself about heaven. From there she now brings forth fruit in the presence of the holy souls: not mortal offspring from marriage, but living offspring from tears. She tastes in heaven the flavor of that whose fragrance she smelled on earth.

I do not grieve for you, my son Eutropius, nor should you complain that you have been cheated of the fruit of your intention by the wealth you left behind. In truth, through those possessions your sister Maura entered more noble marriage chambers and obtained a more solemn union. From the mammon of iniquity she acquired great friends, and a powerful and rich Bridegroom for all who call upon him, one more beautiful than the sons of men: the great friend, the prince of the apostles and keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven; the great Saint Paul, the chosen vessel. In the church of Troyes she dedicated both herself and a considerable portion of her possessions to their service.

Who supplied oil for the lamps? Maura. Who spread the carpets? Maura. Who purchased priestly vestments from her own resources? Maura. I esteem more highly than gold and topaz the linen garment she presented to me, which she prepared, whitened, and humbly requested that I wear during the solemn celebration of the Mass.

O generous and kind virgin, you did these things—and I was silent! I was silent; shall I always be silent? There is a time for silence and a time for speech, now that you rejoice with the Bridegroom in heaven.

I confess, most prudent virgin, that I can no longer keep my mouth closed. In one matter you bestowed two most precious gifts, so that, through the one who gave, nothing could be insignificant or of little value to me; through the one who granted, every gift was pleasing, every thing received welcome, and every rare object precious.

What did I value? I valued the spirit more than the hand, the affection more than the deed, the joy more than the sadness. I give thanks to you, gracious virgin, for your generosity, by which you bestowed so splendid a garment upon one unworthy.

But was it only that? Certainly not. You doubled the gift, and, giving abundantly, gave in abundance. You supplied a twofold adornment: one bodily and the other spiritual; one outward and the other inward; one visible and the other hidden. I no longer wish to conceal the latter, but to reveal it, so that your divine clemency and the hardness of my wretched heart may be made known.

I was dry and parched, and deserved nothing but fire. I had withered like hay, deservedly destined for the furnace. My soul was like land without water, and therefore barren and fruitless. What was I waiting for? Why did I not reveal my misery more plainly?

I handled the sacrament of the Lord’s body with only the scant butter of devotion. When she presented the garment just mentioned, I was eating the Lamb without wild lettuces, and approaching the bread of angels without the bread of tears.

What more can I say? That strong woman sought—not wool, but linen—and worked according to the counsel of her hands. Within a few days she completed the work she had undertaken, in which the skill of its maker shone forth; and at last she gave it to Prudentius, the bishop whom she loved.

I shall no longer hide your mercy, Lord. From my abundant store I shall relate the great things you have done through your servant Maura. For when I received the garment, immediately that ancient virgin’s virtue brought forth a plentiful stream of water from me, harder than stone; and how effective it was afterward, whenever many of us were clothed in it for the solemn celebration of the Mass, is beyond description.

O good Jesus, this is altogether true and tested, and we see it fulfilled in the young Maura: what young women loved, and what was sufficient in advance to have been proclaimed. From the beginning of her life she remained daily in the church of the Apostles from the morning praises until the sixth hour.

You know that the image of the Lord the Savior is painted in three ways: as a child sitting in his mother’s lap; as the great Lord sitting on the throne of majesty; and as a young man hanging on the cross. Blessed Maura observed this practice from tender childhood, so that each day she never ceased to contemplate the entire representation with her bodily eyes.

It is a trite but true saying: where there is love, there is the eye. Loving the Lord with a sincere and undivided affection, the young girl could never be satisfied with looking upon him.

Now, dearest brothers, I wish to open what has remained closed until now, what I have hitherto concealed. I judge it harmful to keep silent about the rest and fruitful to disclose it; the time has come for me freely to explain what I had extracted from her lips by persistent questioning.

The day of her calling was approaching, and the swift laying aside of her tabernacle. Therefore, wishing at last to receive some instruction from her, I asked her—and repeated the question several times—why she slowly prostrated herself before the aforementioned image of the Savior’s speech [i.e. representation], every day and successively.

At last, after being entreated in many ways, she answered, though not without great difficulty:

“Blessed is the church of the Apostles, in which I have often heard the child wailing in his mother’s lap, the young man groaning on the cross, and the king thundering terribly from his throne, yet kindly giving me a golden scepter.”

When I immediately began to put another question to her about the groaning and wailing of our Savior, she clasped my hand in hers and thereby restrained my tongue. Then she added these few words:

“It must be attributed not to nature but to miracles if, in order to recall the wondrous mysteries of our faith and strengthen them in the minds of the faithful, a piece of dry wood produced a groan or a wail.”

O how blessed is our industrious daughter—not fertile in children, but in holy works! O mother, so solicitous and troubled about many things! She cared to assist not only the needs of clerics but also those of monks. Leo the abbot and his holy congregation acknowledge this: she acquired for them, from her own resources, cowls and maniples; diligently sought the favor and assistance of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul in the church of the clerics; and more earnestly implored the patronage of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius in the monastery of the monks.

Although the monastery is about four miles from this city of Troyes, she nevertheless visited it every Wednesday and Friday as a pilgrim, barefoot and fasting, without bread or water.

[scan page 694]

## On the Life and Death of the Blessed Virgin Maura

How great the virtue and efficacy of the maniple that Maura gave to Leo are, the cleric Melanus and the most holy monk Paulinus plainly testify: they were freed from fevers by its touch.

Although some attribute and ascribe this to the merits of the gentle Leo, I nevertheless think it should rather be understood as Leo himself understands it with us: namely, that what her Bridegroom wondrously performs should redound to the glory of the holy virgin, lest anyone else presume to appropriate the golden necklaces which the Beloved wished to present to his beloved as a sign of affection and an ornament of beauty.

Brother Mauritius, I have not yet forgotten what I learned through your [hidden, or “eyewitness”] faith while you were serving. After the matutinal office had been completed, you signaled me to look more closely at Maura, who was embracing more tightly and kissing more sweetly the altar where the body of the blessed virgin Mastidia rests. But when the sixth hour had been sung by the brothers, you displayed at the feet of that same altar a little stream of your tears and washed your own eyes with it. How much that washing benefited you, and that you possess the grace of tears while no longer possessing the blemish of the eye, are proved by certain and irrefutable arguments.

You became, for as long as you live, a most clear, living, and true testimony to the wondrous works of the Lamb and his Bride. For although your tongue is silent, wherever you go your eye never ceases to preach the praises of Christ and Maura.

We all know, dearest Levite Mauritius, that your voice is scarcely audible, so that, when you read the Holy Gospel, you can hardly be heard at the church door. How, then, did that sonority arise which on Good Friday penetrated Maura’s ears, although she was alone and far away?

On that day, between the Sixth and the Ninth Hour, I, a most wretched sinner and such a bishop as I am, was sowing the seeds of holy preaching in the church of Saint Aventinus in the suburb of the city. In fulfillment of my office I cast the hook of divine speech into the hearts of those listening, catching, according to my ability, a few small fish.

Maura was present, listening attentively and sitting among the other hearers. No circumstance could ever draw her away from this holy occupation. But because she was from God, she heard the words of God, inscribing them in her heart as in a book.

When, as the time required, I began to speak about the mystery of the Lord’s Passion, she suddenly rose while the others remained seated, stood upon her feet, and armed herself entirely with the sign of the life-giving cross.

When I asked what had happened to her, and why, contrary to custom, she did not sit with the others, she replied with a modest expression and dove-like simplicity:

“Father, is one to remain seated when the Holy Gospel is being read?”

The Levite Mauritius had begun to read the Passion of the Lord in the church of the Apostles. If it pleases those standing, let us omit other matters for a little while and listen.

Immediately I asked the bystanders whether they had heard anything. When silence had been made, the whole crowd replied that it had heard absolutely nothing. Understanding, therefore, that divine power was present in the distinguished virgin, and that tears were flowing abundantly, I could in no way complete the sermon I had begun.

But immediately, for the sake of those who doubted and in order to establish the great works of God more certainly, we all hurried to the church of the Apostles. There, after making a brief station at the entrance, we could scarcely at last hear the thin and faint voice of Mauritius, who was still reading.

When the Gospel of the Lord’s Passion had been completed, we all together offered glory and honor to the Lord. Offering glory to his name in his temple, we all said, “Glory to him who is glorious in his saints.”

The virgin of God, however, lay trembling at my feet. While the others rejoiced, she wept and beat her breast; and, as though the word of salvation had troubled her, she loudly declared herself the most wretched of sinners.

Soon afterward the day of the calling mentioned above dawned—the day illumined by a great light, namely, the apostle and evangelist Matthew, whose glorious feast was then being celebrated. A lesser light was added to him, namely Maura, the bride of God, wholly pleasing and acceptable to the apostle, who pleases God in the light of the living. Thus there are now two olive trees and two shining lampstands before the Lord, a pair of turtle-doves or two young pigeons.

Blessed Matthew the apostle, you have the power to lead a sister with you as a brother, like the brother of the Lord, James, and Cephas. You surely do not consider the former tax collector less worthy than a best man of Christ’s Bridegroom. You no longer disdain to receive the virgin who calls upon you into your fellowship, for you remember that you were a publican. You truly love Maura’s holiness, since you proclaimed the everlasting salvation of Mauritania; and you gently become mild toward the white-robed virgin, though you were not at all afraid of the dreadful Ethiopians.

When the feast just mentioned arrived, whose joy was doubled by the happiness of blessed Maura’s calling, we saw her raise her head from her sickbed as best she could and incline it toward the four directions. When Leo familiarly asked why she did this, she replied:

“Behold, four strong ones surround my bed on four sides and drive away bloody beasts: Peter and Paul, Gervasius and Protasius, whom I served with whatever devotion I could for as long as I lived.”

Immediately turning to me, she added:

“This final favor I ask of you, Father Prudentius, bishop: that in their presence I may receive from your hand the sacraments of the Eucharist and of extreme unction.”

And this was done. Immediately, when the Lord’s Prayer had begun, after she had completed the petition that says, “Your kingdom come,” she happily departed to the Lord, her heavenly calling fulfilled in jubilation.

At once the matron Mauriciana, Sedulia’s sister, and Mauriciana’s two daughters, Damona and Thecia, snatched a hair-cloth from the holy body and divided it into four pieces. They kept three for themselves and gave me the fourth, which I have preserved as a great treasure.

After washing the body according to custom, they presented to my eyes water that had been changed into milk, a testimony to the virgin’s chastity. Leonicus, Damona’s son, overcome by sweetness and drinking abundantly, was healed of the fever’s burning; and by the touch of the holy cloth, Thecia was freed from a blemish …

[scan page 695]

## Saint Prudentius of Troyes, Bishop

…with a certain mark on her face which she had contracted from her mother’s womb and which therefore displeased her husband, she was freed. At that very hour when the holy virgin departed, Veranus the monk—who had long before completely lost his sense of smell—sensed the same fragrant odor in the monastery of Saint Leontius, which those who were near the holy body also perceived. After she had been suitably committed to burial, in the place where she is now honored by the faithful, countless miracles followed, worked by him who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# Saint Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

## Second Part

### Historical Monuments of Germany

# Annals of Saint Bertinus, or the Annals of Bertin

*(In Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae Historica.)*

## Extracts from Pertz’s Preface to the Annals of Bertin

That the second part of the Annals of Bertin was formerly attributed to Prudentius, the distinguished bishop of Troyes, is clear from the twenty-fifth letter of Hincmar of Reims, addressed to Egilo, archbishop of Sens. He writes as follows:

> “Lord Prudentius, in the Annal of the deeds of our kings which he composed, wishing to confirm his own opinion, inserted under the year of the Lord’s incarnation 859, saying: ‘Pope Nicholas, by the grace of God, concerning free will, the truth of double predestination, and the blood of Christ, that it was poured out for all believers, faithfully confirms and declares this in the Catholic manner; for we have heard it from no other person, nor have we read it elsewhere. Therefore, since the very deeds in which these matters were written have now come into the hands of many, it is necessary that we advise concerning this apostolic lord in such a way that scandal may not arise from it in the Church.… The king possesses the Annal of which I speak; it is the very book which, in your presence, in the church where he commended it to us, I returned to him after he had entrusted it to me before you.’”

The words reported by Hincmar, except for the phrase concerning the blood, are found in our Annals near the end of the year 859. Since Prudentius died in 861, as is stated shortly afterward, he certainly could not have carried his work beyond the beginning of that year. The learned former abbot Lebeuf, in a special dissertation on this matter, demonstrated that the remaining portion, beginning in 861, is entirely different from the earlier part.

First, with regard to individual words, he proposed that Prudentius, who came from Spain, in accordance with his native usage, whenever the occasion arose, called it not “Epiphany” but the *Festum Apparitionis Domini* (“Feast of the Lord’s Manifestation”). He also proposed that Prudentius called the affairs of the Franks, and generally of Christians, *res nostras* (“our affairs”); that, when circumstances required it, he used not the word *hostis* (“enemy”) but *exercitus* (“army”), following Roman usage; and that, following Julius Caesar’s *Commentaries* and the Antonine Itinerary, he referred to Gallic cities by their ancient names: Agedincum of the Senones, Augusta of the Tricasses, Augusta of the Treveri, Augusta of the Veromandui, Caesarodunum of the Turones, Durocortorum of the Remi, Samarobriva of the Ambiani, Lutetia of the Parisii, and Tullum of the Leuci.

By contrast, after 861 the continuator uses *Durocortorum Remorum* only once; employs *hostis* (“enemy”) in place of *exercitus* (“army”), in both masculine and feminine gender; and uses *honores* (“honours”) in place of *beneficia* (“benefices”). Lebeuf therefore argued that Prudentius was concerned chiefly with recording Spanish matters, and that, in describing all noteworthy events, he occupied himself with eclipses of the sun and moon, comets, the northern lights, rains and storms, earthquakes, floods, lightning, winter and pestilence, famine, and the devastation caused by wolves. He touched ecclesiastical affairs only lightly and in expressions used in antiquity, and willingly attributed everything, good or evil, in a pious and benevolent spirit to the divine omnipotence.

The continuator, omitting all these matters, was chiefly concerned to give, as fully as necessary, the history of King Charles and, above all, the deeds of Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, omitting nothing. Since this is evident to anyone who examines the work, it is difficult to doubt that the continuator also held a high rank in the Church.

Lebeuf therefore maintained that Hincmar, after Prudentius’s death, continued the Annals, which had been lent to him by King Charles, and enlarged them. It is consequently easy to understand why the passage concerning Gottschalk, as it now appears in the Annals under the year 849, could not have been written by Prudentius, but has been altered to appear as though it were his.

Hincmar, he believed, corrected the book intended for his own use. Anyone who examines that portion of the Annals more carefully will see that the archbishop was thoroughly versed not only in canon law but also in the events of his own time. He appears in the Bouquet edition as having restored the passage to the form in which he believed it had originally proceeded from Prudentius, and he took considerable risks in doing so. Some of the information he supplied could scarcely have been known to anyone except Hincmar.

Among such matters are the account, under the year 867, of clerics sent by Hincmar to Rome in pilgrims’ clothing; the mention, under the year 845, of the day on which Hincmar received the pope’s letter and read it to King Charles; the account, under the year 861, of Hincmar’s flight when a certain monastery called Sithiu was plundered; and the account, under the year 876, of the dispute over the primacy of Gaul between Hincmar and Ansegisus.

The Annals were not composed in the monastery of Saint Bertinus, as is demonstrated by the mention of that monastery under the year 845 and by the fact that, under the year 853, Hincmar refers to a monastery called Sithiu.

Prudentius and Hincmar begin the year from the Nativity of the Lord.

### Notes

(a) In Hincmar’s works, volume II, p. 292.

# Annals

Could he have wished to undertake such extensive care in setting these matters forth? Nor can it be doubted that, like Prudentius, the continuator too had been raised to the highest ranks in the Church. It is now clear that Hincmar, after Prudentius’s death, wrote out the Annals lent to him by King Charles and enlarged them by a continuation.

If this is admitted, it is readily understood why the passage concerning Gottschalk, in the form in which it now stands under the year 849, could not have been written by Prudentius. Learned men think that it has been altered so as to give that appearance. Even before Abbot Lebeuf, Cardinal Fleury and Bishop de Ravalière had been persuaded of this view; and anyone who examines that part of the Annals attentively will find the archbishop’s character clearly apparent.

In the Bouquet edition Lebeuf attempted to restore the passage to the form which he thought had proceeded from Prudentius, and he did not lack courage in doing so. Some of the material he brought forward could scarcely have been known to anyone but Hincmar. Such matters include the account under the year 867 of clerics sent by Hincmar to Rome in pilgrims’ clothing, the mention under the year 845 of the day on which Hincmar received the pope’s letter and read it to King Charles, the account under the year 881 of Hincmar’s flight when, after a monastery called Sithiu had been plundered, he withdrew to Sparnacum, and the account under the year 876 of the dispute over the primacy of Gaul between Hincmar and Ansegisus.

The Annals were not composed in the monastery of Saint Bertinus, as is shown by the mention of that monastery under the year 845 and by the reference under the year 881 to Hincmar’s flight when, after a certain monastery called Sithiu had been plundered, he withdrew to Sparnacum.

Under the year 880, the work reports that Louis the king traveled from Aachen through the places of Duziacum, Attiniacum, Ercuriacum, and Hibodimonte to Reims, of which the first three are located in the diocese of Reims and are respectively twenty-five, eleven, and only five leagues distant from Reims.

## Saint Prudentius’s Annals, or the Second Part of the Annals of Bertin

### From the Year 835 to the Year 861

After these and other matters useful to the kingdom had been properly arranged, and everything relating to his own affairs had been settled, the emperor celebrated the holy season of Lent in the same palace and the most holy feast of Easter in the aforesaid city with the aforementioned Archbishop Drogo. He then proceeded to the general assembly which he had announced would be held at Stremiacum, near the city of Lyon.

When the assembly had been held there in the month of June, and the annual gifts had been received, after arrangements had been made concerning the marches of Hispania, Septimania, and Provence, he returned to Aachen. While he was staying at the same assembly, however, the Northmen, invading Dorestad at their second incursion, devastated it and plundered it in hostile fashion.

The emperor, returning with difficulty to Aachen, arranged all matters concerning the maritime region, carried out the autumn hunt in the Ardennes, and then returned to Aachen to spend the winter, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 835.

### 836

After the feast of the Nativity of the Lord had been celebrated, he again sent envoys to Lothar, urging him to recognize the agreement and obedience of the Church and to accept peace and concord. To make him more eager to acknowledge this, the emperor ordered that envoys be sent to his father by the man in whom he placed the greatest confidence, so that they might negotiate concerning his honor and safety and faithfully announce his father’s will toward him.

Not entirely resisting his father’s commands, he sent Walo, abbot of the monastery at Theodonis Villa, to the emperor. An agreement was reached with him concerning his arrival: namely, that he would come safely with his own men into his father’s presence and thereafter be allowed to return. It was likewise promised by oath that he would come without delay to his father’s presence at the appointed assembly.

After these matters had been settled, he spent several days hunting near Mount Rumericus and finally came to Worms in September for the announced assembly. There, after receiving the annual gifts as usual and awaiting Lothar, he was informed that Lothar, overcome by fever, could in no way come.

Envoys were sent to him—Abbot Hugh and Count Adalgar—to inquire about his illness, recovery, and intention to come later, and also about the restoration of the property of the churches established in Francia but situated in Italy, which had been seized by his men at their pleasure. They also inquired concerning the bishops and counts who had formerly come from Italy to the emperor with loyal devotion, so that their own sees, counties, benefices, and property might be restored to them.

Lothar replied through his envoys that, because certain conditions had been imposed, he could not agree to everything. At the same time the Northmen again ravaged Dorestad and Frisia. Horic, king of the Danes, also sent envoys to the same assembly, communicating terms of friendship and obedience. He declared that he had in no way consented to their oppressive actions and complained about the killing of his envoys to the emperor, who had previously been slain near Cologne by the presumption of certain men. The emperor took the most just vengeance for their death by sending envoys for that purpose alone.

After completing the autumn hunt at the palace of Frankfurt, he returned to Aachen. There the envoys of Horic also arrived, demanding the total number of those whom the emperor had had killed after capturing them—men who had long been plotting such actions against our borders.

Azenarius, count of Upper Gascony, who had defected from Pippin several years earlier, also died a horrible death. His brother Sancio-Sancius, while Pippin denied him the region, occupied it. At that time Walo, abbot, whose counsel Lothar relied on greatly, also died in Italy.

### Variants

1. Dorestadum: Chesne and Bouquet.

2. *Abbas*: Bouquet.

3. Omitted by Chesne.

4. It is read as *anulo*.

5. Chesne and Bouquet: “having arranged the defense of Frisia.”

6. “Brother of the emperor”; compare the *Life of Louis*, chapter 55.

7. This assembly was held in the previous year, not on the Purification of the Blessed Virgin, but on 6 February, as is shown by the words with which the document begins: “When we bishops had assembled in the palace at Aachen, in the secretarium of the holy basilica of Mary, Mother of God, which is called Lateran, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 836, indiction 14, in the twenty-third year of the reign of the aforesaid Caesar, on the eighth day before the Ides of February.” Bouquet.

8. “Maritime Frisia,” that is, Frisia and Zeeland, in the same way as occurs not rarely in medieval charters.

### 837

After the solemn celebration of the Nativity and the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary, the emperor held an assembly of bishops at Aachen. Much was discussed there concerning the holy churches of God, and what was appropriate to each according to its proper order was disclosed and written down.

A letter was also sent by that venerable assembly of bishops to Pippin. In it they strongly admonished him regarding his salvation and, above all, urged him, mindful of the memory of his ancestors—especially of his most devout father—to restore to their original integrity the property of the churches of God which his men had previously invaded and plundered, lest he provoke the divine wrath against himself even more fiercely.

Moved by the agreement of so many fathers and by their counsel, he restored everything and individually returned the property to each church, confirming the documents with his own seal. The emperor therefore, after arranging the defense of Maritime Frisia, came to Theodonis Villa in May and received the annual gifts. He announced his journey to Rome for the defense of the holy Roman Church and for prayer.

Meanwhile, he sent envoys to Lothar, urging him to receive him with filial reverence and to arrange suitable and timely provisions for the journey. At that time the Northmen, invading Frisia in their customary raid, attacked our people unprepared on the island called Walacria. They killed many and plundered even more.

After remaining there for some time, exacting tribute as they pleased, they reached Dorestad with the same violence and likewise demanded tribute. When the emperor heard this, he abandoned the journey just mentioned and did not delay in hastening to the fortress of Nijmegen, near Dorestad. When the Northmen heard of his arrival, they immediately withdrew.

The emperor then held a general assembly and publicly questioned those princes whom he had appointed to guard the region. The inquiry showed that they had been unable to resist the enemy partly because of impossibility and partly because of the disobedience of certain men. Accordingly, vigorous abbots and counts were sent to suppress the disobedience of the Frisians, and a fleet was ordered to be more carefully prepared in every direction so that their incursions might thereafter be resisted more easily.

Lothar ordered the passes in the Alps to be fortified with the strongest walls. Landbert, Lothar’s foremost follower, and Hugh, his father-in-law, died.

Meanwhile the Britons, moved by a certain insolence, attempted to rebel. The emperor quickly suppressed their movement by sending an expedition. The land was restored to our people, and hostages were given, with promises that they would remain faithful thereafter.

After this, with Louis arriving and consenting, together with the envoys of Pippin and all the people who had been ordered to be present at the palace of Aachen, he gave his son Charles the greater part of the Belgians: namely, from the sea through the borders of Saxony as far as the borders of the Ripuarians, all Frisia, and, along the borders of the Ripuarians, the counties of Moilla, Batua, Hammelant, and Mosagau; then everything between the Meuse and the Seine as far as Burgundy, including the Verdun district; and, from Burgundy, the districts of Toul, Omois, Blesois, Perthois, the two Barrois, Brienne, Troyes, Auxerre, Sens, Gâtinais, Melun, Étampes, Chartres, and Paris; then, along the Seine, as far as the Ocean, and by that same sea as far as Frisia. That is, he gave all bishoprics, abbeys, counties, royal estates, and everything within the aforesaid boundaries, with all their appurtenances, in whatever region they might be situated. Thus, at the emperor’s command, in his presence the bishops, abbots, counts, and royal vassals holding benefices in the places named commended themselves to Charles and confirmed their fidelity by oath.

### Variants

1. “By written instruments”: Chesne and Bouquet.

2. “Island,” without *Maritime custody*; this has been corrupted in the text.

3. “Frisians”: Chesne.

4. “And elsewhere”: omitted by Chesne.

5. “This conjecture will, I trust, defend itself.”

### Notes

(a) I remember having read “Campania” for *Maritima*, not because Zeeland differs entirely from Frisia, or Maritime Frisia from Roman Campania, but because their regions were included within them.

(b) The Northmen withdrew immediately; the account is taken from the chronicle of the deeds of the Northmen in Francia, which follows below.

(c) Walcheren in Zeeland.

(d) “Through the borders” means “from the borders,” since all the counties now to be listed lay outside Burgundy and along its boundaries.

(e) The county of Moilla should be placed on the Waal, on the borders of Frisia and Ripuaria, where the village of Millingen and Schenkenschans are found even today. The counties of Batua, Hammelant, and Mosagau are sufficiently well known.

# Annals

Louis, in accordance with his father’s command, did not delay in presenting himself. After an exchange of words with his father, which proceeded otherwise than it ought, he lost whatever he had usurped from his father’s jurisdiction on either side of the Rhine: namely, Helvetia, Saxony, Thuringia, Austrasia, and Alamannia.

All the bishoprics, abbeys, counties, royal estates, and everything situated within the aforesaid boundaries, together with all that belonged to them, were taken from him. Thus, at the emperor’s command, the bishops, abbots, counts, and royal vassals who held benefices in those places commended themselves to Charles in the emperor’s presence and confirmed their loyalty by oath.

### 838

After the solemn celebrations of the Nativity, Epiphany, and the Lord’s Offering had been completed, and the fasts of Lent had begun, it became known to the emperor that Louis, Lothar’s brother, had sought a meeting with Lothar within the Alpine barriers without the emperor’s knowledge or consultation. The emperor took this badly. He sent messengers in every direction as quickly as possible to summon all the faithful, and, if necessity required it, to have them ready to resist.

When Louis learned of this, he came to his father during the octave of Holy Easter, as his father had commanded. He was carefully examined and finally confirmed by oath, together with those in whom he placed the greatest confidence, that he had planned nothing contrary to his father’s loyalty and honor in that meeting. He was then sent back to his own territory, with instructions to meet the emperor at Nijmegen in May.

The emperor intended to advance according to the agreement, so that the damage caused in previous years by the harassment of pirates and by the negligence of our people might be avoided. After an assembly of the faithful had been held, a large force was distributed along the coast.

Meanwhile, Danish pirates, having left their homeland, were caught by a sudden storm on the sea. Only a very few survived. Pippin, son of the emperor and king of Aquitaine, died on the Ides of December, leaving two sons, Pippin and Charles.

As the emperor was setting out, he was informed that his son Louis had occupied Frankfurt with hostile forces and was attempting not only to take possession of the palace for the winter but also to prevent the crossing of the Rhine. Greatly disturbed by this report, the emperor ordered the faithful to be summoned from every direction. He himself, however, continued as he had begun and reached Mainz, in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 839.

3. Hattuaria.

4. Hammelant.

6. “Into the castles”: Chesne and Bouquet; but there is no doubt that the reading should be “he occupied the whole of Frisia.”

7. Cassel, situated opposite Mainz and founded by the Romans. Compare Meginhard, *Life of Ferrutius*, chapter 5.

9. Concerning the same matter, Rabanus writes in his book *Against the Jews*, chapter 42:

> “We do not remember that this had ever happened before. A certain deacon named Bodo, nobly born, nobly educated, and trained in the offices of the Church, was led astray by them [the Jews]. He abandoned the palace and entirely abandoned the Christian kingdom. Now, among the Saracens in Spain, he was associated with Jews and had been persuaded by them to deny that Christ is the Son of God, to profane the grace of baptism, to accept physical circumcision, and to change his name, so that he who had previously been called Bodo might now be called Eleazar. Thus, having become entirely Jewish in superstition and dress, bearded and married, he daily blasphemes Christ and his Church in the synagogues of Satan.”

# Saint Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

The emperor hastened toward the royal estate called Bodoma. Meanwhile, with immense grief—grief which all the sons of the Catholic Church ought to share—the following matter became known.

Bodo, a deacon of Alamannian origin, had from almost the cradle been instructed in the Christian religion and, to some extent, in the divine and human disciplines of the palace. In the preceding year he had asked the emperor for permission to go to Rome for prayer, and, after being loaded with many gifts, had obtained it.

But, after being deceived by the enemy of the human race, he abandoned Christianity and converted to Judaism. First, he entered into a treacherous and destructive conspiracy with the Jews whom he had brought with him, and did not hesitate craftily to arrange that they should be sold to pagans. After they had been sold, he retained only one, said to be his nephew. Having denied the faith—something we mention with grief—he professed himself a Jew.

After being circumcised, allowing his hair and beard to grow, and adopting, or rather usurping, the name Eleazar, he also girded himself with a military belt. He married the daughter of a certain Jew, compelled his nephew to convert likewise to Judaism, and finally, overcome by greed and in league with the Jews, entered Caesaraugusta, a city of Spain, with their assistance.

How great a joy this was to the emperor and to all those redeemed by the grace of the Christian faith was plainly shown to everyone by the distress with which the emperor could not readily be persuaded to believe it.

Moreover, on the seventh day before the Kalends of January—the day of the passion of the blessed protomartyr Stephen—such an extraordinary inundation, contrary to the customary tides of the sea, occupied almost all Frisia, so that it stood level with the abundant sandbanks there, called dunes, by six [units; the printed reading is uncertain]. Everything that they had enveloped, both human beings and other animals, is said to have perished. The number of those who were carefully counted is reported as 2,437.

In February, fiery formations and other colored signs also appeared in the sky, and fiery stars forming crosses were seen.

After Holy Easter, when the emperor had returned to Francia, the king of the Angles sent envoys to him, asking that permission be granted to pass through Francia on the way to Rome for prayer. He also urged the emperor to take more diligent care of the subjects entrusted to him, for the sake of the salvation of their souls, since a vision had appeared to someone among them which had greatly terrified their minds.

The emperor wished to send him the account of the vision, which was as follows:

## Vision of a Certain Religious Priest from the Land of the Angles

This vision was shown after the Nativity of the Lord to a certain religious priest from the land of the Angles.

One night, while that religious priest was sleeping, a certain man came to him and ordered him to follow. The priest arose and followed him. His guide led him to a land unknown to him, where he saw various and marvelous buildings. Among them was a church, into which the priest and his guide entered. There he saw many boys reading.

When he asked his guide whether he might inquire who the boys were, the guide replied: “Ask whatever you wish, and I will freely tell you.”

As he approached them and saw what they were reading, he realized that their books were written not only in black letters but also in letters of blood: one line was written in black letters and the next in blood-red letters.

When he asked why those books were written in lines of blood, his guide replied:

“The blood-red lines which you see in these books are the various sins of human beings, because they refuse to do and fulfill the things commanded and ordered for them in the divine books. The boys whom you see moving about here as though reading are the souls of the saints. Every day they mourn the sins and crimes of Christians and intercede for them, so that at last they may be converted to repentance. If these holy souls did not cry out to God with such unceasing tears, the end of so many evils among the Christian people would already have come.

“You remember that in the present year crops appeared abundantly not only in the earth but also on trees and vines. Yet, because of human sins, most of them perished and did not reach human use and benefit. If Christian people do not soon repent of their various vices and crimes, and do not observe the Lord’s Day more properly and honorably, the greatest and unbearable danger will quickly come upon them.

“For three days and nights, a very dense fog will spread over their land. Then pagan men will come against them with an immense multitude of ships, and they will lay waste with fire and sword the greater part of the Christian people and their land, together with everything they possess.

“Nevertheless, if they are still willing to practice true repentance and strive to amend their sins according to the Lord’s command by fasting, prayer, and almsgiving, they will then be able, through the intercession of the saints, to escape these punishments and dangers.”

### Variants

1. Omitted by Chesne.

2. “Observe more honorably”: Chesne.

3. Perhaps “incomparably.”

### Notes

(a) Theodosius was a *patricius*, not a bishop, as is testified by the chronicle written at the command of Constantine Porphyrogenitus, book III, no. 37; this is also taught by the works published in the *Patrologia*.

# Annals

Greek envoys also arrived, sent by the emperor Theophilus: namely, Theodosius, metropolitan bishop of Chalcedon, and Theophanes the *spatharius*. They brought gifts and a letter to the emperor. The emperor received them honorably at Ingelheim on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June.

Their embassy concerned the confirmation of the pact and peace, and of perpetual friendship and charity, between the two emperors and their subjects. They asked that the emperor and his subjects offer thanks to the giver of all victories in a spirit of friendship, not boast of the victories which he had gained from heaven against foreign peoples through war.

Theophilus also sent with them certain men who said that they, that is, their people, were called Rhos—men whom, as they asserted, their king, called the Chagan, had sent to Theophilus for the sake of friendship. Through the letter they asked that, by the emperor’s kindness, they might have permission and assistance to return through his entire empire. The routes by which they had come to Constantinople had passed among barbarous and exceedingly savage peoples, and the emperor did not wish them to return by those routes lest they encounter danger.

Investigating the reason for their arrival more carefully, the emperor discovered that they belonged to the people of the Sueones. He judged them more likely to be spies of that kingdom and of ours than seekers of friendship, and decided to retain them until he could establish truthfully whether they had arrived there in good faith.

He did not delay in informing Theophilus of this through the aforementioned envoys and letter. He explained that he had gladly received them out of love for him and that, if they proved faithful, he would send them back with assistance and provide a safe opportunity for their return to their homeland. Otherwise, he would send them together with our envoys into Theophilus’s presence, so that he himself might determine what should be done with such men.

After these matters had been completed, the emperor reached the city of the Vangiones on the third day before the Kalends of June, as agreed. There he received certain faithful men whom he had specifically ordered to hasten to that place. He did not refuse to receive his son Lothar, who was coming from Italy, with paternal affection.

When Lothar openly fell humbly at his father’s feet before everyone and earnestly asked forgiveness for his previous excesses, the emperor, moved by the mercy in which he had always excelled incorporeally, forgave him with paternal kindness for whatever he and his men had done against him in preceding years, provided that thereafter they attempted nothing against him through wicked schemes.

He also granted many of his followers not only estates but also benefice honors. In addition, after dividing his kingdom into nearly equal portions, he gave Lothar the choice of one of them—

### 138B

### S. Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

…whichever of them he preferred, he did not disdain to offer. The formula of this division was as follows:

One portion comprised the kingdom of Italy and part of Burgundy—that is, the Valley of Aosta, the county of Valais, the county of Vaud as far as the Rhône, and thereafter the eastern and northern bank of the Rhône as far as the county of Lyon; the county of Scudingium, the county of Wirascum, the county of Portois, the county of Suentis, the county of Galmont; the duchy of Mosellania, the county of Ardennes, and the county of Gondorust. From there, following the course of the Meuse to the sea, it comprised the duchy of the Ripuarians, Worinafeld, Speyergau, the duchy of Alsace, the duchy of Alemannia, Chur, and the duchy of Austrasia with Swabia, the Nordgau, and Hesse; the duchy of Thuringia with its marches; the kingdom of Saxony with its marches; the duchy of Frisia as far as the Meuse; the county of Hamaland; the county of Batavia; and the county of Testrabent.

The other portion comprised part of Burgundy—that is, the county of Geneva, the county of Lyon, the county of Chalon, the county of Amaus, the county of Hattuaria, the county of Langres, and the county of Tuil; and so onward along the Meuse to the sea; the land between the Meuse and the Seine, and between the Seine and the Loire, with the Breton March; Aquitaine and Gascony with the marches belonging to them; Septimania with its marches; and Provence.

Since the emperor chose the former portion, he assigned the latter to his son Charles, on the condition that, while they faithfully obeyed him, they should, after his death, possess the aforesaid portions. After receiving many oaths from Lotharius, he allowed them to return to Italy.

The emperor, however, at the general assembly appointed for the Kalends of September near Chalon, sent envoys to Louis, ordering him not to presume to leave the boundaries of Bavaria unless commanded by him, and requiring him to confirm this by oath. Otherwise, he was not to doubt that at the beginning of September the emperor would meet him in arms at Augsburg.

Having therefore appointed and dispatched those who were to accompany him into Bavaria, should necessity compel it, and those who, together with his son Charles, were to suppress the Aquitanian disturbances—certain Aquitanians having recently defected from the emperor with Pippin, the son of Pippin—and who were also to oppose, together with the Saxons, the incursions of the Danes and Slavs, which were reported to be imminent, the emperor himself remained at Kreuznach, eagerly occupying himself with hunting in the Ardennes, while he awaited the return of the envoys sent into Bavaria.

When they returned, accompanied by Louis’s envoys as far as the emperor’s presence, they reported that Louis had not been very compliant with his father’s commands, but that he had promised to obey on the condition that the security under oath which he sought should also be granted to him by the emperor’s faithful men. Since the leading men through whom he requested that this security be given happened then to be absent, the emperor chose rather to entrust him to his own faith and to his humble promises until, returning after a divinely granted victory in Aquitaine, he could kindly receive him if he persevered in obeying the commands; but, if he acted otherwise, he would not delay pursuing him with all his strength.

He also granted certain men who had recently separated from him because of those disturbances, and whose proprietary rights had been altered, permission to remain in their estates, provided that they faithfully served the emperor and avoided utterly every discourtesy or evasion in respect of royal fidelity and solicitude.

Envoys were dispatched especially for this purpose to receive from them the security of an oath. The Saxons were also organized against the incursions of the Danes and the Wiltzes, who had recently burned certain villages of that Saxon march; and expeditions of Austrasians and Thuringians were arranged against the Abodrites and those called the Linones. The emperor himself, delighting in hunting at Andernach, ordered the rest of the faithful throughout the kingdom to be present at Chalon around the Kalends of September, as he had commanded.

Certain pirates, entering a part of the Seine, inflicted no small harm upon our territories. Oricus also sent envoys to the emperor—apparently a man whose counsel he trusted and through whom he seemed to conduct everything—bearing gifts customary among gentile peoples, in order to strengthen the peace and confirm the emperor’s favor. They were received and rewarded with good cheer. Since they complained of certain injuries inflicted upon the Frisians, vigorous leaders were appointed to administer justice to them at the appointed time.

After receiving the faithful at Chalon, the emperor turned his entire army toward Aquitaine. Having pitched his camp nearly three miles from the city of the Arverni, he received the Aquitanians who came to meet him and bound them by oath through the intervention of his son. He decided that, together with his son, he would proceed toward Poitiers; he himself then hastened to the fortress commonly called Carlat, since certain associates of Pippin were said to be gathered there.

This fortress had no addition constructed by human workmanship: it stood high upon a natural rock and was defended on every side by steep valleys, except on the eastern side, where it was separated from the mainland by only a very narrow interval. Nevertheless, he compelled those who held it to surrender and, with his customary clemency, granted them life, limb, and inheritance.

From there he turned toward the region of the Touraine, where his faithless opponents were hiding and trying in vain to resist him. But when they scattered in different directions and fled everywhere in small groups, he suffered considerable hardship from the calm weather and the harshness of the sun. For, seized by a severe fever, he lay partly overcome by illness and partly by the most difficult journey.

### Variant readings

- The manuscript reading is corrupt: *Suadga…*. I have attempted to correct it to *Sunalafelda et Norogo, Wlechessi*.
- The manuscript reads *operiri*; this should be corrected to *opperiri*.
- I have emended the passage in this way; Chesne and Bouquet read *fugit*.
- The manuscript reads *nuper in se separatis rerum*.

The Hattuarii lay on the river Arar. In the Chronicle of Saint Benignus, Hugo is mentioned as count of the Hattuarii. In the Chronicle of Besançon the pagus and county of the Hattuarii are frequently mentioned. Valesius believes that the Hattuarii were a Frankish people, captured and transferred by Constantius Chlorus Caesar, and that they gave their name to the pagus. Bouquet. From the division-table itself it appears that the pagi of Amaus and the Hattuarii lay from south to north between the pagi of Chalon and Langres, and from west to east between the pagi of Scudingium, Wirascum, and Portois; indeed, the Hattuarii were counted among the people of Langres.
