### [Scan page 702]

### Annals

The emperor, having sent envoys especially for this purpose, received from these men the security of an oath. He also arranged the Saxons against the incursions of the Danes and the Wiltzes, who had recently burned certain villages of the Saxon March; and he prepared expeditions of Austrasians and Thuringians against the Abodrites and those who are called the Linones. He himself, pleasantly occupying himself in hunting at Andernach, ordered the other faithful men of the entire kingdom to be present at Chalon around the Kalends of September, as he had commanded.

Certain pirates, entering a part of the Seine, inflicted no small damage upon our territories. Oricus also sent envoys to the emperor—apparently a man whose counsel he trusted and through whom he seemed to conduct everything—bearing the gifts customary among gentile peoples in order to strengthen the peace and confirm the emperor’s favor. They were received cheerfully and rewarded. Since they complained of certain injuries inflicted upon the Frisians, vigorous leaders were appointed to administer justice to them at the appointed time.

The emperor, having received the faithful at Chalon, turned his entire army toward Aquitaine. Having pitched his camp nearly three miles from the city of the Arverni, he received the Aquitanians who came to meet him and bound them by oath through the intervention of his son. He decided that, together with his son, he would proceed toward Poitiers; he himself hastened to the fortress commonly called Carlat, because certain companions of Pippin were said to be gathered there.

The fortress, although constructed by no human artifice, was raised upon a natural rock and defended on every side by precipitous valleys, except on the eastern side, where it was separated from the mainland by only a very short interval. Nevertheless, he compelled those who were stationed there to surrender under siege, and with his customary clemency granted them life, limb, and inheritance.

From there he turned toward the region of the Touraine, where his faithless opponents were hiding and attempting to resist him in vain. When they wandered in different directions and fled everywhere in scattered groups, he experienced considerable hardship from the calm weather and the harshness of the sun. For, seized by a severe fever, he lay partly overcome by illness and partly by the most difficult journey.

### DCCCXL

[The opening of the year is badly damaged in the supplied scan.] The surviving text reports that the emperor celebrated the Purification in the city of Poitiers and dealt with the magnates of Aquitaine. As Lent approached, he divided the army. Louis—whom his father had designated king—was sent with a portion toward the Rhine to assert his claim to the kingdom; Charles remained with another part of the army in the city already mentioned. The emperor himself came to the royal palace and, after celebrating the Lord’s Resurrection, crossed the Rhine into Germany. The intervening account of his pursuit and of assistance among the pagan peoples is fragmentary, but it records that his presence caused several opponents to cease their resistance.

An eclipse of the sun was seen in many places on the Nones of May, at about the eighth hour of the day. The emperor, returning from the pursuit of his son, fell ill on an island in the Rhine. He was carried toward Ingelheim and died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July. Perceiving the weakness of his body, he summoned Louis and Charles and urged each concerning the other and the prosperity of both. The final clause records a provisional settlement made according to their father’s arrangement, “under conditions of this kind until the appointed time”; the surrounding words are too damaged to determine more securely.

### DCCCXLI

Louis and Charles—the one on this side of the Rhine, the other beyond it—each subdued or won over all the men belonging to his own side: some by force, some by threats, some by honors, and some by various conditions.

Lotharius, during the days of Lent, led his forces as far as Mainz against Louis; but Louis resisted him, and Lotharius was long prevented from crossing the river. Nevertheless, when Lotharius crossed through a certain stratagem and through the treachery of people attached to Louis, Louis made for Bavaria.

A large force also tried to prevent Charles from crossing the Seine at Lotharius’s side. Yet Charles, crossing the river with manly prudence and prudent courage, twice and even three times put them all to flight. When Lotharius heard of the flight of his men and of Charles’s arrival, he crossed the Rhine again. Having stationed guards against Louis, he set out to meet Charles.

Louis attacked the troops that Lotharius had arranged against him, gave a large part of them over to slaughter, put the rest to flight, and then hastened to bring aid to his brother Charles.

Meanwhile, Danish pirates, carried from the ocean through the Strait of Calais, attacked Rouen. Raging through the city with plunder, sword, and fire, they destroyed the city, the monks, and the remaining populace through slaughter and captivity. They either devastated all the monasteries and every place adjoining the Seine, or, after receiving large sums of money, withdrew in fear.

When Louis finally drew near, his brother Charles came to meet him with the greatest eagerness and affection. Having joined forces, they used both fraternal love and the arrangement of their camps, their common banquets, and their united counsels to send frequent embassies to their brother Lotharius concerning peace and concord and the government of the entire people and kingdom.

Lotharius, however, mocking them with repeated embassies and oaths, eventually received Pippin, the son of his brother Pippin who had long been dead, from Aquitaine. At Fontenay, in the pagus of Auxerre, he attempted to deprive both brothers of their portions of the kingdom by hostile force.

When he could not be recalled to peace and fraternal concord, he was intercepted by the brothers on the seventh day before the Kalends of July, a Saturday morning. Many fell on both sides and many were routed; he was shamefully defeated and fled.

The Palatines were slaughtered everywhere until Louis and Charles, burning with compassion, decided that the killing should cease. Indeed, for the sake of Christianity, they also stopped pursuing those who fled farther from the camps. They ordered the bishops to bury the corpses of the dead on the following day, since they had remained encamped at the same place for this purpose, as the opportunity of time allowed.

In that battle George, bishop of Ravenna, who had been sent by Pope Gregory of Rome to Lotharius and his brothers for the sake of peace, but had been detained by Lotharius and not permitted to come to the brothers, was captured. He was sent back to his own country with honor.

Lotharius turned his back and reached Aachen. He tried to win over the Saxons and the other neighboring peoples in order to renew the war. He went so far as to grant the Saxons called the Stellinga—whose number among that people is very large—the choice of whichever law or ancient Saxon custom they preferred.

They, always inclined toward evil, chose rather to imitate pagan rites than to keep the sacraments of the Christian faith.

To Heriold, who together with the other Danish seafarers had brought such great troubles upon his father’s cause, Lotharius granted Walcheren and other neighboring places as a benefice. It was a deed worthy of every condemnation: those who had inflicted evils upon Christians were preferred to Christian lands and peoples; persecutors of the Christian faith were made lords of Christians; and Christian peoples were made servants of worshipers of demons.

Louis subdued to his authority, partly by terror and partly by favor, many of the Saxons and almost all of the Austrasians, Thuringians, and Alemannians. Charles, having arranged matters in Aquitaine as circumstances permitted, crossed through the lands of the Cenomanni, Parisii, and Bellovaci, entered Francia, and approached the Hasbani, winning them over more by affection than by fear.

Lotharius, having crossed the Rhine and intending to attack Louis in war, was frustrated in his plans and efforts and suddenly turned against Charles, believing that Charles, separated by a considerable distance from his brother Louis, could more easily be defeated.

Charles, returning from Paris, crossed the Seine and for a long time resisted Lotharius’s efforts. Prevented from crossing the river, Lotharius sought its upper regions and entered the pagus of Mauripense through the pagus of the Senones. From there he reached the Cenomanni without difficulty and ravaged everything with plunder, fires, sexual violence, sacrilege, and oaths, to such an extent that he did not spare even the sanctuaries themselves.

Whatever treasures he could find, deposited in the churches or in their treasuries for the sake of salvation—even when priests and clerics of the other orders were bound by oath—he did not hesitate to remove. He also forced the very nuns devoted to divine worship to swear allegiance to him.

Charles, having remained for a long time near Paris, came to Châlons to celebrate there the feast of the Lord’s Nativity.

- Rouen.

- This is taken from the Chronicle concerning the deeds of the Normans.

- The pagus and principality of the Angrians, in which the town of Angers is situated; the place might be understood under the name *Kesigesburck*. Certainly, what follows was first written in the margin and afterward incorporated into the text:

  “While the emperor was compelled to remain at Angers because of the severity of the approaching winter, and was delayed by the harshness of the winter, he reached Poitiers with the remainder of his army. Meanwhile the Saxons, fighting against the Sorabs at the place called Clodfeld, near Kesigesburg, with heavenly assistance obtained victory; after their king Cimusci had been killed, they captured the same city and eleven fortresses. They also recovered the standards taken from their king. When a new disturbance arose among them, they received hostages and exacted a great sum of money. But when the emperor’s envoys were sent to them for the sake of peace, they received the oaths and made an unbreakable agreement.”

The author of the Chronicle of Fulda interprets *Kesigesburg*, or *Resigesburg*, as Moosburg on the right bank of the Saale. The manuscript itself must be consulted on this matter.

### [Scan page 703]

### S. Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

### DCCCXLII

From there he came to Troyes, and, crossing the Alsatian pagus and the city of Toul, crossed the Vosges and joined his brother Louis near Strasbourg.

Lotharius, having laid waste the lower parts of Gaul so extensively that neither he nor his men gained any advantage from it, crossed the Seine near Paris and returned to Aachen. When he heard of the union of his brothers, he bore it with difficulty.

Louis and Charles, in order to bind more firmly to themselves the peoples subject to each of them, bound themselves to one another by oath. They also bound the faithful people of both sides by an equal oath: if either brother attempted anything harmful against the other, all of them, abandoning entirely the author of the dissension, should turn to the defender of brotherhood and friendship.

When these things had been done, they sent envoys to Lotharius for the sake of peace. He prevented their envoys from appearing before him or speaking with him and prepared himself and his men for armed resistance against his brothers.

At the palace of Sentiacum, built about eight miles from the Moselle, Lotharius denied them the opportunity of crossing by stationing guards. Louis therefore reached the fortress of Confluentes by boat and Charles by horse. When they began courageously to cross the Moselle, all Lotharius’s guards quickly fled.

Terrified by the unexpected arrival of his brothers, Lotharius withdrew, removing everything from the palace of Aachen—both the treasures of Saint Mary and the royal treasures, including a silver dish of extraordinary size and beauty. Upon it were represented the description of the whole world, the observation of the stars, and the varied courses of the planets, separated from one another by intervals and shining in relief through sculpted signs.

After cutting it into pieces and distributing it among his men, he fled through Châlons. The men who had been hired at such a price and under such terror nevertheless abandoned him in groups throughout the camps. Having completed the Easter solemnity at Troyes, he made for Lyon.

Louis celebrated the same feast near Cologne; Charles celebrated it at the palace of Herstal.

Meanwhile, the men of the respective sides received into their own ranks those who sought refuge with them and, refraining from pursuing their brother, accepted them in many ways. After receiving them repeatedly, they followed their brother’s departure at a slower pace, because, although unwilling, he was striving for a treaty of peace between the brothers and sent envoys on whom he relied greatly.

For this business, the vicinity of the city of Mâcon was selected. Both sides assembled there, their camps separated by the river Saône, and began to meet and confer on an island in that river.

There, after each side had requested and received pardon for the wrongs committed in the past, they also swore to one another an oath of true peace and brotherhood. They decided that careful arrangements for equal portions of the entire kingdom should be made on the Kalends of October in the city of the Mediomatrici, called Metz.

At that time a fleet of Normans, arriving before dawn unexpectedly at the trading port called Quentovic, raged through it with plunder, captivity, and slaughter of people of both sexes, leaving nothing there except buildings redeemed with money.

Moorish pirates, carried up the Rhône near Arles, likewise plundered everything everywhere and returned unpunished with their ships loaded.

Charles, entering and traversing Aquitaine from Mâcon, did not delay coming to the appointed place and time of the assembly. Lotharius received envoys from the Greeks at Trier and, after dismissing them, took up residence at the palace called Thionville at the time appointed for the assembly.

Louis, having traversed all Saxony, subdued by force and terror all who had until then resisted him. Having seized all the leaders of such great impiety—men who had almost abandoned the Christian faith and had resisted him and his faithful men so greatly—he punished 140 by beheading, hanged 14 on the gallows, made innumerable others disabled by mutilation of their limbs, and left no one at all who opposed him.

Meanwhile, because the people of Benevento were divided among themselves, the Saracens, invited by them from Africa, first as helpers and afterward as violent persecutors, seized many cities by force.

In October Charles set out from the city of the Mediomatrici toward Vangionum and joined his brother Louis. After they had remained there for a long time, sending envoys back and forth to Lotharius and discussing for a long time the portions of the kingdom, it was finally decided that thirty envoys should be chosen throughout the kingdom subject to them. By their diligence, the division of the kingdom was to be carefully completed.

### [Scan page 705]

### S. Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

Having established the division of the kingdom between the brothers, the envoys returned to their respective rulers. Lotharius left the region of the Mediomatrici; Louis returned to Germany; and Charles came to the palace of Carisiacum.

From there he went to the palace of Germaniacum. Coming to the palace of Carisiacum, he placed Ermentrude, daughter of Count Adalard, there in seclusion, and set out for the city of Trier, where, at the shrine of the blessed martyr Quintinus, he was to celebrate the feast of the Lord’s Nativity.

Meanwhile, a war broke out in the lower parts of Gaul.

### DCCCXLIII

Lotharius and Louis restrained themselves within the boundaries of their kingdoms and remained at peace; Charles traversed Aquitaine.

When the appointed time arrived, Nominoë the Breton and Lambert of Nantes, who had recently defected from his allegiance, killed Renaud, duke of Nantes, and captured several others.

Then, when wars arose everywhere and evil followed evil without interruption, the whole of Gaul was afflicted by such a famine that, in many places, people were reduced to such scarcity and want that they ate the earth. It was a lamentable—indeed, utterly detestable—state of affairs: the fodder of rapacious creatures was overflowing, while people needed the cruel admixture of the very earth.

Norman pirates attacked the city of Nantes. After killing the bishop and the clergy and plundering the city indiscriminately, they began to ravage the lower parts of Aquitaine. Finally, having entered a certain island and subdued the mainland, they decided to spend the winter there as though in permanent quarters.

Charles, meeting his brothers at the appointed place, joined them near Verdun. There, after the portions had been distributed, Louis received everything beyond the Rhine, and on this side of the Rhine he received the cities and pagi of the Nemetes, Vangionum, and Mainz.

Lotharius received the land between the Rhine and the Scheldt, which flows into the sea, and then the Cambrai district, Hainaut, the Lommois, Castricius, and the counties contiguous to these on this side of the Meuse, as far as the Saône flowing into the Rhône; and, following the Rhône to the sea, the counties similarly adjoining it on either side.

He assigned the remainder, as far as Spain, to Charles.

After oaths had been exchanged, they finally separated from one another, remaining in concord for a time.

### DCCCXLIV

During the winter, in the month of January, the weather became somewhat milder. Bernard, count of the Spanish March, long since convicted of grave wickedness and breach of faith, underwent the capital sentence in Aquitaine by judgment of the Franks and at Charles’s command.

Gregory, pontiff of the Roman Church, died, and Sergius succeeded him and was established in the same see.

When he had been ordained to the apostolic see, Lotharius sent his son Louis to Rome with Drogo, bishop of the Mediomatrici, and others, so that, when the pope died, no one there should ordain a Roman pontiff without his instruction. When they came to Rome, received suitable honor, and had completed their business, they arranged for Louis to be consecrated king by the Roman pontiff.

He appointed Drogo, his bishop, as his vicar for the Gallican and German regions, and designated Siginulf, duke of the Beneventans, for Lotharius. Having surrendered himself to Lotharius with all his people, Siginulf made himself liable to him for an annual payment of one hundred pounds of gold. The Beneventans, who had formerly been on the other side, joined this same Siginulf. They began to expel from their borders the remnants of the Saracens.

Lambert, together with certain Britons, intercepted and killed some men belonging to Charles’s faction at the bridge of Mâcon.

Pippin, son of the former king Pippin, with several others, hastened from Francia toward Charles, who was surrounding the city of Toulouse with a siege. Meeting him in the pagus of Ecclesiola, he was so swiftly routed, with heavy losses among his own men, that, after the leaders had been killed and the rest put to flight before battle could even be joined, Charles pursued the fugitives and scarcely allowed a few to escape. He captured the rest, despoiled them, bound them by oath, and allowed them to return home.

In this unexpected encounter Hugo, priest and abbot, son of the former emperor Charles the Great, brother of Emperor Louis, and paternal uncle of Kings Lotharius, Louis, and Charles, was killed; so too were the abbot Ridhbold, himself a cousin of the kings and grandson of Emperor Charles through a daughter, Counts Eckard and Raban, and many others; Ebroin, bishop of Poitiers, and Ragenarius were captured.

William, seeking to avenge his father’s death with Pippin’s aid, intercepted Toulouse, which Charles immediately surrounded with a siege. Bouquet.

## 839

Marobrica [Samarobriva, Amiens], bishop of the Ambiani, and Lupus the abbot; also the two sons of Count Eckard, likewise Lokardius, Guntardus, and Ilchuinus, counts, Engilwinus too, and many other nobles. Fulcradus and the other provincials defect from Lothar and usurp for themselves authority over the whole province. Nomenogius the Breton, at the same time insolently overstepping the territories allotted to himself and his predecessors, asserts them for himself and his own.

King Oricus of the Nordmanns directs six hundred ships up the river Elbe into Germany against Hludowic. The Saxons meet them and, battle having been joined, are made victorious through the aid of our Lord Jesus Christ. Departing thence, the Danes attack and take a certain city of the Slavs. A severe famine consumes the interior of Gaul, so that many thousands of people perish as it grows worse. Charles, coming to the estate of Noriacum, where the monastery of Saint Benedict stands, twelve leagues from Orléans, receives Pippin, Pippin’s son. [The surviving text resumes below.]

The Nordmanns, attacking Britain—that part which the Anglo-Saxons inhabit most extensively—are victorious after fighting for three days; making plunder, robbery, and slaughter everywhere, they take possession of the land at will.

Meanwhile, envoys of the brothers—that is, Lothar, Hludowic, and Charles—travel in various directions in turn, out of brotherly affection. In October they meet together near the villa of Theodonis. After several days of friendly and highly necessary conference, they confirm among themselves the rights of brotherhood and charity, never to be violated thereafter. They also promise to be more watchful against the sowers of discord and to punish them, and to restore the condition of the churches, which has been shamefully torn apart by pressing necessities and commonly entrusted to unsuitable persons, that is, to laymen.

Accordingly, they jointly send envoys to Pippin, Landbert, and Nomenogius for the sake of peace, so that they should no longer delay coming to their brother Charles as obedient and faithful men. Otherwise, they declare that, at a suitable time, they will advance against them in force, united against them, to avenge their disloyalty.

The Nordmanns, advancing through Gascony as far as Toulouse, carry out plundering everywhere with impunity. On their return, some of them attack Galicia; some perish through the opposition of the crossbowmen, others are intercepted by a storm at sea. Some also attack the regions of further Spain; after fighting long and fiercely with the Saracens, they are finally defeated and withdraw.

## 845

A very severe winter. One hundred and twenty Nordmann ships travel up and down the Seine in the month of March, devastating everything, while no one at all among the Parisians opposes them. When Charles tries to meet them but sees that his men cannot prevail, he restrains their advance by certain agreements and by a payment of seven thousand pounds, and persuades them to return.

He receives Pippin’s son, and, after receiving from him oaths of loyalty—that henceforth he should be faithful to him as a nephew to his uncle and should offer him assistance to the best of his ability in every necessity—he grants him dominion over all Aquitaine except Poitiers, Saintes, and Angoulême. Consequently, all the Aquitanians who had hitherto been with Charles immediately try to transfer their allegiance to that same Pippin.

The people of Benevento again quarrel with the Saracens, as their old discord flares up anew. The Nordmanns, retracing the channel of the Seine, return to the sea; they plunder and ravage all the places adjoining the sea and then depart.

Although the justice of divine goodness, gravely offended by our sins, has so crushed the lands and kingdoms of the Christians, nevertheless the pagans, whether through extreme folly or certainly through lack of faith, are not to accuse the almighty Lord with impunity for long. For when, after plundering and burning a certain monastery called Sithdiu, they are returning laden with booty to their ships, by divine judgment they are so blinded by darkness and struck with madness that scarcely a few escape to announce to the others the power of almighty God.

Therefore, as is said, Oricus, moved in spirit, sends envoys to Hludowic, king of the Germans, to seek peace, to release the captives, and to restore, according to his ability, the treasures that had been taken.

Lothar, entering Provence, recovers all of it for his authority as far as Arles. The Danes, who in the preceding year had ravaged Aquitaine, on their return attack Saintes, defeat the inhabitants in battle, and remain in their peaceful homes.

Charles, attacking Brittany from Gaul with a small force and without sufficient caution, while all things turn out adversely because of the defection of his allies, hastily returns; having rebuilt his army, he prepares to attack it again.

## 846

Danish pirates, arriving in Frisia, exact tribute according to their pleasure and, also victorious in battle, gain possession of almost the entire province. A north wind blows with extreme violence over the crops and vineyards throughout the whole winter, almost until the beginning of May.

An invasion of wolves boldly devours people in the lower regions of Gaul. In Aquitaine too, they are said to have assembled like an army, nearly three hundred strong, marching in formation along the roads and courageously and unanimously making a stand against those who wished to resist them.

At the villa of Saint Remigius, called Épernay, Charles holds a general assembly of his people in June, contrary to custom. At it, the very necessary admonition of the bishops of his kingdom concerning ecclesiastical affairs is treated with such contempt that never, in Christian times at least, has pontifical authority been so disregarded.

One day a certain young man is found copulating with a mare; by the judgment of the Franks he is burned alive in a fire.

From there Charles proceeds with his army toward Brittany and makes peace with Nomenogius, duke of the Bretons, after oaths of peace have been exchanged on both sides.

In the month of May of this year, so great a flood of rain flows at the city of Auxerre that, penetrating the walls, it carries even casks full of wine into the river Yonne. What is more remarkable, it transports a certain vineyard, with its soil, vines, and all its trees, undamaged and solid as it stands, from one bank of the Yonne to the other, as though it had naturally been in that same field.

In August the Saracens and Moors attack Rome through the Tiber. They devastate the basilica of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, carrying away all its ornaments and treasures, together with the altar that had been placed over the tomb of the aforesaid prince of the apostles. They occupy a strongly fortified mountain one hundred miles from the city.

The troops of the duke of Lothar attack them with insufficient reverence and are destroyed. Another part of the enemy, approaching the church of the blessed apostle Paul, is overwhelmed by the Campanians and completely killed.

Hludowic, king of the Germans, sets out against the Slavs but, terrified both by internal conflict among his own men and by the victory of the enemy, returns.

Hludowic, son of Lothar, king of Italy, fighting with the Saracens, is defeated and scarcely reaches Rome.

## 847

Envoys of Abdirhaman, king of the Saracens, come from Córdoba in Spain to Charles to seek peace and establish a treaty. He receives and dismisses them honorably at Reims, called Durocortorum.

Bodo, who several years earlier had abandoned Christian truth for Jewish perfidy, had advanced so far in wickedness that he tried to incite against all the Christians living in Spain the minds both of the Saracen king and of the Saracen people, so that the Christians should either abandon the religion of the Christian faith and turn to Jewish madness or Saracen folly, or else all be killed.

Concerning this, a tearful petition from all the Christians of that kingdom is sent to King Charles and to the bishops and other orders of his kingdom and our faith, asking that the aforesaid apostate be reclaimed, lest he continue to be either an obstacle or a cause of death to the Christians living there.

The Danes, entering the part of lower Gaul inhabited by the Bretons, defeat them three times in battle. Nomenogius, defeated, flees with his men; afterward, through envoys and gifts, he removes them from his own settlements.

Sergius, Roman pontiff, dies on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, and Leo is elected in his place.

The Saracens, attempting to return by ship with the great quantity of treasure they have carried away from the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, revile God, our Lord Jesus Christ, and his apostles with impious speech while sailing. Suddenly an unavoidable storm arises; the ships collide with one another, and all perish. Some of the treasures are found in the bosoms of the dead whom the sea has cast upon the shores, and are restored to the memorial of the blessed apostle Peter.

The Scots, attacked by the Nordmanns for many years, are made tributary. The Nordmanns remain in possession of the islands situated all around them, since no one resists.

Lothar, Hludowic, and Charles send envoys to Oric, king of the Danes, ordering him to restrain his men from attacking the Christians; otherwise, they do not doubt that they will wage war against him.

At that time the Moors and Saracens invade Benevento and ravage as far as the Roman frontier.

The Danes attack and plunder maritime Aquitaine and besiege the city of Bordeaux for a long time. Others of the Danes occupy and hold the trading settlement called Dorestad and the island of Batavia.

The army of Hludowic, king of the Germans, fights successfully against the Slavs, so that he recovers what he had lost the previous year.

### Variants

- Bouq. long ago combined the reading.
- *statuerit* in Ch.; probably corrupt; perhaps another reading should be adopted.
- *Hlodowic* in Ch.
- Omitted in Ch.
- *Dorastadum* in Ch.

### Notes

- Compare the *Chronicle of the deeds of the Normans*.
- That is, the Church of Reims.
- Épernay.
- Yonne.
- Concerning the cause of this embassy, compare Peter de Marca, *Hispania*, chapter 27.
- Reims.
- Compare above, year 839.
- Compare the *Chronicle of the deeds of the Normans*, year 840.

## 848

The Slavs, invading Hludowic’s kingdom in a hostile manner, are defeated by him in Christ’s name. Charles attacks and vigorously defeats a division of the Nordmanns besieging Bordeaux. Lothar’s army, fighting against the Saracens occupying Benevento, wins a victory. The Danes capture Bordeaux in Aquitaine, plunder and burn it, the Jews having betrayed it.

The Aquitanians, driven by Pippin’s sloth and inactivity, seek Charles and, in Orléans, elect him king with their bishops and abbots and almost all their leading men; they solemnly consecrate him with sacred chrism and episcopal blessing.

Greek pirates ravage Marseilles in Provence unopposed and depart with impunity. The Nordmanns plunder and burn the settlement of Métulum.

The Scots attack the Nordmanns and, victorious through the aid of our Lord Jesus Christ, drive them from their borders. Their king sends envoys and gifts to Charles in pursuit of peace and friendship, asking leave to travel to Rome.

The Moors again invade Benevento.

Guilhelmus, Bernard’s son, takes Ampurias and Barcelona more by treachery than force.

## 849

Lothar and Charles, adopting sounder counsel, return to peace and brotherly concord. At Carisiacum, on 17 February, in the following night while the clergy are offering the Lord their nocturnal prayers, a violent earthquake occurs, but it damages none of the buildings.

Godescalcus, a Gaul, monk and priest of the monastery of Orbais in the diocese of Soissons, inflated with learning and given over to certain superstitions, has entered Italy under pretext of religion. Thence, after being disgracefully expelled, he assails Dalmatia, Pannonia, and Noricum, maintaining by poisonous utterances and writings teachings gravely contrary to our salvation, especially under the name of predestination. Detected and convicted before an episcopal council in the presence of Hludowic, king of the Germans, he is finally compelled to return to the metropolitan city of his diocese, Reims, called Durocortorum, over which the venerable Ingmar presides, there to undergo the judgment deserved by his perfidy.

Charles, a most vigorous champion of God’s holy Church, summons an assembly of the bishops of that diocese and orders Godescalcus to be brought before him. Brought there, he is publicly flogged and compelled to burn the books of his assertions.

Hludowic and Charles meet in brotherly affection and show themselves bound by so great a tie of fraternal love that each publicly gives the other his staff and commends to the survivor the wives and children of the kings.

Charles attacks Aquitaine. Nomenogius the Breton, with his customary perfidy, invades Angers and the neighboring districts. The Nordmanns plunder and burn Périgueux, a city of Aquitaine, and return with impunity to their ships. The Moors and Saracens plunder Luna, a city of Italy, and, with no resistance, devastate all the coasts as far as Provence.

### Variants

- *Metallum* in Chesne and Bouquet; nevertheless *metullum* in Ch.
- “The words printed above should perhaps be restored; I cannot say that this is possible. Bouquet adds: ‘The most learned …’”
- “A certain Gaul named Godescalcus, a priest of the monastery …, censured because he maintained by his sayings and writings certain doctrines contrary to our salvation …”
- *Britto* (“Breton”) in Ch.

### Notes

- Compare the *Chronicle of the deeds of the Normans*.
- Compare the same work.
- Metulum, also called Metullum, a fortified place situated among the Pictones. Bouquet.
- Guillelmus obtained the county of Toulouse from Pippin, king of Aquitaine, either after his father’s death or in the year 845, when Pippin, having made peace with Charles, acquired the greater part of Aquitaine. Bouquet.
- Ampurias.
- Carisiacum. Hincmar, in his *Booklet on Predestination*, chapter 2, says: “At the synodal assembly in the palace at Carisiacum, Gothescalcus was again heard by the bishops and by many other ecclesiastical and religious men who were present at that synod, namely Wenilo, archbishop of Sens; Hincmar, bishop of Reims; and twelve others named there.” Bouquet.
- Compare the *Chronicle of the deeds of the Normans*, year 848.
- Périgueux.
- On this disaster there is a notable letter by Agius, abbot of Vabres, written at the beginning of the tenth century concerning the origin of the monastery of Vabres. Catellus quoted a fragment of the letter in his *History of the Counts of Toulouse*, p. 69:

  “At the time,” says Agius, “when from the northern quarter of Europe there spread the most savage and barbarously cruel people of the Marchomanni, and they entered Gaul, the holy Church suffered grievously beneath their most violent blows. Since no one checked the barbarians’ frenzy, there was no slight affliction: through almost all the districts by the Gallic Ocean churches and cities were scattered and devastated, and monasteries destroyed. Such was the rage of the persecutors that Christians whom they could capture they either killed with the sword or, when horror at killing innocents overcame them, tried to preserve for ransom.

  “Many Christians, having experienced the fiercest persecution, abandoned their estates and left their ancestral lands, giving themselves over to settlements in the eastern regions. Finally, many chose rather to fall beneath spears than to leave their ancestral homes unharmed.

  “Others, indeed more numerous, whose hearts had scarcely taken root in the faith, neglected the bath of holy regeneration; but, cherishing the dark cunning of the pagans, joined themselves to their alliance and vices [the supplied text is lacunose].

  “There was at that time a monastery in the province of Gaul, in the district of Périgueux, called Palnatus, in which worshipers of God continually served Christ, possessing nothing of their own except what the rule of Saint Benedict allowed. Other monasteries in the same province were richer in property; in them, once the aforesaid grievous plague had begun, many monks began to neglect the rule of Saint Benedict through fear of famine, etc.” Bouquet.

### Readings

- Before adopting Bouquet’s conjecture, I attempted to correct the passage as follows: “a certain Gaul named Godescalcus, monk and priest of the monastery of Orbais in the diocese of Soissons, censured because he maintained, especially under the name of predestination, certain doctrines contrary to our salvation by his sayings and writings …” Lebeuf, who suspects that this part of the annals was interpolated into Prudentius, reads it substantially in the same way. Thus the passage first written by Prudentius would be …
- *strenuissimus*: “most vigorous.”
- “A most vigorous champion of the holy Church of God …”
- “Having attacked Dalmatia, Pannonia, and Noricum, he was detected and convicted before the episcopal council in the presence of Hludowic, king of the Germans, and was finally compelled to return to the metropolitan city of his diocese, Reims, called Durocortorum, over which the venerable Ingmar presides …”

## 850

Nomenogius the Breton dies.

Lothar, Hludowic, and Charles come together at the palace of Marsna, where they remain for a few days in brotherly fashion. By the common counsel and agreement of their leading men, they decree and confirm by monograms the following provisions.

**Chapter I.** “So that the abolition of all past evils, disagreements, treacheries, and harmful actions committed among us may be effected, and so that all malice and rancor may be wholly removed from our hearts, so that henceforth nothing of evil, disagreement, or insult may arise in our memory or be repaid among us.”

**Chapter II.** “So that, with the Lord cooperating, true charity may always remain among us hereafter, from a pure heart and a good conscience and an unfeigned faith, without deceit or simulation, so that no one may secretly or through hidden whisperers compose lies or slanders against his equal.”

**Chapter III.** “Let each of us faithfully, wherever necessity requires and he himself is able, assist his brother by himself, through his son, or through his faithful men, with counsel and aid, so that he may duly preserve the kingdom, his faithful men, prosperity, and royal honor. Let each of us demonstrate to the other, truly and faithfully, that if adversity should befall his brother, he grieves in a brotherly manner, and rejoices in his prosperity. And just as we have confirmed that we will henceforth preserve such faith among ourselves, so each of us will preserve the children of his brother if he should die and the survivor remain.”

**Chapter IV.** “And because the peace and tranquility of the kingdom are often disturbed by wandering and disrespectful men, we wish that, if such a man comes to any one of us and wishes to evade giving an account and justice for what he has done, none of us should receive or retain him for any other purpose than to bring him to a proper reckoning and due correction. If he evades a proper reckoning, let all of us jointly, in whatever kingdom he has entered, pursue him until he is brought to account or removed from the kingdom.”

**Chapter V.** “Likewise, the same must be done with one who, excommunicated by any bishop for some capital and public crime, or committing an act deserving criminal condemnation, changes kingdom or ruler: he is to undertake due penance or lawfully complete penance already undertaken. Likewise, if, fleeing, he has taken with him an incestuous close relative, a married woman, a kidnapped woman, or an adulteress whom he was not permitted to have, then, once this has been reported to us by the bishops to whose care he belonged, he shall be diligently sought, lest any of us provide him a place for hiding or remaining in our kingdom and he escape the notice of God and our faithful men; rather, he shall be brought by us or by the royal officers before his bishop, so that, together with the devilish prey which he took with him, he may undergo public penance for the public crime committed or be compelled lawfully to complete penance already undertaken.”

Charles, entering Aquitaine, subdues nearly all its inhabitants to himself, reconciling them to him, with Christ favorable to him; he also arranges the Spanish March according to his pleasure.

Nomenogius the Breton acts with his customary insolence.

## 851

Guilhelmus, son of Bernard, treacherously captures the counts Adalramnus and Isembardus; he himself is captured more treacherously and killed at Barcelona.

The Moors devastate everything as far as Arles, with no one resisting. When they are returning, however, they are turned back by the opposing force and killed.

Lothar sends his son Hludowic to Rome; Pope Leo receives him honorably and crowns him emperor.

Oric, king of the Nordmanns, is attacked in war while his two nephews are fighting one another. He makes peace between them by dividing the kingdom. Roric, nephew of Heriold, who had recently defected from Lothar, gathers the Nordmann armies and, with a multitude of ships, ravages Frisia, the island of Batavia, and other neighboring places along the Rhine and the Waal.

Since Lothar cannot restrain him, he receives him into his allegiance and grants him Dorestad and other counties. The rest of the Nordmanns plunder the Menapii, the Tarvannenses, and other maritime peoples; another part attacks the island of Britain and the English, but they are defeated by them with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ and return to their ships with impunity.

The Moors and Saracens, plundering Luna, a city of Italy, devastate all the coastal places as far as Provence without opposition.

[Continuation of Chapter V; translated above.]

**Chapter VI.** “So that each of our faithful men, in his own order and status, may truly be secure concerning us: henceforth we shall not condemn, dishonor, or oppress anyone against law, justice, authority, or proper reason, nor afflict anyone with unlawful machinations. With the common counsel of those who are truly faithful to us, according to the will of God and the common salvation, we shall give our assent to everything pertaining to the restoration of the holy Church of God, the condition of the kingdom, royal honor, and the peace of the people entrusted to us. We shall do this so that they may not merely fail to contradict and resist us in carrying these things out, but may also be faithful and obedient to us, true helpers and cooperators, with true counsel and sincere assistance, in carrying out what we have promised, just as each person ought, in his own order and status, to be to his prince and lord.”

**Chapter VII.** “So that, being thus joined together—these brothers to one another, we with our faithful men and our faithful men with us—and all of us together with God, we may be reunited; and, that he may be favorable to us, we may offer this to him as a devoted gift: let each of us, without his own excuse or justification, acknowledge in what matters, individually or jointly, we have acted or consented to act against his commands and decrees in the ecclesiastical order and in the condition of the kingdom. Let us truthfully lay each matter openly before a near relative or confederate—indeed, not even conceal it from oneself—so that it may be possible to remove it spiritually from the disgrace of its condition. For, as we promised in the preceding chapter, with true counsel and sincere assistance let us earnestly strive with all our strength to correct these matters jointly, as soon as we can reasonably do so.”

**Chapter VIII.** “And if anyone among the subjects, in whatever order or status, withdraws from this agreement, or retreats, or contradicts this common decree, let the elders, with their truly faithful men, carry out these provisions according to the will of God, the law, and right reason, whether that man wishes it or not—he who has resisted and contradicted the divine counsel and decree and this agreement.

“And if one of the elders withdraws from this agreement or retreats, when many of our faithful elders and the leading men of the kingdoms have come together as one, then, by the counsel of those who have observed these provisions and by the judgment of the bishops, with common agreement, we shall decide, with the Lord’s favor, what should be done concerning him who, after having been duly admonished, persists in being incorrigible.

“And so that you may believe with greater certainty that the aforesaid chapters will be observed by us inviolably, with the Lord’s help, and that we shall observe them, we have signed them with our own hands.”

After this, the pirates of the Danes ravage Frisia and Batavia. They also rage as far as the monastery of Saint Bavo, which they call Ghent, and burn the same monastery. Coming to the city of Rouen, they proceed on foot as far as Beauvais. After burning it and returning, they are defeated and killed by our men.

Nomenogius, coming to Charles in the city of Angers, is received with outstretched hands and is endowed both with royal garments and with the authority of paternal power; moreover, Rennes, Nantes, and Retz are added to him.

The Saracens peacefully possess Benevento and other cities.

Hludowic the king ravages almost all the Slavs and subjects them to his authority.

Pope Leo, fearing the incursions of the Saracens, strengthens the church of the blessed Peter here and there with a wall, carries the same wall as far as the city, and makes it contiguous with the city of Rome.

## 852

The Normans, with 252 ships, arrive in Frisia, and, having received many payments as they themselves determined, proceed to other regions. [The supplied text ends here.]

## Annals

The Moors, betrayed by the Jews, turn against Barcelona, capture it, kill nearly all the Christians, devastate the city, and return without penalty. Charles invites his brother Lothar to a conference at Augusta Viromanduorum, distinguished by the body of the blessed martyr Quintinus. He receives his brother fraternally, treats him honorably and affectionately, rewards him regally, and kindly escorts him on his return.

Lambert and Quamarius, brothers and among the chief parties to the dissension, are killed, one by treachery and the other by accusation. Salomon the Breton becomes faithful to Charles and is given a third of Brittany. Sancho, count of Gascony, captures Pippin, son of Pippin, and keeps him until he can bring him into Charles’s presence. Charles takes the captive to Francia and, after Lothar’s conference, orders him to be tonsured at the monastery of Saint Medard at Soissons.

Louis, son of Lothar, going to Benevento, attacks the city of Bari. Having breached the wall, he abandons his undertaking because of the very bad advice of his counselors. For when they said that a large part of the treasures was there and that he would be completely deprived of them if everyone were indiscriminately allowed to enter, he withdrew into the camp and forbade anyone to storm the city. When they had gone away, the Moors repaired the breach in the wall at night with beams, so that they had no fear whatsoever of the enemy who would come on the following day. Thus Louis, after all his great labor had been expended in vain, returns to his own country with his army.

Abd al-Rahman, king of the Saracens settled in Spain, dies at Córdoba, and his son succeeds him in the kingdom. Godefrid, son of the Dane Heriold, who had once been baptized at Mainz under the emperor Louis, deserts Lothar and goes over to his own people. Having gathered a strong force, he attacks Frisia with a multitude of ships, then enters the neighboring Scheldt and finally the Seine. When Lothar and Charles meet him there with their entire army, they besiege both banks of that river.

### DCCCLII

During this siege they celebrate the feast of the Nativity of the Lord. But because those on Charles’s side were unwilling to join battle, they withdraw without accomplishing anything. Charles wins Godefrid over to himself by certain agreements; the other Danes remain there without any fear until March, plundering, burning, and taking captives all the more ferociously because they act more freely.

Lothar receives Charles’s daughter from the sacred font and, a few days later, attempts to return to his own country.

### DCCCLIII

The Danes, leaving the Seine in July and proceeding up the Loire, ravage the city of Nantes, the monastery of Saint Florentius, and the neighboring places.

In April Charles assembles a synod of bishops near the city of Soissons, in the monastery of Saint Medard. Presiding over the synod himself, he has two priests, monks of that same monastery, degraded at the bishops’ judgment, because they had planned to steal Pippin and flee with him into Aquitaine. Hincmar, bishop of Reims, deposes, at the synod’s judgment, all the priests, deacons, and subdeacons of his church whom Ebo had ordained after his own deposition.

Pippin swears an oath of fidelity to Charles; moreover, he assumes the monastic habit and promises to observe the rule in the customary manner of a monk. Charles then comes to Quierzy and, with certain bishops and monastic abbots, issues four chapters and confirms them by his own subscription.

The first is that no one is predestined by God to punishment, and that there is only one predestination of God, which pertains either to the gift of grace or to the recompense of justice. The second is that free will, which we lost in the first order, is restored to us by the prevenient and assisting grace of Christ. The third is that God wills, in a general sense, all human beings to be saved, although not all are saved. The fourth is that Christ’s blood was shed for all, although not all are redeemed by the mystery of the Passion.

Almost all the Aquitanians desert Charles and send envoys of their submission, with hostages, to Louis, king of the Germans. The same Louis is sharply stirred against Charles on account of certain conditions made between himself and Charles during the time of their disturbances. The Wends deal falsely against Louis with their customary treacheries.

The emperor Lothar, after the death two years earlier of the most Christian queen Ermengard, takes to himself two slave women from the royal estate. By one of them, named Doda, he has begotten a son whom he orders to be called Carloman; his other sons likewise give themselves to adulteries.

Danish pirates, moving upstream from Nantes, come without penalty in November, on the sixth day before the Ides, to the city of Tours and burn it, together with the church of Saint Martin and the other adjacent places. But because this had been foreknown with evident certainty, the body of the blessed Martin had been transferred to Cormery, the monastery of that church, and thence to the city of Orléans.

The Bulgarians, allied with the Slavs and, as is reported, encouraged by gifts from our people, are vigorously stirred up against Louis, king of the Germans, but are defeated with the Lord fighting on our side. The Greeks likewise stir themselves no less against Louis, son of Lothar and king of Italy, because he had been betrothed to the daughter of the emperor of Constantinople but delayed coming to her wedding. The Romans too, worn down by the incursions of the Saracens and Moors, complain to the emperor Lothar that their defense has been utterly neglected.

### DCCCLIV

Charles, suspicious of the fidelity of his brother Louis, comes to Lothar at the village of Leuth. There, after they had long discussed their common friendship and its indissolubility, they finally, in the presence of everyone who was there, repeatedly swore to one another over the holy relics and confirmed their agreement, entrusting to each other their sons, nobles, and kingdoms.

Meanwhile the young Louis, son of Louis king of the Germans, is sought by the Aquitanians from his father. He crosses the Loire and is received by those who had requested him. Charles undertakes an expedition into Aquitaine during Lent and remains there until the Paschal feast. Its people devote all their efforts to plunder, burning, and the capture of human beings, and do not restrain their greed and audacity even from the churches and altars of God.

Lothar addresses his brother Louis on the Rhine concerning his brotherly relationship with Charles. But after first biting one another fiercely, they eventually return to concord and are bound together in the name of peace. Charles, therefore, greatly concerned, returns from Aquitaine without having accomplished anything and invites his brother Lothar to his palace at Attigny. When they meet there, they confirm what they had agreed upon earlier.

The Danes settled on the Loire come as far as the fortress of Blois and burn it, wishing to reach Orléans and do the same there. But when Bishop Ado of Orléans and Count Bouchard prepare ships and warriors against them, they abandon their intention and return to the lower Loire. Other Danish pirates also ravage Frisia adjoining Saxony.

Lothar and Charles send envoys to their brother Louis for the sake of peace and to ask him to recall his son from Aquitaine. Charles again goes into Aquitaine. Pippin, son of Pippin, who had been tonsured at the monastery of Saint Medard, assumed the monastic habit, and sworn an oath to remain there, enters Aquitaine, and the greater part of the country’s people flock to him.

King Charles, setting aside Pippin’s cause, brings his nephew Louis from Aquitaine to Gaul. Charles’s brother Pippin, already ordained a deacon, withdraws from the monastery of Corbie. King Charles dedicates his son Carloman to the ecclesiastical tonsure.

The Danes, fighting among themselves in an internal war, rage with such obstinate fury for three days that, after King Oric and the other kings with him have been killed, almost the entire nobility perishes. The pirates of the Northmen, settled on the Loire, again burn the city of Angers.

### DCCCLV

Lothar gives all Frisia to his son Lothar. Therefore Roric and Godefrid return to their homeland, that is, Denmark, in the hope of obtaining royal power.

Lothar falls ill, and this gives his brothers Louis and Charles an opportunity to return to concord. The Northmen invade Bordeaux, a city of Aquitaine, and roam about at will here and there.

At the request of the Aquitanians, Charles assigns his son Charles to them as their designated king. Charles also honorably receives Æthelwulf, king of the Anglo-Saxons, who is on his way to Rome; he presents him with every kind of royal attire and has him escorted with honors worthy of a king as far as the boundaries of his kingdom.

Lothar complains against Charles on the grounds of suspected disloyalty. Many things contrary to the Catholic faith are stirred up in Charles’s kingdom, even though he himself is not unaware of them.

In August Leo, chief of the Apostolic See, dies, and Benedict succeeds him. In the same month two stars, one larger and one smaller, are seen moving from west toward east. This occurs ten times, alternately, so that while the larger remained visible, the smaller sometimes disappeared entirely.

The emperor Lothar, seized by illness and despairing of life, goes to the monastery of Prüm, established in the Ardennes. Renouncing the world and kingdom completely, he is tonsured and humbly takes up the life and habit of a monk. Having arranged the kingdom among the sons who were staying with him, so that Lothar, his namesake, should obtain Francia while Charles should obtain Provence, he dies within six days, on the third day before the Kalends of October, and receives burial in the same monastery, as he had desired.

In the middle of October the Aquitanians gather at the city of Limoges, generally establish the boy Charles, son of Charles, as king, and, after he has been anointed, the pontiff places the royal crown on him and gives him the scepter.

The Northmen, entering the Loire, leave their ships behind and attempt to reach the city of Poitiers on foot, [the surviving text is materially uncertain: “marked with the name of the royal authority …”]. But when the Aquitanians meet them, they are so thoroughly routed—something previously unfamiliar to them—that only a few of more than three hundred escape.

Roric and Godefrid, not trusting in their own resources, remain at Dorestad and gain possession of the greater part of Frisia.

A harsh and dry winter prevailed, and a pestilence raged in which a great part of the population perished.

Louis, king of Italy and son of Lothar, complained to his uncles Louis and Charles about the portion of his father’s kingdom in Francia that they had taken from his brother Lothar; he asserted that he had obtained Italy through the generosity of Emperor Louis.

Louis, emperor of Italy, and his brother Lothar, king of Francia, met at Orbe. Because frequent Slavic revolts troubled their father’s kingdom, they disputed so sharply over their shares of it that they prepared to decide the matter by arms. Lothar nevertheless apportioned Provence and the duchy of Lyon to his brother Charles as his paternal share. Charles’s nobles then seized him and attempted to tonsure him as a cleric.

In the region of Benevento, forces approaching Naples by treachery seized it and utterly overthrew it [the agents are obscured by the interleaving of the two source columns].

The Aquitanians rejected the boy Charles, whom they had recently made king, and pretended that Pippin—escaped from the monastery of Saint Medard—was their king. King Charles made an agreement with Herispogius of the Bretons, betrothed his daughter to Herispogius’s son Louis, and granted him the duchy of Maine.

The Aquitanians reject Charles, the boy whom they had recently established as king, and drive him away. They bring Pippin, who had escaped from the monastery of Saint Medard, out of monastic custody and pretend that he is king. Charles, with Respogius [or Herispogius] and the Bretons, joins his son.

### DCCCLVII

On the fifth day before the Kalends of January, Danish pirates invade Paris and immediately give it to the flames. Those who were staying on the lower Loire plunder Tours and all the surrounding places as far as the fortress of Blois.

The nobles set up Lothar, son of the former Lothar, as king of Francia, even by sacred anointing. On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May Danish pirates come to the city of Orléans, plunder it, and return with impunity.

Almost all the counts of King Charles’s realm conspire with the Aquitanians against him, inviting Louis, king of the Germans, to carry out their secret plan. Since he is delayed for a long time on the Slavonic expedition, where he also loses a great part of his army, they cannot endure his delay and renounce King Charles. Pippin joins the Danish pirates, devastates the city of Poitiers, and lays waste many other places in Aquitaine.

Lothar, abusing his concubines, casts away his wife. In the city of Cologne, Agilmar, bishop of that city, is present in the church of Saint Peter, while a dense cloud appears above it, sending down frequent flashes of lightning. Suddenly a flash like fire passes through the supports of the church roof, kills one priest and two laymen, and, after these have been carried out, the cloud dissipates.

The Aquitanians, rejecting Pippin, receive again Charles the boy, son of King Charles, whom they had driven away, and bring him back into Aquitaine. Other Danish pirates enter the Seine in the middle of August. They devastate and plunder the cities on both banks of the river, together with monasteries and villas situated far away, as far as the place called Fosse-Gibaud. They establish a station at the island called Ossel, which lies in the Seine, and spend the winter there in peace.

Æthelwulf, king of the West Saxons, returning from Rome, receives in marriage Judith, daughter of King Charles, who had been betrothed to him in July; on the tenth day before the Kalends of October, at the palace of Verberie, he receives her in marriage and takes her to his own country. A dog of extraordinary size is seen running about the altar; it suddenly disappears.

### Variant Readings and Notes

- In some witnesses, **Ludowicus** and elsewhere **Ludoicus**.
- **Abdirhaman.**
- **Sequanam** is absent from manuscript C and from Bouquet; the word **quanam** should have been restored. Nevertheless, it must be **Sequanam**, since this agrees with the year 850.
- At Lothar’s two concubines the source apparatus preserves the damaged Latin *sibi ancillas ex villa regia … Normannorum transportatum est*; the syntax is corrupt, but *ancillas ex villa regia* means “slave women from the royal estate.” It is not a secure statement that he transported them from the Northmen.
- Witness Ch. reads *Maguntiaci* (“at Mainz”).
- *Navium* (“of ships”) is absent from Ch. but plainly required.
- Witness B reads *copulavit* (“joined to himself”) in the sentence about Lothar’s concubines.
- The editor prefers the reading supplied by the *Chronicle of the Deeds of the Northmen* at the adjoining Danish notice.
- Saint-Quentin; compare Valesius, *Notitia Galliarum*, pp. 595–596.
- In September; compare the *Aquitanian or Memmian Chronicle* and the *Angoulême Chronicle* in Bouquet, vol. VII, pp. 222–223.
- The city of Bari is intended.
- The Danes, in July, abandoning the Seine and proceeding to the Loire, ravage Nantes, the monastery of Saint Florentius, and the neighboring places.
- Compare the *Chronicle of the Deeds of the Northmen*.
- Compare Mabillon, *Annals of the Benedictines*, book XXXIV, no. 52.
- That is, the Wends.
- Compare the *Chronicle of the Deeds of the Northmen*.
- This year Æthelwulf, or Æthelwolf, went to Rome, taking with him his son Alfred, as Asser, the contemporary author of the *Life of Alfred*, and the ancient chronicler Æthelweard, book IV, testify. [Bouquet.]

### Source apparatus for scan pages 711–713

- Witnesses vary between *Ludowicus* and *Ludoicus* for Louis, and preserve *Abdirhaman*. At the Seine clause, *Sequanam* is absent from Ch. and Bouquet; the damaged *quanam* must be restored as *Sequanam*, as the annal for 850 confirms.
- In the peace clause the editor supplies *pace* (“peace”); Ch. reads *negocio* for *negotio* (“business”). Ch. and A read *Blisium* (Blois). At Bishop Agius’s preparation against the Danes, the witness has *Budiardo*; Bouquet argues from canon 3 of the second Council of Soissons (853) that *Buchardum* must be read.
- The notes identify Leuth as Liège and Blisium as Blois, and twice compare the *Chronicle of the Deeds of the Northmen* for the year 853.
- Asser, the contemporary author of the *Life of Alfred*, says of Æthelwulf: “After remaining there [at Rome] for a full year, he returned to his country, bringing with him Judith, daughter of Charles, king of the Franks.” Æthelweard, book IV, likewise writes: “When he returned to his country, Charles, king of the Franks, gave him his daughter in marriage; having received her, he took her to his country.” [Bouquet.] Verberie lies on the Oise near Senlis.
- The death date of Lothar is transmitted as the third day before the Kalends of October. Bouquet observes that he may have died on the fourth and been buried on the third, different witnesses reckoning by death or burial; he could also have died during the night between those dates.
- Orbe stands on the Orbe, which flows into Lake Neuchâtel. *Subgrundium* means the projecting part of a roof by which rainwater is shed. The relevant Danish notices are compared with the *Chronicle of the Deeds of the Northmen*.
- Page 713 further preserves *conspirantur* in Ch.; an omitted *rege* (“king”); *ratione* in Ch. and B; and the editorial sequence *reconciliantur. Ex aqui spret[o]*, whose end is damaged. The Chronicle supplies *congruum* (“fitting”). These readings belong respectively to the conspiracy against Charles, Lothar’s royal title, the Aquitanian settlement, and the return of the boy Charles.

### DCCCLVIII

The Danes stationed on the Seine ravage everything freely and attack Paris. They burn the basilica of Saint Peter and that of Saint Genevieve, together with the other buildings, except the house of Saint Stephen, the church of Saint Vincent and Saint Germain, and the church of Saint Denis. For these alone, a large sum of money is paid as ransom.

Other Danes capture the emporium called Dorstad and plunder the entire island of the Batavians and the neighboring places.

Respogius, duke of the Bretons, is killed by Salomon and Almar, Bretons who had long been in conflict with one another. Some of the nobles of King Charles, having joined the Aquitanians, perpetrate many battles and numerous acts of violence. Frotbald, bishop of Chartres, while the Danes are pressing him in that same city, flees on foot and, attempting to reach the river Eure by swimming, is seized by the waters and dies.

When Charles himself entered the island in the Seine called Ossel, where he endured great danger, as many people then learned, and when his brother Louis came against him with all his warlike equipment, he nevertheless withdrew with honor through the mercy of God.

On the feast of the Nativity of the Lord, by night and by day, a strong and very frequent earthquake occurs at Mainz, and it is followed by a severe mortality among human beings.

In the territory of [lacuna] a certain tree, uprooted from its roots, is thrown out. It had previously been unknown in the provinces of Gaul. It was without leaves, but had branches resembling grass, partly broad but longer, and, in place of leaves, certain triangular objects in shape, colored like human fingernails or fish bones. They were thin and adhered to the tips of these branches as though they had been attached from outside. They resembled the ornaments customarily affixed externally to belts or to the harness of men or horses and made from different metals.

In the district of Sens, in the church of Saint Procaire, while Mass is being celebrated on Sunday by a priest, a wolf suddenly enters and disturbs the assembled people as it runs about. At last, repeatedly moving among the women, it disappears.

Æthelwulf, king of the western Saxons, dies. His surviving queen Judith is taken in marriage by his son Æthelbald.

Berno, leader of part of the pirates settled on the Seine, comes to King Charles at his palace in Verberie. Surrendering himself into Charles’s hands, he immediately swears fidelity.

Another part of those same pirates captures Louis, abbot of the monastery of Saint Denis, together with his brother Gauzlenus, and imposes upon them an extremely heavy ransom. For this reason many treasures of the churches of God throughout Charles’s kingdom are exhausted, at the king’s own command. But when these prove wholly insufficient, the king himself, all the bishops, abbots, counts, and other powerful men contribute many gifts in competition with one another to make up the aforesaid sum.

The counts of King Charles, joined with the Bretons and having deserted Charles, compel his son Louis and his followers, who had been prevented from advancing from the region of Le Mans, to cross the Seine and take refuge with his father.

King Lothar, together with his brother Charles, king of Provence, confirms his friendship, giving him two episcopal portions from his kingdom, namely Belley and Tarentaise. Similarly Charles hands over his kingdom to his brother Lothar on the condition that, if Charles dies before taking a wife and fathering sons, Lothar should succeed him by hereditary right.

In May, at the village of Liège, where the body of Saint Lambert rests, such a sudden flood of rain pours down that houses, stone walls, and every kind of building, together with the people and everything else it finds there, are violently swept into the river Meuse, all the way to the very church commemorating Saint Lambert.

The Danes attack Saxony but are driven back. Benedict, the Roman pontiff, dies; Nicholas is substituted for him, chosen more through the favor and support of King Louis and his nobles than by the clergy.

King Lothar, compelled by his own people, takes back the wife whom he had repudiated. Nevertheless, he does not admit her to his bed but hands her over to custody.

King Charles attacks the island in the Seine called Ossel in July, intending to besiege the Danes who are staying there. There his son Charles, the boy, arrives from Aquitaine. With him he receives Pippin, now a layman, and grants him counties and monasteries in Aquitaine.

King Lothar also hurries to the same island in August to offer his uncle assistance. After they remain there without success in the siege until the ninth day before the Kalends of October, they finally return to their own territories.

Meanwhile the counts from King Charles’s kingdom bring Louis, king of the Germans, whom they had been inviting for five years. He arrives at the royal villa of Pontion on the Kalends of September and travels through the territory of Châlons and the land of the Cupedenses to Agedincum of the Senones. From there, entering the region of Orléans, he receives the Aquitanians and Neustrians, as well as the Bretons who had promised to come to him, and returns by nearly the same route as far as the Cupedenses.

When King Charles learns this, he hurries through the territory of Châlons to the villa of Brienne, where the leading men of Burgundy come to him. He awaits Louis, who is pursuing him. But when messengers pass between them and no settlement of peace is reached, finally, on the third day—that is, on the day before the Ides of November—with battle lines prepared on both sides, Charles, seeing that his own men are abandoning him, withdraws and goes toward Burgundy.

Louis, having received those who had deserted Charles, goes to Troyes. There he distributes among those who had invited him counties, monasteries, royal villas, and properties, and returns to the palace at Attigny. King Lothar meets him there and, after confirming the agreements made between them, returns to his own country.

Louis then proceeds through Reims and the district of Laon to Augusta Viromanduorum, that is, the monastery of Saint Quintinus the Martyr, where he enters in order to celebrate the feast of the Nativity of the Lord.

Meanwhile a certain monk from the monastery of Saint Vincent the Martyr or Saint Germain the Confessor, returning from Córdoba, a city of Spain, brings with him the bodies of the blessed martyrs George the deacon and Aurelius, together with the head of Natalia. He places them for preservation in a church at the villa of Aemantus.

### DCCCLIX

The Danes ravage the places beyond the Scheldt. The common people, conspiring together between the Seine and the Loire against the Danes settled on the Seine, resist them bravely. But because their conspiracy was undertaken imprudently, they are easily killed by our more powerful men.

King Charles, having recovered his strength, unexpectedly attacks his brother Louis and drives him from the boundaries of his kingdom. King Lothar hurries to his uncle Charles, and on Sunday, at the beginning of Lent, at the palace of Arcis, they confirm themselves again by oaths publicly exchanged in one another’s presence.

Charles [begins a sentence concerning] certain monasteries which the clergy had previously … [inherited source boundary].

### Notes

This terrible disaster is lamented by Paschasius Radbertus in book VI of his *Commentary on the Lamentations of Jeremiah*:

> Who could ever have believed, or who could ever have imagined, that something of this kind could happen in our regions—that within so short a time we should all have mourned, lamented, and suffered terribly? Even now we fear it no less, since pirates gathered from various families reached the boundaries of Paris and burned the churches of Christ here and there along the shore. Who, I ask, could ever have believed that thieves of mixed origin would ever dare such things? Or who could have imagined that so glorious a kingdom, so fortified, so extensive, so populous, and so strong should be humbled and disgraced by such men? I confess that none of the kings of the earth would have imagined this, nor could any inhabitant of our world have heard that an enemy had entered our Paris.

The anonymous author of the miracles of Saint Genevieve, who lived at this time, writes:

> The most blessed virgin Genevieve remained for five years outside her own shrine because the Normans were ravaging the whole region adjoining the Seine. When they were returning to their own lands, we brought our lady back to the holy place.

He also speaks of the burning of the church of Saint Genevieve by the Normans. Stephen of Tournai, in letter 164 to the bishop of London, writes:

> Among other things, we cannot and should not report without sighing and sobbing that the church of the apostles Peter and Paul, in which the blessed virgin Genevieve rests bodily, built and painted by royal command and workmanship, adorned with mosaic within and without, as the surviving remains still attest, they miserably burned with fire, sparing neither the holy place nor rendering veneration to the blessed virgin and the other saints who rest there.

**L’Eure.**

In the *Necrology of the Church of Chartres*, part of which Mabillon published in volume II of the *Analecta*, p. 550, this slaughter is assigned to the following year, and Frotbald is said to have been killed:

> In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 858, indiction 6, a great slaughter was carried out by the pagan men of the Seine at Chartres, in which Frotbald the bishop, Stephen the priest, and others were killed.

In the chartulary of the monastery of Saint Peter at Chartres, it is stated that he was slaughtered with the canons and monks by bloody swords, namely on the day before the Ides of June. [Bouquet.]

From its resemblance to the nose of a donkey, the place is called, in French, **Nez de Besdan**, otherwise Oissel. [Bouquet.]

Now, that is, in the year 1749, it is an estate called Sainte-Procaire, dependent on the abbey of Pontigny and half a league distant from it. [Bouquet.]

Ingulf, in his account of this marriage, writes:

> Æthelbald, ascending his father’s bed—a thing never heard of among any people—took as his wife Judith, his own stepmother, formerly the daughter of the king of the Franks, whom his father Æthelwulf had married, and led her to the altar amid the greatest astonishment of all his fellow countrymen, who abhorred his crime.

[ Bouq uet.]

Compare the *Chronicle of the Deeds of the Northmen*, year 857.

Louis and Gauzlenus had the same father, Rorico, count of Le Mans, but not the same mother. Louis was the son of Rotrude, daughter of Charles the Bald; Gauzlenus was the son of Bilichildis, who was abbess of Chelles, and so forth. [Bouquet.]

From the side of the monastery of Saint Denis, six hundred and eighty-five pounds of gold and three thousand two hundred and fifty of silver were given, besides their vassals and their wives and children. I read this at the end of the Aachen canonical rule, in a manuscript of Saint Nicaise at Reims written about the year 800; Mabillon notes it in book XXXV of the *Annals of the Benedictines*, no. 33. [Bouquet.]

Belley on the Rhône.

Moustiers.

Compare the *Chronicle of the Deeds of the Northmen*, year 857.

Pontion.

Châlons-sur-Marne.

The highly learned abbot Lebeuf, in a special dissertation (*Memoirs of the Academy of Inscriptions*, vol. XVIII, pp. 282 ff.), proved from a donation by Count Helingaud that there was a hundred of Cupedenses in the Meldic district near Sézanne, and that its chief place was Cubtas, commonly called Queudes.

**Sens.**

**Brienne.**

**Troyes.**

This monk was Usuard, the author of the *Martyrology*. Aimoinus, a monk of the monastery of Saint Germain at Paris, composed the history of this translation. [Bouquet.]

The same Aimoinus, book III, chapter 7, writes:

> We then approached the villa of Aemantus, which belonged to our property and in which at that time the greater part of the brothers were living because of the persecution of the pagans. The monks had fled there with the body of Saint Germain, as is gathered from book II of the *Miracles* of that saint, composed by the same Aimoinus. It is a village commonly called Aimant, near Montereau, at the confluence of the Yonne and the Seine.

[Bo uquet.]

Compare the *Chronicle of the Deeds of the Northmen*.

Arcis, formerly a royal villa between Mézières and Charleville on the river Meuse; today it is a village that retains the old name, Arches. [Bouquet.]

# ANNALS

He used to distribute [them] to laymen. Danish pirates, sailing by a long circuit of the sea—namely, between Spain and Africa—enter the Rhône; after ravaging certain cities and monasteries on an island called Camargue, they establish themselves there.

King Charles holds assemblies with the bishops in various places. But at the fourth milestone from Toul, in the village of Saponaria, while attending a synod of bishops with Lothair and Charles, his grandsons and kings, he presents a written accusation against Gunthion, metropolitan bishop of Sens at Agendicum. This action, however, is postponed because Bishop Gunthion is absent.

From there he hastens to a conference with his brother, King Louis, on an island of the Rhine between Andernach and Confluentes. The outcome of this conference is deferred until the eighth day before the Kalends of November, at the city of Basel. When Louis arrives, Charles, because Lothair is absent, turns back from the journey he had begun.

Nearly all the Aquitanians transfer their allegiance to the young Charles. Pippin joins Count Robert and the Bretons.

Lights are seen in the sky during August, September, and October at night, so that a daylight-like brightness continuously shone from the east toward the north, and columns of blood seemed to emerge from it and extend outward.

The Danes, newly arrived, lay waste by plunder and fire to the monastery of Saint Valery, Samarobriva—the city of Amiens—and other places in the surrounding region. Others of them likewise invade the Rhine island of Batavia with similar fury. Those who are staying on the Seine attack the city of Noyon by night, seize Bishop Immo together with other nobles, both clerical and lay, and, after devastating the city, carry them away with them; they then kill them on the journey.

Two months earlier they had also killed Ermenfrid of Beauvais in a certain village; and in the preceding year they had slain Baltfrid, bishop of Bayeux.

For fear of these same Danes, the bones of the blessed martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius were transported to the district of Maurienne, to Novientum, a village belonging to them, and on the second day before the Kalends of October were carefully placed in a suitable location.

## VARIANTS

2. “Andernach”: Ch.

3. S. Hincmar, Letter 25.
