5. “Scheme”: Ch.

## NOTES

a. Compare the *Chronicle of the Deeds of the Normans*.

b. Camargue, formerly in the mouth of the Rhône. Valesius, *Notes on Gaul*, p. 119.

c. Many remains of this village, which was one league from Toul, still survive. Bouquet.

d. Compare the *Chronicle of the Deeds of the Normans*.

e. Saint Valery.

f. That is, Batavia.

g. Noyon.

h. Beauvais. Nevertheless, it is clear from the acts of the Council of Toul at Tusiacum that Immo, bishop of Noyon, and Ermenfrid of Beauvais were still alive in October of the following year, since both signed those acts. Rainelmus, Immo’s successor, is also found among the names of those signing there. Yet after the synod his acts could have been signed—as often happened—by someone else; certainly two men of Auxerre, Abbo and Christian, signed there. Thus Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, book 35, no. 50. Bouquet.

i. Bayeux.

j. Nogent-sur-Seine.

Lothair assigns to his brother Louis, king of the Italians, a certain portion of his kingdom—namely, what he possessed beyond the Jura Mountains: the cities of Geneva, Lausanne, and Sion, together with their bishoprics, monasteries, and counties, except the hospice situated on Mount Jupiter and the county of Pippin.

### NOTES

a. The cities are Geneva, Lausanne, and Sion.

b. The hospice is on Mount Saint Bernard. On the Kalends of August 1823, returning from Italy, I too stopped there; received most kindly according to the custom of those excellent Fathers, I now render them public thanks here after my private thanks.

c. This is doubtless the county of Pippin, named from the castle of Bipp, on the western slope of the Jura at the sources of the river Birsa. See its map in Schoepflin, *Alsatia Illustrata*, vol. 1, p. 619.

Gunthion, bishop of Sens, is reconciled to King Charles without a hearing before the bishops.

Pope Nicholas, by God’s grace, faithfully confirms and Catholicly decrees the teaching concerning grace and free will, the truth of the twofold predestination, and the blood of Christ, that it was shed for all believers.

## 860

A long winter, severe with continuous snow and frost, lasting from November until April.

Lothair, having come to hate his queen Teutberga with irreconcilable hatred, compelled her to confess before the bishops that she had been involved with her brother Hubert in the crime of sodomy. She was therefore immediately subjected to penance and confined in a monastery.

King Charles, misled by the empty promise of the Danes settled on the Somme, orders a levy to be made from the treasures of the churches and from all estates and merchants, even the poorest, so that their houses and all their utensils were appraised and a fixed tax exacted from them. For those Danes had promised him that, if he gave them three thousand pounds of silver by tested weight, they would march against the Danes who were operating on the Seine and either drive them out or kill them.

On the day before the Nones of April, during the following night—when the new moon had already begun—a certain horn-shaped darkness is said to have appeared, in the same form in which the moon was shining, across the middle of the moon, so that it shone on either side but was dark in the middle.

Likewise, on the seventh day before the Ides of April, the sun is said to have risen with a certain darkness in the middle of its disk. As this darkness descended toward the lower part, another darkness immediately entered it from above and likewise traversed its disk down to the bottom. This occurred on the tenth day of the moon.

The Danes settled on the Somme, since the promised levy was not given to them, take hostages and sail toward Anglo-Saxon territory; defeated and driven back by them, they seek other regions.

The Danes who had been staying in the Rhône advance as far as the city of Valence, ravaging it. After plundering everything in the surrounding area, they return to the island where they had established their settlement.

Kings Louis, Charles, and Lothair meet on the Kalends of June at the castle called Confluentes. After discussing peace among themselves for a long time, they finally confirm their agreement and friendship by oath.

Louis, emperor of Italy, is attacked by a faction of his own people, and he in turn ravages and burns their lands and those of the Beneventans.

The Danes who had been in the Rhône set out for Italy, seize the city of Pisa and other places, plunder them, and lay them waste.

Lothair, fearing his uncle Charles, allies himself with Louis, king of Germany, and, because of that alliance, hands over a part of his kingdom, namely Alsace. Lothair’s wife, fearing her husband’s hatred and plots, flees to her brother Hucbert in Charles’s kingdom. King Charles grants the monastery of Saint Martin to his son Louis.

b. Valence.

## 861

In January the Danes give Paris, the church of Saint Vincent the Martyr, and that of Saint Germanus the Confessor over to fire. They also pursue and capture merchants who are fleeing upstream by boat on the Seine. Other Danish pirates likewise enter the district of Thérouanne and lay it waste.

On the fourth day before the Kalends of April, after the eighth hour of the night, everything is turned into darkness.

King Charles orders his son Lothair the Lame to be tonsured in the monastery of Saint John.

### NOTES

a. Greater credence should be given to Aimoin, monk of Saint-Germain, who flourished at this time. In the *History of the Miracles of Saint Germanus of Paris*, book 2, no. 40, he says that this destruction took place on holy Easter day. Bouquet.

b. That is, in the monastery of Reomay. Lothair was also abbot of that place and likewise of the monastery of Saint-Germain of Auxerre. Bouquet.

## VERSES OF SAINT PRUDENTIUS

*(In Camuzat, the Promptuary or Repertory of the former diocese of Troyes)*

The monks of Saint Augustine established this house,  
once the hands of Romulus had built Rome.  
With the light of the Lord Christ shining throughout the world,  
a lofty house is founded for the Christian people.  
The dust of Peter adorns it, and the revered Paul,  
who by their holiness bear the apostolic summit.

Here I, Prudentius, serving with devoted action,  
gladly discharge this work of the Gospel:  
born in the western land, brought to and raised at *Cehis* [the printed place-name is uncertain],  
and appointed to a bishop’s robes and office.

The four men, inspired by heavenly light,  
composed what I write with a supremely truthful style.  
With different beginnings, but confessing Christ at the end,  
they recount his blessed deeds in a faith that is not different.

Matthew, the Virgin’s son, whom Mary bore,  
reports him instructing and commanding the nations.  
He promises to accompany all the holy ones  
to the end of the age, and always to be with his own.

Mark sings of the Son of the Most High,  
ascending to the heights with the roar of a lion after sleep has been driven away.  
He teaches that the disciples traversed the world preaching  
and confirmed their teaching with new signs.

Luke relates that he was conceived by the Holy Spirit  
and that the offered victim endured the terrible cross.  
But [the corrupt printed lines speak of] the disciples at the celebrated shrine of the threefold temple,  
until they received the heavenly gifts of the Father.

John declares that the Word precedes the first ages,  
and that a human being was made and at the same time was God.  
Flying with swift wings like an eagle,  
he gazes upon the everlasting sun with unwearied sight.

Peter was entrusted with the task of feeding the sheep;  
he tells tranquilly that he too was appointed to this lot.  
Christ is reported by these men as Jesus, Lord, and God,  
preceding all things and freely creating all things.

Eternal and everlasting, flowing from the Father’s breast,  
the almighty Son, begotten from the Almighty.  
We proclaim him created as a human being from a virgin womb,  
free from sin and without an earthly father.

Teaching wonderful things, performing wonderful deeds with power,  
he was handed over to mockery, fastened, and then crucified.  
Sending forth his blessed soul by his own power,  
he loosed and rescued his own from the Tartarean realms.

Then, incorruptible, rising after three days of death,  
he raised his living limbs to the heavenly heights.  
Seated upon the throne and granted the paternal inheritance,  
he rejoices, with all things subjected beneath his feet.

Having briefly set out what the action of this book reports,  
I now turn my prayers to you, good King.  
Look with compassion upon the gifts of your devoted servant,  
and, in pity for me, accept what is pleasing to you.

# FLORILEGIUM FROM SACRED SCRIPTURE

## OF SAINT PRUDENTIUS, BISHOP OF TROYES

*(In Trombellius, *Works of the Ancient Fathers*, Bologna, 1735)*

## TO THE BENEVOLENT READER

What Prudentius of Troyes’s little work is, most kindly reader, I shall explain in the words of the most distinguished Joseph Blanchinus: “A florilegium of passages from the Old and New Testaments, adapted, after the manner of florilegia of the Psalms, for instructing in faith and morals those men who are to be ordained.”

The same most distinguished and most courteous Blanchinus had sent it, copied from Vatican Royal Alexandrine manuscript 191, to the most excellent provost Gori, so that he might publish it in his *Symbols*. But Gori, as he is most obliging and my closest friend, gave it to me as a gift, asking only that I should mention the most distinguished Blanchinus in the work in which he is commemorated. I do this most willingly; for who, unless ungrateful and devoid of all humanity, would be ashamed to make known the man from whose no slight benefit he had received?

What may surprise you, reader, is that in this florilegium abstinence from the blood of animals, and likewise from animals that have died strangled, is counted among the religious precepts imposed upon the Christian people. Certainly this abstinence was enjoined by the apostles at the Council of Jerusalem: “that they abstain from the pollutions of idols, and from fornication, and from things strangled, and from blood” (*Acts* 15:20).

It was very carefully observed at all times by very many in the Church, as you may plainly learn from the Quinisext Council, from the Synod of Worms held under Pope Hadrian II and in the reign of Louis the Pious, and from many penitentials which prescribe and inculcate this very practice. It is therefore not surprising if our Prudentius, a man most celebrated in his age, required this of his people.

Farewell.

## NOTES

a. Canon 67: “Divine Scripture has commanded us to abstain from blood, from things strangled, and from fornication. If thereafter anyone should eat the blood of an animal in any manner, if he is a cleric he shall be deposed; if he is a layman, he shall be separated from communion.” Volume 7 of the Councils, Venetian edition, 1729.

b. Canon 65: “Animals that have been torn by wolves or dogs are not to be eaten, unless pigs, sheep, deer, or goats are found dead. But pigs that, having tasted human blood, have touched it may be eaten; however, if they have eaten a dead corpse, their flesh must not be eaten, since they have been contaminated.” Volume 10 of the Councils, Venetian edition, 1730.

c. See also what is said about Prudentius of Troyes, or rather of Troyes, on p. 1379, where *Gallia Christiana* discusses the bishops of Troyes up to the year 846. Cave, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Prudentius of Troyes, for the year 846, p. 356, volume 1. John Albert Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Latina of the Middle and Later Ages*, book 12, p. 19, volume 6, Padua edition. Finally, not to enumerate everyone, the distinguished Joseph Blanchinus himself, whom I praised in volume 1 of the works of the venerable Cardinal Thomasius, in the appendix, part 2, p. [uncertain].

## THE BOOK BEGINS

Prudentius, bishop of Troyes, collected from both the Old and the New Testament the matters that he ordered to be committed to memory by those hastening toward sacred orders; these are also called **precepts**.

## FROM GENESIS

**[Genesis 9:3–5]** The Lord said to Noah: “You shall not eat flesh with its blood,” and so forth.

You shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister, whether born of your father or your mother. ## Florilegium from Sacred Scripture

…a person, nor gifts; for gifts blind the eyes of the wise and pervert the words of the righteous. Pursue justice, that which is just, so that you may live and possess the land which the Lord your God gives you.

(Deut. 17:8) If you see that the words of a judgment vary, arise and go up to the place which the Lord your God shall choose. You shall come to the priests and to the judge who is in office at that time; you shall inquire of them, and they shall declare to you the truth of the judgment. You shall do whatever those who preside in the place chosen by the Lord tell you, and whatever they teach you according to his law; you shall follow their judgment and not turn aside to the right or to the left. But whoever, in pride, refuses to obey the command of the priest who at that time ministers to the Lord your God, or the decision of the judge, that person shall die; and you shall remove evil from Israel. The whole people, hearing it, shall fear, so that no one thereafter swells with pride.

(Deut. 18:10) Let there not be found among you anyone who makes his son or daughter pass through fire, or who consults soothsayers, observes dreams and omens, practises sorcery or incantation, consults python-spirits or diviners, or seeks truth from the dead.

(Deut. 19:14) You shall not seize or move your neighbour’s boundaries, which those before you have fixed in your possession that the Lord your God will give you in the land which you receive to possess. One witness shall not stand against anyone: whatever sin or offence may have been committed, every matter shall stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses. If a false witness rises against anyone, accusing him, and they find that the witness has spoken a lie against his brother, he shall receive exactly what he intended to do to his brother.

(Deut. 22:5) A woman shall not wear a man’s garment, nor shall a man use a woman’s garment; everyone who does this is abominable before God.

(Ibid., v. 22) If a man sleeps with another man’s wife, both shall die—that is, the adulterer and the adulteress. If a man has betrothed a virgin and someone finds her in a city and lies with her, you shall bring them both out to the gate of that city and stone them to death: the girl, because she did not cry out when she was in the city; the man, because he humbled his neighbour’s wife.

(Deut. 23:9) When you go out against your enemies in battle, guard yourself from every evil thing. If there is among you a man polluted by a nocturnal emission, he shall go outside the camp and not return until, before evening, he has washed himself with water.

(Ibid., v. 16) You shall not hand over to his master a slave who has fled to you; he shall live with you in the place he chooses and which pleases him, and you shall not oppress him. There shall be no prostitute among the daughters of Israel, nor a male prostitute. You shall not lend money at interest to your brother, nor grain, nor any other thing. To your brother, lend without interest whatever he needs, so that the Lord your God may bless you in all your work. When you make a vow to the Lord your God, do not delay to fulfil it, because the Lord your God will require it of you; if you delay, it shall be reckoned to you as sin. But what has once proceeded from your lips you shall observe and do, as you promised the Lord your God of your own will and spoke with your own mouth.

(Deut. 24:10) When you demand from your neighbour something that he owes you, you shall not enter his house to take a pledge, but shall stand outside, and he shall bring out to you whatever he has. But if he is poor, the pledge shall not remain with you overnight; you shall return it to him before sunset, so that, sleeping in his garment, he may bless you and you may have righteousness before the Lord your God. You shall not deny the wage of your needy and poor brother, whether he is a newcomer or a resident in the land; on the same day, before sunset, you shall pay him the price of his labour.

(Ibid., v. 16) Fathers shall not be put to death for sons, nor sons for fathers; each shall die for his own sin. You shall not pervert the judgment of a newcomer or an orphan, nor take a widow’s garment as a pledge. When you reap the harvest in your field and leave a sheaf behind through forgetfulness, you shall not return to take it; you shall allow the newcomer, orphan, and widow to take it up. When you harvest your vineyard, do not gather the remaining clusters; let them go to the newcomer, orphan, and widow.

(Deut. 25:1) If a case arises between persons and they appeal to the judges, the judges shall declare righteous the one whom they perceive to be just and shall condemn the impious one for impiety. But if they judge the offender worthy of stripes, they shall lay him down and have him beaten before them, according to the measure of his offence and the number of stripes—only so that they do not exceed forty.

(Deut. 25:13) You shall not have differing weights in your bag, one greater and one smaller; nor shall there be in your house a measure greater and one smaller. You shall have a just and true weight. For the Lord abominates the one who does these things and detests all injustice.

## Florilegium from Sacred Scripture

(Matt. 19:3) The Pharisees came, saying: “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason?” “For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.”

(Ibid., v. 6) He answered: “Therefore, whoever divorces his wife, except on account of fornication, and marries another, commits adultery; and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.”

(Ibid., vv. 17 ff.) “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments. You shall not murder; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness. Honor your father and mother, and love your neighbor as yourself.” The young man said: “I have kept all these things; what do I still lack?” Jesus said to him: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything that you have and give it to the poor, and come, follow me; then you will have treasure in heaven.”

“Truly I say to you, a rich person will enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty.” And again: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.” With human beings this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.

Peter said: “Look, we have left everything and followed you; what then will there be for us?” Jesus said to him: “Truly I say to you, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel; and everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life.”

(Matt. 25:34) “The king will say to those at his right hand: ‘Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom. For I was hungry, and you gave me food.’”

## From the Epistle to the Romans

(Rom. 1:28) Since they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a depraved mind, to do what is improper: filled with every kind of injustice, wickedness, fornication, greed, malice; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, malignity; whisperers, slanderers, hateful to God, insolent, proud, boastful, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents, foolish, disorderly, without affection, without covenant, without mercy. They know God’s judgment, that those who do such things deserve death; and not only those who do them, but also those who approve of those who do them.

(Rom. 2:11 ff.) There is no partiality with God. For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified.

(Rom. 6:12 ff.) Therefore, do not let sin reign in your mortal body so that you obey its desires; for sin will not rule over you, since you are not under the law but under grace. Do you not know that to whatever you present yourselves as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of the one whom you obey—whether of sin, leading to death, or of obedience, leading to righteousness?

(Rom. 7:2) A woman who is under a husband, while her husband lives, is bound by the law; but if her husband dies, she is released from the law of her husband. Therefore, while her husband lives, she will be called an adulteress if she is with another man.

(Rom. 12:1 ff.) I urge you, brothers, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God: your reasonable service.

(Rom. 13:1) Let every soul be subject to higher authorities; for there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been established by God. Therefore whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance; and those who resist acquire condemnation for themselves.

(Ibid., v. 7) Give to everyone what is owed: tribute to whom tribute is due, taxes to whom taxes are due, honor to whom honor is due, fear to whom fear is due. Owe no one anything except to love one another.

(Ibid., v. 13) Not in feasting and drunkenness, not in bedrooms and indecencies, not in strife and rivalry; but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and do not make provision for the flesh in its desires.

(Rom. 14:3) Let the one who eats not despise the one who does not eat, and let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats; for God has accepted him. Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master.

(Rom. 16:17) I urge you, brothers, to watch those who create dissensions and stumbling-blocks contrary to the teaching that you have learned, and avoid them.

(Ibid., v. 19) I want you to be wise in what is good and simple in what is evil.

## To Timothy I

(1 Tim. 2:9) Likewise, let women adorn themselves in respectable dress, with modesty and sobriety, not with braided hair, gold, pearls, or costly clothing, but as is fitting for women professing godliness through good works. Let a woman learn in silence with all submission. I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man, but to remain silent.

(1 Tim. 3:11) Let women likewise be modest, not slanderers, sober, and faithful in all things.

(1 Tim. 4:7) Avoid profane and old-womanish fables; exercise yourself in godliness. For bodily exercise is useful for a little, having the promise of the life that now is and is to come.

(1 Tim. 5:1) Do not rebuke an older man, but exhort him as a father; younger men as brothers; older women as mothers; younger women as sisters, in all purity.

Honor widows who are truly widows. But if any widow has children or grandchildren, let her first learn to manage her own household and repay her parents, for this is acceptable before God. But she who lives in self-indulgence is dead while living. Command this also, so that they may be irreproachable. If anyone does not provide for his own, especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.

Let a widow be enrolled only if she is at least sixty years old, has been the wife of one husband, and has a testimony of good works: if she has raised children, shown hospitality, washed the feet of the saints, assisted those suffering tribulation, and followed every good work. But avoid younger widows. For when they become wanton against Christ, they wish to marry, having condemnation because they have rejected their first faith. At the same time, being idle, they learn to go around the houses—not only idle, but also talkative and meddlesome, speaking things that ought not to be spoken.

(Ibid., v. 17) Let the presbyters who govern well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in word and teaching. For Scripture says: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing,” and “The laborer is worthy of his wage.”

(1 Tim. 6:1) Let all who are under the yoke as slaves consider their masters worthy of all honor.

Likewise, let older women be in holy conduct, not slanderers, not enslaved to much wine, good teachers, so that they may teach the younger women prudence: to love their husbands, to love their children, to be prudent, chaste, sober, keeping house, kind, and subject to their husbands. Likewise exhort younger men to be sober.

(Tit. 3:1) Remind them to be subject to rulers and authorities, to obey commands, and to be ready for every good work; to slander no one, not to be quarrelsome, but moderate, showing all gentleness toward all people.

*1 Tim. 6:10. Therefore this passage should have been cited earlier.*

*2 Tim. 2:16. The manuscript has “and empty speech,” evidently through the amanuensis’ error.*

## Ancient Rites

(From Martène, *Ancient Ecclesiastical Rites*, vol. I)

### Order for Visiting the Sick

When the priest enters to visit the sick person, he first says:

“Peace to this house.”

**Response:** “And to your spirit.”

Then the antiphon:

“Bless, O Lord, this house.”

And it is sprinkled with blessed water together with the fragrance of incense. Afterwards he says these prayers:

“Lord God, who have spoken through your apostle ...”

Another:

“With every supplication, let us ask the Lord Jesus Christ ...”

Another:

“Come to the aid, O Lord, of this sick person N., and heal him with spiritual medicine, so that, restored to his former health, he may return healthy and offer you acts of thanksgiving. Through ...”

Another:

“O God, who granted your servant Hezekiah fifteen additional years of life ...”

Another:

“Look, O Lord, upon your servant in the infirmity of his body ...”

Another:

“O God, who have provided the human race with the remedy of salvation ...”

Another:

“O God of the heavenly powers, who [from] human bodies ...”

### St. Prudentius

1440

Another:

“Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God ...”

Afterwards he says to the sick person:

“What do you ask of me, brother?”

He answers:

“That you give me penance.”

The priest replies:

“May the Lord Jesus Christ grant you forgiveness. But if the Lord spares you, will you keep it?”

He answers:

“I will keep it.”

Then the priest makes a cross from ashes upon his breast and places a hair shirt upon his head. After this the following prayer is said:

“Let us humbly beseech almighty and merciful God, who does not desire the death of sinners, but that they should be converted and live, most beloved brothers, that, having been converted, he may graciously grant his servant N. forgiveness through his mercy; and if there are any wounds of his faults which he has contracted after the water of sacred washing, may his sins be healed in this public confession, so that no marks of scars remain in him. Through ...”

Another:

“O God, glory of the righteous and mercy of sinners, grant your servant N. complete forgiveness through your indulgence. Entreated in the place of penance, grant it, so that he who mourns his past sins may not experience future evils, nor commit them again while mourning. Forgive him all his crimes, and, appeased, restore him to the paths of righteousness, so that henceforth he may safely deserve to run among your good servants and reach the rewards of eternal peace. Through ...”

Another:

“Almighty, everlasting Lord God, who have placed the forgiveness of sinners in swift confession, come to the aid of those who have fallen and have mercy on the weary, so that those whom the chain of offenses binds may be freed by the compassion of your mercy. Through ...”

Then the sick person says the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed with the sign of the Holy Trinity. The priest questions him as follows:

“Do you wish to forgive all those who have sinned against you, so that God also may forgive you all your sins, as he himself says: ‘If you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins’?”

If he does not wish to forgive, do not receive his confession. And inquire carefully whether he is incestuous; and if he does not wish to renounce the incest itself, give him penance; and if he does not wish to do so, do not give him penance. Afterwards let him confess all his sins, as far as he can remember, and then say these words:

“Many are my sins, O Lord, in words, deeds, and thoughts.”

And let him bend his knees before the priest. Then the priest says the prayer after confession:

“Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, creator and preserver of the human race, who desire the repentance of sinners rather than their death: look upon this servant of yours, who has fallen through the errors of the world and, deceived by the assault of the devil, lies prostrate before the sight of your majesty. You who are kind and merciful, look upon him and raise up the one who has been cast down; release the captive, enlighten the blind, and recall him to salvation. For through the prophet you said: ‘I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should be converted and live.’ Grant also, O Lord, that he may perform worthy fruits of penance and deserve to receive perpetual forgiveness. And, joined to your holy Church, may he rejoice. Through ...”

Another:

“Grant us, O Lord, that just as you were appeased by the prayers and confession of the publican, so you may be appeased toward this servant of yours N.; and graciously incline to his prayers, so that, remaining in tearful confession and continually seeking your clemency in his petition, restored to the sacred altars and sacraments, he may again be devoted to heavenly glory. Through ...”

Another:

“Almighty and merciful God, in your goodness release the offenses of this servant of yours N., who confesses to you, so that the guilt of conscience may not harm him more unto punishment than the indulgence of your mercy benefits him unto forgiveness. Through ...”

Another:

“Look favorably, O Lord, upon this servant of yours N. ...”

Turning to the sick person, he says:

“May almighty God have mercy on you, and may the Lord forgive you your sins, free you from every evil, preserve you in every good, and lead you into eternal life. Amen.”

### Prayer for Communicating the Sick Person

“Our Savior and Redeemer of all, who willingly and mercifully grant forgiveness not only to penitents but also to those who do not even wish to come to you, we earnestly ask you to lead this servant of yours N. to communion in the body and blood of Christ, with forgiveness granted and heavenly blessing. Through ...”

Another:

“Hear us, O Lord our God, and grant that, through the laying on of our hands, the aid of healing may descend upon this servant of yours. You who willingly forgive all who have fallen and, satisfied with their amendment, embrace those who return to you, grant him that, having received the grace of communion, he may bring back victory over the raging enemy, so that, restored to the divine table, he may be filled with heavenly bread. Through ...”

Then the priest orders him to recite the Lord’s Prayer; and when he has finished, he says the following collect:

“With humble mind and devoted charity we ask the immense and merciful invisible God to hear the groans and supplications of those who have fallen, to consign the stains of former deeds to oblivion, and to lead this same N., under the indulgence of his mercy, to participation in sacred communion. Through ...”

From this point the sacrifice is given to the sick person, with these words:

“May the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ be for you unto perpetual salvation, here and in eternity. Amen.”

After this the following prayer is said:

“Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, we faithfully beseech you that, for our brother N. who receives the most holy body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, there may be salvation both of body and of soul. Through the same Lord.”

### Reconciliation of a Penitent at the Point of Death

“Merciful God, gracious God ...”

Here the sick person is to be anointed with holy oil. Then, if a bishop is present, he places his hand upon the head either of the priest or of any sick person; otherwise the priest reconciling a sick priest must not place his hand upon him. Over other sick persons he places his hand and says this prayer:

May the Lord restore to you the joy of his salvation and confirm you with a ruling spirit; may he renew the Holy Spirit within your inward parts and not take him from you. May the blessing of God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit descend upon you, flow abundantly over you, descend to the extremities of your whole body, fill and surround you within and without, and remain always with you. “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, I anoint you with holy oil for the remission of all your sins unto eternal life. Amen.”

While the sick person is being anointed, the antiphon is said: “Heal me, O Lord ...” The following eight psalms are sung in imitation of the eight beatitudes, or for hope of the eighth-day resurrection:

“Turn, O Lord.”

“Save your servant.”

“Lord, preserve him.”

“Lord, send him help upon his bed.”

“Send him, O Lord.”

“Let the enemy gain nothing.”

## II

At nightfall, on the sixth or seventh Sabbath, the signal is not sounded, nor are the day’s offices rung; rather, the boards are struck. On Good Friday—that is, the sixth day—the lector begins the appointed office:

“A reading from the prophet Hosea. Thus says the Lord God in his tribulation ...”

**Response:** “O Lord, I have heard ...”

“A reading from the book of Exodus. In those days the Lord said to Moses and Aaron ...”

**Tract:** “Deliver me, O Lord.”

“The Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ according to John. At that time Jesus went out across the torrent ...”

When the Passion has been finished, prayers are said for the whole Church and its orders. When these have been completed, the body of the Lord, consecrated on the preceding day, is carried in a wooden vessel and placed upon the altar. The priest, approaching the altar, says:

“Let us pray, instructed by saving precepts ...”

And when he has said, “For ever and ever,” he takes some of the sacred host and places it in the chalice without saying anything, because on that day the saving cup is not granted to him. Everything is done in order, and when these prayers have been completed by the priest, as written above:

“Let us pray, most beloved, for the holy Church of God ...”

Meanwhile two singers proceed, carrying the cross beside the position behind the altar, and say in a soft voice:

“O faithless people ...”

Likewise, two stand before the cross; they respond in the same voice with the antiphon:

“Agios ...”

The Greek words are sung in Greek and the Latin words likewise in Latin. The choir begins the same chant again three times:

“Holy God ...”

After the threefold chanting, the cross is stripped of the cloth with which it had been covered. Those who have led it while singing toward the people begin this antiphon in a loud voice:

“Behold the wood of the cross, upon which hung the salvation of the world: come, let us adore.”

Psalm: “Blessed are the undefiled.”

The priest then reverently descends with the presbyters and deacons and kisses the cross after it has been adored; likewise all the others according to their order. Then the priest ascends again to the altar, receives communion, and all the clergy after him, followed by the people. The antiphons follow, and again:

“We adore your cross,”

as in the Roman Missal.

The *Agnus Dei* is not sung, nor is there a communion chant; but when all have communicated, everything is completed.

## III

On Holy Saturday of Easter, the first litany is performed sevenfold, on account of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. The *Agnus Dei* is not sung except in the third litany, which is sung at the introit.

[Several antiphons, psalms, and prayers to be said before and after the burial of the body follow; to these is appended the following rubric.]

On Sunday the offices for the dead are not celebrated, nor are their names celebrated at Mass; only those of kings, princes, and priests are commemorated, or offerings and vows are made for the whole Christian people. But for the dead who die on Sunday, may Christ, the Son of God, himself grant them rest—he who offered himself as a sacrifice for them, or for the whole human race.

Mass for the dead on the third, seventh, and thirtieth day.

# The Breviary of St. Prudentius, Bishop of Trecensis

## Prologue to the Psalter

*I took this prologue of Prudentius, bishop of Trecensis, who flourished in Gaul in the ninth century, from an old Vatican manuscript; I did not, however, judge that the flowers of the psalms themselves, or the little work that follows, should be copied out, since scarcely anything besides Davidic words occurs there. Mai.*

A certain noble matron, having been oppressed by the powerful in the cities or towns and, as many know, being distressed by various accidental tribulations and afflicted by excessive weariness, sent to me, earnestly asking that I write for her, in the briefest verses, something from the praise of the psalms for the consolation of her compassion.

I, grieving not only over her request but also for all who travel through diverse provinces, mountains, and valleys, and for those who traverse rivers and seas, fearing to fall into danger—as Scripture says, dangers in the river, dangers in the sea, dangers in the city, dangers from robbers, dangers in the wilderness, and so forth—and desiring to be delivered and saved by God the governor, have endeavored, as though from a very great meadow, to gather the flowers of the psalms in summary and brevity in this little work of my smallness.

And although there are many who imitate the examples of the holy Fathers—as we have learned by experience—who every day, in divine praises, complete the whole Psalter, nevertheless those who seek this work and who are placed in various dangers cannot complete the whole Psalter, nor are they able to sing at the canonical hours. Let it not displease them to turn these verses over in heart and mouth:

“I have gone through [cod. *revolvi*: ‘I have gone through’] the verses, omitting all those in which, on the part of the Jews or other unbelievers, passages remain most openly and clearly exposed; as the psalm contains the second, third, fifth, thirteenth, twenty-first, thirty-fourth, thirty-fifth, and thirty-sixth; or ‘Why do you boast?’ (Psalm 51), or the sixty-seventh, sixty-eighth, and sixty-ninth, and ‘O God, do not be silent in my praise’ (Psalm 108), and the others which, although suitable in their own meanings, do not pertain to these anxious troubles.

“But lest anyone—God forbid—lose the whole of what he was prevented from doing by active affairs, let him, while he has leisure and ability, not delay in reciting and praying these verses of the psalms. In these, as it is written, the whole may be taken for the part and the part for the whole; with the help of the Lord Christ, one may complete the one hundred and fifty psalms.

“And, so that he may not be forgetful, let him render praise to almighty God seven times a day, at three- and four-hour intervals; as the blessed David says: ‘Seven times a day I have given praise to you,’ and so forth.

“But now I shall undertake the work already begun, joining the first with the last in this manner:

‘Blessed is the man who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night, and whose spirit in the heights praises the Lord from heaven; for every spirit praises ...’”

*Editorial note:* “But we have taken these flowers of the psalms from the Psalter of Thomas. Edition: *Patrologia*, vol. CXV.”

[The source ends here with an incomplete fragment.]

# Saint Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes

[Scan page 733. The damaged introductory rubric preserves these instructions:] …of the Lord. At the beginning of this little work, repeat three times with David, “O God, come to my assistance,” with “Glory be to the Father.” Thereafter, changing the prayer according to what the damaged rubric prescribes, confidently sing the Davidic psalmody with rejoicing, beginning from the first psalm. [Several connecting words in this rubric are illegible.]

## Prayer

May you deign to receive, Lord God almighty, these … [damaged words], these consecrated verses which I, a suppliant, desire to chant in honor of your name, for me, a miserable and unworthy sinner, and for all my offenses, whether committed in deeds or acts, in words, in wicked thoughts, in [a damaged term], or through all my negligences, great and small. May these little verses benefit me unto eternal life, the remission of all sins, time to live well, and the performance of true and worthy repentance. Amen.

## HERE BEGINS THE BREVIARY

Containing verses of the Psalms

Hear my words, O Lord; understand my cry. Give heed to the voice of my prayer, my king and my God. O Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your wrath. Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak. Heal me, O Lord, for all my bones are troubled, and my soul is greatly troubled. And you, O Lord—how long? Turn, O Lord, and deliver my soul. Save me from all those who pursue me, and deliver me. Have mercy on me, O Lord; look upon my humiliation because of my enemies.

Look upon me and hear me, O Lord my God. Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever fall asleep in death. Make my steps firm in your paths, so that my footprints may not be moved. I cried out, for you heard me, O God. Incline your ear to me and hear my words. Make your mercies wonderful, O Lord, for you save those who hope in you.

Guard me, O Lord, as the apple of your eye. Under the shadow of your wings protect me from the face of the ungodly who have afflicted me. Cleanse me from my secret faults, O Lord, and spare your servant from the sins of others. But you, O Lord, do not withhold your mercies from me. Look upon me for my protection. Deliver my soul from the sword, O God, and my only soul from the hand of the dog. Save me from the mouth of the lion, and my humiliation from the horns of unicorns.

Show me your ways, O Lord, and teach me your paths; and guide me in your truth. Remember your mercies, O Lord, and your compassion, which are from eternity. Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorance. According to your great mercy, remember me. For your goodness’ sake, O Lord, and for your name’s sake, O Lord, you will be merciful to my sin, for it is great. See my humiliation and my labor, and forgive all my sins. Do not deliver my soul to the ungodly, O God, nor my life with men of blood.

Hear, O Lord, my voice, with which I have cried to you: have mercy on me and hear me. Do not turn your face from me, and do not reject your servant in anger. You are my helper. Do not abandon me or despise me, O God my savior. Set your law before me, O Lord, in your way, and guide me in the right path because of my enemies.

Do not hand me over to the wills of those who afflict me.

## PSALTER

Containing the words of prayer

Deliver me from my enemies, O God; protect me from those who rise up against me. Do not hand me over to those who persecute my soul. To you, O Lord, I have cried; my God, do not be silent. Do not let me descend with those who go down into the pit. Hear, O Lord, the voice of my supplication, while I pray to you and lift up my hands toward your holy temple.

Do not destroy me with sinners and with those who work iniquity. Save your people, O Lord, and bless your inheritance; rule them and exalt them forever.

In you, O Lord, I have hoped; let me never be confounded. In your justice deliver me. Incline your ear to me; hasten to deliver me. Be for me a protecting God and a place of refuge, that you may save me. Into your hands, O Lord, I commend my spirit. You have redeemed me, O Lord, God of truth.

Deliver me from the hands of my enemies and from those who pursue me. Make your face shine upon your servant, and save me in your mercy. O Lord, let me not be confounded, for I have called upon you. Let your mercy, O Lord, be upon us, just as we have hoped in you.

Judge me, O Lord, and those who harm me; fight against those who fight me. Take up arms and shield; arise to help me. Do not depart from me, O Lord. Arise, O Lord; attend to my judgment. My God and my Lord, take up my cause. Judge me according to your mercy, O Lord my God.

Bring forth your mercy to those who know you, and your justice to those who are upright in heart. Let not the foot of pride come upon me, nor the hand of the sinner move me. Do not abandon me, O Lord my God; do not depart from me. Attend to my help, O Lord, God of my salvation.

Hear, O God, my prayer and my supplication. Receive all my tears; do not be silent toward me, for I am a sojourner with you and a pilgrim like all my fathers. Forgive me, that I may be refreshed before I depart and be no more.

But you, O Lord, do not keep your mercies far from me; your mercy and your truth have always received me, for evils have surrounded me, and there is no number. My iniquities have overtaken me, and I was unable to see. They have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head, and my heart has forsaken me. May it please you, O Lord, to deliver me.

## BREVIARY IN THE PSALMS

Be pleased, O Lord, to deliver me; O Lord, look to my help. Let my mouth be filled with your praise, that I may sing your glory, all day long your magnificence. Do not cast me away in the time of old age; when my strength fails, do not forsake me. O God, do not be far from me. But I am needy and poor: O God, help me. You are my helper and my deliverer, O Lord; do not delay.

I said: O Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you. My God, attend to my help. But I shall always hope in you, O Lord, and I shall add to all your praise; my mouth shall proclaim your justice, your salvation all day long.

Why do you sleep, O Lord? Arise; why do you sleep? Arise, and do not reject us forever. Why do you turn your face away? Do you forget our poverty and our tribulation? Arise, O Lord; help us and deliver us for your name’s sake.

Do not hand over to beasts the souls confessing you, and do not forget forever the souls of your poor. Look upon your covenant, for the dark places of the earth have been filled with the habitations of iniquity. Help us, O God our savior, and for the honor of your name, O Lord, deliver us; be propitious toward our sins for the sake of your name.

Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy; and according to the multitude of your tender mercies blot out my iniquity. Wash me yet more from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin. Turn your face away from my sins and blot out all my iniquities. Create a clean heart in me, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. Do not cast me away from your face, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me. Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a governing spirit. Lord, you will open my lips, and my mouth will proclaim your praise.

God, save me in your name and deliver me in your strength. God, hear my prayer; receive with your ears the words of my mouth. Hear my prayer, O God, and do not despise my supplication; attend to me and hear me.

In God I shall praise the word, and in the Lord I shall praise the utterance. In God I shall hope; I shall not fear what man may do to me. The vows which I shall repay are upon me, O God: praises to you, because you have delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, and my feet from falling, so that I may please the Lord in the light of the living.

Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me, for my soul trusts in you, and under the shadow of your wings I shall hope until iniquity passes away.

Deliver me from my enemies, my God, and free me from those who rise against me. Deliver me from those who work iniquity, and save me from bloodthirsty men, for behold, they have hunted my soul; the mighty have rushed upon me. But I direct my prayer to you, O Lord.

God, at the time of favor, in the abundance of your mercy hear me, in the truth of your salvation. Deliver me from the mire, so that I may not stick fast. Free me from those who hate me and from the depth of the waters. Let no tempest of water submerge me; let not the deep swallow me, nor the pit close its mouth over me. Hear me, O Lord, for your mercy is kind; according to the abundance of your tender mercies look upon me. Do not turn your face from your servant, for I am troubled; hear me quickly. Attend to my soul and free it; because of my enemies deliver me.

O God, attend to my help; O Lord, hasten to assist me. But I am needy and poor: O God, help me. You are my helper and deliverer, O Lord; do not delay. In you, O Lord, I have hoped; let me never be confounded. In your justice free me and deliver me. Incline your ear to me; hasten to deliver me. Be for me a protecting God and a place of refuge, that you may save me. And you, O Lord, are a mighty helper.

Increase, O Lord, your power and come to save us. O Lord God of hosts, convert us and show your face, and we shall be saved. Convert us, O God our savior, and turn your anger away from us, so that you may not be angry with us forever, nor extend your anger from generation to generation. O God, you will turn and revive us, and your people will rejoice in you. Show us, O Lord, your mercy, and grant us your salvation.

Incline your ear to me, O Lord, and hear me, for I am poor and needy. Guard my soul, for I am holy. Save your servant, my God, who hopes in you. Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I have cried to you all day. Gladden the soul of your servant, for to you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul.

But you, O Lord my God, are compassionate and merciful, patient and greatly merciful and true. Look upon me and have mercy on me; give your power to your servant and save the son of your handmaid. Give me a sign for good, so that those who hate me may see it and be confounded, because you, O Lord, have helped me.

O Lord, God of my salvation, by day I have cried out and by night before you. Let my prayer enter your presence; incline your ear to my prayer, O Lord. Where are your ancient mercies, O Lord, as you swore to David in your truth? Remember, O Lord, the reproach of your servants, which I have borne in my breast, the reproach of many nations.

Turn, O Lord, for a little while, and be entreated concerning your servants. And may the splendor of the Lord our God be upon us, and direct the work of our hands for us; indeed, direct the work of our hands.

O Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you. Do not turn your face from me; on whatever day I am troubled, incline your ear to me. On whatever day I call upon you, hear me quickly. Do not take me away in the midst of my days; your years endure through generations and generations.

But you, O Lord, show me mercy for your name’s sake, for your mercy is sweet. Deliver me, for I am poor and needy, and my heart is troubled within me. I have passed away like a declining shadow, and I have been shaken off like a locust. Help me, O Lord my God, and save me according to your mercy.

Repay your servant; vivify me, and I shall keep your words. Open my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law. I am a sojourner on the earth; do not hide your commandments from me. Strengthen me, O Lord, in your words. Remove from me the way of iniquity, and have mercy on me according to your law. Lead me in the path of your commandments, for I have desired it.

Incline my heart to your testimonies and not to avarice. Turn my eyes away, lest they see vanity. Revive me in your way. Establish your word for your servant in your fear. Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge, for I have believed in your commandments.

You are good, O Lord, and in your goodness teach me your ordinances. Let your mercy now come, O Lord, to comfort me according to your word to your servant. Let your mercies come to me, and I shall live, for your law is my meditation. Let my heart be blameless in your ordinances, so that I may not be confounded.

I have been humbled exceedingly, O Lord; revive me according to your word. Let the free offerings of my mouth please you, O Lord, and teach me your judgments. Receive me according to your word, and I shall live; and do not confound me in my expectation. Help me, and I shall be saved, and I shall meditate on your ordinances.

Deal with your servant according to your mercy, and teach me your ordinances. I am your servant; give me understanding, so that I may know your testimonies. Look upon me and have mercy on me according to the judgment of those who love your name.

Direct my steps according to your word, so that no iniquity may rule over me. Redeem me from the calumnies of men, that I may keep your commandments. Make your face shine upon your servant, and teach me your ordinances. Hear my voice according to your mercy, O Lord, and according to your judgment revive me.

See my humiliation and deliver me, for I have not forgotten your law. Judge my judgment and redeem me; for the sake of your word revive me. Let my prayer draw near in your sight, O Lord; according to your word give me understanding. Let my petition enter your sight, O Lord; according to your word deliver me.

My lips will pour forth a hymn when you teach me your ordinances. My tongue will proclaim your words, for all your commandments are just. Let your hand be there to save me, for I have chosen your commandments.

I have longed for your salvation, O Lord, and your law is my meditation. My soul shall live and shall praise you, and your judgments shall help me. I have gone astray like a sheep that is lost. Seek your servant, O Lord, for I have not forgotten your commandments.

Have mercy on us, O Lord, have mercy on us, for we are filled exceedingly with contempt. Do good, O Lord, to those who are good and upright in heart. Turn, O Lord, our captivity, like a torrent in the south.

From the depths I have cried to you, O Lord; O Lord, hear my voice. Let your ears be attentive to the prayer of your servant. On whatever day I call upon you, hear me; you will multiply strength in my soul and lead me, O Lord, in the eternal way.

Place, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips, so that my heart may not incline toward an evil word, to make excuses for sins.

O Lord, hear my prayer; in your truth hear me, in your justice; and do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person shall be justified in your sight. For the enemy has pursued my soul; he has humbled my life to the earth.

Hear me quickly, O Lord; my spirit has failed. Do not turn your face from me, and I shall become like those who descend into the pit. Make me hear your mercy in the morning. Make known to me the way in which I should walk, for to you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul.

Deliver me from my enemies, O Lord; to you I have fled. Teach me to do your will, for you are my God. Your good Spirit will lead me into the right way. For your name’s sake, O Lord, you will revive me in your justice. And you will lead my soul out of tribulation, and in your mercy you will destroy my enemies. You will destroy all who trouble my soul, for I am your servant.

Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit. As it was in the beginning, is now, and always, and for ages of ages. Amen.

I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth. Against you alone have I sinned, and I have done evil before you. I made my sin known to you, and I did not hide my iniquity. I said: I will confess my iniquity against myself to the Lord; and you forgave the wickedness of my sin. For this every holy person shall pray to you at an opportune time.

But you, O Lord, have mercy on me; raise me up, and I shall repay them. By this I have known that you have desired me, because my enemy shall not rejoice over me. But you have received me because of my innocence, and you have established me in your presence forever.

Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, from eternity and forever. Let it be, let it be.

Into your hands, O Lord, I commend my spirit. You have redeemed me, O Lord, God of truth. My salvation is from the hand of the Lord, and my glory is in the sight of God.

## PRAYER IN TRIBULATION

If we set before your eyes, O Lord, the faults we have committed and the wounds we receive, what we suffer is less than what we deserve. We feel the punishment of sin, yet we do not avoid the persistence of sinning. In your scourges our frailty is broken, yet our iniquity is not changed. The sick mind is tormented, and the stiff neck is not bent. Life sighs in pain, and yet it does not amend itself in its conduct.

If you wait, we are not corrected; if you avenge, we do not endure. In correction we confess what we have done; at the visitation we forget what we have bewailed. If you press your hand upon us, we promise that we will do what must be done; if you suspend the blow, we do not fulfill our promises. If you strike, we cry out that you should spare us; if you spare us, we again provoke you to strike.

When distresses come, we ask for time to repent; when mercy intervenes, we abuse the patience that has spared us. The wound recently inflicted has scarcely passed, and already the ungrateful mind does not remember what it suffered. If you hear us quickly, we grow insolent through mercy; if more slowly, we murmur through impatience.

O Lord, we wish to preserve what you have done, but we do not fear to neglect what you have commanded. You have before you guilty people who confess, O Lord; spare us, because you are merciful. We know that, unless you forgive, you rightly punish us. But with you there is abundant compassion and overflowing forgiveness.

Grant without merit what we ask, you who made from nothing those who would ask you. And when we cry out to you, O Lord, have mercy. May a faithful and tearful voice move your mercy, and may that goodness—in which alone we place all our hope—not reckon what we have offended, while it regards what we ask. Though it is a great misery that we are guilty, may it be a greater mercy for you that we are miserable.

As suppliants for your help, we place before you both the evils of our crime and our pains; by prayer we await your mercy, which by sinning we rejected. May indulgence grant what is requested to those whom you recognize as having no confidence in their own righteousness. Raise us up, O Lord our God, and lift us in your mercy, so that, through communion in salvation and the joy of charity, while we ourselves desire to be saved by your gift, we may also rejoice in the faith and peace of all nations. Through.

## PRAYER

### From the Longer Prayer of Saint Ambrose, Bishop

I beseech you, O God, lover of your Church, on behalf of her priests, that by their words and merits alike they may invite the people entrusted to them to the heavenly homeland.

On behalf of kings, rulers, and those set in high places, that they may show themselves fathers of orphans and judges of widows; that they may grieve over the misery of the needy and the groans of the poor; that they may seek nothing in judgment except what is just; and that they may administer present affairs in such a way that they do not lose future goods.

On behalf of virgins, the continent, and those who have renounced the world, that they may despise present things and seek those that are future; that they may not entangle themselves in worldly business, but, serving you, may please him to whom they have proved themselves faithful.

On behalf of married people, that they may pay each other the debt of the flesh in such a way that they do not stray from desire for the heavenly homeland.

But what am I doing, O Lord? As though I had forgotten my own sins, do I presume to pray for others? O how greatly I have offended, and still offend! Yet despair does not steal upon me, since I look to the publican justified in the temple; I behold the thief confessing on the cross and passing from the cross into paradise; I see Mary, after many guilty offenses, washed in the fountain of mercy; I see Peter, after his denial, recovering the grace of the apostolate.

But I ask, ineffable mercy, that since you have permitted me to take confidence from such great examples, you may grant me the publican’s sighs, the thief’s confession, the prostitute’s tears, and the weeping of the denying apostle.

O Lord, if you have determined that my crimes should be punished by temporal scourging, I beseech you with tears that, while you cease in anger against these sins, you may always remember mercy in anger. For whoever you love, you correct; and you scourge every son whom you receive. Although these words clearly threaten the stroke of the rod, they nevertheless reveal the affection of mercy.

Therefore grant endurance amid scourges, lest I incur the mark of murmuring like a bad servant; rather, like a good son, may I repay you with thanksgiving. I ask this also most earnestly: may I always remember the day of death, the day of the final judgment, the condemnation of eternal punishment, and the blessedness of the future kingdom. No one can do this continually except one who has been predestined to eternal life.

And, that this prayer of mine may be effective, I seek the intercession of blessed Mary the virgin. You made her so worthy of merit that, first among women, she offered a new gift, and no one except her received so new a gift. She was the first to offer a new gift, remaining a virgin after childbirth; and no one except her received so new a gift, remaining a virgin after giving birth.

I implore the intercession of the apostles, who, following the footsteps of the Mediator’s most blessed poverty and his sufferings, attained such a height of dignity that whatever they bound on earth was bound in heaven, and whatever they loosed on earth was loosed in heaven; and that they would sit at the end on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

I ask the prayers of the martyrs, who did not hesitate to shed their blood for the Truth, nor love their lives even unto death, so that they might overcome the author of death.

I ask the prayers of the confessors, who, while living piously in Catholic peace, endured the battles of the tempting enemy, or even the struggle with heretics, through prolonged conflict, and—to speak truly—received the palm of a longer and hidden martyrdom.

You never despise the prayers of such people, O Lord God, if you yourself inspire them to intercede for me; you who live and reign throughout all ages and in every age. Amen.

## LETTERS OF SAINT EULOGIUS

**First Letter.** — To Alvarus. It celebrates the martyrdom of the two virgins, Flora and Maria. 841  

**Letter II.** — To Baldegoto. He recounts to Baldegoto the martyrdom of her sister Flora and sends her Flora’s girdle. 844  

**Letter III.** — To Witesindus, bishop of Pamplona. When the blessed Eulogius was traveling to Gaul, he had stayed with this bishop, who had asked him for relics of the blessed Zoilus, martyr of Córdoba. Here he recounts the history of that pilgrimage and also sends the relics of Zoilus and Acisclus, while reviewing the calamities suffered by the Church of Córdoba and the martyrdoms of many others. 845
